determined, which will allow to establish which subunits recruits IRT1 to COPII vesicles. So far, the signals responsible for IRT1 packaging in COPII vesicle are still unknown. However, a diacidic motif (EDD) located in the large cytosolic loop of IRT1 may be implicated, although experimental evidence is needed (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). Parallel to the COPII-mediated anterograde route, a retrograde pathway is driven by coat protein complex I (COPI)-coated vesicles, which allows the continual recycling of proteins and lipids from the Golgi to the ER to maintain an equilibrium (Contreras et  al. 2000; Pimpl et al. 2000; Yorimitsu et al. 2014). Interestingly, coatomer subunits, that are key components of the COPI machinery (Sanchez-Simarro et al. 2020), probably interact with IRT1 since they were found in IRT1 interactome (MartinBarranco et al. 2020). IRT1 may, therefore, be retrieved back from the Golgi apparatus to the ER by COPI vesicles (Fig. 1), even if the relevance of this process remains unclear. The contribution of the IRT1 partners involved in its anterograde and retrograde transport to the establishment of plant metal homeostasis is still uncharacterized, but corresponding mutants will likely have pleiotropic efects. Finally, the later steps of IRT1 trafcking from the Golgi to the PM remain unexplored. This process might involve soluble $N .$ -ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) or the exocyst complex, that were both shown to be implicated in the post-Golgi trafcking of several membrane proteins in plants (Hachez et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2020).


## Endocytosis plays a major role in the regulation of IRT1


In the past decade, numerous studies highlighted the importance of endocytosis in the regulation of IRT1 and metal uptake in Arabidopsis. Early work showed that, under iron limitation and in presence of physiological amounts of non-iron metals, IRT1 cycles between early endosomes (EE)/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and the outer polar domain of the PM, in root epidermal cells (Fig. 1) (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011). A fraction of IRT1 also trafcs through the multivesicular bodies (MVB)/ late endosomes (LE) on the way to the lytic vacuole for constitutive degradation (Barberon et  al. 2011). IRT1 internalization from the PM is at least in part achieved by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and requires the mono-ubiquitination of lysine residues K154 and K179 that are located in the large cytosolic loop of IRT1. Indeed, IRT1 is stabilized at the PM when CME is impaired via the expression of a dominant-negative version of clathrin and when K154 and K179 are mutated (Kerkeb et al. 2008; Barberon et al. 2011, 2014). Importantly, neither ubiquitination nor CME are implicated in IRT1 polar localization. The role of CME in IRT1 internalization is strengthened by the fact that clathrin was recently found to be abundant in IRT1 interactome, suggesting that IRT1 can associate, probably in an indirect manner via adaptor proteins, with clathrin (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The peripheral membrane protein ENHANCED BENDING1 (EHB1) may also be involved in IRT1 endocytosis since: (i) IRT1 protein content increases in ehb1 mutants, (ii) proteins from the same family can induce membrane tubulation in vitro (Khan et al. 2019). Interestingly, EHB1 interacts with and negatively regulates IRT1 in a calciumdependent manner (Fig. 1), leading to a reduction of iron acquisition in plant.

Interestingly, IRT1 intracellular dynamics is not regulated by iron, the primary substrate of IRT1, but is controlled by the non-iron secondary substrates of IRT1 that are toxic when present in excess (Barberon et al. 2014; Dubeaux et al. 2018). Although IRT1 is localized to both EE/TGN and the PM in the presence of physiological concentrations of noniron metals, IRT1 is targeted to MVB/LE and then to the vacuole for degradation upon a cytosolic excess of these metals (Fig. 1) (Dubeaux et al. 2018). The cellular mechanisms involved in the non-iron metal-triggered endocytosis of IRT1 were largely uncovered. Non-iron metal excess is directly sensed by IRT1 via metal binding to a histidine-rich sequence located in the IRT1 large cytosolic loop (Dubeaux et al. 2018). Thus, IRT1 acts as a transceptor, combining transporter and receptor properties (Cointry and Vert 2019). Metal binding on IRT1 allows the recruitment of Calcineurin B-like (CBL)-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 23 (CIPK23) (Fig. 1). Phosphorylation of IRT1 by CIPK23 in turn creates a docking site for the E3 ubiquitin ligase IRT1 DEGRADATION FACTOR1 (IDF1) that converts IRT1 multi-monoubiquitination into K63-type polyubiquitination, a signal that boosts the sorting of IRT1 to the vacuole and its degradation (Dubeaux et al. 2018; Shin et al. 2013). From a physiological point of view, the endocytosis of IRT1 in response to a non-iron metal excess constitutes a protective mechanism for the plant to restrict the absorption of readily available and potentially toxic metals, such as Zn, Mn and Co. Loss of CIPK23, IDF1, or the mutation of ubiquitination targets or metal-binding sites in IRT1 all lead to stabilization of IRT1 at the cell surface, which results in a hypersentivity to non-iron metals (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011; Dubeaux et al. 2018). It should be noted that in addition to this IRT1- mediated protection, non-iron-metal toxicity is also alleviated by tonoplastic transporters such as Metal Tolerance Protein 3 (MTP3) (Arrivault et al. 2006) and Heavy Metal Associated 3 (HMA3) (Morel et al. 2009), which expression is induced under iron defciency in a FIT-dependent manner (Wu et al. 2012), and that allow the sequestration of metals such as Zn and Co into the vacuole.

The recognition of ubiquitin-modifed IRT1 required for its routing to the vacuole is achieved by the MVB/LElocalized FYVE1/FREE1 protein (Fig. 1). FYVE1/FREE1 directly interacts with IRT1 and ubiquitin, and associates with endosomal membrane via phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding (Barberon et al. 2014; Gao et al. 2014). FYVE1/FREE1 is a plant-specifc component of the endosomal sorting complex for transport (ESCRT) that captures ubiquitinated cargos in the MVB/LE membrane and allows their sorting in intraluminal vesicles for subsequent targeting to the vacuole (Isono and Kalinowska 2017; Otegui 2018). Interestingly, overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 in plants leads to an apolar localization of IRT1 in root epidermal cells, which in turn induces defects in metal homeostasis (Barberon et al. 2014). This suggests that the polarization of IRT1 is essential for the radial transport of metals towards the vasculature. So far, it remains unclear why the overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 induces a re-routing of IRT1 to the PM instead of favoring its targeting to the vacuole for degradation. Interestingly, FYVE1/FREE1 protein accumulation is regulated by iron through the action of SINAT1-4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. Expression of these is induced under iron defciency resulting in ubiquitin-mediated degradation of FYVE1/FREE1, thus positively regulating iron uptake (Xiao et al. 2020). Following endocytosis, IRT1 can be recycled to earlier endocytic compartments or the PM. One of these pathways involves the Sorting Nexin 1 (SNX1) protein that partially co-localizes in endosomes with IRT1 (Fig. 1) (Ivanov et al. 2014). snx1 knock-out mutant shows enhanced degradation of IRT1, leading to reduced iron import efciency and hypersensitivity to iron defciency. Although Arabidopsis SNX1 protein works independently of the retrograde transport retromer complex (Pourcher et al. 2010; Zelazny et al. 2013), SNX1 appears to drive the recycling of internalized IRT1 to prevent its premature degradation (Ivanov et al. 2014). Whether SNX1 directly interacts with IRT1 is still undocumented.


## IRT1 is part of an iron acquisition protein complex


Recently, the three main actors of iron uptake in Arabidopsis, IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2, were shown to form tripartite direct interactions, thus creating an iron acquisition protein complex (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). This complex is probably mostly present in the outer PM domain facing the rhizosphere in root epidermal cells, where IRT1 and FRO2 are specifcally localized. The spatial proximity between IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2 among a complex may optimize iron uptake under low iron conditions, by creating a nanoscale environment in the rhizosphere combining low pH, induced by the activity of AHA2, and high concentrations of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ produced by FRO2 (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). Although it remains to be investigated, a channeling mechanism allowing the direct transfer of reduced iron from FRO2 to IRT1 is conceivable. Indeed, channeling of iron was described in yeast between the multicopper oxidase Fet3p, which oxidizes $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , and the iron permease Ftr1p that transports $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ into the cells, both proteins forming a complex (Kwok et al. 2006; Singh et al. 2006).

Characterization of the dynamics of the iron uptake complex revealed that: (i) FRO2 and AHA2 are ubiquitinated but independently of the non-iron metal substrates transported by IRT1, (ii) FRO2 and AHA2 are not largely endocytosed in response to non-iron metal excess, unlike IRT1, (iii) this absence of internalization is due to the dissociation of the complex provoked by the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of IRT1 in response to non-iron metal excess (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The meaning of such dissociation remains to be investigated but released FRO2 and AHA2 may be recruited to other processes than iron uptake, such as copper reduction and membrane energization, respectively (Yi and Guerinot 1996; Robinson et al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2003; Falhof et al. 2016).

## The high-affinity metal Transporters NRAMP1 and IRT1 Team up to Take up Iron under Sufficient Metal Provision


received: 20 June 2016   
accepted: 26 October 2016   
Published: 16 November 2016

Loren Castaings, Antoine Caquot, Stéphanie Loubet & Catherine Curie

Iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) are essential metals which, when scarce in the growth medium, are respectively taken up by the root high affinity transporters IRT1 and NRAMP1 in Arabidopsis thaliana. The molecular bases for low affinity transport however remained unknown. Since IRT1 and NRAMP1 have a broad range of substrates among metals, we tested the hypothesis that they might be functionally redundant by generating nramp1 irt1 double mutants. These plants showed extreme Fedeficiency symptoms despite optimal provision of the metal. Their phenotype, which includes low Fe and Mn contents and a defect of Fe entry into root cells as revealed by Fe staining, is rescued by high Fe supply. Using a promoter swap-based strategy, we showed that root endodermis retains the ability to carry out high affinity Fe transport and furthermore might be important to high-affinity Mn uptake. We concluded that NRAMP1 plays a pivotal role in Fe transport by cooperating with IRT1 to take up Fe in roots under replete conditions, thus providing the first evidence for a low affinity Fe uptake system in plants.

Iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) are essential trace elements for living organisms. Because they can easily loose and gain electrons, these metals are energy-providing catalysers or cofactors for a range of enzymatic reactions. As such, they play important roles in oxidative stress responses, DNA synthesis or pathogen defence1 . In plants especially, Fe and Mn are crucial for photosynthesis as core components of the photosynthetic machinery2,3. Like all transition metals however, Fe and Mn in excess become harmful because they catalyse the formation of reactive oxygen species through the Fenton reaction and the stimulation of the mitochondrial complex II, respectively4,5.

Plant Fe and Mn deficiencies occur in alkaline soils where most of the metals are present as insoluble complexes6–8. Fe deficiency is known to reduce chlorophyll synthesis and photosynthetic activity, leading to leaf interveinal chlorosis and decrease of biomass9,10. Mn deficiency symptoms, yet less documented, are also characterized by growth inhibition and leaf yellowing as well as tissue necrosis induced by the over-production of reactive oxygen species3 .

On the contrary, Fe and Mn phytotoxicity can be reached in flooded areas and acidic soils where metals are readily accessible for plants7 . Excess Fe causes growth arrest and necrotic spots on leaves known as bronzing symptom in rice11,12. Mn toxicity can also lead to chlorosis and necrotic leaf spots13. In higher plants, Fe and Mn are known to be antagonistic so that the excess of one of these metals systematically provokes a secondary deficiency of the other, thus reflecting the competition existing for their absorption7,14.

In non-grass plants, to which the model species Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis here after) belongs, Fe acquisition by Fe-limited roots relies on secretion of phenolic compounds by the root15–18, rhizosphere acidification by a membrane-bound proton ATPase that increases Fe solubility19, reduction of Fe (III) to Fe (II) at the root cell surface and subsequent Fe (II) import into the cell20,21. In Arabidopsis, this last step is mainly performed by the Fe deficiency-induced root plasma membrane transporter IRT1 (IRON-REGULATED TRANPORTER 1), which promotes high affinity Fe uptake under Fe-deficient conditions22,23. IRT1 has a broad range of substrates among divalent metals since it is able to complement yeast strains defective in Mn or zinc $( \mathrm { Z n } )$ uptake24 and since

the irt1-1 loss-of-function mutant fails to accumulate Mn, Zn and cobalt (Co) under Fe-deficient conditions22.   
The exact role of IRT1 in Mn, Zn and Co homeostasis has however not yet been investigated.

Recent studies with rice and Arabidopsis have shown the importance of metal transporters of the NRAMP (NATURAL RESISTANCE-ASSOCIATED MACROPHAGE PROTEIN) family in Mn uptake in plants25,26. NRAMP1 is the major high affinity Mn transporter in Arabidopsis as shown by the hypersensitivity of the nramp1-1 mutant to Mn limitation and its inability to take up Mn in these conditions25. The expression of this plasma membrane transporter is upregulated in roots under Mn deficiency. Interestingly, NRAMP1 is also induced upon Fe deficiency by FIT, the master regulator of the Fe deficiency response27,28 which suggests that it might play a role in Fe homeostasis as well. This hypothesis was further supported by NRAMP1 ability to restore irt1-1 mutant Fe and Co uptakes, indicating that NRAMP1 too has a broad selectivity in vivo25.

Given the obvious yet poorly understood link existing between Fe and Mn uptakes, we sought to shed light on the respective contribution of IRT1 and NRAMP1 to Fe and Mn absorption by plant roots. A reverse genetics approach coupled with a promoter swap strategy allowed us to unravel the functional redundancy of NRAMP1 and IRT1 transporters for the uptake of these two metals under optimal growth conditions and revealed a possible root cell-specificity for Mn absorption.

Knocking out both IRT1 and NRAMP1 has a dramatic impact on plant growth. To assess a possible functional redundancy between IRT1 and NRAMP1 in Mn and/or Fe uptake, we first checked IRT1 and NRAMP1 expression in their respective mutants, namely irt1-1 (Wassilewskija ecotype, Ws) and nramp1-1 (Columbia ecotype, Col). Interestingly, IRT1 was consistently overexpressed in nramp1-1, even under standard growth conditions ( $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn, $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe) (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. S1). This result suggests that compensation mechanisms possibly hide Fe-related phenotypes in the nramp1-1 mutant. In order to investigate this hypothesis, we crossed irt1-1 and nramp1-1 to generate a double nramp1-1 irt1-1 mutant (see Methods). Among the F2 progeny, all homozygous plants for both nramp1-1 and irt1-1 mutations showed slow growth and a strong chlorosis (Supplementary Fig. S2). We therefore selected one of these knock out lines to further investigate the consequence of NRAMP1 and IRT1 simultaneous loss of function (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. S1).

We opted for hydroponic cultures that enable control of the nutrients supply. When grown in that system under standard Mn and Fe supply $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn and $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, see Methods), nramp1-1 developed normally despite a small but significant reduction in the activity of the photosystem II (PSII) (Fig. 1b–d). In these conditions, irt1-1 mutant only harbored a slight reduction in shoot biomass and accession-related morphological specificities such as bigger leaf blades and a wider expanded rosette similar to these of Ws ecotype (Fig. 1b,c and ref. 29). Our standard hydroponic medium provides therefore Mn and Fe in sufficient amounts for nramp1-1 and irt1-1 single mutants to grow nearly as well as wild type plants. In the same hydroponic conditions however, the double mutant developed similar growth defects than those previously observed in soil. Indeed, nramp1-1 irt1-1 displayed a dramatically impaired growth of both shoots and roots (Fig. $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , c } }$ ) and a strong chlorosis associated with a poor photosynthesis efficiency as shown by the reduction of both the energy transfer within the PSII (Fv/Fm) and the light utilization $( \varphi _ { \mathrm { I I } } )$ (Fig. 1b,d).

To confirm this phenotype, we produced a second allele of nramp1 irt1 double mutant using a new mutant allele of NRAMP1 in the Ws ecotype pitched nramp1-2 (Supplementary Fig. S3). The nramp1-2 mutant, despite retaining $2 0 \%$ of the wild-type amount of NRAMP1 transcripts, was hypersensitive to Mn deficiency, similar to the phenotype of nramp1-1 (Supplementary Fig. S3). When grown hydroponically, nramp1-2 irt1-1 plants harbored similar though milder phenotypes than those of nramp1-1 irt1-1. They were smaller and had paler leaves than irt1-1 especially when challenged with limiting Fe supply $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. S4). The difference in phenotype intensity between the two double mutant lines might come from the residual expression of NRAMP1 from the nramp1-2 allele. Also, different genetic backgrounds of the double mutants (Col/Ws for nramp1-1 irt1-1 and Ws for nramp1-2 irt1-1) might be of influence on the phenotype severity. The latter explanation is however less likely since all the independent nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant lines obtained from the initial cross harbored a strong phenotype despite their different Col/Ws allelic combinations (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Altogether these data suggest that NRAMP1 and IRT1 contribute to plant growth under optimal metal supply in a redundant manner.

Fe and Mn levels are reduced in the two different nramp1 irt1 double mutants. In order to further characterize the impact of inactivating both IRT1 and NRAMP1, we measured metal content in nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant plants and compared it to that of wild type plants and parental lines of the single mutants grown under standard metal supply $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn) (Figs 1e–h and $2 \mathrm { b } , \mathsf { c } .$ and Supplementary Table S1). Among the tested metals $Z \mathbf { n } .$ , Cu, Mn and Fe), only Fe and Mn showed significant concentration changes in nramp1-1 irt1-1 (Supplementary Table S1). Indeed, Fe and Mn contents in shoots were respectively $5 0 \%$ and $4 0 \%$ lower in the double mutant compared to the other genotypes (Fig. $^ { 1 \mathrm { e , f } }$ ). Similar results were also obtained in nramp1-2 irt1-1 double mutant (Fig. $^ { 2 \mathrm { b } , \mathrm { c } }$ and Supplementary Fig. S4).

A decrease in metal accumulation in shoots might be the consequence of impaired metal uptake by roots and/or poor metal translocation from roots to shoots. In order to identify which of these two mechanisms is defective in the double mutant, we measured metal content in roots. Mn concentration in nramp1-1 irt1-1 roots was reduced twofold compared to wild type plants (Fig. 1g). The fact that Mn content was decreased in both shoot and root of nramp1-1 irt1-1 plants strongly suggests that Mn uptake is impaired in the double mutant under optimal Mn concentration. Surprisingly, Fe was twice as much concentrated in the roots of nramp1-1 irt1-1 compared to the other genotypes (Fig. 1h). This result was further confirmed by whole-mount roots stained with the Perls histochemical method that showed accumulation of Fe as a blue precipitate in the nramp1-1 irt1-1 root (Fig. 3b). To refine the localization of such accumulated Fe in root tissues of the double mutant, wild type and nramp1-1 irt1-1 root cross-sections were stained with the sensitive Perls-DAB method30. In wild type root sections, Fe deposits were only limited to the rim of a few cells of the cortex, the darker signal in the central cylinder corresponding to light refraction (Fig. 3c). In the root of nramp1-1 irt1-1 however, Fe precipitates dramatically spread to the entire cortical cell layer (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, Fe accumulation was restricted to the apoplast surrounding these cells, a conclusion that is also supported by the observation that Perls-DAB labeling stops halfway through the endodermis where the casparian strip blocks apoplastic transport (Fig. 3d, arrow). This suggests that Fe cannot efficiently enter root cells owing to a defect of Fe uptake.

Taken together these data indicate that NRAMP1 and IRT1 act redundantly in the acquisition of Mn and Fe by the root, over a wide range of concentrations of these metals.

Fe insufficiency is responsible for the poor growth of nramp1 irt1 mutants. We then wanted to know which of the Fe and/or Mn deficiency observed in the nramp1 irt1 double mutant is the most limiting factor for its growth and development. We therefore tested whether growth of the nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant could be restored by increasing Fe or Mn supply. Interestingly, only Fe supplementation significantly improved growth (Fig. 4a). Under high Fe supply $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ or $1 \mathrm { m M }$ ), growth of nramp1-1 irt1-1 was completely rescued and leaf chlorosis fully disappeared (Fig. 4a). Such a situation was not observed when Mn concentration was increased to $1 \mathrm { m M }$ or $2 \mathrm { m M }$ under constant Fe supply $( 2 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . Instead, nramp1-1 irt1-1 developed Mn excess symptoms including growth defect, leaf yellowing and necrotic spots (Fig. 4a).

Under high Fe supply conditions that revert nramp1-1 irt1-1 phenotype, Fe content in leaves of the double mutant increased dramatically to a level exceeding more than threefold that of wild type plants grown in standard conditions, while Mn content slightly decreased (Fig. $^ { \mathrm { 4 b , c } }$ ). This result further strengthens the conclusion that despite being reduced in the double mutant, Mn concentration does not limit its growth. We concluded that Fe deficiency alone is responsible for nramp1-1 irt1-1 poor growth under normal metal supply.

The Fe status of the double mutant under standard Fe supply was evaluated at the molecular level by monitoring root expression of the two iron homeostasis genes FRO2 and FER1 that respond to Fe availability in an opposite manner (Fig. 4d,e). When Fe is scarce, FER1 expression decreases in order to free the pool of immobilized $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 1 }$ . FRO2 is a direct marker of Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis and its expression goes up to increase the ferric reductase activity at the root surface and maximize Fe absorption19. Under standard Fe supply $( 2 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , FRO2 was not significantly deregulated in nramp1-1 but was overexpressed in irt1-1, consistent with the irt1-1 mutant being slightly affected in our standard hydroponic conditions (Figs 1c and 4d). In the nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant, FRO2 expression was further deregulated, showing a twofold higher expression compared to the irt1-1 single mutant, thus confirming that the double mutant experiences a stronger Fe starvation (Fig. 4d). An over-induction of FRO2 was also observed in the nramp1-2 irt1-1 mutant, carrying a NRAMP1 knock-down allele, when grown under limiting Fe supply, especially at $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe where Fe content is the most reduced in the double mutant (Supplementary Fig. S4). As expected, supplementation of the double mutant with high Fe repressed FRO2 expression. Interestingly however, whereas FRO2 expression in wild type plants is minimal at $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$

Fe supply, as much as $1 \mathrm { m M }$ Fe are required to shut FRO2 down in the double mutant (Fig. 4d). Consistently, we found the opposite situation with FER1. FER1 mRNA levels were extremely low in nramp1-1 irt1-1 grown in standard $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe conditions compared to all the other genotypes, thus supporting our previous finding that Fe does not adequately penetrate root cells in these plants. In the double mutant, reversion of FER1 expression to a level equivalent to wild type plants grown in standard medium required up to $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe supplementation, which again points to a defect of Fe entry into root cells (Fig. 4e). Taken together our results show that poor growth and chlorosis symptoms observed in nramp1 irt1 double mutants under Fe and Mn replete conditions are caused by extreme Fe deficiency due to impaired Fe acquisition by root cells.

Assessment of NRAMP1 and IRT1 specificity of transport in various root territories by promoter-swapping. qPCR data and promoter-GUS studies have established that IRT1 and NRAMP1 have expression territories that are both overlapping and distinct22,25. IRT1 is mainly expressed in root epidermis and cortex of the absorption zone and in root hairs while NRAMP1 expression is located more internally in cortex and endodermis from the root tip up to the mature zone as well as in the root meristematic zone22,25. IRT1 and NRAMP1 are also expressed at very low levels in shoots where they conserve a slight induction by Fe and Mn deficiency respectively22,25 (Supplementary Fig. S5). In order to test the importance of these expression patterns for the physiological function of NRAMP1 and IRT1, we carried out a promoter swap strategy. To that aim, pIRT1::NRAMP1 and pNRAMP1::IRT1 constructs were generated and expressed into both nramp1 and irt1 mutants (Fig. 5a, see Methods).

To examine the possibility that the expression territory of NRAMP1 has the potential to carry out optimal iron acquisition in Fe-deficient roots, we tested whether IRT1 expressed under the control of the NRAMP1 promoter could rescue irt1 hyper-sensitivity to Fe deficiency. When the irt1 pNRAMP1::IRT1 transgenic line was grown hydroponically under Fe deficiency, growth of the irt1 mutant was essentially rescued (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. S6). Thus, despite NRAMP1 promoter activity being very weak compared to IRT1 in Fe deficient conditions (Supplementary Fig. S7), it is able to drive sufficient expression of IRT1 in the adequate location to ensure high affinity Fe uptake by the root. As previously reported25, the irt1 phenotype is also rescued by pIRT1::NRAMP1 (Fig. 5b), indicating that NRAMP1 is able to transport Fe when strongly expressed in root epidermis and cortex under the control of the IRT1 promoter. This result was further supported by the observation that pIRT1::NRAMP1 is also able to rescue the Fe-deficiency phenotype of nramp1-1 irt1-1 (Supplementary Fig. S6). Since the plant can be efficiently fed when Fe uptake occurs exclusively in the territories of expression of NRAMP1 and since NRAMP1 can functionally replace IRT1, we concluded that NRAMP1 has the capacity to contribute to Fe acquisition by the root.

Next we asked whether endodermal expression of NRAMP1 is important for its high-affinity Mn transport activity. To that aim, we tested whether NRAMP1 expressed under the control of the IRT1 promoter, which is only active in root outer cell layers excluding endodermis, could rescue nramp1-1. Interestingly, we found that pIRT1::NRAMP1 is unable to restore the tolerance of nramp1-1 to Mn-deficiency (Fig. 5c). Because the functionality of this construct was validated by its ability to successfully complement irt1-1 (Fig. 5b), we concluded that endodermis is essential for high-affinity Mn acquisition by the root. Since root tip also shows differential IRT1 and NRAMP1 expression, it is also possible that root tip plays an important role in Mn uptake under Mn starvation conditions.

At last we evaluated whether IRT1 has the potential to carry out high affinity Mn uptake. To that aim we tested whether the expression of IRT1 under the control of the NRAMP1 promoter was able to complement nramp1-1 hypersensitivity to Mn deficiency. We found that pNRAMP1::IRT1 failed to rescue growth of nramp1- 1 under Mn deficiency (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. S6). Since this construct is functional as shown by its ability to efficiently rescue the irt1 phenotype (Fig. 5b), and since IRT1 transcripts level in this line is high (Supplementary Fig. S7b), we concluded that IRT1 is unable to efficiently take up Mn in the high affinity range. We cannot however exclude the possibility that IRT1 protein is down-regulated at the post-transcriptional level when ectopically expressed in the root.

## Main conclusion IRT1 intracellular dynamics and function are fnely controlled through protein–protein interactions.


Abstract In plants, iron uptake from the soil is tightly regulated to allow optimal growth and development. Iron acquisition in Arabidopsis root epidermal cells requires the IRT1 transporter, which also mediates the entry of non-iron metals. In this mini-review, we describe how protein-protein interactions regulate IRT1 intracellular dynamics and IRT1-mediated metal uptake to maintain iron homeostasis. Recent interactomic data provided interesting clues on IRT1 secretion and the putative involvement of COPI- and COPII-mediated pathways. Once delivered to the plasma membrane, IRT1 can interact with other components of the iron uptake machinery to form an iron acquisition complex that likely optimizes iron entrance in root epidermal cells. Then, IRT1 may be internalized from the plasma membrane. In the past decade, IRT1 endocytosis emerged as an essential mechanism to control IRT1 subcellular localization and thus to tune iron uptake. Interestingly, IRT1 endocytosis and degradation are regulated by its non-iron metal substrates in an ubiquitin-dependent manner, which requires a set of interacting-proteins including kinases, E3 ubiquitin ligases and ESCRT complex subunits. This mechanism is essential to avoid non-iron metal overload in Arabidopsis when the iron is scarce.

Iron is an essential micronutrient for virtually all organisms, but it is not readily available due to its low solubility. In plants, highly specialized systems have evolved in order to acquire iron from the soil. Recent advances have identiWed molecular components of the iron uptake system, both in graminaceous plants (Curie et al. 2001) and in nongraminaceous plants (Eide et al. 1996; Henriques et al. 2002; Robinson et al. 1999; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002).

In Arabidopsis thaliana, upon iron deWciency, expression of a set of genes encoding a proton ATPase, probably of the AHA family (Palmgren 2001), the ferric-chelate reductase FRO2 (Connolly et al. 2003; Robinson et al. 1999) and the metal transporter IRT1 (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2002, 2003) is induced in root epidermal cells. These proteins are responsible for the solubilization of iron through rhizosphere acidiWcation, its reduction from $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and subsequent $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake into the cytoplasm, respectively. Several families of putative iron transporters, including NRAMP, ZIP and YSL have been described in Arabidopsis (Curie and Briat 2003). Although the physiological role of YSL and NRAMP members is associated with distribution, partitioning and remobilization of iron in the plant, the ZIP founding member IRT1 is the only transporter involved in iron uptake (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004). IRT1 was Wrst identiWed through functional complementation of a yeast mutant defective in iron uptake (Eide et al. 1996). Characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis showed that this gene is highly induced by iron starvation in roots and speciWcally expressed in the epidermis and cortex (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2002). Moreover, the identiWcation of a knock-out mutant in the IRT1 gene, irt1-1, demonstrated that in low iron conditions, IRT1 is the main route of iron entry into the plant and mediates the accumulation of additional metal ions (Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1 in Arabidopsis, was previously shown by functional complementation of yeast metal transport mutants to be a transporter of iron and zinc (Vert et al. 2001). Like IRT1, IRT2 is expressed in the outer layers of the root and upregulated, although to a lesser extent than IRT1, by iron deWciency (Vert et al. 2001). Even though IRT2 was suggested to be involved in iron uptake from the soil (Vert et al. 2001), little is known about its biological function. A loss of function En transposon mutant, irt2-1, was isolated and shown to display a slightly reduced stature but no chlorotic phenotype (Varotto et al. 2002). However, transposon insertion in irt2-1 led to concomitant downregulation of the neighboring IRT1 gene, playing itself a major role in iron uptake (Vert et al. 2002), that may result from the loss of an enhancer function acting on both IRT genes (Varotto et al. 2002). Therefore, the analysis of irt2-1 greatly limits the conclusion on the biological role of IRT2.

The present study shows that IRT2 is an intracellular membrane protein whose role in the cellular response to iron deWciency is diVerent from the major root iron transporter IRT1. We propose that IRT1 may compartmentalize iron into vesicles, to prevent toxicity by excess free iron in the cytosol as a result of extracellular iron acquisition by the FRO2/IRT1 system.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ are essential micronutrients that participate in physiological and biochemical processes and promote plant growth and development. $Z \mathrm { n }$ is involved in the synthesis of numerous enzymes, such as alcohol dehydrogenase, copper $( \mathrm { C u } ) – \mathrm { Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, and RNA polymerase. Therefore, Zn deficiency decreases the activity of these enzymes (Hacisalihoglu and Kochian 2003). Recently,

Fe has been used as a cofactor for integrating photosynthesis with various metabolic pathways and regulating gene expression (Imsande 2010). Fe deficiency can affect the growth and yield of fruit trees and other crops, and it affects photosynthesis rate, chlorophyll content, and catalase activity (Fornerginer et al. 2010; Rube´n et al. 2011).

The continuous discovery of metal ion transporters has laid the foundation for studies on factors involved in the absorption, intracellular transport, localization, and efflux of metal ions, such as P1B-type heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family, Zn- and Fe-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) family, normal resistancerelated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and the cation dissemination facilitator (CDF) family (Milner et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2017; Vigani et al. 2013). AtIRT1 was the first ZIP gene identified which is located on the root surface and induced by Fe deficiency in the root of Arabidopsis thaliana L. (Henriques et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a homolog of IRT1, plays a similarly crucial role in A. thaliana. However, under similar Fedeficient conditions, the expression of IRT2 is significantly lower than that of IRT1 (Vert et al. 2001). Their homolog IRT3, which is located in the plasma membrane, increases the uptake of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe to complement the function of both $\mathrm { Z n - }$ and Fe-uptake mutants (Lin et al. 2009). Complementation mutants or knockdown of ZIP1 and ZIP2 in A. thaliana showed that ZIP1 and ZIP2 are involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Mn uptake (Milner et al. 2013). In addition, functional analyses in maize (Zea mays L.) and rice indicated that ZIP3, ZIP4, ZIP5, and ZIP8 play important roles in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in the roots and shoots under Zn-deficient conditions (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, b). In A. thaliana, the function of ZIP9 is similar to that of ZIP12, being induced under $Z \mathbf { n }$ -limiting conditions (Talke et al. 2006; Wintz et al. 2003).

Te zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ -regulated/iron(Fe)-regulated transporterlike family proteins (ZIPs) are membrane-located proteins for cations transport (Eng et  al. 1998; Guerinot 2000). Tey have been found to exist broadly in prokaryotic cells, fungi, plants and mammalians. In plants, ZIPs have been identifed in both dicots and monocots, such as Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998; Milner et  al. 2013), rice (Chen et  al. 2008), maize (Li et  al. 2013), medicago (Lopez-Millan et al. 2004; Stephens et al. 2011) and barely (Tiong et al. 2015). Grotz et al. identifed fve ZIP genes (IRT1, ZIP1-4) in Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998), and later up to 11 ZIP genes from Arabidopsis were detected bioinformatically (Guerinot 2000). Roles of ZIP1-12 from Arabidopsis in Zn transport were explored experimentally (Milner et  al. 2013). More recently, 18 ZIPs from Arabidopsis and 16 ZIPs from rice were annotated (Ivanov and Bauer 2017).

In Arabidopsis and rice, only a small number of ZIPs have been examined for biological functions in plant till now. Arabidopsis IRT1 is a well-studied ZIP gene frst identifed as a crucial transporter for plant Fe uptake (Varotto et  al. 2002; Vert et  al. 2002). Arabidopsis IRT1 can be induced by iron defciency (Korshunova et  al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2002), and may play a role in Mn/ Zn transport as well (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et  al. 2002). Biological functions in $Z \mathrm { n } /$ Fe transport of AtIRT2 (Vert et al. 2001, 2009), AtZIP1/2 (Grotz et al. 1998; Wintz et al. 2003; Milner et al. 2013), OsIRT1 (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Ishimaru et  al. 2006; Bughio et  al. 2002) and OsZIP4/5/8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2008; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Yang et al. 2009) have also been examined in the past decade.

A few studies have also implied that ZIPs may be involved in Cd transport. Yeast cells expressing AtIRT1 showed increased Cd sensitivity (Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2001), and IRT1-dependent $\mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { M n } / Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake was inhibited by excess Cd (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). Te Arabidopsis IRT1 knock-out mutant irt1-1 exhibited reduced Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation (Vert et al. 2002; Fan et al. 2014), while overexpression of AtIRT1 increased Cd sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Connolly et  al. 2002). AtIRT2, phylogenetically similar to AtIRT1, increased Cd uptake when overexpressed in Arabidopsis (Vert et  al. 2009), though the yeast cells expressing AtIRT2 exhibited no altered Cd sensitivity (Vert et  al. 2001). In rice, expression of OsIRT1 and OsIRT2 made the cells more sensitive to Cd and increased Cd accumulation (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009). Nonetheless, we still know little about the roles of most of the ZIPs genes in Cd stress response in Arabidopsis and rice.

In this study, genome-wide ZIPs identifcation in Arabidopsis and rice was performed with rigorous evolutional analysis. A comparative examination of genomewide expression profle of ZIPs in Arabidopsis and rice in response to Cd stress were carried out. Teir role in Cd uptake of typical ZIPs responding to Cd stress was further tested by expressing them in yeast. As expected, most identifed ZIPs gene expression responded remarkably to Cd stress, while unexpectedly it was found that Arabidopsis and rice showed a distinct pattern in ZIPs genes expression profle. Tese results may help to elucidate the plants’ genetic basis for Cd translocation via a ZIPs-dependent pathway.

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.

This family was first identified in plants, taking its name from the founding members as “ZRT, IRT-like protein” [8]. ZRT1 and ZRT2 are the high- and low-affinity zinc-regulated transporters of yeast [9, 10], respectively. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter) is an Arabidopsis transporter expressed in the roots of iron-deficient plants [11]. This family is widely distributed in all organisms, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, animals [12], and plants. A considerably large family of ZIP genes has been currently characterized from various species, such as Arabidopsis [8, 11, 13], rice (Oryza sativa L.) [1, 7], soybean (Glycine max (Linn.) Merr.) The contamination of agricultural soils with heavy metals, including cadmium (Cd), zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , manganese (Mn), and arsenic (As), poses a serious threat to global food safety and human health (Zhao and Wang 2020; Li et al. 2024). Among these heavy metals, Cd is particularly alarming due to its high toxicity, persistence and mobility through the food chain. While Zn, though an essential micronutrient, can become phytotoxic at elevated concentrations (Kaur et al. 2021). Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms governing metal uptake, transport, and accumulation in plants is essential for both complementary goals: mitigating the accumulation of toxic metals in edible crops while ensuring adequate acquisition of essential elements and enhancing the phytoremediation potential of metal-accumulating species (Zhao et al. 2022).

Transmembrane transporters are fundamental to metal homeostasis in plants, the Zn-regulated transporters and iron-regulated transporter-like Proteins (ZRT/IRT-like Proteins, ZIPs), and Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs) families being particularly prominent (Tang et al. 2023). In rice, OsNRAMP5 has been identifed as a major transporter for Cd and Mn uptake (Chang et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2025), while the plasma membrane-localized OsZIP5 and OsZIP9 function synergistically to facilitate Zn and Cd absorption (Tan et al. 2020). Recent studies in Arabidopsis thaliana have further elucidated that several ZIP family members, including AtZIP2, AtZIP3, AtZIP5, and AtZIP8, are predominantly localized to the plasma membrane of root epidermal and cortical cells where they perform redundant yet crucial functions in metal acquisition from the soil environment (Ochoa et al. 2025; Robe et al. 2025).

Notably, the functional roles of ZIP1 orthologs vary considerably across plant species. Early work in rice proposed that OsZIP1 was involved in Zn and Cd uptake under Zndefcient conditions or Cd exposure (Ramesh et al. 2003). While a more recent study re-characterized it as a metal exporter localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane, which reduces cellular Cd and Zn accumulation when overexpressed (Liu et al. 2019). In contrast, Arabidopsis AtZIP1 localizes to both the vacuolar membrane and complements Zn uptake in yeast mutants, indicating its role in intracellular Zn transport (Milner et al. 2013). These functional divergences highlight the importance of characterizing ZIP1 transporter within their specifc plant systems to elucidate their distinct physiological roles.

Brassica juncea, a widely cultivated oilseed and vegetable crop, exhibits a remarkable capacity to accumulate heavy metals, making it as a promising candidate species for phytoremediation applications (Du et al. 2020; Kang et al. 2021; Zeremski et al. 2021). Despite its potential, the specifc transporters responsible for metal uptake in B. juncea remain largely uncharacterized. Our previous transcriptomic analysis revealed that BjZIP1 expression is strongly induced under Cd stress (Zhang et al. 2021); yet, its transport function and subcellular localization have not been experimentally validated. In this study, we functionally characterized BjZIP1 through heterologous expression in yeast, overexpression in A. thaliana, and the B. juncea hairy root transformation system. We demonstrate that BjZIP1 localizes to the plasma membrane and mediates Cd and Zn uptake, thereby contributing to metal accumulation and sensitivity. These fndings highlight BjZIP1 as a key component of metal uptake in $B$ . juncea and a potential molecular target for optimizing phytoremediation efciency.

Iron $( { \mathrm { F e } } )$ and zinc $( \mathrm { Z n } )$ are vital trace elements for plant growth. They play a very important role in the physiological and biochemical processes of plants (Yang, Huang, Jiang, & Zhang, 2009). Zn is involved not only in various metabolic processes in organisms but is also crucial for the stability of biological membranes, gene expression, and other physiological processes. It functions as a key component in many proteins or as a cofactor of more than 300 enzymes in plants (Haydon & Cobbett, 2007). Fe serves as a component of electron transfer complex in cellular respiration, photosynthesis and other biochemical reactions. Deficiency of $\mathrm { Z n }$ or Fe can affect the plant growth and development; however, the oversupply of either element can damage plants (Barberon et al., 2014; Li et al., 2013). Thus, a homoeostatic balance of Zn and Fe in plants is essential. Several Zn and Fe transporter families have been found, including ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter, Iron-regulated transporter-like Protein, ZIP), CDF (Cation-Diffusion Facilitator protein, CDF), NRAMP (Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Protein, NRAMP), YSL (Yellow Stripe-Like, YSL), HMA (Heavy Metal ATPase, HMA) and ATP-binding cassette transporters, which can uptake Zn or Fe from the outside or transport them inside the plant to maintain the homoeostatic balance of these two elements (Li et al., 2013). The first ZIP gene of plants (Iron

Regulated Transporter 1, IRT1) (Eide, Broderius, Fett, & Guerinot, 1996) was cloned from Arabidopsis thaliana. Subsequently, several ZIPs were cloned from rice (Ishimaru, Bashir, & Nishizawa, 2011; Ishimaru et al., 2005; Kavitha, Kuruvilla, & Mathew, 2015; Lee et al., 2010), alfalfa (Lopez-Millan, Ellis, & Grusak, 2004), maize (Li & Chen, 2013) and barley (Pedas, Schjoerring, & Husted, 2009). Plant ZIP family members can transport $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and other metal ions (Milner, Seamon, Craft, & Kochian, 2013; Wang et al., 2012). Different members of ZIP families can transport different metal ions and also respond diversely to various concentrations of metal ions. Therefore, there may be different expression and regulation patterns for these various genes (Huang & Dai, 2015; Milner et al., 2013).

Nasturtium officinale R.Br. is a common aquatic vegetable with a high economic value and is widely cultivated in Guangdong of China (Song, 2008). It is rich in vitamins, cellulose, calcium and Fe, and is beneficial to moisten the lung, suppress cough, build body, and nourish the brain (Yang et al., 2008). Thus in Chinese folk, this vegetable is used in treating diseases such as hypertension and high blood sugar (Cruz, Vieira, & Silva, 2006; Voutsina et al., 2016). Previous studies reported its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities (Bahramikia & Yazdanparast, 2010; Ozen, 2009; Sadeghi et al., 2014). In addition, the plant was abundant in glucosinolates, whose hydrolytic products had anticancer activity (Kopsell, Barickman, Sams, & McElroy, 2007). N. officinale easily adapts to the external environment for growth and is a fast-growing leafy vegetable. During the period of vegetative growth, it poses a high demand for water and fertiliser. It can grow well in eutrophic water. Plenty of roots can quickly absorb large amounts of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and other elements. Furthermore, the plant exhibits high absorption of heavy metals in water (Kisten, Gounden, Moodley, & Jonnalagadda, 2015; Song, 2008). However, the mechanism underlying uptake and transport of heavy metal elements is yet unknown and necessitates further exploration. Are there some ZIPs responsible for absorption and transportation of Zn or Fe on the cell membrane of N. officinale like A. thaliana and rice? How do they express? Constitutive expression or induced expression? Tissue preferential or non-tissue preferential? In this study, we have cloned the full-length coding sequence of NoZIP3 from the roots of N. officinale using RACE method and analysed the sequence using bioinformatics. Additionally, we determined the transcriptional level under different supply of nutrients like Zn and Fe by using qRT-PCR to understand the molecular mechanism of Zn absorption and transportation in N. officinale. All these results could provide a theoretical basis for further exploration of the molecular mechanism of Zn transportation in N. officinale.

Background and aims Dicotyledonous plants, such as Arabidopsis, acquire soil iron using a reduction-based mechanism, named Strategy I, where the final step involves $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ import by the ZIP-family transporter AtIRT1. The universal presence of IRT1-like genes, suggests that Strategy I represents a basic process in the green lineage. However, for some green organisms, like Chlamydomonas and rice, alternative ironacquisition mechanisms are known. We aimed to outline potential interactions between Strategy I and alternative iron acquisition mechanisms.

Methods We investigated gene-coexpression networks in Chlamydomonas, rice and Arabidopsis, and used the sequences of the variable regions of the selected IRT proteins to identify the conservation of key amino acids. Results IRT genes in Chlamydomonas and rice were found to be closely coexpressed with components of alternative available iron-acquisition systems. On protein level, we could observe conservation of potential phosphorylation sites in close proximity to predicted or experimentally-demonstrated ubiquitination sites.

Conclusions Data suggest that the regulation of Strategy I is closely connected to alternative existing iron-acquisition strategies. Transciptional control, together with potential post-transcriptional modifications of IRT transporters, may be involved in finetuning iron import. This study provides a basis for experimentally analyzing the regulation of iron acquisition in an evolutionary context.

## 4.1 Phloem loading and nectar secretion


SWEET proteins are chiefly associated with long-distance sugar translocation via apoplasmic phloem loading. Plasma membrane-localized AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 in phloem cells play a crucial role during apoplasmic phloem loading (Chen et al. 2010; 2012; Giaquinta 1983; Riesmeier et al. 1992; Bush 1993; Sauer and Stolz 1994; Ayre 2011). OsSWEET11, an ortholog of AtSWEET11, is involved in the sucrose efflux in the apoplasm (Antony et al. 2010). Similarly, in Z. mays, ZmSWEET13 is also involved in phloem loading (Bezrutczyk et al. 2018).

Plant nectaries accumulate starch, which is further converted into sucrose. This sucrose is exported to the apoplasmic space via SWEETs localized on the nectary parenchyma (Lin et al. 2014). AtSWEET9, a bidirectional transporter, maintains a concentration gradient inside and outside the nectary, which is essential for

The CWI4 balances a high intracellular-to-extracellular concentration gradient and an increased solute potential outside the nectaries, causing water to flow out into nectar droplets (Lin et al. 2014; Roy et al. 2017). Therefore, the quality and quantity of nectar are vital for honey bees foraging plants. Genetic engineering of SWEETs to improve the quantity of nectar secretion in bee flora like sunflower, pumpkin, rapeseed, and fruit trees can markedly and directly benefit apiculture (figure 3).


## 4.2 Seed development


SWEETs participate in seed filling and embryo nutrition. AtSWEET11, AtSWEET12, and AtSWEET15 play a crucial role in seed filling. The triple mutant atsweet11;12;15 produces wrinkled and defective seeds due to retarded embryo growth, low seed weight, and very low starch and lipid content (Chen et al. 2015b). In maize, ZmSWEET4C plays a role in seed filling (Sekhon et al. 2011; Li et al. 2014; Davidson et al. 2011). RNA sequencing data depicted high expression of ZmSWEET4C in the basal endosperm transfer layer (BETL), a specialized cell layer of endosperm identified by massive increase in the basal membrane surface compared to maternal tissues like the placenta-chalaza (Xiong et al. 2011). Sosso et al. (2015) concluded that ZmSWEET4 is involved in transporting cell wallderived hexose across the BETL, which is critical for importing sugars to the embryo and seed filling in maize. The $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa ortholog of ZmSWEET4c, OsSWEET4, also seems to be involved in grain filling, but its precise functions and cell specificity are not known (Sosso et al. 2015). Another report in maize showed that CLOSED STOMATA1 (CST1), belonging to the SWEET family, was specifically expressed in subsidiary cells. CST1 regulates stomatal opening, photosynthesis, and carbon status in the leaf, and is also involved in promoting grain yield in maize (Wang et al. 2019a). Yang et al. (2018) showed that OsSWEET4 is primarily expressed in the initial stages of seed development, while OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET15 are expressed in the later developmental stages. As expected, a double mutant of OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET15 had defective endosperm development and seed filling. They showed a more severe phenotype, including empty seeds with starch retention in the pericarp. Ma et al. (2017) also reported the involvement of OsSWEET11 in seed filling in O. sativa. OsSWEET11 is a key player for pollen development in the rice cultivars Zhonghua 11 and Kitaake (Chu et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2006). OsSWEET11 was found abundantly in the nucellar epidermis, ovular vascular trace, and cross cells, and it was found to efflux sucrose from the nucellar epidermis at the maternal filial interface (Ma et al. 2017). These findings strongly support the involvement of OsSWEET11 in $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa grain filling, which determines the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of seeds and ultimately, crop yield (figure 3). Wu et al. (2018) showed that the transcription factor OsDOF11 governs SWEET expression in $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa (Wu et al. 2018; Kim et al. 2020). Similarly, GmSWEET15 from Glycine max (soybean) functions in seed development. GmSWEET15 was found to be expressed in the endosperm at the cotyledon stage and to mediate sucrose transport, and gmsweet15 mutants showed a high rate of seed abortion and a low sugar level in the embryo (Wang et al. 2019b). Another report suggested that GmSWEET10a and GmSWEET10b transport sucrose and hexose sugars from the seed coat to the embryo, which determines soybean seed traits such as seed size and oil and protein contents (Wang et al. 2020). We speculate that the alteration of the expression of potential SWEET genes by utilizing the various genome editing approaches may improve crop seed yields.


## 4.3 Fruit development in horticultural crops


Zhen et al. (2018) clarified the involvement of SWEETs in sugar accumulation in apple fruits. Genotyping of an apple cultivar collection indicated that 9 out of 25 MdSWEET genes were highly expressed during fruit development. Three SWEET genes, MdSWEET2e, MdSWEET15a, and MdSWEET9b, were involved in sugar accumulation in apples. Both MdSWEET15a and MdSWEET9b are reported to be clade III members and efficient sucrose transporters (Eom et al. 2015). Similarly, Zhang et al. (2019) demonstrated that the plasma membrane-localized VvSWEET10 from V. vinifera is responsible for the sugar accumulation in grape berries at the onset of ripening. VvSWEET10-overexpressing grapes showed an increased level of glucose, fructose, and other soluble sugars, which highlights the significant role of VvSWEET10 in governing the sugar content of grapes (Zhang et al. 2019). Fruit development in Fragaria vesca (strawberry) showed that different SWEET members have a distinct expression pattern during the transition from young to mature ripened fruit (Liu et al. 2019). FvSWEET1, FvSWEET4, and $F \nu S W E E T 9 b$ were reported to be expressed significantly more in ripening fruit, and FvSWEET1, FvSWEET9c, and FvSWEET7 were also highly expressed during the transition stage of the fruit (Liu et al. 2019). Recently, in Cucumis sativus L. (cucumber), the role of CsSWEET7a was shown in fruit development. High CsSWEET7a expression was found in sink tissues, including fruits, and CsSWEET7a was found to be localized in the plasma membrane of phloem companion cells (Li et al. 2021). CsSWEET7a is involved in phloem unloading in the fruit by transporting sugars from companion cells into the apoplasm, which triggers the metabolism of the raffinose family of oligosaccharides. Hence, more sugars can be unloaded, eventually promoting fruit development (Li et al. 2021). A recent study by Ko et al. (2021) showed that SlSWEET15 in S. lycopersicum was highly expressed in developing fruits as compared to the other vegetative organs. SlSWEET15 was found to be accumulated in the seed coat and vascular tissue and involved in sucrose unloading from the phloem and seed coat for fruit development. These studies provide diverse pictures of overall pathways for sugar accumulation in fruits (figure 3); however, the specific role of SWEETs in these pathways is yet to be delineated.


## 4.4 Tuberization


Extensive changes in resource allocation take place during tuber formation in plants (Abelenda et al. 2014). Abelenda et al. (2019) reported that StSWEET11 from Solanum tuberosum (potato) plays a key role during tuberization. This process involves the switching of sucrose unloading from the apoplasmic to the symplastic route. Tuberization is induced and controlled by an FT-like protein called SP6A (Navarro et al. 2011, 2015; Fernie et al. 2020). StSWEET11 is a putative sucrose transporter located in phloem parenchyma cells, and SP6A was reported to directly interact with the C-terminus of StSWEET11. StSWEET11 releases sugar along the phloem to maintain the sugar supply to radial sinks, including tubers. Abelenda et al. (2019) further showed that

StSWEET11 expression in yeast cells mediated esculin uptake along the concentration gradient, but this uptake was reduced when StSP6A was co-expressed in StSWEET11-expressing yeast cells. Hence, SP6A blocks StSWEET11-dependent apoplastic sucrose flux, and sucrose transport becomes symplastic in tubers (figure 3).

Plants use sunlight to fx carbon dioxide and convert it into sugars during photosynthesis. Sugars are important carbohydrates transported from the synthesized sites in source leaves to sink tissues stems, seeds, and fruits. Sugar transport is key for proper growth and development of plants, especially for agriculturally important organs, such as seeds (Wen et al. 2022). Seed development is related to crop yield. Most importantly, seeds of cereal crops maize, rice, and wheat are major food sources of the most population. Thus, it is imperative to identify and characterize efectors for sugar efux to maintain high yields in a constantly changing environment to meet the demands of an increasing world population (Bailey-Serres et al. 2019).

The frst sucrose transporter was identifed using engineered yeast strains (Riesmeier et al. 1992). Over the past decades, a large number of factors for sugar transport have been reported. Three key classes of transporters have been proved to be responsible for sugar phloem loading and unloading, including monosaccharide transporter (MST), sucrose transporter (SUT), and sugars will eventually be exported transporter (SWEET) (Braun 2022). The MST family can be classifed into several subfamilies, such as polyol transporter (PLT), tonoplast monosaccharide transporter (TMT), and sugar transporter protein (STP). Arabidopsis PLT protein POLYOL TRANSPORTER5 (AtPLT5) has the ability to transport diverse substrates, such as hexoses and pentoses (Klepek et al. 2005). AtTMT1/TMT2 serves as an antiporter to load of glucose and sucrose into the vacuole (Schulz et al. 2011). The suppression of cucumber STP gene CsHT1 results in the inhibition of pollen germination and pollen tube elongation and decreased seed number and seed size (Cheng et al. 2015). For SUT transporters, Arabidopsis SUTs are grouped into three subclades (Reinders et al. 2012). Subclade I SUTs contain fve members (AtSUC1, 2, 5, 8, 9). AtSUC1 is necessary for normal pollen function (Sivitz et al. 2008). Subclade II SUT member AtSUC3 infuences pod dehiscence (Meyer et al. 2000). Arabidopsis SUT subclade III member AtSUC4 in vacuole membrane functions as a sucrose transporter (Weise et al. 2000). In maize, sucrose transporter ZmSUT1 mediates sucrose uptake in a $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient-dependent manner (Carpaneto et al. 2005). Cellular expression and subcellular localization analyses have revealed dual roles of $Z { \mathrm { m S U T 1 } }$ in both phloem loading and apoplasmic recycling (Baker et al. 2016).

The SWEET family is diversifed in nature. Based on SWEET proteins from fifteen plant taxa, SWEETs are divided into four phylogenetic clades. Clades I, II, and IV SWEETs prefer hexoses, while clade III SWEETs are efcient for sucrose transport (Eom et al. 2015). SWEETs are responsible for multiple biological events, from nectar production, biotic and abiotic stress responses, fertility to seed flling. Sucrose is synthesized in nectary and transported by SWEET9. The exported sucrose is then hydrolyzed by invertase to produce sucrose, glucose, and fructose. SWEET9 seems to be important for sucrose secretion from nectary parenchyma. Intriguingly, SWEET9 is essential for nectar secretion in three species Arabidopsis, Brassica, and Nicotiana (Lin et al. 2014). Rice bacterial blight disease gene OsSWEET11/Xa13/Os8N3 is involved in plant-pathogen interaction (Yang et al. 2006). In addition, OsSWEET11 interacts with two copper transporter family member COPT1 and COPT5 to transport copper (Yuan et al. 2010). Two Arabidopsis sucrose transporters SWEET11 and 12 are phosphorylated by drought- and ABA-activated SnRK2 protein kinases. This phosphorylation promotes the sucrose transport activities of SWEET11 and 12 to increase sucrose contents, which leads to the drought tolerance (Chen et al. 2022a). Arabidopsis SWEET13 is vital for pollen nutrition and therefore plant fertility (Sun et al. 2013). In maize, ZmSWEET4c transports hexose across the basal endosperm transfer layer, unique epidermal cells located at the juncture of flial and maternal tissues. Intriguingly, mutants of maize ZmSWEET4c and its rice ortholog OsSWEET4 all result in the defects in seed flling (Sosso et al. 2015).

Roles of SWEETs in abiotic stress adaption have been reported in Arabidopsis (Chen et  al. 2022a). However, SWEETs responses to abiotic stresses in crops remain largely elusive. We previously identifed ZmSWEET1b as a positive regulator of maize salt tolerance using RNA-seq (NCBI accession number GSE128432). To functionally analyze maize ZmSWEET1b gene, we adopted the CRISPR/ Cas9 technique to generate independent ZmSWEET1b knockout lines. Herein, we characterized cereal crop maize SWEET family member ZmSWEET1b, with emphasis on the survey of ZmSWEET1b responses to salinity stress.

 Crop yield depends on efficient allocation of sucrose from leaves to seeds. In Arabidopsis, phloem loading is mediated by a combination of SWEET sucrose effluxers and subsequent uptake by SUT1/SUC2 sucrose $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ symporters. ZmSUT1 is essential for carbon allocation in maize, but the relative contribution to apoplasmic phloem loading and retrieval of sucrose leaking from the translocation path is not known.

 Here we analysed the contribution of SWEETs to phloem loading in maize.

 We identified three leaf-expressed SWEET sucrose transporters as key components of apoplasmic phloem loading in Zea mays L. ZmSWEET13 paralogues (a, b, c) are among the most highly expressed genes in the leaf vasculature. Genome-edited triple knock-out mutants were severely stunted. Photosynthesis of mutants was impaired and leaves accumulated high levels of soluble sugars and starch. RNA-seq revealed profound transcriptional deregulation of genes associated with photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism. Genome-wide association study (GWAS) analyses may indicate that variability in ZmSWEET13s correlates with agronomical traits, especifically flowering time and leaf angle.
