Sugars are the important source of energy for both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Depending on their need organisms have established diferent ways to promote sugar transport across the cell membrane by maintaining the rate of sugar infux and efux. Over the last two decades, various sugar transporters were identifed in bacteria, fungi, plants and humans, which perform an important role in development, metabolism, growth, and homeostasis (Chen et al. 2010). Presently, sugar transporters were categorized into three distinct superfamilies which includes the major facilitator superfamily such as glucose transporters (GLUTs) (Deng et al. 2015), the sodium solute symporter family, such as sodium glucose cotransporters (SGLTs) and Sugar Will Eventually be Exported Transporter (SWEET) proteins (Xuan et al. 2013; Tao et al. 2015). On the basis of genome wide analysis, various number of SWEET genes have been identifed in plants, including 17 in Arabidopsis thaliana (Chen et al. 2010), 21 in Oryza sativa (Yuan and Wang 2013), 23 in Sorghum bicolor (Mizuno et al. 2016), 52 in Glycine max (Patil et al. 2015), 35 in Solanum tuberosum (Manck-Gotzenberger and Requena 2016), 29 in Solanum lycopersicum (Feng and Frommer 2015), 33 in Malus domestica (Wei et al. 2014) and 17 in Vitis vinifera (Chong et al. 2014). Based on the number of 3-TM domain, SWEET proteins have been classifed into three major types, one is semiSWEET which is found in bacteria containing only one 3-TM domain, another one is SWEET which is found in eukaryotes attached via linker element between two 3-TM domains (7-TM) and the third one is extraSWEET which might evolve due to gene duplication of 7-TM (Xuan et al. 2013; Patil et al. 2015). The recently identifed family of SWEET sugar transporters in plants perform crucial roles in various developmental processes such as pollen nutrition (Sun et al. 2013) nectar secretion (Lin et al. 2014), seed flling (Chen et al. 2015), phloem loading function for distance translocation of sucrose (Chen et al. 2012) and regulating gibberellin response (Kanno et al. 2016). SWEET sugar transporter family seemingly translocate carbohydrates to diferent plant tissues, including both monocots and dicots.

The originating members of SWEET sugar transporters were studied to fnd out the function of membrane proteins in plants by using diferent fuorescent sugar sensors techniques. AtSWEET1 and AtSWEET8 are the frst identifed SWEET proteins in Arabidopsis which transport hexose sugars. Similar fuorescent sucrose sensors were used to identify other SWEET members which can transport sucrose (Chen et al. 2012; Lin et al. 2014). SWEET members may also function in the mobilization of carbohydrates mainly glucose, galactose, and fructose, which accumulate on leaves during senescence (Chen et al. 2010). Phylogenetic analysis of SWEET proteins reveals that they are broadly conserved in eukaryotes and ubiquitous in plants. The SWEET protein family is further subdivided into fve diferent clades in which four clades were represented by plants, and one clade is represented by metazoans (Chen et al. 2010). Seven SWEET genes have been identifed in the genome of Caenorhabditis elegans while only a single SWEET gene have been identifed in humans and mice. In Arabidopsis thaliana, a total of 17 SWEET homologs classifed as AtSWEET1 to AtSWEET17 which bidirectionally transport both mono and disaccharides along the substrate concentration gradient and across the plasma membrane (Chen et al. 2015). Interestingly, pathogen infection such as Xanthomonas oryzae causing blight disease in rice directly induces the expression of SWEET genes to utilize sucrose from the plant (Chen et al. 2010). In the past few years, many reviews have been published on sucrose and glucose transporters mainly focussed on its physiological role in plants and animals, but little is known till date about this novel family of SWEETs sugar transporter. In this review, we will be summarizing the structure, evolution, transport mechanism, diverse physiological roles of SWEET proteins and their applications in the feld of agriculture. We also discuss how CRISPR/CAS9 and TALENs based genome editing tools are used to engineer SWEET mutants in plants. This review will provide a strong background for the researchers working in this area. It will facilitate better understanding of the molecular evolution and function of SWEET transporters, while also providing a profound reference for other species.


## Structure and evolution of plant SWEET transporters


Understanding deep aspects about the structural and functional relationship of SWEET transporters are important for studying how eukaryotic SWEETs are involved in the transport of sugars, which may further be advantageous in engineering sugar fux. The SWEET family of sugar transporters is unique in their structure which contains seven multipass TM domains containing two internal THBs. SWEETs possibly originate due to the prokaryotic gene duplication unit which probably adds an inversion linker helix loop (Chen et al. 2015). Structural resolution studies manifest that two individual semiSWEET proteins combines in a parallel orientation to create a translocation pore complex. Visualizing structural basis of semiSWEET proteins confers that a single SWEET unit containing two THBs was intended to create the translocation path (Xu et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2014). Less information is known about the biological signifcance of SWEET homologs in prokaryotes and mammals. However, there is the database known as dbSWEET which consists of more than 2000 SWEET homologs from both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. This database will help researchers to better understand, analyze and predict the function of sugar transporters by designing mutational experiments and simulation studies (Gupta and Sankararamakrishnan 2018).

The SWEET1 family was identifed as a potential sugar transporter with 17 other members found in Arabidopsis and 21 in rice with $2 7 - 8 0 \%$ identity (Chen et  al. 2010). The sequence alignment study of all reported AtSWEETs using Clustal Omega along with their secondary structure is shown in Fig. 1a. It is shown that AtSWEET proteins contain seven TM helixes. The frst TM helix of AtSWEET1, AtSWEET16, and AtSWEET17 starts from N-ter methionine position and covers 30 aminoacid long sequences as compared to other AtSWEETs. The THB (TMs 1–3) from the N-terminal region shows similarity in their structure with C-terminal THB (TMs 5–7). Both the 3-THB parts are arranged in a parallel orientation constituting as a single unit. TM4 act as linker helix which is fused with N and C terminal helix bundles (Fig. 1b). The protein sequence of linker helix is found to be non conserved among various SWEET transporters (Chen et al. 2010). SemiSWEET which is a prokaryotic homolog contain only single THB (Xuan et al. 2013). The membrane dynamics of SWEET proteins reveal diferent integration, including structural TM helix arrangement related to other well known seven pass membrane proteins such as G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) or PnuC vitamin transporters (Yee et al. 2013; Jaehme et al. 2014). Similarly glucose transporter in rice OsSWEET2b found to have an asymmetrical THB pair which is attached via an inversion linker TM helix to form the internal translocation pore complex (Tao et al. 2015). Structural analysis suggests that OsSWEET2b forms inward open state homomeric trimers apparent towards the cytosolic phase. TM4 strongly binds with the frst THB within a protomer region and thus arbitrates key contacts among other proteins to modulate gene expression. Generally, the covalent fusion of two TM bundles through an inversion TM helix creates an asymmetrical sugar transport pathway in eukaryotic SWEETs. This covalent fusion enhance their structural and functional features as compared to the simpler symmetrical semiSWEETs to accommodate diferent substrates or modulate their substrate specifcity.

Introns are the hallmark features of eukaryotic genes which are responsible for providing the genetic diversity through alternative splicing. It was reported in earlier studies that unicellular eukaryotes generally have fewer introns than multicellular eukaryotes (Irimia and Roy 2014; Da Lage et al. 2013). Recently, Hu et al. (2016) has studied 228 SWEET genes and found that unicellular organisms such as fungi or oomycetes have none or few introns per gene compared with multicellular organisms. In contrast, SWEET genes in plants commonly contain 4–5 introns per gene. Structural characteristic features and conserved regions of the tomato SlSWEET genes were mapped to determine the structure of genes containing exons and introns and found that tomato MtN3/saliva/SWEET gene family have introns within their genome sequences. SWEET1d contain eight exons, SWEET3 contain seven exons, SWEET5b, SWEET7a, SWEET7b, SWEET12b contain fve exons and the rest of the gene family members contain six exons (Feng and Frommer 2015). Taking prior hypothesis into the review, Hu et al. (2016) has proposed a fusion hypothesis to explain how SWEET proteins might have been evolved earlier. During evolution, when a methanogenic archaeon engulfs a bacterium lead to the transfer of semiSWEET genes into the host genome. Consequently, bacterial SemiSWEET and host genes combine to form a twin-THB SWEET, but it remains ambiguous that how conserved TM4 was inserted or generated between two THBs (Adams and Palmer 2003; Timmis et al. 2004). Gene duplication and gene fusion are the major driving forces occured during the evolution and distribution of SWEET transporters. The key residues involved in sugar transport by SWEETs were found to be conserved during evolution (Jia et al. 2017). The frst SWEET gene was formed as a result of gene duplication of SemiSWEET and TM4 be a part of a 4-TM transporter intermediate (Fig. 1b). Eukaryotic SWEETs were further amplifed via gene duplication or horizontal gene transfer which results in the simultaneous development of a primordial SWEET. This is in support with the fnding that no prokaryote with more than one SemiSWEET has been identifed till date (Patil et al. 2015). Importantly, plant SWEET proteins actively participates in the intercellular transport and cellular secretion. The insight gained from the structures of SWEET transporters and mutation studies of conserved residues will improve the current knowledge of sugar transport mechanism, also allows the comparative studies of diferent superfamilies involved in the sugar transport and their evolution.


## Transport mechanism and substrate binding pocket of SWEET proteins


Molecular dynamics simulation studies and use of crystal structures are valuable for our understanding the detailed mechanism of sugar transport by SWEET proteins. They have the ability to mediate both cellular uptake and efux. SWEET proteins might function as uniporters due to its low afnity and relative $\mathrm { p H }$ independence in vivo (Chen et al. 2010; Eom et al. 2015). The signifcant role of proline tetrad in sugar transportation has been shown by all the SWEET proteins of Arabidopsis. It might facilitate precise structural rearrangement related to shift between conformational states which potentially act as the centre for gating the sugar transportation. Usually, in semiSWEETs, there is a well conserved PQ motif present at the corresponding site on TM1 (Xu et al. 2014; Lee et al. 2015). The structural organization of semiSWEETs reveals the presence of tryptophan and asparagine pairs which form the binding pocket site thus facilitating sugar transport (Xu et al. 2014). From observation of split-GFP and split-ubiquitin experiment, the structural basis of homo and hetro-oligomerization of SWEET was explained by the trimeric assemblage of OsSWEET2b in rice. In comparison with SemiSWEETs, no tryptophan pairs were found along the cavity of OsSWEET2b. Rather than, $\mathrm { C y s } ^ { 5 8 }$ on THB1 and $\mathrm { P h e ^ { 1 8 1 } }$ on THB2 are present at equivalent positions in OsSWEET2b, while in Arabidopsis AtSWEET1, a $\mathrm { S e r } ^ { 5 4 }$ and $\mathrm { T r p } ^ { 1 7 6 }$ are present at equivalent position (Tao et al. 2015). Crystal structure of AtSWEET13 of $2 . 8 \mathrm { \AA }$ resolution was reported in the inwardfacing conformation with a substrate analog $2 ^ { \prime }$ -deoxycytidine $5 ^ { \prime }$ -monophosphate bound in the central cavity (Han Lei et al. 2017). SWEET transporters function as actual transporters in a way diferent to channels that sustain a rigidbody rocking type movement at the time of transport cycle, related to the movement that occurs in the alternate sugar transporters. In this transport process, glutamine serves as a key element of the cytosolic gate through cross-protomer hydrogen bonds. But in eukaryotic SWEET, the absence of glutamine adjacent to proline shows that similar crossprotomer hydrogen bond is not essential for the formation of the cytosolic gate, which might be due to the presence of covalent linkage between TM4. SWEETs seem to be too small to transport sugars on their own. Functioning of SWEET proteins requires assembly into oligomers, forming a translocation pore which requires at least an SWEET dimer. This was deduced by the mutagenesis study, which leads to the identifcation of dominant negative mutation in AtSWEET1 which suppresses the action of two co-expressed wild type protein (Xuan et al. 2013). After studying a large number of proteins in diferent plant species, it has been concluded that eukaryotic SWEETs contain multiple phosphorylation sites at the cytosolic C terminal end with an average length of $\sim 4 5$ amino acids. Moreover, the cytosolic C terminal acts as the binding site for regulatory elements of diferent proteins. SWEET proteins also act as receptors for sugars, which might play an important role in signal transduction. Therefore revealing the various properties of SWEETs and SemiSWEETs it will be easy to fnd out their afnities, turnover rate and substrate spectrum (Chen et al. 2015). To elucidate the transport mechanism of SWEET proteins in plants, it is necessary to obtain their high-resolution structures and to study the dynamics of SWEETs. Given the importance of sugar transport mechanism in plants, it will be important to study the physiological roles of SWEET transporters and their application in the feld of agriculture.


## Diverse physiological roles of SWEET transporters in plants


SWEETs were thought to play diverse physiological functions in the plant system. Plant genome normally contains about 20 SWEET paralogs which are found to be diferentially expressed in tissues and are involved in the transport of diferent sugar molecules. The SWEET family of sugar transporters in Arabidopsis is divided into four diferent subclades sharing almost $2 7 - 8 0 \%$ identity. Various SWEET transporters belonging to diferent subclades in Arabidopsis preferentially transport distinct sugar moiety. Clade I members of SWEETs mainly transport 2-deoxyglucose moiety while clade II preferentially transports glucose. Clade III members mainly utilize sucrose as a substrate, whereas members of the clade IV (AtSWEET16 and AtSWEET17) mediate unidirectional transport of fructose (Chen et al.

2015). SWEET transporters were confned to distinct cellular compartments, particularly localized in plasma membrane such as SWEET1, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 15 (Kryvoruchko et al. 2016; Seo et al. 2011), the vacuole (SWEET16 and 17) (Chardon et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2014; Klemens et al. 2013) and the Golgi (SWEET9 and 15) (Chen et al. 2015; Lin et al. 2014) which monitors sugar transport in diferent cellular compartments respectively. Diferential expression analysis, localization studies and mutant screening in Arabidopsis has implement researchers to fnd out specialized roles of various SWEET proteins in sugar transport. We have also mentioned distinct physiological roles of diferent SWEET proteins in Table 1. These novel fndings suggest that the members of the SWEET gene family have distinct biological functions which play crucial roles in plant growth and development. The diverse physiological roles of SWEET proteins were further discussed below in detail.


## SWEET proteins are involved in fower, fruit and seed development


In a study, based on RNA sequencing data and expression profle it was found that SWEET genes also have an important role in fruit development and ripening. For example, AnmSWEET5 and AnmSWEET11 from Ananas comosus were found to be highly expressed during the early stages of fruit development (Guo et al. 2018). Similarly in the apple genome, 9 MdSWEET genes were highly expressed throughout the fruit development. Among them, MdSWEET9b and MdSWEET15a are likely to be involved in the regulation of sugar accumulation in apple (Zhen et al. 2018). PsSWEET genes from pea were strongly expressed at the time of germination and seed development (Jameson et al. 2016). Analyses of cis regulatory elements in the promoter regions and expression profles of GhSWEET genes in Gossypium hirsutum revealed that they were likely to be involved in the cotton development and abiotic stresses (Li et al. 2018). AtSWEET8 from Arabidopsis also known as RPG1 is expressed in the tapetum membrane. It was reported that mutation in tapetum expressed AtSWEET8 gene causes male sterility which results in inviable pollen, thus consistent with a role in the transport of glucose for pollen nutrition (Guan et al. 2008). Tomato SlSWEET5b/ Lestd1, a member of low afnity bidirectional glucose transporter is expressed peculiarly in maturing pollen grains (Salts et al. 2005). Likewise, AtSWEET8 and OsSWEET11 in rice also have a prominent role in pollen viability. Gene silencing of OsSWEET11 reduces the pollen starch content, which may lead to male sterility in rice (Yang et al. 2006). Arabidopsis AtSWEET5 (also known as Vegetative Cell Expressed 1, VEX1) is involved in the transport of sugars specially in the vegetative cell of pollen grains and found to be expressed in fully developed, hydrated and germinating pollens (Engel et al. 2005). Also at the tricellular pollen stage, it was found that the expression of AtVEX1 is highest in male gametophytes cells, implying its function in pollen development (Bock et al. 2006). In situ hybridization analysis of Arabidopsis AtSWEET1 suggests that it is highly expressed in stamen primordia and during the early stage of foral development (Wellmer et al. 2006). Similarly one of the study found that the expression level of Arabidopsis AtSWEET15, AtSWEET14, AtSWEET13, AtSWEET8, AtSWEET7, AtSWEET5, AtSWEET4 and AtSWEET1 were higher in fower; AtSWEET14 and AtSWEET13 predominantly in stamen; AtSWEET8 mainly in microspores; AtSWEET15 and AtSWEET1 in petal and AtSWEET4 in sepal (Moriyama et al. 2006). SWEET genes in diverse plant species have been described which have a role in reproductive development and growth. One studied example is the LIM7 (Lily messages Induced at Meiosis) of lily which is a SWEET-type gene found in microsporocytes and was induced during meiotic prophase cell cycle (Kobayashi et al. 1994). Golgi membrane located SWEET9 is a nectar specifc transporter in eudicots which act as sugar efux transporter specifcally involved in nectar production (Lin et al. 2014). Another example of gene silencing, which triggers male sterility is NEC1 from petunia which is a member of clade III SWEET homologous protein is involved in sugar secretion in nectarines. NEC1 is expressed in nacteries and is involved in the regulation of development which negatively correlates with the nectarial starch content (Ge et al. 2000, 2001). In Arabidopsis, plasma membrane localized AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 were highly expressed in developing seeds which are involved in the transport of sucrose from the seed coat to embryo (Chen et al. 2015).


## SWEET proteins functions in the transport of diferent gibberellins


Recent developmental studies of SWEET genes found that some of the SWEET family proteins not only involved in the sugar transport mechanism but also function in plant hormone transport (Kanno et al. 2016). In Arabidopsis, it was studied that AtSWEET13 and AtSWEET14 (member of clade III proteins) are involved in the transport of different gibberellins (GAs). AtSWEET13/AtSWEET14 double mutant plants were unable to transport exogeneous GA and show altered responses during seed germination. Consequent to further observation in the exogenous transport of GA in AtSWEET13/AtSWEET14 double mutants provides the clearest evidence that these SWEET family members have an important role in GA transport (Xu et al. 2014). Recently in pea, it was found that interaction between SWEET and CWINV (cell wall invertase) genes in the presence of plant hormone cytokinins led to the multiple shoot formation and loss of apical dominance during pathogen infection by Rhodococcus fascians (Dhandapani et al. 2016). Although this is the frst study depicting the role of SWEETs in the transport of plant hormone. Therefore, on the basis of current research, it is intriguing to hypothesize that as a companion to sugar transport; SWEET members may also involve in the transport of alternative plant hormones, signaling molecules or some metabolites. Importantly, the higher plants continuously requires balanced transport of nutrients in the phloem which is fulflled by SWEET transporters. The detailed mechanisms of apoplasmic phloem loading have been described.


## SWEET proteins in apoplasmic phloem loading mechanism


Many of the previous dye tracer techniques have revealed about apoplasmic phloem loading in stems, but the specifc transport element that mainly assists the transport of sucrose into the sieve element apoplast is not yet characterized. It has been experimentally proved that phloem loading in the stems is executed by SWEET transporters. These SWEET transporters serve as passive uniporter which discharges sucrose or hexoses along the concentration gradient across the cell membrane (Baker et al. 2012; Braun 2012; Eom et al. 2015; Latorraca et al. 2017). The apoplasmic mechanism of phloem loading suggests that mesophyll cell efux sucrose into the apoplasm which was further transported to phloem parenchyma through plasmodesmata using bundle sheath cell facing phloem (Giaquinta 1983; Ayre 2011). However, to support this hypothesis, there was no direct evidence, until the detection of SWEET efux carriers, which might be restricted in the phloem parenchyma cells (Chen et al. 2012). Once the sucrose efux into the phloem apoplast, it is transported by a sucrose transporter (SUT) and SWEET efux, to the sieve element/companion complex which results in elevating the level of sucrose in the sieve element/companion complex apposing sucrose concentration gradient (Ayre 2011) (Fig. 2).

It has been reported that sucrose transportation across the plasma membrane is carried out by clade III members. Arabidopsis AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 show $8 8 \%$ resemblance and are the closest paralogs among the seven members in clade III. Some SWEETs had been identifed as a pH-independent, bidirectional and low-afnity sucrose transporters. For example, in Arabidopsis AtSWEET12, the Michaelis Constant (Km) of sucrose uptake is $7 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , and the Km of efux was more than $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ (Ayre 2011). OsSWEET11 (Os8N3/Xa13) which is an ortholog of AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 was characterized as a sucrose transporter in rice (Chen et al. 2012). It was studied that OsSWEET11 is located in the plasma membrane of transformed rice callus and conversely expressed in the phloem of leaf tissues. The localization and functional aspects of OsSWEET11 indicates its functional role in phloem loading (Chu et al. 2006). Transcription factors also plays an important role in modulating SWEET gene expression. For example in rice, OsDOF11 (DNA BINDING WITH ONE FINGER 11) modulates sugar transport in the vascular tissues by regulating the expression of SWEET genes (Wu et al. 2018). Leaf phloem parenchymatic cells which are located near the sieve element/companion cell complex where phloem loading take place is the expected expression site for these SWEETs. That’s why the participation of these SWEETs in apoplasmic phloem loading has been strongly determined (Chen et al. 2012). For instance, simultaneous upregulation of AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 in leaves of water defcit plants increased phloem loading (Durand et al. 2018). RNA expression profle of sorghum reveals that three paralogously duplicated genes of SbSWEET13 that is SbSWEET13a, SbSWEET13b and SbSWEET13c are the most expressed SWEET genes of clade III in leaves and stems. These expression patterns were further corroborated with sucrose accumulation in the stem of sweet sorghum cultivar (Makita et al. 2015; Bihmidine et al. 2016). Similarly, the closely related SvSWEET13b gene in green millet was found to be strongly expressed in mature stem tissue during the developmental stage directing the apoplasmic phloem unloading of sucrose (Martin et al. 2016; McGaughey et al. 2016). Apart from the role of SWEETs in phloem unloading, they also allows facilitated difusion of sucrose into the apoplasm of mature stem. In millet, ably located in the plasma membrane of phloem parenchyma cells. Apoplasmic sucrose is converted into glucose and fructose by plant/ microbial invertase for nutrient availability. Finally sucrose is taken up and concentrated in the sieve element/companion cell complex by an $\mathrm { H } +$ coupled sucrose symporter SUT/SUC energized by proton pump ATPase

SvSWEET13b was co-expressed along with the SUTs and various other aquaporin genes. It was hypothesized that $S \nu S \ –$ - WEET13b and aquaporins (like plasma membrane localized, SvNIP and SvPIP and tonoplast localized, SvTIP) play an important role in sucrose and water sorting between cytosol, vacuoles and the apoplasmic storage parenchyma cells for sustaining cell turgidity (McGaughey et al. 2016; Moore and Cosgrove 1991). Triple knockout mutant of ZmSWEET13 paralogues impaired phloem loading in Zea mays. These mutants accumulates high level of soluble sugars and starch (Bezrutczyk et al. 2018). To fulfll these promising roles for SWEETs in mature stem, a lot of information regarding tissue and cell localization is required. Furthermore, it should be administered that how sucrose efux from parenchyma cells is regulated and function in association with other sucrose transporters. Does this coordinated function of SWEETs with other SUTs enhance the rate of sucrose translocation towards sink? Clear mechanism of phloem loading in crop plants mainly in rice is not very clearly understood, which should be taken as future consideration. Structure prediction of SWEET proteins can unravel the mechanism of phloem loading. Can we develop the crystal structure of SWEET proteins to correlate its structure and function? All these queries remain to be answered. Apart from the role of SWEETs in phloem loading, many studies have shown that they also play crucial roles in abiotic stress tolerance.


## SWEET proteins are involved in partitioning sugar transport under diferent osmotic stress conditions


Plants have to maintain a steady regulation on vacuolar sugar transport and storage to sustain with diferent environmental constraints. Vacuole membrane localized sugar transporter CsSWEET16 from the tea plant contributed to sugar compartmentalization across the vacuole and function in modifying cold tolerance in Arabidopsis (Wang et al. 2018). In Arabidopsis AtSWEET17, AtSWEET16, AtSWEET12, AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET4 actively participate in the development of aerial parts or roots and are also involved in abiotic stress tolerance by partitioning sugar transport (Zhou et al. 2014). The Arabidopsis AtSWEET15 also known as SAG29 (senescence-associated genes) putatively encodes a protein containing two MtN3 domains which are found to be expressed specifcally in senescence tissues; however the transcript level gradually increases at the time of natural leaf senescence under diferent osmotic stress conditions including cold, high salinity, and drought mediated by abscisic aciddependent pathway (Quirino et al. 1999). Overexpression lines of SAG29/AtSWEET15 exhibit enhanced leaf senescence in transgenic plant (Seo et al. 2011). Interestingly, the expression of MaSWEETs genes in banana was found to be upregulated, which play an important role in response to cold, salt and osmotic stress (Miao et al. 2017). Recently, genome-wide analysis of BoSWEET genes from Brassica oleracea var. capitata L. report probable candidate genes that promote sugar translocation which further enhance chilling tolerance in plant (Zhang et al. 2019). Heterologous expression of MaRAP2-4, an AP2-ERF transcription factor from Mentha regulates bidirectional sugar transporter AtSWEET10 which modulates water logging stress tolerance in Arabidopsis (Phukan et al. 2014, 2015, 2017). It is also important to understand the molecular mechanism of sugar efux and signaling during pathogen infection in plants.


## Potential role of SWEETs in pathogen nutrition


Most of the pathogens require glucose as a carbon source from their hosts. To fulfll their requirements, pathogens hijack the host sugar efux machinery which is essential for the growth and development of the host. Pathogens presumably monitor sugar efux at the site of infection by modulating SWEET mRNA levels, which have a direct impact on the growth and development of pathogen as well as the host immune system. The best known example is the Xa13 locus in rice (SWEET11/Os8N3) which is responsible for recessive blight disease resistance in rice (Yang et al. 2006; Chu et al. 2006; Yuan et al. 2009). During pathogen infection, the TAL (transcription activator-like) efector molecule precisely binds with the cis regulatory element of the promoter of SWEET gene and modulates transcription. This molecular mechanism enhances the efux of sugars which is utilized by pathogens. For example, rice OsSWEET11 modulates the rate of transcription by binding with the promoter of SWEET genes (Fig. 3). RNAi mediated gene silencing of OsSWEET11 in rice confer resistance against pathogen Xoo (Chu et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2006). Also, inhibition of OsSWEET11 located in mesophyll cells imparts resistance against sheath blight disease caused by Rhizoctonia solani (Gao et al. 2018). Apart from OsSWEET11, other members of SWEETs also perform crucial functions in pathogen nutrition availability. For example, OsSWEET14/Os11N3 which is hijacked by Xoo strain using the TAL efector molecule AvrXa7 or PthXo3 and further activates SWEET gene expression for pathogen nutrition (Zhao et al. 2018). The expression of SWEET genes was also found to be upregulated in leaf tissue of tomato during early infection by root knot nematode (Antony et al. 2010). Since the pathogen TAL efector molecules are extremely vital and peculiar for Xoo infection in plants so that researchers are targeting various properties of TAL efector to develop new approaches to control pathogenicity of Xoo.

TALENs is an artificial nucleases which has been designed by fusing DNA binding domain of the TAL efector molecule with DNA cleavage domain of Fok I restriction endonuclease commonly found in Flavobacterium okeanokoites (Sun and Zhao 2013). By utilizing the TAL efector, a genome editing tool TALENs (TAL Efector Nucleases) has been developed which is used to generate site specifc modifcation in the genome (Li et al. 2012). By utilizing this genome editing tool, several lines of disease resistant rice have been generated (Li et al. 2013; Streubel et al. 2013). This has been supported by the observation that when the TAL efector binding site within the promoter region of OsSWEET14 was disrupted using TALEN editing strategies found that these mutant lines were resistant to AvrXa7 or PthXo3 dependent Xoo strain (Li et al. 2013).

TALEN technology was applied to edit the efector binding elements of susceptible SWEET genes in past few years. Whereas, in recently years, CRISPR/Cas9 is more efcient and easier to operate. CRISPR/Cas9 is used to engineer virus resistance in plants, either by direct targeting/cleaving or by modifying the host plant genome to introduce viral immunity (Zaidi et al. 2016; van Schie and Takken 2014). In fact, problems about exogenous marker introduction in transgenic plants have been solved via transient gene expression, due to which it preferred over the other genome editing technologies. Since the DNA-binding specifcity could be predicted easily, so by utilizing this approach potential binding site of unknown SWEET could be identifed and altered using CRISPR/Cas9 technology to promote research and crop improvement in response to various pathogens. For example, OsSWEET13 mutant using CRISPR/Cas9 technology reveals cryptic resistance gene for bacterial blight of rice (Zhou et al. 2015). Furthermore, interruption of bacterial blight susceptibility genes such as OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET14 has been accomplished in rice (Jiang et al. 2013). OsSWEET11 in rice played an essential role in sucrose efux from maternal tissue during the early stage of caryopsis development based on the phenotypes of CRISPR/ Cas9 edited mutant plants (Ma et al. 2017). CRISPR/Cas9 technology is now efectively applied to create mutations in the efector molecule binding sites in the SWEET promoters, thereby obtaining disease resistant plants without any loss in the productivity (Bi and Yang 2017).

Given the fact that pathogens infect the plants to utilize the required nutrient for efcient growth and reproduction. Recently, it was identified that the pathogen Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. Manihotis TAL efector (TAL20) target MeSWEET10a promoter, which is a clade III hexose and sucrose transporter in cassava thereby enhancing the accumulation of sugars (Cohn et al. 2014). Also, the sugar accumulation in the leaves of Arabidopsis double mutant sweet11/sweet12 triggers the salicylic acid-mediated defense pathway against fungal hemibiotroph Colletotrichum higginsianum (Gebauer et al. 2017). In Ipomoea batatas, plasma membrane localized SWEET transporter IbSWEET10 is responsible for imparting resistant against

Fusarium oxysporum in sweet potato. Expression study found that IbSWEET10 is highly expressed in the vascular tissue of sweet potato (Li et al. 2017). Other sugar transporters of Arabidopsis like AtSWEET2, AtSWEET16, and AtSWEET17 meditates vacuolar sugar transportation. Among these, AtSWEET17 administer the fructose content in leaf vacuoles whereas AtSWEET2 facilitate sugar secretion from roots which also play a vital role in providing resistance against the pathogen Pythium (Chardon et al. 2013; Klemens et al. 2013; Chen et al. 2015).

Above literature supports the evidence of host–pathogen interaction which is mainly involved in the up-regulation the SWEET genes, while in the current study by Asai et al. (2015) reveals that the pathogen attack not only up-regulate the SWEET gene but also down regulate or negatively regulate the SWEET genes. For example, the expression of SWEET15 in tomato was enhanced upon the infection of Botrytis cinerea, which simultaneously down-regulate various other SWEET genes across the four diferent clades. The developmentally regulated glucose transporter of grapevine VvSWEET4 facilitates sugar accumulation during necrotrophic fungal infection of Botrytis cinerea. It was found that VvSWEET4 was overexpressed upon stimulation by ROS and extensive cell death (Chong et al. 2014). There is little information known in the literature about the role of down regulation of various SWEET family genes during plant–pathogen interaction. This down regulation of SWEET genes might be due to the interruption in sugar signaling pathways (Berger et al. 2007; Sade et al. 2013). Also, depth study is required about the diferential expression of SWEET gene during pathogen attack to better understand the physiology of plant–pathogen interaction. Although functional role of SWEET proteins in mycorrhizal symbiosis needs to be established. Based on the earlier research, here we discussed how SWEET proteins play a functional role in response to symbionts and microbiota.


## Involvement of SWEETs in response to symbionts and microbiota


Co-evolution of symbionts with their hosts has increased their range and nutrient availability. The symbionts residing in nodules require continuous energy source either in the form of carbohydrates or as organic acids. Besides plant pathogens, symbionts living inside roots may also target various SWEET genes. A SWEET like gene is highly expressed in the symbiotic tissue of the mycorrhizal protocorm of orchid (Perotto et al. 2014). During symbiotic association between rhizobia and their host legumes, bacteria releases specifc efector molecules which activates the expression of SWEET gene. For microbes or arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus lacking type III secretion system, the secreted efectors may either directly activates the SWEET genes, or by activation of some transcription factors (Fig. 3). In the earlier study, particular MtN3, which is the founder of sweet family protein, was analyzed as nodulin-specifc EST found in the legume plant Medicago truncatula and might be functional in symbiotic association with Rhizobia (Udvardi et al. 1990). Similarly in Arabidopsis SAG29/AtSWEET15 was found to be strongly expressed in the augmentation of club root disease caused by the biotrophic protist Plasmodiophora brassicae (Siemens et al. 2006). Plant SWEET proteins have been found to be involved in providing nutrient to microbes and are, therefore, favorable candidates to play an important role in symbiotic associations. The Mycorrhizal hyphae pose a symbiotic relationship by providing nutrients to their hosts in exchange of sugars (Schussler et al. 2006). Sporadically, mycorrhization induces SWEET proteins which plays an important role in the sugars efux that eventually feeds the symbionts. The microbial community colonizes both the surface and apoplasm of plants (Hacquard et al. 2015). The analysis of the interaction between microbial communities and plant roots eventually helps us to understand that carbon availability is important. In recent years, the potential of SWEETs in controlling the level of nutrients provided to pathogens have been discussed, which determines its ability to contribute towards the enhancement or disease resistance (Bezrutczyk et al. 2017). Plants have the ability to detect pathogen attack by identifying pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) and in turn respond by inducing hexose/ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ symporters, such as STP1, 4 and 13 which counteracts the SWEET-mediated secretion and thus limit apoplasmic sugar accumulation (Fotopoulos et al. 2003; Yamada et al. 2016).


## SWEET genes also act as susceptible genes


SWEET genes are well-know as susceptible genes, and have been a key subject in research of plant disease resistance. All sucrose transporting SWEET proteins in rice act as a susceptibility factor when recruited with the TAL efector molecule in X. oryzae, which is responsible for causing blight disease. Some pathogenic bacteria govern the expression of SWEET genes in diferent plant species. For example, a SWEET gene (UPA) in susceptible pepper plants is transcriptionally induced by TAL efector molecule (AvrBs3) which is mainly secreted by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria (Kay et al. 2009). The TAL efector molecule (Avrb6, a TAL efector determining Xcm pathogenicity) induce the expression of GhSWEET10 confers susceptibility to bacterial blight of cotton (Cox et al. 2017). Designer TAL efectors (dTALEs) were used to study the functional relationship with an advancement of which uncharacterized and with no complementary naturally occurring TAL efector has been analyzed in OsSWEET12 gene. The transcript level of OsS - WEET12 was enhanced during the infection of Xoo strain transformed with dTALEs. These dTALEs were executed to bind with the putative TATA boxes in the promoter region of OsSWEET12 which provides susceptibility to Xoo strain (Streubel et al. 2013). The susceptible Plasmodiophora brassicae infection triggers the expression of specifc BrSWEET genes which further enhance cellular glucose and fructose uptake in Brassica rapa (Li et al. 2018).


## Applications of SWEETs in agriculture


Though SWEET proteins are involved in the transport of distinct sugar molecules in plants and bacteria, it can also be utilized for various biotechnological applications mainly in the feld of agriculture. Various SWEETs were studied which have a role in nitrogen fxation in leguminous plants and involved in pathogen resistance as discussed in the review. These properties of SWEET proteins can be explored and utilized for the sustainable development of agriculture. Symbiotic nitrogen fxation in nodules depends on a continuous supply of carbon to both plants and bacteria. The nodule specifc SWEET proteins in M. truncatula, MtSWEET11 is involved in the transport of sucrose and play critical roles in pathogen susceptibility (Kryvoruchko et al. 2016). Recently studied SWEET transporter from Lotus japonicus, LjSWEET3 has a role in transporting either hexoses or sucrose in nodules and also suggests the presence of multiple routes of carbon accumulation into nodules (Sugiyama et al. 2017). SWEETs also function in determining the seed size by direct translocation of carbohydrates. Seed size was determined by the direct import of carbohydrate, which must be increased through domestication. Though, there are numerous appropriate information regarding domestication of sugar transport and the seed-flling transporters. At the time of seed flling, OsSWEET4 in rice and ZmSWEET4c in maize play key role in hexose transportation across the basal endosperm transfer layer (Sosso et al. 2015). Although the utility of seed-flling mechanisms in rice for higher crop yield, SWEET11 and SWEET15 perform an important role in seed flling and nutrient import (Yang et al. 2018). Recently the role of SWEET genes (HbSWEET10a and 16b) were also studied in sugar transport for latex production in Hevea brasiliensis (Sui et al. 2017).

Background: SWEET is a newly identified family of sugar transporters. Although SWEET transporters have been characterized by using Arabidopsis and rice, very little knowledge of sucrose accumulation in the stem region is available, as these model plants accumulate little sucrose in their stems. To elucidate the expression of key SWEET genes involved in sucrose accumulation of sorghum, we performed transcriptome profiling by RNA-seq, categorization using phylogenetic trees, analysis of chromosomal synteny, and comparison of amino acid sequences between SIL-05 (a sweet sorghum) and $\mathtt { B T } \times 6 2 3$ (a grain sorghum).

Results: We identified 23 SWEET genes in the sorghum genome. In the leaf, SbSWEET8-1 was highly expressed and was grouped in the same clade as AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 that play a role in the efflux of photosynthesized sucrose. The key genes in sucrose synthesis (SPS3) and that in another step of sugar transport (SbSUT1 and SbSUT2) were also highly expressed, suggesting that sucrose is newly synthesized and actively exported from the leaf. In the stem, SbSWEET4-3 was uniquely highly expressed. SbSWEET4-1, SbSWEET4-2, and SbSWEET4-3 were categorized into the same clade, but their tissue specificities were different, suggesting that SbSWEET4-3 is a sugar transporter with specific roles in the stem. We found a putative SWEET4-3 ortholog in the corresponding region of the maize chromosome, but not the rice chromosome, suggesting that SbSWEET4-3 was copied after the branching of sorghum and maize from rice. In the panicle from the heading through to 36 days afterward, SbSWEET2-1 and SbSWEET7-1 were expressed and grouped in the same clade as rice OsSWEET11/Xa13 that is essential for seed development. SbSWEET9-3 was highly expressed in the panicle only just after heading and was grouped into the same clade as AtSWEET8/RPG1 that is essential for pollen viability. Five of 23 SWEET genes had SNPs that caused nonsynonymous amino acid substitutions between SIL-05 and BTx623.

Conclusions: We determined the key SWEET genes for technological improvement of sorghum in the production of biofuels: SbSWEET8-1 for efflux of sucrose from the leaf; SbSWEET4-3 for unloading sucrose from the phloem in the stem; SbSWEET2-1 and SbSWEET7-1 for seed development; SbSWEET9-3 for pollen nutrition.

Keywords: Phloem loading, Phloem unloading, Sugar transporter, Bioethanol, RNA-seq, SNP, Photosynthesis

Due to its chemical stability the disaccharide sucrose represents the main or only compound for source-to-sink transport of carbon in many plants including the model species Arabidopsis thaliana [1, 2]. In species like Arabidopsis where phloem loading with sucrose occurs via an apoplastic route [3] this process requires the activity of sugar transporters to mediate sucrose transport across membranes. The release of sucrose into the apoplast is usually mediated by passive sucrose carriers of the SWEET (SUGARS WILL EVENTUALLY BE EXPORTED TRANSPORTERS) family [4]. The subsequent uptake of sucrose from the apoplast into the sieve element-companion cell complex occurs against the concentration gradient leading to sucrose accumulation and thus needs to be mediated by active transporters. Plant genomes code for small families of both passive SWEET carriers and SUCROSE TRANSPORTERS (SUCs or SUTs; [5]) that work as active $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } /$ sucrose-symporters [6]. In Arabidopsis thaliana, nine different AtSUCs [7–9] and 17 SWEETs [10] have been identified. Of these, only SWEET11, SWEET12 [4], and AtSUC2 [11] are required for phloem loading and have been characterized in detail, whereas the functions of the other sucrose transporters are less understood. A major step in the characterization of sucrose transporters is the determination of their transport activity as especially multi-gene families often contain members that do not encode functional proteins [9, 12, 13]. A frequently used method to determine the sucrose transport activity of a transmembrane protein is the expression of the respective gene in a heterologous system, typically yeast cells or Xenopus oocytes. Sucrose uptake can then be analyzed by uptake measurements with radioactive $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -sucrose or electrophysiological methods, respectively. However, the evolutionary distance between plants and the yeast or animal system may lead to several problems that interfere with uptake measurements: (1) Sometimes targeting signals are not recognized and the transporter is not localized in the plasma membrane [14–16]. The transporter might also lack (2) essential protein modifications or (3) interaction partners and therefore does not show its normal transport activity in the heterologous system [16]. Here we describe an alternative method to analyze sucrose transporter activities in planta that uses Arabidopsis mesophyll protoplasts as expression system. Interestingly, we could show that these cells contain no endogenous sucrose transporters [16]. In addition to their accessibility to transient transformation this makes them an optimal system for the characterization of potential sucrose transporters in planta. Gora et al. (2012) showed that esculin can be used as a fluorescent sucrose analog to indirectly measure the transport activity of type I SUCs in the yeast system [17]. We could show that it is also possible to use the esculin uptake assay with protoplasts [16]. Protoplasts are transformed with the gene for a potential sucrose transporter fused to GFP. This allows the identification of protoplasts containing the transport protein in their plasma membrane by GFP fluorescence. In contrast to non-transformed protoplasts or protoplasts transformed with a control construct, protoplasts containing a functional sucrose transporter in the plasma membrane accumulate esculin in their vacuoles which can be monitored by detection of the esculin fluorescence [16]. It was shown that all type I SUCs tested so far take up esculin, as well as type II SUCs of dicotyledons and sucrosespecific SWEETs [16–18]. The esculin assay therefore can be applied to test a variety of sucrose transporters. Furthermore, uptake activities can be quantified in relation to the amount of protein. As the protein of interest is labeled with GFP and the fluorescent molecule esculin is used as substrate both, the amount of protein in the plasma membrane and the accumulated substrate, can be quantified relative to each other by measuring the fluorescence intensities. This provides the possibility to compare the esculin uptake activity, for example, of different sucrose transporters, splice variants, or point mutants [16]. Furthermore, protoplasts can also be transformed with two or more constructs, allowing the analysis of transporter activities in the presence of interaction partners [16]. The quantification of esculin uptake in the presence of an excess of other compounds additionally provides the possibility to identify other possible substrates as other transported molecules competitively inhibit esculin uptake [16]. Here we describe the design of constructs for the expression of genes of potential sucrose transporters in protoplasts, the isolation and transformation of Arabidopsis mesophyll protoplasts, the setup and imaging of the esculin uptake assay, and the quantitative analysis of the results.

SUT proteins are important carriers for transporting sucrose across the plasma membrane or vacuolar membranes (reviewed by Kühn and Grof 2010). Arabidopsis SUT protein has also been found on the chloroplast membrane (Rolland et al. 2003). Rice OsSUT2 is classified in the same group with Arabidopsis AtSUT4, tomato LeSUT4, potato StSUT4, Lotus japonicus LjSUT4, and barley HvSUT2 (Braun and Slewinski 2009; Kühn and Grof 2010). Some of the above-mentioned SUTs, including AtSUT4, StSUT4, and LjSUT4, have been identified as low-affinity/high-capacity transporters (Weise et al. 2000; Reinders et al. 2008). In addition, AtSUT4, LjSUT4, and HvSUT2 are vacuolar transporters according to a previous analysis of transient SUT–GFP fusion protein expression (Endler et al. 2006; Reinders et al. 2008). On the other hand, LeSUT4 and StSUT4 are located on the plasma membrane of sieve elements (Reinders et al. 2002). OsSUT2 contains 12 transmembrane domains and was localized on plasma membrane. Amino acid alignment showed that the number of amino acids in the central inside loops are similar among OsSUT2 and other SUTs in group 4 (according to the classification by Braun and Slewinski 2009) (Fig. 1); however, the length of the OsSUT2 central loop is shorter than that of SUTs belonging to group 2, i.e., AtSUT2 and LeSUT2. LeSUT2 is considered to function as a putative sucrose sensor (Barker et al. 2000). The conserved domains in the extended cytoplasmic loop of LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 play an important role in signal sensing and transduction (Barker et al. 2000). Because the lengths and amino acid sequences of the central loops are significantly different between OsSUT2 and LeSUT2, the regulatory mechanism and function of OsSUT2 might not be completely identical to that of LeSUT2.

Carbohydrate transport from endosperms and embryos to coleoptiles, shoots, and roots is an important process for supplying developing tissues with a carbon source during seed germination and seedling establishment. The levels of OsSUT2 mRNA gradually increased from 1 to 5 DAI (Fig. 3b). However, our previous report showed that the OsSUT1 transcript significantly increased after 1 to 2 DAI and then quickly decreased at 3 DAI (Chen et al. 2010). The expression level of OsSUT1 was the highest among OsSUT members in embryos at early imbibition stages (i.e., DAI 1), but OsSUT2 was the dominantly expressed OsSUT member 5 DAI (Fig. 3a). Thus, the functions and regulations of individual OsSUT genes are different in the embryos of germinating seeds. As shown by the data in Fig. 8, the expression levels of OsSUT2 in scutellum and vascular bundles were higher than in other embryo ground cells, and the OsSUT2 promoter activity was also significantly observed in aleurone layers. According to the OsSUT2 expression patterns in germinating seeds, it was suggested that OsSUT2 play a role to release sucrose from aleurone layers, transport sucrose into scutellum, and also load sucrose into the phloem in germinating seeds. On the other hand, OsSUT1 gene was expressed in the scutellar vascular bundle of germinating embryos but not in the scutellar epithelial cell layer. Therefore, it was suggested that OsSUT1 functioned to load sucrose into phloem for transport to developing shoot and roots but not play a role to transport sucrose from endosperm to embryos (Scofield et al. 2007).

The increased OsSUT2 expression in isolated embryos (without endosperms) during germination was not obvious in dark conditions; however, the significant up-regulation of OsSUT2 was observed in the embryos of germinating seeds (with endosperms) in dark conditions. Thus, it was suggested that the sugar transported from endosperm was the key factor for promoting OsSUT2 expression. Sugars not only act as nutrients and energy for supporting plant growth but also function as signals controlling plant development and the expression of various genes (reviewed by Gibson 2005; Rolland et al. 2006). The data in Fig. 6 showed that the transcript levels of rice OsSUT2 could be slightly enhanced by glucose and sucrose after 1 day of treatment and significantly enhanced after 5 days of treatment. Moreover, since the OsSUT2 expression was not affected by mannitol, the sugar-enhanced OsSUT2 expression was not caused by osmotic effect. Sugarenhanced expression has also been observed with OsSUT1 (Matsukura et al. 2000; Chen et al. 2010). However, the positive effect of sugar on OsSUT1 expression occurs after 5 days of treatment, and 1-day sugar treatment downregulates OsSUT1 expression (Chen et al. 2010). Thus, the mechanisms of sugar-mediated regulation are different for OsSUT1 and OsSUT2. Sucrose-induced signal transduction for gene regulation could involve sucrose as a direct signal that is sensed by a sensor located on the cell membrane or an intracellular sensor. In addition, sucrose metabolites, such as glucose, could be signals to trigger the downstream transduction pathway (reviewed by Halford et al. 1999). The nonmetabolizable sucrose analog palatinose had a similar effect on OsSUT2 expression in rice embryos as sucrose, suggesting that sucrose acts as a direct molecule for triggering the up-regulation of OsSUT2 expression. In addition, the sensor for sucrose signal transduction is expected to be located on the cell membrane because of the lack of palatinose transport into plant cells (Sinha et al. 2002; Rolland et al. 2006). Moreover, since there was no effect of mannitol on OsSUT2 expressions (Fig. 6), it was suggested that the up-regulation of OsSUT2 expressions by palatinose was not caused by osmotic effect. Moreover, the data showing that 3-OMG can also conduct the same positive effect on OsSUT2 expression in germinating embryos as glucose suggests that the glucose-induced OsSUT2 expression was mediated by a hexokinaseindependent pathway. In contrast, glucose-regulated OsSUT1 expression in germinating embryos was via a hexokinasedependent pathway (Chen et al. 2010). Changes in the transcriptional activity of the OsSUT2 promoter in embryos during germination correlated with the mRNA levels. OsSUT2 promoter activity was also upregulated by glucose in embryos. Thus, promoter regulation was a key step for controlling OsSUT2 expression. The predicted cis-acting elements on the OsSUT2 promoter were searched in the PLACE database (Higo et al. 1999), identifying a SUSIBA2 transcription factor-binding site (WBOXHVISO1; W-box) 477 bp upstream of the ATG translation start codon. SUSIBA2 is a sugar-inducible WRKY protein that can bind the sugar-responsive element on the barley isoamylase 1 promoter (Sun et al. 2003). Further study is needed regarding whether the interaction of SUSIBA2 and the W-box on the OsSUT2 promoter is a key factor to controlling sugar-responsive OsSUT2 expression.

In conclusion, we identified OsSUT2 as a plasma membrane transporter. OsSUT2 expression in germinated embryos correlates with the developmental stage, with regulation depending on the sugar transported from endosperms. The developmental regulation and signaling pathways of sugarresponsive OsSUT2 expression in germinating embryos are different from those of OsSUT1. Glucose-enhanced OsSUT2 expression was mediated by a hexokinase-independent pathway, and sucrose is sensed by a sensor located on the plasma membrane to up-regulate OsSUT2 expression. We also found that promoter activity is the major factor controlling the developmental stage- and sugar-dependent mRNA accumulation of OsSUT2 in the embryos of germinating seeds. Future studies of the activity of the deleted promoter element and finding the factors that interact with the cis-acting element would be helpful for elucidating the molecular mechanism of OsSUT2 expression in germinating rice embryos.
