$\beta$ -pnp-glucoside, $\beta$ -paranitrophenyl glucoside.

Sugarcane (Saccharum ofcinarum), the primary producer of table sugar, is relentlessly challenged by frequent red rot attacks (caused by Colletotrichum falcatum) in India and subtropical regions of the world (Gujjar et al. 2024a). Sucrose, being chief assimilated carbon produced during photosynthesis, functions as an essential plant metabolite during plant growth and development, with additional role as a signaling molecule (Gujjar et al. 2024b). Sucrose is synthesized in the green tissues of plants and is transported to the sink organs either to be metabolized as an energyproducing molecule or to be stored as starch or other organic compounds (Xu et al. 2018). The process called carbohydrate partitioning is fundamental to growth and development, whereby the plants assimilate, transport and distribute the sugars from green leaves (exporting source) to carbon demanding tissues (importing sinks), such as fruits, seeds, fowers, stems, and roots (Wu et al. 2021). Moreover, this process is also associated with tolerance/resistance to abiotic/biotic stress in plants (Julius et al. 2017; Gujjar et al. 2024b). Sugar transporters, besides being indispensable for sugar translocation among adjacent cells in the plant, are also implicated in both biotic and abiotic stress responses (Julius et al. 2017; Hu et al. 2021). Sucrose Transporters (SUTs) basically belong to the class of membrane-bound sucrose–proton symporters present in plants. As a group of primary sugar transporters, they are indispensable for the transport of sucrose from the intercellular apoplast into the cytosol, specifcally when no plasmodesma exists between adjacent cells (Hu et al. 2021; Sun et al. 2022). SUTs generate high turgor pressure through plasma membrane proton motive force to facilitate phloem loading and active transport of sucrose. Sucrose accumulation in sink tissues such as fruits, seeds, stalks during developmental stages is mediated by active transport of sucrose by SUTs (Bavnhøj et al. 2023). In sugarcane, ShSUT1 was the frst SUT identifed in leaves (Rae et al. 2005) and yellow leaf virus infected sugarcane (Saccharum hybrid) stem (ElSayed et al. 2010). Consequently, fve SUT genes, namely SoSUT1, SoSUT2, SoSUT3, SoSUT4, and SoSUT5 were identifed, and their expressions were analyzed in roots, stems, leaves, inforescence, and buds by qRT-PCR in sugarcane (Niu et al. 2019).

Fungal virulence and pathogenicity are stimulated by the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, followed by release of efector molecules by pathogen to facilitate the host invasion (Gujjar et al. 2024a). Disease resistance proteins (DRPs) are accountable for identifying the potential pathogens and triggering appropriate defense responses in host plants. They chiefy comprise of three domains, a nucleotide-binding site (NBS), leucinerich repeats (LRRs), and putative amino-terminal signaling domain (Belkhadir et al. 2004). LRR domain of DRPs is accredited with the role of determining the magnitude of a particular response, and their action leads to plant cell death in case of hypersensitive response (Harris et al. 2013). NanoLC–MS/MS approaches are the most extensively used approaches in recent times for investigating the whole proteome as well as diferential proteome in crop plants under diferent treatment conditions (Gujjar et al. 2020, 2021, 2024c). In one of the previous study, we investigated the impact of $C .$ . falcatum infection on the abundance of proteins and expression of genes implicated in sucrose metabolism in sugarcane (Gujjar et al. 2024b). In the present study, we identifed eight SUT and four DRP proteins in the stalk tissues of sugarcane through nanoLCMS/MS-based proteomics analysis approach. For the frst time, we are reporting the infuence of $C .$ . falcatum infection on the abundance pattern of SUT and DRP proteins in the stalk tissues of red rot resistant and susceptible cultivars of sugarcane.

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are sucrose– $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ symporters, which mediate the active transport of sucrose across plasma membranes. Since sucrose is translocated from source to sink tissues through the phloem, plasma membrane sucrose transporters are believed to play important roles in mediating carbon partitioning in plants (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Over the last decade, genes encoding SUT proteins have been isolated from a wide range of both monocot and dicot plant species, from source and sink tissues and found to be localised in phloem and non-phloem tissues (see reviews by Williams et al. 2000; Truernit 2001; Lalonde et al. 2003).

In cereal species, SUT proteins mainly have been studied in developing grains. For example, in developing rice caryopses, OsSUT1 protein is present in the plasma membrane of the aleurone cell layer surrounding the endosperm (Furbank et al. 2001) and is essential for transport of assimilates into filling grains (Scofield et al. 2002). A similar role in grain filling has been proposed for HvSUT1 protein in barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and for TaSUT1 in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2002). However, cellular localisation of cereal SUT gene expression in vegetative tissues has been less well characterised despite the fact that SUT mRNAs are detectable in these tissues of rice (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003), maize (Aoki et al. 1999), barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). While in dicot plants there is considerable evidence that SUTs play a role in apoplasmic loading of sucrose into the phloem (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003), there is little evidence for this in cereal species. Indeed, there is some debate over whether phloem loading in cereals occurs via symplasmic or apoplasmic pathways (e.g. Russin et al. 1996, also see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Significantly, antisense repression of OsSUT1 expression in transgenic rice did not appear to affect phloem loading (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002).

Previously we reported the isolation of three cDNAs encoding SUT proteins from developing grains of hexaploid wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). The peptide sequences deduced from the three cDNAs showed $9 8 \%$ identity to one another, all with more than $8 5 \%$ similarity to SUT1 proteins from other cereal species. The three wheat SUT1 proteins were encoded individually by single-copy homeologous genes, designated TaSUT1A, 1B and 1D , which are represented once in each of the A-, B- and D-genomes. Northern blot analysis revealed that the TaSUT1 genes were highly expressed not only in developing grains but also in flagleaf blades, flag-leaf sheaths and culms (internodes) at the pre-heading stage.

In the present study, we further investigated expression of TaSUT1 genes in leaves and stems of hexaploid wheat, by semi-quantitative reverse transcription (RT)– PCR, in situ hybridisation and immunolocalisation. Based on the results from these experiments, together with anatomical analysis, the possible role(s) of TaSUT1 proteins in wheat leaves and stems are discussed.

Source leaves export sucrose that, by long distance transport, is released into non-photosynthetic tissues, such as roots, stems, flowers, fruits and seeds (Ludewig and Flügge 2013). The partitioning of sugars in economically important sink organs is governed by several complex physiological processes, including photosynthetic rate, phloem loading in the source leaf, long-distance translocation in the phloem, phloem unloading in sink organs, post-phloem transport and metabolism of imported sugars in sink cells (Nie et al. 2010). Fleshy fruits are a class of terminal reproductive strong storage sinks, but the mechanism of phloem unloading in these organs has received little attention in comparison with vegetative tissues and developing seeds (Zhang et al. 2006).

Peach fruit is an economically important sink in which sugar accumulation is a major determinant of yield and quality. Generally, the average values of soluble solids content obtained in peach commercial cultivars range between 9 and $1 5 \%$ , even if in some cases they reach up to $2 0 \%$ or more (Layne and Bassi 2008, Byrne et al. 2012). Soluble sugars show different accumulation levels throughout fruit growth when individually analyzed. In detail, glucose and fructose are present in nearly equal amounts and mainly during the early stage of growth, sorbitol levels remain low throughout development, whereas sucrose accumulates and becomes the predominant sugar in mature fruit (Vizzotto et al. 1996, Falchi et al. 2013).

Among the sugars synthesized in a plant, only a few move in the phloem over a long distance, regardless of the species and type of phloem loading considered. In all cases, sucrose is the main form of carbon found in the phloem. In addition to sucrose, polyols (mainly sorbitol and mannitol) and oligosaccharides of the raffinose family can also be found (Lemoine et al. 2013). In Prunus persica, like other Rosaceae species, sucrose and sorbitol are both present in phloem sap as form of translocated carbon. Sugars can exit the phloem through either a symplastic or an apoplastic pathway, but the unloading pathway depends on the particular sink involved and its developmental stage (Lemoine et al. 2013). Concerning the apoplastic pathway, the uptake of hexoses resulting from the hydrolysis of the apoplastic sucrose by cell wall invertases has been suggested to predominate in the sink tissues that undergo cell division and elongation, while sucrose transport predominates in the sink storage tissues (Weschke et al. 2000). In this context, sucrose transporters (SUTs) play pivotal roles in mediating sucrose transport within plants, and their activities have a major impact upon plant growth rates and crop yields. The classification of SUT proteins into different subfamilies reflects either an amino acids sequence homology, and similar substrate affinity and function throughout phloem pathway. The SUT genes found in higher plants exhibit distinct expression patterns, depending on tissue, development and plant species (Kühn and Grof 2010). In apoplastically loading plants, membrane-localized sucrose $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime \mathrm { H } ^ { + } }$ symporters mediate the loading of sucrose into the phloem in source tissues, but, interestingly, sucrose $\mathrm { \Delta } H ^ { + }$ symporter transcripts and proteins have also been localized in sink tissues (Geiger 2011). According to a recent classification (Kühn and Grof 2010), SUTs of dicotyledonous species fall into three distinct groups: SUT1, SUT2 and SUT4 subfamilies. In fruit trees, the path of phloem unloading has been elucidated for a small number of species. These investigations often have taken advantage of the fluorescent marker of phloem transport 6(5)-carboxyfluorescein diacetate (CFDA), a membrane-permeable and nonfluorescent compound that, when degraded to 6(5)-carboxyfluorescein (CF) in live cells, becomes a membrane-impermeable fluorescent dye. This technique showed that symplastic and apoplastic mechanism can be interchanged, depending on genotype and developmental stage. In apple, cherry and pear fruit, there is evidence for an apoplastic step in sucrose and sorbitol unloading, involving sugar transporters (Gao et al. 2003, Zhang et al. 2004, Zhang et al. 2014). A similar pattern has been observed in jujube fruit (Zizyphus jujuba), but in this case the predominantly apoplastic unloading mechanism is interrupted by a transient symplastic phase at the middle stage of growth (Nie et al. 2010). The shift of unloading routes in response to sink development has also been observed in grape fruit: a symplastic mechanism occurs at the early stages, while an apoplastic pathway operates at the late stage of development. In grape berry, the turning point has been observed at or just before the onset of ripening, when the fruit begins to store soluble sugars (Zhang et al. 2006). Moreover, in walnut fruit, distinct unloading patterns have been found in two types of tissues: symplastic in seed and apoplastic in fleshy pericarp (Wu et al. 2004). Although the possibility of apoplastic phloem loading through an active transport pathway has been hypothesized as the most important means of exporting carbohydrates from mature leaves in peach (Moing et al. 1997), unloading mechanisms are still a source of debate. However, carrier-mediated transport has been hypothesized for mesocarp of young peaches (Vizzotto et al. 1996). Other attempts to elucidate the mechanism of sugar accumulation in peach fruits have been carried out by the analysis of key enzymes involved in the main sugar conversion pathways (Moriguchi et al. 1990, Nonis et al. 2007, Morandi et al. 2008). Some authors have postulated a preferential utilization of sorbitol in vegetative sink tissues close to the source, such as young sink leaves and cambium (Moing et al. 1992), and a major role of sucrose in fruit growth (Lo Bianco et al. 1999). Recently, the distribution of sugars among different compartments (free space, cytoplasm and vacuole) of peach mesocarp at two different growth stages has been determined, providing evidence for a predominant cytoplasmic localization in young fruit and a vacuolar localization in mature fruit. Moreover, the same authors showed that the permeability through plasma membrane and tonoplast decreased with peach fruit maturation (Jiang et al. 2013).

In this work, we provide the first description of the phloem unloading pathway in peach fruit, by means of microscopy coupled with the symplastic tracer dye CFDA. In addition, three genes encoding SUTs have been identified, and their transcriptional regulation has been examined in different fruit cell types. The results are discussed in order to present a model for the physiological roles that these carriers may play in carbohydrate partitioning in peach fruit.

Sucrose is the major photosynthetic product in plant species, and it can be transported from photosynthetic tissues to storage sink tissues for starch biosynthesis. Sucrose can also be translocated from source tissues to developing sink tissues and function as an energy source to support organ growth. For example, the sucrose synthesized in embryos of rice seeds is transported to developing young shoots and roots during seed germination. In addition, sucrose provides a carbon source for starch biosynthesis in developing pollen during the reproductive stage, and the starch accumulation is a critical indicator for pollen maturation (Datta et al. 2002).

Sucrose is a major transport sugar in plants, and the translocation of sucrose between organs relies on phloem systems. Sucrose transporters carry sucrose across cell membranes and play an important role in loading sucrose into phloem systems. In most plants, sucrose transporters are encoded by a gene family. The five sucrose transporter genes found in the rice genome are OsSUT1, OsSUT2, OsSUT3, OsSUT4, and OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). OsSUT1 was the first SUT gene isolated from rice (Hirose et al. 1997). In rice plants, OsSUT1 expression has been detected in leaf blades, leaf sheaths, panicles, and germinating seeds (Hirose et al. 1997; Scofield et al. $2 0 0 7 \mathrm { a }$ ; Chen et al. 2010). Suppressing OsSUT1 expression reduces the percentage of filled grains (Scofield et al. 2002). During the grain-filling period, OsSUT1 is expressed in the phloem of leaves, the uppermost internode, and the pedicel of the rice plant for sucrose translocation to the filling grains (Scofield et al. 2007b). A recent study showed that the changes in the OsSUT1 expression level could modulate the salt response of rice plants (Siahpoosh et al. 2012). The expression and regulation of both OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 in embryos have been investigated in our previous studies. The antagonism of abscisic acid and gibberellic acid plays a critical role in regulating OsSUT1 expression during embryo germination (Chen et al. 2010). In germinating embryos, OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 expression is also regulated by soluble sugars (i.e., glucose and sucrose). OsSUT1 expression is down-regulated in 1-day sugar treated embryos; however, it is upregulated in 5-day sugar treated embryos. Moreover, the mechanism of glucose-regulated OsSUT1 expression in embryos is mediated by a hexokinase-dependent signal transduction pathway (Chen et al. 2010). However, the upregulation of OsSUT2 in response to glucose occurs through a hexokinase-independent pathway (Siao et al. 2011). In germinating embryos, the expressions of both OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 are significantly lower than those of OsSUT1, 2, and 4 (Siao et al. 2011).

OsSUT4 is expressed in most tissues such as roots, leaves, and panicles (Aoki et al. 2003). Our previous studies showed that OsSUT4 could play a role in sucrose loading into the sheath phloem of the upper leaves during the post-heading period for sucrose transport to developing grains (Chen and Wang 2008). However, little is known about the regulation and functions of the OsSUT4 gene in other rice tissues during different developmental stages. In the analysis of the phylogenetic tree, Braun and Slewinski (2009) demonstrated that OsSUT4 belongs to the same subfamily as Arabidopsis AtSUT2 (or AtSUC3), tomato LeSUT2, and Plantago PmSUC3. According to amino acid analysis, LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 proteins contain extended cytoplasmic domains. Moreover, the structures of LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 are similar to those of yeast glucose sensors, SNF3 and RGT2; thus, it was considered that the LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 could function as sucrose sensors (Barker et al. 2000). The AtSUT2 protein is localized in sieve elements of phloem, and it is expressed in several sink tissues (Meyer et al. 2000, 2004). The sucrose transport activity of AtSUT2 has been detected in AtSUT2-transformed yeast (Meyer et al. 2000). In Plantago major, PmSUC3 was expressed in sieve cells of sink leaves and identified in non-phloem cells (Barth et al. 2003).

In most plant species, sucrose is the major product of carbon assimilation and the major carbon compound translocated. During transport from source organs to sink organs, sucrose may follow a symplasmic pathway, moving from cell to cell via plasmodesmata. Alternatively, sucrose may move apoplasmically through the cell walls and intercellular spaces of the tissue. In most plants, the pathway from source to sink is thought to involve a combination of both symplasmic and apoplasmic transport steps, depending on the tissue type and stage of development (Patrick 1997; Lalonde et al. 2003). Transfer of sucrose between the apoplasmic and the symplasmic compartments is mediated by transporter proteins located in the plasma membrane. Our understanding of the molecular mechanism of sucrose transport was greatly advanced by the isolation of the first plant sucrose transporter from spinach (Riesmeier et al. 1992). Since then, sucrose transporters have been identified in many plant species, including both monocots and dicots (Lemoine 2000; Ku¨ hn 2003; Lalonde et al. 2004). The sequences of these transporters are highly conserved and conform to the consensus structure for members of the Major Facilitator Superfamily (Marger and Saier 1993). Expression of genes from the SUT1 group in yeast mutants has shown that the transporters act as sucrose/proton symporters. Within the sucrose transporter family, functional subgroups can be defined on the basis of kinetic properties and tissue localization.

Phloem loading has been identified as an important role for sucrose transporters. In many plants, the phloem is symplasmically isolated from surrounding tissues due to lack of connecting plasmodesmata, thus necessitating uptake from the apoplasm by transporters. Localization studies have shown that the SUT1 transporter from solanaceous species and the homologous SUC2 transporter from Arabidopsis and Plantago are present in the phloem (Stadler and Sauer 1996; Ku¨ hn et al. 1997). Antisense suppression of transporters from this class provided further evidence of their involvement in phloem loading. Plants with reduced SUT1 activity showed lower growth rates and accumulated sucrose in the leaves (Riesmeier et al.

1994; Bu¨ rkle et al. 1998). More recently, additional sucrose transporters with kinetic properties that differ from SUT1 have also been localized to the phloem in some plant tissues (Reinders et al. 2002). It is likely that these sucrose transporters work cooperatively to control uptake of sucrose in the leaves and retrieval of sucrose that leaks from sieve elements along the transport pathway. However, the involvement of transporters from this family in the transfer of sucrose from vascular tissue to sink organs is less clear. Many of the transporters expressed in the phloem of source leaves are also expressed at lower levels in sink organs (Lemoine 2000). A few transporters are predominantly expressed in sites where loading into sink tissues occurs. For example, DcSUT2 is probably involved in loading of the storage parenchyma of carrot taproots (Shakya and Sturm 1998), and VvSUC12 is expressed in ripening grape berries (Davies et al. 1999). Sucrose transporters appear to have diverse roles in the plant.

Sucrose is the major transported form of sugar in plants. The deposition of starch, which is the main determinant of yield in cereal crops, in seeds is dependent on the supply of this sugar molecule from source tissues through the phloem. The phloem consists of sieve elements (SE) and companion cells (CC) connected by numerous intercellular connections called plasmodesmata and form a SE-CC complex [1]. The SE is responsible for long distance transport of sucrose and other organic materials, whereas the CCs supply proteins and energy to the SEs [2,3]. Phloem loading and unloading of sucrose takes place symplastically and apoplastically. The symplastic transport involves cell to cell movement of sucrose via plasmodesmatal connections, while the apoplastic transport involves active sucrose movement across membranes via sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins [3,4], and mainly takes place in the absence of plasmodesmatal connections. Genes encoding SUTs have been identified from a number of plant species including cereal crops such as rice (Oryza sativa) [5], barley (Hordeum vulgare) [6], maize (Zea mays) [7] and wheat (Triticum aestivum) [8], and form small gene families [9]. All the plant SUTs identified to date are members of the glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family, which is part of the major facilitator superfamily characterized by 12 transmembrane spanning helices [10,11]. Furthermore, the first extracellular loop of plant SUTs contains a histidine residue, such as His-65 of the Arabidopsis SUT1 that serves as a target for diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC) mediated inhibition of sucrose transport activity [12]. It has been shown that this residue is substrate protected from the inhibition reaction induced by DEPC. This along with the ability of eliminating SUTs’ sensitivity to DEPC by substituting histidine with other amino acids without affecting the transport activity of SUTs indicate that the DEPC sensitive histidine residue is localized at or associated conformationally with the sucrose binding site.

Spatiotemporal expression analyses of the SUTs in cereal crops have provided insights into their physiological roles during seed development. For example, SUT1 of maize is highly expressed in leaf blades, leaf sheaths, culms, and husks and pedicels of the ear during reproductive growth of maize; and the expression of ZmSUT1 in the leaf blades was shown to increase as the level of photoassimilates increases, reflecting its role in phloem loading [7,13]. Consistent with this observation, impaired phloem loading in the zmsut1 mutant causes accumulation of carbohydrates in the leaf that led to chlorosis, senescence and reduced plant growth [14]. The three TaSUT1 homeologues, which reside on chromosome 4 of the wheat A, B and D genomes, are found to be expressed at similar levels in flag leaf blades, leaf sheaths and internodes [8], suggesting their equal roles in phloem loading of sucrose. The transcript abundance of TaSUT1 in these tissues was highest before heading and decreased immediately after flowering, when an increased level of its transcript was evident in the developing seeds. A study with symplastic fluorescein tracer has shown the lack of plasmodesmatal connections in the SE-CC complex of wheat flag leaf [15], supporting the hypothesis that TaSUT1 is involved in phloem loading of sucrose. In addition, all SUTs of rice [5,16] and the two known SUT of barley [6] are shown to be expressed in source leaves. Previous studies have also shown that non-foliar tissues of wheat florets, including the glume, lemma and palea, possess photosynthetic ability and contribute $1 0 \%$ to $4 4 \%$ of photoassimilates destined to wheat seeds [17,18]. In agreement with this, transcripts of TaSUT1 were detected in the glumes of wheat ear both before and after heading, although at lower levels than that observed in the flag leaf blades and sheaths [8], suggesting its role in phloem loading of the sucrose produced in the spike.

Leaf sheaths of cereal crops connect leaf blades to the stem nodes, thereby forming phloem conduits that serve as pathways for long distance transport of photoassimilates [15]. Along with internodes, they also act as a temporary storage of excess carbohydrates produced during the early stages of seed filling in the form of water-soluble carbohydrates, mainly fructans. Approximately $5 0 \%$ of the photoassimilates destined to seed filling in wheat appears to be temporarily stored in the leaf sheaths and internodes prior to remobilization during active seed filling, when photoassimilate supply from the leaf is not enough to meet the sink demand [19]. A role for reloading sucrose into the phloem during the remobilization process has been suggested for OsSUT1 and TaSUT1 as their transcripts are present in the leaf sheath and stem tissues of rice and wheat, respectively [5,15,16]. Given that carboxyfluorescein dye moves symplastically out of the phloem in wheat internode [15], the presence of TaSUT1 transcripts in this tissue also suggests its role in retrieving sucrose leaked out into the phloem apoplasm, and thereby providing an efficient photoassimilate translocation mechanism.

Previous studies have shown that SUT1 is highly expressed in the developing seeds of different cereal crops including rice, barley and wheat. In rice, SUT1 is expressed at similar levels from early to late stage of seed filling [20]. Consistently, antisense expression of OsSUT1 resulted in impaired seed filling and retarded germination with no effect on photosynthesis in the flag leaf [21]. The SUT1 of barley, however, exhibited its highest expression during the mid-stage of seed development. The transcripts of OsSUT1 and HvSUT1 are localized mainly in the maternal nucellar projections, aleurone tissues, and filial transfer cells that separate the endosperm cavity from the endosperm [6,20]. Furthermore, anti-OsSUT1 antibody was shown to bind to the plasma membranes of nucellar projections and aleurone tissues of developing wheat seeds [22]. As the maternal and filial tissues of cereal seeds lack symplastic connections; these results suggest the role of SUT1 in the post-phloem transport of sucrose from the maternal to the filial tissues of developing seeds.

Plant SUTs have been classified into five subfamilies, SUT1 to SUT5 [23]. Based on their significant similarity at the amino acid level, OsSUT2 and HvSUT2 are assigned to the SUT4 subfamily rather than to the monocot specific SUT3 or SUT5 subfamilies [9], and these genes are found to be expressed in both source and sink tissues [6,24]. The expression of HvSUT2 in developing seeds was relatively predominant during the earlier and later stages [6], whereas that of OsSUT2 was restricted only to the earlier stages [24]. In developing barley seeds, HvSUT2 has been shown to have almost similar cellular localization as that of HvSUT1 [6]. Recent proteomic and green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion protein studies showed that some members of the SUT4 subfamily including HvSUT2 and OsSUT2, and those derived from other species such as Arabidopsis (AtSUT4), Lotus (LjSUT4) and poplar (PtaSUT4) are localized to the vacuolar tonoplast [25-27], suggesting that these proteins are involved in vacuolar storage of sucrose and its transport across the tonoplast to the cytosol. Consistently, a knockout mutation of OsSUT2 and RNAi mediated suppression of PtaSUT4 caused accumulation of sucrose in source leaves of rice and poplar, respectively, due to a decrease in sucrose transport from the vacuolar to the cytoplasmic compartment [27,28].

Plant SUTs play important roles in the allocation of photoassimilates in the form of sucrose from the source to sink tissues, and thereby determine seed yield. Identifying and characterizing new SUTs, thus, provide insights into the regulation of sucrose transport. Although wheat is one of the most economically important crops of the world, only one wheat SUT gene has been identified and characterized to date [8]. The present study identified a new SUT, designated as TaSUT2, and its homeologous from hexaploid wheat (T. aestivum cv. AC Andrew), and determined their subcellular localization and functionality as SUTs using a yeast heterologous system. Furthermore, the total expression of TaSUT2 and the relative contribution of each of the three genomes were investigated in both source and sink tissues at different stages of development.

Cadmium $\mathrm { ( C d ) }$ is ubiquitously present and represents a major toxic heavy metal to plants and animals; thus, Cd poses serious health hazards to humans worldwide. Although it has been reported as a possible cofactor in a marine diatom, Cd is always regarded as a non-essential metal (Lane and Morel 2000). In many places worldwide, Cd pollution is a major concern because high concentrations of Cd in the soils are detrimental or even lethal to most crop species (Su et al. 2014). Surprisingly, the mechanism underlying Cd toxicity and detoxification remains poorly understood. As a class B metal, Cd can bind with sulfhydryl groups in proteins with high affinity (Villiers et al. 2011). Cadmium can be easily absorbed by plant roots via Ca, Fe and Zn transporters and restrains plant growth by decreasing mineral uptake, inhibiting photosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism and increasing water loss (Villiers et al. 2011; Gallego et al. 2012). At the cellular level, several processes, such as extracellular immobilization, active exclusion from cytoplasm to the apoplasm, chelation in the cytosol and sequestration in vacuoles, contribute to enhancing Cd tolerance in plants (Hall 2002; Villiers et al. 2011). In general, the Cd accumulation and distribution in plants is greatly influenced by increasing the expression of specific transporters or the intracellular binding capacity of the plants (Villiers et al. 2011).

However, the ability to accumulate metals in aboveground tissues has evolved in a few taxa. This interesting phenomenon is known as metal hyperaccumulation, and these plants are called hyperaccumulators (Brooks et al. 1977). Most hyperaccumulators are members of the Brassicaceae family (Kra¨mer 2010). To date, only three plant species have been characterized as Cd hyperaccumulators: Arabidopsis halleri (Bert et al. 2002), Noccaea caerulescens (Brooks et al. 1977; Baker et al. 1994) (formerly Thlaspi caerulescens) and Sedum alfredii Hance (Yang et al. 2004). The first two species belonging to the Brassicaceae family were previously shown to be excellent model systems for Cd hyperaccumulation, allowing researchers to understand the physiology and molecular mechanisms of heavy metal hyperaccumulation (Verbruggen et al. 2009; Kra¨mer 2010). However, as a result of a relatively low biomass, the practical use of Cd phytoextraction in contaminated soils with $N .$ caerulescens and A. halleri is not practically applicable. Therefore, information regarding other Cd hyperaccumulators, particularly non-Brassicaceae species, is essential to better understand intra-family Cd hyperaccumulation mechanisms as well as their potential applications.

The hyperaccumulating ecotype (HE) of S. alfredii Hance, which can accumulate up to $9 0 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { g } } ~ \mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { ~ C ~ }$ d and $2 9 , 0 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { g } ~ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ Zn in its shoots without any toxicity symptoms, is a non-Brassicaceae $\mathrm { Z n / C d }$ co-hyperaccumulator identified from an old $\mathrm { P b / Z n }$ mining area of Quzhou in Zhejiang Province in China (Yang et al. 2002, 2004, 2006; Zhang et al. 2014). This high amount of metals in plant cells requires a powerful detoxification system to protect the plants from the deleterious effects of excess toxic metals. Using radiotracer techniques, Lu et al. (2008) compared Cd uptake between the HE and non-hyperaccumulating ecotype (NHE, identified from a tea garden in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China) of S. alfredii Hance; these ecotypes had contrasting Cd accumulation, and more effective root-to-shoot translocation of Cd was found in the HE than the NHE. Hence, we hypothesized that a highaffinity Cd transporter might be involved in the enhancement of Cd root-to-shoot translocation in the HE of S. alfredii Hance. Furthermore, in a recent study using X-ray microfluorescence $\operatorname { ( \mu - X R F ) }$ and laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS), Tian et al. (2011) found that a large amount of Cd in HE plants was sequestrated at the leaf mesophyll cells. These studies clearly demonstrated the existence of a transporter that is responsible for high-affinity Cd uptake and sequestration in the leaf mesophyll of the HE of S. alfredii Hance. Unfortunately, the transporter responsible for high-affinity Cd sequestration in the leaf mesophyll of this non-Brassicaceae hyperaccumulator plant has not been identified or functionally characterized.

Although some recent studies have been conducted to identify and functionally characterize some genes, e.g., SaMTP1 (Zhang et al. 2011) and SaMT2 (Zhang et al. 2014), the extraordinary Cd translocation and shoot detoxification mechanism of this plant has not yet been studied. The $\mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { 1 B } }$ -type ATPases, also known as Heavy Metal ATPase (HMA), play important roles in heavy metal homeostasis in plant cells (Williams and Mills 2005). In the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, among eight HMA transporters, AtHMA2, AtHMA3 and AtHMA4 belong to the $Z _ { \mathrm { n } } / C \mathrm { d } / P \mathrm { b } / C _ { 0 }$ subgroup, and AtHMA2 and AtHMA4 are essential for $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd translocation from the roots to the shoots (Eren and Arguello 2004; Verret et al. 2004). AtHMA3 is another heavy metal ATPase transporter that is located in the tonoplast and is associated with Cd, Zn and Co tolerance (Morel et al. 2009). It was recently demonstrated that HMA transporters such as AhHMA4 and NcHMA3 (formerly TcHMA3), play critical roles in Zn and Cd hyperaccumulation (Hanikenne et al. 2008; Ueno et al. 2011). AhHMA4 is co-localized with QTL, which is involved in Zn and Cd tolerance in A. halleri. Enhanced expression of AhHMA4 in A. halleri, which has been associated with $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd hypertolerance, is a result of its tandem triplication and altered cis-regulation. The perturbation of the expression of this gene by RNA interference significantly increases the sensitivity to $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd and decreases root-to-shoot translocation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ (Hanikenne et al. 2008). HMA3 is highly expressed in the $\mathrm { Z n / C d }$ hyperaccumulators $A$ . halleri and $N .$ . caerulescens, suggesting that it may be involved in $\mathrm { Z n / C d }$ hyperaccumulation (Becher et al. 2004; Ueno et al. 2011). In $N .$ .

caerulescens, NcHMA3 is a specific Cd transporter gene that is constitutively expressed both in the shoots and roots. The expression of NcHMA3 in the Ganges ecotype is sevenfold higher than that in the Prayon ecotype as a result of the higher copy number in the Ganges genome (Ueno et al. 2011). However, it remains unknown whether the constitutive expression level and substrate specificity of HMA3 are common features in hyperaccumulator species, especially in a non-Brassicaceae hyperaccumulator.

In the present study, a $\mathrm { P } _ { \mathrm { 1 B } }$ -type ATPase gene (SaHMA3) from S. alfredii Hance was isolated and functionally characterized. This gene encoded a tonoplast Cd transporter and the enhanced expression of this gene may be essential for Cd hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance in the HE of S. alfredii Hance.

With the escalation of urban and industrial emissions, mining activities, and the extensive application of pesticides and fertilizers, the levels of hazardous heavy metals, such as cadmium (Cd), lead $\left( \mathrm { P b } \right)$ , and copper $\mathbf { \tau } ( \mathbf { C u } )$ , in soil have been steadily rising (Haider et al. 2021; Edelstein and Ben$\mathrm { H u r } 2 0 1 8$ ; Li et al. 2023b). Notably, according to the ofcial report from the national general survey on soil contamination, announced by the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP) and the Ministry of Land and Resources (MLR) of the People’s Republic of China, $7 \%$ of soil in China is currently contaminated by Cd, making it the most prevalent heavy-metal pollutant (MEP and MLR 2014; Wang et al. 2019b). Cadmium, more mobile than most other heavy metals in soil, enters and accumulates in plants primarily through root absorption, and then translocated to edible parts of crops, posing a signifcant threat to human health as it traverses the food chain (Suhani et al. 2021; Sterckeman and Thomine 2020). As a non-essential metal, Cd enters root cells mainly through nonspecifc transporters responsible for essential metal elements like manganese, iron, zinc, etc. (Tao and Lu 2022).

Cadmium exerts toxic efects on plants even at low concentrations, afecting plant morphology, physiology, and biochemistry (El Rasaf et al. 2022). It disrupts the uptake of essential nutrients, such as iron, zinc, magnesium, calcium, and manganese, causing nutrient imbalances and chlorosis (Qin et al. 2020). Additionally, Cd induces osmotic stress by reducing leaf relative water content, stomatal conductance, and transpiration rates, which leads to dehydration and physiological damage (Hatamian et al. 2020; Deng et al. 2024). One of the most signifcant efects of Cd is the inhibition of lateral root formation and overall plant growth. This occurs through its interference with carbon fxation, reduction of chlorophyll content, and suppression of photosynthetic activity, often culminating in plant necrosis (Hu et al. 2021; Su et al. 2020). Cadmium also disturbs hormonal equilibrium, particularly afecting auxins and cytokinins, which further impedes plant growth and development (Araniti et al. 2023; Bitarishvili et al. 2023). Furthermore, Cd disrupts the antioxidant system, instigating a burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that directly damage cell membranes and organelles, resulting in cell death or even plant mortality (Li et al. 2023b).

To counteract Cd stress, plants have evolved multifaceted strategies, including the establishment of cell wall barriers, inhibition of Cd uptake into root cells and its translocation from root to shoot, sequestration into vacuoles, and formation of chelator–Cd complexes for detoxifcation, among others (El Rasaf et al. 2022). Concurrently, these processes are meticulously regulated by a myriad of regulatory networks, including transcription factors, epigenetic modifcations, and post-translational modifcations (Li et al. 2024b; Chen et al. 2023a; Han et al. 2019). Over the recent decades, numerous studies have been conducted to comprehend the mechanisms underlying plant–Cd interaction. This review will focus on crucial research regarding plant–Cd transport, detoxifcation, and the transcriptional regulatory mechanisms controlled by transcription factors, delving into the latest advancements in this feld. Through these deliberations, our objective is to provide a comprehensive and profound scientifc foundation for the development of more efcacious strategies to mitigate and manage Cd pollution, as well as the cultivation of Cd-resistant plants.


## Plant–Cd transporters


Numerous transporter protein families participate in the processes of Cd absorption and transport from the soil to plants. To date, identifed Cd transport proteins primarily include Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Proteins (NRAMP), Heavy Metal Transporting ATPases (HMA), Zinc-Iron-Regulated Transporters (ZIP), ATP Cassette Transporters (ABC), and Yellow-Stripe-Like Proteins (YSL), among others (Table 1).


## NRAMP family


The NRAMP gene family in plants plays a crucial role in regulating the acquisition, transportation, and homeostasis of various divalent metal ions, including essential nutrients, such as $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ , as well as hazardous metals like $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { H g } ^ { 2 + }$ (Kanwal et al. 2024; Mani and Sankaranarayanan 2022). The initial identifcation of NRAMP proteins and their metal transporter activity began with the discovery of the Mn transporter SMF1 in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) (Supek et al. 1996). Subsequent studies in plants, particularly in rice (Oryza sativa) and Arabidopsis, have provided extensive insights into the roles of NRAMP transporters in metal-ion transport and homeostasis (Belouchi et al. 1997; Vaughan 2004).

Rice possesses seven NRAMP genes, with OsNRAMP1/2/4/5 playing signifcant roles in Cd absorption and transport. Knocking out OsNRAMP1/2/4/5 markedly reduces Cd accumulation in rice grains, enhancing plant resistance to Cd (Chang et al. 2020b, 2022; Hao et al. 2022; Tang et al. 2022). For instance, knocking out OsNRAMP5 dramatically decreases Cd absorption in rice roots, leading to reduced Cd content in stems and grains (Tang et al. 2022). Overexpressing OsNRAMP5 also reduces Cd accumulation in rice grains by disrupting radial Cd transport into the stele for xylem loading but increases Cd content in roots (Chang et al. 2020a). Notably, researchers led by Professor Jianfeng Ma from Okayama University identifed a QTL locus with two copies of OsNRAMP5 in the low-Cd rice variety Pollali as the primary locus responsible for low-Cd accumulation (Yu et al. 2022a). Introducing this QTL into the high-quality Japanese variety Koshihikari successfully bred a new low-Cd variety, demonstrating the signifcant application potential of OsNRAMP5 in breeding low-Cd accumulating rice varieties $\mathrm { T u }$ et al. 2022a). Under Cd stress, mungbean (Vigna radiata L.) mutants of VrNRAMP5 exhibit higher resistance to Cd than the wild type. Overexpression of VrNRAMP5 increases Cd absorption in yeast and Arabidopsis, leading to a hypersensitive response to excessive Cd (Qian et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2024b). The function of NRAMP1 is highly conserved across diferent species. OsNRAMP1 in rice is a close homologue of OsNRAMP5, with Cd-transporting activity. OsNRAMP1 mainly localizes to the plasma membrane and is predominantly expressed in roots and leaves. Knocking out OsNRAMP1 reduces Cd accumulation not only in rice roots but also in shoots and grains (Chang et al. 2020b; Takahashi et al. 2011). Similarly, BcNRAMP1 in pak choi (Brassica rapa L. Chinensis. Shanghaiqing), PcNRAMP1 in silver poplar (Populus $\times$ canescens), and NtNRAMP1 in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) are homologous to OsNRAMP1, localizing to the plasma membrane and primarily expressing in roots, with their transcription induced by Cd stress. Overexpressing BcNRAMP1 in yeast and Arabidopsis increases plant Cd absorption. Non-invasive microelectrode ion fux measurements directly demonstrates the role of BcNRAMP1 in Cd infux into Arabidopsis root cells, revealing its function in Cd transport and absorption (Yue et al. 2021). Overexpressing PcNRAMP1 in silver poplar and NtNRAMP1 in tobacco roots increases Cd content by

$3 9 - 5 2 \%$ and 1.26–2.02 times, respectively (Liu et al. 2022b;   
Yu et al. 2022b).

OsNRAMP2 is localized to the vacuolar membrane and plays a crucial role in facilitating Cd translocation from roots to shoots by regulating Cd efux from root vacuoles. Moreover, it mediates Cd remobilization from vegetative tissues to grains during the flling stage. Disruption of OsNRAMP2 leads to a notable reduction in grain Cd concentration, accompanied by increased Cd levels in leaves and straws, while overexpression of OsNRAMP2 increases grain Cd concentrations by more than $5 0 \%$ (Chang et al. 2022; Yang et al. 2023). Similarly, overexpression of sheepgrass (Leymus chinensis) LcNRAMP2 in rice enhances both Cd accumulation and tolerance (Wang et al. 2024a). Silencing the StNRAMP2 gene increases Cd content in potato (Sola - num tuberosum) tubers but decreases Cd content in other potato tissues, such as roots, stems, and leaves. In contrast, overexpressing the StNRAMP2 gene in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) seedlings causes a threefold increase in Cd content, indicating a crucial role of the StNRAMP2 gene in Cd absorption. More importantly, it may reduce Cd enrich - ment in the main edible part (tubers) of potatoes by enhanc - ing the rate of Cd migration from tubers to leaves (Zhang et al. 2023e). NtNRAMP3 in tobacco exhibits similar characteristics to OsNRAMP2, such as tonoplast localization and Cd transport from vacuoles to the cytoplasm. Knocking out NtNRAMP3 enhances both Cd accumulation and toler - ance (Jia et al. 2022). Current research on the plant NRAMP family primarily focuses on its role in Cd absorption and transport, while the transcriptional regulation mechanism in response to Cd stress requires further investigation.


## HMA family


The Heavy Metal ATPase (HMA), also known as $\mathrm { P _ { 1 b } }$ -ATPases, facilitates the transmembrane transport of metal ions through ATP hydrolysis, contributing to the absorption and transport of heavy-metal ions within plant cells (Keeran et al. 2021; Sinha et al. 2022). Previous studies in Arabidopsis and rice have confrmed the signifcant role of HMA in Cd transport. In recent years, extensive research has focused on HMA in certain Cd hyperaccu - mulator plants. In the Cd hyperaccumulator plant Sedum plumbizincicola, SpHMA1 localizes to the chloroplast envelope. SpHMA1 facilitates the export of Cd from chloroplasts to the cytoplasm, thus protecting the photo - synthetic reaction in leaf cells, ultimately enhancing their resistance to Cd. Knockout mutants and RNAi interference plants of SpHMA1 exhibit a notable increase in Cd accu - mulation in chloroplasts compared to the wild type (Zhao et al. 2019). Through a comprehensive genome-wide asso - ciation analysis of Cd content in 186 chili pepper fruits (Capsicum sp.), Xu et al. (2023) unveiled CaHMA1 as the pivotal gene governing Cd accumulation in pepper fruits. CaHMA1, predominantly localized in the Golgi apparatus and endoplasmic reticulum, exhibits heightened expression levels in pepper fruits. Overexpression of CaHMA1 induced a substantial augmentation in Cd content in Arabidopsis plants. Conversely, silencing the CaHMA1 gene in chili pepper fruits resulted in a signifcant reduction in Cd content. Homologs of HMA2, such as BrpHMA2 in Chinese fowering cabbage (Brassica parachinensis L.H. Bailey) (Liu et al. 2022a), OsHMA2 in rice (Yamaji et al. 2013), and PvHMA2.1 in switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) (Zang et al. 2023), are plasma membrane-localized and induced under Cd stress. The heterologous expression of BrpHMA2 in transgenic Arabidopsis and yeast enhances both Cd accumulation and Cd sensitivity, while knocking out OsHMA2 leads to reduced Cd concentrations in upper nodes and reproductive organs. However, the heterologous expression of $P \nu H M A 2 . I$ mitigates the decline in primary root length and fresh weight in Arabidopsis seedlings subjected to Cd treatment, while concurrently reducing Cd accumulation in roots. The contrasting phenomenon observed, where BrpHMA2 and OsHMA2 enhance Cd accumulation while PvHMA2.1 reduces it, suggests a potential functional divergence in the HMA2 gene during evolution.

It is noteworthy that HMA2 is localized to the plasma membrane, while its homolog HMA3 is located on the tonoplast, indicating diferences in their Cd transport mechanisms. In rice, OsHMA3 sequesters Cd into vacuoles in root cells, limiting Cd transport from roots to shoots and reducing Cd accumulation in grains. In Cd-contaminated soil, overexpression of OsHMA3 reduces Cd concentrations in brown rice by $9 4 - 9 8 \%$ compared to the wild type (Lu et al. 2019). In contrast, OsHMA3 loss-of-function mutants exhibited reduced Cd accumulation in roots but increased Cd accumulation in shoots and grains compared to the WT plants (Yan et al. 2024). ZmHMA3 in maize (Zea mays L.) is a homolog of OsHMA3, and notably, transgenic maize plants overexpressing ZmHMA3a produce Cd-free grains at low $( 1 , 3 \mathrm { p p m } )$ or even extremely high ( $1 8 ~ \mathrm { p p m } )$ Cd levels without loss of yield or quality, demonstrating its potential for low-Cd crop breeding (Chen et al. 2023c). Additionally, by performing grain ionome QTL analysis of recombinant inbred lines (RIL) of sorghum (Sorghum bicolor L.), Wahinya et al. (2022) demonstrated that SbHMA3a was the key loci contributing to low-Cd accumulation in grains by actively limiting the root-to-shoot translocation of Cd. In summary, HMA2 is localized to the cytoplasmic membrane and mainly regulates the Cd homeostasis and redistribution in plants by mediating efux of Cd in diferent species. On the other hand, HMA3 is localized to the tonoplast and plays a vital detoxifcation role in plants by sequestering Cd into vacuoles.


## ZIP family


The ZIP family comprises Zinc-Regulated Transporter Proteins (ZRT) and Iron-Regulated Transporter Proteins (IRT), which typically feature eight transmembrane domains and a conserved metal-ion-binding domain, playing a crucial role in metal-ion transport (Ajeesh Krishna et al. 2020; Huang et al. 2024; Pang et al. 2023). The discovery of AtIRT1 in Arabidopsis thaliana marked the identifcation of the frst ZIP gene in plants (Vert et al. 2021). IRT1 localized to the plasma membrane, and serves as the primary transporter for root iron uptake in plants and exhibits transport capabilities for several other divalent metals like $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ . The Cd-transporting activity of IRT1 is highly conserved across various plant species, including Arabidopsis, rice, wheat (Triticum polonicum L.), lettuce (Lactuca sativa), pak choi (B. rapa, ssp. Chinensis), and Chinese cabbage (B. rapa, ssp. pekinensis) (Jiang et al. 2021; Xu et al. 2024). For example, overexpression of the AtIRT1 gene in rapeseed (Brassica campestris L.) signifcantly enhances Cd accumulation efciency in root hairs and improves Cd tolerance in transgenic roots under Cd stress (Liu et al. 2023). However, overexpression of TpIRT1B in Arabidopsis enhances Cd accumulation but also renders transgenic Arabidopsis plants more sensitive to Cd, suggesting a potential negative regulatory role of TpIRT1 in Cd detoxifcation (Jiang et al. 2021).

Current research on the role of ZRT in Cd transport is predominantly focused on rice. OsZIP1, a metal efux transporter, is localized in the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane. Knockout mutants of OsZIP1 exhibit increased Cd accumulation in roots under Cd stress and heightened sensitivity to Cd. Conversely, OsZIP1 overexpressing lines maintain robust growth under Cd stress with lower Cd content in roots, indicating a protective role of OsZIP1 by limiting Cd accumulation in rice roots (Liu et al. 2019). Furthermore, OsZIP5 and OsZIP9 in rice are also proteins localized to the cytoplasmic membrane, exhibiting infux transport activity, but are mainly expressed in roots. Knockdown mutants of $ { O s Z I P 5 } /  { 9 }$ show reduced Cd absorption, but the double mutants of $ { O s Z I P 5 } /  { 9 }$ signifcantly decrease Cd absorption in roots compared to single mutants, indicating a synergistic efect of these two proteins in promoting Cd absorption in rice roots (Tan et al. 2020). OsZIP16, localized to the endoplasmic reticulum, is also noteworthy. Knocking out OsZIP16 resulted in reduced plant growth and intense cellular damage upon Cd stress, accompanied by a slightly higher Cd translocation from roots to shoots (Li et al. 2024b). Additionally, yeast overexpressing RsZIP1/5/10d/12a from radish (Raphanus sativus) showed better growth than control, implying that these RsZIPs confer enhanced tolerance to excess Cd (Tang et al. 2024). Similarly, overexpression of SmZIP8 from willow (Salix matsudana Koidz) enhances tobacco tolerance to Cd through increased photosynthetic capacity, activation of antioxidant enzymes, and reduction of ROS-induced oxidative damage (Zou et al. 2022). These fndings collectively highlight the diverse roles of ZIP family proteins in Cd transport and tolerance mechanisms across various plant species.


## YSL family


The Yellow Stripe-Like (YSL) protein family represents a class of oligopeptide transporters that play a pivotal role in transporting iron and other metal ions in plants (Chowdhury et al. 2022). Emerging research highlights the role of YSLs in Cd detoxifcation by mediating the reallocation of other metal ions, particularly in the competitive absorption dynamics between iron and Cd. For instance, MsYSL1 in Miscanthus sacchariforus (Chen et al. 2018), SnYSL3 in Solanum nigrum (Feng et al. 2017), and MsYSL6 in alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) (Zhang et al. 2023b) were all located on the cytoplasmic membrane and induced by Cd stress, and have transporting activity of Fe(II)–NA, Zn–NA, Mn–NA, and/or Cd–NA. Heterologous expression of these YSLs in Arabidopsis or tobacco all enhanced their Cd resistance by increasing the root-to-shoot translocation ratios of Fe and other essential metals. In rice, CF1, an allelic variant of the OsYSL2 gene, lacks intrinsic Cd transport activity. However, overexpression of CF1 in rice confers Cd resistance by suppressing the expression of the OsNRAMP5 gene in roots, thereby restricting Cd uptake (Li et al. 2022b).

The ABCG subfamily is a critical subset of ABC family members involved in heavy-metal transport functions. Within this subfamily, AtABCG36/AtPDR8 functions as a heavy-metal efux pump in Arabidopsis, efectively reducing Cd accumulation (Kim et al. 2007). OsABCG36/ OsPDR9 in rice also serves as a Cd-extrusion pump localized to the plasma membrane. OsABCG36 is strongly induced by Cd stress, while knockout of OsABCG36 results in increased Cd accumulation in the root, heightening sensitivity to Cd (Fu et al. 2019). Similarly, PtoABCG36 from Chinese white poplar (Populus tomentosa) and RsPDR8 from radish (Raphanus sativus L.) share functional and subcellular localization characteristics with OsABCG36 and AtABCG36, enhancing Cd efux when overexpressed in yeast and Arabidopsis, thereby leading to reduced Cd accumulation and increased Cd tolerance (Wang et al. 2019a; Zhang et al. 2023c). Additionally, OsABCG48 overexpression in rice reduces Cd accumulation in roots and enhances Cd resistance, as evidenced by improved root length and lateral root numbers (Cai et al. 2021). Another member, OsABCG53/OsPDR20, enhances yeast resistance to Cd when overexpressed, reducing Cd accumulation. Conversely, RNAi knockdown of OsPDR20 increases Cd accumulation in rice roots and aboveground parts, reducing Cd resistance in rice (Li et al. 2024a).


## ABC family


In plants, ABC transporters constitute an indispensable protein family involved in the transport of various molecules, such as heavy-metal ions, secondary metabolites, and phytohormones (Do et al. 2021; Lefèvre and Boutry 2018; Zhang et al. 2023d). Among them, the ABCC subfamily stands out as critical for metal transport processes. Studies on Arabidopsis have highlighted the roles of AtABCC1, AtABCC2, and AtABCC3 in enhancing Cd tolerance by sequestering PC–Cd complexes into vacuoles (Park et al. 2012; Brunetti et al. 2015). In strawberries (Fragaria vesca L.), FvABCC8 and FvABCC11, both localized on the vacuolar membrane, exhibit elevated expression during fruit development and under Cd treatment. Additionally, overexpression of $F { \nu } A B C C I I$ alleviates the inhibitory efect of Cd stress on Arabidopsis root systems and plant growth, enhancing Arabidopsis resistance to Cd (Shi et al. 2020). Similarly, OsABCC9 in rice, also tonoplast-localized, aids in sequestering toxic Cd into root cell vacuoles for detoxifcation purposes. Knockout mutants osabcc9 show heightened sensitivity to Cd stress, with increased Cd concentrations in roots, shoots, xylem sap, and grains compared to the wild


## Plant transcription factor‑mediated gene regulation in Cd stress response


Plant responses to Cd stress are intricately regulated at the transcriptional level by a diverse array of transcription factors (TFs) that orchestrate the expression of stress-responsive genes (Wang et al. 2023a; Kaushik et al. 2024). The coordination of gene expression is essential for plants to mitigate Cd-induced toxicity, maintain metal homeostasis, and activate defense mechanisms against oxidative stress. TFs act as molecular switches that bind to specifc cis-regulatory elements in the promoters of target genes (Liu et al. 2024a), thereby modulating their transcriptional activity in response to Cd stress signals (Sun et al. 2015; Kapoor et al. 2021). Transcriptional regulation in Cd stress response involves a network of TF families that interact synergistically or antagonistically to fne-tune gene-expression profles. Among these TF families, WRKY, ERF (Ethylene Response Factor), HSF (Heat Shock Factor), NAC (NAM, ATAF1/2, CUC2), MYB (Myeloblastosis), and bZIP (basic leucine zipper) families have emerged as key regulators governing various aspects of plant Cd stress responses (Table 2) (Mitra et al. 2023).


## WRKY family


The WRKY TF family, characterized by a highly conserved WRKY domain, is known to play a vital role in regulating plant development and responding to various environmental stresses (Khoso et al. 2022). Studies across various plant species have highlighted the diverse roles of WRKY TFs in modulating Cd tolerance mechanisms. In Arabidopsis, several WRKY TFs exhibit contrasting efects on Cd tolerance. For instance, AtWRKY12 negatively regulates Cd tolerance by suppressing the expression of $\gamma$ -glutamyl cysteine synthetase GSH1, indirectly afecting phytochelatin (PC) synthesis genes and reducing Cd tolerance (Han et al. 2019). Conversely, AtWRKY45 positively regulates Cd tolerance by directly activating PC synthesis-related genes such as PCS1 and PCS2 (Li et al. 2023a). While AtWRKY13, with high amino acid sequence similarity to AtWRKY12, increases Cd tolerance by directly activating the expression of the ABC transporter PDR8 (ABCG36), thereby facilitating Cd efux and reducing Cd accumulation in Arabidopsis (Sheng et al. 2019). Additionally, AtWRKY33 activation under Cd stress in Arabidopsis leads to the ubiquitination and degradation of Cd transporter IRT1 by directly activating the transcription of E3 ubiquitin ligase ATL31, ultimately reducing Cd accumulation and enhancing Cd tolerance (Zhang et al. 2023a).

Similarly, in wheat (Triticum aestivum), WRKY TFs, such as TaWRKY22, TaWRKY74, and TaWRKY13, play crucial roles in Cd tolerance. TaWRKY22 activates the expression of copper transporter TaCOPT3D, thus reducing Cd accumulation in roots, stems, and grains, and alleviating Cd damage (Liu et al. 2022c). TaWRKY74, through transient gene silencing, was shown to enhance Cd resistance by inhibiting the expression of Cd transporters, such as TaNRAMP1/5, TaHMA2/3, and TaIRT1 (Li et al. 2022a). TaWRKY13 activates the expression of TaHMA2 to facilitate Cd uptake, while this process could be repressed by exogenous NaCl, which inhibits Cd uptake by wheat (Wang et al. 2023c). In poplar (Populus alba $\times$ Populus glandulosa), transgenic lines overexpressing PyWRKY48, PyWRKY71, or PyWRKY75 from Populus yunnanensis all grow better than wild type under Cd stress. This phenotype was accompanied by a higher accumulation of photosynthetic pigments and antioxidant enzyme activity (Wu et al. 2023, 2022; Chen et al. 2023b). Moreover, several other WRKY TFs from various plant species, such as maize (ZmWRKY64), potato (StWRKY6), sorghum (SbWRKY54), and soybean (Glycine max L.) (GmWRKY172), have been identifed as positive regulators of Cd resistance. These WRKY TFs modulate Cd uptake and translocation, and enhance the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), peroxidase (POD), and catalase (CAT) to alleviate Cd-induced oxidative stress and damage in plants (Gu et al. 2024; He et al. 2022, 2023; Wang et al. 2023d; Xian et al. 2023).


## MYB family


MYB TFs, characterized by MYB repeat sequences, are involved in plant cell morphogenesis, development, and responses to various environmental stresses (Chen et al. 2019; Ma et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024c). In cotton (Gossypium hirsutum), GhMYB44 has emerged as a key player in Cd stress responses. Acting downstream of the GhRCD1-GhbHLH12 cascade, GhMYB44 not only promotes Cd uptake and accumulation in roots and shoots but also enhances Cd tolerance. This dual function is achieved through direct binding to the promoters of Heavy Metal ATPase (HMA) genes, thereby regulating Cd translocation. Additionally, GhMYB44 interacts with GhPYL8 to recruit abscisic acid (ABA), a phytohormone that generally inhibits bud growth but enhances stress tolerance (Liu et al. 2024b), leading to increased Cd resistance (Wei et al. 2024). In Arabidopsis, AtMYB4 positively regulates Cd resistance by directly binding to the promoters of PCS1 (phytochelatin synthase 1) and MT1C (metallothionein 1C), which are involved in Cd detoxifcation processes (Agarwal et al. 2020). Furthermore, AtMYB4 promotes the expression of MAN3 $\beta$ -mannanase 3) and production of mannose, thus enhancing the binding of mannose to MNB1 (mannose-binding lectin 1), triggering GSH and PC synthesis, ultimately improving Cd tolerance (Yan et al. 2021). In contrast, AtMYB43 attenuates Cd resistance by inhibiting the expression of Cd transporters HMA2/3/4. However, the CRL4PRL1 E3 ligase complex mediates the degradation of AtMYB43, relieving its inhibitory efect under Cd stress (Zheng et al. 2022a). ThRAX2, an R2R3-MYB gene from Tamarix hispida, reduces Cd accumulation in roots and leaves by directly regulating the expression of ion balance-related genes (Wang et al. 2023e). On the other hand, many other MYB TFs were reported to change Cd resistance by regulating the antioxidant system and maintaining reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis under Cd stress conditions. In rice, OsMYB45 expression is induced under Cd stress, and its knockout makes plants highly sensitive to Cd. OsMYB45 regulates Cd resistance by modulating the expression of genes associated with catalase synthesis, reducing excess ROS due to Cd stress (Hu et al. 2017). In Tamarix hispida, ThDIV2 directly targets ThAO1 and ThAO2 encoding ascorbate oxidase by binding to the MYB motifs in their promoters to negatively regulate Cd tolerance by modulating ROS homeostasis (Gao et al. 2023). PsMYB62, isolated from Potentilla sericea, enhances Cd resistance in Arabidopsis by promoting the activity of antioxidant enzymes and increasing the content of antioxidant substances, such as GSH (Feng et al. 2023). Under Cd stress, AtMYB75 in Arabidopsis maintains ROS homeostasis, alleviating oxidative damage and enhancing Cd resistance (Zheng et al. 2022b). Overall, MYB TFs contribute signifcantly to plant responses to Cd stress by modulating ROS balance, regulating Cd transporter genes, integrating hormonal signals, and coordinating stress responses.

Similarly, in Alfalfa, MsbHLH115 directly regulates the iron-defciency response system, indirectly contributing to enhanced Cd detoxifcation responses (Zhang et al. 2024).

In wheat, TabHLH35 binds directly to the promoter of receptor-like kinase TaWAK20, activating its expression. TaWAK20 enhances Cd resistance by boosting the activity of antioxidant enzymes, such as SOD, CAT, and POD. Additionally, TaWAK20 phosphorylates TaSPL5, further increasing plant Cd resistance (Du et al. 2023b). Conversely, TaMYC8 in wheat activates the transcription of TaERF6, which promotes the activities of enzymes involved in the ethylene biosynthetic pathway, such as 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic (ACC) acid synthase (ACS) and ACC oxidase (ACO). Increased ethylene synthesis due to TaMYC8 activity reduces Cd tolerance in wheat plants (Wang et al. 2022). However, TabHLH094 interacts with TaMYC8 at the protein level, and reduces the ability of TaMYC8 to bind to the TaERF6 promoter (Du et al. 2023a). This interaction decreases ethylene production, ultimately enhancing Cd resistance in wheat. Briefy, the bHLH TF family plays a crucial role in modulating plant responses to Cd stress by regulating metal detoxifcation genes, Fe homeostasis, antioxidant activities, and ethylene signaling pathways.


## bHLH family


The bHLH (basic helix–loop–helix) transcription factor (TF) family, widely distributed across plants, is characterized by the presence of the bHLH region in their protein structure. These TFs are pivotal regulators in core plant development and various physiological processes (Gao and Dubos 2023; Guo et al. 2021). In Arabidopsis, the suppression of AtbHLH104 renders mutants sensitive to Cd stress, while its overexpression enhances Cd tolerance. AtbHLH104 positively regulates the expression of metal detoxifcation-related genes, such as IREG2 (Iron-Regulated 2), MTP3 (Metal Tolerance Protein 3), HMA3 (Heavy Metal ATPase 3), and NAS4 (Nicotianamine Synthase 4). IREG2 is involved in the transport and homeostasis of iron and other metals, MTP3 sequesters excess metal ions into vacuoles for detoxifcation, HMA3 transports Cd into vacuoles for detoxifcation, and NAS4 synthesizes nicotianamine, a chelator essential for Cd homeostasis and transport (Schaaf et al. 2006; Morel et al. 2008; Arrivault et al. 2006; Koen et al. 2013). These roles highlight involvement of AtbHLH104 in Cd detoxifcation pathways (Yao et al. 2018). AtbHLH34, also known as AtIDT1, shares homology with AtbHLH104.
