Plant phytohormones are small signaling molecules that are synthesized within plant and control many aspects of plant growth and development, as well as plant responses to environmental cues. Auxin is the most studied and the most important plant hormone. It plays crucial roles in apical meristem maintenance, axillary meristem formation, growth, as well as phototropism, gravitropism and hydrotropism. Executing the multiple roles of auxin is largely dependent on its uneven distribution in plant, which is achieved through an active process called polar auxin transport mediated by plasma membrane auxin transporter proteins [1, 2]. Three major gene families of auxin transporters have been found in plants. Of them the plant specific PIN-FORMED (PIN) auxin efflux facilitators are key players in this process, which work together with the AUXIN1 (AUX1)/LIKE AUX1 (LAX) influx carriers and the phosphoglycoprotein (PGP/MDR⁄ABCB) efflux/influx transporters [3, 4]. The asymmetric subcellular localization of PIN proteins determines the directionality of intercellular auxin flow and the differential distribution of auxin within plant tissue, thereby controlling various plant developmental processes [3, 5, 6].

Our current knowledge about PIN-dependent polar auxin transport in plant mostly comes from the extensive investigation of the PIN gene family in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana), which includes 8 members [7]. Five of the Arabidopsis PINs (PIN1-4 and PIN7) are located in the plasma membrane and they play a prominent role in the directional, cell-to-cell auxin transport [6]. Their spatiotemporal expression patterns and the auxin-dependent cross regulation of their expressions make them functionally redundant and complementary in a variety of plant developmental processes, including embryogenesis, organogenesis, tissue differentiation and tropism [8]. On the contrary, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized PIN5, 6, and 8 are not directly involved in the cell-to-cell auxin transport, but play a role in intracellular regulation of auxin homeostasis by working together with members of the PIN-LIKE auxin efflux carriers [9–13]. Besides their obvious role in many developmental processes, results from Arabidopsis show that PIN proteins are also involved in the crosstalk of auxin, ethylene, cytokinin and strigolactone in root development, where PIN proteins serve as a playground for the integration of hormone signaling through regulation of intracellular PIN protein trafficking and then subcellular polar localization [14]. Recently, the PIN gene family has been characterized from rice, sorghum, maize, and potato [15–19]. Transcriptional profiling analyses in rice, sorghum and maize suggested that some PIN genes from these plant species might mediate the crosstalk between auxin, other hormones and abiotic stresses [15–17].

Soybean is one of the most widely grown crops in the world. It is the most important source of vegetable protein and oil for humans, the most preferable protein source for farm animals, and currently the major feedstock for biodiesel production. With the rapid growth of global population and environmental degradation, improving soybean yield is a crucial task to meet the human demand for food and energy. Considering the importance of PIN genes in plant growth regulation and in plant response to abiotic stress environments, we carried out genome-wide comprehensive analysis of the soybean PIN auxin efflux transporter gene family. Their tissue expression patterns and expression profiling under hormonal treatments such as auxin and abscisic acid (ABA), and abiotic stresses including drought, salt and dehydration were analyzed. Our research identified the soybean PINs associated with abiotic stress responses. Some of them might be ideal candidates for further investigation.

The plant hormone auxin is an essential regulator of growth and development. The principal auxin, indole-3- acetic acid (IAA), is a weak acid $\mathrm { ( p } K _ { \mathrm { a } } = 4 . 7 5 ) $ that is synthesized in meristematic regions at the shoot apex and transported to the root tip. There, it is redirected through root cortical and epidermal tissues to generate a basipetal auxin concentration gradient (i.e. away from the organ apex). Highly sensitive auxin determination methods indicate that additional auxin synthesis takes place in young developing leaves and roots, but auxin both from shoot meristems and from young leaves and roots appears to be transported by similar mechanisms [1,2]. Polarized auxin transport provides essential directional and positional information for developmental processes, such as vascular differentiation, apical dominance, organ development and tropic growth $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 4 , 5 ]$ . Disruption of directional auxin movement by gene mutations or by treatment with transport inhibitors

In apical tissues where auxin concentrations are high, lipophilic diffusion of IAA is augmented by gradientdriven $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symport activity [18]. This activity is associated with the AUX1/LAX family of amino-acid permease-like proteins in Arabidopsis [8,9,19,20]. aux1 mutants exhibit reduced root gravitropism and decreased IAA transport in roots and young leaf primordia; further, aux1 mutants are resistant to inhibitory concentrations of IAA and the synthetic auxin 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), but not of the more lipophilic auxin analog 1-napthalene acetic acid (1-NAA) [19,21]. Because 1-NAA diffuses into the cell more rapidly than IAA, gravitropic growth in aux1 mutants is restored by treatment with 1-NAA but not with 2,4-D, which is taken up at a rate similar to that of IAA uptake but is a poor efflux carrier substrate [21]. The growth phenotypes of aux1 mutants are phenocopied by treatment with the auxin influx inhibitors 1-naphthoxyacetic acid (1-NOA) and 3-chloro-4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid (CHPAA), which do not affect polar auxin efflux or sensitivity to 1-NAA [22]. AUX1 functions both in root basipetal auxin transport and in acropetal transport (i.e. transport toward the organ apex) in a phloem-based auxin transport stream [19]. Consistent with this, AUX1 exhibits a basal PM localization in root protophloem cells, where it appears to function in conjunction with apically localized efflux carriers [19,21].


## PIN proteins characterize auxin efflux carrier complexes


The bias of IAA transport in plant tissues has been attributed to highly regulated, polarly localized efflux complexes that are characterized by the PIN family of proteins (reviewed in [6,23]). PIN proteins are members of the major efflux facilitator family of integral membrane proteins, are essential for polarized auxin movement, and align with the vector of auxin transport (reviewed in [6]). In Arabidopsis, each member of the PIN family displays a unique tissue-specific expression pattern, and pin mutations generally exhibit growth phenotypes that are consistent with the loss of directional auxin transport in the corresponding tissue $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 4 , 1 5 , 2 4 - 2 8 ]$ . PIN1 is localized primarily in the xylem parenchyma, and is essential for basipetal IAA transport in shoot tissues and for acropetal transport in root tissues $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 2 4 ]$ . pin1 mutants exhibit pinformed inflorescences, reduced basipetal auxin transport in inflorescence axes, and defective development of vascular tissue [24,29,30]. The PIN2/AGRAVITROPIC1 [AGR1]/ETHYLENE INSENTIVE ROOT1 (EIR1) is localized apically in root cortical cells, has a basal localization in root epidermal tissues, and functions primarily in the redistribution of auxin involved in root gravitropism $[ 1 4 , 2 5 , 2 6 , 3 1 ^ { \bullet } , 3 2 ^ { \bullet } ]$ . pin2/agr1 mutants display agravitropic root-growth phenotypes and reduced basipetal auxin transport in roots $[ 1 4 , 2 5 , 2 6 , 3 2 ^ { \bullet } ]$ . PIN3 appears to function in the lateral redistribution of auxin that is involved in photo- and gravitropic growth, and has a lateral localization in the cells of the shoot endodermis, in gravi-responding root columella, and in pericycle cells [28]. pin3 mutants exhibit reduced growth, diminished gravi- and phototropic responses, and decreased apical hook formation in etiolated seedlings [28]. PIN4 appears to function in the establishment of an auxin sink below the quiescent center of the root apical meristem [27]. PIN7 plays a role in forming and maintaining apical–basal auxin gradients that are essential for establishing embryonic polarity and functions in root acropetal auxin transport [3,15].

Several recent studies have dissected the complex mechanisms by which PIN-dependent, tissue-specific auxin transport creates localized gradients that are essential for plant organ or meristem formation, patterning, and maintenance $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 4 , 3 3 , 3 4 ^ { \bullet } ]$ . In aerial plant tissues (i.e. cotyledons and leaf primordia), organ formation appears to depend on a ‘reverse fountain’ PIN1-dependent flow of auxin through the outer cell layers of the organ [4]. IAA that has accumulated at the primordium tip is then redirected, or ‘drained’, through newly differentiated vasculature of the organ in a directional PIN1-dependent transport stream [4]. A similar, albeit reversed, mechanism takes place in the formation and maintenance of lateral roots. In these tissues, IAA accumulates in lateral root meristems by PIN1-dependent auxin transport through the central vascular tissues [4]. Analysis of single and combined pin1, pin3, pin4, and pin7 mutations indicates that the PIN1, PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7 proteins function collectively in establishing embryonic polarity and exhibit some functional redundancy in embryonic tissues [15].

More recent analysis of PIN function in Arabidopsis roots indicates that multiple PIN proteins function together to regulate auxin transport, tropic growth, and the maintenance of the root apical meristem $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } ]$ . Analysis of single and combined pin1, pin2, pin3, pin4, and pin7 mutants suggests that PINs function combinatorially to direct auxin flux and reflux in root tissues $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } ]$ . PIN1 appears to be the primary mediator of IAA movement through vascular tissues to the root tip, with PIN3, PIN4, and PIN7 contributing to this transport in adjacent tissues in the lower root $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } ]$ . Once at the root tip, auxin is redistributed basipetally through cortical and epidermal cells in a PIN2-dependent transport stream $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 4 ]$ . In the root elongation zone, PIN2, PIN3, and PIN7 mediate lateral re-direction, or ‘reflux’, of basipetally transported auxin back into the PIN1-dependent stelar auxin transport stream $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } , 1 5 ]$ . Once re-directed, auxin reaches the root tip and the process is repeated, creating a ‘reflux loop’ $[ 3 ^ { \bullet \bullet } ]$ .


## Regulation of auxin transport


Although competitive auxin efflux inhibitors (AEIs) such as triiodobenzoic acid (TIBA), and non-competitive AEIs, such as 1-N-naphthylpthalamic acid (NPA) and cyclopropyl propane dione (CPD), have long been used to define sites of auxin efflux regulation at the plasma membrane, recent evidence suggests that auxin transport is also regulated by cellular trafficking mechanisms [35]. PM localization of PIN1 and PIN3 is regulated by rapid, actin-dependent endocytotic cycling between the PM and endomembrane compartments [6,36,37]. When treated with the membrane-trafficking inhibitor brefeldin A (BFA), PIN1, PIN3, and AUX1 reversibly aggregate in endocytotic juxtanuclear compartments [28,36,38]. BFA washout with TIBA or high concentrations of NPA results in continued internalization of PIN1, indicating that AEIs might disrupt endocytotic trafficking of efflux proteins in addition to inhibiting auxin efflux at the PM [36,39]. Proper PIN1 localization and function are dependent on the GNOM/EMB30 auxin response factor (ARF) GDP/GTP exchange factor (GEF), which mediates BFA internalization of PIN1 [37,40].

The TRANSPORT INHIBITOR RESPONSE 3 (TIR3)/ DARK OVEREXPRESSION OF CAB1 (DOC1)/BIG protein also appears to function in endocytotic trafficking and, perhaps, in the stabilization of efflux complexes that are characterized by PIN1 on the PM. Originally identified in screens for NPA insensitivity, tir3 mutants exhibit reduced auxin transport and delocalization of PIN1 in response to NPA treatment without BFA pre-treatment [41,42]. BIG/TIR3 function does not appear limited to auxin transport, however, as the BIG protein has also been implicated in the responses to both gibberellins and phosphate stress [43,44]. Recent efforts to develop new inhibitors of auxin transport and plant cellular trafficking are expected to allow better dissection of this aspect of auxin transport regulation [45].

The protein kinase PINOID (PID) also appears to regulate PIN-mediated auxin transport. pid mutants are phenotypically similar to pin1 mutants and overexpression of PID results in phenotypes that are associated with increased auxin transport [46,47]. PID overexpression has no effect on PIN localization in epidermal cells, but results in a switch in PIN1 and PIN2 localization in cortical cells at the root tip as well as in a change in the polarity of PIN4 localization in cortical, endodermal, and vascular cells [31 ]. Protein phosphatase activity also appears to regulate auxin transport because the rcn1 mutant, which carries a defective protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit, exhibits decreased gravitropism and increased PIN2-independent basipetal auxin transport in roots [48,49].

Endogenous flavonols are non-essential regulators of auxin transport and appear to interact with the same sites as AEIs such as NPA [16 ,50–52]. In apical tissues, in particular, kaempferol and quercetin negatively regulate auxin efflux, and transparent testa (tt) mutants, which have decreased flavonoid production, show both increased rates of auxin transport and auxin-related phenotypes $[ 1 6 ^ { \bullet } , 5 1 , 5 2 ]$ Further, in flavonoid-deficient mutant backgrounds, flavonols can block the reversal of BFA-induced PIN1 internalization $[ 1 6 ^ { \bullet } ]$ . However, the alterations in PIN protein localization and abundance that are observed in the nonapical tissues of tt mutants can be mimicked by manipulation of wildtype auxin transport, suggesting that these changes result from auxin’s regulation of its own transport rather than from direct flavonoid interactions [16 ].


## The mechanism of auxin efflux


Although the PIN proteins are necessary for directed auxin transport, the mediation of auxin transport by PINs has not been unequivocally demonstrated, perhaps because other components of the efflux complex remain to be identified. To date, only PIN2 has been shown to mediate auxin efflux when expressed in a heterologous system [25], and no evaluation of substrate specificity was included in this work. The most likely candidates for additional auxin transport proteins are the multidrugresistance-like/P-glycoproteins (MDR/PGPs). In mammalian systems, MDR/PGPs (hereafter referred to as PGPs) function in ATP-dependent movement of hydrophobic substrates, and there is increasing evidence that a subset of the 21-member PGP-type ATP-binding cassette ABC transporter family play a similar role in auxin efflux (and possibly influx) in plants [11,53–55]. Defective PGP1 and PGP19 (MDR1) genes result in decreased auxin transport and reduced-growth phenotypes in Arabidopsis ( pgp1 and pgp19), maize (brachytic2 [br2]), and sorghum (dwarf3 [dw3]) [11,53,56]. The dwarf phenotypes are more severe in Arabidopsis double mutants, indicating that PGPs have overlapping, tissue-specific functions [11]. In the context of a chemiosmotically driven auxin transport system, PGPs that function in auxin efflux would be best described as ATP-activated anion carriers.

Biochemical evidence that PGPs function in auxin efflux complexes was obtained when PGP1, PGP2, PGP4, PGP10, and PGP19 were purified from high-affinity NPA-binding complexes. These complexes were solubilized from detergent-resistant membrane microdomains (DRMs) that were isolated from Arabidopsis PM and microsomal fractions ([55]; JJ Blakeslee, AS Murphy, unpublished). PGPs co-purified from PM fractions with proteins that were involved in cellular trafficking and endocytosis, and with the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins TWISTED DWARF1 (TWD1) and FASCICLIN-LIKE ARABINOGALATAN PROTEIN2 (FAGP2)/FASCICLIN2 (FAS2) [11,55]. Subsequent purifications from microsomal fractions also contained PIN1, PIN2, and TIR3/DOC1 (JJ Blakeslee, AS Murphy, unpublished). In mammalian systems, both GPI-anchored proteins and PGPs have been shown to play essential roles in maintaining the sterol-rich DRM microdomains in the PM that are crucial for the formation of multi-protein complexes [57,58]. It is possible that PGPs also play a similar role in Arabidopsis, and that the stabilization of efflux proteins in DRMs is necessary for polar auxin transport. Both cell polarity and the PM localization of PIN1 and PIN3 are disrupted in $o r c ^ { s m t }$ (sterol methyl transferase) mutants that have decreased levels of membrane sterols [59]. The involvement of PGP19 in stabilizing auxin efflux complexes on the PM is suggested by evidence that PIN1 is mislocalized in xylem parenchyma cells of hypertropic Arabidopsis pgp19 hypocotyls after treatment with high levels of the detergent Triton X-100 [54]. This effect is consistent with PGP19-mediated stabilization of PIN1 complexes on the PM, as PIN1 is not mislocalized in pgp1 and is only mislocalized in pgp19 when high detergent concentrations are used (JJ Blakeslee, AS Murphy, unpublished). Recent evidence of direct cellular transport of auxin that is mediated by PGPs in intact Arabidopsis tissues and mesophyll protoplasts, complemented by evidence of PGPmediated transport in yeast and mammalian cells $( [ 6 0 ^ { \bullet \bullet } ]$ ; JJ Blakeslee, AS Murphy, unpublished), suggests that PGPs not only stabilize efflux complexes but also are functional auxin transporters.


## A revised model of auxin efflux


A revised model for auxin transport in which PGPs maintain the stability of efflux complexes in PM DRMs and function as ATP-dependent auxin transporters would suggest that PIN proteins interact with PGPs to establish the transport vector and to enhance the auxin substrate specificity of the efflux complex. Mathematical models in which polarly localized PIN proteins are solely responsible for efflux correctly predict experimental auxin transport only in longer mature cells [34 ]. In small meristematic cells, only the ubiquitous expression of an efflux protein is sufficient to explain the rates of auxin transport seen in planta $( [ 3 4 ^ { \bullet } ] ;$ ; Figure 1). Further, in these smaller cells, auxin concentrations are high and diffusive re-entry of effluxed auxin would impede polar transport. An energy-dependent efflux mechanism, such as that provided by PGPs, would overcome re-diffusion and enhance the net movement of auxin away from the meristematic region. Specific PIN–PGP pairings would provide tissue-specific regulation of auxin transport streams.

The plant hormone auxin plays a central role in almost all aspects of plant development. Unidirectional cell-to-cell transport of auxin generates maxima and minima that are instrumental for tropic growth responses, tissue patterning, and organ initiation (Sabatini et al., 1999; Friml et al., 2002b, 2003; Benkova et al., 2003; Sorefan et al., 2009). The polar auxin flow is accomplished by the concerted action of three families of membrane proteins, the AUXIN RESISTANT1/LIKE AUX1 (AUX1/LAX) influx carriers (reviewed in Parry et al., 2001), the PIN-FORMED (PIN) efflux carriers (reviewed in Paponov et al., 2005), and the P-GLYCOPROTEIN (PGP/ABCB) transporters (reviewed in Geisler and Murphy, 2006). Until now, the role of the PIN auxin efflux carriers in polar auxin transport is most well established. The Arabidopsis thaliana genome encodes eight PIN proteins, named after the pin-formed/pin1 mutant that is defective in polar auxin transport and develops pin-shaped inflorescences (Ga¨ lweiler et al., 1998). The PIN family proteins can be classified into two groups: (1) the PIN1-type proteins (PIN1, 2, 3, 4, and 7) that are plasma membrane (PM) localized and (2) the PIN5-type proteins (PIN5, 6, and 8) that localize to the endoplasmatic reticulum (ER) and seem to be involved in the regulation of auxin homeostasis (Mravec et al., 2009). The PIN1-type proteins have redundant functions, and a loss-of-function mutation in one PIN gene is sometimes compensated for by the ectopic expression of other PINs (Blilou et al., 2005; Vieten et al., 2005). As a result, only mutants in multiple PIN genes show more pronounced phenotypes in embryogenesis, root patterning, and lateral root initiation (Benkova et al., 2003; Friml et al., 2003; Blilou et al., 2005).

The PIN1-type proteins determine the direction of cell-to-cell auxin transport through their asymmetric subcellular localization at the PM (Wis´ niewska et al., 2006), which is dependent not only on tissue-specific factors, but also on the PIN protein sequence (Wis´ niewska et al., 2006). During specific developmental processes, dynamic changes in PIN polarity have been observed (Benkova et al., 2003; Friml et al., 2003; Heisler et al., 2005), and PIN polarity has also been shown to be modulated by environmental cues (Friml et al., 2002b; Harrison and Masson, 2008) and auxin itself (Paciorek et al., 2005; Sauer et al., 2006). Many research efforts have focused on what determines PIN polarity and, thus, what translates upstream developmental and environmental signals into changes in plant architecture by regulating PIN polarity. The current model is that newly synthesized PINs arrive at the PM in a nonpolar fashion and that PIN polarity is established and regulated by subsequent endocytosis,

transcytosis, and recycling back to the PM (Geldner et al., 2001;   
Dhonukshe et al., 2008; Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008).

Background: The plant phytohormone auxin controls many aspects of plant growth and development, which largely depends on its uneven distribution in plant tissues. Transmembrane proteins of the PIN family are auxin efflux facilitators. They play a key role in polar auxin transport and are associated with auxin asymmetrical distribution in plants. PIN genes have been characterized in several plant species, while comprehensive analysis of this gene family in soybean has not been reported yet.

Results: In this study, twenty-three members of the PIN gene family were identified in the soybean genome through homology searches. Analysis of chromosome distribution and phylogenetic relationships of the soybean PIN genes indicated nine pairs of duplicated genes and a legume specific subfamily. Organ/tissue expression patterns and promoter activity assays of the soybean PINs suggested redundant functions for most duplicated genes and complementary and tissue-specific functions during development for non-duplicated genes. The soybean PIN genes were differentially regulated by various abiotic stresses and phytohormone stimuli, implying crosstalk between auxin and abiotic stress signaling pathways. This was further supported by the altered auxin distribution under these conditions as revealed by DR5::GUS transgenic soybean hairy root. Our data indicates that GmPIN9, a legume-specific PIN gene, which was responsive to several abiotic stresses, might play a role in auxin redistribution in soybean root under abiotic stress conditions.

Conclusions: This study provided the first comprehensive analysis of the soybean PIN gene family. Information on phylogenetic relationships, gene structure, protein profiles and expression profiles of the soybean PIN genes in different tissues and under various abiotic stress treatments helps to identity candidates with potential roles in specific developmental processes and/or environmental stress conditions. Our study advances our understanding of plant responses to abiotic stresses and serves as a basis for uncovering the biological role of PIN genes in soybean development and adaption to adverse environments.

Keywords: Soybean, Glycine max, PIN, Auxin efflux carriers, Polar auxin transport, ABA, Abiotic stresses

Auxin is one of the major driving forces of plant development and requires careful regulation of transporter proteins to establish polar auxin transport. The PIN-FORMED (PIN) family plays a pivotal role in plant development by establishing auxin gradients that govern vascular patterning and organogenesis. However, the PIN family remains severely underexplored in Setaria viridis, a well-established model for $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ monocots. In this study, we identified and characterized 13 PIN genes in the S. viridis genome. Phylogenetic and collinearity analyses revealed duplication events in the SvPIN1, SvPIN5 and $S \nu P I N I O$ subfamilies. Structural analysis uncovered unique features, including potential pseudogenization of SvPIN5a. Expression profiling across five developmental stages unveiled the potential developmental roles of SvPINs, with SvPIN1 and SvPIN10 paralogues predominantly expressed in shoots and panicles, SvPIN2 and SvPIN9 in roots, while SvPIN5b showed leaf-enriched expression, suggesting potential involvement in leaf vascular development. Hormonal treatments in callus cultures revealed auxin-mediated upregulation of SvPIN1b, SvPIN2, SvPIN5d, SvPIN8 and SvPIN10a. Our findings provide significant insights into the role of PIN genes in S. viridis and other $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ monocots, establishing a foundation for future functional studies and offering potential targets for crop improvement through auxin transport manipulation.


## Key message


This study characterizes the PIN-FORMED auxin transporter family in the $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ model Setaria viridis, revealing gene duplication, tissue-specific expression, and hormonal regulation that may influence $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ traits.

Besides vascular transport system present in plants,cel to cell transport system also present in the tissues which covers long and short distance auxin distributions across the plant (Zazimalova et al. 2010). Polar auxin efflux carrer (PIN） genes plays important roles in auxin distribution and homeostasis in plants in polarized manner (Friml and Palme 2002; Abas et al. 2006; Barbez et al. 2012). AtPIN1gene was the first PIN gene to be cloned from plant Arabidopsis thaliana (Galweiler et al. 1998). The plant specific PIN gene family of auxin efflux carriers are integral membrane proteins that contain inner and outer transmembrane domain and central hydrophilic domain (Petrasek et al. 2006; Krecek et al.

2009; Mravec et al. 2009). The N-terminal and C-terminal region of PIN proteins are is conserved and the central hydrophilic loop region is very dynamic in nature among diferent PIN proteins (Kramer and Bennett 2006; Mohanta and Mohanta 2013a; Mohanta and Mohanta 2013b). Plant roots serve to fix the plant body in the soil and provide plants with water and nutrients. Roots need to sense and respond appropriately to a diversity of environmental signals, such as gravity, mechanical impedance, light, humidity, oxygen, and essential nutrients, as well as to allelochemicals exuded from neighboring roots, to develop their optimal form or adapt to their environment conditions (Monshausen and Gilroy, 2009). Although phototropic responses in roots were discovered and analyzed some time ago, knowledge of root phototropism is surprisingly poor when compared with that of root gravitropism (Boonsirichai et al., 2002; Correll and Kiss, 2002; Whippo and Hangarter, 2006; Holland et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2009).

The classic Cholodny-Went theory postulates that both gravitropism and phototropism are determined by the asymmetric distribution of the phytohormone auxin. The current discovery and analysis of auxin efflux transporters, the PIN-formed proteins (PINs), supports this hypothesis by describing a sensitive, adjustable network of five PINs (PIN 1, 2, 3, 4, and 7) that drive polar auxin transport in the root apex (Blilou et al., 2005; KleineVehn and Friml, 2008; Balusˇ ka et al., 2010). However, polar PIN localization is not static but undergoes constant recycling between the plasma membrane (PM) and endosomal compartments (Robert and Friml, 2009). Recent studies indicate that blue light (BL) determines the localization and distribution of PIN1 and PIN3 in hypocotyl cells (Blakeslee et al., 2004; Ding et al., 2011) and PIN2 in root cells (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008; Laxmi et al., 2008). Laxmi et al. (2008) reported that a mutation of transcription factor HY5, which is regulated by the blue and red light receptors, phytochromes and cryptochromes, respectively (Lau and Deng, 2010), decreases PM targeting of PIN2 via endosomal trafficking and that the CONSTITUTIVE PHOTOMORPHOGENIC9 complex mediates the proteasome-dependent degradation of PIN2 via its targeting into lytic vacuoles (Laxmi et al., 2008). Retromer components, such as SORTING NEXIN1 and VACUOLAR PROTEIN SORTING29, play a key role in resorting PIN2 into vacuoles under dark conditions and also in retrieving PIN2 from vacuoles back to the PM-targeted recycling pathway under light illumination (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008). PIN2 subcellular relocalization or degradation (or both) is involved in BL-induced root phototropism is unclear. In our previous study, we reported that the BL receptor phot1 is polarly localized on the PM of root cortical cells, showing a localization very similar to that of PIN2 (Rahman et al., 2010), and that the extent of BL-induced phot1 internalization reflects the intensity of BL administered (Wan et al., 2008). Based on these results, we postulated a relationship between BL-induced relocalization of phot1 and endosomal recycling of PIN2 protein.

Plant-specific PIN-formed (PIN) efflux transporters for the plant hormone auxin are required for tissue-specific directional auxin transport and cellular auxin homeostasis. The Arabidopsis PIN protein family has been shown to play important roles in developmental processes such as embryogenesis, organogenesis, vascular tissue differentiation, root meristem patterning and tropic growth. Here we analyzed roles of the less characterised Arabidopsis PIN6 auxin transporter. PIN6 is auxin-inducible and is expressed during multiple auxin–regulated developmental processes. Loss of pin6 function interfered with primary root growth and lateral root development. Misexpression of PIN6 affected auxin transport and interfered with auxin homeostasis in other growth processes such as shoot apical dominance, lateral root primordia development, adventitious root formation, root hair outgrowth and root waving. These changes in auxin-regulated growth correlated with a reduction in total auxin transport as well as with an altered activity of DR5-GUS auxin response reporter. Overall, the data indicate that PIN6 regulates auxin homeostasis during plant development.

The systematic effort of plant molecular biology has integrated the phytohormone auxin in key developmental processes. Auxin (in the most common form, indole-3-acetic acid, IAA) is closely linked with embryogenesis, organogenesis, tissue patterning, regeneration, tropisms [1], and also with a developmental response to stress [2] and other environmental stimuli [3]. Besides auxin signaling, which is located in the nucleus, and controlled IAA synthesis and degradation, which occurs in various cellular compartments, the critical role of the cell-to-cell auxin transport has been classically underlined [4]. In line with this concept, auxin is directionally conveyed by the PIN-FORMED family transporters (PINs) that are typically asymmetrically localized at the plasma membrane (PM) [5]. Besides the PM-located PINs and other auxin transporters present there [6–8], several studies also uncovered intracellularly located transporters WALLS ARE THIN 1 (WAT1) [9], and especially PIN-LIKEs (PILS) that show several structural and phenotypic features related to PINs and are localized on the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) [10,11]. Importantly, there is a functionally and structurally distinct group of PINs located on ER as well [12–15].

The genome of Arabidopsis thaliana encodes eight PIN proteins. Based on their mutual sequence similarity and subcellular localization, they are categorized into two basic sub-clades (Figure 1): plasma membrane (PM- or long) and endoplasmic reticulum (ER- or short) PINs [12,16]. Well-characterized PM-PINs (PIN1, 2, 3, 4, and 7) mediate polar auxin efflux from the cells [4]. In addition, three ER-PINs (PIN5, 6, and 8) show a significant role in maintaining intracellular auxin distribution and homeostasis [12–14].

## 2. Membrane Topology and Structural Properties of ER-PINs 2. Membrane Topology and Structural Properties of ER-PINs

Auxin is a plant hormone that possesses multiple functions that regulate the plant growth and development primarily at the cellular level and in response to diverse environmental stimuli as well [1–5]. Auxin is primarily synthesized in leaf primordium, germinating seeds, root tips, and cambiums. The directional polar auxin transport (PAT) system distributes auxin to the targeted tissues to facilitate apical dominance, embryonic development, vascular tissue development, root meristem maintenance, and organ formation and positioning [6]. The cell–cell polar transport of auxin is mediated by proteins localized in the plasma membrane (PM), and these proteins are members of three distinct gene families: the auxin resistant (AUX) 1/like AUX1 (LAX) influx carriers [7], the pin-formed (PIN) efflux carriers [8], and the ATP-binding cassette B/Multidrug-resistance /P-glycoprotein (ABCB/MDR/PGP) efflux/condition transporters [9]. Unique polar transport of auxin forms auxin gradients that result in asymmetric distribution of PIN, AUX/LAX, and ABCB proteins across cells and tissues. Regulation of the uneven distribution of auxin within tissues and organs or throughout the entire plant body via auxin transporters provides an important strategy to execute the auxin functions in controlling various plant developmental processes and in response to stressful environments.

AUX/LAX influx carriers encompass four highly conversed family members, and AUX1 and LAX1–3 are characterized as multi membrane-spanning transmembrane proteins that facilitated the entry of auxin into cells [10]. The founder member AUX1 is initially identified from Arabidopsis and primarily functions to promote high-affinity cellular auxin uptake in the root tips [11]. The auxin insensitive1 (aux1) mutant exhibits an agravitropic phenotype that is observed in roots after treatment with the auxin influx carrier inhibitor 1- naphthoxyaceticacids (1-NOA), and the gravitropic response in this mutant can be restored by treatment with the membrane-permeable auxin 1-naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA) [12,13]. AtLAX2 participates in the vascular development of cotyledons, and disruption of this gene reinforces cell separation in the quiescent center (QC) and reduces the expression of the auxin response reporter DR5 [14]. LAX3 in combination with AUX1, appears to facilitate lateral root development by targeting the auxin-inducible expression of a selection of cell wall remodeling enzymes. The lax3 mutation in Arabidopsis disrupts lateral root emergence, while the aux1lax3 double mutant exhibits a reduced number of emerged lateral roots [15]. The AUX/LAX gene family has also been described in different monocotyledons and dicotyledons in response to hormonal and abiotic stress at the transcriptional level [16–20].

The PIN family is the most extensively studied of the auxin efflux carriers among the auxin transporters in plants, and these carriers play an essential role in PAT [21]. The PIN genes are first cloned in Arabidopsis, where eight members of this gene family are well characterized. PIN proteins are localized either on the PM (AtPIN1, -2, -3, -4 and -7) or in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (AtPIN5, AtPIN6, and AtPIN8), and corresponding classifications are further divided based on their different structures, which determine their distinct roles in polar intercellular transport and intracellular auxin homeostasis [22]. AtPIN1 is expressed in the vascular bundle of the root, in the inflorescence stem, and the developing organs [23,24]. Loss-of-function mutations in this gene result in defective floral organs and the formation of naked, pin-shaped inflorescences, fused leaves, and other shoot abnormalities [25]. Initially, three identified mutant alleles of PIN2 that possess a strong root agravitropic phenotype were named independently as ethylene-insensitive root1 (eir1), agravitropic1 (agr1), and wavy6 (wav6) [26–28]. AtPIN3 is symmetrically located in the root columella cells; however, this protein rapidly relocalizes laterally in response to gravity stimulation. Mutations in the Arabidopsis gene PIN3 result in reduced growth and tropic response, and apical hook formation is also altered in pin3 mutants [29]. The functional involvement of AtPIN4 during organogenesis and embryogenesis has been also demonstrated. Disruption of AtPIN4 affects pattern formation in both the embryo and the seedling roots. Therefore, AtPIN4 plays an essential role in auxin maximization and redistribution within the root tip [30]. AtPIN7 is expressed in the basal lineage in the embryo and then later in the root tips, and this protein displays an expression pattern that is complementary to that of PIN1 [25]. These loss-of-function phenotypes demonstrate the crucial role of these proteins in these developmental processes.

Arsenic (As), a metalloid commonly present in the soil, primarily exists in sulfdes and other rock-forming minerals. The dissolution of these minerals can lead to the infltration and contamination of groundwater. This poses a signifcant risk to human health including organ damage, clinical complications, and diverse types of cancer (Chen et al. 2019). Similarly, crops irrigated with As contaminated water can accumulate arsenate, potentially compromising the safety of cultivated foods and quality. Furthermore, As induces the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants, adversely afecting crop growth and productivity (Tang et al. 2023). Additionally, arsenic can accumulate in the human body, resulting in organ damage, clinical complications, and diverse types of cancer (Chen et al. 2019).To achieve genetically engineered arsenate-tolerant crops it is crucial to understand how plants absorb the arsenate and the regulatory mechanisms involved to address these implications for human health and food safety.

In soil, As primarily exists as Arsenate As(V), which is structurally similar to phosphate (Pi) and can readily enter plant roots via Pi transporters (Li et al. 2016). The other form is Arsenite As(III) which is interconvertible to As(V) depending upon redox status of the environmental conditions. The absorption of As(III) is primarily facilitated by plant aquaporins or plasma membrane intrinsic proteins, in contrast to the mechanism involved in As(V) uptake (Wang et al. 2018). Members of the membrane receptor PHOSPHATE TRANSPORTER 1 (PHT1) family have been identifed as being involved in As(V) uptake and transport in plants. Recently, a Plant Database SCIPDb showed alterations in PHT1 levels in Cicer arietinum under combined Ralstonia solanacearum and drought stress conditions (Priya et al. 2023). In Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana), AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 were initially discovered to mediate the acquisition of both Pi and As(V) from soils (Shin et al. 2004). Kinases are crucial regulators of both plant and animal development including stresses (Singh et al. 2023a, b; Mishra and Maurya 2023). Studies have demonstrated that CALCIUM-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASES (CPKs), crucial regulators of calcium, are typically engaged in deciphering $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signals induced by stress or stimuli in plants (Harmon et al. 2001; Liu et al. 2017). Arabidopsis harbors 34 CPKs, which play crucial roles in plant growth, development, and response to various abiotic, biotic, and in combined stresses (Yip Delormel and Boudsocq 2019; Priya et al. 2023). In the past, research has demonstrated a signifcant increase in CPKs activity levels when rice plants were subjected to $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress (Huang et al. 2012). which suggests the involvement of CPK in responding to stress induced by arsenate. Recently, it has been demonstrated that CPK31 interacts with the As(III) transporter nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein (NIP1;1), infuencing both the uptake and tolerance of Arabidopsis to arsenic (Ji et al. 2017). Plant NIPs, grouped as NIP1-NIP5, show remarkable conservation across species. NIP1;1, a key As(III) transporter in Arabidopsis, was identifed through a genetics screen, with high expression in roots and plasma membrane localization. Loss-of-function mutants of NIP1;1 exhibited As(III)-tolerant phenotypes, emphasizing its crucial role in mediating toxic As(III) uptake into roots. Beyond arsenic, NIPs are also involved in the transport of various metalloids, such as antimonite, boron, silicon, and selenium, within plants (Kamiya et al. 2009; Kamiya and Fujiwara 2009; Maurel et al. 2015).

Despite this fnding, the specifc regulatory role of CPK31 in modulating NIP1.1 under arsenic stress, particularly As(V)

stress, remains unclear. In the highlighted study, it has been observed that Arabidopsis roots exhibit distinct $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling in response to As(V) stress. Subsequently, the researchers identifed a cpk23 mutant, displaying the most pronounced sensitivity among the 31 CPKs single mutants screened under $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress conditions. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that CPK23 plays a role in modulating As(V) tolerance in Arabidopsis by infuencing the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 through phosphorylation.


## $\pmb { \mathbb { A } s ( \pmb { \mathbb { V } } ) }$ stress, $\pmb { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ signaling and importance of CPK23 in Arabidopsis


$\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ is a celebrated secondary messenger in abiotic stress signaling downstream of the plasma membrane receptor (Dong et al. 2022). In response to As stress, diferential expression of diferent $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensors, such as CaMs, suggests the possible involvement of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent signaling in As tolerance in plants (Chakrabarty et al. 2009). In this regard, CPKs, as essential calcium regulatory proteins, are usually involved in decoding $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signals caused by plant stress or stimuli (Mohanta et al. 2019).

In a recent study, (Liu et al. 2023) discovered that arsenate treatment induced a rapid and transient increase in intracellular calcium levels in Arabidopsis roots. Building upon this fnding, the authors screened and identifed a cpk23 mutant, which displayed the most pronounced sensitivity among 31 CPKs single mutants under As(V) stress, which indicates the involvement of a plasma membrane associated CPK23. Moreover, no change has been observed in the transcript of CPK23 following As(V)-induced stress, leading to speculation that the kinase activity of CPK23 plays a crucial role in its functionality. This is further validated by analyzing the phenotype of CPK23 overexpression (CPK23-OE) transgenic lines and constitutively active CPK23 (CPK23-VK) plants under diferent levels of As(V) stress response (Liu et al. 2023).The authors observed that CPK23-OE plants did not show a tolerance phenotype under As(V) stress. In contrast, all CPK23-VK plants showed a tolerance phenotype under 300, 400, and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress. Furthermore, the authors investigated CPK23's involvement in the phosphate signal response by examining the above mutants (Liu et al. 2023). Despite observing a phosphate defciency phenotype, there was no growth diference between WT plants and mutants, suggesting CPK23 has no role in phosphate defciency response (Liu et al. 2023).Thus, these results suggested that the kinase activity of CPK23 is specifcally required for As(V) tolerance.


## CPK23 orchestrates $\pmb { \mathbb { A } s ( \pmb { \mathbb { V } } ) }$ tolerance by modulating the delocalization of PHT1;1 under As(V) stress


Furthermore, to identify the downstream protein phosphorylated by CPK23, the authors performed co-immunoprecipitation coupled to mass spectrometry (IP-MS) using CPK23-FLAG transgenic seedlings. They identified a peptide corresponding to PHT1;1, a phosphate transporter associated with arsenic transport. Through subsequent protein interaction and phosphorylation experiments, the authors determined that CPK23 interacts with PHT1;1 and phosphorylates the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site at its C-terminus under arsenic stress response (Liu et al. 2023).

Furthermore, to assess the impact of PHT1; $1 ^ { 5 5 1 4 }$ phosphorylation on plant tolerance to $\mathbf { A s } ( \mathbf { V } )$ , the authors generated transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing phospho-dead (ProPHT1;1:PHT1; $1 ^ { \mathrm { S 5 1 4 A } } )$ and phosphoactivated (ProPHT1;1:PHT1;1S514D) versions of PHT1;1 in the pht1;1 mutant background. The phospho-dead variant showed sensitivity to As stress, while the phosphoactivated variant displayed tolerance similar to that of pht1;1 plants response (Liu et al. 2023). These physiological experiments confrmed the importance of PHT1;1S514 phosphorylation for its function in As(V) tolerance. Previously, it has been shown that $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ infuences the localization of the PHT1;1 transporter in the root cell (Navarro et al. 2021). To investigate whether CPK23 regulates the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 via phosphorylation under As(V) stress, the authors expressed PHT1.1 phosphorylation site mutants fused with a green fuorescent protein (GFP) in both wild-type and cpk23 mutant plants lar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration, results in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ spiking which further activates CPK23. Following activation, CPK23 phosphorylates PHT1;1 at the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site. Phosphorylation at $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ promotes the delocalization of PHT1;1 from the plasma membrane, ultimately decreasing $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ uptake and incerases plant tolerance to $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress

(Liu et al. 2023). Furthermore, it has been observed that the localization of PHT1;1 was signifcantly infuenced by the phosphorylation of the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site, with PHT1; $1 ^ { 5 5 1 4 \mathrm { A } }$ - GFP plants exhibiting a more pronounced co-localization with the plasma membrane compared to PHT1; $1 ^ { \mathrm { S 5 1 4 D } }$ -GFP plants. Additionally, authors observed that in WT plants, PHT1;1-GFP undergoes delocalization from the plasma membrane under As (V) stress (Fig. 1), whereas in cpk23 plants, PHT1;1-GFP remains anchored to the plasma membrane in the same conditions response (Liu et al. 2023). These fndings suggest that CPK23 regulates the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 under As (V) stress through phosphorylation of the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site (Fig. 1).

Moreover, CDPK23 and PHT1;1 may orchestrate crucial pathways for As detoxifcation and transport in plants. Understanding their complex mechanisms could open the door to genetic engineering approaches aimed at boosting plant resilience in As-contaminated environments, thereby promoting sustainable agriculture and environmental conservation. This insight into the molecular basis of As tolerance may revolutionize crop production in regions afected by As pollution, addressing a critical global challenge in food security. CPK23 plays a pivotal role in As stress responses, regulating downstream genes involved in detoxifcation mechanisms. PHT1;1, on the other hand, is crucial for As uptake and transport within plants. Thus, manipulating these genes by utilizing CLUSTERED REGULARLY INTERSPACED SHORT PALINDROMIC REPEAT (CRISPR)- CRISPR associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology, RNA interference (RNAi), transgenic approaches, site-directed mutagenesis etc., holds potential to manipulate/modulate the expression or activity of these genes, thereby fortifying crops against As-induced damage. It's noteworthy that kinases are typically not preferentially considered for genetic applications. However, these candidates are particularly intriguing due to their direct involvement in essential As tolerance pathways, making them key players in mitigating the toxic efects of As on crops. Additionally, the interaction between CPK23 and PHT1;1 underscores the importance of these genes in coordinating As detoxifcation and transport within plants. Thus, their manipulation not only addresses As stress directly but also opens avenues for in-depth mechanistic exploration, ofering insights critical for developing resilient and As-resistant crop varieties.

Phosphorus (P) is one of the indispensable macronutrients for many important plant physiological processes,including energy transfer，signal transduction，photosynthesis, and respiration,and is a component of many biomacromolecules,playing a vital role in plant growth and development (Gu et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2016). Soluble inorganic phosphate (Pi) in soil,the predominant source of P for plants,is absorbed by roots and transported into various parts of plant organs for utilization or storage (Nussaume et al.,2011;Remy et al.,2012). Although P is one of the most abundant elements in the earth's crust,ranking 11th among all elements,most of it is present in the form of precipitates with cations,which cannot be directly acquired by plant roots (Blank,2012).Therefore,P is the most commonly limiting nutrient for agricultural production worldwide (Chen et al., 2015).

Uptake of soluble Pi from the soil relies on Pi transporters (PHTs) located in the root cell plasma membrane (Blank, 2012; Gu et al., 2016; Nussaume et al., 2011). Two high-affinity PHTs in the PHT1 family,PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, playa major role in Pi uptake in Arabidopsis (Shin et al., 2004;Wang et al., 2021). The PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 double mutant,pht1;1444,has an extremely low Pi uptake rate,only $2 2 \%$ of that of wild-type plants,and displays severe Pi starvation symptoms under low Pi conditions (Shin et al.,2004)．The expression of PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 is rapidly activated by low Pi to enhance plant Pi uptake,and some important regulators positively or negatively regulating their expression have been identified, including PHR1, WRKY75,WRKY45，WRKY42，WRKY6，MYB62，and ZAT6 (Chen et al.,20o9; Devaiah,Karthikeyan,& Raghothama, 2007; Devaiah，Nagarajan，& Raghothama,2O07；Gu et al., 2016; Nilsson et al.,2007; Rubio et al.,2001; Su et al.,2015;Wang et al.,2014). In addition, the expression of PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 is also epigenetically regulated by chromatin modifications in plants.For example,the inositol pentakisphosphate 2-kinase IPK1 and the nuclear protein actin-related protein 6 (ARP6) are required for deposition of the histone variant H2A.Z at PHT genes and for repression of target gene expression (Kuo et al.,2014; Smith et al., 2010).

In addition to transcriptional control,PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are also modulated at the post-translational level in the plant response to changes inPi availability(Gu et al.,2016)．Phosphate Transporter Traffic Facilitator1 (AtPHF1) in Arabidopsis and its homolog OsPHF1 in rice (Oryza sativa) participate in the trafficking of PHTs from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the plasma membrane, where they mediate Pi transport (Bayle et al., 2011; Chen et al.,2011; Gonzalez et al., 2005)． The phosphorylation status also affects the plasma membrane localization of PHTs.Phosphorylation of PHT1;1 at Ser514 prevents its exit from the ER and subsequent plasma membrane localization in Arabidopsis (Bayle et al., 2011).Further study revealed that CK2 kinase-mediated phosphorylation of OsPHT1;2 and OsPHT1;2 suppresses their interaction with OsPHF1,thus negatively affecting Pi uptake in rice (Chen et al.,2015).In addition,the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme PHOSPHATE2 (PHO2) and the RING-type ubiquitin E3 ligase NITROGEN LIMITATION ADAPTATION (NLA) interact with PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 and facilitate their ubiquitination for vacuolar proteolysis (Huang et al.,2013). Also, endosomal traficking modulates PHT abundance in the plasma membrane for a proper plant response to extracellular Pi availability.It has been reported that the cytosoliclocalized ESCRT-ll-interacting protein ALIX mediates the internalization of PHT1;1 in the multivesicular bodies (MVBs) for degradation in the vacuole,thus the alix mutant has increased PHT1;1 protein stability and enhanced Pi uptake rate and total Pi accumulation (Cardona-Lopez et al., 2015).

Sorting Nexins (SNXs) are endosomal regulatory proteins conserved in mammals,yeast,and plants (Brumbarova& lvanov,2016; Pourcheret al.,2010). In Arabidopsis，three SNX members，SNX1，SNX2a and SNX2b，have been identified and characterized.SNX1 plays a vital role in the plant response to environmental stimuli (Brumbarova & lvanov,2016). For example, SNX1 plays a role in root tip auxin accumulation through affecting the homeostasis of important auxin influx carriers, PIN1 and PIN2 (Jaillais et al., 2006). Also,SNX1 functions in the plant response to limited iron availability by promoting the stability and plasma membrane localization of the principal root iron importer IRON-REGULATED TRANSPORTER1 (IRT1) for increased iron uptake (lvanov et al.,2014).We previously reported that SNX1 afects salt stress-induced nitric oxide (NO) accumulation,thus playing a role in the plant response to high salinity in Arabidopsis (Li et al., 2018).

Recently,it was reported that PLDg2-derived phosphatidic acid (PA) directly binds to SNX1 to promote its accumulation at the plasma membrane, leading to decreased degradation of PIN2, thus promoting root hair development under Pi deficiency (Lin et al., 202O). However, the role of SNX1 in plant Pi uptake,in particular the modulation of PHTs,remains to be elucidated. Here,we report that SNX1 interacts with PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 and decreases their protein stability and plasma membrane accumulation, thus negatively modulating plant Pi uptake under low Pi conditions.

## The snx1-2 mutant is insensitive to low Pi


Plants have evolved sophisticated adaptive mechanisms to respond to limited Pi availability by coordinating growth, development,and metabolic processes.One of the most visible Pi starvation responses (PSRs) is the accumulation of anthocyanin in plant leaves (Ren et al., 2014)． PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 mutants and plants with reduced PHT expression exhibit decreased Pi uptake and increased PSRs,thus usually exhibiting increased leaf anthocyanin accumulation.Therefore，screening and identification of mutants with altered anthocyanin accumulation in response to Pi deficiency may shed some light on plant PSRs.To achieve this,5-day-old wild-type and a collection of Arabidopsis mutant seedlings grown on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium were transferred to medium containing sufficient Pi (MS medium) or deficient Pi (low phosphate [LP] medium with $1 0 ~ \mu \mu$ Pi) for another 5 days,and the leaf anthocyanin levels were examined. Our results show that wildtype leaves exhibited a dark purple color after treatment of lowPi， while the leaves of one mutant， snx1-2 (SALK_O33351),still displayed a green or light purple color, suggesting decreased anthocyanin accumulation in the mutant (Figure 1a). Indeed,the anthocyanin content of the snx1-2 mutant was markedly lower than that of wild-type plants under low Pi conditions (Figure 1b)，revealing decreased PSR of the mutant in response to low Pi.To further investigate the PSR in the snx1-2 mutant, we assayed the expression of some Pi starvation-induced genes, including MYB62, DFR,and LDOX (Huang et al., 2018). Our quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results showed that the expression of these genes was extensively activated in wild-type plants but repressed in the snx1-2 mutant when subjected to low Pi (Figure 1c-e),further supporting the decreased PSR in the mutant.PHR1 is a central transcription factor regulating the expresson of genes correlated with Pi uptake and anthocyanin accumulation.We found that the snx1-2 mutant did not significantly affect PHR1 expression under sufficient Pi or deficient Pi conditions (Figure 1f).

To dissect whether decreased PSR of the snx1-2 mutant is due to increased Pi uptake and Pi content,we assayed the Pi content of mutant and wild-type seedlings under Pisufficient and Pi-deficient conditions. Our results showed that the Pi content in snx1-2 mutant whole seedlings was significantly higher than that in wild-type seedlings (Figure 1g).We also assayed the Pi content in the roots and shoots of the wild type and snx1-2 mutant,and found that the Pi content in the roots and shoots of the snx1-2 mutant was higher than in the wild type (Figure 1g),suggesting that root Pi uptake is promoted in the mutant. Consistently, the snx1-2 mutant showed higher tolerance to low Pi than the wild type in terms of fresh weight (Figure S1a,b).The higher Pi content in snx1-2 mutant shoots than in wildtype shoots raised the possibility that SNX1 modulates PHOSPHATE1 (PHO1),which is implicated in Pi loading into the xylem,thus affecting the Pi distribution in shoots and roots. If this was the case, the shoot-to-root ratio of Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant should be different to that in wild-type plants,but the ratio in the mutant was comparable to that in wild-type plants,under both sufficient Pi and deficient Pi conditions (Figure S1c)，revealing that SNX1 has no effect on the Pi distribution in shoots and roots under different Pi availabilities.

To verify that mutation of SNX1 is the cause for decreased anthocyanin accumulation and increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant under low Pi,a second transfer DNA insertion mutant allele of this gene， snx1-1 (GABI_105C01)，was employed. Similar to the snx1-2 mutant, the snx1-1 mutant also had less anthocyanin accumulation and more Pi content than wild-type plants when treated with deficient Pi (Figure S2),further supporting the key role of SNX1 in anthocyanin accumulation and Pi uptake in the plant response to low Pi.


## The snx1-2 mutant has enhanced Pi uptake


Our above results showed that the snx1-2 mutant had decreased PSR and increased Pi content compared with wild-type plants，suggesting enhanced Pi uptake of the snx1-2 mutant root.To verify this,we tested the sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate,a toxic compound with a similar structure to phosphate that can be absorbed by plant high-affinity PHTs including PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 (Cao et al.,202O; Shin et al., 2004). Arsenate negatively affects plant growth and development such as seed germination, cotyledon greening,and root elongation (Cao et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2014).We found that snx1-2 mutant seeds had comparable germination and cotyledon greening rates to wild-type seeds when grownon arsenate-free medium,while the mutant seeds showed significantly decreased germination and cotyledon greening rates compared to wild-type plants when grown on arsenate-containing medium (Figure 2a-e). The increased sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate was confirmed by assessing its root elongation and fresh weight. Fiveday-old wild-type and snx1-2 mutant seedlings were transferred to arsenate-containing medium and treated for 5 days.As shown in Figure 2(f)， the snx1-2 mutant seedlings exhibited significantly less resistance to arsenate than the wild-type plants,as evidenced by shorter roots. These data indicated increased sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate，revealing enhanced Pi transporter activity in the mutant roots.


## PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 interact with SNX1


Increased Pi content and arsenate sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant suggested higher PHT activity for Pi uptake in roots. Hence，we first examined the expression of the genes encoding the two major high-affinity PHTs，PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants. Our qRTPCR data showed that the expression of both PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 was extensively induced by low Pi in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants,and their expression level in the mutant was similar to that in the wild type (Figure S3), excluding the possibility that increased Pi content in the mutant was due to higher expression of PHT1;1 and PHT1;4.

Considering that SNX1 is a key component of sorting endosomes，we speculated that SNX1 affects plant Pi uptake through modulating endosomal traffickingof PHT1;1 and/or PHT1;4. Thus， we examined the colocalization of SNX1 with PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 by expressing them under the control of their native promoters in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.As shown in Figure 3(a), the fluorescence signals of SNX1-mCherry and PHT1;1-GFP or PHT1;4-GFP were mainly co-localized in vesicles in N. benthamiana leaves,which is in line with a previous report showing that PHT1;1 is localized to sorting endosomes containingSNX1inArabidopsisroottips(Bayle et al.,2011).To further verify such co-localization，we obtained a stable PHT1;1-GFP SNX1-mRFP line by introducing PHT1;1::PHT1;1-GFP into SNX1::SNX1-mRFP plants and observed their localization. Our confocal microscopy results showed that PHT1;1-GFP and SNX1-mRFP mainly co-localized in vesicles in PHT1;1-GFP SNX1-mRFP seedling roots treated with sufficient Pi (Figure 3b)，which is very similar to the previous report (Bayle et al.,2011). However,when treated with deficient Pi,PHT1;1-GFP and SNX1-mRFP exhibited not only vesicular but also plasma membrane localization (Figure 3b)，which is consistent with the recent report that low Pi promotes SNX1 protein accumulation at the plasma membrane (Lin et al., 2020).
