Together with the finding that AtHKT1 was predominantly localized in the phloem tissue, Berthomieu et al. (2003) suggested that AtHKT1 is involved in recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from shoot to root, presumably by promoting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ moving into the phloem in shoots and unloading in roots. The critical role of AtHKT1 in salt tolerance in Arabidopsis was further supported by a study of natural variations (coastal ecotypes Ts-1 and Tsu-1) causing higher accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoots (Rus et al. 2006). Molecular identification of the variant genes revealed that the variations in the AtHKT1 gene are likely to be responsible for the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation phenotype in these two accessions. The distal promoter sequence of AtHKT1 in Col-0 contains a tandem repeat, but only one copy of the repeat is present in Ts-1 and Tus-1 ecotypes. This difference may contribute to lower expression of the AtHKT1 gene and higher accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoots in these two accessions. Baek et al. (2011) further analyzed the features of the AtHKT1 promoter and found that the distal tandem repeat acts as an enhancer element for AtHKT1 expression. In addition, a small RNA target site downstream of the tandem repeat is heavily methylated and both the tandem repeat and the small RNA targeted sequence in the promoter are essential for regulation of AtHKT1 expression and salt tolerance in Arabidopsis (Baek et al. 2011).

The mechanism by which AtHKT1 controls $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ movement in a whole plant became clearer after a number of studies using approaches with combinations of genetic, molecular, and physiological tools (Ma¨ser et al. 2002; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Davenport et al. 2007; review by Horie et al. 2009). The current model for AtHKT1 controlling $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoot states that AtHKT1 functions in unloading of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem to the xylem parenchyma cells in both roots and shoots, thus reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport from root to shoot and decreasing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ movement from xylem into leaf cells. This model is supported by the observation that AtHKT1 is localized in the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells and athkt1 mutant has higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the xylem sap (Sunarpi et al. 2005). This model is also strongly supported by a recent study using an enhancer trap expression system to specifically overexpress AtHKT1 in the root stellar cells. Stellar cell-specific overexpression of AtHKT1 led to a reduction of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ movement from root to shoot, reduced accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoot and enhanced salt tolerance (Møller et al. 2009).

Biological and phylogenetic analyses have suggested two types of HKT transporters in plants: Class 1 and Class 2 (Horie et al. 2009). The Class 1 HKT transporters have high selectivity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ versus $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , and most characterized HKT transporters from Arabidopsis, rice and wheat, belong to this class. Only limited information is available for the Class 2 HKT transporters. The Class 2 HKT transporters are believed to be able to transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ Several studies indicated that the Class 2 HKT transporter genes are induced by low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Wang et al. 1998; Horie et al. 2001; Garciadebla´s et al. 2003), which suggests a role of the Class 2 HKT transporters in response to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency. This notion is strongly supported by a study of OsHKT2;1, a Class 2 HKT transporter in rice. Horie et al. (2007) found that OsHKT2;1 mediates $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -starved conditions for plant growth. This study suggested an interesting fail-safe mechanism of using $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ as a nutritional substitute for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency.


## The vacuolar membrane $N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + }$ antiporter NHX1


Compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuoles has long been proposed as an important salt-tolerance mechanism in plant; however, the molecular identity of the vacuolar membrane transporters for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration was uncovered only in recent years. Gaxiola et al. (1999) isolated the Arabidopsis AtNHX1 and found that this transporter can functionally complement the yeast vacuolar membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter ScNHX1. The important role of AtNHX1 in plant salt tolerance was highlighted by its ability to enhance salt tolerance when overexpressed in plants. Apse et al. (1999) generated more salt-tolerant transgenic plants by overexpressing AtNHX1 in Arabidopsis and found that the improved salt tolerance was attributed to increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ compartmentation in the vacuoles. AtNHX1 was also found to confer salt tolerance in tomato and canola (Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Zhang et al. 2001). Subsequent to these initial findings, a number of studies were undertaken to evaluate the ability of AtNHX1 in improving salt tolerance in other plant species including crops. Many AtNHX1 homologous genes were also isolated from other plants (reviewed by Rodrı´guez-Rosales et al. 2009). However, unlike SOS1 with a unique and large C-terminal tail, AtNHX1 has relatively short C-terminal tail and has several closely related homologous proteins in Arabidopsis genome, which makes it difficult to predict which $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in other plant species is a functional homolog of the Arabidopsis AtNHX1.

Expression of the AtNHX1 gene is induced by ABA and osmotic stress, which suggests a role of AtNHX1 in osmotic adjustment under salt and osmotic stress conditions (Shi and Zhu 2002). By sequestrating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole, the turgor pressure of the cell could be maintained and water loss from the plant cell under salt stress condition could be diminished. Therefore, increasing vacuolar compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is in principle a sound strategy to overcome both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity and osmotic effect caused by high concentrations of salt. However, vacuoles have a limitation for accommodating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ; thus, this salt-tolerance mechanism needs to work with other mechanisms, including limiting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ entry and increasing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion, to effectively reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the cytosol. At the protein level, the transport activity of AtNHX1 is regulated by its C-terminal tail that harbors a CaM-binding domain. Binding of the C-terminal tail with AtCaM15 inhibited the AtNHX1 transport activity (Yamaguchi et al. 2005). Using a forward genetic screening for sos1 suppressors, several dominant gain-of-function mutations in AtNHX1, which suppress salt sensitivity of sos1 have been identified (Shi et al. unpublished; http://www.depts.ttu.edu/ chemistry/Faculty/shi/). Two of the dominant gain-offunction mutations within the AtCaM15-binding domain disrupt interactions between the C-terminal tail of AtNHX1 and AtCaM15, which further supports the inhibitory role of this interaction in AtNHX1 function. Interaction of the C-terminal tail with $\mathbf { C a M }$ also indicates that AtNHX1 activity may be regulated by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ . It is still not clear if this regulatory mechanism for AtNHX1 activity is conserved in other plant species, but it could be used as a criterion to search for functional homologs in other plant species.


## Coordination of SOS1, AtHKT1, and AtNHX1 in salt tolerance


Genetic screenings for sos3 (Rus et al. 2001, 2004) and sos1 suppressors (Shi et al. unpublished; http://www.depts. ttu.edu/chemistry/Faculty/shi/) have identified extragenic mutations in the AtHKT1 gene that suppress the salt sensitivities of sos1 and sos3 mutants. Intriguingly, both sos1 and athkt1 single mutants accumulate more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoot and both are sensitive to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress (Shi et al. 2002; Berthomieu et al. 2003), but sos1/athkt1 double mutant shows reduced salt sensitivity versus sos1 and has lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoot than athkt1 (Shi et al. unpublished data; http://www.depts.ttu.edu/chemistry/Faculty/ shi/). In addition, genetic screening for sos1 suppressor generated seven dominant gain-of-function mutations in the AtNHX1 gene that suppress salt sensitivity of sos1 by enhancing sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuoles (Shi et al. unpublished data). The triple mutant sos1/athkt1/atnhx1 displayed significantly greater suppression of salt sensitivity of sos1. These results indicate that the three transporters, SOS1, AtHKT1, and AtNHX1, function as three independent mechanisms for salt tolerance, while they are coordinated in a whole plant level to effectively remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem and reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoots. We propose the following model for the coordinated function of these three transporters in salt tolerance: under salt stress conditions, AtHKT1 in the plasma membrane transports $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem into the parenchyma cells, thus reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration in the xylem sap; $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulated in the parenchyma cell has two ways to exit: it can be stored in the vacuoles through AtNHX1 function, or it can be excluded from the parenchyma cell into surrounding tissues of the vasculature. In addition to the function in vascular parenchyma cells, SOS1 may also play a crucial role in protecting vigorous diving meritematic cells lacking large central vacuoles. AtNHX1 may also function for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ compartmentation in other mature cells in addition to the parenchyma cells in the vascular tissues.

What we have learned from crops

Effective $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the mesophyll cells of leaves is an important mechanism for salinity tolerance in crop plants (James et al. 2011). In order to reduce the toxicity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaf mesophyll cells, various mechanisms of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion are employed by plants to keep low cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations in leaves. These mechanisms include control of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the xylem, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux from the root, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ compartmentation into the vacuoles, and control of apoplastic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport through bypass flow. Therefore, the ability of crops to maintain low cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaves is regarded as one of the key determinant factors for salt tolerance (Munns et al. 2006; Yeo 1998). Some of the crops are most likely to use more than one mechanism to cope with saline environments (Apse and Blumwald 2007; Flowers 2004). This part of the review will discuss the physiological and molecular mechanisms of salt tolerance identified in crop plants.


## Control of $N a ^ { + }$ uptake and transport


Control of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake is one of the most efficient approaches to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in most crop plants. Upon $\mathrm { N a C l }$ stress, rice OsHKT2;1 transcript was significantly down-regulated in salt-tolerant cv. Pokkali, but not in salt-sensitive cv. BRRI Dhan29 (Kader et al. 2006). Horie et al. (2007) observed that OsHKT2;1-mediated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx is not the cause of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake and toxicity because its expression is rapidly down-regulated upon salt treatment. When overexpressed, the barley HvHKT2;1 resulted in elevated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake, increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations in the xylem sap, and enhanced translocation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to leaves when plants were grown under the conditions with 50 or $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m M } ~ \ N a C l }$ . Interestingly, these responses were correlated with increased salt tolerance in barley (Mian et al. 2011). It was argued that the observed increases in xylem $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations in the tolerant genotypes are required for efficient osmotic adjustment and for support of leaf expansion growth (Shabala et al. 2010).


## $N a ^ { + }$ exclusion from the xylem


$\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ withdrawal from the xylem and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation in the phloem are effective strategies to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoot. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the xylem could take place in different locations of plants including the mature root (Kramer 1983; Yeo et al. 1977), the mesocotyl (Cheeseman 1988; Drew and Lauchli 1987), and the connection part to the shoot or the mature shoot (Matsushita and Matoh 1992; Blom-Zandstra et al. 1998). Recent works have implicated the HKT-type transporters in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ retrieval from the xylem and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation in the phloem in crops. In particular, studies in rice and wheat have pointed out the importance of HKT-type $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the xylem.

Ren et al. (2005) identified a HKT-type transporter named SKC1 as a QTL responsible for salt tolerance in rice. The expression of SKC1 is predominantly in the parenchyma cells surrounding the xylem vessels and the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations in the xylem and shoot were much lower in the tolerant variety than in the sensitive variety (Ren et al. 2005). The SKC1 locus corresponds to OsHKT1;5 in rice. Molecular and physiological studies indicated that OsHKT1;5 mediates $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ removal from the xylem sap into the xylem parenchyma cells, where it could be transported back to the cortex, then moved to the epidermis, and finally effluxed into the soil (Ren et al. 2005). OsHKT1;4 is another HKT-type transporter in rice that controls $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ retrieval into leaf sheath tissue. OsHKT1;4 has high similarity with the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter TrkH (Cao et al. 2011). By comparing the structure of TrkH with the alternative splicing products of OsHKT1;4, Cotsaftis et al. (2012) found that an alternative splicing mechanism is involved in the regulation of functional OsHKT1;4 formation.

In wheat, the Nax1 and Nax2 are two major genes that control $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and tolerance (James et al. 2006). In Durum wheat (Triticum turgidum L. subsp. durum Desf.), an unusual line named Line 149 was identified as a salt tolerance line. This line exhibited low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the leaf blade and was found to contain both Nax1 and Nax2. When the two genes were separated, the lines containing only Nax1 retained $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the sheath and had low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the blade; whereas, the lines containing only Nax2 did not show $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the base although $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the blade was also reduced. Genetic and physiological evidence suggested that Nax1 functions to unload $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem along the leaf base to the blade, leading to a high ratio of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration from sheath to blade. Nax2, however, operates in the root to retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem that is functionally similar to the Kna1 (TaHKT1;5-D1) from bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Lindsay et al. 2004; Davenport et al. 2005; James et al. 2006). The Nax1 was mapped by Huang et al. (2006) to the chromosome 2AL and two putative HKT genes (TmKKT1;4-A1 and TmHKT1;4-A2) in this chromosome co-segregated with Nax1. The TmHKT1;4-A2 gene is expressed in leaf sheath in the Durum wheat Line 149, and this expression pattern provides molecular basis for the role of Nax1 in accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the sheath and decreasing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration in the leaf blades. Therefore, TmHKT1;4-A2 was considered as a candidate for Nax1 (Huang et al. 2006; Lindsay et al. 2004). The Nax2 and its functional analog Kna1 was found to be strongly associated with the HKT transporter TmHKT1;5- A that may be used for unloading of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem (Byrt et al. 2007). HKT1;4-like and HKT1;5-like genes were also mapped to the wheat–barley chromosome groups 2 and 4, respectively (Genc et al. 2010; Huang et al. 2008). The important roles of Nax1 and Nax2 in salt tolerance were further supported by a recent study in which it was found that transferring the TmHKT1;4-A2 and TmHKT1;5-A from durum wheat into bread wheat conferred salt tolerance (James et al. 2011). The increased salt tolerance is correlated with reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the leaf blade. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the leaf blade had 50 and $30 \%$ reduction due to Nax1 and Nax2, respectively, and both genes together conferred $60 \%$ decrease in leaf blade $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration (James et al. 2011). Further study (Munns et al. 2012) showed that TmHKT1;5-A selectively transports $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and is localized in the plasma membrane of the stellar parenchyma and pericycle cells surrounding xylem vessels where TmHKT1;5-A could easily retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem and decrease $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ moving to leaves. In the field trial with saline soils, introducing the TmHKT1;5-A from the wheat relative Triticum monococcum into a cultivated durum wheat significantly decreased leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and increased grain yield by $25 \%$ (Munns et al. 2012).

The cytosolic $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio has been considered as a determinant factor for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance in plants. A comparative study of salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive reed (Phragmites australis) showed that the tolerant variety had a substantially greater $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio than the sensitive variety (Takahashi et al. 2007b). When the plants were grown in the presence of high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in combination with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -starvation, mature PhaHKT1 mRNA was only found in the salt-tolerant reed and was predominant in the roots (Takahashi et al. 2007a). The salt-tolerant reed had low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the aerial parts but higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the roots when compared with the salt-sensitive plants (Takahashi et al. 2007b). An interesting observation in the study by Takahashi et al. (2007b) was the difference in the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulations in the aerial parts between salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive reed plants: the tolerant reed showed a curve of increasing and then decreasing of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, while the sensitive reed displayed a continuous increase in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content during the 10 days of salt treatment. These results suggested that salt-tolerant reed has an ability of retrieval or recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from leaves to roots and that the PhaHKT1 may play a role in this process (Takahashi et al. 2007a).

In addition to the HKT-type transporters, the SOS1-type $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter that was found to control long distance transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in Arabidopsis (Shi et al. 2002) was also studied in crops. The tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) SOS1 homolog SlSOS1 was shown to function in retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from xylem in stem, thus reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in leaves to maximize photosynthesis under saline conditions (Olı´as et al. 2009).


## $N a ^ { + }$ extrusion or efflux from the root


Both physiological and biochemical evidence suggested a role of the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux (DuPont 1992). It is expected that the proton motive force created by the P-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPases would drive $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux from plant cells through the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters (Schachtman and Liu 1999). This process is important for maintaining a high cytosolic $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio under saline conditions (Bartels and Nelson 1994). $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion mechanism may be only operational in certain cells such as the root epidermal cells, as most other cells in plant are surrounded by neighboring cells and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extruded by one cell would bring problems to its neighboring cells (Xiong and Zhu 2002). On the other hand, the energetic cost associated with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion may be a limiting factor for salinity responses (Davenport and Tester 2000). Because the mass flow of solutes is predominantly toward the root and much greater than diffusion away from it (Yeo 1998), $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion from the root would be against an ever increasing gradient, thus becoming more costly and more difficult.

In wheat and barley, a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter across the plasma membrane of the root is likely to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cytoplasm, as suggested from the effects of $\mathrm { p H }$ gradients (Mennen et al. 1990). $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiport activity has also been demonstrated across the plasma membrane of suspension cells in tobacco (Watad et al. 1986). Furthermore, antiport activity was detected in root plasma membrane vesicles of glycophytic plants such as wheat (Allen et al. 1995), tomato (Wilson and Shannon 1995) and cotton (Hassidim et al. 1990), and the halophyte Atriplex (Hassidim et al. 1990). In addition to root tissues, shoot tissues were also found to possess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiport activity in the plasma membrane. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter mediates $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux in exchange with proton and it is the only efflux carrier for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion that has been detected in plants under physiological conditions (Apse and Blumwald 2007). Recently, Martinez-Atienza et al. (2007) identified the rice plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter OsSOS1 and found that OsSOS1 is indeed a functional homolog of AtSOS1 based on its protein sequence, and genetic and biochemical criteria. In wheat, SOS1-like transporter in the plasma membrane was also found to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion in the root epidermal cells. This active $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux requires $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ gradient across the plasma membrane generated by the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase. In consistent with its role in salt tolerance, the expression level of the SOS1-like transporter gene in the salt-tolerant bread wheat cultivar Kharchia 65 was the highest among all cultivars tested (Cuin et al. 2009). Heterologous expression of the durum wheat (Triticum durum) TdSOS1 in a yeast strain lacking endogenous $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux proteins showed complementation of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ - sensitive phenotype by a mechanism involving cation efflux (Feki et al. 2011). In addition, SOS1 may participate in root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis in plants (Oh et al. 2010a). Although there were still debates on the role of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion from the root in plant salt tolerance (Apse and Blumwald 2007; Kronzucker et al. 2006; Tester and Davenport 2003), the role of SOS1-like antiporters in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion in root deserves further study in the future. Moreover, the involvement of other transporters such as ABC transporters in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion and salt tolerance is not clear and requires further investigations.


## Intracellular compartmentation of $N a ^ { + }$ into the vacuoles


The vacuole of a mature plant cell provides a large compartment for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ storage. Sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole is an effective way to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration in the cytosol, which prevents the toxic effects of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ on the cytosolic cellular processes. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration into the vacuole occurs through the function of tonoplast $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHX) that are energized by the proton gradient across the vacuolar membrane generated by the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase (V-ATPase) and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase (V-PPase) (Apse and Blumwald 2007; Gaxiola et al. 2007). Although the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger activity was detected more than two decades ago (Blumwald and Poole 1985), the molecular identity of such exchangers was established only in the recent years when large amount of EST and especially the whole genome sequencing of Arabidopsis were available. The first cloned NHX-type of exchangers was the AtNHX1 (Gaxiola et al. 1999) and it belongs to a subfamily with six members named AtNHX1-6. This group of exchangers was found to transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the vacuoles by using the proton motive force (Apse et al. 1999; Venema et al. 2002; Zhang and Blumwald 2001). In addition to its role in salt tolerance, the NHX transporters have been implicated in many other cellular processes including regulation of endosomal $\mathrm { p H }$ (Yamaguchi et al. 2001), cellular concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Apse et al. 2003), and vesicle trafficking and protein targeting (Bowers et al. 2000; Sottosanto et al. 2004). Since the discovery of NHX exchangers in Arabidopsis, this type of transporters has been found in many other plant species (Pardo et al. 2006). In Avicennia marina, NO enhanced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration by stimulating protein expression of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and NHX1 (Chen et al. 2010). The vacuolar compartmentation mechanism for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ has also been demonstrated by a study in wheat. This study showed that the expression level of NHX1 and the capacity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration into the vacuoles of the root cells were significantly higher in the salt-tolerant bread wheat cultivar Kharchia 65 (Cuin et al. 2009). Besides, the NHX-type of exchangers has also been identified and characterized from other plants, including Atriplex gmelini AgNHX1 (Hamada et al. 2001; Ohta et al. 2002), citrus cNHX1 (Porat et al. 2002), Beta vulgaris BvNHX1 (Xia et al. 2002), Brassica napus BnNHX1 (Wang et al. 2003), Barley Hordeum vulgare HvNHX1 (Fukuda et al. 2004), rice Oryza sativa OsNHX1 (Fukuda et al. 1999), cotton Gossypium hirsutum GhNHX1 (Wu et al. 2004), maize ZmNHX (Zorb et al. 2005), wheat Triticum aestivum TaNHX1 (Brini et al. 2005) and TaNHX2 (Yu et al. 2007), Hordum brevisubulatum HbNHX1 (Lu et al. 2005), Alfalfa Medicago sativa MsNHX1 (Yang et al. 2005), soybean Glycine max GmNHX1 (Li et al. 2006), Agropyron elongatum AeNHX1 (Qiao et al. 2007), Pennisetum glaucum PgNHX1 (Verma et al. 2007), Chenopodium glaucum CgNHX1 (Li et al. 2008b), Populus euphratica PeNHX1-6 (Ye et al. 2009), Zygophyllum xanthoxylum ZxNHX1(Wu et al. 2011), Halostachys caspica HcNHX1 (Guan et al. 2010), Salicornia brachiata SbNHX1 (Jha et al. 2011) and Karelinia caspica KcNHX1 and KcNHX2 (Liu et al. 2012). Since the report of overexpression of AtNHX1 conferring salt tolerance in Arabidopsis (Apse et al. 1999), overexpression of AtNHX1 or other NHX genes conferring stress tolerance has also been achieved in other plants (Table 1).

NHX exchangers transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ by means of the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ gradient across the vacuolar membrane; therefore, it is conceivable that an increase of proton gradient by overexpression of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and/or $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase should enhance $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration through the NHX exchangers. However, due to its multisubunit feature, the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase is not an ideal candidate for overexpression since all subunits have to be overexpressed at similar levels to create a functional overexpression transgenic plant. The vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase (VP) is a better choice for this purpose because it is a single polypeptide protein (Sarafian et al. 1992) and its capacity of generating $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradient is comparable to the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase (Gaxiola et al. 2001). The full-length cDNA sequence of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase, named AVP1 , was first cloned from Arabidopsis (Sarafian et al. 1992). Overexpression of AVP1 conferred drought- and salt-tolerance in the transgenic plants (Gaxiola et al. 2001; Park et al. 2005). Since then, a number of studies have attempted to create salttolerant plants by overexpressing the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPases alone (Table 2) or together with the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Table 3). VP genes have been cloned from many higher plants, such as Barley Hordeum vulgare HVP1 and HVP2 (Tanaka et al. 1993), tobacco Nicotiana tabacum NtVP5, NtVP9 and NtVP31 (Lerchl et al. 1995), rice Oryza sativa OVP1 and OVP2 (Sakakibara et al. 1996), Vigna radiata VVP2 (Nakanishi and Maeshima 1998), Cucurbita moschata CmVP1 (Maruyama et al. 1998), Wheat Triticum aestivum TVP1 (Brini et al. 2005), Hordeum brevisubulatum HbVP1 (Lu¨ et al. 2005), Thellungiella halophila TsVP (Gao et al. 2006), and Suaeda salsa L. SsVP (Guo et al. 2006). A positive relationship between salt tolerance and AtAVP1 expression levels was found through expression-profiling analysis (Jha et al. 2010). Interestingly, a recent study suggested that the major function of the AVP1 is to hydrolyze cytosolic PPi, at least during postgerminative growth (Ferjani et al. 2011).


## Control of apoplastic $N a ^ { + }$ transport through bypass flow


In response to saline conditions, plants evolved mechanisms to prevent excessive $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the apoplast (Anil et al. 2005; Krishnamurthy et al. 2009). In most plants, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ movement from the root epidermis into the xylem occurs via a symplastic pathway across cell layers and involves $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters located at the xylem (Munns et al. 2002). However, rice is an exception in that significant amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ can flow into the stele through an apoplastic pathway (Gong et al. 2006). This apoplastic bypass flow of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is controlled by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (Anil et al. 2005). Rice grown under saline conditions could restrict the apoplastic transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ by enhancing physical barriers through production of suberin, which is detectable within $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ and after several days of salt treatment. The amount of the hydrophobic materials deposited in the apoplastic path was directly correlated with survival rate of rice plants (Krishnamurthy et al. 2009). Another physical barrier that is believed to block apoplastic flow of ions is the Casparian bands (CBs) in the anticlinal walls of root endodermis and exodermis (Lux et al. 2011). The continuity of apoplastic barriers is temporarily interrupted by the emergence of lateral roots, generating sites through which water and minerals could leak into the main root (Yeo et al. 1999; Ma et al. 2001). However, a study by Faiyue et al. (2010b) found that the interruption of the apoplastic barriers by lateral roots did not create sites for bypass flow in rice. Using the tracer trisodium-8-hydroxy1,3,6-pyrenetrisulphonic acid (PTS), Faiyue et al. (2010a) found that the sites of lateral roots allowed PTS to enter into the stele and then move to the shoot, which suggests a possible strategy to improve salt tolerance in rice by limiting the formation of lateral roots and/or enhancing suberin deposition in the apoplastic path. In a recent study, an increase in lateral root densities during salt stress in both salt-tolerant (Pokkali) and -sensitive (IR20) cultivars did not correlate with bypass flow. This suggests that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ bypass flow in rice roots is reduced by the deposition of apoplastic barriers but not related to lateral root formation. The deposition of apoplastic barriers leads to improved plant survival under salt stress conditions (Krishnamurthy et al. 2011).

Silicon deposition in plant cells has been shown to be another defense mechanism for saline conditions. Deposition of silicone in root decreases the bypass flow of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , thus reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio in shoots and influencing the distributions of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and some trophic ions in plants. These changes in turn result in increases in antioxidant production, chlorophyll content, $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase activities, and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ use efficiency, which was observed in rice (Yeo et al. 1999), tomato (Al-Aghabary et al. 2004; Gunes et al. 2007b), cucumber (Zhu et al. 2004), barley (Gunes et al. $2 0 0 7 \mathrm { a }$ ; Liang et al. 2005), spinach (Gunes et al. 2007b), alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) (Wang and Han 2007), wheat (Tuna et al. 2008), Poa pratensis (Chai et al. 2010), and soybean (Glycine max) (Miao et al. 2010). X-ray microanalysis showed that silicon deposition reduced transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ via the apoplastic pathway in the root and decreased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake in rice seedlings under saline conditions (Gong et al. 2006). Two plasma membrane silicon transporters (Lsi1 and Lsi2) responsible for silicon accumulation and deposition have been identified in rice and were found to be preferentially localized in the exodermis and endodermis cells. In contrast to Lsi1, which is localized on the distal side, Lsi2 is localized on the proximal side of the same cells (Ma et al. 2006, 2007). The identification of silicon transporters will provide a new insight into the relationship between salt tolerance and silicon deposition in higher plants.


## Halophytes provide natural mechanisms for salt tolerance


Halophytes are the plant species that can survive and reproduce under growth conditions with above $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl and they comprise $\sim 1 ~ \%$ of the plant kingdom (Flowers and Colmer 2008). Some halophytes, such as Suaeda maritima (Flowers 1972; Wang et al. 2007) and Mesembryanthemum crystallinum (Agarie et al. 2007), require saline environments for optimal growth, while others, such as Puccinellia tenuiflora (Guo et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2009) and Thellungiella halophila (Gao et al. 2006; Gong et al. 2005), do not require saline conditions for optimal growth but can tolerate high concentrations of salts. Although different mechanisms are involved in salt tolerance in halophytes, all halophytes possess active mechanisms to reduce cytosolic salt concentration in mesophyll cells by controlling salt uptake, compartmentalization, and secretion and have high capacity to synthesize organic compatible solutes (Flowers and Colmer 2008). Various types of halophytes may utilize specific mechanisms to adapt to saline conditions (Wang et al.

2002). This part of the review will discuss the common and unique mechanisms employed by halophytes to cope with high salinity.


## Mechanisms of salt tolerance in salt-accumulating halophytes


Sequestration of most toxic ions into the vacuoles is a primary mechanism of salt tolerance in succulent saltaccumulating halophytes (Flowers and Colmer 2008; Wang et al. 2007). This mechanism also contributes to drought tolerance in succulent xerophytes (Ma et al. 2012; Yue et al. 2012). The genus of Suaeda belongs to the succulent halophytes typical of the highly salt-tolerant type that can accumulate ions in their succulent leaves but have no salt glands for salt secretion (Flowers and Colmer 2008). In Suaeda maritima, salts at moderate concentrations can be used as solutes for cell expansion, thus promoting optimal growth; however, at higher salt concentrations, growth reduction can result from a reduced ability for osmotic adjustment (Clipson et al. 1985). Localization of $\mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ in vesicles was observed in the Suaeda species, which suggested that vesicle compartmentation of toxic ions is a salt-tolerance mechanism in these halophytic species (Balnokin et al. 2007; Glenn et al. 1999). In Suaeda salsa, increases in the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity (Qiu et al. 2007) and the activity of the V-ATPase, but not the V-PPase (Wang et al. 2001), were observed. Proteome profiling analysis showed that choline monooxygenase, chloroplastic ATP synthase subunit beta, V-ATPase catalytic subunit A, nucleoside diphosphate kinase 1, chlorophyll a/b-binding protein, and ABC transporter I family member 1 were induced during salt stress (Li et al. 2011). This species also possesses an effective anti-oxidative response system to reduce oxidative damage to chloroplasts caused by $\mathrm { N a C l }$ salinity up to $4 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . This result suggests that SOD in chloroplasts, especially the thylakoidbound SOD which scavenges $\mathrm { O _ { 2 } } ^ { - }$ radicals in situ, plays an important role in resistance to oxidative stress induced by high salinity (Zhang et al. 2005). In Salicornia bigelovii, Ayala et al. (1996) reported that the activities of both the plasma membrane and tonoplast $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPases were elevated upon salt stress treatment. Parks et al. (2002) observed an increased activity of the V-PPase in Salicornia bigelovii in response to salt stress.

Succulent xerophytes Zygophyllum xanthoxylum, and Haloxylon ammodendron were identified as salt-diluting species that accumulate large quantity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ rather than $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the leaves and photosynthesizing branches for osmotic adjustment at moderate soil salinity (Wang et al. 2004b). In Zygophyllum xanthoxylum, $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl resulted in optimal plant growth and alleviated the deleterious impacts on leaf growth by other types of osmotic stresses. Ion analysis showed that drought stress induced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ absorption in Z. xanthoxylum with or without $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { N a C l }$ in the soil. This suggests that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation rather than exclusion may be an effective strategy for adaptation of succulent xerophytes to arid environments (Yue et al. 2012). Further study showed that $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ increased leaf turgor pressure, chlorophyll contents and the activity of photosystem II, resulting in an enhancement of the overall plant photosynthesis rate in Z. xanthoxylum (Ma et al. 2012). Use of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to cope with drought stress is an interesting mechanism and could be utilized for improvement of plant biomass production in arid areas (Janz and Polle 2012).


## Mechanisms of salt tolerance in salt-excluding halophytes


Plant species in the genus of Thellungiella belong to saltexcluding halophytes. These species show high genetic and morphological similarity with Arabidopsis and are close relatives of Arabidopsis. Thellugiella species have been used as an extremophile model for study in salt-tolerance mechanisms. Under salt stress, T. halophila accumulates less sodium, retains more potassium and maintains a higher transpiration rate resulting in higher water uptake than A. thaliana (Volkov and Amtmann 2006). Highly selective transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in T. halophila may contribute to its higher salt tolerance (Alema´n et al. 2009b). This notion is supported by the observation that high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake was reduced to a lesser extent in T. halophila than in $A$ . thaliana when plants were grown with $\mathrm { N a C l }$ . This suggests that high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake under saline conditions plays a role in salt tolerance in salt-excluding halophytes. In fact, the genes encoding $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters are regulated differently in halophytes and glycophytes (Alema´n et al. 2009a). In $5 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl-stressed T. halophila, plastid terminal oxidase acts as an alternative electron sink contributing up to $30 \%$ of the total photosystem II (PSII) electron flow, while electron transport through PSII is inhibited in $A$ . thaliana even under $1 5 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ stress condition (Stepien and Johnson 2009). NaCl treatment caused a significant change in the distribution of aliphatic, aromatic, and indole glucosinolate in different organs of T. salsuginea. This suggests that salt-induced increase in glucosinolate content may be involved in salt stress response in Thellungiella (Pang et al. 2012). A calcineurin B-like (CBL) protein, ThCBL9, was up-regulated in T. halophila leaves by ABA, NaCl, and PEG treatments. Overexpression of ThCBL9 enhanced tolerance to both high salinity and osmotic stress in the transgenic Arabidopsis (Sun et al. 2008). Several genes that play essential roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion and compartmentation (i.e. SOS1, SOS2, NHX1, and HKT1) were expressed at higher levels in T. halophila than in A. thaliana (Taji et al. 2010). Downregulation of ThSOS1 via RNA interference converted T. halophila into a glycophytic plant (Oh et al. 2007). ThSOS1 shares gene structure and sequence similarity with AtSOS1, which includes 11 predicted transmembrane domains and a cyclic nucleotide-binding domain; however, different patterns of simple sequence repeats were found within a 540-bp region upstream of the SOS1 genes in two Thellungiella species (Nah et al. 2009). Gene expression analysis showed that both basal and salt-induced expression of ThSOS1 is higher in Thellungiella parvula and Thellungiella salsuginea than that of the AtSOS1 in Arabidopsis thaliana. This difference was proposed to be resulted from the proximal pyrimidine-rich UTR that is present in the Thellungiella species and other halophytes but absent in Arabidopsis (Oh et al. 2010b). The Arabidopsis athkt1 mutant lines overexpressing TsHKT1;2 were found to be less sensitive to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency than the lines overexpressing AtHKT1. This indicates that maintenance of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake through TsHKT1;2 under salt stress is important for maintaining the halophytic lifestyle of $T .$ . salsuginea (Ali et al. 2012).

The long-term salinity tolerance of $T .$ . halophila is achieved, at least partly, by enhancing defense systems, adjusting energy and metabolic pathways and maintaining RNA structures (Gao et al. 2008). Microarray transcript profiling showed that A. thaliana exhibited a global defense strategy that required bulk protein synthesis, while T. halophila induced genes functioning in protein folding, post-translational modifications and protein redistribution (Gong et al. 2005). A total of 31 and 32 salt induced differentially expressed proteins were identified in Arabidopsis and Thellungiella halophila, respectively; however,

Arabidopsis had more protein changes in abundance than T. halophila did (Pang et al. 2010). Whole genome sequencing of two Thellungiella species was recently attempted. The de novo assembled $\sim 1 4 0 ~ \mathrm { M b }$ genome with 1,496 gap-free contigs was obtained from Thellungiella parvula (Dassanayake et al. 2011). The genome sequence of Thellungiella salsuginea was completed with a coding capacity of at least 28,457 genes, which provides resources and evidence about the nature of defense mechanisms contributing to its success in stressful environments $\mathrm { W u }$ et al. 2012). The completion of the whole genome sequences and analysis of the genome structures of Thellungiella are exciting achievements that will greatly help in understanding of the genetic basis of the extremophile lifestyle.

Puccinellia tenuiflora is a halophytic monocotyledonous species that is widely distributed in the saline–alkali soil in north China (Wang et al. 2004c). Compared to wheat, $P$ . tenuiflora exhibits stronger selective absorption and transport for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Wang et al. 2002, 2004c). $P _ {  }$ . tenuiflora also shows more restricted unidirectional $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx that may contribute to its salinity tolerance (Wang et al. 2009). X-ray microanalysis revealed that selective transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ occurs at the endodermis where the Casparian bands exist, which results in high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in the shoot and large $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ retention in the root (Peng et al. 2004). Expression pattern analysis of PutHKT2;1 in $P$ . tenuiflora implied that PutHKT2;1 might facilitate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake for maintaining a constant $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio under low external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration and in the presence of elevated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Ardie et al. 2009). P. tenuiflora PtNHA1 encodes a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and its expression is predominantly in the roots, which indicates that PtNHA1 may play a role in salt extrusion from the roots (Kobayashi et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2011). $P _ {  }$ . tenuiflora NHX is specifically up-regulated by ${ \mathrm { N a H C O } } _ { 3 }$ rather than $\mathrm { N a C l }$ in roots, which suggests that the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in tonoplast is a player for $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation when a high concentration of alkaline salt is present (Kobayashi et al. 2012). Overexpression of plasma membrane and tonoplast $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters resulted in reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ but increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in shoots under salt stress (Kobayashi et al. 2012). In addition, $P$ . tenuiflora PutPMP3-1 and PutPMP3-2 encoding plasma membrane protein 3 family proteins function to prevent the accumulation of excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions (Chang-Qing et al. 2008). PutAKT1 encodes a plasma membrane-localized $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel family protein that can interact with the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel beta subunits $( \mathsf { K P u t B 1 } )$ to control $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis (Ardie et al. 2010, 2011). PutCAX1 encoding a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter in the vacuolar membrane was proposed to play a role in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { B a } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport (Liu et al. 2009). The study by Guo et al. (2012) suggested a role of $\mathrm { P t S O S 1 }$ in the plasma membrane of the xylem parenchyma cells in controlling $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport into and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ retrieval from the xylem. It was proposed that $\mathrm { P t S O S 1 }$ could be a major player in salt tolerance via selective transport for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in $P$ . tenuiflora. A recent proteomic analysis showed that diverse scavenging mechanisms for reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the leaves of $P$ . tenuiflora are involved in salt stress response. These mechanisms include enhancement of the photorespiration pathway and thermal dissipation, synthesis of the lowmolecular-weight antioxidant R-tocopherol, and accumulation of compatible solutes (Yu et al. 2011).


## Mechanisms of salt tolerance in salt-secreting halophytes


Secretory tissues exist in most vascular plants (Fahn 1988). Some halophytes have the structures of salt glands or ‘‘salt hairs’’ on their leaves serving as secretory tissues for salt excretion. Salt excretion is considered to be an important mechanism that contributes to the resistance of halophytes to salinity (Baumeister and Kloos 1974; Pollak and Waisel 1970; Ramati et al. 1976; Rozema et al. 1981; Waisel et al. 1986). The structurally specialized tissues such as salt glands are relatively dissociated from other living cells and function to transport salts to the leaf surface (Baumeister and Ziffus 1981; Fitzgerald et al. 1992; Waisel 1991). The salts on the leaf surface can form crystals or be naturally removed from the leaf surface by the rain (Balsamo et al. 1995).

Salt glands occur in several families of dicotyledons and in the Gramineae (Liphschitz and Waisel 1974). In dicotyledons, salt glands are characteristic of the Frankeniaceae, Plumbaginaceae and Tamaricaceae, but also occur in some genera of other families, such as Acanthaceae, Chenopodiaceae, Convolvulaceae and Primulaceae. Salt glands are present in many mangrove plants, e.g. Aegialitis (Plumbaginaceae), Aegiceras (Myrsinaceae), Avicennia (Avicenniaceae) and Laguncularia (Combretaceae) (Fahn 1988; Flowers and Colmer 2008; Hill and Hill 1976). Many halophytic grasses have small salt glands, each with two cells for secretion of salts (Amarasinghe and Watson 1989; McWhorter et al. 1995). In Sporobolus virginicus (L.) Kunth, increases in salinity from 0.2 to $20 \%$ of sea water significantly increased secretion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - }$ but had no effect on tissue concentrations of these ions. Further increases in salinity from 20 to $80 \%$ of sea water had no effect on secretion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ but increased tissue concentrations of these ions. High rates of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ secretion and greater retention of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at high salt concentrations resulted in stable $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios in all treatments (Naidoo and Naidoo 1998; Naidoo et al. 1997). In Sporobolus spicatus (Vahl) Kunth, an increase in salt secretion during the night resulted in removal of salts that were accumulated during the day; thus, the plant was ready for the photosynthetic growth under saline environments in the following day (Ramadan 2001). There exists a tight correlation between the capacity of salt glands to secrete salts and the levels of salt tolerance in halophytes (Marcum 1999). The two types of salt secretion apparatus, salt hairs and salt glands, are present in halophytes living in different niches and function differently in adaptation to their living environments. Halophytes in arid areas often have ‘‘salt hairs’’ for salt secretion with limited water loss, which is carried out by the salt hair with only two cells and the outside cell takes up salts and water, swells, and dies eventually (Tester and Davenport 2003). It Atriplex halimus L., the vesiculated hairs play a significant role in removing salt from the leaf, thus preventing accumulation of toxic salts in the parenchyma and vascular tissues (Mozafar and Goodin 1970). Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana Kunth) is known to be a salt-tolerant grass and its tolerance is related to the presence of salt glands that secrete excess salts in the leaves. The salt glands of Rhodes grass reportedly have a high ability to secrete excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Liphschitz et al. 1974; Liphschitz and Waisel 1982) and a low ability to secrete $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ (Kobayashi and Masaoka 2008). A salt-secreting microhair was discovered from a wild relative of rice, Porteresia coarctata Tateoka, which can tolerate salt concentrations of $25 \%$ of sea water (Flowers et al. 1990). Under extremely arid conditions, the xero-halophyte Reaumuria hirtella Jaub. et Sp. (Tamaricaceae) exhibited a diurnal pattern of salt excretion from leaves. Salt secretion gradually decreased toward the midday and showed a negative correlation with the daily transpiration pattern (Ramadan 1998). In Laguncularia racemosa (L.) Gaertn, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accounted for $40 \mathrm { - } 5 3 ~ \%$ of the total secreted salts and the rates of salt secretion were enhanced as soil salinity increased (Sobrado 2004). In Avicennia marina, nitric oxide enhanced salt secretion by increasing net $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux in the salt glands through stimulating protein expression of the plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and SOS1 (Chen et al. 2010).


## Perspectives


Exciting progress toward understanding the molecular mechanisms of salt tolerance has been made since the identification of the plasma membrane and vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters SOS1 and AtNHX1, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter AtHKT1, and the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase AVP1 from Arabidopsis. It has become more and more evident that the cellular mechanisms for salt tolerance operated by these transporters are conserved to some extent in the plant kingdom, and manipulating these transporters could improve salt tolerance. However, the activities of most functional proteins, including membrane transporters, are post translationally modulated by covalent modifications and/or by interactions with other molecules. For instance, CaM binding to the C-terminal tail of the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter AtNHX1 inhibits its transport activity (Yamaguchi et al. 2005), while the biological significance of this interaction and inhibition is not well understood. Another example is the relief of self inhibition of SOS1 by phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail (Quintero et al. 2011). These and other unknown mechanisms being utilized to modulate the activities of these transporters important for salt tolerance could be limiting factors to the overexpression approach. Therefore, understanding the regulatory mechanisms of these transporters and manipulating these transporters to avoid the limiting factors are critical for genetic engineering of salt-tolerant plants. The study in the Shi lab (http://www.depts.ttu.edu/chemistry/Faculty/shi/) has indicated that single amino acid substitutions in AtNHX1, including the changes disrupting CaM binding, resulted in elevated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and enhanced salt tolerance. Also, it has been reported that a single amino acid change could create super active transporters of AtNHX1 (Herna´ndez et al. 2009) and SOS1 (Quintero et al. 2011). These studies provided possibilities of engineering crops by designing and introducing super active $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters that could bypass the requirement of posttranslational activation or avoid interactions with inhibitory molecules. Moreover, the three cellular mechanisms, i.e. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion, and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ compartmentation executed by these three $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters, could be manipulated together to provide even better salt tolerance in plants. However, how these transporters are functionally coordinated at specific locations in a whole plant is still not fully understood, although genetic evidence strongly supports such coordination. Studies have already suggested that, in the case of AtHKT1, tissue specific overexpression conferred salt tolerance (Møller et al. 2009), while overexpression driven by a constitutive promoter resulted in salt hypersensitivity (Baek et al. 2011). Therefore, further physiological and molecular studies are needed to pinpoint the locations and elucidate the coordinated actions of these transporters in plants. Available genetic materials will greatly assist such study, but the technical challenge is the lack of analytical tools that can precisely map the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ distribution at a subcellular level in a whole plant. In addition, the effects of these transporters on other biological processes require further attentions. It seems apparent that these transporters are not only important for salt tolerance, but are also involved in other cellular and physiological processes in Arabidopsis. However, information about the role of these transporters in processes other than salt tolerance in crops is largely obscure. Such information will help assess potential side-effects of overexpressing such transporters for enhanced salt tolerance.

Salt-tolerance study in crop plants, although progressing rapidly in recent years, still largely remains at the level of identifying and manipulating the homologous genes known for salt tolerance in Arabidopsis. Research in rice (Ren et al. 2005; Horie et al. 2007) and wheat (Huang et al. 2006; James et al. 2006, 2011; Byrt et al. 2007) has pointed a direction of elucidating salt-tolerance mechanisms in crops, in particular, the cereal crops. Systemic study using both forward and reverse genetic tools and physiological, molecular and biochemical means in crop plants is still needed. Reverse genetic study of the homologous genes in crops would provide information about the similarity and differences of the functions of the transporters important for salt tolerance in Arabidopsis. Forward genetic screening for mutants sensitive or tolerant to salt stress and identifying salt-tolerance determinants in crops are still not extensively carried out. This approach would identify novel genes and/or salt-tolerance mechanisms unique to crop plants. It is conceivable that unique salt-tolerance mechanisms executed by genes that are not identified from Arabidopsis might exist in crops, especially those monocotyledonous crops due to the different architecture and structural organization of tissues in different plants.

Halophytes provide natural resources for the study of salt-tolerance mechanisms in plants. A very attractive way of elucidating the genetic basis of salt tolerance is to use comparative genomic study between closely related halophytes and glycophytes. This is evidenced by the study by Wu et al. (2012) in which a completed genome sequencing of Thellungiella salsuginea greatly assisted in the identification of plant abiotic stress tolerance mechanisms using comparative genomic approach. Although comparative genomic study requires complete genome sequences, it can be envisioned that more and more genome sequences will be available along with rapid advances in the sequencing technologies and reduction of the associated costs. This approach will also be very useful in identifying the natural variant genes conferring salt tolerance from salt-tolerant lines within a species, which will provide valuable information for molecular breeding in salt tolerance in crops.

Salinity is a major abiotic stress influencing agricultural production around the world and represents a major threat to the maintenance of crop yields, because most crop species are sensitive to the accumulation of sodium in shoot tissues (Tester and Davenport 2003). In the Triticeae, sodium exclusion from roots and leaf tissues is one of the major mechanisms conferring salt tolerance (Gorham et al. 1990; Munns et al. 2006). Modern durum wheat cultivars do not exclude $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the same extent as bread wheat (Triticum aestivum). Two QTLs originating from Triticum monococcum and involved in salinity tolerance, Nax1 $\mathrm { \Delta N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion 1) and Nax2 $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ exclusion 2), were found to correspond to HKT genes [respectively, of HKT1;4 and HKT1;5 types; (Lindsay et al. 2004; Byrt et al. 2007)]. Moreover, HKT genes shown to be associated to QTLs for salinity tolerance belong to subfamily 1. They have been shown to play crucial roles in salinity tolerance in different plant species (Munns et al. 2012; Asins et al. 2013). Nax1 is a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter, a member of the HKT (high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter) family, T. monococcum HKT1;4-A2 (Huang et al. 2006). The Nax1 gene confers a reduced rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and retention of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaf sheath, thus giving a higher sheath-to-blade $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration ratio (James et al. 2006). The second gene, Nax2, also confers a lower rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and has a higher rate of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport, resulting in enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ versus $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ discrimination in the leaf blade (James et al. 2006). The HKT gene family encodes proteins which form part of the $\mathrm { T r k / K t r / H K T }$ group of membrane transporters. These proteins have been shown to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and/or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in bacteria, fungi and plants. HKT genes can be divided into two subfamilies, based on amino acid sequence homology, with members of subfamily 1, which mainly transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ while members of subfamily 2 transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Tester and Davenport 2003). Due to the transporting properties of the encoded HKT proteins, it is likely that a number of HKT proteins play important roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in plants and consequently have direct or indirect roles in determining salinity tolerance (Berthomieu et al. 2003; Haro et al. 2005; Ren et al. 2005; Rus et al. 2004; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Mäser et al. 2003).

Using the GUS reporter strategy and in situ hybridization, HKT gene expression patterns have so far been analyzed in detail in a few plant species aside from rice and Arabidopsis. HKT genes from subfamily 1 have systematically been found to be expressed in vascular tissues in all plants analyzed like rice, wheat, and Arabidopsis plants (Berthomieu et al. 2003, Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Jabnoune et al. 2009; Munns et al. 2012). Some of these genes are essentially expressed in the vasculature system, like HKT1 in Arabidopsis and ice plants and HKT1;5 in rice and wheat. On the other hand, the expression patterns of the rice HKT1;3 and HKT1;4 genes also include the root peripheral cell layers and leaf bulliform cells, similar to the expression pattern of OsHKT2;1. Hence, in addition to root cation uptake, OsHKT2;1 is likely to play a role in long distance cation transport in the plant vasculature between roots and shoots, and in osmoregulatory processes in leaf tissues and bulliform cells, which control leaf rolling upon abiotic constraints (Kadioglu and Terzi 2007). HKT2;4 expression has only been analyzed in rice (Lan et al. 2010). The reported expression pattern is comprised in the root peripheral cell layers, leaf vasculature and mesophyll, so significantly overlaps with that of OsHKT2;1. Thus, the expression patterns of some members of the HKT subfamily 1 can be quite similar to those of members from the HKT subfamily 2. However, important differences in the regulation of expression seem to exist between subfamily 1 and subfamily 2 HKT, suggesting that the two types of genes play specific roles.

Indeed, enhancement of expression in roots in conditions of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ shortage, which has been consistently reported in the HKT subfamily 2, does not seem to occur in subfamily 1. On the other hand, members from both subfamilies can display regulation upon salt stress. This regulation appeared to be variable between tissues (roots and leaves), HKT genes and even between cultivars for some genes (Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005). In this study, we isolated and characterized the promoter sequence of Triticum monococcum TmHKT1;4-A1 gene. The spatio-temporal activity of the PrTmHKT1;4-A1 fused to the gusA gene was investigated in stable transformed Arabidopsis plants under multiple inducible-abiotic-stress treatment and tissue-specific manner.

Salinity stress affects crop production worldwide, particularly by limiting plant growth and reducing potential yield. Plants have three mechanisms for tolerating soil salinity, including tolerance of the osmotic effects of salt; a tolerance in leaf tissues of the negative effects of sodium ions (Na+ ) on cellular function through compartmentalisation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in specific tissues, cells, or cellular organelles; and exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the sensitive shoot tissue [1]. Of these mechanisms, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot is best understood and is, therefore, the current best candidate for a targeted genetic modification approach to improving salinity tolerance.

The HKT gene family encodes one of the most widely studied groups of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters in plants. Current understanding indicates that AtHKT1; $I$ from Arabidopsis is expressed primarily in the stele and has a role in the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream [2,3]. Reduced activity of this transporter leads to increased transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the root to the shoot, leading to a higher shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and a decrease in salinity tolerance [4]. More recently, it was demonstrated that OsHKT1;5 in rice [5] and the $H K T l { ; } 5$ gene from wheat [6] are crucial in maintaining low shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations via a similar mechanism of $\mathrm { N a + }$ retrieval from the transpiration stream into cells within the stele. A second HKT gene that is involved in sodium exclusion in cereal species is HKT1;4. The encoded transporter appears to function in combination with HKT1;5, by retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the shoot transpiration stream and sequestering Na+ in the sheath tissue [7]. The endogenous function of the family of HKT transporters and their role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and provision of salinity tolerance to plants has been reviewed recently [8].

An obvious strategy for improving the salinity tolerance of plants is to increase the expression of HKT genes. Constitutive overexpression of plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters, however, has been unsuccessful in producing salinity tolerant plants [9]. It was hypothesized that such overexpression increases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes into all cells of the plant, this being, on balance, counter-productive to the reduction of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport to the shoot [9,10]. In contrast, it was shown that overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the root xylem parenchyma cells of Arabidopsis leads to improved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and salinity tolerance [9]. Interestingly, the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the root resulting from the improved Na+ exclusion from the shoot was stored within the cortical cells of the root [9].

The aim of experiments described in the current work was to determine if overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the outer cells (epidermis and cortex) of the root would result in opposite effects to overexpression in the stele, or whether a similar improvement of Na+ exclusion and salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis and rice would be observed. A secondary goal was to determine if expression of AtHKT1; $\mathit { \Pi } _ { l }$ in the epidermal and cortical cell layers of the root is the reason for the deleterious effects observed when AtHKT1;1 is constitutively overexpressed, as described previously [9].

In both species, we found that transgenic plants overexpressing AtHKT1;1 in mature root cortex had greater shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and thus increased salinity tolerance.

The High-Afnity Potassium Transporter (HKT) has been considered as the major determinant of salt stress tolerance in several crops (Pardo et al. 2006; Munns and Tester 2008; Ali et al. 2019). At cellular level, when the cytosolic sodium concentration gains a toxic level, HKT transporters contribute to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion by mediating high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in leaf blades (Gorham et al. 1990; Garciadeblas et al. 2003; Horie et al. 2009; Suzuki et al. 2016). Based on their functional properties, HKT transporters have been divided into two subfamilies. The subfamily 1 comprises transporters displaying a strong selectivity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ against $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , while subfamily 2 comprises members permeable to both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Platten et al. 2006; Véry et al. 2014; Xu et al. 2018). This selectivity has been linked to the presence of a serine residue at the frst pore-loop domain of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters against a glycine residue for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ transporters $\mathrm { { X u } }$ et al. 2018; Li et al. 2019).

Compared with the only one gene present in Arabidopsis, cereals possess much larger and variable HKT genes (Platten et al. 2006). For instance, there are 9HKT genes in rice and $6 { - } 2 4 H K T$ genes in barley and wheat (Huang et al. 2008). In wheat, HKT transporters from subfamily 1 have been shown to be associated with quantitative trait locus (QTL) of salt stress tolerance (Byrt et al. 2007; Genc et al. 2019). Kna1 is a major sodium exclusion locus which corresponds to a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter gene TaHKT1;5, located on the chromosome 4DL of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum). It has been shown that Kna1 plays a crucial role in maintaining a high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in leaves via shoot sodium exclusion, upon salt stress conditions (Gorham et al. 1990; Huang et al. 2006; Byrt et al. 2007, 2014; Shavrukov et al. 2009; Hmidi et al. 2019; Hartley et al. 2020). It was reported that TaHKT1;5-D is predominantly expressed in the root stele of bread wheat and that transgenic plants down-expressing this gene signifcantly accumulate a high leaf sodium content compared with WT plants (Byrt et al. 2014). This phenotype observed under control and salt stress conditions, which suggested that TaHKT1;5-D is a key determinant of salt tolerance, controlling the amount of sodium delivered to shoot in bread wheat.

Two other candidates for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion, Nax1 and Nax2, were found in the A genome of diploid wheat (T. monococcum) and mapped to chromosome 2AL and 5AL, respectively (James et al. 2006; Byrt et al. 2007). The second locus Nax2 corresponds to TmHKT1;5-A, which is proposed as a close homolog of TaHKT1;5- $D$ (Kna1) from bread wheat (Byrt et al. 2014; Xu et al. 2018). Despite the high level of sequence identity between them, TmHKT1;5-A and TaHKT1;5-D displayed distinctive functional properties when they were expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
