The non-essential element cadmium (Cd) is toxic to both plants and animals.Excess Cd in soils can be absorbed by plant roots,which inhibits plant growth and diminishes crop yields [1].Importantly,the Cd absorbed by roots can be transported to the shoots and deposited in grains or friuts.Through the dietary intake,plant-derived Cd can enter the human body.Due to its long biological half-life,the Cd level in the body progressively accumulates by low-dose chronic exposure,which can cause various diseases such as renal dysfunction and osteoporosis [2, 3].Therefore,it is desirable to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of Cd detoxification and accumulation in plants,which will enable the development of low-Cd crops,thus reducing dietary intake of Cd by humans.

Cd enters root cells mainly through transport systems responsible for the uptake of essential elements [4,5],such as the manganese transporter OsNramp5 (natural resistance-associated macrophage protein 5) functioning as the major pathway for Cd entry into rice [6-8]. Once adsorbed into the root cels, Cd can cause serious cellular injuries [1,5]. Plants have evolved a series of strategies to cope with Cd toxicity, including extrusion,complexation with thiol-rich compounds such as glutathione (GSH) and phytochelatins (PCs),and vacuolar compartmentalization [5,9].During these biological processes,transporters from different families play important roles.For example,some efflux transporters localized in the plasma membrane can extrude Cd out of root cells [1O,11].AtPDR8(AtABCG36) has been identified as a Cd exporter in Arabidopsis.Its overexpression increases Cd extrusion and reduces the Cd content in the engineered plants,thus conferring resistance to Cd[11].Inaddition,Cd or its complexes can also be sequestered in vacuoles by transporters localized on the tonoplast. Several types of transporter, including HMA (Heavy Metal ATPases),ABC (ATP-binding cassette) and CAX (cation/proton exchanger) transporters,have been demonstrated to be involved in this process [12].In rice,OsHMA3 is the major transporter mediating Cd transport into root cell vacuoles,and the non-functional OsHMA3 fails to sequester Cd into vacuoles,consequently increasing the root-to-shoot Cd translocation [13,14]. Together, the extrusion and vacuolar sequestration of Cd in root cells can not only alleviate Cd toxicity,but also restrict Cd translocation and accumulation in shoots and seeds.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute a large,diverse gene superfamily found in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.Plant ABC transporters are grouped into eight major subfamilies (A-G,I) according to domain structure and evolutionary relationships [15].ABC proteins exhibit wide substrate profiles,including lipids,metals/metalloids,and phytohormones [16]. For example,OsABCC1 can sequester arsenic-PC conjugates in the vacuoles,thereby participating in arsenic detoxification and limiting its transport to the rice grains [17].Multiple ABC transporters have been reported to be capable of transporting Cd or Cd complexes [l2].The first ABC transporter that has been described as a Cd transporter is HMT1 in the fission yeast,which can transport PC-Cd complex into the vacuole for Cd detoxification [18,19]. Subsequently, additional ABC transporters involved in Cd (conjugate) transport have been found in various species [11,2O,21]．In Arabidopsis,besides AtABCG36 [11],three C-type ABC transporters,AtABCC1,AtABCC2 and AtABCC3,are also implicated in Cd tolerance by sequestering PC-Cd complexes into vacuoles [21,22].

133 genes have been annotated as ABC transporters in the whole rice genome [16],and two of them have been shown to participate in Cd tolerance so far. OsABCG43 is induced by Cd treatment in rice roots and confers Cd tolerance in yeast [23],but its exact function in rice remains unclear.Recently，involvement of another rice ABC transporter, OsABCG36,in Cd tolerance has been reported by Fu et al.[1O]. OsABCG36 can be induced in rice roots by brief Cd exposure and is localized to the plasma membrane.Heterologous expression of OsABCG36 in yeast showed an efflux activity for Cd, so itis thought to be required for Cd tolerance by exporting Cd or Cd complexes from the root cells in rice [1O].High-throughput analyses such as microarray and RNA sequencing have shown that OsABCC9 is also up-regulated by Cd treatment [24,25],suggesting its possible involvement in Cd tolerance in rice.However,it has not yet been established what role it plays in Cd tolerance in rice.In this study,we have investigated the role of OsABCC9 in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.The results showed that OsABCC9 was mainly expressed in the root stele under Cd stress,and was localized on the tonoplast.Disruption of OsABCC9 enhanced the Cd sensitivity of rice and the Cd content in the xylem sap and grains. Furthermore,its heterologous expression in yeast resulted in enhanced Cd tolerance along with a higher intracellular Cd content.We therefore propose that OsABCC9 is a vacuolar transporter that confers Cd tolerance and affects Cd accumulation in rice.

ABC proteins are powerful transporters driving the exchange of compounds across many diferent biological membranes and the C-subfamily of ABC proteins is an important component77. In human, ABCC transporters have been studied extensively on substrate specifcity, tissue expression and transport kinetics to provide insights into cellular functions, drug discovery and development52,78. In plants, ABCC transporters are originally defned as vacuolar pumps of GS conjugates, and deemed to associate with detoxifcation, PTEs sequestration, chlorophyll catabolite transport and ion channel regulation76,79.

As a plant hyperaccumulating Cd, S. alfredii Hance harbors numerous genes related to metal transport or detoxifcation and requires intense attentions. Several characterized transporter genes include SaHMA334, $S a Z I P 4 ^ { 3 8 }$ and SaNramp636. Recent reports from Arabidopsis confer the roles of ABCC transporters as major detoxifers sequestering metal-chelators into the plant vacuoles57,58, suggesting that ABCC proteins might contribute to PTEs hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance. However, the physiological functions of ABCC proteins are still scarce in metal hyperaccumulators, and it is of great importance to address their roles in S. alfredii Hance. In the present study, the composition and diversifcation of ABCC subfamily in S. alfredii Hance were identifed using bioinformatics tools and their expression profles were characterized for their possible roles in Cd tolerance and accumulation.

Among the identifed ten proteins belonging to the ABCC subfamily, Sa45F39 is largest (1630 aa) and Sa48F96 is the smallest one (1024 aa). Similar size distribution is observed in Arabidopsis45, rice46 and wheat62. However, the number of ABCC genes in S. alfredii Hance is fewer than those reported species. For instance, there are

15 ABCC proteins in Arabidopsis45, 17 in rice45, 18 in wheat62, 26 in Vitis vinifera80 and 47 in Brassica napus81. Terefore, we presume that S. alfredii Hance may adopt a more economic strategy of assembling multi-functional genes rather than expanding gene family to cope with the external PTEs stress during the adaptive evolution. Tis phenomenon is also observed for leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinase (LRR-RLK) gene family which is also smaller in S. alfredii Hance than other plant species82. Nevertheless, these results are obtained from the transcriptomics rather than a complete genome sequencing data, which limits more precise evaluation of gene numbers especially for gene families composed by long proteins such as ABCC subfamily.

Te analysis on phylogeny and protein structure provides hints on the possible functions of SaABCC genes. Categorized into the division of AtABCC clade (Fig. 1), SaABCC genes are members of ABCC subfamily. All SaABCCs have similar distribution of TMD and NBD as that of AtABCCs, possessing similar protein length and spacer region (Fig. 2). However, it is worth noticing that members of SaABCCs and AtABCCs fall in diferent clades (I, II and III)76, and SaABCCs are only in clade I and II, suggesting the possibilities of multi-functionality in S. alfredii Hance. Additionally, SaABCCs have the identical numbers of MEME motifs and possess uniform distribution except for Sa23221 and Sa45F39 (Fig. 2C), demonstrating a higher conservation than AtABCCs. Tis may imply that under severe surroundings with PTEs stress, members of ABCC subfamily have prior functions to detoxify PTEs than other roles.

Te transcript abundance of ABCC genes across tissues helps in understanding their molecular functions. In the present study, six SaABCC genes exhibited tissue-specifc expression patterns in the absence of Cd, fve (Sa88F144, Sa23221, Sa48F96, Sa12F279 and Sa14F98) in roots and one (Sa14F190) in leaves (Fig. 3). Among them, Sa14F98 may participate in the plant growth and development as it is clustered with AtABCC6 which shows a similar root-specifc expression62. Sa14F190 showing the similar expression specifcity in leaves as TaABCC14 and $T a A B \bar { C } C l 5 ^ { 6 2 }$ may serve as candidate transporters in leaves. Although the clustering of SaABCCs and AtABCCs hints their functional similarity, there might be functional divergences as well. For example, though Sa88F144 and Sa13F200 are clustered together with AtABCC4, Sa13F200 was abundantly expressed in all three tissues and Sa88F144 exhibited a root-specifc expression pattern, neither consistent with the low expression level of AtABCC4 in all tissues83. ABCCs in wheat are reported to show preferential expression in specifc tissues, e.g., TaABCC3 in roots, TaABCC1 in stems, TaABCC14 and TaABCC15 in fag leaves62. As TaABCC3 clustered with AtABCC6 is a gene highly expressed at the initiation point of secondary roots84, it is suggested to play roles in root architecture development62. Such diferent expression patterns imply the possibilities of performing other functions apart from getting involved in the control of stomatal movements as $\bar { _ { A t A B C C } } 4 ^ { 8 3 }$ .

Cd-responsive expression of SaABCC genes hints their roles in Cd hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance in S. alfredii Hance. In the presence of Cd, Sa14F190 and Sa18F186 genes were mostly induced in roots (Fig. 4). Sa18F186 is segregated with AtABCC5 which is involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and salt stress tolerance85. Although AtABCC5 is regarded as a central regulator of guard cell ion channel59, guard cell signaling and phytate storage86, rare studies report the participation of AtABCC5 in Cd response. Te functional discrepancy between Sa18F186 and AtABCC5 may arise from the diferent leaf structures that S. alfredii has feshy leaves and Sa18F186 therefore might enroll to combat Cd stress rather than water loss. Sa14F190 gene falls into the same clade with AtABCC3 and AtABCC7, and AtABCC3 is important vacuolar transporters conferring Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis57. In addition, a Cd-responding cluster is found comprising AtABCC3, AtABCC6, AtABCC7 and SAT3 (serine acetyltransferase gene) on chromosome $\mathrm { I I I } ^ { 8 4 , 8 7 }$ . Although Sa45F39 did not respond signifcantly to Cd stress, it is clustered with AtABCC1/AtABCC2, which are reported to confer the tolerance to $\mathrm { A } s ^ { 5 6 }$ , Cd and $\mathrm { H g }$ in Arabidopsis55. AtABCC2 is particularly involved in vacuolar transport of chlorophyll catabolites58 and the uptake of cyanidin 3-O-glucoside (C3G)88. In rice, OsABCC1 closely related to AtABCC1/AtABCC2 does not confer Cd tolerance; instead, it is involved in As detoxifcation and reduces the allocation of As in grains63. Terefore, Sa45F39 is also speculated with roles in PTEs tolerance.

Han et al. proposed a comparative analysis of S. alfredii Hance transcriptomic datasets and characterized numerous hub genes strongly associated with Cd stress64. However, there are lack of details about SaABCC hub genes and their connections with other genes. In the present study, a co-expression network was reconstructed and uncovered fve SaABCC hub genes (Sa14F190, Sa13F200, Sa12F279, Sa23221 and Sa45F39). Te overlapping in the edge genes hints the internal connections among SaABCC hub genes. For Sa14F190 gene, the edge genes are associated with metabolic process, cellular process, biological regulation activity, transporter activity, response to stimuli and transcription factor (Fig. 5). To be more precise, the edge genes performing transporter activity include multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) efux family protein, zinc/iron transporter, ABC transporter B family member and sulfate transporter. Tose participating in metabolic process and cellular process consist of respiratory burst oxidase homolog protein D, CBL-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase (CIPK), plant cysteine oxidase, endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductin-1, phospholipid-transporting ATPase 1, GDSL esterase/lipase, and heavy metal-associated isoprenylated plant protein (HIPP). Representative transcription factors include bZIP and WRKY transcription factors. Among them, MATE efux family protein harbors multitasking abilities in encompassing regulation of plant development, secondary metabolite transport, xenobiotic detoxifcation, Al tolerance, and disease resistance89. Zinc/iron transporters difers in substrate range and specifcity, involved in the transport of $Z \mathrm { n }$ , Fe, Mn and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 9 0 , 9 1 }$ . Members belonging to HIPP, CIPK and WRKY transcription factor are reported to confer Cd tolerance in yeasts92. Terefore, the functions of Sa14F190 are activated or magnifed through either direct or indirect interactions with these edge genes.

Taking Cd-responsive profles and co-expression network together, we chose Sa14F190 to further assess its roles in Cd tolerance and accumulation by heterologous expression in Cd-sensitive yeasts. Under Cd stress, Cd content in ∆ycf1_Sa14F190 was $3 5 . 4 8 \%$ higher than that in ∆ycf1_EV (Fig. 6), indicating the vital roles of Sa14F190 gene in Cd accumulation. However, Sa14F190 increased the sensitivity of transformed yeasts instead of enhancing Cd tolerance, evidenced by the retarded growth which may be due to more Cd accumulation. Similar fndings are observed for other transporters in S. alfredii Hance which all enhanced the Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation of transformed yeasts, and the increase of cellular Cd content was $2 2 . 2 \%$ by SaNramp636, $2 5 . 2 \%$ by $S a H M A 3 ^ { 3 4 }$ and $1 6 . 4 \%$ by $S a \dot { C } A X \mathcal { 2 } h ^ { 3 9 }$ . It has been reported that AtABCC3 could confer Cd tolerance in yeast cells, but not Cd accumulation93, consistent with another study on AtABCC3 in Arabidopsis57. Tese fndings suggested that members of ABCC subfamily closely located in the phylogenetic tree might have functional divergence, and Cd tolerance and accumulation are mediated by diferent pathways.

In summary, the ABCC transporter Sa14F190 gene is responsible for Cd hyperaccumulation and other SaABCCs might have diverse roles in the tolerance or accumulation of PTEs. Members of ABCC transporter are a genetic pool of candidates encompassing strong ability to transport, tolerate or accumulate Cd and other PTEs for phytoremediation. Tis work applies bioinformatic analysis to provide a preliminary study uncovering the interesting functions of ABCCs members in S. alfredii Hance, and these functions need further experimental evidence to enrich our knowledge.

## The atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout plant is impaired in vacuolar sequestration of Cd


To examine whether AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 confer Cd(II) tolerance by vacuolar sequestration of this non-essential ion, the cellular distribution of Cd(II) was compared in the wild-type and the double mutant using a Cd-indicator dye. Wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant plants were grown in the presence or absence of $5 ~ { \mu \mathsf { M } } ~ { \mathsf { C d } } ( { \mathsf { I I } } )$ for 2 weeks, and protoplasts were isolated and loaded with a Cd(II)- and Pb(II)-sensitive fluorescent probe, Leadmium- Green. In the absence of Cd(II), protoplasts from wild-type plants showed a negligible Leadmium- Green fluorescence signal (Figure 2a–c). When grown in Cd(II)-containing medium, strong green fluorescence was emitted from the vacuole of most wild-type protoplasts (Figure 2d–f). This observation is in agreement with a previous report that used another Cd-sensitive fluorescent dye (Morel et al., 2009) and a study that demonstrated the accumulation of Cd in central vacuoles (Vo¨ geli-Lange and Wagner, 1990). However, in atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants, the majority of cells (approximately $8 6 \%$ of the total) exhibited a markedly different LeadmiumGreen fluorescence pattern; namely, a strong signal at the margin of the cell and a much weaker signal in the vacuole (Figure 2g–j). The green signal was probably derived from the cytoplasm, because it surrounded but did not overlap with the red fluorescence emitted from chloroplasts. Furthermore, measurement of fluorescence intensity in the vacuolar region of wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout protoplasts revealed a significant reduction in Cd accumulation in the vacuole of the mutant (Figure 2k). These results suggest that sequestration of Cd into the vacuole is remarkably reduced in the atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutant.

The possibility that the observed difference in Leadmi$\mathsf { u m } ^ { \mathrm { T M } }$ Green fluorescence intensity in atabcc1 atabcc2 and wild-type protoplasts was due to different concentrations of dye in the vacuole , rather than that of Cd(II), was tested by comparing the fluorescence intensity in the vacuoles of plants treated with Pb(II) (Figure S4). As AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 did not confer Pb tolerance (Figure S1), we predicted that there would be no difference in vacuolar $\mathsf { P b }$ concentration and thus no difference in the fluorescence intensity, if the permeability of the tonoplast to the dye was not altered in the double knockout mutant. Indeed, the distribution of Pb visualized by Leadmium- Green did not differ between the wild-type and the mutant (Figure S4), supporting our conclusion that the difference in Cd fluorescence observed in Figure 2 represents a real difference in Cd content in the vacuole. These results support the hypothesis that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in vacuolar accumulation of Cd.


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 enhance the Hg(II) tolerance of yeast producing PCs


To determine the molecular mechanism by which AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in heavy metal tolerance, we used a heterologous system comprising a mutant strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae that we engineered to express a PC synthase gene of wheat (Triticum aestivum). We expressed TaPCS1 in yeast strain SM4, which lacks four vacuolar ABC transporters including ScYCF1, and named the resulting yeast SM7 (Song et al., 2010). Introduction of AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 enhanced Hg(II) tolerance in SM7 compared to a control transformed with the empty vector (EV; Figure 3a). In the SM4 strain, which does not produce PCs, AtABCC1 conferred Hg(II) tolerance over a narrow range of concentrations, while AtABCC2 improved the growth of yeast in medium containing a broad range of Hg(II) concentrations (Figure 3b). The results indicated that both AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 transport PC–Hg(II) as well as $\mathsf { G S } _ { 2 } \mathsf { - H g } ( | | )$ , and that AtABCC1 is more dependent on PCs than is AtABCC2. Cd(II) tolerance was not improved by expressing either AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 in the SM7 yeast strain (Figure S5).


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate the translocation of Cd from root to shoot


To assess whether the distribution of metal ions is altered by loss of function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, the Cd content of wild-type and mutant plants was measured. After 2 weeks of growth on half-strength MS agar plates containing Cd(II), the shoots and roots of wild-type, atabcc1 and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants were collected separately and their Cd content was measured. The shoots of atabcc1 knockout plants accumulated more Cd than the wild-type (Figure 4a), leading to an increased shoot-to-root ratio of Cd (Figure 4b). In the double knockout plants, the shoot Cd content was similar to that of the wild-type, and the root Cd content was lower, resulting in an increased shoot-to-root Cd ratio even though the total Cd accumulation was lower than that in the wild-type (Figure 4). This result implies that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate translocation of Cd from the root to the shoot. Determination of Hg(II) levels in the double knockout plants yielded similar results as for Cd (Figure S6), supporting the putative function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 in regulation of heavy metal flux between the root and shoot.


## Over-expression of AtABCC1 enhances tolerance to and accumulation of Cd


Increasing the vacuolar storage capacity may dramatically improve the ability of the plant to accumulate and tolerate toxic metal ions, because vacuoles are the main storage organelle for heavy metals and metalloids. We predicted that over-expression of AtABCC1 (Geisler et al., 2004), which plays an important role in Cd tolerance (Figure 1), is a good candidate for increasing the vacuolar storage capacity. We generated AtABCC1 over-expressing Arabidopsis plants, and selected two lines that showed the highest AtABCC1 transcript levels (M-1 and M-2, with 1.2- and 1.4-fold higher transcript levels than the wild-type, respectively; Song et al., 2010). The growth of the two transgenic lines overexpressing AtABCC1 was similar to that of the wild-type on control half-strength MS medium (Figure 5a). However, plants over-expressing AtABCC1 grew better than the wildtype in the presence of Cd(II). The shoot fresh weights of the two over-expressing lines were higher than those of the wild-type on two Cd(II) concentrations (Figure 5b). Furthermore, Cd accumulation in both the shoot and the root, as well as the total Cd content per plant, were higher in the lines over-expressing AtABCC1 than in the wild-type (Figure 5c,d). We tested whether over-expression of AtPCS1 together with AtABCC1 further increased Cd tolerance, as, in the case of arsenic, only plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 exhibited increased tolerance relative to the wild-type (Song et al., 2010). However, the Cd tolerance of plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 did not exceed that of plants only over-expressing AtPCS1 (Figure S7).

For the past two decades, phytochelatins have been known to play a central role in the detoxification of diverse metals/ metalloids, including Cd(II), Hg(II) and As(III), in plants (Grill et al., 1987; Ha et al., 1999). However, it was uncertain whether a common transporter exists for PCs chelated to different metals/metalloids. In the case of fission yeast, the PC transporter SpHMT1 has a high substrate specificy; it can efficiently detoxify Cd(II) (Ortiz et al., 1995), but not As(III) (Preveral et al., 2009). We previously reported that the two ABC transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, which act as apo $\mathsf { P C } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathsf { P C } _ { 2 } \mathsf { - A s } ( | | | )$ transporters, play a central role in arsenic tolerance (Song et al., 2010). The aim of the present study was to investigate whether the same ABC transporters function in the detoxification of Cd(II) and Hg(II) in plants. The growth of atabcc1 and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants was significantly more impaired in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II) than that of wild-type plants, suggesting that the same ABC transporters are responsible for the transport of all three phytochelatin complexes. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 play a major role in Cd sequestration, as vacuolar accumulation of Cd was decreased in atabcc1 atabcc2 protoplasts to $5 . 5 \%$ of wild-type levels (Figure 2). The remaining sequestration activity may result from the presence of other ABCC proteins, such as AtABCC3 and AtABCC6, which were previously implicated in Cd tolerance (Tommasini et al., 1998; Gaillard et al., 2008), or AtABCC11 and AtABCC12, which are the closest homologs of AtABCC1. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 also play a crucial role in Hg (II) tolerance. The fact that both the PC synthase mutant and the transporter mutants (Figure 1f) exhibited such a high sensitivity to Hg(II) indicates that conjugation of Hg(II) to PCs and vacuolar sequestration of PC–Hg(II) are critical steps in Hg(II) detoxification.

AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 confer tolerance to As(III), Cd(II) and Hg(II), but not to Pb(II). The substrate specificity of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 is distinct from that of ScYCF1, a well-characterized ABCC transporter, which confers tolerance to Pb(II) as well as to As(III), Cd(II) and Hg(II) in yeast and/or Arabidopsis (Li et al., 1997; Ghosh et al., 1999; Gueldry et al., 2003; Song et al., 2003). One explanation for this difference may be that ScYCF1 transports GS-conjugated metals (Li et al., 1997), whereas AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 transport PC conjugates (Song et al., 2010). In line with this explanation, the PC-deficient cad1 mutant did not exhibit decreased Pb(II) tolerance (Figure S1), suggesting that Pb tolerance in Arabidopsis does not depend on PCs. As the GSH-deficient cad2 mutant exhibited compromised Pb(II) tolerance (Figure S1), GSH appears to be important in Pb tolerance, either by facilitating Pb sequestration and/or functioning as an anti-oxidant.


## The importance of the ABC transporters in Cd(II) tolerance is different from that in Hg(II) and As(III) tolerance


Although the absence of the two ABC transporters rendered the plant nearly as sensitive to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ or $\mathsf { H g } ( \mathsf { I I } )$ as plants lacking PC synthase, this was not true for Cd(II). The double knockout plant was hypersensitive to Cd(II), but to a lesser degree than the PC synthase mutant, cad1. What could cause the difference in sensitivity between Cd(II) and As(III)/ Hg(II)? One possible explanation is that the PC–metal/metalloid complexes have different stabilities at different pHs. In the case of Cd, it has been reported that the PC–Cd(II) complex is more stable at neutral pH and less stable under acidic conditions, while the PC–As(III) complex is most stable in an acidic environment (Delnomdedieu et al., 1994; Schmo¨ ger et al., 2000; Dorcˇa´k and Kre˛zel, 2003). In cases where a_ PC–metal/metalloid complex is more stable at acidic pH, efficient transport into the acidic vacuole is required to avoid release of the toxic metal/metalloid from the complexes in the cytosol. If a PC–metal/metalloid complex is more stable at a neutral or slightly basic pH, as is the case for Cd(II), release of the metal/metalloid ions would be lower within the cytosol, resulting at least partial detoxification even in the absence of vacuolar sequestration. Therefore, in atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout plants, Cd(II) toxicity may be attenuated by chelation to PCs, resulting in less severe sensitivity than for As(III) or Hg(II). This hypothesis is supported by Cd speciation analysis (Figure S8), which showed that Cd in the mutant is exclusively associated with sulfur detected at a retention time that corresponds with that of PCs.

Furthermore, the level of total low-molecular-weight sulfur compounds, including PCs and GSH, in the wild-type and the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant exposed to Cd(II) was very similar (Table S1). Since GSH concentrations remain constant during long-term exposure of Arabidopsis to Cd after a slight initial reduction (Xiang and Oliver, 1998), this result suggests that PC content in the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant does not differ much from that in the wild-type. This observation is in contrast to that made in a study of plants exposed to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ , in which atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant plants contained a lower amount of PCs than the wild-type (Song et al., 2010). These contrasting results suggest again that Cd is more efficiently complexed to PCs at a cytosolic pH than As is. Tight binding of PCs and Cd in the cytosol may maintain apo PC at low levels, which cannot exert significant feedback inhibition of PC synthesis (Loeffler et al., 1989), even in the absence of vacuolar transport. In contrast, As is less efficiently complexed to PCs at cytosolic pH, and thus plant cells exposed to As may have a high level of apoPC in the cytosol, causing feedback inhibition on PC synthesis. This feedback inhibition is likely to be much higher in the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant than in the wild-type, because the mutant plants lack the transporters that remove As–PC and apoPC from the cytosol.

When AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 were expressed in a yeast strain that produces PCs, resistance to Hg(II) was increased (Figure 3), but not resistance to Cd(II) (Figure S5). The difference in response to the two metals may be explained by the high stability of the PC–Cd(II) complex at cytosolic pH, as described above. Furthermore, the high concentration of

PCs produced in the yeast system could enable the cells to tolerate intracellular Cd even in the absence of the transporters. In a previous report (Song et al., 2010), we showed that SM7 yeast produced more PCs than Arabidopsis plants. Double knockout mutant plants grown in the presence of $1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ As contained 10–15 nmol PCs $\mathfrak { g } ^ { - 1 }$ FW, while SM7 yeast transformed with the empty vector control produced 3 nmol $\mathsf { P C s \mathsf { m } q } ^ { - 1 }$ protein. Assuming that, in the mutant plants and yeast, all PCs are localized in the cytosol [10 and $50 \%$ of the cell volume for plants and yeast, respectively, according to Winter et al. (1993) and Biswas et al. (2003)] and that yeast contain $5 0 ~ \mathsf { m g }$ protein per g FW $( 5 \% )$ , the cytosolic PC concentration is estimated to be $1 0 0 { - } 1 5 0 ~ \mu \mu \mu \mu$ in plants and at least $3 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ in yeast. As Cd is more efficient at inducing PC synthesis than As is, it is likely that SM7 yeast produces more PCs when grown in the presence of Cd(II) than in the presence of As. Such a high PC concentration could be enough to complex and detoxify Cd efficiently in the cytosol, in which case the presence of either ABC transporter would not enhance tolerance to Cd.


## Root-to-shoot translocation of Cd(II) is dependent on AtABCC1 and AtABCC2


Translocation of Cd from the root to the shoot was greater in the double knockout than in the wild-type (Figure 4). This suggests that vacuolar sequestration of the PC–Cd(II) complexes by AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 decreases the cytosolic concentration of the metal in root cells, and thereby reduces translocation to the shoot. In agreement with this explanation, several reports have demonstrated preferential accumulation of Cd and other non-essential heavy metals in the root, and have shown that translocation to the shoot is limited (Kim et al., 2002; Puig and Penarrubia, 2009; Verbruggen et al., 2009) and that xylem loading of Cd is an important factor in controlling shoot metal content (Uraguchi et al., 2009; Conn and Gilliham, 2010). The increased shoot-to-root ratio of Cd in the atabcc1 atabcc2 double mutant in this study is not as pronounced as that reported for rice plants (Oryza sativa) that have reduced OsHMA3 activity (Ueno et al., 2010). However, to our knowledge, the translocation ratio of the corresponding Arabidopsis mutant has not yet been investigated. Further studies are required to understand the relative importance of AtABCC1, AtABCC2, AtHMA3 and other candidate transporters, such as AtCAX2 and AtCAX4 (Hirschi et al., 2000; Korenkov et al., 2009; Ueno et al., 2010), in retaining Cd(II) in the root of Arabidopsis.


## Vacuolar sequestration can be engineered to increase heavy metal tolerance and accumulation


Over-expression of AtABCC1 driven by the 35S promoter enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation in Arabidopsis (Figure 5). This is probably the result of an increased vacuolar storage capacity, as shown for ScYCF1-expressing Arabidopsis plants (Song et al., 2003). However, this was different from the case of arsenic, in which tolerance was enhanced only upon over-expression of both AtABCC1 and PC synthase (Song et al., 2010), indicating that the transport and synthesis of PCs are both required for arsenic tolerance. This difference may originate from the different extents of induction of PC synthesis by different metals. Cd(II) is known to be a more efficient inducer of PC synthesis than As(V) or As(III), and results in a two- to four-fold higher level of PCs (Grill et al., 1989; Vatamaniuk et al., 2000; Oven et al., 2002). In plants over-expressing AtABCC1, it is likely that Cd(II) induces the production of sufficient amounts of PCs, such that transport of PC–Cd(II) determines the tolerance to Cd(II), rather than the PC synthesis.

Among several dozen AtABCC1 transgenic plant lines examined, we did not find any plants with transcript levels higher than $12 0 { - } 1 5 0 \%$ of the wild-type levels (Song et al., 2010). Increasing the expression level to above this level may improve the heavy metal tolerance of the plant further. To test whether a further increase in the level of PCs may have a synergistic effect on the Cd tolerance mediated by AtABCC1, we compared the Cd tolerance of plants over-expressing AtPCS1 alone or both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1, but did not find much difference between them (Figure S7). This may be due to the strong effect of AtPCS1 (an 8.6- to 32-fold increase in transcript level), which produces high levels of PCs that stabilize Cd in the cytosol, whereas AtABCC1 transcript levels were not increased much above wild-type levels.

Understanding the expression control mechanism of AtABCC1, and application of this knowledge may therefore be useful in phytoremediation projects that aim to produce plants with enhanced heavy metal accumulation and tolerance. The broad range of substrates transported by the ABC transporters is a further advantage of using these genes, because many sites are contaminated by a mixture of toxic ions (Vangronsveld et al., 2009). Furthermore, manipulation of these genes in a tissue-specific manner, e.g. in roots or stems, may reduce the accumulation of Cd in the edible parts of plants, such as fruits or grains.

Cadmium (Cd) is a highly toxic element to living organisms,and its accumulation in the edible portions of crops poses a potential threat for human health.The molecular mechanisms underlying Cd detoxification and accumulation are notfullunderstood in plants.In this study,the involvementofa C-type ABC transporter,OsABCC9, in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice was investigated.The expression of OsABCC9 was rapidly induced by Cd treatment in a concentration-dependent manner in the root.The transporter,localized on the tonoplast, was mainly expressd in the root stele under Cd stress. OsABCc9 knockout mutants were more sensitive to Cd and accumulated more Cd in both the root and shoot compared to the wild-type.Moreover,the Cd concentrations in the xylem sap and grain were also significantly increased in the knockout lines,suggesting that more Cd was distributed from root to shoot and grain in the mutants.Heterologous expresion of OsABCC9 in yeast enhanced Cd tolerance along with an increase of intracelllar Cd content.Taken together,these results indicated that OsABCC9 mediates Cd tolerance and accumulation through sequestration of Cd into the root vacuoles in rice.

OsABCC9 (LOC_Os04g13210) was annotated to contain 1278 and 1207 amino acids (aa) in the Rice Annotation Project Database (RAP-DB, http://rapdb.dna.affrc.go.jp/) and the MsU rice genome annotation project database (RGAP， http://rice.plantbiology.msu.edu/)， respectively.When searching in NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information) database,two splice variants of OsABCC9 (1545 and 1603 aa) were obtained,both of which are longer than the sequences in RAPDB and RGAP at the ${ \boldsymbol { 5 } } ^ { \prime }$ terminus.Since the OsABCC9 sequence in NCBI was updated more recently,it may represent the genuine OsABCC9 sequence.Thus,based on the OsABCC9 sequence in NCBI, the full-length ORF(open reading frame) of OsABCC9 was obtained from the model japonica rice variety Nipponbare by high-fidelity PCR.This OsABCC9 ORF is 4638 bp,encoding a predicted protein of 1545 aa. Gene structure analysis showed OsABCC9 has 11 exons and 10 introns (Fig. S1A).A conserved domain search revealed that OsABCC9 harborstwo nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) and two transmembrane domains (TMDs),so it belongs to the full-size ABC transporter (Fig.S1B). Phylogenetic analysis with the C-type ABC transporters in rice and Arabidopsis showed that OsABCC9 is most closely related to OsABCC10 with $6 7 \%$ identity.Among the Arabidopsis ABCC subfamily,AtABCC14 is the closest homolog of OsABCC9 with $5 5 \%$ identity (Fig. S1C, Supplementary data 2).


## 3.2.Expression pattern of OsABCC9


Previous high-throughput analysis revealed that OsABCC9 is upregulated by Cd treatment [24,25],and we examined its expression pattern in more detail by quantitative RT-PCR analysis.Compared with the control,OsABCC9 was significantly induced by Cd treatment in roots,but not in shoots (Fig.lA).The roots were further divided into root tips $\left( 0 - 1 \ \mathrm { c m } \right)$ and basal region roots $( 1 - 2 ~ \mathrm { c m } )$ ,and stronger induction by Cd was observed in the root tips (Fig.1B).Moreover, the time-dependent alterations in the expression of OsABCC9 were examined.As shown in Fig.1C,an increase in the transcriptlevel of OsABCC9 was detected after 1 h exposure to $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd and it continued to increase over $^ { 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of the same treatment,whereas the extent of induction was decreased at 12 and $2 4 \ \mathrm { h }$ after Cd exposure.The transcript level of OsABCC9 was also detected in the presence of different Cd concentrations.As shown in Fig.1D, OsABCC9 expression was elevated in roots treated with $1 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ Cd,and continued to increase with higher Cd exposure,suggesting that OsABCC9 is responsive to external Cd in a concentration-dependent fashion.Furthermore,the responsiveness of OsABCC9 to other metals including zinc $\mathbf { ( } \mathbf { Z n } )$ ,aluminium (Al),and lanthanum (La),was also detected. It was also induced by Zn toxicity, albeit with a lower degree of induction relative to Cd treatment (Fig.1E),suggesting that OsABCC9 is not specifically induced by Cd exposure.


## 3.3． Tissue and subcellular localization of OsABCC9


To analyze the tissue localization of OsABCC9,we generated a transgenic rice line carrying the $2 . 0 \mathrm { k b }$ promoter of OsABCC9 fused with the GFP gene.Immunostaining with an anti-GFP antibody showed weak GFP signals in the epidermis,exodermis,and stele of roots without exposure to Cd (Fig.2C-E),pointing to low expression of OsABCC9 in the absence of Cd.However, in roots treated with Cd, the GFP signal intensity was increased,especially in the stele (Fig.2F-H).These results suggested that the OsABCC9 promoter activity is elevated under Cd exposure,which is consistent with the OsABCC9 expression pattern (Fig.1A).As the negative control, the anti-GFP antibody was also reacted with wild-type roots, but no signal was detected (Fig.2A and B), indicating the specificity of the antibody.

To determine the subcellular localization of OsABCC9,the fusion construct OsABCC9-GFP was co-transformed with the tonoplast marker AtTPK1 (AT5G55630) [28] into rice protoplasts.The green fluorescence signal of OsABCC9-GFP overlapped neatly with the red fluorescence signal generated by AtTPKl-mCherry (Fig.3).By contrast, the green fluorescence signal was visible in the cytosol when GFP alone was expressed (Fig.3)．These results indicated that OsABCC9isa tonoplast-localized transporter.


## 3.4.Cd transport activity of OsABCC9 in yeast


To test whether OsABCC9 possesses transport activity for Cd, it was cloned into the yeast expression vector pYES2 and expressed in the Cdsensitive yeast strain △ycf1 that lacks the vacuolar C-type ABC transporter YCF1 [29].Yeast harboring OsABCC9 and empty vector were cultured on galactose-containing medium with or without Cd.On Cd-free medium,the OsABCC9-expressing yeast grew similarly to those transformed with the empty vector.However,on medium containing Cd (5or $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ ，the OsABCC9 transformants grew better than the vector-transformed yeast (Fig.4A).As negative controls, the transformants were also grown on glucose-containing medium.There was no difference in growth between yeast with OsABCC9 and the empty vector independent of Cd conditions (Fig.S2).These results indicated that OsABCC9 confers Cd tolerance in the yeast mutant △ycf1.

The Cd tolerance conferred by OsABCC9 might be due to sequestration of Cd into vacuoles or extrusion of Cd out of cells.To test these possibilities,the Cd content in OsABCC9-expressing yeast and controls was measured after exposure to Cd for 2 and $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 4 h }$ 、Asa result,the OsABCC9 transformants had higher Cd content than controls after treatment with Cd for $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ ,and the difference in Cd content increased after treatment with Cd for 4h (Fig.4B).Therefore,the Cd tolerance conferred by OsABCC9 is most likely due to vacuolar sequestration of Cd rather than Cd extrusion.

Additionally,several C-type ABC transporters have been shown to participate in arsenic (As) tolerance and accumulation in plants [17,30, 31],so the possible role of OsABCC9 in As tolerance was also examined in △ycf1 yeast.However,no difference in growth between OsABCC9 transformants and controls was observed on medium containing 100 or $2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ NaAsO2 (Fig.S3),demonstrating that OsABCC9 did not affect the As tolerance when expressed in △ycf1.


## 3.5.Knockout of OsABCC9 enhanced Cd sensitivity of rice


To investigate the role of OsABCC9 in Cd tolerance in planta,we created osabcc9 knockout mutants using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.

Two independent mutants,osabcc9-1 and osabcc9-2,were identified by sequencing analysis,each of which contained a 1-bp insertion (A or T) in the target site,respectively (Fig.S4).These insertions resulted in frameshift mutations in OsABCC9.Both mutant plants were used for growth analysis under different Cd conditions.At O and $1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, no growth difference was observed between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Fig. 5A and B). When exposed to 5 and $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, however,root growth of the OsABCC9 knockout mutants was more inhibited relative to the wild-type plants (Fig.5C and D). Quantitative analysis also showed that both the root and shoot dry weight (DW) of osabcc9 mutants were significantly lower than those of the wild type when grown with 5 and $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd (Fig.5E and F).These results indicated that loss of function of OsABCC9 led to sensitivity to Cd in rice.

The sensitivity of osabcc9 mutants to As was also examined.No visible difference in growth was observed between the osabcc9 mutants and wild-type plants,regardless of the As conditions (Fig. S5A and B).

Moreover,quantitative analysis of the dry weight and As content of the roots and shoots showed no differences between osabcc9 mutants and the wild-type (Figs.S5C and D, S6A and B).These results indicated that OsABCC9 may not participate in As tolerance and accumulation in rice.


## 3.6.Knockout of OsABCC9 increased rice plant and grain Cd content


To examine the effect of knockout of OsABCC9 on Cd accumulation, we measured the Cd content in wild-type and osabcc9 mutant plants grown hydroponically with 1,5,and $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd.Under low-Cd $( 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ conditions,the Cd concentrations in roots and shoots did not differ significantly between the mutant and wild-type plants (Fig. 6A and B). However,at5 and $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd,the osabcc9 plants had higher Cd concentrations in their roots and shoots than the wild type (Fig.6A and B), suggesting that loss-of-function of OsABCC9 enhanced Cd accumulation in rice.Meanwhile,the concentrations of other microelements such as Fe, Cu, Mn,and Zn were also determined. S7B and C, S8B and C).No significant difference in Fe concentration was detected between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Figs.S7D, S8D).

Furthermore,we measured the concentrations of Cd and other essential microelements (Zn,Cu,Mn,and Fe) in the grains of osabcc9 mutants and wild-type rice grown in Cd-containing soil $( 2 . 0 \mathrm { m g } / \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { C d } )$ . The Cd concentration was sharply increased in osabcc9 grains by up to

2-3 fold compared with the wild type (Fig. 6C). However, there was no significant difference in the concentration of other microelements in the grains between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Fig.S9).It has been reported that xylem-mediated Cd transfer from root to shoot is the key process determining Cd accumulation in rice shoots and grains [32].We, therefore,measured the Cd levels in the xylem sap of the osabcc9 mutant and wild-type plants treated with $5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd for $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 8 d }$ .We foundamarked increase of the Cd concentration in the xylem sap of the osabcc9 plants relative to the wild type (Fig.6D).These results demonstrated that root-to-shoot transport of Cd was significantly enhanced in osabcc9 mutants, thus increasing Cd accumulation in the grain.

Heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd) and mercury (Hg) are toxic pollutants that are detrimental to living organisms. Plants employ a two-step mechanism to detoxify toxic ions. First, phytochelatins bind to the toxic ion, and then the metal–phytochelatin complex is sequestered in the vacuole. Two ABCC-type transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, that play a key role in arsenic detoxification, have recently been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, it is unclear whether these transporters are also implicated in phytochelatindependent detoxification of other heavy metals such as Cd(II) and Hg(II). Here, we show that atabcc1 single or atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutants exhibit a hypersensitive phenotype in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II). Microscopic analysis using a Cd-sensitive probe revealed that Cd is mostly located in the cytosol of protoplasts of the double mutant, whereas it occurs mainly in the vacuole of wild-type cells. This suggests that the two ABCC transporters are important for vacuolar sequestration of Cd. Heterologous expression of the transporters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae confirmed their role in heavy metal tolerance. Over-expression of AtABCC1 in Arabidopsis resulted in enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation. Together, these results demonstrate that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 are important vacuolar transporters that confer tolerance to cadmium and mercury, in addition to their role in arsenic detoxification. These transporters provide useful tools for genetic engineering of plants with enhanced metal tolerance and accumulation, which are desirable characteristics for phytoremediation.

Keywords: vacuolar sequestration, heavy metal tolerance, phytoremediation, ABC transporter, phytochelatin transporter, heavy metal detoxification.

Cadmium $\mathrm { ( C d ) }$ is one of the naturally occurring heavy metals that is highly toxic to all organisms, including plants. Cd excess in plants can cause the disruption of nutrient homeostasis, dysfunction of proteins, DNA and membrane damage, and an accumulation of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), consequently resulting in significant reduction of crop growth and production (Sandalio et al., 2001; Hall, 2002; crops potentially threatens human health.

To adapt to the Cd-contaminated environment, plants have evolved diverse mechanisms to cope with Cd stress, such as Cd extrusion, chelation, and sequestration (Hall, 2002; Weber et al., 2006; Lin and Aarts, 2012). Among them, several studies have showed that ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters may play important roles in Cd tolerance in plants (Kim et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2007; Oda et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Brunetti et al., 2015). For example, AtABCG36/AtPDR8 was reported to be essential for Cd resistance in Arabidopsis (Kim et al., 2007). It is localized at the plasma membrane of root cells and functions as an efflux transporter for Cd or Cd conjugates. On the other hand, two ABCC-type transporters; AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, are involved in vacuolar sequestration of Cd in Arabidopsis (Park et al., 2012). Knockout of these genes resulted in hypersensitivity to Cd. Recently, another ABCC-type transporter AtABCC3 was also reported to be involved in Cd tolerance by transporting PC-Cd complexes into the vacuoles in Arabidopsis (Brunetti et al., 2015). In rice, there are at least 120 members of ABC transporter (Garcia et al, 2004), but only few has been characterized in terms of Cd tolerance. One of them, OsABCG43 is a Cd-inducible transporter (Oda et al., 2011). Its expression in yeast increased Cd tolerance although its exact role in rice is unknown. Another ABCG-type transporter gene, OsABCG36/OsPDR9, was also reported to be induced by Cd and was suggested to play a possible role in heavy metal stress (Moons, 2003, 2008). However, the role of OsABCG36/OsPDR9 in Cd tolerance has not been investigated. In the present study, we functionally characterized OsABCG36 in terms of the gene expression, cellular and subcellular localization, transport activity. We also obtained two independent mutant lines of OsABCG36 by the CRISPR/Cas9 technique and compared their Cd tolerance and accumulation with the wild-type rice. Our results showed that OsABCG36 is involved in Cd tolerance by effluxing Cd from the root cells.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are one of the largest known superfamilies of membrane transporters in all living organisms [1,2]. ABCC transporters, which belong to one subclass of the ABC transporter superfamily, are well known for their roles as multidrug resistance-associated proteins (MRPs), which are found in all eukaryotic organisms [3–7]. These proteins shuttle substrates as diverse as glutathione conjugates, xenobiotic compounds, intermediate metabolites and hormones across a variety of biological membranes [2,5,8,9].
