## Responses of BnNRT2 gene expression to drought or waterlogging stress


Cis-acting regulatory element analysis of BnNRT2 promoter regions revealed a great abundance of light responsive element (Fig. 3), which implies that BnNRT2 gene expression is closely associated with photosynthesis and might be diurnally regulated. Previous studies with Arabidopsis have elucidated up-regulation of $A t N R T 2 . I$ in daylight and down-regulation during the night, which can be inhibited by sucrose [28, 29]. Taking our results together with past reports supports the conclusion that, as light and sucrose regulated mediators of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and transport, rapeseed NRTs are key members of systems coordinating carbon and $_ \mathrm { N }$ metabolism. Furthermore, the duplication of BnNRT2.1 genes and variation in their responses to N, P and K deficiency treatments, suggests that NRT genes are involved in modulating multiple nutrient response pathways.

Several previous studies have suggested that limited external ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ supplies can promote lateral root elongation through regulation of meristematic activity in mature root tips, where, in rapeseed, cells in the meristematic region are packed more densely than in the elongation zone [30]. In Arabidopsis, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2, two nitrate transporter genes mainly expressed in the root, play key roles in the promotion of lateral root elongation [31, 32]. Recent research has also demonstrated that knock-down of CsNRT2.1 in cucumber strongly reduces root length and lateral root numbers under low $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ conditions [33]. In the present study, $B n N R T 2 . I s$ were predominantly expressed in roots, and most were up-regulated during N deficiency stress (Figs. 5 and 6). Plus, lateral root lengths and root tips also increased in response to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Fig. S3C, D). Therefore, we conclude that BnNRT2.1 family members are likely involves in the regulation of the lateral root elongation under N limited conditions.

More recently, EXO70A3 was identified as a downstream target of PIN4, an auxin efflux carrier, in adaptive drought responses that lead to the production of a deeper root system architecture (RSA) [34]. Analogously, a deeper RSA induced by N deficiency might be modulated by EXO70A3, with NRT2.1 genes possibly involve downstream of auxin pathway related RSA modulation, which is supported by the fact that in CREs analysis, IAA responsive elements were found in the promoter sequences of $B n N R T 2 . 1 s$ (Fig. 3).

In Arabidopsis, Orsel [35] have outlined expression profiles of NRT2 family members, with AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.4,

AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.6 being preferentially expressed in roots, AtNRT2.7 specifically expressed in aerial parts, AtNRT2.3 expression intermediate between the previous two profiles, and AtNRT2.2 undetectable in either roots or shoots. Similarly, in the rapeseed expression profiles observed herein, $B n N R T 2 . l s$ and $B n N R T 2 . 4 s$ were mainly expressed in the root, while $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ were detected only in aerial parts, including leaves, seeds, flowers and stems (Fig. 4b, c). On the other hand, in contrast to the observations of Orsel [35], $B n N R T 2 . 2 a$ transcripts were mainly detected in roots, and no BnNRT2.3 transcripts were detected in either roots or shoots. We did observe that $B n N R T 2 . S s$ were like $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ and expressed mainly in the shoots of adult plants (Fig. 4b, c). However, in the seedlings reared in hydroponics cultures, $B n N R T 2 . S s$ were mainly expressed in the root (Fig. 4d). This could be an artefact of the hydroponics system, or it might suggest that $B n N R T 2 . S s$ expression in roots changes as the plant matures. Finally, $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ were the only BnNRT2s detected in seeds (Fig. 4b), which is consistent with Chopin’s [14] finding that AtNRT2.7 plays a specific role in nitrate accumulation in the seed.

To date, a number of NRT2.1-homologous genes have been cloned and characterized in higher plant species including Arabidopsis thaliana [10, 36], Glycine max [37], Triticum aestivum [38], Oryza sativa [39], Zea mays [40, 41], Cucumber [33], and Chinese cabbage [42], many of which have been demonstrated to be major HATS-type genes involved in root $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake under N limitation. In accordance with previous reports, the mRNA levels of $B n N R T 2 . l s$ in the roots observed in this study were upregulated with declines in N supply (Fig. 5). What’s more, recent research has identified the gene BnaA06g04560D $( B n N R T 2 . I d )$ as a key factor in NUE through genomic and transcriptomic analysis experiments involving two Brassica napus genotypes contrasting in NUE [43]. Additionally, BnNRT2.5 expression profiles vary between seedlings and adult plants, though expression increased with decreases in external N supply (Figs. 5 and 6). Coincidentally, previous research with NRT2.1, NRT2.2, NRT2.4 and NRT2.5 mutants has indicated that AtNRT2.5, which is expressed in the epidermis and the cortex of lateral roots in young seedlings and the minor veins of mature leaves in adult plants, works in combination with these other NRT2s to modulate efficient uptake of nitrate, as well as, to participate in nitrate loading into the phloem during nitrate remobilization under N-starvation conditions [13]. $B n N R T 2 . 5 s$ might perform similar functions in rapeseed as AtNRT2.5 does in Arabidopsis, which could be a worthwhile subject of future investigations.

The absorption of N directly impacts crop yield, and, therefore, maintaining appropriate N fertilizer supplies is an important component of managing crop yields. However, numerous stresses, such as waterlogging, drought and nutrients deficiencies, may reduce crop yields. As expected, in the present study, it was found that waterlogging, drought, P deficiency and K deficiency suppress the expression of rapeseed NRT2 gene members (Figs. 6, 7 and 8). Specifically, BnNRT2.1a was up-regulated under waterlogging stress and K deficiency conditions, BnNRT2.7 members were up-regulated under waterlogging stress and P or K deficiencies conditions (Figs. 6 and 8), and BnNRT2.5 members were up-regulated in roots under waterlogging stress (Fig. 8). This is consistent with the previous findings of some Pi, Fe transporters [44, 45], which were also regulated by different nutrient stresses, and it is well-documented that the cross-talk exist among ion signals when plant respond to different nutrient stresses [45–47]. The enhanced expressions of BnNRT2s genes under P or K deficiencies probably because the $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake or metabolism would be influenced by these deficiencies, we speculated that these NRT2 genes could sense the status of external P or K level. However, the synergistic regulation mechanisms of different nutrients homeostasis need to be further investigated. Additionally, the enhanced expression of BnNRT2s might contribute to efficient $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and transport of rapeseed under waterlogging stresses. Thus, it is reasonable to infer that BnNRT2.1a, BnNRT2.5 s and $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ might play key roles in modulating $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake and transport in rapeseed plants experiencing multiple stresses.

Nitrogen (N), which is an important component of biological macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, provides nutrients and energy for plant growth and development (Gojon 2017). Nitrate and ammonium are the most readily absorbed forms of N in soil by plant roots, especially nitrate, which is the preferred N source in soil for assimilation by most terrestrial plants (Kiba and Krapp 2016). The lack of $\mathbf { N }$ in the natural environment could lead to intense competition between plants and soil microorganisms (Norman and Friesen 2017). To further adapt to changes in diferent N levels, plants have evolved several absorption and transport systems to optimize the availability of nitrate for their own growth, including the low-afnity nitrate transporter system (LATS) and high-afnity nitrate transporter system (HATS) (Fang et  al. 2021). Among them, the NRT1/PTR family (NPF) and nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) are responsible for the functions of the LATS and HATS systems, respectively. The NRT2 family is responsible for the uptake of low nitrate from the soil by roots. Thus, understanding the functions of NRT2 members will be benefcial to the sustainable development of agriculture in the future.

NRT2 members have been isolated and characterized in many species, including seven NRT2 proteins in Arabidopsis (Okamoto et al. 2006), seven to ten NRT2 in barley (Vidmar et  al. 2000), and fve NRT2 in rice (Cai et al. 2008). Among the members of the NRT2 family, NRT2.1 plays a major role in nitrate uptake by roots in the HATS system. There was a strong association between HATS activity and NRT2.1 transcription, which was highly induced by nitrate depletion and repressed by abundant nitrate (Wirth et  al. 2007). OsNRT2.1 overexpression in rice signifcantly increased biomass and yield, and improved agricultural N use efciency (Yan et  al. 2011). Moreover, NRT2.1 played a key role in the regulation of nitrate signaling pathways by lateral root mediation, which was independent of its highafnity nitrate uptake function (van Gelderen et  al. 2021). Though the function of NRT2.1 has been thoroughly studied in herbaceous plants, it is still lacking in woody plants. Therefore, understanding more functions of NRT2.1 in diferent species could play a signifcant role in regulating N absorption.

Plant transporter genes have been well studied in mycorrhizal symbiosis processes. For example, some plant nitrate transporters have been induced by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) colonization with the host plant. A study reported that one NRT gene (TC79437) was down-regulated with Funneliformis mosseae colonization in Medicago truncatula roots (Burleigh 2001). In addition, the expression of NRT genes was also afected by AM colonization in grapevine (Balestrini et  al. 2017), Solanum lycopersicum (Ruzicka et  al. 2012), tomato (Hildebrandt et  al. 2002) and Lotus japonicus (Guether et al. 2009a). Dark septate endophytes (DSEs) are a type of dematiaceous and septate fungal hyphae that are commonly found in the roots of host plants from natural environments (Jumpponen and Trappe 1998). Studies have reported that several DSEs are benefcial for their host plants’ N assimilation (Upson et al. 2009; Vergara et al. 2019; Wu et  al. 2021). However, the impacts of DSEs on plant $\mathbf { N }$ uptake through the regulation of NRT genes are poorly understood.

Sweet cherry (Prunus avium L.) is one of the most popular fresh fruits in the world. However, the molecular mechanism of its N uptake is poorly understood. A previous study found that the DSE fungus S16 could promote the growth of sweet cherry and upregulate the expression of nitrate transporters (Wu et al. 2021). Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the role of the nitrate transporter PaNRT2.1 during colonization by S16 and to determine the function of PaNRT2.1 in N uptake in sweet cherry. This would broaden our understanding of the molecular mechanism of $\mathbf { N }$ uptake with nitrate transporters in DSE symbiosis.

Background: High-affinity nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) genes have been implicated in nitrate absorption and remobilization under nitrogen (N) starvation stress in many plant species, yet little is known about this gene family respond to various stresses often occurs in the production of rapeseed (Brassica napus L.).

Results: This report details identification of 17 NRT2 gene family members in rapeseed, as well as, assessment of their expression profiles using RNA-seq analysis and qRT-PCR assays. In this study, all BnNRT2.1 members, BnNRT2.2a and BnNRT2.4a were specifically expressed in root tissues, while BnNRT2.7a and BnNRT2.7b were mainly expressed in aerial parts, including as the predominantly expressed NRT2 genes detected in seeds. This pattern of shoot NRT expression, along with homology to an Arabidopsis NRT expressed in seeds, strongly suggests that both BnNRT2.7 genes play roles in seed nitrate accumulation. Another rapeseed NRT, BnNRT2.5 s, exhibited intermediate expression, with transcripts detected in both shoot and root tissues. Functionality of BnNRT2s genes was further outlined by testing for adaptive responses in expression to exposure to a series of environmental stresses, including N, phosphorus (P) or potassium (K) deficiency, waterlogging and drought. In these tests, most NRT2 gene members were up-regulated by N starvation and restricted by the other stresses tested herein. In contrast to this overall trend, transcription of BnNRT2.1a was up-regulated under waterlogging and K deficiency stress, and BnNRT2.5 s was up-regulated in roots subjected to waterlogging. Furthermore, the mRNA levels of BnNRT2.7 s were enhanced under both waterlogging stress and P or K deficiency conditions. These results suggest that these three BnNRT2 genes might participate in crosstalk among different stress response pathways.

Conclusions: The results presented here outline a diverse set of NRT2 genes present in the rapeseed genome that collectively carry out specific functions throughout rapeseed development, while also responding not just to N deficiency, but also to several other stresses. Targeting of individual BnNRT2 members that coordinate rapeseed nitrate uptake and transport in response to cues from multiple stress response pathways could significantly expand the genetic resources available for improving rapeseed resistance to environmental stresses.

Keywords: High-affinity nitrate transporter, NRT2, Rapeseed, Various stresses

NRT2 family of nitrate transporters normally require a partner protein, NAR2 (nitrate assimilation related protein), to transport nitrate to a high-affinity (high affinity nitrate transport system, HATS), although its role is still not well understood. In this study, the $C c N R T 2 . I$ and CcNAR2 cDNAs from of Capsicum chinense were cloned and characterized in terms of their structure, phylogeny, and their organ-specific transcriptional regulation, and by ligh/dark cycle, N and sucrose. CcNRT2.1 (putative molecular mass $5 7 . 5 \mathrm { k D a }$ and CcNAR2 $2 2 . 6 6 \mathrm { k D a } )$ retained the characteristic domains of NRT2 and NAR2 family, respectively. CcNRT2.1 is expressed exclusively in the root, and both western blot and protein immunolocalization, demonstrated its exclusive location in root epidermal and cortical cells. CcNAR2 is expressed mainly in the root, but also in fruits of 25 days postanthesis (DPA). The presence of two protein bands ( $\mathord { \sim } 6 0$ and ${ \sim } 8 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ ) detected in the western blot, suggested that CcNRT2.1 monomer and $\mathrm { C c N R T } 2 . 1 / \mathrm { C c N A R } 2$ heterodimer work together for nitrate transport function in roots. Both genes were induced by ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ and glutamate, and CcNRT2.1 was induced by sucrose. The co-expression of both genes in the specific zone of the root $2 \mathrm { - } 4 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ from the apex) in which the high-affinity nitrate transport occurs (evaluated by root $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ endogenous content, extracellular $\mathrm { p H }$ alkalinization, and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ net flux by MIFE technique), strongly supports that $C c N R T 2 . I / C c N A R 2$ belong to a HATS, with a functional similarity to AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 of Arabidopsis. These are the first components of a HATS characterized in the Capsicum genus.

NRT2, as a high-affinity nitrate transporter protein, plays an important role in nitrate uptake and transport in plants, and it is expressed in roots, phloem, epidermis, leaves, seeds, and other organs of plants35. The NRT2 genes has been studied in many species, however, little is known about the NRT2 gene family in alfalfa. In this study, we identified three NRT2 genes using bioinformatics methods. It has been found that seven, four, five, and four NRT2 genes were identified from A. thaliana36, O. sativa37, G. max38, and Populus tomentosa39, respectively. The reason for the difference in the number of genes among species may be due to the difference in the degree of gene amplification among species40. Three genes were distributed on chromosomes 4 and 8 (Fig. 2C). Despite alfalfa is better adapted to infertile soils, the number of NRT2 was not significantly expanded.

To explore the evolutionary relationships of MsNRT2 members with other species, this study analyzed the phylogenetic trees of NRT2 members of M. sativa, A. thaliana and O. sativa. Phylogenetic analysis of these genes revealed that these genes can be classified into three categories, while MsNRT2.2 and MsNRT2.3 in alfalfa were classified into the same category, and MsNRT2.1 was classified into another branch closer to A. thaliana NRT2s (Fig. 1). Based on a phylogenetic tree analysis of the MsNRT2 genes revealed that different evolutionary branches of the MsNRT2 genes contain common or specific motifs. Although the number of motif members varies across branches, the group motif patterns are strongly conserved. Comparison of novel functional structural domains or motif sequences across multiple homologous proteins has become a widely used method for predicting protein function based on evolutionary conservation41. Protein motif analysis showed that all MsNRT2 genes contain nine conserved elements that constitute the MFS_1 structural domain. The existence of these conserved motifs provides a guarantee for MsNRT2 protein family to function and play a role in nitrate absorption and transport, which is of great significance. For example, when following Atnrt2.1/ Atnrt2.2 double mutants, the function of the protein can be significantly affected by disruption of the conserved motifs, resulting in reduced nitrate uptake42. However, MsNRT2.1 motifs differ mainly in motif 10, and it is hypothesized that the difference in protein motifs may be the main reason for the functional differences between $M s N R T 2 . 2 / 2 . 3$ and MsNRT2.1 (Fig. 2B). These results suggest that during the evolution of the MsNRT2 family, internal structural differentiation may have led to functional differentiation.

When plants are stimulated by external factors, some transcription factors are activated, and the activated factors combine with the cis-acting elements of the downstream target gene promoters to change the expression pattern of genes. The study of gene cis-acting elements is particularly important for mining the potential function of genes. To date, many cis-acting elements have been well characterized and divided into distinct groups43. In Malus domestica, all NRT2s were found to contain jasmonic (JA) and ABA motifs except MdNRT2.4 and MdNRT $2 . 5 ^ { 4 4 }$ . The cis-acting regulatory element of Brassica napus NRT2 genes can be categorized into four groups: abiotic stress response elements, developmental regulatory elements, MYB binding sites, and oilseed rapeassociated elements21. By analyzing the action elements in the promoter region of alfalfa NRT2 family members, a large number of light-responsive and stress elements were found (Fig.  3A, C and D), which suggests that the expression of MsNRT2 genes may be regulated by light and stress. In addition, many hormone-responsive elements were found, such as ABRE, AuxRR-core, TATC-box and TCA-element. These results indicate that the MsNRT2 genes might respond to a variety of hormone signals and involved in alfalfa growth and developmental activities (Fig.  3B). Reported studies have found that phytohormones play a role in nitrogen regulation and signaling, including auxin (IAA), cytokinin (CTK), as well as abscisic acid (ABA) and epibrassinolide $( \mathrm { B R } ) ^ { 4 5 }$ . Broad spectrum cis-acting regulatory elements possessed by the NRT2 genes may support an active role for the gene family in cellular metabolic pathways, particularly hormone signaling pathways.

To explore the role of MsNRT2 genes in the growth and development of alfalfa, the expression levels of MsNRT2 genes in different tissues of alfalfa were analyzed, and it was found that the spatiotemporal and temporal expression patterns of MsNRT2 genes differed in various tissues of alfalfa. For example, MsNRT2.1 was expressed only in roots and rhizomes. MsNRT2.3 was expressed in all tissues with differences (Fig. 4). Although the present study did not knockout experiments to demonstrate that the MsNRT2 genes could enhance the stress tolerance of alfalfa, the changes in the expression of these genes under stress suggested that they might be involved in the stress response. Zhao et al.46 found that the Cl/NO3 co-transport system is critical for salt tolerance in plants, and that this system may be controlled through NRT2s, especially in Cl-sensitive plants. The SlNRT2 gene also influences Solanum lycopersicum response to drought and salinity. The SlNRT2 gene responds to drought and salt stress in a variety of ways, with neither stress specificity nor tissue specificity24. In rice, the expression of OsNRT2.3 gene were increased under high temperature stress, thereby improving high temperature tolerance and nitrogen absorption levels47. Overall, it can be concluded that NRT2 genes play active roles in different tissues, organs and developmental stages.

Based on tissue-specific and cis-acting element analysis studies, we analyzed the expression of the alfalfa MsNRT2 genes in roots and leaves using ABA, SA, PEG, and $\mathrm { \Delta N a C l }$ treatment (Figs. 5, 6, 7 and 8). The results showed that the MsNRT2 genes were mainly expressed in roots (Figs. 7 and 8). ABA and SA treatment increased the expression of MsNRT2.1 and MsNRT2.2 and decreased the expression level of MsNRT2.3, suggesting that

ABA and SA stimulated the up-regulation of MsNRT2.1 and MsNRT2.2 activities and increased nitrogen assimilation during nitrate uptake in alfalfa. Several studies indicate nitrate can regulate biosynthesis, deconjugation, degradation, transport, and signaling of different phytohormones, adjusting nitrogen availability and plant growth and development48–50. In contrast, hormonal signaling feedback controls nitrate regulatory networks and metabolism51–53. Apparently, nitrate and hormone signaling are closely related in coordinating plant morphology and function. Hormone signaling exerts feedback control on nitrate regulatory networks and metabolism to align plant nutrient-adapted growth and development with existing environmental conditions (Fig. 9). Tong et al. found that the expression of BnNRT2.7 and BnNRT2.1a in the NRT2 family of oilseed rape was up-regulated under drought stress21. In this study, the expression of MsNRT2.1 and MsNRT2.2 was also up-regulated under drought and salt stress, suggesting that the expression of MsNRT2 genes was associated with abiotic stress response and affected nitrogen uptake and translocation. Therefore, the specific functions of MsNRT2 genes require further in-depth research. Figure 9 shows the potential regulatory model of MsNRT2s. Here, we highlight the link between different hormones and abiotic stress and nitrate signaling pathways. External conditions affect the expression of key genes involved in nitrogen uptake, transport, assimilation and signal transduction, thereby affecting nitrogen uptake efficiency in alfalfa. NRT2.1, NRT2.2, and NRT2.3 may also regulate the expression of hormone- and abiotic stress-related genes that they affect nitrogen uptake efficiency. In summary, the study of MsNRT2 gene will provide excellent candidate genes for further genetic improvement of nitrogen utilization efficiency in alfalfa.

## Cloning of chrysanthemum highaffinity nitrate transporter family (CmNRT2) and characterization of CmNRT2.1


Chunsun Gu, Aiping Song, Xiaoxue Zhang, HaibinWang, Ting Li, Yu Chen, Jiafu Jiang, Fadi Chen & Sumei Chen

The family of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2 (NRT2) proteins belongs to the high affinity transport system (HATS) proteins which acts at low nitrate concentrations. The relevant gene content of the chrysanthemum genome was explored here by isolating the full length sequences of six distinct CmNRT2 genes. One of these (CmNRT2.1) was investigated at the functional level. Its transcription level was inducible by low concentrations of both nitrate and ammonium. A yeast two hybrid assay showed that CmNRT2.1 interacts with CmNAR2, while a BiFC assay demonstrated that the interaction occurs at the plasma membrane. Arabidopsis thaliana plants heterologously expressing CmNRT2.1 displayed an enhanced rate of labeled nitrogen uptake, suggesting that CmNRT2.1 represents a high affinity root nitrate transporter.

Plants have evolved both a high (HATS) and a low (LATS) affinity transport system, which act together to determine nitrate uptake from the soil. The genes involved in HATS and LATS belong to three distinct gene families, namely the nitrate transporter/peptide transporters (NPFs), the nitrate transporters (NRT2s) and the nitrate assimilation related genes (NAR2s)1 . The NRT2 family is part of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). The Arabidopsis thaliana (A. thaliana) genome harbors the seven NRT2 genes, referred to as AtNRT2.1 through $2 . 7 ^ { 2 , 3 }$ . NRT2 homologs are also known in other plant species: five have been identified in barley4 , four in rice5 and six in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii6 . NRT2 was initially identified as a putative high affinity transport gene in barley7 and tobacco8 before their presence was revealed in other species including A. thaliana9–11. On the basis of their transcriptional response to the provision of nitrate, the AtNRT2s have been classified into three types: those which are inducible (AtNRT2.1, 2.2 and 2.4), those which are constitutively transcribed (2.3, 2.6 and 2.7), and the repressible gene $2 . 5 ^ { 1 2 }$ . AtNRT2.1 encodes a high affinity nitrate transporter which functions at low external nitrate concentrations, acting as either a nitrate sensor or a signal transducer in the root13. Although the AtNRT2.1 product is an important contributor to the inducible component of high affinity nitrate transport14, AtNRT2.2 acts as an alternative when AtNRT2.1 is disrupted15.

The evidence which implied a functional interaction existed between NRT and NAR proteins was initially acquired in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, but it has also been shown that both the A. thaliana mutants atnrt2.1 and atnar2.1 lack inducible HATS activity at low levels of nitrate. Direct evidence for the AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 interaction has also been generated via yeast two hybrid, Xenopus oocyte and blue native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis technologies. The loss-of-function of both the rice gene OsNAR2. $l ^ { 1 6 }$ and AtNAR2. $I ^ { \mathrm { i } 7 }$ leads to a drastic reduction in plant growth.

Chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum morifolium) is a leading ornamental species, particularly in China, where the heavy application of nitrogenous fertilizer is a common practice pursued by growers, despite its known deleterious effect on the environment. So far, only one CmNRT2 (AB921547 renamed CmNRT2.4 in this study) gene has been isolated; its product interacts with CmNAR218. Here, a description is given of the isolation of a further six CmNRT2s and a more detailed analysis of the function of CmNRT2.1 has been given. In particular, its inducibility by both nitrate and ammonium has been characterized, and its interaction with CmNAR2 further detailed.

Finally, a demonstration is given that the heterologous expression of CmNRT2.1 in A. thaliana resulted in an increased rate of nitrate uptake into the root.

Nitrogen (N), crucial to plant growth and development, is engaged in numerous physiological and molecular processes (Liu et  al. 2022b; Shi et  al. 2023). Nitrate, the primary N form in aerated soils, is recognized and transported by intricate sensors or transporters from environment into plants. Many transporters, such as nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1) /peptide transport family (NRT1/ NPF), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel family (CLC), and slow anion channel-related homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been confrmed to involve in nitrate transfer and utilization across various tissues and cells (von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2010; Krapp et al. 2014; Maierhofer et al. 2014; Léran et al. 2014). As reported, NRT2 belongs to high-afnity transporter that is indispensable for nitrate uptake during environmental N defciency, i.e., $< 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. For instance, NRT2s have been extensively verifed to promote nitrate uptake and utilization under nitrogen limitation in many plant species including but not limited to Arabidopsis (Wang et al. 2018), rice (Chen et al. 2016, 2020), wheat (Sigalas et al. 2023), barley (Guo et al. 2020), maize (Jia et al. 2023), and pea (Chen et al. 2024). Positive regulation on highafnity nitrate transporters improves plant adaptability to harsh environments and improves crop yields or nitrogenuse efciency under moderate nitrogen levels (Alam et al. 2023; Iqbal et al. 2023).

Over the past several decades, numerous studies have identified various regulators or transcription factors (TFs) involved in regulating NRT2s in plants (reviewed in (Vidal et al. 2020). Regulators or TFs modulate NRTs through binding to nitrate-responsive cis-elements (NRE) in NRT’s promoter (Choi et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022a). For instance, the nitrate regulation master, nodule inception (NIN)-like proteins such as AtNLP7, ZmNLP5, MdNLP7, and HvNLP2, have been implicated in promoting NRT2.1/NRT2.2 via NREs binding (Castaings et al. 2009; Alvarez et al. 2020; Feng et al. 2022; Ge et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2022). Recently, AtNLP7 has been identifed to participate in nitrate transportation in Arabidopsis (Liu et al. 2022a). In addition, TGA1 and TGA4 directly bind to NREs in NRT2.1 or NRT2.2 promoter to infuence lateral root development and nitrate response in Arabidopsis (Alvarez et al. 2014; Zhong et al. 2015). TaNAC2 and OsSNAC1 regulate NRT2 via NRE to participate in seed vigor and nitrogen defciency adaptation (Li et al. 2020; Qi et al. 2023). PdGNC, induced by low nitrate levels, directly activates $P d N R T 2 . 4 b$ through NRE binding in poplar (Shen et al. 2022). AtBES1 enhances NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 through NRE under nitrogen defciency, linking brassinosteroid signaling and nitrate defciency in

Arabidopsis (Wang et  al. 2023). In apple, MdMYB10 transcriptionally activates MdNRT2.4–1 depending on NRE binding to enhance nitrate uptake (Liu et al. 2022c). Moreover, multiple regulators interact each other to modulate the same target gene through binding diverse NREs in promoter (Guan et al. 2017; Alvarez et al. 2020). For instance, TCP20 and NLP7&NLP6 bind to the diferent NRE of nitrate reductase gene (NIA1) and interacts to increase nitrate assimilation in Arabidopsis (Guan et al. 2017).

The presence of NREs in $_ 5 \cdot$ or $_ 3 \cdot$ terminal fanking regions is of utmost importance in advancing the regulation of regulators or TFs on their targets. NREs usually act as enhancer elements to improve the specifc binding, for instance, $\mathsf { S ^ { 3 } - T G A t / c C C N } _ { 1 2 } \mathrm { A a }$ L $/ \mathrm { t G g G a } - 3 ^ { \prime }$ in OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.3 (Wu et al. 2021), $_ 5 \cdot$ -CTATC/TGAGCTT $\mathrm { N _ { 1 0 } T / A A G G A } { - 3 } ^ { , }$ in ZmNRT2.1 and ZmNRT2.2 (Meng et al. 2020), and $\mathrm { 5 ^ { \circ } - G A C t C T T N _ { 1 0 } A A G - 3 ^ { \circ } }$ in AtNIA1 and nitrite reductase gene (AtNiR1) (Konishi and Yanagisawa 2014). However, motif analysis revealed that these putative NREs are not commonly conserved across plant species.

Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is a crucial tropical root crop that provides sustenance for over 800 million individuals worldwide, predominantly in South America and Africa. Starch from the root tubers are utilized in diverse applications, including food production to pharmaceuticals, textiles, plywood, paper, and adhesives, as well as a source of ethanol for biofuel production (Mohidin et al. 2023). In tropical regions, cassava thrives in marginal areas with erratic rain, acidic soils, poor native fertility, and challenging terrains, where other crops typically fail (Reinhardt Howeler and Thomas 2013). As previously reported, most MeNRT2 genes in cassava were induced by nitrate defciency, with MeNRT2.2 exhibiting the highest expression level. Moreover, MeNRT2.2-overexpressing Arabidopsis exhibited enhanced adaptation to low nitrate $( 0 . 3 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 } )$ ) (You et al. 2022). However, the potential regulators on MeNRT2.2 and the putative NREs remain unexplored in cassava.

This study reveals MeZFP29 and MebZIPW influence MeNRT2.2 expressions by binding to adjacent NREs (TGCATT and CAGATG) in its promoter. Two regulators interact each other via conserved ANK repeat domains in vivo and in vitro. Interestingly, MeZFP29 and MeZFP29&MebZIPW exhibit a nitrate-dependent distribution, i.e., nitrate defciency results in extensive distribution in cytoplasm and nucleus, whereas sufcient nitrate restricts them to nucleus, although MebZIPW distributes in both compartments irrespective of nitrate conditions. Overexpression of MeZFP29 in seedlings notably enhanced plant growth under low nitrate, while MebZIPW did not, demonstrating their diferent roles in nitrogen utilization in plant.

Of the four NRT2 family genes extracted from the rice genome database, three genes were nitrate inducible and one gene was expressed before the nitrate induction. In roots, nitrate induced the expression of both OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 and the apparent nitrate uptake within $0 . 5 \mathrm { h }$ after N-starvation (Fig. 3). The amounts of nitrate uptake increased with prolongation of nitrate treatment (Fig. 5). This short induction period of nitrate uptake in rice is coincident with previous reports (Sasakawa and Yamamoto 1978, Hasegawa et al. 1989, Kronzucker et al. 2000). Nitrate induction occurred more rapidly in rice than in barley, which is known as a highly efficient nitrate user (reviewed in Kirk and Kronzucker 2005). On the other hand, the time-lag of apparent nitrate uptake induction in the seedlings pretreated with ammonium (Fig. 5) could be caused by transient negative feedback regulation.

An interesting and important feature found is that OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 have the same ORF with different sequences of $5 ^ { \prime }$ -UTR and $3 ^ { \prime }$ -UTR and their expression in response to nitrogen status are different in planta. The expression patterns of OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 after transfer of the seedlings to nitrate solution from N-free solution were similar. Therefore, OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 are both nitrate-inducible genes as mentioned by Okamoto et al. (2003). However, the expression patterns in the seedlings pretreated with ammonium were different, suggesting a difference in the response to the negative feedback regulation by ammonium pretreatment between OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2. As OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 encode the same amino acid sequence, it is difficult to assess the contribution of their gene products for nitrate uptake. In several higher plants, nitrate uptake has been shown to be positively correlated with the amounts of NRT2 transcripts in nitrate induction (Krapp et al. 1998, Amarasinghe et al. 1998, Zhuo et al. 1999, Vidmar et al. 2000a, Okamoto et al. 2003). As the OsNRT2.1 was expressed in parallel with the increase of apparent nitrate uptake index, it is concluded that OsNRT2.1 is a key gene for the induction of nitrate uptake in rice. However, the result of the gene expression analysis implied that the products of OsNRT2.2 also play an important role in nitrate uptake in the presence of nitrate and ammonium.

Nitrate has been proposed to be a signal molecule for transcription of genes related to nitrate assimilation (Crawford 1995, Wang et al. 2004). The difference in the expression of OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 might be attributed to the $5 ^ { \prime }$ -UTR up-stream region. Although, at present, the nitrate signal transduction pathway and its transcription factor in higher plants are still unclear, the high nitrogen status produced by ammonium pretreatment probably influences the transcription pathway of OsNRT2.1 even where nitrate could be perceived as a signal by the seedlings.

The functional nitrate transport mediated by NRT2 has been shown to require the product of NAR2 in C. reinhardtii and barley using the Xenopus oocyte expression system (Quesada et al. 1994, Zhou et al. 2000, Tong et al. 2005). The expression of OsNAR2.1 was induced by nitrate treatment and repressed by ammonium pretreatment as demonstrated in OsNRT2.1. In addition, the expression of OsNAR2.1 was clearly associated with an increase in the apparent nitrate uptake following pretreatment with or without ammonium (Fig. 5). However, the expression of OsNAR2.1 and OsNRT2.2 did not show a synchronous pattern when the seedlings were pretreated with ammonium (Fig. 3). These results suggest that $O s N A R 2 . I$ is also one of the key genes in nitrate uptake in rice.

The difference in gene expression between OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 was also found in shoots. The transcripts of OsNRT2.1 were barely detectable (Fig. 4), suggesting that OsNRT2.1 is a root-specific gene. On the other hand, the expression of OsNRT2.2 was induced by nitrate treatment, indicating that nitrate induction occurred in shoots (Fig. 4). Unlike the expression in roots, the repression of the OsNRT2.2 expression by ammonium pretreatment was found in shoots. OsNAR2.1 was barely detectable and expressed synchronously with OsNRT2.1 in shoots, suggesting that OsNAR2.1 is also a root-specific gene.

Differentiation of the NRT2 family was demonstrated in rice as shown in the AtNRT2 family (Fig. 2) (Orsel et al. 2002b). Phylogenic analysis demonstrated that OsNRT.2.1 and OsNRT2.2 were categorized in a monocotyledonous group. On the other hand, OsNRT2.3 and OsNRT2.4 were categorized in other NRT2 clusters including AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.7 (Orsel et al. 2002b), which are nitrate-repressible and constitutively expressed genes, respectively (Okamoto et al. 2003). OsNRT2.3, expressed constitutively, affected neither the nitrate uptake nor expression of OsNRT2.4 in roots and shoots. Therefore, OsNRT2.3 and OsNRT2.4 are considered to be minor high-affinity nitrate transporters in rice.

In conclusion, it is important to consider OsNAR2.1, OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.2 when breeding for efficient use of nitrogen in rice. Further investigations on OsNRT2.2 are necessary to understand the regulation of nitrate uptake mechanisms in rice.

Nitrogen is an essential element for nucleotide, amino acid, chlorophyll, and alkaloid metabolites [1]. It plays an important role in the construction of plant cells, and tissues, and in yield formation and is also the primary factor limiting plant growth and yield [2]. Potato is an important noncereal food crop and a highly heterozygous autotetraploid species [3, 4]. In China, the planting area is 4.67 million hectares per year, with an annual output of approximately 90 million tons. In actual production, the nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is less than $4 0 \%$ [5]. Cultivating varieties with high nitrogen use efficiency is an important way to improve nitrogen use efficiency, including nitrogen absorption, assimilation, and reallocation processes [2]. Nitrate is the main form of nitrogen absorbed by potato, which is taken up and transported by nitrate transporters in the roots. The NRT family (Nitrate Transporter and Peptide transporter family, NRT/NPF) plays an important role in the absorption, transport and distribution of nitrate nitrogen in plant cells and tissues [6]. It is one of the largest transporter families in the plant kingdom [7] and plays a crucial role in nitrogen use efficiency and crop production.

Various studies have focused on characterizing and cloning different members of this gene family in various plant species. In Arabidopsis, the NRT1.8 gene functions in nitrate removal from xylem sap and mediates cadmium tolerance [8]. Additionally, the NRT2.4 gene in Arabidopsis plays a dual role in the roots and shoots of nitrogen-starved plants [9]. The NRT2 gene family has been characterized in Arabidopsis, with studies showing interactions between different components of the nitrate uptake system. A total of fifty-three NPF genes, seven NRT2 genes, and two NAR2 genes were identified in Arabidopsis Thaliana [6, 10]. AtNRT1.1 is the first nitrate transporter identified and cloned in plants. It has the functions in nitrate absorption and transport, and auxin transport and regulates nitrate-mediated root development. AtNRT1.1 can respond to changes in the environmental nitrate concentration by changing its level of phosphorylation to regulate nitrate transport activity [11], and it is a receptor that senses nitrate signals [12]. Most NPFs have low nitrate affinity, whereas AtNRT1.1 and OsNRT1.1B have dual affinities [13]. In rice, 93 nitrate transporters were identified, including 70 NPFs. The OsNRT1.1A gene, a member of the nitrate transporter 1/peptide transporter family, has been identified as a key regulator of nitrogen utilization and flowering, leading to high yield and early maturation [14]. NRT1.1B participates in regulating the establishment of root microbial communities and promotes the mineralization of organic nitrogen, thereby mediating the interaction between plants and microorganisms. The rhizosphere of indica rice is richer in microbial communities involved in nitrogen metabolism than that of japonica rice is, resulting in higher nitrogen use efficiency in indica rice varieties than in japonica rice [15, 16]. The natural variation of the NRT1.1B protein is that the 327th amino acid of indica rice is methionine (Met), whereas that of japonica rice is threonine (Thr). The NPF family facilitates the transport of a multiple substrates, encompassing phytohormones such as abscisic acid (ABA) and gibberellins (GAs), as well as metabolites including jasmonic acid-isoleucine (JA-Ile), dipeptides, and polypeptides. OsNPF3.1 is an important low-affinity nitrate and plant hormone transporter gene, that is crucial for rice tillering and nitrogen use efficiency. This gene is strongly induced by nitrate, ABA and gibberellin 3 (GA3) in the roots, stems and leaves of rice and has a significant effect on rice tillering and nitrogen use efficiency. The expression of the OsNPF3.1 gene is positively correlated with the number of tillers. Its overexpression significantly promotes the accumulation of ABA in the roots and GA at the base of the plant, thereby inhibiting the growth of lateral buds and rice tillering, especially under high nitrate concentrations [17, 18]. Experiments have shown that OsNPF3.1 is a pH-dependent low-affinity nitrate transporter and is also a transporter of ABA and GA3. Most NRT2s are high-affinity nitrate transporters [6], and the high-affinity transport system is activated at low nitrate concentrations. NAR2 interacts with AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.5, OsNRT2.1 and $O s N R T 2 . 3 a$ on the cell membrane to improve nitrate transport efficiency [6, 19]. The overexpression of OsNAR2.1 can significantly improve nitrogen absorption and drought resistance in rice, whereas OsNAR2.1 knockout plants have the opposite effect [20]. Studies in tomato have shown that the expression of a cluster of genes encoding NPF members is downregulated in a mutant with a low-SGA phenotype, indicating the importance of these genes in plant growth and development [21]. Furthermore, 77 NPFs, 7 NRT2s, and 1 NAR2 were found in Solanum lycopersicum [22].

Overall, a comprehensive understanding the nitrate and peptide transporter (NRT/NPF) gene family is crucial for elucidating nitrogen metabolism and stress responses in various crops species, including potato. While Zhang et al. [23] identified 39 StNRT genes using PGSC DM v4.03 genome, our study significantly expands this number to 81 leveraging the SolTub_3.0 genome. The objectives of this research were (i) to conduct a more comprehensive identification of NRT genes in the potato genome; (ii) to systematically analyze gene structure, chromosomal distribution, promoter sequences, conserved protein domains and motifs; (iii) to perform a phylogenetic analysis of StNRT genes within potato species; (iv) to compare the homology and phylogenetic relationships of potato StNRT proteins with NRT proteins from other species; (v) to investigate the tissue-specific expression patterns of StNRT genes in potato; and (vi) to examine the expression dynamics of StNRT genes in response to nitrogen stress. To date, no comprehensive whole-genome analysis of the NRT gene family in potato has been reported. In this study, we used whole-genome analysis to identify members of the StNRT gene family. Through bioinformatics and expression analysis, our findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for further research on potato nitrate transporter genes and pave the way for functional studies of these genes. Further investigations into the regulatory mechanisms and functional roles of these genes will offer valuable insights into improving crop yield and nutrient utilization efficiency.

Nitrogen (N) is a primary constituent of proteins and nucleotides that are essential for life. Nitrogen accounts for approximately $2 \mathrm { - } 5 \%$ of the total dry biomass of plants (Xu et  al., 2012). Nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right)$ is a major source of nitrogen in most plants grown in agricultural and natural systems (Wang et  al., 2018). As plants have adapted to variable soil nitrate concentrations, sophisticated nitrate transporter systems have evolved. During the past two decades, four families of nitrate transport proteins, namely, nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel (CLC), and slow anion channel associated homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been identified in higher plants (Krapp et  al., 2014). Among these, NRT1.1, which has multiple functions, is one of the most well-studied. Initially, NRT1.1 was characterised as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter involved in nitrate uptake by roots, as well as root-to-shoot nitrate translocation in Arabidopsis (Liu et  al., 1999; Léran et  al., 2013). Independent of its transport function,

NRT1.1 was later shown to serve as a main nitrate sensor that regulates many aspects of physiological and developmental responses to nitrate, including regulating the expression levels of nitrate-related genes, modulating root system architecture, and relieving seed dormancy (Bouguyon et al., 2015). Moreover, NRT1.1 displays auxin transport activity, which relies largely on external nitrate availability in Arabidopsis (Maghiaoui et  al., 2020a). In recent years, specific topics associated with the transport and sensing functions of NRT1.1 have been discussed in several excellent reviews (Sun and Zheng, 2015; Maghiaoui et  al., 2020b; Vidal et  al., 2020; Wang et  al., 2020b). A series of studies on NRT1.1 have also provided new insights into its function in multiple abiotic stresses in plants. In this review, we briefly summarise the important milestones in the discovery process, dual-affinity features, and structural basis of the dual transport/sensing function of NRT1.1  in Arabidopsis. More importantly, we highlight the most recently characterised functions of NRT1.1  in plant abiotic stress resistance and the correlation between NRT1.1-mediated nitrate transport/signalling and different abiotic stresses, mainly in Arabidopsis (Table  1).

## Discovery of NRT1.1

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ , as the essential element of amino acid, nucleic acid, chlorophyll, and among other biologically important molecules, is vital to plant growth and development. In aerated soils, plants take up nitrogen mainly in the form of nitrate due to intensive nitrification processes. In plants, nitrate can be absorbed and translocated through transmembrane proteins, which mainly consist of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF) and NRT2 (see excellent reviews by $\mathrm { X u }$ et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2018b). There are 53, 93, and 91 NPF genes in Arabidopsis, rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Leran et al. 2014). Most NPFs are responsible for low-affinity nitrate transporter activity $\mathrm { ~ ( > ~ 0 . 5 ~ m M } _ { \mathrm { ~ , ~ } }$ (Epstein et al. 1963; Noguero and Lacombe 2016), except for CHL1/NRT1.1/ AtNPF6.3, which was the first NPF to be found and cloned, displays a dual affinity property (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999). There are 7, 4, 7, and 5 NRT2 genes in Arabidopsis, rice, Brachypodium, and Sorghum, respectively (Orsel et al. 2002, Cai et al. 2008; Massel et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018a, b). In general, all of NRT2s are responsible for high-affinity nitrate transport $( < 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ). Additionally, a third family, named as NAR2/NRT3, requires interacting with most NRT2 members to transport nitrate (Zhou et al. 2000; Orsel et al. 2006; Yan et al. 2011; Kotur et al. 2012), except for AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al.

2012). There are 2, 2, and 3 NRT3 members in Arabidopsis, Rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Plett et al. 2010; Massel et al. 2016). Beside nitrate, NPF family transport diverse components as substrates, including dipeptides, glucosinolate, IAA, ABA, GA, and JA (Leran et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2018a). By contrast, NRT2 members have been only reported to transport nitrate so far.

Based on a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis from 31 fully sequenced plant genomes (Lee et al. 2011), NPF family can be classified into 8 unambiguous clades. Members from NPF1 subfamily have been shown to be involved in redistributing nitrate to developing tissues. For example, AtNPF1.1/NRT1.12 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.11 are expressed in companion cells (CC) of the primary vein, and their double mutant is deficient in remobilizing nitrate to younger leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013). Similarly, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7 is expressed in the phloem of the minor vein in mature leaves and is responsible for nitrate remobilization under nitrogen deficiency (Fan et al. 2009). Additionally, many other NPF2 family members (including AtNPF2.3, AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, OsNPF2.2, and OsNPF2.4) are involved in nitrate translocation from root to shoot (Wang and Tsay 2011; Li et al. 2015; Taochy et al. 2015; Xia et al. 2015). AtNPF2.12/NRT1.6 can mediate nitrate influx to premature embryos (Almagro et al. 2008). In addition to nitrate, two NPF2 members (AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5) are able to transport chloride (Li et al. 2016, 2017); five NPF2 members (AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, AtNPF2.10/ GTR1, AtNPF2.11/GTR2, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7, and AtNPF2.14) are able to transport glucosinolate, which is one of the important secondary metabolites for plant defense (Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). AtNPF3.1, originally identified as a nitrate/nitrite transporter, is found to be a GA transporter which is also affected by nitrate availability (Sugiura et al. 2007; Pike et al. 2014; David et al. 2016; Tal et al. 2016). AtNPF4.6/NRT1.2 has been characterized as a constitutive nitrate transporter (Huang et al. 1999), as well as an ABA transporter (Kanno et al. 2012). As the largest subfamily, three NPF5 members (AtNPF5.11, AtNPF5.12, AtNPF5.16) are responsible for nitrate efflux from tonoplast (He et al. 2017), AtNPF5.5 is involved in nitrate accumulation in embryos (Leran et al. 2015). Moreover, AtNPF5.2/PTR3 can transport dipeptide, which is important for plant pathogen defense (Karim et al. 2007). AtNPF6.3 is the most heavily studied member of the family, and it is a dual-affinity nitrate transporter (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999), auxin transporter (Krouk et al. 2010); it affects stomata opening (Guo et al. 2003) and also serves as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). Interestingly, indica rice OsNRT1.1B/OsNPF6.5, one of the closest orthologous genes of AtNPF6.3 with only a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) with japonica rice $O s N R T I . I B /$ OsNPF6.5, is responsible for better nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in indica rice (Hu et al. 2015). Recently, OsNRT1.1B is reported to facilitate Selenomethinone (Se) translocation in both roots and leaves, and the overexpression lines exhibit a higher Se accumulation in grains (Zhang et al. 2018b). AtNPF6.2/NRT1.4 is specifically expressed in leaf petiole, which is critical for nitrate storage in petiole (Chiu et al. 2004). AtNPF7.2/NRT1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 expressed in close proximity of xylem and their functions are antagonistic upon stress challenges (Li et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2014). The NPF8 subfamily (NPF8.1/PTR1, NPF8.2/PTR5, and NPF8.3/PTR2) in Arabidopsis transports dipeptide and has no detectable nitrate transport activity (Komarova et al. 2009), whereas OsNRT1/ NPF8.9 is a putative nitrate transporter in rice (Lin et al. 2000).

Compared to the large and complex NPF family, NRT2 and NRT3 families in plants are relatively small. There is a clear divergence between monocots and dicots of NRT2 family genes, suggesting NRT2 in monocots may function differently from heavily-studied AtNRT2 (Plett et al. 2010; Wang et al. 2018a, b). It has been well-documented that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are nitrate-inducible transporters, which are major components for high-affinity root nitrate uptake (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 are also involved in high-affinity root nitrate uptake but mainly upon nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Besides, AtNRT2.1 can serve as a signal transducer to regulate lateral root growth (Little et al. 2005). NRT2.7 is the only NRT2 member located on the tonoplast membrane and is responsible for nitrate transport in seeds (Chopin et al. 2007). In rice, OsNRT2.3b responds to pH changes and its overexpression leads to grain yield increase (Fan et al. 2016). Additionally, overexpressing OsNRT2.1 driven by the NAR2.1/NRT3.1 promoter is also able to enhance grain yield in rice (Chen et al. 2016). The importance of NRT3/NAR2 is underlined by their coexpression and interaction with NRT2 genes. All AtNRT2 members except for AtNRT2.7 can interact with NRT3.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Nevertheless, AtNRT3.1 is not indispensable for nitrate uptake mediated by AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al. 2012).

Sugarcane is one of the most productive crops in the world (FAOSTAT, 2016; http://www.fao.org/statistics/en/) and it accounts for $80 \%$ of world sugar supply and $40 \%$ of ethanol production (Zhang et al. 2013). N deficiencies can cause a decreased chlorophyll synthesis as well as a reduced biomass. Together with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, N makes up $90 \%$ of sugarcane dry matter (Brandes 1952). Sugarcane mainly absorbs N through $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilizers or biological nitrogen fixation owing to microbial nitrogen fixers (Boddey et al. 2003). Unfortunately, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is low for agronomic crops, especially for sugarcane, more than $50 \%$ of nitrogen is lost through surface run-off, leaching, denitrifications or volatilizations (Garnett et al. 2009). Only $20 \%$ (or less) of input N can be found in dry biomass of sugarcane at harvest (Franco et al. 2011). Therefore, understanding nitrogen uptake, translocation and utilization is key to improve NUE by conventional breeding and genetic engineering strategy. However, the genetic information for nitrate transporters is still missing in sugarcane, largely due to the lack of a complete genome information. Recently, an allele-defined genome of sugarcane Saccharum spontaneum L. became available (Zhang et al. 2018a), offering an excellent opportunity to identify nitrate transporter families at a genome-wide scale. In this study, we carried out a BLAST search using Arabidopsis and Sorghum NPF/NRTs against newly available sugarcane genome. Phylogenetic analysis, gene structure as well as protein motif analysis were conducted to understand molecular and evolutionary relationships between subfamilies and species. Moreover, RNA-Seq data were analyzed to investigate tissue-specific expression pattern across all NPF/ NRT genes in S. spontaneum. Our results presented a comprehensive characterization of sugarcane NPF/NRT genes, which laid the foundation for future investigations of these nitrogen transporters in sugarcane.

In the present study, we isolated an NRT2 family gene, BraNRT2.1, from non-heading Chinese cabbage, and we sought to characterize the expression pattern and the tissuespecific expression of the BraNRT2.1 gene as well as the subcellular localization of the protein encoded by

BraNRT2.1. We then performed functional experiments to analyze potential roles for BraNRT2.1 in mediating nitrate uptake.

Most steps in the nitrate assimilation pathway are nitrate-inducible (Cai et al. 2008). Changes in gene expression can be elicited by nitrate rapidly (within $5 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m i n } )$ ) for nearly $10 \%$ of the transcriptome (Krouk et al. 2010). In addition, it is well-known that according to the nitrogen demands of plant, inducible high-affinity nitrate transport system (iHATS) is subject to negative feedback from nitrate assimilation products. In the present study, following exposure of the plants to $0 . 2 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ , the transcription of BraNRT2.1 peaked rapidly and then decreased and stabilized. The increase in the expression of BraNRT2.1 demonstrates that BraNRT2.1 can be induced by nitrate, and the subsequent decrease in expression suggests that BraNRT2.1 is feedback-repressible by downstream metabolites. Similarly, after exposure to $2 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate, the maximum rate of high-affinity nitrate uptake was observed at $4 5 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ during the period of nitrate induction, with the rates then declining substantially. The downregulation of NRT2.1 by an elevated supply of nitrogen might result from the concerted action of two different signaling pathways: one pathway is the feedback repression caused by the accumulation of nitrate metabolites (Gansel et al. 2001; Gojon et al. 2009), and the other pathway is the inhibition of NRT2.1 by NRT1.1, which occurs through the local inhibition of transcript accumulation under high nitrate conditions (Krouk et al. 2006). A recent study showed that a 150-base pair region in the promoter of NRT2.1 mediates the induction and repression of the gene (Castaings et al. 2011), providing evidence that this region is a key factor of BraNRT2.1 gene expression.

The expression of NRT2.1 in Arabidopsis has been shown to be affected by fluctuations in the availability of sucrose and by variations in light exposure (Bartsch et al.

1988; Lejay et al. 1999; Vidal and Gutierrez 2008), and the diurnal regulation of nitrate uptake has been demonstrated in many plant species (Lejay et al. 1999; Delhon et al. 1995; Ono et al. 2000). In the present study, BraNRT2.1 was observed to be regulated by nitrate induction, but whether BraNRT2.1 can be regulated by other factors such as light exposure and sucrose availability remains to be examined.

Previous studies have demonstrated in barley (Palechar et al. 2004; Tong et al. 2005) and Arabidopsis (Okamoto et al. 2006) that some NRT2 proteins require a partner protein, NAR2, to mediate nitrate transport. The function of NAR2.1, a member of the NAR2 gene family, is not yet understood clearly, but in nar2.1 mutants, the attainment of nitrate through HATS is defective (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006), and the AtNRT2.1 protein does not localize to the plasma membrane (Wirth et al. 2007). It was then proposed that the active nitrate transporter is actually a complex of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 localized together in the plasma membrane (Yong et al. 2010). Thus far, evidence suggests that NAR2.1 is required for the expression and/or the correct trafficking of NRT2.1. Although preliminary evidence suggests that NAR2.1 is a cofactor involved in the targeting of the NRT2.1 proteins to the plasma membrane in some species, whether the plasma membrane localization of BraNRT2.1 requires a NAR2 family protein will need to be examined.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that BraNRT2.1 is inducible by nitrate and is localized at the plasma membrane. In addition, we found that BraNRT2.1 is expressed primarily in the root and that it promotes nitrate uptake. Together, our results demonstrate that BraNRT2.1 is a high-affinity nitrate transporter which participates in nitrate uptake. These findings contribute to our knowledge of the functions and characteristics of the BraNRT2.1 gene and provide a foundation for future studies and plant breeding to improve the efficiency of nitrogen use and to reduce the accumulation of nitrates in vegetables.

Nitrogen (N) is an essential macronutrient for sustaining plant growth and development (Hawkesford et al. 2023). N is commonly taken up from the soil in one of two inorganic forms: ammonium and nitrate (Glass et al. 2002; S. Guo et al. 2007). Of the two forms, nitrate is the main nitrogen source for most plants, which is absorbed by plant roots through nitrate transporters (NRTs) by sensing external nitrogen signals and then translocated in plants (Glass 2009; Wang et al. 2012a). Plant roots have developed highafnity transport system (HATS) and low-afnity transport system (LATS) to cope with low $\mathrm { ( < 1 ~ m M ) }$ or high $\mathrm { ( > 1 ~ m M ) }$ concentrations of nitrate in soil, respectively (Dechorgnat et al. 2011; Wang et al. 2012a). The transporters protein involved in those system were segregated.

With evolution and gene duplication, most plants have a large gene family wihch encode NRTs. Usually, NRT family is composed of NRT1/PTR (nitrate/peptide transporters, also known as nitrate transporter1/ peptide transporter family, NPF), NRT2, and NRT3 members, which play multifunctional roles in nitrate uptake and transportation from soil to plant (Dechorgnat et al. 2011; O’Brien et al. 2016). In Arabidopsis genome, 62 NRT genes were identifed, of which 53 members belong to NRT1/PTR subfamily, 7 and 2 members belong to NRT2 and NRT3 family, respectively (Okamoto et al. 2003). NRT1 proteins were thought to normally function as components of the LATS, which was activated in high nitrate concentrations (Tsay et  al. 2007). The first identified NRT1 gene in Arabidopsis was AtNRT1.1 (CHL1/AtNPF6.3), which was a dual-afnity nitrate transporter in both low- and highnitrate concentrations, and was modulated when response to fuctuations of nitrate level (Liu et al. 1999). NPF7.2/NRT1.8 and NPF7.3/NRT1.5 were shown to be involved in nitrate uptake by the roots and root-to-shoot nitrate transport in Arabidopsis (Cui et al. 2019), while another root transporter NPF2.3 was proved contributing to nitrate translocation to shoots under salt stress (Taochy et al. 2015). In addition, some NRT1 members, such as AtNPF6.2/AtNRT1.4, AtNPF2.13/AtNRT1.7, and AtNPF1.2/AtNRT1.11, were demonstrated to function in leaf nitrate homeostasis. For example, AtNRT1.7 was reported to participate in nitrate transport from old leaves to new leaves (Fan et al. 2009). NRT2 and NRT3 members were commonly joining with each other in HATS to implicate in nitrate absorption and remobilization under N starvation stress in many plant species. (Okamoto et al. 2006).

In rice, members of NRT1 gene family also had an important role of nitrogen use in the feld. Two NRT1 genes were identifed that were homologous to AtNRT1.1 in rice with diferent functions (Plett et al. 2010). OsNRT1.1A/OsNPF6.3 is plastid localized and induced by ammonium (Wang et al. 2018a).  Protein encoded by OsNRT1.1B gene was localized to cell membrane, and sensed an external nitrate signal, and contributed for grain yield and nitrogen use efciency (NUE) in rice (Hu et al. 2015). There were two more OsNRT1 subfamily genes involved in nitrate transport and encoded low-afnity nitrate transporter. OsNPF2.2/OsPTR2 that function in nitrate transport from root to stem and vascular development (Li et al. 2015), whiling OsNPF4.5 participated in nitrogen acquisition by a conserved mycorrhizal pathway (Wang et al. 2020). With the rapid accumulation of plant genome data, NRT genes were characterized in many more plants, such as poplar (Bai et al. 2013), cucumber (Migocka et al. 2013), apple (Wang et al. 2018b), sugarcane (Wang et al. 2019) and spinach (Wang et al. 2021).

Bamboo belongs to  the subfamily Bambusoideae of Poaceae family, and is widely distributed in tropical and subtropical zones in Asia, Africa and America (Soreng et  al. 2015; Yen 2016). Woody bamboos have tree-like lignifed culms, and exhibit the property of rapid growth and high output, therefore they are considered as one of the most important lignocellulose feedstocks in biofuel industry (Engler et al. 2012; Nayak & Mishra 2016). The fast growth of bamboo shoot and the potential ecosystem benefits including carbon sequestration, soil and water conservation (Nath et al. 2015) are highly concerned. Bamboo needs high amount of nitrogen from the outside to support its rapid growth, therefore the availability of nitrogen in the soil is an important factor for bamboo morphogenesis and biomass (McIntyre 1987; Long et al. 2020).

In recent years, several bamboo speices were genome sequenced and all of them exhibit obvious variation in ploidy levels, comprising diploid herbaceous (Olyra latifolia and Raddia guianensis, HH), tetraploid woody lineages ( $G$ . angustifolia BBCC, Phyllostachys edulis CCDD), and hexaploid woody lineages (Bonia amplexicaulis, Dendrocalamus latiforus, AABBCC) (Guo et al. 2019; Peng et al. 2013; Zheng et al. 2022). Dendrocalamus farinosus is a sympodial woody bamboo and considered as a preferable wood substitute for chemical pulping because of its high cellulose content and good fber quality (Du et al. 2021). In our previous research, we generated a chromosome-scale genome of $D$ . farinosus using the PacBio Sequel platform and Hi-C chromosome conformation capture, and found that the $D$ . farinosus genome was hexaploid AABBCC $2 \mathrm { n } { } = 6 \mathrm { x } { } = 7 0$ ), corresponded well with the closely related species $D$ . latiforus (Zheng et al. 2022). As perennial sympodial bamboo, D. farinosus mostly grow on mountains whose nitrogen nutrition are hard to get replenished without applying extra nitrogen fertilizer. Thus, in the present study, a genomewide identifcation and evolution analysis of NRT genes in $D$ . farinosus was performed. Moreover, the expression profles of DfNRTs in response to diferent nitrate supplies were detected. Our results present a comprehensive characterization of DfNRT genes, and ofer the foundation for the complex genetic dissection of nitrate transport system in $D$ . farinosus.

Immunological detection of AtHKT1 in the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells

The membrane targeting of AtHKT1 or monocot HKT homologs has not yet been analyzed. To directly determine the location of AtHKT1 protein expression at the subcellular and plant cell-type levels, anti-AtHKT1 antibodies were generated. The hydrophilic 15-amino-acid sequence, located in the first pore-forming region, $\mathsf { P _ { A } }$ (Kato et al., 2001; Ma¨ ser et al., 2002a), was chosen as an epitope. The specificities of the anti-AtHKT1 antibodies were tested using AtHKT1 epitope–GST (glutathione-S-transferase) fusion constructs expressed in Escherichia coli or insect cells confirming antibody specificity (Supplementary Figure S1). Since the AtHKT1 antibodies probed against Arabidopsis plant extracts did not show any interaction, we predicted that AtHKT1 expression was restricted to a few cell types and/or the amount of natively expressed AtHKT1 protein was relatively small (data not shown). Therefore, we analyzed the tissue and subcellular localization of the AtHKT1 protein by immunoelectron microscopic studies. A cross-section of the vascular tubes of leaves of Arabidopsis plants grown in $1 / 2$ MS medium showed immunological detection in the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells when the antiserum was used at a 1:20000 dilution (Figure 1). Gold particles were located at the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells, but not significantly found in other cellular membranes (Figure 1c). There were no significant immunological detection signals in other cells of the leaf. The plasma membrane localization of AtHKT1 was also supported by expression of green fluorescent protein (GFP)–AtHKT1 fusions in tobacco BY2 cells. These cells showed a GFP signal localized in the region of the plasma membrane compared with control tobacco cells expressing only the GFP protein, which showed expression throughout the cell and nucleus (Supplementary Figure S2).
