PttSLAH3 of poplar is not activated by protein kinase phosphorylation to absorb nitrate and chloride ions [19]. These studies indicate that SLAC/SLAHs has the nitrate selectivity and permeability and can regulate stomatal closure by regulating anion efflux from guard cells in response to ABA signals.

At present, more and more studies have focused on the slow anion channel proteins, especially those involved in the absorption and transport of nitrate. SLAC/SLAH family members have been identified and studied in several species such as Arabidopsis [9], rice [15], maize [17], barley [16], tobacco [20], poplar [19], and pear [21]. However, Brassica napus (B. napus), an important oil crop, has not been reported on SLAC/SLAHs. B. napus has a higher nitrogen requirement than other crops [22]. It was reported earlier that SLAC/SLAHs were highly expressed in roots and had the nitrate-permeable channel activity [9], we thus hypothesized that SLAC/SLAH family members in B. napus might be involved in nitrate uptake and transport. Therefore, the main objective of this study is to identify the SLAC/SLAH gene family of B. napus and analyze the structure, physicochemical properties, evolutionary relationships and expression profiles of corresponding genes through bioinformatics analysis. It is hoped to provide reference for further research on the biological functions of key candidate genes in nitrogen uptake and utilization of rapeseed.

Anion channels have crucial roles in plant functions (Zifarelli and Pusch 2010) by selectively conducting anions across the cell membrane, leading to intracellular signal transduction processes and other physiological regulators (Roelfsema et al. 2012). In the past few decades, a large body of studies have revealed the functions and basic properties of various ion channels (Kanwar et al. 2020; Medeiros et al. 2018; Vahisalu et al. 2008; Ward et al. 2009; Zifarelli and Pusch 2010). Plant growth, development, reproduction, signaling, and stress response require the frequent transmembrane fow of diferent anions (Saito and Uozumi 2019), which is accurately tuned by anion channels (Pantoja 2021). Each anion channel mediates one or more types of anions for anion efux and infux and their dynamic distribution in the plant cell (Barbier-Brygoo et al. 2011). Even though many anion channels were confrmed using classical and patch-clamp electrophysiology (Barbier-Brygoo et al. 2011), however, some anion channels and transporters are difcult to characterize at the level of molecular (Hedrich and Geiger 2017).

$\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , $\mathrm { S O } 4 ^ { 2 - }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ are the main inorganic anions, while malate $( \mathrm { m a l } ^ { 2 - } )$ is the major organic anions in plant cells (Saito and Uozumi 2019). These anions balance the cations in various proportions depending on the species, growth conditions and cell type, forming a major part of cellular osmosis (Muller et al. 2017). Moreover, each of these anions has unique role in plants. For instance, phosphorus and sulfur are used to synthesize biomolecules (Wang et al. 2021) and malate is main intermediate in carbohydrate metabolism and for pH and osmotic regulation of plant cells (Barbier-Brygoo et al. 2011; Chen et al. 2012; Hills et al. 2012). Therefore, the coordination of anion channels can regulate the concentration of diferent anions in cells for specifc and common functions in the plant kingdom (Feng et al. 2020).

There are several families of anion channels such as slow anion channel 1 (SLAC1)/SLAC1 homolog (SLAH), aluminum-activated malate transporter (ALMT), chloride channel (CLC), voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC), and mechanosensitive-like anion channel (MSL) that mediate the fow of anion across membranes and control the transport anions such as ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and malate across the membranes (Kanwar et al. 2020). For instance, the ALMT transporters encode rapid activation channels (R-type) while SLAC/SLAH anion channels are identifed via slow voltage dependent activation (S-type). Both R-type and S-type channels are accumulated in guard cells by abscisic acid (ABA), $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , reactive oxygen species (ROS), NO, and phosphorylation (Chen et al. 2010b, 2016; Roelfsema et al. 2012; Zhao et al. 2019). Also, the CLC family is mainly found in the intracellular system (Nedelyaeva et al. 2020) and VDACs are conserved proteins in the mitochondria (Sanyal et al. 2020) of plant cells.

However, the evolution of anion channels has not been entirely explored in terms of environmental stresses (Chen and Soltis 2020) such as those caused by climate change (e.g. heat, elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , drought, fooding). Therefore, new research focuses and progresses to modify plant stress tolerance to adapt in a changing environment (Saito and Uozumi 2019) are essential to ensure the sustainable plant production in the future. In this paper, we extensively review the molecular functions and evolutionary features of anion channels, which will help to understand the mechanisms of cellular adaptation against the changing environmental constraints. For the molecular functions and evolution of anion channels, the readers are referred to the excellent reviews elsewhere (Basu and Haswell 2017; Hedrich and Geiger 2017; Kanwar et al. 2020; Medeiros et al. 2018; Pantoja 2021).


## Function and evolution of major anion transport systems in green plants



## Slow anion channels (SLAC1/SLAHs)


Plasma membrane slow anion channel SLAC1 was discovered through electrophysiology in the 1990s (Schroeder and Keller 1992; Schroeder et al. 1993) and its molecular identify, function, and structure were published almost 20  years later (Chen et  al. 2010a; Geiger et  al. 2010; Negi et al. 2008). SLAC1 responds to diverse environmental factors through a variety of signal transduction pathways (Figs. 1, S4) (Hedrich and Geiger 2017; Pantoja 2021; Roelfsema et al. 2012). The modulation of the SLAC1 activity is mainly via the interaction with protein kinases including SNF1-related kinases (SnRKs), Calcium-dependent kinases (CPKs), Calcineurin B-like (CBL)-CBL-interacting protein kinase (CIPK), and the inactivation of protein phosphatases 2C (PP2C) (Fig. 1). (Barbier-Brygoo et al. 2011; Li et al. 2020a; Nejat and Mantri 2017; Pantoja 2021; Roelfsema et al. 2012; Saito and Uozumi 2019). SLAC1 regulates stomatal closure via modulating the efux of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ (Fig. 1, Table S1) (Pantoja 2021), which is a key component in the signaling pathway of ABA, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , NO, plant elicitor peptides, and microbe-associated molecular patterns (Fig. S1) (Roelfsema et al. 2012).

Given the importance of SLAC1/SLAHs, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis of this anion channel family in a number of evolutionarily key green plants and algal species (Figs. 2, S1, S2). In 41 green plant lineages, the potential orthologous proteins for the signaling are identifed through comparative genetic analysis of the genomic datasets (Figs. 2, S2) (Cai et al. 2021; Chen et al. 2021b; Deng et al. 2020; Hu et al. 2020; Zhao et al. 2019). Interestingly, putative orthologs of SLAC1 have been characterized in Chlorophyta Volvox carteri and Rhodophyta Cyanidioschyzon merolae (Fig. 2), which likely to have evolved from Chromista (e.g. Petalonia fascia, Colpomenia sinuosa, and Dictyopteris undulata) (Fig. S1). A wide variety of tellurite-resistance/dicarboxylate transporters have evolved in the aquatic conditions, but only one protein classes survived during plant terrestrialization, leading to the origin of SLAC channels (Hedrich and Geiger 2017). Evolutionary analysis indicated that SLAC1 exists in major green plants (Zhao et al. 2019) and is signifcantly conserved in the Embryophyte (Lind et al. 2015). For the regulatory components of SLAC1, genetic similarity analysis reveals that MPKs display the highest similarity across the green plants, followed by CPKs, ABAs, $\beta$ -carbonic anhydrases (CAs), and SLACs (Fig. 2). The lower similarity of ortholog was found among guard cell hydrogen peroxide-resistant 1 (GHR1), blue light signaling 1 (BLUS1), and resistant to high $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } 1$ (RHC1), which showed the evolutionary origin from the lycophytes and ferns (Fig. 2). Molecular and genetic evidence revealed that the core SLAC signaling pathway consisting of open stomata 1 (OST1), abscisic acid-insensitive (ABIs), CPKs, and CAs might be originated from algae (Chen et al. 2017; Hedrich and Geiger 2017). Thus, the SLAC signaling network evolved early during plant evolution and played a signifcant role in stress response.

We investigated the origins of genes participated in SLAC pathway in Arabidopsis. Our results indicate that 12 (except GHR1, RHC1, BLUS1, SIF2, and LYKs) out of the 17 regulatory components of the SLAC pathway have orthologs in ancestral Embryophyte (Fig. S2). BLUS1 was originated from gene duplication during angiosperm evolution (Fig. S2), it has obviously related and quite conserved pre-duplication orthologue tracing back to ancestral Embryophyte (Harris et al. 2020). Therefore, the analysis implied that the BLUS1-PHOT (NPH, non phototropic hypocotyl) -SLAC1 and HT1 (high leaf temperature 1) -GHR1-SLAC1 pathway might be conserved in vascular plants. Extensive phylogenetic analysis of stomatal function genes indicated that pyrabactin resistance-like proteins (PYLs), PP2Cs, and OST1 present in the most green plants (Sussmilch et al. 2019). In addition, the PYLs, OST1, and SLACs proteins show high similarity (over $4 8 \%$ ) among all the land plants (Chen et al. 2017).

Following the transition to land, SLAC1s are found in plant lineages from streptophyte algae to seed plants such as

Streptophytes (Klebsormidium faccidum, Spirogloea muscicola, and M. endlicherianum), liverworts (M. polymorpha), mosses (Sphagnum fallax), lycophytes (Selaginella moellendorfi) and ferns (Salvinia cucullata) (Fig. 2). The molecular mechanism of interaction between OST1 and SLAC1 was conserved in stomatal closure regulation via control the plasma membrane anion efux (Chater and Gray 2015). Surprisingly, OST1 could not activate the SLAC1 channels in the M. polymorpha and K. faccidum (Lind et al. 2015). Nevertheless, the OST1 homologous of the mosses and algae could activate the AtSLAC1 (Hedrich and Geiger 2017). Besides, lycophyte SmOST1s could activate the AtSLAC instead of SmSLACs (McAdam et al. 2016). In Spermatophyta, SLAC1 channel appeared basal in gymnosperms, then there was a significant separation between monocot and dicot SLACs in angiosperm (Hedrich and Geiger 2017). After split in dicots, monocot SLAC1s developed the nitrate-dependent gating feature (Schafer et al. 2018). At the cytosolic termini of SLAC1, it co-opted the ABA-signaling pathway via developing ten amino acids (LFPNDLAIAI) right after the last transmembrane domain (Fig. 3A), which protein kinases, CERK1 chitin elicitor receptor kinase 1, LYKs lysine motif (LysM) receptor kinases, CPKs Calcium-dependent kinases, CBLs Calcineurin B-like protein, ABIs abscisic acid-insensitive, SIZ1 E3 SUMO-protein ligase, STOP1 sensitive to proton rhizotoxicity 1, RAE1 regulation of AtALMT1 expression 1, GABAs gammaaminobutyric acid, MATEs multidrug and toxic compound extrusion proteins, ABCBs ABC transporter B family member, TDT tonoplast dicarboxylate transporter, VCCNs voltage-dependent chloride channel, CCC1 cation-chloride cotransporter 1, SULTRs sulfate transporters, CFTRs cystic fbrosis transmembrane conductance regulator

permit ABA-activated OSTs to mediate SLAC1 activity during the origin of early Embryophyte (Lind et al. 2015). SLAC1 from the monocots (e.g. maize and rice) is more selective for ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ than $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ compared to Arabidopsis (Qi et al. 2018a; Sun et al. 2016). However, the SLAC1 of Phoenix dactylifera is $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ permeability anion channel activated by ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ (Muller et al. 2017). Consequently, the anion selectivity of SLAC1 is not entirely consistent in diferent vascular plants. Therefore, Tracheophytes may employ diferent combinations of channels and transporters to modulate stomatal closure (Harris et al. 2020).

In Arabidopsis, SLAC1 family consists of SLAC1 and its homologous proteins SLAH1, 2, 3, and 4 (Fig. 4, Table S1). Each SLAC1 subunit has ten transmembrane regions in the form of a trimer to form a functional anion channel (Chen et al. 2010a). Also, the regulation of SLAH3 activity by SLAH1 could be achieved by forming heterotrimer with SLAH3 (Maierhofer et al. 2014). SLAH2 is a ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ selective transporters with weak permeability to $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ (Maierhofer et al. 2014). Furthermore, AtSLAH1 regulates $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ transport from the root to the stem by modulating the activity of AtSLAH3 (Cubero-Font et al. 2016). In terms of ion selectivity and permeability, both AtSLAC1 and AtSLAH3 are signifcantly permeable to $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , but signifcantly more permeable to ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ than $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ (Brandt et al. 2012). SLAH3 is located in guard cells, which drives stomatal closure by regulating ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ efux as well (Geiger et al. 2011). Although the malic acid was found obvious accumulation in guard cells, both SLAC1 and SLAH3 have no obvious permeability to malate. Previously study showed that the opening of anion channels was enough to mediate stomatal closure (Huang et al. 2021). Therefore, stomatal closure should result from the coordination of multiple plasma membrane anions, including SLAC1, ALMT12, and CLCc (Fig. 1) (Saito and Uozumi 2019).


## Aluminum‑activated malate transporters (ALMTs)


About 30 years ago, the R-type anion channels (QUACs) on plasma membrane (PM) of Vicia faba stamata were discovered by patch-clamp technique (Hedrich et al. 1990), which are in the same gene family encoding the ALMTs (Meyer et al. 2010; Roelfsema et al. 2012). ALMTs are typical anion channel in terms of structure and function and each ALMT subunit has six or seven transmembrane regions. ALMT is widely distributed in various plant tissues with diverse biological functions such as aluminum (Al) resistance (Pereira and Ryan 2019), stomatal regulation (Fig. 1), symbiotic nitrogen fxation, mineral nutrition, anion homeostasis, fruit favor, and $\gamma$ -aminobutyric acid (GABA) signaling (Medeiros et al. 2018). ALMTs are regulated by multiple factors, including phosphorus and aluminum in the soil, soil acidifcation, phytohormones, and ROS (Fig. 1) (Kobayashi et al. 2013). The modulation of the ALMT activity is mainly via the interaction with protein including SIZ1 (encoding the SUMO E3 LIGASE) (Xu et al. 2021), STOP1 (sensitive to proton rhizotoxicity 1) (Xu et al. 2021), RAE1 (AtALMT1 Expression 1) (Fang et al. 2021), GABA (Ramesh et al. 2017). In addition, TDT (tonoplast dicarboxylate transporter) and ABCB14 (ATP-binding cassette B 14) could transport malate (Medeiros et al. 2018).

Previous investigations demonstrated that ALMT orthologs were identifed in the Chlorophyte algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Dreyer et al. 2012). Comparative genetic analysis revealed that eight tested gene families crucial for ALMT pathway are evolutionarily conserved in green plants and may have evolved from Streptophyte algae—the sister group to the land plants (Fig. 2). We also identifed the orthologs of anion transporters and regulatory protein families (i.e. ALMTs, SIZ1, STOP1, RAE1, GABAs, MATEs, ABCBs, and TDT) from 41 plant and algal genomes (Figs. 2, S2). All MATEs, ABCBs, and TDT transporters have been confrmed across major land plants and some algal species (Fig. 2). The orthologs of SIZ1, STOP1, and RAE1 were mainly identifed in Streptophyte alga K. faccidum and land plants but not in Rhodophyte and Chlorophyte algal species. Previous study showed SIZ1- STOP1-ALMT module respond to Al stress (Xu et al. 2021), while our analysis implicated that the pathway is likely to be conserved in green plants (Fig. 2). The GABA binding motif was conserved from most algae (except C. reinhardtii) to high plants in ALMT family (Fig. 3B). Thus, GABAALMT signaling pathway may be a vital player for plant development and environmental response in plant (Ramesh et al. 2017).

The frst two identifed ALMTs were ALMT1 from Triticum aestivum (Sasaki et al. 2010) and Arabidopsis (Hoekenga 2006). The N-terminal and transmembrane regions are required for functional ion channels, while the C-terminal region mainly regulates the activity of ion channels (Sharma et al. 2016). ALMTs are permeable to $\mathrm { m a l } ^ { 2 - }$ , $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ (Sharma et al. 2016). For instance, ALMT1 play a signifcant role in secreting malic acid into the soil in multiple plants roots, including Arabidopsis (Hoekenga 2006), oilseed rape (Ligaba et al. 2006), soybean (Liang et al. 2013), and common velvet grass (Chen et al. 2013). In the soil, malic acid secreted by plants can immobilize the ionic aluminum to protect plants from aluminum toxicity and reduce soil $\mathrm { p H }$ to promote the plant to absorb phosphorus for better growth (Xu et al. 2021). In addition, ALMT4 of legume was expressed in vascular cells of root nodules, which induced by $\hbar g 2 2$ and involved in plant–microbe interactions by mediating the transmembrane fow of organic acids (Takanashi et al. 2016). Interestingly, ZmALMT1 mainly mediates the fow of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , and ${ \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ across the PM (Piñeros et al. 2008).

Al and malic acid may enhance the ion channel activity of ALMT1 by directly binding to the channel. Moreover, a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -activated channel AtALMT6 (Meyer et al. 2011) modulates malate infux and efux by tonoplast hyperpolarization and depolarization, respectively (Table S1) (Saito and Uozumi 2019). AtALMT9, a malate-induced $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channel (Medeiros et al. 2018), is regulated by cytoplasmic malic acid for stomatal opening (Fig. 1) (Pantoja 2021). Besides, AtALMT4 is regulated via phosphorylation at Ser382 residue and almt4 displays distinct disablement in ABA-induced guard cells closure (Eisenach et al. 2017). In addition, coexpression of AtOST1 in Xenopus oocytes increased the current of AtALMT12, which functions as voltage sensor for rapid inactivation of membrane hyperpolarization (Saito and Uozumi 2019). ALMTs have complex tissue distribution and diferent biological functions in plant species. For example, HvALMT1 is located at guard cells, roots and seeds for stomatal closure and plant development (Xu et al. 2015). ALMT6 of apple (Malus pumila) mediates the accumulation of malic acid in the vacuole, which afects the acid content and taste of M. pumila (Bai et al. 2012). In grape (Vitis vinifera), ALMT9 mediates the accumulation of malic acids in the vacuole, which afects the quality and yield of wine (De Angeli et al. 2013). These studies demonstrated that ALMTs are diverse in terms of ion selectivity (Table S1), complexity of tissue distribution, subcellular localization and biological functions, which require further research investigations.


## Chloride channels (CLCs)


In CLC protein family, a voltage-gated chloride channel, was frst identifed from the organ of Torpedo (electric ray) approximately 40 years ago (White and Miller 1979), and its function was studied in Xenopus oocytes ten years later (Jentsch et al. 1990). CLCs are participated in a large body of distinct functions in diverse cell types, including regulation of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradients in thylakoid membranes (Hechenberger et al. 1996; Pottosin and Schönknecht 1995), $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } / \mathrm { C l } ^ { - }$ homeostasis (Fig. 1), the regulation of transmembrane electrical potential, and luminal $\mathrm { p H }$ (Subba et al. 2021). Homologous of the CLC were characterized ubiquitously among green plants (Fig. 2) (Saito and Uozumi 2019), including anion channels and anion/proton antiporters.

Here, we explored the evolution of CLC in plants and algae and found a probably evolution of CLCs from Chromista Colpomenia sinuosa and Punctaria latifolia (Fig. S1). There are 350 orthologs of CLCs from the 41 representative genomes consisting of Chlorophyta, Streptophyta, and Embryophyta (Fig. S2), indicating the important roles of CLCs in adapting to the aquatic and terrestrial environments. The Ser/Pro for anion selectivity motif (GSGIP) was conserved from algae to land plants (Fig. 3C), signifying the role of these two residues in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - } / \mathrm { C l } ^ { - }$ selectivity in CLC family (Subba et al. 2021). In CLC channels, the gating glutamate was proposed to permit $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ transport via protonation of its side chain, which may have been evolutionarily conserved in examined green plants (Fig. 3C) and shown physically distinct routes for both $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ transport (Subba et al. 2021). However, Rhodophyta $C .$ . merolae could not show the conserved proton glutamate compared to other plants (Fig. 3C).

CLCs have been characterized in diverse tissues and multiple types of membranes throughout the plant kingdom (Nedelyaeva et al. 2020). In addition, this family has been proved to participate in the distribution of newly synthesized proteins for plant tolerance to stresses (Liu et al. 2020). The AtCLC family habors seven members, which is from AtCLCa to $\mathrm { { A t C L C g } }$ (Fig. 4, Table S1). AtCLCa was nitially characterized as a tonoplast $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter, which plays fundamental role in stomatal closure (Fig. 1) (De Angeli et al. 2006). The activity of AtCLCa could be resumed by OST1 phosphorylation, indicating a possible crosstalk among the three main anion channels—CLCa, SLAC1, and ALMT12 (Cubero-Font and De Angeli 2021; Eisenach and De Angeli 2017). AtCLCc is located at guard cell tonoplast (Fig. 1) and the phenotype of Atclcc mutants suggest that it is involved in guard cells response to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and ABA by modulating the homeostasis of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ (Jossier et al. 2010). Other CLCs of Arabidopsis and CLCs in many evolutionarily important lineages need to be functionally analyzed in the future to understand the diverse role of these highly conserved plant anion channels.


## Voltage‑dependent anion channels (VDACs)


Mitochondrial porins were frst confrmed in Paramecia of the ciliate group in the 1970s (Schein et al. 1976) as proteins capable of forming voltage-dependent anion-selective channels, which was not be obvious anion channel (Young et al. 2007). VDACs form a $\beta$ -barrel pore similar to the bacterial porins (Mannella 1997), which were normal in eukaryotes (Homble et al. 2012). VDACs are mainly located at the mitochondria outer membrane (Fig. 1, Table S1) for the transportation of solutes and the progress of programmed cell death (PCD) (Shoshan-Barmatz et al. 2010). There are several conserved motifs (e.g. mitochondrial porin signature and $\beta$ -signal) in plant VDACs (Balleza and Gomez-Lagunas 2009). Multiple numbers of isoforms of VDACs are present in various species and their secondary structures are signifcantly conserved (Zhang et al. 2015). VDACs are also localized at outer membranes except mitochondrial and have interactions with a range of molecular partners, implying functional diversity of the VDAC protein family (Kanwar et al. 2020). VDACs were found in Rhodophyta C. merolae and $P .$ . yezoenesis, Chlorophyta $C .$ . reinhardtii and $V .$ carteri, Streptophyta $K$ . faccidum and Chara braunii (Fig. 2). Our phylogenetic analysis showed that VDAC1 are found in all tested land plants and algal species (Fig. S1), indicating the important roles of VDACs in adaptation to the aquatic and terrestrial conditions in land plants and algae. The eukaryotic porn signature motif and GLK motif were highly conserved among algae, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta, and Spermatophyta in VDACs (Fig. 3E) (Young et al. 2007).

It was reported that VDACs are participated in a changing environment (Table S1) (Kanwar et al. 2020). VDACs also show signifcant diferences in the expression of diverse organs, developmental stages, and stress conditions (Fig. 4) (Li et al. 2013), which play a fundamental role in defense responses and regulate development and fertility (Hemono et al. 2020). For instance, it was indicated that overexpression of Pennisetum glaucum VDAC confers salt tolerance in Oryza sativa (Desai et al. 2006). Moreover, VDACs were induced by salt stress in roots of maize, Solanum chilense, and Hordeum vulgare (Fig. 4), indicating their essential role in the accumulation and redistribution of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Zorb et al. 2010). Interestingly, mitochondrial VDAC1 in caulifower was downregulated during cold stress and cold recovery, while the expression of VDAC2 was only afected after heat recovery (Rurek et al. 2018). Overexpression of AtVDAC2 increased drought tolerance in ABA-dependent manner in plants (Yan et al. 2009), but expression of TaVDAC1 relieved tolerance to drought conditions in wheat (Guo et al. 2019). The spectra count of VDAC was also induced under fooding stress in beetroots (Rojas-Méndez et al. 2021). Therefore, these investigations on plant VDACs have considerable signifcance for enhancing crop yield and quality (Kanwar et al. 2020). Given the highly evolutionary conservation of VDACs and their key function in stress tolerance (Figs. 2, 3, and 4), it is probable that VDACs can be an important target genetic engineering and gene editing towards improvement of plant tolerance to climate change factor including heat, cold, fooding, drought, and high $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ in the future.


## Mechanosensitive anion channels (MSLs)


Members of the mechanosensitive-like anion channel were frst characterized in yeast Escherichia coli over 30 years ago (Martinac et al. 1987) and its structure was identifed a varying number from 3 to 12 of N-terminal transmembrane helices and a hydrophilic cytoplasmic domain (Bass et al. 2002). Based on the amino acid residue sequences, it was predicted that MSL proteins have multiple transmembrane regions and possess the basic structural features to form ion channels (Hamilton et al. 2015). When the plasma membrane is stretched, the activation of MSL changes the structure by mechanical stress, then the pore that the anions pass is pulled apart (Basu and Haswell 2017).

Here, evolutionary analysis further indicated that MSLs are found in all tested land plants and most algal species expect four algae such as $C$ . braunii and Volcox carteri (Figs. 2, S2), indicating their important roles in adaptation to both aquatic and terrestrial contions in green plants. The transmembrane 3 motif in MSL proteins was conserved from Chlorophyta to Spermatophyta (Fig. 3D) (Balleza and

Gomez-Lagunas 2009). Using 10 Arabidopsis MSLs as the reference, we identifed 358 orthologs from 37 representative genomes consisting of Rhodophyta, Chlorophyta, Streptophyta, and Embryophyta (Fig. S2). Two and four MSLs homologues were identifed in $P .$ yezoensis and M. polymorpha (Silvia et al. 2016), respectively, while the numbers are rapidly expanded to 13 in Physcomitrella patens and 26 in Eucalyptus grandis (Fig. S2).

AtMSL1 is localized at the mitochondria, whereas AtMSL2 and AtMSL3 channels are located at the inner plastid membrane (Table S1) (Li et al. 2020b). In the grain and pollen tube, AtMSL8 channel is located at the PM and endomembrane, which is weakly selective for $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ when expressed in Xenopus laevis oocyte (Pantoja 2021). AtMSL9 and AtMSL10 were the frst identifed MSL family members by electrophysiology, which are located on the PM (Table S1) and activated upon plasma membrane tension to selectively mediate the transmembrane fow of anions (Haswell et al. 2008; Maksaev and Haswell 2012). Also, it was reported that AtMSL10 is involved in plant mechanical damage signaling and jasmonic acid (JA) accumulation (Veley et al. 2014; Zou et al. 2016). In addition, some Arabidopsis MSL members are located on organelle membranes, which regulates the size and shape of organelles (Veley et al. 2012). A total of 10 putative HvMSLs were proved in barley (Kaur et al. 2020) and their expression levels are particularly induced under drought and heat conditions (Fig. 4C). The roots of Hordeum marinum might control $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ ions under high salinity, due to one of the MSLs (HORVU.MOREX. r2.6HG0458520.1) was downregulated in roots after salinity and osmotic treatments (Isayenkov et al. 2020). Nevertheless, the biological functions of the MSL family remain poorly understand (Tran et al. 2021). It is necessary to investigate the structure of constituent ion channel proteins, the molecular mechanism of sensing cell membrane tension and diverse biological functions in green plants (Li et al. 2020b; Vothknecht and Szabo 2020).


## Other anion transport systems in green plants


In plant development, sulfate have been known as an essential macronutrient, which is taken up from roots through sulfate transporters (SULTRs) (Gigolashvili and Kopriva 2014). SULTRs are found in the Rhodophyta C. merolae, Chlorophyta Ostreococcus sp. and V. carteri, Streptophyta K. faccidum, and all land plants examined (Fig. 2). Using 14 Arabidopsis SULTRs as the reference, we identifed 509 homologues from 40 representative genomes, except Rhodophyta $P .$ . yezoensis (Fig. S2). Three and fve SULTRs orthologs are identifed in $K .$ . faccidum, C. braunii, respectively, while the numbers are rapidly expanded to 35 in $G$ . max (Fig. S2). SULTRs participate in abiotic stress response, as sulfate induces the ABA synthesis in guard cell, which is likely to involve chloroplastic SULTR3;1 transporter (Saito and Uozumi 2019).

As a dual-afnity nitrate transporter (NRT), CHL1/ AtNRT1.1/AtNPF6.3 plays a fundamental role in guard cells opening and stomata nitrate accumulation (Guo et al. 2003). CBL1/CBL9-CIPK23 phosphorylates AtNRT1.1 (Table S1), which causes the shift of nitrate from lowafnity to high-afnity mode to increase nitrate uptake under nitrate defciency (Leran et al. 2013). The regulation of AtNRT1.1 and AtSLAH by CBL1/9-CIPK23 may also indicate a potential crosstalk in the two anion transporters in nitrate homeostasis (Table S1) (Saito and Uozumi 2019). NRTs are found in the Rhodophyta $P .$ . yezoensis and C. merolae, Chlorophyta Ostreococcus sp. and V. carteri, and all examined land plants (Zhao et al. 2019). NRTs displayed overwhelming diversifcation in Embryophyte (Zhao et al. 2019), suggesting an important role for NRTs transporters during transition to land and adaptation to terrestrial living and the symbiosis with nitrogen fxing bacteria (Fichtner et al. 2020). However, the signaling role of NRTs and their ability to transport hormones has only been tested mostly in angiosperms (Barbier-Brygoo et al. 2011). For instance, knockout of nitrate reductase improved drought tolerance via the regulation of expression of NRTs and reduced ABA-enhanced slow anion channel current in the Arabidopsis nia1nia2 mutant (Chen et al. 2016).

ATP-binding cassette transporters are ancient and present in most of the organisms with activities in transport of many substances including anions (Kim et al. 2010). Compared with animals, plant genomes are enriched in ABC proteins, which could have occurred diversifcation and multiplication events during evolution, allowing plants to adapt in a changing environment (Fig. S2) (Hwang et al. 2016). For example, AtABCB14 participates in stomatal opening via mediating malate infux across the PM of guard cell (Fig. 1) (Lee et al. 2008). In Arabidopsis, MRP5/ABCC5 shows anion channel activities in plasma membrane of stamata (Suh et al. 2007). Cystic fbrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) was ATP-gated chloride channel belong to ABCC transporter (Geisler and Hegedus 2020), which were found in moss S. fallax, lycophyte S. moellendorfi, fern S. cucullata, gymnosperm Picea abies, and all examined angiosperms (Fig. 2). Besides, HvCFTR1 shows a high expression level in response to the climate change related stresses (Fig. 4C), indicating its important role in physiological functions in barley.

It is thus interesting to determine whether the SULTRs, NRTs and ABCs in other plant lineages and algae participate in signaling pathways that are responsive to environmental stresses associated with climate change.


## Comparative evolutionary and gene expression analysis of anion transport system genes in the model eudicot, monocot, and moss


Studies on the anion channels response to climate change are quite limited, but this is an important area for securing our future food production and protecting the environment. Here, we summarized the current progress of the efect of temperature, elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , drought and fooding on anion channels and the interaction among cellular signaling pathways in plants. We also conducted a comprehensive transcriptome analysis of those anion channels in $P .$ patens, Arabidopsis, and barley to confrm their roles in climate change related environmental stresses (Fig. 5).

In total, 5 SLAC/SLAH genes, 6 ALMT genes, 9 CLC genes, 4 VDAC genes, and 17 MSL genes were characterized in $P .$ . patens (Fig. 4A). Expression of anion channels genes was investigated by based on studies of heat (Elzanati et al. 2020), cold, and drought (Khraiwesh et al. 2015) treatments. PpSLAH2, PpALMT3, PpCLC2/4/5, $P p V D A C I / 2 / 3$ , and PpMSL4/5 displayed high expression in response to heat, cold, and drought treatments (Fig.  4A). The transcripts of four genes $( P p S L A C I . 2$ , PpVDACI , PpMSL8/17) were upregulated by drought in $P .$ patens (Khraiwesh et al. 2015). Similarly, the expression PpCLC3 , $P p S L A C l . 4$ , and PpMSL4 of was elevated in $P .$ . patens subjected to cold stress (Fig. 4A). A dramatically induced expression of $P p S L A C l . 2 , P p C L C9$ , and PpMSLI was observed in protonemal tissue under high temperature, but the transcription of $P p S L A C l . 4 , P p C L C 3 / 5$ , and PpMSL9 was inhibited in $P .$ patens in high temperature conditions (Elzanati et al. 2020). Except PpVDACI was increased under drought stress, $P p V D A C 2 / 3$ were reduced expression in the examined stresses, while no signifcant diference in the expression of PpVDACI was detected both cold and heat conditions (Fig. 4A). Although molecular and physiological evidence of these genes in abiotic stresses have not been unraveled in $P .$ . patens, a number of omics studies were performed of $P .$ . patens under cold (Arif et  al. 2018; Wang et  al. 2009), drought stresses (Wang et  al. 2012; Widiez et  al. 2014), indicating the involvement of anion channel genes to abiotic stress.

Uniprot database showed that Arabidopsis comprised 5 SLAC/SLAH genes, 14 ALMT genes, 7 CLC genes, 6 VDAC genes, and $1 0 ~ M S L$ genes (Fig.  4B). Expression of anion channels genes was investigated by based on studies of high temperature (Blair et al. 2019), cold (Sharma et al. 2018), waterlogging (Yang et al. 2021), and drought (Chen et al. 2021c) stresses. AtSLAC1, AtSLAH3, AtALMT4/5/9, AtCLC-A, AtVDAC1/3, and AtMSL2/3 showed high expression under temperature, waterlogging and drought treatments, while AtCLC-D, AtMSL7/10 were hardly expression under examined stresses (Fig.  4B). SLAC/SLAH genes were expressed in stomata relative to leaves in Ceratopteris richardii, Arabidopsis, and barley (Sussmilch et al. 2021), and the expression of AtSLAH3 was induced with drought stress (Fig. 4B). In addition, AtSLAH3 was repressed under waterlogging, indicating AtSLAH3 expression level relate to fooding (Lehmann et al. 2021). The abundance of AtALMT9 transcripts was hardly altered under heat stress, but it was slightly induced with drought stress (Fig. 4B). AtCLC-A, AtCLC-G, and AtCLC-B were significantly increased under drought, waterlogging, and heat stresses, respectively. Although

AtCLC- $C$ and AtCLC-G demonstrated similar expression patterns in drought and heat stresses, they had not redundant functions (Nguyen et al. 2016). AtVDAC1 was slightly reduced under cold treatments, which was consistent with previous study that atvdac1 plants showed more tolerance than wild type under low temperature (Li et al. 2013). Besides, AtVDAC3 increased the germination and growth under cold stress (Yang et al. 2011), and also were upregulated by abiotic stresses (Zhang et al. 2015) except waterlogging stress (Fig.  4B). AtMSL1 was increased under drought and waterlogging treatments (Fig. 4B) and atmsl1 plants exacerbate mitochondrial glutathione pool oxidation in heat conditions, indicating that MSL1 could improve mitochondrial redox status in diverse environment (Lee et al. 2016). Thus, it might be indicated that these anion channel genes could be direct targets of abiotic stress.

A total of 11 SLAC/SLAH genes, 10 ALMT genes, 12CLC genes, 11 VDAC genes, 10 MSL genes, 11 SPX genes, 28 PHT genes, and 226 NPF/NRT/MFS genes were identifed in barley (Fig. S3B). Expression of anion channels genes in barley was investigated through studies of low temperature (Haas et al. 2020), drought (Harb et al. 2020), heat stress (Pacak et al. 2016), and waterlogging (Borrego-Benjumea et al. 2020) treatments (Fig. 4C). Except $H \nu S L A H 2 . 3 / 3 . 3$ and HvSLAH4.1, HvSLACs showed low expression under heat, cold, drought and flooding stresses (Fig. 4C), but HvSLAC1 was linked to high grain yield in the saline feld (Liu et al. 2014). HvALMT1 exhibited low expression levels in the four stresses (Fig. 4C), but has important roles in grain metabolism and guard cells closure (Gruber et al. 2010; Xu et al. 2015). The expression of $H \nu A L M T 4$ and HvALMT8 were reduced by drought, cold, and heat stresses, while HvALMT6 and $H \nu A L M T I O$ display high expression in waterlogging (Fig.  4C), implying the significance of ALMTs in climate change related abiotic stresses. Moreover, HvCLC1, HvCLC3, HvCLC8 and HvCLC9 demonstrated similar expression patterns and $H _ { \nu } V D A C s$ (e.g. $H _ { \nu } V A D C I$ , HvVADC4, HvVADC6) showed high expression under abiotic stresses (Fig. 4C). Both cold and heat stresses afected the transcript levels of $H _ { \nu } V D A C I$ and $H _ { \nu } V D A C l O$ in barley (Fig. 4C). Although HvMSL3 and HvMSL7 show segmental duplication events (Fig. S3C), HvMSL3 was not expressed in the majority growth stages (Kaur et al. 2020). Furthermore, the gene pair of segmentally duplicated in $H .$ . vulgare (HvMSL4 and HvMSL10) exhibited pseudo-functionalization, where the insignifcant expression of HvMSL10 and $H \nu M S L 4$ is increased by drought (Fig. 4C). In addition, HvNRT family contains three subgroups including NRT1 (NPF), NRT2, and NRT3 (Guo et al. 2020) and the NRT1 group has the most members with signifcant collinear relationship in seven chromosomes of barley (Fig. S3D).

Consistently, most VDACs showed high expression, while most SLAC/SLAHs and ALMTs displayed low expression in $P .$ . patens, Arabidopsis, and barley under heat, cold, drought, waterlogging stresses. Compared to waterlogging and cold stress, more anion channel genes were induced under drought and heat conditions (Fig. 4). In P. patens and barley, MSLs (e.g. HvMSL3/6/7/8 and PaMSL4/10/16) were strongly upregulated, while AtALMT2/8/10/14 were signifcantly increased in Arabidopsis under low temperature stress. Besides, under drought stress, PaMSL8/10/11/17 were obviously increased (more than 21-fold change), while HvCLC6/7/8/9 were mostly upregulated in barley (Fig. 4), indicating distinct plants harbor diverse anion channel genes under drought treatment. However, HvVDAC5 and AtVDAC5, HvMSL3 and AtMSL3 were illustrated similar expression pattern (upregulated over 1.7-fold change) in waterlogging stress, implying their signifcant role in multiple plants under hypoxia. Similarly, HvMSL8 and PpMSL8 , $P p C L C G / 7 / 8 / 9$ and $A t C L C { \cdot } B / F$ were upregulated by heat stress. Taken together, these results implied that there might be a crosstalk among anion channels under abiotic stresses caused by changing climate (Figs. 1, 4, S3).


## Anion transport system and abiotic stress tolerance



## Temperature


Heat and cold stresses are detrimental threats to plant growth and yield (Gong et al. 2020; Jiang et al. 2020). Cold stress activates CPKs, CIPKs, and the mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, thus inducing C-repeat-binding factor (CBF) and cold-regulated (COR) expression (Chen et al. 2021a). Also, plants initiate a series of defense mechanisms to heat stress, including the heat shock protein (HSP) and heat stress response (HSR) to counteract heat efects (Gong et al. 2020). For instance, overexpression of ZmCLC-d and TaVDAC1 in Arabidopsis increased tolerance to cold stress (Guo et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2015). CLC protein in mitochondria may operate in conjunction with a VDAC in seedlings of Z. mays populations for cold tolerance (Tampieri et al. 2011). Therefore, cold and heat stresses operate in multiple modes and exert some associations, implying a more complex model of stresses on plant mitochondrial anion channels (Rurek et al. 2018). Moreover, under moderate heat stress, the signifcance of MSL1 was proved in atmsl1-1 mutants (Lee et al. 2016).


## Elevated ${ \bf { C O } } _ { 2 }$


Carbon dioxide $( \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 ) }$ is the carbon donor of photosynthesis and an external signal that controls stomatal development and movement (Tian et al. 2015). In the atmosphere, increasing $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ levels have increased signifcantly in the last 50 years, leading to global metabolic changes in various plant species (Li et al. 2020a). During meso-proterozoic and paleozoic, the content of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ might have infuenced the evolution and duplication of anion channel genes in green plants (Fig. 5). $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ frst converts into bicarbonate $\left( \mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right)$ by $\beta { \mathrm { C A } } 1 / \beta { \mathrm { C A } } 4$ , which is then perceived and transported through the MATE type transporter RHC1 (Noctor and Mhamdi 2017). Afterwards, ${ \mathrm { H C O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ binds to the transmembrane domain of SLAC1 (Yamamoto et al. 2016), while MPK4 and MPK12 inhibit HT1 through activating OST1/ GHR1, which facilitates the SLAC1 to mediate anion efux, causing in stomatal closure (Fig. 1) (Ma and Bai 2021). The additional activation of SLAC1 is caused by ${ \mathrm { H C O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ in response to increasing concentrations in guard cells (Saito and Uozumi 2019). Also, AtALMT12, a chloride, malate, and nitrate selective channel at guard cell PM, is involved in $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ -induced stomatal closure via controlling malic acid efux (Fig. 1) (Meyer et al. 2010).


## Drought and fooding


Drought is a frequent environmental stress, which causes more annual crop yield loss than all pathogens combined (Gupta et al. 2020). In Gossypium hirsutum, GhSLAC1 plays a fundamental role under drought treatment during stomatal movement (Ren et al. 2021) and AmSLAC1 of Ammopiptanthus mongolicus is induced by ABA and PEGinduced drought stress (Junlin et al. 2019). Under drought stress and ABA treatment, ZmCLC-d showed up-regulation in maize (Wang et al. 2015). OsCLC1 can promote drought tolerance, resulting to increase grain yield in $o$ . sativa (Um et al. 2018). Moreover, overexpression of AtABCG36 confers drought stress tolerance (Kim et al. 2010) and Atabcg9 Atabcg31 knockout mutants showed reduced viability of mature pollen under drought stress in plants (Choi et al. 2014). Approximately one billion hectares of global land area sufer from fooding worldwide, leading to acute crop growth inhibition and yield loss (Pan et al. 2019). Flooding often causes anoxic soils and severe hypoxia within plant roots (Herzog et al. 2016). For instance, in wheat, waterlogging stress increased the expression of TaVDAC and adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT) (Qi et al. 2018b). Waterlogging also decreases the photosynthetic capacity, which attribute to AtSLAH3-mediated PM depolarization (Lehmann et al. 2021).

Therefore, the impact of climate change especially elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ on the function anion channels will potentially lead to a complex interaction with drought and heat conditions through regulating stomatal function. For instance, ABA plays a fundamental role in controlling stomatal aperture under drought condition, while elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ may disrupt that mechanism by delaying the stomatal response to the shortage of water (Li et al. 2020a). These fndings also imply that anion channel genes are potential candidate genes for future studies for crop improvement in abiotic stresses.

Firstly, future work should focus on the function of anion channel in early divergent plants and integration of temperature and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ signals into the regulatory mechanism and the identifcation the critical members of anion channels responsible for climate change related abiotic stress. Secondly, we should also characterize the putative anion channels in major clades of Embryophyte via electrophysiology, X-ray crystallography, molecular biology and next-generation sequencing. Last but not least, investigation the functional divergence of the anion channel gens needs to be conducted by genetic engineering and gene editing in some model green plants including Arabidopsis (Eudicot), O. sativa (Monocot), C. richardii (Pteridophyte), P. patens (Bryophyte), and K. faccidum (Strptophyte alga). These will shed light on the comprehension of the evolution and molecular of anion channel genes in the changing environmental constraints.

## The atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout plant is impaired in vacuolar sequestration of Cd


To examine whether AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 confer Cd(II) tolerance by vacuolar sequestration of this non-essential ion, the cellular distribution of Cd(II) was compared in the wild-type and the double mutant using a Cd-indicator dye. Wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant plants were grown in the presence or absence of $5 ~ { \mu \mathsf { M } } ~ { \mathsf { C d } } ( { \mathsf { I I } } )$ for 2 weeks, and protoplasts were isolated and loaded with a Cd(II)- and Pb(II)-sensitive fluorescent probe, Leadmium- Green. In the absence of Cd(II), protoplasts from wild-type plants showed a negligible Leadmium- Green fluorescence signal (Figure 2a–c). When grown in Cd(II)-containing medium, strong green fluorescence was emitted from the vacuole of most wild-type protoplasts (Figure 2d–f). This observation is in agreement with a previous report that used another Cd-sensitive fluorescent dye (Morel et al., 2009) and a study that demonstrated the accumulation of Cd in central vacuoles (Vo¨ geli-Lange and Wagner, 1990). However, in atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants, the majority of cells (approximately $8 6 \%$ of the total) exhibited a markedly different LeadmiumGreen fluorescence pattern; namely, a strong signal at the margin of the cell and a much weaker signal in the vacuole (Figure 2g–j). The green signal was probably derived from the cytoplasm, because it surrounded but did not overlap with the red fluorescence emitted from chloroplasts. Furthermore, measurement of fluorescence intensity in the vacuolar region of wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout protoplasts revealed a significant reduction in Cd accumulation in the vacuole of the mutant (Figure 2k). These results suggest that sequestration of Cd into the vacuole is remarkably reduced in the atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutant.

The possibility that the observed difference in Leadmi$\mathsf { u m } ^ { \mathrm { T M } }$ Green fluorescence intensity in atabcc1 atabcc2 and wild-type protoplasts was due to different concentrations of dye in the vacuole , rather than that of Cd(II), was tested by comparing the fluorescence intensity in the vacuoles of plants treated with Pb(II) (Figure S4). As AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 did not confer Pb tolerance (Figure S1), we predicted that there would be no difference in vacuolar $\mathsf { P b }$ concentration and thus no difference in the fluorescence intensity, if the permeability of the tonoplast to the dye was not altered in the double knockout mutant. Indeed, the distribution of Pb visualized by Leadmium- Green did not differ between the wild-type and the mutant (Figure S4), supporting our conclusion that the difference in Cd fluorescence observed in Figure 2 represents a real difference in Cd content in the vacuole. These results support the hypothesis that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in vacuolar accumulation of Cd.


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 enhance the Hg(II) tolerance of yeast producing PCs


To determine the molecular mechanism by which AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in heavy metal tolerance, we used a heterologous system comprising a mutant strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae that we engineered to express a PC synthase gene of wheat (Triticum aestivum). We expressed TaPCS1 in yeast strain SM4, which lacks four vacuolar ABC transporters including ScYCF1, and named the resulting yeast SM7 (Song et al., 2010). Introduction of AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 enhanced Hg(II) tolerance in SM7 compared to a control transformed with the empty vector (EV; Figure 3a). In the SM4 strain, which does not produce PCs, AtABCC1 conferred Hg(II) tolerance over a narrow range of concentrations, while AtABCC2 improved the growth of yeast in medium containing a broad range of Hg(II) concentrations (Figure 3b). The results indicated that both AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 transport PC–Hg(II) as well as $\mathsf { G S } _ { 2 } \mathsf { - H g } ( | | )$ , and that AtABCC1 is more dependent on PCs than is AtABCC2. Cd(II) tolerance was not improved by expressing either AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 in the SM7 yeast strain (Figure S5).


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate the translocation of Cd from root to shoot


To assess whether the distribution of metal ions is altered by loss of function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, the Cd content of wild-type and mutant plants was measured. After 2 weeks of growth on half-strength MS agar plates containing Cd(II), the shoots and roots of wild-type, atabcc1 and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants were collected separately and their Cd content was measured. The shoots of atabcc1 knockout plants accumulated more Cd than the wild-type (Figure 4a), leading to an increased shoot-to-root ratio of Cd (Figure 4b). In the double knockout plants, the shoot Cd content was similar to that of the wild-type, and the root Cd content was lower, resulting in an increased shoot-to-root Cd ratio even though the total Cd accumulation was lower than that in the wild-type (Figure 4). This result implies that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate translocation of Cd from the root to the shoot. Determination of Hg(II) levels in the double knockout plants yielded similar results as for Cd (Figure S6), supporting the putative function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 in regulation of heavy metal flux between the root and shoot.


## Over-expression of AtABCC1 enhances tolerance to and accumulation of Cd


Increasing the vacuolar storage capacity may dramatically improve the ability of the plant to accumulate and tolerate toxic metal ions, because vacuoles are the main storage organelle for heavy metals and metalloids. We predicted that over-expression of AtABCC1 (Geisler et al., 2004), which plays an important role in Cd tolerance (Figure 1), is a good candidate for increasing the vacuolar storage capacity. We generated AtABCC1 over-expressing Arabidopsis plants, and selected two lines that showed the highest AtABCC1 transcript levels (M-1 and M-2, with 1.2- and 1.4-fold higher transcript levels than the wild-type, respectively; Song et al., 2010). The growth of the two transgenic lines overexpressing AtABCC1 was similar to that of the wild-type on control half-strength MS medium (Figure 5a). However, plants over-expressing AtABCC1 grew better than the wildtype in the presence of Cd(II). The shoot fresh weights of the two over-expressing lines were higher than those of the wild-type on two Cd(II) concentrations (Figure 5b). Furthermore, Cd accumulation in both the shoot and the root, as well as the total Cd content per plant, were higher in the lines over-expressing AtABCC1 than in the wild-type (Figure 5c,d). We tested whether over-expression of AtPCS1 together with AtABCC1 further increased Cd tolerance, as, in the case of arsenic, only plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 exhibited increased tolerance relative to the wild-type (Song et al., 2010). However, the Cd tolerance of plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 did not exceed that of plants only over-expressing AtPCS1 (Figure S7).

Multiple ABC transporters have been shown to transport metal/ metalloid-ligand complexes,regulating metal detoxification and accumulation within plants [17,30,31,33].In rice, two G-type ABC transporters,OsABCG43 and OsABCG36,have been shown to be associated with Cd tolerance [10,23].The eflux transporter OsABCG36 is suggested to function in exporting Cd or Cd conjugates from root cells,while the exact role of OsABCG43 in Cd detoxification in rice remains obscure [10,23]．Three C-type ABC transporters，AtABCC1，AtABCC2 and AtABCC3,have been shown to confer Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis by sequestering PC-Cd in vacuoles [21,22].However, there is no report on the involvement of C-type ABC transporters in Cd tolerance in rice until now.In the present study,we have reported that OsABCC9 participates in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.

In the previous studies, microarray and RNA-seq data showed that

OsABCC9 is up-regulated in rice under Cd stress [24,25].In this study, the induction of OsABCC9 by Cd treatment was verified by qRT-PCR and immunostaining (Fig.1A,2C,F). Besides Cd toxicity,we found that transcript levels of OsABCC9 were also elevated upon high Zn exposure (Fig.1E), indicating that it was a non-specific Cd-responsive gene and might play roles in multiple metal detoxification.

Furthermore,we examined the time-course induction of OsABCC9 in response to Cd.The up-regulation of OsABCC9 could be detected within $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 1 h }$ of Cd exposure in rice roots and continued to increase until $^ { 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ However, the transcript levels of OsABCC9 gradually declined from12 to $\mathbf { 2 4 h }$ of Cd treatment (Fig.1C),indicating that OsABCC9 belongs to the ‘early’gene that respond rapidly and often non-continuously to Cd toxicity.The temporal expression pattern of OsABCC9 is similar to the rice Cd exporter OsABCG36 [1O].Furthermore,knockout of OsABCC9 and OsABCG36 affected the Cd sensitivity of plants only at relatively high Cd concentrations (Fig.5).These similarities suggested that OsABCC9 may cooperate with OsABCG36 in Cd detoxification under high Cd conditions in rice.However,knockout of OsABCC9 resulted in higher Cd accumulation in both roots and shoots (Fig.6A and B), whereas the Cd content of shoots was unaffected by the OsABCG36 knockout [1O].At the reproductive stage,we also found that the Cd concentration in the grain was markedly elevated in osabcc9 mutants relative to the wild type grown in Cd-contaminated soil (Fig. 6C). These results indicated that loss-of-function of OsABCC9 had a significant impact on Cd accumulation in rice,especially in grains.Therfore, different from OsABCG36, OsABCC9 also plays a role in Cd accumulation in rice.

After long-term Cd treatment, the Cd concentration in the xylem sap was significantly increased in osabcc9 plants (Fig. 6D),suggesting that more Cd had been transported from root to shoot in the mutant. Two heavy metal ATPases,OsHMA2 and OsHMA3,have been reported to be implicated in root-to-shoot translocation of Cd in rice through different mechanisms [13,14,34,35]. OsHMA2 is shown to contribute to $\mathtt { Z n }$ and Cd loading into the xylem,so a reduction of its activity diminishes Zn and Cd translocation from root to shoot,and their accumulation in shoot [34-36]，which is different from the effect caused by OsABCC9 knockout.Furthermore,we also examined the expression level of OsHMA2 in osabcc9 and wild-type plants exposed to Cd.The result showed that OsHMA2 expression did not differ between the two lines (Fig.SlO),suggesting that the high root-to-shoot Cd translocation seen in the osabcc9 mutants might not be associated with OsHMA2. OsHMA3 exerts control over the Cd distribution between root and shoot by sequestration of Cd into root cell vacuoles.Rice varieties harboring the non-functional allele of OsHMA3 exhibit increased root-to-shoot Cd translocation and thus higher Cd accumulation in shoots and grains [13, 14,37],which is similar to the effect produced by knockout of OsABCC9 (Fig.6C and D). Given that OsABCC9 is localized to the tonoplast in rice cells and has transport activity for Cd (complex) in yeast cells (Figs. 3 and 4),we suppose that it might also function in sequestering Cd or Cd-thiol complexes in root vacuoles.Thus,disruption of OsABCC9 led to enhanced Cd levels in the xylem sap and Cd accumulation in the shoot and grain (Fig.6B-D).However,a slight increase in Cd levels in osabcc9 roots was also observed (Fig.6A),which differs from the OsHMA3 knockdown lines [14].This indicates that OsABCC9 might play a minor role in Cd sequestration in root cell vacuoles,as it is expressed only in some cells of the root (Fig.2C and F),while OsHMA3 is detected in all root cells [14].Considering that Zn and Cu concentrations are also elevated in osabcc9 roots (Fig. S7),other transporters responsible for Zn and/or Cu absorption might be induced in the mutant,which resulted in enhanced uptake of Zn and Cu. Since some Zn transporters also display Cd uptake activity [38],the up-regulation of these transporters might also contribute to inadvertent uptake of Cd, thereby leading to an increase of the Cd levels in osabcc9 roots.

Several ABC transporters have been shown to transport Cd in the form of thiol complexes [19,22,29,39]. Such thiol ligands can be GSH or PCs.For instance,the ABCC-type transporter YCF1 from budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) can catalyze the transport of GSH-Cd conjugates [29],while another C-type transporter Abc2 from fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe) is able to transport PC-Cd complexes [39]. Expression of OsABCC9 can enhance the Cd tolerance and content in the yeast mutant△ycfl (Fig.4A and B),so we suppose that OsABCC9 possesses Cd transport activity. Since the budding yeast(△ycf1) lacks PCs [12],the GSH-Cd complexes may be the substrate of OsABCC9 in the △ycfl strain.However,we cannot rule out the possibility that OsABCC9 mediates the transport of PC-Cd complexes in rice. Unlike the budding yeast,rice has phytochelatin synthases (PCS),which can catalyze the synthesis of PCs from GSH [4O,41].Moreover, the OsPCS1 has been suggested to be crucial for Cd tolerance in rice [4O]. Taken together, PC-Cd may be also the substrate of OsABCC9 in rice,which needs to be explored in future studies.

Two C-type ABC transporters,OsABCC1 and OsABCC7,have been shown to be involved in As accumulation in rice by mediating vacuolar sequestration or efflux of As-thiol complexes for xylem loading [17,31]. However,neither of the two transporters seems to participate in Cd tolerance or accumulation in rice [17,31].Besides evaluating the Cd sensitivity and accumulation,we also examined As sensitivity and accumulation in the OsABCC9 knockout mutants.However,loss of function of OsABCC9 did not change either the As sensitivity or accumulation in rice (Figs.S5A-D,S6A and B).In addition,OsABCC9 expression in yeast had no impact on the As tolerance of the cells (Fig.S3).Therefore,in contrast to OsABCC1 and OsABCC7,OsABCC9 might be implicated only in Cd, but not As,tolerance and accumulation in rice.Taken together,these findings indicate that,despite their grouping into one subfamily,each C-type ABC transporter may have distinct roles in rice.

In conclusion, OsABCC9 is a tonoplast-localized ABC transporter for Cd or its complex.It functions to sequester toxic Cd into the root cell vacuoles,and thus is an important component for Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.

Heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd) and mercury (Hg) are toxic pollutants that are detrimental to living organisms. Plants employ a two-step mechanism to detoxify toxic ions. First, phytochelatins bind to the toxic ion, and then the metal–phytochelatin complex is sequestered in the vacuole. Two ABCC-type transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, that play a key role in arsenic detoxification, have recently been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, it is unclear whether these transporters are also implicated in phytochelatindependent detoxification of other heavy metals such as Cd(II) and Hg(II). Here, we show that atabcc1 single or atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutants exhibit a hypersensitive phenotype in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II). Microscopic analysis using a Cd-sensitive probe revealed that Cd is mostly located in the cytosol of protoplasts of the double mutant, whereas it occurs mainly in the vacuole of wild-type cells. This suggests that the two ABCC transporters are important for vacuolar sequestration of Cd. Heterologous expression of the transporters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae confirmed their role in heavy metal tolerance. Over-expression of AtABCC1 in Arabidopsis resulted in enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation. Together, these results demonstrate that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 are important vacuolar transporters that confer tolerance to cadmium and mercury, in addition to their role in arsenic detoxification. These transporters provide useful tools for genetic engineering of plants with enhanced metal tolerance and accumulation, which are desirable characteristics for phytoremediation.

Cadmium $\mathrm { ( C d ) }$ is one of the naturally occurring heavy metals that is highly toxic to all organisms, including plants. Cd excess in plants can cause the disruption of nutrient homeostasis, dysfunction of proteins, DNA and membrane damage, and an accumulation of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS), consequently resulting in significant reduction of crop growth and production (Sandalio et al., 2001; Hall, 2002; crops potentially threatens human health.

To adapt to the Cd-contaminated environment, plants have evolved diverse mechanisms to cope with Cd stress, such as Cd extrusion, chelation, and sequestration (Hall, 2002; Weber et al., 2006; Lin and Aarts, 2012). Among them, several studies have showed that ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporters may play important roles in Cd tolerance in plants (Kim et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2007; Oda et al., 2011; Park et al., 2012; Brunetti et al., 2015). For example, AtABCG36/AtPDR8 was reported to be essential for Cd resistance in Arabidopsis (Kim et al., 2007). It is localized at the plasma membrane of root cells and functions as an efflux transporter for Cd or Cd conjugates. On the other hand, two ABCC-type transporters; AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, are involved in vacuolar sequestration of Cd in Arabidopsis (Park et al., 2012). Knockout of these genes resulted in hypersensitivity to Cd. Recently, another ABCC-type transporter AtABCC3 was also reported to be involved in Cd tolerance by transporting PC-Cd complexes into the vacuoles in Arabidopsis (Brunetti et al., 2015). In rice, there are at least 120 members of ABC transporter (Garcia et al, 2004), but only few has been characterized in terms of Cd tolerance. One of them, OsABCG43 is a Cd-inducible transporter (Oda et al., 2011). Its expression in yeast increased Cd tolerance although its exact role in rice is unknown. Another ABCG-type transporter gene, OsABCG36/OsPDR9, was also reported to be induced by Cd and was suggested to play a possible role in heavy metal stress (Moons, 2003, 2008). However, the role of OsABCG36/OsPDR9 in Cd tolerance has not been investigated. In the present study, we functionally characterized OsABCG36 in terms of the gene expression, cellular and subcellular localization, transport activity. We also obtained two independent mutant lines of OsABCG36 by the CRISPR/Cas9 technique and compared their Cd tolerance and accumulation with the wild-type rice. Our results showed that OsABCG36 is involved in Cd tolerance by effluxing Cd from the root cells.

Key message Vacuolar sequestration via tonoplast-targeted MerC enhances Cd tolerance; expression in roots plays a primary role, while expression in mesophyll is also crucial for protecting the chloroplasts.

Abstract Targeting metal transporters to the vacuole via genetic engineering ofers a strategy to enhance plant tolerance to toxic metals like cadmium (Cd) by promoting vacuolar sequestration. Understanding the infuence of diferent expression patterns of metal transporters is crucial for elucidating Cd-tolerance mechanisms. This study investigated how ubiquitous (p35S promoter) versus mesophyll-specifc (pRBCS1A promoter) expression of a tonoplast-targeted bacterial metal transporter, MerC-AtVAM3 (CV), impacts Cd tolerance, nutrient homeostasis, and subcellular Cd distribution in Arabidopsis. While the short-term plate assays revealed only slight tolerance improvements, the long-term hydroponic Cd treatments ${ \mathrm { 7 } } 0 . 5 { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ and $1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ ) resulted in signifcant enhancement in the CV-expressing lines. Notably, the p35S-CV line, which ubiquitously expresses the transgene, exhibited stronger tolerance (improved growth, mitigated chlorosis confrmed by higher SPAD values) compared to the mesophyll-specifc pRBCS1A-TCV lines, particularly under $1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd. Nutritional profling indicated that CV expression alleviated some Cd-induced nutrient imbalances. Although root Cd accumulation was similar across lines, p35S-CV shoots displayed approximately $3 0 \%$ lower Cd concentration compared to the wild-type (Col-0) and pRBCS1A lines under $1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd conditions. In Col-0 mesophyll cells, subcellular analysis using the Leadmium Green dye showed Cd was preferentially localized in the peripheral cytoplasm. The Leadmium Green signal also exhibited strong colocalization with chloroplasts. Conversely, CV expression efectively redirected Cd to the central vacuole, confrming efcient sequestration by the tonoplast-targeted MerC. The superior tolerance of the p35S-CV line strongly suggests that vacuolar Cd sequestration in roots plays a primary role in conferring robust Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis, while vacuolar sequestration in shoots provides supportive protection.

ABC transporters constitute a large superfamily of proteins described in all kingdoms of life. Some families have a restricted distribution, like the ABC subclass C (or multidrug resistance associated protein, MRP) which is limited to eukaryotes. In plants, ABCC/MRPs are subdivided in three phylogenetic clusters (Kolukisaoglu et al. 2002, Schulz and Kolukisaoglu 2006), two of which are fairly well characterized in Arabidopsis.

Cluster I contains four genes including AtMRP1 and AtMRP2 which are involved in cellular detoxification processes. These transporters display a ubiquitous expression in plants, mediate metal/metalloid tolerance and transport various compounds, such as phytochelatins (Song et al. 2010), glutathione conjugates (Lu et al. 1997), folate (AtMRP1), as well as chlorophyll catabolites (AtMRP2, Lu et al. 1998). The two other members of cluster I (AtMRP11 and AtMRP12) have been poorly investigated; they share transport properties of cluster I MRPs except for chlorophyll catabolites, which seems to be specific to AtMRP2 within this cluster (Frelet-Barrand et al. 2008).

Ten of the fifteen Arabidopsis ABCC/MRPs belong to cluster II. The AtMRP3 expression is induced in leaf and root under cadmium or several other metal treatments (Bovet et al. 2003), and confers tolerance to cadmium in yeast (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP3 exhibits glutathione S-conjugate transport activity, and as described for AtMRP1 and AtMRP2, chlorophyll catabolites transport activity has also been reported (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP6 and AtMRP7 have the highest sequence similarity to AtMRP3 and are also upregulated by $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments. In AtMRP6 mutants, leaf development is more sensitive to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment than in wild type. However, the expression pattern of AtMRP6 suggests that it is not only involved in $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance but also in developmental processes. Indeed, AtMRP6 is expressed during early seedling development, in root apical meristem and in lateral root initiation (Gaillard et al. 2008). AtMRP7 is constitutively expressed in roots and leaves and the protein was localized to both plasmalemma and tonoplast (Wojas et al. 2009). Overexpression of AtMRP7 in tobacco slightly enhances plant resistance to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment and modifies $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ rootto-shoot translocation. These observations suggest that AtMRP3 and its closest homologues may behave as cellular metal detoxifiers although additional functions in planta cannot be ruled out. AtMRP4 and AtMRP5, which also belong to cluster II, have a low sequence similarity, but their stomatal-specific expression patterns suggest a role in plant adaptation to water stress rather than cell detoxification. Indeed, AtMRP4 knock-out mutants display an increased water loss due to a larger constitutive stomata aperture. Considering its strong expression in guard cells and localization in plasmalemma, AtMRP4 is suggested to be involved in a stomata ion channel regulation (Klein et al. 2004). AtMRP5 is also expressed in guard cells but localizes to tonoplast (Nagy et al. 2009). Interestingly, Nagy et al. (2009) demonstrated that AtMRP5 is a high affinity inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) transporter, a molecule that modulates $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 \dagger }$ signaling and $\bar { \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in guard cells. AtMRP5 mutants are impaired in the export of InsP6 into vacuole resulting in constitutive stomata closure and a reduced water loss (Klein et al. 2003, Suh et al. 2007).

Cluster III genes have not been functionally characterized so far. In Arabidopsis (AGI 2000) it was revealed a single MRP/ABCC gene belonging to cluster III, AtABCC13/MRP11 $( \mathrm { A t } 2 \mathrm { g } 0 7 6 8 0 )$ . In this study, we investigated in-depth the expression pattern of AtABCC13 in Arabidopsis. The $\beta$ -glucuronidase (GUS) reporter gene approach revealed that the AtABCC13 expression was related to vascular elements, seed maturation, and seedling development.

Heavy metals such as zinc, iron, nickel, and copper are essential micronutrients for the plant growth and development, while other metals like lead, cadmium, arsenic are toxic. Plants have developed various mechanisms for metal uptake and transfer from soil to root cells. Various transporters are used for uptake and detoxification of metal ions. As a first line of defense, plants that are often exposed to concentrations of heavy metal ions prevent or minimize their absorption into root cells by trapping metal ions into apoplast, binding to the cell wall or preventing their transfer into the cell. The plants utilize metal transport detoxification techniques, chelation, and metal sequestration into the vacuole. If nonessential metals exceed concentrations, then an active metabolic mechanism results in the production of chelating compounds such as metallothioneins and phytochelatins. The complexes of metals are then sequestered to vacuoles via specific transporters.

Crop fields polluted with toxic heavy metals have an increased risk of yielding agricultural products that contain toxic levels of the pollutants. Phytoremediation is an approach in which higher plants are employed to extract the pollutants from soils. For efficient application of the plant-employing method to pollution sites, a deeper understanding of plant reactions to heavy metals is needed. Cadmium (Cd) is one of several toxic heavy metals to which plant reactions are being intensively studied at the molecular level. The best characterized reaction to Cd is the production of phytochelatins. Phytochelatins are cystein (Cys)-rich polypeptides enzymatically synthesized (not translated from gene messages) by phytochelatin synthase. They are thought to bind to Cd incorporated into plant cells and sequester it to vacuoles. Numerous studies have indicated a correlation between the capability of producing these Cys-rich compounds and the degree of tolerance to Cd (for review Cobbett 2000). On the other hand, a more recent study using a Cd hyperaccumulator, Thlaspi caerulescens, presented a novel picture of a developmentally regulated detoxification system in addition to the synthesis of phytochelatins (Ku¨pper et al. 2004). Further analysis of Cd hyperaccumulators such as Thlaspi caerulescens and Arabidopsis halleri (Ku¨pper et al. 2000; Pence et al. 2000; Zhao et al. 2002; Cosio et al. 2004; Plaza et al. 2007) and comparative studies with the model plant, Arabidopsis thaliana (Weber et al. 2004; Hanikenne et al. 2008), have provided insights into the transporters that play a major role in Cd hyperaccumulation in plants.

Despite such progress in the molecular dissection of plant reactions to Cd, many aspects still remain unclear. It is generally believed that Cd is incorporated, without being recognized, by plant roots along with other metals such as Zn. However, various questions are yet to be answered: through what routes is Cd incorporated into roots and then transported to aboveground tissues and seeds? How complicated are the transport pathways for the heavy metal inside the plant? Is there any possibility that plant roots might be able to discriminate Cd in soils from other heavy metals? One possible route to answering these questions might be to identify and analyze Arabidopsis mutants, which have proved to be a powerful tool for the molecular dissection of heavy metal responses. Thus, for example, isolation of two Cd-sensitive mutants in Arabidopsis (Howden and Cobbett 1992; Howden et al. 1995a, 1995b) led to the identification of genes coding the enzymes that catalyze phytochelatin synthesis (Cobbett et al. 1998; Ha et al. 1999). However, other than these pioneering studies, few other Arabidopsis mutants have been identified to date that influence sensitivity to Cd. In the present study, therefore, we attempted to isolate novel Arabidopsis mutants that varied in their tolerance and response to high concentrations of Cd. We termed these Cd-related Arabidopsis mutants as MRCs (mutants altered in the reaction to Cd). To aid identification of novel mutants, we employed a new type of agar plate as a screening tool; this plate has a gradient of Cd concentration. As anticipated, use of the Cd-gradient agar plates enabled us to isolate novel Arabidopsis mutants that exhibited distinctively different reactions to Cd. Here, we describe this new screening procedure for Arabidopsis mutants and characterize the phenotypes of three distinctly different MRCs.

## Early high-Cd responsive transporters in rice roots

Additionally, one C2H2-type zinc finger protein (ZFP182) was significantly enhanced even at the lowest Cd concentration [48], and it was strongly induced from FPKM of 5 to 858 after the short-term high-Cd treatment (Table 2, Additional file 2: Table S2).

To elucidate the rice early response to high-Cd stress, we performed pair-end RNAseq of rice roots with replicates treated with high Cd concentrations $( 1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ for $1 \ \mathrm { h } ,$ , in parallel with control samples at the same time point. As expected, 702 of the 1772 DEGs were uniquely identified in our rice roots treated by short-term highCd treatment (Additional file 5: Figure S2, Additional file 2: Table S2), which differed from previous transcriptomic studies using short-term and moderate or low Cd treatment [21, 27].

Metal transporters play key roles in the acquisition, distribution, and homeostasis of Cd in plants [5]. Several Arabidopsis ABC transporters are suggested to mediate vacuolar sequestration of Cd-phytochelatin conjugates [15, 49]. In this study, all of the 6 Cd-upregulated ABCGs/PDRs were from one of the most highly represented subfamilies of ABC transporters (Table 1, Additional file 7: Figure S3).

In Arabidopsis, ABC transporter of the mitochondria AtATM3 [50] and AtABCC1–3 [15, 49] transported Cd into the vacuoles to increase Cd tolerance. AtABCC3 confers Cd tolerance by transporting phytochelatin (PC)-Cd complexes into the vacuoles to detoxify Cd [15]. In rice, the Cd-inducible OsABCG43 is likely to sequester Cd at the subcellular level [51], similar to vacuolar sequestration mediated by OsHMA3 [17].

Among the Cd-upregulated ABCG-type transporter genes, ABCG36/OsPDR9 is reported induced rapidly and markedly in rice roots by Cd and Zn [52]. Taking its homologs in Arabidopsis into consideration, AtPDR12 and AtPDR8 are all involved in heavy metal resistance, and the Cd-inducible AtPDR8 can export multiple functionally unrelated substrates, including auxinic compounds and Cd; thus, it confers heavy metal resistance as a Cd extrusion pump [12], strengthening the potential of employing ABCG36/OsPDR9 for genetic improvement of Cd tolerance in rice. Besides its mechanism as a pump to exclude lead, AtPDR12 functions as a plasma-membrane ABAuptake transporter [53].

In addition to the upregulated PDR-type transporters, 4 members of the MATE efflux family were rapidly upregulated in 1-h Cd-treated rice roots (Table 1).

MATE proteins play a role in aluminum tolerance by mediating citric acid efflux from root cells to chelate Al [54]. Functional MATE homologs associated with Al tolerance were identified in Arabidopsis [55], Medicago truncatula [56], sorghum [57], barley [58, 59], wheat [60], maize [61], and rice (OsFRDL4, Os01g69010) [62].

In Arabidopsis, the MATE-related transporter DETOXIFICATION 1 (AtDTX1) has been described as an efflux transporter that detoxifies plant-derived or exogenous toxic compounds including Cd from the cytoplasm [63]. Interestingly, a recent study on mammalian MATEs has provided the first evidence that MATE transporters are involved in the cellular transport and detoxification of Cd [64]. Therefore, it would be worth investigating the role of the Cd-induced plant MATE transporters in combating Cd toxicity in planta.

Ten of 11 heavy metal-associated domain containing proteins (HMADs) were rapidly upregulated in Cd-treated rice roots (Table 1).

HMADs, such as AtHMAD1 [65] and heavy metalassociated isoprenylated plant proteins (HIPPs) metallochaperones [66], have been suggested play roles in metal binding and/or transport, thus regulating various processes under (a) biotic stress [65].
