## The Nine Arabidopsis Channels Share a Similar Structure


The multiple alignment of the protein sequences of Arabidopsis channels shows that several blocks are highly conserved along the channels (Fig. 1). Six regions, named R1 to R6, could be defined. R1 is the region upstream from the membrane domain, R2. R1 regions share few similarities with each other and have a variable length (from 62 to 91 amino acids). R2 is composed of six transmembrane segments, named S1 to S6, and a pore domain, P, present between S5 and S6. This region is the most conserved one. R3 is defined as a junction domain linking R2 and R4. R4 shares similarities with cyclic nucleotide binding domains found in various proteins: e.g., $30 \%$ identity with the cAMP binding domain of kinase regulatory subunits (Jahnsen et al. 1986) and $2 5 \%$ identity with the cyclic nucleotide binding domain of cationic channels regulated by cGMP (Kaupp et al. 1989). In six channels, namely AKT1, SPIK, AKT5, AKT2, SKOR, and GORK, R5 contains an ankyrin domain that is composed of five repetitions of the consensus ankyrin motif (Lux et al. 1990), with a sixth incomplete repeat. Ankyrin domains are found in several kinds of proteins (e.g., cytoskeleton binding proteins and transcription factors) and are likely to mediate protein–protein interactions (Hoffman 1991; Sedgwick and Smerdon 1999; Rubtsov and Lopina 2000). In the other three channels (KAT1, KAT2, and AtKC1), R5 does not harbor any ankyrin repeat or display any similarity to other proteins. R5 sequences are highly variable in length: approximately 300 amino acids in AKT1, SPIK, and AKT5, 250 in SKOR and GORK, 220 in AKT2, 130 in KAT1 and KAT2 and 80 in AtKCl (Fig. 1). The sequence of R6 is conserved in the nine channels. This region has been named ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { { \mathrm { H A } } }$ , because of its richness in hydrophobic and acidic residues (Ehrhardt et al. 1997). Two-hybrid experiments have suggested that this region interacts with R3 and R4 (Daram et al. 1997). Experiments using chimerical constructs, fusing a channel to the GFP, have led to the conclusion that R6 could also allow channel clustering on the membrane (Ehrhardt et al. 1997).


## Phylogenetic Analysis of the Coding and Protein Sequences From Arabidopsis


R1 regions share the least in common and the ankyrin domain is not present in every polypeptide (see above). We removed these parts of the sequences to construct phylogenies from sequences present in all proteins. The same procedure was followed for the nucleic sequences. An animal channel that is related to the plant channels, the Mus musculus ERG3 channel (CAC14797; $50 \%$ similarity to AKT1), was used as an outgroup to root the trees constructed from the protein sequences by CLUSTAL X, PROTDIST/FITCH, PROTPARS, and PAUP (Fig. 2). The trees generated using parsimony or distance methods from cDNA sequences (the ERG3 channel sequence not being taken into account) have the same topology, the lengths of the branches and bootstrap values hardly differing (data not shown).

In all the trees the channels were distributed into five groups. Group I contains AKT1, SPIK, and AKT5, which share more than $86 \%$ amino acid sequence similarity (Table 3). Group II contains KAT1 and KAT2 $9 5 \%$ sequence similarity; Table 3), and group $\mathrm { v }$ contains SKOR and GORK $90 \%$ sequence similarity; Table 3). AtKC1 and AKT2 are not included in any of these three groups, cannot be gathered within a single group, and have homologues in other plant species (see below). The whole set of data indicates that AKT2 and AtKC1 define two distinct groups, groups III and IV, respectively.


## Phylogenetic Relationships of the Shaker Channels Identified in Plants


Presently (September 2002), 44 plant DNA sequences encoding (nearly) full-length Shaker channels are available in the databases. The encoded protein sequences were aligned, showing that their structures are similar to those identified in Arabidopsis channels: R1 is poorly conserved and of variable length and some channels do not contain any ankyrin domain R5 (data not shown).

Trees were constructed from the sequences of the R2 to R4 domains using the PROTDIST/FITCH, CLUSTAL X, Darwin, PAUP, and PROTPARS programs, and rooted with the ERG3 sequence. These trees all have the same topology, composed of five subfamilies, strictly corresponding to the five groups defined for Arabidopsis Shaker channels (Fig. 3). The bootstrap values associated with group nodes are always over $94 \%$ . Monocot channels (Fig. 3) are included in all groups. They are located in an independent branch inside each group except in group V. These branches are often associated with high bootstrap values. On the contrary, a Shaker-like channel sequence isolated from the moss Physcomitrella patens $( \mathrm { P p K } 1 )$ ) does not fit in any of the previously identified groups. The weak bootstrap value of the corresponding node emphasizes the fact that this sequence is not strongly associated with any particular group.

To check if the repartition in groups can be found at the level of each region of the proteins, trees were constructed independently from regions R2, R3, R4, R5, and R6 considered individually, with PROTPARS and PROTDIST/FITCH. The groupings were always similar to the one presented in Fig. 3 (for the analysis of R5, group II and IV proteins were removed, as they contain no ankyrin domain). Bootstrap values were always over $80 \%$ for groups III, IV, and V whatever the region considered, whereas they were slightly lower for groups I and II when the R4 and R6 regions were analyzed (data not shown).

Database searching enabled us to find plant ESTs that are likely to encode potassium channels. Some of these ESTs can be assembled to form a contig and were thus considered to correspond to the same gene. A tree was constructed from the translated sequences of the 30 resulting contigs and the full-length sequences of the plant Shaker channels, increasing the total number of sequences to 74 (data not shown; sequences and accession numbers of the ESTs available upon request). All angiosperm ESTs integrate in the five previously defined groups. Because this tree was constructed from proteins of different lengths, its significance is questionable. Nevertheless, it suggests that the distribution in five groups is still conserved when increasing the number of channels from angiosperm species. The two available gymnosperm ESTs (from pine; accession Nos. BG318414 and BG832435) could not be surely associated with any group, as the trees constructed with DARWIN, PROTDIST/FITCH, and PROTPARS are not in accordance to each other (data not shown).


## Description of the Intron Characteristics


The genes encoding Shaker-like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels available up to now were identified in Arabidopsis thaliana, Vitis vinifera, and Oryza sativa. For Arabidopsis and grapevine genes, intron positions, lengths, and sequences were deduced by comparing the genes and the corresponding cloned cDNA. For rice, intron data were determined in silico while extracting the protein sequences from the genomic DNA. As the predicted $O s K 2 . 2$ and $O s K 5 . I$ sequences may be incomplete (see Materials and Methods), it is possible that putative introns located in the missing parts have not been detected. Interestingly, no intron is present in the $O s K 4 . 3$ gene. As postulated for intronless members of multigenic families, this gene could result from the reverse transcription of an mRNA and integration back into the genome (Boudet et al. 2001). Since the origin of $O s K 4 . 3$ is likely to be different from that of the other genes, this gene has not been taken into account in the analysis. No intron was found in the $5 ^ { \prime }$ and $3 ^ { \prime }$ untranslated region (UTR) of Arabidopsis and Vitis genes. Only a few $5 ^ { \prime }$ or $3 ^ { \prime }$ UTRs have been identified in rice genes (see Materials and (S55349); KZM1 (CAD18901); LKT1 (CAA65254); Mkt1 (AAF81249); NpKT1 (BAA84085); PpK1 (from the cDNA AX181028); PtK2.1 (CAC87141); PTK2 (CAC05489); PTORK (CAC05488); SKOR (CAA11280); SKT1 (T07651); SKT2 (T07052); SPICK1 (AAD16278); SPICK2 (AAD39492); SPORK1 (CAC10514); TaAKT1 (AAF36832); VFK1 (CAA71598); ZmK1 (CAA68912); $\mathrm { Z m K } 2$ (CAB54856); VvSIRK (AAL09479); VvSOR (AJ490336). The origin of rice sequences is given in Table 2. The MtK4.1 sequence originates from the translation of the overlapping sequences of the following Medicago truncatula ESTs: AW256430, AW256327, AW299025, AW683944, AW687023, AW736140, BG646059, and AW256736. The different groups are numbered (Roman numeral) in accordance with the numbering in Fig. 2.

Methods). No intron is present in these regions. The following analysis was therefore carried out only on introns interrupting the coding sequences.

The 20 Shaker genes $V { \nu } S I R K$ and the genes from Arabidopsis and rice) contain between 8 and 12 introns (Table 4). Many positions are common to several genes. Twenty-one different intron positions can be identified within the genes. As done previously (Frugoli et al. 1998), the introns were numbered by taking into account their position (from $5 ^ { \prime }$ to $3 ^ { \prime }$ ) in the sequence alignment rather than their position in each gene (Fig. 1). Positions 1 and 2 are separated by only 9 bp, and only group V genes contain an intron at position 1 (Table 4). The short distance between position 1 and position 2 suggests that the intron at position 2 ‘‘slid’’ to position 1 during the evolution of group V genes. Intron sliding is indeed classically put forward to explain this kind of observation (see Stolzfus et al. 1997). In other words, position 1 can be thought to derive directly from position 2.

Intron lengths in the potassium channel genes range from 66 to 1381 bp in Arabidopsis and from 73 to 3222 bp in rice. The introns smaller than 200 bp represent $92 \%$ of the introns in $A$ . thaliana (85 of 92) and $8 5 \%$ in rice (90 of 107). The size of these smaller introns is roughly in the same range ( $9 6 ~ \pm ~ 2 5$ bp and $1 1 6 ~ \pm ~ 5 2$ bp, respectively, in Arabidopsis and rice). The introns over 200 bp are distributed all along the genes in rice (from position 1 to position 21), whereas they are located in the four first positions in Arabidopsis. In relation to their unusual length in Arabidopsis (Hawkins 1988; Brown et al. 1996; The Arabidopsis Genome Initiative 2000), it is tempting to speculate that, in this plant, these longer introns play a role in the regulation of transcription.

$\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is an important ion that plays roles in cellular functions such as turgor adjustment, cell elongation, movement of stomata and leaves, and regulation of enzyme activity (Gierth and Maser 2007). Among stress responses, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ likely plays roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance because the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio is the most important factor in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance (Adams and Shin 2014). In addition, the outward-rectifying potassium channel GORK functions in stomatal closure and therefore is an important factor in drought tolerance (Ache et al. 2000). There are more than 77 genes encoding putative $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels in Arabidopsis. Among them, 15 genes encode $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } ,$ -selective channels and the others are non-selective cation channels (NSCC). Shaker-like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels are the major gene family of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -selective channels (Ward et al. 2009). Previously, we identified the inward-rectifying shaker like potassium channels of rice and found that OsKAT2 is a prevalent potassium channel functioning in guard cells (Hwang et al. 2013). In this study, we found two candidate outward-rectifying potassium channels in the rice genome based on amino acid sequence similarity. However, we could not classify the rice genes based on only the phylogenic tree with AtSKOR and AtGORK of Arabidopsis because the genes encode very similar amino acid sequences and the two rice genes were not grouped separately with AtSKOR or AtGORK in the phylogenetic tree. In addition, the rice genes encode the same functional domains as found in AtSKOR and AtGORK, including cyclic nucleotide binding domain (CNBD), ankyrin repeat domain and acidic domain. However, OsGORK and OsSKOR showed conservation not only in amino acid sequence but also in gene expression pattern compared with the proteins of Arabidopsis, even though the anatomical structure of roots and stomata complexes are quite different between monocots and dicots. In Arabidopsis, AtSKOR is expressed in root stelar cells and AtGORK is expressed in guard cells. Thus, the cell-specific expression patterns of these channels might be indispensable for survival of the plant and important in their functions. Accordingly, we could classify the likely functions of the rice genes based on their gene expression patterns (Gaymard et al. 1998; Ache et al. 2000).

AKT1 is activated by phosphorylation of the C-terminal region, and a single amino acid mutation of AtSKOR can change the outward-rectifying potassium channel into an inward-rectifying channel (Lee et al. 2007; Li et al. 2008). SKOR and GORK proteins share the CNBD and ankyrin repeat functional domains with AKT1. The ankyrin repeat domain of the AKT1 channel is the region of interaction with CIPK23. AKT1 is activated by calcium signaling mediated by calcium sensors CBL1 and 9, and by CIPK23 interaction (Cheong et al. 2007). Calcium signaling not only activates the inward-rectifying potassium channels, but also inhibits outward-rectifying potassium channel activity. Thus, OsGORK and OsSKOR might have a similar channel activity regulation system as AKT1.

In summary, we identified OsSKOR and OsGORK based on amino acid sequence, gene expression patterns and subcellular localization in rice. These results provide valuable information to study $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ regulation in monocots.

$\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is the most abundant cation in the cytosol of the cell and is involved in several major functions, such as neutralization of nondiffusible negative charges of biomolecules and control of the ionic strength, regulation of turgor pressure, and long- and short-term control of cell membrane polarization.

Plants play a major role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry into the biosphere and the trophic chain. The combination of molecular approaches and electrophysiological analyses performed in planta has revealed that several families of transporters and channels are in charge of $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake from the soil solution and subsequent transports within the plant. Among these proteins, the Shaker channels have been shown to play crucial roles in several key steps of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ nutrition: e.g., the AKT11 channel, along with AtKC1, is involved in $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ absorption from the soil solution (Hirsch et al. 1998; Reintanz et al. 2002), SKOR mediates $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ secretion into the xylem sap toward the shoots (Gaymard et al. 1998) and AKT2 has been suggested to allow both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ loading and unloading into/from the phloem sap (Marten et al. 1999; Lacombe et al. 2000b). Also, evidence has been obtained indicating that some Shaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels play a role in the control of stomatal opening and thereby in the regulation of plant water loss: KAT1 and KAT2 are thought to be involved in $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx into the guard cell, allowing an increase in turgor and stomatal opening (Ichida et al. 1997; Pilot et al. 2001; Szyroki et al. 2001), while GORK may contribute to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux during stomatal closure (Ache et al. 2000).

The first plant Shaker channels identified at the molecular level, AKT1 (Sentenac et al. 1992) and KAT1 (Anderson et al. 1992) from Arabidopsis, were cloned by functional complementation of yeast strains deficient in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake. Completion of the Arabidopsis genome sequencing program (The Arabidopsis Genome Initiative 2000; http://www. arabidopsis.org/info/agi.html) has revealed that the Shaker family is composed of nine members in this model plant (see Table 1 and Materials and Methods). Plant Shaker channels share sequence and structure similarities with the Shaker channels identified in Drosophila melanogaster and mammals (Warmke et al. 1991; Warmke and Ganetzky 1994; Zhong and Wu 1991), particularly with those belonging to the EAG subfamily. All the channels of the Shaker superfamily are characterized by a typical hydrophobic core with six transmembrane segments, named S1 to S6, and a pore-forming domain, P, located between S5 and S6 (Jan and Jan 1994). The N- and C-terminal regions, surrounding this transmembrane domain, are cytoplasmic. The similarities between animal and plant Shaker-type channels reside mainly in the hydrophobic core. The most conserved sequence is that of the $\mathrm { P }$ domain, which contains a hallmark motif, GYGD, the signature of highly selective $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels. In the functional protein, which is homo- or heterotetrameric, the P domains of the four subunits line the aqueous pore and control ion permeation. The S4 segment contains conserved acidic and basic residues and forms the voltage sensor of the channel:

## Identification of Shaker Channels Subfamilies


The comparison of the protein sequences shows that the plant Shaker channels possess the same conserved structure. The main structural difference lies in the presence of an ankyrin domain in group I, III and V channels. This led initially to the classification of the Arabidopsis family into two subgroups (Che´ rel et al. 1996; White 2002): the AKT (with ankyrin repeats) and the KAT (without ankyrin repeats) groups. But all the trees constructed from protein or cDNA sequences (Figs. 2 and 3) and from gene structure (Fig. 4) clearly reveal the existence of more than two groups. This phylogenic classification is not based on the structural similarities of the proteins (e.g., consider the distance between group I and group II channels, which are structurally different, and between group I and group V channels, whose structures are similar). Moreover the grapevine VvSIRK channel, undoubtedly included in group II (Fig. 3) (Pratelli et al. 2002), contains two repetitions of the ankyrin motif in the R5 region. This emphasizes the fact that the grouping of the proteins according to sequence data seems, at present, to be the most relevant and universal criterion of classification. Furthermore, this classification is related to the diversity of the functional properties of the channels (see below). The renaming of AtKC1 as KAT3 decided by Maser et al. (2001), based on the fact that, like KAT1 and KAT2, AtKC1 does not possess any ankyrin domain, is not supported by the evolutionary data and should therefore be avoided. It would be smart to use the five-group classification as a basis for renaming the plant Shaker-like potassium channels (as done for rice channels in the present study; see Table 2), the nomenclature of which is currently poorly understandable.


## Relationships Between the Phylogeny and the Function of the Channels


In an attempt to decipher the significance of the phylogenetic grouping in relation to the roles of the channels in the plant, we compared the locations in the trees and the expression patterns of the channels (summarized in Table 1 for the Arabidopsis channels). Interestingly, all group II channels whose expression has been examined to date are expressed in guard cells (KAT1 [Nakamura et al. 1995], KAT2 [Pilot et al. 2001], KST1 [Mu¨ ller-Rober et al. 1995], VvSIRK [Pratelli et al. 2002]). However, the expression patterns of the genes of groups I and III do not seem to be strongly conserved between species, and the expression patterns of too few members of groups IV and V have been investigated until now to draw any conclusion. Concerning the channels’ functional properties (summarized in Table 1 for the Arabidopsis channels), it appears that groups I and II are composed of inward rectifiers, which, moreover, share similar sensitivities to external and internal pH, ATP, cGMP (AKT1 [Gaymard et al. 1996], SPIK Mouline et al. 2002], KAT1 [Anderson et al. 1992; Bertl et al. 1995; Hedrich et al. 1995; Hoshi 1995; Ve´ ry et al. 1995; Marten et al. 1996], KAT2 [Pilot et al. 2001], KST1 [Mu¨ ller-Ro¨ ber et al. 1995; Hoth et al. 1997], SKT1 [Zimmermann et al. 1998], $Z { \mathrm { m K } } 1$ [Philippar et al. 1999], LKT1 [Hartje et al. 2000], VvSIRK [Pratelli et al. 2002]). Channels from group III are characterized by weak rectifying properties and are able to mediate both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux (depending on the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ electrochemical gradient) as shown for AKT2, $Z { \mathrm { m K } } 2$ , and VFK1 (Marten et al. 1999; Lacombe et al. 2000b; Philippar et al. 1999; Ache et al. 2001). Group V channels appear to be outward rectifiers, as shown for SKOR (Gaymard et al. 1998; Lacombe et al. 2000a), GORK (Ache et al. 2000), and VvSOR (R. Pratelli, unpublished data). In group IV, KDC1 (Downey et al. 2000) has been characterized as an inward rectifier in a heterologous system. AtKC1 is an electrophysiologically silent channel when expressed in heterologous systems, but it has been shown that this subunit can modify the functional properties of AKT1 in vivo (Reintanz et al. 2002). No unequivocal characteristic of group IV channels can thus be deduced from the analyses performed up to now. In summary, surveying the available data does not reveal any correlation between the phylogenetic grouping and the channel expression pattern. On the other hand, a relationship between the grouping and the functional properties is suggested, with an apparent exception for group IV. It is tempting to speculate that the separation of groups $\mathrm { I } + \mathrm { I I }$ , III, and V during the evolution of the higher plants was driven by selection pressure to produce channels with different rectification properties (inward, weak inward, or outward, respectively). The available data are not yet sufficient to discuss the meaning of the functional differences between group I and group II, and between group II and group IV.


## Dating of the Major Events in the Evolution of the Shaker Family


The sequencing of the Arabidopsis thaliana genome has enabled the identification and analysis of duplicated and translocated chromosome regions (Blanc et al. 2000; Vision et al. 2000). AKT1, AKT2, and GORK are located in nonduplicated regions. AtKC1 and SKOR are located in regions that have been duplicated, but no similar channel can be found in the corresponding twin region, suggesting that one copy of each pair may have disappeared during evolution (Ku et al. 2000). This could signify that these five genes appeared before the most ancient detectable duplication event, i.e., more than 200 million years ago (Mya) (Vision et al. 2000). Only the two members of the pairs $S P I K / A K T 5$ and $K A T I / K A T 2$ are located in duplicated regions; the corresponding duplication events are considered to have happened 125 and 150 Mya, respectively (Vision et al. 2000). This is in good agreement with the short evolutionary distances separating the members of these two pairs in the phylogenetic trees.

The tree in Fig. 3 shows that the sequences corresponding to Shaker channels from monocots (maize, rice, and wheat) do not form specific groups but are included in the five groups previously defined by the analysis of the Arabidopsis sequences. On the contrary, the protein encoded by a cDNA from $P$ . patens does not fall into the previously identified groups. This suggests that the divergence between the five groups occurred before the monocot– dicot separation (180–220 Mya [see Vision et al. 2000]) and after the separation of the bryophytes and the tracheophytes ${ \sim } 4 2 0$ Mya [Kenrick and Crane 1997]). The completion of the sequencing of other plant genomes and the isolation of complete sequences of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels from gymnosperms and ferns would help to refine the date of the separation of the groups.

The number of members of each group is not conserved across the species, as there are three group II members in rice, two in Arabidopsis, and one in grapevine (Pratelli et al. 2002), at least two group III members in S. saman (SPICK1 and SPICK2) and one in Arabidopsis and rice, and two group I members in rice and three in Arabidopsis. The dating of the duplications in Arabidopsis showed that the $K A T I /$ KAT2 and SPIK/AKT5 separations are relatively recent and may have happened long after the separation of the various angiosperm species (and after the monocot/dicot separation). The SPICK1 and SPICK2 proteins are closely related. Therefore, it can also be postulated that the SPICK1 and SPICK2 genes separated only recently. It is interesting to note that they are expressed in pulvinus cells of Samanea saman and may thus be involved in rhythmic leaf movements (Moshelion et al. 2002). This role is different from that of the other characterized group II members (AKT2, $Z { \mathrm { m K } } 2$ , VFK1), expressed in phloem cells and supposed to be involved in phloem loading and unloading (Marten et al. 1999; Lacombe et al. 2000b; Bauer et al. 2000; Ache et al. 2001). Such a difference in expression patterns and roles of close homologues can also be observed in group I. This emphasizes the fact that during evolution some channels, despite retaining overall functional properties similar to those of the channels of the same group, have also acquired specific features (regulation and localization of expression) corresponding to plant needs. This kind of divergence could have happened in very closely related plants, namely, tomato and potato, as the close homologues LKT1 and SKT1 are endowed with identical functional properties but different expression patterns and functions (Hartje et al. 2000; Zimmermann et al. 2001).


## Evolution from an Ancestral Gene: The Particular Evolution of Groups IV and $V$


The evolution of several multigenic families is thought to involve successive duplications of an ancestral gene. The sequences of these genes diverged and the intron positions changed by insertion and deletion processes (Frugoli et al. 1998; Matthews and Trotman 1998; Robertson 1998). As mentioned previously, the Physcomitrella patens PpK1 channel may have diverged before the determination of the five groups. This sequence is of interest for finding some characteristics of a Shaker-like ancestor common to the present higher plants. Unfortunately, the sequence of the gene encoding the $\mathrm { P p K } 1$ channel is not identified and the intron positions cannot be localized. Nevertheless, the structure of the ancestral gene can be hypothesized from the data currently available. This gene is likely to possess introns at the positions that are currently common to different groups in monocot and dicot genes, namely, positions 1/2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10,11, 12, 13, 16, 17, and 21. These positions are also predicted to be ancestral features by the two phylogeny programs we used. Also, the comparison of the sequence and the structure of $\mathrm { P p K } 1$ with the angiosperm channels provides insight into what could have been the structure of the ancestral polypeptide. PpK1 possesses the six regions identified in the higher plant genes. Its R5 region contains a clear ankyrin domain, composed of five and a half repetitions of the ankyrin motif. This suggests that the structure of the ancestor was similar to that of the present proteins of groups I, III, and V, with an ankyrin domain in R5. With regard to this hypothesis, the two repetitions of the ankyrin motif of VvSIRK (in group II, it is the only ankyrin motif-displaying channel identified so far) might be seen as a remainder of the ancestral ankyrin domain of group II (and IV) channels.

We showed a relationship between the distances that separates the various proteins and the corresponding genes: the conservation of intron positions between two genes increases with the similarity of the encoded proteins (if the postulated ‘‘anomaly’’ of group $\mathrm { I I / I V }$ is not taken into account; see below). This is not a unique fact in Arabidopsis. In at least four multigenic families, the genes can be classified in to similar groups according to their splicing pattern or to protein sequence similarities (thioredoxins [Sahrawy et al. 1996; Meyer et al. 2002], cytochromes P450 [Paquette et al. 2000], syntaxins [Sanderfoot et al. 2000], DEAD-box helicases [Boudet et al. 2001], expansins [Li et al. 2002]). It cannot be said whether the relationships between gene structures and protein sequences are as conserved in these families as in the Shaker family, as no such analysis has been published.

When considering the relationships linking the distances between protein sequences and gene structure, it can be postulated that group I, III, and V genes evolved in the same way because the datapoints are situated on the same line (Fig. 4B). The distance separating the structure of the present genes and the common ancestor (defined above) has been calculated. Groups I, II/IV, and III are all situated at approximately the same distance from this ancestral state, whereas group V genes are more distant. One can imagine either that group V separated before the determination of the other groups or that group V genes evolved more rapidly than the other ones. The latter hypothesis implies that the evolution rates of coding sequences and intron positions have been enhanced together in the same way. This seems improbable because the evolution of the intron position is thought to be slower than that of the coding sequence (Betts et al. 2001). This particular evolution of group $\mathrm { v }$ is probably related to the totally different functional properties of the channels in this group (outward rectifiers).

In the trees constructed from the Shaker polypeptides, group IV sequences are clearly separated from the others and close to group V channels (Fig. 3). On the contrary, the intron patterns of the genes of groups II and IV are very close (Fig. 4A). It has been shown that conserved introns can be the track of an ancient common origin of genes, even if there is little sequence similarity between the encoded proteins (Betts et al. 2001). Several other characteristics suggest a common origin for groups II and IV: the corresponding channels are the only ones in the family that do not harbor any ankyrin domain, although it is probably an ancestral trait (see above); it has been shown that KDC1 (group IV) has inward rectifying properties, like group II proteins (Downey et al. 2000); and the graph in Fig. 4B shows clearly that the relation between these two groups is different from the relations between the other groups. This means that the protein sequences of the channels of these two groups diverged from each other much more rapidly than did the intron positions. This evolution scheme is different from what has been shown for the other groups in the family. The causes and the implications of this fact remain to be examined. More functional data on group IV channels are needed to validate this hypothesis and to understand in what fashion group IV channels are different from, or similar to group II channels. The identification of full sets of Shaker channel families from plant species belonging to other phyla (ferns, gymnosperms, etc.) will help to characterize and to date the evolution of group II/IV and the evolution of group V.


## Evolution of the Plant Shaker Family in Relation to the Other 6TM Channel Families


This attempt to investigate the evolution of the Shaker-like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels in Arabidopsis and in the plant kingdom should also be considered as part of an analysis that aimed at understanding the evolution of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels in the living world (i.e., taking into account other plant, animal, and prokaryotic channels).

The plant Shaker-like channels display similarities to the other 6TM $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels only in the membrane domain and often exclusively in the transmembrane segments (S1–S6 and the pore domain). We used the most conserved sequences (the sequences of the pore and of the S6 segment) to construct a reliable phylogeny. Interestingly, all the proteins in the closest families (KCNH, HCN, CNG, and CNGC families) identified by this analysis possess a cyclic nucleotide binding domain in their C-terminal part which is similar to that of the plant Shaker-like channels. This suggests that the latter channels evolved from an ancestor common to all these families, different from the one that led to the Kv, KCNQ, and KCNN families. It is noteworthy that in most of the animal Shaker-like families, the channels are endowed with outward rectification (KCNN, KCNQ, Kv, KCNH, KCNM), whereas few of them are composed of inward rectifiers (HCN family). On the contrary, the plant family is the only one presenting a particular evolution that led to either inward, weak, or outward rectifiers, all of them sharing a similar structure and high sequence similarities.

The eukaryotic 6TM $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels are thought to have arisen from a prokaryotic channel (Derst and Karschin 1998). The evolution, diversification, and modification of this ancestral gene led to great diversity in the structures and functions of cationic channels, i.e., not only $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels, but also $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels, which are considered to come from the tandem duplications of ancestral 6TM channel genes (Anderson and Greenberg 2001). In this context, it would be interesting to analyze whether other channel families evolved in the particular way of the plant Shaker channels or whether this family really represents a specific and unusual evolution scheme.

Potassium $( \mathrm { K } ^ { + } )$ is the most prevalent cation and constitutes approximately $1 0 \%$ of the dry weight of plants. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ plays roles in multiple processes, including electrical neutralization of anionic groups, control of membrane polarization, and regulation of osmotic pressure in the cell. Water potential and turgor pressure of plant cells is regulated mainly by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and release. Thus, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake, transport, export and storage have to be regulated elaborately in response to environmental changes.

Over the past decades several different families of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters have been identified, such as shaker-like, KCO, and KUP/HAK/KT transporters and HKTs in plants (Maser et al. 2001; Very and Sentenac 2003). Among them, shakerlike $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels mainly regulate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in plants (Hedrich 2012). AtKAT1, of the shaker-like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel family, was the first channel for which the cDNA was cloned in plants (Anderson et al. 1992). The shaker-like gene family consists of nine members in Arabidopsis. The members are classified into three subgroups based on their current rectification properties in Arabidopsis: inward, weakly inward, or outward (Very and Sentenac 2003). KAT1, KAT2, AKT1 and SIPK are inward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels. KAT1 regulates stomatal opening by uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , which increases the osmotic pressure in guard cells (Very and Sentenac 2003). AKT1 is involved in high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake through the root in Arabidopsis (Nieves-Cordones et al. 2014). SIPK is involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in pollen and pollen tube development (Mouline et al. 2002). Seven of nine shaker-like $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels have characteristics of inward rectifiers and only two channels, stelar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ outward rectifier (SKOR) and guard cell outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel (GORK) are known to be outwardrectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Very and Sentenac 2003). SKOR is expressed in root stelar tissues and loads $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the xylem, whereas GORK is expressed in guard cells and induces stomatal closing through $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ export from guard cells in Arabidopsis (Gaymard et al. 1998; Ache et al. 2000).

Although more than 30 genes from ${ \sim } 1 0$ plant species have been identified for inward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels, only 5 genes from 4 species are known for outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels. These comprise GORK and SKOR in Arabidopsis thaliana, PTORK (Populous tremula outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel), SPORK (Samanea saman pulvinus outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel) and ZORK (Zea mays outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel) ( Gaymard et al. 1998; Ache et al. 2000; Moshelion and Moran 2000; Langer et al. 2002; Buchsenschutz et al. 2005). To characterize outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels in rice, a model plant for monocots, we isolated two candidate outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels based on amino acid similarity and analyzed their tissue-specific expression patterns and subcellular localization. Our findings supported the classification of two outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels, OsGORK and OsSKOR, in rice.

Aluminum (Al)-induced organic acid excretion has been convincingly demonstrated as a major mechanism of Al resistance through Al exclusion in many plant species (Ma et al. 2001; Kochian et al. 2015). The first resistance gene in plants was cloned from wheat as

TaALMT1 (aluminum-activated malate transporter) encoding an ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate channel (Sasaki et al. 2004). Citrate transporters responsible for Alactivated citrate efflux were later identified by positional cloning in sorghum (SbMATE, multidrug and toxic compound extrusion, Magalhaes et al. 2007) and barley (HvAACT1,aluminum-activated citrate transported 1, Furukawa et al. 2007), respectively; these transporters are the members of the multi-drug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family. Transgenic Arabidopsis and tobacco showed enhanced Al resistance with the overexpression of SbMATE (Magalhaes et al. 2007) and HvAACT1 (Furukawa et al. 2007), respectively. The transporter genes of the MATE and ALMT families can provide effective ways to enhance the Al resistance of plants. Unravelling additional genes encoding organic acid anion transporters will help more crops to adapt to Al-stresses under acidic soil environments.

MATE transporters are proposed to be involved in a wide range of biological events including xenobiotic efflux, accumulation of alkaloids and flavonoids, iron translocation, Al detoxification and plant hormone signalling (Takanashi et al. 2014). The identified citrate transporter genes in the MATE family have been suggested to function in Al resistance or iron uptake or both. First, SbMATE (Magalhaese et al. 2007), AtMATE (Liu et al. 2009), BoMATE (Wu et al. 2014), EcMATE1 and EcMATE3 (Sawaki et al. 2013), OsFRDL4 (ferric reductase defective like 4, Yokosho et al. 2011), OsFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2016a) and ScFRDL2 (Yokosho et al. 2010), VuMATE1 (Yang et al. 2011), VuMATE2 (Liu et al. 2018), ZmMATE1 (Maron et al. 2010; Maron et al. 2013), FeMATE1 (Lei et al. 2017) were reported to be responsible for Al-activated citrate efflux under Al stress. Second, members such as AtFRD3 (Durrett et al. 2007), GmFRD3b (Rogers et al. 2009), OsFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2009) and ScFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2010), LjMATE1 (Takanashi et al. 2013) were found to be localized to either the root pericycle cell or the nodules and were responsible for Fe supply by assisting the translocation of Fe by providing citrate. Thirdly, it was reported that HvAACT1 and TaMATE1b were involved in both Fe translocation and ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxification (Fujii et al. 2012; Tovkach et al. 2013; Takanashi et al. 2014).

Various regulatory systems were found to control citrate transporter expression and thus function. The first group is represented by ZmMATE1. Its gene duplications determined their expression and thus citrate efflux (Maron et al. 2013). The second group is represented by HvAACT1 and TaMATE1b. HvAACT1, a citrate transporter in barley, provides primary transport of citrate into the root xylem for Fe translocation to the shoot as a Fe-citrate complex in the mature root zones (Fujii et al. 2012). The insertion of a $1 \ \mathrm { k b }$ transposon in the $5 ^ { \prime }$ upstream region of $H _ { { \nu } A A } { \cal A } C T I$ changed its distribution and density to facilitate citrate secretion from the root apex to the rhizosphere for Al detoxification (Fujii et al. 2012). Fujii et al. (2018) also found that retrotransposon insertion and DNA methylation in the upstream genomic region are involved in regulating the expression of $H _ { { \nu } A A } { \cal A } C T I$ then Al resistance in barley especially distributed in European areas with acid soil. A transposonlike element in Triticum aestivum increased citrate transporter TaMATE1B expression in root apex, where it facilitates citrate efflux and enhances Al tolerance (Tovkach et al. 2013). The third group is represented by AtMATE and VuMATE1. Their expression is regulated by Cys2His2 zinc finger-type transcription factor STOP1 (sensitive to proton rhizotoxicity1). The expression of AtMATE is regulated by the transcription factor AtSTOP1 (Liu et al. 2009). Yeast one-hybrid examination has shown that there is an interaction between VuSTOP1 and the promoter region of VuMATE1and VuMATE2 (Yang et al. 2011; Fan et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2018). A $1 . 2 \ \mathrm { k b }$ insertion in the OsFRDL4 promoter region in the rice japonica subspecies increased the number of cis-acting elements of ART1 then enhanced OsFRDL4 expression level, but did not alter its spatial expression or cellular localization (Yokosho et al. 2016b).

Multiple Al resistance mechanisms have been suggested to be involved in Al resistance in soybean (Nian et al. 2004). Correspondingly, multigenetic traits have been suggested to relate to mechanisms underlying Al resistance in soybean by genetic studies (Bianci-Hall et al. 1998, 2000). Compared with the progress made in other important crops and model plant species, little was known about the molecular mechanisms of Al resistance in soybean. Al-induced citrate efflux has been well established as an Al resistance mechanism in soybean (Yang et al. 2000, 2001; Silva et al. 2001). Liu et al. (2016) identified and named a total of 117 genes encoding MATE transporters in the whole soybean genome, which are unevenly distributed on the 20 soybean chromosomes. However, the citrate transporter responsible for citrate efflux from soybean under Al stress has not been identified until now.

Rogers et al. (2009) showed that GmFRD3a and GmFRD3b were induced by iron deficiency in an ironefficient soybean cultivar. GmFRD3b , but not GmFRD3a, was expressed at higher levels in the ironefficient cultivar than its iron-inefficient near-isogenic line, and thus GmFRD3b is suggested to function similarly to AtFRD3 to mediate citrate efflux into the xylem. Their function has not been further characterized until now. Our previous microarray analysis found a MATEfamily transcript (GmMATE75) was up-regulated by Al treatment in the Al-tolerant genotype Jiyu 70 (You et al. 2011) which was also predicated to be the candidate Al tolerance gene according to its gene expression pattern and cis-elements (Liu et al. 2016). The expression of GmALCT1 (GmMATE 79) was also highly induced in soybean root apices under Al stress (Xu et al. 2010). In the present study, we compared three genes in the MATE family, GmMATE75, GmMATE79 and GmMATE87 (GmFRD3a), to reveal their functions in the process of Al-induced citrate efflux from soybean root apices.

Almost half of the world’s arable land has acidic pH. Aluminum salts present in acid soils dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution that inhibit root growth causing severe loss in crop yields. Aluminium toxicity accounts for the second highest loss in plant productivity after drought. Aluminium in high doses causes damage to the plant cell wall, cytoskeleton and DNA. One of the ways by which plants alleviate aluminium toxicity is by the exudation of citrate from the roots that chelates the free $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and prevents its entry into the plant. In several crop plants Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporters regulate citrate exudation from the roots. The MATE proteins are ubiquitously present in bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants. The origin and evolution of these membrane transporters in plants is not well known. Here, using protein sequence information we identify MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors. Our study indicates that the MATE family members expanded in number and functionally diverse among the land plants. We also identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade and a conserved aspartate residue that might regulate citrate exudation. This study can provide leads to engineer MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance in acid soils.

The sessile lifestyle of plants makes them susceptible to multiple biotic and abiotic stresses. Abiotic stresses like high temperature, drought, flooding, nutrient scarcity, xenobiotics, drugs and metal toxicity in soil can severely affect plant growth and reduce yields. While the role of low or high temperature, water availability and nutrients has been studied a lot, an aspect that has comparatively received less attention is the role of soil $\mathrm { p H }$ on agricultural productivity. Almost $50 \%$ of the land used for food production is acidic in nature. Aluminium salts that are very abundant in the soil dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution, which inhibit root elongation and severely affect plant growth and productivity. This is known as Aluminium toxicity and accounts for the second highest loss in yields after drought (Kochian et al. 2004; Bojo´rquez-Quintal et al. 2017). Aluminium-mediated inhibition of root elongation primarily involves damage to the cell wall (pectin, hemicellulose), cytoskeleton elements (actin, microtubules) and also double stranded breaks in the nuclear DNA (Kar et al. 2021).

Plants adopt several morphological and biochemical modifications to counter different stresses. Plants enhance tolerance to aluminium toxicity by either sequestration or exclusion of aluminium. Several membrane-localized transporters play an important role in these tolerance responses. The ABC transporters, vacuolar ATPases and aquaporins mediate aluminium sequestration inside the vacuoles. Exudation of carboxylates like malate and citrate by the Aluminium Activated Malate Transporter (ALMT) and the Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporter respectively, helps the plant to exclude aluminium. The MATE proteins are ubiquitous in nature and present across all life forms including bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Here we have used the protein sequence information to identify the presence of MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors (Fig. 2). While the MATE family members expanded in the land plants we identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade. We observed a conserved aspartate residue responsible for cation efflux one of the motifs that might play an important role in citrate exudation (Table 1, Figs. 2, 3). Future prospects of engineering MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + - }$ in acid soils are also discussed here.

MATE transporters play important roles in cellular detoxification mechanisms in several species. They belong to the multidrug transporter family consisting of the ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) superfamily, major facilitator superfamily (MFS), small multidrug resistance (SMR) family, resistance nodulation cell division (RND) family, and proteobacterial antimicrobial compound efflux (PACE) family (Putman et al. 2000). NorM from Vibrio parahaemolyticus and YdhE its homologue in $E$ . coli, were found to be topologically different from MFS transporters, and were identified as the first MATE transporters (Morita et al. 1998; Brown et al. 1999). In bacteria, MATEs were classified under multidrug/ oligosaccharidyl lipid/ polysaccharide (MOP) exporter superfamily (Hvorup et al. 2003). Since its discovery in bacteria, multiple research on this newly identified transporter family have identified the presence of MATE transporters in archaea as well as eukaryotes including fungi, plants and animals (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Though these genes share a weak sequence similarity, they can be identified using the MatE domain (PF01554). The MATE proteins are membrane embedded and consist of about 400–700 amino acids residues generally forming 12 transmembrane helices. MATEs are further classified in terms of their structure into three distinct types, NorM, DinF and eukaryotic MATES (eMATEs). NorM and eMATE share conserved acidic residues at the C-terminal end whereas NorM and DinF share conserved acidic residues at the N-terminal end of the MATE proteins (Miyauchi et al. 2017). The ubiquitous presence of MATEs in unicellular and multicellular life forms might suggest its importance in the basic cellular processes. These membrane localized transporters primarily mediate cationic efflux (Morita et al. 2000). They regulate cation transport utilizing the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ electrochemical gradient as their driving force. Norfloxacin, ethidium bromide (EtBr), berberine, tetraphenylphosphonium, acriflavine are some of the cationic substrates transported by bacterial MATEs (Morita et al. 2000; Braibant et al. 2002; Chen et al. 2002).

In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, ERC1 type MATE transporter confers resistance to ethionine (Shiomi et al. 1991). In humans, presence of two MATE transporters hMATE1 and hMATE2 are involved in the transport of tetraethylammonium using proton gradient (Otsuka et al. 2005a). In plants they function in transport of secondary metabolites, phytohormones, organic acids along with roles in developmental processes and xenobiotic detoxification (Upadhyay et al. 2019).

We further looked at the expansion and distribution of MATE family of proteins in different bacterial and plant species (Fig. 1). (Fig. 1b). In Pseudomonas aeruginosa there are two MATE subtype transporters under MOP superfamily, while Escherichia coli has three. On the other hand, Arabidopsis thaliana and Glycine max contain 58 and 117 MATE transporters respectively. This might be correlated to the genome size. The small prokaryote genomes have relatively less number of genes coding for these transporters whereas the larger eukaryotic genomes have a greater number of paralogs resulting in expansion of the MATE family (Ren and Paulsen 2005). With the increasing cellular complexity, plants MATEs might have evolved to transport a broader range of substrates from cations to phytohormones, secondary metabolites, organic acids and anions. Regardless of the number of MATE proteins present, the evolutionary conservation of this group of proteins suggests its pivotal role in multidrug resistance and developmental roles across life forms (Fig. 1).

In order to understand better the expansion of the MATE family of proteins among different groups of land plants and their algal ancestors we used available genome sequences from red algae to angiosperms and identified the number of MATE genes in them. For each genome the retrieved genes were verified using a domain search in Pfam database. Only hits with the MatE domain (Pf01554) were considered as potential MATE genes. We observed the expansion of MATE family of transporters specifically in plants. There was an increase in the number of MATE genes from rhodophyta to flowering plants across the evolutionary timeline (Table 1). Red algae have 1–2 MATEs, while members of chlorophyta and charophyta have an average of 10 and 15 MATEs respectively. Chlamydomonas and Chara both have 16 MATE genes in their genome. Among the bryophytes, the first non-vascular land plants, Marchantia has 15 while Physcomitrella has 20 MATE proteins. The MATE family in the lycophyte Selaginella moelendorfii expands to 41 members and in the flowering plants the numbers are even higher. The expansion of the MATE family shows enormous variation both within the monocots and dicots. Rice and Wheat have 54 and 224 MATE proteins while Arabidopsis and Soybean have 58 and 117 of these transporters (Table 1). The change in habitat (movement of plants from water to land) exposed plants to multiple stresses inducing many developmental and genetic modifications. Whole genome duplications in plants might account for the rapid expansion of the MATE family across the evolutionary timeline. A report by Wang et al. (2016) suggests that the expansion of MATEs in Arabidopsis and rice might be a result of tandem and segmental duplication. The mapping of such tandem duplicated genes date back to the monocot dicot split (Wang et al. 2016). Despite a larger genome size, animal kingdom has not seen expansion of this family. Humans and rats have 2 MATE genes specifically involved in extrusion of toxic compounds from the body (Table 1). Hence, the expansion of MATE transporters in plants might be to allow plants to cope better while being sessile (Table 2).

MATE proteins in plants regulate a diverse array of functions, which involve transport of several substrates like secondary metabolites, xenobiotics, hormones, various cations and anions (Upadhyay 2019). A subset of MATE proteins regulates citrate efflux to promote aluminium detoxification. The organic acid exudation function of MATE transporters is well reported in plants like Arabidopsis, sorghum, barley, wheat, rice and soybean (Magalhaes et al. 2007; Liu et al. 2009, 2016; Yokosho et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2013; Qiu et al. 2019). Although the primary function of the exuded citrate in several of these species is to alleviate aluminium toxicity, citrate might play other roles like phosphate mobilization especially in species that are inherently aluminium tolerant like rice. A citrate exuding motif has been identified in 28 MATE proteins in angiosperms that regulate citrate efflux in response to aluminium toxicity (Upadhyay et al. 2019). Furthermore, all the citrate exuding MATEs contain a conserved aspartate (D) residue within the motif (Doshi et al. 2017). Since we identified several MATE proteins in early land plants, we next wanted to examine the conservation of this D-containing motif in early plants. Since MATEs share a weak sequence similarity in the early plants the hits were checked for the presence of Pfam domain (PF01554) also. We then performed the motif scan in MEME with default parameters (number of motifs set to 3) using these orthologs, AtMATE, AtFRD3 and SbMATE (Bailey and Elkan 1994). Our search identified three motifs containing conserved D residues in all the AtMATE orthologs (Fig. 2). This included a N-terminal motif indicated in red and $2 \textrm { C }$ -terminal motifs indicated in blue and green respectively (Fig. 2). The D residue located within the N-terminal motif (red) that was conserved in citrate exuding flowering plants was found to be present from Chlamydomonacae $C .$ . reinhardtii) onwards (Fig. 3). The two C-terminal motifs containing the D residues were even found in the red algal lineages. The conservation of these motifs and the D residue across evolution of land plants suggests that citrate exudation might have a critical functional relevance in land plant adaptation. We further wanted to know if the position of this conserved motif and the D residue is similar in all AtMATE orthologs. We performed sequence homology modeling of these orthologs using Phyre (Kelley et al. 2015). The pdb structures were then opened using PyMOL and the D residue was selected to denote its position (Fig. 3b). The structural modeling of these orthologous proteins also showed a similar location of the motif and the conserved D residue suggesting similar mode of functioning. We further proceeded in obtaining clarity about the posirtion of this Asp residue. We used TOPCONS, a transmembrane helix predicting software to predict the number of transmembrane helices in these orthologs and also the exact amino acid distribution in the helix orientations (inside to outside or vice-versa) (Tsirigos et al.

2015). We looked for the MATEs from $P$ . patens to S.bicolor, and we identified 12 transmemebrane helices in all the transporters (Fig. 3d). The tool also predicted that the Asp residue is located in the outer loop of the first transmembrane helix of all the selected MATE transporters from bryophytes to angiosperms (Fig. 3c). This prediction suggests further conservation of the location of the Asp residue to retain its function throughout the evolutionary timeline.

Citrate permeable MATEs with a mutated Asp residue had a reduced organic cation efflux rate than the wild type allele (Doshi et al. 2017). This residue was homologous to NorM $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ driven MATE cation efflux transporter. In prokaryotes, the Asp36 from NorM of Vibrio chlorae is highly conserved among NorM and DinF types. Though Asp36 was not found to be directly involved in substrate transport using $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ gradient, mutation of this residue resulted in impaired transport activity (Otsuka et al. 2005b;

Jin et al. 2014; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Also, Asp41of Pyrococcus furiosus MATE $( P f M A T E )$ from DinF subtype is conserved among NorM and DinF types. This residue when mutated results in reduced drug and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport (Tanaka et al. 2013; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Hence, this ability of all citrate permeable MATEs to permit both efflux of cations and anions indicated the broad substrate specificity of this transporter family. In plants, the citrate permeable MATEs are generally localized at the cell membrane of roots. It is probable that the AtMATE orthologs in early plants might have undergone selection pressure when plants colonized land and started developing roots to anchor and assimilate nutrients at the same time exclude toxic substances. This study provides an insight on how MATE transporters retain some of the conserved function from their bacterial ancestors while expanding and diversifying in plants. In the future, studies involving mutations in some of the conserved residues can help elucidate the functional relevance of these traditional transporters. It would be exciting how we might be able to engineer the MATE transporters to enhance stress resilience in plants growing under acidic conditions. As (Kawasaki et al. 2021) has shown the effects of root exudates on root microbiome affecting the growth of plant by altering the expression of ALMT and MATE in O.sativa further transporter engineering can also be used to induce synthetic signaling approaches to alleviate the effects of abiotic stress created by enhanced anthorpogenic activity and changing climatic conditions.

## GmMATE75, GmMATE79 and GmMATE87 are all citrate transporters conferring citrate efflux from soybean roots


The 22 reported citrate transporters in the MATE family were conserved between dicots and monocots, but loosely correlated with their known biological functions, such as Al resistance or Fe acquisition (Fig. S1, Fig. S2). GmMATE79, GmMATE75 and GmMATE87 showed the highest similarities to AtMATE (Liu et al. 2009), VuMATE1 (Liu et al. 2013) and LjMATE (Takanashi et al. 2013) respectively (Fig. S2). The former two are Al-activated citrate transporters that conferred Al-induced citrate efflux in Arabidopsis andrice bean, respectively (Liu et al. 2009; Yang et al. 2011), and the latter was a citrate transporter responsible for iron supply to the nodule infection zone of Lotus japonicus (Takanashi et al. 2013).

Consistent with the above multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree, subcellular localization analysis in Arabidopsis protoplast verified that GmMATE79, GmMATE75 and GmMATE87 are all localized to the plasma membrane (Fig. 4). CaMV 35S promoter-driven overexpression of GmMATE75, GmMATE79 or GmMATE87 in soybean hairy roots, Arabidopsis or Arabidopsis mutant all resulted in increased citrate efflux under either –Al or + Al stress (Figs. 5, 6, and 7). Thus, we speculated each of GmMATE79, GmMATE75 or GmMATE87 have the capability to release citrate. The lower Al content in GmMATE75-OE, GmMATE79-OE or GmMATE87-OE soybean hairy roots (Fig. 5g), and higher relative root elongation in Arabidopsis GmMATE75-OE, GmMATE79-OE, GmMATE87-OE (Fig. 6) or GmMATE75-CE, GmMATE79-CE, GmMATE87-CE (Fig. 7) also indicated their acquirement of Al exclusion and Al resistance.

There existed an approximately $4 \textrm { h }$ lag phase preceding a large amount of citrate efflux and Al exposure in soybean (Yang et al. 2001), which was clearly classified in pattern II (Ma et al. 2001). Citrate exudation was non-detectable by HPLC when soybean was grown in the absence of Al (Silva et al. 2001; Yang et al. 2001). A small amount of citrate efflux from soybean roots can be detected after $^ { 2 \mathrm { h } }$ or $^ { 3 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ Al treatment (Silva et al. 2001; Yang et al. 2001). However, in the present study, the more sensitive enzymatic assay detected some citrate efflux from both wild-type and transgenic hairy roots without Al treatment. GmMATE75-OE, GmMATE79- OE or GmMATE87-OE hairy roots each with higher transcript levels of GmMATEs (Fig. 5a-c), secreted more citrate without Al treatment compared to the untransformed hairy roots (Fig. 5d-f). GmMATE75, GmMATE79 and GmMATE87 constitutively contribute to citrate efflux and do not require Al activation, which is similar to AtFRD3 overexpression in barley but different from $H { \nu } A A C T I$ or SbMATE with necessarity of Al to activate citrate efflux (Zhou et al. 2014).

CaMV 35S was used to constitutively express the MATE proteins, thus abrogating the tissue specific localization factor, which has been regarded as critical in determining their biological functions in Fe acquisition or Al detoxification (Yokosho et al. 2011; Maron et al. 2010; Fujii et al. 2012). For example, AtFRD3 functions as a citrate transporter mainly facilitating Fe acquisition (Durrett et al. 2007), but its CaMV 35S -driven overexpression can enhance Al resistance in Arabidopsis (Durrett et al. 2007) and barley (Zhou et al. 2014). VuMATE1 was proven as citrate transporter conferring Al resistance (Fan et al. 2015). But, complementation of frd3–1 with CaMV 35S mediated VuMATE1 expression could restore its Fe deficiency phenotype (Liu et al. 2016). Thus, tissue expression or Cis-regualtion of citrate transporters seemed to play more important role in determining their biological function.

Considering that citrate need to release to rhizosphere to protect Al injury, GmMATE75 and GmMATE79 might be more important in Al detoxifying for soybean. MATE family citrate transporters are complex. STOP1/ ART1 type transcription was reported to regulate citrate transporter genes such as AtMATE (Liu et al. 2009), VuMATE1and VuMATE2 (Yang et al. 2011; Fan et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2018) and OsFRDL4 (Yokosho et al. 2016b). Its regulation was affected by other factors. WRKY22 was found to function together with ART1 in regulation of OsFRDL4 (Li et al. 2018). An F-box protein-encoding gene regulation of Atalmt1 expression 1 (RAE1) was reported to interact with and promote the degradation of AtSTOP1 via the ubiquitin-26S proteasome pathway (Zhang et al. 2018). Even Jiyu 70 and Jiyu 62 displayed same GmSTOP1a sequence and very similar expression pattern under Al stress (Data not shown). We can’t ensure the homologies of GmSTOP1a or other genes such as WRKY or RAE1 displayed same sequence and expression pattern between Jiyu 70 and Jiyu 62; (2) The capacity of GmMATEs regulation also depended on promoter length. Typically, very important regulatory elements including transponson insertion or DNA methylation localized at more than 5000 bp upstream of $5 '$ UTR of HvAACT1 (Fujii et al. 2012, 2018). More effective regulatory elements were expected to reveal in promotor regions of GmMATEs.

Fine-tuning root citrate secretion with two separate root citrate transport systems was reported in rice bean to regulate biphasic Al-induced citrate efflux (Liu et al. 2018). The constitutively expressed VuMATE2 and Alincreased expressed VuMATE1 were respectively suggested to be responsible for the early phase of minor citrate secretion and late phase of large amount citrate efflux under Al stress (Liu et al. 2018). In present study, the rapid and strong induction of GmMATE75 is similar to or even greater than that of OsFRDL4 (Yokosho et al. 2011). Its expression was greatly induced at $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ A l treatment (near 100-fold) and reached approximately 500-fold at $^ { 8 \mathrm { h } }$ (Fig. 1a). GmMATE79 (Fig. 1b) was also induced after $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 2 b }$ Al treatment with lower level as AtMATE (Liu et al. 2009), ZmMATE1 (Maron et al. 2010) and ScFRDL2 (Yokosho et al. 2010), but decreased its expression in the following Al treatment duration. According to their expression patterns, we propose as follows: the constitutive expression and smaller increase of GmMATE79 and GmMATE75 expression resulted in minor citrate efflux from soybean roots under no Al or less than $^ { 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ Al treatment. However, the large amount of Al-induced citrate efflux after $^ \mathrm { ~ 4 ~ h ~ }$ might result from the strong induction of GmMATE75. The higher expression of GmMATE75 in

Jiyu70 (Fig. 1) could also partially explain the genotypic difference that Jiyu 70 secreted more citrate than Jiyu 62 after $^ { 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ Al treatment (Zhou et al. 2018a).

The origin of the Al-induced citrate efflux pattern in soybean roots is complex. (1) The contribution of citrate metabolism to citrate efflux can not be neglected. Our previous study has shown that cytosolic malic enzyme (GmME1) contributed to internal citrate content then Alinduced citrate efflux from soybean (Zhou et al. 2018a). GmME1 displayed higher expression in Jiyu70 in comparison to Jiyu62 under Al stress (Zhou et al. 2018a) (2) The contribution of the other putative soybean citrate transporters has not been clarified; (3) More effective regulatory elements might exist in 5’UTR-uptream of GmMATEs to promote the high expression of GmMATEs under Al stress. Jiyu 70 was bred from Jilin province of China with less acidic soils and exhibited moderate Al resistance. Efficient regulation of GmMATEs mechanisms deserved to be revealed in soybean cultivars with higher Al resistance capability. The genetics studies have revealed the complexity of Al-induced citrate efflux mechanisms in soybean. Some quantitative trait loci analyses have indicated that Al tolerance in soybean is a multigene trait (Abdelhaleem et al. 2014; Sharma et al. 2010; Qi et al. 2008). Using recombinant inbred lines (RILs) derived from the cross of ‘Essex’ with ‘Forrest’ identified two major loci encompassing genes implicated in citrate metabolism (Sharma et al. 2010). The population originating from $\mathrm { Y o u n g } \times \mathrm { P I } 4 1 6 9 3 7$ identified sixteen single nucleotide polymorphisms in the citrate synthase homologue on chromosome $\mathrm { G m 0 8 }$ (Abdelhaleem et al. 2014). However, no genetic report has stated the loci or genes conferring citrate transport implicated in Al resistance in soybean until now.

In summary, GmMATE75, GmMATE79 and GmMATE87 are proposed as plasma-membranelocalized citrate transporters, having capability to release citrate efflux under $- \mathbf { A l } \mathbf { \Pi } _ { 0 \mathbf { r } + \mathbf { A l } }$ stress. Their additive effects might contribute to Al-induced citrate efflux from soybean. Their expression levels were also affected under iron deficiency conditions, but their functions in iron acquisition are not discussed here.
