## Transport of $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ (Rb+ ) fits a three-compartment model in Arabidopsis


To characterize the transport processes that underlie root and shoot accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , we first measured time courses of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ uptake. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into Arabidopsis roots resembled typical measurements of cation uptake into excised roots and storage tissues. We therefore fitted a three-compartment model comprising the root cytosol, root vacuole and the shoot (as previously described in wheat, Davenport et al. 2005). The model was based on the classical ‘four-compartment’ model used to describe fluxes in algal cells and in roots with a xylem compartment, where uptake into an initial root compartment is followed by uptake in parallel into two compartments (in our model the vacuole and shoot) (Walker & Pitman 1976). The initial linear phase of uptake was attributed to unidirectional $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx across the plasma membrane of root cells, resulting in rapid labelling of the root cytosol. The second, slower linear phase of uptake was attributed to influx across the tonoplast to root vacuoles (which assumed a constant rate once the cytosol was approximately fully radioactively labelled). This model assumes that tonoplast fluxes of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ were much slower than fluxes across the plasma membrane, as is commonly assumed for plant cells. Alternatively the second linear phase could represent a second compartment within the root, such as the stele. We think that this is unlikely, given the relative sizes of the first and second compartments and the kinetics of uptake to the shoot. The first, rapidly saturating compartment was clearly small in volume compared to the slower compartment, which continued to fill over many hours (Fig. 3b). It is most likely that the first compartment represents the cytosol, or some portion of the cytosol that includes a stelar component, because it appears that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transported to the shoot derived from this compartment.

Transport of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ into the shoot occurred with a lag coinciding with the period required for labelling of the first compartment (Fig. 3a). Shoot uptake subsequently became linear (indicating full labelling of the compartment from which shoot loading occurred) and approximated the rate of unidirectional transfer from root to shoot. Root and shoot uptake continued for at least $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ with no evidence of saturation (Fig. 3b). The lag and then linearity in shoot uptake indicate that the first, rapidly exchanging compartment comprised the symplast from which xylem loading occurred, indicating that this compartment included a stelar component. The data also suggest that the second phase of root uptake did not contribute to shoot uptake, consistent with a vacuolar identity. A similar phenomenon was observed for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake in Spergularia marina (Lazof & Cheeseman 1986) and wheat (Davenport et al. 2005). It is of course possible that the apparently simple kinetics of uptake represented the summed contribution of many heterogeneous compartments; however, we think that there was a clear functional difference between the first ‘compartment’ that was in contact with the external medium and contributed to shoot uptake, and the second ‘compartment’ that did not have these characteristics. A similar model could describe $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -starved plants (Supplementary Fig. S1).


## AtHKT1;1 is not a ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ influx mechanism but affects root vacuolar $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ uptake


The rate of unidirectional influx into roots of intact control and $h k t l { ; } l$ plants (measured over the first $5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ of uptake) was similar in both genotypes (Fig. 4a). In contrast, the rate of vacuolar influx, estimated from the second linear component of root uptake $\left( { 2 0 - 6 0 \mathrm { m i n } } \right)$ , was much lower in hkt1;1 plants than controls (Fig. 4a).

Measurements of influx over $1 \mathrm { { h } }$ showed that the reduction of vacuolar accumulation in the hkt1;1 mutant was evident in low $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ but was more pronounced at high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (Fig. 4b). The plants were exposed to different $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ levels with only $1 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ pre-treatment, so $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ effects were probably not mediated by changes in gene expression. Rus et al. (2001, 2004) have shown that hkt1;1 mutations were more effective in suppressing the sos salt sensitivity phenotypes in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and attributed this to the lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake rates in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ conditions. $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ partially inhibits $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx into Arabidopsis roots, and this $\mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ -sensitive component has been attributed to influx via non-selective cation channels (Essah et al. 2003). One explanation of the present results is that the rate of vacuolar influx controlled by HKT1 was relatively constant (as suggested by the constancy of the absolute difference between control and hkt1;1 in the different $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments in Fig. 4b) and therefore comprised a larger fraction of vacuolar uptake in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ conditions, when total $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake and cytosolic $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were lower.

The inhibition of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake in hkt1;1 roots led to an almost $5 0 \%$ difference in root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation over $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ (Fig. 4c) and was also evident in excised roots of hkt1;1 (data not shown). The lower rate of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx into root vacuoles was consistent with the lower root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ content of hkt1;1 plants measured after $1 0 { \mathrm { d } } ^ { \prime }$ exposure to NaCl (Fig. 2c).

It should be noted that there were some differences in fluxes between different experiments. It is our experience that Arabidopsis is a difficult plant for physiological experimentation compared to, for example, wheat. As a result, there was a degree of variation from experiment to experiment, possibly because of differences in growth rates between hydroponic batches and in experimental conditions such as humidity (which was not controlled). Despite this, we found the relative differences between hkt1;1 mutants and controls to be highly reproducible, although the absolute rates of transport varied between experiments.


## AtHKT1;1 affects xylem transport of ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ , not recirculation


The unidirectional flux of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ to the shoot was much more rapid in hkt1;1 plants than controls (Fig. 5a). Because the kinetics of initial root influx and saturation of the cytosolic phase of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ accumulation appeared similar in both hkt1;1 and control (Fig. 4a), it was assumed that the specific activity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loaded into the xylem (from the cytosolic phase) was similar in both genotypes, and therefore that the measured fluxes represented actual rates of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ translocation. hkt1;1 plants accumulated approximately five times more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoot within $1 \mathrm { { h } }$ , and this difference was maintained and did not increase significantly over $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ (Fig. 5b), indicating that shoot $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ hyperaccumulation in hkt1;1 was the result of processes occurring early in the pathway of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake. The difference in the rate of unidirectional transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot between genotypes was sufficient to explain the differences in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content (Fig. 2c), without recourse to explanations involving recirculation.

To test whether recirculation could contribute to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration, the plants were loaded for $4 0 \mathrm { h }$ with $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ and were then transferred to unlabelled solution of the same composition and sampled over $^ { 5 2 \mathrm { h } }$ . Shoot $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ content declined by only $1 3 \%$ over $^ { 5 2 \mathrm { h } }$ in the control plants (although this difference was statistically not significant), and showed little change in hkt1;1 plants (Fig. 5c). These results suggest that recirculation, if it occurs at all, does not significantly affect total shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in Arabidopsis. Certainly, the elimination of a possible recirculation rate of $5 \mathrm { - } 1 0 \%$ per day in hkt1;1 plants could not account for the fivefold difference observed in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation between hkt1;1 and control plants over $4 0 \mathrm { { h } }$ of labelling. Root $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ content was low compared to shoot $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ and did not change after $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ of rinsing; therefore, translocation of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ from the roots to the shoot during the unlabelled rinse period could not have masked retranslocation.


## AtHKT1;1 affects ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ retrieval from the xylem


The rate of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivery to the shoot depends on the rate of efflux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the xylem from stelar cells, the rate of withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream back into root stelar cells, and the transpiration rate. The hkt1;1 mutant sas2 has been shown not to differ from control plants in transpiration rate under a range of humidity (Berthomieu et al. 2003). When only the apical portion of the root was exposed to $^ { 2 2 } \mathbf { N a } ^ { + } .$ -labelled solution (Fig. 6a), control and hkt1;1 plants exported approximately the same amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the apical root to the rest of the plant, suggesting that there was no difference in xylem loading, at least in this part of the root (Fig. 6b, ‘translocated’).

However, the amount translocated to the shoot was twofold greater in hkt1;1 compared with wild type (Fig. 6b, ‘shoot’) because twofold more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was withdrawn into the upper root in the control compared with hkt1;1 (Fig 6c, ‘unlab root’). Control plants were able to withdraw $4 4 \%$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the xylem before it reached the shoot, compared to $2 1 \%$ in hkt1;1 mutants (Fig. 6c, ‘unlab/translocated’), indicating that hkt1;1 plants were defective in the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem.


## Modelling $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ fluxes in control and hkt1;1 plants


Knockout of AtHKT1;1 produced two effects on $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport; a reduction in root putative vacuolar uptake and a reduction in $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ withdrawal from the xylem, and these effects were sufficient to explain the hkt1;1 phenotype of low root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Because $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes are interdependent, it was not possible to judge whether these effects arose from alteration of a single transport process or were independent without modelling the total transport system. The root was modelled as two compartments, cytosolic and vacuolar, and the root cytosol exchanged $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ with a third compartment representing the shoot. To model xylem retrieval, it was necessary to add a compartment to the model to represent xylem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ (Fig. 7). It was assumed that the fluxes between compartments depended on the amount of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in the source compartment (e.g. root vacuolar influx represented the proportion of root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transported to the vacuole per unit time, in the range 0.01– 0.5). We first determined a number of sets of parameter values (‘control’ sets) that yielded estimates of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation that approximated the kinetics observed in control plants (Figs 3a & 8a,c).We then mimicked the effect of mutation by altering a single flux over a wide range of values and estimated the effect on the rates of other fluxes and the content of compartments for each control set of parameters to determine whether a ‘mutation’ affecting a single flux could produce the mutant phenotype.

The model indicated that alteration of root vacuolar influx did reduce root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ but had little effect on shoot uptake (Fig. 8a,b).This was because altering vacuolar fluxes did not cause root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to rise, which was required to raise the rate of xylem loading or decrease retrieval (the latter could occur if the xylem: cytosol gradient became unfavourable for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ re-uptake – this was not explicitly modelled because the lack of change in cytosolic $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ precluded this possibility). Cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ did not rise because a reduction in vacuolar influx reduced vacuolar accumulation and produced a corresponding reduction in vacuolar efflux. This is usually the case in real plants, where root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration is often fairly constant over time in high NaCl (Tester & Davenport 2003), and therefore vacuolar fluxes must be in balance.

Alterations of xylem loading, xylem retrieval and recirculation were all able to reproduce the mutant phenotype to some degree (Fig. 8c,d).A reduction in xylem withdrawal caused a large increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation but only a small reduction in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into root vacuoles, too small to account for the nearly $5 0 \%$ reduction in root uptake measured in hkt1;1 plants. Moreover, the phenotype of reduced root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was evident even in excised roots, where there would be no removal of root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in the transpiration stream. The model therefore suggests that hkt1;1 mutations affected the two processes of vacuolar influx and xylem retrieval independently.


## AtHKT1;1 and SOS1 are not involved in root uptake of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (Rb+ )


The sos1 mutants have been reported to show inhibition of root growth in low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ on agar media and reduced $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake into whole seedlings fully immersed in $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ solution (Wu et al. 1996). Because AtHKT1;1 showed some evidence of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport activity (Uozumi et al. 2000), and because knockout of AtHKT1;1 rescued the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype (Rus et al. 2004), we compared $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation conditions in hydroponically grown control, sos1, hkt1;1 and sos1-hkt1;1 plants. There was no difference in uptake of $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ between genotypes from high or low RbCl solutions (Supplementary Fig. S2). It is possible that $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ was not transported in a manner fully analogous to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ; however, these data contradict the earlier report of reduced $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake in whole sos1 seedlings $\mathrm { W u }$ et al. 1996). In our hydroponic conditions, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation for $^ { 5 \mathrm { d } }$ did not produce a clear sos1 phenotype (data not shown) and therefore it is possible that we missed an effect of sos1 and hkt1;1 mutations on $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport that is only exhibited under certain conditions. Qi & Spalding (2004) were also unable to reproduce the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype of sos1 on agar plates except in the presence of millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . We found that we could reliably reproduce the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype in sos1 mutants grown on agar plates only when we supplied sucrose in the medium (Supplementary Fig. S3), but that millimolar $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were not required to produce the phenotype.

Salinization of soils represents a major threat to the maintenance of crop yields, because most crop species are sensitive to the accumulation of sodium $\left( \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \right)$ in shoot tissues (Tester & Davenport 2003). One focus of salinity research therefore is the mechanisms by which plants accumulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , a non-essential ion. Figure 1 shows the main pathways presumed to operate in the accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoot tissues. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ enters roots passively, via non-selective cation channels and possibly other $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters such as HKTs (Amtmann & Sanders, 1999; Tester & Davenport 2003; Haro et al. 2005). It is likely that most of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ that enters root cells in the outer part of the root is pumped back out again via plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Tester & Davenport 2003), and such a function has been demonstrated for the Arabidopsis protein SOS1 at the root apex (Qiu et al. 2003). $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ remaining in the root can be sequestered in vacuoles or transported to the shoot. Compartmentation in vacuoles is achieved by tonoplast $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters such as those belonging to the NHX family in Arabidopsis. Membranes exhibit bidirectional transport, and there is passive leakage of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ back to the cytosol from vacuoles (possibly via tonoplast non-selective cation channels), requiring constant re-sequestration of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ into vacuoles. Overexpression of NHX1 or the tonoplast pyrophosphatase AVP1 that contributes to the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradient for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ storage in the vacuole increases both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance in Arabidopsis, suggesting that more efficient sequestration may improve osmotic tolerance and/or reduce cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels (Apse et al. 1999; Gaxiola et al. 2001).

Transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot is poorly understood. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ moves in the symplast across the endodermis (where it is intact) and is released from mainly xylem parenchyma cells into the apoplastic xylem. The electrochemical gradient for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ release into the xylem is likely to vary and may even favour passive release under conditions where the xylem is relatively dilute (during high transpiration) and cells loading the xylem are depolarized (as is possible in saline conditions). Passive release of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the xylem can involve non-selective cation channels and/or other uniport mechanisms. Under conditions of low transpiration or in mature parts of the root where $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ has accumulated along the xylem pathway, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux to the xylem may require active transport.The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter SOS1 is expressed in stelar cells and has been implicated in active $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loading of the xylem. Re-uptake from the xylem back into root cells may also occur, and this would reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivery to the shoot. In this case, the thermodynamic conditions would be reversed, and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ could be retrieved passively in mature parts of the root where xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is at high concentration. SOS1 has also been proposed to act in xylem retrieval (Shi et al. 2002) but requires some stoichiometric plasticity to overcome the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradient favouring $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux (Tester & Davenport 2003).

The rate of delivery to the shoot depends on root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport processes and, to some extent, on the rate of transpiration (if xylem loading rates are influenced by xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration, as previously suggested). Once delivered to the shoot in the xylem, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is accumulated in shoot cells probably by processes similar to those described in roots.A final factor affecting shoot concentrations of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ apart from the shoot growth rate, is the rate of recirculation of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ to the roots. Recirculation can occur via the phloem, but the contribution of recirculation to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis remains in question. Little is known about the thermodynamics of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loading and unloading of the phloem, but AtHKT1;1 has been proposed to function in both processes (Berthomieu et al. 2003).

Despite decades of intensive research, the kinetics of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport remains poorly understood, and the proteins catalysing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport are largely unknown. However, research in a number of species is now converging on HKT-type proteins as major controllers of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ transport to the shoot. Here we address the role of AtHKT1;1 in Arabidopsis.

The HKT family of proteins has been implicated in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in a number of species, and members of the family have been demonstrated to function as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symporters and as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -selective transporters of both high and low affinity (Rubio, Gassmann & Schroeder 1995; Garciadeblás et al. 2003; Haro et al. 2005). The wheat TaHKT2;1 functions as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symporter when expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Rubio et al. 1995), and down-regulation of expression in planta reduces root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and improves growth in saline conditions (Laurie et al. 2002). The rice OsHKT1;5 functions as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -selective transporter in Xenopus oocytes and is hypothesized to control shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and influence shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by withdrawing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem stream into the xylem parenchyma cells (Ren et al. 2005). The Arabidopsis genome contains a single HKT homolog, AtHKT1;1. AtHKT1;1 appears to function as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -selective uniporter when expressed in Xenopus oocytes and yeast, but it also complements an Escherichia coli $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake-deficient mutant and increases its $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation, suggesting some role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport (Uozumi et al. 2000). hkt1;1 mutants are salt sensitive compared to wild type and hyperaccumulate $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in the shoot, but show hypoaccumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the root (Maser et al. 2002; Berthomieu et al. 2003; Rus et al. 2004).

In addition to the evidence for a direct role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in Arabidopsis, there is also evidence that AtHKT1;1 plays a more complex role in controlling ion fluxes. Although hkt1;1 knockout plants are more salt sensitive than wild type, knockout of AtHKT1;1 partially restores salt resistance in the salt overly sensitive (sos) mutants $( s o s I , s o s 2 , s o s 3 )$ (Rus et al. 2001, 2004). The SOS2 and SOS3 proteins function in a signalling pathway, one of the outputs of which is activation of SOS1, a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. SOS1 is transcribed (at least in non-saline conditions) in the root tip and vasculature, and is hypothesized to efflux $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from roots to the external solution and to pump $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ into or retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem, depending on $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradients in the stele (Shi et al. 2002). sos1, 2 and 3 mutants are more salt sensitive than wild type and show hypo- or hyperaccumulation of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ depending on growth conditions (Wu, Ding & Zhu 1996; Ding & Zhu 1997; Shi et al. 2002), and inhibition of root growth in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation conditions (Wu et al. 1996; Rus et al. 2004). Interestingly, knockout of AtHKT1;1 rescues both the $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sensitivity phenotypes (Rus et al. 2001, 2004).

Several hypotheses have been advanced concerning AtHKT1;1 function in Arabidopsis. Because hkt1;1 mutations ameliorate the sos phenotypes and reduce whole seedling $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in sos3, Rus et al. (2001) proposed that AtHKT1;1 was an influx pathway for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into the root. However, Berthomieu et al. (2003) and Essah, Davenport & Tester (2003) showed that hkt1;1 mutants did not have lower root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx (in excised roots), and Berthomieu et al. (2003) proposed instead that AtHKT1;1 functioned in $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ recirculation from shoots to roots by loading $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the shoot into phloem and then unloading it into the roots for efflux. This hypothesis accounted for the shoot $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ hyperaccumulation and reduced root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ observed in hkt1;1 mutants, and was supported by evidence for reduced phloem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the hkt1;1 (sas2) mutant and apparent phloem localization of AtHKT1;1 transcripts (Berthomieu et al. 2003). Subsequently, Rus et al. (2004) demonstrated that plants overexpressing AtHKT1;1 under the control of the putative native AtHKT1;1 promoter were also salt sensitive, and argued that AtHKT1;1 plays a role in regulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis that is disrupted by knockout or misexpression. Most recently, Sunarpi et al.

(2005) demonstrated that AtHKT1;1 was localized to the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells in the shoot. They found both reduced phloem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and elevated xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoot of hkt1;1 mutants and proposed that AtHKT1;1 functioned primarily to retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem, at least in the shoot, and that retrieval of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ into the symplast had a knock-on effect on phloem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels.

Hypotheses regarding the role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport have relied mainly on measurements of tissue ion contents, which are the net result of a number of different transport processes (Fig. 1), or on disruptive measurements of phloem and xylem contents. In addition, many of the previous experiments have been conducted in plants grown on agar plates (where transpiration is extremely limited) or in soil (where the activity of nutrient and toxic ions is difficult to control), and this makes it difficult to compare results between experiments. For the present study, we developed a hydroponic growth system and minimal media that would allow us to perform a range of physiological experiments under standardized growth conditions, so that we could be confident that a biomass or ion accumulation phenotype observed in a growth experiment could be reproduced in plants grown for short-term flux experiments. We used radioactive tracers to dissect the individual transport processes contributing to $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in intact, transpiring plants in order to test whether AtHKT1;1 was involved in (1) root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx, (2) recirculation from shoot to root, (3) $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ retrieval from the xylem and (4) $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx.

## AtHKT1;1 controls root vacuolar uptake and withdrawal of $\mathbb { N } \bar { \mathbf { a } } ^ { + }$ from the xylem


AtHKT1;1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } .$ -selective transporter that plays a central role in distribution of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ within the plant. While the hkt1;1 phenotype of low root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is well established, the $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ transport processes causing this phenotype remain controversial. We used radioactive tracers to measure unidirectional fluxes of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + } \left( \mathbf { R } \mathbf { b } ^ { + } \right)$ through intact plants, and found that hkt1;1 mutants showed two distinct differences in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes: reduced root vacuolar uptake and reduced root retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem. These defects in unidirectional $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ fluxes were consistent with the net $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation phenotype of the hkt1;1 mutant. There was no evidence to support the hypotheses that AtHKT1;1 was involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into roots or recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from shoots to roots. It appears that if recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from shoot to root occurs at all in Arabidopsis, then it occurs at rates too low to contribute significantly to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels.We were not able to determine the function of AtHKT1;1 in the shoot using radioactive techniques; however, the role of AtHKT1;1 in the roots in controlling unidirectional transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot was sufficient to account for the net differences in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ between control and hkt1;1 plants.

The question then arose of whether AtHKT1;1 was involved in both vacuolar influx and xylem retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or whether perturbation of one of these processes was sufficient to cause the hkt1;1 phenotype. Net accumulation of ions depends on the sum of ion fluxes, but the fluxes themselves are interdependent, so alteration of one flux has effects both on net accumulation and on other fluxes.Therefore, it was necessary to model the movements of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ within the plant to estimate how alterations of single fluxes could impact on other transport processes. Our very simple model was able to describe the observed fluxes and, in conjunction with the experimental evidence, indicated that the effects of the hkt1;1 mutation on vacuolar uptake and xylem retrieval of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were independent.

The dual effects of AtHKT1;1 on root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport support the hypothesis of Rus et al. (2004) that AtHKT1;1 functions to control ion homeostasis. How can these results be reconciled with those of Berthomieu et al. (2003), who found a fivefold elevation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the phloem of hkt1;1 (sas2) mutants compared to wild type and evidence for AtHKT1;1 localization to the phloem? Sunarpi et al. (2005) also found lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the phloem of hkt1;1 mutants, but found that the reduction in phloem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ between hkt1;1 and controls ranged between approximately sixfold and twofold depending on the hkt1;1 allelic mutant. A key question is whether the rate of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ export from the shoot in the phloem is high enough to have a significant effect on shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration. Berthomieu et al. (2003) compared only relative amounts of phloem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ using the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ : glutamine ratio; however, Sunarpi et al. (2005) reported the amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extruded from the phloem. They measured approximately $3 0 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ leaf DW, collected over a $^ { 4 \mathrm { h } }$ period, from plants exposed to $7 5 \ : \mathrm { m M } \ : \mathrm { N a C l }$ for $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ d ~ } }$ . Xylem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ content in the controls was approximately $6 \mu \mathrm { m o l }$ $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } m L ^ { - 1 } }$ xylem sap. The transpiration rate was not reported so it is difficult to compare these two measures. However, if we assume a transpiration rate of $0 . 3 \mathrm { m L g ^ { - 1 } }$ leaf fresh weight (FW) $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ (Hosy et al. 2003), then the delivery of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the leaf would be $2 \mu \mathrm { { m o l } \ N a ^ { + } / g ^ { - 1 } \ F W h ^ { - 1 } }$ . The retranslocation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ via the phloem would be $0 . 7 5 \mu \mathrm { m o l }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ FW $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ (assuming a 10:1 leaf FW : DW ratio), suggesting that the phloem could remove as much as $4 0 \%$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivered in the xylem. This is much higher than indicated in the recirculation experiment presented in Fig. 5. If the average transpiration rate were $1 \mathrm { m L g ^ { - 1 } }$ leaf FW $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ ,then the phloem would remove only $1 2 . 5 \%$ of xylem-delivered $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , closer to our estimates for control plants (Fig. 5c). However, even if the phloem removed as much as half the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivered in the xylem, a mutation causing a fivefold reduction in phloem export would result in only a 1.8-fold increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, which is too low to account for the three- to ninefold excess accumulation usually found in hkt1;1 mutants (Fig. 2c; Maser et al. 2002; Berthomieu et al. 2003; Gong et al. 2004). For a fivefold reduction in phloem export to cause a fivefold increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, phloem export would have to constitute around $8 5 \%$ of xylem import. We could find no evidence of such significant recirculation. By contrast, genotypic differences affecting xylem delivery would have a directly proportional effect on shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Although Berthomieu et al. (2003) measured only a statistically insignificant doubling of xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the hkt1;1 (sas2) mutant, Sunarpi et al. (2005) found large and significant increases in xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in hkt1;1 mutants compared with wild-type controls, and concluded that withdrawal of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ from the xylem constituted the most significant function of AtHKT1;1 with respect to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in the shoot. While it is very likely that hkt1;1 mutants have lower rates of phloem transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , the more critical effect on shoot $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ is the early effect of the hkt1;1 mutation in roots on unidirectional transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot in the xylem. There is little evidence for a significant contribution of recirculation to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in any species (Tester & Davenport 2003).

The localization of AtHKT1;1 remains problematic. Berthomieu et al. (2003) presented evidence from RNA in situ hybridization and promoter fusion for phloem localization of AtHKT1;1 transcripts. While the images presented did not localize AtHKT1;1 unequivocally to the phloem, AtHKT1;1 transcripts appeared to be concentrated in cells around the phloem rather than the xylem (Berthomieu et al. 2003). However, using an antibody raised to AtHKT1;1, Sunarpi et al. (2005) demonstrated localization of the protein to the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells in the shoot, commensurate with a direct role for AtHKT1;1 in withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem in the shoot. It remains unclear, therefore, whether AtHKT1;1 participates directly in retrieval of xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in roots or controls the process indirectly. Plasma membrane localization of AtHKT1;1 is not compatible with a direct involvement in vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes, and the effect of the hkt1;1 mutation in reducing vacuolar $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx is likely to be indirect (unless the AtHKT1;1 protein has several intracellular locations). Overexpression of AtHKT1 under control of its likely native promoter increased salt sensitivity (Rus et al. 2004), indicating that the role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport involves more than simply a reduction of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport to the shoot.


## How does hkt1;1 rescue sos1?


In hydroponic growth conditions, sos1 accumulated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the same concentration as hkt1;1 and sos1-hkt1;1 mutants in the shoot, and showed little reduction in shoot growth in saline conditions (although the shoot displayed visible symptoms of stress). Therefore, high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was not the cause of sos1 salt hypersensitivity, in accord with previous evidence (Ding & Zhu 1997; Shi et al. 2002). However, sos1 plants showed a strong reduction in root growth and hyperaccumulated $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in roots. Root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was partially reduced in the sos1-hkt1;1 double mutant relative to sos1, in conjunction with partial relief of growth inhibition. Because knockout of AtHKT1;1 caused a reduction in root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation (via inhibition of vacuolar influx), these results suggest that hkt1;1 mutations relieve sos1 salt sensitivity by reducing root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation.

The mechanism by which the hkt1;1 mutation rescues sos1 growth in limiting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ conditions remains unclear. We found no evidence for a role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport.

We also found no evidence that the sos1 mutant was defective in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx or net accumulation). This may have been because the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -specific defect in sos1 is only evident in certain growth conditions. Qi & Spalding (2004) could not reproduce the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype except in the presence of millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and speculated that excess root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in sos1 plants inhibited $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake via $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels. This would be compatible with our results showing that the hkt1;1 mutation reduced root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in sos1 and restored root growth. However, sos1 did not demonstrate reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation under saline conditions (although $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ distribution was perturbed, with sos1 plants accumulating higher shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and lower root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ than controls) (Fig. 2d). Tissue $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels were not critical in determining salt sensitivity because the sos1-hkt1;1 mutant resembled sos1 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation but was less salt sensitive. When we attempted to replicate previous studies using agar plates, we found no genotypespecific inhibitory effect of low millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ (which blocks high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake) on sos1 growth on low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ agar plates, and could only reliably reproduce the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ phenotype in the presence of sucrose (Supplementary Fig. S3). Qi & Spalding (2004) did not include sucrose in their media, whereas sucrose was always present in experiments demonstrating a clear sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ phenotype (Wu et al. 1996; Ding & Zhu 1997; Rus et al. 2001, 2004; Shi et al. 2002). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is known to be important in sucrose transport (Deeken et al. 2002), and it is possible that indirect effects of mutations of SOS1 and AtHKT1;1 on intra-root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport perturb phloem transport processes.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that AtHKT1;1 is not involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation via the phloem and is not responsible for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx into roots. Rather, AtHKT1;1 appears to control both retrieval of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ from the xylem and root vacuolar loading.This paper demonstrates the utility of measurements of unidirectional fluxes with radioactive tracers and the use of simple mathematical models to test intuitive descriptions of plant transport processes.

## 3.1. CmHKT1;1 Is a Pumpkin $N a ^ { + }$ -Selective Class I HKT


HKTs are crucial for salt tolerance in plants along with other transporters. They are responsible HKTs are crucial ffor ion homeostasis and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ lt tolerance in plants along with other transporters. They are responsibdistribution within plants [33,34]. HKT transporters are divided into two groups, class I and class II, depending on their roles in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport within plants [7,34]. The presence of Ser instead of Gly in the PA-loop is a key feature that determines preferential $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ conductance in class I HKTs [5,33–36]. We isolated two HKT1-like isoforms from pumpkin, namely, CmHKT1;1 and CmHKT1;2. Following sequence and phylogenetic analysis, both are classified as class I HKTs (Figure 2). These class HKTs have been described as low-affinity and specific $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters responsible for unloading ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { } } { \mathrm { } } } { { \mathrm { } } } ^ { + }$ from the xylem, thus preventing ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ accumulation in the shoots [3,6,8,10,12,37]. However, TsHKT1;2 in the halophytic Thelungiella salsuginea belongs to class I, showing strong $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter activity and selectivity over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ [29]. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport capacity was attributed to the presence of two aspartic residues, D207 and D238, in the transmembrane (M2B) and pore (PB) domains. In these locations, Asn $( \mathrm { N } )$ residues were found in Arabidopsis and all other known plant sequences [29]. These residues are absent in the sequence of any pumpkin isoforms, indicating that both are similar in sequence to typical $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters (Figure 2). Following heterologous expression experiments in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -sensitive yeast mutant cells (G19) and endogenous $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport-defective yeast mutant cells (W∆6), we can conclude that pumpkin CmHKT1;1, similar to AtHKT1;1 [3], is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter and not a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter (Figure 5). With respect to CmHKT1;2, long fragment amino acids lost in the N-terminal were observed, and the first M1A-PA-M1B transmembrane domains were incomplete (Figure 1). Even the mRNAs were not differentially expressed under salt stress and thus were not given focus in this study.

HKT family proteins primarily promote the exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the leaves via the withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root-to-shoot-flowing xylem sap [6,10,12,38]. In monocot plants, HKT1 location was intensively studied, and analysis of transgenic rice lines containing the GUS reporter gene under the control of the OsHKT1;1 promoter or in situ hybridization experiments showed that OsHKT1;1 is expressed mainly in the phloem of leaf blades [39,40]. In bread wheat, tissue-specific expression of TaHKT1;5-D mRNA in the roots is predominantly observed by in situ PCR within the stele, particularly within xylem parenchyma and pericycle cells adjacent to the xylem vessels [13,38]. In Sorghum bicolor, SbHKT1;4 is expressed in the roots, sheath, and leaf veins [41]. In the dicotyledonous plant Arabidopsis, tissue-specific expression analyses of AtHKT1;1 showed its expression in the root stele and leaf vasculature [5]. Further biochemical immunolocalization analyses found that the AtHKT1;1 protein is targeted to the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells suggesting that AtHKT1;1 functions in the removal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem sap [10]. In tomato, in situ PCR results showed that SlHKT1;1 and SlHKT1;2 are expressed in vascular bundle cells of leaves, but only SlHKT1;2 expression could be detected in stellar cells of roots [42]. In the present study, CmHKT1;1 was strongly expressed in the root system and significantly highly upregulated under $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress (Figure 3). In situ hybridization showed that CmHKT1;1 was mainly expressed in pumpkin root stellar cells (Figure 4). These results suggest that CmHKT1;1 is ideally localized to withdraw $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the root xylem sap, thus reducing the root-to-shoot flow of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and decreasing shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation.


## 3.2. CmHKT1;1 Enhances Salinity Tolerance in Transgenic Cucumber


Salt tolerance and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion mechanisms vary in different plant species. Previous studies used genetic engineering to address HKT function. In bread wheat, the RNAi lines reducing TaHKT1;5-D transcripts in planta increase leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration [13]. In barley, loss of HvHKT1;2 function in a mutant plant reduces $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx and growth under saline conditions, and HvHKT2;1 overexpression increases leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and salt tolerance [43,44]. AtHKT1;1 overexpression in the mature root stele of $A$ . thaliana decreases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots [9], and AtHKT1;1expression in the root cortex of rice increases salinity tolerance and decreases shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation [15]. In tomato, SlHKT1;2 silencing promotes $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots and reduces plant growth under salt stress [42]. In woody plants, VisHKT1;1 is a major gene controlling $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion in grapevine rootstocks [45]. Interestingly, the constitutive expression of AtHKT1;1 in WT Arabidopsis driven by the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter causes high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and poor growth [9], and overexpressing AtHKT1;1 in the mutant athkt1-3 under the control of 35S, also suppresses plant growth [29]. However, overexpression of AtHKT1 and SlHKT1;2 in the Arabidopsis mutant athkt1;1, which is driven by the AtHKT1 promoter region, a 5 kb DNA fragment upstream of the ATG start codon of the AtHKT1;1 gene containing the promoter region, the tandem repeat, and the small RNA target region [46], could reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots [47]. These results indicate that HKT1 genes need to be expressed in a specific cell type or tissue in transgenic plants to improve salinity tolerance. However, transgenic barley plants overexpressing HvHKT2;1, which is driven by a strong constitutive ubiquitin promoter, demonstrate increased salt tolerance [44]. The novel soybean gene GmHKT1;4 driven by the CaMV35S promoter enhances the root growth of the tobacco transgenic line and increases the salinity tolerance of tobacco [16]. Ectopic expression of the Mesembryanthemum crystallinum sodium transporter McHKT2, which encodes for the Arabidopsis sodium transporter ortholog AtHKT1 driven by 35S, confers strong salt tolerance in Arabidopsis [48]. SsHKT1;1 is an HKT1 homolog isolated from C3 halophyte Suaeda salsa L. and is a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -selective transporter. Driven by 35S, SsHKT1;1 overexpression in Arabidopsis enhances salt tolerance and increases shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration [49]. In maize, two alternative splicing variants ZmHKT1;1 confer salt tolerance in transgenic tobacco plants and decrease the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the shoots [4]. In the present study, the ectopic expression of CmHKT1;1 in cucumber enhanced the salt tolerance in transgenic cucumber and decreased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots (Figures 6 and 7). The functional differences in different species might be explained by the variations in amino acid sequences, and HKT proteins might enhance salt tolerance through different mechanisms. The regulatory network and the role in long-distance transport of HKTs remain unclear [50].

3.3. CmHKT1;1 Is Critical for Regulation of Shoot $N a ^ { + }$ Accumulation in Grafted Cucumber through Limiting $N a ^ { + }$ Transport from the Roots to the Shoots

Grafting onto tolerant rootstocks is a cost-effective and efficient approach to reduce the effect of salinity on some horticultural crops, such as tomato, cucumber, watermelon, melon, citrus, and grapevine [19,45,51–54]. The use of salt-resistant rootstocks can improve salinity tolerance in shoots. In Arabidopsis, mutant hkt1 and WT $C o l { - } O$ reciprocal grafting experiments showed that the loss of AtHKT1;1 expression in the roots increases the shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content [32]. Reciprocal grafting between cucumber and pumpkin demonstrates the roles of the rootstock in determining $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in cucumber [24]. In the current study, we used the CmHKT1;1 transgenic line as the rootstock and WT cucumber as the scion. Grafting of the plants decreased the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the shoots and improved the growth of the grafted cucumber seedlings under salt stress (Figures 8 and 9).

The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion accumulation in the leaves is controlled predominantly by the genotype of the rootstock, and the characteristics of the rootstock to induce salt tolerance in the shoots depend on the salt tolerance mechanism of the shoot genotype [55]. In cucumber and tomato, which are the reciprocal grafted plants, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoots and roots is also impacted by the rootstock and scion with different levels of salt tolerance [24,56]. Hence, the interaction between the scion and the rootstock is complicated. Previous studies on HKT function mainly focused on the changes in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, and few studies demonstrated the changes in root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content. In the present study, the CmHKT1;1-expressing cucumber had significant reduction in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, relatively higher root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in TG-2, and lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in TG-3 compared with the WT (Figure 7B). However, in the grafting combinations, the rootstock $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content of the transgenic line was significantly lower than that of the WT rootstock under salt stress (Figure 9B). Whether the different results due to the different genotypes of the shoot needs further investigation in the future.

In conclusion, CmHKT1;1 plays an important role in the ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { } } { \mathrm { } } } { { \mathrm { } } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis and salinity tolerance of pumpkin, especially in the grafted cucumber plants. The finding may be useful for engineering salt tolerance in cucurbit crops.

Soil salinity is an environmental stress of major concern, causing significant loss of global agricultural productivity, particularly in irrigated soils [1,2]. Plant growth under salt stress requires the tight control of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake, long-distance transport, and accumulation. Excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is toxic to the plant-cell cytosol and must be excluded from the cytoplasm [3]. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ enters roots passively, via nonselective cation channels and possibly other $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters, such as high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters (HKTs) [4]. HKTs, permeable either only to ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \tt { a } } ^ { + } }$ (class I) or to both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (class II), are thought to play major roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ absorption and transport. In Arabidopsis, the HKT family comprises a single member, AtHKT1;1 $( \mathrm { A t 4 g 1 0 3 1 0 } )$ , which is permeable only to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ [5,6]. However, reported physiological roles and the expression profile of AtHKT1;1 are controversial. Berthomieu et al. [7] concluded that AtHKT1;1 is involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation from shoots to roots by mediating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loading into the phloem sap in shoots and unloading in roots. On the other hand, Davenport et al. [8], based on their experiments using radioactive tracers, concluded that AtHKT1;1 contributes to the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem, but is not involved in recirculation in the phloem. Sunarpi et al. [9] proposed that AtHKT1;1 contributes to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ removal from the ascending xylem sap and recirculation from the leaves to the roots via the phloem vasculature, based on the expression profile and analysis of AtHKT1;1 mutants. An et al. [10] confirmed with reciprocal grafting experiments between wild type (WT) and mutants that, in roots, AtHKT1;1 plays a role in Arabidopsis salt tolerance. Therefore, the major function of AtHKT1;1 remains to be determined in terms of salt tolerance in Arabidopsis: unloading $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root xylem to xylem parenchyma cells, or uploading $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into phloem cells, followed by its recirculation to roots. The expression of AtHKT1;1 has mainly been detected in roots [5], in the root stele, and vascular tissue in leaves [11], in the phloem of every organ [7], and in the xylem parenchyma and phloem cells in roots and shoots [9]. It was also reported that the expression of AtHKT1;1 mRNA did not change in response to NaCl [5,7,10]; however, the AtHKT1;1 gene was reported to be induced with $2 5 { - } 3 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a ^ { + } }$ [9,12]. As the expression characteristics of a gene are closely related to the functions of the product, detailed analysis of the expression profile is important in elucidating function. In addition, the accurate characterization of the promoter is necessary if one wants to utilize this promoter to express transgenes in transgenic plants.

In this study, I analyzed spatial and developmental gene expression patterns, and responsiveness to moderate salt-stress of the AtHKT1;1 promoter using a reporter gene. The results provide useful information on this promoter and reveal novel insights into the functions of AtHKT1;1.

Salinity affects approximately $7 \%$ of the world’s land including agricultural lands and is a crucial factor limiting over $3 0 \%$ of irrigated and $7 \%$ of dryland agriculture worldwide [1]. ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ is a common salt ion that is toxic to most crops [2]. Regulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx, efflux, allocation, and compartmentation is important for plants to cope with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots. This process involves a complex network of channels and transporters that participate in ion uptake and compartmentation in plant cells and tissues.

High-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter-1 (HKT1) encodes a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ preferential transporter that principally controls root-to-shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivery via the withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem sap [3–6]. Members of the HKT family can be divided into two subfamilies, namely, HKT1 and HKT2; the former subfamily functions as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uniporter, whereas the latter serves as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ symporter [7]. HKT1 transporters are involved in retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream [8–10] by mediating the influx of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the xylem parenchyma cells in the roots [3]. HKT1 genes play a crucial role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in several plant species, such as Arabidopsis, rice, wheat, and maize [5,8,9,11–14]. AtHKT1;1 is localized at the plasma membrane of the xylem parenchyma cells in the shoots [10] and at the phloem tissues of both roots and shoots [11]. Therefore, AtHKT1;1 might be involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation from the shoots to roots via phloem and/or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ unloading from the xylem into xylem parenchyma cells [10,11]. An enhancer trap system overexpressing AtHKT1;1 in the mature root stele of Arabidopsis decreases ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \tt { a } } ^ { + } }$ accumulation by $3 7 { - } 6 4 \%$ in the shoots [9]. These changes in the shoots are caused by the augmented influx of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into stellar root cells mediated by AtHKT1;1, which reduces the root-to-shoot transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ [9]. In rice, AtHKT1;1 expression in the roots is affected by low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration in the shoots [15]. In soybean, GmHKT1;4 overexpression significantly enhances the tolerance of transgenic tobacco plants to NaCl stress by promoting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation and inhibiting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots [16].

Cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) is an important vegetable crop worldwide, which is sensitive to salt stress [17]. Saline soils or saline irrigations often limit cucumber production [18–22]. Pumpkin is often used as the rootstock of cucumber, and it is relatively salt-tolerant [23–25]. Grafting onto salt-tolerant pumpkin rootstock can effectively improve the growth of cucumber plants grown under salt conditions [19,23,24]. Our previous study showed limited radial transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the stele by using pumpkin as rootstock, thereby restricting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport from the roots to shoots [26]. However, the function of pumpkin HKT in this process remains unclear.

Salinity stress affects crop production worldwide, particularly by limiting plant growth and reducing potential yield. Plants have three mechanisms for tolerating soil salinity, including tolerance of the osmotic effects of salt; a tolerance in leaf tissues of the negative effects of sodium ions (Na+ ) on cellular function through compartmentalisation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in specific tissues, cells, or cellular organelles; and exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the sensitive shoot tissue [1]. Of these mechanisms, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot is best understood and is, therefore, the current best candidate for a targeted genetic modification approach to improving salinity tolerance.

The HKT gene family encodes one of the most widely studied groups of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters in plants. Current understanding indicates that AtHKT1; $I$ from Arabidopsis is expressed primarily in the stele and has a role in the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream [2,3]. Reduced activity of this transporter leads to increased transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the root to the shoot, leading to a higher shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and a decrease in salinity tolerance [4]. More recently, it was demonstrated that OsHKT1;5 in rice [5] and the $H K T l { ; } 5$ gene from wheat [6] are crucial in maintaining low shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations via a similar mechanism of $\mathrm { N a + }$ retrieval from the transpiration stream into cells within the stele. A second HKT gene that is involved in sodium exclusion in cereal species is HKT1;4. The encoded transporter appears to function in combination with HKT1;5, by retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the shoot transpiration stream and sequestering Na+ in the sheath tissue [7]. The endogenous function of the family of HKT transporters and their role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and provision of salinity tolerance to plants has been reviewed recently [8].

An obvious strategy for improving the salinity tolerance of plants is to increase the expression of HKT genes. Constitutive overexpression of plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters, however, has been unsuccessful in producing salinity tolerant plants [9]. It was hypothesized that such overexpression increases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes into all cells of the plant, this being, on balance, counter-productive to the reduction of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport to the shoot [9,10]. In contrast, it was shown that overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the root xylem parenchyma cells of Arabidopsis leads to improved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and salinity tolerance [9]. Interestingly, the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the root resulting from the improved Na+ exclusion from the shoot was stored within the cortical cells of the root [9].

The aim of experiments described in the current work was to determine if overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the outer cells (epidermis and cortex) of the root would result in opposite effects to overexpression in the stele, or whether a similar improvement of Na+ exclusion and salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis and rice would be observed. A secondary goal was to determine if expression of AtHKT1; $\mathit { \Pi } _ { l }$ in the epidermal and cortical cell layers of the root is the reason for the deleterious effects observed when AtHKT1;1 is constitutively overexpressed, as described previously [9].

In both species, we found that transgenic plants overexpressing AtHKT1;1 in mature root cortex had greater shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and thus increased salinity tolerance.

Salinity is a major abiotic stress influencing agricultural production around the world and represents a major threat to the maintenance of crop yields, because most crop species are sensitive to the accumulation of sodium in shoot tissues (Tester and Davenport 2003). In the Triticeae, sodium exclusion from roots and leaf tissues is one of the major mechanisms conferring salt tolerance (Gorham et al. 1990; Munns et al. 2006). Modern durum wheat cultivars do not exclude $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the same extent as bread wheat (Triticum aestivum). Two QTLs originating from Triticum monococcum and involved in salinity tolerance, Nax1 $\mathrm { \Delta N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion 1) and Nax2 $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ exclusion 2), were found to correspond to HKT genes [respectively, of HKT1;4 and HKT1;5 types; (Lindsay et al. 2004; Byrt et al. 2007)]. Moreover, HKT genes shown to be associated to QTLs for salinity tolerance belong to subfamily 1. They have been shown to play crucial roles in salinity tolerance in different plant species (Munns et al. 2012; Asins et al. 2013). Nax1 is a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter, a member of the HKT (high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter) family, T. monococcum HKT1;4-A2 (Huang et al. 2006). The Nax1 gene confers a reduced rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and retention of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaf sheath, thus giving a higher sheath-to-blade $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration ratio (James et al. 2006). The second gene, Nax2, also confers a lower rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and has a higher rate of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport, resulting in enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ versus $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ discrimination in the leaf blade (James et al. 2006). The HKT gene family encodes proteins which form part of the $\mathrm { T r k / K t r / H K T }$ group of membrane transporters. These proteins have been shown to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and/or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in bacteria, fungi and plants. HKT genes can be divided into two subfamilies, based on amino acid sequence homology, with members of subfamily 1, which mainly transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ while members of subfamily 2 transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Tester and Davenport 2003). Due to the transporting properties of the encoded HKT proteins, it is likely that a number of HKT proteins play important roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in plants and consequently have direct or indirect roles in determining salinity tolerance (Berthomieu et al. 2003; Haro et al. 2005; Ren et al. 2005; Rus et al. 2004; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Mäser et al. 2003).

Using the GUS reporter strategy and in situ hybridization, HKT gene expression patterns have so far been analyzed in detail in a few plant species aside from rice and Arabidopsis. HKT genes from subfamily 1 have systematically been found to be expressed in vascular tissues in all plants analyzed like rice, wheat, and Arabidopsis plants (Berthomieu et al. 2003, Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Jabnoune et al. 2009; Munns et al. 2012). Some of these genes are essentially expressed in the vasculature system, like HKT1 in Arabidopsis and ice plants and HKT1;5 in rice and wheat. On the other hand, the expression patterns of the rice HKT1;3 and HKT1;4 genes also include the root peripheral cell layers and leaf bulliform cells, similar to the expression pattern of OsHKT2;1. Hence, in addition to root cation uptake, OsHKT2;1 is likely to play a role in long distance cation transport in the plant vasculature between roots and shoots, and in osmoregulatory processes in leaf tissues and bulliform cells, which control leaf rolling upon abiotic constraints (Kadioglu and Terzi 2007). HKT2;4 expression has only been analyzed in rice (Lan et al. 2010). The reported expression pattern is comprised in the root peripheral cell layers, leaf vasculature and mesophyll, so significantly overlaps with that of OsHKT2;1. Thus, the expression patterns of some members of the HKT subfamily 1 can be quite similar to those of members from the HKT subfamily 2. However, important differences in the regulation of expression seem to exist between subfamily 1 and subfamily 2 HKT, suggesting that the two types of genes play specific roles.

Indeed, enhancement of expression in roots in conditions of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ shortage, which has been consistently reported in the HKT subfamily 2, does not seem to occur in subfamily 1. On the other hand, members from both subfamilies can display regulation upon salt stress. This regulation appeared to be variable between tissues (roots and leaves), HKT genes and even between cultivars for some genes (Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005). In this study, we isolated and characterized the promoter sequence of Triticum monococcum TmHKT1;4-A1 gene. The spatio-temporal activity of the PrTmHKT1;4-A1 fused to the gusA gene was investigated in stable transformed Arabidopsis plants under multiple inducible-abiotic-stress treatment and tissue-specific manner.

Salinity and drought are two major abiotic stress challenges that severely constrain global crop production. High salinity levels cause osmotic stress and ion toxicity, disrupting plant physiological functions and reducing growth and productivity [1, 2]. The prolonged drought led to a water shortage, affecting photosynthesis, nutrient breakdown, and overall plant metabolism, which in turn threatens food security [3]. Potassium $( \mathrm { K } ^ { + } )$ is a vital micronutrient that plays a key role in activating plant stress responses and supporting critical physiological processes such as enzyme activation, protein synthesis, osmoregulation, and ionic balance maintenance [4]. Adequate potassium intake is therefore crucial for plants to withstand abiotic stress, as it helps maintain cell turgor, control stomatal closure, and mitigate oxidative damage.

The high-affinity Potassium Transporter (HKT) plays a crucial role in the uptake and regulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions, which is vital for plant salt tolerance, particularly in conditions with low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and high salinity [5, 6]. Recent studies have demonstrated that members of the HKT family in rice (Oryza sativa) play a pivotal function in enhancing salt tolerance [7]. Among the HKT genes, HKT1;5 stands out as a key player in managing $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ ion levels. It facilitates the removal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the shoot by enhancing their transport from the xylem to the root. This mechanism helps prevent the accumulation of excessive $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions in the aboveground parts of the plant [8]. Previous studies have also highlighted that OsHKT1;5 regulates $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ balance under salinity stress, indicating its potential as a valuable candidate for improving stress tolerance in other plant species. The Saltol/SKC1 gene on chromosome 1 is recognised as the most significant quantitative trait locus (QTL) for salt tolerance in rice, with OsHKT1;5 identified as the key salt tolerance gene. Notably, four specific amino acid changes (140 P/A/T/I, $1 8 4 \ \mathrm { H / R }$ , D332H, and V395L) have been found to markedly influence the efficiency of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport, distinguishing the salt-tolerant cultivar Nona Bokra from the sensitive variety Koshihikari [8]. Previous studies on wheat have also shown that the TmHKT1;5 and TaHKT1;5 genes enhance salinity tolerance by reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion concentrations in leaves [9, 10].

This study explored the effects of overexpressing the OsHKT1;5 gene from $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa in Arabidopsis on its tolerance to both salinity and drought. An investigation of OsHKT1;5 isolated from Oryza sativa L. An overexpression vector of pB2GW7-OsHKT1;5 was generated using Gateway cloning procedures and then introduced into Arabidopsis using the floral dip transformation approach. An evaluation of the functions and roles of OsHKT1;5 in transgenic Arabidopsis thaliana plants was conducted to investigate the effects and phenomena associated with overexpression. Findings revealed that transgenic plants that overexpressed the OsHKT1;5 gene indeed outperformed compared to wild-type plants when exposed to salinity and drought stress. Our findings may the foundation for future endeavors to enhance the genetic resilience of agronomic crops to salt and drought.

Total salt affected land-area was estimated as 955 million hectares and secondary build up of salts affects about 80 million hectares of land in the arid and semiarid regions (Ghassemi et al., 1995). Number of hungry people in the world is estimated as 925 million in 2010 (World Hunger Education Service, 2012). Therefore, extension of cultivation in salt affected area may help to meet the demand for food. In general, plant species are sensitive to high concentrations of sodium $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ , which causes combined ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ toxicity and osmotic stress. Plants have multiple $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport systems to bypass $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ toxicity. Essential physiological functions of major ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ transporters and their mechanisms mediating salinity resistance have been identified in extensively studied plant Arabidopsis, including the SOS1 (Salt Overly Sensitive), AtNHX (Arabdiopsis thaliana $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters) and AtHKT1; $I$ (A. thaliana High-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ Transporter) gene family (Horie et al., 2009). The HKT gene-family is expressed in xylem parenchyma cells and protects leaves from salinity stress by removing sodium from the xylem-sap (Ren et al., 2005; Sunarpi et al., 2005). Therefore, xylem-parenchyma-expressed ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ permeable plant HKT transporters represent a primary mechanism for mediating salt tolerance and ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ exclusion from leaves as observed in Arabidopsis and other monocot crop-plants as well (Horie et al., 2009). Nevertheless, variation in copy number for individual HKT gene members was observed among the barley, wheat, and rice genomes, and among the different wheat genomes (Huang et al., 2008). HKT gene sequences are not closely related (Platten et al., 2006). Phylogenetic trees of each family define the evolutionary relationships of the members to each other. In each family, closely related isoforms and separate subfamilies of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters existed, indicating possible redundancies and specialized functions (Amrutha et al., 2007). To meet this challenge of world hunger, it is important to understand the mechanisms of salt tolerance to utilize the unused salt-affected land. Better understanding of the relationship among the HKT genes may provide a framework for the development of salt tolerance cultivars. Phylogenetic study on HKT gene family is very limited except earlier work of Platten et al. (2006), Heidari et al. (2011) and very recently Porras et al. (2012). In this study, the phylogeny of plant-HKT genes was examined using the available nucleotide sequences in the current databases.

Soil salinity is one of the major factors affecting agriculture and crop productivity. Deleterious effects of salinity on plants tissues are mainly divided into three aspects: osmotic stress, ion toxicity and nutrient deficiencies (Munns and Tester 2008). To cope with the negative effects of high sodium levels, plants have evolved a series of strategies, including sodium exclusion and/or sodium intracellular compartmentalization into the large cell vacuoles. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (NHXs) could mediated the sodium exclusion and the NHXs from several plant species have been shown to enhance salt tolerance (Apse et al. 1999; He et al. 2005; Patel et al. 2015; Mishra et al. 2015). By these strategies, plants could maintain $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ balance by limiting the over-accumulation of sodium in the cytosol (Hasegawa et al. 2000).

The high-affinity potassium transporter (HKT) genes, belonging to the $\mathrm { T r k / K t r / H K T }$ transporter family, have been shown to play a crucial role in the regulation of sodium and potassium transportation in many species (Corratge´-Faillie et al. 2010). Since the first discovery of TaHKT2;1 in Triticum aestivum (Schachtman and Schroeder 1994), more and more HKT transporters from different species have been found. The HKT transporters have four pore domains (PDs), and HKTs are classified into two sub-families according to the amino acid difference in the first PD (Platten et al. 2006). Sub-family 1 HKTs exhibit a preference for sodium permeability; whereas members of sub-family 2 could select either sodium and/or potassium according to their external concentrations.

Both sub-family 1 and sub-family 2 HKTs have been shown to be able to enhance the salt tolerance of plants by overexpression in transgenic plants. Arabidopsis genome has only one HKT gene, AtHKT1;1, which can mediate the sodium exclusion from leaves under salt stress condition (Horie et al. 2009). It was shown that specifically expression of AtHKT1;1 in the mature root stele of Arabidopsis decreased the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, whereas constitutively expression of AtHKT1;1 driven by 35S promoter led to a high accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Moller et al. 2009). When AtHKT1;1 was specifically expressed in the root cortical and epidermal cells, transgenic plants also had significantly improved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion (Plett et al. 2010). Transgenic barley plants overexpressing $H \nu H K T 2 ; I$ could tolerate high concentration of salt (Mian et al. 2011). In these studies, the salt tolerance of transgenic plants are correlated with the significantly lower accumulation $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than WT plants.

The uptake of N nutrients is finely controlled and influenced by the interplay among three main protein classes, namely transporters, receptors, and transceptors. In this review, the term transporter is used as a synonym of selective carrier proteins, while the term transceptor refers to proteins able to fulfil a dual transport/sensing function [18]. Finally, it is worth remembering that the total concentrations of N forms in root cells depend on external availability as well as on the balance among net uptake (defined as the difference between influx and efflux), root metabolization, vacuolar accumulation, and xylem/phloem (un)loading [1].


## 2.1. Nitrate Uptake


Nitrate is the primary N source for plant growth in most agricultural soils, and its availability significantly affects crop productivity [9]. At high external supplies, total ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ concentration in root cells can reach up to $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M } ,$ , mostly stored in the vacuole, while cytosolic concentration is kept low, as measured by selective-microelectrodes in cereals [19]. Electrophysiological studies indicated that ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake by roots is always an active process, mediated by a $2 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } / 1 \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ symport mechanism, while ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ efflux is passive, saturable, and inducible [20,21].

In plants, ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake is mediated by transporters of the NPF family (previously named NRT1/PTR family) and of the NRT2 family, which in Arabidopsis consist of 53 and 7 members, respectively [22,23]. Although there are no sequence homologies between the two families, these transporters share the same topology consisting of 12 transmembrane domains and have both the $\Nu -$ and $C -$ termini lying on the cytosolic side of the membrane [24]. The activity of these proteins is strictly regulated by ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ availability and plant N nutritional status. In N starved plants, renewed availability of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ triggers the typical ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ primary response (NPR), which comprises the rapid induction of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transporters and $_ \mathrm { N }$ assimilating enzymes. This adaptation is followed by later down-regulation of uptake, correlated with the accumulation of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ itself and of its downstream metabolites, such as glutamine (Gln, Figure 1) [25]. A prominent role for the transcriptional control of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transporters was demonstrated in Arabidopsis and crops, and the importance of PTMs was also highlighted [26–28].

In Arabidopsis, three members of the NPF family are located in the PM of root cells and participate in ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake (Table 1).

NRT1.1 (AtNPF6.3) and NRT1.2 (AtNPF4.6) participate in ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx, and the second is the major one responsible for the constitutive influx in the low-affinity range $\left( > 0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m M } \right)$ [33], while NAXT1 (AtNPF2.7) mediates ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ efflux to the external medium [34].

The characterization of NRT1.1, as the first transceptor identified in higher plants, represents a milestone in plant nutrition research [29]. NRT1.1 is an inducible dualaffinity transporter able to participate in the uptake of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ both in the low-affinity $\left( \mathrm { K m } { \sim } 4 \ \mathrm { m M } \right)$ and high-affinity $( \mathrm { K m } { \sim } 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ ranges, depending on the dephosphorylation/phosphorylation of threonine (Thr)-101 [30].
