## The capacity of NIP homologs to transport As(III) and Sb(III) is conserved across plant species


To gain more functional understanding of the NIP proteins, we first performed a phylogenetic analysis including $3 3 \mathrm { \ N I P }$ homologs from various species, using rat AQP9 as an out-group (Figure 4). The phylogenetic analyses support, and refine further, the subdivision of the NIP subfamily of the aquaporin superfamily into the two subgroups NIPI and NIPII [30-33]. Together, the phylogenetic analysis, transport assays, and phenotypic data presented above, suggested that the capacity to facilitate diffusion of As(III) and Sb(III) across membranes is associated with members of the NIPII subgroup. To substantiate our hypothesis, one isoform of subgroup I (OsNIP1;1) and three isoforms of subgroup II (OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2 and OsNIP3;2) from rice were expressed in yeast and tested for their permeability towards As(III). Expression of

OsNIP2;1 and OsNIP3;2 sensitized yeast to As(III) (Figure 5A) and Sb(III) (data not shown), whereas their expression improved growth of Δfps1 Δacr3 Δycf1 on As(V)-containing medium (Figure 5B). Expression of OsNIP2;2 produced moderate As(III) and Sb(III) sensitivities (Figure 5A and data not shown). In contrast, OsNIP1;1 expression did not affect growth at all (data not shown). Finally, direct transport assays confirmed that the increased sensitivity of cells expressing OsNIP2;1 towards As(III) was the result of increased influx into those cells (Figure 5C).


## Lack of competitive uptake between $\pmb { A s } ( \pmb { I I I } )$ and $B ( O H ) _ { 3 } \circ r$ $S i ( O H ) _ { 4 }$ into yeast cells expressing AtNIP5;1 and OsNIP2;1


OsNIP2;1 and AtNIP5;1 were earlier identified as physiologically important $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ and $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ channels in rice [22] and Arabidopsis [21], respectively. When expressed in oocytes, AtNIP5;1 mediated the uptake of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ and OsNIP2;1 mediated the uptake of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ . Here we demonstrated that As(III) is an additional and common substrate for both proteins. To address whether there is selectivity for the uptake of one metalloid over another, we exposed yeast cells expressing OsNIP2;1 to As(III)

alone or together with various concentrations of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ . However, there was no significant difference in the uptake of As(III), even at a 10-fold higher concentration of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ over As(III) (data not shown). Similarly, no significant difference in As(III) uptake through Atnip5; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - }$ $^ { 6 7 }$ could be measured when yeast cells were exposed to both As(III) and $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ even at a 10-fold higher concentration of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ over As(III) (data not shown). Higher concentrations of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ in the uptake assay cannot be used because of polymerization of monosilic acid to polysilicic acid, and higher concentration of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ will lower the $\mathrm { p H }$ of the medium. Thus, at physiologically relevant concentrations of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ and $\mathrm { \sf B ( O H ) } _ { 3 } ,$ no measurable competition for the uptake of As(III) could be detected.


## Proper functional expression of some NIP isoforms in yeast requires deletion of the N-terminal hydrophilic domain


As shown above, N-terminal truncation allows functional expression of certain NIPs in yeast. To test whether truncation is necessary for proper expression of NIPs in yeast, we extracted microsomal membranes from Δfps1 and Δfps1 Δacr3 Δycf1 cells transformed with AtNIP6;1, Atnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 2 9 }$ and Atnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 9 }$ and probed the extracts by Western-blot analysis using an anti-AtNIP6;1 specific antibody (Figure 6). The antibody was raised against a peptide corresponding to a sequence in the C-terminal end of the protein (Per Kjellbom and Urban Johanson, personal communication). Therefore, the signal on a Western blot should reflect the relative abundance of full-length and truncated versions of AtNIP6;1 in these extracts. In microsomal membranes from yeast transformed with fulllength AtNIP6;1 or both truncated versions, a clear signal could be detected between 35 and $5 5 ~ \mathrm { k D }$ , which might represent the oligomeric forms of the respective protein (Figure 6, arrowheads). The bands corresponding to the truncated forms of AtNIP6;1 migrated faster, as expected from the lower molecular weight due to deletion of the Nterminal 28 and 68 aa, respectively and the monomeric forms were also detected (Figure $^ { 6 , }$ arrows). Truncation of aa 2–29 had little effect on protein levels, whereas truncation of aa 2–69 resulted in higher amount compared with full length AtNIP6;1. We note that the various AtNIP6;1 forms did not migrate according to their molecular size, a phenomenon commonly observed for proteins of the aquaporin family [34,35]. The amount of the heterologous proteins was generally lower in the triple mutant Δfps1 Δacr3 Δycf1 than in Δfps1.

Interestingly, the necessity to remove part of the N-terminal domain does not seem to apply to all members of the NIPII subgroup, as AtNIP7;1, OsNIP3;2 and OsNIP2;1 could be functionally expressed in yeast as full-length proteins (Figures 2 and 5). We therefore hypothesized that the necessity to truncate the N-terminal domain for functional expression in yeast applies to a subpopulation within the NIPII subgroup.

To substantiate this notion, we cloned two additional NIPII homologs from the legume L. japonicus. Primers were designed according to Expressed Sequence Tag (EST) sequences of the N- and the C-termini of probable major intrinsic proteins of L. japonicus from the databases [36]. According to their close sequence similarity to Arabidopsis AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 (Figure 4) and because of a missing nomenclature for aquaporins in L. japonicus, we named them LjNIP5;1 and LjNIP6;1. The full-length coding sequences were submitted to GenBank [37] and are available under accession numbers EU294214 and EU294215, respectively. Expression of the N-terminally truncated versions of both LjNIP5;1 and LjNIP6;1 (Ljnip5; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 7 2 }$ and Ljnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 5 9 }$ ) drastically sensitized Afps1 Aacr3 Aycf1 cells to As(II) whereas expression of the corresponding full length clones did not (LjNIP5;1) or only to a moderate extent $\left( L j N I P G ; 1 \right)$ (Figure 7A). The truncated versions also sensitized cells to Sb(III) (data not shown). When As(V) was supplied to the growth medium, the expression of Lotus Ljnip5; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 7 2 }$ and Ljnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 5 9 }$ increased growth compared with control cells transformed with the empty vector (Figure 7B). Hence, truncating the N-terminus of LjNIPs resulted in As(III) transport, similar to what was observed for AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1.

Aquaglyceroporins from bacteria, yeast, protozoa and mammals have been shown to facilitate transport of the metalloids As(III) and Sb(III) across cell membranes (as reviewed in [20]). Here, we demonstrate that members of the NIP subfamily of plant aquaporins, which are believed to be the functional equivalents to microbial and mammalian aquaglyceroporins, mediate As(III) and Sb(III) transport when expressed in yeast. We conclude that the capacity of aquaporins to transport As(III) and Sb(III) is also well conserved in plants.

It has been reported that truncating parts of the hydrophilic N-terminal domain of certain NIPs is necessary to achieve functional expression in yeast and that the N-terminus is not required for the transport activity itself [27]. Our data support these findings as N-terminal truncation of AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 was necessary for functional expression in yeast (Figures 1, 2 and 3). On the other hand, truncation of AtNIP7;1 had little effect on its transport capacity (Figures 1, 2 and 3), supporting the interpretation that the hydrophilic N-terminal domain is not important for basic channel function. Interestingly, the necessity to remove part of the N-terminal domain does not apply to all members of the NIPII subgroup, as AtNIP7;1, OsNIP3;2 and OsNIP2;1 could be functionally expressed in yeast as full-length proteins (Figures 1, 2, 3 and 5). This is in accordance with data from functional expression of another full-length NIPII isoform from Cucurbita pepo (CpNIP) in yeast [38]. Hence, the necessity to truncate the N-terminal domain for functional expression in yeast appears to apply to a subpopulation within the NIPII subgroup.

In contrast to yeast, AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 were successfully expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes as full-length proteins [21,31]. In fact, it is not known why truncation is required for functional expression in yeast. Our Westernblot analysis of AtNIP6;1 suggests that the physical expression could be part of the reason; truncation of aa 2–69 resulted in increased protein levels in yeast membranes when compared with full-length AtNIP6;1. We can, however, not exclude that other reasons may contribute to this phenomenon. Deletion of the N-terminal domain could influence the targeting of the protein in the yeast secretory pathway. Alternatively, the N-terminal domain could function in gating the channel and components of a putative post-translational regulation mechanism displacing an inhibitory domain may be absent in yeast. A function of the N-terminal domain in gating has been ascribed to the yeast endogenous Fps1p [39,40], and phosphoryla

tion affects Fps1p transport activity [25]. Phosphorylation of plant and mammalian aquaporins was also shown to modulate transport function as well as localization [41- 43] and GmNOD26 of Glycine max is phosphorylated during specific developmental stages [44]. Strikingly, all isoforms that need to be truncated for functional expression in yeast contain a consensus Mitogen Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation site [32] consisting of a Pro-X-Ser/Thr-Pro motif in their N-terminus. This motif is missing in other NIPII homologs. The conservation of this site (Table 1) suggests that phosphorylation is required for functional expression and that phosphorylation may have a regulatory role in plants. However, deletion of the conserved MAPK site in the case of AtNIP6;1 $( A t n i p 6 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - }$ 29) and subsequent expression in yeast did not result in As(III) transport activity (Figures 2 and 3). Hence, the phosphorylation site itself is not identical with a potential inhibitory domain.

Based on the amino acids forming the selectivity filter, the NIP subfamily of plant aquaporins has been divided into two subgroups, NIPI and NIPII [30-33]. According to this classification, NIPI group homologs are characterized by the consensus motif W I/V A/G R (Table 2). The NIPII group was initially defined for homologs characterized by the consensus motif A $\mathrm { I } / \mathrm { V } \mathrm { ~ A } / \mathrm { G }$ R. Later, OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2 and OsNIP3;2 were also placed in the NIPII subgroup [32], despite having a slightly different pattern of amino acids in their selective filter. Furthermore, the amino acid motif in the constriction region of LjNIP6;1 is distinct from the aforementioned examples but similar to MtNIP3 and MtNIP4 from Medicago trunculata (Table 2), all of which group to NIPII in our phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4). However, common to all NIPII isoforms, is a small hydrophilic amino acid residue at the first position, where animal, microbial and other plant NIPs have either an aromatic F or a W. The division into NIPI and NIPII also appears to be a valuable grouping from a functional perspective, as OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2 and OsNIP3;2 also proved to channel As(III) and Sb(III) similar to other NIPII proteins tested in this study. However, the diverse patterns of amino acids in the selective filters of all As(III) and Sb(III) transporting aquaporin homologs from various organisms (Table 2) strongly suggests that other features must be important for the selectivity of these channels. Interestingly, NIP isoforms that facilitate the diffusion of other hydroxylated metalloids such as $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ [21] and $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ [22] also belong to the NIPII subgroup (Figure 4). Thus, accumulating evidence suggests that in plants, NIPII aquaporins are metalloid channels. In contrast, none of the isoforms of the NIPI subgroup tested here mediated As(III) transport. Members of the NIPI subgroup are expressed upon symbiosis with rhizobium and localized to the peribacteroid membrane in legume plants [44-46] and in plants interacting with mycorrhizal fungi [47]. Recently, AtNIP2;1, a member of the NIPI subgroup in Arabidopsis was shown to be induced at transcriptional level upon exposure to anoxic conditions [48]. When heterologously expressed in oocytes, AtNIP2;1 significantly increased the permeability for lactic acid, whereas only a minor permeability for water and glycerol, the 'conventional' aquaporin substrates, was recorded [48].

Glycerol has often been used as a substrate to monitor NIP channel activity [27,28,44,49]. Recent studies have shown that As(III) and Sb(III) exist as hydroxylated $\mathrm { A } s ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ and ${ \mathrm { S b } } ( { \mathrm { O H } } ) _ { 3 }$ at neutral pH [50,51]. Moreover, $\mathrm { A } s ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { S b } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ show very strong structural similarity both to each other and to glycerol [50]. Hence, it was proposed that $\mathrm { A } s ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { S b } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ transit through aquaglyceroporins through the same path as glycerol [50]. Similar conclusions could be drawn for NIPs in plants. However, in plants there is no direct evidence for a physiological role of glycerol transport through NIPs. Instead, metalloids may in fact represent the primary substrate of NIPII homologs. Notably, experimental data show that permeability for glycerol does not always coincide with the transport capacity for As(III) and Sb(III): (i) AtNIP1;1 transports glycerol [28] but does not seem to transport either As(III) or Sb(III) (this work); and (ii) OsNIP2;1 is shown here to be permeable for As(III) but is impermeable for glycerol [22]. The variability in the constriction region [33] along with other structural features of the channel path of NIPs seem to play a role in the discrimination between structurally highly similar solutes such as As(III), Sb(III) and glycerol. Interestingly, our phylogenetic analysis with rAQP9 as an out-group suggests that an ancestral NIP was capable of metalloid transport and that this capacity was lost in NIPI proteins (Figure 4). Nevertheless, this inference will require rigorous testing of more NIPs for the presence or absence of metalloid transport.

Due to the close structural similarity between $\mathrm { A } s ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { S b ( O H ) } _ { 3 } ,$ it was proposed that any difference observed in the toxicological properties of these metalloids must be related to processes other than cellular uptake [50]. However, in our study, expression of AtNIP7;1 only had a marginal effect on yeast growth on medium containing As(III), whereas on medium containing Sb(III), growth of the same transformants was strongly impaired (Figure 1). For yeast expressing Atnip5; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 7 }$ and Atnip6; ${ \cal { 1 } } \Delta _ { 2 - 6 9 } ,$ the opposite effects were seen with high sensitivity towards As(III) but only a mild increase in sensitivity towards Sb(III) (Figure 1). Thus, despite the high structural similarity of the two metalloids, our data demonstrate that NIPs can to some extent discriminate between As(III) and Sb(III) for selective transport.

OsNIP2;1 was originally identified as a $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ specific channel without significant permeability for glycerol [22], and AtNIP5;1 was shown to be crucial for the uptake of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ [21]. AtNIP5;1 and OsNIP2;1 are localized to the distal plasma membrane domain of the endodermis in Arabidopsis roots [21], and endodermis and exodermis of rice roots [22]. These cell layers represent a border for apoplastic transport. Nutrients taken up into the shoot via the vascular system have to enter the symplast by transport across the plasma membrane. Here we show that OsNIP2;1 and AtNIP5;1 are also permeable for the toxic metalloids As(III) and Sb(III). From a physiological point of view, the permeability for both beneficial (silicon) and essential (boron) nutrients as well as toxic substrates could pose a major problem for the plant; in the presence of arsenic in the soil solution, the expressed channels could be responsible for the uptake of toxic As(III). This would be problematic for rice, in particular, as rice roots grow in low oxygen soils, favoring the formation of the reduced form As(III). Hence, under conditions of low Si in the soil, leading to induction of OsNIP2;1, and under concomitant presence of As(III), rice roots are likely to take up As(III) via OsNIP2;1. Our data indicate that under physiologically relevant concentrations, $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ does not compete with As(III) for uptake through OsNIP2;1, suggesting that OsNIP2;1 has a high capacity for the transport of both metalloids. It will be important to investigate if OsNIP2;1 and AtNIP5;1 are differentially regulated by As(III) versus $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ and $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ in rice and Arabidopsis, respectively.

Transport of As(III) through NIPs and translocation to the shoot is potentially interesting for strategies of phytoremediation and the removal of arsenic from contaminated sites. In rice, uptake and translocation of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ is achieved by the concerted action of OsNIP2;1 and OsLsi2, the latter displaying homology to plant citrate transporters and to the Escherichia coli ArsB As(III) efflux transporter [22,52]. Rice Lsi2 is localized to the proximal plasma membrane domains of endodermis and exodermis cells. $\mathrm { { S i } ( O H ) _ { 4 } , }$ entering the cells via OsNIP2;1 is actively transported out of the cell and into the apoplastic continuum of the water transporting xylem elements for long-distance transport to the shoot [22]. However, expression of OsLsi2 or its closest homologs Os10g0547500 and At1g02260 did not affect yeast growth in the presence of As(III) or As(V) (data not shown). Although our data do not indicate that OsLsi2 and its homologs transport As(III) in yeast, it will be important to investigate this issue in plants.

Mammalian AQP9 was earlier shown to transport As(III) when expressed in yeast and Xenopus oocytes [26,53,54]. Interestingly, mono-methylated As(III), which is formed inside liver cells, was transported three times more efficiently than inorganic As(III), which led us to suggest that AQP9 could serve a function in arsenic detoxification [20]. Here, rAQP9 was very efficient in the uptake of As(III) but less effective in releasing the As(III) produced by yeast cells through the reduction of As(V). In contrast, NIP isoforms investigated here were less effective than rAQP9 in the uptake of As(III), but proved superior in supporting yeast growth in the presence of As(V). Plant cells primarily take up the oxidized form As(V) via high affinity phosphate transporters at the plasma membrane. It was recently reported that roots of rice and tomato plants have the capacity to efflux As(III) at high rate, when provided with As(V) in the growth medium [55]. The efficiency of some NIPIIs in extruding As(III) seen here supports the hypothesis that NIPII homologs may play a physiological role in arsenic detoxification. Such a role has been ascribed to the aquaglyceroporin AqpS from the legume symbiont Sinorhizobium meliloti [56]. Although this work demonstrates that specific plant aquaporins facilitate As(III) and Sb(III) transport, more work is needed to understand the role of As(III) transport through NIPII homologs in planta and we are currently putting efforts into this.

In conclusion, we demonstrate that specific plant NIPs transport As(III) and Sb(III) across cell membranes. Since the influx and efflux of toxic compounds is intimately linked to toxicity and detoxification, the identification of the proteins involved in this process provides a first important step towards the development of strategies for improving tolerance and remediation by plants.

In Arabidopsis, the nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein (NIP) subfamily of aquaporin proteins consists of nine members, five of which (NIP1;1, NIP1;2, NIP5;1, NIP6;1, and NIP7;1) were previously identified to be permeable to arsenite. However, the roles of NIPs in the root-to-shoot translocation of arsenite in plants remain poorly understood. In this study, using reverse genetic strategies, Arabidopsis NIP3;1 was identified to play an important role in both the arsenic uptake and root-to-shoot distribution under arsenite stress conditions. The nip3;1 loss-of-function mutants displayed obvious improvements in arsenite tolerance for aboveground growth and accumulated less arsenic in shoots than those of the wild-type plants, whereas the nip3;1 nip1;1 double mutant showed strong arsenite tolerance and improved growth of both roots and shoots under arsenite stress conditions. A promoter- $\mathbf { \beta }$ -glucuronidase analysis revealed that NIP3;1 was expressed almost exclusively in roots (with the exception of the root tips), and heterologous expression in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae demonstrated that NIP3;1 was able to mediate arsenite transport. Taken together, our results suggest that NIP3;1 is involved in arsenite uptake and root-to-shoot translocation in Arabidopsis, probably as a passive and bidirectional arsenite transporter.

Strong arsenite tolerance with regard to root growth was also observed in the NIP1;1-knockout mutants, including nip3;1 nip1;1 double mutants and nip1;1 single mutants (Figure 5). These data further confirm that NIP3;1 and NIP1;1 affect predominantly the As(III) tolerance of the aboveground parts and the belowground roots of Arabidopsis, respectively. The nip3;1 nip1;1 double mutant, similar to nip3;1-4, had a significantly reduced level of As in the aboveground tissues under As(III) conditions, indicating that NIP3;1 is the important factor involved in arsenite translocation from roots to shoots (Figure 6). However, it was surprising that the reduction of As in the roots of both nip3;1 nip1;1 and nip1;1 was relatively small at the $4 8 \ \mathsf { h }$ point. The low amount of reduction in As content in nip1;1 mutants was also detected by Kamiya et al. (2009). The mechanism by which NIP1;1 plays a dominant role for high arsenite tolerance with regard to primary root growth is unclear but may be due to the impact of $\mathsf { A s } ( | | | )$ uptake via NIP1;1 on some special cells controlling root growth. Thus, the observation that the nip3;1 nip1;1 double-mutant plants had the phenotype that exhibited the most pronounced arsenite tolerance was likely due to the combination of both the decreased As accumulation in the shoots of the NIP3;1-kockout mutant, and the well-developed root system of the NIP1;1-knockout mutant under arsenite conditions.

Similar to previous reports, analyses in this study showed that NIP1;1 expression under the strong CaMV 35S constitutive promoter complemented the nip1;1 mutation, and transgenic lines showed arsenite-sensitive phenotypes (Kamiya et al., 2009). Therefore, the pronounced root growth arsenite tolerance phenotype of the nip1;1-genotype mutant provided effective material for functionally identifying the arsenite transporter in Arabidopsis. NIP3;1 overexpression, driven by the CaMV 35S promoter, also restored the arsenite sensitivity of primary root growth in the nip1;1 mutant. Although NIPs and aquaglyceroporins can transport methylated As species, such as monomethylarsonic acid (MMA[V]) and trivalent MMAs(III) (Liu et al., 2006; Li et al., 2009), As(III) is the predominant As species, and methylated As species are found in very low concentrations in plant tissues, even when the plants are exposed to arsenate (Dhankher et al., 2002; Quaghebeur and Rengel, 2004; Raab et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2007). These results suggest that NIP3;1, similar to NIP1;1, functions as an As(III) transporter in Arabidopsis, although each has a distinct physiological function in Arabidopsis.

RT–PCR and promoter-GUS (b-glucuronidase) fusion experiments revealed the predominant expression of NIP3;1 in roots. These tissue-specific expression profiles suggest the roles of NIP3;1 in As(III) transport within roots. Interestingly, no GUS staining was detected at the root tips (Figure 4B, 4C, and 4H), indicating that NIP3;1 is not expressed in the key determinant zones for root growth. Considering that overexpression of NIP3;1 under the control of the CaMV 35S promoter can complement the nip1;1 mutant, NIP1;1 may play a key role in arsenite distribution in root-tip cells. In any case, it will be of interest to determine the specific role of NIP1;1 in the uptake and distribution of As(III) in Arabidopsis.

Efflux of solutes toward the xylem is a critical step in the regulation of the quantities and species of ions available for root-to-shoot translocation (Bowling, 1981; Clarkson, 1993). Recent studies have revealed that some NIP aquaporins are capable of bidirectional arsenite transport in yeast, Xenopus oocytes, and rice roots, indicating that NIP arsenite transporters can play a bifunctional role in the uptake and efflux of arsenite in plant cells (Bienert et al., 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis, 2008; Zhao et al., 2010a). Importantly, our heterologous functional assays show that the truncated NIP3;1D266–323 or NIP3;1D2–29, D266–323 also has a profound effect on the uptake and the efflux of arsenite similar to that of other NIP aquaporins mediating bidirectional arsenite transport in yeast (Figure 7), although only the full-length NIP3;1, not the truncated-NIP3;1D266–323, expressed in nip3;1 nip1;1 double mutant could recover its aboveground As(III)-sensitive phenotype similar to nip1;1 mutant (Supplemental Figure 7), showing that the truncated-NIP3;1 and the full-length NIP3;1 are functionally expressed in yeast and in Arabidopsis, respectively, to mediate As(III) transport.

The nip3;1 mutants showed significantly decreased As concentrations in their aboveground parts, but accumulated similar As in their roots under arsenite conditions compared with the wild-types. A cross section through the root hair zone of $N I P 3 ; 1 _ { p r o } { : : } G U S$ transgenic seedlings revealed GUS expression at high levels in epidermal, cortical, endodermal, and pericycle cells, particularly in the endodermal and pericycle cells adjacent to the protoxylem poles (Figure 4I). These endodermal cells, which are opposite to the protoxylem poles, are thin walled and are also known as passage cells, because they provide a pathway into the stele that is characterized by lower resistance to water flow (Peterson and Enstone, 1996; Hamburger et al., 2002). Several channels and transporters involved in xylem loading, such as the SKOR–potassium channel (Gaymard et al., 1998), the BOR1 boron transporter (Takano et al., 2002), the PHO1 Pi transporter (Hamburger et al., 2002), the AtHMA4 Zn/Cd transporter (Verret et al., 2004), and the NRT1.5 nitrate transporter (Lin et al., 2008), are expressed particularly in passage cells and/or the pericycle cells close to the protoxylem. Therefore, NIP3;1 is significantly expressed in epidermal cells as well as root hairs (Figure 4), and the nip3;1 knockout mutants accumulate half or even less As in roots compared with wild-type in short-term experiments (24 h) (Figure 3D), suggesting that NIP3;1 plays a very important role in As(III) uptake. However, in the longer-term experiment, similar As accumulation in roots of mutants and wild-type is observed, and one possible explanation is that reduced As(III) uptake offsets the low root-to-shoot translocation. Moreover, as a passive and bidirectional transporter, NIP3;1 is also significantly expressed in the passage cells and is possibly involved in the efflux of As(III) out of pericycle cells toward the xylem, which is responsible for loading As(III) into the xylem for root-to-shoot translocation.

## Arsenite Uptake and Translocation via AtNIP3;1


In conclusion, we suggest that NIP3;1, a close homolog of NIP1;1, is a new member of arsenite transporters in Arabidopsis. Depending on the tissue- and cell-specificity of expression, NIP3;1 plays an important role in As uptake and root-to-shoot translocation under arsenite stress conditions. NIP channels possibly form a complex network for the uptake, efflux, and distribution of arsenite in Arabidopsis. Furthermore, identifying and elucidating the molecular mechanism underpinning arsenite distribution in plants will facilitate the design and implementation of mitigation strategies to reduce the risk of As contamination (Su et al., 2008; Ali et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2010b). Thus, these findings may also provide new insights into strategies for improving plant tolerance to arsenite or for reducing As accumulation in edible plant parts through the combined application of As transporter genes and related promoters.

## NIP3;1-Knockout Plants Have Enhanced Aboveground Tolerance to Arsenite


In Arabidopsis, the aquaporin subfamily of NIP genes contains nine members, five of which (NIP7;1, NIP5;1, NIP6;1, NIP1;2, and NIP1;1) are permeable to arsenite (Bienert et al., 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis, 2008; Kamiya et al., 2009). To identify the candidate NIPs in Arabidopsis that are likely involved in the root-to-shoot translocation of arsenite, we obtained homozygous knockout lines of the nine NIP T-DNA-insertion mutants and grew them on 1/2 Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium containing various concentrations of arsenite to measure the relative sensitivity of aboveground parts (Supplemental Figure 1). Shoots of the NIP3;1-deletion mutant, nip3;1-1 (FLAG_065A11 in the

Wassilewskija (Ws-4) background), in which a T-DNA was inserted in the third exon (Figure 1A) and the NIP3;1 transcript was not detectable (Figure 1B), grew much better than those of the wild-type Ws-4 under arsenite stress conditions (Figure 1C). However, the primary root growth of both nip3;1-1 and wild-type Ws-4 plants was strikingly retarded under arsenite conditions; thus, no significant difference was observed (Supplemental Figure 2A). Quantitative analyses confirmed that the nip3;1-1 plants had improved resistance to arsenite in their aboveground parts; the shoot fresh weight of nip3;1-1 was 1.5- to 2.0-fold higher than that of wild-type Ws-4 plants grown in As(III)-containing media (Figure 1D).

To further verify the enhanced aboveground tolerance of the phenotype to arsenite in NIP3;1-knockout plants, more independent T-DNA-insertion alleles nip3;1-2, nip3;1-3, nip3;1-4, and nip3;1-5 in the Columbia (Col-0) ecotype for NIP3;1 were obtained, and the T-DNA insertion sites were confirmed to be in the third exon, the second intron, and the fourth exon (for the last two lines) of the NIP3;1 gene (Figure 1A). No NIP3;1 mRNA expression was detected in any T-DNA-insertion mutant by RT–PCR analysis (Figure 1B). As shown in Figure 1E and 1F, the shoot growth of the nip3;1 mutants was also more tolerant to arsenite than the corresponding Col-0 wild-type. Primary root growth did not differ significantly between the mutants and wild-types (Supplemental Figure 2B). These results demonstrate that in both a Ws-4 and Col-0 background, loss of NIP3;1 has a profound influence on the tolerance of Arabidopsis shoot growth for arsenite.


## NIP3;1 Expression Driven by the NIP1;1 Promoter Restores the Arsenite Sensitivity of Root Growth in the NIP1;1-Knockout Mutant


According to alignment and phylogenetic tree analyses of the deduced amino acid sequences (Supplemental Figure 3), NIP3;1 showed a $5 8 . 7 \%$ identity with NIP1;1, a key determinant in the tolerance of root growth to arsenite, and both NIP3;1 and NIP1;1 belonged to the same group (I) (Ali et al., 2009; Kamiya et al., 2009). To investigate whether NIP3;1 was, like NIP1;1, also an arsenite transporter in Arabidopsis, we used NIP1;1- knockout mutants with a root-growth phenotype that was highly tolerant to arsenite. The T-DNA-homozygous mutant nip1;1 (SALK_016617) of NIP1;1 was selected, and the high arsenitetolerant primary root growth phenotype was confirmed in nip1;1 (Figure 2), as reported by Kamiya et al. (2009). Therefore, we generated the NIP3;1 expression construct under the control of the NIP1;1 promoter and introduced it into the nip1;1 mutant plant. To test whether expression of NIP3;1 using NIP1;1 promoter modified the tolerance to arsenite in nip1;1 mutants, wild-type (Col-0), NIP1;1pro::NIP3;1 (nip1;1), and nip1;1 were examined for growth differences under arsenite condition. The NIP1;1pro::NIP3;1 (nip1;1) showed significantly reduced root growth compared with nip1;1 (Figure 2). Two constitutively expressed NIP3;1 and NIP1;1 constructs under the control of the CaMV 35S promoter were also generated and introduced into nip1;1 mutants. Both 35S-NIP1;1(nip1;1) and 35SNIP3;1(nip1;1) also exhibited enhanced arsenite sensitivity phenotypes (Supplemental Figure 4). These results indicate that the efficiency of NIP3;1 for arsenite transport is similar to that of NIP1;1.

 Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) play essential roles in transporting the nutrients silicon and boron in seed plants, but the evolutionary origin of this transport function and the co-permeability to toxic arsenic remains enigmatic. Horizontal gene transfer of a yet uncharacterised bacterial AqpN-aquaporin group was the starting-point for plant NIP evolution.  We combined intense sequence, phylogenetic and genetic context analyses and a mutational approach with various transport assays in oocytes and plants to resolve the transorganismal and functional evolution of bacterial and algal and terrestrial plant NIPs and to reveal their molecular transport specificity features.   
 We discovered that aqpN genes are prevalently located in arsenic resistance operons of various prokaryotic phyla. We provided genetic and functional evidence that these proteins contribute to the arsenic detoxification machinery. We identified NIPs with the ancestral bacterial AqpN selectivity filter composition in algae, liverworts, moss, hornworts and ferns and demonstrated that these archetype plant NIPs and their prokaryotic progenitors are almost impermeable to water and silicon but transport arsenic and boron. With a mutational approach, we demonstrated that during evolution, ancestral NIP selectivity shifted to allow subfunctionalisations.

 Together, our data provided evidence that evolution converted bacterial arsenic efflux channels into essential seed plant nutrient transporters.

Silicon (Si) is the second most abundant element in the earth crust. It is an essential element for animals and has been implicated in optimal bone and connective tissue development in the human body [1]. For plants, Si is a beneficial element. The beneficial effects are characterized by protecting plants from various biotic and abiotic stresses [2]. For example, Si enhances resistance of plants to diseases, pests, and lodging, improves the light-interception ability by keeping leaves erect, thereby, stimulating canopy photosynthesis in rice, alleviates metal toxicity, and minimizes transpiration losses.

Plants take up Si from the roots in the form of silicic acid $\mathrm { ( S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } ) }$ , an uncharged molecule [3]. Recently, by using a rice mutant defective in Si uptake, the first transporter of silicic acid, Lsi1 (OsNIP2;1), has been identified in rice, which is a highly Si-accumulating species [4]. This transporter is mainly expressed in the roots and localized at the plasma membranes of both exodermis and endodermis. Interestingly, this transporter showed polar localization at distal side of the cells in all types of the roots including main, lateral, and crown roots [4, 5]. This transporter plays a crucial role in Si uptake in rice because disruption of this transporter resulted in a significant reduction of Si uptake and subsequently of rice yield [4, 6]. Blast search showed that this transporter belongs to nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein (NIP), which is one of the four subfamilies in plant aquaporin. Lsi1 has a common structure as other aquaporins, which is characterized by six membrane-spanning $\propto$ - helices and highly conserved NPA (Asn-Pro-Ala) motifs [7]. NIPs are unique to plants, which have nine members in arabidopsis and 10 to 13 members in rice [8]. Functional analysis of NIPs has revealed diversity in their transport substrates. For example, soybean nodulin 26 transported not only water but also glycerol [9], whereas AtNIP2;1 showed a transport activity for lactic acid [10]. Some NIPs are permeable to larger solutes such as urea [11], formamide [11], and boric acid [12], depending on the NIP proteins. Our previous study showed that Lsi1 is not permeable to glycerol [4]. However, it is unknown whether this transporter is permeable to other solutes. In the present study, we further characterized Lsi1 in terms of flux direction, substrate specificity, and phosphorylation by using the Xenopus laevis oocyte expression system. The substrate specificity of NIPs is discussed in relation to the ar/R selectivity filter, which is an important constriction for solute permeability.

Further characterization in the present study showed that Lsi1 was permeable to both water and silicic acid (Fig. 2). In addition, the transport activity for silicic acid was inhibited by $\mathrm { H g } \mathrm { C l } _ { 2 }$ (Fig. 3, 4). It is well known that aquaporin-mediated water flux is inhibited by the mercury by blocking the protein via oxidation of cysteine residue(s). For example, arabidopsis δ-TIP (tonoplast intrinsic protein) has a mercury-sensitive cysteine residue placed in the third transmembrane domain [17]. Lsi1 also has three cysteine residues, and one of them Cys139 is located at the third transmembrane domain. These results indicate that Lsi1 has a common feature similar to most other aquaporins. Furthermore, Lsi1 is a bidirectional transporter (Figs. 3 and 4), which can mediate both influx and efflux of silicic acid in the oocyte expression system, although it only functions as an influx transporter in rice roots [4].

The transport activity of Lsi1 for silicic acid was not affected by the low-temperature treatment (Fig. 3). This result is contrary to that reported in rice. In rice, the Si uptake by the roots was significantly reduced under low temperature [16]. Recently, an efflux transporter (Lsi2) of silicic acid was identified [15]. This transporter is also localized at the exodermis and endodermis, but in contrast to Lsi1, Lsi2 is localized at the proximal side and responsible for the transport of silicic acid out of the cells. This transporter is driven by the proton gradient, and the efflux transport activity was inhibited at low temperature [15]. Therefore, the reduction of Si uptake in rice under low temperature is attributed to the inhibited transport activity of Lsi2 rather than Lsi1.

Substrate specificity of Lsi1

Aquaporin was first identified as water channel proteins [18]. However, subsequent studies have shown that some aquaporins also transport other substrates such as $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ , glycerol, urea, and boric acid [19]. Lsi1 is the first aquaporin identified that transports silicic acid [4], which is present in the form of uncharged molecule at a $\mathrm { p H }$ under 9.0. Lsi1 was not permeable to glycerol [4]. The substrate specificity of Lsi1 was further investigated in the present study by comparing the transport activity for silicic acid with that for two other uncharged solutes: urea and boric acid. Although Lsi1 also showed transport activity for urea and boric acid (Figs. 5 and 6), competition experiments showed that the transport activity for silicic acid was not affected by the presence of an equimolar concentration urea and was decreased only slightly by boric acid (Figs. 5 and 6). In addition, in soil solutions, the concentration of silicic acid is much higher than that of boric acid. It is, therefore, unlikely that Lsi1 functions as a transporter of boric acid. The evidence obtained in the present study indicates that Lsi1 is a highly specific transporter for silicic acid.

In the NIP subfamily, OsNIP2;2 showed a transport activity for silicic acid as Lsi1 (OsNIP2;1) (Fig. 7), whereas two other members (OsNIP1;1 and OsNIP3;1) did not, although both of them are also suggested to be localized in the plasma membrane (Fig. 7). The substrate selectivity of aquaporins is controlled by the NPA (Asn-Pro-Ala) motif and the ar/R (aromatic/arginine) selectivity filter [7, 8]. The NPA region is formed by the close apposition of the asparagines of the two NPA motifs in the loops B and E at the center of the pore. These asparagine residues form hydrogen-bond contacts with the transported water or solute molecules and are proposed to block proton transport by interrupting the hydrogen-bonding network of the water chains by dipole reorientation of transported water [20, 21]. In NIP subfamily, there are several types of NPA motifs including NPV, NPS, and NPG in addition to NPA (Fig. 1); however, it seems that NPA motif is not a crucial factor in the substrate selectivity in NIPs. For example, both OsNIP1;1 and OsNIP2;1 have the same NPA motif (Fig. 1), but only the latter showed transport activity for silicic acid (Fig. 7). On the other hand, nodulin 26 and AtNIP6;1 have different NPA motifs but both showed similar water and glycerol permeability [11].

A second pore constriction is the ar/R region, which is located in the narrowest region on the extra-membrane mouth of the pore. It is formed by four residues including aromatic residues and Arg residues, one each from helix 2 (H2) and helix 5 (H5), as well as two residues from loop E (LE1 and LE2) [22]. The properties of the four residues making up the ar/R selectivity filter appear to govern the substrate specificity of the pore. For example, the selectivity filter residues of water-specific aquaporins tend to be smaller (pore diameter, $2 . 8 \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ }$ ) and more hydrophilic [23, 24], whereas those of glycerol transporter form a larger $( 3 . 4 \mathrm { ~ \AA } )$ , more hydrophobic pore [25]. Based on the ar/R regions of arabidopsis, NIPs have been divided into two groups, NIPs I and II [22] (Fig. 1). However, the identification of Lsi1 (OsNIP2;1) leads us to propose a third group (NIP III) with a distinct ar/R region (Fig. 1). Different from other groups of NIPs (Fig. 1), the ar/R region of NIP III consists of Gly (G), Ser (S), Gly (G), and Arg (R). It is predicted that the smaller size of the residues in the NIP III form a larger constriction size compared with other NIP groups [8, 25], which allows silicic acid with a larger diameter $( 4 . 3 8 \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ } )$ to permeate. This prediction is consistent with our transport activity results for OsNIPs (Fig. 7). Although other members from maize and zucchini in the NIP III have not been tested in terms of their transport activity of silicic acid (Fig. 1), both maize and zucchini are known to accumulate high levels of Si, although less than in rice [15]. Therefore, it is likely that NIP III group is unique to Si-accumulating plant species so far and functions as a silicon transporter. By contrast, NIP I proteins in arabidopsis have been reported to transport water, glycerol [9], and lactic acid [10], whereas NIP II proteins are permeable to larger solutes than NIP I protein, such as urea [11], formamide [11], and boric acid [12]. The evidence so far indicates that the ar/R selectivity filter plays an important role in determining the substrate specificity in the NIP subfamily.

The larger pore size formed in the NIP III group can explain why Lsi1 was also permeable to water, urea, and boric acid (Figs. 2, 5, and 6), which have a smaller diameter than silicic acid. However, although the molecule size of glycerol is smaller than that of silicic acid, Lsi1 was not permeable to glycerol [4]. This suggests that other unknown factors may also be involved in the substrate specificity.

Involvement of phosphorylation in the regulation of Lsi1

A number of studies indicated that the activity of both plant and animal aquaporins may be regulated by phosphorylation [19, 26]. For example, closure of the spinach plasma membrane aquaporin SoPIP2;1 (formally called PM28A) was triggered by the dephosphorylation of two serine residues: Ser115 in the cytosolic loop B and Ser274 in the carboxy-terminal region [26]. Phosphorylation of soybean nodulin 26 on ${ \tt S e r 2 6 2 }$ enhanced water permeability [27]. It is suggested that serine residues located on the N-terminal, C-terminal, and loop B, which are candidate phosphorylation sites, are important for gating [19]. According to the sequence of Lsi1, there are three possible phosphorylation sites, Ser267, 273, and 281. The involvement of phosphorylation site in the regulation of Lsi1 was investigated using two inhibitors: okadaic acid and K252a as protein phosphatase and protein kinase inhibitors, respectively. Both inhibitors have been used in the phosphorylation studies of aquaporins. For example, the water permeability of spinach plasma membrane aquaporin PM28A was inhibited by $50 \%$ with K252a but activated by $30 \%$ with okadaic acid [26]. The water permeability by nodulin 26 was also increased by okadaic acid [27]. On the other hand, the water permeability of HvPIP2;1 was unaffected by these inhibitors [28]. Our results showed that neither okadaic acid nor K252a affected the transport activity for silicic acid in oocytes (Fig. 8). There are two possibilities for this result. One is that, in the oocyte system, Lsi1 could not be phosphorylated by oocyte protein kinase. However, this possibility was ruled out by a previous study with nodulin 26 [27]. Although nodulin 26 was phosphorylated by calciumdependent protein kinase in plants [29, 30], which is not present in animals, it was also phosphorylated by an animal kinase, protein kinase C, when expressed in the oocytes [27]. Further studies are needed to examine whether the phosphorylation of Lsi1 occurs in plants. The other possibility is that phosphorylation is not involved in the regulation of Lsi1. Different from other minerals, Si does not show excess toxicity to plants because silicic acid autopolymerizes at higher concentrations [31]. Furthermore, the beneficial effects of Si on plant growth are enhanced with more accumulation of Si. Therefore, it may not be necessary to regulate the activity of Si transporters by phosphorylation. In fact, Lsi1 is constitutively expressed in the rice roots, and the expression level is not markedly affected by Si level [4, 5].

In conclusion, although Lsi1 is also permeable to water, urea, and boric acid, it is a highly specific bidirectional transporter for silicic acid. The substrate specificity of Lsi1 is largely controlled by a distinct ar/R selectivity filter formed by four small amino acid residues.

Nodulin-26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) of the aquaporin family are involved in the transport of diverse solutes, but the mechanisms controlling the selectivity of transport substrates are poorly understood. The purpose of this study was to investigate how the aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity filter influences the substrate selectivity of two NIP aquaporins; the silicic acid (Si) transporter OsLsi1 (OsNIP2;1) from rice and the boric acid (B) transporter AtNIP5;1 from Arabidopsis; both proteins are also permeable to arsenite. Native and site-directed mutagenized variants of the two genes were expressed in Xenopus oocytes and the transport activities for Si, B, arsenite, and water were assayed. Substitution of the amino acid at the ar/R second helix (H2) position of OsLsi1 did not affect the transport activities for Si, B, and arsenite, but that at the H5 position resulted in a total loss of Si and B transport activities and a partial loss of arsenite transport activity. Conversely, changes of the AtNIP5;1 ar/R selectivity filter and the NPA motifs to the OsLsi1 type did not result in a gain of Si transport activity. B transport activity was partially lost in the H5 mutant but unaffected in the H2 mutant of AtNIP5;1. In contrast, both the single and double mutations at the H2 and/or H5 positions of AtNIP5;1 did not affect arsenite transport activity. The results reveal that the residue at the H5 position of the ar/R filter of both OsLsi1 and AtNIP5;1 plays a key role in the permeability to Si and B, but there is a relatively low selectivity for arsenite.

Key words: Arsenic, boron, NIP aquaporins, selectivity, silicon, substrate.

Nodulin26-like intrinsic membrane proteins (NIPs), aquaporins that have been initially localized in peribacteroid membrane of nitrogen-fixing root nodules of leguminous plants, are present in plasma membrane of the non-symbiotic plants too (Wudick et al., 2009; Kapilan et al., 2018). Aquaporins identified as nodulin26 proteins were first characterized in soybean and then in other rhizobia-symbiotic vegetables (Rouge and Barre, 2008).

Nodule formation is a result of symbiotic relationship between plant and nitrogen fixing bacteria. During the process of nodule formation, nodulin proteins are expressed by plants and transferred to the membranes. Nodulin 26 proteins are expressed at the symbiosome membrane and have similar sequences to NIP proteins (Kapilan et al., 2018).

NIPs have been classified in five phylogenetic groups (NIP1-NIP5) and in three functional groups (NIP I, NIP II, NIP III), based on similarity of the aromatic/arginine constriction (Mateluna et al., 2018).

Comparatively with other aquaporins, NIPs play a similar role as transporters of water, but in contrast with PIPs and TIPs, NIPs have lower water transport activity (Maurel et al., 2015; Kapilan et al., 2018). However, besides glycerol and water (Kruse et al., 2006),

NIPs are permeable to small organic solutes and mineral nutrients and mediate diffusion of metalloids (boric acid, silicon and selenium) and toxic elements (arsenic) (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014; Maurel et al., 2015; Fox et al., 2017). NIPs transport functions have been established by direct mutagenesis and by expression in oocytes (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014). NIP I proteins are permeable to water, glycerol and ammonia, NIP II proteins transport urea and metalloid nutrients (boron), but have lower water permeability and NIP III proteins transport larger molecules (silicic acid, urea) (Mateluna et al., 2018).

Some structural particularities in NPA motif (alanine is replaced with serine, glycine or valine) might render NIPs capable of transporting substrates other than water (Wudick et al., 2009). NIP2 proteins have a wider pore than those of NIP1 and are permeable to large solutes (urea). Also, AtNIP2;1 is expressed in the endoplasmic reticulum of roots, whereas AtNIP5;1 is expressed in plasma membrane of roots elongation zones. The AtNIP2;1 mediates lactic acid transport, being very important to the adaptation to lactic fermentation under anaerobic stress (Gomes et al., 2009). When NIPs phosphorylation is increased, NIPs have an important role in maintaining plant water balance and in drought and salt stress responses (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014; Kapilan et al., 2018).

NIPs proteins have multifunctional transport properties of water and/or uncharged solutes as glycerol. NIP gene transcripts were found in seed coat, shoot and roots (Kaldenhoff and Fischer, 2006).

Aquaporins play a vital role in uptake and transport of water and many other small solutes in plants. A genome-wide search performed in the carrot genome leads to identification of 47 aquaporins. Subsequent, computational analysis and phylogenetic classification of carrot aquaporins predicted DcNIP2-1 as a silicon transporter. The DcNIP2-1 is a member of NIPIII class of the Nodulin-26 like Intrinsic Protein (NIP) subfamily of aquaporins which is known to regulate uptake of silicon and other metalloids like arsenic and Germanium. Despite having NIP2-1 with functionality defining features like G-S-G-R aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity filter, 108 amino acid spacing between two NPA motif, Mitani’s residue and desired pore morphology, carrot plants found to be silicon poor accumulator. Subsequently, pot-experiments were performed to confirm the uptake of other metalloids, and silicon derived benefits in carrot. Carrot plants were grown with arsenic and with or without silicon supplementation. The results obtained neither showed silicon accumulation, nor any significant benefits to carrot plants under arsenic stress. Similarly, very less accumulation of arsenic was observed in carrot leaves. Such low accumulation of silicon was consistent across different Apiaceae species. The information provided here will be helpful to better understand aquaporin regulation and more particularly silicon uptake and silicon derived benefits in Apiaceae and other plant species.

Keywords Aquaporin $\cdot$ Arsenic $\cdot$ Metalloids $\cdot$ Silicon transporter · Stress alleviation
