## pdr8 Phenotypes Are Suppressed by Blocking IBA-to-IAA Conversion


Genetic evidence indicates that peroxisomal carboxyl side chain shortening of IBA to IAA is required for the auxin activity of IBA in Arabidopsis bioassays (Zolman et al., 2000, 2007). IBA-resistant and IAA-sensitive mutants include peroxisome biogenesis mutants, such as pex5 (Zolman et al., 2000) and pex7 (Woodward and Bartel, 2005a), mutants defective in certain peroxisomal $\beta$ -oxidation enzymes, such as IBR1 (Zolman et al., 2008), IBR3 (Zolman et al., 2007), and IBR10 (Zolman et al., 2008), and mutants defective in the PXA1 transporter that brings $\beta$ -oxidation substrates into the peroxisome (Zolman et al., 2001). Many of these mutants exhibit decreased lateral root production in the absence of exogenous hormone (Zolman et al., 2001; Woodward and Bartel, 2005a), suggesting that IBA conversion to IAA is important for proper lateral root formation. The pdr8 phenotypes of increased lateral root production, increased root hair growth, and increased cotyledon expansion suggest that certain pdr8 cells hyperaccumulate auxin, and the observation that pdr8 root tips hyperaccumulate $[ ^ { 3 } \mathsf { H } ]$ -IBA but not $[ ^ { 3 } \mathsf { H } ]$ -IAA suggests that the auxin that accumulates is IBA. Moreover, the pdr8 developmental phenotypes were all suppressed by blocking IBA-to-IAA conversion in the pdr8 pex5 and pdr8 pxa1 double mutants (Figures 5A to 5C, 6G, and 7B). The suppression of pdr8 developmental phenotypes by mutations expected to block

IBA-to-IAA conversion suggests a model in which IBA accumulates to inappropriate levels in pdr8 and is converted to IAA, which causes increased growth (Figure 10).

## Roles of PDR/ABCG Proteins


Although the pdr8 developmental defects had not been previously noted, PDR8/PEN3/ABCG36 has been implicated in pathogen response; pdr8/pen3 mutants exhibit increased sensitivity to the nonhost pathogens Blumeria graminis f. sp hordei (barley powdery mildew) (Stein et al., 2006), Plectospaerella cucumerina, Erysipha pisa (pea powdery mildew) (Stein et al., 2006), and Phytopthera infestans (potato late blight) (Kobae et al., 2006; Stein et al., 2006), as well as decreased sensitivity to the Arabidopsis pathogens Erysiphe cichoracearum (powdery mildew) (Stein et al., 2006) and Pseudomonas syringae (Kobae et al., 2006). Furthermore, pdr8/pen3 mutants accumulate less extracellular callose in response to the microbe-associated molecular pattern molecule Flg22 (Clay et al., 2009), hyperaccumulate Flg22- or pathogen-elicited 4-methoxyindol-3-ylmethylglucosinolate (Bednarek et al., 2009; Clay et al., 2009), and hyperaccumulate pathogen-elicited camalexin (Bednarek et al., 2009). PDR8 also has been implicated in cadmium efflux (Kim et al., 2007). Whether the developmental roles of PDR8 uncovered here and the roles of PDR8 pathogen response, callose, camalexin, and glucosinolate production, or cadmium extrusion are related or separate functions remains to be explored.

Similar to previously identified auxin effluxers in the ABCB/ MDR/PGP subfamily, the 15-member PDR group of the ABCG subfamily of ABC transporters are full-sized ABC transporters with two transmembrane domains each consisting of six membrane-spanning sequences and two apparent nucleotide binding domains (reviewed in van den Brule and Smart, 2002; Crouzet et al., 2006; Verrier et al., 2008). However, few of these transporters have been functionally characterized. PDR9/ ABCG37 is a likely 2,4-D (Ito and Gray, 2006) and IBA (Strader et al., 2008b) efflux facilitator. PDR8, which is only $5 3 \%$ identical to PDR9, is the second PDR/ABCG family member implicated in IBA efflux, raising the possibility that multiple members of this family may efflux IBA. PDR family members have diverse expression patterns (Crouzet et al., 2006); PDR8 and PDR9 are more highly expressed in roots than most PDR genes (van den Brule and Smart, 2002). Future studies may elucidate whether ABCG subfamily members participate in long-distance IBA transport, similar to the roles of ABCB subfamily members in IAA transport, or are more important for short-distance IBA transport. The latter possibility is supported by the enrichment of PDR8-GFP on the outward face of root epidermal cells, suggesting that PDR8 may remove IBA from the root tip. Analyses of additional PDR/ABCG family members will be required to fully understand the roles that these proteins play in IBA transport and auxin homeostasis.

ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter genes are ubiquitous across the three domains of life: Eukarya, Eubacteria and Archaea [1, 2]. Plant genomes harbor more than 100 ABC transporters which are involved in a broad range of biological functions [3]. ABC transporters comprise at least four domains: two transmembrane domains (TMDs) embedded in the membrane bilayer, and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) located in the cytoplasm [1]. The structure of the TMDs is highly diverse and varies in the number of transmembrane helices, whereas the NBDs have highly conserved helices [4]. The ABC transporters are further categorized into full-size transporters with two NBDs and two TMDs and halfsize transporters with only one of each domain [5]. Therefore, two half-size transporters must form either a homodimer or a heterodimer to be functionally active.

In plant genomes, ABC transporters are categorized into eight different subfamilies (ABCA-ABCG and ABCI) [3]. Proteins belonging to the ABCA-ABCD subfamilies have a forward domain organization (TMDNBD) whereas ABCG and ABCI subfamilies have an inverse domain organization (NBD-TMD) [6]. ABCE and ABCF possess only two NBDs and are designated as soluble proteins [6]. In Arabidopsis, 130 ABC transporter genes have been identified but few have been functionally characterized [7]. Previous studies have shown that ABC transporters participate in a wide range of processes including the transport of ions, carbohydrates, lipids, xenobiotics, antibiotics, drugs, and heavy metals [8–10]. The two members of the ABCB gene family in Arabidopsis (AtABCB1 and AtABCB2) are auxin transporters and the overexpression of AtABCB1 causes the elongation of hypocotyl cells [11, 12]. Several members of the ABCC subfamily are responsible for phytate transport as exemplified in Arabidopsis (AtABCC5) [13], maize (ZmABCC4) [14] and rice (OsABCC13) [15]. Two other ABCC transporters (AtABCC1 and AtABCC2) mediate tolerance to both cadmium (Cd) and mercury by vacuolar sequestration [16]. The ABCF subfamily member AtABCF3 in Arabidopsis is involved in root growth and development [17]. ABCG subfamily members were reported to be involved in cuticle formation and Cd tolerance such as in Arabidopsis (AtABCG32) [18] and rice (OsABCG31 and OsABCG36) [19, 20]. Also, the ABC transporter AtABCG36 in Arabidopsis was shown to mediate Cd uptake in the epidermal cells of roots [21] and to be up-regulated by a Cd treatment [22].

Heavy metal (HM) pollution in food, water, and soil is hazardous to human health. HMs have become one of the major concerns across the globe due to the extensive industrialization and because of their direct and indirect effects on soil and crop productivity [23]. HMs such as zinc, copper, manganese, cobalt, and nickel are essential for various biological processes [24]. In contrast, other HMs such as arsenic, lead, and Cd are highly toxic to plants and negatively affect crop productivity [23]. Many HMA genes have been shown to play specific functions in different plant species. For example, OsHMA2 is associated with vascular tissue loading of zinc and tonoplast localization in rice [25]. OsHMA3, localized in the tonoplasts, translocates Cd to the roots while OsHMA4 transports copper to the roots [26]. HvHMA1 is involved in zinc and Cd translocation into barley grain [27]. In wheat, HMA genes also play an important role in Cd translocation and are localized in the plasma membrane [28]. Overexpression of AtHMA3 in Arabidopsis resulted in a 2- to 3-fold increase in Cd accumulation when compared to wild-type plants [29]. These cited studies provide an overview of the importance of both ABC transporter and HMA genes in various plant species, but no systemic studies have been reported in flax.

The initial draft of the flax genome sequence was produced using whole-genome shotgun (WGS) sequencing with short reads obtained on the Illumina sequencing platform [30]. A de novo assembly generated 88,384 scaffolds, totaling $3 1 8 \mathrm { M b }$ and representing $\sim 8 1 \%$ of the estimated $\sim 3 7 0 \mathrm { M b }$ flax reference genome [31]. Thus, the availability of this recent update of the flax genome (version 2.0) constitutes a genomic resource that allows the identification of gene families, evolutionary relationships, and structural analyses. To date, ABC transporter and HMA gene families have been studied in several plant species including Oryza sativa and Arabidopsis thaliana [32], Zea mays [33, 34], Brassica rapa [7], Brassica napus [35], Triticum aestivum [36], and Vitis vinifera [37]. A previous report on ABC transporters in flax has been published [38], but classification patterns, gene duplications, evolutionary and collinear relationships, structural and correlation analyses of paralogous pairs, and the identification of the Cd-associated genes covered herein were not explored in this prior publication. Several other gene families have also been identified in flax, based on bioinformatics analysis such as aquaporin [39], dirigent [40], chalcone [41], detoxification efflux carriers [42], and a ubiquitous glycosyltransferase [43]. In this research work, we hypothesized that either whole genome duplications (WGDs) or tandem events contributed to the expansion of the ABC transporter and HMA gene families in flax. Therefore, we studied the phylogenetic relationships, gene annotation, physicochemical properties, chromosomal distribution, gene synteny, protein-protein interactions (PPIs), and gene duplications of all predicted ABC transporter and HMA genes of the flax genome to understand their evolution and hypothesize their putative functions. Finally, we examined the gene ontology (GO) and expression profiling of ABC transporter and HMA genes in eight tissues, namely root, seed, ovary, and embryo at five different stages (heart, globular, torpedo, mature and cotyledon). This comprehensive analysis is the first report on ABC transporter and HMA genes in flax, providing gene candidate information for future marker association studies on heavy metal accumulation including Cd.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are an ancient and huge transmembrane protein family that widely exist in natural organisms, and they have attracted extensive attention due to their diverse biological functions. ABC proteins release energy mainly by binding and hydrolyzing ATP, leading to conformational changes of proteins, thus realizing the transmembrane transport of a wide array of substrates, including carbohydrates, lipids, peptides, terpenes, cell metabolites, heavy metal chelates, and metal ions [1].

ABC transporters generally contain two domains: hydrophobic transmembrane domains (TMDs) containing four to six transmembrane helices and nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) containing several highly conserved characteristic motifs, such as Walker A motif [GXXGXGKS/T], Walker B motif $[ ( \mathrm { R K } ) \mathrm { X } _ { 3 } \mathrm { G } \mathrm { X } _ { 3 } \mathrm { L }$ (hydrophobic)3], ABC signature motif, the Q-loop, and the H-loop [2]. TMDs serve as recognition agents and channels for substrate transport lipid bilayers, whereas NBDs provide energy for substrate transport or non-transport processes through ATP binding and ATP hydrolysis.

On the basis of the phylogenetic analysis of ABC transporters, the similarity of conserved sequences, and the organization of their domains, ABC transporters are divided into eight subfamilies: ABCA—ABCG and ABCI. To date, the number of ABC transporter genes identified in plants is much higher than that of animals and microorganisms [3].

Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa [4], Brassica campestris [5], and Lycopersicon esculentum [6] have 129, 121, 314, and 154 putative ABC transporters, respectively. Plants have so many ABC transporters, and a diversity of substrates that promote ABC transporters are involved in many processes of plant life activities, such as regulating the transport of plant hormones, enriching and excreting toxic substances, secreting secondary metabolites, maintaining cell osmotic homeostasis, resisting various stresses, ingesting nutrients, transducing signals, and resistance response. In particular, with the increasingly prominent environmental problems, ABC transporters have attracted wide attention as they play roles in the detoxification of toxic compounds or heavy metals. For instance, AtABCB25 confers heavy metal tolerance, probably as glutathione disulfide transporters [7]. HvMDR2, a homolog of AtABCB27, is responsible for Fe sequestration [8]. CjMDR1 transports berberine [9]. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 are related to cadmium and mercury by vacuolar sequestration [10]. AtABCC3, AtABCC6, AtABCC7, AtABCG32, CrCds1, OsABCG31, and OsABCG36 mediate tolerance to Cd [11–17]. AtPDR11 relates to paraquat tolerance and AtABCG34 contributes to defense against necrotrophic pathogens by mediating the secretion of camalexin [18–20].

At present, approximately $5 0 \%$ of arable soil in the world is acidic, and the degree of soil acidification is further intensified. Aluminum toxicity is one of the most important factors limiting crop yield in acidic soil [21,22]. To adapt to this acidic soil environment, plants have formed corresponding detoxification mechanisms in the long-term historical evolution process. At present, aluminum resistance has two mechanisms. One is aluminum efflux detoxification, and the other is aluminum tolerance detoxification [23]. Regardless of which mechanism, we can see that transmembrane transporters play an important role in the detoxification of aluminum [24–26]. According to research, ABC transporters facilitate the detoxification of aluminum in plants. In Arabidopsis, AtALS3 (AtABCI16), which is involved in plant tolerance to aluminum toxicity, contains only a TMD domain and is an ABC transporter located in the plasma membrane [27]. When interacting with its interactive protein, AtSTAR1 (AtABCI17), containing NBD domain, forms an ABC transporter complex located in the tonoplast and represses STOP1 protein accumulation in the nucleus to inhibit the STOP1-ALMT1 pathway [28,29]. STOP1 directly binds to the ALMT1 promoter to improve plant tolerance to aluminum [30]. AtABCB27 (AtALS1) possibly also chelates Al [31]. OsSTAR1/OsSTAR2 and FeSTAR1/FeSTAR2 also are required for Al tolerance in rice and buckwheat, respectively [32–34]. AtALS1, a half-type ABC transporter, is located in the vacuolar membrane of root cells and is required for root growth in an aluminum-toxic environment by facilitating the vacuolar sequestration of Al [31,35]. OsALS1 (OsABCB25), a homologous protein of AtALS1, is also located in the vacuolar membrane and is involved in the internal detoxification of Al in rice [36]. In wheat, TaMDR1 has been reported to be involved in Al toxicity [14]. FeALS1.1 and FeALS1.2 are required for the internal detoxification of aluminum by sequestering Al into the vacuoles in buckwheat [25,37].

Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.) is an important oil crop worldwide. Aluminum toxicity can seriously affect the growth and physiology of soybean, such as in the Rhizobiumlegume symbiosis system, which is the key system of agricultural nitrogen cycle balance. Plant genotype is also an important factor to establish an effective nodulation and nitrogen fixation under Al stress [38]. However, research on the relationship between ABC transporters and aluminum tolerance in soybean is lacking. Therefore, this study utilized a publicly available whole genome sequence [39] to identify all the putative ABC transporters in soybean. Their phylogenetic relationship, expression patterns, structures of genes and proteins, gene duplication, gene collinearity, and chromosomal distribution were also analyzed. Furthermore, soybean ABC transporter genes related to aluminum detoxification were further investigated by differential gene expression analysis. This study provides useful clues for the further understanding of the biological functions of ABC transporters in soybean.

The ABC transporters are known as the largest family of transporters of various macro- and micro-molecules across plant membranes (Theodolou et al. 2000, Holland et al. 2003). These transporters have a broad substrate specificity and a number of ABC proteins have been implicated in transport of secondary metabolites in different plant species. Most of the identified transporters belonging to the ABC family include ABCB/MDR (multi drug resistance), ABCC/MRP (multidrug resistance protein) and ABCG/PDR (pleiotropic drug resistance) (Table 3 Suppl.). The transporters have a significant role in various physiological and biochemical processes in plant systems (Jeong et al. 2014). The role of transporters is not fully understood due to a limited availability of desired radiolabeled compounds requisite to decipher transport mechanisms. There is no report available on identification of ABC transporter genes and dissecting their role in secondary metabolite biosynthesis in $P .$ . hexandrum. Therefore, the transcriptomes of $P$ . hexandrum were mined to identify and validate ABC transporter genes.

The ABC transporter genes were identified as 252 unigenes in the transcriptome of $P$ . hexandrum. They were further classified into nine sub-families such as ABCA, ABCB, ABCC, ABCD, ABCE, ABCF, ABCG, ABCI, and others (Fig. 2 Suppl.). The phylogenetic analysis of the ABC transporters shows a high homology with the functionally characterized genes of Nicotiana plumbaginifolia, Medicago truncatula, Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays, etc. Clustering ABC transporter genes with the well characterized genes of model plant species further confirmed the function of the identified ABC transporters in $P .$ . hexandrum (Fig. 2 Suppl). Out of 252, 22 genes were selected for validation on the basis of transcript abundance to gain insights into regulation of podophyllotoxin biosynthesis. Transcript abundance for 22 ABC transporter genes was checked by two approaches, FPKM and real time qPCR. Expression analysis of 22 ABC transporter genes revealed 14 genes showing a higher expression in shoots as compared to roots and rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum suggesting their major role in transport of various macro- and micromolecules in shoots (Fig. 1 Suppl.). Shoots are the primary organs for synthesis of sugars and starch (Huber et al. 1989). Expression of ABC transporters in shoots might be due to the their involvement in transporting sugars, amino acids, peptides, polyamines, metal ions, etc., to rhizomes (the storage organs of $P$ . hexandrum). The expression pattern observed by the two approaches was similar. Further, in order to find out suitable candidate genes correlating with podophyllotoxin content in $P$ . hexandrum, Pearson’s correlation coefficient was determined. Two genes, namely PhABC6 and PhABCIII, showed a positive correlation with podophyllotoxin content (Table 2 Suppl.). These genes were suggested to be potential candidates for generation of transgenic plants with enhanced podophyllotoxin content.

Furthermore, common and unique ABC transporter genes were also found in the shoot and rhizome transcriptomes of $P$ . hexandrum: 239 ABC transporter genes were found common in shoots and rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum. Similarly, 16 genes (3 in rhizomes and 12 in shoots) were uniquely present in $P$ . hexandrum. Transcript abundance analysis for unique genes revealed transcript medp_podhe_95366 with the highest abundance with 11.96 FPKM value in $P .$ . hexandrum. Similarly, transcript medp_podhe_20101112|14082 showed the highest abundance (402.88 FPKM) among commonly present ABC transporter genes in shoots and rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum (Fig. 1 Suppl.). Previously, unique and common genes have been identified in plant species, such as Jatropha curcas, Ricinus communis, Arabidopsis thaliana, etc., having a role in plant defense systems (Armisen et al. 2008, Sood et al. 2014). The genes commonly present in shoots and rhizomes of P. hexandrum may be involved in transport of common metabolites. The uniquely present genes in rhizomes might be of much more interest as they were suggested to be involved in transport of specific compounds in P. hexandrum.

Till date, only 22 ABC transporter genes are known and have been functionally characterized in different tissues/organs of Arabidopsis thaliana having diverse roles such as cutin and pollen exine formation, plastid lipid formation, auxin transport, fatty acyl-CoA import to peroxisomes, cuticle formation, stomata regulation, abscisic acid import, metal/metalloid tolerance, folate transport, chlorophyll catabolite transport, kanamycin tolerance, and biotic and abiotic stress tolerance (Kang et al. 2011). Out of these 22 ABC transporters genes from Arabidopsis, 3 genes were found to have orthologs in the transcriptome of $P$ . hexandrum, and the orthologs of 2 ABC transporter genes from Vitis vinifera and Nicotiana plumbaginifolia were also identified (Fig. 2 Suppl.). The identified ABC transporter genes were further validated, and their expression patterns were evaluated across different tissues/organs of $P$ . hexandrum using real time qPCR in order to correlate their expressions with podophyllotoxin content (Fig. 3). PhABCII and PhABCV showed a higher transcript abundance in shoots and PhABCIII in rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum (Fig. 3). The expression pattern of PhABCV was consistent with previous reports where this gene was highly expressed in shoots of Nicotiana plumbaginifolia having a role in terpenoids secretion (Grec et al. 2003). Similarly, PhABCII showed a higher expression in shoots where it was involved in transportation of metabolites, xenobiotics, folates, conjugates of chlorophyll catabolite, phytohelatins, etc., in Arabidopsis thaliana (Raichaudhuri et al. 2009, Song et al. 2010).

Podophyllotoxin biosynthesis occurs in roots/ rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum; however, the transport mechanisms of podophyllotoxin remain to be elucidated. Podophyllotoxin is mainly stored in vacuoles in rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum. The ABC transporters were thought to be involved in transporting podophyllotoxin and its derivatives from different compartments to vacuoles of rhizomes. Several questions need to be answered such as how many transporters are involved in transportation of podophyllotoxin. An attempt has been made by providing preliminary information on ABC transporter genes through their identification and validation in different tissues/organs of $P$ . hexandrum. The ABC transporters are well known for transporting various secondary metabolites including lignins, flavonoids, terpenoids, etc., across the plasmalemma and tonoplast (Sibout and Hofte 2012). To gain insights into podophyllotoxin biosynthesis and accumulation, we also evaluated the expression status of ABC transporters genes in roots and rhizomes with respect to shoots of $P$ . hexandrum (Fig. 1 Suppl.). Five genes, namely PhABC11, PhABC16, PhABC17, PhABCIII, and PhABCIV showed a higher expression ranging from 4.45-folds to 20.53-folds in rhizomes and roots as compared to shoots. PhABCIV showed the highest expression (20.53-folds) in rhizomes suggesting its major role in accumulation and transport of podophyllotoxin into rhizomes of $P$ . hexandrum. PhABCIV is well characterized for transport of anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides into vacuoles in Vitis vinifera (Francisco et al. 2013).

The identified ABC transporter genes are thought to be involved in podophyllotoxin accumulation as their transcript abundance correlated with podophyllotoxin content (Table 2 Suppl). However, the functional validation of these highly correlated genes remains to be deciphered. The present study has set-up a new platform by providing ABC transporter gene sequences to a scientific community for further research. This study would help in elucidating the physiological and biological functions of ABC transporters in P. hexandrum.

ABCG transporter proteins are a group of transmembrane transport proteins that can be found in various plant species and possess a wide range of functions [2]. In plants, the ABCG subfamily is considerably larger than in other kingdoms. One explanation for this phenomenon can be ascribed to the sessile lifestyle, which necessitates the export of toxic substances and the vast array of secondary metabolites generated in plants, and many of which must cross membranes to reach their site of function [30]. The full-size ABCG subfamily members can also be known as PDR transporters. Recently, the release of the A. argyi genome sequence has made it available to explore gene family members. So far, the biological functions of most AarPDRs remain unclear, and the identification of putative orthologs in different species will benefit the functional investigation of AarPDRs. In this study, we identified a total of 68 genes encoding PDR proteins in the A. argyi genome, which could be phylogenetically classified into 5 subfamilies based on phylogenetic analysis (Fig.  1). The findings showed that the $A$ . argyi PDR gene family was larger than the $1 5 ~ P D R$ members reported for A.thaliana. It has been indicated that $N .$ tabacum has $3 2 ~ P D R$ genes [31] and $2 2 ~ P D R$ members in S. lycopersicum [32]. Medicago truncatula and Glycine max have PDRs, with 24 and 29, respectively. Such high levels of protein redundancy/clustering might suggest that the adaptation to new transportation functions has caused the duplication of some PDR genes [33]. Our duplication analysis suggested that duplication events were essential for the PDR gene genomic expansion in A. argyi. In addition, collinearity analysis was performed between $A$ . argyi and A.thaliana, and it was found that several homologous pairs exhibited syntenic relationships. A. thaliana, as a model species of dicotyledons, the collinearity indicated the conservation of the members of the PDR gene family during the evolutionary process, and this finding could provide certain assistance for the functional analysis of the PDR gene family in A. argyi.

The investigation of the PDR distinctive domains and conserved motifs suggested that the 5 different subfamily AarPDR proteins contained the highly conserved NBD domain (a Walker A box, a Walker B box, and an ABC signature), which was essential for binding and hydrolysis of ATP to drive transport. The ABCG transporter is markedly expanded in plants, and this expansion of ABCGs appears to be associated with functional diversification, which may have contributed to plant survival in plant environments during evolution [3, 4]. The ABCG transporters revealed an unusual feature in eukaryotic ABC transporters with reverse organization of domains (NBD-TMD-type), in which not individual helices but the entire TMD rotates as a solid body during the transport of molecules. The MacB-type ABC protein can be regarded as a candidate for the originator of eukaryotic ABCG families. The MacB is a fused NBD-TMD ABC protein with the NBD preceding the TMD [34]. Growing evidence indicated that differences in the promoter region were often associated with variations in gene activity [35]. In gene promoter regions, cis-regulatory elements have a crucial role in modulating gene expression in response to developmental cues and environmental fluctuations. The cis-regulatory elements of the AarPDR genes analysis showed that many AarPDRs contained hormone-responsive elements (abscisic acid -responsiveness, MeJA and salicylic acid response elements, auxin and gibberellin-responsive elements). Meanwhile, the promoter region of AarPDRs was found to contain light-responsive elements, circadian clock regulatory elements, low-temperature response elements, defense- and stress-related regulatory elements, as well as drought-inducibility elements. Accordingly, many AarPDR genes were associated with plant development and responded to various abiotic stressors. The biosynthesis and accumulation of secondary metabolites (SMs) in medicinal plants are significantly influenced by environmental factors such as light intensity, water availability, and temperature conditions etc [36]. Therefore, the analysis of cis-elements provides a clue for further functional studies of AarPDR genes regarding the regulatory mechanism in the growth and development of medicinal plants.

It has been suggested that gene expression patterns correlate with function [6]. It can be considered that light is a crucial environmental factor to produce specialized metabolites in plants [37]. Light intensity has a major impact on the accumulation of SMs in medicinal plants, just like it does on other physiological processes [36]. To explore the secondary metabolites transporter response to light, the gene expression of PDRs was detected under different illumination conditions of A. argyi. The majority of AarPDRs exhibited upregulated expression in the leaf under conditions of low photosynthesis (Fig.  6). Additionally, the qRT-PCR examination revealed that the majority of AarPDRs were significantly up-regulated under overcast conditions. The upregulation of gene expression suggested that AarPDRs might be beneficial in maintaining the supply of SMs to sink cells when the supply derived from photosynthate metabolism was diminished. The tissue-specific expression patterns of AarPDR genes provide valuable insights into their functional sites within the plants. As shown in Fig.  8, we downloaded the RNA-seq data of A. argyi in various organs, i.e., leaf, flower, stem, root, and different developmental stages of leaves. The results of heatmaps indicated that the A. argyi PDR gene had spatiotemporal expression characteristics. For instance, in Arabidopsis, some ABCGs are expressed only in specific plant organs, which may be related to redundant functions [8]. The majority of AarPDRs in cluster I were highly expressed at the late developmental alcohol exporter, suggesting its involvement in transporting phenolic chemicals [17]. AtABCG32/PDR4 has been reported to have a function in cuticle constitution [41]. Furthermore, some ABCG transporters were functionally redundant; for example, both AtABCG36/PDR8 and AtABCG40/PDR12 were involved in the pathogen reaction [42]. Reverse genetics is a major method to provide functional insights into the ABCG gene family. However, the complexity of physiological metabolic pathways in plants, coupled with phenotypic pleiotropy resulting from gene mutations, makes it difficult to confirm the substrate transport specificity. Additionally, overexpression of plant ABCG transporters has been successfully achieved in several systems, including plant cells, yeast, bacteria, mammals, insects, and Xenopus [43]. Investigating the substrate spectrum of PDR proteins is also not a trivial task due to their functional/substrate diversity. Here, only one preliminary functional characterization of AarPDR was performed by GO annotation and KEGG pathway analysis. The functional annotation of AarPDRs highlights their crucial role in regulating the transport of A. argyi metabolites and facilitating environmental adaptation (Fig. 10).

The gene expression profiles of the A. argyi PDR suggested their specific functions in different organs and developmental stages of leaves. In addition, it was found that most AarPDR genes were induced by MeJA, indicating the vital effect of these genes in hormone responses. According to the previously reported works, PDRs as phytohormone transporters perform important functions in regulating plant development and metabolism [38, 39].

The ABCG transporters in Arabidopsis present functional/substrate diversity. For instance, a delayed stomata response to ABA and decreased drought tolerance were found due to the absence of the full-sized AtABCG40/PDR12 [40]. The heterologous expression of AtABCG29/PDR1 confirmed its role as a p-coumaryl

In plants, PDR subgroup proteins have been reported to exhibit a similarly diverse array of functions, including detoxification, the translocation of different secondary metabolites, phytohormone transport, and stomata movement [23, 44]. Secondary metabolites are a class of low-molecular-weight compounds that are essential to the life cycle of plants, influence their interactions with the environment, and contribute to the plant’s response to biotic and abiotic challenges. It has been reported that PDR genes play a crucial role in terpenoid transportation in other plant species [2]. Our correlation analysis results also revealed that 15 candidate AarPDRs had significant correlations with the variation of the primary monoterpene 1,8-cineole under different photosynthetic conditions (Table  2). Furthermore, the AarPDR transporters might be beneficial to the volatile terpenoids traverse the cytosol and cross the plasma membrane to exit the cell by active transport (Fig.  11). It should be noted that there are few reports on AarPDRs involved in secondary metabolite transport in A. argyi, and therefore, further exploration of their functions holds significant research value.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute a versatile family of membrane proteins that play pivotal roles in the transport of various substrates across cellular membranes [1–3]. Tese transporters are characterized by a conserved structural motif comprising two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), forming the core structure responsible for substrate translocation and ATP hydrolysis [4, 5]. ABC transporters are widely distributed across the domains of life, from prokaryotes to eukaryotes, and have been extensively studied for their signifcance in diverse biological processes [6–11].

In various species, extensive research has been devoted to ABC transporters due to their multifaceted roles [6, 9–14]. In mammals, they are renowned for their involvement in drug resistance, exemplifed by the P-glycoprotein encoded by the ABCB1 gene, which confers resistance to anticancer drugs [15–17]. In yeast, transporters like Pdr5p are critical for the efux of xenobiotics, including drugs and toxins, thus contributing to cellular detoxifcation [18, 19]. In plants, ABC transporters have garnered substantial attention due to their vital functions in growth, development, and stress responses [12–14, 20]. For instance, the ABCB19 gene in Arabidopsis thaliana encodes a transporter that regulates the polar transport of the phytohormone auxin, crucial for plant development and tropisms [21–24]. In addition, Arabidopsis ABCG27 plays an essential role in fower and leaf development by modulating abscisic acid content [25]. In wheat, the suppression of the ABCC13 transporter unveils its role in grain development, the accumulation of phytic acid, and the formation of lateral roots [26]. Furthermore, the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter OsABCG3 is essential for pollen development in rice [27]. Tese examples illustrate the diversity of roles ABC transporters play in plant growth and development.

One of the most challenging aspects of plant growth is the ability to withstand environmental stressors such as salinity and drought. Tese stress factors can severely afect plant growth and yield. ABC transporters have emerged as key players in plant stress responses by facilitating the transport of toxic ions, heavy metals, and other stress-related molecules out of the cell, thereby alleviating the detrimental efects of stress [14, 20, 28]. In Arabidopsis, the AtABCC1 gene encodes an ABC transporter involved in the detoxifcation of heavy metals, including cadmium and mercury [29]. Additionally, the ABCG36 gene in rice plays a crucial role in exporting toxic heavy metals such as arsenic from roots to shoots, thereby reducing their accumulation in edible parts of the plant [20]. In Artemisia annua, AaABCG40 enhances artemisinin content and modulates drought tolerance [30]. Furthermore, ABC transporters have been implicated in temperature stress responses. For example, in thellungiella salsugineum, overexpression of TsABCG11 exhibited higher photosynthetic rates and water-use efciency under cold stress $( 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ than control plants [31]. Tese fndings underscore the pivotal role of ABC transporters in plant stress responses.

Pear (Pyrus bretchneideri) stands as an economically signifcant fruit crop with growing global importance. However, the genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying stress responses in pear remain insufciently explored. Given the crucial roles of ABC transporters in stress mitigation and plant growth, comprehensively analyzing the ABC transporter family in pear holds immense potential for advancing our understanding of stress tolerance mechanisms and enhancing pear cultivation. Tis study embarks on a genome-wide identifcation and expression analysis of ABC transporters in pear to shed light on their biological functions, with a particular focus on their involvement in regulating stress responses. Trough this investigation, we aim to provide a theoretical foundation for further research into the biological functions of ABC transporters in pear and their potential applications in stress-resistant pear breeding programs.

Background: The ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter gene superfamily is ubiquitous among extant organisms and prominently represented in plants. ABC transporters act to transport compounds across cellular membranes and are involved in a diverse range of biological processes. Thus, the applicability to biotechnology is vast, including cancer resistance in humans, drug resistance among vertebrates, and herbicide and other xenobiotic resistance in plants. In addition, plants appear to harbor the highest diversity of ABC transporter genes compared with any other group of organisms. This study applied transcriptome analysis to survey the kingdom-wide ABC transporter diversity in plants and suggest biotechnology applications of this diversity.

Results: We utilized sequence similarity-based informatics techniques to infer the identity of ABC transporter gene candidates from 1295 phylogenetically-diverse plant transcriptomes. A total of 97,149 putative (approximately $2 5 \%$ were full-length) ABC transporter gene members were identified; each RNA-Seq library (plant sample) had $8 8 \pm 3 0$ gene members. As expected, simpler organisms, such as algae, had fewer unique members than vascular land plants. Differences were also noted in the richness of certain ABC transporter subfamilies. Land plants had more unique ABCB, ABCC, and ABCG transporter gene members on average $( p < 0 . 0 0 5 )$ , and green algae, red algae, and bryophytes had significantly more ABCF transporter gene members $( p < 0 . 0 0 5 ) $ . Ferns had significantly fewer ABCA transporter gene members than all other plant groups $( p < 0 . 0 0 5 )$ ).

Conclusions: We present a transcriptomic overview of ABC transporter gene members across all major plant groups. An increase in the number of gene family members present in the ABCB, ABCC, and ABCD transporter subfamilies may indicate an expansion of the ABC transporter superfamily among green land plants, which include all crop species. The striking difference between the number of ABCA subfamily transporter gene members between ferns and other plant taxa is surprising and merits further investigation. Discussed is the potential exploitation of ABC transporters in plant biotechnology, with an emphasis on crops.

Keywords: ABC transporter, Transcriptomics, Computational biology, Taxonomic diversity

The ABC-transporter superfamily is one of the largest protein families known (Henikoff et al. 1997). In bacteria,most members of this family are responsible for the high-affinity uptake of small molecules like maltose or histidine (Higgins et al. 1986; Higgins 1992). In contrast,eukaryotic ABC transporters have not yet been shown to transport carbohydrates or amino acids.In mammals,ABC transporters have been found to confer multidrug resistance in cancer cells upon overexpression (Chen et al. 1986; Gottesman and Pastan 1993). These transporters mediate diverse cellular transport processes, such as the excretion (extracellular over the plasma membrane or intracellular into the vacuoles) of potentially toxic compounds, lipid translocation, excretion of the mating factor of yeast, conferring heavy-metal tolerance, and antigen presentation, as well as exhibiting ion channel activity or modulating the activity of ion channels (Kuchler et al. 1989; McGrath and Varshavsky 1989；Kelly et al. 1992；Balzi and Goffeau 1994; Szczypka et al. 1994; Higgins 1995).

Despite the recent completion of the genomic sequencing of Arabidopsis (AGI 20o0), knowledge about the function of this large protein superfamily of ABC transporters in plants is still scarce. Among these proteins the so-called “full-size transporters’ are the best characterised to date.Therefore, this review will include an update of the inventory of plant full-size ABC transporters,a description of which has been started in recent reviews (Rea et al. 1998; Rea 1999; Theodoulou 20oo).A further subject of this paper is the assignment of functions to this particular protein family apart from its described cellular detoxification processes. These recent findings shed new light on the role of ABC transporters in plant growth and development processes.


## Characteristics of ABC transporters


On a functional basis, the transport of substrates by ABC proteins is characterized by (i) direct dependence on $\mathbf { M g A T P }$ ； (ii) the fact that other nucleotides,mainly GTP,can substitute for ATP;and (iii) the fact that transport is inhibited by micromolar concentration of vanadate.In plants, these criteria are easy to confirm for transport processes across the vacuolar membrane since the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase is not inhibited by vanadate. Directly energized transporters are able to accumulate a far higher concentration of compounds in the vacuole than secondarily energized transporters (Kreuz et al. 1996).For transporters localized at the plasma membrane，proof of direct energizing is more difficult to ascertain, due to the vanadate-sensitivity of the plasmamembrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase.

Another way to define an ABC transporter is based on their characteristic structures and motifs: all ABC transporters consist of two pairs of basic structural elements - integral membrane-spanning domains (MSD) and nucleotide-binding folds (NBF） oriented towards the cytoplasm.In bacteria, the four domains can reside on different independent polypeptides,whereas bacterial genes encoding fusions of all four domains have,to date, rarely been found (Linton and Higgins 1998;Braibant et al.2ooo). In contrast, in plants -as in animals and yeast - such proteins are encoded by conserved gene families. The so-called “full-size ABC transporters" can be subdivided into two groups according to their topology: multidrug-resistance proteins(MDRs, also known as PGPs for P-glycoproteins) and multidrug-resistance-related proteins (MRPs),which show a structure of MSD-NBF-MSD-NBF. The mirrored topology (NBF-MSD-NBF-MSD) can be found for PDR(pleiotropic drug resistance） and ABC1-like genes (Higgins 1992; Bungert et al. 2001).

Another characteristic feature of the different ABC transporters can be observed in the NBFs,where an identity of $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ over a region of about 200-400 amino acid residues be found. This domain contains three conserved sequence motifs: an ATP-binding site consisting of a Walker A box and a Walker B box separated by approximately 12O amino acids (Walker et al. 1982)and, between the two boxes,a consensus sequence specific for ABC transporters (Higgins 1992).


## Plant ABC transporters


Through the efforts of the coordinated international Arabidopsis sequencing project of the Arabidopsis Genome Initiative (AGI), the complete genomic sequence and a preliminary annotation approach were published before the end of 2000 (AGI 2000). It was already known that Arabidopsis thaliana $( A t )$ shows a high gene density with about 25,500 genes in $1 2 5 { , } 0 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k b }$ ，which exceeds that of any other completely sequenced genome (human,Drosophila, Caenorhabditis, bacteria). Of the ca. 600 predicted membrane-transport systems found in Arabidopsis,a large number are ABC transporters. A total of 51 genes can be found encoding full-size transporters of the AtPDR,AtMRP and AtPGP subclusters (Fig.1， Table 1). Additionally，two sequences，for ABC1- and PMP70-like genes,were annotated as fullsize transporters (see above).Neither of these genes clusters to any of the three major classes of full-size transporters,which confirms their unique status in the Arabidopsis genome.

Therefore, 53 genes have been found to encode fullsize ABC proteins in the Arabidopsis genome. This number of full-size transporters largely exceeds that reported in Saccharomyces cerevisae (Decottignies and Goffeau 1997) and that of Homo sapiens.In the latter the total number of all putative ABC transporters (irrespective of size and structure) is quoted as 51 (see http://www.humanabc.org). This raises the question about the reasons for the high number of full-size ABCtransporter genes in plants.

It is remarkable that in Arabidopsis several members of the three gene families (MDR,MRP,and PDR-like) could be found, but only one ABC1-likegene $( A t 2 g 4 I 7 0 0 )$ . Interestingly, all other homologous ABCtransporter genes in the Arabidopsis genome are annotated as half-size transporters.In contrast, in the human genome at least 14 full-size transporters of the ABC1- like class are found (see http://www.humanabc.org). Also one PMP70-like sequence $( A t 4 g 3 9 8 5 0 )$ has been described showing structures of a full-size transporter, whereas all other known members of this gene family (also from plants) belong to the class of half-size transporters. The extraordinary structures of the mentioned sequences as full-size transporters,emphasizing their unique position in plants, still await confirmation by experimental data.

The large number of genes in the MDR/MRP and PDR5-like sub-clusters,and the strong sequence homology found in many cases, suggest functional redundancy. One reason for a number of gene duplications is clearly the duplication of large segments of Arabidopsis chromosomes.More than 20 segments,each larger than $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k b }$ ， comprise over half the Arabidopsis genome, suggesting a tetraploid origin for Arabidopsis (AGI 2000).Because of this duplication of entire chromosomal regions,and by means of sequence comparisons, we have recently been able to confirm the duplication of several ABC transporter genes in Arabidopsis (data not shown).

Phylogenetic analysis of all three full-size ABCtransporter families groups the AtPGP genes with their human homologues and TAP1, the transporter associated with antigen processing.Although PGPs have also been cloned from barley (Davies et al. 1997) and potato (Wang et al.1996) their functions in plants are still unclear.Experiments with overexpression and antisense repression of AtPGP1 showed that this protein might be involved not only in xenobiotic resistance (Thomas et al.2OoO) but also in light-signal transduction (Dudler and Hertig 1992; Sidler et al.1998). With 22 members, the AtPGPs are the largest family of ful-size transporter genes in Arabidopsis. Two genes related to this family，however,have to be pointed out. At4g25450 (M7J2.180) is annotated as a multidrug resistance gene of 280 amino acids.Although it shows highest homology to AtPGP genes (about $40 \%$ identity), its genomic structure does not show similarities to this gene family. It consists of just one NBF without any membrane-spanning region and therefore has not been included in the list of full-size transporter genes.For At5g39040 (MXF12.50) the case is similar: It shows homology to the AtPGP gene family with sequence identity scores of around $30 \%$ . But the assignment of this sequence to the PGPs,denoted as PGP8 (Davies and Coleman 20oo),is questionable as it encodes a half-size ABC transporter. Compared with other members of this gene family At5g39040 shows a completely different genomic structure. These findings are also supported by the position of the gene in the phylogenetic tree (Fig. 1, denoted as AtPGPL). Therefore,in our eyes,the AtPGP subfamily consists of 22 genes coding for full-size ABC proteins.

The AtMRP genes are the best-characterized plant ABC transporters to date. These proteins are known to function as vacuolar sequesters of glutathionylated compounds,malonylated chlorophyll catabolites and glucuronides (Martinoia et al. 1993, 2000; Rea et al. 1998; Theodoulou 20oO). From the data available, it is evident that at least some of these transporters have overlapping transport activities. AtMRP1, AtMRP2 and AtMRP3 exhibit glutathione-conjugate transport activity,but only AtMRP2 and AtMRP3 are able to transport chlorophyll catabolites accumulated during leaf senescence (Lu et al. 1997, 1998; Tommasini et al. 1998). Interestingly, transport of glutathione conjugates is only negligibly inhibited by chlorophyll catabolites and vice versa (Lu et al. 1998), as has also been confirmed using intact vacuoles (Hinder et al. 1996). AtMRP2 and AtMRP5 also transport glucuronides (Gaedeke et al. 2001; Liu et al.200i). AtMRP2,which is localized on the vacuolar membrane (Liu et al. 2oo1),exhibits a much stronger activity,and shows more of the characteristics observed for glucuronide transport in intact vacuoles where modulation of glucuronide transport by glutathione conjugates has been demonstrated (Klein et al.1998,2000, 2001). Interestingly, the transport activities of compounds containing more than one glucuronate, and hence carrying more negative charges,are increased by a membrane potential that is positive inside the vacuole. Related to AtMRPs are sulfonylurea-receptor-like proteins that are involved in regulating the conductance of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -channels and which may also control the water-conducting aquaporins (Schreiber et al. 1999) and the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (Akabas 2000).

Expression studies in our laboratory have revealed that most of the AtMRP genes are expressed in leaves, roots,flowers， stems and siliques.Only a few genes showed increased accumulation of mRNA in a specific tissue (data not shown). Some AtMRPs exhibit increased transcript levels if plants are treated with xenobiotics or salicylic acid (Tommasini et al. 1997; Sanchez-Fernandez et al. 1998; and our own data). Besides transport measurements for glutathione conjugates (see below), to our knowledge the only report on an MRP-like ABC transporter from plants was the demonstration that antibodiesraised againstan AtMRP homologue from wheat up-regulated by safhttp://mips.gsf.de/proj/thal/db) with ABC signatures were examined for their structural similarity or sequence homology toward characterized full-size ABC transporters.Secondly, several MRP, PDR and PGP amino acid sequences from Arabidopsis were used for BLAST searches against the entire Arabidopsis genomic sequences deposited in GENBANK.As references for the different ABC transporter genes the corresponding entries from MATDB were used, because this database contains one of the most recent annotations (K.F.X.Mayer,personal communication).In cases where deviating data have been given in the list,explanations are found in the footnotes.To determine the number of ESTs for the different genes,BLAST searches with the predicted CDS were made using all GENBANK ESTs in TAIR (http://arabidopsis.org/Blast/)

The AtMRP gene family consists of 15 members,including one aberrant gene， AtMRP15, which is annotated as a protein with an N-terminal truncation due to $5 ^ { \prime }$ stop codons of about 40o amino acids that are not present in other AtMRPs.Its nucleotide sequence isnearly identical to thatof AtMRP9, even in the non-coding $5 ^ { \prime }$ region. In contrast to all other full-size proteins encoding AtMRPs we have been unable to detect a transcript for this gene in Arabidopsis (data not shown)，raising the possibility that AtMRPi5 is indeed a pseudogene. Another MRPrelated gene is encoded by Atlg71330 (F3I7.2). It seems to encode only one membrane-spanning region with high similarities to AtMRP3 and so cannot be considered as a classical transporter. The arrangement of sequences in the phylogenetic tree suggests that AtMRP1,2, 11 and 12 comprise a group of closely related genes. A similar grouping can be found for all other AtMRP genes with the exception of AtMRP13, which represents an intermediate between the two MRP subgroups. Interestingly, these phylogenetic data are in agreement with the intron-exon structures of the genes.

MDRs and MRPs exhibit the same arrangement of domains but differ at their N-termini where an extremely hydrophobic N-terminal extension (NTE) of around 22O amino acids is observed for MRPs but not for MDRs. A careful study of the membrane topology of human MRP, employing glycosylation-site mutants, indicates that the hydrophobic NTE forms a third MSD of five transmembrane $\mathscr { X }$ -helices and that the N-terminus is most likely situated in the extracytoplasmic side of the membrane bilayer (Hipfner et al.1997).Hydropathy plots of animal and plant MRPs resemble each other to a great extent, suggesting a similar arrangement of the membrane-spanning domains in animals and plants.In contrast, the NTE of MRPs exhibits only weak homology among the different members of MRPlike proteins.

The third group of ful-size ABC transporters is formed by 15 AtPDR-like genes and represents a separate sub-cluster. These proteins are characterized in fungal systems as efflux transporters for cytotoxic compounds such as oligomycin or cyclohexamide (Balzi and Goffeau 1994). A PDR-like ABC transporter also plays a role in the pathogen reaction since it has been shown that plant pathogenic fungi need the activity of PDR5- like genes for expression of pathogenicity or acquired resistance towards fungicides (Urban et al. 1999; Andrade et al. 20oo).In a very recent publication, Jasinski et al (20o1) showed that Nicotiana plumbaginifolia ABC1 (NpABC1)，a member of the PDR5-like family，is also localized in the plasma membrane. NpABC1 is highly expressed in the presence of sclareolide,a close analogue of the antifungal diterpene sclareol.These properties, together with the observation that the cellular sclareolide content decreases in parallel with the induction of the ABC transporter and that inhibitors of ATP synthesis reverse this effect, strongly suggest that this PDR5 homologue is involved the excretion of secondary metabolites playing a role in plant defense.

By performing a differential screening of Spirodela polyrrhiza grown in the absence and presence of abscisic acid (ABA), Smart and Fleming (1996) have identified a PDR5-like ABC transporter (TUR2). The expression of this transporter is increased about 7-fold within $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ after application of ABA. Other treatments that, in contrast to ABA,do not induce turion formation in Spirodela, such as exposure to cycloheximide or salt stress,also resulted in an increased mRNA level for TUR2, indicating that expression of TUR2 is not the cause of turion formation. Compared with the AtPGP and AtMRP classes the AtPDR5-like genes form a relatively tight cluster. This also holds true for the genes AtPDR2 and AtPDR12. AtPDR2 was originally annotated as two separate genes (see MATDB entries AT4gl5230 and AT4g15220,http://www.mips.biochem.mpg.de/proj/ thal/db/index.html). Alignment-based re-annotation of the sequences suggests a single gene coding for a protein of 1,385 amino acids,whose genomic structure is in concord with that of other AtPDR5-like genes. Annotations for AtPDR12 differ between MATDB and GENBANK in such a way that MATDB lists AtPDR12 as a pseudogene and GENBANK presents it as a functional gene. Expressed sequence tags(ESTs) for AtPDRi2 (see Table 1） support the latter suggestion. Furthermore,the described annotations for AtPDR2 and AtPDRi2 are supported by their positions in the phylogenetic analysis (see Fig. 1).

Figure 2 shows a comparison of the Walker motifs and ABC signature of plant full-size ABC transporters. It is obvious that only the Walker A box exhibits perfect conservation in all of these proteins, whereas both of the other consensus motifs exhibit a higher degree of variation. One consequence of this finding is that the definition of this class of proteins by consensus sequences alone could result in misleading interpretations about their functions.On the other hand,these consensus motifs can serve as valuable tools. The mentioned PMP70-like sequence lacks the N-terminal Walker A box and the second ABC motif is situated in the last 12 amino acids of the protein leaving no space for a Walker B box.These facts make a function as an ATP-dependent transporter questionable.

Numbering of AtPGP,AtMRP and AtPDR5 genes is according to Davies and Coleman (2oo0),with the exception of AtMRP8,13,11 (described as MRP6-8 in Davies and Coleman 20oO) and AtPGP8 (see above). Genes not mentioned in that review were numbered successively （AtPGP11-AtPGP22，AtMRP9-AtMRP15 and AtPDR9-AtPDR12). It is worth mentioning that this summary cannot be the final list of the Arabidopsis inventory of full-size ABC transporter genes as the complete coding sequences are published only for a small number of genes. The number of full-size ABC transporter genes was estimated from annotations of genomic data. Only half of the genes in this table are confirmed by experimental data or ESTs (Table 1). The annotations are mostly based on homology to known genes and/or gene-prediction programs. Until these predictions are confirmed by experimental data,such estimations of gene numbers should be treated with caution. This holds especially true for cases where either putatively wrong annotations (AtPDR2), contradictory annotations (AtPGP8,AtPGP22) or no annotations at all （AtPDR13-AtPDR15) have been given. Data sets from sequencing projects of Arabidopsis ful-length cDNAs, like the one recently released by Ceres Inc. in theTiGRdatabase(http://www.tigr.org/tdb/ath1/ htmls/index.html),might clear up the remaining questions.


## ABC-type transport activities for which the corresponding transporter has not been identified


Besides glutathione conjugates,chlorophyll catabolites and glucuronides,for which transport proteins have been identified (see above)，vacuolar uptake of some additional substrates exhibits typical ABC-type transport kinetics:

i.Bile acids (Hörtensteiner et al. 1993),which have not been demonstrated in plants.Interestingly, in animals an MDR-type transporter is responsible for the transport of bile acids (Gerloff et al. 1998 ） while in yeast this activity could be assigned to an MRP-type transporter (Ortiz et al. 1997).   
ii. The sulfonated compound Lucifer Yellow.Several animal MRPs have been shown to transport sulfated compounds and it is probable that one or several of the already-cloned AtMRPs exhibits a transport activity for sulfonated and sulfated compounds.   
ii. Glucosylated compounds are the predominant class of secondary metabolites stored within plant cells. In most cases they are transported into the vacuole by proton antiporter mechanisms (Martinoia et al. 2000).However,it has been shown that vacuolar uptake of a glucosylated herbicide,which is formed during the detoxification process (Kreuz et al. 1996), exhibits kinetics typical of ABC-transporters (Klein et al. 1996).

Recent experiments have shown the great diversity of transporters that recognize compounds synthesized by different plants. Uptake of the main barley flavonoid saponarin into barley vacuoles shows that this compound is taken up by a proton antiporter mechanism.In contrast,work in our laboratories has shown that vacuoles isolated from Arabidopsis,a plant that does not synthesize the flavone glucoside saponarin, exhibit direct energization by an ABC-type transporter (Fragne et al.，in press). It is therefore tempting to speculate that glucosides are only taken up by an antiporter mechanism if structural homologues are present in the plant (or cell).In contrast, glucosides, which have no structural analogues in the plant, may be recognized as modified, potentially toxic compounds and transported into the vacuole using a directly energized ABC-type transporter. However, the fact that barley vacuoles transport aesculin by a proton antiport system indicates that this hypothesis cannot be generalized and is probably only true for large glycosylated compounds.


## ABC transporters regulate ion fluxes


Most ABC transporters couple the hydrolysis of ATP and transport of molecules across a membrane against a concentration gradient. As a consequence, this transport mechanism allows the hyper-accumulation of a molecule in a compartment.However, in two cases ABC transporters,well characterized in animal cells,have been unequivocally shown to be involved in ion transport or ion-channel regulation. These transporters control the flux of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ according to the electrochemical gradient and in response to changes in the concentration of cytosolic nucleotides like ADP or ATP.These ABC transporters are:

i. The K-ATP channels (Bryan and Aguilar-Bryan 1999)，which are heteromultimers constituted by ABC-type sulfonylurea receptors (SUR1, SUR2A or SUR2B) and the potassium inward rectifier $( \mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 1$ or ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2 )$ . Neither SUR1 nor $\mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2$ cDNAs exhibited recognizable K-ATP channel activity when expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,but co-expression generated current characteristics of native KATP channels (Inagaki et al. 1995). Interestingly, when Dsur,a novel Drosophila gene highly homologous to vertebrate SUR but harboring an additional 1.7-kb extension，was expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,a classical K-ATP channel signature was recorded (Nasonkin et al. 1999). This result was not observed with mammalian SUR in the same expression system, suggesting that the sequence extension in Dsur could be responsible for the generation of Kchannel activity.

ii. The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator(CFTR),which functions as a phosphorylation- and nucleotide-regulated small-conductance chloride channel (Akabas 20oo). Besides its function asa $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channel, CFTR acts as a regulator of amiloride-sensitive $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ channels,outward-rectifying $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channels, $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ exchanger and ROMK $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Schwiebert et al. 1999).

CFTR and SUR are unequivocally involved in transport/regulation of ion fluxes and share more similarities with the MRP than the MDR family. They exhibit a defined pharmacology. Some sulfonylureas, like glibenclamide and tolbutamide,are potent inhibitors of K-ATP channels and the CFTR-mediated $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ conductance.K-ATP channels can be activated by a diverse group of compounds collectively referred to as potassium channel openers (KCOs). These compounds have been developed for clinical use in patients with hypertension,asthma or ischemic heart disease and may act as antagonists of the sulfonylureas.In order to test whether such ABC-transporters are also present in plants, Leonhardt et al.(1997) investigated the effect of inhibitors of the K-ATP-channel and CFTR on epidermal strips and guard cells of Vicia faba.Incubation of epidermal strips with glibenclamide or tolbutamide led to a dose-dependent increase in stomatal aperture with a $\mathrm { K } _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $2 . 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for glibenclamide. In contrast, KCOs inhibited stomatal opening and induced stomatal closure in the nanomolar range of concentration. Using guard-cell protoplasts and the patch-clamp technique, the authors observed a partial inhibition of the outward potassium current by glibenclamide.This inhibition was partially reversed by the KCO cromakalim. Since the guard-cell potassium channel is not ATP-sensitive,a similar but not identical system to the one described in animals may be present in guard cells.However, due to the fact that guard cels were investigated in the whole-cell configuration, the efects observed on potassium channels may be indirect. Therefore, Leonhardt et al. (1999) also tested this hypothesis and observed that glibenclamide inhibits the $\dot { \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } }$ -induced stomatal closure caused by slow anion efflux.The phytohormone ABA,however, reversed the glibenclamide effect.From these results the authors postulated that in plants,as in animals,ABC-type proteins are involved in the regulation of ion channel activities. Direct evidence that plant ABC transporters are indeed implicated in ion fluxes has been provided recently (Gaedeke et al. 2001). AtMRP5,like the other AtMRPs,exhibits a high similarity to CFTR and SUR. It is highly expressed in vascular tissue and in stomata. Analysis of a T-DNA-induced mutation of AtMRP5 revealed that glibenclamide triggers stomatal opening in the dark in the wild type but not in mrp5-1 mutant plants (Fig.3). This is a direct hint that ABC transporters are also involved in regulation of stomatal opening.Presently，it is not possible to differentiate whether AtMRP5 controls either $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or anion channels, exhibits channel activities or is a member of the signal transduction pathway leading to stomatal opening. Finally,the fact that the nucleotide-binding domain of

ABC transporters resembles the respective domains of Ras and other G-proteins could raise the possibility that a conformational change in these domains might have regulatory consequences for interacting proteins.


## ABC transporters are involved in plant growth processes


Recent results show that ABC transporters are not only implicated in detoxification and ion-regulation processes but also in plant growth processes.

Sidler et al.(1998) have shown that AtPGP1 is responsible for control of hypocotyl cell elongation under low light. An increase of $50 \%$ in hypocotyl length could be observed at a photon fluence rate of $1 \mathrm { \dot { 0 } ~ } \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { \ s } ^ { - 1 }$ for plants overexpressing AtPGP1, and about $20 \%$ inhibition of hypocotyl length was detected for plants that showed antisense inhibition of AtPGP1 under the same light conditions.However,in darkness,as well as at fluence rates of $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m o l } } ~ { \mathrm { m } } ^ { - 2 } ~ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ ， no difference in cell elongation was observed. The growth response was independent of light quality and could be observed under red and blue light regimes.The response to far-red light (FR) was also different in wild-type and overexpressing plants, but in this case seedling growth in FR was less than $1 0 \%$ of that observed in darkness. In addition,roots of plants overexpressing AtPGP1 were slightly larger than control plants.Very recent data suggest that AtPGP1 might export ATP; however, the reason for the observed phenotype is still unknown (Thomas et al. 2000).

A further example of the involvement of plant ABC transporters in light-regulated growth processes has very recently been presented by Moller et al (2001). It was observed that the gene responsible for the laf6 (long after FR） phenotype,which exhibits reduced responsiveness toward continuous FR,encodes an ABC transporter. This ABC transporter is highly homologous to an ABC transporter of Synechocystis and the cryptophyte alga Guillardia theta. It is interesting to note that in this alga the corresponding ABC transporter is encoded on the chloroplast genome,while in higher plants no chloroplast-encoded ABC transporters can be found.In addition to the highly homologous ABC transporters of Synechocystis and Guillardia, AtABC1 contains an N-terminal transit peptide that targets it to the chloroplast. The mutation in this gene results in protoporphyrin IX accumulation and lower chlorophyll contents.The protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPO) inhibitor flumioxazin results in increased levels of protoporphyrin IX and hence mimicks the laf6 phenotype. Plants overexpressing AtABC1 showed a reduced sensitivity to flumioxazin. In addition,genes known to be light-regulated such as chalcone synthase and ferredoxin ${ \mathrm { N A D P } } ^ { + }$ oxidoreductase are attenuated in laf6 compared with the wild type under high-fluence FR. These results suggest that AtABC1 is associated with a hydrophobic protein localized in the internal envelope of the chloroplast and catalyzes an ATP-dependent import of protoporphyrin IX.

In yeast it has been shown that a mitochondrial halfsize ABC transporter ATM1 is involved in the synthesis of Fe/S clusters (Leighton and Schatz 1995). This function appears to be conserved in eukaryotes, since the human Abc7 and MTABC3 have been shown to be functional orthologues of ATMl (Csere et al. 1998; Mitsuhashi et al. 20o0). Recently, Kushnir et al. (2001) showed that the Arabidopsis mutant starik,which leads to dwarfism and chlorosis, is due to the insertion of a TDNA in an orthologue of ATM1, Stal. Stal complements the yeast mutant △atm1, indicating that this gene, like yeast ATM1 and the corresponding human orthologues, supports the maturation of Fe/S clusters in mitochondria.MeasurementofFeshowedthat mitochondria of the stal mutant contain similar amounts of Fe as the wild-type mitochondria. As in △atml yeast,mitochondria of the Stal mutant cells contain 1.5- to 1.8-fold higher levels of free iron and less iron associated with proteins.A further example of altered plant growth was reported by Gaedeke et al. (2001) who observed that root growth in a T-DNA insertion mutant of AtMRP5 differed from that of control plants. Depending on the potassium concentration in the medium, root growth was reduced or enhanced compared with that of wild-type seedlings.

It is likely that growth processes in plants can be modulated in several ways by ABC transporters. As suggested by Moller et al. (200i), ABC transporters may be directly involved in the transport of a metabolite, or, as shown in the case of Synechocystis,of a metal required as cofactor by some enzymes (Bartsevich and Pakrasi 1995).Phenotypes of plants overexpressing an ABC transporter or where an ABC transporter is knocked-out suggest that the phytohormone balance is disturbed. However,phytohormone transport has not yet been reported for ABC transporters.In the case of MRP-like ABC transporters,a perturbation of phytohormone levels may not result from transport of free phytohormones but from the corresponding conjugates. It is well known that most phytohormones are conjugated to glycosides or amino acids. In the case of auxin, it has been reported that the first conjugation products observed in Arabidopsis are aspartate or glutamate conjugates,which are linked by a peptide bond to auxin (Ostin et al. 1998; Tam et al. 2000). Glutamate conjugates have been shown to be substrates for human MRPs and it is likely that they are also substrates for plant MRPs.Furthermore,it has been shown that some glycosides are recognized by ABC transporters. If such a conjugate is not exported efficiently from the cytosol, free-hormone concentrations may rise due either to feedback inhibition of the conjugation step or hydrolysis of the conjugate accumulating in the cytosol. Such a process would result in higher concentrations of phytohormones and hence the observed changes in the developmental pattern of mrp5-1.

An additional mechanism by which ABC transporters may be involved in developmental processes is through the interaction with other proteins.As discussed above, it was suggested that AtMRP5 interacts with ion channels in stomata. Such interactions may result in distinct phenotypes.

Direct evidence for such an interaction recently demonstrated that ABC transporters also interact with immunophilins.In animals,drugs binding to this class of protein are powerful immunosuppressors due to the fact that the immunophilin-drug complex inhibits the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase calcineurin. In plants,several immunophilins have been identified (Blecher et al 1996;Fulgosi et al. 1998; Vittorioso et al. 1998).We have observed that the FK506-binding(FKBP) immunophilinTWISTED DWARF1 (TWDi) from Arabidopsis shows a pleiotropic knock-out mutant phenotype, including a reduction in cell elongation and disorientated growth of the entire plant (data not shown). Also,using the yeast two-hybrid system we have identified the MDR-like Arabidopsis ABC transporter AtPGPl as an interactant with TWD1 (data not shown). Mapping and biochemical analyses showed that the FKBP-like domain of TWDl mediates AtPGP1 interaction. Since AtPGP1-overexpressing/antisense plants also show a phenotype (see above), it is tempting to speculate that ABC transporters are involved in some signal transduction pathways. Genetic analysis revealed that TWD1 is required for brassinosteroid reception or signal transduction (data not shown). In animal systems, interaction of MDR-like ABC transporters with steroids,as well as transport of steroidal precursors, has been reported (Metherall et al. 1996; Debry et al. 1997; Gruol et al. 1999). Therefore,it is tempting to speculate that plant ABC transporters may also play a role in steroid transport or signal transduction.

ABC (ATP-binding cassette) transporter proteins comprise one of the largest families of proteins discovered to date and are widely found in animals, plants, and microorganisms [1]. ABC transporter proteins can take up a wide range of substances, such as inorganic ions, nutrients, amino acids, and organic matter, to maintain the normal biological activities of the organism [2]. ABC transporter proteins have a highly conserved nucleotidebinding domain (NBD) and transmembrane domain (TMD) with fve or six helices [3]. Tese transporter proteins are categorized into three types of structures: holomolecules, semimolecules, and soluble proteins. Holomolecular transporter proteins contain two NBDs and TMDs, semimolecular transporter proteins contain one NBD and TMD, and soluble proteins have only an NBD and no TMD [4]. Among them, the TMD functions as a recognition substrate to transport substances across the membrane, and the NBD is located on the inner side of the cell membrane, including the conserved Walker A and Walker B sequences and the less conserved LSGGQ motif [5].

To date, ABC transporter proteins have been extensively studied in various species, including humans, insects, microorganisms, and plants [6–9]. According to related research, plant ABC members are typically divided into eight subfamilies: ABCA, ABCB, ABCC, ABCD, ABCE, ABCF, ABCG, and ABCI, with no ABCH subfamily identifed in plants [10]. Currently, the most extensively studied subfamilies in diferent species are the ABCB, ABCC, and ABCG subfamilies [11]. Among these subfamilies, the ABCA (AOH, ABC1 homolog), ABCB (MDR, multidrug resistance protein), ABCC (MRP, multidrug resistance-associated protein), and ABCG (PDR, pleiotropic drug resistance protein) subfamilies are classifed as full-transporter ABC proteins, while the ABCA (ATH, ABC2 homolog), ABCB (ATM, ABC transporter of the mitochondrion), ABCB (TAP, transporter associated with antigen processing), ABCD (PMP, peroxisomal membrane protein 3), and ABCG (WBC, white‒brown complex protein) subfamilies are categorized as half-transporter ABC proteins. Te ABCE (RLI, RNase L inhibitor), ABCF (GCN, general control nonrepressible protein), ABCI (SMC, structural maintenance of chromosome protein), and ABCI (NAP, nonintrinsic ABC proteins) subfamilies are soluble ABC transport proteins [12]. Te ABCA subfamily includes both full-transporter AOH and half-transporter ATH types. For example, A. thaliana contains one AOH and 16 ATH type transporter proteins [13]. Notably, AOH-type genes have only been found in dicotyledonous plants such as Arabidopsis and grapes and are absent in monocotyledonous plants such as maize [14, 15]. Te ABCB subfamily includes three classes of transporter proteins: MDR, ATM, and TAP. In Arabidopsis, 29 members of this subfamily have been identifed [13]. Research has revealed that plant ABCB subfamily members are primarily involved in the regulation and transport of auxins (such as AtPGP1 and OsABCB14) and participate in ion transport and resistance to heavy metal stress (including OsABCB25 and OsABCB23) [16–19]. Te ABCC subfamily encodes MRP-type transporter proteins, which are associated with transport and metabolic functions in plants. For instance, AtABCC4 is involved in folate transport, while VvABCC1 and AtABCC2 participate in anthocyanin transport [20–22]. Additionally, members of this subfamily in plants have detoxifcation functions. AtMRP1 and AtMRP2, among others, are involved in resistance to heavy metals [23, 24]. Te ABCD subfamily encodes PMP-type transporter proteins, with AtPMP2 shown to inhibit seed germination [25]. Te ABCG subfamily includes two classes of transporter proteins: PDR and WBC. Tis is the largest subfamily with members that have diverse functions, including regulating plant terpenoids, alkaloids, lipids, and volatile aromatic compounds [26–28]. Te ABCE, ABCF, and ABCI subfamilies lack transmembrane domains and do not exhibit specifc transport characteristics.

Almond, belonging to the genus Prunus in the family Rosaceae, is a medium-sized tree or shrub. Its kernel is highly nutritious and medicinally important, making it widely cultivated and utilized in various countries worldwide. Xinjiang is a major cultivation area of almonds in China, covering an area of approximately 66,000 hectares, and almonds are an important economic fruit tree in this region. However, a major challenge in almond production in Xinjiang is the low pollen activity and reduced fruit set due to self-incompatibility, which severely hinders the development of the almond industry. Terefore, it is of signifcance to explore the potential functions of ABC genes in diferent foral organs of almond. Additionally, there are other common issues that impact the almond industry, such as early fowering of native almond varieties in Xinjiang, making them vulnerable to late spring frosts, and freezing damage to foral organs in extremely low-temperature conditions during the winter dormancy period. Tis region also faces the challenge of severe soil salinity and alkalinity, which limits the development of the almond industry. To gain insight into the characteristics of ABC gene family members in almond, we conducted a comprehensive analysis based on ‘Wanfeng’ almond whole-genome data.
