Mognoliaceae, Paparerareae, Ranunculaceae, and Rutaceae, out of which cultured cells of Coptis japonica (Ranunculaceae) and Thalictrum minus (Ranunculaceae) have been used to study the transport mechanisms of this alkaloid. These are appropriate models to characterize the transport of berberine, i.e. C. japonica cells accumulate berberine exclusively in the vacuoles and they also actively uptake berberine exogenously added to the medium (Sato et al. 1990, 1993, 1994), whereas T. minus secretes most of the berberine biosynthesized in the cells into the medium (Nakagawa et al. 1984). The characterization of the cellular uptake of berberine into cultured cells of C. japonica suggested the involvement of an ABCtype transporter (Sakai et al. 2002) and accordingly the gene for the berberine importer functioning at the plasma membrane was identified as being an ABCBtype ABC transporter, CjMDR1 (Shitan et al. 2003), whose name was derived from the conventional name for multidrug resistance, although such broad substrate specificity was not observed in this plant ABC protein. In contrast, the characteristics of berberine transport in the vacuolar membrane met the criteria for a proton-antiporter, because inhibition of V-type ATPase by bafilomycin A1 and the disruption of delta $\mathrm { p H }$ across the vacuolar membrane by ammonium ions clearly inhibited berberine uptake, while sodium ortho-vanadate, a general inhibitor of ABC proteins, did not inhibit the uptake (Otani et al. 2005). The iontrap mechanism was also excluded from the berberine accumulation mechanism in the C. japonica vacuoles by the analysis of membrane vesicles (Otani et al. 2005). It is noteworthy that two different types of transport by an ABC transporter and a protonantiporter mediate the membrane transport of berberine in one cell. However, no candidate gene for the proton-berberine antiporter has been identified thus far. For the efflux mechanism of berberine in T. minus cells, we have also demonstrated the involvement of an ABC transporter (Terasaka et al. 2003), and have identified several candidate genes (our unpublished results).

Nicotine is the most abundant alkaloid in tobacco leaves. It is highly toxic to insects and moderately to plants cells and therefore is accumulated in the leaf vacuoles (Fig. 1). We have recently identified some strong candidates for nicotine transporter genes of tobacco by cDNA-AFLP (amplified fragment length polymorphisms) (Goossens et al. 2003), and these genes are classified into the multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE) family transporters (our unpublished results), which are discussed later in further detail.


## Transporters for phenolic compounds


Plant phenols are represented by their aromatic ring structures containing more than one phenol residue. These compounds can be classified into simple phenolic compounds, including phenylpropanes $\left( \mathbf { C } _ { 6 } – \mathbf { C } _ { 3 } \right)$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 } { - } \mathrm { C } _ { 1 }$ compounds, stylbenes, lignans, xanthenes, flavonoids, and tannins as polymers of polyphenols that are classified into two types, i.e., hydrolyzable or condensed tannins. From the viewpoint of transport, flavonoids have been intensively studied. Flavonoids represent one of the largest classes of plant phenolics consisting of more than 7,000 compounds, which are involved in plant pathogen interactions and UV light protection, and also in the variation of flower color. Most flavonoids mainly exist as their glycosylated form in planta, and glycosylation is thought to be a prerequisite for the transport of flavonoid molecules into vacuoles. For example in barley, an endogenous flavonoid glucoside, isovitexin (apigenin 6-C-glucoside), is transported into the vacuoles of barley via an electrochemical-gradient dependent transport mechanism (secondary transport), which showed clear specificity for apigenin derivatives (Klein et al. 1996). In contrast, an abiotic glucoside, hydroxyprimisulfuron-glucoside, was transported into barley vacuoles via a primary transporter. These biochemical characterizations suggest that vacuolar transporters of barley distinguish endogenous glucosides from exogenous glucosides. Moreover, even for the same compound, saponarin (apigenin $6 { - } C .$ -glucosyl-7-O-glucoside), Klein and co-workers reported that this major barley flavonoid glucoside is transported by a proton-antiporter in the vacuolar membrane of barley to be accumulated, while it is recognized by a primary transporter in Arabidopsis, which does not produce this flavonoid glucoside, indicative that saponarin is recognized as a xenobiotic (Frangne et al. 2002).

The barley ant310 mutant has a mutation in the chalcone isomerase gene and therefore contains less than $5 \%$ of the flavonoids of wild-type plants (Reuber et al. 1996). It has been shown very recently that isolated vacuoles of ant310 mutants exhibited strongly reduced transport activity for saponarin and isovitexin (Marinova et al. 2007a); however, the transport activity was restored by the incubation with their flavonoid precursor, naringenin, after which the saponarin contents increased up to wild-type level. These results demonstrate that the abilities of biosynthesis and transport of flavonoids are interconnected. If this correlation is not limited to barley, bioinformatics analysis on the transcriptomics linkage map will provide possible transporter genes for endogenous secondary metabolites.

Among various flavonoid glucosides, anthocyanins, which are colored flavonoids responsible for most of the red, pink, purple, and blue color in flowers according to the in vivo state and derivatization patterns, are one of the most well-studied phenolic compounds. They are accumulated in the vacuoles of various plants and act as an attractant for pollinators and protectant from UV light. The uptake of anthocyanins into the vacuoles was reported by several laboratories with various plant species, but according to systems used, the mechanism may differ, i.e. either by primary or secondary transport. The involvement of a primary transporter that transports anthocyanins in the vacuolar membrane was first suggested in the bronze-2 (bz-2) mutant of maize (Marrs et al. 1995). The bz-2 mutant is defective in glutathione S-transferase and failed to accumulate anthocyanin in the vacuoles. Because glutathione conjugates are recognized as common substrates for multidrug resistance associated protein (MRP/ABCC)-type ABC transporters, the involvement of an ABCC-type ABC transporter has been presumed in the vacuolar transport of anthocyanins. This idea was later strongly supported by the identification of ZmMrp3, a tonoplast localized ABCC-type transporter gene, and its antisense suppression resulted in a reduced level of anthocyanin accumulation (Goodman et al. 2004). In contrast, transport studies with Arabidopsis revealed that a secondary transporter mediated the uptake of anthocyanins into the vacuoles, and this transporter belongs to the MATE family (see the section below for details).

Legume plants synthesize flavonoid aglycons, and secrete some of them into the root exudates as signal molecules for rhizobia leading to the establishment of the symbiotic nitrogen fixation (Smit et al. 1992).

Recently, we have investigated the transport mechanism of flavonoid secretion from the root using soybean and its signal flavonoid genistein. Membrane vesicle transport assays demonstrated that an ABCtype transporter could mediate the secretion of genistein from soybean roots (Sugiyama et al. 2007), although there still remains the possibility for other legume plants that secondary transporters will be responsible for the secretion of their signal molecules.

Transport of phenylpropanoid glucosides was also characterized biochemically. Quinone compounds may be classified into phenolic compounds due to the relevance of their oxidation state, while biosynthetic routes of naturally occurring quinines are rather specialized for some quinones. Accumulation and related membrane transport are not well elucidated for quinines, but among benzo-, naphtho-, and anthraquinone compounds, the secretion of lipophilic red naphthoquinone shikonin derivatives has been characterized, where a vesicle trafficking-like mechanism was reported (Kunst and Samuels 2003; Yazaki 2005). However, protein members involved in the extracellular accumulation of shikonin have not yet been identified.


## Transporters for terpenoids


Terpenoids constitute the largest class of secondary metabolites with more than 25,000 compounds (Croteau et al. 2000). Terpenoids are formed from prenyl diphosphates of different chain length, which are provided by the consecutive elongation of five-carbon isoprene units, such as dimethylallyl diphosphate and isopentenyl diphosphate, forming hemiterpenes (one ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ unit), monoterpenes (two ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), sesquiterpenes (three ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), diterpenes (four ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), sesterterpenes (five ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), triterpenes (six ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), tetraterpenes (eight ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 5 }$ units), and further polymers. Although the biosynthetic pathways and physiological roles of terpenoids have been actively characterized, there has been no report on transporter proteins for terpenoids so far, except for a pleiotropic drug resistance (PDR/ABCG)-type ABC transporter of Nicotiana plumbaginifolia (NtPDR1) that is involved in the secretion of an endogenous antifungal diterpene, sclareol, onto its leaf surface (Jasinski et al. 2001). The smallest terpenoid isoprene is vigorously emitted from the leaves of many plant species, which contributes to the thermotolerance in plants (Behnke et al. 2007; Loivamaki et al. 2007; Sasaki et al. 2007), but it is thought that no transporters are involved in this massive emission from leaf cells to the air (Niinemets et al. 2004). Studies on transporter proteins for mono- or sesquiterpenoid will provide a breakthrough in this research field.


## Transporters for other metabolites


Plant sucrose transporters are proton-symporters, and some of them are reported to mediate the transport of various compounds other than sucrose. For example, $\mathrm { P m } \mathrm { S U C } 2$ of Plantago major and AtSUC5 transported biotin (vitamin H) when expressed in yeast (Ludwig et al. 2000), although biotin is not a plant secondary metabolite. The expression of AtSUC2 in Xenopus oocytes suggested the ability of this transporter to uptake various glucosides including arbutin and salicin (Chandran et al. 2003). The ability of sucrose transporters to mediate the uptake of these structurally divergent metabolites is indicative that this transporter family may contribute to facilitate the movement of various secondary metabolites across membranes in planta.

Urea is a nitrogen-containing metabolite in plants. It was reported that an Arabidopsis transporter belonging to the sodium solute symporters family, AtDUR3, mediates the uptake of urea when expressed in Xenopus oocytes and yeast (Liu et al. 2003), while several plant aquaporins were also reported to transport urea in a channel-like manner (Kojima et al. 2006). The in planta function of AtDUR3 was recently reported as a high-affinity urea transporter involved in the uptake of urea from soil, which was demonstrated by expression analyses and transport studies using atdur3 mutants (Kojima et al. 2007).


## MATE transporters, an emerging transporter family mediating various cellular processes


The MATE family was originally found in prokaryotes and their function as multiple drug efflux carrier was studied in detail. However, orthologues in higher organisms have been characterized only in recent years, and some plant MATE members showed particular physiological functions with strict specificity to transport particular substrates. In the last half of this article, we focus on the MATE members to summarize their functions.


## MATE transporters in bacteria and animals


MATE transporters consist of 400–700 amino acids with 9–12 transmembrane $\mathscr { X }$ -helices (Fig. 2), but no apparent consensus sequence has been identified unlike ABC transporters that contain unique ABC signature(s), although three amino acids conserved in one cluster of the MATE family were reported to be essential for the antiport function of bacterial MATEs (Otsuka et al. 2005b). The first MATE transporter was identified from the screening of Vibrio parahaemolyticus genes that confer resistance for norfloxacin, a widely used antimicrobial compound (Morita et al. 1998). The identified gene product was named NorM and reported to function as a sodium-multidrug antiporter that transport various structurally unrelated compounds (Morita et al. 2000). To data, MATE transporters have been reported in all living organisms characterized, and the functions of some members are being elucidated (Omote et al. 2006). The human genome contains two genes (MATE1 and MATE2) encoding MATE transporters. MATE1 is highly expressed in the liver and kidney, and when expressed in HEK293 cells it transported tetraethylammonium, a typical cationic substrate of this family, and 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium in a proton-coupled manner (Otsuka et al. 2005a), and MATE2 is also reported to transport various organic cations (Masuda et al. 2006). These results, along with the report of a mouse MATE1 transporter (Hiasa et al. 2006), suggest that mammalian MATE transporters function in the excretion of toxic organic cations from renal tubular cells and hepatocytes.

MATE transporters in plants

Arabidopsis contains 56 MATE transporter genes in its genome (Fig. 3). This family size is remarkably large compared to the human counterpart (only two members), although their functions have been only elucidated for some members in recent years. The first report on a plant MATE transporters concerned AtALF5, which was identified from a mutant defective in lateral root formation (aberrant lateral root formation) (Diener et al. 2001). Heterologous expression of AtALF5 in yeast conferred resistance to tetramethylammonium, suggesting its function in detoxification as an efflux transporter for xenobiotics. Another MATE member of Arabidopsis, AtDTX1, was identified from the functional screening of a cDNA complementing the growth of a norfloxacinhypersensitive Escherichia coli mutant (Li et al. 2002). When expressed in E. coli, AtDTX1 conferred multiple tolerance to berberine and cadmium in addition to norfloxacin, which suggests that AtDTX1 is also an efflux carrier for multidrug resistance, although the tested compounds are still limited in number. Recently a unique MATE transporter has been identified by the positional cloning of an Arabidopsis enhanced disease susceptibility (eds) mutant that accumulated little salicylic acid, a second messenger in plant-pathogen interactions and showed hypersensitivity to pathogens (Nawrath et al. 2002). The expression of AtEDS5 was induced by pathogen attack and UV-C treatment. Functional analyses have not been carried out with this MATE transporter, but organic molecules involved in the signal transduction cascade and precursors of salicylic acids are suggested as possible substrates.

Arabidopsis contains flavonoid pigments in the mature seed coat (testa), where proanthocyanidins accumulate exclusively in the endothelium layer (Devic et al. 1999). Several Arabidopsis transparent testa $( t t )$ mutants have been isolated via screening for altered pigmentation in the seed coat, and the responsible genes have been identified as being for the biosynthetic enzymes of flavonoids (Lepiniec et al. 2006), while AtTT12, identified as a T-DNA tag line, was found to encode a MATE-type transporter (Debeaujon et al. 2001). AtTT12 was presumed to be a vacuolar transporter for flavonoids in the seed coat, but its function remained unknown until Klein and co-workers in a collaboration with Debeaujon’s group have recently reported the precise functions of AtTT12 (Marinova et al. 2007b). It was shown that the AtTT12 gene was expressed specifically in cells synthesizing proanthocyanidins, and the AtTT12 polypeptide localized to the vacuolar membrane. They also demonstrated that yeast microsome vesicles expressing AtTT12 mediated the membrane transport of cyanidin-3-O-glucoside but not of procyanidin dimers, quercetin-3- $o$ -rhamnoside, quercetin-3-Oglucoside, or catechin-3- $o$ -glucoside, while catechin3-O-glucoside strongly inhibited the transport of cyanidin-3- $o$ -glucoside in a dose-dependent manner. From these results, Klein and co-authors concluded that AtTT12 is a tonoplast proton-antiporter in proanthocyanidins-synthesizing cells of the seed coat, which mediates the transport of anthocyanin. A similar MATE transporter (MTP77) of tomato has also been reported as a putative anthocyanin transporter at the vacuole (Mathews et al. 2003), but the biochemical function as a transporter is still to be characterized.

Another Arabidopsis MATE transporter was identified from the screening of mutants that constitutively express iron-deficient inducible genes under ironsufficient conditions (Rogers and Guerinot 2002). The MATE transporter named AtFRD3 after ferric reductase defective was expressed predominantly in roots and was necessary for correct iron distribution throughout the plant (Green and Rogers 2004). Further functional analysis of AtFRD3 in Xenopus oocytes has shown recently that AtFRD3 mediates the efflux of citrate to the apoplast and is not directly involved in iron transport (Durrett et al. 2007). Together with the localization of this transporter in the root vasculature, Durrett and colleagues suggested that AtFRD3 effluxed citrate into the root vasculature, which facilitated the translocation of iron-citrate complexes to the leaves. A white lupin homologue of AtFRD3, LaMATE, was reportedly upregulated in phosphorus deficiency conditions and under aluminum stress as well (Uhde-Stone et al. 2005). In fact, RNAi-silencing of LaMATE exhibited the reduction of growth under phosphorous deficiency, but its functions regarding transport of particular substances are still unknown.


## MATE transporters and aluminum resistance


Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust. Although aluminum in the form of aluminosilicates is harmless to plants, aluminum solubilized in the form of ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ in acid soil is highly toxic to plants producing strong growth defect, which is most prominent as rapid inhibition of root elongation (Ma and Furukawa 2003). A well-known mechanism of aluminum resistance in plants is the secretion of organic anions such as citrate, oxalate, and malate from the roots (Ma et al. 2001; Kochian et al. 2005). As an experimental proof, the over-expression of AtFRD3, which enhanced exudation of citrate and malate from roots of transgenic Arabidopsis, led to the higher tolerance to aluminum (Durrett et al. 2007). In accordance with this result, several MATE transporters conferring aluminum tolerance have been reported recently. In barley high-resolution mapping of the Alp locus that conditions aluminum tolerance, a gene encoding MATE transporter (HvMATE) was identified as a candidate controlling aluminum resistance (Wang et al. 2007). This barley MATE transporter gene is essentially the same as $H _ { { \nu } A A } { \cal A } C T I$ , identified from a fine mapping and microarray analysis by

Furukawa and co-workers (Furukawa et al. 2007). When expressed in Xenopus oocytes, HvAACT1 protein mediated the efflux of citrate, and the strict specificity of this MATE was indicated that it did not mediate malate secretion. HvAACT1 was presumed to be localized to the plasma membrane, and transgenic tobacco expressing HvAACT1 also showed higher citrate secretion in the presence of aluminum and exhibited higher tolerance to aluminum, but the citrate secretion was not altered in the absence of aluminum despite the constitutive promoter in the heterologous host (Furukawa et al. 2007). A homologous gene that is involved in aluminum resistance has also been reported recently in sorghum (Magalhaes et al. 2007), while in wheat another type of transporter molecule that did not belong to the MATE family was identified, which mediated malate secretion from the root to generate aluminum tolerance.

Evolution has bestowed plants with genetic machinery to biosynthesize a structurally diverse set of small organic molecules, the secondary metabolites, which are primarily, if not limited to, meant for ecological interactions. Most of these compounds often possess remarkable bioactive properties and are of tremendous pharmaceutical potential (Atanasov et al. 2015). Certain secondary metabolites are of human interest owing to their use as drugs, phytomedicines, phytoceuticals, aroma, dyes, favoring agents, and pesticides (Duan et al. 2012; He and Giusti 2010; Kroymann 2011; Zhao et  al. 2005). The secondary metabolites in plants are often produced in low concentrations and are usually restricted to a particular plant species or distributed amongst restricted taxonomic groups. Considering their ecological roles and economic values, plant biologists have long been interested in elucidating their biosynthetic pathways in terms of enzymes and associated structural and regulatory genes. The biosynthetic machinery of metabolites is often compartmentalized within the cell or in diferent cells, implying the involvement of inter or intracellular trafcking of intermediates and metabolites (Verma et al. 2012; Yu and De Luca 2013). The diferent types of membrane transporters exhibit active engagement in the intracellular, intercellular, as well as in long-distance organ to organ transport of secondary metabolites (Fig. 1). The movement of metabolites, for example, nicotine, a pyrrolidine alkaloid, specifcally biosynthesized in Nicotiana species, involves long-distance organ to organ transport. The nicotine, which is biosynthesized mainly in the roots, is transported to the aerial plant part, such as leaf, where it primarily functions in defense response as an insect neurotoxin against herbivory or pest attack (Hashimoto and Yamada 2003). The compartmentalization and storage in specifc sub-cellular sites, for example, vacuoles are part of cellular strategies to tackle potentially cytotoxic secondary metabolites (Sirikantaramas et al. 2007).

Trafcking and storage of small organic molecules may alter the substrate pool for enzymes and thereby could modulate the fate of the end product (Roze et al. 2011). Longdistance trafcking of secondary metabolites, from one organ to another organ, and thereafter, their storage, has also been well reported (Shitan et al. 2003, 2013). Ecological functions of plant secondary metabolites, for example, plant–insect and plant–microbe interactions, highlight the importance of their transport from locations of biosynthesis/storage to the site of action (Vogt 2010; Vranová et al. 2012). Therefore, the transport mechanisms of these specialized metabolites appear to be linked with their biosynthetic machinery, and thereby contribute towards defning the cellular pool of secondary metabolites. The abovementioned instances mandate the involvement of an elegant transport mechanism allowing the trafcking of secondary metabolites across cellular membranes. Although other mechanisms, for example, passive transport of secondary metabolites have been reported, the membrane-localized transporter proteins have been demonstrated to ofer tightly regulated and highly selective transport of these small organic molecules (Morita et al. 2009). Studies have strongly suggested that transportation of secondary metabolites, like other small organic molecules such as phytohormones, is facilitated by transporters. These transporters function like enzymes and are often specifc to a particular compound or may recognize a specifc chemical backbone, depending upon ligand specifcity.


## Transport of plant secondary metabolites


In general, distinct mechanisms of secondary metabolite transport have been proposed, such as simple difusion, vesicle-mediated transport, and transporter-mediated membrane transport (Nour-Eldin and Halkier 2013; Shitan 2016). Alkaloids, an important class of secondary metabolites have been shown to be transported frst via simple difusion and then followed by membrane trapping. Alkaloids being slightly basic in nature can infltrate the tonoplast membrane, in a restricted fashion, through simple difusion and are protonated in the acidic lumen and fnally remain accumulated in the vacuole. On the other side, vesicle-mediated transport of plant-derived metabolites, particularly those of alkaloids and favonoids, have been supported by microscopic observations. In this particular transport mechanism, an alkaloid or a favonoid containing small vesicles, are proposed to transport organic compounds into the vacuole by fusion between the membranes of diferent cellular compartments. Benzylisoquinoline alkaloids, for example, berberine and sanguinarine, the antimicrobial alkaloids that get accumulated in the vacuoles of opium poppy cultured cells have been reported to be transported by the vesicle-mediated transport mechanism (Alcantara et al. 2005; Bock et al. 2002). Anthocyanins have been found to get transported into the vacuole by anthocyanoplasts, possibly by the fusion of prevacuolar compartments (PVCs), for example, in grapevine epidermal cells (Braidot et al. 2008). Also, structures fairly similar to anthocyanoplasts, known as anthocyanic vacuolar inclusions (AVIs), are found to display active movement in the vacuoles of several plant species. These AVIs have been observed in the petal cells of lisianthus and carnation and also known to exist in the anthocyanin-accumulating cells of grapevine, sweet potato and maize (Zhang et al. 2006). However, mechanisms, as mentioned above do not appear to be competent modes of transport employed in plant secondary metabolite transport because they are not specifc and do not ofer tight regulation.


## Transporter‑mediated transport of secondary metabolites


The biosynthetic machinery of secondary metabolites, as well as their accumulation, is tightly regulated at various levels of gene expression (Gonzalez et al. 2008; Hong et al. 2012; Teng et al. 2005; van der Fits et al. 2000). These regulatory mechanisms defne the spatio-temporal accumulation pattern of secondary metabolites and allow the plant to respond to several ecological factors, including surrounding biotic and abiotic stresses (Olsson et al. 2009; Tholl and Lee 2011). Thus, the inter- and intracellular transport of secondary metabolites and their precursors should be tightly regulated to fne-tune the entire biosynthetic machinery optimally. In this regard, transporter-mediated transport of secondary metabolites is an attractive way that allows highly selective and tightly regulated transport of small organic molecules. Being localized on tonoplast and plasma membrane, these transporters are membrane proteins, which play a pivotal role in controlling the metabolic fux of specialized metabolites between diferent cellular or sub-cellular compartments and thus, function as an integral and essential part of cellular metabolic networks.

During the last decade, notable advancement has been made towards identifcation and functional characterization of transporter genes concerned with the transport of plant specialized metabolites. In a plant cell, a central vacuole that can cover up to $8 0 \%$ volume of the cell acts as the major site for sequestration of secondary metabolites within the plant cell. It is, therefore, not surprising that a large number of transporter proteins, localized on vacuolar membranes, have been identifed and demonstrated to export secondary metabolites of diverse chemical backbone to the outside of the cell or sequester them within the vacuole (Yazaki et al. 2008). The vacuolar transportome of plant specialized metabolites has been reviewed recently (de Brito Francisco and Martinoia 2018). However, since then, several empirical fndings related to the membrane transport in plants have been reported. Thus far, certain members belonging to ABC (ATP-binding cassette), MATE (multidrug and toxic compound extrusion or Multi-antimicrobial extrusion), PUP (purine permease) and NRT (nitrate-peptide transporter) transporter families have been identifed as membrane- localized transporters of plant secondary metabolites (Jelesko 2012; Nour-Eldin et al. 2012; Shoji 2014; Shoji et al. 2009; Takanashi et al. 2017; Verrier et al. 2008). Out of the four families of the transporters, linked to the transport function of secondary metabolites thus far, the majority of the characterized members are from ABC and MATE family of transporters (Nour-Eldin and Halkier 2013; Shitan 2016). The vast repertoire of these transporter families in the genome of higher plants as compared to mammals can be linked to the enormous diversity of plant secondary metabolites. In the following heads, an overview of defning features of each class of these transporter families is given.


## ABC transporters


ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters comprise a large, diverse, and ubiquitous family of proteins found in all three domains of life ranging from bacteria to higher plants (Vasiliou et al. 2009). These proteins display presence of an ATP binding cassette, also called as the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), which includes several highly conserved motifs such as Walker A (GXG-K-[ST]), Walker B ([RK]- ${ \bf X } _ { 3 } – \bf G { - } X _ { 3 }$ -L-[hydrophobic] ) motifs, and ABC signature motif ([LIVMFY]-S-[SG]-G- $X _ { 3 }$ -[RKA]-[LIVMYA]-X[LIVMF]-[AG]) (Ambudkar et al. 2006; Higgins and Linton 2004). In addition to NBDs, they also contain transmembrane domains (TMDs), and each of which is composed of several hydrophobic $\alpha$ -helices. A typical functional ABC transporter has four important domains: two NBDs and two TMDs. The two NBDs co-operate to bind and hydrolyze ATP, thereby providing the driving force for transport, and the TMDs are involved in substrate recognition (Martinoia et al. 2002). An ABC transporter is called as full-size ABC transporters if it contains all the four elements (two TMDs and two NBDs) in a single polypeptide chain, whereas the half-size members contain one TMD and one NBD, which are present as homo-or heterodimers. The ABC transporters are divided into three subfamilies:

The multidrug resistance (MDR) or p-glycoproteins (PGP)/ABCB subfamily with domains organized in the forward orientation (TMD1—NBD1—TMD2—NBD2). The pleiotropic drug resistance (PDR)/ABCG subfamily having domain organization in the reverse orientation (NBD1—TMD1—NBD2—TMD2). The multidrug resistance-associated protein (MRP)/ ABCC subfamily with domains also arranged in the forward orientation, but a few possess fve $\alpha$ -helices at the N terminus (Kang et al. 2011; Nuruzzaman et al. 2014).

Phylogenetically, ABC proteins in higher plants are clustered into eight subfamilies, ABCA–ABCI (ABCH is absent in plants). These transporters display remarkable expansion in the plant kingdom and form large superfamilies containing abundant genes (Kang et al. 2011; Shoji 2014; Verrier et al. 2008). For example, in the case of model plant Arabidopsis thaliana genome, about 130 putative genes encoding ABC protein have been reported (Kang et al. 2011; Verrier et al. 2008).


## MATE transporters


MATE (multidrug and toxic compound extrusion or Multiantimicrobial extrusion) transporters were initially classifed as members of the major facilitator (MFS) family, but owing to the presence of unique topology and ubiquitous occurrence in almost all domains of life results in the designation of MATE transporters as a separate family. Typically, MATE transporters have the topology of 12 putative transmembrane helices (TMs) arranged together as two bundles, having long N- and C-terminal extensions (Hvorup et al. 2003; Matsumoto et al. 2008). These proteins display the absence of “signature sequences” specifc to the other multidrug transporter subfamilies. However, in Arabidopsis, an EDS5 protein constitutes only 9–11 TMs, while FRD3 protein comprises of 14 TMs as exceptions (Green and Rogers 2004; Nawrath et al. 2002). MATE transporters are found to be remarkably abundant in plants refecting its importance in the kingdom and, are, in general, crucial for the detoxifcation of metabolic products such as cationic ions, organic acids and are actively involved in the transport of secondary metabolites (Chen et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2017). The functional role of MATE transporters has been broadened now as certain members have been implicated in the plant hormone transport and regulation of cell and organ size as well as in senescence (Jia et al. 2019; Suzuki et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2014). The MATE proteins function as antiporters that couple substrate movement using electrochemical gradients of either $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ generated by proton pumps (Omote et al. 2006). There are reports of 58 MATE members in the model plant Arabidopsis, where they are also called as DETOXIFICATION (DTX) proteins, and of which a few transporter genes have been functionally characterized (Kitamura 2006). Until recently, with the advancement in crystallography and related atomic molecular simulation techniques, the crystal structure of a frst plant MATE transporter has been reported in Camelina sativa, which provides insights into the diversity of MATE transporters and their substrate recognition specifcity (Tanaka et al. 2017). Also, the crystal structure of an Arabidopsis MATE transporter, namely AtDTX14, was unraveled, which provided some concrete information about the structural as well as mechanistic aspects of MATE transporters protein in plants (Miyauchi et al. 2017).


## Nitrate‑peptide transporter


Nitrate-peptide transporters (NRT) or peptide transporters (PTR) constitute a large family and include NRT1/ PTR, NRT2, and NRT3 members. These proteins were originally recognized as a class of transporters having distinct functions in nitrate uptake and transport in plants (Dechorgnat et al. 2010). The gene family of plant nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1) has been rechristened as the NPF family (Léran et al. 2014). The NPF gene family comprises NPF6.3 (NRT1.1 or CHL1) and covers a vast number of genes, which can be grouped into 8–10 subfamilies. NRT1.1 or CHL1 has been the frst member of the NRT1 family reported in Arabidopsis chlorate resistant mutant, where it comprises 53 members. The NRT1.1 functions in low–afnity and in high-afnity nitrate transport, and has an essential role as a nitrate sensor in the activation of nitrate related gene expression in plants (Ho et al. 2009). Apart from nitrate transport, NRT plant transporter proteins have been demonstrated to function in the transport of a diverse array of substrates including peptides, glucosinolates, IAA, abscisic acid, jasmonoyl-isoleucine, and gibberellins, etc. in comparison to their bacterial and animal counterparts (Chiba et al. 2015; David et al. 2016; Kanno et al. 2012; Komarova et al. 2008; Krouk et al. 2010; NourEldin et al. 2012; Saito et al. 2015; Tal et al. 2016).


## PUP (purine uptake permease)


Previously the purine uptake permease (PUP) transporter family in plants was primarily known to be involved in the transport of purine nucleobase substrates. The PUPlike genes consist of a gene family with moderate size in Arabidopsis consisting of 21 genes, including one pseudogene. Typically, a PUP-like transporter possesses ten predicted transmembrane spanning domains and is proposed to function in substrate infux by possibly acting as proton symporters. PUP transporters primarily transport substrates, which comprise of purine ring-containing compounds (adenine, cytosine, and cytokinins) and pyridine ring-containing compounds like pyridoxine and pyridoxal. AtPUP1 from Arabidopsis has been the frst identifed founding member belonging to PUP-like transporter family that displayed high-afnity adenine uptake activity in yeast (Gillissen et al. 2000). Moreover, a PUP-like homolog has been studied in tobacco, where it shows nicotine uptake permease activity and afects nicotine metabolism and root cell growth (Hildreth et al. 2011). These fndings have broadened the physiological role of PUP-like transporter proteins in the plant secondary metabolism as well.


## Transport of plant secondary metabolites


Plant secondary metabolites are divided into distinct groups based on their chemical structure and biosynthetic origin. This review recapitulates the current updates on the major classes of transporters involved in plant secondary metabolite transport on the basis of the chemical backbone of the substrates (Table 1).


## Transport of Alkaloids


Alkaloids consist of low molecular weight, nitrogencontaining compounds with diverse chemical structures, and participate in plant chemical defense against pests, insects, microbes, and other herbivores (Steppuhn et al. 2004). Owing to their potent biological activity, these compounds constitute a major family of plant natural products with several compounds of potential pharmaceutical uses. Remarkable examples include taxol, vincristine, and vinblastine (VLB), which are recommended prescription anticancer drugs in chemotherapies, and morphine, which functions as an analgesic. The molecular and cellular studies on some important alkaloid biosynthetic pathways demonstrated that alkaloids, as well as their biosynthetic intermediates, are transported within plant tissues in a regulated and dynamic fashion (Shitan and Yazaki 2007; Verma et al. 2012). Three diferent modes of transport have been known to operate in alkaloid biosynthesis and accumulation: inter-organ, intercellular, and intracellular (Shitan and Yazaki 2007). The alkaloid transport has been studied particularly in the model system Nicotiana tabacum in detail. This plant mainly produces a pyridine alkaloid, namely nicotine, which acts as a neurotoxin in defense against herbivory (Dewey and Xie 2013; Shoji et al. 2009). The nicotine is biosynthesized in roots from where it is transported to the aerial plant parts and fnally gets accumulated in the central vacuole of leaf via xylem, where it acts in defense response (Steppuhn et al. 2004). The transporters involved in nicotine transport have been comprehensively reviewed in the recent past (Shitan 2016;

Shitan et al. 2014a). Three tonoplast localized transporters from the MATE family, namely jasmonate-inducible alkaloid transporter1 (JAT1), JAT2, and MATE1, are recognized as well-established nicotine transporters, which possibly acts as nicotine/proton antiporters (Morita et al. 2009; Shitan et  al. 2014a; Shitan and Yazaki 2007). Experimental studies demonstrated that JAT1 and JAT2 transporters are involved in the transport of nicotine into leaf vacuoles, whereas two vacuolar membrane-localized MATE transporters, namely NtMATE1 and NtMATE2, have been reported to possibly function in nicotine transport into root vacuoles (Shoji et al. 2009). The in vitro assays showed that these transporters are not strictly specifc for nicotine, and can transport other structurally related alkaloids like anabasine, and scopolamine. In addition to the above- mentioned tonoplast localized transporters, a plasma membrane-localized transporter belonging to PUP family namely Nicotine uptake permease1 (NUP1) has been demonstrated to be involved in the infux of nicotine at the cell membrane of the root tip (Hildreth et al. 2011; Kato et  al. 2015). Thus, the studies on nicotine transport in tobacco suggested that multiple transporters could be implicated in the transport process of a particular secondary metabolite. Furthermore, it was elucidated that these transporters display a considerable degree of substrate specifcity. Recently, BUP1 transporter, belonging to the PUP family has been implicated in the transport of benzylisoquinoline in Papaver sominferum (Dastmalchi et al. 2019).

In the medicinal plant, Catharanthus roseus, the biosynthesis of two important leaf derived bisindole alkaloids, vinblastine, and vincristine takes place through the dimerization of catharanthine and vindoline (monoterpenoid indole alkaloids) mediated by class III basic peroxidase (Prx1) (Costa et al. 2008; Kumar et al. 2007; Sottomayor and Barceló 2003). During alkaloid biosynthesis in C. roseus, intermediate metabolites display inter- and intracellular transport involving diferent organelles and cells (De Luca et al. 2014; Verma et al. 2012). Previous studies have demonstrated that a plasma-membrane localized ABCG transporter, namely CrTPT2, mediates the efux of catharanthine to the leaf surface (Yu and De Luca 2013). Another study found that important monoterpenoid indole alkaloids (MIAs) from $C$ . roseus, such as vindoline, gets accumulated in the mesophyll cell vacuoles by specifc proton antiport systems (Carqueijeiro et al. 2013). The localization of the two monomeric MIAs (vindoline and catharanthine) in diferent cells ofers an obvious account of the low level of dimeric MIAs accumulated in plants. The knockdown of CrTPT2 transporter gene by VIGS (virus-induced gene silencing) technique displayed a decreased level of catharanthine at the leaf surface, whereas increased catharanthine level was observed in the internal leaf cells which in turn, results in an increased level of catharanthine–vindoline dimers within the leaf. Metabo - lomic and cell-specifc localization studies using Imaging mass spectrometry expounded that TIA precursors such as iridoids are localized in the epidermal cells, while some key TIAs like serpentine and vindoline are found to be localized in the idioblast cells. Also, strictosidine, the central TIA intermediate, has been suggested to be accumulated in both epidermal and idioblast cells. Furthermore, this study also showed that as the leaf expands, the accumulation of vindoline also increases in laticifer cells. Overall, this work sheds light on the complexity of intercellular localization and the accumulation of specialized molecules and their biosynthetic intermediates within the plant system (Yamamoto et  al. 2019). Recently, a tonoplast localized transporter, CrNPF2.9 of nitrate/peptide family (NPF) from C. roseus, has been characterized as a vacuolar exporter of strictosidine, which is a central monoterpene indole alkaloid intermediate (Payne et al. 2017). Strictosidine synthase, an enzyme involved in strictosidine biosynthesis,was reported to be localized in the vacuole (Guirimand et al. 2011). This suggests that for ef - cient strictosidine biosynthesis, strictosidine precursors such as tryptamine and secologanin must get transported into the vacuole from the cytosol. However, until now, no specifc transporter involved in such transport process has been iden - tifed. Furthermore, in C. roseus, three plasma membranelocalized iridoid glucoside transporters have been identifed by functional screening of eight orthologous transporters from the NPF family . The three identifed CrNPF2 trans - porters, namely CrNPF2.4, CrNPF2.5, and CrNPF2.6, have been found to play an important role in the transportation of iridoid glucosides 7-deoxyloganic acid, loganic acid, loga - nin and secologanin. These transporters imported the four iridoid glucosides with distinct relative activity at the pH of the apoplast, i.e., $\mathrm { p H } 5$ (Larsen et al. 2017). A recent study in C. roseus mutant provides concrete evidence about the existence of the inter-organ transport mechanism of secolo - ganin, which facilitates the formation of MIAs in the leaves (Kidd et al. 2019).

Another remarkable example is of berberine, a benzylisoquinoline alkaloid produced by Coptis japonica, a perennial medicinal plant found to be grown in the Asian sub-continent, is synthesized mainly in roots and accu - mulated in the rhizome (Ikezawa et al. 2003). Various biochemical studies reported that ABC transporters of B subgroup family play important functions in berberine transport (Sakai et al. 2002; Shitan and Yazaki 2007). To this end, three members of ABC B subfamily trans - porters, namely CjABCB1 (CjMDR1), CjABCB2, and CjABCB3, have been identifed and characterized (Shitan et al. 2013; Yazaki et al. 2001). Amongst, CjABCB1 rep - resents the founding member of plant secondary metabo - lite specifc transporter (Shitan et al. 2003; Yazaki et al. 2001). Functional analysis indicated the crucial role of

ABC transporters CjABCB1 and CjABCB2 in berberine transport from its site of synthesis (root) to the rhizome by mediating its transport at the plasma membrane of xylem cells of the rhizome (Shitan et al. 2003, 2005). Besides, it was also suggested that berberine is transported in the vacuole of cultured cells via the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ /berberine antiporter systemin in C. japonica (Otani et al. 2005). Thus, proton gradient-driven transporters are thought to mediate the transport of berberine across the tonoplast. The fndings of a recent study in C. japonica demonstrated that a MATE transporter, CjMATE1, functions as a vacuolar transporter of berberine (Takanashi et al. 2017).


## Transport of phenylpropanoids


Phenylpropanoids, commonly called plant phenolics, consist of an aromatic ring with one or few hydroxyl substituents and contain many subgroups, such as favonoids and lignans. Flavonoids are a remarkable class of plant natural compounds chemically exhibiting a common three-membered ring structure (C6–C3–C6). Owing to their ubiquitous occurrence, tremendous structural diversity, and manifold functions in plant biology such as control of auxin transport, protection against UV light, plant–microbe interactions, and in fower color variation, these compounds have been a focus of detailed studies (Falcone Ferreyra et al. 2012). In planta, a majority of favonoids subsist as their glycosylated form in the cell and glycosylation is critically required for their efcient vacuolar transport. The biosynthesis of favonoids occurs in the cytosol of the cell and gets accumulated into the vacuole and display long-distance transport (Buer and Muday 2004; Peer et al. 2001; Saslowsky and Winkel‐Shirley 2001). In the last two decades, several transporter proteins, belonging mostly to ABC and MATE families have been identifed as the transporters of favonoids. For instance, ABC family of transporters have been documented to be involved in the vacuolar transport of favone glucuronide conjugates in rye mesophyll cell vacuoles as well as in favone glucoside uptake in Arabidopsis vacuoles (Frangne et al. 2002; Klein et al. 2000). The genetic studies demonstrated that a C-type ABC transporter protein, ZmMRP3 mediates the vacuolar accumulation of anthocyanin in maize crop (Goodman et al. 2004). Studies found that suppression of ZmMRP3 signifcantly decreased the anthocyanin level indicating its involvement in anthocyanin transport. A tonoplast localized ABC transporter, VvABCC1, expressing in the exocarp of grape berry during ripening stage functions in the vacuolar accumulation of anthocyanins. Biochemical studies showed that the VvABCC1 transporter facilitates the co-transportation of glucosylated anthocyanidin, malvidin 3-O-glucoside with glutathione (GSH) and thus function as an anthocyanin transporter (Francisco et al. 2013). Furthermore, recently, an Arabidopsis ABC transporter, namely AtABCC2 alongside other ABCC transporters, has been suggested to function in the vacuolar transport of anthocyanins and few other favonoids within the vegetative tissue (Behrens et al. 2019). Legumes synthesize and secrete a few favonoid aglycons from the roots, which can act as signal molecules essential for the establishment of symbiotic interaction with soil rhizobia, suggesting a provision of exudation of favonoids in the rhizosphere (Smit et al. 1992). Genomic studies investigated the transport process governing the secretion of favonoids from the soybean roots and provided a clear picture of the key role of ABC type transporters in this secretion (Sugiyama et al. 2007). Moreover, favonoid secretion plays a vital part in the plant defense response against root-infecting pathogens. For instance, MtABCG10, an ABC transporter, has been reported to function in favonoid secretion possibly by mediating the modulation of the isofavone levels in roots of M. truncatula (Banasiak et al. 2013). In addition to this, another ABCG sub-family transporter, AtABCG37 in Arabidopsis root, has been found to mediate the secretion of scopoletin and coumarin to the soil in response to iron defciency (Fourcroy et al. 2014). Apart from ABC proteins, another family of multidrug transporters, MATEs also play a critical role in favonoid transport. An Arabidopsis MATE transporter, namely AtDTX41/AtTT12 (TRANSPARENT TESTA12) functions as a proanthocyanidin (PA)/ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter by controlling the transport of glycosylated favan-3-ol monomers in the seed coat endothelium and has been found to transport epicatechin $3 ^ { \prime }$ -O-glucoside more efciently than anthocyanin cyanidin-3-O-glucoside (Debeaujon et al. 2001; Marinova et al. 2007; Zhao and Dixon 2009). The analysis further showed that mutant tt12 seeds exhibit varied favonoid composition and do not display distinctive bright brown-orange coloration as compared to wild-type seeds (Debeaujon et al. 2001). Another MATE transporter FFT/DTX35, closely related to AtTT12, has been reported to transport favonoid primarily pro-anthocyanin in Arabidopsis, and it was reported that $\mathcal { H } t$ mutant, unlike tt12 mutant, displayed defective reproductive development (Marinova et al. 2007; Thompson et al. 2010). Moreover, recently, FFT/DTX35 MATE transporter in Arabidopsis has been reported to function as a chloride channel in root hair and pollen tube elongation crucial for turgor regulation (Zhang et al. 2017). These fndings indicate that our current knowledge about the exact nature of FFT/DTX35 substrates needs further clarifcation. Furthermore, MATE transporters phylogenetically related to AtTT12 have also been shown to transport favonoids in diferent plants. For example, two MATE transporters, namely MdMATE1 and MdMATE2, identifed in Malus domestica function as vacuolar favonoid $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \mathrm { \left/ H ^ { + } \right. } }$ -antiporters in proanthocyanidin accumulation (Banasiak et al. 2013; Frank et al. 2011). Studies suggested that MtMATE1 transporter from Medicago mediates transport of epicatechin $3 ^ { \prime } .$ -O-glucoside, whereas MtMATE2 transports several anthocyanidin glucosides showing preferential substrate specifcity for malonylated favonoids (Zhao and Dixon 2009; Zhao et al. 2011). MTP77, a MATE transporter and a close homolog of AtTT12, identifed in Solanum lycopersicum has been shown to have a major function in anthocyanin vacuolar transport in the leaf tissue (Mathews et al. 2003). Two grapevine MATE transporters, namely VvAM1, and VvAM3, have been proposed to mediate the anthocyanin accumulation in a small vesicle that display movement towards vacuole (Gomez et al. 2009, 2011). Two MATE type transporters VvMATE1 and VvMATE2 from V. vinifera L., have been identifed as putative proanthocyanidin transporters during the development of berry. Also, subcellular localization studies of these transporters suggested that VvMATE1 is tonoplast localized, whereas VvMATE2 is found to be localized in the Golgi complex, refecting their diferent routes for intracellular proanthocyanidin transport (Pérez-Díaz et al. 2014). Recent studies indicated that a MATE transporter FaTT12, is exclusively involved in the accumulation of proanthocyanidin in strawberry fruits (Chen et al. 2018). Altogether it is evident that diferent classes of transporters might be involved in transporting the same backbone, as discussed above in the case of anthocyanins, which are transported by ABC transporters in maize and grapevine and also by MATE transporters in grape and Medicago. Owing to the fact that these specialized plant metabolites possess a vast structural diversity, it is likely that the provision of multiple transporter families for a particular favonoid backbone could ofer a mechanism to fne-tune their transportation.


## Transport of Terpenoids


Terpenoids are vast and structurally varied class of plant natural products. Based on the number of isoprene units present, these compounds such as monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes, and triterpenes may function as secondary metabolites and play crucial roles in plant-environment interactions (Aharoni et al. 2005; Pichersky and Gershenzon 2002; Staniek et al. 2013; Trapp and Croteau 2001). In addition, certain terpenoid backbones have been reported to function as phytohormones, for example, cytokinins, gibberellic acid, abscisic acid, brassinosteroid, and strigolactones. More than 30,000 isoprenoids, mostly of plant origin, are listed in the Dictionary of Natural Products (Buckingham 2004). Many terpenoids are potentially valuable as phytomedicine. For example, taxol from Taxus baccata shows anti-carcinogenic activity and artemisinin from A. annua is used as antimalarial drug, and some has favoring uses as well. These molecules act as insect attractants, antifeedants, and few of these metabolites are reported to function as electron carriers in respiration and photosynthetic pigments. Therefore, eforts are being made to explicate and engineer the biosynthetic pathway governing these specialized metabolites in plants (Staniek et al. 2013). A few transporters of ABCG subfamily have been reported so far, which are assigned functional roles in the transport of some specifc terpenes. A pleiotropic drug resistance1 (NpPDR1/NpABC1) transporter from Nicotiana plumbaginifolia displaying preferential expression in the leaf glandular trichomes, fower petals, and roots is the frst ABC G sub-family transporter, which was proposed to function in sclareol transport at its leaf surface (Jasiński et al. 2001). Silencing of NpPDR1 in N. plumbaginifolia resulted in high susceptibility to some fungal and oomycete pathogens, which indicates its prominent role in pathogen resistance by facilitating the transportation of antifungal diterpene, sclareol onto the plant surface (Bultreys et al. 2009). In addition to this, similar role in the sclareol secretion have been proposed for two close homologs of NpPDR1 protein namely AtPDR12, and SpTUR2 from Arabidopsis and Spirodela polyrrhiza, respectively (Campbell et al. 2003; Van Den Brûle et al. 2002). Additionally, in N. tabacum, an ABCG transporter namely NtPDR1, which showed $8 4 \%$ similarity with NpPDR1, at the amino acid level has been reported to mediate the transport of anti-fungal diterpenes (manool, sclareol, and macrocyclic cembrene) to the apoplast and function in plant chemical defense but was not found to transport eucalyptol, a monoterpene in tobacco BY2 cells (Crouzet et al. 2013). In A. annua L., (annual wormwood), artemisinin, a unique sesquiterpene lactone is primarily produced in glandular trichomes and gets accumulated within the subcuticular space of the glandular secretory trichomes, and it is apparent that artemisinin itself or its immediate precursors are exported out of the apical cells (Duke 1994; Tellez et al. 1999). Thus, it is enthralling to contemplate that a few G subfamily ABC transporters reside on the plasma membrane of glandular secretory trichome cells and could be involved in the transport of artemisinin. A few of these ABC transporters identifed from A. annua have been proposed to function in DHAA (dihydroartemisinic acid) transport from the apical cells to the subcuticular space of glandular trichomes, where DHAA is oxidized to produce artemisinin (Zhang et al. 2008). Recently studies in A. annua also demonstrated that a plasma membrane-localized trichome specifc PDR transporter, AaPDR3 is involved in the transport of sesquiterpene $\beta$ -caryophyllene (Fu et al. 2017).

Apocarotenoids, which are carotenoid derivatives, play several critical roles in the metabolism of a plant, such as the attraction of pollinators, defense against pathogenic attacks, herbivory, and protection against photo-oxidative stresses. These compounds can get transported and accumulated at diferent locations within or outside the plant cell. The current information about the membrane transportation of apocarotenoids is still limited. Recently, an ABCC subfamily of transporters has been identifed to be involved in the vacuolar transport of crocins in the stigmas of safron (Crocus sativus) using the transportomic approach. The ABC transporter, CsABCC4 was reported to be localized on tonoplast, and its heterologous expression in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves showed enhanced crocin accumulation (Demurtas et al. 2019).


## Transport of glucosinolates


Glucosinolates constitute a diverse group of amino acidderived sulfur and nitrogen-containing compounds present in the Brassicaceae family. Glucosinolates and thioglucosidases (myrosinases) are stored usually at diferent sub-cellular locations. In plants, upon tissue disruption resulting from wounding or insect/pathogen attack, the glucosinolates are released at the site of damage and become hydrolyzed by myrosinase. The hydrolysis catalyzed by the enzyme myrosinase results in isothiocyanates, nitriles, and thiocyanate production. These degradation products serve as deterrents, attractants, and plant defense chemicals against insects, herbivores and certain microbial pathogens (Halkier and Gershenzon 2006). Therefore, the biosynthesis and precise sequestration of glucosinolates at each developmental stage are vital for the ecological interactions of the plants. In Arabidopsis, it has been documented that glucosinolates accumulate within the vacuoles of both root cortex cells and epidermis leaf margins (Andersen et al. 2013; Madsen et al. 2014). These active compounds are found to be transported between the adjacent cells or allocated to distant organs (Andersen et al. 2013; Chen et al. 2001; Madsen et al. 2014; Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). Two high-afnity $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -dependent transporters from the nitrate/peptide (NRT/PTR) sub-family, namely GTR1 and GTR2 have been demonstrated to function as glucosinolate specifc transporters in Arabidopsis. The analysis of gtr1 and gtr2 double mutants showed no accumulation of any glucosinolates in sink tissues, whereas in source tissues such as leaves, glucosinolates were found to be over-accumulated by many folds indicating their crucial role in the long-distance mode of glucosinolate transport (Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). Thus, these two transporters, GTR1 and GTR2, have been proposed to regulate glucosinolate transport from the apoplasm into the phloem in leaves. In addition to glucosinolate transport, studies showed that GTR1 transporter also functions in jasmonoyl-isoleucine and gibberellins transport when expressed heterologously in oocytes and may function in stamen development of Arabidopsis by mediating the supply of gibberellins (Saito et al. 2015). These studies highlight that GTR1, a known glucosinolate transporter, is multifunctional and transports structurally distinct ligands.


## Transport of plant volatiles


A plethora of chemically diverse volatile molecules synthesized by plants function in plant defense, plant-to-plant communication, pollination, allelopathy, and recently, these have been implicated in inter-organ communication and signaling (Boachon et al. 2019; Dudareva et al. 2006; Pichersky and Gershenzon 2002). Volatile compounds are low molecular weight lipophilic molecules having high vapor pressure at ambient temperature and may include phenylpropanoids, terpenoids, fatty acid derivatives, and benzenoids. Earlier it was presumed that volatile compounds are difused out of plant cells through simple difusion (Adebesin et al. 2017; Schuman et al. 2016; Widhalm et al. 2015). However, it was predicted by modeling that emission of volatile compounds exclusively by difusion could result in the accumulation of volatile compounds at toxic levels within the membranes themselves (Widhalm et al. 2015). In the recent past, a transporter from ABC family has been functionally characterized in Petunia hybrida, and it was demonstrated that PhABCG1 actively function in the efux of benzenoid volatile molecules across the cell membrane in petunia fowers (Adebesin et al. 2017). To understand whether PhABCG1 is involved in volatile compound emission, transgenic petunia lines with downregulation of PhABCG1 transporter were generated using interference (RNAi) approach with expression driven by petal-specifc linalool synthase promoter. These downregulated transgenic lines displayed signifcantly decreased volatile compound emission. Also, the transport activity of PhABCG1 protein in the transport of two benzenoid volatile compounds, methyl benzoate and benzyl alcohol in petunia fowers, was demonstrated by expressing it in tobacco BY-2 cells, and it was found that PhABCG1 actively efux out the radiolabeled forms of these volatile compounds. This study provides substantial evidence about the involvement of an active membrane transport system in plant volatile emission (Adebesin et al. 2017). The aromatic plants are reservoirs of these volatile compounds, and it would be fascinating to study whether similar transporters function in the transportation of their volatile compounds. Such studies will help elucidate the membrane transport system in the plant volatile emission, allowing tighter controls on volatile emission rates, which may play a pivotal role in plant volatile communication systems with a higher degree of precision.


## Transporters for metabolic engineering of secondary metabolites


Secondary metabolites ofer advantages to plants under testing environmental conditions such as biotic and abiotic stresses and, therefore, can afect plant survival and productivity (Isah 2019). The role of plant secondary metabolites as insect deterrents is well documented, and thus these compounds confer protection against insect pests (Douglas 2018; Misra et al. 2010; Treutter 2005). In addition, certain secondary metabolites such as favonoid have been implicated in regulation of plant growth (Peer and Murphy 2007). Thus, the modifcation of their content is a promising approach for the development of stress tolerant crop plants. Owing to their interesting pharmacological activities, several of them have been in use as phytomedicines and nutraceuticals. The studies have suggested that the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites is tightly regulated by various temporal and spatial cues including, environmental factors (Tholl and Lee 2011; Yang et al. 2012). The tight regulation of secondary metabolite biosynthesis limits their production and yield in plant tissues. In addition, the biosynthesis of certain highvalue plant natural products, for example, artemisnin, camptothecin, taxol, vinblastine and vincristine is restricted to a specifc plant species or taxonomic group. In view of the role of plant secondary metabolites in plant biology as well as their use as phytopharmaceuticals and aroma compounds, there has been growing interest to modify the biosynthesis of secondary metabolites in plants through the intervention of tools of genetic engineering (O’Connor 2015). To this end, the genetic manipulation of structural and regulatory genes has been instrumental in modulating the content of the secondary metabolites in plants.

The membrane transporters, which play a crucial role in the trafcking of secondary metabolites and their precursors, constitute an important component in molecular machinery involved in the biosynthesis and accumulation of secondary metabolites. The expression of the transporter genes might be tightly regulated by various temporal and spatial cues for fne-tuning of their transport under diverse sets of growth conditions. For obvious reasons, membrane transporters also appear to be promising targets for metabolic engineering program aiming at the development of novel plant genotypes with modifed content of the targeted plant secondary metabolite. Thus, deciphering and unveiling the transport mechanism of these metabolites in plant cells holds great promise in devising strategies to perturb channeling of intermediates and end-products and, thereby improving the yield of the concerned metabolite. Eforts have been made for transporter engineering to enhance the heterologous production of certain highly economically important secondary metabolites (Moses et al. 2013). In A. annua L., the artemisinin biosynthesis is exclusively limited to the glandular trichomes. The blocking of the competitive metabolic steps was demonstrated to improve the content of artemisinin in A. annua (Lv et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2009). A PDR type transporter gene, namely AaPDR3 identifed in the A. annua, was reported to be preferably expressed in T-shape trichomes. Functional analysis revealed that knockdown of AaPDR3 by RNAi strategy led to increased artemisinin and decreased $\beta$ -caryophyllene contents in transgenic plants (Fu et al. 2017). As AaPDR3 transporter was implicated in the transport of $\beta$ -caryophyllene, it was presumed that the altered channelling of farnesyl diphosphate (FPP), a common substrate for sesquiterpenoids might be responsible for enhanced accumulation of artemisinin in AaPDR3 silenced lines. Such observations demonstrate the potential utility of manipulation of transporter genes in the area of metabolic engineering of secondary metabolites. Another example that envisaged the improved production of valuable metabolites in plants by transporter engineering is concerned with catharanthine, an anticancer drug component found in C. roseus. As mentioned in the earlier part of the review, in the recent past, an ABCG family of transporter, CrTPT2 from C. roseus, has been characterized as the transporter of catharanthine, a terpene indole alkaloid. This transporter performs the function of the efux of catharanthine from epidermal cells to the surface of the leaf (Yu and De Luca 2013). Functional studies have shown that knockdown of CrTPT2 led to the decreased level of catharanthine at the leaf surface, whereas in the internal leaf cells, the catharanthine level was found to be increased, which in turn leads to an enhanced level of catharanthine–vindoline dimers in the leaf. In addition to the examples mentioned above, there are several other reports, where transporter engineering has been successfully explored in enhancing the production of important compounds in heterologous hosts. For example, constitutive co-expression of genes encoding carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase $( C s C C D 2 )$ and crocin transporter led to enhanced crocin accumulation in N. benthamiana (Demurtas et al. 2019). The transport mechanism can also be harnessed during metabolic engineering of secondary metabolites in cultured plant cells, where specifc transporters can be expressed to channel the secondary metabolite(s) in the media or other defned sub-cellular locations.

Apart from the plants, the microbes have been demonstrated to be promising systems for metabolic engineering of high-value secondary metabolites (Dziggel et al. 2017; Pyne et al. 2019). Several successful attempts, involving synthetic biology tools have been made to engineer the biosynthetic pathways of several important classes of plant natural products in microbial hosts. One such paradigmatic example of engineering plant biosynthetic pathways is the production of artemsinic acid, a precursor of antimalarial terpenoid drug, in $E$ . coli and yeast (Paddon et al. 2013; Tsuruta et al. 2009). Metabolic engineering of benzylisoqunioline alkaloids has also been successfully carried out in the yeast system (Bourgeois et al. 2018; Pyne et al. 2016). To this end, recently, complete biosynthetic pathway leading to the cannabinoid biosynthesis has been introduced in yeast (Luo et al. 2019). Apart from these, the pathways for the biosynthesis of other classes of secondary metabolites such as favonoids have been engineered in microbial hosts (Lehka et al. 2017). The accumulation of plant secondary metabolites in microbial cells at critical levels could be toxic to the host cell itself, and it can hamper cell growth and afect the fnal yield of plant natural product. Thus, engineering suitable transporters from plants and microbes, mediating sequestration of secondary metabolites, can be a suitable approach for the efcient production of economically valuable natural products in microbial hosts (Liu et al. 2017). For example, over-expression of an ABC transporter, namely SNQ2 in engineered S. cerevisiae resulted in the increased production of a stilbenoid, resveratrol (Katz et al. 2011). Thus, the improved knowledge of transporters involved in the transport of diferent types of plant secondary metabolites, will pave the way towards establishing efective biotechnological interventions for the improved production of highvalue plant-based molecules in microbial system.


## Concluding remarks and future outlook


In the last decade, the research on the transporters of plant secondary metabolites has made major strides. The studies suggested that transporter proteins belonging to diverse families, namely ABC, MATE, PUP, and NRT are concerned with the transportation of a huge repertoire of plant secondary metabolites. In line with the enormous number of phytochemicals, the gene families of transporters have considerably expanded in plants. The studies have also unveiled that the transporter proteins exhibit considerable specifcities to a particular chemical backbone. Despite the accumulating knowledge in the feld; however, there are still some major gaps in our understanding of plant secondary metabolite transport. The transport mechanism of several other secondary metabolites of pivotal medicinal signifcance, such as artemisinin, cannabinoids, glycyrrhizin, camptothecin, etc. remains elusive so far. One of the major hurdles towards the functional characterization of transporters for a particular metabolite is the presence of a huge number of transporter genes in a plant genome. The tissue-specifc and condition-specifc gene expression data provides opportunities to fsh out the complete repertoire of the transporter genes in the plant species under question (Fig. 2). The bioinformatic analysis for identifcation of transporter genes displaying tight co-expression with the structural genes involved in the biosynthesis of secondary metabolite coupled with metabolomics should be useful in fltering out a subset of candidate genes out of a large number of transporter genes in a plant genome. The candidate genes, thus fltered, can be studied for their potential substrates using protein structural biology. Taken together, these combined approaches might be instrumental in the identifcation of a set of candidate transporter genes, which can be further confrmed for their functional attributes using in vitro transport assay and transgenesis. To this end, recent advancements in techniques for in vivo substrate visualization should also be vital. These fndings can provide new profound insights to decipher and disentangle the entire route of the transport mechanism of many valuable molecules in plants. Thus, functionally characterized transporters can be selected as potential targets for targeted metabolic engineering of economically important plant secondary metabolites. Altogether a better understanding of secondary metabolite transport could ofer an attractive and novel system towards developing suitable targeted biotechnological interventions for enhanced production of high-value secondary metabolites in plants and microbial systems. Several pharmaceuticals are known to be transported in the animal system through ABC type transporters, and this mechanism afects their pharmacological outcome. The understanding of the transport function of phytopharmaceutical molecules could provide useful clues about the pharmacology of these compounds in animal system and, therefore, might assist in plant-based drug development.
