In this study, 10 MsMATE proteins predicted to participate in Al detoxification were used to determine the functional and physical relationship through rice and Arabidopsis association model using the STRING software, respectively (Fig. S2). Of these 10 MsMATE proteins, the homologous gene suits the easiest bit score by the way of default. OsFRDL4, at the centre of the network node, is an Al-induced citrate transporter that is involved in Al-induced citrate secretion in rice root cells (Fig. S2A) (Yokosho, Yamaji & Ma, 2011). The Nramp aluminum transporter (NRAT1) encodes a transporter involved in Al uptake from the root tip cell wall into the cell and plays a key function in rice aluminum tolerance (Li et al., 2014; Xia, Yamaji & Ma, 2011). The Al-induced gene STAR1 encodes an ATP-binding protein and a TM domain protein, which are required for Al tolerance (Huang et al., 2009). The OsFRDL4 could potentially interact with at least seven proteins, including (NRAT1 and STAR1), indicating that it plays important role in the regulation Al-induced citrate transporter (Fig. S2A). Furthermore, the dicot plant model of Arabidopsis was further determined (Fig. S2B). Among the 10 MsMATE proteins, MsMATE01, 02, 03, 04, and 05 shared a high similarity to Ferric redictase defective3 (FRD3), which shown to be a citrate efflux transporter, the ectopic expression of FRD3-GFP possessed an enhanced resistance to aluminium in Arabidopsis roots (Durrett, Gassmann & Rogers, 2007). Meanwhile, MsMATE22 shared the highest similarity $( 7 4 \% )$ with AT1G51340, previous studies shown that this protein might be involved in the citrate exudation into the rhizosphere to protect roots from Al toxicity (Liu et al., 2012, 2009).


## Expression profiles of MsMATE genes in different tissues


The expression profiles of all 88 MsMATE genes at six developmental stages, namely, elongating stem internodes (ES), developing flowers, mature leaf, nitrogen fixing nodules, post-elongating stem internodes (PES) and whole root, were analysed using Illumina RNA-seq data (Fig. 4). Depending on the hierarchical clustering, the MsMATE genes have various transcript levels during alfalfa development. Among the 88 MsMATE genes, five (MsMATE 05, 22, 31, 38, and 82) showed an overall coverage among all developmental stages (value ${ > } 1 . 2 7$ ). In contrast, the expression level of 13 MsMATE genes (MsMATE 03, 06, 14, 36, 45, 51, 52, 53, 60, 67, 72, 80, and 83) was relatively low in all tissues (value $< 1 . 2 7$ ) Moreover, among the remaining 70 MsMATE genes, 39, 35, 29, 23, 22, and 14 showed high expression levels (value ${ > } 1 . 2 7$ ) in the mature leaf, developing flowers, nitrogen fixing nodules, ES, whole root, and PES, respectively, implying they may play important roles in the corresponding tissues. Although some MsMATE genes were classified into one subgroup, the distinct tissue expression profiles of these genes in alfalfa showed that they may have exceptional physiological roles. Furthermore, some MsMATE genes had tissue-specific expression, for example, MsMATE 02, 34, and 64 in the developing flowers; MsMATE 01, 25, 26, 46, 62, and 63 in the whole root; and MsMATE 15, 42, 43, 55, 56, 59, 76, 77, and 78 in nitrogen-fixing nodules.


## Expression of the subgroup G1–3 MsMATE genes in response to Al toxicity


As we were interested in the roles of MATE genes involved in Al stress in alfalfa, the expression patterns of 10 MsMATEs that were predicted to be Al detoxification-related based on the sequence similarity were further analysed using qRT-PCR. As shown in Fig. 5, MsMATE05 and MsMATE09 were significantly up-regulated after Al treatment. The expression of MsMATE03, MsMATE07, and MsMATE22 fluctuated across early $( 4 \mathrm { h } )$ , middle $( 8 \mathrm { ~ h } )$ and/or late $( 2 4 \mathrm { ~ h } )$ Al exposure time points. Among these five up-regulated MsMATE genes, MsMATE09 has the highest expression level, nearly up-regulated 18-fold at time point $^ { 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ compared with control. In contrast, the expression of the five remaining genes (MsMATE01, MsMATE02, MsMATE04, MsMATE06, and MsMATE08) was significantly down-regulated after Al treatment.

The multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) protein superfamily includes a large number of transporters involved in transporting cations, organic acids secondary metabolites as well as detoxification of xenobiotic compounds (Yazaki 2005). They have been found to be widely represented in all living organisms from prokaryotes to eukaryotes (Moriyama et al. 2008). Ever since the identification of the first MATE family protein NorM, a sodiummultidrug antiporter conferring resistance to norfloxin in Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Morita et al. 1998, 2000), some putative MATE family transporters have been identified and functionally characterized from different plant species. Although there are about 45 MATE family genes predicted in the rice genome (Wang et al. 2016), only a few of OsMATE family proteins of rice have been characterized for their different roles (Bashir et al. 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2011a, b; Tiwari et al. 2014; Yokosho et al. 2009, 2016). The transcript of $\mathrm { L O C \_ O s 0 5 g 4 8 0 4 0 }$ , one of the OsMATE family genes, was reported to be up-regulated upon As-stress for the first time by Norton et al. (2008). We also found its strong positive correlation between the transcript expression and arsenic content in seven different rice genotypes having diverse parentage (Fig. 1), and assigned this $\mathrm { L O C \_ O s 0 g 4 8 0 4 0 }$ as OsMATE2 (GenBank accession number: KC631818.1). We aimed to understand the physiological role of the OsMATE2 in relation to the transport and accumulation of the arsenic (As) through gain-of-function in tobacco system and loss-of-function in native host rice.

The bioinformatics analyses clearly established that the OsMATE2 derived from the newly cloned gene of IR64 rice cultivar is a member of the plant MATE family (Fig. 2), and predicted to possess 12 transmembrane domains (Supplementary Fig. S1). The derived polypeptide sequence of OsMATE2 also revealed the presence of two conserved amino acids, i.e., E279 and D397 crucial for cation binding and transport (Supplementary Fig. S2). The E279 of OsMATE2 is similar to E255 of NorM (He et al. 2010) and E290 in AtTT12 (Chen et al. 2015), whereas the D397 is similar to D368 of NorMVp (Otsuka et al. 2005). Although the precise structure–function relationship of plant MATE family proteins are yet to be validated, the presence of E279 and D397 in OsMATE2 polypeptide indicates the possible involvement in cation binding and transport across membranes. MATE proteins are ubiquitous in plant kingdom and are present in multiple copies in plant genome without comprehensive sequence information. Therefore, the publicly available database was searched for MATE family proteins from different plant groups, which have been functionally characterized to have defined physiological roles and a phylogenetic tree was constructed (Fig. 2b). The phylogenetic tree clearly distributed the representative MATE family members in five different clusters based on functionality. The OsMATE2 was found to be grouped with toxin exporter DTX1, DTX14 and ALF5 of Arabidopsis along with the nicotine transporter JAT1 of tobacco in the second clade. Since, the substrate specificity of transporter proteins is usually associated with phylogeny, the phylogenetic analysis suggested that the OsMATE2 might be involved in the transport of either secondary metabolites or toxic ions, or detoxification of xenobiotics in rice plant. The hypothesis is strengthened by the previous findings, which indicated that the MATE family members of the same subfamily demonstrate same or similar cellular functions, whereas the members of dissimilar subfamily show different functions (Wang et al. 2016).

Very recently, the crystal structure of an A. thaliana MATE family member, AtDTX14 was solved that provided significant information regarding the molecular functioning of the MATE transporter proteins (Miyauchi et al. 2017). Interestingly, our analysis not only showed that AtDX14 and OsMATE2 occupy the same clade in the phylogenetic tree (Fig. 2b); but also the comparison of amino acid sequences revealed that OsMATE2 and AtDTX14 share a very high similarity and identity values (Supplementary Table 1). Thus, to gain an insight into the function of OsMATE2, a homology model using the AtDTX14 crystal structure as template was prepared (Supplementary Fig. S4A). The in silico analysis of the generated model indicated the presence of a salt bridge formation between the Glu 103 (TM2) and Arg 408 (TM10) (Supplementary Fig. S4B, C), implying the interaction between TM2 and TM8 leading to closure of the internal gate similar to what is seen in AtDTX14 (Miyauchi et al. 2017). This hypothesis is further strengthened by the presence of the Gly residues in the TM2 (Gly112) and TM8 (Gly 334) domains, which can act as the sites for hydrophobic interactions, resulting in tight closure of the internal gate. Furthermore, at the extracellular site, an external gate (Supplementary Fig. S4D, E) composed of the residue pairs Asp 153 and Asn 295, and Ala 81 & Ser 304 along with the Gly 291, which may contribute to the inward open structure similar to AtDTX14 (Miyauchi et al. 2017). Additionally, like AtDTX14, a hydrogen bonding network involving Glu 277, Asp 397, Asn 420 and Gln 457 around the important hinge region Cys 277 is predicted. The presence of this hydrogen bonding region in the C-lobe around the hinge region is highly conserved in the eukaryotic MATE family, signifying its possible importance in the transport process (Miyauchi et al. 2017).

The qRT-PCR based expression analysis of OsMATE2 in different tissues of rice plant upon exogenous As treatment indicated the up-regulation of OsMATE2 expression in both leaves and seeds but down-regulation in roots of indica rice cultivar IR64 (Fig. 2c). However, publicly available microarray data indicate toward consistent up-regulation of OsMATE2 transcript in both root and shoot tissues of indica rice cultivar ensuing As stress (Supplementary Fig. S6). This change in the expression pattern of OsMATE2 may be due to the high concentration (1 ppm) of As used during the microarray experiment. Nevertheless, the expression profile of OsMATE2 clearly suggests that this transporter plays role in both vegetative and reproductive parts of rice plant.

Therefore, to investigate the functional role of OsMATE2 during As stress, heterologous gene expression in tobacco and endogenous gene silencing in rice was carried out in the present work. Transgenic tobacco plant lines were developed through Agrobacterium-mediated transformation with the OsMATE2 gene expression construct (Fig.  3a). The OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco plantlets with intact roots when grown under As stress displayed reduced root growth but improved shoot proliferation (Fig. 4ai) as evident from the increase in the fresh weight (Fig. 4aii) along with the dry weight (Fig. 4aiii), and supported by SPAD values compared to the untransformed control (Fig. 4av). Moreover, the observation of improved fitness in absence of As stress in the transgenic tobacco plants in comparison to the control plants indicated the involvement of OsMATE2 in plant developmental process. Similar to our observations, constitutive overexpression of OsMATE2 in Arabidopsis has also been shown to amend variation in vegetative tissues, including the leaf size and altered pattern of rosette development (Tiwari et al. 2014). Both the findings highlight the importance and involvement of OsMATE2 in the growth and developmental processes of plants. Further, the AAS analysis indicated toward the higher As content in the roots (Fig. 4b) coupled with the reduced As content in the shoots (Fig. 4c) of OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco lines compared with the untransformed control plants. The enhanced effect of As toxicity on the OsMATE2- expressing transgenic tobacco lines was further validated by staining the roots with the trypan blue dye (Fig. 5a) and Hoechst-PI double stains (Fig. 5b, c), which displayed the presence of a higher proportion of non-viable cells in the root tissues compared to the untransformed control plants following exposure to As. Moreover, histochemical staining for the detection of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ , the major ROS molecule using DAB also showed the presence of enhanced production of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ (Fig. 5d), which could be responsible for higher ROS damage and decreased cell viability in the transgenic roots. Since, prolonged exposure to As is known to cause cellular death due to oxidative stress damages (Finnegan and Chen 2012), the results point to the important role played by OsMATE2 in maintaining cellular homeostasis and sensitivity toward As. The constitutive expression of OsMATE2 in tobacco demonstrated interference of the root-to-shoot translocation of arsenic upon As stress by restricting the accumulation of As in roots.

Since the transgenic tobacco seedlings overexpressing OsMATE2 documented oxidative stress damage principally in the roots following As treatment, we wanted to check whether the uptake of As leads to increased oxidative stress in de-rooted plants as well. The aim of this experiment was to investigate the co-regulation of As uptake and oxidative stress response in OsMATE2 overexpressed transgenic plants. Following this, transgenic plants grown on MS media after de-rooting exhibited enhanced arsenic sensitivity and oxidative damage compared to the control plants as evident by the reduced growth of root, shoot and biomass weight (Fig. 6a). The transgenic tobacco plants also demonstrated lesser cell membrane stability, higher electrolyte leakage, higher MDA content (Fig. 6b) and increased APS toxicity (Fig. 6c) following As stress, than the untransformed control plants. The increased production of ROS and subsequent imbalance of cellular redox system resulting in oxidative damage to membrane lipids have been well documented (Srivastava et al. 2009; Hartley-Whitaker et al. 2001). After de-rooting the shoots of OsMATE2-expressing tobacco plants clearly demonstrated greater oxidative stress damage compared to the control tobacco plants under As stress. Previous reports have documented that upon exposure to exogenous As, most plants have the ability to preserve the majority of the As in the roots that act as the first exposed plant tissue toward As, thereby critically inhibiting the proliferation and initiation of roots (Finnegan and Chen 2012). Moreover, the reduction in As transfer coefficient of the transgenic tobacco plants (Table 2) in the present study clearly indicates the functional role of OsMATE2 in accumulation of As. In the presence of roots, the oxidative damage was largely confined in the root system due to increased accumulation of As in roots but because of the reduced As accumulation in shoots, lesser oxidative stress damage was observed in the shoot part of OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco in comparison to the untransformed control (Fig. 5). However, the experiment conducted with de-rooted plants, i.e., in the absence of root system documented that the As accumulated in the shoot system of the OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco and resulted in significant oxidative damages of shoots (Fig. 6). Together, these findings clearly indicate the disruption of As transfer coefficient from root to shoot due to constitutive OsMATE2 overexpression in transgenic tobacco plants.

The MATE family members being primarily efflux transporters, this increased accumulation of As in the roots of the OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco plants was interesting. However, in a recent study of overexpressing the OsMATE2 in Arabidopsis, a prominent sensitivity toward the $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ in transgenic Arabidopsis plants was observed, which was attributed to the flavonoid sequestration ability of this protein leading to the imbalance of cellular flavonoids resulting in perturbation of ROS scavenging activity and As(V) sensitivity (Tiwari et al. 2014). Furthermore, the altered flavonoid content was in turn associated with the increased glutathione-S-transferases (GSTs) levels in the transgenic plants (Tiwari et al. 2014). Since, the GSTs are known to catalyse the conjugation of the reduced glutathione (GSH) to xenobiotic substrates including As (Zhao et  al. 2009) for their detoxification, we anticipate that this increased cellular level of GSTs in turn could lead to the enhanced cellular accumulation of As in the roots of OsMATE2-expressing transgenic tobacco plants. Moreover, we observed that the overexpression of OsMATE2 failed to increase the As accumulation in transgenic tobacco shoots, presumably due to the complexation of As with GSHs in roots, thereby disturbing the transport of As from roots to shoots.

Our findings that the OsMATE2 expression is up-regulated in leaf and seed tissues of rice plant, and the OsMATE2 is functionally involved in the accumulation of As in transgenic tobacco lines foster us to adopt transgenic strategy for the reduced accumulation of As in rice grains through down-regulation of OsMATE2 in grain-specific manner. It is worthy to mention here that the histological GUS staining based analysis of the OsMATE2 promoter in Arabidopsis indicated its expression in the seedling and the flowering stages, including a strong activity at the early stage of embryo and seed development (Tiwari et al. 2014). Therefore, the reported information and our observations together justify the selection of a seedspecific promoter, instead of a constitutive promoter, to drive the hpOsMATE2 gene cassette. Hence in the present study, the seed-specific silencing of OsMATE2 gene was carried out using the endosperm-specific glutelin C (GluC) promoter of rice (Das et al. 2017). Analysis of the results demonstrated that the hpRNA construct (Fig. 7a) was capable of down-regulating the OsMATE2 transcript in the developing seed tissues of the transgenic rice lines (Fig. 7c, d). The transgenic rice plants accumulated reduced level (upto $\sim 4 8 \%$ ) of As in the grains (Fig. 7e), compared to the untransformed control. However, the reduction of only ${ \sim } 4 8 \%$ of As content in the grains of transgenic rice lines clearly indicated the involvement of additional factors in the cellular accumulation of As in rice plant. This hypothesis is further strengthened by the observation in the transgenic line hpL2, where in spite of $\sim 3 8 \%$ reduction of OsMATE2 expression, it failed to reduce the As accumulation in the grain. Interestingly, the grains of the OsMATE2 downregulated transgenic rice plants displayed a significant reduction in grain size (Fig. 8a; Table 3) and early flowering and prematurity (Fig. 8b; Table 4) compared to the untransformed control rice plants without any yield compromise when grown on either As treated or untreated soil. Since the exact reason behind these off-target phenotypes due to down-regulation of OsMATE2 gene is unknown, further insights need to be generated to explain the molecular function of this gene in rice plant.
