## The KT/HAK/KUP gene family in tomato


Using the sequence of Arabidopsis and rice KT/HAK/KUP transporters, candidate KT/HAK/KUP transporters were identified in the tomato genome database. Subsequently, redundant sequences were removed according to the chromosome locations, resulting in a total of 19 putative KT/HAK/KUP genes (Table 1). Chromosomal location analyses showed that SlHAK genes were spread over 10 different chromosomes (Table 1; Fig. 1). Chromosome 2, 4, 5, 9, and 12 were found to possess two to four SlHAK genes each, and chromosome 1, 3, 6, 8, and 10 possessed a single SlHAK gene each (Fig. 1).

The $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter domain (k_trans; PF02705) of the KT/HAK/KUP family, found in bacteria, yeast, and plants, is a conserved domain (Gupta et al. 2008). The putative 19 SlHAK genes were further analyzed using SMART (http:// smart.embl-heidelberg.de/) and Pfam (http://pfam.sanger. ac.uk/) to confirm the presence of the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter domain. As shown in Fig. S1, all the predicted SlHAKs contained the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter domain, indicating that putative SlHAK genes belong to the KT/HAK/KUP family. In maize, ZmHAK proteins have been reported to contain several trans-membrane segments (Zhang et al. 2012). Similarly, SlHAKs contained at least eight trans-membrane segments (Table 1). Because of the difference in the optimal $\mathrm { p H }$ for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake, plant KT/HAK/KUP transporters are localized on different membranes, such as the plasma membrane, tonoplast, and chloroplast thylakoid membrane (Senn et al. 2001; Ban˜uelos et al. 2002; Zhang et al. 2012). In the case of tomato, 18 of the 19 SlHAK proteins were predicted to localize on the plasma membrane by PSORT analysis, and SlHAK12 was located on the chloroplast thylakoid membrane (Table 1). This indicates that SlHAKs are membrane transporters.


## Phylogenetic and gene structure analysis of the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family


To gain an insight into the evolution of the KT/HAK/KUP family in tomato, amino acid sequences of the putative KT/ HAK/KUP proteins in tomato were compared with those in Arabidopsis and rice KT/HAK/KUP proteins. A phylogenetic tree was constructed using the neighbor-joining method. As shown in Fig. S2, phylogenetic tree analysis clearly defined four major groups (I, II, III, and IV). Group II constituted the largest clade containing eight tomato KT/ HAK/KUP proteins, and group III formed the second largest clade containing six tomato KT/HAK/KUP proteins (Fig. 2a). Four rice KT/HAK/KUP proteins belonged to group IV, which was absent in tomato and Arabidopsis genomes (Fig. S2; Gupta et al. 2008). Most of the KT/ HAK/KUP transporters in group I facilitate high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake (Ahn et al. 2004; Gierth et al. 2005; Qi et al. 2008), whereas transporters in group II might play a role in low-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport complementing potassium channels (Senn et al. 2001; Garciadeblas et al. 2002; Gupta et al. 2008), suggesting that the putative tomato KT/HAK/ KUP transporters in group I and II might have functions similar to other plant KT/HAK/KUP transporters.

However, the same phylogenetic clustering does not necessarily mean the same subcellular localization. In group II, AtKUP4 (tonoplast), OsHAK2 (plasma membrane),

OsHAK3 (plasma membrane), OsHAK7 (microbody), OsHAK14 (mitochondrial inner membrane), OsHAK15 (chloroplast thylakoid membrane), and tomato HAKs (plasma membrane; Table 1) were found to have different subcellular localizations (Jaquinod et al. 2007; Gupta et al. 2008). This indicates that these proteins have different cytological functions, although sequence similarity shows that they belong to the same phylogenetic group.

To gain further insight into the structural diversity of tomato HAK genes, we compared the exon/intron organization in the coding sequencing of each SlHAK gene. The coding sequences of all the SlHAKs are disrupted by seven to eleven introns, and most of SlHAK genes comprise eight to nine exons (Fig. 2b). This suggests that the gene structure in tomato is more convergent than that in rice and maize HAK genes, which contain one to nine and two to nine introns, respectively (Gupta et al. 2008; Zhang et al. 2012).

To further identify the conserved motifs in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family, we used the Multiple EM for Motif Elicitation (MEME) program (Bailey et al. 2006). As shown in Fig. 2c, we found a total of 3 conserved motifs, with 50, 45 and 44 amino acids, respectively. Among these, 3 motifs were shared by most tomato KT/HAK/KUP proteins except SlHAK14. In addition, motif 1 appeared twice in SlHAK6, whereas motif 3 was found twice in SlHAK7, 8, and 10 (Fig. 2c).


## Evolutionary patterns and exon structure of SlHAKs


Segmental duplication, tandem duplication, and transposition events, including retroposition and replicative transposition, have been suggested as the main reasons for gene family expansion (Kong et al. 2007). In addition, two paralogs located on the tandem duplicate chromosomal segment are likely to be the result of single-gene duplication (Olinski et al. 2006). Chromosomal localization analysis and amino acid sequence similarity $( > 7 5 ~ \% )$ of the KT/HAK/KUP family in tomato showed that two pairs of SlHAK genes (SlHAK12/13/14 and SlHAK16/17), which lie close together on the same chromosome and display high sequence similarity, are most likely the result of tandem duplication (Fig. 1). Because most plants are diploidized polyploids and retain numerous duplicated chromosomal blocks within their genomes, segmental duplication occurs frequently in plants (Cannon et al. 2004; Cai et al. 2013). In poplar, segmental duplication together with tandem duplication has been identified to play a leading role in the expansion of the KT/HAK/KUP family (He et al. 2012). We downloaded the within-genome duplication information of tomato from the Plant Genome Duplication Database (PGDD; http://chibba.agtec.uga.edu/ duplication/). Five pairs of segmental duplicated paralogs (SlHAK1/15, SlHAK2/3, SlHAK4/9, SlHAK7/8, and SlHAK11/19) were discovered in 19 tomato KT/HAK/ KUP genes (Fig. 3), indicating that segmental and tandem duplication events are important factors governing the expansion of the KT/HAK/KUP family in tomato.

To investigate the evolutionary dates of the segmental duplication events, the PAML software was used to estimate Ks (the number of synonymous substitutions per synonymous site) and Ka (the number of nonsynonymous (amino acid) substitutions per nonsynonymous site) distances, as well as the Ka/Ks ratio. Although SlHAK4/9 was expected to be the result of a segmental duplication event, this gene pair was discarded to avoid saturation effects as described by Wang et al. (2013). Ks in segmental duplication in SlHAK genes ranged from 0.4996 to 0.8738, dating the duplication event to have occurred between 35.89 million years ago (Mya) to 62.77 Mya (Table 2).

Segmental duplications in KT/HAK/KUP genes in poplar (clock-like rate $= 9 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ ; Lynch and Conery 2000) occurred between 10.2 Mya $\mathrm { { ( K s = 0 . 1 8 5 7 } }$ ) and $1 8 . 4 ~ \mathrm { M y a }$ $\mathrm { { K s } } = 0 . 3 3 4 8$ ) (He et al. 2012), indicating that the segmental expansion in the poplar KT/HAK/KUP family can be dated to recent duplication events than the segmental expansion in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family.

In the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family, the ${ \mathrm { K a } } / { \mathrm { K } } s$ ratio of the four segmental duplication pairs was lower than 1, suggesting that these segmental duplication pairs were subjected to purifying selection similar to the poplar KT/HAK/KUP family (He et al. 2012). In order to infer whether duplicated genes evolve at the same rate, the Tajima relative rate test (Tajima 1993) was conducted with amino acid substitutions on pairs of SlHAK paralogs by using the orthologous sequence from Arabidopsis or rice KT/HAK/KUP genes as an outgroup. The results of this analysis indicate that all segmental duplicated pairs in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family evolved at a similar rate (Table 3).

Analysis of the exonic structures determines the conserved gene structure with the same number of nucleotides in the exons and the conserved intron phases, which are indicative of the genetic relatedness of the studied genes (von Schantz et al. 2006). As shown in Fig. 4, exon colored red was conserved in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family. At least four conserved exons were observed in the tandem or segmental duplicated SlHAK pairs. In addition, the same intron phases are shared by each duplicated SlHAK pair. The first intron from the SlHAK gene is a phase 0 intron, which refers to the splicing after the first nucleotide of the codon (Hyun et al. 2011), whereas the second intron is a phase 1 intron that interrupts the codons between the first and second nucleotides (Fig. 4). Taken together, these indicate a common ancestral relationship between each duplicated pair.


## In-silico expression analysis of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes


To characterize the general features of the promoter regions of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes, the $- 1 . 0 \ \mathrm { k b }$ sequences upstream from the start site of genes were used to search against known cis-elements in the PLACE database (http:// www.dna.affrc.go.jp/PLACE/). In the list of motif, five of these cis-regulatory elements, WBOXNTERF3, ARR1AT, WRKY71OS, ACGTATERD1, and GT1CONSENSUS, were found in most of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes. These elements are involved in hormone- and environment stress-response (Terzaghi and Cashmore 1995; Sakai et al. 2000; Simpson et al. 2003; Nishiuchi et al. 2004; Jo and Hyun 2011), indicating that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake might be regulated with hormone and stress response.

To estimate the expression level for each gene, we conducted an analysis in the available Tomato Functional

Genomic database (RNA-seq). Most of SlHAKs, except SlHAK11, 12, and 13, were expressed in all tissues. The expression of SlHAK11, 12, and 13 was determined in anthesis flowers and fruits (10DPA and 20DPA) but not in cotyledons, hypocotyl, whole root, and young leaves (Table 4). ## Phylogenetic and conserved motif analysis of pear ABC proteins


To investigate the evolutionary relationships of ABC transporters, we constructed a neighbor joining phylogenetic tree in MAGA 7.0 using the full-length protein sequences of 177 PbrABCs from pear and 144 AtABCs from Arabidopsis. According to the phylogenetic tree (Fig.  1), the ABC transporters from pear and arabidopsis were divided into seven major groups based on their similarities and relationship with 130 Arabidopsis members. ABCE includes 9 members, ABCF has 8 members, and ABCG stands out as the most substantial subfamily with 80 members.

To unveil the diversifcation among pear ABC genes more efectively, we conducted an analysis of their conserved motifs. We employed the MEME online tool to predict the composition of conserved motifs within the PbrABCs (Fig. 2). Te number of motifs ranged from 3 to 19. Notably, Motif 1, representing the ABC domain, was detected in all PbrABCs. Te PbrABC proteins within each group exhibited signifcant similarity among orthologous members but displayed notable distinctions from members in the other groups, suggesting a divergent evolution from a shared ancestor or their origin from gene duplication events.


## Chromosomal distribution and collinearity analysis of PbrABC genes


Based on the genomic positions of 177 pear ABC genes on pear chromosomes, we assessed the chromosomal distribution of the PbrABC gene family (Fig. 3). Te fndings reveal that among these 177 PbrABC genes, 148 PbrABC genes are heterogeneously distributed across

17 chromosomes, displaying varying quantities on each chromosome. Notably, chromosome 11 emerges as the chromosome harboring the highest number of PbrABC genes, boasting a total of 16 members. Conversely, chromosome 4 hosts the fewest members, containing only 2 PbrABC genes. Te remaining chromosomes exhibit distinct numbers of PbrABC gene members, such as chromosome 1 (4 members), chromosome 2 (6 members), chromosome 3 (15 members), chromosome 5 (8 members), chromosome 6 (7 members), chromosome 7 (6 members), chromosome 8 (4 members), chromosome 9 (12 members), chromosome 10 (15 members), chromosome 12 (13 members), chromosome 13 (5 members), chromosome 14 (7 members), chromosome 15 (7 members), chromosome 16 (7 members), and chromosome 17 (12 members). Tis comprehensive distribution analysis underscores the chromosomal variations in the abundance of PbrABC genes across the pear genome. Moreover, it’s intriguing to note that numerous PbrABC genes are arranged into clusters of diferent sizes, signifying occurrences of gene duplication during the evolutionary journey of PbrABC genes. Te mechanisms potentially contributing to gene expansion during evolution encompass whole-genome duplication, tandem repeats, and dispersed duplication [32]. Tese mechanisms are pivotal in enabling functional diversifcation and gene separation. Scrutinizing the patterns of gene duplication is imperative for comprehending the evolution of gene families.

To reveal the expansion mechanisms of PbrABC genes within the pear genome, we conducted an analysis of gene duplication patterns. Te results indicate that in the pear genome, 177 PbrABC genes partake in 84 $( 4 7 \% )$ WGD duplications and 64 $( 3 6 \% )$ dispersed duplications (Fig. S1), hinting at WGD and dispersed duplication as the predominant driving force behind the expansion of the ABC family in pear. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that chromosomes 3, 10, 11, 12 and 17 exhibit the highest repetition rates, which likely account for the increased abundance of PbrABC genes on these chromosomes. Identifying homologous genes is important for understanding the evolutionary history of gene families. To delve deeper into the origins and evolutionary relationships of PbrABC genes in pear, we conducted a collinearity analysis (Fig. 3). Te outcomes unveil 48 pairs of collinear genes among PbrABC genes in the pear genome, with a heightened concentration of ABC homologous genes identifed on pear chromosome 11. Consequently, this analysis ofers valuable insights into the evolution and expansion of the pear ABC gene family, tailored to the linguistic standards of botanists and biologists.


## Analysis of cis‑acting elements in the promoter region of pear ABC gene family


Cis-regulatory elements (CREs) are a family of noncoding DNA molecules that infuence the transcription of neighboring genes, thereby controlling gene expression during diferent developmental stages [33, 34]. To gain a deeper understanding of the transcriptional regulation mechanisms of PbrABC genes, we characterized cis-regulatory elements within the $2 0 0 0 \mathsf { b p }$ upstream region of transcription start sites using the PlantCARE and PLACE databases (Fig.  4). Our results reveal that these identifed cis-regulatory elements can be categorized into four primary functional groups: light response, hormone response, developmental regulation, and stress response. Notably, all 177 PbrABC genes contain at least one hormone-responsive element, including auxin and gibberellin-responsive elements. Furthermore, 150 cisregulatory elements are associated with responses to abscisic acid, methyl jasmonate, ethylene, and salicylic acid, highlighting the crucial role of the PbrABC gene family in complex hormone regulatory networks. In addition, the promoter sequences of some PbrABC genes also harbor elements related to both biotic and abiotic stress responses, including defense elements (rich in AT and TC repeats), drought-responsive elements (MBS), coldresponsive elements (DRE and LTR), and anaerobic stress elements (ARE). Tis suggests potential functions of PbrABC genes in biological and abiotic stress responses. Tese fndings enhance our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of PbrABC genes, particularly their roles in plant growth and stress responses.

Te gene expression patterns can provide direction and strategies for predicting gene biological functions. Forty-nine PbrABC genes show high expression in petals, implying their potential role in the development of foral organs.


## Expression analysis of PbrABCs in response to drought and salt stress


Te ABC transporters have been reported to be widely involved in response to abiotic stress [20, 29, 31]. To investigate the expression patterns of the pear ABC transporters in response to abiotic stress, we conducted an analysis of expression changes in pear leaf tissues under drought and salt stress, based on the RNA-Seq data. As shown in Fig. 6, for salt stress, 82 of 177 PbrABC genes were sensitive to salt stress, the majority of which exhibited diferent expression profles at diferent stages of salt treatment. For example, 21 PbrABC genes tended to be observably up-regulated at $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ and decreased at $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ . Te qRT–PCR results generally confrmed the RNA-seq results. The present study provided new insights into the regulation of anthocyanin biosynthesis by light. Effects of light on anthocyanin biosynthesis and compartment in grape berry skin and flesh were studied by artificial removal of light from berries of Gamay and its teinturier mutation. Light exclusion decreased anthocyanin concentration, which correlated with reduced transcriptional abundance of structural, regulatory and transporter genes. In addition, light exclusion increased the ratio of dihydroxylated/trihydroxylated anthocyanins in accordance with the transcriptional abundance of $F 3 ^ { \prime } H / F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H .$ . The extent of the aforementioned modifications induced by light exclusion varied depending on cultivars and tissues. Sugar and ABA were both slightly reduced by light exclusion in the three colored tissues, but this reduction seems to play a limited role in regulating anthocyanin synthesis between cultivars.

## Berry size and sugar accumulation


Under light-exposed conditions, Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay had similar skin and flesh weights along berry development (Fig. 1a, b). Light exclusion markedly reduced flesh weight of Gamay Fre´aux but had less effect on the flesh weight of Gamay berries (Fig. 1b).

The time-course of sugar accumulation was different between cultivars and was modified by light conditions (Fig. 1c, d). Under light-exposed condition, hexose (glucose $^ +$ fructose) accumulated faster and reached the plateau earlier in Gamay Fre´aux than in Gamay in both skin and flesh. However, the longer duration of sugar accumulation in the flesh of Gamay compensated for its lower accumulation rate, resulting in a higher hexose concentration $\mathrm { 1 3 0 . 9 ~ m g / g }$ FW) at maturity than in Gamay Fre´aux $1 0 1 . 8 ~ \mathrm { m g / g }$ FW). Light exclusion delayed the onset of sugar accumulation by 1 week in both cultivars compared to the light-exposed berries. However, light exclusion induced different effects on the kinetics of sugar accumulation, significantly lowering hexose concentrations at maturity in light-excluded Gamay (64.3 and $3 9 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m g / g \ F W }$ for flesh and skin, respectively), while similar concentrations were found in Gamay Fre´aux (98.7 and $6 7 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m g / g }$ FW for flesh and skin, respectively), compared to lightexposed berries.


## Anthocyanin concentration and composition


For both cultivars, there were significant differences in total anthocyanin amounts and substantial differences in anthocyanin composition between the light-exposed and - excluded berries (Fig. 2). Under light-exposed conditions, total anthocyanins increased rapidly between 2 and

3 weeks after veraison, and then stayed at a steady level in berry skins of Gamay and Gamay Fre´aux as well as berry flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. 2a, b). At maturity, the skins of Gamay Fre´aux had the highest concentration of anthocyanins $1 3 0 6 . 2 \mathrm { \ m g / 1 0 0 \ g \ F W ) }$ , followed by the skins of Gamay $( 9 3 9 . 3 ~ \mathrm { m g } / 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { g } ~ \mathrm { F W } )$ , and both values were more than one order of magnitude higher than anthocyanin concentration in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux $( 4 8 ~ \mathrm { m g / 1 0 0 ~ g }$ FW). Light exclusion strongly decreased anthocyanin accumulation in berry skin and flesh. At maturity, total anthocyanin concentration in light-excluded skin of Gamay only accounted for $1 4 . 1 ~ \%$ of the light-exposed ones. For the teinturier cultivar Gamay Fre´aux, there was a 51.7 and $5 2 . 3 ~ \%$ reduction in total anthocyanins in light-excluded berry skin and flesh, respectively.

While the total anthocyanin concentration was lower in light-excluded berries, $3 ^ { \prime } , 4 ^ { \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime }$ -trihydroxylated anthocyanins (delphinidin-, petunidin-, and malvidin-derivatives) decreased more than $^ { 3 ^ { \prime } , 4 ^ { \prime } }$ -dihydroxylated (Cy- and $\mathrm { P n }$ -derivatives) anthocyanins (Fig. 2c–f). At maturity, the decrease in trihydroxylated anthocyanin concentration was

90.6, 68.3, and $8 7 . 6 ~ \%$ in light-excluded Gamay skin, Gamay Fre´aux skin and Gamay Fre´aux flesh, respectively, compared to the light-exposed ones. On the other hand, a smaller decrease in dihydroxylated anthocyanin concentration was observed in light-excluded Gamay skin, Gamay Fre´aux skin and flesh (73.4, 21.7, and $3 6 . 5 ~ \%$ , respectively) compared to the light-exposed ones. It was worth noting that the relative content of $\mathrm { P n }$ derivatives was sharply increased in berry skin, while the relative content of malvidin derivatives was greatly decreased in berry pulp (Fig. S3). Thus, the ratio of dihydroxylated to trihydroxylated anthocyanins was higher in light-excluded colored skin and pulp via two ways (Fig. 2g, h). Interestingly, the ratio increased with berry development regardless of cultivar, tissue, and light conditions. Despite this modification, the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux accumulated predominately dihydroxylated anthocyanins under both light-exposed and light-excluded conditions. In contrast, the skins of Gamay and Gamay Fre´aux accumulated predominantly trihydroxylated anthocyanins under light, but dihydroxylated ones under light exclusion.

In addition to changing the hydroxylation level, light exclusion also influenced the acylation and methylation of anthocyanins (Fig. S4). Light exclusion significantly increased the proportion of acylated anthocyanins in the skin of Gamay and the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux, but had minor effect on the skin of Gamay Fre´aux. Similarly, light exclusion only increased the proportion of methylated anthocyanins in the skin of Gamay compared to light-exposed conditions. However, the composition of methylated anthocyanins was modified in all the three colored tissues, with increased $3 ^ { \prime }$ -methylated anthocyanins at the expense of $3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime }$ -methylated ones under light exclusion.


## Transcript abundance of structural genes of anthocyanin biosynthesis


Transcript levels of structural genes involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis and their responses to light conditions were found to be both cultivar and tissue dependent (Figs. 3, 4). Six out of the seven analyzed genes showed higher transcript abundance in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux than that of Gamay under light-exposed conditions. Only AOMT transcript levels were similar in the skins of both cultivars. In the skin of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay, transcript amounts of CHS2, CHI, $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ , and AOMT were all significantly decreased by light exclusion (Figs. 3a, c, g, 4c). However, F30 H, DFR, and UFGT transcripts were reduced by light exclusion only in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux and were unaffected in the skin of Gamay (Fig. 3e, i).

Because this study mainly focused on light effect on anthocyanin content and Gamay Fre´aux was the only cultivar developing color in its flesh, transcript levels were determined only in the flesh of this cultivar (right panels of Figs. 3, 4). Under light-exposed condition, flesh had lower CHI, $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H ,$ , UFGT, and AOMT transcripts, while $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ and DFR transcripts were more abundant, and CHS was not affected, compared to the skin of Gamay Fre´aux. Moreover, the transcript patterns found along development in the flesh differed from skin under light-exposed conditions. The most contrasting pattern was observed for $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ (Fig. 3h), whose transcripts decreased continually over the studied periods in flesh, while they showed a sigmoid curve in the skin. A preliminary PCR analysis showed that there were only 5 genes in the $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ gene family expressed in our samples (data not shown), whose transcripts amounts all continuously declined in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. S5). AOMT also showed a tissue-specific transcript profile, which started to decrease as early as 47 DAF in flesh (Fig. 4d), while it still increased linearly in the skin (Fig. 4c). To a lesser extent, $C H S , C H I , F 3 ^ { \prime } H , D F R$ transcript abundance decreased sharply from 61 DAF to maturity in light-exposed flesh, while they remained constant or decreased slightly in the skin (left panels of Fig. 3). As observed in the skin, light exclusion down-regulated all the genes studied in the flesh during the early developmental stages (before 61DAF). Thereafter, the difference between treatments was reduced and the transcript level reached a similar level between light-excluded and -exposed berries.


## Transcript abundance of regulatory genes of anthocyanin biosynthesis


Transcript abundance of regulatory genes that modulates the expression of the structural genes studied in the skin and flesh was affected by light exclusion (Fig. 5). Transcripts of MybA1, Myb5b, and MybPA1 were less abundant in both skin and flesh of Gamay Fre´aux under light exclusion than under light exposure. Under light exclusion, the transcript levels of Myb5a were not modified in the skin (Fig. 5c), but they increased in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. 5d). Light exclusion had similar effects on transcript abundance of the regulatory genes in Gamay skin, with transcriptional level of MybA1 and Myb5b being decreased while that of Myb5a and MybPA1 were not affected. Regardless of light conditions, the flesh consistently had lower levels of transcripts than that of skin.

The transcript abundance of cytochrome b5 (CytoB5), which modulates the enzymatic activity of $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ enzyme (de Vetten et al. 1999) and plays a different regulatory role than those of abovementioned transcriptional factors, was also studied (Fig. 5i, j). Light exclusion largely reduced the transcript abundance of CytoB5 in the skins of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay. It also decreased the transcript abundance of CytoB5 in the pulp of Gamay Fre´aux from 40 to 60 DAF, thereafter the differences were reduced.


## Transcript abundance of genes encoding anthocyanin transporters


Expression of genes encoding anthocyanin transporters was also affected by light conditions (Fig. 6). Light exclusion decreased the expression level of AM3 and GST in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay and in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux compared to light-exposed berries. AM1 was expressed approximately 40- to 50-fold higher in berry skin than that in berry flesh under light exposure. Light exclusion down-regulated AM1 in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay, but up-regulated it in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. 6a, b). Regardless of light conditions, AM1 transcript amounts exhibited a bell shape while AM3 and GST showed a sigmoid curve in the skin of both cultivars. In contrast to the skin, the transcripts found in the flesh exhibited two distinct temporal profiles, including decreasing throughout the sampling period (AM1) and sigmoid curves (AM3 and GST).


## ABA accumulation and genes of ABA biosynthesis


The concentration of free ABA in the skin and flesh of both cultivars was significantly reduced by light exclusion from 40 to 54 DAF, after which the difference diminished (Fig. 7a, b). In parallel with ABA concentration, light exclusion also down-regulated NCED1 and NCED2 in the skin of both cultivars (Fig. 7c, e). Moreover, light exclusion also decreased the concentration of major ABA catabolites, including ABA glucose ester (ABAGE), phaseic acid, and dihydrophaseic acid (DPA), and the levels of Hyd2 transcripts that code for an enzyme involved in ABA catabolism (Fig. S6).

However, light exclusion had different effects in flesh compared to skin. NCED1 expression level was slightly decreased by light exclusion in the flesh of Gamay, while its accumulation in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux was delayed significantly, peaking at 54 DAF in light-exposed flesh, but at 68 DAF in light-excluded flesh (Fig. 7d). On the other hand, a reverse effect of light exclusion was observed on NCED2, which was up-regulated in the flesh but downregulated by light exclusion in the skin of both cultivars (Fig. 7e, f). It is worth noting that the developmental profiles of free ABA and both NCEDs showed high similarity between the two cultivars under both light conditions. Moreover, only the expression of NCED1 matched closely ABA concentration, whereas NCED2 did not.


## Multivariate analysis to assess cultivar and tissue similarity and specificity


In addition to the point-by-point analysis, principal component analysis (PCA) and correlation network analysis were conducted to gain an integrative view of the spatiotemporal anthocyanin accumulation and gene expressions under both light conditions (Figs. 8, 9, 10). PCA readily discriminated the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux from the skin of both cultivars by the first two PCs, which explained $6 3 . 7 ~ \%$ of the total variance (Fig. 8a). This discrimination between flesh and skin was largely determined by the relative composition between dihydroxylated and trihydroxylated anthocyanins (Di/Tri) and the ratio of gene expression $F 3 ^ { \prime } H / F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ (Fig. 8b; Fig. S7). In addition, the expression of NCED2, AM1 and Myb5a and the concentration of DPA also contributed to separate the flesh from skin (Fig. 8b) in PCA. PCA also discriminated, to a lesser extent, different developmental stages and the two light conditions (Fig. 8a). PC1 separated the flesh of different light conditions and the skin of different development stages, based mainly on changes in total anthocyanin concentration and the transcript levels of $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H ,$ , CHI, Myb5b, CytoB5, and AOMT. PC2 resolved the flesh of different ripening stages and the skin of different light conditions, related mainly to differences in DFR, $F 3 ^ { \prime } H ,$ , MybA1, GST transcript abundances, and the $F 3 ^ { \prime } H / F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ ratio (Fig. 8b).

Correlation networks among metabolites and transcripts were constructed for each cultivar and tissue combination, namely the skin of Gamay (Fig. 9a), and the skin (Fig. 9b) and flesh (Fig. 9c) of Gamay Fre´aux. Only those correlations with a correlation coefficient ${ > } 0 . 6 2$ and an adjusted $P$ value $- 0 . 0 5$ were considered significant. There was similar number of nodes (metabolites and transcripts) in the three networks (32 for Gamay skin, 34 for Gamay Fre´aux skin, and 35 for Gamay Fre´aux flesh). However, the connectivity between nodes differed, with 236 for Gamay Fre´aux skin, 184 for Gamay skin, and 142 for Gamay Fre´aux flesh. In each network, there was a major module accompanied by several minor modules. The major module included total anthocyanins and structural and regulatory genes involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis. Minor modules were mainly related to ABA biosynthesis and catabolism, the ratio between $F 3 ^ { \prime } H / F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H s$ , and the expression between different $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ copies. Network comparison was used to further explore the similarity and specificity among the three colored tissues. It revealed that there were 26 nodes with 60 linkages common in the three colored tissues (Fig. 9; Fig. S8 and S9d). Among them, several unprecedented links were observed, such as ABA with AOMT $( r = 0 . 6 9$ , $P < 0 . 0 5 )$ , CytoB5 with AOMT $( r = 0 . 8 3$ , $P < 0 . 0 0 0 1$ ), and CytoB5 with CHS2 ${ r = 0 . 8 8 }$ , $P < 0 . 0 0 0 1$ ) (Fig. 9; Fig. S9d). Pairwise network comparison showed that the skin of Gamay and Gamay Fre´aux had the highest number of common links (147), while the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux was more identical to the skin of Gamay Fre´aux (94 common links) than to the skin of Gamay (65 common links, Fig. S9). On the other hand, network comparison also revealed that $30 . 3 ~ \%$ of the significant links in flesh of Gamay Fre´aux were specific to this tissue, while there were only 23.3 and $1 7 . 4 ~ \%$ tissue-specific links in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay, respectively (Fig. S8 and S10).

Metabolite and transcript profiles were integrated to study the effect of light on anthocyanin accumulation and composition in three colored grape tissues, including the skin of cv. Gamay, the skin and flesh of cv. Gamay Fre´aux, a teinturier mutant of Gamay. The potential involvement of sugar and ABA in light-induced modifications in anthocyanin was also investigated. The results showed that light exclusion significantly reduced anthocyanin concentration and profoundly modified anthocyanin composition. These modifications were associated with changes in expression of structural and regulatory genes of anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway, as well as in genes of anthocyanin transport, in a cultivar- and tissue-specific manner. Sugar and ABA accumulation were also affected by light exclusion, but seem to play a limited role in mediating the light effect on anthocyanin biosynthesis.


## Comparison of Gamay Fre´aux and Gamay under light-exposed growth condition


Not only does the mutation in Gamay Fre´aux lead to anthocyanin accumulation in its flesh, but it also significantly increases anthocyanin concentration in its skin compared to its wild counterpart Gamay under natural growth conditions (Fig. 2a). The latter difference may be due to higher expression of all the genes (except AOMT) involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis and regulation in Gamay Fre´aux compared to Gamay (Figs. 3, 4, 5). The transcripts of GST, which plays a role in anthocyanin transport from cytosol to vacuole (Conn et al. 2008; Gomez et al. 2011), were also more abundant in the skin of Gamay Fre´aux than in the skin of Gamay (Fig. 6e). Moreover, the expressions of these genes were tightly coordinated along berry development, as revealed by the highly connected correlation networks among them (Fig. 9). This confirms that the pathway is developmentally regulated as a module (Boss et al. 1996). Despite the difference in concentration, the skin of both cultivars had similar anthocyanin compositions in terms of hydroxylation (Fig. 2g), acylation and methylation patterns (Fig. S4). The identical hydroxylation patterns found over berry development most likely result from the similar ratio of the relative expression of $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ and $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ in both cultivars (Fig. S7a), as suggested in previous investigations (Bogs et al. 2006; Jeong et al. 2006; Castellarin and Di Gaspero 2007; Falginella et al. 2010, 2012). The similar expression profile of AOMT could be responsible, at least in part, for the identical methylation pattern (Hugueney et al. 2009; Fournier-Level et al. 2011). In addition, the similar expression of AM1 and AM3, which mediate the specific transport of acylated anthocyanins (Gomez et al. 2009, 2011), may play a role in determining the proportion of acylated anthocyanins.

The anthocyanin concentration is much lower in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux than in the skins of both cultivars (Fig. 2), most likely as a result of the lower expression of $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ and UFGT (Figs. 3, 4). Interestingly, the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux accumulated anthocyanins constitutively from fruit-set to maturity (Fig. S2) and reached a concentration of $2 . 7 ~ \mathrm { m g } / 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { ~ g ~ }$ FW 1 week before veraison (Fig. 2b). This differs from another commonly used teinturier cultivar Alicante Bouschet, which does not accumulate anthocyanins in flesh before veraison (Castellarin et al. 2011). Despite the differences in the onset of coloration, the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux showed a similar anthocyanin composition as in the flesh of other teinturier cultivars (e.g., Alicante Bouschet and its descendants), accumulating predominately dihydroxylated Cy- and Pnderivatives (Ageorges et al. 2006; Castillo-Mun˜oz et al. 2009; He et al. 2010b; Falginella et al. 2012; Guan et al. 2012). Similarly, the commonly used cell suspensions of Gamay Fre´aux accumulate mainly the dihydroxylated anthocyanins (Cormier et al. 1990; Do and Cormier 1991; Saigne-Soulard et al. 2006; Conn et al. 2008, 2010), and should therefore be considered as a representative model system for berry flesh rather than skin.

In parallel with its distinct temporal profile of anthocyanin accumulation, the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux also showed different gene expression profiles under light-exposed conditions in comparison with the skin of both cultivars (Figs. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7). The most distinct profile was observed for $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ transcripts, which decreased continuously in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. 3h; Fig. S5), while it increased from veraison on and reached a plateau at maturity in the skin of both cultivars (Fig. 3g). We then investigated the potential regulatory genes that might be involved in regulating $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ enzyme activity or $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ expression in flesh of Gamay Fre´aux (Fig. 5). De Vetten et al. (1999) observed that a cytochrome b5 can regulate the activity of $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ enzyme in Petunia. Later Bogs et al. (2006) showed that the putative cytochrome b5 encoding gene (CytoB5) is expressed concomitantly with $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ in the skin of Shiraz berry, suggesting CytoB5 may be involved in the control of $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ expression. Our results in skin (Fig. 5i) supported the observation of Bogs et al. (2006); however, in flesh (Fig. 5j), CytoB5 exhibited a more asynchronous pattern of expression with $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ . On the other hand, the expression of $V \nu F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ could be induced 12-fold via separate heterologous overexpression of $V \nu M y b 5 a$ and $V \nu M y b 5 b$ in tobacco petals (Deluc et al. 2008). In spite of a specific regulator of proanthocyanidins (PAs) biosynthesis, VvMybPA1 could induce the promoter of $V \nu F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H I \sim 3 8$ -fold when they were co-expressed in grape suspension cells (Bogs et al. 2007). However, none of the above regulatory gene transcripts, together with MybA1, showed a tight correlation with $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ in flesh of Gamay Fre´aux. These results suggest that other, yet unknown transcriptional factors are involved, or the activity of $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ in flesh of Gamay Fre´aux is not regulated at transcriptional level.


## Light exclusion reduces anthocyanin concentration and increases the ratio between dihydroxylated and trihydroxylated anthocyanins


Light exclusion markedly decreased total anthocyanin concentrations for the three colored tissues (Fig. 2), in agreement with many previous studies (Spayd et al. 2002; Jeong et al. 2004; Koyama and Goto-Yamamoto 2008; Azuma et al. 2012; Guan et al. 2014). However, several authors also reported a lack of modification of total anthocyanin concentration by light exclusion (Downey et al. 2004; Cortell and Kennedy 2006; Ristic et al. 2007). These differences may reflect the cultivar sensitivity to light exclusion (Downey et al. 2004; Zheng et al. 2013). Interestingly, the anthocyanin composition between the skin and flesh largely differs, with trihydroxylated anthocyanins dominant in skin while dihydroxylated anthocyanins prevail in the flesh. As anthocyanins were decreased in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux, despite this, there is no evidence of a correlation between the hydroxylation pattern of anthocyanins and the sensitivity to light exclusion.

In our study, light exclusion caused an increase in the ratio of dihydroxylated/trihydroxylated anthocyanins in all the three colored tissues (Fig. 2), confirming previous reports (Downey et al. 2004; Azuma et al. 2012; Guan et al. 2014). Here, we also suggest that the increased ratio might result from different regulatory pathways in berry skin and pulp: it mainly results from the increased proportion of dihydroxylated anthocyanins in berry pulp, but from the decreased proportion of trihydroxylated anthocyanins in berry skin (Fig. S3). Furthermore, detailed analysis of the temporal profile revealed that light exclusion reduced the biosynthesis of trihydroxylated anthocyanins by $\sim 8 0 \%$ , but reduced the dihydroxylated anthocyanins only by $\sim 4 4 ~ \%$ . These results suggest that the two metabolic branches leading to the biosynthesis of tri- and dihydroxylated anthocyanins have different sensitivities to light exclusion. Interestingly, distinct sensitivities of the two branches were also reported in response to other environmental factors. For example, high temperature decreased the proportion of dihydroxylated anthocyanins (Mori et al. 2007; Tarara et al. 2008) with a reduced total anthocyanin concentration, and water stress also decreased the proportion of dihydroxylated anthocyanins, but with an increased total anthocyanin concentration (Castellarin et al. $2 0 0 7 \mathrm { a }$ , b). Similarly, Kovinich et al. (2014) observed that different environmental conditions triggered distinct sets of anthocyanins in Arabidopsis, providing ‘fingerprints’ that reflect the physiological status of the plants. Deciphering the underlying mechanisms will enable the anthocyanin composition of grapes, or other plants, to be fine tuned by combining different environment factors. For example, the possible regulation of $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ by cytochrome b5 deserves further investigation.


## Coordinated reduction in structural, regulatory and transporter genes by light exclusion is responsible for the reduced total anthocyanin concentration


Seven structural genes, three transport genes, and four regulatory genes were all significantly down-regulated by light exclusion in the skins of Gamay Fre´aux (Figs. 3, 4, 5, 6). This coordinated reduction is in line with the decreased total anthocyanin concentration by light exclusion in the skin of this cultivar. Although previous studies also observed down-regulation of structural and regulatory genes by light exclusion (Jeong et al. 2004; Guan et al. 2014), we further illustrate that the transporters mediating anthocyanin storage were also reduced in concert, which underlines the importance of coordinated regulation to optimize the accumulation efficiency of the pathway. A similar down-regulation of the genes studied was observed in the skin of Gamay, except that $F 3 ^ { \prime } H , D F R$ , and UFGT were not affected (Figs. 3, 4), highlighting the different regulation modes between the two cultivars. Surprisingly, Myb5a was the only gene studied that was not significantly affected by light exclusion in the skins of the two cultivars, as observed by Guan et al. (2014). Myb5a was initially identified as a regulatory gene involved in the control of different branches of the phenylpropanoid pathway in grapevine, including anthocyanins (Deluc et al. 2006). More recently, Cavallini et al. (2014) showed that Myb5a has a more limited influence on the expression of genes directly related to anthocyanin biosynthesis. This may explain why it is not responding to light exclusion.

The flesh of Gamay Fre´aux showed a different and less coordinated response to light exclusion than skins (Figs. 3, 4, 5, 6, 9). Among the 15 genes assayed, 12 were downregulated by light exclusion with different magnitudes, with $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ being the most sensitive as it was almost completely repressed by light exclusion. The down-regulation of these genes is most likely responsible for the observed decrease in total anthocyanin concentration in the flesh. In contrast, Myb5a and AM1 were up-regulated (Fig. 10). The up-regulation of Myb5a may control other pathways than anthocyanin biosynthesis (Deluc et al. 2006, 2008; Cavallini et al. 2014). According to the study of Gomez et al. (2009), the expression of AM1 and AM3 were quite restricted to the pigmented tissue—berry skin, and AM3 was generally more expressed than AM1 in berry skin. The expression of AM1 was independent of anthocyanin content and composition, while AM3 was expressed higher in berry skin containing higher acylated anthocyanins. Similarly, our study indicates that both AM1 and AM3 might contribute greatly to anthocyanin transport in berry skin because of their high expression under light exposure. Their decreased expression under light exclusion related to decreased anthocyanin content in berry skin. On the other hand, AM3 was the main anthocyanin transporter gene in pigmented berry flesh because of its much higher expression compared to AM1. Although AM1 is up-regulated, its much lower expression under light exclusion further suggests that this gene might play limited roles in mediating anthocyanin transport in berry flesh. Moreover, it seems that other flavonoids, such as flavonol and PAs, were likely to be affected by light exclusion (Downey et al. 2004; Ristic et al. 2007). This could be inferred from transcriptional changes of structural and regulatory genes investigated in this study. The expression of Myb5a (general phenylpropanoid pathway, Deluc et al. 2006), Myb5b (anthocyanin and PA biosynthesis, Deluc et al. 2008), MybPA1 (PA biosynthesis, Bogs et al. 2007) and the common structural genes were differently regulated by sunlight. The effect of light exclusion on the biosynthesis of other flavonoids (e.g., flavonols and PAs) warrants further investigation, in order to gain a more in-depth understanding of the phenylpropanoid pathway.


## Different sensitivities of ${ \pmb { F } } { \pmb { 3 } } ^ { \prime } { \pmb { H } }$ and $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ to light exclusion result in fine-tuning the anthocyanin hydroxylation pattern


Anthocyanin hydroxylation is known to be mediated by $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ and $\mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H }$ activities, which lead to the biosynthesis of the $3 ^ { \prime } 4 ^ { \prime }$ -dihydroxylated and $3 ^ { \prime } 4 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime }$ -trihydroxylated anthocyanins, respectively, in plants (Tanaka and Brugliera 2013), including grape berry (Bogs et al. 2006). Our results showed that the two genes have at least two modes of response to light exclusion in the three colored tissues (Fig. 10). In the skin of Gamay, light exclusion only reduced the expression of $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ but not $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ , resulting in a higher ratio of $F 3 ^ { \prime } H / F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ and consequently a higher ratio of dihydroxylated/trihydroxylated anthocyanins (Fig. 10). This agrees with our previous results on the teinturier cultivar Yan73 (a progeny of Muscat Hamburg $\times$ Alicante Bouschet) (Guan et al. 2014). The $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ transcript abundance is relatively stable under various conditions, since water stress did not affect $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ expression, while it up-regulated $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ in Merlot (Castellarin et al. 2007b) and in Cabernet Sauvignon (Castellarin et al. 2007a), resulting in a lower ratio of dihydroxylated/trihydroxylated anthocyanins. However, in the skin and flesh of Gamay Fre´aux, both $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ and $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 H$ were down-regulated by light exclusion, with $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ reduced to a greater extent than $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ , which led to an increase in the dihydroxylated/trihydroxylated anthocyanins ratio in both tissues (Fig. 10). This agrees with the observations made for shaded Cabernet Sauvignon (Koyama and Goto-Yamamoto 2008). The two response modes observed here highlight the complex nature of regulation for the hydroxylation pattern of anthocyanins as a function of genotype and environmental factors.

Our previous results in Yan73 showed that the light transmission through the skin decreased with the accumulation of anthocyanins, and hence the colored skin increases the shading effect on the berry flesh (Guan et al. 2014). The present results and other previous studies consistently show that light exclusion can alter the balance between diand trihydroxylated anthocyanins, by favoring the accumulation of the dihydroxylated anthocyanins. This prompted us to further test the hypothesis that the skinshading on flesh is responsible, to some extent, for the enrichment of dihydroxylated anthocyanins in the flesh. Several lines of evidence support this hypothesis: (i) $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ is very sensitive to light exclusion in the flesh, and its gradual decrease in flesh under light-exposed conditions parallels the increase of anthocyanin concentration in skin; (ii) the accumulation of trihydroxylated anthocyanins stopped once the skin accumulated considerable amount of anthocyanins under light-exposed conditions (around 54 days after flowering), while the less light-sensitive dihydroxylated anthocyanins continued to accumulate in the flesh; (iii) the ratio of di-/trihydroxylated anthocyanins in the flesh increased during berry development; (iv) many structural genes showed a sharp decrease from 61 days after flowering, when skin anthocyanins reached a high level. These facts suggest that the skinshading effect most likely plays a significant role in impacting anthocyanin biosynthesis in the flesh.


## Sugar and ABA play a limited role in regulating anthocyanin synthesis between cultivars


High sugar and ABA concentrations promote anthocyanin accumulation in grape cells cultured in vitro (Vitrac et al. 2000; Hiratsuka et al. 2001). Interestingly, sugars and ABA concentration in both skin and flesh are well correlated in both cultivars under light-exposed conditions (Figs. 1c, d, 7a, b), indicating that the mutation in Gamay Fre´aux does not affect the accumulation of sugar and ABA. Moreover, this excludes the possibility that sugar and ABA control the higher skin anthocyanin concentration observed in Gamay Fre´aux compared to Gamay and the presence of color in the flesh of Gamay Fre´aux. Sugar and ABA were both reduced by light exclusion in the three colored tissues, but this reduction seems to have little causal relationship with the reduction in anthocyanin. In fact, there was no marked difference between Gamay and Gamay Fre´aux in the skin concentrations of hexose and ABA under light exclusion, while the total anthocyanins were quite different. An experiment combining light exclusion, and ABA and sugar feeding with in vitro cultured berry may further clarify the role of sugar and ABA in the modification of anthocyanin pools induced by light exclusion (Azuma et al. 2012; Dai et al. 2014). Moreover, the strong correlation between ABA and AOMT transcript abundance found in all the three colored tissues under both light conditions provides a relevant basis for further functional analysis.

Main conclusion Light exclusion reduces the concentration and modifies the composition of grape anthocyanins, by altering the expression of genes involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis and transport, in a cultivarand tissue-specific manner.

Unlike most grapes, teinturier grapes accumulate anthocyanins both in skin and flesh. However, the concentration and composition of anthocyanins in both tissues differ, providing a valuable system to study tissue-specific regulation of anthocyanin synthesis. Furthermore, little is known about the mechanisms controlling the sensitivity of anthocyanin accumulation to light. Here, light was excluded from Gamay (white-fleshed) and Gamay Fre´aux (teinturier mutant) berries throughout berry development. Under lightexposed conditions, the skin of Gamay Fre´aux accumulated the highest level of anthocyanins, followed by the skin of

Gamay, while the pulp of Gamay Fre´aux had much lower anthocyanins than the skins. Network analysis revealed the same order on the number of significant correlations among metabolites and transcripts in the three colored tissues, indicating a higher connectivity that reflects a higher efficiency of the anthocyanin pathway. Compared to light conditions, light exclusion reduced the total amount of anthocyanins, most severely in the skin of Gamay and to a lesser extent in the flesh and skin of Gamay Fre´aux. Coordinated decrease in the transcript abundance of structural, regulatory and transporter genes by light exclusion correlated with the reduced anthocyanin concentration in a cultivar- and tissue-specific manner. Moreover, light exclusion increased the ratio of dihydroxylated to trihydroxylated anthocyanins, in parallel with $F 3 ^ { \prime } H$ and $F 3 ^ { \prime } 5 ^ { \prime } H$ transcript amounts. Sugars and ABA only play a limited role in the control of anthocyanin synthesis in the berries, in contrast with what has been described in cell suspensions. This study provides novel insights into the regulation of anthocyanin in wild type and teinturier cultivars.

The widespread presence of flavonoids at cellular, tissue and organ level in grape, as described above, indicates that their functions are crucial for the correct development of the plant. Furthermore, flavonoids could also play a major role in plant responses to environmental cues, in particular during biotic and abiotic stresses. In this view, flavonoid synthesis, transport and allocation could be assumed as hallmarks of an adaptive metabolism, to exert protective, antibiotic and modulatory effects [106].


## 8.1. Biotic Stress


In grapevine, the stress signalling molecule methyl jasmonate (MeJA), known to be involved in biotic stress [2] has often been shown to induce an accumulation of secondary metabolites in leaves and berries, such as stilbenes (especially resveratrol and viniferin), which act as anti-microbial compounds [107]. In addition, it has been firstly reported that application of MeJA to grape cell suspension cultures, irradiated with light, increases anthocyanin production [108]. Besides, MeJA treatment, in combination with sucrose, has been studied in grapevine cell suspensions in relation to defence mechanisms. In particular, the treatment induces genes encoding pathogenesis-related (PR) proteins CHIT4c and PIN, as well as up-regulating PAL and STS genes. The latter genes are associated with a strong stilbene production. These compounds, formed starting from the general phenylpropanoid metabolism, have an anti-microbial function. Moreover, MeJA treatment determines an accumulation of CHS and UFGT genes, related to a strong increase of anthocyanins [107], and induces a hypersensitive-like response in grapevine leaves and cell suspensions, together with the accumulation of phenylpropanoid-derived compounds and defence-related products [109].


## 8.2. Abiotic Stress



## 8.2.1. Light and UV Stress


For a long time, flavonoids have been considered only as a generic light filter to protect plant tissues from high energetic wavelengths (UV-B and UV-A). Indeed, they have been shown to protect shade-adapted chloroplast from exposure to high intensity sun flecks [110] and, in addition, can also be considered as UV-B screen, in order to protect PSII. It has been widely reported that the massive accumulation of flavonoids in external appendices is consistent with UV-screening functions in photo-protection [111]. However, recently UV-B-induced flavonoid biosynthesis does not seem to have a primary role in UV-screening [112]. Rather, UV light induces the synthesis of flavonoids with higher hydroxylation levels (dihydroxy B-ring-substituted forms, such as quercetin $_ { 3 - O }$ and luteolin 7-O-glycosides), which perform antioxidant roles, thus contributing to ROS-detoxification through chemical ROS quenching in plant cells [112].

Several studies have shown that modification of light exposure could affect flavonoid accumulation in many cultivars, such as Shiraz [111], Pinot Noir [113], Cabernet Sauvignon [114,115] and Sangiovese [116]. In these works, different methods of sunlight exclusion have been adopted, by either application of opaque boxes to bunches, as designed by Downey and co-workers [111,113,115,117], or leaf removal, and/or moving [114,116].

The expression of some flavonoid genes has been reduced by shading treatments [111,113,114,117]. In particular, the effect of light quality has been investigated [115]. Plant covering with UV-proof film does not affect proanthocyanidin amount, but this treatment remarkably decreases flavonols. Again, the transcript level of FLS4 gene (related to flavonol biosynthesis) is lowered after shading with UV-proof film. Finally, a recent study has focused on the synergistic action between temperature and light on anthocyanin accumulation in grape berry skin [118]. It has been shown that a low temperature $( 1 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and light treatment have a positive effect on anthocyanin accumulation. It should be also underlined that the expression of different MYB-related genes and flavonoid-related genes are regulated independently by the two environmental factors considered [115].


## 8.2.2. Temperature


Several studies have shown the effect of high and low temperatures on the composition or concentration of flavonoids. Low temperature has been shown to induce anthocyanin synthesis in various species [119]. In particular, Choi and co-workers [120] identified an enhanced level of anthocyanin 1 (ela1) mutant of Arabidopsis, which exhibits elevated levels of flavonoids and also a cold stress tolerance to a temperature of $4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . Effects of temperature on the content of anthocyanins in grape berry skins have been extensively studied [121–123]. Nevertheless, the mechanisms responsible for the poor coloration of berry skin at high temperatures have not been completely understood.

The effects of temperature on the biosynthesis of flavonoids and the expression levels of related genes have been examined in an in vitro environmental experiment, using detached grape berries [118]. This paper shows that the accumulation of anthocyanins is dependent on low temperature combined with the presence of light. Mori and co-workers [124], by a microarray analysis, have demonstrated that anthocyanin biosynthetic genes are not strongly down-regulated by high temperatures. On the contrary, the decrease in anthocyanin accumulation, under a high temperature, could result from different causes, such as accelerated anthocyanin degradation and inhibition of mRNA transcription of the anthocyanin biosynthetic genes [124].


## 8.2.3. Water Deficit


It has been shown that plants respond to water deficit accumulating anthocyanins and other phenolics [125–127], although the metabolic inducers of such effects are still unclear [128]. The expression of anthocyanin biosynthetic genes is specifically modulated by the seasonal availability of water throughout the progress of ripening has been demonstrated [29,129]. More than $80 \%$ of the increase in anthocyanin accumulation may be correlated to a mRNA accumulation of the major anthocyanin biosynthetic genes involved in the flavonoid pathway, such as UFGT, CHS and $F 3 H .$ Genes coding for F3'5'H and MT are also up-regulated in berries subjected to water shortage, leading to more hydroxylated and more methoxylated anthocyanin derivatives, such as malvidin and peonidin [29,129].

Previously, it has been shown [129] that anthocyanin accumulation increases after véraison, in either early or late water deprivation. The increase in anthocyanin accumulation results from an earlier and greater expression of the genes associated to the anthocyanin biosynthetic pathway $( F 3 H , D F R$ , UFGT and GST). Manipulation of this abiotic stress, through application of moderate water deficits, can, therefore, be used as an agronomic practice, not only to modulate berry metabolite accumulation during fruit ripening, but also to change the timing of some ripening processes, since early stress determines greater effects than late stress. The onset of anthocyanin biosynthesis appears to be also anticipated. The higher anthocyanin content parallels the up-regulation of related biosynthetic genes, thus indicating that the higher concentration of anthocyanins is not merely a consequence of a higher sap concentration in fruit or of an inhibition of berry growth, but depends on an increased biosynthesis. In addition, a water shortage changes the degree of hydroxylation of anthocyanins, leading to an enrichment of purple/blue pigments, modifying grape and must colour [3]. This modification converts the pigments into moieties that are more resistant to oxidation and with a different colour.

Grimplet and co-workers [100] have also found that water deprivation induces an up-regulation of mRNA involved in several pathways of secondary metabolism. Such a phenomenon is mainly restricted to pulp and skin tissues, while seeds remain scarcely involved. These transcripts are responsible for the biosynthesis of aromatic and coloured compounds within skin and pulp tissues that ultimately impact wine quality.

Water shortage also induces an increased expression of the grape BTL homologue, in parallel with the well-known macroscopic effect on berry pigmentation [99] and the activation of the whole flavonoid biosynthetic pathway [129]. This suggests that stress conditions trigger not only the biosynthetic pathways, but also the expression of proteins involved in flavonoid transport and accumulation. Hence, such a stress seems to activate the whole metabolon involved in flavonoid metabolism, resembling the analogue phenomenon observed at véraison during berry development.

Almost half of the world’s arable land has acidic pH. Aluminum salts present in acid soils dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution that inhibit root growth causing severe loss in crop yields. Aluminium toxicity accounts for the second highest loss in plant productivity after drought. Aluminium in high doses causes damage to the plant cell wall, cytoskeleton and DNA. One of the ways by which plants alleviate aluminium toxicity is by the exudation of citrate from the roots that chelates the free $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and prevents its entry into the plant. In several crop plants Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporters regulate citrate exudation from the roots. The MATE proteins are ubiquitously present in bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants. The origin and evolution of these membrane transporters in plants is not well known. Here, using protein sequence information we identify MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors. Our study indicates that the MATE family members expanded in number and functionally diverse among the land plants. We also identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade and a conserved aspartate residue that might regulate citrate exudation. This study can provide leads to engineer MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance in acid soils.

The sessile lifestyle of plants makes them susceptible to multiple biotic and abiotic stresses. Abiotic stresses like high temperature, drought, flooding, nutrient scarcity, xenobiotics, drugs and metal toxicity in soil can severely affect plant growth and reduce yields. While the role of low or high temperature, water availability and nutrients has been studied a lot, an aspect that has comparatively received less attention is the role of soil $\mathrm { p H }$ on agricultural productivity. Almost $50 \%$ of the land used for food production is acidic in nature. Aluminium salts that are very abundant in the soil dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution, which inhibit root elongation and severely affect plant growth and productivity. This is known as Aluminium toxicity and accounts for the second highest loss in yields after drought (Kochian et al. 2004; Bojo´rquez-Quintal et al. 2017). Aluminium-mediated inhibition of root elongation primarily involves damage to the cell wall (pectin, hemicellulose), cytoskeleton elements (actin, microtubules) and also double stranded breaks in the nuclear DNA (Kar et al. 2021).

Plants adopt several morphological and biochemical modifications to counter different stresses. Plants enhance tolerance to aluminium toxicity by either sequestration or exclusion of aluminium. Several membrane-localized transporters play an important role in these tolerance responses. The ABC transporters, vacuolar ATPases and aquaporins mediate aluminium sequestration inside the vacuoles. Exudation of carboxylates like malate and citrate by the Aluminium Activated Malate Transporter (ALMT) and the Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporter respectively, helps the plant to exclude aluminium. The MATE proteins are ubiquitous in nature and present across all life forms including bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Here we have used the protein sequence information to identify the presence of MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors (Fig. 2). While the MATE family members expanded in the land plants we identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade. We observed a conserved aspartate residue responsible for cation efflux one of the motifs that might play an important role in citrate exudation (Table 1, Figs. 2, 3). Future prospects of engineering MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + - }$ in acid soils are also discussed here.

MATE transporters play important roles in cellular detoxification mechanisms in several species. They belong to the multidrug transporter family consisting of the ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) superfamily, major facilitator superfamily (MFS), small multidrug resistance (SMR) family, resistance nodulation cell division (RND) family, and proteobacterial antimicrobial compound efflux (PACE) family (Putman et al. 2000). NorM from Vibrio parahaemolyticus and YdhE its homologue in $E$ . coli, were found to be topologically different from MFS transporters, and were identified as the first MATE transporters (Morita et al. 1998; Brown et al. 1999). In bacteria, MATEs were classified under multidrug/ oligosaccharidyl lipid/ polysaccharide (MOP) exporter superfamily (Hvorup et al. 2003). Since its discovery in bacteria, multiple research on this newly identified transporter family have identified the presence of MATE transporters in archaea as well as eukaryotes including fungi, plants and animals (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Though these genes share a weak sequence similarity, they can be identified using the MatE domain (PF01554). The MATE proteins are membrane embedded and consist of about 400–700 amino acids residues generally forming 12 transmembrane helices. MATEs are further classified in terms of their structure into three distinct types, NorM, DinF and eukaryotic MATES (eMATEs). NorM and eMATE share conserved acidic residues at the C-terminal end whereas NorM and DinF share conserved acidic residues at the N-terminal end of the MATE proteins (Miyauchi et al. 2017). The ubiquitous presence of MATEs in unicellular and multicellular life forms might suggest its importance in the basic cellular processes. These membrane localized transporters primarily mediate cationic efflux (Morita et al. 2000). They regulate cation transport utilizing the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ electrochemical gradient as their driving force. Norfloxacin, ethidium bromide (EtBr), berberine, tetraphenylphosphonium, acriflavine are some of the cationic substrates transported by bacterial MATEs (Morita et al. 2000; Braibant et al. 2002; Chen et al. 2002).

In plants they function in transport of secondary metabolites, phytohormones, organic acids along with roles in developmental processes and xenobiotic detoxification (Upadhyay et al. 2019).

On the other hand, Arabidopsis thaliana and Glycine max contain 58 and 117 MATE transporters respectively. This might be correlated to the genome size. The small prokaryote genomes have relatively less number of genes coding for these transporters whereas the larger eukaryotic genomes have a greater number of paralogs resulting in expansion of the MATE family (Ren and Paulsen 2005). With the increasing cellular complexity, plants MATEs might have evolved to transport a broader range of substrates from cations to phytohormones, secondary metabolites, organic acids and anions. Regardless of the number of MATE proteins present, the evolutionary conservation of this group of proteins suggests its pivotal role in multidrug resistance and developmental roles across life forms (Fig. 1).

In order to understand better the expansion of the MATE family of proteins among different groups of land plants and their algal ancestors we used available genome sequences from red algae to angiosperms and identified the number of MATE genes in them. For each genome the retrieved genes were verified using a domain search in Pfam database. Only hits with the MatE domain (Pf01554) were considered as potential MATE genes. We observed the expansion of MATE family of transporters specifically in plants. There was an increase in the number of MATE genes from rhodophyta to flowering plants across the evolutionary timeline (Table 1). Red algae have 1–2 MATEs, while members of chlorophyta and charophyta have an average of 10 and 15 MATEs respectively. Chlamydomonas and Chara both have 16 MATE genes in their genome. Among the bryophytes, the first non-vascular land plants, Marchantia has 15 while Physcomitrella has 20 MATE proteins. The MATE family in the lycophyte Selaginella moelendorfii expands to 41 members and in the flowering plants the numbers are even higher. The expansion of the MATE family shows enormous variation both within the monocots and dicots. Rice and Wheat have 54 and 224 MATE proteins while Arabidopsis and Soybean have 58 and 117 of these transporters (Table 1). The change in habitat (movement of plants from water to land) exposed plants to multiple stresses inducing many developmental and genetic modifications. Whole genome duplications in plants might account for the rapid expansion of the MATE family across the evolutionary timeline. A report by Wang et al. (2016) suggests that the expansion of MATEs in Arabidopsis and rice might be a result of tandem and segmental duplication. The mapping of such tandem duplicated genes date back to the monocot dicot split (Wang et al. 2016). Despite a larger genome size, animal kingdom has not seen expansion of this family. Humans and rats have 2 MATE genes specifically involved in extrusion of toxic compounds from the body (Table 1). Hence, the expansion of MATE transporters in plants might be to allow plants to cope better while being sessile (Table 2).

MATE proteins in plants regulate a diverse array of functions, which involve transport of several substrates like secondary metabolites, xenobiotics, hormones, various cations and anions (Upadhyay 2019). A subset of MATE proteins regulates citrate efflux to promote aluminium detoxification. The organic acid exudation function of MATE transporters is well reported in plants like Arabidopsis, sorghum, barley, wheat, rice and soybean (Magalhaes et al. 2007; Liu et al. 2009, 2016; Yokosho et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2013; Qiu et al. 2019). Although the primary function of the exuded citrate in several of these species is to alleviate aluminium toxicity, citrate might play other roles like phosphate mobilization especially in species that are inherently aluminium tolerant like rice. A citrate exuding motif has been identified in 28 MATE proteins in angiosperms that regulate citrate efflux in response to aluminium toxicity (Upadhyay et al. 2019). Furthermore, all the citrate exuding MATEs contain a conserved aspartate (D) residue within the motif (Doshi et al. 2017). Since we identified several MATE proteins in early land plants, we next wanted to examine the conservation of this D-containing motif in early plants. The pdb structures were then opened using PyMOL and the D residue was selected to denote its position (Fig. 3b). 2015). We looked for the MATEs from $P$ . patens to S.bicolor, and we identified 12 transmemebrane helices in all the transporters (Fig. 3d). The tool also predicted that the Asp residue is located in the outer loop of the first transmembrane helix of all the selected MATE transporters from bryophytes to angiosperms (Fig. 3c). This prediction suggests further conservation of the location of the Asp residue to retain its function throughout the evolutionary timeline.

Citrate permeable MATEs with a mutated Asp residue had a reduced organic cation efflux rate than the wild type allele (Doshi et al. 2017). This residue was homologous to NorM $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ driven MATE cation efflux transporter. In prokaryotes, the Asp36 from NorM of Vibrio chlorae is highly conserved among NorM and DinF types. Though Asp36 was not found to be directly involved in substrate transport using $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ gradient, mutation of this residue resulted in impaired transport activity (Otsuka et al. 2005b;

Jin et al. 2014; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Also, Asp41of Pyrococcus furiosus MATE $( P f M A T E )$ from DinF subtype is conserved among NorM and DinF types. This residue when mutated results in reduced drug and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport (Tanaka et al. 2013; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Hence, this ability of all citrate permeable MATEs to permit both efflux of cations and anions indicated the broad substrate specificity of this transporter family. In plants, the citrate permeable MATEs are generally localized at the cell membrane of roots. It is probable that the AtMATE orthologs in early plants might have undergone selection pressure when plants colonized land and started developing roots to anchor and assimilate nutrients at the same time exclude toxic substances. This study provides an insight on how MATE transporters retain some of the conserved function from their bacterial ancestors while expanding and diversifying in plants. In the future, studies involving mutations in some of the conserved residues can help elucidate the functional relevance of these traditional transporters. It would be exciting how we might be able to engineer the MATE transporters to enhance stress resilience in plants growing under acidic conditions. As (Kawasaki et al. 2021) has shown the effects of root exudates on root microbiome affecting the growth of plant by altering the expression of ALMT and MATE in O.sativa further transporter engineering can also be used to induce synthetic signaling approaches to alleviate the effects of abiotic stress created by enhanced anthorpogenic activity and changing climatic conditions.

Acid soils $\mathrm { ( p H } < 5 . 5 )$ , representing up to $5 0 \%$ of arable land, are widely distributed in developing countries in Africa, Asia, and South America [1–3]. Solubilized aluminum (Al), the most toxic trivalent cation $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ which forms an Al complex in aluminosilicate clays $\mathrm { ( p H } < 5 . 5 )$ , is a major limiting factor for plant growth and crop yield in acidic soils [4]. $\mathrm { \ A l ^ { 3 + } }$ toxicity primarily damages the root apex, causing significant reductions in plant growth and development by affecting the plasma membrane structure, inducing root cell death and inhibiting nutrient uptake [5, 6]. To date, two main types of Al-resistance mechanisms have been investigated in most plant species such as maize, wheat, and sorghum. The exclusion mechanism prevents Al from entering the root apex, while tolerance mechanisms detoxify and sequester Al in plants [1, 3]. Under Al stress, plants enhance their resistance to Al toxicity by root exudation of organic acids including malate, citrate and oxalate [7–11]. Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporters have recently become the most categorized multidrug efflux transporter family. These proteins couple with substrate translocation across the plasma membrane with an electrochemical gradient of cations (such as $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ ions) [12]. X-ray crystallography indicated a unique structural topology of the predicted 12 transmembrane (TM) helices in the MATE transporter that was distinct from that of other multidrug resistance transporters [13]. MATE transporters exist widely in bacteria, fungi, mammals and plants [14]. Many MATE genes, which encode proteins that induce citrate efflux in response to aluminum toxicity, have also been investigated and characterized in plants [1]. Using map-based cloning, SbMATE and HvAACT1 were the first MATE transporters shown to be involved in detoxification of Al in sorghum and barley [15, 16]. Since then, a number of MATE genes have been reported to be involved in the Al-induced secretion of citrate in herbaceous plants. These genes include AtMATE in Arabidopsis [6, 17], TaMATE in wheat [18], ZmMATE1 in maize [19], ScFRDL1 in rye [20], HvAACT1 in wheat and barley [21], SbMATE in barley [22], BoMATE in Arabidopsis [23], OsFRDL2 in rice [24], FeMATE1 and FeMATE2 in buckwheat [17], BdMATE in Setaria viridis [25], and MtMATE66 in Medicago truncatula [26]. All these homologous genes encode MATE proteins that are required for external Al-resistance, and are primarily localized to the root epidermis cells [16, 17, 20, 23]. Some plant MATE transporters play diverse roles in iron homeostasis [26–32]; heavy metal [33], and toxin resistance [34]; vacuolar transport of nicotine [35–37]; chloride channels [38]; abscisic acid (ABA) efflux [39]; transport of secondary metabolites such as alkaloids, flavonoids, and anthocyanins [36, 39–42]; hypocotyl cell elongation [43]; export of hydroxycinnamic acid amides [44]; organ initiation [45]; regulation of lateral organ size and initiation rate [46]; plant growth and development [47]; the establishment of plant disease resistance [48]; and resistance to viruses [49], etc.
