## Tonoplast-localized nitrate uptake transporters involved in vacuolar nitrate efux and reallocation in Arabidopsis


Ya-Ni He1,2,3, Jia-Shi Peng1, Yao Cai1,2, De-Fen Liu1,2, Yuan Guan1,3, Hong-Ying Yi1 & Ji-Ming Gong $\Phi ^ { 1 }$

A great proportion of nitrate taken up by plants is stored in vacuoles. Vacuolar nitrate accumulation and release is of great importance to nitrate reallocation and efcient utilization. However, how plants mediate nitrate efux from vacuoles to cytoplasm is largely unknown. The current study identifed NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 as vacuolar nitrate efux transporters in Arabidopsis. Histochemical analysis showed that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were expressed preferentially in root pericycle cells and xylem parenchyma cells, and further analysis showed that these proteins were tonoplastlocalized. Functional characterization using cRNA-injected Xenopus laevis oocytes showed that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were low-afnity, pH-dependent nitrate uptake transporters. In npf5.11 npf5.12 npf5.16 triple mutant lines, more root-fed $^ { 1 5 } { \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ was translocated to shoots compared to the wild type control. In the NPF5.12 overexpression lines, proportionally less nitrate was maintained in roots. These data together suggested that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 might function to uptake nitrate from vacuoles into cytosol, thus serving as important players to modulate nitrate allocation between roots and shoots.

Nitrate is the major nitrogen source for most plants, especially those grown in aerobic soil conditions1 . Once taken up from soil, nitrate is either assimilated or stored in vacuoles. As the largest organelle in fully expanded plant cells, vacuoles are identifed as the major nitrate storage pools and contain up to $9 0 \%$ of the total cellular nitrate2, 3 . However, vacuolar nitrate is not readily accessible to NR (nitrate reductase), thus it has to be reallocated for metabolic use when necessary4, 5 . Vacuolar nitrate release helps to maintain the relative steady level of cytosolic nitrate when external nitrogen supply was limited6, 7 . During the dark-to-light transition, nitrate remobilization from vacuoles was also observed to comply with the new steady state caused by the increased NR activity4 . Terefore, vacuolar nitrate and its remobilization are important for the regulation of nitrogen assimilation and nitrogen use efciency5, 8, 9 .

Transport across the tonoplast is energized by the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (V-ATPase) and the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase (V-PPase), which create the proton gradient and the membrane potential10–12. For nitrate, its accumulation in vacuoles is probably mediated by the nitrate/proton antiport machinery13–16 and the nitrate/ proton symport system may serve to remobilize vacuolar nitrate16–18. However, only a few tonoplast localized nitrate transporters have been identifed up to date. AtCLCa and AtNRT2.7 are two transporters responsible for nitrate accumulation in vacuoles19–21. AtCLCa was a tonoplast localized $2 \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - } / 1 \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ antiporter expressed in both shoots and roots20, 22. Disruption of AtCLCa led to approximately $5 0 \%$ decrease of vacuolar nitrate, suggesting an important role for AtCLCa in vacuolar nitrate accumulation19, 20. AtNRT2.7, however, was a tonoplast localized transporter expressed exclusively in seeds, which regulated the kinetics of seed germination by afecting nitrate storage in seed vacuoles21. AtCLCc was also supposed to be involved in vacuolar nitrate accumulation, because it was tonoplast localized and the related mutants showed lower nitrate contents22, 23. Regarding nitrate efux from vacuoles, however, indirect evidences imply that AtCLCb and OsNPF7.2 might get involved, as they both were tonoplast-localized, and heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes indicated that they mediated nitrate uptake, but no evidence showed that functional disruption of these genes led to nitrate accumulation in vacuoles24, 25. AtCLCa was also implied to get involved in vacuolar nitrate efux, because it mediated anion homeostasis in stomata movement26, while nitrate is one of the anions contributing to stomatal movement27, 28.

In the current study, three tonoplast-localized NRT1/NPF family members NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were identifed by bioinformatics analysis, and functional characterization was performed. Our data suggested that these three transporters were all tonoplast localized, and mediated nitrate uptake in a pH-dependent low-afnity manner when heterologously expressed in oocytes. Further analysis indicated that they possibly modulated nitrate allocation between roots and shoots via vacuolar nitrate release.

Signifcant progresses have been made in clarifying the nitrate uptake and transport in Arabidopsis by the characterization of the transporters in NRT1/NPF, NRT2, CLC and SLAC/SLAH families34. However, our current knowledge about nitrate transport across the tonoplast is quite limited though the signifcance of this process is widely recognized.

Te transporters responsible for vacuolar nitrate efux should be tonoplast-localized and uptake nitrate toward cytoplasm. Our data suggested that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were localized in tonoplast in Arabidopsis (Fig. 1) and plasma membrane in Xenopus laevis oocytes (Supplementary Fig. S2), and in oocytes they could elicit inward currents by external nitrate and uptake nitrate in a $\mathrm { p H }$ dependent way (Fig. 2). When these results were assigned to the topology of the plant tonoplast, the inward currents might represent $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ efux from the vacuole to the cytoplasm24, because the external medium for oocytes corresponds to the vacuole in planta35, 36 and the $\mathrm { p H }$ of vacuole in Arabidopsis is about $5 . 5 ^ { 3 3 , }$ 37. Tus we speculated that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were responsible for vacuolar nitrate release in Arabidopsis.

Considering that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and $\mathrm { N P F } 5 . 1 6$ are predominantly expressed in vacuole membrane of pericycle cells and xylem parenchyma cells in roots (Figs 1, 3). We proposed that they might be involved in the regulation of nitrate long-distance transport by modulating the vacuolar sequestration capacity (VSC) of nitrate in roots. Relationship between VSC and long-distance transport of metals in plant have been well documented38, and accumulating evidences indicated that VSC of essential anions including sulfate and nitrate also regulated their long-distance transport39, 40. Te vacuolar sulfate efux transporters SULTR4;1 and SULTR4;2 played an essential role in delivering sulfate to the xylem vessels by balancing storage and turnover of sulfate in the root vacuoles39. While Han et al., found that the decreased VSC of nitrate in roots would enhance nitrate transport to shoots and contribute to a higher nitrogen use efciency (NUE)40. Our hypothesis about the physiological role of NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 was supported by the observation that more proportion of $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ was translocated to shoots in triple mutant lines (Fig. 4) and overexpression of $N P F 5 . 1 2$ resulted in a lower nitrate contents in roots (Fig. 5c). In the triple mutant lines, root VSC increased but not too much was available to newly absorbed nitrate due to the impaired nitrate efux from vacuoles, resulting in less vacuolar nitrate sequestration and the consequent enhancement of $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ long-distance transport to shoots when fed with $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ for a short time $3 0 \mathrm { m i n } )$ ). In $N P F 5 . 1 2$ overexpression lines, the overall nitrate contents in roots decreased because of the lower VSC of nitrate, thus leading to the higher $\mathrm { S } / \mathrm { R }$ ratios in the overexpression lines (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. S10b).

No signifcant diference of nitrate contents was detected between all the mutants and wild type under various growth conditions we tested (Supplementary Figs S5, S6, S7). We proposed that there might be other transporters or channels that function redundantly with NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16, as the reutilization of vacuolar nitrate is crucial to environmental adaption for plants. Te speculation is according with the observation that more $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ was translocated to shoots in triple mutant but not in single mutant. Similarly, no obvious changes in nitrate allocation was observed in mutants of AtCLCb or $O s N P F 7 . 2 ^ { 2 \bar { 4 } , 2 5 }$ . In addition, considering their specifc tissue localization in roots (Fig. 3), we speculated that physiological efect of NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 in nitrate allocation might be more noticeable specifcally in pericycle cells and parenchyma cells. Tus more defnitive evidences are needed in the future to demonstrate the working model for vacuolar nitrate efux.

Plant NPF (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER FAMILY) proteins display sequence homology with the proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter (POT) family of peptide transporters, belong to the large peptide transporter (PTR) family [1] and are involved in dietary nitrogen absorption in the form of di- and tripeptides [2,3]. In plants, NPF members are initially characterized as nitrate or peptide transporters. AtNPF6.3, known as AtNRT1.1, is the first plant member discovered as a nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis [4], and the crystal structure of AtNPF6.3 recently determined showed the similarity with PTRs in the bacterial [5,6]. Subsequently, some NPF members are identified in different plants and demonstrated that they behave as dipeptide transporters [7,8]. So, nitrate/peptide transport function is believed to be a specific feature of this family in plants over a period of time. However, in recent years, several studies demonstrated that some NPF members could transport an even wider range of substrates, including nitrite, chloride, auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs), and gibberellins (GAs) and glucosinolates [9–12]. Additionally, some of the NPF members are even able to transport more than one different substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, peptides/amino acids, or GA/JA.

After identifying the first nitrate transporter NPF6.3/NRT1.1, Tsay et al. [4,8] subsequently characterized more than half of the NPF nitrate transporters. So far, more than

21 NPF members have been demonstrated to be able to transport nitrate in Arabidopsis, many of which are able to transport other substrates, such as ABA, GA, JA and glucosinolates [8,13]. Screening 45 out of 53 AtNPF members using a modified yeast two-hybrid system with ABA, GA and JA-Ile specific receptor complexes, Chiba et al. [14] confirmed that nine NPF members had an ABA transport function, $1 8 ~ N P F$ members were able to transport GA and 13 NPF members were able to transport the bioactive JA/JA-Ile. NRT1.1/NPF6.3 was confirmed to be able to transport IAA and 2,4-D [15,16]. In addition, PTR3/NPF5.2, PTR1/NPF8.1, PTR5/NPF8.2 and PTR2/NTR1/NPF8.3 were identified as dipeptide and tripeptide transporters using complementation of yeast strains deficient for peptide uptake [17,18].

Based on the phylogenetic relationship, NPF members were divided into eight subfamilies (from NPF1 to NPF8) [1]. In the NPF1 subfamily, MtNPF1.7, from Medicago truncatula, has been characterized to be involved in nodulation and root architecture and behaves as a high-affinity nitrate transporter [19–21]. NPF1.1 and NPF1.2, from Arabidopsis, are confirmed to be important for redistributing xylem-borne nitrate to enhance plant growth [22]. The NPF2 subfamily contains nitrate, phytohormone and glucosinolates transporters, and NPF2 members show a wide range of tissue and developmental specificity in Arabidopsis. AtNPF2.3, as a root stele transporter, contributes to nitrate translocation to shoots under salt stress [23], and the low-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF2.12 is responsible for nitrate-dependent early embryo development [24]. Besides, five AtNPF members that are capable of transporting glucosinolates belong to the NPF2 subfamily [11]. AtNPF3.1 is the only member of the NPF3 subfamily in Arabidopsis and plays the role of nitrite transport [25]. It has been demonstrated that ABA could be transported by NPF4 subfamily members [10], and some members of the NPF4 subfamily are able to transport GA, such as NPF4.1 and NPF4.2. NPF5 is the largest NPF subfamily and contains numerous members involved in nitrate, ABA, GA, JA and di-peptides transport [14,26,27]. In the NPF6 subfamily, most of the members have been demonstrated to be nitrate transporters, including the first identified NPF member AtNPF6.3 [4,28–30]. At least two different substrates were able to be transported by NPF7 subfamily members based on three well functionally characterized proteins: AtNPF7.2/NTR1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NTR1.5 for nitrate transport [31,32], as well as OsNPF7.3 for dipeptide transport [33]. Three Arabidopsis NPF8 subfamily members, AtNPF8.1/PTR1, AtNPF8.2/PTR5 and AtNPF8.3/PTR2, have been proved to be dipeptide transporters, while AtNPF8.1 and AtNPF8.2 are able to transport JA-Ile simultaneously [34,35]. It is noteworthy that 38 and 17 NPF genes have been characterized at the functional level in Arabidopsis and rice, respectively, and more than half of them function on nitrate transport and are distributed on eight NPF subfamilies, and play important roles in nitrate absorption, translocation and utilization [13,31,36,37]. Generally, NPF transporters with a very broad substrate specificity have an important function in plant growth and development, and genome-wide identification has been implemented in poplar [38], alfalfa [36], apple [39] and wheat [13], but a few systematic analyses have been conducted for NPF genes in Brassica species.

B. napus, an allotetraploid evolved from the hybridization between two diploid progenitors (Brassica rapa and Brassica oleracea), is an important oil crop in the world. Compared with Arabidopsis, B. napus has experienced a whole-genome triplication, which occurred between 7.9 and 14.6 million years ago [40], and a hybridization event via the natural crossing of B. rapa and B. oleracea (both of which diverged from a common ancestor $\mathrm { { \sim } \backslash n 4 }$ million years ago) about 7500 years ago [41–43]. Recently, the genomes of ‘Darmor-bzh’ and ‘ZS11’ have been successfully sequenced and assembled [42,44], and Pan-genomes have been constructed based on next-generation sequencing technologies for B. napus, which facilitate systematically excavating NPF genes in rapeseed. Although the NPF genes have been identified in rapeseed [45,46], functional NPF proteins and genes should be excavated, and their expression characteristics and role in the tissues that play an important role in rapeseed oil yield should be further analyzed. In this study, 169NPF genes were excavated in the B. napus, and the expression profiles of BnaNPF genes in diverse tissues, as well as time-serial expression changes in leaf, silique wall and seed, were determined; meanwhile, expression changes induced by vernalization at different development stages and response to nitrate deficiency were analyzed. These results will provide useful information for further investigation of the biological function of BnaNPF genes for growth and development in B. napus.

Nitrogen (N) is a primary constituent of proteins and nucleotides that are essential for life. Nitrogen accounts for approximately $2 \mathrm { - } 5 \%$ of the total dry biomass of plants (Xu et  al., 2012). Nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right)$ is a major source of nitrogen in most plants grown in agricultural and natural systems (Wang et  al., 2018). As plants have adapted to variable soil nitrate concentrations, sophisticated nitrate transporter systems have evolved. During the past two decades, four families of nitrate transport proteins, namely, nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel (CLC), and slow anion channel associated homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been identified in higher plants (Krapp et  al., 2014). Among these, NRT1.1, which has multiple functions, is one of the most well-studied. Initially, NRT1.1 was characterised as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter involved in nitrate uptake by roots, as well as root-to-shoot nitrate translocation in Arabidopsis (Liu et  al., 1999; Léran et  al., 2013). Independent of its transport function,

NRT1.1 was later shown to serve as a main nitrate sensor that regulates many aspects of physiological and developmental responses to nitrate, including regulating the expression levels of nitrate-related genes, modulating root system architecture, and relieving seed dormancy (Bouguyon et al., 2015). Moreover, NRT1.1 displays auxin transport activity, which relies largely on external nitrate availability in Arabidopsis (Maghiaoui et  al., 2020a). In recent years, specific topics associated with the transport and sensing functions of NRT1.1 have been discussed in several excellent reviews (Sun and Zheng, 2015; Maghiaoui et  al., 2020b; Vidal et  al., 2020; Wang et  al., 2020b). A series of studies on NRT1.1 have also provided new insights into its function in multiple abiotic stresses in plants. In this review, we briefly summarise the important milestones in the discovery process, dual-affinity features, and structural basis of the dual transport/sensing function of NRT1.1  in Arabidopsis. More importantly, we highlight the most recently characterised functions of NRT1.1  in plant abiotic stress resistance and the correlation between NRT1.1-mediated nitrate transport/signalling and different abiotic stresses, mainly in Arabidopsis (Table  1).

This study presents the largest NRT/NPF gene family (204 members) analysis to date in a single plant genome, which is due to the highly diversified NPF family, and polyploid characteristics of sugarcane genome. Systematic analysis of NRT family as a whole has been explored in poplar (Bai et al. 2013) and pineapple (Li et al. 2018). Furthermore, a comparative phylogenetic analysis of NRT family has been performed between monocots and dicots (Plett et al. 2010). However, such an analysis has not been satisfactorily carried out on the broader NPF family, of which NRT1 is a member (Leran et al. 2014). Even though substrate specificity varies within NPF family members, studying NRT1 alone may overlook certain NPF members that can also transport nitrate. NPF family is inarguably the main contributor for low-affinity nitrate transport in Arabidopsis, with a notable exception in the well-studied dual-affinity transporter AtNRT1.1/AtNPF6.3 (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999; Ho et al. 2009). However, concerns have been raised that only low-affinity transport currents were recorded when studying AtNRT1.1/AtNPF6.3 in Xenopus oocytes (Noguero et al. 2018). Nevertheless, MtNPF1.7 behaves as a high-affinity nitrate transporter in Medicago truncatula (Bagchi et al. 2012). In contrast to NPF genes, NRT2 genes are all high-affinity transporters. Our study identified $1 7 8 ~ \mathrm { N P F }$ genes and 20 NRT2 genes. Gene structure and motif analysis further confirm their classifications. NPF1 is a contracted subfamily based on phylogenetic analysis as opposed to other expanded subfamilies due to whole genome duplications. As mentioned in the introduction section, NPF1 genes in Arabidopsis are involved in nitrate remobilization from older leaves to younger leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013), the fact that NPF1 is contracted may be explained by lack of need to remobilize nitrate between leaves, because stem is a stable sink in sugarcane that can easily coordinate nitrate distributions. We found SsNPF4.6, SsNPF6.13, and $S s N P F 8 . 2 3$ are preferably expressed in young stems and may contribute to such processes. NRT2 genes with homogenized gene structures and genomic localizations, on the other hand, are expanded in sugarcane, suggesting selective constraint on high-affinity nitrate transport. Similar to the NPF family, NRT3 exhibited highly diverse gene structures as well as gene expression patterns. A tetramer with two of each NRT2 and NRT3 proteins is proposed to be the functional unit for the high-affinity nitrate transporter activity (Yong et al. 2010), and they have been found to play important roles during nitrogenlimited conditions in Sorghum (Gelli et al. 2014). As NRT3 is induced under $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency and is regulated by nutritional cues (Orsel et al. 2006), Allelic diversity may be beneficial for plants growing in sub-optimal conditions. Due to lack of gene expression data from sugarcane root, it is impossible to narrow down the particular SsNPF and SsNRT candidates specifically expressed in shoot or root, which may provide better prediction of NPF/NRT in controlling nitrate store capacity in shoot and uptake efficiency in root. It is worth noting that further interpretation of NRT/NPF gene expression should be undertaken with caution. The low number of replicates in this dataset requires further verification for tissue-specific expression. Overall, Both of SsNPF and SsNRT3 genes showed diversified gene structures as well as expression patterns. This suggests it may be possible for sugarcane to fine-tune the homeostasis of nitrate or other potential substrates, like plant hormones, to cope with the changing environment and especially under N deficient conditions.

Sorghum and Saccharum are close relatives. According to a predictive model, $90 \%$ of the sugarcane gene can be found in Sorghum and $80 \%$ in a collinear position (Paterson et al. 2009). The basic chromosomes number was reduced from 10 to 8 in S. spontaneum, and this can be explained by chromosome fissions and fusions in two ancestral chromosomes homologous to Sorghum chromosomes 5 and 8 (Zhang et al. 2018a, b). These chromosome rearrangements also can be detected when comparing Sorghum and Saccharum NPF genes. For instance, SbNPF2.4 and SbNPF2.5 are located on the second half of sorghum chromosome 8, which later are duplicated and translocated to chromosome 2 as SsNPF2.8, SsNPF2.9, SsNPF2.10, SsNPF2.11, SsNPF2.12, and SsNPF2.13. Therefore, it is particularly relevant to understand the genomic relationships when studying gene functions and regulatory networks from close relatives. Interestingly, some NPF proteins (SsNPF4.22, SsNPF4.27, SsNPF4.28, SsNPF5.3, SsNPF5.15, SsNPF5.39, and SsNPF8.21) possess multiple sets of conserved motif (ranged between 2 and 4 sets, Fig. 2), suggesting multiple events of gene duplications and fusions. This occurs frequently in enzymes like phosphagen kinases (Suzuki et al. 1998) and arginine kinase (Compaan and Ellington 2003). This is also common in transporters, such as SWEET, a class of sugar transporters with two duplicated MtN3-like functional domains (Chen et al. 2012; Xuan et al. 2013). Structural analysis of AtNPF6.3/NRT1.1 suggests that it should functions as a dimer (Parker and Newstead 2014; Sun et al. 2014). Here, it would be interesting to know whether the NPF genes with the duplicated functional domain in sugarcane are functional or not, which will further expand our understandings about the functional units of nitrate (or other substrates) transporters.

Our study mainly focused on the systematic analysis of genes within the NRT/NPF family in the newly sequenced genome of S. spontaneum. Due to limited experimental data gathered from Sorghum’s NRT/NPF family, the vast majority of the sugarcane transporters are functionally unidentified and uncharacterized in sorghum. The NRT/NPF genes discussed herein may not be a complete list for functional studies as suggested in this study. It can be concluded that structural and functional diversity exists in sugarcane NRT/NPF family, and different selection forces are in effect during the course of evolution within each NRT/NPF subfamily. Nitrate is unique among the essential inorganic nutrients in so far as its uptake from soil solution by the major nitrate transporters AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 and AtNPF6.3 (originally named NRT1.1), and subsequent assimilation by enzymes such as nitrate reductase, requires prior exposure to nitrate for several hours to induce expression of the encoding genes. In the absence of external nitrate, genes encoding these transporters and enzymes are not expressed or expressed at low abundance. An exception to this requirement for nitrate induction is the cHATS for nitrate uptake. Behl et al. (1988) suggested that the principal role of this cHATS was to enable roots previously deprived of nitrate to absorb this ion and initiate induction of nitrate-inducible genes. Thus, at low external nitrate concentration, the activity of cHATS represents the first step in the complex pathway of nitrate assimilation. In a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014), it was demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was considerably enhanced, while nitrate influx measured at $0 . 2 \mathrm { m M }$ was reduced by up to $3 0 \%$ in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants. Nitrate influx in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 was reduced by a further $6 3 \%$ suggesting that NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 are the major contributors to nitrate influx under these conditions. Li et al. (2007), however, found that the cHATS influx was reduced by only $3 5 \%$ in Arabidopsis nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutants, suggesting that $\mathrm { N R T } 2 . 1 / 2 . 2$ is not the major transporter responsible for cHATS influx. Indeed, a large contribution to constitutive nitrate influx by NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 is contrary to expectation, in so far as it has been presumed that after several days of nitrate deprivation, these genes are no longer expressed (Okamoto et al. 2003). Nevertheless, our study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present at low abundance even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ of $\mathbf { N }$ starvation (Supporting Information Fig. S3).

The influx data shown in Fig. 6 and Table 2 provide convincing evidence that in A. thaliana AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to the cHATS. The average reduction of influx ( $6 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the two T-DNA knockout mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 is of a similar order of magnitude as was observed for the reduction of iHATS influx ( $7 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the $n r t { 2 . } I n r t { 2 . } 2$ mutants (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). This finding is different in magnitude from results reported by Lezhneva et al. (2014) which indicated only a $3 0 \%$ reduction of influx in NRT2.5 mutants.The difference in present findings may result from the ‘severe starvation’ employed in the Lezhneva study.

Complementation of the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant with AtNRT2.5 cDNA resulted in a statistically significant increase of the cHATS compared with the mutant, but influx failed to reach $1 0 0 \%$ of WT influx (Table 3). Incomplete recovery of the influx in Atnrt2.5-35S:NRT2.5 may be a result of lower AtNRT2.5 mRNA expression in the complemented line compared with WT (Table 3) possibly due to partial gene silencing. Schubert et al. (2004) reported silencing of genes under 35S promoter control in Arabidopsis T-DNA transformants that is controlled by transcript levels of transgenes. Nevertheless, this partial complementation taken together with the documented reduced nitrate influx in two independent Atnrt2.5 mutants provides strong evidence that AtNRT2.5 represents the major component of cHATS influx with primary responsibility for nitrate uptake at low nitrate concentration in nitrate-deprived plants.

The observed reduction of influx resulted in reduced nitrate accumulation in the Atnrt2.5 mutants. Although roots and shoots of the mutants and WT plants contained similar nitrate concentrations after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without N, after $6 \mathrm { { h } }$ of induction by $1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { ~ K N O } _ { 3 }$ , mutants contain significantly lower nitrate concentration than WT roots (Table 4). However, following short-term $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime } 5 \mathrm { \ m i n } )$ ) exposure to $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , no differences were observed in the proportion of tracer transferred to shoots in uninduced or induced plants. Thus, AtNRT2.5 plays an important role in nitrate uptake into roots but not in the transfer of nitrate to shoots of Arabidopsis (Table 2). With respect to the transfer of nitrate to shoots, similar conclusions may be drawn from results reported by Kechid et al. (2013) using plants supplied with $2 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. Lezhneva et al. (2014) found that under conditions of extreme N deprivation (4 weeks without N) phloem nitrate concentrations of NRT2.4 mutants was reduced by $4 0 \%$ , although there were no differences in NRT2.5 single mutants. This is consistent with the pattern of mRNA expression of AtNRT2.5 that was more abundant in roots than in shoots of 6-week-old nitratedeprived WT plants (Fig. 3a). A similar expression profile of AtNRT2.5 during both vegetative and reproductive growth stages of Arabidopsis was observed previously by Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014). However, after $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ of exposure to nitrate in the present study, root AtNRT2.5 expression had decreased to such an extent (with virtually no change of shoot AtNRT2.5 expression) that AtNRT2.5 expression was more abundant in shoots than in roots. Thus, depending on the duration of nitrate deprivation or re-exposure both higher and lower levels of AtNRT2.5 expression may be observed in roots versus shoots. This may account for the apparent differences between reports from Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014), and the reported higher levels of AtNRT2.5 expression in shoots than roots described by Mantelin et al. (2006) and Kechid et al. (2013). Recently,

Garnett et al. (2013) followed responses of nitrate transporters to nitrogen supply in Zea mays over the life cycle and found that ZmNRT2.5 is the only NRT transporter (besides NRT2.1) expressed at significant levels when plants were grown hydroponically in low concentration nitrate solution.

$^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx into roots of uninduced WT plants revealed that cHATS influx conformed to saturable Michaelis– Menten kinetics over the nitrate concentration range from 10 to $2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 6a,b). We have calculated kinetic parameters for the difference flux (WT minus $A t n r t { 2 . 5 }$ mutants) as a measure of influx specifically due to the AtNRT2.5 transporter (Table 1). $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ were estimated to be $2 . 3 \mu \mathrm { m o l \ g F W ^ { - 1 } \ h ^ { - 1 } }$ and $1 1 \ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ , respectively, for the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant, and $1 . 7 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { F W } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ and $7 ~ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ for the Atnrt2.5-2 mutant. These results are consistent with the findings of Behl et al. (1988), Siddiqi et al. (1990), Aslam et al. (1992) and Kronzucker et al. (1995) where cHATS was found to be a low capacity uptake system that exhibited a significantly higher substrate affinity (lower $K _ { \mathrm { m } _ { \mathrm { \ell } } }$ ) than that of the iHATS. However, in these earlier studies, lacking specific mutants, it was not possible to differentiate components of the cHATS flux.

Nevertheless, a significant nitrate flux remains in the two knockout mutants under non-inducing conditions. As noted above, Lezhneva et al. (2014) reported a significant contribution of NRT2.1/NRT2.2 to nitrate uptake by nitrate-starved roots. We have demonstrated that NRT2.1 proteins have a long half-life even after removal of external nitrate, confirmed by Western blots that reveal the presence of traces of NRT2.1 protein even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without nitrate (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Although the iHATS nitrate influx has been attributed to the activities of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001), while examining the double deletion (NRT2.1/NRT2.2) Arabidopsis nrt2 mutant, defective in iHATS, Cerezo et al. (2001) and Li et al. (2007) reported a residual high-affinity influx that was $2 7 \%$ of the WT flux. This remaining high-affinity nitrate uptake in the mutant is not nitrate inducible, is saturable and most likely the result of cHATS activity (Cerezo et al. 2001). Figure 3b shows that the expression of AtNRT2.5 is significantly higher in the double-mutant Atnrt2.1-nrt2.2 (described in Li et al. 2007) compared with WT plants both under induced and uninduced conditions. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in an $A t n r t 2 . I { - } I$ mutant disrupted in both NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 was reported earlier (Orsel et al. 2004, 2006). It is possible that up-regulation of AtNRT2.5 is a compensatory mechanism mitigating the loss of AtNRT2.1.

The reduced cHATS influx in Atnrt2.5-1 plants and diminished nitrate content of roots and shoots of the NRT2.5 mutant (Table 4) were associated with reduced induction/ expression of AtNRT2.1 (which is largely responsible for iHATS) and complete absence of the $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ oligomeric complex of NRT2.5/NAR2.1 in induced Atnrt2.5-1 mutants compared with WT plants (Fig. 4). Accordingly, nitrateinduced $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx (iHATS) was significantly reduced in the Atnrt2.5-1 mutants (Fig. 7b). These observations demonstrate the importance of AtNRT2.5 in optimizing nitrate uptake following resupply of nitrate.

AtNRT2.5 gene expression was strongly suppressed when nitrate or ammonium were supplied to N-starved plants (Fig. 3a, Supporting Information Fig. S1); after prolonged nitrate exposure, mRNA of AtNRT2.5 was almost undetectable. Likewise, Okamoto et al. (2003) observed that the provision of nitrate to WT Arabidopsis suppressed expression of AtNRT2.5. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in roots under conditions of N-deprivation is consistent with its role as the transporter with the primary responsibility for nitrate uptake following a period of nitrate deprivation. Reduced expression of AtNRT2.5 following provision of nitrate is consistent with its principal function having been performed, that is, nitrate has been absorbed; induction of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 is underway and subsequent nitrate uptake is now taken up by these higher capacity, lower affinity transporters (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). Noting that NRT2.5 is subject to downregulation following exposure to nitrate or ammonium raises the question as to the appropriateness of the term cHATS that has long been applied to this system, which is not truly constitutive.

The absence of AtNRT2.1 in Arabidopsis mutant lines has a strong effect on plant growth resulting in smaller plants, especially at low nitrate supply (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al.

2007). AtNRT2.1 also has an important role in morphological and physiological responses of the root system to nitrogen-limited conditions, having direct effect on initiation of lateral root primordia (Remans et al. 2006). In order to examine the effect of AtNRT2.5 mutation on growth, plants were grown on low and high nitrate prior to plant weight and root length measurements. There were no differences between WT and Atnrt2.5-1 root weights of 5-week-old plants or root length of 2-week-old plants (Supporting Information Fig. S2) as observed by Kechid et al. (2013), but shoot growth of the mutants was significantly reduced by comparison with WT plants grown under conditions of low $( 2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { u } )$ nitrate indicating that nitrate deprivation associated with disruption of AtNRT2.5 resulted in increased root to shoot ratio, a clear indication of N deprivation, in $A t n r t 2 . 5$ mutants (Supporting Information Fig. S2b). Under conditions of prolonged growth at limiting nitrate concentration, Lezhneva et al. (2014) also noted that AtNRT2.5 contributed to the maintenance of shoot growth.

AtNRT2.5 is located on chromosome 1 in the forward orientation, on the first half of the chromosome, close to the three most important Arabidopsis nitrate transporters NPF6.3, NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 and a nitrate reductase NR2. Phylogenetic analysis of the AtNRT2 family from different plant species reveals the existence of closely related AtNRT2.5 orthologues in both dicots and monocots (Fig. 1, red). The clade of NRT2.5 proteins is divergent from NRT2.1-like proteins in dicots and monocots, probably stemming directly from a common ancestral nitrate transporter (Fig. 1). Similarly, Plett et al. (2010) found that NRT2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6 genes from dicots sit on an entirely separate phylogenetic tree from grass NRT2s, while NRT2.5 is the only NRT2 gene that has clear orthologues among dicot and monocot species. Interestingly, out of all dicot and monocot species examined in this analysis, only S. tuberosum has no NRT2.5 orthologue. In a similar analysis that included sequences of another Solanaceae species, namely Solanum lycopersicum, the same absence of NRT2.5 orthologue was observed (Supporting Information Fig. S4). This observation is surprising given that S. lycopersicum appears to possess normal cHATS activity (Cárdenas-Navarro et al. 1999). As more plant genome sequences become available, it will be interesting to confirm this phenomenon and explore possible explanations.

Western blot analysis of protein complexes separated by the BN-PAGE indicates that AtNRT2.5 exists in root membranes only as a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex, that is absent in the Atnar2.1-2 mutant (Fig. 4).The complex was separated in the second dimension by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and both AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1 monomers were detected and shown to be derived from the same $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex (Fig. 5). The corresponding complex with AtNAR2.1 was observed for the AtNRT2.1 nitrate transporter (Yong et al. 2010). Based on observed interactions of other NRT2 nitrate transporters with NAR2.1 in heterologous systems (Kotur et al. 2012), the oligomeric polypeptide complex $\left( { \sim } 1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a } \right)$ may be a universal model for NRT2/NAR2.1 interactions and function.

The evidence presented here strongly supports the hypothesis that AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to cHATS in roots of $A$ . thaliana, and that this transporter has a critical role in the induction of iHATS in N-starved plants. Even though the Atnrt2.5 mutants are knockouts, a significant nitrate influx $( 3 7 \%$ of WT) remains in these mutants. The study by Lezhneva et al. (2014) indicates that AtNRT2.1/ AtNRT2.2/AtNAR2.1 is responsible for this remaining flux. The $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex in which NRT2.1 is expressed (Yong et al. 2010) and which is primarily responsible for the iHATS flux has a long half-life of around $3 5 \mathrm { h }$ (Supporting Information Fig. S5) and, in roots of plants deprived of nitrate for 1 week (a treatment that de-induces AtNRT2.1 expression), is still present at around $2 4 \%$ of the abundance found in nitrate-induced plants (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Moreover, cHATS was found to be reduced by $3 5 \%$ in the nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutant compared with WT (Li et al. 2007), signifying a contribution of AtNRT2.1 and/or AtNRT2.2 to the constitutive nitrate influx under the same conditions used in experimental work presented in this paper. In NAR2.1 mutants, from which NRT2 (but not NPF) proteins are absent, $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx is approximately $4 \%$ of WT values. Hence, it is unlikely that the remaining $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx observed in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants receives a significant contribution from NPF6.3 activity (Glass & Kotur 2013).

Clearly, the function of AtNRT2.5 is not limited to nitrate influx associated with cHATS activity. Thus, Kechid et al. (2013) have established that AtNRT2.5 and indeed AtNRT2.6 play an essential role in plant growth promotion induced by the rhizospheric bacterium P. brassicacearum. Interestingly, this effect is nitrate independent.

Nitrogen (N) is an essential plant macronutrient that is often limited in availability, which leads to millions of metric tons of nitrogenous fertilizer being applied at significant cost to agricultural fields worldwide [1, 2]. Furthermore, excessive application of N fertilizer degrades the environment through pollution of water and air, where it also contributes to global warming. Therefore, reducing the requirements for N fertilizer through improvements in crop $_ \mathrm { N }$ use efficiency (NUE) is a worthwhile research objectives for crop breeders and plant scientists [3].

For most plant species, uptake, assimilation, and translocation processes are vital early steps for successful acquisition and utilization of $_ \mathrm { N }$ from soil sources. Nitrogen assimilation requires the reduction of nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } \right)$ to ammonium, followed by incorporation of ammonium into amino acids, which depends on the acquisition and transport of inorganic $_ \mathrm { N }$ sources and transfer of amino acids and proteins between multiple plant organs [4]. Since $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ is the most abundant inorganic $_ \mathrm { N }$ in soils [1], $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and translocation, therefore, play crucial roles in NUE.

The composition of $_ \mathrm { N }$ in the soil is affected by many factors, including mositure, temperature, wind, soil type and $\mathrm { p H } .$ , which has led to large variations in nitrate concentrations among soil environments [3, 5]. In order to cope with the heterogeneity of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ in the soil, plants have evolved two $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ absorption systems, namely a low-affinity transport system (LATS), and a high-affinity transport system (HATS), which are mediated by nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1) and nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), respectively [6]. Overall, NRT2 activity supplants NRT1 activity as N availability diminishes. In one set of comparable results, expression in Xenopus oocytes has led to Km value estimates of $5 . 9 \mathrm { m M }$ for the Arabidopsis LATS transporter AtNRT1.2 and $3 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ for the barley HATS transporter HvNRT2.1 [7, 8]. This nearly 200 fold variation in nitrate affinity suggests that HATS NRT2 may be key targets in efforts to improve NUE, especially under low $_ \mathrm { N }$ availability conditions.

Seven high-affinity nitrate transporters (NRT2.1-NRT2.7) have been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) [6, 9]. To date, AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2 and AtNRT2.4 have been implicated in root ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake [10, 11]. Interestingly, AtNRT2.1 plays a predominant role in $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ absorption, while AtNRT2.2 is capable of compensating for lost $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 }$ uptake when AtNRT2.1 is incapacitated [12]. For its part, AtNRT2.4 not only acts in $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ absorption, but also contributes to loading $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ in shoot phloem vessels [11]. Another high-affinity nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis, AtNRT2.5, is up-regulated under $_ \mathrm { N }$ limiting conditions in both shoots and roots of mature plants, where it supports efficient uptake of nitrate, as well as, nitrate loading into the phloem during nitrate remobilization [13]. AtNRT2.7 has been reported to localize on the vacuolar membrane, it plays specifics roles in seed nitrate accumulation [14]. Neither NRT2.3 nor NRT2.6 have been implicated in $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake or translocation. Similar activities by homologues of Arabidopsis NRT2 genes in crop species have been partially confirmed, though efforts have been limited. Work with rice has revealed five NRT2 genes, including $O s N R T 2 . 3 a .$ , which was found to play a key role in root to shoot nitrate translocation under N limiting conditions [15].

Rapeseed (Brassica napus L.) is a globally important oil crop that is cultivated widely for production of vegetable oil, biofuels and industrial products, such as lubricants and surfactants [16, 17]. As an allotetraploid, the Brassica napus (genome $\mathrm { A _ { n } A _ { n } C _ { n } C _ { n } } )$ is a product of genome doubling in a hybridization between Brassica oleracea (L.) (genome $\mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { o } } \mathrm { C } _ { \mathrm { o } } )$ ) and Brassica rapa (L.) (genome $\mathrm { A _ { r } A _ { r } }$ ) $\sim 7 5 0 0$ years ago [18]. This suggests that the Brassica napus genome might harbor multiple homologs for individual NRT2 members in Arabidopsis [18]. Rapeseed requires substantial amounts of $\mathrm { N _ { i } }$ , and, as a result, is extremely sensitive to changes in soil $_ \mathrm { N }$ availability [19]. Reducing the input of N fertilizer while maintaining yields of rapeseed will, therefore, likely entail improving the NUE of rapeseed. Furthermore, rapeseed is sensitive to various environmental stresses, such as macronutrient deficiencies, waterlogging and drought stresses, these will lead to the nutrients imbanlance, influence the N metabolism or other metabolic pathways, finally suppress the growth and yield of rapeseed [20–25]. It’s necessary to understand the adaptive patterns of NRT2 family genes in response to these stresses which commonly appeared in the production of rapeseed. Thus, the aim of this study is (i) to identify all NRT2s family members in the Brassica napus genome, (ii) analyze the genomic and transcriptomic characteristics of BnNRT2s family members, including exon-intron organization, conserved motifs, phylogeny, gene duplication, tissue specific expression, and their responsive profiles under various stresses, and (iii) determine core gene members contributing to $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ absorption and transportation under N limiting conditions or other environmental stresses. Overall, this report reveals the characteristics of NRT2 genes in rapeseed and also provides candidate gene resources for improving NUE and reducing $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilizer applications to rapeseed fields.

NRT2 proteins are common in bacteria, animals and plants. Though NRT2 gene family members from a number of species have been described in detail, information on nitrate transporters in rapeseed, especially respond to various stresses remains limited. In this study, 17 putative NRT2 genes were identified from the genome of rapeseed, which means that individual Arabidopsis NRT2 genes (7 genes) may have multiple homologs in rapeseed. Indeed, that was observed in this study, but with the less expected outcome that a total of seven BnNRT2.1 genes and two BnNRT2.2 genes were identified based on their respective closest matches in Arabidopsis being the highly similar pair of NRT2 genes, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 (Fig. 1 and Table 1). The extent of BnNRT2.1 genes in rapeseed suggests that this complex gene family might be the product of allopolyploidy or duplication events in the rapeseed evolutionary history [18], and our results indeed found that most gene duplications of the NRT2 gene family resulted from whole-genome duplication (Table S1). In addition, results from the macronutrient deficiency experiment reported herein clearly indicate that duplication of BnNRT2.1 genes has led to divergence of the specific roles played by members of this family in responses to varied macronutrient stress conditions. Conserved domain analysis indicated that all 17 of the putatively identified NRT2 proteins harbor the signature sequence (G-W-G/A-N/D-M/L/VG) of NNP family proteins (Fig. 2), which are also found in other NRT2 transporters, such as the NarK protein in E. coli and NRT2 in Heb. cylindrosporum [9, 27].

Drought and waterlogging have extremely serious impacts on agricultural production, with severe impacts on rapeseed plants often occurring vegetative growth. In this study, drought and waterlogging stresses were simulated in pot cultures in order to investigate the expression patterns of BnNRT2s genes in response to these stresses. Under drought stress conditions, the transcript abundance of all BnNRT2 genes, except $B n N R T 2 . l a ,$ dramatically decreased relative to expression in control pots over the course of 14 days of drought stress, and then restored to control levels upon rehydration (Fig. 7).

## Responses of BnNRT2 gene expression to drought or waterlogging stress


Cis-acting regulatory element analysis of BnNRT2 promoter regions revealed a great abundance of light responsive element (Fig. 3), which implies that BnNRT2 gene expression is closely associated with photosynthesis and might be diurnally regulated. Previous studies with Arabidopsis have elucidated up-regulation of $A t N R T 2 . I$ in daylight and down-regulation during the night, which can be inhibited by sucrose [28, 29]. Taking our results together with past reports supports the conclusion that, as light and sucrose regulated mediators of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and transport, rapeseed NRTs are key members of systems coordinating carbon and $_ \mathrm { N }$ metabolism. Furthermore, the duplication of BnNRT2.1 genes and variation in their responses to N, P and K deficiency treatments, suggests that NRT genes are involved in modulating multiple nutrient response pathways.

Several previous studies have suggested that limited external ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ supplies can promote lateral root elongation through regulation of meristematic activity in mature root tips, where, in rapeseed, cells in the meristematic region are packed more densely than in the elongation zone [30]. In Arabidopsis, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2, two nitrate transporter genes mainly expressed in the root, play key roles in the promotion of lateral root elongation [31, 32]. Recent research has also demonstrated that knock-down of CsNRT2.1 in cucumber strongly reduces root length and lateral root numbers under low $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ conditions [33]. In the present study, $B n N R T 2 . I s$ were predominantly expressed in roots, and most were up-regulated during N deficiency stress (Figs. 5 and 6). Plus, lateral root lengths and root tips also increased in response to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Fig. S3C, D). Therefore, we conclude that BnNRT2.1 family members are likely involves in the regulation of the lateral root elongation under N limited conditions.

More recently, EXO70A3 was identified as a downstream target of PIN4, an auxin efflux carrier, in adaptive drought responses that lead to the production of a deeper root system architecture (RSA) [34]. Analogously, a deeper RSA induced by N deficiency might be modulated by EXO70A3, with NRT2.1 genes possibly involve downstream of auxin pathway related RSA modulation, which is supported by the fact that in CREs analysis, IAA responsive elements were found in the promoter sequences of $B n N R T 2 . 1 s$ (Fig. 3).

In Arabidopsis, Orsel [35] have outlined expression profiles of NRT2 family members, with AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.4,

AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.6 being preferentially expressed in roots, AtNRT2.7 specifically expressed in aerial parts, AtNRT2.3 expression intermediate between the previous two profiles, and AtNRT2.2 undetectable in either roots or shoots. Similarly, in the rapeseed expression profiles observed herein, $B n N R T 2 . l s$ and $B n N R T 2 . 4 s$ were mainly expressed in the root, while $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ were detected only in aerial parts, including leaves, seeds, flowers and stems (Fig. 4b, c). On the other hand, in contrast to the observations of Orsel [35], $B n N R T 2 . 2 a$ transcripts were mainly detected in roots, and no BnNRT2.3 transcripts were detected in either roots or shoots. We did observe that $B n N R T 2 . S s$ were like $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ and expressed mainly in the shoots of adult plants (Fig. 4b, c). However, in the seedlings reared in hydroponics cultures, $B n N R T 2 . S s$ were mainly expressed in the root (Fig. 4d). This could be an artefact of the hydroponics system, or it might suggest that $B n N R T 2 . S s$ expression in roots changes as the plant matures. Finally, $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ were the only BnNRT2s detected in seeds (Fig. 4b), which is consistent with Chopin’s [14] finding that AtNRT2.7 plays a specific role in nitrate accumulation in the seed.

To date, a number of NRT2.1-homologous genes have been cloned and characterized in higher plant species including Arabidopsis thaliana [10, 36], Glycine max [37], Triticum aestivum [38], Oryza sativa [39], Zea mays [40, 41], Cucumber [33], and Chinese cabbage [42], many of which have been demonstrated to be major HATS-type genes involved in root $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake under N limitation. In accordance with previous reports, the mRNA levels of $B n N R T 2 . l s$ in the roots observed in this study were upregulated with declines in N supply (Fig. 5). What’s more, recent research has identified the gene BnaA06g04560D $( B n N R T 2 . I d )$ as a key factor in NUE through genomic and transcriptomic analysis experiments involving two Brassica napus genotypes contrasting in NUE [43]. Additionally, BnNRT2.5 expression profiles vary between seedlings and adult plants, though expression increased with decreases in external N supply (Figs. 5 and 6). Coincidentally, previous research with NRT2.1, NRT2.2, NRT2.4 and NRT2.5 mutants has indicated that AtNRT2.5, which is expressed in the epidermis and the cortex of lateral roots in young seedlings and the minor veins of mature leaves in adult plants, works in combination with these other NRT2s to modulate efficient uptake of nitrate, as well as, to participate in nitrate loading into the phloem during nitrate remobilization under N-starvation conditions [13]. $B n N R T 2 . 5 s$ might perform similar functions in rapeseed as AtNRT2.5 does in Arabidopsis, which could be a worthwhile subject of future investigations.

The absorption of N directly impacts crop yield, and, therefore, maintaining appropriate N fertilizer supplies is an important component of managing crop yields. However, numerous stresses, such as waterlogging, drought and nutrients deficiencies, may reduce crop yields. As expected, in the present study, it was found that waterlogging, drought, P deficiency and K deficiency suppress the expression of rapeseed NRT2 gene members (Figs. 6, 7 and 8). Specifically, BnNRT2.1a was up-regulated under waterlogging stress and K deficiency conditions, BnNRT2.7 members were up-regulated under waterlogging stress and P or K deficiencies conditions (Figs. 6 and 8), and BnNRT2.5 members were up-regulated in roots under waterlogging stress (Fig. 8). This is consistent with the previous findings of some Pi, Fe transporters [44, 45], which were also regulated by different nutrient stresses, and it is well-documented that the cross-talk exist among ion signals when plant respond to different nutrient stresses [45–47]. The enhanced expressions of BnNRT2s genes under P or K deficiencies probably because the $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake or metabolism would be influenced by these deficiencies, we speculated that these NRT2 genes could sense the status of external P or K level. However, the synergistic regulation mechanisms of different nutrients homeostasis need to be further investigated. Additionally, the enhanced expression of BnNRT2s might contribute to efficient $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and transport of rapeseed under waterlogging stresses. Thus, it is reasonable to infer that BnNRT2.1a, BnNRT2.5 s and $B n N R T 2 . 7 s$ might play key roles in modulating $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake and transport in rapeseed plants experiencing multiple stresses.

Soil nutrient scarcity, particularly N availability, often limits crop growth and yield. Excessive N fertilizer usage aiming to high yield usually leads to low nitrogen-use efciency (NUE), which accompanies severe environmental pollution. NUE in crops is determined by a series of intricate processes including N uptake, transport, and assimilation. Many genes linked to N uptake and assimilation have been characterized in diverse plants in recent years. Moreover, deciphering the regulation via regulators on their target genes may be a more efective strategy to improve plant growth and NUE, as these factors can orchestrate gene expression within interconnected processes. Arabidopsis NIN-like protein 7 (NLP7) stimulates the expression of genes associated with nitrate uptake, assimilation, and signaling to improve nitrogen utilization (Marchive et al. 2013). Corresponding to AtANLP7, OsNLP4 in rice signifcantly enhances NUE by $7 0 \%$ and yield by $3 0 \%$ compared with wild type under moderate N level (Wu et al. 2021; Yu et al. 2021). Similarly, ZmNLP5 stimulates ZmNiR1.1 activity and enhances root nitrate content (Ge et al. 2020). Zinc fnger proteins (ZFP) and basic leucine zipper proteins (bZIP) are also essential regulators on N sense, transport, and assimilation across various species (Brooks et al. 2019; Kaur et al. 2022). For instance, OsDST, a C2H2 zinc fnger transcription factor, modulates OsNR1.2 encoding nitrate reductase to play a crucial role for rice NUE (Han et al. 2022). CrNZF1, a zinc fnger tandem protein, is proposed to regulate nitrate signaling and nitrate-dependent growth in algae (Higuera et al. 2014). In wheat, TabZIP60 suppresses TaNADH-GOGAT1-3B (glutamine-2-oxoglutarate aminotransferase, or glutamate synthase) through promoter binding, thereby infuencing N utilization (Yang et al. 2019). Our study frst discloses that MeZFP29 and MebZIPW function as crucial regulators for MeNRT2.2 in cassava, and particularly modulating MeZFP29 may genetically improve MeNRT2.2 expressions, which benefts to the adaptability on N limited soil or high NUE in cassava.

As well as known, nitrate, a signaling molecule, directly affects regulators by altering their distribution in cells. For instance, consistent nitrate supplementation leads to an extracellular dominance of the AtNLP6&7–AtTCP20 heterodimers, whereas insufcient nitrogen implies their dominance inside the nucleus to activate nitrate assimilatory gene AtNIA1, showing an up-regulation of a AtTCP20- and AtNLP6&7-dependent genes under N starvation (Guan et al. 2017). Likewise, the localizations of MeZFP29 and MeZFP29&MebZIPW was determined by nitrate signaling in our study. It is worth noting that under sufcient nitrate, MeZFP29s are exclusively detected in the nucleus, but fails to enhance MeNRT2.2. Research indicates that nitrate-triggered calcium signatures and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent protein kinase (CPK) phosphorylation induce the spatial distribution and function of nitrate-responsive regulators (Wang et al. 2021). For instance, nitrate–CPK signaling phosphorylates a conserved serine (S205) in AtNLP7, triggering its nuclear retention and enhancing N assimilation, while mutation of S205 results in its failed response to nitrate stimulation (Liu et al. 2017). It is interesting that we have preliminarily confrmed that the expression levels of MeZFP29 and MeNRT2.2 are greatly suppressed by $\mathrm { L a C l } _ { 3 }$ (a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ inhibitor) (Supplementary Fig. S8), implying they may be efected by nitratetriggered calcium signatures. Therefore, we speculate that MeZFP29 may be phosphorylated under sufcient nitrate to make them nuclear retention. Moreover, phosphorylation of MeZFP29 may suppress its binding to its NRE, which greatly inhibits the regulation on MeNRT2.2. Conversely, in N limitation, MeZFP29 is kept in a dephosphorylated state, which makes it freely shift between cytosol and nucleus and at the same time improves its binding to the corresponding NRE. The binding of MeZFP29 to the promoter may facilitate the recruitment of MebZIPW to its NRE, resulting in an enhanced MeNRT2.2. On the other hand, MeNRT2.2 may be suppressed by negative regulator and feedback of the saturated N in plant including posttranscriptional histone modifcation under sufcient nitrate. For instance, the negative regulators such as NIGT1 and LBD37/38/39 have been verifed to involve in negative regulation on NRT2 (Rubin et al. 2009; Maeda et al. 2018). In addition, AtIWS1, encoding a RNA polymerase II complex, represses NRT2.1 to respond to high N supply through involving in the accumulation of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 (Widiez et al. 2011). According to our results, we preliminarily develop a model to describe the proposed regulatory mechanism of MeZFP29 and MebZIPW on MeNRT2.2 (Supplementary Fig. S9), but how MeNRT2.2 is depressed under sufcient nitrate is an exciting open question.

The fanking sequence around NRE is crucial for regulator binding and the cis-elements at the $_ 5 \cdot$ or $_ { 3 } ,$ terminals function as enhancer for binding. Through promoter analysis extending to $- 2 0 0 0$ bp from the start codon, we determined 4371 genes with promoters harboring both NREzfp29 and NREbzipw, over 12,000 with NREzfp29, and 3613 with NREbzipw in cassava (Supplementary Table S3). However, Y1H assays revealed that MeZFP29 could not bind to the promoters of MeNR2 and MeNRT2.7 harboring TGCATT at $- 1 8 2 3$ and −1670 bp, indicating the importance of fanking sequence around NREs. For instance, the previous research verifed that an approximately 150 bp fragment within promoter of AtNRT2.2 was identifed as a nitrate-specifc regulatory region (Girin et  al. 2007). In our study, we verify the short nitrateresponsive fragment $( 0 \sim - 4 5 0 \mathrm { b p } )$ triggers the response of MeNRT2.2 to varied nitrate conditions in cassava. As previously reported, CCCH-ZFP usually binds to cis-acting elements like 'TGAGTCA/TGCAAAG' (Chen et al. 2014) or 'GGGAGA' (Chai et al. 2022), and basic leucine zipper proteins (bZIPs) typically recognize ACGT motifs, including CACGTG, GACGTC, and TACGTA or GCN4 (TGA GTCA) (Pysh et al. 1993; Wu et al. 1998). Here, we frst report NREs in cassava, i.e., ‘TGCATT’ and ‘CAGATG’, which broadens the repertoire of binding motifs available for future research.

All in all, our study introduces two novel regulators, MeZFP29 and MebZIPW, providing a signifcant advancement in understanding the regulatory mechanism on the high-afnity nitrate transporter MeNRT2.2. To fully elucidate the mechanism of nitrate signalingMeZFP29&MebZIPW-target genes should be beneft to improve the NUE in cassava under moderate nitrogen as low as possible.
