Nitrogen (N) is an essential element for plant growth, development, and reproduction. Plants have evolved sophisticated transport mechanisms to optimize N uptake and utilization, thereby adapting to fuctuations in environmental availability [1]. Nitrate and ammonium are the primary inorganic N forms absorbed and utilized by higher plants [2], with nitrate typically being the predominant N source in aerobic soils. In Arabidopsis thaliana, Nitrate transporters 1 and 2 (NRT1 s and NRT2 s) are vital in nitrate absorption and transportation. NRT1 belongs to the low-afnity nitrate transport system (LATS) and primarily performs functions when external nitrate concentrations are high; in contrast, NRT2 belongs to the high-afnity nitrate transport system (HATS) and mediates N uptake when external nitrate concentrations are low [3, 4].

Seven NRT2 family members have been identifed in the $A$ . thaliana. AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.4, and AtNRT2.5 exclusively mediate high-afnity nitrate infux. However, external nitrate availability does not afect AtNRT2.3, AtNRT2.6, or AtNRT2.7 [5–7]. AtNRT2.1 is a central component of HATS, and internal HATS activity is reduced by $7 2 \%$ in the $n r t 2 . 1$ mutant. AtNRT2.4 is primarily upregulated in the epidermis of lateral roots and is specifcally localized to the outer layer of the plasma membrane under severe N defciency [6], and demonstrated the greater sensitivity to high N inhibition compared to AtNRT2.1 [8]. Nitrate transport by multiple NRT2 s requires the chaperone protein NRT3.1 (NAR2.1), and they may function as tetramer through an as-yet-unknown mechanism [9–11]. Te Xenopus oocyte experiments demonstrated that AtNRT2.4, unlike AtNRT2.1, can transport nitrate independently of AtNRT3.1 [5, 6]. Furthermore, the nrt2.4 mutant does not afect plant biomass, nitrate infux, or total plant nitrate content but specifcally reduces nitrate levels in the leaf phloem [7]. According to these studies, AtNRT2.4 might have unknown functional roles than those that have been identifed.

Nitrate serves a dual role as an essential nutrient and a signaling molecule that triggers numerous physiological and developmental responses, including primary nitrate responses (PNR) [12, 13]. Plants perceive nitrate signals through several pathways: (i) AtNRT1.1, which mediates the perception of local N signals [14, 15]; (ii) C-terminally encoded peptides (CEPs), which are involved in long-distance systemic signaling [16]; and (iii) NIN-like protein 7 (NLP7), which is responsible for intracellular nitrate sensing [17, 18]. AtNRT1.1 is a dual-afnity nitrate transporter and sensor. Its phosphorylation state, which is regulated by the Calcineurin B-like protein 9 (CBL9) and the CBL-interacting protein kinase23 (CIPK23), afects its afnity for nitrate transport [14, 19]. Plant roots initiate CEP peptides in response to N starvation, which are transported to the shoot via xylem, detected by CEP receptors (CEPRs) on shoot, leading to the synthesis of CEP-derived peptides (CEPDs), which were then transported back to the roots, where they increased AtNRT2.1 expression and pushed nitrate uptake [16]. NLP7 rapidly binds to nitrate within the cell, and its N-terminal HLY residues form coordination bonds with nitrate molecules, inducing conformational changes that enable nuclear translocation and subsequent activation of nitrate-responsive genes [18, 20, 21]. Additionally, under N-defcient conditions, AtNLP7 interacts with teosinte branched1/cycloidea/proliferating cell factor 1–20 (AtTCP20) and upregulate the expression levels of AtNRT1.1 [22].

Te root system architecture (RSA) of A. thaliana has been signifcantly infuenced by both local and systemic N signaling pathways [23]. Under severe N defciency, root elongation and proliferation are suppressed, while mild N defciency stimulates the elongation of lateral roots (LR). High nitrate, ammonium, and organic N sources (such as glutamate) restrict root growth [24–26]. Under N-defcient conditions, plants use"root foraging"to allocate resources to areas with abundant nitrate by promoting LR elongation and proliferation [27–29]. Under uneven nitrate distribution, transcription factors AtTCP20 and AtANR1 respond to systemic nitrate signals, activate LR foraging behavior, and regulate the expression of genes related to primary nitrate uptake, transport, and assimilation [30–32]. Furthermore, specifc kinases (such as CIPK8, CIPK23, and CPK10/30/32) modulate RSA by infuencing the phosphorylation status of AtNRT1.1 [20, 33].

Anthocyanins, favonoid compounds derived from the phenylpropanoid pathway, protect plants from adverse environmental conditions by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby serving as an autoprotective mechanism against adversity [34, 35]. Tese pigments accumulated in diferent plant tissues in response to multiple abiotic stresses such as ultraviolet light [36, 37], drought [38], cold [39], and $_ \mathrm { N }$ defciency [36, 40, 41]. Typically, low N availability facilitates the accumulation of anthocyanins, whereas high $_ \mathrm { N }$ levels suppress this process [42–44]. Early biosynthesis genes (like CHS and F3H), late biosynthesis genes (like DFR and ANS), and regulatory factors (like PAP1/2 and TT8) have all worked together to control the biosynthesis of anthocyanins [45, 46]. An accumulation of anthocyanins was reported by the induction of AtPAP1, AtPAP2, and AtGL3 expression under N-defcient conditions [40]. It has been reported that under N-limited conditions, members of the MYB transcription factor family, such as PAP1 in A. thaliana and MdMYB1 in Malus domestica, regulate anthocyanin biosynthesis by forming MBW complexes with bHLH and WD40-type transcription factors [47, 48].

In A. thaliana, mutations in AtNRT2.4 have been reported not to afect nitrate transport and the normal growth and development of the plant [6, 7], yet the underlying mechanisms have not been fully understood. Trough split-root experiments conducted in this study, we demonstrated that AtNRT2.4 can sense both local and systemic nitrate signals, thereby modulating RSA. Comparing key mutants with the Col-0, we found that the nitrate sensing mechanism of AtNRT2.4 is distinct from the known sensors: the local N signal sensor AtNRT1.1, the systemic signal sensor AtCEP, and the intracellular nitrate sensor AtNLP7. Furthermore, AtNRT2.4 plays a signifcant role in the biosynthesis and accumulation of anthocyanins under N-limited conditions. Tese fndings suggest that AtNRT2.4, in addition to its role as a highafnity nitrate transporter, may also serve as a nitrate sensor.

## AtNRT2.4 can respond to local N‑defciency signal and systemic nitrate signal


It has been reported that the $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant exhibits growth performance similar to that of Col-0 under low nitrate conditions [6, 7]. To further investigate whether AtNRT2.4 can sense nitrate defciency stress and elucidate its response mechanisms, we designed two homogeneous control treatments $\mathrm { ( C . N a C l }$ and ${ \mathrm { C . N a N O } } _ { 3 } ,$ ) and a split-root system $( \mathrm { S p . N a C l / S p . N a N O _ { 3 } } )$ to characterize the nrt2.4 mutant in detail (Fig. 1a). Based on the classifcation by Rufel et al. [13], these signals were categorized into local N-defciency signals, systemic N-defciency signals, and systemic N-sufciency signals, with the latter two collectively referred to as systemic nitrate signals.

In this study, it was found that Col-0 is capable of perceiving local N-defciency signals, promoting root growth under $\mathrm { { C . N a C l } }$ conditions. Additionally, Col-0 can detect systemic N-defciency signals, thereby facilitating LR growth on $\mathrm { S p . N a N O _ { 3 } }$ side. Conversely, it responds to systemic $_ \mathrm { N }$ -sufciency signals by inhibiting LR growth on $\mathrm { S p . N a C l }$ side. Tese root responses of Col-0 to the external nitrate status were consistent with previous reports [13, 49]. As expected, in the homogeneous controls, the nrt2.4 mutant displayed inhibited root elongation under $\mathrm { { C . N a C l } }$ conditions and stimulated LR growth under $\mathrm { C . N a N O _ { 3 } }$ conditions. In the split-root system, the $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant showed reduced LR growth on $\mathrm { S p . N a N O _ { 3 } }$ side (Fig.  1a - c), contrasting sharply with the behavior observed in Col-0. It indicates that the nrt2.4 mutant cannot perceive local N-defciency and systemic nitrate signals, ultimately afecting RSA.

We comprehensively elaborated the efect of local N-defciency and systemic nitrate signals on the RSA, nitrate uptake and transport, and root development related genes expression. Te specifc data are detailed in Table 1 and illustrated in Additional fle 1: Fig. S1. We found that the AtNRT2.4 gene responded to local N-defciency signal, promoted root growth under $\mathrm { { C . N a C l } }$ treatment and up-regulated root development, nitrate uptake, and transport related genes. Additionally, AtNRT2.4 could sense systemic N-defciency signals, primarily by promoting root growth on the $\mathrm { S p . N a N O _ { 3 } }$ side and upregulated the genes involved in root development and the N starvation response. In parallel, AtNRT2.4 also perceives a systemic N-sufciency signal, resulting in inhibited root growth on the $\mathrm { S p . N a C l }$ side and down-regulated the transcription levels of genes linked to root development and nitrate uptake. Signifcantly, the gene expression pattern of AtANR1 responsive to local N-defciency and systemic nitrate signals was most analogous to RSA, with the most signifcant alterations in transcriptional activity, indicating a stronger correlation between the AtANR1 transcriptional activity and AtNRT2.4 presence or absence (Table 1, Additional fle 1: Fig. S1).

In conclusion, AtNRT2.4 can perceive both local N-defciency and systemic nitrate signals. It modulates root growth in response to rapid fuctuations in local nitrate availability by regulating the expression of genes associated with nitrogen sensing and root architecture development.


## AtNRT2.4 is not involved in CEP‑mediated N stress response pathways and does not require AtNRT3.1 as a chaperone


As described above, AtNRT2.4 can sense both local N-defciency and systemic nitrate signals. To elucidate the relationship between the specifc sensing mechanism of AtNRT2.4 with the currently known nitrate signal transduction pathways, we selected Col-0, nrt2.4, cepr2, and nrt3.1 mutants and subjected them to shortterm N starvation and nitrate resupply treatments. Tis experimental design enabled us to analyze the patterns of transcriptional activity of essential genes involved in these mechanisms. Te transcriptional activity changes in all mutants were compared with those in Col-0 throughout our rest investigation.

AtNRT2.4 is not regulated by AtCEPRs as the expression pattern of AtCEPR2 remained consistent between Col-0 and $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant under low nitrate (LN) conditions. However, it was markedly upregulated in nrt2.4 mutant under normal nitrate (NN) conditions (Fig.  2a). AtNRT2.4 might negatively regulate the expression level of AtCEPR2 under NN conditions. Te expression of AtNRT2.1 was signifcantly down-regulated in both nrt2.4 and cepr2 mutants under LN conditions and up-regulated signifcantly in these mutants under NN conditions (Fig.  2b). Quite diferently, the expression of AtNRT2.4 was not signifcantly diferent between cepr2 mutant under LN and NN conditions (Fig.  2c), indicating that the absence of AtCEPR2 does not considerably infuence on the transcription of AtNRT2.4. Tese results suggest that under LN conditions, AtNRT2.1 is induced and up-regulated by AtCEPR2, while AtCEPR2 does not infuence AtNRT2.4.

Transcriptional activity of AtNRT2.4 is not affected by AtNRT3.1 as the expression of AtNRT3.1 was significantly down-regulated in nrt2.4 mutant under LN conditions and showed no significant difference from Col-0 under NN conditions (Fig.  2d), suggesting that the transcription of AtNRT3.1 is suppressed due to an inhibitory effect of AtNRT2.4 under LN conditions. Furthermore, AtNRT2.1 expression was down-regulated as nitrate concentration increased in Col-0, while it was not affected as nitrate concentration increased in nrt2.4 and nrt3.1 mutants (Fig.  2e), indicating that the response of AtNRT2.1 to external nitrate concentration is dependent on the assistance of AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT3.1. In contrast, the expression pattern of AtNRT2.4 remained consistent between Col-0 and nrt3.1 mutant under LN and NN conditions (Fig.  2f ), indicating that the transcriptional activity of AtNRT2.4 is independent of AtNRT3.1. As a pivotal member of the HATS, AtNRT2.1 relies not only on AtNRT3.1 as a chaperone but also has its transcription influenced by AtNRT2.4, whereas AtNRT2.4 itself is not affected by AtNRT3.1.

In summary, AtNRT2.4 does not participate in the CEP-mediated systemic N stress signaling pathway, and its function does not require AtNRT3.1 to be a chaperone protein. In addition to functioning as a nitrate transporter, AtNRT2.4 is involved in the nitrate sensing pathway that is distinct from that of AtNRT2.1.


## AtNRT2.4 is involved in the dual‑afnity transition of AtNRT1.1


To further elucidate the nitrate sensing pathway involving AtNRT2.4, we introduced an additional key mutant, nrt1.1, and subjected it to the same experimental conditions as described above. Our results demonstrated that the expression of AtNRT2.4 was signifcantly down-regulated exclusively in the nrt1.1 mutant under LN condition (Fig.  3a), indicating that under LN conditions, the transcriptional activity of AtNRT2.4 is up-regulated under the infuence of AtNRT1.1. Surprisingly, the expression of AtNRT1.1 was up-regulated in nrt2.4 mutant under both LN and NN conditions (Fig.  3b), suggesting that AtNRT2.4 may apply an unknown negative regulatory efect on the transcriptional activity of AtNRT1.1. Tese fndings indicate that AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.1 exhibit reciprocal regulatory interactions under diferent nitrate concentrations, which may be attributed to their distinct roles in nitrate sensing and transport.

Previous work has demonstrated that the CBL1/9- CIPK23 complex’s phosphorylation of the T101 residue on AtNRT1.1 is essential for efective nitrate uptake in low N conditions [14, 50]. Te detailed transcriptional activities of AtCBL9 and AtCIPK23 were analyzed in different mutants. We observed that AtCBL9 and AtCIPK23 expression levels were both up-regulated in nrt2.4 mutant, with no signifcant diference in nrt1.1 mutant (Fig. 3c, d). It was suggested that AtNRT2.4 may suppress the transcriptional activity of AtCBL9 and AtCIPK23. Tese results suggest that AtNRT2.4 may participate in the dual-afnity transition of AtNRT1.1 by downregulating the transcriptional levels of AtCBL9, AtCIPK23, and AtNRT1.1.


## AtNRT2.4 constrains AtNLP7‑mediated perception of intracellular nitrate signaling


AtNLP7 has been identifed as a principal transcription factor, that directly binds to nitrate ions, sense the intracellular nitrate levels and govern the expression of nitrate signaling genes such as AtNRT1.1, AtNRT2.1, and AtCEPR2, either directly or indirectly [17]. Interestingly, further detailed investigation of the attachment data of Alvarez’s research [17] discovered that AtNRT2.4 expression was consistently unafected among all AtNLP7 genetically modifed materials. Tis fnding pushed us to investigate the unknown but potential relationship between AtNLP7 and AtNRT2.4 in nitrate signaling transduction. Terefore, this study analyzed the diferential expression patterns of AtNLP7 in Col-0, nrt2.4, and nrt1.1 mutants under LN and NN conditions. In contrast to Col-0, the expression level of AtNLP7 was signifcantly elevated in nrt2.4 mutant under both LN and NN conditions, there was no signifcant diference in the nrt1.1 mutant (Fig. 3e). Tese outcomes suggest that AtNRT2.4 might play a critical role in regulating intracellular nitrate signaling transduction by inhibiting the transcriptional activity of AtNLP7.


## The overexpression of AtNRT2.4 can boost the growth of A. thaliana


To elucidate the mechanism by which the deletion of AtNRT2.4 does not adversely afect the growth of $A$ . thaliana and to identify the compensatory genes that functionally substitute for its loss, we successfully produced overexpression lines (OE3, OE16) in the Col-0 background and created complementation lines (Com4, Com9) in the $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant background (Fig. 4a). In line with previous studies, we subjected Col-0, nrt2.4 mutant, and these transgenic lines to short-term N starvation and nitrate resupply experiments.

Te expression levels of the AtNRT2 family members are typically induced by LN concentrations and suppressed by NN concentrations, as exemplifed by

AtNRT2.4, AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, and AtNRT2.5 (Fig. 4a - d). In contrast, AtNRT1.1 is predominantly induced by NN concentrations (Fig.  4e). AtNLP7 primarily detects the presence of nitrate and is less infuenced by the changes in its concentration (Fig.  4f ). Compared to Col-0, the AtNRT2.1 expression was signifcantly reduced in nrt2.4 mutant under LN conditions (Fig.  4b). However, the expression levels of AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.5, AtNRT1.1, and AtNLP7 were considerably higher in nrt2.4 mutant under LN conditions (Fig.  4c, f ). Moreover, these fve genes’expression patterns in the complementation and overexpression lines were largely in accordance with those observed in Col-0. Tese fndings suggest that under LN conditions, the functional defciency of AtNRT2.4 as a high-afnity nitrate transporter is primarily compensated by the upregulation of AtNRT2.2 and AtNRT2.5 in the $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant. Meanwhile, AtNLP7 quickly initiates the transduction of intracellular nitrate signaling.

To further determine the infuence AtNRT2.4 on $A$ . thaliana growth and seed yield, we conducted long-term pot experiments under LN and NN conditions (Additional fle  2: Fig. S2). Te accumulation of nitrate and ammonium in the above-ground parts of various lines, and phenotypic traits were assessed. Under both LN and NN conditions, the rosette leaf diameter of nrt2.4 mutant was signifcantly larger than that of the transgenic lines, but leaf area did not show remarkable diferences among the lines (Additional fle  3: Fig. S3b-d). Under LN conditions, the nitrate and ammonium accumulation were comparable across all lines, indicating that the presence or absence of AtNRT2.4 has little efect on nitrate absorption and transport under LN conditions. However, under NN conditions, the overexpression lines accumulated signifcantly more ammonium than other lines (Fig.  4g, Additional fle  3: Fig. S3a). Under NN conditions, the overexpression lines displayed signifcantly better phenotypic traits, including plant height, number of siliques, biomass, and seed yield, compared to other lines. In contrast, under LN conditions, the nrt2.4 mutant showed a reduced plant height, while no signifcant diferences were observed in silique numbers, biomass, or seed yield (Fig.  4h, i, Additional fle  3: Fig. S3e, f ). Tese results suggest that the overexpression of AtNRT2.4 enhances ammonium accumulation under NN conditions, thereby promoting plant growth and increasing silique number, biomass, and seed yield.

In conclusion, the absence of AtNRT2.4 does not afect nitrate absorption and transport in A. thaliana, but the overexpression of AtNRT2.4 enhances $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake and accumulation, thereby promoting A. thaliana growth and development.


## AtNRT2.4 promote anthocyanin biosynthesis in response to N defciency


In our preliminary experiments, we observed that under LN conditions, the leaves of the nrt2.4 mutant remained green. In contrast, the leaves of in Col-0 exhibited a purple coloration and contained signifcantly higher levels of anthocyanins than in $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant (Additional fle  4: Fig. S4). Based on these observations, it is hypothesized that the absence of AtNRT2.4 may impair the plant’s ability to perceive external nitrate defciency signals, thereby reducing the anthocyanin accumulation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted short-term N starvation and nitrate resupply experiments on the previously mentioned transgenic lines. Under LN conditions, a signifcant purple coloration was evident in Col-0 leaves but absent in the nrt2.4 mutant; the leaf color of the complementation lines was intermediate between that of Col-0 and nrt2.4 mutant, while the overexpression lines exhibited leaf colors similar to or more intense than those of Col-0 (Fig. 5a). Tese reproducible phenotypes further validate the potential connection between AtNRT2.4 and the process of anthocyanin biosynthesis and accumulation.

Tis observation quantifed the expression levels of key genes involved in anthocyanin biosynthesis and accumulation (AtDFR, AtANS, AtTT8, AtPAP2, AtF3H). Under LN conditions, the expression of these genes declined in nrt2.4 mutant and signifcantly increased in both the overexpression and complementation lines (Fig.  5b - e, Additional fle 4: Fig. S4). Tese data strongly support our hypothesis that AtNRT2.4 responds to low nitrate/nitrogen defciency stress and initiates the biosynthesis and accumulation of anthocyanins in leaves.

Nitrate availability fluctuates greatly in soil because of the high turnover rate associated with leaching, denitrification and various seasonal edaphic factors (reviewed in Wolt 1994; Cameron et al. 2013). In order to adapt to these changes of nitrate availability, plants have developed several different transport systems (Siddiqi et al. 1990). Uptake of nitrate at high external concentrations is accomplished mainly by low affinity transport systems (LATS). LATS are encoded by members of the NRT1/PTR Family (NPF) genes, and in Arabidopsis thaliana NPF6.3 (NRT1.1) and NPF4.6 (NRT1.2) are major contributors to nitrate-inducible and constitutive LATS (iLATS and cLATS), respectively (Tsay et al. 1993; Huang et al. 1999). At concentrations below $0 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate, uptake from soil solution is achieved through high-affinity transport systems (HATS), of which there are both constitutive and nitrate-inducible systems, (cHATS) and iHATS, respectively (reviewed in Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998; Wang et al. 2012). The cHATS transporter is active without prior exposure to nitrate and is typically of higher affinity ( $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values $< 2 0 \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ but lower capacity $\left( V _ { \mathrm { m a x } } < 2 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } \right.$ FW $\mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ ) than the iHATS transporters (Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998).

Net ${ } ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake or $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx by the cHATS was first characterized in N-deprived barley roots (Behl et al. 1988; Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992). Siddiqi et al. (1990) found that the nitrate fluxes due to cHATS were saturable at ${ \sim } 0 . 2 \ \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and exhibited $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values that were 27-fold and fourfold lower, respectively, than fluxes associated with iHATS in nitrate-induced plants. The noted high affinity for nitrate exhibited by cHATS transporters in barley and other species (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995) makes this transporter ideally suited to detect and respond to trace quantities of nitrate in the root environment. iHATS transport in Arabidopsis is achieved principally through the activity of AtNRT2.1, whose expression is strongly induced by nitrate, peaking at some hours after first exposure to nitrate (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001; Orsel et al. 2002; Okamoto et al. 2003; Li et al. 2007). In addition to this major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter, expression of a second nitrate-inducible protein (AtNAR2.1) is required for both cHATS and iHATS nitrate uptake (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Yong et al. (2010) have shown that the functional iHATS nitrate transporter is a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1, localized in the plasma membranes (PMs) of Arabidopsis roots. Bimodal patterns of nitrate influx into roots of nitrateinduced plants, when represented as Hofstee or Lineweaver– Burk plots, demonstrate that cHATS and iHATS contribute simultaneously to total nitrate uptake with distinct kinetic properties (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995). Behl et al. (1988) proposed that an important function of the cHATS system of nitrate uptake was to supply trace amounts of nitrate that would set in motion the transcriptional events leading to iHATS induction. In addition, many other genes are activated, including enzymes such as nitrate reductase as well as developmental changes associated with nitrate provision (Wang et al. 2000, 2003, 2004).

Wang & Crawford (1996) isolated an EMS-mutagenized Arabidopsis line that was impaired in cHATS activity. This mutant exhibited a delay in the expression of inducible HATS, and was resistant to $0 . 1 \mathrm { m M }$ chlorate, a toxic nitrate analogue. Electrophysiological studies showed that there was very little response to $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate in the uninduced nrt2 mutant compared with strong initial membrane depolarization in wild-type (WT) plants. However, the gene encoding this putative cHATS was not identified. cHATS is also reduced by $9 0 \%$ in Atnar2.1-2 mutants compared with WT (Okamoto et al. 2006), suggesting that the AtNAR2.1 gene is necessary for the function of the cHATS transporter as was demonstrated for iHATS (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Thus, one clue to the identity of the transporter responsible for cHATS is that it requires co-expression of NAR2.1 for physiological activity.

In an earlier communication we demonstrated that all members of the AtNRT2 family are capable of nitrate uptake in Xenopus oocytes when co-expressed with AtNAR2.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Furthermore, the most prominent $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ enrichment in oocytes was observed for NRT2.5/NAR2.1 co-expression, suggesting that AtNRT2.5 might function in nitrate influx as a PM complex with AtNAR2.1 as was demonstrated for NRT2.1 (Yong et al. 2010). Kechid et al. (2013) showed that AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.6 play an important role in plant growth regulation in response to growthpromoting rhizobacterium Phyllobacterium brassicacearum strain STM196. With respect to AtNRT2.5’s involvement in cHATS, Okamoto et al. (2003) demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was diminished by nitrate provision, while a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression increased continuously during N-starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Measurements of nitrate influx in N-deprived AtNRT2.5 mutants and in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 demonstrated a 30 and $9 3 \%$ reduction, respectively, compared with WT (Lezhneva et al. 2014), suggesting that NRT2.1/NRT2.2 plays a predominant role in nitrate influx in N-starved plants. However, the finding is surprising, given that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are strongly induced by nitrate and expressed at diminished levels following nitrate deprivation. Nevertheless, the present study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present in roots of Arabidopsis after $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ d ~ } }$ of nitrogen starvation.

To investigate the nature of the association between AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1, we have used biochemical methods to isolate and characterize a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex between these two polypeptides, as well as physiological assays of nitrate influx in mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 to evaluate the impact of this disruption upon the kinetics of cHATS influx.

Nitrogen (N), crucial to plant growth and development, is engaged in numerous physiological and molecular processes (Liu et  al. 2022b; Shi et  al. 2023). Nitrate, the primary N form in aerated soils, is recognized and transported by intricate sensors or transporters from environment into plants. Many transporters, such as nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1) /peptide transport family (NRT1/ NPF), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel family (CLC), and slow anion channel-related homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been confrmed to involve in nitrate transfer and utilization across various tissues and cells (von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2010; Krapp et al. 2014; Maierhofer et al. 2014; Léran et al. 2014). As reported, NRT2 belongs to high-afnity transporter that is indispensable for nitrate uptake during environmental N defciency, i.e., $< 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. For instance, NRT2s have been extensively verifed to promote nitrate uptake and utilization under nitrogen limitation in many plant species including but not limited to Arabidopsis (Wang et al. 2018), rice (Chen et al. 2016, 2020), wheat (Sigalas et al. 2023), barley (Guo et al. 2020), maize (Jia et al. 2023), and pea (Chen et al. 2024). Positive regulation on highafnity nitrate transporters improves plant adaptability to harsh environments and improves crop yields or nitrogenuse efciency under moderate nitrogen levels (Alam et al. 2023; Iqbal et al. 2023).

Over the past several decades, numerous studies have identified various regulators or transcription factors (TFs) involved in regulating NRT2s in plants (reviewed in (Vidal et al. 2020). Regulators or TFs modulate NRTs through binding to nitrate-responsive cis-elements (NRE) in NRT’s promoter (Choi et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022a). For instance, the nitrate regulation master, nodule inception (NIN)-like proteins such as AtNLP7, ZmNLP5, MdNLP7, and HvNLP2, have been implicated in promoting NRT2.1/NRT2.2 via NREs binding (Castaings et al. 2009; Alvarez et al. 2020; Feng et al. 2022; Ge et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2022). Recently, AtNLP7 has been identifed to participate in nitrate transportation in Arabidopsis (Liu et al. 2022a). In addition, TGA1 and TGA4 directly bind to NREs in NRT2.1 or NRT2.2 promoter to infuence lateral root development and nitrate response in Arabidopsis (Alvarez et al. 2014; Zhong et al. 2015). TaNAC2 and OsSNAC1 regulate NRT2 via NRE to participate in seed vigor and nitrogen defciency adaptation (Li et al. 2020; Qi et al. 2023). PdGNC, induced by low nitrate levels, directly activates $P d N R T 2 . 4 b$ through NRE binding in poplar (Shen et al. 2022). AtBES1 enhances NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 through NRE under nitrogen defciency, linking brassinosteroid signaling and nitrate defciency in

Arabidopsis (Wang et  al. 2023). In apple, MdMYB10 transcriptionally activates MdNRT2.4–1 depending on NRE binding to enhance nitrate uptake (Liu et al. 2022c). Moreover, multiple regulators interact each other to modulate the same target gene through binding diverse NREs in promoter (Guan et al. 2017; Alvarez et al. 2020). For instance, TCP20 and NLP7&NLP6 bind to the diferent NRE of nitrate reductase gene (NIA1) and interacts to increase nitrate assimilation in Arabidopsis (Guan et al. 2017).

The presence of NREs in $_ 5 \cdot$ or $_ 3 \cdot$ terminal fanking regions is of utmost importance in advancing the regulation of regulators or TFs on their targets. NREs usually act as enhancer elements to improve the specifc binding, for instance, $\mathsf { S ^ { 3 } - T G A t / c C C N } _ { 1 2 } \mathrm { A a }$ L $/ \mathrm { t G g G a } - 3 ^ { \prime }$ in OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.3 (Wu et al. 2021), $_ 5 \cdot$ -CTATC/TGAGCTT $\mathrm { N _ { 1 0 } T / A A G G A } { - 3 } ^ { , }$ in ZmNRT2.1 and ZmNRT2.2 (Meng et al. 2020), and $\mathrm { 5 ^ { \circ } - G A C t C T T N _ { 1 0 } A A G - 3 ^ { \circ } }$ in AtNIA1 and nitrite reductase gene (AtNiR1) (Konishi and Yanagisawa 2014). However, motif analysis revealed that these putative NREs are not commonly conserved across plant species.

Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is a crucial tropical root crop that provides sustenance for over 800 million individuals worldwide, predominantly in South America and Africa. Starch from the root tubers are utilized in diverse applications, including food production to pharmaceuticals, textiles, plywood, paper, and adhesives, as well as a source of ethanol for biofuel production (Mohidin et al. 2023). In tropical regions, cassava thrives in marginal areas with erratic rain, acidic soils, poor native fertility, and challenging terrains, where other crops typically fail (Reinhardt Howeler and Thomas 2013). As previously reported, most MeNRT2 genes in cassava were induced by nitrate defciency, with MeNRT2.2 exhibiting the highest expression level. Moreover, MeNRT2.2-overexpressing Arabidopsis exhibited enhanced adaptation to low nitrate $( 0 . 3 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 } )$ ) (You et al. 2022). However, the potential regulators on MeNRT2.2 and the putative NREs remain unexplored in cassava.

This study reveals MeZFP29 and MebZIPW influence MeNRT2.2 expressions by binding to adjacent NREs (TGCATT and CAGATG) in its promoter. Two regulators interact each other via conserved ANK repeat domains in vivo and in vitro. Interestingly, MeZFP29 and MeZFP29&MebZIPW exhibit a nitrate-dependent distribution, i.e., nitrate defciency results in extensive distribution in cytoplasm and nucleus, whereas sufcient nitrate restricts them to nucleus, although MebZIPW distributes in both compartments irrespective of nitrate conditions. Overexpression of MeZFP29 in seedlings notably enhanced plant growth under low nitrate, while MebZIPW did not, demonstrating their diferent roles in nitrogen utilization in plant.

Nitrogen (N), which is an important component of biological macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, provides nutrients and energy for plant growth and development (Gojon 2017). Nitrate and ammonium are the most readily absorbed forms of N in soil by plant roots, especially nitrate, which is the preferred N source in soil for assimilation by most terrestrial plants (Kiba and Krapp 2016). The lack of $\mathbf { N }$ in the natural environment could lead to intense competition between plants and soil microorganisms (Norman and Friesen 2017). To further adapt to changes in diferent N levels, plants have evolved several absorption and transport systems to optimize the availability of nitrate for their own growth, including the low-afnity nitrate transporter system (LATS) and high-afnity nitrate transporter system (HATS) (Fang et  al. 2021). Among them, the NRT1/PTR family (NPF) and nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) are responsible for the functions of the LATS and HATS systems, respectively. The NRT2 family is responsible for the uptake of low nitrate from the soil by roots. Thus, understanding the functions of NRT2 members will be benefcial to the sustainable development of agriculture in the future.

NRT2 members have been isolated and characterized in many species, including seven NRT2 proteins in Arabidopsis (Okamoto et al. 2006), seven to ten NRT2 in barley (Vidmar et  al. 2000), and fve NRT2 in rice (Cai et al. 2008). Among the members of the NRT2 family, NRT2.1 plays a major role in nitrate uptake by roots in the HATS system. There was a strong association between HATS activity and NRT2.1 transcription, which was highly induced by nitrate depletion and repressed by abundant nitrate (Wirth et  al. 2007). OsNRT2.1 overexpression in rice signifcantly increased biomass and yield, and improved agricultural N use efciency (Yan et  al. 2011). Moreover, NRT2.1 played a key role in the regulation of nitrate signaling pathways by lateral root mediation, which was independent of its highafnity nitrate uptake function (van Gelderen et  al. 2021). Though the function of NRT2.1 has been thoroughly studied in herbaceous plants, it is still lacking in woody plants. Therefore, understanding more functions of NRT2.1 in diferent species could play a signifcant role in regulating N absorption.

Plant transporter genes have been well studied in mycorrhizal symbiosis processes. For example, some plant nitrate transporters have been induced by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) colonization with the host plant. A study reported that one NRT gene (TC79437) was down-regulated with Funneliformis mosseae colonization in Medicago truncatula roots (Burleigh 2001). In addition, the expression of NRT genes was also afected by AM colonization in grapevine (Balestrini et  al. 2017), Solanum lycopersicum (Ruzicka et  al. 2012), tomato (Hildebrandt et  al. 2002) and Lotus japonicus (Guether et al. 2009a). Dark septate endophytes (DSEs) are a type of dematiaceous and septate fungal hyphae that are commonly found in the roots of host plants from natural environments (Jumpponen and Trappe 1998). Studies have reported that several DSEs are benefcial for their host plants’ N assimilation (Upson et al. 2009; Vergara et al. 2019; Wu et  al. 2021). However, the impacts of DSEs on plant $\mathbf { N }$ uptake through the regulation of NRT genes are poorly understood.

Sweet cherry (Prunus avium L.) is one of the most popular fresh fruits in the world. However, the molecular mechanism of its N uptake is poorly understood. A previous study found that the DSE fungus S16 could promote the growth of sweet cherry and upregulate the expression of nitrate transporters (Wu et al. 2021). Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the role of the nitrate transporter PaNRT2.1 during colonization by S16 and to determine the function of PaNRT2.1 in N uptake in sweet cherry. This would broaden our understanding of the molecular mechanism of $\mathbf { N }$ uptake with nitrate transporters in DSE symbiosis.

Nitrogen is considered to be one of the most important factors limiting plant growth in many natural ecosystems and in most agricultural systems. Moderate nitrogen deficiency inhibits shoot growth and even stimulates root growth (Agren and Ingestad 1987). Extreme nitrogen deficiency leads to a general inhibition of growth, but root growth is less affected than shoot growth. The accumulation of nitrate in the shoot seems to act as a signal regulating shoot–root allocation (Scheible et al. 1997).

Many physiological investigations have led to the conclusion that plants have developed at least three different uptake systems to cope with large variations in nitrate concentrations in cultivated soils (Glass and Siddiqi 1995). Two saturable high-affinity transport systems (HATS) are able to transport nitrate at low concentrations (between $1 ~ \mu \mathbf { M }$ and $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ ). One of these systems is constitutive (cHATS); the other is specifically stimulated by nitrate in the external medium, and is consequently assumed to be inducible (iHATS). The low-affinity nitrate transport system (LATS) displays linear kinetics and becomes significant when nitrate concentration increases above $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ .

The molecular basis of root nitrate uptake has been the matter of intensive studies during the last decade (reviewed by Crawford et al. 1988; Forde 2000; Orsel et al. 2002a). So far, two gene families, NRT1 and NRT2, are supposed to code for putative components of the three systems. The first mutant characterized as having a defect in nitrate uptake mediated by the LATS was described in Arabidopsis thaliana, the Chl1 (nrt1) line, and was shown to be mutated in the AtNRT1.1 gene (Tsay et al. 1993). The first members of the NRT2 gene family were identified in lower eukaryotes. The CRNA (NRTA) gene was isolated from the fungus Aspergillus nidulans using a screen for chlorate resistance (Unkles et al. 1991). A second gene, NRTB, has been recently identified in this fungus, and shows $76 \%$ similarity over the whole deduced amino-acid sequence with the NRTA protein (Unkles et al. 2001). Two other genes of this family, CrNRT2.1 and CrNRT2.2 were identified in mutants of the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii deficient in nitrate and/or nitrite transport. Most members of the NRT2 family in higher plants (barley, Nicotiana plumbaginifolia, soybean and A. thaliana) were subsequently identified via their sequence homology with the CRNA and CrNRT2.1 genes. So far, in most species, NRT2 genes are members of a small multigene family: for example, the analysis of the complete genome of A. thaliana has revealed the presence of seven AtNRT2 genes distributed on three of the five chromosomes (Orsel et al. 2002a). The expression patterns of these seven genes have been studied by reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR) with respect to their organ specificity and to adaptative responses of the plant to both spatial and temporal changes in nitrogen availability (Okamoto et al. 2003; Orsel et al. 2002b). However, expression studies only give hints as to gene function while comparative functional studies of specific mutants can quantify the relative contributions of particular members of a gene family.

The first functional evidence supporting the role of the NRT2 genes in the root nitrate uptake process was obtained using a reverse genetic approach. We isolated an $A$ . thaliana knockout mutant in which the T-DNA insertion led to the complete deletion of AtNRT2.1 together with the deletion of the $3 ^ { \prime }$ region of the AtNRT2.2 gene (Filleur et al. 2001). The initial analysis demonstrated that nitrate-induced high-affinity uptake is reduced by $6 3 \%$ in the atnrt2a mutant. No significant changes were detected in low-affinity uptake or in constitutive high-affinity uptake in this mutant. Thus, the AtNRT2.1 and/or AtNRT2.2 genes appear to be essential for the inducible component of the HATS. Further investigations on the atnrt2a mutant have shown that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 play a key role in the regulation of high-affinity nitrate uptake (Cerezo et al. 2001). However, since the NRT2 family is multigenic, the impact of such a mutation on mutant growth rate needs to be evaluated. In fact, it has already been shown that genetic redundancy may provide a phenotypic plasticity in response to environmental conditions. The growth rates of plants affected in one of two related potassium channels depend on the presence of AKT1 but not AKT2 channels when grown in the presence of limiting concentrations of $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Dennison et al. 2001). In the same manner, growth tests with nitrate as the sole nitrogen source show that the nrtA and nrtB single mutants from $A$ . nidulans grow similarly to the wild type (WT) while a double mutant fails to grow at nitrate concentrations up to $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ (Unkles et al. 2001). In some cases, growth conditions must be investigated in order to reveal differences between WT and mutant plants. The disruption of one of the six AMT genes, potentially involved in ammonium transport, led to plants that were indistinguishable from the WT under most growth conditions. However, when grown on ammonium and sucrose, the mutant grew poorly and died (Kaiser et al. 2002).

The aim of our work was to measure the physiological impact of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 disruption on plant growth and N-metabolism. Therefore, the growth phenotype of the atnrt2a mutant has been investigated under different nutritional conditions. In particular, the impact of the mutation on the concentration of Nmetabolites and on the expression of the other AtNRT2 family members and N-metabolism-related genes has been evaluated.

Background: High-affinity nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) genes have been implicated in nitrate absorption and remobilization under nitrogen (N) starvation stress in many plant species, yet little is known about this gene family respond to various stresses often occurs in the production of rapeseed (Brassica napus L.).

Results: This report details identification of 17 NRT2 gene family members in rapeseed, as well as, assessment of their expression profiles using RNA-seq analysis and qRT-PCR assays. In this study, all BnNRT2.1 members, BnNRT2.2a and BnNRT2.4a were specifically expressed in root tissues, while BnNRT2.7a and BnNRT2.7b were mainly expressed in aerial parts, including as the predominantly expressed NRT2 genes detected in seeds. This pattern of shoot NRT expression, along with homology to an Arabidopsis NRT expressed in seeds, strongly suggests that both BnNRT2.7 genes play roles in seed nitrate accumulation. Another rapeseed NRT, BnNRT2.5 s, exhibited intermediate expression, with transcripts detected in both shoot and root tissues. Functionality of BnNRT2s genes was further outlined by testing for adaptive responses in expression to exposure to a series of environmental stresses, including N, phosphorus (P) or potassium (K) deficiency, waterlogging and drought. In these tests, most NRT2 gene members were up-regulated by N starvation and restricted by the other stresses tested herein. In contrast to this overall trend, transcription of BnNRT2.1a was up-regulated under waterlogging and K deficiency stress, and BnNRT2.5 s was up-regulated in roots subjected to waterlogging. Furthermore, the mRNA levels of BnNRT2.7 s were enhanced under both waterlogging stress and P or K deficiency conditions. These results suggest that these three BnNRT2 genes might participate in crosstalk among different stress response pathways.

Conclusions: The results presented here outline a diverse set of NRT2 genes present in the rapeseed genome that collectively carry out specific functions throughout rapeseed development, while also responding not just to N deficiency, but also to several other stresses. Targeting of individual BnNRT2 members that coordinate rapeseed nitrate uptake and transport in response to cues from multiple stress response pathways could significantly expand the genetic resources available for improving rapeseed resistance to environmental stresses.

Keywords: High-affinity nitrate transporter, NRT2, Rapeseed, Various stresses

Nitrate uptake by plant roots from soil solution is mediated by members of three gene families, namely the NitRate Transporter families (NRT1 and NRT2) and the Nitrate Assimilation Related family (NAR2) (see reviews by Miller et al., 2009; Dechorgnat et al., 2011; Tsay et al., 2011). Full activity of the inducible high-affinity nitrate transport system (IHATS) in roots of Arabidopsis thaliana requires expression of two transporters, namely, NRT2.1 and NRT2.2, both of which are members of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). Evidence for this assertion is based upon the high degree of correlation between physiological activity of the IHATS and transcript abundance of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 in wild-type (WT) lines and the reduction of IHATS in mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.1 and or AtNRT2.2 (Zhuo et al., 1999; Filleur et al., 2001; Okamoto et al., 2003; Li et al., 2007). Nevertheless, it was first shown in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii that the NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 genes require simultaneous expression of another gene called NAR2 in order to express high-affinity nitrate transport (Quesada et al., 1994). In A. thaliana also, disruption of NAR2.1 (NRT3.1), in a T-DNA insertional mutant Atnar2.1-1, caused an almost complete loss of inducible high-affinity nitrate influx (Okamoto et al., 2006; Orsel et al., 2006). This observation is now readily explained by the demonstration that AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 form part of a $1 5 0 \mathrm { - k D a }$ plasma membrane (PM) complex (Yong et al., 2010) that was suggested to be a tetramer consisting of two subunits each of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1. Further, it was proposed that the $1 5 0 \mathrm { - k D a }$ complex is the functional high-affinity nitrate transporter in A. thaliana. Interestingly, this complex, as is AtNRT2.1, is absent from PM preparations derived from NAR2.1 mutants (Wirth et al., 2007; Yong et al., 2010), suggesting that AtNRT2.1n only exist in the root PM in association with AtNAR2.1. Membrane interactions between AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 were clearly indicated earlier by heterologous expression in the yeast two-hybrid and Xenopus oocytes systems. Only when oocytes were injected with both AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 RNA was nitrate uptake into oocytes detected (Orsel et al., 2006). In addition to A. thaliana, the two-component nitrate uptake system of NRT2 and NAR2 has been demonstrated to be present in other plant species such as barley (Hordeum vulgare) and rice (Oryza sativa) (Glass, 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2011). Yeast two-hybridization showed that OsNAR2.1 interacted not only with OsNRT2.1 ⁄ OsNRT2.2, but also with OsNRT2.3a (Feng et al., 2011). In a study of NRT2 ⁄ NAR2 interactions in barley, it was suggested that the C-terminus of HvNRT2.1 is possibly involved in binding to the HvNAR2.3 central region and that the Ser463 present in the HvNRT2.1 C-terminus plays a role in the binding ability (Ishikawa et al., 2009).

In addition to AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2, there are five other members of the NRT2 gene family in A. thaliana, NRT2.3 to NRT2.7 (Orsel et al., 2002; Okamoto et al., 2003). Quantitatively, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are responsible for c. $8 0 \%$ of IHATS in A. thaliana (Li et al., 2007). The remaining $2 0 \%$ is probably attributable to expression of a constitutive high-affinity transport system (CHATS) and CHL1 (NRT1.1). Although a role for AtNRT2.7 in seed nitrate accumulation has been proposed (Chopin et al., 2007) and expression patterns of the remaining NRT2 genes have been documented (Orsel et al., 2002; Okamoto et al., 2003), their functions and possible interactions with NAR2 are unknown.

In the present study, therefore, we have used heterologous expression in the yeast two-hybrid system and transient expression in A. thaliana leaf protoplasts to look for possible interactions between AtNAR2.1 and the other NRT2 genes (AtNRT2.2 to AtNRT2.7) and to localize the demonstrated interactions in planta. To explore the physiological functions of the NRT2 polypeptides we have used transient expression of AtNRT2.1 to AtNRT2.7 (plus or minus AtNAR2.1) and $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake into Xenopus oocytes.

A large proportion of the nitrate $( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } )$ ) acquired by plants from soil is actively transported via members of the NRT families of ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters. In Arabidopsis, the NRT1 family has eight functionally characterised members and predominantly comprises low-affinity transporters; the NRT2 family contains seven members which appear to be high-affinity transporters; and there are two NRT3 (NAR2) family members which are known to participate in high-affinity transport. A modified reciprocal best hit (RBH) approach was used to identify putative orthologues of the Arabidopsis NRT genes in the four fully sequenced grass genomes (maize, rice, sorghum, Brachypodium). We also included the poplar genome in our analysis to establish whether differences between Arabidopsis and the grasses may be generally applicable to monocots and dicots. Our analysis reveals fundamental differences between Arabidopsis and the grass species in the gene number and family structure of all three families of NRT transporters. All grass species possessed additional NRT1.1 orthologues and appear to lack NRT1.6/NRT1.7 orthologues. There is significant separation in the NRT2 phylogenetic tree between NRT2 genes from dicots and grass species. This indicates that determination of function of NRT2 genes in grass species will not be possible in cereals based simply on sequence homology to functionally characterised Arabidopsis NRT2 genes and that proper functional analysis will be required. Arabidopsis has a unique NRT3.2 gene which may be a fusion of the NRT3.1 and NRT3.2 genes present in all other species examined here. This work provides a framework for future analysis of ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters and ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport in grass crop species.

Indian mustard (Brassica juncea (L.) Czern and Coss) is an important source of vegetable oil after soybean and palm oil. Brassica requires $4 0 { - } 5 0 ~ \mathrm { k g }$ more $_ \mathrm { N }$ as compared to cereals ( $30 \%$ more than wheat) (Colton and Sykes 1992). However, the NUE in Brassica species varies between 12 and $36 \%$ depending upon $_ \mathrm { N }$ source and water availability (Gan et al. 2008). Poor NUE is of great concern in Brassica species, therefore, improving NUE is an important alternative for sustainable agriculture.

Nitrate uptake into plants from soil via roots involves two basic transport system identified by kinetic studies: high-affinity (HATS), operating under low external concentration $( K _ { m } < 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , and low-affinity (LATS) operating under higher external concentrations $\mathrm { ( > 5 0 ~ m M ) }$ without saturation (Crawford and Glass 1998). In Arabidopsis, entire family of NRT2 genes comprising of seven members that controls the flux of nitrate from soil into root tissues and throughout the plant system has been characterized. AtNRT2.1 belongs to inducible HATS and is strongly expressed in root plasma membrane under nitrate starvation and down-regulated under increasing nitrate concentration (Filleur and Daniel-Vedele 1999). More than 40 full length cDNA sequences encoding NRT2 transport components have been identified sharing $25 \%$ similarity to crnA gene of Aspergillus nidulans (Trueman et al. 1996) and $43 \%$ with CrNRT2 of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Zhou et al. 2000). The NRT2 genes cloned and characterised from crop plants include BnNRT2 (B. napus) (Faure-Rabasse et al. 2002), GmNRT2 (Glycine max) (Amarasinghe et al. 1998), NpNRT2.1 (N. plumbaginifolia) (Fraisier et al. 2000), HvNRT2.1 (BCH1) and HvNRT2.2 (BCH2) from barley (Vidmar et al. 2000) and TaNRT2.1 (Yin et al. 2007) from Triticum aestivum. In the present study, an attempt was made to isolate a fulllength cDNA of high-affinity nitrate transporter from Indian mustard.

Nitrogen (N) is a primary constituent of proteins and nucleotides that are essential for life. Nitrogen accounts for approximately $2 \mathrm { - } 5 \%$ of the total dry biomass of plants (Xu et  al., 2012). Nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right)$ is a major source of nitrogen in most plants grown in agricultural and natural systems (Wang et  al., 2018). As plants have adapted to variable soil nitrate concentrations, sophisticated nitrate transporter systems have evolved. During the past two decades, four families of nitrate transport proteins, namely, nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel (CLC), and slow anion channel associated homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been identified in higher plants (Krapp et  al., 2014). Among these, NRT1.1, which has multiple functions, is one of the most well-studied. Initially, NRT1.1 was characterised as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter involved in nitrate uptake by roots, as well as root-to-shoot nitrate translocation in Arabidopsis (Liu et  al., 1999; Léran et  al., 2013). Independent of its transport function,

NRT1.1 was later shown to serve as a main nitrate sensor that regulates many aspects of physiological and developmental responses to nitrate, including regulating the expression levels of nitrate-related genes, modulating root system architecture, and relieving seed dormancy (Bouguyon et al., 2015). Moreover, NRT1.1 displays auxin transport activity, which relies largely on external nitrate availability in Arabidopsis (Maghiaoui et  al., 2020a). In recent years, specific topics associated with the transport and sensing functions of NRT1.1 have been discussed in several excellent reviews (Sun and Zheng, 2015; Maghiaoui et  al., 2020b; Vidal et  al., 2020; Wang et  al., 2020b). A series of studies on NRT1.1 have also provided new insights into its function in multiple abiotic stresses in plants. In this review, we briefly summarise the important milestones in the discovery process, dual-affinity features, and structural basis of the dual transport/sensing function of NRT1.1  in Arabidopsis. More importantly, we highlight the most recently characterised functions of NRT1.1  in plant abiotic stress resistance and the correlation between NRT1.1-mediated nitrate transport/signalling and different abiotic stresses, mainly in Arabidopsis (Table  1).

## Discovery of NRT1.1

Defoliation is caused by a variety of biotic and abiotic factors and is a major traumatic event which threatens plant’s survival. Large-scale defoliation events in trees are common, especially during periodical outbreaks of defoliating insects such as tent caterpillars (Cooke et al. 2011). In trembling aspen (Populus tremuloides), epidemic outbreaks of forest tent caterpillar (Malacosoma disstria Hbn.) occur on an average at about 10-year intervals (Churchill et al. 1964; Cooke et al. 2011) and can lead to complete defoliation of entire tree stands. Plants which are commonly exposed to defoliation have developed various adaptations to prevent the loss of leaves and to cope with its consequences once defoliation takes place. Fully defoliated aspen trees produce new leaves by precocious break of the lateral buds; however, if defoliation is only partial, lateral buds may remain inhibited until the following growth season (Donaldson and Lindroth 2008).

The loss of photosynthetic area and the resulting depletion of energy reserves are among the main concerns in defoliated trees (Churchill et al. 1964; Landhäusser and Lieffers 2012). In trembling aspen trees, the recovery of root energy reserves may take up to 2 years following partial defoliation (Landhäusser and Lieffers 2012) and affect long-term hydraulic performance of trees (Anderegg and Callaway 2012). On the other hand, compensatory responses which may offset some of the loss of foliage have been reported for plants in which partial defoliation stimulated photosynthetic rates in the remaining leaves (Thomson et al. 2003; Turnbull et al. 2007; Quentin et al. 2012). The transient increase in photosynthesis may be accompanied by an increase in transpiration rates or stomatal conductance (Gálvez and Tyreee 2009; Quentin et al. 2012). However, the signaling pathways leading to these responses remain unclear.

The loss of foliage alters the water and hormonal balance in trees. The water demand of a partly defoliated tree will depend on the degree of the photosynthetic compensation response and the involvement of stomatal conductance in this response. In fully defoliated trees, the demand for water will be greatly reduced until the expansion of leaf primordia commences in lateral buds and new leaves emerge. Partial defoliation lowers the tree’s transpirational area and causes a rapid increase in the root-to-shoot mass ratio. Therefore, adjustments in the energy-costly maintenance processes of root hydraulic conductance could be desirable to reflect changes in the transpirational demand.

Plant water transport is driven by fast, transpirationdriven and slow, osmotically driven forces (Steudle and Peterson 1998). In both cases, water moves along the leastresistance pathways and there is extensive evidence which points to aquaporins as the principal structures responsible for regulating water flow resistance in roots and leaves (Javot and Maurel 2002; Heinen et al. 2009; Shatil-Cohen et al. 2011). The synthesis and opening of aquaporins are energy-demanding (Kamaluddin and Zwiazek 2001). Therefore, adjustments of root hydraulic conductivity to reflect changes in the total transpirational demand may help conserve limited energy resources which are needed in defoliated plants for defense mechanisms, wound repair, and re-growth of new leaves.

The role of leaf aquaporins in regulating water transport processes is still the subject of an intensive debate (Heinen et al. 2009; Shatil-Cohen et al. 2011). If leaf aquaporins play a significant role in regulating leaf water transport in aspen, the effect of defoliation on leaf water flow properties offers an excellent opportunity to study the role of leaf aquaporins since the removal of leaves changes an overall hydraulic balance of the plant. It has been estimated that the resistance of leaves to water transport accounts for as much as $80 \%$ of the total plant hydraulic resistance (Sack and Holbrook 2006). Leaf hydraulic conductance has been often correlated with photosynthetic capacity, maximum stomatal conductance and stomatal pore area per leaf area (Aasamaa and Sõber 2001; Sack et al. 2003; Brodribb et al. 2005). If defoliation triggers an increase in photosynthesis and transpiration of the remaining leaves, it is likely that the increased water transport to the leaves is facilitated by the increased hydraulic conductance, possibly mediated by aquaporins. Increased root (Lee et al. 2008; Laur and Hacke 2013) and leaf (Lee et al. 2009; Lopez et al. 2013) hydraulic conductance has been often reported to accompany increased transpirational demand and may be accompanied by the increased expression of aquaporins (Laur and Hacke 2013; Lopez et al. 2013).

In the present study, we examined the effects of partial and complete defoliation on gas exchange, water transport and aquaporin expression in trembling aspen (Populus tremuloides) seedlings. The study was carried out to examine the adjustments in water relations of trembling aspen seedlings following defoliation and the processes involved in these responses. We examined the hypothesis that defoliation would (1) decrease root hydraulic conductivity to reflect reduced transpirational demand of the partly defoliated plants and (2) increase leaf hydraulic conductance to keep up with the increased water demand of the remaining leaves (compensation response). We also hypothesized that these changes would be accompanied by changes in the aquaporin expression in leaves and roots, which would impact cell-to-cell water transport. To study a possible role of chemical signals originating in shoots on plant hydraulic responses to defoliation, we also girdled stems of plants prior to defoliation to block the basipetal transport through the phloem and vascular cambium.

Plant roots require sufficient amount of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ for respiration and growth [1]. Contrary to anoxia, that is characterized by a total absence of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ plant roots commonly experience periods of hypoxia, especially when $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ availability is reduced due to waterlogging [2] or soil compaction [3, 4]. Even in a normoxic environment, $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ gradients exist across tissues due to the differences in metabolic rates [5].

Although most of the terrestrial plant species cannot survive long-term $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ deficiency, some plants have developed effective strategies to either increase $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ delivery to roots or to tolerate short-term disruptions of the metabolism and the resulting toxicity [6].

Root hypoxia commonly alters plant water relations and may cause wilting [7, 8]. This effect was attributed to changes in the root system architecture [9] and an inhibition of aquaporin-mediated root water transport resulting in a decrease of root hydraulic conductivity [10, 11]. Aquaporins play a central role in plant water relations by regulating water flow resistance, which is especially important for the radial pathway in roots [9]. Aquaporin-mediated and apoplastic water transport interact with each other and regulate plant water balance [7, 12]. In addition to water, aquaporins can transport other small molecules including $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ [13], $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ [14] and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ [15]. Plant aquaporins show high diversity with more than 30 different homologs in all of the examined species [9]. In higher plants, five subfamilies of aquaporins have been described including the PIPs (plasma membrane intrinsic proteins), TIPs (tonoplast membrane intrinsic proteins), NIPs (nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins), SIPs (small intrinsic proteins) and XIPs (uncategorized intrinsic proteins).

Aquaporins mediate root hydraulic adjustments in response to environmental factors [16]. Aquaporin expression [15], membrane trafficking [17], and posttranslational regulation [18] have been implicated in regulating cell-tocell water transport in response to environmental stress. The closure of aquaporins through intracellular acidosis [11] and energy deprivation [19] was also proposed to be among the reasons for the decreased water uptake by hypoxic roots. Recently, a potassium-dependent $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ sensing pathway was proposed in Arabidopsis, which may regulate the aquaporin activity [20]. Although the inhibition of root hydraulic conductivity by hypoxia is a commonly observed phenomenon, it cannot be clearly correlated with the expression levels of water-transporting aquaporins and both decreases and increases of gene expression levels encoding for different PIP2 aquaporins have been reported in hypoxic roots [7, 21]. On the other hand, increased gene expression by root hypoxia of the NIP and PIP1 aquaporins was reported to be involved in the transport of lactate [22, 23], $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ [24], and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ [15] in plants, suggesting a possible role of these aquaporins in hypoxia tolerance.

The inhibitory effects of hypoxia on root water transport in some plants could be partly reversed by the exposure of roots to exogenous ethylene [19]. Ethylene synthesis and accumulation in plants can be induced by various biotic and abiotic stress, including drought [25], wounding [26], and flooding stresses [27], and is produced through the Yang cycle [28]. The effects of ethylene are mediatedby the downstream transcriptional activities of a group of Ethylene Response Factors (ERFs), which are rapidly upregulated following an exposure of plants to hypoxia [29]. Ethylene can improve plant hypoxia tolerance through the stimulation of adventitious roots and aerenchyma formation [29–31], however, only a few studies have focused on the relationship between ethylene and aquaporinmediated water transport [31]. Aquaporins were reported to be involved in the ripening of grape berry and latex yield of rubber tree that were regulated by ethylene [32, 33] and it was recently reported that the cell water transport in Arabidopsis was increased by ethylene through the enhanced C-Terminal phosphorylation of AtPIP2;1 [29].

While these findings provide possible links between ethylene and aquaporin abundance as well as posttranslational regulation of aquaporins, more information is still needed for comprehensive understanding of the processes involved in regulation of root water transport by ethylene.

In the present study, we examined the effects of root hypoxia and exogenous ethylene application on gas exchange, water transport and the expression of ERF and aquaporin genes in trembling aspen (P. tremuloides) seedlings to shed more light on the regulation of aquaporinmediated water transport by $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ deficiency and ethylene. It was hypothesized that the effects of ethylene on root hydraulics under hypoxic conditions involve changes inthe aquaporin gene expression.

Defoliation is a common traumatic event with a major impact on the hydraulic architecture of the affected plant. In our study, aspen plants subjected to partial defoliation decreased $E$ within several minutes following defoliation. However, this initial response was followed by an over twofold increase in $E$ compared with control plants when measured 1 day following defoliation. Changes in $E$ were accompanied by changes in $\mathrm { \Delta P _ { n } }$ , but of a lower magnitude suggesting that the stomatal conductance was not likely the limiting factor to photosynthesis in defoliated plants. Defoliated and non-defoliated plants had similar intercellular $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ concentrations (data not shown). On the other hand, since some of the PIP2 aquaporins were recently demonstrated to be involved in facilitating $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ transport (Mori et al. 2014), we cannot exclude the possibility that the increased PIP2;4 expression in the leaves of partly defoliated plants could facilitate $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ transport and stimulate $\mathrm { \Delta P _ { n } }$ . However, similarly to the barley HvPIP2;4 aquaporin, PIP2;4 from aspen has methionine residue present at position 254 suggesting that it may not have $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ transporting properties (Mori et al. 2014). The photosynthetic compensation response has been frequently observed following defoliation (Tschaplinski and Blake 1995; Quentin et al. 2012; Eyles et al. 2013). The response varies in magnitude between studied plants and may or may not be accompanied by increases in E and (or) stomatal conductance (Gálvez and Tyreee 2009; Quentin et al. 2012). The explanations for the photosynthetic compensation response include changes in source–sink relationship (Tschaplinski and Blake 1995; Pinkard et al. 2011;

Eyles et al. 2013) and the increase in maximum carboxylation rate and RuBP regeneration (Turnbull et al. 2007). Root metabolites (Meinzer and Grantz 1990) and carbohydrates (Eyles et al. 2013) have been implicated as possible signaling molecules for up-regulation of gas exchange in defoliated plants.

Increases in $E$ measured 1 day after partial defoliation in aspen seedlings were accompanied by decreases in leaf water potentials suggesting that the rates of water loss due to increased $E$ likely exceeded the rates of water uptake.

A similar transient decrease in stem water potential which accompanied an increase in stomatal conductance was reported in hybrid poplar (Populus trichocarpa $\times$ deltoides) plants exposed to increased light level (Laur and Hacke

2013). In our study, plant hydraulic adjustments did not take place immediately following defoliation as evidenced by the absence of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ responses when measured $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ following defoliation. However, within 1 day following 50 and $75 \%$ defoliation, $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ decreased to about 75 and $50 \%$ , respectively, compared with the control (non-defoliated) plants. $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ slowly recovered in defoliated plants but the reduction was still present after 3 weeks in plants subjected to $75 \%$ defoliation. In Citrus plants, partial defoliation resulted in higher water potentials and root conductivities, but did not affect stomatal conductance which was probably limited by other factors (Syvertsen 1994). Higher whole plant hydraulic conductance was also reported for defoliated Eucalyptus globulus seedlings (Quentin et al. 2012). Since the resistance of leaves to water transport accounts for $30 \%$ of the total plant hydraulic resistance (Sack and Holbrook 2006), it is likely that the overall effect of defoliation on plant hydraulic conductance may be influenced by the decreased resistance caused by leaf removal and possible changes in leaf hydraulic conductance triggered by defoliation. In our study, $K _ { \mathrm { l a m } }$ increased by about six times in one-day defoliation treatments and returned to the control level 1 week following defoliation. However, 3 weeks after defoliation, $50 \%$ -defoliated plants had again higher $K _ { \mathrm { l a m } }$ and $E$ compared with non-defoliated plants, likely reflecting renewed growth of newly flushed shoots. Diurnal changes in leaf hydraulic conductance largely reflected those in stomatal conductance in Populus trichocarpa and $P .$ nigra leaves suggesting that a regulation of both processes in leaves may be linked (Lopez et al. 2013).

The decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ is a logical rapid response of plants to the large loss of transpiration area and the resulting decrease in water demand in plants which lost 50 or $75 \%$ of their foliage. However, the large increases of $E$ in oneday-defoliated plants at least partly compensated for the lost transpiration area. A similar phenomenon was reported for partly defoliated sugarcane (Meinzer and Grantz 1990). The decrease of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ at the time the transpiration rates increased is in contrast to the commonly observed responses to other environmental stresses where $E$ and stomatal conductance were usually synchronized with $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ (Wan et al. 2001; Kamaluddin and Zwiazek 2001, 2002). The decrease in leaf water potentials of one-day-defoliated plants suggests that the reduction of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ was among the factors which limited water supply to the leaves. To examine whether the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ involved changes in cell-to-cell water flow in roots, we compared $L _ { \mathrm { p c } }$ in root cortical cells of non-defoliated (control) plants and in plants subjected to $75 \%$ defoliation treatment for 1 day. Since the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p c } }$ was of a similar magnitude to the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } } ,$ we concluded that the inhibition of cell-to-cell transport in roots was the principal factor responsible for the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } } .$

The increase in $K _ { \mathrm { l a m } }$ in defoliated plants which accompanied the increase in transpiration rates demonstrates the importance of a dynamic regulation of leaf water transport to a plant’s water balance. The pivotal role of aquaporins in root water transport regulation has been well documented (Maurel et al. 2010; Lee et al. 2012). More recently, the importance of leaf aquaporins in hydraulic responses to environmental cues received considerable attention (Cochard et al. 2007; Voicu et al. 2009; Lopez et al. 2013; Pou et al. 2013). Changes in hydraulic properties of roots and leaves of aspen seedlings that were triggered by defoliation were accompanied by profound changes in the expression of both root and leaf aquaporins. In the roots of one-day-defoliated plants, the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ was accompanied by a large decrease in PIP1;2 expression while in the leaves, the most striking change was the large increase in the expression of PIP2;4. Both PIP1;2 and PIP2;4 were among the highly expressed PIPs in roots and leaves of aspen seedlings, respectively, and following defoliation, PIP2;4 showed higher expression in the leaves than any other PIP. These PIPs were reported to be expressed in all studied organs of $P .$ tremula $\times$ tremuloides rooted cuttings, however, the isoform PIP1;2 showed an increase in mycorrhizal roots where $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ was also increased (Marjanovic´ et al. 2005). Although PIP1 isoforms show very low water permeability in heterologous expression, their water permeability increases when they interact with PIP2 isoforms in a heterotetrameric complex (Fetter et al. 2004; Temmei et al. 2005; Zelazny et al. 2007). In fact, PtPIP1;3 from Populus trichocarpa, which shares $99 \%$ identity with PIP1;2 from $P .$ tremuloides, was shown to play a major role in refilling of embolized vessels (Secchi and Zwieniecki 2010) and was found to be responsive to drought in $P .$ simonii $\times \ b a l$ - samifera (Almeida-Rodriguez et al. 2010).

PIP2 aquaporins have been shown to be the major water channels in plants (Chrispeels et al. 2001). PIP2;4 shows $99 \%$ similarity with $P .$ trichocarpa PIP2;4 which, when expressed in oocytes, increased their permeability by fivefold (Secchi et al. 2009). Putative orthologs of PIP2;4 include JrPIP2;1 and JrPIP2;2 from Junglas regia and AtPIP2;5 from A. thaliana.

There is growing evidence of the importance of leaf and root aquaporins in adjusting plant hydraulic properties to transpirational demand. In J. regia, the increase in PIP transcript levels in response to light was reported to be functionally linked to the increase in leaf hydraulic conductance (Cochard et al. 2007). The increased gene expression of several root aquaporins including PIP1;1, PIP1;2, PIP1;3, PIP2;3; PIP2;4, and PIP2;5 was reported in $P .$ trichocarpa $\times$ deltoids exposed to increased humidity and light levels (Laur and Hacke 2013). In both cases, the changes in root aquaporin expression were accompanied by changes in root water flow (Laur and Hacke 2013). Exposure to light also induced gene expression of several leaf aquaporins and triggered an accumulation of PIP2 proteins in leaves of $P .$ trichocarpa and $P .$ nigra which was accompanied by increases in leaf hydraulic conductance (Lopez et al. 2013). In our study, the reduction in root PIP1;2 levels and the increase in leaf PIP2;4 did not occur in plants after 1 and 3 weeks of defoliation suggesting that the longer term regulation of hydraulic properties also involved other mechanisms. Both root (Laur and Hacke 2013) and leaf (Lopez et al. 2013) PIP aquaporin expression followed a complex pattern in response to light in the studied poplars and it was suggested that they are regulated through adjustments in the levels of transcripts and proteins in response to environmental factors (Lopez et al. 2013).

To investigate possible signals triggering changes in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ and root PIP expression, we girdled the stems of seedlings above the root collar prior to complete defoliation. Similarly to partial defoliation, complete defoliation reduced $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ by about $50 \%$ and was carried out to remove a possible source of chemical signals (Schachtman and Goodger 2008; Eyles et al. 2013) transported in the phloem from the leaves and which could affect $L _ { \mathrm { p r } } .$ Girdling treatment did not affect $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ in non-defoliated plants and did not prevent the reduction of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ in plants defoliated for 1 and 10 days. Therefore, it is unlikely that the carbohydrates (Eyles et al. 2013) or other phloem-transported signaling molecules (Schachtman and Goodger 2008) could be responsible for the inhibition of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ in defoliated aspen seedlings. It is also unlikely that sparse wood axial parenchyma (Ache et al. 2010) could provide a significant alternative pathway for basipetal transport to roots in girdled seedlings (Wan et al. 2006).

In conclusion, partial and complete defoliation of aspen seedlings triggered a decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } } .$ One day after the defoliation treatment, the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ was proportional to the degree of defoliation and was accompanied by the decrease in $L _ { \mathrm { p c } }$ of root cortical cells as well as a profound reduction in the root expression levels of PIP1;2. Partial (50 and $7 5 \ \%$ ) defoliation also increased $K _ { \mathrm { l a m } }$ in one-daydefoliated seedlings and the magnitude of this increase was similar in both defoliation treatments. The increase in $K _ { \mathrm { l a m } }$ was accompanied by an over $100 \%$ increase in E and a five- to tenfold increase in the leaf expression of PIP2;4. The decrease of $L _ { \mathrm { p r } }$ in defoliated plants could not be prevented by girdling suggesting that the response was not likely due to chemical signals which originated in the shoots. The results point to the importance of root and leaf aquaporins in the coordination of plant hydraulic responses to defoliation and in adjustments of plant hydraulic properties to changes in transpirational demand.
