[61] showed the efficiency of chitosan treatment in enhancing the salt tolerance of saffron and okra plants. The obtained results show that, if applied under proper dosages, chitosan enhanced growth performance and up-regulated the ZmPIP gene expression, which could promote a more effective root apparatus able to better take up and retain water. Additionally, chitosan reduces transpiration rates, thereby maintaining higher relative water content in leaves under adverse conditions. These observations align with the current study’s results, indicating that chitosan’s modulation of ZmPIP expression and its positive effects on root development contribute significantly to improved plant water status during stress. Moreover, chitosan has shown metabolic balance regulation and accumulation of polyamines, which increased plant tolerance against salt stress. For example, in one study conducted on tomato plants, chitosan application resulted in a higher level of gene expression related to stress responses and thus facilitated better growth under saline conditions [62]. This, in a nutshell, means that chitosan plays an important role in enhancing ZmPIP gene expression for the improvement of root system efficiency as a biostimulant against salt stress in plants. Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase $( P A L )$ is a crucial enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, playing a significant role in plant responses to abiotic stresses, including salinity. In Brassica napus (rapeseed), the PAL1 gene has been observed to be upregulated under salt stress conditions, contributing to the synthesis of phenolic compounds that aid in stress mitigation. PAL is an important regulatory enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, which plays a crucial role in the responses of plants to abiotic stresses, including salinity. The PAL1 gene in Brassica napus (rapeseed) was induced under salt stress, thus contributing to the synthesis of phenolic compounds involved in stress mitigation [63]. The effects of chitosan treatment under saline conditions in rapeseed have been associated with the increased expression of the PAL1 gene, hence synergistic enhancement of plant defense responses. This contributes to better growth performance and improved stress resilience through enhanced antioxidative capacity and structural maintenance at the cellular level [64]. The interaction of chitosan treatment and the expression of the PAL1 gene play critical roles in the rapeseed responses to salt stress. Enhanced activities of PAL elevate the phenolic content, becoming indispensable for countering oxidative damage and keeping physiological functions alive under severe conditions. This work contributes to pointing out the chitosan effectiveness as a biostimulant product in order to enhance resilience to salinity stress of crops.

Enzymes involved in plant defense, such as phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), chitinase, and $\beta$ -1,3-glucanase, along with reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging enzymes like catalase, peroxidase, and polyphenol oxidase, are all stimulated by chitosan [64]. The results indicated that, at 45 days after sowing (DAS), chitosan pretreatment increased PAL activity in sweet basil plants at concentrations ranging from 0.1 to $1 \%$ . However, at lower chitosan concentrations of $0 . 0 1 { - } 0 . 0 5 \%$ , PAL activity was comparable to control values [65]. These findings align with the results of this study. Rashidi et al. [66]. examined the effect of chitosan on gene expression, as well as some morphological and physiological traits of sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum L.) under salinity stress. Their findings demonstrated that chitosan enhanced growth parameters in both stressed and non-stressed conditions compared to the controls. In this context, chitosan increased the levels of protein and chlorophyll, along with the expression of the COVMT and PAL genes, resulting in an increase in phenolic compounds. These results are consistent with those observed in this study.

Plants subjected to salt stress may alter their protein composition or produce new proteins as a means of adapting to changing environmental conditions. Certain metabolites are generated under stress that mitigate the damage caused by salt stress. Variations in the expression of the PAL1 gene drive this mechanism, resulting in either a decrease or increase in structural or enzymatic proteins [67]. Numerous studies demonstrate the connection between PAL1 and the phenolic pathway, particularly in plants experiencing abiotic stressors such as salinity [68]. Salinity stress affects various aspects of plant growth, biological activities, and chlorophyll content. Reports indicate a decrease in chlorophyll content during salt stress, attributed to increased oxidation and degradation of chlorophyll caused by the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Furthermore, the reduction in chlorophyll is correlated with the level of salinity [69–70, 71].

In the present study, the amounts of total chlorophyll, carotenoids, and chlorophyll a, b, and c in rapeseed plants decreased under salt stress. The results indicated a significant decline in chlorophyll content when salinity stress reached a threshold of $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . This reduction in chlorophyll biosynthesis may be attributed to the increased utilization of glutamate, a precursor in both the chlorophyll and proline synthesis pathways. During salinity stress, competition between glutamine kinase (the enzyme responsible for proline production) and glutamate ligase (the first enzyme in the chlorophyll biosynthesis pathway) can lead to diminished chlorophyll biosynthesis [72–73]. These findings are consistent with our research. The results indicated that chitosan treatment led to an increase in the levels of chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, total chlorophyll, and carotenoids in rapeseed. In research conducted by Abu-Muriefah [74]. water stress resulted in a decline in photosynthetic pigments in bean plants (Phaseolus vulgaris L.); however, the application of chitosan increased pigment concentrations in these plants. Additionally, Zayed et al. [75]. demonstrated that chitosan mitigated the negative effects of salt stress in Phaseolus vulgaris L., resulting in enhanced levels of carotenoids and chlorophyll a and b. Alenazi et al. [40]. investigated the effects of chitosan (Cs) and chitosan nanoparticles (CsNPs) on Phaseolus vulgaris L. under salinity stress. Their findings revealed that the application of either Cs or CsNPs significantly improved yield, pigment content, carbohydrate content, proline levels, and the antioxidant system in plants subjected to salt stress. Furthermore, these treatments reduced hydrogen peroxide levels, lipid peroxidation, and electrolyte leakage. Similarly, Jiao et al. [76]. reported that chitosan positively influenced root development, photosynthetic traits, and the antioxidant system, thereby enhancing salinity tolerance in maize plants. These findings collectively support the recommendation to utilize chitosan as an effective strategy for improving salinity tolerance in crops.

Ullah et al. [77]. investigated the reduction of the negative effects of salt stress on tomato yield through the exogenous application of chitosan. Their findings demonstrated that foliar spraying of chitosan at a concentration of $1 5 0 \mathrm { m g / L }$ positively influenced tomato yield under $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ salt stress; however, various salinity applications adversely affected nearly all evaluated parameters. Additionally, Moradbeygi et al. [78] examined the enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defense mechanisms in Dracocephalum moldavica L. in response to salt stress using iron oxide nanoparticles. Their results indicated that plants treated with a $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ solution exhibited higher levels of total phenolic compounds, flavonoids, and anthocyanins, along with increased activities of guaiacol peroxidase, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and glutathione reductase. Furthermore, Frary et al. [79] reported that the flavonoid content in Solanum pennellii increased in response to salt stress, corroborating the findings of the present study.

Consistent with the findings of this study, Ali et al. [80] examined the impact of salinity on Origanum majorana and found an increase in flavonoid content. Similarly, Bistgani et al. [81] investigated the effects of salt on two types of thyme, Thymus vulgaris L. and Thymus daenensis Celak, and reported that flavonoid levels rose under saline conditions. Research has also demonstrated that rice plants exposed to salt stress exhibit higher total flavonoid content, suggesting that flavonoids may play a protective role under stress by accumulating in plant tissues to shield them from damage [82].

Furthermore, Coqueiro et al. [83]. found that chitosan application led to an increase in flavonoid content in tomato plants. A study on the effects of chitosan under water stress in white clover (Trifolium repens) revealed that flavonoid content also increased with chitosan treatment during drought conditions. This accumulation is thought to be associated with the antioxidant defense and osmotic regulation of stressed plants [71]. Additionally, Emami et al. [84]. documented an increase in flavonoid compounds when thyme (Thymus daenensis Celak) was treated with chitosan. Moreover, studies on Isatis tinctoria L. and Salvia officinalis L. hair cultures demonstrated that chitosan enhances the concentration of flavonoid components in these plants [85–86].

In this study, rapeseed plants were cultivated for 20 days under saline conditions with chitosan pretreatment, which significantly increased proline levels in both the aerial and root regions of the plants. Shams Peykani et al. [87]. demonstrated that coating seeds with chitosan enhanced the growth parameters of seedlings, specifically in Triticum aestivum L. and Zea mays L., while mitigating the negative effects of salt stress. The application of low concentrations of chitosan resulted in improved proline content and antioxidant enzyme activity, along with reduced malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation. In conclusion, an adequate dose of chitosan improved growth performance and biochemical marker variations under salinity stress. According to Sheikha and Al-Maliki [88]. and Khan et al. [89]., the application of varying concentrations of chitosan enhances plant defense mechanisms against various stresses, thereby promoting the growth and yield of beans and peas. In addition to its role as a beneficial biomolecule, chitosan is also recognized as a signaling molecule and a growth regulator [90]. According to a study by Sadak and Talaat [91]., complete soluble sugars (TSS), proline content, and phenolic compounds significantly increased when chitosan or calcium carbonate was applied to wheat plants. Research on proline levels in wheat plants under stress, including studies by Ku et al. [92] on Nicotiana benthamiana, El-Bassiouny and Sadak [93] on flax, and Ibrahim et al. [94] on sunflower, corroborated the observed increase in proline. Proline and TSS, two major components of organic osmolytes, are elevated in plants under stress. This increase may facilitate the adjustment of cellular osmotic potential, resulting in improved water absorption and translocation under salinity stress [95]. Additionally, proline acts as a scavenger of free radicals, protecting various enzymes and cellular structures from oxidative damage [96]. Data from Aazami et al. [97]. demonstrated that foliar spraying of grape plants with chitosan-starch nanocomposites (CS-SA NCs) significantly influenced proline levels. Proline’s ability to inhibit the growth of reactive oxygen species (ROS), enhance osmotic regulation, and protect membrane structures explains the observed improvement in cellular protection [80].

One of the most significant roles of amino acids in plants is their ability to withstand salt stress. They accomplish this through various mechanisms, such as regulating osmotic pressure (with proline and glycine being prominent examples) and eliminating reactive oxygen species [98–99]. Free amino acids can be regarded as a unique water reservoir for plants during salt stress. They aid in regulating [100]. In this investigation, the concentration of free amino acids in rapeseed increased significantly in response to salt stress. Xie et al. [101] demonstrated that Phragmites australis exhibited higher levels of proline and amino acids when exposed to saline conditions. In this study, chitosan at a concentration of $1 0 \mathrm { \ m g / }$ liter significantly increased the free amino acid content. Notably, the levels of free amino acids increased in other treatments, although they decreased at a concentration of $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ in the combined treatment of salinity and chitosan. Rabêlo et al. [102]. investigated the effects of chitosan on maize plants subjected to water stress and found that chitosan application enhanced the concentrations of proline and amino acids. Furthermore, Li et al. [71]. reported that chitosan application on white clover (Trifolium repens) under water stress led to the accumulation of specific amino acids, corroborating the findings of the present investigation. The increase in these compounds, facilitated by chitosan, activates the plants’ antioxidant defense system, promoting osmotic regulation under stress conditions.

Active oxygen species are produced by plants under salinity stress, which subsequently leads to oxidative damage. This oxidative stress causes membrane damage and lipid peroxidation, with the plasma membrane being the first organ to experience salt stress [103]. To gauge the membrane damage induced by oxidative stress from salinity, the production of malondialdehyde (MDA) should be evaluated [104]. In this study, malondialdehyde levels in rapeseed under salt stress increased. Similarly, Taïbi et al. [105]. found that the bean plant (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) exhibited elevated levels of malondialdehyde. In the current study, plants exposed to salt stress showed a decrease in malondialdehyde levels with the application of chitosan, while an increase in malondialdehyde in the aerial portions was observed. Consistent with our findings, research by Jabeen and Ahmad [106]. demonstrated that low concentrations of chitosan reduced malondialdehyde levels in safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.) and sunflower (Helianthus annuus L.). Furthermore, Turk [107] reported that maize seedlings subjected to salt stress exhibited increased malondialdehyde levels, which were significantly reduced to normal levels upon chitosan application. Salinity stress disrupts the natural growth and development of plants due to increases in sodium and potassium ions in the soil environment [108]. This disruption can affect water absorption and lead to ion imbalances. Salinity also impairs the absorption, transfer, and distribution of nutrients, exacerbating the ion imbalance [109]. The findings of this study align with previous research, suggesting that the competition between potassium and sodium during salinity stress results in reduced potassium absorption. Potassium ions are accessed through ion channels in the cell membrane. Due to the similar ionic radii of potassium and sodium, sodium enters the cell under salinity stress, causing a decrease in potassium levels and an increase in sodium levels [110]. In this investigation, the concentration of chlorine in the rapeseed plants increased, whereas phosphorus and nitrogen levels decreased. According to Wahome et al. [111]., elevated chlorine levels disrupt cellular metabolism and impair the absorption of essential components, such as nitrates.

According to the findings of Abdel-Aziz et al. [112], the addition of chitosan to wheat resulted in higher levels of potassium, phosphorus, and nitrogen. Conversely, Rasheed et al. [113] reported that the treatment of pea plants (Pisum sativum L.) with chitosan under cadmium stress led to a decrease in the concentrations of phosphorus, potassium, and calcium. The notable impact of chitosan on plant development may be attributed to the enhanced activity of nitrogen metabolism enzymes, including glutamine synthase, reductase, and protease, as well as improved photosynthesis, which drives plant growth [114–115]. Additionally, gibberellins and other plant hormones are synthesized in response to chitosan, promoting growth by enhancing several auxin biosynthesis-related signaling pathways through a tryptophanindependent mechanism [116–93]. Moreover, the effects of chitosan may be linked to an elevation in cell osmotic pressure, which facilitates the supply and uptake of water and essential nutrients. This increase in osmotic pressure, coupled with enhanced antioxidant and enzyme activities, contributes to the reduction of harmful free radical accumulation [117].

Tolerance to drought stress in plants is a complex phenomenon and involves many changes at both biochemical and physiological levels (Ingram and Bartels, 1996). Mechanisms of osmotic adjustment and modulation of tissue hydraulic conductivity are required to maintain tissue water potential (Bohnert et al., 1995). Such mechanisms, which regulate water flux, are likely to be mediated, in part, by aquaporins (Maurel, 1997).

The discovery of aquaporins has lead to the realization that water flow across membranes may be regulated not only by osmotic pressure differences, but also by modulating the abundance and/ or the activity of aquaporins (Martre et al., 2002). Water that is lost from the leaves through transpiration is replenished by an apoplastic and transcellular water flow from cells that have a higher water potential. Transcellular flow requires the movement of water across the tonoplast and the plasma membrane and such transmembrane water movement is facilitated by aquaporins (Maurel, 1997; Scha¨ ffner, 1998; Luu and Maurel, 2005). It has been proposed that regulation of PIPs in the plasma membrane of root cells may play a key role in controlling radial water uptake, whereas TIPs may rather determine a general role of the vacuole in buffering osmotic fluctuations in the cytoplasm (Maurel et al., 2002).

PIP aquaporins have been shown to be regulated by drought at the transcript level (Mariaux et al., 1998). In this study, all the genes studied showed the highest sequence homology to PIP aquaporins. We aimed to investigate if the AM symbiosis alters the pattern of PIP gene expression as a mechanism to improve plant tolerance to drought stress. Previous studies have shown that the AM fungi can take up water from soil and transfer such water to the host plant. This has been proposed as a mechanism that can help the plant to cope with drought stress (Hardie, 1985; Faber et al., 1991; Ruiz-Lozano and Azco´ n, 1995; Marulanda et al., 2003; Porcel et al., 2003). If AM fungi are transferring water to the root of the host plants, it is expected that the plant must increase its permeability for water and that aquaporin genes should be up-regulated in order to allow a higher rate of transcellular water flow (Javot and Maurel, 2002). In fact, aquaporins are enriched in zones of fast cell division and expansion, or in areas where water flow or solute flux density would be expected to be high. This included biotrophic interfaces between plants and symbiotic bacteria or fungi, as is the case of the AM symbiosis (Tyerman et al., 2002).

In contrast, to the above hypothesis, our results show that the genes studied here are downregulated both in soybean and lettuce under drought stress and that such down-regulation is even more severe in AM plants than in nonAM plants. A similar result has been obtained very recently by Ouziad et al. (2005) regarding the expression of PIP and TIP genes in roots of AM tomato plants subjected to salt stress. The down regulation of the aquaporin genes is not as evident in soybean plants from the first experiment, since the down-regulation of both GmPIP genes in AM and in noninoculated plants is of a similar magnitude (Figures 1A and 4). However, when the expression of GmPIP2 is analyzed in a timecourse, it is clearly visible that AM plants already down-regulated that gene significantly at 5 and 12 dai, while both nonAM control plants still maintained GmPIP2 gene expression almost unaltered. At 20 dai, the more intense down-regulation of that gene in AM plants than in both nonAM plants was still clearly visible. Finally, at 35 days all treatments had the same level of GmPIP2 gene expression. This effect of the AM symbiosis anticipating the down-regulation of GmPIP2 gene may have a physiological importance to help AM plants to cope with drought stress. In fact, according to Aharon et al. (2003), the overexpression of a PIP aquaporin in transgenic tobacco improves plant vigor under favorable growth conditions, but the over-expression of such PIP gene has no beneficial effect under salt stress, and has even negative effect during drought stress, causing fast wilting. Hence, the decreased expression of plasma membrane aquaporin genes during drought stress in AM plants can be a regulatory mechanism to limit the water lost from the cells (Barrieu et al., 1999). In support of this hypothesis, data on leaf $\Psi$ and RWC show that AM plants (soybean and lettuce) had a less negative $\Psi$ and also higher water content than nonAM plants.

The up- or down-regulation by drought stress of mRNAs encoding aquaporins homologues has been described in the roots of many plant species (Javot and Maurel, 2002). There are currently two opposite descriptions of the role of aquaporins in response to dehydration stress (Smart et al., 2001). The first is based on evidence that expression of some aquaporins is induced under dehydration stress (Fray et al., 1994; Yamada et al., 1997; Barrieu et al., 1999; Jang et al., 2004), which is predicted to result in greater membrane water permeability and facilitated water transport. The second is based on the fact that aquaporin activity is down-regulated under dehydration stress, which should result in decreased membrane water permeability and may allow cellular water conservation (Yamada et al., 1995; Johansson et al., 1998; Smart et al., 2001) during periods of dehydration stress.

Data obtained with lettuce plants also colonized by G. mosseae point in the same direction, namely that under drought stress conditions there is a higher down-regulation of the PIP genes studied (and also at the protein level, as revealed by western blot) in AM plants than in nonAM plants. In contrast to G. mosseae, plants colonized by $G$ . intraradices do not exhibit such downregulation of PIP gene expression or protein accumulation. The expression of PIP genes under drought stress in these plants is similar to control nonAM plants. However, functional diversity among different AM fungi has been widely observed in several aspects of the symbiosis. Burleigh et al. (2002) showed that the functional diversity between AM fungal species occurs not only at the level of mycorrhiza formation, plant nutrient uptake or plant growth, but also at the molecular level. These authors studied seven AM fungal species and found that the seven species widely varied in their influence on the root expression of MtPT2 and Mt4 genes from Medicago truncatula and also of LePT1 and TPSI1 genes from Lycopersicon esculentum involved in plant $\mathrm { P }$ nutrition. In the same way, previous studies from our research group showed a differential regulation by both AM fungi of the expression of genes encoding late embryogenesis abundant proteins (Porcel et al., 2005b).

The exact reason for the different influence of G. mosseae and $G$ . intraradices on lettuce PIP gene expression is not known. However, in a previous study, also with lettuce, we evaluated the ability of six AM fungal species, including $G$ . mosseae and $G$ . intraradices, to enhance the amount of soil water uptake by these plants (Marulanda et al., 2003). The study demonstrated that there were substantial differences among the six AM fungi used. One of the most efficient fungi stimulating water uptake by plants was $G$ . intraradices, while G. mosseae showed a reduced ability to improve plant water uptake. This may suggest that the strategy of both fungi to protect the host plant against water deficit is different. G. intraradices seems to have an important capacity to enhance the rate of water uptake by lettuce roots. This means that the water movement in these roots must be enhanced and thus, the root water permeability must also increase, maybe by maintaining high levels of PIP aquaporin gene expression as we observe in this study. Contrarily, $G$ . mosseae seems to direct its strategy for plant protection against water deficit toward the conservation of the water existing in the plant and by that reason down-regulates the expression of PIP genes. Such down-regulation of PIP genes has been interpreted as a mechanism to decrease membrane water permeability and to allow cellular water conservation (Yamada et al., 1995; Johansson et al., 1998; Smart et al., 2001). In any case, both strategies seems to protect the host plant in a similar way since lettuce plants had similar RWC and leaf $\Psi$ regardless of the fungus colonizing their roots.

A curious result obtained in this study concerns the reduced GmPIP2 gene expression in Br plants under well-watered conditions. Apart from the studies describing the soybean Nodulin)26 aquaporin (Dean et al., 1999; Niemietz and Tyerman, 2000), we do not know of any other study describing an effect of Rhizobia on the expression of aquaporins or its meaning for the biological nitrogen fixation. In any case, it is likely that this symbiosis can affect the expression of aquaporin genes as consequence of the changes that the root cells must undergo to accommodate the nodules. In addition, it must be considered that aquaporins not only are water channels, but they also allow passage to small neutral molecules such as glycerol or urea, or small gases such as ammonia or $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ (Luu and Maurel, 2005). Hence, it cannot be discarded that the rhizobial symbiosis can be also regulating the PIP gene expression under well-watered conditions.

In conclusion, results from this study suggest that AM plants respond to drought stress by down-regulating the expression of the two PIP genes studied and anticipating its down-regulation as compared to nonAM plants, rather than by maintaining high levels of these PIP genes expression. This down-regulation of PIP genes is likely to be a mechanism to decrease membrane water permeability and to allow cellular water conservation. It must be considered, however, that as PIP are members of a multi-gene family, other PIP isoforms in soybean and lettuce plants may be regulated differently.

In acid soils the soluble Al ions exist mainly in the trivalent $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ form which damages membranes and rapidly inhibits root growth [29]. A widespread mechanism for Al resistance in many plant species relies on the release of organic anions from roots apices (the sensitive region of the root for Al toxicity). The organic anions, such as malate, citrate and oxalate, are able to chelate $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to prevent it from binding in the cell wall and membranes and from entering the cytosol. This chelation reduces harmful interactions from occurring in the apoplast and in the cytosol of the root apex [30]. The first member of the family identified was TaALMT1 from wheat where it controls the major mechanism for aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ resistance [1]. TaALMT1 is constitutively expressed in the root apices and activated by the $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ cations prevalent in acid soils to release malate anions into the apoplast. Malate chelates the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ which reduces damage to the cell wall, membranes and other cellular components. Other members of the family perform similar functions in Arabidopsis [3,31], rape (Brassica napus L.) [4], rye (Secale cereale L.) [2], soybean (Glycine max L.) [32], alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) [33], and Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus L.) [34]. Regulation of these vary and some show more complex interactions [35]. For instance, AtALMT1 is not constitutively expressed in Arabidopsis roots but induced by low pH and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [3] and GmALMT1 in soybean shows complex interactions with Al stress and phosphorus nutrition [32].

Most members of the ALMT family are not involved in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance but perform other functions on different membranes [21,36]. For example, four members in Arabidopsis (AtALMT4, AtALMT6, AtALMT9 and AtALMT12) and one in barley (Hordeum vulgare L., HvALMT1) are involved in guard cell regulation. This is consistent with the involvement of anion transport in signal transduction and osmotic adjustment in modulating stomatal aperture [5–7,10,18,20]. Electrophysiological studies in Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802) oocytes revealed similarities between the currents generated by AtALMT12 and the previously characterised rapid or R-type/QUAC anion currents which propose that AtALMT12 anion channels are responsible for these currents [6,37]. AtALMT6 localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and facilitates calcium and pH-dependent movement of malate into the vacuole [8], but knockout mutations show little or no phenotype indicating some redundancy in these functions. AtALMT9 also localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and knock-out mutations show impaired stomatal opening in the light and delayed wilting [8,9]. AtALMT9 is activated by cytosolic malate and appears to facilitate chloride movement into the vacuole during stomatal opening. VvALMT9 is a homolog of AtALMT9 in grape (Vitis vinifera L.) and reportedly controls the acidity of berries during fruit maturation by facilitating tartrate, malate and succinate accumulation in the vacuoles of mesocarp cells [15]. A recent study also indicated that the ABA induced anion channel AtALMT4 of mediates $\mathrm { M a l } ^ { 2 - }$ efflux from the vacuole during stomatal closure and its activity depends on phosphorylation [38].

Acidity in apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) similarly relies on the ALMT transporter Ma1 which mediates malate accumulation into the vacuoles of developing fruit cells [14]. In maize (Zea mays L.), ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2 are mainly expressed in root tissues and likely function to assist in balancing charges during nutrient uptake [12,13]. Both proteins localise to the plasma membrane and both are permeable to inorganic anions but ZmALMT2 is also permeable to organic anions as demonstrated by the constitutive release of malate from the roots of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing ZmALMT2 [13]. OsALMT4 is a member of the ALMT family in rice (Oryza sativa L.). OsALMT4 is widely expressed in rice and encodes a malate-permeable anion channel on the plasma membrane. Enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins [39].

Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. SlALMT15 (Solyc11gO6897O) was found to be related to a stomatal density trait that functions in stomatal formation in tomato leaves,and further affects photosynthesis and drought tolerance in tomato (J.Ye,Wang, et al.,2021). Z.Wang et al. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.

Thisreport provides evidence suggesting that SlALMT11 (SolycO8g0o699O) expressed in tomato leaf guard cells is involved in stomatal closure induced by external malate,but not by abscisic acid.This study also highlights how the guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (SlALMT11 and AtALMT12)are activated by external organic acids and identifies the amino acid residues of the ALMT proteins involved in the voltage-dependent channel activity.

The aluminium activated malate transporter (ALMT) gene family is named after the first member of the family identified in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) [1]. The product of this gene controls resistance to aluminium (Al) toxicity. TaALMT1 was the first member of this novel family of genes encoding anion channels. Although widely spread in plants, relatively little information is available on the roles performed by other members of this family. However those that have been characterised show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13], fruit acidity [14,15], microbe interactions [16,17] and seed development [18].

ALMT genes encode transmembrane proteins that function as anion channels and perform multiple functions involving the transport of organic anions (e.g., carboxylates) and inorganic anions in cells [19–21]. Carboxylic acids such as malic and citric acids are important metabolites in plant cells due to their involvement in photosynthesis, the tricaboxylic acid pathway, carbohydrate metabolism, cytosolic pH regulation, contribution to the maintenance of electroneutrality and nutrition [22–24]. These organic anions also confer resistance to Al toxicity in acid soils because when released from roots their carboxyl groups chelate the trivalent Al cations $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ rendering them less toxic [22]. Carboxylic anions can also bind with other multivalent metal ions [21].

Anion channels are integral membrane proteins that form aqueous pores to selectively allow the rapid transport of anions across membranes down their electrochemical gradients [25]. Therefore, anion channels are passive transporters located on many plant membranes including the plasma membrane, tonoplast, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial and chloroplast membranes. Some also perform signalling roles and function as master switches in stress responses [25–27]. The development of the patch-clamping technique provided a method for detailed research on the functioning of ion channels. The patch-clamp technique has been used to investigate the function of some members of the ALMT family. Some are permeable to malate anions while others are also permeable to other organic inions (such as fumarate) or inorganic inions (such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , $\mathrm { N O } ^ { 3 - }$ and less to $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ ). Other useful methods for studying ion channels also include the analysis of substrate concentrations in native and heterologous expression systems. In plants, the guard cells that regulate stomatal aperture have become a popular model system for characterising membrane transport and signal transduction. For instance, in Vicia faba L. guard cells, researchers have identified two types of anion channel considered important for stomatal closure: the rapid-type (R-type) and the slow-type (S-type) [28]. The R-type anion channels can be activated rapidly within $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ by depolarisation and activates potassium release when the membrane potential falls below the equilibrium potential for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ while S-type channels showed a much slower (seconds) voltage-dependent activation and deactivation [20,28].

## 3.1丨 Screening of SIALMT genes expressed in guard cells


Previous studies revealed that the AtALMT12/QUAC1 gene is involved in stomatal closure (Meyer etal., 201O; Sasaki et al., 2010).

To determine which SlALMT genes are expressed in tomato guard cells，the expression levels of 16 SIALMT genes were compared between the epidermis and whole leaves by semi-quantitative RTPCR (Figure 1a and Supporting Information: Figure S1).Three SIALMT genes，SIALMT4，SIALMT5，and SIALMT11，were found to be expressed in guard cell-enriched epidermis.The expression level of the SIALMT11 gene relative to that of the SlUBQ gene was higher than those of the SIALMT4 and SIALMT5 genes (Figure 1a and Supporting Information: Figure S1).The SlALMT11 protein is categorized as being in Clade 3 of the ALMT-protein family that also includes AtALMT12 (Sasaki et al.，201O； Sasaki，Tsuchiya，Ariyoshi, Nakano,et al., 2016).The SIALMT11 gene was expressed in leaves, but much less in roots (Figure 1b). Moreover,analysis of transgenic plants expressing GUS or GFP under the control of the SIALMT11 promoter (3187bp upstream of the first ATG) showed that staining or fluorescence was detected in guard cells (Figure 1c and Supporting Information: Figure S2a,b). In contrast，SIALMT4 and SIALMT5 expression was not apparent in the guard cells of plants transformed with the promoter:GUS constructs (Figure 1c).

The subcelllar localization of SlALMT11 was determined by transient expression of the protein fused to GFP in Arabidopsis protoplasts (see Section 2)，where the fluorescence was mainly observed at the surface of the protoplasts (Figure 1d and Supporting Information: Figure S3a).This finding was confirmed by comparing the localization of SlALMT11 protein directly with that of AtPIP2;1 protein that is known to be localized to the plasma membrane (Sorieul et al.,2011).The AtPlP2;1::mCherry could be co-expressed with GFP because of its distinct excitation and emission wavelengths. The fluorescence from GFP::SIALMT11 nearly overlapped with that from the AtPlP2;1:mCherry signals (Figure 1d).These results indicate that SlALMT11 is highly expressed in guard cells and isa plasmamembrane localized protein.Weak fluorescence was observed inside the cells that we attribute to strong autofluorescence from chlorophyll (Figure 1d and Supporting Information: Figure S3b).


## 3.2丨Physiological function of SlALMT11 in stomatal movement


We hypothesized that SlALMT11 might be involved in stomatal closure as is AtALMT12 (Meyer et al., 201O; Sasaki etal., 2010).To examine this hypothesis,we compared stomatal closure in leaves from the wild type with that from two independent RNAi lines suppressing SlALMT11 gene expression (see Section 2). Levels of the SIALMT11 transcript in leaves of two RNAi lines were 1O times lower than that in the wild type (Figure 2a).The density of stomata on the leaves of the two tomato RNAi lines was not different from that of the wild type (Figure 2b).Stomatal aperture in response to exogenous ABA indicated no difference between the RNAi lines and the wild type (Figure 2c,d).Because AtALMT12 expression in Xenopus oocytes showed enhanced inward currents by exogenous malate (Meyer et al.,2010; Mumm et al., 2013), we tested the effect of exogenous malate on stomatal closure.As the malate concentration increased, wild-type stomata closed (Figure 2e,f and Supporting Information: Table S4).In contrast,SIALMT11 RNAi lines were impaired in stomatal closure at $\mathsf { 3 m M }$ malate (Figure 2e,f). Similarly,exogenous malate $( 3 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { M } )$ induced stomatal closure in the Arabidopsis wild type but not in the atalmt12 knock-down line (Supporting Information: Figure S4). Taken together,these results suggested that stomatal closure in response to ABA is different between SIALMT11 and AtALMT12; however, these results also showed that SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 are involved in stomatal closure regulated by apoplastic malate concentrations.


## 3.3|Electrophysiological properties of SIALMT11


Electrophysiological measurements in Xenopus oocytes revealed that AtALMT12 has a bell-shaped current-voltage (I/V) pattern that is dependent on the endogenous and exogenous malate concentrations (Mayer et al.，201O; Mumm et al.，2013)．To elucidate the electrophysiological function of SIALMT11,we injected SlALMT11 cRNA in Xenopus oocytes and used the two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC)method to measure the current magnitude at different membrane voltages (Figure 3a,b).

In oocytes expressing SlALMT11 without malate pre-injection and exposed to a malate bath solution,the inward currents were slightly higher than those in the control oocytes (Figure 3a,b).The inward currents of malate in pre-injected oocytes increased and showed a characteristic bell-shaped I/V pattern (Figure 3b) similar to that of AtALMT12 (Supporting Information: Figure S5；Mumm et al.，2013).Furthermore,in the SIALMT11-expressing oocytes, the peak of the inward current shifted toward a more negative voltage potential in the malate bath solution than in the gluconate bath solution (Figure 3b).In addition,the reversal potentials $( E _ { \mathrm { r e v } } )$ of SIALMT11-expressing oocytes shifted more to the positive direction than that of the water-control oocytes.The positive shift in the reversal potential is remarkable in the malate pre-injected oocytes expressing SlALMT11 (Figure 3b,indicated with arrowheads).These results demonstrated that SlALMT11 is involved in malate efflux that is similar in function to AtALMT12.The malate efflux currents of SIALMT11at the peak voltage $( - 6 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { V } )$ in the bath solution $( 1 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { M }$ sodium gluconate at $\mathsf { p H } 4 . 5$ were not significantlydifferent (with $\mathbf { t } \cdot \mathbf { \tau }$ test) between replicates with $1 0 0 \mu \mathsf { M } \mathsf { A } \mathsf { I C l } _ { 3 }$ $( - 3 0 8 \mathsf { n A } \pm 5 7 \mathsf { S E }$ , $n = 9$ and replicates without ${ \mathsf { A l C l } } _ { 3 }$ $( - 4 3 4 \mathsf { n A } \pm 6 7 \mathsf { S E }$ ， $n = 5$ Thisresult indicates that the transport function of SlALMT11 is not activated by $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ ions.


## 3.4丨Exogenous solution-dependent malate efflux


Because the function of AtALMT12 is regulated by the exogenous malate concentration (Mumm et al.,2013),the effects of several exogenously added organic and inorganic anions on the malate efflux from oocytes expressing SIALMT11 or AtALMT12 were examined (Figure 4).

Malate efflux derived from SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 were activated and generated high，bell-shaped I/V patternsby exogenous fumarate and citrate,as well as malate in the bath solutions (Figure 4a,d),whereas inorganic anions,sulphate, nitrate, and chloride had similar current patterns as the gluconate-based bath solution (Figure 4b,e). Similar to the malate bath solution, fumarate and citrate shifted the relative open probability $( P _ { \mathrm { O } } )$ of the channel to more negative membrane potentials following Boltzmann characteristics (Figure 4c,f)．Malate, fumarate，and citrate shifted the half-maximal activation potential $( V _ { 1 / 2 } )$ to more negative values (about $- 4 0 \mathsf { m V } )$ ）compared to inorganic bath solutions (Figure $_ { 4 \mathrm { g } ) }$ .These results suggest that SlALMT11 and AtALMT12 channels open the channel gate at a more negative membrane potential in bath solutions containing malate,fumarate and citrate，than in bath solutions containing gluconate and inorganic anions.

Next,we also examined the activation of both ALMT proteins by isomers of malate and fumarate as exogenously supplied organic acids (Supporting Information: Figure S6a).L-Malic acid occurs naturally,and D-malic acid is an enantiomer of malate.As shown in Supporting Information:Figure S6a,inward currents derived from the oocytes expressing SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 showed similar inward currents depending on the malate efflux in the bath solution，including both L- and D-malic acid，and caused a hyperpolarized peak of the bell-shaped curve in oocytes expressing both ALMT genes.These results suggest that two carboxyl groups of dicarboxylic acids,regardless enantiomers,are required for full activation of malate efflux by both ALMT proteins.In contrast, maleic acid did not produce a current pattern similar to that of fumaric acid. Maleic acid [2-butenedioic acid: $\mathsf { C } _ { 2 } \mathsf { H } _ { 2 } ( \mathsf { C O O H } ) _ { 2 } ]$ isa geometric isomer (cis-form) of fumaric acid (trans-from) and may form two adjacent carboxyl groups at $\mathsf { p H } ~ 5 . 6$ (see Supporting Information: Figure S6b).

Taken together，our results indicate that SlALMT11 and AtALMT12 are activated by extracellular di-and tri-carboxylic acids.


## 3.5| Substrate specificity of guard-cell ALMTs


There is evidence that ALMT-family proteins are involved in malate permeation (Ryan et al.，2O11)；however，several organic anions (fumarate and succinate) can be transported via some ALMT-family proteins (Kovermann et al.，20O7；Meyer et al.,2011；Takanashi et al.,2O16).Therefore,we investigated the organic acid specificity as transport substrates for SIALMT11 and AtALMT12.In Supporting Information:Figure S7.oocytes were injected with several organic acids and exposed to a malate-based bath solution as shown in the illustration.Our results showed that fumarate and succinate were secreted and resulted in the characteristic bell-shaped inward currents similar to the profile when malate was pre-injected (Supporting Information: Figure S7); however,pre-injection of citrate into the oocytes did not result in high and bell-shaped inward currents.


## 3.6丨 The C-terminal region of SIALMT11 is involved in generating a current pattern related to malate efflux


Mumm et al. (2O13) reported that inward currents increased with hyperpolarization in oocytes expressing YFP fused to the C-terminus of AtALMT12.To characterize the properties of SlALMT11 channel protein,the effect of GFP fusion to the N-or C-terminus (indicated as GFP:SIALMT11 or SIALMT11:GFP，respectively） on the inward currents was analysed (Figure 5a and Supporting Information: Figure S8).We confirmed that both GFP fusions were localized to the plasma membrane of Xenopus oocytes (Figure 5b).Oocytes expressing GFP::SlALMT11 had a similar bell-shaped pattern of inward current with the native SlALMT11 protein (Figures 3b and 5a). In contrast，oocytes expressing the C-terminus fusion of GFP, SIALMT11:GFP,had a higher negative-going voltage dependent on inward currents under our measurement conditions compared to those in the water-injected control oocytes.These patterns are similar to those of AtALMT12 as reported by Mumm et al. (2013). Additionally,our results indicated that the inward currents were higher in a malate-based bath solution than those in gluconate-based solutions (Figure 5a).

Mumm et al. (2013)also explored a series of C-terminal truncations of AtALMT12 and reported that many truncated proteins were not functional in oocytes,except for △377-448 which is absent in SIALMT11 (Supporting Information: Figure S9a). To compare AtALMT12 with SlALMT11,we also examined C-terminal truncations of SlALMT11,especially at the end of the C-terminal region.In our experiments,the oocytes expressing SlALMT11 and its mutants were pre-injected with malate and exposed to a bath solution that included $1 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { M }$ sodium malate (see Section 2).The truncated mutation of GFP:SIALMT11 at the N-terminus,△504-536,resulted in ohmic current-voltage behaviour in the malate bath solution， but GFP:SIALMT11△422-504had nocurrents(Supporting Information:Figure S9b,c),although both mutant proteins localized to oocyte plasma membranes (Supporting Information: Figure S9e). Disturbance of the bell-shaped currents by the C-terminal truncation of SIALMT11 led us to confirm a C-terminal truncation in AtALMT12. Truncation of 28 amino acids from AtALMT12 (△533-560)also resulted in the disappearance of the bell-shaped currents (Supporting

Information: Figure S9d).This result is inconsistent with a previous report by Mumm et al. (2013).


## 3.7| C-terminal acidic amino acids are required to generate the bell-shaped I/V pattern


To explore the C-terminal region of ALMT proteins involved in generating the bell-shaped current-voltage patterns,we re-evaluated the amino acid alignments of AtALMT12,SIALMT11 and BdALMT12 orthologs.BdALMT12 is also reported to be an ALMT that is expressed in guard cells of Brachypodium distachyon (Luu etal., 2019). The alignment showed that two acidic amino acids,aspartic acid (Asp, D) or glutamic acid (Glu,E) are conserved at the C-terminus among these orthologs，except for the ALMT in Gossypium arboretum (XP_017625576) (Supporting Information: Figure S10a,b).

We next tried to assess whether the C-terminal Asp or Glu residue are involved in generating the bell-shaped patterns in SIALMT11 and AtALMT12,by truncating these amino acids from C-terminus of each ALMT.C-terminal truncations of SIALMT11 △D536 and AtALMT12 △E560 resulted in the disappearance of the bell-shaped pattern,especially in a malate-based bath solution (Figure 6 and Supporting Information: - Figure S11a).This observation was also true for ALMT proteins fused to GFP at the C terminus (Figure 5) and for proteins in which the 28-32 amino acids from the C terminus were truncated (Supporting

Information: Figure S1Oa).These results suggested that C-terminal Asp and Glu are critical for keeping the bell-shaped current-voltage patterns. In contrast,current magnitudes in oocytes expressing SlALMT11 △D536 in a gluconate-based solution were small, although the current patterns of AtALMT12 △E56O were similar in malate-and gluconate-based bath solutions (Figure 6 and Supporting Information: Figure S1la).Furthermore,we confirmed that the I/V properties from oocytes expressing SIALMT11 △D536 and GFP::SIALMT11 △D536 were similar (Figure 6 and Supporting Information: Figure S11b)，and the fluorescence from GFP:SIALMT11 △D536 was observed on oocyte plasma membranes (Supporting Information: Figure S11b).Taken together, these results imply that C-terminal acidic amino acids (Asp or Glu) are required to maintain the bell-shaped current-voltage pattern during malate-activated malate efflux through the SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 channels.

## 4.1| Physiological roles of rapid- and slow-anion channels in stomatal movement


The apoplastic malate concentration induces stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Araujo et al., 2011; Hedrich et al.,1994). In this study,we showed that guard-cell-type ALMT proteins playa crucial role in stomatal closure induced by exogenous malate in tomato and

Arabidopsis (Figure 2 and Supporting Information: Figure S4). SIALMT11-dependent inward currents associated with malate efflux from the cells were activated by extracellular malate aswas AtALMT12/QUAC1,suggestinga functional similarity between the two proteins (Figure 3 and Supporting Information: Figure S5).The activation of bell-shaped $1 / V$ patterns associated with SlALMT11 and AtALMT12 coincided with the negative shift of the $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ and was brought about not only by malate but other organic acids (Figure 4 and Supporting Information: Figure S6).Malcheska et al. (2017) reported that the $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ shifted to a more negative membrane potential by extracellular sulphate than chloridein oocytes expressing both AtALMT12 and OST1. In our study, $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ and $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ in oocytes expressing AtALMT12 or SIALMT11 in the absence of OST1 were similar to sulphate-and chloride-based bath solutions (Figure 4).This difference in channel activity in the presence of sulphate may be explained by the requirement for OST1 interaction.The bell-shaped voltage dependency of these ALMTs indicates a hyperpolarized repression of these channel activities, which might be beneficial for accelerating the hyperpolarization of the plasma membrane enhanced by ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ -ATPase during stomatal opening (lnoue & Kinoshita,2017).

The anion efflux associated with SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 occurred when dicarboxylic acids (fumarate,succinate,and malate) were preinjected into the oocytes (Supporting Information: Figure S7); however, anion effux was not observed when citrate,a tricarboxylic acid,was preinjected.This finding indicates that dicarboxylic anions are substrates for these guard-cell-type ALMTs. Similar selectivity has been reported for other ALMT proteins,AtALMT6,AtALMT9 and LjALMT4 (Kovermann et al.,2007；Meyer et al.，2011；Takanashi et al.，2016)，although ZmALMT1 was shown not to be an organic acid specific (Pineros, Cancado，Maron，et al.，2OO8).In contrast，S-type anion channels mediated by AtSLAC1 in Xenopus oocytes permeated $\mathtt { C l }$ and ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } { \mathsf { \bar { \ } } }$ rather than malate (Geiger et al., 20O9; Lee et al.,2009). Another study reported that cytosolic malate activated SLAC1-channel function using patch-clamp measurements of guard cellsand TEVC in Xenopus oocytes, although malate might not interact directly with SLAC1 (C.Wang et al.,2018).We hypothesize that the activity of SLAC-type and ALMTtype anion channels in guard cells are differently regulated by intra-and extracellularmalate.

In this study,we did not observe ABA-induced stomatal closure mediated by SlALMT11 (Figure 2c,d),of which the closest ortholog in Arabidopsis,AtALMT12,does mediate ABA-induced closure (Sasaki et al.,201O).Therefore,the ABA-dependent ALMT activation pathway may be different in tomato and Arabidopsis.ABA-induced stomatal closure in tomato is possibly mediated by an S-type anion channel, in an OST1-mediated manner,as suggested by Shi et al. (2015).


## 4.2| Functional motifs of guard-cell-type ALMT channels


Several functional domains in anion channels have been acknowledged.For example，arginine residue‘R256' located on the cytoplasmic side between the second and third transmembrane domains of AtSLAC1 is required for $\mathsf { C O } _ { 2 }$ -regulated stomatal movement in planta and S-type anion channel activation by ${ \mathsf { H C O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ ， but not for ABA-induced closure (J. Zhang et al., 2018). Cytosolic Nterminal and C-terminal domains are reported to contain important sites for SLAC1/OST1 function,and a conserved 1O amino acid region is found as a C-terminal OST1 interaction region in SLAC1 channels from many plant species (Hedrich & Geiger,2017；Lind et al., 2015).

A few functional domains have been identified for the guard-celltype ALMT proteins. Luu et al. (2019) reported that a calmodulinbinding domain was present in the C-terminal half (amino acid position 334-351) of the BdALMT12 protein from B.distachyon. These investigatorshypothesized that extra malate-sensitive BdALMT12 channel activity was coregulated by calmodulin as a primary modulator for cytosolic ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ ．Other investigators have reported that the C-terminal half of AtALMT12 is oriented to the cytoplasmic side and is important for actively maintaining the voltage-gating mechanisms when conducting analyses in Xenopus oocytes (Mumm et al.,2013).Truncation of residues 533-560 in the C-terminus of AtALMT12 completely abolished the channel activity (Mumm et al.,2O13)； however,our study indicated that the same deletion increased inward currents,although the mutation lost the bell-shaped I/V pattern observed with the native protein (Supporting Information:Figure S9d).The difference in the currents observed with the same AtALMT12 △533-560 protein may be attributed to different measurement parameters，like malate pre-injection or perhaps other unknown reasons.

Our results suggested that the negatively charged amino acids in the C-terminal ends of AtALMT12 and SIALMT11 are essential for regulating the voltage dependency of guard-cell type ALMT channels. Furthermore, the conserved motifs were present in the C-terminal regions among many plant species(Supporting Information: Figure S1Oa).In several plant families the conserved motif was ‘A-A-E' (Motif Il,and Ill in Supporting Information:Figure S10b); however， the C-terminus of the truncated mutants,SlALMT11 △504-536 and AtALMT12 △533-560, had Lys (K) followed by Glu (E)residues at the C-terminal end.The conserved motif for these mutants was ‘A-H/S-F-K-E' (Supporting Information: Figure S10a), although these mutations did not have the bell-shaped patterns intheir mean current-voltage curves (Supporting Information: Figure S9b,d).These results suggest that neutral amino acid residues might be necessary before ‘D/E'to maintain the characteristic bellshaped I/Vpatterns of the ALMT channels.Therefore,theaddition of a peptide tag,including GFP,at the C-terminus of SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 disrupted the native bell-shaped patterns (Figure 5, Mumm et al.,2013).Interestingly,the addition of GFP at the end of TaALMT1 did not affect inward currents derived from $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux in Xenopus oocytes (Sasaki et al.,2014),indicating that the relationship between the C-terminal structure and functions vary among respective ALMT proteins.

Most recently,the structures of two ALMT proteins, Arabidopsis AtALMT1 and soybean (Glycine max) GmALMT12/QUAC1，were analysed by cryo-electron microscopy.AtALMT1 (categorized as a Clade 1 ALMT) contains putative $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -binding sites and forms a pore involved in malate recognition (J.Wang et al.,2022),however, the putative sites are not conserved in guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (Clade 3). In contrast, two pairs of Arg residues (R8O and R165 of AtALMT1) involved in malate recognition are conserved among other ALMT proteins (J.Wang et al., 2022).

Analysis of GmALMT12 supported the hypothesis that malate activates the channel via regulating the conformation of tryptophan W90 (Qin et al., 2022),although no direct evidence for GmALMT12- mediated stomatal closure has been reported in soybean.Moreover, the tryptophan residue in this position is not only conserved among almost all Clade 3 ALMTs but all ALMT proteins.Both reports only mention malate permeable pore formation but do not discuss the selectivity of other substrates，inorganic and organic anions.Moreover，these structures do not reveal how C-terminal amino acids are involved in voltage sensing in each type of ALMT protein $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activating or guardcell type ALMTs).Therefore，further studies will be necessary to characterize how the C-terminal acidic amino acid residues generate the bell-shaped I/V pattern in SIALMT11 and AtALMT12.

In summary,our results demonstrate similarities in extracellular malate-induced stomatal closure in tomato and Arabidopsis,and both plants require guard-cell-type ALMT channels.Which organic acids enhance the ALMT channel in the apoplastic spaces of guard cells remain unknown.We hypothesize that the ALMT channels might be activated by ‘malate'released from mesophyll cells,since malate is the most abundant organic anion in plant cells (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2OoO).As for the malate response shared between AtALMT12 and SLALMT11,the apoplastic malate concentration increases in response to an elevated ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ concentration leading to stomatal closure in Vicia faba (Hedrich et al.,1994),although this response has not yet been recognized in other plant species.Jalakas et al. (2021) reported that the coordinated activation of $\mathsf { R } ^ { - }$ and S-type anion channels is needed for stomatal stress signalling,usinga series of single,double and triple mutants of atalmt12,slac1,and slah3 in Arabidopsis.Further studies of ALMT/QUAC and SLAC/SLAH channels might enhance our understanding of how stomatal movements in response to environmental stresses (e.g.，drought and water loss)are controlled in each plant species.

chunks.section: 3.ALMTs Are Widely Distributed in the Ge
chunks.text:
The characterised ALMT members show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13,39], microbe interactions [16,17], fruit acidity [14,15], and seed development [18]. Members which have been characterised are widely distributed in higher plant families of Poaceae, Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Rutaceae, Rosaceae, Vitaceae and Solanaceas (Table 1).


## 3.1. ALMT Members in Poaceae


The Poaceae species which have characterised ALMT members include wheat TaALMT1, rye ScALMT1, goatgrass AetALMT1, Yorkshire fog HlALMT1, maize ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2, rice OsALMT4 and barley HvALMT1. ALMT genes in wheat, rye, goatgrass and Yorkshire fog facilitate resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley HvALMT1 was related to stomatal functions (Figure 1).

By using a cDNA subtractive hybridisation technique, Sasaki et al. [1] cloned a cDNA which was more highly expressed in the root apices of an Al-resistant wheat line (ET8) than in a near-isogenic but Al-sensitive line (ES8). TaALMT1 was mapped to chromosome 4DL and the relative expression of this gene among various genotypes of wheat was strongly correlated with Al-activated malate efflux capacity and Al resistance [40]. Electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus laevis oocytes indicated that TaALMT1 encodes an Al-activated transporter that can mediate both inward and outward currents. The malate transport permeability is enhanced by external Al but it is also permeable to a lesser degree to other physiologically relevant anions such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ [1,41]. Transgenic rice, Arabidopsis, barley and tobacco cultured cell lines expressing TaALMT1 all showed an Al-activated malate efflux. In the later three cases, TaALMT1 also increased Al resistance [1,42]. The higher expression of TaALMT1resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley in resistant than sensitive wheat genotypes is due to a series of repeated blocks in the promoter [43].

Among cereal crops, rye is the most Al resistant species. Researchers have mapped Al-resistance loci on chromosomes 3R (Alt2), 4RL (Alt3), 6RS (Alt1) and 7RS (Alt4) by using segregating populations and wheat-rye addition lines [44–48]. Using primers to the TaALMT1 gene, Fontecha et al. [49] cloned a 1359 bp cDNA called ScALMT1 from rye and showed that it co-segregated with the Al resistance locus Alt4. ScALMT1 is mainly expressed in roots and expression is upregulated by exogenous Al treatment. Collins et al. [2] showed that the Alt4 resistance locus contains a cluster of ALMT genes. Although − −there are some mRNA splice variations that might affect protein function, the M77.1 promoter and ScALMT1-M39.1 gene are sufficient to explain most of the Al resistance in that line. As the ancestor of the wheat D genome, goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii Coss.) contains more genetic variation than bread wheat perhaps because it experienced less artificial selection. Ryan et al. [50] screened 760 accessions in a total of seven progenitor species of hexaploid wheat and other early relatives. Of these only five of 29 Aegilops tauschii tested showed a moderate level of resistance to Al. The coding sequences of the AetALMT1 genes in the five resistant genotypes were identical to TaALMT1 and resistance was correlated with AetALMT1 expression level and with Al-activated malate efflux. Unlike TaALMT1, all the Aegilops tauschii genes lacked any of the tandem repeats in the promoter region—even the moderately resistant ones [50]. Yorkshire fog is a grass that shows a large genotypic variation in acid soil tolerance. Chen et al. [34] cloned the HlALMT1 gene and found that plants from plots with acidic soil (HL-A) had significantly higher HlALMT1 expression levels in their roots than plants from plots with neutral pH soil (HL-N). The higher expression in HL-A plants was linked with a greater number of the cis-acting elements which recognise an Al-responsive transcription factor (HlART1) [34]. Furthermore, the HL-A roots secreted approximately twice as much malate as the HL-N roots, but there was no difference in citrate secretion. These results indicated that cis elements in the promoter of the HvALMT1 gene generated higher expression of HlALMT1 leading to higher malate efflux and greater Al resistance.

In maize, ZmALMT1 was initially considered a candidate for an Al resistance gene due to its sequence homology with TaALMT1 [12]. Although ZmALMT1 localises to the plasma membrane, is mainly expressed in root tissue, and shows increased expression with Al treatment, other results indicated that this gene was not involved with the mechanism of Al resistance. Firstly, electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus oocytes showed that ZmALMT1 had greater permeability to ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ than malate and these anions would not bind with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to reduce its activity in the apoplast. Furthermore, ZmALMT1 expression was low in the root tips where protection from $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress by organic anions is crucial. Lastly, transport activity of ZmALMT1 was independent of exogenous Al [12]. Linkage analysis of Al resistance genes in maize identified another ALMT gene, ZmALMT2, that is associated with net root growth under Al stress [51]. However, once again, ZmALMT2 is more permeable to inorganic anions $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right.$ , $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ ) than organic anions such as malate. Furthermore, ZmALMT2 is mainly expressed in mature roots and not root apices, expression levels are similar in Al-sensitive and resistant genotypes. Therefore, this gene is also unlikely to be involved with Al resistance despite its genetic linkage with that trait. Instead the authors suggested ZmALMT2 is involved with mineral nutrition [13].

There are nine members of the ALMT family rice but only OsALMT4 has been examined in detail. OsALMT4 localises to the plasma membrane and is expressed widely in roots and shoots, especially in the vasculature. Transgenic plants over-expressing OsALMT4 released malate from roots which is consistent with OsALMT4 encoding a malate-permeable anion channel. The over-expressing (OX) lines developed distinct symptoms on their leaves which consisted of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins which did not appear on null segregant plants or RNAi lines with reduced OsALMT4 expression. The partitioning of Mn within the leaf tissue was altered in the transgenic since the OX lines had a greater proportion of Mn residing in the apoplast of the leaves compared to the null plants. OX lines also had higher concentrations of malate in the xylem sap and increased expression of genes encoding Mn transporters (OsNramp5 and OsYSL2) and B transporters (OsBOR1 and OsNIP3.1). Growth studies found that the OX lines were more sensitive to Mn toxicity but more tolerant of B toxicity than null plants. The authors conclude that enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms [39].

Barley is another important plant in Triticeae and the barley ALMT1 gene was shown to be involved in facilitating anion efflux from guard cells during stomatal closure and seed development [5,11,18]. HvALMT1 is located on chromosome 2H. Tissue localisation showed that this protein was expressed in guard cells and in emerging lateral roots, the nucellar projection, aleurone layer and the scutellum of developing barley grain [5,18]. Intracellular localisation of HvALMT1 included the plasma membrane and small motile vesicles in the cytosol but the identity and function of those vesicles is unknown. Heterologous expression in Xenopus oocytes showed that this protein could mediate both inward and outward currents. HvALMT1 is permeable to malate and its activity is sensitive to $\mathrm { p H }$ [5]. The transgenic plants over-expressing HvALMT1 released more malate from roots than the control plants and they took significantly longer to close their stomata under low light than null controls. They also tended to reach a lower stomatal conductance under low light but the results were not significant. Combined with the finding that HvALMT1 is highly expressed in guard cells these results provided evidence that this channel contributes to stomatal function [11]. Interestingly, overexpressing HvALMT1 to high levels with a constitutive promoter affected plant growth and grain formation. Further experiments showed that malate release measured from isolated aleurone layers of grain was significantly lower in transgenic lines in which HvALMT1 expression was reduced by RNAi compared to control plants [18]. Therefore, HvALMT1 function affects stomatal aperture, grain development and plant growth. This shows that a single ALMT gene may perform multiple functions [5,11,18].

## 3.4. ALMT Members in Fruit Plants


In many acid soils it is common for Al toxicity to be linked with phosphorus (P) deficiency. This is because the soluble P is likely to be in a complex with iron or Al or fixed in other less soluble forms. Indeed some plants very efficient at taking up P from highly P-fixing soils, such white lupin (Lupinus albus L.), rely on organic anion release from roots (especially citrate release) to access more P [22]. Research indicates that members of the ALMT family might also contribute to greater P-use efficiency. For instance, the Al resistant species of citrus ‘Xuegan’ (Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck, CsALMT1) displayed more resistance to P-deficiency than a sensitive species ‘Sour pummelo’ (Citrus grandis (L.) Osbeck, $C g A L M T 1 )$ . Evidence was presented that ALMT genes in these species might contribute to the resistance of citrus to Al and/or P-deficiency [61].

Some ALMT proteins appear to affect fruit acidity by transporting malate across the tonoplast membrane (Figure 3). This was revealed when Bai et al. [14] narrowed down the Ma locus to a $6 5 { - } 8 2 \mathrm { k b }$ region on chromosome 16 of the apple cultivar Golden Delicious. The Ma locus is associated with fruit acidity in apple and the genomic region contains 12–19 predicted genes. By aligning these genes with two BACs covering different haplotypes of the Ma locus (high and low acidity), they identified two ALMT homologues and named them Ma1 and Ma2. Phylogenetic analysis using these two apple ALMT members against the Arabidopsis proteins indicated that these two members from apple were most similar to AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 which mediate anion transport across the tonoplast [14]. Ma1 was shown to localise on the tonoplast and heterologous expression in yeast increased malate influx into yeast cells. Quantitative RT-PCR experiments predicted that expression of Ma1, but not Ma2, is significantly linked with fruit acidity (high Ma1 expression was correlated with more acidic fruit). Moreover, a natural mutation in Ma1 leading to a truncation of the gene was also associated with low fruit acidity. The Ma1 genotype is closely related to apple fruit acidity suggesting Ma1 is associated with the accumulation of malic acid in apple fruits [62]. Similarly, De Angeli et al. [15] cloned an AtALMT9 homolog from grape called VvALMT9. VvALMT9 expression increased as the berry matured. The VvALMT9 protein has $6 4 \%$ identity with AtALMT9 and also localises to the tonoplast. VvALMT9 is not only permeable to malate, but also displays a low permeability to tartrate. The authors predicted that VvALMT9 is a tonoplast channel that contributes to malate and tartrate accumulation in grape berries [15].

Similar conclusions were reported by Sasaki et al. [53] who generated chimeric proteins from TaALMT1 of wheat and AtALMT1 of Arabidopsis and examined their transport function in Xenopus oocytes. Firstly they detected transport activity only for TaALMT1 but not for AtALMT1. However where the N- and C-terminal halves of TaALMT1 and AtALMT1 were swapped (Ta::At and At::Ta) they found transport activity whenever the N-terminal half of TaALMT1 was present [53]. Moreover, they identified a putative helical domain on the N-terminal and another on the C-terminal ends of TaALMT1 which are important for its transport activity [53].

In fact, the topology of ALMT transporters remains unclear and doubt still remains whether the N and the C-terminal ends are intracellular or extracellular [6,8,20,70,72,79]. Recently Ramesh et al. [80] showed that the transport activity of several ALMTs expressed in Xenopus oocytes is very sensitive to inhibition by gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and muscimol, an agonist of $\mathrm { G A B A _ { A } }$ receptor. Subsequent studies suggest that ALMT proteins may be GABA receptors in plants and underlay novel signalling pathways associated with stress responses. Although the ALMTs have a low overall sequence similarity with the $\mathrm { G A B A _ { A } }$ receptors in animal cells, ALMTs contain a conserved motif that is similar to the GABA binding site on $\mathrm { G A B A _ { A } }$ receptors. This intriguing result suggests that ALMTs may perform many other functions in plants which are still to be discovered [80].

Guard-cell-type aluminium-activated malate transporters (ALMTs) are involved in stomatal closure by exporting anions from guard cells. However, their physiological and electrophysiological functions are yet to be explored. Here,we analysed the physiological and electrophysiological properties of the ALMT channelsin Arabidopsis and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum). SIALMT11 was specifically expressed in tomato guard cells. External malate-induced stomatal closure was impaired in ALMT-suppressed lines of tomato and Arabidopsis, although abscisic acid did not influence the stomatal response in SIALMT11-knock-down tomato lines. Electrophysiological analyses in Xenopus oocytes showed that SIALMT11 and AtALMT12/ QUAC1 exhibited characteristic bell-shaped current-voltage patterns dependent on extracellular malate, fumarate，and citrate. Both ALMTs could transport malate, fumarate,and succinate, but not citrate, suggesting that the guard-cell-type ALMTs aredicarboxylic anion channels activated by extracellular organic acids. The truncation of acidic amino acids, Asp or Glu, from the C-terminal end of SlALMT11 or AtALMT12/QUAC1 led to the disappearance of the bell-shaped current-voltage patterns.
