Starch reserved in seed serves as the primary carbon and energy source for seed germination and early seedling establishment. In cereal seeds, $\mathscr { X }$ -amylase digests starch granules stored in endosperm after seed imbibition, and then $\mathscr { X }$ -glucosidase generates maltose and linear/shortbranch chain oligosaccharides for further degradation to glucose. Subsequently, the glucose or maltose is transferred into embryos and further re-synthesized to sucrose in scutellums (Nomura et al. 1969; Aoki et al. 2006). The sugar is then transported to growing young radicles and shoots via vascular bundles connecting embryos and their derived roots and shoots. Phloem functions as a dominant systemic network for carbon source transport among various plant tissues, and sucrose is the major transported carbohydrate molecule in phloem.

Cell-to-cell remobilization of sucrose is mediated either through a symplastic pathway involving plasmodesmata or via apoplastic transport performed by sucrose transporters (SUTs). SUT is a 12 membrane-domain containing protein that functions as the machinery in charge of transporting sucrose across membranes. Changes in carbohydrate allocation and photosynthesis inhibition have been observed in transgenic plants with SUT activity reduced using the antisense technique; these results indicate that SUT plays an important role in carbohydrate partitioning combined with physiological processing (Ku¨hn et al. 1996; Bu¨rkle et al. 1998). SUT genes of most plant species constitute a multiple-gene family. For example, the Arabidopsis genome contains nine SUT genes, and the rice genome has five (Braun and Slewinski 2009). According to sequence homology, Aoki et al. (2003) have classified SUT genes into three types, and Sauer (2007) have grouped them into four clades. Recently, since completion of genome sequencing in some grasses such as sorghum and identification of more SUT gene sequences, the SUT gene families of both dicot and monocot species were reclassified into five groups (Braun and Slewinski 2009).

The five SUT genes in rice are designated as OsSUT1 to OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). Based on the phylogenetic tree developed by Braun and Slewinski (2009), the first SUT gene isolated from rice (Hirose et al. 1997), OsSUT1, was classified into group 1. All SUT genes included in group 1 have been isolated from monocots. The sucrose transport ability of several group 1 SUTs, i.e., ZmSUT1, HvSUT1, ShSUT1, and TaSUT1, have been, respectively, identified using Xenopus oocytes or yeast expression systems (Carpaneto et al. 2005; Rae et al. 2005; Sivitz et al. 2005; Aoki et al. 2006). According to gene expression patterns and protein localization, maize ZmSUT1 and wheat TaSUT1 were suggested to involve in phloem loading in source leaves (Aoki et al. 1999, 2004; Carpaneto et al. 2005). On the other hand, the ShSUT1 protein of sugarcane was also detected in mature leaves but did not localize in phloem cells; instead, it was observed in cells around vascular bundles (Rae et al. 2005). In germinating wheat seeds, TaSUT1 mRNA and proteins have been detected in aleurone layer and scutellum cells (Aoki et al. 2006). In rice plants, OsSUT1 expression has been detected in leaf blades, leaf sheaths, panicles, and germinating seeds, but almost never in roots (Hirose et al. 1997). OsSUT1 expression has been investigated during the grain-filling period using OsSUT1 promoter/GUS fusion gene analysis and immunolocalization (Scofield et al. 2007b). The results indicated that OsSUT1 is expressed in the phloem of leaf, uppermost internode, and pedicel for sucrose transport to filling grains. In developing rice caryopses, the expression levels of OsSUT1 gradually increased from 1 to 7 days after flowering, and then began to decrease (Aoki et al. 2003). Furthermore, the OsSUT1 mRNA levels in the leaf sheaths of upper position leaves at the pre-heading stage were higher than at the post-heading stage; in other words, OsSUT1 expression in source leaf sheaths is stronger than in sink leaf sheaths (Chen and Wang 2008). In situ hybridization analysis showed that expression of OsSUT1 in rice leaf sheaths was specific to phloem companion cells (Matsukura et al. 2000).

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are sucrose– $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ symporters, which mediate the active transport of sucrose across plasma membranes. Since sucrose is translocated from source to sink tissues through the phloem, plasma membrane sucrose transporters are believed to play important roles in mediating carbon partitioning in plants (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Over the last decade, genes encoding SUT proteins have been isolated from a wide range of both monocot and dicot plant species, from source and sink tissues and found to be localised in phloem and non-phloem tissues (see reviews by Williams et al. 2000; Truernit 2001; Lalonde et al. 2003).

In cereal species, SUT proteins mainly have been studied in developing grains. For example, in developing rice caryopses, OsSUT1 protein is present in the plasma membrane of the aleurone cell layer surrounding the endosperm (Furbank et al. 2001) and is essential for transport of assimilates into filling grains (Scofield et al. 2002). A similar role in grain filling has been proposed for HvSUT1 protein in barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and for TaSUT1 in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2002). However, cellular localisation of cereal SUT gene expression in vegetative tissues has been less well characterised despite the fact that SUT mRNAs are detectable in these tissues of rice (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003), maize (Aoki et al. 1999), barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). While in dicot plants there is considerable evidence that SUTs play a role in apoplasmic loading of sucrose into the phloem (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003), there is little evidence for this in cereal species. Indeed, there is some debate over whether phloem loading in cereals occurs via symplasmic or apoplasmic pathways (e.g. Russin et al. 1996, also see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Significantly, antisense repression of OsSUT1 expression in transgenic rice did not appear to affect phloem loading (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002).

Previously we reported the isolation of three cDNAs encoding SUT proteins from developing grains of hexaploid wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). The peptide sequences deduced from the three cDNAs showed $9 8 \%$ identity to one another, all with more than $8 5 \%$ similarity to SUT1 proteins from other cereal species. The three wheat SUT1 proteins were encoded individually by single-copy homeologous genes, designated TaSUT1A, 1B and 1D , which are represented once in each of the A-, B- and D-genomes. Northern blot analysis revealed that the TaSUT1 genes were highly expressed not only in developing grains but also in flagleaf blades, flag-leaf sheaths and culms (internodes) at the pre-heading stage.

Sucrose transporters (SUTs) are important for both phloem loading in source tissue and sucrose uptake into some sink cells [1]. SUTs are considered to be the control points for sucrose storage in plant because they can carry sucrose across cell membranes and play an important role in loading sucrose into phloem systems in a series of steps [1]. Plant SUTs belong to the glycoside-pentosidehexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family (TC2.A.2) that is part of the major facilitator super-family (MFS) [2]. Transporters in the GPH family have the primary characteristics of MFS proteins that contain 12 transmembrane spanning domains with $\Nu _ { - }$ and C-termini in the cytoplasm [3]. Since the first plant sucrose transporter SoSUT1 was functionally identified using an elegant yeast complementation strategy from spinach (Spinacea Oleracea) [4], SUTs have been demonstrated to effect on the multiple aspects of plant development such as biomass partitioning, pollen germination, restraining plant growth, fruit size reduction and ethylene biosynthesis [5–9].

Comprehensive understanding of the molecular structure and evolution of a gene family in plant species is the first step towards understanding their physiological roles and metabolic mechanism involved in different growth phases. Recent studies have revealed that SUT was a small gene family that consisted of at least four SUT genes in the most plant species. The SUT family members have been identified from a number of plant species such as Arabidopsis [10], rice (Oryza sativa) [11], wheat (Triticum aestivum) [12], populus [8], sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) [13] and pineapple (Ananas comosus) (Unpublished, Zhang and Ming) as well. Phylogenetic analysis of SUT family suggested that the plant SUT could be divided into five subgroups including two monocot specific subgroups, one dicot specific and two monocot-dicot subgroups. SUT family members in many plant species are divergent in function and deferentially expressed in different tissues types or at different plant developmental stages. For instance, in rice, OsSUT1 expression has been detected in germinated seeds, leaf blades, leaf sheaths and panicles [14–16]; the expressions of both OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 are dramatically lower in embryos than those of OsSUT1, OsSUT2, and OsSUT4 [17]; OsSUT4 has been detected in most tissues such as roots, leaves, and panicles [11], and could play a role in sucrose loading into the sheath phloem of the upper leaves during the post-heading period for sucrose transport to developing grains [18]. In Arabidopsis [10], AtSUC2 has been detected in phloem and companion cells in source leaves [19, 20] and functions in loading sucrose into the phloem sieve elements (SEs), correspond with the result identified by tissue-specific complementation of different promoters [7, 21] and by $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ labeling studies [22]; AtSUC3 and

AtSUC4 are expressed in minor veins of source leaves of mature plants [23–25].

Sugarcane (Saccharum spp.) is one of the world’s most produced crops (FAOSTAT, 2015), and contributes to about $80 \%$ of the world sugar and about $4 0 \ \%$ of ethanol production worldwide. Modern sugarcane cultivar has one of the most complex genome among all the crops; by being both aneupoid and autopolypoid with an extreme ploidy level that can range from octoploidy $\left( \mathbf { { x } } = 8 \right)$ to dodecaploidy $( \mathbf { x } = 1 2 )$ . Approximately $80 \%$ of cultivars’ chromosomes are derived from S. officinarum and $1 0 - 2 0 \ \%$ is derived from S.spontaneum with the remained from interspecific recombination [26–28]. Sugarcane is not only an economically important crop species, but also serves as an important model crop for studying sucrose transporters because its remarkable ability to accumulate vast amounts of sucrose in its stems that can reach close to $7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ or in excess of $5 0 \%$ of the dry weight (DW) (DW) [29]. But to date, limited works in characterizing these SUT genes have been reported, except for SUT1 (transcripts accession:AY780256.1, GU812864.1 and BU925792). In an earlier study based on sugarcane Expressed Sequence Tag (EST) database survey, SUT1 was revealed to be more abundant in the mature internodes than the other tissues [30]. This result was confirmed by a study for Hawaiian sugarcane cultivar, in which the SUT1 transcript levels increased during maturation and sucrose storage, whereas, SUT1 expression was observed to be not affected by sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) infection in sugarcane [31]. Biochemical analysis of sugarcane SUT1 suggested that SUT1 was highly selective for sucrose, but had a relatively low affinity for sucrose, inhibited by sucralose and played key role in sucrose loading from the vascular tissues into the storage sites in parenchyma cells of sugarcane stems [32, 33]. Besides SUT1, the gene family of SUTs is not understood in sugarcane due to the formidable challenge caused by its high degree of polyploidy and heterozygosity genome.

In this study, to gain comprehensive understandings of the molecular and evolutionary characterization as well as the possible functions of SUT family in sugarcane, based on combination of comparative genomics strategies and high genome coverage of bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) libraries resources, we identified and characterized SUT gene families in Saccharum species and investigated their transcriptional expression patterns. The analysis in this study mainly focused on: (1) identifying the gene members and allele haplotypes of the SUT gene family in sugarcane; (2) analyzing evolutionary relationship, exon/intron organization of the SUT gene family; and (3) characterizing the expression patterns of the SUT gene family in three progenitor Saccharum species.

Background: Sucrose transporters (SUTs) play important roles in regulating the translocation of assimilates from source to sink tissues. Identification and characterization of new SUTs in economically important crops such as wheat provide insights into their role in determining seed yield. To date, however, only one SUT of wheat has been reported and functionally characterized. The present study reports the isolation and characterization of a new SUT, designated as TaSUT2, and its homeologues (TaSUT2A, TaSUT2B and TaSUT2D) in hexaploid wheat (Triticum aestivum L.).

Results: TaSUT2A and TaSUT2B genes each encode a protein with 506 amino acids, whereas TaSUT2D encodes a protein of 508 amino acids. The molecular mass of these proteins is predicted to ${ \mathrm { b e } } \sim 5 4 { \mathrm { ~ k D A } } .$ Topological analysis of the amino acid sequences of the three homeologues revealed that they contain 12 transmembrane spanning helices, which are described as distinct characteristic features of glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide cation symporter family that includes all known plant SUTs, and a histidine residue that appears to be localized at and associated conformationally with the sucrose binding site. Yeast SUSY7/ura3 strain cells transformed with TaSUT2A, TaSUT2B and TaSUT2D were able to uptake sucrose and grow on a medium containing sucrose as a sole source of carbon; however, our subcellular localization study with plant cells revealed that TaSUT2 is localized to the tonoplast. The expression of TaSUT2 was detected in the source, including flag leaf blade, flag leaf sheath, peduncle, glumes, palea and lemma, and sink (seed) tissues. The relative contributions of the three genomes of wheat to the total expression of TaSUT2 appear to differ with tissues and developmental stages. At the cellular level, TaSUT2 is expressed mainly in the vein of developing seeds and subepidermal mesophyll cells of the leaf blade.

Conclusion: This study demonstrated that TaSUT2 is a new wheat SUT protein. Given that TaSUT2 is localized to the tonoplast and sucrose is temporarily stored in the vacuoles of both source and sink tissues, our data imply that TaSUT2 is involved in the intracellular partitioning of sucrose, particularly between the vacuole and cytoplasm.

Keywords: Homeologous genes, TaSUT2, Sucrose transporter, Gene expression, Source tissues, Developing seeds, Wheat

As a major photosynthetic product, sucrose constitutes one of the primary carbohydrates, which is transported between source tissues and heterotrophic sink tissues (Lemoine 2000; Williams et al. 2000). Furthermore, as a signaling molecule, sucrose can significantly influence cellular processes of the plant, particularly with regard to metabolic activity and fruit development. Sucrose metabolism also plays a pivotal role in developmental processes, stress response, and yield formation, primarily by generating a series of sugar metabolites used for energy metabolism and the synthesizing of essential compounds, including proteins, cellulose, and starch (Kühn 2011; Ruan 2014). Sucrose transporters (SUTs) possess 12 transmembrane domains and constitute typical membrane proteins in higher plants. SUTs are responsible for sucrose transport across membranes, including phloem loading in source tissues and sucrose unloading into sink tissues (Kühn et al. 2010; Doidy et al. 2012a).

Since the first SUT gene SoSUT1 was discovered from spinach (Spinacia oleracea) (Riesmeier et al. 1992), numerous SUT genes have been identified and characterized both in dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous species (Aoki et al. 2003; Doidy et al. 2012b; Zanon et al. 2015a; Zhang et al. 2016). All the SUTs in plants can be categorized into five subfamilies (Kühn et al. 2010), of which SUT1, SUT2, and SUT4 subfamilies were identified in dicots, whereas SUT2, SUT3, SUT4, and SUT5 subfamilies were found in monocots. According to the phylogenetic analysis, SUTs were classified into three groups, including Type I, Type II (A and B), and Type III (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type I members, localized to the plasma membrane, are identified as high-affinity sucrose carriers, involving in phloem loading or sucrose import into sink cells (Gottwald et al. 2000; Sauer 2007; Slewinski et al. 2009). They have been detected across various sink organs, including tubers, pollen, flowers, and fruits, suggesting a complex role in sucrose partitioning (Kühn et al. 2010). The Type II group can be divided into two sub-groups, IIA and IIB. Type IIA contains both eudicot and monocot isoforms, whereas Type IIB only represents the monocot-specific SUTs (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type IIA members are characterized by an elongated central loop with an unclear function, and are localized to the plasma membrane, similar with Type I. Several Type IIB members are plasma membrane-localized, high-affinity, and participate in phloem loading (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type III, comprising tonoplast SUTs from both monocots and eudicots, are thought to facilitate sucrose release from vacuoles into the cytoplasm (Schneider et al. 2012; Ruan 2014). Type III SUTs are expressed in various tissues, including the veins of sink and source leaves, roots, anthers, and fruits (Weise et al. 2000; Peng et al. 2011; Zanon et al. 2015a). Furthermore, they are targeted to the plasma membrane or tonoplast depending on the plant species. Dual localization with tonoplast and plasma membrane has been reported for some Type III SUTs in certain species, such as Arabidopsis AtSUT4, potato StSUT4, tomato SlSUT4, and poplar PtaSUT4 (Chincinska et al. 2013).

Heterologous expression in yeast indicated the ability of SUT4 (AtSUT4, LjSUT4, and PpSUT4) to catalyze sucrose uptake with low affinity (Weise et al. 2000; Reinders et al. 2008; Zanon et al. 2015a). The SUT4 homologs in Arabidopsis (AtSUT4), barley (HvSUT2), Lotus Japonica (LjSUT4), and peach (PpSUT4) function as sucrose proton symporters, suggesting that they are most likely involved in the sucrose efflux from the vacuole (Neuhaus 2007; Zanon et al. 2015a). SUT4 has been found to be participated in diverse biological processes in different plant species. In potato, inhibition of the StSUT4 expression results in early flowering, tuberization, and the reducing expression of gibberellic acid and ethylene biosynthetic genes (Chincinska et al. 2008). In poplar plants, PtaSUT4-silenced results in an increased leaf-to-stem biomass ratio with the decreased translocation of sucrose to the sink organs (Payyavula et al. 2010). In pear, PbSUT2 affected sucrose content in sinks and the overexpression of PbSUT2 leads to early flowering (Wang et al. 2016). Previous study showed sucrose not only improves fruit flavor but also relevant to lipid metabolism (Cui et al. 2016). Overexpression of AtSUT2 and/or AtSUT4 in combination with diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) genes can increase seed oil production in both soybean and maize (Allen et al. 2015).

Jatropha curcas, well known as the “purging nut,” is a promising bio-energy perennial oilseed crop, in which the seeds can be processed to produce high-quality biodiesel fuel (Pereira et al. 2017). However, few transcriptome studies had mentioned the SUT genes in J. curcas (Jiang et al. 2012). Therefore, investigating the mechanism of SUTs might provide significant insight into the growth and development of J. curcas. In this study, we cloned JcSUT4 from J. curcas. JcSUT4 was mainly localized to plasma membrane and mediated the sucrose uptake by yeast complementation assay. JcSUT4 was highly expressed in mature source leaves, and gradually increased at early stages of fruit development. Our results identified the primary biological functions of JcSUT4, providing information for exploration of the mechanism that control sucrose accumulation in this bioenergy species.

In plants, carbohydrates translocate from the source to sink tissues through symplastic and apoplastic pathways. Sugar transport between cells in symplasts is mediated by plasmodesmata. In apoplasts, sugar translocators are responsible for carbohydrate uptake into cells. Because sucrose is the major transported form of carbohydrate between plant tissues, sucrose transporter (SUT) plays an important role in long-distance disaccharide transport. SUT1 in sugarcane functions to partition sucrose between the vascular bundle and storage cells (Rae et al. 2005). Maize SUT, ZmSUT1, is responsible for sugar uptake into phloem in source tissues and sugar unloading from phloem into cells in sink tissues (Carpaneto et al. 2005). Changes in carbohydrate allocation and the inhibition of photosynthesis have been observed in transgenic plants with reduced SUT activity due to antisense SUT genes; thus, SUT has been indicated to play an important role in carbohydrate partitioning and physiological processing (Kühn et al. 1996; Bürkle et al. 1998).

To date, SUT genes have been identified from several plants, most belonging to gene families (Lemoine 2000; Lalonde et al. 2004). The SUT gene families of dicot and monocot species were classified into five sequence-based groups by Braun and Slewinski (2009). In rice, the SUT gene family consists of five genes, OsSUT1 to OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). OsSUT1 and 3 were classified into group 1. The group 1 SUT family is composed of several Poaceae SUT members; so far, no dicot SUTs have been found in group 1. OsSUT2 was classified with Arabidopsis SUT4 (AtSUT4) in group 2. AtSUT4 has been demonstrated to be responsible for the low-affinity/high-capacity transport system (reviewed by Lalonde et al. 2004). OsSUT4 and OsSUT5 were classified into group 3 and 5, respectively.

During plant development from seed germination to seed establishment and seedling growth, starch reserved in the seed is the primary carbon and energy source for sprouting and early seedling establishment, and then the sugar sources for later stages of seedling growth come from the photosynthetic shoots. In rice plants, carbohydrate transport from germinating seeds to other developing sink tissues is a fundamental process for plant development and growth. Sugar derived from starch degradation exported to the cytosol from storage organelles is the first step for longdistance carbohydrate translocation. In cereal endosperms, starch granules are attacked by $\propto$ -amylase (Murata et al. 1968), and the maltose and linear/short-branch-chain oligosaccharides are generated for further degradation by $\propto$ -glucosidase (Stanley et al. 2011). The hexoses produced by starch degradation can be taken up by the scutellum cells of the embryo. Hexoses have been suggested to be resynthesized into sucrose in the scutellum (Edelman et al. 1959; Nomura et al. 1969). Sucrose in the scutellum is loaded into the vascular bundle, transported, and then unloaded to growing tissues through apoplastic or symplastic pathways (Aoki et al. 2006). In addition, it was also suggested that sucrose transported from aleurone layers to endosperm at early germination stage could be further uptaked by scutellum (Aoki et al. 2006). Based on our previous work (Liu et al. 2010), soluble sugar can also be converted to starch in scutellum or the cells surrounding vascular bundles at the post-germination stage, and the amount of transitory starch in embryonic tissues was dependent on the demand of growing sink tissues. Phloem functions as an important pathway for carbon source transport among various plant tissues. In rice germinating seeds, OsSUT1 was the first OsSUT family member identified to have a tissue-specific expression pattern (Hirose et al. 1997; Scofield et al. 2007). Developmental expression and regulation of OsSUT1 has been observed in germinating seeds (Chen et al. 2010). However, the regulation of other members of the OsSUT gene family still needs to be established.

Photoassimilated carbohydrates are produced by autotrophic source tissues such as leaves and are translocated to heterotrophic sink tissues such as roots, stems, flowers and seeds. Sucrose is the major transported form of photosynthetically produced sugar in many plant species due to its nonreducing nature and insensitivity to degradation (Lemoine, 2000). Long-distance sucrose transport in the phloem requires transmembrane transport. Sucrose transporters (SUTs or SUCs) play vital roles in transmembrane transport during phloem loading and unloading as well as in sucrose allocation within plants and between pathogens and beneficial symbionts (Kühn & Grof, 2010).

Plant sucrose transporters are members of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS), which typically have 12 transmembrane (TM) domains divided into two regions by a hydrophilic cytoplasmic loop (Lalonde, Wipf & Frommer, 2004; Bush, 1993). All of the transporters in the SUT/SUC family studied to date are sucrose $^ { \prime \mathrm { H + } }$ symporters, including vacuolar SUTs. The first plant SUT gene, SoSUT1, was isolated from spinach using a yeast complementation system (Riesmeier, Willmitzer & Frommer, 1992). With the increasing availability of plant genomes and molecular information, a growing number of SUT s have been identified in many plant species, including both monocot and dicot species, such as Arabidopsis (Weise et al., 2000), rice (Aoki et al., 2003), Populus (Hackel et al., 2006; Payyavula et al., 2011), wheat (Deol et al., 2013), maize (Usha, 2015), pear (Zhang et al., 2013), cacao (Li et al., 2014), tomato (Reuscher et al., 2014), cotton (Li et al., 2018) and various species considered weeds (Misra et al., 2019). However, these genes are absent in the unicellular chlorophyte alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and in Volvox carteri (Reinders, Sivitz & Ward, 2012).

According to the genomes of grasses, SUT genes were originally classified into five groups: SUT1-SUT5 (Kühn & Grof, 2010; Braun & Barker, 2009; Lalonde & Frommer, 2012). The SUT1 clade is dicot specific, with members expressed in the plasma membrane of sieve elements or companion cells (Weise et al., 2000; Stadler et al., 1995; Baker et al., 2016). SUT2 and SUT4 encompass members from both dicot and monocot plants, whereas both SUT3 and SUT5 groups are monocot specific. SUT2 transporters are mainly expressed in the plasma membrane of SEs and are found in vegetative sink organs (Barth, Meyer & Sauer, 2003; Meyer et al., 2004). All members of the SUT4 clade are proposed to be vacuolar SUTs (Endler et al., 2006; Chincinska et al., 2008). Recently, researchers have divided SUT s into two subfamilies (Ancient Group 1 and Ancient Group 2) and three types (type I, type II and type III) (Reinders, Sivitz & Ward, 2012; Peng et al., 2014). SUT family genes play essential roles in phloem loading and unloading, pollen development, fruit ripening, ethylene biosynthesis and seed development and germination in many plant species (Payyavula et al., 2011; Usha, 2015; Chincinska et al., 2008; Sivitz, Reinders & Ward, 2008; Srivastava et al., 2009a). In addition, SUT genes are involved in various physiological processes and sucrose exchange between plants and symbionts, pathogens and fungi (Kühn & Grof, 2010; Doidy et al., 2012; Wittek et al., 2017). For example, in Arabidopsis, AtSUC5 is predominantly expressed in the seeds. AtSUC1 is expressed in seedlings, where it is necessary for normal anthocyanin accumulation. AtSUC1 is also expressed in pollen and required for normal pollen function. AtSUC9 appears to be required for normal floral transition (Sivitz et al., 2007; Sivitz, Reinders & Ward, 2008), and OsSUT2 is expressed in the seeds and is involved in the germination of embryos (Siao et al., 2011; Eom et al., 2016). The activity and expression of sucrose transporters are regulated by genetic, molecular and physiological factors.

Orchidaceae is one of the largest families in angiosperms, with more than 25,000 species and 880 genera, representing ${ \sim } 1 0 \%$ of flowering plants (Sharma & Mukai, 2015). Many of them are economically important due to their unique ornamental and medicinal value. Moreover, orchids are model systems for elucidating floral evolution in angiosperms and symbiotic activities between plants and fungi (Hsiao et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2017). To date, the genomes of three Orchidaceae species, Dendrobium officinale, Phalaenopsis equestris, and Apostasia shenzhenica, have been sequenced and published, which has greatly promoted the understanding of the genetics and genomics of orchids (Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2015). However, the roles of sucrose transporters in orchids are still unknown. In the present study, we performed genome-wide identification and characterization of the members of the SUT gene families in three sequenced Orchidaceae species. Transcriptome sequencing and water-soluble sugar content analysis were also conducted in D. officinale. Our findings provide insight into the evolution, expression, and functions of SUT genes in Orchidaceae.

## Plants exhibit high genetic diversity in SUT gene families


SUTs play a pivotal role in the phloem loading and unloading of sucrose, enabling its long-distance translocation from source to sink tissues and thereby ensuring efcient carbon allocation throughout the plant (Sun et al. 2023a, b; Deng et al. 2023). Furthermore, to their essential function in carbohydrate distribution, SUT genes have also been implicated in plant responses to various abiotic stresses. Their transcriptional regulation under stress conditions suggests a critical role in maintaining energy homeostasis and osmotic balance, supporting plant growth and resilience under adverse environments (Chen et al. 2022a, b; Salvi et al. 2022). High-throughput sequencing technologies have successfully sequenced and assembled several sugarcane genomes, including monoploid and polyploid assemblies. These genomic resources, including S. spp. Hybrid R570 (Garsmeur et al. 2018; Healey et al. 2024), Modern sugarcane cultivar “CC01-1940” (Trujillo et al. 2021), S. Hybrid ZZ1 (Bao et al. 2024), and the two S. spon clones “AP85-441 and Np-X” (Zhang et al. 2018, 2022), ofer valuable references for genome-wide and functional analysis of important gene families in sugarcane. In this study, 37 ShSUT genes were uncovered in the S. spp. Hybrid XTT22 genome (Table 1), highlighting the substantial genetic diversity of the SUT family members in sugarcane and across plant species. Members of SUT family have been extensively characterized in both monocots such as $o$ . sativa (Aoki et al. 2003), Lilium (Huang et al. 2024), Z. mays (Usha et al. 2015), S. bicolor (Milne et al. 2013), S. spontaneum (Dhungana and Braun 2022), S. ofcinarum, E. rufpilus (Akbar et al. 2025), and T. aestivum L. (Hou et al. 2024), and dicots, including A. thaliana (Peng et al. 2014; Durand et al. 2018), H. brasiliensis (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c), B. vulgaris (Sun et al. 2023a, b), and G. hirsutum (Li et al. 2018).

Comparative analysis of gene evolution, structural organization, and conserved motif patterns revealed that ShSUT gene family members within the same clade generally share similar exon–intron organization and domain architecture, although some members exhibit clade-specifc variations (Sun et al. 2023a, b). In our study, inferred from phylogenetic relationships, ShSUT genes were classifed into three major groups “I–III,” with Group-I containing the largest number of genes. Groups-II and Group-III also comprised closely related members, though notable diferences in gene structure and motif compositions suggest potential functional divergence (Fig. 1). Similar evolutionary classifcations of SUT gene families have been reported in sugar beet (Sun et al. 2023a, b), cotton (Li et al. 2018), bamboo (Deng et al. 2023), and oil-seed camellia (Zhou et al. 2024) indicating evolutionary conversion across diferent plant lineages. Further, the exon–intron structures of ShSUT genes varied from 5 to 14 exons (Fig. 1), consistent with fndings in wheat, where TaSUT genes contain 5–16 exons (Hou et al. 2024).

Notably, conserved motif profling highlighted the structural similarity among genes within the same phylogenetic group often shared specifc motif patterns, suggesting possible subgroup-specifc functions (Sun et al. 2023a, b).

Cis-acting elements are essential components of gene regulatory networks. In this study, numerous stress-responsive and growth-related cis-elements were uncovered within the 1-kb promoter regions of 37 ShSUT genes (Fig. 3). These included a broad range of phytohormone-responsive ciselements, including those responsive to MeJA, ABA, SA, Aux, and GA, which are commonly linked to plant growth regulation and stresses responses (Jiang et al. 2023; Ali et al. 2025). Additionally, stress-responsive elements associated with anaerobic induction, and wound signaling, drought tolerance and defense mechanism were widely present in ShSUT promoters (Chen et al. 2022a, b). Several cis-elements related to growth and development were also detected, including those involved in meristem activity, zein metabolism, endosperm expression, seed-specifc regulation, and light responsiveness (Li et al. 2015; Akbar et al. 2025). Together, these discoveries suggest that ShSUT genes are under complex transcriptional regulation and may play key roles in integrating developmental programs with environmental stress responses.

Genomic duplication event is a key evolutionary mechanism that produces extra gene duplicates, permitting them to develop new functions or refne prevailing ones while preserving vital biological activities. This mechanism facilitates regulatory divergence, enhances genetic complexity, and promotes the emergence of novel traits and adaptive pathways (Li et al. 2018; Qiao et al. 2019; Van de Peer et al. 2021). In this study, frequent gene duplication events were observed among ShSUT genes in the S. spp. XTT22 genome; however, no ShSUT genes underwent tandem duplication within individual chromosomes (Fig. 4). These fndings suggest that, unlike tandem duplication, segmental duplication and transposition primarily drove the expansion of the ShSUT gene family in sugarcane, aligning with patterns observed in other gene families (Sun et al. 2023a, b; Akbar et al. 2025; Ali et al. 2025).

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) function as key post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, facilitating plant development and enabling adaptive responses to various environmental stresses. This study predicted that seven unique miRNAs from seven diferent families target 28 ShSUTs, with “sbi-miR5381” targeting 17 genes, miRNAs sbi-miR 395k and sbi-miR6229- 3p targeting eight and four genes, and miRNAs “sbi-miR169d- ${ \cdot } 3 p$ ,” “sbi-miR5386,” and “sbi-miR821e” targeting two or more genes (Supplementary Figure S2). Previous studies have identifed various miRNAs involved in regulating plant development and stress mechanism (Fan et al. 2024). Notably, DcSUT5 is regulated by “miR397,” which primarily targets laccase (LAC) genes intricate in lignin biosynthesis (Huang et al. 2020). PtaSUT1 in transgenic populus disrupted sucrose partitioning, altered copper homeostasis via sucrose-sensitive Cu-miRNAs, triggered leaf injury, activate defense responses (Xue et al. 2025). Additionally, miR156, miR529, and miR535 target SQUAMOSA promoter-binding protein-like (SPL) genes, thereby negatively regulating plant immunity. Furthermore, “sbi-miR169d- ${ \it 3 p }$ ” and $^ { \bullet \bullet } m i R 6 2 2 3 \ – 5 p ^ { \prime \prime }$ were identifed as key regulators contributing to the diferential response of sweet sorghum genotypes under heavy metal stress (Jia et al. 2021). DcSWEET16 is mainly targeted by “miR156,” whereas DcpGlcT2 is regulated by both “miR156” and “miR172,” which are associated with overall plant development (Fan et al. 2024).

Extensive studies in plants have demonstrated that SUT proteins are integral to the regulation of essential biological processes, including growth, development, and response to various environmental stresses (Sun et al. 2022). The

PPI analysis identifed three key ShSUT proteins such as ShSUT25 (homologous to maize Sut2), ShSUT08 (homologous to maize Umc2347), and ShSUT17 (homologous to maize Sut4) as central network hubs with multiple interactions. Notably, ShSUT25 interacted with proteins such as BZIP113 and IVR1, suggesting roles in diverse pathways, while ShSUT08 showed interaction with the Tdy1 protein (Supplementary Figure S3). In this context, Bitterlich et al. (2014) demonstrated that the SlSUT2 (homolog to ShSUT2) from tomato is involved in brassinosteroid signaling and plays a role in regulating arbuscular mycorrhiza formation (Bitterlich et al. 2014). Similarly, Chai et al. (2025) highlight that, “PsMYB20” and “PsMADS9” directly bind to the promoter region of PsSUT2 (homolog to ShSUT25), thereby upregulating its expression and potentially infuencing sucrose transport through the transcriptional regulation of PsSUT2 (Chai et al. 2025). Furthermore, Wang et al. (2020) proved that, IbSUT4 (homolog to ShSUT17) modulates sweet potato growth and stress responses via ABF-mediated ABA signaling (Wang et al. 2020). Deng et al. (2023) demonstrated that, overexpressing DfSUT4 (homolog to ShSUT17) enhanced photosynthesis, biomass, grain weight, and cellulose content, indicating its role in sucrose transport, hormone signaling, and stress response (Deng et al. 2023). The ShSUT protein interaction analysis suggests that its homology and interactions with known Zea mays proteins may indicate conserved functions in sucrose transport, plant growth, and stress responses; however, additional research is required to validate these functions.


## Expression dynamics of ShSUT and interacting genes under abiotic stress


Members of the ShSUT gene family play central roles in the intricate molecular networks that regulate plant immunity and coordinate defense responses against various environmental stresses (Li et al. 2018; Chen et al. 2022a, b; Sun et al. 2022). This study analyzed the expression patterns of ShSUT genes and their interacting partners under key abiotic stress conditions such as low temperature, drought, and salinity. The results revealed distinct and gene-specifc stress responses. For example, under cold stress, ShRF2a, ShPsbR, and ShSPT were down-regulated, indicating their role as negative regulators in stress response. In contrast, ShSUT01 was signifcantly up-regulated, likely to enhance sugar transport and maintain cellular energy levels under stress conditions. The time-specifc induction of ShSUT04 and ShCOPT5.1 suggests a fnely tuned response, refecting the plant's need to optimize sugar transport and ion homeostasis at diferent stages of cold stress. This temporal regulation likely helps to balance energy allocation and protect cellular functions as the plant adapts to prolonged cold exposure. During drought, ShSUT04 and ShPsbR were signifcantly induced, and meanwhile, under salinity stress, ShSUT01 and ShPsbR showed increased expression despite suppression of other genes, highlighting their positive role in stress adaptation (Figs. 6, 7, and 8). These fndings align with previous reports on SUT gene expression in other plant species under abiotic stress, further supporting the conserved regulatory functions of ShSUTs. For example, OsSUT1, HvSUT1, ZmSUT1, and TaSUT1 (homologs to ShSUT01/ ShSUT02) were highly up-regulated under drought conditions, whereas other SUT genes were down-regulated, indicating functional divergence in stress responses (Al-Sheikh Ahmed et al. 2018; Xu et al. 2018). Similarly, CaSUT1 and CaSUT3 (homologs of ShSUT01 and ShSUT02) were upregulated in roots under cold and heat stress, suggesting involvement in temperature stress adaptation (Chen et al. 2020). In Saccharum species, SUT4 and SUT5 (including ShSUT04) were up-regulated during drought stress, pointing to a role in sugar-mediated osmotic adjustment via ABAdependent pathways, while SUT1 and SUT2 were downregulated (Zhang et al. 2016). This pattern is further supported by fndings in $D .$ . farinosus, where DfSUT4 (homolog to ShSUT04), DfSUT8, DfSUT9, and DfSUT11 were induced under drought and linked to ABA and MeJA signaling, with

DfSUT4 playing a dominant role in environmental adaptability (Deng et al. 2023). Additionally, OsSUT2 (a homolog of ShSUT01/ShSUT04) was signifcantly up-regulated in rice under drought and salinity, implicating it in ABA-mediated stress signaling (Ibraheem et al. 2011). Further, in poplar, silencing of PtaSUT4 expression led to reduced water uptake and prolonged wilting, highlighting its role in regulating hydraulic conductance (Frost et al. 2012). Overexpression of NtSUT1 (homologous to ShSUT01) in tobacco promoted root elongation under aluminum stress, while StSUT4 in potato responded to GA and ethylene signaling (Chincinska et al. 2008; Kariya et al. 2017). Likewise, BnSUC1-2 in oilseed rape was induced by GA, SA, and heat, linking it to hormone-driven stress responses (Jian et al. 2016). More recently, Zhao et al. (2022) proved that heterologous expression of peach PpSUT2 (homologous to ShSUT04) in tobacco may enhance cold and drought tolerance via sugar transport and ABA pathway activation (Zhao et al. 2022). Supporting this, AcSUT1B, regulated by “AcCBF1,” boosted cold tolerance in Arabidopsis, underscoring its role in cold stress signaling (Long et al. 2024). In summary, these results reveal the role of Saccharum SUT genes in abiotic stress tolerance, with further research needed to link sucrose transport to their physiological functions. Notably, ‘ShSUT04’ with its distinct responses to drought, salinity, and cold, may be a promising target for improving stress resilience and developing genetically engineered sugarcane and other crop varieties.

In addition, key genes such as RF2a, PsbR, SPT, and COPT are crucial regulators of stress responses and metabolic processes, yet their complex functions in plants remain insufciently explored, highlighting the need for focused research. Despite their importance, relatively few studies have examined their roles in abiotic stress responses. For instance, in cotton, silencing GhRF2-32 improved drought and salinity tolerance by enhancing antioxidant defense and reducing stress damage, highlighting the RF2 gene family potential for genetic improvement (Gu et al. 2023). Similarly, the RF2 subfamily bZIP gene “TabZIP3” in wheat is triggered by salt and drought stress, and its overexpression in Arabidopsis enhances salt tolerance, confrming its role in stress adaptation (Guangyan et al. 2019). In rice, OsPsbR1 enhances cold tolerance by activating stress-responsive genes without afecting yield, while OsPsbR3 shows stressresponsive expression and OsPsbR2 is largely inactive, highlighting OsPsbR1 as a key target for crop enhancement (Li et al. 2017). Likewise, in wheat, TaCOPT3D, regulated by the TaWRKY22 TF, which binds to its promoter under Cd stress, plays a vital role in adaptation to abiotic stress by enhancing Cd tolerance, making it a hopeful target for abiotic resistance through genetic engineering (Liu et al. 2022a, b). In S. lycopersicum, AGH786-associated plants showed enhanced resistance to copper harmfulness and drought stress, primarily through the upregulation of SlCOPT genes, key regulators of copper transport. Elevated expression of SlCOPT along with SlMT in both root and shoot tissues highlights SlCOPT as a central gene in mediating stress tolerance in this study (Naz et al. 2022). In our study, ShRF2a, ShPsbR, ShSPT, and ShCOPT5.1 were identifed as interacting partners of ShSUT4 and analyzed their responses under abiotic stresses. These genes are critically involved in photosynthesis, stress signaling, sucrose transport, and metal homeostasis. However, their specifc functions in abiotic stress tolerance remain largely uncharacterized, primarily due to gene redundancy and the complex regulatory networks present in polyploid species like sugarcane. Despite these challenges, preliminary data reveal stress-responsive expression patterns, suggesting their potential roles in environmental adaptation. To fully understand their mechanisms and exploit their capabilities for enhancing stress resilience, comprehensive functional studies are essential.

Under conditions of environmental stress, sugars play important roles as osmolytes, reactive oxygen species (ROS) quenchers and signaling molecules involved in stress perception and signaling and regulation of stress-mediated gene expression, contributing to osmotic adjustment responses, elimination of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and regulation of plant growth and development processes, including fruit ripening (Fakher et al. 2022). Among the sugars present in plant species, sucrose is the main product of the photosynthesis process (Kaur et al. 2021). The sucrose generated is transiently accumulated in leaf vacuoles or transported from source to sink tissues to satisfy the plant growth and development requirements (Braun 2022). Sucrose not only functions as a source of carbon and energy for cells, but also acts as an osmotic adjustment agent, participating in the plant adaptive responses to unfavorable environmental circumstances (Salvi et al. 2022). In situations of environmental stress, the efficiency of photosynthesis is inhibited, which affects the supply, transport and partitioning of sucrose and, therefore, stress tolerance (Salvi et al. 2022).

Long-distance sucrose transport and intracellular compartmentalization are mediated by membrane sucrose transporters (SUTs) (Braun 2022). SUTs are involved in the controlled movement of sugars from source tissues (leaves) to sink tissues (i.e. fruits and roots), determining the overall development of the plant (Liang et al. 2023). Genes encoding SUTs have been studied in various crops and categorized into three groups and their subgroups according to phylogenetic analyses. Type I SUTs are present exclusively in eudicots, playing a role in sucrose loading in the phloem of leaves (Hackel et al. 2006). Type II-A and II-B SUTs are specific to mono- and eudicots, with type II-B being involved in sucrose unloading into the phloem and sucrose importing into sink tissues (Salvi et al. 2022). Type III SUTs are present in all land plants (Salvi et al. 2022), acting as low-affinity/high-capacity sucrose transporters (Garg et al. 2022). They are located in the plasma membrane or tonoplast, with that of tonoplast particularly involved in storing sucrose and modulating its cytosolic levels (Salvi et al. 2022).

Three members belonging to the SUT family have been identified in cultivated tomato (Reuscher et al. 2014). SlSUT1 (Solyc11g017010.1.1) is expressed mainly in assimilate source leaves (Hackel et al. 2006), whose protein has been shown to be located in the plasma membrane of sieve tube elements and to play an essential role in loading apoplastic sucrose into the phloem and its long-distance transport (Reuscher et al. 2014), ensuring the redistribution of energy from leaves to other sink organs of the plant, such as fruits and roots. SlSUT2 (Solyc05g007190.2.1) is expressed predominantly in sink organs, such as young leaves, stems and fruits, with its protein localized in the plasma membrane of sieve tube elements and possibly acting in the unloading of sucrose from the phloem (Reuscher et al. 2014). The SlSUT2 protein has also been shown to influence pollen tube growth (Hackel et al. 2006), the formation of mycorrhizae and to interact with hormones such as brassinosteroids (Hansch et al. 2020). The interaction of SlSUT2 with sucrose and other hormonal factors suggests a complex function in the signaling and transport of sugars within the plant (Kanayama 2017). SlSUT4 (Solyc04g076960.2.1) plays a less understood role, being involved in the regulation of flowering and the modulation of gibberellin biosynthesis, transport of sucrose from the vacuole to the cytoplasm and signaling associated with plant growth and development (Garg et al. 2022). It has a potential location in both the plasma membrane and the tonoplast, suggesting a dual function in metabolic regulation and sucrose transport (Schneider et al. 2012).

The roles of SUTs in plant development have been extensively investigated. For example, inhibition of SUT1 expression in tomato has been shown to affect fruit development (Hackel et al. 2006). In potato, SUT4 (type III) silencing causes early flowering (Chincinska et al. 2008, 2013). SUTs genes are also involved in the response to various abiotic stresses such as salinity, drought and low temperatures (Kaur et al. 2021). In Arabidopsis, AtSUC1 and AtSUC2 transcripts were up-regulated in response to low temperature (Lundmark et al. 2006). In rice, OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 were up-regulated under water deficit and salinity (Ibraheem et al. 2011; Siahpoosh et al. 2012). Overexpression of the apple MdSUT2 gene in tomato plants conferred tolerance to drought, salt stress and resulted in earlier flowering and ripening of transgenic tomato fruits compared to wildtype plants (Ma et al. 2017). Another piece of evidence was reported by Zhang et al. (2014), in which the lower sucrose content was one of the crucial factors leading to the late ripening process of the mutant sweet orange. Therefore, the level of sucrose is also important for the regulation of fruit ripening.

The aforementioned studies provide evidence of the crucial role of sucrose transporters in tolerance to environmental stresses and in promoting fruit ripening. It is therefore essential to gain a better understanding of the role of sucrose transporters in these processes. Tomato is an excellent model for these studies, as there are natural mutants for some master genes controlling fruit ripening, such as rin (ripening-inhibitor), Nr (never-ripe), nor (nonripening), Cnr (colorless nonripening), Gr (green-ripe), and gf (green flesh) (Karlova et al. 2014). Thus, this work aimed to characterize the molecular features of the SUT gene family in tomato and the expression of each gene in response to water deficit in both source and sink organs, as well as the effects of rin and Nr mutations that affect fruit ripening.

Sucrose is the major photosynthetic product in plant species, and it can be transported from photosynthetic tissues to storage sink tissues for starch biosynthesis. Sucrose can also be translocated from source tissues to developing sink tissues and function as an energy source to support organ growth. For example, the sucrose synthesized in embryos of rice seeds is transported to developing young shoots and roots during seed germination. In addition, sucrose provides a carbon source for starch biosynthesis in developing pollen during the reproductive stage, and the starch accumulation is a critical indicator for pollen maturation (Datta et al. 2002).

Sucrose is a major transport sugar in plants, and the translocation of sucrose between organs relies on phloem systems. Sucrose transporters carry sucrose across cell membranes and play an important role in loading sucrose into phloem systems. In most plants, sucrose transporters are encoded by a gene family. The five sucrose transporter genes found in the rice genome are OsSUT1, OsSUT2, OsSUT3, OsSUT4, and OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). OsSUT1 was the first SUT gene isolated from rice (Hirose et al. 1997). In rice plants, OsSUT1 expression has been detected in leaf blades, leaf sheaths, panicles, and germinating seeds (Hirose et al. 1997; Scofield et al. $2 0 0 7 \mathrm { a }$ ; Chen et al. 2010). Suppressing OsSUT1 expression reduces the percentage of filled grains (Scofield et al. 2002). During the grain-filling period, OsSUT1 is expressed in the phloem of leaves, the uppermost internode, and the pedicel of the rice plant for sucrose translocation to the filling grains (Scofield et al. 2007b). A recent study showed that the changes in the OsSUT1 expression level could modulate the salt response of rice plants (Siahpoosh et al. 2012). The expression and regulation of both OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 in embryos have been investigated in our previous studies. The antagonism of abscisic acid and gibberellic acid plays a critical role in regulating OsSUT1 expression during embryo germination (Chen et al. 2010). In germinating embryos, OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 expression is also regulated by soluble sugars (i.e., glucose and sucrose). OsSUT1 expression is down-regulated in 1-day sugar treated embryos; however, it is upregulated in 5-day sugar treated embryos. Moreover, the mechanism of glucose-regulated OsSUT1 expression in embryos is mediated by a hexokinase-dependent signal transduction pathway (Chen et al. 2010). However, the upregulation of OsSUT2 in response to glucose occurs through a hexokinase-independent pathway (Siao et al. 2011). In germinating embryos, the expressions of both OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 are significantly lower than those of OsSUT1, 2, and 4 (Siao et al. 2011).

OsSUT4 is expressed in most tissues such as roots, leaves, and panicles (Aoki et al. 2003). Our previous studies showed that OsSUT4 could play a role in sucrose loading into the sheath phloem of the upper leaves during the post-heading period for sucrose transport to developing grains (Chen and Wang 2008). However, little is known about the regulation and functions of the OsSUT4 gene in other rice tissues during different developmental stages. In the analysis of the phylogenetic tree, Braun and Slewinski (2009) demonstrated that OsSUT4 belongs to the same subfamily as Arabidopsis AtSUT2 (or AtSUC3), tomato LeSUT2, and Plantago PmSUC3. According to amino acid analysis, LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 proteins contain extended cytoplasmic domains. Moreover, the structures of LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 are similar to those of yeast glucose sensors, SNF3 and RGT2; thus, it was considered that the LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 could function as sucrose sensors (Barker et al. 2000). The AtSUT2 protein is localized in sieve elements of phloem, and it is expressed in several sink tissues (Meyer et al. 2000, 2004). The sucrose transport activity of AtSUT2 has been detected in AtSUT2-transformed yeast (Meyer et al. 2000). In Plantago major, PmSUC3 was expressed in sieve cells of sink leaves and identified in non-phloem cells (Barth et al. 2003).

Sugarcane (Saccharum sp.) is a vital commodity for global sugar production and biomass generation, with sucrose being the primary sugar accumulated predominantly in the stem. The sucrose transporter protein is essential in facilitating sucrose transport across cells and over long distances within plants, from source to sink tissues. This study focused on the cloning and expression analysis of the SoSUT4 gene in the Bululawang sugarcane variety. A partial coding sequence of SoSUT4, comprising 802 nucleotides and encoding a 267-amino acid protein, was successfully cloned and sequenced. Sequence analysis revealed that the SoSUT4 protein shares high similarity with other SUT4 proteins in monocotyledonous plants, particularly with Saccharum spontaneum and Saccharum hybrid. Bioinformatics predictions indicated that the SoSUT4 protein is localized to the plasma membrane and contains six transmembrane helices. Gene expression analysis further demonstrated that SoSUT4 expression was significantly higher in the middle internodes of the stem compared to the youngest midsection of the leaves. This expression pattern correlates with higher sucrose accumulation in the stem, as reflected by elevated Brix levels in the stem $( 1 9 . 6 1 \% )$ compared to the leaves $( 1 9 . 4 8 \% )$ . This finding suggests that SoSUT4 is essential for sucrose translocation to the stem, which serves as the primary storage site for sugar. The study provides valuable insights into the SoSUT gene family in sugarcane, particularly highlighting the role of SoSUT4 in sugar transport and accumulation. Future research should further investigate the underlying mechanisms of SoSUT4 and related genes to enhance our understanding of their impact on sugarcane yield, with potential applications for genetic engineering aimed at improving crop productivity.

[Keywords: brix, relative expression, SoSUT4]

The sugarcane plant (Saccharum sp.) is a significant commodity for sugar production and has the potential to produce a substantial amount of biomass. The primary sugar in sugarcane is sucrose, which accumulates in the stem. Sucrose is the main product of carbon dioxide fixation during photosynthesis and plays a crucial role in the plant’s allocation of assimilated carbon (Sauer, 2007). According to Subiyakto et al. (2016), sugar is a major source of calories in the Indonesian diet, alongside other staple foods. Its importance is reflected in government policy, which classifies sugar—particularly crystallized sugar—as one of the nine essential foods. As a result, the policy mandates that sugar must be available in sufficient quantities, be of high quality, affordable, and easily accessible to consumers.

The Center for Agricultural Data and Information (2022) reported that global sugarcane productivity has not yet reached optimal levels. In 2022, Indonesia’s sugarcane productivity was around 67 tons per hectare, placing it $3 6 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ in the world. However, domestic production remains insufficient to meet national demand, resulting in sugar imports from countries such as Thailand, India, Brazil, and Australia (Statistics Indonesia, 2023). That year, sugar imports increased to 6.01 million tons, valued at US\$ 2.998 billion, surpassing the previous year’s import levels. This reliance on imports highlights the need for agricultural innovations to improve sugarcane yield and ensure self-sufficiency.

One way to increase sugarcane productivity is through breeding programs that develop new, highyielding varieties. A primary goal of these programs is to enhance the sucrose content in sugarcane stems. Sucrose accumulation is influenced by several factors, including photosynthesis, enzyme activity in sucrose metabolism, transport to storage organs, carbon allocation, and mobilization of sucrose for \*)Corresponding author: dsantosa@indo.net.id vegetative growth (Conradie, 2011). Effective sucrose accumulation requires efficient translocation from source organs (leaves) to sink organs (stems). This process is facilitated by sugar transporter proteins, which regulate, transport, compartmentalize, and store assimilates within the plant. Wang et al. (2017) classified sugar transporter genes into several categories, including SWEET (Sugars Will Eventually Be Exported Transporters), SUT (sucrose transporters), and monosaccharide transporters.

SUT proteins play a crucial role in sucrose translocation through the phloem, particularly in the uptake and accumulation of high levels of sucrose. These proteins are essential for building sucrose reserves in plants. Zhang et al. (2016) reported that most plant species contain at least four types of SUT proteins. SUT protein-encoding genes have been identified in various crops, including pineapple (Rae et al., 2002), rice (Aoki et al., 2003), potato (Leggewie et al., 2003), Arabidopsis (Sivitz et al., 2008), sorghum (Milne et al., 2013), and wheat (Deol et al., 2013). In sugarcane, Niu et al. (2019) successfully cloned five SUT genes (SoSUT1 to SoSUT5) and analyzed their expression in various tissues, including buds, inflorescences, leaves, stems, and roots. The study found that SoSUT4 expression was negatively correlated with sucrose concentration in the stem internodes, while SoSUT1, SoSUT2, SoSUT3, and SoSUT5 were positively correlated. These findings suggest that different SUT genes may have varying roles during sucrose accumulation.

Enhancing sucrose concentration in sugarcane stems can be achieved by silencing SUT genes that negatively affect sucrose content, such as SoSUT4. Studies in other crops have shown that manipulating SUT expression can have significant impacts. For instance, overexpressing SUT genes has resulted in increased tuber yield in potatoes (Sun et al., 2011), higher sugar concentrations in mature tomato fruit (Wang et al., 2016), improved rice yield components (Putri et al., 2020), and enhanced sucrose accumulation in tobacco root cells (Kariya et al., 2017). Additionally, Chincinska et al. (2013) found that suppressing SUT4 improved sucrose efflux from developing tubers and leaves in potatoes.

Despite these advances, SoSUT4 remains underexplored in sugarcane, particularly in Indonesian varieties. This research aims to isolate, clone, and analyze SoSUT4 gene expression in Indonesian sugarcane varieties. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of highyielding sugarcane through genetic manipulation and breeding programs, ultimately reducing Indonesia’s dependence on sugar imports and enhancing the country’s agricultural sustainability.

## Modifications of Zn, Cd, and Fe accumulation in AtHMA4-expressing tomato


The homeostasis of Zn, Cd and Fe is not specific for each metal, but is interconnected by common pathways and is called “metal cross-homeostasis”. In transgenic plants ectopically expressing Zn transporters, this phenomenon contributes to alteration of not only Zn accumulation and distribution, but also that of other metals like Cd or Fe [14]. Therefore, although AtHMA4 (a Zn-transporter) was expressed in tomato to improve the Zn content in shoots, the concentration of Cd and Fe in transgenic and wild-type plants was also examined.

Expression of AtHMA4 facilitates root-to-shoot Zn translocation but in a $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply-dependent manner. In plants grown at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, the expression of AtHMA4 enhanced the translocation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ to shoots and its concentration in leaves, but the differences versus wild-type plants were much more pronounced in line 4. However, upon exposure to $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, there was no difference in Zn accumulation among the studied lines (Fig. 1a-c).

Interestingly, when Cd was added to the control medium (containing $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn), Zn translocation to leaves of transgenic plants was stimulated, especially in line 4 (Fig. 1c). Expression of AtHMA4 significantly increased the Cd concentration in leaves and reduced it in roots, but only in line 4 (Fig. 1d-f). The total Fe concentrations did not differ much between transgenic and wild-type plants, both in the leaves and in the roots for most examined experimental variants (Fig. 1g-i).

In summary, the level of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in the shoots of tomato expressing AtHMA4 (responsible for the control of $Z \mathrm { n }$ translocation to shoots in A. thaliana) depended on $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply, and also on the presence of Cd. This points to the difficulties in engineering a plant displaying the desired Zn level in shoots (e.g. for biofortification or phytoremediation purposes) when grown under differing conditions of metal supply. To better plan future modifications of metal uptake and root/shoot distribution, it is necessary to unravel the molecular mechanisms induced in transgenic plants that are responsible for the detected diverse phenotype of transgenics grown on media of varying mineral compositions. Therefore, detailed expression analysis of transgenic and wild-type plants was performed.

## Microarray-based analysis of the transcription profiles of LCM-derived tissues from roots of transgenic and wild-type tomato exposed to 5 μM Zn


As a first step, microarray analysis was used to identify the endogenous tissue-specific molecular metal-crosshomeostasis pathways that are activated in the roots of tomato expressing AtHMA4 and which accompany increased Zn root-to-shoot translocation. The transcription profiles of root tissues collected by LCM from transgenic line 4 (with $Z \mathrm { n }$ translocation to shoots enhanced more efficiently than in line 15) and wild-type plants grown at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn were compared (Fig. 1a-c). The Zn concentration in the root tissues used for expression analysis is shown in Additional file 6.

Transcript profiles were compared in two root sectors: epidermis $^ +$ cortex (EC) and the stele (S). Gene expression was considered as up- or downregulated if the transcript level showed a minimum of a 1.2-fold change and FDR of ${ < } 0 . 0 5$ (a low value was chosen to avoid overlooking smaller changes which might also be important in modifications of Zn root/shoot distribution in AtHMA4- expressing plants; RT-qPCR was used as final confirmation of a difference) (Additional file 1). The complete dataset is available in the NCBI with accession no. GSE68641 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/projects/geo/ query/acc.cgi?acc $\asymp$ GSE68641), and is also included as Additional file 7). The NCBI Accession Numbers of nucleic acid sequences are given in the appropriate Additional files.

In AtHMA4-expressing tomato, as many as 513 genes were differentially expressed in the EC, whereas a lower number, 230 genes, was detected in the S (Fig. 2). The relative distribution of differentially expressed genes in roots classified by GO (Gene Ontology) of biological processes (using the Tomato Functional Genomics database) (Additional file 8) shows that genes related to categories such as “metabolic processes”, “cellular processes”, “response to stress”, and “transport” constitute a relatively large group, indicating importance in the regulation of a transgenic plant’s response to the applied conditions. Our focus was on differentially expressed genes involved in: (i) metal transport; (ii) transcription factors; (iii) ethylene biosynthesis; (iv) cell wall modifications. The complete sets of genes for these four categories present in the microarray are shown in Additional file 9. The genes selected for further analysis are listed in Additional file 10, and the microarray data were validated by RT-qPCR (Fig. 3) confirming differential expression for most of the selected genes (Additional file 10 and (Fig. 3). Some inconsistencies between the microarray and RT-qPCR expression analyses were most likely due to the lower specificity of the microarray probes than of the gene-specific primers used in RTqPCR. The expression of certain genes selected for detailed analysis was found by microarray to be higher, and by RT-qPCR to be lower than in the wild type. The probes for these genes also recognize other sequences: (i) LeNRAMP2: probe Les.4532.1.S1_at recognizes fragments of chromosomes 05, 07, 10, 12; (ii) LeFER: probe Les.3814.1.S1_at recognizes fragments of chromosomes 02, 05, 07; (iii) LebZIP44: probe Les.3126.1.S1_at also recognizes fragments of chromosome 05. Thus, if the outcome of the RT-qPCR-based expression study differed from that of the microarray experiment, the results of the more sensitive and reliable RT-qPCR analysis were accepted as valid.

Two metal transporters were identified (Fig. 3a, e). The first was LeNRAMP2 (Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Protein), with a slightly lower level of mRNA in the EC of transformants. The second was ABC putative transporter (ATP-Binding Cassette transporter) strongly downregulated in the S of transgenic plants relative to the wild type.

In the category of transcription factors, LeFER (encoding the bHLH protein) was identified as a gene whose mRNA levels in transgenic plants were lower in both root sectors than in the wildtype. On the other hand, LebZIP44 (basic-region leucine-zipper) mRNA remained at the wild-type level (Fig. 3b, f ).

Interestingly, profound downregulation of most identified biosynthesis genes and ethylene receptors was found in transgenic plants relative to the wild type (Fig. 3c, g). Ethylene receptor NR (never-ripe), LeACO4, and LeACO5 (encoding 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate oxidases) were strongly downregulated in the EC and in the S, but LeACO3, in the EC only.

Moreover, in transgenic vs. wild-type plants, microarray data indicated differential expression of numerous genes involved in cell wall remodeling (Additional file 10). Considering the importance of the apoplast in a plant’s response to metals [18, 19], we focused on seven genes with the most pronounced expression modifications. RT-qPCR analysis (Fig. 3d, h) showed downregulation of LeTHT7-1, LeTHT7-8 (N-hydroxycinnamoyl-CoA:tyramine N-hydroxycinnamoyl transferase), LeExp8, LeExp18 (expansins), and LetXET-B1 (xyloglucan endotransglucosylase), and upregulation of LeuJ-2 (an extensin) in both examined tissues. For LeXTH3 (xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydroxylase) the transcript level was higher in the S of transformants than in the wild type.


## RT-qPCR-based analysis of gene expression in LCM-derived tissues from roots of transgenic and wild-type plants exposed to different Zn concentrations and to Cd


At this stage of the research, the aim was to identify the molecular mechanisms behind the Zn- and Cd-supplydependent modifications of Zn and Cd accumulation patterns in transgenic plants (Fig. 1). We examined the possible contribution of metal-homeostasis and ethylene-related genes (except cell wall-remodeling genes) (Fig. 3) that were selected from among the genes identified in the microarray-based analysis. In addition, four metal-homeostasis genes were included in the expression study (Additional file 11): (i) LeIRT1 (Iron Regulated Transporter 1, dependent on FER), the Strategy I Fe-deficiency uptake gene [20] known to mediate uptake of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd; (ii) LeNRAMP1 and LeNRAMP3 involved in metal redistribution [20]; (iii) LeChln (LeNAS), encoding nicotianamine synthase participating in the biosynthesis of nicotianamine (NA), a metal chelator involved in the regulation of Zn and Cd translocation to shoots [20, 21]. In this study two transgenic lines were compared—lines 4 and 15. They differ in the efficiency of Zn translocation to shoots (higher in line 4) (Fig. 1) [13]. The expression pattern of the examined endogenous genes was substantially modified in transgenic plants as compared with the wild type (Fig. 4).

There was also a major difference in the expression pattern between transgenic plants grown at 5 and $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn. In the EC, the expression of ethylenerelated genes LeACO4, LeACO5, the ethylene receptor LeNR, as well as the ethylene-dependent LeChln and the Fe (also Zn and Cd) acquisition system represented by LeFER, LeIRT1 was lower (relative to the wild type) in plants exposed to $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, but higher in those grown at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn (Fig. 4a, b). The expression of NRAMPs in the EC was lower for both tested Zn conditions, but primarily for line 4, except LeNRAMP2.

In the S, the transcript level in transgenics grown at both 0.5 and $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn was lower than in the wild type for most of the tested genes, except differential expression of LeNRAMP2 (Fig. 4d, e).

When $0 . 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd was added to the control medium containing $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, in the EC the expression pattern of LeNR, LeACO4, and LeACO5 remained similar to controls for all tested lines; the opposite was observed, however, for NRAMPs. In the S of transgenic plants lower expression than in the wild type was detected both for ethylene genes (LeNR, LeACO4, and LeACO5) and for ethylene-dependent LeFER, LeChln, and LeNRAMP1 (Fig. 4c, f; Fig. 5c, f ).
