Three of these genes (XTH1, XTH3, XTH7) were differentially expressed in the transgenic plants, however, not in the same fashion. The third class was the endo-1,4-beta-D-glucanases (Cel genes). In both analyzed tissues, lower and higher transcript levels were found in transgenic plants for LeCel2 and LeCel7, respectively.

Thus, ectopic expression of AtHMA4 in tomato modified transcription profiles of the studied genes in a tissue-specific manner with striking differences between the EPP and the ESP in certain cases.

AtHMA4 expression overloads the apoplast of transgenics’ leaves with Zn and modifies Zn distribution in the leaf blade It is known that AtHMA4 exports Zn to the apoplast [2,3,10]. Here we confirmed that expression of AtHMA4 in tomato enhanced the $Z \mathrm { n }$ concentration in the apoplast of leaves (Fig. 8a). Thus, the $Z \mathrm { n }$ status at the cellular level in transgenic plants was different from that of the wild type. The potassium concentration, used as an indicator of cytoplasmic contamination, remained at comparable levels in all tested lines (Fig. 8b).

In our previous study on AtHMA4-expressing tobacco we showed that the enhanced concentration of Zn in the apoplast of leaves from plants grown in the medium containing a high concentration of this metal is related to the initiation of Zn loading into clusters of $^ { \omega } \mathrm { Z n }$ storage” mesophyll cells [19]. Therefore, in this study, finding that expression of AtHMA4 in tomato modifies the expression of endogenous genes and changes the Zn apoplast/symplast status, prompted us to examine the Zn distribution pattern within leaves.

The presence of $Z \mathrm { n }$ was indicated by Zinpyr-1-based green fluorescence (Fig. 9). In the leaves of wild-type plants grown either at 0.5 or $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn in the medium, $Z \mathrm { n }$ was evenly distributed in the mesophyll cells, though its level was higher at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn (Fig. 9b, d).

In contrast, in transgenic leaves, enhanced Zn levels were detected inside groups of cells (Fig. 9a, c). This is especially evident in plants exposed to $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn. Zinpyr1-based intensive fluorescence indicating a high Zn level was detected in groups of mesophyll cells (primarily palisade parenchyma), whereas neighboring groups of cells showed fluorescence of lower intensity (indicating lower Zn concentrations) (Fig. 9c). Thus, similarly as in tobacco [19], expression of AtHMA4 in tomato contributed to the manifestation of heterogeneity in the mesophyll cells with respect to their capacity for $Z \mathrm { n }$ storage.

Zn accumulation due to AtHMA4 expression (increased Zn root-to-shoot translocation at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, no change at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ~ Z \mathrm { n } )$ were accompanied in the roots by tissuespecific expression patterns of metal-homeostasis genes that were different than in the wild type. Importantly, the pattern of modifications detected in transgenic plants (as compared with the wild type) was not the same upon exposure to 0.5 and $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn in the medium. According to the presented model (Fig. 10), changes in the expression of endogenous genes in transgenic plants are induced in response to the mineral imbalance resulting from the export activity of AtHMA4 in transgenic tomato. These alterations contribute to the generation of the phenotype of transgenic plants, including changes in the accumulation and distribution of metal(s) between roots and shoots. It has already been shown [22] that plants grown under different conditions of exposure to metals (metal deficiency, sufficiency, and excess) differ greatly in their expression profiles. Therefore, it was assumed that these very different molecular backgrounds of tomato (used for transformation) grown at varying Zn levels in the medium will interact with the changes in the mineral status at the cellular level (resulting from AtHMA4 export activity), the extent of which is different at lower and higher Zn exposure. As a result, in specific cells/tissues/organs endogenous genes known to respond to the availability of a metal(s) are up- or downregulated in transgenic plants in a tissue-dependent fashion. The activation of endogenous metal cross-homeostasis mechanisms in transgenic plants is considered a key factor that contributes to the generation of their characteristics.

## Zn supply-dependent modification of Zn root/shoot distribution due to expression of AtHMA4 in tomato is accompanied in roots by tissue-specific differential expression of metal-homeostasis genes


Our previous study showed that expression of 35S::AtHMA4 and $A h H M A \mathcal { 4 } _ { p } . . . A h H M A \mathcal { 4 }$ in tobacco and tomato led to changes in Zn and Cd accumulation and root/shoot distribution. The pattern was different, however, at a range of metal concentrations in the medium, indicating involvement of endogenous processes specifically induced in transgenic plants [10–13]. Here it was shown that the Zn supply-dependent modifications of


## Changes specific for the EC (epidermis $^ +$ cortex)


In numerous plant species, Zn excess decreases the Fe level in aerial parts and induces an Fe-deficiency response due to a shoot-born systemic signal [22–24]. In the wild-type tomato, the shoot Fe content was lower at elevated $Z \mathrm { n }$ (10 and $2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ ) compared with $1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn [13]. In line with these observations, here it was shown that in the EC of roots from wild-type tomato grown at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, the expression of transcription factor LeFER, and LeFER-dependent LeIRT1 that mediates Fe, Zn and Cd uptake [20, 25, 26] was higher compared with $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn exposure (Fig. 4a, b; Fig. 5a, b). However, expression of AtHMA4 changed the intracellular Fe status, which was different at the lower and higher Zn levels in the medium.

Thus, expression of the Fe deficiency-inducible Strategy I Fe acquisition genes (LeIRT1 and LeFER), ethylene genes (LeNR, LeACO4, and LeACO5), and Chln found to be higher in transgenic plants than in the wild type grown at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, indicates generation of Fe deficiency status due to AtHMA4 expression. Conversely, the lower expression of these genes in AtHMA4-plants grown at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn indicated that their Fe status had changed to Fe sufficiency. These contrasting changes in the expression of endogenous genes show how deeply the $Z \mathrm { n }$ export activity of HMA4 alters endogenous metal cross-homeostasis mechanisms (Fig. 10). In transgenic plants they did not lead, however, to marked changes in total root and leaf Fe concentrations, except in transgenic line 4 grown at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ~ \mathrm { Z n }$ (Fig. 1g-i), suggesting that in most experimental variants, there occurred the induction of pathways counteracting mineral imbalance generated by the export activity of AtHMA4 in tomato.

Ethylene is necessary for upregulation of Fe-uptake genes [27]. The examined genes included LeNR (an ethylene receptor that responds to environmental stresses), LeACO4, and LeACO5. Ethylene is the product of the reaction catalyzed by 1-aminocyclopropane-1- carboxylate oxidase (ACO), therefore, the site of ACO expression is considered the best indicator of ethylene production [28, 29]. Ethylene affects Fe deficiencyinducible genes, including IRT1, by regulating the FER transcription factor level [30]. Expression of LeIRT1 also depends on the expression of LeChln, the only NAS gene in tomato involved in nicotianamine (NA) synthesis that is known to regulate cross-homeostasis of Fe, Zn, Mn, Cd, and $\mathrm { N i }$ , among others [26, 31, 32]. Upon exposure to 0.5 or $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, in the EC the expression of LeIRT1 in AtHMA4-tomato was higher or lower than in the wild type, respectively, and was accompanied by respectively higher or lower expression of LeChln (Fig. 4a).

Moreover, in the EC of transgenic plants grown at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, the expression of NRAMP1 and NRAMP3 was lower than in the wild type in both lines, whereas at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn—only in line 4 (Fig. 4a; Fig. 10). It cannot be excluded that the detected modified expression of LeNRAMPs could contribute to regulation of the amount of Zn available for radial transport and root-to-shoot translocation, thus, to the difference in Zn and Fe root and shoot concentrations detected between lines 4 and 15 (Fig. 1b-c, h-i). The NRAMPs consist of a group of membrane importer proteins that exhibit functional divergence and broad substrate specificity, including Fe, Mn, Ni, Cd, Zn, Pb [33]. However, up to now the tomato LeNRAMP1 and LeNRAMP 3 localized to the internal membranes have only been shown to mediate Mn transport [20]. Other metals, including $Z \mathrm { n }$ , were not tested, hence it was not determined if $Z \mathrm { n }$ is a substrate. Further research aimed at elucidation of LeNRAMP1 and LeNRAMP3 function is needed to understand the contribution of these proteins to $Z \mathrm { n }$ homeostasis and partitioning in organs.


## Changes specific for the S (stele)


In the S (where $Z \mathrm { n }$ is loaded into xylem vessels) the Zn supply-dependent contribution of AtHMA4 expression to Zn root-to-shoot translocation efficiency (increase at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, no change at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn; Fig. 1c) was accompanied primarily by a distinct expression pattern of LeNRAMP2. In plants exposed to $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, LeNRAMP2 was downregulated, and upregulated at $5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn (Fig. 4d, e). Thus, LeNRAMP2 was found to respond in the S of both transgenic lines in a unique way to the changes in mineral status resulting from AtHMA4 export activity (see model in Fig. 10). This suggests that LeNRAMP2 could be considered a candidate gene for involvement in the Zn supply-dependent efficiency of Zn translocation to shoots, which is distinct in transgenic vs. wild-type plants (Fig. 1c). To corroborate this supposition, it is necessary to characterize LeNRAMP2. Currently only its sequence is known. The highest level of sequence identity was found between LeNRAMP2 and the Arabidopsis NRAMPs from the second sub-family, which include AtNRAMP2-5 (Additional file 14). It shares $7 4 . 2 ~ \%$ amino acid identity with AtNRAMP2 which does not complement the fet3fet4 yeast mutation, indicating the lack of ability to transport Fe [21]. LeNRAMP2 also shows high identity with AtNRAMP3 and TcNRAMP3 $( 7 2 . 1 \ \%$ and $7 1 . 5 ~ \%$ , respectively), and with AtNRAMP4 and TcNRAMP4 $6 9 . 6 ~ \%$ and $6 8 . 2 ~ \%$ , respectively). They encode tonoplast-localized proteins implicated in the release of Fe, Mn, and Cd from vacuoles [21, 34–36]. It cannot be excluded that LeNRAMP2, as an import protein, is localized to the internal membranes and participates in metal redistribution from intracellular stores. Detailed molecular and functional characteristics are needed, however, to conclude about its specific role in the S relating to modifications of Zn supply-dependent alteration of Zn translocation to shoots in the AtHMA4- tomato.


## Cd-dependent modifications of Zn/Cd root/shoot distribution due to expression of AtHMA4 in tomato involves root tissue-specific alteration of LeNRAMP1-3 and LeChln


Expression of AtHMA4 also contributed to enhanced Cd root-to-shoot translocation. Moreover, in the presence of Cd, the efficiency of $Z \mathrm { n }$ translocation was significantly higher, however, the difference was noted primarily in transgenic line 4 (Fig. 1). These changes were accompanied at the molecular level by differences in the abundance of LeNRAMP1-3 mRNA, especially in the EC (Fig. 4c, f; Fig. 10) indicating that they were regulated in a tissue-specific manner directly or indirectly by $Z \mathrm { n } / \mathrm { C d }$ . It is noteworthy that there is a growing amount of data suggesting the involvement of NRAMP transporters in mediating Cd uptake and in intracellular distribution in plants [34, 36, 37]. The changes in Cd and Zn accumulation distinct for line 4 were accompanied by the reduction to a barely detectable level of the expression of LeNRAMP2, LeChln (LeNAS), and yet uncharacterized transcription factors LebZIP44 in the S of transgenics’ roots. The role of NAS in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd translocation to shoots has been shown for AhNAS2 from A. halleri [32, 38]. However, the tissue-specific regulation of LeChln upon exposure to a range of Zn and to Cd had not been investigated thus far. The expression of LeFER and LeChln in the S of transgenics’ roots was lower than in the wild type and corresponded with decreased expression of ethylene-related genes (Fig. 10). In the EC this correlation was not as obvious, however. The role for ethylene in a plant’s response to Cd was indicated in experiments showing higher tolerance to Cd in the Nr tomato mutant [39], as well as in the etr1-1 and ein2-1 Arabidopsis mutants [40].


## In leaves, ectopic expression of AtHMA4 modifies the ethylene-dependent pathway in a tissue-dependent fashion


Expression of HMA4 in tobacco and tomato led to the appearance of necrosis within leaf blades when plants were exposed to elevated $Z \mathrm { n }$ in the medium [11,12]. It was shown that loading of $Z \mathrm { n }$ into $^ { \omega } \mathrm { Z n }$ -storage cells” was initiated upon a high Zn concentration in the apoplast, however, the nature of the signal was not proposed. In this study, in the leaves of AtHMA4-tomato plants grown at moderately toxic $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ~ Z \mathrm { n }$ its accumulation was also restricted to groups of mesophyll $Z \mathrm { n }$ -storage cells, whereas it remained low in neighboring nonaccumulating ones. Upon exposure to a higher $( 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ Zn concentration, necrotic regions developed [13], likely originating from the groups of $Z \mathrm { n }$ -accumulating cells identified in this study. In contrast, in wild-type tomato $Z \mathrm { n }$ was distributed uniformly across mesophyll cells (Fig. 9).

Here we demonstrate that formation of clusters of Znaccumulating cells in leaves of AtHMA4-tomato plants (Fig. 9) is accompanied by dramatically lower, relative to the wild type, expression of two ethylene receptors LeNR, both in the EPP (upper epidermis $^ +$ palisade parenchyma) and in the ESP (lower epidermis $^ +$ spongy parenchyma), and LeETR1 in the ESP (Fig. 7c, g). Lower expression of ethylene receptors in transgenic tomato might indicate fewer receptors within the ER of mesophyll tissues, leading to higher sensitivity to ethylene than in the wild type [41].

These results were the basis for formulating the hypothesis linking the appearance of groups of Znaccumulating mesophyll cells (Fig. 9) with modifications of the expression profiles of genes from the ethylene biosynthesis pathway detected in transgenic tomato plants exposed to $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn (Fig. 7c, g). According to this hypothesis, the combination of higher sensitivity to ethylene than in the wild type with the probably higher production of ethylene (resulting from higher expression of certain ACO genes in the mesophyll) could be involved in the pathway signaling Zn excess in the apoplast, leading to induction of Zn accumulation in groups of mesophyll cells. Our previous research on tobacco expressing AtHMA4 led to the conclusion that until the Zn concentration is sensed as too high, Zn is accumulated uniformly in mesophyll cells, but when the apoplastic Zn reaches a threshold, a signal is generated to redirect Zn to groups of cells (“Zn-storage cells”). The nature of the signal is not known; however, the results of this study suggest that ethylene could be a part of it. These results open a new direction in the search for the mechanisms behind formation of necrotic regions, which, according to our recent data, could be considered a mechanism of tolerance to $Z \mathrm { n }$ , protecting neighboring non-accumulating cells from the toxic effects of $Z \mathrm { n }$ rather than only being a symptom of toxicity [15]. Future research should clarify this issue. Ethylene is involved in the regulation of numerous physiological processes, including the response to biotic and abiotic stresses [42]. Interestingly, in tomato leaves ethylene accounts for formation of ozone-dependent lesions from specific mesophyll cells, which were considered groups of cells disposed to die upon a certain signal resulting from increased ethylene [43]. Moreover, a recent study on ethylene insensitive mutants etr1-1 and ein2-1 indicated that ethylene signaling is involved in the early Cd stress response in A. thaliana leaves [40].


## Expression of AtHMA4 in tomato modifies expression of cell-wall remodeling genes


Plant cell wall composition and structure play a variety of functions in a plant’s response to metals, including regulation of the capacity for metal accumulation and signaling of metal status [44]. These functions might be distinctly affected in different root and leaf tissues of tomato plants due to overloading of the apoplast with Zn as a result of AtHMA4 export activity.


## Roots


Expression of AtHMA4 induced processes leading to strengthening of the cell wall structure by enhanced expression of cell wall structural proteins, extensins, and downregulation of several cell wall-modifying enzymes (Fig. 3d, h). Upregulation of the cell wall structural protein, extensin uJ-2, was noted in both root sectors. Stress-induced expression of extensin genes is usually related to the requirement for a fortified cell wall [45]. Significantly higher expression of uJ-2 in both examined sectors of transgenic roots, with a much higher increase of the transcript level in the EC, indicate hitherto unknown regulation resulting from the high Zn status in the apoplast due to the export activity of the AtHMA4 protein. Increased expression of the cell wall structural gene was accompanied by strong downregulation of expansin-encoding LeEXP8 and LeEXP18 genes that facilitate cell wall extension and contribute to cell wall disassembly [46, 47]. Studies have shown that the mRNA of LeEXP8 accumulates in germinating seeds in the cortical tissue of the root elongation zone [48]. In agreement with this, expression of LeEXP8 in the wild-type tomato was detected at a high level in the EC only, whereas in the S, the transcript level remained almost undetectable (Fig. 3d). In turn, the expression of LeEXP18 was detected in aerial parts of young soilgrown seedlings and not in roots [49]. In our experiments, expression of LeEXP18 decreased to almost zero in transgenics in both sectors, however, in the wild type it was very low in the S, and high in the EC. Thus, this study demonstrates that LeEXP18 in wild-type tomato is expressed specifically in the EC of the roots, and that a high-Zn apoplastic status in transgenic plants contributes to downregulation of its transcript level. Other downregulated genes in transgenics were plant cell wallremodeling genes, THT7-1 and THT7-8, that encode an enzyme responsible for the synthesis of hydroxycinnamoyl tyramines. It has been proposed that they promote accumulation of cell wall-bound phenolic amines, and respond to wounding and ozone [50]. It seems that this is an example of common pathways for biotic and abiotic stresses, including the action of heavy metals. Finally, the XTHs and XET genes involved in modification of the cellulose/xyloglucan network [46, 51] were differentially expressed in transgenic tomato. XTHs encodes xyloglucan endotransglucosylase/hydroxylases with two distinct activities. Most act as transglucosylase referred to as XET, while some XTHs, preferentially as hydrolases. The encoded enzymes participate in a range of physiological processes including wall loosening, wall strengthening, cell-wall remodeling during abiotic stress [46, 51]. Interestingly, the accumulation profiles of these genes were different in AtHMA4-tomato, with moderate downregulation of tXET-B1 in both EC and S root sectors, and very strong upregulation of XTH3, specifically in the S. Compared with the wild type, the lower accumulation of tXET$B { 1 } ~ \mathrm { m R N A }$ in transgenics is in agreement with the overall expression pattern of cell-wall remodeling genes, indicating strengthening of this structure in AtHMA-tomato roots. Transglycosylation by XET can increase or reduce the length of polysaccharides, which could result in either cell wall expansion or disassembly [51].

Expression of the cell wall-remodeling genes was not further analyzed upon longer exposure to the lower $( 0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ Zn concentration and in the presence of Cd, as cell wall modification in response to metals was not the major aim of this study. However, these data constitute a basis for further research with a focus on the specific role of the apoplast in a plant’s response to $Z \mathrm { n }$ .


## Leaves


The genes found to be expressed differently in the leaves of transgenic tomato vs. wild type were, except for LeXTH3, not the same as those found in roots (Figs. 3 and 7). LeXTH3 showed higher transcript levels in leaves, specifically in the EPP. In transgenic tomato, in addition to three XTHs (LeXTH1, LeXTH3, LeXTH7), differential expression of three Cel genes encoding endo1,4-beta-D-glucanases (LeCel2, LeCel5, LeCel7) and LePMEU1 encoding pectin-methyl-esterase (PME) were identified. Endoglucanases are hydrolytic enzymes related to hemicellulose degradation involved in cell wall disassembly during vegetative growth and fruit ripening [46], but also involved in cell wall signaling. Both identified XTHs and Cel genes are ethylene-inducible [52, 53], and their tissue-specific expression in transgenic plants is accompanied by downregulation of LeETR1 and LeNR receptor genes and upregulation of ACO genes, which is very much specific for the EPS and EPP (Fig. 7). In this context, the detected higher expression of LePMEU1 in transgenic leaves in both EPS and EPP, known from its role in cell wall loosening and cell wall signaling by generation of active oligogalacturonides (OGAs) [54, 55], could be related to signaling the modification of the cell wall structure due to the apoplastic Zn excess. Higher expression of LePMEU1 was also detected in tomato exposed to $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn with enhanced Zn concentration in the apoplast due to expression of AhHMA4::AhHMA4 [11]. Not much is known about the role of the identified classes of cell wall proteins in plant responses to metals, nonetheless, our study points to their significance in this process. More detailed analysis is needed to demonstrate the nature and physiological significance of these relationships, and to indicate whether they likely contribute to signaling and/or accommodation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ excess in the cell wall.

The major questions asked in this manuscript are: What makes a transgenic plant resistant to changes introduced by a transgene? What endogenous mechanisms are initiated?

The phenomenon of metal-supply-dependent metal root/shoot distribution is known for wild-type plants. It was expected that engineering a desired level of metal accumulation in a target organ by ectopic expression of a chosen metal-homeostasis gene (especially under a strong constitutive promoter) would lead to a modification that remains qualitatively the same under varying conditions of metal supply. It turned out, however, that overcoming the endogenous system controlling the amount of metal transferred to shoots is very difficult, and underlying mechanisms remain unknown [14]. Understanding the regulation of these processes would help to more successfully engineer desired metal accumulation patterns for phytoremediation and biofortification purposes.

In this study, the detected Zn supply-dependent modification of Zn root/shoot distribution in AtHMA4- tomato (increase $Z \mathrm { n }$ root-to-shoot translocation at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $Z \mathbf { n } _ { i }$ , no change at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ~ Z \mathrm { n } )$ involved distinct expression of LeNRAMP2, primarily in the stele of the root. Moreover, ethylene-dependent pathways, including ethylene-dependent Fe-uptake system (LeIRT1, LeFER, LeChln) and ethylene-related genes (LeNR, LeACO3, LeACO5) likely play an important role in this phenomenon. The expression of the identified genes (LeNR, LeACO3, LeACO5, LeIRT1, LeFER, LeChln) in transgenic plants was different depending on Zn exposure (upregulated at $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, downregulated at $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $Z \mathrm { n } )$ , and also on Cd exposure.

Ethylene is also suggested as an important factor in a pathway induced by high $Z \mathrm { n }$ in the apoplast, which resulted in loading excess $Z \mathrm { n }$ into the mesophyll of $^ { \omega } \mathrm { Z n }$ accumulating cells”, which might protect the entire leaf blade from $Z \mathrm { n }$ toxicity [15]. Furthermore, it was shown that modification of several classes of cell wallremodeling genes due to overloading of the apoplast with $Z \mathrm { n }$ , was organ specific and tissue specific, despite ectopic expression of AtHMA4.

Ectopic expression of AtHMA4 led to deregulation of cellular $Z \mathrm { n }$ -status, and induced endogenous metal crosshomeostasis molecular mechanisms in a tissue-specific fashion, likely to counteract these changes. It is noteworthy that more dramatic alterations in the expression level of metal-homeostasis genes were detected in transgenic plants at lower, $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } _ { : }$ Zn compared with $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn, especially in the EC of the roots. Thus, the export activity of AtHMA4 interfered in metal homeostasis to a larger extent at the lower Zn concentration in the medium.

Moreover, the difference in the efficiency of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd translocation to shoots between line 4 (higher efficiency) and line 15 was accompanied by differences in the expression of LeNRAMP1-3 (primarily in the EC), with the greatest difference in the expression of LeNRAMP2 (both in the EC and S).

## Abbreviations


aRNA, amplified RNA; EC, epidermis $^ +$ cortex; EPP, palisade parenchyma $^ +$ upper epidermis; ESP, spongy parenchyma $^ +$ lower epidermis; LCM, laser capture microdissection; RT-qPCR, reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction; S, stele

Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic heavy metal that naturally exists in earth or artificially occurs as a result of the industrial and agricultural activity. Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is an essential nutrient that plays various physiological and biochemical roles in plants. However, an excess of this essential metal ion is also severely toxic to plant growth, which is another kind of contamination. The excessive heavy metal contamination in soil can be a result of various factors, including mining activities, the use of phosphate fertilizers and manures, and the disposal of municipal sewage waste, urban compost and industrial sludge (Das et al. 1997; Benavides et al. 2005; Grata˜o et al. 2005). Heavy metal pollution of farmland is a big problem of crop production and human health. Heavy metal ions can be easily absorbed through roots and can be translocated into the aerial plant part. As a result, agricultural products cultivated in soil contaminated with heavy metals contain toxic metals. Furthermore, differences in the content and distribution of heavy metals have been observed to be dependent on crop species and in cultivars within the same species (Pulford et al. 2003; Chao et al. 2012; Park et al. 2012).

The Arabidopsis Col-0 ecotype has a single base-pair deletion (Thymine) at position 1626 bp of the HMA3 gene when compared to that of the Ws ecotype cDNA, and this results in a frame shift that produces a premature stop codon and a subsequent truncated protein (Gravot et al. 2004; Hussain et al. 2004; Morel et al. 2009). The difference between the AtHMA3 genes observed in two cultivars (Ws and Col-0) affects the ability of metal translocation (Park et al. 2012). In a recent review (Park and Ahn 2014), we presented the proposed model (Fig. S1) for the difference in the activation of the translocation and compartmentation that is dependent on whether HMA3 is working. Specific transporter-related Cd and Zn uptake results in the absorption of these heavy metals into roots in Arabidopsis, and they are sequestered into the vacuole by some transporter such as tonoplast-located HMA3 protein present in Ws ecotype but not in Col-0 ecotype. The translocation capacity of remaining metals outside the vacuole is involved in some transporter activity such as HMA2 and HMA4 (Park et al. 2012). The sequestration into the vacuole via normal HMA3 protein limits Cd and Zn translocation from the root to shoot, thereby partially could decrease the competition between metals in the Ws shoots, whereas less sequestration caused by an HMA3 mutation in the Col-0 may give rise to severe chlorosis and anthocyanin. In addition, genome-wide association studies have determined that HMA3 mutation leads to natural variation in the Cd concentration in the leaf of Arabidopsis varieties, which are widely present in the world. Grafting study suggested that HMA3 functions in the root govern Cd translocation into the shoot (Chao et al. 2012). These results are consistent with the role of OsHMA3 limiting the Cd translocation from the root to the shoot (Ueno et al. 2010; Miyadate et al. 2011). However, the overexpression of AtHMA3 could increase the Cd content in the shoot (Morel et al. 2009).

The focus of this paper is to provide a discussion on the different metal-related phenotype in Col-0 (with the HMA3 mutation) in comparison to those of Ws (having the full copy of HMA3). In addition, to obtain a definite answer for whether the different metal-related phenotype observed between Col-0 and Ws results only from this mutation, we performed a further investigation with HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background and hma3 mutant in Ws background.

## Generation and confirmation of transgenic Arabidopsis plants


A loss- and gain-of-function analysis was carried out with Arabidopsis to better understand the different metal-related phenotypes in Col-0 (with HMA3 mutation) as compared to that of Ws (having the full copy of HMA3). The T-DNA insertion obtained Flag_485B05 in the second exon region from the ${ 5 ^ { \prime } } \mathrm { U T R }$ of AtHMA3 in the Ws background, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Homozygous knock-out plants (line 5 and 8 in hma3 mutants) were selected by genomic PCR and mutant line 5(named hma3) was used for further analysis, as shown in Fig. 1b. In addition, we generated transgenic Col-0 overexpressing a cauliflower mosaic virus 35S promoter: AtHMA3 (Ws cDNA). The AtHMA3 transcript levels determined by RT-PCR were higher in the AtHMA3-transgenic plants and Ws than in Col-0, and two lines (1 and 3) showing a high expression of AtHMA3 were selected and were named HMA3 OX#1 and HMA3 OX#2, respectively (Fig. 1c).


## HMA3-overexpressing lines in Col-0 background shows more tolerant phenotype than Col-0 and hma3 mutant in Ws background against Cd and Zn


When the plants were grown in agar plates with or without Cd and Zn, no noticeable differences were observed in the germination rates of all plants (data not shown). Then the effect that the metal toxicity had on the growth rate was investigated in Ws and Col-0 ecotypes, two HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in Col-0, hma3 knock-out line in Ws. In a manner consistent with previous results, we also found that the Ws and two HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in Col-0 grew better than $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ and hma3 mutant when these plants were grown in the presence of Cd or Zn (Fig. 2a). The root growth rate and the fresh weight of Ws, HMA3 OX#1 and OX#2 were consistently higher than those of $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ and hma3 mutant in the presence of Cd and Zn (Fig. 2b, c). These data support the finding that Col-0 has a higher sensitivity to Cd and Zn than Ws due to the HMA3 point mutation in Col-0, and HMA3 is important for heavy metal detoxification.


## Col-0 and hma3 mutant exhibit more chlorotic symptoms and anthocyanin accumulation than Ws under Cd or Zn stress


To further study the metal-related leaf phenotype of plants depending on the presence or absence of the function of

HMA3, the plants were grown in soil and were provided $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m l }$ of $3 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M C d }$ or $3 5 ~ \mathrm { m M Z n }$ solution for 2 weeks on alternate days. Two HMA3-overexpressing lines in Col-0 treated with Cd showed a better Cd tolerance phenotype than Col-0, hma3 mutant, along with the Ws ecotype (Fig. 3a). In line with this observation, under a control condition, no significant differences in the chlorophyll A, B and in carotenoid content were observed among all plants. However, the chlorophyll A and B contents in the leaves of Col-0 and hma3 mutant treated with Cd for 14 days were of about 2–3 times lower than those of Ws and HMA3 overexpressing lines leaves. In the same conditions, the carotenoid content was not affected by the Cd stress (Fig. 3b). To elucidate whether the chlorotic symptoms were induced by deficiency of iron (Fe) in leaves, we analyzed the amount of Fe ion in the plants. Interestingly, the Fe concentration in the shoot of Col0 and hma3 mutants decreased under conditions with an excess of Cd, but not of Ws and Col-0 with functional HMA3-expressed lines (Fig. 4).

When all lines were grown in soil under Zn stress, the leaves of the Col-0 and hma3 mutant appeared to be more purplish (Fig. 5a), and the anthocyanin content in their leaves notably increased with Zn treatment when compared to leaves in the Ws- and HMA3-overexpressing lines in Col-0 background (Fig. 5b). To investigate whether anthocyanin accumulation was induced by other abiotic stress, we measured the anthocyanin content in two ecotypes treated with cold, drought or Zn stress. As shown

Fig. S1, the most prominent difference in the anthocyanin content between both ecotypes was observed in the leaves of Col-0 under Zn stress when compared to other stresses. These results suggest that $Z \mathrm { n }$ toxicity promotes the accumulation of anthocyanin in Col-0.


## HMA3-overexpressing lines in Col-0 background reduces the translocation rates of Cd and Zn


To test whether the loss- and gain-of-function in HMA3 affects the heavy metal translocation rate of plants, we measured the Cd and Zn content in all lines grown in solution with

$5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd or $5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Zn for 7 days. The Cd and $Z \mathbf { n }$ contents in the root of two HMA3-overexpressing lines were similar to the content of Ws and were higher when compared to the content of $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ and hma3 mutant. In the shoot, the Cd contents of the hma3 mutants were slightly higher than that of the Ws, and the Cd contents of the HMA3-overexpressing lines were lower than that of Col-0. There was no significant difference in the $Z \mathbf { n }$ contents of the shoot between all lines. The differences in the translocation rates of Cd and Zn between all lines were observed, and the translocation rates of Cd and Zn in hma3 mutant were high when compared to those of the Ws and HMA3-overexpressing lines (Fig. 6).

In our previous studies of the physiological responses in Arabidopsis Ws and Col-0 ecotypes under Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ stress (Park et al. 2012), we found that Col-0 readily translocates Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ to the shoot but not Ws, thereby inducing an alteration in the phenotype of the leaf color. However, there is no clear evidence of what causes the differences in the tolerance or loading of the heavy metals between Ws and Col-0 due to the non-function of HMA3 or some other factor. In this report, we have demonstrated that the difference in the metal-related phenotype observed between Col-0 and Ws is a result of the mutation of HMA3 in Col-0 by carrying out an investigation with HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background, hma3 mutants in Ws background.

It is necessary to investigate the effect of metal on the growth and fresh weight in a concentration-dependent manner to better understand the physiological response to Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ metal toxicity in Ws-, Col-0-, HMA3 (Ws)- overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background, hma3 mutant. In a manner consistent with the results obtained by Morel et al. (2009), we found that Ws grew better than Col0 when the plants were grown in the presence Cd or Zn. In addition, the Col-0 with functional HMA3 expressed by the full cDNA of AtHMA3 also mitigates the sensitivity to Cd and $Z \mathbf { n }$ . The hma3 mutant in the Ws background showed a Col-0-like phenotype that responded to Cd and Zn excess (Fig. 4). The HMA3-overexpressing lines showed higher expression of HMA3 comparing with col-0; however, lower expression of HMA3 comparing with Ws as shown in Fig. 1c. It can be expected that the root elongation of HMA3-overexpressing lines should be between those of Ws and Col-0 under Cd and Zn stress. But our result was not completely consistent with what we expected. Further study is required to find whether the additional genes involved in heavy metal tolerance in HMA3-overexpressing lines were activated. Nevertheless, the difference in root growth depending on the presence or absence of HMA3 function was clearly shown in this study (Fig. 4).

We also observed that the Cd-treated hma3 mutant along with Col-0 showed more severe chlorosis than the Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background (Fig. 5). The Chlorophyll A and B content in the leaves of HMA3 nonfunctional plants significantly decreased when compared to those of the Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background under Cd stress. These results may indicate a blocking of chlorophyll synthesis at the cellular level by heavy metal (Cd) stress (Stobart et al. 1985), and serious chlorosis in Cd-treated Col-0 and mutant (HMA3 nonfunctional plants) may reflect that the competition between Fe and Cd led to less $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake into the leaf (Fig. S1) and also negatively affected the efficiency of photosynthesis (Alca´ntara et al. 1994). The limited translocation of HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background may partially reduce the competition between Cd and Fe. The data suggest that sequestration, detoxification and/or reduction of the competition among the metals in the shoot of Ws and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background may prevent the harmful effects of the Cd stress. Competition between Fe and Cd has been widely recognized to occur in plants (Siedlecka and Krupa 1999; Sharma et al. 2004; Nakanishi et al. 2006; Shao et al. 2007, 2008; Sa´va´ri et al. 2008; Conte et al. 2011). In particular, Nakanishi et al. (2006) proposed that the Fe-uptake system was activated by Fe deficiency and led to an increased uptake of Cd in rice. Chlorosis as a symptom of heavy metal toxicity occurs together with a decrease in Fe content as the heavy metal concentration in the external medium increases (Wallace and Abou-Zamzam 1989; Ren et al. 1993; Bao et al. 2009; Bernard et al. 2009). Supply of Fe solution to leaves could recover a chlorotic leaf (Chaney 1993). These results indicated that symptoms of chlorosis are related to an induced deficiency in Fe.

The observable production of anthocyanin is one of the characteristic responses of plants to various stresses. Anthocyanin and other polyphenolic compounds (e.g., flavonols and condensed tannins) have a wide range of functions in plants related to UV absorption, pathogen attacks, and nutrient stress (Stewart et al. 2001; Kliebenstein 2004).

Several enzymes for anthocyanin synthesis, such as chalcone synthase, chalcone isomerase, flavone-3- $\cdot \hat { a }$ -hydroxylase $( \mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H } )$ , dihydroflavonol-4-reductase, leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase (LDOX; Takos et al, 2006), are well known. Moreover, UDP-Glc-flavonoid 3-O-glucosyl transferase (UF3GT) and PAP1 (for the production of anthocyanin pigment1, AtMYB7) are specific enzymes for anthocyanin synthesis (Borevitz et al. 2000; Takos et al. 2006). In a previous report, we described the positive relationship between the accumulation of anthocyanin under Zn treatment and the increase in the expression of genes ( $F 3 ^ { \prime } H ,$ , LDOX, UF3GT, and PAP1) in Col-0 (Park et al. 2012). Chlorosis and anthocyanin accumulation were observed only in Col-0 and hma3 mutants (Figs. 3, 5). This observation suggests that the plant could increase the metal-related symptom in the leaf when they exhibited a high root-to-shoot translocation rate if the plant has no function for toxic metal detoxification. The $Z \mathbf { n }$ translocation capacity in the plant was affected less than the Cd translocation rate depending on the presence or absence of HMA3. Since zinc is an essential nutrient, probably other factors seem to replace the role of HMA3.

Plants have evolved several effective mechanisms to tolerate high concentrations of toxic metals. In some plants, this tolerance is accomplished by preventing the uptake of toxic metals into the root cells (excluders). Sequestration into the vacuole has been suggested to be responsible for $Z \mathrm { n }$ tolerance in the shoots of the Zn-hyperaccumulator

Thlaspi caerulescens (Lasat et al. 1996, 1998, 2000). However, some plants are very sensitive to the accumulation of metals in the cell. These plants can be used as phytoindicators to indicate the metal concentration in the surrounding soil (Raskin et al. 1994). For instance, previous study showed a different phenotype under Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ stress between two ecotypes (Ws and Col-0) (Park et al.

2012). In addition, OsHMA3 in rice showed a low translocation of Cd from root to shoot due to vacuolar sequestration (Ueno et al. 2010). Therefore, we were interested in finding the effect of the AtHMA3 point mutation on the ability for heavy metal uptake and translocation in Col-0. As shown in Fig. 6, Col-0 and hma3 mutant plants showed a lesser metal accumulation in the roots under high Cd concentrations, and thereby, the translocation rates of the absorbed Cd from the root to shoot were high when compared to those of Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background. Although we are not certain of the mechanism for the increase in the translocation in the Col-0 and hma3 mutant, the HMA4 expression level in $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ was induced, but those of Ws tended to decrease compared to the control (Park et al. 2012) and this evidence suggested that the up-regulation of AtHMA4 gene expression in the Col-0 and hma3 mutant due to the non-function of HMA3 may be responsible for delivering toxic metals into the xylem for translocation in the presence of Cd (Park et al. 2012).

In many genetics experiments, complementation is used to verify whether the observed phenotype is affected by the specific gene mutation (Frandsen 2011). Complementation analyses can either be dependent on the endogenous promoter or a heterologous promoter such as constitutive promoters. The latter promoters direct expression in virtually all tissues and are largely, if not entirely, independent of environmental and developmental factors. As their expression is normally not conditioned by endogenous factors, constitutive promoters are usually active across species and even across kingdoms. It is true that both promoters are used in experiments to express additional copies of an endogenous gene or heterologous genes from ectopic loci in the genome (Frandsen 2011). However, complementation experiments occasionally cannot be completely restored the wild-type trait. This case has been attributed to differences in expression patterns resulting from differences in chromatin structure and epigenetic factors between the endogenous locus and the ectopic integration site (Rep et al. 2004). In this study, our complementation analysis using 35S promoter as a constitutive promoter showed that the normal function of HMA3 was restored successfully (although not completely).

In conclusion, we found that the difference in the AtHMA3 genes observed in two cultivars (Ws and Col-0) affects the metal translocation ability and the metal-related phenotype, such as that related to chlorosis and anthocyanin accumulation, and we then clarified these findings by loss-of-function and gain-of-function in Arabidopsis. The results indicate that Col-0 readily translocates Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ to the aerial parts but not Ws, thereby inducing an alteration in the phenotype in leaf color. HMA3 is important for Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ detoxification in Arabidopsis, possibly by the sequestration of Cd and Zn into root vacuoles, and in the control of translocation from root to shoot. Moreover, the mutation of the AtHMA3 gene is likely to be useful with respect to inhibiting the uptake of toxic metals, such as Cd from contaminated land to the plant root, and in enhancing the translocation of essential nutrients.
