Background: The $\mathsf { P } _ { 1 \mathsf { B } } .$ -ATPase subfamily is an important group involved in transporting heavy metals and has been extensively studied in model plants, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa. Emerging evidence indicates that one homolog in Glycine max is also involved in cadmium (Cd) stress, but the gene family has not been fully investigated in soybean.

Results: Here, we identified 20 heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family members in the soybean genome, presented as 10 paralogous pairs, which is significantly greater than the number in Arabidopsis or rice, and was likely caused by the latest whole genome duplication event in soybean. A phylogenetic analysis divided the 20 members into six groups, each having conserved or divergent gene structures and protein motif patterns. The integration of RNA-sequencing and qRT-PCR data from multiple tissues provided an overall expression pattern for the HMA family in soybean. Further comparisons of expression patterns and the single nucleotide polymorphism distribution between paralogous pairs suggested functional conservation and the divergence of HMA genes during soybean evolution. Finally, analyses of the HMAs expressed in response to Cd stress provided evidence on how plants manage Cd tolerance, at least in the two contrasting soybean genotypes examined.

Conclusions: The genome-wide identification, chromosomal distribution, gene structures, and evolutionary and expression analyses of the 20 HMA genes in soybean provide an overall insight into their potential involvement in Cd responses. These results will facilitate further research on the HMA gene family, and their conserved and divergent biological functions in soybean.

Keywords: Soybean, HMA, P1B-ATPase, Phylogenetic analysis, Cadmium, Expression analysis

Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic element that can affect mineral homeostasis, photosynthesis, water balance, and nutrient uptake in plants [1–3]. The physiological modifications and the dynamics of Cd accumulation and distribution within plant tissues as well as the function of the main heavy metal transporters involved in Cd uptake, translocation, and detoxification are well-known in poplar plants [4–9].

After the mobilization from soil, Cd uptake within plant tissues is determined by plasma membrane transporters located in root cells. When Cd enters in root tissues, translocation to shoot depends on its mobility within the root symplast, across the endodermal barrier, and further within the xylem. Cd accumulation and storage in leaf cells require its uptake from xylem and apoplast, as well as its phloem loading, to mobilize and allocate it among leaves or other organs (i.e., seeds, fruits) [10]. Several putative metal transporter genes are involved in these processes, such as transporters belonging to: (i) Zinc/Ironregulated transporter-like Proteins (ZIPs), (ii) Natural Resistance and Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs), and (iii) plasma membrane Heavy Metal proton-ATPases (HMAs) [10,11]. Members of NRAMP family are considered general metal ion transporters due to their ability to transport several ions, including Cd [12,13]. These transporters play a crucial role in the response, translocation, and accumulation of Cd [14–16].

On the other hand, Cd long-distance transport toward the shoot is primarily driven by the xylem water flux; when inside the stele, the divalent cation is actively translocated to the xylem vessels through transporters belonging to the HMA family [17,18]. In Populus trichocarpa the HMA isoforms PtHMA1–PtHMA4 belong to the $Z \mathrm { n } / { \mathrm { C o } } / { \mathrm { C d } } / { \mathrm { P b } }$ subgroup while $P t H M A 5 - P t H M A 8$ are members of the $\mathrm { C u / A g }$ subgroup [19]. In several species, the HMA1–4 isoforms are crucial for Cd translocation and accumulation [20–23]. Eren and Argüello [24] demonstrated that in Arabidopsis thaliana, HMA2 is an active pump which drives Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and Cd efflux to the extracellular compartment. Metal compartmentalization in plant cell is essential because free Cd within the cytosol causes phytotoxicity and the activation of specific processes of detoxification [25]. Several ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) transporters have vacuolar localization and, in particular, AtABCC3/6/7 are involved in Cd active storage for protection [26]. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 genes play an important role in metal compartmentalization as well [27], and an increase in transcript levels of ABCC10 was found in Cd-exposed roots of $P .$ trichocarpa and Populus deltoides [28]. Recently, a study found that overexpression of the ABCG36 gene of Populus tomentosa is effective in enhancing Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis plants, indicating the function of this transporter as a heavy metal extrusion pump [29].

Plants require a control system for managing metal homeostasis in order to balance the delivery of essential micronutrients (such as zinc, copper, and iron) to various organs while simultaneously preventing non-essential metals such as lead and cadmium from accumulating to toxic concentrations that may adversely affect the plant [35]. Heavy metal ATPase are transmembrane transporters that play a significant role in heavy metal transportation, distribution, detoxification, and accumulation in plants [36]. Previous studies have identified the HMA gene family in various plants, including 8 in A. thaliana [37], 9 in rice (Oryza sativa L.) [38], 11 in maize (Zea mays $L$ .) [21], 11 in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor $L .$ .) [21], 17 in Populus trichocarpa [39], and 20 in soybean (Glycine max L.) [40], 31 in Brassica napus (B. napus) [41], 8 mulberry (Morus) [25], 21 barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) [42], 14 turnip (Brassica rapa) [43], 48 tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) [34], and 27 in wheat (T. aestivum) [22].

However, the heavy metal ATPase gene family within the Arecaceae family remains unreported in existing literature.

In this study, we identified 12 AcHMA genes in Areca. The number of AcHMA genes in A.catechu genome was lower than in tomato and wheat [22, 34] while almost closer to sorghum, rice and maize [21], suggesting a potential shared evolutionary or functional aspect in the context of HMA genes among these plant species. The HMA family members has been divided into several clades in different plant species based on substrate specificity and phylogenetic clustering. HMA proteins in Arabidopsis and potato were categorized into 6 clades [44], 5 in barley [42], 8 in flax [45], 7 in cotton [46], 11 in dragon fruit [47], and 3 in maize [48]. The AcHMA gene family in A.catechu was categorized into two sub-families $\mathrm { ( C u / }$ Ag P1B-ATPase and $\mathrm { Z n / C o / C d / P b }$ P1B-ATPase) and five sub-subfamilies (I-V) based on substrate specificity and phylogenetic clustering among A. catechu, Arabidopsis, O. sative, and C.nucifera. Our investigation into the HMA gene family in A. catechu aligns with the established pattern, suggesting a conserved organizational structure within the HMA gene family across plant species.

The similar structural pattern of HMA genes shows that they might have similar functions and connections in different plants, especially regarding their specific substances [39]. This helps us to understand the various roles these gene family play in different plants and how they adapt to their environments. It has been reported that HMA transporter activities are linked to the subcellular distribution of the HMA transporters. The AtHMA1, OsHMA1, AtHMA6, and AtHMA8 identified both in Arabidopsis and rice, exhibited a chloroplast envelop localization, and were involved in Zinc translocation into the chloroplast [23, 49]. Similarly, AtHMA2, OsHMA2, AtHMA4, AtHMA5, OsHMA5 and OsHAM9 are located in plasma membrane confers tolerance to $Z _ { \mathrm { n / C d / C u } }$ [50–52]. The OsHMA3 and OsHMA4 in Oryza sativa are located at the tonoplast and help in cadmium and copper accumulation in vacule [50, 53].

Furthermore, P1B-ATPases have metal binding domains (MBDs) that act as cell transport regulators [54]. The distinctive cysteine structure $\textstyle ( \operatorname { C x x C } )$ in the HMA domain enables these genes to bind metal ions through thiol groups [55, 56]. P1B-ATPases, a type of transporter, are effective in expelling essential and toxic metal ions out of cells, ensuring a balance of metals (homeostasis) within the cellular environment. This mechanism is vital for maintaining the overall health and functionality of the cell [14, 57]. Understanding the exon-intron structure is crucial in evolution and comprehending the gene family. Significant evolutionary changes occur in eukaryotic genes due to intron gain or loss, which entails inserting and deleting gene segments [58]. Analyzing the exonintron structure of AcHMA genes reveals conservation within the gene family despite divergent exon numbers. Although, the exon/intron count varies even within the same sub-family $( \mathrm { C u } / \mathrm { A g }$ and $\mathrm { Z n / C o / C d / P b }$ P1BATPase). Exon/intron ratio variations within the gene family hint at functional diversification or evolutionary changes [59].

Cis-regulatory elements play a vital role in mediating stress responses, emphasizing their significance in the regulatory network [60]. Cis- regulatory elements and plant hormones, including ethylene (ET), salicylic acid (SA), abscisic acid (ABA), and jasmonic acid (JA), act as crucial signalling molecules that empower plants to adapt to abiotic stresses [60, 61]. The analysis of cis-regulatory elements of AcHMA family genes indicates the presence of multiple abiotic stress-responsive cis-elements. Specifically, elements like MYB, Myc, and STRE, abundant in the promoter region, exhibit a robust response to heavy metal stress, implying a potential role of AcHMA in the plant’s reaction to Cd and other heavy metal stress [62]. Understanding cis-acting elements in gene promoters, like G-box and ABRE, is crucial for unravelling plant stress responses. The abundance of cis-elements suggests that these genes may be triggered in response to various environmental stresses, potentially improving its overall stress tolerance [63].

According to previous studies, HMAs are thought to play a crucial role in detoxifying heavy metals in dicots by inhibiting the efflux of these metals into the cytosol through efflux mechanisms [14]. To understand the role of AcHMAs in A.catechu, we performed RNA-seq data analysis and qPCR to investigate the expression of AcHMA under normal conditions and heavy metal stress.

In normal conditions, the AcHMA1-AcHMA8 genes had high expression levels throughout many tissues. However, the expression pattern of these genes was altered in response to abiotic stimuli, thereby highlighting the diverse function of AcHMA genes. The diverse expression pattern of AcHMA genes suggests that they were widely involved in abiotic stress as well as the growth and development of A.catechu. As a result of heavy metals exposure, both roots and leaves exhibited high levels of AcHMA gene expression at 48 and $7 2 \ \mathrm { h }$ . Notably, AcHMA1 and AcHMA2 genes exhibited the highest upregulation in response to $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ stresses in roots and leaves, while AcHMA5 and AcHMA8 showed significant upregulation in the presence of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ .The higher expression level of AcHMA1 and AcHMA2 against $\mathrm { C } \dot { \mathsf { d } } ^ { 2 + }$ stress indicates their role in cadmium transportation in roots and leaves. Previously, it was revealed that AtHMA3 in Arabidopsis, OsHMA3 in rice and ZmHMA2 and ZmHMA3 from maize has shown cadmium transport capabilities into root vacuoles of plants [1, 26, 30]. Based on these results, it appears that HMA2 and HMA3 genes play a similar role in regulating cadmium transport in diverse plant species, and this supports our conclusion regarding AcHMA1 and AcHMA2. These results provide evidence that genes closely related to each other in plant phylogeny play a similar role in regulating cadmium transport to vacuolar sequestration, as well as subsequent root-to-shoot translocation in various plant species.

Similarly, as a result of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment, our study revealed a notable upregulation of AcHMA1, AcHMA2, AcHMA3, AcHMA7, and AcHMA8 both in leaves as well as in roots, suggesting their involvement in zinc transportation in the tonoplast. Similar gene expression patterns have been identified in both O.sativa and A.thalian, and our findings align with those earlier studies. As a result of zinc stress, previous studies reported elevated levels of AtHMA1, OsHMA1, and OsHMA2 expression in the tonoplast, indicating that these genes play a role in zinc transport [14, 23, 27]. In response to ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ stress, most of the AcHMAs show differential expression patterns. Notably, AcHMA5 and AcHMA8 were upregulated in roots and leaves, suggesting their potential roles in Cu transport or detoxification. Additionally, AcHMA2, AcHMA5, and AcHMA7 exhibited moderate expression in leaves, while AcHMA1, AcHMA2, and AcHMA3 appeared downregulated in roots. Our findings are consistent with those of the existing literature. Noteworthy, AcHMA5 upregulation in roots corresponds to the reported involvement of AtHMA5, OsHMA5, and PtHMA5 in $\mathrm { C u }$ transport from the roots to the shoots and Cu detoxification. Furthermore, the increased expression of AcHMA8 in leaves reflects the recognized roles of AtHMA8,

PtHMA7, and PtHMA8 in Cu transport, emphasizing how these roles were conserved across different plant species throughout evolution. In conclusion, based on the gene expression profiles under different heavy metal stress treatments, we proposed a schematic model, which summarized the key AcHMA genes that play role in response to different heavy metal stress in Areca (Fig. 7). This study comprehensively explores the functional roles and expression patterns within the HMA gene family of A. catechu. Our results will lay a foundation for further analysis of how AcHMA gene responds to heavy metal stress in areca.

Cadmium (Cd) pollution has become a major threat to crop production and quality globally. The heavy metal $\mathrm { \Delta P _ { 1 B } }$ -ATPases (HMAs) play a crucial role in metal transport in plants. In the present study, we investigated the interaction in metal transport by HMAs between Cd and mineral elements in rice plants. Rice seedlings were treated with cadmium nitrate either in the nutrient solution $\bf ( ^ { 6 6 } C d \mathrm { + } M ^ { 3 } )$ ) or in the ultrapure water (“Cd-M”). Result showed that phytotoxicity of Cd to rice seedlings was evident from both Cd treatments, judged by relative growth rate (RGR), where more severe repression $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ of RGR was observed in the “Cd-M” treatments than the $\mathrm { ^ { 6 6 } C d { + } M ^ { \prime } }$ treatments. More Cd $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ was accumulated in rice tissues from the “Cd-M” treatments than the $\mathrm { ^ { 6 6 } C d { + } M ^ { \prime } }$ treatments, while there is a signifcant diference $( p < 0 . 0 5 )$ in distribution and translocation of mineral elements in rice tissues between the $\bf \ddot { \omega } C d { + } M \bf \ddot { \omega }$ and the “Cd-M” treatments. RT-qPCR analysis displayed that the expression patterns of HMAs related genes were quite diferent between $\bf \ddot { \omega } C d { + } M \bf \ddot { \omega }$ and “Cd-M” treatments, suggesting their diferent regulatory efects during the transport of Cd and mineral elements within rice plants. The competition in metal transport by HMAs mainly occurs between Cd and micro-elements of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and $\mathrm { C u }$ in rice tissues during Cd exposure. Overall, this study provides new evidence to clarify the diferent translocation mechanisms of HMAs in metal transport between Cd and mineral elements in rice seedlings during Cd exposure.

Keywords Cadmium $\cdot$ Mineral element $\cdot$ Rice $\cdot$ HMAs $\cdot$ Interaction analysis

The persistence of Cd in agricultural soils poses signifcant ecological risks, owing to its high mobility and tendency for phytoaccumulation. As the primary interface for heavy metal uptake, plant root systems mediate Cd absorption through shared transport pathways for divalent cations, particularly via $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ transporters (Zhou et al. 2021). Our fndings demonstrate that $Z { \mathrm { n } } / \mathrm { M n }$ supplementation efectively decreased Cd accumulation and translocation in cabbage, with the $\mathrm { Z n + C d }$ treatment achieving the lowest root and leaf Cd concentrations, and the ${ \mathrm { Z n M n } }$ $+ \mathrm { C d }$ combination showing minimal translocation efciency (Fig. 1). This mitigation efect likely stems from competitive inhibition at shared cation uptake channels, where $\mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ions interfere with $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ absorption through similarities in ionic radius and charge parity (Fang et  al. 2021; Li et  al. 2022a; Lu et al. 2022). The observed root-to-leaf Cd translocation reduction aligns with the dual-phase metal exclusion mechanism: primary restriction at rhizospheric uptake followed by secondary limitation in xylem loading (Uraguchi et  al. 2011). Our results corroborate previous fndings across multiple species: foliar Zn application reduced rice grain Cd (Wang et  al. 2018), while increasing $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations reduced Cd uptake in rice roots through OsZIP transporter competition (Fahad et  al. 2015). Similarly, Mn supplementation decreased wheat grain Cd by $4 6 \%$ via enhanced Mn-SOD activity and vacuolar Cd sequestration (Huang et al. 2021). Notably, Zn showed better Cd fxation efciency in plant tissues, mainly through enhancing the synthesis and crosslinking of cell wall pectin, thus signifcantly improving the binding ability of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , while Mn-induced chloroplast protection mechanisms in lettuce (Lactuca sp.) suggest that our observed efects may involve both transport competition and potentiation of the antioxidant system (Ramos et al. 2002; Zheng et al. 2024). These collective fndings establish $\mathrm { Z n / M n }$ application as a promising plant management strategy, leveraging essential micronutrient supplementation to disrupt Cd entry routes.

Transcriptomic profling demonstrated its efectiveness in elucidating the transcriptional regulatory networks underlying Cd stress adaptation in plants, while functional annotation analysis further delineated treatment-specifc biological processes through diferential GO enrichment patterns (Li et al. 2022b). The GO annotation analysis revealed that Zn preferentially up-regulated cell wall biosynthesis genes, Mn induced hydrolase activity-related transcripts, and ${ \mathrm { Z n M n } }$ co-treatment enhanced genes associated with plasma membrane integrity.

Zn-induced cell wall reinforcement supports its role as the primary Cd exclusion barrier, with pectin methylesterases and lignin biosynthesis enzymes likely enhancing Cd immobilization through polysaccharide crosslinking and metal–ligand complexation (Loix et  al. 2017). Mn-mediated hydrolase activation (e.g., proteases, lipases) may facilitate metabolic reprogramming, especially in seed germinationrelated pathways (e.g., $\alpha$ -amylase, $\beta$ -glucosidase), supporting the role of hydrolases in heavy metal detoxifcation through protein turnover and toxic metabolite degradation (Zhang et  al. 2008). ZnMn co-treatment induces lipid metabolism genes and alters phosphatidylcholine composition to achieve plasma membrane specialization and enhance membrane stability. This is a key adaptation for maintaining ion homeostasis under Cd stress (Yao et  al. 2020). Specifcally, the enhanced membrane stability resulting from ZnMn co-treatment is due to Zn-facilitated $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ sequestration in plant cell walls through enhanced pectin cross-linking and lipid membrane structure, thereby reducing $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transmembrane absorption efciency (Chande et  al. 2010; Kučerka et al. 2017). Mn blocks the transmembrane transport of Cd by activating the cellular Mn transporter and enzymatic activity associated with lipid synthesis, thereby promoting the synthesis of phospholipids and cuticle in the cell membrane (Salomé et al. 2017; Wei et al. 2018).

Overall, these transcriptional divergences suggest treatment-specifc Cd tolerance mechanisms: Zn treatment results in the highest number of upregulated DEGs in GO terms, particularly enhancing extracellular isolation and efectively reducing Cd uptake by cabbage roots. Mn treatment has relatively few up-regulated DEGs, primarily regulating intracellular protein balance and enhancing intracellular Cd diferentiation. In contrast, ZnMn co-treatment downregulates the expression of  DEGs in the top $2 0 ~ \mathrm { G O }$ terms, thereby suggesting a potential negative impact on cabbage root growth. These fndings advance our understanding of micronutrient-mediated Cd mitigation strategies.

The KEGG annotation results demonstrated that the DEGs were involved in various biological pathways. In this paper, several pathways were selected for further analysis based on the number of enriched genes, aiming to understand potential Cd tolerance mechanisms in cabbage roots (Li et al. 2022b). The results revealed that DEGs were predominantly enriched in three core pathways: phenylpropanoid metabolism (Zn treatment), tryptophan metabolism (Mn treatment), and circadian rhythm regulation (ZnMn co-treatment), with each pathway demonstrating distinct mechanisms of Cd tolerance.

The phenylpropanoid metabolism pathway, a critical plant defense system, confers resistance to abiotic stresses, including salinity, drought, and heavy metal toxicity, through the biosynthesis of protective metabolites (Yadav et  al. 2020). Downstream products such as lignins, favonoids, and procyanidins enhance metal tolerance via chelation, antioxidant activity, and structural reinforcement (Ge et al. 2023). In this study, transcriptomic analysis of Zn-treated cabbage roots revealed pronounced up-regulation of peroxidase (POD) and lignin biosynthesis genes (Supplementary Figure S5 A). POD is an oxidative enzyme widely found in plants; it mediates xylem lignifcation, redox homeostasis, and stress adaptation through the catalytic degradation of reactive oxygen species (Barceló et al. 2007). Lignins, dominant components of secondary cell walls, immobilize heavy metals via carboxyl and phenolic functional groups, efectively restricting cytoplasmic Cd entry (Li et al. 2018; Su et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2022). This aligns with our prior fndings of Zn-induced cell wall-related gene activation, suggesting Zn stimulates endogenous antioxidant systems to mitigate oxidative damage by reducing ROS accumulation (Maleva et  al. 2018). The observed lignin-mediated cell wall compartmentalization may be an important Cd detoxifcation mechanism in both the roots and leaves of cabbage.

Tryptophan biosynthesis in plants is linked to growth and adaptive mechanisms, which synthesize indole-derived secondary metabolites essential for defense and environmental interaction. These include indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), serotonin, and melatonin, which have a wide range of functions in higher plants, including physiological processes such as seed germination, root growth and development, senescence, fowering, or fruit ripening, as well as in the response mechanisms against biotic and abiotic stresses (Corpas et  al. 2021). In this study, Mn treatment specifcally enriched IAA biosynthesis genes in cabbage roots (Supplementary Figure S5B), potentially elevating indolepyruvate, indoleacetate, and other related metabolites levels. IAA is considered a heavy metal bioadsorption regulator, capable of restoring plant growth. It enhances primary metabolite synthesis and antioxidant capacity while inhibiting Cd uptake, possibly through hemicellulose-1-mediated cell wall modifcation (Piotrowska-Niczyporuk et  al. 2012). This mechanism may explain the reduced root Cd absorption observed in Mn-treated plants.

Plants can integrate environmental signals, including temperature and light, and coordinate various physiological processes, such as photoperiodic fowering, hormone signaling, growth, metabolism, and responses to biological and abiotic stresses. Circadian rhythm is a biological rhythm infuenced by many external factors, including abiotic stress (Venkat et al. 2022). In this study, ZnMn co-treatment signifcantly activated the circadian rhythm pathway, up-regulating CDF1 (cycling DOF factors), a unique DOF-family transcription factor that coordinates stress responses (Supplementary Figure S5 C). CDF1 protein is a distinct transcription factor in the plant DOF family, playing an important role in plant growth and development. CDF transcription factors are involved in inducing the expression of stress-response genes, accumulating osmotic regulatory substances, and maintaining the carbon/nitrogen balance and endogenous hormone balance. They also play a crucial role in responding to abiotic stress and improving stress tolerance in crops (Fornara et al. 2009; Corrales et al. 2017; Renau-Morata et al. 2017).

In summary, Zn treatment triggered phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, while Mn treatment enhanced tryptophan metabolism. ZnMn co-treatment activated the circadian rhythm-related detoxifcation metabolic response in cabbage under Cd stress. This may be because, under Cd stress, phenylpropanoids in plants indirectly infuence the oscillatory expression of genes associated with the biological clock by modulating ROS homeostasis and hormone signaling. This, in turn, establishes a bidirectional regulatory network between metabolism and circadian rhythms (Lv et al. 2024). Additionally, indoles derived from tryptophan metabolism interact with circadian clock components via jasmonic acid signaling, promoting the night-specifc activation of defense genes and, consequently, regulating the expression of photoperiodic response genes (Qin et al. 2024). These results indicate that the pathways enriched in KEGG may play a crucial role in maintaining normal conditions in plants under Cd stress.

Plants produce structurally diverse specialized metabolites, including bioactive alkaloids and terpenoids, in response to biotic and abiotic environmental stresses (Shoji et al. 2021). In this study, Zn, Mn, and ZnMn treatments had signifcant efects on lipidrelated metabolism, plant secondary metabolism, and the amino acid metabolism pathways. These results suggest that the above metabolites play an important role in the Cd stress response, which will be the focus of our research.

Lipids are not only an important structural component of the cell membrane and the surface of plant tissues and organs, but also a physiologically active substance and signal molecule, playing a crucial role in plant growth, development, and stress response $( \mathrm { K i m } \ 2 0 2 0$ ; Zhao et  al. 2021). In this study, the results of the KEGG enrichment analysis of DAMs revealed signifcant enrichment in the fatty acid elongation pathway in three comparisons, with notable efects on lipids and lipid-like molecules (C00157, C04230, C01233, C00670), organic nitrogen compounds (C00588), and nucleosides, nucleotides, and analogues (C00307). Some studies have pointed out that increased lipid metabolism directly contributed to maintaining the stability of the cell membrane and reducing cell damage under Cd stress (Feng et  al. 2024). Organic nitrogen compounds, such as phosphocholine, can participate in the synthesis of phospholipids and may promote lipid metabolism in plants (Ulch et al. 2025). CDP-choline, a nucleoside, nucleotide, and analogue, is the precursor of phosphatidylcholine and acetylcholine, key components of the cell membrane. It participates in the formation of the phospholipid bilayer of the cell membrane, regulating membrane fuidity and protecting against oxidative damage to the membrane (Weiss 1995). Therefore, we believe that Zn, Mn, and ZnMn treatments enhance Cd tolerance in cabbage by maintaining normal lipid synthesis and metabolism, thereby improving cabbage’s Cd tolerance.

In plants, the secondary metabolic pathways produce a diversity of compounds called plant secondary metabolites (PSMs), these compounds contain a large group of structurally diverse molecules originating from either primary metabolites or intermediates in the biosynthetic pathways of these primary metabolites (Piasecka et  al. 2015; Pang et  al. 2021). Plant secondary metabolites play a variety of functions, such as in plant growth and developmental processes, innate immunity (Piasecka et  al. 2015), defense response signaling (Isah 2019), and response to environmental stresses (Yang et al. 2018). The results of this study revealed that Zn treatment signifcantly upregulated the biosynthesis of a variety of plant secondary metabolites, mainly phenylpropanoids, polyketides (C01864), and organic acids and derivatives (C00073). Studies have found that Zn can induce the up-regulation of key enzymes in the phenylpropanoid metabolic pathway and promote polymerization of lignin monomers. Meanwhile, Zn can increase the content of favonoids in plant cells and enhance their complexation with $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , thus enhancing the cell wall’s fxation of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ (Marreiro et  al. 2017; Wang et  al. 2023). Zn may reduce cytoplasmic free $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration by promoting the synthesis of organic acids in plants, specifcally chelating $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and transporting it to the vacuole for isolation (Song et al. 2025). Therefore, we believed that plant secondary metabolites are involved in stabilizing cabbage roots during Cd stress and that maintaining normal plant secondary metabolism is an important way to improve the Cd tolerance of cabbage.

Amino acids have a variety of prominent functions in plants, not only as precursors for protein biosynthesis but also as participants in a large number of cellular reactions, infuencing many physiological processes, and playing a key role in signal transduction processes as well as plant stress responses (Hildebrandt et al. 2015). The results of this study revealed that ZnMn co-treatment signifcantly up-regulated the biosynthesis of a variety of organic acids and derivatives (C00791 and C02714) and organic nitrogen compounds (C00179). Some studies have indicated that plants, when exposed to metals, typically synthesize a variety of low-molecular-weight compounds, particularly specifc free amino acids (FAAs), which are recognized as compatible solutes (Mahdavian et al. 2023). These FAAs have been shown to act as signaling molecules and play a crucial role in plant physiology (Dinkeloo et  al. 2018). Notably, the levels of FAAs signifcantly increase in response to both abiotic and biotic stressors, positioning them as reliable biomarkers of stress (Zhu et  al. 2018). From this, we inferred that the regulation of amino acid metabolism is considered the main strategy for plant protection and survival under adverse living conditions. Moreover, the ZnMn co-treatment promotes amino acid metabolism in cabbage roots, which suggests that the treatment may have adverse efects on the roots.

Based on the above, Zn treatment regulated plant secondary metabolism to alleviate Cd toxicity, Mn treatment primarily improved lipid metabolism, which helped to decrease Cd stress, while ZnMn co-treatment may disturb amino acid metabolism in plants under Cd stress. The changes in the metabolism levels mentioned above play a crucial role in the mechanism by which plants adapt to Cd stress.

Metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses were integrated to elucidate coordinated pathway interactions between DEGs and DAMs in cabbage under

Cd stress. To investigate the associations between the metabolome and transcriptome, the KEGG pathways enriched by both were integrated (Du et al. 2024). In this study, DEGs and DAMs were mostly enriched in metabolic pathways, including amino acid metabolism, lipid metabolism, nucleotide metabolism, metabolism of terpenoids and polyketides, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins. Based on KEGG co-enrichment analysis, the fatty acid elongation pathways were signifcantly enriched in the Zn-vsCK and ZnMn-vs-CK comparisons. The tryptophan metabolism, glutathione metabolism, and favonoid biosynthesis pathways were signifcantly enriched in the Mn-vs-CK and ZnMn-vs-CK comparisons.

Lipid metabolism includes systemic biochemical reactions such as fat synthesis, decomposition, and transport. It is the core metabolic pathway for maintaining cell energy homeostasis. The fatty acid elongation pathway plays an important role in lipid metabolism and cell function, converting nutrients into metabolic intermediates for membrane biosynthesis, energy storage, and signaling molecule generation (Rohrig et  al. 2016; Xie et  al. 2020). Our results further suggest that the enrichment of key biosynthetic genes and metabolites involved in the lipid metabolism pathway under Zn and ZnMn cotreatments may play an important role in cabbage’s response to Cd stress.

Tryptophan, the sole indole-containing amino acid, modulates plant stress tolerance through its derivatives, including auxins and melatonin, which regulate oxidative balance and metabolic adaptation (Xue et  al. 2023). The activation of the glutathione metabolism pathway serves as a conserved detoxifcation mechanism in plants under Cd stress. Glutathione efectively reduces the transport of Cd from the roots to the shoots and enhances the resistance of plants to Cd (Nakamura et  al. 2020; Huang et  al. 2022; Li et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2021). Flavonoids are major secondary metabolites derived from the phenylpropane pathway in plants and play an important role in plant development, afecting basic physiological metabolism, as well as stress and disease resistance (Wang et al. 2020b). These fndings suggest that Mn treatment and ZnMn co-treatment are closely related to Cd tolerance in Chinese cabbage. Tryptophan may alleviate Cd stress in cabbage roots by balancing IAA levels. Glutathione maintains intracellular homeostasis by scavenging reactive oxygen species in

Chinese cabbage roots, while favonoid accumulation enhances antioxidant capacity and directly removes Cd-induced ROS.

Therefore, lipids, tryptophan, glutathione, and favonols play a vital role in Zn, Mn, and ${ \mathrm { Z n M n } }$ treatments under Cd stress. In future studies, the identifcation of key genes and the verifcation of potential up-regulated diferential metabolites will be the focus of our research, which will contribute to a deeper understanding of Cd tolerance and accumulation mechanisms in cabbage.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is essential to plants. A large portion of the proteome binds $Z \mathbf { n }$ as a structural component or co-factor, including enzymes and transcription factors (Andreini et  al. 2006). Therefore, $Z \mathbf { n }$ defciency can decrease growth and productivity, which poses a problem for agriculture considering that soils with low $Z \mathbf { n }$ concentrations are widespread (Alloway 2004). On the other hand, excessive Zn uptake by plants can lead to toxicity, reducing photosynthesis and causing oxidative stress (Kaur and Garg 2021). Therefore, (Sinclair and Krämer 2012; Ricachenevsky et al. 2015).

Heavy metal ATPase 3 (HMA3) is a vacuolar transporter that, when overexpressed in A. thaliana, promotes tolerance to cadmium (Cd), Zn, and other divalent cations (Morel et al. 2009). Its physiological role as a Zn transporter was frst proposed by Becher et  al. (2004) for the Zn hyperaccumulator in Arabidopsis halleri. In  rice plants overexpressing a functional allele of OsHMA3 no change in Zn concentrations was detected in shoots; however, the expression of several ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter/Ironregulated transporter-like Protein) transporters was increased  in roots. This evidence suggests the existence of compensatory mechanisms for maintaining Zn concentration in shoots when OsHMA3 transports Zn into root vacuoles (Sasaki et  al. 2014; Cai et  al. 2019). Furthermore, it is well known that elements that are part of the ionome cooperate within crosstalk mechanisms (Pita-Barbosa et  al. 2019b), which deserves careful attention to optimize plant nutrition.

Conclusive evidence for the role of HMA3 in Zn sinking into root vacuoles was only recently provided using A. thaliana Col-0 accessions, which have a nonfunctional allele of AtHMA3, complemented with a functional AtHMA3 allele from a CSHL-5 accession. Transgenic A. thaliana plants expressing AtHMA3 were used to show that expression levels of functional AtHMA3 are correlated with the expression of genes controlling Zn homeostasis, providing direct evidence that changes in Zn accumulation in root vacuoles lead to the bufering of Zn homeostasis in shoots (PitaBarbosa et al. 2019a, b). Natural variations have been explored to identify distinct responses within A. thaliana diversity and  in many  crops (Chao et  al. 2012). However, it is not clear whether natural AtHMA3 expression variations are also bufered by changes in Zn transporters in A. thaliana. In this study, we demonstrate that natural accessions of A. thaliana bufer Zn homeostasis to accommodate AtHMA3 expression variation and maintain $Z \mathrm { n }$ at optimal concentrations.

As a non-essential heavy metal in plants, cadmium (Cd) is toxic and widespread present in the environment [1, 2]. Increasing of Cd levels in the arable soil severely limited the crop yield and harmed human health via the food chain [3]. Cd also exerted adverse impacts on various biochemical and physiological activities of plants, such as growth inhibition, oxidative stresses, protein inactivation and disturbance of nutrient uptake [4, 5]. However, plants have developed a sophisticated arsenal of metabolic “weapons” to combat the Cd-induced stresses, including restriction of intake and transportation, immobilization, chelation and sequestration of Cd in vacuoles, efflux Cd from the cytoplasm [6–8].

Accumulation of Cd in plant shoots is closely related to a myriad of physiological processes, including root uptake, vacuoles sequestration, and xylem and phloem translocation [9]. Generally, Cd can enter plants from soil through either apoplasmic pathway or symplasmic pathway [10]. Plants actively acquire Cd mainly through essential elements uptake systems, involving $\mathrm { F e ^ { 2 + } }$ , $\dot { \mathrm { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { M n ^ { 2 + } }$ [11–13]. It has also been suggested that high-affinity Cd transporters were involved in Cd uptake in Thlaspi caerulescens [14]. After entering the root, Cd is first delivered to the stele via the endodermis [14] and then transported to shoots via the xylem under the driving force of leaf transpiration [10, 15]. Phloem transportation is responsible for further seed or grain Cd accumulation [16, 17].

During the past decade, the continuing expansion of available transcriptional data has led to identification and characterization of the underlying genetic basis behind the above Cd accumulation physiological processes. Such advancement has tremendously enhanced our ability to explore Cd translocation and detoxification in Cd hyperaccumulating plants, such as Arabidopsis halleri [7, 18], Brassica juncea [19, 20], Sedum alfredii [21], and Noccaea caerulescens [22–24], as well as cultivated plants like the pea (Pisum sativum L.) [25], barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) [26, 27], and rice (Oryza sativa L.) [28, 29].

Soybean is a protein- and oil-enriched crop which is a main source of essential amino acids of plant food for humans and animals [30]. Generally, soybean is Cd-sensitive and accumulates Cd even at a low concentration of Cd in soils [31], the risk of Cd accumulation in soybean has raised great concerns [32]. Further, soybean genotypes differ greatly in Cd tolerance and accumulation [33, 34]. The Codex Committee on Food Additives and Contaminants proposed a safe upper limit of $0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { m g / k g ~ C d }$ in soybean seeds[35]. However, the Cd uptake, translocation, and accumulation processes in soybeans are still mostly unknown. In this research, we examined the Cd content in shoots and roots of two soybean varieties and found that Cd accumulation in these two varieties was significantly different. We employed comparative transcriptome analysis for the roots of the two soybean varieties before and after Cd treatment to elucidate the potential genetic reasons for the different physiological traits. Findings from this study may provide new insight into the molecular-assisted breeding methods for soybeans.

The organisms that populated the primordial Earth lived in an anaerobic environment where Fe was predominantly reduced, soluble, and biologically abundant. As photosynthetic organisms proliferated and transformed Earths atmosphere, however, Fe became increasingly oxidized and biologically scarce. Fe bioavailability is thus low in over one-third of the Earths land surface area, particularly in alkaline or calcareous soils (Crowley et al.1987). This has imposed enormous selective pressures on terrestrial plants and microorganisms to develop efficient strategies for solubilizing Fe from the soil.

Most aerobic organisms have evolved mechanisms to solubilize Fe based on the chemical processes of chelation, reduction, and acidification (reviewed in Kochian 1991, 2000). These strategies of Fe acquisition are restricted to discrete phylogenetic groups. Yeast and all plants except the grasses reduce $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ chelates and absorb the more soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ion released by this process. Under Fe deficiency, species of this group induce the activity of a plasma membrane ferric chelate reductase and also stimulate the release of protons, both of which enhance the solubility of soil Fe. Other classes of organisms, including fungi, bacteria, and members of the family Poaceae (the grasses), release high-affinity $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ -chelating compounds, called siderophores, that solubilize $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ and are then recognized for uptake by specific membrane receptors (Ro¨ mheld and Marschner 1986; Chaney 1987; Bienfait 1988).

Previous work has shown that Fe deficiency in many nongrass plant species elicits a stimulated influx of Fe and other divalent cations. Fox et al. (1996) found that Fe-deficient pea seedlings exhibited higher rates of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx compared to Fe-sufficient seedlings. Furthermore, tissue concentrations of Fe and other mineral elements can be influenced by plant Fe status. Welch et al. (1993) demonstrated that the shoot concentrations of several divalent cationic metals, including Cu, Mn, and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g }$ increased in Fe-deficient pea seedlings compared to Fesufficient pea seedlings. Rodecap et al. (1994) also reported that Fe-deficient Arabidopsis plants accumulated higher concentrations of Cd and $\mathrm { M g }$ in racemes and seeds compared to Fe-sufficient plants.

We previously demonstrated that Fe deficiency induced a high affinity Cd influx into roots of pea seedlings, a finding that has implications for the entry of heavy metals into food crops (Cohen et al. 1998a). Our preliminary investigations into the mechanistic basis for this observation suggested that Fe deficiency induces a divalent cation transporter that can facilitate $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. We established that expression of a homolog of the Arabidopsis IRT1 Fe transporter gene (Eide et al. 1996) was induced in roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. When expressed in yeast, it was found that this transporter could mediate $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake (Cohen et al. 1998b). Enhanced expression of this gene could increase IRT1 density in the root-cell plasma membrane and could account for the observed stimulation in root Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake.

IRT1 is a member of the ZIP family of metal transporters that are hypothesized to play a role in micronutrient nutrition, and in particular in Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and transport (Guerinot 2000). The ZIP designation, which stands for ZRT, IRT-like protein, comes from the names of the first members of this family to be identified. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter), a transporter first identified in Arabidopsis, is induced by Fe deficiency in roots, and has been suggested to be an Fe transporter (Eide et al. 1996). ZRT1 and ZRT2 (zinc-regulated transporter) are high and low affinity $Z \mathfrak { n }$ transporters in yeast that are regulated by changes in cellular $Z \mathrm { n }$ status (Zhao and Eide 1996a, 1996b). Some ZIP family members have been cloned from several plant species including Arabidopsis (IRT-1, -2; ZIP 1–4), Thlaspi caerulescens (ZNT-1, -2) and tomato (LeIRT-1 -2) (Eide et al. 1996; Grotz et al. 1998; Pence et al. 2000; Assunc¸ ao et al. 2001; Eckhardt et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2001). In some of these studies, heterologous expression of ZIP genes in yeast mutants defective in specific micronutrient uptake systems have provided researchers with information concerning the transport properties of the ZIP proteins. What is emerging from these studies is the concept that some of these transporters may exhibit a fairly broad specificity with regards to the micronutrient metal transported. For example, based on heterologous expression studies in yeast, it was suggested that IRT1 may transport $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ in addition to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Korshunova et al. 1999). However, caution must be exercised in extrapolating these findings in yeast to higher plants growing in the soil, particularly since the metal concentrations used in these studies were much higher than those found in the soil or rhizosphere.

More recently, studies from three different laboratories using Arabidopsis knockout mutants for IRT1 have provided more direct evidence that IRT1 is a major transporter responsible for Fe uptake and homeostasis in higher plants (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In each of these studies, the IRT1 knockout based on T-DNA insertion yielded plants that had visual shoot symptoms consistent with Fe deficiency (reduced growth, chlorotic leaves) and growth on elevated levels of Fe restored the wild-type phenotype. Furthermore, in the studies of Varotto et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), analysis of Fe accumulation and transport indicated that root Fe uptake and plant Fe accumulation were significantly reduced in the irt1 mutants, strongly suggesting a central role for this transporter in plant Fe nutrition.

The findings described here are a continuation of the work published in Cohen et al. (1998a), and address the mechanistic basis for the ‘‘induction’’ of root Cd and Zn uptake by imposition of Fe deficiency in Pisum sativum. Here, we tested the hypothesis that enhanced expression of a pea IRT1 orthologue could account for the stimulation in divalent cation influx during Fe deficiency. A cDNA clone that confers Fe transport activity was isolated from a library constructed with mRNA collected from roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. The tissuespecific expression of this gene in response to changes in plant Fe status was investigated, along with functional complementation of yeast mutants that are defective in high- and low-affinity iron or zinc transport. In this heterologous system, a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic investigation of Fe, Zn, and Cd uptake was carried out at metal concentrations that are physiologically relevant to plant roots growing in agricultural soils.

The work detailed in this paper follows up on a previous study in which we showed that the imposition of Fe deficiency stimulated both Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ influx in roots of pea seedlings (Cohen et al. 1998a). There have been a number of examples in the plant micronutrient nutrition literature indicating that Fe nutrition is linked, in poorly understood ways, to the transport and nutrition of other micronutrients as well as to heavy metals such as Cd, which are presumed to enter plants via systems normally operating for essential micronutrients. For example, in dicotyledonous plants that employ a reductive-based mechanism for Fe acquisition, it has been shown that the imposition of either Fe or Cu deficiency activated the Fe deficiency responses associated with Fe acquisition: root ferric reductase activity and acidification of the rhizosphere (Welch et al. 1993; Cohen et al. 1997). It is possible that in dicots, as has been shown for yeast, Cu is required for proper Fe utilization and transport. Furthermore, there have been several examples in the literature in which Fe deficiency in dicots induces the stimulated accumulation of a number of micronutrient metals other than Fe (for example, see Welch et al. 1993; Rodecap et al. 1994). More recently, researchers are beginning to understand the molecular basis for micronutrient nutrition from information gained from the cloning and characterization of plant micronutrient transporters from several gene families, including the ZIP family of metal transporters. These findings have led some researchers to suggest that these metal transporters may be relatively promiscuous, and facilitate the transport of several micronutrient metals (Guerinot 2000). In particular for the Arabidopsis ZIP transporter, IRT1, it was originally suggested that it may be a broad specificity metal transporter that can facilitate uptake from the soil of a number of micronutrients (Korshunova et al. 1999). These observations raise important questions about how plants might regulate the homeostasis of specific micronutrients, particularly if the expression of transporters that can mediate the influx of several different metals can also be regulated by changes in the plant status of several micronutrients.

Most of the findings suggesting multiple transport roles for ZIP transporters have come from yeast complementation studies, in which specific defects in micronutrient uptake (Fe, Zn, Mn), which prevent growth of the yeast at low levels of those micronutrients, have been complemented with plant metal transport genes. As researchers begin to extrapolate from these experiments based on heterologous expression in yeast to terrestrial plants in order to better understand plant micronutrient nutrition, it will be important to characterize the properties of the plant micronutrient transporters under conditions that more closely mimic roots functioning in the soil. To investigate the molecular basis for the observed enhancement of Zn and Cd accumulation in Fe-deficient pea seedlings, we isolated a putative iron transporter cDNA from pea. This cDNA, designated RIT1, shows significant nucleotide and amino acid sequence similarity to the Arabidopsis IRT1 cDNA. Expression of RIT1 in the yeast Fe transportdefective mutant conferred enhanced growth under low iron conditions. In this study, we showed that RIT1 mediates high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ that ranges from 54 to $9 3 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ . These findings suggest that RIT1 normally functions to mediate acquisition of Fe in plants. $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values in the nanomolar range measured in the heterologous yeast system are consistent with the significant fluxes observed at nanomolar $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in intact pea roots (Fox et al. 1996). Ferrous ion activities in this range also agree with the estimated critical $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activity required for optimal plant growth $\left( 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \mathrm { n M } \right)$ and the $_ { 0 . 1 - 1 , 0 0 0 \ n M }$ levels of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ typically found in bulk soil solutions (Lindsay 1991). A $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value in the nanomolar range is thus physiologically relevant to the environmental conditions a plant is most likely to encounter.

Therefore, these results, based on kinetic analysis of RIT-mediated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx, provide further support for recent findings from several laboratories based on analysis of Arabidopsis IRT1 knockout mutants, that led those authors to propose that IRT1 is the main transporter mediating plant Fe uptake from the soil (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In all three of these studies, characterization of T-DNA knockout lines for IRT1 produced a mutant phenotype nearly identical to that seen for plant Fe deficiency, and the wild type phenotype was restored by providing elevated levels of Fe in the soil or hydroponic medium. Furthermore, in the studies by Henriques et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), transport studies indicated that the irt1 mutant exhibited significantly reduced uptake of Fe, as well as Zn (in Henriques et al. 2002) and Zn, Mn, and Co (in Vert et al. 2002). Vert et al. (2002) also showed that the mutant phenotype was not overcome by supplementing the plants growth medium with elevated levels of Zn, Mn, or Co; the only mineral that reversed the chlorotic mutant phenotype was elevated Fe.

In the study detailing the original cloning and characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis (Eide et al. 1996), the data from the concentration-dependent kinetics for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in the fet3fet4 yeast expressing IRT1 indicated that the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake was $6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ , indicating that the affinity of IRT1 for $\mathrm { \bar { F e } } ^ { 2 + }$ is approximately 100 times lower than that found in the current study. However, in the former study, the total Fe concentration in the uptake solutions was used for the kinetic analyses (and ranged from 0 to $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } $ , which resulted in a very large overestimation of the actual uptake solution $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 \bar { + } }$ activity, and yielded a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value that was much larger than the actual value.

Our additional findings that RIT1 complements the yeast Zn transport-defective mutant ZHY3, the Mn transport-defective mutant SLY8, and mediates moderately high affinity $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx and lower affinity $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in yeast, suggests that RIT1 may provide a common pathway for the entry of metals besides iron across the root-cell plasma membrane. These findings, along with the result that RIT1 expression is induced by Fe deficiency in roots of pea seedlings, corroborate evidence at the whole-plant level and in intact roots of an Fedeficiency-induced stimulation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake (Fox et al.1996; Cohen et al. 1998a). These results suggest that the Fe-deficiency-induced stimulation of Fe2+, $\mathrm { \bar { C } d } ^ { 2 + }$ and divalent cation influx in intact pea roots may be the result of increased RIT1 expression.

Interestingly, our results demonstrate that RIT1 shows the highest affinity for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ $( 5 4 - 9 3 ~ \mathrm { n M } )$ , moderate affinity for Zn $( 4 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , and much lower affinity for Cd $1 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . It should be noted that we obtained similar kinetics for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx when yeast $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake experiments were conducted with either chelate buffered or standard, non-chelate buffered uptake solutions. This finding indicates that the results are not due to any artifact resulting from the use of chelate-buffered uptake solutions. Thus, RIT1 may exhibit a high specificity for Fe but still may be promiscuous, in that it will transport other micronutrient metals or their analogues if the metal concentrations in the soil are high enough. Variable charge-density ratios of the metals $( { \mathrm { F e } } > { \mathrm { Z n } } > { \mathrm { C d } } )$ could account for, or contribute to, differences in binding affinity to the transporter.

The $Z \bar { \mathrm { n } } ^ { 2 + }$ influx values measured in our heterologous systems from uptake solutions containing micromolar Zn concentrations may be meaningful in a physiological context, as we have previously measured significant $^ { 6 5 } { \cal Z } \mathrm { n }$ influx from solutions containing 1 mM Zn using intact pea roots (Cohen et al.1998a). More recently, our laboratory conducted a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic analysis for root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficient and inefficient cultivars of wheat (Hacisalihoglu et al. 2001). In that study, we described a $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport system with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ that was very similar to the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1-mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx reported here $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ in wheat: $2 { \ - } 5 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1: $4 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ ). It is possible that a wheat RIT homolog may be mediating this moderately high affinity root $\bar { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. However, Hacisalihoglu et al. (2001) uncovered a second very high affinity root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake system, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\dot { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 \mp }$ influx of $0 . 6 { - } 2 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ The transport properties of this second $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporter are more in line with what would be expected for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx from the rhizosphere of agricultural soils. The estimated critical activity of $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ required for optimal plant growth ranges from 0.01 to $0 . 1 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ (Norvell and Welch 1993; Welch and Norvell 1993), and the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in a typical soil solution ranges from 1 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ (Lindsay 1991; Hodgson et al.1966). When we used chelate buffer techniques to control $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in the nanomolar range, we did not see significant RIT1- mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ fluxes (data not shown), suggesting that RIT1 does not normally play a role in root $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake at physiologically relevant soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ levels.

In conclusion, the findings reported here suggest that, in typical agricultural soils, RIT1 functions primarily as a high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter that mediates root Fe acquisition. However, the ability of RIT1 to facilitate $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake when these metals are present at elevated concentrations suggests that RIT1 may be one pathway for the entry of toxic metals into the food chain. These findings are consistent with those presented recently in the literature indicating that Arabidopsis IRT1 plays a major role in mediating root Fe uptake from the soil, but also may facilitate the uptake of other divalent metals (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). Furthermore, the finding that plant Fe deficiency status may promote heavy metal uptake via increased expression of this transporter could have implications both for human nutrition and also for phytoremediation—the use of terrestrial plants to sequester toxic metals from contaminated soil. A more comprehensive understanding of the regulation and function of RIT1 may contribute to further progress in these areas.

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.

This family was first identified in plants, taking its name from the founding members as “ZRT, IRT-like protein” [8]. ZRT1 and ZRT2 are the high- and low-affinity zinc-regulated transporters of yeast [9, 10], respectively. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter) is an Arabidopsis transporter expressed in the roots of iron-deficient plants [11]. This family is widely distributed in all organisms, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, animals [12], and plants. A considerably large family of ZIP genes has been currently characterized from various species, such as Arabidopsis [8, 11, 13], rice (Oryza sativa L.) [1, 7], soybean (Glycine max (Linn.) Merr.) [5], Medicago truncatula [6, 14], the hyperaccumulation plant Thlaspi caerulescens [4, 15], Th. japonicum [16], etc.

In recent years, much progress has been made towards understanding molecular mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$

Functional analysis indicated that members of the ZIP gene family play a prominent role in the cytosolic zinc import, transporting this nutrient from outside the cell [4] or within an intracellular compartment [12];

they can transport a variety of divalent cations, including $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ [3, 17] and differ in their substrate range and specificity [17]. The expression of these genes was detected in various tissues, including roots, shoots, nodules, and flowers, and it seems likely that these genes were transcriptionally regulated by metal levels [1, 7, 13]. The proteins encoded by ZIP genes are predicted to have eight transmembrane domains (TM) with the amino- and carboxyl-terminal ends located on the outer surface of the plasma membrane [3]. Their overall length varies considerably due to a variable region between TM-3 and TM-4 containing a potential histidine-rich metal-binding domain. The most conserved region of these proteins occurs in TM-4 that is predicted to form an $\alpha$ -helix with a fully conserved histidine residue [17]. The transport function is eliminated when the conserved residues are replaced by mutation [18].

Rice, a species sensitive to zinc deficiency and a model plant for grasses, is the most important food crop in the world, feeding over half of the global population. However, rice yield is often limited by the low levels of soil Zn, especially in calcareous soils of arid and semiarid regions [19]. There is significant genetic variation both within and between plant varieties in their ability to maintain significant growth and yield under conditions of Zn deficiency [20]. In recent years, research has been carried out in several laboratories to elucidate the physiological mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficiency in plants; however, these mechanisms are still poorly understood [21]. An accurate map-based blueprint for all chromosomes and two shotgun sequences of rice genome have been published in the last three years, which provide an encouraging opportunity to study the interplay between various gene family members in a single organism [21]. Although several ZIP genes have been identified and functionally characterized at the molecular level [1, 7], the complete gene family and their role in metal homeostasis is not fully understood. To investigate new Zn transporters and Zn transporters probably associated with the Zn efficiency in rice, we exploited the current bioinformatics resources with the aim of achieving a comprehensive characterization of the ZIP family. We also studied the expression patterns of OsZIP1, OsZIP3, and OsZIP4 , which have been established as $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters in rice [1, 7], in different parts of $Z \mathrm { n }$ -efficient and Zn-inefficient rice genotypes (IR8192 and Erjiufeng) grown under different $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activity conditions. Our results suggest that the ZIP gene expression may partly explain the differences in zinc efficiency between IR8192 and Erjiufeng.
