Nitrogen, a critical macronutrient for plant growth and productivity, is assimilated from inorganic nitrate and ammonium into amino acids—its primary organic form [1, 2]. Amino acids not only serve as macronutrients and primary constituents of nitrogen-containing macromolecules but also function as signaling molecules that regulate leaf development, seed germination, root architecture, flowering, and developmental transitions [1]. The limited capacity of amino acids to diffuse across cellular membranes necessitates the involvement of membranebound amino acid transporters to mediate their intercellular and systemic translocation via vascular networks [3, 4]. While the xylem facilitates unidirectional upward transport of amino acids, the phloem governs bidirectional source-to-sink redistribution, a process fundamental to nitrogen allocation and metabolic homeostasis in plants [4]. Crucially, amino acid transporters directly regulate nitrogen assimilation efficiency and its integration into macromolecular biosynthesis (e.g., proteins, nucleic acids), thereby critically shaping plant physiological processes such as leaf senescence, grain yield, fruit quality, root architecture remodeling, pathogen resistance, drought adaptation, and cadmium detoxification [5, 6]. Therefore, understanding the function of amino acid transporters is crucial for decoding the regulatory mechanisms of nutrient metabolism and stress adaptation in many plants.

In plants, three major families of amino acid transporters have been identified: the Amino Acid/Auxin Permease (AAAP) family, the Amino Acid-Polyamine Organocation (APC) family, and the Usually Multiple Acids Move In and Out Transporters (UMAMIT) family [7, 8]. Among them, the AAAP family not only demonstrates broader functional significance but also comprises the largest number of members compared to the APC and UMAMIT families, and this gene family plays pivotal roles in amino acid transport, stress adaptation, auxin signaling, and crop yield optimization [9, 10]. The AAAP family includes eight subfamilies: amino acid permease (AAP), γ-aminobutyric acid transporter (GAT), lysine histidine transporter (LHT), putative auxin transporter (AUX), proline transporter (ProT), similar to ANT1-like aromatic and neutral amino acid transporter (ANT), and amino acid transporter-like (ATLa and ATLb) [11]. They all have identical Aa_trans conserved structural domain (PF01490) [12].

The AAAP family plays critical roles in hormone crosstalk, pathogen resistance, and nutrient signaling [6, 9]. In Arabidopsis, AtLHT1 modulates broad-spectrum defense responses by regulating cellular redox homeostasis through salicylic acid (SA) signaling [5]. Overexpression of GmAAP6-like gene enhances jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis in soybean [13]. By restricting amino acid availability in the apoplast, AAAPs limit pathogen access to nitrogen-rich metabolites—a key strategy for resisting microbial invasion [14]. These findings underscore AAAPs’ multiple roles in plant defense, coordinating amino acid transport and immune signaling pathways. However, the interplay between AAAPs and JA/SA signaling remains poorly characterized in woody plants. In grapes, drought and salt stress alter the expression of 12 VvAAAP genes in the shoot apex [15]. In pepper, eight AAAP genes are upregulated in roots under cold, heat, osmotic, oxidative, and salt stress but downregulated in leaves [11]. The AAAP-mediated adaptation to abiotic stresses has been documented in many plant species, including wheat, cotton, poplar, moso bamboo, foxtail millet, and Liriodendron chinense [9, 10, 12, 16–18]. In contrast, AAAP responses to nutrient deficiency remain understudied. For instance, GmAAP6a enhances nitrogen deficiency tolerance in both Arabidopsis and soybean [19], while in maize, ZmPHRs (central regulators of lowphosphate signaling) suppress ZmAAP2 and ZmLHT1 expression via P1BS cis-element binding [20, 21]. Nevertheless, the mechanisms by which AAAPs mediate adaptation to nitrogen, phosphate, and boron deficiencies in woody plants remain largely unexplored.

Belonging to the dicot family Myrtaceae, Eucalyptus encompasses three genera (Eucalyptus, Angophora, and Corymbia), comprising 1,239 taxa (869 species and 370 subspecies) naturally occurring across Australasia and Southeast Asia [22]. Renowned for their exceptional growth velocity (reaching up to $\sim 1 0 \mathrm { ~ m ~ }$ annually), high-quality timber, and resilience to diverse conditions, these trees have been introduced to over 100 nations and regions, representing approximately $2 3 \%$ of global plantation forests [22]. In China, this genus supplies over $3 3 \%$ of industrial timber output and thrives in the acidic soils prevalent in southern regions, where limited free phosphorus bioavailability (phosphate, Pi) results from interactions with aluminum/iron cations [21, 22]. These edaphic challenges underscore the urgency to investigate molecular mechanisms enabling nitrogen and phosphorus utilization efficiency in Eucalyptus. Notably, AAAPs remain functionally uncharacterized in Eucalyptus, and their transcriptional dynamics under JA/SA induction or nutrient deprivation (nitrogen, phosphate, boron) remain unexplored.

This study conducted phylogenetic analyses and functional characterization of the 78 EgAAAPs identified in Eucalyptus grandis, a model species within the Eucalyptus spp. Comprehensive transcriptional profiling was performed to investigate EgAAAPs expression across tissues, developmental stages, and under hormonal treatments (JA/SA) or nutrient deprivation. These findings establish foundational insights for elucidating AAAPmediated stress tolerant mechanisms in woody species. Additionally, the work reveals stress-responsive patterns of AAAPs in perennial plants and offers candidate genetic resources for engineering trees with enhanced nutrientuse efficiency.

As many of the bioactive compounds used for crop protection, especially pesticides, are toxic, efforts to reduce their usage are necessary, in the interests of both safeguarding human health and minimizing collateral damage to the environment1. Major losses are incurred by spray drift, run-off and photodegradation, and it has been estimated that less than $0 . 1 \%$ of the bioactive material applied actually reaches its target2,3.

An attractive strategy to improve pesticide efficacy is to modify bioactive compounds in order to encourage their ability to cross the plasma membrane and be subsequently translocated through the plant's vascular system to reach the site of pest/pathogen damage2. The addition of either amino acids, amino acid esters or sugar moieties to a pesticide structures has been found to measurably improve mobility in plants, especially through the phloem, presumably through the involvement of the plant's native transporter machinery4-9. These conclusions have been primarily based on physiological experiments, for example, concentration-dependent kinetics, competition and inhibit studies. With the acquisition of extensive DNA sequence, it is increasingly possible to identify the carriers responsible for the movement of pesticide conjugates. The in silico identification of Ricinus communis sugar transporter genes and the monitoring of their transcriptional behavior has led to the identification of the GTF (glucose-fipronil conjugate) induced gene RcSTP1. Functional analysis based on the expression of this gene in Xenopus laevis oocytes has demonstrated that its product has a high affinity for GTF. Long-distance root-to-shoot transport of GTF was found to be enhanced by introducing a transgene which constitutively expressed RcSTP110. More recently studies were able to show that the distinctive tissue distribution of a glycine/fipronil conjugate (GlyF) is governed by the activity of four amino acid transporters, and one of them, RcANT15, has the ability to significantly increase the uptake of serine-fipronil conjugate in Xenopus oocytes significantly11,12.

The Arabidopsis thaliana genome harbors a minimum of 67 genes encoding proteins likely involved in amino acid transport; several of these have been have been functionally characterized13. While AtLHT1 was initially held to be a high-affinity transporter for both lysine and histidine, in the meantime it has been shown to have much broader specificity14-16. Thus AtLHT1 appears not only responsible for the uptake of amino acids into the root, but also in their cycling within mesophyll cells15,16. AtLHT1 was also reported to negatively regulate aspects of the plant's pathogen defense response by altering the availability of glutamine17. Analysis of are2 mutant has revealed that AtLHT1 is the gene responsible, indicating that AtLHT1 is involved in the transport of ACC (1- aminocylopropane carboxylic acid)18, and implying that AtLHT1 has a broad substratespecificity. Given that AtLHT1 makes a major contribution to the uptake of amino acids into roots, as well as that of some amino acid derivatives, it was therefore of interest to test whether its functionality could be exploited to actively take up a pesticide/amino acid conjugate.

The organisms that populated the primordial Earth lived in an anaerobic environment where Fe was predominantly reduced, soluble, and biologically abundant. As photosynthetic organisms proliferated and transformed Earths atmosphere, however, Fe became increasingly oxidized and biologically scarce. Fe bioavailability is thus low in over one-third of the Earths land surface area, particularly in alkaline or calcareous soils (Crowley et al.1987). This has imposed enormous selective pressures on terrestrial plants and microorganisms to develop efficient strategies for solubilizing Fe from the soil.

Most aerobic organisms have evolved mechanisms to solubilize Fe based on the chemical processes of chelation, reduction, and acidification (reviewed in Kochian 1991, 2000). These strategies of Fe acquisition are restricted to discrete phylogenetic groups. Yeast and all plants except the grasses reduce $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ chelates and absorb the more soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ion released by this process. Under Fe deficiency, species of this group induce the activity of a plasma membrane ferric chelate reductase and also stimulate the release of protons, both of which enhance the solubility of soil Fe. Other classes of organisms, including fungi, bacteria, and members of the family Poaceae (the grasses), release high-affinity $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ -chelating compounds, called siderophores, that solubilize $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ and are then recognized for uptake by specific membrane receptors (Ro¨ mheld and Marschner 1986; Chaney 1987; Bienfait 1988).

Previous work has shown that Fe deficiency in many nongrass plant species elicits a stimulated influx of Fe and other divalent cations. Fox et al. (1996) found that Fe-deficient pea seedlings exhibited higher rates of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx compared to Fe-sufficient seedlings. Furthermore, tissue concentrations of Fe and other mineral elements can be influenced by plant Fe status. Welch et al. (1993) demonstrated that the shoot concentrations of several divalent cationic metals, including Cu, Mn, and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g }$ increased in Fe-deficient pea seedlings compared to Fesufficient pea seedlings. Rodecap et al. (1994) also reported that Fe-deficient Arabidopsis plants accumulated higher concentrations of Cd and $\mathrm { M g }$ in racemes and seeds compared to Fe-sufficient plants.

We previously demonstrated that Fe deficiency induced a high affinity Cd influx into roots of pea seedlings, a finding that has implications for the entry of heavy metals into food crops (Cohen et al. 1998a). Our preliminary investigations into the mechanistic basis for this observation suggested that Fe deficiency induces a divalent cation transporter that can facilitate $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. We established that expression of a homolog of the Arabidopsis IRT1 Fe transporter gene (Eide et al. 1996) was induced in roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. When expressed in yeast, it was found that this transporter could mediate $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake (Cohen et al. 1998b). Enhanced expression of this gene could increase IRT1 density in the root-cell plasma membrane and could account for the observed stimulation in root Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake.

IRT1 is a member of the ZIP family of metal transporters that are hypothesized to play a role in micronutrient nutrition, and in particular in Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and transport (Guerinot 2000). The ZIP designation, which stands for ZRT, IRT-like protein, comes from the names of the first members of this family to be identified. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter), a transporter first identified in Arabidopsis, is induced by Fe deficiency in roots, and has been suggested to be an Fe transporter (Eide et al. 1996). ZRT1 and ZRT2 (zinc-regulated transporter) are high and low affinity $Z \mathfrak { n }$ transporters in yeast that are regulated by changes in cellular $Z \mathrm { n }$ status (Zhao and Eide 1996a, 1996b). Some ZIP family members have been cloned from several plant species including Arabidopsis (IRT-1, -2; ZIP 1–4), Thlaspi caerulescens (ZNT-1, -2) and tomato (LeIRT-1 -2) (Eide et al. 1996; Grotz et al. 1998; Pence et al. 2000; Assunc¸ ao et al. 2001; Eckhardt et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2001). In some of these studies, heterologous expression of ZIP genes in yeast mutants defective in specific micronutrient uptake systems have provided researchers with information concerning the transport properties of the ZIP proteins. What is emerging from these studies is the concept that some of these transporters may exhibit a fairly broad specificity with regards to the micronutrient metal transported. For example, based on heterologous expression studies in yeast, it was suggested that IRT1 may transport $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ in addition to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Korshunova et al. 1999). However, caution must be exercised in extrapolating these findings in yeast to higher plants growing in the soil, particularly since the metal concentrations used in these studies were much higher than those found in the soil or rhizosphere.

More recently, studies from three different laboratories using Arabidopsis knockout mutants for IRT1 have provided more direct evidence that IRT1 is a major transporter responsible for Fe uptake and homeostasis in higher plants (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In each of these studies, the IRT1 knockout based on T-DNA insertion yielded plants that had visual shoot symptoms consistent with Fe deficiency (reduced growth, chlorotic leaves) and growth on elevated levels of Fe restored the wild-type phenotype. Furthermore, in the studies of Varotto et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), analysis of Fe accumulation and transport indicated that root Fe uptake and plant Fe accumulation were significantly reduced in the irt1 mutants, strongly suggesting a central role for this transporter in plant Fe nutrition.

The findings described here are a continuation of the work published in Cohen et al. (1998a), and address the mechanistic basis for the ‘‘induction’’ of root Cd and Zn uptake by imposition of Fe deficiency in Pisum sativum. Here, we tested the hypothesis that enhanced expression of a pea IRT1 orthologue could account for the stimulation in divalent cation influx during Fe deficiency. A cDNA clone that confers Fe transport activity was isolated from a library constructed with mRNA collected from roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. The tissuespecific expression of this gene in response to changes in plant Fe status was investigated, along with functional complementation of yeast mutants that are defective in high- and low-affinity iron or zinc transport. In this heterologous system, a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic investigation of Fe, Zn, and Cd uptake was carried out at metal concentrations that are physiologically relevant to plant roots growing in agricultural soils.

Micronutrients are essential for both plant growth and human health, and a deficiency in such nutrients may reduce the yield and quality of crop plants and lead to nutritional deficiency syndrome in mammals such as anaemia, hypophrenia, and stagnation of growth and development. It was reported that deficiencies in bio-available iron, zinc, and other essential minerals affect a large proportion of the global population [1–3]. Besides, zinc and iron are essential metal nutrient factors for plants since they play critical roles in the process of growth and development, including photosynthesis, respiration, and other biochemical reactions that require Zn or Fe as co-factors.

In plants, zinc deficiency leads to internode shortening, reduction in leaf size and other morphological changes [4–6], while iron deficiency can cause severe chlorosis and growth arrest. A deficiency in Zn and Fe repress plant growth and reduces the yield and quality [7], although too much Zn and Fe may result in considerable biochemical toxicity [8, 9]. To avoid excessive absorption and facilitate adequate intake, plants have created a balanced network to regulate the uptake, utilisation, and storage of these metal ions [10, 11]. Actually, such adjustments rely on genes that control ion homeostasis in plants. Recently, several metal transporters that contribute to metal-ion homeostasis in plants have been identified, including the zinc-regulated transporter (ZRT), iron-regulated transporter (IRT)-like protein (ZIP), natural resistance-associated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and yellow stripe-like protein (YSL).

Zn exhibits low solubility, and its solubilisation is thought to occur via acidification of rhizosphere and secretion of organic chelators such as nicotianamine (NA) and citric acid. Subsequently, as a free ion, zinc is uptake into the root cells by ZIPs [12]. Zn can then be transported into vacuoles and immobilised in the root symplast or it can be translocated into the vascular cylinder through plasmodesmata [12]. The translocation of Zn from roots to shoots requires the export of zinc from root cells and loading of zinc into the apoplastic xylem [13, 14]. Inside the xylem, zinc flux from roots to shoots is massflow driven and ionic zinc is chelated by lowmolecular-weight ligands to avoid $\mathrm { Z n }$ retention. Then, $\mathrm { Z n }$ is taken up from the xylem of shoots and transported across the plasma membranes of adjacent cells via membrane zinc transporters [15]. Two different mechanisms are involved in iron acquisition in plants. Strategy I is specifically used by nongraminaceous plants, which contains the reduction of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ on the root surface and the acquisition of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ into root cells by $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters, including ZIPs [12]. Furthermore, phenolics are secreted to facilitate iron acquisition during Fe starvation. These substances serve as iron chelators or electron donors for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ reduction during iron uptake [16]. Graminaceous plants such as rice and corn use strategy II, which involves the synthesis and secretion of phytosiderophores (PS) to facilitate iron uptake. The chelated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ is then translocated into roots cell by YS proteins. The transportation of iron in graminaceous plants is mediated by NA and YSL proteins. These results indicated that ZIPs play essential roles in both absorption and translocation of Zn and Fe in nongraminaceous plants, while their functions in graminaceous plants remain less understood.

ZIPs function in ion homeostasis as they can transport cations into the cytoplasm [17]. AtIRT1 was the first cloned member of ZIP family and encodes a major Fe transporter at the root surface [18–21]. Further studies showed that irt1 had lower Ni accumulation than the wild-type plants under Fe-deficiency status, indicating that AtIRT1 play essential roles in Fe and Ni translocation in Arabidopsis [22]. AtIRT2 localized to intracellular vesicles, suggesting it may play roles in compartmentalisation and remobilising of iron into internal storage vesicles to avoid metal toxicity [23]. Additionally, the accumulation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in reproductive organs correlate with expression levels of $V \nu Z I P 3$ during the reproductive growth stage, indicating that ZIPs may be associated with Zn distribution in embryo and endosperm [6]. It has also

been reported that overexpression of ZIPs may result in elevated metal ion content. Overexpressing AtZIP1 in Hordeum vulgare increases the Zn and Fe contents in seeds [24]. Similarly, Fe and Zn levels were increased in shoots, roots and seeds when overexpressing OsIRT1 in rice [25]. However, overaccumulating OsZIP4, result in increased Zn contents in roots, while Zn levels in seeds was significant lower than in non-transgenic plants [26]. Since it was reported that OsZIP4 was expressed in the phloem cells of stem, and vascular bundles of leaves and roots [27], it can be assumed that the endogenous expression profiles of ZIP genes may be critical for appropriate Zn and Fe distribution and metal homeostasis in plants.

The contribution of ZIP genes in the uptake and translocation of iron and zinc has been investigated extensively in Arabidopsis and rice. However, our understanding of the functions of ZIPs in maize remains limited. In this study, two ion transporters, ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3, were cloned from maize and showed distinctive expression patterns. It was demonstrated that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 showed different activity of yeast complementation, and the expression level of ZmIRT1 was induced by Fe deficiency [28]. To explore the physiological function of ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 in plants, transgenic Arabidopsis lines overexpressing ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 were generated. The contents of Zn and Fe in transgenic plants were then measured using ICP-OES and Zinpyr-1 staining. We analysed the phenotype of overexpression lines under excess and deficient Zn and Fe conditions, and detected the transcription levels of key genes that play a role in the uptake and translocation of Zn and Fe in transgenic Arabidopsis plants. It was shown that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 are functional metal transporters, and ectopic overexpression of ZmIRT1 stimulated endogenous Fe uptake mechanisms, which may facilitate metal uptake and homeostasis.

The work detailed in this paper follows up on a previous study in which we showed that the imposition of Fe deficiency stimulated both Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ influx in roots of pea seedlings (Cohen et al. 1998a). There have been a number of examples in the plant micronutrient nutrition literature indicating that Fe nutrition is linked, in poorly understood ways, to the transport and nutrition of other micronutrients as well as to heavy metals such as Cd, which are presumed to enter plants via systems normally operating for essential micronutrients. For example, in dicotyledonous plants that employ a reductive-based mechanism for Fe acquisition, it has been shown that the imposition of either Fe or Cu deficiency activated the Fe deficiency responses associated with Fe acquisition: root ferric reductase activity and acidification of the rhizosphere (Welch et al. 1993; Cohen et al. 1997). It is possible that in dicots, as has been shown for yeast, Cu is required for proper Fe utilization and transport. Furthermore, there have been several examples in the literature in which Fe deficiency in dicots induces the stimulated accumulation of a number of micronutrient metals other than Fe (for example, see Welch et al. 1993; Rodecap et al. 1994). More recently, researchers are beginning to understand the molecular basis for micronutrient nutrition from information gained from the cloning and characterization of plant micronutrient transporters from several gene families, including the ZIP family of metal transporters. These findings have led some researchers to suggest that these metal transporters may be relatively promiscuous, and facilitate the transport of several micronutrient metals (Guerinot 2000). In particular for the Arabidopsis ZIP transporter, IRT1, it was originally suggested that it may be a broad specificity metal transporter that can facilitate uptake from the soil of a number of micronutrients (Korshunova et al. 1999). These observations raise important questions about how plants might regulate the homeostasis of specific micronutrients, particularly if the expression of transporters that can mediate the influx of several different metals can also be regulated by changes in the plant status of several micronutrients.

Most of the findings suggesting multiple transport roles for ZIP transporters have come from yeast complementation studies, in which specific defects in micronutrient uptake (Fe, Zn, Mn), which prevent growth of the yeast at low levels of those micronutrients, have been complemented with plant metal transport genes. As researchers begin to extrapolate from these experiments based on heterologous expression in yeast to terrestrial plants in order to better understand plant micronutrient nutrition, it will be important to characterize the properties of the plant micronutrient transporters under conditions that more closely mimic roots functioning in the soil. To investigate the molecular basis for the observed enhancement of Zn and Cd accumulation in Fe-deficient pea seedlings, we isolated a putative iron transporter cDNA from pea. This cDNA, designated RIT1, shows significant nucleotide and amino acid sequence similarity to the Arabidopsis IRT1 cDNA. Expression of RIT1 in the yeast Fe transportdefective mutant conferred enhanced growth under low iron conditions. In this study, we showed that RIT1 mediates high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ that ranges from 54 to $9 3 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ . These findings suggest that RIT1 normally functions to mediate acquisition of Fe in plants. $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values in the nanomolar range measured in the heterologous yeast system are consistent with the significant fluxes observed at nanomolar $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in intact pea roots (Fox et al. 1996). Ferrous ion activities in this range also agree with the estimated critical $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activity required for optimal plant growth $\left( 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \mathrm { n M } \right)$ and the $_ { 0 . 1 - 1 , 0 0 0 \ n M }$ levels of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ typically found in bulk soil solutions (Lindsay 1991). A $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value in the nanomolar range is thus physiologically relevant to the environmental conditions a plant is most likely to encounter.

Therefore, these results, based on kinetic analysis of RIT-mediated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx, provide further support for recent findings from several laboratories based on analysis of Arabidopsis IRT1 knockout mutants, that led those authors to propose that IRT1 is the main transporter mediating plant Fe uptake from the soil (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In all three of these studies, characterization of T-DNA knockout lines for IRT1 produced a mutant phenotype nearly identical to that seen for plant Fe deficiency, and the wild type phenotype was restored by providing elevated levels of Fe in the soil or hydroponic medium. Furthermore, in the studies by Henriques et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), transport studies indicated that the irt1 mutant exhibited significantly reduced uptake of Fe, as well as Zn (in Henriques et al. 2002) and Zn, Mn, and Co (in Vert et al. 2002). Vert et al. (2002) also showed that the mutant phenotype was not overcome by supplementing the plants growth medium with elevated levels of Zn, Mn, or Co; the only mineral that reversed the chlorotic mutant phenotype was elevated Fe.

In the study detailing the original cloning and characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis (Eide et al. 1996), the data from the concentration-dependent kinetics for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in the fet3fet4 yeast expressing IRT1 indicated that the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake was $6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ , indicating that the affinity of IRT1 for $\mathrm { \bar { F e } } ^ { 2 + }$ is approximately 100 times lower than that found in the current study. However, in the former study, the total Fe concentration in the uptake solutions was used for the kinetic analyses (and ranged from 0 to $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } $ , which resulted in a very large overestimation of the actual uptake solution $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 \bar { + } }$ activity, and yielded a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value that was much larger than the actual value.

Our additional findings that RIT1 complements the yeast Zn transport-defective mutant ZHY3, the Mn transport-defective mutant SLY8, and mediates moderately high affinity $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx and lower affinity $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in yeast, suggests that RIT1 may provide a common pathway for the entry of metals besides iron across the root-cell plasma membrane. These findings, along with the result that RIT1 expression is induced by Fe deficiency in roots of pea seedlings, corroborate evidence at the whole-plant level and in intact roots of an Fedeficiency-induced stimulation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake (Fox et al.1996; Cohen et al. 1998a). These results suggest that the Fe-deficiency-induced stimulation of Fe2+, $\mathrm { \bar { C } d } ^ { 2 + }$ and divalent cation influx in intact pea roots may be the result of increased RIT1 expression.

Interestingly, our results demonstrate that RIT1 shows the highest affinity for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ $( 5 4 - 9 3 ~ \mathrm { n M } )$ , moderate affinity for Zn $( 4 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , and much lower affinity for Cd $1 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . It should be noted that we obtained similar kinetics for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx when yeast $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake experiments were conducted with either chelate buffered or standard, non-chelate buffered uptake solutions. This finding indicates that the results are not due to any artifact resulting from the use of chelate-buffered uptake solutions. Thus, RIT1 may exhibit a high specificity for Fe but still may be promiscuous, in that it will transport other micronutrient metals or their analogues if the metal concentrations in the soil are high enough. Variable charge-density ratios of the metals $( { \mathrm { F e } } > { \mathrm { Z n } } > { \mathrm { C d } } )$ could account for, or contribute to, differences in binding affinity to the transporter.

The $Z \bar { \mathrm { n } } ^ { 2 + }$ influx values measured in our heterologous systems from uptake solutions containing micromolar Zn concentrations may be meaningful in a physiological context, as we have previously measured significant $^ { 6 5 } { \cal Z } \mathrm { n }$ influx from solutions containing 1 mM Zn using intact pea roots (Cohen et al.1998a). More recently, our laboratory conducted a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic analysis for root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficient and inefficient cultivars of wheat (Hacisalihoglu et al. 2001). In that study, we described a $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport system with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ that was very similar to the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1-mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx reported here $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ in wheat: $2 { \ - } 5 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1: $4 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ ). It is possible that a wheat RIT homolog may be mediating this moderately high affinity root $\bar { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. However, Hacisalihoglu et al. (2001) uncovered a second very high affinity root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake system, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\dot { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 \mp }$ influx of $0 . 6 { - } 2 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ The transport properties of this second $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporter are more in line with what would be expected for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx from the rhizosphere of agricultural soils. The estimated critical activity of $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ required for optimal plant growth ranges from 0.01 to $0 . 1 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ (Norvell and Welch 1993; Welch and Norvell 1993), and the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in a typical soil solution ranges from 1 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ (Lindsay 1991; Hodgson et al.1966). When we used chelate buffer techniques to control $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in the nanomolar range, we did not see significant RIT1- mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ fluxes (data not shown), suggesting that RIT1 does not normally play a role in root $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake at physiologically relevant soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ levels.

In conclusion, the findings reported here suggest that, in typical agricultural soils, RIT1 functions primarily as a high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter that mediates root Fe acquisition. However, the ability of RIT1 to facilitate $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake when these metals are present at elevated concentrations suggests that RIT1 may be one pathway for the entry of toxic metals into the food chain. These findings are consistent with those presented recently in the literature indicating that Arabidopsis IRT1 plays a major role in mediating root Fe uptake from the soil, but also may facilitate the uptake of other divalent metals (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). Furthermore, the finding that plant Fe deficiency status may promote heavy metal uptake via increased expression of this transporter could have implications both for human nutrition and also for phytoremediation—the use of terrestrial plants to sequester toxic metals from contaminated soil. A more comprehensive understanding of the regulation and function of RIT1 may contribute to further progress in these areas.

To investigate the main expression tissues of IRT1, thereby its potential location and function, we have analyzed the gene expression profiles of the IRT1 gene in A. thaliana and S. lycopersicum using Genevestigator. At anatomical part level, Arabidopsis IRT1 have been identified to be expressed in flowering parts and in many root-related structures such as roots, primary roots, root tip, lateral root, maturation zone, radicle, root phloem companion cell etc. During the development, Arabidopsis IRT1 was mainly expressed in seedling, germinated seeds and young rosette stages (Suppl. 1 Fig.1). Moreover, Fe-deficiency in Arabidopsis plants has greately affected the expression profile of IRT1. Under iron deficiency, the IRT1 gene has been identified to be up-regulated with high fold-change (Suppl. 1 Fig. 2). In tomato (S. lycopersicum), IRT1 has also demonstrated the similar tissue expression pattern to that of Arabidopsis, with an expression mainly in root, seedling and flowering parts (Suppl. 1 Fig. 3). The expression profiles of Arabidopsis and tomato plants indicated that IRT1 could mainly function in root and flowering parts of plants. This also supports the function of IRT1 transporters at root for Fe uptake . Overall, general physico-chemical properties of identified IRT1 proteins and expression profile data analysis of IRT1 genes in Arabidopsis and tomato supported that identified proteins could possibly function in

Fe uptake at root.

In motif 1, two rows of thoroughly conserved histidine residues were detected (Fig. 1A); in motif 2, one row of histidine residues with partially disrupted by other residues detected (Fig. 1B), and in motif 3, one row of thoroughly conserved histidine residues detected (Fig. 1C). Thus, motif 1 and 3 were the two motifs with thoroughly conserved histidine residues. When membrane topologies of IRT1 proteins for transmembrane domain IV analyzed, motif 1 seemed more potential candidate for most conserved region in IRT1s. ZIP proteins also contain a variable cytoplasmic region between transmembrane domains 3 and 4 (Guerinot, 2000). This variable region was also clearly observed in transmembrane topology analysis in B. distachyon, C. reinhadrtii, S. lycopersicum and P. trichocarpa (Suppl. 2).

Gene organization analysis showed that AtIRT1 has 2 exons; BdIRT1 has 2 exons; BrIRT1 has 2 exons; CrIRT1,2 have 5 exons; CsIRT1 has 2 exons; EgIRT1 has 2 exons; GmIRT1-3 have 3, 2 and 3 exons, respectively; GrIRT1 has 2 exons; MtIRT1,2 have 2 and 3 exons, respectively; OsIRT1,2 have 2 and 3 exons, respectively; PvIRT1,2 have 3 and 2 exons, respectively; PhpIRT1,2 have 5 and 2 exons, respectively; PtIRT1,2 have 2 exons; SlIRT1 has 2 exons; SbIRT1 has 2 exons; VvIRT1,2 have 4 and 2 exons, respectively and ZmIRT1 has 2 exons (Fig. 2). Exon numbers of species usually varied between 2 and 3, except for C. reinhardtii, and one member of $P$ . patents and $V .$ . vinifera. Exon/intron variations (loss or gains) in these species might have occurred during the development of orthologous genes (Rogozin et al., 2005), and may be related with the species-specific functional diversities. Koralewski and Krutovsky (2011) report that shorter exons increase the potential for alternative splicing (AS) and genomic complexity but AS rate does not always correlate with the species complexity. When the data in Fig. 2 was analyzed, it was observed that CrIRT1 and 2, MtIRT2, OsIRT2, PhpIRT1 and VvIRT1 genes include some relatively shorter exons in comparison with other species but there was no relationship between exon length and genomic complexity observed since two lower plants $C .$ . reinhardtii and $P$ . patents contained relatively shorter exons. In general, this shows that reliability of obtained results is directly related with the number of species analyzed. Therefore, studies regarding the evolutionary development of exons/introns; their contribution to speciation and species complexity necessitate to analyze the large number of inter-and-intra species sets.

Predicted interaction partner analysis was performed for AtIRT1/ZIP6 (AT2G30080.1) protein. Ten putative interaction partners were found, including HMA4, AT1G51610, AtCDF1, ZAT, NAS3, AT3G20870, AT3G08650, NAS4, KEA3 and

NRAMP2 for AtIRT1 (Fig. 4). Among these interaction partners, nicotianamine synthase (NAS) 4 is required for proper response to iron deficiency and distribution of iron (Koen et al., 2013). Perturbation studies showed that the NAS4 gene is significantly up-regulated under Fe-deficiency, supporting its possible function in iron deficiency and its distribution (Suppl. 1 Fig. 4). Nicotianamine synthase (NAS) 3 functions as a sensor for iron status within the plant and involved in the transport of iron (Inoue et al., 2003). Although Fe-deficiency has led to slightly induce the up-regulation of NAS3 at root, it is mainly down-regulated in leaf and shoot as response to Fe-deficiency (Suppl. 1 Fig. 5). This implicitly may indicate the presence of a relationship between cellular iron concentration and NAS3 expression. NRAMP2 is an iron transporter protein functioning in iron metabolism in plants (Gruenheid et al., 1999). In addition, NRAMP family is a kind of broad range plant metal transporter carrying $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { N i } ^ { \bar { 2 } + }$ ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ , ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ , ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ (Thomine et al., 2000; Nevo and Nelson, 2006; Xia et al., 2010). Under Fe-deficiency, the expression of NRAMP2 gene did not show any significant change (Suppl. 1 Fig. 6). Thus, its expression could be related with the presence of cellular iron or iron related-uptake of other metals. AT3G20870 and AT3G08650 are ZIP family proteins functioning in metal ion transport (Wang et al., 2011). AtCDF1/ZAT are metal ion transmembrane transporters mediating Zn ion homeostasis in plants (Bloß et al., 2002). AT1G51610 (MTPC4) is a cation efflux family protein functioning in sequestration of excess metal in the cytoplasm into vacuoles to regulate metal homeostasis (Mäser et al., 2001). HMA4 is a cadmium ion transmembrane transporter, and involved in cadmium and zinc transport (Miyadate et al., 2011). KEA3 is a potassium ion transmembrane transporter (Kunz et al., 2014). Although AT3G20870, AT3G08650, AtCDF1/ZAT, AT1G51610 (MTPC4), HMA4 and KEA3 genes have been induced upon iron-deficiency, no significant differentially expression pattern has been demonstrated (Suppl. 1 Fig. 7-12). However, presence of their expression under Fe-deficiency indicates that these genes could be in a cross-talk with Fe-metabolism in a way. Moreover, all the interaction partners of Arabidopsis IRT1 are ion transporter proteins. When taken into account that many metal ion transporters are a type of broad-range metal transporter (Guerinot, 2000) carrying a range of metal ions, it is understandable that AtIRT1 proteins have an interaction with different types of transporter proteins.

## qRT-PCR analysis and expression patterns of MdZIP genes


The seedlings of M. hupehensis showed significant phenotypic changes under Zn and Fe deficiency. Young leaves exhibited chlorosis, and the plants were shorter and the length, tip number, surface area, average diam and volume of roots of seedlings decreased under Fe deficiency; under Zn deficiency, the plants were shorter and the length, tip number, surface area, average diam and volume of roots of seedlings decreased (Figs. S2–S4). In order to study this phenomenon, we conducted analysis of qRT-PCR and expression patterns of MdZIP genes.

MdZIP genes expression patterns varied among the different stress conditions studied. Previous phylogenetic analyses enabled the prediction of gene function (Fu et al. 2017; Li et al. 2013). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that MdZIP9, MdZIP17, and MdZIP10 image of iron coloring according to the Prussian blue reaction in apical and steles, and whole seedlings of 12-days-old WT and transgenic OX-26 lines of A. thaliana grown on standard MS medium $\mathrm { ( p H } 5 . 7 \mathrm { ) }$ , obtained using fluorescence microscope

clustered with AtZIP9, AtIRT3, and AtZIP4, which were induced by Zn-deficient conditions (Fig. 2) (Talke et al. 2006; Grotz et al. 1998). The expression of MdZIP9, MdZIP17, and MdZIP10 was highly induced in the roots and shoots of plants exposed to Zn deficiency, indicating that these three MdZIPs might be functional orthologs of AtZIP9, AtIRT3, and AtZIP4, respectively (Fig. 5). Four MdZIPs (MdZIP15, MdZIP16, MdZIP6, and MdZIP18) and two AtZIPs (AtIRT1 and AtIRT2), which are closely related (Fig. 2), were induced by Fe deficiency (Vert et al. 2002). In the present study, these ZIPs were also induced by Fe deficiency (Fig. 5), indicating that these genes enhanced the uptake and soil-to-root translocation of Fe when Fe availability was low. The phylogenetic analysis showed that MdZIP7, MdZIP3, MdZIP11, and MdZIP13 were closely related to AtZIP6 and AtZIP1 (Fig. 2), which were induced under Zn-deficient conditions (Grotz et al. 1998;

Bauer and Bereczky 2004). In the present study, the expression of MdZIP7, MdZIP3, MdZIP11, and MdZIP13 in the roots and shoots of plants exposed to Zn deficiency was sensitive to increases in Zn concentration (Fig. 5), indicating that the high transcription levels of these four MdZIP genes were responsible for the higher uptake and root-to-shoot translocation of Zn. The phylogenetic analysis revealed that MdZIP14 and MdZIP1 clustered with

AtZIP2 and AtZIP11 (Fig. 2). A previous study reported that AtZIP11 and AtZIP2 might be expressed in the root of A. thaliana (Milner et al. 2013; Olsen and Palmgren 2014). In the present study, Zn deficiency enhanced the expression of MdZIP14 and MdZIP1 in the roots, suggesting that they might be functional orthologs of AtZIP2 and AtZIP11, respectively (Fig. 5a). These results indicated that MdZIP family members respond to $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe deficiency.

Expressing MdZIP10 in Arabidopsis increases its Zn and Fe contents

To evaluate the biological functions of MdZIP genes, MdZIP10 was further analyzed, because it its expression was induced in the roots and shoots of plants under Fe- and Zn-deficient conditions. Previous studies have shown that the overexpression of ZmIRT1, ZmZIP3 and ZmZIP7 increases the accumulation of Zn and Fe in A. thaliana (Li et al. 2015, 2016). In the present study, MdZIP10-overexpressing transgenic plants accumulated more Fe and Zn in their shoots and roots than did the WT plants (Fig. 6a, b). We colored iron in plant tissues according to the Prussian blue reaction. As shown in Fig. 7e, the roots (steles and apical) of MdZIP10-overexpressing transgenic plants were bluer than in the roots of WT plants, and transgenic leaves were bluer than WT leaves (Fig. 6c). Visualization of Zinpyr-1 revealed that fluorescence signals were considerably stronger in the roots (lateral and apical) of transgenic plants than in the roots of WT plants (Fig. 7d–i). In addition, fluorescence intensity was weaker in WT seedlings than in transgenic OX-26 line seedlings (Fig. 7a–c). The stronger the fluorescence intensity, the more zinc was contained (Li et al. 2016). These results showed that MdZIP10 overexpression increased the Zn content of A. thaliana, and enhanced Fe storage in its roots and leaves. Thus, MdZIP10 seems to have a direct role in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in apple.


## Yeast complementation and overexpression of MdZIP10 enhances tolerance to Zn and Fe deficiencies


To determine the metal transport specificities of the MdZIP10, we performed yeast functional complementation experiment for the MdZIP10. The result showed that MdZIP10 grew well on Zn-sufficient and Znlimited mediums (Fig. 8a). Similarly, in the presence of $0 . 0 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ or $0 . 0 2 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ BPDS, the fet3fet4 mutant could be complemented by MdZIP10 (Fig. 8b). These results showed that MdZIP10 were able to complement zrt1zrt2 and fet3fet4 mutant and transport Zn and Fe.

The overexpression of MdZIP10 alleviated Fe and Zn deficiency symptoms, and the roots were considerably longer in transgenic than in WT lines under normal conditions (Fig. 9a–c). However, the roots of both WT and transgenic lines exhibited no significant differences in the expression of MdZIP10 when exposed to excess Zn and Fe (Fig. 9d–f). The overexpression of MpZIP3 has been reported to increase the content of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe in M. polymorpha and alleviate Fe-deficiency symptoms (Lo et al. 2016); moreover, the increased uptake of Fe by roots and transport in response to Fe deficiency and immanently high active Fe content are important mechanisms of tolerating low Fe stress (Zha et al. 2014). Thus,

MdZIP10 transgenic $A$ . thaliana might enhance the uptake and root-to-shoot translocation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe, when the available contents of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe are low.

Changes in the expression of genes related to the uptake and transport Fe and Zn are closely associated with changes in endogenous metal contents and phenotypes of transgenic plants (Li et al. 2015). Under Fe-deficient conditions, the bHLH transcription factor AtFIT exhibits a positive effect on the Fe uptake mechanism of A. thaliana (Lo et al. 2016). Under Zndeficient conditions, the transcription factors bZIP19 and bZIP24 regulate the expression of some ZIP transporters, including ZIP1 in the root of A. thaliana (Assunc¸a˜o et al. 2010; Inaba et al. 2015). Additionally, IRT1 was induced in Fe-deficient roots (Klatte et al. 2009), and HMA2 played important roles in maintaining intracellular metal homeostasis (Hussain et al. 2004). In the present study, the expression of FIT, bZIP19, bZIP24, FRO2, IRT1, HMA2, IRT3, and ZIPs increased under Zn-deficient conditions (Fig. S5). We found that the expression of FIT, bZIP19, bZIP24, FRO2, IRT1, HMA2, IRT3, and ZIPs also increased in MdZIP10-transgenic plants under Fe-deficient conditions (Fig. S6). These results suggest that the upregulation of these genes in the MdZIP10-overexpressing plants might not only facilitate the uptake and transport of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe, but also contribute to the changes observed in root architecture to a certain extent, thus alleviating the symptoms of Zn and Fe deficiencies.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is an essential micronutrient for living organisms including plants and humans playing diverse roles in various cellular processes. In plants zinc exists only as $Z \mathrm { n } ( \mathrm { I I } )$ and does not take part in oxidoreduction reactions (Marschner 1995). The non redox active property of Zn combined with its geometry makes it suitable cofactor for an array of enzymes involved in DNA transcription, protein, nucleic acid, carbohydrate, and lipid metabolism (Broadley et al. 2007; Ishimaru et al. 2011; Palmer and Guerinot 2009). In addition, Zn is critical to the control of gene transcription and the coordination of other biological processes regulated by proteins containing DNA-binding Zn-finger motifs (Rhodes and Klug 1993), RING fingers, and LIM domains (Vallee and Falchuk 1993). Several molecules associated with DNA and RNA synthesis are also Zn metalloenzymes, such as RNA polymerases (Wu et al. 1992), reverse transcriptases, and transcription factors (Wu and Wu 1987). Besides being essential, Zn could be potentially toxic when in excess. Symptoms of Zn toxicity may include inhibition of root elongation and chlorosis in young leaves (Godbold et al. 1983; Marschner 1995; Ruano et al. 1988). Although the mechanisms of Zn toxicity is not completely understood, the possible reasons may include, but not limited to, inappropriate binding to intracellular ligands and competition with other metal ions for enzyme active sites or transporters.

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) provides energy to almost half of the world’s population. Thus, increasing the Zn content of rice has a great potential to mitigate wide spread Zn deficiency problem in humans (Graham et al. 1999; Ruel and Bouis 1998; Welch and Graham 2004). Therefore, it is essential to understand the molecular mechanism through which plants mobilize, take up, translocate, and store Zn. Plants acquire Zn from rhizosphere and the absorbed Zn must be transported into aerial parts as well as to the intracellular compartments of the cell where it is required for the Zn-dependent processes.

In plants, mugineic acid family phytosiderophores (MAs) and nicotianamine (NA), are well characterized for their role in iron (Fe) uptake and homeostasis (Bashir et al. 2010; Mori 1999; Takagi 1976). MAs also play a role in $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and translocation (Suzuki et al. 2006; Suzuki et al. 2008b; Takagi 1976; Welch and Shuman 1995). NA is present in all higher plants, whereas MAs are specifically synthesized in graminaceous plants (Marschner 1995). MAs are synthesized from Methionine (Met) and NA and $2 ^ { \prime }$ -deoxymugineic acid (DMA) share the biosynthetic pathway from LMet (Mori and Nishizawa 1987). NA synthase (NAS)

catalyzes the trimerization of S-adenosyl Met to NA (Higuchi et al. 1994; Higuchi et al. 1999). In graminaceous plants, NA is then converted to a $3 ^ { \prime \prime }$ -keto intermediate through the transfer of an amino group by NA aminotransferase (NAAT; (Kanazawa et al. 1993)). The subsequent reduction of the $3 ^ { \prime \prime }$ -keto group by DMA synthase (DMAS) produces DMA, which is the first species of MAs synthesized in this conserved pathway (Bashir et al. 2006; Bashir and Nishizawa 2006; Shojima et al. 1990). The MAs are then released to rhizosphere through transporter of MAs 1 (TOM1, (Nozoye et al. 2011)) where they bind to metals and the resultant MAs-metal complex is taken up through yellow stripe 1 like (YSL) family transporters (Curie et al. 2001; Inoue et al. 2009; Murata et al. 2006). The expression of genes for MAs biosynthesis changes in diurnal rhythm and MAs are also secreted in diurnal fashion with a peak in the morning to avoid bacterial degradation (Nagasaka et al. 2009; Takagi et al. 1984). The secretion of MAs increases under Zn deficiency in wheat (Triticum spp.) and barley (Hordeum vulgare) (Cakmak et al. 1994; Suzuki et al. 2006; Walter et al. 1994; Zhang et al. 1989). All the genes of DMA biosynthesis pathway have been cloned from rice and barley (Bashir et al. 2006; Bashir et al. 2010; Bashir and Nishizawa 2006; Herbik et al. 1999; Higuchi et al. 1994; Higuchi et al. 1999; Inoue et al. 2003; Inoue et al. 2008; Takahashi et al. 1999). The expression of NASHOR2, a NAS in barley (Herbik et al. 1999), and HvNAAT-B increase under Zn-deficiency in barley shoots (Suzuki et al. 2006). Moreover, the expression of HvNAS1, HvNAAT-A, HvNAAT-B (barley NAATs) increase in Zn- and Fe-deficient roots, while the expression of these genes was not observed in Fe-deficient shoots (Suzuki et al. 2006). It was suggested that $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency induces DMA synthesis in barley shoots, while both $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe deficiency induce MAs synthesis and secretion in barley roots (Ishimaru et al. 2011; Suzuki et al. 2006). Thus NA and DMA are suggested to play a significant role in plant $Z \mathrm { n }$ mobilization. In addition to NA and DMA a series of transporters belonging to different families are also suggested to be involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and translocation in rice.

Several members of the $Z \mathrm { n }$ -regulated transporters and iron (Fe)-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) gene family (Guerinot 2000) have been characterized and shown to be involved in metal uptake and transport in plants (Connolly et al. 2002; Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). The ZIP proteins are predicted to have eight transmembrane domains, with their amino- and carboxyl-terminal ends situated on the outer surface of the plasma membrane (Guerinot 2000). These proteins vary considerably in overall length due to a variable region between the transmembrane domains (TM) TM-3 and TM-4. In rice several ZIPs have been reported e.g. OsIRT1, OsIRT2, OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5, OsZIP7, and OsZIP8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Yang et al. 2009). IRT1 is a key $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in plants with representatives in Arabidopsis (IRT1) and rice (OsIRT1) localized to the plasma membrane and functioning to transport $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from the rhizosphere to root cells (Bughio et al. 2002; Connolly et al. 2002; Conte and Walker 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2005; Ishimaru et al. 2006). The expression of OsIRT1 in rice is regulated by Fe availability and to some extent by Zn deficiency (Ishimaru et al. 2005). The Arabidopsis IRT2 localizes to vesicles within root epidermal cells, while OsIRT2 localizes to the plasma membrane (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Vert et al. 2001). Like IRT1, IRT2 also transports $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and its expression is also regulated by Fedeficiency both in rice and Arabidopsis (Bughio et al. 2002; Connolly et al. 2002; Conte and Walker 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2006). When expressed heterologously in yeast, OsIRT1 does not transport Zn and is mainly involved in Fe transport (Ishimaru et al. 2006). OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are reported to encode rice plasma membrane Zn transporters and are induced by Zn deficiency (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Suzuki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2009).

Although the understanding of Zn uptake and translocation in rice is increasing, the information regarding expression of different $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporters during different developmental stages is scarce. Here we discuss the mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake in rice and expression pattern of ZIP transporters through different developmental stages of rice from root to stem, leaves and reproductive parts. The data regarding expression of OsZIPs through different developmental stages of rice was acquired from the RiceXPro:http://ricexpro. dna.affrc.go.jp/ (Sato et al. 2011a, b). This data was generated by microarray analysis of rice plants (Oryza sativa L. cv. Nipponbare) grown under natural field condition (Sato et al. 2011a, b). The RixeXPro database provides information about expression of genes in different tissue such as root, stem, leaves, anther, ovary, embryo and endosperm through different growth stages. Understanding the expression pattern of these transporters offers a significant advance for manipulating the Zn absorption and translocation to the shoots and ultimately seed and to mitigate the human Zn deficiency problem.


## Expression of Zn transporters during germination


The germination of rice seed is governed by various factors such as temperature, light, water, and hormonal signaling. During this process nutrients are directed to the developing tissue like roots and shoots. The first source of nutrients for the germinating rice seed are the ones stored in grain itself during seed development. In mature rice seed, Zn is unevenly distributed to all of parts of the seed, with a significantly high value for the aleurone layer and embryo (Takahashi et al. 2009). Rice seeds contain not only Zn but also NA and DMA (Masuda et al. 2009; Usuda et al. 2009), and during germination, NA, DMA and Zn are mobilized (Takahashi et al. 2009). During germination, Zn flow is quite dynamic compared to Fe, Mn and $\mathrm { C u }$ and the $Z \mathrm { n }$ stored in the endosperm is transported to the embryo resulting in a high Zn localization in the radicle and leaf primordium (Takahashi et al. 2009). As the germination further proceeds, localization of $Z \mathrm { n }$ increases in the scutellum and the vascular bundle of the scutellum. This localization of Zn matches to Fe localization to some extent (Bashir et al. 2010; Ishimaru et al. 2011; Takahashi et al. 2009). In rice seeds the expression of ZIP family members decrease or remain unchanged during germination (Nozoye et al. 2007). In particular the expression of OsZIP4 and OsZIP7 significantly decrease during germination. In meristematic tissue Zn localizes to the embryo and a decrease in OsZIP family transcripts might be necessary for this type of partial localization of $Z \mathrm { n }$ (Nozoye et al. 2007; Takahashi et al. 2009).


## Zn uptake through root


In barley, Zn-DMA is preferred over $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ for uptake through roots (Suzuki et al. 2006). In contrast rice plants absorb, less $Z \mathrm { n }$ -DMA compared to $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Suzuki et al. 2008b). Similarly the secretion of mugineic acids (MAs)

increases in Zn deficient barley, while it decreases in rice (Suzuki et al. 2006; Suzuki et al. 2008b). Despite this, $Z \mathrm { n }$ -DMA is suggested to be the preferred form for the long distance transport in rice (Suzuki et al. 2008b). Difference in secretion of DMA is suggested to increase tolerance in rice (Widodo et al. 2010). Recently a modeling study also proposed a strong correlation between DMA secretion and rooting density, and suggested a role of DMA for Zn absorption in rice (Ptashnyk et al. 2011). The data revealed by microarray analysis through different growth stages of rice grown under natural filed conditions was utilized to check the expression of DMA biosynthesis related genes in root ((RiceXPro;http://ricexpro.dna. affrc.go.jp/ (Sato et al. 2011a, b)). The expression of OsNAS1 increased from 27 days after transplantation (DAT) to 76 DAT and decreased at 27 and 76 DAT during noon while opposite trend is reported for samples collected at midnight (Fig. 1). Expression of OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 was higher during noon compared to midnight at 27 DAT, however the expression was is not regulated diurnally at 76 DAT (Fig. 1). The expression of OsNAAT1 increased from 27 DAT to 76 DAT, while the expression of OsDMAS1 did not changed from 27 to 76 DAT. The DMA biosynthesis genes are up-regulated by Fe deficiency (Bashir et al. 2006; Inoue et al. 2003; Inoue et al. 2008) and the expression of DMA biosynthesis genes is reported to be regulated in a clear diurnal fashion in barley, however in rice these genes are not regulated in a clear diurnal fashion ((Nagasaka et al. 2009; Negishi et al. 2002; Nozoye et al. 2004). Among the OsZIP genes, OsIRT1, OsIRT2, OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are expressed in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Sato et al. 2011b; Yang et al. 2009). Microarray analysis (Suzuki et al. 2012) revealed that among the ZIP family genes OsZIP4, OsZIP5, and $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ are upregulated by Zn deficiency in roots and shoots, while the expression of OsZIP7 is upregulated only in shoots. OsZIP1, OsZIP3, and OsZIP4 are expressed in the vascular bundles and epidermal cells in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a; Ramesh et al. 2003; Yang et al. 2009). Expression of OsZIP1 is induced in roots 24 to $9 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ after Zn deficiency treatment. Under Zn deficiency, the OsZIP2, and OsZIP3 transcripts are visible in roots (Ramesh et al. 2003). While in plants subjected to Zn deficiency for two weeks the expression of OsZIP1-3 is not upregulated by Zn deficiency (Suzuki et al. 2012). The expression of OsZIP4 is also induced by Zn deficiency in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Suzuki et al. 2012). In Zn-deficient rice, OsZIP4 is expressed in the root apical meristem and vascular bundles of Zn-deficient roots especially in the phloem cells (Ishimaru et al.

2007; Ishimaru et al. 2005). The OsZIP genes are not regulated by diurnal rhythm in root tissue (Fig. 1). The expression of OsZIP1 and OsZIP5 decreases from 27 DAT to 76 DAT. On the other hand the expression of OsZIP8 significantly increased from 27 DAI to 76 DAT. The expression of OsZIP4 does not change significantly with time. The data obtained by microarray analysis of root samples prepared by laser micro dissection reveals that The OsZIP genes are expressed in different parts of the root tissue (RiceXPro;http://ricexpro.dna.affrc.go. jp/). OsZIP5, OsZIP7 and OsZIP8 were expressed in the root sections consisting of epidermis, exodermis and sclerenchyma (Fig. 2). OsZIP4 mainly expresses in the vascular tissue (Ishimaru et al. 2005). OsZIP1 and OsZIP3 are suggested to be involved in Zn uptake from rhizosphere (Lee et al. 2010a; Ramesh et al. 2003), while OsZIP4 and OsZIP5 are suggested to be involved in phloem Zn transport (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Ishimaru et al. 2005; Lee et al. 2010a). Although the role of DMA in Zn uptake from root has been discussed, the transporter involved in Zn-DMA uptake in rice has not been characterized yet. The yellow stripe 1 (ys1) gene was first identified in maize and was shown to be critical for the uptake of Fe(III)-MAs (Curie et al. 2001). ZmYS1 transports MAs-bound metals, including Zn, Cu, and nickel (Murata et al. 2006; Schaaf et al. 2004)), while there is controversy if $Z { \mathrm { m Y S 1 } }$ transports $Z \mathrm { n }$ -MAs ((Roberts et al. 2004). In rice 18 YSL homologs are reported which exhibit $3 6 - 7 6 \%$ sequence similarity to maize YS1 (Koike et al. 2004). Among these, OsYSL2 expresses specifically in the phloem and transports $\mathrm { F e ( I I ) }$ -NA and $\mathrm { M n } ( \mathrm { I I } )$ -NA, suggesting that. OsYSL2 is a $\mathrm { { M n } ( I I ) }$ - and Fe (II)-NA transporter responsible for phloem transport of metals. OsYSL15 and OsYSL18 transports Fe(III)- DMA (Aoyama et al. 2009; Inoue et al. 2009).

In addition to the upregulation of several genes involved in Zn uptake, recently the upregulation of genes involved in starch synthesis and transport and accumulation of starch in Zn deficient plants has also been reported (Suzuki et al. 2012). These results suggest that starch accumulation may also be helpful to mitigate Zn deficiency.


## Zn transport in stem


In the stem, OsZIP3 expresses in the vascular bundles and epidermal cells (Ramesh et al. 2003), While OsZIP4 expresses mainly in the phloem (Ishimaru et al. 2005). OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are also expressed in stem at 83 and 90 DAT (Fig. 3). The expression of OsZIPI and OsZIP5 decreases from 83 DAT to $9 0 \mathrm { D A T }$ and the expression of OsZIP3 and OsZIP8 increases, while the expression of OsZIP4 remain unchanged (Fig. 3). Recently, it was reported that in rice phloem sap Zn predominantly exists as Zn-NA (Nishiyama et al. 2012). The expression of OsNAS1-3, OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 is not significantly regulated in diurnal rhythm. The expression of OsNAS3 decreases from 83 to $9 0 \ \mathrm { D A T }$ , while the expression of OsDMAS1 increased from 83 to 90 DAT (Fig. 3). As OsZIP proteins do not transport ZnNA complex, it is possible that rice YSL (OsYSL) family is involved in this transport of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ . Although, a Zn-NA transporter or Zn-DMA transporter involved in Zn translocation has not been identified in rice plants yet, the existence of Zn-NA complexes in rice phloem sap (Nishiyama et al. 2012) suggests that YSLs could be involved in the transport of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ or Zn-DMA in rice.


## Zn transport in rice leaves


In rice leaves, the expression of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 as well as the amount of endogenous DMA increase in shoots of Zn deficient rice (Suzuki et al. 2008b). As the expression of OsNAAT1 dramatically increases in $Z \mathrm { n }$ -deficient shoots, the amount of endogenous NA in shoots reduces remarkably by $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency. Furthermore, positron-emitting tracer imaging system (PETIS) experiment demonstrated that more $Z \mathrm { n }$ is translocated to the newest leaf when $^ { 6 2 } \mathrm { Z n - D M A }$ is supplied compared to the conditions when $^ { 6 2 } \mathrm { Z n }$ is supplied. At the bottom of the leaf sheath an opposite trend was observed, (Suzuki et al. 2008b), suggesting that Zn-DMA is the preferred form for long-distance transport of Zn in Zn-deficient rice. The expression of NA and DMA biosynthesis related genes changes significantly in leaves from 27 to $1 2 5 \mathrm { \ D A T }$ through 76 DAT (Fig. 4). In leaf blade, the expression of OsNAS3 is higher compared to OsNAS1 and OsNAS2 ((Fig. 4 & (Inoue et al. 2003)). The expression of OsDMAS1 was high at midnight compared to the expression at noon and increased from 27 to 76 DAT and then decreased slightly at 124 DAT particularly at noon. It clearly suggests a role of DMA for Zn transport in leaves. As Zn predominantly exists as Zn-NA in phloem sap (Nishiyama et al. 2012), the role of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ and OsYSLs in leaf $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport and mobilization seems to be very important.

OsZIP1 expresses in the vascular bundle of leaves. In leaves, OsZIP4 expresses in all parts of vascular bundles and mesophyll cells of Zn deficient plants (Ishimaru et al. 2005). Strong expression of OsZIP4 could also be observed in shoot meristem. The expression of ZIPs changes significantly in rice leaf blade from 27 to 76 and 125 DAT (Fig. 3). The expression of OsZIP1 significantly increases from 27 to 76 DAT and then slightly decreases at 125 DAT. Expression of OsZIP3 and OsZIP4 do not change significantly from 27 to 76 and 125 DAT. The expression of OsZIP4 is comparatively high during noon compared to midnight at 27, 76 and $1 2 5 \mathrm { \ D A T }$ . The expression of OsZIP5 was low at 27 DAT, then increases at 76 DAT during midnight and then decreases to a level comparable to 27 DAT during midnight. During noon it increases slowly from 27 DAT to 125 DAT. Significant diurnal rhythm was observed for OsZIP8. The expression of $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ was high during noon compared to midnight at 76 and 125 DAT. These changes in expression indicate that these genes could play an important role in Zn transport during the growth cycle of rice. In leaves, the expression of $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ is high compared to other ZIP transporters. The expression of OsZIPs in rice leaves and changes in the expression of these genes with developmental stages indicate their role in Zn translocation in leaf tissue. We suggest that OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are important for $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport in leaves.


## Expression of ZIP transporters during flowering and seed development


The DMA biosynthesis genes are expressed during flowering and seed development and are expressed in anther, ovary, embryo and endosperm (Figs. 5–8). In Ovary the expression of OsNAS1 decreased from 1 to 3 days after flowering (DAF) and then increased at 5 and 7 DAF (Fig. 6). The expression pattern of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 increased from 1 to 5 DAF, and then the expression of OsNAS3 decreased, while the expression of OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 did not changed significantly. In embryo, the expression of OsNAS1 decreased from 7 to 28 DAF, while the expression of OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 remain unchanged (Fig. 7). The expression of OsNAAT1 decreased slowly from 7 to 42 DAF, while expression of OsDMAS1 decreased from 7 to 10 DAF and then increased from 14 to 28 DAF. Slight changes for the expression of these genes were also observed in endosperm (Fig. 8). The information about the expression of OsZIP genes during different stages of flowering and seed development is scarce. OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 express in the anther. The expression of OsZIP3 varies significantly from $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ from base of anther to $1 . 2 \mathrm { - } 1 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ from base (Fig. 5). The expression of OsZIP5 is slightly higher at the bottom of anther compared to the top.

In ovary, the expression of OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 changes significantly. The expression of OsZIP3 varies significantly from 3 DAF to 5 DAF (Fig. 6). The expression of OsZIP4 and OsZIP8 is higher compared to OsZIPI and OsZIP3. The expression of OsZIP5 increases from 1 to 3 DAF and then decreases at 5 and 7 DAF. In embryo, the expression of OsZIP4 is significantly high compared to other OsZIPs (Fig. 7). The expression of OsZIPI , OsZIP3, OsZIP4, and OsZIP5 increases slowly from 7 to 42 DAF (Fig. 8). OsZIPs also express in endosperm. Again the expression of OsZIP4 is significantly high compared to other OsZIPs (Fig. 8). The expression of OsZIP4 increases slowly from 7 to 28 DAF and then decreases slightly. The expression of OsZIP5 decrease slowly from 7 to 42 DAF. As OsZIPs are expressed during all the flowering and seed developmental stages, it is reasonable to conclude that these genes play an important role in $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport to developing seed. The role of OsZIP4 seems particularly important in transporting the Zn to the developing seed.


## Increasing the seed Zn concentration


Zn deficiency is serious nutritional problem for humans and is particularly prevalent among children and pregnant women, especially in developing countries (World Health Organization 2002). The uptake of Zn depends on various factors including soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ concentration which is often low in soils (Cakmak 2008; Cakmak et al. 1999). The concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in rice seeds ranges from 8.9– $9 5 ~ { \mu \mathrm { g } } / \mathrm { g }$ dry weight (Yang et al. 1998) or $0 . 4 7 \mathrm { - } 0 . 7 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }$ per seed (Wissuwa et al. 2006). In another report the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in seeds was reported from 15.9– $5 8 . 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / g }$ dry weight (Graham et al. 1999) and depends upon external $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply and soil conditions (Wissuwa et al. 2008; Wissuwa et al. 2006). Increasing the Zn content and bioavailability of cereals such as rice seeds is an important target for breeders and offers the potential benefits to a large proportion of human population (Cakmak 2008; Palmgren et al. 2008; Zhu et al. 2007). Different strategies such as plant breeding, foliar or soil application of $Z \mathrm { n }$ fertilizers has been suggested and demonstrated to increase the Zn content of cereals (Cakmak 2008; Cakmak et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2012). Foliar application of Zn is shown to increase the Zn content of cereal up to two times (Cakmak et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2012). It is obvious that various Zn transporters transport this Zn to the developing seeds; however the detailed role of these transporters has to be characterized yet. Moreover, various transgenic approaches have been adopted to increase the Zn content of rice grains. The most common approach used by different research groups is to increase the expression of NAS genes. Rice lines expressing HvNAS1 under the control of CaMV35S or Actin1 promoter accumulate more Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ in seeds suggesting that NA overproduction have the potential to increase the Fe and Zn translocation to rice grains (Masuda et al. 2009). Increasing the expression of OsNAS2, through activation tagging, increased the expression of DMA biosynthetic pathway genes as well as genes related to Zn-uptake (Lee et al. 2011). Thus increasing the amount of NA increases DMA secretion from roots and stimulates Zn uptake and translocation to seed. Moreover, the enhanced NA and DMA in endosperm increased the content of bio-available Zn as revealed by feeding trials in mice (Lee et al. 2011). Increasing the expression of OsNAS3 through activation tagging also increases the Fe and Zn content of rice seeds (Lee et al. 2009). Similarly rice plants over expressing OsNAS1, OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 accumulated more Fe and Zn in the seed indicating that NA is important for Fe and Zn transport and could be successfully deployed for bio-fortification of Zn (Johnson et al. 2011). The overexpression of OsNAS1 not only increases the concentration of Zn in rice seeds but also increases its bio-availability (Zheng et al. 2010). Overexpression of barley dioxygenase gene, IDS3, involved in the biosynthesis of MAs also increased the rice seed Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ concentration (Masuda et al. 2008; Nakanishi et al. 2000; Suzuki et al. 2008a).

On the other hand regulating the expression of ZIPs to increase the seed Zn content was not successful. Transgenic rice plants over-expressing OsZIP4 under the control of the CaMV35S promoter accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots while the shoot Zn contents decreased significantly (Ishimaru et al. 2007). Similarly OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 overexpression rice also accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots at the expense of shoot Zn (Lee et al. 2010a). The OsZIP5 overexpression rice lines were sensitive to $Z \mathrm { n }$ excess, while the oszip5 knock out plants were tolerant to $Z \mathrm { n }$ excess (Lee et al. 2010a). Rice sucrose promoter (OsSUT1), is highly expressed in the mature phloem of all the vegetative tissues involved in the long-distance assimilate transport pathway during grain filling, in addition to the flag leaf blade and sheath prior to heading (Hirose et al. 2002; Scofield et al. 2007). The expression of OsYSL2 when controlled by the sucrose transporter promoter increased the Fe concentration in polished rice up to 4.4-fold compared to WT (Ishimaru et al. 2010). These results suggest that the controlling the temporal and spatial expression of OsZIP genes could be effective to increase the $Z \mathrm { n }$ in rice seeds.

In this study, we demonstrated that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 are involved in the uptake and translocation of metal ions in plants, and our results suggested that they might be associated with metal homeostasis by regulating the expression of genes involved in metal uptake and transportation.

It was reported that transgenic plants overexpressing OsIRT1 exhibited less chlorosis and had higher chlorophyll content than the wild-type under Fe-deficient conditions. Moreover, the Fe content was also increased in mature seeds of OsIRT1 overexpression plants [25]. In addition, overexpression of MxIRT1 enhanced Fe and Zn contents in rice seeds [41]. Likewise, overexpression of AtZIP1 in barley lead to an elevated level in the short-term Zn uptake, and enhanced Zn and Fe contents in seeds [24]. However, overexpression of OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 in rice leads to increased Zn levels in roots, although the Zn content was reduced in shoots and mature seeds of overexpression lines [29, 42]. These data suggested that the metal transportation activity of ZIP proteins may differ, or ectopic accumulation of ZIPs may disrupt the endogenous metal homeostasis due to incongruous in vivo ion transporter gradients. It was found that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 showed strongly and relatively weaker reverse the yeast complement activity. Moreover, the expression of ZmIRT1 was significantly upregulated in roots and shoots under Fe-deficiency, and it was induced in shoots at $9 6 \mathrm { { h } }$ after $\mathrm { Z n }$ -deficiency. These results suggested that ZmIRT1 might be essential for both uptake and translocation of Fe and Zn. On the contrary, ZmZIP3 was induced by Zn deficiency, indicating that ZmZIP3 may be important for Zn uptake [28]. In this study, we examined the expression pattern of ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 in various organs. ZmIRT1 was predominantly expressed in silk and embryo, while ZmZIP3 is a leaf-specific gene. The different expression pattern of ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 indicated that they might play distinct roles in metal uptake and translocation. To analyse the physiological roles of the ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 in plants, we generated transgenic Arabidopsis and examined whether ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 could transport Zn or Fe in plants. It was found that overexpression of ZmIRT1 in Arabidopsis enhanced Fe and Zn contents in both roots and seeds (Fig 4A and 4E), suggesting that ZmIRT1 is a functional Fe and Zn transporter, and it may be associated with the translocation of metals toward seeds. Additionally, we found that ZmIRT1-overexpressing plants grew longer roots than the wild-type under Zn- and Fe-excess conditions (Fig 2E and 2G), which indicates that the transgenic plants are more tolerant to excess zinc and iron. ZmIRT1 is localized to the plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum in maize (S1 Fig) and Arabidopsis mesophyll protoplasts [28]. Therefore, ZmIRT1 may function in translocating excess subcellular free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ into the endoplasmic reticulum. Moreover, ZmIRT1 may play an essential role in storage and detoxification of Zn and Fe. On the contrary, ZmZIP3-overexpression plants developed more lateral roots and longer roots than wild-type under Fe-deficient conditions (Fig 3F), indicative of a stronger Fe deficiency

It is noteworthy that the growth of ZmZIP3 transgenic plants was better than the wild-type, despite the Fe-deficiency response in roots (Fig 3F). This is probably because over-accumulation of ZmZIP3 facilitated the uptake of Zn in the roots, which alleviated the symptoms of Fe deficiency.
