Besides the morphological changes, the expression of many genes associated with Fe/Zn deficiency and excess responses were also altered in the ZmIRT1- and ZmZIP3-overexpressing plants. It was reported that the expression profiles of genes associated with Fe and Zn uptake and translocation were regulated in accordance with the internal and environmental metal conditions. OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 encode enzymes for the biosynthesis of NA and $2 ^ { \circ }$ -deoxymugineic acid (DMA), which plays important roles in chelating and distributing metal ions within plants. The expression of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 are enhanced in the overexpression lines under $\mathrm { Z n }$ -deficient conditions [29]. In addition, the activation of OsNAS3 resulted in increased Zn and Fe contents in rice grains, suggesting that OsNAS3 contributes to ion homeostasis [43]. In our study, the transcription levels of genes associated with $\mathrm { Z n / F e }$ uptake and transportation may reflect the endogenous metal status; thus, we investigated the expression of 12 Arabidopsis genes known to be involved in the homeostasis of Zn and Fe (Fig 7). The results showed that the expressions of genes involved in the uptake of Fe and Zn were altered in both ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 transgenic lines. The transcript levels of AtNAS1, 2, which are associated with NA synthesis, AtFRO2 that plays a role in ferric reduction, and AtIRT1 that is related to ferrous uptake were up-regulated in ZmIRT1-overexpressing plants (Fig 7). The enhanced expression of these genes may be due to the root absorbed too much iron that stimulated the expression of NAS, FRO and IRT1, which associated with iron uptake. In contrast, AtFRO2 and AtIRT1 were reduced in the ZmZIP3 transgenic lines (Fig 8), possibly due to the iron content was decreased so suppressed the expression of these genes. These results suggest that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 play different roles in metal homeostasis. The stimulation of these genes in ZmIRT1-overexpressing lines may be due to the increased expression of transcription factors that regulate ion homeostasis. It has been demonstrated that Fe homeostasis is controlled by conserved transcriptional networks in both grasses and non-grasses [44, 45]. Under Fe-deficiency, FIT (FER-like iron-deficiency-induced transcription factor) interacts with bHLH038 and bHLH039 to regulate the expression of IRT1 and FRO2 in Arabidopsis [37]. It was also reported that FIT, IRT1, FRO2, and BHLH100 are iron deficiency induced genes in roots [15]. Although there are no orthologs of FIT in rice, OsIRO2 is a regulator of the Fe deficiency-responsive gene, which is highly similar to bHLH38/39. OsIRO2 regulates the expression of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS translocation-related genes, with the exception of OsIRT1 [46]. Co-overexpression of FIT and bHLH38 or bHLH39 results in increased expression of NAS1 and NAS2, which enhanced NA accumulation and increased transport of Fe from roots to shoots [47]. We found that the expression of FIT was stimulated in the ZmIRT1 transgenic plants, indicating that a transcriptional cascade was activated as a result of ectopic accumulation of ZmIRT1. Besides, pleiotropic effects may also contribute to the activation of gene expression since a greater quantity of Fe and Zn was absorbed into the cytoplasm when ZmIRT1 was overexpressed. The expression of NRAMPs, YSLs, and endogenous ZIPs were suppressed in both ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 lines (Figs 7 and 8), suggesting that over-accumulation of ZIP proteins may inhibit the expression of endogenous genes that function in metal transportation. Taking this into consideration, our results suggested that overexpressing ZmIRT1 may facilitate Zn and Fe uptake by inducing genes associated with strategy I (ferric reduction and ferrous uptake) and strategy II (ion-chelator synthesis) iron uptake systems, although the expression of genes involved in intercellular ion transportation was suppressed.

Fe uptake mechanisms were classified into two strategies. Strategy I, a reduction-based strategy, is used by non-grasses such as Arabidopsis [44, 45]. It begins with acidification of the rhizosphere and increases the solubility of ferric in the soil [48–50]. The reduction of ferric irons then occurs on the membrane by a membrane-bound ferric-chelate reductase AtFRO2, and ferrous is taken into root epidermal cells by transmembrane transporters, such as AtIRT1 [21, 22]. On the contrary, strategy II, a chelation-based strategy is used by grasses such as barley, rice, and maize. Phytosiderophores are released into the rhizosphere to chelate ferric [51], and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS can be absorbed into root cells by YSLs [52, 53]. The main distinction between these two strategies is different oxidation and reduction forms of iron absorbed into the root cells, as non-grasses prefer ferrous and grasses absorb ferric. It is generally considered that the iron uptake mechanisms used by these two strategies do not overlap. The identification of two functional $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters, OsIRT1 and OsIRT2, indicates that strategy I may be used by

graminaceous plants [54, 55]. It was proposed that rice uses a combined strategy including strategy II and partial strategy I to uptake Fe from the soil. TOM1/OsZIFL4 and OsYSL15 were reported to be involved in the release of PS and uptake of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS as strategy II, while OsIRT1 translocated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ into root cells through strategy I. However, the genes responsible for acidification and ferric reduction seemed to be lost in the rice genome [54, 56, 57]. As a graminaceous plant, maize was considered to apply strategy II for Fe uptake. However, ZmIRT1 was identified as a functional $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in yeast and transgenic Arabidopsis. ZmIRT1 overexpression plants contain increased amounts of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe in roots and seeds (Fig 4A and 4E), as well as elevated Zn levels in seedlings (Figs 5 and 6). In addition, ZmZIP3-overexpressing transgenic plants accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots. These results indicated that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 are functional ion transporters. Moreover, we identified putative FRO and AHA genes in the maize genome (data not shown) using the reported AtFRO and AtAHA ( $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase) as TBLASTN queries, and suggested that the ferric reducing and rhizosphere acidification capacities may be retained through evolution. Thus, further investigations are required to determine whether maize use strategy I as a complementary Fe uptake mechanism, and determine why it has been maintained during evolution.

It was previously reported that although AtIRT1 was expressed constitutively in 35S-IRT1 transgenic plants, the protein was present only in iron-limited roots. This result suggested that the accumulation of IRT1 is influenced by post-transcriptional regulation [58]. It was also reported that post-transcriptional regulation did not play a significant role in OsIRT1 overexpression rice, as both OsIRT1 and metals were accumulated under metal-sufficient conditions and the transgenic plants showed visible morphological changes when grown under standard conditions [25]. In this study, the ZmIRT1-overexpressing Arabidopsis exhibited increased levels of zinc and iron in different tissues, and the transgenic plants showed an enhanced resistance against excess-iron and zinc. These results indicated that ZmIRT1 might escape posttranscriptional control because ZmIRT1 is highly homologous with OsIRT1 $7 3 . 0 4 \%$ identity) and they share low sequence similarity with AtIRT1 $5 0 . 9 2 \%$ identity for ZmIRT1 and $4 8 . 9 3 \%$ identity for OsIRT1, respectively).

The contamination of agricultural soils with heavy metals, including cadmium (Cd), zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , manganese (Mn), and arsenic (As), poses a serious threat to global food safety and human health (Zhao and Wang 2020; Li et al. 2024). Among these heavy metals, Cd is particularly alarming due to its high toxicity, persistence and mobility through the food chain. While Zn, though an essential micronutrient, can become phytotoxic at elevated concentrations (Kaur et al. 2021). Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms governing metal uptake, transport, and accumulation in plants is essential for both complementary goals: mitigating the accumulation of toxic metals in edible crops while ensuring adequate acquisition of essential elements and enhancing the phytoremediation potential of metal-accumulating species (Zhao et al. 2022).

Transmembrane transporters are fundamental to metal homeostasis in plants, the Zn-regulated transporters and iron-regulated transporter-like Proteins (ZRT/IRT-like Proteins, ZIPs), and Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs) families being particularly prominent (Tang et al. 2023). In rice, OsNRAMP5 has been identifed as a major transporter for Cd and Mn uptake (Chang et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2025), while the plasma membrane-localized OsZIP5 and OsZIP9 function synergistically to facilitate Zn and Cd absorption (Tan et al. 2020). Recent studies in Arabidopsis thaliana have further elucidated that several ZIP family members, including AtZIP2, AtZIP3, AtZIP5, and AtZIP8, are predominantly localized to the plasma membrane of root epidermal and cortical cells where they perform redundant yet crucial functions in metal acquisition from the soil environment (Ochoa et al. 2025; Robe et al. 2025).

Notably, the functional roles of ZIP1 orthologs vary considerably across plant species. Early work in rice proposed that OsZIP1 was involved in Zn and Cd uptake under Zndefcient conditions or Cd exposure (Ramesh et al. 2003). While a more recent study re-characterized it as a metal exporter localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane, which reduces cellular Cd and Zn accumulation when overexpressed (Liu et al. 2019). In contrast, Arabidopsis AtZIP1 localizes to both the vacuolar membrane and complements Zn uptake in yeast mutants, indicating its role in intracellular Zn transport (Milner et al. 2013). These functional divergences highlight the importance of characterizing ZIP1 transporter within their specifc plant systems to elucidate their distinct physiological roles.

Brassica juncea, a widely cultivated oilseed and vegetable crop, exhibits a remarkable capacity to accumulate heavy metals, making it as a promising candidate species for phytoremediation applications (Du et al. 2020; Kang et al. 2021; Zeremski et al. 2021). Despite its potential, the specifc transporters responsible for metal uptake in B. juncea remain largely uncharacterized. Our previous transcriptomic analysis revealed that BjZIP1 expression is strongly induced under Cd stress (Zhang et al. 2021); yet, its transport function and subcellular localization have not been experimentally validated. In this study, we functionally characterized BjZIP1 through heterologous expression in yeast, overexpression in A. thaliana, and the B. juncea hairy root transformation system. We demonstrate that BjZIP1 localizes to the plasma membrane and mediates Cd and Zn uptake, thereby contributing to metal accumulation and sensitivity. These fndings highlight BjZIP1 as a key component of metal uptake in $B$ . juncea and a potential molecular target for optimizing phytoremediation efciency.

ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter, Iron-regulated transporter-like Protein, ZIP) plays an important role in uptake or transport Zn or Fe in plants. So studying ZIPs in plant can help to elucidate the molecular mechanism for Zn and Fe transportation. Herein, we have cloned a novel Zn transporter gene NoZIP3 from Nasturtium officinale root using rapid-amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) method, evaluated its function by functional complementation assay and determined its relative transcriptional level by quantitative real-time Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (qRT-PCR). The results showed that the full-length cDNA of NoZIP3 was 1029 bp, which encoded a polypeptide of 342 amino acids with a conserved domain of the typical ZIPs. NoZIP3 sequence shared a high similarity $( 5 7 - 8 9 \% )$ with that of other plant species. NoZIP3 could complement a mutant yeast deficient in Zn transportation; however, it could not complement that of Fe transportation. qRT-PCR revealed that the transcriptional level of NoZIP3 in roots was much higher than that in leaves under Zn deficiency, Fe deficiency or sufficient nutrition. These results suggested that NoZIP3 might be preferentially expressed in roots and had roles in Zn transportation, which could provide the foundation for further studying the characteristics and function of this gene.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ are essential micronutrients that participate in physiological and biochemical processes and promote plant growth and development. $Z \mathrm { n }$ is involved in the synthesis of numerous enzymes, such as alcohol dehydrogenase, copper $( \mathrm { C u } ) – \mathrm { Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, and RNA polymerase. Therefore, Zn deficiency decreases the activity of these enzymes (Hacisalihoglu and Kochian 2003). Recently,

Fe has been used as a cofactor for integrating photosynthesis with various metabolic pathways and regulating gene expression (Imsande 2010). Fe deficiency can affect the growth and yield of fruit trees and other crops, and it affects photosynthesis rate, chlorophyll content, and catalase activity (Fornerginer et al. 2010; Rube´n et al. 2011).

The continuous discovery of metal ion transporters has laid the foundation for studies on factors involved in the absorption, intracellular transport, localization, and efflux of metal ions, such as P1B-type heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family, Zn- and Fe-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) family, normal resistancerelated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and the cation dissemination facilitator (CDF) family (Milner et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2017; Vigani et al. 2013). AtIRT1 was the first ZIP gene identified which is located on the root surface and induced by Fe deficiency in the root of Arabidopsis thaliana L. (Henriques et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a homolog of IRT1, plays a similarly crucial role in A. thaliana. However, under similar Fedeficient conditions, the expression of IRT2 is significantly lower than that of IRT1 (Vert et al. 2001). Their homolog IRT3, which is located in the plasma membrane, increases the uptake of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe to complement the function of both $\mathrm { Z n - }$ and Fe-uptake mutants (Lin et al. 2009). Complementation mutants or knockdown of ZIP1 and ZIP2 in A. thaliana showed that ZIP1 and ZIP2 are involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Mn uptake (Milner et al. 2013). In addition, functional analyses in maize (Zea mays L.) and rice indicated that ZIP3, ZIP4, ZIP5, and ZIP8 play important roles in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in the roots and shoots under Zn-deficient conditions (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, b). In A. thaliana, the function of ZIP9 is similar to that of ZIP12, being induced under $Z \mathbf { n }$ -limiting conditions (Talke et al. 2006; Wintz et al. 2003).

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.

This family was first identified in plants, taking its name from the founding members as “ZRT, IRT-like protein” [8]. ZRT1 and ZRT2 are the high- and low-affinity zinc-regulated transporters of yeast [9, 10], respectively. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter) is an Arabidopsis transporter expressed in the roots of iron-deficient plants [11]. This family is widely distributed in all organisms, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, animals [12], and plants. A considerably large family of ZIP genes has been currently characterized from various species, such as Arabidopsis [8, 11, 13], rice (Oryza sativa L.) [1, 7], soybean (Glycine max (Linn.) Merr.) [5], Medicago truncatula [6, 14], the hyperaccumulation plant Thlaspi caerulescens [4, 15], Th. japonicum [16], etc.

In recent years, much progress has been made towards understanding molecular mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$

Functional analysis indicated that members of the ZIP gene family play a prominent role in the cytosolic zinc import, transporting this nutrient from outside the cell [4] or within an intracellular compartment [12];

they can transport a variety of divalent cations, including $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ [3, 17] and differ in their substrate range and specificity [17]. The expression of these genes was detected in various tissues, including roots, shoots, nodules, and flowers, and it seems likely that these genes were transcriptionally regulated by metal levels [1, 7, 13]. The proteins encoded by ZIP genes are predicted to have eight transmembrane domains (TM) with the amino- and carboxyl-terminal ends located on the outer surface of the plasma membrane [3]. Their overall length varies considerably due to a variable region between TM-3 and TM-4 containing a potential histidine-rich metal-binding domain. The most conserved region of these proteins occurs in TM-4 that is predicted to form an $\alpha$ -helix with a fully conserved histidine residue [17]. The transport function is eliminated when the conserved residues are replaced by mutation [18].

Rice, a species sensitive to zinc deficiency and a model plant for grasses, is the most important food crop in the world, feeding over half of the global population. However, rice yield is often limited by the low levels of soil Zn, especially in calcareous soils of arid and semiarid regions [19]. There is significant genetic variation both within and between plant varieties in their ability to maintain significant growth and yield under conditions of Zn deficiency [20]. In recent years, research has been carried out in several laboratories to elucidate the physiological mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficiency in plants; however, these mechanisms are still poorly understood [21]. An accurate map-based blueprint for all chromosomes and two shotgun sequences of rice genome have been published in the last three years, which provide an encouraging opportunity to study the interplay between various gene family members in a single organism [21]. Although several ZIP genes have been identified and functionally characterized at the molecular level [1, 7], the complete gene family and their role in metal homeostasis is not fully understood. To investigate new Zn transporters and Zn transporters probably associated with the Zn efficiency in rice, we exploited the current bioinformatics resources with the aim of achieving a comprehensive characterization of the ZIP family. We also studied the expression patterns of OsZIP1, OsZIP3, and OsZIP4 , which have been established as $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters in rice [1, 7], in different parts of $Z \mathrm { n }$ -efficient and Zn-inefficient rice genotypes (IR8192 and Erjiufeng) grown under different $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activity conditions. Our results suggest that the ZIP gene expression may partly explain the differences in zinc efficiency between IR8192 and Erjiufeng.

Te zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ -regulated/iron(Fe)-regulated transporterlike family proteins (ZIPs) are membrane-located proteins for cations transport (Eng et  al. 1998; Guerinot 2000). Tey have been found to exist broadly in prokaryotic cells, fungi, plants and mammalians. In plants, ZIPs have been identifed in both dicots and monocots, such as Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998; Milner et  al. 2013), rice (Chen et  al. 2008), maize (Li et  al. 2013), medicago (Lopez-Millan et al. 2004; Stephens et al. 2011) and barely (Tiong et al. 2015). Grotz et al. identifed fve ZIP genes (IRT1, ZIP1-4) in Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998), and later up to 11 ZIP genes from Arabidopsis were detected bioinformatically (Guerinot 2000). Roles of ZIP1-12 from Arabidopsis in Zn transport were explored experimentally (Milner et  al. 2013). More recently, 18 ZIPs from Arabidopsis and 16 ZIPs from rice were annotated (Ivanov and Bauer 2017).

In Arabidopsis and rice, only a small number of ZIPs have been examined for biological functions in plant till now. Arabidopsis IRT1 is a well-studied ZIP gene frst identifed as a crucial transporter for plant Fe uptake (Varotto et  al. 2002; Vert et  al. 2002). Arabidopsis IRT1 can be induced by iron defciency (Korshunova et  al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2002), and may play a role in Mn/ Zn transport as well (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et  al. 2002). Biological functions in $Z \mathrm { n } /$ Fe transport of AtIRT2 (Vert et al. 2001, 2009), AtZIP1/2 (Grotz et al. 1998; Wintz et al. 2003; Milner et al. 2013), OsIRT1 (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Ishimaru et  al. 2006; Bughio et  al. 2002) and OsZIP4/5/8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2008; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Yang et al. 2009) have also been examined in the past decade.

A few studies have also implied that ZIPs may be involved in Cd transport. Yeast cells expressing AtIRT1 showed increased Cd sensitivity (Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2001), and IRT1-dependent $\mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { M n } / Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake was inhibited by excess Cd (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). Te Arabidopsis IRT1 knock-out mutant irt1-1 exhibited reduced Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation (Vert et al. 2002; Fan et al. 2014), while overexpression of AtIRT1 increased Cd sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Connolly et  al. 2002). AtIRT2, phylogenetically similar to AtIRT1, increased Cd uptake when overexpressed in Arabidopsis (Vert et  al. 2009), though the yeast cells expressing AtIRT2 exhibited no altered Cd sensitivity (Vert et  al. 2001). In rice, expression of OsIRT1 and OsIRT2 made the cells more sensitive to Cd and increased Cd accumulation (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009). Nonetheless, we still know little about the roles of most of the ZIPs genes in Cd stress response in Arabidopsis and rice.

In this study, genome-wide ZIPs identifcation in Arabidopsis and rice was performed with rigorous evolutional analysis. A comparative examination of genomewide expression profle of ZIPs in Arabidopsis and rice in response to Cd stress were carried out. Teir role in Cd uptake of typical ZIPs responding to Cd stress was further tested by expressing them in yeast. As expected, most identifed ZIPs gene expression responded remarkably to Cd stress, while unexpectedly it was found that Arabidopsis and rice showed a distinct pattern in ZIPs genes expression profle. Tese results may help to elucidate the plants’ genetic basis for Cd translocation via a ZIPs-dependent pathway.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , as an essential micronutrient, is a component of more than 300 enzymes involved in plant biological processes. It plays important roles in gene expression and cellular development. However, a pre-requisite to developing zinc biofortified foods is the understanding of the molecular mechanism of zinc uptake by root, transport through stem, and loading to the specified organs such as seed and fruit.

Maize is an important cereal in the world with high production and productivity. Maize is grown in more than 166 countries for various uses, and in diverse seasons and agroecological conditions due to its high yield potential. In India, while $25 \%$ of the maize produce is consumed as food, the remaining $75 \%$ is used as livestock and poultry feed. Thus, micronutrient-deficient maize not only affects human beings but also livestock and poultry. Therefore, biofortified maize will be immensely helpful for the eradication of malnutrition as it is sustainable and affordable for the poorest of the poor. It is well documented that several genes control the Zn homeostasis in strategy II model plant rice (Ramesh et al. 2003; Ishimaru et al. 2006, 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, 2010b; Bashir et al. 2012). However, genes responsive to zinc uptake as well as loading in the kernel of maize have not so far been studied, which is a prerequisite for understanding the molecular mechanism of Zn uptake. Members of the ZRT-IRT-like protein (ZIP) family were the first metal transporters to be identified in plants (Eide et al. 1996). Along with other factors, the expressions of ZIP genes are regulated by the tissue metal status of the plant (Grotz et al. 1998). Genes with the ZIP domain have also been identified and characterized from other plant species including soybean, Medicago truncatula , Noccaea caerulescens and Thlaspi japonica (Pence et al. 2000; Assunção et al. 2001; Burleigh et al. 2003; Mizuno et al. 2005; Moreau et al. 2002; Plaza et al. 2007). For instance, NcZNT1 from Noccaea caerulescens was shown to mediate high-affinity $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and low-affinity Cd uptake in yeast (Pence et al. 2000). Homologous genes TjZNT1 and TjZNT2 isolated from the Ni hyper-accumulator Thlaspi japonica were shown to enhance the transport of Zn, Cd, and Mn (Mizuno et al. 2005).

The complete genome sequences derived from large-scale sequencing projects are important for comparative and functional genomics research, providing the opportunity to scan various gene families. Like any other sequencing project, the complete maize genome sequence also provides a valuable resource for comparative analysis of the gene families. With decoding of the maize genome sequence, several gene families have already been characterized in maize (Liu et al. 2013a, b; Zhang et al. 2013). Although individual zinc-regulated transporters (ZRT) and iron-regulated transporter-like (IRT) protein (ZIP) genes have been extensively studied in yeast (Wu et al. 2011), as well as in higher plants such as rice (Lee et al. 2010b; Lan et al. 2013), genome-wide analysis of the members of this family has yet to be studied in maize.

Therefore, the objectives of present studies were, (1) identification of non-redundant members of maize ZIP family genes, (2) characterization of their biochemical properties, genomic organization, motif analysis, and phylogenetic relationship, and (3) expression analysis of these genes in different genotypes of maize. The results of this work provide a foundation to better understand functional and evolutionary history of the ZIP gene family in angiosperms. In the present study, we identified 12 putative members of maize ZIP genes $( Z m Z I P s )$ on the basis of ZIP domain and validated their expression among the two inbred lines which differ in $Z \mathrm { n }$ use efficiency. This is the first attempt to describe the ZIP gene family along with their expression in maize.

 High expression of zinc (Zn)-regulated, iron-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) genes increases root Zn uptake in dicots, leading to high accumulation of Zn in shoots. However, none of the ZIP genes tested previously in monocots could enhance shoot Zn accumulation. In this report, barley (Hordeum vulgare) HvZIP7 was investigated for its functions in Zn transport.

 The functions of HvZIP7 in planta were studied using in situ hybridization and transient analysis of subcellular localization with a green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter. Transgenic barley lines overexpressing HvZIP7 were also generated to further understand the functions of HvZIP7 in metal transport.

 HvZIP7 is strongly induced by Zn deficiency, primarily in vascular tissues of roots and leaves, and its protein was localized in the plasma membrane. These properties are similar to its closely related homologs in dicots. Overexpression of HvZIP7 in barley plants increased Zn uptake when moderately high concentrations of Zn were supplied. Significantly, there was a specific enhancement of shoot Zn accumulation, with no measurable increase in iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu) or cadmium (Cd). HvZIP7 displays characteristics of low-affinity Zn transport.

In living organisms, a variety of enzymatic and electron transport processes employ iron due to its property as a transition metal to change in between different redox states. Iron deficiency leads to severe biochemical and developmental alterations and may cause death. In order to cope with their iron demand, all organisms have developed efficient mechanisms for acquiring iron from the environment. One mechanism is based on the reduction of ferric iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ to ferrous iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ , which is then imported into the cell through the action of bivalent metal transporters. This mechanism, termed Strategy I, is well studied in dicotyledonous flowering plants and especially the model plant Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana). Recent gene expression, mutant analysis and functional complementation data suggest that Strategy I is employed throughout the green lineage including green algae, bryophytes, dicot and monocot flowering plants (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Lo et al. 2016; Urzica et al. 2012).

Central to this reduction-based strategy is the function of the ZRT, IRT-like Protein (ZIP)-family transporters (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2002). They are predicted to have eight transmembrane domains and to translocate ions, such as $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and others, across membranes in the direction of the cytoplasm (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000). The founding member of this family is the Arabidopsis IRON-REGULATED TRANSPORTER1 (AtIRT1), whose main function is the import of rhizosphere iron (Eide et al. 1996; Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT proteins have been identified in other organisms, such as Chlamydomonas (Chlamydomonas reinhardtii), rice (Oryza sativa), tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), apple (Malus xiaojinensis), and others, based on the consistent upregulation of their genes in response to iron deprivation and sequence homology to AtIRT1 (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Li et al. 2006; Urzica et al. 2012) (summarized in Table 1). Studies on AtIRT1 have revealed three potential metal coordination sites in the structure of the protein. The loop between transmembrane domains II and III is one of these, predicted to be oriented towards the extracellular space. It was shown to coordinate $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and mutations in it change the transporter substrate specificity (Potocki et al. 2013; Rogers et al. 2000). Transmembrane domains IV and V contain histidine residues which, together with the polar residues in the vicinity may act as intramembrane metal binding sites (Eng et al. 1998). Indeed, mutating any of these amino acids abolishes all AtIRT1 transport activity (Rogers et al. 2000). In the cytoplasmically-exposed part of AtIRT1, the region between transmembrane domains III and IV, referred to as variable region, contains a histidine-rich sequence that is characteristic to all but a few ZIP family members across all kingdoms (Eng et al. 1998). The function of this region in metal transport is at present not clear. Arabidopsis AtIRT1 loss-of-function plants or fet3fet4 iron-deficient yeast can be fully complemented by an AtIRT1 protein with mutated histidines (Kerkeb et al. 2008), while another study using the fet3fet4 yeast only, reported that the MxIRT1 protein from Malus xiaojinensis is only fully functional with all histidines intact (Zhang et al. 2013).

AtIRT1 gene expression was shown to be suppressed by the presence of sufficient iron in the rhizosphere and its expression can be modulated in response to a great variety of stimuli (Blum et al. 2014; Brumbarova et al. 2015; Eide et al. 1996). Under iron limitation, AtIRT1 is strongly upregulated in a tissue- and cell-specific manner and this correlates with the enhanced AtIRT1 protein abundance and iron uptake (Blum et al. 2014; Eide et al. 1996; Marques-Bueno et al. 2016; Vert et al. 2002). At the same time, the protein is subjected to strict posttranslational regulation. It was found to localize at the plasma membrane, as well as in the early endosomes/transGolgi Network as a result of active processes of secretion and clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Barberon et al. 2011). The AtIRT1 localization at the plasma membrane of root epidermis cells depends on the availability of zinc, manganese and cobalt. In their absence, AtIRT1 localizes predominantly to the outer domain facing the rhizosphere (Barberon et al. 2014). Endocytosed AtIRT1 is retrieved from the degradation pathway and recycled to the plasma membrane. Two proteins, FYVE1/FREE1, a plant-specific ESCRT complex subunit (Gao et al. 2014), and SORTING NEXIN1 (SNX1), a stress-responsive trafficking regulator (Brumbarova and Ivanov 2016), have thus far been implicated in this recycling process (Barberon et al. 2014; Ivanov et al. 2014). The variable region of IRT1 contains two lysine residues that are targets for ubiquitination by at least one E3 ubiquitin ligase, IDF1 (Barberon et al. 2011; Kerkeb et al. 2008; Shin et al. 2013). The classical degradation pathway through the multivesicular body/prevacuolar compartment might not be the only way for degrading iron transporters. Studies in yeast grown under excessive iron showed that heterologously expressed MxIRT1 can be a target for autophagy (Li et al. 2015).

Additional iron-acquisition mechanisms are found in the green lineage. The green alga Chlamydomonas employs a reduction-oxidation-based mechanism that is similar to that of budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae). There, iron is reduced by a FRE-family ferric reductase, which is followed by oxidation by the multicopper oxidase FOX1 and import into the cell as $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ by the high-affinity FTR1 transporter (Allen et al. 2007; Glaesener et al. 2013; Herbik et al. 2002). Plants of the Poaceae family employ a chelation-based strategy, also known as Strategy II, where potent iron chelators of the mugineic acid family are secreted from the root through the action of the TRANSPORTER OF MUGINEIC ACID FAMILY SIDEROPHORES1 (TOM1). The mugineic acid-iron complexes are then taken up by YELLOW STRIPE (YS)-family transporters (Kobayashi and Nishizawa 2012). Iron chelation may be important to sustain the Strategy I as well. Species-specific substances, such as flavins and phenolic compounds, secreted by dicotyledonous plants were found critical for the acquisition of iron (Fourcroy et al. 2014; Fourcroy et al. 2016; Jin et al. 2007; RodriguezCelma et al. 2011; Schmid et al. 2014). The role of these chelators is not entirely clear, however it was proposed that they maintain iron in an accessible form, might have weak iron reduction activity and may affect the growth of beneficial siderophore-producing rhizosphere microflora (Mladenka et al. 2010; Romheld and Marschner 1983; Siso-Terraza et al. 2016).

Since iron import is tightly controlled to balance iron requirements and iron toxicity, we assumed that different types of iron acquisition mechanisms should be controlled in a similar manner. To test this, we investigated gene regulation interaction between Strategy I and alternative iron-acquisition mechanisms and IRT1 protein structure analysis in Arabidopsis, rice and Chlamydomonas. Our data suggest that alternative strategies for iron acquisition in Chlamydomonas and plants are closely coordinated and protein modifications, such as phosphorylation, might play a role in the regulation of the iron import process.

In a previous work, we had shown that the Arabidopsis IRT2 gene encodes a putative transporter of iron and zinc which, like its close homolog the major root $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter IRT1, is expressed in root epidermal cells in response to iron deWciency (Vert et al. 2001). Preliminary investigations suggested that IRT2 may have a minor function in iron uptake (Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). It is now clear that IRT2 is not directly involved in iron uptake. Indeed, we show that irt2 null mutants show no apparent phenotype, in contrast to the dramatic chlorosis and growth defect displayed by the irt1-1 mutant (Fig. 1c; Vert et al. 2002). Furthermore, overexpression of IRT2 in irt1-1 plants does not reduce their chlorotic symptoms, thus showing that IRT2 is not able to replace IRT1 in the function of iron uptake from the soil (Fig. 1e; Varotto et al. 2002). We also show here that an IRT2-GFP fusion protein is addressed to the membrane of internal vesicles in transfected Arabidopsis cells (Fig. 2b), whereas using the same experimental system we had previously observed a plasma membrane localization of a similar IRT1-GFP fusion (Vert et al. 2002). Because IRT2 is upregulated by iron deWciency, a tempting hypothesis is that IRT2 function in epidermal cells would be to remobilize iron stores from internal storage vesicles when cytosolic iron is low. As yet, we have found no evidence to support this hypothesis. On the contrary, it is contradicted by the fact that 35S::IRT2 plants show a clear upregulation of IRT1 (Fig. 4), arguing in favor of a depletion of cytosolic iron by IRT2.

In addition to the deregulation of IRT1 in 35S::IRT2 genetic backgrounds shown in the present study, we had previously observed that IRT2 is upregulated in the irt1-1 knock-out line (Vert et al. 2002). This indicates that the activity of these two transporters is integrated in the root epidermal cell. Expression of IRT1 is controlled by the FIT bHLH transcription factor, as attested by the low level of IRT1 mRNA accumulation in the Wt-1 mutant (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004; Jakoby et al. 2004; Seguela et al. 2008; Yuan et al. 2008). Our results show that IRT2 is also controlled by FIT (Fig. 5a). Furthermore, we show in this study, through a split-root experiment, that as previously demonstrated for IRT1 and FRO2 in Arabidopsis and other species (Schikora et al. 2006; Vert et al. 2003), IRT2 expression is controlled both locally and systemically by the iron status (Fig. 5b), further supporting the strict co-regulation with IRT1. The co-regulation of the IRT2 gene with the genes encoding the two major components of the iron uptake machinery argues for the implication of IRT2 in the same cellular process, i.e. iron absorption from the soil, although not involved in iron uptake per se.

The investigation of the intracellular localization of the IRT2-GFP fusion protein revealed an endomembrane localization. How to reconcile the fact that IRT2 expression complements the growth defect of yeast mutants aVected in metal uptake (Vert et al. 2001) whereas it is localized to an endomembrane compartment in planta? The strong overexpression resulting from the use of a yeast expression vector carrying a $2 \mu$ replication origin and the strong phosphoglycerate kinase promoter may lead to mis-sorting of proteins in the cell. This was already reported for the AtNRAMP3/4 vacuolar iron transporters that complement the fet3fet4 iron uptake mutant (Lanquar et al. 2005; Thomine et al. 2003). Therefore, functional heterologous expression in yeast does not necessarily provide information about the intracellular targeting of the protein in its native environment. Other non-plant members of the ZIP family of metal transporters are targeted, as described in the present study for IRT2, to endomembrane compartments and allow sequestration or release of metals in and from such compartments (Huang et al. 2005; Kumanovics et al. 2006). However, we cannot exclude that IRT2 might dynamically localize to diVerent membranes in response to a given stimulus, as reported for several ZIP transporters in mammals (Dufner-Beattie et al. 2004). This signal appears to be independent of iron since (1) IRT2-GFP localization in protoplasts is not aVected by iron (data not shown) and (2) IRT2 overexpression in the strongly chlorotic irt1-1 mutant did not rescue its phenotype (Fig. 1e).

If not involved in external iron uptake through the plasma membrane, what is then the role of IRT2 in the iron deWciency response? It is possible that speciWc processes requiring iron take place in the IRT2-localized vesicles, that are either necessary to the iron deWciency response or to the metabolism of iron-limited cells. A second explanation could reconcile the fact that IRT2 is both involved in iron compartmentalization and synthesized in iron-deWcient roots. Low iron levels, that trigger the iron deWciency response of the roots, lead to fast and strong expression of FRO2 and IRT1. As a result, cytosolic iron content is likely to rapidly rise to ranges that are toxic for the cell. The coinduction of IRT2 with the genes responsible for iron uptake could prevent toxicity through rapid sequestration of iron into vesicles. This phenomenon is known as a proactive adaptation to environmental change. The involvement of such a proactive mechanism was Wrst reported for the control of zinc homeostasis in yeast (MacDiarmid et al. 2003). Under low zinc, plasma membrane zinc uptake transporters are highly expressed, which leads to a rapid accumulation of large amounts of zinc when the metal is re-supplied to the cells, a condition referred to as “zinc shock”. The ZRC1 vacuolar $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporter, that is induced prior to the shock in $Z \mathbf { n }$ limited cells, is required for tolerance to this $Z \mathrm { n }$ shock. A similar scenario was reported in Arabidopsis where the tonoplastic AtMTP3 protein that accumulates in the root epidermis under iron deWciency conditions was proposed to contribute to basic cellular Zn tolerance, particularly under conditions of high $Z \mathrm { n }$ inXux into the root symplasm such as $\mathrm { - F e }$ (Arrivault et al. 2006). Although we favor this model for a role of IRT2 in planta, we were unable to monitor signiWcant resistance or hypersensitivity to re-supply of iron after starvation in 35S::IRT2 and irt2 plants, respectively.

During the past decade, reverse genetics provided a wealth of information on iron homeostasis genes. The next challenge will be to understand how the diVerent actors of the iron homeostasis are integrated in the plant to optimize iron uptake, distribution and storage to ensure proper growth and development of the plant.

Dynamic observation of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride via PET revealed that FEX is involved in the movement and accumulation of fuoride throughout the plant. FEX appears to be responsible for directed fuoride movement in the plant and that fuoride movement with the transpiration stream is the basis for WT fuoride tolerance (Fig. 6). In WT plants, $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ Fluoride accumulated in all terminal tissues. From the patterns of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride movement, the roots do not appear to be the primary locus of FEX action nor does it seem that FEX directed $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to a specifc tissue or immediately sequester $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride into the vacuoles. The data are most consistent with FEX acting in each individual cell to provide overall fuoride tolerance to the whole plant.

The PET experiments allowed the evaluation of several models for the function of FEX in fuoride tolerance as described: vacuolar localization, avoidance, selective tissue targeting, and each cell for itself.

It is well-established that many toxins are shunted to the vacuoles, which function as depositories for harmful substances, including toxic ions. The PET data indicate that vacuole detoxifcation is not a primary mechanism of fuoride resistance in Arabidopsis, at least not in the frst three hours of exposure. This model predicts that $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride would not move with the transpiration stream in WT plants, but would be shunted to the vacuoles and appear to be stationary. The anion $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ has been shown to be shunted into barley vacuoles on the order of $1 2 \mathrm { m i n }$ (Martinoa et al. 1986). We observe the opposite for $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in WT Arabidopsis foral stems. It was not expected that FEX would function in the vacuoles because of the rescue of the membrane FEX in

S. cerevisiae (Li et al. 2013) and because AtFEX has been identifed as a cell membrane protein (SUBA4; Hooper et al. 2017). Yet, a role for FEX in the vacuolar membrane cannot be fully excluded. It might play a role at higher fuoride concentrations, later times, under diferent environmental conditions, or within specifc parts of the plant. It may even vary between diferent plant species. Arabidopsis is an herbaceous annual with a short life cycle. Plants with diferent growth habits might react diferently like tea, a woody evergreen, which does show slow movement of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride from the roots into the stem (Niu et al. 2020). Fluoride has been detected in tea leaf vacuoles (Gao et al. 2014). An alternative interpretation of our cold fuoride experiment is that the higher concentration of fuoride activates a mechanism where fuoride is shunted to the vacuoles and appears to not progress up the stem. Tea has an additional FEX homolog that is expressed when fuoride levels increase and could be responsible for moving fuoride into vacuoles (Song et al. 2020). Another indication that tea might have additional fuoride detoxifcation methods is the fnding that anion inhibitors like NPPB reduce the intake of fuoride (Zhang et al. 2016). We did not observe a similar efect in Arabidopsis, which is less fuoride-tolerant than tea. Further research into FEX expression and cell location in fuoride susceptible and ride movement is that FEX in the cell membrane (orange cylinders) exports fuoride quickly into the transpiration stream. If FEX is not present, fuoride is not efuxed, increasing the steady state concentration of fuoride in the cytoplasm to the detriment of the cell

fuoride tolerant plants will be needed when contemplating the engineering of susceptible plants to tolerate environmental fuoride.

The other three models for fuoride tolerance proposed here assume that FEX functions within the plasma membrane, a location for which there is clear evidence. FEX homologs from several diferent plants all rescued a yeast FEX knockout mutant, where FEX is known to function within the cell membrane (Berbasova et  al. 2017; Zhu et al. 2019; Tausta et al. 2021). Also, GFP-labeled tea FEX appears in the root cell membranes of transformed Arabidopsis (Zhu et al. 2019).

In the ‘avoidance’ model, the roots are expected to provide the primary location of fuoride efux by preventing entry of fuoride into the transpiration stream. Plants often have multiple transporters to maintain optimal levels of a substance within cells. For instance, there are more than 10 known transporters of chloride and some in the nitrate excretion transporter (NXT) family are responsible for chloride efux specifcally from root cells (Li et al. 2017). Roots of some varieties of citrus or grape are so efcient at keeping chloride out of the shoot that they are used as root stock for more susceptible varieties (Brumós et al. 2010; Tregeagle et al. 2010; Henderson et al. 2014). It appears that only the single Arabidopsis FEX gene is responsible for fuoride tolerance. Two results argue against the avoidance strategy. First, both WT and fex plants accumulated similar amounts of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride when the bolus was applied through the intact roots. Second, the pattern of fuoride distribution was not altered for either the WT or fex plants when the fuoride bolus was applied through the roots or directly into the stem. Although we cannot conclude there is no role for the roots in fuoride efux, it does not appear to be the primary mechanism of protection from fuoride toxicity in Arabidopsis.

The third model proposes that FEX directs fuoride to a less vulnerable or dispensable tissue within the plant or selective tissue targeting. An example of this is the accumulation of zinc in the leaf trichomes of Arabidopsis thaliana and the hyperaccumulation of zinc in Arabidopsis halleri (Zhao et al. 2000; Ricachenevsky et al. 2021). Trichomes on leaves are a convenient noncrucial tissue near the end of the transpiration stream with the added beneft of being a deterrent to herbivory. During the period of the PET experiments, there was no evidence of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride being directed to a specifc tissue. $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ Fluoride accumulated into all terminal tissues, including vulnerable reproductive tissues. Thus, the PET data are inconsistent with the selective tissue targeting model, at least during the frst hours of exposure.

The PET results are most consistent with a model in which each cell appears to be acting for itself to keep fuoride moving through the transpiration stream (Fig. 6). This is similar to the action of FEX within single-celled organisms where efux out of each individual cell relieves toxicity. It is also consistent with previous experiments which determined that overexpression of FEX led to increased tolerance to environmental fuoride and that FEX is expressed in most tissues (Zhu et al. 2019; Song et al. 2020; Tausta et al. 2021). FEX expression is prominent in young tissues, as demonstrated by both RT-PCR and promoter GUS experiments, and shows some increase upon fuoride exposure (Zhu et al. 2019; Song et al. 2020; Tausta et al. 2021). In the FEX mutant, the $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride entered the plant vasculature at the same rate as WT, but did not move with the bulk water up the stem of the plant. This same pattern was observed for WT plants exposed to high concentrations of cold fuoride, consistent with a model in which the action of FEX is saturable. In the absence of FEX or upon FEX saturation, fuoride accumulates in cells. The pattern of fuoride immobility suggests that the mutant cells are unable to efux fuoride. Reports using radioactive water showed that much of the water traveling in the xylem actually leaks out horizontally and then re-enters the transpiration stream to continue up the plant (Ohya et al. 2008; Metzner et al. 2010). Fluoride would be expected to stay solvated and travel with the water into surrounding tissues. With a functioning FEX, fuoride localized into xylem-adjacent cells would be efuxed back into nearby vessels, allowing it to continue movement through the plant with the bulk water (Ohya et al. 2008; Metzner et al. 2010). This explains the faster apical movement of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride within the WT plant.

At later time points, $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride did slowly move up the mutant stem and into the terminal fower. When grown for weeks in substrates containing very low $( \sim 1 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ concentrations of fuoride, mutant plants did accumulate fuoride in the fowers (Tausta et al 2021). While the physical half-life of $^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F }$ prevents scanning for multiple days, future work could examine the accumulation of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride with longer time periods (e.g., up to $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ ). Fluoride immobility in fex plants would increase the steady-state fuoride concentration within mutant cells resulting in more cellular damage (Zhu et al. 2019; Tausta et al. 2021). Early experiments have suggested that plants vary in their susceptibility to fuoride toxicity due to diferences in speed of movement within the plant with the slowest (gladiolus) being the most susceptible and the fastest (cotton) being the least (Jacobson et al. 1966).

The accumulation of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride into terminal fowers in the WT plant was an unexpected result given our previous work on the fex mutant. We found that the mutant, and not WT, plants accumulated fuoride in the fowers when grown for long periods (weeks) in low-fuoride-containing substrates. While the ‘each cell for itself’ model establishes how individual cells reduce fuoride damage, there must also be a mechanism to rid the plant of accumulated fuoride once it reaches the terminal tissues.

There are two ways in which water exits the plant; as vapor from the stomata and as liquid from the hydathodes. These are the most likely mechanisms for some fuoride release from the plant. It was previously reported that fuoride accumulation in the tips of cotton leaves was also accompanied by the appearance of more fuoride on the external leaf surface suggesting an ability to release fuoride from internal tissues in cotton (Jacobson et al. 1966). Water vapor released from stomata can contain volatiles like methanol (Hüve et al. 2007). HF, in particular, is highly soluble in water and could be emitted through the stomata. Ions and other substances have also been detected in the guttation exudate and it is considered a method of reducing concentrations from within the plant (Singh and Singh 2013). Our PET experiments establish that there is efcient movement of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to the Arabidopsis WT terminal tissues via the transpiration stream. Although this is consistent with the fact that leaf tips are where fuoride damage is seen in most plants, it could also suggest that, like cotton, fuoride can be released into the atmosphere via hydathodes and/or stomata. Fluoride ions were found in the guttation fuid of maize. However, it was determined that the amount detected there was not sufcient to account for the total loss of fuoride in leaves (Takmaz-Niscancioglu and Davison 1988). The presence of fuoride in the guttation fuid suggests it is possible for elimination to occur via this route (Weinstein 1977).

The comparison of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride movement kinetics in FEX mutant and WT plants has revealed the inability of the mutant to fush fuoride from tissues during transpiration on the time scale of hours, which clarifes how plants deal with this environmental toxin. The PET results are most consistent with a model of FEX action by each cell for fuoride tolerance. These results underscore the importance of this one transporter in protecting the entire plant from fuoride toxicity.

## Multiple sequence alignment revealed the presence of conserved sequence stretches among plant FEXs


Figure  1 represents the multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of FEX sequences from yeast and selected plants. The motifs, GxxTR, ooFooX, ooXooFxxE, PxGTxxxN and YxxxS/T, associated with FEX were found to be conserved in all plants with minor exceptions. According to Berbasova et al. (2017), a conserved Asn (corresponding to N56 in yeast FEX) must be present in the middle of TM2. The plant FEX proteins also contain a conserved Asn (marked with ‘\*’ in Fig. 1) which lies close to N56 of yeast FEX1. Actually, TM2 forms the non-functional Pore I (Berbasova et al. 2017). So, in spite of the sequence shift of this particular Asn in plant FEXs (with respect to yeast FEX1), fluoride transport activity should not be hampered. Following the sequence similarity detected in MSA, Table 2 has been constructed to compare similarly localized residues among plant and yeast FEXs, and the effect of mutation of these residues in yeast, according to Berbasova et al. (2017).

## Post‑translational modifications in plant FEXs


NetPhos 3.1 Server detected a large number of Ser and Thr, and comparatively lesser number of Tyr phosphorylations in plant FEXs. The probable phosphorylations with confidence score above the threshold of 0.5 were represented (Table 3). DISPHOS 1.3 on the other hand predicted only Ser phosphorylations especially towards the N-terminal region of plant FEXs except in phylogenetically closely related B. oleracea and B. rapa FEX sequences (Fig. 3). Table 4 shows the large number of Arg methylations (confidence scores higher than 0.9 except in M. truncatula due to unavailability), Lys acetylations (confidence scores higher than 1.0) and Cys S-nitrosylation among plant FEX sequences. Being membrane proteins, each plant FEX revealed potential fatty acid modifications at target peptide sequences (Table 5).


## Intrinsic disorder and ancestor chart of OsFEX


We next analyzed the intrinsic disorder profile of the OsFEX (as a representative example) and found that mostly the residues from position 1 to 170 (N-terminus) formed disordered secondary structures (coils) (Fig. 4a). The DisEMBL predicted the periodic presence of loops or coils (lacking regular secondary structure) within OsFEX. The disorder probability calculated based on Remark465 (regions that could lack electron density in crystal structure) and hot loops (highly mobile loops) also corroborated with the disordered regions formed by the loops or coils. The probability of occurrence of hot loops was much lower than the cutoff threshold of 0.4 (Fig. 4b). OsFEX was tagged with the Gene Ontology accession, GO:1903424 in UniProtKB. The gene ontology ancestor chart from QuickGO, EMBL-EBI predicted that OsFEX is an anion transmembrane transporter localized in the plasma membrane (Fig. 4c). Analysis in Pfam, EMBLEBI revealed the presence of two CRCB domains ranging between amino acid numbers 176–295 and 368–489 in the OsFEX sequence (Fig. 4d).

## Crystallizability of O. sativa FEX


The OsFEX was predicted to be insoluble upon heterologous overexpression in $E$ . coli with a probability of 0.737985. Multiple parameters were used to assess crystallizability of OsFEX. Length, isoelectric point, gravy index, predicted structural disorder and surface hydrophobicity of OsFEX were not in the optimum crystallizable range (Fig. 8a–d, h). As a result, according to “expert pool” analysis, OsFEX occupied class 5 (least crystallizable). However, “random forest” analysis is an improved version, which uses protein surface entropy, surface ruggedness, instability index, percentage of coil structures, coiled coils and insertion score (Fig. 8e–g, i–k), for predicting the crystallizability class. Since these parameters of OsFEX were in the optimum crystallizable range, “Random forest” analysis revealed that OsFEX protein occupied class 1 (highest probability of being crystallizable) (Fig. 8m).

## Identification of cis‑acting elements in the promoters of plant FEXs


Though bioinformatic characterization of DNA sequence motifs might not justify a functionally active site, the in silico analysis of the probable cis-acting elements in \~ 1 Kbp upstream region of representative plant FEXs provides an idea regarding the nature of stress signals that might regulate their expressions (Table 6). A number of motifs such as TATA, GATA, CAAT, ROOTMOTIFTAPOX1, POLLEN1LELAT52, G-box, EBOXBNNAPA, WRKY71OS, W-box, PYRIMIDINEBOX, GT1CONSENSUS, OSE2ROOTNODULE and CIRCADIANLELHC were detected in all representative FEX promoters. These cis-acting elements provide an insight regarding the inducible nature and tissue-specific expression of FEX gene in plants.

We next analyzed the presence of common cis-acting elements in the promoters of representative FEX genes from plants (Table 6). The cis-acting elements such as TATA boxes and enhancer elements such as GATA and CAAT boxes were detected in the FEX promoters of $o$ . sativa, A. thaliana, M. sativa and V. vinifera. A root-specific cis-acting element, ROOTMOTIFTAPOX1, represented that the FEX genes might be expressed in plant roots along with shoots.

Interestingly, repeats of a pollen-specific element, POLLEN1LELAT52, were also identified (Table 6). Fluoride translocates to the shoots and often accumulates in reproductive parts such as fruits and grains (Mondal 2017). The pollen-specific element probably ensures FEX expression in the pollens to exclude toxic fluoride ions and mediate proper reproductive development.

Phytohormones such as abscisic acid (ABA), gibberellic acid (GA) and salicylic acid (SA) are important regulators of plant growth physiology. ABA is regarded as the universal stress phytohormone (Roychoudhury and Banerjee 2017; Banerjee and Roychoudhury 2018a, b, c, 2019). Thus, the presence of ABA-responsive elements (ABREs) in multiple repeats is common in ABA-inducible genes. The ABREs have an ACGT core consensus sequence (G-box) to which the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors (TFs) bind (Banerjee and Roychoudhury 2017). Another type of ABRE, EBOXBNNAPA, was also identified in multiple copies. EBOXBNNAPA has been regarded as the most welldistributed ABRE in the promoters of calcium-dependent protein kinases in rice (Roychoudhury and Banerjee 2017). We identified multiple ABREs consisting of G-box and EBOXBNNAPA in the upstream region of FEX genes across different plant species (Table 6). ABA and GA are known to work antagonistically during stress. However, GA-responsive elements (GAREs) could be observed in FEX promoters (Table 6). Such cross-regulation of FEX via two antagonistically interacting phytohormones might be interesting. Possibly under control conditions, the GA-responsive silencing factors bind to the GAREs and down regulate unnecessary FEX expression to channelize the metabolic equivalents for plant growth. During fluoride stress, GA levels are reduced (Gadi et al. 2016) probably due to ABA accumulation. The FEX repression is removed in the absence of GA-responsive inhibitors and because of the binding of ABA-dependent bZIP TFs to the ABREs, the gene is up regulated. However, detailed investigations at the molecular level are required for establishing such hypotheses. The reverse regulation, i.e., gene induction by GA and silencing in the presence of ABA has been reported in case of $\alpha$ -amylase gene of Hordeum vulgare (Gubler and Jacobsen 1992). The upstream region of this gene contained both GAREs and ABREs (Gubler and Jacobsen 1992).

WRKY proteins are crucial TFs which regulate several abiotic and biotic stresses. They bind to conserved motifs called W-boxes (Banerjee and Roychoudhury 2015). A large number of WRKY71-binding sites (WRKY71OS) were detected in all the FEX promoters in the selected plant species (Table 6). WRKY71 is an ABA-inducible gene in rice and the encoded TF has been found to block GA-induced $\alpha$ -amylase gene expression in H. vulgare (Zou et al. 2008).

The cis-acting elements such as the ABREs and WRKY71OSs detected in the plant FEX promoters can be present in those of any ABA-responsive gene. FEX, being fluoride-specific transporter, should not be produced abundantly under any sub-optimal condition which induces endogenous ABA levels. This would not be metabolically beneficial for the system. Thus, the presence of a fluoridespecific riboswitch in FEX RNAs is quite evident because it acts as a post-transcriptional regulatory checkpoint. It determines the optimum tertiary RNA structure in presence of fluoride ions to ultimately promote FEX translation. So, in spite of the fact that bioinformatics could not detect a riboswitch in FEX RNA via sequence similarity searches within a limited database, we propose the existence of a robust fluoride sensor within the plant cell.

FEX promoter was also found to contain SA-responsive elements (SAREs) (Table 6). SAREs are recognized by bZIP TFs and though SA is primarily involved in systemic acquired resistance, it also plays a role in developing abiotic stress responses (Roychoudhury et  al. 2016). The presence of an element associated with pathogen infection indicates that FEX expression might represent crosstalk between abiotic and biotic stresses.

Interestingly, a light-responsive element (LRE) associated with the maintenance of circadian rhythm has been detected in single copy in all the FEX promoters. Recent studies have correlated the existence and importance of melatonin as a circadian rhythm associated-phytohormone, actively participating in abiotic stress responses (Nawaz et al. 2016). The LRE might actually act as a melatonin-responsive element and promote the binding of melatonin-responsive TFs to regulate FEX expression. A single LRE was identified in the FEX promoters of all selected plant species (Table 6).

## $[ ^ { 1 8 } \bar { \mathsf { F } } ]$ fuoride administration and imaging in Arabidopsis foral stems


To understand the role that FEX plays in protecting the plant from fuoride toxicity, PET was used to determine if $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride localization and dynamics were diferent between WT and FEX mutant (fex) Arabidopsis plants. Previously, the fex mutant was found to be much more susceptible to fuoride in the growth media becoming stunted, exhibiting tip burn, and unable to produce viable seeds (Tausta et al. 2021). However, fex plants could be grown without any fuoride-induced phenotypes in hydroponics where no fuoride was present. Growth in hydroponics allowed the comparison of WT and mutant plants at the same age with no previous exposure to fuoride.

Arabidopsis presented significant challenges to PET imaging studies due to the small diameter of its stems (Schmidt et  al. 2020). We first tested the feasibility of detecting $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in the Arabidopsis stem tissues and the ability of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to enter the plant via the roots. Following an initial CT scan used for positioning and feature identifcation, the plant roots were placed in a tube containing $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in bufer just out of the feld of view. After $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ , the roots were returned to a tube with plain bufer and the foral stems were monitored. There was ample detected signal in the vegetative tissues (Fig. 1). Movement of the $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride bolus from the roots to the aerial parts of the plant was evident. The source bufer showed negligible loss of radioactivity after administration. These results were consistent with observations made with larger plants which established that movement of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride bolus within plant tissues could be monitored by PET (Glycine max, McKay et al. 1988; rice, Kang et al. 2009; Brassica oleracea, Converse et al. 2015; tea, Niu et al. 2020).

The patterns of fuoride movement were distinctly different between the WT and fex plants near the base of the stem. In WT plants with roots intact, there was a sharp increase in $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride at the bottom of the foral stem (WT15: $1 5 \mathrm { m m }$ from the bottom of the feld of view) that continued throughout the $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ pulse (Sup. Figure 1b). This was followed by a gradual decrease in $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride consistent with washout of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride from the stem section. In contrast, the initial appearance of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in the equivalent foral stem section of the mutant (fex15) was slightly slower. Upon reaching its peak, it did not appear that any of the accumulated $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride cleared out of the tissue segment at later time points during the $1 8 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ of the experiment (Sup. Figure 1b).

Root application of the bolus confrmed the ability of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to enter the transpiration stream through the root tissue bypassing the endodermis. This was consistent with other studies where $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride supplied to the roots of tea (Niu et al. 2020) and cowpea (Furukawa et al. 2001) that also showed upward mobility into the stem and leaves. The observation that the fuoride entered both WT and fex with equally efciency (WT: $2 . 9 \pm 1 . 4 ( \mu \mathrm { C i } / \mathrm { g } ) / \mu \mathrm { C i }$ bolus, fex: $2 . 2 \pm 0 . 9$ $( \mu \mathrm { C i } / \varrho ) / \mu \mathrm { C i }$ bolus), suggested that the main role of FEX was not to keep fuoride out of the root tissue. Thus, while FEX is necessary for fuoride tolerance, it does not act primarily by preventing fuoride from entry via the roots under these conditions.

Application of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to roots followed by washing resulted in continued accumulation of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in both plant genotypes throughout the scanning period $( 1 . 5 \mathrm { h } )$ . This implicated continual uptake of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride from residual radioactivity retained in or on the roots. To better observe the diferences in $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride movement between the WT and mutant plants without the continuous introduction of radioactivity from the roots, which we established was not the main mechanism for resistance, two other methods were tested. First, the $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride bolus was applied to the roots, followed by cutting of the roots and rosette leaves and placing the stem in cold bufer. Application of the bolus to the roots followed by trimming resulted in a sharper bolus pulse and washout (Sup. Figure 1c). The resulting time activity curve (TAC) from cutting of the roots allowed evaluation of the root contribution, but resulted in a cleaner washout without further contribution of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride from the roots after the pulse. The second procedure bypassed the roots by adding the bolus to the cut stem and then recutting the stem and placing it into cold bufer. This resulted in further sharpening of the TAC patterns without altering $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride dynamics (Fig. 2). This result also confrmed that removal of the roots did not change the pattern of movement or accumulation in the vegetative tissues of either the WT or fex plants. Application of the bolus to a cut stem or petiole has been used previously in rice (Kang et al. 2009), Brassica (Converse et al. 2015), and soybean (McKay et al. 1988; Kume et al. 1997). One of these two methods was used for further experiments and kinetic modeling depending on whether the contribution of the root tissue was being tested or not. Removing the roots either before or after the $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride bolus resulted in patterns of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride movement consistent with those seen when the roots were left intact, but were more readily quantifed.


## WT and fex stems have diferent fuoride dynamics


There were distinct differences between $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fluoride movement in the stems of WT and fex plants. Within the WT stem, the bolus of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride entered during the $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ pulse and then progressed quickly to higher sections of the plant. Even at the highest region of the foral stem, the amount of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride peaked after $1 2 \mathrm { m i n }$ and then decreased by $2 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ (Fig. 2a, Sup. Fig. S2). For example, in Fig. 2A the stem region of interest (ROI) at $2 4 \mathrm { m m }$ (distance from the bottom edge of the feld of view) in the WT plant (WT24) peaked around $1 2 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ and only $1 \%$ of the maximum radioactivity remained at $9 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ . In contrast, within the fex foral stem, the majority of the radioactivity remained in the lower stem section and did not continue to travel up the stem (Fig. 2b). In the case of the fex stem at $2 0 \ : \mathrm { m m } \ : ( f e x { 2 0 } ) \ : 8 3 \%$ of the highest $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride peak count was still present at $9 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ (Fig. 2b). In fact, the lowest fex stem section retained the highest amount of radioactivity. This is in contrast to the WT where the lowest stem section had the least amount of radioactivity after $9 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ . This is evident in the video of the time course (Sup. Movie1) of the scan shown in Fig. 1 and in the resulting time activity curves (Fig. 2). At the latest time frames, the upper sections of the fex stem (fex71 and fex76) still showed a slow increase in $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride. This is also in contrast to the WT, which showed a decrease in radioactivity in these regions at later time frames, similar to the bottom of the stem. Note that rainbow colored curves, which denote progressively higher sections of the stem, are reversed between the WT and fex plants (Fig. 2). Biological replicates confrmed these different patterns across multiple test plants (Fig. 2c and d).

The mutant phenotypes of the fex plants were fully rescued with a YFP tagged AtFEX construct under the control of the ALCOHOL DEHYDROGENASE1 (ADH1) promoter (Michniewicz et al. 2015). Under our growth conditions of very low fuoride, robust YFP fuorescence as detected by confocal microscopy was seen in most vegetative plant cells (Sup. Fig. S3), and less fuorescence in root cells. This pattern of expression was sufcient to rescue mutant plants such that they were able to produce viable seeds. When rescued plants were given $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride, the time activity curves were indistinguishable from that of the WT, confrming that rescue was reliant on FEX expression (Fig. 2e).

It was possible that a build-up or malposition of fuoride ions due to loss of FEX caused a decrease in transpiration in the mutant which would appear as a lack of fuoride movement. Although the bolus of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride was only $\sim 1 . 5 \mathrm { n M }$ , this concentration might be enough to inhibit stomatal opening. However, when both genotypes were grown in media with a low amount of fuoride and the mutant showed the phenotypes of fuoride sensitivity, the average transpiration rate was not diferent from WT (Sup. Fig. S4).


## [ 18F]Fluoride kinetic properties in WT and fex stems


Application of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride to the cut stem provided a suitable bolus to evaluate kinetic properties for fuoride uptake. This method was used for the quantifcation of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride initial velocity and clearance. The entry of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride into the vasculature of the cut stem was fast with little lag across all plants whether WT or fex. The total amount of radioactivity measured in the stems of either WT or fex at the end of the experiment was similar (Fig. 3a). Also, the peak amounts of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride were comparable varying from plant to plant regardless of the presence of FEX (Fig. 2). The velocities of initial transport into the stem were similar in WT $( 2 . 2 \pm$ $0 . 8 4 \mathrm { c m / m i n } $ ) and fex $( 2 . 4 \pm 0 . 8 6 \mathrm { c m / m i n }$ ; Fig. 3b), but could be slowed in the WT $( 1 . 3 \pm 0 . 2 8 \mathrm { c m / m i n } )$ ) with the addition of $2 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ cold NaF (Fig. 3b).

The initial velocity of fuoride movement within Arabidopsis was slower than the rate of $3 6 ~ \mathrm { c m / m i n }$ originally calculated in soybean by McKay et al. (1988), the same as $2 . 2 \mathrm { c m / m i n }$ reported for Brassica oleracea (Converse et al. 2015), and faster than tea (Niu et al. 2020). The speed was similar to that $( 1 . 9 { - } 1 . 1 \ \mathrm { c m / m i n } )$ ) calculated for $[ ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { O } ] \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ in rice leaves (Kiyomiya et al. 2001). Although a portion of $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride in the transpiration stream of the fex stem had an initial velocity equivalent to WT $( 2 . 4 \mathrm { c m / m i n } )$ , the vast majority of fuoride remained stationary, which afected the overall bulk movement.

The rate of initial transport up the stem was not afected by the FEX mutation, however the washout kinetics were very diferent. Fluoride clearance rates were calculated for WT and fex plants (Sup. Fig. S5 and S6). To directly compare WT and fex clearance rates, the value closest to $2 0 \mathrm { m m }$ was chosen because it was close to the bolus entry site and it showed a clear pattern in the time activity curves, but it was far enough away to avoid background from the administration site. Comparison of the point directly above and below the $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ value showed the values were consistent, especially in the fex stem (Sup. Fig. S7a). The $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride concentration decreased with time in WT plants, with clearance rates of $0 . 0 2 7 \pm 0 . 0 1 2 \mathrm { { m i n } ^ { - 1 } }$ at $2 0 \mathrm { m m }$ up the stem, consistent with bulk fow. However, within the mutant, $[ ^ { 1 8 } \mathrm { F } ]$ fuoride concentrations remained constant in lower portions of the plant and increased slowly at higher positions (Sup. Fig. S5 and S6). The clearance rate of $0 . 0 0 0 9 5 { \scriptstyle \pm 0 . 0 0 1 } \mathrm { { \ m i n ^ { - 1 } } }$ at the $2 0 \mathrm { m m }$ position on the mutant stem was signifcantly slower than the WT rates $\mathrm { ( P < 0 . 0 0 0 1 ) }$ ) and consistent with a lack of continuous fuoride transport out of the tissue (Fig. 3c).
