In the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family, the ${ \mathrm { K a } } / { \mathrm { K } } s$ ratio of the four segmental duplication pairs was lower than 1, suggesting that these segmental duplication pairs were subjected to purifying selection similar to the poplar KT/HAK/KUP family (He et al. 2012). In order to infer whether duplicated genes evolve at the same rate, the Tajima relative rate test (Tajima 1993) was conducted with amino acid substitutions on pairs of SlHAK paralogs by using the orthologous sequence from Arabidopsis or rice KT/HAK/KUP genes as an outgroup. The results of this analysis indicate that all segmental duplicated pairs in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family evolved at a similar rate (Table 3).

Analysis of the exonic structures determines the conserved gene structure with the same number of nucleotides in the exons and the conserved intron phases, which are indicative of the genetic relatedness of the studied genes (von Schantz et al. 2006). As shown in Fig. 4, exon colored red was conserved in the tomato KT/HAK/KUP family. At least four conserved exons were observed in the tandem or segmental duplicated SlHAK pairs. In addition, the same intron phases are shared by each duplicated SlHAK pair. The first intron from the SlHAK gene is a phase 0 intron, which refers to the splicing after the first nucleotide of the codon (Hyun et al. 2011), whereas the second intron is a phase 1 intron that interrupts the codons between the first and second nucleotides (Fig. 4). Taken together, these indicate a common ancestral relationship between each duplicated pair.


## In-silico expression analysis of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes


To characterize the general features of the promoter regions of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes, the $- 1 . 0 \ \mathrm { k b }$ sequences upstream from the start site of genes were used to search against known cis-elements in the PLACE database (http:// www.dna.affrc.go.jp/PLACE/). The elements presented in the $5 ^ { \prime }$ -UTR regions of the coding strands are listed in Table S1. In the list of motif, five of these cis-regulatory elements, WBOXNTERF3, ARR1AT, WRKY71OS, ACGTATERD1, and GT1CONSENSUS, were found in most of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes. These elements are involved in hormone- and environment stress-response (Terzaghi and Cashmore 1995; Sakai et al. 2000; Simpson et al. 2003; Nishiuchi et al. 2004; Jo and Hyun 2011), indicating that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake might be regulated with hormone and stress response.

To estimate the expression level for each gene, we conducted an analysis in the available Tomato Functional

Genomic database (RNA-seq). Most of SlHAKs, except SlHAK11, 12, and 13, were expressed in all tissues. The expression of SlHAK11, 12, and 13 was determined in anthesis flowers and fruits (10DPA and 20DPA) but not in cotyledons, hypocotyl, whole root, and young leaves (Table 4). In addition, the strong expression of SlHAK9 and 16 was analyzed in roots, whereas SlHAK11, 12, 13, and $^ { l 4 }$ were highly expressed in anthesis flowers (Table 4). Taken together, differential tissue-specific regulation of tomato KT/HAK/KUP genes indicates that they might regulate not only the primary $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in roots, but also the developmental processes in different tissues (Zhang et al. 2012).

## Genome‑wide identifcation of CaHAK gene family members in pepper


We identifed 20 putative HAK/KUP/KT genes in pepper genome basing on the BLAST search results (Table S2). These putative genes were named CaHAK1 to 20, and all of them encoded proteins with, in most cases, similar physicochemical properties. Information about all the putative genes was listed in Table S2, including gene name, ID, protein length, isoelectric point, predicted protein molecular weight, grand average of hydropathicity (GRAVY), and predicted protein subcellular localization. The lengths of the 20 HAK/ KUP/KT putative proteins ranged from 713 to 848 amino acids, the molecular weights and isoelectric points of these proteins varied from 79.2 to $9 4 . 4 \mathrm { k D a }$ and from 6.04 to 9.34, respectively (Table S2). GRAVY analysis showed that all the proteins were hydrophobic, while the predicted subcellular locations of the CaHAK proteins were all at the plasma membrane (PM), the results of both properties suggested that the protein functions were to maintain $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in pepper.


## Phylogenetic analyses of HAK/KUP/KT family genes


To reveal the genetic relationship among the CaHAK genes, a total of 144 plant HAK protein sequences from eight species, namely Capsicum annuum L, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum, Vitis vinifera, Oryza sativa, Arabidopsis, and Physcomitrella patens, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, were aligned using the Clustal X program, and an unrooted tree was constructed using the Neighbor-Joining method using MEGA7 software. According to the phylogenetic tree, CaHAK family genes could be divided into four major clusters (I–IV) (Fig. 1). In cluster I, the six CaHAK members, CaHAK1, CaHAK5, CaHAK9, CaHAK13, CaHAK15, and CaHAK16 belong to cluster IA, and it is worth noting that cluster IB contained only members from rice. In cluster II, the eight CaHAK members, namely CaHAK2, CaHAK3, CaHAK4, CaHAK6, CaHAK7, CaHAK8, CaHAK10, and CaHAK17, were classifed into three sub-clusters (cluster IIA, IIB, and IIC). In cluster III, CaHAK family contained fve members and was composed of sub-cluster IIIA (CaHAK18 and CaHAK19) and III B (CaHAK11, CaHAK12, and CaHAK20). Cluster IV contained only one pepper gene, CaHAK14. Notably, several orthologous CaHAK members were found in tomato genome, indicated that a whole-genome triplication contributed to the expansion of the CaHAK gene family.

To further investigate the evolution of the HAK/KUP/ KT family genes, we identifed 223 HAK/KUP/KT genes in 14 species from algae, lycopodiophyta, early angiosperm, bryophytes, monocotyledons to dicotyledons. The counts of diferent cluster of HAK/KUP/KT genes are shown in Fig. 2. The number of HAK/KT/KUP family gene of algae and bryophyta was less than that in higher plants. Interestingly, the cluster IV was the largest subfamily both in algae and bryophyta species, indicated that the cluster IV began to expand during the plant terrestrialization. In addition, the numbers of cluster II and III family gene were highly conserved in magnoliophyte and mesangiospermae, respectively.


## Chromosomal position and duplication analysis of CaHAK genes


The chromosomal locations of the CaHAK genes were mapped from the pepper genome database, using TBtools. As shown in Fig. S2, apart from CaHAK7, which was located on a scafold chromosome (NW_015960857.1), all the CaHAK genes were mapped onto 9 of the 12 pepper chromosomes. Chromosome 3 carried the most CaHAK genes (fve). Chromosome 2 carried four CaHAK genes, followed by chromosomes 5, 9, and 11 (two CaHAK genes on each chromosome), and chromosomes 1, 6, 8, and 12, each carrying a single CaHAK gene. A similar random distribution model of HAK/KUP/KT gene families was also observed in Arabidopsis and pears (Ahn et al. 2004; Wang et al. 2018).

In addition, the duplication modes of the CaHAK genes were analyzed in pepper, using TBtools. The results identified three segmentally duplicated gene pairs (CaHAK6/CaHAK8, CaHAK15/CaHAK2, and CaHAK4/CaHAK18), and one tandem duplication type gene pair (CaHAK13/CaHAK15) (Table 1). The frequencies of non-synonymous (Ka) and synonymous (Ks) substitutions and the corresponding ratio $\mathrm { ( K a / K s ) }$ can be used to estimate the evolutionary date and the direction of the subsequent selection pressure on these genes (Qiao et al. 2015; Wang et al. 2018). In the present study, the $\mathrm { K a / K s }$ ratios of these duplicated CaHAKs gene pairs were calculated. The results showed that all of the Ka/Ks ratios were $< 0 . 5$ , indicating that purifying (negative) selection played the main force driving for the evolution of HAK genes. The time of divergence of segmentally/tandem CaHAK gene pairs was also estimated. According to the results, the divergence times of duplicated genes occurred between 2.81 and 8.29 million years ago (mya).

To further understand the phylogenetic relationship among pepper CaHAK genes, the collinear relationships with fve other species were constructed, including four dicotyledonous plants (Arabidopsis, grape, eggplant and tomato) and one monocotyledonous plant (rice) (Fig. 3). In total, 27 syntenic gene pairs of CaHAKs with orthologs of the other four species were found in the pepper genome. The CaHAKs genes had eight syntenic gene pairs with tomato (Table S3), nine syntenic gene pairs with eggplant, six syntenic gene pairs with grape, and two syntenic gene pairs with each of A. thaliana and rice. Additionally, the numbers and chromosomal positions of the HAK/KUP/KT family genes in pepper were closely aligned with those of tomato and eggplant, indicating that HAK/KUP/KT genes of solanaceous species were highly conserved during evolutionary divergence.


## Gene structure of HAK/KUP/KT family genes


To gain insights into the structural features of CaHAKs, the exon/intron structures of 20 CaHAKs were analyzed by comparing the corresponding coding sequences (CDS) and genomic sequences (Hu et  al. 2015). As shown in Fig. 4, most HAK/KUP/KT genes in pepper contain 8 – 12 exons, and highly conserved exon/intron structures could be observed in the CaHAKs belonging to the same cluster. Notably, most of the exons common to all of the CaHAKs were 225 bp, 248 bp, 50 bp (or $5 3 \mathrm { \ b p }$ ), and 260 bp in length, a fnding which is consistent with previous results from tomato and pear, indicating that this gene structure was evolutionarily conserved among these species (Liu et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2018). Interestingly, some of the CaHAK genes either lacked one intron (CaHAK6 and CaHAK8) or had gained one intron (CaHAK3, CaHAK10, and CaHAK16).

In general, the function of individual CaHAK proteins was refected in their protein structure. All of the CaHAK proteins contained the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter domain (PF02705), which indicated that all 20 CaHAK genes could perform similar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition functions. The distribution of 10 conserved motifs in the CaHAK proteins was analyzed, and all $2 0 { \mathrm { C a H A K } }$ proteins contained at least eight typical motifs associated with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ potassium acquisition, including motifs 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 (Fig. 4). Although most of the motifs were present and conserved in all 20 CaHAK proteins, some of the motifs were lost from individual CaHAK proteins, such as motif 16, 12 was absent from CaHAK15 and CaHAK10, respectively. This phenomenon had also been reported in HAK/KUP/KT family genes from other species, such as pear and wheat (Cheng et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2018).

## Identification of the HAK/KUP/KT gene family in pear


Using sequences of HAK/KUP/KT transporters from Arabidopsis and rice, candidate HAK/KUP/KT transporters were identified in the genome sequences of $F .$ . vesca, V. vinifera, and P. bretschneideri. Among them, 21 putative HAK/KUP/KT genes (designated PbHAK1-PbHAK21 according to chromosome location) were identified in pear. All putative PbHAK genes contained a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter domain (k_trans; PF02705). The PbHAKs ranged from 584 (PbHAK12) to 2128 (PbHAK11) amino acid residues (aa) in length, corresponding to calculated molecular weights from 64.95 to $2 3 9 . 2 4 4 \mathrm { { k D a } }$ . Estimated isoelectric points ranged from 4.94 (PbHAK20) to 9.4 (PbHAK3). All PbHAKs harbored 8–13 trans-membrane segments and were predicted by Plant-mPLoc to be located predominantly in the plasma membrane (Table S3).


## Phylogenetic distribution and structure of PbHAK genes


96 full-length protein sequences from pear (21), strawberry (17), grapevine (18), Arabidopsis (13) and rice (27) were used to construct a phylogenetic tree. As shown in Fig. 1, the HAK/KUP/KTs separated into five clusters (I–V), consistent with results reported by Nieves-Cordones et al. (2016). 21 PbHAK genes were assigned to clusters I, II, III, and V, with 4, 12, 2, and 3 members, respectively. Cluster I, containing 22 proteins, was further subdivided into Clusters Ia and Ib. Cluster II, containing 44 proteins, was subdivided into Clusters IIa, IIb, and IIc. Clusters consisted of proteins from multiple species rather than from only one species, suggesting that the protein families represented by the clusters are evolutionarily conserved. Notably, pear and Arabidopsis proteins contributed no members to subclades Ib and IV, implying that distinct HAK/KUP/KT families occur in different plant species. An NJ phylogenetic tree was also constructed using a previously published classification of HAK/KUT/

KT proteins from Arabidopsis and rice (Rubio et al. 2000; Gupta et al. 2008). As shown in Fig. S1, the HAK/KUT/KT family was divided into four major groups, and all PbHAKs were distributed into Clusters Ia, IIa, IIb, and III, with 4, 7, 5, and 5 members, respectively. PbHAKs possess 7–12 exons and 6–11 introns (Fig. S2). Most of the 15 conserved motifs identified by MEME in of PbHAK sequences are predicted to components of the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport domain (Fig. S3; Table S4).


## Chromosomal localization and duplication analysis of PbHAK genes


Duplication events in the genome can expand gene families and set the stage for the functional diversification of genes (Maher et al. 2006). To examine the role of duplication in the expansion of the HAK/KUP/KT family, we classified each of the 96 HAK/KUP/KT genes using the MCScanX analysis package. The algorithm assigns genes to one of five different duplication modes: whole-genome duplication (WGD)/segmental, tandem, proximal, dispersed duplication, or singleton. The results show that the duplication modes contribute differently to the expansion of HAK/KUP/KT family in the five plant species (Fig. 2). For example, $6 2 \%$ of PbHAKs were generated by WGD/segmental events, compared with $1 9 \%$ of genes arising from tandem or dispersed duplications. A similarly high proportion $( 5 5 \% )$ of HAK/KUP/KT genes in rice originated from WGD/segmental duplication. In contrast, $6 1 \%$ of HAK/KUP/KT genes in grapevine, $6 4 \%$ in strawberry and $6 2 \%$ in Arabidopsis originated through dispersed gene duplication, suggesting that this duplication mode contributed most to expansion of the HAK/KUP/KT family in these species. PbHAK genes were located on 9 of the 17 pear chromosomes and two scaffolds (Fig. S4). Chromosome 13 contained the largest numbers of PbHAKs (5), while the only one PbHAK was present on chromosomes 5, 9, and 16.


## HAK/KUP/KT orthology between pear and Arabidopsis (or rice)


Orthologs are genes derived from the same ancestral gene locus following speciation. The relationship between orthologous sequences reflects the phylogenetic branching order of the species in which they are found (Altunoglu et al. 2016). Based on the results of phylogenetic and BLAST analyses, orthologous HAK/KUP/KT genes in pear and Arabidopsis were identified and classified into three types (Table 1). In type I, each PbHAK gene corresponded to at least one orthologous AtKUP gene. Six PbHAK genes belonged to this type, suggesting that these genes did not experience additional duplications in pears after they diverged from Arabidopsis. In type II, a cluster of PbHAK genes corresponded to one or more AtKUP gene(s). 14 PbHAK genes belonged to type II. Among them, five clusters of PbHAK genes corresponded to one AtKUP (or OsHAK) gene, while one cluster of PbHAK genes corresponded to two AtKUP genes, implying that there were at least 6 HAK/KUP/KTs in the common ancestor of pear and Arabidopsis. Type III contained PbHAK2, a single gene without any orthologous genes in Arabidopsis (or rice). It is possible that the orthologs have been lost in these species, perhaps because the function provided by PbHAK2 is unnecessary or is performed by other members in the same family.

Orthologous proteins usually have similar sequences and are frequently presumed to perform similar functions (Altunoglu et al. 2016). PbHAK12, PbHAK13, PbHAK14 and PbHAK17 are homologous to AtHAK5, which mediates high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in roots (Table S5). 54, 14, and $5 \%$ of HAK/KUP/KT genes in Arabidopsis have roles in salt, cold and drought stress tolerance, respectively. ## Cis elements associated with PbHAK genes


To explore possible regulatory mechanisms, cis-acting elements in the promoter regions of PbHAK genes were identified and classified using the PLACE database. As shown in Table 2, the promoters of most PbHAK genes harbored multiple potential regulatory elements, such as the G-Box (light response element), HSE (heat stress response element), LTR (low temperature response element), MBS (MYB binding site), TC-rich repeat (a stress-induced cis-acting element), TGACG motif (involved in methyl jasmonate), ERE (ethylene response element), TCA element (involved in salicylic acid responsiveness), ABRE (abscisic acid response element), TGA element (involved in auxin responsiveness), and TATC box (involved in gibberellin responsiveness). Many of these motifs are involved in the response to phytohormones or environmental stresses. However, additional experiments will be required to demonstrate that PbHAKs have roles in these processes.


## Expression of PbHAK genes in different tissues


To investigate PbHAK functions in pear seedlings, expression of the PbHAK gene family was analyzed in three different tissues using qRT-PCR. As shown in Fig. 3, expression patterns varied widely. Nearly all PbHAKs were detected in roots, perhaps because these PbHAKs have a major role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ absorption. Of the 21 PbHAKs, PbHAK2, PbHAK3, PbHAK4, and PbHAK12 were highly expressed in roots. PbHAK5 and PbHAK10 were preferentially expressed in stems, while PbHAK2, PbHAK3, PbHAK4 and PbHAK11 were abundantly expressed in leaves. The tissue-specific expression patterns suggest that members of the PbHAK family are involved in diverse physiological processes.


## Expression of selected PbHAK genes under ${ \pmb K } ^ { + }$ deficiency


PbHAK genes with high levels of tissue-specific expression (PbHAK2 and PbHAK12 in roots, PbHAK10 in stems, PbHAK2, PbHAK3, PbHAK4 and PbHAK11 in leaves) were selected for expression analysis under conditions of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency. PbHAK12, PbHAK13, PbHAK14, and PbHAK17 were also included because of their similarity to AtHAK5, an important high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter. As shown in Fig. 4, PbHAK2, PbHAK12, PbHAK13, PbHAK14, and PbHAK17 had similar expression patterns in roots under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency. Expression markedly increased at $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ , followed by a decline at 3 days and then an increase at 10 days. The increase at $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ suggests that root cells quickly sense and respond to low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels. PbHAK12 (3.4-fold) exhibited the largest increase, followed by PbHAK2 (1.6-fold) and PbHAK13/14/17 (1.3- fold). In stems, PbHAK10 expression increased at $^ { 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ and 3 days in response to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency, but fell below control levels after 10 days. In leaves, PbHAK2 and PbHAK3 transcript levels gradually declined after and reached a minimum at 3 days, followed by an increase at 10 days. In contrast, PbHAK4 and PbHAK11 mRNA levels decreased in response to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency, especially at $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ .


## Subcellular localization of PbHAK12


According to the orthologous relationship to AtHAK5 and the increased expression of PbHAK12 induced by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency, PbHAK12 might be a high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporter from pear. To help characterize the putative function of PbHAK12, its subcellular localization was determined in Arabidopsis mesophyll protoplasts. As shown in Fig. 5, the fluorescence signal from the control vector was detected throughout the cell. However, PbHAK12 tagged with GFP localized at the plasma membrane, consistent with the prediction made by Plant-mPLoc (Table S3). The result supports our speculation that PbHAK12 is an important potassium transporter mediating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in pear roots.


## Expression of PbHAKs under abiotic stresses in roots


Abiotic stresses adversely impact growth in pears. To determine whether salt, cold, and drought affect the expression of PbHAK genes, we measured mRNA levels in pear seedling roots under these conditions. As shown in Fig. 6, nearly all PbHAKs respond at least one of these stresses (PbHAK13 is a notable exception). PbHAK1, PbHAK7, and PbHAK10 were up-regulated by all three stresses, suggesting that they might play crucial roles in stress resistance. In contrast, PbHAK9, PbHAK14, and PbHAK20/21 were down-regulated by all three stresses. Synthetically, seven PbHAKs were significantly up-regulated by salt and cold treatments, whereas five PbHAKs were down-regulated by these stresses. Finally, four PbHAKs were up-regulated by drought stress, while eight PbHAKs were down-regulated.

## Comparative phylogenetic analysis of M. domestica with different plants


Potassium transporters and channel protein sequences were utilized to investigate their phylogenetic and evolutionary relationships among C. arietinum, M. truncatula, G. max, O. sativa, A. thaliana, and M. domestica. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels were divided into both Shaker and TPK subfamilies in agreement with phylogenetic analysis. Shaker channels were categorized into subfamilies called AKT-like, KAT-like, and SKOR-like. In Arabidopsis and rice, AKT (MdAKT1.1, MdAKT1.2, MdAKT1.3, and MdAKT2.1) family members with their counterparts showed a close relationship (Fig. 2). MdAKT1.1 and MdAKT1.2 indicated a paralogous relation in M. domestica. The MdAKT1.1 and MdAKT1.2 genes were duplicated through segmental duplication, indicated by calculations of divergence. In M. domestica, KAT family members MdKAT1.1 and MdKAT1.2 indicated a neighboring relationship with their counterparts (MdKAT1.1 and MdKAT2.1). Since 52.90 million years ago, the evolutionary study demonstrated the duplication through segmental duplication. Around 40.14 million years ago, segmental duplication resulted in the emergence of two TPK family members, MdTPK1.1 and MdTPK1.2, within M. domestica genome. These duplicates exhibit a paralogous relationship within the apple genome and show co-orthologous and orthologous relationships with OsTPK1.1/OsTPK2.1 from O. sativa and AtTPK1.1 from A. thaliana, respectively. In apples, two members of the SKOR subfamily (SKOR1.1 and SKOR1.2) were also identified, which exhibit a neighboring relationship with respective homologs in O. sativa and A.thaliana (SKOR and GORK) (Fig. 3).

Phylogenetic analyses classified $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters into three subfamilies: KUP/HAK/KTs, KEAs, and HKTs (Fig. 2). In M. domestica, only one member of the HKT subgroup, MdHKT1.1, was identified. This gene displayed a paralogous relationship within the species, originating from a tandem duplication event approximately 183.67 million years ago. MdHKT1.1 also showed co-orthologous relationships with OsHKT1.4/OsHKT1.5 and AtHKT1.1 with $4 7 . 6 0 \%$ and $4 6 . 2 2 \%$ identity, respectively, compared to AtHKT1.1. Additionally, 18 KUP/HAK/ KTs were identified from $M$ . domestica genome, revealing a strong relationship with KUP/HAK/KTs from O.

sativa and A. thaliana. Among them, MdKUP/HAK/KT8.1 and MdKUP/HAK/KT6.1 exhibited a paralogous relationship, sharing $4 4 . 1 3 \%$ identity within M. domestica (Fig.  3). The 163.37 MYA (million years ago), Md KUP/HAK/KT8.1 and MdKUP/HAK/KT6.1 were duplicated through tandem duplication. MdKUP/HAK/KT6.1 demonstrated a $7 3 . 1 6 \%$ identity with its ortholog AtKUP/HAK/KT6.1 in Arabidopsis, the highest identity rate observed among paralogous relationships. Similarly, MdKUP/HAK/KT8.1 showed the highest identity of $7 5 . 1 2 \%$ with its ortholog AtKUP/HAK/KT8.1 in Arabidopsis. Around 138.5 MYA, MdKUP/HAK/KT3.1 and 4.1 developed a paralogous relationship due to tandem or segmental duplication. MdKUP/HAK/KT3.1 shares an orthologous relationship with AtKUP/HAK/KT3.1, while MdKUP/HAK/KT4.1 exhibits a close relationship with its homolog, showing $7 6 . 3 \%$ identity. MdKUP/HAK/KT5.1 and 5.3 likely arose from tandem or segmental duplication approximately 178.03 MYA, with MdKUP/HAK/KT5.1 also showing an orthologous relationship with AtKUP/HAK/KT5.1.

Segmental duplication around 67.86 MYA led to a paralogous relationship between MdKUP/HAK/KT10.1 and 10.2. Similarly, AtKUP/HAK/KT9.1, 10.1, and 11 share a co-orthologous relationship with their counterparts. MdKUP/HAK/KT10.1 exhibits a maximum identity of $6 7 . 3 1 \%$ with AtKUP/HAK/KT10. The MdKUP/HAK/ KT12.1 and 12.2, resulting from segmental duplication about $3 0 . 5 4 ~ \mathrm { M Y A }$ , show a co-orthologous relationship with AtKUP/HAK/KT12. MdKUP/HAK/KT7.1 and 7.2, originating from segmental duplication around 40.13 MYA, exhibit a close relationship with AtKUP/HAK/KT7.1, sharing $7 0 . 1 9 \%$ identity.

In M. domestica, there are 7 putative members (MdKEA1.1 to MdKEA6.1) of the KEA family, which show a neighboring relationship with their counterparts in O. sativa and A. thaliana. The MdKEA1.1 and 2.1 exhibit a paralogous relationship, evolving $3 2 . 6 8 \ \mathrm { M Y A }$ through segmental duplication. MdKEA1.1 shows a high identity rate of $7 4 . 4 \%$ and a co-orthologous relationship with AtKEA1.1 and 2. The MdKEA2.1 indicates an orthologous relationship with OsKEA2. Consequently, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters and channels evolved as a result of segmental duplication revealed by the analysis of duplication events. ## Cis-regulatory detection by plant-care database


Cis-regulatory elements are the sites in the upstream regions of transcription start sites (TSS) of genes where transcription factors bind and initiate transcription. In this analysis, some shakers and HKTs sequences found putative cis-elements. To gain insights into tissue-specific and functional regulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport-related genes in M. domestica, we screened promoter regions (1000 bp upstream ATG) of these genes for cis-regulatory elements (CREs). Analysis revealed several potential CREs in the promoter sequences of both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels and transporters, including ABRE, NAC Core motif, W-box, GT-1 motif, MYB/MYC recognition site, and G-box. These findings provide valuable information about gene regulatory networks associated with potassium transport in M. domestica. Furthermore, cis-elements associated with plant response to $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ,$ light signals, and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ were also identified (Table 2).


## Whole transcriptome-based expression profiling


Based on the cis-regulatory element analysis, there was a need to further explore the molecular mechanism of potassium transport-related genes in M. domestica. Therefore, RNA-seq expression profiling of these genes was performed. Two different transcriptomes were chosen to investigate gene expression. Mostly potassium channels in both experiments were known to be up-regulated. MdKEA2.1 was known to be the most upregulated gene in both experiments. Many potassium transporters including members of the HKT-family and KT-family were observed to be downregulated in both experiments (Fig. 5).

In plants, the HAK/KUP/KT family is the largest group of potassium transporters, and it plays an important role in mineral element absorption, plant growth, environmental stress adaptation, and symbiosis. Although these important genes have been investigated in many plant species, limited information is currently available on the HAK/KUP/KT genes for Pepper (Capsicum annuum L.). In the present study, a total of 20 CaHAK genes were identifed from the pepper genome and the CaHAK genes were numbered 1 – 20 based on phylogenetic analysis. For the genes and their corresponding proteins, the physicochemical properties, phylogenetic relationship, chromosomal distribution, gene structure, conserved motifs, gene duplication events, and expression patterns were analyzed. Phylogenetic analysis divided CaHAK genes into four cluster (I–IV) based on their structural features and the topology of the phylogenetic tree. Purifying selection played a crucial role in the evolution of CaHAK genes, while whole-genome triplication contributed to the expansion of the CaHAK gene family. The expression patterns showed that CaHAK proteins exhibited functional divergence in terms of plant $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and salt stress response. In particular, transcript abundance of CaHAK3 and CaHAK7 was strongly and specifcally up-regulated in pepper roots under low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or high salinity conditions, suggesting that these genes are candidates for high-afnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters and may play crucial roles in the maintenance of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ balance during salt stress in pepper. In summary, the results not only provided the important information on the characteristics and evolutionary relationships of CaHAKs, but also provided potential genes responding to potassium defciency and salt stress.
