It is worth noting that phloem and xylem $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations and could range from around 50 to $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ (Kallarackal et al. 2012). As histochemical analysis showed that $C H X I 4 { \because } G U S$ was expressed in the xylem parenchyma of Arabidopsis (Supporting Information Fig. S4), it may be plausible that CHX14 exports high concentrations of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ out of xylem into xylem parenchyma cells. Therefore, low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ affinity and high transport capacity of CHX14 is thus reasonable for such a function. Also, CHX14 appears to have limited expression in the root epidermal cells under normal conditions, and could be induced to express in other tissues under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency and particularly $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ KCl stress. Thus, the transport differences among chx14 mutant and overexpression lines likely result from indirect effects on other $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters. Based on our data, we speculate that in xylem parenchyma CHX14 functions primarily as a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter that is somehow activated by the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ gradient across the plasma membrane. So far, how these $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux transporters, including SKOR and GORK, sense $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and are activated by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fluctuations remains enigmatic (Ache et al. 2000; Ivashikina et al. 2001; Johansson et al. 2006; Liu et al. 2006; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013).


## Mechanisms of CHX14-mediated $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ efflux


CHXs are thought to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in cells via a cation/proton exchange (Cellier et al. 2004; Padmanaban et al. 2007). It is possible that CHX13 has multiple catalytic modes at different $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations and various $\mathrm { p H }$ ranges (Zhao et al. 2008a), and CHX14 may also function at varying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations. We surveyed CHX14 functionality in a range of yeast strains, and obtained evidence to propose a mechanism for CHX14 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux. In the plant uptake assays, the difference in $\mathrm { { \bf R } } { \bf b } ^ { + }$ uptake between 35S::CHX14 lines and vector controls could be diminished by CCCP (Figs $4 \mathrm { g }$ & 6f), suggesting that CHX14-mediated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux may be dependent on the proton gradient. Furthermore, the phenotype of chx14 lines appeared to be pH dependent (Fig. 3, Supporting Information Fig. S5), suggesting CHX14 plays a role in regulating $\mathrm { p H }$ as proposed for CHX20 (Padmanaban et al. 2007). The capacity of CHX14-mediated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux appears to be high, consistent with its function in pH-dependent $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux (Figs 4 & 7).

We postulate that the long C-terminal tail of CHX14 may impede functional assays in yeast. It is possible that this region has multiple regulatory functions analogous to the mammalian transporter NHE1 (Putney et al. 2002) and the yeast Nha1p (Kinclová-Zimmermannova et al. 2006). Another intriguing scenario is that the C-terminus of CHX13 and CHX14 interact with different regulatory molecules in planta. Nevertheless, in our yeast assay conditions, CHX14 appeared to mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux. Decreased kinetic uptake of $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ into yeast cells by expression of CHX14 and diminished amounts of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in CHX14-expressing yeast cells suggest that CHX14 can facilitate $\mathrm { { \bf R } } { \bf b } ^ { + }$ efflux. Future work with CHX13 and CHX14 will be directed at how these transporters are integrated into the signal transduction pathways in response to alterations in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fluctuations.


## Roles of CHX14 in $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ nutrition


The chx14 lines had more robust growth than the control lines under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -deficient conditions, indicating separate function from CHX13 (Fig. 6). Our results also suggest that while CHX13 plays a role in contributing to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition (Zhao et al. 2008a), CHX14 may mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ removal and redistribution. Thus the divergence of one ancestor CHX gene has resulted in two genes, CHX13 and CHX14, with distinct physiological roles in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis.Although both CHX13 and CHX14 are expressed during pollen development, we were not able to find dramatic differences in pollen maturation and in vitro tube growth between chx13, chx14 mutants and wild type. Numerous CHX transport activities expressed in pollen are likely engaged during pollen maturation and subsequent tube growth, suggesting their redundant functions (Sze et al. 2004; Lu et al. 2011). CHX13 is expressed in roots of seedlings (Zhao et al. 2008a). Specifically, CHX14 is localized to root and leaf vascular tissues and junction areas of roots and shoots (Sze et al. 2004). The differential expression patterns of CHX13 and CHX14 imply that these two transporters perform distinct physiological functions. During high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ stress conditions, increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake occurs in roots and CHX14 up-regulation may be required to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from epidermal or cortical cells into the xylem for longdistance transport. Conceivably, during a $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ stress, root and shoot vascular tissues as well as leaves express high levels of CHX14 to attenuate the stress. Functional analysis on both chx14 mutant alleles, overexpression lines, and chx13/chx14 double-knockout lines suggests that loss-offunction on CHX14 results in an increased sensitivity to 100– $2 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ stress, whereas gain-of-function lines are more tolerant to an elevated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ stress. All these observations support the idea that CHX14 transports $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ .

We posit two PM localized CHX homologues transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in opposite directions and therefore regulate plant $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in different ways. These distinct functions may be attributed to a single amino acid difference as this has been shown to alter the vectorial properties of a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel SKOR (Li et al. 2008).The Arabidopsis SKOR conducting outward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ current and is activated by positive membrane potentials and a tomato $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel LKT1 conducting inward current and is activated by negative membrane potentials also share high amino acid sequence similarity; a single amino acid change can convert SKOR into an inward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ rectifier (Li et al. 2008). The C-terminal autoinhibitory domain may also cause these differences. Motif searches revealed potential phosphorylation sites in these domains that could mediate our postulated differences (Sze et al. 2004). It is interesting to note that Arabidopsis CHX17 (1-820aa)-GFP localizes to a prevacuolar compartment (PVC) and to PM in roots, while AtCHX17 (1-472aa), lacking its carboxylic tail, does not appear to associate with PVC or PM in plant cells (Chanroj et al. 2013). In our assays, CHX14- mediated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux in a $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient-dependent manner, and such activity may be highly regulated by other environmental and hormonal stresses through its C-terminal tail (https:// www.genevestigator.com/). Future work will be directed to identify the motifs that determine the functional differences between CHX13 and CHX14.

In summary, results from genetic, molecular and biochemical studies support a model for CHX14 functioning in pH-dependent vascular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport to facilitate the partitioning of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . The redistribution of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ mediated by CHX14 between root, shoots and leaves through xylem parenchyma under high concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in root tissues may be important for balancing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis and nutrition.

Cells have evolved mechanisms to regulate ion and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis in order to respond to developmental cues and to adapt to a constantly changing environment. In prokaryotes, this feat is accomplished with a diverse array of transporters at the plasma membrane. In eukaryotes, cells have increased in size and contain more intracellular membranes, including organelles and various compartments of the secretory and endocytic pathways. Consequently, the number of ion transporters localized to endomembranes has increased considerably. As plant ancestors initially living in an aquatic or marine environment colonized land, we wondered how transport systems required for growth, reproduction, and adaptation evolved in their structure and function. The genomes of diverse plants have been sequenced in recent years offering the first opportunity to understand how plant transporters evolved over one billion years. Here we focus on the monovalent cation/proton antiporter (CPA) superfamily whose members are thought to regulate cation and pH homeostasis (Brett et al., 2005a) by exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ . Prokaryote and eukaryote CPA members fall into two major families designated as CPA1 (2.A.36) and CPA2 (2.A.37; Saier, 2000; Brett et al., 2005a). In plants, CPA1 includes the well-studied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } - }$ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchanger (NHX) family, and the relatively obscure CPA2 family that includes $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux Antiporter (KEA) and Cation– $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchanger (CHX) families. The purpose of this study is to understand the evolutionary relationship of NHX, KEA, and CHX homologs from algae to flowering plants, to use comparative biology to infer functions of uncharacterized plant genes (Chang et al., 2004), and hopefully reveal new model systems to determine functions of KEA and CHX genes which remain largely uncharacterized.

Functional studies of CHX transporters have started recently, so far limited to Arabidopsis (Chanroj et al. 2012); the emerging model suggests that these transporters play important roles in the cellular homeostasis of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ . Although two of these transporters, AtCHX13 (Zhao et al. 2008) and AtCHX21 (Hall et al. 2006), are apparently functional in the plasma membrane, most CHX transporters appears to reside in pre-vacuolar, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi membranes, or in unspecific endomembranes (Padmanaban et al. 2007, Chanroj et al. 2011, Lu et al. 2011). The localization of $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } \mathsf { 1 }$ to the Golgi complex and $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ to the tonoplast and possibly to the plasma membrane is consistent with the Arabidosis model. Some chx mutants of Arabidopsis show defects in the opening of stomata or the guidance of the pollen tube (Padmanaban et al. 2007, Lu et al. 2011, Evans et al. 2012). These defects cannot be studied in protonemal cultures of P. patens, in which these structures do not exist. However, the basic cellular functions mediated by the CHX transporters that are primarily altered in these mutants (e.g. membrane trafficking events that affect protein and cargo sorting; Chanroj et al. 2012) are probably identical or very similar in Arabidopsis and P. patens.


## The mechanism of CHX transporters


The functional expression of PpCHX1 and PpCHX2 in E. coli mutants (Fig. 4) was similar to previous findings with AtCHX17, AtCHX20 (Chanroj et al. 2011) and AtCHX23 (Chanroj et al.

2011, Lu et al. 2011), which demonstrates that all these proteins mediate $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transport. In E. coli, $\mathsf { P p C H X 1 }$ and $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ seem to have identical functions but with different specific activities, as suggested by the different expression levels of the arabinoseresponsive $\mathsf { P } _ { \mathsf { B A D } }$ promoter that are required in each case. For rapid growth on $5 \mathsf { m } N \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ , the PpCHX1 clone required $1 0 0 \mu M$ arabinose while the PpCHX2 clone required $1 3 \mathsf { m } M$ arabinose, which represents ${ > } 1 0$ -fold different transcript expression levels (Guzman et al. 1995). Although $1 3 \mathsf { m } M$ arabinose was toxic for the PpCHX1 clone at $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations of $\geq 5 \mathsf { m } M$ , growth at $2 \mathsf { m } N \mathsf { \Lambda } \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ occurred at $1 3 \mathsf { m } M$ but not at $1 0 0 \mu M$ arabinose. These results and the slow growth of the PpCHX2 and $P p C H X 2 . 1$ clones at $2 \mathsf { m } M \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ can be explained by the rate of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake, which depends on the number of transporters, ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ concentration and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ influx kinetics, i.e. the $K _ { \mathsf { m } }$ and specific activity of the system. If the rate of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ influx is too low or too high, the cells do not grow. These observations are important regarding the mechanism of transport discussed below because they strongly suggest that the growth at low ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ is limited by the kinetics and not by the thermodynamics of the system.

To understand the physiological function of CHX transporters, the study of their functional mechanism is of crucial importance; for this issue, the mechanism underlying the CHXmediated ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ uptake in E. coli constitutes the most basic information. In our experiments (Fig. 3), this uptake may be mediated by either a $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uniporter—‘passive’ transport—or a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symporter—‘active’ transport—but not by an electroneutral $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter, which would mediate $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ efflux. The simplest way to distinguish between the uniport and symport mechanisms is to calculate whether the value of the membrane potential can explain the internal/external ratio of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations in growing cells of E. coli (Rodrı´guez-Navarro et al. 1986). To calculate this ratio, the external $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentration is $2 { \mathsf { m } } M ,$ , because the PpCHX1 clone was found to grow at this concentration. In a medium without ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ , the internal concentration of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ in growing cells of E. coli is $2 1 1 \mathsf { m } M$ (Schultz and Solomon 1961). This concentration might be reduced at $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -limited growth rates, but not very much considering that, even in the presence of ${ \mathsf { N H } } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ and ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ , the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content of chemostat cultures of Enterobacter aerogenes is not greatly reduced (Tempest and Strange 1966). According to these data, an internal $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentration $< 1 5 0 \mathsf { m } M$ is absolutely unlikely, which corresponds to a minimal internal/ external ratio of 75. To obtain this ratio by ‘passive’ uptake would require a membrane potential of $- 1 1 2 \mathsf { m V } ,$ which is unlikely to be generated by E. coli at $\mathsf { p H } 5 . 5$ . The membrane potential in E. coli has been extensively studied (Padan et al. 1976, Zilberstein et al. 1979, Felle et al. 1980, Bakker and Mangerich 1981, Kashket 1982, Setty et al. 1983). According to these studies, a likely value of the membrane potential of E. coli at $\mathsf { p H } 5 . 5$ is between $- 9 0$ and $- 9 5 \mathsf { m V }$ . The most negative value is given in the study of Felle et al. (1980) by microelectrode recording, reporting a measured value of $- 8 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { V }$ that is corrected to $- 1 0 0 \mathrm { m V }$ after calculating the effect of the current leakage through the membrane seal. To interpret these calculations, it is worth noting that a positive growth is an unequivocal proof of fulfilling an energetic requirement, while a negative growth might be the consequence of an influx that is too slow to support a detectable growth rate. We discussed above that the growth of the PpCHX1 and PpCHX2 transformants of TKW4205 at low $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ is probably limited by the kinetics and not by the thermodynamics of the system.

The discussion above can be applied to the Arabidopsis transporter AtCHX20 based on similar growth tests of E. coli transformants (Chanroj et al. 2011). In summary, the thermochemical calculations do not prove, but strongly suggest, that some plant CHX transporters mediate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symport in E. coli. This mechanism is of crucial importance to develop a comprehensive functional model of these transporters that explains the results obtained with the yeast mutants. In contrast, it is worth noting that if the mechanism of the CHX transporters was ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ uniport they would be equivalent to ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ channels (without voltage gating), through which $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ moves but not ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ . Using a different approach, the same issue has been previously discussed by Chanroj et al. (2011) for the Arabidopsis transporters AtCHX17 and AtCHX20.

Both $\mathsf { P p C H X 1 }$ and $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ suppressed the defect of the kha1 ena1-4 nha1 mutant of Saccharomyces cerevisiae at pH 7.5 (Fig. 5), which again coincides with previously reported results for several Arabidopsis CHX transporters (Maresova and Sychrova 2006, Padmanaban et al. 2007, Chanroj et al. 2011). Assuming that the KHA1 gene of S. cerevisiae encodes a $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter, a tentative interpretation of the results obtained with the heterologous expression would be that CHX transporters mediate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symport in E. coli and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } /$ $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiport in S. cerevisiae. However, an alternative explanation would be that $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symporters and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters fulfill similar functions in endosomal compartments and that these two mechanisms show a certain degree of functional redundancy and reciprocal substitution. This means that a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symporter could substitute for KHA1, even if KHA1 mediates $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiport. This reasoning would apply not only to CHX transporters but also to PpHAK2, which also suppresses the kha1 mutation of S. cerevisiae (Haro et al. 2013). The basis of this notion is that these two mechanisms participate in the pH control of organelles.

NHX, HAK and CHX transporters are probably present in the membrane of most organelles (see below). Therefore, the possibility that the functional mechanisms associated with these transporters might be either $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symport or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiport raises the question of how these two mechanisms can participate in the pH control of the organellar lumen. In the most likely model, the organelle pH is established by the steady state that results from $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ pumping into the organelle and returning to the cytosol, in parallel with $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ and ${ \mathsf { C l } } ^ { - }$ conductances (Demaurex 2002, Paroutis et al. 2004, Casey et al. 2010, Ohgaki et al. 2011). $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ pumping and a parallel influx of anions would decrease the organelle pH to very low values, but the effective control of the pH requires the return of ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ to the cytosol. ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ pumping is mediated by the electrogenic V-ATPase, while the return of $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ can be mediated by multiple systems: $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ passive leaks and fluxes coupled to ${ \mathsf { C l } } ^ { - }$ or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ fluxes. In plant cells, a specific type of pyrophosphatase might cooperate with the ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ pump V-ATPase (Segami et al. 2010). The question raised above refers to ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ coupling and can be addressed with a simple model including the pump, the coupled $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ efflux and a ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ channel, if necessary (Fig. 7). Assuming that the membrane potential drives all the other movements, a simple calculation shows that both a ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ antiporter and a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symporter are similarly effective to return $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ from the organelle lumen to the cytosol, assuming the existence of a $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ channel for $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ recirculation. If the equilibrium is reached, which is the limit of the gradient that can generate the system, the organelle pH could be higher than the cytosolic pH $\mathtt { \langle \Delta \Delta \Delta \mathsf { p } H }$ would be 1 for a $\Delta \Psi$ of $- 6 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { V } ,$ ). It is worth noting that the three couplings, antiport plus channel, symport plus channel and antiport plus symport, would be similarly effective to return $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ to the cytosol (Fig. 7), but they would be associated with different ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ contents.


## Functions of PpCHX1 and PpCHX2 in planta


To analyze the function of $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } \mathsf { 1 }$ and $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ in plant cells, we disrupted these genes and also constructed the DPpchx2 DPphak1 double mutant.

PpCHX1 localized to the Golgi complex, and DPpchx1 plants showed no growth defects when growth was tested in a large variety of conditions of $\mathsf { p H } ,$ and ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ , ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ and ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations. This suggests that the function of $\mathsf { P p C H X 1 }$ may be replaced by other transporters. As already discussed, the mechanism of the redundant transporters might be either $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ symport or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiport. PpHAK3 also localizes to the Golgi (Haro et al. 2013), which makes it a candidate substitute for PpCHX1, but there are also other candidates. In Arabidopsis, NHX5 and NHX6 are associated with the Golgi and the transGolgi network (Bassil et al. 2011), and two NHX transporters in P. patens show high sequence homology with AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 (Chanroj et al. 2012). Therefore, it might be possible that CHX, HAK and NHX transporters are working in parallel in the Golgi membrane, returning ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ from the lumen of the Golgi apparatus to the cytosol.

In the case of $\Delta P p c h x 2$ plants, no defects were found that connect CHX2 to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (or $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ ) uptake, but we found that these plants showed a higher cellular retention of $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ . When DPpchx2 plants were exposed to $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ , they showed an increased $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + } / \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ ratio but the same $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ loss. Considering that $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ influx was not increased by the mutation, the increased $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ content of DPpchx2 plants must be the consequence of either a slower $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ efflux through the plasma membrane or a slower vacuole to cytosol $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ transfer, which results in a higher vacuolar $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ retention. Because we did not detect differences in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ contents and the differences in $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ contents between DPpchx2 and wild-type plants were small, the most likely hypothesis is that $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ mediates $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ movements in parallel with other transporters that exhibit a higher ${ \sf K } ^ { + } / { \sf R b } ^ { + }$ discrimination either in the plasma membrane or in the tonoplast. These transporters might fully substitute PpCHX2 for ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ transport, but only partially for $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ transport.

PpCHX2–GFP localized to the tonoplast, but it might also localize to the plasma membrane. The functional difference between these two localizations is mechanistic because $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ efflux $\mathrm { ^ { \prime } K ^ { + } }$ efflux in physiological conditions) across the plasma membrane must be $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiport while vacuole to cytosol $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ transfer $\mathrm { ^ { \prime } K ^ { + } }$ transfer in physiological conditions) must be either $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ uniport or $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + } { - \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ symport, assuming that, in physiological conditions, the vacuole has low pH, high ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ content and a weak membrane potential that is positive with reference to the cytosol. Considering these observations and the previous discussion about the mechanism of CHX transporters, the most likely possibility is that $\mathsf { P p C H } \mathsf { X } 2$ mediates $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (or $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + } ) { - } \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ symport in the tonoplast. Unfortunately, taking into account the large volume of the vacuole, the technical tools to distinguish from a slightly higher $\mathsf { R b } ^ { + }$ content in the cytosol or in the vacuole between mutant and wild-type plants are practically non-existent. Therefore, at the current level of knowledge, a precise conclusion cannot be reached and it is doubtful that it can be reached from biochemical experiments.

Most probably, the identification of the functions of both PpCHX1 and PpCHX2 will come from a genetic approach, by constructing double or triple mutants that show clear defects. However, the problem of this approach is that the number of non-CHX transporters that could substitute for the CHX transporters is high. In the plasma membrane, $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ efflux is mediated by the PpENA1 ATPase (Fraile-Escanciano et al. 2009), and in the Golgi complex, we have already discussed the presence of PpHAK3 and NHX transporters. Regarding the vacuole, P. patens have five NHX transporters showing high sequence homology to the NHX1–NHX4 transporters of Arabidopsis, which play vital $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ exchange roles in vacuoles (Barraga´n et al. 2012, Chanroj et al. 2012).

In conclusion, despite the phylogenetic distance between Arabidopsis and P. patens, the functional basis of CHX transporters in both species seems to be very similar. Taken together, the present study and other studies on CHX, HAK and NHX transporters in P. patens and Arabidopsis provide compelling evidence about the existence of a complex series of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transporters in plant organelles. Although these systems might not be essentially redundant considering their functional conditions, they might replace each other in mutant plants. Although some double CHX mutants in Arabidopsis are clearly defective (Lu et al. 2011, Evans et al. 2012), the construction of double mutants involving two different transporter families seems the only way to unravel the complexity of the individual functions of endomembrane ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ transporters in plant cells.

Intracellular $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ homeostasis is essential for many enzymatic and metabolic processes (Pittman 2012; Casey et al. 2010). $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps such as P-ATPase, V-ATPase, and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ - PPase mediate the establishment of proton gradients across cell membranes (Gaxiola et al. 2007). Recent evidence shows that cation/proton antiporters (exchangers) also contribute to cytosolic $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation (Pittman 2012; Bassil et al. 2011b; Chanroj et al. 2011; Maresova and Sychrova 2005). In Arabidopsis, these antiporters are referred to as the cation/proton antiporter (CPA) family (Maser et al. 2001), which includes the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (NHX), ca$\mathrm { { t i o n / H ^ { + } } }$ exchanger (CHX), and K efflux antiporter (KEA) subgroups.

The roles of these antiporters remain largely unclear; however, the NHX transporters are the best characterized among them. AtNHX1 and AtNHX2 are localized to leaves, root steles, guard cells, inflorescence tissues, and siliques, and both are induced by salt and osmolarity stresses (Barragan et al. 2012; Shi and Zhu 2002; Yokoi et al. 2002). AtNHX1 is an $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (Gaxiola et al. 1999) that contributes to the salt tolerance of Arabidopsis by maintaining shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content and the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pool in the vacuoles (Apse et al. 1999; Barragan et al. 2012; Apse et al. 2003). In addition, the vacuoles of atnhx1atnhx2 double mutant Arabidopsis are more acidic in hypocotyl cells of etiolated seedlings and in root cells (Barragan et al. 2012). AtNHX3 localizes to the vacuolar membrane, and the loss-of-function mutant nhx3 shows hypersensitivity to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency (Liu et al. 2010). AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 colocalize to the Golgi, and mutant Arabidopsis lacking both AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 show reduced growth and enhanced sensitivity to salinity (Bassil et al. 2011a). AtNHX7 (also referred to as SOS1) and AtNHX8 are plasma membrane proteins that play important roles in salinity tolerance and ion homeostasis (Zhu et al. 1998; Zhu 2002, 2003; Shi et al. 2000), and function as $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (An et al. 2007).

Another CPA subgroup, CHX, contains some 28 members in Arabidopsis, and the functions of most have not been elucidated. It has been shown that AtCHX13 and AtCHX17 are involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in the ER (Cellier et al. 2004; Padmanaban et al. 2007; Zhao et al. 2008). Expression analyses indicate that AtCHX13 is induced by potassium-deficient conditions (Zhao et al. 2008), and that AtCHX17 is up-regulated by salt stress and treatments that induce low pH in the roots (Cellier et al. 2004). The third group, the AtKEAs, are putative $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, but are the least understood subgroup of CPA genes, due to a lack of sufficient experimental findings. The six members of the Arabidopsis KEA family (AtKEA1–6) are highly homologous to the bacterial $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters KefC and KefB. In Escherichia coli, KefC is a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -efflux system that is gated by glutathione and is involved in protecting cells from toxicity produced by electrophiles (Douglas et al. 1991, 1994; Munro et al. 1991). The KefB and KefC systems, which are closely related in sequence and regulatory mechanisms, are activated by the formation of oxidative glutathione adducts, which results in cytoplasmic acidification that protects cells from electrophilic attack (Ferguson et al. 1995). The KefB system, despite a high degree of sequence similarity with KefC, shows different effects as a result of identical site-specific mutations (Ness and Booth 1999). YabF is an ancillary protein that is required for KefC activity; deletion of yabF reduces KefC activity tenfold, and readdition of yabF restores activity (Miller et al. 2000). The mode of action of KefC has been elucidated by crystallization (Roosild et al. 2002). Genechip analyses have demonstrated that AtKEA1 was mainly expressed in cotyledons, leaves, petioles, and stems, and only rarely in roots (Sze et al. 2004). Recently, by expressing a truncated AtKEA2 lacking the N-terminal domain, AtKEA2 was functionally assessed and shown to likely be a cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (with preference for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ - $= \mathrm { C s ^ { + } } > \mathrm { L i ^ { + } } > \mathrm { N a ^ { + } } )$ that confers increased tolerance to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ stress in yeast (Aranda-Sicilia et al. 2012). Given its preferential localization to the chloroplasts, AtKEA2 has been suggested to play a role in modulating monovalent cation levels and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis in chloroplasts and plastids. Hans-Henning Kunz found that AtKEA1, AtKEA2, and AtKEA3 were targeted to the chloroplast and had a fundamental role in chloroplast osmoregulation, integrity, and ion and pH homeostasis (Kunz et al. 2014).

With the exception of AtKEA1–3, the functions of the AtKEAs are not well understood. To obtain a better understanding of the roles of the six members of the AtKEA family, we performed promoter activity analyses in transgenic plants and RT-PCR measurements to reveal AtKEA gene tissue localization and transcriptional responses to the experimental conditions. By disseminating this experimental data on the AtKEA family, this study provides insight that is expected to be invaluable to future studies aimed at uncovering the function of putative $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters in Arabidopsis.

Plant $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters function in maintaining cellular ion and $\mathtt { p H }$ homeostasis (Bassil and Blumwald, 2014; Isayenkov et al., 2020).These antiporters play an important role in a variety of cellular and physiological processes,including potassium nutrition, salt tolerance,auxin homeostasis,protein traficking,and growth and development (Bassil and Blumwald, 2014; Qiu, 2016; Fan et al., 2018; Sze and Chanroj, 2018).

Arabidopsis CHX gene family,which is predicated to encode cation/ proton exchangers,consists of 28 members (Chanroj et al.，2012; Isayenkov et al.，2O2O). Studies have shown that plant CHXs are involved in many aspects of growth and development, such as pHand $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis,stomatal movement,male gametophyte development, pollen growth,and plant development (Chanroj et al., 2Ol2; Sze and Chanroj, 2018; Isayenkov et al., 2020). CHX23, which is located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER),is specially expressed in pollen (Lu et al., 2011; Sze and Chanroj, 2O18). CHX23 is critical for pollen ion and pH homeostasis and pollen growth (Lu et al., 2O1l). Studies have shown that CHX21 and CHX23 are involved in the reception or the transduction of female signals that target pollen tube to the ovule (Lu et al., 2011). Pollen of the double mutants chx21 chx23 develops into mature grains, but pollen tubes failed to reach the egg (Lu et al., 2Ol1). However, the mechanism underlying CHX23 function in regulating pollen growth remains to be studied.

Auxin plays an important role in plant growth and development (Mockaitis and Estelle, 2008; Adamowski and Friml, 2015). PIN proteins are auxin efflux transporters that are crucial for auxin asymmetric distribution in tissues (Krecek et al., 2009; Zhou and Luo, 2018). The PIN family contains eight members grouped into two subcategories:PM-PINs and ER-PINs (Viaene et al., 2O13). The PM-PINs, containing PIN1-PIN4 and PIN7,are located in the plasma membrane (PM) (Rakusova et al., 2015;Sauer and Kleine-Vehn, 2O19). The ER-PINs,containing PIN5, PIN6 (also acting at the PM; Simon et al.,2Ol6),and PIN8,are located in the ER (Friml and Jones, 201O; Grones and Friml, 2015).PIN8,which is more highly expressed in the male gametophyte,is critical for pollen growth (Dal Bosco et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2012). However, how PIN8 regulates pollen growth remains elusive.

Recently,progress has been made in understanding the mechanism underlying the regulation of the function of PIN5 and PIN6 in plant growth and development (Fan et al., 2018; Lv et al., 202O). Studies have shown that NHX5 and NHX6,endosomal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters in Arabidopsis,regulate the function of PIN5 and PIN6 and, consequently, cellular auxin homeostasis and plant development (Fan et al., 2O18; Lv et al.,2O2O).NHX5 and NHX6 co-localized in the ER with PIN5 and PIN6,and regulate the function of PIN5 and PIN6 with pH gradients created by their transport activity (Fan et al., 2O18; Lv et al., 2020). Since both CHX23 and PIN8 are localized in the ER,it is interesting to ask whether CHX23 regulates PIN8 function in pollen growth and development.

In this report,we studied the role of CHX23 in regulating PIN8 function and hence pollen growth.Genetic analyses found that the chx23 mutant was affected in pollen growth and pollen morphological development. The pin8 chx23 double mutant was decreased in pollen growth. CHX23 and PIN8 act jointly in maintaining pollen auxin homeostasis. CHX23 and PIN8 co-localized but did not interact.Both chx23 and pin8 chx23 were altered in pollen growth under KCl and NaCl treatments.We demonstrate that CHX23 and PIN8 act coordinately in regulating pollen growth.CHX23 may regulate pollen growth through regulating PIN8 function and hence auxin homeostasis by its transport activity.

The sequencing of the Arabidopsis genome (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000) allowed the identification of large numbers of genes encoding putative membrane-bound transporters (e.g. Ma¨ser et al., 2001). These include members of the CPA (cation proton antiporter) superfamily (Chang et al., 2004) which are considered to be involved in monovalent cation exchange in plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria. In Arabidopsis, the CPA1 group of transporters includes eight NHX (sodium/hydrogen exchanger) proteins. The two most highly characterized are AtNHX1, which is localized in the vacuolar membrane and enables sodium compartmentalization in the vacuole (Apse et al., 1999) and AtNHX7 (SOS1) which is localized in the plasma membrane and is thought to be involved in sodium efflux (Wu et al., 1996; Shi et al., 2000). The CPA2 family consists of two cation transporter families: the KEA (potassium exchange antiporters) and CHX (cation hydrogen exchangers) families. There are six members of the KEA family in Arabidopsis which are thought to function as $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, given their homology to proteins with this function in bacteria. The Arabidopsis CHX family comprises 28 members and these are thought to be involved in cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport (Sze et al., 2004).

The CHX group represents an interesting model for the study of the diversification of protein sequence and function. Many of the CHX proteins exist as pairs of close homologues, such as AtCHX13 and AtCHX14, and AtCHX21 and AtCHX23 (Sze et al., 2004). Such relationships clearly suggest that members of each pair possessed a relatively recent common ancestor. AtCHX21 and AtCHX13 lie close together on chromosome 2. Their nearest homologues are AtCHX23 and AtCHX14, respectively and these two genes lie close together on chromosome 1 (Supplementary Fig. S1 available at JXB online), suggesting that the current situation is a result of the duplication of part of an ancestral chromosome. This proposition is strengthened by the observation that AtCHX8 and AtCHX7 lie next to each other further along chromosome 2 and the closest homologues to these genes are AtCHX6a and AtCHX5 which again lie next to one another on chromosome 1.

To date, only a few of the AtCHX transporters have been characterized in yeast and/or in planta. AtCHX17 is an endomembrane transporter which was shown to transport potassium in yeast and is therefore thought to have a role in potassium homeostasis (Cellier et al., 2004; Maresova and Sychrova, 2006). Similarly, CHX20 has been shown to transport potassium in yeast, but only under alkaline conditions. This transporter is located in the guard cells and is thought to function in osmoregulation (Padmanaban et al., 2007). AtCHX13 restored the growth of yeast lines mutant at both trk1 and trk2 (Zhao et al., 2008). The conclusion of the authors was that AtCHX13 has a role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and that it is involved in high-affinity potassium uptake. The gene is expressed in roots under conditions of potassium deficiency and, using 86Rb as a tracer, the protein has been shown to mediate highaffinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in both Arabidopsis and yeast. Green fluorescent protein (GFP)-tagged versions of the protein were localized within the plasma membrane in both yeast and plant.

Cellier et al. (2004) reported that expression of AtCHX17 could be detected, using northern analysis, in anthers and also in roots that had been subjected to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation, abscisic acid treatment, or low external $\mathrm { p H }$ . Using GUS constructs and in situ reverse transcription-PCR (RT-PCR), they showed that the gene is expressed in the epidermal and cortical cells of mature roots in response to these stresses. Gene knockouts in Arabidopsis accumulated less $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their roots compared with the wild type in response to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation. Their conclusion was that AtCHX17 is involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis. Maresova and Sychrova (2006) were subsequently able to demonstrate that AtCHX17 cDNA complements a growth defect at increased $\mathrm { p H }$ phenotype of Dkha1 in yeast. They showed that a GFP-tagged AtCHX17 protein had a punctuate distribution resembling that of the Golgi apparatus. They speculated that AtCHX17 and

Sckha1p may both function in $\mathrm { p H }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in Golgi cisternae.

AtCHX21 has been shown to be localized on the plasma membrane of root endodermal cells and has been shown to play a role in the transport of sodium into the stele. Genotypes homozygous for a knockout allele of the gene exhibited lower root growth rates in the presence of elevated sodium or potassium ions. When exposed to elevated sodium concentrations around their roots, these genotypes were shown to contain lower levels of sodium within their transpiration stream and lower amounts of sodium accumulated in their leaves (Hall et al., 2006).

Song et al. (2004) reported AtCHX23 expression to be widespread around the plant following experiments employing RT-PCR and a CHX23 promoter–GUS fusion. Work with a GFP fusion protein showed that AtCHX23 is located in the chloroplast envelope. They employed two types of mutant to affect the expression of this gene: an RNA interference (RNAi) line and a mutant produced using ethylmethane sulphonate (EMS) that resulted in a product with a point mutation (Phe761 to lysine). Both mutants displayed a striking phenotype in homozygous lines. Under ‘ideal conditions’ they exhibited a reduced growth rate and had yellower leaves (possessing less chlorophyll) than the wild type, and possessed smaller siliques with fewer seeds. The chloroplasts in the mutants lacked granal stacks and must have been severely compromised with regard to their photosynthetic capacity. Growth of seedlings on MS medium supplemented with $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ KCl increased the growth rate of the mutants and led to higher chlorophyll accumulation. On the basis of this observation, the authors suggested that CHX23 might function in K transport. However, they also reported that chx23 mutants displayed a high sensitivity to NaCl, with seed germination being reduced in elevated salt conditions.

In contrast to the results of Song et al. (2004), Sze et al. (2004) reported that AtCHX23 is preferentially expressed in pollen. This conclusion was based on the use of microarray data, RT-PCR experimentation, and the examination of transgenic plants bearing a AtCHX23 promoter–GUS fusion. They were unable to explain the discrepancy between their results and those of Song et al. (2004). Sze et al. (2004) concluded that 18 of the AtCHX genes are specifically or preferentially expressed in the male gametophyte and speculated that some CHX proteins may play a role in osmotic adjustment and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis as mature pollen desiccates and then rehydrates.

In this study, the role of AtCHX23 in root growth was assessed to determine whether knocking out this gene results in a phenotype similar to that of plants with a mutant allele of AtCHX21 (its closest homologue). Next, crosses were carried out between genotypes bearing mutant alleles of AtCHX21 and AtCHX23 in an attempt to determine the phenotypic characteristics of a double mutant. Since the results indicate that the genes have an overlapping function in reproduction, experiments were carried out to discover which part of this process is blocked when the genes are mutant. Finally, heterologous expression experiments were performed in yeast to determine the ionic specificity of AtCHX23. The experimental approaches used here exploit the gene knockout resources available for two model organisms: Arabidopsis thaliana and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The results provide information about the function of AtCHX23 but also afford an opportunity to consider the processes by which two similar genes (AtCHX21 and AtCHX23) have diverged from one another in recent evolutionary history.

The Arabidopsis genome contains many sequences annotated as encoding $\mathsf { H } ^ { \star }$ -coupled cotransporters. Among those are the members of the cation:proton antiporter-2 (CPA2) family (or CHX family), predicted to encode $\ N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / \hat { \Sigma } ^ { + }$ antiporters. AtCHX17, a member of the CPA2 family, was selected for expression studies, and phenotypic analysis of knockout mutants was performed. AtCHX17 expression was only detected in roots. The gene was strongly induced by salt stress, potassium starvation, abscisic acid (ABA) and external acidic pH. Using the $\beta$ -glucuronidase reporter gene strategy and in situ RT-PCR experiments, we have found that AtCHX17 was expressed preferentially in epidermal and cortical cells of the mature root zones. Knockout mutants accumulated less ${ \pmb { \ K } } ^ { + }$ in roots in response to salt stress and potassium starvation compared with the wild type. These data support the hypothesis that AtCHX17 is involved in ${ \pmb { \ K } } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis.

Keywords: Arabidopsis, salt stress, ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ -starvation, $\ N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / \hat { \Sigma } ^ { + }$ antiporters, $\mathsf { K } ^ { \star }$ transport, CHX transporters.

The Arabidopsis AtHKT1;1 protein was identified as a sodium $( N a ^ { + } )$ transporter by heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. However, direct comparative in vivo electrophysiological analyses of a plant HKT transporter in wild-type and hkt loss-of-function mutants has not yet been reported and it has been recently argued that heterologous expression systems may alter properties of plant transporters, including HKT transporters. In this report, we analyze several key functions of AtHKT1;1-mediated ion currents in their native root stelar cells, including ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ and ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ conductances, AtHKT1;1-mediated outward currents, and shifts in reversal potentials in the presence of defined intracellular and extracellular salt concentrations. Enhancer trap Arabidopsis plants with GFP-labeled root stelar cells were used to investigate AtHKT1;1-dependent ion transport properties using patch clamp electrophysiology in wild-type and athkt1;1 mutant plants. AtHKT1;1-dependent currents were carried by sodium ions and these currents were not observed in athkt1;1 mutant stelar cells. However, ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ currents in wild-type and athkt1;1 root stelar cell protoplasts were indistinguishable correlating with the ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ over $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ selectivity of AtHKT1;1-mediated transport. Moreover, AtHKT1;1-mediated currents did not show a strong voltage dependence in vivo. Unexpectedly, removal of extracellular ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ caused a reduction in AtHKT1;1- mediated outward currents in Columbia root stelar cells and Xenopus oocytes, indicating a role for external ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ in regulation of AtHKT1;1 activity. Shifting the NaCl gradient in root stelar cells showed a Nernstian shift in the reversal potential providing biophysical evidence for the model that AtHKT1;1 mediates passive ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ channel transport properties.

HKT1-type transporters play a crucial role in plant adaptation to salt stress. HKT1-type transporters mediate the distribution of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ within the plant by removing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem, particularly in the roots, to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in the shoots (Munns and Tester, 2008; Hamamoto et al., 2015). HKT1 homologs have been identified in a number of plant species, including Arabidopsis, and their ion selectivity characterized in yeast and Xenopus oocytes (Rubio et al., 1999; Fairbairn et al., 2000; Uozumi et al., 2000; Golldack et al., 2002; Garciadeblás et al., 2003; Su et al., 2003; Haro et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2007; Jabnoune et al., 2009; Asins et al., 2012; Shao et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Ali et al., 2016). HKT1-type transporters are classified into two subclasses, subclass1 and subclass2, based on their protein structure and ion selectivity (Platten et al., 2006). All HKT1s from dicots contain a serine residue at the predicted filter in the pore-loop A domain. Like AtHKT1, EsHKT1;2 (formerly TsHKT1;2) and EpHKT1;2 belong to subclass1 and contain the conserved serine residue in the selectivity filter (Ali et al., 2012). However, the behavior of EsHKT1;2 and EpHKT1;2, which show significantly higher affinity for potassium than for sodium ions, differs from the other subclass 1 proteins (Figures 4, 7; Ali et al., 2016).

Potassium uptake is important for plants during salt stress (Qi and Spalding, 2004; Anschütz et al., 2014). High $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the cytosol leads to severe $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency. One strategy to counteract $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency is to activate high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters to take up $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and thus maintain the ionic balance at the cell level (Maathuis and Amtmann, 1999). Salt stress leads to upregulation of EsHKT1;2 and EpHKT1;2, suggesting their role in salinity stress (Figure 2; Wu et al., 2012). This pattern of upregulation is different from that of AtHKT1 in Arabidopsis, which imports $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ instead of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ under salinity stress (Uozumi et al., 2000; Ali et al., 2012). EpHKT1;2 and EsHKT1;2 will be instrumental in the capture and redistribution of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in $E _ { i }$ . parvula and E. salsuginea, respectively, based on their transcriptional activation in response to high salinity and their permeability to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Figures 2, 3; Ali et al., 2016).

Protein sequence alignment showed that all HKTs from E. parvula and $E _ { i }$ . salsuginea have high similarity to AtHKT1 (Figure 4A). However, AtHKT1 functions as a selective $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter in yeast and $X .$ laevis oocytes (Uozumi et al., 2000), but EsHKT1;2 and EpHKT1;2 function as $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters with lower affinity toward $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Figure 4B; Ali et al., 2016). Therefore, although they are categorized as subclass1 proteins, EsHKT1;2 and EpHKT1;2 do not behave the same as other HKT1 proteins in this subclass (Figure 3; Ali et al., 2012).

High-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters, as well as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, are activated during salt stress (Oh et al., 2009). Other transporters are also involved in partitioning $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole, which can act as the ultimate sink for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions (Kronzucker and Britto, 2011). The localization of AtHKT1 in xylem parenchyma cells relates to its role in reducing the flux of sodium ions to the shoot tip in the presence of excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . For plants such as halophytes that may be exposed to potentially toxic levels of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , the function of some HKT1 isoforms seems to have changed from excluding $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ flux throughout the plant into functioning as $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters. The ability of Eutrema species to maintain a low cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio in the presence of high salinity has been shown (Orsini et al., 2010). Downregulation of EsHKT1;2 by RNA interference (RNAi) leads to a hyperaccumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoots and lower concentrations in the roots compared to the WT, indicating that EsHKT1;2 in E. salsuginea regulates $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake under salt stress. The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio was also disturbed in EsHKT1;2RNAi lines (Ali et al., 2012). We hypothesized that EpHKT1;2, like EsHKT1;2, contributes to salt tolerance based on its ectopic expression in Arabidopsis (Figures 6, 7). EpHKT1;2-overexpressing Arabidopsis plants were more tolerant to salt stress than all other tested plants (Figure 6).

In contrast, EpHKT1;1-overexpressing Arabidopsis plants were sensitive to salt stress, but plants overexpressing AtHKT1 were the most sensitive to salt stress (Figures 5, 6). Analysis of ion contents in transgenic lines also showed enhanced retention of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in Arabidopsis plants overexpressing EpHKT1;2, which is consistent with reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and toxicity (Figure 7; Asins et al., 2012).

These results agree with previous findings on the modeled structures generated for AtHKT1 and EsHKT1;2 showing dissimilar charge distributions at the pore-loop domain (Ali et al., 2016). Aspartate residues in the pore-forming region created a strong negatively charged surface to which $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions were attracted as the result of a strong salt-bridge interaction between the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ion and oxygen atoms in Asp residues, thereby favoring selective $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ permeation through the EsHKT1;2 transporter. The presence of conserved amino acids (Asp and Asn) in the pore-loop region of HKT1 variants from plant species with contrasting salt tolerance underscores their importance in cation selectivity. In this work, we differentiated EpHKT1;2 from EpHKT1;1 based on the amino acid sequence and the pore domain and their ionic selectivity. EpHKT1;2 contains an Asp (D) residue and EpHKT1;1 contains an Asn (N) residue in their selectivity filter positions (Figure 4A). Substitution of these amino acids in the two proteins altered their functions: the addition of Asp residue conferred salt tolerance to yeast expressing mutated EpHKT1;1 (Figure 4B), while its WT form was associated with salt sensitivity in yeast and plants (Figures 4–7).

Soil salinization is a significant threat to the sustainable development of agriculture worldwide (Munns et al. 2020). Grape (Vitis vinifera L.), being an economically important fruit tree, displayed moderate sensitivity to salt stress (Maas and Hoffman 1977). High levels of salt in the environment negatively impact grape growth and yield, while also compromising the quality of fruits and wine due to the accumulation of sodium $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ and chloride (Cl- ) ions in berries (de Loryn et al. 2014; Walker et al. 2003).

The HKT family of proteins has been well-documented to function as a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ symporter (Haro et al. 2010). The members of the HKT family are classified into two groups based on their transport properties: class I and class II. Class I members demonstrate selectivity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport, while class II members exhibit permeability to both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions (Mäser et al. 2002a). Owing to the pivotal role of class

I HKT family proteins in mediating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -selective transport under salt stress conditions, research on these proteins has been extensive. Among the class I HKT family proteins, the HKT1 has been identified as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -preferential transporters that function in retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from xylem sap, thereby preventing the delivery of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from roots to shoots and thus protecting above ground tissues from salt-induced damage (Zhang et al. 2023). Multiple QTLs (quantitative trait loci) and GWAS (Genome-wide association studies) have confirmed the predominant role of HKT1 in conferring salt resistance through enhanced leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion, such as in Arabidopsis thalianaAtHKT1;1 (An et al. 2017), rice OsHKT1;1 (Campbell et al. 2017), and wheat TmHKT1;5 (James et al. 2011). Moreover, the knockout AtHKT1;1 allele in the coastal accession Tsu-1 of A. thaliana or the downregulation of OsHKT1;1 expression in rice (Oryza sativa) resulted in a greater sensitivity to salinity compared to the wild type (An et al. 2017; Campbell et al. 2017). To date, numerous HKT1 transporters have been identified and extensively studied across a range of plant species. Different HKT1 members exhibit varying transport properties, which may contribute to differences in ionic homeostasis and salt tolerance (Wang et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2018, 2023).

It has been shown that the activity of HKT1 alleles significantly influences plant salt tolerance. For example, NSKC1, an allele of OsHKT1;5 (also called SKC1) from a salt-tolerant variety Nona Bokra is more active than KSKC1 from a susceptible variety Koshihikari (Horie et al. 2009; Platten et al. 2013; Ren et al. 2005). This difference in allelic activity results in distinct salt sensitivity phenotypes in rice seedlings (Campbell et al. 2017). Additionally, modulating HKT1 expression patterns can also affect overall plant salt tolerance. The root-specific constitutive expression of TmHKT1;5-A confers lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ leaf content in wheat lines (Munns et al. 2012), while decreasing VcHKT1;1 transcript level in blueberry plants causes higher leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ contents in saline conditions (Song et al. 2023). Remarkably, the vascular-specific expression of AtHKT1;1 confers enhanced salt tolerance by reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoots, as evidenced in literature (Sunarpi et al. 2005). In contrast, the constitutive expression of AtHKT1;1 in A. thaliana renders it hypersensitive to salt stress (Møller et al. 2009). Thus, elucidating expression profiles of HKT1s and regulatory mechanisms of their expression appears to be no less important than identifying HKT1s activity for uncovering HKT1s role in whole-plant salt tolerance.

Despite the extensive exploration of HKT family proteins in model plants and crops, very little attention has been given to grapevine (Vitis vinifera). To date, only six genes within the HKT1 family have been identified in grape rootstock through the mapping of a salt-tolerance QTL associated with leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion (NaE). Among these, VviHKT1;1 has been found as the best candidate gene for controlling leaf $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ exclusion, based on transcript profiling and functional characterization in heterologous systems (Henderson et al. 2018). Furthermore, the analysis of $V \nu i H K T I ; I$ allelic variation between the parent rootstocks has uncovered the highly active $V \nu i H K T I ; I { - } E$ allele, which is responsible for the effective exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the rootstock (Henderson et al. 2018). However, the comprehension of the VviHKT1;1 role and regulatory mechanism of its expression in conferring salt tolerance of grape remains notably incomplete.

Here, VviHKT1;1 transcript profile of salt response was analyzed and the promoter region of $V \nu i H K T I ; I$ was isolated from grape varieties with differential salt tolerance. Most notably, a natural 294-bp InDel (insertion/deletion) was identified in the proximal promoter region of VviHKT1;1, which has been designated as $p V \nu i H K T I ; I ^ { I n }$ and $p V \nu i H K T I ; I ^ { D e l }$ , respectively. Subsequently, we investigated the influence of the InDel region within the VviHKT1;1 promoter on the expression pattern of $V \nu i H K T I ; I$ under both normal and salt stress conditions using a GUS reporter system. Additionally, we examined its impact on salt tolerance in A. thaliana plants overexpressing a highly active VviHKT1;1 allele. The results showed that this natural mutation was likely to modulate the expression profile of $V \nu i H K T I ; I$ , consequently affecting the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ distribution in above-ground tissues. Our findings were expected to allow for a better understanding of the role of VviHKT1;1 in control of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ distribution on a whole plant level.

AcHKT1;1 and AcHKT1;2 from A. canescens are HKT I-type transporters

HKTs belong to the HKT/Trk/Ktr-type $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter superfamily and play a crucial role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport for the regulation of growth and development in plants (Corratgé-Faillie et  al. 2010; Hamamoto et  al. 2015). Polypeptide analysis has revealed that HKT transporters contain 8–12 transmembrane regions and four repeated conserved MPM domains, and each domain is composed of one transmembrane segment (M1), one pore-forming loop (P-loop) and one transmembrane segment (M2) (Hauser and Horie 2010; Cao et al. 2011). The amino acid residue at the frst P-loop flter (P-loop A) is a key site that determines the protein ion selectivity of the HKT family. HKT proteins are endowed with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity in the presence of a serine (Ser) residue, and phylogenetic analysis classifes them as the frst subfamily (HKT I), which is ubiquitously present in higher plant species (Mäser et  al. 2002; Véry et  al. 2014). A single AtHKT1;1 in Arabidopsis is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter with Ser in the P-loop A, though its function changed from $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ permeability in yeast and Xenopus oocyte heterologous expression systems after the Ser was replaced by a glycine (Gly) residue (Mäser et al. 2002). Similarly, DmHKT1 in Dionaea muscipula exhibited pronounced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } ,$ -permeable features with a $7 5 \%$ drop in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ conductance in oocyte recordings after mutation of Ser at P-loop A to Gly (Böhm et al. 2016). Hence, the HKT proteins with Gly residues at the frst pore domain belong to the second subfamily (HKT II) in the phylogenetic relationship and thus far have mainly been identifed in monocotyledonous species (Véry et al. 2014). In our study, two HKT genes, AcHKT1;1 and AcHKT1;2, were isolated from recretohalophyte A. canescens. Their encoded proteins contain 8 and 9 transmembrane regions, respectively, which are in line with the transmembrane characteristics of the HKT family (Supplementary Figure  S3). Moreover, both AcHKT1;1 and AcHKT1;2 have four MPM domains, and the key amino acid residues at P-loop A are Ser, similar to AtHKT1;1 in Arabidopsis (Fig.  2). Phylogenetic analysis showed that these two proteins belong to the HKT I subfamily (Fig. 3). Therefore, it is preliminarily indicated that AcHKT1;1 and AcHKT1;2 are most likely HKT I-type transporters with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity.

AcHKT1;2 is related to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ secretion as a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter

Tissue-specifc expression analysis showed that AcHKT1;1 is expressed primarily in roots of A. canescens (Fig.  4a  and Supplementary Figure  S4). In Arabidopsis and rice, AtHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;5 are preferentially expressed in parenchyma cells bordering root xylem vessels, functioning as a restriction of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport to the above-ground parts (Ren et  al. 2005; Møller et  al. 2009). However, A. canescens can actively absorb a large quantity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and transport it to the shoots, then ultimately excrete it from the plant body through the salt bladders on the leaf surface (Pan et  al. 2016; Guo et  al. 2020). Thus, for recretohalophytes, the HKT protein expressed in roots probably plays a distinct function from the Arabidopsis AtHKT1;1 and rice OsHKT1;5 proteins. What’s exciting is that another gene, AcHKT1;2, from A. canescens was mainly expressed in shoots, especially in mature leaves (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Figure S4), and its expression was strongly induced by NaCl treatments in leaves containing salt bladders (Fig. 8c). In addition, we found that the salt bladders on the surfaces of mature leaves in A. canescens possessed a much stronger ion secretion function than other parts of the leaves, and salt sequestration in mature leaf EBCs was strongly induced by external NaCl (Fig. 1). It is speculated that AcHKT1;2 is highly expressed in mature leaves of A. canescens and is closely related to the salt secretion process of salt bladders. Therefore, attention was focused on the AcHKT1;2 protein in this study.

Transient expression in tobacco epidermis revealed that AcHKT1;2 was localized in the plasma membrane (Fig.  5), which is consistent with the subcellular localization of HKT transporters in most plants (Horie et  al. 2008; Huang et  al. 2020). Yeast complementation experiments confrmed that AcHKT1;2 efciently mediated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake (Fig. 6a) and endowed yeast cells with a weaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake phenotype (Fig.  6b). AcHKT1;2 also exerted robust $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport activity in Xenopus oocytes, but no $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ selectivity (Fig.  7a-c and g). We speculated that AcHKT1;2 may be slightly $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ selective in yeast strain CY162 but not in Xenopus oocytes. The conceivable reason for this phenomenon is unknown at this time and could arise from the increased abundance of AcHKT1;2 protein triggered by the expression of some endogenous genes in CY162 or from some regulatory mechanism. Besides, AcHKT1;2 has a highly conserved serine in P-loop A forming an S-G-G-G motif (Fig.  2) and belongs to the HKT I subfamily with specifc $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity according to phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 3). Taking together these lines of evidence, we conclude that the cation selectivity and characteristics of AcHKT1;2 are consistent with those of Arabidopsis AtHKT1;1 at the cellular level as a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter (Uozumi et  al. 2000). End here, AcHKT1;2 was abundantly expressed in mature leaves with the strongest salt secretion activity, and intensely mediates cell $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake. Hence, this protein is likely to be involved in regulating the spatial distribution of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in $A$ . canescens leaves.


## AcHKT1;2 is a candidate transporter that mediates the entry of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into $A$ . canescens EBCs


The salt bladder (EC-SC-EBC complex) is an important structure for A. canescens to adapt to saline environments and can sequester more than $7 0 \%$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaves (Pan et al. 2016; Guo et al. 2020). The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ excreted from ECs must cross the SCs and fnally enter into the EBCs; consequently, the transporter that mediates the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ infux in the cells plays an indispensable role. Through the EBC transcriptome, several groups have identifed AcHKT1;2 orthologs expressed in M. crystallinum and quinoa, and thus speculated that these transporters might mediate the loading of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into salt bladders in these two species, but there is no further direct evidence (Oh et al. 2015; Böhm et  al.  2018). In this study, the expression of AcHKT1;2 was signifcantly downregulated in young and mature leaves once the EC-SC-EBC complex was removed (Fig.  8a). When the salt bladders were brushed for $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ , the AcHKT1;2 expression levels in all types of leaves rapidly decreased, and showed the maximal decline amplitude in mature leaves since salt bladders on their surface possessed the greatest capacity to accumulate ions (Figs.  1 and 8b). The real-time expression results under diferent NaCl concentration treatments also presented consistent consequences: the expression of AcHKT1;2 was obviously reduced in mature leaves excluding the EC-SC-EBC complex, although it was sharply induced by salt treatments in the presence of the complex (Fig.  8c). These results directly proved that AcHKT1;2 was preferentially expressed in the EC-SC-EBC complex of A. canescens leaves, and the removal of the EC-SC-EBC complex resulted in massive loss of AcHKT1;2 mRNA from the leaf surface, a likely main reason for the sharply reduced AcHKT1;2 transcripts in leaves excluding salt bladders. Combined with the observation mentioned earlier that AcHKT1;2 is a plasma membrane-localized protein and mediates the robust infux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Figs. 5, 6 and 7), we can sufciently speculate that $A$ . canescens AcHKT1;2 is mainly located in the plasma membrane of SCs and EBCs and mediates a high amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport from leaves into EBCs, which provides a direct supporting evidence for the transport system predicted by Shabala et  al. (2014) regarding the involvement of HKT1 in EBC $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ secretion. In addition, the results of our previous work showed that in addition to the genes encoding HKTs, other DEGs related to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport, such as the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter SOS1 and tonoplast $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ antiporter NHX, were signifcantly upregulated in A. canescens leaves after $\mathrm { N a C l }$ treatment (Guo et  al. 2019), which may also play vital roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in salt bladders. In this study, AcHKT1;2 was proposed to be a candidate transporter mediating the infux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into salt bladders. We speculated that SOS1 might mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efux from ECs, and then these $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions transported into salt bladders by AcHKT1;2 might fnally be sequestered in the vacuoles of EBCs by NHX, as described by Shabala et al. (2014) in a predicted transport system mediating salt sequestration in EBC.

HKTs (high-afnity potassium transporters) are crucial for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ long distance transport in plants, and play a key role in their salt tolerances (Adams and Shin 2014; Hamamoto et al. 2015). Although the Cucurbitaceae family contains more than 700 species worldwide and many of them are very important for the health and livelihoods of people (Zhang et al. 2011; Zhao et al. 2019), very few $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters have been identifed in this family, and none to date in melons. In this study, one candidate HKT1,1 gene (CmHKT1,1, GenBank accession number: MK986658) was isolated from melon roots based on genomic similarity with known HKTs, and functional characterization.


## CmHKT1;1 belongs to the HKT transporter Class I and shows ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ specifcity


HKT proteins are characterized using four MPM motifs and can be phylogenetically classifed into three groups in plants (Mäser et al. 2002b; Platten et al. 2006; Su et al. 2015). Classes I and II have been intensively studied, but Class III is relatively under-studied (Su et al. 2015). To date, no HKT Class II homologs have been identifed in dicotyledonous species (Ali et al. 2019). In general, in Class I HKTs, the frst of four glycine amino acids within the predicted selectivity flter is substituted with serine as Ser-Gly-Gly-Gly, conferring $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ specifcity and a lack of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ permeability $( \mathrm { P _ { A } - P _ { D } }$ ; Fig. 1b). Conversely, the selectivity flter of Class II HKTs is usually composed of four glycine residues, as Gly-GlyGly-Gly, which confers $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ symport. However, these specifcity guidelines are not true of all HKTs. For example, the Eucalyptus camaldulensis HKTs EcHKT1;1 and EcHKT1;2 transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ when expressed in X. laevis oocytes (Liu et al. 2001), and the HKT TsHKT1;2 from Thellungiella salsuginea appears to show $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ specifcity in the presence of $\mathrm { N a C l }$ (Ali et al. 2012). HKT2;1 is an

HKT from cereals in which the frst Gly residue has reverted to Ser, but it has been clearly shown to mediate both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ infux into roots (Kronzucker and Britto 2011).

Structurally, the obtained CmHKT1;1 sequence is predicted to form 8 transmembrane segments and 4 pore-forming loops, and it contains a Ser as the frst residue in the selectivity flter of the frst pore-forming loop $\mathrm { ( P _ { A } }$ , Fig. 1). The presence of Ser in the $\mathrm { P _ { A } }$ -loop, as seen in CmHKT1;1, is conserved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ permeable HKT transporters (Class I) (Mäser et al. 2002b; Platten et al. 2006). The CmHKT1;1 protein showed close homology to the CsHKT1;1, AtHKT1;1, and OsHKT1;1 HKTs (Fig.  1). Multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis revealed that these structurally similar transporters all belong to Class I, sharing high sequence identity in their core regions (Figs. 1, 2). Based on these analyses, CmHKT1;1 is also a Class I HKT transporter.

CmHKT1;1 showed $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ specifcity in two heterologous expression systems (Figs. 5, 6). Following heterologous expression experiments in yeast cells, CmHKT1;1 improved the salt sensitive of the transformed strains (Fig. 5). We evaluated the efect of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ on CmHKT1;1-mediated currents in oocytes with varying concentrations of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 6b, c), and these currents were measured in the presence of $0 . 3 \mathrm { \ m M \ N a ^ { + } }$ with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations of 0.3, 3, and $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ (Fig. 6b). The current-voltage relationship stayed almost the same under these treatments, and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ did not show a clear efect on the CmHKT1;1-mediated inward current, or a large shift in the voltage dependence of CmHKT1;1-mediated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ currents, regardless of the external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration (Fig. 6b). Based on the results, the CmHKT1;1-mediated inward current strongly depends on the presence of external $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , but not $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Fig. 6c). In the presence of both cations, the electrophysiological characteristics of $\mathrm { C m H K T 1 ; 1 }$ were similar to those of AtHKT1 when only one cation was present (Uozumi et al. 2000). Electrophysiological evidence from Xenopus oocytes clearly demonstrated that CmHKT1;1 has a special afnity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport through it was not blocked by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ presence at low or high concentrations (Fig. 6). The observed $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -selective transport by CmHKT1;1 is consistent with its predicted $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity as a Class I HKT transporter. All of these observations help confrm that CmHKT1;1 has the ability to transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ .


## CmHKT1;1 regulation at the transcriptional level


In Arabidopsis, AtHKT1;1 showed its expression in the root stele and leaf vasculature (Mäser et al. 2002a). Further biochemical immunolocalization analyses found that its protein was located on the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells, suggesting that they might function in the removal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem sap (Mäser et al. 2002a). In Sorghum bicolor, SbHKT1;4 was expressed in the roots, sheath, and leaf veins (Wang et al. 2014). CmHKT1;1 in Cucurbita moschata demonstrated localization at the plasma membrane, as well as preferential expression in the root stele, helping to demonstrate its capacity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport (Sun et  al. 2018). In this study, the CmHKT1;1 transcripts were the most abundant in roots, whereas only approximately onefourth as much was detected in leaves and stems (Fig. 3a). In line with our data, CmHKT1;1 was strongly expressed in the roots, and its products were targeted to the plasma membrane (Fig. 3a, b), which was consistent with the patterns of HKT localization mentioned above (Uozumi et al. 2000; Sun et al. 2018). The results suggest that CmHKT1;1 is cell membrane-localized and acts as a plasma membrane transporter.

No signifcant efect of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ on AtHKT1 transcription has been observed under diferent culturing conditions (Wang et al. 1998). But rapid up-regulation of HKT1 in barley occurred in response to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -limited conditions after $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 1 d }$ , and its expression in the monocots wheat, barley, and rice was enhanced after $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ withdrawal (Wang et al. 1998). The Eutrema salsuginea genome includes three copies of HKT1 in a tandem array, of which only EsHKT1;2 was dramatically induced at the transcript level under salt stress. The EsHKT1;2 transporter showed a high afnity for potassium, while EsHKT1;1 was more likely a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter (Ali et al. 2012). The genome of Eutrema parvula, a halophytic relative of Arabidopsis, contains two HKT1 genes, of which EpHKT1;2 was induced very rapidly upon salt stress (Ali et al. 2018). The transcripts of HvHKT1;1 were signifcantly upregulated in the roots of Tibetan wild barley when treated with NaCl (Han et al. 2018). This suggests that some HKT1 genes can be regulated by salt stress, and some cannot. In this study, the transcript amount of CmHKT1;1 was signifcantly upregulated by NaCl treatment in melon plants (Fig. 4), which was consistent with the expression patterns of EsHKT1;2, EpHKT1;2, and $H \nu H K T I ; I$ (Ali et al. 2018; Han et al. 2018). We tested the expression of CmHKT1 gene in the roots and shoots of transgenic lines OE-1 and OE6 in order to detect whether the expression amount of this gene would change under diferent salt treatments, although it’s a constitutive expression. The expression of CmHKT1 did change a little (with $\mathrm { 0 \ m M \ N a C l }$ treatment as the control), but it did not reach signifcant diference (Fig. S2) . The results demonstrated that the expression of CmHKT1;1 could be regulated by salt stress in melon plants, but did not change when constitutively expressed in Arabidopsis.

In another experiment, CmHKT1;1 was statistically upregulated in the two melon cultivars under $\mathrm { N a C l }$ treatment (Fig. 4), and its expression in both the salt-tolerant cultivar ‘BXC’ and salt-sensitive cultivar ‘YL’ increased signifcantly after $\mathrm { N a C l }$ treatment within a $^ { 2 4 \mathrm { h } }$ time period. Compared with the salt-sensitive cultivar ‘YL’, CmHKT1;1 was more signifcantly upregulated in the salt-tolerant cultivar ‘BXC’, especially in the roots. In our previous work, when treated with $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ , a lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ level and a higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio was observed in the leaves of the ‘BXC’ cultivar (Wang et al. 2013).
