HKT-transporter mediation of sodium exclusion and maintenance of high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios in leaves under salt stress is a primary salt tolerance mechanism in plants (Hauser and Horie 2010), which is consistent with the higher transcription levels of CmHKT1;1 in ‘BXC’ melons and the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport function of CmHKT1;1. This further confrms that CmHKT1;1 may be regulated at the transcript level and play an important role in melon salt tolerance under high soil salinization.


## Potential roles of CmHKT1;1 in salt tolerance


Plants have evolved various adaptive mechanisms to control ion homeostasis under stress conditions. Among them, HKT1-type transporters regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis by modulating the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels in the cytoplasm, thereby reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc toxicity in plants (Ali et al. 2019). HKTs are crucial for salt tolerance in plants along with other transporters.

Overexpression of HKT1-like genes can improve plant salt tolerance. Constitutive expression of the Mesembryanthemum crystallinum sodium transporter McHKT2 confers salt tolerance in transgenic Arabidopsis (Nishijima et al. 2017). In transgenic tobacco plants, ZmHKT1;1 from maize conferred salt tolerance and decreased the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the shoots (Ren et al. 2015). GmHKT1;4 from soybeans, with the CaMV 35S promoter, improved the root growth of transgenic tobacco lines under salt stress, and increased their salinity tolerance (Chen et al. 2014). Following the former studies, overexpression of some HKT1 genes could enhance transgenic plant growth under stress conditions, potentially ofering a strategy to improve their salt tolerance. In this study, there were no signifcant differences in roots length between OE lines and WT lines under control conditions (Fig. 7). However, when $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was increased to a high level of $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , the root growth of WT plants was signifcantly reduced $\mathrm { ( P < 0 . 0 5 ) }$ . When the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration was increased to $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , the roots of WT were shorter than that of the OE lines (Fig. 7d). The root growth of OE plants under salt stress was signifcantly better than the WT lines (Fig. 7a). The DW and FW of the seedlings also displayed the same phenotype as the root growth (Fig. 7b, c). Overexpression of CmHKT1;1 also enhanced the salt tolerance in adult transgenic Arabidopsis lines with less growth retardation, bigger FW and DW, and also better $\mathrm { F _ { v } / F _ { m } }$ compared with the WT lines, when cultured in substrate (Figs. 8, 9). These data show that the overexpression of CmHKT1;1 improves salt tolerance in transgenic plants during both the seedling and adult stage.

It has been reported that HKT transporters are a possible pathway for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to enter the root vascular system under high salinity conditions (Almeida et al. 2017). AtHKT1;1 was preferentially expressed in the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells, and was suggested to regulate the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ distribution between roots and shoots (Sunarpi et al.

2005; Moller et al. 2009; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). Disruption of its expression reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations in roots and caused a higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the shoots, with little efect on the net $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake (Rus et al. 2004; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). It has also been reported that overexpression of $A t H K T I ; I$ in the mature root stele of Arabidopsis decreases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation by $3 7 - 6 4 \%$ in the shoots (Moller et al. 2009). AtHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;5 were expressed in the parenchyma cells surrounding the xylem vessels, and function to reduce the transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to shoots and thereby increase plant salinity tolerance (Ren et al. 2005; Davenport et al. 2007). HKT transporters mediate sodium exclusion and maintenance of a high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in leaves during salinity stress, which is a conserved salt tolerance mechanism of plants (Hauser and Horie 2010).

In this study, we demonstrated pronounced lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulations and higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios in the shoots of the OE plants compared with WT plants (Fig. 10). The results provide evidence that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in OE plants can be regulated by the CmHKT1;1 transporter. Both of the OE lines showed similarly higher levels of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , lower levels of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , and consequently increased $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios (Fig. 10). This phenotype was diferent from the wild type lines, and also quite diferent from the Arabidopsis hkt1;1 mutant, which was characterized by hyper accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , and a reduction of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in shoots during transpiration (Mäser et al. 2002a). All of our experimental results showed that CmHKT1;1 clearly has similar functions to AtHKT1;1 in Arabidopsis and OsHKT1;5 and OsHKT1;4 in rice (Ren et al. 2005; James et al. 2006). Therefore, CmHKT1;1 transporters are likely to be responsible for unloading $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem and maintaining high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios during salt stress, in order to prevent $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoots and improve melons salt tolerance.

The HKT [high-afnity $( \mathrm { K } ^ { + } )$ potassium transporter] family was named when the frst member of this family was identifed [1]. The gene encoding this protein was cloned from a cDNA library constructed from $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -starved wheat roots, a condition known to induce high-afnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in plants [1, 2]. HKT1, now known as TaHKT2;1, encodes an integral membrane protein that spans the plasma membrane of the outer cell types of Triticum aestivum (bread wheat) roots [1, 3]. As its name suggests, and based on the protein’s transport activity when observed in heterologous expression systems, TaHKT2;1 was proposed to mediate high-afnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in root cells [1, 4]. In both Xenopus laevis oocytes and yeast, TaHKT2;1 functions as a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } N a ^ { + } }$ symport protein facilitating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry when external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is low, using an electrochemical gradient for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ [4]. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uniport into heterologous systems and root cells has also been attributed to the TaHKT2;1 activity when external $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations are in the millimolar range [1, 5, 6]. TaHKT2;1 expression is also downregulated by high external $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ [7], through a mechanism that has been speculated to limit the entry of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into plants, which can be toxic to cells if accumulated to high levels in the cytoplasm—particularly in photosynthetic tissues [8, 9].

More than 20 years after their discovery, it is now clear that HKT proteins are found widely across the plant kingdom, and are in fact members of the high-afnity $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ transporting Ktr/TrK/HKT superfamily of proteins present in bacteria (Ktr and TrK), fungi (TrK), and plants (HKT) [10, 11]. It has recently been suggested that in bacteria, Ktr transporters could be a part of a larger protein complex that directly interact with a pump-like subunit belonging to the superfamily of P-type ATPases [12]. Based on these observations, the authors proposed a new mechanism that repurposes protein channel architecture for active transport across biomembranes.

Of the Ktr/TrK/HKT superfamily, HKT proteins are exceptional as some HKTs can facilitate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport without co-transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . All $\mathrm { K t r / T r K / H K T }$ proteins are predicted to have eight transmembrane $\alpha$ -helices that fold into fourfold pseudo-tetramers around a central pore [13–15]. In plants, HKT proteins have been classifed into two subfamilies: classes $\operatorname { H K T } 1 { \mathrm { ; } } x$ and HKT2;y [3, 16], based on the transport characteristics of HKT proteins that were characterised at that stage, and using sequences predicted to line the entry pore. The class 2 of HKT proteins has thus far only been found in monocots [15, 17], and in general, these proteins can facilitate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } N a ^ { + } }$ symport, or at high external concentrations $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uniport. As also occurs in Ktr and TrK proteins, the selectivity flter lining the entry pore of the class 2 HKT proteins is predicted to be composed of four glycine residues; in TaHKT2;1, these are present at the protein sequence positions 91, 246, 370, and 473. In the class 1 HKT proteins, the frst glycine within the predicted selectivity flter is substituted with a serine residue [13]. For instance, OsHKT1;5 has a glycine present at the positions 264, 391, and 495 and one serine residue at the position 76 [14]. The majority of class 1 HKT proteins have no reported $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ permeability and function as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uniporters only, and this has been linked to the presence of the glycine to serine substitution [3, 13–15, 18].

As the HKT family shares a considerable homology and their genetic variation causes a diferential transport activity in plants, it is clear that subtle changes in their protein sequences can have a profound infuence on transport properties [14, 19–23]. Site-directed mutagenesis has been used previously to probe diferences in HKT transport properties for TaHKT2;1 [24], DmHKT1 [25], SlHKT1;2 and SpHKT1;2 [26, 27], TsHKT1;2, and AtHKT1 [28], making them ideal candidates for detailed structure–function examinations. Three-dimensional (3D) models of two OsHKT1;5 proteins were constructed using the crystal structure of a TrkH protein from Vibrio parahaemolyticus VpTrKH [14, 29], and this model was used to predict functional diferences between two rice alleles; however, no functional validation of residues responsible for the predicted functional diferences was performed [19]. Of the HKT proteins so far characterised in $X .$ laevis oocytes, they catalyse $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in a range of afnities (e.g., $K _ { \mathrm { m } } = \sim 1 { - } 7 6 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ for HKT1;x and $0 . 1 5 { - } 6 . 7 \ \mathrm { m M }$ for HKT2;y) [30–35]. The HKT2;y subfamily members appear to possess a higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -uptake afnity than the HKT1; $\mathbf { \Delta X }$ subfamily; however, HKT1;x proteins are a demonstrated resource for improving salt tolerance in a range of plant species; e.g., AtHKT1;1 in A. thaliana, OsHKT1;5 from Oryza sativa cv. Nona Bokra, TaHKT1;5-D from T. aestivum, and TmHKT1;5-A from $T .$ monococcum [19, 33, 34, 36–38]. The structural elements that result in the diferences in transport afnity of these proteins has not yet been determined.

We have previously shown that HKT genes underpin two major QTL for salt tolerance in wheat; they both encode proteins that reside on the plasma membrane of cells that surround the vasculature and withdraw $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream preventing it from reaching the shoot, where it can do damage to photosynthetic apparatus [33, 34, 39, 40]. Hexaploid bread wheat, T. aestivum, has three genomes; it is the D genome carrying TaHKT1;5-D within the Kna1 locus that confers the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -excluding ability so important to the greater salt tolerance of bread wheat [41]. An ancestral diploid wheat relative, Triticum monococcum (einkorn wheat), carries the homologue TaHKT1;5-A on the A genome. T. monococcum is not a progenitor to modern wheat and was the source of the Nax2 QTL [41]. This represents an additional source of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion that was shown to produce an increase in yield of $2 5 \%$ in saline soil when introgressed into the tetraploid durum wheat that lacks any homologues of this gene [33].

In the current work, we construct new 3D models for HKT proteins using a more recently solved crystal structure of the $\mathrm { K t r B ~ K ^ { + } }$ transporter from Bacillus subtilus [14, 15, 42]. We then use this model to determine the impact of particular amino acid residues on the function of TmHKT1;5-A and TaHKT1;5-D. The model indicates why several mutations abolish the function of TmHKT1;5-A and predicts the residues that result in diferent $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -transport afnities between TmHKT1;5-A and TaHKT1;5-D. The impact of mutations and residue substitutions of interest was confrmed through site-directed mutagenesis and functional characterization of these HKT proteins in $X$ . laevis oocytes.

In Arabidopsis, one AtHKT1.1 transporter has been identifed (Uozumi et al. 2000), which is mainly expressed on the plasma membrane in the xylem cells of roots (Sunarpi et al. 2005). Compared with WT, Arabidopsis athkt1 mutants accumulate more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoots than in roots (Rus et al. 2004). Furthermore, athkt1 mutants have higher xylem sap $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations than WT plants (Sunarpi et al. 2005). Analysis of isotopes $^ { ( 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } ) }$ revealed that AtHKT1;1 regulates the transport rate of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from roots to shoots by retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem sap of roots (Davenport et al. 2007). These fndings basically confrm the main function of AtHKT1.1, which mediates shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion by retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem sap, conferring salt tolerance (van Zelm et al. 2020). In $o$ . sativa, Z. mays, and V. corymbosum, HKT1 transporters similar to AtHKT1.1 have been identifed, including OsHKT1.1, ZmHKT1, and VcHKT1.1 (Wang et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2018, 2023; Song et al. 2024). These studies have indicated that HKT1 transporters play a positive role in improving salt tolerance in plants. Notably, vasculature-specifc expression of AtHKT1;1 is positively associated with salt tolerance, and its constitutive expression (35S promoter) increases salt sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Møller et al. 2009; Ali et al. 2016). In this study, overexpression of SlHKT1.1 severely inhibited root growth by increasing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the roots of transgenic poplar (Fig. 4, 6a). Similarly, overexpression of SlHKT1.1 also afected the root growth of transgenic poplar seedlings under KCl stress (Fig. 5). However, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content in the transgenic seedlings did not show a consistent trend under the two concentrations of KCl (Fig. 6c). NMT measurements showed no signifcant diference in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fux rate in roots of WT and transgenic seedlings under treated and untreated conditions (Fig. 7), suggesting that SlHKT1.1 does not directly transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . Combined with the features of the conserved S residue in PD1, these results suggest that SlHKT1.1 is a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter and that its constitutive expression increases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake and accumulation in the roots (Fig. 8). However, under high concentration of KCl stress (Fig. 5), the roots of transgenic poplar seedlings were inhibited, which may be related to the dynamic balance of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , because more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was accumulated in the roots of transgenic poplar seedlings under normal conditions (Fig. 6a).

Unlike glycophytes, halophytes have evolved strong salt adaptations that may be related to unique or functionally signifcant genes in the body, such as S. salsa and $T .$ halophila (Vera-Estrella et al. 2005; Shao et al. 2008; Taji et al. 2010). For example, TsHKT1.2 from the halophyte $T .$ salsuginea had a stronger positive efect on salt tolerance than AtHKT1.1 (Ali et al. 2016). S. linearistipularis, a halophytic shrub, has extremely strong saline–alkali adaptability, suggesting that its genetic resources are unique. SlHKT1.1 was cloned from S. linearistipularis, and its overexpression caused extreme NaCl sensitivity in transgenic poplar. Under $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ stress, the transgenic poplar seedlings were almost lethal, and the WT seedlings grew normally (Fig. 4). Moreover, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in roots of transgenic poplar seedlings was more than twice that in WT roots under NaClstressed and not-stressed conditions (Fig. 6a). These studies suggest that the function of SlHKT1.1 in the transport and accumulation of $\mathrm { N a C l }$ is remarkable. Further research should attempt to generate transgenic plants with high NaCl tolerance by using the vasculature-specifc expression of SlHKT1.1.

Background High-afnity potassium transporters (HKTs) are crucial in facilitating potassium uptake by plants. Many types of HKTs confer salt tolerance to plants through regulating $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ and ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis under salinity stress. However, their specifc functions in cassava (Manihot esculenta) remain unclear.

Results Herein, an HKT gene (MeHKT1) was cloned from cassava, and its expression is triggered by exposure to salt stress. The expression of a plasma membrane-bound protein functions as transporter to rescue a low potassium $( \mathsf { K } ^ { + } )$ sensitivity of yeast mutant strain, but the complementation of MeHKT1 is inhibited by NaCl treatment. Under low ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ stress, transgenic Arabidopsis with MeHKT1 exhibits improved growth due to increasing shoot $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content. In contrast, transgenic Arabidopsis accumulates more ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ under salt stress than wild-type (WT) plants. Nevertheless, the differences in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content between transgenic and WT plants are not signifcant. Additionally, Arabidopsis expressing MeHKT1 displayed a stronger salt-sensitive phenotype.

Conclusion These results suggest that under low ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ condition, MeHKT1 functions as a potassium transporter. In contrast, MeHKT1 mainly transports ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ into cells under salt stress condition and negatively regulates the response of transgenic Arabidopsis to salt stress. Our results provide a reference for further research on the function of MeHKT1, and provide a basis for further application of MeHKT1 in cassava by molecular biological means.

Keywords Cassava, High-afnity potassium transporter, Potassium starvation, Salt tolerance

High-afnity potassium transporters (HKTs) are known to play an signifcant efect in relieving salt stress in plants31–34. Our research team identifed a high-afnity potassium transporter of AtHKT1gene and cloned it from the leaf of Arabidopsis thaliana in $\mathrm { \Delta N a C l }$ stress, and we found that AtHKT1 gene sequence has an $8 4 . 0 \%$ similarity with Tellungiella HKT1 gene sequence (EF025500). Te phylogenetic tree showed that AtHKT1 and Tellungiella HKT1 (ABK30935.1) were in the same cluster, suggesting that AtHKT1 may have the function of transporting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ under salt stress. A number of studies have demonstrated that AtHKT1 controls $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in shoot23–28, but little has been reported if AtHKT1 might function in adjusting $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ content in heterologous plants. In this research, the AtHKT1 gene was successfully transferred into a tobacco cultivar ‘CV87’. Te AtHKT1gene was detected using several molecular methods, such as PCR, PCR-Southern blot, Southern blot, RT-PCR, and qRT-PCR. Te AtHKT1 has an open reading frame of 1521 bp and encods 506 amino acids. Te gene was a stable alkaline protein with a possible theoretical isoelectric point of 9.33. One TrkH cation transporter protein conserved domain was at the 152–500 amino acids. Te AtHKT1 also had ten transmembrane regions, fve hydrophilic regions and thirteen hydrophobic regions with uniform distribution in the peptide. Our study demonstrated that AtHKT1 was expressed in the root, stem and leaf vein xylem. Large diferences in AtHKT1 gene expression were discovered in the transgenic lines; the T3 line had the greatest AtHKT1 expression, or 1.2 to 4.4 times than other fve transgenic lines. Tese consequents mean that transformation of AtHKT1 gene may give a chance for the enhancement of tobacco plants to salt resistance. Te perspective is supported by the improved biophysicochemical features of the transgenic lines, including total chlorophyll, proline, soluble sugar, MDA, electrolyte leakage, root activity and antioxidant enzyme activities.

Recently, many research have been made to know the role of HKTs expression with the salt hypersensitivity in plant. Zea mays increased accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaves with the natural ZmHKT1 loss-of-function35. Solanum lycopersicum plants become hypersensitivity to salinity with ScHKT1;2 and SlHKT1;2 genes silencing36. In strawberry (Fragaria ananassa), an increase of HKT1expression in roots leads to high tolerance to salinity37. Most of them focused on the HKT1 function on $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation under salt stress. Our results add novel information that the over-expression of AtHKT1 gene in tobacco leads to $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ steady state, reduces $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in leaf, improved physicochemical characters of the whole plant under salt stress; this may serve as a possible mechanism Potential impacts of the protein on the improvement of salt tolerance.

Damage to plants due to high salinity results in reduction of enzyme activity and loss of biomass due to osmotic imbalance caused by water defcit6 . Keeping $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in a high level under high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress conditions is identifed as a strategy to enhance salinity tolerance38. Improving $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content and decreasing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation could retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in leaves39, and this process may help alleviate osmotic imbalance and avoid salt-induced hydraulic failure via stomatal closure and a cascade of downstream efects40. In the present study, we measured $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ contents in the diferent organs with or without AtHKT1 expression under salt stress. We found that the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ content was obviously more in the transgenic lines compared with the control plantlets under NaCl stress. Te line with higher AtHKT1 expression (the T3 line as an example) has stable $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ contents in the diferent organs under the diferent levels of NaCl stress. Under the $2 0 0 \mathrm { m m o l L ^ { - 1 } N a C l }$ stress, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content in the leaves, shoot and roots of the control plants decreased remarkably, while little reduction was shown in the transgenic lines. Furthermore, with increased salt stress, the control plantlets raised $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content signifcantly $( P < \bar { 0 } . 0 5 )$ more compared with the transgenic lines in their leaves and stems. Tese results demonstrate that the transgenic plantlets with high AtHKT1 expression are able to maintain $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ steady state under high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress conditions.

Tis may suggest a possible mechanism that the enhanced tolerance to salt stress in the transgenic tobacco plants is due to the constitutive over-expression of AtHKT1 gene helping keep $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ at a high level to minimize or avoid $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity under salt stress. Also, the AtHKT1 over-expression confers multiple functions, such as the improved activities of antioxidant enzymes SOD, CAT and POD; raised contents of chlorophyll and soluble sugar and root activity; and decreased proline and MDA contents and electrolyte leakage destruction. Tese enhanced physiochemical traits helped minimize cell damage under high salt concentrations, and consequently, increasing plant productivity.

Tis research examined the hypothesis that the over-expression of AtHKT1 in tobacco maintains plantlet $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ accumulation under $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ coercion, thus enhancing salt tolerance. Our results showed that under salinity stress, AtHKT1 gene was expressed in the xylem of stem, root and leaf vein in the transgenic tobacco, which uninstalled $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the shoot and leaves via transporting more $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ , thus, decreased the toxicity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and advanced many biophysicochemical activities that assist decrease the salt-induced hurt. Te constitution of AtHKT1 in tobacco plants promoted a conversion from osmotic imbalance to osmotic balance. An over-expression of the AtHKT1 improved the ability to keep plantlet growth even under high salt stress conditions. Tis study also provide reference for future research of crop salt tolerant improvement, over-expression AtHKT1 gene in heterologous crop may be a useful method on increasing crop production.

Background: Although the HKT transporter genes ascertain some of the key determinants of crop salt tolerance mechanisms, the diversity and functional role of group II HKT genes are not clearly understood in bread wheat. The advanced knowledge on rice HKT and whole genome sequence was, therefore, used in comparative gene analysis to identify orthologous wheat group 11HKT genes and their role in trait variation under different saline environments.

Results: The four group II HKTs in rice identified two orthologous gene families from bread wheat, including the known TaHKT2;1 gene family and a new distinctly different gene family designated as TaHKT2;2. A single copy of TaHKT2;2 was found on each homeologous chromosome arm 7AL, 7BL and 7DL and each gene was expressed in leaf blade, sheath and root tissues under non-stressed and at $2 0 0 ~ { \mathsf { m } } { \mathsf { M } }$ salt stressed conditions. The proteins encoded by genes of the TaHKT2;2 family revealed more than $9 3 \ \%$ amino acid sequence identity but ${ \leq } 5 2 ~ \%$ amino acid identity compared to the proteins encoded by TaHKT2;1 family. Specifically, variations in known critical domains predicted functional differences between the two protein families. Similar to orthologous rice genes on chromosome 6L, TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 genes were located approximately $3 1 \mathrm { k b }$ apart on wheat chromosomes 7AL, 7BL and 7DL, forming a static syntenic block in the two species. The chromosomal region on 7AL containing TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 co-located with QTL for shoot ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentration and yield in some saline environments.

Conclusion: The differences in copy number, genes sequences and encoded proteins between TaHKT2;2 homeologous genes and other group II HKT gene families within and across species likely reflect functional diversity for ion selectivity and transport in plants. Evidence indicated that neither TaHKT2;2 nor TaHKT2;1 were associated with primary root ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ uptake but TaHKT2;1 may be associated with trait variation for ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ exclusion and yield in some but not all saline environments.

Keywords: Group II $H K T ,$ IWGS, Rice genome, ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ exclusion

## 2.1. Function of HKT Transporters Is Important for Plants Tolerating Soil Salinity


Salinity has come to mean the occurrence of salts (primarily sodium chloride, NaCl) in ground water or the soil solution at levels that inhibit the growth of plants [25]. The actual concentration of salts needed to have a negative influence on plant growth varies and is dependent on many factors, including plant species, soil type and water availability [25]. From an agricultural perspective, soil is usually considered saline when the electrical conductivity (ECe) of the soil solution exceeds $4 ~ \mathrm { d S / m }$ [24,25]. Both intra- and inter-specific natural variation in salinity tolerance exists in plants [24,26]. Sensitive species, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa, struggle to survive in the presence of $1 0 0 \ : \mathrm { m M N a C l }$ , whereas Atriplex amnicola (saltbush) can complete its lifecycle in $6 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl [24]. Intraspecific variation is common and probably best documented in cereals [27,28]. The mechanisms that result in salt tolerance and account for variation within and between species are numerous, but unsurprisingly, solute transport proteins are often critical, particularly those involved in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport [24,29].

HKT proteins have been characterised predominantly as monovalent cation transporters [30], although reports of $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ permeability in some members has been proposed sporadically [31,32]. HKT proteins-mediated transport of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ is known to be an important component of salinity tolerance in several species, including Arabidopsis [26,33,34], rice [22,28,35] and wheat [36–38]. HKT genes are frequently discovered underlying quantitative trait loci (QTL) that explain significant variation in salinity tolerance within mapping populations of wheat [37,39,40]. It has been demonstrated that a wide range of alleles for specific HKT genes can be present and that differences in these alleles may explain a component of the natural variation in salinity tolerance in Arabidopsis [26,41]. For example, Baxter and co-workers [26,41] used genome-wide association mapping, genetic complementation and gene expression studies to identify cis-regulatory expression level polymorphisms at the AtHKT1;1 locus. Some reports challenge the assumption that $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ exclusion leads to better salinity tolerance [26,27], with either no correlation or higher $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ concentration in the shoot and lower HKT expression correlating with better salt tolerance, while many other reports find the opposite [28,37]. Regardless, HKT alleles are an important component of salt tolerance conferred by either strategy. This paradox may be explained by simultaneous differences and natural variation in the other components that underpin salinity tolerance, such as the ability to tolerate the effects of salt accumulation in the shoot or cope with the osmotic components of salinity [24].

The important function of HKTs in assisting plants to survive high soil salinity has been confirmed in gene knockout experiments that made plants more sensitive to salt [33,34,42] and through transgenic expression of HKT genes in other plant species, i.e., expression of the AtHKT1;1 gene in rice allowed the rice plants to grow better under saline conditions [35].

While it is clearly very beneficial to manipulate HKT gene expression in crop plants to improve their salinity tolerance in some instances, as recently demonstrated by Munns et al. [36], it is important to properly understand function, regulation and expression patterns of the HKT transporters to achieve the desired result. For example, Møller et al. [43] overexpressed the Arabidopsis HKT1;1 gene using a constitutive promoter and a promoter that was specific for stele cells of roots. Transgenic plants overexpressing AtHKT1;1 constitutively accumulated large amounts of salt in the shoot and were relatively more salt sensitive than control plants, whilst plants over-expressing the same gene specifically in root stele cells accumulated less salt in the shoot and became more salt tolerant [43]. Evidence also exists that different HKT proteins may have different roles within a plant, so it is important to choose the correct allele, when modifying HKT expression to improve salt tolerance. TmHKT1;5-A is located in the cells around the root xylem, where the transporter moves $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ down its electrochemical gradient, which in most physiological circumstances is likely to be out of the xylem [36]. Similarly, AtHKT1;1 is thought to be present around xylem and phloem tissues in the root and shoot, and it also increases $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ retention in the root directly [44]. AtHKT1;1 has also been proposed to recirculate $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ in the phloem, although this function has been questioned [24,30,34]. The possible involvement of HKTs in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ recirculation is still controversial and has been discussed in detail in a recent review by Hauser and Horie [45]. On the other hand, TaHKT2;1, OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;4 appear to be expressed in the outer part of the root, including root hairs, and may actually provide an entry point for $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ into plant roots from the soil solution. In these circumstances, downhill electrochemical gradient for $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ entry into plant cells is proposed to assist with high affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry into roots when $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is at low concentrations in the soil solution [32,46–48]. With this in mind, it is clearly important to have a comprehensive understanding of how a particular HKT protein functions, before attempting to manipulate expression of that HKT or the selection of that allele and its promoter to increase the productivity of a plant species or a variety grown in saline soil.


## 2.2. Ion Selectivity of HKT Transporters


The discovery of plant HKT proteins was made by Schachtman and Schroeder [46], who identified a plant transport protein, which could rescue a mutant yeast strain (Saccharomyces cerevisiae CY162) defective in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport. A cDNA of the wheat-root plasmid encoding the HKT1 gene permitted mutant yeast growing on media containing $3 0 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ [46]. These authors subsequently expressed this HKT1 gene in Xenopus laevis oocytes and showed that the resulting transport protein was selective for the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions, while allowing transport of some $\mathrm { C s } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ , but only of trace amounts of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ . For these reasons, this transport protein was subsequently designated as a “High-affinity Potassium Transporter” (HKT) [46]. However, this protein, now known as TaHKT2;1 [49], is now thought to be a $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ symporter at micromolar concentrations of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and a $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ uniporter at millimolar concentrations of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ , after more detailed analysis in Xenopus oocytes [50,51].

There are numerous HKT genes in commercially important grain species [46], but there is only one in the model plant Arabidopsis, designated AtHKT1;1 [52,53]. Most functional studies have indicated that HKT proteins are monovalent cation transporters, with the cation selectivity varying between individual members of the HKT family [46,54,55], although some findings have suggested divalent cation transport by HKT proteins [31,32]. Some HKT proteins are highly selective for $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ , while others are more promiscuous and will move $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , e.g., OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;2, respectively [55]. Further, some HKT proteins even change their selectivity depending on an ionic environment, e.g., EcHKT1;1 [56]. Many individual HKT genes have now been cloned and expressed in various heterologous systems, to evaluate and characterise transport selectivity and behaviour of the specific HKT transport protein. These includes HvHKT2;1 expressed in yeast [57], AtHKT1;1 in Xenopus oocytes [34], yeast [53] and $E$ . coli [53], EcHKT1;1 and EcHKT1;2 in Xenopus oocytes and $E .$ . coli [56,58] and TaHKT2;1 expressed in yeast and Xenopus oocytes [46,50]. These experiments in heterologous systems describe HvHKT2;1 as a $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ selective uniporter [57] and OsHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;1 as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symporters at low $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ concentrations and a $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ uniporter at high $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ concentrations [34,46,50,53,59]. EcHKT1;1 and EcHKT1;2 have been reported to be permeable to $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ , as well as being $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symporters, even at high $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ concentrations [56,58]. Several authors have observed $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symport by the AtHKT1;1, HvHKT1;5, Ni-OsHKT1;5 and Po-OsHKT1;5 proteins in yeast, which has not been observed in Xenopus oocytes [46,57,60]. These observations lead to uncertainty, as to what would be the actual behaviour of HKT proteins in planta.

This uncertainty is compounded by paucity of direct evidence showing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symport in wheat [61], barley [62] and rice [63] roots, calling into question the putative role of HKT2-type proteins in plants in the uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficient conditions, using the electrochemical gradient for $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ [57,64]. This means that either the results from heterologous systems are incorrect or the activity of the HKTs in planta has been masked in these particular experiments through the activity of other plant proteins or in the specific conditions imposed. At the same time, there is evidence of HKT activity from plants that mirrors the activity found in oocytes and yeast for instance $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symport in Arabidopsis [65] and for OsHKT2;1 in a plant cell expression system [55]. Speculation as to the accuracy of extrapolating HKT function in planta from heterologous systems has been called into question by a number of groups for reasons ranging from artefacts induced by the choice of vector used for protein overexpression to the inadvertent ascribing of endogenous channel activity of heterologous systems to that of HKTs [48,66]. This extends to the observation of divalent cation transport $\left( \mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + } \right.$ and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ) by OsHKT2;4 when expressed in Xenopus oocytes [32], which could not be reproduced in a subsequent study [48]. This is something that the researchers need to be mindful of, when interpreting data from various heterologous expression systems [55,66].

While the transport selectivity of some HKT transporters is well established, the actual mechanism of transport is less clear. Whether HKT predominantly mediates $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , there have been several proposed mechanisms as to how the HKT proteins mediate movement of these ions. It was originally suggested that $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symport may provide the gradient needed to move ions across the plasma membrane [46,67], although subsequent experimental evidence seemed to suggest that this is unlikely. Active transport by HKT proteins powered by the ATP hydrolysis has been ruled out, due to the lack of a recognisable ATP-binding domain [46]. Both in vitro and in planta experiments now indicate that the most likely mechanism of HKT proteins is to facilitate the movement of monovalent cations down their electrophysiological gradient [24,68]. Some HKTs potentially having $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symport capacity when either the $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ gradient allows the other ion to enter cells against its electrochemical gradient [50,56,59]; however, this mechanism is highly dependent on specific ionic conditions imposed on heterologous systems, which may not be relevant to in planta function. Before manipulating HKT-mediated cation movement in planta within the context of altering salinity tolerance in plants, it would be beneficial to describe the characteristics of transport mechanisms of monovalent cations by HKT proteins in general. It would also be useful to know what the structural determinants of selectivity are for specific HKT.

Expression patterns and tissue localisation varies significantly between different HKT transporters, likely reflecting in planta function of the individual proteins [32,34,44]. There is a consensus that all HKT proteins characterised so far are plasma membrane IMPs [24,32,34,44,45]. Tissue localisation however, varies significantly. OsHKT1;5 [22] and TaHKT1;5 [37] are expressed in the cells around the root xylem in rice and wheat, while OsHKT1;4 [22] and TaHKT1;4 [38] are expressed in the corresponding cells in the leaf sheath. AtHKT1;1, on the other hand, is expressed around the phloem and xylem tissues in Arabidopsis [33,34]. TaHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;1 have quite different localisation though, as these proteins appear to be expressed on the exterior of root and root hairs rather than around the vascular tissue [32,46] and assist with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ entry into roots [69].

## 3.1. HKT1 synthesis and characterization


The genomic DNA sequence of FaHKT1 and FcHKT1 were obtained on the basis of the nucleotide HKT1 sequence predicted for $F$ . vesca and cloned. Both genes have three exons with an open reading frame encoding proteins of 534 amino acids. FaHKT1 and FcHKT1 proteins showed identities of $9 9 . 6 \%$ between them and with the predicted protein of the Fragaria plant model $F _ { \cdot }$ . vesca (FvHKT1). Additionally, both proteins showed a similarity of $67 \%$ with the AtHKT1;1 protein (Uozumi et al., 2000) of the dicot plant model

A. thaliana. Supporting information 4 shows the alignment of FaHKT1, FcHKT1, FvHKT1, AtHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;1 from the monocot model Oryza sativa.

Structurally, HKT transporters consist of 8 transmembrane segments and 4 poreforming loops (P1-P4; Supporting Information 4). HKT transporters of higher plants are phylogenetically classified in two classes (Platten et al., 2006). A residue in the selectivity filter of the first pore loop was identified as a class indicator. Members of the class I have a characteristic serine (S) residue in P1, while the other three pore-forming loops (P2, P3, and P4) have glycines (G) at the equivalent positions. The four characteristic residues of the four P-loops form the structural motif SGGG. The Class II has most often only Gs at the respective position of selectivity filter (GGGG) (Mäser et al., 2002; Platten et al., 2006). The presence of S is associated with a preference for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport over other cations, while the presence of G allows HKT transporters to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in addition to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ with varying $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ permeability ratios. (Horie et al., 2007; Mian et al., 2011; Sassi et al., 2012). The obtained HKTs of strawberries have a S $( \mathbf { S } 8 7 )$ as the first residue in the selectivity filter in the first pore-forming loop (Supporting Information 4). According to the sequence and phylogenetic analysis (Supporting Information 4 and 5), FaHKT1 and FcHKT1 are clearly class I HKT transporters (Corratgé-Faillie et al., 2010; Hauser and Horie, 2010; Horie et al., 2009; Platten et al., 2006).


## 3.2. Electrophysiological characterization of FaHKT1


Because the HKT1 transporters obtained from $F$ . x ananassa and $F _ { \cdot }$ . chiloensis differed only in 9 amino acids at positions that are not expected to influence fundamentally transporter properties, we concentrated our study of the functional features of strawberry HKT1s on FaHKT1 after expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes. Electrophysiological analyses showed that this transporter is able to mediate both inward and outward currents (Figure 1), like most other members of the HKT family previously characterized (Jabnoune et al., 2009; Ren et al., 2005; Uozumi et al., 2000). FaHKT1 is highly $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } .$ -selective. Under constant extracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , increasing external $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ between 0.3 and $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ strongly stimulated inward current and shifted the reversal potential towards more positive potentials (depolarization). In contrast, when $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was kept constant and the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration was varied, increases in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ did not affect significantly the reversal potential. Interestingly, external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ appears to block the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ currents through FaHKT1 (Figure 1D). The preference of FaHKT1 for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ over $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ was similar to that reported previously for AtHKT1;1 (Mäser et al., 2002; Uozumi et al., 2000). This becomes also evident when comparing the ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } .$ -dependence and the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -dependence of the reversal potentials of FaHKT1 with the theoretical values of a sodium-selective (Figure 1E, left) and potassium-selective channel (Figure 1E, right). The dashed lines in Figure 1E show perfect "Nernst behavior" ( $5 9 ~ \mathrm { m V }$ change per 10-fold concentration change). The slopes of the experimental curves are zero in the case of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and slightly smaller than that of a perfectly selective channel in the case of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . This divergence indicates that FaHKT1 does not only carry $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , although the transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is clearly favored over other ions. Instead, the voltage-dependent blocking effect of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Figure 1D) points to an influence of this ion on the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ permeation. The absolute values of the reversal potential indicated that the sodium concentration in FaHKT1 expressing oocytes equilibrated with the storage solution as expected for cells that over-express non-regulated open $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ channels. With $9 6 \mathrm { m M }$ internal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ the reversal potentials are predicted to be $- 2 9 \ \mathrm { m V }$ ( $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ external $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ ), and $- 5 7 \mathrm { m V }$ ( $1 0 \mathrm { m M }$ external $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ ). In summary, FaHKT1 mediates the entry of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and marginally also probably other cations including $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ , similar to AtHKT1;1 (Uozumi et al., 2000).

As next, the effects of changes in the extracellular $\mathrm { p H }$ and the application of $\mathrm { L } \mathfrak { a } ^ { 3 + }$ , $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ were evaluated. A change of the external $\mathsf { p H }$ from 7.4 to 5.6 did not influence the FaHKT1-mediated currents (Supporting information 6A). The addition of $1 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { L a } ^ { 3 + }$ to the solution, which is a generic blocker of ion channels (Demidchik and Maathuis, 2010), resulted in a weak block of the transporter (Supporting information 6B). On the other hand, the addition of $1 0 \mathrm { \ m M \ C a } ^ { 2 + }$ slightly reduced the magnitude of the current (Supporting information 6C). It has been reported that some members of the HKT family are blocked by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ as EcHKT1;2 or OsHKT2;1 (Fairbairn et al., 2000; Yao et al., 2010). The addition of $1 0 \mathrm { \ m M \ C s } ^ { + }$ blocked the FaHKT1 current in a voltage-independent manner (Supporting information 6D). The homologous transporter in Arabidopsis (AtHKT1;1) is not permeable to $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ (Uozumi et al., 2000). However, another member of the class I, McHKT1, has been reported to have larger permeability for $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ than for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Su et al., 2003) and some members of the class II as OsHKT2;1 are also permeable for $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ under certain conditions (Jabnoune et al., 2009). Inhibition by $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport was also observed in several HKTs from class I or II (Jabnoune et al., 2009).


## 3.3. FaAKT1 synthesis and characterization


From genomic AKT1 sequences of $F .$ . x ananassa and $F _ { \cdot }$ . chiloensis the coding sequences of FaAKT1 and FcAKT1 were obtained using the “USER cloning” strategy (GeuFlores et al., 2007; Nour-Eldin et al., 2006, 2010). These genes have open reading frames that encode proteins of 893 amino acids. Both encoded proteins, FaAKT1 and FcAKT1 have a very high identity of $9 9 . 7 \%$ and share an identity of $9 9 . 1 \%$ with the predicted protein FvAKT1 from $F .$ . vesca. Moreover, FaAKT1 and FcAKT1 share $6 8 . 1 \%$ identity and $8 0 . 8 \%$ similarity with AtAKT1 from $A$ . thaliana.

Structurally, AKT1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels are tetramers (Dreyer et al., 2004; Dreyer and Blatt, 2009; Dreyer and Uozumi, 2011; Lebaudy et al., 2008) and each subunit is formed by six transmembrane domains. The voltage-sensor comprises the first four segments S1-S4 followed by the pore module formed by transmembrane segments S5 and S6 with the selectivity filter and the pore helix (P) in between them. The selectivity filter, which selects $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over other cations, is formed by the conserved motif TxGYGD (Supporting information 7) (Aqvist and Luzhkov, 2000) and suggests that these channels have a high selectivity towards $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , like other AKT1 channels described in plants (Becker et al., 1996; Bertl et al., 1997; Boscari et al., 2009; Buschmann et al., 2000; Fuchs et al., 2005; Uozumi et al., 1995). Phylogenetic analysis of FaAKT1 and FcAKT1 grouped these proteins within the AKT1 group of Shaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Gomez-Porras et al., 2012; Pilot et al., 2003b; Supporting information 8).


## 3.4. Electrophysiological characterization of FaAKT1


Because FaAKT1 and FcAKT1 differ in only 3 amino acids in the cytosolic C-terminus we focused on the protein from $F .$ . x ananassa in our electrophysiological characterization. The functional properties of FaAKT1 were studied in Xenopus laevis oocytes in coexpression with AtCBL1-AtCIPK23 (Geiger et al., 2009; Li et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006). FaAKT1 currents were activated by membrane hyperpolarization. Currents increased with increasing potassium concentrations (Figure 2). These currents can be completely blocked at voltages more negative than $- 1 4 0 \mathrm { m V }$ by the addition of $1 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { C s C l }$ to the bath (not shown).

Tail currents (Figure 2A, B) were used to study the effect of changes in the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration on the reversal potential of the channel. With a decreasing concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ , the $V _ { r e \nu }$ moves to more negative voltages. Reversal potentials of AKT1 (- $- 3 6 \mathrm { m V }$ for K30 and $- 9 \mathrm { m V }$ for K100) are very similar to those described for channels only selective to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Weber, 1999). They correlate well with theoretical potential of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ balance calculated by the Nernst equation (Hille, 2001), which confirms that FaAKT1 is a channel highly selective to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ .

FaAKT1 is an inward rectifying highly $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ selective and $\mathrm { C s } ^ { + } .$ -sensitive channel like its homologs AtAKT1 from Arabidopsis thaliana (Gaymard et al., 1996; Li et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2013), DKT1 from Daucus carota (Formentin et al., 2004), LKT1 from Solanum lycopersicum (Hartje et al., 2000), HvAKT1 from Hordeum vulgare (Boscari et al., 2009) and OsAKT1 from Oryza sativa (Fuchs et al., 2005).


## 3.5. Expression of AKT1 in Fragaria spp. under NaCl treatment


$F _ { \cdot }$ . x ananassa and $F .$ . chiloensis HKT1 and AKT1 encode functional proteins, with similar properties as HKT1 and AKT1 homologs from other plants. Next, the effect of salt stress on the expression of HKT1 and AKT1 in three genotypes of Fragaria spp. with different ecological adaptations was assessed. The commercial cultivar of $F .$ . x ananassa Camarosa, the cultivated accession of $F .$ . chiloensis Bau and the wild accession of $F$ . chiloensis Cucao were used for that purpose.

Several studies have reported that potassium channels of the AKT1 type are the main pathways for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake by plants (Nieves-Cordones et al., 2014). They are located mostly in the roots, especially in epidermis, cortex and endodermis (Boscari et al., 2009; Hartje et al., 2000; Lagarde et al., 1996; Wang and Wu, 2013). The evaluation of the relative expression of AKT1 in roots of the three strawberry genotypes grown in $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l }$ for 7 days showed differences in gene expression patterns in response to the salinity stress (Figure 3). In roots of $F _ { \cdot }$ . x ananassa cv. Camarosa, the applied salt concentration significantly induced the expression of AKT1 only $6 \textup { h }$ after initiation of the treatment; at all other time points the expression level was similar to that observed initially (Fig. 3A). Also in the roots of $F .$ . chiloensis accession Bau, no changes were observed in the relative expression of AKT1 over time (Fig. 3B), while the expression pattern in the roots of $F .$ . chiloensis accession Cucao showed larger variations. Notable is a significant decrease (by a factor of ${ \sim } 3$ ) at $6 \mathrm { h }$ (Fig. 6C).

Previous studies with both glycophytic and halophytic plants have shown a wide spectrum of changes in the expression of AKT1 genes in response to salt stress (Duan et al., 2015; Fuchs et al., 2005; Golldack et al., 2003; Mekawy et al., 2015; Su et al., 2001). However, several studies on both sensitive and salt tolerant plants report no effect of NaCl treatment on the expression of AKT1 in roots: This was observed in Arabidopsis thaliana (Oh et al., 2010; Pilot et al., 2003a), in the rice variety IR29, which is relatively sensitive to salinity (Golldack et al., 2003), and in the monocot halophyte Puccinellia tenuiflora (Ardie et al., 2010). AKT1-like channels have other regulatory mechanisms that efficiently control its activity (Fig. 4). Apart from its regulation by phosphorylation (Geiger et al., 2009; Li et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006), these are predominantly (i) its voltage-dependent activation and (ii) its ability to form heteromeric channels with other $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel subunits.

Salinity is typically related to relatively little $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the soil, which usually results in a depolarization of the cell caused by the entry of large amounts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Shabala et al., 2003; 2005). Under these conditions, K selective AKT1 channels would mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux rather than influx (Fig. 4; Gambale and Uozumi, 2006; Véry et al., 2014). However, the activation of AKT1-like channels upon hyperpolarization and their deactivation upon depolarization (Véry and Sentenac, 2003) provoke a strong reduction of AKT1 activity under salt stress conditions. Additionally, as shown in Arabidopsis, the expression of the K channel subunit AtKC1 is strongly increased upon salt stress (Pilot et al., 2003a). This subunit negatively regulates AKT1 through heteromerization (Geiger et al., 2009). Thus, several mechanisms different from transcriptional regulation contribute to the downregulation of AKT1 activity to limit $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ loss during salt stress (Fig. 4). It is therefore likely that the role of AKT1 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake by roots in salt stress conditions is limited. For maintaining the levels of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in plants under salt stress, membrane transporters such as KT/KUP/HAK might play more important roles; they have not been studied exhaustively yet, but an increase of their expression at low concentrations of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ has been shown in Arabidopsis (Gierth et al., 2005), as well as in rice and barley (Bañuelos et al., 2002; Rubio et al., 2000).


## 3.6. Expression of HKT1 in Fragaria spp. under NaCl treatment


The HKT transporter of Fragaria spp. characterized in this study belongs to the group I. By analogy to its orthologue from A. thaliana AtHKT1;1, it might be postulated to be also located in xylem parenchyma cells of roots, retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the xylem sap into cells of the xylem parenchyma (Fig. 4). Thereby, it would prevent excessive amounts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to reach the shoot with the transpiration flow, which is related to salinity tolerance (Horie et al., 2005; Møller et al., 2009; Plett et al., 2010). The role of HKT to improve the performance of plants in saline soils has been demonstrated in $A$ . thaliana by silencing AtHKT1;1, which increased the sensitivity of the plants to salinity (Berthomieu et al., 2003; Davenport et al., 2007; Mäser et al., 2002). Additionally, the expression of AtHKT1;1 in rice allowed plants to grow better in saline conditions (Plett et al., 2010). A similar role as AtHKT1; $I$ in $A$ . thaliana has been reported for transporters OsHKT1;4/5 in rice (Cotsaftis et al., 2012; Horie et al., 2005; Ren et al., 2005) and TaHKT1;4/5 in wheat (James et al., 2006).

The evaluation of the relative expression profiles of HKT1 in roots of the three strawberry genotypes showed differences between them in response to salinity (Figure 3DF). In roots of $F$ . $x$ ananassa cv. Camarosa, salt stress induced a slight increase in the expression of HKT1 at 6 and $^ { 1 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ after initiation of treatment with NaCl (Fig. 3D). In roots of $F _ { \cdot }$ . chiloensis accession Bau, no clear trend in the relative expression of HKT1 was observed (Fig. 3E). However, in roots of $F _ { \cdot }$ . chiloensis accession Cucao, a significant increase in the relative expression of HKT1 at 12 and $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ after starting the stress was observed (Fig. 3F). Thereafter, the amount of transcripts returns to the baseline.

A previous study showed that genotype ʻCucaoʼ of $F _ { \cdot }$ . chiloensis was more tolerant to salinity than the other two strawberry genotypes evaluated (Garriga et al., 2015). Therefore, the increase of the relative expression of HKT1 in the roots of ʻCucaoʼ could be related to a greater retention of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the roots, preventing excessive accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in photosynthetic tissues and thereby increasing its tolerance to salinity (Fig. 4). Although in this study the changes in the concentrations of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaves and roots as a result of salt stress could not be determined, in a previous study the effect of a long-term salt stress in these three strawberry genotypes was evaluated. Plants of ʻCucaoʼ grown in $6 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ over 104 days had the lowest sodium accumulation in comparison to unstressed plants. The concentration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ increased 4.9 and 2.7-fold in leaves and roots, respectively. These increases were significantly lower than those observed for instance in plants of ʻCamarosaʼ, where $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ increased 34-fold in leaves and 11-fold in roots (Garriga et al., 2015). The better performance of ´Cucao´ could be related to an increase of active HKT1 proteins, as observed in the analysis of relative gene expression.

Although the “exclusion model” of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem of roots and the major involvement of HKT transporters is well studied in Arabidopsis and other plants of economic importance (Horie et al., 2005; Møller et al., 2009; Plett et al., 2010), the mechanisms that control the levels of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are still largely unknown. There is no evidence in A. thaliana of a direct role of AtHKT1; $I$ in the transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Møller et al., 2009). However, it has been hypothesized that the entry of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem via HKT1;1 results in a depolarization of xylem parenchyma cells, which in turn provokes an activation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux channels that then release $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the xylem (Horie et al., 2005), helping to maintain a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio favorable for plant metabolism.

Trk/Ktr/HKT transporters probably were evolved from simple $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ channels KcsA. HKT transporters, which mediate ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + } .$ -uniport or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ -symport, maintain ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis and increase salinity tolerance, can be classified into three subfamilies in higher plants. In this review, we systematically analyzed the characteristics of amino acids sequences and physiological functions of HKT transporters in higher plant. Furthermore, we depicted the hypothetical models of cations selection and transportation mediated by HKT transporters according to the highly conserved structure for the goal of better understanding the cations transportation processes.
