Plant NPF (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER FAMILY) proteins display sequence homology with the proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter (POT) family of peptide transporters, belong to the large peptide transporter (PTR) family [1] and are involved in dietary nitrogen absorption in the form of di- and tripeptides [2,3]. In plants, NPF members are initially characterized as nitrate or peptide transporters. AtNPF6.3, known as AtNRT1.1, is the first plant member discovered as a nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis [4], and the crystal structure of AtNPF6.3 recently determined showed the similarity with PTRs in the bacterial [5,6]. Subsequently, some NPF members are identified in different plants and demonstrated that they behave as dipeptide transporters [7,8]. So, nitrate/peptide transport function is believed to be a specific feature of this family in plants over a period of time. However, in recent years, several studies demonstrated that some NPF members could transport an even wider range of substrates, including nitrite, chloride, auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs), and gibberellins (GAs) and glucosinolates [9–12]. Additionally, some of the NPF members are even able to transport more than one different substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, peptides/amino acids, or GA/JA.

After identifying the first nitrate transporter NPF6.3/NRT1.1, Tsay et al. [4,8] subsequently characterized more than half of the NPF nitrate transporters. So far, more than

21 NPF members have been demonstrated to be able to transport nitrate in Arabidopsis, many of which are able to transport other substrates, such as ABA, GA, JA and glucosinolates [8,13]. Screening 45 out of 53 AtNPF members using a modified yeast two-hybrid system with ABA, GA and JA-Ile specific receptor complexes, Chiba et al. [14] confirmed that nine NPF members had an ABA transport function, $1 8 ~ N P F$ members were able to transport GA and 13 NPF members were able to transport the bioactive JA/JA-Ile. NRT1.1/NPF6.3 was confirmed to be able to transport IAA and 2,4-D [15,16]. In addition, PTR3/NPF5.2, PTR1/NPF8.1, PTR5/NPF8.2 and PTR2/NTR1/NPF8.3 were identified as dipeptide and tripeptide transporters using complementation of yeast strains deficient for peptide uptake [17,18].

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ , as the essential element of amino acid, nucleic acid, chlorophyll, and among other biologically important molecules, is vital to plant growth and development. In aerated soils, plants take up nitrogen mainly in the form of nitrate due to intensive nitrification processes. In plants, nitrate can be absorbed and translocated through transmembrane proteins, which mainly consist of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF) and NRT2 (see excellent reviews by $\mathrm { X u }$ et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2018b). There are 53, 93, and 91 NPF genes in Arabidopsis, rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Leran et al. 2014). Most NPFs are responsible for low-affinity nitrate transporter activity $\mathrm { ~ ( > ~ 0 . 5 ~ m M } _ { \mathrm { ~ , ~ } }$ (Epstein et al. 1963; Noguero and Lacombe 2016), except for CHL1/NRT1.1/ AtNPF6.3, which was the first NPF to be found and cloned, displays a dual affinity property (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999). There are 7, 4, 7, and 5 NRT2 genes in Arabidopsis, rice, Brachypodium, and Sorghum, respectively (Orsel et al. 2002, Cai et al. 2008; Massel et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018a, b). In general, all of NRT2s are responsible for high-affinity nitrate transport $( < 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ). Additionally, a third family, named as NAR2/NRT3, requires interacting with most NRT2 members to transport nitrate (Zhou et al. 2000; Orsel et al. 2006; Yan et al. 2011; Kotur et al. 2012), except for AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al.

2012). There are 2, 2, and 3 NRT3 members in Arabidopsis, Rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Plett et al. 2010; Massel et al. 2016). Beside nitrate, NPF family transport diverse components as substrates, including dipeptides, glucosinolate, IAA, ABA, GA, and JA (Leran et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2018a). By contrast, NRT2 members have been only reported to transport nitrate so far.

Based on a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis from 31 fully sequenced plant genomes (Lee et al. 2011), NPF family can be classified into 8 unambiguous clades. Members from NPF1 subfamily have been shown to be involved in redistributing nitrate to developing tissues. For example, AtNPF1.1/NRT1.12 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.11 are expressed in companion cells (CC) of the primary vein, and their double mutant is deficient in remobilizing nitrate to younger leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013). Similarly, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7 is expressed in the phloem of the minor vein in mature leaves and is responsible for nitrate remobilization under nitrogen deficiency (Fan et al. 2009). Additionally, many other NPF2 family members (including AtNPF2.3, AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, OsNPF2.2, and OsNPF2.4) are involved in nitrate translocation from root to shoot (Wang and Tsay 2011; Li et al. 2015; Taochy et al. 2015; Xia et al. 2015). AtNPF2.12/NRT1.6 can mediate nitrate influx to premature embryos (Almagro et al. 2008). In addition to nitrate, two NPF2 members (AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5) are able to transport chloride (Li et al. 2016, 2017); five NPF2 members (AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, AtNPF2.10/ GTR1, AtNPF2.11/GTR2, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7, and AtNPF2.14) are able to transport glucosinolate, which is one of the important secondary metabolites for plant defense (Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). AtNPF3.1, originally identified as a nitrate/nitrite transporter, is found to be a GA transporter which is also affected by nitrate availability (Sugiura et al. 2007; Pike et al. 2014; David et al. 2016; Tal et al. 2016). AtNPF4.6/NRT1.2 has been characterized as a constitutive nitrate transporter (Huang et al. 1999), as well as an ABA transporter (Kanno et al. 2012). As the largest subfamily, three NPF5 members (AtNPF5.11, AtNPF5.12, AtNPF5.16) are responsible for nitrate efflux from tonoplast (He et al. 2017), AtNPF5.5 is involved in nitrate accumulation in embryos (Leran et al. 2015). Moreover, AtNPF5.2/PTR3 can transport dipeptide, which is important for plant pathogen defense (Karim et al. 2007). AtNPF6.3 is the most heavily studied member of the family, and it is a dual-affinity nitrate transporter (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999), auxin transporter (Krouk et al. 2010); it affects stomata opening (Guo et al. 2003) and also serves as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). Interestingly, indica rice OsNRT1.1B/OsNPF6.5, one of the closest orthologous genes of AtNPF6.3 with only a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) with japonica rice $O s N R T I . I B /$ OsNPF6.5, is responsible for better nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in indica rice (Hu et al. 2015). Recently, OsNRT1.1B is reported to facilitate Selenomethinone (Se) translocation in both roots and leaves, and the overexpression lines exhibit a higher Se accumulation in grains (Zhang et al. 2018b). AtNPF6.2/NRT1.4 is specifically expressed in leaf petiole, which is critical for nitrate storage in petiole (Chiu et al. 2004). AtNPF7.2/NRT1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 expressed in close proximity of xylem and their functions are antagonistic upon stress challenges (Li et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2014). The NPF8 subfamily (NPF8.1/PTR1, NPF8.2/PTR5, and NPF8.3/PTR2) in Arabidopsis transports dipeptide and has no detectable nitrate transport activity (Komarova et al. 2009), whereas OsNRT1/ NPF8.9 is a putative nitrate transporter in rice (Lin et al. 2000).

Compared to the large and complex NPF family, NRT2 and NRT3 families in plants are relatively small. There is a clear divergence between monocots and dicots of NRT2 family genes, suggesting NRT2 in monocots may function differently from heavily-studied AtNRT2 (Plett et al. 2010; Wang et al. 2018a, b). It has been well-documented that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are nitrate-inducible transporters, which are major components for high-affinity root nitrate uptake (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 are also involved in high-affinity root nitrate uptake but mainly upon nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Besides, AtNRT2.1 can serve as a signal transducer to regulate lateral root growth (Little et al. 2005). NRT2.7 is the only NRT2 member located on the tonoplast membrane and is responsible for nitrate transport in seeds (Chopin et al. 2007). In rice, OsNRT2.3b responds to pH changes and its overexpression leads to grain yield increase (Fan et al. 2016). Additionally, overexpressing OsNRT2.1 driven by the NAR2.1/NRT3.1 promoter is also able to enhance grain yield in rice (Chen et al. 2016). The importance of NRT3/NAR2 is underlined by their coexpression and interaction with NRT2 genes. All AtNRT2 members except for AtNRT2.7 can interact with NRT3.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Nevertheless, AtNRT3.1 is not indispensable for nitrate uptake mediated by AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al. 2012).

Sugarcane is one of the most productive crops in the world (FAOSTAT, 2016; http://www.fao.org/statistics/en/) and it accounts for $80 \%$ of world sugar supply and $40 \%$ of ethanol production (Zhang et al. 2013). N deficiencies can cause a decreased chlorophyll synthesis as well as a reduced biomass. Together with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, N makes up $90 \%$ of sugarcane dry matter (Brandes 1952). Sugarcane mainly absorbs N through $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilizers or biological nitrogen fixation owing to microbial nitrogen fixers (Boddey et al. 2003). Unfortunately, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is low for agronomic crops, especially for sugarcane, more than $50 \%$ of nitrogen is lost through surface run-off, leaching, denitrifications or volatilizations (Garnett et al. 2009). Only $20 \%$ (or less) of input N can be found in dry biomass of sugarcane at harvest (Franco et al. 2011). Therefore, understanding nitrogen uptake, translocation and utilization is key to improve NUE by conventional breeding and genetic engineering strategy. However, the genetic information for nitrate transporters is still missing in sugarcane, largely due to the lack of a complete genome information. Recently, an allele-defined genome of sugarcane Saccharum spontaneum L. became available (Zhang et al. 2018a), offering an excellent opportunity to identify nitrate transporter families at a genome-wide scale. In this study, we carried out a BLAST search using Arabidopsis and Sorghum NPF/NRTs against newly available sugarcane genome. Phylogenetic analysis, gene structure as well as protein motif analysis were conducted to understand molecular and evolutionary relationships between subfamilies and species. Moreover, RNA-Seq data were analyzed to investigate tissue-specific expression pattern across all NPF/ NRT genes in S. spontaneum. Our results presented a comprehensive characterization of sugarcane NPF/NRT genes, which laid the foundation for future investigations of these nitrogen transporters in sugarcane.

The plant NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (NRT1/PTR FAMILY or NPF) encodes membrane proteins involved in various substrates: nitrate, nitrite, amino acids, glucosinolates, peptide, and hormone transport. All these transporters display 12 predicted transmembrane domains. Phylogenetic analysis divides the NPF family into eight clades (Le´ran et al. 2014). The different subfamilies have various substrate specificities, and some members are able to transport more than one substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, or peptides/amino acids. The first plant member identified was the plant transceptor NPF6.3 (NRT1.1/CHL1), able to transport nitrate in low- and high-affinity transport systems (LATS and HATS, respectively) and to sense nitrate (Bouguyon et al. 2015). In addition, NPF6.3 is also able to transport IAA but in competition with nitrate uptake, leading to a role in root architecture development (Krouk et al. 2010). Several other members are involved in lowaffinity nitrate transport, allowing nitrate uptake or root nitrate efflux and long-distance transport in different plant organs (for review, see Krapp et al. 2014).

The smallest subfamily of NPF contains the cucumber CsNPF3.2, the first plant nitrite transporter described, which is localized at the chloroplast inner membrane (Sugiura et al. 2007). Using transient expression, the Arabidopsis orthologue, AtNPF3.1, has been shown to be located at the plasma membrane (Pike et al. 2014), offering a new perspective regarding its function. Electrophysiology measurements of heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocyte characterized the NPF3 proteins of Arabidopsis and Grapevine as a low-affinity nitrate/nitrite transporter (Pike et al. 2014). A modified yeast-two hybrid (Y2H) system with hormone receptor complexes allowed testing the hormone uptake capacity of almost all the NPF family members (Kanno et al. 2012; Chiba et al. 2015). Using this method, NPF3.1 has been shown to transport in yeast different active forms of gibberellins (GAs) $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ (Chiba et al. 2015). Very recently, expression of NPF3.1 in Xenopus oocytes revealed its capacity to transport $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ as well (Tal et al. 2016). In the same study, the use of fluorescently labeled GAs (GA-FI) proved that AtNPF3.1 in responsible for GAs transport in planta as mutants is not able to take up this hormone, while overexpressors accumulate GA-FI in their roots (Tal et al. 2016). Previously, exogenous application of GA-FI has demonstrated that an active GA transport mechanism does exist in planta, since an accumulation of labeled GAs has been observed in elongating endodermal cells (Shani et al. 2013). Thus, this cell type seems to be a target of the bioactive GAs, although they are mainly synthesized in the meristematic and non-meristematic zones (Mitchum et al.

2006). Other numerous examples illustrate the occurrence of GA biosynthesis pathways and GA-regulated events in separated tissues (Hedden and Thomas 2012). In germinating seeds, in situ hybridization analyses demonstrated that the GA-responsive genes are not restricted to the site of active GA biosynthesis (Ogawa et al. 2003). In developing flowers, GA synthesis occurs in stamens, while GAs are required for petals growth (Plackett et al. 2011). All these results indirectly reveal the presence of GA transport mechanisms in plants.

GA hormones are diterpenoids and more than 100 GAs have been identified in plants. $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ , and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 7 }$ are known to be biologically active in plants involved in the regulation of photomorphogenesis, the other forms being precursors or products of catabolism (Yamaguchi 2008). The bioactive forms bind the GID1 receptor to trigger the degradation of DELLA through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (Feng et al. 2008). DELLA proteins repress the cell expansion, whereas GAs promote their development. This antagonist effect has been proved for root growth, leaf expansion, and floral development. GAs are involved in the elongation of hypocotyls in the light and in the dark by influencing cell elongation (de Lucas et al. 2008; Feng et al. 2008). In seeds, light and cold stimulate the GA biosynthesis, leading to the seed germination and counteracting ABA effect (Yamauchi et al. 2004; Oh et al. 2006). In Arabidopsis, nitrate has been described in the control of seed dormancy through the regulation of CYP707A2 expression, a gene involved in the ABA catabolism (Matakiadis et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010), and in hedge, mustard nitrate can also promote the expression of GA3OX2, a gene involved in the production of active GA forms (Carrillo-Barral et al. 2014). Thus, GAs are important molecules acting to promote seed germination and cell elongation particularly in hypocotyl elongation. The aim of this investigation is to understand whether NPF3.1 is involved in these processes through its capacity to transport GAs and nitrate. The capacity of numerous NPF to transport various hormones (Chiba et al. 2015) underlines a redundancy in functioning and raises the question of the substrate specificity. Therefore, to decipher the in planta function of NPF3.1 and its substrate specificity, we analyzed its expression pattern and we characterized two mutant lines at different developmental stages. Then, given these different traits, we discuss the potential role of NPF3.1 within the plant.

Developmental plasticity allows a plant to respond to nutrient availability by changing the architecture of the root system (Zhang and Forde, 2000; Linkohr et al., 2002). Nitrate is one of the major nutrients known to act as a signal molecule involved in the control of root architecture through the regulation of primary root growth and in the emergence and development of lateral roots (LR), as part of an adaptive strategy (Zhang and Forde, 1998; Zhang et al., 1999; Zhang and Forde, 2000; Tian et al., 2008; Vidal et al., 2010b; CelisArámburo et al., 2011). The molecular nature of nitrate sensing and signaling has been extensively studied in A. thaliana in relation to the regulation of LR development. At high nitrate concentrations, a systemic response suppresses LR growth after initiation at the early LR emergence stage (Zhang et al., 1999). In addition, studies have shown that when a plant is subject to nitrate deficiency, followed by the application of a high local nitrate concentration, LR growth is locally stimulated towards this most abundant source of nitrate (Zhang and Forde, 1998; Zhang et al., 1999). The localized effect of nitrate on LR growth was shown to be mediated by the dual-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF6.3 (Remans et al., 2006) and ANR1, a transcription factor of the MADS box family (Zhang and Forde, 1998). Furthermore, the finding that AtNPF6.3 transports nitrate and auxin (indoleacetic acid; IAA), provides a model in which: (i) under low nitrate conditions, AtNPF6.3 transports auxin away from the LR tip and the low content of auxin in the tip inhibits the outgrowth of LR; (ii) under high nitrate conditions, nitrate stimulates LR emergence by inhibiting AtNPF6.3 dependent auxin basipetal transport, leading to auxin accumulation in the LR tip (Krouk et al., 2010). In nonnodulated Medicago truncatula, i.e. in the absence of rhizobia, the modulation of shoot-toroot auxin transport in response to nitrate availability was shown to reduce the density of LR and this effect was mediated by the SUNN (super numeric nodules) gene (Jin et al., 2012).

The effect of nitrate on primary root growth has been less well studied compared to LR growth, although nitrate has been shown in several species to inhibit primary root growth through the alteration of hormone transport or signaling. In maize seedlings, nitrate supply resulted in a decrease in auxin content in the phloem thus decreasing auxin shoot-to-root translocation (Tian et al., 2008). In A. thaliana, nitrate was shown to regulate primary root growth by a pathway involving the auxin receptor AFB3 (Vidal et al., 2010a). Nitrate treatment induced the accumulation of the small RNA miR393 which was shown to specifically direct cleavage of AFB3 transcripts (Vidal et al., 2010a). In M. truncatula, nitrateinduced inhibition of primary root growth was altered in a mutant affected in the high-affinity nitrate transporter MtNPF1.7 also known as LATD/NIP (LATeral root organ Defective/Numerous Infections and Polyphenolics) (Harris and Dickstein, 2010; Yendrek et al., 2010; Bagchi et al., 2012). As the root architecture phenotype of npf1.7 mutants was rescued by the application of exogenous abscisic acid (ABA) (Liang et al., 2007), it is possible that the control of root architecture by nitrate in M. truncatula might involve an interaction with an ABA signaling pathway. Accordingly, the A. thaliana low-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF4.6 was shown to transport both nitrate (Huang et al., 1999) and ABA (Kanno et al., 2012). Three closely related proteins belonging to the NPF family (At1g27040 /AtAIT2 /AtNPF4.5, At3g25260 /AtAIT3 /AtNPF4.1 and At3g25280 /AtAIT4 /AtNPF4.2) were shown to transport ABA (Kanno et al., 2012).

In a previous study, we characterized the dual-affinity nitrate transporter MtNPF6.8 (MtNRT1.3) in M. truncatula (Morère-Le Paven et al., 2011; Léran et al., 2014). Based on

Apple (Malus domestica) is an economically important fruit and is widely planted worldwide. Both genetic and environmental factors affect fruit quality and yield, and nutrient absorption and utilization are very important for apple growth. Nitrogen is the most important nutrient promoting crop productivity1 . In agricultural production, effective utilization of nitrogen is the key to high plant yield, but as a great deal of nitrogen in the soil cannot be absorbed fully by plants, it is necessary to study the mechanisms and genes involved in nitrogen absorption, assimilation, and transport to improve nitrogen use efficiency.

$\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ are the major nitrogen sources in aerobic and anoxic soils, respectively2 . For most crops, nitrate is the major nitrogen source3 , and its uptake and transport by plants have been studied in depth. Nitrate is taken up into plants by nitrate transporters. To adapt to different environmental $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ concentrations in the environment, plants have evolved two $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ absorption systems, low-affinity transport systems, and high-affinity transport systems, with corresponding low affinity (NRT1) and high affinity (NRT2) $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transporters4 . In Arabidopsis, the NRT1/PTR family contains 53 members, while the NRT2 family contains 7 members5,6 . Some NRTs have also been functionally identified. For example, NRT1.1/CHL1 is both a nitrate sensor and dual-affinity nitrate transporter7,8 . NRT1.1, NRT1.2, NRT2.1, and NRT2.2 are involved in nitrate uptake9–11, NRT1.4 regulates leaf nitrate homeostasis11, NRT1.6 participates in the transfer of nitrate from maternal tissue to developing embryos12, NRT1.7 regulates nitrate remobilization from source to sink tissue13, and NRT1.9 is involved in the transport of nitrate from roots to shoots14.

NRT1.5/NPF7.3 and NRT1.8 have been confirmed as two crucial nitrate transporters for long-distance transport15. NRT1.5 is expressed predominantly in root pericycle cells and plays an important role in loading nitrate into the xylem, while NRT1.8 is mainly expressed in xylem parenchyma cells and plays a major role in unloading nitrate from xylem sap10. Under normal conditions, NRT1.5 loads nitrate from roots into xylem vessels (from which it is transferred to aerial tissues), whereas NRT1.8 unloads nitrate into xylem parenchyma cells15. Microarray analysis demonstrated that NRT1.5 and NRT1.8 have opposite regulatory patterns under various abiotic and biotic stresses4 . Nitrate reallocation to plant roots often occurs under stress; a previous study indicated that drought, cadmium, and salt treatments reduced the expression of NRT1.5, and the transcription of the abiotic stress-responsive genes $N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + }$ EXCHANGER1 (NHX1), SALTS OVERLY SENSITIVE1 (SOS1), RESPONSIVE TO DESICCATION29A (RD29A), and nitrate transporter NRT1.8 was upregulated in nrt1.5 mutant plants. These findings indicate that NRT1.5 may be involved in nitrate reallocation to regulate plant stress tolerance16.

In plants, nitrate is one of the most abundant anions, and its absorption and transport are believed to be accompanied by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , NRT1.5 plays a crucial role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ translocation from roots to shoots and is also involved in the coordination of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } / \mathrm { \Delta N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ distribution in plants6,17. In addition to $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , recent research has found that NRT1.5 transports IBA (indole-3-butyric acid) more efficiently than IAA, and IBA is the preferred substrate of NRT1.5 in vivo. NRT1.5-mediated IBA uptake into specific cells is involved in root gravitropism18.

Nitrate is both an important nutrient and signaling molecule for regulating the expression of many genes19. Nitrate inhibits anthocyanin accumulation primarily by suppressing the expression of production of anthocyanin pigments genes which are induced by light in Arabidopsis20. The bZIP transcription factor elongated hypocotyl 5 (HY5), which positively regulates plant photomorphogenesis, is involved in nitrogen signaling by promoting the expression of nitrate uptake genes and assimilation-related genes21. Nitrate signaling pathways for regulating phosphate utilization have been extensively studied. A previous study found that NRT1.1B could perceive nitrate signals and degrade the repressor protein SPX4, with subsequent release of core transcription factors for phosphate and nitrate signaling to ensure coordinated utilization of N and P in rice22. The NIN-like protein NLP7 is a central transcription factor that regulates the expression of NRT1.1 and NRT2.1 in Arabidopsis23. $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling is also involved in the response to nitrate24,25.

Various hormone signals affect plant nitrate contents. For example, the nitrate content of Arabidopsis plants changed when they were treated with ethylene and methyl jasmonate15. ABA is a crucial hormone that regulates many developmental processes and abiotic stress responses26. ABA has been demonstrated to be involved in nitrate signaling, and the expression levels of nitraterelated genes were altered under ABA treatment in Arabidopsis27. Nitrate provisioning following nitrate starvation increased root-tissue ABA accumulation in wheat, and this enhancement affected the expression of NRT2/ NAR genes28. These findings demonstrate that there is some correlation between ABA and nitrate.

In this study, we examined the effect of exogenous ABA on the transport of nitrate in apple seedlings and investigated the pertinent regulatory mechanisms. We found that ABA treatment inhibited the transport of nitrate from roots to shoots, and the transcription factor MdABI5 bound directly to the promoter region of the nitrate transporter MdNRT1.5 and suppressed its expression. In brief, these results indicate that MdABI5 regulates rootto-shoot transport of nitrate by modulating the expression of MdNRT1.5, illuminating the molecular mechanism by which ABA regulates nitrate transport in apples.

Nitrate is unique among the essential inorganic nutrients in so far as its uptake from soil solution by the major nitrate transporters AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 and AtNPF6.3 (originally named NRT1.1), and subsequent assimilation by enzymes such as nitrate reductase, requires prior exposure to nitrate for several hours to induce expression of the encoding genes. In the absence of external nitrate, genes encoding these transporters and enzymes are not expressed or expressed at low abundance. An exception to this requirement for nitrate induction is the cHATS for nitrate uptake. Behl et al. (1988) suggested that the principal role of this cHATS was to enable roots previously deprived of nitrate to absorb this ion and initiate induction of nitrate-inducible genes. Thus, at low external nitrate concentration, the activity of cHATS represents the first step in the complex pathway of nitrate assimilation. In a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014), it was demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was considerably enhanced, while nitrate influx measured at $0 . 2 \mathrm { m M }$ was reduced by up to $3 0 \%$ in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants. Nitrate influx in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 was reduced by a further $6 3 \%$ suggesting that NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 are the major contributors to nitrate influx under these conditions. Li et al. (2007), however, found that the cHATS influx was reduced by only $3 5 \%$ in Arabidopsis nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutants, suggesting that $\mathrm { N R T } 2 . 1 / 2 . 2$ is not the major transporter responsible for cHATS influx. Indeed, a large contribution to constitutive nitrate influx by NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 is contrary to expectation, in so far as it has been presumed that after several days of nitrate deprivation, these genes are no longer expressed (Okamoto et al. 2003). Nevertheless, our study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present at low abundance even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ of $\mathbf { N }$ starvation (Supporting Information Fig. S3).

The influx data shown in Fig. 6 and Table 2 provide convincing evidence that in A. thaliana AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to the cHATS. The average reduction of influx ( $6 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the two T-DNA knockout mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 is of a similar order of magnitude as was observed for the reduction of iHATS influx ( $7 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the $n r t { 2 . } I n r t { 2 . } 2$ mutants (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). This finding is different in magnitude from results reported by Lezhneva et al. (2014) which indicated only a $3 0 \%$ reduction of influx in NRT2.5 mutants.The difference in present findings may result from the ‘severe starvation’ employed in the Lezhneva study.

Complementation of the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant with AtNRT2.5 cDNA resulted in a statistically significant increase of the cHATS compared with the mutant, but influx failed to reach $1 0 0 \%$ of WT influx (Table 3). Incomplete recovery of the influx in Atnrt2.5-35S:NRT2.5 may be a result of lower AtNRT2.5 mRNA expression in the complemented line compared with WT (Table 3) possibly due to partial gene silencing. Schubert et al. (2004) reported silencing of genes under 35S promoter control in Arabidopsis T-DNA transformants that is controlled by transcript levels of transgenes. Nevertheless, this partial complementation taken together with the documented reduced nitrate influx in two independent Atnrt2.5 mutants provides strong evidence that AtNRT2.5 represents the major component of cHATS influx with primary responsibility for nitrate uptake at low nitrate concentration in nitrate-deprived plants.

The observed reduction of influx resulted in reduced nitrate accumulation in the Atnrt2.5 mutants. Although roots and shoots of the mutants and WT plants contained similar nitrate concentrations after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without N, after $6 \mathrm { { h } }$ of induction by $1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { ~ K N O } _ { 3 }$ , mutants contain significantly lower nitrate concentration than WT roots (Table 4). However, following short-term $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime } 5 \mathrm { \ m i n } )$ ) exposure to $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , no differences were observed in the proportion of tracer transferred to shoots in uninduced or induced plants. Thus, AtNRT2.5 plays an important role in nitrate uptake into roots but not in the transfer of nitrate to shoots of Arabidopsis (Table 2). With respect to the transfer of nitrate to shoots, similar conclusions may be drawn from results reported by Kechid et al. (2013) using plants supplied with $2 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. Lezhneva et al. (2014) found that under conditions of extreme N deprivation (4 weeks without N) phloem nitrate concentrations of NRT2.4 mutants was reduced by $4 0 \%$ , although there were no differences in NRT2.5 single mutants. This is consistent with the pattern of mRNA expression of AtNRT2.5 that was more abundant in roots than in shoots of 6-week-old nitratedeprived WT plants (Fig. 3a). A similar expression profile of AtNRT2.5 during both vegetative and reproductive growth stages of Arabidopsis was observed previously by Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014). However, after $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ of exposure to nitrate in the present study, root AtNRT2.5 expression had decreased to such an extent (with virtually no change of shoot AtNRT2.5 expression) that AtNRT2.5 expression was more abundant in shoots than in roots. Thus, depending on the duration of nitrate deprivation or re-exposure both higher and lower levels of AtNRT2.5 expression may be observed in roots versus shoots. This may account for the apparent differences between reports from Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. Garnett et al. (2013) followed responses of nitrate transporters to nitrogen supply in Zea mays over the life cycle and found that ZmNRT2.5 is the only NRT transporter (besides NRT2.1) expressed at significant levels when plants were grown hydroponically in low concentration nitrate solution.

$^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx into roots of uninduced WT plants revealed that cHATS influx conformed to saturable Michaelis– Menten kinetics over the nitrate concentration range from 10 to $2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 6a,b). We have calculated kinetic parameters for the difference flux (WT minus $A t n r t { 2 . 5 }$ mutants) as a measure of influx specifically due to the AtNRT2.5 transporter (Table 1). $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ were estimated to be $2 . 3 \mu \mathrm { m o l \ g F W ^ { - 1 } \ h ^ { - 1 } }$ and $1 1 \ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ , respectively, for the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant, and $1 . 7 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { F W } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ and $7 ~ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ for the Atnrt2.5-2 mutant. These results are consistent with the findings of Behl et al. (1988), Siddiqi et al. (1990), Aslam et al. (1992) and Kronzucker et al. (1995) where cHATS was found to be a low capacity uptake system that exhibited a significantly higher substrate affinity (lower $K _ { \mathrm { m } _ { \mathrm { \ell } } }$ ) than that of the iHATS. However, in these earlier studies, lacking specific mutants, it was not possible to differentiate components of the cHATS flux.

Nevertheless, a significant nitrate flux remains in the two knockout mutants under non-inducing conditions. As noted above, Lezhneva et al. (2014) reported a significant contribution of NRT2.1/NRT2.2 to nitrate uptake by nitrate-starved roots. We have demonstrated that NRT2.1 proteins have a long half-life even after removal of external nitrate, confirmed by Western blots that reveal the presence of traces of NRT2.1 protein even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without nitrate (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Although the iHATS nitrate influx has been attributed to the activities of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001), while examining the double deletion (NRT2.1/NRT2.2) Arabidopsis nrt2 mutant, defective in iHATS, Cerezo et al. (2001) and Li et al. (2007) reported a residual high-affinity influx that was $2 7 \%$ of the WT flux. This remaining high-affinity nitrate uptake in the mutant is not nitrate inducible, is saturable and most likely the result of cHATS activity (Cerezo et al. 2001). Figure 3b shows that the expression of AtNRT2.5 is significantly higher in the double-mutant Atnrt2.1-nrt2.2 (described in Li et al. 2007) compared with WT plants both under induced and uninduced conditions. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in an $A t n r t 2 . I { - } I$ mutant disrupted in both NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 was reported earlier (Orsel et al. 2004, 2006). It is possible that up-regulation of AtNRT2.5 is a compensatory mechanism mitigating the loss of AtNRT2.1.

The reduced cHATS influx in Atnrt2.5-1 plants and diminished nitrate content of roots and shoots of the NRT2.5 mutant (Table 4) were associated with reduced induction/ expression of AtNRT2.1 (which is largely responsible for iHATS) and complete absence of the $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ oligomeric complex of NRT2.5/NAR2.1 in induced Atnrt2.5-1 mutants compared with WT plants (Fig. 4). Accordingly, nitrateinduced $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx (iHATS) was significantly reduced in the Atnrt2.5-1 mutants (Fig. 7b). These observations demonstrate the importance of AtNRT2.5 in optimizing nitrate uptake following resupply of nitrate.

AtNRT2.5 gene expression was strongly suppressed when nitrate or ammonium were supplied to N-starved plants (Fig. 3a, Supporting Information Fig. S1); after prolonged nitrate exposure, mRNA of AtNRT2.5 was almost undetectable. Likewise, Okamoto et al. (2003) observed that the provision of nitrate to WT Arabidopsis suppressed expression of AtNRT2.5. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in roots under conditions of N-deprivation is consistent with its role as the transporter with the primary responsibility for nitrate uptake following a period of nitrate deprivation. Reduced expression of AtNRT2.5 following provision of nitrate is consistent with its principal function having been performed, that is, nitrate has been absorbed; induction of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 is underway and subsequent nitrate uptake is now taken up by these higher capacity, lower affinity transporters (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). Noting that NRT2.5 is subject to downregulation following exposure to nitrate or ammonium raises the question as to the appropriateness of the term cHATS that has long been applied to this system, which is not truly constitutive.

The absence of AtNRT2.1 in Arabidopsis mutant lines has a strong effect on plant growth resulting in smaller plants, especially at low nitrate supply (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al.

2007). AtNRT2.1 also has an important role in morphological and physiological responses of the root system to nitrogen-limited conditions, having direct effect on initiation of lateral root primordia (Remans et al. 2006). In order to examine the effect of AtNRT2.5 mutation on growth, plants were grown on low and high nitrate prior to plant weight and root length measurements. There were no differences between WT and Atnrt2.5-1 root weights of 5-week-old plants or root length of 2-week-old plants (Supporting Information Fig. S2) as observed by Kechid et al. (2013), but shoot growth of the mutants was significantly reduced by comparison with WT plants grown under conditions of low $( 2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { u } )$ nitrate indicating that nitrate deprivation associated with disruption of AtNRT2.5 resulted in increased root to shoot ratio, a clear indication of N deprivation, in $A t n r t 2 . 5$ mutants (Supporting Information Fig. S2b). Under conditions of prolonged growth at limiting nitrate concentration, Lezhneva et al. (2014) also noted that AtNRT2.5 contributed to the maintenance of shoot growth.

AtNRT2.5 is located on chromosome 1 in the forward orientation, on the first half of the chromosome, close to the three most important Arabidopsis nitrate transporters NPF6.3, NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 and a nitrate reductase NR2. Phylogenetic analysis of the AtNRT2 family from different plant species reveals the existence of closely related AtNRT2.5 orthologues in both dicots and monocots (Fig. 1, red). The clade of NRT2.5 proteins is divergent from NRT2.1-like proteins in dicots and monocots, probably stemming directly from a common ancestral nitrate transporter (Fig. 1). Similarly, Plett et al. (2010) found that NRT2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6 genes from dicots sit on an entirely separate phylogenetic tree from grass NRT2s, while NRT2.5 is the only NRT2 gene that has clear orthologues among dicot and monocot species. Interestingly, out of all dicot and monocot species examined in this analysis, only S. tuberosum has no NRT2.5 orthologue. In a similar analysis that included sequences of another Solanaceae species, namely Solanum lycopersicum, the same absence of NRT2.5 orthologue was observed (Supporting Information Fig. S4). This observation is surprising given that S. lycopersicum appears to possess normal cHATS activity (Cárdenas-Navarro et al. 1999). As more plant genome sequences become available, it will be interesting to confirm this phenomenon and explore possible explanations.

Western blot analysis of protein complexes separated by the BN-PAGE indicates that AtNRT2.5 exists in root membranes only as a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex, that is absent in the Atnar2.1-2 mutant (Fig. 4).The complex was separated in the second dimension by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and both AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1 monomers were detected and shown to be derived from the same $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex (Fig. 5). The corresponding complex with AtNAR2.1 was observed for the AtNRT2.1 nitrate transporter (Yong et al. 2010). Based on observed interactions of other NRT2 nitrate transporters with NAR2.1 in heterologous systems (Kotur et al. 2012), the oligomeric polypeptide complex $\left( { \sim } 1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a } \right)$ may be a universal model for NRT2/NAR2.1 interactions and function.

The evidence presented here strongly supports the hypothesis that AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to cHATS in roots of $A$ . thaliana, and that this transporter has a critical role in the induction of iHATS in N-starved plants. Even though the Atnrt2.5 mutants are knockouts, a significant nitrate influx $( 3 7 \%$ of WT) remains in these mutants. The study by Lezhneva et al. (2014) indicates that AtNRT2.1/ AtNRT2.2/AtNAR2.1 is responsible for this remaining flux. The $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex in which NRT2.1 is expressed (Yong et al. 2010) and which is primarily responsible for the iHATS flux has a long half-life of around $3 5 \mathrm { h }$ (Supporting Information Fig. S5) and, in roots of plants deprived of nitrate for 1 week (a treatment that de-induces AtNRT2.1 expression), is still present at around $2 4 \%$ of the abundance found in nitrate-induced plants (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Moreover, cHATS was found to be reduced by $3 5 \%$ in the nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutant compared with WT (Li et al. 2007), signifying a contribution of AtNRT2.1 and/or AtNRT2.2 to the constitutive nitrate influx under the same conditions used in experimental work presented in this paper. In NAR2.1 mutants, from which NRT2 (but not NPF) proteins are absent, $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx is approximately $4 \%$ of WT values. Hence, it is unlikely that the remaining $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx observed in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants receives a significant contribution from NPF6.3 activity (Glass & Kotur 2013).

Clearly, the function of AtNRT2.5 is not limited to nitrate influx associated with cHATS activity. Thus, Kechid et al. (2013) have established that AtNRT2.5 and indeed AtNRT2.6 play an essential role in plant growth promotion induced by the rhizospheric bacterium P. brassicacearum. Interestingly, this effect is nitrate independent.

A current hypothesis to explain the mechanism of Al tolerance in wheat proposes that an Al-dependent efflux of malate chelates and detoxifies Al cations in the rhizosphere (Delhaize and Ryan,1995; Delhaize et al.,1993b;Ma et al., 2001; Ryan et al.,1995,1997,2001; Zhang et al.,2001). We have presented several lines of evidence supporting the conclusion that ALMT1 encodes an Al-activated malate transporter.This finding represents the first isolation and characterization of a plant gene encoding a transporter that facilitates organic anion efflux.The additional findings that ALMT1-1 expression co-segregates with Al tolerance in wheat and that cultured tobacco cells overexpressing ALMT1 show an increase in Al tolerance (Figure 7) suggest that ALMT1-1 is a strong candidate for the Alt1 gene of wheat.

At least two alleles of ALMT1 are present in wheat (ALMT1-1 and ALMT1-2). Expression of these genes in oocytes or in cultured tobacco cells indicates that both are capable of functioning as malate transporters (Figures 5c and 7b),although ALMT1-2 did not appear to be as effective as ALMT1-1. The Al-tolerant line ET8 expresses the ALMT1-1 only at relatively high levels, whereas the Al-sensitive line ES8 expresses the ALMT1-2 only at significantly lower levels. The same pattern of expression was observed in a set of another two lines examined,Altas66 and Scout66. However,a moderately

Al-tolerant cultivar, Chinese Spring,which releases malate at rates between those measured for the Al-tolerant and Alsensitive cultivars (Papernik et al.,20o1),expresses only the ALMT1-2 allele,but at relatively high levels (Figure 2b). These results suggest that the relative Al tolerance afforded by ALMT1 in different wheat cultivars is determined primarily by the level of expression of these alleles rather than the two-amino acid difference between them.Future work will test this hypothesis by correlating Al tolerance with both ALMT1 expression and Al-dependent malate efflux in a range of wheat cultivars.

Previous physiological experiments have described a malate-permeable anion channel in ET8 wheat seedlings with attributes similar to those shown here for ALMT1 (Ryan et al., 1997,2001; Zhang et al., 2001). For example, both are activated by Al,but not by $\mathsf { L } \mathsf { a } ^ { 3 + }$ ，both facilitate malate efflux from cells,both are constitutively expressed, and both are localized to the root apices.As much of the existing physiological evidence indicates that malate efflux from the roots of Al-tolerant wheat cultivars is mediated by anion channels,we can infer that the ALMT1 protein may be the first member of a new family of plant anion channels (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,20oo). However,we acknowledge that without investigating the isolated protein,we cannot exclude the alternative possibility that ALMT1encodes for a receptor that can activate a malate transport protein present in both plant and animal cells.

The finding that Al activates malate efflux from wheat roots,and from plant and animal cells expressing ALMT1is especially intriguing,as Al has been shown to inhibit many other transporters including ion channels (see Ryan et al., 1997).However,some cations can activate transporters, including ion channels,in other plant species,as well as in animal cells.For instance,Al has been shown to activate an anion channel in maize roots in a similar manner to that described in wheat (Kollmeier et al.，20o1;Pineros and Kochian,2001）and ${ \mathsf { H } } { \mathsf { g } } ^ { 2 + }$ can activate the rat aquaporin AQP6 by binding to the protein and trapping it in a conformation that is permeable to water and ions (Yasui et al., 1999).It is still unclear whether Al activates malate efflux by directly interacting with the ALMT1 protein,or whether intermediate steps are involved (Ryan et al.,1995,1997, 2001;Zhang et al.,2001). The observations that ALMT1 expression elicits an Al-activated efflux of malate in plant cells (Figures 6and 7)and an Al-dependent inward current (consistent with malate efflux) in animal cells (Figure 5) suggest that a direct interaction is more likely.Al also appears to directly activate an anion channel in maize roots, because the response has been detected in the outside-out patch configuration for which involvement of secondary messengers is unlikely (Pineros and Kochian,2001).

For future study,we will investigate whether the expression of the ALMT1 gene in Al-sensitive crop and pasture species can increase plant production in acid soils.

In acid soils the soluble Al ions exist mainly in the trivalent $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ form which damages membranes and rapidly inhibits root growth [29]. A widespread mechanism for Al resistance in many plant species relies on the release of organic anions from roots apices (the sensitive region of the root for Al toxicity). The organic anions, such as malate, citrate and oxalate, are able to chelate $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to prevent it from binding in the cell wall and membranes and from entering the cytosol. This chelation reduces harmful interactions from occurring in the apoplast and in the cytosol of the root apex [30]. The first member of the family identified was TaALMT1 from wheat where it controls the major mechanism for aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ resistance [1]. TaALMT1 is constitutively expressed in the root apices and activated by the $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ cations prevalent in acid soils to release malate anions into the apoplast. Malate chelates the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ which reduces damage to the cell wall, membranes and other cellular components. Other members of the family perform similar functions in Arabidopsis [3,31], rape (Brassica napus L.) [4], rye (Secale cereale L.) [2], soybean (Glycine max L.) [32], alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) [33], and Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus L.) [34]. Regulation of these vary and some show more complex interactions [35]. For instance, AtALMT1 is not constitutively expressed in Arabidopsis roots but induced by low pH and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [3] and GmALMT1 in soybean shows complex interactions with Al stress and phosphorus nutrition [32].

Most members of the ALMT family are not involved in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance but perform other functions on different membranes [21,36]. For example, four members in Arabidopsis (AtALMT4, AtALMT6, AtALMT9 and AtALMT12) and one in barley (Hordeum vulgare L., HvALMT1) are involved in guard cell regulation. This is consistent with the involvement of anion transport in signal transduction and osmotic adjustment in modulating stomatal aperture [5–7,10,18,20]. Electrophysiological studies in Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802) oocytes revealed similarities between the currents generated by AtALMT12 and the previously characterised rapid or R-type/QUAC anion currents which propose that AtALMT12 anion channels are responsible for these currents [6,37]. AtALMT6 localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and facilitates calcium and pH-dependent movement of malate into the vacuole [8], but knockout mutations show little or no phenotype indicating some redundancy in these functions. AtALMT9 also localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and knock-out mutations show impaired stomatal opening in the light and delayed wilting [8,9]. AtALMT9 is activated by cytosolic malate and appears to facilitate chloride movement into the vacuole during stomatal opening. VvALMT9 is a homolog of AtALMT9 in grape (Vitis vinifera L.) and reportedly controls the acidity of berries during fruit maturation by facilitating tartrate, malate and succinate accumulation in the vacuoles of mesocarp cells [15]. A recent study also indicated that the ABA induced anion channel AtALMT4 of mediates $\mathrm { M a l } ^ { 2 - }$ efflux from the vacuole during stomatal closure and its activity depends on phosphorylation [38].

Acidity in apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) similarly relies on the ALMT transporter Ma1 which mediates malate accumulation into the vacuoles of developing fruit cells [14]. In maize (Zea mays L.), ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2 are mainly expressed in root tissues and likely function to assist in balancing charges during nutrient uptake [12,13]. Both proteins localise to the plasma membrane and both are permeable to inorganic anions but ZmALMT2 is also permeable to organic anions as demonstrated by the constitutive release of malate from the roots of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing ZmALMT2 [13]. OsALMT4 is a member of the ALMT family in rice (Oryza sativa L.). OsALMT4 is widely expressed in rice and encodes a malate-permeable anion channel on the plasma membrane. Enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins [39].

The aluminium-activated malate transporter (ALMT) family is found ubiquitously in sequenced genomes throughout the plant kingdom [1] and was named when the first member of the family to be discovered was found to be involved in aluminium resistance in wheat [2]–although proteins of this family are channels, rather than transporters as their name suggests. The first characterized homologue in Arabidopsis thaliana, AtALMT1 [3], was similarly found to be involved in Al-resistance. However, in addition to ALMT1, the gene family in this species contains 13 other members suggesting that they are involved in more than just Al-resistance, and some of these have already shown to have a wide range of other roles [4]. To date, the ALMT family has been shown to be central to physiological processes such as control of stomatal aperture [5,6] and anion homoeostasis [7]. Furthermore, increasing attention is being paid due to their potential role in economically valuable traits such as fruit flavour [8] and grain filling [9], and more recently they have been shown to be key mediators of GABA (γ -aminobutyric acid) signalling [10]. Identification of the molecular actors in these processes is already helping guide marker-assisted breeding [11]. The ALMT family is now known to be central to many physiological processes, with scope for even more diversity as many homologues are still to be characterized and thus, a comprehensive review of all currently known functions is a timely addition to the literature.


## Aluminium resistance



## Overcoming aluminium toxicity on acid soils


Acid soils are prevalent worldwide, comprising around half of all potentially arable land [12]. In these soils, aluminium ions become solubilized and damage crops via root growth inhibition [13] and, to compound the problem, nutrients such as phosphate become less available [14]. Several plant species have been identified as aluminium-resistant and they use a variety of mechanisms including thickening of cell walls [15], active transport of aluminium away from sensitive organs [16], or, prominently, organic acid exudation, chiefly either by release of malate or citrate [17,18].

Studies on crosses of near isogenic Al-resistant and Al-sensitive wheat (Triticum aestivum) cultivars alongside electrophysiological studies using Xenopus oocytes [19,2,20] first identified TaALMT1 as the channel responsible for malate exudation from root tips, providing the primary mechanism of aluminium resistance. TaALMT1 is constitutively expressed in the root apices of Al-resistant wheat and malate chelates $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ forming a 2:2 complex with the trivalent aluminium ions, thus encasing the ions and rendering them non-toxic [21]. This allows longer root growth and greater yields compared with a sensitive cultivar grown on acid soils. In addition to protection from $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity, malate extrusion has the benefit of increasing phosphate availability in the soil – since $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ binds and complexes phosphate [22]. This is part of a host of processes activated in plants for improved phosphorous usage [14,23]. Heterologous expression of TaALMT1 in cultured tobacco cells, Xenopus oocytes, and transgenic rice plants has shown efflux of malate activated by the presence of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and expression confers Al-resistance to tobacco cells [2]. Importantly, transgenic expression of TaALMT1 in Al-sensitive barley plants rendered them resistant to aluminium toxicity [24]. In one study, transgenic plants grown on acid soil displayed root growth similar to that seen in neutral soils and a doubling in yield when expressing just the single gene [23], making it a powerful tool for transgenic crop development. A thorough review of transgenic approaches using ALMT1 and other genes can be found in Ryan et al. [25].


## Other ALMTs involved in aluminium resistance


Since the characterization of TaALMT1, several ALMTs from other species including oilseed rape, Arabidopsis, rye, soybean and Yorkshire fog have been shown to be vital for

Al-resistance and characterized (see Figure 1 and Table 1). These channels are activated by $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and in some cases their expression is also up-regulated upon sensing $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [26].

AtALMT1 is a malate channel critical for aluminium resistance in Arabidopsis, expressed at the plasma membrane of the epidermal cells of the root tip [3]. This protein shows $4 1 \%$ sequence identity and $6 3 \%$ similarity to TaALMT1. However, in contrast, AtALMT1 is not constitutively expressed; instead, expression is up-regulated by aluminium [26,27], mediated by the transcription factors STOP1, STOP2 and WRKY, which also regulate other genes critical for tolerance of acid soils [28–30]. In addition, two genes with $9 5 \%$ sequence identity with one another were identified in oilseed rape (Brassica napus) [31,32], as well as GmALMT1 in soybean (Glycene max), and ScALMT1 in rye (Secale cereale) [33,34]. These genes are expressed at root tip plasma membranes, and the corresponding proteins are permeable to malate and are activated by aluminium, showing this mechanism for Al-resistance is widespread among plant species. In addition, GmALMT1 channel activity has also been shown to be regulated by $\mathrm { p H }$ changes and phosphorous concentration [35]. Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus) HlALMT1 has also been identified as an important resistance gene in the model grass species, and has Alactivated expression similar to AtALMT1 controlled by a Alresponsive transcription factor ART1, with expression levels in different accessions controlled by the number of binding regions for ART1 in the promoter region [36].


## Other root-related functions


ZmALMT2 from maize (Zea mays) has been shown to be root localized and to release malate into the soil. Unlike AtALMT1 and TaALMT1, however, this is not correlated with Alresistance, but instead is likely to provide solubilization for soil nutrients, such as phosphate, as discussed above for TaALMT1. As it is also found in vascular tissue, ZmALMT2 could also play a role in the transport of organic acids or mineral anions in the xylem [37].


## Guard cell movements


Another vital role played by some ALMT family members is as molecular components of the guard cell movements that regulate gas exchange across leaf surfaces. Plants control $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ uptake and water loss by regulating the aperture of the stomatal pores. Three family members from Arabidopsis, AtALMT6, AtALMT9 and AtALMT12, are involved in opening and closing of stomata, with movement driven by osmotically active inorganic and organic ions [38]. Upon stomatal opening, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ enters the guard cell via voltagegated inward rectifying potassium channels, driven by the electrochemical gradient maintained by ATP-driven proton pumping. Malate synthesis from stored starch provides a charge-balancing ion, and is taken up into the vacuole via AtALMT6, and similarly AtALMT9 acts to permit entry of chloride counterions into the vacuole. The increase in solutes draws water into the cell down the water potential gradient, swelling the cell. The process is inverted during stomatal closing. The membrane is depolarized, prompted by the action of AtALMT12/QUAC1 (quick anion channel 1) releasing malate rapidly, this allows $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ to flow out of the cell, accompanied by $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } -$ anions via SLAC1 (slow anion channel 1). In addition, AtALMT6 activity is regulated in part by cytosolic malate concentration, and so malate can flow out of the vacuole to either be lost via AtALMT12/QUAC1 or used in metabolism. This loss of osmotica drives a loss of water and closing of the stomata.

AtALMT6 is expressed in guard cell vacuoles and is a malate channel, specific for divalent malate involved in stomatal movements. It is not aluminium activated but instead is controlled by light, ABA [39], $\mathrm { p H }$ and cytosolic malate concentration [4]. As transport is dependent on the concentration of malate in the cytosol and the tonoplast membrane potential, AtALMT6 can mediate both malate uptake into and release from the vacuole in guard cells, with uptake during stomatal opening, and release during stomatal closing as shown in Figure 2. Interestingly, in A. thaliana expression is also seen in floral organs, suggesting another role yet to be elucidated. Knockout plants did not show phenotypic differences, indicating functional redundancy in vacuolar malate channels, perhaps from the action of

$K ^ { + }$ ions enter the cell during opening, and the charge is balanced by malate synthesis from starch, which is then taken up into the vacuole via ALMT6 and activates ALMT9 to permit $\mathbb { C } ^ { | - }$ uptake into the vacuole. This increase in osmotic potential draws water into the cell, leading to swelling and stomatal opening. Stomatal closing, conversely, is driven by release of $K ^ { + }$ ions, which is permitted during membrane depolarization and driven by ALMT12. Additionally, anions are released by SLAC1 over a longer period of time. Loss of osmolytes leads to concomitant loss of water and thus stomatal closing.

AtALMT9 and perhaps also AtALMT5, which has been shown to be expressed in guard cells, and to be closely related to AtALMT6 (see Figure 1).

AtALMT9 is a vacuolar chloride channel in guard cells and Atalmt9 knockouts show impaired stomatal opening [6]. It permits chloride to enter the vacuole, providing a charge-balance for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the same way as malate. Malate in the cytosol (synthesized from starch) activates the channel, meaning malate can act both as an osmolyte and as a signalling molecule in guard cells. Interestingly, kinetic data suggest AtALMT9 is multimeric, with a number of subunits ${ > } 2 . 5$ with more recent work suggesting that it forms a tetramer [40]. Furthermore, cytosolic nucleotides such as ATP block the activity of AtALMT9, competing with malate for a binding site [41]. The $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -V-ATPases that maintain a hyperpolarized tonoplast consume ATP, provoking lowered cytosolic ATP concentrations, removing this block and thus permitting currents via AtALMT9 and facilitating anion uptake into the vacuole.

AtALMT12 (also known as QUAC1) is expressed in guard cell plasma membranes and operates as an R-type (rapid-type) channel crucial for stomatal closing [5], allowing rapid malate release. One study also found localization to endomembranes, although this is possibly an artefact of overexpression [42]. The channel opens with fast kinetics upon membrane depolarization, releasing malate into the apoplasm in parallel with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ release through potassium channels to maintain the depolarization. Moreover, external malate causes increased activation of the channel and thus may represent a positive-feedback loop. Loss-of function mutants confer a wilty phenotype due to their impaired stomatal closing. Rather than being ligand gated, as seen in ALMT1, ALMT12 activity is voltage gated; however, the voltage sensor is yet to be identified, although it is likely in the CTD (C-terminal domain), which has been shown to be vital for regulation [43].


## Other roles



## Malate storage and homoeostasis


AtALMT9, in addition to its role in guard cells (discussed above and summarized in Table 1), has been shown to be permeable to both chloride and malate and expressed strongly throughout leaf mesophyll tissue. It is likely to have a role in homoeostasis: ensuring that the concentration of malate – which plays an essential role in metabolism as part of the citric acid cycle – remains stable within the cytoplasm. Similar to AtALMT6, the channel is likely to work in both directions, by storing excess in the vacuole and releasing it when required to regulate osmotic potential and C-metabolism [44].


## Cell elongation and nutrient storage


Barley (Hordeum vulgare) HvALMT1 is a malate channel expressed in guard cells and the root elongation zone, as well as floral tissues and seeds [45]. Although it has the greatest sequence similarity to TaALMT1 of any barley gene and localizes to the plasma membrane, it is not involved in Al-resistance but seems to have several distinct roles within the plant. HvALMT1 over-expressing lines take longer to close their stomata [46] and RNAi knockouts show a similar phenotype to Atamlt12 knockouts [9], so HvALMT1 is likely to be a functional homologue of AtALMT12. In expanding cells HvALMT1 may help provide an osmotic balance and regulate turgor. Additionally, later studies have shown that this channel plays a role in seed development during acidification of the starchy endosperm, which is required for enzyme activity [9]. Rather than directly causing acidification itself (this is probably caused by a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase pumping protons from the aleurone) release of malate is suggested to act as a counterion for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ and other positively charged nutrients such as $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , helping to maintain electroneutrality and osmotic balance in a similar manner to the role of malate in guard cell movements. The significant difference in function between HvALMT1 and TaALMT1 despite strong sequence similarity again highlights that small differences in sequence can underlie large changes in function.


## Fruit flavour


Malic acid is an important component of apple taste, grape quality and wine production: an economically significant set of traits. A malic acid channel with high homology to AtALMT genes has been shown to be responsible for the acidity of apples, and functions to accumulate malic acid in the vacuole [8,47]. Similarly, grape berries contain an ALMT family member expressed in the tonoplast of berry mesocarp tissue responsible for malate and tartrate accumulation [48]. Understanding of the action of these genes could be valuable for fruit and wine development [47].


## Inorganic anion homoeostasis


ZmALMT1 from maize was one of the first family members to be described that did not have a role in aluminium resistance. It localizes to plasma membranes throughout the plant, but is less permeable to organic anions and instead is probably involved in inorganic anion homoeostasis and mineral nutrition [7].


## GABA signalling


A recently discovered role of ALMTs is in mediating GABA signalling in plants. This is the first evidence for GABA signalling in plants in addition to its established role as a metabolite [10]. GABA – a non-protein amino acid – accumulates in plant tissues in response to biotic and abiotic stresses, and has a central role in pollen tube growth and regulation of root growth [49]. Recently, it has been shown that GABA’s influence is exerted by interaction with ALMT proteins, and a putative GABA-binding motif has been identified in the CTD. GABA binding negatively regulates ion flux through the channel, i.e. decreasing carbon flux from roots in the case of TaALMT1. Additionally, as plant anion equilibrium potentials are strongly positive and plant action potentials are generated by voltage-gated ion channels, GABA inhibition of ALMTs will hyperpolarize membranes and decrease excitability.

Moreover, to advance studies of ALMTs, perhaps parallels can be drawn with the more well-studied GABA(A) receptors from mammals, which have a greater level of structural detail elucidated already. Although they are different gene families, it may be possible to apply insights from mammalian proteins to design experiments to study ALMTs as GABA(A) receptors are predicted to have a similar overall architecture, being ${ \sim } 4 5 0 \mathrm { A A }$ long and divided into a membrane-embedded half and a soluble half [50]. In the mammalian system the channel is formed by a central pore between five monomers, and the GABA-binding site is found at the interface of monomer subunits; perhaps a similar multimeric structure will be found for ALMTs as suggested by recent results from AtALMT9 [40].

Some of these may have similar or redundant roles, for example AtALMT4 and AtALMT5 are closely related to AtALMT6 and so may also have a role in the guard cell vacuolar membrane. Indeed, some of these channels may account for residual activity seen in knockout mutants that still retain some function. Alternatively, ALMTs may form hetero-multimers to provide diversified functions, as seen in GABA(A) receptors in mammals. In addition, several members have expression patterns that show they must have a wider range of roles than is currently known – for example, AtALMT6 has a role in guard cells, but is also expressed in floral tissues with an as-yet undefined function. It is possible that ALMTs are involved in shuttling malate in C4 and CAM metabolism as the channels involved have not yet been identified. However, as Arabidopsis is a C3 plant these experiments will have to be done in another species.

Although there is a growing body of knowledge about the physiological functions of ALMTs, much less is known about their structure and mechanism. Relatively small differences in sequence can lead to large changes in localization, substrate specificity, gating and physiological function. In many cases, evidence is either scant or directly contradictory. No detailed 3D structure is available of any family member, but would help guide biochemical and functional studies and elucidate further details of mechanism and regulation, and thus detailed, high quality structural studies are vital for a full understanding ALMTs.

Finally, the ALMT family has been shown to have many members that are not aluminium activated, to have members permeable to anions other than malate, and to be channels rather than active transporters. Thus, the name aluminiumactivated malate transporters does not fully reflect this family of proteins and is potentially confusing. It is perhaps advisable to take up the previously suggested QUAC nomenclature, which better reflects the characteristics of the family members.

Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.
