Tese include $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiport and uptake by ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters13,14.

Te multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporters appear to be the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporters involved in the vacuolar transport of favonoids. Tere are 58 MATE transporters encoded in the genome of Arabidopsis. However, very few of these have been functionally characterized15. Te involvement of MATE transporters in the vacuolar uptake of favonoids was frst determined through the characterization of TRANSPARENT TESTA12 (TT12). TT12 is a MATE transporter localized to the vacuolar membrane and mechanistically active as a favonoid glucoside $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter in PA synthesizing cells of the seed coat16,17. Te role of MATE proteins in the vacuolar accumulation of PA precursors or anthocyanins has also been demonstrated in Medicago truncatula6,18, tomato19 and grapevine20. TT12, MtMATE1 and MtMATE2, have all been shown to transport cyanidin 3-O-glucoside (C3G; Fig. 1) when heterologously expressed in yeast6,17,18.

Te plant vacuolar membrane also contains ABC transporters that move large organic anions into the vacuole21–23. ABC transporters are directly energized by ATP hydrolysis and therefore do not depend on the transmembrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -electrochemical gradient. ABC transporters are characteristically inhibited by vanadate, a phosphoryl transition-state analogue. Tere are several lines of evidence that ABC transporters are involved in the vacuolar uptake of favonoids, specifcally, the ABCC subclass (previously known as multidrug resistance-associated proteins [MRP]). Te vacuolar uptake of favone glucuronide conjugates by rye mesophyll vacuoles and the uptake of a favone glucoside by Arabidopsis vacuoles were shown to occur through an ABC transporter-type mecha$\mathrm { n i s m } ^ { 1 3 , 2 4 }$ . However, in both cases, a specifc transporter was not identifed and in the case of Arabidopsis, the favone glucosides examined were not synthesized by this species. Genetic studies in maize provided evidence that ZmABCC3 (formerly ZmMRP3) was involved in the vacuolar uptake of $\mathrm { C } 3 \mathrm { G } ^ { 2 5 }$ . ZmABCC4 (formerly ZmMRP4), a homolog of ZmABCC3, was thought to be responsible for the vacuolar localization of anthocyanins in the aleurone25. However, it has never been demonstrated that ZmABCC3 or ZmABCC4 can functionally transport C3G in vitro. More recently, it has been shown that the ABC transporter VvABCC1, is localized to the tonoplast of grape berry exocarp cells and is biochemically capable of co-transporting anthocyanidin 3-O-glucosides and GSH when heterologously expressed in yeast26. Te co-transport of GSH with bile acids, vincristine, and other drugs by a human ABCC transporter has also been previously demonstrated27–29.

Tough it is well known that TT12 is a MATE transporter responsible for the transport of favonoids into the seed coat endothelium of Arabidopsis seeds16,17, and that TT12 can also transport anthocyanins when heterologously expressed in yeast6,17, the transporter(s) involved in vacuolar sequestration of anthocyanins in the vegetative tissue of Arabidopsis has not been determined. Tis is critical since Arabidopsis can form a variety of modifed cyanidin-type anthocyanins that are not found in seeds, but are found in other tissues and organs including stems and leaves30. In this study, using C3G as a model substrate, we demonstrate that anthocyanin uptake by vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles isolated from Arabidopsis cell cultures occurs through both an ABC transporter and an $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter mechanism. Given the fnding that VvABCC1 can serve as an anthocyanin/GSH co-transporter26 and that the ABC-transporters are generally better characterized in Arabidopsis than MATE transporters, we decided to examine which specifc AtABCC transporter is involved in the vacuolar uptake of C3G. Te two best characterized AtABCC transporters include AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 and both can be functionally expressed in yeast31–33. Both have been shown to transport a variety of substrates and are expressed in all Arabidopsis tissue examined32 including cell suspension cultures (Bio-Analytic Resource, ePlant Gene Expression Tool, www.bar.utoronto.ca). From in vitro C3G uptake assays with membrane vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2, we demonstrated that, like VvABCC126, AtABCC2 was a C3G/GSH co-transporter and transport did not depend on the formation of an anthocyanin-glutathione conjugate. We also showed that, in addition to anthocyanins, AtABCC2 could transport favone and favonol glucosides. Besides the biochemical studies, we also performed ligand docking to a homology model of AtABCC2 and investigated the putative binding sites of C3G and GSH through site-directed mutagenesis and functional studies. Tese studies revealed the close proximity of the C3G and GSH binding sites in AtABCC2 and identifed residues important for ligand recognition and transport activity.

C3G transport by vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles from Arabidopsis thaliana. Previously it has been shown that transport competent vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles can be isolated from Arabidopsis cell cultures and fractionated on discontinuous sucrose density gradients14,34,35. Te vacuolar membrane enriched vesicles are collected from the interface between the $1 0 \%$ and $2 3 \%$ (10/23) sucrose gradients while the plasma membrane-enriched vesicles are collected at the interface between the $3 4 \%$ and the $4 0 \%$ (34/40) sucrose gradients14,36. A $2 3 / 3 4 \%$ fraction is typically added between the $1 0 / 2 3 \%$ and the $3 4 / 4 0 \%$ sucrose gradients14,3 6. Examination of C3G uptake activity in each of these fractions showed that the vesicles isolated from the $1 0 / 2 3 \%$ interfaced had the highest ATP-dependent uptake of C3G (Fig. 2a). Tis increase in uptake activity correlated with the vacuolar membrane enrichment as demonstrated by the increase in the immunodetection of the V-ATPase (vacuolar membrane marker; Fig. 2b). Te immunodetection of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (plasma membrane marker) was low in the $1 0 / 2 3 \%$ fraction and high in the $2 3 / 3 4 \%$ and $3 4 / 4 0 \%$ fractions, while that of BiP (ER membrane marker) was unchanged across the three collected fractions (Fig. 2b). Terefore, MgATP-dependent C3G uptake activity was associated with the vacuolar membrane-enriched fraction from Arabidopsis cell cultures and this fraction was used in subsequent experiments.

Tere are generally two solvents that have been used to wash anthocyanins of of flters for HPLC analysis following transport assays. Te frst involves $5 0 \%$ methanol6 and the second involves $5 0 \%$ methanol $\mathrm { / 1 \% H C l ^ { 2 6 } }$ . To test the diference, we added a known amount of C3G in our assay media to the flters and washed the flters with either $5 0 \%$ methanol or $5 0 \%$ methanol $1 \%$ HCl. Te samples were then analyzed by HPLC. Filters washed with $5 0 \%$ methanol as used in our study resulted in $8 3 \%$ recovery following HPLC analysis and flters washed with $5 0 \%$ methanol $7 \%$ HCl resulted in $8 2 \%$ recovery following HPLC analysis. Tese high recovery rates are virtually identical. In addition, we incubated C3G in either $5 0 \%$ methanol or $5 0 \%$ methanol $\%$ HCl at the concentrations used in our study and looked for degradation. However, the amounts recovered following HPLC were identical regardless of the incubation solution. In addition, the variation observed with our replicates was not correlated with the storage time (two days or less) of the flter extracts and we never observed any evidence of degradation during storage of the flter extracts.

In the presence of MgATP, the uptake of C3G into Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles increased with time up to $4 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ (Fig. 3a). In the absence of MgATP, the uptake of C3G was nearly undetectable and did not increase over time (Fig. 3a). Te standard reaction time used for all subsequent C3G uptake assays with Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles was $1 5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ .

Te HPLC retention time of C3G before addition to the uptake assay media (C3G standard) was $1 1 . 8 \mathrm { m i n }$ (Fig. 3b). Following the uptake assays, the C3G that was washed of of the flters eluted as a single peak with the same HPLC retention time as the C3G standard (Fig. 3b). Te retention time of C3G was the same regardless of whether or not the assay included MgATP (Fig. 3b). Terefore, C3G remained unaltered following uptake into the Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles.

Since the presence of MgATP resulted in an increase in the uptake of C3G by Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles, the next goal was to determine the mechanism of this uptake. Directly energized MgATP dependent uptake would likely involve an ABC transporter-type mechanism. Vanadate is a phosphoryl transition-state analog known to be a strong inhibitor of proteins that form a phosphoenzyme intermediate, including ABC transporters. Glybenclamide is a sulfonylurea derivative that efectively inhibits ABC transporters, especially subclass C (ABCC) transporters37. GSH is known to stimulate the ABCC transporter-mediated uptake of some organic compounds27–29. Indirectly energized MgATP dependent uptake would likely involve an antiporter that couples the movement of the substrate with that of a proton. A proton gradient would be formed in the presence of MgATP by the tonoplast localized $\mathrm { v } .$ -type $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase. Baflomycin $\mathbf { A } _ { 1 }$ is a specifc inhibitor of V-type $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPases38 and gramicidin D is a cation-selective ionophore that would disrupt the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient that would otherwise be formed in the presence of MgATP. Te ABC transporter inhibitors vanadate $( 1 \mathrm { m M } )$ ) and glybenclamide $( 1 5 0 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ resulted in strong inhibition of C3G uptake $7 8 . 5 \%$ and $8 9 \%$ inhibition, respectively; Fig. 3c). Baflomycin $\mathbf { A } _ { 1 }$ $( 0 . 4 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ and gramicidin D $( 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ also resulted in strong inhibition of C3G uptake $9 5 \%$ and $8 3 \%$ inhibition, respectively; Fig. 3c). Te presence of GSH $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \mathrm { \prime } } 5 \mathrm { m M } ,$ ) had no efect on C3G uptake (Fig. 3c).

In Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles, the MgATP-dependent uptake of C3G exhibited Michaelis-Menten-type saturation kinetics with C3G concentration with apparent $K _ { m }$ and $V _ { m a x }$ values of $0 . 5 5 \mathrm { m M }$ and $1 . 5 \mathrm { n m o l } \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { \dot { m } g ^ { - 1 } }$ , respectively (Fig. 3d).

C3G transport by AtABCC2. In light of the recent fnding that an ABCC transporter from grapevine (VvABCC1) is capable of C3G and GSH co-transport26, we examined the possibility that one of the known vacuolar membrane localized AtABCC transporters would also be capable of C3G and GSH co-transport. Te two best characterized AtABCC transporters in Arabidopsis are AtABCC1 and AtABCC231–33. In the absence of MgATP, yeast transformed with pYES3, pYES-AtABCC1, or pYES3-AtABCC2 had minimal C3G uptake activity, which increased slightly in the presence of MgATP (Fig. 4). Te most dramatic increase in C3G uptake was observed in the presence of both MgATP and GSH with vesicles isolated from the pYES3-AtABCC2 transformed yeast. Tis uptake activity was 4.6-fold greater than that in the presence of MgATP alone and 6.3-fold higher than the C3G uptake activity in the presence of MgATP and GSH observed with membrane vesicles isolated from pYES3 transformed yeast. Comparable increases in C3G uptake activity were not observed for membrane vesicles isolated from yeast transformed with pYES3-AtABCC1. In addition, the uptake of cyanidin (aglycone) in the presence or absence of MgATP or GSH by membrane vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2 was undetectable.

In the presence of MgATP and GSH, the uptake of C3G into yeast vesicles expressing AtABCC2 increased with time up to $2 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ (Fig. 5a). Unless otherwise indicated, all other assays using yeast vesicles containing heterologously expressed AtABCC2 were conducted for $1 5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ in the presence of both MgATP and GSH.

Following the uptake assays with membrane vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2, the C3G that was washed of of the flters eluted as a single peak with the same HPLC retention time as the C3G standard (Fig. 5b). Te retention time of C3G was the same regardless of whether or not the assay included MgATP or GSH (Fig. 5b). Terefore, as with the assays conducted with Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles, the C3G remained unaltered following transport and there was no evidence of the formation of a C3G-glutathione conjugate even in uptake assays that included GSH.

In order to determine the mechanism of C3G uptake into the yeast vesicles expressing AtABCC2, we examined the uptake in the presence of various transport inhibitors. C3G uptake was completely abolished in the presence of vanadate $( 1 \mathrm { m M } )$ and strongly inhibited $5 5 \%$ inhibition) by glybenclamide $( 1 5 0 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , two known inhibitors of ABCC transporters (Fig. 5c). Te nonhydrolyzable analog of ATP, adenosine $5 ^ { \prime }$ - $\cdot \beta , \gamma$ -imino)triphosphate (AMP-PNP), could not substitute for ATP in the transport assays indicating that ATP hydrolysis is required for transport (Fig. 5c). Te $\mathrm { v }$ -type $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase inhibitor, baflomycin $\mathbf { A } _ { 1 }$ ${ \mathrm { 7 } } 0 . 4 { \mu \mathrm { M } } )$ or the cation-selective ionophore, gramicidin D $( 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ had no efect on C3G uptake (Fig. 5c). Terefore, transport was not dependent on the formation of an $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ gradient. Te pattern of inhibition observed is consistent with C3G transport by AtABCC2 occurring through an ABC-transporter-mediated mechanism.

Te MgATP-dependent uptake of C3G into yeast vesicles expressing AtABCC2 exhibited Michaelis-Menten-type saturation kinetics with C3G concentration with apparent $K _ { m }$ and $V _ { m a x }$ values of $1 . 6 \mathrm { m M }$ and $\mathrm { 1 . 1 n m o l \ m i n ^ { - 1 } m \dot { g } ^ { - 1 } }$ respectively (Fig. 5d).

Substrate specifcity of AtABCC2. To determine the substrate specifcity of AtABCC2, we isolated membrane vesicles from yeast expressing AtABCC2 and conducted uptake assays in the presence of four anthocyanins (C3G, M3G, D3G, and P3G), a favanone glucoside (N7G), two favone glucosides (L7G and A7G), and two favonol glucosides (K3G and Q3G; Fig. 1). A signifcant increase in the uptake activity above that observed for control assays (vesicles from yeast transformed with empty vector) was observed for all substrates tested except N7G (Fig. 6). Te greatest relative increase above the control values was observed for all four anthocyanins; with M3G exhibiting the greatest fold increase. However, the greatest overall uptake activity was observed for L7G. Terefore, it appears that AtABCC2 can transport all of the anthocyanins tested and a variety of other favonoid glucosides.

L7G transport by AtABCC2. Since a high AtABCC2-mediated uptake activity in the presence of MgATP and GSH was observed with L7G (Fig. 6), we investigated the efects of MgATP and GSH on L7G transport by vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2. Compared to the control, the addition of MgATP signifcantly increased L7G uptake (Fig. 7a). Te addition of both MgATP and GSH further increased the L7G uptake of vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2, but no further increase was seen for membrane vesicles isolated from the control. Te addition of MgATP and GSH increased the uptake activity of vesicles from yeast expressing AtABCC2 about 2-fold compared to the addition of MgATP alone and 4.7-fold compared to the uptake observed in the absence of MgATP (Fig. 7a). Following the uptake assays with membrane vesicles isolated from yeast expressing AtABCC2, the L7G that was washed of of the flters eluted as a single peak with the same HPLC retention time as the L7G standard (Fig. 7b). Te retention time of L7G was the same regardless of whether or not the assay included MgATP or GSH (Fig. 7b). Terefore, L7G, like C3G, remained unaltered following transport.

C3G promoted transport of $[ ^ { 3 } \mathsf { H } ] \mathsf { G } \mathsf { S } \mathsf { H }$ by AtABCC2. In the absence of C3G or L7G, we were able to detect the MgATP-dependent uptake of $[ { ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } } ] \mathrm { G S H }$ by yeast vesicles expressing AtABCC2 (Table 1). Tough the MgATP-dependent uptake of $[ { ^ { 3 } \mathrm { \bar { H } } } ] \mathrm { G S H }$ was not increased in the presence of L7G, the inclusion of C3G resulted in a statistically signifcant 3.6-fold increase in $[ { } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { G S H }$ uptake. Neither C3G nor L7G had any efect on the MgATP-dependent uptake of $[ { } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { G S H }$ by membrane vesicles isolated from yeast transformed with the empty vector (pYES3; Table 1). Terefore, AtABCC2 functions as an anthocyanin/GSH co-transporter, but not as a favone/GSH co-transporter. It should also be noted that C3G did not promote the uptake of $[ { } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { G } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { H }$ by vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles isolated from Arabidopsis cell cultures.

Putative binding sites of C3G and GSH in AtABCC2. To determine the putative binding sites of C3G and GSH, we combined molecular modeling, ligand docking, site-directed mutagenesis and in vitro assays of mutants. Through a Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST; https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) search of AtABCC2 against the Protein Data Bank (PDB) database, we found four crystal structures of AtABCC2 homologues: PDB ID 5UAK, 5W81, 5WUA and 6BHU, with sequence identity to AtABCC2 of 28, 31, 32 and $3 8 \%$ , respectively. As the crystal structures represent diferent conformational states of the ABC transporters, ligand docking depended on the substrate cavity space associated with the transporter state. Tus, ligand docking in AtABCC2 homology models based on PDB ID 5W81 and 6BHU failed to provide reasonable solutions.

On the other hand, the AtABCC2 homology model based on PDB ID 5WUA showed two distinct binding sites for C3G and GSH with adequate physicochemical properties (Fig. 8). Te binding site for C3G was found in the same location in the AtABCC2 homology model based on PDB ID 5UAK, whereas the GSH binding site overlapped with the C3G site in the latter homology model. Overlapped binding sites for C3G and GSH would suggest competition between these ligands and are incompatible with the functional data that shows that GSH activates C3G uptake. Terefore, for the structural analysis we used the AtABCC2 homology model based on PDB ID 5WUA. To validate the identifed C3G and GSH binding sites, we mutated residues that putatively interacted with these ligands and examined the activity of the mutants in vitro (Fig. 9). We distinguish three sites composed of residues that interact with: both C3G and GSH (site 1), only C3G (site 2), and only GSH (site 3). E357 is within hydrogen bond distance from both C3G and GSH and can also interact with R426, the other residue close to both C3G and GSH (Fig. 8c). K309 and Y360 make hydrogen bond interactions with C3G, while E1148 and R567 interact with the glucosyl and cyanidin moieties of C3G. Te mutants expressed well (Fig. 9a) and the measured transport activity was normalized based on the level of protein expression as indicated by western analysis (Fig. 9b–d). All six mutants had impaired transport activity and GSH activation, compared to the wild-type protein (Fig. 9d). E357A (site 1) mutation abolished transport activity irrespective of MgATP or GSH addition. Te next group of mutations with the most impact on transport activity (ranging between $1 7 \%$ and $2 6 \%$ of wild-type activity) were R426A (site 1), R567A (site 2), and Y360F (site 3; Fig. 9d). Te mutation with the lowest efect on transport activity was E1148A (retained $3 3 \%$ wild-type activity) despite two possible hydrogen bond interactions with the glucosyl group of C3G. Irrespective of whether the mutants were in the C3G or GSH binding site, they all showed signifcant reduction in GSH transport activation, at a level of $0 { - } 6 0 \%$ of wild-type (Fig. 9f ). On the other hand, MgATP transport activation of the mutants (i.e. transport activity in the presence versus absence of MgATP) was not signifcantly afected (level of $3 0 { - } 9 5 \%$ of the wild-type, Fig. 9e).

Putative binding sites of L7G in AtABCC2. Te Ligand docking of L7G to an AtABCC2 model based on PDB ID 5WUA showed that the L7G binding site spans both the C3G and GSH binding sites identifed above (See Supplementary Fig. S1). Tus, L7G and GSH cannot both bind to the active site simultaneously, consistent with the fnding that AtABCC2 is not a favone/GSH co-transporter.

We demonstrate that the vacuolar membrane-enriched fraction from Arabidopsis cell cultures transports C3G in an MgATP-dependent manner. Tis transport was strongly inhibited by known inhibitors of ABC transporters and $\dot { \mathrm { H } } ^ { + }$ -antiporters, suggesting that both an ABC transporter and an $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter are involved in C3G transport. Surprisingly, in the presence of the ABC transporter inhibitors, the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ antiporter-mediated uptake did not compensate for the inhibition of the ABC transporter and vice versa. Both an ABC transporter and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter were also thought to be involved in the uptake of abscisic acid glucosyl ester (ABA-GE) by Arabidopsis vacuoles39 and salicylic acid 2-O- $\cdot \beta$ -D-glucose by Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles14. Te pattern of inhibition with C3G may suggest that not only are two transport mechanisms involved, but that there might be some interaction where the inhibition of one afects the activity of the other. Tere are numerous examples of ABC proteins interacting with and regulating other transporters40–47. However, further research will be necessary to determine if there is an interaction between tonoplast localized ABCC transporters and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporters during the vacuolar sequestration of anthocyanins.

Given that an ABC transporter appeared to be involved in the uptake of C3G by Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles, it was of interest to determine which specifc ABC protein might be involved. Te vacuolar membrane of Arabidopsis contains 10 ABC subclass C members (AtABCC1-8, 10 and $1 4 ) ^ { 4 8 }$ and the AtABCC proteins are the predominate ABC transporters localized to the vacuolar membrane49. Within this group, AtABCC1 and 2 were the frst plant ABCC transporters identifed and are the best characterized in terms of their in vitro transport activity31–33,39,50,51. Interestingly, both were also thought to be capable of transporting the glutathione conjugate of C3G (C3G-GS)31,32. However, these results were questioned since other investigators10 were unable to replicate the chemical formation of the $[ ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { C } 3 \mathrm { G } { \cdot } \mathrm { G } S$ substrate. It was suggested that the severe chemical conditions (e.g. high pH, heat, long incubation time) used for the synthesis of $[ ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { C } 3 \mathrm { G } { \cdot } \mathrm { G } \mathrm { S }$ from C3G and $[ { } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ]$ GSH resulted in the formation of oxidized $[ { } ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ]$ GSH $( [ ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { G S S G } )$ rather than $[ ^ { 3 } \mathrm { H } ] \mathrm { C } 3 \mathrm { G } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { G } \mathrm { S } ^ { 1 0 }$ . In any case, C3G-GS was tested as a possible substrate for AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 following the discovery of the involvement of both GST enzymes (BZ2) and ABCC transporters (ZmABCC3 and 4) in the vacuolar sequestration of anthocyanins in corn9,25. Te closest ZmABCC3 homolog in Arabidopsis is AtABCC1025,26. However, to the best of our knowledge, AtABCC10 has not been linked to anthocyanin transport in Arabidopsis and it has not been shown to transport anthocyanins in heterologous expression systems. More recently, it has been demonstrated that VvABCC1 is involved in the vacuolar accumulation of anthocyanins in grape berry26. Te in vitro transport of anthocyanins was strictly dependent on GSH though no anthocyanin-GS conjugate was formed; rather, VvABCC1 was a co-transporter for both anthocyanins and GSH. Te obvious involvement of ABCC transporters in the vacuolar sequestration of C3G and the fnding that VvABCC1 was capable of anthocyanin and GSH co-transport, prompted us to reexamine the ability of AtABCC1 and 2 to transport C3G. As with VvABCC1, we were able to demonstrate that AtABCC2, but not AtABCC1, could transport C3G in a GSH dependent manner. During our in vitro assays, there was no chemical change in C3G following transport ruling out the formation of a C3G-GS conjugate. Rather, AtABCC2, like VvABCC1, was an anthocyanin/GSH co-transporter since C3G would promote the uptake of GSH and vice versa. Tis is the frst demonstration that an ABCC transporter from the model organism Arabidopsis is capable of C3G/GSH co-transport.

Te MgATP-dependent transport of C3G by Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles exhibited Michaelis-Menton-type saturation kinetics $\mathrm { \Delta K _ { m } }$ for C3G of $0 . 5 5 \mathrm { m M }$ ) as did the MgATP-dependent uptake of C3G in the presence of GSH by AtABCC2 expressed in yeast $\mathrm { \Delta K _ { m } }$ for C3G of $1 . 6 \mathrm { m M }$ ). Our calculations (see Supplementary Information) indicate that the cyanidin-type anthocyanin concentration can reach $3 4 \mu \mathrm { M }$ in cells of Arabidopsis leaves under typical soil-grown conditions and $0 . 3 8 \mathrm { m M }$ in the cytosol of leaf cells experiencing stress conditions. Tis cytosolic concentration under stress conditions begins to approach the $\mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values for both AtABCC2 expressed in yeast and the vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles. It should also be noted, that the cyanidin-type anthocyanins in Arabidopsis leaves are decorated with xylosyl, malonyl, coumaryl, and sinapoyl moieties52. Tese naturally occurring cyanidin-type anthocyanins are the more likely natural substrates of AtABCC2 and the other possible transporters in the vacuolar membrane and may be transported at a higher afnity than observed for the model substrate C3G. Tis may be similar to what was observed for MtMATE2, which had a kinetic preference for malonylated anthocyanins over the non-malonylated glycosides18.

In addition to anthocyanins, MtMATE2 has also been shown to transport a variety of other favonoids18. Therefore, we were interested in determining if this was also the case for AtABCC2. We demonstrated that AtABCC2 could transport all anthocyanins examined in the presence of MgATP and GSH. We did not observe any signifcant uptake of the aglycones. Terefore, at a minimum, glucosylation is a requirement for transport. In addition to anthocyanins, AtABCC2 had signifcant uptake capacity for favones (L7G and A7G) and favonols (K3G and Q3G), but not the favonone N7G. When MtMATE2 was expressed in yeast it was capable of signifcant anthocyanin (C3G) transport as well as transport of favone glucosides (A7G and L7G) and a favanone glucoside (N7G). However, in vitro MtMATE2 did not transport favonol glucosides. It is signifcant that AtABCC2 can transport favonol glucosides, since in addition to cyanidin-type anthocyanins, quercetin and kaempferol-type favonols are also prevalent in the vegetative tissue of Arabidopsis30,52–54. Te presence of two transporter types (ABCC and MATE transporters) in the vacuolar membrane of Arabidopsis may extend the range of the types of favonoids that are transported into the vacuole. However, it remains to be determined if the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter-mediated uptake of C3G by Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles involves a MATE transporter.

Given the relatively high uptake rate for L7G by AtABCC2, we decided to further explore the transport mechanism of this substrate. Even though L7G is not found in Arabidopsis52, it does have roles in other plants including alfalfa where it may be a nod-gene inducing compound in Rhizobia meliloti55,56. Dietary Luteolin from plants has also been shown to function in animals as an anti-oxidant, anti-infammatory, and anti-cancer agent57. In species that produce luteolin glucosides, ABCC transporters may be involved in the vacuolar sequestration and thus the regulation of the activity of this favonoid. Interestingly, though ABCC2 appeared to be a cotransporter of C3G and GSH, this efect was not observed with L7G; while GSH enhanced L7G transport, L7G did not afect GSH transport. Ligand docking studies showed that the L7G binding site overlaps with the GSH and C3G binding sites, supporting the fnding that AtABCC2 is not a L7G/GSH co-transporter. Regardless of the assay conditions, L7G was not altered afer transport indicating that a GSH conjugate was not formed. A multisite model for AtABCC2 has been proposed that includes semi-autonomous transport pathways and distinct binding sites33. GSH has been shown to stimulate the uptake of $\beta$ -estradiol 17- $\beta$ -D-glucuronide) $( \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } 1 7 \beta \mathrm { G } )$ , but $\mathrm { E } _ { 2 } 1 7 \mathrm { \beta G }$ did not promote GSH transport. Given the similarities, it is possible that the transport of L7G may occur through the same site on AtABCC2 as $\mathrm { E } _ { 2 } 1 7 \mathrm { \beta G }$ .

While we could demonstrate that ABCC2 expressed in yeast was capable of C3G and GSH cotransport, we did not see a diference in transport rates or inhibitor sensitivities between vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles isolated from wild-type or atabcc2 mutants (see Supplementary Fig. S2). In addition, knock-out mutants of AtABCC2 did not show any favonoid-related phenotypes58 and AtABCC2 expression is not infuenced by regulators of anthocyanin formation in Arabidopsis52. Terefore, it is possible that in addition to AtABCC2, other transporters (e.g. ABCC and/or MATE transporters) are also involved in the vacuolar uptake of favonoids including anthocyanins.

GSH stimulation of C3G transport by yeast vesicles expressing AtABCC2 was not replicated in Arabidopsis vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles. It is possible that endogenous factors modulating the activity of C3G uptake by ABCC transporters co-purify with the isolated vacuolar membrane-enriched vesicles. Tese factors would be absent in the yeast used as a heterologous expression system for AtABCC2. The addition of GSH might then substitute for the missing factors in yeast. One possible factor might involve the membrane bound immunophilin-like protein TWISTED DWARF1 (TWD1). TWD1 has been shown to interact with both AtABCC1 and 2 and modulate the activity of organic anion transport by isolated vacuoles in a manner similar to that observed for both glutathione conjugates and $\mathrm { G S H } ^ { 5 9 }$ .

Tough there is now evidence that the uptake of anthocyanins by at least two plant ABCC transporters (i.e. AtABCC2 and VvABCC1; $2 7 . 2 \%$ sequence identity at the amino acid level) can be enhanced by the presence of GSH, the transport mechanism at the protein level has not been explored until now. As indicated by the molecular modeling analysis of AtABCC2 and supported by mutagenesis studies, the central cavity in the membrane part of the transporter contains the C3G and GSH binding sites in close proximity to each other. Mutants of residues from these ligand binding sites show variable degrees of impairment in transport activity and GSH activation; coupling between ATP hydrolysis and transport activity in all the mutants is not signifcantly afected, though slightly lower. Mutations of R426 and E357 residues at the binding sites boundary reduce transport activity signifcantly (R426, $1 9 \%$ of the wild-type activity) or completely (E357). Tey are probably residues important for coordinating and organizing the ligand binding as they can interact with either ligand as well as with each other, with E357 playing a more critical role. Single-site mutations in residues that interact only with one of the ligands (R567 and E1148 for C3G or Y360 and K309 for GSH), decrease transport activity by 30 to $6 0 \%$ of the wild-type, indicating that there is no particular residue essential for ligand binding and that ligand recognition is distributed among the residues forming the binding site. Nevertheless, the larger side-chain residues do seem more important probably because they impose steric constraints besides providing hydrogen-bond interactions to ligand binding. E1148, which comes from the C-terminus half of the transporter, is predicted to make hydrogen bonds with two hydroxyl groups in the glucosyl moiety of C3G, however its mutation still retains $3 3 \%$ of wild-type C3G uptake activity. Most residues in the C3G and GSH binding sites belong to the N-terminus half domain; C-domain residues may move in and out of the ligand binding site in response to ATP hydrolysis. Tus, E1148 may not be involved in the initial binding of C3G to AtABCC2, explaining the modest efect its mutation has on transport activity. In AtABCC2, K309 and Y360 in the GSH binding site are more than $8 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ away from where C3G putatively binds, however their mutations afect C3G uptake even when GSH is absent. Tis coupled with the proximity of the C3G and GSH binding sites, and with the fnding that mutants in the C3G binding site (R567A and E1148A) impair GSH transport activation, suggest that C3G and GSH are not independently recognized, rather C3G and GSH infuence each other’s binding. Whether this is the case for other GSH-dependent ABC transporters remains to be established. In the crystal structure of a GSH-binding ABC transporter, $\mathrm { A t m l } ^ { 6 0 }$ , the GSH binding site is located similarly as in the AtABCC2 model, close to the inner membrane surface in the cavity, but the amino acids involved in GSH binding (R280, R284, S394, and D398) are not conserved in AtABCC2. Tis suggests that while the recognition of GSH may vary, the mechanism by which GSH enhances transport of substrates in ABC transporters may be more general.

In conclusion, we suggest that AtABCC2 along with possibly other ABCC proteins and MATE transporters is involved in the vacuolar transport of anthocyanins and other favonoids in the vegetative tissue of Arabidopsis. Te identifcation of an ABCC transporter in Arabidopsis that is capable of the in vitro anthocyanin transport and the wealth of genetic resources available for this model organism should allow for a more complete investigation of the role of ABCC transporters, GSH, GST (TT19), TWD1, and possible ABCC/MATE protein-protein interactions in the vacuolar sequestration of anthocyanins. In addition, through molecular modeling analysis, site-directed mutagenesis, and functional transport studies of AtABCC2, we suggest that the C3G and GSH binding sites are in the central cavity of the membrane localized portion of the transporter and are in close proximity to one another such that ligand binding is coordinated. Tese studies also allowed us to identify amino acid residues important for ligand recognition and transport activity. Understanding the mechanistic details of GSH transport activation and substrate recognition in AtABCC2 will provide essential insights into the functional versatility of ABC transporters.

The ABC-transporter superfamily is one of the largest protein families known (Henikoff et al. 1997). In bacteria,most members of this family are responsible for the high-affinity uptake of small molecules like maltose or histidine (Higgins et al. 1986; Higgins 1992). In contrast,eukaryotic ABC transporters have not yet been shown to transport carbohydrates or amino acids.In mammals,ABC transporters have been found to confer multidrug resistance in cancer cells upon overexpression (Chen et al. 1986; Gottesman and Pastan 1993). These transporters mediate diverse cellular transport processes, such as the excretion (extracellular over the plasma membrane or intracellular into the vacuoles) of potentially toxic compounds, lipid translocation, excretion of the mating factor of yeast, conferring heavy-metal tolerance, and antigen presentation, as well as exhibiting ion channel activity or modulating the activity of ion channels (Kuchler et al. 1989; McGrath and Varshavsky 1989；Kelly et al. 1992；Balzi and Goffeau 1994; Szczypka et al. 1994; Higgins 1995).

Despite the recent completion of the genomic sequencing of Arabidopsis (AGI 20o0), knowledge about the function of this large protein superfamily of ABC transporters in plants is still scarce. Among these proteins the so-called “full-size transporters’ are the best characterised to date.Therefore, this review will include an update of the inventory of plant full-size ABC transporters,a description of which has been started in recent reviews (Rea et al. 1998; Rea 1999; Theodoulou 20oo).A further subject of this paper is the assignment of functions to this particular protein family apart from its described cellular detoxification processes. These recent findings shed new light on the role of ABC transporters in plant growth and development processes.


## Characteristics of ABC transporters


On a functional basis, the transport of substrates by ABC proteins is characterized by (i) direct dependence on $\mathbf { M g A T P }$ ； (ii) the fact that other nucleotides,mainly GTP,can substitute for ATP;and (iii) the fact that transport is inhibited by micromolar concentration of vanadate.In plants, these criteria are easy to confirm for transport processes across the vacuolar membrane since the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase is not inhibited by vanadate. Directly energized transporters are able to accumulate a far higher concentration of compounds in the vacuole than secondarily energized transporters (Kreuz et al. 1996).For transporters localized at the plasma membrane，proof of direct energizing is more difficult to ascertain, due to the vanadate-sensitivity of the plasmamembrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase.

Another way to define an ABC transporter is based on their characteristic structures and motifs: all ABC transporters consist of two pairs of basic structural elements - integral membrane-spanning domains (MSD) and nucleotide-binding folds (NBF） oriented towards the cytoplasm.In bacteria, the four domains can reside on different independent polypeptides,whereas bacterial genes encoding fusions of all four domains have,to date, rarely been found (Linton and Higgins 1998;Braibant et al.2ooo). In contrast, in plants -as in animals and yeast - such proteins are encoded by conserved gene families. The so-called “full-size ABC transporters" can be subdivided into two groups according to their topology: multidrug-resistance proteins(MDRs, also known as PGPs for P-glycoproteins) and multidrug-resistance-related proteins (MRPs),which show a structure of MSD-NBF-MSD-NBF. The mirrored topology (NBF-MSD-NBF-MSD) can be found for PDR(pleiotropic drug resistance） and ABC1-like genes (Higgins 1992; Bungert et al. 2001).

Another characteristic feature of the different ABC transporters can be observed in the NBFs,where an identity of $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ over a region of about 200-400 amino acid residues be found. This domain contains three conserved sequence motifs: an ATP-binding site consisting of a Walker A box and a Walker B box separated by approximately 12O amino acids (Walker et al. 1982)and, between the two boxes,a consensus sequence specific for ABC transporters (Higgins 1992).


## Plant ABC transporters


Through the efforts of the coordinated international Arabidopsis sequencing project of the Arabidopsis Genome Initiative (AGI), the complete genomic sequence and a preliminary annotation approach were published before the end of 2000 (AGI 2000). It was already known that Arabidopsis thaliana $( A t )$ shows a high gene density with about 25,500 genes in $1 2 5 { , } 0 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k b }$ ，which exceeds that of any other completely sequenced genome (human,Drosophila, Caenorhabditis, bacteria). Of the ca. 600 predicted membrane-transport systems found in Arabidopsis,a large number are ABC transporters. A total of 51 genes can be found encoding full-size transporters of the AtPDR,AtMRP and AtPGP subclusters (Fig.1， Table 1). Additionally，two sequences，for ABC1- and PMP70-like genes,were annotated as fullsize transporters (see above).Neither of these genes clusters to any of the three major classes of full-size transporters,which confirms their unique status in the Arabidopsis genome.

Therefore, 53 genes have been found to encode fullsize ABC proteins in the Arabidopsis genome. This number of full-size transporters largely exceeds that reported in Saccharomyces cerevisae (Decottignies and Goffeau 1997) and that of Homo sapiens.In the latter the total number of all putative ABC transporters (irrespective of size and structure) is quoted as 51 (see http://www.humanabc.org). This raises the question about the reasons for the high number of full-size ABCtransporter genes in plants.

It is remarkable that in Arabidopsis several members of the three gene families (MDR,MRP,and PDR-like) could be found, but only one ABC1-likegene $( A t 2 g 4 I 7 0 0 )$ . Interestingly, all other homologous ABCtransporter genes in the Arabidopsis genome are annotated as half-size transporters.In contrast, in the human genome at least 14 full-size transporters of the ABC1- like class are found (see http://www.humanabc.org). Also one PMP70-like sequence $( A t 4 g 3 9 8 5 0 )$ has been described showing structures of a full-size transporter, whereas all other known members of this gene family (also from plants) belong to the class of half-size transporters. The extraordinary structures of the mentioned sequences as full-size transporters,emphasizing their unique position in plants, still await confirmation by experimental data.

The large number of genes in the MDR/MRP and PDR5-like sub-clusters,and the strong sequence homology found in many cases, suggest functional redundancy. One reason for a number of gene duplications is clearly the duplication of large segments of Arabidopsis chromosomes.More than 20 segments,each larger than $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k b }$ ， comprise over half the Arabidopsis genome, suggesting a tetraploid origin for Arabidopsis (AGI 2000).Because of this duplication of entire chromosomal regions,and by means of sequence comparisons, we have recently been able to confirm the duplication of several ABC transporter genes in Arabidopsis (data not shown).

Phylogenetic analysis of all three full-size ABCtransporter families groups the AtPGP genes with their human homologues and TAP1, the transporter associated with antigen processing.Although PGPs have also been cloned from barley (Davies et al. 1997) and potato (Wang et al.1996) their functions in plants are still unclear.Experiments with overexpression and antisense repression of AtPGP1 showed that this protein might be involved not only in xenobiotic resistance (Thomas et al.2OoO) but also in light-signal transduction (Dudler and Hertig 1992; Sidler et al.1998). With 22 members, the AtPGPs are the largest family of ful-size transporter genes in Arabidopsis. Two genes related to this family，however,have to be pointed out. At4g25450 (M7J2.180) is annotated as a multidrug resistance gene of 280 amino acids.Although it shows highest homology to AtPGP genes (about $40 \%$ identity), its genomic structure does not show similarities to this gene family. It consists of just one NBF without any membrane-spanning region and therefore has not been included in the list of full-size transporter genes.For At5g39040 (MXF12.50) the case is similar: It shows homology to the AtPGP gene family with sequence identity scores of around $30 \%$ . But the assignment of this sequence to the PGPs,denoted as PGP8 (Davies and Coleman 20oo),is questionable as it encodes a half-size ABC transporter. Compared with other members of this gene family At5g39040 shows a completely different genomic structure. These findings are also supported by the position of the gene in the phylogenetic tree (Fig. 1, denoted as AtPGPL). Therefore,in our eyes,the AtPGP subfamily consists of 22 genes coding for full-size ABC proteins.

The AtMRP genes are the best-characterized plant ABC transporters to date. These proteins are known to function as vacuolar sequesters of glutathionylated compounds,malonylated chlorophyll catabolites and glucuronides (Martinoia et al. 1993, 2000; Rea et al. 1998; Theodoulou 20oO). From the data available, it is evident that at least some of these transporters have overlapping transport activities. AtMRP1, AtMRP2 and AtMRP3 exhibit glutathione-conjugate transport activity,but only AtMRP2 and AtMRP3 are able to transport chlorophyll catabolites accumulated during leaf senescence (Lu et al. 1997, 1998; Tommasini et al. 1998). Interestingly, transport of glutathione conjugates is only negligibly inhibited by chlorophyll catabolites and vice versa (Lu et al. 1998), as has also been confirmed using intact vacuoles (Hinder et al. 1996). AtMRP2 and AtMRP5 also transport glucuronides (Gaedeke et al. 2001; Liu et al.200i). AtMRP2,which is localized on the vacuolar membrane (Liu et al. 2oo1),exhibits a much stronger activity,and shows more of the characteristics observed for glucuronide transport in intact vacuoles where modulation of glucuronide transport by glutathione conjugates has been demonstrated (Klein et al.1998,2000, 2001). Interestingly, the transport activities of compounds containing more than one glucuronate, and hence carrying more negative charges,are increased by a membrane potential that is positive inside the vacuole. Related to AtMRPs are sulfonylurea-receptor-like proteins that are involved in regulating the conductance of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -channels and which may also control the water-conducting aquaporins (Schreiber et al. 1999) and the cystic fibrosis transmembrane regulator (Akabas 2000).

Expression studies in our laboratory have revealed that most of the AtMRP genes are expressed in leaves, roots,flowers， stems and siliques.Only a few genes showed increased accumulation of mRNA in a specific tissue (data not shown). Some AtMRPs exhibit increased transcript levels if plants are treated with xenobiotics or salicylic acid (Tommasini et al. 1997; Sanchez-Fernandez et al. 1998; and our own data). Besides transport measurements for glutathione conjugates (see below), to our knowledge the only report on an MRP-like ABC transporter from plants was the demonstration that antibodiesraised againstan AtMRP homologue from wheat up-regulated by safhttp://mips.gsf.de/proj/thal/db) with ABC signatures were examined for their structural similarity or sequence homology toward characterized full-size ABC transporters.Secondly, several MRP, PDR and PGP amino acid sequences from Arabidopsis were used for BLAST searches against the entire Arabidopsis genomic sequences deposited in GENBANK.As references for the different ABC transporter genes the corresponding entries from MATDB were used, because this database contains one of the most recent annotations (K.F.X.Mayer,personal communication).In cases where deviating data have been given in the list,explanations are found in the footnotes.To determine the number of ESTs for the different genes,BLAST searches with the predicted CDS were made using all GENBANK ESTs in TAIR (http://arabidopsis.org/Blast/)

The AtMRP gene family consists of 15 members,including one aberrant gene， AtMRP15, which is annotated as a protein with an N-terminal truncation due to $5 ^ { \prime }$ stop codons of about 40o amino acids that are not present in other AtMRPs.Its nucleotide sequence isnearly identical to thatof AtMRP9, even in the non-coding $5 ^ { \prime }$ region. In contrast to all other full-size proteins encoding AtMRPs we have been unable to detect a transcript for this gene in Arabidopsis (data not shown)，raising the possibility that AtMRPi5 is indeed a pseudogene. Another MRPrelated gene is encoded by Atlg71330 (F3I7.2). It seems to encode only one membrane-spanning region with high similarities to AtMRP3 and so cannot be considered as a classical transporter. The arrangement of sequences in the phylogenetic tree suggests that AtMRP1,2, 11 and 12 comprise a group of closely related genes. A similar grouping can be found for all other AtMRP genes with the exception of AtMRP13, which represents an intermediate between the two MRP subgroups. Interestingly, these phylogenetic data are in agreement with the intron-exon structures of the genes.

MDRs and MRPs exhibit the same arrangement of domains but differ at their N-termini where an extremely hydrophobic N-terminal extension (NTE) of around 22O amino acids is observed for MRPs but not for MDRs. A careful study of the membrane topology of human MRP, employing glycosylation-site mutants, indicates that the hydrophobic NTE forms a third MSD of five transmembrane $\mathscr { X }$ -helices and that the N-terminus is most likely situated in the extracytoplasmic side of the membrane bilayer (Hipfner et al.1997).Hydropathy plots of animal and plant MRPs resemble each other to a great extent, suggesting a similar arrangement of the membrane-spanning domains in animals and plants.In contrast, the NTE of MRPs exhibits only weak homology among the different members of MRPlike proteins.

The third group of ful-size ABC transporters is formed by 15 AtPDR-like genes and represents a separate sub-cluster. These proteins are characterized in fungal systems as efflux transporters for cytotoxic compounds such as oligomycin or cyclohexamide (Balzi and Goffeau 1994). A PDR-like ABC transporter also plays a role in the pathogen reaction since it has been shown that plant pathogenic fungi need the activity of PDR5- like genes for expression of pathogenicity or acquired resistance towards fungicides (Urban et al. 1999; Andrade et al. 20oo).In a very recent publication, Jasinski et al (20o1) showed that Nicotiana plumbaginifolia ABC1 (NpABC1)，a member of the PDR5-like family，is also localized in the plasma membrane. NpABC1 is highly expressed in the presence of sclareolide,a close analogue of the antifungal diterpene sclareol.These properties, together with the observation that the cellular sclareolide content decreases in parallel with the induction of the ABC transporter and that inhibitors of ATP synthesis reverse this effect, strongly suggest that this PDR5 homologue is involved the excretion of secondary metabolites playing a role in plant defense.

By performing a differential screening of Spirodela polyrrhiza grown in the absence and presence of abscisic acid (ABA), Smart and Fleming (1996) have identified a PDR5-like ABC transporter (TUR2). The expression of this transporter is increased about 7-fold within $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ after application of ABA. Other treatments that, in contrast to ABA,do not induce turion formation in Spirodela, such as exposure to cycloheximide or salt stress,also resulted in an increased mRNA level for TUR2, indicating that expression of TUR2 is not the cause of turion formation. Compared with the AtPGP and AtMRP classes the AtPDR5-like genes form a relatively tight cluster. This also holds true for the genes AtPDR2 and AtPDR12. AtPDR2 was originally annotated as two separate genes (see MATDB entries AT4gl5230 and AT4g15220,http://www.mips.biochem.mpg.de/proj/ thal/db/index.html). Alignment-based re-annotation of the sequences suggests a single gene coding for a protein of 1,385 amino acids,whose genomic structure is in concord with that of other AtPDR5-like genes. Annotations for AtPDR12 differ between MATDB and GENBANK in such a way that MATDB lists AtPDR12 as a pseudogene and GENBANK presents it as a functional gene. Expressed sequence tags(ESTs) for AtPDRi2 (see Table 1） support the latter suggestion. Furthermore,the described annotations for AtPDR2 and AtPDRi2 are supported by their positions in the phylogenetic analysis (see Fig. 1).

Figure 2 shows a comparison of the Walker motifs and ABC signature of plant full-size ABC transporters. It is obvious that only the Walker A box exhibits perfect conservation in all of these proteins, whereas both of the other consensus motifs exhibit a higher degree of variation. One consequence of this finding is that the definition of this class of proteins by consensus sequences alone could result in misleading interpretations about their functions.On the other hand,these consensus motifs can serve as valuable tools. The mentioned PMP70-like sequence lacks the N-terminal Walker A box and the second ABC motif is situated in the last 12 amino acids of the protein leaving no space for a Walker B box.These facts make a function as an ATP-dependent transporter questionable.

Numbering of AtPGP,AtMRP and AtPDR5 genes is according to Davies and Coleman (2oo0),with the exception of AtMRP8,13,11 (described as MRP6-8 in Davies and Coleman 20oO) and AtPGP8 (see above). Genes not mentioned in that review were numbered successively （AtPGP11-AtPGP22，AtMRP9-AtMRP15 and AtPDR9-AtPDR12). It is worth mentioning that this summary cannot be the final list of the Arabidopsis inventory of full-size ABC transporter genes as the complete coding sequences are published only for a small number of genes. The number of full-size ABC transporter genes was estimated from annotations of genomic data. Only half of the genes in this table are confirmed by experimental data or ESTs (Table 1). The annotations are mostly based on homology to known genes and/or gene-prediction programs. Until these predictions are confirmed by experimental data,such estimations of gene numbers should be treated with caution. This holds especially true for cases where either putatively wrong annotations (AtPDR2), contradictory annotations (AtPGP8,AtPGP22) or no annotations at all （AtPDR13-AtPDR15) have been given. Data sets from sequencing projects of Arabidopsis ful-length cDNAs, like the one recently released by Ceres Inc. in theTiGRdatabase(http://www.tigr.org/tdb/ath1/ htmls/index.html),might clear up the remaining questions.


## ABC-type transport activities for which the corresponding transporter has not been identified


Besides glutathione conjugates,chlorophyll catabolites and glucuronides,for which transport proteins have been identified (see above)，vacuolar uptake of some additional substrates exhibits typical ABC-type transport kinetics:

i.Bile acids (Hörtensteiner et al. 1993),which have not been demonstrated in plants.Interestingly, in animals an MDR-type transporter is responsible for the transport of bile acids (Gerloff et al. 1998 ） while in yeast this activity could be assigned to an MRP-type transporter (Ortiz et al. 1997).   
ii. The sulfonated compound Lucifer Yellow.Several animal MRPs have been shown to transport sulfated compounds and it is probable that one or several of the already-cloned AtMRPs exhibits a transport activity for sulfonated and sulfated compounds.   
ii. Glucosylated compounds are the predominant class of secondary metabolites stored within plant cells. In most cases they are transported into the vacuole by proton antiporter mechanisms (Martinoia et al. 2000).However,it has been shown that vacuolar uptake of a glucosylated herbicide,which is formed during the detoxification process (Kreuz et al. 1996), exhibits kinetics typical of ABC-transporters (Klein et al. 1996).

Recent experiments have shown the great diversity of transporters that recognize compounds synthesized by different plants. Uptake of the main barley flavonoid saponarin into barley vacuoles shows that this compound is taken up by a proton antiporter mechanism.In contrast,work in our laboratories has shown that vacuoles isolated from Arabidopsis,a plant that does not synthesize the flavone glucoside saponarin, exhibit direct energization by an ABC-type transporter (Fragne et al.，in press). It is therefore tempting to speculate that glucosides are only taken up by an antiporter mechanism if structural homologues are present in the plant (or cell).In contrast, glucosides, which have no structural analogues in the plant, may be recognized as modified, potentially toxic compounds and transported into the vacuole using a directly energized ABC-type transporter. However, the fact that barley vacuoles transport aesculin by a proton antiport system indicates that this hypothesis cannot be generalized and is probably only true for large glycosylated compounds.


## ABC transporters regulate ion fluxes


Most ABC transporters couple the hydrolysis of ATP and transport of molecules across a membrane against a concentration gradient. As a consequence, this transport mechanism allows the hyper-accumulation of a molecule in a compartment.However, in two cases ABC transporters,well characterized in animal cells,have been unequivocally shown to be involved in ion transport or ion-channel regulation. These transporters control the flux of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ according to the electrochemical gradient and in response to changes in the concentration of cytosolic nucleotides like ADP or ATP.These ABC transporters are:

i. The K-ATP channels (Bryan and Aguilar-Bryan 1999)，which are heteromultimers constituted by ABC-type sulfonylurea receptors (SUR1, SUR2A or SUR2B) and the potassium inward rectifier $( \mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 1$ or ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2 )$ . Neither SUR1 nor $\mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2$ cDNAs exhibited recognizable K-ATP channel activity when expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,but co-expression generated current characteristics of native KATP channels (Inagaki et al. 1995). Interestingly, when Dsur,a novel Drosophila gene highly homologous to vertebrate SUR but harboring an additional 1.7-kb extension，was expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,a classical K-ATP channel signature was recorded (Nasonkin et al. 1999). This result was not observed with mammalian SUR in the same expression system, suggesting that the sequence extension in Dsur could be responsible for the generation of Kchannel activity.

ii. The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator(CFTR),which functions as a phosphorylation- and nucleotide-regulated small-conductance chloride channel (Akabas 20oo). Besides its function asa $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channel, CFTR acts as a regulator of amiloride-sensitive $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ channels,outward-rectifying $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channels, $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ exchanger and ROMK $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Schwiebert et al. 1999).

CFTR and SUR are unequivocally involved in transport/regulation of ion fluxes and share more similarities with the MRP than the MDR family. They exhibit a defined pharmacology. Some sulfonylureas, like glibenclamide and tolbutamide,are potent inhibitors of K-ATP channels and the CFTR-mediated $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ conductance.K-ATP channels can be activated by a diverse group of compounds collectively referred to as potassium channel openers (KCOs). These compounds have been developed for clinical use in patients with hypertension,asthma or ischemic heart disease and may act as antagonists of the sulfonylureas.In order to test whether such ABC-transporters are also present in plants, Leonhardt et al.(1997) investigated the effect of inhibitors of the K-ATP-channel and CFTR on epidermal strips and guard cells of Vicia faba.Incubation of epidermal strips with glibenclamide or tolbutamide led to a dose-dependent increase in stomatal aperture with a $\mathrm { K } _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $2 . 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for glibenclamide. In contrast, KCOs inhibited stomatal opening and induced stomatal closure in the nanomolar range of concentration. Using guard-cell protoplasts and the patch-clamp technique, the authors observed a partial inhibition of the outward potassium current by glibenclamide.This inhibition was partially reversed by the KCO cromakalim. Since the guard-cell potassium channel is not ATP-sensitive,a similar but not identical system to the one described in animals may be present in guard cells.However, due to the fact that guard cels were investigated in the whole-cell configuration, the efects observed on potassium channels may be indirect. Therefore, Leonhardt et al. (1999) also tested this hypothesis and observed that glibenclamide inhibits the $\dot { \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } }$ -induced stomatal closure caused by slow anion efflux.The phytohormone ABA,however, reversed the glibenclamide effect.From these results the authors postulated that in plants,as in animals,ABC-type proteins are involved in the regulation of ion channel activities. Direct evidence that plant ABC transporters are indeed implicated in ion fluxes has been provided recently (Gaedeke et al. 2001). AtMRP5,like the other AtMRPs,exhibits a high similarity to CFTR and SUR. It is highly expressed in vascular tissue and in stomata. Analysis of a T-DNA-induced mutation of AtMRP5 revealed that glibenclamide triggers stomatal opening in the dark in the wild type but not in mrp5-1 mutant plants (Fig.3). This is a direct hint that ABC transporters are also involved in regulation of stomatal opening.Presently，it is not possible to differentiate whether AtMRP5 controls either $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or anion channels, exhibits channel activities or is a member of the signal transduction pathway leading to stomatal opening. Finally,the fact that the nucleotide-binding domain of

ABC transporters resembles the respective domains of Ras and other G-proteins could raise the possibility that a conformational change in these domains might have regulatory consequences for interacting proteins.


## ABC transporters are involved in plant growth processes


Recent results show that ABC transporters are not only implicated in detoxification and ion-regulation processes but also in plant growth processes.

Sidler et al.(1998) have shown that AtPGP1 is responsible for control of hypocotyl cell elongation under low light. An increase of $50 \%$ in hypocotyl length could be observed at a photon fluence rate of $1 \mathrm { \dot { 0 } ~ } \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { \ s } ^ { - 1 }$ for plants overexpressing AtPGP1, and about $20 \%$ inhibition of hypocotyl length was detected for plants that showed antisense inhibition of AtPGP1 under the same light conditions.However,in darkness,as well as at fluence rates of $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m o l } } ~ { \mathrm { m } } ^ { - 2 } ~ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ ， no difference in cell elongation was observed. The growth response was independent of light quality and could be observed under red and blue light regimes.The response to far-red light (FR) was also different in wild-type and overexpressing plants, but in this case seedling growth in FR was less than $1 0 \%$ of that observed in darkness. In addition,roots of plants overexpressing AtPGP1 were slightly larger than control plants.Very recent data suggest that AtPGP1 might export ATP; however, the reason for the observed phenotype is still unknown (Thomas et al. 2000).

A further example of the involvement of plant ABC transporters in light-regulated growth processes has very recently been presented by Moller et al (2001). It was observed that the gene responsible for the laf6 (long after FR） phenotype,which exhibits reduced responsiveness toward continuous FR,encodes an ABC transporter. This ABC transporter is highly homologous to an ABC transporter of Synechocystis and the cryptophyte alga Guillardia theta. It is interesting to note that in this alga the corresponding ABC transporter is encoded on the chloroplast genome,while in higher plants no chloroplast-encoded ABC transporters can be found.In addition to the highly homologous ABC transporters of Synechocystis and Guillardia, AtABC1 contains an N-terminal transit peptide that targets it to the chloroplast. The mutation in this gene results in protoporphyrin IX accumulation and lower chlorophyll contents.The protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPO) inhibitor flumioxazin results in increased levels of protoporphyrin IX and hence mimicks the laf6 phenotype. Plants overexpressing AtABC1 showed a reduced sensitivity to flumioxazin. In addition,genes known to be light-regulated such as chalcone synthase and ferredoxin ${ \mathrm { N A D P } } ^ { + }$ oxidoreductase are attenuated in laf6 compared with the wild type under high-fluence FR. These results suggest that AtABC1 is associated with a hydrophobic protein localized in the internal envelope of the chloroplast and catalyzes an ATP-dependent import of protoporphyrin IX.

In yeast it has been shown that a mitochondrial halfsize ABC transporter ATM1 is involved in the synthesis of Fe/S clusters (Leighton and Schatz 1995). This function appears to be conserved in eukaryotes, since the human Abc7 and MTABC3 have been shown to be functional orthologues of ATMl (Csere et al. 1998; Mitsuhashi et al. 20o0). Recently, Kushnir et al. (2001) showed that the Arabidopsis mutant starik,which leads to dwarfism and chlorosis, is due to the insertion of a TDNA in an orthologue of ATM1, Stal. Stal complements the yeast mutant △atm1, indicating that this gene, like yeast ATM1 and the corresponding human orthologues, supports the maturation of Fe/S clusters in mitochondria.MeasurementofFeshowedthat mitochondria of the stal mutant contain similar amounts of Fe as the wild-type mitochondria. As in △atml yeast,mitochondria of the Stal mutant cells contain 1.5- to 1.8-fold higher levels of free iron and less iron associated with proteins.A further example of altered plant growth was reported by Gaedeke et al. (2001) who observed that root growth in a T-DNA insertion mutant of AtMRP5 differed from that of control plants. Depending on the potassium concentration in the medium, root growth was reduced or enhanced compared with that of wild-type seedlings.

It is likely that growth processes in plants can be modulated in several ways by ABC transporters. As suggested by Moller et al. (200i), ABC transporters may be directly involved in the transport of a metabolite, or, as shown in the case of Synechocystis,of a metal required as cofactor by some enzymes (Bartsevich and Pakrasi 1995).Phenotypes of plants overexpressing an ABC transporter or where an ABC transporter is knocked-out suggest that the phytohormone balance is disturbed. However,phytohormone transport has not yet been reported for ABC transporters.In the case of MRP-like ABC transporters,a perturbation of phytohormone levels may not result from transport of free phytohormones but from the corresponding conjugates. It is well known that most phytohormones are conjugated to glycosides or amino acids. In the case of auxin, it has been reported that the first conjugation products observed in Arabidopsis are aspartate or glutamate conjugates,which are linked by a peptide bond to auxin (Ostin et al. 1998; Tam et al. 2000). Glutamate conjugates have been shown to be substrates for human MRPs and it is likely that they are also substrates for plant MRPs.Furthermore,it has been shown that some glycosides are recognized by ABC transporters. If such a conjugate is not exported efficiently from the cytosol, free-hormone concentrations may rise due either to feedback inhibition of the conjugation step or hydrolysis of the conjugate accumulating in the cytosol. Such a process would result in higher concentrations of phytohormones and hence the observed changes in the developmental pattern of mrp5-1.

An additional mechanism by which ABC transporters may be involved in developmental processes is through the interaction with other proteins.As discussed above, it was suggested that AtMRP5 interacts with ion channels in stomata. Such interactions may result in distinct phenotypes.

Direct evidence for such an interaction recently demonstrated that ABC transporters also interact with immunophilins.In animals,drugs binding to this class of protein are powerful immunosuppressors due to the fact that the immunophilin-drug complex inhibits the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase calcineurin. In plants,several immunophilins have been identified (Blecher et al 1996;Fulgosi et al. 1998; Vittorioso et al. 1998).We have observed that the FK506-binding(FKBP) immunophilinTWISTED DWARF1 (TWDi) from Arabidopsis shows a pleiotropic knock-out mutant phenotype, including a reduction in cell elongation and disorientated growth of the entire plant (data not shown). Also,using the yeast two-hybrid system we have identified the MDR-like Arabidopsis ABC transporter AtPGPl as an interactant with TWD1 (data not shown). Mapping and biochemical analyses showed that the FKBP-like domain of TWDl mediates AtPGP1 interaction. Since AtPGP1-overexpressing/antisense plants also show a phenotype (see above), it is tempting to speculate that ABC transporters are involved in some signal transduction pathways. Genetic analysis revealed that TWD1 is required for brassinosteroid reception or signal transduction (data not shown). In animal systems, interaction of MDR-like ABC transporters with steroids,as well as transport of steroidal precursors, has been reported (Metherall et al. 1996; Debry et al. 1997; Gruol et al. 1999). Therefore,it is tempting to speculate that plant ABC transporters may also play a role in steroid transport or signal transduction.

Life is not possible without the exchange of substances and information between cells, therefore macro- and micro-organisms have developed efficient transport systems to control the molecular interaction processes within the colonized environment. Transportation of many molecules through the cell semipermeable membrane against a concentration gradient requires the use of energy that can be provided, for instance, by ATP hydrolysis. Plants, due to their sessile status, have evolved a very complex movement system for molecules, in which proteins belonging to the ABC superfamily play a major role [1].

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily represents one of the largest protein group within the kingdoms of archaea, eubacteria and eukarya. Proteins belonging to this superfamily are ATP powered transporters able to translocate substrates across cellular membranes. The transported molecules, even if secreted from the same ABC protein, may be extremely different, both in terms of chemistry and structure [2].

The canonical architecture of ABC transporters comprises two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two cytosolic nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), also known as ATP-binding cassettes. The structural organisation of the four domains is a dimer of dimers, which can deploy as single polypeptides, or as multisubunit oligomers, reflecting ancient gene duplication events and fusions of the cytosolic catalytic with the membrane-spanning domains [1]. Usually intracytosolic loops are present as extensions of TMDs and function as the interface between the NBDs and TMDs [3]. The NBD contains several highly conserved motifs, including the Walker A and B sequences, the ABC signature motif, the H loop and the Q loop [4].

The ABC signature (alias C motif or LSGGQ motif, ((LIVMFY)S(SG)GX 3(RKA)(LIVMYA)X(LIVFM)(AG)) is situated between the two Walker boxes [5], and is the hallmark that distinguish ABC transporters from other ATP binding proteins.

Due to the complexity and dimension of ABC protein superfamily, a precise classification of all the subfamilies is necessary. The proposed categorisations are various. The transporter classification (TC) system, based on incorporation of both functional and phylogenetic information, includes 53 subfamilies of ABC exporters and 34 of ABC importers (http://www.tcdb.org). Based on sequence comparison, [6,7] three classes of ABC systems, that were probably present in the last common ancestor of archaea, bacteria and eukarya, have been proposed: class 1 comprises transporters with fused TMDs and NBDs (exporters); class 2 includes nontransporter ABCs lacking TMDs; class 3 (which is absent in eukaryotes) includes mainly transporters with NBDs and TMDs formed by separate polypeptide chains (canonical importers), and some bacterial exporters.

Plant genomes encode for a high number of ABC proteins with more than 120 found in both Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa [8,9]. The currently used plant ABC protein classification systems are mainly based on phylogenetic information, domain arrangement or similarities/structure comparison with human and microbial prototypes (eg: Pleiotropic Drug Resistance PDR). Sanchez-Fernandez et al. [10] combined information from different classification systems and identified 13 plant subfamilies, including also membrane-bound ABCs that consist only of those containing soluble NBD domains. In order to unify plant and animal ABC naming systems, the Human Genome Organization (HUGO) proposed a new subfamily designation for vertebrate and invertebrate ABC communities, which is now widely used [11,12]. This system originally comprised seven ABC subfamilies (A–G) based on sequence homology, phylogenetic relationships and domain organization. Subsequently, following a more recent inventory of Drosophila and fish ABC proteins, an additional subfamily (H) (not containing members from plants) has been defined. For plants, a further subfamily (I) has been created to incorporate ‘prokaryotic’- type ABCs that are not present in many animal genomes [9]. Subfamilies ABCA, ABCB, ABCC and ABCD contain “forward orientation” TMD-NBD transporters. Subfamilies ABCG and ABCH, instead, are characterized by a “reverse organization” domain NBD-TMD. Subfamilies E and F show only two domains NBD and thus they are labelled as “soluble”. These proteins are not transporters but their NBDs clearly cluster with those of other ABC proteins.

Plant genome sequences availability is growing fast, resulting in an almost completely unexplored repository. The aim of the present work was to list, compare and phylogenetically classify the ABC proteins of selected vascular plant genomes (A. thaliana, O. sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum, Vitis vinifera), the green alga Volvox carteri and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in order to facilitate future studies on ABC genes and proteins. Identification and classification were based on the work by Verrier and collaborators [9]. Further, a selection pressure study and a customized gene duplication analysis, to identify recent duplication events in vascular plant genomes, have been accomplished. Finally, an expression profile overview of ABC superfamily to detect tissue-specific transporter activation in tomato has been performed as a proof of concept and reported.

## 4.2. Secondary Transporters


This is by far the largest group of transporters in plants and in plant mitochondria (Table 1, Table S1), where they are located in the IMM. These transporters are either symporters or antiporters, and use the electrochemical gradient established across the IMM to move ions into or out of the mitochondrial matrix. The size and diversity of transporters in this family reflect the metabolic complexity of mitochondria and its importance as an energetic conduit for the cell [13,28,29].


## 4.2.1. The Mitochondrial Carrier (MC) Family


The MC family (MCF) is predicted to contain 58–60 members in Arabidopsis [28, TransportDB 2.0] and 50–61 members in rice [24, TransportDB 2.0]. The majority of the MCF members are localized in the IMM, although at least 10 are found in plastids, peroxisomes, endoplasmic reticulum, and plasma membrane [29].

About half of all the MCF members are predicted to be found in the mitochondria of both Arabidopsis (30 out of 60) and rice (33 out of 61) (Table S1). In Arabidopsis, 58 members have been experimentally identified (including all the predicted), in other words, a very satisfying $9 7 \%$ , while in rice 49 have been identified (including 29 of the predicted), producing an $8 0 \%$ ‘’recovery” rate (Tables S1 and S2, Figure 1). The almost $1 0 0 \%$ recovery rate for MCF members in proteomic profiling of isolated mitochondria means that most, if not all, of the MC members localized to other membranes [13,29] have also been found in mitochondria. To what extent this is due to dual localization or to contamination of the mitochondrial preparations is an open question.

The MC members catalyze the transport of numerous metabolic intermediates across the IMM—nucleotides like ADP, ATP, and $\mathrm { N A D ^ { + } }$ ; coenzymes like coenzyme A, thiamine pyrophosphate, and folate; di- and tri-carboxylic acids like malate, oxoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and citrate; amino acids like glutamate, aspartate, ornithine, citrulline, and carnitine; as well as phosphate and protons. All these carriers have been admirably reviewed by Palmieri et al. [28] and Toleco et al. [36], so we will not discuss them any further except briefly in connection with one important metabolite, ascorbate.

Ascorbate is very important in mitochondrial metabolism where it participates in the ascorbate-glutathione cycle that removes $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ produced by the respiratory chain e.g., [37]. The last step in ascorbate biosynthesis takes place on the outer surface of the IMM [38], but to date no ascorbate transporter has been identified in the IMM. Ascorbate transport was measured in plant and rat liver mitochondria by Scalera et al. [39]. The protein responsible was in the size range $2 8 { - } 3 5 \mathrm { k D a } _ { \ r }$ , which is where most of the MC family transporters are found, but the gene was not identified. An ascorbate transporter has been identified in the chloroplast envelope [40], which could in principle be dually targeted to IMM. However, since it is $6 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ it could not be responsible for the transport activity observed by Scalera et al. [39].
