Shallot commodities with high economic value influence the rate of inflation. In Indonesia, shallots are cultivated intensively in 34 provinces with a total harvested area in 2017 of 158,172 ha with the total production of 1,470,154 tons (the Central Bureau of Statistics (BPS, 2018). Several problems still hamper the development of cultivation in Indonesia. Those problems include the unavailability of seeds with good quality throughout the growing season and the presence of seed-borne pathogens. Shallot production using bulbs as the planting materials in the long term causes accumulation of pathogens (Widodo et al., 2011). The availability of bulbs is also limited since it depends on the planting seasons and requires a long storage time (maximum 6-8 months) until the bulbs are ready to be used as planting seeds (Pardjo et al., 2012). These problems can be solved by using True Shallot

Seed (TSS) as an alternative substitution of the bulbs as the planting materials. TSS is known to have higher productivity, fewer seed needs, more efficient distribution and storage of seeds, the longer shelf life of seeds and higher resistance to viruses and seed infectious diseases (Pangestuti and Sulistyaningsih, 2011).

Such cultivars as Tuk Tuk, Sanren and Lokananta are superior shallots cultivars produced by the East West Seed Indonesia Ltd. They have been registered in the Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia with the numbers: 361/Kpts/SR.120/5/2006; 072/Kpts/ SR.120/D.2.7/7/2013; and 059/Kpts/SR.120/ D.2.7/6/2017. Tuk Tuk can adapt well in lowlands with an altitude of 20-220 m.a.s.l. and is very well planted in the dry season (the Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia, 2006). Sanren can be produced well when planted in the dry or rainy season. It has high productivity and requires the medium bulb size. In addition, it is resistant to leaf blight disease which often attacks during the rainy season, adapts well in lowlands with an altitude of 50-100 m.a.s.l (the Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia, 2013). Meanwhile, Lokananta has fusarium wilt resistance and high production and is suitable to be planted in lowlands (the Ministry of Agriculture of the Republic of Indonesia, 2017).

TSS has shoots that do not experience senescence even after entering the harvest season. This means that the shoots still have a high assimilate potential that is large enough to be translocated for bulb formation. Bulb formation is influenced by the balance of stimulator and inhibitor hormones in plants. The presence of growth inhibitors is needed to focus energy on bulbs formation. Paclobutrazol is one of the growth retardants that can be used to regulate shoot growth and transfer photosynthetic energy to bulb formation (Ibrahim et al., 2015).

The paclobutrazol application is known to increase the activities of the sucrose transporter enzyme which plays a role in the translocation of sucrose from source to sink (Lee and Huang, 2013; Dewi and Darussalam, 2018). It decreases chlorophyllase activities because plants synthesize more cytokinins (Tsegaw et al., 2005). High content of chlorophyll and a slow degradation rate cause the photosynthetic activity of plants to run well, and the plants have a longer duration of the photosynthetic activity. The longer duration of the photosynthetic activity is expected to increase the yield on accumulated assimilates which will be translocated for bulbs formation. The increase in cytokinin synthesis is present due to the inhibition of gibberellin biosynthesis resulting in a secondary pathway. Cytokinins are known to be hormones that can support the bulbing process (Ni’mah et al., 2012). Research on several horticultural plants including peanut, mango, corn, carrot, potato and cassava showed that paclobutrazol can regulate shoot growth, biomass distribution, and finally increase yield (Senoo and Isoda, 2003; Nafeeset al., 2010; Lolaei et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015; Mabvongwe et al., 2016; Panyapruek et al., 2016).

Attempts to increase the productivity of shallots in the context of fulfilling national consumption and seed needs have been made by the government. They include sustainable intensification programs, namely cultivation by GAP/SOP (the application of appropriate pesticides and fertilization), seed development, and also extensification with the use of marginal land and off-season cultivation. Increased productivity can also be done through the use of paclobutrazol. Based on the previous studies (Silva et al., 2003; Singh et al., 2005; Kishore et al., 2015), the use of paclobutrazol at the recommended/optimum doses and the right application time has neither affected soil microbial, nor dehydrogenase activity. Application at proper dose will maintain soil health and soil properties so that it will support sustainable farming systems.

However, such attempts to increase shallot productivity can be supported if seeds are available at all times. Therefore, the government encourages farmers to plant shallots using TSS instead of bulbs. Studies to increase the productivity of TSS are essential. This is also based on the fact that currently there is not much research on TSS that has been conducted. Research on the effectiveness of paclobutrazol in influencing growth in TSS has not yet been carried out. Also, previous research on the paclobutrazol application in some plants, particularly on the relationship between and influence of changes in physiological variables and growth of the yield, has not yet been discussed in detail. Therefore, it is necessary to deeply analyze the relationship between variables on the effectiveness of paclobutrazol in influencing plant growth activities to result in optimal TSS production.

True Shallot Seed (TSS) is a planting material for shallots in the forms of seeds. It shows a visual appearance of the fresh green shoot even though in the harvest season. This condition indicates that TSS still has potential assimilates which should be optimized for bulbs formation. Paclobutrazol is increasing assimilate translocation from source to sink by activating the sucrose transporter enzyme and changing the phytohormones balance. The study aimed to find out how paclobutrazol increased bulb yield on TSS by analyzing the closeness in the relationship between and the influence of physiological property variables and growth analysis. The study was conducted at Universitas Gadjah Mada experimental field, Yogyakarta, from September to November 2017. It was arranged in a Randomized Complete Block Design with three replications. The first factor included the paclobutrazol concentration (0, 15, 30 and $4 5 \mathrm { m g L ^ { - 1 } }$ ), while the second one included TSS cultivars (Tuk Tuk, Sanren and Lokananta). Correlation and regression were used in the data analysis. The results revealed that paclobutrazol significantly affected the physiological properties and the growth of TSS, instead of cultivars. Regression analysis showed that the effect of the concentration of the applied paclobutrazol formed quadratic pattern, where most observed variables had a positive correlation with shallot productivity. Paclobutrazol increased bulb yield by maintaining shoot biomass duration (SBD) and chlorophyll content which had a positive and linear effect on plant growth rate (PGR). The PGR might increase bulb yield per planting hole and indirectly increase its productivity. Paclobutrazol application at $1 5 { - } 3 0 \ \mathrm { m g \ L ^ { - 1 } }$ could be used to improve bulb yield in TSS.

The dynamic relationship between sources and sinks changes markedly during the life cycle of the plant. Leaves commence their life cycle initially as sinks, and mature into sources, and the seed, initially a strong sink, becomes the source of energy and nutrients during germination [1]. The availability and partitioning of carbon and nitrogen (N) provide the resources underpinning source-sink dynamics [2,3].

Key to the movement of sucrose around the plant are the Sugar Will Eventually be Exported Transporters (SWEETs), sucrose transporters (SUTs) and cell wall invertases (CWINVs) [1,4,5], and to the movement of amino acids are the amino acid permeases (AAPs) [6,7]. These same proteins are involved in the transport of assimilates to the developing seed [8–12]. However, during germination, as the seed changes from a sink to a source, the question arises as to whether these proteins are involved in the re-mobilisation of the reserves they helped to mobilise to the seed in the first place.

Functional studies have shown that the Arabidopsis AAPs can transport a wide range of amino acids [6,13], and various gene family members are involved in the source to sink translocation of amino acids [7]. In pea, expression of the AtAAP1::PsAAP1 construct increased overall plant biomass and N content, as well as increasing seed yield and seed N [11]. Seed storage proteins are degraded to provide amino acids for the biosynthesis of nucleic acids and new proteins, but may also be metabolised to satisfy the energy demands of the developing seedling [14,15]. Transportation of amino acids within the germinating seed and to the young seedling would appear to be a necessary requirement. In both the legume, Medicago truncatula, and in rice, the AAPs constitute larger gene families than in Arabidopsis [13,16]. We showed previously that of the $1 3 \ : P s A A P$ gene family members detected in a pea transcriptome, the PsAAPs were represented in most of the clusters of AAP orthologues in Arabidopsis and other leguminous species [17]. Multiple sequences were identified in several family members, particularly for PsAAP2 (Cluster 3A) and PsAAP7 (Cluster 1), as previously noted [13]. AtAAP7 has yet to be functionally characterised.

In contrast to the AAPs, SUTs belong to a smaller gene family [18]. SUTs are considered essential to the movement of sucrose from source leaves to sink organs, and to the uploading of sucrose into seeds [9,19,20]. Type I and II SUTs are localised to the plasma membrane [20]. The role of SUTs during early seed germination has been studied in rice [21,22]. In monocots, Type II SUTs (OsSUT1, 3, and 4) are utilised for phloem loading [20,23]. During early seed germination, OsSUT1 is upregulated in the scutellar vascular bundle [21], while OsSUT4 is expressed in the seed aleurone layer, and subsequently in the scutellum and embryonic vascular bundle [22], indicating differential temporal and spatial expression for these gene family members during germination.

In Ricinus communis, sucrose is released from the endosperm to the apoplast and from there taken up by the cotyledons for transfer to the rest of the seedling [24]. RcSUT1 was shown to be expressed more in the cotyledon of the germinating seed than in the endosperm [24]. While the loading of sucrose into developing legume seeds has been studied in detail [8,9,19,25,26], it would appear less attention has been given to the movement of sugars during the germination of non-endospermous seed, such as pea.

SWEETs are the most recent gene family to be designated a key role in sink/source dynamics [27,28]. Dhandapani et al. (2016) [17] showed that the 13 PsSWEET gene sequences identified from a pea transcriptome had members in all four of the SWEET clades described recently [12,29]. SWEETs have been strongly linked to development in reproductive tissues, especially seeds [12,30,31]. Transgenic analysis has indicated that SWEETs may be activated during seed germination. Seeds over-expressing AtSWEET16 (a Clade IV SWEET) germinated faster than controls [31] as did those over-expressing AtSWEET4 (a Clade II SWEET) [32]. However, the expression of endogenous SWEETs during germination has yet to be shown.

Cell wall invertases catalyse the irreversible breakdown of sucrose to fructose and glucose, and are an integral component of the movement of sucrose between sources and sinks [1,33,34]. They have been shown to be up-regulated in several scenarios affecting source-sink relationships, such as the cytokinin-induced delay of senescence [35,36]. However, they appear to have a dual role, being involved also in stimulating the cell cycle through the production of sugar signals, the latter implicating them, along with the cytokinins, in cell division and seed development [37–40]. Cell wall invertases are likely also to be involved in the mobilisation of resources during seed germination.

The cytokinins are clearly implicated in seed development [41]. The cytokinins are biosynthesised by isopentenyl transferase (IPT), degraded by cytokinin oxidase/dehydrogenase (CKX), and conjugated to storage or inactivated forms by glycosidases. The first formed cytokinins are nucleotides, which may be activated to the free base forms by LONELY GUY (LOG) [42]. A signal transduction pathway is activated upon the detection of free base cytokinins by receptors [43], which activate response regulators (RR) downstream (for recent reviews, see [44,45]).

The feeding of radioactively-labelled precursors has shown that germinating lupin and maize seeds are capable of biosynthesising cytokinin, but that this is restricted to the embryo axis [46–49]. In maize, the cytokinin then moves unidirectionally from the embryo to accumulate in the endosperm in maize [48]. The cytokinins synthesized by the embryonic axis of lupin, and which are also transported unidirectionally to the cotyledons [46], were shown to be highly stable and to induce cotyledon expansion and chlorophyll synthesis [47]. Further, the regulation of reserve mobilization in yellow lupin seeds and in germinating chick-peas, appears to be mediated, at least in part, by cytokinin emanating from the embryonic axis [49,50]. Differential activity of different cytokinin forms has also been suggested in germinating chick-pea with zeatin riboside (ZR) affecting the mobilisation of carbohydrate, whereas zeatin $( Z )$ had more impact on the protein in the cotyledons; isopentenyl adenine (iP) affected only the metabolism of carbohydrates, whereas iPR (iP riboside) mainly affected lipid metabolism [50,51]. Interestingly, all enzymes of the isoprenoid pathway have increased in activity within 2 to $6 \textrm { h }$ from the start of imbibition [52], providing precursors to the cytokinin biosynthetic machinery.

As transporter genes (reviewed in [10,53]), and cytokinin biosynthetic and degradative genes (reviewed in [41]) are the targets of transgenic approaches to increasing seed quality and/or quantity, we were interested if these gene families were expressed during germination. Such knowledge is important as changes in the expression of genes in the parental generation may impact seed germination and seedling vigour of the subsequent generation.

We chose to work with pea as it is both an important legume crop and a well-studied model crop. Additionally, pea seeds are non-dormant and non-endospermous, and their covering layers are not a mechanical constraint to radical protrusion [54]. The germination process is divided into an initial rapid imbibition phase during which pea seeds exhibit increased respiration and metabolic activity [55], followed by an activation phase during which stored carbohydrate and protein are mobilised [56]. Our aim was to determine if the gene families known to be involved in sink activity during seed development (SWEETs, SUTs, CWINVs, IPT, LOG, CKX) are also involved in mobilising reserves during germination. Based on gene family members detected in our pea transcriptome [17], we used RT-qPCR to monitor their expression. We show that genes actively expressed when the seed is a strong sink during its development are also actively expressed when the seed is in the reverse role of being an active source during germination.

Sucrose is the primary product of photosynthesis and the most prevalent long-distance translocatable sugar in higher plants. It has been demonstrated that the decrease of sucrose transport from source to sink tissues can suppress photosynthesis and growth of the plant, while the increase of sink demand can enhance photosynthetic activity and crop productivity (Ainsworth and Bush 2011; Ayre 2011; Bihmidine et al. 2013; Grifths and Paul 2017; Hall et al. 1977;

Hodgkinson 1974; Kaschuk et al. 2010; McCormick et al. 2006; Paul and Foyer 2001; Paul and Pellny 2003; Sheen 1990; Stitt et al. 2010). Thus, it has been proposed that crop yields can be enhanced by promoting the photosynthate transport from the source tissue to the sink tissue (Ainsworth and Bush 2011; Ayre 2011; McCormick et al. 2006).

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are energydependent sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporters which mediate the transport of sucrose across plasma membranes, leading the sugar into and out of the source and sink tissues through phloem (Riesmeier et al. 1992; Sauer 2007). This property enables us to genetically regulate the distribution of photosynthesized carbon, thus enhancing the yield of the target product. For example, downregulation of StSUT4 gene in potato resulted in early fowering and increased tuber yield (Chincinska et al. 2008). The use of endosperm-specifc promoter to direct the expression of $H \nu S U T I$ in barley led to an enhanced sugarabsorption capacity of the seeds and an increased content of storage protein in seeds (Weichert et al. 2010). A phloem cell-specifc expression of Arabidopsis AtSUC2 to promote the sucrose load resulted in an increased yield of rice (Wang et al. 2015).

Cotton is a leading natural fber crop and also an important oil crop in the word (Jefrey et al. 2007). Cotton fber is derived from single epidermal cells of seed. The fber is composed of nearly pure cellulose, the naturally occurring polymer of glucose. During the development of cotton seeds, the phloemunloaded sugar is transported outwards to fber cells for cell elongation and cellulose biosynthesis while inwards to flial tissues for the development of embryo and the biosynthesis of oil and starch (Jiang et al. 2012; Ruan 2005; Xu et al. 2012). This opposite transporting direction provides a dilemma to the regulation of the phloem-unloaded assimilate partition between fbers and the seed: in the case of limited carbon supply, enhancing of the abundance of fber usually leads to smaller seeds, while increasing of the seed size often results in a decrease of fber productivity of the seed (Miller et al. 1958; Miller and Rawlings 1967; Zeng et al. 2007; Zhao et al. 2015). To solve this trade-of problem, the best way is providing more supply to meet the demand of both sides.

Zea mays is a $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ crop, which is featured with high water-use efciency and high-yield potential (Usha et al. 2015). Previous studies demonstrated that $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ grasses (e.g., maize and sorghum) display a higher rate of export of photosynthates than $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ grasses (e.g., wheat and barley) (Grodzinski et al. 1998). ZmSut1, a maize sucrose/proton symporter, has an important function in sugar distribution (Aoki 1999; Baker et al. 2016). This sugar transport protein can efectively mediate sucrose uptake into the phloem in source tissue, as well as release the sugar from the phloem vessels into sink tissue (Baker et al. 2016; Carpaneto et al. 2005). Accordingly, Baker et al. (2016) suggest a potential of using SUTs from $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ plants to engineer $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ photosynthesis and carbon transport in $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ plants.

To see whether and how the ectopic expression of a $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ SUT in cotton is able to increase the efcacy of sucrose transport, thus enhancing the fiber and seed yield, in this study, we constructed transgenic cotton in which the ZmSUT1 gene is under control of a senescence-inducible and seed coat-specifc promoter, respectively. Our data demonstrated that seed coat-specifc expression of ZmSUT1 led to an increase of sugar accumulation in fbers and bolls, and elevated both fber and seed yield of cotton; while senescence-induced expression of the gene resulted in an increase of sugar accumulation in leaves and a delay of leaf senescence, but decreased the yield.

In the foreword to his comprehensive book Assimilate Transport in Plants, A.L. Kursanov stated that “Assimilate transport has proven to be a much more complex phenomenon than could have been inferred from the Münch hypothesis,” but also, after mentioning the controversy on interpretations of data on cytology and physiology of the phloem, that this “controversy lost much of its poignancy after the proponents of rival hypotheses had reached a consensus that assimilates are transported over long distances with the aid of a solution flowing in sieve tubes (mass flow) [1].”

Below is a review of work pertinent for our knowledge of the physiology of phloem transport, which includes the uptake and release of translocate, its regulation, and the different mechanisms resulting finally in a mass flow. This short survey cannot be comprehensive. Its goal is to remind the reader about work on the biochemistry of phloem transport completed 30 to 50 years ago. Since the concept “source to sink” was developed at the same period, progress and implications of this topic (“lateral sinks”) will be discussed. Recent progress on the structure and localization of sugar transporters and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPases [2] may at last enhance the “consensus” on the mechanism, and, finally, a “special case” is presented that brings about an unexpected modification of the “Münch-system”.


## EARLIER DATA VERIFYING DEPENDENCYOF PHLOEM TRANSPORT ON METABOLICCONTROL


Among the various hypotheses on phloem transport, only the “Münch-system” meets most of the corresponding experimental data. Münch [3] had consistently applied the theory of Pfeffer to the system of assimilate movement in plants. He also introduced the terms “symplast” and “apoplast,” although he neglected the resistance of plasmodesmata between leaf cells. He rejected the hypothesis of Pfeffer that not only water permeates the plasma membrane: Pfeffer defined in 1880, for the first time, the function of a vehicle located in the membrane, which carries molecules from one side to the other, with or without energy expenditure. This weakness of the Münch-system left most physiologists skeptical until the original hypothesis was gradually modified and restricted to the sievetube-system itself.

Ironically enough, Crafts at Davis, being a strong proponent of Münch, rejected directly Schumacher’s report [4] that he was able to plasmolyze sieve-tubes, a prerequisite for pressure-flow.

Kursanov was one of the physiologists who questioned Münch’s 50-year-old hypothesis. Kursanov’s group had good evidence for the hypothesis that, in the leaves, sugars and amino acids can be taken up from an external medium, a process partially enhanced by energy expenditure. Moreover, by improved cytological and electron-microscopical methods, the complex structure of plant plasmodesmata was discovered [5]: in many species, the connection of leaf parenchyma to the sieve tube-companion cell system by plasmodesmata was ascertained to be scarce or nil. The sieve areas appear to be real obstacles for mass flow unless their pores are open or traversed by only a few fibrils [6]. Occluded sieve pores are supposed to result from fixation procedures.

Using manometric techniques, high respiration activity was reported for isolated bundles of Plantago and Beta vulgaris in 1952 [7]. Among pathways of oxygen consumption, cytochrome oxidase was found to be active. After infiltrating the bundles with $1 0 ^ { - 2 } \mathbf { M }$ K-cyanide, respiration was completely inhibited [8]. Our similar results with isolated bundles from other species reconfirmed these findings in general, although, after calculations per unit protein, the difference in respiration rates of conducting tissue and the parenchyma cells became less significant [9].

In this context, experiments by Kursanov and Brovchenko [10] on uptake of ATP from external solutions into the leaf blades of sugar beet have to be mentioned. The increase of sugar import into the conducting bundles by external ATP was a surprising result. However, it became in principle corroborated by the observation of Ullrich [11] that fluorescein transport along the phloem of Pelargonium was promoted by application of 2 mM ATP.

The basic aim of our efforts was to assess the role of energy in the stage of transport from the release of assimilates from leaf parenchyma to the use of reduced carbon in growing regions. We focused on experiments that show localized inhibition of phloem transport, obviously independent of any effect on membrane semipermeability [9]. In short, on intact plants of Pelargonium zonale grown in a greenhouse, the central bundles of petioles of two leaves, attached to the plant nearly opposite to each other, were isolated for a length of 1 to $2 \mathrm { c m }$ . The cut ends of the marginal bundles were sealed with vaseline. The inhibitors were applied to the bundle via a cotton swab or, in the case of cyanide, as gaseous atmosphere above a solution of the respective KCN-concentration inside a small airtight chamber. Fluorescein was applied to the leaf veins $1 { - } 4 \ \mathrm { h }$ after exposure to the inhibitor [9]. In the case of $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , labeling by photosynthesis started $3 { - } 6 \mathrm { h }$ after inhibitor treatment [12].

Most interesting was whether inhibition caused by the inhibitor can be attributed to a localized upset in the petiole or to a breakdown of transport within the leaf veins. Whereas exposure of the petiolar bundle to $\mathrm { N } _ { 2 } .$ $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ , or even to CO had no effect, $1 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { K C N }$ led to localized inhibition of transport of fluorescein and of labeled assimilates as well. The cyanide-induced inhibition of phloem transport could be demonstrated as being reversible: in the case of $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ , $9 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ after CNremoval labeled translocate was identified in the basal part of the petiole. In the case of fluorescein, restoration of transport was only observed several hours later [8, 13] after CN-removal. Other inhibitors like dinitrophenol and fluoroacetate caused complete inhibition, and plasmolysis/deplasmolysis studies of phloem parenchyma as a criterion for semipermeability failed in these cases. In a third experimental series, response of assimilate transport to local application of more specific inhibitors was studied [14]. Again tests were carried out on semipermeability of the treated bundle section. The powerful uncoupling agent CCCP caused at $0 . 1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ the complete cessation of transport. Antimycin A at $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ led to a $50 \%$ inhibition of transport; atractylate, which blocks the exchange of ATP vs. ADP at mitochondrial membranes, caused $50 \%$ inhibition at $5 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; and valinomycin exerted its inhibitory effect in the range from 25 to $0 . 1 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ , showing $50 \%$ inhibition at $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { \bar { M } } }$ . It should be noted that relatively high concentrations of specific inhibitors have been used. The large difference between results on isolated mitochondria—inhibition of ATP/ADP exchange by $1 \ \mathrm { n M }$ atractylate, a decrease of the ADP/O ratio in the presence of $\check { \mathrm { K } } ^ { + }$ at $0 . 2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ valinomycin—may be due to the extremely low solubility of both substances and the requirements that the isolated bundles be flooded in order to provide the innermost SE contact with the agents.

It is left open whether antimycin A inhibited by uncoupling or directly at the respiratory chain. Atractylate should inhibit the synthesis of ATP in the CC; this is the easiest explanation for the upset of transport. The effect of valinomycin is interesting, but there are three alternatives possible to explain the results as far as our knowledge of phloem metabolism and speculation on the transport mechanism is concerned [14]:

(1) The potential of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ was equilibrated across mitochondrial membranes, which led to uncoupling.

(2) The potential of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ was equilibrated across the SE plasma membrane, changing the ATPase activity [15]. The high concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inside the SE is well-known, and an assumed gradient of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ vs $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ across this membrane could be disturbed, in turn influencing the ATPase activity involved in stabilizing the concentration gradient of a mass-flow [16].

(3) One could speculate on electroosmotic flow, but there are only a few reports in the literature that support this hypothesis and that cannot be assisted by our data. While the result may not fit “nicely” with the pressure flow hypothesis, it may indicate that there are balancing and metabolically-controlled pumps along the translocation system (see below: “lateral sinks”).


## THE MÜNCH MASS-FLOW HYPOTHESIS IS RECONCILED WITH ACTIVE TRANSPORT


As mentioned above, there is consensus among plant biologists on the reality of a mass flow in sieve tubes driven by a pressure difference generated by energy-dependent loading of molecules like sucrose within sources and passive or active unloading in the sink [17]. All other hypotheses, while being attractive and plausible like protoplasmic streaming or electroosmotic forces, have failed thus far to agree with most of the experimental data.

Irrespective of the driving forces for mass flow, the velocity of phloem transport as measured in intact plants exceeds significantly the limits of other mechanisms. Concerning the speed, only two of more than 20 reliable reports (i.e., monitored in vivo, not using artificial sinks like aphids, exudation, etc.) are cited here. In both cases, translocation of $\mathrm { \dot { 1 } 1 } _ { \mathrm { C } }$ after pulselabeling for $3 { - } 6 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ with $^ { 1 1 } { \bf C O } _ { 2 }$ was monitored by a line of NaJ-crystal-detectors. With four-week-old plants of Zea mays, Troughton et al. [18] observed a wide range of speed values from $0 . 2 \bar { 5 }$ to $1 1 \ \mathrm { c m / m i n }$ depending on the light level, partial shading of the plant, and the sucrose and starch content of leaves. On the water fern, Marsilea quadrifolia, Jahnke et al. [19] measured the speed of $^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { C }$ -translocate by monitoring the petiole using three crystal probes at distances of 50, 85, and $1 2 0 \mathrm { m m }$ from the fully developed leaf exposed to ${ } ^ { \mathrm { i l } } { \mathrm { C O } } _ { 2 }$ for 6 min in light and subsequently flushed by an air stream. Speed measured after the “lag”-phase was within the range of 1.0 to $2 . 5 \mathrm { c m / m i n }$ . It was interesting to note that, after flushing the assimilation chamber with nitrogen gas, the normal increase of $^ { 1 1 } \mathrm { C }$ at the monitored sites of the petiole slowed down within 5 min, but replacement of $\mathrm { \bar { N } } _ { 2 }$ by an air stream led to complete restoration of the $^ { \mathrm { i } _ { 1 } } \dot { C } .$ -slope, thus indicating a strong sink action exerted by the growing rhizome.

However, the strongest arguments for strict pressure flow in the phloem are based on experiments, in which the systems cannot be considered undisturbed. In their elegant demonstration of heat transfer along a phloem strand of Heracleum, Ziegler and Vieweg [20] succeeded in obtaining measurable asymmetric heat transfer only after cutting the strand acropetally. And, as far as experiments with aphids are concerned, Dixon [21] had commented on the influence of aphid punctures on the flow of substances within the SE.

However, most of the results of phloem transport studies can be convincingly interpreted by the mass flow hypothesis, even if some obstacles like the sieve plates, ER, P-protein, or sieve pores lined with ER are taken into account (Evert [22]). On the other hand, micrographs of sieve plate pores of Aristolochia presented by Behnke [23] showing protein filaments and ER passing the pore can hardly be rated as artifacts (as compared with more or less harsh procedures resulting in either occluded or open pores). Whether such a filament arrangement will still be compatible with the pressure flow hypothesis is rather doubtful according to the criteria discussed by Weatherley [6]. Due to the obvious complex sieve-tube contents with its divers obstacles against flow of various molecules, only very few papers deal with the serious problem of how the phloem system for rapid transport of 0.3 to $1 . 3 ~ \mathrm { { M } }$ sucrose overcomes resistances to bulk flow. Richmond and Wardlaw [24] emphasize the necessity of such physicochemically based studies and attempt theoretical analysis of sucrose adsorption to structural protein surfaces. On the basis of their calculations using the Lifshitz continuum theory of van der Waals’ forces, the authors comment that movement of hydrated sucrose at the interface between (protein) membrane surfaces and the sugar could significantly minimize the resistance to flow through a confined flow.

In context with mass-flow in the phloem, the movement of xenobiotics, fluorescent dyes like fluorescein (Schumacher [25]), and viruses must be recalled. Earlier reports on protein synthesis in SE, which required the presence of RNA [26], and reports on occurrence of nucleic acids (RNA) also indicate movement of larger molecules in sieve tubes [27]. There is reason to assume that phloem-mobile macromolecules move along with the mass flow towards the assimilate sinks. For details on this aspect, the reader might refer to the recent review of Oparka and Santa Cruz [28].

The driving force for the mass flow of assimilates is generated by energy-dependent uptake. The findings of ATP in the phloem exudate of trees [29] and in the exudate taken from the brown alga Macrocystis integrifolia [30] can be considered an indication of the rapid turnover of the ATP system in the SE as supposed by Ziegler [27]. Evidence for the decisive turnover of ATP for establishment of the Münch-mass flow accumulated within the last two decades. Progress began in 1973 with data on the presence of ATPase [15] in the SE-CC system, which, as a proton pump, energizes uphill transfer of sucrose and probably of distinct amino acids [31] by a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } .$ -cotransport with sucrose (amino acids, respectively) into the sieve tube [32] and is completed by localizing the sucrose transporters that have been identified as SUT1 in Solanaceae and Chenopodiaceae [33] and as SUT2 in Plantago and Arabidopsis [34] by heterologous expression. Both sucrose transporters exhibit a high affinity for sucrose of $K _ { \mathrm { M } }$ about $0 . 3 \mathrm { - }$ $1 . 0 \mathrm { m M }$ . In addition, a third but low-affinity transport seems to be present in the phloem isolated from soybean cotyledons [35]. While SUT1 was detected by immunofluorescence as localized at the plasma membrane (PM) of mature SE [36, 37], SUT2 is localized in CC [38].

Phloem assimilate loading by SUT2 seems to be more directly energized in the CC itself, which are known for their metabolic activities. Until recently, no PM- $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase had been detected in SE. However, by immunofluorescence evaluated with confocal laser scan microscopy, the site of this system is demonstrated [39]. The activity most probably depends on ATP supply by the mitochondria of the CC. This makes the high turnover of ATP in SE now feasible.

In conclusion, the headline of this chapter has been verified by the recent success in molecular analysis and localization of some of the most important and energized transporters in sieve tube elements themselves (for further details, see [40]). The SE system cannot be characterized as pre-mortal anymore: it comprises biochemical activities, which generate mass flow in their final stages.


## IS CONTROL EXERTED BY SOURCE AND SINK, AND BY LATERAL SINKS?


In view of the limited space, the subject “control of phloem transport” cannot be dealt with all its important aspects. Since the physiological background of this chapter has close links to the control of carbon partitioning in plants, the reader might be referred to the corresponding review of Wardlaw [41], which clearly presents the facts and the need for more information (hormonal control, organ initiation, etc.). The long-distance transport through the SE occurs from source to sink. This statement appears self-evident and must include the existence of apical and lateral meristems of both sink and source leaves and of the great variety of sink organs like roots, fruits, etc. Moreover, the network of conduits poses problems if one tries to explain the fact of bidirectional movement of labeled assimilate vs. fluorescein in the same sieve tube as demonstrated in the elegant aphid experiments on Vicia plants by Eschrich [42]. Strong sinks are able to attract translocate from different sources, “normally” via conduits of separate phloem strands.

Loading in photosynthesizing leaves is a prerequisite for the supply of the heterotrophic sink organs. Since loading of assimilates within leaves determines the efficiency of the source, the assimilate transfer from the chlorenchyma towards the conduits still remains the focus of structural and biochemical studies. Over the past 40 years, it has become increasingly accepted that two different ways of loading, symplastic and apoplastic processes, are realized in plants of different taxa. While studies on the inflow of solutes into leaf tissue conducted by Kursanov and colleagues [43–45] and others [46] suggested the dominance of apoplastic loading, the comprehensive work of Gamalei [47] demonstrated the diversity of the structure and function of minor veins “in herbs and trees,” mainly stressing the importance of plasmodesmal junctions between leaf cells and specialized transfer cells. In his review, van Bel [48] presented cytological and biochemical arguments leading to a more flexible concept of loading. However, an exclusive symplastic assimilate transfer, which is proposed by the author [49], is explained by the “polymerization trap mechanism” [50], which might work in cucurbits. But, what about other plants? Evidence for symplastic loading was presented [51] by the microautoradiography of veins in Cucumis melo, which are connected with the mesophyll by plasmodesmata. It is questionable, however, based on cucurbits with low sugar content (i.e., less mass transfer) in SE, to draw conclusions about the loading mechanism in other angiosperms (cf. preceding chapter). It might be mentioned that the Laminariales in their large-sized thalli have evolved a system of a peculiar sieve element system that is characterized by the long-distance transport of assimilates. The photoassimilating meristoderm is connected via a symplastic transport system with the sieve elements [52], where mass-flow supplies sinkslike the holdfast or the growing stem. Concentration and pressure gradients along the route are unknown thus far.

While in angiosperms, active loading of sucrose is bound to at least one apoplastic step at the CC-PM or SE-PM, most of the unloading at sink organs occurs symplastic, which was demonstrated by Farrar [53] on barley roots. Schulz [54] exposed pea roots to osmotic stress by mannitol solution and induced a widening of plasmodesmata which in turn increased unloading. Passive apoplastic unloading along a concentration gradient is also known. The same type of sucrose transporters was probably used as in the source. The apoplastic mode plays a prominent role at the border between generations in seeds, the supply of which has been shown as a sequence of symplastic transport within the maternal tissue followed by an apoplastic step [55].

There is increasing evidence that it is not only the loading at the sources and unloading at the various sinks that control the mass flow, but that lateral sinks also play a role. This observation cannot be explained by passive leakage, because mass flow along a concentration gradient relies on intact conduits. Experiments with Phaseolus showed that sucrose was found in the apoplast of the stem up to 25 to $6 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , under appropriate conditions of free space [56]. The authors propose that an apoplastic pool of assimilates can buffer sudden changes in phloem contents in the case of changes in source–sink configuration, which is the basis for a retrieval system that presupposes active reloading of sucrose along the route. The same conclusion was drawn by Grimm et al. [57] from their data on the uptake and efflux studies using the petioles of the garden plant Cyclamen persicum. The authors demonstrated that the efflux of sucrose in the petiole is compensated by carrier-mediated influx accomplished by $\hat { \mathrm { H } } ^ { + }$ -cotransport. It is therefore reasonable to assume that mass flow along a concentration gradient of sucrose or other solutes depends, along the entire route, on the activity of balancing carriers. The data on sucrose transporters and their activity along the route contribute to this hypothesis.

The well-known parasite Cuscuta, which develops hyphae penetrating cell walls of sieve tubes of the host, resulting in a large contact area, deserves special attention. Solutes from the host sieve tubes are unloaded into the enlarged apoplast from which the parasitic “contact hypha” absorb the solute [58, 59].


## TRANSPORT IN GYMNOSPERMS AS A SUPER RELAY SYSTEM


While, in angiosperms, a more or less continuous pressure gradient seems to drive assimilate flow from source to sink, which is regulated by active transport at the source region and by unloading in sinks, this seems unlikely in gymnosperms. Already in 1891, Eduard Strasburger [60] described not only the extremely long sieve cells ( $\bar { 1 } { - } 3 . 5 \ \mathrm { m m }$ in length!), which are characterized by areas of small pores in their long-tapering end walls, but also “albuminous cells” (rich in protein) that are located along the edges of the pith rays. Each sieve cell has contact with at least one of these specialized parenchyma cells, named later as “Strasburger Zellen,” by symplastic connections, without direct ontogenetic relation (as was well known for the SE-CC system) between both partners. The ultrastructure of the SE, the Strasburger cells, and primarily the sieve area has been thoroughly analyzed by Kollmann and Schumacher [61, 62] on Metasequoia glyptostroboides, a deciduous conifer. The numerous pores of the sieve areas are not only lined by the plasma membrane but also pass by an extended ER system, resulting in extremely narrow pore lumina [63]. Thus, it is feasible to assume an active role of the ER system on control of assimilate translocation in gymnosperm sieve cells. Schulz [64] demonstrated by confocal laser-scanning fluorescence microscopy of living sieve cells of branches of Picea abies the real orientation of the ER system. This in vivo procedure avoids any artificial ER plugging at the sieve area. Therefore, the earlier data on Metasequoia were reconfirmed, in turn bringing the pressure flow hypothesis for conifers into serious question.

The reader should be reminded that, in 1966, transport of $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -labeled assimilates in Metasequoia from ${ \mathrm { ^ { 1 4 } C O } } _ { 2 }$ -assimilating needles to the branches was studied [65]. Sucrose was shown to be the main labeled substance, the velocity of transport monitored at two distinct points along the branch axis was calculated to be $4 8 { - } 6 0 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ per hour. It should be mentioned that the experiments were done in early October when phloem transport from the leaves of Metasequoia is at its peak. We had hints that implied that the youngest differentiated secondary phloem represents the transport zone, but evidence was provided from high resolution microautoradiography [66] and, earlier, by aphids feeding on the youngest sieve cells in Juniperus communis (Kollmann and Dörr [67]).

As opposed to histoautoradiograms from sieve tubes of angiosperms [68, 69], in gymnosperms, $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -translocates, while only scattered in the lamina, appear to accumulate on the sieve areas [70]. In a recent review, Schulz [71] discussed the specific role of the ER as a nonplasmatic compartment, which could regulate a long-distance gradient of assimilates by reestablishing the (sugar) gradient in each SE, a hypothesis proposed by Lang [72] as a “relay mechanism.” In this model, transport is discontinuous from sieve cell to sieve cell. At the sieve area, the translocate becomes unloaded into and reloaded out of the ER tubules into the next sieve cell. It is tempting to speculate that this would generate a sawtooth pressure gradient along a file of sieve elements [73]. Minchin and Thorpe [56] proposed such a continuous leak-pump exchange between SE and apoplast as supposed to be present in angiosperm stems. In the case of the gymnosperm sieve area, a possible, although extremely narrow, symplastic route between the plasmalemma and the ER has to be taken into account (Schulz [64]): ATPase was demonstrated to be localized at the ER-system of sieve elements of Pinus nigra (Sauter [74]), which indicates energy-consuming steps (to reload the translocate) on the sieve area [39].

In summary, conifers are indeed worth studying because of their fascinating and peculiar (“sawtooth”) transport system consisting of lines of individual “Münch cells” bordered by the sieve areas. I would expect that recent progress in molecular biology with respect to immunolocalization of sucrose carriers will not only supplement our present knowledge of sieve elements but provide an answer to this fascinating question. Transport in the young secondary phloem obviously provides an adequate assimilate supply even in case of Sequoia sempervirens, Pseudotsuga menziesii, and Picea sitchensis, species which attain $1 0 0 \mathrm { m }$ or more in height. This is quite a challenge for young scientists!

In higher plants, non-photosynthetic or photosynthetically inactive sink tissues rely on a supply of sugars produced predominantly in mesophyll cells of source leaves through photosynthesis for their nutrition (Williams et al. 2000). Long-distance transport of photosynthetic assimilates between sources and sinks occurs in the phloem sieve elements, mainly in form of sucrose (Lemoine 2000). In sink tissues, unloaded sucrose can get into sink cells symplasmically via plasmodesmata and/or apoplasmically via plasma membrane sugar transporters, i.e. directly via sucrose transporters or via monosaccharide transporters after extracellular hydrolysis by cell wall invertases (EC 3.2.1.26) to glucose and fructose (Bu¨ttner and Sauer 2000).

Plant monosaccharide transporters mediate the membrane transport of a variable range of monosaccharides, which plays a crucial role in the cell-to-cell and long-distance distribution of sugars throughout the plant (Williams et al. 2000). Since the first plant monosaccharide transporter gene was isolated from Chlorella kessleri (Sauer and Tanner 1989), numerous homologous genes have been cloned from a wide range of monocot and dicot plant species. Most of the identified plant monosaccharide transporters are proved or supposed to be located in the plasma membrane (Bu¨ttner and Sauer 2000). Most recently monosaccharide transporters located in chloroplast have been cloned from spinach, Mesembryanthemus crystallinum and olive (Hausler et al. 2000; Weber et al. 2000; Butowt et al. 2003), and the presence of monosaccharide transporters in plant mitochondria, Golgi and vacuole has also been reported (Chiou and Bush 1996; Szarka et al. 2004; Wang et al. 2006).

Plant monosaccharide transporters are encoded by a multigene family, which belongs to the Major Facilitator Superfamily of membrane carriers (Marger and Saier 1993; Pao et al. 1998). For example, a superfamily of monosaccharide transporters containing seven subfamilies and at least 53 members has been predicted by using bioinformatics analysis of the Arabidopsis genome (Schneidereit et al. 2005; Johnson et al. 2006). The situation in rice may be even more complex. However, only five members of the rice monosaccharide transporter gene family have been studied so far (Toyofuku et al. 2000; Takeda et al. 2001; Ngampanya et al. 2003; Mamun et al. 2006).

Expression analyses of plant monosaccharide transporters revealed diverse expression patterns: sink-specific expression for most, both source and sink expression for some, and source-specific expression for AtSTP3 in Arabidopsis, the only one monosaccharide transporter specifically expressed in source tissues (Bu¨ttner et al. 2000). Different expression patterns of plant monosaccharide transporters reflect their diverse physiological functions. In general, plant monosaccharide transporters are thought to play a role in monosaccharide uptake in sink tissues, and in source tissues to play a role in the retrieval of monosaccharides lost to the apoplastic space by passive leakage (Bu¨ttner and Sauer 2000). Plant monosaccharide transporters are also involved in environmental stress responses (Harrison 1996; Ehness and Roitsch 1997;

Bu¨ttner et al. 2000; Fotopoulos et al. 2003), and probably in sugar sensing and sugar-mediated signal transduction (Bu¨ttner et al. 2000). Recent studies on transgenic tobacco indicate that monosaccharide transporter may play an important role in assimilate transport and in morphogenesis (Leterrier et al. 2003).

Developing seeds are net importers of nutrients in plant. Studies in legume and cereals show that both sucrose transporters and monosaccharide transporters are involved in sugar supply for seed development. The route depends on species and developmental stage. In fava bean, a sucrose transporter and a monosaccharide transporter were found to play a cooperative role in sugar supply for developing seeds (Weber et al. 1997). In maize, the cell wall invertase/ monosaccharide transporter pathway seems to be of great importance for the kernel development. When this pathway is blocked in the maize mutant miniature-1, due to the lack of expression of an endosperm-specific cell wall invertase in the pedicel and endosperm, the transport of photoassimilates into developing kernel is interrupted and the seeds are only one-fifth of the normal weight (Miller and Chourey 1992; Cheng et al. 1996). Current studies in barley suggest that the cell wall invertase/monosaccharide transporter pathway predominates in caryopses at the prestorage stage, and the sucrose transporter pathway predominates in caryopses as they switch to storage mode (Weschke et al. 2000, 2003). Since great differences exist in the seed structures and in patterns of assimilate transport in developing seeds between rice, maize and barley (Krishnan and Dayanandan 2003), the molecular biology of sugar transport during seed development in rice may be different from that in maize and barley. Up to now, all members of the rice sucrose transporter gene family OsSUT1-5 have been found to be involved in seed development (Hirose et al. 1997; Aoki et al. 2003), but none of the five cloned rice monosaccharide transporter genes have been shown to be expressed in developing caryopses (Toyofuku et al. 2000; Ngampanya et al. 2003; Mamun et al. 2006).

To investigate whether monosaccharide transporters are involved in rice caryopsis development, blast searches of GenBank (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST/) were carried out with the rice OsMST1-3 sequence (Toyofuku et al. 2000) and a highly homologous expressed sequence tag (EST) (GenBank accession number: AA753003) was found to be obtained from the large-scale sequence analysis of ESTs from rice immature seeds at 5 days after pollination. The corresponding gene of this EST, OsMST4, named after OsMST1-3, was then chosen to be further studied. In this study, we cloned the cDNA of OsMST4, characterized the monosaccharide transportation function of the encoded protein by heterologous expression in yeast and analyzed its expression in relation to its role in caryopsis development. The temporal, spatial and cell type-specific expression of OsMST4 suggested that this gene may play a primary role in monosaccharides supply for developing caryopses during the whole grain filling stage, and the different cell type-specific expression patterns of OsMST4 in developing caryopses and source leaf blades implied different physiological functions it may have in sink and source tissues.

## Identification of a putative plasma membrane-localized sucrose transporter JcSUT4 in J. curcas


Sucrose is the end production of photosynthesis and the major phloem-translocated component in higher plants. SUTs mediate long distance transport of sucrose from source to sink organs (Doidy et al. 2012a). While the function of SUTs has been extensively investigated in some higher plants, information from J. curcas was rarely reported. JcSUT4, the novel SUT gene derived from J. curcas in this study, encoding a protein with predicted topology of 12 transmembrane domains (Figure S3) and belonged to the MFS, in agreement with SUTs from other species (Reinders et al. 2012). The deduced amino acid sequence of JcSUT4 showed $9 0 \%$ identity with HbSUT4 from rubber (Yang et al. 2007) and $7 7 . 7 \%$ identity with PtaSUT4 from poplar (Frost et al. 2012), suggesting that they serve very similar functions among these species. According to the result of the mutant yeast complementary experiment, we infer JcSUT4 can transport sucrose like AtSUT4 (Figure 2). Subcellular localization analysis suggested that JcSUT4 was mainly localized to plasma membrane, which was similar with SUT4 in other species, including Arabidopsis (Schulze et al. 2003), apple (Fan et al. 2009), potato (Chincinska et al. 2008, 2013), tobacco (Okubo-Kurihara et al. 2011; Chincinska et al. 2013), poplar (Nilsson et al. 2010), and pear (Wang et al. 2016). Many members of the Type III SUTs seem to undergo dual targeting to the tonoplast and the plasma membrane, such as Arabidopsis AtSUT4, potato StSUT4, tobacco NtSUT4, tomato SlSUT4, and poplar PtaSUT4 (Chincinska et al. 2013). Previous studies showed that AtSUT4 was located at vacuole (Endler et al. 2006), plasma membrane (Schulze et al. 2003), and probably chloroplast envelope (Rolland et al. 2003) with three different methods. Poplar PtaSUT4 was localized to plasma membrane by plasma membrane proteomics (Nilsson et al. 2010) and vacuole by GFP fusion (Payyavula et al. 2010). JcSUT4 might be also localized to other parts of the cell. But more necessary experiments with different methods will be needed for exploration of localization of JcSUT4.


## JcSUT4 might play a role in sink tissues


SUTs are membrane proteins involved in several crucial steps of assimilate distribution, contributing to the translocation of sucrose (Kühn et al. 2010). Members of the SUT family have diverse functional roles, including sucrose loading into the phloem or companion cells, as well as sucrose efflux into source or sink (Sauer 2007; Reinders et al. 2012).

Type III SUTs, also known as vacuolar sucrose $\boldsymbol { { } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H } ^ { + } }$ symporters, are vital in release sucrose from vacuoles (Kühn et al. 2010). In potato, StSUT4 was found to control circadian gene expression by potentially regulating sucrose export from leaves (Chincinska et al. 2013). High expression levels of the JcSUT4 gene were detected in the mature leaves of J. curcas (Figure 5(a)), consistent with the observation from poplar PtaSUT4. Additionally, PtaSUT4 were readily detected in both conducting and mesophyll cells in source leaves (Payyavula et al. 2010). The high expression of PtaSUT4 indicated it might potentially modulate efflux of sucrose from source leaves (Payyavula et al. 2010).

AtSUC4 seems to play only a minor role in sucrose flux via the tonoplast under physiological conditions. However, PbSUT2, a member of the SUT4 clade localized to the plasma membrane, enhanced sucrose content in sinks and the fruits (Wang et al. 2016). In apple (Malus domestica), MdSUT1 (AY445915) was localized to the plasma membrane and interacted with Cytochrome b5 to enhance the affinity of the sugar transporters for substrate sugar (Fan et al. 2009). If SUT4 is expressed outside of the phloem in sink tissues, it could function directly in sucrose uptake into sink cells and have a role in determining sink strength (Weise et al. 2000; Chincinska et al. 2013). JcSUT4 belonged to the Type III clade of SUTs (Figure 1) and its transcript was expressed throughout fruit development in J. curcas (Figure 4(b) and Figure 5(b)). In our study, it was found that expression of JcSUT4 increased from 10 to 30 DAFB, and then reduced gradually, with lowest levels at 60 DAFB in J. curcas fruit. The expression patterns of JcSUT4 seemed to be positively correlated with the fruit growth rate, which rapid fruit growth in the period of 10–30 DAFB were with higher transcript levels (Figure S4). Likewise, previous report had demonstrated that three SUT genes (JC_C100001823, JC_C100022541, and JC_C100022782) were all expressed at relatively high levels in developing seeds, indicating that these SUTs might play an important role in sucrose transport into sink cells (Jiang et al. 2012). Particularly, the SUT JC_C100022782, also named as JcSUT4 in our study, exhibited higher transcript levels in the seeds from period of 14–29 days after pollination (DAP), and higher starch accumulation rates (Jiang et al. 2012), consistent with the results in our study. Except the oilseed tree species J. curcas, members in type III clade seem to be participated in fruit development for their high expression in several crops. For example, in pear fruit, PbSUT1 transcripts are significantly increase during the ripening process with increasing sucrose levels (Zhang et al. 2013), whereas PpSUT4 from peach displayed the increased expression level at the early phases of fruit growth with the accumulation of soluble sugars (Zanon et al. 2015b). These findings, along with the results in this study, revealed that SUT4 subfamily might play pivotal role in sucrose distribution during fruit development.

Previous studies indicated that overexpression of AtSUT2 and/or AtSUT4 in combination with DGAT genes could increase seed oil production in both soybean and maize (Allen et al. 2015). In the seed of J. curcas, the starch content was raised up in the period of 25–35 DAP, but the oil accumulation rates were high from 29 to 41 DAP (Jiang et al. 2012). Therefore, we speculate that high expression of JcSUT4 might be associated with the change of sugar and oil content in the fruit. In the period of rapid fruit development with high expression of JcSUT4, sucrose stored in fruits and then may convert to lipid in high oil plant. However, the mechanism may be more complex except transferring sucrose into the storage compartment by SUTs. Further functional characterization of JcSUT4 will be carried out to explore the exact role of JcSUT4 in sink tissues.

In summary, in this study a sucrose transporter gene JcSUT4 from J. curcas was identified. The high expression of JcSUT4 in mature leaves and at green immature stage of fruit suggested its potential role in sucrose transported from source leaves to the sink fruits. Our results provided promising gene that involved in sucrose transport between source and sink in J. curcas. However, the regulatory mechanism remains to be elucidated in the future.
