In the light of the above knowledge, B transport molecules NIP5;1 and BOR1 stood out as significant candidates from agricultural perspective to ameliorate the effects of B-deficiency/toxicity and improve the B tolerance in plants. So, this work identified the homologs of these two molecules in the genomes of 18 different plant species, investigated them at primary, secondary and tertiary structural levels, and evaluated the expression profiles under different perturbations and in different plant tissues/organs.

Background: Legumes comprise important crops that offer major agronomic benefits, including the capacity of establishing symbiosis with rhizobia, fixing atmospheric $\mathsf { N } _ { 2 }$ . It has been proven that legumes are particularly susceptible to boron (B) stress, which leads to important yield penalties. Boron (B) deficiency or toxicity in plants causes the inhibition of growth and an altered development. Under such conditions, the participation of two distinct protein families (the major intrinsic protein family MIP and the Boron transporter family BOR) is required to minimize detrimental effects caused by B stress. However, in legumes, little is known about the transport mechanisms responsible for B uptake and distribution, especially under deficiency.

Results: A Medicago truncatula protein, MtNIP5;1 (Medtr1g097840) (homologous to the Arabidopsis thaliana AtNIP5; 1) was identified as a novel legume B transporter involved in B uptake under deficiency. Further analyses revealed that this M. truncatula aquaporin expression was boron-regulated in roots, being induced under deficiency and repressed under toxicity. It localizes at the plasma membrane of root epidermal cells and in nodules, where B plays pivotal roles in symbiosis. Furthermore, the partial complementation of the nip5;1–1 A. thaliana mutant phenotype under B deficiency supports a functional role of MtNIP5;1 as a B transporter in this legume model plant.

Conclusions: The results here presented support a functional role of MtNIP5;1 in B uptake under deficiency and provides new insights into B transport mechanisms in legume species.

Keywords: Boron deficiency, Medicago truncatula, Aquaporins, MtNIP5;1, Boron transport, Legumes

Boron (B) is an essential micronutrient for plants that limits crop productivity worldwide. Its distribution in soils is very heterogeneous and extensive areas suffer from limited B availability including important agricultural lands in Japan, China, United States or Brazil [1]. In soils, B is mainly found uncharged, as boric acid $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ) }$ , and is lost by leaching due to its high solubility [2,3]. This explains why most of the B deficiency areas correspond to areas with high precipitation rates.

In higher plants, B deficiency symptoms predominantly occur in growing tissues, due to its structural role as a cell wall component [4]. B functions as a cross-linker in the cell wall, bonding two apiose molecules of two ramnogalacturonan II (RGII) chains. Consequently, plants subjected to B deficiency normally show altered cell wall phenotypes and growth defects [5,6].

Roots acquire $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ from soils and, depending on its availability, the uptake can take place passively or via a facilitated transport in coordination with an active transport driven by borate transporters [2]. Thus, under optimal B supply conditions, the micronutrient enters the root by passive diffusion crossing the lipid layer. When B availability is limited, the uptake from the soil takes place through a facilitated transport via channel proteins that belong to the Major Intrinsic Proteins family (MIP family) [7]. Then, high affinity active transporters from the BOR family, are responsible for the B efflux into xylem and later, its redistribution within the plant is driven by members of the BOR and the NIP family [2,8–11].

Boron is one of the essential nutrients for plants, and boron deficiency is a major cause of reduced crop production1 . Large quantities of boron are toxic to plants, and boron toxicity is a worldwide problem in food production2 . Two different classes of borate transporters were discovered in Arabidopsis thaliana3 . One of them, a transporter named BOR1, is a plasma membrane borate exporter in Arabidopsis root cells, and is essential for efficient xylem loading of boron4 . BOR1 and its paralogs are also involved in boron toxicity tolerance in plants5,6 .

It was reported that the level of BOR1 is tightly regulated by the concentration of borate in the growth environment7 . At low concentrations of borate, BOR1 is stably localized to the proximal side of plasma membrane in root cells but is degraded upon application of high concentrations of borate7–9 . This degradation occurred after endocytosis of the transporter from the plasma membrane and the endocytosed transporter was transported from early endosome to multivesicular body, ubiquitinated and finally targeted to vacuoles for degradation8–11. A similar boron-dependent decrease in borate transporter levels was also observed in rice12 although in this case the mechanism of the reduction was not elucidated. Thus it was not clarified whether the borate-induced endocytotic degradation of BOR1 that is found in Arabidopsis root cells is conserved among different plant species and different types of plant cells.

The tobacco BY-2 cell line is widely used as a model for the analysis of the cell cycle and protein trafficking in plant cells. This cell line is advantageous for conducting pharmacological studies because of the small size of its cell clumps as well as its ability to grow in liquid suspension13. To obtain an insight into the regulation of borate transporter levels and borate sensing machinery, we investigated the localization and degradation of BOR1-green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion in tobacco BY-2 cells in the presence of high concentrations of borate and analyzed the effect of inhibitors for protein synthesis, protein degradation and intracellular trafficking on its degradation.

We conclude that the experimentally observed swiftness of boron transporters’ boron-mediated downregulation can be understood as a necessary mechanism to maintain optimal constant xylem loading rates over time, while also avoiding DNA damage due to oscillations within cells. One could argue that without a substrate-mediated downregulation of the transporters there would not be the need to avoid traffic jam-like behaviour through swift regulatory dynamics in the first place. However, were the system not to present the regulation, the plant would be unable to shield itself from toxic soil boron levels (Figure 8A) and be much less efficient in growing at low soil boron levels (Figure 8B). Thus, some kind of inhibitory regulation necessarily has to be present, to ensure plant plasticity under different environmental conditions. As a consequence, the speed of the transporter downregulation needs to be sufficiently high. We showed that this is an intrinsic requirement, simply because boron transporters are polarly located: The requirement itself does not depend on external boron fluctuations in the medium, number of cell files composing the root tissue, possible saturable activity of the transporter itself nor the magnitude, location or strength of the xylem flow.

Our study has been based on the well-characterised system of directed boron transport, owing to the richness in quantitative experimental measurements regarding BOR and NIP regulation. However, the implications of our derived insights apply to any system in which the dynamics of polar transport of a given substance relies on an inhibitory feedback between the concentration of that substance and its local transport rate. For example, the phosphate and iron transport systems present both polar transporters as well as substrate-dependent regulation, serving as candidates for such phenomena and dynamical constraint avoidance. In the case of the phosphate transport system, transporters localised to the outer side of the epidermis are responsible for uptake (LePT1 and LePT2, Liu et al., 1998), and they have recently been found to carry a domain possibly involved in phosphate sensing which leads to rapid degradation of phosphate transporter in a phosphatedependent manner (Gu et al., 2016). Similar regulation is also reported for the iron (Fe) transport system, where polar accumulation of IRT1, a major Fe transporter for Fe uptake into roots, is regulated in an Fe-dependent manner (Barberon et al., 2014). Even other transport systems which do not shuttle nutrients might display this sort of instability, such as polar auxin transport, for which stable flows might also require fast response dynamics regarding the activity of auxin importers and efflux facilitators (Robert and Friml, 2009). Indeed, for any polarised tissue in which adaptive regulation of transport levels is necessary we can expect to find intrinsic temporal constraints operating to ensure that steady state flows are maintained and large fluctuations avoided.

In molecular terms, we discovered that although both transporters are predicted to work synergistically and are both required to be effectively similar in regard to rapid regulation, their regulations are biologically encoded in unique ways. We here experimentally focused on the regulatory swiftness of the bidirectional transporter NIP5;1, and found strong evidence that it constitutes a system in which production is maintained high but degradation is rapidly controlled transcriptionally, allowing for the necessarily rapid boron-dependent response. It will be interesting to speculate what underlying reason, if any, has caused the directed exporter, BOR1, which is similarly known and required to be swiftly regulated, to be controlled on a biologically distinct level.

For this work, the analogy with motorway traffic jams was helpful to build an understanding of principles of polarised transport dynamics, albeit both systems obviously deviate in important aspects. Boron concentrations are continuous and can reach arbitrarily high levels, as opposed to (incompressible) cars. Yet, the discrete nature of cells and their regulated polar transporters, combined with the boron-dependent inhibition of the transporters themselves, resembles cars slowing down in response to busy regions along the motorway. Moreover, in both systems highly sensitive responses can prevent jamming (Sugiyama et al., 2008). We therefore propose that the notion of traffic jams can be universally instructive and helpful for biologists considering physiology and regulated growth through polarised transport in plants, as well as for future efforts to enhance plant growth under diverse environmental conditions.

Boron (B) is an essential micronutrient for plants; however, it shows cytotoxicity at high concentrations. A borate transporter BOR1 is required for efficient transport of B toward the root stele in Arabidopsis thaliana. BOR1 shows polar localization in the plasma membrane of various root cells toward the steleside under B limitation. To avoid over-accumulation of B, BOR1 in the plasma membrane is rapidly internalized and transported into the vacuole for proteolysis after high-B supply in an ubiquitinationdependent manner. Although BOR1 has been predicted to be transported into multi-vesicular bodies/ late endosomes (MVB/LEs) via the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT) machinery, experimental evidence was absent so far. In this study, we investigated the intracellular localization of BOR1 by visualizing endomembrane compartments, and tested the involvement of ESCRT-0-like proteins TOM1-LIKEs (TOLs) in the vacuolar sorting of BOR1. Under low-B conditions, a large portion of cytoplasmic BOR1 was localized in the trans-Golgi networks/early endosomes (TGN/EEs) labeled with VHA-a1 subunit. Pharmacological interference of endosomal recycling using brefeldin A-induced colocalization of BOR1 with RabA5D, which labels recycling vesicles associated with the TGN. On the other hand, under high-B conditions, BOR1 was localized in the inside of TOL5-positive MVB/LEs. To examine the roles of TOL proteins in intracellular trafficking of BOR1, we analyzed BOR1-GFP localization in the TOL quintuple mutant (tolQ; tol2-1tol3-1tol5-1tol6-1tol9-1) after high-B supply. In the tolQ mutant, vacuolar sorting of BOR1 was delayed, while the polar localization of BOR1 was not disturbed. Taken together, BOR1 is constantly transported to the TGN/EE by endocytosis and recycled to the plasma membrane likely via RabA5D-positive endomembrane compartments under low-B conditions. On the other hand, BOR1 is transported to the vacuole via TOL5-positive MVB/LEs under high-B conditions. TOL proteins are required for sorting of ubiquitinated BOR1 into MVB/LE for vacuolar degradation.

Background Boron is an essential nutrient for plants and has a largely structural role in development. Globally, there are large tracts of arable land that are deficient in boron, and others where plant growth is restricted by high and toxic boron concentrations. Plants have evolved a range of strategies to cope with deficiency and excess, and considerable genotypic variation exists in responses to variable boron supply.

Scope Boron is available to plants as boric acid, a small molecule with a high membrane permeability compared to other mineral nutrients. As a result, its uptake and distribution in plants can be more difficult to control. This review examines the interconnecting network of processes that are employed by plants to try to achieve optimal growth under conditions where the boron supply may be low, adequate or potentially toxic.

Conclusions The emerging picture of boron movement in plants is of a complex multi-layered system designed to optimise the use of boron over a broad range of concentrations. At the cellular level, plants can switch the direction of boron flow through the polar expression of membrane transporters, while at the whole plant level, integration of xylem and phloem transfer can deliver boron to specific tissues dependent on developmental stage.

Keywords Aquaporins Boron deficiency $\because$ BOR genes . Boron toxicity $\because$ Boron transporter $\ddots$ Efflux pump

Boron (B) is the only nonmetallic element in Group IIIA of the periodic table (boron group elements) and is classified as a quasimetallic or semimetallic element, a substance between metals and nonmetals. B is a vital micronutrient for the growth and development of plants [1] and primarily exists as boric acid $\mathrm { ( H _ { 3 } B O _ { 3 } ) }$ in neutral solutions. The presence of B in both the soil and the water used for irrigation plays a critical role in determining agricultural productivity [2]. In plants, the symptoms of B deficiency occur mainly in the growing or enlarged organs of the plant, including inhibited apical dominance, and reduced B accumulation in flower organs causes reduced fertility [3]. In addition, low B also inhibits leaf expansion and indirectly reduces plant photosynthetic capacity, mainly by disrupting microspore formation and pollen tube growth, reducing fertility and leading to malformed fruit [4, 5]. The typical symptoms of B poisoning occur in the marginal areas of mature leaves, with B accumulation at the ends during transpiration stream transport, resulting in chlorosis or necrosis of these parts. Therefore, excessive or insufficient B content reduces not only crop yield but also quality [6]. In summary, B content is critical to plant growth and development, and B transport genes are indispensable for the uptake and efficient use of boron by plants. There are three main mechanisms of boric acid transmembrane transport: passive diffusion through the lipid bilayer, in which aquaporin (AQP) plays an important role; the promoted transport of the Nodulin 26-like Intrinsic Protein (NIP) channel, which is crucial for promoting the absorption of boron required for plant growth; and root development in a low-boron environment. NIP6;1 and NIP5;1 belong to NIP subgroup II and have similar three-dimensional structures and functions in boron transport in Arabidopsis bud tissue development, both of which play a role in regulating intraplant boron transport [7, 8]. In addition, active transport via BOR transporters [2] plays an important role in the transport of organisms.

Arabidopsis BOR1, an efflux transporter, was the first B transporter found in a biological system [9]. AtBOR1, human Anion Exchanger 1 (hAE1), ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ -coupled acid– base transporter (NBCe1) and Saccharomyces mikatae BOR1 are members of the bicarbonate transport protein superfamily solute carrier 4 (SLC4) [10–14]. To date, a total of 20 BOR transporters have been identified in the Brassica napus genome [15], while 14 TaBOR genes have been identified in common wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) [16]. Additionally, the soybean (Glycine max L.) genome contains 13 distinct GmBOR sequences, the poplar (Populus trichocarpa L.) genome harbors 10 unique PtrBOR gene sequences, and four OsBOR1-like genes have been identified in the rice (Oryza sativa L.) genome [17]. Research has demonstrated that alterations in the maize

ROTTEN EAR (RTE) gene, a functional counterpart of Arabidopsis’s BOR1 protein responsible for boron transport, can lead to severe developmental defects and sterility [18]. In brassica-type rapeseed, boron transporter downregulation reduces the accumulation of B in flower organs, ultimately leading to severe sterility and loss of seed yield [3]. In wheat, unlike AtBOR1 and OsBOR1, TaBOR1 acts as a boron effector transporter, and its mRNA accumulation is regulated by boron status [19]. The overexpression of VvBOR1 in grape can restore the wild-type phenotype in B-deficient Arabidopsis bor1-3 mutants [20]. These observations indicate that B transporters play crucial roles in the growth and development of plants.

Cotton (Gossypium spp.) serves as the most significant natural fiber source globally and as a crucial raw material for China’s textile manufacturing sector, as well as for oilseeds and vegetable protein, and serves as a cornerstone of China’s agricultural economic development [21]. B deficiency has been reported in at least 132 crops and 80 countries, including cotton in 23 countries in Europe, North and South America, and Africa. B deficiency in upland cotton in the United States was first identified in field trials during the period from 1935 to 1937, and cotton was shown to be the crop with the greatest sensitivity to boron application among dicotyledonous plants [22]. The application of B fertilizer was found to significantly increase cotton productivity and lint characteristics in various tropical soils [23]. Additionally, foliar application of silicon and boron enhances boll retention, increases lint yield, and improves fiber quality characteristics in transgenic cotton [24]. In summary, this phenomenon may be related to the further influence of B on plant growth and development through the action of specific transporters. However, research on BOR as a boron transport factor in upland cotton is limited. Therefore, for the first time, in this study, we identified the number of BOR genes in upland cotton, Asian cotton, and Raimondii cotton and analyzed their physical and chemical attributes along with the evolutionary connections between diploid and tetraploid species. Additionally, we examined the cis-acting regulatory elements and performed differential expression analysis of upland cotton. We identified candidate genes associated with flowering time by transcriptome expression profiling and qRT-PCR and investigated the key role of GhBOR1 in upland cotton flowering and fertility via virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS). This integrated approach offers a significant understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of GhBOR1 in cotton reproduction and contributes to the improvement of cotton breeding for increased yield and quality.

Boron (B) is an essential micronutrient for plants, but the molecular mechanisms underlying the uptake and distribution of B in allotetraploid rapeseed (Brassica napus) are unclear. Here, we identified a B transporter of rapeseed, BnaC4.BOR1;1c, which expressed in shoot nodes and involved in distributing B to the reproductive organs. Transgenic Arabidopsis plants containing a BnaC4.BOR1;1c promoter-driven GUS reporter gene showed strong GUS activity in roots, nodal regions of the shoots and immature floral buds. Overexpressing BnaC4.BOR1;1c in Arabidopsis wild-type or in bor1-1 mutants promoted wild-type growth and rescued the bor1-1 mutant phenotype. Conversely, knockdown of BnaC4.BOR1;1c in a B-efficient rapeseed line reduced B accumulation in flower organs, eventually resulting in severe sterility and seed yield loss. BnaC4.BOR1;1c RNAi plants exhibited large amounts of disintegrated stigma papilla cells with thickened cell walls accompanied by abnormal proliferation of lignification under low B conditions, indicating that the sterility may be a result of altered cell wall properties in flower organs. Taken together, our results demonstrate that BnaC4.BOR1;1c is a AtBOR1-homologous B transporter gene expressing in both roots and shoot nodes that is essential for the developing inflorescence tissues, which highlights its diverse functions in allotetraploid rapeseed compared with diploid model plant Arabidopsis.

Key-word: Brassica napus, boron deficiency, BnaC4.BOR1;1c, gene expression, inflorescence growth, seed yield

Both B deficiency and B excess cause inhibited plant growth. BOR1 exhibits polar localization in the plasma membrane toward the stele side and is required for B translocation toward the xylem under low-B conditions (Takano et al., 2002, 2010). Upon high-B supply, BOR1 is inactivated by B-dependent vacuolar sorting via ubiquitination at the K590 residue to avoid overloading with boric acid (Takano et al., 2005; Kasai et al., 2011). These characteristics of BOR1 are consistent with the result that overexpression of BOR1 under control of the 35S promoter improved tolerance to B deficiency in Arabidopsis by enhancing B translocation without affecting growth under high-B conditions (Miwa et al., 2006). In this study, we found that expression of a BOR1 variant unexpectedly enhanced tolerance to excess B. BOR1(K590A)- GFP-HPT showed restricted polar localization and stable accumulation even under excess-B conditions (Figures 2, 3). The ubiquitous expression of BOR1(K590A)-GFP-HPT by the UBQ10 promoter conferred tolerance to excess-B conditions (Figures 4, 5). This consequence is similar to the case of overexpression of BOR4, a borate transporter stably accumulated under high-B conditions (Miwa et al., 2007; Miwa and Fujiwara, 2011).

However, the mechanism by which B-excess tolerance is conferred appears to be different from those in wild-type Arabidopsis plants and in transgenic plants overexpressing BOR4 under control of the 35S promoter. The concentrations of B in the roots and shoots of plants overexpressing BOR4 were three-fold lower than those in the wild-type plants (Miwa et al., 2007), and the B concentration in shoots of bor4 lossof-function mutant plants was greater under high-B conditions (Miwa et al., 2014). These results suggest that BOR4 functions in the exclusion of B from roots to decrease the concentration of B in whole plants under conditions of B-excess. When the plants carrying proUBQ10:BOR1(K590A)-GFP-HPT were grown at $3 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ B supply, the concentration of B in the roots was similar to that in wild-type plants, while the B concentration in the shoots was greater than that of wild-type plants (Figure 6). These results suggest that expression of BOR1(K590A)-GFPHPT does not exclude B from roots under high-B conditions. Instead, it is likely that BOR1(K590A)-GFP-HPT confers excessB tolerance by exclusion of B from the cytosol in various cells in shoots. The excess-B tolerance mechanism by B export from the cytosol was also implicated in the leaves of barley and wheat. B-toxicity typically appears as necrosis in leaves in these species. In the leaves of B-tolerant cultivars of barley and wheat, B concentrations that induce necrosis were more than two-fold higher than in those of sensitive cultivars (Reid and Fitzpatrick, 2009). In addition, B concentration in leaf protoplasts from the B-tolerant barley cultivar, Sahara, was only $5 6 \%$ of that from the intolerant cultivar when incubated with $1 0 \mathrm { m M }$ B. It was also shown that leaching of B from leaves by rain makes significant contribution on growth of roots and shoots of Sahara under excess B conditions. A BOR4 homolog Bot1 was identified as a key factor for excess-B tolerance in Barley. Sahara contains about four times as many Bot1 gene copies and encodes a Bot1 protein that possesses a higher capacity of B export compared to the intolerant cultivar (Sutton et al., 2007). It is conceivable that proUBQ10:BOR1(K590A)- GFP-HPT conferred excess-B tolerance to Arabidopsis plants by a similar B-export mechanism that occurs in the leaves of barley and wheat. In a previous study, overexpression of Arabidopsis TIP5;1, a tonoplast localized aquaporin, under control of the 35S promoter improved tolerance to excess-B conditions in Arabidopsis plants (Pang et al., 2010). Similar to the case with proUBQ10:BOR1(K590A)-GFP-HPT, B concentrations in shoots were increased in the TIP5;1 overexpression lines. Although B-transport activity of TIP5;1 has not been proven, the authors proposed that TIP5;1 conferred excess-B tolerance by vacuolar compartmentalization of B. It is likely that protection of sensitive cytosol is a key process in excess-B tolerance of plants.

Another important finding in our study is that the shoot growth of plants expressing BOR1-GFP-HPT and BOR1(K590A)-GFP-HPT tended to be greater than that of the wild-type under low-B conditions $( 0 . 3 \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ , Figures 4, 5G–L; Supplemental Figure 2). This is attributable to the higher concentration of B in the shoots of the transgenic lines (Figure 6B). Our careful analysis of polar localization showed that BOR1-GFP-HPT and BOR1(K590A)-GFPHPT maintained weak polarity toward the stele side in root epidermal cells and clear polarity in mature endodermal cells (Figures 2A,B). These results suggest that ubiquitous expression of BOR1 variants enhances B translocation toward the stele side, as was the case of BOR1 overexpression by the 35S promoter (Miwa et al., 2006). The difference in polar localization between BOR1-GFP-HPT variants and BOR4- GFP likely determined the direction of B flux toward the stele in the former case and outside the roots in the latter case.

The results from this study reveal the potential for engineering trafficking properties of transporters to develop stress-tolerant plants. The physiological function of wildtype BOR1 is to effect efficient B translocation under low-B conditions. However, ubiquitous expression of an engineered BOR1 variant with restricted polar localization and stable accumulation conferred excess-B tolerance in plants.

Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. SlALMT15 (Solyc11gO6897O) was found to be related to a stomatal density trait that functions in stomatal formation in tomato leaves,and further affects photosynthesis and drought tolerance in tomato (J.Ye,Wang, et al.,2021). Z.Wang et al. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.

Thisreport provides evidence suggesting that SlALMT11 (SolycO8g0o699O) expressed in tomato leaf guard cells is involved in stomatal closure induced by external malate,but not by abscisic acid.This study also highlights how the guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (SlALMT11 and AtALMT12)are activated by external organic acids and identifies the amino acid residues of the ALMT proteins involved in the voltage-dependent channel activity.

Guard-cell-type aluminium-activated malate transporters (ALMTs) are involved in stomatal closure by exporting anions from guard cells. However, their physiological and electrophysiological functions are yet to be explored. Here,we analysed the physiological and electrophysiological properties of the ALMT channelsin Arabidopsis and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum). SIALMT11 was specifically expressed in tomato guard cells. External malate-induced stomatal closure was impaired in ALMT-suppressed lines of tomato and Arabidopsis, although abscisic acid did not influence the stomatal response in SIALMT11-knock-down tomato lines. Electrophysiological analyses in Xenopus oocytes showed that SIALMT11 and AtALMT12/ QUAC1 exhibited characteristic bell-shaped current-voltage patterns dependent on extracellular malate, fumarate，and citrate. Both ALMTs could transport malate, fumarate,and succinate, but not citrate, suggesting that the guard-cell-type ALMTs aredicarboxylic anion channels activated by extracellular organic acids. The truncation of acidic amino acids, Asp or Glu, from the C-terminal end of SlALMT11 or AtALMT12/QUAC1 led to the disappearance of the bell-shaped current-voltage patterns. Our findings establish that malate-activated stomatal closure is mediated by guard-cell-type ALMT channels that require an acidic amino acid in the C-terminus as a candidate voltage sensor in both tomato and Arabidopsis.

## 3.1丨 Screening of SIALMT genes expressed in guard cells


Previous studies revealed that the AtALMT12/QUAC1 gene is involved in stomatal closure (Meyer etal., 201O; Sasaki et al., 2010).

To determine which SlALMT genes are expressed in tomato guard cells，the expression levels of 16 SIALMT genes were compared between the epidermis and whole leaves by semi-quantitative RTPCR (Figure 1a and Supporting Information: Figure S1).Three SIALMT genes，SIALMT4，SIALMT5，and SIALMT11，were found to be expressed in guard cell-enriched epidermis.The expression level of the SIALMT11 gene relative to that of the SlUBQ gene was higher than those of the SIALMT4 and SIALMT5 genes (Figure 1a and Supporting Information: Figure S1).The SlALMT11 protein is categorized as being in Clade 3 of the ALMT-protein family that also includes AtALMT12 (Sasaki et al.，201O； Sasaki，Tsuchiya，Ariyoshi, Nakano,et al., 2016).The SIALMT11 gene was expressed in leaves, but much less in roots (Figure 1b). Moreover,analysis of transgenic plants expressing GUS or GFP under the control of the SIALMT11 promoter (3187bp upstream of the first ATG) showed that staining or fluorescence was detected in guard cells (Figure 1c and Supporting Information: Figure S2a,b). In contrast，SIALMT4 and SIALMT5 expression was not apparent in the guard cells of plants transformed with the promoter:GUS constructs (Figure 1c).

The subcelllar localization of SlALMT11 was determined by transient expression of the protein fused to GFP in Arabidopsis protoplasts (see Section 2)，where the fluorescence was mainly observed at the surface of the protoplasts (Figure 1d and Supporting Information: Figure S3a).This finding was confirmed by comparing the localization of SlALMT11 protein directly with that of AtPIP2;1 protein that is known to be localized to the plasma membrane (Sorieul et al.,2011).The AtPlP2;1::mCherry could be co-expressed with GFP because of its distinct excitation and emission wavelengths. The fluorescence from GFP::SIALMT11 nearly overlapped with that from the AtPlP2;1:mCherry signals (Figure 1d).These results indicate that SlALMT11 is highly expressed in guard cells and isa plasmamembrane localized protein.Weak fluorescence was observed inside the cells that we attribute to strong autofluorescence from chlorophyll (Figure 1d and Supporting Information: Figure S3b).


## 3.2丨Physiological function of SlALMT11 in stomatal movement


We hypothesized that SlALMT11 might be involved in stomatal closure as is AtALMT12 (Meyer et al., 201O; Sasaki etal., 2010).To examine this hypothesis,we compared stomatal closure in leaves from the wild type with that from two independent RNAi lines suppressing SlALMT11 gene expression (see Section 2). Levels of the SIALMT11 transcript in leaves of two RNAi lines were 1O times lower than that in the wild type (Figure 2a).The density of stomata on the leaves of the two tomato RNAi lines was not different from that of the wild type (Figure 2b).Stomatal aperture in response to exogenous ABA indicated no difference between the RNAi lines and the wild type (Figure 2c,d).Because AtALMT12 expression in Xenopus oocytes showed enhanced inward currents by exogenous malate (Meyer et al.,2010; Mumm et al., 2013), we tested the effect of exogenous malate on stomatal closure.As the malate concentration increased, wild-type stomata closed (Figure 2e,f and Supporting Information: Table S4).In contrast,SIALMT11 RNAi lines were impaired in stomatal closure at $\mathsf { 3 m M }$ malate (Figure 2e,f). Similarly,exogenous malate $( 3 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { M } )$ induced stomatal closure in the Arabidopsis wild type but not in the atalmt12 knock-down line (Supporting Information: Figure S4). Taken together,these results suggested that stomatal closure in response to ABA is different between SIALMT11 and AtALMT12; however, these results also showed that SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 are involved in stomatal closure regulated by apoplastic malate concentrations.


## 3.3|Electrophysiological properties of SIALMT11


Electrophysiological measurements in Xenopus oocytes revealed that AtALMT12 has a bell-shaped current-voltage (I/V) pattern that is dependent on the endogenous and exogenous malate concentrations (Mayer et al.，201O; Mumm et al.，2013)．To elucidate the electrophysiological function of SIALMT11,we injected SlALMT11 cRNA in Xenopus oocytes and used the two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC)method to measure the current magnitude at different membrane voltages (Figure 3a,b).

In oocytes expressing SlALMT11 without malate pre-injection and exposed to a malate bath solution,the inward currents were slightly higher than those in the control oocytes (Figure 3a,b).The inward currents of malate in pre-injected oocytes increased and showed a characteristic bell-shaped I/V pattern (Figure 3b) similar to that of AtALMT12 (Supporting Information: Figure S5；Mumm et al.，2013).Furthermore,in the SIALMT11-expressing oocytes, the peak of the inward current shifted toward a more negative voltage potential in the malate bath solution than in the gluconate bath solution (Figure 3b).In addition,the reversal potentials $( E _ { \mathrm { r e v } } )$ of SIALMT11-expressing oocytes shifted more to the positive direction than that of the water-control oocytes.The positive shift in the reversal potential is remarkable in the malate pre-injected oocytes expressing SlALMT11 (Figure 3b,indicated with arrowheads).These results demonstrated that SlALMT11 is involved in malate efflux that is similar in function to AtALMT12.The malate efflux currents of SIALMT11at the peak voltage $( - 6 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { V } )$ in the bath solution $( 1 0 \mathsf { m } \mathsf { M }$ sodium gluconate at $\mathsf { p H } 4 . 5$ were not significantlydifferent (with $\mathbf { t } \cdot \mathbf { \tau }$ test) between replicates with $1 0 0 \mu \mathsf { M } \mathsf { A } \mathsf { I C l } _ { 3 }$ $( - 3 0 8 \mathsf { n A } \pm 5 7 \mathsf { S E }$ , $n = 9$ and replicates without ${ \mathsf { A l C l } } _ { 3 }$ $( - 4 3 4 \mathsf { n A } \pm 6 7 \mathsf { S E }$ ， $n = 5$ Thisresult indicates that the transport function of SlALMT11 is not activated by $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ ions.


## 3.4丨Exogenous solution-dependent malate efflux


Because the function of AtALMT12 is regulated by the exogenous malate concentration (Mumm et al.,2013),the effects of several exogenously added organic and inorganic anions on the malate efflux from oocytes expressing SIALMT11 or AtALMT12 were examined (Figure 4).

Malate efflux derived from SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 were activated and generated high，bell-shaped I/V patternsby exogenous fumarate and citrate,as well as malate in the bath solutions (Figure 4a,d),whereas inorganic anions,sulphate, nitrate, and chloride had similar current patterns as the gluconate-based bath solution (Figure 4b,e). Similar to the malate bath solution, fumarate and citrate shifted the relative open probability $( P _ { \mathrm { O } } )$ of the channel to more negative membrane potentials following Boltzmann characteristics (Figure 4c,f)．Malate, fumarate，and citrate shifted the half-maximal activation potential $( V _ { 1 / 2 } )$ to more negative values (about $- 4 0 \mathsf { m V } )$ ）compared to inorganic bath solutions (Figure $_ { 4 \mathrm { g } ) }$ .These results suggest that SlALMT11 and AtALMT12 channels open the channel gate at a more negative membrane potential in bath solutions containing malate,fumarate and citrate，than in bath solutions containing gluconate and inorganic anions.

Next,we also examined the activation of both ALMT proteins by isomers of malate and fumarate as exogenously supplied organic acids (Supporting Information: Figure S6a).L-Malic acid occurs naturally,and D-malic acid is an enantiomer of malate.As shown in Supporting Information:Figure S6a,inward currents derived from the oocytes expressing SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 showed similar inward currents depending on the malate efflux in the bath solution，including both L- and D-malic acid，and caused a hyperpolarized peak of the bell-shaped curve in oocytes expressing both ALMT genes.These results suggest that two carboxyl groups of dicarboxylic acids,regardless enantiomers,are required for full activation of malate efflux by both ALMT proteins.In contrast, maleic acid did not produce a current pattern similar to that of fumaric acid.
