Aluminum Activated Malate Transporters (ALMTs) are important plant anion channels by playing roles in organic acid transport, stress resistance, growth and development, nutrient absorption, and the GABA response (Hedrich 2012; Ramesh et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2016; Balzergue et al., 2017; Medeiros et al., 2018; Long et al.,

2020). Wheat TaALMT1 was the first identified family member (named due to its activation by aluminium $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ , the main ion causing toxicity to plants in acidic soil) mediates malate efflux to chelate ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ and relieve toxicity (Zhang et al., 2001; Sasaki et al., 2004). Our recent work has shown that TaALMT1 not only participates in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxification but also participates in the GABA response (Ramesh et al., 2015; Long et al., 2020). Arabidopsis has 14 ALMTs, with those characterized having varied roles, and several others yet to be characterized (Hedrich 2012; Sharma et al., 2016; Medeiros et al., 2018). AtALMT1, which is mainly expressed in roots and localized at the plasma membrane (PM), functions in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity resistance, similarly to TaALMT1, low phosphorus (LP) signal transduction, and Fe uptake, by mediating malate efflux in roots (Hoekenga et al., 2006; Balzergue et al., 2017; Mora-Macıas et al., 2017 ́ ). ALMT3 is also involved in the LP response in root hairs (Maruyama et al., 2019). The vacuolar membrane (tonoplast)-localized anion channels ALMT4, ALMT6, and ALMT9 transport anions across the tonoplast to regulate stomatal movement and/or salinity stress resistance (Kovermann et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2011; De Angeli et al., 2013a; Baetz et al., 2016; Eisenach et al., 2017). ALMT12, ALMT13, and ALMT14, are all likely to be Rtype anion channels in the PM, playing roles in malate transport to regulate stomatal opening, stomatal and mesophyll conductance, and pollen tube growth (Meyer et al., 2010; Sasaki et al., 2010; Medeiros et al., 2016; Gutermuth et al., 2018; Domingos et al., 2019). Furthermore, ALMT family members were reported to be involved in physiological and stress response processes in other crops and plants including maize, rice, soybean, apple, grape, tomato, canola, Brachypodium distachyon, and Medicago sativa (Ligaba et al., 2006; Piñeros et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; De Angeli et al., 2013b; Sasaki et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018; Heng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Luu et al., 2019).

Previously, through the use of gene mapping, a mutation in OsALMT7 was found to underpin a panicle apical abortion (paab1) phenotype. The two paab1 transcripts (paab1-t1 and paab1-t2), were found to be transcribed into proteins with Cterminal truncations (containing 163 amino acid residues) that transport anions with a capacity lower than that of the fulllength OsALMT7 (Heng et al., 2018). OsALMT7 (paab1) is expressed in vascular tissues of roots, stems, sheaths, and panicles and localizes to the PM, and it was concluded that it plays an important role in panicle anion transport, panicle development, and grain yield (Heng et al., 2018). Furthermore when wild-type plants were transformed with a genomic fragment containing the paab1 base substitution resulting in a panicle abortion phenotype (Heng et al., 2018). Compare with other ALMTs, OsALMT7 has special molecular characteristicses that it has the ability to mediate malate flux with its transmembrane helices incomplete, and its truncated protein represses the wild-type channel in rice. Here, we investigate the mechanism of these characteristicses with further electrophysiology studies. We proposed and tested the hypothesis that OsALMT7 transports malate as a multimer and that paab1 interaction with OsALMT7 inhibits transport capacity. Furthermore, we extended this to examine whether this is a feature of other ALMTs, specifically TaALMT1.

A number of plant channels are already known to function as homo- or hetero-multimers, and heteromerization is acknowledged to be an important mechanism of channel regulation (Hedrich, 2012). For example, aquaporins of both the PM and tonoplast assemble as homo- or heterotetramers, such as PIP1s with no or weak water permeability with itself, combine with PIP2s and increase their activity in different plant species (Harvengt et al., 2000; Bienert et al., 2012; Fetter et al., 2004; Heinen et al., 2014; Berny et al., 2016). Shaker family potassium (K) channels share a similar structure with ALMTs, 6 transmembrane $\alpha$ -helices with both N-terminal and C-terminal cytosolic domains, and function as homo- or heterotetramers; notably, KC1, the silent channel subunit, forms a heterotetramer with other shaker K channels to change their voltage dependence (Baizabal-Aguirre et al., 1999; Pilot et al., 2001; Véry and Sentenac, 2003; Xicluna et al., 2007; Duby et al., 2008; Lebaudy et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2009; Lebaudy et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Jeanguenin et al., 2011). Cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 2 (CNGC2) and CNGC4 have been proposed to form a heteromeric channel to mediate $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ currents (Tian et al., 2019). For plant anion channels, the S-type channel SLAC1 has been proposed to combine with the shaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2 and inhibit their channel activity (Zhang et al., 2016). Zhang et al. (2013) showed that tonoplast-localized AtALMT9 formed homomultimeric complex by coexpressing the mutant channel and wild-type channel in tobacco leaves; however, it has not been determined whether PM-localized ALMTs, including OsALMT7, and R-type anion channels, such as ALMT12/13/14, function as multimers or monomers.

Here, we determined that OsALMT7 function as multimeric proteins and that combinations of ALMT subunits can contribute to anion channel regulation. This strengthens our understanding of ALMT function. By defining the mechanism by which subunit modification has a dominant effect on channel function, this provides a new avenue by which genetic modification or gene editing can have important effects without first creating knockout mutants, enabling crop stress resistance and grain yield improvements.

 Anion transport by aluminium-activated malate transporter (ALMT) proteins is negatively regulated by gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which increases in concentration during stress.  Here, the interaction between GABA and wheat (Triticum aestivum, Ta) TaALMT1 heterologously-expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes was investigated.

 GABA inhibited anion transport by TaALMT1 in membrane patches from the cytosolic, not extracellular membrane face, via a reduction in open probability $( \mathsf { N P } _ { \mathsf { o p e n } } )$ , not an inhibition of channel current magnitude. TaALMT1 currents in patches frequently exhibited rundown with complete removal of cytosolic factors, but were partially sustained by protein kinase C dependent phosphorylation. When applied to whole oocytes a GABA-analogue-BODIPY conjugate inhibited TaALMT1 anion currents from the cytoplasmic face only, whereas free GABA inhibited from both the inside and outside consistent with GABA traversing the TaALMT1 pore then acting from the inside.

 We propose GABA does not competitively inhibit ALMT conductance through the same pore but rather leads to an allosteric effect, reducing anion channel opening frequency. Across plants GABA is a conserved regulator of anion transport via ALMTs – a family with numerous physiological roles beyond $A | ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance. Our data suggests that a GABA–ALMT interaction from the cytosolic face has the potential to form part of a novel plant signalling pathway.

The aluminium activated malate transporter (ALMT) gene family is named after the first member of the family identified in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) [1]. The product of this gene controls resistance to aluminium (Al) toxicity. TaALMT1 was the first member of this novel family of genes encoding anion channels. Although widely spread in plants, relatively little information is available on the roles performed by other members of this family. However those that have been characterised show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13], fruit acidity [14,15], microbe interactions [16,17] and seed development [18].

ALMT genes encode transmembrane proteins that function as anion channels and perform multiple functions involving the transport of organic anions (e.g., carboxylates) and inorganic anions in cells [19–21]. Carboxylic acids such as malic and citric acids are important metabolites in plant cells due to their involvement in photosynthesis, the tricaboxylic acid pathway, carbohydrate metabolism, cytosolic pH regulation, contribution to the maintenance of electroneutrality and nutrition [22–24]. These organic anions also confer resistance to Al toxicity in acid soils because when released from roots their carboxyl groups chelate the trivalent Al cations $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ rendering them less toxic [22]. Carboxylic anions can also bind with other multivalent metal ions [21].

Anion channels are integral membrane proteins that form aqueous pores to selectively allow the rapid transport of anions across membranes down their electrochemical gradients [25]. Therefore, anion channels are passive transporters located on many plant membranes including the plasma membrane, tonoplast, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial and chloroplast membranes. Some also perform signalling roles and function as master switches in stress responses [25–27]. The development of the patch-clamping technique provided a method for detailed research on the functioning of ion channels. The patch-clamp technique has been used to investigate the function of some members of the ALMT family. Some are permeable to malate anions while others are also permeable to other organic inions (such as fumarate) or inorganic inions (such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , $\mathrm { N O } ^ { 3 - }$ and less to $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ ). Other useful methods for studying ion channels also include the analysis of substrate concentrations in native and heterologous expression systems. In plants, the guard cells that regulate stomatal aperture have become a popular model system for characterising membrane transport and signal transduction. For instance, in Vicia faba L. guard cells, researchers have identified two types of anion channel considered important for stomatal closure: the rapid-type (R-type) and the slow-type (S-type) [28]. The R-type anion channels can be activated rapidly within $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ by depolarisation and activates potassium release when the membrane potential falls below the equilibrium potential for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ while S-type channels showed a much slower (seconds) voltage-dependent activation and deactivation [20,28].

The ALMT (aluminium-activated malate transporter) family comprises a functionally diverse but structurally similar group of ion channels. They are found ubiquitously in plant species, expressed throughout different tissues, and located in either the plasma membrane or tonoplast. The first family member identified was TaALMT1, discovered in wheat root tips, which was found to be involved in aluminium resistance by means of malate exudation into the soil. However, since this discovery other family members have been shown to have many other functions such as roles in stomatal opening, general anionic homoeostasis, and in economically valuable traits such as fruit flavour. Recent evidence has also shown that ALMT proteins can act as key molecular actors in GABA $\dot { \gamma }$ -aminobutyric acid) signalling, the first evidence that GABA can act as a signal transducer in plants.

The plant genome has frequent repetitions of the aluminumactivated malate transporters (ALMT) genes, which is essential for transporting organic acids (OAs) across membranes (Zhang et al., 2014). OAs regulate plant metabolism and modulate adaptational (Sharma et al., 2016) activities like stomatal motion (Meyer et al., 2010a; Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010), aluminum tolerance, pH modulation, and stress response (Sharma et al., 2016). In the last few decades, multiple reports have suggested that the release of OAs (particularly, malic acid) can modulate plant tolerance to metal, while its improvs nutritional stress, ion transport, and cell turgor pressure (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).

Therefore, delineating the underlying mechanism of ALMTs action can provide us with tools to improve plant response to biotic and abiotic stressors.

Evolutionary analysis of ALMTs in bacteria (Takanashi et al., 2016), Arabidopsis (Kovermann et al., 2007), rice (Oryza sativa) (Liu et al., 2017), apple (Ma et al., 2018), and Chinese white pear (Xu et al., 2018) demonstrated that plants ALMTs have distinctive function, for example aluminum tolerance, and fruit acidity in plants. They have also been correlated with resistance response, ion transport, and opening and closing of the stomatal guard cells.

Based on a study on Arabidopsis thaliana, the ALMT family has 14 members, divided into three subgroups, according to their functions. The most representative family member is AtALMT1, which belongs to the first subgroup and is located in the root cell membrane. AtALMT9 represents member of the second subgroup and is primarily expressed in mesophyll cells. AtALMT12 belongs to the third subcategory and is primarily expressed in the plasma membrane and the intima of guard cells. Its function is related to the closure of guard cell type anion channels and stomata (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010).

ALMTs were reported to function as anion channel proteins (Zhang et al., 2014). In particular, the activity and expression profile of the AtALMT12 gene was shown to have significant influence on the anion efflux. In stomatal guard cells, under drought stress, the gene was shown to accelerate guard cell cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, and vacuole anion discharge. A massive exudation of anions altered cell membrane polarity, activated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel proteins, and resulted in the release of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ out of cells, causing reduction in cell turgor pressure, closure of the stomata and minimization of moisture loss.

Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is a highly profitable crop and the largest source of natural fiber for the global textile industry. The demand for enhanced fiber quality is increasing with the rapid growth of modern textile industries. Till now, little is known about the role of the ALMT gene family in upland cotton. Here, we screened the entire genome of the upland cotton ALMT gene family and predicted gene structure, chromosome distribution, cellular localization, and expression pattern. This work will offer new insight into the development of genetically enhanced stress-resistant cotton fiber.

To guarantee appropriate gas exchanges under changing environmental conditions, ion transport and metabolism have to be integrated processes in guard cells. Anions have to meet the metabolic requirements of the cell as well as to keep the ionic balance and the osmotic potential. Chloride has an important role as an osmoticum and charge balance but is metabolically inactive. In contrast, malate is part of several metabolic pathways and through the action on PEPcase regulates the synthesis of oxaloacetate, its precursor31. During stomatal opening concomitantly to potassium uptake, malate and chloride are taken up from the apoplast1,4,6,32. Moreover, malate is also synthesized via starch degradation4,5. The amount of malate in the apoplast is limited and the synthesis of large amounts of malate through starch breakdown and glycolysis is likely to be slower than the uptake. As the cytosolic volume of guard cells is only about $2 0 { - } 3 0 \%$ of the cellular volume when stomata are closed, small increases of cytosolic malate are sufficient to activate the vacuolar chloride channel and consequently allow a rapid opening reaction via chloride accumulation in the vacuole. Consequently, at least in short terms, malate may not have the role as the main osmolyte during stomatal opening but rather exhibit a so far unexplored signalling function: the regulation of anion fluxes across the plasma and the vacuolar membranes, hence participating in the control of the osmotic pressure of guard cells (Fig. 6). We found that AtALMT9 mediates chloride currents activated by cytosolic malate in a physiological concentration range in both heterologous expression system and under native conditions. In Arabidopsis, the relative contribution of AtALMT9 in vacuolar chloride fluxes can be estimated based on our data. We could attribute the relatively weak activation observed in Arabidopsis compared with the measurements in N. benthamiana overexpressing AtALMT9 to the relative high background currents in Arabidopsis vacuoles. However, taking the measured values and deducing the - ICl þ malalmt9 )/(IClCol - 0 - IClalmt9)) lating the ratios of, an activation of the AtALMT9-mediated chloride current of $\sim 3$ could be obtained; a value similar to that observed in tobacco.

At $- 1 2 0 \mathrm { m V }$ and in the presence of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M C l ^ { - } }$ , and $1 \mathrm { m M }$ malate the current through AtALMT9 is $\sim - 3 \mathsf { p A p F } ^ { - 1 }$ . We found that beside AtALMT9 the major current under our experimental conditions is generated by AtCLCa with a current density of $\sim - 3 \mathsf { p A p F A } ^ { - 1 }$ . If one takes into account that AtCLCa is a nitrate, chloride/proton antiporter12,29 and that under our experimental conditions, two protons are exported for each chloride taken up by the vacuole it results that the chloride flux mediated by AtALMT9 is about three times the one mediated by AtCLCa. Nonetheless, it should be mentioned that the relative contributions of AtALMT9 and AtCLCa may differ in function of the given membrane potential and cytosolic chloride concentrations and regulatory factors.

Our results also show that AtALMT9 is required for fast and complete opening of stomata, but has no effect on stomata closure. Mutants of AtALMT9 wilt faster, which is in accordance with the gas exchange data and the measurements made on isolated epidermal strips. AtALMT9 is also expressed in the mesophyll cells18. To exclude indirect effect of the mesophyll, we compared water contents and the osmolarity in the leaves of wildtype and mutant plants. Both parameters were displaying no significant differences between wild-type and knockout plants consequently excluding a role of the mesophyll in the observed phenotype. Therefore, the drought-resistant phenotype of the knockout can be attributed to the impaired stomatal opening resulting from a reduced uptake of chloride in guard cell vacuoles. This is in line with the functional properties of AtALMT9 mediating chloride fluxes directed into the vacuole.

Wang and Blatt33 have recently shown that carboxylates inhibit chloride fluxes across the plasma membrane of Vicia faba guard cells, indicating that carboxylates act as important regulatory elements of chloride fluxes across cellular membranes. In our work, we identified AtALMT9 as target of the carboxylate modulation. Whether the inhibition observed by Wang and Blatt33 is due to an opposite regulatory effect of carboxylates on plasma membrane localized ALMTs or SLACs or whether an inhibition of the plasma membrane chloride efflux was observed due to the activation of the vacuolar chloride currents remains to be established. The discovery that AtALMT9 constitutes a vacuolar chloride channel, which has been sought for over 20 years, assigns a completely novel function to this anion channel. These results may pave the way to get further insights in the regulation of guard cell anion channels and finally to modulate stomatal aperture allowing to produce plants that are more drought tolerant and more productive under certain environmental conditions.

Even after SLAC1 was identified as a guard cell S-type anion channel, the origin of R-type anion channel currents had remained unknown [38,39]. Then in 2010, several researches identified AtALMT12, a member of aluminum-activated malate transporter family, as a major component of the guard cell R-type anion channels [46,162,163]. AtALMT12 represents an anion channel permeable to malate, chloride and nitrate, and unlike SLAC1 it does not require any kinases for activation [162,163]. However, coexpression of OST1 in Xenopus oocytes resulted in further enhancement of AtALMT12 current [97]. AtALMT12 is different from its homologue AtALMT1 in that its activity was not stimulated by $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [163,164]. atalmt12 mutant plants showed partially impaired stomatal closure in response to various stimuli such as $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , ABA and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ [162,163]. AtALMT12 shows rapid inactivation at hyperpolarized membrane potential, in which its cytosolic C-terminal domain serves as a voltage sensor [165].

Three other members of ALMT family reside in Arabidopsis guard cell tonoplast; AtALMT4, 6 and 9 (Figure 1) [95,96,166–168]. AtALMT6 was identified as a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -activated channel permeable to malate and fumarate, and its activity modulated by vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ [95]. This channel can mediate malate influx upon tonoplast hyperpolarization, and efflux upon depolarization [95]. Atalmt6 mutant plant displayed reduced malate current in guard cell vacuole. However, no obvious phenotypic difference was observed compared to WT plants [95]. AtALMT9, on the other hand, acts as a chloride efflux channel activated by cytosolic malate, and the phenotype of the mutant plant evidenced its role in stomatal opening [96]. Recently, AtALMT4 was shown to be another tonoplast ALMT, that can mediate anion influx and efflux, regulated by phosphorylation at ${ \tt S e r 3 8 2 }$ residue [94]. Though its function shows some similarity to AtALMT6, Atalmt4 mutant plant shows obvious impairment in ABA-induced stomatal closure [94].

The significance of malate during stomatal movements has been implied decades before the identification of ALMTs described above [47,169–172]. This includes malate release from mesophyll cells and malate synthesis in guard cells [22,47,171,172]. In 2008, an ABC transporter AtABCB14, was reported to mediate malate influx across guard cell PM, and confirmed to participate in stomatal opening [98]. Together, these data suggest an elaborate regulation of stomatal movement by malate.

Emerging evidence compiled over the last two decades suggests that gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an endogenous signalling molecule in plants [1–10]. In response to both abiotic (acidosis, hypoxia, salinity, drought, and cold) and biotic (pathogens, viruses, and herbivory) stress, GABA concentrations can change rapidly in plants [1,4,11–18]. Micromolar concentrations of GABA (and its analog muscimol) regulate anion currents through the ALMT family of proteins from various plant species [4], and the GABA-induced inhibition of anion transport via an ALMT protein localised to the tonoplast in guard cells can regulate stomatal aperture under drought stress [19]. This modulation of anion flux facilitated by ALMTs presents a probable process by which GABA can function as a stress signal in plants [4], depend on the amino acids present within a putative GABA binding motif in ALMTs, and share homology with the GABA binding site of mammalian GABAA receptors. The site-directed mutagenesis of particular amino acids in the putative GABA binding motif alters the GABA sensitivity of plants [4], and the patch clamping of the wheat ALMT1 (TaALMT1) that is expressed in Xenopus oocytes indicates that GABA is inhibitory on the cytoplasmic side of the protein [20].

It is possible to manipulate the internal GABA concentrations in plant cells using the pharmacological agents (e.g., amino-oxyacetate (AOA) and vigabatrin) that have been used to characterise mammalian GABA receptors [21–25] or according to the mutagenesis of the enzymes involved in GABA synthesis [26,27]. The manipulation of endogenous GABA concentrations using pharmacological agents such as AOA and vigabatrin have provided insights into the association between anion flux and GABA modulation in anion channels, although these agents are also directly manipulated TaALMT1 activity [28]. Malate efflux via ALMTs is negatively correlated with internal GABA concentrations, and in ALMT with mutations in the putative GABA binding site, this relationship is eliminated [28]. In Xenopus laevis oocytes, tobacco BY2 cells, and yeast, TaALMT1 expression decreases endogenous GABA concentrations by facilitating GABA efflux from the cells, and that GABA can also be transported into the cell via ALMTs at low pH levels [28]. The capacity for GABA efflux via ALMTs seems to be higher when compared to malate efflux on a molar basis, and this is expected to have wide-ranging impacts on the carbon/nitrogen balance and signalling in plants.

ALMTs in general, and wheat roots in particular, efflux malate (anions) and GABA via ALMTs upon exposure to aluminium (Al) at low $\mathrm { p H }$ levels [29] and in response to external anions at neutral and high pH levels [4,30,31]. The mechanism for the transport and efflux of GABA across cell membranes and its interaction with malate through ALMT channels is suggestive of these proteins having a dual function [28]. However, the question that arises is whether both malate and GABA are transported through the same pores in ALMT or via a different pathway in the same protein simultaneously. The recently described cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of Arabidopsis thaliana AtALMT1 reveals that the ALMT1 dimers assemble as an anion channel and that trivalent aluminium ions $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ bind on the extracellular side, leading to conformational changes in the transmembrane (TM) 1–2 loop and in the TM5-6 loop that result in the opening of an extracellular gate for malate flux [32]. One permeation pathway for ion flux is predicted with residues D49, E156, and D160 that are important for $\mathrm { \ A l } ^ { 3 + }$ activation. However, the pathway for GABA flux through the protein or binding was not examined for AtALMT1. If a single permeation pathway exists through ALMT1, the protein may have two conformational states that affect selectivity: one that is permeable to malate, and one that is permeable to GABA, with the conformation of the pore depending on whether it is GABA or malate that is binding to the protein. The apoplastic and cytoplasmic concentrations of both malate and GABA may be finely titrated, and each regulates and is regulated by the other in the cells.

In animal studies, plant-derived pharmacological agents have been used extensively to dissect the structure and function of GABA receptors and ion channels. Picrotoxin derived from the seeds of Anamirta cocculus can act on $\mathrm { G A B A _ { A } }$ receptors as either a noncompetitive channel blocker $( \mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ channels) [33,34] or by mediating inhibition via an allosteric mechanism [35–37]. Interestingly, the picrotoxin-mediated inhibition of glycine receptors (GlyR) is competitive [38]. Picrotoxin is not structurally similar to GABA, but it inhibits ion flow via the chloride channels activated by GABA by binding within the ion channel rather than at GABA recognition sites [39]. Picrotoxin may act by preferentially binding to an agonist-bound form of the receptor and reducing the frequency of channel openings [34]. Similarities between the GABA binding region in mammalian $\mathrm { G A B A _ { A } }$ receptors and the putative GABA motif in the ALMT family of anion channels have enabled the use pharmacological agents to dissect and characterise the function of GABA binding site in plants.

In this study, picrotoxin was tested on a near-isogenic line (NIL) of wheat (ET8) that is tolerant to aluminium at low $\mathrm { p H }$ levels [40] as well as on TaALMT1 and ALMT from Vitis vinifera (VvALMT9) expressed in tobacco BY2 cells and Xenopus oocytes, respectively, to assess if it inhibited anion and GABA efflux. The exogenous application of picrotoxin had an inhibitory effect on malate efflux; however, there was no effect on the efflux of GABA mediated by the wheat and grapevine ALMTs. Interestingly, similar results were obtained in the site-directed mutant of TaALMT1, i.e., TaALMTF213C, which is impaired during the GABA-induced regulation of malate transport [4,28]. Continued GABA efflux mediated by ALMTs upon exposure to picrotoxin suggests that ALMTs may exist in two conformational states: one that is permeable to malate and inhibited by picrotoxin, and one that is permeable to GABA and insensitive to picrotoxin.

Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic heavy metal that naturally exists in earth or artificially occurs as a result of the industrial and agricultural activity. Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is an essential nutrient that plays various physiological and biochemical roles in plants. However, an excess of this essential metal ion is also severely toxic to plant growth, which is another kind of contamination. The excessive heavy metal contamination in soil can be a result of various factors, including mining activities, the use of phosphate fertilizers and manures, and the disposal of municipal sewage waste, urban compost and industrial sludge (Das et al. 1997; Benavides et al. 2005; Grata˜o et al. 2005). Heavy metal pollution of farmland is a big problem of crop production and human health. Heavy metal ions can be easily absorbed through roots and can be translocated into the aerial plant part. As a result, agricultural products cultivated in soil contaminated with heavy metals contain toxic metals. Furthermore, differences in the content and distribution of heavy metals have been observed to be dependent on crop species and in cultivars within the same species (Pulford et al. 2003; Chao et al. 2012; Park et al. 2012).

The Arabidopsis Col-0 ecotype has a single base-pair deletion (Thymine) at position 1626 bp of the HMA3 gene when compared to that of the Ws ecotype cDNA, and this results in a frame shift that produces a premature stop codon and a subsequent truncated protein (Gravot et al. 2004; Hussain et al. 2004; Morel et al. 2009). The difference between the AtHMA3 genes observed in two cultivars (Ws and Col-0) affects the ability of metal translocation (Park et al. 2012). In a recent review (Park and Ahn 2014), we presented the proposed model (Fig. S1) for the difference in the activation of the translocation and compartmentation that is dependent on whether HMA3 is working. Specific transporter-related Cd and Zn uptake results in the absorption of these heavy metals into roots in Arabidopsis, and they are sequestered into the vacuole by some transporter such as tonoplast-located HMA3 protein present in Ws ecotype but not in Col-0 ecotype. The translocation capacity of remaining metals outside the vacuole is involved in some transporter activity such as HMA2 and HMA4 (Park et al. 2012). The sequestration into the vacuole via normal HMA3 protein limits Cd and Zn translocation from the root to shoot, thereby partially could decrease the competition between metals in the Ws shoots, whereas less sequestration caused by an HMA3 mutation in the Col-0 may give rise to severe chlorosis and anthocyanin. In addition, genome-wide association studies have determined that HMA3 mutation leads to natural variation in the Cd concentration in the leaf of Arabidopsis varieties, which are widely present in the world. Grafting study suggested that HMA3 functions in the root govern Cd translocation into the shoot (Chao et al. 2012). These results are consistent with the role of OsHMA3 limiting the Cd translocation from the root to the shoot (Ueno et al. 2010; Miyadate et al. 2011). However, the overexpression of AtHMA3 could increase the Cd content in the shoot (Morel et al. 2009).

The focus of this paper is to provide a discussion on the different metal-related phenotype in Col-0 (with the HMA3 mutation) in comparison to those of Ws (having the full copy of HMA3). In addition, to obtain a definite answer for whether the different metal-related phenotype observed between Col-0 and Ws results only from this mutation, we performed a further investigation with HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background and hma3 mutant in Ws background.

In our previous studies of the physiological responses in Arabidopsis Ws and Col-0 ecotypes under Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ stress (Park et al. 2012), we found that Col-0 readily translocates Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ to the shoot but not Ws, thereby inducing an alteration in the phenotype of the leaf color. However, there is no clear evidence of what causes the differences in the tolerance or loading of the heavy metals between Ws and Col-0 due to the non-function of HMA3 or some other factor. In this report, we have demonstrated that the difference in the metal-related phenotype observed between Col-0 and Ws is a result of the mutation of HMA3 in Col-0 by carrying out an investigation with HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background, hma3 mutants in Ws background.

It is necessary to investigate the effect of metal on the growth and fresh weight in a concentration-dependent manner to better understand the physiological response to Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ metal toxicity in Ws-, Col-0-, HMA3 (Ws)- overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background, hma3 mutant. In a manner consistent with the results obtained by Morel et al. (2009), we found that Ws grew better than Col0 when the plants were grown in the presence Cd or Zn. In addition, the Col-0 with functional HMA3 expressed by the full cDNA of AtHMA3 also mitigates the sensitivity to Cd and $Z \mathbf { n }$ . The hma3 mutant in the Ws background showed a Col-0-like phenotype that responded to Cd and Zn excess (Fig. 4). The HMA3-overexpressing lines showed higher expression of HMA3 comparing with col-0; however, lower expression of HMA3 comparing with Ws as shown in Fig. 1c. It can be expected that the root elongation of HMA3-overexpressing lines should be between those of Ws and Col-0 under Cd and Zn stress. But our result was not completely consistent with what we expected. Further study is required to find whether the additional genes involved in heavy metal tolerance in HMA3-overexpressing lines were activated. Nevertheless, the difference in root growth depending on the presence or absence of HMA3 function was clearly shown in this study (Fig. 4).

We also observed that the Cd-treated hma3 mutant along with Col-0 showed more severe chlorosis than the Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background (Fig. 5). The Chlorophyll A and B content in the leaves of HMA3 nonfunctional plants significantly decreased when compared to those of the Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background under Cd stress. These results may indicate a blocking of chlorophyll synthesis at the cellular level by heavy metal (Cd) stress (Stobart et al. 1985), and serious chlorosis in Cd-treated Col-0 and mutant (HMA3 nonfunctional plants) may reflect that the competition between Fe and Cd led to less $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake into the leaf (Fig. S1) and also negatively affected the efficiency of photosynthesis (Alca´ntara et al. 1994). The limited translocation of HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background may partially reduce the competition between Cd and Fe. The data suggest that sequestration, detoxification and/or reduction of the competition among the metals in the shoot of Ws and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background may prevent the harmful effects of the Cd stress. Competition between Fe and Cd has been widely recognized to occur in plants (Siedlecka and Krupa 1999; Sharma et al. 2004; Nakanishi et al. 2006; Shao et al. 2007, 2008; Sa´va´ri et al. 2008; Conte et al. 2011). In particular, Nakanishi et al. (2006) proposed that the Fe-uptake system was activated by Fe deficiency and led to an increased uptake of Cd in rice. Chlorosis as a symptom of heavy metal toxicity occurs together with a decrease in Fe content as the heavy metal concentration in the external medium increases (Wallace and Abou-Zamzam 1989; Ren et al. 1993; Bao et al. 2009; Bernard et al. 2009). Supply of Fe solution to leaves could recover a chlorotic leaf (Chaney 1993). These results indicated that symptoms of chlorosis are related to an induced deficiency in Fe.

The observable production of anthocyanin is one of the characteristic responses of plants to various stresses. Anthocyanin and other polyphenolic compounds (e.g., flavonols and condensed tannins) have a wide range of functions in plants related to UV absorption, pathogen attacks, and nutrient stress (Stewart et al. 2001; Kliebenstein 2004).

Several enzymes for anthocyanin synthesis, such as chalcone synthase, chalcone isomerase, flavone-3- $\cdot \hat { a }$ -hydroxylase $( \mathrm { F } 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { H } )$ , dihydroflavonol-4-reductase, leucoanthocyanidin dioxygenase (LDOX; Takos et al, 2006), are well known. Moreover, UDP-Glc-flavonoid 3-O-glucosyl transferase (UF3GT) and PAP1 (for the production of anthocyanin pigment1, AtMYB7) are specific enzymes for anthocyanin synthesis (Borevitz et al. 2000; Takos et al. 2006). In a previous report, we described the positive relationship between the accumulation of anthocyanin under Zn treatment and the increase in the expression of genes ( $F 3 ^ { \prime } H ,$ , LDOX, UF3GT, and PAP1) in Col-0 (Park et al. 2012). Chlorosis and anthocyanin accumulation were observed only in Col-0 and hma3 mutants (Figs. 3, 5). This observation suggests that the plant could increase the metal-related symptom in the leaf when they exhibited a high root-to-shoot translocation rate if the plant has no function for toxic metal detoxification. The $Z \mathbf { n }$ translocation capacity in the plant was affected less than the Cd translocation rate depending on the presence or absence of HMA3. Since zinc is an essential nutrient, probably other factors seem to replace the role of HMA3.

Plants have evolved several effective mechanisms to tolerate high concentrations of toxic metals. In some plants, this tolerance is accomplished by preventing the uptake of toxic metals into the root cells (excluders). Sequestration into the vacuole has been suggested to be responsible for $Z \mathrm { n }$ tolerance in the shoots of the Zn-hyperaccumulator

Thlaspi caerulescens (Lasat et al. 1996, 1998, 2000). However, some plants are very sensitive to the accumulation of metals in the cell. These plants can be used as phytoindicators to indicate the metal concentration in the surrounding soil (Raskin et al. 1994). For instance, previous study showed a different phenotype under Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ stress between two ecotypes (Ws and Col-0) (Park et al.

2012). In addition, OsHMA3 in rice showed a low translocation of Cd from root to shoot due to vacuolar sequestration (Ueno et al. 2010). Therefore, we were interested in finding the effect of the AtHMA3 point mutation on the ability for heavy metal uptake and translocation in Col-0. As shown in Fig. 6, Col-0 and hma3 mutant plants showed a lesser metal accumulation in the roots under high Cd concentrations, and thereby, the translocation rates of the absorbed Cd from the root to shoot were high when compared to those of Ws- and HMA3 (Ws)-overexpressing lines in the Col-0 background. Although we are not certain of the mechanism for the increase in the translocation in the Col-0 and hma3 mutant, the HMA4 expression level in $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ was induced, but those of Ws tended to decrease compared to the control (Park et al. 2012) and this evidence suggested that the up-regulation of AtHMA4 gene expression in the Col-0 and hma3 mutant due to the non-function of HMA3 may be responsible for delivering toxic metals into the xylem for translocation in the presence of Cd (Park et al. 2012).

In many genetics experiments, complementation is used to verify whether the observed phenotype is affected by the specific gene mutation (Frandsen 2011). Complementation analyses can either be dependent on the endogenous promoter or a heterologous promoter such as constitutive promoters. The latter promoters direct expression in virtually all tissues and are largely, if not entirely, independent of environmental and developmental factors. As their expression is normally not conditioned by endogenous factors, constitutive promoters are usually active across species and even across kingdoms. It is true that both promoters are used in experiments to express additional copies of an endogenous gene or heterologous genes from ectopic loci in the genome (Frandsen 2011). However, complementation experiments occasionally cannot be completely restored the wild-type trait. This case has been attributed to differences in expression patterns resulting from differences in chromatin structure and epigenetic factors between the endogenous locus and the ectopic integration site (Rep et al. 2004). In this study, our complementation analysis using 35S promoter as a constitutive promoter showed that the normal function of HMA3 was restored successfully (although not completely).

In conclusion, we found that the difference in the AtHMA3 genes observed in two cultivars (Ws and Col-0) affects the metal translocation ability and the metal-related phenotype, such as that related to chlorosis and anthocyanin accumulation, and we then clarified these findings by loss-of-function and gain-of-function in Arabidopsis. The results indicate that Col-0 readily translocates Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ to the aerial parts but not Ws, thereby inducing an alteration in the phenotype in leaf color. HMA3 is important for Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ detoxification in Arabidopsis, possibly by the sequestration of Cd and Zn into root vacuoles, and in the control of translocation from root to shoot. Moreover, the mutation of the AtHMA3 gene is likely to be useful with respect to inhibiting the uptake of toxic metals, such as Cd from contaminated land to the plant root, and in enhancing the translocation of essential nutrients.

## 3.1 AtHMA3 controls both cadmium and zinc accumulation in the shoots of A. thaliana natural accessions


Previously, Pita-Barbosa et  al. (2019a, b) considered that Col-0 plants carrying a natural non-functional AtHMA3 allele transformed with a functional AtHMA3 allele from the CSHL-5 accession up-regulated the expression of genes related to Zn homeostatic control. Furthermore, the level of the AtHMA3 transgene was correlated with the expression of the Zn-related genes, demonstrating that plants use such genes to bufer Zn concentration in shoots, implicating AtHMA3 in Zn homeostasis. Here, we performed experiments to verify if this regulatory process is functional in natural accessions of A. thaliana with varying levels of AtHMA3.

We determined the AtHMA3 expression level in roots and the concentration of Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ in shoots of selected A. thaliana natural accessions expressing functional and non-functional/hypofunctional

AtHMA3 copies. It is essential to highlight that the gene expression level of AtHMA3 is not relevant in genotypes with non-functional/hypofunctional copies. On the other hand, expression in those with functional copies might reveal diferences in the transcriptional regulation of Zn homeostasis genes. Comparing all genotypes, CSHL-5 and Touf-1 (functional) showed higher AtHMA3 expression levels, whereas nonfunctional alleles exhibit lower expression than functional ones, except for the functional accession Star-8 (Fig. 1a).

Genotypes with functional AtHMA3 alleles exhibited lower Cd and Zn concentrations in shoots, whereas genotypes with non-functional/hypofunctional AtHMA3 showed higher Cd and Zn concentrations in shoots compared to those with functional copies (Fig. 1b and c). Therefore, we concluded that AtHMA3 is involved in determining shoot Cd and Zn accumulation in the studied natural accessions of A. thaliana, reafrming the efect observed in $A$ . thaliana transgenic plants (Pita-Barbosa et al. 2019a, b) and in natural variations of other species such as rice (Sasaki et al. 2014), Brassica rapa (Zhang et al. 2019) and Sedum plubizincicola (Zhang et al. 2016).

Considering that Zn is an essential micronutrient that can also accumulate and become toxic, its concentrations is fnely tuned in roots and shoots (Ricachenevsky et  al. 2015), in opposition to Cd, a heavy metal with no known biological function (Gallego et  al. 2012). In a previous set of experiments using Col-0 plants complemented with functional copies of AtHMA3 derived from a CSHL-5 accession, we proposed that changes in AtHMA3 function in roots resulted on variations in Cd concentration in shoots, (Pita-Barbosa et al. 2019a, b), possibly due a lack of strict control of Cd concentration We did not fnd alterations in  Zn concentration, suggesting that this element is tightly regulated. However, in the present experiment, Cd concentrations varied similarly to Zn between natural accessions (Fig. 1), suggesting that Cd concentration is at least partially linked to Zn homeostatic control. Moreover, despite the diference in AtHMA3 expression between CSHL5 and the other two functional genotypes (Touf-1 and Star 8), no signifcant diferences were detected between these functional genotypes for Cd and Zn shoot concentration. This suggests a threshold value for AtHMA3 expression, after which the Zn uptake mechanism is upregulated, maintaining Zn under an adequate concentration. Further increases in AtHMA3 expression do not need to be bufered by increased primary uptake.


## $3 . 2 ~ \mathrm { Z n }$ transporters AtZIP3 and AtMTP1 are up-regulated in genotypes with high expression of functional AtHMA3 alleles


We evaluated the expression of fve genes coding for Zn transporters: AtZIP3, AtZIP4, AtMTP1, AtPCR2 and AtZIF1. Regression analyses only including functional genotypes were used to identify correlation between the expression of AtHMA3 and the transcription of each abovementioned gene. While confrming our hypothesis that functional AtHMA3 should afect the transcription levels of Zn-related transporters, as also observed by Pita-Barbosa et  al. (2019a, b), we found signifcant positive correlations between AtHMA3 expression and two important Zn-homeostasis genes: AtZIP3 and AtMTP1. However, no signifcant correlations between AtHMA3 expression and AtZIP4, AtPCR2, and AtZIF1 expression were observed (Fig. 2c–e).

AtZIP3 is predicted to be a Zn-responsive plasma membrane infux transporter predominantly expressed in the roots, which possibly plays a role in the uptake of Zn from the rhizosphere (Grotz et  al. 1998). In agreement with our previous work (PitaBarbosa et  al. 2019a, b), the present work supports the idea that AtZIP3 is induced when cytosolic $Z \mathrm { n }$ is depleted due to high functional AtHMA3 expression in root cells. Curiously, we found no clear physiological function described for AtZIP3. Determining its function in plant physiology would be key to understand the Zn homeostatic control in plants.

AtMTP1 is a Zn vacuolar infux transporter (Fig. 2a and b) and functions similarly to AtHMA3 (Desbrosses-Fonrouge et  al. 2005), probably contributing to “Zn shock” avoidance—the Zn overaccumulation in Zn-limited root cells suddenly resupplied with Zn (MacDiarmid et al. 2003). In silico analysis suggests that AtMTP1 exhibits a high expression in the apical zone of primary roots (Das et  al. 2021), where the Casparian strips are being formed and the apoplastic pathway is open, reducing the selective control of metal ions, and therefore requiring an additional point of control for Zn exclusion. This could explain the redundant function of AtMTP1 and AtHMA3 and the correlation between the expression in these two genes. Therefore, both AtZIP3 and AtMTP1 might be markers of compensatory mechanisms regulating shoot Zn concentration due to increased Zn sinking into root vacuoles.

After identifying the Zn homeostasis genes whose expression levels were afected by the expression of a functional AtHMA3, we performed Pearson’s correlation analysis to fnd other interactions among the studied genes. We found a signifcant correlation in the expression of the following genes: $A t M T P I \times A t Z I P 4$ $( \mathbf { r } = 0 . 5 3 )$ , $A t M T P I \times A t P C R 2$ $( \mathbf { r } = 0 . 6 9 )$ ), $A t M T P I \times A t Z I F I$ $( \mathbf { r } = 0 . 5 2 )$ , $A t Z I F I \times A t P C R 2$ $( \mathbf { r } = 0 . 8 5 )$ (Table 1).

AtZIP4 is a Zn defciency-responsive gene, possibly with a role in transporting Zn from root to shoot and to reproductive tissues (Nishida et al. 2015; Campos et al. 2017; Lee et al. 2021). AtZIP4 was shown to be responsive to local Zn concentration in roots (Sinclair et  al. 2018), suggesting this gene expression might be linked to decreased Zn concentration in root cells due to higher AtHMA3 expression. AtPCR2 is a Zn transporter that has a dual role, acting on both zinc efux from epidermal cells and loading it on the xylem under Zn excess conditions. AtZIF1 is also involved in Zn excess tolerance, with functions towards the partitioning of the Zn-binding molecule nicotianamine, a  metal-chelating molecule, into vacuoles (Haydon et al. 2012).

Except for the correlation between AtMTP1 and AtPCR2, all abovementioned correlations for natural genotypes expressing a functional AtHMA3 were also detected in the transgenic lines, suggesting a conserved strategy for Zn homeostasis in $A$ . thaliana. On the other hand, the lack of correlation between AtHMA3 expression and other tested genes suggests that only a subset of possible transcriptional bufering pathways is present in natural accessions of A. thaliana, therefore, trade-ofs may occur.

We conclude that AtHMA3 has a role in controlling Zn homeostasis in A. thaliana natural genotypes by up-regulating AtZIP3 and AtMTP1. This mechanism is conserved among the studied natural accessions. Zn homeostasis is plastic and other genes may be involved in this process among different genotypes, leading to distinct mechanisms to bufer AtHMA3 expression variation. Changes in the activity of a root-localized vacuolar Zn transporter ensue changes in the expression levels of Zn uptake and detoxifcation genes to maintain Zn concentration in shoots at optimal concentration.

Biofortification of crop plants in $Z \mathrm { n }$ is frequently considered a solution to the problem of low-mineral dietary intake. Molecular approaches to this end include overexpression of metal transport genes to generate plants that more effectively translocate the micronutrient to shoots. The major processes in roots contributing to the regulation of Zn transfer to shoots include (i) in the epidermis and cortex: regulation of metal uptake efficiency; compartmentalization in roots, primarily in vacuoles, which contributes to radial transport, (ii) in the stele: regulation of the efficiency of loading the metal into xylem vessels [1]. Therefore, efforts to biofortify a target species with Zn frequently encompass expression of the metal transporters involved in these processes.

HMA4 (a $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } }$ -ATPase) from A. thaliana and A. halleri participates in $\mathrm { Z n / C d }$ xylem loading, thus in the control of $\mathrm { Z n / C d }$ translocation to shoots [2–7]. High HMA4 expression resulting from tandem triplication is a key element responsible for $Z \mathrm { n } / \mathrm { C d }$ hyperaccumulation in $A$ . halleri [6, 8, 9]. To enhance the efficiency of translocating $Z \mathrm { n }$ to shoots in transformants of non-accumulating species, HMA4 has been expressed either under the constitutive CaMV 35S promoter or under the native promoter from A. halleri [6, 10–13]. Zn root-to-shoot translocation and its concentration in shoots were higher in these transformants than in the wild-type. The rise in the shoot $Z \mathrm { n }$ content depended, however, on the Zn concentration in the medium, thus, the increase did not occur at all tested Zn levels [10–13]. It is thought that the phenomenon of the metal-supply-dependent metal accumulation detected in transgenic plants (which differs from the pattern in the wild-type) results from different transcription profiles (molecular backgrounds) of a given plant species grown at varying metal conditions (low, sufficient, excess), against which the expression of a transgene takes place [14]. The nature of these interactions is very poorly understood.

Overall, this study contributes to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying generation of a transgenic phenotype. The first aim of our research was to identify the metal homeostasis genes in AtHMA4-expressing tomato plants that were differently expressed in selected root tissues compared with wild-type plants and whose expression accompanied Zn supply-dependent changes of $Z \mathrm { n }$ root/shoot distribution. Laser Capture Microdissection (LCM) was used to isolate two root sectors having different functions in the control of metal root-to-shoot translocation, the (i) epidermis $^ +$ cortex and (ii) stele; next, they were used for comparative expression analysis. Moreover, since expression of AtHMA4 in tobacco and tomato leaves leads to development of necrotic areas that begin to form in the palisade parenchyma [15], two leaf sectors, (i) upper epidermis $^ +$ palisade parenchyma and (ii) lower epidermis $^ +$ spongy parenchyma, were also subjected to comparative expression analysis. The aim of the second part of the study was to identify metal-homeostasis pathways modified due to transgene expression accompanying formation of Zn-dependent necrosis in transgenic leaves.

Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic element that can affect mineral homeostasis, photosynthesis, water balance, and nutrient uptake in plants [1–3]. The physiological modifications and the dynamics of Cd accumulation and distribution within plant tissues as well as the function of the main heavy metal transporters involved in Cd uptake, translocation, and detoxification are well-known in poplar plants [4–9].

After the mobilization from soil, Cd uptake within plant tissues is determined by plasma membrane transporters located in root cells. When Cd enters in root tissues, translocation to shoot depends on its mobility within the root symplast, across the endodermal barrier, and further within the xylem. Cd accumulation and storage in leaf cells require its uptake from xylem and apoplast, as well as its phloem loading, to mobilize and allocate it among leaves or other organs (i.e., seeds, fruits) [10]. Several putative metal transporter genes are involved in these processes, such as transporters belonging to: (i) Zinc/Ironregulated transporter-like Proteins (ZIPs), (ii) Natural Resistance and Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs), and (iii) plasma membrane Heavy Metal proton-ATPases (HMAs) [10,11]. Members of NRAMP family are considered general metal ion transporters due to their ability to transport several ions, including Cd [12,13]. These transporters play a crucial role in the response, translocation, and accumulation of Cd [14–16].

On the other hand, Cd long-distance transport toward the shoot is primarily driven by the xylem water flux; when inside the stele, the divalent cation is actively translocated to the xylem vessels through transporters belonging to the HMA family [17,18]. In Populus trichocarpa the HMA isoforms PtHMA1–PtHMA4 belong to the $Z \mathrm { n } / { \mathrm { C o } } / { \mathrm { C d } } / { \mathrm { P b } }$ subgroup while $P t H M A 5 - P t H M A 8$ are members of the $\mathrm { C u / A g }$ subgroup [19]. In several species, the HMA1–4 isoforms are crucial for Cd translocation and accumulation [20–23]. Eren and Argüello [24] demonstrated that in Arabidopsis thaliana, HMA2 is an active pump which drives Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and Cd efflux to the extracellular compartment. Metal compartmentalization in plant cell is essential because free Cd within the cytosol causes phytotoxicity and the activation of specific processes of detoxification [25]. Several ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) transporters have vacuolar localization and, in particular, AtABCC3/6/7 are involved in Cd active storage for protection [26]. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 genes play an important role in metal compartmentalization as well [27], and an increase in transcript levels of ABCC10 was found in Cd-exposed roots of $P .$ trichocarpa and Populus deltoides [28]. Recently, a study found that overexpression of the ABCG36 gene of Populus tomentosa is effective in enhancing Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis plants, indicating the function of this transporter as a heavy metal extrusion pump [29].

Recent studies showed that transmembrane protein transporters play the main role in the inflow and movement of heavy metals (HMs) in plants [1, 2]. Thus, one group of transporters provides for metal ion transport into the cytoplasm from the environment or from intracellular compartments. They include, in particular, representatives of CDF (Cation diffusion facilitator), NRAMP (Natural resistance-associated macrophage protein), and ZIP (Zinc iron permease) families [3–5]. Another group of proteins is involved in HM transport from the cytoplasm through the plasmalemma to conducting vessels or through membranes to the cell organelles. Proteins of HMA (Heavy metal АТFase) family are among them [6, 7].

HMA proteins are related to ATPases of $\mathrm { \bf P } _ { 1 \mathrm { B } }$ -type, and they differ in their localization in the cell and in fulfilled functions [8–10]. For example, HMA2 and HMA3 proteins have similar primary structure, but HMA2 proteins are localized in the plasmalemma and involved in the loading of HM ions, in particular cadmium and zinc, into the conducting vessels and in their transport from the roots to the stems [11], while HMA3 proteins are localized in the tonoplast and transport ions into the vacuole [12].

It should be noted that the majority of studies devoted to HMA proteins and the expression of corresponding genes were performed on plants-hyperaccumulators of HMs, Arabidopsis hallerii and Thlaspi caerulescens [13–15], and they all were focused on the study of the mechanisms of hyperaccumulation and hyperresistance. There are much less studies with plants not belonging to hyperaccumulators, such as those from the family Poaceae, although an increase in the expression of HMA2 and HMA3 genes under the influence of cadmium was detected in these species. Thus, the level of transcripts of these genes increased in the presence of metal in the roots and shoots of wheat [16], rice [7], and barley [17]. At the same time, it was revealed that an increased expression of HMA2 and HMA3 genes in cereals (especially in rice) affected the metal transport from the roots to the stems and respectively the concentration of cadmium in the seeds [7, 18].

The data presented above show the importance of studying the role of HMA family transporters and corresponding genes in the transport of cadmium ions in plants and in the mechanisms of plant metal tolerance. However, despite the obvious progress in this area, there are still a number of unanswered questions, such as a possible contribution of HMA2 and HMA3 genes to an increase in plant tolerance to cadmium, as well as the impact of plant age on the expression of these genes. Although, for example, when studying the action of cadmium ions on plants, it is known that there are pronounced age differences in the content of $H \nu P C S$ gene transcripts involved in the synthesis of phytochelatin synthase in barley roots [19] and those of genes encoding protein transporters belonging to ZIP and CDF families in $T .$ . caerulescens [14].

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is essential to plants. A large portion of the proteome binds $Z \mathbf { n }$ as a structural component or co-factor, including enzymes and transcription factors (Andreini et  al. 2006). Therefore, $Z \mathbf { n }$ defciency can decrease growth and productivity, which poses a problem for agriculture considering that soils with low $Z \mathbf { n }$ concentrations are widespread (Alloway 2004). On the other hand, excessive Zn uptake by plants can lead to toxicity, reducing photosynthesis and causing oxidative stress (Kaur and Garg 2021). Heavy metal ATPase 3 (HMA3) is a vacuolar transporter that, when overexpressed in A. thaliana, promotes tolerance to cadmium (Cd), Zn, and other divalent cations (Morel et al. 2009). Its physiological role as a Zn transporter was frst proposed by Becher et  al. (2004) for the Zn hyperaccumulator in Arabidopsis halleri. In  rice plants overexpressing a functional allele of OsHMA3 no change in Zn concentrations was detected in shoots; however, the expression of several ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter/Ironregulated transporter-like Protein) transporters was increased  in roots. This evidence suggests the existence of compensatory mechanisms for maintaining Zn concentration in shoots when OsHMA3 transports Zn into root vacuoles (Sasaki et  al. 2014; Cai et  al. 2019). Furthermore, it is well known that elements that are part of the ionome cooperate within crosstalk mechanisms (Pita-Barbosa et  al. 2019b), which deserves careful attention to optimize plant nutrition.

Conclusive evidence for the role of HMA3 in Zn sinking into root vacuoles was only recently provided using A. thaliana Col-0 accessions, which have a nonfunctional allele of AtHMA3, complemented with a functional AtHMA3 allele from a CSHL-5 accession. Transgenic A. thaliana plants expressing AtHMA3 were used to show that expression levels of functional AtHMA3 are correlated with the expression of genes controlling Zn homeostasis, providing direct evidence that changes in Zn accumulation in root vacuoles lead to the bufering of Zn homeostasis in shoots (PitaBarbosa et al. 2019a, b). Natural variations have been explored to identify distinct responses within A. thaliana diversity and  in many  crops (Chao et  al. 2012). However, it is not clear whether natural AtHMA3 expression variations are also bufered by changes in Zn transporters in A. thaliana. In this study, we demonstrate that natural accessions of A. thaliana bufer Zn homeostasis to accommodate AtHMA3 expression variation and maintain $Z \mathrm { n }$ at optimal concentrations.
