Cadmium (Cd) contamination poses a signifcant threat to agriculture and human health due to its high soil mobility and toxicity. This review synthesizes current knowledge on Cd uptake, transport, detoxifcation, and transcriptional regulation in plants, emphasizing the roles of metal transport proteins and transcription factors (TFs). We explore transporter families like NRAMP, HMA, ZIP, ABC, and YSL in facilitating Cd movement within plant tissues, identifying potential targets for reducing Cd accumulation in crops. Additionally, regulatory TF families, including WRKY, MYB, bHLH, and ERF, are highlighted for their roles in modulating gene expression to counteract Cd toxicity. This review consolidates the existing literature on plant–Cd interactions, providing insights into established mechanisms and identifying gaps for future research. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for developing strategies to enhance plant tolerance, ensure food safety, and promote sustainable agriculture amidst increasing heavy-metal pollution.

Keywords Cadmium $\cdot$ Metal transporter $\cdot$ Transcription factor $\cdot$ Transcriptional regulation $\cdot$ Plant

As the development of the global economy has progressed, industrialization has developed rapidly. However, one of the negative effects of industrialization is heavy metal pollution. Heavy metal pollution can affect human health via food chains, as heavy metals can pollute water and soil resources. One of the mechanisms of heavy metal toxicity involves irreversible in vivo protein structural changes, and as a result, the function of those proteins is lost or reduced. Heavy metals can lower the activity of enzymes in cells and subsequently affect the function of essential ion carrier proteins (Williams and Mills 2005). For example, cadmium (Cd) preferentially combines with protein molecules that contain hydroxyl, amino, and sulfonyl groups; as such, Cd inhibits many enzyme systems, subsequently affecting the normal function of the organs such as the liver and kidneys (Choppala et al. 2014; Waalkes 2000). Phytoremediation can be an efficient and environmental friendly solution for heavy metal-contaminated soils (Qiu et al. 2004). The mechanisms of plant resistance to heavy metal toxicity is currently being studied. During the complicated heavy metal toxicity resistance mechanisms, membrane transporters have been found to play an important role in the uptake and transport of micronutrients and/or heavy metal cations. At present, many gene families whose members function in metal transport have been discovered and studied (Williams and Mills 2005).

P-type ATPases are heavy metal transporters that exhibit strong affinity for absorbing and pumping heavy metals into plant cells. $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } }$ -type ATPases, which are also known as heavy metal ATPases (HMAs), constitute a subfamily of P-type ATPases. In addition, by hydrolyzing ATP, HMA transporters output mostly metal cations (Argüello 2003; Axelsen and Palmgren 2001; Morel et al. 2009; Palmgren 1999). During the process of plant growth, HMA transporters can selectively uptake and transport not only metal ions such as $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ but also nonessential ions such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ . The function of $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } }$ -type ATPases occurs at a specific site that constitutes the heavy metal-binding domain. Both the N-terminal and C-terminal regions of this specific site contain metal-binding domains that can bind and interact with specific metal ions, such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ (Argüello et al. 2007; Williams and Mills 2005). $\mathrm { P _ { 1 B } }$ -type ATPases also contain a soluble nucleotidebinding domain, phosphorylation domain, and soluble actuator domain. The interactions of these three domains plays an important role in regulating the uptake and transportation of metal ions (Smith et al. 2014).

With respect to their substrate specificity, HMAs can be divided into two phylogenetic subclasses, namely, a $\mathrm { C u / A g }$ subgroup and a $Z n / C o / C \mathrm { d } / \mathrm { P b }$ subgroup. HMAs have been studied at the genomic scale in both Arabidopsis and rice. There are eight members of Arabidopsis HMAs (AtHMAs) and nine members of rice HMAs (OsHMAs). AtHMA1–4 and OsHMA1–3 belong to the $\mathrm { C u / A g }$ subgroup, and AtHMA5–8 and OsHMA4– 9 belong to the $Z _ { \mathrm { n } } / C _ { 0 } / C _ { \mathrm { d } } / \mathrm { P b }$ subgroup (Williams and Mills 2005). AtHMA3 can phenotypically complement the ${ \mathrm { C d } } / { \mathrm { p } } { \mathrm { b } }$ -hypersensitive strain ycf1 but not the Znhypersensitive strain zrc1. Overexpression of AtHMA3 improves plant tolerance to Cd, Co, Pb, and Zn. Compared with wild-type plants, plants overexpressing AtHMA3 exhibited a 2–3-fold increase in Cd accumulation (Morel et al. 2009). HMA4 in Arabidopsis halleri encodes a $Z \mathrm { n } / \mathrm { C d }$ pump that transports metals from the roots to the shoots, and HMA4 has been confirmed to be a genetic determinant for $Z \mathrm { n } / \mathrm { C d }$ tolerance and accumulation (Hanikenne et al. 2008). However, expression of AtHMA4 in tobacco causes a slight decrease in Cd accumulation (Siemianowski et al. 2014). The heterologous expression of OsHMA2 in yeast demonstrated influx-type transport activity for Zn and Cd (Yamaji et al. 2013). In addition, OsHMA5 is involved in $\mathrm { C u }$ loading into the xylem of roots in rice. OsHMA5 expression is specifically up-regulated by excess Cu and not by other metals, such as Zn, Fe, and Mn. The expression of OsHMA5 in a $\mathrm { C u }$ transport-defective mutant yeast strain was shown to restore growth (Deng et al. 2013). The expression of OsHMA9 is induced by high concentrations of Cu, Zn, and Cd and occurs mostly in the vascular bundles and anthers (Lee et al. 2007). In addition, HMA members have been identified in other plant species, including barley and wheat (Deng et al. 2013).

Brassica napus (B. napus) is tolerant to and accumulates Cd. As such, B. napus can potentially be used to remediate heavy metal pollution without compromising the original economic value of the crop (Mwamba et al. 2016; Selvam and Wong 2009). Therefore, the mechanism of Cd transport in $B$ . napus should be studied, and the Cd uptake- and metabolism-related transporter genes in $B _ { \cdot }$ . napus should be identified. Understanding the mechanism and identifying its related genes are highly important for the cultivation of practical Cd-accumulating B. napus crops, which is beneficial for remediating soil pollution. As such, we studied the expression of the Cdrelated homologous genes of $B$ . napus plants under different concentrations of Cd stress and performed a bioinformatic analysis combined with transcriptomic data sequencing. Our results showed that the key functional gene of the $B$ . napus response to Cd stress may be BnHMA2. As a result, a genome-wide analysis of the $B$ . napus HMA gene family was carried out. The results provide insight into the roles of HMA2 in $B .$ . napus in response to Cd stress.

Numerous members of the NPF family are able to transport hormones. In the present study, using a modified yeast Y2H system with a receptor complex for GA or direct transport assays in yeast expressing NPF3.1, we showed that NPF3.1 promoted the transport of $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ , and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ . These results confirmed the previous results obtained with the yeast expression system (Chiba et al. 2015) or with the Xenopus oocyte expression system and fluorescent-labeled GA uptake in planta (Tal et al. 2016). We also described NPF3.1 transport activity for two non-bioactive forms $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 9 } }$ (a precursor of $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ ) and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 8 }$ (a deactivated form of $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ ), while $\mathrm { G A } _ { 2 0 }$ was also transported by NPF3.1 using the Xenopus oocyte system (Tal et al. 2016). These results indicate that NPF3.1 transports preferentially $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ -related forms, especially the precursor $\mathrm { G A } _ { 1 9 }$ , then $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 8 }$ in addition to $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ the active endogenous in Arabidopsis. NPF3.1 has also been described as a low-affinity nitrate/ nitrite transporter using electrophysiological studies in Xenopus oocytes (Pike et al. 2014). A dual transport of nitrate and hormone has been demonstrated for NPF6.3 (NRT1.1), which transports nitrate and auxin (Krouk et al. 2010), NPF4.6 (NRT1.2), a nitrate/abscisic acid transporter (Kanno et al. 2012), and NPF2.10, a multifunctional transporter able to transport nitrate and hormones, such as jasmonoyl-isoleucine and GAs (Saito et al. 2015). While the auxin transport capacity of NPF6.3 is only active at low-nitrate concentrations $( 0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ , nitrate does not compete with abscisic acid transport of NPF4.6 (Kanno et al. 2013). In the case of NPF3.1, we did not observe any influence of a large range of nitrate concentration (up to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate) on the GA uptake capacity in yeast experiments, indicating that nitrate has no effect on the GA-dependent AD-GAI/BD-GID1a interactions in the 2YH system. Accordingly, no GA/nitrate competition has been observed with $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate using the heterologous system Xenopus oocytes (Tal et al. 2016). However, using various heterologous systems might not depict the in planta physiological context, where transporters are potentially subjected to several types of post-transcriptional regulations. To evidence the in planta role of NPF3.1 in GA transport, we pursued studies with loss of function npf3.1 mutants.


## NPF3.1 is a GA transporter involved in hypocotyl elongation under low-nitrogen supply and in seed germination


In this study, the in planta function of NPF3.1 in the GA transport and in the regulation of growth and development was revealed using two allelic npf3.1 mutants. Considering that NPF3.1 is expressed mainly in the endodermis of shoot, hypocotyl and root, or in dry seeds of mature siliques, we performed hypocotyl elongation measurements and germination assays.

Interestingly, we observed a conditional hypocotyl elongation phenotype under low-nitrate supply. The hypocotyl elongation limited by a low-nitrate supply $( 0 . 2 5 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ was not restored by exogenous $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ in the npf3.1 mutants in the light. Consistently, the paclobutrazol inhibition of the hypocotyl elongation was less restored by $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ in npf3.1 mutants grown in low-nitrate conditions and in darkness. The expression level of $N P F 3 . I$ was lower in darkness which might explain the tenuous phenotype observed in this condition. Given that a higher level of NPF3.1 expression was observed also for seedlings grown under limiting nitrate supply, these results support the hypothesis of a role in planta for NPF3.1 in GA. The lack of a phenotype for npf3.1 mutants recently described by Tal et al. (2016) for this trait might be explained by the use of a standard Arabidopsis growth medium containing high, non-limiting levels of nitrate and ammonium $( 2 0 \mathrm { \ m M \ N } )$ and a medium with indeed lower N content ( $\mathrm { 1 0 ~ m M }$ nitrate), but probably not limiting for growth.

Our results highlighted a role for GA transport mediated by NPF3.1 in growth adaptation to low-nitrate supply. Molecular events connecting GA and hypocotyl elongation have been reviewed in Claeys et al. (2014). Several transcription factors involved in the regulation of expansionpromoting genes and auxin transport are regulated transcriptionally by GA. Auxin regulated hypocotyl elongation through the activation of a plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase (Takahashi et al. 2012). A cross-talk between GA, auxin, and nitrate signaling needs to be considered in the future, since low nitrate regulates auxin synthesis and transport (Krouk 2016). Evidence of hormone-signaling events (auxin, cytokinin, ABA) in response to environmental constraints and especially nitrate limitation is increasing (Krouk 2016). N availability has a great impact on growth and development, and plant adaptation to $_ \mathrm { N }$ limitation implies the integration of numerous signaling pathways at the molecular, metabolic, and physiological levels.

In the same manner, in germination assay with paclobutrazol-treated seeds, we observed a clear phenotype linked to GA transport in npf3.1 mutants. The germination of paclobutrazol-treated seeds was less efficiently restored in the presence of exogenous $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ or $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ . Moreover, exogenous nitrate addition ( $\mathbf { \Omega } ^ { \mathrm { ~ ( 1 ~ m M ) ~ } }$ ) leads to an increase in germination rate for all genotypes, according to the signaling role of nitrate in the control hormonal balance between GA and ABA (Matakiadis et al. 2009). Nitrate induces ABA degradation, and GA levels are negatively regulated by ABA and conversely GA negatively regulates ABA level (Seo et al. 2006; Oh et al. 2007). The phenotype of npf3.1 mutants was maintained in the presence of $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ exogenous nitrate, supporting a defect in GA but not in nitrate transport in the mutants. Publicly available transcriptomic data in Arabidopsis eFPbrowser (http://bar.utor onto.ca/efp/cgi-bin/efpWeb.cgi) show a high level of expression in dry seeds followed by a decrease in NPF3.1 expression level after $1 { - } 2 4 ~ \mathrm { h }$ of water imbibitions (Nakabayashi et al. 2005) (Fig. S5). Thus, NPF3.1 is probably present in dry seed even before the synthesis of GA induced by imbibition and nitrate signaling. In germination assay performed by Tal et al. (2016), npf3.1 mutants do not present any phenotype, but the nitrate level in this medium was high $0 . 5 \times$ Murashige-Skoog) compared to our conditions and endogenous GA synthesis was not inhibited by paclobutrazol.

Otherwise, the GUS pattern that we observed in stamen could suggest a role of NPF3.1 in floral tissue development. The GID receptors are also expressed in stamen and siliques (Gallego-Giraldo et al. 2014), and mutants of GA biosynthesis enzymes, GID1 receptor, and DELLA proteins exhibit shorter stamens (Griffiths et al. 2006; Plackett et al. 2011, 2014). However, the absence of any marked stamen phenotype in the npf3.1 mutants might be due to a functional redundancy with NPF2.10 that has been clearly described as the physiological active GA transporter in stamen, and involved in fertility (Saito et al. 2015). It would be interesting to generate and analyze the phenotypes of multiple mutants defective in several GA transporters.

Gibberellins are also involved in responses to abiotic stresses, such as drought or high salinity (reviewed by Colebrook et al. 2014), and it would be interesting to investigate the phenotype for npf3.1 mutants under these conditions. Moreover, GA antagonizes JA signaling but synergizes SA signaling in biotic stress responses (see review Pieterse et al. 2012), and DELLA has been identified in the control of plant immune response (Navarro et al. 2008). The GA transport activity of NPF3.1 might allow a new interpretation of the role of this transporter in the plant pathogen response, as described by Pike et al. (2014).


## There is no evidence for an NPF3.1 nitrate transport activity in planta


Pike et al. (2014) demonstrated that NPF3.1 is a lowaffinity nitrate/nitrite transporter which is active in the range of $1 { - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate in Xenopus oocytes. Since our GUS staining experiments showed an endodermal localization in vascular tissue of roots and shoots, the in planta nitrate transport activity of NPF3.1 was assessed. In our growth conditions with nitrate supply ranging from 0.25 to $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ , no clear differences in nitrate content were observed in mutants. Furthermore, our measurements of net nitrate uptake using $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ methodology did not support a direct role of NPF3.1 in root nitrate uptake (either HATS or LATS) from the outer medium. Although it is still difficult to link the 3D structure to the substrate specificity of NPF, the nitrate binding site of NPF6.3 has been recently revealed, using crystallography studies (Parker and Newstead 2014; Sun et al. 2014). Notably, His 356 has been suggested as a crucial residue for the nitrate binding capacity. Other residues might be important for the nitrate transport activity, notably Phe 571 in association with His 356, but these amino acids are no longer present in other NPF6.3 orthologues as well as in NPF3.1, while the nitrate transport activity has been maintained in several NPF6.3 orthologues. Our results suggested that NPF3.1 was likely not involved in nitrate transport activity in planta at least under the conditions tested. However, several post-transcriptional or post-translational regulations might interfere and mask the nitrate transport activity of NPF3.1 in planta, and we could not reject definitively the hypothesis of a nitrate transport capacity for NPF3.1, especially under other environmental or developmental conditions.

In the conclusion, these results provide that the evidence of the in planta activity of NPF3.1 in GA-mediated phenotypes is modulated by nitrate availability, in relationship with its transcriptional expression. It would be interesting to measure the effect of nitrate supply on endogenous GA levels to better decipher the interaction between nitrate and GA effects on growth. Using public transcriptomic data, a threefold increased of GA3ox1 , the $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ biosynthesis enzymes were observed by $^ { 1 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of nitrate resupply after 10 days of $\mathbf { N }$ deprivation (Krapp et al. 2011, htttp:// urgv.evry.inra.fr/CATdb). In further studies, it will be relevant to focus on the connection between GA and nitrate signaling. Some cross-talk between nitrate and hormone signaling has already been revealed with transcriptomic approaches (Gutie´rrez et al. 2007; Krouk et al. 2010; Vidal et al. 2010) and for the root nitrate uptake mechanism (Ruffel et al. 2014). Currently, nothing is known concerning the interactions between GAs and nitrate signaling pathways, and all these results open the way for future investigations.

NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (NRT1/PTR) homologous proteins are a group of membrane transport proteins present in all major living kingdoms [1–5]. Generally, 12 transmembrane domain (TM) proteins have a conserved structural arrangement connected by short peptide loops, including a large hydrophilic loop between the sixth and seventh TM [5]. In previous studies, homologous proteins were conventionally named according to their first identified substrates, such as NRT (a nitrate transporter), PTR (a peptide transporter), and others [1, 6]. Thereafter, additional substrates of NRT1/PTR homologs were characterized in plants; thus, they were recently and uniformly named as members of the NRT1/PTR family (NPF) [7].

Since AtNPF6.3/AtNRT1.1/CHL1 is characterized as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis [6, 8, 9], many of its homologs are cloned and functionally characterized in many plant species with multisubstrate transporting capacity. To date, the most well known roles of plant NPF genes (NPFs) include low- and/or high-affinity nitrate transportation. For example, Arabidopsis AtNPF1.1/NRT1.11 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.12 proteins are low-affinity nitrate transporters involved in redistributing nitrate into developing leaves [10], while Zea mays (maize) ZmNPF6.6 is a high-affinity nitrate transporter that can rapidly respond to exogenous nitrate supply [11]. Meanwhile, NPF proteins (NPFs) also behave as nitrite transporters, e.g., Arabidopsis AtNPF3.1/Nitr and Vitis vinifera VvNPF3.2 [12]. Additionally, NPFs are key transporters for many other substrates, especially hormones and peptides. For example, AtNPF8.1/PTR1 [13, 14], AtNPF8.2/ PTR5 [14], and AtNPF8.3/PTR2 [15, 16] are di−/tri-peptide transporters that can mediate the process of flowering, as well as seed and root development; AtNPF4.6/ AIT1 transports abscisic acid (ABA) to regulate stomatal aperture [17, 18]; and AtNPF6.3 represses lateral root growth during low nitrate availability by promoting basipetal auxin (IAA) transport [19]. Moreover, members of NPF have been demonstrated to transport secondary metabolites; AtNPF2.10/GTR1 and AtNPF2.11/GTR2 are key transporters for glucosinolate (GLS) [20]. Additionally, a few NPFs display chloride or potassium transport activity: AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5 mediate chloride efflux activity [21, 22], while AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 regulates pH-dependent $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux activity [23].

Brassica napus is a significant source of human-edible vegetable oil and animal protein feed; thus, it is an essential oil crop, extensively cultivated in Asia, North America, and Europe. Given essential roles in plant nitrate, di−/tripeptide, hormone, potassium, chloride, and secondary metabolite transports, NPFs have been systematically identified and analyzed in many species, including Arabidopsis [20], Oryza sativa (rice) [24], Triticum aestivum (wheat) [25], and Malus domestica (apple) [26] at the genome-wide level. Identifying and analyzing this gene family in the B. napus genome will provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential roles in transporting nitrate, hormones, and GLS, among others.

This study identified NPFs in the B. napus genome, accompanied by comprehensive analysis of their gene and protein structural features, chromosomal location, classification, promoter regulation network, and genomic duplication mechanism. Further, we performed systematic expression profile analysis of this gene family in diverse tissues across different developmental stages in Arabidopsis (79 tissues) and $B$ . napus (50 tissues). Additionally, expression patterns of NPF gene family in $B$ napus under five exogenous hormone inductions (IAA, auxin; ABA, abscisic acid; $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 } ,$ , gibberellic acid; 6-BA, cytokinin; and ACC, ethylene) were assessed, based on the RNA-Seq dataset. Moreover, expression patterns of 12 candidate NPFs of the NPF2–1 subfamily in one high- and one low-GLS B. napus variety, as well as their expression profiles under hormone induction, were assessed using qRT-PCR. Our study provides an abundant gene resource for further functional analysis of NPFs in B. napus.

To date, a wide range of NPF family substrates have been characterized in plants, including nitrate/nitrite [6], di/tri-peptides [13, 14], hormones (such as IAA, ABA, GA, MeJA, etc.) [18], chloride [21, 22], potassium [23], and secondary metabolites [20, 49], demonstrating their diverse roles in plants. Previously, the plant NPFs were well known for their important roles in nitrate/nitrite transportation (Table 1). Accordingly, up to 10 of the 11 subfamilies of this gene family (NPF1, NPF2–1, NPF2–2, NPF3, NPF4, NPF5–1, NPF5–2, NPF6–1, NPF7, and NPF8) had been shown to be involved in nitrate transport in plants. Moreover, the majority of functionally characterized NPFs in these 10 subfamilies were lowaffinity nitrate transporters, while a few members of the NPF1 and NPF6–1 subfamilies acted as high-affinity nitrate transporters, such as AtNPF6.3 and its homolog in Medicago truncatula (MtNPF6.8) [6, 11, 13, 69–71]. NPFs were identified as important transporters for hormones as well, with eight subfamilies (NPF1, NPF2–1, NPF2–2, NPF3, NPF4, NPF5–1, NPF6–1, and NPF8) associated with hormone transportation (Fig. 1 and Table 1). Among them, members of the NPF1, NPF2–2, NPF3, NPF4, and NPF5–1 subfamilies have a relatively wider range of substrates and are commonly involved in GA, ABA, and MeJA transports; for example, AtNPF4.1/AIT3 in the NPF4 subfamily can transport ABA, $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 / 3 / 4 / 8 / 2 0 } } ,$ and MeJA [17, 18, 50, 55]. Members of the NPF2–1 subfamily, such as AtNPF2.10, were reported to transport two substrates (GA and MeJA) [18, 54]. On the contrary, members of each of the NPF6–1 and NPF8 subfamilies transport only one kind of hormone: AtNPF6.3 (NRT1.1/CHL1) of the NPF6–1 subfamily is involved in IAA transport [19], while AtNPF8.1 of the NPF8 subfamily is related to MeJA transport [18]. Additionally, NPFs can transport many other substrates, including di−/tri-peptides, chloride, potassium, and secondary metabolites. For instance, AtNPF5.2/PTR3 of the NPF5–1 subfamily, and AtNPF8.1, AtNPF8.2, and AtNPF8.3 of the NPF8 subfamily showed specific dipeptide transport activity [13–16, 60]. In terms of chloride transport, AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5 of the NPF2–2 subfamily mediate chloride efflux activity [21, 22]. Regarding potassium transport, AtNPF7.3 displayed pH-dependent $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux activity and mediated a proton-coupled $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ loading into the xylem [23]. Recently, these gene family members were shown to be involved in secondary metabolite transport [20, 49]. For instance, five NPF2–1 subfamily members (AtNPF2.10, AtNPF2.11, AtNPF2.9, AtNPF2.14, and AtNPF2.13/

NRT1.7) were shown to be the key transporters for GLS [20, 37]. Similarly, an NPF from the same subfamily in Catbarantbus roseus, CrNPF2.9, can transport monoterpene indole alkaloids [49]. Overall, NPFs have diverse substrates in plants, especially for nitrate and multiple hormone transportation.

Notably, NPFs in most subfamilies can generally transport more than one type of substrate (Table 1). For example, NPF2–1 subfamily members can transport four types of substrates: nitrate, GLS, GA, and MeJA (Fig. 1 and Table 1); in Arabidopsis, AtNPF6.3 of the NPF6–1 subfamily transports nitrate as well as auxin [19]. Moreover, many studies have found that the role of NPFs in transporting diverse substrates generally demonstrates hormone-mediated characteristics. For example, AtNPF6.3 of the NPF6–1 subfamily was highly induced by IAA treatment under low nitrogen conditions [72]. AtNPF2.4 was repressed by ABA treatment and then played a role in chlorine transport [21]. AtNPF2.10 was upregulated by MeJA treatment, which then accelerated the transport of gibberellin [54]. AtNPF3.1 was upregulated by ABA to promote the transport of gibberellin [55]. AtNPF5.2 was regulated by SA, MeJA, and ABA treatments against biotic and abiotic stresses [60]. In this study, many CREs involved in hormone responses, such as SA- (103/199 genes), ABA- (93/199 genes), and MeJA-responsive CRE (123/199 genes), were found in a series of BnaNPF promoters (Fig. 2), suggesting their potential hormone-inducing characteristics. Accordingly, the expression of $3 2 . 6 6 \%$ of the BnaNPFs (65/199 genes) were regulated by one or more types of hormone inductions (ABA, IAA, 6-BA, $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ , and ACC) (Fig. 5). Consistent with previous work [72], NPF6–1 subfamily proteins in $B .$ . napus (e.g., BnaNPF6.5, BnaNPF6.7, and BnaNPF6.7) were also highly induced by IAA in our study. Additionally, we revealed that the genes involved in GLS transport are induced by IAA, $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 } ,$ , and 6-BA treatments (Fig. 6). Together, these results support the hypothesis that hormones have an essential role in substrate transport by NPFs.

Given that the role of NPFs in transporting many substrates is crucial for plant development and stress response, genome-wide analyses of the NPF gene family have been performed in many plant species. However, the classification of this gene family is not yet uniform. For example, this gene family was divided into 10 supergroups and 32 groups (subfamilies) based on phylogenetic analysis of 20 plant genomes [73]. In contrast, other research divided this gene family into 8 subfamilies (NPF1-NPF8) based on similar analysis in 33 plant genomes (including Physcomitrella patens and Selaginella moellendorffii) [7]. Subsequent studies generally followed the criteria of the latter division [25, 26, 74]. Recently, in apple, the NPF2 subfamily was further divided into two groups (subfamilies) [26], implying a new classification trend. In this study, we found that three of the eight previously demonstrated subfamilies (NPF2, NPF5, and NPF6) [7] should be divided into two subfamilies with high bootstrap values: NPF2–1/NPF2–2, NPF5–1/NPF5–2, and NPF6–1/ NPF6–2, respectively (Fig. 1). To confirm this result, we further expanded our dataset to include NPFs from O. sativa, Populus trichocarpa, Z. mays, B. rapa, B. oleracea, and Glycine max (Additional file 2: Table S2). Phylogenetic analysis of the NPFs from these different species highly supported that of BnaNPFs (Additional file 15: Figure S7). Moreover, the gene and protein structures (Additional file 4: Figure S2, Additional file 5: Figure S3, and Additional file 6: Figure S4) and expression patterns (Figs. 4 and 5) of BnaNPFs in each subfamily supported our classification, as well. Interestingly, all the NPFs involved in secondary metabolite transport known to date belong to the NPF2–1 subfamily (Table 1). We confirmed that 267 proteins belonging to this subfamily exist in 31 angiosperms, though not in the lower plants $P .$ . patens and S. moellendorffii [7] (Additional file 16: Table S9). Given that currently known members of the NPF2–1 subfamily across different plant species, including lower plants (Table 1), are mainly involved in nitrate transport, we speculated that the secondary metabolite transport feature of this subfamily was newly evolved in a given lineage or species in angiosperms during their evolution, indicating the specific subfunctionalization trend of this gene family.
