Background: Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporters, which exist widely in plants, function as crucial regulators in plant resistance to aluminum (Al) toxicity by inducing citrate efflux. However, the functions of most MATE family members in soybean (Glycine soja) remain to be elucidated.

Results: Expression pattern analysis showed that GsMATE was constitutively expressed in different soybean organs, with the highest level in root compared with those in stem, leaf and cotyledon. In addition, Al stress induced expression of GsMATE in soybean. Temporal analysis indicated that GsMATE expression was greatly enhanced by increasing concentrations of aluminum $[ \mathsf { A } | ^ { 3 + } ]$ after short exposure, reaching the high levels detected in the BW69 (Al-resistant) and the JW81 (Al-sensitive) lines of Glycine soja of wild soybean at 6 h and $8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ respectively. Furthermore, transient GsMATE expression in Arabidopsis protoplasts showed that GsMATE protein localized to the plasma membrane. Overexpression of GsMATE on an Arabidopsis columbia-0 (Col-0) background resulted in increased Al tolerance in transgenic plants. Analysis of hematoxylin staining showed that the roots of GsMATE transgenic lines were stained less intensely than those of the wild-type exposured to the same $\mathsf { A l C l } _ { 3 }$ concentrations. Therefore, GsMATE enhanced the resistance of transgenic plants to Al toxicity by reducing Al accumulation in Arabidopsis roots.

Conclusions: In summary, our results indicate that GsMATE is responsive to aluminum stress and may participate in the regulation of sensitivity to Al toxicity in Arabidopsis. In addition, the GsMATE protein is an Al-induced citrate transporter of the MATE family and exerts an essential role in Al tolerance in Glycine soja.

Keywords: GsMATE, Al tolerance, Glycine soja, Arabidopsis thaliana

Background: Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family is an important group of the multidrug efflux transporters that extrude organic compounds, transporting a broad range of substrates such as organic acids, plant hormones and secondary metabolites. However, genome-wide analysis of MATE family in plant species is limited and no such studies have been reported in soybean.

Results: A total of 117 genes encoding MATE transporters were identified from the whole genome sequence of soybean (Glycine max), which were denominated as GmMATE1 - GmMATE117. These 117 GmMATE genes were unevenly localized on soybean chromosomes 1 to 20, with both tandem and segmental duplication events detected, and most genes showed tissue-specific expression patterns. Soybean MATE family could be classified into four subfamilies comprising ten smaller subgroups, with diverse potential functions such as transport and accumulation of flavonoids or alkaloids, extrusion of plant-derived or xenobiotic compounds, regulation of disease resistance, and response to abiotic stresses. Eight soybean MATE transporters clustered together with the previously reported MATE proteins related to aluminum (Al) detoxification and iron translocation were further analyzed. Seven stress-responsive cis-elements such as ABRE, ARE, HSE, LTR, MBS, as well as a cis-element of ART1 (Al resistance transcription factor 1), GGNVS, were identified in the upstream region of these eight GmMATE genes. Differential gene expression analysis of these eight GmMATE genes in response to Al stress helps us identify GmMATE75 as the candidate gene for Al tolerance in soybean, whose relative transcript abundance increased at 6, 12 and $2 4 ~ \mathrm { h }$ after Al treatment, with more fold changes in Al-tolerant than Al-sensitive cultivar, which is consistent with previously reported Al-tolerance related MATE genes.

Conclusions: A total of 117 MATE transporters were identified in soybean and their potential functions were proposed by phylogenetic analysis with known plant MATE transporters. The cis-elements and expression patterns of eight soybean MATE genes related to Al detoxification/iron translocation were analyzed, and GmMATE75 was identified as a candidate gene for Al tolerance in soybean. This study provides a first insight on soybean MATE family and their potential roles in soybean response to abiotic stresses especially Al toxicity.

Keywords: Abiotic stress, Aluminum toxicity, cis-element, Duplication, Expression analysis, MATE, Phylogenetic analysis, Soybean

Aluminum (Al) toxicity is a major agronomic problem on acidic soil, which comprise $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ of arable soils in the world (Vonuexkull and Mutert 1995). Increasing solubility of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ at low pH $\mathrm { ( p H } < 5 . 5 ) $ in acidic soil inhibits the plant root growth and function, which results in a serious loss of crop yields (Kochian et al. 2004; Delhaize et al. 2007). In plants, Al exclusion and internal tolerance are two main physiological mechanisms to tolerate Al toxicity (Kochian et al. 2004). Some membrane transporters, which either decrease Al concentrations in cytosol or transport compounds, such as organic acids, are the main contributors in exclusion mechanism. Recently, some genes from MATE gene family were identified that encode the transport proteins involved in Al activated citrate release to tolerate Al toxicity in several species (Liu et al. 2009; Maron et al. 2013; Sivaguru et al. 2013).

As a group of secondary active transporters, the MATE gene family consists of multiple genes that widely exist in bacteria, fungi, mammals and plants (Omote et al. 2006). The MATE gene was first reported in Vibrio parahaemolyticus named norM in 1998, which could export several $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ coupled antibacterial agents across the membrane (Morita et al. 1998). Since then increasing MATE members have been researched in a wide range of living organisms. Compared with a fairly small numbers of MATE members in the bacteria and animals, plants have a higher diversity of MATE genes (Omote et al. 2006). Since 56 MATE genes have been isolated in Arabidopsis thaliana and 52 in Oryza sativa (Li et al. 2002; Hvorup et al. 2003; Tiwari et al. 2014). MATE gene family has also been identified in other plant species, such as Sorghum bicolor (Sivaguru et al. 2013), Hordeum vulgare (Fujii et al. 2012), Triticum aestivum (Ryan et al. 2009), Secale cereale (Yokosho et al. 2010) and Lotus japonicus (Takanashi et al. 2013). MATE proteins are characterized by one or two highly conserved MATE domains and about 12 putative transmembrane helical segments (TMSs) (Tiwari et al. 2014). Plant MATE proteins that are regarded as $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ coupled antiporters are involved in the detoxication of endogenous secondary metabolites and exogenous agents (Omote et al. 2006). For example, Arabidopsis MATE protein, TT12 is responsible for the vacuolar sequestration of flavonoids in the seed coat endothelium (Debeaujon et al. 2001). ALF5, encodes a member of the MATE family of integral membrane proteins, which is required for protection of the roots from inhibitory compounds (Diener et al. 2001). Further, increasing reports reveal that MATE-type transporters are involved in Al detoxification in plants. For instance, HvAACT1, a barley MATE gene localized on the plasma membrane of epidermal cells of the roots is responsible for the Al-induced secretion of citrate (Furukawa et al. 2007).

Maize (Zea mays L.), is a major crop worldwide. As yet, only ZmMATE1 and ZmMATE2 have been identified in maize (Maron et al. 2010; Takanashi et al. 2014). With the completion of maize genome sequencing, an excellent opportunity is provided to conduct genomewide analysis of the maize MATE gene family and infer its evolutionary history (Schnable et al. 2009). In the present study, we identified MATE gene family in maize and conducted a relatively detailed research about the phylogenetics, gene structures, chromosomal localization, gene duplications and expression profiles. Our work is expected to pave the way for future cloning and functional studies of MATE proteins in maize and contribute to understand evolutionary history of MATE gene family.

Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family is a new secondary transporter family distinct from any other known multidrug resistance transporters because of the unique topology of the 12 predicted transmembrane (TM) helices (He et al. 2010, Shoji 2014, Takanashi et al. 2014). Their activities depend on the electrochemical gradient of cations (such as $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions) to translocate substrates across the membrane (Kuroda and Tsuchiya 2009). MATE transporters are widely distributed in prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and implicated in various processes of the growth and development.

Multiple studies have shown that the diverse functions of MATE are consistent with the broad range of the transportation of substrates (Zhao and Dixon 2009), such as secondary metabolites, alkaloids, organic acids, flavonoids, and plant hormones (Diener et al. 2001, Zhu et al. 2016, Li et al. 2017). The functions of additional MATE transporters have been clarified and divided into three classes based on their established functions in plants. The first group of MATE transporters is involved in disease resistance. The molecular mechanism of pathogen resistance is illustrated by analyzing some Arabidopsis mutants, such as Ateds5, which encodes AtDTX47 that is localized in the chloroplast and involved in export of salicylic acid out of cells to promote disease tolerance (Serrano et al. 2013, Yamasaki et al. 2013). The second group of MATE proteins generally transports small organic molecules out of cells and acts as ligands or chelating agents. For instance, roots secrete citrate out of cell to chelate aluminum and avoid damage to the plants. The Al is different from other metals. In acidic soil, $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ can produce toxic effects and then inhibit root development. As such, the mechanism of Al toxicity has been widely studied (Yokosho et al. 2016b, Pereira et al. 2019). The first aluminum-activated citrate transporter, namely, SbMATE, in sorghum has been cloned, and SbMATE can secrete citrate, thereby chelating Al to form nontoxic complexes in soil solutions (Magalhaes et al. 2007). Since then, MATE genes encoding citrate transporter proteins participating in Al tolerance have been cloned in Triticum, Hordeum, Secale, Oryza, Phaseolus, Arabidopsis, Zea mays, and Nicotiana tabacum (Furukawa et al. 2007, Liu et al. 2009, Ryan et al. 2009, Maron et al. 2010, Yang et al. 2011, Yokosho et al. 2010, 2011, Tovkach et al. 2013,). The third group of MATE proteins is located in vacuoles and involved in the transport of flavonoids and secondary metabolites. Vacuoles are the main storage components of most conjugated forms of flavonoids, including anthocyanins, flavonols, and flavone glycoside. A kinetic study on vesicles has revealed that the MATE family member AtTT12 can specifically transport glycosidic forms, such as cyanidin 3-O glucoside5 and epicatechin 39-O-glucoside via AtTT12 expressed in yeast (Debeaujon et al. 2001, Zhao and Dixon 2009). The homologous genes of TT12 are cloned from Vitis and Medicago, and the expressed proteins in cell organelles are implicated in the mobilization of flavonoids (Marinova et al. 2007, Gomez et al. 2009, Zhao et al. 2011). In tobacco, MATE proteins can transport alkaloids into vacuoles through a similar mechanism (vacuolar flavonoid sequestration; Morita et al. 2009, Shoji et al. 2009).

Rice is one of the most important crops around the world and a model plant in studies involving the molecular genetics of monocotyledons. Its yields are severely affected by abiotic stresses, such as drought, low temperature, salt damage, heavy metals, and pathogens every year. Many plants, including rice, form various mechanisms of stress tolerance to ensure their normal growth. One of these mechanisms is detoxification, and an example of this mechanism is the excretion of toxic compounds from cells. In this process, MATE proteins play vital roles. In the rice genome, at least 50 MATE genes are available, but only a small number have been analyzed (Yokosho et al. 2009, 2011, 2016b, 2016a). Considering the effects of the reported MATE transporters on plant growth and stress responses, we believe that many unknown MATE transporter members will participate in plant development and stress resistance.

This study aimed to identify the MATE protein gene structure, chromosome localization, subcellular localization, and expression patterns of various subfamily genes in different tissues and organs in rice through bioinformatics tools and to understand the information and function of MATEs. This can study provides useful information on the research of MATE transporters in rice.

Background: Species in the Solanaceae family are known for producing plethora of specialized metabolites. In addition to biosynthesis pathways, a full comprehension of secondary metabolism must also take into account the transport and subcellular compartmentalization of substances. Here, we examined the MATE (Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion, or Multi-Antimicrobial Extrusion) gene family in the tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) genome with the objective of better understanding the transport of secondary metabolites in this model species. MATE membrane effluxers encompass an ancient gene family of secondary transporters present in all kingdoms of life, but with a remarkable expansion in plants. They mediate the transport of primary and secondary metabolites using the proton motive force through several membrane systems of the cell.

Results: We identified 67 genes coding for MATE transporters in the tomato genome, 33 of which are expressed constitutively whereas 34 are expressed in specific cell types or environmental conditions. Synteny analyses revealed bona fide paralogs and Arabidopsis orthologs. Co-expression analysis between MATE and regulatory genes revealed 78 positive and 8 negative strong associations $( \rho { \geq } | 0 . 8 | )$ ). We found no evidence of MATE transporters belonging to known metabolic gene clusters in tomato.

Conclusions: Altogether, our expression data, phylogenetic analyses, and synteny study provide strong evidence of functional homologies between MATE genes of tomato and Arabidopsis thaliana. Our co-expression study revealed potential transcriptional regulators of MATE genes that warrant further investigation. This work sets the stage for genome-wide functional analyses of MATE transporters in tomato and other Solanaceae species of economic relevance.

Keywords: Antiporter, Efflux, Genome evolution, Metabolic gene cluster, Regulatory gene network

## 4.1 Phloem loading and nectar secretion


SWEET proteins are chiefly associated with long-distance sugar translocation via apoplasmic phloem loading. Plasma membrane-localized AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 in phloem cells play a crucial role during apoplasmic phloem loading (Chen et al. 2010; 2012; Giaquinta 1983; Riesmeier et al. 1992; Bush 1993; Sauer and Stolz 1994; Ayre 2011). OsSWEET11, an ortholog of AtSWEET11, is involved in the sucrose efflux in the apoplasm (Antony et al. 2010). Similarly, in Z. mays, ZmSWEET13 is also involved in phloem loading (Bezrutczyk et al. 2018).

Plant nectaries accumulate starch, which is further converted into sucrose. This sucrose is exported to the apoplasmic space via SWEETs localized on the nectary parenchyma (Lin et al. 2014). AtSWEET9, a bidirectional transporter, maintains a concentration gradient inside and outside the nectary, which is essential for

SWEETs can be directly or indirectly genetically manipulated to increase sucrose accumulation in the embryo, which ultimately determines the quantity and quality of seeds and thereby contributes to crop yield, e.g., OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET15 in Oryzae sativa (rice) and GmSWEET15 in Glycine max (soybean). SWEETs contribute to transporting sugars towards microbes involved in root nodulation, which enhances the nitrogen fixation efficiency and productivity of crops, e.g., in Medicago truncatula, MtSWEET11 is involved in sucrose transport to nodules that provide nutrition to rhizobia. SWEETs are involved in sugar accumulation in fruits, e.g., MdSWEET2e, MdSWEET15a, and MdSWEET9b in Malus domestica (apple); VvSWEET10 in Vitis vinifera (grapes); and FvSWEET1 and FvSWEET4 in Fragaria vesca (strawberry). These SWEETs can be exploited for enhancing the yield and quality of fruits. Tissue-specific modulation of SWEETs could be exploited to increase the sugar content of nectaries and nectar secretion to attract a large number of pollinators and increase the chances of pollination and fruit set. The role of AtSWEET9 has been well studied in nectar secretion in A. thaliana. SWEETs can be identified and tweaked in plants serving as honey bee flora, such as sunflower, pumpkins, rapeseed, and fruit trees, to enhance nectar secretion. Further, SWEETs can be targeted for promoting tuber formation in crop plants, which involves the switching of sucrose transportation from the apoplastic to the symplastic route. This may be achieved by stopping SWEET-mediated apoplastic sucrose transport either by downregulating SWEETs via mutagenesis or by overexpressing the regulators that block SWEETs. For example, StSP6A blocks StSWEET11-mediated sucrose flux and stops the apoplastic route, thereby accumulating sucrose for tuber formation. Besides, SWEETs are involved in promoting sugar accumulation in the stems of crop plants like Saccharum officinarum (sugarcane), e.g., SoSWEET4a, SoSWEET4b, and SoSWEET13c, as well as Sorghum bicolor (sorghum), e.g., SbSWEET4-3. Such SWEETs can be manipulated to develop transgenic crops with a high sugar content in the stems as feedstock for bioethanol and sugar production. Finally, SWEETs can be modulated for crop protection against pathogen infection. SWEETs are known to be targeted by pathogens via effectors to acquire sugar for nutrition. CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing of SWEETs can prevent targeting by a pathogen and provide durable disease resistance, e.g., mutation in OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET14 led to a rice line resistant to Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo). Besides, a ‘SWEETR kit’ has been developed to detect Xoo infection in rice, where SWEET primer pairs detect the mRNA accumulation of OsSWEET11, OsSWEET13, and OsSWEET14 genes from leaf samples isolated from rice fields.

nectar secretion (Lin et al. 2014). Sucrose cleavage by nectar-specific cell wall invertase 4 (CWI4) maintains this concentration gradient in the extracellular space. The CWI4 balances a high intracellular-to-extracellular concentration gradient and an increased solute potential outside the nectaries, causing water to flow out into nectar droplets (Lin et al. 2014; Roy et al. 2017). Thus, SWEETs and cell wall invertases have an essential role in maintaining nectar flow and encouraging pollinator visitation, which directly impacts the reproduction and abundance of insect-pollinated species.

Only $1 6 \%$ of the world’s flowering plants act as food sources for honey bees in the form of nectar for honey production (Crane 1990; Roy et al. 2017). Therefore, the quality and quantity of nectar are vital for honey bees foraging plants. Genetic engineering of SWEETs to improve the quantity of nectar secretion in bee flora like sunflower, pumpkin, rapeseed, and fruit trees can markedly and directly benefit apiculture (figure 3).


## 4.2 Seed development


SWEETs participate in seed filling and embryo nutrition. AtSWEET11, AtSWEET12, and AtSWEET15 play a crucial role in seed filling. The triple mutant atsweet11;12;15 produces wrinkled and defective seeds due to retarded embryo growth, low seed weight, and very low starch and lipid content (Chen et al. 2015b). In maize, ZmSWEET4C plays a role in seed filling (Sekhon et al. 2011; Li et al. 2014; Davidson et al. 2011). RNA sequencing data depicted high expression of ZmSWEET4C in the basal endosperm transfer layer (BETL), a specialized cell layer of endosperm identified by massive increase in the basal membrane surface compared to maternal tissues like the placenta-chalaza (Xiong et al. 2011). Sosso et al. (2015) concluded that ZmSWEET4 is involved in transporting cell wallderived hexose across the BETL, which is critical for importing sugars to the embryo and seed filling in maize. The $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa ortholog of ZmSWEET4c, OsSWEET4, also seems to be involved in grain filling, but its precise functions and cell specificity are not known (Sosso et al. 2015). Another report in maize showed that CLOSED STOMATA1 (CST1), belonging to the SWEET family, was specifically expressed in subsidiary cells. CST1 regulates stomatal opening, photosynthesis, and carbon status in the leaf, and is also involved in promoting grain yield in maize (Wang et al. 2019a). Yang et al. (2018) showed that OsSWEET4 is primarily expressed in the initial stages of seed development, while OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET15 are expressed in the later developmental stages. As expected, a double mutant of OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET15 had defective endosperm development and seed filling. They showed a more severe phenotype, including empty seeds with starch retention in the pericarp. Ma et al. (2017) also reported the involvement of OsSWEET11 in seed filling in O. sativa. OsSWEET11 is a key player for pollen development in the rice cultivars Zhonghua 11 and Kitaake (Chu et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2006). OsSWEET11 was found abundantly in the nucellar epidermis, ovular vascular trace, and cross cells, and it was found to efflux sucrose from the nucellar epidermis at the maternal filial interface (Ma et al. 2017). These findings strongly support the involvement of OsSWEET11 in $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa grain filling, which determines the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of seeds and ultimately, crop yield (figure 3). Wu et al. (2018) showed that the transcription factor OsDOF11 governs SWEET expression in $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa (Wu et al. 2018; Kim et al. 2020). Similarly, GmSWEET15 from Glycine max (soybean) functions in seed development. GmSWEET15 was found to be expressed in the endosperm at the cotyledon stage and to mediate sucrose transport, and gmsweet15 mutants showed a high rate of seed abortion and a low sugar level in the embryo (Wang et al. 2019b). Another report suggested that GmSWEET10a and GmSWEET10b transport sucrose and hexose sugars from the seed coat to the embryo, which determines soybean seed traits such as seed size and oil and protein contents (Wang et al. 2020). We speculate that the alteration of the expression of potential SWEET genes by utilizing the various genome editing approaches may improve crop seed yields.


## 4.3 Fruit development in horticultural crops


Zhen et al. (2018) clarified the involvement of SWEETs in sugar accumulation in apple fruits. Genotyping of an apple cultivar collection indicated that 9 out of 25 MdSWEET genes were highly expressed during fruit development. Three SWEET genes, MdSWEET2e, MdSWEET15a, and MdSWEET9b, were involved in sugar accumulation in apples. Both MdSWEET15a and MdSWEET9b are reported to be clade III members and efficient sucrose transporters (Eom et al. 2015). Similarly, Zhang et al. (2019) demonstrated that the plasma membrane-localized VvSWEET10 from V. vinifera is responsible for the sugar accumulation in grape berries at the onset of ripening. VvSWEET10-overexpressing grapes showed an increased level of glucose, fructose, and other soluble sugars, which highlights the significant role of VvSWEET10 in governing the sugar content of grapes (Zhang et al. 2019). Fruit development in Fragaria vesca (strawberry) showed that different SWEET members have a distinct expression pattern during the transition from young to mature ripened fruit (Liu et al. 2019). FvSWEET1, FvSWEET4, and $F \nu S W E E T 9 b$ were reported to be expressed significantly more in ripening fruit, and FvSWEET1, FvSWEET9c, and FvSWEET7 were also highly expressed during the transition stage of the fruit (Liu et al. 2019). Recently, in Cucumis sativus L. (cucumber), the role of CsSWEET7a was shown in fruit development. High CsSWEET7a expression was found in sink tissues, including fruits, and CsSWEET7a was found to be localized in the plasma membrane of phloem companion cells (Li et al. 2021). CsSWEET7a is involved in phloem unloading in the fruit by transporting sugars from companion cells into the apoplasm, which triggers the metabolism of the raffinose family of oligosaccharides. Hence, more sugars can be unloaded, eventually promoting fruit development (Li et al. 2021). A recent study by Ko et al. (2021) showed that SlSWEET15 in S. lycopersicum was highly expressed in developing fruits as compared to the other vegetative organs. SlSWEET15 was found to be accumulated in the seed coat and vascular tissue and involved in sucrose unloading from the phloem and seed coat for fruit development. These studies provide diverse pictures of overall pathways for sugar accumulation in fruits (figure 3); however, the specific role of SWEETs in these pathways is yet to be delineated.


## 4.4 Tuberization


Extensive changes in resource allocation take place during tuber formation in plants (Abelenda et al. 2014). Abelenda et al. (2019) reported that StSWEET11 from Solanum tuberosum (potato) plays a key role during tuberization. This process involves the switching of sucrose unloading from the apoplasmic to the symplastic route. Tuberization is induced and controlled by an FT-like protein called SP6A (Navarro et al. 2011, 2015; Fernie et al. 2020). StSWEET11 is a putative sucrose transporter located in phloem parenchyma cells, and SP6A was reported to directly interact with the C-terminus of StSWEET11. StSWEET11 releases sugar along the phloem to maintain the sugar supply to radial sinks, including tubers. Abelenda et al. (2019) further showed that

StSWEET11 expression in yeast cells mediated esculin uptake along the concentration gradient, but this uptake was reduced when StSP6A was co-expressed in StSWEET11-expressing yeast cells. Hence, SP6A blocks StSWEET11-dependent apoplastic sucrose flux, and sucrose transport becomes symplastic in tubers (figure 3).

Plants use sunlight to fx carbon dioxide and convert it into sugars during photosynthesis. Sugars are important carbohydrates transported from the synthesized sites in source leaves to sink tissues stems, seeds, and fruits. Sugar transport is key for proper growth and development of plants, especially for agriculturally important organs, such as seeds (Wen et al. 2022). Seed development is related to crop yield. Most importantly, seeds of cereal crops maize, rice, and wheat are major food sources of the most population. Thus, it is imperative to identify and characterize efectors for sugar efux to maintain high yields in a constantly changing environment to meet the demands of an increasing world population (Bailey-Serres et al. 2019).

The frst sucrose transporter was identifed using engineered yeast strains (Riesmeier et al. 1992). Over the past decades, a large number of factors for sugar transport have been reported. Three key classes of transporters have been proved to be responsible for sugar phloem loading and unloading, including monosaccharide transporter (MST), sucrose transporter (SUT), and sugars will eventually be exported transporter (SWEET) (Braun 2022). The MST family can be classifed into several subfamilies, such as polyol transporter (PLT), tonoplast monosaccharide transporter (TMT), and sugar transporter protein (STP). Arabidopsis PLT protein POLYOL TRANSPORTER5 (AtPLT5) has the ability to transport diverse substrates, such as hexoses and pentoses (Klepek et al. 2005). AtTMT1/TMT2 serves as an antiporter to load of glucose and sucrose into the vacuole (Schulz et al. 2011). The suppression of cucumber STP gene CsHT1 results in the inhibition of pollen germination and pollen tube elongation and decreased seed number and seed size (Cheng et al. 2015). For SUT transporters, Arabidopsis SUTs are grouped into three subclades (Reinders et al. 2012). Subclade I SUTs contain fve members (AtSUC1, 2, 5, 8, 9). AtSUC1 is necessary for normal pollen function (Sivitz et al. 2008). Subclade II SUT member AtSUC3 infuences pod dehiscence (Meyer et al. 2000). Arabidopsis SUT subclade III member AtSUC4 in vacuole membrane functions as a sucrose transporter (Weise et al. 2000). In maize, sucrose transporter ZmSUT1 mediates sucrose uptake in a $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient-dependent manner (Carpaneto et al. 2005). Cellular expression and subcellular localization analyses have revealed dual roles of $Z { \mathrm { m S U T 1 } }$ in both phloem loading and apoplasmic recycling (Baker et al. 2016).

The SWEET family is diversifed in nature. Based on SWEET proteins from fifteen plant taxa, SWEETs are divided into four phylogenetic clades. Clades I, II, and IV SWEETs prefer hexoses, while clade III SWEETs are efcient for sucrose transport (Eom et al. 2015). SWEETs are responsible for multiple biological events, from nectar production, biotic and abiotic stress responses, fertility to seed flling. Sucrose is synthesized in nectary and transported by SWEET9. The exported sucrose is then hydrolyzed by invertase to produce sucrose, glucose, and fructose. SWEET9 seems to be important for sucrose secretion from nectary parenchyma. Intriguingly, SWEET9 is essential for nectar secretion in three species Arabidopsis, Brassica, and Nicotiana (Lin et al. 2014). Rice bacterial blight disease gene OsSWEET11/Xa13/Os8N3 is involved in plant-pathogen interaction (Yang et al. 2006). In addition, OsSWEET11 interacts with two copper transporter family member COPT1 and COPT5 to transport copper (Yuan et al. 2010). Two Arabidopsis sucrose transporters SWEET11 and 12 are phosphorylated by drought- and ABA-activated SnRK2 protein kinases. This phosphorylation promotes the sucrose transport activities of SWEET11 and 12 to increase sucrose contents, which leads to the drought tolerance (Chen et al. 2022a). Arabidopsis SWEET13 is vital for pollen nutrition and therefore plant fertility (Sun et al. 2013). In maize, ZmSWEET4c transports hexose across the basal endosperm transfer layer, unique epidermal cells located at the juncture of flial and maternal tissues. Intriguingly, mutants of maize ZmSWEET4c and its rice ortholog OsSWEET4 all result in the defects in seed flling (Sosso et al. 2015).

Roles of SWEETs in abiotic stress adaption have been reported in Arabidopsis (Chen et  al. 2022a). However, SWEETs responses to abiotic stresses in crops remain largely elusive. We previously identifed ZmSWEET1b as a positive regulator of maize salt tolerance using RNA-seq (NCBI accession number GSE128432). To functionally analyze maize ZmSWEET1b gene, we adopted the CRISPR/ Cas9 technique to generate independent ZmSWEET1b knockout lines. Herein, we characterized cereal crop maize SWEET family member ZmSWEET1b, with emphasis on the survey of ZmSWEET1b responses to salinity stress.

In higher plants, photosynthesis is the process by which carbon and energy and transformed into sugars in source tissues. These sugars are exported to various sink tissues and organs to support normal growth and development1 . Sugars are an important nutritional component, especially in fruit crop species, and the accumulation of soluble sugars somewhat determines the quality of fruits. However, the accumulation of soluble sugars requires sugar biosynthesis, metabolism, and transport, in which specialized sugar transporters play an indispensable role2–4 .

Tomato is considered an ideal model crop species because of its fleshy fruits that have important economic value5 . Sugar transport and storage are essential for improving tomato quality6,7 . Early studies indicated that sucrose unloading in young tomato pericarps undergoing cell division occurs symplastically8 . The postphloem cellular pathways in the outer pericarps are associated with switching from the symplastic route during the starch accumulation stage to the apoplastic route during the hexose accumulation stage9 . This symplastic-toapoplastic switch is compatible with a facilitated transport process allowing the accumulation of soluble sugars at high concentrations without attenuating phloem unloading9 .

Sucrose is unloaded from the phloem to the fruit apoplast, where it can be either directly transported into storage parenchyma cells by sucrose transporters (SUTs) through the extracellular pathway or hydrolyzed to glucose and fructose by extracellular invertase and then transported into parenchyma cells by hexose transporte rs10,11. Thus, the apoplastic unloading of sugar can facilitate the influx of hexoses across the plasma membranes of storage cells. In contrast, sucrose can accelerate the efflux of sucrose from the phloem sink to the apoplast through sucrose concentration differences9 . Three SUTs and three hexose transporters have been identified in tomato12–14. Immunolocalization assays showed that three of these SUTs colocalized in sieve elements and that LeSUT1 and LeSUT2 are present only in the sieve tube cells of tomato fruits and not in other phloem cells or storage parenchyma cells12,15. However, three hexose transporters (SlHT1, SlHT2, and SlHT3) are expressed in the storage parenchyma cells of tomato fruits16. The cleavage of sucrose by sucrose synthase can save more energy than can cleavage by invertase in growing sink organs17. Therefore, sucrose transmembrane transport may also occur in the parenchyma cells of tomato fruits.

In tomato, the SUTs and monosaccharide transporters identified thus far are energy dependent and sensitive to the activity of proton transporters. These transporters move sucrose across the membrane by coupling with $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase in the cell membrane. Recent studies have shown that the translocation of sucrose is driven by both saturated (possibly via SUTs) and unsaturated phases, but SUTs and other known monosaccharide transporters display low levels of expression in relevant cells despite showing only saturated sucrose transport kinetics18,19. This finding indicates that there are other transporters responsible for the transmembrane transport of sugars, independent of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase. The discovery of SWEETs (Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporters) has provided new insights into sugar transport mechanisms20. SWEET proteins are sugar transporters that do not require energy and are responsible for transporting monosaccharides and/or disaccharides across membranes following a concentration gradient21. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that the SWEET protein family comprises four clades, the members of which have distinct characteristics (clade I and II SWEETs prefer hexoses; clade III members mainly transport sucrose; and clade IV members are involved in the flux of fructose across the tonoplast)21,22. The multiplicity of SWEET genes in higher plants also explains their different functions in essential developmental and physiological processes, including growth and flower, pollen, nectar and seed development 22–29

Passive facilitation plays an important role in the release of sucrose from sieve tube companion cell complexes and other vascular bundle cells to fruit parenchyma cells. Among the tomato SlSWEET genes, only SlSWEET1a and SlSWEET15 have been experimentally researched, and it has been reported that SlSWEET1a is involved in sugar regulation in fruits and leaves and that SlSWEET15 is responsible for fruit and seed development7,30,31. Therefore, it is necessary to explore other candidate SWEET genes involved in sustaining sugar homeostasis in tomato fruits to improve their quality. In this study, SlSWEET7a and SlSWEET14 were selected for further analysis based on the results of a preliminary study32. Here, the putative effects of SlSWEET7a and SlSWEET14 on tomato fruits were explored.

Sugar is the main carbon source and energy-supplying substance in organisms, and it plays an important role in plant growth and development. Sugar is the main product of photosynthesis and carbon dioxide assimilation occurs mainly in stromal cells of chloroplast. The main assimilation product synthesized in chloroplasts is triose phosphate, most of which will be converted to either sucrose in the cytosol or starch in the chloroplast1,2 . Sucrose is commonly translocated to other carbondemanding organs through the long-distance transport occurring in phloem. Hence, sugar transportation is critical for maintaining the source-sink balance3 .

Over the past two decades, various sugar transporters have been identified in living organisms, including plants, animals, humans, and fungi4–6 . These transporters can be categorized into four families: sodium solute symporter transporters; major facilitator superfamily transporters; phosphotransferase system transporters; and sugar will eventually be exported transporters (SWEETs). Among these transporters, SWEETs emerge as a unique and novel class of sugar transporters. SWEETs are conserved evolutionarily and exist widely in eukaryotes, and prokaryotes such as arechaea and eubacteria. The first member of the SWEET gene family, MtN3, was identified in Medicago truncatula, and its expression was induced during root nodule development7 . Later, a homolog of the MtN3 gene, designated Saliva, was identified in Drosophila and displayed salivary gland-specific expression during embryonic development8 . Recently, MtN3/Saliva-type genes were functionally characterized as sugar transporters in both animals and plants, and thus gave the name $^ { \prime \prime } S W E E T ^ { \prime 9 }$ . SWEET proteins are characterized by the MtN3/Saliva motif (also known as the PQ-loop repeat), which comprises three alpha-helical transmembrane domains (3-TMs). Eukaryotic SWEETs consists of a tandem repeat of the basic 3-TM unit separated by a single transmembrane domain, which constitutes a 3-1-3 TM structure. In contrast, prokaryotic SWEETs, also called SemiSWEETs, contain only a single 3-TM unit, suggesting that eukaryotic SWEETs evolved through a duplication of the 3-TM unit10.

In plants, SWEETs function as bidirectional uniporters that mediate influx and efflux of sugars across cell membranes. SWEETs can be divided into four clades11. Clades I, II, and IV SWEETs transport predominantly hexoses, whilst clade III SWEETs appear to be sucrose transporters (SUTs)12–15. For example, the clade I SWEET AtSWEET1 and the clade II SWEET OsSWEET5 mediate the uptake and efflux of glucose or galactose, respectively, across the cell membrane9,16. Two clade III SWEETs, AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12, are involved in efflux of photosynthesized sucrose from phloem parenchyma cells into intercellular space for phloem loading and longdistance translocation of sucrose17. A newly identified clade III SWEET, AtSWEET9, transports sucrose to the apoplast and plays an essential role in nectar secretion18. The clade IV SWEET, AtSWEET17, functions as a fructose-specific uniporter, with a key role in facilitating bidirectional transport of fructose across the tonoplast in leaf and root12,13. In addition, SWEETs have been shown to affect various physiological processes, such as pollen development19,20, seed filling21,22, stress and senescence14,16,23,24, modulating gibberellins response25, and host–pathogen interaction26. Usually, abiotic stress such as cold, high salinity, and drought, and biotic stress caused by fungi or bacteria result in an induction of specific SWEET genes27,28.

The accumulation of carbohydrates in storage organs such as seeds and fruits mainly depends on the supply of photoassimilates from photosynthetic tissues, especially source leaves. In most plants, sucrose is the major carbohydrate transported over a long distance in the veins to support the growth and development of storage organs6 . Sugar transporter genes exhibit divergent evolutionary patterns and play important roles in sugar accumulation in plants29. For example, genes encoding SUT proteins are involved in sugar translocation toward storage organs30–32. Recently, the SWEET4 gene is also found to play an important role in seed filling22. In maize and rice, SWEET4 shows high expression during seed development and contributes to seed filling by enhancing the importation of hexoses into the endosperm. This study sheds light on our understanding on the mechanism by which sucrose is released from maternal tissues such as seed coat to support filial tissues such as embryonic tissue. Since sugar content is an important component of fruit quality, increasing attention has also been paid to investigate the SWEET gene family in fruit crops such as apple33, grapevine34, and banana35. However, the effect of SWEETs on fruit sugar accumulation remains elusive.

The domesticated apple, Malus $_ x$ domestica Borkh., is an economically important fruit crop worldwide. Apple belongs to the family Rosaceae, and the cultivated apple is a diploidized autopolyploid species with a basic chromosome number of $x = 1 7$ . The draft genome sequence of the domesticated apple has been released, and accounts for an approximately $7 5 0 \mathrm { M b }$ per haploid36. In this study, we report the identification of the MdSWEET genes with high expression during apple fruit development. DNA markers for these MdSWEETs were developed to investigate their association with fruit sugar content. Our study not only aids our better understanding of the effect of SWEETs on fruit sugar accumulation but it will also be helpful for genetic improvement of fruit sugar accumulation in apple-breeding programs.

Sugars are the precursor molecules for most cellular carbon and energy sources. In plants, sugars are transported from photosynthetically active source tissues to heterotrophic sink tissues. Sugar will eventually be exported transporters (SWEETs) are a newly discovered class of sugar transporters involved in sugar efflux processes and are widely distributed and highly conserved among all organisms, including plants, metazoans, and humans (Chen et al. 2010, 2012, 2015a, b; Lin et al. 2014). They were first discovered in Medicago truncatula (barrelclover) as being involved in rhizobium-induced nodule development (Gamas et al. 1996) and were named MtN3. Then, in Drosophila melanogaster, a gene named saliva was identified as a homolog of MtN3, and it had a high level of transcripts in the salivary gland. Therefore, these SWEETs were initially referred to as MtN3/ saliva genes. Later, high-throughput screening via a novel mammalian expression system was performed to characterize the putative membrane proteins from the Aramemnon membrane protein database of Arabidopsis thaliana. Fo¨ rster resonance energy transfer-based sensors were used to identify glucose transporters (GLUTs, SGLTs) and their transport activities (Taka

naga and Frommer 2010). Chen et al. (2010) were the first to characterize the glucose efflux transporter in $A$ . thaliana, which they named AtSWEET1. Phylogenetic studies have revealed SWEET homologs in prokaryotes, referred to as semiSWEETs. The structure and phylogenetic analysis of eukaryotic SWEETs hint that they might have evolved from prokaryotic semiSWEETs (Feng and Frommer 2015; Hu et al. 2016).

Sugar is a major carbon source and energy source for higher plants in their growth and development (Walmsley et al. 1998; Lalonde et al. 2004; Chen et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2012). Higher plants can use convert $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into organic carbon in photosynthetic leaves (the source). The source is involved in the storage and transport of nutrients in plants (Ruan 2014; Rolland et al. 2002). However, sugar cannot be transported independently across the plant cell membrane system and requires the assistance of appropriate sugar transporters, such as MSTs (monosaccharide transporters) (Slewinski 2011), SUTs (sucrose transporters) (Kuhn and Grof 2010; Ayre 2011) and SWEETs (sugars will eventually be exported transporters) (Chen et al. 2010).

SWEETs are a new family of sugar transporters discovered in recent years, generally with seven transmembrane domains and two MtN3 motifs (Talbot 2010; Baker et al. 2012). SWEET shows the function of bidirectional reversible transport of sugar, and promotes the diffusion of sucrose to the apoplast pathway through transmembrane across the gradient of concentration on cell efflux (Baker et al. 2012; Lin et al. 2014; Eom et al. 2015). Since SWEET was first discovered using Forster resonance energy transfer (FRET) by optical glucose sensors (Chen et al. 2010), SWEET family members have been identified by genome-wide analyses in different plant species, such as Arabidopsis (Chen et al. 2010), rice (Yuan and Wang 2013), tomato (Feng et al. 2015), soybean (Patil et al. 2015) and cucumber (Hu et al. 2017).

At present, researches on the functions of SWEET genes are carried out mainly in Arabidopsis and rice, while only a small part of them have been functionally characterized. The functions of transporting glucose and sucrose are identified in most well-studied SWEETs currently (Chen et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2012). For example, AtSWEET1 is involved in the regulation of glucose uptake and efflux (Chen et al. 2010; Sonnewald 2011). OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET14 are the low affinity transport sucrose carriers that may be involved in the phloem sucrose loading process (Chen et al. 2012; Chen 2014). AtSWEET1/4/5 may directly involve in the transport of sugar to regulate the osmotic active substances, or participate in cell wall sugar loading (Bauer et al. 2013). Other SWEETs have the function of transporting fructose and galactose (Klemens et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2014; Zhou et al. 2014). AtSWEET16 and AtSWEET17 are highly expressed in roots and involved in the transport of monosaccharides and polysaccharides across tonoplast (Klemens et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2014; Chardon et al. 2013). In addition, SWEETs participate in the transport of sugar and ions. AtSWEET13 is involved in the regulation of aluminum ion balance in plants (Zhao et al. 2009). OsSWEET11 forms a complex with two other copper transporter protein COPT1 and COPT5 in the plasma membrane (Yuan et al. 2009; Yuan et al. 2010), regulating the transport of copper ions and sugars (Yuan et al. 2010).

It has been found that some SWEETs take part in plant reproductive development also. AtSWEET9 transports sucrose into apoplasts for nectar secretion (Lin et al. 2014). AtSWEET8, a glucose transporter expressed in tapetum and embryo sacs, participates in the development of the pollen and anther (Guan et al. 2008; Sun et al. 2013). The silenced AtSWEET11 mutant showed lower pollen viability and even pollen sterility (Sonnewald 2011). Suppression of OsSWEET11 resulted in pollen dysplasia, leading to male infertility (Yuan et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2011; Ge et al. 2000). AtSWEET5 was highly expressed in the female gametophyte during the three-cell pollen stage (Yuan et al. 2010). Some researches have showed that SWEETs plays a role in the process of plant senescence and response to abiotic stresses. AtSWEET15 can be induced by cold, salt and drought stress (Seo et al. 2011). Overexpressing AtSWEET16 improved the tolerance to cold stress, osmotic stress and nitrogen availability in Arabidopsis (Klemens et al. 2013). In addition, SWEETs from other plants (e.g., Hordeum vulgare, tomato, etc.) are also involved in the regulation of abiotic stress (Yuan and Wang 2013).

Although some studies have been reported in cotton, such as, SWEETs are involved in sugar transport during fiber elongation and bacterial blight of cotton (Zhang et al. 2017; Cox et al. 2017; Phillips et al. 2017), the function of SWEET in cotton, especially in stress response and host-pathogen interaction, has not been identified until now. With the release of genomes sequences of two diploid cotton (A2, D5) and two allotetraploid cotton (AD1, AD2) (Phillips et al. 2017; Li et al. 2014; Paterson et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2012; Li et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2015; Yuan et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2015) facilitates the survey of SWEETs in cotton. In this study, we identified the SWEETs in four cotton species by genome-wide analysis. This results will provide insights into the evolution of SWEET genes and more candidates for specific genetic modification, which will be useful in future research.

Sugars are the major carbon and energy source in all plant and animal systems. Occasionally, sugars also function as signaling molecules, thus playing a major role in all essential developmental and physiological processes. In plants, these sugars are synthesized during photosynthesis and are transported to sink organs through phloem. This sugar transport is facilitated by one or more of the following three families of sugar transporters: (i) MSTs (monosaccharide transporters), (ii) SUTs (sucrose transporters) and (iii) SWEETs (Sugars will eventually be exported transporters) [1–4]. Of these three families, SWEET sugar transporters were the last to be described and so named by Chen et al. [5] for the first time. These proteins are membrane-localized uniporters, transporting only sugars along a concentration gradient (they transport no other molecules, as is the case with symporters).

The first two foundation members of the family of SWEET proteins, namely MtN3 and Saliva were identified in late 1990s, much before the sugar transporter SWEET genes were recognized and so named [5]. MtN3 belongs to Medicago truncatula and is involved in nodule development [6], while Saliva belongs to Drosophila and is expressed in salivary glands during embryo development [7]. Therefore, the domain that is a characteristic feature of SWEET proteins in eukaryotes is called MtN3/Saliva or MtN3_slv domain. Therefore, the corresponding SWEET genes are also sometimes described as MtN3/Saliva or MtN3_slv SWEET genes (see review by Yuan and Wang [8]). MtN3_slv domain is a 3-transmembrane helix (TMH) domain that is characteristic of SWEET proteins in prokaryotes, and the corresponding 7-TMHs protein carrying two MtN3_slv domains is a characteristic feature of SWEET proteins in eukaryotes. In Vitis vinifera, a SWEET protein consists of two 7-TMHs structures with four 3-TMH domains, separated by two single TMHs; this has been described as extraSWEET in contrast to semiSWEET with only single 3-TMHs, which is invariably found in prokaryotes (Fig. 1). In a recent analysis of $\sim 3 5 0 0$ SWEET proteins, superSWEET sugar transporters with 18, 23 and 25 TMHs have also been identified in three species of Phytophthora. Thus, a superSWEET carries more than 5–8 repeats of a semiSWEET with 3-TMH [9]. All the four types are known to occur in eukaryotes, although semiSWEET, extraSWEET and superSWEET are not believed to be of common occurrence. However, in a survey of SWEET genes in 25 plant genomes, out of 411 SWEETs, 140 were semiSWEET genes, suggesting that semiSWEET genes are not really uncommon among higher plants [10], as believed by some. The structures of all the four types of SWEET proteins including semiSWEET, SWEET, extraSWEET and superSWEET are shown in Fig. 1.

It has been observed that in the genome of a plant species, many SWEET genes are found, while in the genome of an animal species (including humans), only one SWEET gene is found. The only exceptions are Drosophila with two SWEET genes and the model worm Caenorhabditis elegans with seven SWEET genes. In higher plants, 17 SWEET genes were reported for the first time in Arabidopsis [5], followed by reports of these genes in a number of plant species including the following: Vitis vinifera (17), Oryza sativa (21), Sorghum bicolor (23), Musa acuminata (25), Solanum lycopersicum (29), Brassica rapa (32), Malus pumila (33), Solanum tuberosum (35), Glycine max (52), Gossypium hir ‎ - sutum (55), Brassica napus (68), and Triticum aestivum (71) (figures in parentheses are number of SWEET genes in each case) [8–20].

On the basis of phylogenetic analysis, the members of SWEET gene family in plants were classified into four clades (representing four sub-families). Genes in clades I and II encode proteins, which transport hexose sugar (including glucose and fructose), those in clade III (the most common class) encode proteins, which transport sucrose, those in clade IV (mainly vacuolar transporters and least frequent) are involved in a flux of fructose across the tonoplast [5, 21]. An extra clade V was also reported, which is absent in plants and occurs only in mammals, Chlamydomonas and C. elegans [21].

Multiplicity of SWEET genes in higher plants also explains their diverse roles in essential developmental and physiological processes including growth, senescence and flower/seed/pollen development. More importantly, they are known to play a role in adaptation to abiotic and biotic stresses including host-pathogen interactions [22–27]. As many as 17 types of AtSWEET genes were reported in Arabidopsis, which have been treated as 17 different types for describing SWEET genes in all plant species. These 17 types seem to perform different specific functions. For instance, SWEET11 and SWEET12 are abundant in leaves, and are known to be involved in cellular efflux for phloem loading, thus helping in the transport of sugar from leaves to the roots [23]; these are also involved in seed coat and endosperm efflux for grain filling [22]. Similarly, SWEET4 is associated with increase in plant size, higher accumulation of sugars, and freezing tolerance [27]. SWEET genes of clade III are also known to be particularly involved in pathogen susceptibility/resistance, which is an important function of SWEET proteins (see Feng and Frommer [15] for a review).

It is also known that a pathogen may hijack one or more SWEET genes in the host and make them overexpress to derive nutrition for its own growth [8, 28]. These SWEET genes are actually the targets of pathogen’s effectors, and represent susceptibility (S) genes. For instance, significant upregulation of several Arabidopsis SWEET genes (e.g., AtSWEET4, AtSWEET5, AtSWEET7, AtSWEET8, AtSWEET10, AtSWEET12, and AtSWEET15) was reported after infection by the model pathogen Pseudomonas syringae [5]. Rice SWEET genes including OsSWEET11 (Os8N3/, Xa13), OsSWEET12, OsSWEET13 (Xa25), OsSWEET14, and OsSWEET15 are also known as major bacterial blight (strain Xoo) susceptibility genes of rice [29–32]. In V. vinifera also, SWEET4 protein was shown to facilitate plant pathogen interactions involving the pathogen Botrytis cinerea [17].

Wheat is one of the world’s most important cereal crop [33] that suffers serious losses due to biotic and abiotic stresses like drought [34–36]. In this crop, in a genome-wide search, 71 SWEET genes (including 12 truncated genes; maximum number reported in any species) were identified [20]. This earlier study mainly focused on structure and phylogenetic analysis of 59 genes (12 truncated genes were not included in this analysis); in this study, expression analysis was also conducted for 18 selected genes (each encoding protein with 7-TMHs), and altered expression was observed for five SWEET genes following inoculation by the pathogen, Puccinia graminis triticina $( P g t )$ , causing stem rust.

In the present study, we conducted a detailed study involving genome-wide search of SWEET genes using the recently reported complete whole genome sequence of wheat (IWGSC RefSeq v1.0; IWGSC 2018), which was not available for the above earlier recent study. The present study involved use of SWEET protein sequences from eight species as query sequences [as against only two species (rice and Arabidopsis) used in the earlier study] and allowed identification of 108 putative TaSWEET genes (as against 59 complete genes reported in the above study); three novel types (TaSWEET18–20) were also identified for the first time. Our study included the following additional features, which were not covered in the earlier study by Gao et al. [20]: chromosome mapping; comparative genomics; gene duplication events; detailed analysis of gene structure (including comparative genomics including synteny and collinearity); protein 3D structure (including MD simulation); alignment of amino acid residues; docking analysis with sucrose and glucose; identification of regulatory elements including cis-regulatory elements and targets of miRNAs. In silico expression of all the 108 genes in five different tissues (leaf, stem, grain, root and spike), under water stress and heat stress was also conducted. Using a representative sample of 7 SWEET genes, qRT-PCR analysis was also conducted to study in planta alterations in the expression of these SWEET genes under water/heat stress and after pathogen inoculation. For this purpose, two contrasting wheat genotypes (drought/heat tolerant cvs. C306 and HD2985 and drought/heat sensitive cvs. HD2967 and HD2329 respectively) and two NILs for leaf rust gene Lr28 in the background of HD2329 were utilized. The present study thus provides detailed supplementary information about SWEET genes and proteins, which should prove useful for planning strategies for developing high-yielding wheat cultivars carrying tolerance to a variety of biotic and abiotic stresses.

Background: SWEETs (Sugar Will Eventually be Exported transporters) function as sugar efflux transporters that perform diverse physiological functions, including phloem loading, nectar secretion, seed filling, and pathogen nutrition. The SWEET gene family has been identified and characterized in a number of plant species, but little is known about in Litchi chinensis, which is an important evergreen fruit crop.

Results: In this study, 16 LcSWEET genes were identified and nominated according to its homologous genes in Arabidopsis and grapevine. Multiple sequence alignment showed that the 7 alpha-helical transmembrane domains (7-TMs) were basically conserved in LcSWEETs. The LcSWEETs were divided into four clades (Clade I to Clade IV) by phylogenetic tree analysis. A total of 8 predicted motifs were detected in the litchi LcSWEET genes. The 16 LcSWEET genes were unevenly distributed in 9 chromosomes and there was one pairs of segmental duplicated events by synteny analysis. The expression patterns of the 16 LcSWEET genes showed higher expression levels in reproductive organs. The temporal and spatial expression patterns of LcSWEET2a and LcSWEET3b indicated they play central roles during early seed development.

Conclusions: The litchi genome contained 16 SWEET genes, and most of the genes were expressed in different tissues. Gene expression suggested that LcSWEETs played important roles in the growth and development of litchi fruits. Genes that regulate early seed development were preliminarily identified. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of the SWEET gene family in litchi, laying a strong foundation for further functional studies of LcSWEET genes and improvement of litchi fruits.

Keywords: Litchi chinensis, LcSWEETs, Expression patterns, Seed development

Background: The SWEET (Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporters) gene family is a recently identified group of sugar transporters that play an indispensable role in sugar efflux, phloem loading, plant-pathogen interaction, nectar secretion, and reproductive tissue development. However, little information on Saccharum SWEET is available for this crop with a complex genetic background.

Results: In this study, 22 SWEET genes were identified from Saccharum spontaneum Bacterial Artificial Chromosome libraries sequences. Phylogenetic analyses of SWEETs from 11 representative plant species showed that gene expansions of the SWEET family were mainly caused by the recent gene duplication in dicot plants, while these gene expansions were attributed to the ancient whole genome duplication (WGD) in monocot plant species. Gene expression profiles were obtained from RNA-seq analysis. SWEET1a and SWEET2s had higher expression levels in the transitional zone and maturing zone than in the other analyzed zones. SWEET1b was mainly expressed in the leaf tissues and the mature zone of the leaf of both S. spontaneum and S. officinarum, and displayed a peak in the morning and was undetectable in both sclerenchyma and parenchyma cells from the mature stalks of S. officinarum. SsSWEET4a\4b had higher expression levels than SWEET4c and were mainly expressed in the stems of seedlings and mature plants. SWEET13s are recently duplicated genes, and the expression of SWEET13s dramatically increased from the maturing to mature zones. SWEET16b’s expression was not detected in S. officinarum, but displayed a rhythmic diurnal expression pattern.

Conclusions: Our study revealed the gene evolutionary history of SWEETs in Saccharum and SWEET1b was found to be a sucrose starvation-induced gene involved in the sugar transportation in the high photosynthetic zones. SWEET13c was identified as the key player in the efflux of sugar transportation in mature photosynthetic tissues. SWEET4a\4b were found to be mainly involved in sugar transportation in the stalk. SWEET1a\2a\4a\4b\13a\16b were suggested to be the genes contributing to the differences in sugar contents between S. spontaneum and S. officinarum. Our results are valuable for further functional analysis of SWEET genes and utilization of the SWEET genes for genetic improvement of Saccharum for biofuel production.

Keywords: Gene expression, Gene evolution, Saccharum officinarum, Saccharum spontaneum, Sugar transport, SWEET

Higher plants have evolved well for the ability to employ solar energy to convert $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ into organic carbon in photosynthetic source leaf tissues, and this carbon then travels to various heterotrophic sink organs (such as seeds, roots, and fruits) [1]. The efficient distribution (translocation and partitioning) of sugars between a source–sink system is governed by sugar transporters, and it is crucial for sink organ development and positive feedback to source tissues to ensure sufficient energy allocation and to maintain a trade-off between the different parts of plants [1,2]. Therefore, sugar transporters usually act as bridges, and they are fundamentally pivotal to the cellular exchange of carbon and energy in multicellular organisms to perform further biological functions. Research has shown that membrane-localized sugar transporters in plants can be categorized into MFSs (the major facilitator superfamily) and SWEET (Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporter, PFAM: PF03083) family [3]. The homologs of the SWEET family among the higher plants are structurally characterized by seven transmembrane domains (TMDs) harboring two MtN3/PQ-loop domains connected by a loop, and they are phylogenetically divided into four clades with mono- and disaccharide transport activity by a uniport mechanism [4,5]. Their functions are essential for various activities in plants, such as phloem loading [6], pollen development [7], nectar secretion [8], seed filling [9–11], freezing tolerance [12], pathogen resistance [13–15], and others, and they act by mediating the translocation and partitioning of hexoses and/or sucrose.

SWEETs homologs have not only been found in prokaryotes (semiSWEETs) but have also reportedly appeared in all the eukaryotic kingdoms ranging from fungi to plants and animals [4,16,17]. Plant SWEETs were initially identified as sugar effluxers with glucose or sucrose transport activities in Arabidopsis and rice [5]. Thereafter, additional homologs of SWEETs from different plant varieties were explored and their functions were determined to improve crop survival and yield potential. For example, in the model plant Arabidopsis, plasma membrane (PM)-localized AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 of the clade III sucrose transporters were characterized by their role in the preparation of sucrose apoplastic phloem loading [18]. A double mutation (Atsweet11/12) blocks assimilation exudation, which results in a shorter root, abnormal vascular structure and lower freezing tolerance [6,18]. In addition, AtSWEET11/12/15 are specifically expressed in developing seeds to transfer sugars from the seed coat to the embryo, and the triple mutant (Atsweet11/12/15) resulted in severe seed defects [19]. Like other members of clade III, AtSWEET9 has a demonstrated function as an essential sucrose efflux transporter in nectar production, and its orthologs are functionally conserved as nectary-specific transporters in core eudicots [8]; AtSWEET10 is involved in the stress response, and AtSWEET13 and AtSWEET14 function within the anthers by tangling with the gibberellic acid response [20,21]. Apart from the sucrose transporters in Clade III, AtSWEET1 [5] and AtSWEET2 in clade I, AtSWEET4 [22] and AtSWEET8 [23,24] in clade II, and AtSWEET16 [12] and AtSWEET17 [25] in Clade IV, have been specifically explored for their significant functions in various biological activities through the manipulation of sugar transport. Parallel with the gradual growth of SWEETs research in Arabidopsis, the further study of SWEETs homologs in other plants, including rice [5,24,26,27], tomatoes [11,28,29], grapes [30,31], Medicago truncatula [32], etc., have been reported and rigorously updated. Therefore, given the versatile regulators and obvious yield potential of SWEETs, more detailed and in-depth studies in more abundant species are needed.

The Brassica rapa plant provides a well-established model of the $^ { \prime \prime } \mathrm { U } ^ { \prime \prime }$ triangle in the Brassica genus, which is characterized by broad genetic and morphological diversity that allowed for the domestication of this genus to produce leafy vegetables, vegetable oils, turnip roots, turnip greens, turnip tops, and fodder turnip [33–35]. The release of the B. rapa and B. oleracea genomes confirmed an additional $\gamma$ whole-genome triplication (WGT) event in the Brassica species after they diverged from Arabidopsis thaliana approximately 9–28 million years ago [34–39]. In comparing the ${ \sim } 2 7 { , } 0 0 0$ genes in the A. thaliana genome, the retained genes (\~42,000) in the B. rapa genome are considerably fewer than the theoretical value from a simple WGT event. Approximately $\mathrm { \sim } 7 0 \%$ , ${ \sim } 4 6 \%$ , and $3 6 \%$ of genes remained in the sub-genomes of the least fractionated (LF), medium fractionated (MF1), and most fractionated (MF2) individuals, respectively, and they were distributed into 71 GBs (genetic blocks) comparing 24 conserved ancestral GBs in A. thaliana [34,40]. Previous reports have suggested that the reshuffle process, namely whole-genome duplication/triplication (WGD/WGT), subsequently intertwined the fractionation and re-diploidization that were ubiquitous in the plant kingdom, which had different impacts on the gene sets/family [41,42]. Structural and functional evidence has suggested that having multiple copies of SWEET genes in eukaryotes allows for diversification in metabolic regulation. However, the puzzle of the molecular characteristics of SWEETs in B. rapa remains unresolved.

Sugars, being the primary products of photosynthesis, are one of the main forms of nutrients that are essential for plant growth and development. Sugar molecules play a central role in plant metabolism, as all other primary and many secondary metabolites are biosynthesized from varieties of sugars. For their availability, storage or utilization in the target organs or tissues, sugars are needed to be transported from the source (photosynthetic) tissues to the sink (non-photosynthetic) tissues through the phloem. However, for both the uploading and downloading of these sugars in the source and sink tissues respectively, various transporters are of utmost necessity. The sugars will eventually be exported transporters (SWEETs) constitute a unique class of sugar transporters that are part of the transporter-opsin-G protein-coupled receptor (TOG) superfamily of integral membrane proteins (Yee et  al. 2013). Typically, the SWEET transporters comprise of 7 transmembrane (TM) domains, having the repeat order in a pair of tandem repeats of 3 TM domains which are separated by a single TM (Xuan et al. 2013). The SWEET proteins are distributed amongst various plant species, and an estimated presence of about 20 paralogs is of general occurrence in the genomes of all angiosperms (Eom et al. 2015). It is estimated that sucrose transporters (SUT) and SWEETs play an interlinked role in importing and exporting sugars induced by Oryza sativa L. DNA BINDING WITH ONE FINGER 11 in the developing sink tissues (Wu et  al. 2019). Along with the primary role of hexose and sucrose transport (Eom et al. 2015), the SWEET transporters have been shown to carry out diverse physiological functions ranging from roles in nectar secretion in Arabidopsis, Brassica and Nicotiana (Lin et al. 2014), senescence induction in Arabidopsis and rice (Zhou et al. 2014), phloem loading and seed flling (Jeena et al. 2019), to pollen development (Engel et al. 2005) and nourishment (Sun et al. 2013) in Arabidopsis. Moreover, the SWEET proteins demonstrated signifcant roles in regulating the development of reproductive tissue in soybean, as well as responding to multiple stresses in cotton plant and in latex production in Hevea brasiliensis (Willd. ex A.Juss.) Müll.Arg. (Patil et al. 2015; Sui et al. 2017; Zhao et al. 2018). Similarly, a few other studies have also implicated the role of SWEET transporters in early seed development of litchi, response to pathogenic cues in rice and biofuel production in sorghum (Mizuno et al. 2016; Zaka et al. 2018; Wu et al. 2019; Xie et al. 2019). Additionally, the observation that direct induction of some of the OsSWEET members of rice by transcriptional activator-like proteins (TALs) of pathogens, indicates the involvement of SWEET transporters in biotic stresses on plants (Jeena et al. 2019). TAL-mediated induction of OsSWEET11–15 during Xanthomonas oryzae infestation not only enhanced the levels of sugars in the apoplast around them (Zhou et al. 2015) but also assisted the pathogen’s development on infected rice plants (Streubel et al. 2013). TAL also induced the expression of citrus CsSWEET1 due to infection by $X$ . Citri (Hu et al. 2014). OsSWEET11 and OsSWEET13 were found to induce resistance towards X. Oryzae and further host-microbe interaction study between rice OsSWEET11, OsSWEET14 and OsSWEET13, led insight into how bacterial blight infuences these transporters (Chu et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2006; Antony et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2010; Liu et al. 2011). Although the role of SWEETs in dealing with biotic stresses is more prominent, there is undoubtedly, a notable response of SWEET transporters seen in the case of abiotic stresses as well. Application of cold stress in Arabidopsis, the AtSWEET15 depicted enhanced expression transcriptionally (He et al. 2008). In the tomato plant also, a type of MtN3/saliva/SWEET gene induced resistance to cold stress and pathogen stress via a mediating pepper transcription factor CaPIF1 (Seong 2007). Further, in Hordeum vulgare L., the MtN3/SWEETtype member with Contig8708 demonstrated signifcant up-regulation during salt stress (Walia et al. 2006). Most interestingly, the SWEET transporters in rice have been shown to be able to interact with various ion transporters and regulate ion transport (Yuan and Wang 2013). A signifcant fnding was that SWEETs in rice interacted with copper transporters (COPT/Ctr) and could infuence the copper levels in the plant (Yuan et al. 2010). The OsSWEET11 interacted with COPT1 and COPT5, and their expression helped recover the lack of copper intake in the yeast mutant, MPY7 which is normally defcient in copper (Yuan et al. 2010). The efect on copper-ion-homeostasis induced by SWEET members suggests its involvement in the cellular homeostasis of other micronutrients like iron, zinc and manganese (Yuan et al. 2011).

Rice (O. sativa), is the second most important cereal crop in the world and is used as the primary staple food for more than half of the world (Gross and Zhao 2014; Das et al. 2017). For the rice eating population of the world, it is one of the major sources of carbohydrates along with calcium, folate and vitamin E. Although, the demand for rice is ever increasing due to rapid expansion in population, during the cultivation of this semi-aquatic plant species under lowland fooded anaerobic conditions, they are exposed to various abiotic stresses due to changing climatic conditions or biogeochemical conversions, resulting in low productivity of rice grains. Exposure to various abiotic stresses is estimated to result in reduced photosynthesis, inhibition of water uptake and transport, imbalance of ions, de-stabilizing the membrane and oxidative stress among other unwanted efects in the plant cell, which ultimately lead to the severe reduction in growth, development as well as productivity of the afected plants (Rosa et al. 2009; Krasensky and Jonak 2012; Van den Ende and El-Esawe 2014). Among the diferent abiotic stressors, heavy metal or metalloid toxicity has emerged as one of the major constraints that afect rice crop productivity and quality (Singh et al. 2016). Amidst the different heavy metal (loid) s, cadmium (Cd) and arsenic (As) not only show signifcant bioaccumulation in rice grains but also results in severe toxicity afecting rice productivity. Very recently, carbohydrates have been identifed as potential agents for improved abiotic as well as heavy metal(loid) stress tolerance and mitigation in plants (Gupta and Kaur 2005; Sami et al. 2016; Breia et al. 2021). Although all the diferent classes of carbohydrates can play a signifcant role as antioxidants, it is the disaccharide sucrose, which in spite of possessing moderate antioxidant capacity, is regarded to play a major role in the control of oxidative stress-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plant cells due to its small size and ease of transport (Gangola and Ramadoss 2018). Consequently, it is hypothesized that the hexose and sucrose transporter SWEET proteins may play a signifcant role in the mitigation of abiotic, including heavy metal(loid) stress in rice plants. Therefore, to ascertain the role of SWEET transporters in abiotic and heavy metal(loid) stress tolerance in rice, a comprehensive understanding of the OsSWEET family in relation to abiotic and heavy metal(loid) stresses is of utmost importance to ensure food security for the growing world population.

Therefore, in this study, we have conducted a genomewide in silico analysis of OsSWEET genes of rice highlighting their genomic organization, phylogenetic relationship, gene structure, protein motifs, and the predicted expression of OsSWEET members under diferent abiotic as well as heavy metal(loid) stress conditions. In addition, we have analyzed the cis-regulatory elements of OsSWEEET promoters as well as their putative regulation via heavy metal(loid)- responsive microRNAs (miRNAs). Furthermore, we have characterized the protein-protein interaction networks of OsSWEETs under abiotic and heavy metal(loid) stresses in rice plants. This comprehensive study of the OsSWEET family should facilitate the discovery of functionality of the members with respect to various abiotic, especially heavy metal(loid) stresses, and create a bridge between the genetic regulation and involvement of these sugar transporters for productivity improvement of rice crop in future.

Sugars are the important source of energy for both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Depending on their need organisms have established diferent ways to promote sugar transport across the cell membrane by maintaining the rate of sugar infux and efux. Over the last two decades, various sugar transporters were identifed in bacteria, fungi, plants and humans, which perform an important role in development, metabolism, growth, and homeostasis (Chen et al. 2010). Presently, sugar transporters were categorized into three distinct superfamilies which includes the major facilitator superfamily such as glucose transporters (GLUTs) (Deng et al. 2015), the sodium solute symporter family, such as sodium glucose cotransporters (SGLTs) and Sugar Will Eventually be Exported Transporter (SWEET) proteins (Xuan et al. 2013; Tao et al. 2015). On the basis of genome wide analysis, various number of SWEET genes have been identifed in plants, including 17 in Arabidopsis thaliana (Chen et al. 2010), 21 in Oryza sativa (Yuan and Wang 2013), 23 in Sorghum bicolor (Mizuno et al. 2016), 52 in Glycine max (Patil et al. 2015), 35 in Solanum tuberosum (Manck-Gotzenberger and Requena 2016), 29 in Solanum lycopersicum (Feng and Frommer 2015), 33 in Malus domestica (Wei et al. 2014) and 17 in Vitis vinifera (Chong et al. 2014). Based on the number of 3-TM domain, SWEET proteins have been classifed into three major types, one is semiSWEET which is found in bacteria containing only one 3-TM domain, another one is SWEET which is found in eukaryotes attached via linker element between two 3-TM domains (7-TM) and the third one is extraSWEET which might evolve due to gene duplication of 7-TM (Xuan et al. 2013; Patil et al. 2015). The recently identifed family of SWEET sugar transporters in plants perform crucial roles in various developmental processes such as pollen nutrition (Sun et al. 2013) nectar secretion (Lin et al. 2014), seed flling (Chen et al. 2015), phloem loading function for distance translocation of sucrose (Chen et al. 2012) and regulating gibberellin response (Kanno et al. 2016). SWEET sugar transporter family seemingly translocate carbohydrates to diferent plant tissues, including both monocots and dicots.

The originating members of SWEET sugar transporters were studied to fnd out the function of membrane proteins in plants by using diferent fuorescent sugar sensors techniques. AtSWEET1 and AtSWEET8 are the frst identifed SWEET proteins in Arabidopsis which transport hexose sugars. Similar fuorescent sucrose sensors were used to identify other SWEET members which can transport sucrose (Chen et al. 2012; Lin et al. 2014). SWEET members may also function in the mobilization of carbohydrates mainly glucose, galactose, and fructose, which accumulate on leaves during senescence (Chen et al. 2010). Phylogenetic analysis of SWEET proteins reveals that they are broadly conserved in eukaryotes and ubiquitous in plants. The SWEET protein family is further subdivided into fve diferent clades in which four clades were represented by plants, and one clade is represented by metazoans (Chen et al. 2010). Seven SWEET genes have been identifed in the genome of Caenorhabditis elegans while only a single SWEET gene have been identifed in humans and mice. In Arabidopsis thaliana, a total of 17 SWEET homologs classifed as AtSWEET1 to AtSWEET17 which bidirectionally transport both mono and disaccharides along the substrate concentration gradient and across the plasma membrane (Chen et al. 2015). Interestingly, pathogen infection such as Xanthomonas oryzae causing blight disease in rice directly induces the expression of SWEET genes to utilize sucrose from the plant (Chen et al. 2010). In the past few years, many reviews have been published on sucrose and glucose transporters mainly focussed on its physiological role in plants and animals, but little is known till date about this novel family of SWEETs sugar transporter. In this review, we will be summarizing the structure, evolution, transport mechanism, diverse physiological roles of SWEET proteins and their applications in the feld of agriculture.
