In this study, we provides comprehensive information on the ClLAX, ClPIN and ClABCB gene families and expression patterns of those genes exposed to salt, drought and cold stresses. The distinctive tissuespecific expression patterns of the ClLAX, ClPIN and ClABCB genes, and their differential responses to salt, drought and cold stresses are the molecular basis to increase abiotic stress tolerance in watermelon. Our studies also provide a new insight into the expression of ClLAX, ClPIN and ClABCB gene families at the phase of grafting.

Auxin is a plant phytohormone that is essential for the initiation of tuberization in sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas (L.) Lam.). Auxin exerts these effects via polar auxin transport facilitated by various auxin influx and efflux carriers. It is unclear which members of the auxin transporter families: PIN, PILS, Aux/LAX, and ABCB, are involved in sweet potato tuber initiation and development. Therefore, a genome-wide analysis of the I. batatas auxin transporter genes was conducted, and their expression patterns during storage root initiation and development were analyzed. Five IbLAX, 16 IbPIN, 12 IbPILS, and 34 IbABCB family members were identified. These genes showed high conservation among families based on their intronexon structure, motif composition, and phylogenetic analysis. Additionally, the promoter regions of these genes had various cis-acting regulatory elements involved in hormone, light, and developmental responses. The auxin transporter genes were expressed in various sweet potato tissues, and many were differentially expressed during storage root development. IbLAX1, IbPIN13, IbPILS7, IbABCB1, and IbABCB14 showed up-regulated expression during tuber initiation. This study characterizes these auxin transporter gene families for the first time. These results are an important reference for validation studies to determine the specific functions of these genes and their auxin transporting capability.

Intra- and intercellular gradients of the plant hormone auxin are generated by a plant-specific cell-to-cell transport process that is designated as polar auxin transport (PAT; reviewed in Robert and Friml, 2009; Vanneste and Friml, 2009). Due to the chemical properties of the main relevant auxin, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), PAT is largely under the control of the plasma membrane (PM) efflux complex that is made up of auxin efflux catalysts of the PIN-FORMED (PIN) and the B family of ABC transporter (ABCB)/ PGP/MDR classes (Blakeslee et al., 2007; Mravec et al., 2008). ABCBs and PINs contribute to PAT independently for the most part (Blakeslee et al., 2007; Mravec et al., 2008), and this is reflected by generally distinct mutant phenotypes. Full-length PINs, which arose with the first land plants (Galván-Ampudia and Offringa, 2007), have mainly polar expression patterns and provide the basis for vectorial mass transport of auxin (Geisler and Murphy, 2006). On the other hand, ancient ABCBs are mainly multilaterally expressed and are thought to function primarily in minimizing apoplastic reflux in apical tissues with high auxin content (Geisler et al., 2005; Geisler and Murphy, 2006; Matsuda et al., 2011).

Whereas regulation of PIN-mediated auxin efflux is well characterized on both the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels, significantly less is known for ABCBs. Current work has focused on the interaction of ABC transporter B1/P-GLYCOPROTEIN1 (ABCB1/PGP1) and ABC transporter B19/P-GLYCOPROTEIN19/ MULTIDRUG-RESISTANCE1 (ABCB19/PGP19/MDR1) with the FK506 binding protein42 TWISTED DWARF1 (TWD1; Bailly et al., 2008). Physiological and growth defects in twd1 are caused by strongly reduced auxin efflux capacities in twd1 and abcb1 abcb19 leading to similarly reduced long-range IAA transport, which results in elevated or reduced auxin accumulation in abcb1 abcb19 and twd1 roots and shoots, respectively (Bailly et al., 2008). This is documented by a close overlap between twd1 and abcb1 abcb19 dwarf phenotypes and undirected helical disorientation of overall plant growth. However, abcb1 abcb19 mutants show less severe dwarfism, suggesting malfunction of additional components (Geisler and Bailly, 2007). This holds true also for the stronger disorientation of epidermal layers (twisting) in twd1 roots and hypocotyls (Geisler et al., 2003; Geisler and Bailly, 2007; Bailly et al., 2008). This is, in contrast with alleles carrying mutations in microtubules or microtubule-associated proteins, not fixed-handed (Hashimoto, 2002; Weizbauer et al., 2011), making a direct connection to microtubule dynamics unlikely.

Epidermal twisting in twd1 was recently shown to be partially rescued by application of the diagnostic auxin transport inhibitor 1-N-naphtyl-phthalamic acid (NPA). This suggests that at least a part of this phenotype is the result of defects in PAT (Wu et al., 2010). Interestingly, both ABCBs and TWD1 have been shown to bind NPA resulting in disruption of ABCB–TWD1 interaction and, thus, ABCB inhibition (Bailly et al., 2008). As a consequence, abcb1 abcb19 and twd1 root gravitropism, although reduced, is less sensitive to NPA (Bailly et al., 2008).

A special mechanism for directing auxin through tissues to its sites of action was recognized even before the chemical structure of this important plant hormone was deduced (Went & Thimann,1937). Socalled polar auxin transport was hypothesized to result from channels releasing the auxin anion $( { \mathsf { I A A } } ^ { - } )$ across the plasma membrane,down a large thermodynamic gradient,more so at one end of the cell than the other (Goldsmith,1977；Raven,1975；Rubery & Sheldrake,1974).

Mathematical models indicated that a twofold higher permeability of the membrane to auxin at one end of each cell in a file would produce the auxin transport rates and high degree of directional bias through tissues (Goldsmith et al.,1981;Mitchison,1981).The breakthrough discovery of PIN-FORMED (PIN) proteins accorded well with the theory because their sequences are consistent with a solute transport function, they are localized at the plasma membrane predominantly at the downstream ends of auxin-transporting cells,and mutant analysis showed them to be required for polar auxin transport (Chen et al.，1998;Gälweiler et al.，1998；Krecek et al.，2009；Okada et al.,1991; Wisniewska et al., 2006).When PIN proteins were shown to reduce the amount of radioactive auxin retained in non-plant cells engineered to express them，indicating they were capable of auxin transport (Chen etal.,1998;Petrasek etal.,2006), the mechanism of polar auxin transport through tissues appeared to be well understood.However,a PIN-only explanation became insufficient when members of the B subfamily of ATP-Binding Cassette (ABCB) transporters were also shown to be essential for polarauxin transport (Noh et al.,2O01; Terasaka et al.,2O05),and also capable of promoting auxineflux as indicated by auxin retention assays (Blakeslee et al.，2007；Cho et al.，2007；Geisler et al.，2005；Petrasek et al.,2006;Yang & Murphy,2009).Of the two types of proteins required for polar auxin transport,only PIN proteins are localized predominantly at one end of cells.Yet the uniformly distributed ABCB proteins are also required for directionally biased release of auxin from cells.It is important to understand how the ABCB transporters playan essential role in the polar auxin transport mechanism.The twd1 mutation prevents multiple auxin-related ABCB transporters from reaching the plasma membrane (Wu, Otegui,et al.,201O).The twd1 mutation does not affect the polar localization of PIN transporters in the same cells,yet it severely impairs polar auxin transport (Bouchard et al.，2OO6).Thus,asymmetrically placed PIN proteins appear insufficient to produce polar auxin transport through tissues. ABCB proteins at the plasma membrane are also required.An explanation of this requirement is needed in order to understand the polar auxin transport mechanism.

One published explanation of the requirement for ABCB proteins in polar auxin transport (Noh et al.,2Oo3) required substantial modificationafter further investigation.Mutations in ABCB genes apparently do not grossly affect the localization of PlN proteins,but they appear to make PIN protein localization more sensitive to disruption by the Triton X-1OO detergent, indicating that ABCB proteins may stabilize PIN proteins in some particular membrane contexts (Titapiwatanakun et al.,2008).

A different potential explanation for why ABCB and PIN proteins are required for polar auxin transport is that they function differently when together than either does separately.This synergistic effect would occur where the two protein types co-reside at the downstream face of each cell. Consistent with this synergistic function idea, ABCB and PIN proteins have been shown to interact physically (Blakeslee etal.,2OO7).Fora critical review of the topic of ABCB and PIN functional cooperativity and its implications for polar auxin transport, see Geisler et al.(2017).

A functional synergy,ora new transport property that manifests when ABCB and PIN proteins are co-expressed,may be difficult to detect with an auxin retention assay.A method that directly measures auxin movement across the membrane while controlling the variables that affect transport may be more effective.The electrophysiological patch-clamp technique can be such a method if the transported substance bears an electric charge.At the pH of cytoplasm,essentially all of the auxin is ${ \mathsf { I A A } } ^ { - }$ ,and release of the ${ \mathsf { I A A } } ^ { - }$ from cells is thermodynamically passive (Goldsmith，1977；Raven，1975；Spalding，2013). Therefore,ABCB and PIN proteins are expected to be electrogenic, meaning their transport activities should produce an electric current that the patch-clamp method may be able to measure.This approach is considered to be a rigorous method for characterizing the functions of plant electrogenic transporters (Dreyer et al.,1999).

A previous report established the feasibility of using heterologous expression and patch clamping to study plant ABCB protein activity (Cho et al.，2014). The ABCB19 protein from Arabidopsis was expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells.Whole-cell patch clamp analyses using NaCl-based electrolytes demonstrated that ABCB19 produced electrogenic transport activity.The ABCB19 currents were carried more by $\mathtt { C l } ^ { - }$ than ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ .The Cho et al. (2014) study was not designed to measure transport of ${ \mathsf { I A A } } ^ { - }$ .The present paper extends the approach of Cho et al. (2014) to determine if the patchclamp technique can directly measure ${ \mathsf { I A A } } ^ { - }$ transport by ABCB and PIN proteins and if some synergy resulting from their co-expression can be detected. The experiments used ABCB4 and PIN2 because these members of the two protein families are expressed in the same outer cell layers of the Arabidopsis root;both are required for shootward polar auxin transport through the root epidermis (Band et al.,2014;Kubes et al.,2012),and both participate in the root gravitropism response (Abas et al., 20O6; Lewis et al.,2O07).They are a logical pair of proteins to study separately and together with electrophysiological methods in order to advance our understanding of the polar auxin transport mechanism.

## The specifc amino acid sites of UMAMIT binding subtracts determined the subtracts specifcity


Amino acid synthesis occurs in various organelles within specifc tissues, such as chloroplasts, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and vesicles. For instance, aromatic amino acids (Trp, Phe, and Tyr), branched-chain amino acids (Leu, Ile, Val, Thr, Met, and Lys), His, Asp, and Arg are primarily synthesized in chloroplasts (Binder 2010; Jander and Joshi 2010; Lynch and Dudareva 2020; Maeda and Dudareva 2012; Slocum 2005; Yoo et al. 2013). These require amino acid transport proteins located at diferent sites to transport amino acids synthesized at diferent regions in the cell. In our study, we predicted the subcellular localization of UMAMITs from sixteen species and found that 314 UMAMIT proteins were localized in the cell membrane, 100 proteins in chloroplasts, 20 in the cytoplasm, 6 in the Golgi apparatus, 3 in the nucleus, and only 1 in the mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum respectively (Fig. 1; Table S3). This specifc subcellular localization information suggests the unique types of amino acids transported by diferent UMAMIT proteins. Protein structure predictions of UMAMIT14 and 18 also revealed that the amino acid binding sites of UMAMIT proteins are specifc, despite their overall structural similarity (Fig. 4). Zhao et al. (2021) also reported that mutations with the strongest efect are found in amino acids within both structural repeats, near or in TM5 or TM10 (Zhao et al. 2021). Analysis of expression patterns indicated that members of the same clade coordinate amino acid transport in various tissues and stages of plant growth and development (Fig. 5). This provides new insights into the transport of amino acids between cells and tissues.


## UMAMIT diferent from other amino acid transporters


Amino acid transporters can be classifed into three major families: ATF (Amino acid Transporter Family, also known as AAAP family), APC (Amino acid-Polyamine-Choline transporter family), and UMAMIT. These proteins share common characteristics such as broad expression patterns, wide substrate selectivity, and multiple physiological functions (Yang et al. 2020). Some members of the ATF and APC families, such as AAP1, AAP5, LHT1, LHT6, and ProT2, have been identifed as amino acid input vectors involved in root uptake. Additionally, AAP2, AAP3, AAP5, ProT1, CAT1, CAT6, and CAT9 contribute to phloem loading (Dinkeloo et al. 2018; Mechthild 2014; Rentsch 2010; Tegeder 2012). Unlike these two families, UMAMIT family members are exporter or bidirectional transporter proteins for amino acids. AtUMAMIT18 (SiAR1) is the frst amino acid transporter with clearly established export properties and and AtUMAMIT31 in subfamily I facilitate passive efux from the cytosol to the apoplast along the electrochemical gradient (Xu et al. 2023). Furthermore, the yeast expressing AtUMAMIT24 predominantly secretes Glu and Asp, while AtUMAMIT25 mainly secretes Glu and Arg. AtUMAMIT14 functions as an output protein for various amino acids when expressed in yeast. AtUMAMIT01 is responsible for ALA uptake, and AtUMAMIT18 catalyzes His efux and Gln and Asp uptake in yeast (Besnard et  al. 2016, 2018, 2021; Ladwig et  al. 2012; Zhao et  al. 2021). Further research on the mechanisms and regulation of these transporters will provide valuable insights into their roles in plant biology

bidirectional Gln transport in oocytes (Ladwig et al. 2012). Moreover, UMAMIT transporters also transport other substrates such as auxin (Ranocha et al. 2013; Xu et al. 2023). Our protein prediction of the UMAMIT family in amino acid transport has revealed potential molecular mechanisms and ofers insights into the transportation process of amino acids within plant tissues.


## Functional divergence and evolution of UMAMIT


Previous studies have examined the evolutionary analysis of 180 UMAMITs from 7 species including Arabidopsis, rice, M. truncatula, Selaginella moellendorf, Physcomitrella patens, Pinus pinaster, and Picea abies (Zhao et al. 2021). However, the study by Zhao et al. lacks UMAMITs from algae, which are essential for understanding the gene family’s origin, and gymnosperms, which are considered primitive seed plants. Furthermore, they did not explore the evolutionary history of the EamA structure, which is vital for comprehending its function. In this study, we conducted phylogenetic analysis of 375 UMAMITs across 16 key species in the evolutionary history of plants, ranging from algae to angiosperms. We found that UMAMITs may have originated from green algae and initially diversifed in bryophytes (Fig. 1), followed by a big expansion through gene duplication events in seed plants (Figs. 1 and 6). During evolution, the stabilization of the EamA structure was gradually completed in hornworts (Fig. 3). Our protein structure prediction revealed that the four-helix bundle motif is crucial in controlling the UMAMIT switch for exporting amino acid (Fig. 4). We hypothesize that the specifc amino acids in the amino acid binding region determine the type of amino acids being transported. Additionally, we have also compiled a summary of the functions of all identifed UMAMIT genes to date (Fig. 6; Table S5).

We have attempted to summarize the functions of UMAMIT genes in plant evolution in Fig. 6. In seeds, AtUMAMIT24 in subfamily I is known to transport amino acids such as Glu and Arg from the bead pore through the syncytial seed coat to the developing embryo (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT25 in subfamily I functions as an amino acid exporter, unloading amino acids from endosperm cells for use by the developing embryo (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT29, AtUMAMIT30, and AtUMAMIT31 in subfamily I are involved in exporting glucosinolates in seeds (Xu et al. 2023). AtUMAMIT28 and AtUMAMIT29 in subfamily I export amino acids like Ala and Glu from the phloem to the developing embryo (Müller et al. 2015). The high expression of these subfamily members in siliques, as indicated by the expression patterns analysis (Fig. 5), suggests their crucial role in seed nutrient storage and their potential application in molecular breeding. In subfamily II, AtUMAMIT18 and AtUMAMIT14 are involved in the radial transport of amino acids in roots, and AtUMAMIT14 also plays a role in phloem ofoading. In subfamily III, AtUMAMIT05 is responsible for determining secondary cell wall thickness in wood fbers and promoting growth hormone export from isolated Arabidopsis vesicles (Ranocha et al. 2013). AtUMAMIT05 and AtUMAMIT36 in subfamily III participate in plant immune responses and stress responses (Denancé et al. 2013; Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). The specifc subcellular localization of these subfamily members, as indicated by our data (Fig. 1; Table S3), suggests their specifcity in various activities. In subfamily IV (clade 9), all members are found in green algae, bryophytes, and ferns. Only AtUMAMIT01 was reported to uptake Ala in yeast cell (Zhao et al. 2021). Further research is needed to explore the functions and precise mechanisms of these genes in plants, with the goal of developing crop varieties that have improved nutrient use efciency. For example, multiple mutations within an evolutionary lineage could be constructed to study their function.

Expression pattern analysis is a valuable tool for understanding gene function. We performed a comprehensive expression analysis using RNA-seq data to explore the expression profle of the UMAMITs in Arabidopsis and rice (Fig. S11, S12). The expression level was estimated for all AtUMAMITs detected from 47 tissues during diferent stages, except for ten genes (AtUMAMIT16-psi, AtUMAMIT29, AtUMAMIT35, AtUMAMIT36, AtUMAMIT38, AtUMAMIT39-psi, AtUMAMIT40, AtUMAMIT43-psi, AtUMAMIT45 and AtUMAMIT46) (Fig. S11). Among the expressed AtUMAMIT genes, AtUMAMIT24 and AtUMAMIT25, which are involved in amino acid export from seeds and endosperm, showed high expression levels during seed stages and were grouped into subfamily I (Fig. S11) (Besnard et al. 2021, 2018). Similarly, the majority of OsUMAMIT genes in subfamily I also exhibited expression in seeds, suggesting their potential involvement in seed development (Fig. 1, Fig. S12).

We selected 14 genes for Quantitative real-time PCR analysis according to RNA-seq data (Fig. S11). The results showed that the expression level of AtUMAMIT10, 14, 17 and 20 grouped into clade 3, were higher in the inforescence and siliques which suggested members of this clade are involved in reproductive and embryo development. Studies have showed that AtUMAMIT11, 14, 24, 25 of clade 3 as amino acids exporters play a role in seed loading and phloem unloading during seed development (Besnard et al. 2016, 2018; Müller et al. 2015). AtUMAMIT07 and 08 clustered into clade 7, were highly expressed in the root, inforescence and siliques. AtUMAMIT02-03 clustered into clade 9, and AtUMAMIT33 -34 clustered into clade 5, were highly expressed in the leaves, roots, inforescence and siliques. AtUMAMIT11 belonged to clade 3 and AtUMAMIT30 belonged to clade 2 specifcally predominantly expressed in roots (Fig. 5). These results indicated that the expression patterns of members of the same clade were often similar and the UMAMITs coordinate to transport amino acids at various stages of plant growth and development.

Amino acids are synthesized, utilized, and degraded in different compartments within the cell such as chloroplasts, cytoplasm, mitochondria and vesicles, and therefore amino acid transporters are required for distributing amino acids within the cell compartments and between plant organs (Binder 2010; Jander and Joshi 2010; Maeda and Dudareva 2012; Slocum 2005; Yoo et al. 2013). UMAMIT (2.A.7.4 in TCDB)/MtN21/EamA-like is a class of transporters that can transport multiple acids in plants (Denancé et al. 2014; Gamas 1996). UmamiT had been originally described as MtN21-like nodulins (Medicago truncatula Nodulin 21,

MtN21) which was initially identifed to be induced by nodulation in M. truncatula, belonging to superfamily of drug/metabolite transporters (DMT) (Gamas 1996; Jack et al. 2001). It was later found that homologs of UMAMITs are also present in the genomes of non-nodulated plants (Denancé et al. 2014). Although UMAMITs are named "usually multiple acids move in and out transporter", most of the identifed UMAMITs have been characterized as uniporters that export amino acids (Zhao et al. 2021).

Only a few members of UMAMITs have been characterized, and their precise mechanism not fully understood. NODULIN 21 (MtN21) was initially identified through screening an M. truncatula nodule library and named "nodulin" (Gamas 1996). WAT1 (AtUMAMIT05) was later discovered as a tonoplast-localized auxin transporter in Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) (Ranocha et al. 2013). It was found that AtUMAMIT05 regulates disease resistance and secondary cell wall formation. Homologs of AtUMAMIT05, such as SlWAT1 in Solanum lycopersicum and GhWAT1 in

Gossypium hirsutum, are induced by auxin and promote lignin deposition and xylem diferentiation (Busov et al. 2004; Lee et al. 2021; Ranocha et al. 2013; Tang et al. 2019). Another member, 5NG4 in Pinus taeda, is also induced by auxin and promotes adventitious root formation (Busov et al. 2004). Inactivation of AtUMAMIT05 enhances broad-spectrum resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum, Xanthomonas campestris and Verticillium dahlia (Denancé et al. 2013). SiAR1 (AtUMAMIT18, Siliques Are Red1, SiAR1) is the frst amino acid transporter with clearly established export properties (Denancé et al. 2014). AtUMAMIT18 has been characterized as a bidirectional transporter of amino acids, playing a crucial role in the allocation of organic nitrogen, particularly in the accumulation of amino acids in seeds (Ladwig et al. 2012). AtUMAMIT11, 14, 24, 25, 28, and 29 act as amino acid exporters and are involved in seed loading and phloem unloading during seed development (Besnard et al. 2016, 2018; Müller et al. 2015). AtUMAMIT24 and AtUMAMIT25 are implicated in amino acid transfer within seeds (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT14 and AtUMAMIT18 are also involved in phloem unloading in the roots (Besnard et al. 2016; Ladwig et al. 2012). UMAMIT14 and UMAMIT36 participate in plant immune responses and stress responses (Besnard et al. 2021; Denancé et al. 2013; Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). Overexpression of AtUMAMIT14 promotes the resistance to Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (Besnard et al. 2021). AtUMAMIT36 (Resistance to Phytophthora parasitica 1, RTP1) located in the endoplasmic reticulum, negatively regulates signaling pathways of plant resistance to biotrophic pathogens like Phytophthora parasitica, Golovinomyces cichoracearum, and Pseudomonas syringae (Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). AtUMAMIT29, 30, and 31 have recently been identifed as glucosinolate exporters, and loss-of-function mutants of these transporters show signifcantly reduced levels of seed glucosinolates (Xu et al. 2023). Glucosinolates are sulfur-containing compounds with important roles in plant defense against herbivores and pathogens. In addition, MtUMAMIT14 plays a role in nodule formation and nitrogenfxation in Medicago truncatula (Garcia et al. 2023). AtUMAMIT44 exports glutamate from chloroplasts, which is vital for controlling nitrogen availability within source leaf cells and for sink nutrition (Samantha et al. 2024). TaUMAMIT17 is an amino acid exporter which might promote to grain development in wheat (Fang et al. 2022).

Recently, UMAMITs has been identified at the genome level in some plant species. A total of 47 and 53 UMAMITs were found in Arabidopsis and rice transcriptomes, including 3 and 2 pseudogenes, respectively (Zhao et al. 2021). In wheat (Triticum aestivum), 213 UMAMITs were identifed (Fang et al. 2022). 88 UMAMITs from M. truncatula (MtUMAMITs), 53 from Oryza sativa (rice) (OsUMAMITs), 16 from Selaginella moellendorf, 8 from

Physcomitrella patens, 13 from Pinus pinaster, and 48 from Picea abies were used for phylogenetic analysis (Zhao et al. 2021). Despite the identifcation of UMAMITs in various plant species, their evolutionary history and functional diversity across the plant kingdom has not been fully explored.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the origins of the UMAMIT gene families. We utilized genomic and transcriptome data from numerous plant and algal species to explore the systematic evolution and classifcation of the UMAMIT gene family. By analyzing conserved motifs and predicting protein tertiary structures, we identifed key amino acids and motifs that control the switch of UMAMITs. Additionally, we examined gene expression patterns to gain insights into the potential functions of UMAMIT family genes. Our study also summarized the functions of all identifed UMAMITs, providing valuable information on the evolution of UMAMITs and their potential application in molecular breeding for developing crop varieties with improved nutrient use efciency.

Members of large multi-gene families often display overlapping functions. Since many amino acid transporters act on the same substrates, specificity may derive from their expression patterns and their responses to environmental signals [14]. For example, the Arabidopsis AAP1 and AAP2 transporters display a preference for neutral and acidic amino acids. However, an analysis of promoter–GUS reporter lines revealed that AAP1 was expressed in the developing endosperm and cotyledons, thus strongly suggesting that AAP1 functions in the import of amino acids into the endosperm embryo. By contrast, AAP2 was highly expressed in the vascular tissue of stems and siliques, suggesting a role in amino acid retrieval and uptake into seeds. Moreover, although the Arabidopsis ProT1 and ProT2 proteins both transport the compatible solute proline, the expression pattern of their encoding genes responds differently to water and salt stress [63].

Nonetheless, not all related transporters share the same substrate specificity, as suggested by the characterization of selected amino acid transporters that differ both in their range of substrates and in their site(s) of action. Recently, Choi showed that Arabidopsis LHT2 can transport 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC), a biosynthetic precursor of ethylene, when expressed in Xenopus oocytes [112]. In addition, UMAMIT5, also called WALLS ARE THIN1 (WAT1), has been ascribed the function of indole-3-acetic acid exporter from the vacuole to the cytosol, unlike other UMAMIT members [18,109]. Seven members of the UMAMIT family have been suggested to play a role in the seed loading process, but their individual expression patterns differ during this process, suggesting that they play distinct roles in amino acid translocation from maternal to filial tissues. Indeed, the phenotypes associated with single umamit loss-of-function mutants are relatively benign, consistent with the involvement of multiple exporters in amino acid transport to developing seeds. Similarly, Arabidopsis LHT6 and AAP1 are expressed in root cells and display overlapping functions in root amino acid uptake. However, they also exhibit different substrate preferences. For example, Perchlik showed that LHT6 is involved in the uptake of acidic amino acids, such as glutamine and alanine, and probably phenylalanine, whereas AAP1 transports neutral amino acids and glutamate when amino acids are present at low concentrations [49]. In the feeding experiments, root uptake of the amino acids alanine, glutamine, proline, serine, glutamate, and phenylalanine significantly decreased in lht6 aap1 double mutant plants. Interestingly, the growth of the lht6 aap1 double mutant was not affected when grown on Murashige and Skoog medium, possibly because other amino acid transporters expressed in the root can compensate for their loss [49]. Similarly, Arabidopsis LHT1 and AAP5 assimilate neutral and acidic amino acids, respectively, and displayed non-overlapping specificity in their substrates, suggesting that they have separate roles in amino acid uptake [50].

Here we have identified UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 as glucosinolate exporters with a key role in the accumulation of glucosinolates in seeds as evidenced by less than $6 \%$ of glucosinolates in seeds of umamit29 umamit30 umamit31 exporter mutants compared with the wild-type level. We previously identified the active high-affinity $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled glucosinolate importers (GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3) and showed that the elimination of seed glucosinolates in the gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 triple mutants was accompanied by altered accumulation patterns of glucosinolates in the rest of the plant8–12. The suppression of this phenotype in the umamit29 umamit30 gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 quintuple mutant provides genetic evidence that UMAMITs function as the exporters that deliver glucosinolates to the apoplast.

The biochemical and biophysical characterization of UMAMIT29–31 in oocytes shows that glucosinolates are exported passively along an electrochemical gradient. In Arabidopsis, in which the plasma membrane potential under physiological conditions is within the range of −100 to $- 1 5 0 \mathrm { m V }$ (ref. 31), UMAMIT29–31 are expected to facilitate efficient export of the monovalent anionic glucosinolates out of biosynthetic cells to the acidic apoplast. A recent theory-based study hypothesized that the mechanism for nutrient homeostasis aimed at reaching a desired cytosolic concentration of a given nutrient requires that at least two differently energized transporter types are involved13. The presence of passive UMAMIT exporters and $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled GTR importers fulfils this requirement. Accordingly, the $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled high-affinity GTR importers empty the apoplast for glucosinolates generating a strong outward chemical gradient (from the cytosol to apoplast), which— together with the strong negative membrane potential—promotes efficient export of glucosinolates through the passive uniport mechanism of UMAMIT29–31. Notably, the glucosinolate exporters as well as the exporters of sugars (SUGARS WILL EVENTUALLY BE EXPORTED TRANSPORTERS (SWEETs))32,33 and amino acids (UMAMITs)26,27 are all uniporters, which suggests the presence of a universal passive uniport mechanism for exporting compounds from symplasm in source tissues.

UMAMIT29–31 belong to UMAMIT clade I proteins (UMAMIT26–32) of which UMAMIT26–31 are brassicaceous-specific (Extended Data Fig. 9). This highlights the potential of transporter families involved in primary metabolism to evolve substrate specificity towards specialized metabolites as recently shown for the NPF family34–40. Analogously, the identification of UMAMITs as exporters of glucosinolates suggests that the UMAMIT family may represent a new family of exporters of specialized metabolites. Notably, the substrate specificity of the three UMAMITs exporters, with UMAMIT29 and UMAMIT30 having broad substrate specificity and UMAMIT31 being specific for indolic glucosinolates, is mirrored in the three GTR importers, with GTR1 and GTR2 having broad substrate specificity and GTR3 favouring indolic glucosinolates9 , indicating co-evolution of substrate preferences across these distinct transporter families. Previous studies on the amino acid export activity


## Article


of UMAMITs using Xenopus oocytes27 and Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells29 have reported different outcomes, which may reflect difficulties in measuring transport activity of primary metabolites that are concomitantly being metabolized by the heterologous host expressing the transporter. The minor alteration in free amino acid levels in seeds of various umamit mutants and myb28 myb29 (MYB28 and MYB29 are master regulators of aliphatic glucosinolates), as well as gtr1 gtr2 mutants41, merits future studies to investigate the relationship between glucosinolates and free amino acids in seeds.

On the basis of the overlapping presence of UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 with glucosinolate biosynthetic marker enzymes in the funiculus at the mature green stage, we propose that the funiculus acts as a major glucosinolate source tissue from where UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 export de novo synthesized seed-bound glucosinolates into the apoplast, and that the secondarily activated high-affinity $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled GTRs subsequently import them into the phloem through which the glucosinolates are translocated to the seeds. Generally, understanding the seed loading process has been hampered owing to a lack of tools, as transporter mutants of primary metabolites such as sucrose and amino acids—for which importers and exporters are already known—often have pleiotropic effects42–45. The latter is typically not the case for specialized metabolite transporters. The glucosinolate UMAMIT exporters, along with the GTR importers, are essential for seed accumulation and provide powerful molecular tools to dissect the process of seed loading to the embryo.

Transport engineering that uses altered expression of transporter genes to change metabolite distribution patterns has resulted in the development of improved agronomic traits2–5,46. Here we show that umamit29 umamit30 umamit31 exporter mutants do not alter the overall distribution of glucosinolates in the plant, which contrast with either reduction (roots, stems) or strong overaccumulation (rosette, cauline leaves, silique valves) in the gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 glucosinolate importer mutants. Thus, from an agricultural perspective, UMAMIT exporters have high biotechnological potential as molecular breeding targets for eliminating anti-nutritional glucosinolates in seed cake of brassicaceous oilseed crops through transport engineering without affecting glucosinolate defence in the rest of the plant.

Cation $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (CAXs) mediate vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sequestration and are critical for maintaining cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ homeostasis in plants. Arabidopsis CAX1, a member of the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C }$ ation Antiporter (CaCA) superfamily, features a modular architecture comprising two pseudosymmetrical domains separated by a cytosolic loop called the acidic motif. CAX1 is also regulated by a cytosolic N-terminal autoinhibitory domain. To define the structural basis of CAX1 activity, we characterized truncated constructs of the N-terminal half of CAX1, comprising a 6-transmembrane (TM) module lacking the autoinhibitory domain (½N-sCAX1), using yeast complementation, structural modeling, and protein interaction studies. The $\% \mathrm { N }$ -sCAX1 monomer folded into a stable topology but it failed to interact with itself or with full-length CAX1, or confer transport activity. Functional reconstitution required tethering two ½N-sCAX1 modules via the acidic motif or removal of TM1, which restored partial $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in yeast. Protein interaction assays revealed that the autoinhibitory domain contributes to ½N-CAX1 dimerization, while TM1 interferes with complex assembly. Structural models demonstrated that correct alignment of the conserved GNxxE motif across ½N-sCAX1 monomers, either by artificial tethering or potentially by higher order hexameric oligomerization, is essential to reconstruct a functional $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -binding pocket. These findings show that CAX1 functionality depends on specific topological constraints and modular interactions that guide formation of CAX1 halves. Our results highlight how architectural features such as TM1 and the autoinhibitory domain regulate transporter assembly and activity, offering insight into CaCA biogenesis and providing a framework for engineering transporters with tailored functional properties.


## Key message


We dissect the structure–function mechanisms of the Arabidopsis vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter CAX1 by analyzing its N-terminal half. Modular fragments alone are inactive but can assemble into tethered dimers that restore $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, revealing structural constraints on activity. The study unveils fresh perspectives on the evolutionary dynamics and functional diversity of CAXs, indicating broader implications for calcium transport across various organisms.

Keywords Vacuole $\cdot$ Transport $\cdot$ Calcium $\cdot$ Yeast $\cdot$ Arabidopsis

Calcium $( \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } )$ is essential for plant growth and development, with roles ranging from structural stabilization of cell walls and membranes to acting as a second messenger in many signaling pathways (White and Broadley 2003, Hepler 2005). The transport of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ across biological membranes is central to these physiological processes (Demidchik et al. 2018). While cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ levels are maintained at micromolar concentrations, higher concentrations are compartmentalized in organelles such as the vacuole, through the action of ATP-driven $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ pumps and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchangers (Spalding and Harper 2011; Pittman and Hirschi 2024). Among these, the high-capacity, low-affinity $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchangers, known as cation exchangers (CAX), are key to sequestering $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ into the vacuole and resetting cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signals (Peiter 2011). Because membrane transporters directly control mineral partitioning and hormone homeostasis, understanding their modular architecture provides a foundation for engineering plants with altered nutritional or signaling profiles (Magidin et al. 2003; Hirschi 2003).

Structural studies of bacterial and yeast CaCAs—including VCX1, YfkE, and AfCAX—demonstrate a conserved architecture of two pseudosymmetrical domains comprising 10–12 transmembrane (TM) helices and conserved residues of the ${ \bf { q } } .$ -repeat regions (such as the GNxxE motif) required for cation coordination (Wu et al. 2013; Nishizawa et al. 2013; Waight et al. 2013). The two domains form a core $5 + 5$ TM repeat structure separated by a cytosolic acidic loop, and this organization underpins the transport mechanism conserved throughout CaCA proteins (Mao et al. 2021). While many CaCA proteins, including VCX1 and AfCAX, appear to display a monomeric structural architecture within the lipid bilayer (Nishizawa et al. 2013; Waight et al. 2013), YfkE has been proposed to form a trimeric structure composed of three identical copies of the YfkE monomer (Wu et al. 2013). Recently, a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) structural analysis of CAX1 from Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) has suggested that it also may assemble into a trimer made of three protomers (monomers) of CAX1 (Wang et al. 2025). However, further examination of the two pseudosymmetrical domains that make up a CAX1 protomer has not been performed.

CAX1 is autoinhibited by a cytosolic N-terminal tail before TM1, and removal of this region (to give short-CAX1 or sCAX1) constitutively activates cation transport (Wang et al. 2024). This N-terminal autohibititory region adopts an $\mathfrak { a }$ -helical structure that physically obstructs the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport tunnel, serving as a steric blockade that prevents ion flux (Wang et al. 2025). Functional reconstitution experiments have shown that the N-terminal $( \% \mathrm { N } )$ half comprising TM helices 1–6 and C-terminal $( \% C )$ half comprising TM helices 7 – 11 of a CAX1 protomer can be expressed as separate polypeptides in yeast and can combine to restore transport activity, highlighting a modular basis for function, while ${ } ^ { 1 / 2 \mathrm { N } }$ -CAX1 (containing the first 36 amino acids of the autoinhibitory domain; Sarkar et al. 2024) can interact with and activate full-length CAX1 (Zhao et al. 2009a, b). Building on these earlier findings, we sought to clarify the modular structure–function relationship and mechanistic basis of these interactions.

Here, we focus on the ½N-sCAX1 module (Rhein et al. 2025), which lacks the first 36 amino acids of the autoinhibitory domain but retains TM1–6, to determine whether this module represents a minimal functional unit or an inactive precursor. We hypothesize that lack of the autoinhibitory domain reveals a core structure, potentially resembling an ancestral CaCA architecture that predates regulatory additions. This work thus explores the structural constraints governing CAX1 function but also how modular evolution may have driven the emergence of regulatory complexity in membrane transporters.

In plants, fungi, and bacteria control of cytosolic $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ levels has been attributed in part to a low affinity, high capacity $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchanger. These transporters have been biochemically characterized, and many of the open reading frames have been identified (7, 8, 10). Emerging genomic studies indicate common motifs among the characterized transporters and a burgeoning number of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchanger homologs (10). However, computer modeling studies, which attempt to ascribe transport function based on primary sequence information, are hindered by the lack of any biological studies focusing on the functional domains required for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchange. Utilizing the Arabidopsis CAX transporters and a robust yeast suppression screen, we have probed the structural basis of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchange.

Recently, we have shown that CAX1 may contain an Nterminal autoinhibitory domain (23). CAX2 and CAX3 may also contain N-terminal autoinhibitory domains. Thus, there may be additional elements that modulate plant $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchange; however, in the experiments detailed here, we have uniformly used CAX variants (CAX1 37–463) that do not contain this regulatory region.

Utilizing a yeast screen, a region of 9 amino acids (residues 87–95 in the CAX1 construct utilized here) can account for a large portion of the vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport differences between CAX1 and CAX3 (Figs. 2–4). The fact that CAX1 and CAX3 both appear to be highly expressed in yeast and localize at the yeast vacuole (13) (Fig. 1) suggests that we have identified a domain involved in transport and not protein stability or membrane targeting. Furthermore, the chimeric constructs differed significantly in their transport properties (Figs. 2 and 3) but were all expressed at approximately equal levels (Fig. 2B). The acidic motif (residues 264–282 in CAX1), which has been implicated in $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (7), did not define the majority of differences between the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport properties of CAX1 and CAX3 (Fig. 2). In yeast assays, when the 9-amino acid region from CAX1 was mobilized into CAX3, the chimeric gene product had a low $K _ { m }$ for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ and $3 6 . 5 \%$ of the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport capabilities of CAX1. The CAX3-9 construct differed from CAX1 in terms of ions that could compete with $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (Fig. 3B). $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ uptake by CAX1 was inhibited by $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ and $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ , indicating that it is able to transport both of these metals, whereas it appears that CAX3-9 can transport $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ but not $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ ; this suggests that interchanging this domain does not significantly alter the transport of other ions. Although these experiments certainly imply that this region is important in $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ specificity, the inability to fully confer CAX1-like phenotypes on CAX3 suggests that other regions in CAX1 affect some elements of $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport. However, consistent with the premise that this region defines an important component of the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ recognition differences between CAX1 and CAX3, when the nine-amino acid region from CAX3 was placed into CAX1, it totally inhibited CAX1-mediated vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (Fig. 2). Given these findings, we labeled this nine-amino acid region the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain.

The mechanism by which the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain regulates ion transport is unknown. This region appears to be a hydrophilic loop that separates membrane-spanning domains 1 and 2 (Fig. 6). The CAX1 hydrophobicity plot predicts that the N-terminal regulatory region and the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain are located on opposite sides of the membrane (orientation unknown). Furthermore, our preliminary results suggest that the N-terminal autoinhibitory domain does not directly interact with the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain.2 Thus, these two domains may act independently to regulate ion transport. Given the regulatory role of the N terminus, we favor a model in which the N terminus is cytoplasmic. This orientation would be consistent with the regulatory C terminus for animal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (24). With this membrane topology, the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain would be found inside the vacuole. Given that $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ binding or transport sites are usually acidic amino acids and no acidic amino acids are within this domain, it is unlikely the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain directly binds $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ ions. This region may restrict the movement of the transmembrane-spanning domains so that a $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ ion can either enter or be blocked from the “pore.”

The modifications of the CAX2 $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain further support the role of this region in $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ selectivity. Expression of CAX2 in yeast demonstrates that this transporter has a lower capacity for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport than does CAX1 (9). In our assay conditions in yeast, we found the apparent $K _ { m }$ for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ of both CAX1 and CAX2 to be $\sim 2 0 ~ \pm ~ 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ (data not shown); thus, the difference between these transporters appears to lie in their capacity to transport $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ . In plants, CAX2 localizes to the plant vacuolar membrane and transports metals and $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ into the vacuoles (22). When the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain of CAX1 was fused to CAX2, the result was an increase in vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport with no noticeable change in transport of other ions (Fig. 5).

A single leucine-to-isoleucine change in the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain allowed the CAX3 gene product to weakly suppress the yeast vacuolar transport mutant (Figs. 2 and 3). Furthermore, this single amino acid change conferred a relatively low apparent $K _ { m }$ for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ to the chimeric CAX3 (Fig. 4). This isoleucine may interact with side chains of specific amino acids from various transmembrane segments of CAX3 to aid in co-ordination of $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ or $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ . Thus, the CAX transporters may contain several $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domains that collectively coordinate ion transport. Given that our experimental procedure compared the CAX transporters to each other, we may have simply identified the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ domain that is the most polymorphic between these transporters.

Although structure/function studies of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchangers are limited, other cotransporters such as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters have been extensively studied (25–27). Histidine residues are candidates for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -sensing amino acids in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, and these face the cytoplasmic side. CAX1 contains only six histidine residues, but their role in transport has not been evaluated. Structural studies demonstrate a novel membraneprotein motif for the $E$ . coli $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter, NhaA. Other studies identify the mechanisms involved in $\mathrm { p H }$ sensitivity and cation binding and transport by $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (24). The fundamental mechanism of cotransporters may be conserved, so insights from those studies may help direct future work related to $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchangers.

Only in relatively few structure/function studies of $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ and heavy metal transporters have some of the amino acid residues that determine ion specificity, binding, or transport been identified (5, 6, 14, 28). This study identified residues in one particular domain of a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / C a ^ { 2 + } }$ exchanger that may be important for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ ion specificity. This type of approach may allow researches to alter the duration of cytosolic $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ pulses in different organisms. Some microbial antiporters appear to be able to mediate both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (7, 29). Using the appropriate yeast suppression screens, it may be feasible to map the substrate-determining regions for these transporters. In plant systems, the ability to modulate CAX-mediated transport and ectopically express these modified genes in plants offers the potential to manipulate both nutrient content and signal transduction events.

## Structural modeling of oligomeric CAX1 N-terminal modules


To evaluate whether the N-terminal module of a CAX1 monomer can form a functional transporter as a homodimer, we performed homology modeling using AlphaFold2. A monomeric $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ structure model was generated with high confidence (Table S1), which shares high structural conservation with the first 6 TM helices of the cryoEM CAX1 monomer (Fig. 1A). However, the ½N-sCAX1 dimer model lacked CAX1-like architecture (Fig. 1A) with CAX1 structure not conserved as determined by CAX1 monomer alignment (Fig. S1A). As a consequence, a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ binding pocket defined by the interaction of the $\mathfrak { a }$ -repeat regions, and notably by close proximity of Gly, Asn and Glu residues within the GNxxE motif on TM3 is predicted to be absent in the ½N-sCAX1 dimer model (Fig. 1B). In contrast, a model of a tethered $\mathrm { \Omega _ { / 2 N - s C A X 1 } ^ { 1 } }$ dimer linked by the acidic motif (½N-sCAX1-AM-½N-sCAX1) did resemble full length CAX1 monomer. This tethered ½N-sCAX1 dimer generates a 12-TM protein, in contrast to the 11-TM topology of a typical eukaryotic CAX, due to inclusion of both copies of TM helix 1 and retained CAX1-like structure (Fig. S1B). This ½N-sCAX1-AM-½N-sCAX1 model also has predicted alignment of both copies of TM helix 3 that should allow $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ion binding within a GNxxE pocket (Fig. 1B). A version of the ½N-sCAX1 dimer without TM1 (½N-sCAX1-ΔTM1) was modeled. This gave a structure with $1 0 \mathrm { T M }$ helices, equivalent to many CaCA proteins like the $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ exchanger (NCX) (Pittman and Hirschi 2016a, 2016b). The ½N-sCAX1-ΔTM1 dimer model more closely resemembled the CAX1 monomer but not perfectly, in part due to low confidence modeling of the now exposed TM2 (Fig. S2). Furthermore, the larger distance between the two copies of TM3 may give weak $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ion binding or prevent binding completely.

Since CAX1 has been demonstrated to exhibit a trimeric structure (Wang et al. 2025), it was evaluated whether $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ might also display an equivalent structure by higher order oligomerization. While the ½N-sCAX1 dimer failed to model a structure that would be predicted to transport $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (Fig. 1), a ½N-sCAX1 hexamer model gave a structure with three lobes that were reminiscent of the CAX1 trimer (Fig. 2A). However, structural alignment with CAX1 gave weak similarity with a very low root mean square deviation (RMSD) score of 26.24 Å (Fig. S3A). Likewise, a ½N-sCAX1-AM-½N-sCAX1 trimer model gave a three-lobed structure but also shared poor alignment with the CAX1 trimer (Fig. S3B and Table S1). Yet unlike with the ½N-sCAX1 dimer, each ‘lobe’ of the ½N-sCAX1 hexamer was predicted to possess a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ion binding pocket due the alignment of both copies of TM helix 3 (Fig. 2B).


## Yeast assays of reconstituted CAX1 and N-terminal CAX1 module without TM1


We investigated the growth patterns of mutant K667 yeast, deficient in vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, expressing various CAX variants (Fig. 3A) while exposed to media containing different concentrations of $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ (Cunningham and Fink 1996). Yeast cells expressing ½N-CAX1 or ½N-sCAX1 alone showed almost no growth, similar to the vector control (Fig. 3B), while K667 expressing the truncated and constitutively active sCAX1 demonstrated strong $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance (Hocking et al. 2017). Notably, formation of the CAX1 variant consisting of two half N-terminal modules of sCAX1 tethered by the acidic motif $\mathrm { ‰ }$ -sCAX1-AM-½N-sCAX1) alleviated the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitivity phenotype (Fig. 3B and C). These findings suggest that the tethered fusion of two copies of the N-terminal sCAX1 module resulted in a functional reconstituted CAX1, consistent with the modeling data (Figs. 1 and 2), effectively correcting the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport deficiency of the K667 yeast mutant. This was despite the presence of a second copy of the first TM helix, therefore yielding a CAX-like protein monomer with 12-TM spans.

Considering the structural homology modeling which suggested that the ½N-sCAX1-ΔTM1 dimer resembled an CAX1-like structure (Fig. S2), the engineered $1 / _ { 2 } \mathrm { N - s C A X 1 }$ - ΔTM1 construct (Fig. 3A) gave partial suppression of the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -sensitive phenotype on high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ media (Fig. 3C), indicating that the absence of this first TM helix in ½N-sCAX1 does allow some $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport.

Subsequently, we investigated whether the deletion of TM1 in ½N-sCAX1 would allow for self-assembly or dimerization in yeast, by utilizing the mating-based splitubiquitin assay (mbSUS). Notably, ½N-sCAX1-ΔTM1 could dimerize unlike ½N-sCAX1 (Fig. 3D). Therefore, the N-terminal CAX1 module lacking TM1 exhibited functional activity in yeast, consistent with the previously described model of $5 + 5$ TM core CAX modules (Pittman and Hirschi 2016a, 2016b).


## Potentiality of N-terminal CAX1 module to oligomerize


To elucidate whether ½N-sCAX1 can physically interact with itself, or with ½N-CAX1 (containing the autoinhibitory domain), we carried out split ubiquitin analysis. From the mbSUS assay, ½N-sCAX1 failed to interact with ½N-CAX1 and full-length CAX1 (Fig. 4B and C), apart from strong interaction of $\% \mathrm { N } .$ -sCAX1 with C-terminal half CAX1 module (½C-CAX1) as reported previously (Zhao et al. 2009a). Also, we did not detect any homo-oligomerization between copies of $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N - s C A X 1 }$ , while ½N-CAX1 with the autoinhibitory domain interacts with itself and also with CAX1 (Fig. 4B), suggesting that the N-terminal 36-amino acid regulatory region may mediate N-CAX1 interaction, supporting our previous findings (Zhao et al. 2009a). Furthermore, ½N-sCAX1 did not interact with full-length CAX2 and CAX3 in both the orientations (Fig. 4C).

To further demonstrate that the interactions between the half N-terminal modules of CAX proteins are relevant in plant cells, co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) using proteins from microsomal preparations revealed that ½N-CAX1 with the regulatory domain interacted with itself in the microsomal fraction (Fig. 4D). However, no interaction was observed between ½N-sCAX1 and a copy of itself. Furthermore, ½N-sCAX1 also did not exhibit any interactions with $\% \mathrm { N } .$ -CAX1 (Fig. 4D). Thus, the half N-terminal CAX1 module without the autoinhibitory domain does not possess the capacity for self-assembly into a protein complex.

## Subcellular Localization of CAX3


CAX1 appears to localize and function in both yeast and plant vacuolar membranes (Pittman and Hirschi, 2001; Cheng et al., 2003; Carter et al., 2004). When heterologously expressed in yeast cells, both hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged CAX1 and CAX3 colocalize to the yeast vacuolar membrane (Shigaki et al., 2001). In addition, chimeric CAX3, which harbors the 9-amino acid ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport determinant domain of CAX1, is able to mediate vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ antiport activity (Shigaki et al., 2001). To further investigate the subcellular localization of CAX3 in plants, microsomal membranes from transgenic lines harboring the HA-tagged CAX3 fusion protein (HA-CAX3) were fractionated. Centrifugation through a linear Suc gradient was first used to compare the distribution of the epitope-tagged transporter in transgenic tobacco (Fig. 1) to that of markers for the tonoplast, plasma membrane (PM), and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen. As shown in Figure 1A, when membrane fractions were screened for the presence of HA-CAX3 accumulation, proteins of approximately $5 2 ~ \mathrm { k D }$ peaked in fractions of $2 8 \%$ to $\bar { 3 4 } \%$ Suc. The HA-CAX3 protein accumulated in fractions enriched in tonoplast, as indicated by the sedimentation profiles, which overlap with a resident protein (V-ATPase) from this membrane but did not overlap with marker proteins from the ER (immunoglobulin heavy chain binding protein [BiP]) or the PM (PMA1; Fig. 1A). Furthermore, the membrane profile of the proteins detected by anti-HA and anti-V-ATPase was unchanged in gradients prepared in the presence of $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ , whereas the $\operatorname { E R } ,$ a s detected by anti-BiP, showed a large characteristic $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ shift to heavier density fractions (Fig. 1B). This result, together with the localization analysis in yeast, suggests that CAX1 and CAX3 localize to the same endomembrane system, namely, the vacuole.


## Expression of CAX1:: $\mathbf { \delta B }$ -Glucuronidase and CAX3: $\mathbf { \sigma } : \beta$ -Glucuronidase in Arabidopsis


RNA-blotting analysis indicated that CAX3 transcripts were detected in Arabidopsis roots, stems, and flowers, but rarely in leaf tissues (Shigaki and Hirschi, 2000). In comparison, CAX1 transcripts were highly accumulated in leaf tissues and were also detected in stems and flowers, with low levels of expression in roots (Hirschi, 1999; Cheng and Hirschi, 2003). Given that CAX3 shows $9 3 \%$ similarity to CAX1, cross hybridization might still occur even though gene-specific probes were used in northern-blot analysis (Shigaki and Hirschi, 2000). In order to verify the expression of these two closely related CAX members and to gain a more precise profile of the expression pattern of the genes, we constructed CAX promoter:: $_ { ; \beta }$ -glucuronidase (GUS) reporters for CAX1 and CAX3. A $2 . 0 { \cdot } \mathrm { k b }$ genomic DNA sequences upstream of the translation initiation (AUG) codon were amplified by PCR using the promoter-specific primers corresponding to CAX1 and CAX3, respectively. The constructs CAX3::GUS and CAX1::GUS were transformed into Arabidopsis ecotype Columbia (Col-0). As shown in Figure 2, GUSstaining patterns were comparable to those revealed by RNA-blotting analysis. In CAX1::GUS transgenic plants, CAX1::GUS expression was predominately detected in leaf tissues (Fig. 2, A and C) and in flowers of the mature plants (Fig. 2, K and L). In cotyledons and young leaves, GUS staining was predominant in the vascular cells (Fig. 2A). Weak GUS staining was seen in roots and stems (Fig. 2, E–G; data not shown), and in the root it was mostly in the vasculature. In comparison with CAX1::GUS, strong expression of CAX3::GUS was detected in roots, particularly in growing root tips (Fig. 2, H–J). However, GUS signals were rarely detected in leaf tissues and only occasionally detected in stem tissues (Fig. 2, B and D; data not shown). In mature plants, CAX3::GUS expression was observed in young flower buds as well as open flowers (Fig. 2M). Both CAX1::GUS and CAX3::GUS were also expressed in the flowers and siliques (Fig. 2, K–N).


## Expression of CAX1 and CAX3 in Yeast


Previous findings suggest that the N-terminal region of CAX1 acts as an autoinhibitory domain for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity when expressed in yeast (Pittman et al., 2002a). To further compare the properties of the CAX transporters with (CAX) and without (sCAX) the putative N-terminal autoinhibitory domain, we cloned these open reading frames into high-copy yeast expression plasmids and expressed them in a yeast strain deficient in vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters and lacking functional calcineurin (Cunningham and Fink, 1996; Hirschi et al., 1996). This strain (K667) lacks the endogenous vacuolar $\dot { \mathsf { C } } \mathsf { a } ^ { 2 + }$ -ATPase PMC1 and vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ antiporter VCX1 and thus is defective in vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, making it unable to grow on high ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ media such as $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ to $2 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { C a } \bar { \mathrm { C l } } _ { 2 }$ (Cunningham and Fink, 1996). We examined the growth of yeast cells expressing empty vector control, N-terminally truncated CAX1 and CAX3 (sCAX1 and sCAX3), and full-length CAX1 and CAX3, in media containing $5 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { C a } \mathrm { C l } _ { 2 }$ . Under these semipermissive conditions, the vector control-expressing strain grew, albeit poorly; however, both the full-length CAX1 and truncated sCAX1-expressing cells suppressed the ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitivity, although the suppression by CAX1 was slightly weaker than sCAX1 (Fig. 3A). Interestingly, the CAX3-expressing cells grew weakly under these conditions yet still stronger than vector control, while the sCAX3-expressing cells grew in a manner similar to vector controls (Fig. 3A). In order to determine if there was some association between CAX1 and CAX3, we expressed both transporters simultaneously in this yeast strain, using His- and Ura-selectable yeast expression plasmids, and assayed for phenotypes under conditions that were nonpermissive for growth of each CAX transporter individually. Interestingly, the $\mathrm { C A X 1 + C A X 3 }$ coexpression strain was able to grow at $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , while yeast expressing the full-length CAX1 or CAX3 individually could not grow (Fig. 3B).

CAXs and the functionally equivalent NCXs belong to the CaCA superfamily of transporters (Pittman and Hirschi 2016a). Understanding the structure–function relationships of these transporters could have significant implications for various biological processes, including the regulation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling pathways. All CaCA proteins, including CAXs, share a conserved core structure consisting of ten TM helices, with the α1- and $\mathtt { q 2 }$ -repeat regions forming conserved cation-binding sites (Fig. 1B) and allowing cation translocation through a pore (Pittman and Hirschi 2016b). The crystal structures of CAX proteins from bacteria (Nishizawa et al. 2013) provide insights into the concept that these transporters can form homomeric or heteromeric oligomers (Zhao et al. 2009a). Recently, structural insight of the autoinhibition mechanism governing Arabidopsis CAX1 revealed the spatial organization of the N-terminal $\mathfrak { a }$ -helix and its docking site within the transporter core (Wang et al. 2025). This demonstrates how this plant exchanger is kept in check and subsequently activated via phosphorylationmediated conformational shifts.

The N-terminal autoinhibitory domain of CAX1 is responsible for the post-translational negative regulation of its $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport channel (Pittman et al. 2002; Wang et al. 2024, 2025). Previous work comparing the full-length transporter with N-terminally truncated CAX1 (sCAX1) lacking a 36 amino acid region of the autoinhibitory domain, showed that removal of this region fully activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport when expressed in yeast, and identified specific residues within the domain that are required for autoinhibition such as by interaction between specific residues (Pittman and Hirschi 2001; Pittman et al. 2002). It has also been demonstrated that phosphorylation of four consecutive serine residues within a region of the autoinhibitory domain (Ser-38 to Ser-41) trigger a conformational change that activates the transporter (Wang et al. 2024). The recent cryo-EM studies of CAX1 also evaluated mutations of the Ser-cluster to create structural models of the constitutively active CAX1. It was found that the N-terminal domain becomes unstable upon phosphorylation, dissociates from the core domain and is released from the transport tunnel (Wang et al. 2025). The ½N-sCAX1 monomer lacks the first 36 amino acids of the autoinhibitory domain and fails to dimerize or confer transport activity (Figs. 1, 3, 4). However, $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N - s C A X 1 }$ retains the other region of the domain that includes the Ser-cluster. Therefore it is possible that when modular assembly occurs, such as by tethering of two ½N-sCAX1 modules together via the acidic motif or within the hexameric $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N - s C A X 1 }$ structure, there might be structural interaction involving the Ser-cluster and surrounding residues within each ½N-sCAX1 module, which could mediate some conformational changes.

Our study uncovers a previously uncharacterized structural barrier to individual pseudosymmetrical domains of Arabidopsis CAX1 being able to homodimerize: the isolated N-terminal module (½N-sCAX1) without the autoinhibitory

Homology modeling revealed that while the $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ monomer retains structural conservation with CAX1, a $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N - s C A X 1 }$ dimer model failed to recapitulate the full-length CAX structure (Fig. 1). This structural incompatibility is likely due to the presence of TM1, which may obstruct interaction interfaces required for the reconstitution of a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ binding pocket. Biochemical interaction assays supported the structural predictions. Yeast split-ubiquitin and in planta Co-IP confirmed that ½N-sCAX1 does not interact with itself, but reconstitutes with $\% C$ -CAX1 into a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter (Fig. 4; Zhao et al. 2009a).

It was interesting to predict that six copies of ½N-sCAX1, all containing TM1, would form an oligomeric structure that was reminiscent of the recently described CAX1 trimer, along with a predicted $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ binding pocket (Fig. 2). However, the overall structural alignment score with the CAX1 trimer was very low. The trimeric state of Arabidopsis CAX1 contrasts with the monomeric structure of yeast VCX1 (Waight et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2025), demonstrating that CAX trimerization is not essential for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. Future work will need to determine whether the hexameric model of $\mathrm { \Delta V { - } s C A X 1 }$ can be experimentally validated or whether such a structure can mediate $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. Yeast growth assays revealed that while expression of $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ does not restore growth in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ - sensitive K667 yeast, indicative of a lack of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity, tethering two ½N-sCAX1 modules via the acidic motif (½N-sCAX1-AM- $. \% \mathrm { N } .$ -sCAX1) reinstates full activity (Fig. 3). This finding reinforces the requirement for tight spatial arrangement between GNxxE motifs of the $\mathfrak { a }$ -repeat regions, a hallmark of functional CaCA proteins. Although such an arrangement was predicted for the $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ hexamer (Fig. 2B), the yeast growth assays suggest that the expression of ${ } ^ { 1 / 2 \mathrm { N } }$ -sCAX1 in yeast was not sufficient to produce a hexameric structure that is functionally active, or that such a structure is prevented in the non-plant host cell.

The homology modeling of the acidic motif tethered $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ dimer predicts the presence of an additional copy of the TM1 helix that does not align with any helix within the CAX1 monomer structure (Fig. S1B). The TM1 helix has been considered as a regulatory component (sometimes referred to as TMR or TM0) that is not required for transport function and is not conserved across CaCA proteins (Wu et al. 2013; Waight et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2025). Therefore, $Y _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { - } \mathrm { s C A X } 1$ without TM1 was created and found to partially restore $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -sensitive yeast growth and could dimerize (Fig. 3C and D). This dimerization and partial functionality was also supported by structure modeling (Fig. S2).

This work builds on prior recent research of CAX1 monomer modularity in plants (Sarkar et al. 2024; Rhein et al. 2025). Firstly, the truncated ${ } ^ { 1 / 2 \mathrm { N } } .$ -CAX1 (TM1–6 plus autoinhibitory domain) when expressed in wild-type Arabidopsis Col-0 background, inhibited endogenous CAX activity, resulting in a dominant-negative phenotype (Fig. S4; Sarkar et al. 2024). In that context, truncated CAX1 forms were primarily viewed as regulatory inhibitors rather than independently functional modules. Secondly, the other module ½N-sCAX1 (TM1–6 without autoinhibitory domain), when expressed in the cax1 mutant, restored sensitivity to post-anoxia stress, exhibiting a functional role in anoxia signaling (Fig. S4; Rhein et al. 2025). This distinction demonstrates that modular components of the CAX1 monomer may possess independent signaling properties that contribute to stress adaptation in ways not previously recognized (Fig. S5; Table S4).

From an evolutionary perspective, our results support a conceptual model (Fig. 5) in which CaCA transporters are derived from an ancient fusion of smaller units (Saier 2003), explaining the pseudosymmetry within CAX topology. The N-terminal half of CAX1 may have originated from such a duplication event. Domain fusion would have conferred ion transport capabilities, while later additions—such as TM1 and the autoinhibitory domain—introduced regulatory layers to fine-tune activity and assembly. The requirement to remove TM1 to restore function positions it as a regulatory switch controlling oligomerization, potentially in response to environmental cues. Furthemore, higher-order oligomerization of CAX monomers, such as seen with the trimeric bacterial CAX YfkE (Wu et al. 2013) and the trimeric Arabidopsis CAX1 (Wang et al. 2025), may have aided the fusion and stability of the half-CAX domains (Fig. S6).

Arabidopsis appears to have several putative CAX transporters (Ma¨ser et al., 2001). Using yeast expression studies, our previous work suggested minimal functional overlap between CAX1 and the closely related transporter CAX3 (Shigaki and Hirschi, 2000). Here, using similar yeast studies, we propose that different CAX transporters may associate, possibly to form heteromers, which confer different biological properties. Although CAX1 and CAX3 mutants have subtle morphological phenotypes, we demonstrate that perturbing both CAX1 and CAX3 causes significant alterations in plant growth including stunting and tip necrosis. In total, these perturbations cause dramatic alterations in the ionome. Thus, our present genetic studies in planta suggest functional association between the CAX transporters. The future challenge is to delineate the nature of this association and how the action of endomembrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ antiporters is integrated into shaping how plants acquire nutrients, grow, develop, and adapt.

Using standard phenotypic analysis of cax1 and cax3, our data further demonstrate the importance of these transporters in an array of biological responses. Previously, we catalogued the striking phenotypes of the cax1/cax3 double mutants in order to demonstrate the importance of CAX function within the plant (Cheng et al. 2005); however, those studies failed to distinguish the biological diVerences between CAX1 and CAX3. Here, we have further evaluated hormone and stress phenotypes and biochemical properties of the cax1 and cax3 lines, strengthening the concept that these transporters function in diverse cellular events. The most compelling observation from these studies is the distinct role of CAX3 during salt stress and the opposing roles CAX1 and CAX3 play on P-ATPase activity. In summary, we suggest that functional diVerences between CAX1 and CAX3 explain the responses of these genes to environmental stress. Firstly, CAX1 and CAX3 appear to diVerentially regulate plasma membrane and tonoplast $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps (Fig. 4a; Cheng et al. 2005), which will in turn aVect various cellular functions including $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } .$ -coupled ion transporters and $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation. Secondly, we have shown further evidence that the CAX1 and CAX3 $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activities are diVerentially regulated by environmental stress: CAX1 by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ stress and CAX3 by $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress (Fig. 4c; Cheng et al. 2005). Finally, we suggest that the root-speciWc localization of CAX3, but not CAX1, in older plants is important in the root response to some environmental stresses. Future work will be needed to address the speciWc interactions among the CAX transporters.
