 Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) play essential roles in transporting the nutrients silicon and boron in seed plants, but the evolutionary origin of this transport function and the co-permeability to toxic arsenic remains enigmatic. Horizontal gene transfer of a yet uncharacterised bacterial AqpN-aquaporin group was the starting-point for plant NIP evolution.  We combined intense sequence, phylogenetic and genetic context analyses and a mutational approach with various transport assays in oocytes and plants to resolve the transorganismal and functional evolution of bacterial and algal and terrestrial plant NIPs and to reveal their molecular transport specificity features.   
 We discovered that aqpN genes are prevalently located in arsenic resistance operons of various prokaryotic phyla. We provided genetic and functional evidence that these proteins contribute to the arsenic detoxification machinery. We identified NIPs with the ancestral bacterial AqpN selectivity filter composition in algae, liverworts, moss, hornworts and ferns and demonstrated that these archetype plant NIPs and their prokaryotic progenitors are almost impermeable to water and silicon but transport arsenic and boron. With a mutational approach, we demonstrated that during evolution, ancestral NIP selectivity shifted to allow subfunctionalisations.

 Together, our data provided evidence that evolution converted bacterial arsenic efflux channels into essential seed plant nutrient transporters.

Silicon (Si), a major constituent of the earth’s crust, is the second most abundant element in the soil (Epstein 1994; Richmond and Sussman 2003). Long considered nonessential for plant growth, it is now gaining more attention by plant biologists because of its reported dynamic roles in alleviating biotic and abiotic stresses (Fauteux et al. 2005; Guntzer et al. 2012). Plants absorb Si in the form of silicic acid and accumulate from 0.1 to $10 \%$ of the dry mass depending on the plant species (Epstein 1994). On the basis of percent Si accumulation, plant species have been categorized as accumulators $( > 1 \ \% )$ or excluders (Guntzer et al. 2012). In general, monocots and primitive plant species are considered good accumulators in contrast to dicots that are mostly excluders (Montpetit et al. 2012; Guntzer et al. 2012). The Si influx into plants is mediated through nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs), which are family members of major intrinsic proteins (MIPs; Ma et al. 2006).

MIPs play an important role in many organisms since they form transmembrane channels that facilitate and discriminate transport of different solutes across the membrane. Most plant MIPs have water transport ability and are therefore commonly referred as aquaporins (Maurel et al. 2008). MIPs have been classified in five major classes including NIPs, which constitute a diverse subfamily possessing very high selectivity for different solutes. Back in 1987, a study conducted to analyze proteins associated with symbiotic nitrogen fixation in soybean led to the identification of the first NIP gene (Fortin et al. 1987). This discovery served as the basis for uncovering several other

NIPs in different plant species. The NIPs can be classified into three distinct groups on the basis of similarity at the aromatic/arginine $( \mathrm { A r / R } )$ constriction and selective filters since they dictate solute specificity (Mitani et al. 2008). The NIP functional classes, namely NIP1, NIP2 and NIP3, have a very diverse range of substrate specificities. NIP1 was found to be more permeable to water and glycerol (Dean et al. 1999), whereas NIP3 shows transport activity of relatively larger molecules like urea and formamide (Wallace and Roberts 2005). The NIP2 subgroup can transport Si, a rare feat among living organisms since Si transporters had been reported previously only in diatoms (Ma and Yamaji 2006). In addition, the NIP2 subgroup appears to be specific to high Si absorbing plant species. For instance, most of the NIP2 genes characterized for Si absorption have been cloned from monocots or lower plant species (Ma and Yamaji 2006; Montpetit et al. 2012; Gre´goire et al. 2012). To date, among dicots, only members of the Cucurbitaceae family have been found to have a Si transporting NIP2 gene (Mitani-Ueno et al. 2011). Therefore, our information about the functional, structural and evolutionary dynamics of NIP2s is lacking in dicots in general, and more particularly in leguminous plant species such as soybean where Si absorption has recently been shown to provide great benefits (Shen et al. 2010; Arsenault-Labrecque et al. 2012; Table S1).

Aquaporins (AQPs) are a family of integral membrane proteins facilitating the transport of small molecules (including water, glycerol, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ ) (Uehlein et al. 2003) Numerous studies have revealed that they are widely present in plants, animals and fungi, and play important roles in water balance (Maurel et al. 2015). There are generally many more members of AQPs in plants than in animals (Ishibashi et al. 2009; Maurel et al. 2015). So far, hundreds of AQP genes have been characterized from studies in genome-wide analysis of AQPs in higher plants, such as Arabidopsis thaliana, Brassica rapa ssp. pekinensis, Solanum lycopersicum and Zea mays (Chaumont et al. 2001; Johanson et al. 2001; Venkatesh et al. 2013; Tao et al. 2014). All these AQPs proteins were divided into fve major subfamilies: plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs), tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs), NOD26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs), small intrinsic proteins (SIPs) and $\mathbf { X }$ -intrinsic proteins (XIPs), while XIP subfamily was not identifed in the genomes of monocotyledonous and certain dicotyledonous (Danielson and Johanson 2008; Gupta and Sankararamakrishnan 2009).

As one of the largest subfamilies of AQPs, NIPs possess special sequence homology and selective flter motifs in plants, leading to their specifc selectivity of substrates (Wallace and Roberts 2005; Ma et al. 2006). It has been demonstrated that the formation and activity of waterselective channels are determined by conserved motifs (including NPAs, ar/R selectivity flter and Froger’s positions), which act as size-exclusion barriers that sterically block the transport of bulkier substrates (Fu et al. 2000; Ilan et al. 2004; Deshmukh et al. 2015). Recently, a systematic functional evolution analysis of NIPs among different species revealed that the nutritional demands of terrestrial plants are important causes of the functional divergence of NIPs (Pommerrenig et al. 2020). On the other hand, despite most NIPs are determined to be localized in the plasma membrane (PM), several members of the proteins have been revealed to be localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). In Arabidopsis, AtNIP1;1, also known as AtNLM1, was demonstrated to be localized in ER and enhances the tolerance to arsenite toxicity (Mizutani et al. 2006; Barozzi et al. 2018).

NIPs are generally believed to facilitate the difusion of small solutes, including boron (B) and silicon (Si), but not water. In Arabidopsis, AtNIP6;1 and AtNIP7;1 were suggested to be water-tight boric acid transport channels (Tanaka et al. 2008; Routray et al. 2018). Nonetheless, several members of NIPs have been identifed as water transporters in various plants. AtNIP5;1, which is strongly up-regulated in Arabidopsis root under B limitation, has been revealed to facilitate the difusion of water and boric acid (Takano et al. 2006). Besides, the pollen-specifc AtNIP4;1 and AtNIP4;2 were confrmed to function as water channels through yeast growth assays and oocyte permeability assays (Giorgio et al. 2016). Given that NIPs are metalloid channels, they were found to play an important role in plant growth, development and abiotic stress response. In Arabidopsis, NIP7;1, a gated boric acid channel, was suggested to promote the uptake of micronutrients involving in pollen cell wall formation (Routray et al. 2018). Furthermore, plasma membrane-localized NIP2;1 was demonstrated to enhance the tolerance to Aluminum (Al) toxicity due to its coordinated function with ALMT1 (Wang et al. 2017).

Citrus is one of the most important fruit crops worldwide. A number of studies have indicated that NIPs play important roles in fruit development and stress response in citrus. A NIP5-like gene was found to be dramatically up-regulated after B defcient treatment in the root of citrus (An et al. 2012). (Wei et al. 2019) revealed that most citrus NIPs are signifcantly accumulated under drought treatment in citrus leaves, indicating their important roles in response to water stress. Besides, citrus fruit is confronted with a series of biotic and abiotic stresses, which cause fruit quality deterioration such as loss of nutrients and water after harvest. The network analysis of the postharvest senescence process of citrus fruits revealed that several AQPs (including NIPs ) are up-regulated in citrus fruit during postharvest storage (Ding et al. 2015). However, few studies have been focused on the functions of citrus NIPs. In this study, a citrus NIP aquaporin was amplifed to investigate the function by various molecular biological methods.

Tere are 43 aquaporins including 8 NIP I proteins, 3 NIP II proteins, and 1 NIP III protein in tomato. SlNIP-1 was the reported Si infux transporters SlLsi1. Mutated SlNIP-1 proteins of single amino acid deletion—SlNIP1Δ141T, SlNIP-1Δ142K, SlNIP-1Δ143N, and SlNIP-1Δ144V—resembled the native SlNIP-1 showing plasma membrane localization. Tough polygenetic tree analysis, conserved structure analysis, and gene expression patterns analysis, we predict SlNIP-7, SlNIP-9, SlNIP-12 may be boric acid facilitators, and SlNIP-2, SlNIP-3 and SlNIP-11 may be involved in the pollen development. Considering the important biological functions of NIP subfamily of plant aquaporins, further analysis of the functions of these genes in specifc tissue is deserved. In addition, we also propose that functional identifcation of SlNIP-1, SlLsi2-1 and SlLsi2-2 should be obtained through transgenic plants and furthermore experimental studies.

Background: Arsenic is a toxic and highly abundant metalloid that endangers human health through drinking water and the food chain. The most common forms of arsenic in the environment are arsenate $( \mathsf { A } \mathsf { s } ( \mathsf { V } ) )$ and arsenite $( \mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } ) ) . \mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ is a non-functional phosphate analog that enters the food chain via plant phosphate transporters. Inside cells, $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ becomes reduced to As(III) for subsequent extrusion or compartmentation. Although much is known about As(III) transport and handling in microbes and mammals, the transport systems for $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ have not yet been characterized in plants.

Results: Here we show that the Nodulin26-like Intrinsic Proteins (NIPs) AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 from Arabidopsis thaliana, OsNIP2;1 and OsNIP3;2 from Oryza sativa, and LjNIP5;1 and LjNIP6;1 from Lotus japonicus are bi-directional $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ channels. Expression of these NIPs sensitized yeast cells to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ and antimonite (Sb(III)), and direct transport assays confirmed their ability to facilitate As(III) transport across cell membranes. On medium containing $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ , expression of the same NIPs improved yeast growth, probably due to increased As(III) efflux. Our data furthermore provide evidence that NIPs can discriminate between highly similar substrates and that they may have differential preferences in the direction of transport. A subgroup of As(III) permeable channels that group together in a phylogenetic tree required N-terminal truncation for functional expression in yeast.

Conclusion: This is the first molecular identification of plant $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ transport systems and we propose that metalloid transport through NIPs is a conserved and ancient feature. Our observations are potentially of great importance for improved remediation and tolerance of plants, and may provide a key to the development of low arsenic crops for food production.

Boron (B) is an essential micronutrient for plants as it plays a structural role in plant cell walls, crosslinking two pectin polysaccharides rhamnogalacturonan-II [1, 2]. When B concentrations are below optimum, Bdeficiency symptoms appear and include the inhibition of root elongation and a reduced leaf expansion and fertility, which results in substantial agronomical losses around the world [3–5].

In soils, B is mainly found as uncharged boric acid [B $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) _ { 3 } ]$ $( \mathrm { K a } = 5 . 8 0 \mathrm { X } 1 0 - 1 0$ at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ $( \mathrm { p K a } = 9 . 2 4 )$ ) [6]. At optimal concentrations, B enters the plant through passive diffusion. However, under deficiency, B is transported into and within the plant by the coordinated action of proteins that belong to two protein families: the major intrinsic protein family MIP and the Boron transporter family BOR [7–10]. MIPs are a superfamily of aquaporins made up of several subfamilies, including the nodulin-26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) [11], which are permeable channels to small solutes including [B $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) _ { 3 } ]$ [12–16].

In plants, the best characterized NIP protein described as a B facilitator transporter is the Arabidopsis thaliana (L.) Heynh. NIP5;1, (AtNIP5;1), a cell membrane channel permeable to water, urea and [B $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) _ { 3 } ]$ [17]. AtNIP5;1 is found in epidermal cells of roots, and its transcripts are up-regulated under low B conditions, increasing B permeability and maximizing B uptake from B-deficient soils [15].

On the other hand, BOR proteins constitute a family of boric acid and borate exporters, with seven members identified in A. thaliana (AtBOR1–7) [18, 19]. AtBOR1 accumulates in the root stele under low-B conditions, and is responsible for xylem loading of [B $\left( \mathrm { O H } \right) _ { 3 } ]$ , allowing B distribution to the rest of the plant [7, 18]. It has been proven that the coordinated action of AtNIPs and AtBORs is essential to ensure a proper B distribution within the plant, especially under low-B conditions, what is required for a proper plant growth and development [20].

Various crops of agronomical interest belong to the legume family (Leguminosae or Fabaceae), such as alfalfa, pea, or soybean [17, 21]. These plant species have the ability to interact symbiotically with $\Nu _ { 2 }$ -fixing Rhizobia, triggering the formation of root nodules, where biological nitrogen fixation takes place [22–24]. In this sense, developing more efficient nitrogen-fixing associations is of high importance given the pollution problems associated with the excessive use of chemical fertilizers [25, 26]. This requires a better understanding of the factors that influence the success of the symbiotic process, including nutrient transport [27–29]. In line with this, it has been shown that every step in the establishment of Legume-rhizobia symbioses is severely affected by B deficiency [30–35]. However, B transport has been barely studied in legumes and the MIP protein superfamily seems to harbor putative B transporter candidates. In the model legume Medicago truncatula Gaertn, this superfamily comprises 46 MIPs, 18 of them belonging to the NIP family [36]. However, only one B transporter (a NIP protein) has been characterized so far [37], and none have been associated with B transport under B deficient conditions.

In the present study we use a candidate gene approach combined with a phenotypic analysis and a heterologous complementation assay to characterize MtNIP5;1 as a novel B transporter of M. truncatula, homologous to AtNIP5;1, that functions under low boron conditions. The results presented here will allow gaining further knowledge regarding B nutrition in leguminous plants.

Nodulin26-like intrinsic membrane proteins (NIPs), aquaporins that have been initially localized in peribacteroid membrane of nitrogen-fixing root nodules of leguminous plants, are present in plasma membrane of the non-symbiotic plants too (Wudick et al., 2009; Kapilan et al., 2018). Aquaporins identified as nodulin26 proteins were first characterized in soybean and then in other rhizobia-symbiotic vegetables (Rouge and Barre, 2008).

Nodule formation is a result of symbiotic relationship between plant and nitrogen fixing bacteria. During the process of nodule formation, nodulin proteins are expressed by plants and transferred to the membranes. Nodulin 26 proteins are expressed at the symbiosome membrane and have similar sequences to NIP proteins (Kapilan et al., 2018).

NIPs have been classified in five phylogenetic groups (NIP1-NIP5) and in three functional groups (NIP I, NIP II, NIP III), based on similarity of the aromatic/arginine constriction (Mateluna et al., 2018).

Comparatively with other aquaporins, NIPs play a similar role as transporters of water, but in contrast with PIPs and TIPs, NIPs have lower water transport activity (Maurel et al., 2015; Kapilan et al., 2018). However, besides glycerol and water (Kruse et al., 2006),

NIPs are permeable to small organic solutes and mineral nutrients and mediate diffusion of metalloids (boric acid, silicon and selenium) and toxic elements (arsenic) (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014; Maurel et al., 2015; Fox et al., 2017). NIPs transport functions have been established by direct mutagenesis and by expression in oocytes (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014). NIP I proteins are permeable to water, glycerol and ammonia, NIP II proteins transport urea and metalloid nutrients (boron), but have lower water permeability and NIP III proteins transport larger molecules (silicic acid, urea) (Mateluna et al., 2018).

Some structural particularities in NPA motif (alanine is replaced with serine, glycine or valine) might render NIPs capable of transporting substrates other than water (Wudick et al., 2009). NIP2 proteins have a wider pore than those of NIP1 and are permeable to large solutes (urea). Also, AtNIP2;1 is expressed in the endoplasmic reticulum of roots, whereas AtNIP5;1 is expressed in plasma membrane of roots elongation zones. The AtNIP2;1 mediates lactic acid transport, being very important to the adaptation to lactic fermentation under anaerobic stress (Gomes et al., 2009). When NIPs phosphorylation is increased, NIPs have an important role in maintaining plant water balance and in drought and salt stress responses (Martinez-Ballesta and Carvajal, 2014; Kapilan et al., 2018).

NIPs proteins have multifunctional transport properties of water and/or uncharged solutes as glycerol. NIP gene transcripts were found in seed coat, shoot and roots (Kaldenhoff and Fischer, 2006).

Silicon (Si) is not considered to be an essential element for plants, but its tissue concentration can exceed that of many essential elements in some plant species (Hodson et al., 2005; White and Brown, 2010). The roles of Si as a beneficial element for plants, protecting them from a variety of abiotic stresses and biotic challenges, have been discussed in the literature for a long time (Epstein, 1999; Coskun et al., 2018).

In most circumstances, plant roots take up Si from the soil solution and it is then transported to the aboveground organs via the xylem (Casey et al., 2003; Mitani et al., 2005). The accumulation of Si varies greatly among plant species and those belonging to the commelinid monocot orders Poales (e.g., cereals, grasses, bromeliads, and sedges) and Arecales (e.g., palms) generally accumulate more Si than other plants (Hodson et al., 2005). The identification of genes encoding proteins responsible for Si transport have shown that Si accumulation is the result of an efficient symplastic pathway mediated by Si influx and efflux transport mechanisms in the plasma membrane of root cells (Ma and Yamaji, 2015). Silicon influx proteins, termed Lsi1, are members of the NIP III (nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein III) group of aquaporin-like proteins belonging to the large MIP (major intrinsic protein) superfamily that contains various classes of integral membrane proteins functioning as diffusion facilitators of water and small uncharged solutes (Wallace and Roberts, 2005; Ma and Yamaji, 2015; Pommerrenig et al., 2015; Deshmukh et al., 2016). Aquaporins in the NIP III group contain two hallmark domains: a unique selectivity filter (ar/R filter, also known as GSGR filter) formed by glycine (G), serine (S), glycine (G) and arginine (R) and two NPA motifs (also referred to as NPA boxes) consisting of asparagine (N), proline (P) and alanine (A) separated by 108 amino acids (Deshmukh et al., 2015; Ma and Yamaji, 2015).

Following its uptake by roots, Si can be deposited in plant tissues in various forms, most frequently in silica cells or silica bodies distributed within the leaf epidermis or as a dense layer beneath the cuticle (Datnoff et al., 2001; Coskun et al., 2018). Other common sites of Si deposition are specialized cells termed stegmata that form a sheath around sclerenchyma fibers attached to vascular bundles or individual fiber bundles in species such as palms in the commelinid monocot order Arecales and orchids in noncommelinid monocot order Asparagales (Møller and Rasmussen, 1984). Root tissues are also sites of Si accumulation in some plant species, with the endodermis being the dominant deposition site, especially in monocots (Sangster and Hodson, 1992; Lux et al., 2003).

The effects of silicon (Si) on many flowering plants [1], including poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima Willd.) [2], have been investigated, and the results have demonstrated that Si has an effect on plant development. The horticultural traits of sunflowers [3] and gerberas [4] were improved by Si supplementation. Greater biomass, chlorophyll content, and numbers of lateral shoots of Tagetes patula were obtained when Si was supplied [5]. However, the characteristics and expression patterns of Si transporters are not extensively studied in these plants. Plants accumulate Si through influx transporters (low silicon 1, Lsi1) and efflux transporters (low silicon 2, Lsi2) [6,7]. Lsi1 belongs to the nodulin 26-like intrinsic membrane protein (NIP) subfamily of the major intrinsic protein (MIP) superfamily [8]. The NIPs have three subgroups named NIP-I, NIP-II, and NIP-III, which are specific to their substrates [9]. A precise spacing of 108 amino acids (AAs) between the asparagine-proline-alanine (NPA) domains of Lsi1 is essential for Si permeability [10]. A single allelic variation in Lsi1 will result in a different Si uptake [11]. Moreover, suppression of Lsi1 and Lsi2 expression results in a reduced Si uptake [6,7]. Therefore, specific protein characteristics and Si transporter expressions are vital to Si uptake by plants.

Studies have shown that Si is beneficial to many plant species, especially when plants are under stresses [12]. It was reported that Si increased the activity of major antioxidant enzymes in plants under high temperature stresses [13]. Si was also observed to increase solutes, membrane stability, and photochemical reactions in plants that are under low temperature stresses [14,15]. Si uptake was inhibited by low temperatures in rice [16] and cucumber [17]. The inhibited transport activities of Lsi2 lead to a reduced Si uptake, while the activities of Lsi1 are not affected by low temperatures [9]. In commercial production, poinsettia propagates in summer and flowers in winter, which exposes it to both high and low temperature stresses. Thus, this study aimed to study how the temperature stresses affect Si transporter expressions and Si accumulation in poinsettia.

In rice [6,7], barley [18], and cucumber [19,20], Lsi1 and Lsi2 are expressed mainly in the roots, and their expressions are down-regulated by the Si supplementation. However, the expression of Lsi1 is not affected by the Si supply in maize [21,22]. Tissue-specific examination of expressions showed that Lsi1 and Lsi2 are abundant in the roots and mature leaves, and low in the stems of cucumber [20]. An investigation of Si transporter gene expressions, Si uptake, and Si accumulation has shown that Lsi1 is responsible for the Si transport in the kernel tissues of maize [23]. Moreover, Si distribution and accumulation in the leaves of the grass Brachiaria brizantha indicated that mature leaf blades have the highest Si content, followed, in order, by recently expanded leaf blades and non-expanded leaf blades [24].

## Plant material and cultivation


Seeds of rice plants (Oryza sativa cv. indica 9311) were surface sterilized by $1 \%$ (w/v) sodium hypochlorite. Plastic pots, each containing 80 plants in 1.0 l of nutrient solution, were kept under a $1 4 \mathrm { - h }$ light $( 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ) / 1 0 \mathrm { - h }$ dark $( 2 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ regime with white fluorescent illumination of $1 5 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m o l } } ~ { \mathrm { m } } ^ { - 2 } ~ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ and relative humidity of $70 \%$ . The rice plants were cultivated to 3-leaf seedlings in the next 8 days under the described conditions. The nutrient solution $\mathrm { ( p H ~ 5 . 0 ) }$ contained $1 . 4 3 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ) _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } }$ , $0 . 3 2 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { N a H _ { 2 } P O _ { 4 } } { \cdot } 2 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , $0 . 5 1 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ , $0 . 9 8 \mathrm { \ m M } \mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ $\mathrm { 1 C a C l _ { 2 } , 1 . 6 3 \ m M M g S O _ { 4 } { \cdot } 7 H _ { 2 } O }$ , $8 . 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\mathrm { M n C l } _ { 2 } { \cdot } 4 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , $1 8 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 }$ , $0 . 1 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\mathrm { Z n S O _ { 4 } } .$ - $\mathrm { 7 H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , $0 . 1 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\mathrm { C u S O } _ { 4 } { \cdot } 5 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ , $3 5 . 7 \ \mu \mathrm { M } \ \mathrm { F e C l _ { 3 } } { \cdot } 6 \mathrm { H _ { 2 } O }$ , and $0 . 0 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ $( \mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ) _ { 6 } \mathrm { M o } _ { 7 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 4 } { \cdot } 4 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ . ## Sucrose feeding and spraying treatments


The rice plants (indica 9311) were cultivated under the normal condition for 8 days, and the 3-leaf seedlings were subjected to sucrose feeding or spraying treatments. In the sucrose feeding treatments, 3-leaf rice seedlings were transferred to the renewed nutrient solutions with the addition of $9 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose. In the sucrose spraying treatments, the mature leaves of rice seedlings were sprayed with the solution of $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose. The sucrose concentration used in spraying treatments was chosen according to our preliminary experiments (data not shown). The spraying of $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose solution ensured the maximum sucrose uptake by mature rice leaves without any additives such as Tween-20 and gelatin that would interfere with normal tissue physiological processes. This sucrose concentration also ensured the desirable physiological responses after $4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ treatment, including the change in sugar contents, root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation, and the related carbon metabolism. In the above-mentioned experiments, each treatment had three pots with each pot containing 80 plants. Rice roots and leaves were harvested after $4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ treatments, and all the samples were stored at $- 7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for further analysis.


## DCMU treatment and sucrose replenishment


For DCMU treatment, the 3-leaf seedlings of rice (indica 9311) were transferred to the renewed nutrient solutions with the addition of $2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ DCMU. After $4 8 \ \mathrm { h }$ , the DCMUtreated seedlings were equally divided into two parts with one treated by $2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ DCMU alone (as control) and the other one treated by combination of $2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ DCMU and $9 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose. Each treatment had three pots with 80 plants in each pot. Rice roots and leaves were harvested after $4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ treatments of DCMU alone or combined with sucrose. All the samples were stored at $- 7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for further analysis.

GS (EC 6.3.1.2) activity was measured in a reaction mixture containing imidazole as described by Rhodes et al. (1975). ## RNA extraction and real-time PCR


The samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at $- 7 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ until use. Each sample was ground to a fine powder in liquid nitrogen using a mortar and pestle, and RNA was isolated by the method of Wen and Chase (1999) with Trizol reagent (Invitrogen). The total RNA was subjected to cDNA synthesis by Promega kit using oligodT primers. For real-time PCR analysis, the resulting cDNA was diluted and used as templates. Real-time PCR reactions were processed using the primers as shown in Table S1. Ammonium ions $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } ) }$ have been well documented as a major source of inorganic nitrogen for rice plants grown in paddy soils (Tabuchi et al. 2007). Rice roots, the typical non-photosynthetic tissues, are responsible for taking up and assimilating the $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ nutrients (Kiyomiya et al. 2001). It is now well established that the cycle of glutamine synthetase (GS; EC 6.3.1.2) and NADH-dependent glutamate synthase (NADH-GOGAT; EC 1.4.1.14) is the only route for the primary $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation in rice roots grown under normal conditions (Ireland and Lea 1999; Lea and Miflin 2003). GS catalyzes an ATP-dependent conversion of glutamate-toglutamine, and GOGAT catalyzes net glutamate synthesis using 2-oxoglutarate (2-OG) as the carbon skeletons (Ireland and Lea 1999). Therefore, GS/GOGAT pathway is closely linked with plant carbon metabolism. The carbon availability as well as the enzyme activities involved in 2-OG production, including hexokinase, $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ -dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase $\mathrm { ( N A D P ^ { + } }$ - ICDH), and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC), is required to sustain root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ uptake and assimilation (Yuan et al. 2007; Setie´n et al. 2014; Kanwal et al. 2014).

In higher plants, sucrose, the photosynthesis product, is the predominant carbon source that can be transported to roots to support $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation in the sink tissues (Wind et al. 2010). Sucrose transport from source to sink tissues requires a number of sucrose transporters playing critical roles in phloem loading, long-distance transport, and subsequent tissue-specific unloading (Hummel et al. 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Lemoine et al. 2013). In plant kingdom, rice genome encodes multiple sucrose transporters, referred to as OsSUT1 to OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). The five OsSUTs have been classified to Type II SUTs except for OsSUT2 that belongs to Type III family of tonoplast members (Aoki et al. 2003; Sun et al. 2010). The OsSUTs are extensively involved in various sucrose phloem-loading pathways as well as developmental and physiological regulation. OsSUT1 has been elucidated to function in apoplastic phloem loading of sucrose during seed germination and pollen development (Hirose et al. 1997, 2010; Ishimaru et al. 2007). Like OsSUT1, the plasma membrane-localized OsSUT3, preferentially expressed in the developing pollen, is also responsible of apoplastic phloem loading (Eom et al. 2012; Ngampanya et al. 2002; Takeda et al. 2001). The tonoplast-localized OsSUT2 has been reported to control symplastic passive loading of sucrose and thus influence source-to-sink carbohydrate export (Eom et al. 2011). The transgenic Arabidopsis over-expressing AtSUC2, the gene encoding a phloem-specific sucrose transporter, has been reported to have an accelerated sucrose uptake (Lei et al. 2011). Recently, Wang et al. (2015) reported that over-expression of AtSUC2 in transgenic rice led to enhanced sucrose loading and improved crop yield. In this study, we evaluate the correlation between the OsSUTs mRNA abundances, soluble sugar contents, and root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation in sucrose-treated rice seedlings.

Sucrose phosphate synthase (SPS, EC 2.3.1.14), the major rate-limiting enzyme in sucrose biosynthesis, has been demonstrated to control carbohydrate partitioning in the whole plant (Slewinski and Braun 2010). Five SPSencoding genes have been identified in rice genome and genetically localized to chromosome 1, 2, 6, 8, and 11 (Valdez-Alarcon et al. 1996; Castleden et al. 2004). As reported by Okamura et al. (2011), the five members in rice SPS gene family, OsSPS1, OsSPS2, OsSPS6, OsSPS8, and OsSPS11, played physiologically important roles in modulating sucrose anabolism during the crop development and diurnal changes. OsSPS1 and OsSPS11, both functionally correlated to leaf sucrose contents under continuous light or specific diurnal changes, have been elucidated to be transcriptionally regulated by light and circadian clock, rather than sucrose (Yonekura et al. 2013). The other OsSPSs also contribute to sucrose metabolism and partitioning in rice plants. The total SPS activity in rice leaves has been assessed to modulate source-to-sink export of photosynthetic assimilates in the crop plants, especially at elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ conditions (Li et al. 2008). In this work, we also evaluate the correlation between the OsSPSs mRNA abundances and rice root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation under different sucrose treatments.

Previous studies have documented that sucrose transport and allocation played critical roles in regulating plant nutrient metabolisms (Hummel et al. 2010; Lemoine et al. 2013). However, the effect of photosynthetic sucrose transport on rice root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation has not been investigated. In the present study, sucrose was sprayed to mature rice leaves to mimic the increase of sucrose content in the photosynthetic tissues. The spraying treatment did increase sucrose content in mature leaves, and the increase of photosynthetic sucrose enhanced main carbohydrates contents in roots (Fig. 3). This was similar to the observation in sucrose-treated Arabidopsis cotyledons that the elevated photosynthetic sucrose level accelerated carbohydrate accumulation in roots (Kircher and Schopfer. 2012). Significantly, the increase in the main carbohydrates contents in rice roots, including total soluble carbohydrates (TSC), sucrose, glucose, and fructose (Fig. 3), was accompanied by the activation of some important enzymes involved in non-photosynthetic $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation (Fig. 1). On the other hand, the accelerated decline of hydroponic $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ content (Fig. 2a) and the increased level of root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ (Fig. 2b) also indicated a higher rate of $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ uptake in the sucrose spraying. The obtained results suggested a positive correlation between root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation capacity and photosynthetic sucrose level. Lejay et al. (2003) described the coupling of root nitrate uptake and assimilation with shoot photosynthetic sucrose level in Arabidopsis seedlings. Here, we addressed the very similar correlation between photosynthetic sucrose and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ uptake and assimilation in rice roots.

Quantitative RT-PCR analysis in the present study revealed the mRNA expression of all the five OsSUTs in mature leaves and roots of rice seedlings (Fig. 4), which agreed to the report of Aoki et al. (2003). The significant increase in the transcript accumulation of OsSUT1, OsSUT2, OsSUT3, and OsSUT4 was observed in mature leaves after sucrose spraying (Fig. 4a–d), indicating an activated sucrose export from the photoautotrophic tissues. Rice plants exploited distinct phloem-loading mechanisms to mediate sucrose efflux, including apoplastic transport route via OsSUT1 and OsSUT3, symplastic transport route via OsSUT2, and retrieval route of reloading sucrose via

OsSUT1 (Sun et al. 2008; Eom et al. 2012; Braun et al. 2014). Aoki et al. (2003) classified OsSUT4 to a unique Type III plant SUT protein, preferentially expressed in rice sink leaves. Our results suggested the participation of multiple OsSUTs in sucrose transport from source leaves to support more active root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation. Chen and Wang (2008) reported a concerted up-regulation of OsSUT1 and OsSUT4 in rice panicle exsertion. In the present study, a similar response was observed in rice root organic nitrogen metabolism. Previous studies have focused the function of particular OsSUTs in rice germinating and maturing stages, including OsSUT1 (Scofield et al. 2002, 2007) and OsSUT4 (Chung et al. 2014). Here, we provided the evidence on the OsSUTs function of primary nitrogen metabolism regulation during vegetative growth in rice. Unlike other rice sucrose transporters, OsSUT5 was the only member to be down-regulated during sucrose spraying (Fig. 4e). The negative regulation at mRNA level, under the increased leaf sucrose condition, was very similar to the previous report that sucrose accumulation repressed transcriptional abundance of $B { \nu } S U T I$ , the OsSUT5 ortholog in sugar beet (Takeda et al. 2001; Vaughn et al. 2002). The physiological significance in the negative regulation of OsSUT5 needs further research.

Notably, sucrose feeding also simultaneously induced the leaf OsSUTs mRNA expression, except for OsSUT5, which was very similar to that observed in sucrose spraying (Fig. 4). The OsSUTs mRNA expression profile was also consistent with the change in root enzyme activities (Fig. 1) and leaf sugar contents (Fig. 3). Based on the observations in sucrose feeding experiment, we assumed the up-regulation of OsSUTs as a metabolic response to the stimulated nitrogen assimilation in sink roots. This could be further confirmed by the results from DCMU treatments and sucrose replenishment. The inhibition of DCMU on enzyme activities involved in root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation could not be fully released by sucrose re-supply (Fig. 6). It suggested the carbon availability of root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation was more dependent on sucrose exported from mature leaves than that absorbed by roots. DCMU treatment led to over-expression of OsSUT1, OsSUT3, and OsSUT5 (Fig. 7), but lower carbohydrate content in roots (Table 1).

Thus, the up-regulation of partial OsSUT family could not compensate for the loss of photosynthetic sucrose in mature leaves and the reduced carbon availability in sink roots, suggesting the importance of concerted regulation of all members in OsSUT family. Interestingly, the OsSUTs mRNA expression profile in roots, a typical sink tissue, was fairly similar to that in mature leaves in both sucrose spraying and feeding experiments (Fig. 4). The similar results were also obtained in DCMU treatments (Fig. 7). These observations revealed the involvement of root OsSUTs in regulating the non-photosynthetic $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation. The OsSUTs expressed in roots would function in sucrose unloading and further intracellular transport and allocation in the sink tissue. Here, we emphasized the importance of source-to-sink coordinated expression of OsSUTs in the regulation of root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation.

Sucrose phosphate synthase (SPS, EC 2.4.1.14) has been reported to regulate sucrose biosynthesis and the related source-to-sink allocation (Huber and Huber. 1992; Strand et al. 2000; Okamura et al. 2011; Sun et al. 2011). SPS activity has been well exploited to indicate carbohydrate metabolism status in transgenic Arabidopsis (Strand et al. 2000), developing peach fruits (Zhang et al. 2013), and rice seedlings under aluminum or drought stress conditions (Mishra and Dubey, 2008; Xu et al. 2015). Okamura et al. (2011) described a negative correlation of OsSPS1 and OsSPS6 transcripts with endogenous sucrose in mature rice leaves. In the present work, increased sucrose content in mature rice leaves, as the result of spraying treatment, also down-regulated OsSPS1 mRNA expression (Fig. 5a), but up-regulated OsSPS6 transcriptional abundance (Fig. 5c). The stimulated OsSPS6 mRNA expression might be a specific response of mature rice leaves to sucrose spraying, an experimental manipulation to supply exogenous sucrose to the source tissue. Thus, unlike OsSPS1, OsSPS6 could be differentially regulated by endogenous and exogenous sucrose. On the other hand, sucrose addition to hydroponic medium significantly induced mRNA expression of OsSPS1, OsSPS6, and OsSPS11 (Fig. 5a, c, e), which was different from the observation of Yonekura et al. (2013) that OsSPS1 and OsSPS11 transcript abundances remained almost unchanged after sucrose addition. In the report of Yonekura et al. (2013), detached parts of rice seedlings, rather than the intact plants, were treated by sucrose. Our observation, based on the sucrose-fed intact rice seedlings, was deduced to reflect the response of OsSPSs transcripts in mature rice leaves to root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation.

In the DCMU treatment, the OsSPSs transcriptional abundances were changed in response to the alteration of soluble carbohydrate level (Fig. 8; Table 1), indicating a flexible regulation of carbohydrate allocation in rice leaves. DCMU treatment also sharply inhibited root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation, which could be indicated by enzyme activities (Fig. 6) and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ contents (Table 1). Interestingly, a significant induction on OsSUT1, OsSUT3, and OsSUT5 was observed to be correlated with the over-expression of OsSPS1 and OsSPS2 in the DCMU treatments (Figs. 7, 8), which could be partially reversed by sucrose replenishment. The observed response could be explained as a specific compensation for loss of photosynthetic sucrose in mature leaves and reduced carbon availability in sink roots. The physiological correlation between soluble carbohydrate contents and mRNA abundances of OsSUTs and OsSPSs was also observed in rice HLY6, the hybrid strain exhibiting significantly higher enzyme activities concerning root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation than its parental cultivar indica 9311 (Table S2). The higher accumulation of OsSPS1 and OsSPS2 transcripts in HLY6 leaves was associated with increased mRNA abundances of OsSUT1, OsSUT2, and OsSUT4 (Fig. S1), suggesting a stimulated source-to-sink sucrose transport that led to elevated content of soluble carbohydrates in the hybrid rice roots (Table S3). Accordingly, the Rubisco large subunit abundance in HLY6 leaves was also increased (Fig. S2), agreeing to the observed transcriptional modulation of OsSPSs. The correlated expression of SPS and Rubisco has been described in the SPS-antisense Arabidopsis seedlings (Strand et al. 2000). These evidences suggested a close correlation between photosynthetic carbon assimilation and sucrose allocation that might further regulate non-photosynthetic $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation.

Unexceptionally, the sucrose treatments applied in this study led to concerted changes of internal carbohydrate contents in leaves and roots (Fig. 3; Table 1). Interestingly, compared to spraying treatment, feeding sucrose to hydroponics exerted similar regulating effects on leaf OsSUTs and OsSPSs expression (Figs. 4, 5). The induction or repression effects of sugars on OsSUTs and OsSPSs may depend on the sugar concentration, in particular, of rice tissues. Thus, the transcriptional regulation of OsSUTs and OsSPSs could be coordinated by certain sugar signal(s). Sugars have been reported to act as signaling molecules modulating gene expression involved in nutrient availability as well as resource distribution (Rolland et al. 2006; Smith and Stitt 2007). Sucrose and its metabolized product(s) may act as specific signal(s) to coordinate sugarresponsive gene expression through hexokinase-dependent and/or -independent pathways (Kunz et al. 2014, 2015). The particular sugar signals modulating sugar-responsive gene expression have been dissected at low sugar concentration $( 1 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ) based on a stemcell-like Arabidopsis culture system (Kunz et al. 2014). In contrast, a much higher sucrose concentration $( 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ) was required in our spraying treatment to modulate OsSUTs and OsSPSs mRNA expression. The rapid metabolization of the added sugar(s) should be considered in evaluating specific sugar signals (Osuna et al. 2007; Kunz et al. 2014). In the present study, the sucrose spraying $( 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ and feeding $( 9 0 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ both increased glucose and fructose contents in leaves and roots (Fig. 3). Glucose, rather than fructose, has been recognized in extensively identified plant signaling pathways (Cho et al. 2006). Thus, the sucrose-derived hexose such as glucose might be potential signal to regulate OsSUTs and OsSPSs transcript abundances. The certain enzyme activities involved in hexose phosphorylation and further catabolism were also required in the observed sugar sensing, including hexokinase, $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ -ICDH, and PEPC (Figs. 1, 6). From the obtained evidences, if there did exist sugar signal to coordinate carbon availability and root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation, the signal pathway might be dependent on hexokinase and sugar catabolism.

In conclusion, the higher capacity of rice root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation was well correlated with the transcriptional regulation of OsSUTs and OsSPSs that led to increased carbon availability in the non-photosynthetic tissue. The marked influence of leave OsSUTs and OsSPSs mRNA expression on root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation was also demonstrated in DCMU treatments and sucrose replenishment.

## $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation in rice (indica 9311) roots after sucrose spraying or feeding


In the present study, sucrose treatments, by spraying to leaves (spraying treatment) and feeding in hydroponic media (feeding treatment), were employed to investigate the effects of the exogenously supplied sucrose on ammonium assimilation in rice (indica 9311) roots. In the case of rice roots, as previously reported, the major enzymes involved in glutamine (Gln)/glutamate (Glu) synthesis and carbon skeleton production are GS/NADHGOGAT cycle, HXK, $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ -ICDH, and PEPC (Yuan et al. 2007). Here, the addition of sucrose by spraying or feeding treatments increased these enzyme activities in rice roots (Fig. 1). The increase in GS and NADH-GOGAT activity was about $40 \%$ after sucrose spraying to mature leaves and the further increased activities were observed in sucrose feeding experiment (Fig. 1a, b). In addition, sucrose spraying to leaves enhanced root $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ -ICDH (Fig. 1c), HXK (Fig. 1d), and PEPC activities (Fig. 1e) by 45, 55, and $3 5 \%$ , respectively. In the case of sucrose feeding treatment, activities of these enzymes were similarly elevated (Fig. 1).

Figure 2 shows the $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ contents in rice growth media as well as in plant tissues. $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ concentration in the hydroponic media with $9 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose declined more rapidly than control, reaching at approximately $1 4 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ 1 ^ { - 1 }$ ${ \bf \zeta } 6 0 0 { \ \mu } { \bf m o l \zeta } ^ { - 1 }$ less than the control). Similarly, compared to the control, $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ contents in the growth media also decreased more rapidly after the spraying treatment (Fig. 2a). Hence, both feeding and spraying treatments could accelerate the $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ uptake in rice roots, which was in agreement with the higher capacity of $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation. As shown in Fig. 2b, sucrose feeding promoted an increase in $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ concentration in root tissues; however, little change could be detected concerning root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ content in the spraying treatment. Similarly, no significant increase was found in the leaf $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ concentration after feeding and spraying treatments (Fig. 2c).

Soluble sugars are well known as the major carbon sources that catabolically linked to plant $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation (Kubik-Dobosz et al. 2001). In this study, we determined the content of total soluble carbohydrates (TSC), sucrose, glucose, and fructose to evaluate carbon availability in rice roots and leaves (Fig. 3). The content of soluble sugars in rice roots, including TSC (Fig. 3a), sucrose (Fig. 3b), glucose (Fig. 3c), and fructose (Fig. 3d), was clearly elevated after sucrose spraying or feeding and reached at a significant value point $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ ) as compared to control. Comparatively, the increase of TSC and sucrose in leaves was around $20 \%$ , which was much lower than that in roots (Fig. 3a, b). However, in the both sucrose treatments, the increase fold of leaf glucose and fructose was highly similar to that of roots (Fig. 3c, d).


## Transcriptional expression pattern of OsSUTs and OsSPSs in rice (indica 9311) seedlings


Sucrose is the predominant transport form of photosynthates between source and sink tissues in higher plants and a considerable number of plant proteins play crucial roles in sucrose allocation, including SUTs and SPSs. In this study, rice (indica 9311) seedling samples in different sucrose treatments were collected to investigate the mRNA expression patterns of OsSUTs and OsSPSs by quantitative RT-PCR analysis. The transcript levels of OsSUT1, OsSUT2, OsSUT3, and OsSUT4 were significantly increased in leaves and roots after spraying sucrose on leaves, and the similar changes were observed in the sucrose feeding treatment (Fig. 4a–d). On the contrary, sucrose treatments, irrespective of spraying or feeding, markedly decreased the OsSUT5 mRNA expression in leaves and roots (Fig. 4e). As shown in Fig. 5, spraying treatment decreased OsSPS1, OsSPS2, and OsSPS8 mRNA abundances in leaves, whereas increased OsSPS6 and OsSPS11 mRNA accumulation in the photosynthetic tissues. In contrast, feeding treatment only decreased OsSPS2 and OsSPS8 transcripts and up-regulated the other OsSPSs mRNA expression (Fig. 5).


## DCMU treatment and sucrose replenishment in rice (indica 9311) roots


To assess the contribution of photosynthetic sucrose transport to rice root $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation, 3-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)-1,1-dimethylurea (DCMU), an effective inhibitor of photosynthetic electron transport, was added to hydroponic media, alone or combined with sucrose. The addition of DCMU alone sharply reduced the GS and NADHGOGAT activities in rice roots (Fig. 6a), and similar changes could be detected in enzyme activities involved in carbon skeleton supply, including HXK, $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ -ICDH, and PEPC (Fig. 6b). As shown in Fig. 6, the inhibitory effects of DCMU could be partially reversed by addition of sucrose in growth media. All the enzyme activities in the combined feeding of DCMU and sucrose, except for NADH-GDH, were significantly higher than those in DCMU treatment alone.

C and N metabolites related to $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ assimilation as well as tissue fresh weights were also determined in DCMU experiments. Significantly, fresh weight of tissue, irrespective of leaves or roots, was decreased in DCMU treatment, and could not be effectively reversed by adding sucrose (Table 1). In the case of roots, as shown in Table 1, DCMU treatment caused nearly $60 \%$ reductions in the amounts of total soluble carbohydrates, about $40 \%$ decrease in soluble protein content, and approximately $20 \%$ decline in $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ concentration. However, to a large extent, the negative effects of DCMU on roots could be reversed by sucrose addition. In the case of leaves, changes in the C and N metabolite contents were similar to those in roots, but could not be reversed by sucrose addition (Table 1). In addition, $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ concentration in media was obviously increased after DCMU treatment and decreased to the control level in the sucrose replenishment.

Figure 7 illustrates the change of OsSUTs transcript levels in leaves and roots to DCMU treatment as well as sucrose replenishment. In the case of leaves, DCMU treatment led to a decreased transcript level only for OsSUT4 (Fig. 7d) and increased transcript accumulation for OsSUT1 (Fig. 7a), OsSUT3 (Fig. 7c), and OsSUT5 (Fig. 7e), which could be partially reversed by sucrose supply. Interestingly, such mRNA expression patterns for the mentioned OsSUT isoforms also occurred in roots (Fig. 7a, c–e). In contrast, the change pattern of OsSUT2 transcripts in leaves was different from that in roots, which was observed in DCMU treatment alone or combined with sucrose (Fig. 7b). Sucrose transporter expression in the embryos of germinating seeds

According to the GUS staining results, OsSUT4 was specifically expressed in the aleurone layer and embryos of rice seeds. In germinating embryos, the GUS activity in the scutellum and vascular bundle was higher than that of other embryonic tissues (Fig. 1). The tissue-specific expression pattern of OsSUT4 in the germinating seeds was similar to that of OsSUT2 (Siao et al. 2011). Both OsSUT2 and Os - SUT4 may play a role in sucrose translocation from the scutellum to the young growing shoots and roots. The tissue-specific expression pattern of OsSUT1 in the germinating seeds has also been detected, and the results showed that OsSUT1 was expressed in phloem but not in scutellar epithelial cells and aleurone layers (Scofield et al. 2007a). Because the temporal and spatial expressions of OsSUT genes are various in the germinating seeds, the function and regulation of each OsSUT family gene were considered to be specialized.

Temperature and sucrose effects on OsSUT4 expression in embryos

Based on the characterization of the tissue-specific OsSUT4 expression in embryos, OsSUT4 may play a critical role in sucrose remobilization from the endosperm to the germinating embryos. The results of the RT-PCR and promoter activity assay showed that the expression level of the Os - SUT4 in embryos at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was lower than that at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Fig. 2a, b). However, the temperature effect on OsSUT4 expression was not present in isolated embryos (Fig. 2c). It was considered that molecules supplied from endosperms may be involved in the regulatory mechanism of temperature-dependent OsSUT4 expression in the embryos of germinating seeds. Sugars have been shown to regulate gene expression in several plant species (Thum et al. 2004; Gibson 2005; Rolland et al. 2006). Our previous studies indicated that OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 expressions in embryos occurred in response to sugars (Chen et al. 2010; Siao et al. 2011). In this study, the activity of $\textsf { \textsf { X } }$ -amylase, a key enzyme for reserved starch degradation, in the endosperms of seeds that germinated at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was lower than that at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Fig. 3a). Moreover, soluble sugar content in the embryos of the seeds that germinated at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was lower than in those that germinated at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Fig. 3b). Thus, the reduction of OsSUT4 expression in the germinating embryos at a lower temperature could be the result of a decrease in soluble sugars that were transported from endosperms. This hypothesis was supported by the data shown in Fig. 4 that indicated that soluble sugars function as inducers that promote OsSUT4 expression in isolated embryos. Conversely, the up-regulation of the OsSUT4 gene was not present in the embryos cultured in the medium containing mannitol. Therefore, the OsSUT4 expression in response to sugars did not occur because of osmotic effects. In the rice OsSUT gene family, the expression of the OsSUT2 gene in isolated rice embryos could also be slightly up-regulated by both glucose and sucrose after 1 day of treatment, and the positive sugar effect was considerably enhanced after 5 days of treatment (Siao et al. 2011). However, although the expression of the OsSUT1 gene was enhanced after 5 days of sugar treatment, OsSUT1 expression decreased after 1 day of sugar treatment (Chen et al. 2010). The mentioned results demonstrate that the sensitivity of the individual OsSUT gene in response to sugars was different in the germinating embryos.


## OsSUT4 expression in developing anthers


The promoter activity assay showed that OsSUT4 was expressed in anther tissues during the heading and flowering stages (Fig. 5). Moreover, both the OsSUT4 and the apoplastic invertase (CIN1) genes expressed in anthers increased during the late stage of pollen development (Fig. 6). Sucrose may be exported from anther tissues (e.g., tapetum) and hydrolyzed by CIN1. Consequently, the hexose hydrolyzed from sucrose may be transported into the developing pollen by monosaccharide transporters (MST) for starch biosynthesis. This was supported by the up-regulations of the MST genes at the late stage of pollen maturation in rice and maize plants (Datta et al. 2002; Kong et al. 2007). In addition, OsSUT4 mRNA expression was correlated with that of most starch biosynthesis genes (i.e., SBEI, SBEIII, GBSSI, AGPL2, AGPL4, SSSIII-1, and SSSIII-2) during anther development (Fig. 6). Therefore, OsSUT4 may function to control the import of sucrose for further sucrose–starch conversion in the developing pollen. Starch accumulation is an indicator of pollen maturity (Datta et al. 2002). The results of the promoter activity assay showed that the OsSUT4 gene was not only expressed in anthers but also in pollen (Fig. 7b). Our data demonstrated that the OsSUT4 expression patterns in developing pollen were associated with the starch accumulation (Fig. 7). Thus, it was suggested that sucrose could be either hydrolyzed to monosaccharide before the uptake into pollen cells by MSTs or directly transported into pollen-mediated SUT systems.

Pollen germination requires sugars as an energy source. The SUT expression in pollen tubes has been investigated in tobacco, Arabidopsis, tomato, and $P$ . major plants (Lemoine et al. 1999; Stadler et al. 1999; Hackel et al. 2006; Lauterbach et al. 2007). In Arabidopsis, the AtSUC1 proteins were detected in growing pollen tubes; the SUT was not only play a role in transporting sucrose for supplying energy and but also modulating the water potential of the pollen tube (Stadler et al. 1999). The expression and function of OsSUT1 were investigated in rice pollen during maturation and germination, and the results showed that the pollen germination may be impaired in OsSUT1 mutants (Hirose et al. 2010). In the LeSUT2 antisense transgenic tomato, pollen tube germination was inhibited and the product yield was reduced (Hackel et al. 2006). In this study, the promoter activity of OsSUT4 was detected in germinating rice pollen and growing pollen tubes (Fig. 8); however, further studies are required to reveal whether OsSUT4 functions to control pollen tube growth.


## Temperature effect on OsSUT4 expression in developing anthers


Low starch amounts in pollen cells and weak pollen activity in low-temperature conditions have been observed in rice plants (Oliver et al. 2005; Mamun et al. 2010). Our data showed a lower starch content in pollen in $1 5 / 1 3 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ conditions compared with that in 30/25 and $3 5 / 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ conditions (Fig. 9a). The temperature effect on the expression of several genes encoded proteins involved in sugar metabolism and monosaccharide transport has been investigated in previous studies. For example, anther-specific cell invertase gene (OsINV4) expression was reduced in low-temperature stresses (Oliver et al. 2005). According to Mamun et al. (2006), the expression of an OsMST8 gene, encoded rice monosaccharide transporter, was repressed at a low temperature. In this study, we showed that the $O s .$ - SUT4 mRNA level in low-temperature conditions was substantially lower than that at 30/25 and $3 5 / 3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Fig. 9b). Consistent with the results of the afore-mentioned studies, the low temperature may negatively affect sucrose translocation from anther tissues to developing pollen and repress the process of sucrose–starch conversion.


## Temperature- and sugar-responsive regulatory elements on OsSUT4 promoter


Based on the result of OsSUT4 promoter activity assay in embryos of transgenic rice plants, it was indicated the OsSUT4 promoter activity in germinating embryos was responsive to temperature (Fig. 2a). The promoter sequence analysis showed that several temperature-related regulatory elements were presented on the OsSUT4 promoter. The CRT/DRE element was C-repeat binding factor (CBF) 1 and 2 binding site, and CBF (also named DREB1) functions as a regulator of low temperature-responsive gene expression in several plant species (Jaglo-Ottosen et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998; Dubouzet et al. 2003; Svensson et al. 2006). MYC recognition element was ICE1 (inducer of CBF expression 1) binding site. ICE1 was an MYC-like bHLH transcription factor and functions as an inducer of CBF/DREB1 gene expression in Arabidopsis under lowtemperature condition (Chinnusamy et al. 2003). Moreover, the numbers of sugar-responsive elements were also found on the OsSUT4 promoter. The CGAGC element was a regulatory element found on promoter of rice Amy3D amylase gene, and it was involved in the sugar starvationinduced Amy3D gene expression (Hwang et al. 1998). Gibberellin-response element (GARE) is involved in the sugar-repressed expression of rice alpha-amylase gene (RAmy1A) (Morita et al. 1998), and it was presented on the OsSUT4 promoter. In addition, two copies of SURE element were located on the OsSUT4 promoter sequence. SURE was a sugar-responsive element identified on the promoter of isoamylase 1 gene, and it was recognized by a WRKY transcription factor, SUSIBA2 (Sun et al. 2003). However, whether these temperature- and sugar-related elements were involved in the regulation of temperatureand sugar-dependent OsSUT4 expressions still needs to be further studied.

In conclusion, rice OsSUT4 gene expression in germinating seeds and developing anthers depends on the developing stages and environmental temperature. The data presented here showed that low temperature is a negative factor affecting OsSUT4 expression in both embryos and anthers. These observations indicated that temperature may determine sugar translocation as well as carbohydrate metabolism and biosynthesis within the various tissues of germinating seeds and developing anthers.

OsSUT1 expression in embryos of germinating seeds

To identify the OsSUT1 expression pattern in the embryos of germinating rice seeds, we excised and collected the embryos from dry seeds and 1 through 5 days after imbibition (DAI) seeds, respectively. According to the QRTPCR results, transcript levels of OsSUT1 quickly and significantly increased after 1- to 2-days imbibition (Fig. 1). However, mRNA levels began to decline at 3 DAI, and the transcript levels remained steady until 5 DAI. In addition, although OsSUT1 expression at 3–5 DAI was obviously lower than that detected at 1 and 2 DAI, the average

OsSUT1 mRNA levels of samples at 3 through 5 DAI were still 3- to 4.5-fold higher than in dry embryos (Fig. 1).


## ABA and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ effects on OsSUT1 expression in rice embryos


The data in Fig. 2a demonstrate that ABA accumulated in dry embryos decreased immediately after seeds were imbibed for 1 day. Because the change in ABA content contrasted with the OsSUT1 expression pattern in embryos at the early germinating stage, we considered whether the role of ABA is that of a negative factor regulating OsSUT1 expression. To address this hypothesis, we treated the dry embryos, respectively, with $2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ABA and $2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ fluridone, an ABA biosynthesis inhibitor, for 1 day. The results showed that exogenous ABA downregulated OsSUT1 expression (Fig. 2b). On the other hand, OsSUT1 mRNA levels in fluridone-treated embryos were higher than those of control embryo samples that had just been imbibed in medium (Fig. 2c). To evaluate the effect of $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ on OsSUT1 expression in germinating embryos, we isolated and imbibed rice embryos in 0, 10, 50, and $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ solutions. In 1-day treated samples, OsSUT1 expression was slightly repressed by $1 0 \ \mu \mathrm { M } \ \mathrm { G } \mathrm { A } _ { 3 }$ but slightly enhanced by 50 and $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 3a). However, OsSUT1 transcript levels significantly increased in embryos incubated with various doses of $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ solutions for 5 days (Fig. 3b). These findings indicated that $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ functions as a positive regulator of OsSUT1 expression.


## Sugar effects on OsSUT1 expression


To address sugar effects on OsSUT1 expression, the isolated embryos were cultured in $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ glucose-, sucrose-, and mannitol- containing MS medium, respectively. The expression of OsSUT1 in each treatment was investigated after 1- and 5-day cultures. As shown in Fig. 4a, glucose and sucrose significantly repressed OsSUT1 expression after 1 day of treatment, respectively. In contrast to the results with 1-day treatment, OsSUT1 transcript levels were obviously enhanced in 5-day glucose- and sucrose-feeding embryos compared with the medium-only cultured samples (Fig. 4b). Moreover, because mannitol effect on OsSUT1 expression was significantly weaker than glucose and sucrose, we infer that osmotic effect was not the key factor to conduct the glucose- and sucrose-response of OsSUT1 gene (Fig. 4a, b).

Because of these differing glucose effects on OsSUT1 expression between 1- and 5-day treated embryos, we questioned whether the contrasting results arose because of differences in the treatment period or in the developmental stage. To dissect these possibilities, we conducted another experiment, culturing the isolated embryos in sugar-freemedium for 4 days and then transferring them to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ glucose-containing medium for 1 day before determining OsSUT1 expression levels. Under these conditions, OsSUT1 expression was only 0.5-fold of that in 5-DAI control embryos cultured in sugar-free medium (Fig. 5). This result indicated that 1-day glucose treatment repressed OsSUT1 expression in either 0- or 4-DAI embryos. Therefore, it appeared that duration of treatment rather than embryonic stage determined the glucose effect on OsSUT1 expression.

To elucidate part of the signal transduction pathway of glucose control of OsSUT1 expression in germinating embryos, we added glucose analogs to the culture medium. $N .$ -acetyl-glucosamine (NAG), an inhibitor of hexokinase activity, was used to address any involvement of a hexokinase-dependent pathway in glucose signaling for regulating OsSUT1 expression. As shown in Fig. 6a, NAG did nothing to ameliorate changes in OsSUT1 expression when we used the same dosage as we did for glucose in the 1-day treatment. Because the cellular uptake efficiency of NAG might be only one quarter that of glucose (Marshall et al. 1991), we also compared OsSUT1 mRNA levels in embryos treated with $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ glucose versus those treated with $8 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ NAG for 1 day. The results showed that the negative effect of glucose could be eliminated in a shortterm treatment with fourfold NAG (Fig. 6a). On the other hand, we also found that the glucose-enhanced OsSUT1 expression in 5-day treated embryos was eliminated in the presence of NAG at the same concentration as glucose or at fourfold levels (Fig. 6b). These results suggested that hexokinase-dependent signal transduction is part of the pathway involved in glucose-dependent regulation of OsSUT1 expression.

SUT proteins are important carriers for transporting sucrose across the plasma membrane or vacuolar membranes (reviewed by Kühn and Grof 2010). Arabidopsis SUT protein has also been found on the chloroplast membrane (Rolland et al. 2003). Rice OsSUT2 is classified in the same group with Arabidopsis AtSUT4, tomato LeSUT4, potato StSUT4, Lotus japonicus LjSUT4, and barley HvSUT2 (Braun and Slewinski 2009; Kühn and Grof 2010). Some of the above-mentioned SUTs, including AtSUT4, StSUT4, and LjSUT4, have been identified as low-affinity/high-capacity transporters (Weise et al. 2000; Reinders et al. 2008). In addition, AtSUT4, LjSUT4, and HvSUT2 are vacuolar transporters according to a previous analysis of transient SUT–GFP fusion protein expression (Endler et al. 2006; Reinders et al. 2008). On the other hand, LeSUT4 and StSUT4 are located on the plasma membrane of sieve elements (Reinders et al. 2002). OsSUT2 contains 12 transmembrane domains and was localized on plasma membrane. Amino acid alignment showed that the number of amino acids in the central inside loops are similar among OsSUT2 and other SUTs in group 4 (according to the classification by Braun and Slewinski 2009) (Fig. 1); however, the length of the OsSUT2 central loop is shorter than that of SUTs belonging to group 2, i.e., AtSUT2 and LeSUT2. LeSUT2 is considered to function as a putative sucrose sensor (Barker et al. 2000). The conserved domains in the extended cytoplasmic loop of LeSUT2 and AtSUT2 play an important role in signal sensing and transduction (Barker et al. 2000). Because the lengths and amino acid sequences of the central loops are significantly different between OsSUT2 and LeSUT2, the regulatory mechanism and function of OsSUT2 might not be completely identical to that of LeSUT2.

Carbohydrate transport from endosperms and embryos to coleoptiles, shoots, and roots is an important process for supplying developing tissues with a carbon source during seed germination and seedling establishment. The levels of OsSUT2 mRNA gradually increased from 1 to 5 DAI (Fig. 3b). However, our previous report showed that the OsSUT1 transcript significantly increased after 1 to 2 DAI and then quickly decreased at 3 DAI (Chen et al. 2010). The expression level of OsSUT1 was the highest among OsSUT members in embryos at early imbibition stages (i.e., DAI 1), but OsSUT2 was the dominantly expressed OsSUT member 5 DAI (Fig. 3a). Thus, the functions and regulations of individual OsSUT genes are different in the embryos of germinating seeds. As shown by the data in Fig. 8, the expression levels of OsSUT2 in scutellum and vascular bundles were higher than in other embryo ground cells, and the OsSUT2 promoter activity was also significantly observed in aleurone layers. According to the OsSUT2 expression patterns in germinating seeds, it was suggested that OsSUT2 play a role to release sucrose from aleurone layers, transport sucrose into scutellum, and also load sucrose into the phloem in germinating seeds. On the other hand, OsSUT1 gene was expressed in the scutellar vascular bundle of germinating embryos but not in the scutellar epithelial cell layer. Therefore, it was suggested that OsSUT1 functioned to load sucrose into phloem for transport to developing shoot and roots but not play a role to transport sucrose from endosperm to embryos (Scofield et al. 2007).

The increased OsSUT2 expression in isolated embryos (without endosperms) during germination was not obvious in dark conditions; however, the significant up-regulation of OsSUT2 was observed in the embryos of germinating seeds (with endosperms) in dark conditions. Thus, it was suggested that the sugar transported from endosperm was the key factor for promoting OsSUT2 expression. Sugars not only act as nutrients and energy for supporting plant growth but also function as signals controlling plant development and the expression of various genes (reviewed by Gibson 2005; Rolland et al. 2006). The data in Fig. 6 showed that the transcript levels of rice OsSUT2 could be slightly enhanced by glucose and sucrose after 1 day of treatment and significantly enhanced after 5 days of treatment. Moreover, since the OsSUT2 expression was not affected by mannitol, the sugar-enhanced OsSUT2 expression was not caused by osmotic effect. Sugarenhanced expression has also been observed with OsSUT1 (Matsukura et al. 2000; Chen et al. 2010). However, the positive effect of sugar on OsSUT1 expression occurs after 5 days of treatment, and 1-day sugar treatment downregulates OsSUT1 expression (Chen et al. 2010). Thus, the mechanisms of sugar-mediated regulation are different for OsSUT1 and OsSUT2. Sucrose-induced signal transduction for gene regulation could involve sucrose as a direct signal that is sensed by a sensor located on the cell membrane or an intracellular sensor. In addition, sucrose metabolites, such as glucose, could be signals to trigger the downstream transduction pathway (reviewed by Halford et al. 1999). The nonmetabolizable sucrose analog palatinose had a similar effect on OsSUT2 expression in rice embryos as sucrose, suggesting that sucrose acts as a direct molecule for triggering the up-regulation of OsSUT2 expression. In addition, the sensor for sucrose signal transduction is expected to be located on the cell membrane because of the lack of palatinose transport into plant cells (Sinha et al. 2002; Rolland et al. 2006). Moreover, since there was no effect of mannitol on OsSUT2 expressions (Fig. 6), it was suggested that the up-regulation of OsSUT2 expressions by palatinose was not caused by osmotic effect. Moreover, the data showing that 3-OMG can also conduct the same positive effect on OsSUT2 expression in germinating embryos as glucose suggests that the glucose-induced OsSUT2 expression was mediated by a hexokinaseindependent pathway. In contrast, glucose-regulated OsSUT1 expression in germinating embryos was via a hexokinasedependent pathway (Chen et al. 2010). Changes in the transcriptional activity of the OsSUT2 promoter in embryos during germination correlated with the mRNA levels. OsSUT2 promoter activity was also upregulated by glucose in embryos. Thus, promoter regulation was a key step for controlling OsSUT2 expression. The predicted cis-acting elements on the OsSUT2 promoter were searched in the PLACE database (Higo et al. 1999), identifying a SUSIBA2 transcription factor-binding site (WBOXHVISO1; W-box) 477 bp upstream of the ATG translation start codon. SUSIBA2 is a sugar-inducible WRKY protein that can bind the sugar-responsive element on the barley isoamylase 1 promoter (Sun et al. 2003). Further study is needed regarding whether the interaction of SUSIBA2 and the W-box on the OsSUT2 promoter is a key factor to controlling sugar-responsive OsSUT2 expression.

In conclusion, we identified OsSUT2 as a plasma membrane transporter. OsSUT2 expression in germinated embryos correlates with the developmental stage, with regulation depending on the sugar transported from endosperms. The developmental regulation and signaling pathways of sugarresponsive OsSUT2 expression in germinating embryos are different from those of OsSUT1. Glucose-enhanced OsSUT2 expression was mediated by a hexokinase-independent pathway, and sucrose is sensed by a sensor located on the plasma membrane to up-regulate OsSUT2 expression. We also found that promoter activity is the major factor controlling the developmental stage- and sugar-dependent mRNA accumulation of OsSUT2 in the embryos of germinating seeds. Future studies of the activity of the deleted promoter element and finding the factors that interact with the cis-acting element would be helpful for elucidating the molecular mechanism of OsSUT2 expression in germinating rice embryos.
