Members of the OPT gene family play critical roles in various physiological processes in plants, including growth and development, nutrient uptake, and stress responses, particularly in the transport and homeostasis of metal ions [16, 17]. In this study, a total of $3 0 \ P t O P T$ gene family members were identified in the $P .$ trichocarpa genome, which is comparable to that in other plant species, such as Arachis hypogaea $4 0 \ : O P T$ genes) [12], Solanum tuberosum (21 OPT genes) [58], Panax ginseng (37 OPT genes) [10], and Brassica rapa (28 OPT genes) [7], but considerably smaller than that in wheat (107 OPT genes) [59]. The members of the OPT gene family in $P .$ trichocarpa were identified on the basis of genome data version 1.0, which led to the identification of only $2 0 \ : O P T$ family members (9 YSL subfamily members and 11 OPT subfamily members) [43]. As the first poplar species to be sequenced, the genome data of $P .$ trichocarpa have undergone multiple rounds of resequencing and refinement. The high-quality genome data may have altered the number of members in the OPT gene family. For example, $2 0 0 ~ E R F$ genes were identified in the $P .$ trichocarpa genome data version 1.1 [60], whereas $2 1 0 ~ E R F$ genes were identified in the $P .$ trichocarpa genome data version 4.1 [45]. On the basis of the latest $P .$ trichocarpa genome database version 4.1, a total of 17 YSL subfamily members and 13 OPT subfamily members were identified in this study, which refined the information on the OPT family members in $P .$ trichocarpa. Physicochemical analysis revealed that all the PtOPT proteins were hydrophobic and mostly basic (Table S1). Most of the PtOPT proteins were located in the plasma membrane, which is consistent with observations in rice, turnip, and maize [7, 9, 61], indicating the high conservation of OPT proteins across species. The $3 0 \ : P t O P T$ genes were unevenly distributed across the 19 chromosomes, with 7 chromosomes lacking PtOPT genes. The YSL subfamily members presented a more clustered chromosomal distribution than did the OPT subfamily (Fig. 1). The members of the PtOPT gene family were divided into two major branches according to phylogenetic analysis: the OPT subfamily and the YSL subfamily, which is consistent with previous reports in other species [8, 12, 59]. Genes exhibiting analogous gene and protein structures were primarily observed within the same subfamily and phylogenetic cluster, thereby supporting the classification of PtOPTs .

Gene duplication events facilitate the generation of novel genes and contribute to the acquisition of new functions by these genes [62]. Analysis of gene duplication events suggested that the majority of PtOPT genes experienced gene duplication events. Specifically, 11 duplicated gene pairs were segmental duplications, whereas one duplicated gene pair was a tandem duplication. Thus, segmental duplication may serve as a primary driving force for the expansion of the PtOPT gene family. Similarly, the expansion of the OPT gene family in $B _ { \cdot }$ . rapa is attributed primarily to segmental duplications [7]. The PtOPT genes may have originated from two distinct ancestors, as the gene duplication events occurred exclusively within subfamilies. The Ka/Ks values of the duplicated gene pairs suggested that the PtOPTs had undergone purifying selection throughout their evolutionary history. Duplicated genes are typically functionally redundant before functional divergence [63]. Consequently, the majority of duplicated genes rapidly become pseudogenes and are lost from the genome [64]. To mitigate the risk of gene loss during evolution, the expression levels of duplicated genes tend to be relatively lower than those of their ancestral counterparts [63]. In this study, the duplicated genes PtOPT6.1, PtOPT2, and $P t O P T 5 . I$ presented low expression levels in all tissues, which is consistent with previous studies indicating that low expression levels may facilitate the retention of duplicated genes and their functional redundancy [65]. Numerous studies have demonstrated that members of the OPT family function in the long-distance transport of sulfur, nitrogen translocation, maintenance of metal homeostasis, and heavy metal chelation [14, 16, 34, 36, 66, 67]. For example, ZmYSL2 regulates kernel development and iron distribution in maize kernels [19]. AtOPT6 functions in the translocation of GSH and PCs, as well as in the distribution of Cd in A. thaliana [17]. In addition, the expression of OPT genes is regulated by various transcription factors. For example, PcWRKY1 represses PcYSL3 to negatively regulate the transport of the Cd-NA complex [20, 68]. In this study, most PtOPT promoters contained ABREs, CGTCA motifs, and TGA elements, which are associated with phytohormone responsiveness. Additionally, cis-acting elements such as AREs, MBSs, and TC-rich repeats, which are linked to stress responses, have been identified. These results indicate that the PtOPT genes may be regulated by hormones and play crucial roles in stress responses. The GO and KEGG analyses of the coexpressed genes of PtOPTs revealed that these coexpressed genes were predominantly enriched in pathways related to cellular nitrogen compound metabolism, small molecule metabolism, and protein-containing complexes, suggesting that PtOPTs are involved in the metabolism of small molecule nitrogen-containing compounds. A gene coexpression network revealed that PtOPT4.2 regulated 575 related genes, suggesting its potential involvement in the synthesis and metabolism of nitrogen-containing compounds.

Members of the OPT family play crucial roles in the uptake and transport of Fe in both graminaceous and nongraminaceous plants [12, 33]. Previous studies have investigated the expression patterns of OPT genes under iron-deficient conditions [12]. However, the expression profiles of OPT genes under iron-sufficient conditions remain poorly understood. In maize, ZmYSLs are induced by iron deficiency, thereby increasing iron absorption, transport, distribution, and accumulation [18]. In Arabidopsis, AtYSLs are involved in the transport of metal ions or metal chelates. For example, AtYSL1, AtYSL2, and AtYSL3 are involved in the translocation of Fe-phytosiderophores (PSs) [69]. The expression levels of PtOPTs remained relatively stable under an excessive iron supply, possibly because an appropriately excessive concentration of Fe was insufficient for poplars (Fig.  7). Cd exposure can disturb the uptake and translocation of Fe in most plants, causing Fe deficiency-like symptoms in the leaves of plants [53]. Several OPT genes, including AtYSL3 [68], AtYSL1 [70], OsYSL16 [71], OsYSL9 [72], ZmYSL2 [36], and MsYSL6 [28], have been identified as key transporters of Fe and the Fe-NA complex to leaves in response to environmental stimuli, such as Fe deficiency and Cd stress. Additionally, some OPT genes, such as PcYSL3 [20], BoOPT3 [26], and AtOPT6 [13, 17], have been demonstrated to be involved in the transport of Cd, Cd-GSH, and Cd-PC for long-distance transport and detoxification of Cd. In our previous studies, a high Cd supply increased Cd accumulation and alleviated Cd toxicity [53, 73]. In the present study, ${ P t Y S L 3 . S }$ and PtOPT6.1 were induced by Cd, suggesting that these genes may play important roles in the translocation of Cd and Fe from roots to shoots. The expression patterns of PtYSL6, PtYSL7.4, PtOPT2, PtOPT5.2, and PtYSL3.3 in leaves were completely opposite in response to Cd under different Fe supply levels, indicating that these five genes play important roles in the absorption and translocation of Cd and Fe.

Metal hyperaccumulators can not only tolerate high concentration of heavy metals in the soils but also take them up actively and accumulate and distribute them to appropriate tissues at extreme high levels, thus make them very attractive for the remediation of heavy metal polluted soils [1]. A large amount of different metal hyperaccumulators have been recognized in different regions all over the world [2], among them, Thlaspi caerulescens, a $\mathrm { { C d } / \mathrm { { Z n } / \mathrm { { N i } } } }$ hyperaccumulator, has been used as a model plant to study the physiological and molecular mechanisms of heavy metal hyperaccumulation [3,4].

The efficient metal loading and unloading ability in the vascular systems was regarded as the key step of hyperaccumulating process for hyperaccumulators [5]. Nonetheless, knowledge about the mechanisms and proteins involved in transporting heavy metals from soil via the roots and stems into their storage sites is much limited. Transporter families, including ZIP (ZRT/IRT like Protein), Nramp (Natural Resistance and Macrophage Protein), MTP (Metal Tolerance Protein), HMA (Heavy Metal transporting P-type ATPase), ABC-type (ATP-binding cassette), COPT family CTR/COPT (high-affinity Cu transporters) as well as YSL (Yellow strip1-Like transporters) families have been porved to involve in transit metal movements, they either act at the plasma membrane (PM) to transport metals into cytoplasm or redistribute metals from intracellular compartments into the cytoplasm [6,7,8,9]. Besides the above transporters families, novel transporters related to metal homeostasis are continuously under discovery, oligopeptide transporter (OPT) family is among those being focused recently [10,11,12]. OPT family is one of three families responsible for peptide transport; the other two are the ATPbinding cassette (ABC-type) transporters superfamily and the peptide transporter (PTR) superfamily [10]. Peptides, existing abundantly in xylem and phloem saps, are important for plant growth, development and signaling. Transport of peptides is taken as a more efficient means of nitrogen distribution than transport of individual amino acids, implying the important role of peptide transporters in long-distance transport of nutrients [10]. Besides the peptides, inorganic nutrients and transit metals have been reported as the substrates of peptide transporters in the recent studies. For intances, the ABC transporters AtMRP3 [13], AtATM3 [14] and AtPDR8 [15] are proposed to involve in heavy metal (Cd, Pb) resistance and movement.

The first OPT family is identified in the pathogenic yeast Candida albicans [16] and subsequently in Schizosaccharomyces pombe [17] and Saccharomyces cerevisiae [18]. Later, it is also found in bacteria, plants, and archaea [11], but still not in animals. OPT family is grouped into two distinct subfamilies, the yellow stripe (YS) clade and the peptide transport (PT) clade [11,12]. The function of YS1-like (YSL) transporter on transportation of metalcomplex has been documented well in planta. For example, YSLs mediate long-distance transport of specific Fe species [19,20]. ZmYS1 cloned from Zea mays is the founding member of YSL family, which functions in root Fe-phytosiderophore (Fe-PS) uptake from the soil [21]. HvYS1 encoding a YSL transporter is a specific transporter for iron (III)-PS in barley roots [22]. Since non-Poaceae species do not synthesize phytosiderophores, the substrates of YSL transporters in dicotyledonous plant are suggested to be Fe(II)/Fe(III)-nicotianamine (Fe-NA) functioning in the long-distance transporting system [23,24,25]. NA is a chelator for several micronutrient metals and involves in the movement of micronutrients and heavy metals throughout the plant [26]. Three YSL genes cloned from T. caerulescens express at higher levels as compared with their Arabidopsis thaliana homologs with distinct patterns. TcYSL3 was further confirmed as a Fe/NiNA influx transporter [19]. Functional analysis in yeast demonstrated that TcYSL3 can transport both Ni-NA and Fe-NA complexes into yeast, indicating that TcYSL3 may be involved in the long-distance translocation of Ni in T. caerulescens.

In Arabidopsis, nine putative OPT orthologues (AtOPT1 to AtOPT9) have been identified [27,28]. OPT transporters predominantly recognize tetrapeptides and pentapeptides, thus they are also called peptide transporters, but this is challenged recently as AtOPTs have been proved to play a role in metal homeostasis and movements. Transcript of AtOPT2 is induced in root by iron and zinc deficiency, and that of AtOPT3 by iron, copper and manganese deficiency [28,29]. AtOPT3 is further proved to involve in the movement of iron to the developing seeds [30]. Moreover, both AtOPT6 and AtOPT7 can transport cadmium or cadmium-glutathione conjugates when heterologously expressed in yeast [31,32]. All these studies indicate that OPT family might play important roles in metal uptake and transportation.

In the present study, we isolated a member of the OPT family from a metal hyperaccumulator, Thlaspi caerulescens, named TcOPT3. We characterized its expression in different tissues, and conducted heterologous expression in yeast to investigate the role of TcOPT3 in metal uptake. We demonstrated that TcOPT3 was involved in Fe/Zn/Cd/Cu transportation and it should be a very important component in the metal long-distance transport system, and contribute to heavy metal hyperaccumulation in the shoots.

## Identification, classification, and nomenclature of YSL subfamily in wheat


One hundred seven wheat protein sequences belonging to OPT family were identified in the wheat genome by performing Pfam blast searches. Among these, 98 proteins with amino acid length $> 4 2 0$ were confirmed for the presence of characteristic domain and considered to be valid. The phylogenetic analysis of the identified wheat OPTs was performed in comparison with A. thaliana OPT sequences. The distribution of OPT proteins in phylogenetic tree basically comprised of two major subgroups: the yellow stripe (YS-OPT) and the peptide transporter (PT-OPT; Fig. S1 and Table S2). Out of 98 high-confidence wheat OPT sequences, the 67 sequences correspond to the YS-OPT type subgroup, whereas 31 belong to the PT-OPT group. The sequence similar to the earlier proposed YSL signature sequence K(F/R)L(T/P/A)(Y/F)PSG(T/ L/S)ATA(V/M/H)LIN (Gendre et al. 2007) confirms their classification as YS-OPT member. The PT-OPT-specific NPG and KIPPR-conserved motifs were specifically found in the sequences form PT-OPTs but were absent in YS-OPT and hence validated the classification of genes (Koh et al. 2002; Hu et al. 2012). Finally, 67 wheat YS-OPT sequences were shortlisted and are referred hereafter as TaYSL (Table S3). Due to hexaploid nature of wheat genome, the identified 67 TaYSLs may also include the corresponding homoeolog for wheat YSL genes. Hence, identified 67 TaYSLs sequences represent 26 genes. The nomenclature of wheat YSL proteins has been assigned in accordance with their phylogenetic relatedness to $B$ . distachyon followed by their corresponding location on chromosomes 1–7.


## Genomic distribution of wheat YSLs


All identified wheat YSL genes were subsequently clustered based on the homoeolog information that was derived from the wheat genome database. Based on their genome location, in total, $2 6 ~ Y S L$ genes were identified. The genomic location of all the 26 TaYSL genes was identified on the chromosome groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7 (Fig. 1a). No YSL gene was found on chromosome group 4A, B, D, 5B, D, and 7B. The density of TaYSL genes loci was highest on the chromosome 2B $( 1 2 , \sim$ $1 8 \%$ ), followed by 2A (11, $\sim 1 6 \% )$ , and 2D (ten, $\sim 1 5 \%$ ) and the minimum number of TaYSLs was found on chromosome 5A (two, $\sim 3 \%$ ). Notably, close to half of the YSL genes were located on the chromosome 2 of hexaploid genome (Fig. 1b). Twenty-five YSL genes were found to have homoeologs on colored boxes and numbers 1–15 at the right. Size of the boxes indicates the length of the conserved motifs. The black lines represent the non-conserved sequences

subgenome A, 23 on D, and 19 on B. Three genes (TaYS1B, TaYSL13.1, and TaYSL18) have only two homoeologs, while homoeologs were not found for TaYSL2, TaYSL8, TaYSL21, and TaYSL23 genes (Fig. 1c).


## TaYSLs have close orthologs in other plant species


To gain an insight for the phylogenetic relationship of wheat YSLs with Arabidopsis and other members of graminaceous family, 67 wheat YSLs (including homoeologs), 19 from Brachypodium, and 18 YSL sequences from rice (Table S4)

were considered. These were analyzed by building an unrooted phylogenetic tree through NJ method. Our analysis revealed the distribution of TaYSLs into four distinct clades (clade I–IV) along with arabidopsis, Brachypodium and rice YSLs (Fig. 2). Clade I was the largest (8 genes) and clade II was the smallest (four genes) of the four clades. It was also found that the members of Brachypodium and rice YSLs specific to grass family were mainly clustered in clade IV, suggesting the specificity of this clade to graminaceous plants. Therefore, YSLs that are grouped in this clade should be considered as unique to grass family (Yordem et al. 2011). In general, the clade I comprises of TaYS1A/1B/TaYSL1-3/7-9 genes from chromosome groups 1, 2, 5, 6, and 7, clade II contains TaYSL4/6/19/20 genes from chromosome group 2 and 3, TaYSL5/11-14/18 genes from chromosomal groups 2 and 6 were in clade III, and the TaYSL10/15-17/21-23 genes from diverse chromosome groups 1–3, 5, and 6 belong to graminaceous-specific clade IV. Phylogenetic relationships of 67 TaYSL proteins among themselves validated the clade distribution (Fig. S2).

The synteny analysis was also performed for better understanding of YSL gene subfamily evolution. Therefore, based on phylogeny, a syntenic relationship was built for YSLs from wheat, Brachypodium, and rice (Fig. 3 and Table S5). Majority of YSL genes are distributed on chromosome 5 in Brachypodium and chromosome 4 in rice. While in wheat, YSL genes are predominantly present on chromosome 2. Out of 26 identified TaYSLs, 14 genes have orthologs both in Brachypodium and rice. Whereas, four and two genes were found to have orthologs only in Brachypodium and rice, respectively. Additionally, no orthologs were found for five TaYSL genes (TaYSL 7, 8, 19, 20, 23) (Table S5).


## Transcript and protein motif structure


Sixty-seven high-confidence TaYSL proteins were divided into three groups (group I, II, and III) on the basis of their sequence similarity. The gene structures for the TaYSL gene family were first analyzed by determining the exon-intron arrangement (Fig. S3). The ORF length of wheat YSLs ranged from 1278 to 2247 base pairs (Table S3). The number of exons identified in TaYSL transcripts varied from 1 to 10 and for introns it varied from 0 to 9 (Table S3). TaYS1B-1D possess the maximum number of introns and exons and fall in group I; whereas, TaYSL22-6A having minimum number of exon, intron falls into group III (Fig. S3). Additionally, difference in exon-intron arrangement was also observed within the YSL homoeologs.

The percentage similarity among wheat YSL proteins ranged from 33.3 to $8 9 . 6 \%$ . The length of the TaYSL proteins ranged from 425 to 748 amino acid residues with the predicted molecular weight and PI ranging from 46.5 to $8 1 . 6 \mathrm { K D a }$ and 5.68–9.87, respectively. The subcellular localization tool predicted the presence of most wheat YSL proteins at the plasma membrane $( \sim 7 3 \% )$ . However, few of them were found to be localized in chloroplast $( \sim 1 2 \% )$ , cytoplasm $( \sim 9 \% )$ , vacuole $( \sim 4 \% )$ , and mitochondria $( 2 \% )$ (Table S3). The number of the transmembrane domains varies from 8 to 18 in different TaYSL proteins. About $46 \%$ of YSL proteins have intracellular $\Nu _ { - }$ and C-termini, $24 \%$ have N-termini outside and Ctermini inside, $16 \%$ have N-termini inside and C-termini outside, and only $14 \%$ YSL proteins have both N- and C-termini predicted to be present in extracellular region (Table S3).

The conserved motifs were predicted using MEME program. A total of 15 conserved motifs designated as motifs 1–15 were identified with length varying from 15 to 50 (Fig. 4). Among these motifs, highly conserved sequence similar to YSL signature sequence K(F/R)L(T/P/A)(Y/F)PSG(T/ L/S)ATA(V/M/H)LIN was specifically present in motifs 3 (Table S6).


## Expression of wheat YSL in developing wheat grain tissue


The accumulation of micronutrients like iron and zinc can be correlated to transportation function of seed metal transporters and YSL proteins. Therefore, expression study of wheat YSLs was performed in 14 DAA immature seeds. Out of 14 genes tested, nine of them showed significant transcript accumulation. Among the expressed YSL genes, TaYSL1A, TaYSL2,

TaYSL6, and TaYSL14 showed the highest expression in grains (Fig. S4). Furthermore, in silico expression analysis of previously published data (Pearce et al. 2015) (referred to as GTE: grain tissue-specific expression; Fig. S5) also showed seed-specific expression of TaYSL1-2A, TaYSL12-2B, and TaYSL17-6D in the seed coat. Whereas, high mRNA accumulation for TaYSL3-2A, TaYSL6, TaYSL12-2A, and TaYSL15- 3D was observed in both seed coat and aleurone layer (al) (Table S7). The high expression of TaYSL6, TaYSL15-3D, and other homeolog of TaYSL3-2D in aleurone layer for $2 0 \mathrm { \ d p a }$ was also supported by data for 20 dpa (Pfeifer et al. 2014) (GTDT: grain tissue-specific developmental time course; Fig. S5). In endosperm tissue, high transcript levels for TaYSL13.2-2A and $T a Y S L I 3 . 2 – 2 D$ were observed. Using data from Choulet et al. 2014, (DTCS: developmental timecourse of Chinese Spring), we found that TaYSL13.2 has the highest expression in seed of 2 dpa when compared with all other tissues (Fig. S5). Collectively, these results ensure our speculations about active involvement of plant YSL proteins in micronutrient partitioning among different wheat seed tissues.


## YSL genes respond to iron-limiting conditions in roots and shoots


The YSL transporters are known to be involved in Fe acquisition and subsequent transport in the foliar tissues (Waters et al. 2006). To test the ability of wheat YSL transporters to perceive iron limiting condition, we studied their temporal expression in roots and shoots. As expected, wheat seedlings exposed to a limiting condition showed iron starvation phenotype in form of leaf yellowing. The control root was positive for Perl’s staining suggesting an uptake of Fe from the media (Fig. 5a). Transcript accumulation of TaYS1A, TaYS1B, TaYSL3, TaYSL5, and TaYSL6 showed an early induction in the iron-starved root samples. In contrast, accumulation of these transcripts was either maintained at the basal level or showed decreased expression during 9 to 15 days of starvation (Fig. 5b). Interestingly, the expression of wheat YSL genes was significantly altered in the control roots during the course of experiment. Such expression pattern suggested an important role of wheat YSL genes during the growth and development of the roots.

Multiple wheat YSLs showed high expression at the later stage of the iron-limiting experiment in shoots. Most of the wheat YSLs have higher mRNA level at either 12 or 15 days of the −Fe condition (Fig. 6). For example, TaYS1A, TaYS1B, TaYSL5, TaYSL12, and TaYSL19 showed multiple fold expression only after 9, 12, or 15 days of iron starvation. This delayed expression response in shoots could be accounted for the timedependent relay of signals from roots to the shoots.


## Expression of wheat YSLs in different tissues


To gain an insight into tissue-specific expression, 26 YSLs were studied for their expression values by using expVIP (Borrill et al. 2016) in different tissues and developmental stages (Table S7) (Pearce et al. 2015; Pfeifer et al. 2014; Choulet et al. 2014). Seven YSL genes (TaYSL2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, and $^ { 1 5 }$ ) were expressed in all tissues and developmental stages studied in these experiments. Within the shoot tissues, the highest expression was observed in TaYSL6 and TaYSL14- $\boldsymbol { \delta B }$ whereas TaYSL3-2A, 2D, TaYSL6, and TaYSL15-3D were predominantly expressed in roots (Fig. S5 and Table S7). TaYSL3-2A and TaYSL6 showed the highest abundance of the transcript within leaf, specifically at 2 dpa. These expression patterns suggested the preferred site of their activity. The expression of several TaYSL genes was detected exclusively in root and spike. TaYS1A-6D, TaYS1B-1D, TaYSL3-2D, TaYSL8-5A, TaYSL19, and TaYSL20 genes were root specific with highest expression observed for TaYS1A-6D, TaYSL19, and TaYSL20-2B. Whereas, for genes specifically expressed in spike, TaYSL10-3A and 3B, TaYSL15-3A and 3B, TaYSL16, TaYSL17-6A and $\boldsymbol { \delta B }$ , and TaYSL21-2A were mostly expressed at anthesis stage, while TaYSL11 showed expression at the flag leaf stage.


## Alternative function of YSLs as evident from their expression during abiotic and biotic stress


The homeostatic interaction has been reported previously for Fe uptake under Pi-limiting condition (Wasaki et al. 2003; Lan et al. 2012; Hoehenwarter et al. 2016). To test this correlation in the expression patterns of wheat YSL genes under Pilimiting conditions, 10-day phosphate starvation RNA-Seq data (Oono et al. 2013) for root and shoot tissues was analyzed using ExpVIP (wheat expression browser). Eight wheat YSL genes showed differential expression in roots, with upregulation of TaYS1A-6DL, TaYSL1-2AL, and TaYSL3-2DL and downregulation of TaYSL20-2DS, TaYSL20-2BS, and all the homoeologs of TaYSL19. Significant fold downregulation (\~ 10-folds) was observed for TaYSL19-2DL (Fig. 7a; Table S7). Additionally, the expression pattern of wheat YSLs was also checked during abiotic stresses like heat, drought, and their combination thereof. Thirteen YSL genes show differential expression either in heat, drought, or the combined stress. In general, YSL genes either had no effect or downregulated in abovementioned conditions. This suggests that this subfamily of transporters is generally negatively regulated during abiotic stress conditions. The only exceptions were $T a Y S L 3  – 2 D$ , TaYSL4-2A, TaYSL6-3D, and TaYSL14-6B that showed induction specific to either heat or dual stress of heat and drought (Fig. 7a; Table S7). Earlier, an alternative function for Arabidopsis YSL3 was demonstrated in pathogen defense (Chen et al. 2014). Our in silico analysis suggested upregulaiton of TaYSL6, TaYSL12, and TaYSL13.1 during Septoria tritici infection in the seedling stage. TaYSL12-2A was also upregulated during powdery mildew infection (Fig. 7b; Table S7). Our data pin-point the probable untapped roles of wheat YSL genes during plant pathogen defense.

In plants, the YSL proteins play a pivotal role, especially in long-distance transport and mobilization of the micronutrients from soil to the vegetative and reproductive parts (Curie et al. 2009). Till date, the YSL subfamily has been identified in several plant species including the model plant Arabidopsis, maize, and the members of grass family like rice and Brachypodium (Curie et al. 2001; Gross et al. 2003; Koike et al. 2004; Yordem et al. 2011). Due to the scarcity of the functional information of YSL proteins from hexaploid wheat, we have performed a comprehensive analysis of YSL transporter in Triticum aestivum genome.


## Presence of high number of wheat YSL genes


OPT transporters are a unique group of membrane-localized proteins having a wide range of functions including the transport of metabolites and substrate including metals and therefore contribute to many biological processes (Lubkowitz 2011). Herein, we have identified 107 wheat OPT members. This is by far the largest number compared to rice, Brachypodium, and Arabidopsis; those are having 33, 28, and 17 OPT genes. Also, a total of 26 wheat YSL were systematically identified that correspond to the largest plant YSL genes known so far. By considering the presence of homoeologs in hexaploid wheat genome, here, we are reporting a total of 67 TaYSL sequences that are representing $2 6 ~ T a Y S L$ genes. Characterization of TaYSL genes was done by performing phylogenetic analysis, chromosomal location, synteny analysis, exon-intron arrangement, conserved motif determination, and predicted subcellular localization. Phylogenetic classification of TaYSL genes resulted in four distinct clades that was consistent with the previous reports from other grass species (Yordem et al. 2011; Curie et al. 2009). Moreover, the classified YSL protein transporter members from clade IV were grass specific. Seven TaYSL genes (TaYSL10, 15, 16, 17, 21, 22, 23) are exclusively part of clade IV and share proximity with other transporters from grass family. The closeness of wheat YSL proteins with rice orthologs also provides opportunity to predict the gene functions based on information from studies in rice. For instance, the closest ortholog of TaYSL7 of clade I is OsYSL15 of rice that has been previously reported to be involved in the acquisition of Fe from the soil (Inoue et al. 2009; Lee et al. 2009).

Topological studies have suggested that all the identified wheat YSL transporters are transmembrane proteins. In general, the identified wheat YSL transporters showed presence for $1 0 { - } 1 4 \ \mathrm { T M }$ domains similar to those in rice and Arabidopsis counterparts (Gross et al. 2003; Le Jean et al. 2005). According to our sequence analysis, almost $70 \%$ of wheat YSL transporters were found to be localized on plasma-membrane with cytosolic N-terminal. This further Fig. 7 Heat-map showing the relative expression of putative wheat YSL genes under various abiotic and biotic stresses. a Heat maps of selected wheat YSL genes were generated using wheat expression database expVIP under various abiotic (phosphate starvation, drought, heat, and drought-heat). b Biotic stresses (Fusarium heat blight, Septoriatritici, stripe rust, and powdery mildew). Color bar at the top of the heat-map shows the fold change; thereby, green color represents downregulation, black represents no change, and red color represents upregulation

suggests their role in metal uptake through the plasma-membrane. Earlier reports have experimentally confirmed the presence of YSL transporters on the plasma-membrane of the cell (Inoue et al. 2009; Lee et al. 2009). Very few of the TaYSL proteins were predicted to be localized in chloroplast, vacuole, and mitochondria and thus reflect their specific role in these subcellular compartments. For example, TaYSL proteins predicted to be localized in the vacuole (TaYSL11-2A, TaYSL11- 2B , and TaYSL14-6A) or chloroplast (TaYSL1-2B, TaYSL4-2A, TaYSL7-7D, TaYSL7-7A2, TaYSL14-6D, TaYSL17-6A, TaYSL17-6D, and TaYSL18-6D) might have important functional roles in maintaining metal homeostasis in plants as these two organelles are considered to be the main storage sites for the metals (Lopez-Millan et al. 2016). Interestingly, all the homoeologs of TaYSL19 and TaYSL20 were predicted to be cytoplasmic.


## Expression profiles of wheat YSL genes


Our gene expression data under iron starvation indicated an early induction of wheat YSLs in roots. Expression response showed that some of these YSLs could be also tissue specific suggesting that they help the plant to meet the requirement during the stress condition. Specifically, TaYS1A, TaYS1B, and TaYSL5 show their presence in root as well as shoot under starvation experiments. The closest homolog of TaYS1A in Barley (HvYS1), when overexpressed in rice, enhances iron uptake, translocation, and loading in seed tissue (Banakar et al. 2017). The high expression of wheat YSL genes under –Fe condition suggest their prime importance during different modes (strategy I or II) for iron uptake. During the recent studies in wheat, quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for grain iron and zinc content were co-mapped on chromosome 2A and 7A (Krishnaapa et al. 2017). These QTL are located at the

Xwmc382-Xbarc124 marker intervals. We have scanned the region of the QTL markers for the presence of any metal transporters and identified TaYSL20 on the wheat chromosome 2A between these markers. The TaYSL20 gene belongs to clade II along with OsYSL6 that has been earlier identified as a candidate gene to manipulate the iron and zinc loading in rice grains (Sperotto et al. 2010). Therefore, TaYSL20 could also be an important candidate gene for testing its role for mineral distribution in developing wheat grains. Utilizing the similar strategy resulted in identification of rice YSL1 as one of the candidate genes associated with high iron and zinc (Upadhyaya et al. 2016).

It is known that iron-related transcription factor (IRO2) is a positive regulator for uptake under iron deficiency (Ogo et al. 2007). During promoter analysis, we identified the core IRO2- binding sequence (CACGTGG) in TaYSL3, 6, 19, and 20. Besides this, 12 wheat YSL genes were identified having phosphate-responsive domain referred to as P1BS (PHR1 binding site) in their promoter region (Table 1). Previously, transcriptome analysis and other physiological characterization in crop plants provided an evidence for the possible interlink between the phosphate and iron homeostasis (Saenchai et al. 2015; Zanin et al. 2017). Therefore, we can speculate that wheat YSL transporters are also important molecular players for micronutrient transport from the roots to the sink tissue such as grains and leaves. Although functional evidences are lacking in this direction, this needs to be validated. Our tissue-specific expression data might provide a clue for the site of YSLs function. For example, wheat YSL transcripts highly expressed in the developing grains and flag leaf could be an important candidate to assess their functional activity. Similarly, in wheat, the absorption of Fe from the root rhizospheric region might require either strategy I- or strategy II-based approaches or the combination thereof, but this still needs to be investigated at the molecular level.

In conclusion, our study supports the expanded and diversified role of wheat YSL transporters that is not limited to iron mobilization. Nevertheless, pinpointing specific transporters for Fe remobilization in the developing grains of wheat could be an important area towards addressing micronutrient biofortification. The information generated in the current study will provide the necessary framework for the contribution of these metal transporters in cereal crops especially wheat. Additionally, this work will also provide detailed inventory for the subsequent functional characterization of TaYSLs in combination with the other mineral transporters as a means to enhance micronutrient content specifically in grains.

Background: Thlaspi caerulescensis a natural selected heavy metal hyperaccumulator that can not only tolerate but also accumulate extremely high levels of heavy metals in the shoots. Thus, to identify the transportors involved in metal longdistance transportation is very important for understanding the mechanism of heavy metal accumulation in this hyperaccumulator.

Methodology/Principal Findings: We cloned and characterized a novel gene TcOPT3 of OPT family from T.caerulescens. TcOPT3 was pronouncedly expressed in aerial parts, including stem and leaf. Moreover, in situ hybridization analyses showed that TcOPT3 expressed in the plant vascular systems, especially in the pericycle cells that may be involved in the long-distance transportation. The expression of TcOPT3 was highly induced by iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) deficiency, especially in the stem and leaf. Sub-cellular localization showed that TcOPT3 was a plasma membrane-localized protein. Furthermore, heterogonous expression of TcOPT3 by mutant yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) complementation experiments demonstrated that TcOPT3 could transport $\mathsf { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\dot { Z } \mathsf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ . Moreover, expression of TcOPT3 in yeast increased metal (Fe, Zn, Cu and Cd) accumulation and resulted in an increased sensitivity to cadmium (Cd) and copper (Cu).

Conclusions: Our data demonstrated that TcOPT3 might encode an $\mathsf { F e } / \mathsf { Z n } / \mathsf { C d } / \mathsf { C u }$ influx transporter with broad-substrate. This is the first report showing that TcOPT3 may be involved in metal long-distance transportation and contribute to the heavy metal hyperaccumulation.
