The availability of irt1 knock out mutation affecting the regulation of IRT2, ZIP1 and ZIP2 target genes offers now a suitable system for identification of iron and zinc responsive “regulons” in Arabidopsis. In addition, restoration of deficient phenotype to wild-type by externally added iron and zinc provides a useful internal control to study how iron deficiency induces oxidative stress leading to progressive chlorosis and ultimate death in the irt1 mutant.

## The high-affinity metal Transporters NRAMP1 and IRT1 Team up to Take up Iron under Sufficient Metal Provision


received: 20 June 2016   
accepted: 26 October 2016   
Published: 16 November 2016

Loren Castaings, Antoine Caquot, Stéphanie Loubet & Catherine Curie

Iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) are essential metals which, when scarce in the growth medium, are respectively taken up by the root high affinity transporters IRT1 and NRAMP1 in Arabidopsis thaliana. The molecular bases for low affinity transport however remained unknown. Since IRT1 and NRAMP1 have a broad range of substrates among metals, we tested the hypothesis that they might be functionally redundant by generating nramp1 irt1 double mutants. These plants showed extreme Fedeficiency symptoms despite optimal provision of the metal. Their phenotype, which includes low Fe and Mn contents and a defect of Fe entry into root cells as revealed by Fe staining, is rescued by high Fe supply. Using a promoter swap-based strategy, we showed that root endodermis retains the ability to carry out high affinity Fe transport and furthermore might be important to high-affinity Mn uptake. We concluded that NRAMP1 plays a pivotal role in Fe transport by cooperating with IRT1 to take up Fe in roots under replete conditions, thus providing the first evidence for a low affinity Fe uptake system in plants.

Iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn) are essential trace elements for living organisms. Because they can easily loose and gain electrons, these metals are energy-providing catalysers or cofactors for a range of enzymatic reactions. As such, they play important roles in oxidative stress responses, DNA synthesis or pathogen defence1 . In plants especially, Fe and Mn are crucial for photosynthesis as core components of the photosynthetic machinery2,3. Like all transition metals however, Fe and Mn in excess become harmful because they catalyse the formation of reactive oxygen species through the Fenton reaction and the stimulation of the mitochondrial complex II, respectively4,5.

Plant Fe and Mn deficiencies occur in alkaline soils where most of the metals are present as insoluble complexes6–8. Fe deficiency is known to reduce chlorophyll synthesis and photosynthetic activity, leading to leaf interveinal chlorosis and decrease of biomass9,10. Mn deficiency symptoms, yet less documented, are also characterized by growth inhibition and leaf yellowing as well as tissue necrosis induced by the over-production of reactive oxygen species3 .

On the contrary, Fe and Mn phytotoxicity can be reached in flooded areas and acidic soils where metals are readily accessible for plants7 . Excess Fe causes growth arrest and necrotic spots on leaves known as bronzing symptom in rice11,12. Mn toxicity can also lead to chlorosis and necrotic leaf spots13. In higher plants, Fe and Mn are known to be antagonistic so that the excess of one of these metals systematically provokes a secondary deficiency of the other, thus reflecting the competition existing for their absorption7,14.

In non-grass plants, to which the model species Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis here after) belongs, Fe acquisition by Fe-limited roots relies on secretion of phenolic compounds by the root15–18, rhizosphere acidification by a membrane-bound proton ATPase that increases Fe solubility19, reduction of Fe (III) to Fe (II) at the root cell surface and subsequent Fe (II) import into the cell20,21. In Arabidopsis, this last step is mainly performed by the Fe deficiency-induced root plasma membrane transporter IRT1 (IRON-REGULATED TRANPORTER 1), which promotes high affinity Fe uptake under Fe-deficient conditions22,23. IRT1 has a broad range of substrates among divalent metals since it is able to complement yeast strains defective in Mn or zinc $( \mathrm { Z n } )$ uptake24 and since

the irt1-1 loss-of-function mutant fails to accumulate Mn, Zn and cobalt (Co) under Fe-deficient conditions22.   
The exact role of IRT1 in Mn, Zn and Co homeostasis has however not yet been investigated.

Recent studies with rice and Arabidopsis have shown the importance of metal transporters of the NRAMP (NATURAL RESISTANCE-ASSOCIATED MACROPHAGE PROTEIN) family in Mn uptake in plants25,26. NRAMP1 is the major high affinity Mn transporter in Arabidopsis as shown by the hypersensitivity of the nramp1-1 mutant to Mn limitation and its inability to take up Mn in these conditions25. The expression of this plasma membrane transporter is upregulated in roots under Mn deficiency. Interestingly, NRAMP1 is also induced upon Fe deficiency by FIT, the master regulator of the Fe deficiency response27,28 which suggests that it might play a role in Fe homeostasis as well. This hypothesis was further supported by NRAMP1 ability to restore irt1-1 mutant Fe and Co uptakes, indicating that NRAMP1 too has a broad selectivity in vivo25.

Given the obvious yet poorly understood link existing between Fe and Mn uptakes, we sought to shed light on the respective contribution of IRT1 and NRAMP1 to Fe and Mn absorption by plant roots. A reverse genetics approach coupled with a promoter swap strategy allowed us to unravel the functional redundancy of NRAMP1 and IRT1 transporters for the uptake of these two metals under optimal growth conditions and revealed a possible root cell-specificity for Mn absorption.

Knocking out both IRT1 and NRAMP1 has a dramatic impact on plant growth. To assess a possible functional redundancy between IRT1 and NRAMP1 in Mn and/or Fe uptake, we first checked IRT1 and NRAMP1 expression in their respective mutants, namely irt1-1 (Wassilewskija ecotype, Ws) and nramp1-1 (Columbia ecotype, Col). Interestingly, IRT1 was consistently overexpressed in nramp1-1, even under standard growth conditions ( $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn, $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe) (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. S1). This result suggests that compensation mechanisms possibly hide Fe-related phenotypes in the nramp1-1 mutant. In order to investigate this hypothesis, we crossed irt1-1 and nramp1-1 to generate a double nramp1-1 irt1-1 mutant (see Methods). Among the F2 progeny, all homozygous plants for both nramp1-1 and irt1-1 mutations showed slow growth and a strong chlorosis (Supplementary Fig. S2). We therefore selected one of these knock out lines to further investigate the consequence of NRAMP1 and IRT1 simultaneous loss of function (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. S1).

We opted for hydroponic cultures that enable control of the nutrients supply. When grown in that system under standard Mn and Fe supply $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn and $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, see Methods), nramp1-1 developed normally despite a small but significant reduction in the activity of the photosystem II (PSII) (Fig. 1b–d). In these conditions, irt1-1 mutant only harbored a slight reduction in shoot biomass and accession-related morphological specificities such as bigger leaf blades and a wider expanded rosette similar to these of Ws ecotype (Fig. 1b,c and ref. 29). Our standard hydroponic medium provides therefore Mn and Fe in sufficient amounts for nramp1-1 and irt1-1 single mutants to grow nearly as well as wild type plants. In the same hydroponic conditions however, the double mutant developed similar growth defects than those previously observed in soil. Indeed, nramp1-1 irt1-1 displayed a dramatically impaired growth of both shoots and roots (Fig. $^ { \mathrm { 1 b , c } }$ ) and a strong chlorosis associated with a poor photosynthesis efficiency as shown by the reduction of both the energy transfer within the PSII (Fv/Fm) and the light utilization $( \varphi _ { \mathrm { I I } } )$ (Fig. 1b,d).

To confirm this phenotype, we produced a second allele of nramp1 irt1 double mutant using a new mutant allele of NRAMP1 in the Ws ecotype pitched nramp1-2 (Supplementary Fig. S3). The nramp1-2 mutant, despite retaining $2 0 \%$ of the wild-type amount of NRAMP1 transcripts, was hypersensitive to Mn deficiency, similar to the phenotype of nramp1-1 (Supplementary Fig. S3). When grown hydroponically, nramp1-2 irt1-1 plants harbored similar though milder phenotypes than those of nramp1-1 irt1-1. They were smaller and had paler leaves than irt1-1 especially when challenged with limiting Fe supply $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, Fig. 2a, Supplementary Fig. S4). The difference in phenotype intensity between the two double mutant lines might come from the residual expression of NRAMP1 from the nramp1-2 allele. Also, different genetic backgrounds of the double mutants (Col/Ws for nramp1-1 irt1-1 and Ws for nramp1-2 irt1-1) might be of influence on the phenotype severity. The latter explanation is however less likely since all the independent nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant lines obtained from the initial cross harbored a strong phenotype despite their different Col/Ws allelic combinations (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Altogether these data suggest that NRAMP1 and IRT1 contribute to plant growth under optimal metal supply in a redundant manner.

Fe and Mn levels are reduced in the two different nramp1 irt1 double mutants. In order to further characterize the impact of inactivating both IRT1 and NRAMP1, we measured metal content in nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant plants and compared it to that of wild type plants and parental lines of the single mutants grown under standard metal supply $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe, $2 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Mn) (Figs 1e–h and $2 \mathrm { b } , \mathsf { c } .$ and Supplementary Table S1). Among the tested metals $Z \mathbf { n } .$ , Cu, Mn and Fe), only Fe and Mn showed significant concentration changes in nramp1-1 irt1-1 (Supplementary Table S1). Indeed, Fe and Mn contents in shoots were respectively $5 0 \%$ and $4 0 \%$ lower in the double mutant compared to the other genotypes (Fig. $^ { 1 \mathrm { e , f } }$ ). Similar results were also obtained in nramp1-2 irt1-1 double mutant (Fig. $^ { 2 \mathrm { b } , \mathrm { c } }$ and Supplementary Fig. S4).

A decrease in metal accumulation in shoots might be the consequence of impaired metal uptake by roots and/or poor metal translocation from roots to shoots. In order to identify which of these two mechanisms is defective in the double mutant, we measured metal content in roots. Mn concentration in nramp1-1 irt1-1 roots was reduced twofold compared to wild type plants (Fig. 1g). The fact that Mn content was decreased in both shoot and root of nramp1-1 irt1-1 plants strongly suggests that Mn uptake is impaired in the double mutant under optimal Mn concentration. Surprisingly, Fe was twice as much concentrated in the roots of nramp1-1 irt1-1 compared to the other genotypes (Fig. 1h). This result was further confirmed by whole-mount roots stained with the Perls histochemical method that showed accumulation of Fe as a blue precipitate in the nramp1-1 irt1-1 root (Fig. 3b). To refine the localization of such accumulated Fe in root tissues of the double mutant, wild type and nramp1-1 irt1-1 root cross-sections were stained with the sensitive Perls-DAB method30. In wild type root sections, Fe deposits were only limited to the rim of a few cells of the cortex, the darker signal in the central cylinder corresponding to light refraction (Fig. 3c). In the root of nramp1-1 irt1-1 however, Fe precipitates dramatically spread to the entire cortical cell layer (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, Fe accumulation was restricted to the apoplast surrounding these cells, a conclusion that is also supported by the observation that Perls-DAB labeling stops halfway through the endodermis where the casparian strip blocks apoplastic transport (Fig. 3d, arrow). This suggests that Fe cannot efficiently enter root cells owing to a defect of Fe uptake.

Taken together these data indicate that NRAMP1 and IRT1 act redundantly in the acquisition of Mn and Fe by the root, over a wide range of concentrations of these metals.

Fe insufficiency is responsible for the poor growth of nramp1 irt1 mutants. We then wanted to know which of the Fe and/or Mn deficiency observed in the nramp1 irt1 double mutant is the most limiting factor for its growth and development. We therefore tested whether growth of the nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant could be restored by increasing Fe or Mn supply. Interestingly, only Fe supplementation significantly improved growth (Fig. 4a). Under high Fe supply $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ or $1 \mathrm { m M }$ ), growth of nramp1-1 irt1-1 was completely rescued and leaf chlorosis fully disappeared (Fig. 4a). Such a situation was not observed when Mn concentration was increased to $1 \mathrm { m M }$ or $2 \mathrm { m M }$ under constant Fe supply $( 2 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . Instead, nramp1-1 irt1-1 developed Mn excess symptoms including growth defect, leaf yellowing and necrotic spots (Fig. 4a).

Under high Fe supply conditions that revert nramp1-1 irt1-1 phenotype, Fe content in leaves of the double mutant increased dramatically to a level exceeding more than threefold that of wild type plants grown in standard conditions, while Mn content slightly decreased (Fig. $^ { \mathrm { 4 b , c } }$ ). This result further strengthens the conclusion that despite being reduced in the double mutant, Mn concentration does not limit its growth. We concluded that Fe deficiency alone is responsible for nramp1-1 irt1-1 poor growth under normal metal supply.

The Fe status of the double mutant under standard Fe supply was evaluated at the molecular level by monitoring root expression of the two iron homeostasis genes FRO2 and FER1 that respond to Fe availability in an opposite manner (Fig. 4d,e). When Fe is scarce, FER1 expression decreases in order to free the pool of immobilized $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 1 }$ . FRO2 is a direct marker of Fe deficiency in Arabidopsis and its expression goes up to increase the ferric reductase activity at the root surface and maximize Fe absorption19. Under standard Fe supply $( 2 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , FRO2 was not significantly deregulated in nramp1-1 but was overexpressed in irt1-1, consistent with the irt1-1 mutant being slightly affected in our standard hydroponic conditions (Figs 1c and 4d). In the nramp1-1 irt1-1 double mutant, FRO2 expression was further deregulated, showing a twofold higher expression compared to the irt1-1 single mutant, thus confirming that the double mutant experiences a stronger Fe starvation (Fig. 4d). An over-induction of FRO2 was also observed in the nramp1-2 irt1-1 mutant, carrying a NRAMP1 knock-down allele, when grown under limiting Fe supply, especially at $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe where Fe content is the most reduced in the double mutant (Supplementary Fig. S4). As expected, supplementation of the double mutant with high Fe repressed FRO2 expression. Interestingly however, whereas FRO2 expression in wild type plants is minimal at $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$

Fe supply, as much as $1 \mathrm { m M }$ Fe are required to shut FRO2 down in the double mutant (Fig. 4d). Consistently, we found the opposite situation with FER1. FER1 mRNA levels were extremely low in nramp1-1 irt1-1 grown in standard $2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe conditions compared to all the other genotypes, thus supporting our previous finding that Fe does not adequately penetrate root cells in these plants. In the double mutant, reversion of FER1 expression to a level equivalent to wild type plants grown in standard medium required up to $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Fe supplementation, which again points to a defect of Fe entry into root cells (Fig. 4e). Taken together our results show that poor growth and chlorosis symptoms observed in nramp1 irt1 double mutants under Fe and Mn replete conditions are caused by extreme Fe deficiency due to impaired Fe acquisition by root cells.

Assessment of NRAMP1 and IRT1 specificity of transport in various root territories by promoter-swapping. qPCR data and promoter-GUS studies have established that IRT1 and NRAMP1 have expression territories that are both overlapping and distinct22,25. IRT1 is mainly expressed in root epidermis and cortex of the absorption zone and in root hairs while NRAMP1 expression is located more internally in cortex and endodermis from the root tip up to the mature zone as well as in the root meristematic zone22,25. IRT1 and NRAMP1 are also expressed at very low levels in shoots where they conserve a slight induction by Fe and Mn deficiency respectively22,25 (Supplementary Fig. S5). In order to test the importance of these expression patterns for the physiological function of NRAMP1 and IRT1, we carried out a promoter swap strategy. To that aim, pIRT1::NRAMP1 and pNRAMP1::IRT1 constructs were generated and expressed into both nramp1 and irt1 mutants (Fig. 5a, see Methods).

To examine the possibility that the expression territory of NRAMP1 has the potential to carry out optimal iron acquisition in Fe-deficient roots, we tested whether IRT1 expressed under the control of the NRAMP1 promoter could rescue irt1 hyper-sensitivity to Fe deficiency. When the irt1 pNRAMP1::IRT1 transgenic line was grown hydroponically under Fe deficiency, growth of the irt1 mutant was essentially rescued (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. S6). Thus, despite NRAMP1 promoter activity being very weak compared to IRT1 in Fe deficient conditions (Supplementary Fig. S7), it is able to drive sufficient expression of IRT1 in the adequate location to ensure high affinity Fe uptake by the root. As previously reported25, the irt1 phenotype is also rescued by pIRT1::NRAMP1 (Fig. 5b), indicating that NRAMP1 is able to transport Fe when strongly expressed in root epidermis and cortex under the control of the IRT1 promoter. This result was further supported by the observation that pIRT1::NRAMP1 is also able to rescue the Fe-deficiency phenotype of nramp1-1 irt1-1 (Supplementary Fig. S6). Since the plant can be efficiently fed when Fe uptake occurs exclusively in the territories of expression of NRAMP1 and since NRAMP1 can functionally replace IRT1, we concluded that NRAMP1 has the capacity to contribute to Fe acquisition by the root.

Next we asked whether endodermal expression of NRAMP1 is important for its high-affinity Mn transport activity. To that aim, we tested whether NRAMP1 expressed under the control of the IRT1 promoter, which is only active in root outer cell layers excluding endodermis, could rescue nramp1-1. Interestingly, we found that pIRT1::NRAMP1 is unable to restore the tolerance of nramp1-1 to Mn-deficiency (Fig. 5c). Because the functionality of this construct was validated by its ability to successfully complement irt1-1 (Fig. 5b), we concluded that endodermis is essential for high-affinity Mn acquisition by the root. Since root tip also shows differential IRT1 and NRAMP1 expression, it is also possible that root tip plays an important role in Mn uptake under Mn starvation conditions.

At last we evaluated whether IRT1 has the potential to carry out high affinity Mn uptake. To that aim we tested whether the expression of IRT1 under the control of the NRAMP1 promoter was able to complement nramp1-1 hypersensitivity to Mn deficiency. We found that pNRAMP1::IRT1 failed to rescue growth of nramp1- 1 under Mn deficiency (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. S6). Since this construct is functional as shown by its ability to efficiently rescue the irt1 phenotype (Fig. 5b), and since IRT1 transcripts level in this line is high (Supplementary Fig. S7b), we concluded that IRT1 is unable to efficiently take up Mn in the high affinity range. We cannot however exclude the possibility that IRT1 protein is down-regulated at the post-transcriptional level when ectopically expressed in the root.

Iron is an essential micronutrient for virtually all organisms, but it is not readily available due to its low solubility. In plants, highly specialized systems have evolved in order to acquire iron from the soil. Recent advances have identiWed molecular components of the iron uptake system, both in graminaceous plants (Curie et al. 2001) and in nongraminaceous plants (Eide et al. 1996; Henriques et al. 2002; Robinson et al. 1999; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002).

In Arabidopsis thaliana, upon iron deWciency, expression of a set of genes encoding a proton ATPase, probably of the AHA family (Palmgren 2001), the ferric-chelate reductase FRO2 (Connolly et al. 2003; Robinson et al. 1999) and the metal transporter IRT1 (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2002, 2003) is induced in root epidermal cells. These proteins are responsible for the solubilization of iron through rhizosphere acidiWcation, its reduction from $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and subsequent $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake into the cytoplasm, respectively. Several families of putative iron transporters, including NRAMP, ZIP and YSL have been described in Arabidopsis (Curie and Briat 2003). Although the physiological role of YSL and NRAMP members is associated with distribution, partitioning and remobilization of iron in the plant, the ZIP founding member IRT1 is the only transporter involved in iron uptake (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004). IRT1 was Wrst identiWed through functional complementation of a yeast mutant defective in iron uptake (Eide et al. 1996). Characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis showed that this gene is highly induced by iron starvation in roots and speciWcally expressed in the epidermis and cortex (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2002). Moreover, the identiWcation of a knock-out mutant in the IRT1 gene, irt1-1, demonstrated that in low iron conditions, IRT1 is the main route of iron entry into the plant and mediates the accumulation of additional metal ions (Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1 in Arabidopsis, was previously shown by functional complementation of yeast metal transport mutants to be a transporter of iron and zinc (Vert et al. 2001). Like IRT1, IRT2 is expressed in the outer layers of the root and upregulated, although to a lesser extent than IRT1, by iron deWciency (Vert et al. 2001). Even though IRT2 was suggested to be involved in iron uptake from the soil (Vert et al. 2001), little is known about its biological function. A loss of function En transposon mutant, irt2-1, was isolated and shown to display a slightly reduced stature but no chlorotic phenotype (Varotto et al. 2002). However, transposon insertion in irt2-1 led to concomitant downregulation of the neighboring IRT1 gene, playing itself a major role in iron uptake (Vert et al. 2002), that may result from the loss of an enhancer function acting on both IRT genes (Varotto et al. 2002). Therefore, the analysis of irt2-1 greatly limits the conclusion on the biological role of IRT2.

The present study shows that IRT2 is an intracellular membrane protein whose role in the cellular response to iron deWciency is diVerent from the major root iron transporter IRT1. We propose that IRT1 may compartmentalize iron into vesicles, to prevent toxicity by excess free iron in the cytosol as a result of extracellular iron acquisition by the FRO2/IRT1 system.

Plant growth conditions

The Arabidopsis thaliana ecotypes used in this study were Columbia (Col-0) and Wassileskija (Ws). The irt1-1 and Wt1 mutants used are in the Ws background (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004; Vert et al. 2002). The iron deWciency treatments and split-root experiments were performed exactly as previously described (Seguela et al. 2008; Vert et al. 2003). Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ are essential micronutrients that participate in physiological and biochemical processes and promote plant growth and development. $Z \mathrm { n }$ is involved in the synthesis of numerous enzymes, such as alcohol dehydrogenase, copper $( \mathrm { C u } ) – \mathrm { Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, and RNA polymerase. Therefore, Zn deficiency decreases the activity of these enzymes (Hacisalihoglu and Kochian 2003). Recently,

Fe has been used as a cofactor for integrating photosynthesis with various metabolic pathways and regulating gene expression (Imsande 2010). Fe deficiency can affect the growth and yield of fruit trees and other crops, and it affects photosynthesis rate, chlorophyll content, and catalase activity (Fornerginer et al. 2010; Rube´n et al. 2011).

The continuous discovery of metal ion transporters has laid the foundation for studies on factors involved in the absorption, intracellular transport, localization, and efflux of metal ions, such as P1B-type heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family, Zn- and Fe-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) family, normal resistancerelated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and the cation dissemination facilitator (CDF) family (Milner et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2017; Vigani et al. 2013). AtIRT1 was the first ZIP gene identified which is located on the root surface and induced by Fe deficiency in the root of Arabidopsis thaliana L. (Henriques et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a homolog of IRT1, plays a similarly crucial role in A. thaliana. However, under similar Fedeficient conditions, the expression of IRT2 is significantly lower than that of IRT1 (Vert et al. 2001). Their homolog IRT3, which is located in the plasma membrane, increases the uptake of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe to complement the function of both $\mathrm { Z n - }$ and Fe-uptake mutants (Lin et al. 2009). Complementation mutants or knockdown of ZIP1 and ZIP2 in A. thaliana showed that ZIP1 and ZIP2 are involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Mn uptake (Milner et al. 2013). In addition, functional analyses in maize (Zea mays L.) and rice indicated that ZIP3, ZIP4, ZIP5, and ZIP8 play important roles in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in the roots and shoots under Zn-deficient conditions (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, b). In A. thaliana, the function of ZIP9 is similar to that of ZIP12, being induced under $Z \mathbf { n }$ -limiting conditions (Talke et al. 2006; Wintz et al. 2003).

Te zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ -regulated/iron(Fe)-regulated transporterlike family proteins (ZIPs) are membrane-located proteins for cations transport (Eng et  al. 1998; Guerinot 2000). Tey have been found to exist broadly in prokaryotic cells, fungi, plants and mammalians. In plants, ZIPs have been identifed in both dicots and monocots, such as Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998; Milner et  al. 2013), rice (Chen et  al. 2008), maize (Li et  al. 2013), medicago (Lopez-Millan et al. 2004; Stephens et al. 2011) and barely (Tiong et al. 2015). Grotz et al. identifed fve ZIP genes (IRT1, ZIP1-4) in Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998), and later up to 11 ZIP genes from Arabidopsis were detected bioinformatically (Guerinot 2000). Roles of ZIP1-12 from Arabidopsis in Zn transport were explored experimentally (Milner et  al. 2013). More recently, 18 ZIPs from Arabidopsis and 16 ZIPs from rice were annotated (Ivanov and Bauer 2017).

In Arabidopsis and rice, only a small number of ZIPs have been examined for biological functions in plant till now. Arabidopsis IRT1 is a well-studied ZIP gene frst identifed as a crucial transporter for plant Fe uptake (Varotto et  al. 2002; Vert et  al. 2002). Arabidopsis IRT1 can be induced by iron defciency (Korshunova et  al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2002), and may play a role in Mn/ Zn transport as well (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et  al. 2002). Biological functions in $Z \mathrm { n } /$ Fe transport of AtIRT2 (Vert et al. 2001, 2009), AtZIP1/2 (Grotz et al. 1998; Wintz et al. 2003; Milner et al. 2013), OsIRT1 (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Ishimaru et  al. 2006; Bughio et  al. 2002) and OsZIP4/5/8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2008; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Yang et al. 2009) have also been examined in the past decade.

A few studies have also implied that ZIPs may be involved in Cd transport. Yeast cells expressing AtIRT1 showed increased Cd sensitivity (Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2001), and IRT1-dependent $\mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { M n } / Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake was inhibited by excess Cd (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). Te Arabidopsis IRT1 knock-out mutant irt1-1 exhibited reduced Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation (Vert et al. 2002; Fan et al. 2014), while overexpression of AtIRT1 increased Cd sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Connolly et  al. 2002). AtIRT2, phylogenetically similar to AtIRT1, increased Cd uptake when overexpressed in Arabidopsis (Vert et  al. 2009), though the yeast cells expressing AtIRT2 exhibited no altered Cd sensitivity (Vert et  al. 2001). In rice, expression of OsIRT1 and OsIRT2 made the cells more sensitive to Cd and increased Cd accumulation (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009). Nonetheless, we still know little about the roles of most of the ZIPs genes in Cd stress response in Arabidopsis and rice.

In this study, genome-wide ZIPs identifcation in Arabidopsis and rice was performed with rigorous evolutional analysis. A comparative examination of genomewide expression profle of ZIPs in Arabidopsis and rice in response to Cd stress were carried out. Teir role in Cd uptake of typical ZIPs responding to Cd stress was further tested by expressing them in yeast. As expected, most identifed ZIPs gene expression responded remarkably to Cd stress, while unexpectedly it was found that Arabidopsis and rice showed a distinct pattern in ZIPs genes expression profle. Tese results may help to elucidate the plants’ genetic basis for Cd translocation via a ZIPs-dependent pathway.

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.

Background and aims Dicotyledonous plants, such as Arabidopsis, acquire soil iron using a reduction-based mechanism, named Strategy I, where the final step involves $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ import by the ZIP-family transporter AtIRT1. The universal presence of IRT1-like genes, suggests that Strategy I represents a basic process in the green lineage. However, for some green organisms, like Chlamydomonas and rice, alternative ironacquisition mechanisms are known. We aimed to outline potential interactions between Strategy I and alternative iron acquisition mechanisms.

Methods We investigated gene-coexpression networks in Chlamydomonas, rice and Arabidopsis, and used the sequences of the variable regions of the selected IRT proteins to identify the conservation of key amino acids. Results IRT genes in Chlamydomonas and rice were found to be closely coexpressed with components of alternative available iron-acquisition systems. On protein level, we could observe conservation of potential phosphorylation sites in close proximity to predicted or experimentally-demonstrated ubiquitination sites.

Conclusions Data suggest that the regulation of Strategy I is closely connected to alternative existing iron-acquisition strategies. Transciptional control, together with potential post-transcriptional modifications of IRT transporters, may be involved in finetuning iron import. This study provides a basis for experimentally analyzing the regulation of iron acquisition in an evolutionary context.

Soil is a fundamental and indispensable resource for global agricultural production. However, not all soil conditions are suitable for crop growth and harvest. Soil contamination caused by toxic elements threatens food safety and poses signifcant risks to human health. Among inorganic contaminants, cadmium $\mathrm { ( C d ) }$ is one of the most toxic elements. The National Soil Pollution Survey report demonstrates that Cd is the most prevalent contaminant, with $7 \%$ of soil samples covering over $7 0 \%$ of land exceeding the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP) limit in China. In addition to its natural occurrence in the Earth’s crust, Cd in the environment originates from human activities such as metal mining, industrialization, and wastewater irrigation (Zhao et  al. 2015, 2022). Furthermore, nitrogen fertilizer application accelerates soil acidifcation, increasing Cd solubility and mobility in soil systems, which leads to higher uptake rates in cultivated plants (Zhao et  al. 2015). Cd poses serious risks to plants, animals, and humans. In plants, Cd accumulation inhibits plant growth by disrupting essential metabolic and physiological processes; In humans, Cd accumulation increases the incidence of severe diseases such as osteoporosis, kidney damage, and Itai-Itai disease, with efects reported even at the epigenetic level (Khan et  al. 2020; Lv et  al. 2017; Li et  al. 2021; Horiguchi et  al. 1994; Zhang et  al. 2023). Humans are mainly exposed to Cd via the food chain, particularly through the soil–plant-human continuum. Cd excess in soils is an evident threat to food safety (Clemens et  al. 2013; Zhao et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2021b). In recent years, Cd contamination has worsened, with reports showing a 2.2-fold increase in the Chinese population’s exposure to Cd through the food chain compared to the 1990s (Song et al. 2017).

There is a real need to limit Cd transfer from soil to the food chain, and great efort is directed towards obtaining plants with lower Cd-accumulation rates in the edible parts. For this purpose, many studies have been conducted to reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying Cd absorption and translocation in rice and in the model plant Arabidopsis (Zhao et al. 2022). Primarily, Cd, as a non-essential metal, can enter plants through essential elements’ transporters, such as iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ , zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , manganese (Mn), and calcium $\mathrm { ( C a ) }$ transporters (Clemens and Ma 2016; Zhao et al. 2022). The zinc‐regulated transporter, and the iron‐regulated transporter-like proteins (ZRT-IRT-related protein, ZIP) are present in plants, animals, and microorganisms and are responsible for Zn and Fe translocation. In tobacco, it was reported that NtZIP4B was responsible for Zn and Cd transport (Barabasz et al. 2019). In Arabidopsis thaliana, Cd was found to be absorbed into roots via the broad-spectrum transporter AtIRT1 (iron-regulated transporter 1). Orthologue IRT1 proteins in wheat, Brassica. rapa (B. rapa), and rice also demonstrated Cd transport activity (Zhang et al. 2021a; Wu et al. 2021; Jiang et al. 2021).

Another relevant protein family associated with metal transport is NRAMPs (natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins), a family of proteins found in mammals, plants, and bacteria (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Nramp family members are generally composed of 11 or 12 transmembrane domains (TMs), with the frst 10 forming LeuT structures that contain complex but conserved metal ion-binding sites (Ehrnstorfer et al. 2014). Although NRAMPs are mainly involved in Mn and Fe absorption in plants, they may also contribute to Cd uptake. The presence of cysteine or methionine sulfur in the metal-binding site can even make Cd their preferred substrate (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Six Nramp transporters have been identifed in Arabidopsis thaliana. AtNramp1, $- 2 , - 3$ , and $^ { - 4 }$ participate in Cd, Mn, and Fe transport (Cailliatte et al. 2010; Lanquar et al. 2010; Gao et  al. 2018). AtNramp6 shows a high afnity for Fe and Cd and cooperates with AtNramp1 in Mn utilization (Li et al. 2022). NtNramp5 in Nicotiana tabacum also participates in Mn and Cd transport, while a cultivar possessing truncated NtNramp5 protein lost Cd/Mn transport activity (Tang et  al. 2017). In rice, it has been reported that OsNramp5 plays a major role in Cd uptake, and the mutant plants containing a defective OsNramp5 protein show decreased Cd uptake (Yang et  al. 2014; Sasaki et  al. 2012; Ishikawa et  al. 2012). Furthermore, changes in OsNramp5 expression levels can afect Cd uptake and translocation. For instance, OsNramp5 overexpression reduces Cd accumulation in rice grain by interfering with Cd transport into the stele and subsequent loading into the xylem (Chang et  al.

2020a). Considering that OsNramp5 activity is essential for Mn transport, it has been stated that the knockout of OsNramp5 largely decreases Mn and Cd absorption (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Ishimaru et al. 2012). On the other hand, OsNramp5 duplication in the rice cultivar Pokkali increases Cd and Mn uptake into root cells but simultaneously reduces Cd movement to the xylem (Yu et al. 2022). Kuramata et al. (2022) showed that a specifc amino acid change in the OsNramp5 protein can reduce Cd uptake without disrupting Mn absorption (Kuramata et al. 2022). In barley and buckwheat, HvNramp5 and FeNramp5 mediate Mn and Cd uptake in roots (Yokosho et al. 2020; Wu et al. 2016).

Green leafy vegetables are essential components of the human daily diet due to their high nutritional value and signifcant role in the diet of inhabitants in Asian countries. These vegetables are rich in minerals and vitamins and hold great potential for application in the feld of fortifed foods (Sarkar et al. 2023). While green leafy vegetables provide an adequate intake of essential trace elements, members of the Brassicaceae family are known to accumulate relatively high levels of Cd in their leaves (Kuboi et  al. 1986). Due to this distinctive ability, the B. rapa cultivar Beijingxiaoza 56 has been proposed as a promising plant for phytoremediation (Liu et  al. 2011). However, this characteristic presents a challenge, as leafy vegetable consumption accounts for $1 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ of dietary Cd exposure among the Asian population (Chen et al. 2018; Song et al. 2017; He et al. 2013).

In the present study, we characterized a Nramp orthologue in B. rapa, BrNramp1 (Bra003587), which is mainly expressed in roots and encodes a plasma membrane-localized protein playing an important role in Mn and Cd uptake. BrNramp1 overexpression in atnarmp1 mutant could accomplish Cd absorption. The present study suggests BrNramp1 participant in Cd and Mn accumulation of Brassica rapa, with a 17-amino-acid deletion in TM3 resulting in the loss-of-function in Cd and Mn transport.

## BrNramp1 shows high sequence identity with AtNramp1


The AtNramp1 protein sequence was used to retrieve homologs in the Brassicaceae  database (BRAD). Using the BLAST tool, three candidate orthologous proteins (ID: Bra003587, Bra035149, and Bra008437)

were identifed. Among these proteins, Bra003587 showed the highest sequence identity to AtNramp1 in A. thaliana $( 8 9 . 6 6 \%$ , Supplementary Fig. 1a). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Bra003587 closely clusters with AtNramp1 from A. thaliana (Supplementary Fig.  1b). Regarding the protein sequence, 12 transmembrane domains were predicted (red-underlined), and structural motifs for metal recognition were also identifed (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Motif A in TM1 (DPGN) and motif B in TM6 (AMVM) in Bra003587 were identical to those reported for AtNramp1 (Lu et  al. 2018). Bra003587 matched the predicted protein with ID: XP_009104491.1 in the NCBI database. Based on these results, Bra003587 was named BrNramp1. The BrNramp1 gene contains 1584 nucleotides encoding 328 amino acids. The alignment of the genomic DNA and cDNA sequences of BrNramp1 showed that this gene consists of 11 exons and 10 introns (Supplementary Fig. 1c).


## BrNramp1 is expressed mainly in roots


To explore the expression pattern of BrNramp1, the expression level of BrNramp1 in the roots and shoots was determined by quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR. When $B$ . rapa plants were cultured in 1/2-strength Hoagland nutrient solution (control), BrNramp1 was mainly expressed in the roots, with a much lower expression level in the shoots. The addition of $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd or Mn defciency (no Mn was added in the nutrient solution) resulted in signifcantly higher BrNramp1 expression levels in roots and shoots compared to the control (Fig. 1).

BrNramp1 localizes in the plasmatic cell membrane

To identify the subcellular localization of BrNramp1, BrNramp1-eGFP was constructed under the control of the 35S promoter and inserted into N. benthamiana leaf mesophyll cells via Agrobacterium strain GV3101 injection. GFP fuorescence of $3 5 S { : : } e G F P$ in mesophyll cells was observed all around the cell components, including the cell membrane, the nucleus, and the cytoplasm, while the GFP fuorescence of 35S:: BrNramp1::eGFP product was observed only in the cell plasma membrane; OsNramp5 was used as the cell membrane marker. 35S::BrNramp1::eGFP and 35S::OsNramp5::RFP vectors were co-transformed into N. benthamiana mesophyll cells, confrming that BrNramp1 encodes a plasma membranelocalized protein (Fig. 2).

BrNramp1 shows transport activities for Cd and Mn when expressed in yeast

The BrNramp1 sequence was amplifed using cDNA of B.rapa accession Chiifu roots as template. Compared with BrNramp1 from Chiifu, Bra003587 from the BALST result in the BRAD database has a 51 base-pair deletion, resulting in a deletion of 17 amino acids in TM3 (Supplementary Fig.  2a, d). Secondary structure prediction showed that, despite the 17 amino-acid deletions, Bra003587 still has 12 transmembrane domains (green-underlined). However, diferences in protein sequence composition were observed: BrNramp1 consists of 275 alpha helixes, 20 beta turns, 157 random coils (Supplementary Fig.  2b), while Bra003587 consists of 272 alpha helixes, 18 beta turns, 157 random coils (Supplementary Fig.  2e). Tertiary structure prediction indicated that the 17 amino-acid deletion resulted in structural changes in TM3 (Supplementary Fig. 2c, f).

To determine the specifc function of the 51  bp fragment, we generated BrNramp1d (Bra003587) in which the 51  bp fragment was deleted based on the BrNramp1 sequence and then heterologously expressed BrNramp1 and BrNramp1d in the yeast INVScI and △smf1 mutant, which were further cultivated with two carbon sources (glucose and galactose). The assays were performed in the presence or absence of Cd and EGTA.

With glucose as the carbon source, no signifcant diferences were observed among yeast lines expressing the empty vector, BrNramp1 or BrNramp1d. When the carbon source was galactose, the GAL promoter was induced, and all yeast lines showed similar growth in the absence of Cd. However, in the presence of Cd, yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 displayed higher sensitivity to Cd compared with those expressing the empty vector, while those expressing BrNramp1d did not (Fig.  3a). The growth curve of yeast cells was determined in the presence and absence of $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd. No growth diferences were observed among yeast cultures in the absence of Cd, but the growth of yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 was signifcantly inhibited in the presence of $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd. Yeast carrying the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed similar growth to those cultured without Cd (Fig. 3c). Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 accumulated signifcantly more Cd than those expressing the empty vector, while Cd accumulation in yeast cells expressing BrNramp1d showed no signifcant diference compared with the empty vector (Fig. 3d).

The growth of the △smf1 mutant showed no signifcant diferences among lines when glucose was used as the carbon source. However, when cultured with galactose, the △smf1 mutant expressing BrNramp1 showed signifcantly better growth on the solid medium containing EGTA, which chelates Mn and reduces its availability, than that expressing the empty vector, indicating the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1. Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1d exposed to EGTA showed similar growth sensitivity to those carrying the empty vector (Fig. 3b).


## The heterologous expression of BrNramp1 in the Arabidopsis complements Cd and Mn uptake


To further investigate the metal transport activity of BrNramp1 in plants, the A. thaliana atnramp1 mutant (SALK_053236) was transformed to express BrNramp1 under the control of 35S promoter. Three independent transgenic lines (OX-1, OX-2, OX-3) were selected and identifed (Supplementary Fig. 3). The relative expression levels of AtNramp1 and BrNramp1 were determined in Col-0, atnramp1 and the independent transgenic lines. Expression of AtNramp1 in atnramp1 and the independent transgenic lines was almost undetectable, while BrNramp1 showed much higher and similar expression levels in the transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 4).

To identify the Cd transport activity of BrNramp1, $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd was added in the hydroponic system to culture Col-0, atnramp1, and three independent transgenic lines. Transgenic atnramp1 plants overexpressing BrNramp1 showed a signifcant increase in Cd content. Cd concentrations in the independent transgenic lines were 2.59–3.09-fold in the shoots and 3.90–4.04-fold in the roots compared to the values found in atnramp1 (Figs.  4a,and b). The Cd contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were 3.84–5.42-fold that of atnramp1 (Fig.  4c). Overexpression of BrNramp1 also increased Mn concentrations in the independent transgenic lines, which were even higher than in Col-0. In the shoots, there was a 2.20–3.00-fold increase compared with atnramp1 and a 1.59–2.16- fold increase compared with Col-0. In the roots, Mn concentrations in the independent transgenic lines showed a 2.64–3.48-fold and 1.49–1.96- fold increase compared with atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Figs.  4d, and e). The Mn contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were 3.01–4.40-fold and 1.56–2.28-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig. 4f). Concentrations of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn were also detected, Fe, Zn and $\mathrm { C u }$ concentrations in the shoots, roots and contents of whole plants did not show signifcant diferences (Supplementary Fig. 5). The dry weight of Arabidopsis plants showed no signifcant diferences. The root-to-shoot translocation ratio (shoot content/whole plant content) of Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn and Cd also showed no signifcant diferences among

Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 6).

To identify the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1, Arabidopsis plants were exposed hydroponically to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M } \ \mathrm { M n C l } _ { 2 }$ and Mn defciency treatments, with both treatments showing a similar Mn distribution. When exposed to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M \ M n C l } _ { 2 }$ , Mn concentrations in the shoots of the independent transgenic lines were $4 . 2 6 { - } 5 . 0 1 $ -fold and 2.10–2.47-fold higher compared with those in atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5a). In the roots, Mn concentrations showed a 4.35–5.91-fold and 2.08–2.83-fold increase, respectively (Fig.  5b). The Mn content of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines was signifcantly higher, with 5.88–8.11-fold and 3.17–4.37-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5c). Fe and Cu concentrations in the shoots, roots and contents of whole plants did not show signifcant diferences, while Zn concentrations in the shoots of the independent lines were signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 (Supplementary Fig. 7). For the total content of Fe, Cu and Zn, similar results were observed, two transgenic lines (OX-1 and OX-2) showed no signifcant diferences, while OX-3 showed signifcantly higher contents of $\mathrm { C u }$ and Zn compared with atnramp1. The root-to-shoot translocation ratio of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn showed no signifcant diferences among Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 8).

When exposed to Mn defciency solution, Mn concentrations in the shoots of the independent transgenic lines were 2.30–3.12-fold and 1.34–1.82-fold higher compared with those in atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5d). In the roots, Mn concentrations showed a 1.82–2.18-fold and 1.05–1.26-fold increase compared with atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig. 5e). The Mn contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were signifcantly higher with 3.96–4.16-fold and 1.88–1.98-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5f). Zn concentrations in the shoots of two transgenic lines were also signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 and Col-0 (Supplementary Fig.  9c). However, when calculating the elemental contents of whole plants, all three independent lines showed higher accumulation of Fe, $\mathrm { C u }$ and Zn than atnramp1 and Col-0 (Supplementary Figs. $9 \ \mathrm { g - i } )$ . Analysis of dry weight showed that the dry weights of the three transgenic lines were higher than that of atnramp1(Supplementary Fig.  11). The root-to-shoot translocation ratio of Fe, Mn, Cu and

Zn showed no signifcant diferences among Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 10).

In the present study, we isolated and functionally characterized a Nramp member BrNramp1 in Brassica rapa. We characterized a homologue of AtNramp1 in B. rapa named BrNramp1, and determined the expression pattern and functional role of this protein in Mn and Cd uptake. Through RT-qPCR, we demonstrated that BrNramp1 is mainly expressed in B. rapa roots, and its relative expression level is induced signifcantly in the presence of Cd and the absence of Mn (Fig.  1). We also detected that BrNramp1 encodes a plasma membrane-localized protein (Fig.  2). Heterologous expression in both yeast and A. thaliana verifed Mn and Cd transport activity of BrNramp1 (Figs. 3,4,5).

It is well-known that plants can take up toxic and non-essential Cd cations through divalent metal ion transporters such as Fe, Mn, and Zn transporters (Verret et  al. 2004; Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Ishimaru et  al. 2012). A large body of evidence documents the role of Nramp proteins in the transport of essential divalent transition metals (including $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ ) in many plant species (Bozzi and Gaudet 2021), and it is also known that they contribute to the uptake of toxic and non-essential metals such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ (Sui et  al. 2018; Chang et  al. 2022). The Nramp family members’ sequences are highly conserved, and they share homologous ion transport functions (Ehrnstorfer et  al. 2014), especially in rice and Arabidopsis thaliana: OsNramp5 and AtNramp1 have been shown to participate in Mn and Cd uptake in roots (Chang et  al. 2020a; Ihnatowicz et al. 2014). To explore the orthologous gene in Brassica rapa plants, we used the AtNramp1 protein sequence to perform a BLAST search in the BRAD database. The results demonstrated that three proteins showed high identity to AtNramp1 (ID: Bra003587, Bra035149 and Bra008437). Phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment indicated that Bra003587 has the highest identity and closely clusters with AtNramp1. Therefore, Bra003587 was named BrNramp1 in the present study. BrNramp1 sequence was amplifed to explore the gene structure (Supplementary Fig.  S1c). The expression pattern of BrNramp1 is also conserved, as reported previously. Through RT-qPCR, we demonstrated that BrNramp1 is mainly expressed in $B$ . rapa roots, and its relative expression level signifcantly increased in the presence of Cd and the absence of Mn (Fig.  1), resembling the behavior of the orthologous gene BcNramp1 (Bra008437) (Yue et  al. 2021). Interestingly, previous research showed that Mn defciency may induce the expression of AtNramp1(Cailliatte et al. 2010). This may be because Mn defciency triggers $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling, activating $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent protein kinases, CPK21 and CPK23, which could phosphorylate $\mathrm { T h r } 4 9 8$ of AtNramp1 to facilitate Mn uptake. The expression level of AhNramp1 in peanuts can be induced by Mn and Zn defciency in stems and roots (Wang et al. 2019). All of Arabidopsis thaliana, peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) and Brassica chinensis are dicotyledons. In monocots, the expressions of OsNramp1 and OsNramp5 in rice, showed no inducement by Mn defciency, but OsNramp1 could be induced by Cd addition and Fe defciency (Chang et al. 2020b). HvNramp5 in barley was not afected by Mn, Cu and Zn defciency (Wu et al. 2016). Transcriptional regulation between dicots and monocots showed both conservation and diferences. Based on the above researches, the response of Nramp family members to Mn defciency may be related to plant developmental pathways and their adaptation to environmental changes.

Conformational structure analysis of transmembrane proteins can help in understanding how these molecules recognize and bind their substrates and transport them into cells to fulfll plant nutritional requirements. The Nramp family encompasses proteins with 11 or 12 conserved transmembrane domains (TMs), with TMs 1–10 forming a LeuT fold, which is the structural core unit enabling the transport of a broad range of substrates (Bozzi et al. 2019). The role of these 10 TMs in metal transport has been extensively analyzed in bacteria (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Based on the sequence, we characterized BrNramp1 as consisting of 10 introns and 11 exons, encoding a protein of 328 amino acids (Supplementary Fig. S1). The predicted structure of BrNramp1, based on the amino acid sequence, indicates 12 transmembrane domains with positions similar to those of Nramp protein members in other species. By sequence alignment, we identifed in BrNramp1 the crucial motifs for Mn selectivity: motif A in TM1 (DPGN) and motif $\mathbf { B }$ in TM6 (AMVM), which are identical to those in AtNramp1 (Supplementary Fig.  S1). The full-length ORF of BrNramp1 obtained for $B$ . rapa accession Chiifu revealed a 51  bp diference compared with the Bra003587 sequence from the BRAD database, resulting in the deletion of a 17-amino-acid region in TM3. This deletion did not alter the number or position of transmembrane domains but caused changes in the secondary and tertiary structures of the protein (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Using a heterologous yeast-based expression system, in combination with Cd/Mn addition/depletion assays, we experimentally demonstrated that this 17-amino-acids protein component is necessary to retain Cd and Mn transport activities. Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 showed growth inhibition when exposed to Cd treatment, demonstrating that BrNramp1 can transport Cd from the medium into yeast cells, while yeast expressing the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed no growth inhibition (Fig. 3). When cultured on a medium containing EGTA, which chelates Mn in the medium and prevents $\mathsf { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ mobility, yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 showed signifcantly better growth, demonstrating that BrNramp1 can transport Mn from the medium into yeast cells. In contrast, yeast expressing the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed growth inhibition, indicating that these yeast cells could not transport Mn (Fig. 3). These results demonstrate that BrNramp1 has Cd and Mn transport ability, whereas BrNramp1d, missing the 17-amino-acid component, lost the ability.

Previous studies suggested that the conserved metal-binding site, with methionine sulfur in TM1 and TM6, would prefer Cd as the coordinate substrate to Co and Fe (Bozzi et  al. 2016). It has also been indicated that TM1, TM5, TM6, and TM10 participate in the stage when the binding site switches from outward to inward during Mn transport (Ray S et al. 2023). A similar study indicated that in the TM3, positions E129, D131, and E134 are crucial points determining $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ transport and infuencing pH-dependent transport activity (Ehrnstorfer et  al. 2017). As for BrNramp1d, 17 missing amino acids in TM3 were detected in positions 131 to 148, and this may impair Mn transport by changing the protein structure of BrNramp1.

The overexpression of BrNramp1 in atnramp1 plants complemented Cd and Mn uptake, resulting in a higher accumulation of these ions in both shoots and roots compared with atnramp1 under Cd exposure. Similarly, three transgenic Arabidopsis lines expressing BrNramp1 accumulated signifcantly more Mn than the wild-type Col-0 under both Mnsufcient and Mn-defcient conditions, indicating the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1(Fig.  4). When exposed to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M \ M n C l } _ { 2 }$ and Mn defciency conditions, Mn distribution was similar, but the independent transgenic lines accumulated signifcantly more Mn compared with atnramp1 and Col-0 (Fig.  5). Heterologous expression in Arabidopsis thaliana demonstrated the Mn and Cd transport activity of BrNramp1. In the present study, Zn concentrations in the transgenic lines showed no signifcant diferences under $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd treatment (Supplementary Fig. S5). However, when cultured in Hoagland nutrient solution containing $5 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { M n C l } _ { 2 }$ or under Mn defciency, Zn concentrations in the shoots of the independent lines were signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 and $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ (Supplementary Figs.  S6, S7). One possibility is that under Cd treatment, BrNramp1 preferentially transports Cd and Mn over Zn, while under Mn defciency or without Cd, BrNramp1 may prefer Zn as a substrate. Since Fe, Cu and Zn contents in the transgenic lines were higher than in atnramp1 and Col0, we analyzed dry weight and found that the shoot and root weights of the three transgenic lines were higher than those of atnramp1, resulting in higher Fe, Cu and Zn contents. The diferences in dry weight may explain that under Mn defciency, BrNramp1 expression in atnramp1 could promote plant growth. The dry weight of Arabidopsis is shown in Supplementary Fig.  11. Another possibility is that under Mn defciency, the expression of genes encoding Mn transporters may be induced in response to environmental changes, leading to higher absorption of divalent cations. Several Mn transporters have been reported to exhibit activity for multiple cations. For example, AtIRT1 shows transport activity for Fe, Mn, Zn, Co and Cd (Huang et  al. 2024; Barberon et  al. 2011; Vert et al. 2002), and AtNramp1 transports Fe, Mn and Cd (Cailliatte et  al. 2010). Members of the ZRT/IRT-related proteins (ZIPs) family also show transport activity for Fe, Mn, Zn and Cd (Spielmann et al. 2020). Recent studies have shown that Mn and Fe defciency may trigger $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling, activating $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent protein kinases such as CPK21 and CPK23, which could phosphorylate $\mathrm { T h r } 4 9 8$ and Ser149 of AtNramp1 and AtIRT1, respectively (Fu D et  al. 2022; Wang et  al. 2023). However, these phosphorylation sites specifcally enhance AtNramp1 uptake of Mn and AtIRT1 uptake of Fe, respectively. There may also be other genes responsible for Mn, Fe, Zn and $\mathrm { C u }$ uptake that are induced under Mn defciency. Both the expression pattern and heterologous expression assays indicate that BrNramp1 participates in Mn and Cd uptake in the roots of $B$ . rapa, with conserved functions similar to orthologous proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana, rice, wheat, barley and buckwheat (Cailliatte et  al. 2010; Sui et  al. 2018; Chang et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2016; Yokosho et al. 2020).

In conclusion, we identifed an ortholog of AtNramp1 in Brassica rapa named BrNramp1. This gene encodes BrNramp1, a plasma membrane-localized transporter functional for Mn and Cd. Heterologous expression of BrNramp1 in both yeast and Arabidopsis thaliana demonstrated its transport activity, and a 51 bp nucleotide missing in TM3 caused the loss of transport activity for both Cd and Mn. These fndings are particularly relevant, as BrNramp1 may serve as a valuable target for breeding low-Cd cultivars using molecular marker-assisted methods in the future.

Protein‒protein interactions (PPIs) were projected via the STRING tool. A total of 34 genes were identified, with disconnected nodes obscured from the network visualization. Nodes with higher connectivity are considered more critical for the stability of the entire network. ## Synteny analyses of SlNRAMP genes


Our investigation into the evolutionary mechanisms of the SlNRAMP gene family revealed that the distribution of the five genes was not uniform across 12 chromosomes in the tomato. SlNRAMP1 was located on chromosome 3, while SlNRAMP2 was found on chromosome 11. The SlNRAMP3 gene is situated on chromosome 2, and SlNRAMP4 and SIEIN2 are distributed on chromosome 4 and chromosome 9, respectively. (Fig.  6A). Within the tomato genome, a pair of paralogous genes, SlNRAMP1 and SlNRAMP4, were detected on the same chromosome (Fig.  6B), suggesting a segmental duplication role in the expansion of the SlNRAMP gene family. Furthermore, to elucidate the origin and functional divergence of the SlNRAMP gene family, a comparative collinearity analysis was conducted for NRAMP genes between the tomato and Arabidopsis. A total of seven pairs of NRAMP genes were identified in both tomato and Arabidopsis (Fig. 6C), indicating a high degree of homology and conservation of NRAMP genes across these species.


## SlNRAMP gene expression patterns in a range of tissue types


To elucidate the expression patterns of SlNRAMP genes in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), a comprehensive analysis was conducted across various plant tissues. The results revealed distinct transcript accumulation for each gene. SlNRAMP1 was significantly expressed in flower, root, and fruit, with the highest levels observed in flowers. SlNRAMP2 presented increased transcription in mature root tissues. SlNRAMP3 had substantial transcript abundance in both leaf and root tissues. SlNRAMP4 and SlEIN2 exhibited high expression levels in roots and fruits; however, SlNRAMP4 was more predominant in roots, whereas SlEIN2 was more predominant in fruits. Notably, the transcript levels of SlNRAMP1, SlNRAMP2, SlNRAMP4, and SlEIN2 were generally greater than those of SlNRAMP3 across all the plant tissues examined. Based on these findings, we can better understand how various organs in tomato plants regulate metal ion homeostasis through the SlNRAMP gene family ( Fig. 7)


## Analysis of the expression patterns of SlNRAMPs under cadmium and salt stress


To examine variations in SlNRAMP gene expression in tomato in response to early Cd and salt stress. The first true-leaf unfolded tomato leaves were treated with Cd and $\mathrm { \Delta N a C l }$ , and the expression of four potential transport genes in the tomato roots were assessed via RT‒PCR at various time points (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ ) following cadmium treatment. The expression of the SlNRAMP1 and SlNRAMP2 genes initially increased but then decreased after heavy metal exposure, with maximum expression of SlNRAMP1 and SlNRAMP2 genes observed after $^ { 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ , after which they declined. The maximum expression of SlNRAMP3 occurred at $2 4 \ \mathrm { h } ,$ while SlNRAMP4 reached its peak at $^ { 1 \mathrm { h } }$ . However, the expression of the SlNRAMP3 and SlNRAMP4 genes fluctuated over time. Under Cd treatment, the four genes exhibited distinct response patterns (Fig. 8).

To elucidate the role of SlNRAMP genes in salt stress response, samples were collected at defined time intervals (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ ) post-treatment. Quantitative RT-PCR analysis revealed distinct expression patterns among the four SlNRAMP genes under salt stress conditions. SlNRAMP2 exhibited transient upregulation at $2 \ \mathrm { h } .$ , followed by rapid downregulation after $4 \mathrm { { h } }$ , indicating its potential role in early salt stress adaptation. In contrast, SlNRAMP1 and SlNRAMP4 demonstrated sustained responses, reaching peak expression at 4 and $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ , respectively, before gradually declining. These differential expression profiles suggest specialized temporal roles for SlNRAMP genes in the tomato salt stress response. In fact, SlNRAMP4 expression decreased significantly at $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ , indicating its functional role during the middle phase of salt stress. The expression of SlNRAMP3 remained stable, with a slight decrease at $^ { 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ after salt treatment (Fig. 9).

Elucidating the molecular mechanisms governing metal uptake and translocation is crucial to understanding plant nutrition and stress responses. While NRAMP transporters have been linked to cadmium absorption in certain species [25, 58, 59] and the uptake of other metal ions [60, 61], advancements in this family remain limited, particularly in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum). In this study, we identified four SlNRAMP genes (SlNRAMP1-4) and one SlEIN2 gene in tomato. Sequence analysis revealed variation in protein lengths among the five genes, with SlNRAMP4 encoding the longest polypeptide (773 amino acids) and SlNRAMP3 the shortest (509 amino acids) (Table 1). These findings diverged from the observed diversity patterns reported in a previous tomato NRAMP study [11]. Chromosome-scale genome assembly localizes NRAMP gene positions on chromosomes, and these five genes are distributed across five different chromosomes. Phylogenetic analysis classified the NRAMP and EIN2 genes from six eudicot and monocot species resolved three major clades: Group A (SlNRAMP1 and SlNRAMP2); Group B (SlNRAMP3 and SlNRAMP4); and EIN2 clade (SlEIN2). Consistent with Arabidopsis thaliana [14, 26], the tomato NRAMP family was subdivided into two subfamilies (Fig. 1). Notably, the four SlNRAMP proteins from tomato exhibited sequence similarity to potato StNRAMPs, a finding aligned with their shared taxonomic membership in the Solanaceae family. These suggests conserved evolutionary relationships among NRAMP homologs in solanaceous crops. These integrated findings provide a foundation for dissecting NRAMP-mediated metal transport mechanisms in solanaceous species.

Functionally, the subcellular localization and sequence features of SlNRAMPs suggest potential roles in ion homeostasis. Notably, SlEIN2, previously misclassified as SlNRAMP5 and assigned to the NRAMP family [62], has been reclassified through phylogenetic analysis (Fig.  1), conserved domain (Fig.  2B) and predicted 3D structure (Fig.  3), which confirm its exclusion from the NRAMP NRAMP clade. Despite its sequence alignment with NRAMP family proteins, SlEIN2 clusters exclusively within the EIN2 lineage, supported by its low N-terminal identity $( 2 1 \% )$ with both EIN2 and NRAMP homologs [57]. Structural divergence is further accentuated by the unique motif combination of SlEIN2 (motif 3, motif 2, motif 4, motif 1, and motif 6) and distinct coding and untranslated regions (CDSs and UTRs) (Fig. 2C), which differentiate it from SlNRAMPs. These findings align with functional studies showing that EIN2 does not mediate ion transport but instead acts through ethylene signaling pathways [57]. Transcriptome analysis highlights SlEIN2 as a key regulator of fruit ripening during tomato fruit ripening, influencing the expression of genes associated with ethylene biosynthesis, signal transduction, and defense pathways [63]. Silencing of SlEIN2 results in a non-ripening phenotype and significant variations in the regulation of more than 4,000 genes, underscoring its central role in ethylene signalling. Additionally, protein–protein interaction (PPI) network analysis identified hub proteins in the SlNRAMP (Table  2), providing insights into their potential functional networks. In summary, while SlEIN2 exhibits limited homology to NRAMP family, it exhibits distinct characteristics that suggest a unique functional role in tomato.

The analysis of the conserved motifs and domains of SlNRAMPs helps predict protein roles and clarifies the relationship between protein structure and function.

These findings suggest that the combination of motifs (motif 3, motif 2, motif 5, motif 8, motif 4, motif 7, motif 1, motif 6, and motif 9) is essential for the proper functioning of NRAMP proteins, as they are consistently found across these four NRAMP genes (Fig. 2A). Notably, the consensus transport motif (CTM) between TMD8 and TMD9 is characterized by the conserved sequence GQSSTxTGTYAGQxxQGFLx in Arabidopsis thaliana, and rice (Oryza sativa)—is highly conserved suggesting its critical role in the evolutionary retention of NRAMPs’ metal ion transport function [32].

Most SlNRAMP promoters contain response elements for ABA, jasmonic acid (MeJA), gibberellin (GA), salicylic acid (SA), and auxins, indicating possible hormonal regulation pathways (Fig. 4). Previous studies have shown that plant hormones such as ABA, MeJA, and SA play a role in the plant response to various metal stressors [64]. However, the overall sensitivity of NRAMPs to these hormones and stress treatments can be rather poor, such as BnNRAMPs in rapeseed [14]. Whether the same phenomenon occurs in tomatoes requires further examination. In fact, the modulation of StNRAMP5 expression in hot peppers to increase root absorption of Cd, as well as the upregulation of genes such as NIR1, GLN1, and IAA9 to combat Cd toxicity and restrict its translocation to the above-ground parts, is a strategy that has been reported in recent studies [65]. Furthermore, this review discusses the role of various transcription factors, including those in the MYB family, in regulating plant responses to Cd stress [66]. This research points to the possibility that IAA9, a gene involved in auxin signalling, might be part of a larger transcriptional regulatory network that modulates plant tolerance to heavy metals such as Cd. These genes likely work in concert to increase the ability of plants to absorb essential nutrients, modulate hormone signalling, and alter metal ion transport and compartmentalization.

Recent studies have provided insights into the intricate relationship between heavy metal stress (e.g. Cd) and gene expression dynamics [11, 34].
