Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. SlALMT15 (Solyc11gO6897O) was found to be related to a stomatal density trait that functions in stomatal formation in tomato leaves,and further affects photosynthesis and drought tolerance in tomato (J.Ye,Wang, et al.,2021). Z.Wang et al. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.

Thisreport provides evidence suggesting that SlALMT11 (SolycO8g0o699O) expressed in tomato leaf guard cells is involved in stomatal closure induced by external malate,but not by abscisic acid.This study also highlights how the guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (SlALMT11 and AtALMT12)are activated by external organic acids and identifies the amino acid residues of the ALMT proteins involved in the voltage-dependent channel activity.

## 4.1| Physiological roles of rapid- and slow-anion channels in stomatal movement


The apoplastic malate concentration induces stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Araujo et al., 2011; Hedrich et al.,1994). In this study,we showed that guard-cell-type ALMT proteins playa crucial role in stomatal closure induced by exogenous malate in tomato and

Arabidopsis (Figure 2 and Supporting Information: Figure S4). SIALMT11-dependent inward currents associated with malate efflux from the cells were activated by extracellular malate aswas AtALMT12/QUAC1,suggestinga functional similarity between the two proteins (Figure 3 and Supporting Information: Figure S5).The activation of bell-shaped $1 / V$ patterns associated with SlALMT11 and AtALMT12 coincided with the negative shift of the $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ and was brought about not only by malate but other organic acids (Figure 4 and Supporting Information: Figure S6).Malcheska et al. (2017) reported that the $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ shifted to a more negative membrane potential by extracellular sulphate than chloridein oocytes expressing both AtALMT12 and OST1. In our study, $P _ { \mathrm { O } }$ and $V _ { 1 / 2 }$ in oocytes expressing AtALMT12 or SIALMT11 in the absence of OST1 were similar to sulphate-and chloride-based bath solutions (Figure 4).This difference in channel activity in the presence of sulphate may be explained by the requirement for OST1 interaction.The bell-shaped voltage dependency of these ALMTs indicates a hyperpolarized repression of these channel activities, which might be beneficial for accelerating the hyperpolarization of the plasma membrane enhanced by ${ \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ -ATPase during stomatal opening (lnoue & Kinoshita,2017).

The anion efflux associated with SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 occurred when dicarboxylic acids (fumarate,succinate,and malate) were preinjected into the oocytes (Supporting Information: Figure S7); however, anion effux was not observed when citrate,a tricarboxylic acid,was preinjected.This finding indicates that dicarboxylic anions are substrates for these guard-cell-type ALMTs. Similar selectivity has been reported for other ALMT proteins,AtALMT6,AtALMT9 and LjALMT4 (Kovermann et al.,2007；Meyer et al.，2011；Takanashi et al.，2016)，although ZmALMT1 was shown not to be an organic acid specific (Pineros, Cancado，Maron，et al.，2OO8).In contrast，S-type anion channels mediated by AtSLAC1 in Xenopus oocytes permeated $\mathtt { C l }$ and ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } { \mathsf { \bar { \ } } }$ rather than malate (Geiger et al., 20O9; Lee et al.,2009). Another study reported that cytosolic malate activated SLAC1-channel function using patch-clamp measurements of guard cellsand TEVC in Xenopus oocytes, although malate might not interact directly with SLAC1 (C.Wang et al.,2018).We hypothesize that the activity of SLAC-type and ALMTtype anion channels in guard cells are differently regulated by intra-and extracellularmalate.

In this study,we did not observe ABA-induced stomatal closure mediated by SlALMT11 (Figure 2c,d),of which the closest ortholog in Arabidopsis,AtALMT12,does mediate ABA-induced closure (Sasaki et al.,201O).Therefore,the ABA-dependent ALMT activation pathway may be different in tomato and Arabidopsis.ABA-induced stomatal closure in tomato is possibly mediated by an S-type anion channel, in an OST1-mediated manner,as suggested by Shi et al. (2015).


## 4.2| Functional motifs of guard-cell-type ALMT channels


Several functional domains in anion channels have been acknowledged.For example，arginine residue‘R256' located on the cytoplasmic side between the second and third transmembrane domains of AtSLAC1 is required for $\mathsf { C O } _ { 2 }$ -regulated stomatal movement in planta and S-type anion channel activation by ${ \mathsf { H C O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ ， but not for ABA-induced closure (J. Zhang et al., 2018). Cytosolic Nterminal and C-terminal domains are reported to contain important sites for SLAC1/OST1 function,and a conserved 1O amino acid region is found as a C-terminal OST1 interaction region in SLAC1 channels from many plant species (Hedrich & Geiger,2017；Lind et al., 2015).

A few functional domains have been identified for the guard-celltype ALMT proteins. Luu et al. (2019) reported that a calmodulinbinding domain was present in the C-terminal half (amino acid position 334-351) of the BdALMT12 protein from B.distachyon. These investigatorshypothesized that extra malate-sensitive BdALMT12 channel activity was coregulated by calmodulin as a primary modulator for cytosolic ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ ．Other investigators have reported that the C-terminal half of AtALMT12 is oriented to the cytoplasmic side and is important for actively maintaining the voltage-gating mechanisms when conducting analyses in Xenopus oocytes (Mumm et al.,2013).Truncation of residues 533-560 in the C-terminus of AtALMT12 completely abolished the channel activity (Mumm et al.,2O13)； however,our study indicated that the same deletion increased inward currents,although the mutation lost the bell-shaped I/V pattern observed with the native protein (Supporting Information:Figure S9d).The difference in the currents observed with the same AtALMT12 △533-560 protein may be attributed to different measurement parameters，like malate pre-injection or perhaps other unknown reasons.

Our results suggested that the negatively charged amino acids in the C-terminal ends of AtALMT12 and SIALMT11 are essential for regulating the voltage dependency of guard-cell type ALMT channels. Furthermore, the conserved motifs were present in the C-terminal regions among many plant species(Supporting Information: Figure S1Oa).In several plant families the conserved motif was ‘A-A-E' (Motif Il,and Ill in Supporting Information:Figure S10b); however， the C-terminus of the truncated mutants,SlALMT11 △504-536 and AtALMT12 △533-560, had Lys (K) followed by Glu (E)residues at the C-terminal end.The conserved motif for these mutants was ‘A-H/S-F-K-E' (Supporting Information: Figure S10a), although these mutations did not have the bell-shaped patterns intheir mean current-voltage curves (Supporting Information: Figure S9b,d).These results suggest that neutral amino acid residues might be necessary before ‘D/E'to maintain the characteristic bellshaped I/Vpatterns of the ALMT channels.Therefore,theaddition of a peptide tag,including GFP,at the C-terminus of SIALMT11 and AtALMT12 disrupted the native bell-shaped patterns (Figure 5, Mumm et al.,2013).Interestingly,the addition of GFP at the end of TaALMT1 did not affect inward currents derived from $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux in Xenopus oocytes (Sasaki et al.,2014),indicating that the relationship between the C-terminal structure and functions vary among respective ALMT proteins.

Most recently,the structures of two ALMT proteins, Arabidopsis AtALMT1 and soybean (Glycine max) GmALMT12/QUAC1，were analysed by cryo-electron microscopy.AtALMT1 (categorized as a Clade 1 ALMT) contains putative $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -binding sites and forms a pore involved in malate recognition (J.Wang et al.,2022),however, the putative sites are not conserved in guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (Clade 3). In contrast, two pairs of Arg residues (R8O and R165 of AtALMT1) involved in malate recognition are conserved among other ALMT proteins (J.Wang et al., 2022).

Analysis of GmALMT12 supported the hypothesis that malate activates the channel via regulating the conformation of tryptophan W90 (Qin et al., 2022),although no direct evidence for GmALMT12- mediated stomatal closure has been reported in soybean.Moreover, the tryptophan residue in this position is not only conserved among almost all Clade 3 ALMTs but all ALMT proteins.Both reports only mention malate permeable pore formation but do not discuss the selectivity of other substrates，inorganic and organic anions.Moreover，these structures do not reveal how C-terminal amino acids are involved in voltage sensing in each type of ALMT protein $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activating or guardcell type ALMTs).Therefore，further studies will be necessary to characterize how the C-terminal acidic amino acid residues generate the bell-shaped I/V pattern in SIALMT11 and AtALMT12.

In summary,our results demonstrate similarities in extracellular malate-induced stomatal closure in tomato and Arabidopsis,and both plants require guard-cell-type ALMT channels.Which organic acids enhance the ALMT channel in the apoplastic spaces of guard cells remain unknown.We hypothesize that the ALMT channels might be activated by ‘malate'released from mesophyll cells,since malate is the most abundant organic anion in plant cells (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2OoO).As for the malate response shared between AtALMT12 and SLALMT11,the apoplastic malate concentration increases in response to an elevated ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ concentration leading to stomatal closure in Vicia faba (Hedrich et al.,1994),although this response has not yet been recognized in other plant species.Jalakas et al. (2021) reported that the coordinated activation of $\mathsf { R } ^ { - }$ and S-type anion channels is needed for stomatal stress signalling,usinga series of single,double and triple mutants of atalmt12,slac1,and slah3 in Arabidopsis.Further studies of ALMT/QUAC and SLAC/SLAH channels might enhance our understanding of how stomatal movements in response to environmental stresses (e.g.，drought and water loss)are controlled in each plant species.

The aluminium-activated malate transporter (ALMT) family is found ubiquitously in sequenced genomes throughout the plant kingdom [1] and was named when the first member of the family to be discovered was found to be involved in aluminium resistance in wheat [2]–although proteins of this family are channels, rather than transporters as their name suggests. The first characterized homologue in Arabidopsis thaliana, AtALMT1 [3], was similarly found to be involved in Al-resistance. However, in addition to ALMT1, the gene family in this species contains 13 other members suggesting that they are involved in more than just Al-resistance, and some of these have already shown to have a wide range of other roles [4]. To date, the ALMT family has been shown to be central to physiological processes such as control of stomatal aperture [5,6] and anion homoeostasis [7]. Furthermore, increasing attention is being paid due to their potential role in economically valuable traits such as fruit flavour [8] and grain filling [9], and more recently they have been shown to be key mediators of GABA (γ -aminobutyric acid) signalling [10]. Identification of the molecular actors in these processes is already helping guide marker-assisted breeding [11]. The ALMT family is now known to be central to many physiological processes, with scope for even more diversity as many homologues are still to be characterized and thus, a comprehensive review of all currently known functions is a timely addition to the literature.


## Aluminium resistance



## Overcoming aluminium toxicity on acid soils


Acid soils are prevalent worldwide, comprising around half of all potentially arable land [12]. In these soils, aluminium ions become solubilized and damage crops via root growth inhibition [13] and, to compound the problem, nutrients such as phosphate become less available [14]. Several plant species have been identified as aluminium-resistant and they use a variety of mechanisms including thickening of cell walls [15], active transport of aluminium away from sensitive organs [16], or, prominently, organic acid exudation, chiefly either by release of malate or citrate [17,18].

Studies on crosses of near isogenic Al-resistant and Al-sensitive wheat (Triticum aestivum) cultivars alongside electrophysiological studies using Xenopus oocytes [19,2,20] first identified TaALMT1 as the channel responsible for malate exudation from root tips, providing the primary mechanism of aluminium resistance. TaALMT1 is constitutively expressed in the root apices of Al-resistant wheat and malate chelates $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ forming a 2:2 complex with the trivalent aluminium ions, thus encasing the ions and rendering them non-toxic [21]. This allows longer root growth and greater yields compared with a sensitive cultivar grown on acid soils. In addition to protection from $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity, malate extrusion has the benefit of increasing phosphate availability in the soil – since $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ binds and complexes phosphate [22]. This is part of a host of processes activated in plants for improved phosphorous usage [14,23]. Heterologous expression of TaALMT1 in cultured tobacco cells, Xenopus oocytes, and transgenic rice plants has shown efflux of malate activated by the presence of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and expression confers Al-resistance to tobacco cells [2]. Importantly, transgenic expression of TaALMT1 in Al-sensitive barley plants rendered them resistant to aluminium toxicity [24]. In one study, transgenic plants grown on acid soil displayed root growth similar to that seen in neutral soils and a doubling in yield when expressing just the single gene [23], making it a powerful tool for transgenic crop development. A thorough review of transgenic approaches using ALMT1 and other genes can be found in Ryan et al. [25].


## Other ALMTs involved in aluminium resistance


Since the characterization of TaALMT1, several ALMTs from other species including oilseed rape, Arabidopsis, rye, soybean and Yorkshire fog have been shown to be vital for

Al-resistance and characterized (see Figure 1 and Table 1). These channels are activated by $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and in some cases their expression is also up-regulated upon sensing $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [26].

AtALMT1 is a malate channel critical for aluminium resistance in Arabidopsis, expressed at the plasma membrane of the epidermal cells of the root tip [3]. This protein shows $4 1 \%$ sequence identity and $6 3 \%$ similarity to TaALMT1. However, in contrast, AtALMT1 is not constitutively expressed; instead, expression is up-regulated by aluminium [26,27], mediated by the transcription factors STOP1, STOP2 and WRKY, which also regulate other genes critical for tolerance of acid soils [28–30]. In addition, two genes with $9 5 \%$ sequence identity with one another were identified in oilseed rape (Brassica napus) [31,32], as well as GmALMT1 in soybean (Glycene max), and ScALMT1 in rye (Secale cereale) [33,34]. These genes are expressed at root tip plasma membranes, and the corresponding proteins are permeable to malate and are activated by aluminium, showing this mechanism for Al-resistance is widespread among plant species. In addition, GmALMT1 channel activity has also been shown to be regulated by $\mathrm { p H }$ changes and phosphorous concentration [35]. Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus) HlALMT1 has also been identified as an important resistance gene in the model grass species, and has Alactivated expression similar to AtALMT1 controlled by a Alresponsive transcription factor ART1, with expression levels in different accessions controlled by the number of binding regions for ART1 in the promoter region [36].


## Other root-related functions


ZmALMT2 from maize (Zea mays) has been shown to be root localized and to release malate into the soil. Unlike AtALMT1 and TaALMT1, however, this is not correlated with Alresistance, but instead is likely to provide solubilization for soil nutrients, such as phosphate, as discussed above for TaALMT1. As it is also found in vascular tissue, ZmALMT2 could also play a role in the transport of organic acids or mineral anions in the xylem [37].


## Guard cell movements


Another vital role played by some ALMT family members is as molecular components of the guard cell movements that regulate gas exchange across leaf surfaces. Plants control $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ uptake and water loss by regulating the aperture of the stomatal pores. Three family members from Arabidopsis, AtALMT6, AtALMT9 and AtALMT12, are involved in opening and closing of stomata, with movement driven by osmotically active inorganic and organic ions [38]. Upon stomatal opening, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ enters the guard cell via voltagegated inward rectifying potassium channels, driven by the electrochemical gradient maintained by ATP-driven proton pumping. Malate synthesis from stored starch provides a charge-balancing ion, and is taken up into the vacuole via AtALMT6, and similarly AtALMT9 acts to permit entry of chloride counterions into the vacuole. The increase in solutes draws water into the cell down the water potential gradient, swelling the cell. The process is inverted during stomatal closing. The membrane is depolarized, prompted by the action of AtALMT12/QUAC1 (quick anion channel 1) releasing malate rapidly, this allows $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ to flow out of the cell, accompanied by $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } -$ anions via SLAC1 (slow anion channel 1). In addition, AtALMT6 activity is regulated in part by cytosolic malate concentration, and so malate can flow out of the vacuole to either be lost via AtALMT12/QUAC1 or used in metabolism. This loss of osmotica drives a loss of water and closing of the stomata.

AtALMT6 is expressed in guard cell vacuoles and is a malate channel, specific for divalent malate involved in stomatal movements. It is not aluminium activated but instead is controlled by light, ABA [39], $\mathrm { p H }$ and cytosolic malate concentration [4]. As transport is dependent on the concentration of malate in the cytosol and the tonoplast membrane potential, AtALMT6 can mediate both malate uptake into and release from the vacuole in guard cells, with uptake during stomatal opening, and release during stomatal closing as shown in Figure 2. Interestingly, in A. thaliana expression is also seen in floral organs, suggesting another role yet to be elucidated. Knockout plants did not show phenotypic differences, indicating functional redundancy in vacuolar malate channels, perhaps from the action of

$K ^ { + }$ ions enter the cell during opening, and the charge is balanced by malate synthesis from starch, which is then taken up into the vacuole via ALMT6 and activates ALMT9 to permit $\mathbb { C } ^ { | - }$ uptake into the vacuole. This increase in osmotic potential draws water into the cell, leading to swelling and stomatal opening. Stomatal closing, conversely, is driven by release of $K ^ { + }$ ions, which is permitted during membrane depolarization and driven by ALMT12. Additionally, anions are released by SLAC1 over a longer period of time. Loss of osmolytes leads to concomitant loss of water and thus stomatal closing.

AtALMT9 and perhaps also AtALMT5, which has been shown to be expressed in guard cells, and to be closely related to AtALMT6 (see Figure 1).

AtALMT9 is a vacuolar chloride channel in guard cells and Atalmt9 knockouts show impaired stomatal opening [6]. It permits chloride to enter the vacuole, providing a charge-balance for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the same way as malate. Malate in the cytosol (synthesized from starch) activates the channel, meaning malate can act both as an osmolyte and as a signalling molecule in guard cells. Interestingly, kinetic data suggest AtALMT9 is multimeric, with a number of subunits ${ > } 2 . 5$ with more recent work suggesting that it forms a tetramer [40]. Furthermore, cytosolic nucleotides such as ATP block the activity of AtALMT9, competing with malate for a binding site [41]. The $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -V-ATPases that maintain a hyperpolarized tonoplast consume ATP, provoking lowered cytosolic ATP concentrations, removing this block and thus permitting currents via AtALMT9 and facilitating anion uptake into the vacuole.

AtALMT12 (also known as QUAC1) is expressed in guard cell plasma membranes and operates as an R-type (rapid-type) channel crucial for stomatal closing [5], allowing rapid malate release. One study also found localization to endomembranes, although this is possibly an artefact of overexpression [42]. The channel opens with fast kinetics upon membrane depolarization, releasing malate into the apoplasm in parallel with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ release through potassium channels to maintain the depolarization. Moreover, external malate causes increased activation of the channel and thus may represent a positive-feedback loop. Loss-of function mutants confer a wilty phenotype due to their impaired stomatal closing. Rather than being ligand gated, as seen in ALMT1, ALMT12 activity is voltage gated; however, the voltage sensor is yet to be identified, although it is likely in the CTD (C-terminal domain), which has been shown to be vital for regulation [43].


## Other roles



## Malate storage and homoeostasis


AtALMT9, in addition to its role in guard cells (discussed above and summarized in Table 1), has been shown to be permeable to both chloride and malate and expressed strongly throughout leaf mesophyll tissue. It is likely to have a role in homoeostasis: ensuring that the concentration of malate – which plays an essential role in metabolism as part of the citric acid cycle – remains stable within the cytoplasm. Similar to AtALMT6, the channel is likely to work in both directions, by storing excess in the vacuole and releasing it when required to regulate osmotic potential and C-metabolism [44].


## Cell elongation and nutrient storage


Barley (Hordeum vulgare) HvALMT1 is a malate channel expressed in guard cells and the root elongation zone, as well as floral tissues and seeds [45]. Although it has the greatest sequence similarity to TaALMT1 of any barley gene and localizes to the plasma membrane, it is not involved in Al-resistance but seems to have several distinct roles within the plant. HvALMT1 over-expressing lines take longer to close their stomata [46] and RNAi knockouts show a similar phenotype to Atamlt12 knockouts [9], so HvALMT1 is likely to be a functional homologue of AtALMT12. In expanding cells HvALMT1 may help provide an osmotic balance and regulate turgor. Additionally, later studies have shown that this channel plays a role in seed development during acidification of the starchy endosperm, which is required for enzyme activity [9]. Rather than directly causing acidification itself (this is probably caused by a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase pumping protons from the aleurone) release of malate is suggested to act as a counterion for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ and other positively charged nutrients such as $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , helping to maintain electroneutrality and osmotic balance in a similar manner to the role of malate in guard cell movements. The significant difference in function between HvALMT1 and TaALMT1 despite strong sequence similarity again highlights that small differences in sequence can underlie large changes in function.


## Fruit flavour


Malic acid is an important component of apple taste, grape quality and wine production: an economically significant set of traits. A malic acid channel with high homology to AtALMT genes has been shown to be responsible for the acidity of apples, and functions to accumulate malic acid in the vacuole [8,47]. Similarly, grape berries contain an ALMT family member expressed in the tonoplast of berry mesocarp tissue responsible for malate and tartrate accumulation [48]. Understanding of the action of these genes could be valuable for fruit and wine development [47].


## Inorganic anion homoeostasis


ZmALMT1 from maize was one of the first family members to be described that did not have a role in aluminium resistance. It localizes to plasma membranes throughout the plant, but is less permeable to organic anions and instead is probably involved in inorganic anion homoeostasis and mineral nutrition [7].


## GABA signalling


A recently discovered role of ALMTs is in mediating GABA signalling in plants. This is the first evidence for GABA signalling in plants in addition to its established role as a metabolite [10]. GABA – a non-protein amino acid – accumulates in plant tissues in response to biotic and abiotic stresses, and has a central role in pollen tube growth and regulation of root growth [49]. Recently, it has been shown that GABA’s influence is exerted by interaction with ALMT proteins, and a putative GABA-binding motif has been identified in the CTD. GABA binding negatively regulates ion flux through the channel, i.e. decreasing carbon flux from roots in the case of TaALMT1. Additionally, as plant anion equilibrium potentials are strongly positive and plant action potentials are generated by voltage-gated ion channels, GABA inhibition of ALMTs will hyperpolarize membranes and decrease excitability.

Moreover, to advance studies of ALMTs, perhaps parallels can be drawn with the more well-studied GABA(A) receptors from mammals, which have a greater level of structural detail elucidated already. Although they are different gene families, it may be possible to apply insights from mammalian proteins to design experiments to study ALMTs as GABA(A) receptors are predicted to have a similar overall architecture, being ${ \sim } 4 5 0 \mathrm { A A }$ long and divided into a membrane-embedded half and a soluble half [50]. In the mammalian system the channel is formed by a central pore between five monomers, and the GABA-binding site is found at the interface of monomer subunits; perhaps a similar multimeric structure will be found for ALMTs as suggested by recent results from AtALMT9 [40].
