Some of these may have similar or redundant roles, for example AtALMT4 and AtALMT5 are closely related to AtALMT6 and so may also have a role in the guard cell vacuolar membrane. Indeed, some of these channels may account for residual activity seen in knockout mutants that still retain some function. Alternatively, ALMTs may form hetero-multimers to provide diversified functions, as seen in GABA(A) receptors in mammals. In addition, several members have expression patterns that show they must have a wider range of roles than is currently known – for example, AtALMT6 has a role in guard cells, but is also expressed in floral tissues with an as-yet undefined function. It is possible that ALMTs are involved in shuttling malate in C4 and CAM metabolism as the channels involved have not yet been identified. However, as Arabidopsis is a C3 plant these experiments will have to be done in another species.

Although there is a growing body of knowledge about the physiological functions of ALMTs, much less is known about their structure and mechanism. Relatively small differences in sequence can lead to large changes in localization, substrate specificity, gating and physiological function. In many cases, evidence is either scant or directly contradictory. No detailed 3D structure is available of any family member, but would help guide biochemical and functional studies and elucidate further details of mechanism and regulation, and thus detailed, high quality structural studies are vital for a full understanding ALMTs.

Finally, the ALMT family has been shown to have many members that are not aluminium activated, to have members permeable to anions other than malate, and to be channels rather than active transporters. Thus, the name aluminiumactivated malate transporters does not fully reflect this family of proteins and is potentially confusing. It is perhaps advisable to take up the previously suggested QUAC nomenclature, which better reflects the characteristics of the family members.

Aluminum Activated Malate Transporters (ALMTs) are important plant anion channels by playing roles in organic acid transport, stress resistance, growth and development, nutrient absorption, and the GABA response (Hedrich 2012; Ramesh et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2016; Balzergue et al., 2017; Medeiros et al., 2018; Long et al.,

2020). Wheat TaALMT1 was the first identified family member (named due to its activation by aluminium $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ , the main ion causing toxicity to plants in acidic soil) mediates malate efflux to chelate ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ and relieve toxicity (Zhang et al., 2001; Sasaki et al., 2004). Our recent work has shown that TaALMT1 not only participates in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxification but also participates in the GABA response (Ramesh et al., 2015; Long et al., 2020). Arabidopsis has 14 ALMTs, with those characterized having varied roles, and several others yet to be characterized (Hedrich 2012; Sharma et al., 2016; Medeiros et al., 2018). AtALMT1, which is mainly expressed in roots and localized at the plasma membrane (PM), functions in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity resistance, similarly to TaALMT1, low phosphorus (LP) signal transduction, and Fe uptake, by mediating malate efflux in roots (Hoekenga et al., 2006; Balzergue et al., 2017; Mora-Macıas et al., 2017 ́ ). ALMT3 is also involved in the LP response in root hairs (Maruyama et al., 2019). The vacuolar membrane (tonoplast)-localized anion channels ALMT4, ALMT6, and ALMT9 transport anions across the tonoplast to regulate stomatal movement and/or salinity stress resistance (Kovermann et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2011; De Angeli et al., 2013a; Baetz et al., 2016; Eisenach et al., 2017). ALMT12, ALMT13, and ALMT14, are all likely to be Rtype anion channels in the PM, playing roles in malate transport to regulate stomatal opening, stomatal and mesophyll conductance, and pollen tube growth (Meyer et al., 2010; Sasaki et al., 2010; Medeiros et al., 2016; Gutermuth et al., 2018; Domingos et al., 2019). Furthermore, ALMT family members were reported to be involved in physiological and stress response processes in other crops and plants including maize, rice, soybean, apple, grape, tomato, canola, Brachypodium distachyon, and Medicago sativa (Ligaba et al., 2006; Piñeros et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; De Angeli et al., 2013b; Sasaki et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018; Heng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Luu et al., 2019).

Previously, through the use of gene mapping, a mutation in OsALMT7 was found to underpin a panicle apical abortion (paab1) phenotype. The two paab1 transcripts (paab1-t1 and paab1-t2), were found to be transcribed into proteins with Cterminal truncations (containing 163 amino acid residues) that transport anions with a capacity lower than that of the fulllength OsALMT7 (Heng et al., 2018). OsALMT7 (paab1) is expressed in vascular tissues of roots, stems, sheaths, and panicles and localizes to the PM, and it was concluded that it plays an important role in panicle anion transport, panicle development, and grain yield (Heng et al., 2018). Furthermore when wild-type plants were transformed with a genomic fragment containing the paab1 base substitution resulting in a panicle abortion phenotype (Heng et al., 2018). Compare with other ALMTs, OsALMT7 has special molecular characteristicses that it has the ability to mediate malate flux with its transmembrane helices incomplete, and its truncated protein represses the wild-type channel in rice. Here, we investigate the mechanism of these characteristicses with further electrophysiology studies. We proposed and tested the hypothesis that OsALMT7 transports malate as a multimer and that paab1 interaction with OsALMT7 inhibits transport capacity. Furthermore, we extended this to examine whether this is a feature of other ALMTs, specifically TaALMT1.

A number of plant channels are already known to function as homo- or hetero-multimers, and heteromerization is acknowledged to be an important mechanism of channel regulation (Hedrich, 2012). For example, aquaporins of both the PM and tonoplast assemble as homo- or heterotetramers, such as PIP1s with no or weak water permeability with itself, combine with PIP2s and increase their activity in different plant species (Harvengt et al., 2000; Bienert et al., 2012; Fetter et al., 2004; Heinen et al., 2014; Berny et al., 2016). Shaker family potassium (K) channels share a similar structure with ALMTs, 6 transmembrane $\alpha$ -helices with both N-terminal and C-terminal cytosolic domains, and function as homo- or heterotetramers; notably, KC1, the silent channel subunit, forms a heterotetramer with other shaker K channels to change their voltage dependence (Baizabal-Aguirre et al., 1999; Pilot et al., 2001; Véry and Sentenac, 2003; Xicluna et al., 2007; Duby et al., 2008; Lebaudy et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2009; Lebaudy et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Jeanguenin et al., 2011). Cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 2 (CNGC2) and CNGC4 have been proposed to form a heteromeric channel to mediate $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ currents (Tian et al., 2019). For plant anion channels, the S-type channel SLAC1 has been proposed to combine with the shaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2 and inhibit their channel activity (Zhang et al., 2016). Zhang et al. (2013) showed that tonoplast-localized AtALMT9 formed homomultimeric complex by coexpressing the mutant channel and wild-type channel in tobacco leaves; however, it has not been determined whether PM-localized ALMTs, including OsALMT7, and R-type anion channels, such as ALMT12/13/14, function as multimers or monomers.

Here, we determined that OsALMT7 function as multimeric proteins and that combinations of ALMT subunits can contribute to anion channel regulation. This strengthens our understanding of ALMT function. By defining the mechanism by which subunit modification has a dominant effect on channel function, this provides a new avenue by which genetic modification or gene editing can have important effects without first creating knockout mutants, enabling crop stress resistance and grain yield improvements.

The plant genome has frequent repetitions of the aluminumactivated malate transporters (ALMT) genes, which is essential for transporting organic acids (OAs) across membranes (Zhang et al., 2014). OAs regulate plant metabolism and modulate adaptational (Sharma et al., 2016) activities like stomatal motion (Meyer et al., 2010a; Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010), aluminum tolerance, pH modulation, and stress response (Sharma et al., 2016). In the last few decades, multiple reports have suggested that the release of OAs (particularly, malic acid) can modulate plant tolerance to metal, while its improvs nutritional stress, ion transport, and cell turgor pressure (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).

Therefore, delineating the underlying mechanism of ALMTs action can provide us with tools to improve plant response to biotic and abiotic stressors.

Evolutionary analysis of ALMTs in bacteria (Takanashi et al., 2016), Arabidopsis (Kovermann et al., 2007), rice (Oryza sativa) (Liu et al., 2017), apple (Ma et al., 2018), and Chinese white pear (Xu et al., 2018) demonstrated that plants ALMTs have distinctive function, for example aluminum tolerance, and fruit acidity in plants. They have also been correlated with resistance response, ion transport, and opening and closing of the stomatal guard cells.

Based on a study on Arabidopsis thaliana, the ALMT family has 14 members, divided into three subgroups, according to their functions. The most representative family member is AtALMT1, which belongs to the first subgroup and is located in the root cell membrane. AtALMT9 represents member of the second subgroup and is primarily expressed in mesophyll cells. AtALMT12 belongs to the third subcategory and is primarily expressed in the plasma membrane and the intima of guard cells. Its function is related to the closure of guard cell type anion channels and stomata (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010).

ALMTs were reported to function as anion channel proteins (Zhang et al., 2014). In particular, the activity and expression profile of the AtALMT12 gene was shown to have significant influence on the anion efflux. In stomatal guard cells, under drought stress, the gene was shown to accelerate guard cell cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, and vacuole anion discharge. A massive exudation of anions altered cell membrane polarity, activated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel proteins, and resulted in the release of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ out of cells, causing reduction in cell turgor pressure, closure of the stomata and minimization of moisture loss.

Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is a highly profitable crop and the largest source of natural fiber for the global textile industry. The demand for enhanced fiber quality is increasing with the rapid growth of modern textile industries. Till now, little is known about the role of the ALMT gene family in upland cotton. Here, we screened the entire genome of the upland cotton ALMT gene family and predicted gene structure, chromosome distribution, cellular localization, and expression pattern. This work will offer new insight into the development of genetically enhanced stress-resistant cotton fiber.

In higher plants anion channels have recently been suggested to play key roles in controlling celular functions,including turgor-and osmoregulation,stomatal movements,anion transport,signal transduction and possibly also signal propagation.In guard cels and roots,physiological functions of anion channels have been proposed which willbe discussed here.In initial investigations it was proposed that anion channels in the plasma membrane of guard cells provide a prominent control mechanism for stomatal closing. The proposed model suggests that anion channel activation and the resulting anion efflux from guard cells cause membrane depolarization, thereby driving $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ eflux through outwardrectifying $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ channels required for stomatal closing. This article provides a brief review of new and recent insights into the molecular properties and cellbiological functions of anion channels in guard cells. Furthermore,recently implicated putative functions of anion channels in roots during salt stress, xylem loading and ${ \bf A } | ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance are addressed.


## Plant anion channel types


Anion channels comprise a diverse class of ion channels in animal and plant cells. The first plant anion channels to be described were the $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ channels which contribute to transient depolarization in algae during action potentials [10,25, 40]. With respect to their voltage dependence, anion channels can be separated into at least two major classes which include depolarization- [17, 31,40,44] and hyperpolarization-activated anion channels [41,45,46]. A third class of anion channels is activated by stretching of the membrane [7,9,33]. Furthermore, second messengers including $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and nucleotides have been shown to regulate anion channels [14,31,52]. In this review we will focus on physiological functions and the regulation of guard cell anion channels which have received recent detailed attention and briefly outline recent suggestions for anion channel functions in roots for nutrient transport and metal toxicities [39,45]. Some of the discussed properties and molecular functions discussed here may apply to anion channels in other higher-plant cells.


## Guard cell anion channels


Stomatal closing is mediated by ${ \mathbf { K } } ^ { + }$ and anion release from guard cells and parallel metabolism of malate to osmotically inactive starch [20, 27]. In guard cells,large anion channel-mediated anion efflux currents are activated by elevation in the cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration [31] and by external $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ [14].When anion channels are activated in the plasma membrane of guard cells, anion efflux occurs because of the anion gradient from the cytosol to the extracellular space and because of the negative membrane potential. Anion release in turn causes a shift in the membrane potential to more positive values. This depolarization has been proposed to activate outward-rectifying $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ channels [4,30,35] and to shift the membrane potential positive of the equilibrium potential of ${ \mathbf { K } } ^ { + }$ which would drive ${ \bf K } ^ { + }$ efflux required for stomatal closing. Therefore, $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activation of anion channels may provide a major mechanism for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ mediation of stomatal closing [14, 31].


## Voltage dependence of anion channels


Guard cell anion channels are activated by depolarization of the guard cell plasma membrane. Two highly distinct types of guard cell anion currents were identified in the guard cell plasma membrane.The initially described $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -activated anion channels are expected to produce a slow depolarization of guard cells [31, 34]. These slow and sustained anion channel currents (Stype) can be continuously activated for long-term periods,lasting longer than 1h and therefore can produce sustained depolarizations [19, 31, 34]. Consistent with this finding,early studies showed that $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ enhancement of slow anion currents resulted in a slow and sustained depolarization of guard cells [31]. Single channel recordings show that S-type anion channels have long lasting open times [19,28,36]. The plant hormone abscisic acid causes long-term depolarization [16,18,42] leading to the suggestion that S-type anion channels may be activated by ABA.Therefore, it was proposed that these slow anion channels provide a central controller of long-term anion and ${ \mathbf { K } } ^ { + }$ efflux during stomatal closing. The most compelling evidence for this model was obtained in studies showing that several chemically distinct slow anion channel blockers can completely abolish ABA- and malate-induced stomatal closing [36, 37].

The second type of anion channel identified in guard cells showed very rapid depolarizationinduced activation with activation times of $< 5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ and was therefore named rapid anion channel (or R-type, also named GCAC1)[14,17, 34]. Activation and deactivation half times of rapid anion channels [14] are about $1 0 ^ { 3 }$ times more rapid than slow anion channels in the guard cell plasma membrane [34]. Analysis of the single channel activity under steady-state conditions with multiple channels in the patch indicated that activation upon depolarization is mediated through an apparent decrease in the closed time and an apparent increase in the mean open time of the channel [14]. During prolonged stimulation,anion channels slowly reclose (inactivate) in a voltage-dependent manner [14,34]. Therefore, these anion channels would cause a rapid and transient depolarization rather than a sustained depolarization.In many respects rapid anion channels are very similar to the previously described transient depolarization-activated $\mathbf { C l } ^ { - }$ currents in algae which have been shown in classical studies to contribute to plant action potentials [3,10,25,44; for review 40]. However, this similarity has not yet been further addressed in guard cells. Upon inactivation，R-type anion channel activity is restored again in response to aprolonged hyperpolarization. The voltagedependence and kinetics of rapid anion channels described above are also reminiscent of voltagedependent $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ ， $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ,and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ channels in excitable membranes [15]. The transient nature of rapid anion channel activation suggests a potentially limited importance in mediation of stomatal closing by ABA, which triggers long-term depolarizations. This suggestion is supported by the finding that complete block of rapid anion channels by DIDS [23] has little effect on stomatal closing by ABA and malate [36].


## Anion selectivity


In order to characterize the selectivity filter of guard cell anion channels,patch-clamp experiments were conducted with solutions containing salts of non permeating cations in combination with permeant anions.When chloride in the extracellular or cytosolic solution was substituted by other halides as well as the physiologically occurring anions,malate and nitrate, the shift in current reversal potential of slow and rapid anion channels revealed different absolute selectivities of the two anion currents,with similar permeability sequences relative of $\mathbf { C l } ^ { - }$ of[13,28]:

Differences in permeability ratios may in part be attributed to differences in experimental solutions and the membrane side to which anions are added [15].Determination of accurate anion selectivities requires use of stable electrodes such as platinum wires [28], because of the reactivity of some anions with silver chloride.Furthermore,when relative selectivities of various ions are calculated, the activity of ions in solution needs to be computed [26]. For malate anions only 33 to $40 \%$ of added malate is available as a free anion under the conditions used in these studies [28]. After consideration of these experimental conditions an interesting result is the high permeability ratio of slow anion channels for nitrate over chloride [28]. The selectivity sequences of guard cell anion channels resemble Eisenman Series I, indicating that the size of the hydrated anion contributes to anion channel selectivity and that guard cell anion channels do not discriminate strongly among anions [51]. Since glutamate or gluconate do not pass the channel, the analogy to GABA- and glycine-activated channels [5,29] would predict an open-pore diameter of ca. $0 . 3 \mathtt { n m }$ .The selectivity of guard cell anion channels appears however to be less stringent than GABA-activated $\mathbf { C l } ^ { - }$ channels,as fluoride ions are permeable to slow anion channels in guard cells [28] while fluoride has a very low permeability in GABA channels [29].


## Regulation ofanion channels bycalcium,nucleotides and abscisic acid


Under conditions of drought, plants synthesize the phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) which in turn closes stomatal pores and reduces transpirational water loss. Interestingly, recent studies suggest that ABA can cause stomatal closing by two signal transduction pathways including a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent pathway as well as a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ - independent pathway [1].At present, more is known about $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent signaling components during stomatal regulation.Abscisic acid can cause rises in the cytosolic $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration of guard cells [1,24,32], which can be in part mediated by non-selective $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -permeable channels in the plasma membrane [32] and by release of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ from intracellular stores. Inositol 1,4,5- trisphosphate triggers a rise in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in guard cells and causes stomatal closing [11]. Furthermore, recent data have suggested that further $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ elevations in guard cells may be mediated by $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ 1 induced $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ release from vacuoles via slow vacuolar (S-V) channels [49]. In addition, at alkaline vacuolar $\mathsf { p H }$ an additional class of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ - independent $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ release channel is activated in guard cell vacuoles [2]. These data indicate multiple sources and mechanisms which can trigger rises in cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ，whereby questions of physiological stimulation and signal specificity require further analysis.

Rises in the cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration have been shown to enhance S-type anion currents in the plasma membrane of guard cells,thereby providing a potentially important mechanism for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -induced stomatal closing [31]. Furthermore, rises in the extracellular $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ concentration from $0 . 1 \mathrm { m M }$ to $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ enhance rapid anion channel currents, when weak cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ buffering $\mathbf { \omega } ( 0 . 1 \mathbf { m M }$ EGTA) is applied[14].In the presence of nucleotides extracellular $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ increased anion current amplitudes 5-20-fold [14]. The question whether ABA activates mainly the slow type of anion channel or also the rapid type of anion channel remains to be determined. It is likely that rapid anion currents provide an additional modulatory component to the sustained anion efux via slow anion currents during stomatal closing.The important link by which ABA and cytosolic $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activate slow and rapid anion channels remains unknown. Data indicating $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -independent stomatal closing [1] would further require yet unknown mechanisms of $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -independent anion channel activation.


## Auxin modulation


Auxins which can cause stomatal opening [21] altered the activation potential and current amplitude of R-type anion channels in a dosedependent manner. Furthermore, this auxin action on rapid anion channels was found to be reversible and side-specific (extracellular face of the channel).When auxins reach their target sites, the activation potential of anion channels is shifted negative towards the resting potential of the cell， after correction for access resistance which also would produce an apparent negative shift,due to the auxin-mediated anion current increase [21, 52]. This shift in activation towards hyperpolarized values has been suggested to separate the working range of rapid anion channels and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ efflux channels,such that rapid anion channels cause membrane depolarization rather than salt (KCl) efflux [21]. On the other hand, if rapid anion channels are not completely closed at the anion equilibrium potential,activation of large rapid anion currents would depolarize the membrane towards the anion equilibrium potential, rather than towards the peak anion current potential.Therefore the auxin-induced depolarization could lie positive of the $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ equilibrium potential and cause transient salt efflux. The linking of auxin-induced depolarization and stomatal opening which requires hyperpolarization points to a yet uncharacterized role for rapid anion channels in signal transduction.Conversely,the low specificity by which several acidic compounds modulate rapid anion channels [13,22] has led other researchers [43] to question the hypothesis that rapid anion channels are a physiological target of auxin. The complete and effective DIDS block of rapid anion channels [23] would provide an approach for determining the importance of rapid anion channels during auxin action. For example, 1 mM DIDS has no effect on lightmediated stomatal opening indicating that activation of rapid anion channels is not required for the stimulation of light-specific stomatal opening [38].


## Malate and $\mathbf { C O _ { 2 } }$ sensing?


When the extracellular side of the plasma membrane of guard cells is exposed to malate, the amplitude of rapid anion currents increases while voltage-activation shifts towards hyperpolarized potentials[13],a behavior also reported for auxin action [21]. The increase in current amplitude in the presence of the extracellular effector appears to be a consequence of channel openings at a voltage range of higher driving force for anion release.

Plants which undergo various distinct forms of photosynthetic metabolism show different patterns in their organic assimilation products. Malate concentrations, malate transport and the cellular and subcellular compartmentation of malate are related to the metabolic activity of different cell types. Stomatal closing during an increase in $\mathbf { C O } _ { 2 }$ has been proposed to result from malate released from mesophyll cells lying adjacent to guard cells [13]. However, the large extracellular malate concentrations required to achieve partial stomatal closing are $4 0 \mathrm { m M }$ malate in Vicia faba,Commelina communis and Arabidopsis thaliana with a half-maximal response at ca. $1 7 \mathrm { m M }$ malate in Vicia faba ([f 36], Y.Liao, S.Lindstrom,J. Scheaffer, J. Esser,and J.I. Schroeder,unpublished). The consistently observed requirement of high malate concentrations for induction of stomatal closing in different species in over 50 experiments in the author's laboratory leads us to an alternative suggestion: effluxing malate from guard cells via anion channels [28] may provide a positive feedback mechanism during stomatal closing rather than an initial signal for stomatal closing. Therefore, the revealed malate-sensitivity of anion channels [13] may provide a feedback mechanism for control or modulation water-use efficiency of plants. Furthermore malate stimulation of stomatal closing provides a consistent and useful tool for analyzing guard cell signal transduction mechanisms [36].

The anionic composition of the extracellular space surrounding guard cells contains chloride and malate [6, 20,48].During stomatal action the extracellular salt content can vary considerably [6,27].A rise in the extracellular chloride concentration of guard cells produces an increase in the single-channel conductance of anion channels from ca. 0 to $6 0 { \mathfrak { p } } { \mathfrak { s } }$ [13] with half-maximal saturation at ca. $2 \mathrm { m M }$ chloride.This ‘anion feedback’on rapid anion channels could provide a mechanism to maintain anion fluxes even during the decay of the anion gradient before stomatal apertures reach their final closing position [13].


## Anion channel blockers strongly affect stomatal regulation


Several potent blockers of both rapid and slow anion channels have been described [22,23,36, 37]. Blocker concentrations of chemically distinct compounds causing inhibition of $50 \%$ of S-type or R-type anion channels currents were:

Note that the most significant difference when comparing both anion channels is the $> 1 0 0 0 -$ fold lower sensitivity of S-type anion channels to DIDS for inhibiting anion efflux [36]. Simultaneous exposure of guard cells of Vicia faba to both abscisic acid and malate effectively closes stomatal pores [36]. DIDS, a potent and complete blocker of rapid anion channels $( K _ { \mathrm { i } } { = } 0 . 2 \mu \mathbf { M } )$ [23] does not markedly affect stomatal closure by ABA and malate at concentrations of $1 0 0 \mu \mathbf { M }$ and $1 \mathrm { m M }$ DIDS [36]. These data suggest that the hypothesis that rapid anon channels are the central mediator of stomatal closing[14, 17] does not apply to the combined ABA and malate stimuli. On the other hand, simultaneous block of both slow and rapid anion channels by the benzoic acid derivative,NPPB,completely abolished ABA- and malate-induced stomatal closing, supporting a central rate-limiting role for S-type anion channels in the mediation of stomatal closing [36]. Furthermore, the concentration dependencies of S-type anion channel block by individual blockers are consistent with blocker concentrations which influence stomatal movements [36, 37]. These investigations do however not exclude a secondary contribution of rapid anion channels to stomatal regulation [36] because these blockers also inhibit rapid anion channels [22].

Interestingly,anion channels appear to not only stimulate stomatal closing but to also participate in regulation of stomatal opening. Slow anion channel blockers enhance stomatal opening [36] and partially reverse ABA inhibition of stomatal opening [37]. It appears that partial inhibition of proton pumps and ${ \mathbf { K } } ^ { + }$ uptake channels after ABA exposure is made more effective by block of anion channels. These data show that the downregulation of proton pumps and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake channels by ABA, are not complete and suggest that additional anion channel activation may be required to fully account for ABA-induced inhibition of stomatal opening [37]. Furthermore, these data indicate indirectly that down-regulation of slow anion channels may be important during light-mediated stomatal opening. Further assays using various physiological stimuli, should enable detailed determination of the roles of both S-type and R-type anion currents during stomatal regulation.One interesting observation is that anion channel blockers as well as anion channel activators appear to influence stomatal regulation much more strongly and reproducibly than $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channel blockers,highlighting the rate-limiting role of anion channels for stomatal regulation.


## Rapid and slow anion channels appear to share protein constituents


The time and voltage dependencies of slow and rapid anion channels in guard cells differ strongly from one another [14,31，34].Furthermore, patch-clamp studies on the mode of action of extracellular auxin, the metabolite malate,and anion channel blockers revealed a common feature of these anionic compounds with respect to their ability to alter the voltage sensor of R-type anion channels [14,21,22]. The same blockers applied to slow anion channels show differing effects on voltage- and time-dependent regulation [34],when compared to rapid anion channels [22,23]. Despite these significant and in some cases extraordinary differences in anion channel properties and physiological functions of slow [19,31,34,36] and rapid [14,17,23] anion channels, recent studies suggest that both anion currents may be carried by shared protein subunits [36,52]. For example,when these anion currents were revealed to occur simultaneously in the same cell, apparent transitions among anion conducting states could be observed (see Fig. 1c in [34]). Furthermore,both anion channel types show similar affinities to the blockers IAA-94 and NPPB and similar single-channel conductances of a main conductance state (ca. 35 pS) [13,17, 19,28, 36]. Note however that slow anion channels have multiple single-channel conductance states with an apparent cooperativity among states [28].

The most compelling evidence that slow and rapid anion channels may share structural components was obtained in tobacco protoplasts. In tobacco protoplasts a transition among wholecell anion current types between a rapid and a slow mode is regulated by the ATP content in the cytosol [52]. In single channel recordings transitions from the ‘flickery' openings of putative rapid anion channels to the long openings of slow anion channels have been reported in guard cells [28]. In spite of the observed direct transitions among gating modes of single channels a detailed statistical analysis would be required to further test whether the same channel proteins may contribute to both slow and rapid anion channel types. Biochemical or molecular biological analysis should allow unequivocal analysis of the suggestion that subunits are shared by both channels [36,52]. Preliminary biochemical studies using oxyacetic acid derivative blockers of guard cell anion channels and antibodies to animal Clchannels indicate a binding protein in guard cell plasma membrane fractions [22]. The extraordinary shift of multiple properties of higher-plant anion channels would suggest large conformational changes.Additional subunits may be one possible mechanism for the proposed extreme mode shifts [36, 52]. Analysis of the molecular structure of plant cell anion channels should provide further insight into the molecular basis and the physiology of anion current modulation.


## Putative anion channel functions in roots


Recent studies have shown that different types of anion channels may exist in root cortical and root xylem parenchyma cells [39,50]. In contrast to anion efflux channels in guard cells,a major type of anion channel in root cortical cells allows anion influx [39]. These root anion channels are activated by membrane depolarization and also by extracellular $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ . The enhancement of root anion channel activity by extracellular $\mathbf { C l } ^ { - }$ , and an apparent $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activation, have led to the hypothesis that these anion channels may be important for membrane potential regulation and $\mathbf { C l } ^ { - }$ uptake in response to salt $\mathbf { ( N a C l ) }$ stress [39].

A different type of anion channel was described in root xylem parenchyma cells which allows anion eflux [50]. Xylem parenchyma anion channels showed properties very similar to slow anion channel in guard cells. Therefore these anion channels have been proposed to function during initial phases of xylem loading which requires eflux of solutes from xylem parenchyma cells [50].It is likely that, similar to guard cells,solute unloading of xylem parenchyma cells requires membrane depolarization,which could be mediated by these anion channels.It should be noted however that only a few single slow anion channels were observed in whole-cell recordings from xylem parenchyma cells.Whole-cell recordings showing conditions which give rise to larger anion currents would be required to postulate a significant contribution of these slow anion channels to putative plant physiological functions.

Recent studies indicate an additional potentially important role for root anion efflux channels in aluminum tolerance.Aluminum is the third most abundant compound in the outer lithosphere of the earth [12]. Under acidic soil conditions, ${ \bf A l } ^ { 3 + }$ dissociates and becomes toxic to plants. A recent groundbreaking comparative study of ${ \bf A } ^ { 1 ^ { 3 + } }$ -sensitive and ${ \bf A } ^ { 3 + }$ -tolerant cultivar in wheat has shown that the ${ \bf A } ^ { 3 + }$ -tolerant cultivars extruded significant levels of malate into the cell wall space of roots while ${ \bf A } | ^ { 3 + }$ -sensitive cultivars secrete less malate [8]. Secreted malate can function as a potent chelator and detoxifier of ${ \bf A } ^ { 1 ^ { 3 + } }$ The finding that guard cell anion channels allow malate efflux [28] implicates anion channels as a possible pathway for controlling and mediating malate secretion. Because a major type of anion channel in root allows mainly anion influx [39] the question remains whether root anion channels can also permit malate efflux.Further research on root anion channels will be necessary to determine their functions in higher-plant root physiology and plant soil interactions.

Salinity is one of the most important environmental constraints affecting more than 800 million ha of arable land (Munns and Tester 2008). Salinity limits plant growth and causes significant losses of crop yield. Plants have evolved several mechanisms to cope with salt stress, the most important of which are $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tissue tolerance, and osmotic tolerance. One key mechanism of salinity tolerance is the ability to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the cytosol and its sequestration into the vacuole to limit cell damage. The transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles is thought to be mediated by vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family, which are driven by the electrochemical gradient of protons (Gaxiola et al. 1999; Pardo et al. 2006). The proton motive force used by vacuolar antiporters is generated by the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -translocating enzymes in the tonoplast, which are V-ATPase and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -inorganic pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ~ H ^ { + } }$ -PPiase). The $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase is a single subunit protein located in the vacuolar membrane (Maeshima 2000). It pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ from the cytoplasm into vacuoles with PPi-dependant $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport activity. Zhen et al. (1997) demonstrated that the Arabidopsis $\mathbf { A } t A V P I$ generated a proton gradient across the vacuolar membrane similar in magnitude to that of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase.

The over-expression of AtNHX1, or its homologs from other plant species, has resulted in enhanced plant tolerance not only to salt, but also to drought stress (Apse et al. 1999; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Xue et al. 2004; He et al. 2005; Brini et al. 2007; Chen et al. 2007; Khoudi et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010a). Similarly, the over-expression of AtAVP1 or its homologs in transgenic plants resulted in both drought and salt tolerance (Gaxiola et al. 2001). Interestingly, the enhanced salt tolerance in transgenic plants, over-expressing the AtAVP1 gene, was correlated with the increased ion content. These results suggest that the enhanced vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumping in transgenic plants was responsible for additional energy to support vacuolar sodium accumulation mediated by the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. In line with these results, Duan et al. (2007) demonstrated that the over-expression of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase resulted in an enhanced proton electrochemical gradient across the vacuolar membrane which accelerated the sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole and improved salinity tolerance at cellular level. Thus, it was predicted that co-expression of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase would confer better salt tolerance to transgenic plants than that of the single gene expression. Indeed, Zhao et al. (2006) provided experimental evidence that co-expression of SsNHX1 and AtAVP1 in transgenic rice conferred greater salt tolerance than that of the single SsNHX1. On the other hand, Qiu et al. (2007) reported that the coordinate expression of V-ATPase and vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter was essential for Suaeda salsa salt tolerance.

Salt stress tolerance is a complex trait (Flowers 2004); therefore, better tolerance to salinity might be achieved by pyramiding several genes into a single genotype (Samis et al. 2001). The success of this approach was demonstrated in the above-mentioned examples for pyramiding $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and one of the vacuolar translocating enzymes $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase or $\mathrm { V { - } H ^ { + } A T P a s e ) }$ ). It was also used for stacking various combinations of genes involved in drought and salt stress tolerance (Singla-Pareek et al. 2003; Zhou et al. 2008; Wei et al. 2011). To engineer plants with multiple genes, Schmidt et al. (2008) described several approaches. For example, plants are individually transformed and then crossed together. This method complicates the downstream breeding due to the size of the segregation population needed to obtain all the transgenes in one individual. An alternative approach consists of performing repeated plant transformation with successive transgenes to obtain multi-gene phenotypes. However, this approach is costly, time consuming, and it needs several selectable marker genes to perform the various selection rounds. One practical solution to overcome these limitations is to physically link multiple gene expression cassettes by positioning them contiguously on DNA that will transfer as single entity (Shibata and Liu 2000). This strategy has been used with great success to stack traits in commercial GM crops.

Soil salinity is one of the major threats to agricultural land that restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops (Flowers 1998). High salinity leads to cytosolic osmotic stress and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion specific toxicity in plants while over accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the cytosol causes inhibitory effects on many developmental processes such as protein synthesis, enzymatic reactions and photosynthesis (Murguia et al. 1995; Tsugane et al. 1999). However higher plants have developed multiple mechanisms through evaluation and adaptation involving morphological, physiological, biochemical and molecular responses to survive the harsh abiotic stress conditions (Hirayama and Shinozaki 2010; Krasensky and Jonak 2012). Salinity and drought may influence the plant growth and productivity in various ways. However, the major cause of damage is the excessive toxic accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and the loss of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the cytoplasm (Ali et al. 2016). To cope with such crucial saline conditions and maintain $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis, plant uses a number of transporters that protect them against $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions stress. This cation and $\mathrm { p H }$ homoeostasis is thought to be regulated by monovalent cation/proton antiporters (CPA) by exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ , or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ (Brett et al. 2005a). Prokaryotic and eukaryotic CPA members fall into two major super families designated as CPA1 (2.A.36) and CPA2 (2.A.37) (Brett et al. 2005a). In plants, the CPA1 family includes the well-studied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (NHX), while CPA2 family includes cation/ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchangers (CHX) and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux antiporter (KEA).

The model plant Arabidopsis contains total eight NHX members belonging to three different classes, six intracellular (IC) transporters that are categorized as either localized at tonoplast vacuoles (IC-I), or endosome (IC-II). The IC-I family includes AtNHX1-4, which are plant specific, while IC-II clade includes AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 that are similar to ScNHX1 (yeast) and human isoforms NHE6 and NHE7 (Bowers et al. 2000; Brett et al. 2005a; Chanroj et al. 2012). Two divergent members of the CPA1 family, AtNHX7/SOS1 and AtNHX8, are located at the plasma membrane. Some of these antiporters extrude toxic amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cell (SOS1/NHX7), while other NHX family members regulate cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ by sequestering them in vacuoles inside plant cells (Apse et al. 1999; Barragan et al. 2012).

Beside antiporters another class of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters is the HKT-type transporters (initially defined as high-affinity potassium transporters) that are divided into two subclasses on the basis of their transport properties and amino acid sequences (Platten et al. 2006). Subclass I transporters (ie.,

HKT1) have a serine (S) residue forming S-G-G-G motif while subclass II (ie., HKT2) type transporters have a glycine (G) residue replacing serine (S) in subclass I transporters and thereby contain a G-G-G-G motif (Maser et al. 2002). The presence of either serine (S) or glycine (G) contributes towards the specificity of transporter toward cations selection (Platten et al. 2006). Members of subclass I have strong affinity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ only, while those belonging to subclass II transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depending on the concentration of the two cations (Maser et al. 2002; Platten et al. 2006; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). HKT1-type transporters are believed to retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from xylem stream to protect shoots from $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, retain it in the root and thereby contribute mainly in reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion toxicity in plants (Rubio et al. 1995; Rus et al. 2001, 2006).

Previous studies on vacuolar compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plants are also shown to regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, mediated by tonoplast localized cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters (NHXs). For this process tonoplast $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase) and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } .$ pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ( H ^ { + } }$ -PPase) provide the proton motive force required for NHX function (Apse et al. 1999; Gaxiola et al. 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). In many transgenic plants the overexpression of tonoplast NHXs have enhanced resistance to salt and drought stress with increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles (Apse et al. 1999; Brini et al. 2007; Galvez et al. 2012; He et al. 2005; Jha et al. 2013; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Zhang et al. 2001), thought there are exceptions to this rule (Leidi et al. 2010; Jiang et al. 2010). The class-I NHX family proteins localized in tonoplast function as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, that are involved in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration inside the vacuoles maintaining turgor pressure and drive cell expansion. Recently, the two Arabidopsis vacuole localized homologous NHX proteins, NHX1 and NHX2 in Arabidopsis are shown to redundantly regulating the accurate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in vacuoles (Barragan et al. 2012; Bassil et al. 2011).


## Role of NHX Protein in Plant Growth and Development


Besides the prominent role of NHX proteins in salt and drought resistance in plants, recent advances have shown a series of other novel functions of these proteins including intracellular ions and pH homeostasis, turgor and osmotic regulation, stomatal movement, water uptake, cell expansion and regulation of flowering time (Andres et al. 2014; Bassil and Blumwald 2014; Bassil et al. 2011; Barragan et al. 2012; Pittman 2012; Reguera et al. 2014).

Ionic homeostasis and pH regulation are essential cellular processes necessary for plant growth and development especially during undesirable environmental conditions. The primary action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pumps regulates the cytoplasmic pH, while the

NHX proteins are $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters localized to the plasma membrane and tonoplast that facilitate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and constitute a proton leak thereby maintaining both $\mathrm { p H }$ and ions homeostasis (Rodríguez-Rosales et al. 2009). The best studied example of $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation is the Japanese morning glory (Ipomoea nil) InNHX2 which promotes the vacuolar alkalization in petals that converts the reddish-purple buds into purple flower by increasing the vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ (Ohnishi et al. 2005). Recently the reverse genetic approach has shown that AtNHX1 and AtNHX2 are $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and are required for active $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake (Fig. 1), osmotic and turgor regulation and playing a unique role in cell expansion and stomatal function by sustaining the intracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). In this review we want to highlight the recent advances in ion homeostasis and evidences existing for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and lacking rather than for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in plants by NHX-exchangers, which regulates a diverse set of functions and enzymatic reactions important for survival and growth of plants.


## $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and Signaling Mechanism


The action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ at the plasma membrane creates an electrical potential across the plasma membrane and increases the negative charge inside the cells promoting the passive influx of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions, while the efflux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (i.e., removal from cell) is not a passive process but needs the expenditure of energy (Maathuis et al. 2014). In high salinity the family of NonSelective Cation Channels (NSCCs family) is thought to mediate the spontaneous transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the root cells across the plasma membrane but until now the exact molecular mechanism is unknown (Kronzucker and Britto 2011). Beside NSCC family transporters, the transpirational bypass of water and solutes $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ across the apoplast has an important role in some plant species, such as rice, in which this non-selective pathway is the major port of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ entry and transport across the xylem without crossing the plasma membrane. In most species the casparian strip and suberine layers in plant roots endodermal and exo-dermal layers provide barriers to the apoplast flow (Yeo et al. 1987; Ochiai and Matoh 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ taken up by plant roots is transported to the shoot part in xylem by bulk flow that is driven by the tension in xylem causing continuous movement of water and solute (i.e., $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) from roots to shoot by transpiration (Almeida et al. 2016; Nobel 2009).

Potassium is one of major essential macronutrients which is required for several key biological functions in plants, like enzyme activation, osmotic and turgor generation, opening and closing of stomatal aperture, cytosolic pH regulation and membrane electric potential. The uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by plant roots is thought to be regulated by two independent transport systems with different kinetic parameters and selectivity (Epstein et al. 1963). The saturable system1 is constituted by the high affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake permeases HAK/KUP that operate in the micromolar range and transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the cytoplasm of the root cells against electrochemical gradient (SantaMarıa et al. 1997; Gierth et al. 2005). System 2 or the low affinity pathway, including channels of shaker family, has the characteristic of channel mediated the transport and uptake of external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at concentration of above 0.5 to $1 \mathrm { m M }$ with plasma membrane potential of -120 to $- 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m V } .$ The first isolated plasma membrane $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and AKT1 (hyperpolarization-activated inward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel) and the carrier-type HUP/HAK/KT transporter HAK5 in Arabidopsis displayed $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in heterologous system (Schachtman et al. 1992; Bertl et al. 1995; Gaymard et al. 1998a) indicated that these channels probably function in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake pathway in guard cells for KAT1 and in the root cells in case of AKT1 (Nakamura et al. 1995; Lagarde et al. 1996). Membrane depolarization by excessive cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx have a strong inhibitory effect on transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions into the plant root cells by inhibiting the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005), and increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux by depolarization-activated outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (eg, GORK) and NSSC as well (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005; Sun et al. 2009). Once $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is captured, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is further transported into the vacuole against the electrochemical gradient of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family energized by the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient across the tonoplast (Walker et al. 1996; Carden et al. 2003; Barragan et al. 2012).

Not much is known about how $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are sensed in most of root cellular systems in plants. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ can either be sensed outside, inside of the cell or both. In the case of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { , } }$ , the extracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by plant through membrane receptors in roots, while intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by membrane protein or other cytoplasmic enzymes (Tracy et al. 2008). From recent advances it is thought that the long cytoplasmic tail of plasma membrane localized antiporter SOS1 (SALT OVERLY SENSITIVE1; NHX7) might be responsible for intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sensing (Shi et al. 2000). However, the plasma membrane localized $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase can directly sense the changes in extracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration which led to the proposal that the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters might be the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sensors in plants.

In plants calcium signaling acts as a second messenger connecting various environmental stresses with intracellular responses including nutrient deficiency. Extracellular salt stress $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) transiently increase the free cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ by depolarization- and hyperpolarization-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels and by ROS-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels at the plasma membrane (Tracy et al. 2008). ROS accumulation is also strongly induced by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -starvation in Arabidopsis root cells (Shin and Schachtman, 2004; Shin et al. 2005). Cytosolic calcium elevation can also stimulate NADPH-oxidase mediating ROS-production (Yang and Poovaiah 2002). The increase in ROS further increase $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ influx by decoding $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensor such as Calmodulin (CaM), Calcinurin B-like proteins (CBLs) and CBL-interacting protein kinases (CIPKs), Forming CBL-CIPK complexes and are designated as calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) (Yang and Poovaiah 2003). Intracellular cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensors trigger various signal transduction pathways that are involved in regulation of ion channels activities (e, g., external $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ strongly blocked NSCC), enzymatic reactions, gene transcription and regulation of ion homeostasis (Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Martínez-Atienza et al. 2007; Adams and Shin 2014).


## Discovery and Localization of Arabidopsis NHX Exchangers


One of the predominant strategies that plant cells employ for the sequestration of toxic cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is to compartmentalize it in vacuoles, and NHX-type intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter have appeared to be well characterized transport proteins involved in this process so far (Apse 2003). Sequencing comparison of the yeast genome uncovered a novel gene present on chromosome IV (YDR456w), which encodes a protein of 633 aa, was named as NHX1 on the basis of sequence homology with the family of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHE1–4), that is found in mammals and other vertebrates, as well as in nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans), and euryhaline crab (Carcinusmaenas). Disruption of NHX1 gene led to a significant decrease in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance at $\mathrm { p H } 4$ or 5, indicating its prominent role in mediating tolerance to stress at acidic $\mathrm { p H }$ (Nass et al. 1997). The discovery of vacuolar NHX1, and its homologous protein in Arabidopsis, opened a new concept of intracellular compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions in plants (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000). AtNHX1 can functionally substitute for the endosomal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (ScNHX1) that requires ATPase activity of endosomal/vacuolar V-type ATPase to mediate ions compartmentalization in yeast vacuole (Quintero et al. 2000). Based on protein similarity of predicted amino acid sequence to AtNHX1, six AtNHX gene family members were categorized in Arabidopsis. These NHX $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene family members were named as AtNHX1-6 in order of decreasing phylogenetic relationship to the prototype of AtNHX1. AtNHX2-4 has $5 6 . 0 { - } 8 7 . 5 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1 whereas AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 has $8 7 . 7 \%$ similarity to each other’s and has $2 1 - 2 3 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1-4 isoforms in Arabidopsis (Yokoi et al. 2002). Maser et al. (2001) further expanded the NHX family to include the plasma membrane isoforms NHX7/SOS1 and NHX8.

Northern blot analysis using total RNA from seedlings of Col-0 indicated that AtNHX1 and 2 transcripts were highly abundant in shoots and roots. The transcript of AtNHX3 was highly abundant only in roots, and a low transcript level of AtNHX5 mRNA was detected in roots and shoots. While AtNHX4 and AtNHX6 transcript were not detectable on northern blot, they were detected in roots and shoots using RT-PCR. These findings established that all six genes of AtNHX are transcriptionally active in seedlings, indicating that their function is not only restricted to the later developmental stages (Yokoi et al. 2002).


## Sodium Exclusion and Tissue Tolerance


Soil salinity (mainly NaCl) restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops more than any other toxic substance in soil. By restricting the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx inside the cells can improve the plant growth and survival in saline stress, however, very little is known about the mechanism to inhibit the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx. On the other hand, to tolerate the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the soil plant cell must be capable of either export $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell or sequester it into the vacuoles to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity inside the cell (Xu et al. 2013). The $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ exclusion process energized by the plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ATPase is mainly carried out by the plasma membrane localized SOS1 (AtNHX7) in Arabidopsis, with its interacting component SOS3 (CBL4) and SOS2 kinase (CIPK24) in a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ dependent manner (Shi et al. 2000; Quintero et al. 2002; Qiu et al. 2002). But the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion by this process to outside medium can further increase the imbalance of osmotic and ionic stress across the membrane, therefore this kind of strategy is useful only for temporary resistance and cannot confers long term salt tolerance in the natural environmental conditions (Adem et al. 2014).

Beside the extrusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell, plants have the ability to safely handle large amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in tissues without any deleterious effect on plant metabolism. Such kind of tissues tolerance is mainly achieved by efficient $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles, thereby reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in the cytosol.


## NHX Proteins are Required for Accurate Potassium $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ Compartmentation in Vacuoles


Potassium is the most vital ionic osmoticum in plant cells that is largely distributed in two major pools, cytosol and vacuoles. Cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is an essential activator for many biochemical and enzymatic reactions, cytosolic $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation and plasma membrane electric potential (Fig. 2), requiring the maintenance of basic cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration within the narrow limit of 75 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ regardless of changes in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply (Walker et al. 1996). However, vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pools which is the largest and most dynamic reservoir of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depends on the availability of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . The lowest limit of vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration appears to be 10 to $2 0 \mathrm { m M }$ . The concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inside the plant cell vacuoles requires the active transport from cytosol which could be achieved through nonelecterogenic $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Walker et al. 1996). Biochemical analysis has proved that tonoplast localized NHX exchangers (NHX1 and NHX2) catalyze the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange with an apparent affinity of 12 to $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , which is below the lower cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration limit, and thus are able to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from cytosol to vacuoles (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; ernandez et al. 2009; Barragan et al. 2012). Different evidences have indicated that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (NHX)–type transporters could achieve the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in plant cells (Venema et al. 2002; Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Yoshida et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010; Leidi et al. 2010). So far six NHX genes (NHX1-6) encoding endosomal antiporters have been identified in Arabidopsis genome (Yokoi et al. 2002). RNA gel blot analysis and RT-PCR quantification showed the increased relative abundance of NHX1 and NHX2 transcript level in all the plant tissues which were accumulated in response to the same effectors (NaCl, KCl, LiCl, osmotic stress, and abscisic acid) (Yokoi et al. 2002).

Among all the Arabidopsis NHX transporters, NHX1 and NHX2 are the most closely related NHX family members at protein level $( 8 7 . 5 \%$ sequence identity) and both are localized in the tonoplast (Yokoi et al. 2002; Bassil et al. 2011b). AtNHX1 has been previously shown to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity with similar affinity (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Hernandez et al. 2009). The $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity in tonoplast of WT and nhx1 nhx2 double mutant by $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient created by V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase at $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ and KCl shows less than one-third of total exchange activity in nhx1 nhx2 than WT, demonstrating the combined contribution of NHX1 and NHX2 to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in total cation exchange capacity at tonoplast (Barragan et al. 2012). Research in transgenic tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) indicated that overexpressing vacuolar AtNHX1 or the endosomal LeNHX2 $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter leads to enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation

in cell vacuoles (Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al.   
2010).


## NHX1 and NHX2 Preferentially Regulates ${ { \bf K } } ^ { + }$ Homeostasis as Compared to $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$


The discovery of vacuolar NHX antiporters which mediate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ across the vacuolar membrane in saline environment (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000), was recently challenged on the basis of biochemistry of NHX-proteins, which do not differentiate between $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or even having stronger affinity for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport as compared with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; RodrıguezRosales et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010). Recent reports have conclusively demonstrated that vacuolar proteins NHX1 and NHX2 of Arabidopsis preferentially mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration as compared to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). Since the AtNHX1 protein regulates vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ level and $\mathrm { p H }$ to control cell expansion and tissue elongation, overexpression of AtNHX1 in transgenic tomato increased the vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration while depleting cytosolic ${ \mathrm { K } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { p o o l } }$ up regulation of HAK5 and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake was increased as compared to WT (Leidi et al. 2010). Notably, the double mutant nhx1 nhx2 of Arabidopsis is more sensitive to moderate KCl stress (10 to $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ concentration) but did not show much greater sensitivity to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ as compared with the WT (Barragan et al. 2012). Remarkably, the nhx1 nhx2 mutant accumulated larger amounts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ upon salt treatment treatment and moderate amounts of NaCl improved the growth of the mutant plant. These results signify that tonoplast NHX proteins are dispensable for the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and that this ion can substitute as osmoticum for the otherwise reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pool in vacuoles of the nhx1 nhx2 mutant (Barragan et al. 2012). These results have raised many questions on how exactly $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is compartmentalized if vacuolar NHX-proteins are specific only for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration, as nhx1nhx2 mutants accumulates more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the plant shoots as compared to WT. It is now clear that in Arabidopsis the ion exchangers other than NHX1 and NHX2 may mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration (Barragan et al. 2012).


## Predominant Role of NHX Proteins in Stomata and Cell Expansion


In early 1970’s, it was proved that potassium has a vital role in regulation of stomata movements. However, with recent research advances the role of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in stomata and guard cell regulation is explained in more detail (Humble et al. 1971; Talbott et al. 1996; Cochrane TT and Cochrane TA 2008). The main solute in osmo-regulation of guard cells are $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , sucrose, and the anions malate and chloride. Guard cells store $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ salts in large quantities which is a cheap and highly mobile solute that regulates opening of stomata (MacRobbie 2006). In Arabidopsis’s guards cells the strong $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fluxes mediates by channels sustain the stomatal movement, i,e opening of stomata is mainly driven by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry through $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2, whereas stomatal closing is facilitated by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux through outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels activated by membrane depolarization (Ache et al. 2000). However, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ must be further routed to the vacuole while keeping the cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at homeostatic values. NHX1 and NHX2 have shown an extensive overlapping expression and subcellular localization pattern including guard cells and other organs, and they share with similar transport properties (Barragan et al. 2012). The best studied example for the role NHX-proteins in stomata is the inactivation of NHX1 and NHX2 genes (nhx1 nhx2) which reduce the total $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ contents in the leaf guard’s cells, with stunted stomata development and function (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). The double mutant of nhx1nhx2 results in wrinkled shaped and thinner stomata as compared with WT. This also explains the role of NHX-proteins in cell expansion. However, the stomata in nhx1nhx2 mutant is not completely dysfunctional but rather exhibit delayed stomatal closure, leaf turgor loss and reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration in guard cells vacuoles as compared with WT (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). Delayed stomata closure and leaf turgor loss was also observed in mutants of Snf1 Related Kinase, OST1 (OPEN STOMATA1) and SLOW EFFLUX ANION CHANNEL-ASSCIATED1. These proteins function as to regulate membrane depolarization of guard cells in response to ABA by releasing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and closing stomata (Ache et al. 2010).

The reduced cell expansion and tissue elongation in double mutant of nhx 1nhx2 was not only limited to the cells of leaves, but the hypocotyl of etiolated seedlings also displayed shorter length phenotype in nhx 1nhx2 mutants as compared to WT (Bassil et al. 2011b). This phenomenon was previously shown by (Apse et al. 2003) in nhx1 single knockout mutant mediating improper $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange and reduced cell expansion in normal physiological condition.
