In this study, we demonstrated that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 are involved in the uptake and translocation of metal ions in plants, and our results suggested that they might be associated with metal homeostasis by regulating the expression of genes involved in metal uptake and transportation.

It was reported that transgenic plants overexpressing OsIRT1 exhibited less chlorosis and had higher chlorophyll content than the wild-type under Fe-deficient conditions. Moreover, the Fe content was also increased in mature seeds of OsIRT1 overexpression plants [25]. In addition, overexpression of MxIRT1 enhanced Fe and Zn contents in rice seeds [41]. Likewise, overexpression of AtZIP1 in barley lead to an elevated level in the short-term Zn uptake, and enhanced Zn and Fe contents in seeds [24]. However, overexpression of OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 in rice leads to increased Zn levels in roots, although the Zn content was reduced in shoots and mature seeds of overexpression lines [29, 42]. These data suggested that the metal transportation activity of ZIP proteins may differ, or ectopic accumulation of ZIPs may disrupt the endogenous metal homeostasis due to incongruous in vivo ion transporter gradients. It was found that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 showed strongly and relatively weaker reverse the yeast complement activity. Moreover, the expression of ZmIRT1 was significantly upregulated in roots and shoots under Fe-deficiency, and it was induced in shoots at $9 6 \mathrm { { h } }$ after $\mathrm { Z n }$ -deficiency. These results suggested that ZmIRT1 might be essential for both uptake and translocation of Fe and Zn. On the contrary, ZmZIP3 was induced by Zn deficiency, indicating that ZmZIP3 may be important for Zn uptake [28]. In this study, we examined the expression pattern of ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 in various organs. ZmIRT1 was predominantly expressed in silk and embryo, while ZmZIP3 is a leaf-specific gene. The different expression pattern of ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 indicated that they might play distinct roles in metal uptake and translocation. To analyse the physiological roles of the ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 in plants, we generated transgenic Arabidopsis and examined whether ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 could transport Zn or Fe in plants. It was found that overexpression of ZmIRT1 in Arabidopsis enhanced Fe and Zn contents in both roots and seeds (Fig 4A and 4E), suggesting that ZmIRT1 is a functional Fe and Zn transporter, and it may be associated with the translocation of metals toward seeds. Additionally, we found that ZmIRT1-overexpressing plants grew longer roots than the wild-type under Zn- and Fe-excess conditions (Fig 2E and 2G), which indicates that the transgenic plants are more tolerant to excess zinc and iron. ZmIRT1 is localized to the plasma membrane and endoplasmic reticulum in maize (S1 Fig) and Arabidopsis mesophyll protoplasts [28]. Therefore, ZmIRT1 may function in translocating excess subcellular free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ into the endoplasmic reticulum. Moreover, ZmIRT1 may play an essential role in storage and detoxification of Zn and Fe. On the contrary, ZmZIP3-overexpression plants developed more lateral roots and longer roots than wild-type under Fe-deficient conditions (Fig 3F), indicative of a stronger Fe deficiency

It is noteworthy that the growth of ZmZIP3 transgenic plants was better than the wild-type, despite the Fe-deficiency response in roots (Fig 3F). Besides the morphological changes, the expression of many genes associated with Fe/Zn deficiency and excess responses were also altered in the ZmIRT1- and ZmZIP3-overexpressing plants. It was reported that the expression profiles of genes associated with Fe and Zn uptake and translocation were regulated in accordance with the internal and environmental metal conditions. OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 encode enzymes for the biosynthesis of NA and $2 ^ { \circ }$ -deoxymugineic acid (DMA), which plays important roles in chelating and distributing metal ions within plants. The expression of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 are enhanced in the overexpression lines under $\mathrm { Z n }$ -deficient conditions [29]. In addition, the activation of OsNAS3 resulted in increased Zn and Fe contents in rice grains, suggesting that OsNAS3 contributes to ion homeostasis [43]. In our study, the transcription levels of genes associated with $\mathrm { Z n / F e }$ uptake and transportation may reflect the endogenous metal status; thus, we investigated the expression of 12 Arabidopsis genes known to be involved in the homeostasis of Zn and Fe (Fig 7). The results showed that the expressions of genes involved in the uptake of Fe and Zn were altered in both ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 transgenic lines. The transcript levels of AtNAS1, 2, which are associated with NA synthesis, AtFRO2 that plays a role in ferric reduction, and AtIRT1 that is related to ferrous uptake were up-regulated in ZmIRT1-overexpressing plants (Fig 7). The enhanced expression of these genes may be due to the root absorbed too much iron that stimulated the expression of NAS, FRO and IRT1, which associated with iron uptake. In contrast, AtFRO2 and AtIRT1 were reduced in the ZmZIP3 transgenic lines (Fig 8), possibly due to the iron content was decreased so suppressed the expression of these genes. These results suggest that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 play different roles in metal homeostasis. The stimulation of these genes in ZmIRT1-overexpressing lines may be due to the increased expression of transcription factors that regulate ion homeostasis. It has been demonstrated that Fe homeostasis is controlled by conserved transcriptional networks in both grasses and non-grasses [44, 45]. Under Fe-deficiency, FIT (FER-like iron-deficiency-induced transcription factor) interacts with bHLH038 and bHLH039 to regulate the expression of IRT1 and FRO2 in Arabidopsis [37]. It was also reported that FIT, IRT1, FRO2, and BHLH100 are iron deficiency induced genes in roots [15]. Although there are no orthologs of FIT in rice, OsIRO2 is a regulator of the Fe deficiency-responsive gene, which is highly similar to bHLH38/39. OsIRO2 regulates the expression of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS translocation-related genes, with the exception of OsIRT1 [46]. Co-overexpression of FIT and bHLH38 or bHLH39 results in increased expression of NAS1 and NAS2, which enhanced NA accumulation and increased transport of Fe from roots to shoots [47]. We found that the expression of FIT was stimulated in the ZmIRT1 transgenic plants, indicating that a transcriptional cascade was activated as a result of ectopic accumulation of ZmIRT1. Besides, pleiotropic effects may also contribute to the activation of gene expression since a greater quantity of Fe and Zn was absorbed into the cytoplasm when ZmIRT1 was overexpressed. The expression of NRAMPs, YSLs, and endogenous ZIPs were suppressed in both ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 lines (Figs 7 and 8), suggesting that over-accumulation of ZIP proteins may inhibit the expression of endogenous genes that function in metal transportation. Taking this into consideration, our results suggested that overexpressing ZmIRT1 may facilitate Zn and Fe uptake by inducing genes associated with strategy I (ferric reduction and ferrous uptake) and strategy II (ion-chelator synthesis) iron uptake systems, although the expression of genes involved in intercellular ion transportation was suppressed.

Fe uptake mechanisms were classified into two strategies. Strategy I, a reduction-based strategy, is used by non-grasses such as Arabidopsis [44, 45]. It begins with acidification of the rhizosphere and increases the solubility of ferric in the soil [48–50]. The reduction of ferric irons then occurs on the membrane by a membrane-bound ferric-chelate reductase AtFRO2, and ferrous is taken into root epidermal cells by transmembrane transporters, such as AtIRT1 [21, 22]. On the contrary, strategy II, a chelation-based strategy is used by grasses such as barley, rice, and maize. Phytosiderophores are released into the rhizosphere to chelate ferric [51], and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS can be absorbed into root cells by YSLs [52, 53]. The main distinction between these two strategies is different oxidation and reduction forms of iron absorbed into the root cells, as non-grasses prefer ferrous and grasses absorb ferric. It is generally considered that the iron uptake mechanisms used by these two strategies do not overlap. The identification of two functional $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters, OsIRT1 and OsIRT2, indicates that strategy I may be used by

graminaceous plants [54, 55]. It was proposed that rice uses a combined strategy including strategy II and partial strategy I to uptake Fe from the soil. TOM1/OsZIFL4 and OsYSL15 were reported to be involved in the release of PS and uptake of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -PS as strategy II, while OsIRT1 translocated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ into root cells through strategy I. However, the genes responsible for acidification and ferric reduction seemed to be lost in the rice genome [54, 56, 57]. As a graminaceous plant, maize was considered to apply strategy II for Fe uptake. However, ZmIRT1 was identified as a functional $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in yeast and transgenic Arabidopsis. ZmIRT1 overexpression plants contain increased amounts of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe in roots and seeds (Fig 4A and 4E), as well as elevated Zn levels in seedlings (Figs 5 and 6). In addition, ZmZIP3-overexpressing transgenic plants accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots. These results indicated that ZmIRT1 and ZmZIP3 are functional ion transporters. Moreover, we identified putative FRO and AHA genes in the maize genome (data not shown) using the reported AtFRO and AtAHA ( $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase) as TBLASTN queries, and suggested that the ferric reducing and rhizosphere acidification capacities may be retained through evolution. Thus, further investigations are required to determine whether maize use strategy I as a complementary Fe uptake mechanism, and determine why it has been maintained during evolution.

This result suggested that the accumulation of IRT1 is influenced by post-transcriptional regulation [58]. In this study, the ZmIRT1-overexpressing Arabidopsis exhibited increased levels of zinc and iron in different tissues, and the transgenic plants showed an enhanced resistance against excess-iron and zinc. Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ are essential micronutrients that participate in physiological and biochemical processes and promote plant growth and development. $Z \mathrm { n }$ is involved in the synthesis of numerous enzymes, such as alcohol dehydrogenase, copper $( \mathrm { C u } ) – \mathrm { Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, and RNA polymerase. Therefore, Zn deficiency decreases the activity of these enzymes (Hacisalihoglu and Kochian 2003). Recently,

Fe has been used as a cofactor for integrating photosynthesis with various metabolic pathways and regulating gene expression (Imsande 2010). Fe deficiency can affect the growth and yield of fruit trees and other crops, and it affects photosynthesis rate, chlorophyll content, and catalase activity (Fornerginer et al. 2010; Rube´n et al. 2011).

The continuous discovery of metal ion transporters has laid the foundation for studies on factors involved in the absorption, intracellular transport, localization, and efflux of metal ions, such as P1B-type heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family, Zn- and Fe-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) family, normal resistancerelated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and the cation dissemination facilitator (CDF) family (Milner et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2017; Vigani et al. 2013). AtIRT1 was the first ZIP gene identified which is located on the root surface and induced by Fe deficiency in the root of Arabidopsis thaliana L. (Henriques et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a homolog of IRT1, plays a similarly crucial role in A. thaliana. However, under similar Fedeficient conditions, the expression of IRT2 is significantly lower than that of IRT1 (Vert et al. 2001). Their homolog IRT3, which is located in the plasma membrane, increases the uptake of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe to complement the function of both $\mathrm { Z n - }$ and Fe-uptake mutants (Lin et al. 2009). Complementation mutants or knockdown of ZIP1 and ZIP2 in A. thaliana showed that ZIP1 and ZIP2 are involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Mn uptake (Milner et al. 2013). In addition, functional analyses in maize (Zea mays L.) and rice indicated that ZIP3, ZIP4, ZIP5, and ZIP8 play important roles in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in the roots and shoots under Zn-deficient conditions (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, b). In A. thaliana, the function of ZIP9 is similar to that of ZIP12, being induced under $Z \mathbf { n }$ -limiting conditions (Talke et al. 2006; Wintz et al. 2003).

Te zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ -regulated/iron(Fe)-regulated transporterlike family proteins (ZIPs) are membrane-located proteins for cations transport (Eng et  al. 1998; Guerinot 2000). Tey have been found to exist broadly in prokaryotic cells, fungi, plants and mammalians. In plants, ZIPs have been identifed in both dicots and monocots, such as Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998; Milner et  al. 2013), rice (Chen et  al. 2008), maize (Li et  al. 2013), medicago (Lopez-Millan et al. 2004; Stephens et al. 2011) and barely (Tiong et al. 2015). Grotz et al. identifed fve ZIP genes (IRT1, ZIP1-4) in Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998), and later up to 11 ZIP genes from Arabidopsis were detected bioinformatically (Guerinot 2000). Roles of ZIP1-12 from Arabidopsis in Zn transport were explored experimentally (Milner et  al. 2013). More recently, 18 ZIPs from Arabidopsis and 16 ZIPs from rice were annotated (Ivanov and Bauer 2017).

In Arabidopsis and rice, only a small number of ZIPs have been examined for biological functions in plant till now. Arabidopsis IRT1 is a well-studied ZIP gene frst identifed as a crucial transporter for plant Fe uptake (Varotto et  al. 2002; Vert et  al. 2002). Arabidopsis IRT1 can be induced by iron defciency (Korshunova et  al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2002), and may play a role in Mn/ Zn transport as well (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et  al. 2002). Biological functions in $Z \mathrm { n } /$ Fe transport of AtIRT2 (Vert et al. 2001, 2009), AtZIP1/2 (Grotz et al. 1998; Wintz et al. 2003; Milner et al. 2013), OsIRT1 (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Ishimaru et  al. 2006; Bughio et  al. 2002) and OsZIP4/5/8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2008; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Yang et al. 2009) have also been examined in the past decade.

A few studies have also implied that ZIPs may be involved in Cd transport. Yeast cells expressing AtIRT1 showed increased Cd sensitivity (Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2001), and IRT1-dependent $\mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { M n } / Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake was inhibited by excess Cd (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). Te Arabidopsis IRT1 knock-out mutant irt1-1 exhibited reduced Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation (Vert et al. 2002; Fan et al. 2014), while overexpression of AtIRT1 increased Cd sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Connolly et  al. 2002). AtIRT2, phylogenetically similar to AtIRT1, increased Cd uptake when overexpressed in Arabidopsis (Vert et  al. 2009), though the yeast cells expressing AtIRT2 exhibited no altered Cd sensitivity (Vert et  al. 2001). In rice, expression of OsIRT1 and OsIRT2 made the cells more sensitive to Cd and increased Cd accumulation (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009). Nonetheless, we still know little about the roles of most of the ZIPs genes in Cd stress response in Arabidopsis and rice.

In this study, genome-wide ZIPs identifcation in Arabidopsis and rice was performed with rigorous evolutional analysis. A comparative examination of genomewide expression profle of ZIPs in Arabidopsis and rice in response to Cd stress were carried out. Teir role in Cd uptake of typical ZIPs responding to Cd stress was further tested by expressing them in yeast. As expected, most identifed ZIPs gene expression responded remarkably to Cd stress, while unexpectedly it was found that Arabidopsis and rice showed a distinct pattern in ZIPs genes expression profle. Tese results may help to elucidate the plants’ genetic basis for Cd translocation via a ZIPs-dependent pathway.

Iron is an essential micronutrient for virtually all organisms, but it is not readily available due to its low solubility. In plants, highly specialized systems have evolved in order to acquire iron from the soil. Recent advances have identiWed molecular components of the iron uptake system, both in graminaceous plants (Curie et al. 2001) and in nongraminaceous plants (Eide et al. 1996; Henriques et al. 2002; Robinson et al. 1999; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002).

In Arabidopsis thaliana, upon iron deWciency, expression of a set of genes encoding a proton ATPase, probably of the AHA family (Palmgren 2001), the ferric-chelate reductase FRO2 (Connolly et al. 2003; Robinson et al. 1999) and the metal transporter IRT1 (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2002, 2003) is induced in root epidermal cells. These proteins are responsible for the solubilization of iron through rhizosphere acidiWcation, its reduction from $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and subsequent $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake into the cytoplasm, respectively. Several families of putative iron transporters, including NRAMP, ZIP and YSL have been described in Arabidopsis (Curie and Briat 2003). Although the physiological role of YSL and NRAMP members is associated with distribution, partitioning and remobilization of iron in the plant, the ZIP founding member IRT1 is the only transporter involved in iron uptake (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004). IRT1 was Wrst identiWed through functional complementation of a yeast mutant defective in iron uptake (Eide et al. 1996). Characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis showed that this gene is highly induced by iron starvation in roots and speciWcally expressed in the epidermis and cortex (Eide et al. 1996; Vert et al. 2002). Moreover, the identiWcation of a knock-out mutant in the IRT1 gene, irt1-1, demonstrated that in low iron conditions, IRT1 is the main route of iron entry into the plant and mediates the accumulation of additional metal ions (Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1 in Arabidopsis, was previously shown by functional complementation of yeast metal transport mutants to be a transporter of iron and zinc (Vert et al. 2001). Like IRT1, IRT2 is expressed in the outer layers of the root and upregulated, although to a lesser extent than IRT1, by iron deWciency (Vert et al. 2001). Even though IRT2 was suggested to be involved in iron uptake from the soil (Vert et al. 2001), little is known about its biological function. A loss of function En transposon mutant, irt2-1, was isolated and shown to display a slightly reduced stature but no chlorotic phenotype (Varotto et al. 2002). However, transposon insertion in irt2-1 led to concomitant downregulation of the neighboring IRT1 gene, playing itself a major role in iron uptake (Vert et al. 2002), that may result from the loss of an enhancer function acting on both IRT genes (Varotto et al. 2002). Therefore, the analysis of irt2-1 greatly limits the conclusion on the biological role of IRT2.

The present study shows that IRT2 is an intracellular membrane protein whose role in the cellular response to iron deWciency is diVerent from the major root iron transporter IRT1. We propose that IRT1 may compartmentalize iron into vesicles, to prevent toxicity by excess free iron in the cytosol as a result of extracellular iron acquisition by the FRO2/IRT1 system.

Iron (Fe) is an essential element for plant growth since required for various cellular processes, such as respiration and photosynthesis. Although abundant in soils, Fe is often available in limited amounts to plants because it is mostly found in rather insoluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ complexes (Colombo et al. 2014; Palmer and Guerinot 2009). Therefore, plants have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to efciently take up iron from the soil. In non-graminaceous plants, including the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, iron uptake by root epidermal cells requires three successive steps (solubilization-reduction-transport) involving plasma membrane (PM) proteins. Under Fe defciency, the solubilization of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ complexes is mainly achieved by Arabidopsis plasma membrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase2 (AHA2)-mediated proton extrusion, which results in local rhizosphere acidifcation (Santi and Schmidt 2009). Solubilized $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ is then reduced to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ by the reductase Ferric Reduction Oxydase2 (FRO2) and ultimately transported into epidermal cells by the Iron Regulated Transporter1 (IRT1) protein (Palmer and Guerinot 2009; Thomine and Vert 2013; Jeong et al. 2017). Interestingly, AHA2, FRO2 and IRT1 gene expression is induced under iron defciency through the direct action of the same basic Helix-Loop-Helix (bHLH) transcription factor named FER-like Iron Defciency-Induced Transcription Factor (FIT) that can heterodimerize with other bHLH proteins (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004; Jakoby et al. 2004; Yuan et al. 2008; Sivitz et al. 2012). IRT1 is a major actor in the regulation of plant iron homeostasis, as attested by the severe chlorosis and lethality of an irt1-1 knockout mutant (Vert et al. 2002; Henriques et al. 2002). IRT1 is poorly selective and, in addition to iron, mediates the uptake of non-iron metals such as zinc, manganese, cobalt or cadmium that are toxic when present in excess in the plant (Eide et al. 1996; Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2002; Korshunova et al. 1999). Considering the crucial role of IRT1 in iron uptake, a great deal of attention was devoted to the mechanisms regulating IRT1 activity. The regulatory processes driving the delivery and removal of IRT1 from the cell surface emerge as crucial for metal homeostasis.  In this mini-review, we focus on the role of IRT1-interacting proteins in the control of IRT1 exit from the ER, its function at the cell surface, and its degradation, as well as highlight their contribution to plant metal homeostasis.


## Clues about the mechanisms of IRT1 secretion to the plasma membrane


In eukaryotic cells, proteins addressed to the cell surface are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and trafc along the secretory pathway. Membrane proteins are exported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus via vesicles coated with coat protein complex II (COPII) (Hanton et al. 2009; Takagi et al. 2013; Chung et al. 2016). Recruitment in COPII vesicles is mediated by physical interactions between subunits of COPII complex and cargo proteins that carry export signals, such as diacidic motifs corresponding to $\left( \mathrm { D / E } \right) \mathbf { x } ( \mathrm { D / E } )$ (Sieben et al. 2008; Zelazny et al. 2009; Sorieul et al. 2011). Recently, the COPII subunits SEC13a and SEC31b were identifed in Arabidopsis IRT1 interactome (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). This suggests that IRT1 exits the ER via the COPII machinery (Fig. 1), which is in line with a previous work proposing that IRT1 from Malus xiaojinesis is exported in COPII vesicles (Tan et al. 2018). Whether the interactions between Arabidopsis IRT1 and COPII components are direct remains to be and FRO2 are also found in EE/TGN, probably associated with IRT1. EHB1 protein can interact with and negatively regulate IRT1 at the PM. Although not indicated on the scheme, AHA2 and FRO2 can also be ubiquitinated, but the cellular outcome of such modifcations remains to be determined. When non-iron metal cations are abundant in the cytosol (right panel), they are directly sensed by IRT1. ## Endocytosis plays a major role in the regulation of IRT1


In the past decade, numerous studies highlighted the importance of endocytosis in the regulation of IRT1 and metal uptake in Arabidopsis. Early work showed that, under iron limitation and in presence of physiological amounts of non-iron metals, IRT1 cycles between early endosomes (EE)/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and the outer polar domain of the PM, in root epidermal cells (Fig. 1) (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011). A fraction of IRT1 also trafcs through the multivesicular bodies (MVB)/ late endosomes (LE) on the way to the lytic vacuole for constitutive degradation (Barberon et  al. 2011). IRT1 internalization from the PM is at least in part achieved by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and requires the mono-ubiquitination of lysine residues K154 and K179 that are located in the large cytosolic loop of IRT1. Indeed, IRT1 is stabilized at the PM when CME is impaired via the expression of a dominant-negative version of clathrin and when K154 and K179 are mutated (Kerkeb et al. 2008; Barberon et al. 2011, 2014). Importantly, neither ubiquitination nor CME are implicated in IRT1 polar localization. The role of CME in IRT1 internalization is strengthened by the fact that clathrin was recently found to be abundant in IRT1 interactome, suggesting that IRT1 can associate, probably in an indirect manner via adaptor proteins, with clathrin (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The peripheral membrane protein ENHANCED BENDING1 (EHB1) may also be involved in IRT1 endocytosis since: (i) IRT1 protein content increases in ehb1 mutants, (ii) proteins from the same family can induce membrane tubulation in vitro (Khan et al. 2019). Interestingly, EHB1 interacts with and negatively regulates IRT1 in a calciumdependent manner (Fig. 1), leading to a reduction of iron acquisition in plant.

Interestingly, IRT1 intracellular dynamics is not regulated by iron, the primary substrate of IRT1, but is controlled by the non-iron secondary substrates of IRT1 that are toxic when present in excess (Barberon et al. 2014; Dubeaux et al. 2018). Although IRT1 is localized to both EE/TGN and the PM in the presence of physiological concentrations of noniron metals, IRT1 is targeted to MVB/LE and then to the vacuole for degradation upon a cytosolic excess of these metals (Fig. 1) (Dubeaux et al. 2018). The cellular mechanisms involved in the non-iron metal-triggered endocytosis of IRT1 were largely uncovered. Non-iron metal excess is directly sensed by IRT1 via metal binding to a histidine-rich sequence located in the IRT1 large cytosolic loop (Dubeaux et al. 2018). Thus, IRT1 acts as a transceptor, combining transporter and receptor properties (Cointry and Vert 2019). Metal binding on IRT1 allows the recruitment of Calcineurin B-like (CBL)-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 23 (CIPK23) (Fig. 1). Phosphorylation of IRT1 by CIPK23 in turn creates a docking site for the E3 ubiquitin ligase IRT1 DEGRADATION FACTOR1 (IDF1) that converts IRT1 multi-monoubiquitination into K63-type polyubiquitination, a signal that boosts the sorting of IRT1 to the vacuole and its degradation (Dubeaux et al. 2018; Shin et al. 2013). From a physiological point of view, the endocytosis of IRT1 in response to a non-iron metal excess constitutes a protective mechanism for the plant to restrict the absorption of readily available and potentially toxic metals, such as Zn, Mn and Co. Loss of CIPK23, IDF1, or the mutation of ubiquitination targets or metal-binding sites in IRT1 all lead to stabilization of IRT1 at the cell surface, which results in a hypersentivity to non-iron metals (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011; Dubeaux et al. 2018). It should be noted that in addition to this IRT1- mediated protection, non-iron-metal toxicity is also alleviated by tonoplastic transporters such as Metal Tolerance Protein 3 (MTP3) (Arrivault et al. 2006) and Heavy Metal Associated 3 (HMA3) (Morel et al. 2009), which expression is induced under iron defciency in a FIT-dependent manner (Wu et al. 2012), and that allow the sequestration of metals such as Zn and Co into the vacuole.

The recognition of ubiquitin-modifed IRT1 required for its routing to the vacuole is achieved by the MVB/LElocalized FYVE1/FREE1 protein (Fig. 1). FYVE1/FREE1 directly interacts with IRT1 and ubiquitin, and associates with endosomal membrane via phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding (Barberon et al. 2014; Gao et al. 2014). FYVE1/FREE1 is a plant-specifc component of the endosomal sorting complex for transport (ESCRT) that captures ubiquitinated cargos in the MVB/LE membrane and allows their sorting in intraluminal vesicles for subsequent targeting to the vacuole (Isono and Kalinowska 2017; Otegui 2018). Interestingly, overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 in plants leads to an apolar localization of IRT1 in root epidermal cells, which in turn induces defects in metal homeostasis (Barberon et al. 2014). This suggests that the polarization of IRT1 is essential for the radial transport of metals towards the vasculature. So far, it remains unclear why the overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 induces a re-routing of IRT1 to the PM instead of favoring its targeting to the vacuole for degradation. Interestingly, FYVE1/FREE1 protein accumulation is regulated by iron through the action of SINAT1-4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. Expression of these is induced under iron defciency resulting in ubiquitin-mediated degradation of FYVE1/FREE1, thus positively regulating iron uptake (Xiao et al. 2020). Following endocytosis, IRT1 can be recycled to earlier endocytic compartments or the PM. One of these pathways involves the Sorting Nexin 1 (SNX1) protein that partially co-localizes in endosomes with IRT1 (Fig. 1) (Ivanov et al. 2014). snx1 knock-out mutant shows enhanced degradation of IRT1, leading to reduced iron import efciency and hypersensitivity to iron defciency. Although Arabidopsis SNX1 protein works independently of the retrograde transport retromer complex (Pourcher et al. 2010; Zelazny et al. 2013), SNX1 appears to drive the recycling of internalized IRT1 to prevent its premature degradation (Ivanov et al. 2014). Whether SNX1 directly interacts with IRT1 is still undocumented.


## IRT1 is part of an iron acquisition protein complex


Recently, the three main actors of iron uptake in Arabidopsis, IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2, were shown to form tripartite direct interactions, thus creating an iron acquisition protein complex (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). This complex is probably mostly present in the outer PM domain facing the rhizosphere in root epidermal cells, where IRT1 and FRO2 are specifcally localized. The spatial proximity between IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2 among a complex may optimize iron uptake under low iron conditions, by creating a nanoscale environment in the rhizosphere combining low pH, induced by the activity of AHA2, and high concentrations of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ produced by FRO2 (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). Although it remains to be investigated, a channeling mechanism allowing the direct transfer of reduced iron from FRO2 to IRT1 is conceivable. Indeed, channeling of iron was described in yeast between the multicopper oxidase Fet3p, which oxidizes $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , and the iron permease Ftr1p that transports $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ into the cells, both proteins forming a complex (Kwok et al. 2006; Singh et al. 2006).

Characterization of the dynamics of the iron uptake complex revealed that: (i) FRO2 and AHA2 are ubiquitinated but independently of the non-iron metal substrates transported by IRT1, (ii) FRO2 and AHA2 are not largely endocytosed in response to non-iron metal excess, unlike IRT1, (iii) this absence of internalization is due to the dissociation of the complex provoked by the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of IRT1 in response to non-iron metal excess (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The meaning of such dissociation remains to be investigated but released FRO2 and AHA2 may be recruited to other processes than iron uptake, such as copper reduction and membrane energization, respectively (Yi and Guerinot 1996; Robinson et al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2003; Falhof et al. 2016).

In the present study, two cDNAs, designated LeIRT1 and LeIRT2, were isolated from a library constructed from Fe-starved tomato root RNA. When introduced into Fe uptake-deficient yeast strains, these cDNAs restored colony growth on Fe-limited media. We therefore conclude that both cDNAs encode Fe transporters. In accordance with the basic observations by Chaney et al. (1972), the LeIRT-mediated transport of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 \dot { + } }$ was largely preferred over $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , implicating that ferric reduction is a prerequisite for Fe uptake. This mechanism has been observed in all plant species examined with the exception of the grasses (Bienfait, 1988) and has also been found in unicellular algae (Eckhardt and Buckhout, 1998). The rate-limiting step is either ferric chelate reduction or ferrous transport, depending on the species analysed.

The apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ of the LeIRT proteins, measured in yeast, were below $1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ . Although this is somewhat lower than found for IRT1 from Arabidopsis $\mathrm { \Delta } ^ { \prime } 6 { \pm } 1 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; Eide et al., 1996), these concentrations are in the physiological range with respect to the iron demand of most higher plants (about

$1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; Epstein, 1972). Thus, LeIRT1 and LeIRT2 appear to be high-affinity Fe transporters.

Calculating the activities of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ with the Geochem-PC program (http://envisci.ucr.edu/Faculty/ dparker/default.htm) revealed that they were below $0 . 1 \%$ of the total concentrations supplied to the assay. This might indicate that the actual $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values for the two transporters were much less than those reported.

It is well established that under Fe-limited growth and in mutants impaired in Fe uptake regulation, the shoot content of a number of transition metals, particularly Mn, increases in higher plants (Scholz et al., 1985; Welch et al., 1993; Yi and Guerinot, 1996; Delhaize, 1996). This observation could be explained if the Fe carrier also transported metal ions other than Fe.

When expressed in yeast, the Fe uptake mediated by both LeIRT proteins was stongly inhibited by a 10-fold excess $( 2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ of Zn, Ni, and Cd. It is not likely that this uptake inhibition was the result of metal toxicity, because Dix et al. (1994) have shown that incubation of yeast in as much as $5 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd or Co over $5 { \mathrm { - } } 1 5 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ did not impair the viability of the cells. Rather, we propose that the LeIRT proteins also transport these metals. Cd has no essential function in any living system thus far investigated. However, similar inhibitory effects of Cd on Fe transport mediated by IRT1 from Arabidopsis were observed (M.L. Guerinot, personal communication). Furthermore, yeast expressing IRT1 were more sensitive to Cd toxicity (D. Eide, personal communication), suggesting that Cd is taken up to the cell, probably due to its chemical similarities to zinc.

Like Cd, Zn strongly inhibited Fe transport by the LeIRT proteins. This inhibitory effect was even higher than the effect of unlabelled Fe supplied to the uptake assays (not shown). Consistent with the finding that both LeIRT proteins complemented a zinc uptake mutant, as did IRT1 from Arabidopsis (Korshunova et al., 1999), we propose that LeIRT1 and 2 are $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporters as well. The apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transport mediated by IRT1 from Arabidopsis was about twice that for $Z \bar { \bf n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, whereas $\nu _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ values were similar (Eide et al., 1996; Korshunova et al., 1999).

Interestingly, the LeIRT-mediated Fe uptake was strongly and reproducibly inhibited by $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 \bar { + } }$ . Similar inhibition was not observed in Arabidopsis. Although nickel was shown to be essential for higher plants (Zonia et al., 1995), Ni transporters have not yet been identified from higher plants. Very recently, a fission yeast mutant, deficient in an open reading frame designated Nic1p was characterized that was impaired in $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake in the presence of high concentrations of $\mathrm { M g }$ (Eitinger et al., 2000). The Nic1 protein supplies $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ to the fission yeast cells operating with high affinity $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ below $5 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ , O. Degen and T. Eitinger, personal communication). At nonphysiologically high concentrations, Ni was found to be transported via Mg uptake systems. With regard to the inhibition of Fe uptake by $\mathrm { N i }$ ions, we propose that the LeIRT1 and LeIRT2 proteins represent lowspecificity transporters that could transport $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ when their physiological substrates are unavailable.

The inhibitory effect of Mn on $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transport was small when supplied in a 10-fold excess over Fe. However, a smf1 mutant was clearly complemented by LeIRT1 and LeIRT2. $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ is therefore likely to be transported by the LeIRT proteins. We suggest that the weak inhibitory effect of Mn on $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transport was due to a low affinity compared to Fe. Therefore, Mn transport may be significant at higher concentrations.

The copper uptake-deficient yeast mutant $6 4 \mathrm { p }$ (1ctr1; Dancis et al., 1994) was also complemented by over-expression of the LeIRT proteins. In parallel, the effect of high concentrations of $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } }$ on $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake assays was inhibitory, while at lower concentrations the effect was complex (data not shown). It therefore appears that the LeIRT proteins could also transport $\mathrm { C u }$ ; however the details of the uptake mechanism remain to be investigated.

In northern blot analyses, it was not possible to distinguish between transcripts of the two LeIRT genes, due to the high overall nucleotide sequence identity between LeIRT1 and LeIRT2. Semi-quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR analyses allowed specific detection of each gene. These analyses revealed that both genes were predominantly expressed in tomato roots, LeIRT1 being strongly induced by Fe deficiency while LeIRT2 was not affected by the iron status of the plant. We therefore assume that LeIRT1 is an Feregulated cation transporter, whereas the function of LeIRT2 is uncertain. It remains to be analysed whether the LeIRT2 gene is induced by other metal deficiencies (e.g. zinc). In parallel with ferric reductase and ferrous transport capacities, the transcript levels of IRT1 in Arabidopsis (Eide et al., 1996) and of a similar gene in pea (Cohen et al., 1998) increased under Felimited growth. Low-level transcription of LeIRT1 was also identified in flowers of 8-week old tomato plants. During the life cycle of peas, the activity of the root $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -chelate reductase was strongly induced during the development of seeds, even under Fe-sufficient conditions (Grusak, 1995). This increase in activity is thought to meet the higher demands for iron during seed development. The faint transcription signal of LeIRT1 in tomato flowers could reflect the expression of a metal transporter that ensures the delivery of Fe and other trace elements to developing seeds. LeIRT1 appears to be an Fe transporter regulated either by Fe deficiency in the roots or by increased Fe demand by developing seeds. To confirm this hypothesis, more detailed spatial and temporal analyses by in situ hybridization or immuno-histochemical staining experiments will be necessary.

Sequence comparisons revealed that the deduced LeIRT proteins are members of the large family of ZRT/IRT-like proteins (ZIP family), spread over the eukaryotic kingdom, including plants, mammals, yeasts, insects and nematodes (Eng et al., 1998). The ZIP metal transporters contain eight putative transmembrane (TM) domains and a histidine cluster between the TM domains 3 and 4. This cytosolic region was designated as the variable region as it displays low sequence conservation. In the fourth TM domain, a highly conserved region was found, containing the ZIP signature sequence (Eng et al., 1998). Histidine residues in the $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ , $4 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ and $5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ TM domains that are highly conserved throughout the entire ZIP family were thought to be essential for metal transport (Gaither and Eide, 2000). All features characteristic of the ZIP family were found in the LeIRT proteins (Figure 2). In eight cases, the transport activities of the ZIP proteins were analysed, i.e. IRT1 (Eide et al., 1996) and the ZIP1-3 proteins from Arabidopsis (Grotz et al., 1998), ZNT1 from Thlaspi caerulescens (Pence et al., 2000), the yeast ZRT1 and 2 proteins (Zhao and Eide, 1996a and b) and the human zinc transporter hZIP2 (Gaither and Eide, 2000). They are either Fe or Zn transporters, most of which are transcriptionally induced by substrate deficiency. With the exception of the human hZIP2, which displays largely different physiology than the plant and yeast Zn transporters (Gaither and Eide, 2000), it appears that the Fe-regulated transporters transport Fe and Zn, whereas the Zn-regulated transporters transport Zn but probably not Fe (Eide et al, 1996; Zhao and Eide, 1996a, b; Grotz et al., 1998; Korshunova et al., 1999). This observation raised the question whether one could discriminate between Fe- and $Z \mathrm { n }$ -regulated transporters. We therefore looked for phylogenetic traces of Zn and Fe transporters (Figure 11). When using ZIP sequences from only plants and yeast, four clades were evident (indicated by circles): the yeast Zn transporter group, the plant Fe transporter group, the plant Zn transporter group and a group containing the ZIP4 protein from Arabidopsis which was proposed to be plastidic (Grotz et al., 1998). Based on the phylogenetic analyses, the Fe-regulated transporters and the Zn-regulated transporters from Arabidopsis appear to be in two different structural clades. The LeIRT proteins are clustered in the group of Fe-regulated but not Zn-regulated transporters (Figure 11), leading us to the assumption that the LeIRT proteins are Fe- but not Zn-regulated. Physiological analyses are under way to confirm this hypothesis.

Parts of the LeIRT genes were isolated by PCR experiments. They are neighbouring genes with a tailto-tail orientation (Figure 10). Even the exon-intron borders are at conserved positions, suggesting that the two genes arose from a duplication event. Similar genetic structures were found in Arabidopsis: the designated IRT2 gene is located adjacent to IRT1, the introns are at conserved positions. In contrast to tomato, however, in Arabidopsis the orientation of the two genes is head-to-tail, suggesting that independent gene duplications have taken place. The transcriptional starting point of LeIRT1 is located at an adenine base, 79 nucleotides upstream of the translational start codon. A sequence that matches well to the consensus of eucaryotic TATA boxes was found 22–30 bp upstream of the transcriptional start, and a putative CAAT box at $- 1 2 0$ to $- 1 2 5$ was also identified. In contrast to tomato, however, in Arabidopsis the orientation of the two genes is head-to-tail, suggesting that independent gene duplications have taken place. The transcriptional starting point of LeIRT1 is located at an adenine base, 79 nucleotides upstream of the translational start codon. A sequence that matches well to the consensus of eucaryotic TATA boxes was found 22–30 bp upstream of the transcriptional start, and a putative CAAT box at $- 1 2 0$ to $- 1 2 5$ was also identified. In mobile signal molecules (Grusak, 1995). Knowledge of the regulation of the Fe assimilation is a prerequisite for genetic alteration of plants in order to achieve higher Fe efficiency.

When exposed to saline or water-deprived condition, plants respond in various ways to increase their survival rate. Stomatal movement is one of the key features of this response. Whenever plant senses salt or drought stress, and the consequent demand for saving water, rapid stomatal closure is induced to prevent water loss. In addition, pathogen attack can also trigger stomatal closure, for stomata can be a pathway for bacterial infestation. It is well known that light induced stomatal opening is controlled by inward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels localized in guard cell PM (plasma membrane), such as KAT1, KAT2, AKT1, and AKT2 [1–8]. In contrast, stomatal closure consists of guard cell expressed outward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels and anion channels. Particularly, when plants are exposed to the stressful conditions mentioned above, activation of guard cell anion channels holds the key to defending themselves by inducing rapid stomatal closure.

Plant cells contain several types of anions including chloride, nitrate, sulfate, and organic acids like malate. Chloride is a major component of salt in soil, alongside with sodium, a major inflictor of salt damage to plants. While chloride acts as an essential nutrient, accumulation of chloride in the shoot (even without the presence of sodium) causes a decreased rate of transpiration and photosynthesis, leading to reduced crop yield and quality [9–11]. Nitrate works as an essential nitrogen source for amino acid synthesis. The process starting from direct uptake of nitrate from the soil, followed by enzymatic reactions and consequent production of glutamate, is an exclusive feature for plants (nitrogen assimilation) [12,13]. Nitrate also acts as an antagonist against chloride and could be applied to prevent Cl over-accumulation in shoots. Malate is important as an intermediate of TCA-cycle, essential storage carbon molecules and major photosynthate in CAM and C4 plants [14–23]. It also participates in the biosynthesis of amino acids and fatty acids, root growth, and aluminum tolerance [24–26]. Sulfate is an essential source for the biosynthesis of cysteine. Cysteine can either be directly incorporated into a protein or a peptide such as glutathione (GSH), or can be used as a sulfur donor for various coenzymes like molybdenum cofactor required for ABA synthesis [27–30].

These anions, once produced or uptaken, are immediately transferred to appropriate tissues and cell compartments by various anion transport systems, anion channels and transporters. The anion membrane transport system is distributed in each cell of the entire plant, and, in particular, many types of anion channels function intensively in guard cells, since the cell volume fluctuates in response to frequent environmental changes. The mechanism of stress-induced stomatal closure thus relies on these guard cell expressed anion channels. Under stress conditions, they drive anions either outside the cell or into the vacuole, triggering change in cell turgor pressure and consequently reducing the volume of guard cells. In this review, we focus on the function and regulation of such anion channels in guard cell.

Early patch clamp studies in the 1980s revealed two types of anion channels present in guard cell PM: R (rapid)-type and S (slow)-type. R-type channel activated rapidly within $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ by depolarization, while S-type channel showed slow voltage-dependent activation and deactivation [31–34]. Then, 2008 saw a breakthrough: an ozone-sensitive Arabidopsis mutant named rcd3 (radical-induced cell death3) was isolated, showing constitutively higher stomatal conductance and deficit in the well-known activations of S-type guard cell anion channels by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ or abscisic acid (ABA) [31,32,35–38]. This mutant was renamed SLAC1 (slow anion channel-associated 1), and afterwards, SLAC1 gene was shown to encode a guard cell expressed S-type anion channel [38,39].

SLAC1 is predicted to be a membrane protein with ten transmembrane helices which, based on the structure of its bacterial homologue, forms a symmetrical trimer [38,40,41]. Usually in its inactive state, in which a phenylalanine residue at position 450 (Phe450) blocks its channel pore, SLAC1 is only activated when it is phosphorylated by certain kinases and a conformational change allows the removal of the Phe450 residue [40,42–44]. Various kinases are involved in this activation of SLAC1, including SnRK (sucrose non-fermenting-related kinase), LRR-RLK (leucine-rich repeat kinase), MPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase), CPK/CDPK (calcium dependent kinase), CBL (calcineurin-B like protein) and CIPK (CBL-interacting protein kinase) (Table 1; Figure 1) [45–55].

Drought/salt responsive stomatal closure occurs by drought-driven synthesis of ABA, which is an essential signaling hormone for some activators of SLAC1. SnRK2.6 also known as OST1 (Open stomata 1), identified through functional screening of Arabidopsis mutants, was the first reported kinase to activate SLAC1 [56,57]. Activity of OST1 is usually suppressed by the protein phosphatase ABI1. Application of ABA induces protein complex formation of ABI1 and ABA receptor proteins PYR/PYL/RCAR, which subsequently inactivates ABI1 and allows OST1 to phosphorylate Ser120 residue of SLAC1 [45,46,56–61]. OST1 also possesses the ability to phosphorylate and inactivate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in channel KAT1, further emphasizing its significance in the closing of stomata [62,63]. In addition to this, a member of LRR-RLK named GHR1 (guard cell hydrogen peroxide-resistant 1) was identified as an alternative key kinase in ABA-dependent regulation of SLAC1 activity. In contrast to OST1, GHR1 interacts with protein phosphatase ABI2 and not ABI1, suggesting that GHR1 acts in parallel with OST1 upon ABA-induced stomatal closure [64]. OST1, activated by ABA, is also capable of promoting ROS (reactive oxygen species) production in guard cell by phosphorylating NADPH oxidase RbohD and RbohF [63,65,66]. Two MPKs, MPK9 and MPK12, are known to mediate ROS-induced S-type channel activation in guard cell [54,67]. Murata et al. reported that ABI2, not ABI1, was inhibited by ROS, suggesting a ROS-mediated indirect enhancement of GHR1 activity [51,58,64]. In a recent study, another kinase BAK1 (Brassinosteroid insensitive 1-associated receptor kinase 1) was shown to directly form a complex with OST1 and stimulate stomatal closure in an ABA-dependent manner. BAK1 functions upstream of ROS production, and its complex formation with OST1 is inhibited by ABI1 [68]. In addition, accumulation of ROS (particularly $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ ) enhances synthesis of nitric oxide (NO) by NR1 (nitrate reductase 1) [69,70]. NO can provide both positive or negative feedback in stomatal closure [70–73]. NO induces phosphatidic acid (PA) production via activation of phospholipase C or D, which in turn inhibits ABI1 and activates RbohD/RbohF [74–77]. On the other hand, accumulation of NO triggers degradation of ABA receptors PYR/PYL/RCAR via tyrosine nitration, and attenuation of OST1 and RbohD activity by S-nitrosylation [78–80].

ABA also stimulates increases in cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration. This is achieved by the release of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ from intracellular stores and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ influx into the cell via inward $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters [31,113–118]. One of the known mechanisms is the activation of hyperpolarization-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -permeable $\mathrm { I } _ { \mathrm { C a } }$ channels by ROS (which is in turn increased by ABA, as described above) [58,119,120]. The elevated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration activates CBL1 or CBL9, both of which form a complex with CIPK26 and phosphorylate RbohF, forming a positive feedback loop in ROS production [48,121]. Another group of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -activated kinases, CPK4, 5, 6 and 11, regulates RbohD in a similar manner [122,123]. Accumulation of ROS promotes synthesis of NO, which is capable of releasing $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ from intracellular $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ stores [72,124,125]. These mechanisms allow the increase of cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration and the activation of various $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ dependent kinases in guard cell, which subsequently phosphorylate and activate SLAC1. To date, the following kinases are known to participate in activation of SLAC1: CPK3, 6, 21, 23, CIPK23 (with CBL1 or CBL9) and CIPK11 (with CBL5) [55,61,82,83,126]. All these kinases are confirmed to activate SLAC1 in Xenopus oocyte, and they recognize different phosphorylation sites from OST1 (for instance, CPK6 phosphorylates Ser59 of SLAC1) [61,83]. However these kinases, like OST1, are confirmed to be inhibited by ABI1 and ABI2, suggesting a complex crosstalk between SLAC1-activating kinases [61,82,83,127]. The four CPKs seem to display differences in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ affinity, since CPK6 and CPK23 enable SLAC1 to emit anion currents at resting $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration in oocytes, while CPK3 and CPK21 requires deletion of their EF-hands (which renders them constitutively active) [82,126]. Patch clamp analysis revealed the severe reduction of S-type anion channel current amplitude in guard cell of cpk23 [82]. In addition, the ABA-induced activation of guard cell S-type anion channels was disrupted in cpk3cpk6 double or cpk5cpk6cpk11cpk23 quadruple mutant [128,129]. While cpk3cpk6 and cpk5cpk6cpk11cpk23 mutant plants showed impaired ABA-induced stomatal closure, stomatal behavior in cipk23 and cbl1cbl9 was somehow the opposite, displaying reduced leaf water transpiration and enhanced drought tolerance [55,109,128,129]. The effect of cpk23 mutation is still under debate since conflicting results are reported [130,131]. cpk21 mutant showed enhanced tolerance in osmotic stress and no change in stomatal conductance, even though CPK21 was confirmed to activate GORK, an outward guard cell $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel that works synergistically with SLAC1 upon stomatal closure [111,131,132]. These somewhat confusing results can be explained by functional overlapping and compensation of CPKs. For example, gene expression of CPK23 is upregulated in cpk21 mutant plant [132]. As for CIPK23, this kinase is known to activate various channels other than SLAC1, including inward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel AKT1 [108–110]. It was therefore speculated, that CIPK23 activates other channels like AKT1 rather than SLAC1 in vivo, resulting in negative regulation of ABA signaling in guard cells [3,45]. Recently, $N$ -myristoylation and S-acylation at the N-terminus of CPK or CBL, was identified as an essential modification of CPK6 and CBL5-CIPK11 upon their activation of SLAC1, in terms of their PM recruitment [55]. Conservation of $N .$ -myristoylation and S-acylation motif among CPKs and CBLs suggest this mechanism as a common requirement for ion channel regulation by these kinases at the membrane [133–137].

In addition to ABA, methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and salicylic acid (SA) also induces stomatal closure via the regulation of S-type anion channel (Figure 1). MeJA-induced stomatal closure is dependent on the activation of guard cell $\mathrm { P M H ^ { + } } .$ -ATPase, a process that is mediated by F-box protein COI1 (Coronatine-insensitive 1) [138]. This promotes hyperpolarization of PM and activation of PM $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels, resulting in an increase of cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ . The elevated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ level results in activation of CPK6, though not of CPK3, 4 or 11, and the consequent SLAC1 activation [139]. MPK9, MPK12 and GHR1 also participate in SLAC1 activation in this pathway, possibly as a consequence of RbohD/RbohF-mediated ROS production by elevated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ [49,64]. Similarly, SA-induced stomatal closure involves ROS production, followed by SLAC1 activation via CPK3, 6, MPK9, MPK12, and GHR1 [54,64,140]. However, this pathway is unique in the way that ROS is produced: it features extracellular ROS produced by SHAM (salicylhydroxamic acid)-sensitive peroxidase, which is then diffused into guard cells [141].

Because stomata work as a major gateway for $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ influx, elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ levels also promote stomatal closure (Figure 1) [39,45]. In this regulation pathway, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ imported from stomatal pore is first converted into $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ by two kinds of carbonic anhydrases (CAs), $\mathsf { \beta C A 1 }$ and $\beta \mathrm { C A 4 }$ . Exposure to high $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ condition elevates the intracellular $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentration, stimulating an $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ sensing component named RHC1 (Resistant to high carbon dioxide 1). This induces the formation of a complex between CA and RHC1, which enables the interaction with, and the subsequent inactivation of HT1 kinase (High leaf temperature 1e), an inhibitor of OST1 and GHR1 [45,81,142–146]. This mechanism would allow SLAC1 activation and the consequent stomatal closure under high $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ condition. In a recent study, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ -permeable aquaporin PIP2;1 was identified as an upstream regulator of $\mathsf { \beta { C A 1 } }$ and $\beta { \mathrm { C A 4 } } ,$ , and MPK4 and MPK12 as additional intermediates for HT1 regulation by− $\mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ [81,147].
