Boron (B) is a micronutrient that is critical for crop growth and quality (Wimmer et al. 2020). It is required for the crosslinking of rhamnogalacturonan II, a pectic polysaccharide, during cell wall development (Funakawa and Miwa 2015). B defciency causes signifcant yield loss in many crop plants worldwide (BrdarJokanović  2020; Rerkasem et  al. 2020). It generally afects fower development and seed set. Low soil B is most prevalent in regions with high rainfall, including parts of China, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Brazil (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Shorrocks 1997). Excess soil B having detrimental efects on plants is also found in arid and semi-arid areas, including parts of India, the USA,

Pakistan, Malaysia, Chile, Peru, Hungary, Serbia, Italy, and the Middle East (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Nable et al. 1997). Excess B concentrations cause double-strand breaks of DNA (Sakamoto et al. 2011) and afect cellular metabolism, likely through binding to ribose moieties of ATP, NADH, and NADPH in cells (Reid 2014). Binding to ribose, both as a free sugar and as an RNA constituent, can inhibit cell division and development (Reid 2014). Symptoms of B toxicity include chlorosis and necrosis, which spread from leaf tips, leaving brown lesions at the margins. Reductions in biomass and seed yield are commonly observed under prolonged B toxicity (BrdarJokanović 2020; Landi et al 2019).

Plant roots take up B mainly in the form of boric acid $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ) }$ , which is a weak Lewis acid, with a pKa of 9.24 $[ \mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } + \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O = B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 4 } ^ { - } + \mathrm { H } ^ { + } ]$ (Power and Woods 1997). B is the only essential nutrient taken up in its uncharged form at physiological $\mathrm { p H }$ . Due to the theoretically high membrane permeability coeffcient of boric acid, it was once widely believed that B transport in plants was a mainly passive process. However, using the plasma membranes of giant internodal cells of the charophyte alga Chara corallina and plasma membrane vesicles isolated from squash roots, the membrane permeability of boric acid was determined to be higher than its theoretical value (Dordas et al. 2000; Stangoulis et al. 2001). Later, plants were found to facilitate the difusion of boric acid through major intrinsic protein (MIP) channels. Plants also use borate transporters (BORs) to export borate out of cells against a concentration gradient of soluble B (Yoshinari and Takano 2017). In this review, we describe the mechanisms of B transport, with an emphasis on membrane transport proteins and their regulation.


## B transport through MIPs


MIPs, including water channels (aquaporins), are universal to all kingdoms of life. Plant MIPs are channels for the bidirectional difusion of water and other small uncharged molecules (Bienert and Chaumont 2014). Based on sequence similarity and subcellular localization, MIPs in seed plants have been classifed into fve subclasses: plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs), tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs), small basic intrinsic proteins (SIPs), NIPs, and X intrinsic proteins (XIPs) (Maurel et al. 2016).

Plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs)

PIPs are plasma membrane-localized aquaporins that are mainly involved in water transport. They are further categorized into two subgroups, PIP1 and PIP2 (Bienert and Bienert 2017). PIP1 proteins possess an inherent capacity for water transport but require the help of PIP2s in plasma membrane trafcking in Arabidopsis and maize (Hachez et  al. 2013; Bienert et  al. 2018). Some PIP proteins have been shown to permeate boric acid in addition to water. In an early study, maize PIP1 expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes enhanced boric acid uptake into the cells (Dordas et  al. 2000). In a later study, the expression of barley (Hordeum vulgare) PIP1;3 and PIP1;4 in yeast led to increased B accumulation and enhanced sensitivity to high B (Fitzpatrick and Reid 2009). In rice roots, PIP expression was induced under high-B treatment (Kumar et  al. 2018). The expression of rice PIP1;3, PIP2;4, and PIP2;7 enhanced B infux and accumulation, and OsPIP2;6 enhanced B efux in yeast cells (Kumar et  al. 2014; Mosa et  al. 2016). Transgenic Arabidopsis plants overexpressing OsPIP1;3, OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OsPIP2;7 enhanced plant tolerance to excess B concentrations (Kumar et al. 2014; Mosa et al. 2016). Tracer experiments using $^ { 1 0 } \mathrm { { B } }$ -enriched boric acid at 2.5 or $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ showed that B uptake and efux from roots were both increased in transgenic plants. These results suggest the possible functions of PIPs in plant B tolerance of high B levels, although further studies using knockout plants are desired.

Tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs)

TIPs function in water transport across the vacuolar membrane, turgor regulation, osmo-sensing, cell growth, and vacuolar diferentiation (Maurel et  al. 2016). TIP isoforms have highly variable sequences within the aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity flter, to transport small molecules including urea, $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ glycerol, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ , and boric acid (Sudhakaran et  al. 2021). The heterologous expression of grape TIPs (VvTnTIP1;1, VvTnTIP2;2, and VvTnTIP4;1) and maize TIPs (ZmTIP1;1 and ZmTIP1;2) in yeast led to higher sensitivity to toxic B conditions (Barzana et al. 2014; Sabir et al. 2014). Overexpression of AtTIP5;1 in Arabidopsis promoted hypocotyl elongation and increased silique production under excess B (Pang et  al. 2010). Transcription profling of B-efcient citrus rootstock showed the upregulation of TIP2;2 and TIP4;1 under B limitation, with diferent temporal patterns (Zhou et  al. 2015). However, the physiological signifcance of B transport across the vacuolar membrane and its relationship to TIPs remain obscure.

Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs)

NIPs were frst reported to be localized in the symbiosome membrane of soybean (Glycine max L.) nodules, and to possess water and glycerol transport properties (Fortin et  al. 1987; Roberts and Routray. 2017). Phylogenetic analyses revealed that NIPs cluster together with aquaporin $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Z } }$ or glycerol uptake facilitator proteins in bacteria (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). This close relationship supports horizontal gene transfer from the bacterial AqpN–aquaporin group to plant NIPs. AqpN is predominantly positioned in arsenic resistance operons of various prokaryotic phyla to contribute to the arsenic detoxifcation machinery (Pommerrenig et al. 2020). Ar/R selectivity flter residues of bacterial AqpN are conserved in NIPs in algae, liverworts, moss, hornworts, and ferns. Bacterial AqpN, KnNIP6;1 in the flamentous terrestrial alga Klebsormidium nitens, and PpNIP5;1, NIP5;2, and NIP5;3 in the moss Physcomitrella patens are impermeable to water and silicic acid but permeable to arsenite and boric acid in Xenopus oocytes. These fndings along with mutational analysis results suggest that bacterial arsenic efux channels are converted into silicic acid and boric acid channels for the efcient uptake and translocation of these nutrients in seed plants (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). Plant NIPs are categorized as NIP-I (AtNIP1–4 s and others), NIP-II (AtNIP5–7 s and others), and NIPIII (OsNIP2;1 and others) based on similarities in their pore constriction regions, which consist of ar/R selectivity flters (Mitani-Ueno et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑Is in B transport


NIP-I proteins are aquaglyceroporins that mediate the transport of water and small neutral molecules such as glycerol (Roberts and Routray 2017). Although their physiological functions are unclear, Brassica napus NIP-Is (NIP2–4) transport B in Xenopus oocytes (Diehn et  al. 2019; see a later section on  Brassica napus for details).

Among NIP-Is in Arabidopsis, AtNIP4;1 is permeable to boric acid, ammonia, urea, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , as shown in Saccharomyces cerevisiae growth assays (Giorgio et  al. 2016). AtNIP4;1 and AtNIP4;2 are localized to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles of pollen tubes (Bock et  al. 2006; Giorgio et  al. 2016). In nip4;1 and nip4;2 mutants and amiRNA-mediated double knockdown plants, fertility was reduced, and pollen tube growth was afected under low B supply but normal under high B supply. These results suggest the roles of NIP4;1 and NIP4;2 in pollen tube growth via B transport.


## Roles of NIP‑IIs as major boric acid channels


The NIP-II protein AtNIP5;1 was the frst boric acid channel identifed to be involved in B uptake into roots, as the abundance of AtNIP5;1 mRNA increased after B starvation (Takano et al. 2006). In the plasma membrane of epidermal, cortical, and endodermal cells of roots, NIP5;1 showed polar localization towards the soil, increasing the efciency of boric acid uptake (Takano et  al. 2010; Wang et  al. 2017). B uptake and accumulation in roots and shoots of nip5;1  T-DNA insertion lines were signifcantly reduced when plants were grown under B limitation compared to wild-type (WT) plants. Due to defective B uptake, nip5;1 mutants showed severe root and shoot growth impairment under B limitation (Takano et al. 2006).

AtNIP6;1, the closest paralogue of AtNIP5;1, is involved in B xylem–phloem transfer for preferential translocation in shoots (Tanaka et  al. 2008). Unlike AtNIP5;1, the expression of AtNIP6;1 was confned to the phloem regions in nodes, including sieve elements (Tanaka et  al. 2008). The nip6;1 mutants showed inhibition of rosette leaf expansion and apical dominance under B limitation. Xenopus oocyte transport analyses indicated that NIP5;1 and NIP6;1 facilitate boric acid uptake into cells but difer in water transport activity (Takano et  al. 2006; Tanaka et al. 2008) with NIP5;1 but not NIP6;1, showing signifcant water permeability. The water-tight nature of NIP6;1 is likely important for phloem function.

AtNIP7;1 is a third member of the NIPII subclass; it plays a role in pollen development under B limitation and shows anther-specifc expression and localization in the plasma membrane of tapetum cells (Routray et  al. 2018). Loss-of-function nip7;1 mutants showed reproductive growth retardation characteristics including decreased fertility, petite siliques, and increased seed abortion compared to WT plants under B limitation (Routray et al. 2018). NIP-II subclass proteins such as AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 possess conserved ar/R pore-forming residues, including the transmembrane helix 2 (H2) region. Alanine at the H2 region is considered a characteristic residue for NIP-II boric acid channels including AtNIP7;1 (Wallace and Roberts 2004, 2005). However, AtNIP7;1 showed lower permeability to boric acid in Xenopus oocytes (Li et al. 2011). The substitution of tyrosine 81 in H2 with a cysteine residue (characteristic of AtNIP6;1) resulted in significantly higher boric acid transport than in WT NIP7;1 and NIP5;1 (Li et  al. 2011). Boric acid transport by AtNIP7;1 was proposed to be controlled by a channel gate function of the conserved tyrosine residue in the pore (Li et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑IIIs in the transport of silicic acid and boric acid


The NIP-III proteins in rice (OsLsi1/OsNIP2;1) and barley (HvLsi1/HvNIP2;1) are silicic acid channels, facilitating its uptake (Ma et  al. 2007; Chiba et  al. 2009). In Xenopus oocytes, OsNIP2;1 and HvNIP2;1 showed signifcant boric acid transport activity along with silicic acid, germanic acid, arsenite, and water (Schnurbusch et  al. 2010; Mitani-Ueno et  al. 2011). The physiological functions of silicic acid channels in B transport in rice and barley are discussed in a later section.


## X intrinsic proteins (XIPs)


XIPs were frst identifed during whole-genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens (Danielson and Johanson 2008). XIP proteins are present in a range of organisms, from unicellular eukaryotes to plants but absent in monocots and members of the Brassicaceae family (Abascal et  al. 2014), likely due to their functional complementation by other MIP subfamilies in these taxa. Based on amino acid residues of the ar/R flter, XIPs are predicted to form a wider and hydrophobic pore, similar to those in the NIP III group (Bienert et  al. 2011). Consistent with this prediction, the heterologous expression of Solanaceae XIP1;1s in oocytes $( \mathrm { S t X I P 1 } ; 1 \alpha$ and StXIP1;1β, SlXIP1;1α, and SlXIP1;1β) resulted in glycerol and urea transport. SlXIP1;1s expressed in yeast (S. cerevisiae) cells showed growth inhibition/sensitivity on media containing ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ or excess boric acid, indicating $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } /$ boric acid infux activity (Bienert et  al. 2011). Grape $V \nu X I P I$ and tobacco $N b \mathrm { X I P 1 ; 1 \alpha }$ also showed increased sensitivity to excess boric acid media in the yeasts S. cerevisiae and Pichia pastoris (Ampah-Korsah et al. 2016; Noronha et  al. 2016). The expression of NtXIP1;1 under the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter complemented a growth defect in an Arabidopsis nip5;1 knockout mutant under B limitation, demonstrating its function as a boric acid channel in planta (Bienert et  al. 2019). However, NtXIP1;1 overexpression in Nico‑ tiana tabacum and Arabidopsis under the En2pPMA4 or 35S CaMV promoter, respectively, resulted in B defciency symptoms such as diminished shoot apical meristem, sterile fowers, and contracted leaves. This result was probably caused by heterogeneous B distribution, prompted by the ectopic expression of NtXIP1;1. Further investigation of the physiological functions of XIP-mediated B transport is required.


## B transport through BORs


Under B limitation, plants use BOR-type borate exporters for efcient translocation of B (Takano et al. 2012; Yoshinari and Takano 2017). Borate exporters are also involved in lowering B concentrations in tissues for excess B tolerance (Miwa et al. 2007). Similarly, in S. cerevisiae, Bor1p functions as a borate exporter for excess B tolerance (Nozawa et al. 2006; Takano et  al. 2007). BOR transporters appear to be able to pump B out against a concentration gradient. For example, WT yeast cells maintained $< 2 5 \%$ of the intracellular B compared to bor1 deletion mutant cells in medium containing $0 . 0 5 { - } 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ boric acid (Takano et al. 2007). Under these conditions, B concentrations in WT cells were estimated to be lower than in the treatment medium. Electrophysiological studies of Bot1, a BOR transporter in barley, in Xenopus oocytes and proteoliposomes showed electrogenic borate anion transport in a Nernstian manner (Nagarajan et al. 2016). The Km for borate was calculated to be $1 0 4 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ using patch-clamped proteoliposomes. Bot1 also transported chloride, phosphate, nitrate, and sulfate but with much lower afnity than borate. Therefore, it is most likely that BOR transporters are anion uniporters with high afnity with borate (Fig.  1). Boric acid taken up into cells via MIPs or passive diffusion is partly converted into borate anions in cytosol with higher pH, which are then exported by BORs dependent on the concentration gradient and negative membrane potential. In the acidic apoplasm, borate anions are converted back into boric acid, generating an uphill boric acid gradient across the plasma membrane.

The Arabidopsis genome encodes seven BORs (BOR1–7). In angiosperms, BORs are classifed into two separate clades (Wakuta et  al. 2015). It is likely that Clade I BORs (AtBOR1–3) and their homologs pH $( \sim 7 . 5 )$ . Then borate anions are exported by borate transporters (BORs) and converted into boric acid at lower $\mathrm { p H }$ $( \sim 5 \ – 6 )$ . Borate anions that are transported to secretion vesicles by AtBOR2 are hypothesized to form diester bonds with two RGII monomers to create B-RGII dimers in these small compartments. b. Considering the higher concentration of B in marine than in terrestrial environments and the low requirement of B due to low pectin content in nonvascular plants, it has been speculated that clade II may have been a prototype of clade I in plant evolution (Onuh and Miwa 2021).


## Clade I BORs


AtBOR1 was the frst BOR to be characterized with a physiological function in B translocation (Takano et  al. 2012). The boric acid transport activity of AtBOR1 was demonstrated by its heterologous expression in the yeast S. cerevisiae (Takano et  al. 2012). Under B limitation, the Arabidopsis bor1–1 loss-of-function mutant showed reduced vegetative growth and sterility compared to the WT (Noguchi et al. 1997; Takano et al. 2010, 2012). These efects were caused by defects in B root-to-shoot translocation and preferential B transport to young leaves and reproductive tissues. AtBOR1 was localized to the stele side of the plasma membrane domain in various root cell types and the apical plasma membrane domain in protovascular cells in the root tip (Takano et  al. 2010; Yoshinari et  al. 2016). The polar localization of BOR1 is assumed to be essential for efcient B transport from the root surface to the xylem, in collaboration with boric acid channels. In the cotyledon, AtBOR1 is expressed in the epidermal cell layer on the top side and polar localization in the plasma membrane toward the inner (downward) side (Yoshinari et al. 2016). This fnding suggests the involvement of AtBOR1 in B uptake at the surface of the cotyledon.

AtBOR2, a close paralog of AtBOR1, has a similar B translocation function to BOR1, and also functions in root cell elongation (Miwa et  al. 2013). BOR2 is an efux B transporter localized in the plasma membrane that exhibits stele-side polarity in root cells including lateral root cap and epidermis cells in the elongation zone. BOR2-GFP was stably localized in the plasma membrane and was also observed in endosomal membrane compartments (Miwa et  al. 2013). AtBOR2 T-DNA insertion mutants showed reduced root growth under B limitation. There were no signifcant diferences in total B concentrations between roots of bor2 mutants and WT plants, but the ratio of RG-II-B dimer formation to that of total RG-II was reduced to $4 5 \%$ when plants were supplied with $0 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ boric acid. These results indicate the involvement of BOR2 in B-RGII crosslinking to enhance the cell elongation for root growth. When B was resupplied to B-deprived Rosa cells, only freshly synthesized RG-II was cross-linked by borate (Chormova et al. 2014), suggesting that crosslinking does not occur in the cell wall. Because pectin chains are assumed to be synthesized in Golgi and Golgiderived secretory vesicles, BOR2 has been proposed to aid RG-II-B dimer formation by transporting boric acid/borate from the cytosol into secretory vesicles (Miwa et al. 2013; Fig. 1).


## Clade II BORs


AtBOR4 and barley BotI are clade II BORs that are important for excess B tolerance (Miwa et al. 2007; Sutton et al. 2007). BOR4 is localized on the distal sides of epidermal cells for the directional export of B from roots to soil under excess B conditions (Miwa et al. 2007). BOR4 T-DNA insertion mutants showed slowed growth and higher shoot B accumulation than WT plants under excess B supply (Miwa et al. 2014).


## Systems controlling B transport proteins


B transport proteins are regulated at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels in response to B conditions to maintain B homeostasis. In this section, we review the regulatory systems controlling the abundance and polar localization of B transport proteins.

Polar localization of B transport proteins

The polar localization of AtNIP5;1 and AtBOR1 in the plasma membrane toward the soil and stele sides of roots cells is important for directional B transport (Wang et  al. 2017; Yoshinari et  al. 2019). The mechanisms of polar localization have been examined using BOR1-GFP and GFP-NIP5;1. Polar localization of BOR1 was disturbed by the expression of a dominant negative variant of the dynaminrelated protein DRP1A, which plays an important role in pinching of clathrin-coated vesicles, and by the loss of function of the clathrin Adaptor Protein2 (AP2) complex (Yoshinari et al. 2016, 2019; Fig. 2). In these cases, BOR1-GFP endocytosis was compromised, indicating the importance of endocytosis for the polar localization of BOR1. Coated vesicle formation is facilitated by small GTPase ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF1), which is activated by a small group of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (ARF-GEFs) (Donaldson and Jackson 2011). GNOM is an ARFGEF that plays an important role in endocytosis and the maintenance of BOR1 polar localization (Yoshinari et al. 2021a; Fig. 2).

The polar localization of NIP5;1 requires the phosphorylation of threonine residues in the conserved factor GNOM. In root cells, internalized BOR1 is hypothesized to undergo transcytosis to the stele-side domain of the cell. NIP5;1 endocytosis is also dependent on the AP2 complex. Phosphorylation in the N-terminal region of NIP5;1 accelerates endocytosis. NIP5;1 is hypothesized to be distributed to the soil side of the cell domain via transcytosis from the TGN/ EE

TPG repeats present in the N-terminal cytosolic region (Wang et  al. 2017). The substitution of alanine in place of threonine at these phosphorylation sites (T18A.T21A.T24A) resulted in reduced endocytosis and weak polar localization. In AP2 subunit mutants, GFP-NIP5;1 showed low endocytosis rates coupled with compromised polar localization (Wang et  al. 2017). These results indicate that continuous polar cycling between the plasma membrane and endosomal compartments through clathrin-mediated endocytosis is required for the maintenance of polar localization of both BOR1 and NIP5;1 against lateral difusion in the plasma membrane. Importantly, expression of a weak polar variant (GFP-NIP5;1 T18A.T21A.T24A) only partially rescued the defects of the nip5;1 mutant in B transport and growth under B limitation. This fnding demonstrated the physiological importance of polar localization in directional nutrient transport. Consistently, AP2 subunit mutants in which polar localization of NIP5;1, BOR1, and BOR2 was compromised showed poor growth under B limitation (Yoshinari et al. 2019).


## Endocytic degradation of AtBOR1


When Arabidopsis plants are transferred from limited B to sufcient B conditions, AtBOR1 is traffcked from the plasma membrane to the endosomes, and then into vacuoles for degradation (Takano et al. 2005). Several other nutrient transporters in plants also have been found to be downregulated via endocytic degradation under high nutrient concentrations to avoid nutrient toxicity (Rodriguez-Furlan et  al. 2019). K63-linked polyubiquitination at the lysine 590 residue is critical for the high B-induced endocytosis and degradation of BOR1; it triggers AP2-independent and dynamin-related protein 1A (DRP1A)- dependent endocytosis (Kasai et  al. 2011; Yoshinari et  al. 2016, 2019, 2021a; Fig.  3). Target of Myb1 (TOM)-like ubiquitin receptor TOL proteins have also been shown to be involved in the vacuolar transport of BOR1 (Yoshinari et  al. 2018; Fig.  3). A forward genetic study showed that BOR1 residues involved in borate transport activity were critical for high B-induced ubiquitination and degradation (Yoshinari et al. 2021b). Further, targeted mutagenesis and comparison to a model of substrate-dependent ubiquitination of yeast amino acid permeases suggested that conformational transition during the borate transport cycle leads to BOR1 ubiquitination. Based on these results, BOR1 was proposed to be a transceptor regulating its own ubiquitination and degradation dependent on its borate transport activity.


## B-dependent regulation of mRNA accumulation and translation


The accumulation of AtBOR1 protein is regulated by B-dependent translational suppression and endocytic degradation (Aibara et al. 2018). The $5 ^ { \prime }$ -untranslated region (UTR) alone is sufcient for the B-dependent translational suppression of BOR1, and at least two independent upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are responsible for this suppression. An analysis of proBOR1:BOR1- GFP constructs lacking 5’UTR with and without K590A substitution demonstrated that BOR1 accumulation was downregulated mainly by ubiquitination-dependent protein degradation under sufcient B conditions and further decreased by translational suppression at higher B concentrations (Aibara et  al. 2018). Using these transgenic lines expressing BOR1 constructs defective for translational suppression and/or endocytic degradation, both of these post-transcriptional mechanisms were shown to contribute to preventing B overloading under high-B conditions.

NIP5;1 mRNA levels are downregulated under higher B supply, dependent on its 5’UTR (Tanaka et  al. 2011). The $5 '$ UTR of NIP5;1 containing AUG-stop sequences was shown to play an important role in B-dependent mRNA degradation. High B enhances ribosome stalling at AUG-stop, which leads to translation suppression and mRNA degradation (Tanaka et al. 2016). Using transgenic lines expressing NIP5;1 constructs with and without the 5’UTR, post-transcriptional regulation dependent on the 5’UTR was found to contribute to preventing excessive B uptake under high-B conditions (Tanaka et al. 2011). Recently, a comparison of RNA sequencing and ribosome profling data revealed that transcripts with reduced translational efciency at high B concentrations were rich in uORFs (Sotta et  al. 2021). Among B transport proteins, only NIP5;1, BOR1, and BOR2, which possess AUG-stop in their $_ 5 '$ -UTR but not others, exhibited B-dependent translational suppression (Sotta et al. 2021). This regulation is primarily based on cytosolic boric acid concentration. Using the AtNIP5;1 5’UTR, genetically encoded B sensors were developed to visualize relative B concentrations in various plant cells (Fukuda et al. 2018).

AtBOR4 functions to export B from root under excess B conditions (Miwa et al. 2007). The mRNA levels of BOR4 in roots increased twofold after highB treatment, and transgenic Arabidopsis with a ProBOR4 (including the promoter and $_ 5 '$ -UTR)-GUS construct showed increased GUS activity after highB treatment (Miwa et  al. 2014). An Arabidopsis sensitive to high-level B 1 (shb1) mutant bearing a point mutation in a gene encoding heme oxygenase 1 (HO1) showed hypersensitivity to excess B (Lv et al. 2017). In the shb1 mutant, BOR4 mRNA levels were reduced and B concentrations in roots were higher than in the WT under high-B conditions. Therefore, AtBOR4 expression is regulated at the mRNA level and dependent on SHB1/HO1.

Transcription factors controlling B transport

The transcription factor NGAL1/abnormal shoot 2 (NGATHA-like 1) was regulated by B-dependent ribosomes stalling at an AUGUAA sequence, similar to the case of NIP5;1 (Tanaka et  al. 2016). Mutant analysis showed that NGAL1 positively regulates the mRNA abundance of BOR1, NIP5;1, NIP6;1, and NIP7;1 under low-B conditions (Tsednee et al. 2022). The mRNA of NGAL1 was induced under excess B conditions as well as under B limitation. NGAL1 positively regulates the mRNA abundance of BOR4 and contributes to excess B tolerance by reducing shoot B accumulation (Tsednee et al. 2022).

WRKY transcription factors (TFs) in plants are involved in the regulation of various biotic/abiotic stresses. The AtWRKY6 gene has higher mRNA accumulation under low-B conditions. Mutant analysis showed that WRKY6 contributes to root growth under B limitation (Kasajima et al. 2010). In Brassica napus, BnaA9.WRKY47 was associated with higher mRNA accumulation under low-B conditions (Feng et  al. 2020). BnaA9.WRKY47 is involved in low-B tolerance through the activation of boric acid channel BnaA03.NIP5;1b (see a later section on Brassica napus). The Arabidopsis homolog AtWRKY47 is also involved in B homeostasis, although its physiological signifcance remains unclear. Under excess B conditions, the mRNA level of AtWRKY47 was downregulated in shoots. Atwrky47 mutants accumulated less shoot B and showed increased growth compared to WT Col-0 plants under excess B (Feng et al. 2021). These results suggest a negative role of AtWRKY47 in excess B tolerance.


## Role of soluble B complexes in B transport


In many plant species that produce sucrose as a photosynthetic product, B mobility in the phloem is limited and thus long-distance B transport mainly follows the transpiration stream (Reid 2014). This phenomenon is thought to be caused by high membrane permeability to boric acid. However, in plant species that produce sugar alcohols, B is mobile in the phloem as cis-diol esters of sugar alcohols and boric acid/borate (Hu et al. 1997; Du et al. 2020). The contribution of sugar alcohols to phlolem B mobility was demonstrated in transgenic tobacco and rice plants expressing a gene for sorbitol synthesis (Bellaloui et  al. 1999, 2003; Brown et  al. 1999). Moderate phloem mobility has also been observed in sucrose-producing plant species. Bis-sucrose borate and bis-N-acetyl-serine borate complexes were identifed in phloem exudates of wheat and canola, which explained the moderate phloem mobility of B in these species (Stangoulis et al. 2010).


## B transport and regulation in crop plants


In this section, we describe the mechanisms and regulation of B transport in fve well-studied crop plants. We focus on B transport proteins for which physiological functions have been genetically verifed or strongly supported by ortholog analyses.


## Brassica napus


Brassica napus is an allotetraploid that is the third most cultivated oilseed crop worldwide. It requires high B levels for production; low soil B $( \leq 0 . 5 \ \mathrm { m g \ B / }$ kg soil) severely afects its seed set and seed yield, leading to a phenotype that fowers without seed setting (Zhang et al. 2014).

Growth rates vary widely among B. napus genotypes under B limitation (Zhang et  al. 2014). Among 210 genotypes in China, eight B-efcient and two B-inefcient genotypes were identifed through seedling biomass and seed yield analyses (Xu et al. 2002). More recently, among 234 spring and 356 winter accessions from Asia and Europe, $^ { 3 \mathrm { ~ B ~ } }$ -efcient accessions from Asia were selected in an automated high-throughput phenotyping facility using a soil substrate-based cultivation system (Pommerrenig et  al. 2018). These genotypes showed better biomass, root growth, and seed yield than B-inefcient genotypes and had very low B demand (Pommerrenig et al. 2018).

Under B limitation, the B-efcient Chinese genotype Qingyou 10 (QY10) showed better growth and seed yield accompanied by lower cell wall B-binding sites and efcient B uptake and translocation than B-inefcient genotypes (Zhang et  al. 2014). Under B limitation, the B-inefcient genotype Westar 10 (W10) accumulates more RG-II monomers than the B-efcient genotype QY10, which renders more cell wall B-binding sites in W10, thereby increasing its B requirement for normal growth and development. QY10 also showed higher BOR2 expression than W10 under B limitation (Zhou et  al. 2017). In Arabidopsis, BOR2 is responsible for efective RG-II crosslinking in the cell wall (Miwa et  al. 2013). An RG-II dimerization assay showed higher rates of borate-crosslinked RG-II dimers in B-efcient QY-10 than in B-inefcient W10 under B limitation (Zhou et  al. 2017). These results suggest that low cell wall B binding sites and higher RG-II dimerization rates confer low-B tolerance in B. napus (Zhou et al. 2017).

Six BOR1 genes have been identifed in B. napus (Chen et  al. 2018). The expression patterns of the BOR1 genes difered between Asian and European winter B. napus genotypes (Chen et  al. 2018; Diehn et  al. 2019). For example, BnaC04.BOR1;1c showed the highest similarity to AtBOR1 and exhibited low B-induced mRNA expression in roots, shoots, and fowers of B-efcient QY10 (Asian winter type). However, there was no upregulation of $B n a C O 4 . B O R I ; I c$ under B limitation in the European winter type (Diehn et  al. 2019). In addition, BnaA05BOR1; $\imath _ { c }$ and $B n a A O 3 . B O R I ; 3 a$ were upregulated under B limitation in QY10 but not in Darmor-PBY018 (Diehn et  al. 2019). Subcellular localization using GFP fusion revealed that BnaC04. BOR1;1c is localized on the plasma membrane (Zhang et al. 2017). Knockdown of BnaC04.BOR1;1c in the B-efcient genotype QY10 reduced B accumulation in fower organs, eventually resulting in fower drooping, severe sterility, and seed yield loss. By contrast, overexpression of BnaC04.BOR1;1c in the B-inefcient genotype W10 led to shorter roots and taller shoots under low-B conditions than in the nontransgenic W10 (Chen et al. 2018). BnaC04.BOR1;1c mRNA expression was later found to be regulated in a $_ 5 '$ -UTR-dependent manner, similar to that of AtNIP5;1 (Wang et  al. 2021). Results from in  situ polymerase chain reaction, immunofuorescence, and GFP fusion analyses showed that BnaC04.BOR1;1c was polarly localized towards the stele side of the plasma membrane in root vascular cells, presumably for efcient xylem loading (Wang et  al. 2021). BnaC04.BOR1;1c was also localized in the plasma membrane of cambium cells in shoot nodes, in a polar manner toward the phloem, presumably for xylemphloem transfer (Wang et al. 2021).

The involvement of boric acid channels in the B efciency of $B$ . napus was frst demonstrated by the identifcation of a major quantitative trait locus (QTL) for B efciency using B-efcient QY10 and B-inefcient W10 populations. Fine-mapping and diferential gene expression analyses revealed the $B n a A O 3 . N I P 5 ; I b$ gene in the QTL (Hua et al. 2016; Zhang et al. 2014). The BnaA03.NIP5;1b is localized in the plasma membrane in a polar manner toward the soil in the lateral root cap, and is required for efcient B uptake into the root tip (He et al. 2021). Although there were no diferences in the amino acid sequences of BnaA03.NIP5;1b between B-efcient (QY10) and B-inefcient (W10) genotypes, their expression levels difered. BnaA03.NIP5;1b expression was higher in roots and leaves of QY10 than in those of W10 under low-B conditions (Yuan et al. 2017). A QY10 allele with a single tandem repeat (CTTTC) in the 5’UTR showed higher expression than a W10 allele with two tandem CTTTCs. Further genetic analysis showed that higher BnaA03.NIP5;1b expression in the QY10 allele was associated with low-B tolerance and high seed yield in diferent genotypes (He et  al. 2021). This fnding opened a path for marker-assisted breeding of low-B tolerance genotypes.

BnaA02NIP6;1a is a close homolog of AtNIP6;1, the boric acid transport activity of which was demonstrated in both yeast and oocytes (Diehn et al. 2019). Unlike AtNIP6;1, the expression of BnaA02NIP6;1a in B. napus was observed in the roots (matured root zone), stems, leaves, shoot nodal region, buds, and foral organs (Diehn et al. 2019; Song et al. 2021). B defciency symptoms in the BnaA02NIP6;1a RNAi lines were prominent in fower buds, indicating that BnaA02NIP6;1a plays an important role in B transport to the developing inforescence (Song et  al. 2021).

In a European winter genotype, NIP3 and NIP4 proteins (NIP-Is) and NIP5, NIP6, and NIP7 proteins (NIP-IIs) were highly expressed in various reproductive organs including fowers, rachises, peduncles, and pedicels under B limitation (Diehn et  al. 2019). A boric acid uptake assay in Xenopus oocytes showed that NIP2, NIP3, and NIP4 proteins showed boric acid transport activity in oocytes, in addition to NIP5, NIP6, and NIP7 proteins (Diehn et  al. 2019) An in-planta growth complementation assay of the Arabidopsis mutant Atnip5;1 under the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter showed that BnaNIP4s, NIP5s, NIP6s, and NIP7s function as boric acid channels in plants (Diehn et al. 2019). The identifcation of these new B-transporting NIP-I proteins (NIP2, NIP3, and NIP4) suggested their contribution to B homeostasis.

The involvement of transcription factor WRKY in B efciency was established in B. napus (Feng et  al. 2020). The promoter regions of BnaNIP5; ls and BnaBOR1s have many W boxes (T/CTGACC /T), which are the typical binding sites of WRKY. Y1H assays demonstrated the binding of BnaWRKYs to these W boxes of B-responsive BnaNIP5;1s and BnaBOR1s (Feng et  al. 2020). The mRNA level of BnaA03.NIP5;1b was signifcantly upregulated and downregulated in BnaA9.WRKY47 overexpressing lines and their null mutants, respectively, although the expression of other BnaNIP5;1s and BnaBOR1s was less afected. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutants of BnaA9.WRKY47 displayed severe B-defciency phenotypes under low-B conditions, and BnaA9.WRKY47 overexpressing lines showed higher tolerance to low B than the WT, indicating that BnaWRKYs play a vital role in the response of $B$ . napus to B defciency (Feng et al. 2020).


## Oryza sativa


As a monocotyledon, rice (Oryza sativa) has less pectin in its cell walls and requires less B for optimal growth than dicotyledons (Rerkasem et al. 2020). Therefore, rice is relatively tolerant to B limitation at the seedling stage. However, continual low B supply visibly reduces rice yield by impairing reproductive growth. The application of optimal B fertilizers increased straw yield, panicle yield, panicle fertility, and individual kernel weight in rice grown in Pakistan (Atique-ur-Rehman et al. 2018).

B stored in the seed endosperm contributes signifcantly to low-B tolerance during the seedling stage in rice (Uraguchi and Fujiwara 2011). Although rice seedlings without endosperm showed greatly reduced plant growth after 10 days under B limitation, plants with endosperm began to show visible B-defciency symptoms after 5 weeks.

Rice has four BORs; among these, OsBOR1 showed the highest similarity to AtBOR1 and exhibited borate export activity when expressed in yeast cells (Nakagawa et  al. 2007). OsBOR1 insertion mutants showed lower xylem sap B concentration and shoot growth rates under B limitation, indicating the important function of B translocation in rice plants (Nakagawa et al. 2007). Immunofuorescence analysis showed that OsBOR1 was localized in a polar manner to the proximal sides of exo- and endodermis cells in the plasma membrane in mature roots (Shao et al. 2021) and was subjected to high B-induced degradation in these cells within several hours (Huang et al. 2022). In shoots, OsBOR1 is expressed in nodes and leaf sheaths under B limitation (Shao et al. 2021).

OsNIP3;1, an NIP II protein showing the highest similarity to AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1, functions as a boric acid channel (Hanaoka et al. 2014). The expression of OsNIP3;1 mRNA was detected in both shoots and roots, and was induced under low-B conditions. OsNIP3;1 RNAi knockdown plants showed reduced growth and altered distribution of B in shoots (Hanaoka et al. 2014).

Transport studies using knockout mutants and immunofuorescence analyses have characterized the functions of OsBOR1 and OsNIP3;1 in preferential B distribution to developing tissues. In basal nodes, OsNIP3;1 and OsBOR1 work cooperatively for the intravascular transfer of B from the xylem of enlarged vascular bundles to that of difuse vascular bundles, whereas in newly developing leaves, they function in xylem unloading (Shao et al. 2018, 2021). By contrast, in developed leaves, OsBOR1 functions in preventing B release from xylem (Shao et al. 2021). OsBOR1 showed polar localization toward the distal sides of mestome sheath cells in developing leaves and the proximal side of bundle sheath cells in developed leaves. Diferential polar localization of OsNIP3;1 and OsBOR1 in the plasma membrane of diferent cell types is apparently critical to directional transport pathways (Shao et al. 2018, 2021).

OsLsi1/OsNIP2;1 belongs to the NIP III subfamily, and was frst identifed as a silicic acid channel polarly localized to the distal side of exo- and endodermis in roots for silicic acid uptake (Ma and Yamaji 2006). However, OsLsi1/OsNIP2;1 transported boric acid in addition to silicic acid in Xenopus oocytes (Mitani et al. 2008). In OsLsi1 knockout lines, more severe B defciency symptoms and reduced B uptake were observed (Shao et  al. 2018). These results showed that OsLsi1 is a major boric channel responsible for B uptake in mature rice roots (Shao et  al. 2018). Unlike in Arabidopsis, in rice, B uptake is not controlled in response to B conditions due to the dual function of the silicic acid channel, although B translocation is controlled through post-transcriptional regulation of OsNIP3;1 and OsBOR1.

OsBOR4 is similar to AtBOR4 and is preferentially expressed in mature pollen. An OsBOR4 insertion mutant showed poor pollen germination and reduced pollen tube growth. These results showed that OsBOR4 is involved in B homeostasis in pollen for fertilization (Tanaka et al. 2013).


## Hordeum vulgare and Triticum aestivum


The cereal crops wheat (Triticum aestivum L) and barley (Hordeum vulgare L.) require relatively low amounts of B during vegetative growth and higher amounts for reproductive growth. Yield losses due to B defciency have been widely reported in various countries (Rerkasem et al. 2020).

Three OsBOR1 orthologous B efux transporters, Bot-A4a (TaBOR1.2), Bot-B4a (TaBOR1.3), and Bot-D4a (TaBOR1.1), have been identifed in wheat (Leaungthitikanchana et  al. 2013). These B efux transporters show plasma membrane localization and B-dependent expression changes. TaBOR1.1 and TaBOR1.3 showed higher mRNA levels under low-B conditions, whereas TaBOR1.2 showed higher mRNA levels under excess B (Leaungthitikanchana et  al. 2013).

In a recent genome-wide association study, HvNIP2;2/HvLsi6 was identifed as a major gene responsible for grain B concentration (Jia et al. 2021). HvNIP2;2/HvLsi6 is an NIP III protein showing silicic acid and boric acid transport activity in Xen‑ opus oocytes (Jia et  al. 2021; Yamaji et  al. 2012). HvNIP2;2 is expressed in roots during the vegetative stage; however, it also shows high expression in the fag leaf, rachis, and developing grains during the reproductive stage (Jia et al. 2021). In numerous genotypes, variation in the mRNA expression levels of HvNIP2;2 is strongly associated with root and shoot B concentrations and root biomass under B limitation (Jia et al. 2021).

Excess soil B afects the yield of barley and wheat in arid and semi-arid regions including South Australia (Brdar-Jokanović, 2020; Schnurbusch et  al. 2010), where barley varieties with agronomical characteristics including high-B tolerance are promoted to help farmers select appropriate varieties to attain high yield (Paynter and Trainor 2017). The unadapted North African barley landrace Sahara 3771 has been considered breeding material for excess B tolerance (Hayes et  al. 2015). Physiological studies have shown that the high B-tolerant Sahara 3771, but not the B-sensitive ‘Schooner’ variety, maintains root B concentrations that are lower than that of the external medium (Hayes et al. 2015). QTL analysis of Sahara 3771 and the B-sensitive Clipper variety identifed HvBot1/HvBOR2, which encodes an ortholog of Arabidopsis BOR4, as the gene responsible for active B export and high-B tolerance (Sutton et  al. 2007). A high-B tolerance assay in yeast cells showed that Bot1 from Sahara 3771 has higher B export capacity than Clipper. The B-tolerant genotype Sahara 3771 contains fourfold more gene copies and \~ 160- to 180-fold higher Bot1 mRNA levels in roots and leaf blades, respectively, than Clipper (Sutton et al. 2007). Among Australian barley germplasm, all high B-tolerant genotypes were found to have tandemly duplicated Sahara 3771 HvBot1 alleles (Hayes et al. 2015).

QTL analysis identifed second B tolerance gene, HvNIP2;1 (also known as HvLsi1), which is a close ortholog of the NIP III-class protein OsLsi1/ OsNIP2;1. Heterologous expression of HvNIP2;1 in Xenopus oocytes showed signifcant boric acid transport activity along with that of silicic acid, germanium acid, arsenite, and water (Schnurbusch et al. 2010). HvNIP2;1/HvLsi1 is localized to the distal side of the plasma membrane in the epidermal and cortical cells of seminal roots, and has been suggested to be a major silicic acid channel responsible for silicic acid uptake in barley (Chiba et  al. 2009). Genetic analysis revealed that reduced HvNIP2;1/ HvLsi1 expression in Sahara 3771 confers tolerance to high-B conditions by decreasing B uptake (Schnurbusch et al. 2010). The coding sequence of HvNIP2;1 is highly conserved among germplasm. However, Sahara 3771 HvNIP2;1 alleles contain a singlenucleotide polymorphism in the $_ 5 '$ UTR that creates a small uORF, and an in vitro luciferase assay showed that the $_ 5 '$ UTR sequence of Sahara 3771 alleles inhibited translation (Hayes et al. 2015).

In wheat, the major QTLs for excess B tolerance were HvBot1-like Bot-B5/D5 alleles (Pallotta et  al. 2014). A wheat genotype containing the strong B tolerance allele Bot-B5b was bred for adaptation to the high-B environment in South Australia. Strong tolerance alleles have not been identifed for other wheat varieties from various agronomic zones worldwide (Pallotta et  al. 2014), which is consistent with the penalty associated with strong B export from tissues in low-B environments.

In barley and wheat, activity in root and leaf cells for exporting B to the apoplast was shown to contribute to excess B tolerance (Reid and Fitzpatrick 2009). Leaching during rain was also shown to reduce B concentrations in leaves and improve growth.


## Zea mays


Similar to most cereals, the vegetative growth of maize (Zea mays L.) is relatively insensitive to B limitation (Matthes et al. 2020). In the 1960s, B defciency symptoms were frst observed in feld-grown maize in the USA and the application of B fertilizer increased yield by $> 1 0 \%$ . The reproductive growth of maize plants was severely afected by decreased shoot apical meristem, smaller tassels, repressed ear development, dried anthers, and poor pollen vitality when grown under B-limited soil and hydroponic conditions (Lordkaew et  al. 2011; Woodruf et  al. 1987). Studies conducted using two maize mutants with defective inforescence development, tassel-less1 (tsl1) and rotten ear (rte), have increased our understanding of B transport in maize.

The causal gene of the tsl1 mutant encodes the NIP II protein ZmNIP3;1, which is an ortholog of AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1, and OsNIP3;1. ZmNIP3;1 functions as a boric acid channel and is necessary for B transport under B limitation for vegetative and reproductive growth (Durbak et  al. 2014; Leonard et  al. 2014). A recent study showed that mutation of thick tassel dwarf 1 (td1), a gene involved in the CLAVATA-WUSCHEL meristem development pathway, partially suppressed the defects of tls1 tassel meristems (Matthes et al. 2022).

The causal gene of rte encodes an ortholog of AtBOR1 (Chatterjee et  al. 2014). RTE and its close homolog RTE2 are expressed in both roots and shoots (Chatterjee et  al. 2017). Compared to single rte mutants, double rte;rte2 mutants showed greater defects in both vegetative and reproductive development under B limitation (Chatterjee et al. 2017). This fnding suggests functional redundancy of the RTE gene in maize under B limitation. Considering the physiological efects of the rte;rte2 double mutant and tls1 mutant, RTE and RTE2 have been hypothesized to work synergistically with TLS1 (ZmNIP3;1) in B uptake and xylem loading in roots (Chatterjee et al. 2017).


## Generation of transgenic plants to alleviate B defciency and toxicity


The extensive understanding of B transport mechanisms provides opportunities to improve crops for better B utilization under varied soil B conditions. Overexpression of AtBOR1 under the control of Caulifower mosaic virus 35S RNA increased root-toshoot B translocation, shoot growth, and seed yield (Miwa et al. 2006). Enhanced expression of AtNIP5;1 or AtBOR2 using chimera 35S and AtNIP5;1/BOR2 promoters improved root elongation under B limitation in transgenic Arabidopsis (Kato et  al. 2009; Takada et  al. 2014). Transgenic tomato (Solanum lycopersium L.) and rice overexpressed with AtBOR1 and OsBOR1, respectively, showed improved growth and yield under low-B conditions (Uraguchi et  al. 2009, 2014). As mentioned earlier, increased production of B-complexing sugar alcohol resulted in increased B uptake and mobility, in turn increasing tolerance to B limitation in tobacco and rice (Bellaloui et al. 1999, 2003; Brown et al. 1999).

Overexpression of BOR4 in Arabidopsis enhanced growth under excess B conditions, which was attributed to reduced B concentration in the cells of roots and shoots (Miwa et  al. 2007; Miwa and Fujiwara 2011). Transgenic rice plants expressing AtBOR4 also showed growth enhancement under excess B (Kajikawa et  al. 2014). The expression of a BOR1 K590A mutant fused with hygromycin phosphotransferase under the control of the ubiquitin 10 promoter showed weak polar localization and stabilized expression under high-B conditions, and had excess B tolerance in Arabidopsis (Wakuta et  al. 2016). In transgenic plants, enhanced B export from root cells was visualized using a genetically encoded biosensor for cytosolic boric acid (Fukuda et  al. 2018). These results demonstrate the potential of genetic engineering in the development of crop plants tolerant to B limitation and excess.

Boron (B) is one of the essential micronutrients that play multiple crucial physiological functions in higher plants, such as cell wall formation, cell division, cell elongation, fowering, fruiting, rooting, nutrient uptake, ion fux, carbohydrate metabolism, nitrogen metabolism, and hormone regulation [1]. However, high B levels are hazardous to plant development [2]. Diferent parts of a plant have unique requirements and functions of B [1]. Furthermore, various plant species, varieties, and plants of various ages respond diferently to B shortage or toxicity [2]. Te primary source of B in plants is from the soil, which can be found as borate or boric acid $\left( \mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } \right)$ in soil solutions. Plants absorb boric acid using three different methods, depending on its accessibility: difusion, major intrinsic proteins (MIP), and B exporters (BOR) transporters [3]. Passive difusion and MIP transport are used when B is adequately available, whereas BOR transporters are used when B is absent. Previous studies revealed B transport in Arabidopsis thaliana plant occurs not just by passive difusion but is also regulated by transport proteins such as boric acid channels (nodulin-26-like intrinsic proteins or NIPs) and B exporters (BORs) [4]. NIPs and BORs work together to keep plant development regular in high and low B environments.

Longan (Dimocarpus longan Lour.) is a prominent subtropical fruit tree native to South China, holding 70 and $6 0 \%$ of the world’s Longan cultivation feld and yield in 2010 [5]. Tere are over 400 varieties of Longan cultivars in China [6], and the majority $( 6 8 \% )$ of them grow during the mid-season (August-September) [5]. Tis season is presided by the rainy season of southeast Asia that depletes relatively soluble B in the soil by leaching it with the rainfall [2]. B efect on Longan’s fruit quality is well studied and practised [5]. A foliar spray of boric acid and applying B fertilizer have increased fruit size, quality, and soluble sugar [3] and reduced fower and fruit drops [7]. For optimal Longan harvesting, it is necessary to understand and employ the proper dose of B. However, the molecular mechanism for B uptake and translocation in various Longan species are not fully understood. We studied two commonly cultivated Longan varieties, the traditional cultivar Shixia (SX), with 140 years of cultivation history in China [5], and the newer Yiduo (YD) cultivar, with better fruit quality [6, 7]. YD was introduced to China from Tailand, making up $9 0 \%$ of the Tai Longan yield [7].

In this study, we observed cellular structural diferences, the sugar content of their leaf cells, the fower’s Jasmonic acid (JA) content, the fruit-setting rate, and the B content of diferent plant organs after foliar B treatment. We also identifed the genes of the BOR and NIP gene families and studied their evolutionary relation, cis-acting elements, and level of expression in diferent tissues. Depending on this analysis, genes that expressed most in various organs of SX and YD were selected for further study. Subcellular localization of this gene product was studied by creating versatile green fuorescent protein (GFP)-gene expression vectors and transforming SX pollen. B tolerance of the GFP-gene transformed pollens was studied, and Longan plants were pollinated using this pollen to check the germination rate. Te unilateral cross incompatibility (UCI) between SX and YD was reported to hinder the attempt to generate successful crossbreeding [6]. So, we established a crossing of $\mathrm { Y D } \mathscr { Q } \times \mathrm { S X } \mathscr { d }$ using hybrid pollen to study the fruit-setting rate of the hybrid panicle.

## Research progress on Boron transporters (BORs) in different species


Boron, as a trace element, is crucial for the growth of higher plants and is involved in all metabolic and cellular functions, especially in the formation and stabilization of cell walls [32]. RG-II, a highly intricate pectin-based polysaccharide, serves as a vital structural element within the primary cellular matrix of plants. It is composed of a variety of sugar residues that are connected by different glucoside bonds. RG-II exists as a dimer in the cell wall and is connected through borate diester bonds. This boron crosslinking connects two homogalacturonic acid chains to form a three-dimensional pectin network, which is essential for preserving the structural integrity and functional strength of the cell wall. Boron deficiency reduces the cross-linking of pectin, affecting the properties of the cellular matrix. This may lead to various symptoms associated with boron deficiency in plants [32]. In recent years, with our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of plant nutrition deepening and the identification of BOR protein as a key carrier of boron transmembrane transport, its function analysis has achieved important progress in a variety of model plants. For example, Arabidopsis AtBOR1 has been shown to maintain intracellular boron homeostasis through efflux transport [33], whereas rice OsBOR4 regulates normal pollen germination and pollen tube elongation [17]. Citrus CmBOR1, as a xylem boron-carrying transporter, encodes a boric acid/borate transporter related to plant boron deficiency tolerance [34]. These studies indicate that the domain of the BOR protein is closely related to its transport activity and that functional differentiation occurs among different species. However, as an important global cash crop, cotton prematurity may be partly affected by the dynamic remodeling ability of the cell wall, and the transmembrane transport of boron directly affects the formation of RG-II dimers in the cell wall. At present, the conservation and evolutionary relationships of BOR family genes and their intrinsic domains have been analyzed in Arabidopsis and other crop species, but this gene has not been reported in cotton. Therefore, a systematic analysis of the evolutionary characteristics, domain conservation, and boron transport function of the BOR gene family in cotton will help elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the response of cotton to boron stress and provide a theoretical basis and candidate gene resources for the exploration of key genes that regulate early maturity traits.


## Characterization and conserved evolution of the BOR gene family in cotton


In this study, we comprehensively identified the ${ \mathrm { H C O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ domain-containing BORs within the genomes of cotton species, including a total of 23 GhBORs in allotetraploid upland cotton, 13 in diploid Asian cotton, and 14 in Raimondii cotton. The quantity of BORs found in the tetraploids was nearly double that found in the diploids. The physicochemical parameters and structural characteristics of the members of the BOR family were similar across the three cotton varieties (Table  1). We classified these genes into four classes on the basis of their evolutionary relationships with GhBOR in upland cotton. Subfamilies I and III included both continuous and independent interspecific clades, indicating that BOR evolution was relatively conservative and ancient (Fig.  1), with cotton BOR genes showing a close phylogenetic relationship to those in soybean, cocoa, and Arabidopsis. Subfamily II contained the BOR genes from rice and wheat, which are monocotyledonous plants. Polyploidy represents a major driving force in evolutionary processes, fostering species diversification and increasing genomic variability [35]. Tetraploid upland cotton originated through chromosome doubling following the interspecific hybridization of diploid Asian cotton and Raimondii cotton [36, 37]. Nevertheless, compared with Asian cotton and Raimondii cotton, upland cotton presented fewer $B O R s _ { \mathrm { { \scriptsize { B } } } }$ which may have been due to chromosome loss and rearrangement during evolution. We discovered no significant difference in the Ka/Ks ratio between diploid and tetraploid cotton, and the ratio was less than 1 in all species, indicating the stability of these gene sequences across evolution in this family. To further confirm the selection pressure on this gene, a Ka/Ks ratio analysis was conducted (Fig.  3). The results demonstrated that the ratio was less than 1, concentrated at 0.2, and that all the genes underwent negative selection, indicating that the evolutionary pattern was similar and conservative within this family.


## GhBOR1 regulates the reproductive development of cotton by coordinating flowering-related gene expression


Given the critical role of boron in plant development, especially during seed formation, the anion exchange activity of the BOR protein is crucial. The basic feature of the BOR protein is its anion exchange activity, and the ${ \mathrm { H C O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ domain plays an essential role in the anion transport process [38–41]. Previous investigations have shown that the nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right)$ concentration significantly affects the B concentration in leaves and BOR1 gene expression in roots. Under high- $\mathrm { \cdot N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ conditions, the growth of the BOR1 mutant is negatively affected by B restriction, whereas this effect is weak under normal $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ conditions, indicating that BOR1 is involved in the growth regulation of plants under high- $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ environments [42]. In addition, BOR1 is transported to vacuoles for degradation via K63-linked polyubiquitination to prevent excessive B accumulation [43]. A previous study revealed that BOR1 interacts with the calcium-dependent protein kinase CPK10 in plants, which regulates BOR1 activity in the absence of B [44]. OsBOR1 in rice plays a similar role in B absorption and xylem transport, and its expression varies in a time- and tissue-dependent manner under different B supply conditions [45]. These studies revealed the key role of BOR1 in the regulation of plant B nutrition. Moreover, the protein encoded by the BOR gene is a key factor in plant reproductive growth. It plays a vital role in plant cell wall synthesis, pollen germination, pollen tube elongation, and seed yield [3, 17, 20, 46]. In this study, we identified candidate flowering genes in upland cotton via qRT-PCR and RNA-seq and subsequently validated the gene function by VIGS (Figs. 6 and 7). In grapes, preferential expression of the VvBOR1 gene is observed within floral tissues, and this gene participates in the accumulation of B in berries [20]. Similarly, the rapeseed BnaC4.BOR1;1c gene, a homolog of Atbor1, is expressed in roots and stem segments and is critical for inflorescence tissue development [3], confirming that GhBOR1 is a key regulatory gene in cotton flowering. Our study revealed that silencing GhBOR1 delayed bud emergence and flowering, as VIGS inhibition of GhBOR1 expression led to boron transport blockage, resulting in boron deficiency that affected flower organ development and the timing of flowering (Fig.  7A). Additionally, pollen viability measurements in control and silenced plants suggested that the loss of GhBOR1 led to pollen abortion (Fig.  7D). These findings are consistent with those from previous studies of the effects of OsBOR4, a boron effector transporter in rice, during pollen germination and tube elongation [17]. Several key flowering genes in G. hirsutum, including GhAP1 and GhFT, which positively regulate flowering, have been reported [47, 48]. In this study, we revealed that silencing the GhBOR1 gene in upland cotton resulted in significantly reduced relative transcriptional levels of the key flowering-related genes GhAP1, GhFT, and GhLFY, thereby regulating the flowering period, which is consistent with the findings of previous studies. Furthermore, the expression level of GhSVP markedly increased in the silenced lines, which is consistent with the findings of prior studies demonstrating that SVP inhibits the expression of floweringassociated integrons such as FT and SOC1 under specific conditions (Fig.  7F). These results suggest that GhBOR1 may regulate flowering by influencing the expression of key genes, possibly through a complex network involving both positive and negative regulation. Additionally, to elucidate the potential mechanism underlying the regulatory function of GhBOR1 in flowering, we constructed a GhBOR protein interaction network and identified 10 putative interacting proteins (Fig. S1). Among them, NPI5-1, which is known to be similar to BOR1, was previously shown to be the main plasma membrane channel involved in boron (or boric acid) transport in plants [7, 43]. Similarly, although NPI6-1 plays a role in different tissues, its expression pattern is similar to that of NPI5- 1, suggesting that they may share a common regulatory pathway [49]. We speculate that GhBOR1 and NPI5-1 coregulate boron homeostasis in plants, thereby further modulating plant flowering.

Despite having a short speciation time of about 7500 yrs, B. napus displays an impressive genetic diversity (Chalhoub et al., 2014). This is due to the fact that this allopolyploid species formed probably several times independently through interspecific crosses between B. rapa and B. oleracea. Thereafter, several genetically distinct variants have been developed in adaption to geographic, environmental, and nutritional demands and according to breeding objectives. This resulted in European winter-, Asian semi-winter-, Canadian-, Australian-, Asian-, and European spring-type cultivars. All B. napus types have a high demand for B in common. European rapeseeds have been cultivated from the Middle Age onwards and spread throughout the world. Since the 1970, ‘double low’ alleles from Canadian and Polish genotypes have been introgressed into European cultivars. Cv. Darmor-bzh shares this history (Chalhoub et al., 2014). Cv. ZS11 is a Chinese semi-winter-type ‘double low’ variety. Chinese rapeseeds probably derive from European cultivars. Subsequently, they were modified by introgression of B. rapa cultivars which had been cultivated for more than 1000 yrs in Asia. These introgression events amplified their genetic diversity. From the 1970/80s, European ‘double low’ cultivars have been introgressed into the Chinese B. napus gene pool. Cv. ZS11 belongs to this latter pool of cultivars. Due to their separate breeding history, adaptions to different soils and climates (Chalhoub et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2017), we expected a different B transporter composition between ZS11 and Darmor-bzh, but found a very similar configuration and a high protein sequence identity of transporters encoded by syntenic gene pairs. In future, comparison of the herein described B transporters with those of Asian cultivars existing prior to the introgression of ‘double low’ traits from non-Asian cultivars will help to understand evolution of B transport during domestication of B. napus and to identify B efficiency transport traits which can be used for the breeding of modern elite lines.

To shed light into the scarcely elucidated molecular functions and regulations of B transporters of rapeseed, we cloned a large set of selected NIPs (from different subfamilies) and BOR1s, tested their transport selectivity and characterized them at the molecular level.


## BOR characteristics


Using the ∆atr1 and ∆bor1 yeast mutant strains, we demonstrated that all six BOR1s of rapeseed are functional B transporters. The fact, that rapeseed kept all six BOR1 isoforms, which have formed by genome multiplications since the evolutionary split from Arabidopsis, underlines their importance for a tightly operated B transport regulation. We then investigated the tissue- and B-dependent expression to understand when and where BOR1s may play a role in B transport.

Under B-deficient growth conditions, BnaC04.BOR1;2c and BnaA04.BOR1;1a were significantly up-regulated in roots and leaves at the peduncle. Our expression map significantly advanced the state-of-the-art knowledge on BOR1 expression patterns, especially in floral tissues. Besides their root expression, all BOR1s showed highest expression in the rachis and in open flowers suggesting that these isoforms are particularly important to deliver B to these highly B deficiency sensitive organs. In contrast to Chen et al. (Chen et al., 2018), no B deficiency-mediated up-regulation of BnaC04.BOR1;1c, BnaA05.BOR1;2a and BnaA03BOR1;3a was detected, neither in the roots, the shoots nor the diverse floral tissues. This indicates that different rapeseed cultivars developed a cultivar-specific BOR1 expression pattern, which may result from the adaptation to different environmental demands. The quantified constitutive high expression of BOR1s might help to constantly ensure B delivery to flowers even under suddenly occurring B-limiting periods when a de novo translation might be too late to prevent detrimental effects.

## NIP characteristics


Experimental data on NIPs of different plant species suggest that they are either impermeable or only weakly permeable to water (Roberts and Routray, 2017). This is in agreement with our results, namely that only BnaC08.NIP3;1c, BnaC04.NIP4;1a, BnaC06.NIP5;1b, and BnaA02.NIP6;1a showed a slightly increased water permeability. The $\mathsf { P _ { f } }$ values of the oocytes expressing these four isoforms are however very low compared to that of oocytes expressing typical ZmPIP2;5 water channel.

Performing B isotope-discrimination uptake assays in oocytes, we detected significant B permeability for all tested NIP2 to NIP7 isoforms except for BnaA05.NIP3;1b and BnaA04.NIP4;1a. Our quantitative assays provided functional evidence that, in addition to members of the NIP5, NIP6 and NIP7 groups, also members of the NIP2, NIP3 and NIP4 groups facilitate the transmembrane diffusion of B. These results indicate that also the latter isoforms that have not been assayed for B transport before, have an impact on the B nutritional status of rapeseed plants and have to be considered in further studies dealing with B transport processes in plants. Interestingly, all assayed NIP2 to NIP7 isoforms were permeable to As, also BnaA05.NIP3;1b and BnaA04.NIP4;1a which did not significantly increase the uptake of B into oocytes. This observation is in agreement with other studies suggesting that As permeability is widespread amongst NIP aquaporin subgroups and that the restrictions for As passage through NIP channels appear to be lower than those for other metalloids such as B (Zhao et al., 2009; Mitani-Ueno et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2015). Interestingly, permeability to As had not been demonstrated for NIP2s and NIP4s, previously.

Transport assays with AtNIP7;1 expressed in Xenopus oocytes showed extremely low B transport rates due to a suggested gating function of a conserved tyrosine in helix 2 (Li et al., 2011). In contrast, BnaA05.NIP7;1a exhibited significantly higher B and As transport rates compared to the negative controls, providing evidence for the activity of the native NIP7 isoforms also in biological membranes despite the presence of the Tyr81 in helix 2. Together, our direct transport assays in oocytes suggest that the tested NIP2 to NIP7 group isoforms are functional B and As channels in rapeseed and have therefore an impact on the distribution of B and As in this high-B-demanding crop.

We experimentally confirmed the B transport ability of BnaNIPs in in planta growth complementation assays using Atnip5;1 knockout lines expressing different BnaNIPs under the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter. Obvious growth defects and B deficiency symptoms of the Atnip5;1 mutants were not observed during the vegetative growth stage of AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \mathcal { I } } _ { p r o }$ :BnaC04.NIP4;1b, AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ :BnaC04.NIP4;1a, AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ :BnaLOC106388529 (NIP5), AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ :BnaC06.NIP6;1a, or AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ :BnaC05.NIP7;1a expressing transformants. These results strikingly demonstrated that the assayed BnaNIP4, BnaNIP5, BnaNIP6 and BnaNIP7 isoforms are also functional metalloidoporins in plants. Unexpectedly, all NIP transformants, including the AtNIP5; $\pmb { 1 } _ { p r o } . A t N I P 5 ; \pmb { 1 }$ ones, had lower shoot fresh weights than the Col-0 wild-type plants and depended on a surplus of B during the vegetative growth stage to be able to develop fertile flowers even under standard growth conditions. For NIP4 and NIP7 transformants one may speculate that a lacking polar localization of these isoforms was responsible for the incomplete recovery of the wild-type growth behavior, since only correctly polar-localized Arabidopsis NIPs, such as AtNIP5;1 or AtNIP6;1 totally complement Atnip5;1 mutants (Wang et al., 2017). The AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ fragment that we used differs slightly from the AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle { \pmb { 1 } } _ { p r o }$ constructs which was used in earlier studies due to cloning specification (Takano et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2017). Additionally, our constructs contained the coding- and not the genomic AtNIP5;1 sequence for expression. Why the NIP5 transformants in this study did not fully rescue the mutant phenotype remains to be elucidated in future. We speculate that this might be due to either missing promoter or enhancer elements located upstream and not integrated in our promoter, or harsher B limiting soil conditions than used in Takano et al. (2006).

In contrast to previous studies on B transporter expression patterns in plants, we particularly focused on the expression of B transporters under B-deficient and B-sufficient conditions in floral tissues. This was possible as we successfully managed to set-up a soil-substrate based growth conditions in which plants can grow phenotypically identical until the flowering stage (BBCH60) under B-sufficient and B-deficient conditions. At this growth stage, the first flowers developed normally without any obvious B deficiency phenotypes, though the plants possessed intrinsic B levels, which are typical for severely B-deficient rapeseed plants (Figure S1). Thereupon, from BBCH61 onwards, typical B deficiency symptoms appeared and finally resulted in the ‘flowering without seed setting’ syndrome. This growth set-up allowed us to investigate in detail the B-dependent expression of B transporters under controlled and reproducible B-deficient conditions during the onset of flowering, when the inflorescences are particular susceptible to B deficiency. As flowering is the developmental stage, which is most prone to B deficiency and subsequent yield losses, it is highly important to understand how B logistics are regulated there and to spot transport bottlenecks, firstly in flowers themselves but also in tissues supplying nutrients to the flowers such as the rachis, peduncles and pedicels. This knowledge provides the basis to potentially enhance transport efficiency in rapeseed and prevent B deficiency caused yield losses. Using this growth setup, we determined tissue- and B-dependent expression patterns at $\geq$ BBCH60 to understand when and where NIPs might play a role in floral B transport fluxes. Thereby, we demonstrated that the previously root-specific defined BnaA02.NIP6;1a isoform (Yuan et al., 2017) is actually highly expressed in the inflorescence (Figure 5b). Moreover, we demonstrated that BnaC05.NIP3;1b, BnaA05.NIP3;1b and NIP7 isoforms are strongly expressed in various inflorescence tissues including the rachis and the open- and closed flowers. Diverse B-permeable NIP4s were also detected in the inflorescence. In addition, several NIP3 and NIP4 genes were either significantly up-or down-regulated dependent on the tissue and the plants’ B nutritional status, indicating that these channel-types are actively regulated by this micronutrient and impact on its distribution. Especially our observations that BnaNIP4s are (i) permeable to B and (ii) expressed dependent on the plants’ B status are interesting with respect to the fact that in Arabidopsis, AtNIP4;1 and AtNIP4;2 seem to be required for pollen development and pollination, two processes which are highly dependent on sufficient B supply also in rapeseed (Di Giorgio et al., 2016). Whether the importance of Arabidopsis NIP4s in pollen development and pollination is due to their B transport function remains unknown to date.

In contrast to the root-specific expression of AtNIP5;1, but in agreement with expression data from B. napus cvs. Q10 and W10 (Yuan et al., 2017), we detected NIP5 transcripts also in shoot tissues and, so far not detected, in floral tissues. Four out of six Darmor-PBY018 NIP5s were strongly up-regulated in roots and shoots under B-deficient conditions. BnaA02.NIP5;1b and BnaC02NIP5;1b were up-regulated in closed flower buds under Bdeficient conditions. No up-regulation under limited B supply was observed for BnaA07.NIP5;1c and BnaC06.NIP5;1c under all tested condition (Figure 6b). Despite their high sequence similarity (Figure 1), this pair displays a completely differential expression pattern (Figure 5b). Together our results suggested that NIP5s are key transport regulators under B-limiting conditions and ensure B fluxes throughout the plant body. BnaA03.NIP5;1a, which significantly contributes to B-efficiency in cv. Q10 (Hua et al., 2016a), was the B transporter with the highest total up-regulation under B-deficient conditions, namely 57-fold in roots. Moreover, compared to the expression of other NIP5s, BnaA03NIP5;1a was almost exclusively detected in roots. The strong B-deficiency-responsiveness of BnaNIP5s in roots and shoots was confirmed in Arabidopsis plants expressing three different $B n a N I P 5 _ { p r o }$ :GUS constructs. For instance, the promoter activity of BnaA03.NIP5;1b but also of BnaC02.NIP5;1a, which were both found in B-efficiency QTLs in cv. Q10 (Hua et al., 2016a), were strongly enhanced under our B-limiting conditions.

This specific regulation of BnaNIP5 expression under B-deficient conditions goes well in line with the existence of a minimum open reading frame (ORF), ATG-Stop, in all six BnaNIP5 promoters (Figure S2). It has been shown that this minimum ORF is crucial for controlling AtNIP5;1 mRNA levels in dependence of the B supply conditions in Arabidopsis (Tanaka et al., 2016) and we hypothesize that the minimum ORFs of BnaNIP5 promoters have a similar conserved function in B. napus. Our qPCR data, obtained for BnaA07.NIP5;1c and BnaC06.NIP5;1c, demonstrated that further tissue- and developmental transcriptional control mechanisms must exist to regulate the activity of these two promoters in addition to the ATG-Stop motif.

Together, with the provided evidence that these isoforms are highly permeable to B (Figure 2), these observations underlined the importance of these isoforms for B uptake transport processes in rapeseed. Interestingly, while we did not detect a significant up-regulation of BnaA07.NIP5;1c by RT-qPCR under B-deficient conditions, we observed an obvious induced promoter activity in the GUS assays. This indicates that BnaA07.NIP5;1c transcript abundance is additionally developmentally regulated. NIP5 promoter activity was strongly enhanced in the vasculature of root tips and in zones were lateral roots emerged. Whether BnaNIP5 isoforms play a role in lateral root emergence or whether this promoter activity is due to the fact that the activity was tested in a heterologous plant expression system will be further investigated. Moreover, in contrast to the AtNIP5; $\scriptstyle 1 _ { p r o }$ , the BnaNIP5;1 promoters were not active in the root epidermis of Arabidopsis.

The results of the GUS staining time series (Figure 7 and S3) indicate that the detected BnaNIP5;1 promoter signals are not caused by a methodological artifact but indeed represent the BnaNIP5;1 promoter activities in the heterologous expression host Arabidopsis.

With this study, we provide comprehensive experimental evidence for B transport functions of six BOR1- and twelve NIP-type B. napus B transporters exploiting transport assays in yeast (BOR1s) and oocytes (NIP2, NIP3, NIP4, NIP5, NIP6 and NIP7) as well as B transport complementation assays in Arabidopsis (NIP4, NIP5, NIP6 and NIP7). In combination with the generated tissue-specific, developmental-, and B-status-dependent expression maps for BOR and NIP genes, these results suggest that in particular NIP5s are key players in the routing of B fluxes throughout the plant. Additionally, we uncovered that members of other NIP subfamilies, such as NIP2, NIP3 and NIP4s, which have not yet been associated with B transport processes, have an impact on B transport regulation. Many BOR1s and NIPs are highly expressed within diverse tissues of the inflorescence or some are even flower-specific such as BnaC05.NIP7;1a, BnaA05.NIP7;1a and BnaA04NIP4;1b. This indicates that the delivery of B to and its allocation within the flowers is tightly managed by both NIPs and BORs and further highlights the role of B for the fertility of plants. Comparing our DarmorPBY018 expression results to previous studies on QY10 or W10 (Yuan et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018), we can conclude that cultivar-specific B transporter expression characteristics exist. Such a diversity is fundamental for breeding strategies aiming at improving the B efficiency of Brassica crops to face future agricultural challenges.
