## Effect of Different Induction Systems on Expression of Nitrate Transporter Genes


All high-affinity nitrate transporter genes (TaNRT2.1, TaNRT2.3, and TaNRT2) were up-regulated in root tissues ranging from 4 to 40-fold, which were exposed with lower external nitrate concentrations $\mathrm { 0 . 0 4 } \mathrm { m M }$ and $0 . 4 \mathrm { m M }$ ) compared to NI root tissues. Except in the case of TaNRT2.3 (down-regulated by almost eight times), the $2 \ \mathrm { m M }$ condition induced the expression of two other high-affinity nitrate transporter genes as compared to NI root tissues. The $\mathrm { 8 ~ m M }$ induction system always down-regulated gene expression of all transporters except TaNRT2.1. As far as C and N metabolite inclusion in the $2 \mathrm { m M }$ induction system is concerned, $+ \cal S$ and $+ \mathrm { S G A }$ caused up-regulation of TaNRT2.3 as compared to $2 \mathrm { m M }$ root tissues. $+ \mathrm { G }$ , $+ \mathbf { A }$ and their combinations with sucrose down-regulated the expression of TaNRT2.3. In the case of TaNRT2.1, all N and C combinations cause downregulation of the gene when included in the $2 \mathrm { m M }$ induction system but independently these sources have positive regulations. These systems, however, down-regulated TaNRT2, except $+ \mathrm { G }$ and $+ \cal S$ , when included in the $2 \mathrm { m M }$ induction system. The low-affinity nitrate transporter TaNRT1.1 was down-regulated in $0 . 0 4 \mathrm { m M }$ , $2 \mathrm { m M }$ , and $\mathrm { 8 ~ m M }$ root tissues, but interestingly in the case of the $0 . 4 \mathrm { m M }$ induction system it was up-regulated. In this case except $+ \mathbf { A }$ and $+ \mathrm { { S G } }$ , other C and $\mathbf { N }$ systems caused up-regulation of TaNRT1.1 expression when included in the $2 \mathrm { m M }$ induction system (Fig. 6).

Nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \right)$ , a primary source of inorganic nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ , is essential for plant growth and developmen, and efficient $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake is an integral part of N cycling (Konishi and Yanagisawa 2014). To ensure crop productivity, massive quantities of N fertilizers are applied worldwide each year. This practice consumes large amounts of energy and poses a great threat to the environment (McAllister et al. 2012). Therefore, the enhancement of plant N use efficiency (NUE) is imperative for the sustainable development of agriculture (Hu et al. 2015b; Wang et al. 2018).

To contend with heterogeneous soil $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ availabilities, plants have evolved at least three $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake systems responsible for efficient $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ acquisition: constitutive and inducible high-affinity transport systems (cHATS and iHATS), operating at submillimolar $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ - concentrations, and the low-affinity transport system (LATS), functioning in the millimolar $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ -concentration range (Wang et al. 2012). The $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ HATS play major roles in the efficient N uptake and transport under N limitations, which are pivotal for NUE enhancement and N fertilizer reduction in crops (Chen et al. 2016).

In plants, all of the $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ HATS members with nitrate-nitrite-porter (NNP) domains belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). High-affinity $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake by plant roots is mediated by nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) with seven members (NRT2.1-NRT2.7) in A. thaliana (Dechorgnat et al. 2011; Forde 2000; Léran et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2012). NRT2.1 is the key contributor of iHATS to facilitating $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ into root cells (Filleur et al. 2001; Forde 2000). In contrast, NRT2.2 makes only a small contribution to iHATS; when NRT2.1 is lost, this contribution increases, resulting in a partial compensation (Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 is involved in root $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake at very low $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations and in shoot phloem $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ loading (Kiba et al. 2012). AtNRT2.5 is essential for efficient $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake and remobilization in adult plants by participating in phloem $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ loading under severe $_ \mathrm { N }$ starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Unlike the four NRT2 transporters above-mentioned, AtNRT2.7 is localized in the tonoplast and is specifically expressed in the seeds, where it is responsible for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ accumulation in the vacuoles (Chopin et al. 2007). However, neither NRT2.3 nor NRT2.6 has not yet been identified to be N transporters implicated in $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake or translocation (Okamoto et al. 2003).

For $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transport, AtNRT2s, except AtNRT2.7, require a second accessory protein, AtNAR2.1 (nitrate assimilation related 2.1)/AtNRT3.1, in a $2 \times 2$ tetramer configuration (Kotur et al. 2012; Kotur and Glass 2015; Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). In rice, OsNRT2.1, OsNRT2.2, and OsNRT2.3a of the OsNRT2 family, are transcriptionally up-regulated by $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ supply and require a partner protein, OsNAR2.1, for $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake at different concentration ranges (Cai et al. 2008; Feng et al. 2011; Tang et al. 2012; Tsay et al. 2007; Yan et al. 2011). Similarly, in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, NAR2 is essential for the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport activity of CrNRT2.1 and CrNRT2.2 (Zhou et al. 2000a). Nevertheless, not all members of the NRT2 family require a protein partner to be able to function. For example, a related gene from Aspergillus nidulans shows highaffinity nitrate transport when alone expressed in oocytes (Zhou et al. 2000b).

Oilseed rape (Brassica napus L.), a high-value crop species, is widely cultivated and harvested for the production of vegetable oil, livestock protein meal and biodiesel (Blackshaw et al. 2011). The allotetraploid $B .$ . napus $\mathrm { ( A _ { n } A _ { n } C _ { n } C _ { n } , }$ ${ \sim } 1 3 4 5 \ \mathrm { M b }$ , $2 n = 4 \times = 3 8$ ) originated from spontaneous interspecific hybridization of the diploid progenitors Brassica rapa $( \mathrm { A _ { r } A _ { r } } ,$ ${ \sim } 4 8 5 \ \mathrm { \ M b }$ , $2 n = 2 \times = 2 0$ ) (Wang et al. 2011) and Brassica oleracea $\mathrm { { C } _ { o } C _ { o } }$ , ${ \sim } 6 3 0$ Mb, $2 n = 2 \times = 1 8$ (Liu et al. 2014) $\sim 7 5 0 0$ years ago (Bayer et al. 2017; Chalhoub et al. 2014; Sun et al. 2017). When compared with A. thaliana $( \sim 1 2 5 \ \mathrm { M b }$ , $2 n = 2 \times = 1 0$ ) (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative 2000), also a member of Brassicaceae, the allopolyploidy events occurring in $B$ . napus generated many duplicated segments and homoeologous regions within the genome (Chalhoub et al. 2014).

B. napus has a higher nutrient requirement for optimum yield than cereals (Grant and Bailey 1993), whereas it is extremely susceptible to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Rathke et al. 2005). However, the molecular mechanisms underlying efficient N uptake and transport remain poorly understood because of the genome complexity. The objectives of the present study were to: (i) identify the genome-wide Brassica NRT2s/NAR2s family members, (ii) determine the genomic and transcriptomic characteristics of the THATS genes, (iii) characterize the core THATS members. In this study, genome-wide identification and molecular characterization of the core THATS transporters provide elite gene resources for crop NUE improvement, and the transcriptomics-assisted gene co-expression network analysis provides novel insights regarding the rapid identification of central members within large gene families of plant species with complex genomes.

The first eukaryotic $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporter gene was isolated over 15 years ago from the fungus, Aspergillus nidulans (Unkles et al., 1991). A few years later a gene encoding an Arabidopsis $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporter was isolated and although this gene also had 12 putative trans-membrane domains it was phylogenetically unrelated to the earlier fungal gene (Tsay et al., 1993). These two types of genes each define the types of transporters that mediate $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake from external sources, and they have become known as the NRT1 and NRT2 families. Both families transport $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ together with a proton $\mathrm { ( H ^ { + } ) }$ in a symport mechanism that is driven by the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradients across membranes. Although other membrane proteins that can transport $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ have been identified, these two families are the best characterized and are therefore the main topic of this review. Most of the information for these gene families has been obtained for Arabidopsis and so much of what is discussed refers to the situation in this plant. In this review, consideration is given as to how well our molecular and physiological knowledge can be integrated and what the key questions and opportunities are for the future is discussed. The transporters that might be key targets for future improvement of nitrogen use by crops are discussed along the way, but to understand $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ acquisition by land plants the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ availability in the soil must be considered and this is where we start.


## Nitrate in the soil


Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ can be available to plant roots in several different forms, including $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , ammonium $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } ) }$ , and organic forms chiefly amino acids. Nitrate is usually the most abundant source of $\mathbf { N }$ but in this anionic form is readily dissolved in soil water and so is very mobile in the soil profile. Nitrate is generated by the microbial conversion of other soil $\mathbf { N }$ forms and this process occurs via intermediates, such as $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ and nitrite, that are usually only found in the soil at very low concentrations. Nitrate is lost from the soil by microbial conversion to $\Nu _ { 2 }$ gas or leaching of soil water carrying dissolved $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ . The conversion to gaseous $\Nu _ { 2 }$ usually only occurs under oxygen-depleted conditions when soil bacteria can use $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ rather than oxygen for respiration. Nitrate availability to roots is therefore ephemeral and the concentrations of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the soil can rapidly change depending on rainfall and factors influencing microbial activity such as $\mathrm { p H }$ , temperature, and oxygen concentrations. Perhaps the single most important soil physical characteristic for determining $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ availability is soil water content. Nonetheless, in models of $\mathbf { N }$ uptake by crops, soil water and $\mathbf { N }$ supply are usually always considered as independent parameters (SUNDIAL SimUlation of Nitrogen Dynamics In Arable Land http://www.rothamsted.ac.uk/aen/sundial/ sundial.htm). There is scope for more research to check if water flux is a good predictor of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake. When soil is sampled there can be large changes in physical properties over relatively short distances. For example, in a transect across four arable fields with $4 \textrm { m }$ sampling intervals, soil $\mathrm { p H }$ varied by $2 \ \mathrm { \ p H }$ units and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentration by almost 100-fold (Fig. 1). Ammonium concentrations were much lower and less variable than $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ with values differing by 10-fold. To some extent, this range of values reflects the soil types and cultivation differences across the transect, but nonetheless the amount of heterogeneity is surprising. At this sampling scale this could be the situation under a single crop of one species and therefore requires considerable root plasticity to achieve maximal yields from each plant. Another interesting aspect of these measurements is the relative ratios of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ to $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ . Within a field this ratio was typically between 10 and 20:1, but on the margins the ratio could be much higher (Fig. 1). Clearly, plant roots need to be able to adapt to these changing supplies to optimize interception of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the soil. An appreciation of these soil processes is important background information and sets the scene for considering the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake processes by plant roots.


## Nitrate uptake by roots


This $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport step is the best understood because it is easier to study than other steps. Arabidopsis seedlings can be conveniently grown on agar Petri dishes or in hydroponics and root $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake is easily assayed (Orsel et al., 2006). Physiological investigations of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake by the roots of many different types of plants have led to the conclusion that plants have developed three types of transport system to cope with the variations in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations in cultivated soils (Crawford and Glass, 1998). Two saturable high affinity transport system (HATS) are able to take up $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ at low external concentrations $\mathbf { \Gamma } _ { \mathrm { ~ 1 ~ \mu N } }$ to $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ ). The constitutive system (cHATS) is available even when plants have not been previously supplied with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ . The inducible system (iHATS) is stimulated by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the external medium. The low affinity transport system (LATS) displays linear kinetics and its contribution to $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake becomes significant at external $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations above $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ (Crawford and Glass, 1998).

Although, in principle, both types of HATS can contribute to nitrate uptake at external concentrations above $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ , their transport activity is saturated and expression is down-regulated such that they actually contribute marginally to $\mathbf { N }$ acquisition. In Arabidopsis, the borders between these various physiological measures of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake are vague and the explanation for this may be due to experimental design. For example, these parameters can depend on the plant developmental stage, time of day, and the ecotype used but this has yet to be carefully described.

Two gene families have been identified in Arabidopsis that potentially encode transporters responsible for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake by roots or distribution within the plant; NRT1 with 53 members and NRT2 with seven members. These gene families for transport of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ have been extensively reviewed and the NRT1 family includes amino acid and peptide transporters and should more correctly be called NRT1/PTR (Forde, 2000; Orsel et al., 2002). The use of Arabidopsis mutants that have disruptions in specific transporter genes has been a powerful tool for the identification of key transporters involved in uptake.


## Genes responsible for LATS


Figure 1 showed that the concentration of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ that is available in the soil is chiefly found in the mM range and yet there is much less knowledge of the molecular identity of LATS when compared with HATS. AtNRT1.1 (formerly called CHL1) was originally identified as a contributor to LATS (Tsay et al., 1993), but deletion mutants only showed a deficiency in low affinity uptake when growing on a mixed $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ supply (Touraine and Glass, 1997). This result led to the suggestion that there may be a second LATS that can only compensate when plants are grown with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ as the only $\mathbf { N }$ source. A later comparison between gene expression levels and LATS activity reckoned that AtNRT1.1 was mainly responsible for influx at $5 ~ \mathrm { \ m M }$ external concentrations of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ (Okamoto et al., 2003). However, LATS is assumed to be constitutively present in roots and AtNRT1.1 expression is $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -inducible. Furthermore, the expression of AtNRT1.1 occurs in very specific tissues at primary and lateral root tips and in stomata where it has a role in water stress responses (Guo et al., 2003). A further complication arises from the fact that the protein was actually described as being dual affinity, with a phosphorylation switch between high and low affinity ranges of nitrate uptake (Liu and Tsay, 2003). By contrast, AtNRT1.2 is constitutively expressed in root epidermal cells and has a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ around $6 \ \mathrm { m M }$ in oocytes (Huang et al., 1999). However, Arabidopsis antisense lines of AtNRT1.2 were characterized by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ depletion assays and electrophysiology that showed a $5 0 { - } 7 0 \%$ decrease in LATS, but these changes did not correlate with the drop in expression across the lines (Huang et al., 1999). Gene deletion lines of

AtNRT1.1 were used for comparison in these experiments and these also showed a $45 \%$ decrease in LATS. Better methods for characterizing the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ influx, such as $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ influx should be used to check LATS in these phenotypes or gene disrupted lines. Taken together these data seem to suggest a complicated role for both AtNRT1.1 and ATNRT1.2 in LATS, but this result requires re-examination especially as AtNRT1.1 is not strongly expressed in the epidermis and cortex of roots (Guo et al., 2001). AtNRT1.4 has a very specific pattern of expression in the leaf petiole where it has a role in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ accumulation within these tissues (Chiu et al., 2004). Expression of AtNRT1.3 was $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -induced in the leaf, but repressed in the root and does not seem to be a significant contributor to LATS (Okamoto et al., 2003). There are many other candidate genes among the NRT1/PTR family. One aspect of the thermodynamics of LATS is the fact that the transport system need not always be coupled to two protons (Miller and Smith, 1996). Therefore the components of LATS may belong to another gene family that are as yet uncharacterized. Clues to identifying the genes responsible for LATS may come from the fact that it is a constitutively expressed system. However, this may also mean that it may be of fundamental importance to plants and gene disrupted mutants may be lethal. The molecular identity of LATS remains a key target for future research especially for uptake by crops.


## Genes responsible for HATS


Arabidopsis mutants with impaired expression of AtNRT2.1 and ATNRT2.2 genes are defective in HATS activity (Filleur et al., 2001; Orsel et al., 2004). These two genes lie end to end in the Arabidopsis genome and encode very similar proteins, sharing $90 \%$ identity (Orsel et al., 2002). Interestingly, parallel gene pairs of NRT2s that are also located closely within the genome are found in other species, for example, Chlamydomonas (Quesada et al., 1994) and rice (Araki and Hasegawa, 2006) and this may be a more general pattern. In rice, the two sequences appear to be identical, but the UTR flanking sequences result in different patterns of gene expression (Araki and Hasegawa, 2006). This information may suggest that functionally homologous genes encoding major components of HATS may have evolved early in plant development by a gene duplication event. Recently, another Arabidopsis mutant has been described that is uniquely disrupted in expression of AtNRT2.1 and this has been used to dissect the relative contributions of these two genes to iHATS and cHATS and to define AtNRT2.1 as the major contributor to both systems (Li et al., 2007).


## Regulation of transporters


At the whole plant level, it has long been recognized that net $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake by roots is regulated by demand and this, in turn, can be measured by the concentrations of $\mathbf { N }$ metabolites including $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the tissue (Vidmar et al., 2000, and references therein). Feedback from the leaf to the root occurs more specifically via the concentrations in the phloem, frequently amino acids and often glutamine are implicated although this is likely to depend on the species (Tillard et al., 1998). At the cellular level, a number of molecular mechanisms that may be used to regulate the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake can now be identified.


## The two component NRT2/NAR2.1 system


Unlike the fungal transporters nrtA/B or YNT1, but similar to some Chlamydomonas NRT2s, AtNRT2.1 requires a second protein to mediate $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport (Orsel et al., 2006). In Xenopus oocytes, AtNRT2.1 and NRT2 homologues from Chlamydomonas and barley all need to be co-expressed with a NAR2 protein, to yield $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport (Zhou et al., 2000a ; Tong et al., 2005; Orsel et al., 2006). This has been confirmed by in planta studies that have used mutant plants disrupted in the expression of the second component AtNAR2.1 (Okamoto et al., 2006; Orsel et al., 2006). One of these mutants (atnar2.1-1) shows a stronger phenotype (greater deficiency in HATS) than the NRT2.1 mutants in Arabidopsis (Orsel et al., 2006). In wild-type plants the expression pattern of AtNAR2.1 appears to parallel that of AtNRT2.1 exactly in the results from RT-PCR and microarray experiments and interaction occurs between the two proteins in yeast split ubiquitin assays (Orsel et al., 2006). However, the expression of AtNAR2.1 is not essential for that of AtNRT2.1, but the level of expression is modulated by the presence of the gene, probably as a consequence of the $\mathbf { N }$ status of the plant. The AtNAR2.1 protein is predicted to be much smaller than AtNRT2.1, and analysis of the sequence predicts an N-terminal ‘secretory pathway signal’ (Orsel et al., 2006). Taken together this information suggested that NAR2s were involved in targeting NRT2s to the plasma membrane, rather like a reported phosphate transporter traffic facilitator (Gonzalez et al., 2005); but unlike the phosphate model the NAR2s share no sequence similarities to SEC12 proteins. Tagging the AtNRT2.1 protein with GFP suggest that in the atnar2.1-1 mutant background the transporter protein is not correctly targeted to the plasma membrane (Orsel et al., 2007). Taken together these results suggest that the NAR2 proteins are not themselves a new type of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters (Okamoto et al., 2006), but rather they facilitate targeting of some NRT2s to the plasma membrane.

A mutation in AtNAR2.1 that replaces an aspartate residue with an asparagine in a highly conserved region of the protein greatly decreases $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake (Kawachi et al., 2006). This mutant was called rnc1 and it has a dwarf phenotype when growing on $5 \mathrm { m M N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , the LATS range of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentration, and this result is different from the other AtNAR2.1 mutants (Okamoto et al., 2006; Orsel et al., 2006). Figure 2 shows wild-type and atnar2.1-1 mutant plants (Orsel et al., 2006) growing in two different hydroponic $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations, $0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { \ m M }$ and $6 ~ \mathrm { \ m M }$ $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ . The dwarf plant phenotype was evident when the plants were grown on soil that was not supplemented with fertilizer (comparing Figs 2A, B, C). However, when supplied with N fertilizer there was no difference between the growth of wild-type and the atnar2.1-1 mutant plants. The fact that the threshold $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentration for the phenotype seems to have been altered by a point mutation in AtNAR2.1 suggests that the gene may alter the affinity of AtNRT2.1 for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ which is also worthy of further investigation. However, another difference between the plants used in these experiments is the Arabidopsis wild-type background, the atnar2.1-1 mutant was in a Wasselewskija (WS) background while the rnc1 was in Columbia (Col-0). These ecotype backgrounds may be important for the HATS/LATS $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentration boundary. The ecotype WS is known to have faster growing roots when compared with other Arabidopsis ecotypes (see Table II in Beemster et al., 2002). These possible differences in the LATS/HATS system of different ecotypes require further investigation and in early papers on $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport in Arabidopsis the wild-type background was not always reported.


## Gene expression


The regulation of NRT2.1 expression has been thoroughly investigated at the mRNA level. NRT2.1 transcript accumulation mainly occurs in epidermis and cortex of the mature root regions (Nazoa et al., 2003), and is strongly influenced by a range of different environmental factors. Expression of NRT2.1 is induced by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , repressed by high $\mathbf { N }$ status through a negative feedback regulation involving reduced $\mathbf { N }$ metabolites such as $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ or amino acids (Zhou et al., 1999; Nazoa et al., 2003), and stimulated by light and sugars (Lejay et al., 2003). The expression pattern of AtNAR2.1 almost exactly parallels that of AtNRT2.1 and is similarly repressed by feedback regulation from N metabolites (Krouk et al., 2006). More recently, AtNRT2.1/NAR2.1 has been shown to be downregulated by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ itself, through a mechanism independent of the feedback repression exerted by N metabolites, but specifically triggered by the dual-affinity transporter NRT1.1 (Munos et al., 2004; Krouk et al., 2006). There is generally a strong positive correlation between changes in NRT2.1 transcript level and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ HATS activity, suggesting that the transcriptional regulation of NRT2.1 expression plays a major role in governing root high-affinity $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake. Over-expression of the endogenous NpNRT2.1 gene driven by either the 35S or RolD promoter did not stimulate $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ HATS influx in $N$ . plumbaginifolia plants (Fraisier et al., 2000). However, when HATS influx was measured in plants supplied with $1 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ there was less feedback inhibition of HATS in the over-expressing lines when compared with the wild type (Fraisier et al., 2000). This work has been cited as an example of the over-expression of a $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporter gene resulting in altered uptake by plants, but actually the plants did not accumulate any more $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ than the wild type and no growth differences were reported. These plants may have lacked a necessary second NAR2-type component and over-expression of both components may be more likely to result in increased $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ accumulation.


## Post-translational regulation of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters


The use of chemical inhibitors in physiological studies had long ago suggested that protein synthesis was important for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake (Agu¨era et al., 1990) and the transporters may turn over relatively slowly. In barley roots, the application of inhibitors showed that the iHATS had a relatively long half-life when compared with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport to the xylem and with potassium uptake (Behl et al., 1988). Recently, in the yeast Hansenula polymorpha it was shown that degradation of a NRT2-type protein (YNT1) in the vacuole was associated with the removal of this transporter from the plasma membrane (Navarro et al., 2006). The YNT1 protein is ubiquitinylated when glutamine is supplied to the cells, and is transferred to the vacuole where it is rapidly degraded by a specific proteinase A. Recently, a similar mechanism for Arabidopsis AtNRT2.1 degradation has been suggested (J Wirth et al., unpublished data) and this could provide a direct molecular mechanism for feedback by a N metabolite.

The presence of a number of conserved protein kinase C recognition motifs in the N- and C-terminal domains of HvNRT2.1 (Forde, 2000) may suggest that phosphorylation events are involved in regulating AtNRT2.1 activity in response to environmental cues, as was shown to be the case for AtNRT1.1 (Liu and Tsay, 2003). Sequence analysis of the NRT2s has identified some possible 14- 3-3 regulatory sites; this is particularly interesting because of the role of these proteins in the regulation of key N assimilatory enzymes. The C-terminus of the tobacco NRT2.1 gene has a perfect 14-3-3 binding consensus (G Moorhead, personal communication). Using this sequence to compare with the Arabidopsis NRT2s identifies four genes with some consensus. In particular, AtNRT2.4 has a perfect 14-3-3 binding motif, consensus sequence RSXSXP, but in contrast to the tobacco gene this region is not present in the C-terminus of the protein. As 14-3-3 binding and regulation involves phosphorylation of the protein, this aspect of the NRT2s is worth further investigation. The 14-3-3 proteins can regulate the activity of both $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ reductase and glutamine synthetase and so it is tempting to speculate that a common regulatory mechanism may exist for the uptake and assimilation of N. It was shown there may be several different forms of the NRT2.1 protein, some that are truncated, phosphorylated, or modified in some way and it is possible that the protein has different functions in each of these states (J Wirth et al., unpublished data).

Finally, one aspect of regulation that is overlooked is the fact that the physical parameters of the cell can have a major effect on $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport. Nitrate transport is driven by co-transport with two protons and is therefore electrically sensitive. Xenopus oocyte expression experiments have shown that membrane voltage can have a direct effect on the activity of the transporter protein. If the electrical potential difference across the cell membrane is decreased there is less energy for transport, but also the protein’s affinity for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ $( K _ { \mathrm { m } } )$ can change (Zhou et al., 1998). Indeed membrane-potential dependent changes in $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ can explain why measurements in oocytes may appear to give kinetic parameters that seem at odds with in planta measurements. Trans-membrane gradients of potential and $\mathrm { p H }$ can have a major effect on $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport into a cell and these may be very different in oocytes and plant cells. The importance of changes in cytosolic $\mathrm { p H }$ and membrane potential as regulators of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake really depends on how much and how fast these parameters might change for cells in planta and it is very difficult to get accurate measurements of these physical parameters for roots growing in soil.


## Nitrate efflux from cells


In general, $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ efflux systems have been much less studied than influx systems; however, it is known that efflux is protein-mediated, passive, saturable, and selective for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ (Aslam et al., 1996). Aquaporins, or more likely, anion channels are an obvious route for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ efflux because they are thermodynamically downhill. However, it is worth noting that one member of the NRT2 gene family was demonstrated to have both a proton-cotransport and passive mechanism (Zhou et al., 2000b). The $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ efflux system is under a degree of regulation, induced by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ (Aslam et al., 1996) and it is also proportional to whole tissue $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations (Teyker et al., 1988; van der

Leij et al., 1998). It can be predicted that the membrane protein mediating $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ efflux must be $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -inducible.

Concentrations of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the xylem sap can be quite high $\mathbf { \left( 1 0 { - } 3 0 \ m M \right) }$ especially in plants which transport most of the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ taken up to the shoot for reduction. Nonetheless the entry of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ into the xylem can be mediated by anion channels assuming cytosolic $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations and membrane potentials in xylem parenchyma cells similar to those measured in epidermal and cortical cells (Miller and Smith, 1996). Genome analysis has identified several different anion channel families that may fulfil this function. Candidate quickly-activating anion channels have been characterized for barley roots (Kohler et al., 2002), but their molecular identity has not yet been determined. Nitrate in the xylem exerts positive feedback on its loading through a change in the voltage dependence of the channel. Interestingly, this effect was specific for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and was not found for $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ . By transport through this channel, $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ efflux into the xylem can be maintained with high $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations in the xylem sap; a situation which can occur during the night. There is a clear diurnal change in xylem sap concentrations (Siebrecht et al., 2003) of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , related to changes in the transpiration rate. In maize xylem parenchyma cells, the activity of a quickly activating anion channel was altered by changes in the water status of plants and the addition of ABA to protoplasts inhibited the channels activity (Gilliham and Tester, 2005).


## Nitrate storage and remobilization from the vacuole


Nitrate storage in the vacuole is important for osmotic balance and as an $\mathbf { N }$ reserve. Tissue levels are indicators of N status and this is the basis of tissue testing for crops. Interestingly, land plants accumulate $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the vacuole but aquatic plants may have either lost this ability or never developed it. Cells of the algae Chara do not accumulate $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the vacuole above passive transport levels after growing in high $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations for many months (Miller and Zhen, 1991). Seven members of the CLC gene family have been identified in the Arabidopsis genome (De Angeli et al., 2006) and disruption of one of these genes was shown to alter the accumulation of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in leaf tissues (Geelen et al., 2000). An earlier paper had reported that some members of the CLC family were localized in endomembranes (Heckenberger et al., 1996), but mammalian examples have been localized to the mitochondria (Jentsch et al., 2002). Studying the activity of mammalian CLCs has been made easier by the fact that the proteins have been characterized by expression in Xenopus oocytes (Jentsch et al., 2002), but this has been unsuccessful for plant homologues (Heckenberger et al., 1996). GFPtagging of the proteins in Arabidopsis and rice has localized them to the tonoplast where they are implicated in the storage and remobilization of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and chloride in the vacuole (De Angeli et al., 2006; Nakamura et al., 2006). Much earlier studies with isolated vacuoles (Schumaker and Sze, 1987) and intracellular measurements of $\mathrm { p H }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ gradients had used thermodynamic calculations to predict an antiport mechanism for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ accumulation in the vacuole (Miller and Smith, 1992). These results are consistent with the new finding that AtCLCa is able specifically to accumulate nitrate in the vacuole and behaves as a $2 \ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (De Angeli et al., 2006). This family of transporters are important for further studies to understand and manipulate N use efficiency in crops. Nitrate storage pools in the leaves and stems of crop plants are important for several quite different reasons; firstly, increased storage in tissue enables overwintered crops in the mopping up of soil $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ that would otherwise cause environmental damage through leaching in rainwater. Secondly, when leafy vegetables are eaten there is medical evidence to suggest that it is beneficial to health to decrease tissue $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations. Finally, this family of transporters may have a role in salt tolerance as these genes can also transport chloride, resulting in accumulation in the vacuole to avoid any possible harmful effects of the anion in the cytoplasm.


## Nitrate transporters, root morphology, and signalling


As $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ is not only a major $\mathbf { N }$ source for nutrition of plants, but also acts as a signal to modulate plant metabolism and development (Crawford and Glass, 1998) this had led to the hypothesis that plant cells must have a sensor for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ availability. One way that this hypothesis can be demonstrated is through the use of Arabidopsis root growth assays on Petri dishes. These experiments have compared the root growth pattern of wild type (WT) with mutant plants that have a gene disruption in specific $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters. The initiation and elongation of lateral root (LR) development is stimulated by local availability of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and it has been proposed in Arabidopsis roots that NRT2.1 may itself be a $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ signal transducer or sensor (Little et al., 2005). This function of the transporter is reckoned to be independent from $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ influx (Little et al., 2005; Remans et al., 2006a). The many regulatory processes that might change the activity of this protein (e.g. phosphorylation, the two components system etc) described previously seems to fit with the idea that the protein may have multiple functions. Furthermore, AtNRT1.1 has been implicated in the signalling pathway triggering root colonization of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -rich patches and this has been linked to changes in the expression of a putative transcription factor MADS box gene (Remans et al., 2006b).

A key aspect of these signalling functions for transporters is the assumption that this effect is independent of the proteins transport function (Little et al., 2005; Remans et al., 2006a, b). This result is fundamental to the proposed separation of the signalling and transport functions of these proteins and so this aspect of the experimental system needs careful examination. For AtNRT2.1, the case rests on the fact that a point mutation in the protein results in a loss of the normal LR repression that occurs in WT growing on high sucrose and low nitrate (Little et al., 2005). The mutant phenotype is actually independent of exogenous $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and is even seen in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ - free conditions when obviously no influx is occurring. As AtNAR2.1 interacts with AtNRT2.1 at the protein level and it is required for membrane targeting, it would be important to know if the protein–protein interaction can still occur with the mutated AtNRT2.1. In another paper for AtNRT2.1, measurements of cumulative $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake were used to show that the LR phenotype was independent of the total amount of nitrate taken up (Remans et al., 2006a). Both types of experiments actually measure whole root nitrate influx, but LR initiation occurs at very specific discrete regions of root and there may be subtle changes at localized regions that get hidden within measures of whole root influx. Of course, there are important practical reasons why these assays are performed on whole roots: in order to obtain sufficient $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ enrichment to detect the influx in the tissue samples. These Petri dish experiments provide a good assay tool and the concentrations of nitrate used are appropriate for the soil ranges (Fig. 1). However, when interpreting the experiments it is necessary to remember how this environment may differ from that experienced by a root growing in soil. For example, $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ patchiness may be much greater in the soil. Recent experiments to investigate the signalling role of AtNRT1.1 have recognized this problem and used split root treatments to offer localized $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -rich patches (Remans et al., 2006b). Clearly, under low levels of supply Arabidopsis roots are very good at growing to forage for N, and this is relevant to breeding new varieties adapted to lower fertilizer inputs. For example, wheat QTL analysis has identified that root architecture is important for $\mathbf { N }$ foraging under deficiency (Laperche et al., 2006).

Another example of nitrate signalling has been demonstrated in the breaking of seed dormancy. In Arabidopsis, a role for AtNRT1.1 has been specifically implicated in this response (Alboresi et al., 2005). Like root development, seed dormancy can provide another useful model system for studying nitrate signalling in plants.

Nitrate availability fluctuates greatly in soil because of the high turnover rate associated with leaching, denitrification and various seasonal edaphic factors (reviewed in Wolt 1994; Cameron et al. 2013). In order to adapt to these changes of nitrate availability, plants have developed several different transport systems (Siddiqi et al. 1990). Uptake of nitrate at high external concentrations is accomplished mainly by low affinity transport systems (LATS). LATS are encoded by members of the NRT1/PTR Family (NPF) genes, and in Arabidopsis thaliana NPF6.3 (NRT1.1) and NPF4.6 (NRT1.2) are major contributors to nitrate-inducible and constitutive LATS (iLATS and cLATS), respectively (Tsay et al. 1993; Huang et al. 1999). At concentrations below $0 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate, uptake from soil solution is achieved through high-affinity transport systems (HATS), of which there are both constitutive and nitrate-inducible systems, (cHATS) and iHATS, respectively (reviewed in Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998; Wang et al. 2012). The cHATS transporter is active without prior exposure to nitrate and is typically of higher affinity ( $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values $< 2 0 \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ but lower capacity $\left( V _ { \mathrm { m a x } } < 2 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } \right.$ FW $\mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ ) than the iHATS transporters (Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998).

Net ${ } ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake or $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx by the cHATS was first characterized in N-deprived barley roots (Behl et al. 1988; Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992). Siddiqi et al. (1990) found that the nitrate fluxes due to cHATS were saturable at ${ \sim } 0 . 2 \ \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and exhibited $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values that were 27-fold and fourfold lower, respectively, than fluxes associated with iHATS in nitrate-induced plants. The noted high affinity for nitrate exhibited by cHATS transporters in barley and other species (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995) makes this transporter ideally suited to detect and respond to trace quantities of nitrate in the root environment. iHATS transport in Arabidopsis is achieved principally through the activity of AtNRT2.1, whose expression is strongly induced by nitrate, peaking at some hours after first exposure to nitrate (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001; Orsel et al. 2002; Okamoto et al. 2003; Li et al. 2007). In addition to this major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter, expression of a second nitrate-inducible protein (AtNAR2.1) is required for both cHATS and iHATS nitrate uptake (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Yong et al. (2010) have shown that the functional iHATS nitrate transporter is a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1, localized in the plasma membranes (PMs) of Arabidopsis roots. Bimodal patterns of nitrate influx into roots of nitrateinduced plants, when represented as Hofstee or Lineweaver– Burk plots, demonstrate that cHATS and iHATS contribute simultaneously to total nitrate uptake with distinct kinetic properties (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995). Behl et al. (1988) proposed that an important function of the cHATS system of nitrate uptake was to supply trace amounts of nitrate that would set in motion the transcriptional events leading to iHATS induction. In addition, many other genes are activated, including enzymes such as nitrate reductase as well as developmental changes associated with nitrate provision (Wang et al. 2000, 2003, 2004).

Wang & Crawford (1996) isolated an EMS-mutagenized Arabidopsis line that was impaired in cHATS activity. This mutant exhibited a delay in the expression of inducible HATS, and was resistant to $0 . 1 \mathrm { m M }$ chlorate, a toxic nitrate analogue. Electrophysiological studies showed that there was very little response to $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate in the uninduced nrt2 mutant compared with strong initial membrane depolarization in wild-type (WT) plants. However, the gene encoding this putative cHATS was not identified. cHATS is also reduced by $9 0 \%$ in Atnar2.1-2 mutants compared with WT (Okamoto et al. 2006), suggesting that the AtNAR2.1 gene is necessary for the function of the cHATS transporter as was demonstrated for iHATS (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Thus, one clue to the identity of the transporter responsible for cHATS is that it requires co-expression of NAR2.1 for physiological activity.

In an earlier communication we demonstrated that all members of the AtNRT2 family are capable of nitrate uptake in Xenopus oocytes when co-expressed with AtNAR2.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Furthermore, the most prominent $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ enrichment in oocytes was observed for NRT2.5/NAR2.1 co-expression, suggesting that AtNRT2.5 might function in nitrate influx as a PM complex with AtNAR2.1 as was demonstrated for NRT2.1 (Yong et al. 2010). Kechid et al. (2013) showed that AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.6 play an important role in plant growth regulation in response to growthpromoting rhizobacterium Phyllobacterium brassicacearum strain STM196. With respect to AtNRT2.5’s involvement in cHATS, Okamoto et al. (2003) demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was diminished by nitrate provision, while a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression increased continuously during N-starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Measurements of nitrate influx in N-deprived AtNRT2.5 mutants and in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 demonstrated a 30 and $9 3 \%$ reduction, respectively, compared with WT (Lezhneva et al. 2014), suggesting that NRT2.1/NRT2.2 plays a predominant role in nitrate influx in N-starved plants. However, the finding is surprising, given that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are strongly induced by nitrate and expressed at diminished levels following nitrate deprivation. Nevertheless, the present study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present in roots of Arabidopsis after $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ d ~ } }$ of nitrogen starvation.

To investigate the nature of the association between AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1, we have used biochemical methods to isolate and characterize a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex between these two polypeptides, as well as physiological assays of nitrate influx in mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 to evaluate the impact of this disruption upon the kinetics of cHATS influx.

Nitrate uptake by plant roots from soil solution is mediated by members of three gene families, namely the NitRate Transporter families (NRT1 and NRT2) and the Nitrate Assimilation Related family (NAR2) (see reviews by Miller et al., 2009; Dechorgnat et al., 2011; Tsay et al., 2011). Full activity of the inducible high-affinity nitrate transport system (IHATS) in roots of Arabidopsis thaliana requires expression of two transporters, namely, NRT2.1 and NRT2.2, both of which are members of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). Evidence for this assertion is based upon the high degree of correlation between physiological activity of the IHATS and transcript abundance of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 in wild-type (WT) lines and the reduction of IHATS in mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.1 and or AtNRT2.2 (Zhuo et al., 1999; Filleur et al., 2001; Okamoto et al., 2003; Li et al., 2007). Nevertheless, it was first shown in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii that the NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 genes require simultaneous expression of another gene called NAR2 in order to express high-affinity nitrate transport (Quesada et al., 1994). In A. thaliana also, disruption of NAR2.1 (NRT3.1), in a T-DNA insertional mutant Atnar2.1-1, caused an almost complete loss of inducible high-affinity nitrate influx (Okamoto et al., 2006; Orsel et al., 2006). This observation is now readily explained by the demonstration that AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 form part of a $1 5 0 \mathrm { - k D a }$ plasma membrane (PM) complex (Yong et al., 2010) that was suggested to be a tetramer consisting of two subunits each of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1. Further, it was proposed that the $1 5 0 \mathrm { - k D a }$ complex is the functional high-affinity nitrate transporter in A. thaliana. Interestingly, this complex, as is AtNRT2.1, is absent from PM preparations derived from NAR2.1 mutants (Wirth et al., 2007; Yong et al., 2010), suggesting that AtNRT2.1n only exist in the root PM in association with AtNAR2.1. Membrane interactions between AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 were clearly indicated earlier by heterologous expression in the yeast two-hybrid and Xenopus oocytes systems. Only when oocytes were injected with both AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 RNA was nitrate uptake into oocytes detected (Orsel et al., 2006). In addition to A. thaliana, the two-component nitrate uptake system of NRT2 and NAR2 has been demonstrated to be present in other plant species such as barley (Hordeum vulgare) and rice (Oryza sativa) (Glass, 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2011). Yeast two-hybridization showed that OsNAR2.1 interacted not only with OsNRT2.1 ⁄ OsNRT2.2, but also with OsNRT2.3a (Feng et al., 2011). In a study of NRT2 ⁄ NAR2 interactions in barley, it was suggested that the C-terminus of HvNRT2.1 is possibly involved in binding to the HvNAR2.3 central region and that the Ser463 present in the HvNRT2.1 C-terminus plays a role in the binding ability (Ishikawa et al., 2009).

In addition to AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2, there are five other members of the NRT2 gene family in A. thaliana, NRT2.3 to NRT2.7 (Orsel et al., 2002; Okamoto et al., 2003). Quantitatively, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are responsible for c. $8 0 \%$ of IHATS in A. thaliana (Li et al., 2007). The remaining $2 0 \%$ is probably attributable to expression of a constitutive high-affinity transport system (CHATS) and CHL1 (NRT1.1). Although a role for AtNRT2.7 in seed nitrate accumulation has been proposed (Chopin et al., 2007) and expression patterns of the remaining NRT2 genes have been documented (Orsel et al., 2002; Okamoto et al., 2003), their functions and possible interactions with NAR2 are unknown.

In the present study, therefore, we have used heterologous expression in the yeast two-hybrid system and transient expression in A. thaliana leaf protoplasts to look for possible interactions between AtNAR2.1 and the other NRT2 genes (AtNRT2.2 to AtNRT2.7) and to localize the demonstrated interactions in planta. To explore the physiological functions of the NRT2 polypeptides we have used transient expression of AtNRT2.1 to AtNRT2.7 (plus or minus AtNAR2.1) and $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ uptake into Xenopus oocytes.

Nitrate is unique among the essential inorganic nutrients in so far as its uptake from soil solution by the major nitrate transporters AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 and AtNPF6.3 (originally named NRT1.1), and subsequent assimilation by enzymes such as nitrate reductase, requires prior exposure to nitrate for several hours to induce expression of the encoding genes. In the absence of external nitrate, genes encoding these transporters and enzymes are not expressed or expressed at low abundance. An exception to this requirement for nitrate induction is the cHATS for nitrate uptake. Behl et al. (1988) suggested that the principal role of this cHATS was to enable roots previously deprived of nitrate to absorb this ion and initiate induction of nitrate-inducible genes. Thus, at low external nitrate concentration, the activity of cHATS represents the first step in the complex pathway of nitrate assimilation. In a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014), it was demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was considerably enhanced, while nitrate influx measured at $0 . 2 \mathrm { m M }$ was reduced by up to $3 0 \%$ in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants. Nitrate influx in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 was reduced by a further $6 3 \%$ suggesting that NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 are the major contributors to nitrate influx under these conditions. Li et al. (2007), however, found that the cHATS influx was reduced by only $3 5 \%$ in Arabidopsis nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutants, suggesting that $\mathrm { N R T } 2 . 1 / 2 . 2$ is not the major transporter responsible for cHATS influx. Indeed, a large contribution to constitutive nitrate influx by NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 is contrary to expectation, in so far as it has been presumed that after several days of nitrate deprivation, these genes are no longer expressed (Okamoto et al. 2003). Nevertheless, our study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present at low abundance even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ of $\mathbf { N }$ starvation (Supporting Information Fig. S3).

The influx data shown in Fig. 6 and Table 2 provide convincing evidence that in A. thaliana AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to the cHATS. The average reduction of influx ( $6 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the two T-DNA knockout mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 is of a similar order of magnitude as was observed for the reduction of iHATS influx ( $7 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the $n r t { 2 . } I n r t { 2 . } 2$ mutants (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). This finding is different in magnitude from results reported by Lezhneva et al. (2014) which indicated only a $3 0 \%$ reduction of influx in NRT2.5 mutants.The difference in present findings may result from the ‘severe starvation’ employed in the Lezhneva study.

Complementation of the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant with AtNRT2.5 cDNA resulted in a statistically significant increase of the cHATS compared with the mutant, but influx failed to reach $1 0 0 \%$ of WT influx (Table 3). Incomplete recovery of the influx in Atnrt2.5-35S:NRT2.5 may be a result of lower AtNRT2.5 mRNA expression in the complemented line compared with WT (Table 3) possibly due to partial gene silencing. Schubert et al. (2004) reported silencing of genes under 35S promoter control in Arabidopsis T-DNA transformants that is controlled by transcript levels of transgenes. Nevertheless, this partial complementation taken together with the documented reduced nitrate influx in two independent Atnrt2.5 mutants provides strong evidence that AtNRT2.5 represents the major component of cHATS influx with primary responsibility for nitrate uptake at low nitrate concentration in nitrate-deprived plants.

The observed reduction of influx resulted in reduced nitrate accumulation in the Atnrt2.5 mutants. Although roots and shoots of the mutants and WT plants contained similar nitrate concentrations after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without N, after $6 \mathrm { { h } }$ of induction by $1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { ~ K N O } _ { 3 }$ , mutants contain significantly lower nitrate concentration than WT roots (Table 4). However, following short-term $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime } 5 \mathrm { \ m i n } )$ ) exposure to $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , no differences were observed in the proportion of tracer transferred to shoots in uninduced or induced plants. Thus, AtNRT2.5 plays an important role in nitrate uptake into roots but not in the transfer of nitrate to shoots of Arabidopsis (Table 2). With respect to the transfer of nitrate to shoots, similar conclusions may be drawn from results reported by Kechid et al. (2013) using plants supplied with $2 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. Lezhneva et al. (2014) found that under conditions of extreme N deprivation (4 weeks without N) phloem nitrate concentrations of NRT2.4 mutants was reduced by $4 0 \%$ , although there were no differences in NRT2.5 single mutants. This is consistent with the pattern of mRNA expression of AtNRT2.5 that was more abundant in roots than in shoots of 6-week-old nitratedeprived WT plants (Fig. 3a). A similar expression profile of AtNRT2.5 during both vegetative and reproductive growth stages of Arabidopsis was observed previously by Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014). However, after $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ of exposure to nitrate in the present study, root AtNRT2.5 expression had decreased to such an extent (with virtually no change of shoot AtNRT2.5 expression) that AtNRT2.5 expression was more abundant in shoots than in roots. Thus, depending on the duration of nitrate deprivation or re-exposure both higher and lower levels of AtNRT2.5 expression may be observed in roots versus shoots. This may account for the apparent differences between reports from Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014), and the reported higher levels of AtNRT2.5 expression in shoots than roots described by Mantelin et al. (2006) and Kechid et al. (2013). Recently,
