Evolution of KEA in plants. Protein phylogenetic analyses showed that all plants, from unicellular algae to flowering plants, had three types of KEAs classified as clades Ia, Ib, and II (Figure 5). Green algae, like C. reinhartdii and V. carteri, contain only one gene in each group. In other plants, diversification occurred in clades KEA-Ia, KEA-II, or both.

Clade Ia KEAs possess a long N-terminal domain. Phylogenetic analysis showed that plant KEAs in clade I diverged into two types that differ in their protein organization. Within clade Ia, all plant sequences from moss to monocot and dicots have an long hydrophilic N-terminal domain of ${ \sim } 5 7 0 { \mathrm { - } } 7 7 0$ amino acids (Figure 6) that is often missed in preliminary gene annotations. This domain is typically rich in negatively charged glutamate residues, and predicted coiled coil structures (Figure S4 in Supplementary Material). The role of this unusual extra sequence is unknown (Rose et al., 2004). The N-terminal domain of green algae Cre and Cva share some similarity $( 4 6 \% )$ and are slightly shorter than that of higher plants (Figure 6). The absence of this region in prokaryotes would indicate that the N-terminal domain is a recent acquisition that gained increasing relevance in land plants.

In contrast, proteins in clade Ib, such as AtKEA3, do not harbor the N-terminal extension, instead they have gained specific insertions between predicted membrane helices 4 and 5 and in the Rossman fold glycine motif of the KTN domain (Figures 4 and 6). Although all hydrophobic regions are conserved in the clade Ib proteins, transmembrane helices are poorly identified by transmembrane prediction programs (Figure 6). In general, only one gene of this type is present per plant, except in G. max and P. patens, where two genes are present (Table 4; Table S3 in Supplementary Material; Figure 5).

Recent diversification of clade II KEAs. Genes encoding AtKEA4– 6 have a hydrophilic N-terminal domain of ${ \sim } 1 5 7 { - } 2 3 5$ residues that is predicted to include a signal peptide (Figures 4 and 6). Green algal sequences found in $V .$ carteri and C. reinhartdii have an anomalous $\mathrm { N a \mathrm { \_ H } }$ exchanger domain that is interrupted by a similar sequence in both species (Figure 5). Interestingly, clade KEA-II has diversified further in angiosperms where AtKEA5 is clearly separate from AtKEA4 and AtKEA6 indicating this occurred recently after the evolution of early land plants.

Function of KEA. Nearly nothing is known about plant KEA function, so bacterial homologs could provide insights. KefB and KefC in E. coli are glutathione regulated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux transporters, that are important for bacterial survival during exposure to toxic metabolites (Booth, 2003). Electrophiles react with glutathione to form glutathione adducts, thereby releasing KefC and KefB inhibition by GSH, and eliciting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ uptake. Cytoplasmic acidification is suggested to prevent DNA damage (Ferguson et al., 2000; Miller et al., 2000). Reduced GSH stabilizes the association of the two KTN domains, whilst the larger adducts disrupt this interaction (Roosild et al., 2010). Based on mutagenesis studies, a short central hydrophilic regulatory loop was proposed to interact with the KTN domain. This regulatory loop is partially conserved in the plant KEA1–3 sequences, but the residues forming the glutathione-binding pocket are less conserved in the plant sequences (Figure 2), indicating that plant KEA1–3 are regulated in a different way (Roosild et al., 2010). Although originally proposed to function as $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels, recent studies indicate KefC has $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiport activity (Fujisawa et al., 2007).

Recently, AtKEA1 and AtKEA3 peptides were detected by mass spectroscopy in Arabidopsis chloroplast preparations (Zybailov et al., 2008). Moreover, localization to thylakoid membrane of SynNha3 (Tsunekawa et al., 2009), a Synechocystis protein closely related to KEA-I and KEA-II proteins (Figure 1), would suggest a role of plant KEA in chloroplast ion homeostasis. So far only one cyanobacterium, Gloeobacter violaceus, has a gene encoding a KEAI homolog (Figure 3). Perhaps ancestral primary plastids originated just after the separation of primitive cyanobacterium, like Gloeobacter, from present-day lineages (Criscuolo and Gribaldo, 2011). In Gloeobacter, thylakoids are absent and photosystems reside at the plasma membrane (Vothknecht and Westhoff, 2001). We hypothesize that the long N-terminal sequence of AtKEA1/2 has a role in chloroplast-specific processes in plant (Vothknecht and Westhoff, 2001). These and other possibilities need to be tested.


## Evolutionary origin of CHX clade in plants


The CHX clade is populated by genes from higher plants, but none from metazoa so far. Nearly all deduced proteins from plants have ${ \sim } 8 0 0$ residues (Table S4 in Supplementary Material) that consist of a hydrophobic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain of ${ \sim } 4 0 0$ residues at the amino terminus, and a carboxyl hydrophilic domain of $3 0 0 -$ 400 residues. The long hydrophilic C-tail does not contain any known conserved motifs, so its role is a complete mystery. NhaS4 from the cyanobacterium Synechocystis PCC 6803 encodes a much shorter protein of 410 residues, though the predicted protein from Synechococcus elongatus PCC 6301 has 715 residues.

Based on analyses using the TM domain alone, we show that the present-day NhaS4 from cyanobacteria, shares the highest similarity with AtCHX16–CHX20 (Figure 1; Sze et al., 2004). NhaS4 gene is found in single-celled Synechocystis PCC 6803 (Inaba et al., 2001) as well as filamentous Anabaena variabilis (Ava1632). Many noncyanobacteria do not have genes that cluster with the CHX/NhaS4 clade. One exception is MyxxaNhaS4 (Table S1 in Supplementary Material) from the gliding bacterium Myxococcus xanthus (a member of Myxococcales) which form fruiting body in response to nutrient starvation (Mauriello et al., 2010). Intriguingly, the mechanisms of motility and establishment of cell polarity in M. xanthus and eukaryotes share several similarities (Leonardy et al., 2010). Although genes from metazoa are absent from this clade, Dictyostelium discoideum (a protist and slime mold) has two members, Nhe3 and Nhe4, of unknown function that cluster with NhaS4 (Figure 1). The function and membrane location of cyanobacterial NhaS4 are still unclear. Interestingly, all fungi examined have a single gene KHA1 that encodes a homolog of Synechocystis NhaS4 as seen in Figure 1. Fungi include unicellular Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and filamentous fungi such as Neurospora crassa, Aspergillus oryzae, and Ustilago maydis (Figure 1; Table S1 in Supplementary Material). Mutants of ScKHA1 have served as a useful heterologous system to test functions of Arabidopsis CHX16–20 (Chanroj et al., 2011; Table 3).

Comparative analyses of full-length protein sequences revealed additional insights on the origin of plant CHX members. One CHX homolog was found in Spirogyra pratensis, a Zygnematales, though none was detected in Chlamydomonas reinhartdii, Volvox carteri (Figures 1 and 7), or red algae (not shown). Early land plants, like Physcomitrella and Selaginella, had four and three genes, respectively encoding CHX homologs (Figure 1). Interestingly, all these proteins cluster in one subclade closest to Arabidopsis CHX20 (Figure 7) and CHX16–19. Results suggest that AtCHX16–CHX20 genes arose early in CHX gene family diversification. In Arabidopsis, these genes are expressed in leaves and roots, especially in dermal tissues, such as root epidermis (Cellier et al., 2004; Chanroj, 2011), root cap, and guard cells (Padmanaban et al., 2007; see Table 3).

Multiple subclades within the CHX family. Analysis of CHX homologs from 14 higher plants unveiled the diversification of this family in flowering plants (Figure 7). In general, CHX genes diverged less in monocots than in dicots. First, the average number of CHX genes (16) per monocot genome is less than that seen in many dicots $( > 2 6 ;$ Table 4). Second, Figure 7 shows that CHX members in Arabidopsis and other dicots can be separated into eight subclades, and five of these are conserved in monocots (Table 5). For example, orthologs of AtCHX20 and AtCHX16–CHX19 were evident in rice, corn, and sorghum, as shown by the blue branches in Figure 7 (Table S4 in Supplementary Material). Furthermore, monocot orthologs of AtCHX15, AtCHX1/2, and AtCHX28 were suggested by their close association with these subclades. Many of these genes in Arabidopsis are preferentially expressed in pollen (Sze et al., 2004; Table 5). Oddly, homologs of AtCHX21/23 were not obvious in monocot

Most dicots had additional CHX homologs that clustered with AtCHX24/25 (V), 26/27, and 13/14 (III). AtCHX3–12 proteins (subclade II) are specific to A. thaliana and A. lyrata. genomes. However, rice had four other genes (OsCHX5–8) that clustered near AtCHX24/25, though none were closely related to 16 additional Arabidopsis gene products, CHX3–12, 13/14, or 26/27. Three to four CHX genes from other monocot plants including Brachypodium, a model of an energy grass, sorghum, and corn also clustered with rice OsCHX5–8, suggesting these represent a monocot subclade of CHX homologs (Figure 7).

In contrast, some dicot plants shared additional genes that are potential orthologs of AtCHX24/25, 13/14, and 26/27. Other dicot CHXs from poplar, Citrus clementina, Mimulus, and Manihot esculenta (cassava) formed clusters that were separate from AtCHX13/14 or 24/25, 26/27 subclades, suggesting these genes had diverged later in speciation. Notably, AtCHX3–8 and AtCHX9–12 proteins were in general specific to Arabidopsis genus, indicating diversification of CHX genes during Arabidopsis speciation. Medicago truncatula also had a cluster of 12 genes that could be a result of additional duplications during speciation.

Functions of plant CHX proteins. Functional studies of plant CHX proteins are just beginning and so far limited to Arabidopsis thaliana. According to results from the founding members of the family, AtCHX16–AtCHX20, these proteins are implicated in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis of dynamic endomembranes. First, expression of AtCHX17 or its homologs CHX16–CHX20, rescued alkaline-sensitive growth phenotype of the host yeast strain (Chanroj et al., 2011). Second, CHX20 caused acidification and alkalization of the cytosol and vacuole of yeast, respectively; although CHX17 did not alter cytoplasmic or vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ (Chanroj et al., 2011). Third, AtCHX17 restored growth of bacteria defective in several $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake systems, and tracer studies demonstrated that CHX17, CHX20, and CHX23 mediated monovalent cation transport with a preference for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Table 3). Thus CHXs, including plasma membrane-localized CHX13, transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Zhao et al., 2008), though their ability to restore yeast growth depends on different external $\mathrm { p H } ^ { \prime } \mathbf { s } .$ . Interestingly, these findings of plant CHX are consistent with mutant studies that suggest Synechocystis NhaS4 probably transported $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , but not $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Inaba et al., 2001).

The association of AtCHX proteins with endomembranes and their role in $\mathrm { p H }$ and cation homeostasis would suggest they perform important roles in membrane trafficking events that affect protein and cargo sorting. Two lines of evidence support this idea. First, AtCHX17, AtCHX18, or AtCHX19, but not CHX20, conferred tolerance to hygromycin B in yeast lacking multiple cation-handling mechanisms (Chanroj et al., 2011). Sensitivity to aminoglycosides in yeast has been related to altered intracellular $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis and membrane trafficking. Second, Chanroj et al. (2011) showed that yeast mutants expressing CHX17 secreted less vacuolar-destined carboxypeptidase Y (CPY) to the external medium similar to cells expressing NHX1. Thus cation and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis in endosomes, such as PVC, appeared to influence sorting and trafficking of proteins in the endomembrane system. Based on these findings and analysis of Atchx20 mutants (Padmanaban et al., 2007), we propose that CHX20 affects endomembrane dynamics and osmoregulation needed for guard cell swelling and stomatal opening.

The multiplicity of CHX genes in Arabidopsis pollen and possibly other plants is surprising and not understood. The first study on pollen CHX proteins showed that AtCHX21 and AtCHX23 are functionally related and that they are involved in either the reception or the transduction of female signals that target pollen tube to the ovule (Lu et al., 2011). Pollen carrying double mutant chx21chx23 developed into mature grains, extended a tube into the transmitting tract, however the tube failed to find the egg (Lu et al., 2011). Pollen tube elongates by tip growth and failure to shift the axis of polarity in the double mutant suggests that localized cation and pH homeostasis by CHX has a role in the establishment, or maintenance of polarity or both. Homologs of Arabidopsis CHX21 and CHX23 are present in dicot, but not in monocot, plants (Figure 7; Table 5; Table S4 in Supplementary Material). Whether they influence pollen tube guidance of dicots in general or have other roles in reproductive fitness will need to be investigated.

Till now, soil salinization-alkalization has become a worldwide problem limiting agricultural production. Salt stress results in increased cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and disrupts ion homeostasis. Consequently, excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ inhibits enzyme activity27. Terefore, once upon salt stress, plants have to start a series of signaling pathways to maintain low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ but high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ content26, 28–30. For this reason, research on CHX family is of great importance to understand the responsive mechanism of saline-alkaline stress.

Te CHX family has been gradually studied in Arabidopsis2 , rice8, 31, and Physcomitrella patens32. However, no systematical study was performed for CHXs in legume plants. Glycine soja, as a sibling species of Glycine max, exhibits high carbonate tolerance and has become one of the most popular materials to study saline-alkaline stress signaling pathway21, 33, 34. In this study, we identifed a total of 34 CHXs in soybean genome and found that soybean possessed about 1.2 times CHXs as many as Arabidopsis. Gene duplications were one of the reasons to force gene family expansion and generate homologous genes with similar structures and functions35. Soybean experienced twice gene duplications during evolution, but only once in Arabidopsis36, which probably contributed to more CHXs in soybean than Arabidopsis.

Studies have shown that CHX family contains a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange domain in the N terminus and an AANH_ like domain close to the C terminus7, 8, 12. Besides, in this study, through searching conserved motifs, we also found another conserved domain in the long C tail of soybean CHXs (Fig. 3B). Although the function of this domain was mysterious, we posited that it might be involved in phosphorylation or protein localization, like NHX family37. Previous reports also showed that deletion of AtCHX17 C terminus inhibited its localization in endomembrane system11. Here, we proved that GsCHX19.3 also localized on plasma membrane in plants (Fig. 5). Terefore, further experiments are needed to investigate the role of the C-terminal domain of GsCHX19.3 in protein localization or activity.

Date to now, studies on CHX family genes were mainly focused on plant growth and development, but it has been reported that CHX family genes responded to adversity stress6, 11, 12, 32, 34, 38–40. Combined with our previous

RNA-seq data15, we found that expression of fve GsCHXs from Group IV responded to carbonate alkaline stress (Fig. S2). Interestingly, even though three GsCHX19s showed high sequence identity and close evolutionary relationship, only GsCHX19.3 displayed a greatly increased expression under carbonate alkaline treatment (Fig. 4A). Further qRT-PCR results verifed its up-regulated expression under both carbonate alkaline and high salt stress (Fig. 4B,C). Besides, AtCHX16/17/18/19 from Group IV in Arabidopsis were all highly expressed in fower, leaf and root8 . Here, we also found that GsCHX19.3 was highly expressed in fower and leaf (Fig. 4D), indicating its roles in reproductive tissue development. Above fndings suggested the involvement of GsCHX19.3 in plant responses to salt-alkaline stress.

In this study, we further demonstrated the positive role of GsCHX19.3 in salt-alkaline stress responses by mediating ion transport. To identify the ion transport activity and specifcity, we used a yeast mutant AXT4K, in which the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (ScENA1-4), plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (ScNHA1), vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter $( S c N H X I ) ^ { 2 2 }$ , and endoplasmic reticulum $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger $( S c K H A I ) ^ { 1 0 }$ were knockout. Here, we proved that GsCHX19.3 expression could rescue the growth of AXT4K on the medium with normal $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ( $1 \mathrm { m M } )$ or low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } \left( 0 . 0 1 \mathrm { m M } \right)$ at $\mathrm { p H } 7 . 5$ (Fig. 6C). In previous studies, CHXs were functionally associated with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport, especially when $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ defciency met with high external $\mathrm { p H } ^ { 8 , 1 1 , 1 2 , 3 2 }$ . We also showed that GsCHX19.3 overexpression in Arabidopsis increased the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ uptake under normal growth condition (Fig. 8A). When $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ was limited, active transport through $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -cotransporters is needed to assist $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake41. Tus, when the medium pH was slightly alkaline, cells could use a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter to accumulate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in cytosol and release $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ to extracellular to remit the alkaline damage.

Interestingly, GsCHX19.3 expression in AXT4K couldn’t confer tolerance to high KCl or $\mathrm { N a C l } _ { \mathrm { \ell } }$ , even it made AXT4K more sensitive to high salt (Fig. S3). Similarly, previous studies have shown that AtCHX20 and AtCHX17 expression in yeast mutants also led to increased sensitivity to high salt stress5, 12. In contrast, NHX1 from grape was able to rescue the growth of nhx1 yeast mutant under high salt stress42, and AtKEAs could mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport under high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at normal pH $( \mathrm { p H } 5 . 8 ) ^ { 5 }$ . Tus, the function of GsCHX19.3 was distinct from that of NHX and KEA.

However, in plants, high salt stress up-regulated the expression of GsCHX19.3 (Fig. 4C), and its overexpression also enhanced salt tolerance of transgenic Arabidopsis (Fig. 7C,E). Hence, it was worth noting that GsCHX19.3 functioned under salt stress in plants, which was diferent from yeast. Previous studies have shown that $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pump could generate $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient and thereby drive secondary transporters43, 44. Recent studies showed that the proton pumped out by $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase could act as substrates of SOS1 (an NHX subfamily member) to promote $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efux, and this cooperation thereby is critical for salt stress responses at high $\mathrm { p H } ^ { 4 5 }$ . Tus, we speculated the phenomenon of decreased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content found in transgenic Arabidopsis might be secondary efects of GsCHX19.3 transporter activity. Terefore, further work need be carried out to identify whether GsCHX19.3 could cooperate with other genes to defense salt stress in plants.

We further suggested the biological function of GsCHX19.3 under carbonate alkaline stress. First, AXT4K expressed GsCHX19.3 grew much better than AXT4K under ${ \mathrm { N a H C O } } _ { 3 }$ stress. At the same time, GsCHX19.3 overexpression in Arabidopsis also enhanced carbonate tolerance (Fig. 7D,F,G,H). As we know, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration in cytoplasm of plant cells will dramatically increase under stress condition46. On one hand, plants will take efective measures to exclude excess cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and lower cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration. On the other hand, plants absorb more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ to maintain the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ balance. In this study, we found that carbonate alkaline stress increased cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, but GsCHX19.3 OX lines showed lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content than WT (Fig. 8B). Tis fnding suggested that GsCHX19.3 overexpression could help to exclude cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , and result in a relative higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ values under salt-alkaline stress (Fig. 8D). However, till now, no electrophysiology evidence for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporting by CHX proteins was reported. Further studies are needed to directly characterize the ion transport activity and specifcity of GsCHX19.3 by using electrophysiology technologies, such as two-electrode, giant-patch, patch-clamp and double-barreled proton-selective microelectrode.

## GsCHX19.3, a member of cation/H+ exchanger superfamily from wild soybean contributes to high salinity and carbonate alkaline tolerance


Bowei Jia1,2, Mingzhe Sun1,2, Huizi DuanMu1, Xiaodong Ding1, Beidong Liu 3, Yanming Zhu1   
& Xiaoli Sun2

Cation/H+ exchangers (CHX) are characterized to be involved in plant growth, development and stress responses. Although soybean genome sequencing has been completed, the CHX family hasn’t yet been systematically analyzed, especially in wild soybean. Here, through Hidden Markov Model search against Glycine soja proteome, 34 GsCHXs were identifed and phylogenetically clustered into fve groups. Members within each group showed high conservation in motif architecture. Interestingly, according to our previous RNA-seq data, only Group IVa members exhibited highly induced expression under carbonate alkaline stress. Among them, GsCHX19.3 displayed the greatest up-regulation in response to carbonate alkaline stress, which was further confrmed by quantitative real-time PCR analysis. We also observed the ubiquitous expression of GsCHX19.3 in diferent tissues and its localization on plasma membrane. Moreover, we found that GsCHX19.3 expression in AXT4K, a yeast mutant lacking four ion transporters conferred resistance to low $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ at alkali pH, as well as carbonate stress. Consistently, in Arabidopsis, GsCHX19.3 overexpression increased plant tolerance both to high salt and carbonate alkaline stresses. Furthermore, we also confrmed that GsCHX19.3 transgenic lines showed lower $\ N \widehat { \mathsf { e } } ^ { + }$ concentration but higher ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } I { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ values under salt-alkaline stress. Taken together, our fndings indicated that GsCHX19.3 contributed to high salinity and carbonate alkaline tolerance.

Soil salt-alkalinity, one of the most important environmental stresses, not only reduces soil fertility, but also abates the amount of agricultural production. Salt-alkaline stress has severely limited the sustainable development of agriculture and economy. Also, with the growing population and increasing demand for food, soil salinization and alkalization has become one of the severest problems. Tus, it is necessary and urgent to study the molecular responses to salt-alkaline stress in crops.

As sessile organisms, plants have developed a variety of physiological and biochemical mechanisms to cope with saline-alkaline stress during their long-term evolution process. It has been well studied that under salt-alkaline stress, cation/proton antiporters (CPAs) serve to maintain lower cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and cellular pH homeostasis1 . Te CPA superfamily is structurally characterized by a conserved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain, and could be divided into CPA1 and CPA2 subfamilies. Te CPA1 subfamily consists of NHAP and NHX clades, while CPA2 is composed of NHA, KEA, and CHX clades2 . Among them, CPA1 have been suggested to function in exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ , and maintaining pH balance under adverse conditions, such as ABA, salt and hyperosmotic stresses3, 4 . Compared with CPA1, research concerning the CPA2 family is very limited until now. Recently, studies of KEAs from the CPA2 family have been gradually begun. For instance, AtKEAs were functionally characterized as $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and functioned under high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ stress5 . However, studies about CHXs are limited in plant growth and development6, 7 , while little is known about their function in response to salt and alkaline stress.

In Arabidopsis, the CHX family was divided into fve groups (Group I-V)8 . Group IV was the largest one, and consisted of 8 members (AtCHX15–21 and AtCHX23). Among them, AtCHX16–20 were all endomembrane transporters9–11. AtCHX 16–19 shared overlapping roles in reproduction and seed development11. AtCHX20 was highly expressed in guard cells, and functioned in osmoregulation of stomatal open by regulating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ movement and pH homeostasis12. AtCHX21 was a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter, regulating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ balance in xylem and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in leaves13. AtCHX23 functioned in cytosol pH adjustment. In atchx21chx23 mutants, pollen tubes failed to target ovules, which resulted in impaired pollen fertility6 . However, date to now, studies on CHXs are mainly limited in Arabidopsis, the function of CHXs from other species, in carbonate stress responses is still unclear.

Glycine soja is a related species of Glycine max, which can survive in severely saline-alkaline areas14. In previous studies, from a total of 345 wild soybean lines, we screened out G. soja 07256, which showed the highest resistance to carbonate stress14. By using microarray and RNA-seq data, we constructed the gene expression profles in response to carbonate alkaline stress15, and further excavated several stress resistant genes, such as $\bar { G } s C B R L K ^ { 1 6 }$ , $G s S K P 2 l ^ { 1 7 }$ , GsACA118, GsGSTU1319 and so on. Considering the potential roles of CHXs in stress responses, in this study, we focused on the CHX family genes of G.soja. A total of 34 GsCHXs were identifed and clustered into fve groups. Expression profles of Group IVa members were investigated in detail, and one of them GsCHX19.3 was demonstrated to mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and positively regulate plant responses to high salt and carbonate alkaline stresses.

Genome-wide identifcation and characterization of the CHX family genes in G. soja. To identify the CHX family genes in G. soja, we carried out Hidden Markov Model (HMM) search against G. soja proteome to identify all CPA superfamily members. A total of 55 non-redundant CPA genes were obtained, and were used to construct a phylogenetic tree with Arabidopsis CPAs $\mathrm { ( A t C H X s ^ { 8 } }$ , AtKEAs5 and AtNHXs). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that 34 of the G. soja CPA genes formed a cluster with AtCHXs, belonging to GsCHXs (Fig. 1). Ten these GsCHXs were designated according to their homologous and evolutionary relationship to AtCHXs. Basic information of all GsCHXs (including gene name, DNA, CDS, protein length, molecular weight, isoelectric point, transmembrane number, predicted localization and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain) is provided in Table S1. Notably, all these GsCHXs contained a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain in their N-terminus. What’s more, they all shared 7–13 transmembrane domains and were predicted to localize on plasma membrane or other membrane-containing organelles, indicating their potential function as membrane transporters.

Phylogenetic and structural analysis of soybean CHXs. To explore the evolutionary relationship of GsCHXs, a phylogenetic tree was constructed with CHX protein sequences from G. soja and Arabidopsis. As depicted in Figs 1 and 2, similar to AtCHXs, GsCHXs were also classifed into fve groups (Group I–V)8 . Among them, Group II could be further divided into two subgroups Group IIa (AtCHX3–12) and Group IIb (GsCHX3– 4.4). Group IIa were previously reported to be specifc to Arabidopsis2 , we speculated that Group IIb might be peculiar to soybean, indicating the diversifcation of CHXs during soybean speciation.

To further examine the conservation of GsCHX protein sequences and structures, the MEME program was used to predict conserved motifs (Figs 3 and S1). Expectedly, GsCHXs displayed high similarity in protein sequences, and GsCHXs within each individual group shared common motif architecture. Among the checked 15 motifs, motif 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12 and 15 in the N-terminus were fragments of the well-known $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / \bar { H } ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain. Motif 2, 5, 10 and 11 composed the AANH-like domain7 , which is beside the C-terminus of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / \bar { H } ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain. Besides, another four conserved motifs (Motif 1, 3, 13, 14) were identifed in the C terminus, but their functions were still unknown. Taken together, CHX family was evolutionarily conserved in terms of motif distribution, especially in each individual group.

Expression profles of GsCHXs under carbonate alkaline stress. Te CHX family genes are found to be involved in plant growth and development and it has been documented that CHX family genes functioned in response to adversity stress4, 5, 12, 16. However, little is known about the roles of GsCHXs in carbonate alkaline stress. Hence, we analyzed the expression profles of GsCHX family genes under carbonate alkaline stress ( $\mathrm { 5 0 m M }$ ${ \mathrm { N a H C O } } _ { 3 }$ , pH8.5) based on our previous RNA-seq data (Fig. S2 and Table S2). As depicted in Figs S2 and 4A, only fve genes from Group IVa (GsCHX18.1, GsCHX18.2, GsCHX19.2, GsCHX19.3, GsCHX20) exhibited high expression levels and responded to carbonate alkaline stress (Figs S2 and 4A). Among them, GsCHX19.3 exhibited the greatest induction by carbonate alkaline stress, and the value was up to 12 fold (Fig. 4A). Terefore, we focused on GsCHX19.3 for further study.

Examination of GsCHX19.3 expression characteristics in G. soja seedlings. To get better understanding of GsCHX19.3 expression, we frstly confrmed the induction of GsCHX19.3 under carbonate alkaline stress. In accordance with the RNA-seq data, GsCHX19.3 expression was greatly induced by carbonate alkaline stress ${ \mathrm { 5 0 ~ m M ~ N a H C O _ { 3 } } } )$ (Fig. 4B). Afer carbonate alkaline treatment, the transcript levels of GsCHX19.3 increased within $^ { 6 \mathrm { { h } } }$ to nearly 10 folds, and then decreased at $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ (Fig. 4B). Considering the fact that high salt stress always occurred simultaneously with carbonate alkaline stress, we further checked the expression of GsCHX19.3 under high salt treatment $( 2 0 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l } )$ ). As expected, the expression of GsCHX19.3 showed an obvious increase afer high salt treatment (Fig. 4C). Overall, results represented here showed that GsCHX19.3 expression was greatly induced by both carbonate alkaline and high salt stresses (Fig. 4B,C), suggesting an important role of GsCHX19.3 in plant responses to salt-alkaline stress.

It has been reported that CHXs exhibited diverse expression patterns in diferent tissues during plant growth and developmental processes8, 13. Ten we carried out qRT-PCR to detect the expression patterns of GsCHX19.3 in diferent tissues of G. soja (including old shoot, young shoot, old leaf, young leaf, hypocotyl, root, old pod and fower). Te results showed that GsCHX19.3 expressed in all detected tissues, and exhibited higher expression levels in fower and young leaf (Fig. 4D). Tis result was accordant with that of AtCHX19, which also displayed high expression levels in fower and leaf8 .

GsCHX19.3 localized to the plasma membrane in onion epidermal cells. As ion transporters, CHXs usually localize on the endomembrane system to regulate cation and pH homeostasis. Hence, to localize GsCHX19.3 protein, we constructed expression vector with GsCHX19.3 tagged at the N-terminus of yellow fluorescent protein (YFP). The AtPIP2-CFP construct was used as plasma membrane marker20. Then GsCHX19.3-YFP and AtPIP2-CFP were transiently co-expressed in onion epidermal cells. As shown in Fig. 5, the signal of GsCHX19.3-YFP protein was exactly overlapped with AtPIP2-CFP on plasma membrane, which was consistent with the result of PSORT prediction (Table S1). Tis fnding was also consistent with previous report that AtCHX19 protein localized on plasma membrane21.

Functional complementation assays of GsCHX19.3 in yeast mutant. To test the transport activity of GsCHX19.3, we performed the functional complementation analyses by using the Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain AXT4K. Strain AXT4K was generated by deleting plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (ScENA1–4), plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter $\left( S c N H A I \right)$ , vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter $( S c N H X I ) ^ { 2 2 }$ , and endoplasmic reticulum $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger $( S c K H A I ) ^ { 1 0 }$ in the W303-1B background. AXT4K was sensitive to high salt and low potassium with alkali $\mathrm { p H } ^ { 5 }$ . Besides, AXT4K was also sensitive to hygromycin B, an aminoglycosidic antibiotic produced by Streptomyces hygroscopicus, which inhibits protein synthesis in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells23. It has been reported that ScNHX1 and AtNHX1 expression could restore AXT4K tolerance to hygromycin $\mathrm { B } ^ { 5 }$ . In this study, to express GsCHX19.3 in AXT4K, its CDS region was cloned into the pDR196 expression vector and introduced into AXT4K. Growth performance of yeast cells revealed that GsCHX19.3 expression in AXT4K could also recover its hygromycin B resistance (Fig. 6A), indicating GsCHX19.3 could function normally in AXT4K.

We further checked the efects of GsCHX19.3 on ion transporting. To do this, transformed yeasts were grown on Arg phosphate (AP) or YPD medium with diferent levels of KCl and NaCl. As shown in Fig. S3, GsCHX19.3 expression didn’t restore yeast tolerance to high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress under normal $\mathrm { p H }$ condition. We also observed that all transformants showed no growth diference on mediums with 0.01 (low $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ ), 0.1 (low $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ ) and 1mM KCl (normal) at normal pH (pH5.8) (Fig. 6B). Tese fndings suggested GsCHX19.3 didn’t function under either low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , or high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , or high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress.

Previous studies have shown that AtCHX19 functioned at low $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ alkalinity condition9, 11. Hence, to further explore the function of GsCHX19.3 at low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and high $\mathrm { p H }$ , the transformed yeasts were grown on low-KCl AP medium (0.01 and $0 . 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ KCl) at either $\mathrm { p H } 4 . 5$ (acidic), or $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 8$ (normal), or $\mathrm { p H } 7 . 5$ (alkali). As shown in Fig. 6C, all yeasts exhibited no growth diference on normal AP medium $\mathrm { \Phi _ { p H } } 5 . 8$ with $1 \mathrm { m M K ^ { + } }$ ). When $\mathrm { p H }$ lowered to 4.5, no signifcant diference was observed for the growth performance of diferent transformed yeasts. However, when the pH value was up to 7.5, only GsCHX19.3 expressed yeasts grew as well as W303-1B. Especially, only GsCHX19.3 and W303-1B could survive on AP medium with $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { m M }$ KCl at pH7.5. Based on these results, we believe that GsCHX19.3 functions as an active $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporter under alkali pH.

In the view of induced expression of GsCHX19.3 under carbonate stress, we further tested the yeast growth on YPD medium with 0, 7 or 11 mM ${ \mathrm { N a H C O } } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 6D). When supplemented with $1 1 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { N a H C O } _ { 3 }$ , W303-1B and GsCHX19.3 transformed yeasts grew much better than other yeast cells, which implied that GsCHX19.3 expression in AXT4K could also facilitate yeast tolerance to carbonate stress. In conclusion, results from yeast complementation assays revealed that GsCHX19.3 functioned as a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporter at alkali $\mathrm { p H }$ , and also participated in carbonate stress responses in yeast cells.

GsCHX19.3 overexpression in Arabidopsis increased plant tolerance to salt-alkaline stress. Te stress induction of GsCHX19.3 expression in G. soja and its functional complementation in yeast mutant AXT4K preliminarily indicated its potential roles in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and stress responses. Hence, to further evaluate the function of GsCHX19.3 in plants, its CDS region was cloned into pCAMBIA $3 3 0 0 3 5 \mathrm { S u } ^ { 2 4 }$ , and transformed into wild type Arabidopsis (Columbia background) through foral dip method (Fig. 7A). Tree overexpression (OX) transgenic lines were identifed through semi-quantitative RT-PCR analyses (Fig. 7B), and two of them (#2 and $\# 6$ ) with diferent expression levels were used for further phenotypic assays.

By using the root length assay, we checked whether GsCHX19.3 overexpression in WT could alter high salt (NaCl) and carbonate alkaline $\mathrm { ( N a H C O _ { 3 } ) }$ ) tolerance. As shown in Fig. 7C,D, all seedlings (WT, and OX lines) showed similar growth under normal condition. Under salt and alkaline stresses, primary roots of OX seedlings were signifcantly longer than those of WT (Fig. 7E,F) $( \mathtt { p } < 0 . 0 5$ by one-way ANVOA).

To further evaluate the salt-alkaline tolerance at the adult stage, the 4-week-old WT and OX plants were watered with $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M N a H C O _ { 3 } } ( \mathrm { p H } = \mathfrak { s }$ . Afer salt-alkaline treatment for 15 days, WT exhibited chlorosis and wilting, even death, but OX plants appeared relatively healthy (Fig. 7G). Quantifcation analysis of the survival rate revealed that only $3 9 . 8 \%$ of WT plants survived, while the survival rates for OX lines were $7 0 . 9 \%$ (line 2) and $6 2 . 5 \%$ (line 6) (Fig. 7H) $( \mathtt { p } < 0 . 0 5$ by one-way ANVOA). Above all, GsCHX19.3 plays a positive role in response to salt-alkaline stress in plants.

GsCHX19.3 mediates $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and $\pmb { { \mathsf { N } } } \hat { \mathbf { q } } ^ { + }$ excretion under carbonate alkaline stress in plants. During the long term evolution, plants have developed unique mechanisms to resist salt-alkaline stress. When sufering salt stress, plants would promote $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ absorbtion in order to alleviate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxic and maintain $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a } ^ { + 2 5 , 2 6 }$ . Considering the function of CHXs in cation transporting, we further examined the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content in WT and OX plants under both normal and salt-alkaline stress. Under normal growth condition, GsCHX19.3 OX lines exhibited signifcantly higher $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content than WT, but showed similar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation to WT (Fig. 8A,B) $^ { ( \ast } \mathrm { p } < 0 . 0 5$ , $^ { * * } \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1$ by Student’s t-test). Tis implied a positive role of $G s C H X 1 9 . 3 $ in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in plants.

Afer carbonate alkaline treatment, all plants showed an obvious decrease in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content, but a great increase in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation (Fig. 8A,B) $^ { ( \ast } \mathrm { p } < 0 . 0 5$ , $^ { * * } \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1$ by Student’s t-test). Compared with WT, OX lines displayed much lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content under stress treatment (Fig. 8B) $^ { \ast } \mathrm { { p } } < 0 . 0 5$ , $^ { * * } \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1$ by Student’s $t$ -test). However, the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ content of WT is similar to that of OX lines (Fig. 8A). As a consequence, under normal condition, WT displayed lower $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ratio, compared with OX lines (Fig. 8C). Afer carbonate alkaline treatment, all plants showed decreased $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ratio, but the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } } / \mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ratio of OX was remarkably higher than WT (Fig. 8D) $( ^ { * * } \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1$ by Student’s $t { \cdot }$ -test).

In conclusion, above results indicated that GsCHX19.3 overexpression could increase $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ absorbtion under normal condition, and reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ absorbtion or increase $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ excretion to alleviate ion poison caused by salt-alkaline stress.

## AtCHX17 belongs to the $N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + }$ antiporter family


The complete AtCHX17 coding region was cloned and sequenced. AtCHX17 is predicted to encode a polypeptide of 820 amino acids with a molecular weight of $8 9 \ \mathsf { k D a }$ . Hydrophobicity plot analysis showed that AtCHX17 has 11 predicted transmembrane domains in a highly hydrophobic N-terminal region (Figure 1a,b). AtCHX17 contains no predicted organellar-targeting sequence. Database searches revealed substantial similarities between the transmembrane region of AtCHX17 and ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ or $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ putative antiporters of microbial or yeast origin. Of these, only KHA1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Ramirez et al., 1998) and NAPA from Enterococcus hirae (Waser et al., 1992) have been functionally characterized. Over a stretch of 420 amino acids (1–420), AtCHX17 share $3 5 \%$ identity and $58 \%$ similarity with KHA1 from S. cerevisiae and $2 6 \%$ identity and $50 \%$ similarity with NAPA from E. hirae (Figure 1a). Phylogenic analysis showed that AtCHX17 clusters with other Arabidopsis members of the CPA2 family, but not with the CPA1 or NhaD antiporter families (Figure 1c).


## AtCHX17 is induced by salt stress and $K ^ { + }$ starvation


A probe, corresponding to the 335 bp fragment located upstream of the stop codon of AtCHX17, was synthesized by RT-PCR. This probe detected a unique restriction fragment on Southern blot with Arabidopsis thaliana ecotype Col-0 or WS genomic DNA, and therefore was considered to be specific for AtCHX17 (data not shown).

Variations of AtCHX17 expression in response to salt stress was investigated by Northern blot experiments (Figure 2a). Arabidopsis thaliana plants grown hydroponically were transferred in nutrient solution containing $1 0 0 \mathrm { \ m m \ N a C l }$ for 2, 4 or 6 days. Plant growth was inhibited in response to the treatment, but no visible damage of the plant tissues was observed. Plant response to salt stress was monitored by measuring ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ content in shoots (Figure 2c). As expected, sodium accumulated in shoots during the treatment. Total RNA was extracted from roots and shoots and analyzed by northern hybridization (Figure 2a). AtCHX17 transcripts were not detected in shoots in any conditions. In roots, AtCHX17 expression was not detected in control plants but was strongly enhanced by salt stress. The level of transcripts accumulated increased with the duration of the treatment and was correlated to salt accumulation in shoots. Such results indicate that salt-induced AtCHX17 expression is likely to be related to progressive salt accumulation in plant rather than to the initial osmotic shock in roots due to the treatment.

Salinity stress interferes with $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ nutrition by limiting the acquisition of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ by cells due to $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } / \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ competition (review in Hasegawa et al., 2000). Therefore, the expression of AtCHX17 was also investigated in response to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation in the absence of ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ . Arabidopsis thaliana plants cultivated in a nutrient solution containing $2 \mathsf { m m } \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ were rinsed 5 min in a $0 . 2 \mathrm { \ m w } \mathrm { \ C a S O } _ { 4 }$ solution and transferred in a nutrient solution without ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ added. Only traces of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + } \left( < 1 5 \mu \mathsf { M } \right)$ were measured in this solution. Plants were maintained during 5 or 2 days in the ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ -free medium then returned to a nutrient solution containing $2 \mathsf { m m } \mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ for two additional days. Rosette growth was not completed at the beginning of the treatment and inhibition of plant growth in response to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation was observed. A decrease in shoot $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was measured indicating a severe limitation of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ for the plant (Figure 2c). However, $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ resupply of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -starved plants restored the shoot $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content at a level similar to control plants indicating that the starvation effects were fully reversible (Figure 2c). Total RNA was extracted from roots and shoots and analyzed by northern hybridization. AtCHX17 transcripts were not detected in leaves of starved plants. In roots, AtCHX17 was strongly induced by $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation and the level of transcripts accumulated increased with the duration of the treatment (Figure 2b). The induction was reversed by the addition of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (Figure 2b).

Because both treatments may result in reduction of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content, the shoots and roots $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content of plant subjected to salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation were compared. Arabidopsis plants grown as previously described were transferred either in nutrient solution containing $1 0 0 \mathrm { \ m m } \mathrm { \ N a C l }$ or in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -free nutrient solution. Six days after the transfer, shoots and roots were collected and washed 5 min in $0 . 2 \mathsf { m m } \mathsf { C a S O } _ { 4 }$ before ion content determination. In both shoots and roots, the decrease in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was equivalent in NaCl-treated and ${ \sf K } ^ { + } .$ -deprived plants (Figure 2d), suggesting that AtCHX17 salt-induction might be a consequence of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation.


## AtCHX17 is induced at acidic external pH and in response to ABA treatment


To gain further insights toward AtCHX17 function in planta, we tested whether a control by external pH might contribute to the regulation of AtCHX17. Plants of A. thaliana cultivated in hydroponic conditions were transferred to nutrient solution maintained at pH 5, 6 or 7 in the presence of organic buffers. Four days after the transfer, total RNA was extracted from roots and shoots and analyzed by northern hybridization (Figure 3a). AtCHX17 transcripts were never detected in shoots. In roots, AtCHX17 expression was induced by acidic external pH (pH 5). As AtCHX17 expression was influenced by the external pH, we have monitored the external pH of the nutrient solutions during salt stress and ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ starvation treatments. For both treatments, the pH of the nutrient solution, initially at 6, was always comprised between 6.2 and 6.4 the day of the harvest. Thus, AtCHX17 induction in response to salt stress and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation was not triggered by acidification of the nutrient solution.

## Expression of AtCHX17 in yeast


The functional characterization of AtCHX17 was investigated by yeast complementation studies. The full-length coding sequence of AtCHX17 was cloned in the yeast expression vector pYES under the control of the inducible GAL promoter and used to transform the S. cerevisiae nhx1:ena1, trk1-2 and kha1 yeast strains. The nhx1:ena1 strain is salt-sensitive, defective in ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ extrusion at the plasma membrane and ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ compartmentalization into the vacuole (Gaxiola et al., 1999). The trk1-2 stain is defective in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -uptake (Ko and Gaber, 1991). The kha1 strain overaccumulate $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (Ramirez et al., 1998). We failed to observe any complementation of these mutants when grown on medium containing high ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ or various $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations (data not shown). Because regulatory sequences/element might be missing for proper AtCHX17 targeting or functioning in yeast, such negative results do not necessarily imply that AtCHX17 is not involved in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ or ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ transport. For example, many $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transporters of the plant HAK family such as AtHAK5 (Rubio et al., 2000), HvHAK2 (Senn et al., 2001), CnHAK1 and CnHAK2 (Garciadeblas et al., 2002) or OsHAK7 and OsHAK10 (Ban˜ uelos et al., 2002), failed to compensate the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transport defect of the yeast trk1-2 strain. The Arabidopsis inward $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ channel SPIK was also unable to complement the trk1-2 strain (F. Gaymard, personal communication, INRA, Montpellier, France), but has been demonstrated to mediate $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in planta (Mouline et al., 2002).

## Phenotypic characterization of chx17 knockout mutants


Morphological phenotypes of chx17-1 were analyzed under various growth conditions. When grown in vitro or in hydroponic conditions in basal nutrient medium or under salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation, no differences in germination time, primary root length, root branching and shoot growth were observed between the wild-type (Col-0) and chx17-1 (data not shown). Phenotypic characteristics of chx17-1 were further investigated by determining ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content in response to salt stress and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation (Figures 7 and 8). Wild-type and mutant plants were grown in hydroponic conditions in the same tanks in basal nutrient solution. After 6 weeks of culture, plants were transferred in nutrient solution containing 100 mM NaCl or in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -depleted nutrient solution. Six days after the transfer, the second fully expanded rosette leaves and the mature zone of the roots (without the root tip) were collected and washed for 5 min in

$0 . 2 \mathrm { \ m M } \mathrm { C a S O } _ { 4 }$ before ion content determination. In control conditions ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ contents were equivalent in both genotypes (Figure 7 and 8). In response to both treatments, the differences between the mutant and the wild type were systematically observed in three independent series of experiments. As expected, the NaCl treatment led to an increase in ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ content (Figure 7a) and to a decrease in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content in shoots and roots of both genotypes, indicating that the plants were $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -deprived (Figure 7b). In shoots of salt-treated plants, the ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was similar in both genotypes (Figure 7a,b). In roots, the ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ content was also equivalent in both genotypes (Figure 7a), but the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was reduced by $2 4 . 3 \%$ in chx17-1 compared with the wild type (Figure 7b). In wild-type roots, 6 days of NaCl treatment led to a loss of $0 . 3 2 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } { 0 } | ~ \mathrm { m g } ^ { - 1 }$ dry weight (DW) of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ . The reduction of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was increased by $40 \%$ in the mutant $1 0 . 4 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ \mathsf { m g } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathsf { D } ^ { 1 }$ W). Interestingly, the root $\mathsf { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ content was found to be similar in both genotypes (Figure 7c), indicating that alteration in ion content was specific for $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ in the mutant. As expected, the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation experiment led to a decrease in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content in shoots and roots (Figure 8a). This decrease was similar in shoots of both genotypes. However, in roots the ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ content was reduced by $2 2 . 8 \%$ in the mutant compared with the wild type (Figure 8a). Again, this difference was specific to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ , the root $\mathsf { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ content being similar in both genotypes in response to the treatment (Figure 8b). Under conditions of reduced $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ availability (salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation), the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content is decreased in chx17-1 roots compared with the wild type, suggesting that AtCHX17 function is related to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis.

To rule out the possibility that the observed phenotype was caused by an unknown point mutation unlinked to chx17-1, an homozygous line (named chx17-1bc) resulting from the back-cross of chx17-1 with Col-0 was selected and analyzed. Furthermore, to confirm that the observed phenotype was the result of loss of function of AtCHX17 and was not specific to the chx17-1 allele, we have analyzed a second mutant with a T-DNA inserted within AtCHX17 (sequencedindexed line Salk-060180, SIGnal database). In this mutant (chx17-2 allele) the T-DNA was inserted within the third exon. A homozygous line was selected, selfed and used for phenotypic analysis. Phenotypic characteristics of chx17-1bc and chx17-2 were investigated by determining the root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content in response to salt stress and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation (Figure 9). As in the mutant chx17-1, the root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was reduced in both mutants compared with the wild type in response to both treatments (Figure 9). Two independent mutants within the AtCHX17 gene led to an equivalent phenotype regarding root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content. Therefore, we conclude that AtCHX17 function relates to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis in Arabidopsis.

## AtCHX17 is homolog of $N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + }$ antiporters


Plant members of the CPA2 (or CHX) family were proposed to encode cation/proton antiporters (Ma¨ ser et al., 2001). So far, no plant members of this family have been characterized. It was predicted that cation $/ \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters extrude cations from the cytosol to the outside or into intracellular compartments such as the vacuole, because of protons pumps at the plasma membrane and endomembranes of plant cells (Sze et al., 1999). AtCHX17 shows substantial similarities with $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } , \mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters from other organisms, particularly with KHA1 from S. cerevisiae. KHA1 was proposed to function as a ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ antiporter localized at the plasma membrane involved in the regulation of intracellular pH, $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ efflux and cell volume control (Ramirez et al., 1998). These homologies suggest that AtCHX17 function as a $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } , \mathsf { K } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter.


## AtCHX17 regulation upon salt stress and potassium starvation suggest a role in $K ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis


AtCHX17 expression was strongly induced in roots in response to salt stress. Plant responses under salinity are not only direct results of ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ toxicity but may be also the consequence of a reduced $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ availability due to the competition between ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ . Indeed, in response to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation or NaCl treatment, similar reduction of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was observed (Figure 2d). Consistent with this hypothesis of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ limitation having a major role in salt-induced AtCHX17 expression, is the strong induction of AtCHX17 in roots of plants under $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation, in the absence of sodium. Therefore, ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ is not required for the expression of the gene. Very recently, using transcriptome analysis, conflicting data were reported regarding AtCHX17 induction by salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation. Consistent with our data, AtCHX17 was found to be overexpressed in roots of Arabidopsis plant treated with NaCl $1 0 0 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ (Kreps et al., 2002). In a second report, AtCHX17 upregulation was not observed in response to salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation (Maathuis et al., 2003). These differences are likely to be explained by the growth stage of the plants. In our experiments, at the beginning of each treatment rosette growth was not completed (stage 3.50– 3.90 according to Boyes et al., 2001) and we clearly observed an inhibition of rosette growth in response to salt stress or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation. In the work of Maathuis et al. (2003) plants have almost completed their growth (stage 5.10 according to Boyes et al., 2001) and whole plant $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ demand might be low at the time of the treatment. Consistent with this interpretation, the root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content was not affected in response to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation in this experiment. All together our expression data point out that the function of AtCHX17 might be related to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transport rather than to ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ transport as predicted by sequence analysis.

Upregulation of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in plants under $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -limitation is an adaptative response to adjust the uptake capacity to the whole plant demand. In split-root experiments, withdrawal of external $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ from one part of the root system leads to an increase of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ influx into the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -deprived roots as well as into the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -supplied roots suggesting that the control is exerted by nutritional status of the whole plant through inter-organ signaling pathway (Drew and Saker, 1984). Increase in high affinity $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in response to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -deprived roots has been shown to involve an increase in the number of carriers and protein synthesis (Drew et al., 1984; Fernando et al., 1990). To our knowledge, upregulation of plant transporters by both salt stress and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation was only reported for two members of the HAK $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -transporters family in common ice plant (Su et al., 2002). These transporters were proposed to be major contributors to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis under high salinity conditions both by facilitating uptake and by transport through the vasculature. Similarly, AtCHX17 is induced upon salt stress and ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ starvation suggesting that AtCHX17 might also contribute to $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis under high salinity in Arabidopsis.

In roots, AtCHX17 expression is strongly induced by ABA treatment. The transport and accumulation of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ was reported to be at least in part ABA-regulated. ABA regulation of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transport has been extensively evidenced in guard cells (review in Schroeder et al., 2001). In higher plant roots, there is evidence of modulation of ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ channel activity in stelar cells by ABA (Roberts, 1998; Roberts and Snowman, 2000). Additionally, treatment with ABA has been shown to downregulate the expression of the pericycle-localized root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ channel SKOR (Gaymard et al., 1998). However, ABA regulation of other root $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transporters was never reported. Whether the induction of AtCHX17 by ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ starvation might be ABA-mediated remains to be elucidated.

Together, these results show that various environmental stresses, including high salt, $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ deficiency, ABA and acidic medium, upregulate AtCHX17 transcript suggesting that this gene has a role in adaptative response to those stresses. Whether AtCHX17 acts directly or indirectly to modulate $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis remains to be clarified.


## Role of AtCHX17 in $K ^ { + }$ homeostasis


The localization of AtCHX17 expression in root cells is consistent with a role in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition. The tissue localization of AtCHX17 expression was determined using a GUS reporter gene strategy and confirmed by in situ RT-PCR experiments. AtCHX17 was expressed in root cell types specialized in ions uptake. AtCHX17 expression is strong along the mature root in epidermal and cortical cells and absent at the root tip. In roots, AtCHX17 is expressed in zones (epidermis and cortex) where ions can reach cell surface by apoplastic diffusion. In the mature root, the Casparian strip present at the endodermis blocks such diffusion into the stele (Pitman, 1982). Therefore, root epidermal and cortical cells mediate the net uptake of ions into the root symplasm, whereas the stelar cells of the root mediate the net loss of ions from the root symplasm into the xylem vessels (Clarkson, 1988).

The phenotype of chx17 knockout mutants supports a role in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis. The functional characterization of AtCHX17 was investigated in two T-DNA insertional mutants (chx17-1 and chx17-2) of Arabidopsis. The mutant plants were compared with the wild type, in response to salt stress and potassium starvation. In response to both treatments, the root ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ content was found to be lower in the mutants compared with the wild type whereas no differences were detected for other cations such as ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ . These data give further support to the hypothesis of a role of AtCHX17 in increasing net $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake. It is unclear whether this is due to an increase in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake or a reduction in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ loss especially in the roots.

In the absence of functional characterization of AtCHX17 protein, direct evidence is lacking regarding the mechanism of AtCHX17 function. However, our data provide circumstantial evidences for stimulating working hypothesis to further investigate the role of this gene. Potassium could enter root cells via $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ channels or ${ \sf K } ^ { + } , { \sf H } ^ { + }$ symporters (review in Ve´ry and Sentenac, 2003) and is then accumulated into vacuoles by a ${ \sf K } _ { \mathrm { i n } } ^ { + } / { \sf H } _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { + }$ exchange. Long-distance transport could involve export of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ from xylem parenchyma cells to the apoplast by a $\sf K _ { o u t } ^ { + } / \sf H _ { i n } ^ { + }$ exchange at the plasma membrane.

Assuming a working model of AtCHX17 as a ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ exchanger, different hypothesis might be proposed. Plant cells contain two major pools of ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ , one in the vacuole and one in the cytosol. In conditions of ${ \sf K } ^ { + }$ sufficiency, it was reported that, in epidermal and cortical cells the net uptake of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ into vacuoles is mediated by ${ \sf K } _ { \mathrm { i n } } ^ { + } / { \sf H } _ { \mathrm { o u t } } ^ { + }$ antiporters (walker 96), and AtCHX17 may be part of this mechanism. However, in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -deficient cells the net $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ release out of the vacuole is proposed to be achieved by ${ \sf H } ^ { + } , { \sf K } ^ { + }$ symporters (Walker et al., 1996). The hypothesis of AtCHX17 being a ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ antiporter localized at the tonoplast activated under $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation is somehow not consistent with this model. In plants there is some biochemical evidence suggesting the existence of ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ antiporter at the plasma membrane (Cooper et al., 1991; Hassidim et al., 1990). These antiporters are proposed to fulfill functions in the control of cellular pH and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content such as those described for fungi (review in Rodrı\`guez-Navarro, 2000). Such antiporters would exclude $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ from the cytosol to the apoplasm. However, AtCHX17 being involved in such a role, is not consistent with the mutant phenotype. According to such a hypothesis, a loss of function mutation is not expected to reduce tissue $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content. Recently, a tomato ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ antiporter, LeNHX2, was reported to be located in the intracellular compartment (Venema et al., 2003). This exchanger is proposed to maintain higher $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ concentration in intracellular compartments under salt-stress conditions and might be involved in intracellular $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis. The contribution of AtCHX17 in such a function in Arabidopsis may be an alternate hypothesis but remains to be elucidated.

In experiments presented in this paper, we have monitored the accumulation of ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ , that is the end result of processes involving multiple transporters. We cannot rule out that compensation by other transporters involved in ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ or $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis, including other CHX members, and/or deregulation mechanisms, occurred in the mutant leading to the phenotype observed. This concerns specially other members of the CHX family closely related to AtCHX17 (AtCHX15, AtCHX16, AtCHX18, AtCHX19 and AtCHX20 shares more than $50 \%$ identities). Excepted AtCHX18, all of them were found to be expressed using RT-PCR experiments (F. Cellier, unpublished data). We also consider a model where activation of AtCHX17 modulates activities of other $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ transporters, such as high-affinity ${ \sf K } ^ { + } , { \sf H } ^ { + }$ symporters, that bring in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ into plants under $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -deficient conditions (Maathuis and Sanders, 1994; Rodrı\`guez-Navarro, 2000; Walker et al., 1996).

This study shows that AtCHX17 has a role in $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis and that it may assist plants to withstand various environmental stresses. Clearly, further investigations are required to determine the membrane location of AtCHX17 protein and to test whether it affects $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ content in roots mainly via a ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } / { \mathsf { H } } ^ { + }$ exchange, a ${ \sf K } ^ { + } , { \sf H } ^ { + }$ symport or a combination of several mechanisms.


## Experimental procedures



## Plant material and culture conditions


Arabidopsis thaliana ecotypes Wassilewskija (Ws) and Columbia (Col-0) were used in this study. The Salk-002039 mutant line is of the ecotype Columbia and was provided by ABRC Arabidopsis stock center as segregating T3 lines. Plants were grown in hydroponic conditions, in vitro or in the greenhouse. For hydroponic culture, seeds were sown on sand laid on a mesh floating on tap water in a 10 l tank. After 2 weeks, the culture system was transferred on aerated basal nutrient solution containing $1 \mathsf { m m } \mathsf { C a } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 } ,$ 1 mM ${ \mathsf { K H } } _ { 2 } { \mathsf { P O } } _ { 4 }$ 1 mM ${ \sf K N O } _ { 3 } ,$ 1 mM ${ \sf M g S O _ { 4 } } ,$ $5 0 ~ \mu \mu$ Na-Fe-EDTA, $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ $\mathsf { H } _ { 3 } \mathsf { B O } _ { 3 } ,$ $0 . 0 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ CoCl, $0 . 0 5 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathsf { C u S O } _ { 4 }$ , 15 lM $Z n S O _ { 4 }$ , $5 0 ~ \mu \mu$ $\mathsf { M n S O } _ { 4 } ,$ $3 ~ \mu \mu$ MoNa, pH adjusted to 6 with KOH if needed. The growthchamber environmental parameters were as follows: light/dark cycle $8 / 1 6 ~ \mathrm { h }$ , light intensity $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ \ s e c ^ { - 1 } \ \mathsf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ PAR, temperature $2 2 ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } } / 2 0 ^ { \circ } { \mathsf { C } } _ { \iota }$ , $70 \%$ hygrometry. The nutrient solution was renewed twice a week during the first part of the culture, and daily the last week before the experiment and during the experiment.

For $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation experiment, roots were rinsed in $0 . 2 \mathrm { \ m M } \mathrm { C a S O } _ { 4 }$ before being transferred to a $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -free medium. In $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ -free medium, ${ \sf K H } _ { 2 } { \sf P O } _ { 4 }$ and ${ \mathsf { K N O } } _ { 3 }$ were replaced by $1 \ \mathsf { m m } \ \mathsf { N a H } _ { 2 } \mathsf { P O } _ { 4 }$ and $0 . 5 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ $\mathsf { C a } ( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ) _ { 2 }$ and the pH was adjusted to 6 with MES-Tris $\left( { \mathsf { p H } } \thinspace 6 \right)$ . For medium maintained at pH 5, 6 or 7, the basal nutrient solution was buffered with 4.4 mM MES (pH 5 or 6 with Tris) or $4 . 4 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ BES (pH 7 with Tris). For all experiments, plants of the same age cultivated in various conditions were harvested at the same time in the middle of the light period. At the beginning of each treatment, plants were at a vegetative stage corresponding to rosette growth (between stage 3.50 and 3.90 according to Boyes et al., 2001) and rosette growth was not completed. When necessary, treatments were initiated for various times before the harvest. During all the experiments, the pH of the nutrient solution was monitored daily. During salt stress, $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation or ABA treatments, the pH of the nutrient solution (initially at 6) was always comprised between 6.3 and 6.6 the day of the harvest.

For in vitro culture, seeds were surface-sterilized by soaking in a solution containing $1 . 5 \%$ (w/v) Bayrochlor (Indusco France, Gargenville, France) in $50 \%$ ethanol for 30 min under strong agitation, rinsed three times in $100 \%$ ethanol and dried overnight under a sterile air flow. Seeds were sown on the same basal nutrient solution containing $0 . 7 \%$ agar and supplemented with $1 \%$ sucrose. After 10 days of culture, seedlings were transferred to the appropriate agar-solidified medium depending on the treatment as described above. For $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ starvation experiment, agar was replaced by agarose. The in vitro growth conditions were as follows: light/ dark cycle $1 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } / 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ , light intensity $1 5 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ \ s e c ^ { - 1 } \ \mathsf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ PAR, temperature $2 1 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C / 1 8 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ , $6 5 \%$ hygrometry.

In the greenhouse, plants were grown on compost (Neuhaus Humin Substrat N2; Klasman-Deilmann GmbH, Geeste, Germany) and subirrigated with tap water. Greenhouse culture conditions were as follows: light/dark cycle $1 6 \mathrm { ~ h } / 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ , sunlight intensity limited to $3 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ \ s e c ^ { - 1 } \ \mathsf { m } ^ { - 2 }$ PAR, temperature $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } / 2 4 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ .

Potassium $( \mathrm { K ^ { + } } )$ plays an essential role in plant growth and development by affecting nutrition, membrane potential, pH homeostasis, cell osmotic pressure, enzyme function and photosynthesis (Pardo et al. 2006; Lebaudy et al. 2007; Dreyer & Blatt 2009; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is present in higher concentrations in plant cells, in the $1 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ range, than in the soil solution, which is typically in the 0.1– $1 . 0 \mathrm { m M }$ range (Ashley et al. 2006; Chérel et al. 2014). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation causes a strong and rapid decrease in total plant $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content; $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels in roots decreases more rapidly than that in shoots, and plant growth can only be maintained for several days after $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation (Pardo et al. 2006; Lebaudy et al. 2007; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013). Moreover, prolonged starvation results in growth inhibition and chlorosis that is usually initially visible on older leaves (Armengaud et al. 2004; Zhao et al. 2008a,b). These observations suggest plants have evolved a protective mechanism that may take up, recirculate and redistribute $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx and efflux transporters to buffer against $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deficiencies or stresses and ensure sustained growth during periods of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation.

Many $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters regulate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in different plant tissues through uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from the soil, transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ among organelles inside of cells,efflux of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ out of root cells, or translocation and/or recirculation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ between roots and shoots (Rodriguez-Navarro & Rubio 2006;Schachtman & Shin 2007).To date, a comprehensive understanding of transporters orchestrating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis remains elusive. However, an array of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters and channels have been characterized (Anderson et al. 1992; Gassmann & Schroeder 1994; Maathuis et al. 1997; Quintero & Blatt 1997; Hirsch et al. 1998; Elumalai et al. 2002; Rodriguez-Navarro & Rubio 2006; Schachtman & Shin 2007; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013), such as root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -uptake transporters with dual-affinities (Fu & Luan 1998; Kim et al. 1998) and some vascular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters functioning as outwardly rectifying transporters (Marten et al. 1999; Lacombe et al. 2000). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is taken up by various inward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels or transporters in root epidermal cells and then transported into the xylem sap (Gaymard et al. 1998). Through the xylem, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is transported into shoots and leaves to support plant growth and development. An Arabidopsis Shaker-type $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel (SKOR) is expressed in the root pericycle and xylem parenchyma cells to sense low extracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and direct an outward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ flux (Gaymard et al. 1998; Johansson et al. 2006; Liu et al. 2006). SKOR may be involved in xylem loading of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx into the xylem. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ can also be transported from leaves and stem cells into phloem (Rodriguez-Navarro & Rubio 2006).Phloem $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentrations tend to be significantly higher than xylem $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and probably range from around 50 to $1 5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ (Kallarackal et al. 2012). Phloem $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport is accomplished by transporters such as AKT2/3 that mediate both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx and efflux owing to its weak rectification properties. Given the vascular expression of this transporter, AKT2/3 may play roles in both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ loading in source leaves and unloading in sink organs (Lacombe et al. 2000; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013).The Arabidopsis guard cell outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel (GORK) mediates $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ release from the guard cells (Ache et al. 2000),GORK is also expressed in the root hairs and root epidermal cells and releases $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from these root cells into the medium in response to stimuli, therefore, it is regarded as a root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sensor (Ivashikina et al. 2001; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013). The $\mathrm { p H }$ environment alters membrane potential and outward or inward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ rectifying activities.The proton gradient, electrochemical potential of the membrane and pH can control $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport activity (Véry & Sentenac 2003; Collins & Larson 2005; Zhao et al. 2008a). In turn, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inward- or outwardrectification affects pH (Walker et al. 1998; Collins & Larson 2005; Dreyer and Uozumi 2011). More regulatory mechanisms of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters, involving $\mathrm { p H }$ , redox status, or phosphorylation status and interaction with other small regulatory factors,are emerging (Schachtman & Shin 2007;Dreyer & Blatt 2009; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013; Latz et al. 2013;Takahasi et al., 2013). Although $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters and inward channels have been extensively studied, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux mechanisms and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ redistribution in plants are still poorly understood (Vergani et al. 1998; Xu et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2007; Dreyer & Blatt 2009; Ahmad & Maathuis 2013; Latz et al. 2013).

The plant cation $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchanger (CHX) transporters contain 10–12 membrane spanning domains and a carboxy tail of variable length. Detailed phylogenetic analysis indicates the CHXs can be separated into five subclades (Sze et al. 2004). Among them, CHX17 (At4g23700), CHX20 (At3g53720), CHX21 (At2g37910) and CHX23 (At1g05580) belong to subclade IV, and CHX13 (At2g30240) belongs to subclade III (Sze et al. 2004).CHX transporters have been implicated in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ homeostasis during growth and development.Mutant studies show that CHX17 is an endomembrane transporter that can suppress yeast endosomal defects in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport (Maresova & Sychrova 2006) and plays a role in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis (Cellier et al. 2004; Chanroj et al. 2011, 2013). CHX20 is also an endomembrane localized transporter that alters yeast growth at low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ when the $\mathrm { p H }$ is alkaline and plays a critical role in osmoregulation in guard cells (Padmanaban et al. 2007; Lu et al. 2011). CHX21 resides on the plasma membrane and appears to have a role in regulating xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations and $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ accumulation in the leaf when the plant is under salt stress (Hall et al. 2006; Evans et al. 2012). Several different functions for CHX23 have been reported (Song et al. 2004; Lu et al. 2011; Evans et al. 2012).
