Interestingly, the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in the roots and shoots of the transgenic plants was higher than that in the WT plants and was in the following order: TP3 (bicistronic) $> T N H X S I > T V P I > \mathbf { W T }$ , suggesting that the over-expression of TNHXS1 antiporter alone or in combination with TVP1 may be effective in the accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in vacuoles.


## Leaf discs of TP3 transgenic lines showed faster $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake than monotransgenic lines


Accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in shoot is controlled by multiples mechanisms. These include exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from uptake by roots, vacuolar compartmentation in root tissue and control of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loading into the xylem. To eliminate the contribution of these mechanisms, we measured the speed of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake using leaf discs derived from transgenic plants grown under normal conditions. Leaf discs from the TP3 transgenic plants showed faster uptake of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than that of the TNHXS1 and TVP1 transgenic plants. The calculated speed of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake by the leaf discs was 0.70, 1.70 and 2.26 $\mathrm { ( p p m ~ h ^ { - 1 } }$ per disc) for the TVP1, TNHXS1 and the TP3 transgenic plants, respectively.

TP3 plants exhibited better performance under greenhouse-based salt stress

To evaluate further the salinity tolerance conferred by the dicistronic construct, we conducted a greenhouse experiment and scored different growth parameters such as plant fresh weight, plant height, number of leaves per plant, root lengths and seed production. Under non-stress conditions, the different transgenic lines showed normal phenotypes and their growth parameters were even superior to those of the WT plants (Fig. 6 and Table 1). When subjected to $2 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt stress, the TP3 and the TVP1 transgenic plants exhibited similar fresh weight production, plant heights, and seed production. However, TP3 and TVP1 transgenic lines significantly outperformed the WT and the TNHXS1 transgenic plants with regard to these parameters (Table 1). The TP3 plants were also found to produce significantly more leaves than the monotransgenic lines and the WT plants (Table 1). It is worth mentioning here that under both conditions (salt and non-salt stress), the TP3 plants showed better developed root systems (Fig. 6 and Table 1). To confirm further the improved salt stress tolerance of the transgenic lines, we calculated the percentage reduction compared with the respective unstressed control for the various parameters. At $2 5 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ , a reduction of $80 \%$ in plant fresh weight was registered in WT plants, whereas in TNHXS1, TVP1 and TP3 transgenic lines, the plant fresh weight percentage reduction was 61, 61 and $54 \%$ , respectively. The percentage reduction in plant height was $76 \%$ for the WT, whereas in TNHXS1, TVP1 and TP3 transgenic lines, the plant height percentage reduction was 63, 52 and $32 \%$ , respectively. The number of leaves per plant followed the same trend with the highest percentage reduction registered in WT plants and the lowest in TP3 transgenic plants.


## TP3 transgenic plants retained more chlorophyll under salt stress


Non-stressed plants grown in the greenhouse were analysed for tolerance to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ stress by leaf disc senescence assay. Incubation of leaf discs of the WT, the TP3, the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 transgenic plants on 300, 500 mM NaCl and water for $^ { 7 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ showed an early bleaching of the WT leaf discs compared with transgenic plants as shown in Fig. 7a.

At both concentrations of salt, the decrease in chlorophyll content in the transgenic plants was less pronounced than in the WT plants.

We also measured the total chlorophyll content of the various transgenic seedlings grown in vitro and found that without salt treatment, TP3 transgenic lines exhibited slightly higher chlorophyll contents compared with the TNHXS1, TVP1 and the WT plants (Fig. 7b). Salt treatment quickly decreased total chlorophyll content of the WT, TNHXS1 and TVP1 transgenic plants. However, the extent of this decline was much less in the TP3 transgenic plants. For example, at $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { { m M } ~ \ N a C l }$ treatment, chlorophyll content in TP3 (line 44) was similar to that recorded in the absence of salt treatment (Fig. 7b). Although TP3 trangenic plants retained less chlorophyll at $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt treatment than at $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , their chlorophyll content was still higher than that of the other transgenic lines and the WT (Fig. 7b). Taken together, these results indicated that the photosynthetic capacities of the TP3 transgenic plants remained higher during salt treatment than those of the transgenic plants over-expressing TNHXS1 or TVP1 genes individually.


## TP3 transgenic plants maintained high catalase activity under salt stress


Salt stress induces cellular accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) which can damage membrane lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Catalase enzymes that can remove the ROS produced by the salt stress play an important role in tolerance. Thus, we measured CAT activity in the leaves of the WT and the various transgenic lines subjected to salt stress. The results indicated that in the absence of salt stress, the TNHXS1 and TVP1 transgenic plants exhibited over threefold more CAT activity in leaf crude extracts compared with the WT plants. The TP3 transgenic lines had over 1.5-fold more CAT activity than the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 transgenic lines (Fig. 8a). When subjected to $2 5 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ salt treatment, CAT activity decreased in both the WT and the different transgenic lines, but CAT activity remained highest in the TP3 transgenic lines (Fig. 8a). Compared with control conditions (absence of salt), the decrease in CAT activity was $84 \%$ in the WT plants, $44 \%$ in the TNHXS1, $33 \%$ in the TVP1 transgenic plants, and only $2 5 \%$ in the TP3 transgenic plants.


## TP3 transgenic plants exhibited minimal membrane damage under salt stress


To study the stability of membrane in transgenic plants under salt stress, we determined the electrolyte leakage $( \% )$ which represents the degree of cell membrane damage under stress. The results indicated that membrane permeability increased when plants are subjected to $2 5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt stress, but it showed a faster rise in the WT plants than that in the transgenic lines. The damage to the TP3 transgenic lines was less than to the single transgenic lines, TNHXS1 and TVP1, which had significantly less damage than the WT (Fig. 8b). In fact, after 1 month of salt treatment, the electrolyte leakage was $83 \%$ for the WT. However, it was

$70 \%$ in the TNHXS1transgenic lines, $60 \%$ in the TVP1 and only $45 \%$ in the TP3 lines.

TP3 plants retained more water than mono-transgenic lines under salt stress

In order to assess the water status of both the TP3 and the mono-transgenic plants, we measured the relative water content (RWC) of plants. As shown in Fig. 8c, no significant difference in RWC was observed between the WT and the various transgenic lines before application of salt stress. When exposed to salt treatment of $2 5 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ significant differences in RWC were detected between the WT and the different transgenic lines, indicating greater water retention capacity in the transgenic plants than in the WT. Under salt treatment, the RWC of the TP3 and the mono-transgenic plants declined, but this decline was more important in the TNHXS1 and TVP1 transgenic plants compared with the bicistronic TP3 lines.

Salinity is one of the most important environmental constraints affecting more than 800 million ha of arable land (Munns and Tester 2008). Salinity limits plant growth and causes significant losses of crop yield. Plants have evolved several mechanisms to cope with salt stress, the most important of which are $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tissue tolerance, and osmotic tolerance. One key mechanism of salinity tolerance is the ability to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the cytosol and its sequestration into the vacuole to limit cell damage. The transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles is thought to be mediated by vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family, which are driven by the electrochemical gradient of protons (Gaxiola et al. 1999; Pardo et al. 2006). The proton motive force used by vacuolar antiporters is generated by the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -translocating enzymes in the tonoplast, which are V-ATPase and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -inorganic pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ~ H ^ { + } }$ -PPiase). The $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase is a single subunit protein located in the vacuolar membrane (Maeshima 2000). It pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ from the cytoplasm into vacuoles with PPi-dependant $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport activity. Zhen et al. (1997) demonstrated that the Arabidopsis $\mathbf { A } t A V P I$ generated a proton gradient across the vacuolar membrane similar in magnitude to that of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase.

The over-expression of AtNHX1, or its homologs from other plant species, has resulted in enhanced plant tolerance not only to salt, but also to drought stress (Apse et al. 1999; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Xue et al. 2004; He et al. 2005; Brini et al. 2007; Chen et al. 2007; Khoudi et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010a). Similarly, the over-expression of AtAVP1 or its homologs in transgenic plants resulted in both drought and salt tolerance (Gaxiola et al. 2001). Interestingly, the enhanced salt tolerance in transgenic plants, over-expressing the AtAVP1 gene, was correlated with the increased ion content. These results suggest that the enhanced vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumping in transgenic plants was responsible for additional energy to support vacuolar sodium accumulation mediated by the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. In line with these results, Duan et al. (2007) demonstrated that the over-expression of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase resulted in an enhanced proton electrochemical gradient across the vacuolar membrane which accelerated the sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole and improved salinity tolerance at cellular level. Thus, it was predicted that co-expression of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase would confer better salt tolerance to transgenic plants than that of the single gene expression. Indeed, Zhao et al. (2006) provided experimental evidence that co-expression of SsNHX1 and AtAVP1 in transgenic rice conferred greater salt tolerance than that of the single SsNHX1. On the other hand, Qiu et al. (2007) reported that the coordinate expression of V-ATPase and vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter was essential for Suaeda salsa salt tolerance.

Salt stress tolerance is a complex trait (Flowers 2004); therefore, better tolerance to salinity might be achieved by pyramiding several genes into a single genotype (Samis et al. 2001). The success of this approach was demonstrated in the above-mentioned examples for pyramiding $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and one of the vacuolar translocating enzymes $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase or $\mathrm { V { - } H ^ { + } A T P a s e ) }$ ). It was also used for stacking various combinations of genes involved in drought and salt stress tolerance (Singla-Pareek et al. 2003; Zhou et al. 2008; Wei et al. 2011). To engineer plants with multiple genes, Schmidt et al. (2008) described several approaches. For example, plants are individually transformed and then crossed together. This method complicates the downstream breeding due to the size of the segregation population needed to obtain all the transgenes in one individual. An alternative approach consists of performing repeated plant transformation with successive transgenes to obtain multi-gene phenotypes. However, this approach is costly, time consuming, and it needs several selectable marker genes to perform the various selection rounds. One practical solution to overcome these limitations is to physically link multiple gene expression cassettes by positioning them contiguously on DNA that will transfer as single entity (Shibata and Liu 2000). This strategy has been used with great success to stack traits in commercial GM crops.

Soil salinity is one of the major threats to agricultural land that restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops (Flowers 1998). High salinity leads to cytosolic osmotic stress and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion specific toxicity in plants while over accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the cytosol causes inhibitory effects on many developmental processes such as protein synthesis, enzymatic reactions and photosynthesis (Murguia et al. 1995; Tsugane et al. 1999). However higher plants have developed multiple mechanisms through evaluation and adaptation involving morphological, physiological, biochemical and molecular responses to survive the harsh abiotic stress conditions (Hirayama and Shinozaki 2010; Krasensky and Jonak 2012). Salinity and drought may influence the plant growth and productivity in various ways. However, the major cause of damage is the excessive toxic accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and the loss of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the cytoplasm (Ali et al. 2016). To cope with such crucial saline conditions and maintain $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis, plant uses a number of transporters that protect them against $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions stress. This cation and $\mathrm { p H }$ homoeostasis is thought to be regulated by monovalent cation/proton antiporters (CPA) by exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ , or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ (Brett et al. 2005a). Prokaryotic and eukaryotic CPA members fall into two major super families designated as CPA1 (2.A.36) and CPA2 (2.A.37) (Brett et al. 2005a). In plants, the CPA1 family includes the well-studied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (NHX), while CPA2 family includes cation/ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchangers (CHX) and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux antiporter (KEA).

The model plant Arabidopsis contains total eight NHX members belonging to three different classes, six intracellular (IC) transporters that are categorized as either localized at tonoplast vacuoles (IC-I), or endosome (IC-II). The IC-I family includes AtNHX1-4, which are plant specific, while IC-II clade includes AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 that are similar to ScNHX1 (yeast) and human isoforms NHE6 and NHE7 (Bowers et al. 2000; Brett et al. 2005a; Chanroj et al. 2012). Two divergent members of the CPA1 family, AtNHX7/SOS1 and AtNHX8, are located at the plasma membrane. Some of these antiporters extrude toxic amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cell (SOS1/NHX7), while other NHX family members regulate cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ by sequestering them in vacuoles inside plant cells (Apse et al. 1999; Barragan et al. 2012).

Beside antiporters another class of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters is the HKT-type transporters (initially defined as high-affinity potassium transporters) that are divided into two subclasses on the basis of their transport properties and amino acid sequences (Platten et al. 2006). Subclass I transporters (ie.,

HKT1) have a serine (S) residue forming S-G-G-G motif while subclass II (ie., HKT2) type transporters have a glycine (G) residue replacing serine (S) in subclass I transporters and thereby contain a G-G-G-G motif (Maser et al. 2002). The presence of either serine (S) or glycine (G) contributes towards the specificity of transporter toward cations selection (Platten et al. 2006). Members of subclass I have strong affinity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ only, while those belonging to subclass II transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depending on the concentration of the two cations (Maser et al. 2002; Platten et al. 2006; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). HKT1-type transporters are believed to retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from xylem stream to protect shoots from $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, retain it in the root and thereby contribute mainly in reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion toxicity in plants (Rubio et al. 1995; Rus et al. 2001, 2006).

Previous studies on vacuolar compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plants are also shown to regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, mediated by tonoplast localized cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters (NHXs). For this process tonoplast $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase) and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } .$ pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ( H ^ { + } }$ -PPase) provide the proton motive force required for NHX function (Apse et al. 1999; Gaxiola et al. 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). In many transgenic plants the overexpression of tonoplast NHXs have enhanced resistance to salt and drought stress with increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles (Apse et al. 1999; Brini et al. 2007; Galvez et al. 2012; He et al. 2005; Jha et al. 2013; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Zhang et al. 2001), thought there are exceptions to this rule (Leidi et al. 2010; Jiang et al. 2010). The class-I NHX family proteins localized in tonoplast function as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, that are involved in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration inside the vacuoles maintaining turgor pressure and drive cell expansion. Recently, the two Arabidopsis vacuole localized homologous NHX proteins, NHX1 and NHX2 in Arabidopsis are shown to redundantly regulating the accurate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in vacuoles (Barragan et al. 2012; Bassil et al. 2011).


## Role of NHX Protein in Plant Growth and Development


Besides the prominent role of NHX proteins in salt and drought resistance in plants, recent advances have shown a series of other novel functions of these proteins including intracellular ions and pH homeostasis, turgor and osmotic regulation, stomatal movement, water uptake, cell expansion and regulation of flowering time (Andres et al. 2014; Bassil and Blumwald 2014; Bassil et al. 2011; Barragan et al. 2012; Pittman 2012; Reguera et al. 2014).

Ionic homeostasis and pH regulation are essential cellular processes necessary for plant growth and development especially during undesirable environmental conditions. The primary action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pumps regulates the cytoplasmic pH, while the

NHX proteins are $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters localized to the plasma membrane and tonoplast that facilitate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and constitute a proton leak thereby maintaining both $\mathrm { p H }$ and ions homeostasis (Rodríguez-Rosales et al. 2009). The best studied example of $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation is the Japanese morning glory (Ipomoea nil) InNHX2 which promotes the vacuolar alkalization in petals that converts the reddish-purple buds into purple flower by increasing the vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ (Ohnishi et al. 2005). Recently the reverse genetic approach has shown that AtNHX1 and AtNHX2 are $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and are required for active $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake (Fig. 1), osmotic and turgor regulation and playing a unique role in cell expansion and stomatal function by sustaining the intracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). In this review we want to highlight the recent advances in ion homeostasis and evidences existing for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and lacking rather than for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in plants by NHX-exchangers, which regulates a diverse set of functions and enzymatic reactions important for survival and growth of plants.


## $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and Signaling Mechanism


The action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ at the plasma membrane creates an electrical potential across the plasma membrane and increases the negative charge inside the cells promoting the passive influx of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions, while the efflux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (i.e., removal from cell) is not a passive process but needs the expenditure of energy (Maathuis et al. 2014). In high salinity the family of NonSelective Cation Channels (NSCCs family) is thought to mediate the spontaneous transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the root cells across the plasma membrane but until now the exact molecular mechanism is unknown (Kronzucker and Britto 2011). Beside NSCC family transporters, the transpirational bypass of water and solutes $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ across the apoplast has an important role in some plant species, such as rice, in which this non-selective pathway is the major port of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ entry and transport across the xylem without crossing the plasma membrane. In most species the casparian strip and suberine layers in plant roots endodermal and exo-dermal layers provide barriers to the apoplast flow (Yeo et al. 1987; Ochiai and Matoh 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ taken up by plant roots is transported to the shoot part in xylem by bulk flow that is driven by the tension in xylem causing continuous movement of water and solute (i.e., $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) from roots to shoot by transpiration (Almeida et al. 2016; Nobel 2009).

Potassium is one of major essential macronutrients which is required for several key biological functions in plants, like enzyme activation, osmotic and turgor generation, opening and closing of stomatal aperture, cytosolic pH regulation and membrane electric potential. The uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by plant roots is thought to be regulated by two independent transport systems with different kinetic parameters and selectivity (Epstein et al. 1963). The saturable system1 is constituted by the high affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake permeases HAK/KUP that operate in the micromolar range and transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the cytoplasm of the root cells against electrochemical gradient (SantaMarıa et al. 1997; Gierth et al. 2005). System 2 or the low affinity pathway, including channels of shaker family, has the characteristic of channel mediated the transport and uptake of external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at concentration of above 0.5 to $1 \mathrm { m M }$ with plasma membrane potential of -120 to $- 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m V } .$ The first isolated plasma membrane $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and AKT1 (hyperpolarization-activated inward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel) and the carrier-type HUP/HAK/KT transporter HAK5 in Arabidopsis displayed $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in heterologous system (Schachtman et al. 1992; Bertl et al. 1995; Gaymard et al. 1998a) indicated that these channels probably function in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake pathway in guard cells for KAT1 and in the root cells in case of AKT1 (Nakamura et al. 1995; Lagarde et al. 1996). Membrane depolarization by excessive cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx have a strong inhibitory effect on transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions into the plant root cells by inhibiting the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005), and increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux by depolarization-activated outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (eg, GORK) and NSSC as well (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005; Sun et al. 2009). Once $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is captured, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is further transported into the vacuole against the electrochemical gradient of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family energized by the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient across the tonoplast (Walker et al. 1996; Carden et al. 2003; Barragan et al. 2012).

Not much is known about how $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are sensed in most of root cellular systems in plants. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ can either be sensed outside, inside of the cell or both. In the case of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { , } }$ , the extracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by plant through membrane receptors in roots, while intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by membrane protein or other cytoplasmic enzymes (Tracy et al. 2008). From recent advances it is thought that the long cytoplasmic tail of plasma membrane localized antiporter SOS1 (SALT OVERLY SENSITIVE1; NHX7) might be responsible for intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sensing (Shi et al. 2000). However, the plasma membrane localized $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase can directly sense the changes in extracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration which led to the proposal that the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters might be the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sensors in plants.

In plants calcium signaling acts as a second messenger connecting various environmental stresses with intracellular responses including nutrient deficiency. Extracellular salt stress $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) transiently increase the free cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ by depolarization- and hyperpolarization-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels and by ROS-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels at the plasma membrane (Tracy et al. 2008). ROS accumulation is also strongly induced by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -starvation in Arabidopsis root cells (Shin and Schachtman, 2004; Shin et al. 2005). Cytosolic calcium elevation can also stimulate NADPH-oxidase mediating ROS-production (Yang and Poovaiah 2002). The increase in ROS further increase $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ influx by decoding $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensor such as Calmodulin (CaM), Calcinurin B-like proteins (CBLs) and CBL-interacting protein kinases (CIPKs), Forming CBL-CIPK complexes and are designated as calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) (Yang and Poovaiah 2003). Intracellular cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensors trigger various signal transduction pathways that are involved in regulation of ion channels activities (e, g., external $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ strongly blocked NSCC), enzymatic reactions, gene transcription and regulation of ion homeostasis (Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Martínez-Atienza et al. 2007; Adams and Shin 2014).


## Discovery and Localization of Arabidopsis NHX Exchangers


One of the predominant strategies that plant cells employ for the sequestration of toxic cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is to compartmentalize it in vacuoles, and NHX-type intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter have appeared to be well characterized transport proteins involved in this process so far (Apse 2003). Sequencing comparison of the yeast genome uncovered a novel gene present on chromosome IV (YDR456w), which encodes a protein of 633 aa, was named as NHX1 on the basis of sequence homology with the family of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHE1–4), that is found in mammals and other vertebrates, as well as in nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans), and euryhaline crab (Carcinusmaenas). Disruption of NHX1 gene led to a significant decrease in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance at $\mathrm { p H } 4$ or 5, indicating its prominent role in mediating tolerance to stress at acidic $\mathrm { p H }$ (Nass et al. 1997). The discovery of vacuolar NHX1, and its homologous protein in Arabidopsis, opened a new concept of intracellular compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions in plants (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000). AtNHX1 can functionally substitute for the endosomal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (ScNHX1) that requires ATPase activity of endosomal/vacuolar V-type ATPase to mediate ions compartmentalization in yeast vacuole (Quintero et al. 2000). Based on protein similarity of predicted amino acid sequence to AtNHX1, six AtNHX gene family members were categorized in Arabidopsis. These NHX $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene family members were named as AtNHX1-6 in order of decreasing phylogenetic relationship to the prototype of AtNHX1. AtNHX2-4 has $5 6 . 0 { - } 8 7 . 5 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1 whereas AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 has $8 7 . 7 \%$ similarity to each other’s and has $2 1 - 2 3 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1-4 isoforms in Arabidopsis (Yokoi et al. 2002). Maser et al. (2001) further expanded the NHX family to include the plasma membrane isoforms NHX7/SOS1 and NHX8.

Northern blot analysis using total RNA from seedlings of Col-0 indicated that AtNHX1 and 2 transcripts were highly abundant in shoots and roots. The transcript of AtNHX3 was highly abundant only in roots, and a low transcript level of AtNHX5 mRNA was detected in roots and shoots. While AtNHX4 and AtNHX6 transcript were not detectable on northern blot, they were detected in roots and shoots using RT-PCR. These findings established that all six genes of AtNHX are transcriptionally active in seedlings, indicating that their function is not only restricted to the later developmental stages (Yokoi et al. 2002).


## Sodium Exclusion and Tissue Tolerance


Soil salinity (mainly NaCl) restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops more than any other toxic substance in soil. By restricting the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx inside the cells can improve the plant growth and survival in saline stress, however, very little is known about the mechanism to inhibit the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx. On the other hand, to tolerate the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the soil plant cell must be capable of either export $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell or sequester it into the vacuoles to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity inside the cell (Xu et al. 2013). The $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ exclusion process energized by the plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ATPase is mainly carried out by the plasma membrane localized SOS1 (AtNHX7) in Arabidopsis, with its interacting component SOS3 (CBL4) and SOS2 kinase (CIPK24) in a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ dependent manner (Shi et al. 2000; Quintero et al. 2002; Qiu et al. 2002). But the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion by this process to outside medium can further increase the imbalance of osmotic and ionic stress across the membrane, therefore this kind of strategy is useful only for temporary resistance and cannot confers long term salt tolerance in the natural environmental conditions (Adem et al. 2014).

Beside the extrusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell, plants have the ability to safely handle large amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in tissues without any deleterious effect on plant metabolism. Such kind of tissues tolerance is mainly achieved by efficient $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles, thereby reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in the cytosol.


## NHX Proteins are Required for Accurate Potassium $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ Compartmentation in Vacuoles


Potassium is the most vital ionic osmoticum in plant cells that is largely distributed in two major pools, cytosol and vacuoles. Cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is an essential activator for many biochemical and enzymatic reactions, cytosolic $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation and plasma membrane electric potential (Fig. 2), requiring the maintenance of basic cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration within the narrow limit of 75 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ regardless of changes in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply (Walker et al. 1996). However, vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pools which is the largest and most dynamic reservoir of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depends on the availability of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . The lowest limit of vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration appears to be 10 to $2 0 \mathrm { m M }$ . The concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inside the plant cell vacuoles requires the active transport from cytosol which could be achieved through nonelecterogenic $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Walker et al. 1996). Biochemical analysis has proved that tonoplast localized NHX exchangers (NHX1 and NHX2) catalyze the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange with an apparent affinity of 12 to $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , which is below the lower cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration limit, and thus are able to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from cytosol to vacuoles (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; ernandez et al. 2009; Barragan et al. 2012). Different evidences have indicated that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (NHX)–type transporters could achieve the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in plant cells (Venema et al. 2002; Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Yoshida et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010; Leidi et al. 2010). So far six NHX genes (NHX1-6) encoding endosomal antiporters have been identified in Arabidopsis genome (Yokoi et al. 2002). RNA gel blot analysis and RT-PCR quantification showed the increased relative abundance of NHX1 and NHX2 transcript level in all the plant tissues which were accumulated in response to the same effectors (NaCl, KCl, LiCl, osmotic stress, and abscisic acid) (Yokoi et al. 2002).

Among all the Arabidopsis NHX transporters, NHX1 and NHX2 are the most closely related NHX family members at protein level $( 8 7 . 5 \%$ sequence identity) and both are localized in the tonoplast (Yokoi et al. 2002; Bassil et al. 2011b). AtNHX1 has been previously shown to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity with similar affinity (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Hernandez et al. 2009). The $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity in tonoplast of WT and nhx1 nhx2 double mutant by $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient created by V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase at $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ and KCl shows less than one-third of total exchange activity in nhx1 nhx2 than WT, demonstrating the combined contribution of NHX1 and NHX2 to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in total cation exchange capacity at tonoplast (Barragan et al. 2012). Research in transgenic tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) indicated that overexpressing vacuolar AtNHX1 or the endosomal LeNHX2 $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter leads to enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation

in cell vacuoles (Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al.   
2010).


## NHX1 and NHX2 Preferentially Regulates ${ { \bf K } } ^ { + }$ Homeostasis as Compared to $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$


The discovery of vacuolar NHX antiporters which mediate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ across the vacuolar membrane in saline environment (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000), was recently challenged on the basis of biochemistry of NHX-proteins, which do not differentiate between $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or even having stronger affinity for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport as compared with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; RodrıguezRosales et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010). Recent reports have conclusively demonstrated that vacuolar proteins NHX1 and NHX2 of Arabidopsis preferentially mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration as compared to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). Since the AtNHX1 protein regulates vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ level and $\mathrm { p H }$ to control cell expansion and tissue elongation, overexpression of AtNHX1 in transgenic tomato increased the vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration while depleting cytosolic ${ \mathrm { K } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { p o o l } }$ up regulation of HAK5 and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake was increased as compared to WT (Leidi et al. 2010). Notably, the double mutant nhx1 nhx2 of Arabidopsis is more sensitive to moderate KCl stress (10 to $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ concentration) but did not show much greater sensitivity to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ as compared with the WT (Barragan et al. 2012). Remarkably, the nhx1 nhx2 mutant accumulated larger amounts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ upon salt treatment treatment and moderate amounts of NaCl improved the growth of the mutant plant. These results signify that tonoplast NHX proteins are dispensable for the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and that this ion can substitute as osmoticum for the otherwise reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pool in vacuoles of the nhx1 nhx2 mutant (Barragan et al. 2012). These results have raised many questions on how exactly $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is compartmentalized if vacuolar NHX-proteins are specific only for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration, as nhx1nhx2 mutants accumulates more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the plant shoots as compared to WT. It is now clear that in Arabidopsis the ion exchangers other than NHX1 and NHX2 may mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration (Barragan et al. 2012).


## Predominant Role of NHX Proteins in Stomata and Cell Expansion


In early 1970’s, it was proved that potassium has a vital role in regulation of stomata movements. However, with recent research advances the role of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in stomata and guard cell regulation is explained in more detail (Humble et al. 1971; Talbott et al. 1996; Cochrane TT and Cochrane TA 2008). The main solute in osmo-regulation of guard cells are $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , sucrose, and the anions malate and chloride. Guard cells store $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ salts in large quantities which is a cheap and highly mobile solute that regulates opening of stomata (MacRobbie 2006). In Arabidopsis’s guards cells the strong $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fluxes mediates by channels sustain the stomatal movement, i,e opening of stomata is mainly driven by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry through $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2, whereas stomatal closing is facilitated by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux through outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels activated by membrane depolarization (Ache et al. 2000). However, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ must be further routed to the vacuole while keeping the cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at homeostatic values. NHX1 and NHX2 have shown an extensive overlapping expression and subcellular localization pattern including guard cells and other organs, and they share with similar transport properties (Barragan et al. 2012). The best studied example for the role NHX-proteins in stomata is the inactivation of NHX1 and NHX2 genes (nhx1 nhx2) which reduce the total $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ contents in the leaf guard’s cells, with stunted stomata development and function (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). The double mutant of nhx1nhx2 results in wrinkled shaped and thinner stomata as compared with WT. This also explains the role of NHX-proteins in cell expansion. However, the stomata in nhx1nhx2 mutant is not completely dysfunctional but rather exhibit delayed stomatal closure, leaf turgor loss and reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration in guard cells vacuoles as compared with WT (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). Delayed stomata closure and leaf turgor loss was also observed in mutants of Snf1 Related Kinase, OST1 (OPEN STOMATA1) and SLOW EFFLUX ANION CHANNEL-ASSCIATED1. These proteins function as to regulate membrane depolarization of guard cells in response to ABA by releasing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and closing stomata (Ache et al. 2010).

The reduced cell expansion and tissue elongation in double mutant of nhx 1nhx2 was not only limited to the cells of leaves, but the hypocotyl of etiolated seedlings also displayed shorter length phenotype in nhx 1nhx2 mutants as compared to WT (Bassil et al. 2011b). This phenomenon was previously shown by (Apse et al. 2003) in nhx1 single knockout mutant mediating improper $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange and reduced cell expansion in normal physiological condition.

Plant species have adopted different molecular and physiological mechanism to regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and the homeostasis of other essential mineral nutrients under ionic stresses (Ali et al. 2017). In last few years several molecular and biochemical studies have uncovered the strong involvement of different transport proteins (NHXs, HKTs, CHXs, KEAs, NHDs) in regulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange for ion homeostasis, cell growth and development in salt stress. Hundreds of genes are involved in regulation of these processes and manipulation of these genes in model plants is so far very successful but the applications in natural agriculture conditions has always been a challenge. The development of salt tolerant varieties is unlikely to be successful until the applications of new molecular techniques like CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats). But again, this technique is very successful only in model plant Arabidopsis, and a lot of efforts are needed to make multiplegene targeting in agricultural crops through CRISPR/cas9 genome editing. The specific transporters for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions sequestration in vacuoles are yet to be identified, as it was recently reported that vacuolar localized NHX proteins (NHX1 and NHX2) are specific only to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ compartmentation. Therefore, a deep insight for increasing salt tolerance in crop plants, future research should be directed to understand molecular and biochemical mechanisms underlying the exact regulation of these transporters in ionic stress conditions and improve crop production.


## Author's Contributions


IUK and DJY designed this work, IUK, AA and DJY collected information from literature and wrote the paper.

Salinity tolerance is a complex, multi-genic trait which involves many physiological and biochemical mechanisms. Fortunately, a large number of potentially important genes which confer salinity tolerance have been identified using forward and reverse genetics, yeast complementation and transcriptomics approaches. Although the overexpression of a single salt-responsive gene can contribute to the improvement of salinity tolerance to some extent, the level of salt resistance is still below the level needed for practical agriculture production. In addition, it has been observed that in many cases, the overall stress tolerance imparted by over-expression of a single gene may not sustain itself under field conditions (Singla-Pareek et al. 2007). Therefore, more integrated approaches are urgently needed. One approach consists of simultaneous up-regulation of extruding mechanisms through over-expression of systems such as vacuolar pumps, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHXs and SOS1) and loss-of-function mutations in uptake pathways such as non-selective ion channels and HKTs. This is feasible through the use of polycistronic expression vectors and gene stacking methodology. In the present study, we used a dicistronic vector for the co-expression of two wheat genes, TNHXS1 and TVP1, in transgenic tobacco plants. We demonstrated that simultaneous overexpression of these two tonoplast proteins conferred better salt tolerance in transgenic tobacco plants than the overexpression of single genes.

The main objective of our cloning strategy was to physically link the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes and positioning them contiguously on DNA that will transfer as a single entity into tobacco genome. We also aimed to express those genes from a single 35S promoter to avoid the repetitious promoter use that leads, in some cases, to negative impact on transgene stability and expression (Peremarti et al. 2010). This strategy needs an important element known as internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs) which are usually viral sequences that can directly recruit ribosomes to internal positions within mRNAs and initiate translation in a cap-independent manner. Various IRES elements of different origins were described in the literature (Halpin 2005). We have chosen and used an IRES element which was previously shown to be functionally active in tobacco protoplasts and human Hela cells transgenic for dicistronic constructs involving the two reporter genes GFP and GUS (Dorokhov et al. 2002). Thus, we expected the IRES to be effective in co-ordinating the expression of the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes in transgenic tobacco plants. Indeed, molecular analysis of the transgenic tobacco plants demonstrated the integration of the transgenes and the production of the full-length bicistronic mRNA which contains the first cistron TNHXS1, the IRES element essential for the internal translation of the second cistron and the second cistron TVP1. More important, the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase activity measured in the double transgenic plants was twice that of the WT and the single TVP1 transformants, which demonstrates that the IRES element used in the present study was very efficient. In a previous study, dicistronic analysis of IRES activity of the ${ 5 ^ { \prime } } \mathrm { U T R }$ of NtHSF1 mRNA (used in this study) in tobacco protoplasts revealed activity comparable to those mediated by IRES of crucifer-infecting tobamovirus (CrTMV) (Dorokhov et al. 2002). CrTMV promotes the translation of a second cistron at $21 \%$ of the levels of the first cistron when a bicistronic construct is expressed in transgenic tobacco plants (Dorokhov et al. 2002). Recently, Ha et al. (2010) have also demonstrated that the IRES of CrTMV can coordinate the expression of two biosynthetic genes in transgenic rice.

The prevailing view is that the compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the plant vacuoles represents an efficient mechanism to avoid toxic effects of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion in the cytosol (Apse and Blumwald 2007). The transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles is mediated by cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters that are driven by electrical gradient of protons generated by the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumps. A large number of genes encoding NHX-like vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters have been isolated from diverse plants and successfully used to enhance salt tolerance in transgenic plants (reviewed in Ashraf and Akram 2009; Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010). However, the salt tolerance imparted by these antiporters varied with the source of antiporter and the plant species engineered. A recent study (Liu et al. 2010a) reported the expression, in Arabidopsis thaliana, of five NHXs from different origins including one from yeast ScNHX1, two from dicotyledons (Arabidopsis thaliana, AtNHX1 and Gossypium hirsutum, GhNHX1) and two from monocotyledons (Triticum aestivum, TaNHX1 and Suada salsa, SsNHX1). It was found that the ectopic expression of these NHXs in Arabidopsis thaliana caused growth retardation in transgenic Arabidopsis compared with wild type plants under normal growth conditions. Under stress conditions, the various NHX proteins conferred higher salt tolerance to transgenic Arabidopsis plants compared to wild type plants, but the TaNHX1 from wheat was less efficient than the other antiporters. Here, the ectopic expression of TNHXS1 in tobacco did not cause any growth retardation in transgenic lines compared to wild type plants. It is worth mentioning that TNHXS1 has $99 \%$ identity to TaNHX1 used in Liu et al. (2010a). Transgenic TNHXS1 plants exhibited better growth and physiological parameters than the wild type plants (Fig. 6 and Table 1) under both normal and salt stress conditions. Interestingly, under high salt conditions, TNHXS1 transgenic plants were able to complete their life cycle and to produce viable seeds whereas WT plants died at the vegetative stage. In addition, TNHXS1 was found to complement a salt-sensitive yeast mutant, and to be able to transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the vacuole of yeast strains, indicating that TNHXS1 is a functional antiporter (Fig. 1). These results indicated that TNHXS1 was a likely candidate gene for enhancing the salt tolerance of transgenic plants.

In the present study, it was observed that the various transgenic lines exhibited better growth than WT plants under normal conditions (Table 1). These transgenic lines expressed constitutively, under the control of the strong 35S promoter, an NHX-type antiporter or a vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ - pyrophosphatase, singly or in combination. These results are not surprising, since it was previously demonstrated that plant vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase plays an important role in plant organogenesis through control of auxin transport and distribution (Li et al. 2005). In fact, overexpression of plant vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase enhanced both shoot and root development in transgenic plants of tomato (Park et al. 2005; Khoudi et al. 2009), cotton (Asad et al. 2008) corn (Li et al. 2008), and bentgrass (Li et al. 2010). A robust root system facilitates water uptake when plants are subjected to abiotic stresses such as drought and salinity. Thus, the TP3 plants described in the present investigation would also be drought tolerant. In addition, the protons pumped into the central vacuole by the tonoplast pyrophosphatase are used for cation accumulation which drives the cell growth. On the other hand, Bassil et al. (2011) demonstrated the role of NHXs in plant growth and development using reverse genetics. It was shown that NHXs control cell expansion in vegetative tissues and male reproductive organs and are required for normal flower development. In fact, nhx1 nhx2 double mutant plants were significantly smaller than wild type, and this was associated with a decrease in cell size rather than defects in tissue organization. According to these authors, NHX-type transporters participate in cation accumulation in the central vacuole leading to water uptake and thus to cell expansion and growth.

Although NHX proteins are generally regarded as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, recent evidence indicates that they catalize substantial $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in plants (Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al. 2010). Interestingly, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the leaves of the TNHXS1 transgenic plants was significantly lower than that of the wild type plants, whereas the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content increased compared to wild type plants under saline stress (Fig. 5a, c). Notably, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content in leaves of salt-stressed TP3 plants more than doubled compared to these plants in the absence of NaCl. In contrast, roots of the TNHXS1 transgenic plants contained higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content than roots of the wild type plants. Similar findings by several authors (Liu et al. 2010b; Xue et al. 2004; Zhao et al. 2007), reporting over-expression of NHX proteins, were regarded as a consequence of higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport into root vacuoles of the transgenic lines which led to a lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ level in the cytosol and intracellular fluid of roots for transport into the shoot through the xylem transpiration stream. However in the light of recent reports (see below) it is more likely that over-expression of TNHXS1 led to a greater control of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis that minimised $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake mechanisms in the first place. In the present study, we found that, under $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt treatment, TNHXS1 and TP3 roots accumulated 2.2 and 2.7 times, respectively, more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than wild type plants, whereas they accumulated 3.1 and 4.5 times, respectively, more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ than wild type plants (Fig. 5). Again, TP3 lines accumulated more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their roots in the presence of $\mathrm { N a C l }$ than in control conditions, opposite to what happened to wild type plants (Fig. 5d). Our results on $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation are in disagreement with the most recent study, Liu et al. (2010a), who reported a higher accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaves of transgenic plants, including transgenics harbouring TaNHX1, compared to WT plants under $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt treatment. However, our results are in line with those reported by Islam et al. (2010) who demonstrated that the over-expression of Pennisetum glaucum vacuolar antiporter gene $( P g N H X I )$ in rice led to significantly higher leaf content of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in transgenic plants as compared to wild type plants. Similar results were also reported by Zhao et al. (2007) and Wei et al. (2010). The over-expression of HvNHX2 from barley in transgenic potato (Bayat et al. 2010) affected ion accumulation in a similar way to that of the over-expression of TNHXS1 in transgenic tobacco (this study). Interestingly, sequence analysis revealed $99 \%$ similarity between HvNHX2 and TNHXS1.

Our results for TVP1 transgenic plants are also in disagreement with previous studies (Gao et al. 2006, Guo et al. 2006; Li et al. 2010) dealing with ectopic expression of V-PPiase proton pumps. In fact, all these authors reported an enhanced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the leaves of transgenic plants compared to wild type plants, following salt treatment. In our hands, the analysis of ion contents indicated that under stress treatments, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in wild type plants was significantly higher than that in TVP1 transgenic plants (Fig. 5a). Our results are in good agreement with Liu et al. (2010b) who reported less accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaves of transgenic rice plants overexpressing rice pyrophosphatase gene OsVP1 singly or in combination with sodium antiporter gene OsNHX1.

Ion transport analyses with tonoplast vesicles isolated from transgenic lines confirmed that single-transgenic lines TVP1cl19 and TNHXS1cl7 had greater $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -PPiase and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity, respectively, than the WT. Interestingly, the double-transgene line TP3cl38 co-expressing both TNHX1 and TVP1 showed even greater $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase activity (Fig. 3). This enhancement did not appear to be caused by different expression levels of the TVP1 transgene among lines based on RT-PCR analyses (Fig. 2). Moreover, the single-transgene line TVP1cl19 also showed increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity relative to non-transformed WT plants (Fig. 3c) and the co-expression of TVP1 and TNHXS1 induced the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumping activity of the endogenouus V-ATPase (Fig. 3b). Thus, it appeared that ectopically expressed TVP1 and TNHXS1 interacted in a synergistic manner to potentiate both $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps, the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase and the V-ATPase. Activation of the V-ATPase could further contribute to the enhanced stress tolerance of line TP3cl38. Indeed, many studies have demonstrated that the enhancement of V-ATPase activity contributes to the improvement of salt stress tolerance in plants (Kluge et al. 2003; Padmanaban et al. 2004; Guo et al. 2006; Batelli et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2011; Hu et al. 2012). Thus, transgenic TP3 plants, which over-expressed simultaneously TNHXS1 and TVP1 genes, exhibited the best salinity tolerance compared to control plants when challenged with salt treatment in vitro or under greenhouse conditions.

The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ selectivity of the TNHXS1 is not yet known. Comparison of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange activity in WT and TP3 plants showed that whereas the tonoplast vesicles from WT had greater $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange than $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange, both activities were commensurately enhanced in the TNHXS1 expressing plants (Fig. 3d), suggesting that this exchanger might have a preference for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . When exposed to salt treatment $( 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ , elemental analysis revealed that TP3 plants accumulated 20 and 4.5 times more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their leaves and roots, respectively, compared to wild type plants (Fig. 5c, d). In addition, TP3 transgenic plants accumulated less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in their leaves but only 2.7 times more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in their roots when compared to wild type plants. The $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in the leaves and roots was enhanced in TP3 transgenic plants following the increase in salt concentration in the medium whereas it was decreased in the case of the wild type plants (Fig. 5c, d). The unusual accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the leaves of TP3 plants, as NaCl concentration increased in the culture medium, could be due to the activity of TNHXS1 alone or because additional mechanisms involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis were activated following the ectopic expression of TNHXS1. It has been established that AtNHX1 influenced the expression of several genes including ion transporters (Sottosanto et al. 2004). Significantly higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in transgenic tobacco leaves is a strong indication of salt tolerance. Maintenance of higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in the transgenic TNHXS1 and TP3 lines under salt stress can be attributed to improved $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis caused by over-expression of vacuolar antiporter (Gao et al. 2007).

The results obtained in this study raise the question of whether the TNHXS1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and whether it is playing any significant role in salinity tolerance trough vacuolar sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Clearly, our results indicate that the enhanced salt tolerance exhibited by TNHXS1 and TP3 transgenic plants is more related to a stronger control of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis than to increased vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration. In other words, TNHXS1 facilitates $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation which in turn leads to salinity tolerance. This is very plausible given the fact that the role of NHX proteins in salinity tolerance through $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ vacuolar sequestration was revisited and an updated model was proposed (Jiang et al. 2010). According to this model, NHX proteins fulfil a protective function to minimize salt-related stress mainly through the vacuolar compartmentlization of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and, in some cases of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ as well, thereby preventing toxic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ ratio in the cytosol while acquiring solutes for osmotic balance (Jiang et al. 2010). Many lines of evidence are in support of this model. First, the founding member of NHX-like antiporters, AtNHX1 from Arabidopsis, was found to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in tonoplast vesicles from transgenic tomato (Zhang and Blumwald 2001), in artificial proteoliposomes (Venema et al. 2002) and in vacuoles of yeast mutant lacking the endogenous $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ activities at the tonoplast (Hernandez et al. 2009). Second, in an experiment aiming at the determination of cation dependant $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchange using lipid vesicles system, the AtNHX1, which is localised in the tonoplast, showed equal transport rates for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange whereas the tomato, LeNHX2, which is targeted to the prevacuolar compartment, showed a strong preference for $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ (Jiang et al. 2010). Third, mutants of AtNHX1 with improved $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ – $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity conferred halotolerance to yeast cells presumably by averting sodic poisoning of the endomembrane network and preserving endosome/prevacuolar functions (Hernandez et al. 2009). In tomato, over-expression of NHX proteins imparted salt tolerance through a mechanism involving $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ compartmentation (Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al. 2010). On the other hand, it was demonstrated that NHX proteins mediate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange for turgor and $\mathrm { p H }$ control especially in petal expansion and flower colour development (Yoshida et al. 2009). The results obtained herein are therefore more easily explained based on the model proposed by Jiang et al. (2010) and indicate that TNHXS1 is mainly a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ antiporter, although it may also mediate some $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration activity.

The co-expression of the TNHXS1 and TVP1 genes conferred higher tolerance to salt stress than single expression of the TNHXS1 or TVP1 genes. Our results are, therefore, in agreement with previous studies reporting the co-expression of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and pyrophosphatase genes (Zhao et al. 2006; Liu et al. 2010b). Interestingly, our results seem to indicate that ectopically expressed TVP1 and TNHXS1 interacted in a synergistic manner to potentiate both $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps. This would result in an increased electrochemical gradient to promote the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } - }$ $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ activity leading to the sequestration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by TNHXS1. In a recent study on the salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis ecotypes, Jha et al. (2010) have shown that the up-regulation of AtNHX1 and AtVP1 was positively correlated in response to salt stress in both shoots and roots. In this study, the TP3 plants exhibited the least $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in leaves, the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in roots, and the highest level of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their leaves and roots when compared to single TNHXS1 or TVP1 transgenic plants. In addition they had the highest $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in their leaves. This may have contributed to their best salt tolerance.

The increased accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and, at lesser extent, of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plant tissues could lead to decreased cell osmotic potential, enhancing plant water uptake and maintaining leaf turgor under salt stress. In the present study, the bicistronic transgenic plants exhibited significantly higher leaf water retention than the single TNHXS1 or TVP1 transgenic lines under salt stress (Fig. 8c). In addition, the TP3 transgenic plants had higher chlorophyll content and greater biomass under salinity conditions. This is probably due to a greater leaf turgor resulting from more balanced osmotic potential which contributes to achieving higher plant photosynthesis and consequently improved growth in the TP3 plants compared to the single-transgenic plants (Table 1).

An important consequence of salinity stress is the generation of excessive ROS which leads to cell toxicity, membrane dysfunction and cell death. Plants defend against the ROS by enhancement of anti-oxidative enzymes. Catalase, which is involved in the degradation of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ into water and oxygen, is the major $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ scavenging enzyme in all aeorobic organisms (Yang and Poovaiah 2002). Catalase is critical for maintaining the redox balance during oxidative stress. It was reported that salinity decreases CAT activity through stressinduced damage to the enzyme (Khedr et al. 2003). Salt tolerant cotton cultivars exhibited significantly greater CAT activity as compared to salt-sensitive ones (Gossett et al. 1994). The over-expression of bacterial CAT gene conferred greater salt tolerance to transgenic rice plants (Moriwaki et al. 2008). In this study, CAT activity was shown to be higher in transgenic plants compared to wild type plants. Interestingly, the TP3 plants retained the highest CAT activity under salt stress. The higher antioxidant capacity of the TP3 transgenic plants may have contributed their less degree of cell membrane damage under salt stress (Fig. 8a, b).

Overall, our results demonstrated the usefulness of coexpression of the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes using a dicistronic system involving IRES in the improvement of salt and drought tolerance in transgenic plants. Also, our results seem to indicate that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation and increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport are prerequisites for plant salt tolerance. Based on these encouraging results, we intend to transform some economically important crops such as wheat and other crops using this bicistronic vector. In addition, the preparation of different bicistronic constructs, involving potentially important genes which confer drought and salinity tolerance to plants in combination with stress-inducible promoters, is in progress.
