In the SOS1expand structure, two extra lipids were determined to be buried in the dimerization interface, leading to extracellular expansion of the TMD. However, the differences in bound lipids did not result in significant conformational changes in the intracellular ends of TM helices and in the intracellular domains. According to the structural comparison, we found that SOS1 is locked in an occluded state by shifting of TM5b toward the dimerization domain, stabilized by interactions between TM5b and HC7-HC8 helices from the other subunit (Fig. 6). We proposed that TM5b may function as a lateral gate to control the accessibility of the ion binding pocket from the intracellular side. Moreover, HC1 directly connects TM13 from the core domain. As reported in a previous study, the core domain is supposed to undergo upward or downward movement relative to the dimerization domain during the transport cycle23. We speculate that the close packing between TMD and intracellular domain would prohibit the core domain from sliding across the membrane, thus inhibiting the activity of SOS1.

Two discrete fragments, C-loop (residues 1007–1017) and C-helix (residues 1030–1048), were determined to interact with intracellular domains from different subunits. We speculate that interactions of C-loop and C-loop with other domains might contribute to stabilize dimerization of the intracellular domains. Deletion of C-loop and/or C-helix $( { \mathsf { S O S I } } ^ { \Delta \mathsf { C } \cdot \mathsf { h e l i x } }$ , $\mathsf { S O S 1 } ^ { \Delta \mathsf { C } \cdot \mathsf { h e l i x } } )$ ) and mutation of W1013 or F1042 significantly stimulate the transport activity of SOS1, demonstrating C-loop and C-helix serve as a crucial molecular switch to regulate the activity of this antiporter. To gain insights into the activation mechanism of SOS1, we also made a constitutively active construct by truncating C-terminal autoinhibitory tail $( \mathsf { S O S 1 } ^ { \Delta 9 9 8 } )$ and carried out cryo-EM study. It turns out that intracellular domains are completely blurred during 2D and 3D classification, preventing us from obtaining a high-resolution map and suggesting that intracellular domains may become highly mobile upon SOS1 activation. Interestingly, we found that the surface electrostatic potential of the intracellular domains is negatively charged (Supplementary Fig. 14). Considering the critical roles of C-loop/C-helix and phosphorylation of C terminal tail in activation of SOS1, we further hypothesis that the phosphorylation of the C-terminal tail would introduce additional negative charge(s) that would repel negatively charged intracellular domains, reducing binding affinity of the C-loop and C-helix to the intracellular domain and destabilizing dimerization of the intracellular domain, thereby activating the SOS1. Previous studies have identified S1138 as the phosphorylation site and highlighted the role of S1136 in localizing SOS2 to the phosphorylation site7 . However, we found that the serine-toalanine mutant SOS1S1136A/S1138A conferred the same degree of salt tolerance in yeast as the wild-type SOS1 in the presence of the SOS2-SOS3 complex (Supplementary Fig. 15). This finding strongly suggests the existence of additional potential phosphorylation site(s) involved in SOS1 activation by the SOS2-SOS3 complex that have not yet been clearly identified. Further investigations are required to map the specific locations of these additional phosphorylation sites and gain valuable insights into the activation mechanism.

We have cloned two SOS1 cDNAs from the seagrass C. nodosa, CnSOS1A, and CnSOS1B, and detected the presence of additional CnSOS1 genes. The expression of CnSOS1A and CnSOS1A-1 in the yeast mutant defective in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux (Dena1-4 Dnha1) makes it clear that $\mathrm { C n S O S 1 A }$ is a system very similar to AtSOS1; the complete protein showed very little activity in suppressing the defect of the mutant, but the suppression was evident when the C-terminus of the protein was truncated, eliminating a residue that can be phosphorylated and which acts as a regulator of the activity (F. J. Quintero, personal communication). Remarkably, again as in AtSOS1, the clear improvement in the growth induced by CnSOS1A-1, of the defective yeast strain induced was not accompanied by a clear increase in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux. Unlike AtSOS1 (Quintero et al. 2002), $\mathrm { C n S O S 1 A }$ was not activated by the AtSOS2/SOS3 system, but this could be explained if the AtSOS2/ SOS3 proteins are specific for the Arabidopsis SOS1 transporter. In summary, the CnSOS1A transporter may fulfill similar functions to AtSOS1 and CnSOS1B might carry out a slightly different function.

The $C .$ nodosa SOS1 transporters were expressed in $E .$ . coli, but this approach could not be used for functional studies of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ efflux due to the toxicity of the CnSOS1A and CnSOS1B proteins in the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux mutant. In contrast, expression in an $E .$ . coli $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -uptake mutant led to the finding that CnSOS1A and CnSOS1B mediate low-affinity ${ \mathrm { { K } } } ^ { + }$ uptake in bacteria. This finding goes against the accepted paradigm, which purports that AtSOS1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (Shi et al. 2000, 2002, 2003; Qiu et al. 2002, 2003). However, the notion that SOS1 mediates ${ \mathrm { { K } } } ^ { + }$ uptake is an old proposal, because Arabidopsis sos1 plants are defective in highaffinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake ( $\mathbf { W } \mathbf { u }$ et al. 1996). This phenotype of sos1 has been explained by the indirect effect of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ on AKT1, which is more inhibited in sos1 than in wild type plants because of the higher $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ content of the former (Qi and Spalding 2004). This is a convincing explanation if SOS1 does not transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ but it does not rule out the possibility that SOS1 is a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter, and it does not contradict our findings.

It has also been reported that the AtSOS1 cDNA does not suppress the defect of the yeast $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport mutant $\left( \Delta t r k l \ \Delta t r k 2 \right)$ (Shi et al. 2002). Even cotransformation of AtSOS1 with AtSOS2/SOS3, which makes AtSOS1 fully active in suppressing the defect of a $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ efflux mutant, was not effective in the yeast $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake mutant (Quintero et al. 2002). Consistent with this, we found that CnSOS1A-1, which suppressed the defect of the yeast $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux mutant (Fig. 3), failed to suppress the defect of the yeast $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport mutant (Dtrk1 Dtrk2). These results rule out the possibility that AtSOS1 and CnSOS1A-1 mediate high-affinity ${ \mathrm { { K } } } ^ { + }$ uptake in yeast, but they do not negate the possibility that these transporters mediate low-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake. It is important to note that it is unlikely that a low-affinity transporter would suppress the defect of a yeast Dtrk1 Dtrk2 mutant, which maintains a very rapid intrinsic low-affinity ${ \mathrm { { K } } } ^ { + }$ uptake (Santa-Marı´a et al. 1997; Madrid et al. 1998; Rubio et al. 2000). The partial loss of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange capacity of plasma membrane vesicles of salt-treated Arabidopsis sos1 plants with reference to wild type plants (Qiu et al. 2003) supports that SOS1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger, but not that it is exclusively a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger. Remarkably, AtSOS1 might also mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake (Ding and Zhu 1997; Shi et al. 2002).

In conclusion, neither those results that support the hypothesis that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange is the main function of SOS1 transporters nor our present results in yeast contradict the possibility that SOS1 transporters mediate low-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake. Moreover, the capacity to mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in $E .$ . coli does not seem to be a peculiarity of $\mathrm { C n S O S 1 }$ transporters because AtSOS1 also performs this function. It is worth noting that, in ${ { \bf K } } ^ { + }$ -limiting growth experiments, $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ was always present: $9 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ in solid $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -free minimal medium (Fig. 5) and $8 7 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ in LB liquid medium (Fig. 8). In $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } \mathbf { b } ^ { + } }$ uptake experiments, the bacterial cells were $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starved for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ in a medium with a very low- $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ content $( 1 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , but they had been grown in LB medium that contained $8 7 ~ \mathrm { m M } ~ \mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ . Therefore, in our experiments, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake mediated by SOS1 transporters could be linked to the $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ efflux activity of the transporter.

Assuming that some SOS1 transporters, including AtSOS1, mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in bacteria, the question becomes, what is the physiological relevance of that function and its relationship with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange. Although the possibility of an artifact attributable to bacterial expression cannot be completely ruled out, it seems unlikely that the expression of a plant protein in bacteria could create a new function that is not present, in any form, in the plant. An alternative possibility is that the expression in bacteria, which may lack important posttranslational modifications relative to eukaryotic cells, may exhibit an abnormal high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ - uptake activity that exaggerates the physiological relevance of it. On the other hand, SOS1 transporters are phylogenetically related to prokaryotic NhaP transporters, and more distantly to animal NHE, tonoplast NHX, and bacterial KefC transporters (Shi et al. 2000; Hamada et al. 2001; Inaba et al. 2001; Waditee et al. 2001). Remarkably, various functions have been reported for NhaP transporters. Although their most firmly established function is $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux mediated by a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange (Shi et al. 2000; Hamada et al. 2001; Inaba et al. 2001; Waditee et al. 2001; Qiu et al. 2003), ApNhaP mediates $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchange (Waditee et al. 2001) and the Synechocystis transporter (Sll0273/ SynNhaP2/NhaS2) mediates $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ uptake (Mikkat et al. 2000). The role of the C-terminal hydrophilic tail in the variability of the functions of these transporters has been well established (Hamada et al. 2001; Waditee et al. 2001). In the case of CnSOS1A, a drastic truncation of this tail only changed the $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ of $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } \mathbf { b } ^ { + } }$ influx, which gives further support to the notion that $\mathrm { C n S O \cdot }$ S1A is a genuine $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter in $E .$ coli.

A mechanism that might simultaneously support the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -efflux and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -uptake functions is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in which ${ { \bf K } } ^ { + }$ substitutes for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ in certain circumstances. An electrogenic mechanism of this type has been proposed for the Gram-positive Tet proteins (Guffanti et al. 1998). More similar to our findings is the function of the GerN protein of Bacillus cereus (Thackray et al. 2001) (GerN shows more sequence similarity to CHX and KEA than to SOS1). GerN can exchange $1 \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / 2 \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or $1 \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / 1 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } { - } 1 \mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and, similarly to our findings, GerN complements the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sensitivity of a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux mutant and the low- $\cdot \mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ sensitivity of a $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake mutant of $E$ . coli (Southworth et al. 2001). Unfortunately, we have been unable to find experimental support for any of the abovementioned two mechanisms. Everted membrane vesicles of $E$ . coli expressing CnSOS1A that were fully active in developing a $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient were insensitive to the addition of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , in either choline or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ loaded vesicles [experiments that were performed similarly to those described by (Hamada et al. 2001; Inaba et al. 2001; Southworth et al. 2001; Waditee et al. 2001) are not shown].

Atsos1 plants show a notorious defect in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance (Wu et al. 1996) and this suggests that SOS1 may be the most important $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux system in Arabidopsis. The same conclusion would not apply to seagrasses if we assume that SOS1 transporters mediate an electroneutral $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange (Qiu et al. 2003), because, as mentioned above, $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ efflux in the epidermal cells of seagrasses has to be electrogenic. However, our results indicate that the transport mechanism of SOS1 transporters is more complex than a mere electroneutral $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange.

One key mechanism of salinity tolerance is the ability to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the cytosol via plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters. SOS1 is the only plant $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ efflux protein in the plasma membrane reported to date. Using root-bending assays, sos1 mutants were identified and the first SOS1 gene from Arabidopsis was cloned (Wu et al. 1996), and then, many SOS1 genes from other plants were isolated and characterized (Shi et al. 2000; Martinez-Atienza et al. 2007; Xu et al. 2008; Olias et al. 2009; Feki et al. 2011; Fraile-Escanciano et al. 2010; Tang et al. 2010; Wang et al. 2011; Quintero et al. 2011; An et al. 2014; Nie et al. 2015). Our present study showed that SpSOS1 was a PM-bound $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in the halophyte S. portulacastrum, and its expression could increase the salt tolerance of transgenic yeast by transporting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of cells (Zhou et al. 2015), suggesting that $\mathrm { S p S O S 1 }$ may be involved in plant salt tolerance. To test the salt tolerance function of SpSOS1 in plants, the SpSOS1 gene was transformed into Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants. The results showed that the SpSOS1 expression in the Arabidopsis sos1 mutant not only complemented the salt sensitivity of the sos1 mutant plants under middle salt stress but the growth of SpSOS1 -transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants was also better than that of the wild-type plants under higher NaCl concentration. The transgenic plants accumulated less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ relative to the wild-type plants under NaCl treatment. These results suggest that the PM $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter SpSOS1 from the halophyte $S .$ . portulacastrum may more efficiently extrude $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than AtSOS1 from the glycophyte Arabidopsis.

Potassium $( \mathrm { K } ^ { + } )$ is an essential macronutrient that plays an important role in plant growth and development (Barragan et al. 2012). Because $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ have similar physicochemical properties, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ competes with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for major binding sites in key physiological and biochemical processes in the cytoplasm, and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in particular inhibits the activity of many enzymes that require $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for their function (Duggleby and

Dennis 1973), so the excessive $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the cytosol can interfere with the essential roles of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . It has been suggested that a high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in the cytosol is necessary for improving plant salt tolerance. SOS1 is generally regarded as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter, and it can improve $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ nutrition by protecting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport under saline conditions (Qi and Spalding 2004). The overexpression of SOS1 could improve the salt tolerance of plants by maintaining a higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio (An et al. 2014). In the present study, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content was lower in the SpSOS1 -transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants than in the sos1 mutant and wild-type Arabidopsis, while the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content was highest in the transgenic plants under salt stress (Fig. 4). The results are consistent with a previous report in which tobacco-expressing SbSOS1 and Arabidopsis-expressing TdSOS1 accumulated more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ during salt stress (Yadav et al. 2012; Feki et al. 2014). These results suggest that SpSOS1 could increase the plant’s salt tolerance by controlling the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis, which is a strong indication of salt tolerance.

Salinity induces oxidative stress, leads to reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and can damage the membrane structure and destroy membrane integrity because it leads to lipid peroxidation (Borsani et al. 2001; Munns 2005; Zhang and Shi 2013). The content of MDA, a membrane lipid peroxidation product, represents the degree of cell membrane damage by ROS (Draper and Hadley 1990). The electrolyte leakage level is an important indicator of membrane injury (Yadav et al. 2012). Radical-induced cell death (RCD1) protects cells against the oxidative injuries imposed by some ROS, Arabidopsis AtSOS1 increases the oxidative tolerance of Arabidopsis by interacting with RCD1, and the Arabidopsis sos1 mutant is hypersensitive to oxidative stress (Katiyar-Agarwal et al. 2006). In the present study, SpSOS1-transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants had the lowest electrolyte leakage and accumulated less MDA relative to the sos1 mutant and wild-type plants (Figs. 5 and 6), indicating that the SpSOS1 transgenic plants might have healthier characteristics and a high capacity for removing ROS under salt stress. These findings suggest that one of the salt tolerance mechanisms of SpSOS1 is to protect the plasma membrane against oxidative damage under salt stress.

Excessive cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is toxic to some important biochemical and physiological processes, and thus, plant cells must be able to transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cytoplasm to the external medium or to compartmentalize it into vacuoles to tolerate high levels of sodium ions, maintaining the cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration at a non-toxic level. Sodium transport out of the cell or into the vacuoles can be accomplished by the operation of plasma membrane- and tonoplast-bound $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Pardo et al. 2006). $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion through SOS1 is regulated through protein phosphorylation by the SOS2/ SCaBP8 kinase complex in the roots (Quan et al. 2007); the SOS2-SOS3 complex regulates the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange activity of SOS1 in the shoots (Quintero et al. 2011). In the present study, SpSOS1 -transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants had higher transcriptional levels of AtSOS2 and AtSCABP8 than in sos1 mutant and wild-type plants under NaCl treatment (Fig. 7c, e), suggesting that the SpSOS1 protein might induced AtSOS2 and AtCBL10 expression in transgenic plants. SpSOS1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter at the plasma membrane in S. portulacastrum, and it has similar structures relative to the reported SOS1 proteins, including the phosphorylation site recognized by the SOS2 kinase complex (Fig. 8) (Zhou et al. 2015), suggesting that the kinase complexes SOS2/SOS3 or SOS2/ScaBP8 should regulate the SpSOS1 activity, and correspondingly, the ability of SpSOS1 to extrude $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ might be stronger in the transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants with increased levels of SOS2 and SCaBP8 (Fig. 7c, e), such that SpSOS1-transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants had stronger salt tolerance relative to the sos1 mutant and wild-type plants (Figs. 2 and 3). SOS2 can reportedly also mediate the sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles by regulating the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange at the tonoplast (Qiu et al. 2004), and the increased SOS2 level might be helpful for compartmentalizing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles in the Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants expressing SpSOS1. In addition, the greater amount of AtNHX1 induced by SpSOS1 protein might transport more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuoles from the cytoplasm (Fig. 7f). Therefore, the higher activity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration into the vacuoles mediated by activated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters at the tonoplast might be one of the salttolerant mechanisms of SpSOS1 -transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants. Oh et al. (2010) reported that SOS1 protein plays an important role in membrane traffic and vacuole functions by controlling the pH homeostasis in Arabidopsis cells. These findings suggest that besides its function as a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter, SpSOS1 may increase plant salt tolerance by regulating other biochemical and physiological processes.

Taken together, these results such as the higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio, lower MDA accumulation, and upregulated expressions of some salt-tolerant genes in SpSOS1-transgenic Arabidopsis sos1 mutant plants compared with the sos1 mutant plants and complementation of SpSOS1 on salt sensitivity of the sos1 mutant have indicated that in addition to its $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange function, SpSOS1 can increase plant salt tolerance by regulating other key metabolic processes. Furthermore, the PM $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter SpSOS1 could not only complement the saltsensitive phenotype of the Arabidopsis sos1 mutant under middle salt stress, but its expression also conferred stronger salt tolerance to the sos1 mutant plants relative to the wildtype while the tested plants were treated with high concentrations of NaCl. Therefore, these results suggest that the $\mathrm { S p S O S 1 }$ from the halophyte S. portulacastrum may be a candidate gene that can be used to develop more salt-tolerant transgenic crops.

Background: ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ extrusion from cells is important for plant growth in high saline environments. SOS1 (salt overly sensitive 1), an $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter located in the plasma membrane (PM), functions in toxic ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ extrusion from cells using energy from an electrochemical proton gradient produced by a PM-localized $\nvdash ^ { + }$ -ATPase (AHA). Therefore, SOS1 and AHA are involved in plant adaption to salt stress.

Results: In this study, the genes encoding SOS1 and AHA from the halophyte Sesuvium portulacastrum $( { \mathsf { S p S O S } } { \mathsf { 1 } }$ and SpAHA1, respectively) were introduced together or singly into Arabidopsis plants. The results indicated that either SpSOS1 or SpAHA1 conferred salt tolerance to transgenic plants and, as expected, Arabidopsis plants expressing both SpSOS1 and SpAHA1 grew better under salt stress than plants expressing only SpSOS1 or SpAHA1 . In response to NaCl treatment, ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ and $\nvdash ^ { + }$ in the roots of plants transformed with SpSOS1 or SpAHA1 effluxed faster than wild-type (WT) plant roots. Furthermore, roots co-expressing SpSOS1 and SpAHA1 had higher ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ and $\nvdash 1 ^ { + }$ efflux rates than single $S p S O S 1 / S p A H A l$ -expressing transgenic plants, resulting in the former amassing less ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ than the latter. As seen from comparative analyses of plants exposed to salinity stress, the malondialdehyde (MDA) content was lowest in the cotransgenic SpSOS1 and SpAHA1 plants, but the $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ level was the highest.

Conclusion: These results suggest SpSOS1 and SpAHA1 coordinate to alleviate salt toxicity by increasing the efficiency of ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + }$ extrusion to maintain $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis and protect the PM from oxidative damage induced by salt stress.

Keywords: $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase, $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter, Plasma membrane, Salt tolerance, Sesuvium portulacastrum

Soil salinity is one of the major threats to agricultural productivity because it disturbs intracellular ion homeostasis and reduces metabolic activities in plants [1]. Excess sodium ions $\left( \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \right)$ lead to water deficiency, membrane dysfunction, and ionic toxicity in plant cells [2]. Thus, it is essential for plants to maintain a low level of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ in the cytosol under salt stress. Plants have three mechanisms to prevent excessive ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the cytosol: restricting influx, increasing efflux, and increasing ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ sequestration into vacuoles [3]. Maintaining a low level of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ in the cytosol is largely mediated through transporters localized on the plasma membrane and tonoplasts [4].

In Arabidopsis, the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene AtSOS1 was identified as one component of the Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) signal transduction pathway [5]. The SOS pathway comprises three components, SOS1, SOS2, and SOS3, which play important roles in maintaining ion homeostasis and controlling salt tolerance in plants [6]. SOS1 plays a critical role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extrusion and controlling the long-distance transport of ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot[5]. SOS2 is a serine/threonine protein kinase [7] that interacts with and is activated by SOS3 [8]. SOS3, as a myristoylated EF-hand calcium-binding protein, senses and interprets the cellular calcium signal elicited under salt stress [9]. The SOS2/SOS3 protein kinase complex phosphorylates and activates SOS1 [10]. Recently, a series of SOS1 homologs have been identified and cloned from a number of other plant species, such as Populus euphratica [11], rice (Oryza sativa) [12], wheat (Triticum aestivum) [13], tomato (Lycopersicon esculentum) [14], Thellungiella salsuginea [15], Physcomitrella patens [16], Chrysanthemum crissum [17], and Helianthus tuberosus [18]. SOS1 can partially suppress the salt-sensitive phenotype of yeasts without ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ efflux transporters[13–18] and transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of plant cells. The SlSOS1-silenced transgenic tomato plants accumulated more ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ in the leaves and roots [14], but HtSOS1 overexpression in rice could exclude more ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ and accumulate more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ [18]. The sos1 mutant lines of Thellungiella salsuginea [15] and Physcomitrella patens [16] showed excessive ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ accumulation in cells.

Upland cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is an economically important crop that provides natural fiber and foodstuffs worldwide. As a glycophytic plant, cotton shows higher salt and drought tolerance than other major crops[19, 20]. However, the limitation of water and salinization of cotton cultivation areas are a challenge for cotton production. Studies on the salt tolerance genes of cotton will benefit improvements in productivity under saline conditions and have great economic value. However, information on the cotton SOS pathway is limited. With the recent availability of upland cotton reference genome sequences [21], the functional study of cotton genes has become very effective and convenient.

In the present study, we isolated and characterized the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene GhSOS1 in upland cotton and demonstrated that the encoded protein was localized to the plasma membrane and its expression was upregulated under salt, drought and cold treatments. Furthermore, GhSOS1 overexpression enhanced tolerance to high salt stress in transgenic Arabidopsis through maintaining a low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio and activating salt stress-related genes in cells. Hence, GhSOS1 may be a target gene for enhancing the salt tolerance of transgenic plants.

Background and aims Two major adaptive strategies used by Zygophyllum xanthoxylum, a $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ succulent xerophyte, against arid environments are absorbing a great quantity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from low-salinity soil which is efficiently transported to the leaves, and maintaining the stability of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration in those leaves. The plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter SOS1 has been suggested to be involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and correlated with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ nutrition in glycophytes. In this study, we investigated the function of the plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter $Z \mathrm { x S O S 1 }$ in long-distance transport and spatial distribution of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the xerophyte Z. xanthoxylum.

Methods The responses of ZxSOS1 to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ , KCl treatments and osmotic stress were investigated by semiquantitative RT-PCR, then the role of $Z \mathrm { x S O S 1 }$ in regulating plant growth and $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport and spatial distribution in $Z .$ xanthoxylum was studied by using posttranscriptional gene silencing.

Results We found that ZxSOS1 was preferentially expressed in roots and was induced and regulated by salt treatments and osmotic stress. Using post-transcriptional gene silencing, we found that ZxSOS1 -silenced plants exhibited reduced growth rate compared to wild-type (WT) plants under both normal and saline conditions. ZxSOS1 -silenced plants accumulated more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in their roots but less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in leaves and stems than WT under $5 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l }$ . Furthermore, ZxSOS1 -silenced plants had a lower net $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake rate than WT plants under both normal and saline conditions, and more interestingly, accumulated less $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in leaves under normal conditions than WT plants. ZxSOS1 -silenced plants also showed a decreased concentration and spatial distribution of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in leaves and roots than WT under $5 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l } .$ In addition, ZxSOS1 -silenced plants possessed an increased selective transport (ST) capacity for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ from root to stem while a decreased ST value from stem to leaf compared with WT plants when both were grown in $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { N a C l }$ . Conclusions These results demonstrate that $Z \mathrm { x S O S 1 }$ is not only essential in long-distance transport and spatial distribution of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and even $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , but also vital for regulating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport system and maintaining $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in $Z .$ xanthoxylum, thereby regulating its normal growth.

Keywords Zygophyllum xanthoxylum $\cdot$ Plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter $\because$ Long-distance transport Sodium $\cdot$ Potassium

The salt-sensitive phenotype of sos1 mutants has been well documented (Wu et al., 1996; Shi et al., 2000, 2002), but the impact of this mutation on the level of cellular structure or on gene expression in the most affected cells has received less attention. The responses to salt stress in Arabidopsis wild type and sos1-1 root cells were compared here. Based on the function of SOS1 as a sodium extruder from cells in which it is expressed, it was expected that cellular events and gene expression patterns in sos1-1 roots would mirror a magnification of events that have often been observed in wild-type plants under salt stress. However, not only was a much more pronounced salt stress response than in the wild type observed, but there were at least three distinct cellular events that were specific to the sos1-1 mutant plants, suggesting additional, other than sodium/proton antiport, roles for SOS1.


## Disrupted vacuolar functions in sos1-1 root cells under salt stress


An early and conspicuous difference between Col3 and sos1-1 root cells under salt stress concerned the morphology of the central vacuoles (Fig. 1A, B). Differences in CoroNa Green fluorescence intensity of the vacuoles was observed after prolonged stress (Fig. 2A, B), accompanying cell death in the sos1-1 root cells (Fig. 2D, F). Earlier, shrinkage of vacuoles had started in sos1-1 root cells (Figs 1B, 2J), resembling the observed loss of turgor and water potential in the vacuole (Kutsuna and Hasezawa, 2005), suggesting that sos1-1 root cells suffer a stress based on the disruption of the water potential equilibrium, even before the higher accumulation of sodium due to the lack of extrusion became significant. Consistent with this observation is a dramatic down-regulation of the expression of plasma membrane and tonoplast aquaporins only in sos1-1 within $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 8 h }$ (Fig. 6C; see Supplementary Table S1 at JXB online). Prolonged stress also resulted in the failure of vacuolar sodium confinement only in sos1-1 root cells (Fig. 2H). The leakage of CoroNa Green fluorescence from vacuoles was mainly observed in cells adjacent to damaged cells which became permeable to propidium iodide, suggesting vacuolar disintegration as a last step in sos1-1 root cells preceding cell death. To address the question whether the observations on sos1-1 root cells resulted from a higher accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ due to the absence of a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ excluder function, the wild-type Col3 root cells were treated with a higher concentration of NaCl. After $1 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ treatment with $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl, the older part of the wild-type root exhibited cell damage (arrows in Supplementary Fig. S1, at JXB online) and CoroNa Green fluorescence intensities were comparable with or even higher than those found in sos1-1 root cells in Fig. 2B. However, the vacuoles of Col3 root cells maintained normal morphology, suggesting that the vacuolar deformation observed in sos1-1 root cells is not a result of higher intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation (see Supplementary Fig. S1 at JXB online).


## Inhibition of membrane trafficking in sos1-1 under salt stress


Another difference between Col3 and sos1-1 root cells at the earlier stages of salt stress was observed by counterstaining the membranes with FM4-64. Both inclusion and intensity of membrane staining of FM4-64 decreased in sos1-1 after 8 h of stress (Fig. 1C–F). A possible explanation can be found in the reports of $\mathrm { p H }$ and salinity-dependent changes in lipid and sterol composition in fungal species (Turk et al., 2004, 2007). The observed inhibition of membrane trafficking was also reflected in the down-regulation of transcripts for GNOM and KNOLLE in the sos1-1 root cells (Fig. 5B), indicating the inhibition of trafficking, auxin transport (Kleine-Vehn et al., 2008) and cell division (Reichardt et al., 2007). By contrast, SYP121 and SYP122, which are SNAREs specifically involved in the secretory pathway to the plasma membrane (Tyrrell et al., 2007), were dramatically induced only in sos1-1 roots. There was also the induction of transcripts of at least two members of the exocyst family, EXO70B1 and EXO70H7 (Hala et al., 2008), suggesting an activation of a secretory or an exocytosis pathway in the sos1-1 root cells under salt stress.


## Changes of vacuolar pH in wild type and sos1-1 under salt stress


Ion accumulation and expression of ion transporters in sos1-1 generally mirrored a more severe salt stress than the wild type. Removal of the SOS1 extruder function resulted in higher sodium ion accumulation in the sos1-1 vacuole after prolonged stress (Fig. 2A, B). SOS1 mutations led to more severe potassium deficiency than that experienced by the wild type under the same stress conditions (Wu et al., 1996), which might be explained by a more drastic decline of HKT1 (Rus et al., 2001, 2004) and TPK1 (Gobert et al., 2007) expression and/or activity in sos1-1 under salt stress (Fig. 6C). Salt stress leads to an increase in free intracellular Ca2+ mainly in root cells (Tracy et al., 2008). The accumulation of vacuolar free $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and transcripts of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters were significantly higher in sos1-1 (Figs 4, 6B), suggesting increased and chronic stress signalling in sos1-1 root cells, which then experienced an amplified version of salt stress. Changes in vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ were fundamentally different in sos1-1 cells compared to the wild type under salt stress. In another study using salt-tolerant quince protoplasts, adding NaCl higher than $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { \ m M }$ to the media increased the cytosolic pH (D’Onofrio and Lindberg, 2009). A study using the Arabidopsis wild type showed significant increases in vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ after incubation in $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ for $1 8 { \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ (Leshem et al., 2006). The accumulation of sodium to the vacuole via $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX-type is expected to result in the vacuoles becoming more alkalinized than the cytoplasm (Fig. 3C, E; see Supplementary Fig. S2 at JXB online). However, sos1-1 cells showed more acidic vacuoles than their cytoplasm (Fig. 3D, E), although sos1-1 plants showed a higher accumulation of sodium in their vacuoles (Fig. 2A, B). The unexpected result seems to indicate the involvement of SOS1 in a function other than the anticipated function of a $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter in pH homeostasis. Significantly, members of genes involved in $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation at both plasma membranes and tonoplasts (Martinoia et al., 2007) were down-regulated only in sos1-1 root cells (Fig. 5A).


## Novel functions of SOS1 other than sodium exclusion


The distinct cellular events in sos1-1 root cells under salt stress are summarized in juxtaposition with wild-type cells (Fig. 7). The removal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cytoplasm into the extracellular space is the expected SOS1 function (Fig. 7A), but the lack of SOS1 also affects the confinement of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles, supporting the previously stated regulatory influence of the SOS pathway on at least some vacuolar ion transporters (Cheng et al., 2004; Qiu et al., 2004). In wildtype root cells, the vacuoles became more alkaline (Leshem et al., 2006), but this was not observed in the mutant. In sos1-1 plants (Fig. 7B), the initial loss of vacuolar turgor and functioning, followed by excessive sodium ion entry into the vacuoles and the inhibition of membrane trafficking, resulted in membrane defects and death of root cells. Consequently, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ flux into the transpiration stream increased via an apoplastic pathway. Disruption of vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ and down-regulation of AVP1 (Fig. 7B, red circle) might be at the core of the observations. Inhibition of AVP1 expression will affect endocytosis and auxin transport (Li et al., 2005) as well as the vacuolar sequestration of sodium ion (Gaxiola et al., 2001) in sos1-1 cells under salt stress (Fig. 7B, a). Acidic vacuoles affect the activity of NHX1 by enhancing the binding of an inhibitory regulator, AtCaM15, to the luminal c-terminus (Yamaguchi et al., 2005), partially explaining the failure of vacuolar sodium sequestration after prolonged stress (Fig. 7B, b).

An effect of SOS1 on the regulation of proton flux in the root tip (Shabala et al., 2005) notwithstanding, our results add another dimension. The mechanism(s) by which the SOS pathway is at the basis of salt tolerance (Zhu, 2001), and how SOS1 determines halophytism (Oh et al., 2009) also seem to include the mediation of vacuolar functions and pH homeostasis. In essence, the SOS pathway, and SOS1 in particular, appear to be more complex than expected. The involvement of a plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ - antiporter in $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis has been documented in animals. The NHE protein family consists of nine antiporters with long C-terminal cytoplasmic tails (Orlowski and Grinstein, 2007), comparable to the plant NHX family of ight members, including SOS1 and NHX1. The Cterminal of the animal NHE1 acts as a scaffold for the assembly of a signalling complex (Baumgartner et al., 2004) and NHE3 travels along the plasma membrane and endosomes, regulating endosomal $\mathrm { p H }$ and trafficking (Orlowski and Grinstein, 2007). Among the plant proteins, only SOS1 includes a C-terminal extension comparable to the animal proteins. The C-terminal tail of SOS1 appears to interact with a regulatory protein, RCD1, involved in oxidative stress (Katiyar-Agarwal et al., 2006), but detailed studies on in vivo interacting partners are still lacking. The distinct cellular events observed in sos1-1 mutant plants identify as yet unknown functions of SOS1 in mediating vacuolar integrity, membrane trafficking, and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis under salt stress, suggesting a more dynamic role of the SOS1 protein in which the $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter describes only one function.

Salinity is one of the most important environmental constraints affecting more than 800 million ha of arable land (Munns and Tester 2008). Salinity limits plant growth and causes significant losses of crop yield. Plants have evolved several mechanisms to cope with salt stress, the most important of which are $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tissue tolerance, and osmotic tolerance. One key mechanism of salinity tolerance is the ability to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions from the cytosol and its sequestration into the vacuole to limit cell damage. The transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles is thought to be mediated by vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family, which are driven by the electrochemical gradient of protons (Gaxiola et al. 1999; Pardo et al. 2006). The proton motive force used by vacuolar antiporters is generated by the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -translocating enzymes in the tonoplast, which are V-ATPase and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -inorganic pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ~ H ^ { + } }$ -PPiase). The $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase is a single subunit protein located in the vacuolar membrane (Maeshima 2000). It pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ from the cytoplasm into vacuoles with PPi-dependant $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport activity. Zhen et al. (1997) demonstrated that the Arabidopsis $\mathbf { A } t A V P I$ generated a proton gradient across the vacuolar membrane similar in magnitude to that of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase.

The over-expression of AtNHX1, or its homologs from other plant species, has resulted in enhanced plant tolerance not only to salt, but also to drought stress (Apse et al. 1999; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Xue et al. 2004; He et al. 2005; Brini et al. 2007; Chen et al. 2007; Khoudi et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010a). Similarly, the over-expression of AtAVP1 or its homologs in transgenic plants resulted in both drought and salt tolerance (Gaxiola et al. 2001). Interestingly, the enhanced salt tolerance in transgenic plants, over-expressing the AtAVP1 gene, was correlated with the increased ion content. These results suggest that the enhanced vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumping in transgenic plants was responsible for additional energy to support vacuolar sodium accumulation mediated by the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. In line with these results, Duan et al. (2007) demonstrated that the over-expression of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase resulted in an enhanced proton electrochemical gradient across the vacuolar membrane which accelerated the sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the vacuole and improved salinity tolerance at cellular level. Thus, it was predicted that co-expression of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase would confer better salt tolerance to transgenic plants than that of the single gene expression. Indeed, Zhao et al. (2006) provided experimental evidence that co-expression of SsNHX1 and AtAVP1 in transgenic rice conferred greater salt tolerance than that of the single SsNHX1. On the other hand, Qiu et al. (2007) reported that the coordinate expression of V-ATPase and vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter was essential for Suaeda salsa salt tolerance.

Salt stress tolerance is a complex trait (Flowers 2004); therefore, better tolerance to salinity might be achieved by pyramiding several genes into a single genotype (Samis et al. 2001). The success of this approach was demonstrated in the above-mentioned examples for pyramiding $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and one of the vacuolar translocating enzymes $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPase or $\mathrm { V { - } H ^ { + } A T P a s e ) }$ ). It was also used for stacking various combinations of genes involved in drought and salt stress tolerance (Singla-Pareek et al. 2003; Zhou et al. 2008; Wei et al. 2011). To engineer plants with multiple genes, Schmidt et al. (2008) described several approaches. For example, plants are individually transformed and then crossed together. This method complicates the downstream breeding due to the size of the segregation population needed to obtain all the transgenes in one individual. An alternative approach consists of performing repeated plant transformation with successive transgenes to obtain multi-gene phenotypes. However, this approach is costly, time consuming, and it needs several selectable marker genes to perform the various selection rounds. One practical solution to overcome these limitations is to physically link multiple gene expression cassettes by positioning them contiguously on DNA that will transfer as single entity (Shibata and Liu 2000). This strategy has been used with great success to stack traits in commercial GM crops.

Salinity tolerance is a complex, multi-genic trait which involves many physiological and biochemical mechanisms. Fortunately, a large number of potentially important genes which confer salinity tolerance have been identified using forward and reverse genetics, yeast complementation and transcriptomics approaches. Although the overexpression of a single salt-responsive gene can contribute to the improvement of salinity tolerance to some extent, the level of salt resistance is still below the level needed for practical agriculture production. In addition, it has been observed that in many cases, the overall stress tolerance imparted by over-expression of a single gene may not sustain itself under field conditions (Singla-Pareek et al. 2007). Therefore, more integrated approaches are urgently needed. One approach consists of simultaneous up-regulation of extruding mechanisms through over-expression of systems such as vacuolar pumps, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHXs and SOS1) and loss-of-function mutations in uptake pathways such as non-selective ion channels and HKTs. This is feasible through the use of polycistronic expression vectors and gene stacking methodology. In the present study, we used a dicistronic vector for the co-expression of two wheat genes, TNHXS1 and TVP1, in transgenic tobacco plants. We demonstrated that simultaneous overexpression of these two tonoplast proteins conferred better salt tolerance in transgenic tobacco plants than the overexpression of single genes.

The main objective of our cloning strategy was to physically link the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes and positioning them contiguously on DNA that will transfer as a single entity into tobacco genome. We also aimed to express those genes from a single 35S promoter to avoid the repetitious promoter use that leads, in some cases, to negative impact on transgene stability and expression (Peremarti et al. 2010). This strategy needs an important element known as internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs) which are usually viral sequences that can directly recruit ribosomes to internal positions within mRNAs and initiate translation in a cap-independent manner. Various IRES elements of different origins were described in the literature (Halpin 2005). We have chosen and used an IRES element which was previously shown to be functionally active in tobacco protoplasts and human Hela cells transgenic for dicistronic constructs involving the two reporter genes GFP and GUS (Dorokhov et al. 2002). Thus, we expected the IRES to be effective in co-ordinating the expression of the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes in transgenic tobacco plants. Indeed, molecular analysis of the transgenic tobacco plants demonstrated the integration of the transgenes and the production of the full-length bicistronic mRNA which contains the first cistron TNHXS1, the IRES element essential for the internal translation of the second cistron and the second cistron TVP1. More important, the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase activity measured in the double transgenic plants was twice that of the WT and the single TVP1 transformants, which demonstrates that the IRES element used in the present study was very efficient. In a previous study, dicistronic analysis of IRES activity of the ${ 5 ^ { \prime } } \mathrm { U T R }$ of NtHSF1 mRNA (used in this study) in tobacco protoplasts revealed activity comparable to those mediated by IRES of crucifer-infecting tobamovirus (CrTMV) (Dorokhov et al. 2002). CrTMV promotes the translation of a second cistron at $21 \%$ of the levels of the first cistron when a bicistronic construct is expressed in transgenic tobacco plants (Dorokhov et al. 2002). Recently, Ha et al. (2010) have also demonstrated that the IRES of CrTMV can coordinate the expression of two biosynthetic genes in transgenic rice.

The prevailing view is that the compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the plant vacuoles represents an efficient mechanism to avoid toxic effects of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion in the cytosol (Apse and Blumwald 2007). The transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles is mediated by cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters that are driven by electrical gradient of protons generated by the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumps. A large number of genes encoding NHX-like vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters have been isolated from diverse plants and successfully used to enhance salt tolerance in transgenic plants (reviewed in Ashraf and Akram 2009; Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010). However, the salt tolerance imparted by these antiporters varied with the source of antiporter and the plant species engineered. A recent study (Liu et al. 2010a) reported the expression, in Arabidopsis thaliana, of five NHXs from different origins including one from yeast ScNHX1, two from dicotyledons (Arabidopsis thaliana, AtNHX1 and Gossypium hirsutum, GhNHX1) and two from monocotyledons (Triticum aestivum, TaNHX1 and Suada salsa, SsNHX1). It was found that the ectopic expression of these NHXs in Arabidopsis thaliana caused growth retardation in transgenic Arabidopsis compared with wild type plants under normal growth conditions. Under stress conditions, the various NHX proteins conferred higher salt tolerance to transgenic Arabidopsis plants compared to wild type plants, but the TaNHX1 from wheat was less efficient than the other antiporters. Here, the ectopic expression of TNHXS1 in tobacco did not cause any growth retardation in transgenic lines compared to wild type plants. It is worth mentioning that TNHXS1 has $99 \%$ identity to TaNHX1 used in Liu et al. (2010a). Transgenic TNHXS1 plants exhibited better growth and physiological parameters than the wild type plants (Fig. 6 and Table 1) under both normal and salt stress conditions. Interestingly, under high salt conditions, TNHXS1 transgenic plants were able to complete their life cycle and to produce viable seeds whereas WT plants died at the vegetative stage. In addition, TNHXS1 was found to complement a salt-sensitive yeast mutant, and to be able to transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the vacuole of yeast strains, indicating that TNHXS1 is a functional antiporter (Fig. 1). These results indicated that TNHXS1 was a likely candidate gene for enhancing the salt tolerance of transgenic plants.

In the present study, it was observed that the various transgenic lines exhibited better growth than WT plants under normal conditions (Table 1). These transgenic lines expressed constitutively, under the control of the strong 35S promoter, an NHX-type antiporter or a vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ - pyrophosphatase, singly or in combination. These results are not surprising, since it was previously demonstrated that plant vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase plays an important role in plant organogenesis through control of auxin transport and distribution (Li et al. 2005). In fact, overexpression of plant vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase enhanced both shoot and root development in transgenic plants of tomato (Park et al. 2005; Khoudi et al. 2009), cotton (Asad et al. 2008) corn (Li et al. 2008), and bentgrass (Li et al. 2010). A robust root system facilitates water uptake when plants are subjected to abiotic stresses such as drought and salinity. Thus, the TP3 plants described in the present investigation would also be drought tolerant. In addition, the protons pumped into the central vacuole by the tonoplast pyrophosphatase are used for cation accumulation which drives the cell growth. On the other hand, Bassil et al. (2011) demonstrated the role of NHXs in plant growth and development using reverse genetics. It was shown that NHXs control cell expansion in vegetative tissues and male reproductive organs and are required for normal flower development. In fact, nhx1 nhx2 double mutant plants were significantly smaller than wild type, and this was associated with a decrease in cell size rather than defects in tissue organization. According to these authors, NHX-type transporters participate in cation accumulation in the central vacuole leading to water uptake and thus to cell expansion and growth.

Although NHX proteins are generally regarded as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, recent evidence indicates that they catalize substantial $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in plants (Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al. 2010). Interestingly, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the leaves of the TNHXS1 transgenic plants was significantly lower than that of the wild type plants, whereas the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content increased compared to wild type plants under saline stress (Fig. 5a, c). Notably, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content in leaves of salt-stressed TP3 plants more than doubled compared to these plants in the absence of NaCl. In contrast, roots of the TNHXS1 transgenic plants contained higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content than roots of the wild type plants. Similar findings by several authors (Liu et al. 2010b; Xue et al. 2004; Zhao et al. 2007), reporting over-expression of NHX proteins, were regarded as a consequence of higher $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport into root vacuoles of the transgenic lines which led to a lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ level in the cytosol and intracellular fluid of roots for transport into the shoot through the xylem transpiration stream. However in the light of recent reports (see below) it is more likely that over-expression of TNHXS1 led to a greater control of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis that minimised $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake mechanisms in the first place. In the present study, we found that, under $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt treatment, TNHXS1 and TP3 roots accumulated 2.2 and 2.7 times, respectively, more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than wild type plants, whereas they accumulated 3.1 and 4.5 times, respectively, more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ than wild type plants (Fig. 5). Again, TP3 lines accumulated more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their roots in the presence of $\mathrm { N a C l }$ than in control conditions, opposite to what happened to wild type plants (Fig. 5d). Our results on $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation are in disagreement with the most recent study, Liu et al. (2010a), who reported a higher accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaves of transgenic plants, including transgenics harbouring TaNHX1, compared to WT plants under $2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ salt treatment. However, our results are in line with those reported by Islam et al. (2010) who demonstrated that the over-expression of Pennisetum glaucum vacuolar antiporter gene $( P g N H X I )$ in rice led to significantly higher leaf content of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in transgenic plants as compared to wild type plants. Similar results were also reported by Zhao et al. (2007) and Wei et al. (2010). The over-expression of HvNHX2 from barley in transgenic potato (Bayat et al. 2010) affected ion accumulation in a similar way to that of the over-expression of TNHXS1 in transgenic tobacco (this study). Interestingly, sequence analysis revealed $99 \%$ similarity between HvNHX2 and TNHXS1.

Our results for TVP1 transgenic plants are also in disagreement with previous studies (Gao et al. 2006, Guo et al. 2006; Li et al. 2010) dealing with ectopic expression of V-PPiase proton pumps. In fact, all these authors reported an enhanced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the leaves of transgenic plants compared to wild type plants, following salt treatment. In our hands, the analysis of ion contents indicated that under stress treatments, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in wild type plants was significantly higher than that in TVP1 transgenic plants (Fig. 5a). Our results are in good agreement with Liu et al. (2010b) who reported less accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaves of transgenic rice plants overexpressing rice pyrophosphatase gene OsVP1 singly or in combination with sodium antiporter gene OsNHX1.

Ion transport analyses with tonoplast vesicles isolated from transgenic lines confirmed that single-transgenic lines TVP1cl19 and TNHXS1cl7 had greater $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -PPiase and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity, respectively, than the WT. Interestingly, the double-transgene line TP3cl38 co-expressing both TNHX1 and TVP1 showed even greater $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase activity (Fig. 3). This enhancement did not appear to be caused by different expression levels of the TVP1 transgene among lines based on RT-PCR analyses (Fig. 2). Moreover, the single-transgene line TVP1cl19 also showed increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity relative to non-transformed WT plants (Fig. 3c) and the co-expression of TVP1 and TNHXS1 induced the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumping activity of the endogenouus V-ATPase (Fig. 3b). Thus, it appeared that ectopically expressed TVP1 and TNHXS1 interacted in a synergistic manner to potentiate both $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps, the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -PPiase and the V-ATPase. Activation of the V-ATPase could further contribute to the enhanced stress tolerance of line TP3cl38. Indeed, many studies have demonstrated that the enhancement of V-ATPase activity contributes to the improvement of salt stress tolerance in plants (Kluge et al. 2003; Padmanaban et al. 2004; Guo et al. 2006; Batelli et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2011; Hu et al. 2012). Thus, transgenic TP3 plants, which over-expressed simultaneously TNHXS1 and TVP1 genes, exhibited the best salinity tolerance compared to control plants when challenged with salt treatment in vitro or under greenhouse conditions.

The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ selectivity of the TNHXS1 is not yet known. Comparison of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange activity in WT and TP3 plants showed that whereas the tonoplast vesicles from WT had greater $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange than $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange, both activities were commensurately enhanced in the TNHXS1 expressing plants (Fig. 3d), suggesting that this exchanger might have a preference for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . When exposed to salt treatment $( 2 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ , elemental analysis revealed that TP3 plants accumulated 20 and 4.5 times more $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their leaves and roots, respectively, compared to wild type plants (Fig. 5c, d). In addition, TP3 transgenic plants accumulated less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in their leaves but only 2.7 times more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in their roots when compared to wild type plants. The $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in the leaves and roots was enhanced in TP3 transgenic plants following the increase in salt concentration in the medium whereas it was decreased in the case of the wild type plants (Fig. 5c, d). The unusual accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the leaves of TP3 plants, as NaCl concentration increased in the culture medium, could be due to the activity of TNHXS1 alone or because additional mechanisms involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis were activated following the ectopic expression of TNHXS1. It has been established that AtNHX1 influenced the expression of several genes including ion transporters (Sottosanto et al. 2004). Significantly higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in transgenic tobacco leaves is a strong indication of salt tolerance. Maintenance of higher $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in the transgenic TNHXS1 and TP3 lines under salt stress can be attributed to improved $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis caused by over-expression of vacuolar antiporter (Gao et al. 2007).

The results obtained in this study raise the question of whether the TNHXS1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter and whether it is playing any significant role in salinity tolerance trough vacuolar sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Clearly, our results indicate that the enhanced salt tolerance exhibited by TNHXS1 and TP3 transgenic plants is more related to a stronger control of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis than to increased vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration. In other words, TNHXS1 facilitates $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation which in turn leads to salinity tolerance. This is very plausible given the fact that the role of NHX proteins in salinity tolerance through $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ vacuolar sequestration was revisited and an updated model was proposed (Jiang et al. 2010). According to this model, NHX proteins fulfil a protective function to minimize salt-related stress mainly through the vacuolar compartmentlization of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and, in some cases of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ as well, thereby preventing toxic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ ratio in the cytosol while acquiring solutes for osmotic balance (Jiang et al. 2010). Many lines of evidence are in support of this model. First, the founding member of NHX-like antiporters, AtNHX1 from Arabidopsis, was found to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in tonoplast vesicles from transgenic tomato (Zhang and Blumwald 2001), in artificial proteoliposomes (Venema et al. 2002) and in vacuoles of yeast mutant lacking the endogenous $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ activities at the tonoplast (Hernandez et al. 2009). Second, in an experiment aiming at the determination of cation dependant $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchange using lipid vesicles system, the AtNHX1, which is localised in the tonoplast, showed equal transport rates for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange whereas the tomato, LeNHX2, which is targeted to the prevacuolar compartment, showed a strong preference for $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange over $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ (Jiang et al. 2010). Third, mutants of AtNHX1 with improved $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ – $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selectivity conferred halotolerance to yeast cells presumably by averting sodic poisoning of the endomembrane network and preserving endosome/prevacuolar functions (Hernandez et al. 2009). In tomato, over-expression of NHX proteins imparted salt tolerance through a mechanism involving $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ compartmentation (Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al. 2010). On the other hand, it was demonstrated that NHX proteins mediate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange for turgor and $\mathrm { p H }$ control especially in petal expansion and flower colour development (Yoshida et al. 2009). The results obtained herein are therefore more easily explained based on the model proposed by Jiang et al. (2010) and indicate that TNHXS1 is mainly a $\mathrm { K ^ { + } { - } H ^ { + } }$ antiporter, although it may also mediate some $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration activity.

The co-expression of the TNHXS1 and TVP1 genes conferred higher tolerance to salt stress than single expression of the TNHXS1 or TVP1 genes. Our results are, therefore, in agreement with previous studies reporting the co-expression of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and pyrophosphatase genes (Zhao et al. 2006; Liu et al. 2010b). Interestingly, our results seem to indicate that ectopically expressed TVP1 and TNHXS1 interacted in a synergistic manner to potentiate both $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps. This would result in an increased electrochemical gradient to promote the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } - }$ $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ activity leading to the sequestration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by TNHXS1. In a recent study on the salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis ecotypes, Jha et al. (2010) have shown that the up-regulation of AtNHX1 and AtVP1 was positively correlated in response to salt stress in both shoots and roots. In this study, the TP3 plants exhibited the least $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in leaves, the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in roots, and the highest level of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in their leaves and roots when compared to single TNHXS1 or TVP1 transgenic plants. In addition they had the highest $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio in their leaves. This may have contributed to their best salt tolerance.

The increased accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and, at lesser extent, of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plant tissues could lead to decreased cell osmotic potential, enhancing plant water uptake and maintaining leaf turgor under salt stress. In the present study, the bicistronic transgenic plants exhibited significantly higher leaf water retention than the single TNHXS1 or TVP1 transgenic lines under salt stress (Fig. 8c). In addition, the TP3 transgenic plants had higher chlorophyll content and greater biomass under salinity conditions. This is probably due to a greater leaf turgor resulting from more balanced osmotic potential which contributes to achieving higher plant photosynthesis and consequently improved growth in the TP3 plants compared to the single-transgenic plants (Table 1).

An important consequence of salinity stress is the generation of excessive ROS which leads to cell toxicity, membrane dysfunction and cell death. Plants defend against the ROS by enhancement of anti-oxidative enzymes. Catalase, which is involved in the degradation of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ into water and oxygen, is the major $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ scavenging enzyme in all aeorobic organisms (Yang and Poovaiah 2002). Catalase is critical for maintaining the redox balance during oxidative stress. It was reported that salinity decreases CAT activity through stressinduced damage to the enzyme (Khedr et al. 2003). Salt tolerant cotton cultivars exhibited significantly greater CAT activity as compared to salt-sensitive ones (Gossett et al. 1994). The over-expression of bacterial CAT gene conferred greater salt tolerance to transgenic rice plants (Moriwaki et al. 2008). In this study, CAT activity was shown to be higher in transgenic plants compared to wild type plants. Interestingly, the TP3 plants retained the highest CAT activity under salt stress. The higher antioxidant capacity of the TP3 transgenic plants may have contributed their less degree of cell membrane damage under salt stress (Fig. 8a, b).

Overall, our results demonstrated the usefulness of coexpression of the TNHXS1 and the TVP1 genes using a dicistronic system involving IRES in the improvement of salt and drought tolerance in transgenic plants. Also, our results seem to indicate that $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation and increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport are prerequisites for plant salt tolerance. Based on these encouraging results, we intend to transform some economically important crops such as wheat and other crops using this bicistronic vector. In addition, the preparation of different bicistronic constructs, involving potentially important genes which confer drought and salinity tolerance to plants in combination with stress-inducible promoters, is in progress.
