Soil salinity is one of the major threats to agricultural land that restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops (Flowers 1998). High salinity leads to cytosolic osmotic stress and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion specific toxicity in plants while over accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the cytosol causes inhibitory effects on many developmental processes such as protein synthesis, enzymatic reactions and photosynthesis (Murguia et al. 1995; Tsugane et al. 1999). However higher plants have developed multiple mechanisms through evaluation and adaptation involving morphological, physiological, biochemical and molecular responses to survive the harsh abiotic stress conditions (Hirayama and Shinozaki 2010; Krasensky and Jonak 2012). Salinity and drought may influence the plant growth and productivity in various ways. However, the major cause of damage is the excessive toxic accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and the loss of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the cytoplasm (Ali et al. 2016). To cope with such crucial saline conditions and maintain $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis, plant uses a number of transporters that protect them against $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions stress. This cation and $\mathrm { p H }$ homoeostasis is thought to be regulated by monovalent cation/proton antiporters (CPA) by exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ , or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ (Brett et al. 2005a). Prokaryotic and eukaryotic CPA members fall into two major super families designated as CPA1 (2.A.36) and CPA2 (2.A.37) (Brett et al. 2005a). In plants, the CPA1 family includes the well-studied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (NHX), while CPA2 family includes cation/ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchangers (CHX) and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux antiporter (KEA).

The model plant Arabidopsis contains total eight NHX members belonging to three different classes, six intracellular (IC) transporters that are categorized as either localized at tonoplast vacuoles (IC-I), or endosome (IC-II). The IC-I family includes AtNHX1-4, which are plant specific, while IC-II clade includes AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 that are similar to ScNHX1 (yeast) and human isoforms NHE6 and NHE7 (Bowers et al. 2000; Brett et al. 2005a; Chanroj et al. 2012). Two divergent members of the CPA1 family, AtNHX7/SOS1 and AtNHX8, are located at the plasma membrane. Some of these antiporters extrude toxic amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cell (SOS1/NHX7), while other NHX family members regulate cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ by sequestering them in vacuoles inside plant cells (Apse et al. 1999; Barragan et al. 2012).

Beside antiporters another class of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters is the HKT-type transporters (initially defined as high-affinity potassium transporters) that are divided into two subclasses on the basis of their transport properties and amino acid sequences (Platten et al. 2006). Subclass I transporters (ie.,

HKT1) have a serine (S) residue forming S-G-G-G motif while subclass II (ie., HKT2) type transporters have a glycine (G) residue replacing serine (S) in subclass I transporters and thereby contain a G-G-G-G motif (Maser et al. 2002). The presence of either serine (S) or glycine (G) contributes towards the specificity of transporter toward cations selection (Platten et al. 2006). Members of subclass I have strong affinity for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ only, while those belonging to subclass II transport both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depending on the concentration of the two cations (Maser et al. 2002; Platten et al. 2006; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). HKT1-type transporters are believed to retrieve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from xylem stream to protect shoots from $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, retain it in the root and thereby contribute mainly in reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ion toxicity in plants (Rubio et al. 1995; Rus et al. 2001, 2006).

Previous studies on vacuolar compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plants are also shown to regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity, mediated by tonoplast localized cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters (NHXs). For this process tonoplast $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ pumps $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase) and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } .$ pyrophosphatase $\mathrm { ( H ^ { + } }$ -PPase) provide the proton motive force required for NHX function (Apse et al. 1999; Gaxiola et al. 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). In many transgenic plants the overexpression of tonoplast NHXs have enhanced resistance to salt and drought stress with increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles (Apse et al. 1999; Brini et al. 2007; Galvez et al. 2012; He et al. 2005; Jha et al. 2013; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Zhang et al. 2001), thought there are exceptions to this rule (Leidi et al. 2010; Jiang et al. 2010). The class-I NHX family proteins localized in tonoplast function as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, that are involved in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration inside the vacuoles maintaining turgor pressure and drive cell expansion. Recently, the two Arabidopsis vacuole localized homologous NHX proteins, NHX1 and NHX2 in Arabidopsis are shown to redundantly regulating the accurate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in vacuoles (Barragan et al. 2012; Bassil et al. 2011).


## Role of NHX Protein in Plant Growth and Development


Besides the prominent role of NHX proteins in salt and drought resistance in plants, recent advances have shown a series of other novel functions of these proteins including intracellular ions and pH homeostasis, turgor and osmotic regulation, stomatal movement, water uptake, cell expansion and regulation of flowering time (Andres et al. 2014; Bassil and Blumwald 2014; Bassil et al. 2011; Barragan et al. 2012; Pittman 2012; Reguera et al. 2014).

Ionic homeostasis and pH regulation are essential cellular processes necessary for plant growth and development especially during undesirable environmental conditions. The primary action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pumps regulates the cytoplasmic pH, while the

NHX proteins are $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters localized to the plasma membrane and tonoplast that facilitate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and constitute a proton leak thereby maintaining both $\mathrm { p H }$ and ions homeostasis (Rodríguez-Rosales et al. 2009). The best studied example of $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation is the Japanese morning glory (Ipomoea nil) InNHX2 which promotes the vacuolar alkalization in petals that converts the reddish-purple buds into purple flower by increasing the vacuolar $\mathrm { p H }$ (Ohnishi et al. 2005). Recently the reverse genetic approach has shown that AtNHX1 and AtNHX2 are $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and are required for active $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake (Fig. 1), osmotic and turgor regulation and playing a unique role in cell expansion and stomatal function by sustaining the intracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). In this review we want to highlight the recent advances in ion homeostasis and evidences existing for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and lacking rather than for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in plants by NHX-exchangers, which regulates a diverse set of functions and enzymatic reactions important for survival and growth of plants.


## $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and Signaling Mechanism


The action of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ at the plasma membrane creates an electrical potential across the plasma membrane and increases the negative charge inside the cells promoting the passive influx of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions, while the efflux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (i.e., removal from cell) is not a passive process but needs the expenditure of energy (Maathuis et al. 2014). In high salinity the family of NonSelective Cation Channels (NSCCs family) is thought to mediate the spontaneous transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the root cells across the plasma membrane but until now the exact molecular mechanism is unknown (Kronzucker and Britto 2011). Beside NSCC family transporters, the transpirational bypass of water and solutes $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ across the apoplast has an important role in some plant species, such as rice, in which this non-selective pathway is the major port of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ entry and transport across the xylem without crossing the plasma membrane. In most species the casparian strip and suberine layers in plant roots endodermal and exo-dermal layers provide barriers to the apoplast flow (Yeo et al. 1987; Ochiai and Matoh 2002; Kronzucker and Britto 2011). The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ taken up by plant roots is transported to the shoot part in xylem by bulk flow that is driven by the tension in xylem causing continuous movement of water and solute (i.e., $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) from roots to shoot by transpiration (Almeida et al. 2016; Nobel 2009).

Potassium is one of major essential macronutrients which is required for several key biological functions in plants, like enzyme activation, osmotic and turgor generation, opening and closing of stomatal aperture, cytosolic pH regulation and membrane electric potential. The uptake of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by plant roots is thought to be regulated by two independent transport systems with different kinetic parameters and selectivity (Epstein et al. 1963). The saturable system1 is constituted by the high affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake permeases HAK/KUP that operate in the micromolar range and transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the cytoplasm of the root cells against electrochemical gradient (SantaMarıa et al. 1997; Gierth et al. 2005). System 2 or the low affinity pathway, including channels of shaker family, has the characteristic of channel mediated the transport and uptake of external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at concentration of above 0.5 to $1 \mathrm { m M }$ with plasma membrane potential of -120 to $- 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m V } .$ The first isolated plasma membrane $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and AKT1 (hyperpolarization-activated inward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel) and the carrier-type HUP/HAK/KT transporter HAK5 in Arabidopsis displayed $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake in heterologous system (Schachtman et al. 1992; Bertl et al. 1995; Gaymard et al. 1998a) indicated that these channels probably function in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake pathway in guard cells for KAT1 and in the root cells in case of AKT1 (Nakamura et al. 1995; Lagarde et al. 1996). Membrane depolarization by excessive cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx have a strong inhibitory effect on transport of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions into the plant root cells by inhibiting the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake transporters (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005), and increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux by depolarization-activated outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (eg, GORK) and NSSC as well (Hirsch et al. 1998; Fuchs et al. 2005; Sun et al. 2009). Once $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is captured, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is further transported into the vacuole against the electrochemical gradient of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters of the NHX family energized by the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient across the tonoplast (Walker et al. 1996; Carden et al. 2003; Barragan et al. 2012).

Not much is known about how $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ are sensed in most of root cellular systems in plants. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ can either be sensed outside, inside of the cell or both. In the case of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { , } }$ , the extracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by plant through membrane receptors in roots, while intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ may be sensed by membrane protein or other cytoplasmic enzymes (Tracy et al. 2008). From recent advances it is thought that the long cytoplasmic tail of plasma membrane localized antiporter SOS1 (SALT OVERLY SENSITIVE1; NHX7) might be responsible for intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sensing (Shi et al. 2000). However, the plasma membrane localized $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase can directly sense the changes in extracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration which led to the proposal that the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters might be the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sensors in plants.

In plants calcium signaling acts as a second messenger connecting various environmental stresses with intracellular responses including nutrient deficiency. Extracellular salt stress $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ) transiently increase the free cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ by depolarization- and hyperpolarization-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels and by ROS-activated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channels at the plasma membrane (Tracy et al. 2008). ROS accumulation is also strongly induced by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -starvation in Arabidopsis root cells (Shin and Schachtman, 2004; Shin et al. 2005). Cytosolic calcium elevation can also stimulate NADPH-oxidase mediating ROS-production (Yang and Poovaiah 2002). The increase in ROS further increase $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ influx by decoding $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensor such as Calmodulin (CaM), Calcinurin B-like proteins (CBLs) and CBL-interacting protein kinases (CIPKs), Forming CBL-CIPK complexes and are designated as calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) (Yang and Poovaiah 2003). Intracellular cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensors trigger various signal transduction pathways that are involved in regulation of ion channels activities (e, g., external $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ strongly blocked NSCC), enzymatic reactions, gene transcription and regulation of ion homeostasis (Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Martínez-Atienza et al. 2007; Adams and Shin 2014).


## Discovery and Localization of Arabidopsis NHX Exchangers


One of the predominant strategies that plant cells employ for the sequestration of toxic cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is to compartmentalize it in vacuoles, and NHX-type intracellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter have appeared to be well characterized transport proteins involved in this process so far (Apse 2003). Sequencing comparison of the yeast genome uncovered a novel gene present on chromosome IV (YDR456w), which encodes a protein of 633 aa, was named as NHX1 on the basis of sequence homology with the family of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (NHE1–4), that is found in mammals and other vertebrates, as well as in nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans), and euryhaline crab (Carcinusmaenas). Disruption of NHX1 gene led to a significant decrease in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ tolerance at $\mathrm { p H } 4$ or 5, indicating its prominent role in mediating tolerance to stress at acidic $\mathrm { p H }$ (Nass et al. 1997). The discovery of vacuolar NHX1, and its homologous protein in Arabidopsis, opened a new concept of intracellular compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions in plants (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000). AtNHX1 can functionally substitute for the endosomal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (ScNHX1) that requires ATPase activity of endosomal/vacuolar V-type ATPase to mediate ions compartmentalization in yeast vacuole (Quintero et al. 2000). Based on protein similarity of predicted amino acid sequence to AtNHX1, six AtNHX gene family members were categorized in Arabidopsis. These NHX $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene family members were named as AtNHX1-6 in order of decreasing phylogenetic relationship to the prototype of AtNHX1. AtNHX2-4 has $5 6 . 0 { - } 8 7 . 5 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1 whereas AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 has $8 7 . 7 \%$ similarity to each other’s and has $2 1 - 2 3 \%$ similarity to AtNHX1-4 isoforms in Arabidopsis (Yokoi et al. 2002). Maser et al. (2001) further expanded the NHX family to include the plasma membrane isoforms NHX7/SOS1 and NHX8.

Northern blot analysis using total RNA from seedlings of Col-0 indicated that AtNHX1 and 2 transcripts were highly abundant in shoots and roots. The transcript of AtNHX3 was highly abundant only in roots, and a low transcript level of AtNHX5 mRNA was detected in roots and shoots. While AtNHX4 and AtNHX6 transcript were not detectable on northern blot, they were detected in roots and shoots using RT-PCR. These findings established that all six genes of AtNHX are transcriptionally active in seedlings, indicating that their function is not only restricted to the later developmental stages (Yokoi et al. 2002).


## Sodium Exclusion and Tissue Tolerance


Soil salinity (mainly NaCl) restricts plant growth and thereby decreases the yield and quality of crops more than any other toxic substance in soil. By restricting the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx inside the cells can improve the plant growth and survival in saline stress, however, very little is known about the mechanism to inhibit the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx. On the other hand, to tolerate the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the soil plant cell must be capable of either export $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell or sequester it into the vacuoles to reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity inside the cell (Xu et al. 2013). The $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ exclusion process energized by the plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ATPase is mainly carried out by the plasma membrane localized SOS1 (AtNHX7) in Arabidopsis, with its interacting component SOS3 (CBL4) and SOS2 kinase (CIPK24) in a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ dependent manner (Shi et al. 2000; Quintero et al. 2002; Qiu et al. 2002). But the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion by this process to outside medium can further increase the imbalance of osmotic and ionic stress across the membrane, therefore this kind of strategy is useful only for temporary resistance and cannot confers long term salt tolerance in the natural environmental conditions (Adem et al. 2014).

Beside the extrusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ out of the cell, plants have the ability to safely handle large amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in tissues without any deleterious effect on plant metabolism. Such kind of tissues tolerance is mainly achieved by efficient $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration in vacuoles, thereby reducing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity in the cytosol.


## NHX Proteins are Required for Accurate Potassium $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ Compartmentation in Vacuoles


Potassium is the most vital ionic osmoticum in plant cells that is largely distributed in two major pools, cytosol and vacuoles. Cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is an essential activator for many biochemical and enzymatic reactions, cytosolic $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation and plasma membrane electric potential (Fig. 2), requiring the maintenance of basic cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration within the narrow limit of 75 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ regardless of changes in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply (Walker et al. 1996). However, vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pools which is the largest and most dynamic reservoir of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ depends on the availability of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . The lowest limit of vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration appears to be 10 to $2 0 \mathrm { m M }$ . The concentration of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ inside the plant cell vacuoles requires the active transport from cytosol which could be achieved through nonelecterogenic $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (Walker et al. 1996). Biochemical analysis has proved that tonoplast localized NHX exchangers (NHX1 and NHX2) catalyze the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange with an apparent affinity of 12 to $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ , which is below the lower cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration limit, and thus are able to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ from cytosol to vacuoles (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; ernandez et al. 2009; Barragan et al. 2012). Different evidences have indicated that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (NHX)–type transporters could achieve the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in plant cells (Venema et al. 2002; Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Yoshida et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010; Leidi et al. 2010). So far six NHX genes (NHX1-6) encoding endosomal antiporters have been identified in Arabidopsis genome (Yokoi et al. 2002). RNA gel blot analysis and RT-PCR quantification showed the increased relative abundance of NHX1 and NHX2 transcript level in all the plant tissues which were accumulated in response to the same effectors (NaCl, KCl, LiCl, osmotic stress, and abscisic acid) (Yokoi et al. 2002).

Among all the Arabidopsis NHX transporters, NHX1 and NHX2 are the most closely related NHX family members at protein level $( 8 7 . 5 \%$ sequence identity) and both are localized in the tonoplast (Yokoi et al. 2002; Bassil et al. 2011b). AtNHX1 has been previously shown to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity with similar affinity (Venema et al. 2002; Yamaguchi et al. 2005; Hernandez et al. 2009). The $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter activity in tonoplast of WT and nhx1 nhx2 double mutant by $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient created by V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase at $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ and KCl shows less than one-third of total exchange activity in nhx1 nhx2 than WT, demonstrating the combined contribution of NHX1 and NHX2 to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange in total cation exchange capacity at tonoplast (Barragan et al. 2012). Research in transgenic tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) indicated that overexpressing vacuolar AtNHX1 or the endosomal LeNHX2 $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter leads to enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation

in cell vacuoles (Rodrıguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Leidi et al.   
2010).


## NHX1 and NHX2 Preferentially Regulates ${ { \bf K } } ^ { + }$ Homeostasis as Compared to $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$


The discovery of vacuolar NHX antiporters which mediate the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ across the vacuolar membrane in saline environment (Apse et al. 1999; Quintero et al. 2000), was recently challenged on the basis of biochemistry of NHX-proteins, which do not differentiate between $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or even having stronger affinity for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport as compared with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 1) (Venema et al. 2002; RodrıguezRosales et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010). Recent reports have conclusively demonstrated that vacuolar proteins NHX1 and NHX2 of Arabidopsis preferentially mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration as compared to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Bassil et al. 2011b; Barragan et al. 2012). Since the AtNHX1 protein regulates vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ level and $\mathrm { p H }$ to control cell expansion and tissue elongation, overexpression of AtNHX1 in transgenic tomato increased the vacuolar $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration while depleting cytosolic ${ \mathrm { K } } ^ { + } { \mathrm { p o o l } }$ up regulation of HAK5 and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake was increased as compared to WT (Leidi et al. 2010). Notably, the double mutant nhx1 nhx2 of Arabidopsis is more sensitive to moderate KCl stress (10 to $2 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ concentration) but did not show much greater sensitivity to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ as compared with the WT (Barragan et al. 2012). Remarkably, the nhx1 nhx2 mutant accumulated larger amounts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ upon salt treatment treatment and moderate amounts of NaCl improved the growth of the mutant plant. These results signify that tonoplast NHX proteins are dispensable for the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and that this ion can substitute as osmoticum for the otherwise reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pool in vacuoles of the nhx1 nhx2 mutant (Barragan et al. 2012). These results have raised many questions on how exactly $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is compartmentalized if vacuolar NHX-proteins are specific only for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration, as nhx1nhx2 mutants accumulates more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the plant shoots as compared to WT. It is now clear that in Arabidopsis the ion exchangers other than NHX1 and NHX2 may mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration (Barragan et al. 2012).


## Predominant Role of NHX Proteins in Stomata and Cell Expansion


In early 1970’s, it was proved that potassium has a vital role in regulation of stomata movements. However, with recent research advances the role of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in stomata and guard cell regulation is explained in more detail (Humble et al. 1971; Talbott et al. 1996; Cochrane TT and Cochrane TA 2008). The main solute in osmo-regulation of guard cells are $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , sucrose, and the anions malate and chloride. Guard cells store $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ salts in large quantities which is a cheap and highly mobile solute that regulates opening of stomata (MacRobbie 2006). In Arabidopsis’s guards cells the strong $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fluxes mediates by channels sustain the stomatal movement, i,e opening of stomata is mainly driven by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ entry through $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2, whereas stomatal closing is facilitated by $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux through outward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels activated by membrane depolarization (Ache et al. 2000). However, cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ must be further routed to the vacuole while keeping the cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ at homeostatic values. NHX1 and NHX2 have shown an extensive overlapping expression and subcellular localization pattern including guard cells and other organs, and they share with similar transport properties (Barragan et al. 2012). The best studied example for the role NHX-proteins in stomata is the inactivation of NHX1 and NHX2 genes (nhx1 nhx2) which reduce the total $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ contents in the leaf guard’s cells, with stunted stomata development and function (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). The double mutant of nhx1nhx2 results in wrinkled shaped and thinner stomata as compared with WT. This also explains the role of NHX-proteins in cell expansion. However, the stomata in nhx1nhx2 mutant is not completely dysfunctional but rather exhibit delayed stomatal closure, leaf turgor loss and reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ sequestration in guard cells vacuoles as compared with WT (Barragan et al. 2012; Andres et al. 2014). Delayed stomata closure and leaf turgor loss was also observed in mutants of Snf1 Related Kinase, OST1 (OPEN STOMATA1) and SLOW EFFLUX ANION CHANNEL-ASSCIATED1. These proteins function as to regulate membrane depolarization of guard cells in response to ABA by releasing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and closing stomata (Ache et al. 2010).

The reduced cell expansion and tissue elongation in double mutant of nhx 1nhx2 was not only limited to the cells of leaves, but the hypocotyl of etiolated seedlings also displayed shorter length phenotype in nhx 1nhx2 mutants as compared to WT (Bassil et al. 2011b). This phenomenon was previously shown by (Apse et al. 2003) in nhx1 single knockout mutant mediating improper $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange and reduced cell expansion in normal physiological condition.

Plant species have adopted different molecular and physiological mechanism to regulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and the homeostasis of other essential mineral nutrients under ionic stresses (Ali et al. 2017). In last few years several molecular and biochemical studies have uncovered the strong involvement of different transport proteins (NHXs, HKTs, CHXs, KEAs, NHDs) in regulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange for ion homeostasis, cell growth and development in salt stress. Hundreds of genes are involved in regulation of these processes and manipulation of these genes in model plants is so far very successful but the applications in natural agriculture conditions has always been a challenge. The development of salt tolerant varieties is unlikely to be successful until the applications of new molecular techniques like CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats). But again, this technique is very successful only in model plant Arabidopsis, and a lot of efforts are needed to make multiplegene targeting in agricultural crops through CRISPR/cas9 genome editing. The specific transporters for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions sequestration in vacuoles are yet to be identified, as it was recently reported that vacuolar localized NHX proteins (NHX1 and NHX2) are specific only to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ compartmentation. Therefore, a deep insight for increasing salt tolerance in crop plants, future research should be directed to understand molecular and biochemical mechanisms underlying the exact regulation of these transporters in ionic stress conditions and improve crop production.

The lack of all three transporters in AB11c leads to a mild depolarization of cell plasma membranes under basal conditions (Kinclova-Zimmermannova et al., 2005). AB11c cells also show sensitivity to hygromycin and this has been attributed to a defective sequestration of toxic cations in intracellular compartments (KinclovaZimmermannova et al., 2005). Overexpression ofPcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 appears to exacerbate the hygromycin sensitive phenotype of

AB11c cells, possibly increasing toxic cation accumulation in cells. Overexpression of OsjNHX1 in yeast R100 (Δnhx1) cells confers hygromycin tolerance (Fukuda et al., 2011), similar to PcNHX1 overexpression in YDR456w (Δnhx1:kanMX; EUROSCARF; data not shown). Overexpression of PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 cells partially restores growth under increasing NaCl concentrations at $\mathrm { p H } 4 . 0$

All cells grew equally in medium lacking NaCl, also at $\mathrm { p H } ~ 4 . 0$ , suggesting the effect is not related to the acidic pH of the medium. No differential growth phenotype of AB11c cells overexpressing PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 was observed in medium containing $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ relative to mutant AB11c cells. Cation transporter function has been linked to the presence of two consecutive amino acids, ‘ND’, in the fifth transmembrane (TM) domain of Populus euphratica NHX3 (PeNHX3; Wang et al., 2014), also conserved in PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 (Supplementary Fig. S3). Overexpression of PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 (AP medium; $\mathrm { p H } 4 . 0 $ ) exacerbates the $\mathrm { L i } ^ { + }$ sensitive phenotype of AB11c cells. Further, PcNHX1 appears to enhance the $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ sensitive phenotype significantly more than either OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1. Wang et al. (2014) have implicated the eleventh TM domain of PeNHX3 in $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ transport. Alignment of the PeNHX3 sequence with PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 sequences suggests that the eleventh TM domain sequence is largely conserved (Supplementary Fig. S3). PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1show three amino acid changes from the PeNHX3 sequence in TM11 domain: Ile400 (PcNHX1) Met398(PeNHX3); ${ \tt S e r } _ { 4 1 0 }$ (PcNHX1) $\ P$ Ala408 (PeNHX3); Gln414 (PcNHX1)→Asn412 (PeNHX3). Of these, the $\mathrm { S e r } _ { 4 1 0 \ ( \mathrm { P c N H X 1 } ) } {  } \mathrm { A l a } _ { 4 0 8 }$ (PeNHX3) may have more significance, as ‘Ala’, a hydrophobic residue in PeNHX3 is replaced by a polar residue in PcNHX1, OsjNHX1 or OsiNHX1 and may contribute to breaking a transmembrane helical domain.

The PcNHX1 gene was overexpressed in transgenic tobacco under the transcriptional control of the previously characterized PcNHX1 promoter (Kizhakkedath et al., 2015). PcNHX1 tobacco seedlings (PcNHX1 promoter) show significant growth advantage under increasing concentrations of NaCl and MS salts (increased ionic strength). PcNHX1 expression in transgenic seedlings was confirmed by RT-PCR (Supplementary Fig. S5). This growth advantage was clearly visible in the absence of stress application (faster germination, increased fresh weight, first leaf pair span). Upon application of NaCl stress, seedlings showed increased fresh weight, root length and first leaf pair span. Increased hypocotyl elongation in PcNHX1 transgenic seedlings under salinity limiting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ conditions was also $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -dependent. Replacing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the medium did not confer the hypocotyl elongation phenotype in etiolated PcNHX1 seedlings, suggesting the effect was $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -specific (data not shown). AtNHX1 knockout mutants show delayed seedling establishment and impaired leaf development in the presence of NaCl (Apse et al., 2003). More recently, AtNHX1 and AtNHX2 have been established as vacuolar $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchangers, sequestering $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the vacuoles to drive turgor-related growth processes (Bassil et al., 2011b; Barragán et al., 2012). In Arabidopsis nhx1 nhx2 mutants, inclusion of NaCl in the growth medium restores flowering and seed setting partially. Hypocotyls of nhx1 nhx2 seedlings grown in $3 0 \mathrm { m M N a } ^ { + }$ elongate more than nhx1 nhx2 grown in control media with limiting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Bassil et al., 2012b). Further, nhx1 nhx2 mutants show increased shoot growth in minimal $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ medium containing sub-toxic $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ ion content (Barragán et al., 2012). Vacuolar localization of PcNHX1 has been shown previously (Kizhakkedath et al., 2015). The above data suggests that $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ ions can partially substitute for the lack of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in contributing to vacuolar cell expansion related processes (increased leaf span and hypocotyl length) in PcNHX1 overexpressing lines. Maintaining high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in the cytoplasm is essential for a number of enzymatic activities (Zeng et al., 2015). Under salinity stress, $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ competes with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ to enter plant cells, mainly through $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport pathways at the plasma membrane (Zeng et al., 2015). In halophytes, $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ serves as an energetically cheap osmoticum that helps balance the plant's osmotic potential against the hypertonic soil solution, thereby alleviating the water deficit that is imposed due to a saline environment (Shabala, 2013).P. coarctata grows in soils constantly exposed to fluctuating salinity (coastal-riverine interface; Sengupta and Majumder, 2010). P. coarctata leaves secrete excess NaCl through specialized microhairs found on the adaxial leaf surface (Flowers et al., 1990). $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -specific activity in yeast cells expressing PcNHX1 and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ - dependent growth observed in PcNHX1 transgenic seedlings suggests that it functions in vacuolar sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in P. coarctata.

Incremental salinity treatment of PcNHX1 transgenic lines resulted in lowered leaf $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, unaltered root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and increased stem $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content (and unaltered $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ratios). PcNHX1p-directed GUS activity is detectable in all plant parts and is highest in stem and roots (inducible by salinity in both tissues) followed by leaf tissues (Kizhakkedath et al., 2015). In root tissues, salinity-induced PcNHX1pdirected GUS expression is detected in the cortex, vasculature and root tips. In transgenic PcNHX1 plants, PcNHX1 expression is also induced by salinity treatment in roots (The variation in expression in PcNHX1 transgenic lines L2 (root) and L7 (leaf) vis-à-vis other lines under salinity may be due to (i) differential post transcriptional regulation of PcNHX1 mRNA in the lines. (ii) promoter methylation (ii) differential influences of flanking plant DNA sequences (position effect) superimposed on basic promoter activity (especially if the flanking DNA sequence harbours silencer/enhancer elements (van Leuween et al., 2001; Kohli et al., 2006). Salinity also upregulates PcNHX1 expression in P. coarctata. The data presented above suggests that root-specific expression of PcNHX1 during salinity plays a role in initial storage following uptake. However, since root $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ is unaltered in salinity treated PcNHX1 lines, it is possibly transferred in the transpiration stream to the stem by other $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporting systems (eg. SOS1, HKT1,4; Olías et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2016) where it is stored. Increased stem specific $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ content in PcNHX1 lines under salinity is consistent with elevated PcNHX1p - directed GUS activity in stems of tobacco plants under salinity (Kizhakkedath et al., 2015). In PcNHX1p:GUS promoter fusion lines, PcNHX1 expression is unaltered by salinity and shows a diurnal rhythm that is damped by NaCl treatment in P. coarctata leaves (Kizhakkedath et al., 2015). Lowered $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in leaves of PcNHX1 lines correlates with reduced GUS activity in leaves of PcNHX1p:GUS transgenic lines under salinity (relative to stem and root). Stem specific $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ storage in PcNHX1 lines contributes to reduced $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ content in actively photosynthesizing tissues (leaves). In tomato, the plasma membrane antiporter SiSOS1 directs stem specific $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, preventing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from reaching leaf tissues (Olías et al., 2009). Increased stem specific PcNHX1 expression also correlates with increased $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ - specific hypocotyl elongation in etiolated PcNHX1 seedlings. Thus, differential tissue-specific expression of PcNHX1 directed by the PcNHX1 promoter (both derived from halophytic P. coarctata) under salinity controls $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ partitioning in plant organs and reduces leaf $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ accumulation in a glycophytic species like tobacco (Supplementary Fig. S7).

Salinity is a kind of abiotic stress affecting the growth of many crop plants. Approximately about $20 \%$ of total world land is salt-affected in more than 100 countries (Rengasamy 2006). Plants greatly differ in their tolerance to salinity. Besides osmotic stress tolerance and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ exclusion, the tolerance of tissue to accumulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ is a vital type for plant adaptation to salinity (Munns and Tester 2008). Memrane proteins, such as vacuole $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters (NHX), play key roles in the tolerance of tissue to accumulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into vacuoles. The plant NHX proteins mediated the compartmentation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in vacuoles to confer salt tolerance of various plants species (Apse et al. 1999; Gaxiola et al. 1999; Blumwald et al. 2000). However, more recent evidence supports the hypothesis that plant NHX also plays crucial roles in $\mathrm { p H }$ regulation (Yoshida et al. 2009) and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis (Leidi et al. 2010). Although the vacuolar storage via NHX is still some lingering questions (Kronzucker and Britto 2011), numerous studies have shown that overexpression of the AtNHX1 gene confers salt tolerance to Arabidopsis plants and various other plant species (Apse et al. 1999; He et al. 2005; Leidi et al. 2010; Li et al. 2011). Furthermore, overexpession of AtNHX1 orthologs, such as OsNHX1 of Oryza sativa L. (Chen et al. 2007), TaNHX2 of wheat (Jian et al. 2009), MdNHX1 of Malus (Li et al. 2010c) and AmNHX2 of Ammopiptanthus mongolicus (Wei et al. 2011), confers high salt tolerance to transgenic plants.

Soybean [Glycine max (L.) Merr.] is a predominant plant source for human diet, animal feeds and biodiesel. Its productivity is significantly reduced by salt stress. To cope with salt stress, soybean developed several salt tolerance mechanisms, including maintenance of ion homeostasis, adjustment in response to osmotic stress, restoration of osmotic balance and other metabolic and structural adaptations (Phang et al. 2008). Many salt tolerance related genes in soybean have been reported (Li et al. 2006; Phang et al. 2008; Zhou et al. 2010). Since the entire genome of soybean has been sequenced using shot-gun sequencing (Schmutz et al. 2010), and more recently, 31 wild and cultivated soybean genomes have been resequenced using the Illumina Genome Analyzer II platform (Lam et al. 2010), more salinity related genes will be used for soybean improvement.

In order to improve the efficiency of soybean transformation, several strategies have been used (Zhang et al. 1999, 2004; Olhoft et al. 2003; Paz et al. 2004, 2006; Rech et al. 2008). However, these methods are still labor-intensive, inefficient, and special trained personnel are required to perform the work. If only one performer can produce at least 300 transgenic lines every year, the needs of existing soybean genomics initiatives will be met (Olhoft et al. 2003). Obviously, few laboratories can hit this target to date. In addition, it always takes several months to a year to regenerate a mature plant with the transformation process, which limits the investigation of gene function in soybean.

The AtNHX1 gene encodes the most abundant vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter in Arabidopsis thaliana, and mediates the transport of both $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ into the vacuole [1,2]. Constitutive over-expression of AtNHX1 and homologues from other plants have been shown to confer significant salt tolerance in a variety of plant species as a result of increased vacuolar sequestration of sodium ions ([3], and references therein). The importance of AtNHX1 to salt stress tolerance was further demonstrated when T-DNA insertional mutant nhx1 'knockout' plants lacking a functional antiporter were shown to be more salt sensitive than wild-type Arabidopsis [4]. Additionally, it was found that nhx1 mutants exhibit an altered phenotype under normal growth conditions, including smaller cells, smaller leaves, and other developmental irregularities, associated with altered $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis brought about by the lack of AtNHX1. These results suggested that AtNHX1 is associated with other cellular processes that are not necessarily related to salt tolerance. Subsequently, the AtNHX1 coding region driven by the CaMV 35S promoter was introduced into the nhx1 knockout line. These 'rescued' plants (NHX1::nhx1) displayed AtNHX1 activity, and a phenotype similar to that of wild-type plants [4].

The transcriptional profile of the AtNHX1 'knockout' (nhx1) line has been analyzed previously [5]. That study examined the differences in transcript level using the Affymetrix $^ { \infty } 2 3 \mathrm { ~ k ~ }$ 'Full Genome' GeneChips® to look at the differences of expression levels between wild-type and nhx1 plants grown in the absence of salt stress, and also to examine the difference in relative gene expression changes that occurred after exposure to two weeks of salt stress. It was found that there was little overlap between the two comparisons suggesting that the role of the antiporter as part of the salt stress response machinery is distinct from its role under normal growing conditions. The previous study [5] also suggested that AtNHX1 is important to the expression of several cellular processes, including components of cell structure, protein processing and trafficking, and energy balance, although AtNHX1 did not appear to dramatically affect the expression of many other transporters.

This report further establishes and clarifies the influence of AtNHX1 on gene expression, limiting the analysis to only those transcripts that respond to salt stress, and including an analysis of the influence of both shorter (12 h and $^ { 4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ ) and longer (one week and two weeks) salt stress treatments. Additionally we have employed an NHX1::nhx1 'rescued' line to determine transcripts whose expression levels correlate with the expression of AtNHX1. This approach provides evidence of the influence of a single gene on the expression of other genes while helping to eliminate some of the non-specific effects that result from the mutation of the antiporter.

Plant NHX-type cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters expressed in the membranes of vacuole and vesicles have been shown to mediate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } ( K ^ { + } ) / H ^ { + } }$ exchange for salinity tolerance and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homoeostasis (Brett et al. 2005; Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Chanroj et al. 2012). Even though NHX transporters are involved in maintaining the cellular pH homeostasis (Sze and Chanroj 2018), it is not known if these transporters contribute to plant tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and to low pH soil. We have shown that ectopic expression of Helianthus tuberosus HtNHX1 or HtNHX2 improved rice tolerance to salinity (Zeng et al. 2018). Also, expression of HtNHX2, but not HtNHX1, improves rice growth under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ -limited, salt stress or general nutrient defcienct conditions (Zeng et al. 2018). The possible explanation for this functional diference may be a diference in the subcellular localization, e.g. the fact that HtNHX2 is located at the endomembrane while HtNHX1 is confned to the tonoplast (Zeng et al. 2018).

In this study, we demonstrated that ectopic expression of HtNHX1 or HtNHX2 improved the rice tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and acidic soil as indicated by alleviating the root growth inhibition (Fig. 1), diminishing the plasticity injury of root apex cells (Fig. 5), and increasing both root and shoot growth (Figs. 7, 8). However, it is notable these two genes show diferent mechanisms in altering $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ transport as well as cell wall structure.

Expressing HtNHX1 alleviated $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress in rice (Fig. 1), which is at least in part due to its enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake of rice and/or retention in the roots under normal $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply levels (Fig. 2a). Given that the vacuole occupies about $9 0 \%$ volume of a mature plant cell, the enhanced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } ( K ^ { + } ) / H ^ { + } }$ transporter activity in the tonoplast has been shown to change cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ in both tomato and Arabidopsis (Leidi et al. 2010; Barragán et al. 2012). The activity of HtNHX1 unavoidably changes the cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ homeostasis, and thus in turn alters the activities of the respective transporters in the plasma membrane. The activities of both plasma membrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporters are modifed by external $\mathrm { p H }$ and the presence of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Ahn et al. 2002; Wherrett et al. 2005). Low $\mathrm { p H }$ in the culture solution can stimulate $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ infux into the root tissue (Shabala et al. 1997) and depolarize membrane potential, thus activating outward rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Babourina et al. 2001). Non- invasive MIFE measurements, Bose et al. (2010) showed that $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ quickly inhibited low $\mathrm { p H }$ -induced $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ infux in the distal elongation zone, concomitantly reducing low pH-induced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efux or even favoring $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ infux into the root tissue in

Arabidopsis. We also detected the low pH-induced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efux and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ infux currents recorded at the elongation zone of rice root tips (Fig. 2, the initial current). Adding $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to the bath medium impaired the net $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efux and net $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ infux from all these roots (Fig. 2) showing nearly the same efect as in Arabidopsis roots (Bose et al. 2010). Notably, only HtNHX1 expression could prevent $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -induced root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efux when $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply was at the normal level $\left( 1 \mathrm { m M } \right)$ , but not at $0 . 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . It is likely that the activity of HtNHX1 at the tonoplast (Zeng et al. 2018) drives more cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ into the vacuole in exchange of $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ , and the changed $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ homeostasis in the cytosol in turn induced change in the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel as well as in the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase activity in the plasma membrane (Figs. 2a, 3b, e). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels are able to mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake at low external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ conditions at extreme membrane hyperpolarization conditions (Hirsch et al. 1998; Hampton et al. 2004). However, the recording bath of low $\mathrm { p H }$ (the leak of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ into the cell) in this study prevented extreme hyperpolarization of the membrane potential, and thus the inward $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels were not likely to be activated when the bath $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ concentration was as low as $0 . 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ . Therefore, the HtNHX1 contribution to reduce ${ \bf A } ^ { 1 ^ { 3 + } }$ -induced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efux was much less signifcant at low external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ conditions (Fig. 2b). The HtNHX1 transgenic lines were coupled with quick $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake but not with increased $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ efux at the plasma membrane (Fig. 2a, c). Nevertheless, the rhizosphere pH of HtNHX1 rice was much lower after prolonged $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ exposure (Fig. 3b, e).

Another important feature of HtNHX1 enhancing rice tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress is the stimulation of root secretion of citric acid (Fig. 4). Secretion of organic acids such as citrate, oxalate and malate for chelating $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ in the exterior has long been recognized as a major mechanism of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxifcation (Ma et al. 2001; Kochian et al. 2004). Some plant species secrete predominantly one type of organic acid, such as oxalate by buckwheat, citrate by rice and bean (Ma et al. 1997; Ma 2000; Liu et al. 2018). We detected only citrate in the rice exudations (Fig. 4), which is consistent with a previous report (Ma et al. 2002).

HtNHX2-located endomembrane systems take a small fraction of the cell volume; therefore, the activity of HtNHX2 would change $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ homeostasis of cytosol much less than the HtNHX1. As expected, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ fux in HtNHX2-expressing lines was similar to that in WT (Fig. 2a). It is intriguing that external $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ only inhibited $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ infux slightly in the root of HtNHX2 lines in comparison to the rapid inhibition in WT and HtNHX1 lines when $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ supply was sufcient (Fig. 2c), which may relate to HtNHX2 change of the luminal $\mathrm { p H }$ and ion-homeostasis of the endomembrane system, and this change afects endosome secretion, thus causing $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase delivery to plasma membrane (Sze and Chanroj 2018).

The initial phase of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity is associated with accumulation of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ in the root apex, which binds mostly to the negatively charged pectin of the cell wall and reduces cell wall extensibility (Tabuchi and Matsumoto 2001; Ma et al. 2004; Jones et al. 2006; Yang et al. 2008). We found that the value of FDC that can be used as a proxy for the cell wall extensibility or deformation was small and nearly the same for WT and the transgenic lines under control conditions (Fig. 5a, c). This indicates that the freeze–thaw treatment did not signifcantly change cell wall structure. However, the transgenic lines showed much more tolerance to freeze–thaw disruption after $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ treatment (Fig. 5b, c). After examining the total amount of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ accumulated at the root apex and its apoplastic or intracellular distribution (Fig. 6), it was obvious that enhancement of cell wall extensibility by these two genes was not due to the less $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ accumulation in the apoplast. Yet the increase of root tip $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ content by HtNHX1 expression is difcult to be explained, and may need to be further characterized in future. The enhancement of the cell wall extensibility by HtNHX1 may be explained by the acid growth theory (Rayle and Cleland 1970), HtNHX1 expression could reduce extracellular pH, making cell wall more fexible. However, the similar phenomenon of HtNHX2 on root FDC is not fulflled with this theory (Fig. 5). It is easy to understand HtNHX1 enhanced cell wall fexibility, since this gene enhanced extracellular acidifcation after $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ treatment (Fig. 3b, e).

The improved mechanical resistance in HtNHX2 overexpressing plants most likely occurred via a diferent mechanism. HtNHX2 at early endosome/trans Golgi network/prevacuolar membranes certainly contributes little to cytosolic $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ homeostasis, but accumulated evidences show that the efect of endosome located NHXs on luminal pH of endomembrane system is critical for endosome trafcking (Pardo et al. 2006; Rodriguez-Rosales et al. 2009; Bassil et al. 2012; Reguera et al. 2014). The cell expansion requires the recruitment of membranes and cell wall. In Arabidopsis, mutation of AtNHX5 and AtNHX6 impaired the endosome secretion pathway (Bassil et al. 2011a). In contrast, HtNHX2 expression in rice likely enhanced endosome secretion and, therefore, more membrane and cell wall would be delivered to cell surface and apoplast.

Impairing nutrients uptake is a major consequence of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity. In our previous studies, we have noticed that HtNHX2 not only enhanced N, P and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake, but also improved their translocation from root to shoot at low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or limited nutrient supplies, thus largely increasing rice yield in comparison to WT and HtNHX1 lines (Zeng et al. 2018). These results indirectly suggest that HtNHX2 may enhance the delivery of transporter proteins to plasma membrane under $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress conditions, and thus beneft nutrient uptake. Moreover, phosphorus $( \mathrm { P } )$ is an important counterion of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity. Al and P can form insoluble complexes like $\mathrm { { A l P O } _ { 4 } }$ in cell wall, cytosol and vacuoles (Zheng et al. 2005; Magalhaes et al. 2018). The elevated $\mathrm { \bf P }$ content in HtNHX2-expressing rice also likely contributes to its $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance.

In conclusion, both HtNHX1 and HtNHX2 play a signifcant role in improving rice tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and acidic soil by diferent means. Due to their diferent subcellular locations, they show a non-redundant function in improving the plant tolerance to salinity (Zeng et al. 2018) and acidic stress (Fig. 7). Their co-expression resulted in additive capacity to stimulate rice growth and tolerate the stresses (Fig. 8). We suggest that such a biotechnological strategy to combine the use of type-I and type-II NHX transporters may be adapted to enhance crop tolerance to other abiotic stresses.

With respect to the affected square area and its negative impact on crop productivity, soil salinity is one of the most serios abiotic stress factors [1]. Elucidation of mechanisms of plant adaptation allowing them to survive in saline environments is an important topic of plant physiology.

High sodium content or high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio in the cytoplasm inactivates many enzymatic reactions of the dark stage of photosynthesis, respiration, protein and polysaccharide syntheses [1, 2].The vacuolar NHX-type transporters transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the cytoplasm into the vacuole in exchange for $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ; thus, in salt stress conditions the toxic effect of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the cytoplasm is alleviated and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is used in vacuole as an osmotic agent for lowering the water potential of the cell [3].

The plant vacuolar NHX antiporters were originally described as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters [4], and later they were shown to mediate $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange across the tonoplast driven by the proton gradient established by the V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pyrophosphatase [5].

Agricultural productivity is seriously affected by soil salinity in many areas around the world. The damage of salinity to crops is mainly caused by sodium ion accumulation, a high concentration of which causes water deficit and enzyme inactivity in most plant organs and cells (Blumwald 2000; Zhu 2000). In plants, the $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter located at the plasma and vacuolar membrane can actively exclude excessive $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ from the cytosol or compartmentalize it into tonoplast to remove $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity (Apse et al. 1999; Hasegawa et al. 2000; Shi et al. 2002). In particular, the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter had been demonstrated to play a key role in salt tolerance of plants (Blumwald 2000). The vacuolar $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter is a transmembrane protein which can catalyze the exchange of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ across the vacuolar membrane and maintains cellular $\mathrm { p H }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis in plants (Apse et al. 1999; Shi and Zhu 2002). Recently, many vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter genes (NHX1) have been characterized and identified from different plant species, including Helianthus annuus (Ballesteros et al. 2006), Arabidopsis thaliana (Apse et al. 1999), Hordeum vulgare (Fukuda et al. 2004a), Atriplex gmelili (Hamada et al. 2001), Thellungiella halophila (Wu et al. 2009), Brassica napus (Wang et al. 2003), Beta vulgaris (Xia et al. 2002), Gossypium hirsutum (Wu et al. 2004), Oryza sativa (Fukuda et al. 2004b), and Medicago sativa (Yang et al. 2005). The analysis and comparison of these genes showed that they were highly homologous with similar structural features and conserved domains, and their primary function conferring salt tolerance had been manifested by transgenic events in many plants (Apse et al. 1999; Zhang and Blumwald 2001; Zhang et al. 2001; Ohta et al. 2002; Wu et al. 2004, 2005; Xue et al. 2004; Chen et al. 2007, 2008; Zhao et al. 2007). These transgenic events clearly demonstrated the possibility and feasibility of breeding salt-tolerant crops using the vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene.

Alfalfa (M. sativa L.) is one of the most important herbage worldwide, and it not only supplies abundance of forage for animals but also improves soil fertility. However, the growth and yield of alfalfa are severely affected by soil salinization in some traditional pastures. It is believed that salt-tolerant alfalfa could be a good alternative for restoring ecosystem and improving soil fertility in such degradation areas. Theoretically, salt-tolerant alfalfa cultivar can be generated through genetic engineering methods. However, alfalfa has been regarded as a recalcitrant plant because its transformation and regeneration in vitro are highly genotype-specific and only rarely cultivated varieties are amenable to regeneration (Somers et al. 2003). Only two transgenic salt-tolerant alfalfa events have been reported with Alfin1 transcriptional factor up to date (Winicov and Bastola 1999; Winicov 2000).

In this study, we cloned a novel vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter gene from a halophyte, Salsola soda, using the rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) method and introduced it into alfalfa. The salt-tolerant ability of transgenic alfalfa was enhanced up to $4 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l } .$ It is suggested that there is an enormous potential for the novel vacuolar $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter gene transferred to other plants. Those that obtained high salt-tolerant alfalfa materials could effectively work for exploiting and utilizing severe saline soil.

Plant genetic engineering has recently placed a lot of emphasis on the expression of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger genes (NHX) to create crops that can withstand salt, in particular, the creation of transgenic plants.

Arabidopsis NHX1 transgenes incorporated into other crops such as (Wheat, Barley, Soybean, Poplar, Fescue, Petunia hybrid, and Alfalfa) are shown to have the potential to mitigate salinity (Table 1). The transgenic plants mentioned above demonstrated normal growth performance under salt stress conditions, with no flaws, due to their enhanced tolerance to salinity stress. It has demonstrated a successful strategy for increasing the output of vegetable and fodder legume crops in salinity-prone locations. Transgenic plants expressing AtNHX1 showed considerable improvements in ion homeostasis, ROS scavenging ability, antioxidant enzyme activities, and osmolyte production with unhindered photosynthetic machinery (Fig. 2). These findings suggest that this gene regulates plant defense mechanisms under stressful conditions.
