## Phosphate Transporter Gene from Masson Pine May Function in Angiosperm


Our previous studies provided the first insights into the molecular nature of phosphate transporter gene (PmPT1) involvement in phosphate transport in the masson pine. As a member of the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters in masson pine, PmPT1 has a strictly conserved sequence and a homology of $74 \% - 7 8 \%$ with the phosphate transporter genes from other angiosperm species, such as $74 \%$ similar to phosphate transporters from Nicotiana tabacum (AAF74025.1) (Zhang et al. 2017). The deduced transp o r t e r p r o t e i n s h a r e d t h e c o n s e r v e d s e q u e n c e GGDYPLSATIMSE, typical of the Pht1 family, a member of the major facilitator super-family, composed of monomeric proteins with 12 transmembrane domains (Guan et al. 2006). Further, it was demonstrated that PmPT1 was predominately expressed in the roots of the masson pine in response to Pi starvation, and PmPT1 protein was classified into the gymnosperm and dicotyledon types (Zhang et al. 2017). Thus, PmPT1 may presumably play a broad role in Pi uptake, translocation, and internal transport so as to enabling the plant to acclimatize to P-status change of the soil.

Earlier, several cis elements in pine genes were reported to function similarly in pine and angiosperms (Wu et al. 1997; Mouradov et al. 1999). Recently, Overexpression of two cambium-abundant Chinese fir (Cunninghamia lanceolata) $\propto$ -expansin genes ClEXPA1 and ClEXPA2 was proved to affect growth and development in transgenic tobacco, and increase the amount of cellulose in stem cell walls (Wang et al. 2011), further the expression of a conifer COBRA-like gene ClCOBL1 from this gymnosperms was justified to alter the leaf architecture in tobacco (Gao et al. 2013), reflecting that genes from gymnosperms can play roles in angiosperm. In the present case, PmPT1 gene from masson pine was transferred into tobacco through Agrobacterium-mediated method, and the two PmPT1-overexpressed transgenic lines demonstrated enhanced tolerance to Pi deficiency. Therefore, phosphate transporter gene from gymnosperm possibly function in angiosperm, and the herbaceous angiosperms such as tobacco would be useful ‘hosts’ to compare cis elements involved in masson pine gene regulation since the transgenic system has not been established in this species so far.

Pht1 family genes are highly homologous, indicating functional cooperation between their members (Nussaume et al. 2011; Jia et al. 2011). For instance, Arabidopsis double mutants of Pht1;1 and Pht1;4 showed significantly the reduced uptake and accumulation of phosphorus in both high-phosphorus and low phosphorus environments, mirroring a compensatory relationship between the two transporters (Misson et al. 2004; Shin et al. 2004). Currently, besides the overexpression of the exogenous PmPT1 gene, the higher expressions of both NtPT1 and NtPT2, two high-affinity phosphate transporter genes of the tobacco Pht1 phosphate transporter family, were also detected in the PmPT1-overexpressed transgenic lines, and they were upregulated in both transgenic lines as compared to that of the WT, irrespective of phosphorus treatments (Fig. 2). Furthermore, the expression of the both genes was higher under low-Pi conditions in comparison with that of the stress-free (Fig. 3C-D). A genomewide transcription analysis of Arabidopsis showed that with the exception of Pht1;6, all other Pht1 family genes were mainly expressed in root tissues and induced by low-phosphorus stress (Misson et al. 2005; Morcuende et al. 2007; Thibaud et al. 2010). Similarly, under low-phosphorus stress, the Pht1;8 and Pht1;9 genes synergistically regulated the Pi uptake in Arabidopsis roots (Remy et al. 2012). Thereby molecular mechanism underlying the enhanced tolerance to Pi-deficiency of PmPT1- overexpressed transgenic tobacco is much complex, however, the available evidences provided useful insights into significance vis-à-vis the functional mechanism of this gene. Further interaction between the exogenous and endogenous phosphate transporter genes from the gymnosperm and angiosperm respectively, remains unclear, which is our ongoing work.


## Overexpression of PmPT1 in Tobacco Enhanced the Tolerance to Low-Pi Stress Via Improvement of P Accumulation and Oxidant Alleviation


Phosphorus, a vital mineral nutrient for plants, is required in large amounts to guarantee growth and development. The most direct effect of phosphorus deficiency is retarded growth, as well as leads to dwarfing, reduction in branches and leaf blades, and weakening root, etc. (Rosolem and Tavares 2006). Many plants have consequently evolved the response mechanisms to adapt to low-phosphorus stress (Cai et al. 2012). One of mechanism was the mobilization of Pi and total phosphorus that got accumulated in various tissues of the plant (Hammond et al. 2003). The phosphate transporters promoted the uptake and accumulation of Pi and total phosphorus in plants, especially under low-Pi stress. Phenotypically, it is generally accepted that, abiotic stresses might alter the growth of shoots and roots, therefore root/ shoot ratio was employed to evaluate the tolerance responses herein. In the present case, the PmPT1-overexpressed transgenic tobacco had higher root/shoot ratios and longer roots in comparison to the WT (Fig. 5B), which was considered to be their adaptive responses to the low phosphorus stress. Further, the transgenic lines also gave the significant increases in total $\mathrm { P }$ and Pi status as subjected to the Pi deficiency stress (Fig. 6), which was consistent with the findings in rice and Arabidopsis (Jia et al. 2011; Ren et al. 2014).

Phosphorus is also an important structural component of chloroplasts, and since chloroplast integrity determines the strength of photosynthesis, phosphorus deficiency decreases photosynthetic rate (Kalaji et al. 2016). The plant responses to Pi deficiency also leads to the hinder of sugar and protein biosynthesis (Yuan and Liu 2008). In the current case, the transgenic tobacco plants demonstrated significantly the higher contents of chlorophyll, soluble sugar and soluble protein compared to the WT under lowphosphorus stress, suggesting that overexpressed-PmPT1 could alleviate the effects of phosphorus deficiency by promoting photosynthesis and other biosynthetic pathways, which was similar with the finding in marigold where a greater efficiency of phosphorus uptake resulted in increased content of soluble sugar and soluble protein in the leaves (Liu et al. 2011). Low-phosphorus stress also triggers the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the cells, which disrupts the free-radical balance and increases cell membrane permeability (Chacónlópez et al. 2011). It was generally accepted that high levels of antioxidant enzyme activities can help the plant from ROSinduced oxidative damage (Mittova et al. 2002). More recently, Aluminum toxicity and phosphate deficiency activates antioxidant systems and up-regulates expression of phosphate transporters gene in ryegrass (Lolium perenne L.) plants (Leyla et al. 2018). In the current case, PmPT1-overexpressed tobacco plants displayed higher SOD, CAT, and POD activities and lower MDA accumulation under low $\mathrm { P }$ condition in comparison to that of the WT (Fig. 7), reflecting that overexpression of PmPT1 could improve the functions of the cellular protection enzyme systems. Also, the activities of antioxidant enzymes (Fig.7) showed the tendency to be positively correlated to the contents of both total $\mathrm { P }$ and inorganic Pi (Fig. 6) of transgenic plants. Therefore, overexpressed-PmPT1 greatly enhanced the tolerance of the transgenic tobacco to lowPi stress, which a least chiefly was ascribed to the improvement of $\mathrm { P }$ accumulation and oxidant alleviation.

Phosphorus (P) is an essential macronutrient for growth and development of all living organisms. It serves various basic biological functions as a structural element in nucleic acids and phospholipids, in energy metabolism, and in the activation of metabolic intermediates, as a component in signal transduction cascades, and the regulation of enzymes. The prevalent form of available $\mathrm { \bf P }$ in the environment is the oxidised anion phosphate. Although the total amount of $\mathrm { \bf P }$ in the soil may be high, the preferred form for assimilation, orthophosphate $( \mathrm { P i } )$ , is not easily accessible to most plants and microbes, because of its adsorption to soil particles and clay minerals and surfaces of calcium $\mathrm { ( C a ) }$ and magnesium $\mathbf { \Pi } ( \mathbf { M } \mathbf { g } )$ carbonates, its conversion to organically bound forms or the formation of insoluble precipitates with common cations like iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ , aluminium (Al), and Ca (Welp et al. 1983; Holford 1997). More-soluble minerals such as nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ move through the soil via bulk flow and diffusion, whereas Pi is moved mainly by diffusion in the soil solution. Since the rate of diffusion of $\mathrm { P i }$ in soils is slow $1 0 ^ { - 1 2 }$ to $1 0 ^ { - 1 5 } ~ \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ~ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } ,$ ), higher-plant $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake rates create a Pi-depletion zone around the root (see Fig. 2A; Marschner 1995; Jungk 2001). Therefore, the low availability of $\mathrm { P i }$ in the bulk soil affects its uptake into roots.

Plants have developed numerous morphological, physiological, biochemical and molecular responses to cope with growth under Pi-limiting conditions, including changes in root morphology and architecture, accumulation of anthocyanin pigments, secretion of phosphomonoesterases and organic acids into the rhizosphere, improved Pi uptake efficiency, and changes in metabolism (for a review, see Raghothama 1999). The ultimate goals of these adaptive changes are increased Pi availability in the rhizosphere, enhanced Pi uptake and maintenance of plant metabolism. To optimally exploit the soil Pi, plants respond with an increased root-toshoot ratio and an enlargement of the absorptive surface area relative to the root volume (Marschner 1995). The increase in absorptive surface area can be attributed in part to the enhanced production of root hairs, their length being especially important for Pi uptake (Bates and Lynch 1996; Jungk 2001). In certain plant species, the formation of cluster roots (bottlebrush-like clusters of rootlets densely covered with root hairs) is another type of response to Pi deficiency. Cluster roots have been functionally linked with efficient mechanisms for the chemical mobilisation of sparingly available Pi sources in the rhizosphere, involving the excretion of large amounts of organic chelators (e.g. citrate, malate and phenolics) and ectoenzymes (acid phosphatase) (for a review, see Neumann and Martinoia 2002). Alternatively, ecto- and endomycorrhizal associations between symbiotic soil fungi and plant roots have to be taken into consideration. In these associations the absorbing surface area of the colonised roots is extended due to the large extraradical mycelium exploiting soil volumes which are otherwise not accessible to the non-colonised plant root (Smith and Read 1997). The increased concentration in available P effected by the plant requires an efficient uptake and transport system.

Plants are able to selectively and actively accumulate Pi and other mineral nutrients in their cells. Selective transport of compounds across cellular and intracellular membranes is mediated by membrane-spanning transporter proteins with specific binding sites. Nutrient allocation on the cellular, tissue and organ levels occurs via short- and long-distance transport, including several membrane transport steps, and plays an essential role in the life cycle of a plant.


## Pi transport mechanisms


Uptake into a living cell: short-distance transport

In order to cope with fluctuating concentrations of external Pi, plants respond to $\mathrm { P i }$ deficiency by increasing their activity of Pi uptake. In their pioneering work, Epstein and Hagen (1952) demonstrated that the kinetics of ion absorption by barley roots were in close agreement with classical enzyme kinetics. $\textrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { { R b } ^ { + } }$ absorption rates followed Michaelis–Menten kinetics and transport of a single ionic species was found to be dual-phasic, operating at high or low affinity, dependent on either low or high external ion concentrations, respectively, thus following two absorption isotherms (Epstein et al. 1963). Most interpretations in the literature concerning Pi uptake kinetics into plant cells under varying $\mathrm { P i }$ concentrations propose the presence of two independent Michaelis–Menten type systems, although the presence of up to seven transport kinetics was suggested, e.g. for $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake into maize roots (Nandi et al. 1987). In Lemna gibba, two Pi uptake systems exhibiting different apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values at varying $\mathrm { P i }$ availability were described with elevated $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ values of both systems during $\mathrm { P i }$ depletion (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1984), while only an enhanced activity of the high-affinity Pi uptake system was detected in suspension-cultured Catharanthus roseus protoplasts without any significant change in $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ of the low-affinity system (Furihata et al. 1992). Assuming that the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ is a characteristic feature of a single transport protein, a change in $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for Pi implies that the molecular species has also changed. On the other hand, changes in $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ may occur either by changes in the nature of the molecular species or by changes in the number of the same species, e.g. providing more transport sites for Pi uptake per root surface area. The existence of high- and low-affinity Pi transport systems has been shown by molecular and/or biochemical methods not only for plant cells, but also for bacteria (Harris et al. 2001), yeast (Persson et al. 1998; Zvyagilskaya et al. 2001), Neurospora crassa (Burns and Beever 1977), arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi (Thomson et al. 1990) and mammals (Olah et al. 1994).

The uptake of Pi into living cells poses a problem for plants, as Pi concentrations in the soil solution rarely exceed $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ (Marschner 1995), while the Pi concentration within most plant cells is 10,000-fold higher $1 { - } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m M }$ ; Bieleski 1973). Thus, under normal physiological conditions the plants have to acquire $\mathrm { P i }$ against this steep concentration gradient (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983). Pi exists in several different forms in solution and the concentration of each form varies as a function of pH. The pK values for the dissociation of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { P O } } _ { 4 }$ into $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ and then into $\mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ are 2.1 and 7.2, respectively. Therefore, below $\mathrm { p H } 6 . 0$ most Pi will be present as the monovalent $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ species, while the other two species will be only present in minor proportions (Sentenac and Grignon 1985). Several studies on the pH dependency of Pi uptake into plant cells have demonstrated that uptake rates are highest between $\mathrm { p H } 4 . 5$ and 6.0, where the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ species is predominant (UllrichEberius et al. 1981; Furihata et al. 1992; Mitsukawa et al. 1997). Thus, it has been suggested that Pi is taken up as $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ across the plasma membrane into the plant cell (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1981). Root cells absorb Pi not only against the steep concentration gradient between the soil solution and the cytosol, as the monovalent Pi anion additionally has to overcome the negative membrane potential that is characteristic for plant cells. The combination of both factors emphasises the requirement for energised transport of $\mathrm { P i }$ across the plasma membrane (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983). Making use of the water-plant duckweed (Lemna gibba G1), evidence was provided for an energy-dependent Pi uptake which proceeds via $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ co-transport dependent on the electrochemical proton gradient and therefore on the activity of an $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -extrusion pump such as the P-type $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1981, 1984). Pi transport transiently depolarises the plasma membrane, which indicates that $\mathrm { P i }$ does not simply enter the cell as $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ or as $\mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ , both of which would lead to a membrane hyperpolarisation if Pi were to be transported alone (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1984). Three other independent lines of evidence further support the idea of an $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ co-transport. First, investigations with suspension-cultured cells of Catharanthus roseus demonstrated that Pi uptake was coupled to an increase in $\mathrm { p H }$ of the extracellular medium (from $\mathrm { p H } 3 . 5$ to 5.8; Sakano 1990), while the cytoplasm acidified (0.2 to $0 . 3 \textrm { \ p H }$ units; Sakano et al. 1992). Similarly, cytoplasmic acidification was measured in barley leaves (Mimura et al. 1992) and root hairs of Limnobium stoloniferum (Ullrich and Novacky 1990). Secondly, inhibitors that dissipate the electrochemical gradient for protons inhibit $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake across the membrane in corn roots (Lin 1979). The third line of evidence is based on the biochemical analysis of plant Pi transporters either expressed in the heterologous yeast system (Leggewie et al. 1997; Daram et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998b) or in cultured plant cells (Mitsukawa et al. 1997). In these experiments, application of protonophores inhibited Pi uptake into cultured cells ectopically expressing a distinct Pi transporter gene. The stoichiometry of Pi uptake is not resolved, but calculations and experimental data suggest that two to four protons are co-transported with each $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ (UllrichEberius et al. 1981, 1984; Sakano 1990).

It has been suggested that one of the major differences between plants and animals is the activity of an $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -dependent transport system in animal cells (Escoubet et al. 1989; Werner et al. 1998; Werner and Kinne 2001), whereas $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ -coupled Pi transport systems occur in plants. However, recent evidence for plant Pi uptake via $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ co-transport was provided from studies with the green algae Chara corallina, demonstrating both $\mathrm { N a } ^ { \bar { + } }$ -dependence of Pi uptake and the reciprocal $\mathrm { P i }$ -dependence of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ uptake (Reid et al. 2000). Both $\mathrm { ~ H ~ } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ and $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ transport processes were found in fungal species (Versaw and Metzenberg 1995; Martinez and Persson 1998; Persson et al. 1998; Zvyagilskaya et al. 2001). While $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ -driven Pi transport in yeast and $N$ . crassa was reported to exhibit a $\mathrm { p H }$ optimum between 4.5 and 6.0, which is in the range of apoplastic $\mathrm { p H }$ values in plants, $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -coupled co-transport had a $\mathrm { p H }$ optimum of 8.0 and higher (up to 10.0) (Versaw and Metzenberg 1995; Martinez and Persson 1998; Zvyagilskaya et al. 2001). This suggests high flexibility of these organisms to changing environmental conditions. Dependence of Pi uptake on $\mathrm { \tilde { N a } ^ { + } }$ has so far not been demonstrated in vascular plants, but the existence of such a transport system can not be excluded, e.g. in halophytes, which have developed mechanisms for salt resistance, or in plants living in alkaline soils.


## Pi translocation on the whole-plant level: long-distance transport


In the soil solution, Pi moves towards the root via diffusion (Marschner 1995) and is subsequently taken up into the root symplasm via rhizodermal cells, including root hairs (Drew et al. 1984; Sentenac and Grignon 1985; Ullrich and Novacky 1990). After uptake into the root symplasm, Pi faces five possible fates: (i) it may enter the metabolic pool (cell cytoplasm plus its organelles), where the main entry for $\mathrm { P i }$ into organic compounds occurs via anhydride bond formation as the c-phosphate group of ATP (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983); (ii) a small fraction of Pi may enter the biosynthetic pathways of P-lipids, DNA, and RNA, respectively, thus becoming structural components of the cell (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983); (iii) variable amounts of Pi are lost from the cell via efflux especially under highPi conditions, an activity which is decreased under Pistarvation conditions (Mimura 1999); (iv) Pi influx and storage occur in the vacuole to regulate Pi homeostasis within the cell (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983; Mimura 1995, 1999); (v) Pi is transported symplasmically to the xylem parenchyma cells and subsequently secreted into the xylem (apoplast) for long-distance translocation to the above-ground organs (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983; Jeschke et al. 1997). Xylem transport is driven by the gradient in hydrostatic pressure and by the gradient in the water potential. The gradient in water potential between roots and shoots is particularly steep during the day when the stomata are open and solute flow in the xylem is therefore unidirectional (Marschner 1995). The mechanism of xylem loading with Pi (or unloading from the symplast to the inner apoplast of the root) could be studied after the identification of a suitable mutant. The Arabidopsis mutant pho1 was isolated based on reduced total Pi concentrations in the leaf tissue and was shown to have root Pi uptake rates that were similar to wild-type plants, whereas translocation rates to the shoot were reduced (Poirier et al. 1991). This suggested a defect in the ability to load/release Pi into the xylem for translocation to the shoot and implies the presence of a specialised transport mechanism for the transfer of Pi to the xylem (Poirier et al. 1991). Recently, the PHO1 gene was identified and characterised (Hamburger et al. 2002) and was shown to be involved either directly or indirectly in Pi transport across membranes (see below for more details).

Several studies provide a picture of Pi distribution patterns on the whole-plant level (Koontz and Biddulph 1957; Biddulph et al. 1958; Linck and Swanson 1960; Jeschke et al. 1997). Pi is described as a phloem-mobile element (Marschner 1995) and it was suggested that Pi is the primary form in which $\mathrm { \bf P }$ moves in the phloem (Bieleski 1969; Jeschke et al. 1997). However, organic Pi compounds, such as nucleotides (including ATP) and hexose-phosphates, were also detected in phloem sap (Bieleski 1969; Kluge et al. 1970). In Pi-sufficient plants, most of the Pi absorbed by the root is transported in the xylem to the young leaves. Pi mobilisation, net export, and re-translocation from older leaves to the root via the phloem were calculated to greatly exceed the requirements of the root under high Pi supply; thus massive transfer of Pi from phloem to xylem for Pi transport back to the shoot was expected to occur in the root (Jeschke et al. 1997). In Pi-deficient plants, the restricted supply of Pi from the roots to the shoot via the xylem is supplemented by increased mobilisation of stored $\mathrm { P i }$ in the older leaves and re-translocation to both younger leaves and growing roots. This process involves the depletion of $\mathrm { P i }$ stores and the breakdown of organic Pi in the older leaves (Jeschke et al. 1997). Another wellcharacterised Arabidopsis mutant (pho2) has higher levels of Pi in leaves (Delhaize and Randall 1995), which could result from a defect or alteration of Pi-transporter function(s) in the shoot or of regulatory genes involved in $\mathrm { P i }$ sensing and homeostasis. Thus, Pi loading of, or transport via, the phloem for allocation to other plant organs could be affected in this mutant (Dong et al. 1998).

Pi homeostasis on the cellular level and Pi transport into organelles

Pi homeostasis plays an important role within plant cells and this may require monitoring of the Pi concentration in each compartment, such as cytoplasm, vacuole, plastids, and mitochondria. In vacuolated cells of higher plants, the vacuole acts as a storage pool, or ‘non-metabolic pool’, of Pi, and at adequate Pi supply of the plants about $8 5 { - } 9 5 \%$ of the total $\mathrm { P i }$ is located to the vacuoles (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983). In contrast, in leaves of Pi-deficient plants virtually all Pi is found in the cytoplasm and chloroplasts, representing parts of the ‘metabolic pool’ of Pi in the plant (Bieleski and Ferguson 1983; Marschner 1995). $^ { 3 1 } \mathrm { P }$ -Nuclear magnetic resonance ( $\mathrm { ^ { 3 1 } P }$ -NMR) measurements with maize roots showed that under Pi deficiency, the vacuole acts as a Pi reservoir to maintain the cytoplasmic Pi pool constant and the latter does not decline until $\mathrm { P i }$ stress becomes severe (Lee et al. 1990). Preceding any detectable change in the cytoplasmic Pi content of the roots during Pi starvation, an increased capacity for Pi influx into the vacuole was found to develop (Lee et al. 1990). Vacuolar $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake activities after incubation of barley protoplasts with $^ { 3 2 } \mathrm { { P i } }$ were very slow in controls, while $^ { 3 2 } \mathrm { { P i } }$ appeared rapidly in vacuoles isolated from Pi-deficient protoplasts (Mimura et al. 1990). Studies of $^ { 3 2 } \mathrm { { P i } }$ uptake, in which isolated vacuoles were directly incubated in the uptake medium, revealed that the increase in Pi uptake into vacuoles of Pi-depleted cells was only detectable in the presence of ATP, which would indicate the involvement of a secondary activated transport system (Mimura et al. 1990). However, no saturation of uptake was observed within a concentration range $\mathrm { 0 { - } } 2 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ which is at the upper end of measured cytoplasmic Pi concentrations in plants (Mimura et al. 1990; Mimura 1999). These results open the question as to which molecular mechanisms regulate Pi transport across the tonoplast. Recently, the identification of a slowly activated, outward rectifying channel with a high permeability for $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ was demonstrated by applying the patch-clamp method to the vacuolar membrane (Dunlop and Phung 1998). However, the authors themselves point out that their patch-clamp experiments do not necessarily correspond to the physiological conditions in the cell and that this Pi-permeable channel would have a low probability of being open in vivo (Dunlop and Phung 1998). Thus, the physiological significance of the Pi channel has yet to be elucidated. Massonneau et al. (2000) readopted the idea of measuring Pi uptake across the tonoplast of intact vacuoles, making use of vacuoles isolated from suspension-cultured cells of Catharanthus roseus. Pi uptake into the vacuoles showed saturation kinetics with an apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of about $\boldsymbol { 5 } \mathrm { m M }$ and a highaffinity uptake system in the micromolar range was never observed. Uptake of Pi was strongly stimulated by both ATP and pyrophosphate (PPi), indicating that the respective $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -pumps are involved in $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake across the tonoplast. Making use of inhibitors of vacuolar $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ - ATPase and agents destroying the electrical component of the vacuolar membrane or affecting the $\Delta \mathrm { p H }$ across the tonoplast, the authors suggest that the electrical component is the driving force for Pi uptake into the vacuole, whereas the DpH plays only a minor role. Interestingly, several anion-channel inhibitors had no effect on $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake (Massonneau et al. 2000). Mobilisation of vacuolar $\mathrm { P i }$ under conditions of deficiency involves controlled efflux of Pi across the tonoplast. Incubation of isolated barley vacuoles in Pi-free medium did not result in a Pi release comparable to that of other anions, suggesting that efflux of Pi from the vacuole may be very slow (Martinoia et al. 1986). However, $^ { 3 1 } { \dot { \mathrm { P } } } .$ NMR spectroscopical measurements in pea leaves under anoxia revealed that Pi moved rapidly between vacuole and cytoplasm (Bligny et al. 1997). Thus, the molecular and biochemical mechanisms of Pi transport into and out of the vacuole are still unclear and further investigations are needed.

During Pi deficiency in leaves, cytoplasmic Pi concentrations may drop from about $\boldsymbol { 5 } \mathrm { m M }$ (or more) to less than $0 . 2 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . Photosynthesis and carbon partitioning in the light–dark cycle are strongly affected by Pi concentrations in the cytosol and the chloroplasts (Walker and Sivak 1986; Marschner 1995) and these processes require Pi transport across the chloroplast inner envelope membrane. The role of $\mathrm { P i }$ in carbon partitioning has been demonstrated by making use of isolated chloroplasts. It was shown that increased Pi concentrations in the external medium to up to $1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ stimulated net photosynthesis, but decreased the production of starch in the chloroplasts. In contrast, Pi limitation within the cytosol led to increased starch synthesis and hence an accumulation of starch in the organelles despite a simultaneous depression of photosynthesis (Heldt et al. 1977; Flu¨ gge 1999). Pi transport across the chloroplast membrane is mainly mediated by the triose-phosphate/phosphate translocator (TPT) with a passive counter-exchange mechanism, i.e. for each molecule of Pi transported in one direction, one molecule of triose-phosphate (dihydroxyacetone-phosphate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate) or glycerate-3-phosphate is transported in the opposite direction. This counter-exchange is strictly coupled, the unidirectional transport of Pi being at least 1,000-fold slower than the rate of counter-exchange. The strict stoichiometry is important, because it ensures that every molecule of phosphoester exported from the chloroplast is counterbalanced by the uptake of a Pi molecule into the chloroplast. Thus, when the Pi concentrations in the cytosol are low, the TPT activity is restricted, which leads to an accumulation of metabolites in the chloroplast, a depletion of $\mathrm { P i }$ in the stroma and starch production (Stitt 1997). Four different groups of phosphate translocator (PT) proteins have been described so far in the inner envelope membrane of plastids and all of them function as antiport systems using Pi or phosphorylated C3 and C6 compounds as counter-substrates (Eicks et al. 2002). The above-mentioned TPT proteins form the first group of PT proteins identified. The phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)/PT (PPT) belongs to the second group of PT proteins in plastids. It mediates the transport of PEP into the organelles, where it is used as a substrate in a variety of metabolic processes, e.g. as a precursor for the shikimate pathway leading to the synthesis of the aromatic amino acids and several secondary compounds. The biosynthesis of aromatics is compromised in cue1, an Arabidopsis mutant defective in PPT-mediated transport, and the reticulate leaf phenotype observed in the mutant can be rescued by feeding aromatic amino acids (Streatfield et al. 1999). In contrast to the TPT, the PPT protein transports Pi out of the chloroplasts into the cytosol under most physiological conditions, a mechanism also performed by the last two groups of PT proteins. The glucose 6-phosphate (Glc-6-P)/PT (GPT) imports Glc-6-P into amyloplasts in exchange for either triose-phosphate or Pi. In the nongreen plastids, Glc-6-P is a precursor for the synthesis of starch and fatty acids and a substrate of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (Flu¨ gge 2001). The first characterised member of the fourth group of PT proteins, XPT, translocates pentose xylulose 5-phosphate (Xul-5-P) in exchange for triose-phosphate or Pi into plastids. The XPT protein is assumed to provide the plastidic pentose phosphate pathway with carbon skeletons under high demand for intermediates of the cycles (Eicks et al. 2002). These data demonstrate the importance of a controlled Pi transport into and out of plastids within the context of cellular Pi homeostasis.

Little is known about plant Pi transporters in the inner mitochondrial membrane. However, the uptake of Pi into the mitochondrial matrix is essential for the oxidative phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. The resulting ATP is transported by the ADP/ATP translocase out of the matrix into the cytosol in exchange for ADP, and Pi is finally returned to the mitochondrial matrix via its respective transporter protein (Phelps et al. 1996). Sequence analysis of the first cloned members of the mitochondrial Pi transporter family from plants revealed high amino acid sequence identity and a proposed polypeptide structure of six membrane-spanning domains (Kiiskinen et al. 1997; Takabatake et al. 1999). Based on experiments with the phosphate carrier (PiC) from mammals and the Pi transport protein (PTP) from yeast, the plant protein is expected to catalyse Pi influx as a homodimer (Schroers et al. 1998) either by a $\mathrm { P i / H ^ { + } }$ symport (Pratt et al. 1991; Phelps et al. 1996) or a $\mathrm { P i / O H ^ { - } }$ antiport (Stappen and Kramer 1994) mechanism. It is generally thought that the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient across the membrane generated by the mitochondrial electron transport chain is the driving force for Pi uptake (Laloi 1999; Takabatake et al. 1999). Several mitochondrial carrier systems function in a heterologous $\mathrm { ( P i / H ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { P i / O H ^ { - } }$ , as described above) as well as in a homologous $\mathrm { P i } / \mathrm { P i }$ exchange mode, especially under conditions of high Pi concentrations on both sides of the membrane (Mcintosh and Oliver 1994). This mode of $\mathrm { P i } / \mathrm { P i }$ exchange activity was used to confirm the Pi transport properties of many putative mitochondrial Pi transporter proteins (including those isolated from plants) with ${ \dot { 3 } } 2 _ { \mathrm { { P i } } }$ import studies into proteoliposomes via the reconstituted carrier proteins (Mcintosh and Oliver 1994; Stappen and Kramer 1994; Silva et al. 1999; Takabatake et al. 1999). However, further studies are needed to evaluate the involvement of the plant mitochondrial Pi transporters in the Pi homeostasis of plant cells.


## Molecular biological analysis of Pi transport systems


Molecular biological studies in recent years have finally made it possible to identify and investigate high- and low-affinity Pi transporters and Pi translocators in membranes of organelles in more detail. The typical features of the different Pi transporter/translocator families are summarised below, including the recently proposed Pht3 family of mitochondrial Pi transporters.


## The Pht1 family of plant Pi transporters


The first genes encoding putative plant Pi transporters were isolated from Arabidopsis and Solanum tuberosum cDNA libraries (Muchhal et al. 1996; Leggewie et al. 1997; Mitsukawa et al. 1997) or via reverse transcription– polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR; Smith et al. 1997) based on sequence similarities to a partial cDNA in the Arabidopsis expressed sequence tag (EST) database. This partial cDNA exhibited similarities to genes encoding Pi transporters from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (PHO84; Bun-Ya et al. 1991), N. crassa (PHO5; Versaw 1995) and Glomus versiforme (GvPT; Harrison and Van Buuren 1995). Meanwhile, additional Pi transporter genes from Lycopersicon esculentum (Daram et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998a), Medicago truncatula (Liu et al. 1998b) and several other plant species have been isolated and the number of cloned genes is steadily increasing. All the members of the Pht1 family of plant Pi transporters and the above-mentioned fungal Pi transporters exhibit high sequence similarity with each other. The putative proteins are similar in size, contain 12 putative transmembrane domains (TMs), as predicted by computer analysis, and have both their Nand C-termini oriented towards the inside of the cell (Raghothama 1999; Smith 2001). Another typical feature is a large hydrophilic loop between TM6 and TM7, resulting in the characteristic $6 + 6$ configuration of many transporter proteins belonging to the major facilitator superfamily MFS (Pao et al. 1998). Pht1 transporters and the related fungal transporters are suggested to utilise the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -gradient at the plasma membrane to drive the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ symport activity. Functional analysis of plant Pi transporters in the yeast mutant defective in the PHO84 gene (Bun-Ya et al. 1991) produced $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values much higher than expected by physiologists (Leggewie et al. 1997; Liu et al. 1998b). However, experimental data obtained via complementation of a yeast mutant disrupted in both high-affinity $\mathrm { P i }$ transporter genes PHO84 and PHO89 (Martinez and Persson 1998) resulted in the determination of an apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { P i }$ of $3 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for LePT1 from tomato (Daram et al. 1998). A $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value of $3 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ was measured in cultured tobacco cells expressing the gene encoding PHT1 from Arabidopsis (Mitsukawa et al. 1997), thus leading to the assumption that the members of the Pht1 family are high-affinity Pi transporters (Bucher et al. 2001).

As a result of extensive studies on the two Pi transporters LePT1 and LePT2 from Lycopersicon esculentum, a broad overview of their gene expression, as well as their mRNA and protein localisation was obtained (Daram et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998a; Muchhal and Raghothama 1999; Rosewarne et al. 1999; Bucher et al. 2001). LePT1 mRNA was detectable in both root and shoot tissues, and transcript levels increased in both tissues upon Pi starvation. Within $2 4 ~ \mathrm { h }$ after re-supply of Pi in the medium, transcript abundance decreased again to control levels. In contrast, $L e P T 2 \ \mathrm { m R N A }$ was exclusively detectable in roots, its concentration was strongly enhanced during Pi deprivation and was also strongly reduced after Pi resupply (Liu et al. 1998a). Using antibodies specific for LePT1, Muchhal and Raghothama (1999) demonstrated that the fluctuations in LePT1 transcripts under changing Pi supply to the plant were concurrent with the levels of the transporter protein. These data strongly suggest a predominantly transcriptional regulation of Pi acquisition, although post-translational modification of Pi transport activity cannot be excluded. In situ hybridisation studies localised the LePT1 transcript to rhizodermal cells, including root hairs and root cap cells (Daram et al. 1998), and mRNA signals were also detected in leaf palisade parenchyma cells (Liu et al. 1998a). LePT1 transcripts and protein accumulated along the entire root and the respective protein was detected primarily in the plasma membrane (Daram et al. 1998; Muchhal and Raghothama 1999). During Pi starvation, a marked increase in transcript abundance was detected in the central cylinder of the root proximal to the root tip (Daram et al. 1998). LePT2 transcripts were primarily observed in root epidermal cells under Pi-limiting conditions (Liu et al. 1998a). The expression pattern of the two Pi transporters from tomato and the protein localisation of LePT1 support a primary role of at least some Pht1 transporters in Pi acquisition at the root–soil interface. Chiou et al. (2001) confirmed the predominant transcriptional regulation and the rhizodermal localisation of another member of the Pht1 family, MtPT1 from $M .$ . truncatula. Enhanced Pitransporter gene expression under Pi-limiting conditions leads to an increased number of transport sites and thus most likely to an increase in $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ of $\mathrm { P i }$ uptake per root area, which is in agreement with data obtained in physiological experiments. In analogy to the situation in tomato, two Pht1 transporter genes were isolated each from M. truncatula (Liu et al. 1998b) and white lupin (Liu et al. 2001), while three Pht1 transporters were characterised in potato (Leggewie et al. 1997; Rausch et al. 2001). The relatively low number of identified Pht1 transporter genes in plant species like Medicago, tomato and potato stays in contrast to the nine different Pht1 genes detectable in the Arabidopsis genome. Recently a nomenclature of Pht1 proteins in Arabidopsis based on the sequences present in the whole Arabidopsis genome has been proposed (Poirier and Bucher 2002; F.A. Smith, personal communication) and includes all nine Pht1 proteins numbered Pht1;1 to Pht1;9 (see Table 1 and http://ukcrop.net/perl/ace/tree/ Mendel-CPGN?name $=$ Pht1&class $=$ GeneFamily).

Presumably, each member has a distinct function during plant growth and development or in a changing environment. Therefore, more Pht1 members may be identified in the future in plants other than Arabidopsis.


## Pi transport in mycorrhizae


The mutualistic symbiosis between fungi and plant roots was given the name mycorrhiza. In the arbuscular mycorrhizae, the fungal hyphae grow inter- and intracellularly and produce arbuscules (branched tuft-like hyphal structures) within the cells. Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi are obligate biotrophs that form such a mutualistic association with a wide range of plant species. Their longterm compatible interaction is based on bidirectional nutrient transfer between the symbionts, where the host plant derives mainly $\mathrm { \bf P }$ from the fungus, which in turn benefits from plant carbohydrates (Smith and Read 1997). In some cases, Pi uptake from the soil by the root is almost totally suppressed in the mycorrhizal symbiosis. Under these circumstances, initial Pi uptake into the fungus/ plant community is almost entirely due to uptake by the extraradical fungal hyphae (Pearson and Jakobsen 1993). Nutrients are taken up by AM fungal extraradical hyphae in soil areas distant from the root surface, from where they are transported to the symbiotic interfaces within the root cortex (Li et al. 1991). Interestingly, similar Pi transport systems exist in plants and AM fungi. Thomson et al. (1990) kinetically identified two transport systems for Pi in the germ-tubes of Gigaspora margarita grown in the absence of Pi. The high-affinity system analysed had an apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of $1 . 8 \mathrm { - } 3 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ and the low-affinity system exhibited a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of $1 0 { - } 1 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ . Due to a reduced Pi uptake rate of the high-affinity system after treatment of the germ tubes with carbonylcyanide $m \cdot$ -chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation, the authors suggested that the high-affinity system exhibits a

$2 \mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ co-transport activity driven by an $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ - translocating ATPase (Thomson et al. 1990). This view was strongly supported by the cloning of the Pi transporter $G \nu P T$ from the AM fungus Glomus versiforme (Harrison and Van Buuren 1995). The deduced GvPT protein shared high sequence similarity with the yeast PHO84 high-affinity Pi transporter and with members of the plant Pht1 family (Fig. 1, Table 1). The function of GvPT as a high-affinity $\mathrm { ~ \bar { ~ } H ^ { + } ~ }$ -dependent $\mathrm { P i }$ transporter $K _ { \mathrm { m } } { = } 1 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ) was confirmed by complementation of the pho84 yeast mutant and via application of CCCP, which prevented uptake of ${ } ^ { 3 3 } \mathrm { \mathbf { P i } }$ into complemented yeast cells. Expression of the corresponding gene in the extraradical hyphae of $G$ . versiforme is consistent with a role of GvPT in the initial uptake of Pi from the soil (Fig. 2A; Harrison and Van Buuren 1995). Recently, a $\mathrm { P i }$ transporter from the AM fungus $G$ . intraradices was isolated based on its homologies to GvPT (Maldonado-Mendoza et al. 2001). GiPT transcripts were detected in the extraradical mycelium and gene expression was influenced by the Pi concentration in the environment surrounding the extraradical hyphae. Thus, extraradical hyphae in a mycorrhiza are involved in the absorption of Pi (and probably other nutrients) from the soil, its translocation through the surrounding soil and its final transport through the mycelium into the fungal structures within the root (Fig. 2A; Smith and Read 1997). Suggested mechanisms of Pi translocation within the AM fungal hyphae from the place of uptake to the fungus–root interfaces involve processes based on both mass flow and cytoplasmic streaming (Cooper and Tinker 1981). Pi uptake into the mycorrhizal plant cells takes place at a specialised interface between the AM fungus and the host plant: the arbuscule (Fig. 2A, B). When a fungal hypha penetrates a cortical cell and differentiates into an arbuscule, the plant cell plasma membrane extends to surround it with the socalled periarbuscular membrane, localising the arbuscule essentially to the plant apoplast. The extended periarbuscular membrane is separated from the fungal wall and the underlying membrane of the arbuscule by a narrow compartment, the interface matrix (Fig. 2B; Harrison 1999). Consequently, two Pi transport steps are required for the transfer of Pi from the fungus into plant cells: (i) the transfer of Pi from the fungus into the apoplastic space (the interface matrix), and (ii) the subsequent uptake of Pi into the cortical cells of the root (Fig. 2B). The molecular components involved in this (active or passive) efflux of Pi across the arbuscular membrane are not known and the mechanisms underlying the process are not understood (Smith and Read 1997), while Pi uptake into the cortical cells was suggested to involve a $\mathbf { \hat { H } } ^ { + }$ -coupled symport mechanism. A lead-precipitation method used to visualise

ATPase activity (Gianinazzi-Pearson et al. 1991), immunolabelling of $\dot { \mathrm { ~ H ~ } } ^ { + }$ -ATPase protein, and $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ -ATPasepromoter–GUS assays (Gianinazzi-Pearson et al. 2000) revealed that the periarbuscular membrane contains high $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase activity. Additionally, it was shown that arbuscules inhabit an acidic compartment within plant roots, which can be destroyed by treatment with a protonophore or by membrane rupture (Guttenberger 2000). These results supported the idea of a plant Pi transporter being active at the periarbuscular membrane surrounding the arbuscule (Fig. 2B). The recent cloning and characterisation of a novel Pi transporter, StPT3 from potato, provides molecular and biochemical evidence for plant Pi uptake at the AM fungus–root interface in mycorrhizae. Sequence analysis revealed the close relationship between the StPT3 protein and other members of the plant Pht1 family and high-affinity Pi transporters of fungal origin (Rausch et al. 2001). Biochemical evidence for the function of StPT3 was obtained by complementation of a yeast mutant defective in the two high-affinity Pi transporter genes PHO84 and PHO89. Pi uptake mediated by StPT3 in the mutant yeast cells followed Michaelis–Menten kinetics, exhibiting an apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value of $6 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ (Rausch et al. 2001). In accordance with previous work (Daram et al. 1998) it was concluded that StPT3 functions as a high-affinity Pi transporter at the plasma membrane. StPT3 expression was shown to be locally induced upon colonisation by the AM fungus $G$ . intraradices and mRNA levels correlated with arbuscule formation in the roots. Additionally, in situ hybridisation studies resulted in $S t P T 3 \ \mathrm { m R N A }$ labelling in arbuscule-containing cells, which is consistent with the presumed function of StPT3 as a mycorrhiza-inducible Pi transporter localised at the periarbuscular membrane.

StPT1 mRNA levels were high in non-mycorrhizal roots, independent of the Pi fertilisation during the experiment, while StPT2 transcript amounts were reduced under high-Pi conditions. In mycorrhizal roots, StPT1 and $S t P T 2 \ \mathrm { m R N A }$ concentrations were reduced independent of the Pi treatment. A reduction in Pi-transporter mRNA levels upon AM fungal colonisation has previously been reported for MtPT1 and MtPT2 (Liu et al. 1998b; Chiou et al. 2001). The authors argued that it seems unlikely that these transporters are involved in Pi transfer at the arbuscular interface, as it is reasonable to assume that the genes encoding transport proteins involved in Pi transfer across the symbiotic interfaces will be up-regulated during the association, which was later confirmed by the identification of StPT3 in potato. Thus, the reduced mRNA levels, especially of StPT2 in potato and the MtPTs in M. truncatula, after colonisation of the root could either be due to the plant/AM fungus interaction (local), or the increased $\mathrm { P i }$ status of the root (local or systemic) or of the whole shoot (systemic), respectively (Rausch et al. 2001).

Recently, another Pi transporter, LePT1 from tomato, has been described as being involved in Pi uptake into the plant from a vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus (Rosewarne et al. 1999). While StPT3 gene expression is strongly induced due to AM fungal colonisation of the potato root, LePT1 transcript levels remained relatively constant in roots of mycorrhizal tomato plants. However, LePT1 cRNA used as a labelled probe led to the detection of signals in arbusculecontaining cortical cells in thin sections of mycorrhised roots. This reported pattern of LePT1 expression is in contrast to that of LePT1 transcript accumulation in rhizodermal cells, root hairs, root cap cells and young stelar tissue of tomato root tips under Pi deprivation (Daram et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998a). It remains to be shown whether the LePT1 gene is indeed expressed in cortical cells colonised by AM fungi or whether LePT1 cRNA cross-hybridised with transcripts of a third Pht1 gene yet to be identified in tomato.


## The Pht2 family of plant Pi transporters


Subsequent to Pi uptake at the root–soil interface, it can be expected that (at least) three additional transport systems participate in Pi translocation within the plant: (i) secretion of Pi into the root xylem; (ii) loading of leaf cells with $\mathrm { P i }$ from the vascular system; and (iii) loading of the phloem required for cycling of Pi within the plant. The first member of the Pht2 family of plant Pi transporters, ARAth;Pht2;1, (see Table 1) was cloned from an Arabidopsis cDNA library using specific primers based on mRNA sequence information from an 81-kb contig of Arabidopsis chromosome III (Quigley et al. 1996; Daram et al. 1999). The predicted Pht2;1 protein with its 12 TMs is structurally similar to the members of the Pht1 family, but distinct from them in sequence and in having a large hydrophilic loop between TM8 and TM9 (Daram et al. 1999). Interestingly, the putative polypeptide has similarities to $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -coupled Pi transporters found in $S$ . cerevisiae (PHO89; Martinez and Persson 1998), N. crassa (PHO4; Versaw and Metzenberg 1995), animals (e.g. Ram-1 and GLVR1; Kavanaugh et al. 1994), as well as to archaebacterial and eubacterial sequences (Daram et al. 1999). Despite the homologies to $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ -dependant $\mathrm { P i }$ transporters, functional analysis of the Pht2;1 protein in mutant yeast cells indicated that it is a $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { P i }$ symporter dependent on the electrochemical gradient across the plasma membrane. Its high apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for Pi $( 0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ and its preferential expression in the shoot, especially in the rosette leaves, suggests a role of Pht2;1 in $\mathrm { P i }$ transport into leaves. This is supported by the presence of relatively high transcript levels around the vascular tissue in leaves as was demonstrated by in situ hybridisation (Daram et al. 1999). Recent investigations demonstrate a chloroplastic localisation of Pht2;1 protein in Arabidopsis and an altered Pi distribution pattern in a Pht2;1 gene knock-out mutant $( p h t 2 ; I { - } I )$ dependent on the availability of Pi to the plant (Ferro et al. 2002; Versaw and Harrison 2002). An unrooted phylogenetic tree shows the relationship between ARAth;Pht2;1, its orthologous protein, MEScry;Pht2;1, from Mesembryanthemum crystallinum and similar Pi-transporter proteins from different kingdoms in relation to several Pht1 proteins (Fig. 1). It shows that the plant Pht2 transporters ARAth;Pht2;1 and MEScry;Pht2;1 are more closely related to the putative Pi transporters from bacteria, C. elegans and the $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { { P i } } }$ symporters characterised from both mammals and fungi than to the plant Pht1 transporters and the yeast $\mathrm { H ^ { \mp } / P i }$ symporter PHO84. The structurally close relationship between the plant Pht2 transporters and the putative bacterial Pi transporters together with the chloroplastic localisation of ARAth;Pht2;1 (Versaw and Harrison 2002) stay in accordance with the proposed endosymbiotic origin of plant chloroplasts. Sequence similarities between Arabidopsis Pht2;1 and translated sequences from cyanobacterial genomes (e.g. Nostoc sp. and Anabaena sp.) further strengthen this argument.


## The Pht3 family of plant Pi transporters in mitochondria


Sequence analysis of the first cloned putative mitochondrial Pi transporters from plants (Kiiskinen et al. 1997; Takabatake et al. 1999) in addition to the results of genome and EST sequencing attempts allowed the proposal to be put forward that there is a third family (Pht3) of Pi transporter genes in plants, the members of which are highly conserved within the mitochondrial transporter family. ## The Pi translocator (PT) family in chloroplasts


All proteins of the four different PT groups identified so far (TPT, PPT, GPT and XPT) are highly hydrophobic and contain information for the integration of the protein into the inner envelope membrane. The proteins contain about six to eight hydrophobic domains (Eicks et al. 2002), which are assumed to form transmembrane $\mathscr { X }$ -helices. The PTs are thought to act as dimers, and may therefore belong to the group of translocators with a $6 + 6$ helix folding pattern (Flu¨ gge 1999).
