PHT1;1 protein stability and plasma membrane abundance in Arabidopsis.As members of the Sorting Nexin family, SNX2a and SNX2b function with SNX1 in plant cellular endosomal trafficking through forming homodimers or heterodimers (Pourcher et al., 2010).Whether SNX2a and SNX2b play a role in plant Pi uptake and PSR remains unknown. Our results showed that snx2a-2 and snx2b-1 mutants had similar anthocyanin accumulation and Pi content to wild-type plants when subjected to sufficient or deficient Pi (Figure S4),revealing that SNX2a or SNX2b is not necessary for plant Pi uptake.

In the present study,we showed that SNX1 is a negative modulator of Pi uptake by facilitating PHT1;1 protein degradation in Arabidopsis. How plants modulate SNX1- mediated PHT1;1 protein degradation under different Pi conditions remains unclear.We examined the expression of SNX1 in plant seedlings treated with sufficient or deficient Pi by qRT-PCR,and found that low Pi treatment significantly downregulated SNX1 expression,consistent with increased PHT1;1 protein stability in low Pi-treated plants. To investigate whether this low Pi-repressed SNX1 expression is mediated by PHR1,the master transcription factor in plant low Pi signaling,we assayed SNX1 expression in wild-type and phr1 mutant plants. Our result showed that the phr1 mutant had comparable levels of SNX1 expression to the wild type (Figure S5)，revealing that SNX1 expression is not affected by PHR1. How plants modulate SNX1 expression to fine-tune PHT1;1 protein stability remains elusive,and extensive experiments are required to explore the underlying mechanism.We speculate that identification of the upstream factors of SNX1 may shed more light on how plants coordinate mechanisms to increase and reduce Pi uptake under different Pi availabilities.

Endosomal traficking controls the localization,degradation,storage,or reutilization of membrane proteins,thus playing a fundamental role in plant membrane protein turnover and responses to environmental stimuli.ALiX in Arabidopsis interacts with the ESCRT-Il component SNF7 and mediates PHT1;1 trafficking from the plasma membrane to the vacuole for degradation through MVBs. Thus, the alix mutant displays reduced vacuolar degradation of PHT1;1 and increased Pi content compared to wild-type plants.Similar to the alix mutant,our study showed that the snx1-2 mutant also has increased PHT1;1 stability and Pi content,raising the possibility that SNX1 acts upstream of ALIX in the endosomal trafficking of PHT1;1 as SNX1 acts in the sorting center for protein trafficking.We speculated that the cytoplasmic PHT1;1 protein is recognized by SNX1 via their interaction,subsequently sorted into ALIXassociated MVBs,and finally degraded in the vacuole in the plant response to sufficient Pi.

In addition to PHT1;1，a series of proteins have been identified as ALIX cargos，including the ABA receptor PYL4/RCAR10 and the brassinosteroid receptor brassinosteroid-insensitive 1，which are modulated by ALIX-mediatedvacuolardegradation(Cardona-Lopez et al., 2015; Garcia-Leon et al., 2019). Thus,alix null mutation can retard plant growth and even result in lethality,in contrast to the snx1-2 mutant,which exhibits relatively normal growth and development, suggesting that ALIX and SNX1 have common as well as different target cargos involved in plant growth and stress responses.The complicated relationship between SNX1-mediated protein sorting and ALIX-mediated protein degradation in diverse plant biological processes remains to be further experimentally elucidated.

It has been reported that the microtubule-associated protein CLASP interacts with SNX1 to mediate an association between endosomes and microtubules; clasp-1 mutant plants exhibit enhancedPlN2 degradation (Ambrose et al., 2013)，indicating that CLASP represses PIN2 degradation via SNX1. Another previous report also documented that both BLOC-1 complex components BLOS1 and BLOS2 interact with SNX1 on sorting endosomes and that BLOS1 knockdown lines exhibit increased PIN2 protein levels (Cui et al., 2010),revealing that BLOS1 promotes PIN2 degradation via SNX1. These reports imply that SNX1 lies at the switch point of the two routes, retrograde transport for protein recycling and protein vacuolar degradation (Cui et al.,2010). The present study demonstrates that SNX1 negatively modulates plant Pi uptake under Pi deficiency by sorting PHT1;1 into endosomes for vacuolar degradation，suggesting the possible involvement of BLOS1 in SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation in plants.Unraveling the role of BLOS1 in the plant response to limited Pi conditions shall shed more light on how SNX1 functions in Pi uptake through modulating PHT1;1 protein stability. Previous reports also showed that SNX1 facilitates iron acquisition by suppressing IRT1 degradation and increasing its plasma membrane localization (Brumbarova & lvanov,2016; lvanov et al.,2014). Considering the antagonistic interaction between iron and P in plantnutritionacquisition， wewonderedwhether increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant was partially due to altered iron uptake. However,we noticed that compared to wild-type plants, the snx1-2 mutant has similar ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under ironsufficient conditions and lower ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under iron-deficient conditions (lvanov et al.,2014). Thus,we speculate that increased Pi uptake in the snx1-2 mutant is independent of IRT1 under low Pi but suficient iron conditions. In addition,these reports show distinct effcts of SNX1 on its targets， suggesting that SNX1 differentially affects sorting and stability of the target proteins in an environmental stimuli-dependent manner via complicated mechanisms.

We previously reported that SNX1 functions in plant salt stress tolerance by affecting NO accumulation and the activities of antioxidant enzymes (Li et al., 2018). It is widely reported that NO significantly affects plant root development and responses to environmental stresses by inhibiting primary root elongation but promoting lateral root and root hair development in plants (Lombardo et al.,20o6; Schlicht et al.,2013),similar to the effect of low Pi on plant root architecture (Liu et al., 2009,2017),suggesting a possible role of NO in the plant response to low Pi conditions.

A recent study documented that low Pi restrains SNX1 accumulation in the cytoplasm but stimulates its plasma membrane localization in a PA-dependent manner (Lin et al.,2020). Combined with our observations,we further speculated that under sufficient Pi,SNX1 interacts with PHT1;1 in cytosolic vesicles to promote its protein degradation, thereby reducing root Pi uptake,while low Pi facilitates SNX1 localization at the plasma membrane in a PAdependent manner and also represses SNX1 expression, thus relieving SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation and increasing root Pi uptake.

Phosphorous (P) is an essential plant macronutrient for life cell growth and development. However, the assimilable inorganic phosphate (Pi) form of $\mathrm { P }$ for plants is often limited in the soil due to its low mobility in the soil solution and its rapid conversion to organic forms (Marschner 1995). Hence, Pi is often a limiting factor for plant growth in both natural and agricultural ecosystems (OropezaAburto et al. 2012). Although fertilizer application has increased crop productivity by $30 \mathrm { - } 5 0 ~ \%$ , its manufacture is an energy-intensive process. Moreover, over-application of fertilizers leads to runoff and pollution of waterways, causing a host of environmental problems. One approach to reducing the application of fertilizers in agriculture is to optimize their efficient use by crop plants (Holford 1997; Raghothama 1999; Yang and Finnegan 2010; Secco et al. 2012).

Phosphate starvation response 1 (PHR1), a key transcriptional regulator of Pi starvation responses (Rubio et al. 2001; Bari et al. 2006; Bustos et al. 2010), directly regulates the expression of IPS1, a non-coding RNA that mimics the target of miR399 to block the cleavage of PHO2 under Pi-deficient conditions (Franco-Zorrilla et al. 2007). PHO2 functions as an ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzyme (UBC24) and modulates Pi acquisition by regulating the abundance of phosphate transporter 1s (PHT1s) in the secretory pathway destined for plasma membranes (Huang et al. 2013). The RING-type ubiquitin E3 ligase nitrogen limitation adaptation (NLA), as the target of miR827, recruits PHO2 for the degradation of Pi transporters in the cellular Pi homeostasis process (Kant et al. 2011; Lin et al. 2013; Park et al. 2014). In the Pi-starvation signaling pathway, PHR1 is sumoylated by an SIZ1-dependent mechanism (Miura et al. 2005). SIZ1 is a plant small ubiquitinlike modifier (SUMO) E3 ligase that is a focal controller of Pi-starvation-dependent responses. In addition, the function of PHR proteins is suppressed by SPX (SYG/PHO81/ XPR1)-domain proteins, which are involved in plant Pi homeostasis (Wang et al. 2009a, b, 2014; Liu et al. 2010; Shi et al. 2014; Lv et al. 2014). In Arabidopsis, AtPHR1 also binds to the promoters of SULTR1;3 and SULTR3;4, regulating shoot-to-root flux of sulfate upon phosphate starvation (Rouached et al. 2011).

Pi uptake across the plant is mediated by Pi transporters belonging to the phosphate transporter 1 (PHT1) class (Poirier and Bucher 2002) of plant $\mathrm { P i / H ^ { + } }$ symporters of the major facilitator superfamily (Pao et al. 1998). In Arabidopsis, there are nine PHT1 family members and among them, PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are reported to be the major players in Pi acquisition under Pi-sufficient conditions (Shin et al. 2004). All nine Arabidopsis PHT1 genes have the P1BS cis-element motif in their promoters, and the mRNA expression of PHT1;1 is dramatically decreased in the double mutant of phr1/phl1 (Bustos et al. 2010), consistent with PHR regulation of PHT1 of expression. In rice, aside from OsPHT1;1 and OsPHT1;4, the other 11 PHT1 family members contain the P1BS motif in the promoter, and OsPHT1;2 (OsPT2) has been confirmed as a direct target of OsPHR2 (Liu et al. 2010). OsPHT1;11 and OsPHT1;13 have the P1BS motif but are arbuscular mycorrhiza-specific Pi transporters and are not involved the Pi starvation response (Paszkowski et al. 2002; Gutjahr et al. 2008; Kobae and Hata 2010; Yang et al. 2012). This finding leads to the speculation that the P1BS motif alone might not sufficient for the DNA binding of PHR proteins. In the posttranslational regulation of PHT1 proteins, phosphate transporter traffic facilitator 1 (PHF1), encoded by a downstream gene of PHR1, assists the trafficking of PHT1s to the plasma membrane (PM) (González et al. 2005; Bayle et al. 2011). Both Arabidopsis and rice phf1 mutants exhibit decreased Pi content and retarded growth (González et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2011).

We have shown that the expression of three $\mathrm { P }$ transporter genes from barley, wheat and maize are strongly induced by mycorrhizal colonisation and expressed in root cortical cells containing mycorrhizal structures. The identification of these three $\mathrm { P }$ transporters (HORvu;Pht1;8,TRIae;Pht1;myc and ZEAma;Pht1;6) increases both the number of mycorrhiza-induced P transporters and the range of plant species in which they have been found. The amino acid sequences of HORvu;Pht1;8, TRIae;Pht1;myc and ZEAma;Pht1;6 can be processed to determine the 3D topology of the proteins. All three $\mathrm { P }$ transporters conform to the Pht1 family topology of 12 hydrophobic membrane-spanning regions divided into two groups of six by a large intracellular hydrophilic charged domain (not shown). This topology is typical of the members of the major facilitator super family (Marger and Saier 1993; Smith et al. 1999).

The findings add to the growing body of evidence that AM host plants have P transporters that are increased in expression when plants are colonised by AM fungi. The role of these transporters is likely to be scavenging $\mathrm { P }$ from the cortical apoplast surrounding mycorrhizal structures. Specificity of these transporters appears variable and the relevance of specificity not yet clear. The potato transporter SOLtu;Pht1;3 (StPT3) was first thought to be specifically induced in mycorrhizal roots (Rausch et al. 2001), but has now been shown by RTPCR to be expressed at a low level in potato shoots (Karandashov et al. 2004). LYCes;Pht1;1 is not upregulated in mycorrhizal roots at the tissue level, but expression does appear to be relocated from epidermis to cells containing arbuscules (Rosewarne et al. 1999).

The expression patterns of HORvu;Pht1;1 andHOR$\nu u ; P h t I , 2$ shown here confirm previous results and support the suggestion that these P transporters are involved with Pi acquisition directly from the soil and mobilisation in roots (Schu¨ nmann et al. 2004; Smith et al. 1999). Reduced expression of $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; I$ and $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; 2$ in roots of plants colonised by AM fungi suggests that these $\mathrm { P }$ transporters are not so important when the alternative mycorrhizal P uptake pathway is activated by any of the three AM fungi tested. This hypothesis is strengthened by the localisation of transcripts in cortical cells containing mycorrhizal structures. The possibility that $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; I , H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; 2$ and $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; \delta$ are coordinately regulated in response to colonisation and that this is quantitatively related to relative importance of different $\mathrm { P }$ uptake pathways will require investigation using both physiological and molecular approaches.

We have a preliminary indication that reduced expression of $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; I$ and 1;2 is related to mycorrhizal colonisation, rather than plant $\mathrm { P }$ status because $\mathrm { P }$ concentrations in low $\mathrm { P }$ plants was similar to $\mathrm { P }$ concentrations in mycorrhizal plants, and lower than in high $\mathrm { P }$ plants. The expression patterns of the remaining $\mathrm { P }$ transporters in barley do not appear to be influenced by AM colonisation and seem unlikely to be involved in $\mathrm { P }$ acquisition from soil, but rather in remobilisation of P in different tissues including shoots (see Mudge et al. 2002; Rae et al. 2003).

The expression patterns observed for HORvu;Pht1;8 are similar to those seen with ORYsa;Pht1;11 (Glassop

2004; Paszkowski et al. 2002), SORtu;Pht1;3, LYCes;Pht1;1 and MEDtr;Pht1;4, P transporters that have previously been implicated in Pi acquisition via mycorrhizal fungi (Harrison et al. 2002; Rausch et al. 2001; Rosewarne et al. 1999). The expression patterns of TRIae;Pht1;myc and ZEAma;Pht1;6 revealed by RT-PCR and in-situ hybridisation are consistent with those observed with $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; \delta$ .

There is now some doubt about the mycorrhizaspecificity of $\mathrm { P }$ transporters previously reported to be expressed only in mycorrhizal roots (Karandashov et al. 2004). Low levels of expression of both SORtu;Pht1;3 (Rausch et al. 2001) and HORvu;Pht1;8 and ZEAma;Pht1;6 (this paper) have been detected in non-mycorrhizal tissues by real-time RT-PCR. In fact MEDtr;Pht1;4 (Harrison et al. 2002; Karandashov et al. 2003) and $O R Y s a ; P h t I ; I I$ (Paszkowski et al. 2002) appear to be the only $\mathrm { P }$ transporter genes so far identified for which ‘mycorrhiza-specificity’ (demonstrated by real-time RT-PCR) seems in any way certain. The sensitivity and stringency of methods of detection are clearly crucial.

Molecular and physiological evidence indicating that mycorrhizal colonisation results in marked changes in $\mathrm { P }$ uptake pathways is strengthening. The changes not only involve up-regulation of mycorrhiza-inducible $\mathrm { P }$ transporters, but also changes in the site of expression of $\mathrm { P }$ transporters from non-mycorrhizal root cells to cells containing mycorrhizal structures (Harrison et al. 2002; Rosewarne et al. 1999) and down-regulation of genes normally expressed in epidermal cells and root hairs in the ‘direct’ root uptake pathway. Furthermore, active uptake of P across the periarbuscular membrane (PBM) requires proton motive force generated by $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ ATPases, in addition to activity of $\mathrm { P }$ transporters (GianinazziPearson et al. 2000). Demonstration of specific localisation of gene expression and immunolocalisation of protein in mycorrhizal cortical cells containing arbuscules adds significantly to the evidence for arbuscules as a key site for $\mathrm { P }$ transfer from AM fungi to plants (GianinazziPearson et al. 1991, 2000). Intracellular hyphal coils have also been implicated in $\mathrm { P }$ transfer from fungus to plant (Cavagnaro et al. 2001; Smith et al. 2004) and is strongly supported by the localised expression of $S O R t u ; P h t I ; 3$ associated with coils formed by Gigaspora margarita in roots of potato (Karandashov et al. 2004). Expression of HORvu;Pht1;8, TRIae;Pht1;myc (as shown here) and ORYsa;Pht1;11 (Glassop 2004) in cortical cells colonised by S. calospora also suggests that the arbusculate coils produced by this fungus may also be a site of $\mathrm { P }$ transfer. More work in the form of immunolocalisation would provide strong evidence to support this hypothesis.

The physiological and molecular changes resulting in operation of the ‘mycorrhizal uptake pathway’ occur not only in mycorrhiza-responsive plants such as medic, but also in the less responsive tomato and in cereals (as shown here). The changes in $\mathrm { P }$ transporter gene expression are in line with the physiological demonstration that the mycorrhizal network in soil can supply up to $1 0 0 \%$ of the $\mathrm { P }$ acquired both responsive medic and unresponsive tomato (Smith et al. 2003, 2004), as well making a major contribution to non-responsive barley (Zhu et al. 2003). These results imply not only up-regulation of the mycorrhizal $\mathrm { P }$ uptake pathway (mediated by mycorrhiza-induced $\mathrm { P }$ transporters in cortical cells) but also down-regulation of direct uptake via epidermal cells.

Understanding how the two pathways of $\mathrm { P }$ uptake work in combination to maximise $\mathrm { P }$ acquisition will help determine how soil $\mathrm { P }$ and $\mathrm { P }$ fertilisers are used by plants and how to maximise the roles of AM fungi. It already seems unlikely that genetic engineering to increase expression of $\mathrm { P }$ transporters in root epidermis and roots hairs will increase $\mathrm { P }$ acquisition from soil because overexpression of $H O R \nu u ; P h t I ; I$ had no effect on $\mathrm { P }$ uptake by barley from soil (Rae et al. 2004). Of key importance will be the determination of which $\mathrm { P }$ transporters are active in field-grown plants, including those that are influenced by AM fungi and proceed to determine the signals that regulate their expression.

## Activity and overall structure of SUC1


To examine the transport mechanism of SUCs, we screened a range of SUC transporters and identified that A. thaliana SUC1 is stable and well expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Extended Data Fig. 2a–d). In oocyte uptake assays, SUC1 shows robust uptake of sucrose with an apparent Michaelis constant $( K _ { \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \mathsf { a p p } } )$ of $1 . 2 8 \mathsf { m M }$ (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 3a), comparable with previous results6,34. Purified SUC1 protein was reconstituted into liposomes and transport was measured using capacitive coupling by solid supported membrane (SSM) electrophysiology. This showed a similar robust but low affinity for sucrose in vitro, with a $K _ { \mathfrak { m } } ^ { \mathsf { a p p } }$ (SSM-based electrophysiology assays in Methods) of $1 9 \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathsf { p H } 5 . 5$ (Fig. 1b). We found a strong pH dependence, with transport being stimulated by increased proton concentration in vivo and with a functional optimum in vitro at symmetrical $\mathsf { p H } 5 . 5$ (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

We proceeded to solve the structure of SUC1 using crystallography at $2 . 7 \mathring { \mathsf { A } }$ resolution (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 2a–d). In the asymmetrical unit, SUC1 forms a non-physiological inverted dimer, with both monomers in the same conformation (root mean square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of Cɑ atoms $= 0 . 1 \mathring \mathrm { A } \big )$ ). Excellent map density allowed the construction of a final atomic model containing residues 25–500 (of 513 residues) with a free $R$ factor $( R _ { \mathrm { f r e e } } )$ of $2 9 . 3 \%$ (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 1). Overall, SUC1 adopts the canonical MFS transporter fold with twelve transmembrane helices arranged into two pseudosymmetrical halves consisting of two six-helix domains, the N-terminal domain (N domain, M1–M6) and C-terminal domain (C domain, M7–M12) (Fig. 1d,e). The two domains are connected by a short cytoplasmic linker region of 26 residues, which are well defined in the experimental map. Of note, the cytoplasmic linker contains a 9 residue amphipathic ɑ-helix (named intracellular helical region (IHR)) (Fig. 1c–e and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5a,b). Extracellularly, a short helical region (named extracellular helical region (EHR)), which also has clear amphipathic properties, is present in the loop connection between M5 and M6. The EHR is anchored to the side of the N domain by a disulfide bridge between the strictly conserved residues Cys216 and Cys220 (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Figs. 4, 5a,c and 6). We explored the roles of the IHR and EHR by mutagenesis and found that transport activity in oocytes appears indifferent to mutagenesis of the hydrophobic residues in the IHR (Extended Data Fig. 5b,d). However, the EHR at the extracellular side is very sensitive to changes. Disrupting the short EHR–M6 link by mutating Cys216 of the disulfide bridge results in loss of transport. Mutation of the three residues (Leu204, Met207 and Phe208) of the EHR, which appear buried in the membrane leaflet, to polar serine residues gives a similar loss of transport, implying an important role during transport for this extracellular region (Extended Data Fig. 5e).

The structure captures SUC1 in an outward open conformation with a conserved electrostatic network between the N and C domains at the cytosolic side (Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7). A large and clearly defined V-shaped cavity, which spans approximately two thirds of the membrane plane between the N and C domain, is open to the extracellular side (Fig. 2a). Overall, the cavity is electronegative, but it becomes electropositive towards the enclosing bottom. Despite the presence of sucrose during crystallization, no defined density for sucrose binding can be observed in the cavity.


## The proton-binding site of SUC1


The active transport of sucrose by SUC1 is proton driven and sensitive to the proton uncoupler carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazone in oocyte assays (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In transporters, acidic residues buried in the transmembrane region are generally essential for proton transport35. In the transmembrane domains of SUC1, the only acidic residue is Asp152(M4), which is strictly conserved in SUCs and therefore the prime candidate as the proton donor/acceptor residue during symport (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Figs. 1 and 6). Asp152 is exposed to the cavity solvent without any close contacts to other residues (Fig. 2b). Mutating Asp152 to an asparagine resulted in loss of transport activity without affecting plasma membrane localization in vivo (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 9). As expected, this mutant also disrupts the current response otherwise observed for wild-type SUC1 in liposomes, supporting its key role as the central proton donor/acceptor (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 8b). Another general requirement for transmembrane proton translocation is $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { a } }$ control of the proton donor/acceptor, which is often mediated by a positively charged residue35–38. However, there are no obvious candidates for this function in the outward open state of SUC1.

To obtain an inward-facing state, we tried to use different artificial intelligence (AI)-based protein structure prediction tools, but obtained only outward-facing conformations similar to our experimental structure (r.m.s.d. of Cɑ 1.6–2.5 Å). However, in the structure, we identified a network of salt bridges between the N and C domain at the intracellular side that stabilizes the outward open state (Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7a). Disrupting these interactions led to inactive or greatly diminished transport activity (Extended Data Fig. 7b). We inferred that the protein had been stabilized in the inward-facing state by these mutations, and used this information to guide an AI-based protein structure prediction tool to generate the inward open conformation (Extended Data Fig. 7a)39,40. Based on this inward open conformation prediction, we suggest that the strictly conserved Gln50(M1) is the probable candidate to control the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { a } }$ of Asp152 (Extended Data Fig. 7c). Despite being $8 . 2 \mathring { \mathsf { A } }$ away from aspartate in the structure, Gln50 shifted by movements of M1 to make hydrogen bonds to the Asp152 in the predicted inward open model (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 7c). Substituting Gln50 to alanine led to loss of transport activity, comparable in magnitude to D152N in oocytes (Fig. 2c). Mutating other residues in the vicinity either did not display any reduced transport activity (Cys74) or showed a somewhat reduced transport activity (Ser78 or Gln456), except for the substitution of Trp47, which led to loss of transport comparable to the Q50A mutant (Fig. 2c). In addition, similar to the D152N mutant, the Q50A mutant also showed the same loss of current response and pH dependence compared with wild-type SUC1 in liposomes (Fig. 2d). Based on this, we propose that Asp152 is the proton acceptor/donor responsible for proton translocation during symport that may involve Gln50 for controlling $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { a } }$ changes in the proton site.


## Sucrose binding is coupled to protonation


From here we focused our interest towards the sucrose binding site located in the V-shaped cavity. There are clearly a range of residues from both the N and C domain in the cavity and close to the proton site that could participate in sucrose binding (Fig. 3a).

To assess the binding mode of sucrose and the functional roles of the residues in the central binding pocket, MD simulations with a sucrose molecule were performed to identify a stable binding pose of sucrose. We performed ten and five independent simulations of ${ \tilde { \mathbf { \Gamma } } } ^ { 1 \mu \mathbf { s } }$ each $( 1 4 . 3 \mu s$ in total) on SUC1 with either a protonated Asp152 (Asp152(H)) or a deprotonated Asp152 (Asp152(−)) and a sucrose placed in the MelB-inspired pose. In all repeats, the protein showed a stable behaviour (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b).

Most of these simulations did not capture a static sucrose binding pose and sucrose would move freely around the cavity. However, in one of the repeats with Asp152(H), the glucosyl moiety of the sucrose stabilized in a static pose towards the N domain for over 1,050 ns (Extended Data Fig. 10c). To examine whether this pose resembles a stable initial binding event of the sucrose molecule, and if this is dependent on

Asp152 being protonated, five new simulations with Asp152(H) or Asp152(−) (10.6 µs in total) were performed with sucrose placed in this new binding position (Extended Data Fig. 10d). In four of five repeats with Asp152(H), the sucrose maintained a stable binding pose, whereas it was readily and rapidly released in the Asp152 $( - )$ repeats (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 10e). Also, in the repeats with Asp152(H), the sucrose would return to the identified binding pose after a dissociation event. Mapping the contacts from the independent simulations shows that, in this initial stable binding pose, sucrose interacts specifically and directly with its glucosyl moiety at the Asp152(H) and residues Trp47, Gly75, Asn155 and Asn156 (Fig. 3c–e and Extended Data Fig. 10d). The contact analysis shows clearly that there are no other binding sites that are remotely comparable in scale. The contact map shows that hydrogen bonds are formed with the glucosyl hydroxyls at positions O2, O3 and O4, and this confers substrate recognition. In addition, hydrophobic interactions contribute to binding with the glucosyl and, to some extent, also the fructosyl initially. Altogether, the simulations pinpoint the glucosyl group of sucrose as the trigger of the initial binding event, creating initial selectivity, and hence suggest that a Asp152(H) is crucial for stabilizing sucrose binding directly within the transporter.


## Sucrose binding requires initial glucosyl moiety recognition


To test the interactions suggested by MD and probe their functional importance for transport, we next determined the biochemical characterizations of the proposed residues and other residues lining the cavity (Fig. 3a,d–f). Our results confirm that the residues predicted to be central for initial binding are essential for transport. Mutating Asn156 led to complete loss of transport in oocytes, consistent with its prominent role in coordinating the glucose part of sucrose (Fig. 3f). For the glucosyl moiety, the contact map also identified the backbone of Gly75, as well as the side chains of Trp47 and Asp152(H), leading to loss of transport activity when mutated (Fig. 2c). For the fructosyl contacts identified, mutagenesis of Asn155 had little apparent effect on transport activity, indicating the hydrogen bond to this residue, and any specific interactions to the fructosyl moiety in the initial binding pose, is of less importance for overall transport. For the other contacts identified, mutation of Gln159 had no effect, whereas mutating Asn449 eliminates transport (Fig. 3c,f). We also targeted residues in the identified binding site that was close to, but not yet engaged in, sucrose binding (Fig. 3a). Mutation of the polar residues Gln83 and Thr290 had no negative effects, whereas mutating the polar residues Gln44, Ser431 and Gln456 substantially reduced transport (Fig. 3f). In addition, mutagenesis of the hydrophobic residues Phe184, Trp294, Phe298, Phe423, Phe427 or Ile452 likewise reduced transport (Fig. 3f). Of interest, mutation of Arg163 or Met188 led to complete loss of transport, similar to Asn449 which is also located at the bottom of the cavity, together indicating a role for these three residues in the fully occluded state (Fig. 3f). Together, these data support that the stable sucrose binding pose observed in the MD simulations of protonated SUC1 represent an initial binding event. Initial substrate recognition by SUC1 is focused on hydrogen bonds to the glucosyl moiety, whereas other residues constituting the central binding pocket have roles in later stages of the transport cycle.

To further support these results, we tested the substrate specificity of SUC1 with a wide range of different putative ligands, using both oocyte assays and SSM-based electrophysiology (Fig. 4a–c). We tested molecules both with and without a glucosyl and found that a glucosyl moiety is a required asset for substrates, whereas the fructosyl moiety can be substituted more readily with cyclic groups that have partial polar properties (Fig. 4). These results are consistent with the binding model that SUC1 interacts with the glucose unit of the sucrose in the initial stable binding pose, and that specific recognition of the fructose unit is less important for transport activity.

SUTs can be grouped into three types or subfamilies (see Fig. 1). The transport function and substrate specificity of a number of type I and type II SUTs has been studied in detail (Boorer et al. 1996; Carpaneto et al. 2005; Chandran et al. 2003; Reinders et al. 2006; Sivitz et al. 2005, 2007). Type I and II SUTs are plasma membrane-localized sucrose uptake transporters with roles in phloem loading or loading of sucrose into sink tissues (Gottwald et al. 2000; Sivitz et al. 2008; Weschke et al. 2000). Much less is currently known about type III SUTs. We tested several type III SUTs by expression in oocytes and TEVC, a technique that depends on localization of the transporter in the plasma membrane. AtSUT4, OsSUT2, and HvSUT2 did not produce large enough sucrose-dependent inward currents for analysis (data not shown). In plants, AtSUT4, HvSUT2 (Endler et al. 2006) and LjSUT4 (Figs. 6, 7) are localized to the vacuole. Therefore, the successful analysis of LjSUT4 by TEVC was due to the fortuitous mislocalization of LjSUT4 to the plasma membrane in oocytes. Similarly, AtSUT4 mislocalization to the plasma membrane in yeast allowed analysis of that transporter (Weise et al. 2000).

Addition of sucrose to LjSUT4-expressing oocytes induced inward currents, indicating the co-transport of a coupling cation. This was further investigated by replacing the sodium and/or potassium in the bath solution. In either case sucrose transport remained unchanged, suggesting that the coupling ion is indeed a proton and not a sodium or potassium ion (Fig. 3a). In addition, sucrose induced membrane depolarization in LjSUT4-expressing oocytes and $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C } .$ -sucrose uptake was sensitive to the protonophore CCCP. This indicates that the proton electrochemical gradient drives sucrose uptake and that LjSUT4 does not function as a sucrose-activated proton channel.

As for most SUTs described, the transport activity of LjSUT4 is pH-dependent, with the highest transport rates at the lowest $\mathrm { p H }$ tested $\mathrm { \Phi _ { p H } } 5 . 0$ ; Fig. 4). In addition, the kinetic properties of LjSUT4 were investigated and the apparent affinity determined at three different $\mathrm { p H }$ values, pH 5.0, 5.3 and 5.6. Based on these experiments, LjSUT4 is a low affinity SUT, similar to AtSUT4 (Weise et al. 2000), with a $K _ { 0 . 5 }$ of $1 2 . 9 \pm 2 . 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathrm { p H } ~ 5 . 0$ $1 6 . 4 \pm 4 . 2 \ \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 3$ and $2 0 . 9 9 \pm 1 . 9 6 \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 6$ (Fig. 4).

LjSUT4 was found to be less selective than type II SUTs but not as unspecific as type I SUTs. Like AtSUC2, a type I SUT previously described (Chandran et al. 2003), LjSUT4 transports both $\varnothing$ - and $\beta$ -linked glucosides, with a preference for $\mathscr { X }$ -linked glucosides. However, unlike AtSUC2,

LjSUT4 does not transport arbutin. In that respect it resembles more closely the type II SUTs HvSUT1 and ShSUT1 (Reinders et al. 2006; Sivitz et al. 2005). These results indicate that type III SUTs have a unique substrate specificity that is intermediate between types I and II.

Our data are consistent with LjSUT4 being a protoncoupled symporter. LjSUT4 therefore had the same transport mechanism as was found for AtSUT4 (Weise et al. 2000) and all other SUTs analyzed to date, with the exception of PsSUF4. The closely related pea sucrose transporter PsSUF4 was described as an uncoupled facilitator (Zhou et al. 2007). It should be pointed out that in that study a different heterologous system was used and coupling was not measured directly. It is certainly possible that some type III SUTs have different transport mechanisms. At this time it is not known what residues constitute the substrate binding-site for either sucrose or protons. It is conceivable that small changes to the protein sequence could change the coupling mechanism. This was found to be the case for the human glucose transporter hSGLT1 where a change of one amino acid residue changed the transporter from a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ /glucose symporter to a glucosegated proton channel (Quick et al. 2001).

There has also been some discussion about the subcellular localization of type III SUTs. While the type III SUT LeSUT4 from tomato was localized to the plasma membrane of sieve elements (Weise et al. 2000), it has recently been shown that the type III SUTs from barley, HvSUT2 and from Arabidopsis, AtSUT4, are present in the vacuole membrane (Endler et al. 2006). For another Solanaceous species, potato, it has been shown that its type III SUT, StSUT4, is localized to the plasma membrane when expressed as a GFP-fusion protein in tobacco or potato epidermis cells. Interestingly, StSUT4-GFP was also detected in a perinuclear ring in these samples (Chincinska et al. 2008). In the same study, using an antibody raised against an StSUT4-specific peptide the protein was only detected in the plasma membrane fraction. In our study we show that even though LjSUT4 is functional on the plasma membrane of Xenopus oocytes as evidenced by our TEVC results, it localizes to the vacuole membrane in plant cells (Figs. 6 and 7). Mistargeting of plant vacuole membrane proteins to the plasma membrane in Xenopus oocytes is not uncommon (see for example Maurel et al. 1993). It is also possible that the type III subfamily contains proteins that localize to either the plasma membrane or the vacuole membrane. Specific sequences for vacuolar targeting have been identified for some proteins but there does not seem to be any general consensus sequence that is present in all vacuolar proteins.

Figure 8 shows a model for the proposed function of LjSUT4 in plant cells. Based on the localization data and the transport mechanism determined by TEVC we propose that LjSUT4 functions in sucrose uptake into the cytoplasm, i.e. sucrose uptake from the vacuole. This activity is different from the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /sucrose antiporter that conducts sucrose uptake into the vacuole (Briskin et al. 1985; Greutert and Keller 1993) and is a novel function for a SUT. A similar transport mechanism has been suggested for both AtSUT4 and HvSUT2 based on their membrane localization (Neuhaus 2007). The in planta physiological role of LjSUT4 as a sucrose exporter from the vacuole remains to be determined. Since LjSUT4 was able to transport a number of glucosides besides sucrose it is interesting to speculate that LjSUT4 may have a role in exporting glucose-conjugates from the vacuole into the cytoplasm. Many plant glucosides are accumulated in the vacuole. For example, the aroma compound 2-phenylethanol is produced in flowers and fruit (Hayashi et al. 2004; Tieman et al. 2007) and is found in a glucosylated form (2-phenylethyl- $\boldsymbol { \cdot } \beta$ -D-glucopyranoside). Flavonoid-glucosides in Arabidopsis are transported into the vacuole by TT12 using a $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled antiporter mechanism (Marinova et al. 2007). Less is known concerning the mechanism of glucoside transport from the vacuole into the cytoplasm although there is some evidence for regulation of vacuolar efflux of phenylpropanoid glycoconjugates during defense responses (Farag et al. 2008). Since LjSUT4 was shown to transport a range of glucosides, it may serve an important role in a variety of pathways.

The only report of the effect of loss-of-function of a type III SUT is from potato. In that case, RNA-interferenceinactivation of the type III SUT StSUT4 resulted in early flowering and increased tuber yield (Chincinska et al. 2008). However, unlike LjSUT4, StSUT4 does not seem to be a vacuolar transporter. No loss-of-function mutant of a vacuolar SUT has been described to date.

LjSUT4-expression has previously been shown to be induced in maturing nodules (14 dpi; Flemetakis et al. 2003) where the mRNA was localized both in the central and the peripheral tissue. In the legume-Rhizobium symbiosis the plant supplies the bacteroids with photosynthetic carbon in the form of malate (Rosendahl et al. 1990). Sucrose is the main transport form of carbon for the plant, and nodules from $L .$ . japonicus have been shown to contain large amounts of sucrose (Lopez et al. 2008). In leaves of different plant species up to $80 \%$ of the sucrose was stored inside the vacuole (Nadwodnik and Lohaus 2008). LjSUT4 may have a role in controlling sucrose release from the vacuole that is required for growth of the nodule and as a supply of carbon to the symbiont. It is somewhat surprising that sucrose release from the vacuole is coupled with protons (rather than using a channel mechanism). Although proton symport is energy dependent, this mechanism is, in theory, capable of reducing sucrose concentration in the vacuole to a lower level compared to a channel mechanism. It is also expected that LjSUT4 expression or activity is regulated to prevent a futile cycle of vacuolar sucrose transport with sucrose $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \mathrm { \left/ H \right. } \mathrm { \Omega } ^ { + } }$ antiporters. A symport mechanism for vacuolar release is novel but may also be important for other solutes that are transiently stored in vacuoles. For example, AtINT1 was recently identified as a vacuolar inositol- $\cdot \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporter and a function for AtINT1 in transport of inositol from the vacuole into the cytoplasm was suggested (Schneider et al. 2008).

Sucrose transporters (SUTs, also called SUCs) are encoded by a small gene family in plants. Arabidopsis has nine homologous SUT genes and rice has five. SUTs are integral membrane proteins with twelve transmembrane spanning domains and are part of the glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family within the major facilitator superfamily (MFS; Chang et al. 2004). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the plant SUT family can be divided into three distinct types (type I, II and III; Aoki et al. 2003; Fig. 1). By determining the substrate specificity and affinity, localization and expression pattern of members of each type of SUT, the question of whether each type has a distinct function can be addressed. Type I and II SUTs have been characterized by expression in Xenopus oocytes and two electrode voltage clamping (Boorer et al. 1996; Carpaneto et al. 2005; Chandran et al. 2003; Reinders et al. 2006; Sivitz et al. 2005, 2007; Zhou et al. 1997). Type I SUTs such as AtSUC2 (Chandran et al. 2003) and AtSUC9 (Sivitz et al. 2007) showed strong differences in substrate specificity compared to HvSUT1 (Sivitz et al. 2005) and ShSUT1 (Reinders et al. 2006). No type III SUTs have been analyzed by this method and available functional data is limited.

Based on available sequence information, one type III SUT gene is found in each eudicot as well as each monocot genome. Arabidopsis AtSUT4 (type III SUT) was expressed in yeast and found to encode a proton-coupled sucrose transporter (Weise et al. 2000). However, the type III SUT from pea (PsSUF4) was recently suggested to be a facilitator rather than a proton-coupled transporter (Zhou et al. 2007). HvSUT2 (type III from barley) and AtSUT4 were shown to localize to the plant vacuole (Endler et al. 2006). This is surprising since all other SUTs have been found in the plasma membrane. Therefore, significant uncertainty exists concerning the transport mechanism and the subcellular localization of type III SUTs.

LjSUT4 is a type III SUT from Lotus japonicus, a legume that forms a symbiotic interaction with Mesorhizobium loti. A special organ is formed during this interaction, the root nodule. The cDNA for LjSUT4 was cloned from maturing root nodules and its expression was shown to be upregulated during nodule development (Flemetakis et al. 2003). LjSUT4 expression was also found in uninfected roots and in green seedpods and hypocotyls (Flemetakis et al. 2003). No information on the transport activity or subcellular localization of LjSUT4 is known. We have expressed LjSUT4 in Xenopus oocytes and provide a detailed analysis of its transport activity. The substrate specificity is distinct from type I or II SUTs. LjSUT4 was localized to the vacuole membrane and we suggest that it functions in the proton-coupled transport of sucrose, and possibly other glucosides, from the vacuole into the cytoplasm.

Our structural analysis, functional studies and MD simulation data provide a model for how sucrose is recognized by SUC1, and identify key structural elements, such as the proton-binding site, that are required for function. The presumed proton acceptor/donor Asp152 is strictly conserved in members of the SUT/SUC family (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 6) and has been reported previously as critical for sucrose-induced transport currents of SUC1 and for the corresponding rice ortholog OsSUT1 (refs. 31,41). SUC1 displays clear differences from other known proton-coupled symporters and presents a unique model for symport. First, the direct coupling between proton site and substrate binding site. Second, Gln50 on the M1 helix that we suggest controls the $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { a } }$ of Asp152 on the M4 helix, breaking with the generic pattern of using a basic residue for this function as observed in other proton transporters14,35,42. Because of these two factors, sugar binding becomes linked directly to proton binding, allowing sugar release into an environment with very high sucrose concentration, as long as the proton dissociates. The set up suggests a tight 1:1 coupling ratio between proton and sucrose, in accordance with previously reported kinetic models34,43. Our data suggest that the protonation of Asp152 is necessary to allow a tight polar interaction from the N domain to the glucosyl moiety of the substrate.

This tight and direct coupling provides a central pivot for explaining how members of the SUT/SUC family can operate at extreme molar-level sucrose concentrations. The low affinity of SUC1 is a prerequisite for high-capacity sucrose transport and is evident from the challenges in capturing a substrate-bound state in both crystallography and MD. Nevertheless, our work suggests that initial recognition of sucrose is mediated by interactions of the glucosyl to the protonated N domain. This is in agreement with previous findings that the glucosyl hydroxyl groups are central to substrate recognition44–47. We also find that residues in both N and C domains have important roles in the central binding pocket during the full transport cycle. Changing the apoplast pH may be used in a responsive manner by the plant to regulate and optimize the transporter activity of SUC1, which is supported by the low passive buffer capacity of the apoplast51. Acidifying the apoplast when competing with sugar transporters of invasive pathogens would increase both SUC1 transport capacity and apparent affinity, while simultaneously facilitating reduction of pathogen transporter activity.

This initial low-affinity binding to the glucosyl moiety is dependent on the protonation of Asp152. After sucrose and proton binding, Arg163 and other binding pocket residues create further sucrose contacts in later stages of substrate recognition. This forms a two-step recognition scheme involving an initial glucosyl recognition site and later involvement of Arg163 in sucrose translocation, consistent with previous studies57. This recognition setup also explains the broader substrate promiscuity toward the secondary saccharide of the substrate. Although the glucosyl is relatively invariant, the fructosyl can be exchanged more readily (Fig. 4). During transporter transition, the intracellular network of salt bridges is broken, whereas, at the extracellular side, charged and polar residues probably form contacts between helices to ensure closure of the cavity from the apoplastic side and stabilization towards the inward state, as supported by predicted models and oocyte mutagenesis studies (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). After opening to the inside, $\mathsf { p } K _ { \mathrm { a } }$ changes directed by Gln50 lead to deprotonation of Asp152 to favour sucrose release.

In conclusion, our work pinpoints Asp152 as the proton-binding site in the SUT/SUC family and shows how sucrose binding, with initial recognition of the glucosyl, is achieved through a direct coupling to proton binding at this site. We identify key elements and properties of transporter function and explain a central molecular mechanism behind sugar signalling, stress responses and the central driving force behind vascular movement of sucrose and other solutes in vascular plants.

Plant sucrose transporters (SUTs) are members of the glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family (TC2.A.2) that is part of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). All plant SUTs characterized to date function as proton-coupled symporters and catalyze the cellular uptake of sucrose. SUTs are involved in loading sucrose into the phloem and sink tissues, such as seeds, roots and flowers. Because monocots are agriculturally important, SUTs from cereals have been the focus of recent research. Here we present a functional analysis of the SUT ShSUT1 from sugarcane, an important crop species grown for its ability to accumulate high amounts of sucrose in the stem. ShSUT1 was previously shown to be expressed in maturing stems and plays an important role in the accumulation of sucrose in this tissue. Using two-electrode voltage clamping in Xenopus oocytes expressing ShSUT1, we found that ShSUT1 is highly selective for sucrose, but has a relatively low affinity for sucrose $( K _ { 0 . 5 } = 8 . 2 6 \ : \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathbf { p H _ { \lambda } 5 . 6 }$ and a membrane potential of $\mathbf { - 1 3 7 m V }$ ). We also found that the sucrose analog sucralose (4,1¢,6¢-trichloro-4,1¢,6¢-trideoxygalacto-sucrose) is a competitive inhibitor of ShSUT1 with an inhibition coefficient $\mathbf { \left( K _ { i } \right) }$ of $\mathbf { 1 6 . 5 \ m M }$ . The presented data contribute to our understanding of sucrose transport in plants in general and in monocots in particular.

Sucrose is the major transported form of sugar in plants. The deposition of starch, which is the main determinant of yield in cereal crops, in seeds is dependent on the supply of this sugar molecule from source tissues through the phloem. The phloem consists of sieve elements (SE) and companion cells (CC) connected by numerous intercellular connections called plasmodesmata and form a SE-CC complex [1]. The SE is responsible for long distance transport of sucrose and other organic materials, whereas the CCs supply proteins and energy to the SEs [2,3]. Phloem loading and unloading of sucrose takes place symplastically and apoplastically. The symplastic transport involves cell to cell movement of sucrose via plasmodesmatal connections, while the apoplastic transport involves active sucrose movement across membranes via sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins [3,4], and mainly takes place in the absence of plasmodesmatal connections. Genes encoding SUTs have been identified from a number of plant species including cereal crops such as rice (Oryza sativa) [5], barley (Hordeum vulgare) [6], maize (Zea mays) [7] and wheat (Triticum aestivum) [8], and form small gene families [9]. All the plant SUTs identified to date are members of the glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family, which is part of the major facilitator superfamily characterized by 12 transmembrane spanning helices [10,11]. Furthermore, the first extracellular loop of plant SUTs contains a histidine residue, such as His-65 of the Arabidopsis SUT1 that serves as a target for diethyl pyrocarbonate (DEPC) mediated inhibition of sucrose transport activity [12]. It has been shown that this residue is substrate protected from the inhibition reaction induced by DEPC. This along with the ability of eliminating SUTs’ sensitivity to DEPC by substituting histidine with other amino acids without affecting the transport activity of SUTs indicate that the DEPC sensitive histidine residue is localized at or associated conformationally with the sucrose binding site.

Spatiotemporal expression analyses of the SUTs in cereal crops have provided insights into their physiological roles during seed development. For example, SUT1 of maize is highly expressed in leaf blades, leaf sheaths, culms, and husks and pedicels of the ear during reproductive growth of maize; and the expression of ZmSUT1 in the leaf blades was shown to increase as the level of photoassimilates increases, reflecting its role in phloem loading [7,13]. Consistent with this observation, impaired phloem loading in the zmsut1 mutant causes accumulation of carbohydrates in the leaf that led to chlorosis, senescence and reduced plant growth [14]. The three TaSUT1 homeologues, which reside on chromosome 4 of the wheat A, B and D genomes, are found to be expressed at similar levels in flag leaf blades, leaf sheaths and internodes [8], suggesting their equal roles in phloem loading of sucrose. The transcript abundance of TaSUT1 in these tissues was highest before heading and decreased immediately after flowering, when an increased level of its transcript was evident in the developing seeds. A study with symplastic fluorescein tracer has shown the lack of plasmodesmatal connections in the SE-CC complex of wheat flag leaf [15], supporting the hypothesis that TaSUT1 is involved in phloem loading of sucrose. In addition, all SUTs of rice [5,16] and the two known SUT of barley [6] are shown to be expressed in source leaves. Previous studies have also shown that non-foliar tissues of wheat florets, including the glume, lemma and palea, possess photosynthetic ability and contribute $1 0 \%$ to $4 4 \%$ of photoassimilates destined to wheat seeds [17,18]. In agreement with this, transcripts of TaSUT1 were detected in the glumes of wheat ear both before and after heading, although at lower levels than that observed in the flag leaf blades and sheaths [8], suggesting its role in phloem loading of the sucrose produced in the spike.

Leaf sheaths of cereal crops connect leaf blades to the stem nodes, thereby forming phloem conduits that serve as pathways for long distance transport of photoassimilates [15]. Along with internodes, they also act as a temporary storage of excess carbohydrates produced during the early stages of seed filling in the form of water-soluble carbohydrates, mainly fructans. Approximately $5 0 \%$ of the photoassimilates destined to seed filling in wheat appears to be temporarily stored in the leaf sheaths and internodes prior to remobilization during active seed filling, when photoassimilate supply from the leaf is not enough to meet the sink demand [19]. A role for reloading sucrose into the phloem during the remobilization process has been suggested for OsSUT1 and TaSUT1 as their transcripts are present in the leaf sheath and stem tissues of rice and wheat, respectively [5,15,16]. Given that carboxyfluorescein dye moves symplastically out of the phloem in wheat internode [15], the presence of TaSUT1 transcripts in this tissue also suggests its role in retrieving sucrose leaked out into the phloem apoplasm, and thereby providing an efficient photoassimilate translocation mechanism.

Previous studies have shown that SUT1 is highly expressed in the developing seeds of different cereal crops including rice, barley and wheat. In rice, SUT1 is expressed at similar levels from early to late stage of seed filling [20]. Consistently, antisense expression of OsSUT1 resulted in impaired seed filling and retarded germination with no effect on photosynthesis in the flag leaf [21]. The SUT1 of barley, however, exhibited its highest expression during the mid-stage of seed development. The transcripts of OsSUT1 and HvSUT1 are localized mainly in the maternal nucellar projections, aleurone tissues, and filial transfer cells that separate the endosperm cavity from the endosperm [6,20]. Furthermore, anti-OsSUT1 antibody was shown to bind to the plasma membranes of nucellar projections and aleurone tissues of developing wheat seeds [22]. As the maternal and filial tissues of cereal seeds lack symplastic connections; these results suggest the role of SUT1 in the post-phloem transport of sucrose from the maternal to the filial tissues of developing seeds.

Plant SUTs have been classified into five subfamilies, SUT1 to SUT5 [23]. Based on their significant similarity at the amino acid level, OsSUT2 and HvSUT2 are assigned to the SUT4 subfamily rather than to the monocot specific SUT3 or SUT5 subfamilies [9], and these genes are found to be expressed in both source and sink tissues [6,24]. The expression of HvSUT2 in developing seeds was relatively predominant during the earlier and later stages [6], whereas that of OsSUT2 was restricted only to the earlier stages [24]. In developing barley seeds, HvSUT2 has been shown to have almost similar cellular localization as that of HvSUT1 [6]. Recent proteomic and green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion protein studies showed that some members of the SUT4 subfamily including HvSUT2 and OsSUT2, and those derived from other species such as Arabidopsis (AtSUT4), Lotus (LjSUT4) and poplar (PtaSUT4) are localized to the vacuolar tonoplast [25-27], suggesting that these proteins are involved in vacuolar storage of sucrose and its transport across the tonoplast to the cytosol. Consistently, a knockout mutation of OsSUT2 and RNAi mediated suppression of PtaSUT4 caused accumulation of sucrose in source leaves of rice and poplar, respectively, due to a decrease in sucrose transport from the vacuolar to the cytoplasmic compartment [27,28].

Plant SUTs play important roles in the allocation of photoassimilates in the form of sucrose from the source to sink tissues, and thereby determine seed yield. Identifying and characterizing new SUTs, thus, provide insights into the regulation of sucrose transport. Although wheat is one of the most economically important crops of the world, only one wheat SUT gene has been identified and characterized to date [8]. The present study identified a new SUT, designated as TaSUT2, and its homeologous from hexaploid wheat (T. aestivum cv. AC Andrew), and determined their subcellular localization and functionality as SUTs using a yeast heterologous system. Furthermore, the total expression of TaSUT2 and the relative contribution of each of the three genomes were investigated in both source and sink tissues at different stages of development.

Sucrose transporters (SUTs) are crucial for plant growth, development, and stress responses. Despite sugarcane’s importance as a sugar and biofuel crop, genomic data on its SUT genes under abiotic stress are limited. In this study, 37 ShSUT genes were identifed through bioinformatic analysis. Phylogenetic classifcation grouped them into three major clades (I–III), with conserved motifs and gene structures supporting their evolutionary relationships. Promoter analysis revealed 15 key cis-elements related to hormone response, stress, development, and light regulation. All ShSUT genes were mapped on three contig regions and seven chromosomes. Collinearity and gene duplication analysis identifed 15 segmentally duplicated gene pairs, indicating evolutionary expansion. Additionally, 7 putative ‘sbi-miRNAs’ were predicted to target 28 ShSUT genes, with sbi-miR5381 alone targeted 17 ShSUTs. For functional characterization, ShSUT04 was chosen due to its evolutionary signifcance, crucial role in sucrose transport, and potential involvement in regulating abiotic stress responses. Eighteen potential interactors were identifed, with confrmed interactions for ShPsbR, ShRF2a, ShCOPTS.1, and ShSPT, validated through BiFC and Y2H assays. qRT-PCR analysis demonstrated stress-responsive expression patterns. Under cold stress, ShRF2a, ShPsbR, and ShSPT were down-regulated, indicating negative regulatory roles, while ShSUT04 and ShCOPT5.1 were up-regulated at specifc time points, and ShSUT01 showed strong induction, suggesting a positive role in defense. Under drought, ShSUT04 and ShPsbR showed signifcant upregulation, suggesting positive regulatory roles. In salinity stress, while several genes were suppressed, ShSUT01 and ShPsbR were induced, refecting their potential in stress adaptation. This study reveals the evolutionary and functional roles of sugarcane SUT genes in abiotic stress regulation, with ShSUT04 showing dual roles, positive under drought and negative under salinity and cold stresses.

As a major photosynthetic product, sucrose constitutes one of the primary carbohydrates, which is transported between source tissues and heterotrophic sink tissues (Lemoine 2000; Williams et al. 2000). Furthermore, as a signaling molecule, sucrose can significantly influence cellular processes of the plant, particularly with regard to metabolic activity and fruit development. Sucrose metabolism also plays a pivotal role in developmental processes, stress response, and yield formation, primarily by generating a series of sugar metabolites used for energy metabolism and the synthesizing of essential compounds, including proteins, cellulose, and starch (Kühn 2011; Ruan 2014). Sucrose transporters (SUTs) possess 12 transmembrane domains and constitute typical membrane proteins in higher plants. SUTs are responsible for sucrose transport across membranes, including phloem loading in source tissues and sucrose unloading into sink tissues (Kühn et al. 2010; Doidy et al. 2012a).

Since the first SUT gene SoSUT1 was discovered from spinach (Spinacia oleracea) (Riesmeier et al. 1992), numerous SUT genes have been identified and characterized both in dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous species (Aoki et al. 2003; Doidy et al. 2012b; Zanon et al. 2015a; Zhang et al. 2016). All the SUTs in plants can be categorized into five subfamilies (Kühn et al. 2010), of which SUT1, SUT2, and SUT4 subfamilies were identified in dicots, whereas SUT2, SUT3, SUT4, and SUT5 subfamilies were found in monocots. According to the phylogenetic analysis, SUTs were classified into three groups, including Type I, Type II (A and B), and Type III (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type I members, localized to the plasma membrane, are identified as high-affinity sucrose carriers, involving in phloem loading or sucrose import into sink cells (Gottwald et al. 2000; Sauer 2007; Slewinski et al. 2009). They have been detected across various sink organs, including tubers, pollen, flowers, and fruits, suggesting a complex role in sucrose partitioning (Kühn et al. 2010). The Type II group can be divided into two sub-groups, IIA and IIB. Type IIA contains both eudicot and monocot isoforms, whereas Type IIB only represents the monocot-specific SUTs (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type IIA members are characterized by an elongated central loop with an unclear function, and are localized to the plasma membrane, similar with Type I. Several Type IIB members are plasma membrane-localized, high-affinity, and participate in phloem loading (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type III, comprising tonoplast SUTs from both monocots and eudicots, are thought to facilitate sucrose release from vacuoles into the cytoplasm (Schneider et al. 2012; Ruan 2014). Type III SUTs are expressed in various tissues, including the veins of sink and source leaves, roots, anthers, and fruits (Weise et al. 2000; Peng et al. 2011; Zanon et al. 2015a). Furthermore, they are targeted to the plasma membrane or tonoplast depending on the plant species. Dual localization with tonoplast and plasma membrane has been reported for some Type III SUTs in certain species, such as Arabidopsis AtSUT4, potato StSUT4, tomato SlSUT4, and poplar PtaSUT4 (Chincinska et al. 2013).

Heterologous expression in yeast indicated the ability of SUT4 (AtSUT4, LjSUT4, and PpSUT4) to catalyze sucrose uptake with low affinity (Weise et al. 2000; Reinders et al. 2008; Zanon et al. 2015a). The SUT4 homologs in Arabidopsis (AtSUT4), barley (HvSUT2), Lotus Japonica (LjSUT4), and peach (PpSUT4) function as sucrose proton symporters, suggesting that they are most likely involved in the sucrose efflux from the vacuole (Neuhaus 2007; Zanon et al. 2015a). SUT4 has been found to be participated in diverse biological processes in different plant species. In potato, inhibition of the StSUT4 expression results in early flowering, tuberization, and the reducing expression of gibberellic acid and ethylene biosynthetic genes (Chincinska et al. 2008). In poplar plants, PtaSUT4-silenced results in an increased leaf-to-stem biomass ratio with the decreased translocation of sucrose to the sink organs (Payyavula et al. 2010). In pear, PbSUT2 affected sucrose content in sinks and the overexpression of PbSUT2 leads to early flowering (Wang et al. 2016). Previous study showed sucrose not only improves fruit flavor but also relevant to lipid metabolism (Cui et al. 2016). Overexpression of AtSUT2 and/or AtSUT4 in combination with diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) genes can increase seed oil production in both soybean and maize (Allen et al. 2015).

Jatropha curcas, well known as the “purging nut,” is a promising bio-energy perennial oilseed crop, in which the seeds can be processed to produce high-quality biodiesel fuel (Pereira et al. 2017). However, few transcriptome studies had mentioned the SUT genes in J. curcas (Jiang et al. 2012). Therefore, investigating the mechanism of SUTs might provide significant insight into the growth and development of J. curcas. In this study, we cloned JcSUT4 from J. curcas. JcSUT4 was mainly localized to plasma membrane and mediated the sucrose uptake by yeast complementation assay. JcSUT4 was highly expressed in mature source leaves, and gradually increased at early stages of fruit development. Our results identified the primary biological functions of JcSUT4, providing information for exploration of the mechanism that control sucrose accumulation in this bioenergy species.

Sucrose is a major product of photosynthesis in plants, and the most common form of carbohydrate transported through the phloem from source leaves to sink organs such as roots and fruits. Extensive research has been conducted in the last three decades on sucrose transport in plants and sucrose transporters (SUTs) are deemed to be essential for the export and efficient movement of sucrose from source to sink [1]. SUTs contain the typical 12 transmembrane (TM) $\alpha$ -helices of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) proteins [2–4]. Most SUTs are characterized as energy-dependent proton sucrose $\mathrm { ^ { \prime H ^ { + } } }$ symporters that utilize the proton motive force across the membrane to transport sucrose against its concentration gradient [5, 6].
