petroleum-derived synthetic rubber. Currently, ${ > } 9 8 \%$ of all natural rubber comes from one single tropical tree species – Hevea brasiliensis (para rubber tree). Rubber is synthesized in the cytoplasm (latex) of highly specialized cells called laticifers that are differentiated from the cambium and arranged in rings (d’Auzac et al. 1997; Hao & Wu 2000). After the maturation process, the laticifers in each ring anastomose together into a reticulate laticiferous network. During rubber harvesting, this ring structure facilitates the exudation of a large amount of latex in a single tapping. The latex-exploitation process consists of tapping, which involves periodically (commonly every 3 d) cutting the bark on the trunk of the tree, hence severing the laticifer rings.

Although the physiological roles of laticifers in the rubber tree remain poorly understood (Ko, Chow & Han 2003), this process has contributed to the welfare of human beings for more than a century by serving as a ‘natural green rubber factory.’ Rubber biosynthesis is the laticifer’s primary metabolic activity. Rubber usually constitutes $3 0 { - } 5 0 \%$ of the weight of fresh latex and over $9 0 \%$ of its dry weight (Jacob & Prevot 1992). The biosynthesis of rubber begins with the precursor molecule, sucrose, running through more than 20 enzymatic reactions that result in the first isoprenoid isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP), which then serves as the fundamental building block for the formation of the final high-molecular weight rubber molecule $( 1 0 ^ { 5 } -$ $1 0 ^ { 6 } \mathrm { D a } )$ ) (Sando et al. 2008). In regularly tapped rubber trees, the laticifers in the bark of the trunk represent a strong sink for sucrose, which provides the carbon skeleton and energy demands for latex regeneration (Silpi et al. 2007). Understanding the mechanisms of sucrose transport and partitioning are of fundamental importance for improving Hevea productivity (Tupy 1989). The cloning and identification of the key genes involved in the loading of sucrose into laticifers will not only facilitate the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms underlying sucrose uptake and its regulation but will also provide solid data for the rational regulation of carbon partitioning between rubberproducing sinks and other competing sinks, such as vegetative growth.

Sucrose transporters (SUT) belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS), and they have 12 typical transmembrane-spanning domains separated by a central cytoplasmic loop (Sauer 2007). To date, the majority of the identified plant SUTs are plasma membrane-localized, energy-dependent proton $\left( \mathrm { H } ^ { + } \right)$ /sucrose symporters. These symporters are responsible for apoplastically loading sucrose into cells, and play a central role in sucrose partitioning between its site of synthesis (source leaf mesophyll) and its numerous sink tissues (Sauer 2007; Braun & Slewinski 2009). In Hevea, the symplasmic isolated nature of the laticifer from its neighbouring cells (Hébant 1981) suggests that SUTs might play an active role in the transmembrane sucrose uptake by laticifers. Several pieces of evidence support this speculation. The flow of sucrose into laticifers occurs not by diffusive entry, but by an energyconsuming system (Tupy 1985). The activity of sucrose loading is also sensitive to some inhibitors and shows carrier-mediated kinetics. Other evidence comes from an electrophysiological sugar-labelling experiment, in which multiple $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } .$ -sugar symport systems with high sucrose affinity (1 mm) were found to exist in the plasma membrane of laticifers (Bouteau et al. 1999). More recently, a number of full-length cDNAs encoding putative Hevea sucrose transporters have been isolated either by degenerate RT-PCR and RACE technologies (Yang et al. 2007) or by library screening (Dusotoit-Coucaud et al. 2009), yet nothing is known about their functions in regularly exploited Hevea trees. In fact, the first set of data was only obtained from unexploited (virgin) trees (DusotoitCoucaud et al. 2009) that are characterized by very lower rubber production compared to exploited trees. In addition, these data mainly account for the effect of ethylene on the expression pattern of HbSUTs, but not for the high metabolic activity related to the combined effect of tapping and ethylene treatment. Tapping represents a serious abiotic mechanical stress for exploited trees as it consistently deeply wounds the bark causing the latex cells to completely regenerate their cytoplasm after latex expulsion. This situation creates a higher carbon demand in the laticifers of exploited trees compared to those of unexploited trees. Our preliminary results from exploited trees revealed that one SUT member, HbSUT3, was not only the predominant member expressed in the latex as compared to other SUT members but also displayed a relatively latex-specific pattern of expression (to be presented in the Results). These results prompted us to further investigate whether HbSUT3 encodes a functional sucrose transporter and plays a role in sucrose loading into the laticifer.

Here, the expression of HbSUT3 under different conditions was investigated mainly in regularly tapped trees of a metabolically active clone Reyan7-33-97 (SCATC7-33-97) (Huang et al. 1994). Using a baker’s yeast system, the functionality and sucrose uptake kinetics of HbSUT3 were determined. Our results demonstrate both the functionality of HbSUT3 and its active role in sucrose loading into the laticifer and the resultant rubber productivity.

## Expression of the SUT genes in Hevea tissues


Previously, we cloned six distinct full-length cDNAs encoding putative SUTs, viz. HbSUT1 (DQ985466), HbSUT2A (DQ985467), HbSUT2B (DQ985465), HbSUT3 (EF067334), HbSUT4 (EF067335) and HbSUT5 (EF067333) from H. brasiliensis (Yang et al. 2007). Later, Dusotoit-Coucaud et al. (2009) identified two new isoforms, HbSUT1B (AM492537) and HbSUT2C (AM491808). Sequence alignments showed that, except for the difference in the length of the untranslated regions, HbSUT1B and HbSUT3 share very high nucleotide sequence identity $( 9 9 . 2 \% )$ , demonstrating that they are the same allele from different Hevea clones. As shown in Fig. S2, except for an 83-bp-long excess sequence near the $3 ^ { \prime }$ -end of its coding regions, HbSUT2C is almost identical $( 9 9 . 6 \% )$ to HbSUT2B. In addition, the excess sequence contains the ${ 5 } ^ { \prime } .$ - and $3 \mathrm { ^ { \prime } - }$ splicing core sites (Lorkovic´ et al. 2000; Ast 2004), supporting the notion that HbSUT2C is an intron-retention splicing variant of HbSUT2B. The expression of HbSUT2C in the latex was also demonstrated in our study but was much less abundant than HbSUT2B (unpublished data). Given these results, only six distinct SUT genes can thus far be identified in H. brasiliensis.

To determine the dominant member of the Hevea SUT family in the rubber-containing cytoplasm of laticifer, i.e. the latex, the mRNA levels of different SUT genes were compared by reverse Northern blot analysis. The results showed that the expression of HbSUT3 was significantly higher than that of any other SUT genes (Fig. 1a), demonstrating that HbSUT3 is the predominant SUT member in the latex.To further study the abundance of HbSUT3 in the latex relative to that in other Hevea tissues, semiquantitative RT-PCR was used, with 18S-rRNA as internal control, to compare the expression of HbSUT3 in 12 tissues including latex, bark (trunk or green branch), bud, leaf (red young, pale-green or mature), flower (female or male), root (small or feeder) and mature seed. As shown in Fig. 1b, HbSUT3 was transcribed in all the tissues tested, suggesting a functional redundancy of this gene, but of the 12 Hevea tissues tested, it revealed a preferential expression in the latex and female flowers, suggesting its major role in these 2 tissues.

The latex-dominant expression character of HbSUT3 suggests the importance of its role in sucrose loading into the laticifer; the following studies were therefore focused on this SUT gene.


## Functional characterization of the HbSUT3 expressed in yeast


To determine whether HbSUT3 cDNA encodes a functional sucrose transporter and to understand the kinetics of its sucrose uptake, the HbSUT3 cDNA was expressed in a yeast strain (SEY6210) that carries a mutation in an invertase gene (SUC2). This strain works well for $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -sucrose uptake assays (Reinders &Ward 2001; Rae, Perroux & Grof 2005).

As shown in Fig. 2a, the full-length cDNA of HbSUT3 conferred markedly higher rates of sucrose uptake to yeast cells compared with the pDR196 empty vector alone, indicating it to be an active sucrose transporter. Under similar conditions, the potato transporter StSUT1 was used as a positive control and accumulated sucrose at a rate approximately five times greater than HbSUT3 (data not shown).

When assayed at $1 \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose, a concentration that is usually used in studying other plant SUTs, the transport activity of HbSUT3 was strongly pH-dependent, showing a $\mathrm { p H }$ optimum at approximately $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 0$ (Fig. 2b). This characteristic of the pH-dependent transport suggested that HbSUT3 mediates proton-driven sucrose uptake, which was supported by the fact that this SUT was sensitive to a protonophore (2, 4-dinitrophenol) (Table 1).

The sucrose affinities of HbSUT3 were measured at $\mathrm { p H }$ 4.0 or 5.5 under a sucrose substrate range of $0 . 5 { - } 8 \mathbf { m } \mathbf { M }$ (Fig. 2c), and the data were used to perform the MichaelisMenten analysis. The Eadie-Hofstee double-reciprocal plots of the data (Fig. 2d) revealed that at pH 4.0, HbSUT3 had a $K \mathrm { m }$ of $1 . 2 4 \mathrm { m M }$ and a transport rate $V { \bmod { \mathbf { X } } }$ of $1 . 0 8 \mathrm { n m o l }$ sucrose $\operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ $( 1 0 ^ { 8 } ~ \mathrm { c e l l s } ) ^ { - 1 }$ . When assayed at an elevated $\mathrm { p H }$ value (5.5), HbSUT3 displayed lower sucrose affinity $\mathrm { \Delta } K \mathrm { m } = 3 . 6 5 \mathrm { \ m m }$ ), whereas its $V { \bmod { \mathbf { X } } }$ increased to $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { n m o l }$ sucrose $\mathrm { \ m i n ^ { - 1 } }$ $1 0 ^ { 8 }$ cells)-1 . Overall, HbSUT3 belongs to the category of high sucrose affinity SUTs.

The substrate specificity of HbSUT3 was assessed in the presence of various unlabeled sugars supplied at a ten-fold greater concentration. Of the investigated potential substrates, only sucrose and maltose competed notably with the $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -sucrose uptake (Table 1), indicating that HbSUT3 is relatively substrate-specific. Lactose was found to slightly stimulate sucrose uptake by HbSUT3.

Consistent with other sucrose $\mathrm { \Delta H _ { \Omega } ^ { + } }$ symporters, the transport activity of HbSUT3 decreased significantly in the presence of the protonophore dinitrophenol (DNP) (Table 1), further confirming the proton/sucrose co-transport characteristic. HbSUT3 was also sensitive to the thiol reagent $N$ -ethylmaleimide (NEM), a character repeatedly observed in other plant SUTs.


## The effect of Ethrel stimulation on HbSUT3 expression


Ethrel (2-chloroethylphosponic acid, an ethylene releaser) application stimulated latex (rubber) yield, and this stimulating effect is partially due to its acceleration of sugar loading into the laticifers (Coupe & Chrestin 1989). To determine whether HbSUT3 contributes to this process, Ethrel treatment was performed to understand its effect on HbSUT3 expression. Initially, different concentrations (0.1– $6 . 0 \%$ ) of Ethrel were used. The results revealed that Ethrel at concentrations of more than $0 . 5 \%$ was effective in stimulating the expression of HbSUT3 (Fig. 3a,b), and $0 . 5 \%$ was also the threshold concentration showing a marked effect in stimulating latex production (Fig. 3c). Next, the speed of HbSUT3 expression response to stimulation was examined at $1 . 5 \%$ Ethrel by real-time RT-PCR. The results showed that the expression of HbSUT3 was significantly upregulated at $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ after treatment, and expression levels increased with time thereafter (Fig. 4a). At $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ after treatment, mRNA accumulated at levels nearly seven-fold that of the untreated controls $( 0 \mathrm { h } )$ . After Ethrel treatment, the latex production revealed similar kinetics that were significantly higher at $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ after treatment than untreated controls, and increased further after the treatment for $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ (Fig. 4b). However, in unexploited (virgin) trees, the expression of HbSUT3 displayed an obvious decreasing trend after Ethrel treatment (Dusotoit-Coucaud et al. 2009). Contrary to the HbSUT3 expression pattern and latex production, the sucrose concentration of the latex decreased progressively with time, reaching barely one seventh that of the control at $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ after Ethrel treatment (Fig. 4c). The rapidly decreasing latex sucrose levels are likely due to the rapidly elevated activity of cytoplasmic invertase after Ethrel treatment (data not shown; Tupy & Primot 1976). The sucrose concentration recovered thereafter, and at $1 0 8 \mathrm { { h } }$ after treatment attained levels nearly twofold greater than the control (data not shown).


## Expression of HbSUT3 in response to tapping and wounding


To assess the respective effect of tapping and wounding on the expression of HbSUT3, experiments were conducted on virgin trees. The first tapping of a virgin rubber tree produced very little latex. The latex yield increased progressively with successive tappings at regular intervals, and it reached a relatively steady equilibrium after 7–10 tappings (Fig. 5a; Pakianathan et al. 1992). Genes related to latex regeneration were expected to be affected by tapping at the transcriptional and/or post-transcriptional levels. HbSUT3 displayed striking responses to tapping (Fig. 5b). HbSUT3 was expressed at a low level at the first tapping and increased with subsequent tappings. Its expression reached a plateau at the third tapping and then declined and fluctuated at the following tappings while maintaining a level significantly higher than that of the initial tapping.

Tapping brought about two inclusive effects: the sink effect resulting from the exudation of latex, which requires latex regeneration before the next tapping; and the wounding effect, which may induce ‘wound ethylene’ release (d’Auzac et al. 1997). To better understand the effect of tapping on HbSUT3 expression, wounding treatments (without latex flow) were applied to the bark of virgin trees (Fig. S1). As shown in Fig. 5c, the expression of HbSUT3 was markedly up-regulated at $1 2 \mathrm { h }$ after wounding, but the effect was much less conspicuous than tapping. Collectively, the above results suggest that the effect of tapping on HbSUT3 expression originated mainly from the sink effect, although wounding contributed.

Unfortunately, the response of HbSUT3 expression to tapping and wounding could not be extended to other Hevea SUT genes. The expression of HbSUT5 was depressed by tapping, while wounding contributes substantially to the effect of tapping on its expression (unpublished data).


## Expression of HbSUT3 among rubber trees with different yields


HbSUT3 encodes a functional sucrose transporter and plays a role in sucrose loading into laticifers. To further support its role in latex production, its expression in latex was monitored in three groups of clone PR107 trees that exhibited different yields. Although these trees were vegetatively propagated by budding from the same clone (variety), their yields were quite different (Fig. 6a), with an average of $0 . 3 2 \mathrm { k g }$ latex per tree per tapping for the first group of trees (designated as 107A), $0 . 8 3 \mathrm { k g }$ for the second group (107B), and $4 . 1 \mathrm { k g }$ for a super-high yielding tree (SY107). As shown in Fig. 6b, the expression of HbSUT3 correlated well with the rubber yields; HbSUT3 was expressed at the highest levels in SY107, at intermediate levels in 107B and the least in 107A.

Hevea brasiliensis exploits sucrose as the primary substrate for rubber synthesis, and the economic product (the rubbercontaining cytoplasm) is regularly harvested from the trunk bark at intervals of several days. The rubber-producing laticifers in trunk bark represent a strong artificially created sucrose sink. Rubber productivity will depend on sufficiently regenerating the expelled latex before the next exploitation, which then requires an efficient sucrose supply (Tupy 1985). Thus, understanding the mechanisms of sucrose transport, partitioning and metabolism is of fundamental importance in improving Hevea productivity.Within this context, we studied the function of one putative Hevea SUT gene, HbSUT3, in regularly tapped rubber trees, from which rubber yield is ultimately realized. Collectively, our findings support the role of HbSUT3 in sucrose loading into the laticifer and latex production in exploited trees.


## HbSUT3 encodes a functional H+ /sucrose symporter


In baker’s yeast, the full-length cDNA construct of HbSUT3 was revealed to encode a functional sucrose transporter (Fig. 2a). However, when the cDNA construct containing the CDS alone was used, the transformed yeast barely showed detectable transport activity (Fig. S3). Moreover, the native UTRs of another Hevea SUT member (HbSUT1) were found to have a negative effect on its expression in yeast (Fig. S3). To our knowledge, this is the first report regarding the effect of native UTRs on the heterogeneous expression of SUT genes, although such a phenomenon has been observed in the cDNAs of two common plantain (Plantago major) polyol transporters (Ramsperger-Gleixner et al. 2004). We propose that the native non-translated flanking sequences of the introduced SUT cDNAs should be replaced with sequences that are ideal for yeast translation machinery when determining the functionality and sucrose uptake kinetics of SUT cDNAs in baker’s yeast, as previously performed for the two PmPLTs (Ramsperger-Gleixner et al. 2004).

Based on the sucrose affinity and transport capacity, SUTs can be classified into two categories: high-affinity/lowcapacity (HALC) and low-affinity/high-capacity (LAHC).

According to the classification system proposed by Sauer (2007),HbSUT3 belongs to group 2 SUT genes (Fig. S4),and many members of this group function in phloem loading and sucrose uptake into different sink cells (Braun & Slewinski 2009). The SUTs of group 2 are reported to encode HALC transporters, showing $K \mathrm { m }$ values of 0.3 to $2 \mathrm { m M }$ (Sauer 2007). Consistent with the many well-characterized SUT genes of this group,HbSUT3 also showed high sucrose affinity,revealing a $K \mathrm { m }$ value of $1 . 2 4 \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathrm { p H } ~ 4 . 0$ (Fig. 2d). With the exception of a few SUFs (sucrose facilitators) (PsSUF1,

PvSUF1 and PsSUF4), the majority of the plant SUTs identified to date have been found to be sucrose $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ symporters (Zhou et al. 2007). The $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ -sucrose uptake of HbSUT3 was pH-dependent when assayed at $1 \mathrm { m M }$ sucrose (Fig. 2b), strongly competed with unlabeled sucrose and was sensitive to a protonophore (DNP) and a thiol reagent (NEM) (Table 1). Therefore, HbSUT3 is a typical sucrose $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ symporter.


## Latex-dominant expression pattern implies the role of HbSUT3 in sucrose loading into the laticifer


The absence of plasmodesmatal connections between laticifers and the surrounding cells in the inner bark implies that assimilates must cross their plasma membrane as they do for others cells such as companion cells (Braun & Slewinski

2009) and vessel-associated cells (Decourteix et al. 2006). In regularly-tapped Hevea trees of a metabolically active clone Reyan 7-33-97, HbSUT3 was revealed to be the dominant SUT member expressed in latex, as compared with other SUT genes (Fig. 1a), suggesting its role in metabolic function of laticifers. The predominant presence of HbSUT3 in latex was also confirmed in a recent report from DusotoitCoucaud et al. (2009), although they used a different technique (real time RT-PCR) to analyse the expression of SUT genes in virgin trees of a different clone (PB217, a low metabolic clone). In their studies, the presence of Hevea SUT1 group (HbSUT1 and 3) transcripts was observed in laticifers through in-situ hybridization, supporting the notion of the possible function of HbSUT3 in sucrose loading into the laticifer. When the expression of HbSUT3 was compared among twelve different Hevea tissues, it was detectable in each tissue examined, suggesting that there is functional redundancy (Fig. 1b). HbSUT3 expression differed markedly among different tissues, with dominance in latex and female flowers. This implies a preferential role in sucrose loading into laticifers and flower organs.


## Ethrel-induced HbSUT3 expression is involved in the latex-stimulating effect of Ethrel


The artificial application of Ethrel onto trunk bark enhances latex regeneration, improves rubber productivity and has become a common practice in modern rubber production (d’Auzac et al. 1997). Although the stimulating mechanisms are not clearly understood, an increase in sucrose metabolism (Tupy & Primot 1976; Silpi et al. 2007), sucrose influx (Tupy 1989) and water influx (Tungngoen et al. 2009) have been reported to occur after Ethrel treatment in the laticifers or across their plasma membranes, and constitutes the factors leading to the stimulated latex production.

The literature indicates that transcriptional regulation in SUT genes is critical for the sucrose transport activity (Weber et al. 1997; Aldape et al. 2003; Zhou et al. 2007; Decourteix et al. 2008), and is linked to exogenous (Meyer et al. 2004) as well as endogenous signals, including hormones (Chincinska et al. 2008). In this study, HbSUT3 expression was found to be up-regulated markedly by ethylene treatment (Figs 3a,b and 4a). The effective threshold concentration of Ethrel was found to be the same $( 0 . 5 \%$ W/W) for inducing HbSUT3 expression and stimulating latex production (Fig. 3). In addition, the time-course kinetics after Ethrel treatment are also similar for HbSUT3 expression and for the stimulating effect on latex production (Fig. 4a,b). These findings clearly support the involvement of HbSUT3 in the stimulating effect of Ethrel, mainly through increased sucrose importation into the laticifers. Interestingly, this data cannot be extended to unexploited Hevea trees for which HbSUT3 was down-regulated by ethylene application, although the predominant nature of basal expression was also demonstrated in the latex as compared with other SUT members (Dusotoit-Coucaud et al. 2009). The difference between unexploited and exploited trees is due to the high sustained carbon demand specific to the exploitation process, which consists of severe wounding, combined with constitutive high metabolic activity necessary for latex regeneration between consecutive tappings (Eschbach et al. 1984; Tupy 1989). Therefore, the sucrose demand of latex cells is much higher in exploited trees than in unexploited ones, and this high expression of HbSUT3 in exploited tree indicates the ability of laticifers to finetune sugar transport equipment according to their carbon demand. The same adjustment of sugar transporters was reported in many active sink organs including the berries (Hayes, Davies & Dry 2007), pollen (Scholz-Starke, Büttner & Sauer 2003) and seeds (Weber et al. 1997). The characterization of HbSUT3 expression in other exploited clones of Hevea trees would open the possibility to underpin the generic role of this sucrose transporter isoform in the ethylene stimulation of latex production.

It is not possible to determine the precise mechanism by which Ethrel regulates the expression of HbSUT3 from these data. There are at least two scenarios. The first suggests that ethylene may directly regulate HbSUT3 expression at the transcriptional level. In this case, the promoter sequence of HbSUT3 may harbour ethylene-responsive elements as is the case for the carrot transporter gene cSUT (Yang et al. 2004) or Hevea aquaporins (Tungngoen et al. 2009). The second assumption may be that ethylene indirectly regulates HbSUT3 expression through feedback controlled by sucrose, by stimulating sucrose metabolism mainly through a rapidly elevated activity of invertase in latex and thereby decreasing sucrose level as observed (Fig. 4c; data not shown). This fits well with many reports showing a sucrose transporter that is down-regulation by a high concentration of its own substrate (Chiou & Bush 1998;Vaughn, Harrington & Bush 2002, Ransom-Hodgkins, Vaughn & Bush 2003).


## HbSUT3 expression is implicated in latex regeneration


The act of tapping stimulated latex production, and the effect was especially conspicuous in virgin Hevea trees (Fig. 5a; Pakianathan et al. 1992). The laticifers in the trunk bark from virgin Hevea trees are characterized by both low metabolic activity and low latex production. With tapping, sucrose absorption into laticifers is accelerated, laticiferous metabolism is activated, and ultimately, the latex yield increases (Pakianathan et al. 1992). This property makes virgin trees an ideal model to identify and characterize latex regeneration-related genes. In virgin Hevea trees, the expression of HbSUT3 was up-regulated markedly with tapping, especially after the second tapping (Fig. 5b). Tapping results in two effects on the trunk bark that is used to harvest rubber: the sink and the wound (d’Auzac et al. 1997). By comparison, wounding alone (without latex exudation) affected the expression of HbSUT3 much less markedly (Fig. 5c), implying that tapping up-regulated HbSUT3 expression mainly through the sink effect, i.e. the requirement for the regeneration of the expelled latex. This response of HbSUT3 expression to tapping is different from that of HbSUT5, which was the only other SUT gene responsive to this treatment. HbSUT5 expression was depressed by tapping (unpublished data). It is interesting to investigate whether these two SUT genes interact with each other in determining the efficiency of sucrose loading into the laticifer. Another piece of evidence supporting the potential role of HbSUT3 in latex production came from the expression analysis among rubber trees with different yields. The expression of HbSUT3 in latex correlated positively with the yields of rubber trees within the same clone (PR107) (Fig. 6).

In addition to Ethrel, jasmonic acid (JA) was also found to markedly up-regulate the expression of HbSUT3 (Fig. S5). JA is the sole phytohormone known to efficiently induce laticifer differentiation (Hao & Wu 2000). Laticifer differentiation leads to the formation of a new carbon sink (the laticifer) and constitutes one of the key factors restricting sustainable rubber production (Gomez, Narayanan & Chen 1972). Therefore, HbSUT3 appears to function in supplying sucrose for laticifer differentiation, and in this manner, it contributes to latex regeneration.

Taken together, we conclude that HbSUT3, a functional sucrose transporter, plays an active role in determining sucrose loading into the laticifer and subsequent latex (rubber) productivity in response to ethylene treatment. Its promoter will now be cloned and functionally characterized using report gene experiments to elucidate how HbSUT3 expression is regulated by this treatment.

In plants, carbohydrates translocate from the source to sink tissues through symplastic and apoplastic pathways. Sugar transport between cells in symplasts is mediated by plasmodesmata. In apoplasts, sugar translocators are responsible for carbohydrate uptake into cells. Because sucrose is the major transported form of carbohydrate between plant tissues, sucrose transporter (SUT) plays an important role in long-distance disaccharide transport. SUT1 in sugarcane functions to partition sucrose between the vascular bundle and storage cells (Rae et al. 2005). Maize SUT, ZmSUT1, is responsible for sugar uptake into phloem in source tissues and sugar unloading from phloem into cells in sink tissues (Carpaneto et al. 2005). Changes in carbohydrate allocation and the inhibition of photosynthesis have been observed in transgenic plants with reduced SUT activity due to antisense SUT genes; thus, SUT has been indicated to play an important role in carbohydrate partitioning and physiological processing (Kühn et al. 1996; Bürkle et al. 1998).

To date, SUT genes have been identified from several plants, most belonging to gene families (Lemoine 2000; Lalonde et al. 2004). The SUT gene families of dicot and monocot species were classified into five sequence-based groups by Braun and Slewinski (2009). In rice, the SUT gene family consists of five genes, OsSUT1 to OsSUT5 (Aoki et al. 2003). OsSUT1 and 3 were classified into group 1. The group 1 SUT family is composed of several Poaceae SUT members; so far, no dicot SUTs have been found in group 1. OsSUT2 was classified with Arabidopsis SUT4 (AtSUT4) in group 2. AtSUT4 has been demonstrated to be responsible for the low-affinity/high-capacity transport system (reviewed by Lalonde et al. 2004). OsSUT4 and OsSUT5 were classified into group 3 and 5, respectively.

During plant development from seed germination to seed establishment and seedling growth, starch reserved in the seed is the primary carbon and energy source for sprouting and early seedling establishment, and then the sugar sources for later stages of seedling growth come from the photosynthetic shoots. In rice plants, carbohydrate transport from germinating seeds to other developing sink tissues is a fundamental process for plant development and growth. Sugar derived from starch degradation exported to the cytosol from storage organelles is the first step for longdistance carbohydrate translocation. In cereal endosperms, starch granules are attacked by $\propto$ -amylase (Murata et al. 1968), and the maltose and linear/short-branch-chain oligosaccharides are generated for further degradation by $\propto$ -glucosidase (Stanley et al. 2011). The hexoses produced by starch degradation can be taken up by the scutellum cells of the embryo. Hexoses have been suggested to be resynthesized into sucrose in the scutellum (Edelman et al. 1959; Nomura et al. 1969). Sucrose in the scutellum is loaded into the vascular bundle, transported, and then unloaded to growing tissues through apoplastic or symplastic pathways (Aoki et al. 2006). In addition, it was also suggested that sucrose transported from aleurone layers to endosperm at early germination stage could be further uptaked by scutellum (Aoki et al. 2006). Based on our previous work (Liu et al. 2010), soluble sugar can also be converted to starch in scutellum or the cells surrounding vascular bundles at the post-germination stage, and the amount of transitory starch in embryonic tissues was dependent on the demand of growing sink tissues. Phloem functions as an important pathway for carbon source transport among various plant tissues. In rice germinating seeds, OsSUT1 was the first OsSUT family member identified to have a tissue-specific expression pattern (Hirose et al. 1997; Scofield et al. 2007). Developmental expression and regulation of OsSUT1 has been observed in germinating seeds (Chen et al. 2010). However, the regulation of other members of the OsSUT gene family still needs to be established.

Sucrose transporters (SUTs) are important for both phloem loading in source tissue and sucrose uptake into some sink cells [1]. SUTs are considered to be the control points for sucrose storage in plant because they can carry sucrose across cell membranes and play an important role in loading sucrose into phloem systems in a series of steps [1]. Plant SUTs belong to the glycoside-pentosidehexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family (TC2.A.2) that is part of the major facilitator super-family (MFS) [2]. Transporters in the GPH family have the primary characteristics of MFS proteins that contain 12 transmembrane spanning domains with $\Nu _ { - }$ and C-termini in the cytoplasm [3]. Since the first plant sucrose transporter SoSUT1 was functionally identified using an elegant yeast complementation strategy from spinach (Spinacea Oleracea) [4], SUTs have been demonstrated to effect on the multiple aspects of plant development such as biomass partitioning, pollen germination, restraining plant growth, fruit size reduction and ethylene biosynthesis [5–9].

Comprehensive understanding of the molecular structure and evolution of a gene family in plant species is the first step towards understanding their physiological roles and metabolic mechanism involved in different growth phases. Recent studies have revealed that SUT was a small gene family that consisted of at least four SUT genes in the most plant species. The SUT family members have been identified from a number of plant species such as Arabidopsis [10], rice (Oryza sativa) [11], wheat (Triticum aestivum) [12], populus [8], sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) [13] and pineapple (Ananas comosus) (Unpublished, Zhang and Ming) as well. Phylogenetic analysis of SUT family suggested that the plant SUT could be divided into five subgroups including two monocot specific subgroups, one dicot specific and two monocot-dicot subgroups. SUT family members in many plant species are divergent in function and deferentially expressed in different tissues types or at different plant developmental stages. For instance, in rice, OsSUT1 expression has been detected in germinated seeds, leaf blades, leaf sheaths and panicles [14–16]; the expressions of both OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 are dramatically lower in embryos than those of OsSUT1, OsSUT2, and OsSUT4 [17]; OsSUT4 has been detected in most tissues such as roots, leaves, and panicles [11], and could play a role in sucrose loading into the sheath phloem of the upper leaves during the post-heading period for sucrose transport to developing grains [18]. In Arabidopsis [10], AtSUC2 has been detected in phloem and companion cells in source leaves [19, 20] and functions in loading sucrose into the phloem sieve elements (SEs), correspond with the result identified by tissue-specific complementation of different promoters [7, 21] and by $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { C }$ labeling studies [22]; AtSUC3 and

AtSUC4 are expressed in minor veins of source leaves of mature plants [23–25].

Sugarcane (Saccharum spp.) is one of the world’s most produced crops (FAOSTAT, 2015), and contributes to about $80 \%$ of the world sugar and about $4 0 \ \%$ of ethanol production worldwide. Modern sugarcane cultivar has one of the most complex genome among all the crops; by being both aneupoid and autopolypoid with an extreme ploidy level that can range from octoploidy $\left( \mathbf { { x } } = 8 \right)$ to dodecaploidy $( \mathbf { x } = 1 2 )$ . Approximately $80 \%$ of cultivars’ chromosomes are derived from S. officinarum and $1 0 - 2 0 \ \%$ is derived from S.spontaneum with the remained from interspecific recombination [26–28]. Sugarcane is not only an economically important crop species, but also serves as an important model crop for studying sucrose transporters because its remarkable ability to accumulate vast amounts of sucrose in its stems that can reach close to $7 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ or in excess of $5 0 \%$ of the dry weight (DW) (DW) [29]. But to date, limited works in characterizing these SUT genes have been reported, except for SUT1 (transcripts accession:AY780256.1, GU812864.1 and BU925792). In an earlier study based on sugarcane Expressed Sequence Tag (EST) database survey, SUT1 was revealed to be more abundant in the mature internodes than the other tissues [30]. This result was confirmed by a study for Hawaiian sugarcane cultivar, in which the SUT1 transcript levels increased during maturation and sucrose storage, whereas, SUT1 expression was observed to be not affected by sugarcane yellow leaf virus (SCYLV) infection in sugarcane [31]. Biochemical analysis of sugarcane SUT1 suggested that SUT1 was highly selective for sucrose, but had a relatively low affinity for sucrose, inhibited by sucralose and played key role in sucrose loading from the vascular tissues into the storage sites in parenchyma cells of sugarcane stems [32, 33]. Besides SUT1, the gene family of SUTs is not understood in sugarcane due to the formidable challenge caused by its high degree of polyploidy and heterozygosity genome.

In this study, to gain comprehensive understandings of the molecular and evolutionary characterization as well as the possible functions of SUT family in sugarcane, based on combination of comparative genomics strategies and high genome coverage of bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) libraries resources, we identified and characterized SUT gene families in Saccharum species and investigated their transcriptional expression patterns. The analysis in this study mainly focused on: (1) identifying the gene members and allele haplotypes of the SUT gene family in sugarcane; (2) analyzing evolutionary relationship, exon/intron organization of the SUT gene family; and (3) characterizing the expression patterns of the SUT gene family in three progenitor Saccharum species.

Under conditions of environmental stress, sugars play important roles as osmolytes, reactive oxygen species (ROS) quenchers and signaling molecules involved in stress perception and signaling and regulation of stress-mediated gene expression, contributing to osmotic adjustment responses, elimination of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and regulation of plant growth and development processes, including fruit ripening (Fakher et al. 2022). Among the sugars present in plant species, sucrose is the main product of the photosynthesis process (Kaur et al. 2021). The sucrose generated is transiently accumulated in leaf vacuoles or transported from source to sink tissues to satisfy the plant growth and development requirements (Braun 2022). Sucrose not only functions as a source of carbon and energy for cells, but also acts as an osmotic adjustment agent, participating in the plant adaptive responses to unfavorable environmental circumstances (Salvi et al. 2022). In situations of environmental stress, the efficiency of photosynthesis is inhibited, which affects the supply, transport and partitioning of sucrose and, therefore, stress tolerance (Salvi et al. 2022).

Long-distance sucrose transport and intracellular compartmentalization are mediated by membrane sucrose transporters (SUTs) (Braun 2022). SUTs are involved in the controlled movement of sugars from source tissues (leaves) to sink tissues (i.e. fruits and roots), determining the overall development of the plant (Liang et al. 2023). Genes encoding SUTs have been studied in various crops and categorized into three groups and their subgroups according to phylogenetic analyses. Type I SUTs are present exclusively in eudicots, playing a role in sucrose loading in the phloem of leaves (Hackel et al. 2006). Type II-A and II-B SUTs are specific to mono- and eudicots, with type II-B being involved in sucrose unloading into the phloem and sucrose importing into sink tissues (Salvi et al. 2022). Type III SUTs are present in all land plants (Salvi et al. 2022), acting as low-affinity/high-capacity sucrose transporters (Garg et al. 2022). They are located in the plasma membrane or tonoplast, with that of tonoplast particularly involved in storing sucrose and modulating its cytosolic levels (Salvi et al. 2022).

Three members belonging to the SUT family have been identified in cultivated tomato (Reuscher et al. 2014). SlSUT1 (Solyc11g017010.1.1) is expressed mainly in assimilate source leaves (Hackel et al. 2006), whose protein has been shown to be located in the plasma membrane of sieve tube elements and to play an essential role in loading apoplastic sucrose into the phloem and its long-distance transport (Reuscher et al. 2014), ensuring the redistribution of energy from leaves to other sink organs of the plant, such as fruits and roots. SlSUT2 (Solyc05g007190.2.1) is expressed predominantly in sink organs, such as young leaves, stems and fruits, with its protein localized in the plasma membrane of sieve tube elements and possibly acting in the unloading of sucrose from the phloem (Reuscher et al. 2014). The SlSUT2 protein has also been shown to influence pollen tube growth (Hackel et al. 2006), the formation of mycorrhizae and to interact with hormones such as brassinosteroids (Hansch et al. 2020). The interaction of SlSUT2 with sucrose and other hormonal factors suggests a complex function in the signaling and transport of sugars within the plant (Kanayama 2017). SlSUT4 (Solyc04g076960.2.1) plays a less understood role, being involved in the regulation of flowering and the modulation of gibberellin biosynthesis, transport of sucrose from the vacuole to the cytoplasm and signaling associated with plant growth and development (Garg et al. 2022). It has a potential location in both the plasma membrane and the tonoplast, suggesting a dual function in metabolic regulation and sucrose transport (Schneider et al. 2012).

The roles of SUTs in plant development have been extensively investigated. For example, inhibition of SUT1 expression in tomato has been shown to affect fruit development (Hackel et al. 2006). In potato, SUT4 (type III) silencing causes early flowering (Chincinska et al. 2008, 2013). SUTs genes are also involved in the response to various abiotic stresses such as salinity, drought and low temperatures (Kaur et al. 2021). In Arabidopsis, AtSUC1 and AtSUC2 transcripts were up-regulated in response to low temperature (Lundmark et al. 2006). In rice, OsSUT1 and OsSUT2 were up-regulated under water deficit and salinity (Ibraheem et al. 2011; Siahpoosh et al. 2012). Overexpression of the apple MdSUT2 gene in tomato plants conferred tolerance to drought, salt stress and resulted in earlier flowering and ripening of transgenic tomato fruits compared to wildtype plants (Ma et al. 2017). Another piece of evidence was reported by Zhang et al. (2014), in which the lower sucrose content was one of the crucial factors leading to the late ripening process of the mutant sweet orange. Therefore, the level of sucrose is also important for the regulation of fruit ripening.

The aforementioned studies provide evidence of the crucial role of sucrose transporters in tolerance to environmental stresses and in promoting fruit ripening. It is therefore essential to gain a better understanding of the role of sucrose transporters in these processes. Tomato is an excellent model for these studies, as there are natural mutants for some master genes controlling fruit ripening, such as rin (ripening-inhibitor), Nr (never-ripe), nor (nonripening), Cnr (colorless nonripening), Gr (green-ripe), and gf (green flesh) (Karlova et al. 2014). Thus, this work aimed to characterize the molecular features of the SUT gene family in tomato and the expression of each gene in response to water deficit in both source and sink organs, as well as the effects of rin and Nr mutations that affect fruit ripening.

Sugarcane (Saccharum ofcinarum), the primary producer of table sugar, is relentlessly challenged by frequent red rot attacks (caused by Colletotrichum falcatum) in India and subtropical regions of the world (Gujjar et al. 2024a). Sucrose, being chief assimilated carbon produced during photosynthesis, functions as an essential plant metabolite during plant growth and development, with additional role as a signaling molecule (Gujjar et al. 2024b). Sucrose is synthesized in the green tissues of plants and is transported to the sink organs either to be metabolized as an energyproducing molecule or to be stored as starch or other organic compounds (Xu et al. 2018). The process called carbohydrate partitioning is fundamental to growth and development, whereby the plants assimilate, transport and distribute the sugars from green leaves (exporting source) to carbon demanding tissues (importing sinks), such as fruits, seeds, fowers, stems, and roots (Wu et al. 2021). Moreover, this process is also associated with tolerance/resistance to abiotic/biotic stress in plants (Julius et al. 2017; Gujjar et al. 2024b). Sugar transporters, besides being indispensable for sugar translocation among adjacent cells in the plant, are also implicated in both biotic and abiotic stress responses (Julius et al. 2017; Hu et al. 2021). Sucrose Transporters (SUTs) basically belong to the class of membrane-bound sucrose–proton symporters present in plants. As a group of primary sugar transporters, they are indispensable for the transport of sucrose from the intercellular apoplast into the cytosol, specifcally when no plasmodesma exists between adjacent cells (Hu et al. 2021; Sun et al. 2022). SUTs generate high turgor pressure through plasma membrane proton motive force to facilitate phloem loading and active transport of sucrose. Sucrose accumulation in sink tissues such as fruits, seeds, stalks during developmental stages is mediated by active transport of sucrose by SUTs (Bavnhøj et al. 2023). In sugarcane, ShSUT1 was the frst SUT identifed in leaves (Rae et al. 2005) and yellow leaf virus infected sugarcane (Saccharum hybrid) stem (ElSayed et al. 2010). Consequently, fve SUT genes, namely SoSUT1, SoSUT2, SoSUT3, SoSUT4, and SoSUT5 were identifed, and their expressions were analyzed in roots, stems, leaves, inforescence, and buds by qRT-PCR in sugarcane (Niu et al. 2019).

Fungal virulence and pathogenicity are stimulated by the activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway, followed by release of efector molecules by pathogen to facilitate the host invasion (Gujjar et al. 2024a). Disease resistance proteins (DRPs) are accountable for identifying the potential pathogens and triggering appropriate defense responses in host plants. They chiefy comprise of three domains, a nucleotide-binding site (NBS), leucinerich repeats (LRRs), and putative amino-terminal signaling domain (Belkhadir et al. 2004). LRR domain of DRPs is accredited with the role of determining the magnitude of a particular response, and their action leads to plant cell death in case of hypersensitive response (Harris et al. 2013). NanoLC–MS/MS approaches are the most extensively used approaches in recent times for investigating the whole proteome as well as diferential proteome in crop plants under diferent treatment conditions (Gujjar et al. 2020, 2021, 2024c). In one of the previous study, we investigated the impact of $C .$ . falcatum infection on the abundance of proteins and expression of genes implicated in sucrose metabolism in sugarcane (Gujjar et al. 2024b). In the present study, we identifed eight SUT and four DRP proteins in the stalk tissues of sugarcane through nanoLCMS/MS-based proteomics analysis approach. For the frst time, we are reporting the infuence of $C .$ . falcatum infection on the abundance pattern of SUT and DRP proteins in the stalk tissues of red rot resistant and susceptible cultivars of sugarcane.

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are sucrose– $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ symporters, which mediate the active transport of sucrose across plasma membranes. Since sucrose is translocated from source to sink tissues through the phloem, plasma membrane sucrose transporters are believed to play important roles in mediating carbon partitioning in plants (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Over the last decade, genes encoding SUT proteins have been isolated from a wide range of both monocot and dicot plant species, from source and sink tissues and found to be localised in phloem and non-phloem tissues (see reviews by Williams et al. 2000; Truernit 2001; Lalonde et al. 2003).

In cereal species, SUT proteins mainly have been studied in developing grains. For example, in developing rice caryopses, OsSUT1 protein is present in the plasma membrane of the aleurone cell layer surrounding the endosperm (Furbank et al. 2001) and is essential for transport of assimilates into filling grains (Scofield et al. 2002). A similar role in grain filling has been proposed for HvSUT1 protein in barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and for TaSUT1 in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2002). However, cellular localisation of cereal SUT gene expression in vegetative tissues has been less well characterised despite the fact that SUT mRNAs are detectable in these tissues of rice (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003), maize (Aoki et al. 1999), barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). While in dicot plants there is considerable evidence that SUTs play a role in apoplasmic loading of sucrose into the phloem (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003), there is little evidence for this in cereal species. Indeed, there is some debate over whether phloem loading in cereals occurs via symplasmic or apoplasmic pathways (e.g. Russin et al. 1996, also see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Significantly, antisense repression of OsSUT1 expression in transgenic rice did not appear to affect phloem loading (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002).

Previously we reported the isolation of three cDNAs encoding SUT proteins from developing grains of hexaploid wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). The peptide sequences deduced from the three cDNAs showed $9 8 \%$ identity to one another, all with more than $8 5 \%$ similarity to SUT1 proteins from other cereal species. The three wheat SUT1 proteins were encoded individually by single-copy homeologous genes, designated TaSUT1A, 1B and 1D , which are represented once in each of the A-, B- and D-genomes. Northern blot analysis revealed that the TaSUT1 genes were highly expressed not only in developing grains but also in flagleaf blades, flag-leaf sheaths and culms (internodes) at the pre-heading stage.

Sucrose, synthesized in mature leaves via photosynthesis, is the primary carbohydrate transported to sink tissues such as roots, young leaves, fowers, and seeds (Wang et al. 2021). This transport is mediated by sucrose transporters (SUTs), which are sucrose– $\mathbf { \cdot H ^ { + } }$ symporters located on the plasma or vacuolar membranes and belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) with 12 transmembrane helices (Deng et al. 2023; Akbar et al. 2025). SUT genes play essential roles in sucrose loading and unloading through the phloem, infuencing key processes such as hormone biosynthesis, stress responses, photosynthesis, and reproductive and fber development (Li et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2021; Hou et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024).

Understanding the molecular structure and evolution of a plant gene family is crucial for comprehending their physiological roles and metabolic mechanisms during diferent growth phases. Recent studies have shown that the SUT gene family is relatively small, typically comprising of fewer members in most plant species. However, the number of SUT genes can vary considerably among taxa. For instance, 06 SUTs have been identifed in Sorghum bicolor (Mizuno et al. 2016), 06 in Saccharum spontaneum (Zhang et al. 2016), 07 in Zea mays (Sun et al. 2023a, b), 09 in Beta vulgaris L. (Sun et al. 2023a, b), 05 in Triticum aestivum (Prasad et al. 2023), 12 in Dendrocalamus farinosus (Deng et al. 2023), and up to 05 and 07 in Erufpilus and Saccharum ofcinarum (Akbar et al. 2025), respectively. Studies on the functions of the SUT family genes in plants have shown that they are involved in various aspects of plant growth and development (Misra et al. 2019), including the transportation and distribution of sucrose (Deng et al. 2023), carbohydrate partitioning (Al-Sheikh Ahmed et al. 2020), germination of pollen (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c), fruit development (Jiang et al. 2023), plant growth (Wang et al. 2020), and biosynthesis of ethylene (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c). For example, AtSUC2 is essential for sucrose loading and root development in Arabidopsis (Gong et al. 2014), while AtSUC4, located on the tonoplast, mediates sucrose-induced inhibition of root elongation (Liu et al. 2022a, b). Tonoplast-localized transporters like PtaSUT4 in poplar and OsSUT2 in rice facilitate sucrose efux from source leaves (Eom et al. 2011; Sun et al. 2022). Notably, suppression of PtaSUT4 increases sucrose accumulation in leaves and alters biomass distribution, highlighting its role in source-to-sink transport (Payyavula et al. 2011). In addition, OsSUT1 is the most studied SUT gene in rice and its inhibition delays seed germination and reduces seed setting without signifcantly afecting leaf carbohydrate levels. OsSUT1 also facilitates sucrose recovery from plastids to support grain flling (Sun et al. 2022; Yingqing et al. 2025). Furthermore, overexpression of GmSUT4.2 in soybean boosts sucrose uptake and promotes sucrose-stimulated hairy root growth, thereby contributing to overall plant growth, development, and yield (Wu et al. 2024). Multiple studies have demonstrated the critical roles of SUT genes in regulating plant growth, sugar metabolism, and stress responses. For example, GmSUT4 infuences plant development through sugar metabolic pathways (Chen et al. 2022a, b), while overexpression of RuSUT2 increases sucrose accumulation in blackberry leaves, suggesting its role in sucrose distribution (Yan et al. 2021). Extensive research has also shown that SUTs mediate responses to phytohormones and environmental stresses (Li et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2020; Hou et al. 2024). Genes like AtSUC4 and AtSUC9 respond to ABA signaling and contribute to drought and cold tolerance (Jia et al. 2015). Similarly, MdSUT2 in tomato and IbSUT4 in sweet potato enhance tolerance to abiotic stress, the latter through an ABF-dependent ABA pathway (Ma et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2020). In peach, PpSUT2 overexpression improved cold and drought tolerance by modulating proline, soluble sugars, and oxidative stress markers (Zhao et al. 2022). More recently, SlSUT4 was shown to regulate sucrose partitioning between vacuole and cytosol, thereby afecting tomato drought responses (Liang et al. 2023).

Sugarcane (Saccharum spp. hybrids), a member of the grass family (Gramineae), is the world’s leading crop for sugar production and a key raw material for biofuel (Zhou et al. 2020, Ali et al. 2025). Commercial sugarcane cultivars are genetically complex, exhibiting allopolyploidy and aneuploidy, with large, highly variable genomes (Zhou et al. 2014; Healey et al. 2024). In China, the hybrid variety ROC22 (derived from $\mathsf { R O C 5 } \times 6 9 - 4 6 3 )$ has been the dominant cultivar over the past two decades, covering approximately $6 0 \%$ of the total sugarcane cultivation area (Su et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2020). Previous studies have identifed numerous SUT family genes in sugarcane (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c; Akbar et al. 2025) and examined their expression under various stress conditions; however, no such analyses have been reported for the Saccharum spp. Hybrid XTT22 (ROC22) genome. This study presents the first identifcation of ShSUT genes in the XTT22 genome, using bioinformatics to examine their physicochemical properties and evolutionary relationships. Transcription factors interacting with ShSUT4 were identifed through BiFC, and Y2H assays, and the expression of ShSUT genes was analyzed under Cold, Drought and Salinity, stressors. These fndings provide key insights into sugar transport, gene evolution, and the genetic basis for improving sugarcane through molecular breeding.

Plant sucrose transporters (SUTs) are members of the glycoside-pentoside-hexuronide (GPH) cation symporter family (TC2.A.2) that is part of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). All plant SUTs characterized to date function as proton-coupled symporters and catalyze the cellular uptake of sucrose. SUTs are involved in loading sucrose into the phloem and sink tissues, such as seeds, roots and flowers. Because monocots are agriculturally important, SUTs from cereals have been the focus of recent research. Here we present a functional analysis of the SUT ShSUT1 from sugarcane, an important crop species grown for its ability to accumulate high amounts of sucrose in the stem. ShSUT1 was previously shown to be expressed in maturing stems and plays an important role in the accumulation of sucrose in this tissue. Using two-electrode voltage clamping in Xenopus oocytes expressing ShSUT1, we found that ShSUT1 is highly selective for sucrose, but has a relatively low affinity for sucrose $( K _ { 0 . 5 } = 8 . 2 6 \ : \mathrm { m M }$ at $\mathbf { p H _ { \lambda } 5 . 6 }$ and a membrane potential of $\mathbf { - 1 3 7 m V }$ ). We also found that the sucrose analog sucralose (4,1¢,6¢-trichloro-4,1¢,6¢-trideoxygalacto-sucrose) is a competitive inhibitor of ShSUT1 with an inhibition coefficient $\mathbf { \left( K _ { i } \right) }$ of $\mathbf { 1 6 . 5 \ m M }$ . The presented data contribute to our understanding of sucrose transport in plants in general and in monocots in particular.

Key-words: cotransporter; symport; Xenopus oocytes.
