In wheat, grain filling is a key phase of development that is reliant on carbohydrate supply from photosynthesis in green leaves as well as from reserve carbohydrate pools, mainly in stems, that have accumulated during vegetative and early reproductive growth (Pheloung and Siddique 1991; Kobata et al. 1992). Stem water soluble carbohydrates (WSC) can account for $5 0 \%$ of the stem dry weight, and this becomes a highly important source for grain filling especially when wheat is exposed to stress (Zhang et al. 2015). Under unfavourable environments, stem WSC provides a major contribution to final grain yield (Schnyder 1993; Yang et al. 2001). Sucrose is the main form of carbohydrate translocated from the source to sinks such as seeds and roots (Ruan 2012). Thus, sucrose transport to the grain is a critical determinant for harvest yield and grain quality (Halford 2011). Three sugar transporter families have been reported, namely, monosaccharide transporters (MSTs), sucrose transporters (SUTs), and hexose and sucrose transporters (SWEETs) (Eom et al. 2015). Sucrose accumulation and degradation are closely linked with the gene expression levels of sucroseassociated genes which include both metabolic pathways and membrane transport (Mizuno et al. 2018). Sugar transporter genes contribute more to sugar accumulation than sugar metabolism genes (Wang et al. 2016).

The distribution of sucrose is dependent on the expression of a number of sucrose transporters (SUT) which play active roles in phloem loading and unloading of sucrose (Hirose et al. 1997; Rosche et al. 2002; Aoki et al. 2004). So far, the cereal SUT family has been detected in rice, barley, maize and wheat (see below). OsSUT1 was first identified by Hirose et al. (1997) in rice and was highly expressed in the leaf blade and leaf sheath before heading, and in the panicle after heading. Rice contains four additional SUT genes OsSUT2, OsSUT3, OsSUT4 and OsSUT5 which are differentially expressed in parts of the shoot and developing grain, and this suggests that the SUT family multifunctions in translocation of sucrose (Aoki et al. 2003). In transgenic rice, AtSUC2 plants had up to $1 6 \%$ increased grain yield (Wang et  al. 2015). In barley, $H \nu S U T I$ is preferentialy expressed in the developing grain at sites where sucrose exchange occurs whereas $H \nu S U T 2$ is expressed widely in both source and sink tissues (Weschke et al. 2000) indicating that $H \nu S U T I$ and $H \nu S U T 2$ play different roles in grain filling. Two SUTs have been identified in maize, ZmSUT1 in vegetative tissues of source organs (Aoki et al. 1999) and ZmSUT2 in the developing tassel, stem, and leaves (Leach et al. 2017). Furthermore, ZmSUT2 plays a role in sucrose remobilization from the vacuole for leaf growth (Leach et al. 2017).

To our knowledge, information for SUT gene regulation is very limited. Recent research investigated the expression of a number of SUT genes in seedlings of nine species under different abiotic stress conditions (Xu et al. 2018). In their study, OsSUT1, HvSUT1, ZmSUT1 and TaSUT1 were all highly up-regulated while other SUT genes studied were down regulated under drought. These results did not show consistency with the findings in a SUT gene study in rice where OsSUT2 was up-regulated under drought and salinity treatments indicated that OsSUT2 may play an important role in tolerance to abiotic stress in rice (Ibraheem et al. 2011). Seedling materials were used in both studies. Whether SUT gene expression is impacted by drought during grain filling in wheat has not been investigated to date.

In wheat, four SUTs have been reported (Aoki et al. 2002, 2004; Deol et al. 2013; Mukherjee et al. 2015). TaSUT1 is expressed in the developing grain 8–32 days after anthesis (DAA), and in leaf and stem tissues from 4 days before heading to 16 days after heading (Aoki et al. 2002). They suggested that TaSUT1 participated in grain growth and starch biosynthesis because of the capability of moving sucrose to the developing grain (Aoki et al. 2002, 2004). Unlike TaSUT1, TaSUT2 is expressed almost equally across vegetative tissues (flag leaf blade and sheath, peduncle, glume, palea and lemma at $8 { \mathrm { - } } 3 0 \ \mathrm { D A A }$ ) and the grain (5–30 DAA) (Deol et al. 2013). These workers proposed that TaSUT2 is a housekeeping gene similar to OsSUT2 and HvSUT2. Recently, Mukherjee et al. (2015) detected the expression of TaSUT1, TaSUT2, TaSUT4 and TaSUT5 at all stages of grain development between 4 and 30 DAA. The higher expression of TaSUT1 between 8 and 25 DAA indicates the important role of TaSUT1 for the developing grain. However, there is no information on TaSUT3 presence or function in wheat. Moreover, there is very limited information for SUT gene regulation in stem WSC remobilization during grain filling under drought. Therefore, the aim of this study was to determine the structure of the SUT1-5 genes in wheat AA, BB and DD genomes, and to determine any differential SUT gene expression in the shoot (stem, sheath, rachis, lemma) and grain during grain filling under irrigated and drought field environments.

Sucrose is the primary product of photosynthesis and the most prevalent long-distance translocatable sugar in higher plants. It has been demonstrated that the decrease of sucrose transport from source to sink tissues can suppress photosynthesis and growth of the plant, while the increase of sink demand can enhance photosynthetic activity and crop productivity (Ainsworth and Bush 2011; Ayre 2011; Bihmidine et al. 2013; Grifths and Paul 2017; Hall et al. 1977;

Hodgkinson 1974; Kaschuk et al. 2010; McCormick et al. 2006; Paul and Foyer 2001; Paul and Pellny 2003; Sheen 1990; Stitt et al. 2010). Thus, it has been proposed that crop yields can be enhanced by promoting the photosynthate transport from the source tissue to the sink tissue (Ainsworth and Bush 2011; Ayre 2011; McCormick et al. 2006).

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are energydependent sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporters which mediate the transport of sucrose across plasma membranes, leading the sugar into and out of the source and sink tissues through phloem (Riesmeier et al. 1992; Sauer 2007). This property enables us to genetically regulate the distribution of photosynthesized carbon, thus enhancing the yield of the target product. For example, downregulation of StSUT4 gene in potato resulted in early fowering and increased tuber yield (Chincinska et al. 2008). The use of endosperm-specifc promoter to direct the expression of $H \nu S U T I$ in barley led to an enhanced sugarabsorption capacity of the seeds and an increased content of storage protein in seeds (Weichert et al. 2010). A phloem cell-specifc expression of Arabidopsis AtSUC2 to promote the sucrose load resulted in an increased yield of rice (Wang et al. 2015).

Cotton is a leading natural fber crop and also an important oil crop in the word (Jefrey et al. 2007). Cotton fber is derived from single epidermal cells of seed. The fber is composed of nearly pure cellulose, the naturally occurring polymer of glucose. During the development of cotton seeds, the phloemunloaded sugar is transported outwards to fber cells for cell elongation and cellulose biosynthesis while inwards to flial tissues for the development of embryo and the biosynthesis of oil and starch (Jiang et al. 2012; Ruan 2005; Xu et al. 2012). This opposite transporting direction provides a dilemma to the regulation of the phloem-unloaded assimilate partition between fbers and the seed: in the case of limited carbon supply, enhancing of the abundance of fber usually leads to smaller seeds, while increasing of the seed size often results in a decrease of fber productivity of the seed (Miller et al. 1958; Miller and Rawlings 1967; Zeng et al. 2007; Zhao et al. 2015). To solve this trade-of problem, the best way is providing more supply to meet the demand of both sides.

Zea mays is a $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ crop, which is featured with high water-use efciency and high-yield potential (Usha et al. 2015). Previous studies demonstrated that $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ grasses (e.g., maize and sorghum) display a higher rate of export of photosynthates than $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ grasses (e.g., wheat and barley) (Grodzinski et al. 1998). ZmSut1, a maize sucrose/proton symporter, has an important function in sugar distribution (Aoki 1999; Baker et al. 2016). This sugar transport protein can efectively mediate sucrose uptake into the phloem in source tissue, as well as release the sugar from the phloem vessels into sink tissue (Baker et al. 2016; Carpaneto et al. 2005). Accordingly, Baker et al. (2016) suggest a potential of using SUTs from $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ plants to engineer $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ photosynthesis and carbon transport in $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ plants.

To see whether and how the ectopic expression of a $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ SUT in cotton is able to increase the efcacy of sucrose transport, thus enhancing the fiber and seed yield, in this study, we constructed transgenic cotton in which the ZmSUT1 gene is under control of a senescence-inducible and seed coat-specifc promoter, respectively. Our data demonstrated that seed coat-specifc expression of ZmSUT1 led to an increase of sugar accumulation in fbers and bolls, and elevated both fber and seed yield of cotton; while senescence-induced expression of the gene resulted in an increase of sugar accumulation in leaves and a delay of leaf senescence, but decreased the yield.

Sucrose is the main product of carbon photoassimilation in source leaves of plant species, and is transported to sink organs to support growth and storage. It is a metabolically inert molecule, and thus ideally suited for long-distance transport from source to sink organs. Phloem loading of sucrose produced in source leaves is an important longdistance transport process, as a high concentration of sucrose in the phloem creates a hydrostatic pressure gradient that enables the mass flow of sucrose to sink organs (van Bel 2003; Turgeon 2010). Of the well characterized phloem loading strategies, the apoplastic loading process relies on the function of phloem plasma membrane-localized sucrose transporter (SUT) to load sucrose from the apoplastic space into the phloem. This type of phloem loading requires energy, since sucrose needs to be moved against its concentration gradient from lower concentrations in the apoplastic space to higher into the phloem companion cell/sieve element complex. In contrast, in the diffusion strategy, the higher sucrose levels in mesophyll cells than phloem tissues is a driving force of sucrose loading in the phloem (Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012).

Since the discovery of the first SUT genes, Spinacia oleracea SUT1 and Solanum tuberosum SUT1 (StSUT1) from spinach and potato, respectively, a large number of SUTs have been subsequently identified throughout the plant kingdom (Riesmeier et al. 1994; Kühn et al. 1996; Gottwald et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Slewinski et al. 2009; Srivastava et al. 2009; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012). The critical role of SUTs in phloem loading has been examined in characterizations of SUT transgenic or mutant plants. For instance, reduced expression of StSUT1 in potato led to accumulation of high soluble sugars and starch, thus resulting in a significant reduction in root development and tuber yield (Riesmeier et al. 1994). Arabidopsis atsuc2, a mutant of sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporter Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose carrier 2 (AtSUC2) showed severe growth retardation (Gottwald et al. 2000; Srivastava et al. 2009). In maize, the Zea mays SUT1 mutant accumulated high concentrations of sugars, and showed growth retardation including reduced plant height, fewer leaves, and stunted tassel development (Slewinski et al. 2009).

To date, a large number of SUTs in dicot plant species have been extensively studied, but cereal SUTs including rice have not been well characterized. To understand the function of the rice SUT genes, Oryza sativa SUT1 (OsSUT1) to OsSUT5, we employed a simple and efficient growth restoration assay by introducing OsSUTs into the heterologous mutant atsuc2, which shows the typical growth retardation phenotype of apoplastic phloem loading mutants. To this end, we generated 10 constructs by combining five OsSUT genes and two different promoters, the native phloem-specific promoter of AtSUC2 (pAtSUC2) and the constitutive Cauliflower Mosaic Virus 35S promoter (pCaMV35S). We phenotypically and metabolically characterized all $p A t S U C 2 { : } O s S U T s$ and $p C a M V 3 5 S { : } O s S U T s$ in transgenic atsuc2 plants. On the basis of these results, we provide clear evidence that OsSUT1 has a phloem loader function.

In this study, to identify rice SUTs that can function as phloem loaders, we introduced OsSUT1 to OsSUT5 genes under the control of two different promoters, pAtSUC2 and pCaMV35S , into the Arabidopsis atsuc2-1 mutant that lacks the Arabidopsis major phloem loader AtSUC2 and displays a severe growth retardation phenotype. Our phenotype restoration assay clearly revealed that of the tested ten constructs, only pAtSUC2:OsSUT1 can complement the Arabidopsis atsuc2-1 mutant (Figs. 1 and 2). We found that strong expression of OsSUT1 in pAtSUC2:OsSUT1 transgenic atsuc2-1 fully complemented the growth defect, while weak expression partially rescued atsuc2-1. In fully complemented lines, levels of soluble sugars, glucose, fructose, and sucrose, and starch were nearly restored to those of WT (Fig. 3). Levels of primary carbohydrate metabolites in the partial complementation lines were intermediates between those of WT and atsuc2-1 (Fig. 3). Thus, our current data provide clear evidence that rice OsSUT1 is an ortholog of the Arabidopsis AtSUC2 functioning as an apoplastic phloem loader.

None of the other OsSUTs, OsSUT2, OsSUT3, OsSUT4, or OsSUT5, was able to rescue atsuc2-1. Previous studies showed that types I and II SUTs are localized to the plasma membrane, while type III SUTs are associated with the tonoplast. Dicot and monocot plants utilize type I SUTs and type II SUTs, respectively, for phloem loading (Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012). The present study showed that OsSUT1, a type II SUT, rescued the growth defect of the Arabidopsis mutant atsuc2, a type I SUT. This further supports the idea that type I and II SUTs evolved similar phloem loading transporter capabilities (Reinders et al. 2012). Of the five rice SUTs, four OsSUTs are categorized as type II, while OsSUT2 belongs to type III. Type II OsSUTs are further divided into two subcategories, IIA (OsSUT4) and IIB (OsSUT1, OsSUT3, and OsSUT5). The monocot type IIB branch of SUTs shows similar high-affinity uptake to the eudicot type I SUTs, including AtSUC2, which are high-affinity/low-capacity transporters. In contrast, type IIA branch members, including OsSUT4, possess a longer Nterminal and central loop sequence with a lower affinity for sucrose (Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012).

Of the rice type IIB SUTs, OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 did not rescue atsuc2, unlike OsSUT1. OsSUT5 can be further classified to a subgroup of monocot SUTs (Kühn and Grof 2010). In biochemical analysis, OsSUT5 showed a higher substrate affinity, less substrate specificity and less pH dependence compared with all type II SUTs (Sun et al. 2010). This may suggest a divergent function of OsSUT5 distinct from phloem loading of OsSUT1. OsSUT3 was found to be highly expressed in pollen development in an in situ localization assay (Ngampanya et al. 2002; Takeda et al. 2001) and its biochemical kinetic properties remain largely unknown. Nonetheless, currently we cannot exclude the possibility that OsSUT3 and/or OsSUT5 can function in phloem loading in planta.

It is also noteworthy that pCaMV35S:OsSUT1, as well as the other pCaMV35S:OsSUT transgenic lines, did not rescue atsuc2-1. It has been reported that organ/tissue-specific promoters can enhance transgene function by activating its expression in the particular areas. For instance, the seedspecific expression of the potato sucrose symporter, StSUT1, under the control of the pea Vicilin promoter enhanced sucrose uptake and thereby growth of pea cotyledon (Rosche et al. 2002; Zakharov et al. 2004). Expression of the barley (Hordeum vulgare) SUT, HvSUT1 under the control of the endosperm-specific Hordien B1 promoter in wheat (Triticum aestivum) increased grain weight by enhancing sucrose uptake capacity (Weichert et al. 2010). A recent study demonstrated that expression of the AtSUC2 under the control of the phloem companion cell-specific PP2-A1 promoter in rice enhanced phloem loading and thereby sucrose transport capability, resulting in high yield (Wang et al. 2015). pCaMV35S is a well-documented constitutive promoter with expression in all different tissues. Thus, our results suggest that phloem-specific rather than ubiquitous localization of SUTs is a prerequisite for their phloem loading capability in planta.

That OsSUT1 can function as a phloem loader is consistent with previous observations that OsSUT1 is confined to the phloem of the vegetative tissues involved in long-distance transport via phloem reloading of sucrose leaked from the phloem during grain filling (Scofield et al. 2007a, b). Antisense transgenic rice plants of OsSUT1 did not accumulate sucrose, lacking any visible symptoms (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002). In the present study, we similarly found that the anther culture-derived ossut1 homozygous mutants were indistinguishable from WT during vegetative growth, and did not accumulate soluble sugars and starch (Fig. 4). Thus, previous studies and our data suggest that the OsSUT1 apoplastic loading process may not be the predominant form of phloem loading in source leaves of rice under normal growth conditions. Nonetheless, it is probable that this apoplastic loading by OsSUT1 may function as an alternative loading mechanism that can compensate symplastic loading by OsSUT2 (see below) under environmental stress or other conditions that have not been tested.

In this regard, it is noteworthy that the ossut2 rice mutant of tonoplast-localized OsSUT2 displayed a severe growth defect, and accumulated sucrose in the leaves. Thus, the decreased transport of sucrose from the vacuole lumen to the cytosol in ossut2 can interfere with its translocation to sink organs and plant growth (Eom et al. 2011, 2012). Our current data also supports the diffusion process of phloem loading in rice in which the tonoplast SUT, OsSUT2, controls mesophyll cytosolic sucrose concentration, and therefore functions as a valve regulating sucrose flux into the phloem (Eom et al. 2012). Nevertheless, detailed characterization of single and multiple mutants of the as-yet-uncharacterized OsSUT3, OsSUT4, and OsSUT5 we generated is needed to determine their precise function.

Sucrose is the main product of carbon photoassimilation in source leaves of plant species, and is transported to sink organs to support growth and storage. It is a metabolically inert molecule, and thus ideally suited for long-distance transport from source to sink organs. Phloem loading of sucrose produced in source leaves is an important longdistance transport process, as a high concentration of sucrose in the phloem creates a hydrostatic pressure gradient that enables the mass flow of sucrose to sink organs (van Bel 2003; Turgeon 2010). Of the well characterized phloem loading strategies, the apoplastic loading process relies on the function of phloem plasma membrane-localized sucrose transporter (SUT) to load sucrose from the apoplastic space into the phloem. This type of phloem loading requires energy, since sucrose needs to be moved against its concentration gradient from lower concentrations in the apoplastic space to higher into the phloem companion cell/sieve element complex. In contrast, in the diffusion strategy, the higher sucrose levels in mesophyll cells than phloem tissues is a driving force of sucrose loading in the phloem (Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012).

Since the discovery of the first SUT genes, Spinacia oleracea SUT1 and Solanum tuberosum SUT1 (StSUT1) from spinach and potato, respectively, a large number of SUTs have been subsequently identified throughout the plant kingdom (Riesmeier et al. 1994; Kühn et al. 1996; Gottwald et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003; Lim et al. 2006; Slewinski et al. 2009; Srivastava et al. 2009; Kühn and Grof 2010; Eom et al. 2012; Reinders et al. 2012). The critical role of SUTs in phloem loading has been examined in characterizations of SUT transgenic or mutant plants. For instance, reduced expression of StSUT1 in potato led to accumulation of high soluble sugars and starch, thus resulting in a significant reduction in root development and tuber yield (Riesmeier et al. 1994). Arabidopsis atsuc2, a mutant of sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporter Arabidopsis thaliana sucrose carrier 2 (AtSUC2) showed severe growth retardation (Gottwald et al. 2000; Srivastava et al. 2009). In maize, the Zea mays SUT1 mutant accumulated high concentrations of sugars, and showed growth retardation including reduced plant height, fewer leaves, and stunted tassel development (Slewinski et al. 2009).

To date, a large number of SUTs in dicot plant species have been extensively studied, but cereal SUTs including rice have not been well characterized. To understand the function of the rice SUT genes, Oryza sativa SUT1 (OsSUT1) to OsSUT5, we employed a simple and efficient growth restoration assay by introducing OsSUTs into the heterologous mutant atsuc2, which shows the typical growth retardation phenotype of apoplastic phloem loading mutants. To this end, we generated 10 constructs by combining five OsSUT genes and two different promoters, the native phloem-specific promoter of AtSUC2 (pAtSUC2) and the constitutive Cauliflower Mosaic Virus 35S promoter (pCaMV35S). We phenotypically and metabolically characterized all $p A t S U C 2 { : } O s S U T s$ and $p C a M V 3 5 S { : } O s S U T s$ in transgenic atsuc2 plants. On the basis of these results, we provide clear evidence that OsSUT1 has a phloem loader function.

In silico analyses revealed that the three members of the tomato SUT family are structurally conserved but have significant differences in sequence, including their predicted subcellular localization, exon-intron and promoter region organizations. It suggests a functional specialization within this gene family. Only SlSUT4 was characterized as a vacuolar localized SlSUT, probably due to the stretch of hydrophobic amino acids at the first 35 residues in the N-terminus and the NAYF motif at position 175, which seems to be reminiscent of NPIR/NXYF motifs known in vacuolar targeting (Xiang et al. 2013). SlSUT1 has 4 exons, while its potato ortholog StSUT1 has a similar structure with 5 exons (Liesche et al. 2011). In contrast, SlSUT2 has 14 exons, compared to potato StSUT2, which has 9 exons, while the SlSUT4 potato ortholog StSUT4 has 6 exons (Liesche et al. 2011). These variations in the gene structure of SUTs suggest specific adaptations to the physiological and functional demands in each species and can be attributed to evolutionary adaptations, such as selective pressure in different environmental contexts, or that influence the way the plants manage the transport and distribution of sucrose (Chincinska et al. 2008; Grof and $\mathrm { K u } 2 0 1 0$ ).

Phylogenetic analyses suggest that SlSUT4 and SlSUT2 are closer to each other than to SlSUT1, reflecting structural and functional similarities that indicate a closer evolutionary relationship (Reinders et al. 2012). SlSUT1 is mainly involved in phloem loading (efflux) from source tissues such as leaves, facilitating the export of sucrose to other parts of the plant (Reuscher et al. 2014). SlSUT2 participates in the transport (unloading/influx) of sucrose to cells of sink tissues, such as fruits and roots, while SlSUT4 has a less clear function, but with reported involvement in both efflux and influx of sucrose in the plasma membrane and tonoplast of cells of sink tissues, probably contributing to the storage of sucrose in the vacuole and regulation of sugar levels in the cytosol (Schneider et al. 2012; Garg et al. 2022; Salvi et al. 2022).

All the SlSUTs contain the conserved domain of the GPH_sucrose superfamily. The GPH_sucrose domain is essential for the binding and transport of sucrose across cell membranes. These domains have evolved to specifically recognize and translocate the sucrose molecule, using the proton gradient to facilitate transport (Salvi et al. 2022). The transmembrane domains found are essential for anchoring the transporters in the cell membrane, creating a channel through which sucrose can be transported. They form a hydrophobic pathway that allows the controlled movement of sucrose, coupled to the transport of $\mathrm { H } +$ ions (protons). The presence of the conserved GPH_sucrose domain and the transmembrane domains in their sequences indicates that all the SlSUT are functional proteins and play a role in the import and export of sucrose to sink and source organs, respectively (Arefin et al. 2020). Another conserved motif found is the diacid (DTD), located in the seventh transmembrane domain, which plays a role in the dimerization of transporters and their functional activity (Garg et al. 2022). Mutation of this motif can affect transport efficiency, suggesting that interactions mediated by this motif are essential for the functionality of transporters.

Protein interaction network analysis indicates that SlUTs play a central role in plant adaptation to water deficit, facilitating both transport and metabolic regulation of carbohydrates. The ability to connect different clusters, which represent distinct biological processes, suggests that the SlSUTs, especially SlSUT1 and SlSUT4, function as control points in the network, optimizing the response to water stress in tomato plants. This metabolic and functional interconnectivity highlights the importance of SUTs in the adaptive response of plants, evidencing that a coordinated regulation between transport and metabolism is crucial for survival in environments with low water availability. The SlSUT1-associated SUS3 is an enzyme that cleaves sucrose into UDP-glucose and fructose, playing a central role in sucrose metabolism, especially under abiotic stress conditions. In tomato, overexpression of SUS3 has been shown to increase cold resistance during the seedling stage (Khan et al. 2023).

The presence of cis-acting regulatory elements responsive to water deficit (ABRE, TC-rich repeats, MBS) and hormonal regulation (ERE, G-BOX, TATC-box, TCA-element and TGA-element) in the promoter region of SlSUTs corroborates with other data previously reported in S. lycopersicum, Oryza sativa and A. thaliana (Ibraheem et al. 2010; Arefin et al. 2020) and our expression data. These elements play a role in drought-inducible gene expression related to drought response and response to hormonal control (Arefin et al. 2020).

WT, rin, and Nr Micro-Tom phenotyping revealed the elicitation of acclimation responses by water deficit treatment at the fruit ripening stage in all plants. The $A , g s$ , and $E$ values significantly decreased as water deficit progressed, concomitantly with a significant increase in the activity of antioxidant enzymes and soluble sugars in leaves and fruits, with some variations observed between WT and mutants. In response to water scarcity, plants close their stomata to reduce water loss, limiting the entry of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ for photosynthesis (Gururani et al. 2015). This effect leads to an accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which in turn induces the activation of antioxidant systems, such as the activity of the enzymes APX, GPX and SOD, to minimize cellular damage (Rai et al. 2021). Plants also accumulate osmoprotectants, including soluble sugars such as glucose, fructose and sucrose, to maintain osmotic homeostasis and mitigate damage to cellular components induced by water stress (Ripoll et al. 2016). Our results demonstrated that fruits and leaves accumulated significantly higher levels of glucose, fructose and sucrose under water deficit conditions, with the rin and Nr mutations abrogating this effect for fructose and glucose in leaf and fruit, respectively. This suggests an increase in the synthesis and transport of sugars to tolerate stress (Cai et al. 2019).

Gene expression analysis revealed that all SlSUT genes were significantly up-regulated in response to water deficit in fruits and leaves of the different genotypes, except for rin that showed no significant water deficit effect on SlSUT1 and SlSUT4 expression. These results suggest that the three SlSUTs contribute to the increased concentration of soluble sugars observed in fruits and leaves of the different Micro-Tom genotypes in response to water deficit, favoring the metabolic adjustment in these organs and the plant acclimatization responses under drought stress. Consistent with these observations are the previous studies demonstrating an up-regulation of (i) SlSUT4 and its potato StSUT4 and Arabidopsis AtSUC4 orthologs in leaves of seedlings subjected to water deficit and high temperature treatments, which correlated with the regulation of sugar status in leaves and stress signaling (Xu et al. 2018), (ii) AtSUC4 and AtSUC1, the respective ortholog of SlSUT1, in leaves, roots and whole seedlings in response to osmotic, high salinity, dehydration, low temperature and ABA treatments, whose loss-of-function mutations were revealed to act as important regulators in tolerance to abiotic stresses through the ABAdependent signaling pathway (Gong et al. 2015), and (iii) VvSUC27, VvSUC12 and $V \nu S U C I I$ , the respective orthologs of SlSUT1, − 2 and − 4, in grapevine seedling leaves treated with PEG-6000, which promoted sucrose metabolism and phytohormone synthesis (Cai et al. 2019).

Sucrose signaling has been shown to interact with several phytohormones, including ethylene, abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonic acid and gibberellin, triggering complex and interconnected sucrose signaling cascades (DuránSoria et al. 2020; Fei et al. 2020). In tomato fruits treated with exogenous sucrose, this sugar positively regulated the ripening process, mainly by triggering ethylene synthesis, consequently accelerating fruit ripening (Li et al. 2016). In kiwifruit, exogenous sucrose also promoted fruit ripening and the expression of the sucrose transporter genes AcSUT1 and AcSUT4, resulting in increased sucrose accumulation during fruit ripening (Fei et al. 2020). The significant correlation between SlSUT4 and SlETR2 expression from our co-expression analysis supports this relationship between ethylene perception and sucrose metabolism. Such a potential relationship is also implied by the simultaneous expression of AtETR2 and the sucrose synthase AtSUS4 in Arabidopsis (Garg et al. 2022). ETR2 is one of the ethylene receptors in plants that also plays a fundamental role in the signaling pathway of this hormone, acting as one of the receptors that perceive the presence of the hormone and trigger a series of events that lead to the activation of genes and specific cellular responses (Liu et al. 2020). For example, ethylene, perceived by receptors such as ETR2, regulates fruit ripening in species such as tomato, promoting the activation of genes that produce enzymes responsible for fruit softening and color changes (Binder 2020; Wilson et al. 2014). In addition, ethylene also induces senescence, activating genes that cause the degradation of chlorophyll and other cellular components, leading to yellowing of the leaves. In stress situations, signaling via ETR2 modulates the expression of defense and adaptation genes (Barry and Giovannoni 2007; Shakeel et al. 2013). Therefore, it is expected that the coexpression of SlSUT4 and SlETR2 contributes to processes such as fruit ripening and stress response, in which ethylene plays an important role in regulating the biochemical and molecular processes involved.

An integrated analysis of SlSUT gene expression, physiological parameters, and sugar accumulation reveals a clear interdependence between genotype and response to water deficit. In WT plants, water stress induced the expression of SlSUT1, SlSUT2, and SlSUT4 in both leaves and fruits, promoting the accumulation of glucose, fructose, and sucrose in these tissues, along with the increased activity of antioxidant enzymes, such as APX, GPX, and PAL, thus facilitating osmotic adjustment. In the rin mutant, the transcriptional response to stress was null in leaves for SlSUT1 and SlSUT4, which coincided with the absence of a significant increase in fructose and a reduction in PAL activity, suggesting that this mutation compromises the plant’s ability to respond to water stress in its source organs. In contrast, in the Nr mutant, SlSUT2 was also induced in roots, a pattern not observed in the other genotypes, and this was accompanied by increased APX, GPX, and PAL activities in fruits. This suggests a compensatory role in osmotic regulation and a possible genotype-specific adaptive response, potentially mediated by ethylene signaling. These findings indicate that hormonal regulation of fruit ripening may directly affect the differential expression of SlSUTs and, consequently, the plant’s physiological capacity to tolerate drought stress, particularly through modulation of sugar transport and accumulation in source-sink organs.

The identification of the conserved domains and motifs in all SlSUT proteins suggests that they share functions related to the transport of sucrose through cell membranes, with possible variations in the efficiency and specificity of this transport. The variations observed in their sequences reveal possible evolutionary and functional adaptations. Their interactions with other proteins involved in the carbohydrate metabolism and transport, together with their regulation by cis-acting regulatory elements associated with responses to abiotic stresses, highlight the role of these transporters in the response to abiotic stress in tomato. Their differentially regulated expression in response to water deficit in different source-sink organs and coexpression with the ethylene receptor SlETR2 also indicate an interconnection between sucrose and ethylene signaling, especially in the context of fruit ripening and stress response. A model of the effects of water deficit on SlSUTs is proposed in Fig. 9. According to the proposed model, water deficit induces the transcriptional activation of SlSUTs mainly in fruits and leaves, which contributes to the accumulation of soluble sugars in these organs necessary for osmoregulation and synthesis of other osmoprotectants in these organs, evidencing their function in the metabolic adjustment and plant acclimation responses. The rin and Nr mutations are able to abolish the drought stress effects on the expression of specific SlSUTs in leaves and roots, but not in fruits. These results provide a basis for future investigations into the functionality of each member of the SlSUT family in response to different environmental conditions and developmental stages of tomato fruit. Detailed functional studies using gene silencing and genome editing approaches will be essential to unravel the exact mechanisms by which each transporter influences sucrose metabolism and the response to drought stress. In addition, the connection between sucrose and ethylene signaling through the coexpression of SlSUT4 and SlETR2 deserves further investigation, given its potential in controlling fruit ripening and adaptation to drought stress.

## Drought tolerant varieties achieved by different mechanisms


Both Westonia and Kauz showed similar high levels of stem WSC. Previously, the stem WSC remobilization to grain under drought has been studied and the $I { - } F E H w 3$ gene was identified as a major gene involved in stem fructan degradation and the $I { - } F E H w 3$ Westonia allele contributed to high stem WSC remobilization efficiency to grain under terminal drought conditions. Kauz is also a drought tolerant variety with significantly higher seed number per spike compared to Westonia. Under irrigated and some drought conditions, the grain weight for both varieties did not show significant differences. The phenology shows that Westonia and Kauz had different mechanisms to achieve high yield under drought.

In the 2014 late sowing trial, based on the harvest data of $1 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ plots, the drought stress significantly reduced the final grain yield in both varieties and the total above ground biomass in Kauz. The GW of Kauz was relatively higher than that of Westonia (Fig. 1a) although there was no significant changes between varieties under both drought and irrigated conditions. Similar to previous results, Kauz showed higher kernel number per spike whereas Westonia remained a higher TGW (Fig. 1b).

In the current experiment, Kauz showed slightly higher levels of stem WSC at 12 and 19 DAA compared with Westonia (Fig. 1c). The sequence of different levels of stem WSC between varieties at 19 DAA coincided with the comparison results of the final grain yield. Our previous results proved that $I { - } F E H w 3$ Westonia type was one of the major contributors for high efficiency of stem WSC remobilization due to the speed of fructan degradation (Zhang et al. 2015). The high GW and stem WSC level in Kauz indicate that there should be other mechanisms in the process of stem WSC remobilization for Kauz to achieve high GW under drought and irrigated conditions.


## TaSUT1‑5 gene structures


To classify wheat SUTs, rice SUTs were used as anchors. Based on a similarity analysis at the amino acid sequence level to five SUTs in rice (Fig. 2), five groups of wheat SUTs (TaSUT1, TaSUT2, TaSUT3, TaSUT4 and TaSUT5) were identified. As previously described (Aoki et al. 2002), the TaSUT1 wheat group, including TaSUT1A, TaSUT1B, and TaSUT1D located on chromosome 4A, 4B and 4D, grouped together with OsSUT1 (Fig. 3). The rice SUT1 gene shows 14 exons and 13 introns while in the wheat genome, TaSUT1 group members show 13 exons and 12 introns (Fig. 4a). Unlike in rice (Aoki et al. 2002), the last two exons in SUT1 were not split in wheat. As previously reported (Deol et al. 2013), the TaSUT2 group including TaSUT2A, TaSUT2B and TaSUT2D located on chromosome 5A, 5B and 5D (Fig. 4b) were similar to OsSUT2. In rice, OsSUT2 included six exons and five introns, whereas the TaSUT2 family had five exons and four introns. Among the five SUT genes in rice, OsSUT3 was the largest gene being $9 . 8 \mathrm { ~ k b }$ . It included 12 exons and 11 introns (Fig. 4c). Most likely, the homologue genes (TaSUT3 group) to OsSUT3 in wheat are located on chromosome 1A and 1D (Figs. 3, 4c). TaSUT3 showed 11 exons and 10 introns. TaSUT3_1A had $4 7 \mathrm { k b }$ and $T a S U T 3 \_ I D$ had $3 4 \mathrm { k b }$ . The homologous gene in 1B was not identified. Similar to OsSUT1, the OsSUT4 gene had 14 exons and 13 introns (Fig. 4d). Correspondingly, the homologue gene family in wheat (TaSUT4 group) also had 14 exons and 13 introns and were located on 6A, 6B and 6D (Figs. 3, 4d). TaSUT4_6BL had the longest intron 1 among these three isoforms of TaSUT4. OsSUT5 had 13 exons and 12 introns. In wheat, the most identical genes to OsSUT5 were located on 2A, 2B and 2D (Figs. 3, 4e). TaSUT5 group showed nine exons and eight introns. Exons 4, 5 and 6 in OsSUT5 appeared to be combined as exon 4 in TaSUT5; similarly, exons 8 and 9 combined to exon 6, and exons 11 and 12 combined to exon 8 in TaSUT5, respectively.


## Different gene expression levels of TaSUT1–5 in shoot parts


For identifying the gene functions of the five SUT gene families in wheat, the gene expression levels of each SUT gene family in different organ samples during the grain filling period were investigated. Five specific pairs of primers to each of the five SUT gene groups located in a conserved sequence region within the group were used for gene expressions.

In the stem, among these five SUT gene groups, TaSUT1, TaSUT2 and TaSUT3 showed higher gene expression levels relative to TaSUT4 and TaSUT5 (Fig. 5a, f). The transcript fragment of TaSUT5 was not visible while that of TaSUT4 was evident at 3, 12, 19 and 31 DAA. TaSUT1 had consistently high expression levels compared to the other SUTs in the stems during grain filling (Fig. 5a, f). By contrast, TaSUT2, TaSUT3 and TaSUT4 tended to be expressed more in the middle grain filling period (Fig. 5a, f). The expression levels of TaSUT2 and TaSUT4 were markedly reduced at 25 DAA (Fig. 5f). Overall, these results present strong evidence that TaSUT1 is predominant in wheat stems.

As the sheath is the major organ for sucrose transportation from the leaf blade (carbon source) to the stem, sheath SUT gene expression was investigated. TaSUT1, TaSUT2 and TaSUT4 showed consistent expression levels across all sampling times and TaSUT1 and TaSUT2 were most strongly expressed overall. Similar to the stem, the highest gene expression of TaSUT3 occurred at 12 DAA, whereas gene expression of TaSUT5 was not detectable during the measurement period (Fig. 5b, f).

The rachis is the closest organ to the spikelets. Similar to the stem and sheath, the gene expression levels of TaSUT1 in the rachis were very pronounced and consistent across the sampling period. TaSUT3 also showed relatively high expression level to TaSUT1 before 19 DAA, wheras TaSUT2 was expressed strongly up to 12 DAA (Fig. 5c, f). TaSUT4 showed consistent low expression levels during grain filling. TaSUT5 was not detected.

The lemma is the second closest photosynthetic organ to the developing grain. During the early stage of grain filling, the lemma probably is a carbon source for seed development. During the period of grain filling, the predominant gene expression level of TaSUT1 in the lemma was similar to that in other organs. Unlike the stem, sheath, and rachis, TaSUT3 was highly expressed at 4 days before anthesis (DBA) and only weakly expressed after anthesis. TaSUT2 was highly expressed before 19 DAA as compared to TaSUT4, and the expression was greatly reduced at 25 DAA (Fig. 5d, f). The expression levels of TaSUT4 were consistent through the sampling time but at relatively low levels. TaSUT5 was not detected in the lemma.

During grain development, cell metabolism and rapid starch accumulation requires continued sucrose supply. Different from the other organs above, TaSUT1 gene expression levels were much more outstanding in grains (e.g. compare SUT1 to GAPDH expression in Fig. 5a–e) during all growth stages while the other SUT gene groups were poorly expressed (Fig.  5e, f). The TaSUT2 and TaSUT4 groups showed consistent gene expression levels whereas the expression of TaSUT3 was only noticeable at 12 DAA (Fig. 5e). Gene expression levels of TaSUT5 were detected at 25 and 31 DAA although the levels were very weak.

The gene expression levels of individual gene isoforms of SUT gene groups were revealed in an RNAseq analysis using stem tissues from the 2011 drought experiments (Fig. 6). Overall, SUT1 gene group exhibited the highest gene expression level among the five SUT gene groups (SUT5 group was not detect in the experiment). On average, SUT1_4D expression level was 12 and $4 9 \%$ higher than SUT1_4A and $S U T I \_ { 4 B }$ , respectively (Fig. 6a). Interestingly, SUT1 gene Westonia type was upregulated at 20 DAA under drought whereas there was no change in Kauz type (Fig. 6a). At 30 DAA, SUT1_4D of both varieties had significantly higher gene expression levels under drought compared to irrigated plots.

Relative to SUT1 genes, the expression levels of SUT2 gene group was 2.5 to sixfolds lower (Fig. 6b). Among the three isoforms of TaSUT2 genes, the gene expression levels of $T a S U T 2 _ { - } S D$ was 2 and 3 times higher than TaSUT2_5A and $T a S U T 2 \_ S B$ , respectively.

Only $S U T 3 _ { - } I D$ gave gene expression readings while $S U T 3 _ { - } I A$ was not detected (Fig. 6c). The gene expression levels of $T a S U T 3 \_ I D$ were almost tenfolds lower compared to the SUT1 gene group, and no difference was evident between varieties and treatments. The gene expression levels of SUT4 group was as low as the levels of $S U T 3 _ { - } I D$ (Fig. 6d). There was a slight difference in SUT4 gene expression between varieties. The SUT4 gene in Kauz was expressed at a slightly higher level under irrigated conditions compared to drought while SUT4_6B in Westonia was the opposite.


## Genotypic variations in SUT1 gene expression and grain assimilation


The results of the semi-qRT-PCR and RNA-seq above revealed that SUT1 was the predominant sucrose transporter in all tissues analysed in Westonia under irrigation. In parallel, the five SUT gene families were examined in Kauz under the same irrigated condition. The significant high levels of SUT1 gene expression were also present in semi-qRT-PCR results (data not shown). Therefore, for further investigating the roles of SUT1 gene in the stem WSC remobilization system, materials from the drought experiments in 2014 were used for qRT-PCR study. Since the wheat stem is the major carbon source for grain filling, stem (sheath included) and grain were examined in this study.

In the stem, SUT1 gene expression was higher in Kauz than in Westonia at 19 DAA under drought treatment (Fig.  7a). Nevertheless, under the same treatment, the reverse results appeared at 25 DAA. Greater expression level was detected in Westonia while it was significantly repressed in Kauz under drought. Under irrigation, the SUT1 gene expression of Kauz increased significantly at 25 DAA whereas it remained unchanged in Westonia.

In grain, the SUT1 gene expression level in Kauz increased to a significantly high level under irrigation at 25 DAA and was retained at 31 DAA, while it increased gradually until 31 DAA then declined under drought (Fig. 7b). Different patterns were found in Westonia. Under drought, SUT1 gene expression was upregulated to a high level at 25 DAA then maintained at the same level whereas under irrigation the level increased later (31 DAA). Overall, SUT1 gene expression in the grain was 1.5 to twofolds higher than that in the stem, and in Kauz. It was greater than that in Westonia under irrigation.

In Westonia, the grain weight of the main spike highly increased under drought compared with the irrigated treatment and the SUT1 gene was upregulated at 25 DAA. On the other hand, in Kauz, the peak value of GW was at 31 DAA and the SUT1 gene expression level was maintained on a high plateau for 2 weeks in irrigated plants (Fig. 7c). The patterns of TGW were similar to the GW in both varieties and treatments. Meanwhile, the KN of Kauz was significantly higher under irrigation than under drought while it was similar between treatments in Westonia (Fig. 7d, e).

The grain weight, TGW and KN were significantly associated with the levels of the SUT1 gene expression (Fig. 8). Under drought, in Westonia, the significantly positive correlations between the levels of SUT1 gene expression and GW, TGW and KN were $0 . 6 2 ^ { * * }$ $( \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1 )$ , $0 . 6 3 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $( \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1 )$ , and $0 . 3 ^ { * }$ $\mathrm { ( P < 0 . 0 5 ) }$ , respectively, whereas, under irrigation, the correlation levels were relatively lower being $0 . 3 5 ^ { * }$ $( \mathrm { P } { < } 0 . 0 1 )$ and $0 . 2 7 ^ { * }$ $( \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1 )$ for GW and TGW, respectively. No correlation was detected in KN under irrigation (Fig. 8a, c, e). In contrast, higher correlations were observed in irrigated Kauz plants. For example, the correlations between the levels of SUT1 gene expression and GW, TGW and KN were $0 . 7 7 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $( \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1 )$ ), $0 . 8 1 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $\mathrm { ( P < 0 . 0 1 ) }$ , $0 . 5 5 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $( \mathrm { P } < 0 . 0 1 )$ under irrigation in Kauz, compared to $0 . 5 5 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $( \mathrm { P } { < } 0 . 0 1 )$ , $0 . 6 1 ^ { \ast \ast }$ $( \mathrm { P } { < } 0 . 0 1 )$ and $0 . 2 9 ^ { * }$ $\mathrm { ( P < 0 . 0 5 ) }$ , respectively, under drought (Fig. 8b, d, f).

## New sucrose transporter genes revealed in wheat


The homologous genes and partial cDNA sequences of the rice SUT genes (Aoki et al. 2003) were located in wheat in public databases and the corresponding SUT gene families, named TaSUT1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, were identified. This is the first study to identify the gene structures of TaSUT3, 4 and 5 in wheat while TaSUT1 and 2 have been described previously (Aoki et al. 2002; Deol et al. 2013).

## Main contributor—TaSUT1


Among the SUT gene family, the SUT1 gene function was essential in phloem loading and storage uptake (Wang et al. 2016). In our semi-qRT-PCR experiments, we examined stem, leaf sheath, rachis, lemma, and grain during grain filling time with GAPDH as the internal standard. TaSUT1 showed consistent high expression levels in all sampled organs and across all growth stages from pre-anthesis to grain maturity, and the expression was particularly high in developing grain. The RNA-seq results in stems under drought and irrigated treatments enabled individual gene expression patterns of each isoform of four SUT gene families (no information was obtained for the SUT5 group due to very low signals) to be obtained. The results provide further evidence of the importance of the SUT1 gene group in wheat development. In rice, high expression of OsSUT1 was observed in the leaf blade and leaf sheath before anthesis, and in developing grains until 15 DAA (Hirose et al. 1999; Aoki et al. 2003). In barley, HvSUT1, the homologous gene to OsSUT1, showed similar high expression patterns to OsSUT1 during grain development (Weschke et al. 2000). In maize, ZmSUT1 was highly expressed in the seedling root and leaf (Usha et al. 2015). The high transcription level of TaSUT1 was also found in wheat grain in glasshouse experiments (Mukherjee et al. 2015). Our qRT-PCR results further confirmed the high gene expression level of TaSUT1 in developing grain in comparison to the stem. This indicates the important function of TaSUT1 in sucrose transportation. In rice, antisense RNA repression of OsSUT1 did not influence plant growth, photosynthesis, or carbohydrate assimilation, indicating that OsSUT1 seriously affected grain yield, but it may not be essential for sucrose loading into the phloem (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002). In contrast, a mutation of ZmSUT1 resulted in a defective phenotype in which leaves accumulated leaf carbohydrates and senesced early, flowering was delayed and plants were shortened (Slewinski et al. 2009). The decreased sucrose export from the leaves of the mutated Zmsut1 plants indicated that the ZmSUT1 gene functions in phloem loading in mature leaves (Slewinski et al. 2009). Taken together, these results suggest that the homologous family of the SUT1 gene may have different functions in different cereal species. In barley, the $H \nu S U T I$ is mainly localized in the endospermal transfer layer and the cells of the nucellar projections that serve as sites of sucrose exchange between the maternal and the filial organs (Weschke et al. 2000). The high gene expression level of TaSUT1 in developing wheat grain may mirror the function of $H \nu S U T I$ in barley since wheat and barley are closely related.


## The second contributor—TaSUT2


Compared with TaSUT1, the gene expression level of TaSUT2 was lower in the stem, sheath, rachis, and developing grain across the whole sampling period. The RNA-seq results showed that the TaSUT2 gene exprssion was 2.5 to sixfolds lower relative to the TaSUT1 family in the stem. In the study of Deol et al. (2013), TaSUT2 expression was very low in grain (1.4 unit), about 2 and 3 units in the peduncle and sheath, respectively, and ranged from 3 to 5 units in the lemma (Deol et al. 2013). Except for the functional flag leaf (8–10 units), the TaSUT2 gene expression levels in the lemma were the highest of the plant parts measured (Deol et al. 2013). Similar results were found in barley, where HvSUT2 gene expression level was $2 5 \%$ less than that of HvSUT1 before 15 DAA in developing grain (Weschke et al. 2000). In maize leaves, the expression level of ZmSUT2 showed similar high levels to ZmSUT1 (Usha et al. 2015). Recently, Leach et al. (2017) revealed that ZmSUT2 is highly expressed in a range of tissues and a diurnal cycling pattern of gene expression was observed in leaves. In rice, OsSUT2 is located in leaf tonoplasts (Eom et al. 2011). Deol et al. (2013) suggest that the localized expression in mesophyll cells indicates an intracellular translocation function. The high expresson level in the flag leaf during early grain filling in previous studies, and the relatively high gene expression levels as compared to TaSUT3 and TaSUT4 in the stem, sheath, rachis, and lemma in our study, suggesting that the TaSUT2 gene may compensate TaSUT1 function in sucrose loading and unloading. In rice, a high sugar level was detected in the mutated OsSUT2 leaf and the shortage of sugar translocation resulted in a large reduction in plant height, TGW and tiller number (Eom et al. 2011). These results indicate that the TaSUT2 group may have crucial roles in regulating sucrose remobilization between the vacuole and the cytosol.


## Expression of TaSUT3, TaSUT4 and TaSUT5


TaSUT3 exclusively showed significant expression before anthesis in the lemma and relative high expression at 12 DAA in the caryopsis and the other parts assayed. These results hint that TaSUT3 may have specific functions in pollination and seed setting. In general, compared to TaSUT1, the expression levels of TaSUT3 and 4 were relatively lower. TaSUT4 consistently displayed similar low gene expression patterns in all the shoot parts at each sampling time (Fig. 5). The transcript level of TaSUT5 was not noticeable in most organ samples except for very low levels that were detected in late developing grains. Low gene expression levels of TaSUT4 and 5 were also reported previously (Mukherjee et al. 2015). However, the expression levels of TaSUT3, 4 and 5 in wheat were different from the gene expression of OsSUT3, 4 and 5 since their transcript levels, in general, were similar to OsSUT1. In rice, OsSUT3 and OsSUT5 were expressed similarly at high levels in different parts of the shoot and developing grain while OsSUT4 gene expression level was high only in sink leaves (Aoki et al. 2003). These results further suggested different SUT roles in sucrose translocation (Aoki et al. 2003). In maize, ZmSUT4 showed similar gene expression levels for leaves and roots while ZmSUT5 was more highly expressed in roots (Usha et al.

2015). The results suggested that ZmSUT4 may act as a housekeeper gene.


## Yield contributions based on genotypic variation of TaSUT1


The results of our study revealed that the SUT1 gene expression levels changed with genotype, growth stage, and treatment. Drought stress could upregulate the SUT1 of Westonia type at 25 DAA in the stem and grain but could repress the SUT1 of Kauz type at the same growth stage in comparison with irrigated plants. The upregulated gene expression levels of TaSUT1_4A, 4B and 4D also were evident at 20 DAA in Westonia stems under drought in our RNA-seq data. Under irrigation, significant differences in SUT1 gene expression levels appeared between varieties. The SUT1 gene expression levels were significantly associated with the grain weight, TGW and KN in Kauz under both irrigation and drought conditions and the correlation values were all higher in irrigated plants. On the other hand, the correlation values in Westonia were higher under drought than under irrigated conditions. The results indicate that the SUT1 gene contributes to high grain yield in Kauz in irrigated environments while the SUT1 Westonia type contributes more to grain filling under drought stress. For improving grain yield under both drought and well-watered conditions, SUT1 gene markers of the Westonia and Kauz types should be generated for high sucrose remobilization efficiency.

Two contradicting results were reported in seedling drought studies. In rice seedlings, among OsSUT1-5 genes, only OsSUT2 was up-regulated in rice seedlings under drought stress (Ibraheem et al. 2011). In contrast, in a similar seedling drought experiment, all SUT1 genes of rice, wheat, maize and barley were upregulated (Xu et al. 2018). The inconsistent results indicate likely different mechanisms being induced in different drought experiments. In a recent water lodging study in sorghum, SUT gene expression levels remained the same while the gene expression levels of one of the sweet transporters increased notably between treatments (Mizuno et al. 2018). The gene functions of sweet transporters should be investigated under drought in wheat (Eom et al. 2015).

In our previous study, the sucrose levels in the stem were similar between treatments and varieties (Zhang et al. 2015). Thus, the stem sucrose level might not be the cause for the different levels of SUT1 gene expression in stems. However, the growth stage for the high level of SUT1 gene expression in Westonia under drought coincided with that of $I { - } F E H w 3$ . The $\jmath _ { - } F E H w 3$ high gene expression occurred at $2 4 ~ \mathrm { D A A }$ in Westonia, which was the same time for significant stem fructan decline and fructose increase (Zhang et al. 2015). The increased fructose level may promote the enhanced SUT1 gene expression in Westonia. Nevertheless, the explanation did not apply to Kauz. Alternatively, SUT1 gene expression could be driven by the level of ABA in grain as the expression level was more pronounced in grain and the ABA levels were almost ten times higher in wheat grain compared to leaves (Guóth et al. 2009).

Drought stress induced ABA accumulation and the ABA level was positively associated with high grain-filling rates (Guóth et  al. 2009). The appropriate level of ABA can enhance sucrose uptake while high ABA levels can reduce sucrose uptake (Zhu et al. 2011). In developing grain, the exogenous ABA significantly reduced the transcription level of TaSUT1_4A and TaSUT1_4B, but not TaSUT1_4D which was the major transporter (Mukherjee et al. 2015). The high level of SUT1 gene expression in grain indicates that sucrose reloading to grain is crucial to the transporting roles of vegetative tissues.

In agreement with the study of Mukherjee et al. (2015), the highest gene expression levels of TaSUT1_4D were also detected in our stem tissues. However, gene expression levels for individual isoforms of TaSUT1 and TaSUT2 differed slightly in stems. For example, different from grain, the gene expression level of TaSUT1_4A was higher than that of TaSUT1_4B. Similar trends were found for TaSUT2 in the D genome which were expressed the most, followed by the A and B genomes. Differences in SUT1 and 2 gene expression levels between stems and grain need further investigation.

In this study on wheat, since samples were taken during the day between 11:00 to 17:00, their gene expression patterns over the diural cycle were not investigated. Whether sucrose transport may be more active during the evening and night, as recently reported in maize (Leach et al. 2017), requires investigation.

It is hypothesised that TaSUT3 may contribute to pollination and seed setting. Group TaSUT5 does not seem to have an important role in wheat plants during the growth stages analysed. The high gene expression of TaSUT1 in grain and the correlation with the grain filling demonstrated the crucial role for TaSUT1 in sucrose reloading to grain and high yield. Significant differences in TaSUT1 gene expression between treatments and varieties indicate the genotypic variations towards two different soil moisture levels. Further molecular study is required for gene identification. Overall, our study provides increased understanding of gene functions of five SUT groups in wheat and builds a base for further SUT studies. The revealed SUT gene structure and the different gene expression levels require further SUT gene marker development for the purpose of high efficiency of stem WSC remobilization to grain under drought, and high grain yield.

Sucrose, synthesized in mature leaves via photosynthesis, is the primary carbohydrate transported to sink tissues such as roots, young leaves, fowers, and seeds (Wang et al. 2021). This transport is mediated by sucrose transporters (SUTs), which are sucrose– $\mathbf { \cdot H ^ { + } }$ symporters located on the plasma or vacuolar membranes and belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) with 12 transmembrane helices (Deng et al. 2023; Akbar et al. 2025). SUT genes play essential roles in sucrose loading and unloading through the phloem, infuencing key processes such as hormone biosynthesis, stress responses, photosynthesis, and reproductive and fber development (Li et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2021; Hou et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024).

Understanding the molecular structure and evolution of a plant gene family is crucial for comprehending their physiological roles and metabolic mechanisms during diferent growth phases. Recent studies have shown that the SUT gene family is relatively small, typically comprising of fewer members in most plant species. However, the number of SUT genes can vary considerably among taxa. For instance, 06 SUTs have been identifed in Sorghum bicolor (Mizuno et al. 2016), 06 in Saccharum spontaneum (Zhang et al. 2016), 07 in Zea mays (Sun et al. 2023a, b), 09 in Beta vulgaris L. (Sun et al. 2023a, b), 05 in Triticum aestivum (Prasad et al. 2023), 12 in Dendrocalamus farinosus (Deng et al. 2023), and up to 05 and 07 in Erufpilus and Saccharum ofcinarum (Akbar et al. 2025), respectively. Studies on the functions of the SUT family genes in plants have shown that they are involved in various aspects of plant growth and development (Misra et al. 2019), including the transportation and distribution of sucrose (Deng et al. 2023), carbohydrate partitioning (Al-Sheikh Ahmed et al. 2020), germination of pollen (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c), fruit development (Jiang et al. 2023), plant growth (Wang et al. 2020), and biosynthesis of ethylene (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c). For example, AtSUC2 is essential for sucrose loading and root development in Arabidopsis (Gong et al. 2014), while AtSUC4, located on the tonoplast, mediates sucrose-induced inhibition of root elongation (Liu et al. 2022a, b). Tonoplast-localized transporters like PtaSUT4 in poplar and OsSUT2 in rice facilitate sucrose efux from source leaves (Eom et al. 2011; Sun et al. 2022). Notably, suppression of PtaSUT4 increases sucrose accumulation in leaves and alters biomass distribution, highlighting its role in source-to-sink transport (Payyavula et al. 2011). In addition, OsSUT1 is the most studied SUT gene in rice and its inhibition delays seed germination and reduces seed setting without signifcantly afecting leaf carbohydrate levels. OsSUT1 also facilitates sucrose recovery from plastids to support grain flling (Sun et al. 2022; Yingqing et al. 2025). Furthermore, overexpression of GmSUT4.2 in soybean boosts sucrose uptake and promotes sucrose-stimulated hairy root growth, thereby contributing to overall plant growth, development, and yield (Wu et al. 2024). Multiple studies have demonstrated the critical roles of SUT genes in regulating plant growth, sugar metabolism, and stress responses. For example, GmSUT4 infuences plant development through sugar metabolic pathways (Chen et al. 2022a, b), while overexpression of RuSUT2 increases sucrose accumulation in blackberry leaves, suggesting its role in sucrose distribution (Yan et al. 2021). Extensive research has also shown that SUTs mediate responses to phytohormones and environmental stresses (Li et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2020; Hou et al. 2024). Genes like AtSUC4 and AtSUC9 respond to ABA signaling and contribute to drought and cold tolerance (Jia et al. 2015). Similarly, MdSUT2 in tomato and IbSUT4 in sweet potato enhance tolerance to abiotic stress, the latter through an ABF-dependent ABA pathway (Ma et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2020). In peach, PpSUT2 overexpression improved cold and drought tolerance by modulating proline, soluble sugars, and oxidative stress markers (Zhao et al. 2022). More recently, SlSUT4 was shown to regulate sucrose partitioning between vacuole and cytosol, thereby afecting tomato drought responses (Liang et al. 2023).

Sugarcane (Saccharum spp. hybrids), a member of the grass family (Gramineae), is the world’s leading crop for sugar production and a key raw material for biofuel (Zhou et al. 2020, Ali et al. 2025). Commercial sugarcane cultivars are genetically complex, exhibiting allopolyploidy and aneuploidy, with large, highly variable genomes (Zhou et al. 2014; Healey et al. 2024). In China, the hybrid variety ROC22 (derived from $\mathsf { R O C 5 } \times 6 9 - 4 6 3 )$ has been the dominant cultivar over the past two decades, covering approximately $6 0 \%$ of the total sugarcane cultivation area (Su et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2020). Previous studies have identifed numerous SUT family genes in sugarcane (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c; Akbar et al. 2025) and examined their expression under various stress conditions; however, no such analyses have been reported for the Saccharum spp. Hybrid XTT22 (ROC22) genome. This study presents the first identifcation of ShSUT genes in the XTT22 genome, using bioinformatics to examine their physicochemical properties and evolutionary relationships. Transcription factors interacting with ShSUT4 were identifed through BiFC, and Y2H assays, and the expression of ShSUT genes was analyzed under Cold, Drought and Salinity, stressors. These fndings provide key insights into sugar transport, gene evolution, and the genetic basis for improving sugarcane through molecular breeding.

In higher plants, photoassimilates are transported from source organs to sink organs mainly in the form of sucrose. The synthesis, storage, transportation, and utilization of sucrose are some of the major determinants of the cell activity, organ and tissue development, and crop yield [1]. Sucrose transportation is mediated by various proteins, of which sucrose transporters or carriers (called SUTs or SUCs) mediate sucrose movement across membranes.

Plant SUTs belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) and are integral membrane proteins with 12 transmembrane-spanning regions [2]. SUTs are assumed to be $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -sucrose transporters involved in cellular protoncoupled sucrose uptake and may serve two main functions in the apoplastic pathway: loading sucrose into the phloem in source leaves and unloading sucrose into the cells of sink organs, such as the storage roots, tubers, fruits, and developing tissues [3]. Several SUTs have been identified and characterized in plants. For example, Riesmeier et al.

(1992) first cloned spinach SUT cDNA and verified its transport function in yeast [4]. Subsequently, the SUTs of Arabidopsis thaliana were reported. Sauer and Stolz (1994) used spinach SUT cDNA as a probe to screen the Arabidopsis thaliana cDNA library, isolating SUT1 and SUT2 [5]. The AtSUCs were analyzed and found to consist of three distinct subfamilies. The low substrate specificity protein encoded by AtSUC2 is highly expressed in the collection phloem, and is involved in phloem loading and the retrieval of leaked sucrose in the transport phloem [6, 7]. In the absence of sucrose, AtSUC2 mutant seedlings were smaller than wild-type (WT) seedlings [8]. Compared to other SUCs, AtSUC9 has an ultrahigh affinity for sucrose. Plants with AtSUC9 mutations are sensitive to low sucrose levels and have an early flowering phenotype under shortday conditions, suggesting that AtSUC9 is associated with floral induction [9]. In contrast to AtSUC9, AtSUC4, which belongs to the SUT4 clade, has low sucrose affinity and is the only Arabidopsis SUC known to be localized in the tonoplast, releasing sucrose from the vacuole [10]. In addition to Arabidopsis thaliana, SUCs in other plants have also been studied. Inhibition of the StSUT4, mainly expressed in sink organs such as tubers, sink leaves, and flowers, leads to early flowering, increased tuber yield, and decreased in sensitivity toward a far-red light, which may be owing to increased sucrose export from the leaves at the end of the light period [11]. Transgenic poplars with RNAi-suppressed PtaSUT4 had increased leaf-to-stem biomass ratios, elevated sucrose in the source leaves and stems, and altered carbohydrate-active enzymes [12]. Together, these studies demonstrate that SUTs are involved in the carbohydrate partitioning of source and sink organs.

SUTs are also involved in the plant’s response to various abiotic stressors; environmental factors impact the source-sink relationship, carbon allocation, and plant growth [1]. The loss-of-function mutation in AtSUC2 and AtSUC4 leads to hypersensitivity to drought, salt, and cold stress, while abscisic acid (ABA) treatment during seed germination and seedling growth lead to high sucrose content in the shoots but low sucrose content in the roots [13]. Compared to WT Populus plants, in those silenced for SUT4, acute drought conditions resulted in reduced water uptake rates and delayed wilting [14]. A recent global analysis of publicly available gene expression data was conducted to assess the regulation of SUT genes in response to different environmental stimuli [15]. The results indicated that SUTs respond to abiotic stressors, but the stress-induced effects on the sucrose distribution and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unexplored.

ABA is a broad-spectrum phytohormone involved in the regulation of stomatal opening, growth and development, and coordination of various stress signal transduction pathways during abiotic stress [16, 17]. To date, several ABA-pathway genes responsible for plant tolerance to abiotic stress have been identified, including the ABA receptor PYL8/RCAR3 and the regulatory factors SNF1 (SNF1-activated protein kinase) and PP2C (2C protein phosphatases) [18–21]. Moreover, it has been reported that ABA is associated with the sugar response pathway in plants [22]. Jia et al. (2015) found that low sucrose levels induced AtSUC9, which accumulates ABA through the ABA-pathway ABAinducible genes, to enhance abiotic stress resistance [23].

Sweetpotato is a dicotyledonous crop, with underground storage organs. Its yield is closely related to the transport and distribution of photosynthetic products. The sweetpotato SUT genes IbSUT1 and IbSUT2 were previously isolated, and an immunolocalization study found that IbSUT2 is localized in the SE-CCs (sieve element-companion cells) [24, 25]. However, the characteristics and functions of the sweetpotato SUTs and the mechanisms by which they mediate sucrose transport to support the growth and development of sink organs in response to environmental stimuli are unknown. Here, we report the double-membrane localization of a novel sweetpotato SUT gene, IbSUT4, and demonstrate its involvement in the abiotic stress response through the ABF-dependent ABA signaling pathway.

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are sucrose– $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ symporters, which mediate the active transport of sucrose across plasma membranes. Since sucrose is translocated from source to sink tissues through the phloem, plasma membrane sucrose transporters are believed to play important roles in mediating carbon partitioning in plants (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Over the last decade, genes encoding SUT proteins have been isolated from a wide range of both monocot and dicot plant species, from source and sink tissues and found to be localised in phloem and non-phloem tissues (see reviews by Williams et al. 2000; Truernit 2001; Lalonde et al. 2003).

In cereal species, SUT proteins mainly have been studied in developing grains. For example, in developing rice caryopses, OsSUT1 protein is present in the plasma membrane of the aleurone cell layer surrounding the endosperm (Furbank et al. 2001) and is essential for transport of assimilates into filling grains (Scofield et al. 2002). A similar role in grain filling has been proposed for HvSUT1 protein in barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and for TaSUT1 in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2002). However, cellular localisation of cereal SUT gene expression in vegetative tissues has been less well characterised despite the fact that SUT mRNAs are detectable in these tissues of rice (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003), maize (Aoki et al. 1999), barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). While in dicot plants there is considerable evidence that SUTs play a role in apoplasmic loading of sucrose into the phloem (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003), there is little evidence for this in cereal species. Indeed, there is some debate over whether phloem loading in cereals occurs via symplasmic or apoplasmic pathways (e.g. Russin et al. 1996, also see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Significantly, antisense repression of OsSUT1 expression in transgenic rice did not appear to affect phloem loading (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002).

Previously we reported the isolation of three cDNAs encoding SUT proteins from developing grains of hexaploid wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). The peptide sequences deduced from the three cDNAs showed $9 8 \%$ identity to one another, all with more than $8 5 \%$ similarity to SUT1 proteins from other cereal species. The three wheat SUT1 proteins were encoded individually by single-copy homeologous genes, designated TaSUT1A, 1B and 1D , which are represented once in each of the A-, B- and D-genomes. Northern blot analysis revealed that the TaSUT1 genes were highly expressed not only in developing grains but also in flagleaf blades, flag-leaf sheaths and culms (internodes) at the pre-heading stage.

Active transport of sucrose across plant cell membranes is mediated by sucrose–proton symporter proteins. A number of sucrose transporters from dicot plant species have previously been identified, characterized and functionally analysed, most recently reviewed by Lemoine (2000) and Williams et al. (2000). Evidence from northern analysis, immunoblotting, cellular localization and functional analysis suggests that the principal role of many of these sucrose transporters (SUTs) is in the apoplastic loading of assimilate from the leaf mesophyll cells into the phloem. However, some SUTs are thought to be involved in pollen germination (Stadler et al. 1999), transport of sucrose into the dicot embryo (Harrington et al. 1997; Weber et al. 1997), and possibly in sugar sensing (Barker et al. 2000). Antisense suppression of gene expression has been used to determine the function of the dicot SUT1 sucrose transporter (Riesmeier et al. 1994; Kühn et al. 1996; Lemoine et al. 1996). These workers introduced antisense constructs of the potato SUT (StSUT) into potato with the result that transgenic plants showed retention of carbohydrate in the leaves and a subsequent inhibition of photosynthesis, along with a reduction in root development and tuber yield. Bürkle et al. (1998) also used antisense suppression to determine the function of the tobacco sucrose transporter NtSUT1. Again, accumulation of assimilates in the leaves and a reduction of photosynthesis was observed, along with reduction in root development and disrupted flowering. Similar data has recently been obtained using knockout mutants of Arabidopsis where SUC2, the gene encoding a similar SUT1-type transporter, was disrupted (Gottwald et al. 2000). These observations confirm the model of apoplastic phloem-loading transport mechanism of assimilates in the species examined, mediated by the SUT. However, to date, no such experiments have been done in cereal species.

In a previous study, we reported the isolation of a cDNA encoding the rice SUT, OsSUT1, the first to be identified from a monocot species (Hirose et al. 1997). Since then,

SUT genes have been isolated from other monocot species including maize and barley (Aoki et al. 1999; Weschke et al. 2000). Organ-specific mRNA expression patterns suggest that OsSUT1, unlike the dicot SUT1, does not play a major role in phloem loading of assimilate from the mesophyll cells of mature source leaves (Hirose et al. 1997). High expression levels of OsSUT1 in panicles after heading led us to propose that OsSUT1 is involved in transport of sucrose into the filling grain (Hirose et al. 1997), fulfilling a function analogous to SUT1 in Vicia faba (Harrington et al. 1997; Weber et al. 1997). This conclusion is supported by high-level expression of OsSUT1 mRNA and functional OsSUT1 protein in aleurone cell layers and in some of the maternal cell layers of developing grain (Furbank et al. 2001). The role of SUT1 in transport of sucrose to the filial tissue of developing grain has also been supported by studies in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000) and barley (Weschke et al. 2000). In addition to its role in grain filling, OsSUT1 may have some role in the transport of sucrose remobilized from temporary starch reserves in the leaf sheath and stem during grain filling (Hirose et al. 1997, 1999). It also appears that OsSUT1 plays a role in loading remobilized carbohydrate into the phloem of young sink leaves during seed germination (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000).

While the data described above suggests that OsSUT1 encodes a protein involved in active transport of sucrose into the filling grain, the evidence is only correlative. In the present study, we probe the function of OsSUT1 using antisense suppression in transgenic rice plants. The effect of reducing OsSUT1 expression on plant growth, photosynthesis, grain filling and seed germination is examined.
