## Full-Length ZIP1 Transporter Is Obtained from Wild Emmer Wheat


In an attempt to identify ZIP1 transporter gene homolog in wild emmer accessions, two primer sets were designed using the modern wheat ZIP1 protein sequence to target specifically the UTR and the start codon regions of wild emmer accessions. PCR amplifications using these primer sets gave fragments at the expected sizes, $1 { , } 2 0 0 \ \mathrm { k b }$ , for all wild emmer accessions, and further sequencing verified the sequences as the ZIP1 transporter gene. Full-length cDNA encoding a ZIP transporter protein was obtained from the roots of MM 5/4 (GeneBank ID: GU825948), 33–48 (GU825947), 19–36 (GU825946), and Balcali85 (GU825945). Molecular weight and theoretical PI value of the isolated sequences are presented in Supplementary Table 1. The PI value of Balcali 85 (modern durum wheat) has a PI of 7.23 while all the other accessions have a PI of 6.92. All of the sequences show approximately $100 \%$ sequence identity to T. aestivum ZIP1 transporter with one or two complementary substitutions and/or deletions (for illustrative purposes, TdZIP1 sequence obtained from the root of MM 5/4 accession was chosen and this accession has two single nucleotide polymorphisms, relative to TaZIP1, one of which was reflected with an amino acid substitution at position 97 from methionine to isoleucine; Fig. 1). A rooted phylogenetic tree that was constructed from the comparison of 20 known plant ZIP family members also revealed the most closely related transporter as the $T .$ aestivum ZIP1 (Fig. 2).

Comparison of the protein sequences of seven ZIP1 transporters from various plant species with the obtained full-length TdZIP1 sequences revealed that the characteristic structural features are conserved, but variations between these different plant species and wild emmer wheat occur mostly in the predicted solvent exposed extracytosolic and cytoplasmic regions (Fig. 1). We analyzed the structural elements of the functionally characterized MM 5/4 accession in detail as the representative sequence from all of the obtained wild emmer wheat accessions. The encoded 360 amino acid long ZIP1 protein sequence from this genotype was predicted to cover the entire signal peptide sequence as well as the eight transmembrane domains with the terminal flanking regions (Fig. 1). ZIP1 proteins vary in size from 223 to 447 amino acids due to either the differences in the N-terminal sequences or the histidine-rich variable regions in the cytoplasmic loop between TM 3 and 4. In TdZIP sequence, a long loop region between $\mathrm { ~ T M ~ } 3$ and four spanning from residues 142 to 208 (shaded yellow in Fig. 1) exists with eight histidines, six of which are found in a tandem arrangement $\mathrm { ( H X H ) } _ { 3 }$ (shown as red-colored capitals in Fig. 1). Since the occurrence of $\mathrm { ( H X H ) } _ { n }$ type sequences within the cytoplasmic loop of ZIP transporters was postulated as putative metal binding sites that facilitate macromolecular interactions (Eng et al. 1998), it is also possible to anticipate a similar function for the isolated ZIP1 from T. dicoccoides. The conserved amphipathic residues, His 217 and Ser 218, and His 245 and Glu 249 (colored in yellow capitals in Fig. 1), which are predicted to lie in $\mathrm { T M } ~ 4$ and 5, respectively, were also identified in the obtained sequence. These residues are expected to be involved in the metal transport by becoming exposed and available for metal binding when a pore or cavity is formed within the membrane (Guerinot 2000). Based on mutational studies done earlier for the Fe transporter protein, Irt1, of Arabidopsis, the extracellular loop between $\mathrm { T M } ~ 2$ and 3 of ZIP transporters was postulated to involve a substrate sensing function before the transport of Fe through the membrane (Rogers et al. 2000). Three residues in Irt1 sequence play roles in this function, His 96, Asp 100, and Glu 103, which show particular selectivity for specific metals. A histidine residue at position 100 that is corresponding to His 96 is conserved in wild emmer wheat sequence and colored in red within TM 2 in Fig. 1. An alanine residue, A104, was sequenced for wild emmer wheat at the expected position of Asp 100. In the deduced sequence at the predicted Glu 103 position, a complementary amino acid Asp 107 was detected, which should not affect the function of this residue. Having changes at these specific residues compared to that of Irt1 sequence suggests preferential difference in metal selectivity for wild emmer wheat. Furthermore, the obtained cDNA has a potential 24 amino acid long signal peptide sequence (colored cyan in Fig. 1) predicted both by PSORT (Claros and von Heijne 1994) and Signal IP (Nielsen et al. 1997) algorithms. This signal sequence is $100 \%$ identical to the signal peptide sequence of ZIP1 from T. aestivum (Fig. 1). Thus, based on the conservation of all the characteristic features of ZIP family members as well as the very high sequence similarity between ZIP1 from wild emmer wheat and durum wheat, we conclude that the deduced TdZIP1 sequence belongs to the ZIP family of transporters.


## Expression of ZIP1 in the Roots of Wild Emmer Accessions Under Zn Deficiency


ZIP transcript showed increase level in response to the decrease of Zn application suggesting that as plants suffer more from Zn deficiency, ZIP transcription was induced to increase root uptake of Zn. For accurate quantification of the ZIP transcript levels, we performed quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) that also showed the elevation of ZIP transcript levels with low level of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in all wild emmer accessions (Fig. 3, four accessions were chosen for illustration). However, the reduction of Zn supply beyond $1 0 ^ { - 7 }  { \mathrm { ~ M ~ Z n } }$ does not cause a significant increase in ZIP expression, setting $1 0 ^ { - 7 } \textnormal { M Z n }$ concentration as the critical dose. Since the threshold cycle values for 18S RNA levels, which were used as a standard, are the same across the genotypes, we compared ZIP transcript accumulation levels in the roots of the genotypes upon a decrease in $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply. According to our comparisons, the least $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency tolerant species, $1 9 -$ 36, showed the highest level of ZIP transcript expression; on the other hand, the most tolerant accession, MM 5/4, showed the lowest level. The other two genotypes, 33–48 and 24–39, showed intermediary expression levels between the two extremes observed for 19–36 and $\mathbf { M M } \mathbf { \Lambda } 5 / 4$ . These findings suggest that the more severe state of $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency observed in 19–36, as reflected by its lower Zn efficiency ratio and low dry matter production under Zn deficiency (Table 1), results in an increased expression of ZIP1 in the root cells.


## TdZIP1 Reveals Zn Specificity


The interaction between elements may affect their uptake by roots. For instance, the high concentration of one element may cause a plant to suffer from deficiency of another element through an antagonistic effect during uptake. It was previously reported that Cd can induce Fe or Zn deficiency at physiological levels and thus affects expression of genes associated with Fe or Zn deficiency in plants (Siedlecka and Baszynsky 1993). Relatively high soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ application contributed to reduction of Cd content in durum wheat where Zn and Cd act antagonistically to each other (Choudhary et al. 1995). Moreover, IRT1, which is a ZIP protein from Arabidopsis thaliana, was shown to be a metal transporter with broad range substrate specificity as it transports Zn, Mn, Cd, and Co (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et al. 2002). In this study, at $1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { M } Z \mathrm { n }$ , the transport of other elements such as Fe might have been inhibited due to high level of Zn concentration in growth medium for plant roots, revealing a Fe deficiencyindependent regulation of ZIP expression. Because some of the ZIP transporters are capable of transporting several divalent cations nonspecifically, the expression of a ZIP protein transporting divalent cations other than Zn was also expected to be high under Zn toxicity. However, qRT-PCR results in this study showed that ZIP1 expression levels were not upregulated at toxic Zn level (Fig. 3), which may be due to the $Z \mathrm { n }$ specificity of the transporter.


## TdZIP1 Complements Zn Uptake in Mutant Yeast Cells


To understand the metal transporting capacity of the identified ZIP1 from T. dicoccoides, we analyzed the constructed cDNAs’ functional expressions in a yeast iron (fet3fet4) and extracellular Zn transporter (zrt1zrt2) deletion strain, ZHY3 (all used mutant yeast strains are given in Table 3). We also aimed to differentiate the yeast growth complementation strengths of the susceptible and tolerant genotypes of TdZIP1 under Zn limitation and availability.

We used ZIP1 genes from 19 to 39 and 24 to 39 accessions of T. dicoccoides for $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency susceptible and tolerant genotypes, respectively.

In the absence of zinc supply and both the high and low affinity extracellular Zn transporters, ZRT1 and ZRT2, respectively, the growth of the mutants was aborted. Expression of the TdZIP1 transporter (from the susceptible genotype) under the control of constitutively expressed yeast promoter was able to restore the growth of the ZHY3 mutant under limiting $Z \mathrm { n }$ -supplied medium, revealing the Zn transport ability of this protein (Fig. 4a). On the other hand, the TdZIP1 from the tolerant genotype, when also expressed constitutively, could not complement the growth of the Zn uptake defective yeast strain under low Zn conditions, barely showing complementation like the mock-transformed cells. This difference in the complementation strengths between the tolerant and susceptible genotypes can emerge by the functional adaptation of the plant to Zn deficiency. The functional complementation of these genotypes under normal Zn supply conditions was also analyzed. There was not any qualitative difference between the expression of neither the vector-only control strain nor the susceptible and tolerant transporters (Supp. Fig. 4).


## TdZIP1 Transporter Is with a Relatively Low Strength Capable of Complementing the Fe Uptake Defective Mutant Under Limiting Zn Conditions


Wild-type strain in the study was Fe uptake defective (fet3fet4 mutants). Although IRT1 of $S .$ cerevisiae was regarded to be induced under Fe deficiency (Vert et al. 2002; Reid and Hayes 2003), it was suggested that it may also allow for the transport of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ . IRT1-mediated accumulation of other divalent metals is reasonable since, to some extent, low affinity zinc transporters are known to provide Fe for some cellular processes under low Fe conditions. Transformation of T. dicoccoides ZIP1 into Fe transporter mutants and the growth on LZM were observed. The results showed that the limitation on the growth due to Fe uptake deficiency can be weakly restored after the ZIP1 complementation in these mutants (Fig. 4b), suggesting substrate preference of $T .$ dicoccoides ZIP1 to Zn rather than Fe. Both tolerant and susceptible Zn transporters showed comparable functional complementation. We also observed growth rescue for the TdZIP1 overexpressing cells, though there was no obvious difference on the complementation strength of the two ZIP1 clones (Fig. 4c). However, the growth rate of the mutant yeast cells when TdZIP1 is constitutively expressed is lower compared to that of the inductively expressed ones (Fig. 4b, c). This difference was anticipated and proved the higher expression levels under the control of an inducible promoter. Taken together, these results not only reveal the Zn selectivity of TdZIP1 but also demonstrate an ability of TdZIP1 to transport Fe for the cells supplied with minimum levels of this nutrient, thereby sustaining basal growth under limiting $Z \mathrm { n }$ medium. To our knowledge, this is the first report showing the non-specific transport ability of, particularly, ZIP1 under low divalent metal containing medium. Moreover, supplementation of EDTA and relevant buffer systems in order to trap $Z \mathrm { n }$ cations may have resulted in a decrease of the available Fe of the medium. The Fe transporter defective strains therefore lose a deal of their ability to grow.

Overexpression of TdZIP1 Under Normal $Z \mathrm { n }$ -Supplied Conditions Causes Toxicity to the Mutant Yeast Cells

TdZIP1 overexpressing vectors were used to study the functional role of the ZIP1 transporter under extreme availability. Overexpression of the susceptible and tolerant transporters shows similar growth rescue ability under depleted Zn conditions (Fig. 5a). Under limiting $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply, the strain was not able to grow in the absence of the recombinant TdZIP1 expression regardless of the originating accession of the clone. Interestingly, when $Z \mathrm { n }$ is supplied, under the expression of a strong promoter, the strains transformed with both of the TdZIP1 clones showed diminished growth compared to the mock-transformed cells (Fig. 5b). We reasoned these growth declines by the enhanced function of the TdZIP1 that leads to growth restoration under limiting $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply and causes toxicity to the cells under normal $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply.

Partial TdZIP1-GFP Localizes at the Endoplasmic Reticulum

To determine the TM domains that are responsible for $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport capacity in TdZIP1, we truncated the last 20 amino acids of TM 8 at the C terminus and constructed a GFP-tagged mutant of TdZIP1. Earlier findings suggested that TM 3 and 4 are responsible for Zn transport capacity (Eng et al. 1998; Guerinot 2000; Rogers et al. 2000). There are known variants of Zn transporters that have five membrane spanning domains. Yet, to maintain the proper folding in the bilayer, the protein should conserve its optimum conformation. Therefore, we kept TM 6 and 7 and deleted only the part of TM 8 whose function is not yet determined. Interestingly, we observed localization of our TdZIP1-GFP construct at the ER membrane (Fig. 6). This result contradicts with the earlier findings where human transporters were shown to be localized at the plasma membrane of the cells (Eide 2000). However, our observation may exhibit a role for TdZIP1 in the subcellular transport of $Z \mathrm { n }$ rather than to/from the extracellular compartment. In recent studies with the Ni hyperaccumulating plant, Thlaspi japonicum, it was shown that in addition to the plasma membrane, TjZIP1 could localize at the perinuclear and vacuolar membranes (Nishida et al. 2008). The constructed ZIP1 in the present study was from the 19 to 36 accession of wild emmer wheat, which was identified as the susceptible genotype to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency. The observed high expression levels of ZIP1 for this accession, as measured by qRT-PCR (Fig. 3), may correlate with the ER localization of this transporter. Upregulation of this transporter may be necessary for the $Z \mathrm { n }$ partitioning out of the roots, thus enabling the transport of $Z \mathrm { n }$ to the xylem stream of the plant. These results together may provide a glimpse into the stress response mechanism to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in wild emmer wheat because under $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency stress, Zn has to be transported to the ER to maintain its critical functions such as protein folding, degradation, and secretion. These processes all depend on the direct interactions of Zn ions with the ER proteins, such as calnexin, calreticulin, DnaJ homolog Scj1, and secreted alkaline phosphatases (Galperin and Jedrzejas 2001; Mann and Sevlever 2001; Nishikawa et al. 2001; Leach et al. 2002).

One other way explanation for the ER localization of TdZIP1-GFP protein could be the improper folding of the protein due to the missing sequence of TdZIP1 at the C terminus. This deleted region is a part of the predicted TM 8 which might be important for keeping the proper protein folding integrity. Therefore, in the absence of this sequence, improper 3D structure of the transporter could have resulted, and the protein might have been retained at the ER, preventing its translocation to the plasma membrane.

ER localization of the transporter may emerge due to the presence of the GFP tag at the C terminus. GFP is a rather large protein molecule with an intrinsic distribution to the cell cytoplasm as well as nucleus and due to its polarity it does not prefer to be located trans- or in contact to the membrane. The ZIP transporters have been known to expose their C-terminal tails as well as their N-terminals out of the cell. Since GFP is localized at the C terminus of the transporter, its exposure to the extracellular matrix might not be possible, and therefore, the proper positioning of the transmembrane domains in order to create the 3D pore structure does not take place. Moreover, due to the size of GFP, the protein might have encountered a tension on its C terminus that would cause a loss of the transporter proper delivery from the ER to the membrane. Nonetheless, TjZNT1 localization experiments were performed using a GFP tag in yeast cells and that study demonstrated plasma, perinuclear, and vacuolar membrane localization of the transporter (Nishida et al. 2008). The authors claimed that trafficking of all expressed TjZNT1-GFP protein to the plasma membrane might not occur in yeast due to heterologous expression (Nishida et al. 2008), which may also be the case for the ER residency of TdZIP1 in yeast. Because from the complementation analysis we have securely concluded the functional expression of TdZIP1, another strategy such as smaller fluorescent tags (other than GFP) will be needed for cellular compartmentalization studies in wild emmer wheat.

Iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ and zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ are essential nutrients for all organisms, which are involved in the function of numerous key enzymes in metabolism [1, 2]. It has been reported that low consumption of foods rich in bio-available $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe is one of the main causes of Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiencies in human beings [3]. Zn and Fe deficiencies are probably the most widespread micronutrient deficiencies limiting cereal production and grain quality [4]. Metal ion transporters provide an efficient tool to transport metal ions from the soil solution into the root, and then distribute them throughout the plant. In recent years, a number of genes involved in metal transport in plants have been identified [5]. They belong to several different transporter families, including CAX family involved in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H }$ , $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H }$ or $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } /$ H anti-transportor, CDF (cation diffusion facilitator) family involved in Zn homeostasis, Nramp (natural resistance associated macrophage protein) family possibly to be involved in Cd, Fe homeostasis and ZIP $\mathrm { \Delta } Z \mathrm { r t }$ , Irt-like protein) family [5]. Members of the ZIP gene family identified in plants are capable of transporting Cd, Fe, Mn and Zn [5, 6]. The hallmark features of ZIP proteins consist of 309–476 amino acid residues with eight putative TM domains and a similar membrane topology, in which the amino- and carboxyl-terminals of the protein are located on the outside surface of plasma membrane [6]. There is a variable region between the TM domains III and IV, containing a potential metal-binding domain rich in conserved histidine residues. The highly conserved signature motif exists in the TM domain IV [6]. The ZIP family has representatives in several plant species, including Arabidopsis, pea, tomato, soybean, rice and alfalfa [7–17], as well as in archaea, yeast, bacteria and animals [18].

The OsIRT1 cDNA was isolated from a cDNA library prepared from Fe-deficient rice roots, which was highly homologous to Arabidopsis Fe (II) transporter gene IRT1 [13]. OsIRT1 was predominantly expressed in rice roots and up-regulated in Fe-deficient rice roots. OsIRT1 reversed the growth defect of yeast mutant YH003 (Dftr1, Dfet4, Dfre1) on Fe-depleted media [13]. The OsZIP1, OsZIP2 and OsZIP3 genes were identified from rice by searching GenBank with amino acid sequences of Arabidopsis ZIP transporter ZIP1 [14]. OsZIP1 and OsZIP3 were up-regulated in rice roots and shoots after Zn deprivation, while OsZIP2 up-regulated only in rice roots by $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency. OsZIP1 and OsZIP3 could complement the growth defect of yeast mutant ZHY3 on low Zn medium [14]. The OsZIP4, OsZIP5, OsZIP6 and OsZIP7 isolated from rice were found to be homologous with OsIRT1 [15]. Among these genes OsZIP4 was up-regulated in rice roots and shoots by Zn deficiency, OsZIP5 and OsZIP7 upregulated in rice shoots by Zn deficiency. The OsZIP4 may complement a $Z \mathbf { n }$ -uptake-deficient yeast mutant [15]. Here we reported the cloning of another two members OsZIP7a and OsZIP8 of ZIP gene family from rice, their expression patterns in various rice organs and seedlings under Fe or Zn deficiency treatment, as well as functional complementation of OsZIP7a and OsZIP8 in the yeast mutants.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ is an essential micronutrient for living organisms including plants and humans playing diverse roles in various cellular processes. In plants zinc exists only as $Z \mathrm { n } ( \mathrm { I I } )$ and does not take part in oxidoreduction reactions (Marschner 1995). The non redox active property of Zn combined with its geometry makes it suitable cofactor for an array of enzymes involved in DNA transcription, protein, nucleic acid, carbohydrate, and lipid metabolism (Broadley et al. 2007; Ishimaru et al. 2011; Palmer and Guerinot 2009). In addition, Zn is critical to the control of gene transcription and the coordination of other biological processes regulated by proteins containing DNA-binding Zn-finger motifs (Rhodes and Klug 1993), RING fingers, and LIM domains (Vallee and Falchuk 1993). Several molecules associated with DNA and RNA synthesis are also Zn metalloenzymes, such as RNA polymerases (Wu et al. 1992), reverse transcriptases, and transcription factors (Wu and Wu 1987). Besides being essential, Zn could be potentially toxic when in excess. Symptoms of Zn toxicity may include inhibition of root elongation and chlorosis in young leaves (Godbold et al. 1983; Marschner 1995; Ruano et al. 1988). Although the mechanisms of Zn toxicity is not completely understood, the possible reasons may include, but not limited to, inappropriate binding to intracellular ligands and competition with other metal ions for enzyme active sites or transporters.

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) provides energy to almost half of the world’s population. Thus, increasing the Zn content of rice has a great potential to mitigate wide spread Zn deficiency problem in humans (Graham et al. 1999; Ruel and Bouis 1998; Welch and Graham 2004). Therefore, it is essential to understand the molecular mechanism through which plants mobilize, take up, translocate, and store Zn. Plants acquire Zn from rhizosphere and the absorbed Zn must be transported into aerial parts as well as to the intracellular compartments of the cell where it is required for the Zn-dependent processes.

In plants, mugineic acid family phytosiderophores (MAs) and nicotianamine (NA), are well characterized for their role in iron (Fe) uptake and homeostasis (Bashir et al. 2010; Mori 1999; Takagi 1976). MAs also play a role in $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and translocation (Suzuki et al. 2006; Suzuki et al. 2008b; Takagi 1976; Welch and Shuman 1995). NA is present in all higher plants, whereas MAs are specifically synthesized in graminaceous plants (Marschner 1995). MAs are synthesized from Methionine (Met) and NA and $2 ^ { \prime }$ -deoxymugineic acid (DMA) share the biosynthetic pathway from LMet (Mori and Nishizawa 1987). NA synthase (NAS)

catalyzes the trimerization of S-adenosyl Met to NA (Higuchi et al. 1994; Higuchi et al. 1999). In graminaceous plants, NA is then converted to a $3 ^ { \prime \prime }$ -keto intermediate through the transfer of an amino group by NA aminotransferase (NAAT; (Kanazawa et al. 1993)). The subsequent reduction of the $3 ^ { \prime \prime }$ -keto group by DMA synthase (DMAS) produces DMA, which is the first species of MAs synthesized in this conserved pathway (Bashir et al. 2006; Bashir and Nishizawa 2006; Shojima et al. 1990). The MAs are then released to rhizosphere through transporter of MAs 1 (TOM1, (Nozoye et al. 2011)) where they bind to metals and the resultant MAs-metal complex is taken up through yellow stripe 1 like (YSL) family transporters (Curie et al. 2001; Inoue et al. 2009; Murata et al. 2006). The expression of genes for MAs biosynthesis changes in diurnal rhythm and MAs are also secreted in diurnal fashion with a peak in the morning to avoid bacterial degradation (Nagasaka et al. 2009; Takagi et al. 1984). The secretion of MAs increases under Zn deficiency in wheat (Triticum spp.) and barley (Hordeum vulgare) (Cakmak et al. 1994; Suzuki et al. 2006; Walter et al. 1994; Zhang et al. 1989). All the genes of DMA biosynthesis pathway have been cloned from rice and barley (Bashir et al. 2006; Bashir et al. 2010; Bashir and Nishizawa 2006; Herbik et al. 1999; Higuchi et al. 1994; Higuchi et al. 1999; Inoue et al. 2003; Inoue et al. 2008; Takahashi et al. 1999). The expression of NASHOR2, a NAS in barley (Herbik et al. 1999), and HvNAAT-B increase under Zn-deficiency in barley shoots (Suzuki et al. 2006). Moreover, the expression of HvNAS1, HvNAAT-A, HvNAAT-B (barley NAATs) increase in Zn- and Fe-deficient roots, while the expression of these genes was not observed in Fe-deficient shoots (Suzuki et al. 2006). It was suggested that $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency induces DMA synthesis in barley shoots, while both $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe deficiency induce MAs synthesis and secretion in barley roots (Ishimaru et al. 2011; Suzuki et al. 2006). Thus NA and DMA are suggested to play a significant role in plant $Z \mathrm { n }$ mobilization. In addition to NA and DMA a series of transporters belonging to different families are also suggested to be involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and translocation in rice.

Several members of the $Z \mathrm { n }$ -regulated transporters and iron (Fe)-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) gene family (Guerinot 2000) have been characterized and shown to be involved in metal uptake and transport in plants (Connolly et al. 2002; Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). The ZIP proteins are predicted to have eight transmembrane domains, with their amino- and carboxyl-terminal ends situated on the outer surface of the plasma membrane (Guerinot 2000). These proteins vary considerably in overall length due to a variable region between the transmembrane domains (TM) TM-3 and TM-4. In rice several ZIPs have been reported e.g. OsIRT1, OsIRT2, OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5, OsZIP7, and OsZIP8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Yang et al. 2009). IRT1 is a key $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in plants with representatives in Arabidopsis (IRT1) and rice (OsIRT1) localized to the plasma membrane and functioning to transport $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from the rhizosphere to root cells (Bughio et al. 2002; Connolly et al. 2002; Conte and Walker 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2005; Ishimaru et al. 2006). The expression of OsIRT1 in rice is regulated by Fe availability and to some extent by Zn deficiency (Ishimaru et al. 2005). The Arabidopsis IRT2 localizes to vesicles within root epidermal cells, while OsIRT2 localizes to the plasma membrane (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Vert et al. 2001). Like IRT1, IRT2 also transports $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ and its expression is also regulated by Fedeficiency both in rice and Arabidopsis (Bughio et al. 2002; Connolly et al. 2002; Conte and Walker 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2006). When expressed heterologously in yeast, OsIRT1 does not transport Zn and is mainly involved in Fe transport (Ishimaru et al. 2006). OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are reported to encode rice plasma membrane Zn transporters and are induced by Zn deficiency (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Suzuki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2009).

Although the understanding of Zn uptake and translocation in rice is increasing, the information regarding expression of different $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporters during different developmental stages is scarce. Here we discuss the mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake in rice and expression pattern of ZIP transporters through different developmental stages of rice from root to stem, leaves and reproductive parts. The data regarding expression of OsZIPs through different developmental stages of rice was acquired from the RiceXPro:http://ricexpro. dna.affrc.go.jp/ (Sato et al. 2011a, b). This data was generated by microarray analysis of rice plants (Oryza sativa L. cv. Nipponbare) grown under natural field condition (Sato et al. 2011a, b). The RixeXPro database provides information about expression of genes in different tissue such as root, stem, leaves, anther, ovary, embryo and endosperm through different growth stages. Understanding the expression pattern of these transporters offers a significant advance for manipulating the Zn absorption and translocation to the shoots and ultimately seed and to mitigate the human Zn deficiency problem.


## Expression of Zn transporters during germination


The germination of rice seed is governed by various factors such as temperature, light, water, and hormonal signaling. During this process nutrients are directed to the developing tissue like roots and shoots. The first source of nutrients for the germinating rice seed are the ones stored in grain itself during seed development. In mature rice seed, Zn is unevenly distributed to all of parts of the seed, with a significantly high value for the aleurone layer and embryo (Takahashi et al. 2009). Rice seeds contain not only Zn but also NA and DMA (Masuda et al. 2009; Usuda et al. 2009), and during germination, NA, DMA and Zn are mobilized (Takahashi et al. 2009). During germination, Zn flow is quite dynamic compared to Fe, Mn and $\mathrm { C u }$ and the $Z \mathrm { n }$ stored in the endosperm is transported to the embryo resulting in a high Zn localization in the radicle and leaf primordium (Takahashi et al. 2009). As the germination further proceeds, localization of $Z \mathrm { n }$ increases in the scutellum and the vascular bundle of the scutellum. This localization of Zn matches to Fe localization to some extent (Bashir et al. 2010; Ishimaru et al. 2011; Takahashi et al. 2009). In rice seeds the expression of ZIP family members decrease or remain unchanged during germination (Nozoye et al. 2007). In particular the expression of OsZIP4 and OsZIP7 significantly decrease during germination. In meristematic tissue Zn localizes to the embryo and a decrease in OsZIP family transcripts might be necessary for this type of partial localization of $Z \mathrm { n }$ (Nozoye et al. 2007; Takahashi et al. 2009).


## Zn uptake through root


In barley, Zn-DMA is preferred over $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ for uptake through roots (Suzuki et al. 2006). In contrast rice plants absorb, less $Z \mathrm { n }$ -DMA compared to $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Suzuki et al. 2008b). Similarly the secretion of mugineic acids (MAs)

increases in Zn deficient barley, while it decreases in rice (Suzuki et al. 2006; Suzuki et al. 2008b). Despite this, $Z \mathrm { n }$ -DMA is suggested to be the preferred form for the long distance transport in rice (Suzuki et al. 2008b). Difference in secretion of DMA is suggested to increase tolerance in rice (Widodo et al. 2010). Recently a modeling study also proposed a strong correlation between DMA secretion and rooting density, and suggested a role of DMA for Zn absorption in rice (Ptashnyk et al. 2011). The data revealed by microarray analysis through different growth stages of rice grown under natural filed conditions was utilized to check the expression of DMA biosynthesis related genes in root ((RiceXPro;http://ricexpro.dna. affrc.go.jp/ (Sato et al. 2011a, b)). The expression of OsNAS1 increased from 27 days after transplantation (DAT) to 76 DAT and decreased at 27 and 76 DAT during noon while opposite trend is reported for samples collected at midnight (Fig. 1). Expression of OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 was higher during noon compared to midnight at 27 DAT, however the expression was is not regulated diurnally at 76 DAT (Fig. 1). The expression of OsNAAT1 increased from 27 DAT to 76 DAT, while the expression of OsDMAS1 did not changed from 27 to 76 DAT. The DMA biosynthesis genes are up-regulated by Fe deficiency (Bashir et al. 2006; Inoue et al. 2003; Inoue et al. 2008) and the expression of DMA biosynthesis genes is reported to be regulated in a clear diurnal fashion in barley, however in rice these genes are not regulated in a clear diurnal fashion ((Nagasaka et al. 2009; Negishi et al. 2002; Nozoye et al. 2004). Among the OsZIP genes, OsIRT1, OsIRT2, OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are expressed in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Ramesh et al. 2003; Sato et al. 2011b; Yang et al. 2009). Microarray analysis (Suzuki et al. 2012) revealed that among the ZIP family genes OsZIP4, OsZIP5, and $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ are upregulated by Zn deficiency in roots and shoots, while the expression of OsZIP7 is upregulated only in shoots. OsZIP1, OsZIP3, and OsZIP4 are expressed in the vascular bundles and epidermal cells in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2010a; Ramesh et al. 2003; Yang et al. 2009). Expression of OsZIP1 is induced in roots 24 to $9 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ after Zn deficiency treatment. Under Zn deficiency, the OsZIP2, and OsZIP3 transcripts are visible in roots (Ramesh et al. 2003). While in plants subjected to Zn deficiency for two weeks the expression of OsZIP1-3 is not upregulated by Zn deficiency (Suzuki et al. 2012). The expression of OsZIP4 is also induced by Zn deficiency in roots (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Suzuki et al. 2012). In Zn-deficient rice, OsZIP4 is expressed in the root apical meristem and vascular bundles of Zn-deficient roots especially in the phloem cells (Ishimaru et al.

2007; Ishimaru et al. 2005). The OsZIP genes are not regulated by diurnal rhythm in root tissue (Fig. 1). The expression of OsZIP1 and OsZIP5 decreases from 27 DAT to 76 DAT. On the other hand the expression of OsZIP8 significantly increased from 27 DAI to 76 DAT. The expression of OsZIP4 does not change significantly with time. The data obtained by microarray analysis of root samples prepared by laser micro dissection reveals that The OsZIP genes are expressed in different parts of the root tissue (RiceXPro;http://ricexpro.dna.affrc.go. jp/). OsZIP5, OsZIP7 and OsZIP8 were expressed in the root sections consisting of epidermis, exodermis and sclerenchyma (Fig. 2). OsZIP4 mainly expresses in the vascular tissue (Ishimaru et al. 2005). OsZIP1 and OsZIP3 are suggested to be involved in Zn uptake from rhizosphere (Lee et al. 2010a; Ramesh et al. 2003), while OsZIP4 and OsZIP5 are suggested to be involved in phloem Zn transport (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Ishimaru et al. 2005; Lee et al. 2010a). Although the role of DMA in Zn uptake from root has been discussed, the transporter involved in Zn-DMA uptake in rice has not been characterized yet. The yellow stripe 1 (ys1) gene was first identified in maize and was shown to be critical for the uptake of Fe(III)-MAs (Curie et al. 2001). ZmYS1 transports MAs-bound metals, including Zn, Cu, and nickel (Murata et al. 2006; Schaaf et al. 2004)), while there is controversy if $Z { \mathrm { m Y S 1 } }$ transports $Z \mathrm { n }$ -MAs ((Roberts et al. 2004). In rice 18 YSL homologs are reported which exhibit $3 6 - 7 6 \%$ sequence similarity to maize YS1 (Koike et al. 2004). Among these, OsYSL2 expresses specifically in the phloem and transports $\mathrm { F e ( I I ) }$ -NA and $\mathrm { M n } ( \mathrm { I I } )$ -NA, suggesting that. OsYSL2 is a $\mathrm { { M n } ( I I ) }$ - and Fe (II)-NA transporter responsible for phloem transport of metals. OsYSL15 and OsYSL18 transports Fe(III)- DMA (Aoyama et al. 2009; Inoue et al. 2009).

In addition to the upregulation of several genes involved in Zn uptake, recently the upregulation of genes involved in starch synthesis and transport and accumulation of starch in Zn deficient plants has also been reported (Suzuki et al. 2012). These results suggest that starch accumulation may also be helpful to mitigate Zn deficiency.


## Zn transport in stem


In the stem, OsZIP3 expresses in the vascular bundles and epidermal cells (Ramesh et al. 2003), While OsZIP4 expresses mainly in the phloem (Ishimaru et al. 2005). OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are also expressed in stem at 83 and 90 DAT (Fig. 3). The expression of OsZIPI and OsZIP5 decreases from 83 DAT to $9 0 \mathrm { D A T }$ and the expression of OsZIP3 and OsZIP8 increases, while the expression of OsZIP4 remain unchanged (Fig. 3). Recently, it was reported that in rice phloem sap Zn predominantly exists as Zn-NA (Nishiyama et al. 2012). The expression of OsNAS1-3, OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 is not significantly regulated in diurnal rhythm. The expression of OsNAS3 decreases from 83 to $9 0 \ \mathrm { D A T }$ , while the expression of OsDMAS1 increased from 83 to 90 DAT (Fig. 3). As OsZIP proteins do not transport ZnNA complex, it is possible that rice YSL (OsYSL) family is involved in this transport of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ . Although, a Zn-NA transporter or Zn-DMA transporter involved in Zn translocation has not been identified in rice plants yet, the existence of Zn-NA complexes in rice phloem sap (Nishiyama et al. 2012) suggests that YSLs could be involved in the transport of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ or Zn-DMA in rice.


## Zn transport in rice leaves


In rice leaves, the expression of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1, and OsDMAS1 as well as the amount of endogenous DMA increase in shoots of Zn deficient rice (Suzuki et al. 2008b). As the expression of OsNAAT1 dramatically increases in $Z \mathrm { n }$ -deficient shoots, the amount of endogenous NA in shoots reduces remarkably by $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency. Furthermore, positron-emitting tracer imaging system (PETIS) experiment demonstrated that more $Z \mathrm { n }$ is translocated to the newest leaf when $^ { 6 2 } \mathrm { Z n - D M A }$ is supplied compared to the conditions when $^ { 6 2 } \mathrm { Z n }$ is supplied. At the bottom of the leaf sheath an opposite trend was observed, (Suzuki et al. 2008b), suggesting that Zn-DMA is the preferred form for long-distance transport of Zn in Zn-deficient rice. The expression of NA and DMA biosynthesis related genes changes significantly in leaves from 27 to $1 2 5 \mathrm { \ D A T }$ through 76 DAT (Fig. 4). In leaf blade, the expression of OsNAS3 is higher compared to OsNAS1 and OsNAS2 ((Fig. 4 & (Inoue et al. 2003)). The expression of OsDMAS1 was high at midnight compared to the expression at noon and increased from 27 to 76 DAT and then decreased slightly at 124 DAT particularly at noon. It clearly suggests a role of DMA for Zn transport in leaves. As Zn predominantly exists as Zn-NA in phloem sap (Nishiyama et al. 2012), the role of $Z \mathrm { n - N A }$ and OsYSLs in leaf $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport and mobilization seems to be very important.

OsZIP1 expresses in the vascular bundle of leaves. In leaves, OsZIP4 expresses in all parts of vascular bundles and mesophyll cells of Zn deficient plants (Ishimaru et al. 2005). Strong expression of OsZIP4 could also be observed in shoot meristem. The expression of ZIPs changes significantly in rice leaf blade from 27 to 76 and 125 DAT (Fig. 3). The expression of OsZIP1 significantly increases from 27 to 76 DAT and then slightly decreases at 125 DAT. Expression of OsZIP3 and OsZIP4 do not change significantly from 27 to 76 and 125 DAT. The expression of OsZIP4 is comparatively high during noon compared to midnight at 27, 76 and $1 2 5 \mathrm { \ D A T }$ . The expression of OsZIP5 was low at 27 DAT, then increases at 76 DAT during midnight and then decreases to a level comparable to 27 DAT during midnight. During noon it increases slowly from 27 DAT to 125 DAT. Significant diurnal rhythm was observed for OsZIP8. The expression of $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ was high during noon compared to midnight at 76 and 125 DAT. These changes in expression indicate that these genes could play an important role in Zn transport during the growth cycle of rice. In leaves, the expression of $ { O s Z I P 8 }$ is high compared to other ZIP transporters. The expression of OsZIPs in rice leaves and changes in the expression of these genes with developmental stages indicate their role in Zn translocation in leaf tissue. We suggest that OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 are important for $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport in leaves.


## Expression of ZIP transporters during flowering and seed development


The DMA biosynthesis genes are expressed during flowering and seed development and are expressed in anther, ovary, embryo and endosperm (Figs. 5–8). In Ovary the expression of OsNAS1 decreased from 1 to 3 days after flowering (DAF) and then increased at 5 and 7 DAF (Fig. 6). The expression pattern of OsNAS3, OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 increased from 1 to 5 DAF, and then the expression of OsNAS3 decreased, while the expression of OsNAAT1 and OsDMAS1 did not changed significantly. In embryo, the expression of OsNAS1 decreased from 7 to 28 DAF, while the expression of OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 remain unchanged (Fig. 7). The expression of OsNAAT1 decreased slowly from 7 to 42 DAF, while expression of OsDMAS1 decreased from 7 to 10 DAF and then increased from 14 to 28 DAF. Slight changes for the expression of these genes were also observed in endosperm (Fig. 8). The information about the expression of OsZIP genes during different stages of flowering and seed development is scarce. OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 express in the anther. The expression of OsZIP3 varies significantly from $1 \ \mathrm { m m }$ from base of anther to $1 . 2 \mathrm { - } 1 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m m }$ from base (Fig. 5). The expression of OsZIP5 is slightly higher at the bottom of anther compared to the top.

In ovary, the expression of OsZIP1, OsZIP3, OsZIP4, OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 changes significantly. The expression of OsZIP3 varies significantly from 3 DAF to 5 DAF (Fig. 6). The expression of OsZIP4 and OsZIP8 is higher compared to OsZIPI and OsZIP3. The expression of OsZIP5 increases from 1 to 3 DAF and then decreases at 5 and 7 DAF. In embryo, the expression of OsZIP4 is significantly high compared to other OsZIPs (Fig. 7). The expression of OsZIPI , OsZIP3, OsZIP4, and OsZIP5 increases slowly from 7 to 42 DAF (Fig. 8). OsZIPs also express in endosperm. Again the expression of OsZIP4 is significantly high compared to other OsZIPs (Fig. 8). The expression of OsZIP4 increases slowly from 7 to 28 DAF and then decreases slightly. The expression of OsZIP5 decrease slowly from 7 to 42 DAF. As OsZIPs are expressed during all the flowering and seed developmental stages, it is reasonable to conclude that these genes play an important role in $Z \mathrm { n }$ transport to developing seed. The role of OsZIP4 seems particularly important in transporting the Zn to the developing seed.


## Increasing the seed Zn concentration


Zn deficiency is serious nutritional problem for humans and is particularly prevalent among children and pregnant women, especially in developing countries (World Health Organization 2002). The uptake of Zn depends on various factors including soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ concentration which is often low in soils (Cakmak 2008; Cakmak et al. 1999). The concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in rice seeds ranges from 8.9– $9 5 ~ { \mu \mathrm { g } } / \mathrm { g }$ dry weight (Yang et al. 1998) or $0 . 4 7 \mathrm { - } 0 . 7 9 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }$ per seed (Wissuwa et al. 2006). In another report the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in seeds was reported from 15.9– $5 8 . 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / g }$ dry weight (Graham et al. 1999) and depends upon external $Z \mathrm { n }$ supply and soil conditions (Wissuwa et al. 2008; Wissuwa et al. 2006). Increasing the Zn content and bioavailability of cereals such as rice seeds is an important target for breeders and offers the potential benefits to a large proportion of human population (Cakmak 2008; Palmgren et al. 2008; Zhu et al. 2007). Different strategies such as plant breeding, foliar or soil application of $Z \mathrm { n }$ fertilizers has been suggested and demonstrated to increase the Zn content of cereals (Cakmak 2008; Cakmak et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2012). Foliar application of Zn is shown to increase the Zn content of cereal up to two times (Cakmak et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2012). It is obvious that various Zn transporters transport this Zn to the developing seeds; however the detailed role of these transporters has to be characterized yet. Moreover, various transgenic approaches have been adopted to increase the Zn content of rice grains. The most common approach used by different research groups is to increase the expression of NAS genes. Rice lines expressing HvNAS1 under the control of CaMV35S or Actin1 promoter accumulate more Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ in seeds suggesting that NA overproduction have the potential to increase the Fe and Zn translocation to rice grains (Masuda et al. 2009). Increasing the expression of OsNAS2, through activation tagging, increased the expression of DMA biosynthetic pathway genes as well as genes related to Zn-uptake (Lee et al. 2011). Thus increasing the amount of NA increases DMA secretion from roots and stimulates Zn uptake and translocation to seed. Moreover, the enhanced NA and DMA in endosperm increased the content of bio-available Zn as revealed by feeding trials in mice (Lee et al. 2011). Increasing the expression of OsNAS3 through activation tagging also increases the Fe and Zn content of rice seeds (Lee et al. 2009). Similarly rice plants over expressing OsNAS1, OsNAS2 and OsNAS3 accumulated more Fe and Zn in the seed indicating that NA is important for Fe and Zn transport and could be successfully deployed for bio-fortification of Zn (Johnson et al. 2011). The overexpression of OsNAS1 not only increases the concentration of Zn in rice seeds but also increases its bio-availability (Zheng et al. 2010). Overexpression of barley dioxygenase gene, IDS3, involved in the biosynthesis of MAs also increased the rice seed Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ concentration (Masuda et al. 2008; Nakanishi et al. 2000; Suzuki et al. 2008a).

On the other hand regulating the expression of ZIPs to increase the seed Zn content was not successful. Transgenic rice plants over-expressing OsZIP4 under the control of the CaMV35S promoter accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots while the shoot Zn contents decreased significantly (Ishimaru et al. 2007). Similarly OsZIP5 and OsZIP8 overexpression rice also accumulated more $Z \mathrm { n }$ in roots at the expense of shoot Zn (Lee et al. 2010a). The OsZIP5 overexpression rice lines were sensitive to $Z \mathrm { n }$ excess, while the oszip5 knock out plants were tolerant to $Z \mathrm { n }$ excess (Lee et al. 2010a). Rice sucrose promoter (OsSUT1), is highly expressed in the mature phloem of all the vegetative tissues involved in the long-distance assimilate transport pathway during grain filling, in addition to the flag leaf blade and sheath prior to heading (Hirose et al. 2002; Scofield et al. 2007). The expression of OsYSL2 when controlled by the sucrose transporter promoter increased the Fe concentration in polished rice up to 4.4-fold compared to WT (Ishimaru et al. 2010). These results suggest that the controlling the temporal and spatial expression of OsZIP genes could be effective to increase the $Z \mathrm { n }$ in rice seeds.

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.

This family was first identified in plants, taking its name from the founding members as “ZRT, IRT-like protein” [8]. ZRT1 and ZRT2 are the high- and low-affinity zinc-regulated transporters of yeast [9, 10], respectively. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter) is an Arabidopsis transporter expressed in the roots of iron-deficient plants [11]. This family is widely distributed in all organisms, including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, animals [12], and plants. A considerably large family of ZIP genes has been currently characterized from various species, such as Arabidopsis [8, 11, 13], rice (Oryza sativa L.) [1, 7], soybean (Glycine max (Linn.) Merr.) [5], Medicago truncatula [6, 14], the hyperaccumulation plant Thlaspi caerulescens [4, 15], Th. japonicum [16], etc.

In recent years, much progress has been made towards understanding molecular mechanisms of $Z \mathrm { n }$

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ and iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ are essential micronutrients that participate in physiological and biochemical processes and promote plant growth and development. $Z \mathrm { n }$ is involved in the synthesis of numerous enzymes, such as alcohol dehydrogenase, copper $( \mathrm { C u } ) – \mathrm { Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, and RNA polymerase. Therefore, Zn deficiency decreases the activity of these enzymes (Hacisalihoglu and Kochian 2003). Recently,

Fe has been used as a cofactor for integrating photosynthesis with various metabolic pathways and regulating gene expression (Imsande 2010). Fe deficiency can affect the growth and yield of fruit trees and other crops, and it affects photosynthesis rate, chlorophyll content, and catalase activity (Fornerginer et al. 2010; Rube´n et al. 2011).

The continuous discovery of metal ion transporters has laid the foundation for studies on factors involved in the absorption, intracellular transport, localization, and efflux of metal ions, such as P1B-type heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family, Zn- and Fe-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) family, normal resistancerelated macrophage protein (NRAMP), and the cation dissemination facilitator (CDF) family (Milner et al. 2013; Fu et al. 2017; Vigani et al. 2013). AtIRT1 was the first ZIP gene identified which is located on the root surface and induced by Fe deficiency in the root of Arabidopsis thaliana L. (Henriques et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). IRT2, a homolog of IRT1, plays a similarly crucial role in A. thaliana. However, under similar Fedeficient conditions, the expression of IRT2 is significantly lower than that of IRT1 (Vert et al. 2001). Their homolog IRT3, which is located in the plasma membrane, increases the uptake of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe to complement the function of both $\mathrm { Z n - }$ and Fe-uptake mutants (Lin et al. 2009). Complementation mutants or knockdown of ZIP1 and ZIP2 in A. thaliana showed that ZIP1 and ZIP2 are involved in $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Mn uptake (Milner et al. 2013). In addition, functional analyses in maize (Zea mays L.) and rice indicated that ZIP3, ZIP4, ZIP5, and ZIP8 play important roles in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in the roots and shoots under Zn-deficient conditions (Ishimaru et al. 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, b). In A. thaliana, the function of ZIP9 is similar to that of ZIP12, being induced under $Z \mathbf { n }$ -limiting conditions (Talke et al. 2006; Wintz et al. 2003).

ZIP (Zinc-regulated transporter, Iron-regulated transporter-like Protein, ZIP) plays an important role in uptake or transport Zn or Fe in plants. So studying ZIPs in plant can help to elucidate the molecular mechanism for Zn and Fe transportation. Herein, we have cloned a novel Zn transporter gene NoZIP3 from Nasturtium officinale root using rapid-amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) method, evaluated its function by functional complementation assay and determined its relative transcriptional level by quantitative real-time Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (qRT-PCR). The results showed that the full-length cDNA of NoZIP3 was 1029 bp, which encoded a polypeptide of 342 amino acids with a conserved domain of the typical ZIPs. NoZIP3 sequence shared a high similarity $( 5 7 - 8 9 \% )$ with that of other plant species. NoZIP3 could complement a mutant yeast deficient in Zn transportation; however, it could not complement that of Fe transportation. qRT-PCR revealed that the transcriptional level of NoZIP3 in roots was much higher than that in leaves under Zn deficiency, Fe deficiency or sufficient nutrition. These results suggested that NoZIP3 might be preferentially expressed in roots and had roles in Zn transportation, which could provide the foundation for further studying the characteristics and function of this gene.

Te zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ -regulated/iron(Fe)-regulated transporterlike family proteins (ZIPs) are membrane-located proteins for cations transport (Eng et  al. 1998; Guerinot 2000). Tey have been found to exist broadly in prokaryotic cells, fungi, plants and mammalians. In plants, ZIPs have been identifed in both dicots and monocots, such as Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998; Milner et  al. 2013), rice (Chen et  al. 2008), maize (Li et  al. 2013), medicago (Lopez-Millan et al. 2004; Stephens et al. 2011) and barely (Tiong et al. 2015). Grotz et al. identifed fve ZIP genes (IRT1, ZIP1-4) in Arabidopsis (Grotz et  al. 1998), and later up to 11 ZIP genes from Arabidopsis were detected bioinformatically (Guerinot 2000). Roles of ZIP1-12 from Arabidopsis in Zn transport were explored experimentally (Milner et  al. 2013). More recently, 18 ZIPs from Arabidopsis and 16 ZIPs from rice were annotated (Ivanov and Bauer 2017).

In Arabidopsis and rice, only a small number of ZIPs have been examined for biological functions in plant till now. Arabidopsis IRT1 is a well-studied ZIP gene frst identifed as a crucial transporter for plant Fe uptake (Varotto et  al. 2002; Vert et  al. 2002). Arabidopsis IRT1 can be induced by iron defciency (Korshunova et  al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2002), and may play a role in Mn/ Zn transport as well (Korshunova et al. 1999; Rogers et al. 2000; Connolly et  al. 2002). Biological functions in $Z \mathrm { n } /$ Fe transport of AtIRT2 (Vert et al. 2001, 2009), AtZIP1/2 (Grotz et al. 1998; Wintz et al. 2003; Milner et al. 2013), OsIRT1 (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009; Ishimaru et  al. 2006; Bughio et  al. 2002) and OsZIP4/5/8 (Ishimaru et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2008; Lee et al. 2010a, b; Yang et al. 2009) have also been examined in the past decade.

A few studies have also implied that ZIPs may be involved in Cd transport. Yeast cells expressing AtIRT1 showed increased Cd sensitivity (Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2001), and IRT1-dependent $\mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { M n } / Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake was inhibited by excess Cd (Eide et al. 1996; Korshunova et al. 1999). Te Arabidopsis IRT1 knock-out mutant irt1-1 exhibited reduced Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation (Vert et al. 2002; Fan et al. 2014), while overexpression of AtIRT1 increased Cd sensitivity in Arabidopsis (Connolly et  al. 2002). AtIRT2, phylogenetically similar to AtIRT1, increased Cd uptake when overexpressed in Arabidopsis (Vert et  al. 2009), though the yeast cells expressing AtIRT2 exhibited no altered Cd sensitivity (Vert et  al. 2001). In rice, expression of OsIRT1 and OsIRT2 made the cells more sensitive to Cd and increased Cd accumulation (Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Lee and An 2009). Nonetheless, we still know little about the roles of most of the ZIPs genes in Cd stress response in Arabidopsis and rice.

In this study, genome-wide ZIPs identifcation in Arabidopsis and rice was performed with rigorous evolutional analysis. A comparative examination of genomewide expression profle of ZIPs in Arabidopsis and rice in response to Cd stress were carried out. Teir role in Cd uptake of typical ZIPs responding to Cd stress was further tested by expressing them in yeast. As expected, most identifed ZIPs gene expression responded remarkably to Cd stress, while unexpectedly it was found that Arabidopsis and rice showed a distinct pattern in ZIPs genes expression profle. Tese results may help to elucidate the plants’ genetic basis for Cd translocation via a ZIPs-dependent pathway.

 High expression of zinc (Zn)-regulated, iron-regulated transporter-like protein (ZIP) genes increases root Zn uptake in dicots, leading to high accumulation of Zn in shoots. However, none of the ZIP genes tested previously in monocots could enhance shoot Zn accumulation. In this report, barley (Hordeum vulgare) HvZIP7 was investigated for its functions in Zn transport.

 The functions of HvZIP7 in planta were studied using in situ hybridization and transient analysis of subcellular localization with a green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter. Transgenic barley lines overexpressing HvZIP7 were also generated to further understand the functions of HvZIP7 in metal transport.

 HvZIP7 is strongly induced by Zn deficiency, primarily in vascular tissues of roots and leaves, and its protein was localized in the plasma membrane. These properties are similar to its closely related homologs in dicots. Overexpression of HvZIP7 in barley plants increased Zn uptake when moderately high concentrations of Zn were supplied. Significantly, there was a specific enhancement of shoot Zn accumulation, with no measurable increase in iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), copper (Cu) or cadmium (Cd). HvZIP7 displays characteristics of low-affinity Zn transport.

Zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , as an essential micronutrient, is a component of more than 300 enzymes involved in plant biological processes. It plays important roles in gene expression and cellular development. However, a pre-requisite to developing zinc biofortified foods is the understanding of the molecular mechanism of zinc uptake by root, transport through stem, and loading to the specified organs such as seed and fruit.

Maize is an important cereal in the world with high production and productivity. Maize is grown in more than 166 countries for various uses, and in diverse seasons and agroecological conditions due to its high yield potential. In India, while $25 \%$ of the maize produce is consumed as food, the remaining $75 \%$ is used as livestock and poultry feed. Thus, micronutrient-deficient maize not only affects human beings but also livestock and poultry. Therefore, biofortified maize will be immensely helpful for the eradication of malnutrition as it is sustainable and affordable for the poorest of the poor. It is well documented that several genes control the Zn homeostasis in strategy II model plant rice (Ramesh et al. 2003; Ishimaru et al. 2006, 2007; Lee et al. 2010a, 2010b; Bashir et al. 2012). However, genes responsive to zinc uptake as well as loading in the kernel of maize have not so far been studied, which is a prerequisite for understanding the molecular mechanism of Zn uptake. Members of the ZRT-IRT-like protein (ZIP) family were the first metal transporters to be identified in plants (Eide et al. 1996). Along with other factors, the expressions of ZIP genes are regulated by the tissue metal status of the plant (Grotz et al. 1998). Genes with the ZIP domain have also been identified and characterized from other plant species including soybean, Medicago truncatula , Noccaea caerulescens and Thlaspi japonica (Pence et al. 2000; Assunção et al. 2001; Burleigh et al. 2003; Mizuno et al. 2005; Moreau et al. 2002; Plaza et al. 2007). For instance, NcZNT1 from Noccaea caerulescens was shown to mediate high-affinity $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and low-affinity Cd uptake in yeast (Pence et al. 2000). Homologous genes TjZNT1 and TjZNT2 isolated from the Ni hyper-accumulator Thlaspi japonica were shown to enhance the transport of Zn, Cd, and Mn (Mizuno et al. 2005).

The complete genome sequences derived from large-scale sequencing projects are important for comparative and functional genomics research, providing the opportunity to scan various gene families. Like any other sequencing project, the complete maize genome sequence also provides a valuable resource for comparative analysis of the gene families. With decoding of the maize genome sequence, several gene families have already been characterized in maize (Liu et al. 2013a, b; Zhang et al. 2013). Although individual zinc-regulated transporters (ZRT) and iron-regulated transporter-like (IRT) protein (ZIP) genes have been extensively studied in yeast (Wu et al. 2011), as well as in higher plants such as rice (Lee et al. 2010b; Lan et al. 2013), genome-wide analysis of the members of this family has yet to be studied in maize.

A current hypothesis to explain the mechanism of Al tolerance in wheat proposes that an Al-dependent efflux of malate chelates and detoxifies Al cations in the rhizosphere (Delhaize and Ryan,1995; Delhaize et al.,1993b;Ma et al., 2001; Ryan et al.,1995,1997,2001; Zhang et al.,2001). We have presented several lines of evidence supporting the conclusion that ALMT1 encodes an Al-activated malate transporter.This finding represents the first isolation and characterization of a plant gene encoding a transporter that facilitates organic anion efflux.The additional findings that ALMT1-1 expression co-segregates with Al tolerance in wheat and that cultured tobacco cells overexpressing ALMT1 show an increase in Al tolerance (Figure 7) suggest that ALMT1-1 is a strong candidate for the Alt1 gene of wheat.

At least two alleles of ALMT1 are present in wheat (ALMT1-1 and ALMT1-2). Expression of these genes in oocytes or in cultured tobacco cells indicates that both are capable of functioning as malate transporters (Figures 5c and 7b),although ALMT1-2 did not appear to be as effective as ALMT1-1. The Al-tolerant line ET8 expresses the ALMT1-1 only at relatively high levels, whereas the Al-sensitive line ES8 expresses the ALMT1-2 only at significantly lower levels. The same pattern of expression was observed in a set of another two lines examined,Altas66 and Scout66. However,a moderately

Al-tolerant cultivar, Chinese Spring,which releases malate at rates between those measured for the Al-tolerant and Alsensitive cultivars (Papernik et al.,20o1),expresses only the ALMT1-2 allele,but at relatively high levels (Figure 2b). These results suggest that the relative Al tolerance afforded by ALMT1 in different wheat cultivars is determined primarily by the level of expression of these alleles rather than the two-amino acid difference between them.Future work will test this hypothesis by correlating Al tolerance with both ALMT1 expression and Al-dependent malate efflux in a range of wheat cultivars.

Previous physiological experiments have described a malate-permeable anion channel in ET8 wheat seedlings with attributes similar to those shown here for ALMT1 (Ryan et al., 1997,2001; Zhang et al., 2001). For example, both are activated by Al,but not by $\mathsf { L } \mathsf { a } ^ { 3 + }$ ，both facilitate malate efflux from cells,both are constitutively expressed, and both are localized to the root apices.As much of the existing physiological evidence indicates that malate efflux from the roots of Al-tolerant wheat cultivars is mediated by anion channels,we can infer that the ALMT1 protein may be the first member of a new family of plant anion channels (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,20oo). However,we acknowledge that without investigating the isolated protein,we cannot exclude the alternative possibility that ALMT1encodes for a receptor that can activate a malate transport protein present in both plant and animal cells.

The finding that Al activates malate efflux from wheat roots,and from plant and animal cells expressing ALMT1is especially intriguing,as Al has been shown to inhibit many other transporters including ion channels (see Ryan et al., 1997).However,some cations can activate transporters, including ion channels,in other plant species,as well as in animal cells.For instance,Al has been shown to activate an anion channel in maize roots in a similar manner to that described in wheat (Kollmeier et al.，20o1;Pineros and Kochian,2001）and ${ \mathsf { H } } { \mathsf { g } } ^ { 2 + }$ can activate the rat aquaporin AQP6 by binding to the protein and trapping it in a conformation that is permeable to water and ions (Yasui et al., 1999).It is still unclear whether Al activates malate efflux by directly interacting with the ALMT1 protein,or whether intermediate steps are involved (Ryan et al.,1995,1997, 2001;Zhang et al.,2001). The observations that ALMT1 expression elicits an Al-activated efflux of malate in plant cells (Figures 6and 7)and an Al-dependent inward current (consistent with malate efflux) in animal cells (Figure 5) suggest that a direct interaction is more likely.Al also appears to directly activate an anion channel in maize roots, because the response has been detected in the outside-out patch configuration for which involvement of secondary messengers is unlikely (Pineros and Kochian,2001).

For future study,we will investigate whether the expression of the ALMT1 gene in Al-sensitive crop and pasture species can increase plant production in acid soils.
