## Recovery of Al resistance in the AtALMT1P::AtMATE transgenic line


To evaluate the functions of the promoter-swapped transgenes, we compared the levels of Al resistance for the wild-type, AtALMT1-KO, AtMATE-KD and double-KO/KD mutants, and the two promoter-swap transgenic lines. We found that, after 6 days of Al exposure, root growth was inhibited by approximately $50 \%$ for the wild-type plants relative to control root growth in the absence of Al. Compared to the wild-type, the Al resistance measured as a percentage of relative net root growth $( \mathsf { R R G } \mathsf { \Lambda } ^ { \mathrm { o } } )$ of AtALMT1- KO, AtMATE-KD and double-KO/KD decreased by $6 6 \%$ , $7 \%$ and $7 5 \%$ respectively, confirming our previous findings that AtALMT1 plays a major role and AtMATE plays a smaller role in Al resistance in Arabidopsis (Figure 4 and Table 1).

Transformation of the $A t A L M T \mathcal { 1 } _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ promoterswap construct into the double-KO/KD background dramatically increased Al resistance for the transgenic plants. As seen in Figure 4, Al resistance $( \mathsf { R R G } \mathsf { \Lambda } ^ { \mathrm { o } } )$ of the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } \because A t -$ MATE line increased 4.5-fold compared to the double-KO/KD line, achieving a level of Al resistance comparable to wild-type plants. However, expression of the other promoter-swap construct, $A t M A T E _ { P } . . . A t A L M T \mathcal { I } ,$ in the same background led to only a small increase in Al resistance (Figure 4).


## The AtALMT1P::AtMATE transgenic line uses less carbon than the wild-type to achieve the same level of Al resistance


To estimate the carbon-use efficiency for Al resistance in the various genotypes, we normalized Al resistance measured as ${ \tt R R G \% }$ to the total carbon released by the roots under Al stress due to malate and citrate efflux. As shown in Table 1 and Figure 5, after Al treatment, the roots of wild-type plants released a mean of 0.52 nmol citrate and 2.05 nmol malate per plant per day. This is equivalent to a release of 3.12 nmol carbon per plant per day from citrate, which has six carbon atoms, and 8.2 nmol carbon per plant per day originating from malate, which has four carbon atoms, giving a total of 11.3 nmol carbon released per plant per day (Table 1). Thus, the carbon-use efficiency for wild-type plants was estimated as 4.6 units of Al resistance $( \mathsf { R R G } \mathsf { \Lambda } ^ { \mathrm { o } } )$ per nmol carbon lost from roots per plant per day (Table 1).

Carbon-use efficiency was also calculated for all of the transgenic lines used in this study, including AtALMT1-KO, AtMATE-KD, double-KO/KD, $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ and AtMATE ::AtALMT1. As shown in Table 1, compared to the AtALMT1-KO, AtMATE-KD and double-KO/KD lines, the wild-type line was the most Al-tolerant. However, there was a significant carbon cost for this higher Al resistance, and the carbon use efficiency in wild-type plants was as much as $50 \%$ lower than that calculated for the AtALMT1-KO and AtMATE-KD lines (4.6 versus 6.8 in wild-type and double-KO/KD lines, respectively) (Table 1).

Even more interesting, in the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ line, a significant increase in carbon-use efficiency was seen, almost threefold higher than in wild-type (11.9 versus 4.6) and almost twofold higher than the $A t M A T E _ { P } . . . A t A L M T \ i$ line (11.9 versus 6.3). As the difference between the double-KO/ KD and $A t A L M T \mathcal { 1 } _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ lines is due to the presence of the transgenic promoter-swap construct in the latter, the increase in Al resistance in the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ line is the result of the 3.0-fold increase in Al-activated root citrate exudation mediated by the transgenic AtMATE citrate transporter whose gene expression is driven by the stronger AtALMT1 promoter (Figure 3 and Table 1).

The much higher carbon-use efficiency in the AtAL$M T 1 _ { P } { \mathrel { \mathop : } } A t M A T E$ line was due to the fact that, although Al resistance and the rate of root citrate exudation for this transgenic line are comparable to that of wild-type, the level of root malate exudation in this $A t A L M T \mathcal { 1 } _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ line is negligible compared with that in wild-type plants, leading to a $5 8 \%$ decrease in total root carbon release in the AtAL$M T 1 _ { P } { \mathrel { \mathop : } } A t M A T E$ line compared to the wild-type (Table 1).

As described above, the root malate exudation resulting from expression of the AtALMT1 gene driven by its own native AtALMT1 promoter in wild-type plants, and the root citrate exudation resulting from AtMATE expression driven by the transgenic AtALMT1 promoter in the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } \therefore A t -$ MATE line, are the major determinants for Al resistance in each line (Table 1). Due to the differences in promoter strength of the native and transgenic AtALMT1 promoters (Figure 1), the rate of root malate exudation in the wild-type was 3.6 times higher than that of root citrate exudation in the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } . . . A t M A T E$ line (Figure 5 and Table 1). Both lines exhibited similar levels of root citrate exudation; however, both lines displayed comparable levels of Al resistance (Table 1). This is quite interesting, and, as discussed below, is due to the efflux of citrate, a much more effective chelator than malate, being more localized to the growing root tip in the $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } { \because } A t M A T E$ line and not expressed more diffusely throughout the mature root region as it is in wild-type plants. These findings also suggest that the carbon loss due to the large malate efflux in wild-type plants is a significant carbon cost on root growth, and the same level of Al resistance in the AtALMT1P::AtMATE line with similar citrate and much less malate exudation than wild-type may be due in part to a reduction in this carbon cost.

The primary mechanism of Arabidopsis aluminum (Al) resistance is based on root Al exclusion, resulting from Al-activated root exudation of the $A | ^ { 3 + }$ -chelating organic acids, malate and citrate. Root malate exudation is the major contributor to Arabidopsis Al resistance, and is conferred by expression of AtALMT1, which encodes the root malate transporter. Root citrate exudation plays a smaller but still significant role in Arabidopsis Al resistance, and is conferred by expression of AtMATE, which encodes the root citrate transporter. In this study, we demonstrate that levels of Al-activated root organic acid exudation are closely correlated with expression of the organic acid transporter genes AtALMT1 and AtMATE. We also found that the AtALMT1 promoter confers a significantly higher level of gene expression than the AtMATE promoter. Analysis of AtALMT1 and AtMATE tissue- and cell-specific expression based on stable expression of promoter–reporter gene constructs showed that the two genes are expressed in complementary root regions: AtALMT1 is expressed in the root apices, while AtMATE is expressed in the mature portions of the roots. As citrate is a much more effective chelator of $A | ^ { 3 + }$ than malate, we used a promoter-swap strategy to test whether root tip-localized expression of the AtMATE coding region driven by the stronger AtALMT1 promoter $( A t A L M T \bar { \imath } _ { P } . . . A t M A T E )$ resulted in increased Arabidopsis Al resistance. Our results indicate that expression of $A t A L M T 1 _ { P } ;$ :AtMATE not only significantly increased Al resistance of the transgenic plants, but also enhanced carbon-use efficiency for Al resistance.

Keywords: aluminum resistance, transporter protein, organic acid exudation, promoter swap, carbon-use efficiency, Arabidopsis thaliana.

Background: A major limiting factor for plant growth is the aluminum (Al) toxicity in acidic soils, especially in tropical regions. The exclusion of Al from the root apex through root exudation of organic acids such as malate and citrate is one of the most ubiquitous tolerance mechanisms in the plant kingdom. Two families of anion channels that confer Al tolerance are well described in the literature, ALMT and MATE family.

Results: In this study, sugarcane plants constitutively overexpressing the Sorghum bicolor MATE gene (SbMATE) showed improved tolerance to Al when compared to non-transgenic (NT) plants, characterized by sustained root growth and exclusion of aluminum from the root apex based on the result obtained with hematoxylin staining. In addition, genome-wide analysis of the recently released sugarcane genome identified 11 ALMT genes and molecular studies showed potential new targets for aluminum tolerance.

Conclusions: Our results indicate that the transgenic plants overexpressing the Sorghum bicolor MATE has an improved tolerance to Al. The expression profile of ALMT genes revels potential candidate genes to be used has an alternative for agricultural expansion in Brazil and other areas with aluminum toxicity in poor and acid soils.

Keywords: Aluminum, Sugarcane, MATE, ALMT, Abiotic stress, Hydroponic system

Malate efflux from root apices plays a critical role in aluminum (Al) tolerance in wheat. Malate prevents the inhibition of root elongation by chelating Al ions, thus reducing phytotoxicity to the root apex (Delhaize et al. 1993b). Differences in the amounts of Al-induced malate efflux are correlated with differences in Al tolerance among wheat cultivars (Ryan et al. 1995b). Malate efflux has been shown to be regulated by the permeability of plasmamembrane anion channels or transporters in wheat apical root cells (Ryan et al. 1997; Zhang et al. 2001). It is important to identify the components that mediate such malate efflux because selection for the Al-tolerance genes is expected to improve crop productivity on Al-toxic acid soils (Kochian et al. 2004).

Physiological characteristics of Al-responsive malate efflux provide strong evidences for the identification of malate transporters in wheat (see Ryan et al. 2001, 2003; Kochian et al. 2004). For instance, observations that Al triggers malate release within a few minutes implied that the Al-inducible gene expression of malate transporters is not necessary for the response (Ryan et al. 1995a; Osawa and Matsumoto 2001). In agreement with this assumption, a recent differential screening for gene transcripts with constitutively high expression in an Altolerant wheat cultivar and genotype resulted in the discovery of an Al-tolerance gene (Sasaki et al. 2004). This gene, Al-responsive malate transporter (ALMT1), conferred Al-responsive malate release to transgenic crops and cell lines including rice, tobacco, and barley (Delhaize et al. 2004; Sasaki et al. 2004). An electrophysiological study using Xenopus laevis oocytes showed that ALMT1 functions as an Al-activated malate efflux transporter (Sasaki et al. 2004), although its kinetics are not fully understood. One major obstacle to the characterization of this transport is that malate is widely distributed in living cells and is readily metabolized by endogenous enzymes (Martinoia and Rentsch 1994).

To overcome such problems, alternative traceable substrates that are resistant to catabolism have been employed in detailed transport analysis. For example, the rubidium ion $( \mathrm { R b } ^ { + } )$ is often used as an alternative substrate to trace the movement of the potassium ion $( \mathbb { K } ^ { + } )$ across the cell membrane via $\mathrm { K } ^ { \bar { + } }$ channels or transporters (e.g. Gassmann and Schroeder 1994; Uozumi et al. 1995). Frequently yeasts have been used as model systems. The use of yeast mutants that lack the ability to excrete certain toxic compounds, such as drugs, toxic metals, and weak acids, has led to the identification of substrates for several efflux transporters including ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters, metal transporters and organic anion transporters (Cui et al. 1996; Li et al. 1996; Piper et al. 1998).

Aluminum Activated Malate Transporters (ALMTs) are important plant anion channels by playing roles in organic acid transport, stress resistance, growth and development, nutrient absorption, and the GABA response (Hedrich 2012; Ramesh et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2016; Balzergue et al., 2017; Medeiros et al., 2018; Long et al.,

2020). Wheat TaALMT1 was the first identified family member (named due to its activation by aluminium $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ , the main ion causing toxicity to plants in acidic soil) mediates malate efflux to chelate ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ and relieve toxicity (Zhang et al., 2001; Sasaki et al., 2004). Our recent work has shown that TaALMT1 not only participates in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxification but also participates in the GABA response (Ramesh et al., 2015; Long et al., 2020). Arabidopsis has 14 ALMTs, with those characterized having varied roles, and several others yet to be characterized (Hedrich 2012; Sharma et al., 2016; Medeiros et al., 2018). AtALMT1, which is mainly expressed in roots and localized at the plasma membrane (PM), functions in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity resistance, similarly to TaALMT1, low phosphorus (LP) signal transduction, and Fe uptake, by mediating malate efflux in roots (Hoekenga et al., 2006; Balzergue et al., 2017; Mora-Macıas et al., 2017 ́ ). ALMT3 is also involved in the LP response in root hairs (Maruyama et al., 2019). The vacuolar membrane (tonoplast)-localized anion channels ALMT4, ALMT6, and ALMT9 transport anions across the tonoplast to regulate stomatal movement and/or salinity stress resistance (Kovermann et al., 2007; Meyer et al., 2011; De Angeli et al., 2013a; Baetz et al., 2016; Eisenach et al., 2017). ALMT12, ALMT13, and ALMT14, are all likely to be Rtype anion channels in the PM, playing roles in malate transport to regulate stomatal opening, stomatal and mesophyll conductance, and pollen tube growth (Meyer et al., 2010; Sasaki et al., 2010; Medeiros et al., 2016; Gutermuth et al., 2018; Domingos et al., 2019). Furthermore, ALMT family members were reported to be involved in physiological and stress response processes in other crops and plants including maize, rice, soybean, apple, grape, tomato, canola, Brachypodium distachyon, and Medicago sativa (Ligaba et al., 2006; Piñeros et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2013; De Angeli et al., 2013b; Sasaki et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018; Heng et al., 2018; Li et al., 2020; Luu et al., 2019).

Previously, through the use of gene mapping, a mutation in OsALMT7 was found to underpin a panicle apical abortion (paab1) phenotype. The two paab1 transcripts (paab1-t1 and paab1-t2), were found to be transcribed into proteins with Cterminal truncations (containing 163 amino acid residues) that transport anions with a capacity lower than that of the fulllength OsALMT7 (Heng et al., 2018). OsALMT7 (paab1) is expressed in vascular tissues of roots, stems, sheaths, and panicles and localizes to the PM, and it was concluded that it plays an important role in panicle anion transport, panicle development, and grain yield (Heng et al., 2018). Furthermore when wild-type plants were transformed with a genomic fragment containing the paab1 base substitution resulting in a panicle abortion phenotype (Heng et al., 2018). Compare with other ALMTs, OsALMT7 has special molecular characteristicses that it has the ability to mediate malate flux with its transmembrane helices incomplete, and its truncated protein represses the wild-type channel in rice. Here, we investigate the mechanism of these characteristicses with further electrophysiology studies. We proposed and tested the hypothesis that OsALMT7 transports malate as a multimer and that paab1 interaction with OsALMT7 inhibits transport capacity. Furthermore, we extended this to examine whether this is a feature of other ALMTs, specifically TaALMT1.

A number of plant channels are already known to function as homo- or hetero-multimers, and heteromerization is acknowledged to be an important mechanism of channel regulation (Hedrich, 2012). For example, aquaporins of both the PM and tonoplast assemble as homo- or heterotetramers, such as PIP1s with no or weak water permeability with itself, combine with PIP2s and increase their activity in different plant species (Harvengt et al., 2000; Bienert et al., 2012; Fetter et al., 2004; Heinen et al., 2014; Berny et al., 2016). Shaker family potassium (K) channels share a similar structure with ALMTs, 6 transmembrane $\alpha$ -helices with both N-terminal and C-terminal cytosolic domains, and function as homo- or heterotetramers; notably, KC1, the silent channel subunit, forms a heterotetramer with other shaker K channels to change their voltage dependence (Baizabal-Aguirre et al., 1999; Pilot et al., 2001; Véry and Sentenac, 2003; Xicluna et al., 2007; Duby et al., 2008; Lebaudy et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2009; Lebaudy et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2010; Jeanguenin et al., 2011). Cyclic nucleotide-gated channel 2 (CNGC2) and CNGC4 have been proposed to form a heteromeric channel to mediate $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ currents (Tian et al., 2019). For plant anion channels, the S-type channel SLAC1 has been proposed to combine with the shaker $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels KAT1 and KAT2 and inhibit their channel activity (Zhang et al., 2016). Zhang et al. (2013) showed that tonoplast-localized AtALMT9 formed homomultimeric complex by coexpressing the mutant channel and wild-type channel in tobacco leaves; however, it has not been determined whether PM-localized ALMTs, including OsALMT7, and R-type anion channels, such as ALMT12/13/14, function as multimers or monomers.

Here, we determined that OsALMT7 function as multimeric proteins and that combinations of ALMT subunits can contribute to anion channel regulation. This strengthens our understanding of ALMT function. By defining the mechanism by which subunit modification has a dominant effect on channel function, this provides a new avenue by which genetic modification or gene editing can have important effects without first creating knockout mutants, enabling crop stress resistance and grain yield improvements.

Aluminum (Al) is the most abundant metal element in the earth's crust. At low $\mathsf { p H }$ ,dissolution of Al-containing compounds is enhanced,and the release of toxic Al cations (particularly $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } \mathsf { I }$ into the soil solution can rapidly inhibit root growth.Poor root development reduces nutrient and water uptake,explaining why Al toxicity is the major limiting factor for crop and pasture production in acid soils. Soil acidity limits plant production on over $30 \%$ of the world's arable land,and the increasing area of arable land affected by acidity poses a serious threat to global food production (von Uexkull and Mutert,1995).Some plant species and even cultivars within certain species (e.g.wheat and maize) have evolved mechanisms that minimize the harmful effects of Al ions (Kochian,1995; Matsumoto,2000;Taylor,1991), and the nature of these mechanisms has attracted considerable interest. In wheat (Triticum aestivum L.),this phenomenon has been investigated using near-isogenic lines (ET8 (Al-tolerant) and ES8 (Al-sensitive)) that differ in Al tolerance at a single dominant locus designated as Alt1 (Delhaize et al.,1993a).The Alt1 locus co-segregates with an Al-activated malate efflux from root apices (Delhaize et al., 1993a,b)and it is hypothesized that the released malate protects the sensitive growing zone by chelating Al in the soil to form non-toxic complexes (Delhaize and Ryan,1995; Delhaize et al.,1993b; Ma et al.,2001; Ryan et al.,2001).As malate efflux is mediated by Al-activated anion channels in theplasmamembrane ofrootcells,theAlt1genecouldencode a malate-permeable anion channel ora protein that modulates the activity of such a channel (Delhaize and Ryan,1995; Delhaize et al.,1993b;Ma et al.,2001; Ryan et al.,1995,1997, 2001; Zhang et al., 2oo1). However, the gene that controls this Al-activated malate efflux has not been previously isolated.In this study,we describe the isolation and characterization of a gene from wheat that confers an Al-activated efflux of malate,when expressed in Xenopus oocytes, rice (Oryza sativa L.),and cultured tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) cells.

Many plant species cope with the aluminum $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ present in acid soils $\mathrm { ( p H } \leq 5 . 5 ) $ using mechanisms classified as resistance (exclusion of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ from root and shoot tissues) or tolerance (safe accommodation of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ once it enters the cell). An $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance mechanism present in many species is the efflux of organic acids (citrate, malate or oxalate) from root apices into the apoplasm (Liu et al. 2014). This mechanism relies on the formation of a complex between the organic acid(s) released by the root tips and the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ present in the soil; these complexes are less damaging to the root tip, consequently reducing $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity to the plant (Kochian et al. 2015).

In wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), two organic anions (malate and citrate) have been reported to detoxify the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ around the root tip (Delhaize et al. 1993; Ryan et al. 2009), and the membrane transporters encoded by the genes TaALMT1 (chromosome 4D) and TaMATE1B (chromosome 4B) are responsible for the efflux of these anions by the root apex (Sasaki et al. 2004; Raman et al. 2005; Tovkach et al. 2013). Although differences in the TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B structural region can be detected (Sasaki et al. 2004; Raman et al. 2005, 2008; Tovkach et al. 2013), it is the level of gene expression that shows higher correlation to the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance/sensitivity. For instance, the overexpression of those genes have been reported to transgenically enhance the amount of malate or citrate released by the root tip (Sasaki et al. 2004; Delhaize et al. 2004; Zhang et al. 2008; Pereira et al. 2010; Ryan et al. 2011; Tovkach et al. 2013). Ultimately, the increase in organic acid release enhances the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. The link between higher TaALMT1 expression and higher $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance was also observed in conventional wheat lines of non

Japanese origin where the number of repeats of four blocks (A, B, C and D) in the TaALMT1 promoter was correlated with the level of TaALMT1 expression, malate efflux, and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance (Sasaki et al. 2006). It is the presence of these tandem repeated elements in the TaALMT1 promoter region that contribute directly to the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance of hexaploid wheat (Ryan et al. 2010). Similarly, greater $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance in wheat has also been correlated with citrate efflux from root tips and the expression of the TaMATE1B gene (Tovkach et al. 2013). Genotypes with a transposon-like insertion upstream of the TaMATE1B coding region have stronger expression at the root apex and greater citrate efflux (Tovkach et al. 2013; Garcia-Oliveira et al. 2014). The transposon-like insertion near TaMATE1B as well as the repeated elements in the TaALMT1 promoter can be discriminated by PCR (Sasaki et al. 2006; Garcia-Oliveira et al. 2014). Up to date, nine alleles for the TaALMT1 promoter have been described this way (Sasaki et al. 2006; Raman et al. 2008; Ryan et al. 2010; Delhaize et al. 2012b), while the transposon insertion in the TaMATE1B promoter can be distinguished by the presence or absence of a PCR product (Tovkach et al. 2013; Garcia-Oliveira et al. 2014). In general, genotypes with the Type V and Type VI alleles of TaALMT1 (greater number of repeats in the promoter) show intermediate to high levels of expression and are more resistant to ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ (Sasaki et al. 2006; Raman et al. 2008). The transposon-like insertion near TaMATE1B is associated with constitutive citrate efflux by the root tip and higher $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance (Tovkach et al. 2013; GarciaOliveira et al. 2014).

Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. SlALMT15 (Solyc11gO6897O) was found to be related to a stomatal density trait that functions in stomatal formation in tomato leaves,and further affects photosynthesis and drought tolerance in tomato (J.Ye,Wang, et al.,2021). Z.Wang et al. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.

Thisreport provides evidence suggesting that SlALMT11 (SolycO8g0o699O) expressed in tomato leaf guard cells is involved in stomatal closure induced by external malate,but not by abscisic acid.This study also highlights how the guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (SlALMT11 and AtALMT12)are activated by external organic acids and identifies the amino acid residues of the ALMT proteins involved in the voltage-dependent channel activity.

Acid soils account for about $30 \%$ of the world’s total land area and over $50 \%$ of the world’s potentially arable lands (von Uexkull and Mutert, 1995; Kochian€ et al., 2004). As the third most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, aluminum (Al) is solubilized from aluminosilicate clay minerals to the toxic species $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ in soils with pH values of 5 or below (Kochian et al., 2004). As micromolar concentrations of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ can rapidly inhibit root elongation (Kochian, 1995; Poschenrieder et al., 2008), Al stress has been considered as one of the most important constraints for agricultural production in acid soils (Kochian et al., 2004). Therefore, enhancing Al resistance in crops becomes a key to increasing crop productivity on these soils, which would subsequently help solve the problem of food shortage and biofuel production.

The Al-resistant mechanism employed by plants can be classified into external exclusion and internal detoxification, depending on whether Al is detoxified out of or within the plant cell. Although several mechanisms for the external exclusion of Al have been proposed (Kochian et al., 2004; Poschenrieder et al., 2008), the most wellstudied strategy is the secretion of organic acid anions, including citrate, oxalate and malate, from the root apices (Ma et al., 2001; Ryan et al., 2001; Kochian et al., 2004). These organic acid anions prevent Al from binding to root cells via chelating Al externally, and thereby detoxify Al outside the cells (Ma et al., 2001; Ryan et al., 2001). Many transporter-encoding genes responsible for the Al-activated secretion of malate and citrate have been identified (Ryan et al., 2011; Delhaize et al., 2012). The malate transporter gene ALMT1 that conferred Al resistance was first cloned in wheat (Sasaki et al., 2004), and its homologous genes have been isolated in Arabidopsis and oilseed rape (Hoekenga et al., 2006; Ligaba et al., 2006); however, the HvALMT1 in Hordeum vulgare (barley) has been proven to be an anion channel to facilitate organic anion transport in stomatal function and expanding cells, but not to be associated with Al resistance (Gruber et al., 2010). Genes involved in the Al-induced or -activated citrate secretion (multidrug and toxic compound extrusion, MATE) have also been identified in barley, Sorghum, Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays (maize), Secale cereale (rye), Oryza sativa (rice) and Vigna umbellata (ricebean) (Furukawa et al., 2007; Magalhaes et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009; Maron et al., 2010; Yokosho et al., 2010, 2011; Yang et al., 2011). But in Triticum spp. (wheat), the TaMATE1B is constitutively expressed and citrate secretion does not require Al activation (Ryan et al., 2009; Tovkach et al., 2013). In Arabidopsis, Al stress induces a high level of root malate exudation and a lower level of root citrate exudation. Using mutants of ALMT1 and MATE demonstrated that ALMT1 is a major contributor to Arabidopsis Al resistance, and MATE makes a significant but smaller contribution (Liu et al., 2009). Moreover, the two transporters function independently to confer Al resistance in Arabidopsis; however, the regulatory mechanisms of expression of these genes are still poorly understood.

Recently, two zinc-finger proteins, sensitive to proton rhizotoxicity 1 (STOP1) in Arabidopsis and $A | ^ { 3 + }$ resistance transcription factor 1 (ART1) in rice, respectively, were identified by mutant analysis (Iuchi et al., 2007; Yamaji et al., 2009). The two proteins share significant sequence similarity and appear to act as transcription factors to enhance the expression of a range of Al resistance genes (Sawaki et al., 2009; Yamaji et al., 2009). In the absence of STOP1, Al-induced ALMT1 and MATE expression were completely suppressed in Arabidopsis (Liu et al., 2009). Nevertheless, the transcriptional regulation of Al resistance genes is largely unknown. Moreover, both STOP1 and ART1 are not Al-inducible genes (Iuchi et al., 2007; Yamaji et al., 2009), indicating that there may be other Al-responsive factors involved in the regulation of Al resistance genes.

The plant-specific WRKY domain-containing proteins comprise one of the largest transcription factor families in plants (Eulgem et al., 2000; Rushton et al., 2010). There are 74 members in Arabidopsis (Rushton et al., 2010). WRKY proteins contain one or two domains composed of the conserved amino acid sequence WRKYGQK, together with a novel zinc-finger-like motif (Ulker and Somssich, 2004). With the domains, they can activate or repress transcription through directly binding to the W–box, which has a core sequence (T)(T)TGAC(C/T) present in promoters of the target genes (Eulgem et al., 2000). WRKY transcription factors play critical roles in a great number of processes in Arabidopsis or other species (Ulker and Somssich, 2004; Rushton et al., 2010). In particular, they are involved in regulating responses to biotic stress, such as pathogen invasion, or abiotic stress, such as drought and high salinity (Rushton et al., 2010). In this study we found that Arabidopsis WRKY46, which was previously reported to participate in basal resistance against the pathogen Pseudomonas syringae (Hu et al., 2012), is responsive to Al. Furthermore, we demonstrated that it functions in Al sensitivity through regulating the expression of ALMT1.

In acid soils the soluble Al ions exist mainly in the trivalent $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ form which damages membranes and rapidly inhibits root growth [29]. A widespread mechanism for Al resistance in many plant species relies on the release of organic anions from roots apices (the sensitive region of the root for Al toxicity). The organic anions, such as malate, citrate and oxalate, are able to chelate $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to prevent it from binding in the cell wall and membranes and from entering the cytosol. This chelation reduces harmful interactions from occurring in the apoplast and in the cytosol of the root apex [30]. The first member of the family identified was TaALMT1 from wheat where it controls the major mechanism for aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ resistance [1]. TaALMT1 is constitutively expressed in the root apices and activated by the $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ cations prevalent in acid soils to release malate anions into the apoplast. Malate chelates the $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ which reduces damage to the cell wall, membranes and other cellular components. Other members of the family perform similar functions in Arabidopsis [3,31], rape (Brassica napus L.) [4], rye (Secale cereale L.) [2], soybean (Glycine max L.) [32], alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) [33], and Yorkshire fog (Holcus lanatus L.) [34]. Regulation of these vary and some show more complex interactions [35]. For instance, AtALMT1 is not constitutively expressed in Arabidopsis roots but induced by low pH and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ [3] and GmALMT1 in soybean shows complex interactions with Al stress and phosphorus nutrition [32].

Most members of the ALMT family are not involved in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance but perform other functions on different membranes [21,36]. For example, four members in Arabidopsis (AtALMT4, AtALMT6, AtALMT9 and AtALMT12) and one in barley (Hordeum vulgare L., HvALMT1) are involved in guard cell regulation. This is consistent with the involvement of anion transport in signal transduction and osmotic adjustment in modulating stomatal aperture [5–7,10,18,20]. Electrophysiological studies in Xenopus laevis (Daudin, 1802) oocytes revealed similarities between the currents generated by AtALMT12 and the previously characterised rapid or R-type/QUAC anion currents which propose that AtALMT12 anion channels are responsible for these currents [6,37]. AtALMT6 localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and facilitates calcium and pH-dependent movement of malate into the vacuole [8], but knockout mutations show little or no phenotype indicating some redundancy in these functions. AtALMT9 also localises to the tonoplast of guard cells and knock-out mutations show impaired stomatal opening in the light and delayed wilting [8,9]. AtALMT9 is activated by cytosolic malate and appears to facilitate chloride movement into the vacuole during stomatal opening. VvALMT9 is a homolog of AtALMT9 in grape (Vitis vinifera L.) and reportedly controls the acidity of berries during fruit maturation by facilitating tartrate, malate and succinate accumulation in the vacuoles of mesocarp cells [15]. A recent study also indicated that the ABA induced anion channel AtALMT4 of mediates $\mathrm { M a l } ^ { 2 - }$ efflux from the vacuole during stomatal closure and its activity depends on phosphorylation [38].

Acidity in apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) similarly relies on the ALMT transporter Ma1 which mediates malate accumulation into the vacuoles of developing fruit cells [14]. In maize (Zea mays L.), ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2 are mainly expressed in root tissues and likely function to assist in balancing charges during nutrient uptake [12,13]. Both proteins localise to the plasma membrane and both are permeable to inorganic anions but ZmALMT2 is also permeable to organic anions as demonstrated by the constitutive release of malate from the roots of transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing ZmALMT2 [13]. OsALMT4 is a member of the ALMT family in rice (Oryza sativa L.). OsALMT4 is widely expressed in rice and encodes a malate-permeable anion channel on the plasma membrane. Enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins [39].

Background Aluminum (Al) toxicity has limited the productivity and expansion of cereal crops on acid soils; however, a number of plant species or cultivars have developed different strategies for detoxifying aluminum both internally and externally.

Scope This review focuses on recent progress on molecular mechanisms of Al tolerance in gramineous plants.

Conclusions A common mechanism in all gramineous plants is the secretion of organic acid anions (citrate and malate) from the roots. Genes belonging to ALMT (for Aluminum-activated malate transporter) and MATE (Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion) family involved in the secretion have been identified in several plant species; however, different plant species show different gene expression patterns including Alinduction, spatial and temporal expression, and tissue localization. Furthermore, the mechanisms regulating the gene expression also differ with plant species, which are achieved by increased tandem repeated element, increase of copy number, insertion of transposon, or alteration of cis-acting element. In addition to these common Al exclusion mechanisms, rice as a highly Al-tolerant species has developed a number of other mechanisms for detoxification of Al. A transcription factor for Al tolerance ART1 identified in rice regulates at least 30 genes implicated in internal and external detoxification of Al. These multiple genes may contribute to the high Al tolerance of rice. In the future, regulation mechanisms of Al-tolerance genes need to be further investigated.

Keywords Aluminum $\cdot$ Anion transporter $\because$ Citrate . Gramineous plant $\cdot$ Malate $\cdot$ Tolerance

Al is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element, making up around $7 \%$ of the earth’s crust (Tesfaye et al., 2001). When the soil $\mathrm { p H }$ value is lower than 5.0, the soluble aluminum in soil solutions is mostly present as the toxic $\bar { \mathsf { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ , which inhibits root growth at micromolar concentrations in many species (Kochian et al., 2005). Micromole levels of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ can remarkably inhibit root elongation, and impair the absorption, of water and nutrients (Kochian et al., 2005). The well-known mechanism of plant Al tolerance is the Al-induced secretion of organic acids (OA) from the root tips. The OAs chelate $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and form the non-toxic compound OA-Al (Kochian et al., 2004; Horst et al., 2010; Ryan et al., 2011). The most common OAs involved in the Al detoxification process are malate, citrate, and oxalate, depending on the plant. For example, malate is used in wheat (Delhaize et al., 1993) and Arabidopsis (Hoekenga et al., 2003), citrate is secreted in maize (Pellet et al., 1995), and oxalate is used in buckwheat (Zheng et al., 2005) and tomato (Yang et al., 2008).

Wheat TaALMT1 (ALMT, for Al-activated Malate Transporter) encoding a malate transporter was the first plant gene involved in Al tolerance and the first ALMT family gene. In Al-tolerant wheat genotypes, TaALMT1 is specifically expressed in the root tips (Sasaki et al., 2004; Raman et al., 2005). Overexpression of TaALMT1 in wheat, barley, and tobacco-cell suspension increases the efflux of Al-activated malate and enhances tolerance to Al stress (Delhaize et al., 2004; Sasaki et al., 2004; Pereira et al., 2010). TaALMT1 homologs have now been isolated in Arabidopsis (Hoekenga et al., 2006), oilseed rape (Ligaba et al., 2006), rye (Collins et al., 2008), soybean (Liang et al., 2013), and Medicago sativa (Chen et al., 2013). Multi-antimicrobial extrusion (MATE) proteins are a family of proteins that function as drug/sodium or proton antiporters. MATE proteins can secrete organic anions to contribute to the Al tolerance in plants (Furukawa et al., 2007; Magalhaes et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2009). In Arabidopsis, the zinc finger transcription factor STOP1 (known as ART1 in rice) plays a critical role in plant Al tolerance by regulating the Al-inducible expression of ALMT and MATE (Liu et al., 2009). In rice, multiple genes implicated in Al tolerance, including MATE transporter family members, are regulated by the transcription factor ART1 (Yamaji et al., 2009).

Cabbage (Brassica oleracea) is one of the most important vegetable crops around the world (Wu et al., 2014). Our previous study has shown that BoMATE encodes a citrate transporter and is induced by Al and enhances aluminum tolerance in Arabidopsis (Wu et al., 2014). Here we report that cabbage BoALMT1 is located in the plasma membrane and induced by Al. A reverse genetic approach was used to characterize the functions of BoALMT1. Overexpressing BoALMT1 in Xenopus oocytes and Arabidopsis facilitated $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ efflux. Overexpressing BoALMT1 in Arabidopsis resulted in enhanced Al tolerance and increased malate secretion. These results suggested that BoALMT1 has an important role in Al tolerance in cabbage.

Strain B6 promoted soil nutrient cycling and $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability

Inoculation with strain B6 enhanced $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability, while reducing soil $\mathrm { p H }$ from 8.21 to 7.87 (Table S1). Soil $\mathrm { p H }$ is often inversely correlated with heavy metal bioavailability, as lower $\mathrm { p H }$ increases the solubility of various metals (Cui et al. 2023). The decrease of soil $\mathrm { p H }$ may be result from nitrogen conversion by strain B6, which increased ammonium and nitrate nitrogen (Table  S1), displacing $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ ions from soil colloids to soil solution. Additionally, inoculation with strain B6 upregulated amino acid and citric acid expression in rhizosphere soil, further reducing soil $\mathrm { p H }$ and altering heavy metal bioavailability (Sheng et al. 2008; Rojjanateeranaj et al. 2017; Manoj et al. 2020). Bacillus has been shown to enhance heavy metal bioavailability through producing organic acids and polysaccharides (Sheng et  al. 2008). Furthermore, root exudates, including proteins, polysaccharides, low-molecular-weight organic acids, secondary metabolites, and sugars, infuenced heavy metal bioavailability (Ali et al. 2020; Jeyasundar et al. 2021).

Inoculation with strain B6 signifcantly improved soil nutrients cycling and enzyme activity (Table  S1). Bacillus megaterium can solubilize phosphorus, thereby enhancing availability of this nutrient (Esringü et al. 2014; Guo et al. 2021). Soil enzymes were involved in nutrient cycling (Lin et  al. 2021). For instance, acid phosphatase, protease, and sucrase activity were enhanced following strain B6 inoculation, playing crucial roles in the phosphorus, nitrogen, and carbon cycles, respectively (Yang et  al. 2020a; Lin et  al. 2021; Ge et  al. 2023). However, no signifcant change in biomass was observed despite the increase in available soil nutrients following inoculation, likely due to the short duration of the experiment.

Soil nutrient elements, including nitrogen, organic matter and available phosphorus, also infuenced heavy metal chemical forms. Nitrogen-containing oxides formed from available nitrogen can undergo nitration reaction, increasing heavy metal bioavailability in soil (Yang et  al. 2020b). Organic matter promoted the formation of heavy metal adsorption sites and chelators, inhibiting their availability (Tang et  al. 2020). Similarly, available phosphorus can directly react with heavy metal ions in soil to induce the transformation of heavy metals to a more stable form, thus reducing the content of available heavy metals in soil (Li et al. 2023b). Although individual nutrient elements afected $\mathrm { P b }$ chemical forms diferently, the combined efects ultimately enhanced $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability in soil after strain B6 inoculation.

## Strain B6 colonization recruited benefcial strains for soil remediation


Bacillus possesses several advantages, including rapid growth, efcient reproduction, stability, and strong stress resistance, and is widely distributed in various natural environments (Huang et  al. 2020). After inoculation with strain B6, Bacillus abundance signifcantly increased in both the rhizosphere and endosphere microbial community (Fig.  3C), indicating strain B6’s competitive advantage in $\mathrm { P b }$ -polluted environments. The diversity of bacterial communities enhanced in both the rhizosphere and endosphere (Fig.  2C and D). Introducing benefcial microorganisms can improve nutrient utilization by plants, thereby increasing microbial community diversity (Shi et  al. 2022). This is consistent with the results of this experiment, inoculation of endophytes accelerated the soil nutrient cycling and improved rhizosphere environment, signifcantly promoting microbial diversity in rhizosphere soil (Wang et al. 2020).

However, the endosphere microbial community exhibited more pronounced changes than the rhizosphere microbial community (Fig.  2C and D). Wang et  al. found similar results after Brassica juncea inoculation with endophytes of Serratia PRE01 and Arthrobacter PRE05 in V-contaminated soil (Wang et  al. 2020). This may be due to the relatively simple internal environment and microbial community of plant roots, which have a lower bufering capacity compared to soil against exogenous microorganisms. Therefore, we hypothesize that strain B6 exerts divergent efects on rhizosphere and endosphere bacterial communities, playing distinct roles in facilitating Pb transport in S. integra. Additionally, the endosphere microbial community, due to its greater variability, may possess higher potential for phytoremediation (Weyens et al. 2009; Eljounaidi et al. 2016).

Proteobacteria, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria were the three most abundant phyla in the rhizosphere and endosphere bacterial community both before and after inoculation for their adaptation to the heavy metal environment, while the abundance of these phyla was signifcantly altered after inoculation with strain B6 (Fig.  3A). Proteobacteria exhibit high tolerance to heavy metals, likely due to their extensive ability for degradation metabolism and adaptability to a wide range of habitats (Sinkko et al. 2013). As the main microbial group, Firmicutes, a dominant microbial group, are widely found in mining soils, where they decompose organic matter and possess genomes conferring heavy metal tolerance (Zhao et  al. 2019; Li et al. 2021a; Wang et al. 2021b).

Furthermore, strain B6 colonization increased the relative abundance of Fictibacillus and Paenibacillus in the rhizosphere, while the relative abundance of Rhizobium, Acidovorax and Hydrogenophaga increased in the endosphere (Fig.  3C). Fictibacillus and Paenibacillus contained heavy metal resistance genes and contribute to the remediation of heavy metal contaminated soil (Zhang et  al. 2012; Jroundi et  al. 2020). Additionally, Rhizobium promoted plant growth and alleviated biochemical stress caused by heavy metals. Acidovorax and Hydrogenophaga wereassociated with heavy metals and exhibited tolerance to complex heavy metal environments (Lin et  al. 2021; Wang et  al. 2021a; Gan et  al. 2022). Thus, the introduction of strain B6 shaped microbial community structure by altering the ecological niche, and infuencing microbial communication through metabolites, ultimately increasing the relative abundance of benefcial microorganisms involved in soil remediation.


## Diferential metabolites promoted $\mathrm { P b }$ transport and bioavailability


Metabolic substances in the rhizosphere soil originated from plant root exudates and rhizospheric organisms, including bacteria, fungi and soil fauna (Petriacq et al. 2017). Fatty acids and phospholipids exhibited the highest abundance in the rhizosphere soil following inoculation with strain B6 (Table S2). The levels of CL (I-12:0 / i-12:0/18:2 (z) $_ { 9 \mathrm { ~ z ~ } }$ , $1 1 ~ /$ I-24:0) and LysoPC (22:0/0–0) in phospholipids signifcantly increased by $3 0 . 6 6 \%$ and $2 7 . 7 4 \%$ , respectively (Fig.  4B), which were crucial components of the lipid membrane, and lipid membrane is the primary defense against heavy metals (Jung et al. 2015). This was consistent with the increase of $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability and the relative abundance of heavy metalresistant microorganisms (Fig. 3C).

Furthermore, the pathways of “Starch and sucrose metabolism” and “Phosphotransferase system (PTS)” were enriched in the rhizosphere soil after inoculation with strain B6 (Fig. 4D), with the function of regulating acid phosphatase and sucrase, which enhanced available phosphorus and organic matter content. Therefore, inoculation of strain B6 improved the rhizosphere environment of S. integra, such as promoting nutrient cycling (Table S1), consistent with previous studies (Wang et al. 2020). SEM results showed that diferential metabolites indirectly regulate $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability by altering soil chemical properties in the soil (Fig. 6A).

In the roots, amino acids and organic acids were most abundant, withthe expression of L-histidine, L-tryptophan, citric acid, glutaric acid, cis-aconitic acid and oxaloacetate signifcantly up-regulated after inoculation with strain B6 (Fig.  4A). It’s reported that endophytic bacteria can alter metal accumulation capacity in plants by excreting organic acids and biosurfactants to improving mobility of heavy metal (Ma et al. 2016). Furthermore, heavy metals frst enter the central cylinder of the root before being transported to aboveground parts. Inoculation with Pseudomonas putida CZ1 stimulated the secretion of organic acids and other metabolites in Elsholtzia splendens, promoting $\mathrm { C u }$ transport to the central cylinder and thus improving $\mathrm { C u }$ transfer coefcient (Xu et al. 2015).

Additionally, amino acids could efectively chelate metal ions to reduce heavy metals toxicity in plants (Singh et al. 2015). Metal ions exist in diferent chemical forms in xylem vessels, such as organic acid, amino acid and sulfur compound state (Zhai et al. 2022), and Cd-GSH transport form is one of the mechanisms involved in hyperaccumulating Sedum (Lu et al. 2014). Similarly, citric acid, tartaric acid and histidine in the xylem sap of rice promoted Cd transport from the root to the aboveground part (Fu et al. 2019). Moreover, the endosphere microbial community exhibited strong correlations with metabolite changes in the root of S. integra (Fig. 5B). In summary, we hypothesize that strain B6 could change metabolites expression in S. interga by regulating endosphere microbial community structure either directly or indirectly, thus reducing $\mathrm { P b }$ toxicity and promoting $\mathrm { P b }$ mobility to accelerate its continuous transport to the aboveground part.

Metabolic pathways describe molecular interactions, physiological and biochemical reactions, and the relationships between gene products. Endophytes can enhance heavy metals transport from roots to aboveground part by promoting transporters expression in the symplast pathway (Chi et al. 2022; Du et al. 2022). Compared with uninoculated groups, the diferential metabolites were signifcantly enriched in metabolic pathways of “ABC transporters” and “Alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism” in the root (Fig. 4C). ABC transporters, such as ABCC, ABCG35 and ABCG36, are involved in $\mathrm { P b }$ and Cd absorption and transport in poplar and willow (Han et al. 2020). Additionally, in the pathway of “Alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism”, aspartic acid and asparagine have been reported to be involved in complexation with heavy metals (Li et al. 2021b), which may explain how strain B6 inoculation reduced $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ complexation and promoted its transport to the aboveground part. Therefore, these results once again proved that inoculating strain B6 promoted directly $\mathrm { P b }$ transport from root to aboveground by afecting the metabolism of S. integra and its endosphere microbes. Our SEM result proved that diferential metabolites played a paramount role in regulating Pb transport pathway directly, and their impact on $\mathrm { P b }$ transport was more pronounced compared to their contribution in enhancing $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability.

The KEGG database was used to perform an enrichment analysis of diferential metabolites in rhizosphere soil and roots. As shown in Fig. 4C and Fig. 4D, the pathways with high enrichment and $P -$ -value corrected less than 0.05 in the two comparison groups of rhizosphere soil and roots. Compared with uninoculated groups, 16 pathways were signifcantly enriched in the rhizosphere soil, whereas 14 pathways were signifcantly enriched in the roots. Among them, "Purine metabolism" and "ABC transporters" were enriched in both rhizospheres soil and roots and associated with a more enriched degree in roots. "Starch and sucrose metabolism" and "phosphotransferase system (PTS)" were found to be enriched exclusively in the rhizosphere soil, while "Carbon fxation in photosynthetic organisms" and "Citrate cycle (TCA cycle)" showed enrichment exclusively in the roots.


## The correlation analysis of metabolites and preponderant microbe


After inoculation of strain B6, signifcant changes were observed in both the metabolites and microbial diversity. However, the interaction between them remains to be seen. We analyzed the correlation between seven genus with high relative abundance and nineteen diferential metabolites in the rhizosphere soil. Bacillus showed a signifcantly positive correlation $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with deoxyguanosine $( \mathrm { r } > 0 . 8 2 )$ , while Paenisporosarcina exhibited a signifcant correlation $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with all of nineteen diferential metabolites, including ten negative correlations and nine positive correlations (Fig. 5A).

Meanwhile, the correlation was studied between thirteen genus with high relative abundance and twenty-two diferential metabolites in the roots (Fig.  5B). The relationship of genus and diferential metabolites was much closer and more complex in the endosphere microbial community. Bacillus was signifcantly associated $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with nineteen metabolites, comprising eleven positive and eight negative correlations. Actinoplanes, Acidovorax, Devosia, Nocardioides, Pelomonas and Pseudomonas showed signifcant associations $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with all metabolites. Hydrogenophaga was signifcantly associated $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with sixteen metabolites, ten positive and six negative correlations. Rhizobium was positively associated $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ with l-tryptophane $( \mathrm { r } > 0 . 8 5 )$ and negatively associated $( P { < } 0 . 0 5 )$ with linoleic acid $\left( \mathbf { r } < - 0 . 8 3 \right)$ and guanosine $\left( \mathbf { r } < - 0 . 8 1 \right.$ ) (Fig. 5B).

The analysis of the regulatory mechanism of $\mathrm { P b }$ transport

A structural equation model (SEM) was constructed, which were consisted of inoculation with Bacillus megaterium B6, soil chemical properties, microbial community, diferential metabolites, bioavailability of soil Pb (Fig. S5) and $\mathrm { P b }$ transport coefcient (Fig.  6A). Soil chemical properties, microbial community, and diferential metabolites were characterized by the frst principal component of principal component analysis. Inoculation with Bacillus megaterium B6 afected the expression of metabolites by altering the microbial community structure. Pb transport coefcient was directly regulated by diferential metabolites in the root.

While, diferential metabolites regulate the bioavailability of $\mathrm { { \mathrm { P b } } }$ through direct and indirect action in the soil, which of the indirect action was through regulating soil chemical properties, and ultimately afect the transport of Pb. Besides, diferential metabolites played more pronounced role in regulating $\mathrm { P b }$ transport compared to their contribution in enhancing $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability (Fig.  6B). According to the SEM, we made a schematic of B6 facilitating $\mathrm { P b }$ transport (Fig. 6C).

Aims This study seeks to elucidate the mechanisms by which Bacillus megaterium B6 (strain B6) enhances lead $\left( \mathrm { P b } \right)$ transport from roots to branches in Salix integra by approximately one time.

Methods Variations in rhizosphere/endosphere microbes, along with changes in metabolites profles in rhizosphere soil and roots, were assessed using amplicon sequencing and LC–MS, respectively, after inoculation with strain B6 in a controlled pot experiment.

Results Inoculation with strain B6 signifcantly enhanced species richness and diversities of microbes in both the rhizosphere and endosphere after inoculation with strain B6. The relative abundance of

Bacillus, particularly within endosphere microbes, increased markedly. Benefcial microbes, essential for soil remediation, became the dominant species, especially within endosphere communities. Diferential metabolites, for example up-regulated amino acids, chelated $\mathrm { P b }$ , reducing its toxicity. These metabolites signifcantly enriched in "ABC transporters" pathway, promoting $\mathrm { P b }$ transport directly in the root. In the soil, these metabolites either increased $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability directly or indirectly by regulating soil properties. Additionally, diferential metabolites were significantly correlated with dominant microbes, especially in root, and they played a crucial role in enhancing $\mathrm { P b }$ transport than in $\mathrm { P b }$ bioavailability.

Conclusion After colonization, strain B6 recruited benefcial microbes for soil remediation, altered metabolites expression in plant roots and rhizosphere soil, and consequently enhanced $\mathrm { P b }$ transfer, either directly or indirectly. Furthermore, endosphere microbes played a more signifcant role in facilitating $\mathrm { P b }$ transport. These fndings provide new insights into microbe-assisted phytoremediation in heavy metalcontaminated soil.

Cadmium (Cd) is not an essential element and is toxic to plants (Jia et al. 2013). Cd can enter the food chain by plant accumulation and endanger human health, resulting in Cd pollution that is a widespread environmental problem. Phytoremediation is a potentially cost-effective and environmentally friendly technique to sequester heavy metals from water and soil (Gupta et al. 2013). One of the main objectives of phytoextraction is to achieve the highest possible accumulation of heavy metals in aboveground plant parts (Borisev et al. 2016). Plant growth promoting bacteria (PGPB) can promote plant growth, enhance heavy metal uptake, and increase phytoremediation efficiency (Long et al. 2011; Leung et al. 2013; Ma et al. 2015). As a good method to strengthen phytoremediation techniques, PGPB has received increased attention.

Being a non-essential element, it is generally acknowledged that there would be no specific uptake and transport proteins for Cd. Instead, Cd would enter plant cells via uptake systems for other essential cations (Clemens 2006), competing with some nutrient ions, such as iron (Fe), zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , and magnesium $\mathrm { ( M g ) }$ (Thomine et al. 2000; White and Broadley 2003; Plaza et al. 2007; Menguer et al. 2013). Cd is often thought to be transported using Fe translocation routes (Vert et al. 2002). Under Cd stress, a study of Fe accumulation in poplar roots revealed that Cd blocked Fe translocation and acquisition (Fodor et al. 2005). Zinc-regulated transporters, iron-regulated transporter (ZRT/IRT)-like protein (ZIP) family, were proven to be the main $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake system in Arabidopsis thaliana root cells (Vert et al. 2002). IRT1- overexpressing A. thaliana accumulated more Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ in the root tissue under Fe-deficient conditions (Connolly et al. 2002). Plant homologs of the natural resistance-associated macrophage protein (NRAMP) family are regarded as other metal transporters, allowing Cd entry into plant cells. Research has shown that AtNramp1, AtNramp3, and AtNramp4 conferred Cd uptake activity when expressed in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Liu et al. 1997). The heavy metal ATPase (HMA) family is a member of the $\mathrm { P _ { 1 } }$ -ATPase heavy metal transporting P-type ATPase subfamily and is the major transporter involved in the root to shoot translocation of Zn in A. thaliana (Hussain et al. 2004). Later reports showed that HMA3 is mainly involved in the natural variation in leaf Cd accumulation of A. thaliana (Chao et al. 2012), and HMA4 is another key transporter responsible for loading $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd into the xylem vessels in Arabidopsis halleri (Hanikenne et al. 2008).

Sedum alfredii Hance, as a hyperaccumulator, can accumulate high concentrations of heavy metals, especially Cd and Zn. Our previous studies showed that the endophytic bacterium Sphingomonas SaMR12 could enhance plant heavy metal accumulation (Zhang et al. 2013; Chen et al. 2014a, b) and increase the root-soil contact area (Chen et al. 2014a), organic acid secretion (Chen et al. 2014a,b), and glutathione biosynthesis (Pan et al. 2016); however, the effects of SaMR12 on metal ion uptake and its possible influences on the expression of metal transporters are still unknown.

Based on RNA sequencing (Gao et al. 2013), we designed the primes of the possible genes involved in metal transportation in S. alfredii (Table 1), and the aim of this study was to elucidate the effects of SaMR12 on (1) essential metal ion uptake and (2) the gene expression levels of three metal transporter families in plants.

Heavy metals (HMs),having long biological half-life and nondegradability,are a kind of widespread trace metal possessing a hazardous impact on living organisms (Lal et al.， 2O19; Migocka et al., 2017).Due to the natural, industrial and agricultural sources, the arable soil contamination with several HMs,such as cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb) and chromium $\mathrm { ( C r ) }$ ,has becoming one of the most vital environmental and agricultural issues for crop production and safety (Zhao et al., 2021; Yokosho et al.,2021).Excess absorption of Cd by plants could cause serious nutrition and oxidative stress,protein degradation and inhibition of photosynthesis and transpiration,resulting into dramatically impeding plant growth and development (Zhao et al., 2O21). Moreover, Cd can accumulate in human body via food chain,which might lead to chronic health hazards such as lung cancer and kidney damage (Jablonska et al.，2017； Larsson et al.，2015). Therefore，how to genetically achieve effective control of Cd in edible plant organs is pivotal for crop improvement and human health.

A range of heavy metal transporters,including the ATP-binding cassete (ABC), natural resistance-associated macrophage protein (Nramp)and P1BATPases,are vital participators involved in HMuptake, accumulation and translocation in plants (Zheng et al., 2O22; Liu et al., 2020).The ABC transporters,comprising two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) and two transmembrane domains (TMDs),represent one of the most critical membrane transport proteins that are ubiquitously existed in plants (Gani et al., 2021; Kuromori et al., 2017).Among seven subfamilies of the ABC proteins (ABCA-ABCG),the ABC transporters with the reverse organization of domains on the polypeptide chain are grouped into the ABCG subfamily (Yokosho et al., 2021;Mills et al., 2010).Many previous studies reported that the ABCG subfamily transporters were extensively involved in a variety of physiological and biological processes as well as biotic and abiotic stress responses in


## plants (Bessire et al., 2011; He et al., 2019; Migocka et al., 2017).


The pleiotropic drug resistance (PDR) proteins,belonging to the fullsize ABCG subfamily,are capable of transporting a number of substrates, including lipids,phytohormones,inorganic acids and heavy metals (Zhang et al., 2020; Lefevre et al., 2018). Several ABCG transporters, such as AtABCG36,AtABCG40, OsABCG36 and OsABCG37,have been proven to play critical roles in HM extrusion,sequestration and homeostasis in plants (Ashraf et al.,202l； Ziegler et al.,2017). Overexpression of AtPDR8 resulted in reduced Cd accumulation in Arabidopsis plants,whereas loss-of-function of PDR8 led to Cd sensitivity and increased Cd accumulation (Kim et al., 20O7).The OsPDR20 was involved in reducing cellular Cd concentration in rice (Li et al., 2022). Overexpression of OsABCG36/OsPDR9 enhanced Cd tolerance via transporting Cd out of the root cels in rice (Fu et al., 2Ol9). Increasing evidences indicated that the HM stress (e.g. Cd and Pb) can trigger overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and induce oxidative stress in plants (He etal.,202O; Yang etal., 2022). The activity of several crucial antioxidant enzymes such as catalase (CAT) and ascorbate peroxidase (APX) were increased to mitigate or eliminate Cd-induced ROS production in Impatiens glandulifera (Coakley et al., 2O21). Moreover,a few HM transporters,including the NRAMPs and YSLs,can activate CAT and superoxide dismutase (SOD) to achieve ROS scavenging under HM stress in plants (Yang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2020). However,whether the antioxidant defense system that motivated by HM stress could be mediated by the PDRs still awaits further investigation in plants.

Radish (Raphanus sativus L.) is an important economical root vegetable worldwide,whose taproot is highly sensitive to HM stress (Xu et al.,202O; Tang et al., 2021). In face of arable soil with HM contamination,HM stress has developed as a main limiting factor that hampers taproot formation and enlargement,which consequently dismissing radish yield and quality.In recent years,a variety of PDR family members acting as HM efflux pumps have been identified in some model or crop species such as Arabidopsis and rice (Kim et al., 2OO7; Fu et al., 2019; Li et al., 2O22).Nevertheless, the isolation and functional characterization of PDR genes awaits comprehensively explored in radish. Currently,a few available radish genome sequences (Jeong et al., 2016; Zhang et al.，2021; Xu et al.,2023) provided fundamental basis to globally characterize the PDR family genes in radish.In this study, basing on characterizing the phylogenetic relationship,gene structure and differential expression of RsPDRs,we aimed to assess the metal transport capacity of RsPDR8 in yeast cells,and explore the functional role of RsPDR8 in mediating the Cd accumulation and ROS scavenging in radish.These results would facilitate unraveling the RsPDR8-mediated HM stress regulatory network in radish,and pave the way for genetic engineering of low-Cd-accumulating cultivars in radish breeding program.

ABC transporters constitute a large superfamily of proteins in bacteria, animals, and plants (Guidotti, 1996). ABC proteins are able to transport various substrates such as hormones, lipids, glutathione conjugates, inorganic acid, xenomolecules and heavy metals (Rea, 2007; Verrier et al., 2008). There are more than 120 members in both Arabidopsis and rice, which are classified into seven subfamilies (ABCA to ABCG) (Garcia et al, 2004). Several ABC transporters, including AtABCC1, AtABCC2, AtABCC3, and AtABCG36, have been reported to play a role in Cd tolerance by Cd extrusion or vacuolar sequestration (Kim et al., 2007; Park et al., 2012; Brunetti et al., 2015). However, the exact functions of most ABC transporters in plants are still unknown. In the present study, we functionally characterized an ABCG-type transporter gene, OsABCG36, which encodes a plasma membrane-localized protein (Fig. 3). OsABCG36 is expressed in both roots and shoots, but only expression in the roots was rapidly and greatly up-regulated in response to Cd (Fig. 1A, D). Knockout of OsABCG36 resulted in decreased tolerance to Cd, but did not alter the tolerance to other metals including Zn, Cu, Al, and Pb (Fig. 5F; Supplementary Fig. S7). Furthermore, loss of function of OsABCG36 resulted in more Cd accumulation in the roots and root cell sap (Fig. 5G). Although the cell sap data alone couldn’t be used for a quantitative analysis of symplastic vs. apoplastic Cd because release of weakly bound Cd or Cd conjugates from the cytosol and vacuoles may be able to contact with the cell walls and partially binds there after breaking the root cells by the freeze-thaw procedure, the difference was also found in the total Cd concentration of the roots (Fig. 5H). Given that OsABCG36 showed an efflux transport activity for Cd in yeast (Fig. 4B), the higher Cd accumulation in the root cell sap of the mutants is the result of loss of Cd efflux from the root cells. This may be associated with enhanced Cd toxicity in the mutants (Fig. 5D, F; Fig. 6B). Although the transport substrate of OsABCG36 remains to be identified in future, it could be ionic Cd or Cd-conjugates.

Similar to most full-size G-type ABC transporters, OsABCG36 consists of two nucleotide-binding domains (NBD) and two $\mathrm { A B C } _ { 2 }$ transmembrane domains (TMD) (Supplementary Fig. S1B). OsABCG36 is not the closest homolog of AtABCG36 (Supplementary Fig. S1C), but OsABCG36 functions similarly to AtABCG36 (Kim et al., 2007). Both of them are efflux transporters of Cd or Cd conjugates, contributing absence of Cd, the expression level of OsABCG36 was low in the root and shoot (Fig. 1A), whereas that of AtABCG36 was high (Kim et al., 2007). In the presence of Cd, the expression of OsABCG36 only in the roots is rapidly and greatly induced (Fig. 1A). Furthermore, the expression level increased with increasing the external Cd concentrations (Fig. 1B), whereas that of AtABCG36 was slightly enhanced by Cd in both the roots and shoots of Arabidopsis (Kim et al., 2007). Under normal conditions, OsABCG36 was expressed in the root cells at a low level, whereas AtABCG36 was some functions of OsABCG36 and AtABCG36 diverged during evolution. Additionally, AtABCG36 was also suggested to play a role in Pb tolerance (Kim et al., 2007). However, we found that knockout of OsABCG36 did not affect the tolerance to other metals including Pb (Fig. 5F; Supplementary Fig. S7). Such difference between rice and Arabidopsis was also reported for other ABC transporters. For example, AtABCC1/2 is involved in both Cd and As tolerance in Arabidopsis (Song et al., 2010; Park et al., 2012), whereas OsABCC1 is only involved in As tolerance, but not Cd tolerance (Song et al., 2014).

Detoxification of toxic metals could be achieved by a variety of mechanisms including compartmentalization (vacuolar sequestration), chelation by metal ligands such as phytochelatins and metallothioneines, and efflux of toxic metals from the cells (Hall, 2002). The present work provides evidence that OsABCG36 is involved in effluxing Cd from the root cells. However, the effect of knockout of OsABCG36 on Cd tolerance was only observed at relatively high Cd concentration (Fig. 5D-F; Fig. 6B). Furthermore, the root elongation in the mutants was not completely inhibited in the presence of Cd (Fig. 5D-F; Fig. 6B). These results suggest that OsABCG36-mediated efflux of Cd is one of the components of Cd tolerance in rice and that its contribution is not very large.

Although knockout of OsABCG36 decreased the tolerance to 6B), it did not affect Cd accumulation in the shoots ( suggesting that Ma, 2016; Wang et al., 2019). OsNramp5, a Nramp (natural resistance-associated macrophage protein) member, was identified as a major pathway for Cd uptake in rice (Ishimaru et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2012). Two P-type ATPase transporters, OsHMA3 and OsHMA2, were reported to be responsible for the vacuolar sequestration of Cd in the root cell and root-to-shoot translocation of Cd, respectively (Ueno et al., 2010; Miyadate et al., 2011; Satoh-Nagasawa et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2012; Yamaji et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2018). At the reproductive stage, OsLCT1, a (Uraguchi et al., 2011, 2014). OsHMA2 expressed in the rice nodes is also involved in Cd distribution to the grain (Yamaji et al., 2013). Among these transporters, only OsHMA3 was demonstrated to play an important role in Cd tolerance through vacuolar sequestration of Cd in the roots (Sasaki et al., 2014). Therefore, at least there are three pathways for Cd in the root cells taken up by OsNramp5; vacuolar sequestration mediated by OsHMA3, efflux from the root cells by OsABCG36 and root-to-shoot translocation by OsHMA2. No difference in shoot Cd accumulation between mutants and wild type suggests that the contribution of OsABCG36 to shoot Cd accumulation is very small. One possible explanation for this is presence of redundant genes with similar functions to OsABCG36 in rice. Phylogenic analysis showed that OsABCG36 was closely related to OsABCG32, OsABCG34, OsABCG35, OsABCG37 and OsABCG44 and shared high identity $( 7 6 - 8 5 \% )$ ) with analysis also showed that OsABCG37 and OsABCG44 was up-regulated in roots by high-Cd stress (Tan et al., 2017). These data suggested that OsABCG37 and OsABCG44 possibly play a similar function as OsABCG36 in roots although the exact future.

In conclusion, our results indicate that OsABCG36 localized at the plasma membrane is involved in Cd tolerance through effluxing Cd out of the root cells in rice.
