Organisms transport broad range of substrates either organic or inorganic across plasma membrane from the extracellular environment to cell as a source of nutrients. Micronutrients such as heavy metals (either essential or non-essential) are vital for various physiological and biological processes in plants such as chlorophyll biosynthesis, nitrogen assimilation, photosynthesis, and respiration (Morrissey & Guerinot, 2009). The heavy metals pollution is one of the negative effects of industrialization, which is dexterous not only to human health but also to environment. However, excess amount of heavy metal uptake causes cellular toxicity by inhibiting protein binding activity or enzyme functions through binding with sulfhydryl groups of protein, disturbance in cellular transportation system, and oxidative damages (Williams & Miller, 2001). Therefore, plants have evolved various mechanism on heavy metal ion toxicity tolerance and metal scavenging systems (Li et al., 2015). In past few decades, molecular biology techniques have enabled in identification and characterization of different metal transportation gene families (Williams & Miller, 2001).

In plants, different substrate specific transporters are localized in plasma membrane and are associated with active transportation of sucrose, peptides, amino acids, and metals (Koh et al., 2002). The peptide transporters are proteins that transport peptides into cell as source of amino acids for protein biosynthesis or as a nitrogen and carbon (Lubkowitz et al., 1997). The peptide transporters are divided into various classes such as the oligopeptide transporters (OPT), nitrate transporters (NRT), and the ABC-type transporter family (Rentsch et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2010). The membrane proteins, OPT, can transport a wide range of substrate across membrane and play pivotal role in various biological processes. The OPT proteins are first characterized in yeast (Lubkowitz et al., 1997) and later in bacteria (Lubkowitz et al., 1998) and plants (Koh et al., 2002).

The OPT proteins are multifunctional proteins and may involve in four biological processes; (i) nitrogen assimilation or mobilization (Koh et al., 2002; Pike et al., 2009), (ii) long distance metal transportation (Stacey et al., 2008), (iii) glutathione transporters (Zhang et al., 2004), (iv) heavy metal sequestration (Cagnac et al., 2004). The plants OPT proteins are classified into two sub families based on phylogeny; the peptide transporter (PT) subfamily and yellow stripe-like (YSL) sub-family (Curie et al., 2001). The PT sub-family contained 18 or 11-14 amino acid highly conserved NPG (Asn-Pro-Gly) or KIPPR (LysIle-Pro-Pro-Arg) motifs and considered to transport tetrapeptide or pentapeptides (Koh et al., 2002; Osawa et al., 2006), while YSL lack these motifs and function in metal transport (Inoue et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009).

The PT subfamily proteins has been identified and characterized in Arabidopsis, Brassica, and rice (Bogs et al., 2003; Osawa et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2009) and have been involved in metal detoxification (Bogs et al., 2003), seeds germination (Müntz, 1998), embryo development (Stacey et al., 2008), nitrogen transportation (Williams and Miller, 2001), and glutathione transporter (Bogs et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004). The YSL subfamily is considered to function in metal transportation such as $\mathrm { M g } .$ , Fe, Cd and so on (Inoue et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009) and multiple YSL transporter genes have been identified from Brachypodium distachyon (Yordem et al., 2011), Arabidopsis thaliana (Gross, 2003), Zea mays (Yordem et al., 2011), and Oryza sativa (Koike et al., 2004). In maize, ZmYSL1 demonstrated as Phyto siderophore transporter (Curie et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2004). In rice, various YSL (OsYSL2, OsYSL15, OsYSL18) are orthologs to $Z { \bmod { \mathrm { S L } } } 1$ , in that they facilitate to transport metal-nicotianamine (Koike et al., 2004; Aoyama et al., 2009; Inoue et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009). Moreover, some OPT members of rice (OsOPT1, OsOPT3, OsOPT4, OsOPT5, OsOPT7) have ability to transport nicotianmine bound iron (Vasconcelos et al., 2008).

To understand the potential role of OPT gene family, it is important to identify OPT gene family members in tomato genome. In this study, we are presenting identification of OPT gene family in tomato, including chromosome distribution, gene structure analysis, motif analysis, cis regulatory elements prediction, in silico subcellular location prediction, and phylogenetic analysis. In addition, the tissue/organ specific expression profile analysis under normal conditions as well as under various heavy metal stresses were performed. The systematic analysis of OPT gene family in tomato can lay a foundation for future functional studies in tomato as well as other plant species.

The contamination of agricultural soils with heavy metals, including cadmium (Cd), zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , manganese (Mn), and arsenic (As), poses a serious threat to global food safety and human health (Zhao and Wang 2020; Li et al. 2024). Among these heavy metals, Cd is particularly alarming due to its high toxicity, persistence and mobility through the food chain. While Zn, though an essential micronutrient, can become phytotoxic at elevated concentrations (Kaur et al. 2021). Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms governing metal uptake, transport, and accumulation in plants is essential for both complementary goals: mitigating the accumulation of toxic metals in edible crops while ensuring adequate acquisition of essential elements and enhancing the phytoremediation potential of metal-accumulating species (Zhao et al. 2022).

Transmembrane transporters are fundamental to metal homeostasis in plants, the Zn-regulated transporters and iron-regulated transporter-like Proteins (ZRT/IRT-like Proteins, ZIPs), and Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Proteins (NRAMPs) families being particularly prominent (Tang et al. 2023). In rice, OsNRAMP5 has been identifed as a major transporter for Cd and Mn uptake (Chang et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2025), while the plasma membrane-localized OsZIP5 and OsZIP9 function synergistically to facilitate Zn and Cd absorption (Tan et al. 2020). Recent studies in Arabidopsis thaliana have further elucidated that several ZIP family members, including AtZIP2, AtZIP3, AtZIP5, and AtZIP8, are predominantly localized to the plasma membrane of root epidermal and cortical cells where they perform redundant yet crucial functions in metal acquisition from the soil environment (Ochoa et al. 2025; Robe et al. 2025).

Notably, the functional roles of ZIP1 orthologs vary considerably across plant species. Early work in rice proposed that OsZIP1 was involved in Zn and Cd uptake under Zndefcient conditions or Cd exposure (Ramesh et al. 2003). While a more recent study re-characterized it as a metal exporter localized to the endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane, which reduces cellular Cd and Zn accumulation when overexpressed (Liu et al. 2019). In contrast, Arabidopsis AtZIP1 localizes to both the vacuolar membrane and complements Zn uptake in yeast mutants, indicating its role in intracellular Zn transport (Milner et al. 2013). These functional divergences highlight the importance of characterizing ZIP1 transporter within their specifc plant systems to elucidate their distinct physiological roles.

Brassica juncea, a widely cultivated oilseed and vegetable crop, exhibits a remarkable capacity to accumulate heavy metals, making it as a promising candidate species for phytoremediation applications (Du et al. 2020; Kang et al. 2021; Zeremski et al. 2021). Despite its potential, the specifc transporters responsible for metal uptake in B. juncea remain largely uncharacterized. Our previous transcriptomic analysis revealed that BjZIP1 expression is strongly induced under Cd stress (Zhang et al. 2021); yet, its transport function and subcellular localization have not been experimentally validated. In this study, we functionally characterized BjZIP1 through heterologous expression in yeast, overexpression in A. thaliana, and the B. juncea hairy root transformation system. We demonstrate that BjZIP1 localizes to the plasma membrane and mediates Cd and Zn uptake, thereby contributing to metal accumulation and sensitivity. These fndings highlight BjZIP1 as a key component of metal uptake in $B$ . juncea and a potential molecular target for optimizing phytoremediation efciency.

It is well known that transport, chelation, and sequestration processes in living organisms function in regulating concentrations of essential metal ions in different cellular compartments and minimizing the damage caused by heavy metal ions entering the cytosol (O’Halloran and Culotta 2000; Clemens 2001). Important components of heavy metal homeostasis and detoxification systems are membrane-localized heavy metal transporters (Williams et al. 2000) and chelation processes (Cobbett 2000). Membrane transport systems are likely to play a central role in the regulation of metal concentrations within different cells and organelles. The ATP binding cassette (ABC) protein superfamily is the largest membrane protein family, well known in plants. Members of this superfamily catalyze the Mg ATP-energized transport of a broad range of substrates across biological membranes. ABC transporters mediate diverse cellular transport processes such as excretion of potentially toxic compounds and conferring of heavy metal tolerance (Martinoia et al. 2002). Once metal ions enter the cell, they are bound by chelators. Metallothioneins (MTs) are the best characterized heavy metal-binding ligands in plant cells. They belong to the superfamily of thiol-containing metal-binding proteins which modulate internal levels of metal concentrations between deficient and toxic concentrations by binding to the toxic metals through closely spaced cysteinthiol groups (Cobbett 2000).

Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) are an important component of the rhizosphere and have been well documented to enhance phytoremediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils (Gonzalez-Chavez 2000; Davies et al. 2001). Environmental stress conditions, such as accumulation of heavy metals, typically impose severe difficulties for plant survival and growth. The AMF symbiosis can alleviate abiotic stresses through improvement of plant growth as a result of enhanced nutrient and water uptake (Davies et al. 2002; Carpio et al. 2005) and by stimulating or modifying specific physiological mechanisms related to the adaptation to stressful environments (Porcel et al. 2003; Auge et al. 2004).

AMF can influence certain plant physiological mechanisms, such as metal avoidance or tolerance to increase plant phytoremediation capability (Perotto and Martino 2001). There is evidence showing that plant-encoded metal transporters and chelators are expressed in mycorrhizal plants when grown under conditions of heavy metal contamination (Rivera-Becerril et al. 2005; Gohre and Paszkowski 2006; Hildebrandt et al. 2007). On the other hand, it has been shown that nickel (Ni) can form chelated compounds, which may replace other heavy metals from physiologically important centers in plant metabolism (Cammack et al. 1988; Kramer et al. 1996). The aim of the present study was to investigate the physiological and molecular mechanisms involved in Ni tolerance of mycorrhizal tall fescue plants inoculated with Funneliformis mosseae. Ni translocation and the expression levels of MT and ABC genes in response to four concentrations of Ni were investigated.

We found 20 members of the ALMT transporter family on the $P .$ trichocarpa genome, which were most similar, according to the selection criteria, to the 12 ALMTs that are functionally characterized in diferent species (Table S1 and File S1). These factors are responsible for increasing the expression of AtALMT1, as well as indoleacetic acid (IAA) and abscisic acid (ABA) (Kobayashi et  al. 2013). In Holcus lanatus (HlALMT1) and Secale cereale (ScALMT1), the transport of malate through the membrane protein ALMT is critical for tolerance to toxic Al in soil (Fontecha et al. 2007; Chen et al. 2013). TaALMT1, from Triticum aestivum, is a membrane protein responsible for providing greater tolerance to Al, as observed when the gene was inserted into other plants (Sasaki et al. 2004). Although the $P .$ trichocarpa proteins PoptrALMT1, PoptrALMT2, PoptrALMT3, PoptrALMT4, and PoptrALMT5 are not in the same subclade, they are phylogenetically closer Al stress-responsive transporters, an indication that they could intermediate malate transport in response to the same stress.

Not all genes from clade A are related to Al stress. For example, the HvALMT1 transporter of Hordeum vulgare $L .$ , despite its high protein similarity with TaALMT1, is not directly involved with Al tolerance, and it is expressed in cells of the expanding root and guard cells (Gruber et al. 2010). The overexpression of HvALMT1 revealed that this gene is involved in diferent metabolic pathways of the plant; the protein may be related to the transport of other OAs, such as fumarate and succinate, but the main functions of this gene are stomatal opening and closure and osmotic balance of expanding cells (Gruber et al. 2011). No P. trichocarpa protein was fitted to this ALMT group, but four $P .$ . trichocarpa sequences, PoptrALMT9, PoptrALMT10, PoptrALMT11, and PoptrALMT12, were grouped separately.

The only characterized gene of clade B, AtALMT12, is associated with stomatal opening and closure; AtALMT12 is localized on the plasma membrane of the guard cell, where it is responsible for the rapid activation ( $R$ -typr) of the ion channel (QUAC) that allows the passage of nitrates and hydrochlorides (Sasaki et al. 2010). The protein sequences of PoptrALMT15, PoptrALMT14, and especially PoptrALMT13, were similar to that of AtALMT12, an indication that they could be related to the same process.

The ALMTs in clade C, as well as the other members of the family, are located in the plasma membrane; the already characterized ALMTs from this clade are specifcally located on the tonoplast. The MdMA1 and VvALMT9 proteins are involved in apple and grapefruit acidity, regulating the transport of OAs into the vacuole; consequently, the accumulation of these acids is related to the fnal quality of the fruit (de Angeli et al. 2013). VvALMT9 is related to the transport of malic acid $\mathrm { ( C _ { 4 } H _ { 6 } O _ { 5 } ) }$ and tartaric acid $\mathrm { ( C _ { 4 } H _ { 6 } O _ { 6 } ) }$ , and its expression increases with fruit maturity (de Angeli et al. 2013). This clade included fve $P .$ trichocarpa sequences; of these, the proteins PoptrALMT19 and PoptrALMT20, which would be interesting to further analyse to fgure if they are involved on OA accumulation on vacuoles of fruit cells.


## Syntenic and ALMT gene duplication analyses in P. trichocarpa


One characteristic that distinguishes angiosperms from mammals, in general, is the process of genome expansion through duplication and even triplication, as well as the reduction of ploidy, making the angiosperm genome more structurally complex than that of mammals (Wang and Paterson 2011). This increase, followed by decreasing genome size, was important for the creation of new functions for genes, a process called neofunctionalization, as well as for subdivision of their biological activities, or subfunctionalization. In addition, gene duplication is the primary source for the generation of new genes (He and Zhang 2005). During evolution, approximately 8000 pairs of duplications have resisted the process of ploidy reduction in the Populus genome (Tuskan et al. 2006).

To determine the number of paralogs of the ALMT family, a microsynteny analysis was performed to compare the P. trichocarpa genome with itself (Fig. 2a), and the number of gene duplications was then determined (Fig. 2c). To establish an evolutionary comparison and to identify the orthologues, a systematic analysis was carried out between the P. trichocarpa and Arabidopsis thaliana genomes, as the latter species has the highest number of characterized ALMT genes (Fig. 2b).

For the ALMT transporter family, eight pairs of paralogs were found on $P .$ . trichocarpa genome. Of those, fve pairs were present in clade A of the phylogenetic tree, a clade composed mainly of ALMTs responsive to Al stress. The number of paralogs of a transporter family tends to be greater when related to abiotic stresses (Ramakrishna and Ravishankar 2011). The highest concentration of paralogs was among the genes PoptrALMT9, PoptrALMT10, PoptrALMT11, and PoptrALMT12, which are phylogenetically located in the Al stress response clade, although they did not exhibit high similarity with any characterized ALMT protein. Paralogs were also observed in clade B (one pair) and clade C (two pairs).

The establishment of orthologues between the A. thaliana and $P .$ trichocarpa genomes is important for future studies, as this is a yet poorly characterized transporter family. Five pairs of orthologues were found between the ALMT family and the A. thaliana genome. Regarding Al-responsive members, four genes had orthologues with ALMT family members in A. thaliana; however, these genes have not yet been functionally characterized. The gene PoptrALMT20, which according to the phylogenetic tree is involved with fruit malate content, had two orthologues in A. thaliana (AtALMT4 and AT1G68600) that have not yet been functionally characterized. Because the PoptrALMT13 gene is an orthologue of AtALMT12, it can be inferred that it is related to the transport of nitrate and hydrochlorides in guard cells.

On the $P$ trichocarpa genome, the observed gene duplications were only related to the phylogenetic clade related to Al stress. They were divided into three groups, and all members of this group were phylogenetically close to GmALMT1.

## P. trichocarpa ALMT genes expression in diferentRNA‑seq libraries


Using the PopGenIE online platform (Sundell et al. 2015), an analysis of ALMT gene expression was performed in 24 libraries, and 15 of the 20 family members were expressed on at least one of the libraries (Fig. 3). The genes PoptrALMT1, PoptrALMT2, PoptrALMT7, PoptrALMT9, and PoptrALMT12 were not expressed in any of the libraries and were located in clade A of the phylogenetic tree (Fig. 1).

The genes were grouped on the expression map accordingly to their expression profle, and genes that are in different phylogenetic clades were grouped in the same clade in the expression map due to the diference between the expression and phylogenetic analyses. In the phylogenetic tree, the genes were grouped according to their primary protein structure, indicating an afnity for a given substrate. In the expression map, the genes were grouped according to the expression profle in the diferent libraries, correlating their expression with a given tissue or stress, such that genes that transport diferent substrates may be involved in the same tissue and/or stress.

The putative Al-responsive ALMT family members in $P .$ trichocarpa had a lower mean expression when compared to other clades. The only member not expressed in the roots was PoptrALMT3, which exhibited high expression in libraries related to reproductive organs such as fower bud, fower and ovary. PoptrALMT6 exhibited expression in diferent libraries, indicating that it might be related to several metabolic pathways in the plant.

Some ALMT family members are indirectly related to the efux of diferent compounds, including nitrate and chloride, important signalling molecules in the plant that are involved in the dormancy stage and seed germination (Alboresi et al. 2005). PoptrALMT14 had a high expression on the fower dormancy sample, which is in agreement with the phylogenetic tree analysis.


## P. trichocarpa MATE genes expression in diferentRNA‑seq libraries


In the $P .$ trichocarpa genome, 56 MATE transporters were identifed that exhibited similarity to the 43 members of this family characterized by diferent species (Table S1 and File S2). The phylogenetic tree was divided into clades and subclades accordingly to the distribution of the already characterized MATE transporters (Fig. 4). To better understand the functions of this family in $P .$ tricocharpa, the 56 PoptrMATE transporters were analyzed on a database of transcripts available on the PopGenIE.org platform (Sundell et al. 2015). Only 43 were expressed in the tested libraries, and nine had high and constitutive expression (Fig. 5). The phylogenetic tree and the heat map are not sufcient to defne the biological function of a protein but are strong indications of a possible function.

Clade I (dark green) had the highest number of $P .$ . trichocarpa members, with a total of 24 transporters, located on four subclades. Subclade I.1 comprised transporters PoptrMATE1 to PoptrMATE9 grouped together with OsPEZ1 and OsPEZ2, which are transporters of phenolic compounds involved with iron (Fe) precipitation and Al detoxifcation in Oryza sativa (Bashir et al. 2011; Ishimaru et al. 2011). NtMATE1, which is involved with nicotine transport in the Nitotiana tabacum root (SHOJI et al., 2009), and ZmMATE2, which is associated with a quantitative trait locus (QTL) in Zea mays related to Al tolerance (Maron et al. 2010), were mostly expressed in the root. However, in clade I.1, only PoptrMATE8 was expressed in the root, and the others were highly expressed in libraries related to the plant shoot, mainly leaf and fower. Clade I.2 comprised three Populus members (PoptrMATE10, PoptrMATE11 and PoptrMATE12) that are almost constitutively expressed in several libraries. In addition to these members characterized for the transport of favonoids in the vacuole, this subclade also comprised AtTT12 from A. thaliana (Debeaujon et al. 2001), BrTT12 from Brassica rapa (Chai et al. 2009), MtMATE1 from Medicago truncatula (Zhao and Dixon 2009), and MdMATE 1 and MdMATE2 from Malus domestica (Frank et al. 2011).

When overexpressed in A. thaliana, OsMATE1 caused several morphological and physiological changes, with a negative response to biotic stress (Tiwari et al. 2014). This transporter was grouped in subclade I.3 together with PoptrMATE13, PoptrMATE14, PoptrMATE15, and PoptrMATE16. PoptrMATE13 was the only one that was expressed in the libraries tested, and was highly expressed in diferent tissues and in response to diferent stresses. On the other hand, subclade I.4 grouped alkaloid transporters located in the vacuole, including CjMATE1 from Coptis japônica (Takanashi et al. 2017) and NtJAT2 from N. tabacum (Shitan et al. 2014), as well as favonoid transporters such as MtMATE2 from Medicargo truncatelo (Zhao et al. 2011), AtFFT from A. thaliana (Thompson et al. 2010), and VvAM1 and VvAM2 from Vitis vinífera (Pérez-Díaz et al. 2014). This subclade also contained eight MATE transporters from P. trichocarpa; of these, PoptrMATE18, PoptrMATE21 and PoptrMATE22 were constitutively expressed and PoptrMATE23 exhibited low expression in all libraries. PoptrMATE19 was more responsive to drought.

Clade II, presented in mustard colour, has $1 2 ~ P .$ trichocarpa members and three already characterized members. AtADX1 is involved in the transport of alkaloids and toxic compounds (Li et al. 2002). OsMATE1 and OsMATE2 are involved in diferent pathways of plant growth and development (Tiwari et al. 2014). NtJAT1 is related to the transport of nicotine in the plant (Morita et al. 2009). According to the expression data in diferent libraries, most $P .$ trichocarpa genes in this clade had increased expression in mature seeds and expanded fower libraries. PoptrMATE28 also had high expression in the mechanical shock library.

Clade III comprises fve P. trichocarpa genes grouped with an already characterized MATE transporter, AtALF5, which is responsible for plant defence against toxic compounds that come in contact with the A. thaliana root (Diener et  al. 2001). The genes PoptrMATE37, PoptrMATE38 and PoptrMATE39 had increased expression on the beetle attack libraries, and PoptrMATE38 and PoptrMATE39 on a mechanical damage library. All of the genes were expressed in the roots; however, expression was higher in the shoot than in the root.

Clade IV grouped eight P. trichocarpa genome sequences that were phylogenetically close to three MATE transporters characterized in the literature as involved with Fe homeostasis (AtBCD1) (Seo et al. 2012), efux of abscisic acid (AtDTX50) (Zhang et al. 2014) and plant defence mechanisms (AtADS1) (Sun et al. 2011) in A. thaliana. Under osmotic stress conditions such as high salinity and drought, a large number of genes involved in the tolerance and stress response process are activated due to the accumulation of abscisic acid (ABA), a key hormone in signalling processes (Yoshida et al. 2014). The genes PoptrMATE45 and PoptrMATE47 exhibited the highest expression in water stress-related libraries, and these genes may be related to the transport of abscisic acid. PoptrMATE45 also had high expression in response to the beetle attack and mechanical damage. All P. trichocarpa genes from this clade exhibited increased expression in young leaf growth libraries.

Clade V comprised seven P. trichocarpa sequences with high phylogenetic similarity and 19 already characterized Populus sequences. This is one of the most concordant clades in the tree in terms of the transported substrate due to a large number of MATE family members characterized. This clade was subdivided into two subclades: clade V.1, which comprised two P. trichocarpa sequences and a MATE characterized as a salicylic acid transporter in A. thaliana (AtEDS5) (Nawrath et al. 2002), and clade V.2, which comprised several genes characterized as citrate transporters, both in response to the Al present in the soil and to Fe defciency, in addition to fve Populus sequences. In subclade V.1, the PoptrMATE50 gene exhibited maximum expression in mature leaf RNA-seq libraries; because it has a high identity with the AtEDS5 gene, it is likely responsible for the transport of salicylic acid. ## Gene co‑expression network among MATE and ALMT family members in P. trichocarpa


A correlation network was constructed with P. trichocarpa members of the MATE and ALMT families (Fig. 6), using 24 public libraries available in the PlantGenie.org database (Sundell et al. 2015), using the Pearson’s method with a correlation coefcient of $\rho \geq | | 0 . 7 |$ . The thickness of the lines (edges) connecting the genes (nodes) is proportional to the degree of correlation between the genes, where the thin line corresponds to a correlation closer to |0.7| and the thicker line to a correlation close to | 1 |. The correlation network between transporter families is important to understand how they are connected and how members of transporter families are correlated.

The co-expression network between the transporter families yielded 32 MATE members and 13 ALMT members with higher than minimum correlation with another member of both families. This network demonstrated that although most transporters are transcriptionally correlated to some degree, indicating a probable participation in similar metabolic pathways, it was also possible to observe isolated groups, suggesting that these genes might be involved on more specifc pathways. In the co-expression network between MATE and ALMT families, it was possible to observe the formation of four subgroups of genes: one large subgroup containing 25 genes (17 MATE and 8 ALMT), one smaller subgroup (right side; 10 MATE and 4 ALMT), and two small subgroups

containing three genes, one composed exclusively of MATE members.

One of the small networks contained phylogenetically close genes, such as the genes PoptrMATE1, PoptrMATE2, and PoptrMATE3, which are candidates to transport alkaloids and phenolic compounds. Another network comprised more distant genes, such as PoptrMATE19, PoptrALMT13, and PoptrMATE15, which have the potential involvement on the transport of alkaloids, stomatal opening and closure, and plant development and growth, respectively. Another group of genes with few connections contained the PoptrMATE4, PoptrMATE6, and PoptrMATE7 genes of the MATE family, which might be related to the transport of secondary metabolites, and the PoptrALMT4, PoptrALMT14, and PoptrALMT18 genes of the ALMT family, possibly involved in Al stress, stomatal opening and closure, and fruit acidity, respectively.

One network, composed of 10 members of the MATE family and four members of the ALMT family, was separated from the others. The members of the MATE family might be related to plant defence mechanisms, as well as abscisic acid transport, maintenance of Fe homeostasis and citrate transport in response to Al toxicity. Members of the ALMT family are those close to characterized members related to malate transport in response to the presence of toxic Al in the soil. Therefore, these two families may be involved in the response to Al. Thus, it is possible to relate these genes to Al stress because in the presence of toxic Al, defcient Fe absorption is observed, with consequent release of OAs to neutralize Al (Kochian et al. 2015). In eucalyptus, Al accumulates in old leaves, which are later eliminated through leaf abscission (Silva et al. 2004).

The expression of the genes PoptrALMT10, PoptrALMT11, PoptrMATE53, and PoptrMATE54 was analysed in diferent P. trichocarpa tissues to determine the expression profle of these genes in the plant. These genes were selected because they are similar to those characterized as Al stress-responsive and had the highest degree of correlation in the co-expression network. The relative expression of these genes was analyzed in the following tissues: young and mature leaves, node, internode and root. Both members of the ALMT family were highly expressed in the root, as well as PoptrMATE54. PoptrALMT10 was the only one with greater expression in mature leaves compared to young ones; for the other transporters, there were no signifcant diferences between the leaf tissues of diferent ages.

PoptrMATE53 exhibited high expression in the internode and low expression in the leaves.


## Correlation network between the PoptrALMT10and PoptrMATE54 genes in P starvation and Altoxicity stress samples


The genes PoptrALMT10 and PoptrMATE54 were evaluated in Al toxicity and P starvation libraries to determine which genes were correlated with these stresses in root and leaf tissues, using a Spearman correlation of $\rho { \geq } | | 0 . 8 |$ (Fig. 7). Under phosphorus defciency, these genes had unrelated transcriptional profles in the leaf and the root. In the root, both under phosphorus defciency and Al toxicity, PoptrALMT10 had the highest number of correlated genes. The same was observed for PoptrMATE54 on the leaf samples (Table S2).

In the root exposed to low phosphorus concentration, the PoptrALMT10 gene was connected to 2757 genes and the PoptrMATE54 gene was connected to only 680 genes; there were no genes in common on the network between the ALMT and MATE genes. In contrast, under the same stress on the leaf, a much smaller number of genes correlating to the two members of these families was observed. PoptrALMT10 was connected to 49 genes, and PoptrMATE54 was connected to 85 genes and three other genes shared connections with both of them.

Under phosphorus deficiency and Al toxicity, PoptrALMT10 had the highest number of correlated genes in the root, whereas in the leaf, PoptrMATE54 had the highest number of correlated genes. In A. thaliana, AtALMT1 is responsible for conferring tolerance to Al, although AtMATE has a small contribution to tolerance (Liu et al. 2009). PoptrALMT10 and PoptrMATE54 only had correlated genes in common on root samples under Al stress, although it is well established in the literature that Al toxicity is closely related to phosphorus defciency (Ryan and Delhaize 2001; Kochian et al. 2015; Carvalho et al. 2016).

When the root was exposed to Al, a diferent profle was observed compared to P defciency stress. PoptrALMT10 was connected to 203 genes, whereas PoptrMATE54 was connected to 81 genes. However, the most interesting result was 35 shared genes, of which three are putative transcription factors belonging to Trihellix, NF-YB and bHLH families. One transcription factor family predominant in Al stress in A. thaliana was bHLH (Kumari et al. 2008). In addition, this family is essential for gene regulation in Oryza sativa under Fe defciency (Ogo et al. 2007).

To obtain more information about the genes connected to PoptrALMT10 and PoptrMATE54, enrichment was done using the BLAST2GO software (Table S3). The genes that were connected with PoptrMATE54 and PoptrALMT10 are related to the transport of primary and secondary ions through the membrane, mainly of the nucleus, cytoplasm and vacuole, respectively (Fig. S2). Therefore, it is possible to speculate that the genes PoptrALMT10 and PoptrMATE54 share the same pathways associated genes in Al stress, whereas in P defcienty stress, they act in an unrelated manner.

chunks.section: 3.ALMTs Are Widely Distributed in the Ge
chunks.text:
The characterised ALMT members show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13,39], microbe interactions [16,17], fruit acidity [14,15], and seed development [18]. Members which have been characterised are widely distributed in higher plant families of Poaceae, Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Rutaceae, Rosaceae, Vitaceae and Solanaceas (Table 1).


## 3.1. ALMT Members in Poaceae


The Poaceae species which have characterised ALMT members include wheat TaALMT1, rye ScALMT1, goatgrass AetALMT1, Yorkshire fog HlALMT1, maize ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2, rice OsALMT4 and barley HvALMT1. ALMT genes in wheat, rye, goatgrass and Yorkshire fog facilitate resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley HvALMT1 was related to stomatal functions (Figure 1).

By using a cDNA subtractive hybridisation technique, Sasaki et al. [1] cloned a cDNA which was more highly expressed in the root apices of an Al-resistant wheat line (ET8) than in a near-isogenic but Al-sensitive line (ES8). TaALMT1 was mapped to chromosome 4DL and the relative expression of this gene among various genotypes of wheat was strongly correlated with Al-activated malate efflux capacity and Al resistance [40]. Electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus laevis oocytes indicated that TaALMT1 encodes an Al-activated transporter that can mediate both inward and outward currents. The malate transport permeability is enhanced by external Al but it is also permeable to a lesser degree to other physiologically relevant anions such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ [1,41]. Transgenic rice, Arabidopsis, barley and tobacco cultured cell lines expressing TaALMT1 all showed an Al-activated malate efflux. In the later three cases, TaALMT1 also increased Al resistance [1,42]. The higher expression of TaALMT1resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley in resistant than sensitive wheat genotypes is due to a series of repeated blocks in the promoter [43].

Among cereal crops, rye is the most Al resistant species. Researchers have mapped Al-resistance loci on chromosomes 3R (Alt2), 4RL (Alt3), 6RS (Alt1) and 7RS (Alt4) by using segregating populations and wheat-rye addition lines [44–48]. Using primers to the TaALMT1 gene, Fontecha et al. [49] cloned a 1359 bp cDNA called ScALMT1 from rye and showed that it co-segregated with the Al resistance locus Alt4. ScALMT1 is mainly expressed in roots and expression is upregulated by exogenous Al treatment. Collins et al. [2] showed that the Alt4 resistance locus contains a cluster of ALMT genes. Although − −there are some mRNA splice variations that might affect protein function, the M77.1 promoter and ScALMT1-M39.1 gene are sufficient to explain most of the Al resistance in that line. As the ancestor of the wheat D genome, goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii Coss.) contains more genetic variation than bread wheat perhaps because it experienced less artificial selection. Ryan et al. [50] screened 760 accessions in a total of seven progenitor species of hexaploid wheat and other early relatives. Of these only five of 29 Aegilops tauschii tested showed a moderate level of resistance to Al. The coding sequences of the AetALMT1 genes in the five resistant genotypes were identical to TaALMT1 and resistance was correlated with AetALMT1 expression level and with Al-activated malate efflux. Unlike TaALMT1, all the Aegilops tauschii genes lacked any of the tandem repeats in the promoter region—even the moderately resistant ones [50]. Yorkshire fog is a grass that shows a large genotypic variation in acid soil tolerance. Chen et al. [34] cloned the HlALMT1 gene and found that plants from plots with acidic soil (HL-A) had significantly higher HlALMT1 expression levels in their roots than plants from plots with neutral pH soil (HL-N). The higher expression in HL-A plants was linked with a greater number of the cis-acting elements which recognise an Al-responsive transcription factor (HlART1) [34]. Furthermore, the HL-A roots secreted approximately twice as much malate as the HL-N roots, but there was no difference in citrate secretion. These results indicated that cis elements in the promoter of the HvALMT1 gene generated higher expression of HlALMT1 leading to higher malate efflux and greater Al resistance.

In maize, ZmALMT1 was initially considered a candidate for an Al resistance gene due to its sequence homology with TaALMT1 [12]. Although ZmALMT1 localises to the plasma membrane, is mainly expressed in root tissue, and shows increased expression with Al treatment, other results indicated that this gene was not involved with the mechanism of Al resistance. Firstly, electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus oocytes showed that ZmALMT1 had greater permeability to ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ than malate and these anions would not bind with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to reduce its activity in the apoplast. Furthermore, ZmALMT1 expression was low in the root tips where protection from $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress by organic anions is crucial. Lastly, transport activity of ZmALMT1 was independent of exogenous Al [12]. Linkage analysis of Al resistance genes in maize identified another ALMT gene, ZmALMT2, that is associated with net root growth under Al stress [51]. However, once again, ZmALMT2 is more permeable to inorganic anions $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right.$ , $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ ) than organic anions such as malate. Furthermore, ZmALMT2 is mainly expressed in mature roots and not root apices, expression levels are similar in Al-sensitive and resistant genotypes. Therefore, this gene is also unlikely to be involved with Al resistance despite its genetic linkage with that trait. Instead the authors suggested ZmALMT2 is involved with mineral nutrition [13].

There are nine members of the ALMT family rice but only OsALMT4 has been examined in detail. OsALMT4 localises to the plasma membrane and is expressed widely in roots and shoots, especially in the vasculature. Transgenic plants over-expressing OsALMT4 released malate from roots which is consistent with OsALMT4 encoding a malate-permeable anion channel. The over-expressing (OX) lines developed distinct symptoms on their leaves which consisted of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins which did not appear on null segregant plants or RNAi lines with reduced OsALMT4 expression. The partitioning of Mn within the leaf tissue was altered in the transgenic since the OX lines had a greater proportion of Mn residing in the apoplast of the leaves compared to the null plants. OX lines also had higher concentrations of malate in the xylem sap and increased expression of genes encoding Mn transporters (OsNramp5 and OsYSL2) and B transporters (OsBOR1 and OsNIP3.1). Growth studies found that the OX lines were more sensitive to Mn toxicity but more tolerant of B toxicity than null plants. The authors conclude that enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms [39].

Barley is another important plant in Triticeae and the barley ALMT1 gene was shown to be involved in facilitating anion efflux from guard cells during stomatal closure and seed development [5,11,18]. HvALMT1 is located on chromosome 2H. Tissue localisation showed that this protein was expressed in guard cells and in emerging lateral roots, the nucellar projection, aleurone layer and the scutellum of developing barley grain [5,18]. Intracellular localisation of HvALMT1 included the plasma membrane and small motile vesicles in the cytosol but the identity and function of those vesicles is unknown. Heterologous expression in Xenopus oocytes showed that this protein could mediate both inward and outward currents. HvALMT1 is permeable to malate and its activity is sensitive to $\mathrm { p H }$ [5]. The transgenic plants over-expressing HvALMT1 released more malate from roots than the control plants and they took significantly longer to close their stomata under low light than null controls. They also tended to reach a lower stomatal conductance under low light but the results were not significant. Combined with the finding that HvALMT1 is highly expressed in guard cells these results provided evidence that this channel contributes to stomatal function [11]. Interestingly, overexpressing HvALMT1 to high levels with a constitutive promoter affected plant growth and grain formation. Further experiments showed that malate release measured from isolated aleurone layers of grain was significantly lower in transgenic lines in which HvALMT1 expression was reduced by RNAi compared to control plants [18]. Therefore, HvALMT1 function affects stomatal aperture, grain development and plant growth. This shows that a single ALMT gene may perform multiple functions [5,11,18].

## 3.4. ALMT Members in Fruit Plants


In many acid soils it is common for Al toxicity to be linked with phosphorus (P) deficiency. This is because the soluble P is likely to be in a complex with iron or Al or fixed in other less soluble forms. Indeed some plants very efficient at taking up P from highly P-fixing soils, such white lupin (Lupinus albus L.), rely on organic anion release from roots (especially citrate release) to access more P [22]. Research indicates that members of the ALMT family might also contribute to greater P-use efficiency. For instance, the Al resistant species of citrus ‘Xuegan’ (Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck, CsALMT1) displayed more resistance to P-deficiency than a sensitive species ‘Sour pummelo’ (Citrus grandis (L.) Osbeck, $C g A L M T 1 )$ . Evidence was presented that ALMT genes in these species might contribute to the resistance of citrus to Al and/or P-deficiency [61].

Some ALMT proteins appear to affect fruit acidity by transporting malate across the tonoplast membrane (Figure 3). This was revealed when Bai et al. [14] narrowed down the Ma locus to a $6 5 { - } 8 2 \mathrm { k b }$ region on chromosome 16 of the apple cultivar Golden Delicious. The Ma locus is associated with fruit acidity in apple and the genomic region contains 12–19 predicted genes. By aligning these genes with two BACs covering different haplotypes of the Ma locus (high and low acidity), they identified two ALMT homologues and named them Ma1 and Ma2. Quantitative RT-PCR experiments predicted that expression of Ma1, but not Ma2, is significantly linked with fruit acidity (high Ma1 expression was correlated with more acidic fruit). Moreover, a natural mutation in Ma1 leading to a truncation of the gene was also associated with low fruit acidity. The Ma1 genotype is closely related to apple fruit acidity suggesting Ma1 is associated with the accumulation of malic acid in apple fruits [62]. Similarly, De Angeli et al. The VvALMT9 protein has $6 4 \%$ identity with AtALMT9 and also localises to the tonoplast. VvALMT9 is not only permeable to malate, but also displays a low permeability to tartrate. The authors predicted that VvALMT9 is a tonoplast channel that contributes to malate and tartrate accumulation in grape berries [15].
