The AtMRP gene family consists of 15 members,including one aberrant gene， AtMRP15, which is annotated as a protein with an N-terminal truncation due to $5 ^ { \prime }$ stop codons of about 40o amino acids that are not present in other AtMRPs.Its nucleotide sequence isnearly identical to thatof AtMRP9, even in the non-coding $5 ^ { \prime }$ region. In contrast to all other full-size proteins encoding AtMRPs we have been unable to detect a transcript for this gene in Arabidopsis (data not shown)，raising the possibility that AtMRPi5 is indeed a pseudogene. Another MRPrelated gene is encoded by Atlg71330 (F3I7.2). It seems to encode only one membrane-spanning region with high similarities to AtMRP3 and so cannot be considered as a classical transporter. The arrangement of sequences in the phylogenetic tree suggests that AtMRP1,2, 11 and 12 comprise a group of closely related genes. A similar grouping can be found for all other AtMRP genes with the exception of AtMRP13, which represents an intermediate between the two MRP subgroups. Interestingly, these phylogenetic data are in agreement with the intron-exon structures of the genes.

MDRs and MRPs exhibit the same arrangement of domains but differ at their N-termini where an extremely hydrophobic N-terminal extension (NTE) of around 22O amino acids is observed for MRPs but not for MDRs. A careful study of the membrane topology of human MRP, employing glycosylation-site mutants, indicates that the hydrophobic NTE forms a third MSD of five transmembrane $\mathscr { X }$ -helices and that the N-terminus is most likely situated in the extracytoplasmic side of the membrane bilayer (Hipfner et al.1997).Hydropathy plots of animal and plant MRPs resemble each other to a great extent, suggesting a similar arrangement of the membrane-spanning domains in animals and plants.In contrast, the NTE of MRPs exhibits only weak homology among the different members of MRPlike proteins.

The third group of ful-size ABC transporters is formed by 15 AtPDR-like genes and represents a separate sub-cluster. These proteins are characterized in fungal systems as efflux transporters for cytotoxic compounds such as oligomycin or cyclohexamide (Balzi and Goffeau 1994). A PDR-like ABC transporter also plays a role in the pathogen reaction since it has been shown that plant pathogenic fungi need the activity of PDR5- like genes for expression of pathogenicity or acquired resistance towards fungicides (Urban et al. 1999; Andrade et al. 20oo).In a very recent publication, Jasinski et al (20o1) showed that Nicotiana plumbaginifolia ABC1 (NpABC1)，a member of the PDR5-like family，is also localized in the plasma membrane. NpABC1 is highly expressed in the presence of sclareolide,a close analogue of the antifungal diterpene sclareol.These properties, together with the observation that the cellular sclareolide content decreases in parallel with the induction of the ABC transporter and that inhibitors of ATP synthesis reverse this effect, strongly suggest that this PDR5 homologue is involved the excretion of secondary metabolites playing a role in plant defense.

By performing a differential screening of Spirodela polyrrhiza grown in the absence and presence of abscisic acid (ABA), Smart and Fleming (1996) have identified a PDR5-like ABC transporter (TUR2). The expression of this transporter is increased about 7-fold within $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ after application of ABA. Other treatments that, in contrast to ABA,do not induce turion formation in Spirodela, such as exposure to cycloheximide or salt stress,also resulted in an increased mRNA level for TUR2, indicating that expression of TUR2 is not the cause of turion formation. Compared with the AtPGP and AtMRP classes the AtPDR5-like genes form a relatively tight cluster. This also holds true for the genes AtPDR2 and AtPDR12. AtPDR2 was originally annotated as two separate genes (see MATDB entries AT4gl5230 and AT4g15220,http://www.mips.biochem.mpg.de/proj/ thal/db/index.html). Alignment-based re-annotation of the sequences suggests a single gene coding for a protein of 1,385 amino acids,whose genomic structure is in concord with that of other AtPDR5-like genes. Annotations for AtPDR12 differ between MATDB and GENBANK in such a way that MATDB lists AtPDR12 as a pseudogene and GENBANK presents it as a functional gene. Expressed sequence tags(ESTs) for AtPDRi2 (see Table 1） support the latter suggestion. Furthermore,the described annotations for AtPDR2 and AtPDRi2 are supported by their positions in the phylogenetic analysis (see Fig. 1).

Figure 2 shows a comparison of the Walker motifs and ABC signature of plant full-size ABC transporters. It is obvious that only the Walker A box exhibits perfect conservation in all of these proteins, whereas both of the other consensus motifs exhibit a higher degree of variation. One consequence of this finding is that the definition of this class of proteins by consensus sequences alone could result in misleading interpretations about their functions.On the other hand,these consensus motifs can serve as valuable tools. The mentioned PMP70-like sequence lacks the N-terminal Walker A box and the second ABC motif is situated in the last 12 amino acids of the protein leaving no space for a Walker B box.These facts make a function as an ATP-dependent transporter questionable.

The nomenclature for all described full-size ABC transporter genes in Arabidopsis is summarized in Table 1. Numbering of AtPGP,AtMRP and AtPDR5 genes is according to Davies and Coleman (2oo0),with the exception of AtMRP8,13,11 (described as MRP6-8 in Davies and Coleman 20oO) and AtPGP8 (see above). Genes not mentioned in that review were numbered successively （AtPGP11-AtPGP22，AtMRP9-AtMRP15 and AtPDR9-AtPDR12). It is worth mentioning that this summary cannot be the final list of the Arabidopsis inventory of full-size ABC transporter genes as the complete coding sequences are published only for a small number of genes. The number of full-size ABC transporter genes was estimated from annotations of genomic data. Only half of the genes in this table are confirmed by experimental data or ESTs (Table 1). The annotations are mostly based on homology to known genes and/or gene-prediction programs. Until these predictions are confirmed by experimental data,such estimations of gene numbers should be treated with caution. This holds especially true for cases where either putatively wrong annotations (AtPDR2), contradictory annotations (AtPGP8,AtPGP22) or no annotations at all （AtPDR13-AtPDR15) have been given. Data sets from sequencing projects of Arabidopsis ful-length cDNAs, like the one recently released by Ceres Inc. in theTiGRdatabase(http://www.tigr.org/tdb/ath1/ htmls/index.html),might clear up the remaining questions.


## ABC-type transport activities for which the corresponding transporter has not been identified


Besides glutathione conjugates,chlorophyll catabolites and glucuronides,for which transport proteins have been identified (see above)，vacuolar uptake of some additional substrates exhibits typical ABC-type transport kinetics:

i.Bile acids (Hörtensteiner et al. 1993),which have not been demonstrated in plants.Interestingly, in animals an MDR-type transporter is responsible for the transport of bile acids (Gerloff et al. 1998 ） while in yeast this activity could be assigned to an MRP-type transporter (Ortiz et al. 1997).   
ii. The sulfonated compound Lucifer Yellow.Several animal MRPs have been shown to transport sulfated compounds and it is probable that one or several of the already-cloned AtMRPs exhibits a transport activity for sulfonated and sulfated compounds.   
ii. Glucosylated compounds are the predominant class of secondary metabolites stored within plant cells. In most cases they are transported into the vacuole by proton antiporter mechanisms (Martinoia et al. 2000).However,it has been shown that vacuolar uptake of a glucosylated herbicide,which is formed during the detoxification process (Kreuz et al. 1996), exhibits kinetics typical of ABC-transporters (Klein et al. 1996).

Recent experiments have shown the great diversity of transporters that recognize compounds synthesized by different plants. Uptake of the main barley flavonoid saponarin into barley vacuoles shows that this compound is taken up by a proton antiporter mechanism.In contrast,work in our laboratories has shown that vacuoles isolated from Arabidopsis,a plant that does not synthesize the flavone glucoside saponarin, exhibit direct energization by an ABC-type transporter (Fragne et al.，in press). It is therefore tempting to speculate that glucosides are only taken up by an antiporter mechanism if structural homologues are present in the plant (or cell).In contrast, glucosides, which have no structural analogues in the plant, may be recognized as modified, potentially toxic compounds and transported into the vacuole using a directly energized ABC-type transporter. However, the fact that barley vacuoles transport aesculin by a proton antiport system indicates that this hypothesis cannot be generalized and is probably only true for large glycosylated compounds.


## ABC transporters regulate ion fluxes


Most ABC transporters couple the hydrolysis of ATP and transport of molecules across a membrane against a concentration gradient. As a consequence, this transport mechanism allows the hyper-accumulation of a molecule in a compartment.However, in two cases ABC transporters,well characterized in animal cells,have been unequivocally shown to be involved in ion transport or ion-channel regulation. These transporters control the flux of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ according to the electrochemical gradient and in response to changes in the concentration of cytosolic nucleotides like ADP or ATP.These ABC transporters are:

i. The K-ATP channels (Bryan and Aguilar-Bryan 1999)，which are heteromultimers constituted by ABC-type sulfonylurea receptors (SUR1, SUR2A or SUR2B) and the potassium inward rectifier $( \mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 1$ or ${ \mathrm { K } } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2 )$ . Neither SUR1 nor $\mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { I R } } 6 . 2$ cDNAs exhibited recognizable K-ATP channel activity when expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,but co-expression generated current characteristics of native KATP channels (Inagaki et al. 1995). Interestingly, when Dsur,a novel Drosophila gene highly homologous to vertebrate SUR but harboring an additional 1.7-kb extension，was expressed alone in Xenopus oocytes,a classical K-ATP channel signature was recorded (Nasonkin et al. 1999). This result was not observed with mammalian SUR in the same expression system, suggesting that the sequence extension in Dsur could be responsible for the generation of Kchannel activity.

ii. The cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator(CFTR),which functions as a phosphorylation- and nucleotide-regulated small-conductance chloride channel (Akabas 20oo). Besides its function asa $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channel, CFTR acts as a regulator of amiloride-sensitive $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ channels,outward-rectifying $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ channels, $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H C O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ exchanger and ROMK $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels (Schwiebert et al. 1999).

CFTR and SUR are unequivocally involved in transport/regulation of ion fluxes and share more similarities with the MRP than the MDR family. They exhibit a defined pharmacology. Some sulfonylureas, like glibenclamide and tolbutamide,are potent inhibitors of K-ATP channels and the CFTR-mediated $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ conductance.K-ATP channels can be activated by a diverse group of compounds collectively referred to as potassium channel openers (KCOs). These compounds have been developed for clinical use in patients with hypertension,asthma or ischemic heart disease and may act as antagonists of the sulfonylureas.In order to test whether such ABC-transporters are also present in plants, Leonhardt et al.(1997) investigated the effect of inhibitors of the K-ATP-channel and CFTR on epidermal strips and guard cells of Vicia faba.Incubation of epidermal strips with glibenclamide or tolbutamide led to a dose-dependent increase in stomatal aperture with a $\mathrm { K } _ { 1 / 2 }$ of $2 . 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for glibenclamide. In contrast, KCOs inhibited stomatal opening and induced stomatal closure in the nanomolar range of concentration. Using guard-cell protoplasts and the patch-clamp technique, the authors observed a partial inhibition of the outward potassium current by glibenclamide.This inhibition was partially reversed by the KCO cromakalim. Since the guard-cell potassium channel is not ATP-sensitive,a similar but not identical system to the one described in animals may be present in guard cells.However, due to the fact that guard cels were investigated in the whole-cell configuration, the efects observed on potassium channels may be indirect. Therefore, Leonhardt et al. (1999) also tested this hypothesis and observed that glibenclamide inhibits the $\dot { \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } }$ -induced stomatal closure caused by slow anion efflux.The phytohormone ABA,however, reversed the glibenclamide effect.From these results the authors postulated that in plants,as in animals,ABC-type proteins are involved in the regulation of ion channel activities. Direct evidence that plant ABC transporters are indeed implicated in ion fluxes has been provided recently (Gaedeke et al. 2001). AtMRP5,like the other AtMRPs,exhibits a high similarity to CFTR and SUR. It is highly expressed in vascular tissue and in stomata. Analysis of a T-DNA-induced mutation of AtMRP5 revealed that glibenclamide triggers stomatal opening in the dark in the wild type but not in mrp5-1 mutant plants (Fig.3). This is a direct hint that ABC transporters are also involved in regulation of stomatal opening.Presently，it is not possible to differentiate whether AtMRP5 controls either $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ or anion channels, exhibits channel activities or is a member of the signal transduction pathway leading to stomatal opening. Finally,the fact that the nucleotide-binding domain of

ABC transporters resembles the respective domains of Ras and other G-proteins could raise the possibility that a conformational change in these domains might have regulatory consequences for interacting proteins.


## ABC transporters are involved in plant growth processes


Recent results show that ABC transporters are not only implicated in detoxification and ion-regulation processes but also in plant growth processes.

Sidler et al.(1998) have shown that AtPGP1 is responsible for control of hypocotyl cell elongation under low light. An increase of $50 \%$ in hypocotyl length could be observed at a photon fluence rate of $1 \mathrm { \dot { 0 } ~ } \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { ~ m } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { \ s } ^ { - 1 }$ for plants overexpressing AtPGP1, and about $20 \%$ inhibition of hypocotyl length was detected for plants that showed antisense inhibition of AtPGP1 under the same light conditions.However,in darkness,as well as at fluence rates of $1 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m o l } } ~ { \mathrm { m } } ^ { - 2 } ~ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ ， no difference in cell elongation was observed. The growth response was independent of light quality and could be observed under red and blue light regimes.The response to far-red light (FR) was also different in wild-type and overexpressing plants, but in this case seedling growth in FR was less than $1 0 \%$ of that observed in darkness. In addition,roots of plants overexpressing AtPGP1 were slightly larger than control plants.Very recent data suggest that AtPGP1 might export ATP; however, the reason for the observed phenotype is still unknown (Thomas et al. 2000).

A further example of the involvement of plant ABC transporters in light-regulated growth processes has very recently been presented by Moller et al (2001). It was observed that the gene responsible for the laf6 (long after FR） phenotype,which exhibits reduced responsiveness toward continuous FR,encodes an ABC transporter. This ABC transporter is highly homologous to an ABC transporter of Synechocystis and the cryptophyte alga Guillardia theta. It is interesting to note that in this alga the corresponding ABC transporter is encoded on the chloroplast genome,while in higher plants no chloroplast-encoded ABC transporters can be found.In addition to the highly homologous ABC transporters of Synechocystis and Guillardia, AtABC1 contains an N-terminal transit peptide that targets it to the chloroplast. The mutation in this gene results in protoporphyrin IX accumulation and lower chlorophyll contents.The protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPO) inhibitor flumioxazin results in increased levels of protoporphyrin IX and hence mimicks the laf6 phenotype. Plants overexpressing AtABC1 showed a reduced sensitivity to flumioxazin. In addition,genes known to be light-regulated such as chalcone synthase and ferredoxin ${ \mathrm { N A D P } } ^ { + }$ oxidoreductase are attenuated in laf6 compared with the wild type under high-fluence FR. These results suggest that AtABC1 is associated with a hydrophobic protein localized in the internal envelope of the chloroplast and catalyzes an ATP-dependent import of protoporphyrin IX.

In yeast it has been shown that a mitochondrial halfsize ABC transporter ATM1 is involved in the synthesis of Fe/S clusters (Leighton and Schatz 1995). This function appears to be conserved in eukaryotes, since the human Abc7 and MTABC3 have been shown to be functional orthologues of ATMl (Csere et al. 1998; Mitsuhashi et al. 20o0). Recently, Kushnir et al. (2001) showed that the Arabidopsis mutant starik,which leads to dwarfism and chlorosis, is due to the insertion of a TDNA in an orthologue of ATM1, Stal. Stal complements the yeast mutant △atm1, indicating that this gene, like yeast ATM1 and the corresponding human orthologues, supports the maturation of Fe/S clusters in mitochondria.MeasurementofFeshowedthat mitochondria of the stal mutant contain similar amounts of Fe as the wild-type mitochondria. As in △atml yeast,mitochondria of the Stal mutant cells contain 1.5- to 1.8-fold higher levels of free iron and less iron associated with proteins.A further example of altered plant growth was reported by Gaedeke et al. (2001) who observed that root growth in a T-DNA insertion mutant of AtMRP5 differed from that of control plants. Depending on the potassium concentration in the medium, root growth was reduced or enhanced compared with that of wild-type seedlings.

It is likely that growth processes in plants can be modulated in several ways by ABC transporters. As suggested by Moller et al. (200i), ABC transporters may be directly involved in the transport of a metabolite, or, as shown in the case of Synechocystis,of a metal required as cofactor by some enzymes (Bartsevich and Pakrasi 1995).Phenotypes of plants overexpressing an ABC transporter or where an ABC transporter is knocked-out suggest that the phytohormone balance is disturbed. However,phytohormone transport has not yet been reported for ABC transporters.In the case of MRP-like ABC transporters,a perturbation of phytohormone levels may not result from transport of free phytohormones but from the corresponding conjugates. It is well known that most phytohormones are conjugated to glycosides or amino acids. In the case of auxin, it has been reported that the first conjugation products observed in Arabidopsis are aspartate or glutamate conjugates,which are linked by a peptide bond to auxin (Ostin et al. 1998; Tam et al. 2000). Glutamate conjugates have been shown to be substrates for human MRPs and it is likely that they are also substrates for plant MRPs.Furthermore,it has been shown that some glycosides are recognized by ABC transporters. If such a conjugate is not exported efficiently from the cytosol, free-hormone concentrations may rise due either to feedback inhibition of the conjugation step or hydrolysis of the conjugate accumulating in the cytosol. Such a process would result in higher concentrations of phytohormones and hence the observed changes in the developmental pattern of mrp5-1.

An additional mechanism by which ABC transporters may be involved in developmental processes is through the interaction with other proteins.As discussed above, it was suggested that AtMRP5 interacts with ion channels in stomata. Such interactions may result in distinct phenotypes.

Direct evidence for such an interaction recently demonstrated that ABC transporters also interact with immunophilins.In animals,drugs binding to this class of protein are powerful immunosuppressors due to the fact that the immunophilin-drug complex inhibits the calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein phosphatase calcineurin. In plants,several immunophilins have been identified (Blecher et al 1996;Fulgosi et al. 1998; Vittorioso et al. 1998).We have observed that the FK506-binding(FKBP) immunophilinTWISTED DWARF1 (TWDi) from Arabidopsis shows a pleiotropic knock-out mutant phenotype, including a reduction in cell elongation and disorientated growth of the entire plant (data not shown). Also,using the yeast two-hybrid system we have identified the MDR-like Arabidopsis ABC transporter AtPGPl as an interactant with TWD1 (data not shown). Mapping and biochemical analyses showed that the FKBP-like domain of TWDl mediates AtPGP1 interaction. Since AtPGP1-overexpressing/antisense plants also show a phenotype (see above), it is tempting to speculate that ABC transporters are involved in some signal transduction pathways. Genetic analysis revealed that TWD1 is required for brassinosteroid reception or signal transduction (data not shown). In animal systems, interaction of MDR-like ABC transporters with steroids,as well as transport of steroidal precursors, has been reported (Metherall et al. 1996; Debry et al. 1997; Gruol et al. 1999). Therefore,it is tempting to speculate that plant ABC transporters may also play a role in steroid transport or signal transduction.

Background: ATP-binding cassette proteins have been recognized as playing a crucial role in the regulation of growth and resistance processes in all kingdoms of life. They have been deeply studied in vertebrates because of their role in drug resistance, but much less is known about ABC superfamily functions in plants.

Results: Recently released plant genome sequences allowed us to identify 803 ABC transporters in four vascular plants (Oryza. sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum and Vitis vinifera) and 76 transporters in the green alga Volvox carteri, by comparing them with those reannotated in Arabidopsis thaliana and the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Retrieved proteins have been phylogenetically analysed to infer orthologous relationships. Most orthologous relationships in the A, D, E and F subfamilies were found, and interesting expansions within the ABCG subfamily were observed and discussed. A high level of purifying selection is acting in the five ABC subfamilies A, B, C, D and E. However, evolutionary rates of recent duplicate genes could influence vascular plant genome diversification. The transcription profiles of ABC genes within tomato organs revealed a broad functional role for some transporters and a more specific activity for others, suggesting the presence of key ABC regulators in tomato.

Conclusions: The findings achieved in this work could contribute to address several biological questions concerning the evolution of the relationship between genomes of different species. Plant ABC protein inventories obtained could be a valuable tool both for basic and applied studies. Indeed, interpolation of the putative role of gene functions can accelerate the discovering of new ABC superfamily members.

Keywords: ATP-binding cassette transporters, Multidrug resistance, Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Solanum tuberosum, Vitis vinifera, Volvox carteri, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Gene duplication, Evolutionary dynamics

## Identification of ABC transporters in B. tabaci


A total of 55 ABC transporters was identified in B. tabaci Q genome (Table 1). The number of ABC transporters in B. tabaci $\mathrm { Q }$ is comparable with other arthropod species;

however, subfamilies G and $_ \mathrm { H }$ expanded in phloem- and blood-sucking arthropods (Table 2 and Additional file 1: Figure S1). For example, ABCG and ABCH account for $5 8 \%$ (42 and $1 6 \%$ , respectively) of ABC transporters in the phloem-sucking $B _ { \cdot }$ . tabaci, and $4 9 \%$ (45 and $4 \%$ respectively) in the blood-sucking Cimex lectularius. The percentage reduces to $2 1 \%$ $( 1 8 \% + 3 \% )$ in the red flour beetle, T. castaneum. The expansion of ABCG and ABCH subfamilies in these polyphagous and phloem-sucking arthropods, including the whitefly $B _ { \cdot }$ . tabaci, the wheat aphid $D _ { * }$ . noxia and the spider mite $T .$ urticae, suggest the potential contribution of ABC transporters to their adaptability and invasiveness. Phylogenetic analysis categorized the 55 B. tabaci ABC transporters into eight subfamilies (Fig. 1). To further understand the evolutionary placement of $B$ tabaci ABC transporters, in-depth phylogenetic analyses were conducted for each subfamily. The results of these analyses were described and discussed in the following sections.


## ABCA subfamily


A phylogeny tree of the eight ABCA proteins identified in B. tabaci and other organisms was presented in Additional file 2: Figure S2. All of the B. tabaci ABCA proteins are full-transporters (Table 1), which is consistent with $D$ . pulex and T. urticae [10, 13]. The silkworm ABCA subfamily, in contrast, contains two full-transporters, one half-transporter and three incomplete ABC transporters [8]. Furthermore, no ABCA protein has been identified in yeast [26].

The B. tabaci ABCA subfamily has one of the largest B. tabaci ABC transporters, Btabq008198.1, encoding 1730 amino acids (Table 1). Btabq008198.1 clustered with the ABCA5 group, including Anopheles gambiae AGAp010416-PA, D. noxia DnXP_01537 5463.1 and H. sapiens ABCA5 cluster (hABCA5, 6, 8, 9 and 10) (Additional file 2: Figure S2). Although these ABCA5-related genes in mammalians (human, dog and mouse) cluster with ABCA5 on the same chromosomes [6, 27], no counterpart of the ABCA5- related genes has been identified in invertebrates, such as B. mori [8] and T. urticae [10]. Besides Btabq008198.1, the other seven B. tabaci ABCA genes (Btabq017043.1, Btabq003223.3, Btabq003232.1, Btabq 009375.1, Btabq009376.1, Btabq022409.1, and Btabq 022410.1) form a sister-group with a high bootstrap support. This sister-group clustered with $D$ . noxia DnXP_015366480.1 (ABCA3), T. japonicas TjABCA3 and seven $T .$ urticae genes. These genes then clustered with $D$ . melanogaster DmCG31731 with a moderate bootstrap support. DmCG31731 was down-regulated in the salivary glands of a $D _ { \ast }$ . melanogaster E93 mutant [28]. As an early ecdysone responsive gene, E93 was a primary regulator of programmed cell death in $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster development [29]. Injection of dsRNAs synthesized from the two ABCA genes, TcABCA-9A and TcABC A-9B, led to approximately $3 0 \%$ mortality in the red flour beetle, T. castaneum [17].


## ABCB subfamily


In B. tabaci Q, we identified three ABCB half-transporters but no full-transporters (Table 1). These B. tabaci halftransporters (Btabq001304.1, Btabq013065.1 and Btabq 013065.1) belong to three clades, indicating that these genes are homologous to ABCB genes in human, fruit fly and other insects (Additional file 3: Figure S3). Btabq001304.1 clustered with ABCB6 proteins from other species, including $D _ { * }$ . noxia DnXP_015376167.1, An. gambiae AGAP002278, D. melanogaster DmCG4225, T. japonicas TjABCB6, and H. sapiens hABCB6. Similarly, Btabq028971.1 formed an ABCB7 clade with D. noxia DnXP_015378905.1, D. melanogaster DmCG7955, T. japonicas TjABCB7, and H. sapiens hABCB7. Meanwhile, Btabq013065.1 was clustered with ABCB8 from $D$ melanogaster (DmCG1824), T. urticae $( \mathrm { T u 1 7 g 0 2 0 0 0 } )$ , T. japonicas (TjABCB8) and $H .$ sapiens (hABCB8).

In H. sapiens, hABCB6, hABCB7 and hABCB8/ MABC1 are mitochondrial transporters with roles in iron metabolism and transportation of Fe/S protein precursors [30, 31]. Drosophila melanogaster DmCG4225 (ABCB6) was tolerant to cadmium [32]. Disruption of C. elegans ABTM- 1, a homologue of ABCB7, induced oxidative stress and premature cell death [33]. Furthermore, a homologous gene of $H .$ sapiens ABCB7 in Aedes aegypti was up-regulated in an insecticide resistant strain [34]. Disruption of mouse ABCB8 decreased mitochondrial iron export and led to cardiomyopathy [35]. Similar to $D _ { * }$ . pulex, B. tabaci Q do not have homologous genes of human ABCB half-transporters that were associated with antigen processing (hABCB2, hABCB3, and hABCB9) [13].


## ABCC subfamily


Insects typically have different number of ABCC transporters (Table 2). In B. tabaci $\mathrm { Q } ,$ we identified six ABCC full-transporters, including Btabq019529.2, Btabq000311.1, Btabq008004.1, Btabq026695.3, Btabq004618.1 and Btabq 003933.1. ABCC subfamily proteins are full-transporters with diverse functions, such as cell-surface receptor, ion transport and translocation of a broad range of substrates including drugs and endogenous compounds [36–39]. Due to their diverse functions, human ABCC subfamily members refer to multidrug resistance associated proteins (MRPs), which function as transporters; the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR, ABCC7), which forms a chloride channel; and sulfonylurea receptors (SUR1/2, ABCC8/9), which function as regulators of potassium channels [40]. In $H _ { \ast }$ sapiens, “long” MRPs like

ABCC1, 2, 3, 6 and 10 (MRP1, 2, 3, 6 and 7, respectively) have a TMD0, the third N-terminal transmembranespanning domain, while “short” MRPs like ABCC4, 5, 11 and 12 (MRP4, 5, 8 and 9, respectively) lack TMD0 [40].

In our phylogenetic analysis, two B. tabaci ABCC1 genes, Btabq019529.2 and Btabq000311.1, clustered with $D$ . noxia DnXP_015366208.1, DnXP_015366209.1, D. melanogaster DmCG6214, T. japonicus ABCC1 and a group of $H .$ sapiens “long” MRPs (MRP1, 2, 3 and 6) (Additional file 4: Figure S4). MRP1/ABCC1 transports a structurally diverse range of endogenous substances (e.g. leukotrienes and estrogen conjugates), xenobiotics and their metabolites [41]. These MRPs have been extensively studied as transporters of natural product drugs such as anthracyclines and plant alkaloids [42]. As a homologous gene to $H .$ sapiens MRP1, MRP2, MRP3 and MRP6, DmCG6214 functions as a high capacity ATP-dependent organic anion transporter and acts as a transporter of ecdysteroid and juvenile hormone conjugates [43]. The other two ABCC genes in B. tabaci, Btabq008004.1 and Btabq026695.3, gathered with a large clade of ABCC4 in $D _ { * }$ . noxia, An. gambiae and a cluster of Drosophila ABCC proteins, including DmCG10505, DmCG14709 and others. MRP4/ABCC4 can remove a wide range of endogenous and exogenous molecules from cells [44]. The ABCC transporter encoded by CG10505 in $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster was regulated by heavy metals and was involved in biochemical detoxification of zinc and copper [45]. Drosophila DmCG14709 gene, a homologue of H. sapiens MRP4/ABCC4, was tightly regulated by oxygen [46]. The human body louse ABCC4 gene, PhABCC4, was up-regulated after exposed to the pesticide ivermectin. Injection of female lice with PhABCC4 dsRNA significantly increased their sensitivity to ivermectin [47].

Btabq004618.1 clustered with $D$ . noxia DnXP_01537 3973.1, T. japonicas TjABCC7, $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster DmCG 7806, H. sapien hABCC10/MRP7 and $T .$ . urticae $\mathrm { T u 0 3 g }$ 07840. hABCC10/MRP7 was able to transport amphipathic anions and conferred resistance to some antitumor drugs [48]. In addition, Btabq003933.1 clustered with sulfonylurea receptors (SURs) in $D$ . noxia, $D$ . melanogaster, T. japonicas, T. urticae and $H .$ sapiens. Unlike other ABCC subfamily genes, SURs help form ATPsensitive potassium $( \mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { A T } }$ P) channels [38, 49]. Although SUR was considered to be a direct target of chitin synthesis inhibitors [50], it did not express in $D$ . melanogaster epidermis, where chitin disruption was observed [51]. Moreover, data obtained from $D$ melanogaster suggested that chitin synthesis was independent of SUR [52]. Similarly, RNAi knockdown of SUR homologue in T. castaneum did not result in a phenotype [17]. ABCC subfamily is not only involved in detoxification and multidrug resistance in

Manduca sexta but also participate in host plant selection in T. urticae [10, 53].


## ABCD subfamily


Bemisia tabaci Q has two ABCD transporters, Btabq026746.1 and Btabq017051.1 (Table 1). The same amount of ABCDs have also been found in other insects [8], while more ABCDs were identified in $D _ { * }$ . pulex, $H .$ sapiens and C. elegans. Members of ABCD subfamily are half-transporters and involve in the import of fatty acids and acyl-CoAs into this organelle [55]. ABCD transporters participated in peroxisome-related developmental progress in C. elegans [56]. Mutations in hABCD1/ALDP gene resulted in adrenoleukodystrophy, a genetic disorder that occurs primarily in males [57]. Our phylogenetic analysis suggested that three clades of ABCDs in metazoans, with the two B. tabaci ABCDs distributed in two clades (Additional file 5: Figure S5). Btabq026746.1 clustered with $D _ { * }$ noxia, DnXP_015374078.1, An. gambiae AGAP 002071, D. melanogaster DmCG216, T. japonicas TjAB CD2, $H .$ sapiens hABCD2 and hABCD1. Meanwhile, Btabq017051.1 belongs to ABCD3 clade.


## ABCE and ABCF subfamilies


ABCE and ABCF subfamilies contain atypical ABC transporters characterized by a pair of linked NBDs with no TMDs [1]. Their structure implied their roles in biological processes other than transportation. ABCE1 is one of the most evolutionarily conserved proteins and expressed in all organisms except eubacteria. Because of its role in translation and ribosome biosynthesis, ABCE1 is essential for all life stages [58]. Homo sapiens ABCE1/ RNase L was initially identified as an inhibitor of RNase L [58]. Members of the ABCE subfamily in human and yeast also have a role in translation initiation [59]. However, the ABCE and ABCF transporters have not been well characterized in invertebrates. RNAi knockdown of an ABCE gene, TcABCE-3A, resulted in significant mortality in penultimate T. castaneum larvae [17]. ABCE subfamily has only one member in all metazoans studied to date [9, 60], and B. tabaci follows this rule (BtabqABCE1, Table 1 and Additional file 6: Figure S6).

For ABCF subfamily, three transporters, Btabq009873.1, Btabq014578.1, and Btabq016264.1, were annotated and showed well-supported sister clades (Additional file 7: Figure S7). Btabq009873.1, Btabq014578.1, and Btabq 016264.1 were placed within the ABCF1, ABCF2, and ABCF3 clades, respectively. In human and yeast, ABCF proteins participated in gene regulation systems and ribosome assembly [14]. Mutations in the yeast GCN20 gene, which was involved in the initiation and control of translation, reduced Eif2α phosphorylation and translation in the ribosome [61].

Knockdown of TcABCF-2A led to $1 0 0 \%$ mortality in penultimate T. castaneum larvae [17].


## ABCG subfamily


ABCGs have a typical reverse domain architecture, with a NBD localized at the N-terminus and a TMD at the Cterminus (NBD-TMD). The ABCG transporters in metazoans are half-transporters and can be a functional transporter only after dimerization. In plants and fungi, however, ABCGs are full-transporters, also called pleiotropic drug resistance proteins (PDRs) [16, 62]. Because of their duplicated domain structure, yeast PDRs were not included in the phylogenetic analyses in this study.

ABCG proteins represent the largest ABC subfamily (23 members) in B. tabaci (Table 1) and also form the largest ABC subfamily in $D _ { * }$ . noxia [63], An. gambiae [7], bed bug (Cimex lectularius) [64], human body louse (Pediculus humanus humanus) [65], Drosophila [1] and A. mellifera [8] (Table 2). According to Sturm et al. [13], the expansion of ABCG transporters in $D _ { * }$ pulex and D. melanogaster genomes was resulted from extensive lineage specific gene duplications.

Among the 23 ABCG members in B. tabaci $\mathrm { Q } ,$ 17 are ABCG1 and ABCG4 transporters. These ABCG1 and ABCG4 proteins clustered with those in $D _ { * }$ . noxia, An. gambiae, T. urticae, and $D$ . melanogaster (DmCG9664, DmCG32091, DmCG4822, DmCG31689, DmCG9663, DmCG17646, DmCG5853 and DmCG3164) (Additional file 8: Figure S8). The ABCG4 gene has the same intron/ exon structure as ABCG1, suggesting that they arose by a relatively recent gene duplication event [66]. Similar to ABCG1, ABCG4 can be inducible by oxysterols and retinoids [67]. In $H .$ sapiens, hABCG1 and hABCG4 were involved in cellular cholesterol efflux [68]. In addition, the elevated expression of ABCG4 in An. stephensi suggested its involvement in the degradation of a pyrethroid insecticide [18, 69].

Btabq001288.1 and Btabq001290.1 clustered with DnXP_01579755.1, DnXP_015379710.1, DmCG11069, DmCG31121, Tu01g16280, TjABCG5, hABCG5 and hABCG8. hABCG5 and hABCG8 mediated the intestinal and biliary efflux of cholesterol and sterols [68]. A clear subclass was formed with Btabq023890.1, D. melanogaster DmCG3327, and T. urticae tetur17g02510. DmCG3327 (also named E23), a 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E)-induced ABC transporter, regulated metamorphosis, probably by removing 20E from cells [70]. Similarly, ABCG expression in silkworm midgut was also regulated by 20E [8]. RNAibased functional study confirmed a similar role in metamorphosis of TcABCG-8A, a homologue of E23 in T. castaneum [17].

Among invertebrates, the functions of ABCGs were first characterized in Drosophila as pigment precursor transporters (brown, scarlet and white genes) [71, 72]. In our phylogenetic analysis, four B. tabaci ABCG proteins, Btabq014028.1, Btabq015484.1, Btabq002474.1 and Btabq022510.1, showed homologous relationships with these pigment precursor transporters in $D _ { * }$ . noxia, An. gambiae and $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster. Besides transporting pigment precursors, these transporters also function in courtship behavior [73], transport of biogenic amines [74] and up-take of uric acid [75]. RNAi-mediated suppression and genetic linkage analysis confirmed that down-regulation of Pxwhite gene was tightly linked to Cry1Ac resistance in Plutella xylostella [76].

Based on a recent review, $8 0 \%$ of the peer-reviewed publications involving arthropod ABC transporters (50) linked ABC transporters with insecticides-resistance [77]. Members of ABCG subfamily were over-expressed in thiamethoxam-resistant $B .$ . tabaci, suggesting the involvement of these genes in insecticide resistance [78]. In addition, ABCG subfamily not only participated in multipesticide resistance in $T .$ urticae but also reduced the chemical defense from host plants [10]. In $B .$ mori, at least five ABCG genes acted as 20-hydroxyecdysone (20E)-response genes and participated in hormonal regulation [8]. These results suggested that members of the ABCG subfamily play significant roles in the development and the removal of amphiphilic xenobiotics. Although ABC transporters in subfamilies B, C, and G are involved in the metabolic resistance to various xenobiotics, $B .$ . tabaci $\mathrm { Q } ,$ however, contains predominantly G, but few B and C family members (Table 2). This bias reflects the importance of ABCG subfamily in $B _ { * }$ . tabaci to fend off xenobiotic offences derived from host plants as well as agroecosystems.


## ABCH subfamily


As inverse half-transporters, ABCH proteins share the same domain architecture as ABCG transporters. ABCH transporters were first discovered in $D _ { \ast }$ . melanogaster and have only annotated in arthropods and zebrafish [6, 8, 10, 11, 13, 17]. ABCH proteins have not been identified in fungi, C. elegans, plants and mammals [1, 16, 54, 62]. ABCH subfamily was documented in zebrafish but not in catfish, fugu or cod [79].

A total of nine ABCH transporters were identified in B. tabaci. Phylogenetic analysis showed that ABCH subfamily members were species-specific. Bemisia tabaci ABCH clustered with genes in $D$ . noxia with a high bootstrap value (Additional file 9: Figure S9). An RNAi screen of $D _ { * }$ melanogaster genes revealed that silencing of $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster CG9990 was lethal [80, 81]. In two insecticide-resistant $P .$ . xylostella strains, an ABCH $( P x O I 4 9 5 5 )$ , was the most up-regulated ABC transporter [82]. Knockdown of TcABCH-9C, an ABCH in T. castaneum, resulted in $1 0 0 \%$ larval mortality and a significant reduction of fecundity and hatching rate. In addition, T. castaneum larvae injected with TcABCH-9C dsRNA showed a lack of lipids in their epicuticle, indicating that TcABCH-9C may be required for the formation of a waterproof barrier in the epicuticle [17]. In the cotton bollworm Helicoverpa armigera and Manduca sexta, the expression of ABCH subfamily was highly induced after larvae fed with secondary metabolites [19, 53].


## Expression profiles across developmental stages


Based on RNA-seq data, all 55 ABC transporters were expressed with a RPKM (Reads Per Kilobases per Million reads) ${ > } 1$ in at least one of the $B .$ . tabaci life stages (Additional file 10: Table S1). Members from ABCE and ABCF subfamilies were ubiquitous and expressed highly throughout B. tabaci developmental stages (Fig. 2). In the polyphagous spider mite, T. urticae, an ABCE (tetur30g01400), showed high expression level throughout the life cycle [10]. Moreover, TcABCE-3A transcripts were abundant in all developmental stages of T. castaneum [17]. The expression profile of ABCE genes in the intertidal copepod, T. japonicas, and sea lamprey, Petromyzon marinus, showed similar trends as well [83, 84]. Btabq014578.1 (ABCF2) had the highest expression level throughout the life cycle. ABCE1, ABCF1 and ABCF2 were highly expressed in all developmental stages of $B _ { \cdot }$ . tabaci. ABCF3, also ubiquitously expressed, exhibited a lower expression level. These gene expression patterns were consistent with the fundamental functions in ribosome biogenesis and translation regulation [17, 85, 86]. The results suggest that ABCE and ABCF transporters were possibly essential to maintain “housekeeping” function in B. tabaci.

The expression levels for ABCA transporters in $B$ tabaci were relatively low with the exception of Btabq003232.1 (ABCA3), which was highly expressed in all life stages (Fig. 2). ABCA3 is critical for the proper formation of lamellar bodies and surfactant function and may participate in surfactant phospholipid metabolism [87]. Btabq001304.1 (ABCB6) expressed in all life stages of B. tabaci and highly expressed in eggs and nymphs. Btabq028971.1 (ABCB7) expressed in all developmental stages, especially in the fourth nymph stage and adult. Btabq013065.1 (ABCB8) expressed in all stages but at a lower level than other ABCB genes. Homo sapiens ABCB half-transporters, ABCB6, ABCB7, ABCB8 and ABCB10, were localized at mitochondria and functioned in iron metabolism [88].

Expression levels of all ABCC members were documented in each developmental stage of $B .$ . tabaci $\mathrm { Q } ,$ and the expression patterns were different among these genes (Fig. 2). Only Btabq008004.1 was highly expressed throughout life stages (Fig. 2). The two $B .$ tabaci ABCDs, Btabq026746.1 and Btabq017051.1, showed stable expressional level among different developmental stages (Fig. 2). Btabq026746.1 was highly expressed while

Btabq017051.1 showed slight lower expression level. Because the two ABCDs are homologous to those of mammal and insect transporters, similar functions such as roles in fatty acid metabolism can be inferred in $B _ { \cdot }$ tabaci Q.

Members of the ABCG subfamily showed different expression patterns in B. tabaci Q. Btabq003568.1, Btabq029281.1 and Btabq007131.3 were ubiquitously with high expression profiles. Expression levels were also high for Btabq006006.1, Btabq007377.1, Btabq029952.1 and Btabq000844.1. Overall, ABCG1 and ABCG4 members in B. tabaci Q had moderate to high expressional levels in all developmental stages. The ABCG4 in An. stephensi showed an increased expressional level in defense against the pyrethroid insecticide [18, 69]. Btabq001288.1 (ABCG5) and Btabq001290.1 (ABCG8)

showed high expression in all stages of $B$ . tabaci. Homologues of ABCG5 and ABCG8 in $D _ { * }$ . melanogaster and $T .$ castaneum function, respectively, in metamorphosis [17] and may have a similar function in $B .$ . tabaci. Furthermore, Btabq022510.1 was annotated as a white gene and its expression level in nymph and adult stages was especially high. Recently, a Pxwhite gene was shown to be tightly linked to Cry1Ac resistance in $P .$ . xylostella [76].

ABCH transporters differed in expression patterns during $B .$ . tabaci development. Btabq027409.1 and Btabq 026264.1 were highly expressed in all developmental stages. Moreover, Btabq015123.1, Btabq009745.1, and Btabq019352.1 also showed high expression level, especially in the $4 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ -instar nymphs and adults. One ABCH subfamily gene, CG9990, was presumed to be involved in mortality [81]. Silencing of $T .$ . castaneum TcABCH-9C reduced oviposition and pupal molting [17]. ABCH transporters are highest expressed in the head of $H .$ armigera when the larvae were ingested secondary metabolism [19].

Expansion of ABCG and ABCH subfamilies do exist in B. tabaci Q. Combined with their expressional profiles, we suspect that these ABCG and ABCH genes are involved in development-related metabolism and in the detoxification of xenobiotics including insecticides and secondary metabolites from host plant.

Within ABCA subfamily, Btabq003232.1 had the highest expressional level, followed by Btabq008198.1 and Btabq017043.1. This trend is consistent with RNA-seq analysis. Similarly, gene expression level of ABCB genes from high to low was Btabq028971.2, Btabq001304.1 and Btabq013065.1. ## Transcriptional response to imidacloprid treatments


A total of five genes were significantly up-regulated in imidacloprid-treated $B .$ . tabaci (Fig. 4, Additional file 11: Table S4). Btabq008198.1, an ABCA5 gene, can regulate accumulation of cholesterol [89]. The other four belong to ABCG subfamily, including Btabq003568.1 (ABCG1), Btabq020594.1 (ABCG1), Btabq007131.3 (ABCG4), and Btabq029281.1 (ABCG4).

The metabolic detoxification of xenobiotics likely involves a set of detoxification enzymes, which are general classified into three categories. Besides Phase I (e.g., cytochrome P450 monooxygenases) and Phase II (e.g., glutathione S-transferases), ABC transporters represent a major class of Phase III enzymes.

ABC transporters, especially those in the ABCG subfamily, facilitated $H .$ armigera defense against secondary metabolites such as nicotine and tomatine [19]. The high expression of ABCG11 in $H .$ armigera was the results of nicotine ingestion [19]. In addition, ABCG4 in An. stephensi was up-regulated in response to pyrethroid insecticide [18, 69]. The expression levels of three ABC transporters, ABCG20-3, ABCG23-5 and ABCH-B, were higher in fieldcollected resistant populations of C. lectularius [90]. Then knockdown of ABCG20-3 reduced deltamethrin resistance [90]. ABC transporters, particularly ABCG1 and ABCG4, may have important role in response to xenobiotics. Moreover, ABCG4 gene has the same intron/exon structure as ABCG1, suggesting that they arose by a relatively recent gene duplication event [66]. Overall, feeding on imidacloprid significantly affected the expression of ABC transporters especially those in ABCG subfamily, suggesting the potential involvement of these genes in the B. tabaci metabolic resistance.

Boron (B) is a micronutrient that is critical for crop growth and quality (Wimmer et al. 2020). It is required for the crosslinking of rhamnogalacturonan II, a pectic polysaccharide, during cell wall development (Funakawa and Miwa 2015). B defciency causes signifcant yield loss in many crop plants worldwide (BrdarJokanović  2020; Rerkasem et  al. 2020). It generally afects fower development and seed set. Low soil B is most prevalent in regions with high rainfall, including parts of China, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Brazil (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Shorrocks 1997). Excess soil B having detrimental efects on plants is also found in arid and semi-arid areas, including parts of India, the USA,

Pakistan, Malaysia, Chile, Peru, Hungary, Serbia, Italy, and the Middle East (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Nable et al. 1997). Excess B concentrations cause double-strand breaks of DNA (Sakamoto et al. 2011) and afect cellular metabolism, likely through binding to ribose moieties of ATP, NADH, and NADPH in cells (Reid 2014). Binding to ribose, both as a free sugar and as an RNA constituent, can inhibit cell division and development (Reid 2014). Symptoms of B toxicity include chlorosis and necrosis, which spread from leaf tips, leaving brown lesions at the margins. Reductions in biomass and seed yield are commonly observed under prolonged B toxicity (BrdarJokanović 2020; Landi et al 2019).

Plant roots take up B mainly in the form of boric acid $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ) }$ , which is a weak Lewis acid, with a pKa of 9.24 $[ \mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } + \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O = B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 4 } ^ { - } + \mathrm { H } ^ { + } ]$ (Power and Woods 1997). B is the only essential nutrient taken up in its uncharged form at physiological $\mathrm { p H }$ . Due to the theoretically high membrane permeability coeffcient of boric acid, it was once widely believed that B transport in plants was a mainly passive process. However, using the plasma membranes of giant internodal cells of the charophyte alga Chara corallina and plasma membrane vesicles isolated from squash roots, the membrane permeability of boric acid was determined to be higher than its theoretical value (Dordas et al. 2000; Stangoulis et al. 2001). Later, plants were found to facilitate the difusion of boric acid through major intrinsic protein (MIP) channels. Plants also use borate transporters (BORs) to export borate out of cells against a concentration gradient of soluble B (Yoshinari and Takano 2017). In this review, we describe the mechanisms of B transport, with an emphasis on membrane transport proteins and their regulation.


## B transport through MIPs


MIPs, including water channels (aquaporins), are universal to all kingdoms of life. Plant MIPs are channels for the bidirectional difusion of water and other small uncharged molecules (Bienert and Chaumont 2014). Based on sequence similarity and subcellular localization, MIPs in seed plants have been classifed into fve subclasses: plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs), tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs), small basic intrinsic proteins (SIPs), NIPs, and X intrinsic proteins (XIPs) (Maurel et al. 2016).

Plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs)

PIPs are plasma membrane-localized aquaporins that are mainly involved in water transport. They are further categorized into two subgroups, PIP1 and PIP2 (Bienert and Bienert 2017). PIP1 proteins possess an inherent capacity for water transport but require the help of PIP2s in plasma membrane trafcking in Arabidopsis and maize (Hachez et  al. 2013; Bienert et  al. 2018). Some PIP proteins have been shown to permeate boric acid in addition to water. In an early study, maize PIP1 expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes enhanced boric acid uptake into the cells (Dordas et  al. 2000). In a later study, the expression of barley (Hordeum vulgare) PIP1;3 and PIP1;4 in yeast led to increased B accumulation and enhanced sensitivity to high B (Fitzpatrick and Reid 2009). In rice roots, PIP expression was induced under high-B treatment (Kumar et  al. 2018). The expression of rice PIP1;3, PIP2;4, and PIP2;7 enhanced B infux and accumulation, and OsPIP2;6 enhanced B efux in yeast cells (Kumar et  al. 2014; Mosa et  al. 2016). Transgenic Arabidopsis plants overexpressing OsPIP1;3, OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OsPIP2;7 enhanced plant tolerance to excess B concentrations (Kumar et al. 2014; Mosa et al. 2016). Tracer experiments using $^ { 1 0 } \mathrm { { B } }$ -enriched boric acid at 2.5 or $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ showed that B uptake and efux from roots were both increased in transgenic plants. These results suggest the possible functions of PIPs in plant B tolerance of high B levels, although further studies using knockout plants are desired.

Tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs)

TIPs function in water transport across the vacuolar membrane, turgor regulation, osmo-sensing, cell growth, and vacuolar diferentiation (Maurel et  al. 2016). TIP isoforms have highly variable sequences within the aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity flter, to transport small molecules including urea, $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ glycerol, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ , and boric acid (Sudhakaran et  al. 2021). The heterologous expression of grape TIPs (VvTnTIP1;1, VvTnTIP2;2, and VvTnTIP4;1) and maize TIPs (ZmTIP1;1 and ZmTIP1;2) in yeast led to higher sensitivity to toxic B conditions (Barzana et al. 2014; Sabir et al. 2014). Overexpression of AtTIP5;1 in Arabidopsis promoted hypocotyl elongation and increased silique production under excess B (Pang et  al. 2010). Transcription profling of B-efcient citrus rootstock showed the upregulation of TIP2;2 and TIP4;1 under B limitation, with diferent temporal patterns (Zhou et  al. 2015). However, the physiological signifcance of B transport across the vacuolar membrane and its relationship to TIPs remain obscure.

Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs)

NIPs were frst reported to be localized in the symbiosome membrane of soybean (Glycine max L.) nodules, and to possess water and glycerol transport properties (Fortin et  al. 1987; Roberts and Routray. 2017). Phylogenetic analyses revealed that NIPs cluster together with aquaporin $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Z } }$ or glycerol uptake facilitator proteins in bacteria (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). This close relationship supports horizontal gene transfer from the bacterial AqpN–aquaporin group to plant NIPs. AqpN is predominantly positioned in arsenic resistance operons of various prokaryotic phyla to contribute to the arsenic detoxifcation machinery (Pommerrenig et al. 2020). Ar/R selectivity flter residues of bacterial AqpN are conserved in NIPs in algae, liverworts, moss, hornworts, and ferns. Bacterial AqpN, KnNIP6;1 in the flamentous terrestrial alga Klebsormidium nitens, and PpNIP5;1, NIP5;2, and NIP5;3 in the moss Physcomitrella patens are impermeable to water and silicic acid but permeable to arsenite and boric acid in Xenopus oocytes. These fndings along with mutational analysis results suggest that bacterial arsenic efux channels are converted into silicic acid and boric acid channels for the efcient uptake and translocation of these nutrients in seed plants (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). Plant NIPs are categorized as NIP-I (AtNIP1–4 s and others), NIP-II (AtNIP5–7 s and others), and NIPIII (OsNIP2;1 and others) based on similarities in their pore constriction regions, which consist of ar/R selectivity flters (Mitani-Ueno et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑Is in B transport


NIP-I proteins are aquaglyceroporins that mediate the transport of water and small neutral molecules such as glycerol (Roberts and Routray 2017). Although their physiological functions are unclear, Brassica napus NIP-Is (NIP2–4) transport B in Xenopus oocytes (Diehn et  al. 2019; see a later section on  Brassica napus for details).

Among NIP-Is in Arabidopsis, AtNIP4;1 is permeable to boric acid, ammonia, urea, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , as shown in Saccharomyces cerevisiae growth assays (Giorgio et  al. 2016). AtNIP4;1 and AtNIP4;2 are localized to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles of pollen tubes (Bock et  al. 2006; Giorgio et  al. 2016). In nip4;1 and nip4;2 mutants and amiRNA-mediated double knockdown plants, fertility was reduced, and pollen tube growth was afected under low B supply but normal under high B supply. These results suggest the roles of NIP4;1 and NIP4;2 in pollen tube growth via B transport.


## Roles of NIP‑IIs as major boric acid channels


The NIP-II protein AtNIP5;1 was the frst boric acid channel identifed to be involved in B uptake into roots, as the abundance of AtNIP5;1 mRNA increased after B starvation (Takano et al. 2006). In the plasma membrane of epidermal, cortical, and endodermal cells of roots, NIP5;1 showed polar localization towards the soil, increasing the efciency of boric acid uptake (Takano et  al. 2010; Wang et  al. 2017). B uptake and accumulation in roots and shoots of nip5;1  T-DNA insertion lines were signifcantly reduced when plants were grown under B limitation compared to wild-type (WT) plants. Due to defective B uptake, nip5;1 mutants showed severe root and shoot growth impairment under B limitation (Takano et al. 2006).

AtNIP6;1, the closest paralogue of AtNIP5;1, is involved in B xylem–phloem transfer for preferential translocation in shoots (Tanaka et  al. 2008). Unlike AtNIP5;1, the expression of AtNIP6;1 was confned to the phloem regions in nodes, including sieve elements (Tanaka et  al. 2008). The nip6;1 mutants showed inhibition of rosette leaf expansion and apical dominance under B limitation. Xenopus oocyte transport analyses indicated that NIP5;1 and NIP6;1 facilitate boric acid uptake into cells but difer in water transport activity (Takano et  al. 2006; Tanaka et al. 2008) with NIP5;1 but not NIP6;1, showing signifcant water permeability. The water-tight nature of NIP6;1 is likely important for phloem function.

AtNIP7;1 is a third member of the NIPII subclass; it plays a role in pollen development under B limitation and shows anther-specifc expression and localization in the plasma membrane of tapetum cells (Routray et  al. 2018). Loss-of-function nip7;1 mutants showed reproductive growth retardation characteristics including decreased fertility, petite siliques, and increased seed abortion compared to WT plants under B limitation (Routray et al. 2018). NIP-II subclass proteins such as AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 possess conserved ar/R pore-forming residues, including the transmembrane helix 2 (H2) region. Alanine at the H2 region is considered a characteristic residue for NIP-II boric acid channels including AtNIP7;1 (Wallace and Roberts 2004, 2005). However, AtNIP7;1 showed lower permeability to boric acid in Xenopus oocytes (Li et al. 2011). The substitution of tyrosine 81 in H2 with a cysteine residue (characteristic of AtNIP6;1) resulted in significantly higher boric acid transport than in WT NIP7;1 and NIP5;1 (Li et  al. 2011). Boric acid transport by AtNIP7;1 was proposed to be controlled by a channel gate function of the conserved tyrosine residue in the pore (Li et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑IIIs in the transport of silicic acid and boric acid


The NIP-III proteins in rice (OsLsi1/OsNIP2;1) and barley (HvLsi1/HvNIP2;1) are silicic acid channels, facilitating its uptake (Ma et  al. 2007; Chiba et  al. 2009). In Xenopus oocytes, OsNIP2;1 and HvNIP2;1 showed signifcant boric acid transport activity along with silicic acid, germanic acid, arsenite, and water (Schnurbusch et  al. 2010; Mitani-Ueno et  al. 2011). The physiological functions of silicic acid channels in B transport in rice and barley are discussed in a later section.


## X intrinsic proteins (XIPs)


XIPs were frst identifed during whole-genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens (Danielson and Johanson 2008). XIP proteins are present in a range of organisms, from unicellular eukaryotes to plants but absent in monocots and members of the Brassicaceae family (Abascal et  al. 2014), likely due to their functional complementation by other MIP subfamilies in these taxa. Based on amino acid residues of the ar/R flter, XIPs are predicted to form a wider and hydrophobic pore, similar to those in the NIP III group (Bienert et  al. 2011). Consistent with this prediction, the heterologous expression of Solanaceae XIP1;1s in oocytes $( \mathrm { S t X I P 1 } ; 1 \alpha$ and StXIP1;1β, SlXIP1;1α, and SlXIP1;1β) resulted in glycerol and urea transport. SlXIP1;1s expressed in yeast (S. cerevisiae) cells showed growth inhibition/sensitivity on media containing ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ or excess boric acid, indicating $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } /$ boric acid infux activity (Bienert et  al. 2011). Grape $V \nu X I P I$ and tobacco $N b \mathrm { X I P 1 ; 1 \alpha }$ also showed increased sensitivity to excess boric acid media in the yeasts S. cerevisiae and Pichia pastoris (Ampah-Korsah et al. 2016; Noronha et  al. 2016). The expression of NtXIP1;1 under the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter complemented a growth defect in an Arabidopsis nip5;1 knockout mutant under B limitation, demonstrating its function as a boric acid channel in planta (Bienert et  al. 2019). However, NtXIP1;1 overexpression in Nico‑ tiana tabacum and Arabidopsis under the En2pPMA4 or 35S CaMV promoter, respectively, resulted in B defciency symptoms such as diminished shoot apical meristem, sterile fowers, and contracted leaves. This result was probably caused by heterogeneous B distribution, prompted by the ectopic expression of NtXIP1;1. Further investigation of the physiological functions of XIP-mediated B transport is required.


## B transport through BORs


Under B limitation, plants use BOR-type borate exporters for efcient translocation of B (Takano et al. 2012; Yoshinari and Takano 2017). Borate exporters are also involved in lowering B concentrations in tissues for excess B tolerance (Miwa et al. 2007). Similarly, in S. cerevisiae, Bor1p functions as a borate exporter for excess B tolerance (Nozawa et al. 2006; Takano et  al. 2007). BOR transporters appear to be able to pump B out against a concentration gradient. For example, WT yeast cells maintained $< 2 5 \%$ of the intracellular B compared to bor1 deletion mutant cells in medium containing $0 . 0 5 { - } 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ boric acid (Takano et al. 2007). Under these conditions, B concentrations in WT cells were estimated to be lower than in the treatment medium. Electrophysiological studies of Bot1, a BOR transporter in barley, in Xenopus oocytes and proteoliposomes showed electrogenic borate anion transport in a Nernstian manner (Nagarajan et al. 2016). The Km for borate was calculated to be $1 0 4 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ using patch-clamped proteoliposomes. Bot1 also transported chloride, phosphate, nitrate, and sulfate but with much lower afnity than borate. Therefore, it is most likely that BOR transporters are anion uniporters with high afnity with borate (Fig.  1). Boric acid taken up into cells via MIPs or passive diffusion is partly converted into borate anions in cytosol with higher pH, which are then exported by BORs dependent on the concentration gradient and negative membrane potential. In the acidic apoplasm, borate anions are converted back into boric acid, generating an uphill boric acid gradient across the plasma membrane.

The Arabidopsis genome encodes seven BORs (BOR1–7). In angiosperms, BORs are classifed into two separate clades (Wakuta et  al. 2015). It is likely that Clade I BORs (AtBOR1–3) and their homologs pH $( \sim 7 . 5 )$ .
