(2014) demonstrated that ABA restores root length in the latd mutant by reducing ROS accumulation levels and by increasing cell length demonstrating an important role of MtRbohC (encoding a NADPH oxidase) as a negative regulator of root elongation. Zhang et al. (2014) propose that one hypothesis to explain this finding could be that MtNPF1.7 and ABA act in parallel to regulate ROS levels and root elongation (Fig. 4).

Nitrate perceived by a NPF transporter and nitrate impact on root architecture have been studied in M. truncatula. In this species, nitrate has an inhibitory effect on primary root growth at low and high concentrations in two different ecotypes, A17 and R108 (Yendrek et al. 2010; More\`re-Le Paven et al. 2011; Pellizzaro et al. 2014). A quantitative genetic approach allowed us to identify a major QTL involved in the control of M. truncatula radicle elongation in post-germination phase in both N-free medium and medium supplied with $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. The MtNPF6.8 gene, which coincided with the peak of the QTL, appeared to be a significant candidate involved in the control of primary root growth and nitrate-sensing (More\`re-Le Paven et al. 2011). Further experiments using npf6.8 mutants indicated that MtNPF6.8 has the hallmarks of a nitrate sensor (Fig. 4), which can regulate primary root growth via control of primary root cell elongation (Pellizzaro et al. 2014). The fact that MtNPF6.8 expression was stimulated by ABA, which also restored the inhibitory effect of nitrate on primary root growth in npf6.8 mutants, allowed us to hypothesize that ABA acts downstream MtNPF6.8 in this nitrate-signaling pathway. MtNPF6.8 was also demonstrated to be an ABA facilitator/transporter when expressed in Xenopus oocytes, confirming the ability of a single protein to transport both nitrate and ABA as previously shown for the AtNPF4.6 transporter of A. thaliana (Huang et al. 1999; Kanno et al. 2012). However, no direct link between a nitrate signal mediated by MtNPF6.8 acting on the primary root growth and ABA transport has been demonstrated.

In summary, in M. truncatula, two nitrate transporters, MtNPF1.7 and MtNPF6.8, are implicated in primary root growth by regulating root cell length, both in connection with ABA signaling. As noted by Harris (2015), it is surprising that $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ABA rescues the wild type phenotype either by increasing (for latd mutants) or decreasing (for nitrate-treated npf6.8 mutants) root length, suggesting contradictory results (Fig. 4). However, the genotypes used in both cases were different. It is also important to note that studies on MtNPF6.8 concern nitrate effect on primary root length, since MtNPF6.8 was shown to function as a nitrate sensor. The role of MtNPF1.7 in nitrate sensing is still unknown. Finally, whether MtNPF6.8 and MtNPF1.7 contribute to the same signaling pathway in root growth control is still to be unravelled.


## Nitrate transporters and their possible roles in rhizobial symbiosis


In legumes, it has been determined that nitrate is involved in the regulation of nodulation (Heath et al. 2010; Saito et al. 2014). Nitrate transporters are thus likely to have important roles to play during symbiosis establishment. Indeed, in a recent study, Damiani et al. (2016) analysed the root hair transcriptome from roots of control M. truncatula or following treatment with nod-factors (NF). NF are signaling molecules produced by rhizobia, inducing many of the plant responses during the early stages of plant-bacteria interaction. The authors paid particular attention to proteins likely to play a role in nutrient ion uptake. Medtr5g012290 (also named MtNPF6.7; Le´ran et al. 2014), a homolog of AtNPF6.3, was the most highly expressed NPF member in M. truncatula root hairs, while MtNPF1.7 expression was 6 times lower than that of MtNPF6.7 and MtNPF6.8 was not expressed. Upon NF treatment, the expression of MtNPF6.7 was up-regulated (Damiani et al. 2016). In the NRT2 family, MtNRT2.1 and MtNRT2.2 are also expressed in root hairs and up-regulated upon NF treatment (Damiani et al. 2016). In the present study, the microarray data analysis showed that many M. truncatula NPF genes are expressed in nodules (Fig. 2). For some genes (NPF4.7, NPF3.2, NPF7.4, NPF5.4, NPF7.6, NPF3.3, NPF1.4, NPF5.11, NPF1.2 and NPF5.6), the expression in nodules (Fig. 2B) is higher than in other plant tissues (Fig. 2A), or during seed development (Fig. 2C). Furthermore in M. truncatula, MtNRT2s and MtNAR2s are expressed in mature nodules (Criscuolo et al. 2012; Pellizzaro et al. 2015). This expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in nodules raise the question of a possible role of the corresponding transporters in nitrate transport inside the nodule. However, direct involvement of nitrate transporters in the exchange of nutrients between roots and nodules has never been reported.

One might ask, what are the roles attributed to these transporters in nodules, if they are not involved in transporting nitrate? In M. truncatula, it has been shown that MtNPF1.7 is essential in the formation and maintenance of nodule meristems and in rhizobial invasion during nodulation (Veereshlingam et al. 2004; Harris and Dickstein 2010). Using different mutants of MtNPF1.7, Bagchi et al. (2012) proposed that the ability of MtNPF1.7 to transport nitrate is correlated with the abilities of mutants to form and maintain nodules. However, these same authors also proposed that MtNPF1.7 should have another unknown activity, besides nitrate transport, in nodule development and in root architecture. MtNPF1.7 may be important for nitrate redistribution within the plant or could transport nitrate that would be useful as a precursor for the synthesis of nitric oxide (NO), a potent signaling molecule shown to be an important regulatory player in the Rhizobium-legume symbiotic interaction (Hichri et al. 2015). Otherwise, since new nodule formation is partially dependent on the suppression of lateral root emergence, MtNPF1.7, which is expressed in both of these organs, could play a role in coordinating development of lateral roots and nodules (Harris and Dickstein 2010). Alternatively, the role of MtNPF1.7 in ABA signaling in root meristem function, as shown by Liang et al. (2007), suggests that nodule formation, controlled by MtNPF1.7, may require ABA (Harris and Dickstein 2010). High expression of MtNRT2.1 and MtNRT2.3 in M. truncatula nodules indicates that nitrate transporters of the MtNRT2 family could also be involved in signaling pathways governing nodule formation, development and/or function (Pellizzaro et al. 2015). The involvement of nitrate transporters in the establishment of the symbiotic interaction has also been proposed after studying some members of the NPF and NRT2 families in another species of legume, L. japonicus (Criscuolo et al. 2012). These authors suggested the possible involvement of LjNRT2 and LjNPF in the high and/or low nitrate-signaling pathways affecting nodule formation, but also a possible role for a LjNPF, named CM0826.370, in mature nodules. All these data provide a basis for future experiments that will help to understand the possible roles of these nitrate transporters in the nodule.

NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (NRT1/PTR) homologous proteins are a group of membrane transport proteins present in all major living kingdoms [1–5]. Generally, 12 transmembrane domain (TM) proteins have a conserved structural arrangement connected by short peptide loops, including a large hydrophilic loop between the sixth and seventh TM [5]. In previous studies, homologous proteins were conventionally named according to their first identified substrates, such as NRT (a nitrate transporter), PTR (a peptide transporter), and others [1, 6]. Thereafter, additional substrates of NRT1/PTR homologs were characterized in plants; thus, they were recently and uniformly named as members of the NRT1/PTR family (NPF) [7].

Since AtNPF6.3/AtNRT1.1/CHL1 is characterized as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis [6, 8, 9], many of its homologs are cloned and functionally characterized in many plant species with multisubstrate transporting capacity. To date, the most well known roles of plant NPF genes (NPFs) include low- and/or high-affinity nitrate transportation. For example, Arabidopsis AtNPF1.1/NRT1.11 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.12 proteins are low-affinity nitrate transporters involved in redistributing nitrate into developing leaves [10], while Zea mays (maize) ZmNPF6.6 is a high-affinity nitrate transporter that can rapidly respond to exogenous nitrate supply [11]. Meanwhile, NPF proteins (NPFs) also behave as nitrite transporters, e.g., Arabidopsis AtNPF3.1/Nitr and Vitis vinifera VvNPF3.2 [12]. Additionally, NPFs are key transporters for many other substrates, especially hormones and peptides. For example, AtNPF8.1/PTR1 [13, 14], AtNPF8.2/ PTR5 [14], and AtNPF8.3/PTR2 [15, 16] are di−/tri-peptide transporters that can mediate the process of flowering, as well as seed and root development; AtNPF4.6/ AIT1 transports abscisic acid (ABA) to regulate stomatal aperture [17, 18]; and AtNPF6.3 represses lateral root growth during low nitrate availability by promoting basipetal auxin (IAA) transport [19]. Moreover, members of NPF have been demonstrated to transport secondary metabolites; AtNPF2.10/GTR1 and AtNPF2.11/GTR2 are key transporters for glucosinolate (GLS) [20]. Additionally, a few NPFs display chloride or potassium transport activity: AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5 mediate chloride efflux activity [21, 22], while AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 regulates pH-dependent $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux activity [23].

Brassica napus is a significant source of human-edible vegetable oil and animal protein feed; thus, it is an essential oil crop, extensively cultivated in Asia, North America, and Europe. Given essential roles in plant nitrate, di−/tripeptide, hormone, potassium, chloride, and secondary metabolite transports, NPFs have been systematically identified and analyzed in many species, including Arabidopsis [20], Oryza sativa (rice) [24], Triticum aestivum (wheat) [25], and Malus domestica (apple) [26] at the genome-wide level. Identifying and analyzing this gene family in the B. napus genome will provide a solid foundation for exploring its potential roles in transporting nitrate, hormones, and GLS, among others.

This study identified NPFs in the B. napus genome, accompanied by comprehensive analysis of their gene and protein structural features, chromosomal location, classification, promoter regulation network, and genomic duplication mechanism. Further, we performed systematic expression profile analysis of this gene family in diverse tissues across different developmental stages in Arabidopsis (79 tissues) and $B$ . napus (50 tissues). Additionally, expression patterns of NPF gene family in $B$ napus under five exogenous hormone inductions (IAA, auxin; ABA, abscisic acid; $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 } ,$ , gibberellic acid; 6-BA, cytokinin; and ACC, ethylene) were assessed, based on the RNA-Seq dataset. Moreover, expression patterns of 12 candidate NPFs of the NPF2–1 subfamily in one high- and one low-GLS B. napus variety, as well as their expression profiles under hormone induction, were assessed using qRT-PCR. Our study provides an abundant gene resource for further functional analysis of NPFs in B. napus.

The plant NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (NRT1/PTR FAMILY or NPF) encodes membrane proteins involved in various substrates: nitrate, nitrite, amino acids, glucosinolates, peptide, and hormone transport. All these transporters display 12 predicted transmembrane domains. Phylogenetic analysis divides the NPF family into eight clades (Le´ran et al. 2014). The different subfamilies have various substrate specificities, and some members are able to transport more than one substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, or peptides/amino acids. The first plant member identified was the plant transceptor NPF6.3 (NRT1.1/CHL1), able to transport nitrate in low- and high-affinity transport systems (LATS and HATS, respectively) and to sense nitrate (Bouguyon et al. 2015). In addition, NPF6.3 is also able to transport IAA but in competition with nitrate uptake, leading to a role in root architecture development (Krouk et al. 2010). Several other members are involved in lowaffinity nitrate transport, allowing nitrate uptake or root nitrate efflux and long-distance transport in different plant organs (for review, see Krapp et al. 2014).

The smallest subfamily of NPF contains the cucumber CsNPF3.2, the first plant nitrite transporter described, which is localized at the chloroplast inner membrane (Sugiura et al. 2007). Using transient expression, the Arabidopsis orthologue, AtNPF3.1, has been shown to be located at the plasma membrane (Pike et al. 2014), offering a new perspective regarding its function. Electrophysiology measurements of heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocyte characterized the NPF3 proteins of Arabidopsis and Grapevine as a low-affinity nitrate/nitrite transporter (Pike et al. 2014). A modified yeast-two hybrid (Y2H) system with hormone receptor complexes allowed testing the hormone uptake capacity of almost all the NPF family members (Kanno et al. 2012; Chiba et al. 2015). Using this method, NPF3.1 has been shown to transport in yeast different active forms of gibberellins (GAs) $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ (Chiba et al. 2015). Very recently, expression of NPF3.1 in Xenopus oocytes revealed its capacity to transport $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ as well (Tal et al. 2016). In the same study, the use of fluorescently labeled GAs (GA-FI) proved that AtNPF3.1 in responsible for GAs transport in planta as mutants is not able to take up this hormone, while overexpressors accumulate GA-FI in their roots (Tal et al. 2016). Previously, exogenous application of GA-FI has demonstrated that an active GA transport mechanism does exist in planta, since an accumulation of labeled GAs has been observed in elongating endodermal cells (Shani et al. 2013). Thus, this cell type seems to be a target of the bioactive GAs, although they are mainly synthesized in the meristematic and non-meristematic zones (Mitchum et al.

2006). Other numerous examples illustrate the occurrence of GA biosynthesis pathways and GA-regulated events in separated tissues (Hedden and Thomas 2012). In germinating seeds, in situ hybridization analyses demonstrated that the GA-responsive genes are not restricted to the site of active GA biosynthesis (Ogawa et al. 2003). In developing flowers, GA synthesis occurs in stamens, while GAs are required for petals growth (Plackett et al. 2011). All these results indirectly reveal the presence of GA transport mechanisms in plants.

GA hormones are diterpenoids and more than 100 GAs have been identified in plants. $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ , and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 7 }$ are known to be biologically active in plants involved in the regulation of photomorphogenesis, the other forms being precursors or products of catabolism (Yamaguchi 2008). The bioactive forms bind the GID1 receptor to trigger the degradation of DELLA through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (Feng et al. 2008). DELLA proteins repress the cell expansion, whereas GAs promote their development. This antagonist effect has been proved for root growth, leaf expansion, and floral development. GAs are involved in the elongation of hypocotyls in the light and in the dark by influencing cell elongation (de Lucas et al. 2008; Feng et al. 2008). In seeds, light and cold stimulate the GA biosynthesis, leading to the seed germination and counteracting ABA effect (Yamauchi et al. 2004; Oh et al. 2006). In Arabidopsis, nitrate has been described in the control of seed dormancy through the regulation of CYP707A2 expression, a gene involved in the ABA catabolism (Matakiadis et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010), and in hedge, mustard nitrate can also promote the expression of GA3OX2, a gene involved in the production of active GA forms (Carrillo-Barral et al. 2014). Thus, GAs are important molecules acting to promote seed germination and cell elongation particularly in hypocotyl elongation. The aim of this investigation is to understand whether NPF3.1 is involved in these processes through its capacity to transport GAs and nitrate. The capacity of numerous NPF to transport various hormones (Chiba et al. 2015) underlines a redundancy in functioning and raises the question of the substrate specificity. Therefore, to decipher the in planta function of NPF3.1 and its substrate specificity, we analyzed its expression pattern and we characterized two mutant lines at different developmental stages. Then, given these different traits, we discuss the potential role of NPF3.1 within the plant.

Plant NPF (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER FAMILY) proteins display sequence homology with the proton-coupled oligopeptide transporter (POT) family of peptide transporters, belong to the large peptide transporter (PTR) family [1] and are involved in dietary nitrogen absorption in the form of di- and tripeptides [2,3]. In plants, NPF members are initially characterized as nitrate or peptide transporters. AtNPF6.3, known as AtNRT1.1, is the first plant member discovered as a nitrate transporter in Arabidopsis [4], and the crystal structure of AtNPF6.3 recently determined showed the similarity with PTRs in the bacterial [5,6]. Subsequently, some NPF members are identified in different plants and demonstrated that they behave as dipeptide transporters [7,8]. So, nitrate/peptide transport function is believed to be a specific feature of this family in plants over a period of time. However, in recent years, several studies demonstrated that some NPF members could transport an even wider range of substrates, including nitrite, chloride, auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs), and gibberellins (GAs) and glucosinolates [9–12]. Additionally, some of the NPF members are even able to transport more than one different substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, peptides/amino acids, or GA/JA.

After identifying the first nitrate transporter NPF6.3/NRT1.1, Tsay et al. [4,8] subsequently characterized more than half of the NPF nitrate transporters. So far, more than

21 NPF members have been demonstrated to be able to transport nitrate in Arabidopsis, many of which are able to transport other substrates, such as ABA, GA, JA and glucosinolates [8,13]. Screening 45 out of 53 AtNPF members using a modified yeast two-hybrid system with ABA, GA and JA-Ile specific receptor complexes, Chiba et al. [14] confirmed that nine NPF members had an ABA transport function, $1 8 ~ N P F$ members were able to transport GA and 13 NPF members were able to transport the bioactive JA/JA-Ile. NRT1.1/NPF6.3 was confirmed to be able to transport IAA and 2,4-D [15,16]. In addition, PTR3/NPF5.2, PTR1/NPF8.1, PTR5/NPF8.2 and PTR2/NTR1/NPF8.3 were identified as dipeptide and tripeptide transporters using complementation of yeast strains deficient for peptide uptake [17,18].

Based on the phylogenetic relationship, NPF members were divided into eight subfamilies (from NPF1 to NPF8) [1]. In the NPF1 subfamily, MtNPF1.7, from Medicago truncatula, has been characterized to be involved in nodulation and root architecture and behaves as a high-affinity nitrate transporter [19–21]. NPF1.1 and NPF1.2, from Arabidopsis, are confirmed to be important for redistributing xylem-borne nitrate to enhance plant growth [22]. The NPF2 subfamily contains nitrate, phytohormone and glucosinolates transporters, and NPF2 members show a wide range of tissue and developmental specificity in Arabidopsis. AtNPF2.3, as a root stele transporter, contributes to nitrate translocation to shoots under salt stress [23], and the low-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF2.12 is responsible for nitrate-dependent early embryo development [24]. Besides, five AtNPF members that are capable of transporting glucosinolates belong to the NPF2 subfamily [11]. AtNPF3.1 is the only member of the NPF3 subfamily in Arabidopsis and plays the role of nitrite transport [25]. It has been demonstrated that ABA could be transported by NPF4 subfamily members [10], and some members of the NPF4 subfamily are able to transport GA, such as NPF4.1 and NPF4.2. NPF5 is the largest NPF subfamily and contains numerous members involved in nitrate, ABA, GA, JA and di-peptides transport [14,26,27]. In the NPF6 subfamily, most of the members have been demonstrated to be nitrate transporters, including the first identified NPF member AtNPF6.3 [4,28–30]. At least two different substrates were able to be transported by NPF7 subfamily members based on three well functionally characterized proteins: AtNPF7.2/NTR1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NTR1.5 for nitrate transport [31,32], as well as OsNPF7.3 for dipeptide transport [33]. Three Arabidopsis NPF8 subfamily members, AtNPF8.1/PTR1, AtNPF8.2/PTR5 and AtNPF8.3/PTR2, have been proved to be dipeptide transporters, while AtNPF8.1 and AtNPF8.2 are able to transport JA-Ile simultaneously [34,35]. It is noteworthy that 38 and 17 NPF genes have been characterized at the functional level in Arabidopsis and rice, respectively, and more than half of them function on nitrate transport and are distributed on eight NPF subfamilies, and play important roles in nitrate absorption, translocation and utilization [13,31,36,37]. Generally, NPF transporters with a very broad substrate specificity have an important function in plant growth and development, and genome-wide identification has been implemented in poplar [38], alfalfa [36], apple [39] and wheat [13], but a few systematic analyses have been conducted for NPF genes in Brassica species.

B. napus, an allotetraploid evolved from the hybridization between two diploid progenitors (Brassica rapa and Brassica oleracea), is an important oil crop in the world. Compared with Arabidopsis, B. napus has experienced a whole-genome triplication, which occurred between 7.9 and 14.6 million years ago [40], and a hybridization event via the natural crossing of B. rapa and B. oleracea (both of which diverged from a common ancestor $\mathrm { { \sim } \backslash n 4 }$ million years ago) about 7500 years ago [41–43]. Recently, the genomes of ‘Darmor-bzh’ and ‘ZS11’ have been successfully sequenced and assembled [42,44], and Pan-genomes have been constructed based on next-generation sequencing technologies for B. napus, which facilitate systematically excavating NPF genes in rapeseed. Although the NPF genes have been identified in rapeseed [45,46], functional NPF proteins and genes should be excavated, and their expression characteristics and role in the tissues that play an important role in rapeseed oil yield should be further analyzed. In this study, 169NPF genes were excavated in the B. napus, and the expression profiles of BnaNPF genes in diverse tissues, as well as time-serial expression changes in leaf, silique wall and seed, were determined; meanwhile, expression changes induced by vernalization at different development stages and response to nitrate deficiency were analyzed. These results will provide useful information for further investigation of the biological function of BnaNPF genes for growth and development in B. napus.

Nitrogen plays a crucial role in plant life, influencing growth, development, and participating in various signaling pathways [1]. Early-diverging land plants primarily relied on atmospheric deposition and symbiotic nitrogen fixation for nitrogen acquisition. However, with the emergence of roots during the Devonian period, plants gradually evolved root-mediated nitrogen uptake [2, 3]. In seed plants, the well-developed root system has become the primary means of obtaining nitrogen. Thus, the establishment of efficient nitrogen uptake and transport systems in roots has been essential for plant adaptation to terrestrial environments. Nitrate is the principal form of nitrogen absorbed by most plant roots. During the evolutionary transition from algae to land plants, the nitrate transporter gene family, NPF (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER FAMILY), underwent rapid expansion and functional divergence [4]. Concurrently, the continuous recruitment of multilevel regulatory components enhanced the complexity of nitrate signaling regulatory network (NSRN), ultimately evolving an efficient and sophisticated nitrate transport system in plant roots [5–7].

NPF6.3, also known as NRT1.1 and CHL1 (CHLORATE RESISTANT 1), is a member of the NPF family and functions as a dual-affinity transceptor that initiates and dominates the entire NSRN [8–11]. This network involves numerous transcription factors, protein kinases, and other regulatory factors. In Arabidopsis thaliana, CIPK23 and CBL1/9 regulate the phosphorylation status of NPF6.3(NRT1.1/CHL1), thereby modulating its nitrate affinity [10]. Upon nitrate perception, NPF6.3(NRT1.1/ CHL1) triggers the accumulation of $\mathrm { I P } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { { C a } ^ { 2 + } }$ . The calcium signal is subsequently decoded by CPK10/30/32, which phosphorylates the master regulator NLP7, facilitating its nuclear retention and activation of nitrate responsive genes [12]. NLP7 further interacts with TCP20 [13, 14], and NRG2 [15] to coordinately regulate the expression of more downstream nitrate responsive genes. In addition to NPF6.3(NRT1.1/CHL1), NLP7 and NRT2.1 has been proposed as a nitrate sensor contributing to NSRN [16–20]. Furthermore, myriad TFs have been identified as key regulators of nitrate responsive gene expression or signal integration, including: bZIP1 [21], TGA1/4 [17, 22, 23], SPL9 [24], FIP1 [25], CPSF30 [25], LBD37/38/39 [26], HHO1/HRS1 [27, 28], ANR1 [29, 30], BT1/2 [31, 32], NAC4 [33, 34], AFB3 [33], and ARF8 [35], etc. (Fig. 1).

Previous studies have demonstrated that NPF orthologs were present in chlorophytes and streptophytes with limited copy numbers, while their abundance markedly increased in land plants through multiple lineage-specific duplication events [36, 37]. Due to the complexity of terrestrial environments, NPFs have undergone neofunctionalization in substrate- or tissue-specificity, which benefits plants [4, 36, 38]. The NRT2 gene family existed throughout Archaeplastida, with the ancestral $\zeta$ whole-genome duplication (WGD) event in seed plants giving rise to two clades [37]. In A. thaliana, members of these two clades subsequently differentiated into inducible and constitutive high-affinity transport systems (iHATS and cHATS), exhibiting distinct expression patterns [39, 40]. CPK orthologs are widely distributed among plants and have undergone extensive duplications. An ancestral duplication event in charophytes led to the formation of five clades in streptophytes, and subsequent WGDs in seed plant ancestors likely further increased copy numbers within these clades [37]. The orthologs of TCP20 and NRG2, which originated in charophytes, have also undergone expansion and functional divergence in land plants [37]. While the origins and evolutionary histories of several gene families involved in nitrogen transport and signal transduction have been extensively studied, it remains unclear whether these genes have acquired the conserved functions characteristic of model plants, especially A. thaliana, in algae or early-diverging land plants, and when they were integrated into NSRN.

Here, we systematically identified orthologs of 20 key components of the NPF6.3(NRT1.1/CHL1)-centered NSRN in plant roots and elucidated their evolutionary histories across land plant evolution. Our analyses demonstrated that the three major evolutionary innovations of six core components have promoted the gradual optimization of NSRN: (1) the emergence of putatively functional clade, (2) the acquisition of root-preferential expression patterns, and (3) the establishment of proteinprotein interactions. Ultimately, we speculate a relatively complete NSRN was established at the ancestral node of seed plants. Additionally, the ongoing recruitment of non-core components might further reshape the complexity of NSRN. These findings provide new insights into the molecular adaptations underlying nitrogen utilization since plant terrestrialization.

Since nitrate transporters are mainly responsible for the uptake and transport of nitrate and limited nitrogen/nitrate condition occurs frequently, there are quite a few nitrate transporters coping with this abiotic stress.


## 2.1. NRT2 Family in Response to Nitrate/Nitrogen Limitation


The NRT2 proteins belong to high-affinity transport system which is responsible for transporting nitrate at low concentration and plays an important role in conditions with limited nitrogen [6,16]. To date, four of seven Arabidopsis NRT2 transporters have been shown to be involved in plant low nitrogen adaptation. Those four transporters are AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.4, and AtNRT2.5, with different spatio-temporal distributions in root [8,9,15,16,44]. AtNRT2.1 is derepressed by nitrogen deprivation and is mainly localized in cortex cells of the root’s mature regions [8,9]. Under low nitrogen conditions, AtNRT2.1 mediates apoplastic nitrate absorption, IHATS (nitrate-inducible high-affinity transport system), and root system architecture [10–13]. It has been demonstrated that AtNRT2.1 was the major contributor to IHATS, because phenotypes related to IHATS were preferentially observed in atnrt2.1 mutants and could be partially compensated by AtNRT2.2 [14]. Different from AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 were responsible for nitrate uptake from soil into plants, and were induced in epidermal cells of young roots by long-term nitrogen starvation [8,15,16]. Using nrt2.1 nrt2.2 double mutants and nrt2.1 nrt2.2 nrt2.4 triple mutants, further comparative analyses showed that AtNRT2.4 contributed essentially to plant biomass production under low nitrate supply [15]. Moreover, researchers found that AtNRT2.5 was a key component along with AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, and AtNRT2.4 for adult plants to cope with severe nitrogen starvation [8,16].

In rice, it has been shown that the partner protein OsNAR2.1 (nitrate assimilation related protein) was needed for the three plasma membrane localized nitrate transporters OsNRT2.1, OsNRT2.2, and OsNRT2.3a, and they worked together to absorb nitrate [18,19]. As the osnar2.1 RNAi knockdown plants with synchronously suppressed expression of OsNRT2.1, OsNRT2.2, and OsNRT2.3a showed reduced plant growth and lower total nitrogen concentration under either low or high nitrate treatments compared with wide type plants [18], it was indicative that those three proteins were likely to be involved in ensuring optimal plant growth under various nitrate levels.


## 2.2. NPF Transporters in Response to Nitrate/Nitrogen Limitation


Besides the NRT2 proteins mentioned above, several NPF proteins also participate in low nutrient response. NRT2 proteins are exclusively responsible for nitrate uptake, while NPF proteins are involved in more transport processes such as nitrate distribution between different tissues.

The low-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF7.3/AtNRT1.5 is localized on plasma membrane of root pericycle cells surrounding the xylem, and functions in xylem nitrate loading [45]. AtNPF7.3/AtNRT1.5 is required for suppressing the nitrate deficiency-induced leaf senescence, most likely by promoting foliar potassium accumulation [26,27]. Moreover, AtNPF7.3/AtNRT1.5 was proved to play an essential role in repressing leaf chlorosis and preventing growth retardation when external potassium was limited [28]. AtNPF2.12/AtNRT1.6 is expressed in the vascular tissue of the silique and funiculus, and functions to deliver nitrate to the developing embryo. Disruption of AtNPF2.12/AtNRT1.6 reduces nitrate accumulation in seeds, and further leads to higher seed abortion rate. However, nitrate starvation treatment decreased the seed abortion rate of npf2.12 mutants, indicating that the requirement of nitrate during early embryo development could be alleviated when external nitrogen was limited [31]. Furthermore, the study on AtNPF2.13/AtNRT1.7 revealed the details of nitrate remobilization from source leaves and elucidated its role in plant growth under nitrogen starvation conditions [32]. Expression of AtNPF2.13/AtNRT1.7 was detected in the phloem of the leaf minor vein and was increased as leaves aged. However, AtNPF2.13/AtNRT1.7 hardly affects plant growth under nutrient sufficient conditions. Long-term nitrogen starvation retarded growth of npf2.13 mutant plants, and one of the mutant lines even showed early senescence in older leaves when nitrogen was removed at reproductive stage [32]. Further study found that the AtNPF2.13/AtNRT1.7 modulating low nitrogen adaptation was negatively regulated by the protein ubiquitination pathway, which was mediated by NLA (Nitrogen Limitation Adaptation) [46].

OsNPF6.3/OsNRT1.1A, OsNPF6.5/OsNRT1.1B, OsNPF2.4, and OsNPF8.9b have been demonstrated to contribute to plant growth, yield production, and/or NUE under diverse nitrogen conditions, but with different underlying mechanisms. OsNPF6.3/OsNRT1.1A is a tonoplast-localized protein and was reported as a target to simultaneously manipulate rice yield and maturation. OsNPF6.3-overexpressing plants exhibited significantly improved growth, yield, and NUE under both low and high nitrogen conditions, mainly because of the upregulated expression of nitrogen utilization-related genes [38]. OsNPF6.5/OsNRT1.1B was reported to transport nitrate under both low and high nitrate concentrations and had an essential single-nucleotide polymorphism between indica and japonica rice. The OsNPF6.5/OsNRT1.1B-indica variation was shown to improve grain yield and NUE, probably by enhancing nitrate uptake and translocation and upregulation of nitrate response, especially when under relatively low nitrate conditions [39]. OsNPF2.4 is a low-affinity nitrate transporter involved in acquisition and long-distance transport of nitrate, including nitrate redistribution from old leaves to nitrogen-starved roots and young leaves. Dry weight of npf2.4 mutants was always lower compared with the wide type plants under either normal or nitrate deficiency conditions [40]. $O s N P F 8 . 9 b$ (refer to OsNRT1.1b to avoid confusion [7]) is one of the splicing forms of OsNPF8.9, encoding a protein with six transmembrane domains, but it showed nitrate transport activity when expressed in oocytes. Overexpression of $O s N P F 8 . 9 b$ could increase nitrogen accumulation in plants and improve rice growth under various nitrogen conditions, including low nitrogen supply [41]. When overexpressed, OsNPF8.20/OsPTR9 improved grain yield under the condition of no fertilizer or low ammonium supply [42], but the exactly underlying mechanism is still an open question.

Low nitrogen (N) use efficiency (NUE) is a serious problem impeding the sustainable development of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) production worldwide (Zhang et al. 2015). Breeding wheat cultivars with a high N uptake ability is a promising option for improving N fertilizer use efficiency; however, breeding for improved N uptake cannot be achieved without a full understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying N uptake by wheat plants. Nitrate is the major N source in aerobic soils (Fan et al. 2017a). There are generally two nitrate transport systems in higher plants: the lowaffinity transport system (LATS) and the high-affinity transport system (HATS). LATS is the main nitrate uptake system at ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ concentrations ranging from 0.25 to $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ and HATS exhibits a Km of $1 0 \sim 2 5 0$ $\mu \mathrm { M }$ and is encoded by NRT2 family genes (Okamoto et al. 2003). LATS is encoded by NPF (nitrate transporter 1 and peptide transporter family) genes belonging to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS). Some NPF genes encode peptide transporters (Leran et al. 2014), but may not be able to transport nitrate due to the absence of the specific binding sites for nitrate in some of these proteins. In addition to nitrate and peptides, NPF genes were also involved in the transport of nitrite, chloride, glucosinolates, auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs), and gibberellins (GAs). Some of these transporters are even capable of transporting more than one substrate (Corratge-Faillie and Lacombe 2017). In Arabidopsis thaliana, the AtNRT1.1 (AtNPF6.3) protein can act as a dual-affinity transporter when its affinity is altered by phosphorylation (Liu and Tsay 2003); in this way, AtNPF6.3 acts as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). By contrast, NRT2 proteins are more specific to nitrate. Moreover, most NRT2 proteins require another protein, NAR2 (nitrate assimilation-related protein, also known as NRT3), to transport nitrate, with a few exceptions like AtNRT2.7 (Kotur et al. 2012), OsNRT2.3b (Liu et al. 2014) and OsNRT2.4 (Wei et al. 2018). In recent years, an increasing number of studies have shown that overexpression of NPF and NRT2 genes can significantly improve the yield, shoot biomass or NUE of crops (Fan et al. 2017b; Hu et al. 2015), suggesting great application potential of NPF and NRT2 genes during N-efficient wheat cultivar breeding.

NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat have been largely uncharacterized compared with those in model plants due to the large and complex genome of wheat and the difficulty of its genetic transformation (Paux et al. 2008). Some studies have investigated the responses of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Buchner and Hawkesford 2014), drought stress (Duan et al. 2016) and fungal colonization (Tian et al. 2017). TaNRT2.1, which was mainly expressed in the roots of wheat, can be induced by N starvation and ABA (Guo et al. 2014; Xiong et al. 2019; Yin et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2020), and may play a major role in post-flowering ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake (Taulemesse et al. 2015). Recently, the overexpression of TaNRT2.5, which was mainly expressed in the tonoplasts of grain cells, increased grain nitrate uptake, seed vigor and yield (Li et al. 2020). Nevertheless, function of most of the wheat NPF and NRT2 genes have mainly been predicted based on DNA or protein sequence homology. Although basic phylogenetic analyses of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat have been conducted (Bajgain et al. 2018), the analyses were based on an old wheat genome version and some key information such as gene collinearity, detailed location on chromosomes, nitrate transport characteristics and evolution is still largely unknown.

It has been reported that the NAC transcription factor $T a N A C 2  – 5 \ A$ can positively regulate the expression of multiple NPF or NRT2 genes in wheat by directly binding their promoter regions (He et al. 2015). In rice, the NAC transcription factor OsNAC42 binds and activates the promoter of an elite NPF gene OsNPF6.1, and the NAC42-NPF6.1 signaling cascade is a strategy for high NUE and yield breeding in rice (Tang et al. 2019). A MYB transcription factor (AtMYB59) has been shown to directly bind to the promoter of the AtNPF7.3 gene and enable the regulation of its expression in Arabidopsis (Du et al. 2019). Members of other transcription factor families such as Dof, MADS-box, WRKY, ZFP, RWP-RK and bZIP may also regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in plants (Kumar et al. 2018; Mu and Luo 2019; Vidal et al. 2020). The overexpression of some wheat transcription factors, such as TaZFP593;l(Chen et al. 2017), TabHLH1(Yang et al. 2016) and TaNBP1(Liu et al. 2018), in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) led to differences in the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in tobacco, suggesting that the genes in wheat may also be regulated by these transcription factors. Nevertheless, direct evidence of the roles of these transcription factors in regulating NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat is lacking. In addition, it is unknown whether other unrecognized transcription factors may also regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat.

Natural variations in NPF and NRT2 genes may greatly alter the N uptake ability of plants; for example, in rice, a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) (T/C) of $\mathit { O s N P F 6 . 5 }$ contributes to the divergence in nitrate use between indica and japonica subspecies (Hu et al. 2015). The first green revolution beginning in the mid20th century led to a great increase in the production of wheat grain due to the introduction of dwarf genes into wheat cultivars and the application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. The dwarf trait, biotic or abiotic stress resistance and high quality have become the main target traits in wheat cultivar breeding since the first green revolution. It has been reported that the N utilization efficiency of wheat did not change significantly from 1958 to 2007 but that $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake efficiency increased with the year of cultivar release (Sadras and Lawson 2013). The increase in N uptake efficiency may be due to the natural variation in NPF and NRT2 genes during the artificial selection of wheat cultivars in recent decades, which requires further investigation.

In the present study, we firstly identified putative NPF and NRT2 genes at the whole-wheat-genome level; and then verified the nitrate transport function of two NPF and one NRT2 genes via a heterologous expression system. We also investigated transcription factors that may regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat via weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA). More specially, we analyzed polymorphisms of NPF and NRT2 genes in a natural wheat population composed of 254 wheat accessions collected worldwide. We aimed to test the following hypotheses: (1) just like some other gene families in wheat, duplication events are ubiquitous in NPF and NRT2 gene families in the wheat genome; (2) unrecognized transcription factors regulating the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes exist in wheat; (3) wheat orthologues of the previously characterized NPF or NRT2 genes reported in other plant species have similar characteristics in nitrate transport; and (4) cultivar selection is the main driver of polymorphism accumulation in NPF and NRT2 genes.

Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plant growth and development, as it is a building block for proteins, nucleic acids, and other biomolecules [1]. Most plants take up nitrogen mainly in the form of nitrate $( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } )$ , which is the most abundant nitrogen source in soil [2]. Plants have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to adjust to diferent concentrations of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ acquisition, which is mainly carried out via three models: low-afnity transport system (LATS), high-afnity transport system (HATS), and dualafnity transport system (DATS) [3–5]. $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPases pump $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ across the plasma membrane under electrochemical potential gradients, which is then carried by NITRATE TRANSPORTERS (NRTs) to store in the vacuole or assimilate into amino acid in the cytoplasm.

Nitrate transporters are divided into four families, NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) (NPF), NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2 /

Nitrate-Nitrite Porter (NNP) (NRT2) [6], CHLORIDE CHANNEL (CLC) [7], and the SLOW ANION ASSOCIATED CHANNEL HOMOLOG (SLAC/SLAH) [8]. Te NPF and NRT2 families were involved in the primary nitrate reaction [9]. NPF is also known as SOLUTE CARRIER 15 (SLC15), PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PepT/PTR), or PROTON-COUPLED OLIGOPEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (POT) [10]. Te NPF family in plants is highly homologous in sequence but diverse in functions. Due to its diverse substrate selectivity, NPF can transport protons, peptides, and various nitrogenous organic solutes [11–14]. Léran [10] compared the phylogeny of the NPF family in 33 fully sequenced plant genomes and found that the original NRT1 family clustered into the NPF1-NPF7 subfamilies, while the PTR family grouped in the NPF8 subfamily. NRT2 is a two-component nitrate uptake system requiring the additional NITRATE ASSIMILATION-RELATED PROTEIN 2 (NAR2), also known as NRT3 [15]. NRT2 and NAR2 are closely clustered as nitrate-associated genes [16], forming functional units to maintain NRT2 plasma membrane targeting and protein stability [14]. However, not all NRT2 require NAR2, such as AtNRT2.4 [17], OsNRT2.3b [18], and OsNRT2.4 [19]. Previous studies have shown that NPF is primarily responsible for LATS, while NRT2 is primarily responsible for HATS. Tey operate at nitrate concentrations above or below $1 \mathrm { m M }$ [20]. For example, AtNPF2.12/NRT1.9, which is involved in early embryonic development, is a low-afnity nitrate transporter [21]. However, NIP/LATD from Medicago truncatula, classifed as NPF1, was a nitrate transporter with high afnity [22]. AtNPF6.3/NRT1.1 has been proven to belong to dual-afnity nitrate transporters [6]. Moreover, the dual-afnity nitrate transporters could be switched by phosphorylation of the key residue Tr101 [23]. MtNPF6.8 [24] and OsNRT2.4 [19] have been confrmed to encode proteins in Xenopus laevis oocytes as dual-afnity nitrate transporters. Terefore, identifying NPF and NRT2 as LATS and HATS is complicated, and the function of each member needs further research and verifcation.

Browning is one of the major issues in woody plant regeneration in vitro, as more phenolic compounds may accumulate during lignin biosynthesis. Numerous studies have revealed a link between browning and nitrogen. Reduction of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ in the medium could inhibit browning during callus induction in Bacopa monnieri [25]. In Paeonia sufruticosa, callus browning was also well controlled when the basal salt changed from MS to $1 / 4 \times \mathrm { M S }$ [26]. Daigen et al. (2000) revealed that reducing the content of $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ) _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } }$ in the medium can signifcantly reduce the browning degree in rice [27]. Chopin et  al. found that the seed coat of NRT2.7 mutants was brown [28]. Cristóbal investigated the potential link between N and browning in sweet cherries after harvest. Te study found that the phenolic composition and the oxidative states of the cherries, which were infuenced by N treatment, could afect the fruit’s post-harvest shelf life [29].

Ginkgo is a gymnosperm species whose callus tends to brown within three months [30]. Te transgenic hairy roots were also susceptible to browning due to slow growth [31]. It is essential to prevent browning to develop a highly efcient regeneration and suspension production system in Ginkgo. We treated calluses with various concentrations of $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and found that browning was more severe in higher concentrations. Nitrogen is the primary regulator of this process, so we investigated the role of NRTs during nitrogen treatment. To better understand the relationship between NRTs and callus browning, we identifed the NRTs gene family in the Ginkgo genome and systematically analyzed the physicochemical properties, conserved domains, and conserved motifs of GbNRTs proteins. We also analyzed the gene structure, phylogenetic relationships between genes, replication patterns, election pressures, cis-acting elements(CREs), and transcription factor binding sites of the promoter fraction. Furthermore, we detected the expression of GbNRTs under diferent nitrate concentration treatments by RNA-seq and Quantitative Real-Time PCR (qRT-PCR) assay during calluses induction. Tis study may be the frst step in understanding the molecular mechanism of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and utilization in the process of Ginkgo tissue culture and identifying the gene family associated with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transport in Ginkgo biloba. In conclusion, understanding the role of NRTs during $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake and utilization in  vitro culture and identifying the genes associated with $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transport is crucial to prevent browning and develop a highly efcient regeneration and suspension production system in Ginkgo.

Nitrate transporters have been reported in Arabidopsis, rice, wheat, tomato and other species [10, 27–29]. However, only VvNPF3.2 was identified in grapevines, which functions as a low-affinity transporter for both nitrate and nitrite and plays a role in host nutrient distribution during powdery mildew infection [30]. In this study, we characterized another nitrate transporter, VvNPF6.5, as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter mainly expressed in roots and stems, and demonstrated that VvNPF6.5 is responsible for nitrate uptake and allocation in grapevines.

VvNPF6.5 belongs to the family of NRT1/PTR/NPF. In this family, only CHL1 and its homology proteins MtNRT1.3 and OsNRT1.1B behave as dual-affinity nitrate transporters, while other members are all characterized as low-affinity nitrate transporters [31, 32]. The high- and low-affinity nitrate uptake activities of VvNPF6.5 were assessed by analyzing $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ uptake activity of cRNA-injected Xenopus oocytes at $1 0 \mathrm { m M }$ and $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m M }$ (Fig. 3). Interestingly, VvNPF6.5 also functions as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter. Sequence alignment revealed that $\mathrm { R X X T ^ { 1 0 0 } }$ in VvNPF6.5 is identical to the phosphorylation site $\mathrm { R X X T ^ { 1 0 1 } }$ in CHL1, which is responsible for the shift between low- and high-affinity (Fig. 1). The regulatory mechanism allows plants to change the affinity of nitrate uptake rapidly, which might be critical when competing for limited nitrate [14]. However, the site is also found in other low affinity nitrate transporters, indicating there might be additional regulatory mechanisms.

The expression of VvNPF6.5 was induced by nitrate (Fig. 4b), similar to those nitrate transporter genes which regulate nitrate uptake, like CHL1, AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.1 [11]. The strong correlation between the transcript abundance of these nitrate transporter genes and nitrate uptake activities suggests that transcriptional regulation plays important role in modulating nitrate uptake activities [11]. In addition to its absorption properties, VvNPF6.5 was found to participate in nitrate longdistance transport because the expression level of VvNPF6.5 was relatively high in stems and the $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ content in shoots of overexpression lines was also increased after $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ feeding (Fig. 5a). It is of great significance to identify the transporter involved in nitrate longdistance transport because the process determines nitrate distribution and subsequent assimilation between different tissues and further influence the nutrient use efficiency [33].

Several nitrate transporters have been reported to contribute to nitrogen use efficiency. OsNRT1.1B is an important player in NUE improvement for crop breeding because its polymorphism could result in NUE difference [31]. Coordinate regulation of BnNRT1.5 and BnNRT1.8 could promote nitrate allocation to aerial parts and contribute to higher NUE in Brassica napus [24]. Increasing the expression of OsNRT2.1, especially under the control of OsNAR2.1 promoter, can improve the yield and NUE in rice [34]. In this study, VvNPF6.5 was proved to play role in regulating NUE in grapevines because transgenic plants showed higher NUE compared to wild type in Arabidopsis (Fig. 5c). These studies showed that nitrate transporters could improve NUE by regulating nitrate uptake or long-distance translocate, indicating that nitrate acquisition was very important and providing a new perspective for the study of NUE.

Nitrate functions as not only a nutrient but also a signaling molecule. Nitrate signaling participates in regulating many physiological processes like root development, shoot growth, ABA-independent stomatal opening, flowering time and seed dormancy [17, 35]. The primary nitrate response is the best known nitrate-induced response, in which the expression of several nitrate transporters and nitrate assimilatory enzymes is rapidly induced under nitrate treatment [36]. Time-course analysis of VvNPF6.5 expression showed that $V \nu N P F 6 . 5$ was rapidly and highly induced by nitrate (Fig. 4b), which was consistent with the primary nitrate response. Therefore, the effect of VvNPF6.5 on nitrate signaling was further detected. In VvNPF6.5 overexpression lines, the rapid nitrate-induced expression of the two known primary nitrate response genes, NIA1 and NiR, was enhanced (Fig. 6), suggesting that VvNPF6.5 might be involved in nitrate signaling. CHL1 was proved to function as a nitrate sensor for nitrate signaling in the primary nitrate response [16]. It has been speculated that such a function may not be restricted to CHL1 and may concern other NRT1/PTR/NPF proteins from different species [37]. VvNPF6.5 is an interesting candidate in grapevines, while further research is required to test whether VvNPF6.5 is also a nitrate sensor.

Given that the $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ content in roots and shoots was increased (Fig. 5a, b) and the primary nitrate response was enhanced when VvNPF6.5 was overexpressed (Fig. 6), it is a possibility that grapevines roots utilize a transporter responsible for nitrate uptake and translocate, such as VvNPF6.5, to monitor changes of nitrate concentrations in soil and in turn this could induce the expression of nitrate-related genes and then regulate nitrogen metabolism. Therefore, the results indicate that the higher NUE of overexpression lines might be achieved by regulating nitrate uptake, root-to-shoot nitrate long-distance transport and nitrate signaling.

Nitrogen (N) is a major component of amino acids, proteins, nucleic acid, chlorophyll and hormones [1]. It is a key macronutrient required for plant growth and development of watermelon. The availability of N affects plant architecture, flowering, fruit development, photosynthesis, and allocation of photosynthates in plants [2–4]. N is absorbed by the roots in the form of nitrate $\left( \mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } \right)$ and ammonium $\mathrm { ( N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } ) }$ through the nitrate and ammonium transporters. After uptake these ions are transported to the shoot. During the process of assimilation, ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ is converted to $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ through cytosolic nitrate reductase. Then, $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ is converted to glutamine, glutamate, or glutamate dehydrogenease. These synthesized $_ \mathrm { N }$ compounds serve as precursor for amino acids, proteins, and other N-containing metabolites that are utilized for plant growth and development [4, 5]. Understanding the plant response to nitrogen availability is crucial for sustainable agricultural development [6]. According to a report, under low $_ \mathrm { N }$ conditions plant growth (dry weight) and relative chlorophyll content are substantially reduced compared with optimum N supply [4]. N starvation also reduces leaf area and photosynthetic assimilation capacity leading to reduced plant growth, dry matter accumulation and yield [7, 8].

The absorption of nitrate from the external environment, and transportation and translocation among cells, tissues and organs requires transmembrane proteins. Four protein families are involved in nitrate transport that includes NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF), NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2 (NRT2), CHLORIDE CHANNEL (CLC) family, and SLOWELY ACTIVATING ANION CHANNEL. In Arabidopsis and rice 53 and 93 NPF genes has been found. Most of these genes display low nitrate affinities but a few have dual affinities [9]. Most of the NRT2 display high-affinity nitrate transport activity; Arabidopsis genome includes 7 NRT2 genes while rice genome has only 4 NRT2 genes. The nitrate transporters play a vital role in nitrate uptake, nitrate signaling, plant growth, lateral root formation, leaf development, stomatal regulation, bud formation, flowering, nitrogen storage, seed development, seed nitrate content, and seed dormancy [9]. The overexpression of nitrate transporters from NRT1 (NPF) and NRT2 families enhances the nitrogen use efficiency of plants. For example, the overexpression of rice OsNRT2.3b enhanced the nitrate and iron uptake and improved the yield under low and high $_ \mathrm { N }$ availability under field condition [10]. N containing fertilizers are applied to all important agronomic and horticultural crops to fulfill their requirement, however, only $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ of that fertilizers are utilized by the crops while rest of $_ \mathrm { N }$ is lost through leaching or volatilization and causes environmental pollution along with loss of resources [11]. This situation requires attention, and it becomes important to understand the underlying molecular regulatory mechanism in addition to morphological and physiological plants responses to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficient conditions. Watermelon is cultivated on a commercial scale across the world, China being the leading producer constitute $6 6 . 5 \%$ of the world watermelon production. According to National Bureau of Statistics of China, annual use of nitrogenous fertilizer exceeds 24 million tons [12]. A fair share of this nitrogenous fertilizer is utilized for watermelon production.

RNA-Seq is one of the next-generation high throughput sequencing technologies, and it is widely used for transcription profiling, because of low background noise, high sensitivity, reproducibility, dynamic range of expression, and base pair resolution [13]. This technique is utilized to study transcriptomic profiles of different plants under biotic and abiotic stress conditions such as heat and drought stress [14, 15]. Whole transcriptome analyses using RNA-Seq to examine genes involved in N deficiency have been done for Arabidopsis [16], maize [17], sorghum [18], cucumber [12, 19], rice [20, 21] and wheat [3]. However, the transcriptome responses of watermelon to low $_ \mathrm { N }$ are not studied yet. Considering the importance of $_ \mathrm { N }$ for plant growth and development, and yield, we executed this study to examine the effect of different levels of N on plant growth; N concentration in different parts of plant, photosynthetic assimilation, and root and leaf transcriptome responses of watermelon seedlings. So far as we know, this is the first study that provides information regarding root and leaf transcriptome responses of watermelon to low N. This study has the potential to reveal novel genes and pathways responsible for adaptation to low $_ \mathrm { N }$ in watermelon. This study can be utilized in crop improvement of watermelon, understanding the mechanism of N metabolism and enhancing the N use efficiency of watermelon plants.

Nitrogen (N) is a crucial nutrient essential for both plant growth and crop yield. The production of N fertilizers consumes $1 \%$ of the total energy used by humankind in the world (Chen et al. 2020). However, only approximately $3 3 \%$ of $\mathbf { N }$ fertilizer application is taken up by crops, which is accompanied by increased agricultural production costs and environmental pollution (Raun and Johnson 1999; Good et al. 2004). As a result, there is an urgent need to focus on the development of new crop varieties that combine high yields with enhanced NUE, which will pave the way for a more sustainable form of agriculture that requires minimal N input (Liu et al. 2022).

Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is one of the most important staple crops, feeding half of the world’s population; therefore, it is very important to improve wheat NUE to ensure food security (Habash et al. 2007). Various strategies have been attempted to increase wheat NUE and multiple exogenous genes have also been manipulated to cultivate wheat with high NUE through transgenic methods (BaileySerres et al. 2019). For example, introducing the rice transcription factor OsGRF4 can improve wheat grain yield and NUE at low N supply by coordinating N assimilation, carbon fxation, and growth (Li et al. 2018). Likewise, the overexpression of rice OsDREB1C in wheat, an integrator of photosynthesis, NUE and early fowering, resulted in a notable increase in grain yield per plant, ranging from $1 7 . 2 \%$ to $2 2 . 6 \%$ . This enhancement was accompanied by elevated photosynthetic capacity and earlier fowering (Wei et al. 2022). Therefore, the use of genes from other species with known functions to improve the NUE of wheat is an efective approach.

Recent research shows that specialized plant membrane transporters are essential for transporting mineral nutrients and controlling low N tolerance, which can be used to enhance crop yield (Schroeder et  al. 2013). Nitrate $( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } )$ availability in the soil varies drastically over space and time, and crops have evolved strategies to adapt to low $\mathbf { N }$ conditions. N uptake from soil by plant roots mainly relies on nitrate transport proteins (NRTs) located on the cell membrane (Wang et al. 2012; Krapp et al. 2014). NRTs developed high-afnity ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transport systems (HATS) and low-afnity ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transport systems (LATS) to ensure the efciency of the infux of ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ into roots. AtNRT1.1/ AtNPF6.3 is the initial ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transporter identifed through chlorate resistance screening and functions as a nitrate sensor triggering the primary nitrate response (Ho et al. 2009). AtNRT1.1 is a member of the NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family, also known as the NPF protein family. In Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) and rice (Oryza sativa L.), this family encompasses 53 and 93 members, respectively. These members can be further categorized into 8 \~ 10 subfamilies, each exhibiting a wide range of substrate specifcities (Léran et al. 2014). While NPF members are recognized as the primary constituents of the LATS under high ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ concentrations (Fan et al. 2017), specifc members such as NRT1.1 in Arabidopsis and MtNRT1.3 in Medicago truncatula serve as dual-afnity transporters, participating in both the HATS and LATS (Morere-Le Paven et al. 2011). Furthermore, under conditions of N starvation, the nitrate remobilization facilitated by NRT1.7 plays a crucial role as a mechanism allowing plants to optimize N utilization and maintain robust growth (Chen et al. 2020). In rice, there are three putative homologs of AtNRT1.1, including OsNRT1.1A/OsNPF6.3, OsNRT1.1B/OsNPF6.5, and OsNRT1.1C/OsNPF6.4 (Plett et al. 2010). Recent work has shown that overexpression of the OsNRT1.1A gene in rice can signifcantly promote fowering and increase yield, which has great potential in cultivating high-yield and early-maturing crop varieties (Wang et al. 2018a).

Through a genome-wide analysis, a total of 292 TaNPF members were identifed in wheat. These members could be categorized into eight subgroups (TaNPF1 to TaNPF8) based on the presence of conserved domains. Among these, 32 genes exhibited noteworthy alterations in their expression patterns in response to N starvation and/or N recovery, which suggests their involvement in N uptake and assimilation processes (Kumar et al. 2022). With the whole genome sequencing and de novo assembly of Kenong 9204, genes related to N uptake and metabolism in wheat were identifed, which is of great signifcance for analyzing the molecular mechanism of NUE in wheat (Shi et al. 2022). Using a comparative genome-wide association study (GWAS) between wheat and barley under varying N inputs, researchers pinpointed the $N P F 2 . I 2$ gene, encoding low-afnity nitrate transporters. The study also revealed that the expression of a rare natural allele of $N P F 2 . I 2$ was linked to a marked improvement in root growth and the translocation of ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ from roots to shoots in both crops under low ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ conditions (Siddiqui et al. 2023).

OsNRT1.1A is a key gene for improving crop NUE, accelerating crop maturation, and increasing rice yield. In addition, the overexpression of OsNRT1.1A in Arabidopsis can signifcantly advance fowering and increase the biomass and seed amount (Wang et al. 2018a). However, the potential application of the gene in the improvement of other crops, such as wheat, has not been evaluated. In this study, we created transgenic wheat overexpressing the OsNRT1.1A gene and found that it not only promoted wheat heading but also improved the NUE and grain yield per plant of wheat under low N conditions, which further expands the application of the OsNRT1.1A gene in species other than rice and provides a candidate gene for improving NUE in wheat.

In this study, we genetically dissected the seed loading route of glucosinolate specialized metabolites. Re-introduction of the main glucosinolate exporter UMAMIT29 and the main importer GTR2 in specific tissues revealed that glucosinolates move across four plasma membrane barriers en route from their source in reproductive organs to the embryo (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, our data suggest that the mobile form of glucosinolates matches the source tissue profile.

De novo glucosinolate synthesis in the funiculus happens when the seeds reach the mature green stage and coincides with the expression of both UMAMIT glucosinolate exporters and GTR importers7 . After biosynthesis, UMAMIT29, localized in biosynthetic cells in the funiculus, has been proposed to export seed-bound glucosinolates along the electrochemical gradient into the apoplast7,19. Upon arrival at the phloem unloading zone, glucosinolates are exported by UMAMITs to the apoplast and diffuse towards the embryo, where GTRs import the glucosinolates into the embryo symplasm. As GTR2 driven by the SUC2 promoter fully complemented seed glucosinolate levels, our data suggest that after export from biosynthetic cells, glucosinolates move through the phloem to the seed. This is consistent with previous studies reporting the presence of glucosinolates in the leaf phloem sap20 and strong expression of GTR2 in phloem companion cells12.

As the embryo is symplasmically isolated from the maternal tissues, another export/import event can be expected in connection with unloading from maternal seed tissue and import into filial tissue (endosperm and embryo). Indeed, the strong expression of UMAMIT29 in the chalazal seed coat and the strong reduction of seed glucosinolate levels when UMAMIT29 is not expressed in this tissue show that export of glucosinolates in the chalazal seed coat is important for seed loading. Export of glucosinolates through the chalazal seed coat is similar to what has been observed for amino acids, where chalazal-localized UMAMIT11, 14 and 18 are required to export amino acids from the phloem unloading zone to seeds3 . Interestingly, sucrose, which is also transported via the phloem, probably enters the outer integument of the seed coat through plasmodesmata at the early developmental stages4 . Among the sucrose exporters, the SUGARS WILL EVENTUALLY BE EXPORTED TRANSPORTERs (SWEETs) SWEET11, SWEET12 and SWEET15 are involved in the release of sucrose to the embryo through the integuments4 . In this study, our experimental design does not address the contribution of integuments to seed glucosinolate accumulation. Since UMAMIT29 is present in integuments (Fig. 1a), we do not exclude that export of glucosinolates from integuments to endosperm and embryo may contribute to seed accumulation.

Following release to the apoplast by UMAMIT29 in the chalazal seed coat, it can be expected that importers are needed for glucosinolates to enter the embryo. Interestingly, GTR2 is also highly expressed in the chalazal seed coat (Fig. 2a). However, this expression of GTR2 is not required to achieve full complementation of seed glucosinolate levels, as evidenced by the data from the SUC2 promoter-driven GTR2 complementation lines in which full complementation was achieved despite the SUC2 promoter not leading to GTR2 expression in the chalazal seed coat (Fig. 2d). In sucrose and amino acid seed loading, SWEET and UMAMIT transporters localize to specific subregions in the unloading zone and seed coat integuments4,9,21,22. The ARR22 promoter drives expression in all cells in the chalazal seed coat and integuments (Fig. 2c), and may thus target cells that do not natively express GTR2 or UMAMIT29. Transporter mislocalization to the wrong cell type might have impacted the level of complementation that we observed in the lines where UMAMIT29 and GTR2 were expressed by the ARR22 promoter (Figs. 1c and 2e). Further studies, such as single-cell transcriptomics in seeds at the mature green stage, are needed to determine whether GTR2 and UMAMIT29 function in different subpopulations of cells forming a transport cascade within the chalazal seed coat and whether GTR2 in this region plays a role in glucosinolate seed loading.

Downstream from the chalazal seed coat, specific elimination of GTRs from the embryo leads to significant reduction of glucosinolates in seeds. Thus, active uptake by the embryo is a critical step in glucosinolate seed loading as the re-introduction of GTR2 in the embryo increases the sink strength and enables wild-type levels to be reached. However, we identified embryo-specific benzoyloxyalkyl glucosinolates in the absence of GTRs in the embryo (Fig. 3c), which suggests that glucosinolates can be loaded into the embryo symplasm through other importers. Furthermore, this shows that the elimination of glucosinolates in gtr mutants8 must be caused by lack of import before the glucosinolates reach the seeds.

In Arabidopsis Col-0, the vegetative tissues mainly contain methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates, while seeds accumulate the methylthioalkyl and benzoyloxyalkyl forms15. This discrepancy in profiles has prompted speculation into which of these glucosinolates are translocated from source tissues to seeds6 . When GTR2 is available in source tissues but absent from the embryo, seeds accumulate methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates, presumably in the apoplast (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4). This suggests that glucosinolates are unloaded from phloem predominantly as methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates and that the seed-specific profile is subsequently established by sidechain modifying enzymes inside the embryo symplasm (Fig. 3d). The latter includes hydroxylation of methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolates by AOP3 and subsequent BZO1- and SCPL17-dependent conversion to benzoyloxyalkyl glucosinolates17,18, as well as the reduction of methylsulfinylalkyl to methylthioalkyl glucosinolates by a yet unknown reaction. Phloem sap from leaves contains high methylsulfinylalkyl glucosinolate levels20, which supports a model in which the profile of the glucosinolates being transported in the phloem is similar to that of the surrounding source tissues. Alternatively, GTR2 may function as a filter to enrich methylthioalkyl glucosinolates in the mobile fraction through a substrate preference for methylthioalkyl glucosinolates, analogous to previously reported substrate preferences among GTRs23–25. Identifying and characterizing enzymes capable of reducing methylsulfinylalkyl to methylthioalkyl glucosinolates or engineering of transporter substrate preference would serve to further test these hypotheses for the mobile glucosinolate profile.

In apoplastic loaders, primary metabolites such as amino acids and sucrose are exported to the apoplast in source tissues via passive uniporters and imported into phloem companion cells by active importers. This is exemplified by the Arabidopsis SWEET-SUC2 and UMAMIT-AMINO ACID PERMEASE (AAP) passive/active transporter pairs for sucrose and amino acids, respectively21. Within the seed, UMAMIT–AAP pairs carry out unloading of amino acids in the seed coat and loading into the embryo9,26, suggesting that the four-step transporter route mediated by the UMAMIT–GTR passive/active transporter pair represents a universal mechanism for seed loading of metabolites. For sucrose, SWEETs play a role in phloem unloading within the seed4 , while the mechanism behind loading into the embryo has remained unclear. In agreement with publicly available expression data27,28, we observe SUC2 promoter-driven expression in the epidermal cells of embryo cotyledons in addition to the well-known expression in phloem companion cells (Extended Data Fig. 3). This suggests that SUC2 may contribute to sucrose loading into the embryo during seed maturation. It would be interesting to test the role of SUC2 in embryo loading. However, the Arabidopsis suc2 mutant is severely stunted and sterile29, which makes it difficult to determine whether SUC2 has other roles in sucrose transport to seeds beyond phloem loading, such as loading into the embryo.

Lack of viable mutants of primary metabolite transporters hampers the ability to study the transport route of primary metabolites through genetic studies, especially when the same transporter is required at multiple places. By contrast, eliminating seed glucosinolates in transporter mutants does not affect plant viability, making this system a unique tool for studying the transport route of a metabolite from the site of synthesis to storage in seeds. Our study suggests that the very low glucosinolate accumulation in seeds of both the umamit29/30/31 exporter and gtr1/2/3 importer mutants can be explained by the blockage of essential barriers within the maternal tissue before seed loading. Thus, the knowledge gained here can guide transport engineering at specific sites to improve the nutritional value of seeds with minimum interruption of other cellular processes. We anticipate that the experimental strategies developed here— expression-guided re-introduction of transporters at specific barriers and embryo-specific knockouts through selection marker-based seed sorting—are applicable to the study of seed loading systems for both primary and specialized metabolites.
