The plant NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (NRT1/PTR FAMILY or NPF) encodes membrane proteins involved in various substrates: nitrate, nitrite, amino acids, glucosinolates, peptide, and hormone transport. All these transporters display 12 predicted transmembrane domains. Phylogenetic analysis divides the NPF family into eight clades (Le´ran et al. 2014). The different subfamilies have various substrate specificities, and some members are able to transport more than one substrate: nitrate/IAA, nitrate/ABA, nitrate/glucosinolates, or peptides/amino acids. The first plant member identified was the plant transceptor NPF6.3 (NRT1.1/CHL1), able to transport nitrate in low- and high-affinity transport systems (LATS and HATS, respectively) and to sense nitrate (Bouguyon et al. 2015). In addition, NPF6.3 is also able to transport IAA but in competition with nitrate uptake, leading to a role in root architecture development (Krouk et al. 2010). Several other members are involved in lowaffinity nitrate transport, allowing nitrate uptake or root nitrate efflux and long-distance transport in different plant organs (for review, see Krapp et al. 2014).

The smallest subfamily of NPF contains the cucumber CsNPF3.2, the first plant nitrite transporter described, which is localized at the chloroplast inner membrane (Sugiura et al. 2007). Using transient expression, the Arabidopsis orthologue, AtNPF3.1, has been shown to be located at the plasma membrane (Pike et al. 2014), offering a new perspective regarding its function. Electrophysiology measurements of heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocyte characterized the NPF3 proteins of Arabidopsis and Grapevine as a low-affinity nitrate/nitrite transporter (Pike et al. 2014). A modified yeast-two hybrid (Y2H) system with hormone receptor complexes allowed testing the hormone uptake capacity of almost all the NPF family members (Kanno et al. 2012; Chiba et al. 2015). Using this method, NPF3.1 has been shown to transport in yeast different active forms of gibberellins (GAs) $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ (Chiba et al. 2015). Very recently, expression of NPF3.1 in Xenopus oocytes revealed its capacity to transport $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ as well (Tal et al. 2016). In the same study, the use of fluorescently labeled GAs (GA-FI) proved that AtNPF3.1 in responsible for GAs transport in planta as mutants is not able to take up this hormone, while overexpressors accumulate GA-FI in their roots (Tal et al. 2016). Previously, exogenous application of GA-FI has demonstrated that an active GA transport mechanism does exist in planta, since an accumulation of labeled GAs has been observed in elongating endodermal cells (Shani et al. 2013). Thus, this cell type seems to be a target of the bioactive GAs, although they are mainly synthesized in the meristematic and non-meristematic zones (Mitchum et al.

2006). Other numerous examples illustrate the occurrence of GA biosynthesis pathways and GA-regulated events in separated tissues (Hedden and Thomas 2012). In germinating seeds, in situ hybridization analyses demonstrated that the GA-responsive genes are not restricted to the site of active GA biosynthesis (Ogawa et al. 2003). In developing flowers, GA synthesis occurs in stamens, while GAs are required for petals growth (Plackett et al. 2011). All these results indirectly reveal the presence of GA transport mechanisms in plants.

GA hormones are diterpenoids and more than 100 GAs have been identified in plants. $\mathrm { G A _ { 1 } }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { G A } _ { 4 }$ , and $\mathrm { G A } _ { 7 }$ are known to be biologically active in plants involved in the regulation of photomorphogenesis, the other forms being precursors or products of catabolism (Yamaguchi 2008). The bioactive forms bind the GID1 receptor to trigger the degradation of DELLA through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (Feng et al. 2008). DELLA proteins repress the cell expansion, whereas GAs promote their development. This antagonist effect has been proved for root growth, leaf expansion, and floral development. GAs are involved in the elongation of hypocotyls in the light and in the dark by influencing cell elongation (de Lucas et al. 2008; Feng et al. 2008). In seeds, light and cold stimulate the GA biosynthesis, leading to the seed germination and counteracting ABA effect (Yamauchi et al. 2004; Oh et al. 2006). In Arabidopsis, nitrate has been described in the control of seed dormancy through the regulation of CYP707A2 expression, a gene involved in the ABA catabolism (Matakiadis et al. 2009; Liu et al. 2010), and in hedge, mustard nitrate can also promote the expression of GA3OX2, a gene involved in the production of active GA forms (Carrillo-Barral et al. 2014). Thus, GAs are important molecules acting to promote seed germination and cell elongation particularly in hypocotyl elongation. The aim of this investigation is to understand whether NPF3.1 is involved in these processes through its capacity to transport GAs and nitrate. The capacity of numerous NPF to transport various hormones (Chiba et al. 2015) underlines a redundancy in functioning and raises the question of the substrate specificity. Therefore, to decipher the in planta function of NPF3.1 and its substrate specificity, we analyzed its expression pattern and we characterized two mutant lines at different developmental stages. Then, given these different traits, we discuss the potential role of NPF3.1 within the plant.

## Unveiling NRTs in G. biloba: phylogenetic insights and evolutionary signifcance


Nitrate serves as the primary nitrogen source for most plants, and NRTs are responsible for nitrate allocation across a wide range of $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ concentrations [35]. While previous studies primarily focused on angiosperms, our investigation shines a light on the unique NRT landscape in Ginkgo, an evolutionarily distinct gymnosperm [36]. Tis study identifed 74 GbNRT proteins, including 68 NPFs, 4 NRT2s, and 2 NRT3s. NPF and NRT2 have been shown to co-code the NRT gene family, but they are two distinct families with high sequence similarity [37]. NRT3/NAR2 is a chaperone protein to assist NRT2 in nitrate transport.

Te classifcation of the NPF subfamily has been a matter of ongoing discussion, with difering approaches proposed by various researchers. Wittgenstein [38] divided the NPF family into 10 supergroups based on the phylogeny of NPF from 20 plant species. In this study, we follow the classifcation proposed by Léran et al. [10], which split the NPF family into 8 subfamilies across various species. However, our analysis found interesting patterns that challenge this classifcation. Notably, subfamilies previously considered homogenous, such as AtNPF2, AtNPF5, and AtNPF6, showed subdivision in our analysis. Similar patterns emerged in PtNPF2 and PtNPF5, as well as PpNPF6 and PpNPF7, indicating a need for revised classifcation methodologies. Other studies have seen a similar trend. For instance, when characterizing the genome-wide profle of the NPF gene family in Malus × domestica Borkh., 15 MdNPF2 were further divided into two groups [39]. Similarly, In Brassica napus, BnNPF2, BnNPF5, and BnNPF6 were all divided into two groups [40], as well as CsNPF2, CsNPF5, and CsNPF6 in Camellia sinensis [41].


## Key structural features of the GbNPF family indicated dynamic proton transporting ability


Analyzing the conserved motifs of the NPF family uncovers crucial structural features infuencing proton transport across cell membranes. NPF has three relatively conserved motifs that vary among diferent members and across diferent plants [39]. Te $\mathrm { E _ { 1 } X _ { 1 } X _ { 2 } E _ { 2 } R }$ motif, with its distinct variations in the NPF family, plays a critical role in proton coupling and active transport. Te "X" residues within this motif exert an infuence on the electrochemical gradient, thereby afecting the transport function of NPF proteins [42, 43].

In the GbNPF4 subfamily, most members have a complete $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } [ \mathrm { R } / \mathrm { K } ]$ motif, but 32 members lack or have an incomplete motif. Notably, GbNPF4 and GbNPF7 deviate from this pattern. In the GbNPF4 subfamily, most members retain only $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } \mathrm { X } _ { 3 } ,$ or $\mathrm { X _ { 1 } X _ { 2 } X _ { 3 } E _ { 2 } X _ { 4 } } ,$ while GbNPF4.7 exhibits a complete motif replacement. Similarly, the $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } [ \mathrm { R } / \mathrm { K } ]$ motif in the GbNPF7 subfamily is entirely substituted by QGLAT, which is also observed in the NPF7 subfamily of other plants [29].

Te variability in the E1X1X2E2R motif, central to proton coupling and active transport, presents intriguing possibilities. In Arabidopsis, this motif has two variants, with arginine or lysine at the ends $( \mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } \mathrm { R } /$ $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } \mathrm { K } )$ . Te $\mathrm { E } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 1 } \mathrm { X } _ { 2 } \mathrm { E } _ { 2 } \mathrm { K }$ motif is essential for glucosinolate transport in NPF2.11 [44]. Furthermore, AtNPF7.3, characterized by an entirely altered E1X1X2E2[R/K] motif, orchestrates potassium ion homeostasis by promoting the expression of potassium ion transporter under low nitrate conditions [45]. However, GbNPF5.8, GbNPF6.4 and GbNPF8.2 lack this motif. More research is needed to fgure out their actual roles and how they transport nitrogen compounds. Our study unveils variations in this motif among GbNPF members, suggesting potential variations in their ability to transport protons and their functional diversity. Tis emphasizes the complex ways the NPF family works across diferent plants.


## Expression profle and cis‑elements analysis revealed the potential role of GbNRTs in callus browning regulation


Browning is a major challenge in plant tissue culture. Ginkgo, a gymnosperm known for its favonoid production, faces challenges in establishing regeneration and production systems due to browning [30, 46]. In this study, we treated zygotic embryos with varying nitrate concentrations during callus induction, revealing that higher nitrate concentrations resulted in deeper browning of Ginkgo calluses (Fig. 5). Many studies have indicated a connection between browning and nitrogen levels [47–49]. In Camptotheca acuminata, Zhang et  al. [50] discovered that using Schenk & Hildebrandt (SH) basal salt is less likely to brown compared to using Murashige & Skoog (MS) basal salt. Te SH basal salt contains a lower nitrogen concentration than MS. Daigen [33] observed that using reduced nitrogen compounds like $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } N O _ { 3 } }$ can decrease browning in rice. Moreover, Chopin found that the seed coat of the nrt2.7 mutant in Arabidopsis exhibited brown coloring [28]. Ogawa et  al. [51] hypothesized that low nitrite reductase activity could lead to high levels of nitrate, causing browning and stopping growth.

NPFs are responsible for transporting various substrates across cell membranes, such as nitrate, peptides, amino acid, and other organic compounds [52, 53]. In plants, NPFs play a critical role in nitrogen uptake and utilization, which is essential for plant growth, development, and stress responses [54]. Among the 53 NPF proteins in Arabidopsis, 20 have been shown to transport nitrate, while peptide transport activity has only been demonstrated in the NPF8 subfamily. In addition, NPF proteins could transport other substrates, such as nitrite [55], chloride [56], glucosinolate, auxin (IAA [57], 2,4-D [58]), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs) [59] and gibberellins (GAs) [60, 61]. Tis diverse range of functions highlights the importance of the NPF family in plant physiology, growth and development, and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses.

Analysis of the promoter regions of the GbNRTs also revealed several hormone-related CREs. Among the 72 GbNRTs genes, 30 of their promoter regions contained Auxin-associated CREs (AuxRR-core, TGA-box, TGA-element) (Table S7). Expression analysis revealed that out of the diferentially expressed 21 genes, 14 were higher expressed in calluses under LN treatment, and only 7 were higher expressed in calluses under HN treatment (Table S8). Tese fndings suggest that auxin may afect the calluses’ browning in Ginkgo. Previous studies have shown that adding 1-Naphthylacetic acid (NAA) promoted the proliferation of jasmine callus, increased the total phenol, favonoid content, and free radical clearance, and inhibited browning compared to 2,4-D [62]. Additionally, studies in maize and Arabidopsis have exhibited that the inhibition of root growth under high nitrogen conditions is due to the decrease of root IAA level [63, 64], and root growth was promoted after switching from high nitrogen to low nitrogen conditions [64]. Furthermore, Krouk et  al. [57] found that Arabidopsis NRT1.1 inhibited auxin accumulation at low nitrate concentrations. Tese results indicate that there is a signaling regulation between nitrogen and auxin, and nitrate may indeed afect plant growth and development by afecting auxin.

Enzymatic browning occurs when polyphenols, such as phenolic acids, favonoids, and tannins, undergo oxidation [65, 66]. Te synthesis of these polyphenols is regulated by transcription factors activated by various plant hormones, such as methyl jasmonate [67], abscisic acid [68], auxin [69], and ethylene [70]. Te promoter region of GbNRTs contains numerous transcription factor binding sites, such as MYB and bHLH (Fig.  3), suggesting their potential role in regulating polyphenol synthesis. In red-feshed apple, MdMYB10 is a key transcription factor that determines the fruit coloration [71, 72] and is associated with increased accumulation of anthocyanins due to enhanced nitrate uptake through the activation of MdNRT2.4–1 [73]. However, recent research has shown that brassinolide inhibits favonoid biosynthesis and coloration in apples through a MdBEH2.2-MdMYB60 complex [74]. In Arabidopsis, the interaction between Teosinte branched1/ Cycloidea/ Proliferating cell factors (TCP) protein and V-myb avian myeloblastosis viral oncogene homolog (R2R3-MYB) protein promoted favonoid biosynthesis while negatively regulating the auxin response [75]. Overall, the regulation of polyphenol synthesis is a complex and dynamic process that involves multiple factors and pathways.

Our fndings suggest that GbNPFs, acting as nitrate sensors and transporters, infuence the signaling pathways of nitrate uptake and assimilation, as well as auxin and polyphenol biosynthesis, to control browning during callus induction in Ginkgo. However, additional research is necessary to explore the mechanisms through which nitrates impact phenolic substance formation and how nitrates and auxins infuence plant browning.

Fundamental studies to understand mechanisms that govern nitrate transport and signaling offer prospects to better control nitrogen use efficiency in plants. Mining of extant datasets enables identification of candidate genes and consideration of their possible roles in planta. To date, few studies of legume nitrate transporters have been undertaken, and thus much remains undiscovered, in particular the role of these transporters in nodules.

Experimental characterization of nitrate transporters is usually performed under optimal or at least unchallenging conditions. However, plants are continuously subjected to ever changing environmental conditions. Their sessile lifestyle exposes them to unavoidable frequent and severe climatic changes and attacks by herbivores and microorganisms. It is well known that legume plants adapt their root architecture and their metabolism to abiotic stress through signaling pathways involving ABA and NO (Planchet et al. 2011, 2014). Given that studies on both characterized nitrate transporters, MtNPF1.7 and MtNPF6.8, connect these NPFs with root architecture and ABA, it will be valuable to fully investigate the role of legume NPFs in response to challenging environmental conditions.

Because nitrogen is an essential nutrient for plants, we have developed functional screens in heterologous systems (yeast and xenopus oocytes) to identify new nitrogen transporters in Arabidopsis. In one family of nitrogen transporters, NPF (NRT1/PTR Family6 ), several proteins have been identified as dipeptides, amino-acids and nitrate transporters, three main forms of nitrogen for nutrition of the plants. We expressed in both yeast and xenopus oocytes 26 of the 53 Arabidopsis NPF CDS. While we were unable to identify new dipeptide (Leu-Leu) transporters in yeast, our screen in xenopus oocytes identified two as yet uncharacterized nitrate transporters: NPF5.5 and NPF5.10. While the NPF5 subfamily is the largest one in plants (663 members out of 2384 in 31 fully sequenced plant genomes6 ), only one member AtNPF5.2/PTR3 has been functionally characterized in Arabidopsis, and shown to be a dipeptide transporter33. None of the NPF5 members (NPF5.1, 3–5, 7, 9–14, 16) tested in this study complemented yeast deficiency in Leu-Leu uptake. Nevertheless, NPF5.5 and NPF5.10 are the first nitrate transporters identified in this subfamily (Figure 2).

Human and animal feeding relies on organic nitrogen produced by plants. Plant seeds provide an important source of this nitrogen. Several nitrate transporters have been demonstrated to be expressed in the seed2 . For example, NRT2.7 is a high-affinity vacuolar nitrate transporter, highly expressed in seeds and embryos and involved in nitrate accumulation in the seed34. NPF2.12/NRT1.6 is expressed in vascular tissues of the silique and in funiculus, and is important for embryo development35. Several organic nitrogen (peptide) transporters are involved in nitrogen accumulation in embryos18,36.

NPF5.5 is expressed in different tissues within the plant29 but is the first NPF transporter gene so far showing an expression in the embryo. Transcriptomic analyses on embryos isolated at different stages showed that NPF5.5 level is rather stable during embryo maturation31. Its expression in the embryo (at bent cotyledon stage) has been confirmed by Q-RT-PCR (Figure 3b). To assess the role of NPF5.5 in the embryo, we have isolated two homozygous KO lines in which no full-length $N P F 5 . 5 \ \mathrm { m R N A }$ was found (Figure 3b). Nitrogen content (as $\%$ of dry weight) was determined for WT and the $2 ~ \mathrm { K O }$ lines on 5 batches of 75 isolated embryos. Embryo nitrogen content is $7 - 8 \%$ lower in both KO lines compared to WT (Figure 3c), demonstrating an effect of NPF5.5 function on the embryo nitrogen content. Since NPF5.5 gene was knock out in all the plant, we cannot exclude that part of this phenotype involves expression of NPF5.5 in other tissues.

NPF5.5 is one of the Arabidopsis genes for which there is no cDNA sequence available in databases but we have identified two different mRNAs transcribed from this gene. These different forms most likely arise from different transcription initiation site (instead of alternative splicing). Both proteins encoded by these two different transcripts are nitrate transporters (Figure 4c). Further experiments are needed to identify the role of these different transcripts. Two non-exclusives kind of regulation could exist. The first one is a post-transcriptional regulation due to different $5 ^ { \prime }$ -UTR. The second one is a post-translational regulation involving the 22 amino acids extended N-terminus of NPF5.5b that contains phosphorylable residues (2 serines and 2 threonines).

Iron (Fe) is an essential element for plant growth since required for various cellular processes, such as respiration and photosynthesis. Although abundant in soils, Fe is often available in limited amounts to plants because it is mostly found in rather insoluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ complexes (Colombo et al. 2014; Palmer and Guerinot 2009). Therefore, plants have evolved sophisticated mechanisms to efciently take up iron from the soil. In non-graminaceous plants, including the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, iron uptake by root epidermal cells requires three successive steps (solubilization-reduction-transport) involving plasma membrane (PM) proteins. Under Fe defciency, the solubilization of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ complexes is mainly achieved by Arabidopsis plasma membrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase2 (AHA2)-mediated proton extrusion, which results in local rhizosphere acidifcation (Santi and Schmidt 2009). Solubilized $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ is then reduced to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ by the reductase Ferric Reduction Oxydase2 (FRO2) and ultimately transported into epidermal cells by the Iron Regulated Transporter1 (IRT1) protein (Palmer and Guerinot 2009; Thomine and Vert 2013; Jeong et al. 2017). Interestingly, AHA2, FRO2 and IRT1 gene expression is induced under iron defciency through the direct action of the same basic Helix-Loop-Helix (bHLH) transcription factor named FER-like Iron Defciency-Induced Transcription Factor (FIT) that can heterodimerize with other bHLH proteins (Colangelo and Guerinot 2004; Jakoby et al. 2004; Yuan et al. 2008; Sivitz et al. 2012). IRT1 is a major actor in the regulation of plant iron homeostasis, as attested by the severe chlorosis and lethality of an irt1-1 knockout mutant (Vert et al. 2002; Henriques et al. 2002). IRT1 is poorly selective and, in addition to iron, mediates the uptake of non-iron metals such as zinc, manganese, cobalt or cadmium that are toxic when present in excess in the plant (Eide et al. 1996; Rogers et al. 2000; Vert et al. 2002; Korshunova et al. 1999). Considering the crucial role of IRT1 in iron uptake, a great deal of attention was devoted to the mechanisms regulating IRT1 activity. The regulatory processes driving the delivery and removal of IRT1 from the cell surface emerge as crucial for metal homeostasis.  In this mini-review, we focus on the role of IRT1-interacting proteins in the control of IRT1 exit from the ER, its function at the cell surface, and its degradation, as well as highlight their contribution to plant metal homeostasis.


## Clues about the mechanisms of IRT1 secretion to the plasma membrane


In eukaryotic cells, proteins addressed to the cell surface are synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and trafc along the secretory pathway. Membrane proteins are exported from the ER to the Golgi apparatus via vesicles coated with coat protein complex II (COPII) (Hanton et al. 2009; Takagi et al. 2013; Chung et al. 2016). Recruitment in COPII vesicles is mediated by physical interactions between subunits of COPII complex and cargo proteins that carry export signals, such as diacidic motifs corresponding to $\left( \mathrm { D / E } \right) \mathbf { x } ( \mathrm { D / E } )$ (Sieben et al. 2008; Zelazny et al. 2009; Sorieul et al. 2011). Recently, the COPII subunits SEC13a and SEC31b were identifed in Arabidopsis IRT1 interactome (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). This suggests that IRT1 exits the ER via the COPII machinery (Fig. 1), which is in line with a previous work proposing that IRT1 from Malus xiaojinesis is exported in COPII vesicles (Tan et al. 2018). Whether the interactions between Arabidopsis IRT1 and COPII components are direct remains to be and FRO2 are also found in EE/TGN, probably associated with IRT1. EHB1 protein can interact with and negatively regulate IRT1 at the PM. Although not indicated on the scheme, AHA2 and FRO2 can also be ubiquitinated, but the cellular outcome of such modifcations remains to be determined. When non-iron metal cations are abundant in the cytosol (right panel), they are directly sensed by IRT1. Consequently, the CIPK23 kinase is recruited to and phosphorylates IRT1, which triggers the dissociation of the IRT1-AHA2-FRO2 complex. CIPK23-dependent phosphorylation also enhances the recruitment of IDF1 that in turn converts monoubiquitin moieties into K63-polyubiquitin chains, which sorts IRT1 into MVB/LE. Such endosomal sorting requires interaction with the ESCRT protein FYVE1/FREE1 that allows IRT1 targeting to intraluminal vesicles for subsequent degradation in the vacuole. IRT1 may be saved from degradation and recycled to earlier endocytic compartments via the action of SNX1 protein. Grey and black arrows indicate the secretion and the endocytosis/recycling of IRT1, respectively. determined, which will allow to establish which subunits recruits IRT1 to COPII vesicles. So far, the signals responsible for IRT1 packaging in COPII vesicle are still unknown. However, a diacidic motif (EDD) located in the large cytosolic loop of IRT1 may be implicated, although experimental evidence is needed (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). Parallel to the COPII-mediated anterograde route, a retrograde pathway is driven by coat protein complex I (COPI)-coated vesicles, which allows the continual recycling of proteins and lipids from the Golgi to the ER to maintain an equilibrium (Contreras et  al. 2000; Pimpl et al. 2000; Yorimitsu et al. 2014). Interestingly, coatomer subunits, that are key components of the COPI machinery (Sanchez-Simarro et al. 2020), probably interact with IRT1 since they were found in IRT1 interactome (MartinBarranco et al. 2020). IRT1 may, therefore, be retrieved back from the Golgi apparatus to the ER by COPI vesicles (Fig. 1), even if the relevance of this process remains unclear. The contribution of the IRT1 partners involved in its anterograde and retrograde transport to the establishment of plant metal homeostasis is still uncharacterized, but corresponding mutants will likely have pleiotropic efects. Finally, the later steps of IRT1 trafcking from the Golgi to the PM remain unexplored. This process might involve soluble $N .$ -ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) or the exocyst complex, that were both shown to be implicated in the post-Golgi trafcking of several membrane proteins in plants (Hachez et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2020).


## Endocytosis plays a major role in the regulation of IRT1


In the past decade, numerous studies highlighted the importance of endocytosis in the regulation of IRT1 and metal uptake in Arabidopsis. Early work showed that, under iron limitation and in presence of physiological amounts of non-iron metals, IRT1 cycles between early endosomes (EE)/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and the outer polar domain of the PM, in root epidermal cells (Fig. 1) (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011). A fraction of IRT1 also trafcs through the multivesicular bodies (MVB)/ late endosomes (LE) on the way to the lytic vacuole for constitutive degradation (Barberon et  al. 2011). IRT1 internalization from the PM is at least in part achieved by clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) and requires the mono-ubiquitination of lysine residues K154 and K179 that are located in the large cytosolic loop of IRT1. Indeed, IRT1 is stabilized at the PM when CME is impaired via the expression of a dominant-negative version of clathrin and when K154 and K179 are mutated (Kerkeb et al. 2008; Barberon et al. 2011, 2014). Importantly, neither ubiquitination nor CME are implicated in IRT1 polar localization. The role of CME in IRT1 internalization is strengthened by the fact that clathrin was recently found to be abundant in IRT1 interactome, suggesting that IRT1 can associate, probably in an indirect manner via adaptor proteins, with clathrin (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The peripheral membrane protein ENHANCED BENDING1 (EHB1) may also be involved in IRT1 endocytosis since: (i) IRT1 protein content increases in ehb1 mutants, (ii) proteins from the same family can induce membrane tubulation in vitro (Khan et al. 2019). Interestingly, EHB1 interacts with and negatively regulates IRT1 in a calciumdependent manner (Fig. 1), leading to a reduction of iron acquisition in plant.

Interestingly, IRT1 intracellular dynamics is not regulated by iron, the primary substrate of IRT1, but is controlled by the non-iron secondary substrates of IRT1 that are toxic when present in excess (Barberon et al. 2014; Dubeaux et al. 2018). Although IRT1 is localized to both EE/TGN and the PM in the presence of physiological concentrations of noniron metals, IRT1 is targeted to MVB/LE and then to the vacuole for degradation upon a cytosolic excess of these metals (Fig. 1) (Dubeaux et al. 2018). The cellular mechanisms involved in the non-iron metal-triggered endocytosis of IRT1 were largely uncovered. Non-iron metal excess is directly sensed by IRT1 via metal binding to a histidine-rich sequence located in the IRT1 large cytosolic loop (Dubeaux et al. 2018). Thus, IRT1 acts as a transceptor, combining transporter and receptor properties (Cointry and Vert 2019). Metal binding on IRT1 allows the recruitment of Calcineurin B-like (CBL)-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 23 (CIPK23) (Fig. 1). Phosphorylation of IRT1 by CIPK23 in turn creates a docking site for the E3 ubiquitin ligase IRT1 DEGRADATION FACTOR1 (IDF1) that converts IRT1 multi-monoubiquitination into K63-type polyubiquitination, a signal that boosts the sorting of IRT1 to the vacuole and its degradation (Dubeaux et al. 2018; Shin et al. 2013). From a physiological point of view, the endocytosis of IRT1 in response to a non-iron metal excess constitutes a protective mechanism for the plant to restrict the absorption of readily available and potentially toxic metals, such as Zn, Mn and Co. Loss of CIPK23, IDF1, or the mutation of ubiquitination targets or metal-binding sites in IRT1 all lead to stabilization of IRT1 at the cell surface, which results in a hypersentivity to non-iron metals (Barberon et al. 2014, 2011; Dubeaux et al. 2018). It should be noted that in addition to this IRT1- mediated protection, non-iron-metal toxicity is also alleviated by tonoplastic transporters such as Metal Tolerance Protein 3 (MTP3) (Arrivault et al. 2006) and Heavy Metal Associated 3 (HMA3) (Morel et al. 2009), which expression is induced under iron defciency in a FIT-dependent manner (Wu et al. 2012), and that allow the sequestration of metals such as Zn and Co into the vacuole.

The recognition of ubiquitin-modifed IRT1 required for its routing to the vacuole is achieved by the MVB/LElocalized FYVE1/FREE1 protein (Fig. 1). FYVE1/FREE1 directly interacts with IRT1 and ubiquitin, and associates with endosomal membrane via phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate binding (Barberon et al. 2014; Gao et al. 2014). FYVE1/FREE1 is a plant-specifc component of the endosomal sorting complex for transport (ESCRT) that captures ubiquitinated cargos in the MVB/LE membrane and allows their sorting in intraluminal vesicles for subsequent targeting to the vacuole (Isono and Kalinowska 2017; Otegui 2018). Interestingly, overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 in plants leads to an apolar localization of IRT1 in root epidermal cells, which in turn induces defects in metal homeostasis (Barberon et al. 2014). This suggests that the polarization of IRT1 is essential for the radial transport of metals towards the vasculature. So far, it remains unclear why the overexpression of FYVE1/FREE1 induces a re-routing of IRT1 to the PM instead of favoring its targeting to the vacuole for degradation. Interestingly, FYVE1/FREE1 protein accumulation is regulated by iron through the action of SINAT1-4 E3 ubiquitin ligases. Expression of these is induced under iron defciency resulting in ubiquitin-mediated degradation of FYVE1/FREE1, thus positively regulating iron uptake (Xiao et al. 2020). Following endocytosis, IRT1 can be recycled to earlier endocytic compartments or the PM. One of these pathways involves the Sorting Nexin 1 (SNX1) protein that partially co-localizes in endosomes with IRT1 (Fig. 1) (Ivanov et al. 2014). snx1 knock-out mutant shows enhanced degradation of IRT1, leading to reduced iron import efciency and hypersensitivity to iron defciency. Although Arabidopsis SNX1 protein works independently of the retrograde transport retromer complex (Pourcher et al. 2010; Zelazny et al. 2013), SNX1 appears to drive the recycling of internalized IRT1 to prevent its premature degradation (Ivanov et al. 2014). Whether SNX1 directly interacts with IRT1 is still undocumented.


## IRT1 is part of an iron acquisition protein complex


Recently, the three main actors of iron uptake in Arabidopsis, IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2, were shown to form tripartite direct interactions, thus creating an iron acquisition protein complex (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). This complex is probably mostly present in the outer PM domain facing the rhizosphere in root epidermal cells, where IRT1 and FRO2 are specifcally localized. The spatial proximity between IRT1, FRO2 and AHA2 among a complex may optimize iron uptake under low iron conditions, by creating a nanoscale environment in the rhizosphere combining low pH, induced by the activity of AHA2, and high concentrations of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ produced by FRO2 (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). Although it remains to be investigated, a channeling mechanism allowing the direct transfer of reduced iron from FRO2 to IRT1 is conceivable. Indeed, channeling of iron was described in yeast between the multicopper oxidase Fet3p, which oxidizes $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , and the iron permease Ftr1p that transports $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ into the cells, both proteins forming a complex (Kwok et al. 2006; Singh et al. 2006).

Characterization of the dynamics of the iron uptake complex revealed that: (i) FRO2 and AHA2 are ubiquitinated but independently of the non-iron metal substrates transported by IRT1, (ii) FRO2 and AHA2 are not largely endocytosed in response to non-iron metal excess, unlike IRT1, (iii) this absence of internalization is due to the dissociation of the complex provoked by the CIPK23-mediated phosphorylation of IRT1 in response to non-iron metal excess (Fig. 1) (Martin-Barranco et al. 2020). The meaning of such dissociation remains to be investigated but released FRO2 and AHA2 may be recruited to other processes than iron uptake, such as copper reduction and membrane energization, respectively (Yi and Guerinot 1996; Robinson et al. 1999; Connolly et al. 2003; Falhof et al. 2016).

The work detailed in this paper follows up on a previous study in which we showed that the imposition of Fe deficiency stimulated both Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ influx in roots of pea seedlings (Cohen et al. 1998a). There have been a number of examples in the plant micronutrient nutrition literature indicating that Fe nutrition is linked, in poorly understood ways, to the transport and nutrition of other micronutrients as well as to heavy metals such as Cd, which are presumed to enter plants via systems normally operating for essential micronutrients. For example, in dicotyledonous plants that employ a reductive-based mechanism for Fe acquisition, it has been shown that the imposition of either Fe or Cu deficiency activated the Fe deficiency responses associated with Fe acquisition: root ferric reductase activity and acidification of the rhizosphere (Welch et al. 1993; Cohen et al. 1997). It is possible that in dicots, as has been shown for yeast, Cu is required for proper Fe utilization and transport. Furthermore, there have been several examples in the literature in which Fe deficiency in dicots induces the stimulated accumulation of a number of micronutrient metals other than Fe (for example, see Welch et al. 1993; Rodecap et al. 1994). More recently, researchers are beginning to understand the molecular basis for micronutrient nutrition from information gained from the cloning and characterization of plant micronutrient transporters from several gene families, including the ZIP family of metal transporters. These findings have led some researchers to suggest that these metal transporters may be relatively promiscuous, and facilitate the transport of several micronutrient metals (Guerinot 2000). In particular for the Arabidopsis ZIP transporter, IRT1, it was originally suggested that it may be a broad specificity metal transporter that can facilitate uptake from the soil of a number of micronutrients (Korshunova et al. 1999). These observations raise important questions about how plants might regulate the homeostasis of specific micronutrients, particularly if the expression of transporters that can mediate the influx of several different metals can also be regulated by changes in the plant status of several micronutrients.

Most of the findings suggesting multiple transport roles for ZIP transporters have come from yeast complementation studies, in which specific defects in micronutrient uptake (Fe, Zn, Mn), which prevent growth of the yeast at low levels of those micronutrients, have been complemented with plant metal transport genes. As researchers begin to extrapolate from these experiments based on heterologous expression in yeast to terrestrial plants in order to better understand plant micronutrient nutrition, it will be important to characterize the properties of the plant micronutrient transporters under conditions that more closely mimic roots functioning in the soil. To investigate the molecular basis for the observed enhancement of Zn and Cd accumulation in Fe-deficient pea seedlings, we isolated a putative iron transporter cDNA from pea. This cDNA, designated RIT1, shows significant nucleotide and amino acid sequence similarity to the Arabidopsis IRT1 cDNA. Expression of RIT1 in the yeast Fe transportdefective mutant conferred enhanced growth under low iron conditions. In this study, we showed that RIT1 mediates high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ that ranges from 54 to $9 3 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ . These findings suggest that RIT1 normally functions to mediate acquisition of Fe in plants. $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values in the nanomolar range measured in the heterologous yeast system are consistent with the significant fluxes observed at nanomolar $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in intact pea roots (Fox et al. 1996). Ferrous ion activities in this range also agree with the estimated critical $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activity required for optimal plant growth $\left( 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \mathrm { n M } \right)$ and the $_ { 0 . 1 - 1 , 0 0 0 \ n M }$ levels of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ typically found in bulk soil solutions (Lindsay 1991). A $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value in the nanomolar range is thus physiologically relevant to the environmental conditions a plant is most likely to encounter.

Therefore, these results, based on kinetic analysis of RIT-mediated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx, provide further support for recent findings from several laboratories based on analysis of Arabidopsis IRT1 knockout mutants, that led those authors to propose that IRT1 is the main transporter mediating plant Fe uptake from the soil (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In all three of these studies, characterization of T-DNA knockout lines for IRT1 produced a mutant phenotype nearly identical to that seen for plant Fe deficiency, and the wild type phenotype was restored by providing elevated levels of Fe in the soil or hydroponic medium. Furthermore, in the studies by Henriques et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), transport studies indicated that the irt1 mutant exhibited significantly reduced uptake of Fe, as well as Zn (in Henriques et al. 2002) and Zn, Mn, and Co (in Vert et al. 2002). Vert et al. (2002) also showed that the mutant phenotype was not overcome by supplementing the plants growth medium with elevated levels of Zn, Mn, or Co; the only mineral that reversed the chlorotic mutant phenotype was elevated Fe.

In the study detailing the original cloning and characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis (Eide et al. 1996), the data from the concentration-dependent kinetics for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in the fet3fet4 yeast expressing IRT1 indicated that the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake was $6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ , indicating that the affinity of IRT1 for $\mathrm { \bar { F e } } ^ { 2 + }$ is approximately 100 times lower than that found in the current study. However, in the former study, the total Fe concentration in the uptake solutions was used for the kinetic analyses (and ranged from 0 to $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } $ , which resulted in a very large overestimation of the actual uptake solution $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 \bar { + } }$ activity, and yielded a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value that was much larger than the actual value.

Our additional findings that RIT1 complements the yeast Zn transport-defective mutant ZHY3, the Mn transport-defective mutant SLY8, and mediates moderately high affinity $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx and lower affinity $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in yeast, suggests that RIT1 may provide a common pathway for the entry of metals besides iron across the root-cell plasma membrane. These findings, along with the result that RIT1 expression is induced by Fe deficiency in roots of pea seedlings, corroborate evidence at the whole-plant level and in intact roots of an Fedeficiency-induced stimulation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake (Fox et al.1996; Cohen et al. 1998a). These results suggest that the Fe-deficiency-induced stimulation of Fe2+, $\mathrm { \bar { C } d } ^ { 2 + }$ and divalent cation influx in intact pea roots may be the result of increased RIT1 expression.

Interestingly, our results demonstrate that RIT1 shows the highest affinity for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ $( 5 4 - 9 3 ~ \mathrm { n M } )$ , moderate affinity for Zn $( 4 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , and much lower affinity for Cd $1 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . It should be noted that we obtained similar kinetics for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx when yeast $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake experiments were conducted with either chelate buffered or standard, non-chelate buffered uptake solutions. This finding indicates that the results are not due to any artifact resulting from the use of chelate-buffered uptake solutions. Thus, RIT1 may exhibit a high specificity for Fe but still may be promiscuous, in that it will transport other micronutrient metals or their analogues if the metal concentrations in the soil are high enough. Variable charge-density ratios of the metals $( { \mathrm { F e } } > { \mathrm { Z n } } > { \mathrm { C d } } )$ could account for, or contribute to, differences in binding affinity to the transporter.

The $Z \bar { \mathrm { n } } ^ { 2 + }$ influx values measured in our heterologous systems from uptake solutions containing micromolar Zn concentrations may be meaningful in a physiological context, as we have previously measured significant $^ { 6 5 } { \cal Z } \mathrm { n }$ influx from solutions containing 1 mM Zn using intact pea roots (Cohen et al.1998a). More recently, our laboratory conducted a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic analysis for root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficient and inefficient cultivars of wheat (Hacisalihoglu et al. 2001). In that study, we described a $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport system with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ that was very similar to the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1-mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx reported here $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ in wheat: $2 { \ - } 5 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1: $4 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ ). It is possible that a wheat RIT homolog may be mediating this moderately high affinity root $\bar { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. However, Hacisalihoglu et al. (2001) uncovered a second very high affinity root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake system, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\dot { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 \mp }$ influx of $0 . 6 { - } 2 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ The transport properties of this second $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporter are more in line with what would be expected for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx from the rhizosphere of agricultural soils. The estimated critical activity of $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ required for optimal plant growth ranges from 0.01 to $0 . 1 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ (Norvell and Welch 1993; Welch and Norvell 1993), and the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in a typical soil solution ranges from 1 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ (Lindsay 1991; Hodgson et al.1966). When we used chelate buffer techniques to control $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in the nanomolar range, we did not see significant RIT1- mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ fluxes (data not shown), suggesting that RIT1 does not normally play a role in root $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake at physiologically relevant soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ levels.

In conclusion, the findings reported here suggest that, in typical agricultural soils, RIT1 functions primarily as a high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter that mediates root Fe acquisition. However, the ability of RIT1 to facilitate $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake when these metals are present at elevated concentrations suggests that RIT1 may be one pathway for the entry of toxic metals into the food chain. These findings are consistent with those presented recently in the literature indicating that Arabidopsis IRT1 plays a major role in mediating root Fe uptake from the soil, but also may facilitate the uptake of other divalent metals (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). Furthermore, the finding that plant Fe deficiency status may promote heavy metal uptake via increased expression of this transporter could have implications both for human nutrition and also for phytoremediation—the use of terrestrial plants to sequester toxic metals from contaminated soil. A more comprehensive understanding of the regulation and function of RIT1 may contribute to further progress in these areas.

## 2.1.Analysis ofa Predicted Signal Peptide on the Malus xiaojinensis Iron-Regulated Transporter 1 (Mx IRT1) N-Terminus


The $N .$ -terminal SPs of ER-processed eukaryotic membrane and secretory proteins share similar canonical features，including a region containing polar and often charged amino acids at the $N .$ -terminus (N-region), a hydrophobic core ( $H .$ region） region at the center,and a polar region at the $C$ -terminal $C \mathrm { \cdot }$ region） portion [11,18].The SPs are typically cleaved from the mature protein during transport/processing through the ER. A comparative analysis of the $N .$ -termini of IRT1 proteins from several plant species with known cleavable SPs in other organisms indicated that these characteristic SP regions are present in the plant iron transport proteins as well (Figure 1A). For this study, we have focused primarily on the $N .$ -terminus of Mx IRT1. Using SignalP4.1 for analysis, it was found that amino acids located between the $N .$ -terminal and residue 30 of Mx IRT1 showed the highest $S \mathrm { . }$ -scores, with a maximum of 0.882, and a mean $S \mathrm { . }$ -score of O.674. This indicates that the first 29 residues occur before the cleavage site. The Q residue at position 30 had a high $C \mathrm { \cdot }$ -score of 0.815 (Figure 1B), suggesting a likely cleavage site between the 29th (S:Ser) and 30th(Q:Gln) residues.These results are consistent with the presence of a cleavable 1-29 amino acid SP at the $N .$ -terminus of Mx IRT1 (Figure 1B).

While most $N .$ -terminal peptides with these characteristic features have been shown to be responsible for correct membrane sorting through the ER,and are cleaved from the mature protein during this process, there are some exceptions. For example, the $N .$ -terminus of the G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) CRF2a (Figure 1A), predicted by SignalP [17] to posses features typical of a cleavable SP, has been found by functional analysis to a“pseudo”SP that cannot mediate ER traficking and is not cleaved from the mature protein [20]. Furthermore, while SignalP4.1 has predicted that almost all IRT1 family members contain a putative cleavable $N .$ -terminal SP,an alignment of their actual amino acids sequences reveals only weak conservation (Figure 1C). Therefore,to understand the precise intracelllar trafficking of Mx IRT1, it is important to confirm that its predicted $N .$ -terminal SP does in fact function as a bona fide, cleavable sorting peptide that mediates its ER trafficking, membrane localization,and ultimately its efficient iron uptake capability [8,10].

2.2. Deletion of the N-Terminal Mx IRT1 Signal Peptide (SP) Reduces Iron Uptake Ability in Arabidopsis and Yeast

To understand the role of the putative SP as a determinant of Mx IRT1 function, we used genetic complementation to comparatively analyze the metal uptake ability of Arabidopsis plants and yeast cells expressing a Mx IRT1, or a modified Mx IRT1 in which the predicted SP had been deleted (designated Mx DsIRT1) (Figure 2A). For expression in plants, these Mx IRTl,and Mx DsIRTl constructs were inserted into the expression vector pCAMBIA1301-35Spro-NOSterminator. A GFP (green fluorescent protein） tag at the $C \mathrm { \cdot }$ -terminal end of both proteins allowed for visualization of their trafficking through the plant cells by confocal fluorescence microscopy (please see Section 2.3). For complementation in yeast cells, these same constructs (without the GFP tag） were inserted into the expression vector pDBLeu. Genetic complementation/expression assays were performed using an Arabidopisis irtl iron uptake mutant, as well as the yeast mutant DEY 1453 (fet3fet4) that has impaired iron uptake ability.

Mx IRTl and Mx DsIRTl (and as a control, the vector alone) were introduced into an Arabidopisis irtl mutant that shows a lethal chlorotic phenotype associated with an iron deficiency condition. This severe chlorotic phenotype is not observed when WT(wild type) plants are grown under the same conditions. Furthermore, the irtl mutation can be complemented by constitutive expression of the endogenous At IRT1 from a 35S promoter (35S:At IRT1)，with transformed plants showing the WT growth phenotype [3]. In this experiment, wild type (WT), irtl:vector (vector alone), irt1:Mx IRTl,and irt1:Mx DsIRTl Arabidopsis lines were grown in $1 / 2 ~ \mathrm { M S }$ for 7 days,and then transferred to 1/2 MS medium supplemented with Fe (CK medium) or deficient in Fe (-Fe medium) for 10 days. On Fe-supplied media (CK), the growth of transgenic lines expressng the heterologous Mx IRT1 transporter was comparable to that of the WT seedlings (Figure 2B, top row). ## 2.4. The N-Terminal 1-29 Amino-Acid Sequence Contributes to ER Targeting


Based on the effect of the Mx IRT1 SP deletion on its localization,and in view of previous findings that some PM membrane proteins are sorted to the PM through the SP-dependent ER secretory pathway [13,18,25], we systematically studied whether Mx IRT1 $N .$ -terminus is in fact an authentic SP capable of guiding the intact Mx IRT1 to the ER for synthesis and PM sorting.

ER-mCherry (red) is a fluorescent marker protein that is targeted to the ER of plant cels [22]. When transiently expressed together with Mx IRT1-eGFP in protoplasts,both of these fluorescent labeled proteins were found to co-localize (yellow), showing a mesh-like pattrn characteristic of ER localized proteins (Figure 5A,toprow, white arrow indicates co-localization).This co-localization confirms that the full-ength Mx IRT1 was guided to and translated in the ER. However, in the case of Mx DsIRT1-eGFP, the green eGFP fluorescence signal was detected diffusely throughout the cytoplasm, showing no co-localization with the mCherry-ER. The lack of co-localization indicates that the SP-deleted Mx DsIRT1-eGFP did not enter the ER for translation and sorting (Figure 5A, botom row). For a more precise comparative determination of Mx IRT1-eGFP and Mx DsIRT1-eGFP distribution in protoplast, we used laser scanning for visualization of fluorescence at different cell depths using multiple focal planes (depth increases from left to right in Figure 5B). This multi-focal plane scanning revealed that a mesh-like structure associated with Mx IRT1-eGFP occurred throughout the cell(Figure 5B, top row), while the Mx DsIRT1-eGFP was evenly distributed throughout the cytosol in a highly diffuse pattern (Figure 5B, middle row), in a pattern indistinguishable from the eGFP alone (Figure 5B,bottom row). From the Figures 3B and 5A,B, we found the Mx IRT1-eGFP localized both to the ER and the PM in the same cell. As reported, At IRT1 was also observed both in the intracellular compartment and PM in the same root hair cell 8]. Interestingly,At IRT1 accumulated under metal-depleted conditions at the outer polar domain of the PM facing the rhizosphere [10]. These results indicate the IRT1 protein experiences a dynamic location according to the environmental change，which process may control ion absorption. Therefore, it is conceivable that the significant accumulation of Mx IRTlin the ER may keep the rate of export from this compartment for the balance of iron uptake.

## 2.5. The SP Remains on the Mature Mx IRT1 Protein


For most ER target proteins, the $N .$ -terminal SP is cleaved from the protein by the ER-resident signal peptidase while it is still growing on the ribosome. If the functional $N .$ -terminal SP is in fact cleaved from mature Mx IRT1, then the Mx IRT1-eGFP and Mx DsIRT1-eGFP proteins from the expression constructs should co-migrate when separated by SDS-PAGE (dodecyl sulfate， sodium salt Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis). Unexpectedly， the mature MxIRT1-GFP showed a higher molecular weight than Mx DsIRT1-GFP when purified from the transgenic plants and yeast. By extending the time of SDS-PAGE electrophoresis for clear separation, it was found that the protein band for Mx IRT1-eGFP was approximately $3 ~ \mathrm { \ k D a }$ larger than that of Mx DsIRT1-eGFP (69 vs. 66 kDa, respectively) in both plant and yeast cells (Figure 6A).Meanwhile, we compared the molecular weight of SP(1-54)-eGFP with $\Delta \mathrm { S P - e G F P } ( 3 0 - 5 4 )$ in transformed yeast.Per the molecular weight, the SP(1-54)-eGFP $( \sim 3 1 \ \mathrm { k D a } )$ was ${ \sim } 3 \ \mathrm { k D a }$ larger than △SP-eGFP(30-54) $( 2 8 \mathrm { k D a } )$ (Figure 6A). These results provide evidence that the signal peptide of the Mx IRT1 is not cleaved from the mature protein.

For further evidence that the $N .$ -terminal SP is retained on the mature protein, a cMyc-tag was added to the $N .$ -terminus end of Mx IRT1, upstream of the SP region. Two constructs were prepared for expression in yeast (Figure 6B). The first， designated pYES-cMyc-Mx IRT1-eGFP, lacked the Mx IRT1's ATG initiation codon. The second,designated pYES-cMyc-ATG-Mx IRT1-eGFP,contained the initiator ATG codon (Figure 6B). These were transformed into yeast cells for analysis of $N .$ -terminal cleavage. Proteins were extracted by phase partitioning into two distinct fractions (a reagent kit “Thermo Mem-PER Eukaryotic Membrane Protein Extraction"), a hydrophilic fraction containing soluble protein and a hydrophobic fraction that included the membrane proteins. As a positive control, anti-GFP detected all three proteins, including Mx IRT1-eGFP (without the cMyc-tag, as a positive control) only in the membrane fraction (Figure 6C, middle row). Similarly, the PM marker Pmalp was found only in the membrane fraction and not in the soluble component (Figure 6C, bottom row). We also extracted intact membrane fractions from yeast transformed with pYES-cMyc-Mx RT1-eGFP using an Optiprep density gradient described before and detected cMyc using the cMyc antibody. As shown in Figure 6D,cMyc signals were mainly present in fractions 1 and 2, similar to

Pmalp.This result further demonstrates that the SP is present on the mature Mx IRT1. Taken together, the data shown in Figure 6 support that the $N .$ -terminal region of Mx IRT1, shown in this study to be a bona fide functional SP,remains intact on the mature PM-associated Mx IRT1 molecule.

Since the discovery of SPs,the SP hypothesis of secretory proteins has predicted the co-translational targeting, processing, and removal of the $N .$ -terminal signaling sequence, a process mediated through cytoplasmic chaperones such as HSP70/40 that promote SP interactions with a signal-recognition particle located within the rough ER membrane [26-29]. In addition, a better understanding of the mechanisms by which integral proteins interact with the ER was provided [30]. Integral membrane proteins located in the PM, Golgi,lysosomes (tonoplast), and peroxisomal membrane are allsynthesized on the rough ER membrane. Numerous studies have demonstrated a paradigm in which $N .$ -terminal SPs of PM integral proteins were cleaved by signal peptidases during translocon-mediated insertion into the ER membrane [13,18,25]. However, there are some exceptions, such as sucrase-isomaltase (type ) [31], prion protein [32], CD18,and the $\beta$ -subunit of $\beta _ { 2 }$ -integrins [14],in which the SP has been found to be uncleaved. In this study, we presented another exception to the canonical pathway [30] by showing that an essential plant membrane protein, Mx IRT1 has a non-cleavable SP protein that mediates its entry into the ER and trafficking to the PM, thereby enabling its critical iron transport function.

It is not yet known why some PM proteins require that an uncleaved SP be retained at their $N .$ -terminus, whereas most others do not. Recent work suggests that the uncleaved SPs do not only serve the classical mediators ofER targeting,but might in fact have additional role(s)as well. As one example, the uncleaved SP of the PM protein CD18 has been found to be a factor in rendering ruminants susceptible to leukotoxin of the pathogen Mannheimia haemolytica [14]. As to the uncleaved SP of Mx IRT1, we can speculate that it might play additional roles as well such as participating in regulation of the protein stability, maintaining correct the protein location, mediating interaction with other proteins, or in binding of as yet unknown ligands. Our results also suggest that Mx IRT1 likely possesses nine TMDs instead of eight. Interestingly, our results also suggest that Mx IRT1 likely possesses nine TMDs instead of the predicted eight, possibility indicating an insertional or positional role for the attached SP peptide.

To date, the identification of the $N .$ -terminus of IRT1 family members as a functional SP has only been predicted based on sequence analysis. In this study, we have experimentally analyzed properties of the Mx IRT1 of the $N .$ -terminus and shown it to be a bona fide signal peptide for ER sorting,a property shared with other well characterized ER markers such as the signal peptide of Arabidopsis wall-associated kinase 2 [22]. What makes Mx IRT1 unique from other known plant PM proteins is its uncleaved $N .$ -terminal SP peptide. Consistent with our localization experiments, the lost of its correct transport capability for the truncated Mx IRT1 protein was due to its improper trafficking and localization within the cell We found that the full-length Mx IRT1 could rescue the growth of Arabidopsis IRTl mutant, but Mx DsIRT1, which lacked the SP,could not. Interestingly,immunoblot analysis detected both the ful-ength Mx IRT1 as wellas the truncated version of Mx DsIRT1 in transgenic Arabidopsis IRT1, indicating that there are several other factors that contribute to the lack of degradation of the truncated Mx DsIRT1. With the yeast heterologous complementation experiments, we verified the ability of Mx IRT1 to transport bivalent iron and cadmium, as has been demonstrated for the related iron transport protein At IRT1 [2,33,34]. Recently, there has been some controversy related to the functional necessity of the His-box region in the At IRT1 and Mx IRT1 proteins. The His-box has been shown to be essential for iron transport in Mx IRT1,but not in At IRT1 [35,36].Therefore,the exact mechanism of divalent metal transport utilized by the IRT family members warrants further study. Based on findings presented here, it would be highly interesting to determine if the attched SP sequence of MxIRT1 plays a role in mediating the metal absorption efcacy of this important PM-localized iron transport protein.

Iron is an essential nutrient for plants and other organisms. It is critical for many processes in plants, including serving as a cofactor for redox enzymes involved in photosynthesis and respiration, as well as a catalyst for chlorophyllbiosynthesis [1]. Although naturally very abundant in soils, iron is not easily absorbed by plant roots due to its insolubility under neutral or alkaline conditions [1]. Previous studies have used reverse genetics to demonstrate that iron-regulated transporter 1 (IRT1) is a major multi-pass plasma membrane (PM) importer responsible for iron uptake from soil under conditions of iron deficiency [2-4]. Most significantly，severe chlorosis and lethality due to reduced iron uptake have been observed in an Arabidopsis irtl-1 knockout mutant [4]. The IRT1 protein family is widespread, occurring in a variety of dicots and monocots including but not limited to Arabidopsis [2], maize [5], rice [6], and Malus xiaojinensis [7]. A series of studies with Arabidopsis have provided significant new insights on the sorting, trafficking and localization of IRT1 within plant cells. Surprisingly, IRT1 has been found to be predominantly localized to the trans-Golgi network and early endosomes of root hairs [8]. Additional findings have demonstrated that members of the sorting nexinl (SNX1) family of proteins are necessary for the correct trafficking of At (Arabidopsis thaliana) IRT1，and for modulating overall iron uptake activity [9]. A recently identified endosomal protein， FYVE1 (a phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate-binding protein recruited to late endosomes), was found to control IRT1 recycling and polar delivery to the PM outer domain [10]. Together these findings indicate that efficient iron uptake mediated by IRT1 ultimately relies on precise intracellular traficking of this essential transporter to the outer PM domain. However, specific protein sequences or domains within the IRT1 protein itself that interact with celular trafficking components to meditate its transport to this domain are currently not well understood. It is known that two Lys residues located within a cytosol-exposed loop domain aect the ubiquitination, endocytosis,and degradation of IRT1 [8]. It is clear that further studies of the domain-based sorting signals are needed to understand how the complex sorting pathway of IRT1 functions,and how this pathway might be modified for improving iron uptake and bioavailability in plants.

Trafficking of multi-pass PM proteins such as IRT1 typically require an $N .$ -terminal signal peptide (SP) which enables their incorporation into the ER (endoplasmic reticulum) endomembrane transport system,and an internal membrane-anchor stop transfer sequence that delineates a transmembrane region. The ER-targeting SPs of such proteins vary somewhat in their primary sequence and length, but are typically 15-3O residues long,with polar or charged residues at the $N .$ -terminal， followed by a 6-15 amino acid region of hydrophobic residues and a polar $C \mathrm { \cdot }$ -terminal region containing the cleavage site for signal peptidase [11,12]. As these ER targeted proteins are being translated in the cytoplasm,the signal recognition particle (SRP） recognizes the newly synthesized $N .$ -terminal signal peptide, represses translation, and attches the nascent protein-ribosome complex to an SRP receptor on the ER membrane. The SRP then disassociates,allowing translation to continue,and the protein is brought into the ER lumen through a translocator channel as it is being synthesized [11,13]. Typically, the SP will then be cleaved from the $N .$ -terminal protein by an ER-resident signal peptidase. This mature protein, lacking the signal sequence, is then trafficked through the ER and inserted into the PM. However, a very small minority of mature ER processed proteins located at the surface of animal cells have been shown to retain their intact $N .$ -terminal SP,such as CD18, the $\beta$ -subunit of $\beta _ { 2 }$ -integrins [14]. Multi-pass PM proteins that retain an uncleaved $N .$ -terminal signal peptides have not yet been reported in plants.

Malus xiaojinensis is an iron-efficient plant species in the genus Malus [15,16]. Its inducible iron transporter Mx IRTl has been shown to be highly expressed in roots under Fe deficiency,and is considered to be a key determinant ofiron-efficiency for this species [7]. We report here that the mature ER-transported Mx IRT1 protein retains its $N .$ -terminal signal peptide when inserted into the PM. Analysis using the bioinformatics tool SignalP4.1 [17] indicates the presence of a putative SP with domains characteristic of a cleaved SP at $N .$ -terminal 1-29 amino acids of Mx IRT1. The goal of this study was to identify the function of this putative SP through complementation and location analysis, using transgene complementation of an Arabidopsis IRTl mutant and the iron uptake deficient yeast mutant fet3fet4. Findings presented here demonstrate that mature Mx IRT1 iron transporter retains the bona fide $N .$ -terminal SP that directs ER entry and transport through the PM secretory pathway to the cell surface. This study provides the first evidence for a functional uncleaved SP in plants.

IRT1, the founding member of ZIP transporter family, was identified by a powerful suppressor screen based on the complementation of yeast fet3 multicopper oxidase and fet4 Fe(II)-transporter mutations that block high and low affinity iron transport, respectively (Askwith et al., 1994; Dix et al., 1994;

Eide et al., 1996). IRT1 was also found to suppress the zrt1zrt2 mutations of high and low-affinity zinc transporters and the smf1 $\Delta$ mutation of a high-affinity Nramp manganese transporter, as well as to increase cadmium sensitivity, when expressed in yeast (Korshunova et al., 1999; Rogers et al., 2000). Nonetheless, IRT1 turned out to differ both structurally and functionally from these yeast transporter proteins, but shows homology to numerous putative membrane proteins in eukaryotes, including predicted products of $1 5 ~ Z I P$ genes in the sequenced Arabidopsis genome (Guerinot, 2000; Mäser et al., 2001). Characterization of other members of ZIP family indicated that IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1, facilitates iron and zinc uptake, whereas ZIP1, ZIP2 and ZIP3 mediate only zinc transport in yeast. YS1 (yellow strip 1) gene in Arabidopsis suggests that even further transporters are implicated in the control of iron homeostasis in plants (Curie et al., 2001).

This high redundancy raises the logical question whether reverse genetics, producing single recessive or dominant gene mutations, would be helpful in the dissection of physiological functions of individual plant metal transporters. Our pulse-labeling experiments with $^ { 5 9 } \mathrm { F e }$ seem to contradict the data of Yi and Guerinot (1996), who found very little iron accumulation in shoots within the first hour of $^ { 5 5 } \mathrm { F e }$ trace labeling.
