fact that nitrogen transport is difficult to measure. Some studies rely on the analysis of the depletion of the medium, others use stable isotopes, or the $\mathsf { \Omega } ^ { 1 3 } \mathsf { N } .$ -isotope, which has a short half-life time of ${ \sim } 1 0$ min and requires access to a suitable supply source (Wang et al., 1993; Clarkson et al., 1996). Most of these techniques lack spatial resolution, that is information on which cell layers and which root zones absorb the nutrient. Electrophysiological assays can provide spatial information; however, they are mostly used at accessible surfaces. Spatial information has been provided in a few studies by methods such as vibrating electrodes (Henriksen et al., 1990, 1992), positron-emitting tracer imaging systems (Matsunami et al., 1999; Kiyomiya et al., 2001), or secondary ion mass spectrometers (Clode et al., 2009). We also know little about differences in the distribution of the nitrogen forms in different root cell types or zones and with respect to cellular compartmentation. Classical approaches average total ion/metabolite levels over all cells in the sample, for example, in whole roots. Nitrate levels differ dramatically between root cell types (Zhen et al., 1991; Karley et al., 2000). Recently, a GFP-labeled protoplast-sorting platform was used to compare metabolomes of individual cell types in roots (Moussaieff et al., 2013). This study found that the levels of small oligopeptides were comparatively higher in the epidermis and endodermis compared to other root cell types. Compartmental analyses indicated that the nitrate concentration of root vacuoles is ∼10-fold higher compared to the cytosol (Zhen et al., 1991).

Transporters are placed in strategic positions to control which and how much of a specific nitrogen form can enter a given cell at a given point of time. The progress in identifying transporter genes provided a new handle for addressing the mechanisms and the spatial and temporal regulation of nitrogen acquisition from a new level of detail. Three major families of transporters for inorganic nitrogen uptake (and distribution) have been identified: the NPF/POT nitrate transporter family (Leran et al., 2013), NRT2 nitrate transporters (Kotur et al., 2012), and the ammonium transporters of the AMT/ MEP/Rh family (von Wirén et al., 2000; Andrade and Einsle, 2007). In addition to their role in nitrate uptake, members of the NPF/POT (Leran et al., 2013) family play important roles also in the transport of histidine, dicarboxylates, oligopeptides, and glucosinolates, and surprisingly at least three major plant hormones: auxin, ABA, and gibberellin (Krouk et al., 2010; Kanno et al., 2012; Boursiac et al., 2013). Genes are valuable tools for exploring physiological functions. Analysis of RNA levels allows us to study gene regulation (Gazzarrini et al., 1999), for example, transcriptional GUS-fusions for determining organ and cell type specific expression and translational GFP-fusions for subcellular localization. Both classical and novel methods, including cell-specific transcriptional profiles and ‘translatomes’ provide us with new insights into differences in the expression of transporters in roots (Brady et al., 2007; Mustroph et al., 2009). Analysis of cell type-specific expression profiles showed that the majority of changes in nitrate-induced gene expression are cell-specific (Gifford et al., 2008). Expression and purification of the proteins followed by reconstitution in vesicles or expression in heterologous systems to interrogate biochemical properties include $\mathsf { K } _ { \mathsf { m } }$ and transport mechanisms. The genes can be used as a basis for structure function studies (Loqué et al., 2007) and to obtain crystal structures (Andrade et al., 2005; Doki et al., 2013). We can use the genes to identify interacting proteins (Lalonde et al., 2010). Importantly, the availability of genes enables us to generate specific mutants (Yuan et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2009) that provide insights into their physiological roles. However, even with this massive amount of detailed data, the key information is missing, namely the information on the activity state of a given protein in vivo. In vivo activity depends mainly on two additional parameters beyond protein abundance at a given membrane: the local concentration of the substrate/s, the status of the cell (e.g., the membrane potential and local pH as key determinants for ion transporter activity), and the status of cellular regulatory networks required for the activity of the protein in question. Again, genes can help us to find regulators and study the effect of mutations on nitrogen acquisition, but ultimately we need to be able to quantify the activity of the transporters in individual cells in vivo.

Nitrogen uptake is controlled by many factors, such as nitrogen level, energy status of the plant, assimilation status of imported nitrogen, N-demand, and involved mobile signals between shoots and roots as well as between different parts of the root system (von Wirén et al., 1997). Nitrate transporters are regulated through phosphorylation, mediated by calcium-dependent calcineurin-like kinases (Calcineurin B-like, CBL and CBL-interacting protein kinase, CIPK) (Ho et al., 2009; Hu et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2009). Major breakthroughs were findings that indicate both the members of the AMT and NPF/POT family function as transporters and receptors (transceptors) (Ho et al., 2009; Lima et al., 2010; Rubio-Texeira et al., 2010). However, despite broad progress, at present, we have only a limited understanding of signaling pathways that control nitrogen acquisition.

It is important to develop tools for monitoring the activity of individual transporters in specific locations in individual cells of plant roots in a minimally invasive manner. A minimally invasive tool that has proven valuable for monitoring ions and metabolite levels with high spatial and temporal resolution is genetically encoded fluorescent nanosensors (Okumoto, 2012). These sensors rely on substrate binding–dependent conformational rearrangements in a sensory domain. The rearrangements are reported by changes in Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) efficiency between two fluorescent proteins, which act as FRET donor and acceptor due to spectral overlap. Sensors for glucose, sucrose, and zinc have successfully been used in Arabidopsis to monitor steady state levels as well as accumulation and elimination under both static and dynamic conditions where roots were exposed to pulses of the respective analytes (Deuschle et al., 2006; Chaudhuri et al., 2008; Okumoto et al., 2008; Chaudhuri et al., 2011; Lanquar et al., 2014).

The recent progress in obtaining crystal structures for transporters, and more importantly the availability of transporter structures in multiple configurations, has provided insights into the conformational rearrangements occurring during the transport cycle (Doki et al., 2013; Guettou et al., 2013; Henderson and Baldwin, 2013; Madej et al., 2013). Biochemical and structural analyses have shown that many transporters undergo conformational changes during the transport cycle (Shimamura et al., 2010; Jiang, 2012a; Krishnamurthy and Gouaux, 2012). Important in this context is that such rearrangements have been observed for many members of the MFS superfamily, including members of the NPF/ POT family (Doki et al., 2013). We therefore hypothesized that it should be possible to ‘record’ the conformational rearrangements that occur during the transport cycle in a similar manner as used for the engineering of the FRET sensors. The first prototype for transport activity sensors, named AmTrac, uses ammonium transporters as sensory domains for engineering transport activity sensors by inserting a circularly permutated EGFP (cpEGFP) into a conformation-sensitive position of an ammonium transporter (De Michele et al., 2013). Addition of ammonium to yeast cells expressing the AmTrac sensor triggers concentration-dependent and reversible changes in fluorescence intensity (De Michele et al., 2013). Whether this approach is transferable to other family proteins in different species remained to be shown. To create nitrate and peptide transport activity sensors, we fused CHL1 and four PTRs to fluorescent protein pairs, expressed the fusions in yeast, and tested their response to substrate addition (named NiTrac for nitrate transport activity and PepTrac for peptide transport activity). The five sensors responded to the addition of nitrate or peptides, respectively. The kinetics of the NiTrac1 sensor response was strikingly similar to the transport kinetics of the native CHL1; the response was specific and reversible. The new sensors were used to study structure/function relationships, to correlate effects of mutations in CHL1 and NiTrac1 on activity and sensor responses, and to observe the effect of potential regulators on the conformation of the transporter. The successful use of the sensors in yeast indicates that these new tools can be used for in planta analyses.

The non-essential element cadmium (Cd) is toxic to both plants and animals.Excess Cd in soils can be absorbed by plant roots,which inhibits plant growth and diminishes crop yields [1].Importantly,the Cd absorbed by roots can be transported to the shoots and deposited in grains or friuts.Through the dietary intake,plant-derived Cd can enter the human body.Due to its long biological half-life,the Cd level in the body progressively accumulates by low-dose chronic exposure,which can cause various diseases such as renal dysfunction and osteoporosis [2, 3].Therefore,it is desirable to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of Cd detoxification and accumulation in plants,which will enable the development of low-Cd crops,thus reducing dietary intake of Cd by humans.

Cd enters root cells mainly through transport systems responsible for the uptake of essential elements [4,5],such as the manganese transporter OsNramp5 (natural resistance-associated macrophage protein 5) functioning as the major pathway for Cd entry into rice [6-8]. Once adsorbed into the root cels, Cd can cause serious cellular injuries [1,5]. Plants have evolved a series of strategies to cope with Cd toxicity, including extrusion,complexation with thiol-rich compounds such as glutathione (GSH) and phytochelatins (PCs),and vacuolar compartmentalization [5,9].During these biological processes,transporters from different families play important roles.For example,some efflux transporters localized in the plasma membrane can extrude Cd out of root cells [1O,11].AtPDR8(AtABCG36) has been identified as a Cd exporter in Arabidopsis.Its overexpression increases Cd extrusion and reduces the Cd content in the engineered plants,thus conferring resistance to Cd[11].Inaddition,Cd or its complexes can also be sequestered in vacuoles by transporters localized on the tonoplast. Several types of transporter, including HMA (Heavy Metal ATPases),ABC (ATP-binding cassette) and CAX (cation/proton exchanger) transporters,have been demonstrated to be involved in this process [12].In rice,OsHMA3 is the major transporter mediating Cd transport into root cell vacuoles,and the non-functional OsHMA3 fails to sequester Cd into vacuoles,consequently increasing the root-to-shoot Cd translocation [13,14]. Together, the extrusion and vacuolar sequestration of Cd in root cells can not only alleviate Cd toxicity,but also restrict Cd translocation and accumulation in shoots and seeds.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute a large,diverse gene superfamily found in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.Plant ABC transporters are grouped into eight major subfamilies (A-G,I) according to domain structure and evolutionary relationships [15].ABC proteins exhibit wide substrate profiles,including lipids,metals/metalloids,and phytohormones [16]. For example,OsABCC1 can sequester arsenic-PC conjugates in the vacuoles,thereby participating in arsenic detoxification and limiting its transport to the rice grains [17].Multiple ABC transporters have been reported to be capable of transporting Cd or Cd complexes [l2].The first ABC transporter that has been described as a Cd transporter is HMT1 in the fission yeast,which can transport PC-Cd complex into the vacuole for Cd detoxification [18,19]. Subsequently, additional ABC transporters involved in Cd (conjugate) transport have been found in various species [11,2O,21]．In Arabidopsis,besides AtABCG36 [11],three C-type ABC transporters,AtABCC1,AtABCC2 and AtABCC3,are also implicated in Cd tolerance by sequestering PC-Cd complexes into vacuoles [21,22].

133 genes have been annotated as ABC transporters in the whole rice genome [16],and two of them have been shown to participate in Cd tolerance so far. OsABCG43 is induced by Cd treatment in rice roots and confers Cd tolerance in yeast [23],but its exact function in rice remains unclear.Recently，involvement of another rice ABC transporter, OsABCG36,in Cd tolerance has been reported by Fu et al.[1O]. OsABCG36 can be induced in rice roots by brief Cd exposure and is localized to the plasma membrane.Heterologous expression of OsABCG36 in yeast showed an efflux activity for Cd, so itis thought to be required for Cd tolerance by exporting Cd or Cd complexes from the root cells in rice [1O].High-throughput analyses such as microarray and RNA sequencing have shown that OsABCC9 is also up-regulated by Cd treatment [24,25],suggesting its possible involvement in Cd tolerance in rice.However,it has not yet been established what role it plays in Cd tolerance in rice.In this study,we have investigated the role of OsABCC9 in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.The results showed that OsABCC9 was mainly expressed in the root stele under Cd stress,and was localized on the tonoplast.Disruption of OsABCC9 enhanced the Cd sensitivity of rice and the Cd content in the xylem sap and grains. Furthermore,its heterologous expression in yeast resulted in enhanced Cd tolerance along with a higher intracellular Cd content.We therefore propose that OsABCC9 is a vacuolar transporter that confers Cd tolerance and affects Cd accumulation in rice.

OsABCC9 (LOC_Os04g13210) was annotated to contain 1278 and 1207 amino acids (aa) in the Rice Annotation Project Database (RAP-DB, http://rapdb.dna.affrc.go.jp/) and the MsU rice genome annotation project database (RGAP， http://rice.plantbiology.msu.edu/)， respectively.When searching in NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information) database,two splice variants of OsABCC9 (1545 and 1603 aa) were obtained,both of which are longer than the sequences in RAPDB and RGAP at the ${ \boldsymbol { 5 } } ^ { \prime }$ terminus.Since the OsABCC9 sequence in NCBI was updated more recently,it may represent the genuine OsABCC9 sequence.Thus,based on the OsABCC9 sequence in NCBI, the full-length ORF(open reading frame) of OsABCC9 was obtained from the model japonica rice variety Nipponbare by high-fidelity PCR.This OsABCC9 ORF is 4638 bp,encoding a predicted protein of 1545 aa. Gene structure analysis showed OsABCC9 has 11 exons and 10 introns (Fig. S1A).A conserved domain search revealed that OsABCC9 harborstwo nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) and two transmembrane domains (TMDs),so it belongs to the full-size ABC transporter (Fig.S1B). Phylogenetic analysis with the C-type ABC transporters in rice and Arabidopsis showed that OsABCC9 is most closely related to OsABCC10 with $6 7 \%$ identity.Among the Arabidopsis ABCC subfamily,AtABCC14 is the closest homolog of OsABCC9 with $5 5 \%$ identity (Fig. S1C, Supplementary data 2).


## 3.2.Expression pattern of OsABCC9


Previous high-throughput analysis revealed that OsABCC9 is upregulated by Cd treatment [24,25],and we examined its expression pattern in more detail by quantitative RT-PCR analysis.Compared with the control,OsABCC9 was significantly induced by Cd treatment in roots,but not in shoots (Fig.lA).The roots were further divided into root tips $\left( 0 - 1 \ \mathrm { c m } \right)$ and basal region roots $( 1 - 2 ~ \mathrm { c m } )$ ,and stronger induction by Cd was observed in the root tips (Fig.1B).Moreover, the time-dependent alterations in the expression of OsABCC9 were examined.As shown in Fig.1C,an increase in the transcriptlevel of OsABCC9 was detected after 1 h exposure to $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd and it continued to increase over $^ { 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of the same treatment,whereas the extent of induction was decreased at 12 and $2 4 \ \mathrm { h }$ after Cd exposure.The transcript level of OsABCC9 was also detected in the presence of different Cd concentrations.As shown in Fig.1D, OsABCC9 expression was elevated in roots treated with $1 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ Cd,and continued to increase with higher Cd exposure,suggesting that OsABCC9 is responsive to external Cd in a concentration-dependent fashion.Furthermore,the responsiveness of OsABCC9 to other metals including zinc $\mathbf { ( } \mathbf { Z n } )$ ,aluminium (Al),and lanthanum (La),was also detected. It was also induced by Zn toxicity, albeit with a lower degree of induction relative to Cd treatment (Fig.1E),suggesting that OsABCC9 is not specifically induced by Cd exposure.


## 3.3． Tissue and subcellular localization of OsABCC9


To analyze the tissue localization of OsABCC9,we generated a transgenic rice line carrying the $2 . 0 \mathrm { k b }$ promoter of OsABCC9 fused with the GFP gene.Immunostaining with an anti-GFP antibody showed weak GFP signals in the epidermis,exodermis,and stele of roots without exposure to Cd (Fig.2C-E),pointing to low expression of OsABCC9 in the absence of Cd.However, in roots treated with Cd, the GFP signal intensity was increased,especially in the stele (Fig.2F-H).These results suggested that the OsABCC9 promoter activity is elevated under Cd exposure,which is consistent with the OsABCC9 expression pattern (Fig.1A).As the negative control, the anti-GFP antibody was also reacted with wild-type roots, but no signal was detected (Fig.2A and B), indicating the specificity of the antibody.

To determine the subcellular localization of OsABCC9,the fusion construct OsABCC9-GFP was co-transformed with the tonoplast marker AtTPK1 (AT5G55630) [28] into rice protoplasts.The green fluorescence signal of OsABCC9-GFP overlapped neatly with the red fluorescence signal generated by AtTPKl-mCherry (Fig.3).By contrast, the green fluorescence signal was visible in the cytosol when GFP alone was expressed (Fig.3)．These results indicated that OsABCC9isa tonoplast-localized transporter.


## 3.4.Cd transport activity of OsABCC9 in yeast


To test whether OsABCC9 possesses transport activity for Cd, it was cloned into the yeast expression vector pYES2 and expressed in the Cdsensitive yeast strain △ycf1 that lacks the vacuolar C-type ABC transporter YCF1 [29].Yeast harboring OsABCC9 and empty vector were cultured on galactose-containing medium with or without Cd.On Cd-free medium,the OsABCC9-expressing yeast grew similarly to those transformed with the empty vector.However,on medium containing Cd (5or $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ ，the OsABCC9 transformants grew better than the vector-transformed yeast (Fig.4A).As negative controls, the transformants were also grown on glucose-containing medium.There was no difference in growth between yeast with OsABCC9 and the empty vector independent of Cd conditions (Fig.S2).These results indicated that OsABCC9 confers Cd tolerance in the yeast mutant △ycf1.

The Cd tolerance conferred by OsABCC9 might be due to sequestration of Cd into vacuoles or extrusion of Cd out of cells.To test these possibilities,the Cd content in OsABCC9-expressing yeast and controls was measured after exposure to Cd for 2 and $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 4 h }$ 、Asa result,the OsABCC9 transformants had higher Cd content than controls after treatment with Cd for $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ ,and the difference in Cd content increased after treatment with Cd for 4h (Fig.4B).Therefore,the Cd tolerance conferred by OsABCC9 is most likely due to vacuolar sequestration of Cd rather than Cd extrusion.

Additionally,several C-type ABC transporters have been shown to participate in arsenic (As) tolerance and accumulation in plants [17,30, 31],so the possible role of OsABCC9 in As tolerance was also examined in △ycf1 yeast.However,no difference in growth between OsABCC9 transformants and controls was observed on medium containing 100 or $2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ NaAsO2 (Fig.S3),demonstrating that OsABCC9 did not affect the As tolerance when expressed in △ycf1.


## 3.5.Knockout of OsABCC9 enhanced Cd sensitivity of rice


To investigate the role of OsABCC9 in Cd tolerance in planta,we created osabcc9 knockout mutants using the CRISPR/Cas9 approach.

Two independent mutants,osabcc9-1 and osabcc9-2,were identified by sequencing analysis,each of which contained a 1-bp insertion (A or T) in the target site,respectively (Fig.S4).These insertions resulted in frameshift mutations in OsABCC9.Both mutant plants were used for growth analysis under different Cd conditions.At O and $1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, no growth difference was observed between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Fig. 5A and B). When exposed to 5 and $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, however,root growth of the OsABCC9 knockout mutants was more inhibited relative to the wild-type plants (Fig.5C and D). Quantitative analysis also showed that both the root and shoot dry weight (DW) of osabcc9 mutants were significantly lower than those of the wild type when grown with 5 and $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd (Fig.5E and F).These results indicated that loss of function of OsABCC9 led to sensitivity to Cd in rice.

The sensitivity of osabcc9 mutants to As was also examined.No visible difference in growth was observed between the osabcc9 mutants and wild-type plants,regardless of the As conditions (Fig. S5A and B).

Moreover,quantitative analysis of the dry weight and As content of the roots and shoots showed no differences between osabcc9 mutants and the wild-type (Figs.S5C and D, S6A and B).These results indicated that OsABCC9 may not participate in As tolerance and accumulation in rice.


## 3.6.Knockout of OsABCC9 increased rice plant and grain Cd content


To examine the effect of knockout of OsABCC9 on Cd accumulation, we measured the Cd content in wild-type and osabcc9 mutant plants grown hydroponically with 1,5,and $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd.Under low-Cd $( 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ conditions,the Cd concentrations in roots and shoots did not differ significantly between the mutant and wild-type plants (Fig. 6A and B). However,at5 and $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd,the osabcc9 plants had higher Cd concentrations in their roots and shoots than the wild type (Fig.6A and B), suggesting that loss-of-function of OsABCC9 enhanced Cd accumulation in rice.Meanwhile,the concentrations of other microelements such as Fe, Cu, Mn,and Zn were also determined. Compared with the wild type, osabcc9 mutants accumulated more $\mathrm { Z n }$ in their roots,but not shoots, independent of Cd conditions (Figs.S7A, S8A),suggesting that OsABCC9 may also be involved in Zn accumulation in rice roots.The Cu and Mn concentrations were slightly increased in the root, but notin the shoot of the osabcc9 mutants grown in the presence of 5 and $1 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd (Figs. S7B and C, S8B and C).No significant difference in Fe concentration was detected between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Figs.S7D, S8D).

Furthermore,we measured the concentrations of Cd and other essential microelements (Zn,Cu,Mn,and Fe) in the grains of osabcc9 mutants and wild-type rice grown in Cd-containing soil $( 2 . 0 \mathrm { m g } / \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { C d } )$ . The Cd concentration was sharply increased in osabcc9 grains by up to

2-3 fold compared with the wild type (Fig. 6C). However, there was no significant difference in the concentration of other microelements in the grains between osabcc9 mutants and the wild type (Fig.S9).It has been reported that xylem-mediated Cd transfer from root to shoot is the key process determining Cd accumulation in rice shoots and grains [32].We, therefore,measured the Cd levels in the xylem sap of the osabcc9 mutant and wild-type plants treated with $5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd for $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 8 d }$ .We foundamarked increase of the Cd concentration in the xylem sap of the osabcc9 plants relative to the wild type (Fig.6D).These results demonstrated that root-to-shoot transport of Cd was significantly enhanced in osabcc9 mutants, thus increasing Cd accumulation in the grain.

Multiple ABC transporters have been shown to transport metal/ metalloid-ligand complexes,regulating metal detoxification and accumulation within plants [17,30,31,33].In rice, two G-type ABC transporters,OsABCG43 and OsABCG36,have been shown to be associated with Cd tolerance [10,23].The eflux transporter OsABCG36 is suggested to function in exporting Cd or Cd conjugates from root cells,while the exact role of OsABCG43 in Cd detoxification in rice remains obscure [10,23]．Three C-type ABC transporters，AtABCC1，AtABCC2 and AtABCC3,have been shown to confer Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis by sequestering PC-Cd in vacuoles [21,22].However, there is no report on the involvement of C-type ABC transporters in Cd tolerance in rice until now.In the present study,we have reported that OsABCC9 participates in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.

In the previous studies, microarray and RNA-seq data showed that

OsABCC9 is up-regulated in rice under Cd stress [24,25].In this study, the induction of OsABCC9 by Cd treatment was verified by qRT-PCR and immunostaining (Fig.1A,2C,F). Besides Cd toxicity,we found that transcript levels of OsABCC9 were also elevated upon high Zn exposure (Fig.1E), indicating that it was a non-specific Cd-responsive gene and might play roles in multiple metal detoxification.

Furthermore,we examined the time-course induction of OsABCC9 in response to Cd.The up-regulation of OsABCC9 could be detected within $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 1 h }$ of Cd exposure in rice roots and continued to increase until $^ { 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ However, the transcript levels of OsABCC9 gradually declined from12 to $\mathbf { 2 4 h }$ of Cd treatment (Fig.1C),indicating that OsABCC9 belongs to the ‘early’gene that respond rapidly and often non-continuously to Cd toxicity.The temporal expression pattern of OsABCC9 is similar to the rice Cd exporter OsABCG36 [1O].Furthermore,knockout of OsABCC9 and OsABCG36 affected the Cd sensitivity of plants only at relatively high Cd concentrations (Fig.5).These similarities suggested that OsABCC9 may cooperate with OsABCG36 in Cd detoxification under high Cd conditions in rice.However,knockout of OsABCC9 resulted in higher Cd accumulation in both roots and shoots (Fig.6A and B), whereas the Cd content of shoots was unaffected by the OsABCG36 knockout [1O].At the reproductive stage,we also found that the Cd concentration in the grain was markedly elevated in osabcc9 mutants relative to the wild type grown in Cd-contaminated soil (Fig. 6C). These results indicated that loss-of-function of OsABCC9 had a significant impact on Cd accumulation in rice,especially in grains.Therfore, different from OsABCG36, OsABCC9 also plays a role in Cd accumulation in rice.

After long-term Cd treatment, the Cd concentration in the xylem sap was significantly increased in osabcc9 plants (Fig. 6D),suggesting that more Cd had been transported from root to shoot in the mutant. Two heavy metal ATPases,OsHMA2 and OsHMA3,have been reported to be implicated in root-to-shoot translocation of Cd in rice through different mechanisms [13,14,34,35]. OsHMA2 is shown to contribute to $\mathtt { Z n }$ and Cd loading into the xylem,so a reduction of its activity diminishes Zn and Cd translocation from root to shoot,and their accumulation in shoot [34-36]，which is different from the effect caused by OsABCC9 knockout.Furthermore,we also examined the expression level of OsHMA2 in osabcc9 and wild-type plants exposed to Cd.The result showed that OsHMA2 expression did not differ between the two lines (Fig.SlO),suggesting that the high root-to-shoot Cd translocation seen in the osabcc9 mutants might not be associated with OsHMA2. OsHMA3 exerts control over the Cd distribution between root and shoot by sequestration of Cd into root cell vacuoles.Rice varieties harboring the non-functional allele of OsHMA3 exhibit increased root-to-shoot Cd translocation and thus higher Cd accumulation in shoots and grains [13, 14,37],which is similar to the effect produced by knockout of OsABCC9 (Fig.6C and D). Given that OsABCC9 is localized to the tonoplast in rice cells and has transport activity for Cd (complex) in yeast cells (Figs. 3 and 4),we suppose that it might also function in sequestering Cd or Cd-thiol complexes in root vacuoles.Thus,disruption of OsABCC9 led to enhanced Cd levels in the xylem sap and Cd accumulation in the shoot and grain (Fig.6B-D).However,a slight increase in Cd levels in osabcc9 roots was also observed (Fig.6A),which differs from the OsHMA3 knockdown lines [14].This indicates that OsABCC9 might play a minor role in Cd sequestration in root cell vacuoles,as it is expressed only in some cells of the root (Fig.2C and F),while OsHMA3 is detected in all root cells [14].Considering that Zn and Cu concentrations are also elevated in osabcc9 roots (Fig. S7),other transporters responsible for Zn and/or Cu absorption might be induced in the mutant,which resulted in enhanced uptake of Zn and Cu. Since some Zn transporters also display Cd uptake activity [38],the up-regulation of these transporters might also contribute to inadvertent uptake of Cd, thereby leading to an increase of the Cd levels in osabcc9 roots.

Several ABC transporters have been shown to transport Cd in the form of thiol complexes [19,22,29,39]. Such thiol ligands can be GSH or PCs.For instance,the ABCC-type transporter YCF1 from budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) can catalyze the transport of GSH-Cd conjugates [29],while another C-type transporter Abc2 from fission yeast (Schizosaccharomyces pombe) is able to transport PC-Cd complexes [39]. Expression of OsABCC9 can enhance the Cd tolerance and content in the yeast mutant△ycfl (Fig.4A and B),so we suppose that OsABCC9 possesses Cd transport activity. Since the budding yeast(△ycf1) lacks PCs [12],the GSH-Cd complexes may be the substrate of OsABCC9 in the △ycfl strain.However,we cannot rule out the possibility that OsABCC9 mediates the transport of PC-Cd complexes in rice. Unlike the budding yeast,rice has phytochelatin synthases (PCS),which can catalyze the synthesis of PCs from GSH [4O,41].Moreover, the OsPCS1 has been suggested to be crucial for Cd tolerance in rice [4O]. Taken together, PC-Cd may be also the substrate of OsABCC9 in rice,which needs to be explored in future studies.

Two C-type ABC transporters,OsABCC1 and OsABCC7,have been shown to be involved in As accumulation in rice by mediating vacuolar sequestration or efflux of As-thiol complexes for xylem loading [17,31]. However,neither of the two transporters seems to participate in Cd tolerance or accumulation in rice [17,31].Besides evaluating the Cd sensitivity and accumulation,we also examined As sensitivity and accumulation in the OsABCC9 knockout mutants.However,loss of function of OsABCC9 did not change either the As sensitivity or accumulation in rice (Figs.S5A-D,S6A and B).In addition,OsABCC9 expression in yeast had no impact on the As tolerance of the cells (Fig.S3).Therefore,in contrast to OsABCC1 and OsABCC7,OsABCC9 might be implicated only in Cd, but not As,tolerance and accumulation in rice.Taken together,these findings indicate that,despite their grouping into one subfamily,each C-type ABC transporter may have distinct roles in rice.

In conclusion, OsABCC9 is a tonoplast-localized ABC transporter for Cd or its complex.It functions to sequester toxic Cd into the root cell vacuoles,and thus is an important component for Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.

Heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd) and mercury (Hg) are toxic pollutants that are detrimental to living organisms. Plants employ a two-step mechanism to detoxify toxic ions. First, phytochelatins bind to the toxic ion, and then the metal–phytochelatin complex is sequestered in the vacuole. Two ABCC-type transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, that play a key role in arsenic detoxification, have recently been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, it is unclear whether these transporters are also implicated in phytochelatindependent detoxification of other heavy metals such as Cd(II) and Hg(II). Here, we show that atabcc1 single or atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutants exhibit a hypersensitive phenotype in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II). Microscopic analysis using a Cd-sensitive probe revealed that Cd is mostly located in the cytosol of protoplasts of the double mutant, whereas it occurs mainly in the vacuole of wild-type cells. This suggests that the two ABCC transporters are important for vacuolar sequestration of Cd. Heterologous expression of the transporters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae confirmed their role in heavy metal tolerance. Over-expression of AtABCC1 in Arabidopsis resulted in enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation. Together, these results demonstrate that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 are important vacuolar transporters that confer tolerance to cadmium and mercury, in addition to their role in arsenic detoxification. These transporters provide useful tools for genetic engineering of plants with enhanced metal tolerance and accumulation, which are desirable characteristics for phytoremediation.

Keywords: vacuolar sequestration, heavy metal tolerance, phytoremediation, ABC transporter, phytochelatin transporter, heavy metal detoxification.

## The atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout plant is impaired in vacuolar sequestration of Cd


To examine whether AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 confer Cd(II) tolerance by vacuolar sequestration of this non-essential ion, the cellular distribution of Cd(II) was compared in the wild-type and the double mutant using a Cd-indicator dye. Wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant plants were grown in the presence or absence of $5 ~ { \mu \mathsf { M } } ~ { \mathsf { C d } } ( { \mathsf { I I } } )$ for 2 weeks, and protoplasts were isolated and loaded with a Cd(II)- and Pb(II)-sensitive fluorescent probe, Leadmium- Green. In the absence of Cd(II), protoplasts from wild-type plants showed a negligible Leadmium- Green fluorescence signal (Figure 2a–c). When grown in Cd(II)-containing medium, strong green fluorescence was emitted from the vacuole of most wild-type protoplasts (Figure 2d–f). This observation is in agreement with a previous report that used another Cd-sensitive fluorescent dye (Morel et al., 2009) and a study that demonstrated the accumulation of Cd in central vacuoles (Vo¨ geli-Lange and Wagner, 1990). However, in atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants, the majority of cells (approximately $8 6 \%$ of the total) exhibited a markedly different LeadmiumGreen fluorescence pattern; namely, a strong signal at the margin of the cell and a much weaker signal in the vacuole (Figure 2g–j). The green signal was probably derived from the cytoplasm, because it surrounded but did not overlap with the red fluorescence emitted from chloroplasts. Furthermore, measurement of fluorescence intensity in the vacuolar region of wild-type and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout protoplasts revealed a significant reduction in Cd accumulation in the vacuole of the mutant (Figure 2k). These results suggest that sequestration of Cd into the vacuole is remarkably reduced in the atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutant.

The possibility that the observed difference in Leadmi$\mathsf { u m } ^ { \mathrm { T M } }$ Green fluorescence intensity in atabcc1 atabcc2 and wild-type protoplasts was due to different concentrations of dye in the vacuole , rather than that of Cd(II), was tested by comparing the fluorescence intensity in the vacuoles of plants treated with Pb(II) (Figure S4). As AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 did not confer Pb tolerance (Figure S1), we predicted that there would be no difference in vacuolar $\mathsf { P b }$ concentration and thus no difference in the fluorescence intensity, if the permeability of the tonoplast to the dye was not altered in the double knockout mutant. Indeed, the distribution of Pb visualized by Leadmium- Green did not differ between the wild-type and the mutant (Figure S4), supporting our conclusion that the difference in Cd fluorescence observed in Figure 2 represents a real difference in Cd content in the vacuole. These results support the hypothesis that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in vacuolar accumulation of Cd.


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 enhance the Hg(II) tolerance of yeast producing PCs


To determine the molecular mechanism by which AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 function in heavy metal tolerance, we used a heterologous system comprising a mutant strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae that we engineered to express a PC synthase gene of wheat (Triticum aestivum). We expressed TaPCS1 in yeast strain SM4, which lacks four vacuolar ABC transporters including ScYCF1, and named the resulting yeast SM7 (Song et al., 2010). Introduction of AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 enhanced Hg(II) tolerance in SM7 compared to a control transformed with the empty vector (EV; Figure 3a). In the SM4 strain, which does not produce PCs, AtABCC1 conferred Hg(II) tolerance over a narrow range of concentrations, while AtABCC2 improved the growth of yeast in medium containing a broad range of Hg(II) concentrations (Figure 3b). The results indicated that both AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 transport PC–Hg(II) as well as $\mathsf { G S } _ { 2 } \mathsf { - H g } ( | | )$ , and that AtABCC1 is more dependent on PCs than is AtABCC2. Cd(II) tolerance was not improved by expressing either AtABCC1 or AtABCC2 in the SM7 yeast strain (Figure S5).


## AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate the translocation of Cd from root to shoot


To assess whether the distribution of metal ions is altered by loss of function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, the Cd content of wild-type and mutant plants was measured. After 2 weeks of growth on half-strength MS agar plates containing Cd(II), the shoots and roots of wild-type, atabcc1 and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants were collected separately and their Cd content was measured. The shoots of atabcc1 knockout plants accumulated more Cd than the wild-type (Figure 4a), leading to an increased shoot-to-root ratio of Cd (Figure 4b). In the double knockout plants, the shoot Cd content was similar to that of the wild-type, and the root Cd content was lower, resulting in an increased shoot-to-root Cd ratio even though the total Cd accumulation was lower than that in the wild-type (Figure 4). This result implies that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 regulate translocation of Cd from the root to the shoot. Determination of Hg(II) levels in the double knockout plants yielded similar results as for Cd (Figure S6), supporting the putative function of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 in regulation of heavy metal flux between the root and shoot.


## Over-expression of AtABCC1 enhances tolerance to and accumulation of Cd


Increasing the vacuolar storage capacity may dramatically improve the ability of the plant to accumulate and tolerate toxic metal ions, because vacuoles are the main storage organelle for heavy metals and metalloids. We predicted that over-expression of AtABCC1 (Geisler et al., 2004), which plays an important role in Cd tolerance (Figure 1), is a good candidate for increasing the vacuolar storage capacity. We generated AtABCC1 over-expressing Arabidopsis plants, and selected two lines that showed the highest AtABCC1 transcript levels (M-1 and M-2, with 1.2- and 1.4-fold higher transcript levels than the wild-type, respectively; Song et al., 2010). The growth of the two transgenic lines overexpressing AtABCC1 was similar to that of the wild-type on control half-strength MS medium (Figure 5a). However, plants over-expressing AtABCC1 grew better than the wildtype in the presence of Cd(II). The shoot fresh weights of the two over-expressing lines were higher than those of the wild-type on two Cd(II) concentrations (Figure 5b). Furthermore, Cd accumulation in both the shoot and the root, as well as the total Cd content per plant, were higher in the lines over-expressing AtABCC1 than in the wild-type (Figure 5c,d). We tested whether over-expression of AtPCS1 together with AtABCC1 further increased Cd tolerance, as, in the case of arsenic, only plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 exhibited increased tolerance relative to the wild-type (Song et al., 2010). However, the Cd tolerance of plants over-expressing both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1 did not exceed that of plants only over-expressing AtPCS1 (Figure S7).

ABC transporters constitute a large superfamily of proteins described in all kingdoms of life. Some families have a restricted distribution, like the ABC subclass C (or multidrug resistance associated protein, MRP) which is limited to eukaryotes. In plants, ABCC/MRPs are subdivided in three phylogenetic clusters (Kolukisaoglu et al. 2002, Schulz and Kolukisaoglu 2006), two of which are fairly well characterized in Arabidopsis.

Cluster I contains four genes including AtMRP1 and AtMRP2 which are involved in cellular detoxification processes. These transporters display a ubiquitous expression in plants, mediate metal/metalloid tolerance and transport various compounds, such as phytochelatins (Song et al. 2010), glutathione conjugates (Lu et al. 1997), folate (AtMRP1), as well as chlorophyll catabolites (AtMRP2, Lu et al. 1998). The two other members of cluster I (AtMRP11 and AtMRP12) have been poorly investigated; they share transport properties of cluster I MRPs except for chlorophyll catabolites, which seems to be specific to AtMRP2 within this cluster (Frelet-Barrand et al. 2008).

Ten of the fifteen Arabidopsis ABCC/MRPs belong to cluster II. The AtMRP3 expression is induced in leaf and root under cadmium or several other metal treatments (Bovet et al. 2003), and confers tolerance to cadmium in yeast (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP3 exhibits glutathione S-conjugate transport activity, and as described for AtMRP1 and AtMRP2, chlorophyll catabolites transport activity has also been reported (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP6 and AtMRP7 have the highest sequence similarity to AtMRP3 and are also upregulated by $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments. In AtMRP6 mutants, leaf development is more sensitive to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment than in wild type. However, the expression pattern of AtMRP6 suggests that it is not only involved in $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance but also in developmental processes. Indeed, AtMRP6 is expressed during early seedling development, in root apical meristem and in lateral root initiation (Gaillard et al. 2008). AtMRP7 is constitutively expressed in roots and leaves and the protein was localized to both plasmalemma and tonoplast (Wojas et al. 2009). Overexpression of AtMRP7 in tobacco slightly enhances plant resistance to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment and modifies $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ rootto-shoot translocation. These observations suggest that AtMRP3 and its closest homologues may behave as cellular metal detoxifiers although additional functions in planta cannot be ruled out. AtMRP4 and AtMRP5, which also belong to cluster II, have a low sequence similarity, but their stomatal-specific expression patterns suggest a role in plant adaptation to water stress rather than cell detoxification. Indeed, AtMRP4 knock-out mutants display an increased water loss due to a larger constitutive stomata aperture. Considering its strong expression in guard cells and localization in plasmalemma, AtMRP4 is suggested to be involved in a stomata ion channel regulation (Klein et al. 2004). AtMRP5 is also expressed in guard cells but localizes to tonoplast (Nagy et al. 2009). Interestingly, Nagy et al. (2009) demonstrated that AtMRP5 is a high affinity inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) transporter, a molecule that modulates $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 \dagger }$ signaling and $\bar { \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in guard cells. AtMRP5 mutants are impaired in the export of InsP6 into vacuole resulting in constitutive stomata closure and a reduced water loss (Klein et al. 2003, Suh et al. 2007).

Cluster III genes have not been functionally characterized so far. In Arabidopsis (AGI 2000) it was revealed a single MRP/ABCC gene belonging to cluster III, AtABCC13/MRP11 $( \mathrm { A t } 2 \mathrm { g } 0 7 6 8 0 )$ . In this study, we investigated in-depth the expression pattern of AtABCC13 in Arabidopsis. The $\beta$ -glucuronidase (GUS) reporter gene approach revealed that the AtABCC13 expression was related to vascular elements, seed maturation, and seedling development.

ABC transporters hydrolyze ATP to transport substrate molecules across cellular membranes. All membrane-bound ABC proteins consist of a double set of two basic structural modules: a transmembrane domain (TMD), typically containing six membrane-spanning segments, and a cytoplasmic nucleotidebinding domain (NBD), containing the ABC. The so-called full-size ABC transporters contain all four elements in a single polypeptide chain, while half-size transporters combine two TMD-NBD units as homo- or heterodimers (Higgins et al., 1986). In plants, full-size ABC transporters have been better studied. Of the 53 Arabidopsis full-size members, all but two can be divided into three groups: the multidrug resistance (MDR) or P-glycoproteins (PGP) belonging to the ABCB subfamily, the multidrug resistance-associated protein (MRP)/ABCC subfamily, and the pleiotropic drug resistance (PDR) of the ABCG subfamily (Sanchez-Fernandez et al., 2001).

ABC transporters came into spotlight when the MDR1 PGP was found to determine MDR of cancer cells (Chen et al., 1986), and in fact early studies of plant ABCs focused on a potential role in cell detoxification. The sole MDR-like transport mechanism reported in plants so far arose from the functional characterization of one of the 21 full-size members of the ABCB family, the Arabidopsis AtABCB1 gene, whose cloning disclosed the occurrence of ABCs in plants (Dudler and Hertig, 1992). Indeed, ectopic expression of AtABCB1 in Arabidopsis conferred enhanced resistance to multiple xenobiotics, namely to various classes of herbicides including dicamba, pendimethalin, oryzalin, or monosodium acid methanearsonate, pointing to a resistance mechanism relying on decreased retention or increased active xenobiotic efflux from cells (Thomas et al., 2000; Windsor et al., 2003). Several detailed studies also demonstrated that AtABCB1 and the closely related AtABCB19 are required for polar transport of auxin, the major growth phytohormone, by facilitating cellular efflux of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), its predominant endogenous form (Noh et al., 2001, 2003; Lin and Wang, 2005; Lewis et al., 2007). Another extensively studied ABCB transporter, AtABCB4, was implicated in root shootward auxin transport and appears to function in both cellular IAA efflux and influx (Santelia et al.,

2005; Terasaka et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2007; Lewis et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2007; Yang and Murphy, 2009). Interestingly, recent findings indicate that AtABCB4 is also able to mediate cellular influx of 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), rendering the carrier a target of the herbicidal activity of this synthetic auxin (Kubes et al., 2012). An Arabidopsis AtABCB4 homolog, AtABCB21, has also been described to mediate IAA import/export, depending on the cytoplasmic concentration of the phytohormone (Kamimoto et al., 2012), while AtABCB14 and AtABCB15 have been associated with polar auxin transport (PAT) in inflorescence stems (Kaneda et al., 2011). Thus, all plant full-size ABCB (MRP/PGP)

transporters characterized to date contribute to PAT in vegetative tissues, directing long-distance auxin transport in mature plants. Nevertheless, AtABCB14 was first reported as a malate importer regulating stomatal closure (Lee et al., 2008), suggesting that full-size ABCB carriers may play important roles in other key processes.

ABCC (MRP) transporters, which have been typically associated with detoxification processes, were first identified in human drug-resistant cancer cells (Cole et al., 1992). Most of the 15 Arabidopsis members are localized at the vacuolar membrane (Rea, 2007), representing the only tonoplastic full-size ABC transporters described to date (Kang et al., 2011). A common cellular detoxification strategy in plants is to sequester toxic compounds in the vacuole to avoid deleterious effects on cytosolic metabolism. Early studies showed that plant vacuolar accumulation of glutathionated xenobiotics is ATP-dependent (Martinoia et al., 1993), prompting the identification of the first plant ABCC transporters. Indeed, AtABCC1, AtABCC2, and AtABCC3 are implicated in vacuolar sequestration of conjugated xenobiotics such as herbicides, with the latter two transporters functioning also in endogenous chlorophyll catabolite detoxification (Lu et al., 1997, 1998; Tommasini et al., 1998). Importantly, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 were recently described as phytochelatin transporters with overlapping functions in plant tolerance to the metalloid arsenic and the heavy metals cadmium and mercury (Song et al., 2010; Park et al., 2012). There is also evidence pointing to a role of AtABCC3 and AtABCC6 in responses to cadmium stress (Tommasini et al., 1998; Gaillard et al., 2008). Furthermore, both AtABCC1 (Raichaudhuri et al., 2009) and AtABCC4 (Klein et al., 2004) are involved in vacuolar sequestration of excess folates, whereas AtABCC5 is a high-affinity inositol hexakisphosphate $\mathrm { ( I n s P _ { 6 } ) }$ ) transporter modulating seed phytate content (Nagy et al., 2009) as its maize homolog ZmMRP4 (Shi et al., 2007). Interestingly, both AtABCC4 (Klein et al., 2004) and AtABCC5 (Gaedeke et al., 2001; Klein et al., 2003; Suh et al., 2007) regulate stomatal movements, which in the case of AtABCC5 could be linked to its $\mathrm { I n s P } _ { 6 }$ transport activity (Kang et al., 2011). Finally, ZmMRP3 was shown to affect vacuolar anthocyanin accumulation (Goodman et al., 2004), and a recent study implicated AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 in vacuolar sequestration of a conjugate of the phytohormone abscisic acid (ABA) (Burla et al., 2013). It is therefore clear that plant ABCC transporters are involved in a range of processes beyond detoxification, such as the transport of primary and storage compounds or hormones and the control of stomatal apertures.

PDR proteins are specific to plants and fungi and in Arabidopsis comprise the 15 full-size members of the ABCG subfamily, which uniquely among ABCs feature a reverse organization of the NBD and TMD domains in each unit (Crouzet et al., 2006). All PDRs characterized so far are plasma membrane transporters (Kang et al., 2011), and the first to be identified in plants, the Spirodella polyrhiza SpTUR2 and the Nicotiana plumbaginifolia NpPDR1, mediate the transport of terpenes (Jasinski et al., 2001; van den Brule et al., 2002). SpTUR2 expression in Arabidopsis confers resistance to the diterpenoid sclareol, as does the Arabidopsis AtABCG40 (Campbell et al., 2003) later shown to function in cellular uptake of the sesquiterpenoid ABA (Kang et al., 2010). Intriguingly, AtABCG40 also mediates detoxification of the heavy metal lead via a glutathione-independent process (Lee et al., 2005). Another PDR transporter, AtABCG36, is involved in cadmium (Kim et al., 2007) and sodium toxicity (Kim et al., 2010) resistance. Following the findings that NpPDR1 secretes antifungal terpenoids (Jasinski et al., 2001) and contributes to basal plant defense (Stukkens et al., 2005), AtABCG36 was identified as a key factor in the resistance to fungal and bacterial pathogens (Kobae et al., 2006; Stein et al., 2006; Underwood and Somerville, 2013; Xin et al., 2013). Moreover, both AtABCG36 and AtABCG37 excrete a range of synthetic auxins, including 2,4-D, and indole-3-butyric acid (IBA), the natural IAA precursor (Ito and Gray, 2006; Strader and Bartel, 2009; Ruzicka et al., 2010). Interestingly, AtABCG36, AtABCG37, and AtABCG30 are involved in root exudation of phytochemicals (Badri et al., 2009, 2012). Recent studies implicate the tobacco NtPDR5 in herbivore defense (Bienert et al., 2012), while the wheat PDR carrier LR34 confers resistance to fungal pathogens (Krattinger et al., 2009; Risk et al., 2013). Thus, plant full-size ABCG proteins play a preponderant role in metal and xenobiotic detoxification as well as in biotic stress resistance, but also fulfill functions in phytohormone transport.

ABC super families of transporters are expressed in microorganisms and mammals and are involved in the transport of chemically diverse compounds across membranes. ABCC (MRP) is a subfamily among the ABC transporters shown to have important functions across evolution. Mutations in ABCC1 (MRP1) cause drug resistance and immune response in humans. In plants, Arabidopsis thaliana ABCC1 is present in vacuolar membranes and is known to transport glutathione (GSH) conjugate and folates (Rea, 2007;

Raichaudhuri et al., 2009). Early studies with AtMRP1 showed MgATP-energized, vanadate-inhibitable, uncoupler-insensitive uptake of several glutathione (GSH) conjugates (GS-conjugates) like N-ethylmaleimide-GS (NEM-GS), S-(2,4-dinitrophenyl)-GS (DNP-GS), glutathionylated chloroacetamide herbicides, (metolachlor-GS), folates and antifolates (methotrexate MTX) mediated by this protein in isolated vacuoles (Martinoia et al., 1993) or in vacuolar membrane vesicles purified from plants (Li et al., 1995; Rea, 2007; Raichaudhuri et al., 2009). In addition, AtMRP1 was shown to have a role in tolerance and detoxification of heavy metal and metalloids (Rea, 2007; Song et al., 2010). MRP proteins are classified based on the presence of one or two ATP-binding cassettes or nucleotide binding domains (NBDs). Each NBD encompasses \~200 amino acid residues and contains three idiotypic sequence motifs. These are a Walker A motif $\cdot G X _ { 4 } \mathrm { G K } ( \mathrm { S T } ) )$ and a Walker B motif $( \mathrm { R K } ) X _ { 3 } \mathrm { G } X _ { 3 } \mathrm { L }$ (hydrophobic)3), that are separated by \~120 amino acid residues (Walker et al., 1982), and an ABC signature (alias C motif, ((LIVMFY)S(SG)GX3(RKA)(LIVMYA)X(LIVFM)(AG)) (Bairoch, 1992).

In addition to two NBDs, AtMRP transporters contain two or three hydrophobic integral membrane spanning domains (MSDs), each of which contains multiple (usually four to six) transmembrane $\pmb { \mathscr { L } }$ -helices. The MSDs form the pathway for solute amovement across the phospholipid bilayer.

In south Asia, particularly in parts of Indian subcontinent, arsenic in ground water is a hazardous environmental pollutant. Arsenic content in water used for drinking and irrigation has been reported to cross the accepted limits of $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / L }$ proposed by the mWorld Health Organization in several areas of South Asia. Arsenic is taken up by plant roots and is sequestered in plant vacuoles. Two transporters in Arabidopsis, from ABCC (MRP) family AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, were shown to contribute to arsenic tolerance via vacuolar sequestration of As (III)-phytochelatin conjugates. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Yeast Cadmium Factor 1 (Ycf1), an ABC transporter localized to the vacuolar membrane originally identified for its role in vacuolar cadmium sequestration, was shown to detoxify arsenic by transporting As(glutathione $) _ { 3 }$ complexes into vacuoles (Szczypka et al., 1994; Li et al., 1996; Ghosh et al., 1999). AtMRP1 is the Ycf1 homolog in A. thaliana. AtMRP1 is localized at the vacuolar membrane and transports substrates to the vacuolar lumen thereby effectively sequestering them from cytosol (Li et al., 1997; Rea et al., 1998). Over expression of Ycf1 (35S::ycf1) was shown to confer both accumulation and enhanced resistance to lead and cadmium in Arabidopsis plants (Song et al., 2003). The most common forms of arsenic available in the environment for uptake by plants are arsenate (AsV) and arsenite (AsIII). Arsenate is acquired by plant roots through endogenous transport systems for phosphate and is reduced to the thiol-reactive form As III inside the cell (Asher and Reay, 1979). At equimolar concentrations, AsIII is more toxic than AsV.

Ycf1p (the yeast homolog of AtMRP1) shows several potential phosphorylation sites. Genetic evidence in yeast suggested that yeast casein kinase $_ { 2 \alpha }$ (Cka1p) may regulate Ycf1p function athrough phosphorylation of $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 2 5 1 }$ either directly or indirectly (Paumi et al., 2008). Ycf1p phosphorylation at $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 9 0 8 }$ and $\mathrm { T h r } ^ { 9 1 \bar { 1 } }$ was found to be required for cadmium detoxification (Eraso et al., 2004), and phosphorylation at $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 2 5 1 }$ negatively regulated transport activity (Paumi et al., 2008). Six additional sites of phosphorylation were identified within the linker region by studies aimed at examining the complete yeast phosphoproteome via highthroughput analysis (Li et al., 2007; Smolka et al., 2007; Albuquerque et al., 2008).

The experiments described here were directed towards understanding the role of phosphorylation events controlling AtMRP1 transporter function both under AsIII stress as well as under antifolate treatment. There are several potential phosphorylation sites in AtMRP1. Using mutational analysis and heterologous expression in yeast, the role of phosphorylation, especially in the serine triad, has been investigated.

The data presented here shows that AtMRP1 C-terminal NBD2 phosphorylation is important in the presence of As III and antifolate MTX. A potential signaling event in response to As III is also indicated.

ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter genes are ubiquitous across the three domains of life: Eukarya, Eubacteria and Archaea [1, 2]. Plant genomes harbor more than 100 ABC transporters which are involved in a broad range of biological functions [3]. ABC transporters comprise at least four domains: two transmembrane domains (TMDs) embedded in the membrane bilayer, and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs) located in the cytoplasm [1]. The structure of the TMDs is highly diverse and varies in the number of transmembrane helices, whereas the NBDs have highly conserved helices [4]. The ABC transporters are further categorized into full-size transporters with two NBDs and two TMDs and halfsize transporters with only one of each domain [5]. Therefore, two half-size transporters must form either a homodimer or a heterodimer to be functionally active.

In plant genomes, ABC transporters are categorized into eight different subfamilies (ABCA-ABCG and ABCI) [3]. Proteins belonging to the ABCA-ABCD subfamilies have a forward domain organization (TMDNBD) whereas ABCG and ABCI subfamilies have an inverse domain organization (NBD-TMD) [6]. ABCE and ABCF possess only two NBDs and are designated as soluble proteins [6]. In Arabidopsis, 130 ABC transporter genes have been identified but few have been functionally characterized [7]. Previous studies have shown that ABC transporters participate in a wide range of processes including the transport of ions, carbohydrates, lipids, xenobiotics, antibiotics, drugs, and heavy metals [8–10]. The two members of the ABCB gene family in Arabidopsis (AtABCB1 and AtABCB2) are auxin transporters and the overexpression of AtABCB1 causes the elongation of hypocotyl cells [11, 12]. Several members of the ABCC subfamily are responsible for phytate transport as exemplified in Arabidopsis (AtABCC5) [13], maize (ZmABCC4) [14] and rice (OsABCC13) [15]. Two other ABCC transporters (AtABCC1 and AtABCC2) mediate tolerance to both cadmium (Cd) and mercury by vacuolar sequestration [16]. The ABCF subfamily member AtABCF3 in Arabidopsis is involved in root growth and development [17]. ABCG subfamily members were reported to be involved in cuticle formation and Cd tolerance such as in Arabidopsis (AtABCG32) [18] and rice (OsABCG31 and OsABCG36) [19, 20]. Also, the ABC transporter AtABCG36 in Arabidopsis was shown to mediate Cd uptake in the epidermal cells of roots [21] and to be up-regulated by a Cd treatment [22].

Heavy metal (HM) pollution in food, water, and soil is hazardous to human health. HMs have become one of the major concerns across the globe due to the extensive industrialization and because of their direct and indirect effects on soil and crop productivity [23]. HMs such as zinc, copper, manganese, cobalt, and nickel are essential for various biological processes [24]. In contrast, other HMs such as arsenic, lead, and Cd are highly toxic to plants and negatively affect crop productivity [23]. Many HMA genes have been shown to play specific functions in different plant species. For example, OsHMA2 is associated with vascular tissue loading of zinc and tonoplast localization in rice [25]. OsHMA3, localized in the tonoplasts, translocates Cd to the roots while OsHMA4 transports copper to the roots [26]. HvHMA1 is involved in zinc and Cd translocation into barley grain [27]. In wheat, HMA genes also play an important role in Cd translocation and are localized in the plasma membrane [28]. Overexpression of AtHMA3 in Arabidopsis resulted in a 2- to 3-fold increase in Cd accumulation when compared to wild-type plants [29]. These cited studies provide an overview of the importance of both ABC transporter and HMA genes in various plant species, but no systemic studies have been reported in flax.

The initial draft of the flax genome sequence was produced using whole-genome shotgun (WGS) sequencing with short reads obtained on the Illumina sequencing platform [30]. A de novo assembly generated 88,384 scaffolds, totaling $3 1 8 \mathrm { M b }$ and representing $\sim 8 1 \%$ of the estimated $\sim 3 7 0 \mathrm { M b }$ flax reference genome [31]. Thus, the availability of this recent update of the flax genome (version 2.0) constitutes a genomic resource that allows the identification of gene families, evolutionary relationships, and structural analyses. To date, ABC transporter and HMA gene families have been studied in several plant species including Oryza sativa and Arabidopsis thaliana [32], Zea mays [33, 34], Brassica rapa [7], Brassica napus [35], Triticum aestivum [36], and Vitis vinifera [37]. A previous report on ABC transporters in flax has been published [38], but classification patterns, gene duplications, evolutionary and collinear relationships, structural and correlation analyses of paralogous pairs, and the identification of the Cd-associated genes covered herein were not explored in this prior publication. Several other gene families have also been identified in flax, based on bioinformatics analysis such as aquaporin [39], dirigent [40], chalcone [41], detoxification efflux carriers [42], and a ubiquitous glycosyltransferase [43]. In this research work, we hypothesized that either whole genome duplications (WGDs) or tandem events contributed to the expansion of the ABC transporter and HMA gene families in flax. Therefore, we studied the phylogenetic relationships, gene annotation, physicochemical properties, chromosomal distribution, gene synteny, protein-protein interactions (PPIs), and gene duplications of all predicted ABC transporter and HMA genes of the flax genome to understand their evolution and hypothesize their putative functions. Finally, we examined the gene ontology (GO) and expression profiling of ABC transporter and HMA genes in eight tissues, namely root, seed, ovary, and embryo at five different stages (heart, globular, torpedo, mature and cotyledon). This comprehensive analysis is the first report on ABC transporter and HMA genes in flax, providing gene candidate information for future marker association studies on heavy metal accumulation including Cd.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are one of the largest known superfamilies of membrane transporters in all living organisms [1,2]. ABCC transporters, which belong to one subclass of the ABC transporter superfamily, are well known for their roles as multidrug resistance-associated proteins (MRPs), which are found in all eukaryotic organisms [3–7]. These proteins shuttle substrates as diverse as glutathione conjugates, xenobiotic compounds, intermediate metabolites and hormones across a variety of biological membranes [2,5,8,9].
