## Identification of AtDUR3 as a Urea Transporter in Plants


Urea transporter genes from different unicellular organisms, such as cyanobacteria and yeast, have been identified on the basis of screening and recomplementation of urea uptake– defective mutants (ElBerry et al., 1993; Valladares et al., 2002). Urea transporters from higher eukaryotes have been identified mainly by genetic approaches and heterologous expression in oocytes (Leung et al., 2000; Smith and Rousselet, 2001). Using the BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) search algorithm, we searched for ESTs from higher plants that encode proteins homologous with microbial or mammalian urea transporters. We identified a group of plant ESTs (Arabidopsis AV524336, maize BQ164112, rice AU056606, soybean AW164789, barley BF256473, wheat BF202504, and oilseed rape H07563) that showed weak homology with the ScDUR3 gene from yeast (ElBerry et al., 1993). ScDUR3 is a member of the sodium-solute symporter (SSS) gene family, which is widespread in microorganisms, animals, and humans. Members of the SSS family have been described to transport sugars, amino acids, nucleosides, inositols, vitamins, anions, and urea (Reizer et al., 1994; Turk and Wright, 1997; Saier, 2000).

A putative full-length coding sequence of AV524336 from Arabidopsis was deduced from a genomic clone (At5g45380), isolated from a cDNA library (Minet et al., 1992) using genespecific primers, and cloned into the yeast expression vector pHXT426 carrying a hexose transporter promoter (Wieczorke et al., 1999). The sequence-verified 2428-bp cDNA contained an open reading frame of 2085 bp with an ATG start codon at position 214 and a termination codon at position 2298. An in-frame termination codon 18 bp upstream of the translational initiation codon indicated that the cDNA represented the complete coding region of the respective protein, which was named AtDUR3.

A yeast complementation assay was set up by substituting the ScDUR3 gene in Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain 23346c (ura3) for a marker gene by PCR-based gene disruption. The resulting mutant, YNVW1 (dur3, ura3), was defective in urea uptake and growth on ${ < } 5 \mathsf { m M }$ urea as a sole nitrogen source when transformed with the empty vector pHXT426 (Figure 2). Heterologous expression of AtDUR3 enabled the yeast mutant to grow efficiently on $2 \mathsf { m M }$ urea (Figure 2). Growth complementation of the yeast mutant by AtDUR3 depended on medium pH. pHXT426-AtDUR3 transformants attained better growth than the control transformants on 2 mM urea at $\mathsf { p H } 6 . 0$ and below but showed weak complementation at pH 7.0 (Figure 2). By contrast, wild-type yeast (23346c) also grew better at higher pH, most likely attributable to a different regulation of ScDUR3 gene expression and/or different biochemical properties of the ScDUR3 protein. The pH-dependent growth complementation by AtDUR3 suggested that urea transport is stimulated by external protons.

Phylogenetic analysis indicated the closest relationship between DUR3 proteins from plants and yeast (S. cerevisiae and Schizosaccharomyces pombe). These DUR3 proteins form a subfamily that has not been functionally characterized (Figure 3). Among the SSS members from other organisms, urea transport activity has been demonstrated for the low-affinity ${ \mathsf { N a } } ^ { + } .$ Glc cotransporter rbSGLT1, the $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ -iodide cotransporter rNIS, and the $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ -Cl	-

Proteins from the SSS family possess between 400 and 700 amino acid residues and are predicted to form 12 to 15 transmembrane-spanning domains (Reizer et al., 1994). Computerbased analysis of the hydrophobicity profile indicated that the AtDUR3 polypeptide represents an integral membrane protein with 14 transmembrane-spanning domains (www.cbs.dtu.dk; Sonnhammer et al., 1998), which are arranged in two stretches of six and an additional stretch of two transmembrane-spanning domains. The N and C termini were predicted to protrude into the extracellular space (Figure 4). No transit peptides for chloroplasts or mitochondrial targeting were indicated. An outside-oriented domain between transmembrane helices 8 and 9 contains a consensus sequence for a P-loop, also designated a “Walker A” motif (Saraste, 1990).

Upon urea addition, small and reversible currents were detected that were absent in noninjected or water-injected control oocytes (Figure 5A). Currents induced by urea were time independent and corresponded to the net influx of positive charge. Weaker currents were observed by superfusion with the structural urea analog thiourea (data not shown). Because urea and thiourea both were uncharged, the current had to be ascribed to another, most likely cotransported ion. No currents were detectable when the following substrates were tested, which have been described as substrates for SSS transporters (Turk and Wright, 1997): Glc, Gal, myo-inositol, and Pro. Urea-induced currents were voltage dependent. The current-voltage relationship was nonlinear, with larger currents at more negative membrane potentials (Figure 5B). Urea-induced currents in AtDUR3-expressing oocytes also were investigated for their dependence on external urea application. Currents increased steeply at lower micromolar concentrations of urea and saturated at $> 5 0 ~ \mu \mathsf { M }$ (Figure 5C).


## Urea Transport by AtDur3 Is pH and Concentration Dependent


$^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -labeled urea uptake into AtDUR3-injected oocytes was investigated at different external pH values. $^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -urea uptake into noninjected oocytes showed no difference from that into waterinjected oocytes and served as a control. At $\mathsf { p H } ~ 5 . 0$ , urea uptake was stimulated approximately threefold in AtDUR3- expressing oocytes but not in control oocytes (Figure 6A). The stimulation of $^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -urea uptake by AtDUR3 became less prominent at higher pH, in agreement with the weak growth complementation of yeast by AtDUR3 on 2 mM urea at $\mathsf { p H } > 6$ (Figure 2). This finding indicated that AtDUR3 transports urea in a $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ - dependent manner. Because some SSS family members from bacteria and animals were described as $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ -coupled cotransporters, we additionally tested if $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ influences urea transport by AtDUR3. However, in choline-based solutions at $\mathsf { p H } 5$ , the presence of $3 \mathsf { m M N a ^ { + } }$ did not affect $^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -urea uptake into oocytes (Figure 6B).

$^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -labeled urea uptake by oocytes was used further to determine concentration-dependent transport by AtDUR3. Uptake periods of 20 min allowed tracer accumulation in oocytes that was sufficient for reliable determination (data not shown) (Leung et al., 2000). $^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -urea transport was saturable at low concentrations of urea, and the urea concentration that permitted half-maximal uptake was ${ \sim } 3 ~ { \mu } { \sf M }$ (Figure 6C). Extended uptake periods of up to $^ { 2 \mathfrak { h } }$ yielded similar $K _ { \mathfrak { m } }$ values. Both concentration-dependent transport of $^ { 1 4 } \mathsf { C }$ -labeled urea and ureainduced currents in AtDUR3-expressing oocytes saturated similarly at $\sim 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ (Figures 5C and 6C).


## Transcriptional Regulation of AtDUR3 by Nitrogen


Nitrogen-dependent regulation of AtDUR3 gene expression was studied in Arabidopsis plants cultured hydroponically in Magenta boxes for 29 days and then subjected to nitrogen deficiency for 3 days. AtDUR3 was expressed in both shoots and roots under all nitrogen treatments tested (Figure 7). Transcript levels in shoots were not altered significantly under nitrogen starvation. In roots, however, AtDUR3 transcript levels were low under adequate nitrogen supply and increased continuously during 3 days of nitrogen starvation. The same observation was made when roots were analyzed from plants grown in nonaxenic nutrient solution (data not shown).

Because urea represents not only a nitrogen form available in the environment but also an important intermediate from the secondary nitrogen metabolism, AtDUR3 expression was monitored during germination and leaf aging, when nitrogen remobilization processes become prominent. Under these conditions, AtDUR3 was only weakly detectable by RNA gel blot analysis; therefore, reverse transcriptase-mediated (RT) PCR was performed. Using RNA from germinating seeds over a 5-day period allowed us to observe an increase in AtDUR3 expression levels between days 2 and 3 (Figure 8A). From day 3 onward, AtDUR3 transcripts were maintained at a higher level, similar to transcript levels of the ammonium transporter gene AtAMT1;1 (Gazzarrini et al., 1999) and cytosolic Gln synthetase (Oliveira and Coruzzi, 1999). In germinating seedlings, AtDUR3 gene expression apparently was not coregulated with the expression of UREG, which encodes a urease accessory protein (Freyermuth et al., 1999). On the other hand, AtDUR3 mRNA was at a similar level in Arabidopsis leaves of different ages, except in the youngest leaves (Figure 8B, leaf 16). Thus, AtDUR3 expression levels also were altered under conditions in which nitrogen remobilization processes were prominent.

## The snx1-2 mutant is insensitive to low Pi


Plants have evolved sophisticated adaptive mechanisms to respond to limited Pi availability by coordinating growth, development,and metabolic processes.One of the most visible Pi starvation responses (PSRs) is the accumulation of anthocyanin in plant leaves (Ren et al., 2014)． PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 mutants and plants with reduced PHT expression exhibit decreased Pi uptake and increased PSRs,thus usually exhibiting increased leaf anthocyanin accumulation.Therefore，screening and identification of mutants with altered anthocyanin accumulation in response to Pi deficiency may shed some light on plant PSRs.To achieve this,5-day-old wild-type and a collection of Arabidopsis mutant seedlings grown on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium were transferred to medium containing sufficient Pi (MS medium) or deficient Pi (low phosphate [LP] medium with $1 0 ~ \mu \mu$ Pi) for another 5 days,and the leaf anthocyanin levels were examined. Our results show that wildtype leaves exhibited a dark purple color after treatment of lowPi， while the leaves of one mutant， snx1-2 (SALK_O33351),still displayed a green or light purple color, suggesting decreased anthocyanin accumulation in the mutant (Figure 1a). Indeed,the anthocyanin content of the snx1-2 mutant was markedly lower than that of wild-type plants under low Pi conditions (Figure 1b)，revealing decreased PSR of the mutant in response to low Pi.To further investigate the PSR in the snx1-2 mutant, we assayed the expression of some Pi starvation-induced genes, including MYB62, DFR,and LDOX (Huang et al., 2018). Our quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) results showed that the expression of these genes was extensively activated in wild-type plants but repressed in the snx1-2 mutant when subjected to low Pi (Figure 1c-e),further supporting the decreased PSR in the mutant.PHR1 is a central transcription factor regulating the expresson of genes correlated with Pi uptake and anthocyanin accumulation.We found that the snx1-2 mutant did not significantly affect PHR1 expression under sufficient Pi or deficient Pi conditions (Figure 1f).

To dissect whether decreased PSR of the snx1-2 mutant is due to increased Pi uptake and Pi content,we assayed the Pi content of mutant and wild-type seedlings under Pisufficient and Pi-deficient conditions. Our results showed that the Pi content in snx1-2 mutant whole seedlings was significantly higher than that in wild-type seedlings (Figure 1g).We also assayed the Pi content in the roots and shoots of the wild type and snx1-2 mutant,and found that the Pi content in the roots and shoots of the snx1-2 mutant was higher than in the wild type (Figure 1g),suggesting that root Pi uptake is promoted in the mutant. Consistently, the snx1-2 mutant showed higher tolerance to low Pi than the wild type in terms of fresh weight (Figure S1a,b).The higher Pi content in snx1-2 mutant shoots than in wildtype shoots raised the possibility that SNX1 modulates PHOSPHATE1 (PHO1),which is implicated in Pi loading into the xylem,thus affecting the Pi distribution in shoots and roots. If this was the case, the shoot-to-root ratio of Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant should be different to that in wild-type plants,but the ratio in the mutant was comparable to that in wild-type plants,under both sufficient Pi and deficient Pi conditions (Figure S1c)，revealing that SNX1 has no effect on the Pi distribution in shoots and roots under different Pi availabilities.

To verify that mutation of SNX1 is the cause for decreased anthocyanin accumulation and increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant under low Pi,a second transfer DNA insertion mutant allele of this gene， snx1-1 (GABI_105C01)，was employed. Similar to the snx1-2 mutant, the snx1-1 mutant also had less anthocyanin accumulation and more Pi content than wild-type plants when treated with deficient Pi (Figure S2),further supporting the key role of SNX1 in anthocyanin accumulation and Pi uptake in the plant response to low Pi.


## The snx1-2 mutant has enhanced Pi uptake


Our above results showed that the snx1-2 mutant had decreased PSR and increased Pi content compared with wild-type plants，suggesting enhanced Pi uptake of the snx1-2 mutant root.To verify this,we tested the sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate,a toxic compound with a similar structure to phosphate that can be absorbed by plant high-affinity PHTs including PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 (Cao et al.,202O; Shin et al., 2004). Arsenate negatively affects plant growth and development such as seed germination, cotyledon greening,and root elongation (Cao et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2014).We found that snx1-2 mutant seeds had comparable germination and cotyledon greening rates to wild-type seeds when grownon arsenate-free medium,while the mutant seeds showed significantly decreased germination and cotyledon greening rates compared to wild-type plants when grown on arsenate-containing medium (Figure 2a-e). The increased sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate was confirmed by assessing its root elongation and fresh weight. Fiveday-old wild-type and snx1-2 mutant seedlings were transferred to arsenate-containing medium and treated for 5 days.As shown in Figure 2(f)， the snx1-2 mutant seedlings exhibited significantly less resistance to arsenate than the wild-type plants,as evidenced by shorter roots. These data indicated increased sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant to arsenate，revealing enhanced Pi transporter activity in the mutant roots.


## PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 interact with SNX1


Increased Pi content and arsenate sensitivity of the snx1-2 mutant suggested higher PHT activity for Pi uptake in roots. Hence，we first examined the expression of the genes encoding the two major high-affinity PHTs，PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants. Our qRTPCR data showed that the expression of both PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 was extensively induced by low Pi in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants,and their expression level in the mutant was similar to that in the wild type (Figure S3), excluding the possibility that increased Pi content in the mutant was due to higher expression of PHT1;1 and PHT1;4.

Considering that SNX1 is a key component of sorting endosomes，we speculated that SNX1 affects plant Pi uptake through modulating endosomal traffickingof PHT1;1 and/or PHT1;4. Thus， we examined the colocalization of SNX1 with PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 by expressing them under the control of their native promoters in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.As shown in Figure 3(a), the fluorescence signals of SNX1-mCherry and PHT1;1-GFP or PHT1;4-GFP were mainly co-localized in vesicles in N. benthamiana leaves,which is in line with a previous report showing that PHT1;1 is localized to sorting endosomes containingSNX1inArabidopsisroottips(Bayle et al.,2011).To further verify such co-localization，we obtained a stable PHT1;1-GFP SNX1-mRFP line by introducing PHT1;1::PHT1;1-GFP into SNX1::SNX1-mRFP plants and observed their localization. Our confocal microscopy results showed that PHT1;1-GFP and SNX1-mRFP mainly co-localized in vesicles in PHT1;1-GFP SNX1-mRFP seedling roots treated with sufficient Pi (Figure 3b)，which is very similar to the previous report (Bayle et al.,2011). However,when treated with deficient Pi,PHT1;1-GFP and SNX1-mRFP exhibited not only vesicular but also plasma membrane localization (Figure 3b)，which is consistent with the recent report that low Pi promotes SNX1 protein accumulation at the plasma membrane (Lin et al., 2020).

To explore the genetic relationship between SNX1 and PHT1;1,we obtained an snx1-2 pht1;1 double mutant by genetically crossing the two mutants and assessed its Pi content. ## SNX1 decreases PHT1;1 protein stability


The above results showed that SNX1,as an interacting partner of PHT1;1 and PHT1;4，, negatively affects plant Pi uptake，raising the possibility that SNX1 affects PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 protein stability through their interaction.To evaluate the stability of PHT1;1 or PHT1;4 in the snx1-2 mutant，we first generated PHT1;1-GFP-overexpressing transgenic plants in the snx1-2 mutant background by genetic crossing 35S:PHT1;1-GFP with the snx1-2 mutant. Five-day-old 35S::PHT1;1-GFP and 35S::PHT1;1-GFP snx1-2 seedlings were transferred to Pi-sufficient or -deficient medium for 5 days and then treated with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX).Our immunoblot assays showed that CHX treatment resulted in decreased PHT1;1-GFP accumulation in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant background plants,while the PHT1;1-GFP level decreased faster in the CHX-treated wild-type plants than in the snx1- 2 mutant,indicating increased PHT1;1 stability in the mutant (Figure 4a,b).We also found that although low Pi treatment suppressed the degradation of PHT1;1-GFP in both wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants,the stability of PHT1;1 in the mutant was still higher than that in the wild type as evidenced by higher PHT1;1-GFP accumulation in the mutant (Figure 4a,b),further indicating that SNX1 negatively modulates PHT1;1 protein stability in plants.

To further confirm the role of SNX1 in the modulation of PHT1;1 stability,we performed in vivo and in vitro protein degradation experiments. PHT1;1-GFP (target protein) and mCherry (control） were co-expressed with SNX1-Flag or Flag tag in N.benthamiana leaves for 3 days,and then the PHT1;1-GFP and mCherry proteins were detected.As shown in Figure 4(c,d),PHT1;1-GFP transcript levels were similar in the leaves expressing SNX1-Flag and Flag，but the PHT1;1-GFP protein level was significantly lower in the SNX1-Flag-expressing leaves than in the Flag-expressing leaves,while mCherry protein levels were not significantly altered,revealing that SNX1 facilitates PHT1;1 degradation in vivo.In addition,we also extracted total proteins from N. benthamiana leaves expressing PHT1;1-GFP,mCherry, and SNX1-Flag and incubated the protein mixture containing similar amounts of mCherry but different ratios of

PHT1;1-GFP and SNX1-Flag. Our immunoblot results showed that the protein accumulation of mCherry was similar but the PHT1;1-GFP level significantly decreased as the SNX1-Flag protein level increased (Figure 4e,f), indicating that SNX1 also promotes the degradation of PHT1;1 in vitro. Together,these results demonstrate that SNX1 decreases PHT1;1 protein stability.


## SNX1 reduces PHT1;1 plasma membrane accumulation


Increased PHT1;1 stability in the snx1-2 mutant suggested higher PHT1;1 protein accumulation in the mutant.We further generated transgenic wild-type and snx1-2 mutant plants expressing PHT1;1-GFP driven by its native promoter (PHT1;1:PHT1;1-GFP and PHT1;1::PHT1;1-GFP snx1- 2)and treated them with sufficient or deficient Pi.Our immunoblot results showed that the amount of PHT1;1- GFP protein in PHT1;1::PHT1;1-GFP snx1-2 plants Was significantly higher than that in PHT1;1:PHT1;1-GFP plants treated with either sufficient or deficient Pi (Figure 5a), indicating that the snx1-2 mutant had more PHT1;1 protein than the wild-type plant. Furthermore,we compared the abundance of PHT1;1 in wild-type and snx1-2 mutant roots in the plant response to sufficient or deficient Pi. Using FM4-64 to stain the plasma membrane，we found that PHT1;1-GFP was mainly localized in the cytoplasm as well as at the plasma membrane in roots under sufficient Pi, while low Pi stimuli significantly reduced PHT1;1-GFP cytoplasmic localization but increased its plasma membrane localization in PHT1;1:PHT1;1-GFP roots (Figure 5b)，suggesting that low Pi promotes PHT1;1 plasma membrane localization by affecting its endosomal trafficking. When PHT1;1:PHT1;1-GFP snx1-2 roots Were observed，more PHT1;1-GFP was localized at the mutant root plasma membrane than in the wild-type root plasma membrane,under either deficient Pi or sufficient Pi (Figure 5b), implying a role of SNX1 in the modulation of PHT1;1 accumulation at the plasma membrane.This view was verified by fractionation experiments，which revealed that PHT1;1 protein levels at the plasma membrane-enriched fractions were higher in PHT1;1:PHT1;1-GFP snx1-2 roots than in PHT1;1:: PHT1;1-GFP roots under suficient or deficient Pi conditions (Figure 5c),further supporting that SNX1 decreases PHT1;1 levels in the plasma membrane.

Taken together，our study reveals that SNX1 interacts with PHT1;1 and facilitates its degradation via endosomal trafficking to reduce its accumulation inat the plasma membrane,thus negatively modulating plant Pi uptake in roots.

PHT1;1 protein stability and plasma membrane abundance in Arabidopsis.As members of the Sorting Nexin family, SNX2a and SNX2b function with SNX1 in plant cellular endosomal trafficking through forming homodimers or heterodimers (Pourcher et al., 2010).Whether SNX2a and SNX2b play a role in plant Pi uptake and PSR remains unknown. Our results showed that snx2a-2 and snx2b-1 mutants had similar anthocyanin accumulation and Pi content to wild-type plants when subjected to sufficient or deficient Pi (Figure S4),revealing that SNX2a or SNX2b is not necessary for plant Pi uptake.

In the present study,we showed that SNX1 is a negative modulator of Pi uptake by facilitating PHT1;1 protein degradation in Arabidopsis. How plants modulate SNX1- mediated PHT1;1 protein degradation under different Pi conditions remains unclear.We examined the expression of SNX1 in plant seedlings treated with sufficient or deficient Pi by qRT-PCR,and found that low Pi treatment significantly downregulated SNX1 expression,consistent with increased PHT1;1 protein stability in low Pi-treated plants. To investigate whether this low Pi-repressed SNX1 expression is mediated by PHR1,the master transcription factor in plant low Pi signaling,we assayed SNX1 expression in wild-type and phr1 mutant plants. Our result showed that the phr1 mutant had comparable levels of SNX1 expression to the wild type (Figure S5)，revealing that SNX1 expression is not affected by PHR1. How plants modulate SNX1 expression to fine-tune PHT1;1 protein stability remains elusive,and extensive experiments are required to explore the underlying mechanism.We speculate that identification of the upstream factors of SNX1 may shed more light on how plants coordinate mechanisms to increase and reduce Pi uptake under different Pi availabilities.

Endosomal traficking controls the localization,degradation,storage,or reutilization of membrane proteins,thus playing a fundamental role in plant membrane protein turnover and responses to environmental stimuli.ALiX in Arabidopsis interacts with the ESCRT-Il component SNF7 and mediates PHT1;1 trafficking from the plasma membrane to the vacuole for degradation through MVBs. Thus, the alix mutant displays reduced vacuolar degradation of PHT1;1 and increased Pi content compared to wild-type plants.Similar to the alix mutant,our study showed that the snx1-2 mutant also has increased PHT1;1 stability and Pi content,raising the possibility that SNX1 acts upstream of ALIX in the endosomal trafficking of PHT1;1 as SNX1 acts in the sorting center for protein trafficking.We speculated that the cytoplasmic PHT1;1 protein is recognized by SNX1 via their interaction,subsequently sorted into ALIXassociated MVBs,and finally degraded in the vacuole in the plant response to sufficient Pi.

In addition to PHT1;1，a series of proteins have been identified as ALIX cargos，including the ABA receptor PYL4/RCAR10 and the brassinosteroid receptor brassinosteroid-insensitive 1，which are modulated by ALIX-mediatedvacuolardegradation(Cardona-Lopez et al., 2015; Garcia-Leon et al., 2019). Thus,alix null mutation can retard plant growth and even result in lethality,in contrast to the snx1-2 mutant,which exhibits relatively normal growth and development, suggesting that ALIX and SNX1 have common as well as different target cargos involved in plant growth and stress responses.The complicated relationship between SNX1-mediated protein sorting and ALIX-mediated protein degradation in diverse plant biological processes remains to be further experimentally elucidated.

It has been reported that the microtubule-associated protein CLASP interacts with SNX1 to mediate an association between endosomes and microtubules; clasp-1 mutant plants exhibit enhancedPlN2 degradation (Ambrose et al., 2013)，indicating that CLASP represses PIN2 degradation via SNX1. Another previous report also documented that both BLOC-1 complex components BLOS1 and BLOS2 interact with SNX1 on sorting endosomes and that BLOS1 knockdown lines exhibit increased PIN2 protein levels (Cui et al., 2010),revealing that BLOS1 promotes PIN2 degradation via SNX1. These reports imply that SNX1 lies at the switch point of the two routes, retrograde transport for protein recycling and protein vacuolar degradation (Cui et al.,2010). The present study demonstrates that SNX1 negatively modulates plant Pi uptake under Pi deficiency by sorting PHT1;1 into endosomes for vacuolar degradation，suggesting the possible involvement of BLOS1 in SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation in plants.Unraveling the role of BLOS1 in the plant response to limited Pi conditions shall shed more light on how SNX1 functions in Pi uptake through modulating PHT1;1 protein stability. Previous reports also showed that SNX1 facilitates iron acquisition by suppressing IRT1 degradation and increasing its plasma membrane localization (Brumbarova & lvanov,2016; lvanov et al.,2014). Considering the antagonistic interaction between iron and P in plantnutritionacquisition， wewonderedwhether increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant was partially due to altered iron uptake. However,we noticed that compared to wild-type plants, the snx1-2 mutant has similar ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under ironsufficient conditions and lower ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under iron-deficient conditions (lvanov et al.,2014). Thus,we speculate that increased Pi uptake in the snx1-2 mutant is independent of IRT1 under low Pi but suficient iron conditions. In addition,these reports show distinct effcts of SNX1 on its targets， suggesting that SNX1 differentially affects sorting and stability of the target proteins in an environmental stimuli-dependent manner via complicated mechanisms.

We previously reported that SNX1 functions in plant salt stress tolerance by affecting NO accumulation and the activities of antioxidant enzymes (Li et al., 2018). It is widely reported that NO significantly affects plant root development and responses to environmental stresses by inhibiting primary root elongation but promoting lateral root and root hair development in plants (Lombardo et al.,20o6; Schlicht et al.,2013),similar to the effect of low Pi on plant root architecture (Liu et al., 2009,2017),suggesting a possible role of NO in the plant response to low Pi conditions.

A recent study documented that low Pi restrains SNX1 accumulation in the cytoplasm but stimulates its plasma membrane localization in a PA-dependent manner (Lin et al.,2020). Combined with our observations,we further speculated that under sufficient Pi,SNX1 interacts with PHT1;1 in cytosolic vesicles to promote its protein degradation, thereby reducing root Pi uptake,while low Pi facilitates SNX1 localization at the plasma membrane in a PAdependent manner and also represses SNX1 expression, thus relieving SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation and increasing root Pi uptake.

High-affinity phosphate (Pi) transporters (PHTs) PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are necessary for plant root Pi uptake especially under Pi-deficient conditions,but how their protein stability is modulated remains elusive. Here, we identified a Ttransfer DNA insertion mutant of Sorting Nexin1(SNX1),which had more Pi content and less anthocyanin accumulation than the wild type under deficient Pi. By contrast,the snx1-2 mutant displayed higher sensitivity to exogenous arsenate in terms of seed germination and root elongation,revealing higher Pi uptake rates. Further study showed that SNX1 could co-localize and interact with PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 in vesicles and at the plasma membrane. Genetic analysis showed that increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant under low Piconditions could be extensively compromised by mutating PHT1;1in the double mutant snx1-2 pht1;1,revealing that SNX1 is epistatic to PHT1;1.In addition,SNX1 negatively controls PHT1;1 protein stability; therefore,PHT1;1 protein abundance in the plasma membrane was increased in the snx1-2 mutant compared with the wild type under either sufficient or deficient Pi. Together,our study (i) identifies SNX1 as a key modulatorof the plant response to low Pi and (ii unravels its role in the modulation of PHT1;1 protein stability,PHT1;1 accumulation at the plasma membrane,and root Pi uptake.

Keywords: SNX1, PHT1, phosphate, protein stability, plasma membrane localization.

Phosphorus (P) is one of the nutrients that are essential for all organisms. It is required for cellular constituents, including nucleic acids, membranes and ATP, and is a key component in regulating enzyme reactions, metabolic pathways and signal transduction processes (Chiou and Lin, 2011; Nussaume et al., 2011; Baek et al., 2017). Cells acquire P mainly in the form of inorganic phosphate (Pi, orthophosphate) by Pi transporters at plasma membranes. In plants, Pi is initially acquired by roots, moved towards the stele, transported up to the above-ground tissues, and subsequently distributed among different tissues. The acquisition and allocation of Pi mainly relies on the activities of plasma membrane-localized Pi transporters. Regulation of Pi transport activities by coordinating the environmental Pi supply with the demand of plants is a prerequisite to sustain plant growth and development and to ensure reproductive success.

The members of the phosphate transporter 1 (PHT1) family located at the plasma membranes are conserved in plant species and are responsible for Pi acquisition from the rhizosphere as well as for Pi remobilization among different tissues (Nussaume et al., 2011; Johri et al., 2015). In Arabidopsis thaliana, nine genes (AtPHT1;1 - AtPHT1;9) in the PHT1 family were identified. Several of them are preferentially expressed in the root epidermal or cortical cells, supporting their roles in Pi uptake (Mudge et al., 2002; Poirier and Bucher, 2002). In particular, AtPHT1;1 plays a predominate role in Pi acquisition under Pi replete conditions because pht1;1 mutants showed less Pi accumulation than wild-type plants as a result of reduced Pi uptake activity (Shin et al., 2004; Ayadi et al., 2015). The PHT1 genes are transcriptionally upregulated by Pi starvation and PHT1 proteins are post-translationally regulated via intracellular trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the plasma membrane and ubiquitin-mediated degradation (González et al., 2005; Bayle et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013). The Pi transport activities of several PHT1 members have been detected in transformed oocytes, yeast mutants, or plant cells (Muchhal et al., 1996; Mitsukawa et al., 1997; Ai et al., 2009). The Pi transport activity of AtPHT1 was enhanced under low pH but inhibited by protonophores, indicating the nature of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled Pi symporters (Mitsukawa et al., 1997). Expression of AtPHT1;1 in the BY-2 tobacco cell line exhibited a high-affinity Pi transport property $( \mathrm { K } _ { \mathrm { m } } = 3 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ (Mitsukawa et al., 1997). Furthermore, it has been recently suggested that AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 could form a homomeric or heteromeric complex, which modulates Pi transport activity (Fontenot et al., 2015). Site-directed mutagenesis at Y312D residue of AtPHT1;1 enhanced Pi transport likely due to the disruption of homomeric interactions (Fontenot et al., 2015). Despite the above-mentioned work, our knowledge on the structure-function relationship of PHT1 proteins is still limited.

PHT1 proteins belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) whose members could transport many kinds of small solutes (Pao et al., 1998). MFS represents the largest secondary transporter group using the electrochemical potential gradient generated by ATPase across membranes. They are typically 400 to 600 amino acids long consisting of 12 transmembrane (TM) $\mathfrak { a }$ -helices and share similarities in transmembrane topology with both $\mathrm { N } -$ and C-termini facing cytosol (Pao et al., 1998; Yan, 2015; Quistgaard et al., 2016). All MFS transporters contain a characteristic core folding, by which 12 TMs are divided into 3 groups depending on spatial arrangement at the plasma membrane, including the core helices (TMs 1, 4, 7, and 10), the middle helices (TMs 2, 5, 8, and 11), and the outer helices groups (TMs 3, 6, 9, and 12) (Yan, 2015). A general transport mechanism of MFS has been suggested based on the structure analysis of several representative members whose distinct conformational states include initial ligand-free occluded, outward open, ligand-bound occluded, and final inward open states (Yan, 2015; Quistgaard et al., 2016). These conformational states could be modulated by substrate interactions via hydrogen bonds and by the gating residues of A-motifs, GX3-(D/E)-(R/K)-X-G-[X]-(R/K)-(R/K), via internal salt bridges (Jiang et al., 2013; Quistgaard et al., 2016). Moreover, the A-motif between TM2 and TM3 in the N-domain and/or between TM8 and TM9 in the C-domain are/is able to form internal salt bridges with residues on TM5 or TM10 (Jiang et al., 2013; Quistgaard et al., 2016).

The phosphate: $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporter (PHS) family, belonging to MFS Family 9, has been identified in yeasts, fungi, and plants, including PHO84 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, GvPT from Glomus versiforme, and PHT1 members from plants (Bun-ya et al., 1991; Harrison and Buuren, 1995; Muchhal et al., 1996; Pao et al., 1998). The first crystal structure of a fungal Pi transporter PiPT (Piriformospora indica PT) with an inward-facing ligand-bound occluded state was resolved (Pedersen et al., 2013). In PiPT, several residues such as Y150, F174, Q177, W320, D324, Y328, N431, and K459 residues were found in the Pi binding pocket and D45, D48, E108, R139, and

D149 residues have been suggested to be involved in $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transfer (Pedersen et al., 2013). The transport mechanism of PiPT was proposed to be mediated by conformational changes through protonation and deprotonation of D324 residue, triggering off an outward open state to a ligand-bound occluded state (Pedersen et al., 2013). The functional analysis of ScPHO84 suggested the involvement of R168 and D178 residues (corresponding to R139 and D149 residues in PiPT) in $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transfer and Y179, D358 and K492 residues (corresponding to Y150, D324 and K459 residues in PiPT) in the Pi-binding pocket (Samyn et al., 2012, 2016). Nevertheless, the importance of these amino acid residues is not validated experimentally in vivo.

To further elucidate the structure-function relationship of Pi transporters, in this study, we were thus prompted to identify the key amino acid residues of AtPHT1;1 engaged in the course of Pi transport, which shows protein sequence homology $30 \%$ identity and $48 \%$ similarity) with PiPT. The selected candidate residues were subjected to alanine scanning mutagenesis, followed by functional complementation analysis in the yeast pam2 mutant defective in two high-affinity Pi transporters and in Arabidopsis pht1;1 mutants, respectively. Together with the structure information, our study offers experimental evidence to validate the importance of potential residues that may participate in $\mathrm { P i / H ^ { + } }$ transport, maintain structural stability, or facilitate conformational changes. A working model is accordingly proposed to illustrate in a detailed manner the mechanism through which Pi transporters act.

Phosphorus (P) is one of the essential macronutrients for plant growth and development, and it takes part in cellular macromolecules, energy transfer reactions, and cellular metabolism. Efficient acquisition of phosphate (Pi) from soil combined with efficiency translocation of Pi within plants is essential for plants to maintain adequate levels of cellular Pi necessary for normal function (Raghothama and Karthikeyan, 2005). Although total P in soils is abundant, the soluble phosphate (Pi) is often low (Bieleski, 1973; Rausch and Bucher, 2002), and therefore plants often encounter a scarcity of Pi in soils of both agricultural and natural systems (Raghothama, 1999, 2000). As there is a large difference between Pi levels in plant cells (mM) and soil solution $( \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , plants need to acquire Pi against a steep concentration gradient across the plasma membrane (Smith et al., 2003; Raghothama and Karthikeyan, 2005). The transmembrane transport of Pi from soils into plant cells requires a high-affinity, energy-driven transport mechanism (Smith et al., 2003). The PHT1 family of plant Pi transporters is assumed to play the predominant roles in this transmembrane transport process. These proteins are characterized by 12 membranespanning domains which are similar to PHO84, a high-affinity Pi transporter from yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) (Muchhal et al., 1996; Rausch and Bucher, 2002).

There are four PHOSPHATE TRANSPORTER (PHT) families in plants: PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, and PHT4 which are located on plasma membrane, plastid inner membrane, mitochondrial inner membrane, and Golgi-compartment, respectively (LopezArredondo et al., 2014). Under the stress of P-starvation, the expression of PHT1 genes are strongly induced to increase the ability of the roots in acquiring P from soils and remobilize P within plants (Smith et al., 2003; Raghothama and Karthikeyan, 2005). A large number of PHT1 transporters have been identified in many plant species and show differences in expression locations and affinities for Pi (Nussaume et al., 2011). Nine PHT1 genes in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) have been identified. AtPHT1.1 and AtPHT1.4 are highly expressed at the root–soil interface, including the epidermis, root hair cells, and the root cap under low P conditions (Mudge et al., 2002), and they are the major genes responsible for Pi acquisition by roots in both high and low P supplies (Misson et al., 2004; Shin et al., 2004; Catarecha et al., 2007). AtPHT1.8 and AtPHT1.9 are likely to act sequentially in the interior of the plant during the root-to-shoot translocation of Pi and are involved in rootto-shoot translocation of Pi (Lapis-Gaza et al., 2014). There are 13 PHT1 members in the rice (Oryza sativa) genome, and some of them have been functionally characterized, including OsPHT1.1 (Sun et al., 2012), OsPHT1.2 and OsPHT1.6 (Ai et al., 2009), OsPHT1.4 (Ye et al., 2015), and OsPHT1.8 (Jia et al., 2011; Li et al., 2015). For example, OsPHT1.6 is expressed in both epidermal and cortical cells of the younger primary and lateral roots and encodes as a high-affinity transporter with a broad role in Pi uptake and translocation throughout the plant, whereas OsPHT1.2 is localized exclusively in the stele of primary and lateral roots and functions as a low-affinity transporter responsible for Pi translocation (Ai et al., 2009). Barley (Hordeum vulgare) is a close relative to wheat (Triticum aestivum). To date, 11 PHT1 genes have been reported in barley. The HvPHT1.1 and HvPHT1.2 promoters drive the expression of $\beta$ -glucuronidase (GUS) and green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter genes in epidermal and cortex cells as well as vascular tissues of roots (Schunmann et al., 2004). When expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes, HvPHT1.1 is confirmed to be a high-affinity transporter with a very low $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value $( 1 . 9 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ for Pi transport (Preuss et al., 2011). The expression locations and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value for Pi transport indicate the possible role of HvPHT1.1 in $\mathrm { P }$ uptake. HvPHT1.6 is expressed in both roots and shoots (Huang et al., 2008). Also, it is highly expressed in old leaves compared to young leaves, especially in the leaf phloem tissue (Rae et al., 2003). HvPHT1.6 shows the linear transport activity for Pi-stimulated inward current over a concentration range of 5 to $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ in Xenopus laevis oocytes (Preuss et al., 2010). These results suggest that HvPHT1.6 function as a low-affinity Pi transporter responsible for Pi remobilization in the whole plant. Huang et al. (2011) investigated the expression of PHT1 genes and its relationship with $\mathrm { P }$ acquisition efficiency and $\mathrm { P }$ utilization efficiency (the amount of biomass produced per unit of acquired P) in four barley genotypes. They did not find a clear pattern in the expression of the four HvPHT1.1 paralogs (HvPHT1.1, 1.2, 1.9, 1.10) among the four barley genotypes, but observed that the expression of HvPHT1.3 and 1.6 positively correlated with P utilization efficiency. HvPHT1.8 and HvPHT1.11 (known as HvPT11) have been demonstrated to be specifically activated by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi (Glassop et al., 2005; Sisaphaithong et al., 2012), indicating their possible roles in the mycorrhizal pathway of Pi uptake.

Wheat is one of the most important crops. However, limited attempts have been made to dissect the role of Pi transporters in wheat (Secco et al., 2017). Davies et al. (2002) isolated the first full-length sequence of a wheat PHT1 gene (TaPHT1.10-U, formerly known TaPT2) and partial clones of several other putative PHT1 genes. TaPHT1.10-U was induced by P-deficiency in roots, and had higher transcript abundance in P-efficient wheat varieties than in inefficient ones (Davies et al., 2002). In yeast, TaPHT1.10-U can complement highaffinity phosphate transporter gene PHO84 function (Zeng et al., 2002) and shows an apparent mean $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of $2 3 . 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Pi (Guo et al., 2014). Overexpression of TaPHT1.10- $U$ increases plant dry weight and $\mathrm { P i }$ acquisition, whereas knock-down of TaPHT1.10-U has the opposite effect (Guo et al., 2014). These results suggest that TaPHT1.10-U functions as a high-affinity Pi transporter and mediates Pi uptake. A recent study observed that TaPHT1.12-7A (former name TaPHT1.4) was root-specific and P-deficiency inducible. Yeast complement analysis showed that TaPHT1.12-7A encodes a high-affinity Pi transporter with an apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of $3 5 . 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ . Overexpressing TaPHT1.12-7A significantly improves growth traits and accumulates more Pi than the wild-type plant and those with downregulated TaPHT1.12-7A expression (Liu et al., 2013). A recent study also revealed the relationships between PHT1 expression and $\mathrm { P }$ use efficiency in wheat (Aziz et al., 2014). The highly P-efficient wheat cultivar Chinese 80-55 has a higher Pi acquisition in the presence of Pi and accumulates higher Pi concentrations in all organs upon Pi withdrawal compared with the less-efficient cultivar Machete. These differences correlate with differential organspecific expression of Pi transporters TaPHT1.10-4A (reported as TaPHT1.2, GenBank: AY293828), TaPHT1.6-5A (reported as TaPHT1.5, GenBank: AF110180) and TaPHT1.4-5B (reported as TaPHT1.8, GenBank: AK333026) (Aziz et al., 2014). Shukla et al. (2016) found that aleurone accumulates more Pi with higher expression of TaPHT1 genes compared to endosperm. TaPHT1.8- 6A (known as TRIae; Pht1; myc, Glassop et al., 2005, GenBank: AJ830009), TaPHT1.11-4A (known as TRIae; Pht1; 12, GenBank: AB753271), TaPHT1.11-4B (known as TRIae; Pht1;11, GenBank: AB753270), and TaPHT1.11-4D (known as TRIae; Pht1; 10, GenBank: AB753269) have been found to be induced by AM fungi (Glassop et al., 2005; Sisaphaithong et al., 2012). Although expression of some PHT1 genes has displayed correlation with P use-related traits in wheat and its close relative barley under controlled conditions, an on-farm field-scale investigation is required to explore the PHT1 genes contributing to $\mathrm { P }$ uptake and utilization, as the response of PHT1 genes to P supply level under controlled conditions greatly differed from that under field conditions. Our recent study showed that the expression of TaPHT1.1, 1.2, 1.9, and 1.10 in roots at the flowering stage under low $\mathrm { P }$ conditions was lower than that under high P conditions in a field experiment (Teng et al., 2013). The inhibition of these four wheat genes by P-deficiency could be, at least partially, explained by the upregulated AM colonization under P-deficiency, considering that AM colonization has been found to inhibit the response of HvPHT1.1 and HvPHT1.2 to P deficiency in barley (Glassop et al., 2005).

The transportation and translocation of essential inorganic nutrient Pi is mainly mediated by phosphate transporters (PTs). During this process, the coupled proton gradient that is generated by plasma membrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } .$ -ATPase provides the energy needed in the processes (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1981).

Plant PT members are categorized into four groups: PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, and PHT4 (Rausch and Bucher 2002). They are responsible for diverse phosphate transport processes. PHT1 members are responsible for absorbing Pi from growth media and for mediating Pi transportation across tissues (Mudge et al. 2002; Ai et al. 2009), whereas PHT2 members are responsible for Pi translocation across cells and tissues (Daram et al. 1999). PHT3 and PHT4 members are mainly involved in cellular Pi transportation to distinct subcellular localizations, such as chloroplasts, mitochondria, and Golgi bodies (Karandashov and Bucher 2005; Rouached et al. 2010). PHT1 members share 12 conserved membrane-spanning domains in which two regions of six transmembrane domains are separated by a hydrophilic loop (Henderson 1993; Petersson et al. 1999). Most PHT1 members are targeted to the cytoplasmic membrane after ER sorting (Bucher 2007; Lambers et al. 2008). In the present study, characterization analysis of TaPT2 revealed that it shares common features with previously identified PHT1 members (Riesmeier et al. 1992). At the nucleic acid level, TaPT2 is highly similar to PHT1 genes in diverse plant species. Its translated product contains 12 membrane-spanning domains and is targeted to the cytoplasmic membrane after ER sorting. Therefore, TaPT2 is one of the PHT1 family members in wheat.

Kinetic characteristics, such as $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value, are important factors for understanding the regulatory functions of PHT1 members in Pi uptake or Pi translocation across tissues. Two types of PHT1 members can be classified according to the $K \mathrm { m }$ value: high affinity and low affinity. High-affinity PHT1 members have micromolar $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values (Raghothama 1999), whereas low-affinity PHT1 members have higher $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values than high-affinity Pi transporters (Ai et al. 2009). To date, the determined $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values in several PHT1 family members were largely varied, including 280 and $1 3 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for two of the potato PHT1 transporters (Muchhal et al. 1996; Leggewie et al. 1997; Liu et al. 1998b), 97 and $2 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for the rice OsPT6 and OsPT8 (Ai et al. 2009; Jia et al. 2011), $1 9 2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for Medicago MtPT1 (Liu et al. 1998b), and $2 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ for wheat TaPHT2;1 (Guo et al. 2013). In the present study, functional complement analysis of TaPT2 was performed in MB192, a yeast mutant defective in high-affinity Pi transporter system. TaPT2 can endow the yeast mutant with growth under Pi deprivation $( 5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { \ p i }$ ), with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value of $2 3 . 6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ on Pi acquisition. These findings suggest that TaPT2 is a high-affinity PHT1 member in wheat.

Most members of the PHT1 family in various plant species, such as those classified into monocots and dicots, exhibit strong expression levels in roots (Muchhal et al. 1996; Leggewie et al. 1997; Smith et al. 1997; Schu¨nmann et al. 2004a; Koyama et al. 2005; Nagy et al. 2006; Xiao et al. 2006; Jia et al. 2011; Liu et al. 2013). Numerous PHT1 genes are root specific, and their expression levels are induced by Pi deprivation, with more transcripts located at the root epidermal cells and root hairs (Mudge et al. 2002; Rae et al. 2003; Bucher 2007; Lambers et al. 2008; Liu et al. 2013). Most PHT1 members are specifically or predominantly expressed in the roots, with an upregulated pattern under Pi starvation. This finding is consistent with their regulatory function in nutrient acquisition (Muchhal et al. 1996; Leggewie et al. 1997; Smith et al. 1997; Liu et al. 1998). In the present study, TaPT2 was specifically expressed in the roots, and its expression levels were dramatically elevated upon exposure to Pi deprivation. These results are consistent with the expression characterizations of the PHT1 genes reported previously. Distinct cis-regulatory elements such as the PIBS-like motifs are reported to be crucial in PHT1 genes in response to Pi deprivation (Schu¨nmann et al. 2004a, b; Glassop et al. 2005). Further identification of the cis-regulatory elements in the TaPT2 promoter and promoter–reporter system analysis can elucidate the transcriptional mechanism of this wheat PHT1 gene.

Enhancement of Pi uptake capacity by Pi deprivation has been documented in various plant species (Bucher 2007). Moreover, induction of high-affinity PHT1 gene expression is one strategy that plants adapt under Pi deprivation (Raghothama 1999; Liu et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2013). The increased amount of Pi uptake under Pi deprivation can be partly associated with the activation of existing PHT1s or with the synthesis of other PHT1 members (Dunlop and Gardiner 1993). In Arabidopsis, two PHT1 genes, AtPht1;1 and AtPht1;4, are highly expressed in the epidermis and root hair cells. These genes are involved in Pi uptake over a wide range of external Pi concentrations. The double mutant of both AtPht1;1 and AtPht1;4 exhibited a $75 \%$ reduction in the amount of Pi uptake compared with the WT plants (Shin et al. 2004). The rice high-affinity PHT1 gene OsPT1 has redundant function with other Pi starvation-upregulated PHT1 genes in the acquisition and transportation of Pi (Qin et al. 2012). Overexpression and downregulation of wheat TaPht1;4 significantly altered the plant phenotypic features under Pi deprivation, wherein more significantly improved growth traits and accumulated Pi were observed in TaPT2-overexpressing plants than in TaPT2-downregulating plants (Liu et al. 2013). In the current study, TaPT2 overexpression and downregulation exhibited similar functions to TaPht1;4. The plants overexpressing TaPT2 had significantly improved plant growth traits based on their significantly higher Pi uptake under Pi deprivation. By contrast, the plants downregulating TaPT2 had dramatically reduced plant growth, with lower plant dry mass, Pi acquisition amounts, and photosynthetic behaviors than the control plants under Pi deprivation. Previous studies confirm that $\mathrm { \bf P }$ deficiency limits photosynthetic rate by altering leaf chlorophyll and protein contents (Plesnicˇar et al. 1994; Usuda 1995), causing decreased photosynthetic rate $( P _ { n } )$ (Brooks 1986; Rao and Terry 1989). By contrast, available intracellular Pi plays an important role in maintaining high efficiency of photosynthesis reaction system, resulting in improved net photosynthetic assimilation capacity (Liu et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2013). Therefore, TaPT2 has critical functions in plant Pi acquisition under Pi deprivation, supported by its induced expression patterns under Pi deprivation and high-affinity features on Pi acquisition. Our findings suggest that the improvement of Pi acquisition by TaPT2 can lead to increased plant photosynthesis which further enhances the plant dry mass production under Pi deprivation.

Several PHT1 members in plant species have important functions in Pi acquisition under both Pi sufficiency and deprivation. For example, AtPht1;1 and AtPht1;4 are involved in Pi uptake over a wide range of external Pi concentrations (Shin et al. 2004). In the present study, upregulated or downregulated TaPT2 expression did not affect Pi uptake, plant growth, morphological characteristics, and photosynthetic behaviors under Pi sufficiency. In this case, PHT1 members such as those belonging to lowaffinity PHT1 members possibly function as the main regulators of Pi uptake and transportation. Moreover, TaPT2 exhibited similar expression patterns in response to Pi deprivation, kinetic features on Pi acquisition, and biological functions in Pi uptake in transgenic plants to TaPht1;4, another high-affinity PHT1 gene in wheat that we characterized previously (Liu et al. 2013). Although TaPT2 and TaPht1;4 are genetically divergent $( 5 6 . 5 ~ \%$ identity at the nucleic acid level), their biochemical properties in Pi affinity, distinct biological functions in plant Pi uptake, and synergistic response to external Pi deprivation need to be further characterized.

P is an essential macronutrient in plant growth, development, and high crop productivity (Zebrowska et al. 2012; Cai et al. 2013; Yang et al. 2013; Hajong et al. 2013; Bargaz et al. 2013). A large amount of Pi fertilizers is frequently applied to achieve high crop yields because of the low availability of $\mathrm { \bf P }$ in arable fields. However, P fertilizers applied in the agricultural soils can transport to ground water through leaching, causing the environmental concern and a potential risk to human health (Vance et al. 2003). Therefore, improved P use efficiency in wheat and other cereals through the molecular breeding approach is crucial for sustainable agriculture and food security worldwide (Godfray et al. 2010; Parry and Hawkesford 2010). Our findings suggest that the high-affinity PHT1 wheat gene TaPT2 can be used as an important genetic marker and valuable gene resource for enhancing plant P use efficiency because of its high affinity in Pi acquisition and efficient regulation of external Pi uptake under Pi deprivation.

In conclusion, TaPT2 is a key member of the PHT1 family in wheat. It was specifically expressed in the roots, and its expression was upregulated under Pi deprivation. TaPT2 possesses typical molecular characteristics of a phosphate transporter gene, is targeted to the cytoplasmic membrane, and has important functions in plant Pi uptake under P deprivation. These findings provided insights into the Pi acquisition mechanism mediated by PHT1 family members in plants under P deprivation.
