Plant growth requires a large amount of P, which is not only an important component of nucleic acids, phospholipids, ATP, ADP and sugars, but also participates in various metabolic and material transportation pathways [1–3]. Phosphorus, as one of the most limiting nutrient elements for plant growth and crop production in the world [4–7], plays an irreplaceable role in plant growth. Although the total amount of $\mathrm { P }$ in the soil is very high, most of it exists in the form of an organic state that cannot be absorbed by plants [8], and the mobility of $\mathrm { P }$ in the soil is low, the effective utilization rate is poor, and it is easy to be adsorbed and fixed by cations or organic compounds in the soil that convert $\mathrm { P }$ into insoluble and organic forms that cannot be absorbed and utilized by plants [9–17]. Phosphate transporters are the main transporters involved in the uptake of Pi (refers to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ^ { - }$ in this paper) from the soil and its reuse and distribution in plants [18,19], they can also enable plants to resist the damage caused by various stresses by regulating the absorption and transportation of $\mathrm { P i }$ under a variety of abiotic stress conditions to maintain the normal growth and development of plants [20].

The phosphate transporter family contains many members. According to the different gene protein structures, subcellular localizations and functions in plants, they can be divided into four subfamilies, named PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, PHT4 [15,21–26]. Different families of phosphate transporter genes play different roles in the process of plant growth and development [1,26,27]. PHT1 is the family with the most research results at present. It plays an important role in the process of Pi absorption, transport, distribution and reuse in plants [9,28–31]. PHT1 subfamily proteins belong to the 9th branch of the major facility superfamily (MFS) in structure. They usually have 12 transmembrane-spanning domains [8,15,16,32,33]. They are located on the plasma membrane and use the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -gradient at the plasma membrane to provide energy to drive the absorption of Pi by plants [15,16]. In general, the absorption and transport of one Pi by PHT1 family genes requires 2\~4 protons to enter the plasma membrane together with the change in membrane potential [16,34].

The first plant phosphate transporter gene (PHT1) was cloned from Arabidopsis [35]. It is a high-affinity phosphate transporter gene located on the cytoplasmic membrane and has a structure and function similar to those of PHO84 cloned from Saccharomyces cerevisiae [8,23,33,36]. With increasing attention given to phosphate transporter genes, many related studies have been conducted, and this type of phosphate transporter gene has been found in rice, maize, tomato, sorghum, soybean, millet, poplar, wheat, pepper, tobacco, potato and other plants [3,19,21,23,26,37–44]. Among them, 13 PHT1 genes were identified in rice (Oryza sativa) and maize (Zea mays) [40,45,46], 8 PHT1 genes in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) [43], 11 PHT1 genes in sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) [42], 14 PHT1 genes in soybean (Glycine max) [44], 12 PHT1 genes in millet (Setaria italica) [3,47], 14 PHT1 genes in poplar (Populus trichocarpa) [23], 35 PHT1 genes in wheat (Triticum aestivum) [21]and 49 PHT1 genes in oilseed rape (Brassica napus) [48], and 8 PHT1 genes in potato (Solanum tuberosum) [19,49]. Different phosphate transporter genes involve different functions. At present, the molecular mechanism of the PHT1 genes in Arabidopsis and rice is relatively clear. AtPHT1;1, AtPHT1;2 AtPHT1;3 and AtPHT1;4 genes in Arabidopsis, are mainly involved in the uptake of Pi; AtPHT1;5 gene is responsible for the mobilization of Pi from the source to sink organs; AtPHT1;8 and AtPHT1;9 genes are likely to act sequentially in the interior of the plant during the root-to-shoot translocation of Pi [8,22,25,50–53]. In rice, OsPHT1; 4 is mainly expressed in roots and leaves, OsPHT1; 8 is mainly expressed in roots and stems, among which OsPHT1;1, OsPHT1;4 and OsPHT1;8 all plays in rice Pi uptake and translocation [25,26,37]. At the same time, OsPHT1; 8 also plays an important role in redistribution of Pi from source to sink organs [38].

The potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) is an annual herb of Solanaceae. It is the fourth largest food crop in the world after rice, wheat and maize. Because of its high yield, wide distribution and strong adaptability, it has become the main food crop in many countries and regions. Phosphorus plays a key role in potato root development, tuber formation, nutritional quality and resistance to some diseases [54,55]. The lack of available phosphorus in the soil will inhibit the growth and development of potatoes and reduce the yield and quality of potatoes. However, at present, there are few studies on the function of potato PHT1 gene. Therefore, the study of potato PHT1 gene is of great significance to explore the molecular response mechanism of Pi stress and improve the utilization efficiency of Pi in potato. In this study, potato hydroponic seedlings were used as experimental materials to clone potato phosphate transporter PHTI family member $S t P H T I ; I / I ; 6 / I ; 9 / I ; I 0 / I ; I 2 / I ; I 3$ and analyzed the expression pattern of potato PHTI family gene in different tissues and organs under Pi stress. The purpose of this study was to elucidate the function of potato phosphate transporter, explore the molecular response mechanism of potato under Pi stress, screen efficient Pi germplasm resources and provide basis for molecular breeding.

Phosphorus (P) is an essential macronutrient required for many physiologic and metabolic processes (Li et al. 2011a, b). It is integral to several molecules, such as nucleic acids, phospholipids, and ATP, as well as to intermediates of signal transduction events (Schachtman and Shin 2007; Rouached et al. 2010). Plants must balance $\mathrm { \bf P }$ uptake, mobilization, and partitioning in various organs to modulate P homeostasis.

In vascular plants, the acquisition of inorganic phosphate $( \mathrm { P i } )$ by plant roots is accomplished through active absorption via the phosphate transporters (PTs) into the epidermal and cortical cells of the roots. Pi could then be loaded into the apoplastic space of the xylem and transported to the shoot mediated by the PTs after taken up in the root cortical cells (Marschner 1995).

PHO84 and PHO89 derived from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae were the first reported PTs in living cells. Functional analysis verified that they are two high-affinity phosphate $( \mathrm { P i } )$ permeases mediating Pi transport across the plasma membrane (Bun-Ya et al. 1991; Martinez and Persson 1998). PHO84 is a $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / P i }$ co-transporter and PHO89 mediates in sodium-dependent Pi transport activity. Homologues of PHO84 and PHO89 have been identified in the fungus Neurospora crassa, referred to as PHO5 and PHO4, respectively (Versaw and Metzenberg 1995). Over the past two decades, several plant PT genes were identified in plants based on amino acid homology with PHO84. They were functionally characterized based on complement analysis of yeast mutants with defective endogenous high-affinity PTs (Raghothama 1999; Rausch and Bucher 2002; Rae et al. 2003). The Xenopus laevis oocyte expression system has been used for detecting the Pi transport kinetics of plant PTs (Ai et al. 2009; Preuss et al. 2010, 2011).

Computational modeling of the encoded PT proteins in vascular plants predicts a conserved secondary structure containing 12 transmembrane (TM) domains with a large hydrophilic loop between TM6 and TM7 and both of the hydrophilic N and C termini located in the cytoplasm. Expression analysis of the plant PT genes revealed that most of them, especially Pht1 family members, are generally more numerous in roots than in shoots and the transcripts are enhanced in response to Pi deprivation in most cases (Leggewie et al. 1997; Liu et al. 1998a). Kinetic measurements and in situ localization of mRNA transcripts in rhizodermal cells indicate a key regulatory role of at least some of the plant PHO84-related proteins with highaffinity Pi uptake at the root–soil interface (Mitsukawa et al. 1997; Daram et al. 1998; Liu et al. 1998a).

In addition to the Pi uptake system, three distinct transport systems possibly participate in Pi translocation within the plant, including one that secretes Pi into the xylem in the root, another that loads Pi from the vascular system to the leaf cells, and one that cycles Pi within the plant. The Arabidopsis mutant pho1 is defective in the Pi loading of the xylem, which suggests that this gene has a similar role as PTs, which secretes Pi from the xylem parenchyma cells into the xylem vessels (Poirier et al. 1991; Delhaize and Randall 1995). By contrast, a second mutant, pho2, exhibits defective Pi loading in the phloem (Delhaize and Randall 1995). However, the genes corresponding to the respective phenotypes of the mutants have not been determined.

The identified plant PT genes are classified into four families, namely, Pht1 to Pht4, according to their molecular characterizations and subcellular targeting positions. The subcellular localizations of Pht1, Pht2, Pht3, and Pht4 are targeted to the plasma membrane, chloroplast, mitochondria, and Golgi apparatus, respectively, suggesting their diverse biological functions in plant growth and development (Rausch and Bucher 2002). PT members belonging to the Pht1 family, which are presumed as highaffinity PTs, are studied more intensively (Paszkowski 2006; Bucher 2007; Ai et al. 2009; Preuss et al. 2011). In Arabidopsis, AtPht1;1 and AtPht1;4, two high-affinity PT members, have significant roles in plant Pi acquisition under low and high Pi conditions (Shin et al. 2004; Catarecha et al. 2007). In rice, 13 putative high-affinity Pi transporter genes that belong to the Pht1 family (OsPT1– OsPT13) have been identified (Goff et al. 2002). Two of them, OsPT11 and OsPT13, are exclusively induced in roots by inoculation with Arbuscular mycorrhiza fungi (Paszkowski et al. 2002; Glassop et al. 2005; Gu¨imil et al. 2005). The others, such as OsPT2 and OsPT6 , have different functions and kinetic properties in Pi uptake and translocation (Ai et al. 2009). In barley, eight PHT1 genes have been described (Smith et al. 1999). The promoter::reporter fusions of HvPHT1;1 and HvPHT1;2 show that reporters are expressed in root hairs, epidermal and cortex cells, and vascular tissues of roots (Schu¨nmann et al. 2004; Glassop et al. 2005). Recently, HvPHT1;1 was confirmed to be a high-affinity Pi transporter with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ of $1 . 9 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ when expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes (Preuss et al. 2011), suggesting its involvement in Pi acquisition. In contrast to HvPHT1;1 and HvPHT1;2, HvPHT1;6 was expressed in both shoots and roots (Huang et al. 2008) and localized in the leaf phloem tissue (Rae et al. 2003). It displayed unsaturated uptake in a millimolar range of Pi concentrations when expressed in oocytes (Preuss et al. 2010), indicating its crucial function in Pi retranslocation within plants.

Compared with extensive studies on Pht1 family members in diverse plant species (Schu¨nmann et al. 2004; Glassop et al. 2005; Catarecha et al. 2007; Ai et al. 2009; Preuss et al. 2010), few investigations on Pht2 family members in vascular plants have been performed. Daram et al. (1999) functionally characterized an Arabidopsis Pht2 family member referred to as Pht2;1. Pht2;1 are predominantly expressed in green tissue. PHT2;1–green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusion analysis indicated that it is present in the chloroplast envelop (Versaw et al. 2002). Functional analysis of the $\mathrm { P h t } 2 ; 1$ protein in mutant yeast cells indicated that it is a proton/Pi symporter dependent on the electrochemical gradient across the plasma membrane with fairly high apparent $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for Pi $( 0 . 4 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ . In addition, analysis of the mutant revealed that PHT2;1 activity affected Pi allocation within the plant, especially in leaves, and modulated Pi starvation responses, including the expression of Pi starvation response genes and the translocation of Pi within leaves (Daram et al. 1999; Versaw et al. 2002). The data suggest that Arabidopsis $\mathrm { P h t } 2 ; 1$ acts as a low-affinity Pi transporter in the shoot and plays an indispensable role in Pi translocation within tissues in plants.

Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a cereal with worldwide importance. Therefore, improvement of $\mathrm { \bf P }$ efficiency in wheat through genetic breeding is crucial for sustainable agriculture and worldwide food security (Godfray et al. 2010; Parry and Hawkesford 2010). However, although several wheat PT members have been reported (Davies et al. 2002; Miao et al. 2009), only one of them belonging to the Pht1 family designated as TaPHT1;2D1 has been characterized (Miao et al. 2009). In this study, we report the characterization of the novel wheat Pi transporter gene TaPHT2;1. Its molecular characterization, expression pattern, subcellular location, and endowing capacity of Pi acquisition for a yeast mutant, together with its homologous relation to Arabidopsis PHT2;1 and function of transferring Pi from the cytosol to the chloroplast, suggest that TaPHT2;1 is a member of the $\mathrm { P h t } 2$ family. Moreover, knockdown expression analysis indicated that TaPHT2;1 has an essential role in the regulation of plant Pi homeostasis and plant growth under various Pi supply conditions. It is also a useful gene resource on genetic improvement of phosphorus usage efficiency in wheat.

Arsenic (As), a metalloid commonly present in the soil, primarily exists in sulfdes and other rock-forming minerals. The dissolution of these minerals can lead to the infltration and contamination of groundwater. This poses a signifcant risk to human health including organ damage, clinical complications, and diverse types of cancer (Chen et al. 2019). Similarly, crops irrigated with As contaminated water can accumulate arsenate, potentially compromising the safety of cultivated foods and quality. Furthermore, As induces the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants, adversely afecting crop growth and productivity (Tang et al. 2023). Additionally, arsenic can accumulate in the human body, resulting in organ damage, clinical complications, and diverse types of cancer (Chen et al. 2019).To achieve genetically engineered arsenate-tolerant crops it is crucial to understand how plants absorb the arsenate and the regulatory mechanisms involved to address these implications for human health and food safety.

In soil, As primarily exists as Arsenate As(V), which is structurally similar to phosphate (Pi) and can readily enter plant roots via Pi transporters (Li et al. 2016). The other form is Arsenite As(III) which is interconvertible to As(V) depending upon redox status of the environmental conditions. The absorption of As(III) is primarily facilitated by plant aquaporins or plasma membrane intrinsic proteins, in contrast to the mechanism involved in As(V) uptake (Wang et al. 2018). Members of the membrane receptor PHOSPHATE TRANSPORTER 1 (PHT1) family have been identifed as being involved in As(V) uptake and transport in plants. Recently, a Plant Database SCIPDb showed alterations in PHT1 levels in Cicer arietinum under combined Ralstonia solanacearum and drought stress conditions (Priya et al. 2023). In Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana), AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 were initially discovered to mediate the acquisition of both Pi and As(V) from soils (Shin et al. 2004). Kinases are crucial regulators of both plant and animal development including stresses (Singh et al. 2023a, b; Mishra and Maurya 2023). Studies have demonstrated that CALCIUM-DEPENDENT PROTEIN KINASES (CPKs), crucial regulators of calcium, are typically engaged in deciphering $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signals induced by stress or stimuli in plants (Harmon et al. 2001; Liu et al. 2017). Arabidopsis harbors 34 CPKs, which play crucial roles in plant growth, development, and response to various abiotic, biotic, and in combined stresses (Yip Delormel and Boudsocq 2019; Priya et al. 2023). In the past, research has demonstrated a signifcant increase in CPKs activity levels when rice plants were subjected to $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress (Huang et al. 2012). which suggests the involvement of CPK in responding to stress induced by arsenate. Recently, it has been demonstrated that CPK31 interacts with the As(III) transporter nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein (NIP1;1), infuencing both the uptake and tolerance of Arabidopsis to arsenic (Ji et al. 2017). Plant NIPs, grouped as NIP1-NIP5, show remarkable conservation across species. NIP1;1, a key As(III) transporter in Arabidopsis, was identifed through a genetics screen, with high expression in roots and plasma membrane localization. Loss-of-function mutants of NIP1;1 exhibited As(III)-tolerant phenotypes, emphasizing its crucial role in mediating toxic As(III) uptake into roots. Beyond arsenic, NIPs are also involved in the transport of various metalloids, such as antimonite, boron, silicon, and selenium, within plants (Kamiya et al. 2009; Kamiya and Fujiwara 2009; Maurel et al. 2015).

Despite this fnding, the specifc regulatory role of CPK31 in modulating NIP1.1 under arsenic stress, particularly As(V)

stress, remains unclear. In the highlighted study, it has been observed that Arabidopsis roots exhibit distinct $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling in response to As(V) stress. Subsequently, the researchers identifed a cpk23 mutant, displaying the most pronounced sensitivity among the 31 CPKs single mutants screened under $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress conditions. Furthermore, the authors demonstrated that CPK23 plays a role in modulating As(V) tolerance in Arabidopsis by infuencing the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 through phosphorylation.


## $\pmb { \mathbb { A } s ( \pmb { \mathbb { V } } ) }$ stress, $\pmb { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ signaling and importance of CPK23 in Arabidopsis


$\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ is a celebrated secondary messenger in abiotic stress signaling downstream of the plasma membrane receptor (Dong et al. 2022). In response to As stress, diferential expression of diferent $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensors, such as CaMs, suggests the possible involvement of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent signaling in As tolerance in plants (Chakrabarty et al. 2009). In this regard, CPKs, as essential calcium regulatory proteins, are usually involved in decoding $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signals caused by plant stress or stimuli (Mohanta et al. 2019).

In a recent study, (Liu et al. 2023) discovered that arsenate treatment induced a rapid and transient increase in intracellular calcium levels in Arabidopsis roots. Building upon this fnding, the authors screened and identifed a cpk23 mutant, which displayed the most pronounced sensitivity among 31 CPKs single mutants under As(V) stress, which indicates the involvement of a plasma membrane associated CPK23. Moreover, no change has been observed in the transcript of CPK23 following As(V)-induced stress, leading to speculation that the kinase activity of CPK23 plays a crucial role in its functionality. This is further validated by analyzing the phenotype of CPK23 overexpression (CPK23-OE) transgenic lines and constitutively active CPK23 (CPK23-VK) plants under diferent levels of As(V) stress response (Liu et al. 2023).The authors observed that CPK23-OE plants did not show a tolerance phenotype under As(V) stress. In contrast, all CPK23-VK plants showed a tolerance phenotype under 300, 400, and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress. Furthermore, the authors investigated CPK23's involvement in the phosphate signal response by examining the above mutants (Liu et al. 2023). Despite observing a phosphate defciency phenotype, there was no growth diference between WT plants and mutants, suggesting CPK23 has no role in phosphate defciency response (Liu et al. 2023).Thus, these results suggested that the kinase activity of CPK23 is specifcally required for As(V) tolerance.


## CPK23 orchestrates $\pmb { \mathbb { A } s ( \pmb { \mathbb { V } } ) }$ tolerance by modulating the delocalization of PHT1;1 under As(V) stress


Furthermore, to identify the downstream protein phosphorylated by CPK23, the authors performed co-immunoprecipitation coupled to mass spectrometry (IP-MS) using CPK23-FLAG transgenic seedlings. They identified a peptide corresponding to PHT1;1, a phosphate transporter associated with arsenic transport. Through subsequent protein interaction and phosphorylation experiments, the authors determined that CPK23 interacts with PHT1;1 and phosphorylates the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site at its C-terminus under arsenic stress response (Liu et al. 2023).

Furthermore, to assess the impact of PHT1; $1 ^ { 5 5 1 4 }$ phosphorylation on plant tolerance to $\mathbf { A s } ( \mathbf { V } )$ , the authors generated transgenic Arabidopsis plants expressing phospho-dead (ProPHT1;1:PHT1; $1 ^ { \mathrm { S 5 1 4 A } } )$ and phosphoactivated (ProPHT1;1:PHT1;1S514D) versions of PHT1;1 in the pht1;1 mutant background. The phospho-dead variant showed sensitivity to As stress, while the phosphoactivated variant displayed tolerance similar to that of pht1;1 plants response (Liu et al. 2023). These physiological experiments confrmed the importance of PHT1;1S514 phosphorylation for its function in As(V) tolerance. Previously, it has been shown that $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ infuences the localization of the PHT1;1 transporter in the root cell (Navarro et al. 2021). To investigate whether CPK23 regulates the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 via phosphorylation under As(V) stress, the authors expressed PHT1.1 phosphorylation site mutants fused with a green fuorescent protein (GFP) in both wild-type and cpk23 mutant plants lar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration, results in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ spiking which further activates CPK23. Following activation, CPK23 phosphorylates PHT1;1 at the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site. Phosphorylation at $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ promotes the delocalization of PHT1;1 from the plasma membrane, ultimately decreasing $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ uptake and incerases plant tolerance to $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ stress

(Liu et al. 2023). Furthermore, it has been observed that the localization of PHT1;1 was signifcantly infuenced by the phosphorylation of the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site, with PHT1; $1 ^ { 5 5 1 4 \mathrm { A } }$ - GFP plants exhibiting a more pronounced co-localization with the plasma membrane compared to PHT1; $1 ^ { \mathrm { S 5 1 4 D } }$ -GFP plants. Additionally, authors observed that in WT plants, PHT1;1-GFP undergoes delocalization from the plasma membrane under As (V) stress (Fig. 1), whereas in cpk23 plants, PHT1;1-GFP remains anchored to the plasma membrane in the same conditions response (Liu et al. 2023). These fndings suggest that CPK23 regulates the subcellular localization of PHT1;1 under As (V) stress through phosphorylation of the $\mathrm { S } ^ { 5 1 4 }$ site (Fig. 1).

Moreover, CDPK23 and PHT1;1 may orchestrate crucial pathways for As detoxifcation and transport in plants. Understanding their complex mechanisms could open the door to genetic engineering approaches aimed at boosting plant resilience in As-contaminated environments, thereby promoting sustainable agriculture and environmental conservation. This insight into the molecular basis of As tolerance may revolutionize crop production in regions afected by As pollution, addressing a critical global challenge in food security. CPK23 plays a pivotal role in As stress responses, regulating downstream genes involved in detoxifcation mechanisms. PHT1;1, on the other hand, is crucial for As uptake and transport within plants. Thus, manipulating these genes by utilizing CLUSTERED REGULARLY INTERSPACED SHORT PALINDROMIC REPEAT (CRISPR)- CRISPR associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology, RNA interference (RNAi), transgenic approaches, site-directed mutagenesis etc., holds potential to manipulate/modulate the expression or activity of these genes, thereby fortifying crops against As-induced damage. It's noteworthy that kinases are typically not preferentially considered for genetic applications. However, these candidates are particularly intriguing due to their direct involvement in essential As tolerance pathways, making them key players in mitigating the toxic efects of As on crops. Additionally, the interaction between CPK23 and PHT1;1 underscores the importance of these genes in coordinating As detoxifcation and transport within plants. Thus, their manipulation not only addresses As stress directly but also opens avenues for in-depth mechanistic exploration, ofering insights critical for developing resilient and As-resistant crop varieties.

Phosphorous (P) is an essential plant macronutrient for life cell growth and development. However, the assimilable inorganic phosphate (Pi) form of $\mathrm { P }$ for plants is often limited in the soil due to its low mobility in the soil solution and its rapid conversion to organic forms (Marschner 1995). Hence, Pi is often a limiting factor for plant growth in both natural and agricultural ecosystems (OropezaAburto et al. 2012). Although fertilizer application has increased crop productivity by $30 \mathrm { - } 5 0 ~ \%$ , its manufacture is an energy-intensive process. Moreover, over-application of fertilizers leads to runoff and pollution of waterways, causing a host of environmental problems. One approach to reducing the application of fertilizers in agriculture is to optimize their efficient use by crop plants (Holford 1997; Raghothama 1999; Yang and Finnegan 2010; Secco et al. 2012).

Phosphate starvation response 1 (PHR1), a key transcriptional regulator of Pi starvation responses (Rubio et al. 2001; Bari et al. 2006; Bustos et al. 2010), directly regulates the expression of IPS1, a non-coding RNA that mimics the target of miR399 to block the cleavage of PHO2 under Pi-deficient conditions (Franco-Zorrilla et al. 2007). PHO2 functions as an ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzyme (UBC24) and modulates Pi acquisition by regulating the abundance of phosphate transporter 1s (PHT1s) in the secretory pathway destined for plasma membranes (Huang et al. 2013). The RING-type ubiquitin E3 ligase nitrogen limitation adaptation (NLA), as the target of miR827, recruits PHO2 for the degradation of Pi transporters in the cellular Pi homeostasis process (Kant et al. 2011; Lin et al. 2013; Park et al. 2014). In the Pi-starvation signaling pathway, PHR1 is sumoylated by an SIZ1-dependent mechanism (Miura et al. 2005). SIZ1 is a plant small ubiquitinlike modifier (SUMO) E3 ligase that is a focal controller of Pi-starvation-dependent responses. In addition, the function of PHR proteins is suppressed by SPX (SYG/PHO81/ XPR1)-domain proteins, which are involved in plant Pi homeostasis (Wang et al. 2009a, b, 2014; Liu et al. 2010; Shi et al. 2014; Lv et al. 2014). In Arabidopsis, AtPHR1 also binds to the promoters of SULTR1;3 and SULTR3;4, regulating shoot-to-root flux of sulfate upon phosphate starvation (Rouached et al. 2011).

Pi uptake across the plant is mediated by Pi transporters belonging to the phosphate transporter 1 (PHT1) class (Poirier and Bucher 2002) of plant $\mathrm { P i / H ^ { + } }$ symporters of the major facilitator superfamily (Pao et al. 1998). In Arabidopsis, there are nine PHT1 family members and among them, PHT1;1 and PHT1;4 are reported to be the major players in Pi acquisition under Pi-sufficient conditions (Shin et al. 2004). All nine Arabidopsis PHT1 genes have the P1BS cis-element motif in their promoters, and the mRNA expression of PHT1;1 is dramatically decreased in the double mutant of phr1/phl1 (Bustos et al. 2010), consistent with PHR regulation of PHT1 of expression. In rice, aside from OsPHT1;1 and OsPHT1;4, the other 11 PHT1 family members contain the P1BS motif in the promoter, and OsPHT1;2 (OsPT2) has been confirmed as a direct target of OsPHR2 (Liu et al. 2010). OsPHT1;11 and OsPHT1;13 have the P1BS motif but are arbuscular mycorrhiza-specific Pi transporters and are not involved the Pi starvation response (Paszkowski et al. 2002; Gutjahr et al. 2008; Kobae and Hata 2010; Yang et al. 2012). This finding leads to the speculation that the P1BS motif alone might not sufficient for the DNA binding of PHR proteins. In the posttranslational regulation of PHT1 proteins, phosphate transporter traffic facilitator 1 (PHF1), encoded by a downstream gene of PHR1, assists the trafficking of PHT1s to the plasma membrane (PM) (González et al. 2005; Bayle et al. 2011). Both Arabidopsis and rice phf1 mutants exhibit decreased Pi content and retarded growth (González et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2011).

DNA cis-elements are important regulators of gene expression (Segal and Widom 2009) and considerable effort is currently being invested to decipher the rules governing gene expression. The fine structure of the PHO5 promoter from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) was mapped, revealing that Pho4 binding affinity was ruled by E-box flanking sequences (Rajkumar et al. 2013). In Arabidopsis, PHR1 was found to bind an imperfect palindromic sequence (GNATATNC) that is found in the promoter regions of many phosphate starvation induced (PSI) genes (Franco-Zorrilla et al. 2004; Rubio et al. 2001). Bustos et al. (2010) reported that a B-motif (GAWGATNC) was essential for AtPHR1 to bind an adjacent P1BS site in the AtIPS1 promoter. In addition, our previous research showed that most PSI genes have a P1BS-like motif, which is similar in structure to P1BS, in the region adjacent to their P1BS motif (Wu et al. 2013).

In this study, we found that OsPHR2 DNA binding affinity is regulated by the P1BS flanking sequences and P1BS variable bases, and that the most efficient P1BS constitution for OsPHR2 binding is ‘GaATATtC’, herein named the A–T-type P1BS. Further, we used the highest affinity P1BS combination (HA-P1BS) for modification of the OsPHF1 promoter and generated phosphate-efficient transgenic plants (OsPHF1-HA-P1BS) with obviously increased yield under low-phosphate conditions. Our research thus provides a new approach to modify crops without largescale changes to the original expression pattern of modified genes, which can avoid energy waste and other possible
