Arsenic and antimony are highly toxic and can only permeate cells through the transporters evolved for accumulation of essential ions and nutrients using the molecular mimicry. In aqueous solution at the physiological $\mathrm { p H }$ , trivalent arsenite $\left[ \mathrm { A s } ( \mathrm { I I I } ) \right]$ and antimonite [Sb(III)] exist mainly in the trihydroxylated uncharged forms, $\mathrm { A s ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ and $\mathrm { S b ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ , which structurally resemble glycerol [9,10]. Thus, in all domains of life organisms easily accumulate As(III) and Sb(III) by the aquaglyceroporins, a ubiquitous family of membrane proteins, which are permeable for water and glycerol (Figures 1–3) [11,12]. In addition, As(III) and Sb(III) can enter the cells via hexose transporters. Arsenate [As(V)] behaves as a chemical analogue of inorganic phosphate and is taken up by the phosphate transporters (Figures 1–3) [6,7]. In contrast antimonate $[ \mathrm { S b ( V ) } ]$ exists as $\left[ \mathrm { S b } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 6 } \right] ^ { - }$ anion and does not compete with the phosphate uptake [13,14]. The pathway of Sb(V) entry into the cells has not been determined yet.


## 2.1. Uptake of As(V) via Phosphate Transporters


In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae two high-affinity, Pho84 and Pho89, and three low-affinity, Pho87, Pho90 and Pho91, phosphate transporters have been identified [15]. Deletion of PHO84 and PHO87 genes resulted in increased As(V) tolerance strongly, suggesting that As(V) uptake is mediated by phosphate transport system in yeast (Figure 1) [16,17]. Moreover, cells lacking the membrane protein Pho86, which is required for targeting Pho84 to the plasma membrane, and the phosphate transporter-associated proteins, Gtr1 and Pho88, which regulate positively transport activity of Pho84, also exhibited increased resistance to As(V) [16–18].

Figure 1. Pathways for arsenic uptake and detoxification in the yeast S.cerevisiae. In yeast cells uptake of As(III) is facilitated mainly via the aquaglyceroporin Fps1 but in the absence of glucose As(III) also enters the cell through the hexose permeases Hxt (Hxt1-Hxt17, Gal2). As(V) is taken up by the phosphate transporters (Pho), such as Pho84 and Pho87, followed by reduction to As(III) by the arsenate reductase Acr2 in the cytoplasm. Next, As(III) is transported out of the cell by the $\mathrm { \ A s ( I I I ) / H } ^ { + }$ antiporter Acr3 against the concentration gradient or by the aquaglyceroporin Fps1, especially during As(V) exposure, when the internal concentration of As(III) is higher than the outside. In addition, As(III) is conjugated with glutathione (GSH) and sequestrated into the vacuole by the ABC transporters Ycf1 and $\mathrm { V m r } 1$ .

Since the As(V)-tolerant plants display constitutive suppression of high-affinity phosphate uptake system [19,20] and As(V) import is inhibited by the presence of phosphate [21], it has been generally accepted that plants accumulate $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ via the phosphate transporters. However, the involvement of particular phosphate transporters in As(V) intake has not been demonstrated. Recently, based on the genetic data, two phosphate transporters, Pht1;1 and Pht1;4, have been proposed to be responsible for As(V) uptake in Arabidopsis thaliana (Figure 2) [22,23]. The A. thaliana mutant lacking both Pht1;1 and Pht1;4 exhibited high resistance to As(V) [22]. In addition, mutation in the A. thaliana PHF1 gene, which blocks Pht1;1 trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum to the plasma membrane resulted in increased tolerance to As(V) [23]. In a more recent report, it has been presented that the rice Pht1 (OsPht1;8) mediates high-affinity transport of As(V) and transgenic lines overexpressing OsPht1;8 accumulated high-levels of As(V) [24].

Figure 2. Routes for arsenic transport in higher plants. In plant cells As(III) is accumulated through the aquaporins of Nodulin26-like intrinsic protein subfamily (NIPs) and plasma membrane intrinsic protein subfamily (PIPs), while As(V) uptake is catalyzed by the phosphate transporters (PHT1). In the cytoplasm $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ is rapidly reduced to As(III) by the arsenate reductase ACR2/CDC25. Upon binding to phytochelatins (PCs), $\mathrm { P C } _ { 2 }$ -As(III) complexes are compartmentalized into the vacuole by two A. thaliana ABC transporters, ABCC1 and ABCC2. As(III) can also leak out of the plant root cell via the NIP and PIP channels down the concentration gradient to external medium. On the other hand, in rice the silicon transporter Lsi2 localizing to the proximal side of root cells extrudes As(III) to the xylem contributing to metalloid accumulation in shoots and grain.

Transporters responsible for As(V) uptake has been recently identified in vertebrates. Five rat sodium/phosphate transporters NaPiIIa, NaPiIIb, NaPiIIc, Pit-1 and Pit-2, which constitute the mammalian phosphate uptake system, were expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes to analyze directly transport of radioactive As(V) [25]. NaPiIIa, NaPiIIc, Pit-1 and Pit-2 occurred to have 10-fold lower affinity for $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ than for inorganic phosphate, suggesting their negligible role in $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ accumulation. In contrast, NaPiIIb from rat, mouse and human showed high affinity for $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ and was proposed to be a major entry for $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ in the intestine (Figure 3) [25]. Similarly, NaPi-IIb1 from zebrafish is also involved in As(V) transport [26].

Figure 3. Summary of arsenic transport pathways in mammalian cells. As(V) uptake is mediated by the high-affinity phosphate transporter NaPiIIb. Next, As(V) is reduced to As(III) by CDC25 phosphatases/arsenate reductases. As(III) is transported into the mammalian cells via multiple pathways: the aquaglyceroporins (AQP3, AQP7, AQP9, AQP10), the glucose permeases (GLUT1, GLUT2, GLUT5) or the organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATPB, OATPC). The AQP9 and GLUT2 transporters are also responsible for the transport of methylated species of As(III) out of the cells. The ABC transporters from the ABCB (MDR1/P-gp) and ABCC (MRP1 and MRP2) subfamilies are the major pathways of As(III) extrusion. Both MRP1 and MRP2 are able to transport inorganic and monomethylated forms of As(III) conjugated with glutathione. In addition, MRP2 mediates efflux of seleno-bis $S \mathrm { \cdot }$ -glutathionyl) arsinium ion. The exact form of As(III) recognized by MDR1/P-gp is uncertain but it is not glutathione-S-conjugate.

The first evidence suggesting that the aquaglyceroporins are the entry pathway for metalloids comes from the study of Sanders et al. [27] showing that inactivation of Escherichia coli glpF gene, encoding for the glycerol facilitator, led to Sb(III) resistance phenotype. Later, based on the genetic data and direct transport measurements of radioactive As(III), Wysocki et al. [28] have demonstrated that the $S$ . cerevisiae glycerol facilitator Fps1 mediates uptake of As(III) and Sb(III) (Figure 1). Both glycerol facilitators GlpF and Fps1 belong to the family of major intrinsic proteins (MIP) that comprises the membrane channel proteins, which are selective for either water only (aquaporins) or water and other uncharged solutes, like glycerol and urea (aquaglyceroporins) [11].

The physiological role of Fps1 is the regulation of intracellular level of glycerol in response to changes in osmolarity [29]. In response to hyperosmotic stress Fps1 closes to allow glycerol accumulation in the cytosol and opens to release glycerol out of the cell under hypoosmotic conditions. Gating of Fps1 channel is mediated by the cytosolic N-terminal tail, and its truncation renders Fps1 constitutively open and allow an unregulated bidirectional transport of glycerol. Thus, yeast overexpressing of fps1-Δ1 allele lacking N-terminal extension were hypersensitive to As(III) and Sb(III) and accumulated more As(III), while deletion of FPS1 gene or high-osmolarity conditions profoundly increased resistance to As(III) and Sb(III) [28]. Interestingly, transport of metalloids via Fps1 is regulated at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level. After As(III) and Sb(III) addition to the media, transcription of the FPS1 gene is rapidly downregulated to reduce the Fps1 protein level [28]. Besides, activity of Fps1 is negatively regulated by the mitogen-activated protein kinase Hog1, which phosphorylates Fps1 at treonine 231 located in the N-terminal tail [30]. Deletion of HOG1 or expression of Fps1-T231A resulted in increased sensitivity to As(III) and Sb(III) due to upregulation of metalloid intake. Thus, we proposed that As(III) and Sb(III) activate Hog1 kinase to phosphorylate N-terminal tail of Fps1 which results in channel closing and restriction of metalloid accumulation. Beese et al. [31] have shown that the pleckstrin homology (PH) domain proteins Rgc1 and Rgc2 positively regulate transport activity of Fps1 by yet unknown mechanism. Interestingly, deletion of RGC1 and RGC2 genes caused resistance to As(III) in both wild type and the hog1Δ mutant background suggesting that Hog1 may also effect activity of Fps1 by targeting Rgc1 and Rgc2. Indeed, As(III)-induced phosphorylation of Rgc2 was partially decreased in the absence of Hog1 but it has not been established whether Rgc2 is a substrate for Hog1.

A heterologous expression system using the yeast mutants lacking metalloid transporters, including Fps1, was successfully employed to identify plant aquaporins responsible for metalloid uptake [32–34]. Plant aquaporins are classified into four subfamilies corresponding to distinct subcellular localizations: small basic intrinsic proteins (SIP) located in the endoplasmic reticulum, plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIP) and tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIP) responsible for water transport, and Nodulin26-like intrinsic membrane proteins (NIP), which are localized to plasma and intracellular membranes to mediate transport of $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ , $\mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 }$ or $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ [35–37]. Based on the plasma membrane localization and structural similarity between their physiological substrates and $\mathrm { A s ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ or $\mathrm { S b ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ , NIPs were obvious candidates for testing their ability to transport As(III) and Sb(III) into the cells. Bienert et al. [32] have shown that $A$ . thaliana AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1 and AtNIP7;1, Oryza sativa OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2 and OsNIP3;2, Lotus japonicus LjNIP5;1 and LjNIP6;1 increased sensitivity to As(III) and Sb(III) when expressed in $S _ { \cdot }$ . cerevisiae lacking the aquaglyceroporin Fps1, thus highly resistant to metalloids. Importantly, decreased accumulation of As(III) in yeast cells expressing NIPs from A. thaliana and $O _ { \ l }$ . sativa was confirmed in direct transport studies [32]. Several other reports independently demonstrated a significant role of NIPs in As(III) uptake in A. thaliana (AtNIP1;1, AtNIP1;2, AtNIP5;2 and AtNIP7;1) and $O$ . sativa (OsNIP1;1, Lsi1/OsNIP2;1, Lsi6/OsNIP2;2, OsNIP3;1) by showing their permeability to As(III) in $X .$ . laevis oocytes or increased As(III) tolerance and accumulation in the plant nip mutants [33,34,38]. In addition, the rice aquaporin Lsi1/OsNIP2;1 is also permeable to methylarsonic acid $\left[ \mathrm { M A s } ( \mathrm { V } ) \right]$ and dimethylarsinic acid [DMAs(V)] [39], while NIP1;1 in Arabidopsis contributes to $\operatorname { S b } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ uptake and sensitivity [40]. In sum, above findings suggest that all NIPs are permeable to $\operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ and $\operatorname { S b } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ and some of them, like OsNIP1;1 and Lsi1/OsNIP2;1 in rice, constitute a major pathway for $\operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ accumulation into roots and determine level of As(III) tolerance in plants (Figure 2). However, three members of rice PIP subfamily of aquaporins have been recently reported to mediate As(III) transport [41]. OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OsPIP2;7 facilitated As(III) uptake in $X .$ laevis oocytes, while overexpression of these proteins in Arabidopsis resulted in increased As(III) resistance. Moreover, the transgenic Arabidopsis lines expressing OsPIP2;6 exhibited both influx and efflux of As(III) depending on the outside concentration of this metalloid. This suggests that in plants both NIPs and PIPs are involved in As(III) transport down the concentration gradient (Figure 2).

It is believed that the active form of Sb(V)-based drugs used in the treatment of leishmaniasis is actually Sb(III), which is formed after reduction of ${ \mathrm { S b } } ( { \mathrm { V } } )$ inside macrophages. Thus, the role of aquaglyceroporins in metalloid uptake and tolerance was investigated in Leishmania parasites [42]. The Leishmania major AQP1 (LmAQP1), the closest homologue of human AQP9, has been shown to be responsible for As(III) and Sb(III) accumulation. Overexpression of LmAQP1 gene in $L$ . tarentolae, $L$ . infantum, and $L$ . major facilitated As(III) and Sb(III) uptake and resulted in hypersensitivity to both metalloids. Moreover, mutation in one of LmAQP1 alleles in $L$ . major increased resistance to Sb(III). Importantly, LmAQP1 expression in wild type and antimony-resistant $L$ . donovani strains could increase sensitivity to antimonials. Downregulation of AQP1 RNA level seems to be a major mechanism of antimony resistance found in field and clinical isolates of Leishmania [43,44].

Human genome encodes thirteen aquaporins (AQP0-12), out of which AQP3, AQP7, AQP9, and AQP10 are permeable for glycerol [45]. First, ability to transport As(III) and Sb(III) was demonstrated for two mammalian aquaglyceroporins, AQP7 and AQP9 (Figure 3) [46]. Expression of rat AQP9 in the yeast fps1Δ mutant reversed resistance to As(III) and Sb(III) and increased transport of As(III) and Sb(III) into the cells. Both mouse AQP7 and rat AQP9 were able to mediate As(III) uptake when expressed in $X .$ laevis oocytes. Similarly, human aquaglyceroporins AQP7 and AQP9 were also shown to mediate As(III) uptake into oocytes, while no significant As(III) accumulation was observed when human AQP3 and AQP10 were expressed [47]. In this study, AQP9 proved to be the most efficient aquaglyceroporin in As(III) transport. Analysis of serial mutants of rat AQP9 in the pore region allowed to establish that $\mathrm { A s ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ and glycerol use the same translocation pathway in AQP9 [47]. Based on the fact that AQP9 is primarily expressed in liver, spleen, testis and leukocytes [45], it has been proposed that AQP9 constitutes a major pathway for As(III) uptake from blood to liver, which plays a primary role in arsenic metabolism [45]. In addition, AQP9 contributes to As(III) sensitivity in leukemia cells [46]. Overexpression of AQP9, sensitized leukemia cells to metalloids, while As(III)-resistant leukemic cell lines displayed low level of AQP9 [48,49]. Analysis of aquaglyceroporin levels in an As(III)-resistant cell line (R15) derived from a human lung adenocarcinoma cell line (CL3) revealed that in the AQP7 and AQP9 non-expressing cells AQP3 may contribute to As(III) uptake and sensitivity [50]. Silencing of AQP10 expression with iRNA in the human colon adenocarcinoma Caco-2 cell line resulted in increased As(III) uptake, which suggests that AQP10 may be involved in intestinal absorption of As(III) [51]. Recently, involvement of seven aquaglyceroporins present in the zebrafish Danio rerio has been examined for metalloid transport [52]. Five of them, Aqp3, Aqp3l, Aqp9a, Aqp9b, and Aqp10, were able conduct both As(III) and Sb(III), with the exception of Aqp3, which was not permeable to Sb(III). Interestingly, both zebrafish and mammalian aquaglyceroporins were also shown to conduct organic methylated arsenicals, like methylarsonous acid [MAs(III)], MAs(V) and DMAs(V), however instead of the role in uptake, contributing to metalloid efflux and detoxification (see below) [52–54].


## 2.3. Role of Hexose Transporters in As(III) and Sb(III) Accumulation


Liu et al. [55] found that the yeast fps1Δ mutant accumulated As(III) at high rate when the transport experiments were performed in the absence of glucose. This observation led to the hypothesis that hexose transporters may be permeable to metalloids (Figure 1 and 3). Indeed, no accumulation of As(III) was observed in the yeast mutant devoid of all eighteen hexose transporter, whereas addition of glucose and other sugars inhibited As(III) uptake in wild type cells. Later, it has been shown that rat and human hexose transporter GLUT1, which belongs to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS), mediate As(III) accumulation when expressed in yeast cells and $X .$ laevis oocytes [56]. The question was how glucose transporters could recognize As(III) as a substrate. It was suggested that three $\mathrm { A s ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ molecules could polymerize to a ring structure that mimics the hexose molecule [55]. However, it seems to be unlikely in a view of the observation that GLUT1 can also catalyze transport of MAs(III), which did not compete with glucose transport [55]. This suggested that arsenicals and hexoses are differently translocated through GLUT1. Indeed, Jiang et al. [57] have shown that mutations in GLUT1 amino acid residues, which are critical for glucose uptake, increased the transport rate of MAs(III), while inhibitors of glucose transport did not affect MAs(III) flow. It has been speculated that arsenicals may use the water pathway for translocation via mammalian GLUT1, which is different from the glucose pathway [57]. Two more glucose permeases, GLUT2 in hepatocytes [58] and GLUT5 in the human colon adenocarcinoma Caco-2 cell line [51], were also reported to participate in uptake of As(III). Finally, OATPB [51] and OATPC [59], two human members of the organic anion transporting polypeptide family (OATP) involved in the transport of a wide range of amphipathic endogenous and exogenous organic compounds [60], were identified as the additional pathways for As(III) influx.

This review addresses one of the most important functions of roots — the uptake of nutrients and their subsequent redistribution throughout plant tissues. The fundamental mechanism involved in these processes is the transport of mineral nutrients that are usually charged across lipid membranes. The most widely studied of these transport systems is movement across the plasmalemma of the epidermal and cortical cells of plant roots. This membrane provides the biological interface between the apoplast and the symplast. Ions entering the plant symplast traverse the plasmalemma. The physiological and biophysical characteristics of transport of charged nutrient ions across this membrane have been known for a long time. Both highaffinity and low-affinity transport systems, each of which could be described by first-order kinetics, were demonstrated by Epstein and colleagues (Epstein and Hagen, 1952; Epstein, 1953) over 40 years ago. For ions such as phosphate and sulphate these transport processes occur against large concentration gradients since concentrations of these ions in the rhizosphere of typical soils are often less than $2 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ , whilst concentrations in the plant cytoplasm are of the order of $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ (Mimura, 1999). Further, transport of anions such as phosphate and sulphate across the plasmalemma must overcome a large electrical gradient as the interior surface of the membrane is normally negatively charged. Physiological and biophysical evidence indicates that transport of these ions against the electrochemical gradients is mediated by the operation of proton-coupled cotransporter proteins.

Use of molecular tools by nutritional physiologists over the past 7 years has resulted in the identification and characterisation of genes that encode the transporter proteins from a number of plant species. Specific genes have been identified that encode transporters for many essential plant nutrients and studies on the regulation of these genes is improving our understanding of the way in which plants interact with the soil in the rhizosphere. Considerable attention has been devoted to phosphate and sulphate because of the agricultural and physiological significance of these nutrients. Identification within a single plant species of multiple genes that encode different phosphate and sulphate transporters highlights the fact that transport occurs through membranes other than the plasmalemma of root cells. Movement of sulphate and phosphate between different organs and organelles during plant growth and development necessitates transport across different membranes and the involvement of a number of transporter proteins and, possibly, ion channels. The roles of these different transporters and the way in which they are regulated are beginning to emerge (Hawkesford, 2000; Raghothama, 1999, 2000; Saito, 2000; Smith, 1999; Smith et al., 2000). Advances in our understanding of phosphate and sulphate transport systems in plants that have resulted from these molecular advances in recent years are reviewed in this paper.


## Identification of plant sulphate and phosphate transporters


Genes encoding proteins involved in the transport of sulphate and phosphate were among the first ion transporters to be cloned from plants. A yeast complementation strategy was initially used to identify genes that encode plant sulphate transporters. This strategy involved creation of the YSD1 yeast mutant in which the gene encoding the yeast SUL1 highaffinity sulphate transporter had been deleted (Smith et al., 1995a). This mutant was then used to screen root cDNA libraries for genes that restored the capacity of the YSD1 mutant to take up sulphate. These screens resulted in the isolation of the SHST1, SHST2 and SHST3 genes from Stylosanthes hamata (Smith et al., 1995b) and the HVST1 gene from barley (Smith et al., 1997a). Heterologous expression of these genes in the yeast YSD1 mutant revealed that SHST1, SHST2 and HVST1 encode high-affinity sulphate transporters with $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ values for sulphate of 10, 11.2 and $6 . 8 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ respectively, whilst SHST3 encodes a lower-affinity sulphate transporter with a $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for sulphate of $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ The sequences of these genes have since been used to identify genes encoding sulphate transporters from other plant species (Kouchi and Hata, 1993; Ng et al., 1996; Yamaguchi et al., 1997) including seven different genes encoding sulphate transporters from Arabidopsis thaliana (Takahashi et al., 1996, 1997, 1999a, b, 2000).

The first reported genes encoding plant phosphate transporters (Muchhal et al., 1996; Smith et al., 1997a) were isolated by use of their sequence similarities to a partial cDNA in the Arabidopsis EST database. This partial cDNA bore similarities to genes encoding phosphate transporters in yeast and fungi. These genes, isolated from Arabidopsis, belong to the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters. Since then additional members of the Pht1 family have been isolated from potato (Leggewie et al., 1997), tomato (Daram et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1998a), Arabidopsis (Mitsukawa et al., 1997a), Catharanthus (Kai et al., 1997), Medicago (Liu et al., 1998b) and barley (Smith et al., 1999). Eight different genes belonging to the Pht1 family have been isolated from barley, indicating that members of this family are involved in a number of different phosphate transport roles in plants.

A member of a different family of plant phosphate transporters, Pht2, has recently been isolated from Ar abidopsis (Daram et al., 1999). The $P h t 2 ; I$ cDNA was amplified from a library by polymerase chain reaction using primers specific to an open reading frame within Arabidopsis Chromosome III. This open reading frame encodes a polypeptide that has similarities to sodium-dependent phosphate transporters found in archaebacteria, fungi, yeasts and mammals. The protein encoded by $P h t 2 ; I$ is quite different in structure to those encoded by the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters. Its function as a plant phosphate transporter has been clearly demonstrated.


## Topology of sulphate and phosphate transporters


The plant sulphate transporters are typically 635–685 amino acids in length and $6 9 { - } 7 5 \mathrm { k D a }$ in size. Depending upon the constraints used, hydrophobicity analyses predict they contain 10–14 membrane-spanning domains (MSDs). The hydrophobic regions that make up these MSDs are separated by more hydrophilic regions that form the loops on the inside or outside of the membrane. The consensus is that the plant sulphate transporters contain 12 MSDs and both the N-terminal and C-terminal are oriented towards the inside of the membrane (Hawkesford and Smith, 1997b). Unlike members of the major facilitator superfamily of proteins (Marger and Saier, 1993; Pao et al., 1998; Saier and Reizer, 1991), the sulphate transporters do not possess a long central inner loop. This topology is common among sulphate transporter proteins from filamentous fungi, yeast, plants, mammals and humans (Smith et al., 1995b). It has therefore been highly conserved during evolution.

Plant phosphate transporters belonging to the Pht1 family contain 520–550 amino acids and are approximately $5 8 ~ \mathrm { k D a }$ in size. They also contain 12 MSDs and have both the N-terminal and C-terminal oriented towards the inside of the membrane (Smith, 1999). However, the phosphate transporter proteins contain a long inner loop between MSDs 6 and 7 that results in a $_ { 6 + 6 }$ configuration (Smith et al., 1997a). This configuration is characteristic of the major facilitator superfamily of proteins (Marger and Saier, 1993; Pao et al., 1998; Saier and Reizer, 1991) and is shared by proteins involved in the transport of many organic anions, sugars, amino acids and inorganic anions across biological membranes. Recent data indicate that the long central cytoplasmic loop is required for proper insertion of these transporter proteins into the membrane (Weinglass and Kaback, 2000). Again, there has been a high level of conservation during evolution of the topology found in the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters (Smith et al., 1997a; Pao et al., 1998) with similar proteins also being found in fungi and yeasts. A segment containing 39 amino acids from proteins of the plant Pht1 family and closely related phosphate transporters from yeast and filamentous fungi contain 11 fully conserved residues (Pao et al., 1998). These residues may provide a signature for this family of transporters and suggest these amino acids may be important to the phosphate transport function of the proteins.

The recently isolated Pht2 family of plant phosphate transporters has quite a different topology to the Pht1 family. The ARAth;Pht2;1 member of this family from Arabidopsis (Daram et al., 1999) encodes a 61- kDa protein containing 587 amino acids. Analyses of the protein sequence predict 12 MSDs with both the N-terminal and C-terminal oriented to the outside of the membrane. Other features of this protein include a long hydrophilic N-terminal region and a long hydrophilic loop between MSDs 8 and 9. The Pht2 family of plant phosphate transporters also appears to have been conserved during evolution since it contains features that are similar to eubacterial and eukaryotic type III sodium-dependent phosphate transporters.

Yet another family of proteins involved in phosphate transport has been isolated from plastids (Fischer et al., 1994, 1997; Kammerer et al., 1998). A detailed discussion of this family is beyond the scope of this review.


## Functional analysis of phosphate and sulphate transporters


Heterologous expression in yeast mutants of fulllength cDNAs encoding plant transporter proteins has proven to be a valuable technique for functional analysis of these genes. The YSD1 mutant in which the gene encoding the yeast high-affinity SUL1 sulphate transporter has been deleted (Smith et al., 1995a) has been successfully used to study the functions of plant sulphate transporters. Another mutant CP154- 7A which contains disruptions to the genes encoding both the SUL1 and SUL2 yeast sulphate transporters has become available more recently (Cherest et al., 1997). Complementation of these mutants with plant cDNAs has enabled both high-affinity and low-affinity functional subgroups to be identified. Using this expression system for kinetic studies, the SHST1 and SHST2 transporters from Stylosanthes (Smith et al., 1995b), the HVST1 transporter from barley (Smith et al., 1997b) and the Sultr1;1 transporter from $A r -$ abidopsis (Takahashi et al., 2000) have been shown to be high-affinity sulphate transporters with apparent $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ values for sulphate in the range of $3 \mathrm { - } 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . In similar studies the SHST3 transporter from Stylosanthes and the Sultr2;1 transporter (formerly AST68) from Arabidopsis have been shown to be low-affinity sulphate transporters with apparent $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ values of 100 and $4 0 0 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ , respectively. Functional analyses using heterologous expression in yeast has also revealed that sulphate uptake rates are sensitive to $\mathrm { p H }$ , declining as the extracellular $\mathrm { p H }$ increases from 5.5 to 7.5 (Smith et al., 1995b, 1997b). Increasing the buffer concentration in the external solution has also been shown to reduce sulphate uptake rates. These data indicate that the plant sulphate transporters rely upon the maintenance of a proton gradient across the membrane. They therefore function as $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } / \mathrm { S O _ { 4 } } ^ { 2 - }$ symporters, the proton gradient being provided by a proton pump.

Functional analyses of plant phosphate transporters has been more difficult. Although a yeast mutant defective in the PHO84 gene encoding a yeast phosphate transporter has been available (Bun-ya et al., 1991), complementation of this mutant with plant cDNAs encoding phosphate transporters has been disappointing. $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ values for plant phosphate transporters arising from such heterologous expression studies have been much higher than physiologists would have expected (Leggewie et al., 1997; Liu et al., 1998b). Availability of mutants in which genes encoding both the PHO84 phosphate transporter and the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -coupled PHO89 transporter have been disrupted (Martinez and Persson, 1998) have permitted more reliable functional analyses. Using such mutants an apparent $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for phosphate of $3 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ was obtained for the tomato LePT1 phosphate transporter from the Pht1 family (Daram et al., 1998). An apparent $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for phosphate of $3 9 5 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ was obtained for the $\mathrm { P h t } 2 ; 1$ phosphate transporter from Arabidopsis (Daram et al., 1999), indicating that this is a low-affinity transporter.

Expression of the gene encoding the PHT1 phosphate transporter from Arabidopsis in cultured tobacco cells has yielded the most reliable kinetic data (Mitsukawa et al., 1997b). The apparent $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for phosphate of $3 . 1 \ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ measured with this system is similar to the $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ values derived for high-affinity phosphate uptake from physiological experiments.

Again, studies in yeast indicate that phosphate transport is dependent upon the proton gradient across the membrane (Daram et al., 1998, 1999). Further, measured decreases in cytoplasmic pH during phosphate uptake (Mimura et al., 1992; Sakano et al., 1992; Ulrich and Novacky, 1992) are consistent with the plant phosphate transporters functioning as $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / H _ { 2 } P O _ { 4 } } ^ { - }$ symporters. The $\mathrm { P h t } 2 ; 1$ phosphate transporter from Arabidopsis is interesting since, although it is very similar to sodium-dependent phosphate transporters in other organisms, Pht2;1 is a proton/phosphate symporter in plants.


## Regulation of plant phosphate and sulphate transporters


The expression of genes encoding transporters involved in sulphate and phosphate by plants roots is transcriptionally regulated by signals that respond to the nutrient status of the plants. Thus, when the external supply of sulphate is restricted, there is a rapid increase in mRNA transcripts in roots corresponding to high-affinity sulphate transporters (Smith et al., 1995b, 1997b; Takahashi et al. 2000; Vidmar et al., 1999). Similarly, when the external phosphate supply becomes limiting there is an increase in mRNA transcripts in roots corresponding to highaffinity phosphate transporters (Liu et al., 1998a, b; Muchhal and Raghothama, 1999; Smith et al., 1997a). These increases in steady state mRNA levels are accompanied by increases in the capacities of the root to take up sulphate or phosphate. In the case of sulphate deprivation they are also accompanied by decreases in the sulphate, cysteine and glutathione levels in the plant tissues. Upon resupplying sulphate to sulphate deprived plants or phosphate to phosphate-deprived plants, mRNA levels corresponding to the high affinity sulphate or phosphate transporters decline rapidly. This rapid decline is accompanied by reduced capacities of the plants to take up sulphate or phosphate and increases in the levels of assimilatory products in the plant tissues. The expression of genes encoding these transporters is therefore closely regulated by negative feedback loops. These loops, the physiological significance of which had been recognised before the molecular evidence was available (Clarkson and Scattergood, 1982; Clarkson et al., 1983; Cogliatti and Clarkson, 1983; Clarkson and Luttge, 1991; Lefebvre and Glass, 1982), serve to maintain the concentration of sulphur and phosphorus in plant tissues within limits that are necessary to maintain ion homeostasis (Mimura, 1995, 1999; Mimura et al., 1992).

The feedback regulation of sulphate or phosphate uptake by plant roots result from systemic signals rather than localised effects. Physiological studies involving split root experiments indicate that sulphate or phosphate uptake rates in those sections of the root system deprived of sulphate or phosphate respond to the overall sulphate or phosphate status of the whole plant (Clarkson et al., 1983; Drew and Saker, 1984). They do not respond to the localised concentration of nutrient adjacent to that particular root. These physiological studies are now being confirmed by molecular data (Lappartient et al., 1999; Liu et al., 1998a). Thus, the signals responsible for transcriptional regulation of these transporters are themselves likely to be delivered via some inter-organ transport system. Evidence for such signalling is emerging from studies implicating glutathione, translocated via the phloem, in the regulation of the gene encoding the Sultr2;1 sulphate transporter in plant roots (Lappartient et al., 1999).

There is also evidence of positive transcriptional regulation of genes encoding high-affinity sulphate transporters. This emerges from studies with barley in which the roots of plants adequately supplied with sulphate were exposed to $o$ -acetylserine, a precursor in the synthesis of cysteine (Hawkesford and Smith,

1997a; Smith et al., 1997b). Under these conditions transcription of the gene encoding the HVST1 highaffinity sulphate transporter was derepressed. Rapid increases were observed in the levels of HVST1 mRNA transcripts, sulphate uptake rates and cysteine and glutathione concentrations in the plant tissues. Thus, the negative feedback that normally occurs in plants grown on an adequate sulphate supply was partially over-ridden by an increase in the supply of a key C/N precursor of the sulphur assimilatory pathway. Genes encoding high-affinity sulphate transporters are therefore transcriptionally regulated by signals that respond to the demand for sulphate to synthesise reduced sulphur compounds and the supply of key precursors in the assimilatory pathway. Such controls are included in the regulatory sequence proposed by Hawkesford (2000).

These types of transcriptional regulation control the numbers of transporters in the membranes. The rates at which both mRNA transcripts corresponding to high-affinity sulphate transporters decay and the sulphate uptake function declines when sulphate is re-supplied to sulphate-starved plants (Smith et al., 1997b) has led to the conclusion that both the mRNA transcripts and the transporter proteins in the membrane turn over rapidly. The view that is emerging is that the membrane is a very dynamic structure with embedded transporter protein molecules continuously appearing and disappearing. In addition to this regulation of the number of transporter proteins, it is also very likely that the activity of these transporters is regulated by post-transcriptional modifications of the protein and by allosteric regulatory processes. The presence of highly conserved potential phosphorylation sites within the sequences of plant phosphate transporters (Smith, 1999; Smith et al., 1997a) suggest that phosphorylation may be important in the regulation of these transporters. It is known that a number of interacting proteins are involved in regulating phosphate transport in yeast (Bun-ya et al., 1992, 1996; Yompakdee et al., 1996a, b). The existence of homologues of these proteins seems likely in plants, but to date, such homologues have not been identified.

Expression of genes encoding the lower-affinity sulphate transporters SHST3 and Sultr2;1 is also transcriptionally regulated by the sulphate status of the plants (Smith et al., 1995b; Takahashi et al., 1997, 2000). Although there appears to be fewer transcripts of these types than of the high-affinity types in the roots, they are similarly regulated by the sulphate status of the plants. That is, feedback loops result in increased levels of expression in sulphate-deprived roots. However, these lower affinity types are also expressed in shoot tissues where they appear to be downregulated as a result of sulphate deprivation (Smith et al., 1995b). A possible explanation for this is provided when the role of this type of sulphate transporter is discussed in a later section.

The Pht2;1 family of phosphate transporters is primarily expressed in shoot tissues (Daram et al., 1999). Highest levels of expression were found in Arabidopsis in non-senescent rosette leaves and there was very little expression detected in roots. Levels of expression in leaves responded little to depriving the plants of phosphate. In contrast to the Pht1 family of transporters (Smith et al., 1995a) there is only limited up-regulation of expression of $P h t 2 ; I$ in the roots of plants deprived of phosphate. Studies of $P h t 2 ; I$ expression in the pho1 (Poirier et al., 1991) and pho2 (Delhaize and Randall, 1995; Dong et al., 1998) mutants of Arabidopsis confirm that the phosphorus status of the shoot appears to have little influence on the regulation of the Pht2;1 gene.


## Roles of different phosphate and sulphate transporters


The availability of information from plant genome sequencing projects and attempts to screen libraries for genes encoding plant phosphate and sulphate transporters are revealing that most species have a number of different transporters involved in the transfer of these ions across membranes. To date six members of the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters have been identified in Arabidopsis (Okumura et al., 1998), eight in barley (Smith et al., 1999) and seven genes encoding sulphate transporters have been identified from Arabidopsis (Takahashi et al., 2000). It is also interesting to note that some of the phosphate transporters that have been identified have almost identical sequences and appear to be similarly regulated (Smith et al., 1997a, 1999). The close physical proximity of some of these genes within the genome (Okumura et al., 1998) suggests they may be recent evolutionary duplications. However, differences in the sequences of the noncoding regions of these genes may ultimately reveal subtle differences in the regulation of their expression.

The physiological functioning of whole plants requires the co-ordinated operation of a number of phosphate and sulphate transport systems (Clarkson, 1993). It is not surprising, therefore, that there are multiple members of gene families encoding these transporters. We can probably expect that, as in the case of the recent identification of the Pht2 family of genes encoding phosphate transporters, additional families of these genes will be found. The challenge then becomes one of assigning physiological roles to the different transporters and developing an understanding of how they are regulated.

Perhaps the best information currently available on the roles of different transporters is that related to sulphate transport in dicotyledon species (Takahashi et al., 2000). Putative roles of a number of these transporters have been derived by bringing together information on their phylogenetic relationships, their kinetics, their regulation and the cell and tissue types in which they are expressed. Based upon the phylogenetic relationships between all of the presently known plant sulphate transporters, four major groups have been suggested (Hawkesford, 2000; Takahashi et al., 2000). The functional significance of these groups is enhanced by the fact that members of these groups are also expressed in similar tissue types.

The first group includes the high-affinity sulphate transporters that are primarily expressed in roots. The best documented of these are the SHST1 and SHST2 transporters from Stylosanthes (Smith et al., 1995b), the HVST1 transporter from barley (Smith et al., 1997b) and the Sultr1;1 transporter from Arabidopsis (Takahashi et al., 2000). All of these transporters have a $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for sulphate of $3 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 \ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . The genes encoding them are up-regulated during sulphate stress so the root cells in which they are expressed will have an enhanced capacity to take up any sulphate that becomes available to them. Reporter gene studies using green fluorescent protein indicate that, at least within the dicotyledon species, the genes encoding these transporters are primarily expressed in cells in the outer layers of plant roots: around the root tip, in epidermal cells and root hairs and in the outer layers of the cortex (Takahashi et al., 2000). Transporters in this group are therefore well placed and have the necessary high-affinity kinetic characteristics to transport sulphate from the low sulphate concentrations in the external soil solution across the plasmalemma and into the symplasm of plant roots. Taken together, these data suggest that these transporters play a primary role in the initial uptake by plant roots of sulphate from the soil solution. The amount of sulphate entering the plant can be controlled by the regulatory characteristics of these transporters. As indicated in a previous section, important among these is up-regulation by feedback control circuits that respond to the sulphate status of the whole plant and to the availability of C/N precursors in the sulphate assimilatory pathway.

A second phylogenetic grouping includes the SHST3 transporter isolated from Stylosanthes (Smith et al., 1995b) and the Sultr2;1 transporter isolated from Arabidopsis (Takahashi et al., 1997). These are lower affinity types with a $\mathrm { K } _ { m }$ for sulphate in the range $1 0 0 { - } 4 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ . They are expressed in both roots and shoots (Hawkesford, 2000, Takahashi et al., 2000). In situ hybridisation and reporter gene studies indicate these genes are expressed within the vascular tissues, primarily in the pericycle and xylem parenchyma, although there may be some expression in phloem cells as well (Takahashi et al., 2000). During sulphate stress their expression is up-regulated in root tissues, but appears to be down-regulated in plant shoots (Smith et al., 1995b). The role of the members of this group of sulphate transporters is not clear at present. A transport system within the vascular tissues involved in the loading of xylem vessels is required, but this would be an efflux process. Although it is possible that transporters of the SHST3 and Sultr2;1 types could also have a sulphate efflux function, heterologous expression in yeast (Smith et al., 1995b; Takahashi et al., 2000) suggests they are primarily involved in influx of sulphate. This raises the question of what role a lowaffinity influx transporter may have in these cell types within the stele. One possible explanation is that they may be involved in scavenging for sulphate that may be leaking back from xylem vessels into apoplastic spaces within the stele. Such a process might be particularly important in roots during periods of sulphate stress and therefore up-regulated when plants are deprived of sulphur. Conversely, in order for sulphate to be transported to leaf cells during periods of sulphate stress it may need to be down-regulated in the vascular tissues of plant shoots as has been reported by Smith et al. (1995b).

The gene encoding the sulphate transporter Sultr2;2 (formerly AST56) from Arabidopsis is also a member of this phylogenetic group. When expressed in yeast this transporter has a lower affinity for sulphate than either the Sultr2;1 or SHST3 members of this group. Sultr2;2 is primarily expressed in leaves where promoter-GFP reporter studies indicate that it is mainly localised in the bundle sheath cells that surround the leaf veins (Takahashi et al., 2000). It is therefore likely that a primary role of this transporter is the re-adsorption of sulphate being delivered to leaves after its release from xylem vessels within the leaf veins. It might be expected that the bundle sheath cells would then transfer that sulphate on to the leaf mesophyll cells. The third phylogenetic grouping of plant sulphate transporters is comprised of members that are also expressed in leaves (Takahashi, 1999b). Little work has been done on the members of this group to date. Presumably they are involved in the storage of sulphate in leaves and its transfer between various pools.

Genes encoding sulphate transporters within the fourth phylogenetic grouping are more distantly related to the other members of the family of plant sulphate transporters. The amino acid sequence derived from the full-length clone of the gene from Arabidopsis within this group contains a characteristic chloroplast targeting peptide. Studies fusing this peptide to GFP indicate that the Sultr4;1 gene encoding this sulphate transporter is most likely expressed in the chloroplast (Takahashi et al., 1999a) where the protein could play a role in transport to the site of reduction.

A useful framework for delineating the role of sulphate transporters in dicotyledon plants is emerging. There are big gaps, particularly with respect to the identity and regulation of transporters that mediate the transfer of sulphate across membranes other than the plasmamembrane. There is also a quandry regarding sulphate transport in monocotyledon plant species where fewer genes encoding sulphate transporters have been isolated to date. Further, data that is emerging on the localisation of expression of the high-affinity sulphate transporter in monocotyledons suggests there may be significant differences between the sulphate transport systems of monocotyledon and dicotyledon species.

At this time it is not possible to reliably ascribe roles to many of the phosphate transporters that have been isolated from plants. Progress on these has been hampered by the high degree of similarity that exists between many members of the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters. This similarity continues to cause problems when trying to use techniques such as in situ hybridisation to localise the sites of expression of specific members of the Pht1 family in some species. It is also likely that additional members will be added to the Pht2 family of phosphate transporters and different roles ascribed to them.


## Phosphate transport and mycorrhiza-plant interactions


The symbiotic relationships between endomycorrhizal fungi and most plants used in commercial agriculture is of particular interest to this Symposium. This symbiosis provides an important mechanism for the acquisition of phosphate by plant roots (Harrison, 1999). Following colonisation of roots, endomycorrhizal fungi form structures known as arbuscules in the cortical cells of the roots. The arbuscules are involved in the exchange of carbon compounds from the plant to the fungus and the exchange of phosphate, as well as some other nutrients on occasions, from the fungus to the plant. Arbuscules develop when hyphal branches penetrate the cell wall. The associated hyphal network through which phosphate is taken up from the soil may extend several centimetres from the root surface. This hyphal network therefore significantly increases the volume of soil that the plant root can access for phosphate.

Uptake of phosphate from the soil solution by fungal hyphae is mediated by a proton coupled phosphate transporter very similar to the Pht1 family of phosphate transporters from plants and the PHO84 phosphate transporter from yeast. The gene encoding one of these transporters has been cloned from hyphae of the mycorrhizal fungus Glomus versiforme (Harrison and van Buuren, 1995). This is a high-affinity phosphate transporter capable of transporting phosphate into the hyphae from the low concentrations that occur in most soil solutions.

Release of phosphate to the plant at the arbuscule/cortical cell interface will involve two transport processes. The first will be an efflux of phosphate into the apoplast across the fungal membrane that surrounds the arbuscule. The second will be an influx of phosphate from the apoplast into the plant symplast and will be mediated by phosphate transporters in the peri-arbuscular membrane that is formed when the growing arbuscule displaces the plant plasma membrane. The transporter involved in efflux from the arbuscule has not been identified. Progress has been made in identifying a plant transporter likely to be involved in uptake of phosphate into the plant through the peri-arbuscular membrane. In situ hybridisation studies have suggested that the gene encoding the LePT1 phosphate transporter or a gene homologous to LePT1 is highly expressed in cortical cells containing arbuscules (Rosewarne et al., 1999).

Work on Medicago truncatula has identified genes encoding two phosphate transporters of the Pht1 family that are expressed in plant roots (Liu et al., 1998). The expression of both of these genes is up-regulated when the phosphate status of the plant declines. In

M. truncatula plants infected with mycorrhizae, however, the degree to which the expression of these two genes is up-regulated is reduced in plants infected with mycorrhizae. Whilst this may be due in part to the improved phosphate status of mycorrhizal plants, there are indications that mycorrhizal colonisation itself may restrict expression of genes that encode phosphate transporters in the plasma membranes of root cells. There is clear evidence that, quite early in the process of mycorrhizal colonisation before the phosphate status of the plant is significantly altered, there are signals that influence the expression of genes that are normally induced in the host plant during phosphorus starvation (Burleigh and Harrison, 1997, 1999; Liu et al., 1998). This signalling and its effect on phosphorus transport processes is likely to be important to both the success of the mycorrhizal symbiosis and to the phosphate nutrition of the plant. It is therefore an important area for future research.

The aluminium activated malate transporter (ALMT) gene family is named after the first member of the family identified in wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) [1]. The product of this gene controls resistance to aluminium (Al) toxicity. TaALMT1 was the first member of this novel family of genes encoding anion channels. Although widely spread in plants, relatively little information is available on the roles performed by other members of this family. However those that have been characterised show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13], fruit acidity [14,15], microbe interactions [16,17] and seed development [18].

ALMT genes encode transmembrane proteins that function as anion channels and perform multiple functions involving the transport of organic anions (e.g., carboxylates) and inorganic anions in cells [19–21]. Carboxylic acids such as malic and citric acids are important metabolites in plant cells due to their involvement in photosynthesis, the tricaboxylic acid pathway, carbohydrate metabolism, cytosolic pH regulation, contribution to the maintenance of electroneutrality and nutrition [22–24]. These organic anions also confer resistance to Al toxicity in acid soils because when released from roots their carboxyl groups chelate the trivalent Al cations $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ rendering them less toxic [22]. Carboxylic anions can also bind with other multivalent metal ions [21].

Anion channels are integral membrane proteins that form aqueous pores to selectively allow the rapid transport of anions across membranes down their electrochemical gradients [25]. Therefore, anion channels are passive transporters located on many plant membranes including the plasma membrane, tonoplast, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial and chloroplast membranes. Some also perform signalling roles and function as master switches in stress responses [25–27]. The development of the patch-clamping technique provided a method for detailed research on the functioning of ion channels. The patch-clamp technique has been used to investigate the function of some members of the ALMT family. Some are permeable to malate anions while others are also permeable to other organic inions (such as fumarate) or inorganic inions (such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ , $\mathrm { N O } ^ { 3 - }$ and less to $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ ). Other useful methods for studying ion channels also include the analysis of substrate concentrations in native and heterologous expression systems. In plants, the guard cells that regulate stomatal aperture have become a popular model system for characterising membrane transport and signal transduction. For instance, in Vicia faba L. guard cells, researchers have identified two types of anion channel considered important for stomatal closure: the rapid-type (R-type) and the slow-type (S-type) [28]. The R-type anion channels can be activated rapidly within $5 0 \mathrm { m s }$ by depolarisation and activates potassium release when the membrane potential falls below the equilibrium potential for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ while S-type channels showed a much slower (seconds) voltage-dependent activation and deactivation [20,28].

The characterised ALMT members show a range of functions including Al resistance [1–4], stomatal function [5–11], mineral nutrition [12,13,39], microbe interactions [16,17], fruit acidity [14,15], and seed development [18]. Members which have been characterised are widely distributed in higher plant families of Poaceae, Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Rutaceae, Rosaceae, Vitaceae and Solanaceas (Table 1).


## 3.1. ALMT Members in Poaceae


The Poaceae species which have characterised ALMT members include wheat TaALMT1, rye ScALMT1, goatgrass AetALMT1, Yorkshire fog HlALMT1, maize ZmALMT1 and ZmALMT2, rice OsALMT4 and barley HvALMT1. ALMT genes in wheat, rye, goatgrass and Yorkshire fog facilitate resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley HvALMT1 was related to stomatal functions (Figure 1).

By using a cDNA subtractive hybridisation technique, Sasaki et al. [1] cloned a cDNA which was more highly expressed in the root apices of an Al-resistant wheat line (ET8) than in a near-isogenic but Al-sensitive line (ES8). TaALMT1 was mapped to chromosome 4DL and the relative expression of this gene among various genotypes of wheat was strongly correlated with Al-activated malate efflux capacity and Al resistance [40]. Electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus laevis oocytes indicated that TaALMT1 encodes an Al-activated transporter that can mediate both inward and outward currents. The malate transport permeability is enhanced by external Al but it is also permeable to a lesser degree to other physiologically relevant anions such as $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ [1,41]. Transgenic rice, Arabidopsis, barley and tobacco cultured cell lines expressing TaALMT1 all showed an Al-activated malate efflux. In the later three cases, TaALMT1 also increased Al resistance [1,42]. The higher expression of TaALMT1resistance to Al, members in maize and rice functions on mineral nutrition, while the barley in resistant than sensitive wheat genotypes is due to a series of repeated blocks in the promoter [43].

Among cereal crops, rye is the most Al resistant species. Researchers have mapped Al-resistance loci on chromosomes 3R (Alt2), 4RL (Alt3), 6RS (Alt1) and 7RS (Alt4) by using segregating populations and wheat-rye addition lines [44–48]. Using primers to the TaALMT1 gene, Fontecha et al. [49] cloned a 1359 bp cDNA called ScALMT1 from rye and showed that it co-segregated with the Al resistance locus Alt4. ScALMT1 is mainly expressed in roots and expression is upregulated by exogenous Al treatment. Collins et al. [2] showed that the Alt4 resistance locus contains a cluster of ALMT genes. Although − −there are some mRNA splice variations that might affect protein function, the M77.1 promoter and ScALMT1-M39.1 gene are sufficient to explain most of the Al resistance in that line. As the ancestor of the wheat D genome, goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii Coss.) contains more genetic variation than bread wheat perhaps because it experienced less artificial selection. Ryan et al. [50] screened 760 accessions in a total of seven progenitor species of hexaploid wheat and other early relatives. Of these only five of 29 Aegilops tauschii tested showed a moderate level of resistance to Al. The coding sequences of the AetALMT1 genes in the five resistant genotypes were identical to TaALMT1 and resistance was correlated with AetALMT1 expression level and with Al-activated malate efflux. Unlike TaALMT1, all the Aegilops tauschii genes lacked any of the tandem repeats in the promoter region—even the moderately resistant ones [50]. Yorkshire fog is a grass that shows a large genotypic variation in acid soil tolerance. Chen et al. [34] cloned the HlALMT1 gene and found that plants from plots with acidic soil (HL-A) had significantly higher HlALMT1 expression levels in their roots than plants from plots with neutral pH soil (HL-N). The higher expression in HL-A plants was linked with a greater number of the cis-acting elements which recognise an Al-responsive transcription factor (HlART1) [34]. Furthermore, the HL-A roots secreted approximately twice as much malate as the HL-N roots, but there was no difference in citrate secretion. These results indicated that cis elements in the promoter of the HvALMT1 gene generated higher expression of HlALMT1 leading to higher malate efflux and greater Al resistance.

In maize, ZmALMT1 was initially considered a candidate for an Al resistance gene due to its sequence homology with TaALMT1 [12]. Although ZmALMT1 localises to the plasma membrane, is mainly expressed in root tissue, and shows increased expression with Al treatment, other results indicated that this gene was not involved with the mechanism of Al resistance. Firstly, electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus oocytes showed that ZmALMT1 had greater permeability to ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ than malate and these anions would not bind with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ to reduce its activity in the apoplast. Furthermore, ZmALMT1 expression was low in the root tips where protection from $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress by organic anions is crucial. Lastly, transport activity of ZmALMT1 was independent of exogenous Al [12]. Linkage analysis of Al resistance genes in maize identified another ALMT gene, ZmALMT2, that is associated with net root growth under Al stress [51]. However, once again, ZmALMT2 is more permeable to inorganic anions $\left( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } \right.$ , $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ ) than organic anions such as malate. Furthermore, ZmALMT2 is mainly expressed in mature roots and not root apices, expression levels are similar in Al-sensitive and resistant genotypes. Therefore, this gene is also unlikely to be involved with Al resistance despite its genetic linkage with that trait. Instead the authors suggested ZmALMT2 is involved with mineral nutrition [13].

There are nine members of the ALMT family rice but only OsALMT4 has been examined in detail. OsALMT4 localises to the plasma membrane and is expressed widely in roots and shoots, especially in the vasculature. Transgenic plants over-expressing OsALMT4 released malate from roots which is consistent with OsALMT4 encoding a malate-permeable anion channel. The over-expressing (OX) lines developed distinct symptoms on their leaves which consisted of dark brown spots and stripes and occasionally necrotic margins which did not appear on null segregant plants or RNAi lines with reduced OsALMT4 expression. The partitioning of Mn within the leaf tissue was altered in the transgenic since the OX lines had a greater proportion of Mn residing in the apoplast of the leaves compared to the null plants. OX lines also had higher concentrations of malate in the xylem sap and increased expression of genes encoding Mn transporters (OsNramp5 and OsYSL2) and B transporters (OsBOR1 and OsNIP3.1). Growth studies found that the OX lines were more sensitive to Mn toxicity but more tolerant of B toxicity than null plants. The authors conclude that enhancing OsALMT4 expression affected the compartmentation of malate within the tissues which increased Mn concentrations in the apoplast and caused the toxicity symptoms [39].

Barley is another important plant in Triticeae and the barley ALMT1 gene was shown to be involved in facilitating anion efflux from guard cells during stomatal closure and seed development [5,11,18]. HvALMT1 is located on chromosome 2H. Tissue localisation showed that this protein was expressed in guard cells and in emerging lateral roots, the nucellar projection, aleurone layer and the scutellum of developing barley grain [5,18]. Intracellular localisation of HvALMT1 included the plasma membrane and small motile vesicles in the cytosol but the identity and function of those vesicles is unknown. Heterologous expression in Xenopus oocytes showed that this protein could mediate both inward and outward currents. HvALMT1 is permeable to malate and its activity is sensitive to $\mathrm { p H }$ [5]. The transgenic plants over-expressing HvALMT1 released more malate from roots than the control plants and they took significantly longer to close their stomata under low light than null controls. They also tended to reach a lower stomatal conductance under low light but the results were not significant. Combined with the finding that HvALMT1 is highly expressed in guard cells these results provided evidence that this channel contributes to stomatal function [11]. Interestingly, overexpressing HvALMT1 to high levels with a constitutive promoter affected plant growth and grain formation. Further experiments showed that malate release measured from isolated aleurone layers of grain was significantly lower in transgenic lines in which HvALMT1 expression was reduced by RNAi compared to control plants [18]. Therefore, HvALMT1 function affects stomatal aperture, grain development and plant growth. This shows that a single ALMT gene may perform multiple functions [5,11,18].


## 3.2. ALMT Members in Brassicaceae


The Arabidopsis ALMT gene family contains 14 members and five of them were detailed characterised (Figure 2). AtALMT1 is mostly expressed in Arabidopsis roots and knock-out mutants are more sensitive to Al stress [3]. Expression studies showed that AtALMT1 expression is induced by Al treatment and low pH [3]. Electrophysiological characterisation in Xenopus oocytes indicated that AtALMT1 functions as a malate-permeable channel [3,52]. However other researchers couldthat AtALMT1 functions as a malate-permeable channel [3,52]. However other researchers could not not demonstrate AtALMT1 function in oocytes [53]. Interestingly, AtALMT1 expression is not only induced by external Al but also by lowinduced by external Al but also by low p $\mathrm { p H } ,$ , hydrogen peroxide and phytohormones such as ABAydrogen peroxide and phytohormones such as ABA and and IAA [54]. Furthermore, AtALMT1 might also be involved in biotic interactions. A transgenic Arabidopsis line in which GUS expression was driven by the promoter of AtALMT1 showed an increase in GUS expression in the roots when the leaves were treated with the foliar pathogenincrease in GUS expression in the roots when the leaves were treated with the foliar pathogen Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato (Pst DC3000). This same treatment also induced malate release from thePseudomonas syringae pv tomato (Pst DC3000). This same treatment also induced malate release from roots. The authors found that the malate release helped recruit the beneficial bacterium Bacillus FB17 around the roots [16,31]. Furthermore, AtALMT1 expression was induced by flg22, a kind of MAMPFB17 around the roots [16,31]. Furthermore, AtALMT1 expression was induced by flg22, a kind of (microbe-associated molecular pattern) in a manner that was independent of the salicylic acid and jasmonic acid pathways [55]. A recent study with Arabidopsis, which also relies on malate efflux via aand jasmonic acid pathways [55]. A recent study with Arabidopsis, which also relies on malate efflux ALMT1 channel, proposes that the Al:malate complex is taken up by the root cells and transported to shoot by NIP1;2 to maintain low Al concentrations in the apoplast shoots [56]. These results indicate that AtALMT1 expression could contribute to plant-pathogen interactions [16] and that a single ALMT gene can perform multiple functions.

Initial reports disagreed as to the sub-cellular localisation and function of AtALMT12. Sasaki et al. [7] localised this protein to endomembranes and plasma membrane and predicted that AtALMT12 can mediate $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ fluxes but not malate. They also concluded that this protein was not responsible for either the R-type not S-type anion currents [7]. By contrast, Meyer et al. [6] found that the protein localised to the plasma membrane and concluded that AtALMT12 can mediate malate transport and likely functions as the R-type anion channel. Further studies confirmed that AtALMT12 is a malate-dependent R-type channel in guard cells and interacts with the kinase Open Stomata 1 to regulate stomatal closure [6,37,57]. Similarly, a recent report mentions that the ALMT4 is required for stomatal closure in response to abscisic acid (ABA). AtALMT4 functions as an ion channel that mediates ${ \bf M a l } ^ { 2 - }$ release from the vacuole. ALMT4 is localised to the vacuolar membrane and is expressed in leaf mesophyll and guard cells. Electrophysiological result indicates that ALMT4 can mediate $\mathrm { M a l } ^ { 2 - }$ efflux and the channel activity is dependent on a phosphorylatable C-terminal serine. Knock-out mutants showed impaired stomatal closure in response to the drought-stress hormone ABA and increased whole-plant wilting in response to drought and ABA [38].

Malate movement can also be important to balance the accumulation of cations in the vacuole such as potassium during stomatal opening. Therefore, ALMTs probably contribute to balancing anion movement across the tonoplast as well. For instance, in Arabidopsis the AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 proteins localise to the tonoplast. AtALMT6 is expressed in guard cells of leaf, stem and flower tissues. An AtALMT6-GFP fusion protein was targeted to the vacuolar membrane both in transient and stable expression systems [8]. Meyer et al. [8] concluded that AtALMT6 is a $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -activated malate channel as its transport activity was significantly altered by cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ . Moreover, AtALMT6 activity can be regulated by vacuolar pH and cytosolic malate. The atalmt6 T-DNA knockout mutant showed reduced malate current density across the tonoplast membrane [8]. Kovermann et al. [10] cloned the AtALMT9 gene and 1785 bp upstream of the coding region. Subcellular localisation in both Arabidopsis and onion epidermal tissue showed localisation to the tonoplast. Tissue-specific localisation using the promoter to drive GUS expression showed the gene is expressed in many organs including leaves (mesophyll tissue), roots and flower tissues [10]. Malate currents were inhibited across the tonoplast of AtALMT9 knock-out lines compared to WT controls but enhanced in tobacco lines expressing AtALMT9. AtALMT9 appears to function primarily as a malate channel although it exhibits weak conductance to fumarate and chloride [10]. More recently, De Angeli et al. [9] confirmed that AtALMT9 is an anion channel located on the tonoplast and is involved with stomatal opening. Unlike AtALMT6, AtALMT9 is not sensitive to cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ but can be activated by malate in the cytosol but not by malate in the vacuole [9]. Further research also demonstrated that AtALMT9 transport can be modulated by cytosolic nucleotides and other vacuolar anions [58].

Unlike other plant species, rape releases both malate and citrate when exposed to Al [59]. Ligaba et al. [4] cloned two TaALMT1 homologs from rape. These proteins only have $4 0 \%$ similarity with the wheat gene, but they still proved to be related to Al resistance. Similar with other Al related members, BnALMT1 is localised in the plasma membrane [4]. The expression of BnALMT1 and BnALMT2 was detected mainly in root but not shoots and their expression can be enhanced by Al treatment and to a lesser degree by other multivalent cations (such as lanthanum, ytterbium, and erbium). Transgenic tobacco culture cells expressing these genes showed increased malate efflux when exposed to Al and some other cations such as ytterbium and erbium [4].


## 3.3. ALMT Members in Fabaceae


Medicago sativa (lucerne or alfalfa) is an Al-sensitive pasture legume species. Nevertheless transcript analysis using a cDNA library from cultivar YM1 SSH indicated that MsALMT1 expression was up-regulated by a $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ treatment with $5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Al [60]. Transgenic tobacco expressing MsALMT1 showed malate efflux and the rate correlated with MsALMT1 transcription level. Under Al stress, these transgenic tobacco plants also had better root growth than control lines which suggests that this gene could be involved with Al resistance in Medicago even though it was cloned from a sensitive genotype [33].

GmALMT1 from soybean has been cloned by Liang et al. [32]. Sub-cellular localisation of the protein indicated that it is located in the plasma membrane. Heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis cells shows that this gene encodes a protein that mediates inward and outward currents. GmALMT1 is mainly expressed on root tips with expression and malate efflux altered by both low $\mathrm { p H }$ and Al treatments. Arabidopsis plants overexpressing GmALMT1 show better malate efflux and higher Al resistance. Additionally, increasing and decreasing the expression of this gene in transgenic hairy roots of soybean indicated that accumulation of Al in the root tissues was inversely correlated with relative GmALMT1 expression level. Together these results demonstrate that GmALMT1 is also likely to function as an Al resistance gene in soybean [32].

Of the seven ALMT proteins expressed in Lotus japonicus LjALMT4 is highly expressed in nodules. When expressed in Xenopus laevis oocytes, this protein was found to mediate the efflux of dicarboxylates, including malate, succinate, and fumarate, but not tricarboxylates such as citrate. Moreover, LjALMT4 was found to be specifically expressed in the parenchyma cells of nodule vascular bundles, suggesting that LjALMT4 is not a transporter at the peribacteroid membrane but is involved in transporting [17].


## 3.4. ALMT Members in Fruit Plants


In many acid soils it is common for Al toxicity to be linked with phosphorus (P) deficiency. This is because the soluble P is likely to be in a complex with iron or Al or fixed in other less soluble forms. Indeed some plants very efficient at taking up P from highly P-fixing soils, such white lupin (Lupinus albus L.), rely on organic anion release from roots (especially citrate release) to access more P [22]. Research indicates that members of the ALMT family might also contribute to greater P-use efficiency. For instance, the Al resistant species of citrus ‘Xuegan’ (Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck, CsALMT1) displayed more resistance to P-deficiency than a sensitive species ‘Sour pummelo’ (Citrus grandis (L.) Osbeck, $C g A L M T 1 )$ . Evidence was presented that ALMT genes in these species might contribute to the resistance of citrus to Al and/or P-deficiency [61].

Some ALMT proteins appear to affect fruit acidity by transporting malate across the tonoplast membrane (Figure 3). This was revealed when Bai et al. [14] narrowed down the Ma locus to a $6 5 { - } 8 2 \mathrm { k b }$ region on chromosome 16 of the apple cultivar Golden Delicious. The Ma locus is associated with fruit acidity in apple and the genomic region contains 12–19 predicted genes. By aligning these genes with two BACs covering different haplotypes of the Ma locus (high and low acidity), they identified two ALMT homologues and named them Ma1 and Ma2. Phylogenetic analysis using these two apple ALMT members against the Arabidopsis proteins indicated that these two members from apple were most similar to AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 which mediate anion transport across the tonoplast [14]. Ma1 was shown to localise on the tonoplast and heterologous expression in yeast increased malate influx into yeast cells. Quantitative RT-PCR experiments predicted that expression of Ma1, but not Ma2, is significantly linked with fruit acidity (high Ma1 expression was correlated with more acidic fruit). Moreover, a natural mutation in Ma1 leading to a truncation of the gene was also associated with low fruit acidity. The Ma1 genotype is closely related to apple fruit acidity suggesting Ma1 is associated with the accumulation of malic acid in apple fruits [62]. Similarly, De Angeli et al. [15] cloned an AtALMT9 homolog from grape called VvALMT9. VvALMT9 expression increased as the berry matured. The VvALMT9 protein has $6 4 \%$ identity with AtALMT9 and also localises to the tonoplast. VvALMT9 is not only permeable to malate, but also displays a low permeability to tartrate. The authors predicted that VvALMT9 is a tonoplast channel that contributes to malate and tartrate accumulation in grape berries [15].
