Salinity stress affects crop production worldwide, particularly by limiting plant growth and reducing potential yield. Plants have three mechanisms for tolerating soil salinity, including tolerance of the osmotic effects of salt; a tolerance in leaf tissues of the negative effects of sodium ions (Na+ ) on cellular function through compartmentalisation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in specific tissues, cells, or cellular organelles; and exclusion of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the sensitive shoot tissue [1]. Of these mechanisms, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from the shoot is best understood and is, therefore, the current best candidate for a targeted genetic modification approach to improving salinity tolerance.

The HKT gene family encodes one of the most widely studied groups of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters in plants. Current understanding indicates that AtHKT1; $I$ from Arabidopsis is expressed primarily in the stele and has a role in the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream [2,3]. Reduced activity of this transporter leads to increased transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the root to the shoot, leading to a higher shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and a decrease in salinity tolerance [4]. More recently, it was demonstrated that OsHKT1;5 in rice [5] and the $H K T l { ; } 5$ gene from wheat [6] are crucial in maintaining low shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations via a similar mechanism of $\mathrm { N a + }$ retrieval from the transpiration stream into cells within the stele. A second HKT gene that is involved in sodium exclusion in cereal species is HKT1;4. The encoded transporter appears to function in combination with HKT1;5, by retrieving $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the shoot transpiration stream and sequestering Na+ in the sheath tissue [7]. The endogenous function of the family of HKT transporters and their role in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport and provision of salinity tolerance to plants has been reviewed recently [8].

An obvious strategy for improving the salinity tolerance of plants is to increase the expression of HKT genes. Constitutive overexpression of plasma membrane $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters, however, has been unsuccessful in producing salinity tolerant plants [9]. It was hypothesized that such overexpression increases $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes into all cells of the plant, this being, on balance, counter-productive to the reduction of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport to the shoot [9,10]. In contrast, it was shown that overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the root xylem parenchyma cells of Arabidopsis leads to improved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and salinity tolerance [9]. Interestingly, the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the root resulting from the improved Na+ exclusion from the shoot was stored within the cortical cells of the root [9].

The aim of experiments described in the current work was to determine if overexpression of AtHKT1;1 specifically within the outer cells (epidermis and cortex) of the root would result in opposite effects to overexpression in the stele, or whether a similar improvement of Na+ exclusion and salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis and rice would be observed. A secondary goal was to determine if expression of AtHKT1; $\mathit { \Pi } _ { l }$ in the epidermal and cortical cell layers of the root is the reason for the deleterious effects observed when AtHKT1;1 is constitutively overexpressed, as described previously [9].

In both species, we found that transgenic plants overexpressing AtHKT1;1 in mature root cortex had greater shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and thus increased salinity tolerance.

Background Rice is subjected to various environmental stresses, resulting in significant production losses. Abiotic stresses, particularly drought and salinity, are the leading causes of plant damage worldwide. The High-affinity Potassium Transporter (HKT) gene family plays an important role in enhancing crop stress tolerance by regulating physiological and enzymatic functions.

Methods and results This study investigates the effect of overexpressing the rice HKT1;5 gene in Arabidopsis thaliana on its tolerance to salinity and drought. The OsHKT1;5 gene was introduced into Arabidopsis under the control of $3 5 \mathrm { S }$ promoter of CaMV via floral dip transformation method. PCR confirmed the integration of the transgene into the Arabidopsis genome, while $\mathsf { q P C R }$ analysis showed its expression. Three transgenic lines of OsHKT1;5 were used for stress treatment and phenotypic studies. The overexpressed lines showed considerably higher germination rates, increased leaf counts, greater fresh and dry weights of the roots and shoots, higher chlorophyll contents, longer root lengths, and reduced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels together with increased $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions levels after salt and drought treatments, in comparison to wild-type plants. Furthermore, overexpressed lines exhibited higher antioxidant levels than wild-type plants under salinity and drought conditions. In addition, transgenic lines showed higher expression levels of the OsHKT1;5 gene in both roots and shoots compared to wild-type plants.

Conclusions In conclusion, this study revealed OsHKT1;5 as a promising candidate for enhancing tolerance to salinity and drought stresses in rice, marking a significant step toward developing a new rice variety with improved abiotic stress tolerance.

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is a hyperaccumulator of silicon (Si) which may account for more than $10 \%$ of shoot dry weight (Ma et al. 2002; Sasaki et al. 2016). Si provides several benefits (e.g., protection from abiotic and biotic stresses) and is required for optimal productivity (Savant et al. 1997; Yamaji and Ma 2007). Uptake and distribution of Si in rice primarily involves two different transporters encoded by the Lsi1 (Low silicon 1) and Lsi2 (Low silicon 2) genes (Ma and Yamaji 2015). The Lsi1 transporter is a Si selectively permeable channel and a member of the nodulin 26-like major intrinsic protein (NIP) III subgroup of aquaporins (Ma et al. 2006; Ma and Yamaji 2015). Lsi2 is a Si efflux transporter that belongs to an uncharacterized putative anion transporter family (Ma et al. 2007; Ma and Yamaji 2015; Sasaki et al. 2016). Both Lsi1 and Lsi2 were initially identified using a forward genetic screen of chemically-induced rice mutants grown in the presence of germanium (Ge), an analogue of Si. Ge is toxic to plants but is indistinguishable from Si with regard to uptake by roots (Ma et al. 2001). Identification of mutants which were tolerant to Ge, and thus presumably defective in $\mathrm { G e } / \mathrm { S i }$ uptake, led to the cloning of the Lsi1 and Lsi2 genes (Ma et al. 2006, 2007).

Plants take up Si in the form of silicic acid, an uncharged monomeric molecular at $< \mathrm { p H } ~ 9$ . Under the anaerobic conditions in flooded rice paddies, arsenic (As) is predominantly found as arsenite (AsIII), which has similar chemical properties to silicic acid. Based on the similarities between silicic acid and arsenite, Ma et al. (2008) hypothesized that arsenite uptake was also mediated by the Lsi1 and Lsi2 transporters. Indeed, lsi1 mutants were found to be defective in arsenite uptake while lsi2 mutants exhibit significant reductions in arsenite transport to the xylem and accumulation in shoot tissues and seeds (Ma et al. 2008). Due to the high expression of the Lsi1 and Lsi2 genes in rice roots and their distinct locations in the root exodermis and endodermis, uptake of Si and As in rice is more efficient than other cereals (Song et al. 2014). Lsi1 transporters are localized to the distal sides of both cell layers while Lsi2 is located on the proximal sides and the two work in concert to facilitate the accumulation of high levels of Si and As (Song et al. 2014; Ma and Yamaji 2015; Sasaki et al. 2016). The uptake and accumulation of As in rice is a significant global concern due to the importance of rice as a major staple and the toxic and carcinogenic nature of As and As compounds (Sohn 2014).

While other transporters of arsenite and arsenate (AsV, the major form of As in aerobic soils), have been identified (Chen et al. 2017), Lsi1 and Lsi2 have the largest impact on arsenite uptake in rice due to their high expression in roots (Song et al. 2014). Analysis of As uptake and accumulation in rice straw and grains of lsi1 and lsi2 knockout mutants has revealed that while both transporters contribute to As content in rice straw, Lsi2 plays a significant role in grain As content but Lsi1 appears to have little to no effect (Ma et al. 2008). More recently, Song et al. (2014) reported the characterization of OsABCC1, a ATP binding cassette (ABC) subfamily C transporter, that is involved in detoxifying and decreasing As in rice grains. OsABCC1 appears to function by sequestering As in the vacuoles of phloem companion cells in rice nodes, thus limiting transport to the grain. T-DNA insertion lines in which the OsABCC1 gene is knocked out exhibit greater sensitivity to As and accumulate less As in shoot tissues compared to wild type. These mutants also had increased As accumulation in their grain.

Arsenic (As), an acute toxin, is the number one carcinogen (Centre international de recherche sur le cancer 2012). Arsenic poisoning has been associated with different health problems, such as, but not limited to, lung, bladder, and liver cancers (Aposhian et al. 2003; Hong et al. 2014; Rossman et al. 2004). Additionally, arsenic has been linked to obesity among those exposed to As (Castriota et al. 2018). Arsenic occurs in nature and is distributed in various types of rocks, such as volcanic, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. The volcanic activities, use of fossil fuels, and several industrial processes and activities contribute to a rise in As in the atmospheric air, eventually reaching surface water, groundwater, and soil (Bednar et al. 2002).

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the second largest food staple crop for more than half of the world’s population (Hashim et al. 2024). Rice is mostly grown in paddies, which are flooded with water. Flood conditions are suitable for As dissolution and release from minerals in the soil; thus, compared to other crops, rice is best equipped to accumulate As (Zhao et al. 2010; Muehe et al. 2019; Meselhy et al. 2024). This poses a significant risk to consumers, particularly infants, because infant nourishment relies heavily on rice products. Several recent reports highlighted the presence of high levels of As, cadmium (Cd), lead $\left( \mathrm { P b } \right)$ , and chromium (Cr) in baby foods (Srivastava et al. 2024).

Arsenic is taken up by plants with non-specificity, leading to the co-transport of As along with other elements due to chemical and structural similarities. As a result, AsV and AsIII can be taken by plants via phosphate (Pi) and silicon (Si) transporters, respectively (Ullrich-Eberius et al. 1989; Meharg and Macnair 1990; Ma et al. 2008), making As transporters potential targets to restrict As accumulation in crops’ edible parts. Aquaporins (AQPs) are the major contributor to As uptake and transport (Deng et al. 2020). Based on sequence homology, AQP proteins fall into four common and conserved groups among plant species: plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs), tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIP), nodulin-26-like intrinsic proteins (NIP), small basic intrinsic proteins (SIP) (Maurel et al. 2008). Aquaporins are $2 3 { - } 3 1 \ \mathrm { k D a }$ proteins with six membrane-spanning domains and five loops (A to E) forming a central aqueous pore, characterized by conserved Asn-Pro-Ala (NPA) motif, allowing for substrate specificity by size exclusion at pore constrictions and stereospecific recognition via hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions (Maurel et al. 2008). Given their structure characteristics, AQPs facilitate the passage of water, small uncharged solutes, and metalloids (Kumar et al. 2018).

Increased efforts have been directed to identify and characterize different As transporters in other plant species to produce safe and clean food and develop non-destructive technology to remediate the contaminated soils using phytoremediation technology. Different AQPs are involved in As uptake and transport. Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana L.) AtNIP1;1 and AtNIP7;1 were proved to facilitate As transport, and their mutants atnip1;1 and atnip7;1 show tolerance to arsenite (AsIII) with decreased As accumulation (Isayenkov and Maathuis 2008; Kamiya et al. 2009). Similarly, AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 when expressed in fps1Δ yeast cells caused AsIII sensitivity as an evidence of As uptake (Bienert et al. 2008). Further, AtNIP3;1 was reportedly involved in As uptake and translocation from root to shoot in Arabidopsis (Xu et al. 2015). In rice, OsNIP1;1 and OsNIP3;3 overexpression resulted in decreased As accumulation in the shoots and grains, indicating their role in restricting As translocation from roots to shoots (Sun et al. 2018).

Nutrients and other chemicals, including As, move through root cells toward the xylem to be loaded into by lateral polarity (Barberon and Geldner 2014). Different nutrients use lateral polarity to move across the root (Alassimone et al. 2010; Chiba et al. 2009; Gordon-Weeks et al. 2003; Mitani et al. 2009; Miwa et al. 2007; Takano et al. 2010; Ueno et al. 2009). One good example of AsIII transporters is OsLsi1 (OsNIP2;1) and OsLsi2, originally characterized as silicon transporters, which are involved in the influx and efflux of AsIII in rice roots, respectively, permitting AsIII to cross the CS barrier in the root exodermis and endodermis (Ma et al. 2006, 2007) Similarly, As translocation to aboveground tissues requires specific transporters, like other NIPs proteins and the ABC protein family, such as OsABCC7 (Ma et al. 2008; Tang et al. 2019). Having As transporters exclusively transporting As would be advantageous for genetic manipulation; however, this is challenging because the same transporters also transport other elements such as silicon and phosphate. For instance, oslsi1 mutation adversely impacted rice productivity with a $9 0 \%$ decline in grain yield and showed susceptibility to pests and diseases (Ma et al. 2006).

Mosa et al. (2012) showed that rice PIPs share sequence similarities with well-known As transporters from bacteria (GlpF), yeast (Fps1p), and mammalian AQP7 and AQP9 (Liu et al. 2002; Mosa et al. 2012; Sanders et al. 1997; Wysocki et al. 2001), which introduce PIPs as potential targets to restrict As uptake and transport in rice. Heterologous expression of rice PIPs in Xenopus Levies, yeast, and Arabidopsis have proved that PIPs facilitate AsIII transport (Mosa et al. 2012). Overexpression of rice OsPIP2;4, $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ , and OsPIP2;7 in Arabidopsis provided tolerance to As toxicity by functioning as an AsIII bidirectional channel (Mosa et al. 2012). Recently, we demonstrated that OsPIP2;6, localized in the vasculature tissues in the root, is involved in As transport from root to shoot in rice (Meselhy et al. 2024).

The current research demonstrated that OsPIP1;3 transport AsIII and contribute to AsIII transport from root to shoots. We showed that knocking down of OsPIP1;3 expression using RNAi approach decreased As accumulation in the shoot of OsPIP1;3 RNAi (Ri) seedlings and shoot and flag leaves of mature ospip1;3 Ri plants compared to WT. In contrast, the overexpression (OE) of OsPIP1;3 increased As accumulation in seedlings shoot and in shoots, flag leaves, and grains of mature OE plants compared to WT.

Potentially toxic elements (PTEs) negatively affect the environment as well as plants, animals and humans. Most of them are toxic causing abiotic stress; reduce plant growth and affecting food quality by entering the food chain, and ultimately threatening human health (F. J. ZHAO et al., 2009). Among the PTEs, arsenic (As) is considered as one of the most hazardous metalloid causing serious health diseases including cancer (CHANDRAKAR et al., 2016). The source of these elements can be natural or anthropogenic, like industrial emissions, application of fertilizers and pesticides, sewage irrigation, mining etc (ALAM, 2005). As-contaminated groundwater occurs in many regions of the world, the most severe problems reported from Bangladesh, West Bengal, China and Taiwan (WHO, 2001) (ABEDIN & MEHARG, 2002). Also reported groundwater contaminated with arsenic from Chile, Argentina, Mexico United States, India Italy and Hungary (PIGNA et al., 2009). The main forms of As in groundwater are inorganic, like arsenate $( \mathrm { A s } ( \mathrm { V } ) )$ and arsenite (As(III)) with neglected amounts of methylated As-species including monomethylarsonic acid (MMA) and dimethylarsinic acid (DMA) (BAKHAT et al., 2017).

Paddy rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the main agricultural crop grown in arsenic-affected areas of Asian countries. Therefore, As accumulation in rice grown in those soils is a concern (ABEDIN et al., 2002b). There are different international standards or regulatory limits for As in food and drinking water. Recommended maximum level (MLs) for inorganic arsenic (iAs) in white rice is $0 . 2 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ , in parboiled rice and husked rice $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ , in rice waffles, rice wafers, rice crackers, and rice cakes $0 . 3 0 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ and in rice destined for the production of food for infants and young children $0 . 1 0 \mathrm { ~ m g ~ k g ^ { - 1 } }$ (FAO, 2016). In aerobic conditions, the As(V) form is dominated which is analogous to the phosphate $\left( \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 3 - } \right)$ . One of the mechanisms to uptake As by rice roots using high affinity $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 3 - }$ transporters (ABEDIN et al., 2002a). In rice paddy soils the As bioavailability is high because of the flooded conditions. Anaerobic circumstances contribute to the reduction of $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ to As(III), which is more soluble therefore can be easily uptaken by rice roots via the silicic acid transporters (X. CHEN et al., 2012; MA et al., 2008). The As(III) is a silicic acid analogous element, therefore its uptake happens through Si transporter aquaporin channels of the plant root cells. Methylated As species (MMA and DMA) can also be taken up similarly (R.-Y. LI et al., 2009b; MA et al., 2008).

Once As get into plants, they may affect many important biological processes inhibiting plant growth and reducing crop yields. As-toxicity causes oxidative stress and inhibits the ATP formation, which leads to lower grain yield (PANAULLAH et al., 2009). Phytotoxic symptoms were also observed by KHAN et al. such as stunted growth, brown spots, and scorching on leaves of plants in soils containing ${ > } 6 0 \ \mathrm { m g \ k g ^ { - 1 } }$ total As (KHAN et al., 2010). Other studies showed that excess As-exposure in the soil could negatively affect seed germination, plant shoot, and root growth. It can cause wilting and necrosis of leaf blades, reduces leaf area and photosynthesis (ABEDIN et al., 2002a).

ABEDIN et al. (2002a) also found that the As accumulation in rice tissues increased significantly with increasing soil As concentration. The highest amount of As concentrated in the root followed by straw, husk and grain. Similarly, in KÁDÁR and LEHOCZKY (2008) study, the higher As contaminated soil resulted in higher As accumulation in plant organs. For all the investigated plants, the concentration of As in the roots was higher than that of the above ground parts. In FODOR and SZEGEDI (2015) plot experiment As content was not detected in the grain of wheet, maize and sunflower, even the application of $2 7 0 \ \mathrm { k g \ h a ^ { - 1 } }$ As treatment, however in the straws 5.2, 1.5 and $3 . 3 ~ \mathrm { m g ~ k g ^ { - 1 } }$ were measured, respectively.

As accumulation and speciation in rice depend on both environment and genotype (NORTON et al., 2009a). The As level and As speciation of the grain are influenced by the redox value, pH, phosphate concentration of the soil, the formation of iron plaque in the rhizosphere, microbial activity and the rice variety. The oxidative rhizosphere in paddy soil modifies As forms associated with rice root surface (LIU et al., 2005).

Williams et al. found large varietal variation in As uptake and transport (WILLIAMS et al., 2005). The study of GENG et al. showed cultivar differences in the growth due to the As exposure (GENG et al., 2006). Based on these findings, the As content of rice grain can be reduced by choosing As-tolerant varieties. In addition, there are some agrotechnical methods for reducing As content in rice, including water management strategies and the application of different minerals e.g. phosphorus (P), silicon (Si), sulfur (S) and iron (Fe). These practices can change the As solubility in soil solution (FAROOQ et al., 2016).


## Strategies for producing low As containing rice



## Genetical variation in As accumulation


Recent field studies have shown substantial genetic variation in rice grain As concentration and speciation. NORTON et al. (2009b) examined As concentration in the grains of 76 rice cultivars grown in two fields. The two sites had different levels of As in the soils and in the irrigation water. A strong correlation $( \mathrm { r } = 0 . 8 0 2 )$ was found in grain As concentrations of the 76 cultivars between the two locations, despite the different environments, suggesting stable genetic variations in As accumulation (NORTON et al., 2009b). However, in another study by NORTON et al. (2009a), among six sites, the environment made the most significant contribution to the variation in grain As concentration $( 6 1 \% )$ , followed by genotype $( 6 \% )$ and genotype x environment interaction $( 1 9 \% )$ (NORTON et al. 2009a). In the studies of NORTON et al. (2009a, b) there was also a significant genotype effect in the percentage of iAs and DMA in grain, but the environmental influence was higher. Similarly, AHMED et al. (2011) investigated 38 Bangladeshi cultivars grown in ten different agroecological zones of Bangladesh. They reported large environmental effect $( 6 9 - 8 0 \% )$ of the variation in grain As concentration, whereas genotype and genotype x environment interactions accounted for only $9- 1 0 \%$ and $10 { - } 2 1 \%$ of the observed variability (AHMED et al., 2011). Pillai et al. (2010) investigated 25 diverse rice cultivars at one field site over three growing seasons. They reported that the concentrations of total grain As and As species (As(III) and DMA) varied widely among the varieties. The effect of genotype on the As concentration and speciation of the rice grain accounted for about $70 \%$ of the variation, and the interaction between year and genotype accounted for about $20 \%$ (PILLAI et al., 2010). Comparing the studies of PILLAI et al. (2010), AHMED et al. (2011) and NORTON et al. (2009a), it can be concluded that genetic stability is greater across seasons than in different sites. A study by WILLIAMS et al. (2005) showed that the main As species of the rice grain were As(III) and DMA(V). The proportion of DMA in the grains significantly depended on the variety $\mathrm { P } { = } 0 . 0 2 6$ ) (WILLIAMS et al., 2005).

Our previous study examined the As content of shoots of four rice varieties in different irrigation systems (flooded and aerobic). No significant differences were recognized among the varieties in aerobic conditions. In one case, however, we found a significant difference between two tested varieties $\mathrm { ~ \ r ~ { ~ M ~ 4 8 8 } ~ }$ and ‘Nembo’) in flooded conditions on soil treated with Humin Power G soil conditioner (SZALÓKI et al., 2022).


## Water management


As discussed above, the anaerobic conditions in paddy soils support the reductive mobilization of As, so the As uptake is can be enhanced greatly by rice roots, leading to excessive As accumulation in rice grain and straw.In contrast, in aerobic treatments, the bioavailability of As reduces dramatically (R. Y. LI et al., 2009a). In a pot experiment, LI et al. (2009a) measured the concentration of total and iAs of rice grains in different water management systems. The continuously flooded rice showed the highest concentration of As in grain compared with the other treatments, followed by flooded-aerobic, aerobic-flooded and continuously aerobic conditions, where the iAs reductions were $2 5 \%$ , $46 \%$ and $87 \%$ , respectively (R. Y. LI et al., 2009a). In Arao et al. pot study, the results of water management treatments prove that the flooded condition increases the As concentration in the soil solution. The aerobic treatment for 3 weeks before and after heading was the most effective in decreasing the As content in grain, although the concentration of Cd in the grain increased considerably in anaerobic circumstances (ARAO et al., 2009). According to SPANU et al. (2020), intermittent irrigation methods effectively reduce the total amount of toxic elements including As in rice grain. Sprinkler irrigation was more effective method in reducing toxic elements in rice grain $( 9 0 \% )$ than the saturation irrigation $( 3 0 \% )$ compared to the continuous flooding. Moreover, the As concentration of the rice grain was decreased by $9 8 . 4 \%$ with sprinkler irrigation instead of flooded condition (SPANU et al., 2020). NORTON et al. (2019) also found strong correlation between the irrigation practices and As concentration of rice plants. For all tested cultivars, alternate wetting and drying (AWD) significantly reduced the As content of grain and shoot by more than 15 and $27 \%$ , respectively, compared to the plants grown under continuous flooding (NORTON et al., 2019).

The water-saving cultivation methods were described by BOUMAN et al. (2007), such as aerobic rice, alternate wetting and drying (AWD) and raised bed cultivation (BOUMAN et al., 2007). These cultivation methods can also prevent excessive arsenic accumulation in rice. In addition, there is less input of As-contaminated irrigation water into the soil, so the rice absorbs less As (MEHARG & ZHAO, 2012).

A field experiment by TAKAHASHI et al. (2004) verified that As, Fe, and Mn concentrations of soil solution increased under flooded conditions. They also examined the oxidation state of As in soil and water using in-situ spectroscopic method. It was found that the As(III) concentration of soil enhanced from $30 \%$ (non-flooded conditions) to $70 \%$ under flooded conditions. The higher proportion of As(III) in the aqueous phase compared to $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ suggests that $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ is reduced to As(III), which explains the increased As(III) concentration in groundwater (TAKAHASHI et al., 2004).

In our previous greenhouse pot experiment, the As concentration of the above-ground biomass was significantly higher in flooded than in aerobic conditions, as Figure 1. shows (SZALÓKI et al., 2022).


## Role of phosphate


The application of phosphate fertilizers plays a major role in the control of As uptake by rice in As-contaminated soils (FAROOQ et al., 2016; GENG et al., 2005).

$\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ is chemically analogous of phosphate (Pi) and the major arsenic form of aerobic soils, therefore enters plant root tissues through Pi-transporters (OsPht1;8) (WU et al., 2011). KAMIYA et al. (2013) also demonstrated the role of OsPT1 transporter in $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ uptake of rice from the soil (KAMIYA et al., 2013). Although As(III) is the main species of the soil solution of flooded paddy fields (TAKAHASHI et al., 2004; XU et al., 2008; LI et al., 2009), $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ is also considered to be present (STROUD et al., 2011).

In a research by ABEDIN et al. (2002a) rice plants were irrigated with As-contaminated water and two phosphate doses were applied to observe the effect of $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 3 - }$ on As uptake and toxicity. The As content of rice parts (root, straw, husk and grain) as well as the agronomic parameters of the plants were not significantly affected by the $\mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 3 - }$ application in flooded (anaerobic) conditions (ABEDIN et al., 2002a).

Several studies showed that the As concentration of the soil solution increases with the application of higher doses of phosphorus fertilizer. The additional phosphate reduces the adsorption capacities of As(V) because of the competition between the two elements (LEE et al., 2016; LIU et al., 2004; ZENG et al., 2012). However, in different soils, the influence of P application on As(V) adsorption may vary (SIGNES-PASTOR et al., 2007). In that study, As solubility increased upon As(V) reduction and Fe was mobilized too. Under highly oxidative conditions, As and Fe solubilities were low and mainly associated with adsorption or coprecipitation onto amorphous Fe oxides. Under aerobic and moderately anaerobic conditions, almost all of the total As was As(V). In contrast, in anaerobic soil solution, the As(V) content was low.

Beside the redox potential, pH also played an important role in controlling the effects of the addition of P-fertilizers on As chemistry (SIGNES-PASTOR et al., 2007).

PIGNA et al. (2009) reported lower As toxicity in wheat according to Pi applications (PIGNA et al., 2009). In LU et al. (2010) study the higher P/As molar ratio in rice shoot resulted in lower As concentration of rice grain (LU et al., 2010). Additionally, the mobility of As can be reduced by co-application of Ca and Pi, as Ca-P-As complex is formed (NEUPANE & DONAHOE, 2013).


## Role of silicon


Silicon (Si) is the second most abundant element in soil. Although Si is not considered an essential element for higher plants, it has a beneficial effect on overcoming stresses (W. CHEN et al., 2011).

It has been reported that Si alleviates the stress caused by salinity, drought, high temperature, and exposure to heavy metals by amplifying the antioxidant enzyme activity, helping to bind heavy metal sequestration in the vacuoles and co-precipitating or chelating with heavy metalloids (W. CHEN et al., 2011; LIMMER et al., 2018; Ma, 2004).

Since As(III) is chemically analogous to Si, it enters rice roots via silicon transporters. These transporters were identified as Nodulin26-like Intrinsic Proteins (NIPs) subfamily of plant aquaporins. OsNIP2;1 (Lsi1) in rice plants have been localized to the plasma membrane, and its main function is silicic acid transport in rice roots (MA et al., 2006). It has been studied that in addition the As(III), methylated As species, i.e., monomethylarsinic acid (MMA) and dimethylarsinic acid (DMA) were also taken up by rice roots via silicon transporter Lsi1 (LI et al. 2009b). While Lsi1 is responsible for As(III) influx to the rice root cells, another transporter, Lsi2 mediates As(III) efflux toward the xylem. Moreover, As(III) transport to the xylem and accumulation in the shoots was inhibited in wild-type rice by addition of Si fertilizer to the nutrient solution (MA et al., 2008). In a greenhouse experiment of LI et al. (2009a) the applied Si fertilizer decreased the total As concentration of rice straw, husk and grain in flooded conditions by 78, 50 and $16 \%$ , respectively. Si treatment also affected As speciation decreasing the content of iAs forms, but increasing the DMA in rice grain. This efficiency of silicic acid/arsenite assimilation and mobilization of As(III) under reduced conditions differentiates rice from crops grown under aerobic soil conditions for high grain As loading (ZHAO et al., 2010).


## Role of Sulfur


Sulphur (S) can influence the regulation and mobility of As within plants due to its complexation with As, resulting in the formation of thio-rich compounds such as glutathione (GSH) and phytochelatins (PCs) (ZHAO et al., 2010). These nonprotein thiol complexes play a crucial role in the detoxification of As (TRIPATHI et al., 2007). SONG et al. (2010) investigated the subcellular localization of thiol compounds in the roots of rice plants and after As exposure, the complexes were localized to the vacuoles (SONG et al., 2014). In a research by DUAN et al. (2011) PCs concentration of rice shoots correlated negatively with the As accumulation of rice grains (DUAN et al., 2011). In DIXIT et al. (2016) study enhanced S doses resulted in enhanced As accumulation in root, but reduced the concentration of As in shoots. It means the translocation factor (root/shoot) of As was decreased by increasing S supplementation indicating less As translocation from root to shoot in $5 \mathrm { m M }$ than $0 . 5 \mathrm { \ m M \ S }$ treatment. In addition, higher S level can relieve the As-caused oxidative stress by decreasing $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ accumulation in both root and shoot. The activities of arsenate reductase (AS) and ascorbate oxidase (AAO) enzymes were enhanced by the addition of more S. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity increased in roots with elevated S levels, but decreased in shoots at the same level of As treatment, as did APX activity. Relative expression of As transporter Lsi1 was upregulated and Lsi2 was downregulated with increasing As content and the S treatments decreased both of Lsi1 and Lsi2 gene expression compared to the $0 \mathrm { { S } }$ application (DIXIT et al., 2016). Another effect is the application of S increased concentrations of extractable $\mathrm { F e / M n }$ in iron plaque formation without As addition. In As treatments the addition of $\mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ reduced the concentration of As in dithionite-citrate-bicarbonate (DCB) extracts (HU et al., 2007).

## 2.1. Uptake and Transport of Inorganic Arsenic Species


The uptake of inorganic species of arsenic by rice roots occurs by two mechanisms. The transport of $\mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ from soil solution to aerial parts of the plants occurs through high affinity phosphate transporter (PT) [37,38]. The phosphate transporter gene family of rice includes 13 OsPT genes encoding the transporters range from OsPT1to OsPT13 [39]. Among them, the roles of OsPT1 and OSPT8 in arsenic transport have been investigated in details by Kamiya et al. [40] and Wang et al. [41], respectively. OsPT1 mediates arsenate transport from root to shoot [40]. Whereas, OsPT8 is a key transporter protein for arsenate uptake into rice roots, and a profound toxic effect on root elongation was exerted after arsenate uptake mediated by OsPT8 [41]. In addition, overexpression of OsPT8 resulted in an enhanced arsenic accumulation in plants [41]. The second route by which ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ is taken-up by root cell is aquaporin channels [32,42]. In root cells of rice, ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ enters through Lsi1, a nodulin 26 like intrinsic protein (OsNIP2;1), a major influx transporter for silicic acid [43,44], while another protein Lsi 2, a silicon efflux transporter mediate ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ efflux to the xylem in rice plant [45]. In the rice cultivars Oochikara, T-65, and Koshihikari ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ is transported in the form of arsenous acid $\mathrm { A s ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ through Lsi1 and Lsi2 transporters [42,46]. In the rice mutant for Lsi2, a significantly decreased rate of ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ transport to xylem and accumulation in shoots and grain were found [42]. After ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ is taken up by the root cells, some of it is instantly released into the rhizosphere by the bidirectional function of Lsi1protein channel [47]. Inside plant tissues, $\mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ is reduced to ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ ; ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ is sequestered into root vacuoles or is translocated to the shoots and it is disseminated to various organs [46,47]. Rice is unable to methylate inorganic arsenic species, thus methylated species of arsenic most likely come from the rhizosphere via microbial methylation [48].


## 2.2. Uptake and Transport of Organic Arsenic Species


Arsenite is the predominant species in the submerged soil and microbial transformation of inorganic species to organic form produces considerable quantities of methylated arsenic species dimethylarsinic acid (DMA) and smaller amounts of monomethylarsonic acid (MMA) in the paddy soil [11]. This transformation to organic form is beneficial because methylated arsenic species are less toxic than the pentavalent arsenic species. The uptake mechanisms of methylated species are less extensively studied than inorganic arsenic species. MMA and DMA are taken up through the nodulin 26-like intrinsic protein. Inorganic arsenic species $( \mathsf { A } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ and $\mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } } .$ ) are more efficiently taken up by roots than methylated arsenic species (DMA and MMA), but the translocation rate in plant shoot of inorganic arsenic species is much lower than methylated arsenic species [49]. The reduced complex formation of methylated arsenic-species with the ligands (glutathione/phytochelatin) may be the reason for the better translocation of methylated-arsenic species [49]. ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ was found to be the most abundant species in the rice grain, followed by DMA with low concentrations of $\mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ , MMA, and other two unidentified arsenic species, as suggested by analysis of 121 samples of 12 rice types [50]. On the other hand, in rice straw, $\mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ is a predominant species followed by ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ and DMA [15].


## 2.3. Accumulation of Arsenic in Rice Grain


Rice is one of the most efficient transporters of Si among all crop plants and inadvertently passes arsenite through silicic acid transporter [51]. This factor contributes to higher concentrations of arsenic in rice grain, greater than the recommended safe limit [12,52,53].

However, Yamaji and Ma [54] observed that transportation of arsenic in rice through Lsi1 and Lsi2 are restricted in the root, and xylem loading of arsenic mainly contributes to the accumulation in vegetative parts but not in the grains. More than $9 0 \%$ of ${ \mathsf { A } } s ^ { \mathrm { I I I } }$ uploading into the grain is contributed from phloem transport [55].

Reduction of arsenate may be the first step of arsenic detoxification in rice plants. Researchers have identified different arsenate reductases in rice, like, OsHAC1;1, OsHAC1;2, [56], and OsHAC4 [57], which regulate the conversion of arsenate to arsenite. These genes are expressed mainly in the roots, and catalyse the reaction in the outer cell layer of root, thereby, facilitating arsenite efflux from the root to soil. OsHAC1;1 is abundant in epidermis, root hair, and pericycle, while OsHAC1;2 being predominant in epidermis, outer cortex layer, and endodermis [56]. OsHAC4 is localized mainly in root elongation and mutation zone in epidermis and exodermis [57]. Overexpression of OsHAC1;1 and OsHAC1;2 significantly increased arsenite efflux into external medium and decreased arsenic accumulation in rice [56]. On the other hand, mutation of OsHAC1;1, OsHAC1;2, and OsHAC4 led to decrease arsenate reduction in root, lessen arsenite efflux, and increase arsenic accumulation in root and grain [56,57].

Besides arsenate reduction, phytochelatin-arsenite complexation and subsequent sequestration into the vacuoles constitute another important pathway of arsenic detoxification in plants [58]. Being the precursor compound of phytochelatin (PC) synthesis, glutathione (GSH) plays a crucial role in arsenic tolerance. GSH is synthesized by ATP dependent reaction from Gly and G-glutamylcysteine (G-EC). The intermediate G-ECs are synthesized within plastid and are exported from plastid to cytosol by CRT like transporter protein (CLT) in plants [59]. Similar transporter OsCLT1 in rice plays a role in GSH homeostasis by mediating transport of $\mathrm { \Delta V }$ -EC and GSH form plastid to cytoplasm. Under arsenic treatment OsCLT1 mutant rice plants exhibit lower concentration of PC content when compared to wild type plants, resulting in lower arsenic accumulation in roots but higher arsenic accumulation in shoots [60].

The presence of a tonoplast transporter in phloem companion cells (OsABCC1) increase the arsenic sequestration in vacuoles, which help in reduced arsenic translocation into rice grains [58]. However, methylated arsenic species, especially DMA is mobilized at a higher rate than inorganic species [55,61] and its redemption in aleurone, endosperm, and embryo may reduce the seed setting rate and induce spikelet sterility and a reduced yield [62]. Arsenic accumulation in rice grain varies according to the genotype of the plant [51]. The genotypes TD71 and Yinjingruanzhan contain less inorganic arsenic in their grains than genotypes IAPAR9 and Nanyangzhan [63]. More than 1700 rice varieties are investigated around the world for their differences in arsenic accumulation, and about 20 fold variations was found among various strains of rice [64]. Arsenic concentration in rice grains vary to 6 and 7 folds in different countries, while this concentration varies up to 40-folds in rice varieties within same country. The findings help in hypothesizing that both the genotypes and environmental factors play very important roles to control arsenic accumulation in rice grains [65]. The major factors that influence the arsenic accumulation in rice grain include the type of the rice cultivar, plant physiology, the place where the plant was cultivated, and the method of processing of rice [10]. It was found that concentration of arsenic in brown rice was higher than white rice [10].

In the present study, rice showed the highest As accumulation in shoots among the three cereal species tested, regardless whether the plants were supplied with arsenate or arsenite (Fig. 2b). Arsenic accumulation in plant shoots is determined by both root uptake and root-to-shoot translocation; both processes differed significantly between the three species and between the two forms of As supplied to the plants (Figs. 2, 3).

Arsenic uptake per unit root weight was the highest in rice supplied with arsenite, which was approximately double of the uptake by barley and wheat in the arsenite treatment (Fig. 2c). This result supports our hypothesis that rice is more efficient in the uptake of arsenite than wheat or barley, and is in accordance with the fact that rice is a strong accumulator of Si and that arsenite is taken up mainly through the Si transporters in rice (Ma et al. 2008). Based on a metaanalysis of the data reported in the literature, Hodson et al. (2005) showed that the mean relative concentration of Si in the rice shoots is approximately double of that in wheat and barley. In both rice and barley, the aquaporin Lsi1 (NIP2;1) is responsible for the influx of Si (as silicic acid) into the root cells (Chiba et al. 2009; Ma et al. 2006). The rice Lsi1 is permeable to arsenite (as arsenous acid) (Ma et al. 2008). Although the permeability of the barley Lsi1 to arsenite has not been tested yet, this protein has exactly the same NPA (Asn-Pro-Ala) motif and the amino acid composition in the aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity filter as the rice Lsi1; these are the two key structural features that govern the substrate specificity in aquaporins (Maurel et al. 2008). Therefore, it is highly likely that the barley Lsi1 can also mediate the influx of arsenite. No information is yet available on the influx transporters for Si in wheat. Variation in Si uptake among rice or barley cultivars was found to correlate with the expression level of Lsi1 in roots (Chiba et al. 2009; Ma et al. 2007b). Differences in expression of Lsi1 may also partly explain the difference in arsenite uptake among rice, wheat and barley observed in the present study. It is also important to recognise that As is greatly mobilised as arsenite under the anaerobic conditions in submerged paddy soil (Li et al. 2009; Marin et al. 1993; Xu et al. 2008); this, coupled with the high arsenite uptake ability, leads to excessive As accumulation in rice.

In the case of arsenate treatment, the difference in uptake among the three plant species was smaller, with rice and wheat being about $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ higher than barley (Fig. 2c). This result is also in agreement with our initial hypothesis. It is well established that arsenate is taken up by the phosphate transporters (reviewed by Zhao et al. 2009). Therefore, the variation in arsenate uptake is possibly related to the expression level of phosphate transporters in roots and/or the relative affinity of the transporters to arsenate. In our experiment, phosphate was present in the nutrient solution $( 0 . 1 ~ \mathrm { \ m M } )$ , which would compete with arsenate uptake.

Except for As hyperaccumulators, plants generally have a low efficiency of As translocation from roots to shoots, possibly due to the complexation of arsenite by thiol compounds and subsequently sequestration in the root vacuoles (Zhao et al. 2009), or to the strong efflux of arsenite to the external medium (see below). After one-day exposure to arsenate or arsenite, only $3 . 6 { - } 2 0 . 3 \%$ of the As taken up by plants was distributed to shoots. Rice had a higher efficiency of As translocation from roots to shoots than wheat and barley (Fig. 3). The difference among plant species in the efficiency of As translocation was maintained in both arsenate and arsenite treatments, although the efficiency was higher with the latter. This difference may also be related to the Si pathway. Following influx of Si into root cells mediated by Lsi1, Si is effluxed into the apoplast towards the stele for xylem loading. This efflux is mediated by the carrier protein Lsi2 in rice, which is localised in the proximal side of the plasma membranes of both exodermis and endodermis cells (Ma et al. 2007a). Mutation in Lsi2 resulted in a marked reduction of both arsenite concentration in the xylem sap and of As accumulation in rice shoots, indicating that Lsi2 is also able to mediate arsenite efflux (Ma et al. 2008). Lsi2 is highly expressed in rice roots, thus explaining the efficient translocation of both Si and arsenite in this plant species. Lsi2 homologues in wheat and barley have not been characterised yet.

Both arsenite and arsenate were present in the xylem sap, but their relative proportions depended on plant species and the form of As supplied (Fig. 4). In rice, arsenite was found to be the predominant form of As transported in the xylem sap in both the arsenite and arsenate treatments (Fig. 4). This means that arsenate was mostly reduced in roots prior to efflux and xylem loading. In wheat and barley, most of the As in the xylem sap from the arsenite-treated plants was also arsenite. However, in the arsenate treatment, arsenate accounted for higher proportions of the As in the xylem sap of wheat $( 5 5 \% )$ and barley $( 3 7 \% )$ than of rice $( 1 6 \% )$ . Therefore, the phosphate transport pathway may play a more important role in As translocation in wheat and barley than in rice. Our initial hypothesis predicts similar translocation efficiency among the three plant species in the arsenate treatment. This aspect of the hypothesis is not supported by the experimental results, because rice still showed greater translocation efficiency than wheat and barley in the arsenate treatment, similar to the pattern observed in the arsenite treatment. This discrepancy can be explained by the fact that arsenite is also the main form of As translocated in rice fed with arsenate, and rice is inherently more efficient than wheat and barley in arsenite translocation as a result of its strong pathway for Si accumulation.

In agreement with previous studies with tomato, rice, Holcus lanatus and the duckweed Wolffia globosa (Logoteta et al. 2009; Xu et al. 2007; Zhang et al. 2009), substantial amounts of arsenate added to the nutrient solution were reduced to arsenite after 24- h exposure, especially in wheat (Fig. 1). Xu et al. (2007) showed that this conversion was mediated mainly by plant roots rather than by microbes or root exudates. The evidence available to date indicates that arsenate is taken up into root cells via the phosphate transporters, reduced to arsenite by arsenate reductase (s) and then effluxed to the external medium (Zhao et al. 2009). Assuming that the decrease in the solution arsenate concentration and the increase in the solution arsenite concentration represent arsenate uptake and arsenite efflux, respectively, when normalised on root weight, arsenite efflux accounted for a major proportion of the arsenate uptake by the three plant species within the 24-h exposure period $6 3 \%$ , $74 \%$ and $8 6 \%$ in rice, barley and wheat, respectively). Arsenate uptake was the highest in wheat, although it also had the highest arsenite efflux among the three plant species tested. It is possible that arsenite efflux towards the external medium is a basal mechanism of As detoxification in plants (Logoteta et al. 2009; Zhao et al. 2009), as has been demonstrated in microorganisms (Bhattacharjee and Rosen 2007), and that the efflux would result in less translocation of arsenite to shoots. Arsenite effluxed from roots may be re-absorbed, but the extent of the reabsorption would depend on the concentration gradient of arsenite between the root cytosol and the external medium. In the arsenite treatment, a small proportion of arsenite in the medium was oxidised to arsenate. These results emphasise the need to monitor As speciation in the experimental medium even in relatively short-term experiments, as transformation of As species can occur rapidly.

In conclusion, the present study has shown that rice is more efficient in both the uptake of arsenite and the translocation of arsenite from roots to shoots than wheat and barley. This enhanced ability of uptake and translocation, coupled with arsenite mobilisation in submerged paddy soil, is an important reason why rice accumulates excessive levels of As in straw and grain, thus posing a significant health risk to animals and humans (Abedin et al. 2002a; Meharg et al. 2009; Zhu et al. 2008b).

Human activities, such as wood preservatives (chromate copper arsenate [CCA] chemicals), extraction of arsenopyrite, pesticides, insecticides, weed controllers, disposal of wastewater and industrial materials, paint products and natural climate changes have made arsenic (As) an important factor in polluting the environment [1, 2]. As can be present in different oxides (i.e., AsIII and AsV) and is a carcinogen that poses a serious risk to food security [3, 4]. Rice grown under high As concentrations was found to absorb As with varied capacities in endosperm, bran and husk [5].

Arsenic dramatically reduces the fresh weight of plant roots [6] and photosynthesis [7], and allows plants to accumulate reactive oxygen species in excess [8]. As accumulation at nodes is much higher than in internodes and blades, which can be used as an important storage site for As transportation [9]. In Arabidopsis, inositol transporters, phosphate transporters, arsenate reductase CRT-like transporters, and ACR3 transporters mediate As absorption, transport, and metabolism. In rice, aquaporins (AsIII transport), glutaredoxin, phytochelatin synthase, NRAMP transporter, ACR3 transporter, and inositol transporters (As transport), CRT-like transporters mediate As absorption, transportation, and metabolism [10]. Arsenic (III) and As (V) are absorbed by rice roots through aquaporin (AQP) and phosphate transporter (Pht) respectively. Sodium arsenite $( \mathrm { N a A s O _ { 2 } } )$ is more toxic than arsenate. As (V) groups can replace phosphate groups to interfere with phosphates; arsenite binds to thiol groups and affects the structure of coenzyme factors and proteins, inhibiting their catalytic function [11]. High-As contaminated agricultural soils are associated with decreased rice yields, while soil inversion techniques have the potential to enhance rice yields [12].

Arsenic (III) can trigger plant defense mechanisms by being sequestered in vacuoles and by arsenic methylation and volatilization facilitated by ArsM expression, which helps lower the amount of As accumulation in rice grains [13–15]. Plants have many transporters that control the accumulation of arsenic, including plasma membrane transporters OsPT1, OsPT4, and OsPT8 ; vacuole transporter AtABCC1; synthase GSH1; arsenate reductase OsHAC1; transcription factor OsPHR2; and small RNA miRNA528 [16–23]. In rice, expression of vacuole-chelated As genes ScYCF1 and OsABCC1 reduced As accumulation in brown rice by $7 0 \%$ [24]. Overexpression of OsHAC4 can improve the tolerance of As in rice [25]. As (V) is more easily absorbed by soil components than As (III), but As (III) is more toxic. Microorganisms, algae, and fungi offer the potential for mitigating As contamination in plants [26–28]. Mineral elements, such as iron and silica, can compete for arsenic binding sites, influencing adsorption and uptake [29–31]. As-resistant plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria have also been explored for reducing the crop As toxicity [32]. However, microbial remediation has limitations, and its effectiveness may vary depending on environmental conditions, and scalability for large-scale agriculture poses challenges. Mineral competition with As is context-dependent, making results inconsistent across soil types and arsenic levels. Furthermore, using As-resistant rhizobacteria requires optimization and may have specificity and long-term sustainability limitations. Although these strategies hold promise for alleviating heavy metal stress in plants, there is a need for ongoing refinement to address the complexities of As contamination effectively to improve agricultural productivity.

Studies have revealed that nitric oxide (NO) can alleviate As toxicity in rice roots and aerial parts [33]. Hydrogen sulfide $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 2 } S )$ signaling and NO co-studies have demonstrated that they independently mitigate arsenic toxicity at the seedling stage of rice [34]. NO plays a mitigating role in various abiotic stresses and pathogen infestations, such as salt stress, drought, and metal stress [35–37]. NO alleviates As-induced oxidative stress by activating multiple enzymes in metabolic processes [38]. However, different rice varieties do not consistently adapt to the environment; tetraploid rice demonstrated stronger cadmium stress resistance than diploid rice [39]. According to previous studies on As toxicity, selecting rice varieties resistant to As toxicity or absorbing less arsenic is a good strategy. Therefore, this experiment tried to use tetraploid rice as a material to study the alleviation of As toxicity and the foliar application of NO on As toxicity.

Studies have indicated that wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) faces a higher risk of As contamination than rice at equivalent concentrations [40]. The benefits of tetraploid rice are primarily evident in its robust growth, strong stress resistance, large grain size, substantial biomass, and high nutrient content [41–44]. Tetraploid exhibited greater tolerance to cadmium by augmenting antioxidant enzyme activity to preserve normal cell shape compared to diploid [45]. Tetraploid rice exhibited reduced arsenic absorption and oxidative damages under similar growing circumstances compared to diploid line [46]. Chromosome doubling induces methylation variations, influencing gene expression and aiding novel tetraploids in adapting to dose effects [47]. DNA hypomethylation in tetraploid rice enhances the expression of salt-tolerant genes [48]. While numerous studies have explored As accumulation in plants and its influence on various physiological processes, more attention should be directed toward understanding the unique responses of different rice cultivars, particularly focusing on tetraploid rice in the context of As toxicity. Furthermore, despite previous research scrutinizing the capacity of NO to mitigate As toxicity in rice, a gap remains, necessitating more comprehensive investigations into the multifaceted effects of NO in this context.

The present study explored the potential of tetraploid rice as a more resilient crop in As-contaminated environments and assessed the impact of NO application on mitigating arsenic toxicity across different rice lines. This study offered a new perspective on As stress mitigation in rice, specifically concentrating on tetraploid rice and the potential role of NO. The primary objective was to evaluate and compare how diploid and tetraploid rice responded to arsenic stress. Crucially, the study delved into As absorption, transportation, and metabolism in rice, focusing on potential differences between diploid and tetraploid lines. The research also examined gene expression patterns associated with arsenic accumulation and detoxification, emphasizing variations between rice types. Tetraploid rice was hypothesized to demonstrate enhanced resilience to As contamination compared to diploid rice and shed light on the unique attributes of tetraploid rice in As-contaminated environments, making it a promising candidate for As-affected agricultural regions. Nonetheless, the limited study of tetraploid rice’s response to arsenic toxicity underscores the need for further research to refine appropriate strategies for mitigating heavy metal stress in plants.

Arsenic (As) contamination in soils and water has become a serious environmental problem, especially in South and Southeast Asia [1, 2]. Mining and industrial activities are the main sources of As contamination to the environments [3–5]. The As content in rice grains produced from contaminated sites in China, India and Korea can be as high as $0 . 7 7 { - } 0 . 8 5$ $\mathrm { m g / k g }$ [6, 7]. In paddy soil, arsenite (As(III), $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { A s O } _ { 3 } )$ is the predominant species of As that is taken up by rice [8–10]. Understanding the regulations and key period of $\operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ uptake and transport by rice is important to developing control strategies for safe rice production in As-contaminated soils.

To date, genes that have been identified to be associated with As(III) uptake and transport in rice plants are the same as those for silicon (Si) uptake and transport because arsenite is a chemical analogue of silicic acid. In rice roots, As(III) is inadvertently taken up and transported via the silicic acid transporters OsLsi1 and OsLsi2 [8, 11, 12]. OsLsi1 is preferentially distributed on the distal side of Casparian bands, passively transporting As(III) into root cells; OsLsi2, localized on the proximal side of Casparian bands, actively transports As(III) from root cells to apoplast toward xylem [8, 13, 14]. Once transported into the root cells, As(III) can be either complexed with phytochelatins (PCs) and then sequestered in vacuoles for detoxification [15, 16] or transported to stems and leaves by transpirational flow through the xylem vessels of rice [17]. OsABCC1, a Ctype ABC (ATP-binding cassette) transporter localized in the tonoplast, is responsible for As vacuolar compartmentalization [16]. OsABCC1 can be expressed in roots, stems, leaves and husks of rice, and sequestering As in vacuoles is important in reducing the allocation of As to rice grains [16].

Nodes in graminaceous plants control the distribution of mineral elements in different tissues of shoots, including essential and toxic elements [18, 19]. In the nodes of rice, three transporters (i.e., OsLsi6, OsLsi2, and OsLsi3) are involved in the intervascular transport of As(III) from nodes to panicles [20–22]. OsLsi6, a plasma membrane-localized Si/As(III) channel, is mainly expressed at the xylem transfer cells of enlarged vascular bundles (EVBs) [23]. OsLsi2 and OsLsi3 are localized at the distal side of the bundle sheath of EVBs and parenchyma cells between EVBs and diffuse vascular bundles (DVBs), respectively [22]. As(III) in the xylem of EVBs can be selectively unloaded by OsLsi6 and then reloaded to the xylem of DVBs by OsLsi2 and OsLsi3, leading to preferential As distribution to panicles through xylem vessels [22, 23]. In addition, OsLsi6 can be found in leaves and nodes and is responsible for As(III) transport out of xylem into the tissues of leaf and node [8].

A number of studies have explored As(III) uptake and transport in rice plants [19, 22, 24], the majority of which mainly focused on the seedling or maturing stage of rice growth [25–27]. For example, many experiments implemented to identify the As(III) transporters in rice (e.g., OsLsi1 and OsLsi2) were performed during the seedling stage [25–27]. Arsenic is mainly transported into caryopsis during the grain filling stage [28], which is considered to be the key stage to take measures to reduce As uptake in rice [29]. However, As(III) can be taken up by rice during the whole growth period, and As(III) transport in different organs and/or tissues of rice is mediated by various transporters, as mentioned above. The expression of genes for these transporters is important to regulating As accumulation in grains. However, gaps in our understanding remain with regard to the dynamics in gene expression of As(III) uptake and transport during the whole growth period. Thus, the aim of the present study was to investigate the dynamics of gene expression of As(III)-related transporters as well as the characteristics of As(III) uptake and accumulation in different organs of rice during the whole growth period. The results obtained can provide a better understanding of the As(III) uptake and transport regulated by gene expression in different parts of rice, which would be useful to guide As mitigation strategies in As-contaminated paddy soil.

Arsenic (As) contamination in rice presents a daunting global challenge, particularly in regions like South and Southeast Asia, where rice is a dietary staple (Chowdhury et al. 2024). This problem stems from the high natural presence of As in the earth’s crust, with subsequent release and uptake by rice plants. Prolonged exposure to As via rice-based diets imposes severe health risks on potentially, 200 million people worldwide, encompassing conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, developmental issues, and compromised immune function (Bjørklund et al. 2020). Ensuring the safety of rice from As contamination is paramount owing to its role as staple food for a substantial segment of the global populace. Despite extensive research endeavors aimed at understanding the mechanisms underlying As uptake by rice and associated health impacts and its mitigation, gaps persist at tail end of research eforts. Studies have shown signifcant genetic variation among rice genotypes in sequestering As into grains. While certain cultivars like Shatabdi, Gobindbhog (Khanam et al. 2021) and Kalijira (Paulelli et al. 2019) exhibit reduced As accumulation in grain, others such as Rajalaxmi, IR 64 and BRRI dhan 47 tend to accumulate higher levels (Khanam et  al. 2021; Islam et  al. 2016), albeit having other economically desirable traits.

Rice roots absorb both As(III) and As(V) species through diferent uptake pathways. Arsenic(III), a chemical analog of silicic acid, is absorbed and translocated through the silicate uptake transporters via OsLSi1 and OsLSi2, respectively. OsLSi1 transporter is predominantly located on the distal side of casparian bands, where it passively transports As(III) into root cells. Conversely, OsLSi2 is situated on the proximal side of casparian bands, actively facilitating the transport of As(III) from root cells into the apoplast toward the xylem (Pan et al. 2019). Whereas, As(V) is an analog of phosphates (P), and P transport pathways have been identifed for As(V) uptake in rice plants. The transporters OsPT1 and OsPT8 are involved in the absorption of As(V) from the soil into the roots, while OsPT2 transporters are primarily responsible for transferring As(V) from the roots to the aboveground parts of the plant (Geng et al. 2024). Additionally, As detoxifcation in rice involves the complexation of As with phytochelatins (PCs) and subsequent sequestration in vacuoles via ABC transporters, notably OsABCC1 (Song et al. 2014; Ma et al. 2008).

The synthesis of PCs is further regulated by S supply to the plant from soil and water system. Biochar application can enhance soil organic carbon and increase microbial activity, promoting the solubilisation of native S into sulphate $\mathrm { ( S O _ { 4 } ) }$ . However, the functions of these genes in regulating As accumulation in rice plants under different water management regimes are poorly understood. Improving water footprint of rice is a global research priority. Water management has a signifcant impact on redox potential, $\mathrm { p H }$ , available iron (Fe), Si, P, S, microbial activity in paddy soils, and the formation of Fe-plaque on rice roots, infuencing As bio-availability in soil to rice plants (Fang et al. 2023). The question arises whether the movement of As from soil to root, root to shoot, and ultimately to the grain can be regulated by manipulating the related transporters through modifcations in the soil and water system in the rhizosphere.

Of late, use of biochar has been recommended for cultivation of rice for improving its carbon footprints and some other benefts including availability of nutrients (Munda et al. 2018) Further, addition of biochar in soil resulted in a substantial reduction in carbon foot print by $4 9 \%$ during the spring season and $3 8 \%$ during the summer season paddy, compared to conventional residue practices (Mohammadi et al. 2016).

Despite extensive research on As contamination in rice, signifcant gaps remain in understanding the mechanistic efects of biochar application on As uptake under diferent water management regimes. Preliminary reports on the use of biochar to reduce As loading in rice grains are contradictory. Some studies observed a signifcant reduction in grain As by $2 5 \%$ (Wu et al. 2022), while others reported an increase of $2 0 { - } 2 5 \%$ (Mandal et al. 2024). The alkaline properties of biochar increased solution $\mathrm { p H }$ , leading to decreased As solubility (Chatzimichailidou et al. 2023). Additionally, biochar enhanced root triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) reductive intensity, reduced root $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentration, and promoted Fe-plaque formation, which in turn increased the accumulation of As onto the root surface. The rice biomass also increased by $2 8 \%$ with biochar addition, suggesting that rice plants became more tolerant to As toxicity (Xu et al. 2022). Contrastingly, researchers (Mandal et al. 2024) reported that the availability of As in contaminated soils increased with higher doses of rice straw and bean stalk biochar amendments, likely due to competition between phosphate released from biochars and $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ on the surface of soil solid phases.

Comprehensive research on the efects of diferent biochar application rates under varying water regimes is currently lacking. This research aims to investigate whether a specifc biochar dosage, combined with a suitable water management regime, can efectively alter the soil environment. This alteration may result in changes in balance between Si/As, P/As, S, and Fe concentrations impacting the competition among As, Si and P for uptake. Furthermore, it could infuence the expression of relevant transporters (such as OsLSi1, OsLSi2, OsPT1, OsPT2, OsABCC1, OsNIP 3;3, and $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ , afect the synthesis and sequestration of As-phosphate complexes, and infuence Fe-plaque formation. Ultimately, this could lead to changes in As uptake and transport to the rice grains. The primary focus of this investigation is to addresses the gap in understanding how biochar, combined with water management, afects As uptake in diferent rice cultivars. Previous research shows conficting results on biochar’s impact on As levels, lacking mechanistic insights. This study uniquely explores the interaction between biochar dosage and water regimes, focusing on their efects on As dynamics in soil, nutrient competition, and key transporter gene expressions.

Due to the accumulation and toxicity of arsenic (As) in irrigated areas, As contamination as an environmental problem is a serious concern to sustainable crop production. In Asian countries such as Bangladesh, India, and Iran, increased As contamination of soil through natural and anthropogenic resources has caused great concern that threatens human health by entering the food chain (Zhao et al. 2010). The two predominant inorganic forms of As are arsenite $( \mathbf { A } \mathbf { s } ^ { \mathrm { I I I } } )$ and arsenate $( \mathrm { A s } ^ { \mathrm { V } } )$ forms that exist in the environment. Due to the structural similarity of arsenate with phosphate, most arsenate in plants is transported through phosphate transporters (high-afnity). Due to the anaerobic conditions of the paddy feld, the predominant form of As is arsenite. Further, most of the As absorbed by the plant roots is reduced and stored as arsenite (Kumar et al. 2015). Two major arsenite transporters were identifed in rice plants; Lsi1 and Lsi2. Lsi1 and Lsi2 are localized on the distal and proximal sides of both exodermis and endodermis cells, respectively. Lsi1 mediates the infux of arsenite; while Lsi2 transports arsenite to the aerial parts of the rice plant (Ma et al. 2008). Arsenite inhibits the function of enzymes and proteins through thiol interactions; while arsenate disrupts energy fow through phosphate replacement (Ma et al. 2008). Two mechanisms accomplish iron (Fe) uptake in plants: Strategies I and II, specifc to non-graminaceous and graminaceous plants, respectively (Römheld and Marschner 1986). Rice, as a plant of the Gramineae family, uptakes Fe by the YSL transporters by secreting mugineic acid (MA) in the root and forming an $\mathrm { { M A { - } F e ^ { 3 + } } }$ complex (Kobayashi and Nishizawa, 2012). Other Fe transporters that absorb Fe through strategy II ${ \mathrm { F e } } ^ { 3 + }$ -chelate) include OsNRAMP5, OsYSL2, and OsFRDL1. However, the rice plant can absorb $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ directly by the root due to its unique transporter OsIRT1 (Ishimaru et al. 2006). OsNRAMP5 transporters, along with the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ , also transport Cd (cadmium) and Mn ions in the rice plant (Ishimaru et al. 2012). Arsenite $( \mathbf { A } \mathbf { s } ^ { \mathrm { I I I } } )$ is one of the most phytotoxic forms of As ion which inactivates proteins and enzymes by binding to their sulfhydryl groups. As also produces a variety of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and induces oxidative stress in plants (Dave et al. 2013), which damages the function and structure of macromolecules such as proteins, DNA and lipids (Petrov et al. 2015). Plants also have a defense system, including enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidants, to counteract the efects of ROS. However, the antioxidant system of the plant may not play a sufcient role in reducing the effects of heavy metal-induced oxidative stress under severe toxicity. In recent years, much research has been done to increase plant tolerance to heavy metal toxicity using exogenous plant growth regulators (Li et al. 2014; Ali et al. 2015).

Methyl jasmonate (MJ) is one of the most important phytohormones that plays a key role in plant responses to stressful conditions. Several reports have shown that endogenous level of MJ increases significantly under adverse conditions such as pathogen infection, wounding, heavy metals and ozone stress (Piotrowska et al. 2009; Farooq et al. 2016; Kanna et al. 2003). Several studies have reported that MJ in various plant species plays an important role in reducing the efects of heavy metals (Keramat et al. 2010; Yan et al. 2013). However, studies on the understanding of the response mechanism induced by MJ under As toxicity, especially at the transcriptional level of As transporters, are insufcient.

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the staple food for more than half of the world’s population (more than 3 billion people), which provides about $2 0 \%$ of protein and $2 7 \%$ of the dietary energy of developing countries. For a long time, rice is cultivated in an area of nearly 600,000 hectares mainly in the two provinces of Mazandaran and Guilan in northern Iran. The Tarom hashemi and Fajr varieties are the most popular native and aromatic varieties in Mazandaran province (Ghorbani et al. 2009). Therefore, given the importance of both T. hashemi and Fajr varieties and increased As contamination in the paddy felds of northern Iran, in this study, the efects of diferent concentrations of MJ on morphological, physiological and, molecular traits, as well as the yield of two varieties of rice under varying levels of As were investigated hydroponically. It will also determine which variety is more tolerant to arsenic toxicity.

Arsenic (As) is one of the most toxic metalloid that can enter the food chain through ingestion of As contaminated water or food, posing a serious threat to human health. Among cereals, rice could contain the highest amount of As because of the special growing conditions. Therefore, the importance of the reduction of As concentration in rice is essential. Many studies have been conducted to understand the mechanism of arsenic uptake, accumulation and translocation. The interactions between As and plants are influenced by soil type and other factors such as $p H ,$ mineral contents and redox status of the soil, As speciation, and microbial activity. Different nutrients including phosphates, iron, silicon and sulfur effectively regulate the uptake and accumulation of As in different parts of plants. Genetic variation has also effect on As accumulation of rice grain. Water management practices can help to decrease As content of rice plants due to changing the redox status of the soil. Phosphate and silicon transporters can be used by As to enter the rice root cells, therefore detoxification mechanisms of As in rice greatly depend on the activity of these transporters. In this review, we covered the main factors that affect the uptake, accumulation, and translocation of As in different plant organs in rice. We investigated the different soil factors and plant cell transporters needed to understand the mechanisms. This study may be useful for further research to develop strategies that inhibit As entry and transport in plant cells and contribute to safe food production.

Keywords: arsenic, varietal variation, water management, mineral nutrients application
