Az arzén (As) az egyik legmérgezőbb félfém, amely a szennyezett vizekkel és élelmiszerekkel bekerülhet az emberi szervezetbe is, és ott súlyos egészségügyi problémákat okozhat. A gabonafélék között a rizs az egyik, amely a legmagasabb koncentrációban tartalmazhat arzént. Ezért az arzéntartalom csökkentése alapvetően fontos a termelés során. Az arzén felvételének, felhalmozásának és a növényen belüli transzportjának a mechanizmusait számos tudományos publikációban vizsgálták. Az arzén felvételét számos tényező befolyásolja, mint a talajtípus, a pH, az ásványi anyagok mennyisége, a talajok redox tulajdonsága, az arzén kémiai formája és a talajok mikrobiológiai aktivitása. A különböző tápanyagok, mint a foszfor, a vas, a szilícium és a kén hatékonyan szabályozzák az arzén felvételét és felhalmozódását a különböző növényi részekben. Emellett a fajták közötti genetikai különbségek is befolyásolják az arzén beépülését a szemekbe. Az agrotechnikai lépések között a megfelelő vízgazdálkodási gyakorlatok segíthetnek az arzénfelvétel csökkentésében a talaj redox tulajdonságainak szabályozása által. A foszfor és szilícium transzporterek segítségével juthat az arzén a rizs gyökérsejtekbe, ezért az arzén detoxifikáció folyamata nagyban függ ezektől a transzporterektől. Ebben az áttekintésben sorra vesszük az arzén felvételében, felhalmozásában és a rizsnövényen belüli transzportjában szerepet játszó főbb tényezőket. Megvizsgáljuk a különböző talajtulajdonságok és a sejttranszporterek szerepét is. Jelen tanulmányunk alapja lehet az arzénfelvétel csökkentését célzó új kutatási programok kidolgozásának és ezáltal hozzájárulhat a biztonságosabb élelmiszerellátáshoz.

Kulcsszavak: arzén, fajtakülönbségek, vízgazdálkodás, ásványi tápanyag alkalmazás

Arsenic contamination is widespread, and exposure occurs through multiple sources, including food, drinking water, and air, posing a serious threat to human and environmental health (Chung et al. 2014). To develop strategies to reduce As ingestion through food, it is crucial to investigate and understand the mechanisms associated with uptake, transport, fate, and metabolism in plants. Earlier studies revealed that AsIII is prevalent under anaerobic conditions common to rice growth in paddy felds and is mostly accumulated and transported radially across root cells via the highly specialized Si transporters, Lsi1 and Lsi2 (Feng Ma et al. 2008; Zhao et al. 2009). However, the fact that Si, a crucial element for rice, is primarily taken up and transported by these same transporters does complicate assessment (Jian et al. 2006). To avoid the possible negative impacts on plant productive that could be associated with altering Si transporters, signifcant eforts have been directed towards discovering alternate As transporters. Recently, we identifed and characterized some rice PIPs and showed their role in metalloid transport, including AsIII and boron (B) (Mosa et al. 2012, 2016; Kumar et al. 2014). Specifcally, the expression of OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OspIP2;7 in Xenopus oocytes, yeast, and Arabidopsis, resulted in bidirectional As and B transport (Mosa et al. 2012, 2016; Kumar et al. 2014). However, the in-planta role of PIPs in As transport in rice and other plants remains unknown. Here we report that OsPIP2;6 is in fact an As transporter and contributes to As translocation from roots to shoots. RNAi knockdown and overexpression approaches were used to characterize the in-planta function of OsPIP2;6 in As transport in rice.

Protein spatiotemporal function is controlled by its structure, localization, and abundance (Feng Ma et al. 2008). The transcript levels and abundance of genes will afect its intracellular functional rate (Rocca et al. 2015). Therefore, we measured the $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ transcript abundance, which showed expression in both roots and shoots, although levels were signifcantly higher in shoot tissue (Fig. 1c), which aligns with Sakurai et al. (2005). The diferential regulation of genes is one of the initial in-planta defense mechanisms against toxic substance exposure (Li et al. 2016). In a previous study, we reported that $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ expression was downregulated in response to AsIII over $^ { 2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ exposure, possibly as a physiological response to inhibit As transport (Mosa et al. 2012).

Mutants are a powerful tool for studying the mechanisms of in-planta physiology and biochemistry as they provide insights into the function of specifc gene(s) (Østergaard and Yanofsky 2004). Transgenic OsPIP2;6 RNAi plants responded to As exposure diferently than WT and accumulated less shoot As. This was also evident in the calculated arsenic TF, which was much lower in RNAi lines compared to WT (Fig. 2); these fndings may also explain why $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ expression was downregulated in response to AsIII. Conversely, no diference in As accumulation was observed in the roots compared with WT (Fig. 2), suggesting that OsPIP2;6 does not signifcantly contribute to AsIII uptake; indeed, this role is fulflled by OsLsi1 (Feng Ma et al. 2008). It appears that the diference in As accumulation between WT and OsPIP2;6 RNAi lines is due to the ability of WT plants to translocate more As from roots to shoots, as is evident from the lower As TF in the transgenic RNAi plants (Fig. 2c, d). Our hypothesis that OsPIP2;6 plays a role in root-to-shoot translocation of As was further supported by As accumulation pattern in mature Ospip2;6 RNAi plants; a signifcant decrease in shoot As content was evident with no signifcant increase in root levels and slight reductions in the fag leaves and grain (Fig. 4).

Previous studies have shown that overexpression of $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ in Arabidopsis confers tolerance to AsIII with no appreciable diference in As accumulation in roots and shoots between transgenic and WT plants; however, transgenic plants show As infux and efux activity, suggesting that OsPIP2;6 function as a bidirectional channel (Mosa et al. 2012). Here we report that OsPIP2;6 in rice is likely unidirectional channel since independent $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ overexpression lines at the seedling stage accumulated more As in shoots when exposed to AsIII under hydroponics conditions (Fig. 3a). Conversely, As accumulation in roots does not change (Fig. 3b), which again supports our contention that OsPIP2;6 is involved in root-to-shoot translocation of AsIII but does not contribute to AsIII uptake from media or soil to roots. Again, this diference was supported by the increased As translocation from root-to-shoot as arsenic TF was higher in OsPIP2;6 OE independent lines compared with WT (Fig. 3c). Similarly, the mature overexpression plants showed an increase in As accumulation in shoots and fag leaves but again, not in the roots and grains (Fig. 5).

Our hypothesis that OsPIP2;6 is mediating the directional transport of As to the stele was supported by the GUS reporter studies, which showed tissue-specifc expression of OsPIP2;6 in the vascular tissues of roots and leaves (Fig. 6). The distribution of OsPIP2;6 in the roots and veins of leaves supports the proposed function as an aquaporin to facilitate the transport of water and non-charged solutes across cell membranes. This pattern of tissue-specific expression is in accordance with many PIP2s proteins, which are localized in the endodermis; for example, ZmPIP2;1 and ZmPIP2;5 are localized in the endodermis near the xylem and have a potential role in water transport (Hachez et al. 2006; Sakurai-Ishikawa et al. 2011). Experimental evidence from both in vivo and in vitro studies has confrmed that the proper localization of PIP1s to the membrane necessitates a direct interaction between PIP2s and PIP1s (Zelazny et al. 2007). Since PIP1 and PIP2 proteins are known to interact for their proper functions, we cannot rule out the possibility that the reduced As transport from roots to shoots in Ospip2;6 Ri lines could be attributed to the impaired function of PIP1s, which may have been afected by the absence of interaction with OsPIP2s (specifcally, OsPIP2;6 in our study). However, evaluating that potential interaction was beyond the scope of the current study. Examples from various species, including maize ZmPIP2s PIP1s, rice OsPIP2;2 and OsPIP1;3, Mimosa pudica MpPIP1;1 and MpPIP2;1, and strawberry FaPIP1;1 and FaPIP2;1, have provided evidence that PIP2s enhances the activity of PIP1s in a manner that is concentration dependent (Fetter et al. 2004; Temmei et al. 2005; Zelazny et al. 2007; Yanef et al. 2014).

We noted a signifcant efect of OsPIP2;6 on As transport during both the seedling stage and at maturity; the impact was evident in As content in the shoots and to a lesser extent the grains. We were unable to provide a clear explanation for this observation, although there are several possibilities. For example, it is possible that alternative transporters or mechanisms become more infuential as the plant develops. Other possibility is that for maturity assays in soil, AsIII may bind to the soil particles and hence less As become available to mature plant, or mature plants have more biomass and hence the total As in terms of per unit biomass is lower and hence less As is translocated in grains at maturity. Further investigation is required to gain a thorough understanding of this process and its signifcance relative to toxic metal accumulation and food safety.

We hypothesize that the observed phenotype in $O s P I P 2 ; 6$ RNAi and OE plants under AsIII stress can be attributed to the combined efect of the two proposed factors: tissuespecifc transport activity and direct interaction between PIP1s and PIP2s. However, further investigation is required to accurately examine the interaction between various PIPs and their impact on membrane targeting and incorporation, ultimately facilitating As transport.

It is becoming increasingly clear that plant aquaglyceroporins of the NIP subgroup such as the rice AQP Lsi1 catalyse the uptake of As(III) into roots12,13, and that the rice ArsB family member Lsi2 is responsible for the movement of As(III) from roots to shoots through the xylem12. The final piece of the puzzle is how arsenic is loaded from the shoots into the seeds of plants6 . In this study, we show that the A. thaliana inositol transporters AtINT2 and AtINT4 catalyse As(III) loading into phloem and are necessary for arsenic accumulation in the seeds of this model plant. We speculate that knowledge of the pathway of arsenic accumulation in Arabidopsis seeds will shed light on the corresponding mechanism in rice, the main source of dietary arsenic for the majority of the world’s population. Understanding the loading mechanism of As(III) into rice grains, fruits or seeds of other crops is critical for enhancing food safety.

As(III) is the predominant arsenic species found in seeds, especially in rice grains3,36. A survey of arsenic speciation in Chinese rice showed that in market rice, $5 0 \mathrm { - } 6 0 \%$ arsenic was present as As(III), and in rice collected from farmers’ fields in mining areas, $6 0 { - } 7 0 \%$ was $\mathrm { A } s ( \mathrm { I I I } ) ^ { 3 5 }$ . Approximately $9 0 \%$ of As (III) in rice grains is delivered via the phloem19–23. However, prior to the present study, little was known about the mechanisms of arsenic loading and unloading during phloem transport6 . Generally, solutes load into and unload from phloem through either the apoplastic or symplastic pathway. Apoplastic loading is driven thermodynamically via the proton motive force and conducted by plasma membrane transporters37. Symplastic loading is passive and conducted through plasmodesmata between adjacent cells38,39. In A. thaliana, AtINT2 and AtINT4 are located in the plasma membrane. Organ and tissue specificity of AtINT2 and AtINT4 expression showed that both AtINT2 and AtINT4 are strongly expressed in the vasculature, primarily in the companion cells of phloem, although there is also a little expression in root tissue28,30. Functional analyses further demonstrated that AtINT2 and AtINT4 are $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled symporters that are responsible for loading of inositol into the phloem to supply the developing seeds. In the present study we demonstrate that AtINT2 and AtINT4 also transport $\operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ (Figs 1 and 2). Myo-inositol in the growth medium inhibited the uptake of As(III) by AtINT2 and AtINT4 (Fig. 3). The disruption of AtINT2 or AtINT4 significantly decreased arsenic concentration in phloem exudates (Fig. 5a), and subsequently significantly decreased arsenic concentration in shoots, siliques and seeds (Fig. ${ 5 } \mathrm { b } , { c } )$ ). Most importantly, arsenic accumulation in siliques and seeds decreased by half (Fig. 5c), but the ratios of each arsenic species in plants tissues were similar between the mutants and WT (Supplementary Fig. 4). Additionally, when plants were feed with arsenite through leaves, arsenic accumulation in shoots and siliques of mutants was significantly lower than those of WT (Fig. 5b). In contrast to that, arsenic concentrations in the xylem sap did not vary between WT and mutant plants (Fig. 5d). These results clearly demonstrate that inositol transporters AtINT2 and AtINT4 are responsible for arsenite loading into phloem, and essential for arsenite accumulation in A. thaliana seeds.

We conclude that AtINT2 and AtINT4 are responsible for the loading of arsenic from the apoplast into the phloem (Supplementary Fig. 5). Our results are consistent with the tissue and cell specificity of expression28,30. Nevertheless, a single mutation of AtINT2 or AtINT4 did not totally suppress translocation of arsenic into seeds (Fig. 5). This could be contributed to by AtINT4 in Atint2 or AtINT2 in Atint4, or other transporters may be also involved in arsenic loading to phloem. AtINT2 and AtINT4 are not expressed in young sink leaves28,30, so it was anticipated that neither AtINT2 nor AtINT4 mutations would affect arsenic accumulation in seedlings treated with As(III) (Supplementary Fig. 3). Once entry into the companion cells of the phloem, arsenic passively diffuses through the plasmodesmata into the sieve elements and is finally released into the sink cells of seeds (Supplementary Fig. 5). As is the case for nutrients, unloading of arsenic from the phloem into the sink cells of plant seeds is likely to be mediated by specific transport proteins40, and identification of these transporters should be a priority of future research.

In summary, we demonstrate here that inositol transporters AtINT2 and AtINT4 adventitiously catalyse loading of $\operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { I I I } )$ into the phloem, a possible pivotal step of arsenic translocation to the seeds of higher plants. To our knowledge, this is the first identification of transporters responsible for arsenic loading into phloem. If these findings prove to be applicable to rice, then inositol transporters may be candidates for future genetic modification to reduce the arsenic content in rice grain. If so, this discovery will enable development of new cultivars that accumulate lower amounts of arsenic in their grain without affecting yield production, a major advance toward mitigation of health risks posed by arsenic in rice.

## Received 03 May 2015; accepted 16 November 2015; published 21 December 2015

Arsenic (As) is one of the most toxic heavy metal pollutants which afects plants, animals, and humans all over the globe; and impose a threat to mankind as it can contaminate the groundwater supply and irrigation system of many countries (Guha and Dasgupta 2011; Milton et al. 2005; Smith et al. 2002; Taylor and Mukherjee 2003). Apart from being one of the most abundant elements of earth, the sources of arsenic can be diverse. In recent times, arsenic has been used in pesticides which are a potent source to pollute water sources. Prolong arsenic exposure can induce neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular complications, and can also appear as a carcinogenic in certain cases (Li et al. 2017; Argos et al. 2010; Chen et al. 2011). There are two major ways of arsenic exposure which include use of arsenic-contaminated water and crops. Another potential way of exposure of arsenic is from livestock and other products derived from the vegetation of arsenic-contaminated areas. Apart from the use of direct contaminated water, the arsenic in crops and livestock end up in the food chain, which is due to the arsenic uptake by the crop plants. Arsenic in plant systems translocates through phosphate transporter proteins and accumulates in shoot and root tissue; in case of crop plants like rice, arsenic accumulates in shoot and grain through silicon transporters (Jian et al. 2008).

There are diferent valence states in which arsenic can exist in nature; and arsenic salts have a wide range of solubility which frmly rely on the pH condition and ionic environment (Tripathi et al. 2007). Two major forms of inorganic arsenic are abundant in environment arsenate (AsV) and arsenite (AsIII); among them, arsenate (AsV) is dominant in oxygenated condition but arsenite (AsIII) is in stable form in reducing environment (Mitra et al. 2017). However, organic forms of arsenic like monomethylarsonic acid (MMA) and dimethyl arsenic acid (DMA) also exist in nature but they are not abundant as inorganic forms (Tripathi et al. 2007). Arsenate (AsV) enters the plant system through root phosphate transporters as an analog of inorganic phosphate (Srivastava et al. 2007). On the other hand, arsenite (AsIII) is taken up by plants through aquaglyceroporins because it exists predominantly as arsenous acid $[ \mathrm { A s } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } ]$ in nature (Ali et al. 2009). Upon entering the cell, arsenate (AsV) and arsenite (AsIII) interact diferently with the cellular processes, as a phosphate analog, arsenate (AsV) interferes with the ATP synthesis process and oxidative phosphorylation process while arsenite (AsIII) has an inclination to bind with thiol group which ultimately afects the normal enzyme activity of regular cellular processes (Németi et al. 2010; Tripathi et al. 2007). In bacterial, fungal, and also in plant systems, the arsenate (AsV) is readily reduced to arsenite (AsIII) by arsenate reductase enzyme (Mukhopadhyay and Rosen 2002). After conversion to arsenite (AsIII), it is transported out of the cytoplasm by diferent transporters (Achour et al. 2007). There are diferent types of transporters involved; frst type belonging from the Major Facilitator Superfamily, ArsB antiporters which extrude antimonite (SbIII) and arsenite (AsIII) from cell through ATP hydrolysis or by electrochemical gradient (Dey and Rosen 1995; Garbinski et al. 2019); second are ABC “ATP-binding cassette” type transporter family present in eukaryotes which export sulfhydrylated antimonite (SbIII) and arsenite (AsIII) out of the plant cell (Maciaszczykdziubinska et al. 2011; Song et al. 2010) and last type is from BART (bile/arsenite/transporter) Superfamily, Acr3 which extrude arsenite (AsIII) from cytoplasm; present in bacteria, archaea, fungi, and ferns (Indriolo et al. 2010; Ordoñez et al. 2015; Wysocki et al. 1997). These Acr3 permeases type proteins contain ten transmembrane domains and present in tonoplast as well as plasma membrane (Gil et al. 2009). Acr3 transporters play a major role in arsenic exclusion from plant cytoplasm (Indriolo et al. 2010).

Plants have diferent strategies in place to cope up with the arsenic accumulation. In Pteris vittata, the Acr3 is found in the tonoplast of their fronds where vacuolar sequestration of arsenite takes place (Indriolo et al. 2010; Sundaram et al. 2008). Interestingly, to date, no Acr3 has been reported in angiosperms. Transgenic approaches have been made by overexpressing the ACR3 gene in rice and Arabidopsis plants to generate more tolerant and low-arsenic-accumulating plants (Ali et al. 2012; Duan et al. 2012). In this review, we aimed to discuss the diversity and importance of Acr3 transporter protein.


## Arsenic transporters in plants



## Transporters involved in arsenic uptake



## Phosphate transporter


The predominant form of arsenic in soil is mineral from including oxides of arsenite like Arsenolite $( \mathrm { A s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } )$ , Claudetite $( \mathrm { A s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } )$ , and oxides of arsenate arsenic pentoxide $( \mathrm { A s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } )$ which in turn act as a source of arsenate $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ (Shrivastava et al. 2015). Arsenate or As(V) $[ \mathrm { A s } _ { 4 } ] ^ { 3 }$ is a chemical analog of phosphate $[ \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } ] ^ { 3 }$ , so arsenate enters the plant system through the phosphate transporters (Wang et al. 2002). Several phosphate transporters have been reported in Arabidopsis thaliana like AtPHT1;1, AtPHT1;4, AtPHT1;5, AtPHT1;7, AtPHT1;8, AtPHT1;9, and AtVPT1 which are involved in $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ uptake; phosphate transporter 1;1 (AtPHT1;1), is the most predominant $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -coupled phosphate cotransporter found in the root (Liao et al. 2019) (Fig. 1). Mutation in AtPHT1;1 showed an increase in tolerance to As(V) by lower uptake by plant; however, an increase in As(V) uptake is reported during overexpression of AtPHT1;1 (Catarecha et al. 2007; LeBlanc et al. 2013; Shin et al. 2004). Along with this, a vacuolar phosphate transporter AtVPT1 is also responsible for altering As(V) tolerance; mutation in AtVPT1 results in elevated levels of phosphate in the cytosol which in turn suppresses the expression of the PHT1-type transporter which ultimately reduced the As(V) uptake in cell (Luan et al. 2018). Further, in rice plants also, several phosphate transporters like OsPHT1;1, OsPHT1;4, and OsPHT1;8 have been reported which actively take part in As(V) transport and uptake (Cao et al. 2017; Kamiya et al. 2013; Shi et al. 2016). In arsenic hyper-accumulators like Pteris vittata, arsenate have been taken up by phosphate transporters like PvPht1;3 and PvPht1;4 (Ditusa et al. 2016; Sun et al. 2020) (Table 1).


## Aquaporins


Arsenite As (III) predominantly exists in nature as arsenous acid $[ \mathrm { A s } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } ]$ (Ali et al. 2009) and due to this neutral state of the arsenite, it is transported by aquaporins which belong to the superfamily major intrinsic protein (MIP) of plants (Mosa et al. 2012). Depending on the subcellular localization, plant aquaporins are divided into four subfamilies; in endoplasmic reticulum small basic intrinsic protein (SIP), in vacuolar membrane tonoplast intrinsic protein (TIP), in plasma membrane intrinsic protein (PIP), and in plasma membrane and intercellular membrane Nodulin26-like intrinsic proteins (NIP) (Jian et al. 2006; Maurel 2007; Takano et al. 2006).


## Nodulin26‑like intrinsic proteins


It has been reported that Nodulin26-like intrinsic proteins (NIP) like AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1, and AtNIP7;1 of

Arabidopsis thaliana, and OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2, and OsNIP3;2 of Oryza sativa are responsible for uptake of As(III) (Bienert et al. 2008). The NIP sub-family of Arabidopsis has total of nine members in the genome; of them,

AtNIP1;1, AtNIP1;2, AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1 and AtNIP7;1 which encode the corresponding transporters are all responsible for arsenite uptake (Bienert et al. 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis 2008; Kamiya et al. 2009). OsNIP2;1 was previously reported only as silicon(Si) transporter but recent studies depicted that it also takes part in As(III) uptake, but the expression level and the sub-cellular localization of the transporter also contribute to the diferent degrees of transportability of arsenite (Jian et al. 2008) (Fig. 1).


## Plasma membrane intrinsic protein


Plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIP) have been reported to be conserved and sub-divided into two phylogenetic groups PIP1 and PIP2 (Vajpai et al. 2018). Of these two types of PIPs, in rice, OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OsPIP2;7 are reported to be involved in As(III) transport (Mosa et al. 2012).


## Tonoplast intrinsic protein


Among major aquaporins, tonoplast intrinsic proteins or TIPs are mainly located on tonoplast but further studies have suggested a diverged sub-cellular distribution (He et al. 2016). Recent report suggested a member of tonoplast intrinsic protein (TIP), PvTIP4;1 from Pteris vittata might be responsible for arsenite uptake (He et al. 2016).


## Transporters involved in arsenite detoxifcation



## Chelation and vacuolar sequestration


Phytochelation of As in plant cells follows several major necessary steps like phytochelation, translocation, sequestration, and efux of As (Yamazaki et al. 2018). The detoxifcation of arsenic in cell depends upon the phytochelatins (PCs) and glutathione (GSH) which are responsible for the vacuolar sequestration; on one hand, phytochelatins (PCs) bind with As(III) with their thiol group and then create As(III)–PC complex, and on the other hand, glutathione (GSH) makes conjugate with As(III) and forms arsenite triglutathione complex $( \operatorname { A s } ( \operatorname { G S } ) _ { 3 } )$ , both of which are transported to the vacuole for sequestration by ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters (Liu et  al. 2010; Song et  al. 2010, 2014; Yamazaki et al. 2018). Two major ABC transporters have been reported in Arabidopsis, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, which are involved in the sequestration of GSH-conjugate as well as in the sequestration of As(III)–PC complex into the vacuole (Song et al. 2010; Wanke and Üner Kolukisaoglu 2010). In rice, OsABCC1 which is a member of the C-type ABC transporter (OsABCC) family, is responsible for the vacuolar sequestration of As in the phloem companion cells which, in turn, contributes to the reduction of total accumulation of As in rice grain (Song et al. 2014).


## Translocation and phloem loading


In rice, As(III) is transported to xylem through OsLsi1 (OsNIP2;1), the silicon efux transporter which corresponds to the root-to-shoot arsenic transport (Jian et al. 2008). Along with the C-type ABC transporter family, OsABCC7 also has been reported to be responsible for root-to-shoot arsenic translocation (Tang et al. 2019). OsABCC7 is predominantly expressed and localized in the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma which, in turn, is capable of As(III)–PC and $\mathrm { A s } ( \mathrm { G S } ) _ { 3 }$ efux from the cell which mainly contributes to xylem loading of As (Tang et al. 2019). A member of multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) protein family is reported to be responsible for As accumulation in rice, OsMATE2; silencing of endogenous OsMATE2 showed a reduced accumulation in rice grain (Das et al. 2018). On the other hand, in Arabidopsis, inositol transporters (INT) have been reported to play a part in the phloem loading of arsenite. Particularly, AtINT2 and AtINT4 are involved in transport of As(III) into the phloem (Duan et al. 2015). Recent studies indicated an intricate pathway for arsenic tolerance in $P .$ vittata, in which As(V) upon entering the cell might convert by GLYCERALDEHYDE 3-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (PvGAPC1) to 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate (1-As-3-PG) and then the sequestration of this “chemically trapped” As takes place by ORGANIC CATION TRANSPORTER 4 (PvOCT4) into arsenic metabolizing vesicles (Cai et al. 2019).


## Efux and sequestration


Along with chelation, translocation, and vacuolar sequestration, efux of As(III) from plant cells is also an immensely important step for arsenic detoxifcation. Apart from OsLsi1 (OsNIP2;1), all these transporters discussed above are involved in unidirectional transport of As(III), i.e., uptake and translocation within plant system but the aquaporins like OsLsi1 mediate bidirectional transport of As(III) depending on the concentration gradient (Jian et al. 2008). But transporters only showing As efux properties have not been found in fowering plants. In some bacteria and in yeast, ArsB and Acr3 transporters have been found, respectively, to have As(III) efux properties (Meng et al. 2004; Wysocki et al. 1997). These antiporters belong to the bile/arsenite/ ribofavin transporter (BART) superfamily (Mansour et al. 2007). No copies of these transporters have been found in higher plants, and in Pteris vittata, two copies of ACR3; PvACR3 and PvACR3;1, have been reported (Indriolo et al. 2010). Primarily, it was postulated that As(III) only be sequestered in vacuoles after being chelated by PC or GSH. Later it was identifed that As(III) as itself can be sequestered in vacuoles of $P .$ vittata where transporters are found in tonoplast but further studies indicated that PvACR3 transporters are also responsible for efux of As(III) (Chen et al. 2013; Indriolo et al. 2010). Heterologous expression of $P \nu A C R 3$ in Arabidopsis shows the localization of PvACR3 transporter to plasma membrane and an increased efux of arsenic to the external media; moreover, the result indicated a reduction of As concentration in root but an elevation of As concentration in the shoot (Chen et al. 2013).


## ACR3 as an As(III) efux transporter in plants


Plants adapted to two diferent mechanisms for As stress tolerance responses. First, they developed detoxifcation processes of biologically active inorganic arsenic within the cell and second, they used an exclusion mechanism of arsenic from the cell by diferent transporters. In plants’ arsenic stress resistance mechanisms, the efux transporters play a very crucial role and such transporters have been found in Pteris vittata named Arsenic Compound Resistance (ACR3) (Indriolo et al. 2010). The ACR genes were frst discovered in yeast chromosome XVI in a $4 . 2 \mathrm { k b }$ region; namely ACR1, ACR2, and ACR3 (Bobrowicz et al. 1997).


## ACR1 and ACR2


Arsenic sensing and signaling corresponding genes to defend the organism are the central dogma for arsenic tolerance mechanism. ACR1 gene is the responsible factor for arsenic sensing in the tolerant organisms; in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, ACR1 which encodes a transcription factor called ACR1, also known as Yap8, is involved in arsenic sensory mechanism (Kumar et al. 2016a, 2016b; Wysocki et al. 1997). Yap8 is a yeast AP-1 family transcription factor containing conserved cysteine residue and basic leucine-zipper (bZIP) for arsenic sensing (Toone and Jones 1999; Di and

Tamás 2007; Wysocki et al. 2004). In arsenic-exposed cells, the AsIII binds with the aforementioned conserved cysteine residues Cys 132, Cys 137, and Cys 274, which changes the Yap8 conformation and subsequently leads to the ACR2 and ACR3 expression (Kumar et al. 2016a, 2016b). The primary stage of arsenic detoxifcation is the conversion of As(V) to As(III), although this process takes place in prokaryotic as well as eukaryotic organism but the non-enzymatic reduction of arsenate is considered to be too slow to have any signifcant role in physiological process (Bleeker et al. 2006). On the other hand, the enzymatic reduction of arsenate to arsenite is the key frst step in arsenic tolerance of tolerant organisms (Bobrowicz et al. 1997). This enzymatic conversion employs ACR2 protein which is from protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTPase) family 1 (Fauman et al. 1998). The arsenite reductase protein ACR2 which converts cellular As(V) to As(III) is encoded by ACR2 (Mukhopadhyay and Rosen 1998). But primarily a homologue of ACR2 was identifed in Arabidopsis thaliana as CDC25 (Landrieu et al. 2004a). This CDC25 is a dual-specifcity phosphatase and further studies have suggested that the phosphatase activity is present in Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa, but absent in Pteris vittata and yeast (Ellis et al. 2006; Duan et al. 2007). Although the ACR2 expression is very important for the arsenic biotransformation process and subsequently important for As tolerance, a recent study has suggested the existence of several alternative pathways in arsenate reduction in yeast and plants (Liu et al. 2012).

Arsenic (As), a metalloid, is a non-essential and highly toxic element to most organisms, including humans and plants (Abernathy et al., 2003; Tchounwou et al., 2004). Both organic and inorganic As exist in the environment, but the latter is predominant. The International Agency for Research on Cancer has classified inorganic As as a group I human carcinogen (ATSDR, 2007; IARC, 2012).

Inorganic As species exist in two different oxidation states, known as fully oxidized pentavalent arsenate (As[V]) and reduced trivalent arsenite (As[III]). In plants, As can be taken up from soil and water and leads to an inhibition of plant growth, development, and photosynthesis as well as reduced crop yields. The phosphate transporters, Arabidopsis PHT1;1 and PHT1;4, take up $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ from the environment (Shin et al., 2004). In recent years, some members of the subfamily of nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) of plants, which are similar in structure and function to microbial and mammalian aquaglyceroporins, have been discovered to be permeable to arsenite (Bienert et al., 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis, 2008; Ma et al., 2008; Kamiya et al., 2009). OsNIP2;1 (Lsi1), a silicon (Si) transporter (Ma and Yamaji, 2006), also contributes to the uptake of arsenite in monocot rice (Ma et al., 2008). In Arabidopsis, the NIP subfamily consists of nine members in the genome. Based on yeast and oocyte expression systems, NIP5;1, NIP6;1, NIP7;1, and NIP1;2 are all capable of As(III) transport (Bienert et al., 2008; Kamiya et al., 2009). Furthermore, a strong root-growth arsenite-tolerant phenotype has been found in NIP1;1 loss-of-function mutants (Kamiya et al., 2009).

Across As hyperaccumulator and non-hyperaccumulator plant species, $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ is rapidly reduced to As(III) after it enters root cells


## Molecular Plant


(Pickering et al., 2000; Bleeker et al., 2006; Dhankher et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2010). In the As hyperaccumulating fern, Pteris vittata, a PvACR3 As(III) efflux transporter gene has recently been discovered and likely functions to efflux arsenite into vacuoles for detoxification (Indriolo et al., 2010). However, in non-hyperaccumulator plants, including Arabidopsis, sequestration of As(III)-thiol complexes into vacuoles and extrusion of arsenite out of cells are the two primary systems for As detoxification. Glutathione-based phytochelatins (PCs) are unique in plants and are used to create complexes with heavy metals and arsenite for detoxification (Grill et al., 1987; Sneller et al., 1999; Raab et al., 2004; Srivastava et al., 2007; Schulz et al., 2008). Recently, Song et al. (2010) identified the PC transporters AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, which are responsible for transporting $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } ) { \mathsf { \Pi } } \mathsf { - P C } _ { 2 }$ into vacuoles. The complexation of As(III) with PCs contributes to As sequestration in roots, whereas $\mathsf { A s } ( | | | )$ is extruded out of cells into the external medium and even into the xylem for root-to-shoot translocation (Liu et al., 2010). In a recent report, the Lsi2 Si efflux carrier, with a motif similar to that of the arsenite efflux transporter ArsB in Escherichia coli, was shown to permit arsenite efflux toward the stele from the exodermis and endodermis cells in rice roots, and to affect the accumulation of As in shoots (Ma et al., 2008). Some NIP aquaporins also mediate arsenite efflux (Bienert et al., 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis, 2008; Zhao et al., 2010a). The expression of several NIPs from different plants, including Arabidopsis NIP5;1, NIP6;1, and NIP7;1, enhances the ability of yeast cells to extrude As(III) (Bienert et al., 2008; Isayenkov and Maathuis, 2008). The rice NIP aquaporin OsNIP2;1 (Lsi1) is also able to efflux arsenite out of rice root cells into the external medium (Zhao et al., 2010a). These studies suggest that NIPs facilitate the bidirectional movement of As(III) in plants. However, the role of NIPs in arsenite root-to-shoot translocation in Arabidopsis remains unknown. Both NIP5;1 and NIP6;1 are permeable to boric acid (B) in Arabidopsis. NIP5;1 is responsible for B uptake in roots from soils, whereas NIP6;1 is involved in the xylem–phloem transfer of B at the nodal regions that promote shoot growth (Takano et al., 2006; Tanaka et al., 2008). It is possible that some NIPs may also function to extrude arsenite into the xylem for long-distance distribution in Arabidopsis. Here, we report on an as yet uncharacterized NIP gene, NIP3;1, which shows a root-predominant expression pattern and is involved in As uptake and root-to-shoot translocation in Arabidopsis under arsenite conditions.

Rice is the main diet for more than half of the world’s population; thus, it gains special interest to ensure it is safe for consumption. Growing rice, especially in flooded paddy fields where the soil or irrigation water is contaminated with Arsenic (As) favors rice to accumulate it in biomass and edible grains. Thus, rice is the primary source of dietary As contamination, which is a major health hazard. Understanding the mechanism of As uptake and developing approaches to restrict the movement of As from soil to different plant tissues are necessary to limit As accumulation in rice. This study investigates the role of rice plasma membrane intrinsic protein, OsPIP1;3, in As transport and translocation from root to shoot in rice. Suppression of OsPIP1;3 expression using RNAi (Ri) technology decreases As accumulation in the shoots of transgenic OsPIP1;3 Ri plants by $( 4 5 . 3 { - } 4 5 . 6 \% )$ , with no noticeable effect on root arsenic levels. In contrast, constitutive overexpressing (OE) OsPIP1;3 increased As in shoots of rice seedlings by $8 - 2 9 \%$ , with no significant change in root As content compared with WT. At the maturity stage, OsPIP1;3

Ri plants accumulated $( 2 9 - 3 6 \% )$ and $( 5 - 2 1 \% )$ less As in shoot and flag leaves, respectively, while grains show a slight reduction. Similar to the seedling stages, OsPIP1;3 OE mature plants accumulated significantly high As levels in their shoots, flag leaves, and grains compared to WT. Together, these results suggest that OsPIP1;3 contribute to As transport from root to shoot in rice. This finding could add to the current knowledge of As transporters, which are collectively considered a major genetic source for manipulation to reduce As accumulation in rice and other food crops for improved human and environmental health.

Orchids, like many terrestrial plants, often form a symbiotic relationship with specific fungi, known as orchid mycorrhiza (OM) [1]. This mutually beneficial partnership enhances the orchid’s ability to access essential mineral nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen. In return, the orchid transfers part of its synthesized organic carbon, such as carbohydrates, to the fungus, providing it with nutrition [2]. The fungus utilizes this organic carbon as an energy source to meet its energy requirements [3].

The orchid-fungal symbiosis is unique compared to other mycorrhizal associations like ectomycorrhiza and arbuscular mycorrhiza, primarily due to the orchid’s distinct life cycle and diverse trophic strategies [4]. During the early stages of seed germination and seedling development, orchids rely on the mycorrhizal fungus for essential nutrients. The fungus aids in the uptake of minerals and possibly provides organic compounds while receiving limited or no direct nutritional resources from the orchids [5]. This phase of the symbiotic relationship is often referred to as the “fungus-dependent” or “mycoheterotrophic” stage [6].

After infecting the plant, OM fungi form mycorrhizal structures and develop dense rolls of mycelium called pelotons in the cortical cells of the embryo stalk. The digestion of these pelotons by the host plant is a significant mechanism for capturing fungus-derived compounds in OM [7]. According to previous research, Dearnaley and Cameron [8] summarized the bidirectional nutrient flow model of OM symbionts. The mycorrhizal fungus transfers nutrients including carbon (C), phosphorus (P), and nitrogen (N) across the interfacial matrix. Fungal nutrients like P, N, and C also pass to the orchid as the pelotons are digested [9]. As the orchid matures and becomes photosynthetic, the flow of carbon from the plant to the fungus is established, marking the transition from a heterotrophic juvenile to an autotrophic adult [10]. While the mechanisms of nutrient exchange in ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular mycorrhizal associations have been extensively studied, orchid mycorrhizal (OMF) interactions remain less understood, presenting a fascinating area for ongoing research.

There is growing evidence that the colonization of symbiotic fungi in plants creates new carbon reservoirs and significantly influences carbon allocation and sugarrelated metabolic processes in both the above-ground and root tissues [11, 12]. For example, Zhao et al. [12] demonstrated that inoculation by “Rhizophagus irregularis” or “Glomus aggregatum with high arbuscular mycorrhizal” colonization increased sucrose, glucose, and fructose levels in both the above-ground parts and roots of soybean compared to uninoculated controls. In a previous investigation, Shachar-Hill et al. [13] employed isotope-labeled sugars alongside comprehensive nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic analyses, demonstrating the direct transfer of glucose from the host plant to the fungus.

SWEET proteins, a family of bidirectional sugar transporters independent of proton pump activity, are predominantly located in the plasma membrane, tonoplast, or Golgi membrane [14, 15]. Additionally, various SWEET genes are transcriptionally activated by biotrophic bacteria and fungi, which modulate SWEET protein expression to extract carbon from the host plant [16, 17]. In Solanum tuberosum (potato) and Glycine max (soybean), specific SWEET transporter genes have shown upregulation during mycorrhizal symbiosis [12], indicating that certain SWEET family members may play a role in providing sugars to arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Manck-Götzenberger and Requena [18] also observed that the promoter regions of SWEET genes in potatoes were highly active near cells containing arbuscules, suggesting that SWEET proteins may facilitate sugar transport from the plant to these specialized fungal structures. In light of this, the current study aims to investigate the role of SWEET sugar transporters in the mycorrhizal symbiosis of Dendrobium officinale.

In brief, this study explored the molecular role of the SWEET14 gene in the mutualistic relationship between Dendrobium officinale and the OM fungus during the colonization phase. The findings revealed that the expression of the DoSWEET14 gene was significantly upregulated during mycorrhizal symbiosis, indicating increased gene activity in the presence of the OM fungus. This suggests that DoSWEET14 plays a crucial role in the symbiotic interaction. Additionally, this research provides valuable insights into the specific interactions between Dendrobium officinale and the OM fungus, while also establishing a theoretical basis for understanding the regulatory mechanisms governing sugar transporter gene expression in the Orchidaceae family, particularly in green orchid species.

Sugar is the main carbon source and energy-supplying substance in organisms, and it plays an important role in plant growth and development. Sugar is the main product of photosynthesis and carbon dioxide assimilation occurs mainly in stromal cells of chloroplast. The main assimilation product synthesized in chloroplasts is triose phosphate, most of which will be converted to either sucrose in the cytosol or starch in the chloroplast1,2 . Sucrose is commonly translocated to other carbondemanding organs through the long-distance transport occurring in phloem. Hence, sugar transportation is critical for maintaining the source-sink balance3 .

Over the past two decades, various sugar transporters have been identified in living organisms, including plants, animals, humans, and fungi4–6 . These transporters can be categorized into four families: sodium solute symporter transporters; major facilitator superfamily transporters; phosphotransferase system transporters; and sugar will eventually be exported transporters (SWEETs). Among these transporters, SWEETs emerge as a unique and novel class of sugar transporters. SWEETs are conserved evolutionarily and exist widely in eukaryotes, and prokaryotes such as arechaea and eubacteria. The first member of the SWEET gene family, MtN3, was identified in Medicago truncatula, and its expression was induced during root nodule development7 . Later, a homolog of the MtN3 gene, designated Saliva, was identified in Drosophila and displayed salivary gland-specific expression during embryonic development8 . Recently, MtN3/Saliva-type genes were functionally characterized as sugar transporters in both animals and plants, and thus gave the name $^ { \prime \prime } S W E E T ^ { \prime 9 }$ . SWEET proteins are characterized by the MtN3/Saliva motif (also known as the PQ-loop repeat), which comprises three alpha-helical transmembrane domains (3-TMs). Eukaryotic SWEETs consists of a tandem repeat of the basic 3-TM unit separated by a single transmembrane domain, which constitutes a 3-1-3 TM structure. In contrast, prokaryotic SWEETs, also called SemiSWEETs, contain only a single 3-TM unit, suggesting that eukaryotic SWEETs evolved through a duplication of the 3-TM unit10.

In plants, SWEETs function as bidirectional uniporters that mediate influx and efflux of sugars across cell membranes. SWEETs can be divided into four clades11. Clades I, II, and IV SWEETs transport predominantly hexoses, whilst clade III SWEETs appear to be sucrose transporters (SUTs)12–15. For example, the clade I SWEET AtSWEET1 and the clade II SWEET OsSWEET5 mediate the uptake and efflux of glucose or galactose, respectively, across the cell membrane9,16. Two clade III SWEETs, AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12, are involved in efflux of photosynthesized sucrose from phloem parenchyma cells into intercellular space for phloem loading and longdistance translocation of sucrose17. A newly identified clade III SWEET, AtSWEET9, transports sucrose to the apoplast and plays an essential role in nectar secretion18. The clade IV SWEET, AtSWEET17, functions as a fructose-specific uniporter, with a key role in facilitating bidirectional transport of fructose across the tonoplast in leaf and root12,13. In addition, SWEETs have been shown to affect various physiological processes, such as pollen development19,20, seed filling21,22, stress and senescence14,16,23,24, modulating gibberellins response25, and host–pathogen interaction26. Usually, abiotic stress such as cold, high salinity, and drought, and biotic stress caused by fungi or bacteria result in an induction of specific SWEET genes27,28.

The accumulation of carbohydrates in storage organs such as seeds and fruits mainly depends on the supply of photoassimilates from photosynthetic tissues, especially source leaves. In most plants, sucrose is the major carbohydrate transported over a long distance in the veins to support the growth and development of storage organs6 . Sugar transporter genes exhibit divergent evolutionary patterns and play important roles in sugar accumulation in plants29. For example, genes encoding SUT proteins are involved in sugar translocation toward storage organs30–32. Recently, the SWEET4 gene is also found to play an important role in seed filling22. In maize and rice, SWEET4 shows high expression during seed development and contributes to seed filling by enhancing the importation of hexoses into the endosperm. This study sheds light on our understanding on the mechanism by which sucrose is released from maternal tissues such as seed coat to support filial tissues such as embryonic tissue. Since sugar content is an important component of fruit quality, increasing attention has also been paid to investigate the SWEET gene family in fruit crops such as apple33, grapevine34, and banana35. However, the effect of SWEETs on fruit sugar accumulation remains elusive.

The domesticated apple, Malus $_ x$ domestica Borkh., is an economically important fruit crop worldwide. Apple belongs to the family Rosaceae, and the cultivated apple is a diploidized autopolyploid species with a basic chromosome number of $x = 1 7$ . The draft genome sequence of the domesticated apple has been released, and accounts for an approximately $7 5 0 \mathrm { M b }$ per haploid36. In this study, we report the identification of the MdSWEET genes with high expression during apple fruit development. DNA markers for these MdSWEETs were developed to investigate their association with fruit sugar content. Our study not only aids our better understanding of the effect of SWEETs on fruit sugar accumulation but it will also be helpful for genetic improvement of fruit sugar accumulation in apple-breeding programs.

In this study we found that MtSWEET1b encodes a glucose transporter that is strongly upregulated in arbuscule-containing cells compared to roots and which localizes to the peri-arbuscular membrane surrounding the arbuscules (Fig. 7). Overexpression of MtSWEET1b increased the fungal mass in symbiotic roots, further suggesting that MtSWEET1b may play a role in exporting sugar from arbuscule-containing cells to AM fungi (Fig. 7). However, mycorrhization did not seem to be significantly affected in two $M .$ . truncatula lines where the MtSWEET1b gene is mutated to produce a truncated protein that is incapable of glucose transport in yeast. Intriguingly, overexpression of dominant-negative alleles of MtSWEET1b impaired arbuscule maintenance, implying that MtSWEET1b might form hetero-oligomers with other (SWEET) transporters.

M. truncatula has 26 SWEET genes, of which only MtSWEET1b showed strongly induced expression in root cortex cells colonized by the AM fungus. Several other MtSWEET members did show differential expression upon mycorrhization, however none of them exhibited induced expression in the root cortex cells where nutrient/sugar delivery is thought to occur (Roth & Paszkoswki, 2017). Phylogenetic analyses showed that MtSWEET1b is a homolog of AtSWEET1, a glucose transporter mainly active in flowers (Chen et al., 2010). M. truncatula has two homologs in this clade, of which MtSWEET1a is highly expressed in the flowers. There are at least two closely related SWEET1 homologs in O. sativa, L. japonicus or S. tuberosum. Interestingly, at least one SWEET1 in each plant species was found to be induced upon mycorrhization (Handa et al., 2015; Manck-Götzenberger & Requena, 2016; Sugimura & Saito, 2017). It seems likely that Arabidopsis, a non-host for AM fungi, has lost the AM regulated gene. In potato, several additional SWEET genes were found to be induced upon mycorrhization in arbuscule-containing cells, including clade II and clade III (sucrose This article is protected by copyright. Furthermore, in potato a clade I homolog of AtSWEET2 was also found to be induced in arbuscule-containing cells, which is thought to function at the tonoplast (Chen et al., 2015). This indicates that regulation of SWEET gene expression in different plant species may differ, and we speculate that it will influence the symbiotic efficiency of different plant-fungal combinations. Besides increased expression in arbuscule-containing cells, MtSWEET1b is also highly expressed in root nodules, seeds and pods (Kryvoruchko et al., 2016), raising the suggestion that it may play an important role in both AM and rhizobium symbioses.

The phylogenetic analyses suggested that MtSWEET1b is a glucose transporter. This was confirmed in yeast, as MtSWEET1b could complement the glucose transport defect of the EBY.VW4000 mutant (Wieczorke et al., 1999). So far, all the functionally characterized SWEET family members from different plant species were confirmed to have both sugar efflux and influx activity (Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2014; Eom et al., 2015). As uniporters SWEETs transport sugars along a concentration gradient, which raises the question whether MtSWEET1b exports glucose towards the fungus, or whether it imports glucose in competition with the fungus to support the high metabolic activity of arbuscule-containing cells or to avoid defense responses caused by high levels of glucose in the apoplast (Schaarschmidt et al., 2007; Helber et al., 2011; Moore et al., 2015; Bezrutczyk et al., 2018). Several studies indicate that arbuscules-containing cells form a strong sink for hexoses. For example, a hexose transporter (MtHEX1) likely involved in the uptake of hexose from the apoplast and a sucrose transporter (MtSUT1) thought to be involved in the export of sucrose from the vacuole as well as genes encoding amylase and secreted invertases showed the highest level of expression in root cortex cells adjacent to arbuscule-containing cells (Gaude et al., 2012a, b). The observation that plasmodesmata between arbuscule-containing cells and adjacent cells are enlarged (Blee & Anderson, 1998), suggests that cortical cells adjacent to arbuscule-containing cells supply carbohydrates to arbuscule-containing cells via symplastic transport (Gaude et al., 2012b). In the arbuscule-containing cells, a strongly induced cytoplasmic sucrose synthase (MtSucS1) This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

converts the sucrose to glucose. When knocked-down, this gene impaired fungal colonization and caused an early collapse of arbuscules (Baier et al., 2010). Therefore, we consider it likely that the glucose concentration inside arbuscule-containing cortex cells is higher than in the peri-arbuscular space and that MtSWEET1b facilitates the export of glucose across the peri-arbuscular membrane for subsequent uptake by the fungus through the monosaccharide transporter MST2 (Helber et al., 2011) (Fig. 7). Recently, it has been shown that the expression of MtSWEET1b is consistent with a carbon allocation to the fungal side during AM symbiosis (Kafle et al., 2019), which strengthens the possibility that MtSWEET1b indeed exports sugars to AM fungi. However, formal proof that MtSWEET1b indeed exports glucose across the peri-arbuscular membrane remains to be shown, which is complicated by the fact that the fungus also obtains carbon in the form of fatty acids that can be converted into sugars by the fungus (Jiang et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).

The observation that overexpression of MtSWEET1b increased the mycorrhization level may suggest that more glucose was supplied to the AM fungi thereby promoting the growth of the fungus inside the roots. However, the absence of any effect on arbuscule formation or mycorrhization levels in the Tnt1 MtSWEET1b insertion lines challenged the importance of glucose efflux into AM fungi during AM symbiosis. The insertion lines could still produce truncated MtSWEET1b proteins, which may still retain certain transport activity that could explain the lack of mycorrhization phenotypes. However, we consider it very unlikely, since the predicted deletion of transmembrane domains would seriously disrupt the protein configuration in the membrane. Expression of such a truncated MtSWEET1b protein did not allow the hexose-transport deficient EBY.VW4000 yeast strain to grow on glucose-containing medium, indicating that at least the glucose transport ability of MtSWEET1b is indeed lost. Thus, our genetic data indicate that the AM fungus is still able to obtain sufficient carbohydrates to sustain fungal growth in host plants in which glucose transport activity derived from MtSWEET1b is lost. This further implies that there is functional redundancy between MtSWEET1b and other related SWEET family members or that there is compensation through sugar uptake from the apoplast by the intraradical hyphae This article is protected by copyright.
