Salinity affects plant growth and development and causes low crop productivity [1]. Salinity can give rise to osmotic stress, nutritional imbalance, and ionic toxicity in the plant [2,3]. Among major cereal crops, rice (Oryza sativa) is the most sensitive to salinity stress [2,4].

The high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter (HKT) gene family has been found to be relevant to salt stress tolerance in plants [5,6]. The first HKT gene in plants, TaHKT2;1 from bread wheat Triticum aestivum, was reported to be a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ co-transporter [7]. HKTs can be classified into at least two subfamilies [5,8]. Subfamily 1 HKTs (HKT1s) are found in monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous species, and they are $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selective transporters. So far, only monocotyledonous species contain the subfamily 2 HKTs (HKT2s) that are selective for both $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ [9]. Interestingly, both HKT1 and HKT2 proteins were suggested to exhibit features of a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ channel when the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration at extracellular spaces are high [7,10,11]. In fact, AtHKT1;1 in Arabidopsis, belongs to the subfamily 1, has been demonstrated to show a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ channel activity by comparative patch clamping analyses using wild-type and athkt1;1 loss-of-function mutants [12]. In a japonica cultivar of rice, seven functional OsHKT genes have been identified [13]. Four of them were grouped in the HKT1 gene subfamily and those products, OsHKT1;1,

OsHKT1;3, OsHKT1;4 and OsHKT1;5, were shown to be $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ selective by the two-electrode voltage clamp experiment using Xenopus laevis oocytes [14–17].

Salinity is a major abiotic stress influencing agricultural production around the world and represents a major threat to the maintenance of crop yields, because most crop species are sensitive to the accumulation of sodium in shoot tissues (Tester and Davenport 2003). In the Triticeae, sodium exclusion from roots and leaf tissues is one of the major mechanisms conferring salt tolerance (Gorham et al. 1990; Munns et al. 2006). Modern durum wheat cultivars do not exclude $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the same extent as bread wheat (Triticum aestivum). Two QTLs originating from Triticum monococcum and involved in salinity tolerance, Nax1 $\mathrm { \Delta N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion 1) and Nax2 $\mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ exclusion 2), were found to correspond to HKT genes [respectively, of HKT1;4 and HKT1;5 types; (Lindsay et al. 2004; Byrt et al. 2007)]. Moreover, HKT genes shown to be associated to QTLs for salinity tolerance belong to subfamily 1. They have been shown to play crucial roles in salinity tolerance in different plant species (Munns et al. 2012; Asins et al. 2013). Nax1 is a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter, a member of the HKT (high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter) family, T. monococcum HKT1;4-A2 (Huang et al. 2006). The Nax1 gene confers a reduced rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and retention of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the leaf sheath, thus giving a higher sheath-to-blade $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration ratio (James et al. 2006). The second gene, Nax2, also confers a lower rate of transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from root to shoot and has a higher rate of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport, resulting in enhanced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ versus $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ discrimination in the leaf blade (James et al. 2006). The HKT gene family encodes proteins which form part of the $\mathrm { T r k / K t r / H K T }$ group of membrane transporters. These proteins have been shown to transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and/or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in bacteria, fungi and plants. HKT genes can be divided into two subfamilies, based on amino acid sequence homology, with members of subfamily 1, which mainly transport $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ while members of subfamily 2 transport $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Tester and Davenport 2003). Due to the transporting properties of the encoded HKT proteins, it is likely that a number of HKT proteins play important roles in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in plants and consequently have direct or indirect roles in determining salinity tolerance (Berthomieu et al. 2003; Haro et al. 2005; Ren et al. 2005; Rus et al. 2004; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Mäser et al. 2003).

Using the GUS reporter strategy and in situ hybridization, HKT gene expression patterns have so far been analyzed in detail in a few plant species aside from rice and Arabidopsis. HKT genes from subfamily 1 have systematically been found to be expressed in vascular tissues in all plants analyzed like rice, wheat, and Arabidopsis plants (Berthomieu et al. 2003, Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005; Sunarpi et al. 2005; Jabnoune et al. 2009; Munns et al. 2012). Some of these genes are essentially expressed in the vasculature system, like HKT1 in Arabidopsis and ice plants and HKT1;5 in rice and wheat. On the other hand, the expression patterns of the rice HKT1;3 and HKT1;4 genes also include the root peripheral cell layers and leaf bulliform cells, similar to the expression pattern of OsHKT2;1. Hence, in addition to root cation uptake, OsHKT2;1 is likely to play a role in long distance cation transport in the plant vasculature between roots and shoots, and in osmoregulatory processes in leaf tissues and bulliform cells, which control leaf rolling upon abiotic constraints (Kadioglu and Terzi 2007). HKT2;4 expression has only been analyzed in rice (Lan et al. 2010). The reported expression pattern is comprised in the root peripheral cell layers, leaf vasculature and mesophyll, so significantly overlaps with that of OsHKT2;1. Thus, the expression patterns of some members of the HKT subfamily 1 can be quite similar to those of members from the HKT subfamily 2. However, important differences in the regulation of expression seem to exist between subfamily 1 and subfamily 2 HKT, suggesting that the two types of genes play specific roles.

Indeed, enhancement of expression in roots in conditions of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ shortage, which has been consistently reported in the HKT subfamily 2, does not seem to occur in subfamily 1. On the other hand, members from both subfamilies can display regulation upon salt stress. This regulation appeared to be variable between tissues (roots and leaves), HKT genes and even between cultivars for some genes (Su et al. 2003; Ren et al. 2005). In this study, we isolated and characterized the promoter sequence of Triticum monococcum TmHKT1;4-A1 gene. The spatio-temporal activity of the PrTmHKT1;4-A1 fused to the gusA gene was investigated in stable transformed Arabidopsis plants under multiple inducible-abiotic-stress treatment and tissue-specific manner.

Maintaining low intracellular $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ concentrations is an essential physiological strategy in salt stress tolerance in most cereal crops. Here, we characterized a member of the high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter (HKT) family in barley (Hordeum vulgare), HvHKT1;5, which negatively regulates salt tolerance and has different functions from its homology in other cereal crops. HvHKT1;5 encodes a plasma membrane protein localized to root stele cells, particularly in xylem parenchyma cells adjacent to the xylem vessels. Its expression was highly induced by salt stress. Heterogenous expression of HvHKT1;5 in Xenopus laevis oocytes showed that HvHKT1;5 was permeable to ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } .$ , but not to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , although its $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport activity was inhibited by external $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ . HvHKT1;5 knockdown barley lines showed improved salt tolerance, a dramatic decrease in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ translocation from roots to shoots, and increases in the $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratio when compared with wild-type plants under salt stress. The negative regulation of HvHKT1;5 in salt tolerance distinguishes it from other HKT1;5 members, indicating that barley has a distinct $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ transport system. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the functions of HKT family members and the regulation of HvHKT1;5 in improving salt tolerance of barley.

Key words: high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter, Hordeum vulgare, ion homeostasis, $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ loading, salt tolerance

An important trait associated with the salt tolerance of wheat is the exclusion of sodium ions $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ from the shoot. We have previously shown that the sodium transporters TmHKT1;5-A and TaHKT1;5-D, from Triticum monoccocum (Tm) and Triticum aestivum (Ta), are encoded by genes underlying the major shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -exclusion loci Nax1 and Kna1, respectively. Here, using heterologous expression, we show that the afnity $( K _ { \mathrm { m } } )$ for the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport of TmHKT1;5-A, at $2 . 6 6 \mathrm { m M }$ , is higher than that of TaHKT1;5-D at $7 . 5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ . Through 3D structural modelling, we identify residues $\mathrm { D ^ { 4 7 1 } / a }$ gap and $\mathrm { D } ^ { 4 7 4 } /$ $\mathrm { G } ^ { 4 7 3 }$ that contribute to this property. We identify four additional mutations in amino acid residues that inhibit the transport activity of TmHKT1;5-A, which are predicted to be the result of an occlusion of the pore. We propose that the underlying transport properties of TmHKT1;5-A and TaHKT1;5-D contribute to their unique ability to improve $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion in wheat that leads to an improved salinity tolerance in the feld.

The efects of abiotic stresses are intensifying as a result of global warming, increased greenhouse gas emissions, and increased human activity, resulting in a $5 0 \%$ decrease in average cereal crop yields (Kole 2021). Salinity stress is one of the major abiotic stresses, and it is estimated that more than half of the global cultivable land will be in danger of salinization by 2050 (Kole 2021). Hence, an improved understanding of salt tolerance mechanisms in plants has become a key issue in abiotic stress physiology, and it is necessary to ensure optimal growing conditions and avoid crop yield and quality loss. Particularly, a high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio in the cytoplasmic, produces a series of intracellular alterations that afect the function of several transmembrane ion transport proteins (Davenport et al. 2007). Therefore, the ability of plants to maintain a balanced $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ratio therefore has a direct impact on their salt-tolerant ability. The highafnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter (HKT) is an important ion transporter in plants, which can improve salt tolerance by transferring $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or limiting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation by promoting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation (Riedelsberger et al. 2021). Based on the selectivity flter sequence and physiological features, the HKT gene family is divided into two subgroups. In the frst pore loop (P-loop; $\mathrm { P _ { A } }$ ), members of class I have Ser residues (S-GG-G), while members of class II have Gly residues (G-GG-G), which mostly infuence ion conduction. Generally, class I HKTs (S-G-G-G) are $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uniporters, whereas class II HKTs (G-G-G-G) mediate the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ symport (Platten et al. 2006; Riedelsberger et al. 2021). Nomenclature of HKT genes according to their subfamily membership, the names

HKT1;x or HKT2;y belonging to subfamily I or II, respectively (Platten et al. 2006).

In the study of salt tolerance mechanisms in plants, this unique transport ability has attracted a lot of attention. The frst HKT gene was cloned from wheat (Triticum aestivum) in 1994 (Schachtman and Schroeder 1994), and it has since been studied in Arabidopsis (Davenport et al. 2007), rice (Oryza sativa) (Riedelsberger et al. 2021), barley (Hordeum vulgare) (Huang et al. 2020), grape (Vitis vinifera) (Li et al. 2019), and other plants. The HKT gene family is the most comprehensive investigation in rice. There are now nine members of the HKT gene family discovered in rice, with two considered pseudogenes (Garciadeblás et al. 2003). However, the HKT gene family in foxtail millet has not been reported, and there is a lack of systematic study.

Foxtail millet is an important $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ cereal crop, with barren tolerance, strong adaptability, and a small diploid genome (Kole 2021; Li et al. 2022b). In addition, the germplasm resources of foxtail millet are rich in genetic diversity and contain a variety of excellent genes that can be used (Li et al. 2022b). Therefore, it is advantageous to cultivate salttolerant varieties and has far-reaching signifcance for the improvement of saline-alkali soil by exploring the HKTs in foxtail millet. The rapid-cycling mini foxtail millet mutant xiaomi has become a suitable $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ model plant, which lays the foundation for further exploration of millet genetic resources (Yang et al. 2020). Due to the potential functions of the HKT gene family to salt stress, we thoroughly characterized the HKT genes in foxtail millet. In this study, 7 SiHKT genes were identifed in the xiaomi genome and comprehensively analyzed, including their sequence features, chromosomal locations, phylogenetic relationships, and expression patterns in response to salt stress, which can help to identify the function of HKT genes in foxtail millet. In addition, the potential genes regulating SiHKTs were mined by WGCNA, which laid the foundation for further understanding the modulation mechanism of HKT expression in foxtail millet under salt stress.

## Chromosomal mapping, multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis


The distributions of SiHKTs on chromosomes were plotted with MG2C (http://mg2c.iask.in/mg2c_v2.0). Multiple sequence alignments of SiHKTs were performed by using ClustalX (https://www.genome.jp/tools-bin/clustalw) with default parameters (Thompson et al. 2002). Visualization of ClustalX results by ESPript 3.0 (https://espript.ibcp.fr/ ESPript/ESPript/index.php). The protein sequences of HKT in Arabidopsis, soybean, rice, sorghum, and maize were obtained from the Phytozome database (https://phytozomenext.jgi.doe.gov) (Supplementary Table 2). Multi-sequence alignment of the HKT protein sequences was conducted by ClustalW, and the phylogenetic tree was constructed by the Neighbor-Joining (NJ) method, the Jones-Taylor-Thornton (JTT) model and a bootstrap of 1000 in MEGA 11.0 (Tamura et al. 2021). The phylogenetic tree was displayed with Evolview (https://www.evolgenius.info/evolview).

Salinity and drought are two of the most common abiotic stresses that plants frequently encounter and cause a negative impact on their growth, development, and production due to ion toxicity and physiological drought (Munns and Tester 2008; Tang et  al. 2016). High-afnity potassium transporter (HKT) family proteins are anticipated to play an essential role in plant salt stress tolerance. HKTs were frst identifed as high-afnity potassium $( \mathrm { K ^ { + } } )$ transporters and were proven to transport sodium $\left( \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \right)$

via channels with other cations (Horie et al. 2009). HKTs are also responsible for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport as well as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ homeostasis in plants during plant development, making them potential goals for the development of salt tolerance in crops. Most of the research on the functional study of HKT family genes has focused on yeast and model plants such as Arabidopsis, as well as crops like wheat, maize, sorghum, barley, and eucalyptus (Liu et al. 2001; Rus et al. 2001; Haro et al. 2005; Munns et al. 2012; Ren et al. 2015; Li et al. 2019). However, a more thorough investigation needs to be into HKT family genes in rice.

In this study, we identifed nine HKT genes, whereas eight are functional depending on the japonica and indica cultivars from the rice genome database. Based on the conserved domain search, we confrmed that TrkH is conserved in all the HKT genes (Fig.  2). Te TrkH domain is a hydrophobic membrane protein vital in controlling $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ movement in higher plants, contributing to enhanced salinity tolerance (Horie et  al. 2009; Su et  al. 2015). All OsHKT proteins have similar physiological properties, comprising equal transmembrane helices, and are mainly localized in the plasma membrane (Table 1). Tese fndings indicate that HKT proteins have a close evolutionary connection with plants during biological evolution. Te paralogous pairs of OsHKT genes found in subfamily 1 and 2 of the monophyletic tree also indicate that each subfamily’s HKT genes undergo the same evolutionary process and serve the same functions, and potentially retain plant resistance to salt stress (Maser et al. 2002; Li et al. 2019). Furthermore, ten distinct motifs were discovered, and most of the motifs appeared in rice HKT proteins (Fig. 3B), suggesting that they are relatively conserved and have a strong evolutionary relationship (Singh et al. 2002). HKT genes have three exons and two introns (Fig. 4), demonstrating even more clearly that HKT genes in plants have been evolutionary conserved because the exon–intron arrangement has been utilized as supporting proof for developmental relationships between genes (Koralewski and Krutovsky 2011). In addition, gene duplication events are one of the critical factors that could provide a profound explanation for gene family expansion in plants (Moore and Purugganan 2005). Te chromosomal location ofers valuable information about tandem and segmental duplications of a specifc family gene. Two or more genes located on the same chromosome reveal the possibility of tandem duplication, while genes situated on diferent chromosomes indicate segmental duplication events (Zhu et  al. 2014; Nasim et al. 2016). Notably, two pairs of paralogous OsHKT genes (OsHKT1;4/OsHKT1;5 and OsHKT2;3/ OsHKT2;4) are segmentally duplicated, including OsHKT2;1/Po_OsHKT2;2 was discovered to be tandemly duplicated due to gene distributions on the same chromosome (Fig.  5). To understand functional sites and functional protein alterations, selective pressure investigations are generally required as they reveal selective benefts for changing amino acid sequences in the protein (Morgan et  al. 2010). Te $\mathrm { K a } / \mathrm { K } s$ value $< 1$ indicates the purifying selection, while the Ka/Ks ratio $> 1$ proposes the probability of a positive selection (Yang and Bielawski 2000; Bowers et al. 2003). Based on the $\mathrm { K a } / \mathrm { K } s$ values for both segmental and tandem, they indicated that rice HKT genes have undergone intense purifying selection pressure (Table  2). Te phylogenetic tree (Fig.  6) indicated that rice HKT proteins were related to monocot and dicot; however, they were more closely related to wheat and maize HKT proteins. Te highly conserved cluster of HKT genes provided evidence that they perform similar functions rather than being the result of a series of evolutionary events (Zhang et al. 2013). One pair of orthologous OsHKT genes with maize (OsHKT1;5/ Zm00008a011700) revealed the purifying selection and showed the same intron numbers, which means conserved gene organization (Table  2). Tese fndings suggest that the orthologous pair arose from the common inherited genes that existed before the divergence of the monocots and dicots. It is also mentioned that purifying selection played a vital role in the evolution of the HKT genes in other crop species (Zhang et al. 2019).

Transcription factors are pivotal in regulating the plant’s response to abiotic stress by modulating the gene expression (Lindemose et al. 2013). Regulatory elements are crucial for detecting gene expression patterns, as regulatory elements control the expression of many genes through distinct binding sites (Mariño-Ramírez et  al. 2009). WRKY, bHLH, bZIP, MYB, AP2/ERF, GATA, B3, Dof, and C2H2 type important binding sites that were highly distributed in all the promoter regions of OsHKT genes. TFs like WRKY, NAC, bHLH, bZIP, MYB, and AP2/ERF play vital roles in the responses to abiotic and biotic stress in many plant species (Lindemose et  al. 2013; Das et  al. 2019). Moreover, B3, a plant-specifc transcription factor, has a variety of roles in the growth and development of plants (Peng and Weselake 2013), GATA is involved in light responsiveness (Behringer and Schwechheimer 2015), C2H2 type transcription factor plays a diverse role in plant growth and development as well response to stress (Yin et al. 2020) and Dof transcription factor also participates in many plant development stages and the response to diferent environmental stressors (Khan et al. 2021). Te OsHKT genes possess a high abundance of stress-responsive cis-regulatory elements (CREs) such as MYB, MYC, MBS, W-box, ARE, STRE and DRE core. Te expression of MBS, which is a binding site for MYB TF, changes in many plants when exposed to salt, suggesting that these plants are responding to salt stress (Hua et al. 2006). Moreover, members of this TF also infuence the abscisic acid (ABA), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and SA-signalling pathways, which confer resistance to abiotic stresses (Ambawat et  al. 2013). TGACG, CGTCA-motif, ERE, and ABRE were also abundant in the rice HKT promoter region. Te next most common type of cis-acting elements were those that regulated growth and development, hormones, and light. Te GT1-motif, as1, G-box, TCCC, and Box-4 are more frequently present in rice HKT promoters that were responsive to light. On the other hand, TGACG and CGTCA-motif were responsive to methyl jasmonate, ERE was responsive to ethylene, ABRE was responsive to abscisic acid (ABA), TCA was responsive to salicylic acid, TGA was responsive to auxins and P-box and GAREmotif were responsive to gibberellin. Plant hormones and other signalling pathways are important for adequate and integrated stress responses (Ryu and Cho 2015). ABA, methyl jasmonate, and ethylene have been suggested as factors governing adaptive responses to abiotic stimuli, while auxin, salicylic acid, and gibberellin are essential in growth and development. Te presence of TGACG and CGTCA motifs suggests that methyl jasmonate may be involved in the regulation of the OsHKT gene. In line with this, a signifcant concentration of methyl jasmonate has been found in salt-tolerant rice cultivars (Kang et al. 2005). ERE-containing genes are regulated in the context of ethylene. It has been proposed that ethylene controls salt-responsive gene expression under salt stress (Verma et al. 2016). Most abiotic stress-responsive gene promoter regions comprise two cis-regulating elements, namely ABA-responsive elements (ABRE) and dehydration-responsive elements (DRE), both of which contain the core sequences ACGTGG/TC and TACCGA CAT or A/GCCGAC, respectively (Kobayashi et al. 2004; Yamaguchi-Shinozaki and Shinozaki 2006) and the ABRE motif participates in the ABA-dependent gene expression under high-stress situations (Finkelstein 2013). According to previous research, there are interactions between ABA and methyl jasmonate at the MYC2 transcription factor, which is implicated in the control of gene expression under salt stress (Moons et  al. 1997). Tus, cis-elements pertaining to ABA, ethylene, and methyl jasmonate suggest that these hormones have roles in OsHKTs in response to abiotic stresses. Various elements, such as W-box, WUN-motif, LTR, and TC-rich repeat also present in OsHKT promoter regions, are implicated in the salt stress response and defence (Gao et  al. 2010; Li et  al. 2013; Manimaran et  al. 2017). According to promoter analysis, OsHKTs may respond to environmental stress and stimuli to regulate plant growth and development. On the other hand, we have discovered that a wide range of transcription factors control OsHKT gene expression. Tese include C2H2 zinc fnger protein, Myb transcription factor, Dof zinc fnger domain-containing protein, DNA binding domain-containing protein, B3 domain-containing RAV and trihelix family-type protein, ARF, and dehydration-responsive transcription factors. Recent fndings have reported that the expression of OsHKT1;1 has been positively regulated by OsMYBc. It binds to specifc conserved DNA regions in the OsHKT1;1 promoter, modulating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and preventing sodium toxicity in leaf blades (Wang et al. 2015). Knocking out OsMYBc also led to a decrease in the salt-induced expression of OsHKT1;1, and modifcations in specifc promoter regions resulted in reduced OsHKT1;1 promoter activity. To increase the expression of OsHKT1;5, the stable complex of OsSUVH7, OsMYB106, and OsBAG4 binds to the promoter of OsHKT1;5 (Wang et  al. 2020). It has been shown that the bHLH transcription factor OsbHLH035 controls the expression of the genes OsHKT1;3 and OsHKT1;5. Tese fndings indicate that OsbHLH035 positively infuences the expression of OsHKT1;3 and OsHKT1;5 (Chen et al. 2018). Chen and his team identifed a popular TF, PalERF109, as a positive regulator of the PalHKT1 gene expression (Chen et  al. 2020b). In Arabidopsis, several TFs, such as AtbZIP24, ARR1, ARR12, and ABI4, have been found to regulate AtHKT1;1 expression (Yang et al. 2009; Mason et al. 2010; Shkolnik-Inbar et al. 2013). Te observation indicated that AtbZIP24, ARR1, and ARR12 are negative regulators of AtHKT1;1 gene expression. Additionally, ABI4 TF also negatively regulates AtHKT1;1 gene expression, and the involvement of the abscisic acid signal transduction pathway in salt responses in Arabidopsis suggests that OsHKT1;5 may play a similar function in rice. Te GT factors are a family of transcription factors found exclusively in plants and share a common DNA-binding trihelix domain. GT elements have A/T-rich core sequences and are highly degenerate ciselements. OsGTγ-1, OsGTγ-2, and OsGTγ-3 genes were upregulated in response to high salinity and other abiotic stimuli, suggesting a role for this subfamily transcriptional regulation of stress responses. At the vegetative stage, transgenic rice with an overexpression of OsGTγ- 1 demonstrated an improvement in their salt tolerance (Fang et al. 2010). On the other hand, DREB TFs, which mainly bind with C-repeat/DRE (A/GCCGAC), infuence the expression of several cold or drought-inducible genes in an ABA-independent route, enhancing plant abiotic stress tolerance (Chen et al. 2008). Tus, these TFs have roles in OsHKTs in response to abiotic stresses.

In our study, OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;5 had higher expression levels in both vegetative and reproductive tissues. On the other hand, OsHKT1;3, OsHKT2;1, and OsHKT2;4 had higher expression in the vegetative stage, while OsHKT1;4 had lower expression in the vegetative stage (Fig.  11A). Also, both salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive genotypes have higher expression of OsHKT1;5, OsHKT1;1, OsHKT1;3, and OsHKT2;1 (Fig.  11B). Our real-time PCR results have confrmed that OsHKT1;5, OsHKT1;1, OsHKT1;3, OsHKT2;1, and OsHKT2;3 are crucial genes responsible for rice salinity tolerance (Fig. 12). Te previous study on OsHKT1;4 also reported lower expression in a vegetative stage during stress (Suzuki et al. 2016). A rice QTL, SKC1, corresponded to OsHKT1;5 and maintained $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ion homeostasis under salt stress (Ren et  al. 2005), and OsHKT1;5 mutants also showed $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and protected leaf blades under salt stress (Kobayashi et  al. 2017). OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;4 contribute to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from leaf blades under salt stress (Cotsaftis et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2015; Suzuki et al. 2016). OsHKT2;1/2 is also involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ co-transport under high salt concentrations and has been reported to maintain an appropriate ionic balance in Nona bokra (Oomen et  al. 2012). Te previous report also suggested that HKT genes play a vital role in response to salt stress in many plant species like wheat (Munns et  al. 2012; Schachtman and Schroeder 1994), Arabidopsis (Sunarpi et al. 2005), maize (Ren et al. 2015) and barley (Mian et  al. 2011). Tus, HKT genes in rice may be excellent candidate genes for accelerating transgenic research for salinity stress management in plant growth and development.

Proteins rarely function alone. A protein’s activity can be activated, inhibited, or otherwise regulated through its interactions with other proteins or biological components. So far, no study has been disclosed identifying interaction partners for any HKT protein. Te protein– protein interaction exhibited exciting facts about the substantial contribution of OsHKT to numerous physiological functions (Fig.  13). Our fndings show that rice HKT genes (OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT2;1) interact with the P5CS, which participates in salt stress tolerance and plays a vital role in proline biosynthesis (Zhang et  al. 2014; Funck et  al. 2020). Likewise, the OsHKT gene interacted with NHX1 and NHX2, a sodium/hydrogen exchanger-related protein that plays a central role during plant exposure to $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ defciency and high salinity (Fukuda et al. 2011; Barragán et al. 2012; Teng et al. 2017); HAK1, HAK23, and HAK27 are related to high-afnity potassium transporters that also transport rubidium. Furthermore, Os01g0893400 is a putative BTB and TAZ domain protein, and TPKC is an inward-rectifying potassium channel family protein that is known to be important in plant growth and development (Bhattacharjee et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018). Interestingly, a small heat shock family protein, Hsp20/alpha-crystallin family protein, also interacts with rice HKT genes. Small HSPs are hypothesized to act as chaperones, protecting their targets against denaturation and aggregation when organisms are exposed to diverse biotic and abiotic stimuli. A recent study indicated that OsHSP20 exhibits molecular chaperone functions in  vitro, and overexpression has been shown to improve heat and salt stress tolerance in E. coli, $P .$ pastoris, and transgenic rice plants. It was also found that the N-terminal part of OsHSP20 is tightly linked to both in vivo stress tolerance and in vitro chaperone activity (Guo et al. 2020). Our results highlighted the signifcance of HKT transporters in rice salinity tolerance via their interactions with other proteins.

Plant cellular responses to abiotic stresses such as salinity, cold, and dehydration were revealed to be regulated by microRNA. Several miRNAs target genes that are actively involved in gene regulation or their associated transcription factors in response to stress. MiRNAs may play an essential role in reactions triggered by stress (Cheng and Long 2007; Sunkar et al. 2008). Fifteen OsamiR11339 (bona fde mRNAs from rice) found in rice HKT genes represent lipid metabolisms in rice by targeting the terpene synthase gene (LOC_Os07g11790) (Baldrich et  al. 2015) and also revealing the role in protein and starch metabolisms during grain flling under high day time temperature (HDT) stress (Payne et  al. 2023). Four Osa-miR11343 genes found in rice HKT genes are involved in biotic stress by targeting the MLO domaincontaining protein (LOC_Os10g39520) in rice. One novel Osa-miR5819 has three target sites found in rice HKT gene-targeted CPuORF -containing bZIP38 TF and lipid transfer protein (LTPL118) subject to translational control via regulation by sucrose (Baldrich et  al. 2015). Sucrose is a signal molecule that is involved in the activation of plant defense mechanisms. Another miR444 found in the rice HKT gene specifcally targets the MADS-box transcription factors, which play an essential role in the HDT-induced caryopsis development, (Payne et al. 2023). Evidence has also shown that heat stress has been demonstrated to induce an upregulation of miR444 in maize (He et  al. 2019). Interestingly, we found two microRNAs, Osa-miR1846 and Osa-miRN45, have several target sites in rice HKT genes. In both CDT and HDT, Osa-miR1846 was found to be strongly expressed during grain flling in the spikelets and its targeting of a heat shock factor (HSF) (Kushawaha et  al. 2021). HSFs may cause chalkiness by increasing the expression of heat shock proteins (Kaneko et al. 2016). Terefore, it is probable that increased amounts of Osa-miR1846 in the Cypress inhibit this HSF, resulting in less chalkiness. On the other hand, Osa-miRN45 has a particular function to play throughout the diferentiation process at the time of grain flling in rice (Peng et  al. 2013). Together, these fndings lay the groundwork for future genetic studies of OsHKT genes and facilitate the breeding of novel rice cultivars.

Phylogenetic analysis and gene structure of MdZIPs

Although ZIP family proteins have been reported in various species, the genes of this family have not been reported in apple. Complete genome sequencing of apple has provided a possibility for studying gene families in this species (Velasco et al. 2010). In the present study, we identified 18 candidate ZIP gene family members, which were designated MdZIP1-18, based on their chromosomal locations (Table 1). To characterize the evolutionary relationships among ZIP family proteins, sequences of all the ZIP proteins of apple were phylogenetically analyzed (Fig. 1a). MdZIPs were divided into four groups (I–IV): MdZIP8, MdZIP7, MdZIP12, MdZIP11, MdZIP3, MdZIP13, and MdZIP2 belonged to group I, MdZIP6, MdZIP18, MdZIP16, and MdZIP15 belonged to group II, MdZIP1, MdZIP14, MdZIP5, and MdZIP4 belonged to group III, and MdZIP9, MdZIP10, and MdZIP17 belonged to group IV, consistent with a precious study on ZmZIPs and PtZIPs (Fu et al. 2017; Li et al. 2013). The survey on the structure of MdZIP genes revealed that the number of exon/intron-containing ZIP genes ranged from 1 to 11 (Fig. 1b).

Furthermore, MdZIP family members within the same cluster exhibited similar gene structures. To characterize the evolutionary history of the ZIP gene family further, the reported ZIP gene sequences of various species were used for phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 2). The phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that some MdZIP genes analyzed in the present study were closely related to those of dicotyledons, whereas the others were closely related to those of monocotyledons, consistent with the previous reports on maize and Marchantia polymorpha L. (Li et al. 2013; Lo et al. 2016). These findings suggested that ZIP family proteins were conserved across clades. The 18 MdZIP genes were mapped to eight apple chromosomes (Fig. 3). Additionally, most members in the phylogenetic tree exhibited closely related protein structures (Fig. 4). The protein structure of each member of MdZIP proteins was different. Most of which contain 6–9 motifs, while MdZIP1 and MdZIP14 protein contains two domains. In addition, sequence analysis showed that all identified MdZIP proteins contained (TM) domains 8 and motifs information analysis showed that the motif1, motif2, motif3, motif4, motif5, motif6 and motif9 had transmembrane domain (Fig. S1, Table S2). It was usually considered that a variable region it may be related to the binding and transport of metal ions.

## qRT-PCR analysis and expression patterns of MdZIP genes


The seedlings of M. hupehensis showed significant phenotypic changes under Zn and Fe deficiency. Young leaves exhibited chlorosis, and the plants were shorter and the length, tip number, surface area, average diam and volume of roots of seedlings decreased under Fe deficiency; under Zn deficiency, the plants were shorter and the length, tip number, surface area, average diam and volume of roots of seedlings decreased (Figs. S2–S4). In order to study this phenomenon, we conducted analysis of qRT-PCR and expression patterns of MdZIP genes.

MdZIP genes expression patterns varied among the different stress conditions studied. Previous phylogenetic analyses enabled the prediction of gene function (Fu et al. 2017; Li et al. 2013). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that MdZIP9, MdZIP17, and MdZIP10 image of iron coloring according to the Prussian blue reaction in apical and steles, and whole seedlings of 12-days-old WT and transgenic OX-26 lines of A. thaliana grown on standard MS medium $\mathrm { ( p H } 5 . 7 \mathrm { ) }$ , obtained using fluorescence microscope

clustered with AtZIP9, AtIRT3, and AtZIP4, which were induced by Zn-deficient conditions (Fig. 2) (Talke et al. 2006; Grotz et al. 1998). The expression of MdZIP9, MdZIP17, and MdZIP10 was highly induced in the roots and shoots of plants exposed to Zn deficiency, indicating that these three MdZIPs might be functional orthologs of AtZIP9, AtIRT3, and AtZIP4, respectively (Fig. 5). Four MdZIPs (MdZIP15, MdZIP16, MdZIP6, and MdZIP18) and two AtZIPs (AtIRT1 and AtIRT2), which are closely related (Fig. 2), were induced by Fe deficiency (Vert et al. 2002). In the present study, these ZIPs were also induced by Fe deficiency (Fig. 5), indicating that these genes enhanced the uptake and soil-to-root translocation of Fe when Fe availability was low. The phylogenetic analysis showed that MdZIP7, MdZIP3, MdZIP11, and MdZIP13 were closely related to AtZIP6 and AtZIP1 (Fig. 2), which were induced under Zn-deficient conditions (Grotz et al. 1998;

Bauer and Bereczky 2004). In the present study, the expression of MdZIP7, MdZIP3, MdZIP11, and MdZIP13 in the roots and shoots of plants exposed to Zn deficiency was sensitive to increases in Zn concentration (Fig. 5), indicating that the high transcription levels of these four MdZIP genes were responsible for the higher uptake and root-to-shoot translocation of Zn. The phylogenetic analysis revealed that MdZIP14 and MdZIP1 clustered with

AtZIP2 and AtZIP11 (Fig. 2). A previous study reported that AtZIP11 and AtZIP2 might be expressed in the root of A. thaliana (Milner et al. 2013; Olsen and Palmgren 2014). In the present study, Zn deficiency enhanced the expression of MdZIP14 and MdZIP1 in the roots, suggesting that they might be functional orthologs of AtZIP2 and AtZIP11, respectively (Fig. 5a). These results indicated that MdZIP family members respond to $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe deficiency.

Expressing MdZIP10 in Arabidopsis increases its Zn and Fe contents

To evaluate the biological functions of MdZIP genes, MdZIP10 was further analyzed, because it its expression was induced in the roots and shoots of plants under Fe- and Zn-deficient conditions. Previous studies have shown that the overexpression of ZmIRT1, ZmZIP3 and ZmZIP7 increases the accumulation of Zn and Fe in A. thaliana (Li et al. 2015, 2016). In the present study, MdZIP10-overexpressing transgenic plants accumulated more Fe and Zn in their shoots and roots than did the WT plants (Fig. 6a, b). We colored iron in plant tissues according to the Prussian blue reaction. As shown in Fig. 7e, the roots (steles and apical) of MdZIP10-overexpressing transgenic plants were bluer than in the roots of WT plants, and transgenic leaves were bluer than WT leaves (Fig. 6c). Visualization of Zinpyr-1 revealed that fluorescence signals were considerably stronger in the roots (lateral and apical) of transgenic plants than in the roots of WT plants (Fig. 7d–i). In addition, fluorescence intensity was weaker in WT seedlings than in transgenic OX-26 line seedlings (Fig. 7a–c). The stronger the fluorescence intensity, the more zinc was contained (Li et al. 2016). These results showed that MdZIP10 overexpression increased the Zn content of A. thaliana, and enhanced Fe storage in its roots and leaves. Thus, MdZIP10 seems to have a direct role in the uptake and transport of Zn and Fe in apple.


## Yeast complementation and overexpression of MdZIP10 enhances tolerance to Zn and Fe deficiencies


To determine the metal transport specificities of the MdZIP10, we performed yeast functional complementation experiment for the MdZIP10. The result showed that MdZIP10 grew well on Zn-sufficient and Znlimited mediums (Fig. 8a). Similarly, in the presence of $0 . 0 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ or $0 . 0 2 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ BPDS, the fet3fet4 mutant could be complemented by MdZIP10 (Fig. 8b). These results showed that MdZIP10 were able to complement zrt1zrt2 and fet3fet4 mutant and transport Zn and Fe.

The overexpression of MdZIP10 alleviated Fe and Zn deficiency symptoms, and the roots were considerably longer in transgenic than in WT lines under normal conditions (Fig. 9a–c). However, the roots of both WT and transgenic lines exhibited no significant differences in the expression of MdZIP10 when exposed to excess Zn and Fe (Fig. 9d–f). The overexpression of MpZIP3 has been reported to increase the content of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe in M. polymorpha and alleviate Fe-deficiency symptoms (Lo et al. 2016); moreover, the increased uptake of Fe by roots and transport in response to Fe deficiency and immanently high active Fe content are important mechanisms of tolerating low Fe stress (Zha et al. 2014). Thus,

MdZIP10 transgenic $A$ . thaliana might enhance the uptake and root-to-shoot translocation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe, when the available contents of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Fe are low.

Changes in the expression of genes related to the uptake and transport Fe and Zn are closely associated with changes in endogenous metal contents and phenotypes of transgenic plants (Li et al. 2015). Under Fe-deficient conditions, the bHLH transcription factor AtFIT exhibits a positive effect on the Fe uptake mechanism of A. thaliana (Lo et al. 2016). Under Zndeficient conditions, the transcription factors bZIP19 and bZIP24 regulate the expression of some ZIP transporters, including ZIP1 in the root of A. thaliana (Assunc¸a˜o et al. 2010; Inaba et al. 2015). Additionally, IRT1 was induced in Fe-deficient roots (Klatte et al. 2009), and HMA2 played important roles in maintaining intracellular metal homeostasis (Hussain et al. 2004). In the present study, the expression of FIT, bZIP19, bZIP24, FRO2, IRT1, HMA2, IRT3, and ZIPs increased under Zn-deficient conditions (Fig. S5). We found that the expression of FIT, bZIP19, bZIP24, FRO2, IRT1, HMA2, IRT3, and ZIPs also increased in MdZIP10-transgenic plants under Fe-deficient conditions (Fig. S6). These results suggest that the upregulation of these genes in the MdZIP10-overexpressing plants might not only facilitate the uptake and transport of $Z \mathbf { n }$ and Fe, but also contribute to the changes observed in root architecture to a certain extent, thus alleviating the symptoms of Zn and Fe deficiencies.

The organisms that populated the primordial Earth lived in an anaerobic environment where Fe was predominantly reduced, soluble, and biologically abundant. As photosynthetic organisms proliferated and transformed Earths atmosphere, however, Fe became increasingly oxidized and biologically scarce. Fe bioavailability is thus low in over one-third of the Earths land surface area, particularly in alkaline or calcareous soils (Crowley et al.1987). This has imposed enormous selective pressures on terrestrial plants and microorganisms to develop efficient strategies for solubilizing Fe from the soil.

Most aerobic organisms have evolved mechanisms to solubilize Fe based on the chemical processes of chelation, reduction, and acidification (reviewed in Kochian 1991, 2000). These strategies of Fe acquisition are restricted to discrete phylogenetic groups. Yeast and all plants except the grasses reduce $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ chelates and absorb the more soluble $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ ion released by this process. Under Fe deficiency, species of this group induce the activity of a plasma membrane ferric chelate reductase and also stimulate the release of protons, both of which enhance the solubility of soil Fe. Other classes of organisms, including fungi, bacteria, and members of the family Poaceae (the grasses), release high-affinity $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ -chelating compounds, called siderophores, that solubilize $\mathrm { F e ( I I I ) }$ and are then recognized for uptake by specific membrane receptors (Ro¨ mheld and Marschner 1986; Chaney 1987; Bienfait 1988).

Previous work has shown that Fe deficiency in many nongrass plant species elicits a stimulated influx of Fe and other divalent cations. Fox et al. (1996) found that Fe-deficient pea seedlings exhibited higher rates of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx compared to Fe-sufficient seedlings. Furthermore, tissue concentrations of Fe and other mineral elements can be influenced by plant Fe status. Welch et al. (1993) demonstrated that the shoot concentrations of several divalent cationic metals, including Cu, Mn, and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { g }$ increased in Fe-deficient pea seedlings compared to Fesufficient pea seedlings. Rodecap et al. (1994) also reported that Fe-deficient Arabidopsis plants accumulated higher concentrations of Cd and $\mathrm { M g }$ in racemes and seeds compared to Fe-sufficient plants.

We previously demonstrated that Fe deficiency induced a high affinity Cd influx into roots of pea seedlings, a finding that has implications for the entry of heavy metals into food crops (Cohen et al. 1998a). Our preliminary investigations into the mechanistic basis for this observation suggested that Fe deficiency induces a divalent cation transporter that can facilitate $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. We established that expression of a homolog of the Arabidopsis IRT1 Fe transporter gene (Eide et al. 1996) was induced in roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. When expressed in yeast, it was found that this transporter could mediate $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake (Cohen et al. 1998b). Enhanced expression of this gene could increase IRT1 density in the root-cell plasma membrane and could account for the observed stimulation in root Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake.

IRT1 is a member of the ZIP family of metal transporters that are hypothesized to play a role in micronutrient nutrition, and in particular in Fe and $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake and transport (Guerinot 2000). The ZIP designation, which stands for ZRT, IRT-like protein, comes from the names of the first members of this family to be identified. IRT1 (iron-regulated transporter), a transporter first identified in Arabidopsis, is induced by Fe deficiency in roots, and has been suggested to be an Fe transporter (Eide et al. 1996). ZRT1 and ZRT2 (zinc-regulated transporter) are high and low affinity $Z \mathfrak { n }$ transporters in yeast that are regulated by changes in cellular $Z \mathrm { n }$ status (Zhao and Eide 1996a, 1996b). Some ZIP family members have been cloned from several plant species including Arabidopsis (IRT-1, -2; ZIP 1–4), Thlaspi caerulescens (ZNT-1, -2) and tomato (LeIRT-1 -2) (Eide et al. 1996; Grotz et al. 1998; Pence et al. 2000; Assunc¸ ao et al. 2001; Eckhardt et al. 2001; Vert et al. 2001). In some of these studies, heterologous expression of ZIP genes in yeast mutants defective in specific micronutrient uptake systems have provided researchers with information concerning the transport properties of the ZIP proteins. What is emerging from these studies is the concept that some of these transporters may exhibit a fairly broad specificity with regards to the micronutrient metal transported. For example, based on heterologous expression studies in yeast, it was suggested that IRT1 may transport $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ in addition to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Korshunova et al. 1999). However, caution must be exercised in extrapolating these findings in yeast to higher plants growing in the soil, particularly since the metal concentrations used in these studies were much higher than those found in the soil or rhizosphere.

More recently, studies from three different laboratories using Arabidopsis knockout mutants for IRT1 have provided more direct evidence that IRT1 is a major transporter responsible for Fe uptake and homeostasis in higher plants (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In each of these studies, the IRT1 knockout based on T-DNA insertion yielded plants that had visual shoot symptoms consistent with Fe deficiency (reduced growth, chlorotic leaves) and growth on elevated levels of Fe restored the wild-type phenotype. Furthermore, in the studies of Varotto et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), analysis of Fe accumulation and transport indicated that root Fe uptake and plant Fe accumulation were significantly reduced in the irt1 mutants, strongly suggesting a central role for this transporter in plant Fe nutrition.

The findings described here are a continuation of the work published in Cohen et al. (1998a), and address the mechanistic basis for the ‘‘induction’’ of root Cd and Zn uptake by imposition of Fe deficiency in Pisum sativum. Here, we tested the hypothesis that enhanced expression of a pea IRT1 orthologue could account for the stimulation in divalent cation influx during Fe deficiency. A cDNA clone that confers Fe transport activity was isolated from a library constructed with mRNA collected from roots of Fe-deficient pea seedlings. The tissuespecific expression of this gene in response to changes in plant Fe status was investigated, along with functional complementation of yeast mutants that are defective in high- and low-affinity iron or zinc transport. In this heterologous system, a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic investigation of Fe, Zn, and Cd uptake was carried out at metal concentrations that are physiologically relevant to plant roots growing in agricultural soils.

IRT1, the founding member of ZIP transporter family, was identified by a powerful suppressor screen based on the complementation of yeast fet3 multicopper oxidase and fet4 Fe(II)-transporter mutations that block high and low affinity iron transport, respectively (Askwith et al., 1994; Dix et al., 1994;

Eide et al., 1996). IRT1 was also found to suppress the zrt1zrt2 mutations of high and low-affinity zinc transporters and the smf1 $\Delta$ mutation of a high-affinity Nramp manganese transporter, as well as to increase cadmium sensitivity, when expressed in yeast (Korshunova et al., 1999; Rogers et al., 2000). Nonetheless, IRT1 turned out to differ both structurally and functionally from these yeast transporter proteins, but shows homology to numerous putative membrane proteins in eukaryotes, including predicted products of $1 5 ~ Z I P$ genes in the sequenced Arabidopsis genome (Guerinot, 2000; Mäser et al., 2001). Characterization of other members of ZIP family indicated that IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1, facilitates iron and zinc uptake, whereas ZIP1, ZIP2 and ZIP3 mediate only zinc transport in yeast. IRT1 and IRT2 are induced by iron depletion, whereas ZIP1, ZIP2 and ZIP3 are activated by zinc deficiency specifically in Arabidopsis roots (Eide et al., 1996; Grotz et al., 1998; Vert et al., 2001). By contrast ZIP4, carrying a putative chloroplast signal peptide, was suggested to function as leaf specific zinc-regulated transporter (Grotz et al., 1998). In addition to the ZIP family, however, 3 members of the Arabidopsis NRAMP (natural-resistanceassociated macrophage protein) family were also identified to respond to iron depletion and to mediate iron and cadmium uptake (Curie et al., 2000; Thomine et al., 2000). Recent finding of homologs of maize

YS1 (yellow strip 1) gene in Arabidopsis suggests that even further transporters are implicated in the control of iron homeostasis in plants (Curie et al., 2001).

This high redundancy raises the logical question whether reverse genetics, producing single recessive or dominant gene mutations, would be helpful in the dissection of physiological functions of individual plant metal transporters. The knock-out of IRT1 function described above provides an encouraging answer suggesting that quantitative differences in the contribution of individual metal transporters, as well as differences in their spatial and temporal regulation, may result in characteristic phenotypes of individual transporter mutants. Thus, our data show that inactivation of IRT1 results in shoot iron deficiency leading to severe chlorosis and lethality. However, it is likely that the reduction of zinc uptake in the irt1 mutant contributes to the phenotype, as the irt1 mutant shows also bleaching in zinc-depleted iron-sufficient medium (unpublished). Characteristic changes in the differentiation of specific cell layers in leaf, stem and root may thus reflect consequences of a combined iron and zinc deficiency in the irt1 mutant. Due to functional redundancy of iron and zinc transporters, the irt1 knock-out does not completely abolish iron and zinc uptake by the roots, thus the otherwise unviable chlorotic irt1 mutant can be rescued to wild-type by providing external iron and zinc. However, the dramatic phenotype of the irt1 mutant demonstrates that the contribution of IRT1 to the maintenance of iron and zinc homeostasis is essential, despite a redundancy of root-specific iron and zinc transporters. Thus, neither IRT2 nor other IRT-like and ZIP genes listed in the Arabidopsis genome database seem to be able to compensate for the reduction of iron and zinc accumulation caused by the loss of IRT1 function, although the expression of the IRT2 gene is considerably higher in irt1 roots than in wild-type. To classify IRT1, e.g. based on a comparison to IRT2 in yeast, as highaffinity iron transporter is nevertheless premature as detailed biochemical characterization of these proteins is further awaited in Arabidopsis. This should also help to define the quantitative contribution of IRT1 and IRT2 to iron accumulation in the roots and further iron transport into the shoots. Our pulse-labeling experiments with $^ { 5 9 } \mathrm { F e }$ seem to contradict the data of Yi and Guerinot (1996), who found very little iron accumulation in shoots within the first hour of $^ { 5 5 } \mathrm { F e }$ trace labeling. As in our case, however, similar quantities of $^ { 5 5 } \mathrm { F e }$ were detected upon $4 8 \mathrm { h }$ uptake in shoots and roots of wild-type plants. More importantly, Yi and Guerinot (1996) demonstrated that frd1 mutations of the Arabidopsis $F R O 2 \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -chelate reductase gene significantly reduce iron uptake and transport by the roots indicating that FRO2 is obligatorily required to satisfy $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ -specificity of root iron transporters. How iron and zinc are transported from the epidermis via the cortex and endodermis of roots through the vascular tissues into the shoots is an intriguing question. Recently, the expression of IRT2 has been localized to the root epidermal (i.e. rhizodermal) layer by monitoring the activity of a promoter-GUS reporter gene fusion (Vert et al., 2001). Nonetheless, to understand how IRT1 and IRT2 regulate the transport of iron and zinc between root cell layers and from roots to shoots, further studies of IRT1 expression pattern and stability of IRT1 and IRT2 transporters in reciprocal knock-out mutants are required.

An intriguing aspect of iron and zinc uptake studies is the regulation of gene expression under deficiency stress conditions. Recent transcript profiling experiments using microarrays of Arabidopsis cDNAs indicate that a battery of genes involved in anaerobic respiration in roots, as well as in gluconeogenesis, starch degradation, phloem loading, tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative pentose phosphate pathway in shoots, are induced in response to iron deficiency stress (Thimm et al., 2001). Analogous transcript profiling experiments in yeast have identified 46 genes controlled by the transcription factor ZAP1 that binds to zinc-responsive elements of promoters regulated by zinc deprivation (Lyons et al., 2000). Yeast Aft1 and Aft2 were similarly defined as transcription factors required for resistance to oxidative stress and regulation of genes induced by iron deficiency (Blaiseau et al., 2001). The availability of irt1 knock out mutation affecting the regulation of IRT2, ZIP1 and ZIP2 target genes offers now a suitable system for identification of iron and zinc responsive “regulons” in Arabidopsis. In addition, restoration of deficient phenotype to wild-type by externally added iron and zinc provides a useful internal control to study how iron deficiency induces oxidative stress leading to progressive chlorosis and ultimate death in the irt1 mutant.

IRT1 and IRT2 are members of the Arabidopsis ZIP metal transporter family that are specifically induced by iron deprivation in roots and act as heterologous suppressors of yeast mutations inhibiting iron and zinc uptake. Although IRT1 and IRT2 are thought to perform redundant functions as root-specific metal transporters, insertional inactivation of the IRT1 gene alone results in typical symptoms of iron deficiency causing severe leaf chlorosis and lethality in soil. The irt1 mutation is characterized by specific developmental defects, including a drastic reduction of chloroplast thylakoid stacking into grana and lack of palisade parenchyma differentiation in leaves, reduced number of vascular bundles in stems, and irregular patterns of enlarged endodermal and cortex cells in roots. Pulse labeling with $^ { 5 9 } \mathrm { F e }$ through the root system shows that the irt1 mutation reduces iron accumulation in the shoots. Short-term labeling with $^ { 6 5 } \mathrm { Z n }$ reveals no alteration in spatial distribution of zinc, but indicates a lower level of zinc accumulation. In comparison to wild-type, the irt1 mutant responds to iron and zinc deprivation by altered expression of certain zinc and iron transporter genes, which results in the activation of ZIP1 in shoots, reduction of ZIP2 transcript levels in roots, and enhanced expression of IRT2 in roots. These data support the conclusion that IRT1 is an essential metal transporter required for proper development and regulation of iron and zinc homeostasis in Arabidopsis.

The work detailed in this paper follows up on a previous study in which we showed that the imposition of Fe deficiency stimulated both Cd and $Z \mathrm { n }$ influx in roots of pea seedlings (Cohen et al. 1998a). There have been a number of examples in the plant micronutrient nutrition literature indicating that Fe nutrition is linked, in poorly understood ways, to the transport and nutrition of other micronutrients as well as to heavy metals such as Cd, which are presumed to enter plants via systems normally operating for essential micronutrients. For example, in dicotyledonous plants that employ a reductive-based mechanism for Fe acquisition, it has been shown that the imposition of either Fe or Cu deficiency activated the Fe deficiency responses associated with Fe acquisition: root ferric reductase activity and acidification of the rhizosphere (Welch et al. 1993; Cohen et al. 1997). It is possible that in dicots, as has been shown for yeast, Cu is required for proper Fe utilization and transport. Furthermore, there have been several examples in the literature in which Fe deficiency in dicots induces the stimulated accumulation of a number of micronutrient metals other than Fe (for example, see Welch et al. 1993; Rodecap et al. 1994). More recently, researchers are beginning to understand the molecular basis for micronutrient nutrition from information gained from the cloning and characterization of plant micronutrient transporters from several gene families, including the ZIP family of metal transporters. These findings have led some researchers to suggest that these metal transporters may be relatively promiscuous, and facilitate the transport of several micronutrient metals (Guerinot 2000). In particular for the Arabidopsis ZIP transporter, IRT1, it was originally suggested that it may be a broad specificity metal transporter that can facilitate uptake from the soil of a number of micronutrients (Korshunova et al. 1999). These observations raise important questions about how plants might regulate the homeostasis of specific micronutrients, particularly if the expression of transporters that can mediate the influx of several different metals can also be regulated by changes in the plant status of several micronutrients.

Most of the findings suggesting multiple transport roles for ZIP transporters have come from yeast complementation studies, in which specific defects in micronutrient uptake (Fe, Zn, Mn), which prevent growth of the yeast at low levels of those micronutrients, have been complemented with plant metal transport genes. As researchers begin to extrapolate from these experiments based on heterologous expression in yeast to terrestrial plants in order to better understand plant micronutrient nutrition, it will be important to characterize the properties of the plant micronutrient transporters under conditions that more closely mimic roots functioning in the soil. To investigate the molecular basis for the observed enhancement of Zn and Cd accumulation in Fe-deficient pea seedlings, we isolated a putative iron transporter cDNA from pea. This cDNA, designated RIT1, shows significant nucleotide and amino acid sequence similarity to the Arabidopsis IRT1 cDNA. Expression of RIT1 in the yeast Fe transportdefective mutant conferred enhanced growth under low iron conditions. In this study, we showed that RIT1 mediates high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ that ranges from 54 to $9 3 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ . These findings suggest that RIT1 normally functions to mediate acquisition of Fe in plants. $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values in the nanomolar range measured in the heterologous yeast system are consistent with the significant fluxes observed at nanomolar $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in intact pea roots (Fox et al. 1996). Ferrous ion activities in this range also agree with the estimated critical $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ activity required for optimal plant growth $\left( 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \mathrm { n M } \right)$ and the $_ { 0 . 1 - 1 , 0 0 0 \ n M }$ levels of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ typically found in bulk soil solutions (Lindsay 1991). A $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value in the nanomolar range is thus physiologically relevant to the environmental conditions a plant is most likely to encounter.

Therefore, these results, based on kinetic analysis of RIT-mediated $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx, provide further support for recent findings from several laboratories based on analysis of Arabidopsis IRT1 knockout mutants, that led those authors to propose that IRT1 is the main transporter mediating plant Fe uptake from the soil (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). In all three of these studies, characterization of T-DNA knockout lines for IRT1 produced a mutant phenotype nearly identical to that seen for plant Fe deficiency, and the wild type phenotype was restored by providing elevated levels of Fe in the soil or hydroponic medium. Furthermore, in the studies by Henriques et al. (2002) and Vert et al. (2002), transport studies indicated that the irt1 mutant exhibited significantly reduced uptake of Fe, as well as Zn (in Henriques et al. 2002) and Zn, Mn, and Co (in Vert et al. 2002). Vert et al. (2002) also showed that the mutant phenotype was not overcome by supplementing the plants growth medium with elevated levels of Zn, Mn, or Co; the only mineral that reversed the chlorotic mutant phenotype was elevated Fe.

In the study detailing the original cloning and characterization of IRT1 in Arabidopsis (Eide et al. 1996), the data from the concentration-dependent kinetics for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in the fet3fet4 yeast expressing IRT1 indicated that the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake was $6 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ , indicating that the affinity of IRT1 for $\mathrm { \bar { F e } } ^ { 2 + }$ is approximately 100 times lower than that found in the current study. However, in the former study, the total Fe concentration in the uptake solutions was used for the kinetic analyses (and ranged from 0 to $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } $ , which resulted in a very large overestimation of the actual uptake solution $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 \bar { + } }$ activity, and yielded a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value that was much larger than the actual value.

Our additional findings that RIT1 complements the yeast Zn transport-defective mutant ZHY3, the Mn transport-defective mutant SLY8, and mediates moderately high affinity $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx and lower affinity $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in yeast, suggests that RIT1 may provide a common pathway for the entry of metals besides iron across the root-cell plasma membrane. These findings, along with the result that RIT1 expression is induced by Fe deficiency in roots of pea seedlings, corroborate evidence at the whole-plant level and in intact roots of an Fedeficiency-induced stimulation of $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake (Fox et al.1996; Cohen et al. 1998a). These results suggest that the Fe-deficiency-induced stimulation of Fe2+, $\mathrm { \bar { C } d } ^ { 2 + }$ and divalent cation influx in intact pea roots may be the result of increased RIT1 expression.

Interestingly, our results demonstrate that RIT1 shows the highest affinity for $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ $( 5 4 - 9 3 ~ \mathrm { n M } )$ , moderate affinity for Zn $( 4 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , and much lower affinity for Cd $1 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . It should be noted that we obtained similar kinetics for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx when yeast $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake experiments were conducted with either chelate buffered or standard, non-chelate buffered uptake solutions. This finding indicates that the results are not due to any artifact resulting from the use of chelate-buffered uptake solutions. Thus, RIT1 may exhibit a high specificity for Fe but still may be promiscuous, in that it will transport other micronutrient metals or their analogues if the metal concentrations in the soil are high enough. Variable charge-density ratios of the metals $( { \mathrm { F e } } > { \mathrm { Z n } } > { \mathrm { C d } } )$ could account for, or contribute to, differences in binding affinity to the transporter.

The $Z \bar { \mathrm { n } } ^ { 2 + }$ influx values measured in our heterologous systems from uptake solutions containing micromolar Zn concentrations may be meaningful in a physiological context, as we have previously measured significant $^ { 6 5 } { \cal Z } \mathrm { n }$ influx from solutions containing 1 mM Zn using intact pea roots (Cohen et al.1998a). More recently, our laboratory conducted a detailed concentration-dependent kinetic analysis for root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx in $Z \mathrm { n }$ efficient and inefficient cultivars of wheat (Hacisalihoglu et al. 2001). In that study, we described a $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport system with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ that was very similar to the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1-mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx reported here $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ in wheat: $2 { \ - } 5 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ ; $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for RIT1: $4 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ ). It is possible that a wheat RIT homolog may be mediating this moderately high affinity root $\bar { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx. However, Hacisalihoglu et al. (2001) uncovered a second very high affinity root $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ uptake system, with a $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ for $\dot { Z } \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 \mp }$ influx of $0 . 6 { - } 2 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ The transport properties of this second $Z \mathrm { n }$ transporter are more in line with what would be expected for $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ influx from the rhizosphere of agricultural soils. The estimated critical activity of $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ required for optimal plant growth ranges from 0.01 to $0 . 1 { \mathrm { ~ n M } }$ (Norvell and Welch 1993; Welch and Norvell 1993), and the concentration of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in a typical soil solution ranges from 1 to $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { n M }$ (Lindsay 1991; Hodgson et al.1966). When we used chelate buffer techniques to control $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ activities in the nanomolar range, we did not see significant RIT1- mediated $Z \mathfrak { n } ^ { 2 + }$ fluxes (data not shown), suggesting that RIT1 does not normally play a role in root $Z \mathrm { n }$ uptake at physiologically relevant soil $Z \mathrm { n }$ levels.

In conclusion, the findings reported here suggest that, in typical agricultural soils, RIT1 functions primarily as a high-affinity $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter that mediates root Fe acquisition. However, the ability of RIT1 to facilitate $Z \mathrm { n }$ and Cd uptake when these metals are present at elevated concentrations suggests that RIT1 may be one pathway for the entry of toxic metals into the food chain. These findings are consistent with those presented recently in the literature indicating that Arabidopsis IRT1 plays a major role in mediating root Fe uptake from the soil, but also may facilitate the uptake of other divalent metals (Henriques et al. 2002; Varotto et al. 2002; Vert et al. 2002). Furthermore, the finding that plant Fe deficiency status may promote heavy metal uptake via increased expression of this transporter could have implications both for human nutrition and also for phytoremediation—the use of terrestrial plants to sequester toxic metals from contaminated soil. A more comprehensive understanding of the regulation and function of RIT1 may contribute to further progress in these areas.

IRT1, the founding member of ZIP transporter family, was identified by a powerful suppressor screen based on the complementation of yeast fet3 multicopper oxidase and fet4 Fe(II)-transporter mutations that block high and low affinity iron transport, respectively (Askwith et al., 1994; Dix et al., 1994;

Eide et al., 1996). IRT1 was also found to suppress the zrt1zrt2 mutations of high and low-affinity zinc transporters and the smf1 $\Delta$ mutation of a high-affinity Nramp manganese transporter, as well as to increase cadmium sensitivity, when expressed in yeast (Korshunova et al., 1999; Rogers et al., 2000). Nonetheless, IRT1 turned out to differ both structurally and functionally from these yeast transporter proteins, but shows homology to numerous putative membrane proteins in eukaryotes, including predicted products of $1 5 ~ Z I P$ genes in the sequenced Arabidopsis genome (Guerinot, 2000; Mäser et al., 2001). Characterization of other members of ZIP family indicated that IRT2, a close homolog of IRT1, facilitates iron and zinc uptake, whereas ZIP1, ZIP2 and ZIP3 mediate only zinc transport in yeast. IRT1 and IRT2 are induced by iron depletion, whereas ZIP1, ZIP2 and ZIP3 are activated by zinc deficiency specifically in Arabidopsis roots (Eide et al., 1996; Grotz et al., 1998; Vert et al., 2001). By contrast ZIP4, carrying a putative chloroplast signal peptide, was suggested to function as leaf specific zinc-regulated transporter (Grotz et al., 1998). In addition to the ZIP family, however, 3 members of the Arabidopsis NRAMP (natural-resistanceassociated macrophage protein) family were also identified to respond to iron depletion and to mediate iron and cadmium uptake (Curie et al., 2000; Thomine et al., 2000). Recent finding of homologs of maize

YS1 (yellow strip 1) gene in Arabidopsis suggests that even further transporters are implicated in the control of iron homeostasis in plants (Curie et al., 2001).

This high redundancy raises the logical question whether reverse genetics, producing single recessive or dominant gene mutations, would be helpful in the dissection of physiological functions of individual plant metal transporters. The knock-out of IRT1 function described above provides an encouraging answer suggesting that quantitative differences in the contribution of individual metal transporters, as well as differences in their spatial and temporal regulation, may result in characteristic phenotypes of individual transporter mutants. Thus, our data show that inactivation of IRT1 results in shoot iron deficiency leading to severe chlorosis and lethality. However, it is likely that the reduction of zinc uptake in the irt1 mutant contributes to the phenotype, as the irt1 mutant shows also bleaching in zinc-depleted iron-sufficient medium (unpublished). Characteristic changes in the differentiation of specific cell layers in leaf, stem and root may thus reflect consequences of a combined iron and zinc deficiency in the irt1 mutant. Due to functional redundancy of iron and zinc transporters, the irt1 knock-out does not completely abolish iron and zinc uptake by the roots, thus the otherwise unviable chlorotic irt1 mutant can be rescued to wild-type by providing external iron and zinc. However, the dramatic phenotype of the irt1 mutant demonstrates that the contribution of IRT1 to the maintenance of iron and zinc homeostasis is essential, despite a redundancy of root-specific iron and zinc transporters. Thus, neither IRT2 nor other IRT-like and ZIP genes listed in the Arabidopsis genome database seem to be able to compensate for the reduction of iron and zinc accumulation caused by the loss of IRT1 function, although the expression of the IRT2 gene is considerably higher in irt1 roots than in wild-type. To classify IRT1, e.g. based on a comparison to IRT2 in yeast, as highaffinity iron transporter is nevertheless premature as detailed biochemical characterization of these proteins is further awaited in Arabidopsis. This should also help to define the quantitative contribution of IRT1 and IRT2 to iron accumulation in the roots and further iron transport into the shoots. Our pulse-labeling experiments with $^ { 5 9 } \mathrm { F e }$ seem to contradict the data of Yi and Guerinot (1996), who found very little iron accumulation in shoots within the first hour of $^ { 5 5 } \mathrm { F e }$ trace labeling. As in our case, however, similar quantities of $^ { 5 5 } \mathrm { F e }$ were detected upon $4 8 \mathrm { h }$ uptake in shoots and roots of wild-type plants. More importantly, Yi and Guerinot (1996) demonstrated that frd1 mutations of the Arabidopsis $F R O 2 \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ -chelate reductase gene significantly reduce iron uptake and transport by the roots indicating that FRO2 is obligatorily required to satisfy $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ -specificity of root iron transporters. How iron and zinc are transported from the epidermis via the cortex and endodermis of roots through the vascular tissues into the shoots is an intriguing question. Recently, the expression of IRT2 has been localized to the root epidermal (i.e. rhizodermal) layer by monitoring the activity of a promoter-GUS reporter gene fusion (Vert et al., 2001). Nonetheless, to understand how IRT1 and IRT2 regulate the transport of iron and zinc between root cell layers and from roots to shoots, further studies of IRT1 expression pattern and stability of IRT1 and IRT2 transporters in reciprocal knock-out mutants are required.

An intriguing aspect of iron and zinc uptake studies is the regulation of gene expression under deficiency stress conditions. Recent transcript profiling experiments using microarrays of Arabidopsis cDNAs indicate that a battery of genes involved in anaerobic respiration in roots, as well as in gluconeogenesis, starch degradation, phloem loading, tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative pentose phosphate pathway in shoots, are induced in response to iron deficiency stress (Thimm et al., 2001). Analogous transcript profiling experiments in yeast have identified 46 genes controlled by the transcription factor ZAP1 that binds to zinc-responsive elements of promoters regulated by zinc deprivation (Lyons et al., 2000). Yeast Aft1 and Aft2 were similarly defined as transcription factors required for resistance to oxidative stress and regulation of genes induced by iron deficiency (Blaiseau et al., 2001). The availability of irt1 knock out mutation affecting the regulation of IRT2, ZIP1 and ZIP2 target genes offers now a suitable system for identification of iron and zinc responsive “regulons” in Arabidopsis. In addition, restoration of deficient phenotype to wild-type by externally added iron and zinc provides a useful internal control to study how iron deficiency induces oxidative stress leading to progressive chlorosis and ultimate death in the irt1 mutant.

Zinc is an essential micronutrient that plays many important roles in various physiological and metabolic processes of plants and humans, serving as a cofactor for many enzymes and as the key structural motif in transcriptional regulatory proteins [1]. Zinc shortage in soil is a widespread micronutrient deficiency limiting crop production and reducing $Z \mathrm { n }$ content in agronomic products, which ultimately leads to $Z \mathrm { n }$ deficiency in human diet [2]. Despite the importance of $Z \mathrm { n }$ in both plant and human nutrition, the knowledge of how plants acquire, transport, store, and utilize this metal at the molecular level is quite limited.
