This might suggest that an increased uptake of water by the roots is needed to cool the temperature of leaves by increasing transpiration.


## 3.2. Cold Stress


Plants are exposed to a wide range of environmental conditions, and in addition to heat, cold stress is also a factor that shapes the physiology of cereals [99]. Low soil temperatures inhibit water uptake by roots [100]. A decrease in water permeability across the root (i.e., a decrease in the root hydraulic conductivity, Lpr) is expected to affect the plant water status, stomatal conductance, photosynthesis, growth and, lastly, productivity [94,101–104]. In rice, a decrease in the Lpr under cold stress was linked to the role of aquaporins [105]. A 96-h treatment at $4 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was enough to cause a decrease in the expression of eight PIP and two TIP genes in rice (Table 2) [63]. Interestingly, the differences in the profiles of the AQP genes (nine PIPs and three TIPs) expression was also detected in rice when whole plants were chilled compared to when only the roots of the plants were chilled at $1 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for five days. When only the roots were chilled, there was an increased expression of OsPIP1;3, OsPIP2;4 and $O s P I P 2 ; 5$ compared to the control conditions (Table 2) [79]. The authors observed that a low room temperature treatment (LRT) for a prolonged length of time induced a gradual increase the root osmotic hydraulic conductivity Lpr(os), which suggests that LRT-treated roots acclimate to low temperatures by acquiring a water uptake mechanism that is not present at the normal growth temperature of $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ [79]. This might suggest that a cold acclimation process for the root water uptake functions in rice and that is possibly regulated via aquaporins [79]. Furthermore, the low temperature causes changes in the amount of AQP transcripts not only in roots but also in leaves. Recently, it was shown that temperature of growth was a significant factor influencing the level of accumulation of HvPIP1 transcript and protein in barley leaves. The level of accumulation of HvPIP1 transcript decreased at $5 ^ { \circ } C$ (compared to $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ) but was higher at $2 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ than at $2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in the analysed genotypes [106].


## 3.3. Salinity


Soil salination and a high salt accumulation affect the growth, development, metabolism and yield of plants [107]. A wide range of physiological and biochemical alterations in plants is induced by salinity, which causes a lower water potential in the soil solution and ionic disequilibrium, as well as a higher accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) [107]. This is why the salt stress tolerance trait has multi-component nature [108]. Among cereals, barley is highly tolerant for salinity, while wheat and maize display a high sensitivity [34]. AQPs could play a role in the mechanism by which plants cope with saline concentration because it leads to changes in the AQP gene expression profiles, which has been shown in many plant species including cereals (Table 2). In barley (Hordeum vulgare L.), foxtail millet (Setaria italica L.) and rice (Oryza sativa L.), different concentrations of NaCl from 150 till $2 5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ were used for the salt treatment, as well as different durations of the treatment (Table 2). During the early research on barley, the opposite profile of the expression of the HvPIP2;1 gene was detected in the roots and shoots after $4 8 \mathrm { h }$ of treatment with $2 0 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l } _ { \ l }$ , which decreased and increased compared to the control conditions, respectively (Table 2) [109]. The HvPIP2;1 protein was confirmed to be localised in the plasma membrane. The functional expression of this gene in Xenopus oocyte indicated that HvPIP2;1 has a water transport activity [83]. Other research on both barley and rice also showed that after $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ of NaCl treatment, there was a decrease in the expression of many members of the PIP subfamily in the roots (Table 2) [81,84]. Severe salinity stress $( 2 0 0 \mathrm { m M N a C l } )$ ) also significantly reduced the root hydraulic conductivity (Lpr) in rice [84].

However, under relatively mild salt stress $\mathrm { \Delta ^ { \prime } 1 0 0 ~ m M ~ N a C l ) }$ , there was only a moderate decrease in the Lpr with no significant difference in the HvPIP mRNA levels [84]. The biological significance of such a regulation may increase the prevention of an excessive water loss from cells during the early stages (the osmotic stress phase) of salinity stress, and the Lpr decrease might represent the mode of change in barley plants from the rapid growth stage, which requires a high water absorption to the protected stage, which requires less water uptake [84]. Conversely, under salinity stress some TIP genes were detected whose expression increased compared to the control conditions such as OsTIP1;1 and OsTIP1;2 (Table 2) [75]. OsTIP1;2 had a water and glycerol transport activity [58]. The upregulation of some of the OsTIPs genes might be connected with water transport from the vacuole to the cytoplasm to perform an osmotic adjustment [75].

3.4. Comparison between Genotypes, Which Are Characterised as Tolerant or Resistant to Specific Abiotic Stress

An extremely interesting aspect of an expression study of AQP genes under abiotic stress conditions is the comparison between the cultivars, which are characterised by the opposite phenotype in terms of their tolerance to specific abiotic stresses. This kind of research could lead to identifying the important players among AQPs in stress tolerance. The genes that would be identified in such a way could serve as potential candidates for further downstream characterisation studies in order to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie abiotic stress tolerance. Two contrasting cultivars of the foxtail millet (Setaria italica L.), which is a naturally abiotic stress-tolerant crop, were investigated in terms of their abiotic stress tolerance. The study showed that SiPIP3;1 and SiSIP1;1 were differentially expressed in both of the cultivars in response to salinity, heat and dehydration stresses [66]. In the stress-tolerant cultivar, the expression of these genes in roots were higher compared to the resistant ones. Their role in providing salinity and dehydration stress tolerance was also validated via the heterologous overexpression of these genes in the S. cerevisiae system in which the overexpression lines were found to be tolerant to abiotic stresses [66]. In turn, in rice, the expression of the aquaporin RWC3 gene (PIP1) was investigated in upland and lowland rice. Upland rice is traditionally regarded as having drought avoidance, which is one of the mechanisms of drought resistance [110]. The expression of RWC3 mRNA was higher in the upland rice in the early response (up to four hours) to a $2 0 \%$ polyethylene glycol (PEG) 6000 treatment in the roots, whereas there were no significant changes in its expression in the lowland rice. The protein levels increased in the upland rice and decreased in the lowland rice after a ten-h water deficit. An analysis with the Xenopus oocyte expression system showed that RWC3 has a water transport activity. The authors suggested that a high level of RWC3 improves water uptake under a water deficit and therefore maintains the plant water balance [111]. Another interesting example of an AQP gene expression study in two inbred lines that contrast in their water use efficiency, root hydraulic conductivity (Lpr) and AQP contribution to the Lpr was performed on pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum (L) R. Br.). This is a key cereal for food security in arid and semi-arid regions of the world, which is heat and drought adapted [112]. Increased water use efficiency (WUE) can alleviate drought stress [67]. The line with a lower WUE had a significantly higher AQP contribution to the Lpr and also had a higher $P g P I P 1 - 3$ and $P g P I P 1 \ – 4$ gene expression compared to the line with a higher WUE that was grown in hydroponic conditions. The authors suggested that a downregulation of the PgPIP genes might induce inhibition of transpiration and water savings. However, an investigation of the expression patterns of the AQP genes under abiotic stress conditions could be a very important subject for further research. Additionally, treating roots with a common AQP inhibitor (azide) suggested that AQP contributed up to $8 4 \%$ of the root hydraulic conductivity (Lpr) in pearl millet [67]. Furthermore, in the same cereal, four recombinant inbred lines that vary in their transpiration rate $( \mathrm { T r } )$ response to vapour pressure deficit (VPD) conditions were selected for an expression study of the AQP genes [113]. Some of the water-saving traits were the capacity of certain genotypes to restrict plant transpiration when the evaporative requisition was high [114]. The differences in the transpiration response phenotype were accompanied by diverse AQP gene abundances between the VPD-sensitive and VPD-insensitive genotypes. The expression pattern of the PgAQP genes indicated that the VPD-insensitive genotypes had a slightly higher expression of AQPs, including $P g P I P 1 ; 1$ and $P g P I P 2 ; 6$ in the root tissue, than in the VPD-sensitive genotypes under low VPD conditions $( 1 . 2 \mathrm { k P a } )$ , when there was no high evaporative demand from the atmosphere [113]. The last example is from wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) for which the profiles of the AQP genes were investigated using accessions with contrasting responses to drought according to the yield tolerance index (YTI). In the leaves, as stress intensity increased, some of the AQP genes of the PIP1 and PIP2 subfamilies such as TaPIP1-1, TaPIP1-5 or TaPIP2-24 were clearly upregulated in the tolerant genotype. In the case of the TIP family, TaTIP2-4, TaTIP3-4 and TaTIP4-1 also increased their expression levels during severe stress. On the other hand, in the roots, the tolerant genotype had a lower level of expression compared to the susceptible ones for the TaPIP1-1, TaPIP1-5, TaAQP7, TaPIP2-1C1, TaTIP1-2, TaTIP3-4 and TaTIP4-1 genes under moderate stress [61].

Plants being sessile and autotrophic in nature are restricted to their specific site for growth and development. They are dependent on the soil for their water and mineral requirements (Singh et al., 2020). Water uptake and distribution to all the parts of the plants is crucial process for various physiological processes of vascular plants (Oniosun et al., 2019). Recent studies provides as interesting breakthrough to understand the basic mechanism of water and mineral transport inside the plant system. The water molecules or solutes after uptake from the roots, passes through many cellular layers such as cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem parenchyma cells and reaches the vessels (xylem and phloem) (Medina-Velo et al., 2017). During 1920s the flow of water across the membranes was believed to be carried out by diffusion, but the process of diffusion was too slow to maintain an adequate supply of water to carry out various physiological activities of plants. Later in 1993, it was reported that the water channel proteins named as aquaporins (AQPs) present in the roots, facilitates the trans-cellular water movements (Maurel et al., 1997). AQPs are small membrane proteins having molecular weights in range from 21kD to $3 4 \mathrm { k D }$ , found in majority of the living organism (Shivaraj et al., 2019). AQPs were first come into attention when Maurel and his coworkers placed Xenopus laevis oocytes in hyposmotic medium for a cell swelling experiment in 1993. They also expressed the Arabidopsis thalliana water channel proteins (AtTIP1;1) in Xenopus oocytes and found that the water permeability was increased by 6–8 folds. Plant AQPs have a large and diverse protein family of 30–70 homologues present in rice, maize, tomato, poplar, cotton and soybean (Reuscher et al., 2013). On the basis of their sequence similarity, they are classified into five subfamilies which includes, plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIP), tonoplast intrinsic protein (TIP), small basic intrinsic protein (SIP), Nodulin 26 like intrinsic protein (NIP) and XIP (X intrinsic proteins). The PIP, NIP and XIP proteins are present on the entire surface of the plasma membranes. SIP and some NIP are localized in endoplasmic reticulum and TIPs are present on the vacuolar membrane known as tonoplast. TIP and PIP proteins are also localized in the inner membrane of the thylakoids present in the chloroplast (Singh et al., 2020).

The detailed studies and researches on structure of AQPs led us to have first insights of the selectivity mechanism which is the basis of water and solutes transportation. Selectivity mechanism of aquaporins is based on the conserved NPA motifs and the amino acid residues (Hub & De Groot, 2008). The NPA motifs are highly conserved in PIPs and TIPs in which the PIP contributes to the water, glycerol, urea, $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ transport and also participated in the response to abiotic stresses. The NPA motifs constitute asparagine, proline and alanine amino acids (Hub & De Groot, 2008). These motifs also possess side chains of asparagine residues which are directed towards the pore. The aromatic/arginine (ar/R) forms the narrowest part of the pore and is considered to be an important for selectivity of water and various solutes (Hub & De Groot, 2008). The residues in ar/R region differ in their respective sizes and hydrophobicity. Water and other solutes such as $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ , glycerol and urea strongly differ with each other in relation to their respective hydrophobicity and sizes. When a solute passes inside the AQP the favorable interactions between water and protein (ARG195 or Cys189 or His 180) is reduced and replaced by solute protein interactions. The stronger the interaction, more favorable will be the passing of solutes from the selectivity barrier of AQP (Hub & De Groot, 2008). TIP is also involved in regulating the cell turgor by exchanging the water inside and outside of the vacuoles through the tonoplast. Besides the water transport it is also known to regulate the availability of glycerol, ammonia, urea in the vacuoles. In recent year’s scientist have paid attention towards the role of

AQPs in maintaining the carbon and nitrogen status inside the plant system. C-N ratio coordinates the functioning for normal plant growth and yield. Proper balance of carbon and nitrogen leads to favorable increase in biomass (Gao et al., 2018). Role of AQPs in maintaining the C-N ratio is speculated by various researchers all across the world (Maurel et al., 2008; Gao et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2018). Various researchers have reported that stressful condition rapidly reduces the water transportation rates (Arif et al., 2019; Biyani et al., 2019; Vishwakarma et al., 2019; Tripthi et al., 2020; Vaculík et al., 2020). The AQPs effectively regulates the water circulation inside the plant system during normal as well as stressful conditions (Ding et al., 2020; Ding & Chaumont, 2020). AQPs have shown their importance in maintaining water and ionic homeostasis in normal as well as stressful environmental conditions throughout the life of the plants exposed to diverse types of stressful conditions (Chaumont & Tyerman, 2017; Kourghi et al., 2018). The stressful conditions can be very crucial for plants because stresses such as drought, temperature extremities, salinity, heavy metal stress negatively impacts several metabolic dysfunctions such as seed germination, root-shoot development, flowering and fruiting that leads to senescence and death (Gautam et al., 2019a, 2019b; Pandey et al., 2019a, 2019b). Plants adapt to the harsh condition by inducing changes in the expression of many genes via regulating micro RNAs expression and post translational modifications (Pandey et al., 2020b; Gautam et al., 2020a). Changes in the expression of AQPs can effectively regulate the water availability in the plant during harsh conditions. Some AQPs are expressed in specific parts of the plants while some are expressed throughout the plants. PIP and TIP are expressed throughout the plants and are abundantly present in ER, Golgi, endosomes, autophagosomes and vacuoles while some aquaporins such as SIP are specifically expressed in ER and chloroplast and NIP are confined in nitrogen fixing symbiosome (Wudick et al., 2009; Uehlein et al., 2007; Maurel et al., 2015). Members of XIP AQPs are likely to be localized in cytoplasm, nucleus and in chloroplast. Additionally AQP are not expressed in peroxisomes and mitochondria for which the reason is yet not explored (Maurel et al., 2008). Scientists use comparative transcriptomics studies and molecular analysis to understand the role of different AQPs isoforms in regulating the plant water status during a number of harsh conditions. The complex expression patterns of different isoforms of AQPs revealed the importance of AQPs in conferring tolerance to abiotic stress. System biology approaches is needed extensively in order to explore the various interactions of aquaporins with its different isoforms and other molecules to understand the molecular mechanism behind the aquaporins functioning pattern in plant system (Pandey et al., 2020).

Nowadays scientists have gained attention on AQPs far beyond the level of membrane water transport. AQPs are targeted for producing crops with more efficient water and solute transporting activities and improved AQPs functioning to develop stress tolerant crops (Hussain et al., 2016; del Carmen Martinez-Ballesta & Carvajal, 2014). This review presents comprehensive insights on involvement of various homologs of aquaporins and their diverse role in providing tolerance to various environmental constraints. Recent studies provide evidences of timely up-regulation and downregulation of aquaporins which is critical to ensure the availability of water for stress acclimation and maintaining plant water relations. Additionally the recent discoveries regarding types, cellular localization and structure and functions of aquaporins are also elaborated in detail.


## Plant Aquaporins: Structure and Functions


The AQPs are the transmembrane proteins that play a role in rapid movement of water molecules by formation of channels in the intracellular spaces and plasma membrane (Maurel et al., 2015). Water molecules move in both the directions of the water channel pore along its potential gradient using protein electrostatic forces (Chrispeels et al., 2001). Characteristic aquaporins consist of six transmembrane alpha helices with C and N termini which face towards the cytosol. A loop between second-third and fourth-fifth transmembranes occurs in cytosol while the loops present between the first- second, third-fourth and fifth-sixth transmembranes occur outside the cytosol. These loops contain Asparagine-Proline-Alanine (NPA) motifs that form water selectivity pore/filter. This sequence is generally conserved but in some Arabidopsis and maize species the alanine residues is absent and is replaced by other amino acids such as valine, serine, cysteine, leucine or threonine residues. These AQPs exist as tetramers by assembling four AQPs monomers and each monomer forms its individualistic water transfer channel. The structural analysis of plant AQPs has been done in kidney bean and spinach which has confirmed tetramers conformations of AQPs (Maurel et al., 2015; Stahlberg et al., 2001; Kapilan et al., 2018; Chaumont & Tyerman, 2014).

The fundamental role of AQPs in plants is to coordinate the flow of water molecules inside and outside of the cell. Therefore this is present in almost all the parts of the plants such as roots, stems, leaves, flower, fruits and seeds (Kapilan et al., 2018). AQPs are reported to be highly expressed in roots because they mediate transcellular (across membranes) root water transport (Chaumont & Tyerman, 2014). Mercury acts as AQP blocker as it binds with the cysteine residues present in the loops of the AQPs and alters its functions. In an experiment performed on a tomato plant, mercury was used as AQP blocker it was observed that AQPs contributed to greater than $70 \%$ of root hydraulic conductivity (Balarynova & Fellner, 2019). This experiment was repeated with many other plant species and supporting results were obtained (Pei et al., 2016; Maurel & Prado, 2017; Shekoofa & Sinclair, 2018; Kshetrimayum et al., 2017). Several other AQPs inhibitors such as azide and weak acids also showed similar results (Quiroga et al., 2019; Gambetta et al., 2017; Grondin et al., 2016). The AQPs are reported to be highly expressed not only in roots but also in shoot so that they can play an important role in maintaining the hydraulic conductance. This fact was proved in an AQPs blocking experiment using mercuric chloride in a sunflower. However the hydraulic conductance in roots was more determined by AQPs (greater than $70 \%$ ) rather than that in leaves $( 2 5 \% )$ (Adiredjo et al., 2014).

The functioning of AQPs also depends on interactions with other physiological and metabolic activities. In the last two decades multiple studies have unveiled the different functions of AQPs. In addition to water transport they aid in transport of different solutes having considerable importance in physiological and metabolic activities of plants (Fig. 1) (Chaumont & Tyerman, 2014; Gao et al., 2018). It plays an important role in mineral and nutrient transport such as boron and silicon which are necessary for plant growth and development. Seed germination process requires deposition of storage proteins and oligosaccharides which are also reported to be accompanied by AQPs (Gao et al., 2018; Groszmann et al., 2017). Critical role of AQPs was observed when mercury derivatives deprived the seed germination process by interfering with the cysteine residues and hence blocking the AQPs (Hukin et al., 2002). AQPs are also involved in cell expansion, root emergence, stomatal regulation and $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ conductance through the mesophyll of the plant cell (Gao et al., 2018; Pawłowicz & Masajada, 2019).


## Plant Aquaporins Family and their Subcellular Localization


As the AQPs are involved in regulation of water transport through the transmembranes, they are localized in almost different tissues of plants (Kapilan et al., 2018). It is reported that it controls the water flow by altering the rate of flow of water or by changing the AQP abundance across the cell membranes (Kapilan et al., 2018). The AQPs are classified into five subfamilies on the basis of their localizations and sequences of amino acids. These are plasma membrane intrinsic protein, tonoplast intrinsic protein, nodulin 26 like intrinsic proteins, small basic intrinsic proteins and X intrinsic proteins (Fig. 2) (Afzal et al., 2016).


## Plasma Membrane Intrinsic Proteins


Plasma membrane intrinsic protein (PIPs) is largest AQPs family having a molecular weight of $3 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ and is located in plasma membranes of organs involved in high efflux and influxes of water like guard cells, vascular tissues and flowers (Maurel & Prado, 2017). As it composes of $40 \%$ of total AQPs, it has a large role in regulation of water transport (Yaneff et al., 2014). The two types of PIPs are PIP1s and PIP2s which are having differences in length of amino acids, amino acid substitution and water permeability (Bienert et al., 2018). PIP 1 subgroup has five isoforms PIP1;1, PIP1;2, PIP1;3, PIP1;4, PIP1;5 while PIP2 subgroup has eight isoforms PIP2;1, PIP2;2, PIP2;3, PIP2;4, PIP2;5, PIP2;6, PIP2;7, PIP2;8. PIP1 and PIP 2 subgroups share $80 \%$ common amino acids identity (Yaneff et al., 2015). PIP1 proteins are usually present in plasma membranes and provide less water permeability. PIP also tends to work along with

PIP2 proteins forming a hetero-tetramer when unable to work independently (Bienert et al., 2018). The two subgroups are reported to interact by hetero-oligomerization in which one extracellular loop of PIP2 forms hetero-tetramers with PIP1 AQPs. As an illustration, when PIP1and PIP2 proteins are expressed separately in plants or oocytes or yeast cells, the PIP1 proteins cling to intracellular membranes such as endoplasmic reticulum and PIP2 proteins are expressed at plasma membrane but when the two proteins are co-expressed, both are expressed on plasma membrane (Bienert et al., 2018). This is due to their interaction and formation of hetero-tetramer. Further the hetero-oligomerization were reported in Zea mays (ZmPIP2;6/ZmPIP2;1 and ZmPIP1;1/ZmPIP1;2), Beta vulgaris, Phaseolus vulgaris and Oryzae sativa (BvPIP2;1/BvPIP1;1, OsPIP2;3/OsPIP1;3, and PvPIP2;3/PvPIP1;1) (Yaneff et al., 2015; Bienert et al., 2018).


## Tonoplast Intrinsic Proteins


AQPs present in vacuolar membranes with water permeability activities were first identified in Arabidopsis and are known as tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs). The molecular weight of TIPs is around $2 8 \mathrm { k D a }$ , an isoelectric point of 6.0 and contributes to nearly $40 \%$ of the proteins of vacuolar membrane or tonoplast (Fox et al., 2017). TIPs are present in every land plant in which mosses have single types of TIPs. Other types of TIPs have evolved in higher plants (Pawłowicz et al., 2017). TIP AQPs exist in more divergent forms in comparison to PIPs. The TIPs are further divided into five isoforms TIP1, TIP2, TIP3, TIP4 and TIP5 on the basis of their sequence homologies (Kapilan et al., 2018). TIP1 and TIP2 isoforms are expressed in vegetative tissues, TIP 3 isoforms are largely located in seeds and TIP 5 isoforms are associated with pollen grains. The tonoplast intrinsic proteins play an important role in maintaining the water movement across the vacuolar membrane along with maintaining an osmotic balance inside the vacuolar compartment. The osmotic balance is maintained by movement of small solutes and gases (Vitali et al., 2016). Higher water permeability in tonoplast leads to osmotic adjustment which thereby maintains the cell turgor pressure (Vitali et al., 2016). As these proteins are found in tonoplast, these can be used as vacuolar markers (Vitali et al., 2016). Apart from water conductivity it also contributes to ammonia transport and helps in maintaining the nitrogen level, performing key roles in cell growth and tissue elongation as reported in transcriptional analysis (Kirscht et al., 2016). For instance, in maize plants the TIP 1;1 homologues are largely expressed in growing roots, leaves and reproductive organs of the plants. It is associated with elongating tissues of soybean, castor bean and radish (Maurel et al., 2015; Feng et al., 2019; Rodrigues et al., 2016; Yue et al., 2017).


## Nodulin like Intrinsic Proteins


Leguminous plants such as peas, beans, peanuts involved in nitrogen fixation have nodules like structures in roots that occur due to symbiotic relationship of rhizobacteria and the plant (Roberts & Routray, 2017). The plant and bacteria are associated with a symbiosome membrane where nodulin like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) proteins are expressed. The NIP proteins are reported to be the essential as well as major integral channel protein as it forms $10 \%$ of the total symbiosome membrane protein (Roberts & Routray, 2017). The NIP proteins regulate water and small uncharged solutes permeability across the plant. The NIP proteins were first reported in Glycine max (GmNOD26) that is involved in the symbiotic relationship of soybean and rhizobia and constitutes $1 0 { - } 1 5 \%$ of the total membrane protein (Lu et al., 2018). NIP proteins are also present in divergent forms as they are divided into five subgroups (NIP1, NIP2, NIP3, NIP4 and NIP). In Arabidopsis NIP isoforms includes AtNIP1;1, AtNIP1;2, AtNIP2;1, AtNIP3;1, AtNIP4;1, and AtNIP4;2 (Yuan et al., 2017). The NIP subgroups are ubiquitously occurring in all higher plants in which NIP3 occurs largely in monocots (Lu et al., 2018). During initial years of discovery, NIP was suggested to be involved in malate transportation across the symbiosome membrane but in 1997 it was recognized as a water channel and finally it is now accepted as functional water channel along with transporter of solutes such as ammonia and urea that are nutritionally important nitrogenous molecules (Pommerrenig et al., 2015). The NIP transporters may be speculated as metalloid transporters because boron which is a metalloid is needed for the proper development of nodules (Pommerrenig et al., 2015). It is also reported that NIP not only facilitates the diffusion of metalloids but also play a key role in transporting them within the plant (Pommerrenig et al., 2015). Hence it is reasonable to think that the NIP family contributes towards uptake, translocation and extrusion of metalloids, thus regulating metalloid homeostasis in the plant system.


## Small Basic Intrinsic Proteins and X-Intrinsic Proteins


SIP proteins can be expanded as small basic intrinsic proteins and are considered to be very basic and small sized proteins present in plants. They are small sized proteins because they have short cytosolic $_ \mathrm { N }$ terminal region (Chaumont & Tyerman, 2017). The N terminal tail is reported to be shorter in comparison to other AQPs while the C terminal tail is of the same size with those of other AQPs (Bienert et al., 2007). Arabidopsis has three isoforms which includes SIP1;1, SIP1;2 and SIP2;1 while rice has two (OsSIP1;1 and OsSIP2;1) (Johanson et al., 2001; Sakurai et al., 2005). It is reported that it has different solute permeability due to different characteristic structural residues (Kumar et al., 2018) The NPA motifs are replaced by NPT, NPC and NPL in SIP1;1, SIP1;2, and SIP 2;1 respectively (Ishibashi, 2006). This variation directs the substrate selectivity and velocity of transportation of the water molecules (Ishibashi, 2006). These AQPs are composed of basic residues like lysine and have higher isoelectric points (Johanson & Gustavsson, 2002). The Green fluorescence study revealed the presence of SIP members in endoplasmic reticulum while no members were discovered on plasma membrane or tonoplast (Hanton et al., 2005). The XIPs (X or Unknown intrinsic proteins) are newly discovered protein subfamily which is present in dicots, fungi, protozoa and mosses. Till now 41 XIP members are discovered in which 8 in Solanum tuberosum, 6 in Solanum lycopersicum, 6 in Hevea brasiliensis, 5 are present in populus, 3 in Jatropha curcus, 3 in Linun usitatissimum, 3 in Citrus sinensis, 2 in Glycine max, 2 in Sellaginella moellendorffii, 1 is present in Beta vulgaris, 1 in Gossypium hirsutum and 1 in Physcomitrella patens (Zargar et al. 2017; Kapilan et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2018, Bezerra-Neto et al., 2019). XIP is generally found in plasma membranes and is known to be permeable for the largest uncharged solutes such as urea, boric acid, glycerol and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ etc. Based on computational and experimental studies scientists have made it possible to understand the molecular mechanism behind the transportation of diverse solutes (Hub & de Groot, 2006; Brunner et al., 2004). The signature of XIP family is the highly conserved NPARC motif in which a cysteine residue is located after NPA motif and the aromatic/ arginine selectivity filter (Danielson & Johanson, 2008). The selectivity filter is reported to consist of four residues approximately $8 \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ }$ away from the NPA region in the extracellular side. The members of this AQP family are least characterized and need to be further investigated.


## AQPs in Regulating Carbon Status


Role of AQP in regulation of photosynthesis has been studied. Water is photolysed into oxygen and undergoes a series of reactions to convert light energy to chemical energy. The electrons are extracted from the water and directed towards $\mathrm { N A D P ^ { + } }$ that drives carbon dioxide fixation into carbohydrates (Xuan et al., 2017). The water is provided inside the chloroplast through the AQP present in thylakoids. A consistent amount of water is needed across the thylakoids membrane so as to fulfill the need of photosynthetic activities (Beebo et al., 2019). Proteomics tools have been used to identify the location of TIP protein in the thylakoids and chloroplast membranes. TIP2;1 and TIP1;2 are detected in chloroplast and thylakoids. PIP1;2, PIP1;3, PIP2;4 and PIP2;7 are also detected in chloroplast membranes (Gao et al., 2018). Carbon dioxide also diffuses from stomata pores to internal cavities and to chloroplast. $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ diffusion rate also affects the rate of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ fixation (Wang et al., 2018). Expression of AQP in carbonic anhydrase exposed Xenopus oocytes membranes resulted in increased $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ permeability which proves that AQP acted as a $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ channel. Additionally when mercuric chloride (AQP inhibitor) was applied on oocytes the $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ permeability was decreased by $6 0 \% - 7 0 \%$ (Endeward et al., 2017). The beneficial role of AQPs in facilitating $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ uptake were also studied in Arabidopsis thalliana, Hordeum vulgare, Oryzae sativa, Zea mays and Pisum sativum (Groszmann et al., 2017; Coffey et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2016;Quiroga et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2017).


## AQPs in Regulating Nitrogen Status


Major nitrogen sources such as ammonium and nitrate are uptake by roots involving nitrate transporter (NRT) and ammonium transporter (AMT) families (Tyerman et al., 2017). After reaching the xylem nitrogen is distributed to different parts of the plants via transpiration stream (Gao et al., 2018). Therefore it is reasonable to think that N acquisition to different parts of the plants is accomplished by adequate water availability to the plants (Tyerman et al., 2017). As the water supply is maintained by the aquaporins, they become critical for the nitrogen availability to the plants. The key role of AQPs in maintaining the water and nitrogen availability in the plants is largely supported by studies involving over expression of AQPs which leads to enhanced transpiration rates and nitrogen uptake (Maurel et al., 2016). Further AQP inhibitors induce decreased transpiration rates and nitrogen content of the plant. AQPs such as TIP2;1, TIP2;3, TIP1;1, TIP1;2 are involved in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ transport as reported in studies on Arabidopsis and Zea mays, (Quiroga et al., 2020; Srivastava et al., 2016). Apart from TIP, NIPs are involved in urea transport. In rice roots the AQPs including OsPIP1;1, OsPIP2;2, OsPIP2;3, OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;5, OsPIP2;6, OsTIP1;1 and OsTIP2;2 was upregulated when nitrogen was provided for $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ (Madrid-Espinoza et al., 2018). further PIP2;1, PIP2;2, PIP1;2, PIP1;3 genes in Arabidopsis were downregulated on nitrogen starvation for 6 days (Clarkson et al., 2000).


## Aquaporins during Adverse Abiotic Conditions


Abiotic stress components are considers as s serious constraint across the globe and hence affect growth of plants at different physiological stages and ultimately reduces yield. Abiotic streses mainly include salinity, drought, chilling and heavy metal stresses (Vishwakarma et al., 2019; Biyani et al., 2019; Arif et al., 2019; Vaculík et al., 2020; Tripthi et al., 2020). Various studies report that AQPs is regulated by these environmental factors along with phytoharmones and signaling molecules (Fig. 1). Therefore plants need to maintain water and minerals levels under stressful conditions (Afzal et al., 2016). AQP maintains water and ionic homeostasis by changing the gene expression in the plants exposed to different abiotic stresses (Fox et al., 2017; Ghorbani et al., 2019). Studies reported that reduced expression of AQPs limits the water permeability while overexpression leads to increased hydraulic conductivity of the membranes (Li et al., 2020; Gambetta et al., 2017; Gitto & Fricke, 2018; Ding et al., 2020).

#

Salinity is excess ion stress that limits crop yield by affecting growth and development of the plant. Sodium Chloride (NaCl) is the most prevalent amongst various types of salts present in the soil that renders it saline (Zeeshan et al., 2020). Salinity affects the nutrient bioavailability by competing during uptake and translocation and precipitating with other ions such as $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ , and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Guarino et al., 2020). It also interferes with the ammonium and nitrate uptake by interacting with them and immobilizing them. Later change in the plasma membrane integrity also leads to reduced uptake of ammonia and nitrate inside the cell. Salinity leads to cellular dehydration due to reduced turgor pressure in the cells (Evelin et al. 2019; Etesami & Alikhani, 2019; Bidalia et al., 2019).

Plants maintain the turgor by accumulation of osmolytes and regulation of water uptake. Enhanced photosynthesis, ROS detoxification and induction of phytohormones are other different strategies to combat the stress (Sharma et al., 2019; Ahanger et al., 2019; Rohman et al., 2019). Aquaporins are crucial for transporting water across the membranes and regulates the hydraulic conductance (Singh et al., 2020). Literature reports regarding the role of AQP in salinity stress are consistent with that of drought. As an example, up regulation of PIP1;2 and PIP1,2 in bananas results in increased tolerance to salt as well as drought stress (Xu et al., 2020a, 2020b). Similarly salinity leads to over expression of PIP2;1 gene in shoot while down regulation in roots of barley plant (Horie et al., 2011). Salt stress induces $6 5 \mathrm { - } 7 0 \%$ lowered expression of PIPs and TIPs in Arabidopsis (Shekhawat & Ganapathi, 2013). Some plants like Hordeum vulgare showed varying expression of PIP genes on exposure to salinity. The PIP1;1 expression was lowered in roots while it was uplifted in shoots (Katsuhara et al., 2002). PIP2;1 gene was also expressed in leaves of Glycine soja on exposure to salinity while it was downregulated in roots on the same treatment (Wang et al., 2015). Several PIP genes and one TIP gene was also downregulated in $M .$ . crystallinum plants due to salinity (Kirch et al., 2000). Salt stress tolerant plant species such as rice plants showed down regulation of different families of PIP and TIP genes on exposure to salt stress (Yamada et al., 1995). In addition to PIPs many TIPs are also reported to be involved in maintaining ionic homeostasis in plants by accumulating ions in addition to their role in transporting water across vacuoles (Afzal et al., 2016). It is supported by the study in which over-expression of TIP5;1 gene leads to enhanced tolerance to boron toxicity thereby suggesting its involvement in maintaining the level of boron inside the vacuoles (Pang et al., 2018). Transgenic tobacco lines showed tolerance to salt stress in addition to increased antioxidant activities (Chang et al., 2016). The mutants having loss of TIP functioning are reported to be less sensitive to NaCl, PEG and mannitol in comparison to the wild type plants (Feng et al., 2018). There are fewer reports in literature regarding the expression of NIP AQPs in salinity induced responses. However, transgenic Arabidopsis plant in which TaNIP from wheat plant was overexpressed showed tolerance to salinity (Gao et al., 2010) (Table 1).


## Heavy Metals/ Metalloid


Rapid industrialization and excessive use of chemicals in modern agricultural practices have led to increased heavy metal contamination in the soil water and air. This contributes to a major abiotic stress as it induces major cytotoxic, genotoxic and genomic instability in plants (Gautam & Dubey, 2018). Heavy metal such as arsenic, chromium, nickel, manganese, cadmium, lead etc. mediates growth inhibition, enhanced production of reactive oxygen species such as superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals (Pandey and Gautam 2020; Pandey et al., 2020, 2020b; Gautam et al., 2019a, 2019b; Pandey et al., 2019a, 2019b; Rajpoot et al., 2016; Srivastava et al., 2014). The heavy metals reduces the photosynthetic activity, damages the protein by attacking the thiol groups and inducing protein carbonylation (Gautam et al., 2019a, 2019b). These events gradually disrupt various physiological and metabolic processes in the plants. Under extreme conditions this may severely affect the health of the plant which finally leads to cell death (Pandey et al., 2019a, 2019b).

Besides these some metals which are essential nutrients such as boron and silicon are required for plant growth are uptake by the plant through the roots (Farooq et al., 2019). AQPs have an important role in transporting solutes necessary for cellular processes in plants such as boric acid, silicon, lactic acid, hydrogen peroxide, ammonia, nitrates, urea, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, selenium etc. (Mitra, 2017). NIP5;1 gene lacking mutant Arabidopsis showed lowered boron supply in plants and hence growth retardation as it is an important growth regulatory element (Yoshinari & Takano, 2017). Additionally NIP6;1 and NIP7;1 play important roles in the distribution of boron from roots to shoots and various organs of the plant system (Diehn et al., 2019). In another study, boron toxicity tolerant transgenic barley plants was observed to show lowered expression of NIP2;1 genes (Schnurbusch et al., 2010). Silicon is an important element involved in plant defense against various stresses. The knockout NIP 2;2 gene from rice showed defective Si uptake by the plant which further supports that NIP transporters are involved in Si uptake (Mitani et al., 2009). Deshmukh et al. (2015) performed an extensive study and found that Si permeability in plants relies on a precise spacing of 108 amino acids between the NPA domains of AQPs. The mutated variants of Poplar having a spacing of 109 or 107 amino acids between the NPA domains lacked the Si permeability. NIP genes are not only involved in nutrient transport but they are also involved in transport and response to toxic metals and metalloids such as arsenic and antimony (Bienert & Bienert, 2017). In Arabidopsis thalliana AtNIP1;1 and NIP3;1 has been known to be involved in As transport and knock down of NIP genes lead to tolerance to As due to reduced As transport activities (Gautam et al., 2020b). Transport of antimony by NIP1;1 and tolerance towards its toxicity by knockdown of NIP genes has also been reported (Sharma et al., 2018). Aluminum toxicity along with water deficit is reported as a major limiting factor for crop yield (Pandey et al. 2016) Plants have even developed an exclusion and detoxification mechanism to tolerate the aluminum toxicity. The NIP subfamily of AQPs is a bidirectional transporter present in the root tips facilitates the aluminum transport inside and outside of the plant. Wang et al., 2017 revealed the role of NIP1;2 transcripts in translocating aluminum in the form of aluminum malate complex from root cell wall to the root symplasm (Table 1).


## Drought


Drought is prolonged shortages of water that leads to low water availability and affects growth and development of plants. It occurs due to lowering of rainfall, temperature extremities such as low or high temperature, salinity etc. it alters various physiological, morphological and biochemical processes of plants (Fathi & Tari, 2016). As AQPs are water channels, its function in relation to drought is interesting to study. The expression patterns and alteration in subcellular localization is observed in drought exposed plants. During drought, the activity of AQPs is increased to absorb more and more water but the activities slow down at the later stages so as to inhibit the reverse transport of water molecules from root to the soil (Shekoofa & Sinclair, 2018). Water uptake and transcellular distribution is largely mediated by PIPs and TIPs which are also considered as most abundant AQPs in plasma membrane and tonoplast respectively (Kapilan et al., 2018). The NIP genes are found to be least expressed during desiccation (Alexandersson et al., 2005). Exposure to drought stress leads to differential expression of aquaporin homologues. Expression of 35 aquaporin homologues were studied by Alexandersson et al., 2005 in Arabidopsis exposed to drought stress (Afzal et al., 2016). Increased expression of PIP and TIP while decreased expression of NIP genes was found in drought exposed plants samples (Afzal et al., 2016). Similar results were obtained in drought exposed olive plants (Secchi et al., 2007). Comparative transcriptomic studies of cotton revealed drought induced up regulation of PIP1;3, PIP2;5 gene (Alexandersson et al., 2010). Contrasting results were also obtained in studies on Vitis vinifera in which the VvPIP1;1 was upregulated and VvPIP2;1 gene was downregulated on drought exposure to plants (Vandeleur et al., 2009). Osmotic stress in rice showed null effects on OsPIP1;3 gene but OsPIP1;1 and OsPIP1;2 were up regulated (Abdelkader et al., 2012). Many PIP genes were also reported to be downregulated in roots of tobacco and olive and fruits of peach (Mahdieh et al., 2008; Secchi et al., 2007).. The polyethylene glycol (PEG) treated rice plants induced the expression of OsPIP1;1 and OsPIP1;2 while no change was noticed in OsPIP1;3 (Guo et al., 2006) (Table 1).

Many factors are considered on over expressing of AQPs in development of transgenic plants as some AQP are not much beneficial in providing tolerance against drought in crops as up regulating PIP1;2 genes in tobacco plants leads to increased wilt on exposure to drought. Similarly PIP2;1 gene in rice was also found to show increased water loss by leaf on exposure to drought (Afzal et al., 2016; Šurbanovski et al., 2013). Over-expression of PIP1;1 and PIP1;2 genes showed elevated tolerance to drought in Banana while over-expression of SlTIP2;2 induced tolerance to drought in tomato plants (Xu et al., 2014; Sade et al., 2009). The drought stress in combination with heat stress imposes severe damage to crops in comparison with their individual stress. The combination of drought and heat are extensively studied from time to time. Rizhsky et al., 2004 studied the impact of combination of heat and drought on Arabidopsis. The transcription analysis revealed that 454 transcripts were expressed specifically in the plants exposed to combined stress. Moreover sugars such as maltose and gulose were found to be accumulated in the plants exposed to combined stress. Exposure of combined heat and drought stress on tobacco plants revealed the stomatal closure, reduced photosynthesis, increased photorespiration and expression of heat shock proteins (Rizhsky et al., 2002). Expression of ascorbate peroxidase was suppressed in combined stress while transcripts encoding dehydrin catalase and glycolate oxidase were induced in drought exposed plants. Some other transcripts that were up-regulated due to the combined effect of stress include alternative oxidase, glutathione peroxidase and phenylalanine ammonia lyase. The photosynthetic genes were down-regulated while transcripts playing a role in glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathway were found to be up-regulated in plants exposed to combined stress. The response of tobacco plants on combined stress strongly suggests that the combined effect is very much contrasting with the individual effects.

#

Cold stress is an important abiotic stress that limits plant growth and development. Excessive falling of temperatures modifies the metabolism of the plant due to changes in the structure and catalytic properties of the enzymes (Zhu, 2016). Phenotypic symptoms include reduced expansion of leaf, yellowing of leaf due to chlorosis, wilting of leaves followed by necrosis and death of the plant (Wang et al., 2016). Major effects of the chilling stress at reproductive stages include pollen sterility that leads to lowered grain yield of the crops (Hossain et al., 2018). Plasma membrane damage due to transition from semi fluid state to crystalline state leads to cell death. Contrary to this cold resistant plant can withstand the transition due to presence of unsaturated fatty acids as this solidifies slower than saturated fatty acid that is present in cold sensitive plant species (Zhang et al., 2019).

Transcriptomic studies report reduction in expression of PIP genes in plants when exposed to cold stress and an increased expression on recovery from the stress. In Oryzae sativa the expression of OsPIP2;5 was up regulated and increased expression of PIP and TIP AQPs (MaPIP1;1, MaPIP1;2, MaPIP2;4, MaPIP2;6, MaTIP1;3) was found in banana (Murai-Hatano et al., 2015). Transgenic plants that showed enhanced drought stress on over expression of PIP genes also showed tolerance to cold. For example transgenic banana and wheat plant over expressing PIP2 genes showed tolerance to drought as well as cold (Ayadi et al., 2019; Sreedharan et al., 2013). Transgenic Arabidopsis became tolerant to cold stress when AtPIP1;4 or AtPIP2;5 genes were over expressed (Nguyen et al., 2013). Similarly transgenic tobacco plants showed cold and drought tolerance when AQP7 gene was overexpressed (Zhou et al., 2012). In contrast, the transgenic Arabidopsis plants over-expressing PIP1;4 and PIP1;5 genes were resistant to cold stress but showed rapid dehydration on exposure to drought. This speculates that there is no such uniformity of AQP expression under cold and drought conditions among the crops (Ahamed et al., 2012). Cold stress exposure also caused suppression of TIP genes as seen in Oryzae sativa. The expression of OsTIP1;1 and OsTIP2;2 were down-regulated in rice on exposure of cold stress (Sakurai et al., 2005). It is interesting to report that among different isoforms of PIP AQPs only PIP2;5 and PIP2;6 were over-expressed (Table 1). These genes also exhibit a complex regulatory network with ABA dependent and ABA independent pathway of AQP regulation. The response of AQPs varies with ABA treatment which indicates key role of ABA dependent and ABA independent signaling cascades in AQP expression (Li et al., 2015).


## AQPs and Plant Hormones


Plant hormones such as gibberellins (GA), abscisic acid (ABA), cytokinins and auxins play an important role in AQPs regulation (Table 2). The ABA regulates plant AQPs by altering the root hydraulic conductivity and induces stomatal closure. The GA regulated the expression of TIP1;1 AQP transcript and increased the plant growth rate, photosynthetic efficiency, transpiration rate and stomatal density (Phillips & Huttly, 1994). Hu et al. (2007) extensively studied the role of plasma membrane AQPs (OsRWC3) in inducing gravitropism in the lower side of the Oryzae sativa leaves. The expression of the AQP was confirmed to be induced by GA because when rice leaves were exposed to ancymidol, a GA biosynthetic inhibitor, the expression of OsRWC3 was markedly reduced. Moreover the osmotic potential in the lower side of the leaves consequently decreased thus reducing its gravitropic curvature. Auxin is known to be an important growth regulator for lateral root development in plants. Péret et al. (2012) have reported the role of auxin in reduction of root hydraulic conductivity and emergence of lateral roots through PIPs. Mutant plants having disrupted PIP genes showed reduced lateral root development.

Ethylene hormone regulates cell expansion which is a crucial step for growth of plants. It also regulates the seed germination, organ growth, flowering, ripening of fruits and senescence (Iqbal et al., 2017). In a study on Rosa hybrida the leaf expansion was found to be associated with PIP1;1 and PIP2;1 genes (Pei et al., 2013). The ethylene hormone induces the transcription of RhNAC100 gene that directs the cell expansion process in Rosa hybrida (Pei et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2008). Chen et al. (2013) demonstrated that RhPIP1;1 gene silencing significantly decreased the petal expansion in comparison to control. Apart from GA, auxin and ethylene, another important phytohormone known as abscisic acid (ABA), critically control the water level in plants (Fig. 2). The role of AQP has been studied in regulating the osmotic potential of the guard cell. Mutant Arabidopsis thalliana plant lacking PIP 2;1 genes showed deformity in stomatal closure (Grondin et al., 2015). ABA also induces twice the increase in osmotic water permeability in guard cells. This study supports the ABA induced guard cell derived stomatal closure using PIP mediated regulatory mechanism (Grondin et al., 2015).


## AQPs and Signaling Molecules


Several studies have demonstrated that aquaporins facilitate the transport of various signaling molecules that are essential for proper functioning of the plant (Table 1). Different cellular processes like stomatal movement, photosynthesis, photorespiration, cell growth and differentiation and senescence require quick transport of the regulatory molecules across the plasma membrane (Conner & Schmid, 2003). It is very important to understand the role of aquaporins as transporting molecules to facilitate transport of these key regulatory molecules to carry out important processes in the plant system. One of the key regulatory molecule, hydrogen peroxide $( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ , although diffuses across the membrane but some membranes that are less permeable requires a specific channel protein PIP to facilitate the transport. Jang et al., 2012 studied the role of Arabidopsis thalliana isoforms AtPIP2;2, AtPIP2;4, AtPIP2;5, and AtPIP2;7 in facilitating $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ transport in yeast cells.

Several studies have reported the role of Hydrogen sulfide in abiotic stress tolerance including heat, salinity, cold and heavy metal stress (Fotopoulos et al., 2013; Jin, 2015; Pandey et al., 2020; Paul & Roychoudhury, 2020). In an experiment when plants were exposed to heat stress $( 4 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ showed a marked upregulation of heat shock protein along with an up regulation of PIP AQP suggesting that heat exposure induces PIP expression (Jin, 2015). When plants were treated with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ using NaHS $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ donor, sodium hydrogen sulphide) the PIP expression was delayed in comparison to the plants not treated with NaHS. Overall data confirms the role of AQPs in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S }$ mediated abiotic stress tolerance. Nitric oxide or NO is another gaseous regulatory molecule that readily diffuses through the plasma membrane and carries out several biological processes including seed germination (Liu et al., 2007). The expression and regulation of PIPs has been studied by Liu et al., 2007 and their data concludes the role of NO in regulating the PIP expression during the seed germination process (Fig. 2). OsPIP1;1, OsPIP2;8, OsPIP1;3 were found to be expressed at the germination stage in rice seedlings. Mutant plants lacking OsPIP genes showed reduced seed germination. The results also suggest that NO promotes seed germination and the AQPs function as downstream effectors of NO signaling pathway.


## Tolerance Strategies of AQPs


One of the important ways of crop improvement is to improvise the use of resources like maximizing the uptake of water and essential nutrients through roots (Khan et al., 2017; Badr et al., 2018). AQPs are nowadays targeted for genetic engineering and the transgenic plants that are designed to over express AQPs to improve the uptake of water and minerals and providing tolerance in plants exposed to stressful conditions (del Carmen Martinez-Ballesta & Carvajal, 2014). Genetic manipulation of AQPs, gene silencing and T-DNA insertion are promising strategies to study the role of AQPs in maintaining plant water relations. Over-expression of AQP genes and production of transgenic plants leads to improved stress tolerance in plants. Suppression of AQP genes, knockouts or over-expressions are some novel tools implied to understand the functioning of different isoforms of AQPs under wide range of abiotic stresses. Neri and his co-workers over-expressed aqua 1 gene in Populas alba, a well known cadmium tolerant plant species and found improved cadmium translocation and lowered cadmium sensitivity in transgenic plants. Exposure to higher levels of cadmium to the wild type as well as aqua1 transgenic plants did not showed any morphological symptoms even after 2 months of treatment. This further confirms the role of AQPs in heavy metal transport in plant (Neri et al. 2021). Xu et al., 2020a cloned the PIP2 isoforms of AQPs and reported that over-expression of the PIP2 isoforms improved tolerance to a multiple stresses including drought, salt and cold in transgenic banana species. Transgenic banana plants exhibited reduced membrane injury, maintained osmotic balances by elevated $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ ratios and enhanced ABA levels. Xu and his coworkers in another experiment demonstrated that AQP gene, SIP2–1, when overexpressed in bananas provided tolerance to osmotic, cold and salt stresses. The transgenic lines not only exhibited higher chlorophyll, proline, soluble sugar and ABA content but also lowered $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and malondialdehyde contents (Xu et al., 2020b). Hence SIP2–1 isoforms of AQP proved to have potential of improving abiotic stresses in plants. Over-expressing PIP2;4 isoforms of AQPs in Oryzae sativa (Giza178 and IR64 species) resulted in significantly improved root hydraulic conductivity which eventually led to increased growth, relative water content, gaseous exchanges and grain yield in drought exposed transgenic lines (Nada & Abogadallah, 2020).

Various research efforts have been made to enhance the efficiency of AQP such as PIP and TIP so that more water and solutes can be taken in the stressful conditions (Xu et al., 2020a, 2020b; Wang et al., 2019; Song et al., 2018). The transgenic Arabidopsis plant expressing Vicia faba PIP1 (VfPIP1) showed improved tolerance to drought by inducing stomatal closure and decreased water loss by transpiration (Cui et al., 2008). The SlTIP2;1 was over expressed in tomato plant conferred drought and salt tolerance (Li et al., 2016). In addition over expression of AQPs in one plant from another plant species also improves the tolerance. For instances expression of TdPIP1;1 genes from wheat in tobacco plant lead to increased root growth and leaf area (Ayadi et al., 2011). It was also observed that over expressing wheat AQPs in tobacco lead to increased activity of detoxification enzymes such as SOD, CAT and reduces the level of ROS including $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ in addition of enhancing the plant water relations (Zhou et al., 2012). Similarly the over expression of TIP AQPs from enhanced the plant transpiration in tomato and $\mathrm { P g T I P 1 }$ expression from Panax ginseng increased root shoot growth in Arabidopsis under drought stress (An et al. 2017). The tonoplast AQPs TIP5;1 also increased the uptake of boron in addition of improving water transport (Pang et al., 2010). In addition, the wheat AQPs TaNIP enhanced salinity tolerance by increasing potassium and calcium influx and sodium efflux from the cytoplasm to extracellular matrix (Almeida et al., 2017) (Fig. 2). Some phytohormones not only play a key role in regulating the AQPs and up regulating the expression of associated transporters genes but also help in portraying architecture of the roots. For instance, cytokinins, a phytohormone, helps in improving shoot growth of plants through increasing uptake of water through AQPs (Pavlů et al., 2018; Calvo-Polanco et al., 2019). The structure of root depends on its interaction with the environment (Sah et al., 2016). Water scarcity leads to significant alteration in root structure and growth pattern (Sah et al., 2016). Abscisic acid play role in response to inconsistent water availability in the soil and stimulates the ion flux and water flow to regulate the turgor pressure into the roots (Sah et al., 2016). It also decreases the rate of transpiration to reduce the water loss (Sah et al., 2016). Moreover ABA is reported to induce the growth of roots in comparison to the growth of shoots in the plants during water stress (Spollen et al., 2000). Spollen and his coworkers reported accumulation of ABA induced root elongation in maize during water stress. The roots also became thinner and longer so as to search water carrying moist soils in its surroundings.

## Analysis of the HvTIP promoter reveals the presence of stress- and hormone-related elements


The EnsemblePlants database was used to identify the promotor sequences of the HvTIP genes and the mRNA sequences that are deposited in the NCBI database were used as the query. The HvTIP genes in the barley genome were previously identified by Hove and coworkers [12]. A genetic similarity tree was created based on the amino acid sequences of the barley aquaporins from the TIP subfamily using the Neighbour Joining Clustering method. The three main clusters are shown: a): HvTIP4;3, HvTIP4;1, HvTIP4;2 and HvTIP5;1, b): HvTIP1;1, HvTIP1;2, HvTIP3;1 and HvTIP3;2 and c): HvTIP2;1, HvTIP2;2 and HvTIP2;3, which are further subdivided into smaller groups in which the isoforms that have the same main number occur (Fig 2).

The $H \nu T I P$ genes are located in all barley chromosomes except for 5H (Table 1). The number of splice variants for individual genes that were found in EnsemblePlants ranged from 2 to 18. These data are provided by the International Barley Genome Sequencing Consortium and are based on a deep RNA sequencing project (RNA-seq) [31]. The abundant amount of alternative splicing for some of the HvTIP genes suggest that post-transcriptional processing might be their important regulatory mechanism. There was no high confident hit for HvTIP5;1 during the BLAST analysis using an amino acid sequence as the query in the Ensemble database (Table 1).

The multiple sequence alignment of the partial amino acid sequences of the HvTIP in barley showed the presence of both conserved and specific motifs. The dual NPA (AsparagineProline-Alanine) motifs were conserved among all 11 HvTIP. However, the ar/R (aromatic/

Arginine) selective filters, which consist of four residues, were highly variable and contained the following amino-acids at these positions: [H/Q]–[I/T/V]–[A/G]–[V/R] (Fig 3).

To identify the putative stress-responsive cis-elements in the promoter regions of the $H \nu T I P$ genes, one kb of the upstream sequences relative to the transcription start sites were searched against the PlantCARE database. The presence of several putative cis-regulatory elements that are mainly connected with abiotic stress (Table 2) and phytohormone (Table 3) responses were revealed. A total of four types of stress-related cis-elements were detected, including LTR (low temperature-responsive elements), DRE (dehydration-responsive element), TC-rich repeats (defense and stress-responsive elements) and MBS (the MYB binding site that is involved in drought-inducibility). Additionally, the cis-elements that are recognised by transcription factors (TF) from the MYB and MYC family, which may play a role in the response to abiotic stress were detected in the promoters of HvTIP (Table 2). Furthermore, four types of elements that possibly participate in the response to hormones, such as abscisic acid (ABA), methyl jasmonate (MeJA), gibberellins (GA) and auxin, were also identified (Table 3).

All of the 11 genes contained at least one cis-element that is connected with the stress or hormone response. The best represented were two regulatory elements: the TGACG-motif and CGTCA-motif, which were found in all of the promoters that were investigated. These elements are implicated in plant responses to methyl jasmonate (MeJA), a well-known primary signal in plant defense and stress response. All of the HvTIP promoter regions, except for $H \nu T I P 2 ; I$ , contained at least one ABA-responsive element (ABRE), which is involved in the ABA response and in ABA-mediated abiotic stress signalling. Conversely, only some of the $H \nu T I P$ promoters contained an auxin- or gibberellin-responsive element (Table 3). Other well-represented elements were: DRE (dehydration responsive), which was detected in 6 of the $1 1 H \nu T I P$ promoters and MBS (a MYB binding site that is involved in drought-inducibility), which was found in 4 of the 11 promoters. The functionality of the predicted cis-elements requires experimental validation.

We first assessed the number of HvTIP transcripts in the seedlings that were grown in the optimal soil moisture conditions. Our analysis showed that most of the $H \nu T I P$ genes, except for HvTIP3;2, HvTIP4;3 and HvTIP5.1, were transcribed in the leaves of the ten-day-old barley seedlings. As is shown in the Fig 6, the most highly expressed genes were: HvTIP2;3, HvTIP1;2 and HvTIP1;1, which could indicate they are indispensable during this stage of leaf development. Conversely, the HvTIP3;1 gene was expressed at the lowest level, followed by the

HvTIP2;1 and HvTIP2;2 genes. The expression level of HvTIP3;1 was much lower and the expression level of HvTIP2;3 was slightly higher compared to the reference ADP gene encoding ADP-ribozylation factor 1.

Because all $1 1 H \nu T I P$ genes had the drought-responsive cis-elements in their promoters, we decided to evaluate their transcriptional activity in seedlings that were exposed to ten days of severe drought stress followed by 14 days of re-watering. Three genes: HvTIP3;2, HvTIP4;3 and $H \nu T I P 5 . 1$ , which were not transcribed in the leaves of the ten-day-old seedlings under optimal moisture conditions, were also not induced by drought treatment. However, the majority of the HvTIP genes that were transcriptionally active in the control, had significant changes in their expression level in response to the drought stress that was applied and the return to the optimal water conditions. The timing and magnitude of the observed changes were diverse among the analysed genes. Based on their expression profiles, we distinguished two main groups of HvTIP: the first group of five genes that were down-regulated after drought stress $( H \nu T I P I ; I , H \nu T I P I ; 2 , H \nu T I P 2 ; I , H \nu T I P 2 ; 2$ and HvTIP2;3) and the second group of two genes $( H \nu T I P 3 ; I , H \nu T I P 4 ; I )$ that were up-regulated after the drought treatment. The transcriptional activity of only one gene (HvTIP4;1) was not affected by the drought stress (Fig 7). The highest reduction of the expression under drought stress was detected for the $H \nu T I P { \cal I } ; 2$ and HvTIP2;1 genes, a 142- and 30-fold lower expression level in the droughttreated seedlings than in the control seedlings, respectively. For three other genes, HvTIP1;1, HvTIP2;3 and HvTIP2;2, this decrease was much lower– 7-, 5- and 1.5-fold, compared to the control, respectively. The greatest change in transcriptional activity was observed for the HvTIP3;1 gene, which showed more than a 5000-fold increase in expression in the leaves of the stress-treated seedlings. Interestingly, rehydration caused the return of the expression of many genes to the level that was observed under optimal moisture conditions or at least a change in this direction (Fig 7). For the $H \nu T I P { I } ; I$ and HvTIP1;2 genes, the expression increased again, while for the $H \nu T I P 3 ; 1$ and $H \nu T I P 4 ; I$ genes, it dropped to the control level. After the re-watering period, only three of the eight genes (HvTIP2;3, HvTIP2;1 and HvTIP2;2) had a change in their expression level compared to the control growth. One of these genes–HvTIP2;3 exhibited a further decrease in expression level after the significant decrease that was caused by the drought treatment and its expression after re-watering was reduced 59-fold lower compared to control. That was the only gene that showed a specific profile than
