The AtCLCc is predominantly expressed in stomatal cells and pollen grains. The treatment of leaf epidermis with ABA induced the expression of AtCLCc in epidermal cells and stomatal guard cells [30].

The clcc knockout mutants (Col-0, Ws) were distinguished by the impaired regulation of stomatal conductance under the action of light and ABA. After 2-h illumination, the aperture of stomata in the mutants was one-third lower than in the WT plants. The ABA treatment did not induce stomatal closure in the mutant. Because of misregulated stomatal movements, the leaf temperature was higher in clcc than in the WT plants. The intracellular $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ content in stomata of the mutant was lower than in the WT plants [30].

The clcc mutation had no influence on plant development and morphology or on pollen fertility. However, clcc mutants were characterized by increased sensitivity to $\mathbf { N a C l }$ [30]. The aboveground organs of mutant plants exposed to salinity contained larger quantities of chloride than the WT plants [29].

The application of QTL (Quantitative Trait Loci) analysis for the search of chromosomal loci responsible for nitrate accumulation revealed that AtCLCc participates in the homeostasis of this anion [45]. The supporting evidence is that the content of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and citrate was reduced in the shoots of clcc A. thaliana ecotype No-0, while the content of malate was raised [45].

The AtCLCc (Col-0) protein contains two phosphorylation sites, namely, serines $\mathbf { S } ^ { 2 7 }$ and $\mathbf { S } ^ { 6 7 2 }$ at the ${ \bf N } _ { - }$ and C-terminal parts, respectively [40, 46]. Phosphorylation of $\mathbf { S } ^ { 6 7 2 }$ was induced by treating the plants with sodium chloride [46]. The N-terminal (1–92) and C-terminal (562–779) segments of the AtCLCc protein were shown to interact with the C5 subunit of phosphatase PP2A [41]. This finding suggests that the activity of AtCLCc is regulated by phosphorylation– dephosphorylation of its amino acid sequence.

AtCLCd was the first plant anion transporter identified in the compartments engaged in the endocytic membrane trafficking. The AtCLCd transporter is found in the trans-Golgi membranes, where it is colocalized with the $\mathrm { v . }$ -type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase [19, 20, 27, 28]. The AtCLCd is likely involved in regulation of pH and chloride concentration in the lumen of the trans-Golgi network and in late endosomes. This protein is assumingly transports $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ into the endosomal lumen. $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ influx neutralizes positive charges that accumulate in the lumen due to functioning of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase and, thereby, stimulates lumenal acidification required for endocytic and secretory events [20].

The activity of the AtCLCd gene promoter was observed in all organs and tissues; the promoter activity level was organ-specific and depended on the stage of plant development. The activity of the AtCLCd promoter was most conspicuous in seedling roots, cotyledons, hydathodes, flowers, and, particularly, in anthers and pollen grains [20]. The use of Western blot analysis revealed the presence of AtCLCd protein in all plant organs; the largest amount of this protein was detected in seedpods [27].

The clcd knockout mutants did not differ from the WT plants in morphology, growth parameters, and ion content at various $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations in the medium. However, the root growth in the mutants was suppressed at weakly acidic media $( \mathrm { p H } 6 . 8 - 6 . 2 )$ . The clcd mutants showed an increased sensitivity to concanamycin A, a known blocker of $\mathrm { v . }$ -type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase [20].

It was found that AtCLCd acts as a negative regulator of plant immunity induced by pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP); this effect was apparently due to the participation of FLS2 receptor (FlagellinSensitive 2) in vesicle trafficking [47]. The clcd mutants were more resistant to the virulent strain of bacteria Pseudomonas syringae. The clcd mutation enhanced the early and late responses to the action of elicitors (f lg22, elf18, or chitin). The treatment with elicitors elevated the level of reactive oxygen species in tissues and resulted in a larger deposition of callose in clcd mutants compared to WT plants. At the same time, the treatment with the f lagellin peptide f lg22 enhanced the expression of PAMP-induced genes— Flg22-induced Receptor-like Kinase 1 (FRK1), At1g51890, and At2g17740—and Pathogenesis-Related gene 1 (PR1, the late response gene) much higher in clcd mutant than in WT plants. Overexpression of AtCLCd in A. thaliana plants led to the opposite effects: the plants became more susceptible to the pathogen impact. Guo et al. [47] showed that the expression of AtCLCd is regulated by signaling complexes, including the PAMP-recognizing receptor FLS2 and kinases SERK3 and SERK4 (Somatic Embryogenesis Receptor-like Kinase). The binding of elicitors to these complexes suppressed the expression of both AtCLCd and other representatives of the A. thaliana CLC family [47].

AtCLCe is located in the chloroplast thylakoid membranes [28]. Analysis of chlorophyll fluorescence in clce mutants and WT plants revealed the involvement of AtCLCe protein in light reactions of photosynthesis [19, 28]. At the same time, the clce mutation did not affect plant growth parameters [28]. Analysis of fluorescence induction kinetics and dark relaxation of chlorophyll a excited states in clce mutant revealed no significant changes in light-dependent electron transport in chloroplasts. However, the ratio of lightinduced electrical $( \Delta \Psi )$ and chemical $\mathrm { ( \Delta p H ) }$ components of the proton-motive force $( \Delta \rho )$ in mutants, as well as the chloroplast ultrastructure, was disturbed [48]. The authors proposed that AtCLCe participates in the export of chloride from the thylakoid lumen during the light–dark transition and plays only a minor role in the transport of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ into the thylakoid lumen during light reactions of photosynthesis [48].

In addition, there is evidence that the AtCLCe protein is involved in nitrate homeostasis. The phenotypic manifestations of clce mutation are similar to those in clca mutant plants. Compared to wild-type plants, the clce mutants are characterized by reduced $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ content and the increased content of nitrite and malate. A possible role of AtCLCe protein in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ homeostasis was also supported by the search of the chromosomal loci responsible for nitrate accumulation in A. thaliana (QTL analysis) [45]. Nevertheless, the functions of AtCLCa and AtCLCe proteins are not redundant, as indicated by a particular role of AtCLCe in the ionic homeostasis of thylakoids [38]. The AtCLCe gene is expressed mainly in aerial organs, such as leaf rosettes, rosettes, and seedpods. The level of AtCLCe expression is comparable with the expression of AtCLCf and is substantially lower than the expression of AtCLCa– AtCLCd genes [19, 38]. The existence of a “cross-talk” between the AtCLCe, AtCLCa genes and the genes of nitrate transporter families was proposed [38].

AtCLCf is localized predominantly in cis-Golgi compartments and, to a lesser extent, in the transGolgi network [28]. When the AtCLCf gene was introduced into the mutant strain Δgef1 of Saccharomyces cerevisiae (this yeast contains only one CLC family gene encoding the chloride transporter Gef1p), the product of the AtCLCf gene was apparently able to transport chloride ions [28]. AtCLCf is expressed in all organs of A. thaliana [19]. According to Lv et al. [19], the content of AtCLCf gene transcripts in organs depends on plant age: it increases during plant growth and development. This protein is thought to participate in intracellular vesicular trafficking, apparently, by facilitating ionic homeostasis in the Golgi apparatus and the trans-Golgi network. The functions of AtCLCf and AtCLCd may partly overlap [28]. Along with these findings, the data of QTL analysis reveal the possible role of AtCLCf gene product in nitrate accumulation in A. thaliana [45]. The AtCLCf transporter currently remains the least studied protein of the AtCLC family: its transport function and physiological roles are not yet fully clarified.

AtCLCg is localized in the tonoplast and participates in the sequestration of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ in the vacuole under salt stress [19, 29]. Knockout mutants for this gene have a pronounced phenotype. Under growing at elevated salinity, the plant fresh weight, root length, and the number of lateral roots were lower in clcg mutants than in the WT plants. Under salinity conditions, the mutants accumulated larger amounts of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ in aerial organs and higher quantities of $\mathsf { S O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ in roots [29].

The AtCLCg protein is most similar to AtCLCc in terms of amino acid sequence. The expression of AtCLCg was suppressed in the clcc mutant; conversely, the expression of AtCLCc was weakened in clcg mutant, which suggests the interaction of both genes [29]. Physiological functions of the AtCLCg and AtCLCc proteins do not duplicate each other; each of them makes a specific contribution to salt tolerance: the sensitivity of the double mutant clcc-clcg to NaCl was not higher than that of the plants with a single gene mutation, clcc or clcg [29].

The highest activity of the AtCLCg promoter was observed in mesophyll cells, phloem, parenchymal cells of the root hair zone, hydathodes, and the leaf blade areas adjacent to hydathodes. The high activity of AtCLCg promoter in hydathodes may indicate the participation of $\mathbf { \Delta A t C L C g }$ in $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ excretion into external medium at elevated salinity. The activity of gene promoter in phloem cells and high $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ content in shoots of mutant plants suggests that $\mathbf { \Delta } \mathbf { A } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { L } \mathbf { C } \mathbf { g }$ might be involved in $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ recirculation. It is also possible that this protein participates in xylem loading with chloride. When the roots are exposed to excessive salinity, AtCLCg of parenchymal cells in the root hair zone might regulate cytosolic $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ concentration and promote this anion sequestration into the vacuole [29].


## CLC PROTEIN FAMILYIN OTHER PLANT SPECIES


Full-length gene sequences of the CLC family were cloned not only from A. thaliana but also from other plants, such as tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum) [21, 49, 50], rice (Oryza sativa) [51, 52], soybean (Glycine max) [16, 53], wild soybean (Glycine soja) [16], maize (Zea mays) [54–56], trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliate) [57, 58], salt-excreting halophyte Thellungiella halophila [59], and an euhalophyte Suaeda altissima [60, 61].

The first cloned CLC gene from plants was NtCLC1, whose product is similar in amino acid sequence to AtCLCc [49]. The gene NtCLC1 was expressed in all organs of $N .$ . tabacum. The highest expression was observed in stems. When the NtCLC1 protein was expressed in frog oocytes, it mediated a slowly activated inward current in response to plasma membrane hyperpolarization, and it was permeable to $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ , $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { I } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { B r ^ { - } }$ , and, to a lesser extent, malate, sulfate, and glutamate [49, 50]. The NtCLC1 protein is localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (EPR). Experiments with a $\mathsf { p H }$ -sensitive fluorescent dye pHluorin conjugated with HDEL tetrapeptide (pHluorin– HDEL sensor targeted to EPR), have shown that the NtCLC1 protein contributes to the regulation of lumenal pH in EPR and accounts for alkalinization of the lumen [21]. Using the secreted form of GFP (secGFP), Sun et al. [21] established the importance of NtCLC1 for protein secretion. The promoter activity of NtCLC1 was detected in all plant organs. The NtCLC1 protein is probably involved in plant growth and development. This view stems from the observations with N. benthamiana (a close relative of tobacco) that simultaneous knockout of two homologous NtCLC1 genes in nbclca nbclcb mutants decreased the plant height and flower size as compared to these parameters in WT plants [21]. The implication of NtCLC1 in viral pathogenesis in tobacco plants was also reported. The NtCLC1 transporter was found to interact with the 6K2 protein of PVY potyvirus (Potato virus Y). It was proposed that PVY virus binds to and activates the NtCLC1 transporter, which alters the lumenal pH in EPR and promotes the subsequent release from EPR of virus-containing vesicles that deliver virus particles to the plasmalemma, thus contributing to the systemic infection [21].

The relation of the CLC family proteins to viral pathogenesis was also found with Solanum lycopersicum (tomato) plants infected by potato spindle tuber viroid. The transcription of SlCLCb , an AtCLCb homolog in tomato, was silenced by small viroid RNAs due to the mRNA degradation of SlCLCb [62]. The virusinduced silencing of SlCLCb caused growth retardation and leaf curl symptoms [62], which implies the important role of the SlCLCb protein in plant growth and development. However, the function of SlCLCb at the cellular level awaits further studies.

Apart from NtCLC1, the genome of N. tabacum contains 16 more genes (NtCLC2–NtCLC17) attributed to the CLC family [17]. However, Zhang et al. [17] did not find the transcripts of five of them (1, 4, 11, 14, 16) in plant organs and tissues. Genes 6, 7, 9, 10, and 17 were mainly expressed in the stem; genes 3, 5, 8, 12, and 13 in buds; and gene 15 in the pistil. Under salt stress conditions, the level of transcripts increased for all genes in the aerial organs and increased for genes 2, 3, and 12 in the roots. When the genes homologous to genes 2 and 13 from $N .$ . tabacum were separately silenced in N. benthamiana plants, the chloride content in the aerial organs decreased and increased, respectively [17], which points to the participation of these genes in the long-distance $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ transport.

Two genes of the CLC family, OsCLC-1 and OsCLC-2, homologous to the NtCLC1 gene were cloned from rice ( $O .$ . sativa). OsCLC-1 was expressed in all tissues, whereas OsCLC-2 was expressed only in roots, nodes, and stem internodes as well as in the leaf sheath. Proteins OsCLC-1 and OsCLC-2 are localized in the tonoplast and are involved in the transport of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ across the vacuolar membrane [52]. These proteins are crucial for growth and development of rice plants, as indicated by the inhibited growth of mutants knocked out on OsCLC-1 and OsCLC-2 genes. The level of OsCLC-1 transcripts in roots and leaves of rice seedlings increased when NaCl was present in the medium, whereas the expression of OsCLC-2 was independent of the presence of external NaCl. It has been suggested that OsCLC-1 plays a role in the mechanism of salt tolerance, apparently, by compartmentalizing $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ in the vacuole [52]. The physiological role of OsCLC-2 remains undisclosed.

All members of the chloride channel family were successfully cloned from the moderately salt-tolerant cultivated soybean $G .$ . max and the salt-tolerant wild soybean species $G .$ soja [16]. The family includes eight genes: CLC1, b1, b2, c1, c2, d1, d2 , and $g .$ . All genes of the CLC family of $G .$ . max and $G$ . soja were expressed in roots, stems, and leaves. The expression of genes CLC1, b1, b2, c1, and $^ { c 2 }$ in soybean organs was induced under salt shock conditions, which suggests that these gene products participate in the formation of salt tolerance [16].

The properties of GmCLC1 were studied in more detail [53, 63, 64]. Electrophysiological experiments with frog oocytes have shown that GmCLC1 is a $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. The GmCLC1 protein is localized in the tonoplast. It accounts for the compartmentalization of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ in vacuoles and plays an important role in salt tolerance of soybean plants. The protein GmCLC1 transports $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ [16, 63]. Expression of GmCLC1 improved the salt tolerance of transgenic A. thaliana plants because it retarded the entry of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ into aerial organs [64]. The increased resistance to salt stress was also observed in poplar plants expressing GmCLC1 [65].

The GsCLCc2 protein is a voltage-gated vacuolar transporter carrying $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ into the vacuole and conferring salt resistance to $G .$ . max plants. The conductance of $\mathbf { G s C L C c } 2$ for anions decreased in the following row: $\mathbf { B } \mathbf { r } ^ { - } \geq \mathbf { I } ^ { - } > \mathbf { C } \mathbf { l } ^ { - } > \mathbf { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ . The transgenic $G .$ . max plants showing overexpression of GsCLCc2 featured a comparatively high salt tolerance [16]. Despite the presence of both conservative glutamates in the GsCLCc2 protein sequence, the ion transport mediated by this transporter was independent of $\mathrm { p H }$ . The GsCLCc2 protein operated as an anion channel [16].

Full-length sequences coding $Z { \bmod { C } } \mathrm { L C c }$ and ZmCLCd proteins are cloned from maize [54–56]. ZmCLCc is localized in mitochondria and is presumably involved in $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ transport. This view stems from the suppression of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { I } ^ { - }$ fluxes through the inner mitochondrial membrane under the action of antibodies to this protein. The importance of $Z { \bmod { C } } \mathrm { L C c }$ for cold tolerance in $Z .$ mays was concluded, because expression of this protein was induced in cold-stressed maize seedlings. An enhanced expression of ZmCLCc was observed in maize lines featured an increased cold tolerance during seed germination and plant development [54].

The expression of ZmCLCd in leaves, roots, and stems was documented. The highest level of ZmCLCd transcription was observed in leaves. A. thaliana plants overexpressing ZmCLCd were more tolerant to cold stress, salinity, drought, and oxidative stress compared with WT plants [56]. The transport function and localization of $Z { \bmod { C } } \mathrm { L C d }$ have not been investigated.

Six genes of the CLC family (PtrCLC1–PtrCLC6) found in the genome of the trifoliate orange (P. trifoliata) have been cloned [57, 58]. The PtrCLC genes were expressed in all tissues; the highest expression was observed in leaves, and the smallest expression was in roots. The level of PtrCLC expression depended on nitrate concentration in the medium and changed in response to salinity [58]. Heterologous expression of

PtrCLC2 in wild-type A. thaliana plants and clcc knockout mutant decreased the $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ content in shoots, thus improving salt tolerance of transgenic plants compared to nontransformed plants. Proteins of the PtrCLC family are presumably involved in ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ homeostasis [57].

The salt-excluding halophyte Thellungiella halophila is from the same Brassicaceae family as A. thaliana. From this plant, a ThCLC-a gene was cloned [59]. ThCLC-a is localized in the vacuolar membrane, where it apparently transports $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and accounts for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ accumulation in vacuoles. The ThCLC-a gene was expressed in all organs; its expression level in roots was higher than in shoots. The ThCLC-a expression was induced by $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ added to the culture medium. In T. halophila plants featuring the reduced expression of ThCLC-a, the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ content in shoots and roots was lower than in WT plants. The $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ content in tissues of $A$ . thaliana plants overexpressing ThCLC-a was higher than in WT plants under conditions of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ deficiency [59].

Sequencing of the leaf transcriptome of the saltand drought-tolerant plant Arabidopsis pumila allowed the identification of ApCLCa, ApCLCc, and ApCLCd genes. Based on the fact that ApCLCa expression was considerably induced in response to salt stress, the product of this gene was assumed to be essential for the acquisition of salt tolerance in A. pumila [66].

Two genes (SaCLCa1 and SaCLCc1) of the chloride channel family have been cloned from the eugalophyte Suaeda altissima [60, 61]. The protein SaCLCc1 is involved in $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ transport [60], whereas SaCLCa1 is likely to participate in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport [61]. Expression of SaCLCc1 in the Δgef1 mutant cells of $S .$ . cerevisiae resulted in complementation of Δgef1 mutation [60], whereas the expression of SaCLCa1 did not restore the growth of mutant yeast on selective media. The replacement of proline with serine (P188S) in the selective filter of SaCLCa1 partially restored the growth of Δgef1 cells [61]. The genes SaCLCa1 and SaCLCc1 are expressed in roots and leaves of $S .$ . altissima. The expression of SaCLCa1 in roots was induced by nitrate-deficient media or by sodium chloride salinity, which suggests the role of SaCLCa1 in the control of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ supply into aboveground organs. Expression of SaCLCc1 in leaves increased in response to NaCl salinity, which may be relevant to SaCLCc1-mediated accumulation of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ in the aerial organs [61].

Three identified genes in the genome of cucumber (Cucumis sativus)—CsCLCa, CsCLCc, and CsCLCg— were homologous to the genes of Arabidopsis vacuolar proteins AtCLCa, AtCLCc, and AtCLCg [67]. In cucumber roots, the highest level of expression was observed for CsCLCa and CsCLCg , while the lowest level for CsCLCc. The deficiency of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in the medium diminished the expression of CsCLCa and CsCLCg but did not affect the expression of CsCLCc.

The addition of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ to the growth medium after a period of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -deficiency led to the induction of CsCLCa and CsCLCc in roots [67]. The authors concluded that CsCLCa plays a leading role in the vacuolar accumulation of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ in cucumber cells [67], a function similar to that of AtCLCa.

In the genome of tea plant Camellia sinensis, eight representatives of the CLC family, $( C s C L C I - \mathcal { 8 } )$ were found [68]. C. sinensis plants are tolerant to $\mathrm { F ^ { - } }$ and belong to the hyperaccumulators of fluoride. It is assumed that proteins of the CLC family participate in the accumulation of $\mathrm { F ^ { - } }$ ions in tea leaves. [68]. Analysis of CsCLC gene expression during the treatment of plants with $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ or $\mathrm { F ^ { - } }$ ions suggest that the subclass CsCLC4-8, including CsCLC6 and $\mathrm { C s C L C 7 }$ , ensures the transport and sequestration of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ in vacuoles, whereas the subclass CsCLC1-3 accounts for the fluoride transport. Further studies are needed to confirm the putative functions of CsCLC proteins [68].

In the genome of allotetraploid rape Brassica napus (B. rapa $\times \textit { \textbf { B } }$ . oleracea), 22 genes of the CLC family were found: BnaCLCa1-4, BnaCLCb1-4, BnaCLCc1-4, BnaCLCd1-2, BnaCLCe1-2, BnaCLCf1-4, and BnaCLCg1-2 [18]. Their exon–intron structures, the putative cis-acting elements in the gene promoters and conservative motifs of the respective proteins were identified. [18]. The proteins BnaCLCa and BnaCLCb, like proteins AtCLCa and AtCLCb, apparently play an important role in nitrate homeostasis. Similarly to expression of AtCLCa, the expression of BnaCLCa1-4 in roots and shoots was induced by the addition of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ to the nitrate-free medium. The BnaCLCa3 protein, similarly to AtCLCa, plays a primary role in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport across the vacuolar membrane, which was evidenced by stronger $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -induced expression of this gene compared to the expression of other BnaCLCa genes [18]. The addition of nitrate to the medium also induced the expression of BnaCLCb in shoots. In plants grown on $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ -deficient media, the expression of BnaCLCb1, BnaCLCb3, and BnaCLCb4 genes in roots was high and decreased in response to $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ addition to the medium [18]. The induction of BnaCLCb4 expression in roots under nitrate deficit was also demonstrated with the B. napus line featuring high nitrogen use efficiency [69].

Table 1 summarizes the above data on CLC family proteins in A. thaliana and other plants.


## SUPPOSED INVOLVEMENT OF ENDOSOMAL $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ ANTIPORTERS IN PLANT RESISTANCE TO NaCl


The $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ - and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporters localized in the endosomal membranes, such as AtCLCd, AtCLCf [19, 20, 27, 28], AtNHX5, and AtNHX6 [70] might directly contribute to $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis in the plant cell cytoplasm under salt stress conditions.

Endosomes that accumulate $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ by means of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } } .$ - and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporters can fuse with the tonoplast and/or plasma membrane, thus exporting $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , respectively, to the vacuole and/or the apoplast.

We demonstrated the electrogenic activity of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter using a membrane fraction enriched in the Golgi apparatus (GA) that was isolated from the euhalophyte $S .$ . altissima roots [71]. Pyranin was loaded into vesicles as a fluorescent $\mathsf { p H }$ indicator and safranin $\mathrm { o }$ was used as an indicator of the transmembrane electric potential $( \Delta \Psi )$ . When the $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ concentration gradient $( \Delta \mathsf { p C l } )$ was imposed to drive $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ entry from the medium to the lumen of isolated vesicles, we observed the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ eff lux (alkalinization of the lumen) and the generation of $\Delta \Psi$ with the negative potential inside the vesicles. A long-lasting operation of $\Delta { \mathsf { p } } { \mathsf { C l } }$ -driven $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport from the vesicles was attained under the condition that the membranepermeable tetraphenylphosphonium $\left( \mathrm { T P P ^ { + } } \right)$ or Tris+cations were added to the medium in order to neutralize negative charges accumulated in the lumen during $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ exchange [71].

In consistency with the assumed vesicular mechanism of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ transport involving $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ transporters, the electron microscopic examination of $S .$ . altissima plants grown at high salinity revealed that the cytoplasm contains numerous membrane structures of various sizes, including multivesicular bodies. The majority of these structures accumulated in close vicinity to the tonoplast and plasmalemma. Using a cytochemical electron-microscopy method based on the formation of electron-dense $\mathbf { A g C l }$ granules in tissues treated with silver ions, Balnokin et al. [72] detected $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ accumulation in these boundary zones, which probably indicates the NaCl-stimulated fusion of the outer membrane of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } } .$ -loaded endosomes with the tonoplast and plasmalemma.

The stimulatory effect of NaCl on the formation of membrane structures in the cytoplasm and their fusion with vacuoles was also shown in intact plant cells and suspension cultures of $A$ . thaliana [73–76], suspension cultures of the mangrove plant Bruguiera sexangula and barley [77], and in the intact plant cells of Chenopodium album [78]. The Golgi membranes and post-Golgi vesicles in which AtCLCd [20], AtNHX-5, and AtNHX-6 [70] were localized made up an essential part of these membrane structures.

The above data suggest the following scheme of the coordinated operation of $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter, and the $\mathrm { v . }$ -type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase in endosomes (Fig. 4). The V-type ATPase transports $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ into the endosomes, thus generating the gradients of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ concentration $\mathrm { ( \Delta p H ) }$ and the electric potential $( \Delta \Psi )$ across the endosomal membrane. For the sustained operation of ATPase, positive charges accumulating on the inner side of endosomal membranes should be neutralized. This function is performed by the $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter that transfers negatively charged chloride into vesicles and transports positively charged protons in the opposite direction. As a result, the electric potential $\Delta \Psi$ generated by the ATPase is converted to $\Delta \mathrm { p H }$ . The latter is used by the electrically neutral $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ -antiporter as energy source to accumulate $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ by early endosomes. After maturation of the early endosomes into the late endosomes, the latter are transferred to the respective target membranes where they merge with these membranes, thus excreting $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ from the cytoplasm. The involvement of postGolgi structures in various pathways of vesicular trafficking is apparently significant for the homeostasis of $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in cytoplasmic organelles under salt stress conditions. The trans-Golgi network represents a cellular compartment where endocytic and secretory pathways intersect: the trans-Golgi network mediates the recycling of endocytic vesicles back to the plasma membrane; in addition, the primary transport vesicles produced from the plasma membrane during endocytosis merge with the membranes of the trans-Golgi network. Part of the early endosomes and the products of their fusion with transport vesicles mature into the late endosomes/multivesicular bodies (MVB)/prevacuolar compartments (PVC); these structures sort the membrane proteins and lipids for their delivery to the tonoplast or plasma membrane and for carrying soluble substances to the vacuole or periplasm [79–81]. The excess of cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ accumulated under salt stress conditions is compartmentalized by endosomal ion transporters, such as AtCLCd [20], AtNHX-5, and AtNHX-6 [70], into the trans-Golgi network and its derivatives. Thereafter, these ions are exported by endosomes from the cytoplasm into the vacuole or periplasmic space.

Chloride channels (CLCs) are ubiquitously expressed from bacteria to animals and make significant contributions to various biological processes. Studies on prokaryotic CLCs provided a substantial progress in the understanding of the CLC family (Matulef and Maduke 2007). In higher plants, CLC proteins also appear as key players in regulation of cell pressure potential, stomatal movement, generation of action potentials, nutrient transport, and metal tolerance (Zifarelli and Pusch 2010). The first plant CLC genes have been cloned independently in tobacco and Arabidopsis (Hechenberger et al. 1996, Lurin et al. 1996). Since then, many plant CLCs have been isolated from rice, soybean, and other plant species (Diedhiou and Golldack 2005, Li et al. 2006, Zhou and Qiu 2010). Among these plant CLCs, Arabidopsis CLCs are the most thoroughly investigated proteins. Seven CLC genes exist in Arabidopsis genome, named AtCLCa-g. The AtCLC proteins are targeted to various membranes including the vacuolar membrane (AtCLCa, AtCLCb, AtCLCc, and AtCLCg), Golgi vesicles (AtCLCd and AtCLCf), or chloroplast membrane (AtCLCe). Physiological characterization of Arabidopsis mutants suggests the involvement of AtCLCa and AtCLCb in controlling $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ exchange across the tonoplast (Geelen et al. 2000, Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2010). Application of patch-clamp technique to isolated vacuoles has revealed that AtCLCa is able to accumulate nitrate in the vacuole and functions as a $2 \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ { - } / 1 H ^ { + } }$ antiporter (De Angeli et al. 2006). This provides a direct evidence that AtCLCa plays a major role in $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ homeostasis, probably partly in cooperation with AtCLCe which is postulated to be an $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ channel/ transporter on thylakoid membranes (Monachello et al. 2009). The AtCLCc is also suggested as another major component for $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ accumulation. Harada et al. (2004) has reported that clcc-1 mutant plants show a reduced $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ content in shoots as compared with wild-type shoots. However, in contrast with AtCLCa mutants, the plants have also an altered Cl- content indicating a broader anion specificity of AtCLCc compared with AtCLCa. Indeed, AtCLCc were recently reported to be related to the movement of Cl- across the tonoplast and hence contributes to opening stomata or salt resistance of plants (Wege et al. 2010). The localization of AtCLCd is coincident with that of V-type ATPase VHA1a in agreement with a functional link between these two proteins (Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2007). The expression of the plant AtCLCd and AtCLCf proteins, both residing in Golgi vesicles, complements the gef1 yeast mutant phenotype (Hechenberger et al. 1996, Gaxiola et al. 1998, Marmagne et al. 2007) suggesting a functional similarity with gef1. The AtCLCg has been suggested to have vacuole localization, but its functional properties are still unknown.

Although CLC genes in Arabidopsis have been studied extensively, a comprehensive analysis of the CLC gene family in other plant species has not been conducted. Citrus is a major world horticultural commodity and it is sensitive to NaCl stress, particularly to Cl- toxicity. We previously reported that a citrus CLC homologue $( C s C L C c )$ can alleviate NaCl stress in CsCLCc -overexpressing Arabidopsis by controlling Cl- accumulation (Wei et al. 2013). This impels us to gain more knowledge about the CLC genes in citrus. Recently, the genome sequence of citrus has been published (Xu et al. 2013) and provided an excellent opportunity for systematic study of citrus CLCs. In the present study, we identified CLC genes in the genome of trifoliate orange which is widely used as rootstock in citrus-producing regions. Then we report on comprehensive sequence analysis and phylogenetic construction. Organ expression profiles and gene expression patterns under abscisic acid or stress treatments were also examined using real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) method.

In plant cells, electrophysiological analyses have revealed the presence of anion channels in most investigated membranes (plasma membrane, tonoplast, organelle membranes), where they participate in cell signalling, osmoregulation, plant nutrition and metabolism, and contribute to metal tolerance (Barbier-Brygoo et al., 2000; De Angeli et al., 2007). To date, very few of the associated proteins have been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana at the molecular level. Recently, at the plasma membrane, the SLAC1 protein has been shown to be an essential component of the slow-type anion channel in guard cells (Negi et al., 2008; Vahisalu et al., 2008). At the tonoplast, two anion transport systems have been clearly identified: the malate channel ALMT9 (Kovermann et al., 2007) and AtClCa, one of the seven members of the ChLoride Channel (CLC) family (De Angeli et al., 2006). The AtClCa protein acts as a $2 \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } / 1 \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchanger, a feature which supports the physiological characterization of a T

DNA insertion mutant in the AtClCa gene (clca-1), which displays an under-accumulation of nitrate in root and shoot tissues (by approximately $5 0 \%$ ) and hypersensitivity to chlorate (Geelen et al., 2000). Three other members of the CLC family are targeted to endomembranes: AtClCe and AtClCf to thylakoid membranes and cis-Golgi vesicles, respectively, (Marmagne et al., 2007) and AtClCd to trans-Golgi vesicles (Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al., 2007). Although some evidence of biological roles in agreement with the subcellular localization has been reported, direct evidence for the transport activity of these proteins could not be found in their native membranes, which are not easily amenable to electrophysiological techniques. In Arabidopsis, quantitative trait locus (QTL) analyses have provided a further genetic basis to correlate water and anion contents with nitrogen availability, driven by the hypothesis that nitrate acts osmotically to increase water uptake (Loudet et al., 2003), but the genes contributing to these QTLs are unknown. In a similar QTL analysis of nitrate storage, Harada et al. (2004) identified AtClCe, AtClCc and AtClCf as candidate genes contributing to quantitative variations in nitrate accumulation. Indeed, they showed that a clcc mutant displayed altered endogenous nitrate levels, demonstrating a role for at least one of these candidate genes. Together, these data suggest that AtCLC proteins participate in the control of the intracellular nitrate content in a manner which remains to be understood.

To gain an insight into the biological function of CLCs in plants, we focused on two members of the family, AtClCa and AtClCe. Previous data have demonstrated the role of AtClCa in vacuolar nitrate storage (De Angeli et al., 2006) and have suggested a putative role for AtClCe in controlling the ionic strength in the lumen of grana stacks in chloroplasts (Marmagne et al., 2007). In this article, we report further phenotypic analyses of T-DNA insertion mutants within the AtClCa and AtClCe genes, which reveal new nitrate-related traits in addition to nitrate under-accumulation already shown for clca (Geelen et al., 2000). We provide evidence for the interconnected contributions of the AtClCa and AtClCe proteins to nitrate homeostasis involving two types of endomembrane. We also show cross-talk between different families of nitrate transporters participating in the regulation of nitrate transport and assimilation pathways.

In plant cells, anion channels and transporters are essential for key functions. Members of the chloride channel (CLC) family located in intracellular organelles are required for anion accumulation, pH adjustment, and salt tolerance. Here, we cloned a maize (Zea mays L.) CLC gene, named ZmCLC-d, and found that its transcription was up-regulated under cold, drought, salt, and heat stresses, and after hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ and abscisic acid (ABA) treatments. The overexpression of $Z m C L C { - } d$ in Arabidopsis conferred tolerance to cold, drought, and salt stresses; this tolerance was primarily displayed by an increased germination rate, root length, plant survival rate, antioxidant enzyme (catalase, peroxidase, and superoxide dismutase) activities, and a reduced accumulation of Cl- in transgenic plants as compared with wild type (WT) plants. The accumulation of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and superoxide anion in leaves of the ZmCLC- $d$ -overexpressing plants is much less than that of the WT plants. The expressions of some stress related genes, such as CBF1, CBF2, CBF3, DREB2A, and RCI2A, increased to a greater extent in the ZmCLC- $\cdot d$ -overexpressing plants than in the WT. Our results strongly suggest that ZmCLC-d played an important role in stress tolerance.

Additional key words: catalase, cold, heat, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , peroxidase, superoxide dismutase, water stress, Zea mays.

In this study, we described molecular cloning chloride channel ZmCLC-d from maize and the improvement of stress tolerance of Arabidopsis transgenic plants overexpressing ZmCLC-d. ZmCLC- $d$ is homologous to Arabidopsis AtCLC-d, and previous studies have demonstrated that AtClC-d is expressed in the trans-Golgi network (Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2007). Eight putative transmembrane domains were predicted in the N-terminal of ZmCLC-d suggesting ZmCLC-d may localize in the plasma membrane or membranes of organelles.

NaCl stress involves two distinct phases, a rapid osmotic phase in response to the osmotic effect of salt, followed by a slow ionic phase resulting from a toxic accumulation of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ and Cl- in the cytoplasm. Studies on NaCl tolerance have mainly focused on $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ , as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ reaches a toxic concentration in many species before Cldoes (for review, see Munns and Tester 2008). Although Cl- is an essential micronutrient for higher plants (White and Broadley 2001, Hänsch and Mendel 2009), it can become toxic if accumulates in the cytoplasm. Indeed, for some species, such as soybean, citrus, and grapevine, Cl- is more toxic than $\mathrm { N \bar { a } ^ { + } }$ (Läuchli 1984, Storey and Walker 1999). CLCs may be involved in responses to salt stress. In soybean, GmCLC-1, which is located at the tonoplast and induced by NaCl treatment, allows better tolerance to NaCl probably by accumulating chlorides in the vacuole as it is in transgenic BY2 cells (Li et al. 2006). In rice, OsCLC-1, which is also located at the tonoplast, is expressed in response to NaCl treatment (Nakamura et al. 2006). In Physcomitrella patens, a member of the CLC family was identified in response to NaCl treatment by proteomic analyses (Wang et al. 2008). An Arabidopsis vacuolar anion transporter, AtCLCc, is involved in the regulation of stomatal movements and contributes to salt tolerance (Jossier et al. 2010). The lumen pH in the trans-Golgi network was adjusted by AtCLC-d-mediated transport of Cl- or $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \overline { { \Omega } } }$ , meanwhile root growth and cell elongation were also impaired in the AtCLC-d loss function mutant (Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2007). To investigate the biological function of ZmCLC-d, we overexpressed it in Arabidopsis. We found the transgenic plants have a higher tolerance to abiotic stresses. The transgenic Arabidopsis seedlings expressing ZmCLC-d grown on the MS medium containing $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ for 7 d exhibited higher germination rates and longer roots than the control seedlings (Table 5). This might happen because the overexpressing ZmCLC-d Arabidopsis had a lower Clcontent than the controls. Drought, heat, and chilling stresses are also accompanied by changes in ion concentrations. ZmCLC- $^ { . d }$ might be directly or indirectly involved in these resistance responses because we found the Arabidopsis seedlings overexpressing ZmCLC-d were more tolerant to these stresses. Our data indicate that ZmCLC- $d$ played an important role in plant stress tolerance, especially in the salt stress.

In the present study, ZmCLC-d was also shown to be up-regulated by the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and ABA treatments (Table 3). Furthermore, the ZmCLC- $d \cdot$ -overexpressing seeds showed a difference from the control plants during germination on MS plates that were supplemented with different concentrations $( 0 ~ - ~ 2 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ of ABA (data not shown) suggesting that $Z m C L C { - } d$ induced stress tolerance may be ABA-dependent, and in addition, the second messenger, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , might participate in ZmCLC-d tolerance response processes.

Certain stress-induced proteins have been shown to impart stress tolerance. The overexpression of genes, such as CBF/DREB1, OSISAP1, and HVA1 was able to confer stress tolerance to transgenic plants $( \mathrm { X i n } ~ 2 0 0 1$ , Dubouzet et al. 2003, Mukhopadhyay et al. 2004). These examples provide a target for improving the stress tolerance of crop plants and provide an opportunity to elucidate the function of previously uncharacterized genes. The ZmCLC-d expression in maize was induced following the exposures to the cold, drought, heat, and salt stresses (Table 3). In Arabidopsis, the overexpression of ZmCLC-d led to increased tolerance to the cold, dehydration, and salt stresses. Our data suggest that the overexpression of ZmCLC- $^ { \cdot d }$ resulted in the enhanced transduction of stress-response signals. Furthermore, an elevated stress tolerance displayed by the 35S::ZmCLC-d plants coincided with the up-regulation of stressresponsive genes including DREB2A, CBF1, CBF2, CBF3, and RCI2A (Table 7). CBFs are thought to function in cold-responsive gene expression, whereas DREB2s are involved in high salinity- and droughtresponsive gene expression (Liu et al. 1998). RCI2A protein is neither regulated by CBF/DREB1 nor involved in the CBF/DREB1-independent pathways that modulate stress signaling (Medina et al. 2005). The hydrophilic RCI2A protein contributes to increased stress tolerance in transgenic plants (Thomashow 1998, Hasegawa et al. 2000). Thus, the enhanced stress tolerance displayed by the $Z m C L C { - } d$ transgenic plants might partially depend on changes in the expression of these genes. However, the mechanisms how $Z m C L C { - } d$ regulated the transcription of stress induced genes are not clear.

In conclusion, we used RT-qPCR to examine the expression patterns of $Z m C L C { - } d$ under different stress conditions. These results clearly suggest that $Z m C L C { - } d$ was transcriptionally up-regulated in response to the cold, drought, heat, $\mathrm { { N a C l } }$ , ABA, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ . The overexpression of ZmCLC- $\mathbf { \nabla } \cdot d$ in Arabidopsis enhanced its tolerance to the cold, drought, heat, and salt stresses by increasing the germination rate, root length, plant survival rate, antioxidant enzymes (CAT, POD, and SOD) activities, and reducing the accumulation of Cl- compared with the WT plants. These results demonstrate that $Z m C L C { - } d$ might be a positive regulator of cold, drought, heat, and salinity tolerances. The enhanced stress tolerance of the 35S::ZmCLC-d Arabidopsis plants reveals that ZmCLC-d was involved in stress response pathways.

Although the detailed mechanism by which $\mathrm { Z m C L C { \ - - d } }$ is involved in stress has not yet been elucidated, the characterization of $Z m C L C { - } d$ function provides new insights into stress pathways. This report broadens knowledge of the function of $C L C – d$ in plants and provides beneficial information regarding molecular breeding that could lead to improved stress tolerance of agricultural crops.

Chilling stress is a major environmental factor that limits agricultural productivity. Chloride channel proteins comprise a protein family that mediates chloride transport across the plasma membrane and intracellular membranes. The chloride channel (CLC) family are ubiquitous proteins present in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, and, unusually, comprise both channel proteins and transporters (Mindell and Maduke 2001, Jentsch 2008). The roles of plant anion channels include nutrient homeostasis, signaling, and responses to biotic and abiotic stresses (Isayenkov et al. 2010). Seven AtCLC genes (AtCLCa-g) have been identified in the Arabidopsis genome (Hechenberger et al. 1996, Lv et al. 2009). Intracellular localization of some of these proteins shows that AtCLCs are present in various membranes including the vacuolar membrane (AtCLCa and AtCLCb) (De Angeli et al. 2006, Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2010), Golgi vesicles (AtCLCd and AtCLCf), or chloroplast membranes (AtCLCe) (Marmagne et al. 2007, Von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2007).

Physiological characterization of Arabidopsis mutants suggested the involvement of AtCLCa, AtCLCb, and AtCLCc in the regulation of nitrate content in plants (Geelen et al. 2000, Harada et al. 2004, Von der FechtBartenbach et al. 2010). AtCLCa is located at the tonoplast in Arabidopsis mesophyll cells and functions as $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { \dot { ^ { \circ } } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter. In agreement, an AtCLCa knockout mutant accumulates $50 \%$ less nitrate than wild-type plants (Geelen et al. 2000, De Angeli et al. 2006). Thus, AtCLCa plays a major role in nitrate homeostasis, probably partly in cooperation with AtCLCe which is localized in the chloroplast (Monachello et al. 2009). It has also been proposed that AtCLC proteins located in cellular organelles participate in the establishment of acidic intra-organellar pH. AtCLCd has been shown to be targeted to the trans-Golgi network (TGN), to co-localize with V-type ATPase, and to be involved in adjustment of the luminal $\mathrm { p H }$ of this compartment (Von der FechtBartenbach et al. 2007).

AtCLCa plays a role in the translocation of nitrate into the vacuole, but all the other characterized CLCs in bacteria and mammals are involved in chloride transport. It was recently shown that this difference in selectivity is due to an amino acid change in the selectivity filter (Bergsdorf et al. 2009, Wege et al. 2010). Three of other AtCLCs (AtCLCc, AtCLCd, and AtCLCg) possess a selectivity filter in favour of chloride transport (Zifarelli and Pusch 2010). It has been suggested that these proteins could be involved in processes that require Cl- transport, such as stomatal movement or salt tolerance (Hänsch and Mendel 2009, Teakle and Tyerman 2010). In response to salt stress, the transcription of the chloride channel gene OsCLC1 is repressed in the salt-sensitive rice line IR29 which accumulates Cl- ; however, the transcription is transiently induced in the salt tolerant rice line Pokkali which excludes Cl- (Diédhiou and Golldack 2006).

In contrast to the detailed knowledge regarding the molecular regulation of $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ homeostasis and the metabolism of osmo-protective compounds (Sun et al. 2010), the regulation of anion transporters and particularly of Cl- transport systems in plants remain poorly understood. Maize is one of the most important crops worldwide, but its growth and yield are severely limited by high salinity or low temperature (Kizis 2002). It has been reported that ZmCLC-d was induced in maize by chilling stress (Yang et al. 2011), and the CLC protein in mitochondria is divergently selected for cold tolerance in maize populations (Tampieri et al. 2011). In the present study, we showed the expression patterns of the $Z m C L C { - } d$ gene under cold, drought, salt, and heat stresses, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and abscisic acid (ABA) treatments. We also studied transgenic Arabidopsis plants that constitutively expressed ZmCLC-d and their responses to multiple stresses.

This review summarizes evidence for the involvement of CLC family proteins in multiple processes and physiological functions in plants. The most important function is homeostasis of nitrate and chloride; the role of CLC proteins in this process at the cell and whole organism levels is well proven. Homeostasis of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ is necessary for plant growth and development; it also confers resistance to chloride salinity, water deficit, and other adverse environmental factors. One of the most challenging tasks is the search for CLC isoforms localized in the Golgi membranes and post-Golgi vesicles, which participate in intracellular vesicular trafficking of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ . The vast majority of studies on the transport of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ by CLC proteins were carried out with the model plant A. thaliana. The studies on functional and physiological roles of CLC family members in other plant species are just in the beginning stage. There is only fragmentary information about the participation of these proteins in the distribution of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ and $\mathbf { C l ^ { - } }$ ions in the whole plant system. There is no complete knowledge on the mechanisms by which CLC proteins regulate the transmembrane electric potential $( \Delta \Psi )$ and the inner $\mathsf { p H }$ in plant organelles, including those of $A$ . thaliana and yeasts. The proposed hypotheses based on available information are still contradictory. The mechanisms by which such regulation is carried out obviously warrant further investigation. The regulation of lumenal $\mathrm { p H }$ in cytoplasmic compartments, particularly in the trans-Golgi network responsible for the intracellular sorting of proteins, is extremely important for the vesicular transport. The latter plays a key role in remodeling the composition of membrane protein and lipids, which occurs in response to internal and environmental stimuli, including biotic and abiotic stress factors. The regulation of vesicular trafficking by CLC family proteins is therefore an important component of the processes that determine plants' resistance to stress factors. The study of the role of CLC family proteins in regulation of vesicular transport is therefore one of the urgent tasks in cell physiology.

Chloride channels (CLCs) play pivotal roles in plant development and anion transport. However, little research has been conducted about the CLC in fruit-bearing plants. Here we provide an insight into the evolution and expression patterns of CLC gene family members in various tissues of trifoliate orange [Poncirus trifoliata (L.) Raf.] and their responses to several treatments. Genome-wide analysis identified six PtrCLC genes. The predicted proteins had similar numbers of amino acids, but shared a low sequence identity. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that PtrCLC were classified into two separate subgroups, and PtrCLC4 and PtrCLC6 in subgroup II were more closely related to bacterial CLCs. Sequence comparison with EcCLCA from Escherichia coli reveals that PtrCLC showed amino acid divergence in anion selectivity of CLC proteins. Real time qPCR analysis shows that PtrCLC genes, particularly PtrCLC6 , preferentially expressed in leaves. Nitrogen deficiency irreversibly inhibited expression of PtrCLC genes except for PtrCLC1 . In contrast, NaCl stress profoundly induced expression of PtrCLC genes, particularly PtrCLC2 and PtrCLC4, both of which were also upregulated by ABA treatment. The results presented here provide a solid foundation for a future functional research on citrus CLC genes.

Additional key words: abscisic acid, gene expression, nitrogen supply, Poncirus trifoliata, salt stress, sequence analysis.

Background: The anionic toxicity of plants under salt stress is mainly caused by chloride $( \mathsf { C l } ^ { - } )$ . Thus $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ influx, transport and their regulatory mechanisms should be one of the most important aspects of plant salt tolerance studies, but are often sidelined by the focus on sodium $\left( \mathsf { N a } ^ { + } \right)$ toxicity and its associated adaptations. Plant chloride channels (CLCs) are transport proteins for anions including ${ \mathsf { C l } } ^ { - }$ and nitrate $( \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } ) _ { i }$ , and are critical for nutrition uptake and transport, adjustment of cellular turgor, stomatal movement, signal transduction, and $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ and ${ \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ homeostasis under salt stress.

Results: Among the eight soybean CLC genes, the tonoplast-localized c2 has uniquely different transcriptional patterns between cultivated soybean N23674 and wild soybean BB52. Using soybean hairy root transformation, we found that GsCLC-c2 over-expression contributed to ${ \mathsf { C l } } ^ { - }$ and ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ homeostasis, and therefore conferred salt tolerance, through increasing the accumulation of $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ in the roots, thereby reducing their transportation to the shoots where most of the cellular damages occur. Also, by keeping relatively high levels of ${ \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ in the aerial part of the plant, GsCLC-c2 could reduce the $\mathsf { C l } ^ { - } / \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ ratio. Wild type GsCLC-c2, but not its mutants (S184P, E227V and E294G) with mutations in the conserved domains, is able to complement Saccharomyces cerevisiae △gef1 $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ sensitive phenotype. Using two-electrode voltage clamp on Xenopus laevis oocytes injected with $G s C l C – C 2 \mathsf { c R N A } ,$ we found that GsCLC-c2 transports both $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ and $N O _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ with slightly different affinity, and the affinity toward ${ \mathsf { C l } } ^ { - }$ was pH-independent.

Conclusion: This study revealed that the expression of GsCLC-c2 is induced by NaCl-stress in the root of wild soybean. The tonoplast localized GsCLC-c2 transports $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ with a higher affinity than ${ \mathsf { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ in a pH-independent fashion. GsCLC-c2 probably alleviates salt stress in planta through the sequestration of excess $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ into the vacuoles of root cells and thus preventing $\subset \joinrel ^ { - }$ from entering the shoots where it could result in cellular damages.

Keywords: Chloride, Chloride channels, ${ \mathsf { C l } } { \mathsf { C s } } ,$ Differential expression, GsCLC-c2, Nitrate, Salt stress, Soybean, Wild soybean

In addition to the channels described above, several anion channels from other families have been shown to compete in stress-induced stomatal movement. CLC is a family of chloride channels that can be found ubiquitously among bacteria, animals, and plants [46,173–176]. Seven members of CLC gene, AtCLCa-g, are present in Arabidopsis genome [177,178]. Among these seven, AtCLCc is particularly expressed in guard cell tonoplast. Though its detailed function remains unveiled, the phenotype of clcc mutants postulate its participation in stomatal response to ABA and NaCl through modulation of chloride/nitrate homeostasis [102]. Wege et al. stated that another CLC member AtCLCa, originally identified as a tonoplast nitrate/proton antiporter, was required for ABA-induced stomatal closure or inhibition of stomatal opening [99,100]. AtCLCa mediates nitrate influx at hyperpolarization and efflux upon depolarization [99,100]. Although ATP binding to the C-terminus of AtCLCa inhibits its transport activity, its activity can be resumed by phosphorylation via OST1, suggesting some crosstalk between SLAC1 and AtALMT12 regulation [100,101,168]. Two members from Arabidopsis detoxification efflux carrier (DTX)/Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family, DTX33 and 35, were recently identified as an additional anion channel residing in guard cell tonoplast [103–105]. Both channels exhibit vacuolar chloride influx in various types of cells, including guard cell, and mutation of their genes results in impaired stomatal opening [105]. Andrés et al. reported that the dynamic structure change of guard cell vacuole itself is necessary for proper regulation of stomata movement, and that this is mediated by tonoplast $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter NHX1 and NHX2, and, possibly, by the yet unidentified $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ antiporter [179]. It was later proposed that CBL2, CBL3, CIPK9 and CIPK17 might contribute in this NHX1/2-mediated convolution of vacuole [112].

Studies from the 1980s demonstrated that $S O _ { 2 }$ can also promote stomatal closure, which was most recently concluded as being a result of non-apoptotic cell death caused by the accumulation of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 }$ [180–182]. Another research implicates sulfate as an important element for drought-induced stomatal closure [106]. Sulfate, uptaken from roots through sulfate transporter SULTRs, had long been known as an essential macronutrient for plant growth and development [27,28,183]. SULTR family is divided into five groups [184]. Recently the essential role of sulfate in ABA synthesis was elucidated, suggesting the participation of SULTRs in abiotic stress response [29,30,185,186]. Malcheska et al. reported stomatal closure induced by apoplastic sulfate, and activation of AtALMT12 by sulfate application [106]. This study also proposed that sulfate induces enhanced ABA synthesis inside the guard cell, possibly involving chloroplastic SULTR3;1 as a key transporter (Figure 1) [106].

Key message We propose that anion channels are essential players for green plants to respond and adapt to the abiotic stresses associated changing climate via reviewing the literature and analyzing the molecular evolution, comparative genetic analysis, and bioinformatics analysis of the key anion channel gene families.

Abstract Climate change-induced abiotic stresses including heatwave, elevated $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ , drought, and fooding, had a major impact on plant growth in the last few decades. This scenario could lead to the exposure of plants to various stresses. Anion channels are confrmed as the key factors in plant stress responses, which exist in the green lineage plants. Numerous studies on anion channels have shed light on their protein structure, ion selectivity and permeability, gating characteristics, and regulatory mechanisms, but a great quantity of questions remain poorly understand. Here, we review function of plant anion channels in cell signaling to improve plant response to environmental stresses, focusing on climate change related abiotic stresses. We investigate the molecular response and evolution of plant slow anion channel, aluminum-activated malate transporter, chloride channel, voltage-dependent anion channel, and mechanosensitive-like anion channel in green plant. Furthermore, comparative genetic and bioinformatic analysis reveal the conservation of these anion channel gene families. We also discuss the tissue and stress specifc expression, molecular regulation, and signaling transduction of those anion channels. We propose that anion channels are essential players for green plants to adapt in a diverse environment, calling for more fundamental and practical studies on those anion channels towards sustainable food production and ecosystem health in the future.

Keywords Ion channel $\cdot$ Membrane transport $\cdot$ Stomata $\cdot$ Comparative genomics $\cdot$ Gene family evolution

Aluminum (Al)-induced organic acid excretion has been convincingly demonstrated as a major mechanism of Al resistance through Al exclusion in many plant species (Ma et al. 2001; Kochian et al. 2015). The first resistance gene in plants was cloned from wheat as

TaALMT1 (aluminum-activated malate transporter) encoding an ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate channel (Sasaki et al. 2004). Citrate transporters responsible for Alactivated citrate efflux were later identified by positional cloning in sorghum (SbMATE, multidrug and toxic compound extrusion, Magalhaes et al. 2007) and barley (HvAACT1,aluminum-activated citrate transported 1, Furukawa et al. 2007), respectively; these transporters are the members of the multi-drug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family. Transgenic Arabidopsis and tobacco showed enhanced Al resistance with the overexpression of SbMATE (Magalhaes et al. 2007) and HvAACT1 (Furukawa et al. 2007), respectively. The transporter genes of the MATE and ALMT families can provide effective ways to enhance the Al resistance of plants. Unravelling additional genes encoding organic acid anion transporters will help more crops to adapt to Al-stresses under acidic soil environments.

MATE transporters are proposed to be involved in a wide range of biological events including xenobiotic efflux, accumulation of alkaloids and flavonoids, iron translocation, Al detoxification and plant hormone signalling (Takanashi et al. 2014). The identified citrate transporter genes in the MATE family have been suggested to function in Al resistance or iron uptake or both. First, SbMATE (Magalhaese et al. 2007), AtMATE (Liu et al. 2009), BoMATE (Wu et al. 2014), EcMATE1 and EcMATE3 (Sawaki et al. 2013), OsFRDL4 (ferric reductase defective like 4, Yokosho et al. 2011), OsFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2016a) and ScFRDL2 (Yokosho et al. 2010), VuMATE1 (Yang et al. 2011), VuMATE2 (Liu et al. 2018), ZmMATE1 (Maron et al. 2010; Maron et al. 2013), FeMATE1 (Lei et al. 2017) were reported to be responsible for Al-activated citrate efflux under Al stress. Second, members such as AtFRD3 (Durrett et al. 2007), GmFRD3b (Rogers et al. 2009), OsFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2009) and ScFRDL1 (Yokosho et al. 2010), LjMATE1 (Takanashi et al. 2013) were found to be localized to either the root pericycle cell or the nodules and were responsible for Fe supply by assisting the translocation of Fe by providing citrate. Thirdly, it was reported that HvAACT1 and TaMATE1b were involved in both Fe translocation and ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ detoxification (Fujii et al. 2012; Tovkach et al. 2013; Takanashi et al. 2014).

Various regulatory systems were found to control citrate transporter expression and thus function. The first group is represented by ZmMATE1. Its gene duplications determined their expression and thus citrate efflux (Maron et al. 2013). The second group is represented by HvAACT1 and TaMATE1b. HvAACT1, a citrate transporter in barley, provides primary transport of citrate into the root xylem for Fe translocation to the shoot as a Fe-citrate complex in the mature root zones (Fujii et al. 2012). The insertion of a $1 \ \mathrm { k b }$ transposon in the $5 ^ { \prime }$ upstream region of $H _ { { \nu } A A } { \cal A } C T I$ changed its distribution and density to facilitate citrate secretion from the root apex to the rhizosphere for Al detoxification (Fujii et al. 2012). Fujii et al. (2018) also found that retrotransposon insertion and DNA methylation in the upstream genomic region are involved in regulating the expression of $H _ { { \nu } A A } { \cal A } C T I$ then Al resistance in barley especially distributed in European areas with acid soil. A transposonlike element in Triticum aestivum increased citrate transporter TaMATE1B expression in root apex, where it facilitates citrate efflux and enhances Al tolerance (Tovkach et al. 2013). The third group is represented by AtMATE and VuMATE1. Their expression is regulated by Cys2His2 zinc finger-type transcription factor STOP1 (sensitive to proton rhizotoxicity1). The expression of AtMATE is regulated by the transcription factor AtSTOP1 (Liu et al. 2009). Yeast one-hybrid examination has shown that there is an interaction between VuSTOP1 and the promoter region of VuMATE1and VuMATE2 (Yang et al. 2011; Fan et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2018). A $1 . 2 \ \mathrm { k b }$ insertion in the OsFRDL4 promoter region in the rice japonica subspecies increased the number of cis-acting elements of ART1 then enhanced OsFRDL4 expression level, but did not alter its spatial expression or cellular localization (Yokosho et al. 2016b).

Multiple Al resistance mechanisms have been suggested to be involved in Al resistance in soybean (Nian et al. 2004). Correspondingly, multigenetic traits have been suggested to relate to mechanisms underlying Al resistance in soybean by genetic studies (Bianci-Hall et al. 1998, 2000). Compared with the progress made in other important crops and model plant species, little was known about the molecular mechanisms of Al resistance in soybean. Al-induced citrate efflux has been well established as an Al resistance mechanism in soybean (Yang et al. 2000, 2001; Silva et al. 2001). Liu et al. (2016) identified and named a total of 117 genes encoding MATE transporters in the whole soybean genome, which are unevenly distributed on the 20 soybean chromosomes. However, the citrate transporter responsible for citrate efflux from soybean under Al stress has not been identified until now.

Rogers et al. (2009) showed that GmFRD3a and GmFRD3b were induced by iron deficiency in an ironefficient soybean cultivar. GmFRD3b , but not GmFRD3a, was expressed at higher levels in the ironefficient cultivar than its iron-inefficient near-isogenic line, and thus GmFRD3b is suggested to function similarly to AtFRD3 to mediate citrate efflux into the xylem. Their function has not been further characterized until now. Our previous microarray analysis found a MATEfamily transcript (GmMATE75) was up-regulated by Al treatment in the Al-tolerant genotype Jiyu 70 (You et al. 2011) which was also predicated to be the candidate Al tolerance gene according to its gene expression pattern and cis-elements (Liu et al. 2016). The expression of GmALCT1 (GmMATE 79) was also highly induced in soybean root apices under Al stress (Xu et al. 2010). In the present study, we compared three genes in the MATE family, GmMATE75, GmMATE79 and GmMATE87 (GmFRD3a), to reveal their functions in the process of Al-induced citrate efflux from soybean root apices.

## Functional characterization and discovery of modulators of SbMATE, the agronomically important aluminium tolerance transporter from Sorghum bicolor


Rupak Doshi1,5,6, Aaron P. McGrath1, Miguel Piñeros2, Paul Szewczyk1,7, Denisse M. Garza1, Leon V. Kochian3 & Geofrey Chang1,4

About $50 \%$ of the world’s arable land is strongly acidic $( \mathsf { p H } \leq 5 )$ . The low pH solubilizes root-toxic ionic aluminium $( A | ^ { 3 + } )$ species from clay minerals, driving the evolution of counteractive adaptations in cultivated crops. The food crop Sorghum bicolor upregulates the membrane-embedded transporter protein SbMATE in its roots. SbMATE mediates efux of the anionic form of the organic acid, citrate, into the soil rhizosphere, chelating $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ ions and thereby imparting Al-resistance based on excluding $\mathsf { A l } ^ { + 3 }$ from the growing root tip. Here, we use electrophysiological, radiolabeled, and fuorescence-based transport assays in two heterologous expression systems to establish a broad substrate recognition profle of SbMATE, showing the proton and/or sodium-driven transport of 14C-citrate anion, as well as the organic monovalent cation, ethidium, but not its divalent analog, propidium. We further complement our transport assays by measuring substrate binding to detergent-purifed SbMATE protein. Finally, we use the purifed membrane protein as an antigen to discover native conformationbinding and transport function-altering nanobodies using an animal-free, mRNA/cDNA display technology. Our results demonstrate the utility of using Pichia pastoris as an efcient eukaryotic host to express large quantities of functional plant transporter proteins. The nanobody discovery approach is applicable to other non-immunogenic plant proteins.

Nearly $3 0 \%$ of all cellular genomes code for integral membrane proteins, such as receptors, channels, and transporters. Tese proteins contain multiple membrane-spanning segments that traverse the phospholipid bilayer. Transporters are cellular gate-keepers, moving a wide variety of specifc molecules and ions in both directions across the plasma membrane as well as other endomembrane-bound compartments. Importers allow the cellular uptake of essential nutrients and metabolic reactants, while exporters mediate the efux of metabolic byproducts, defense agents, toxic compounds, and xenobiotics. As a result, transporters are crucial in shaping the ability of cells to adapt and survive in their surrounding environment.

Active transporters move substrates against their concentration or electrochemical (for ions) gradients utilizing energy, derived either from the binding and hydrolysis of ATP (primary active) or by using other transmembrane electrochemical potential gradients (secondary active). Te Multidrug And Toxic compound Extrusion (or

MATE) family of secondary-active transporters was initially identifed from bacterial isolates that appeared to be resistant to antibiotics, drugs, and cationic dyes. Since then, MATE transporters have been identifed in almost all organisms, including humans and plants. In humans, MATE transporters play a key role in secreting organic drugs, toxins, and metabolites into the renal tubular lumen1 . In plants, MATE transporters are involved in a wide variety of physiological process, including xenobiotic efux, accumulation of secondary metabolites including alkaloids and favonoids, iron (Fe) translocation, plant hormone signaling, and aluminum $( \mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ resistance2 .

Given that aluminum (Al) is the most abundant metal in the earth’s crust, plants have evolved in a soil environment where their root system can frequently be exposed to high levels of this toxic metal. Acid soils constitute approximately $3 0 \%$ of the land presently under cultivation and over $5 0 \%$ of the world’s potentially arable lands3,4 . At soil $\mathrm { p H } < 5 . 0$ , Al solubilizes as the phytotoxic species, $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ , causing a strong inhibition of root growth and function, ultimately resulting in severe reductions in crop yield. Aluminum toxicity is, therefore, a signifcant global agricultural problem, prevalent in many regions where food security is already tenuous, with $3 8 \%$ of the farmland in Southeast Asia, $3 1 \%$ of Latin America, and $2 0 \%$ of the arable lands in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa currently being impacted. Te ability to adapt/fortify crops to tolerate high soil Al thus has the potential to enormously increase food production in many at-risk regions.

Sorghum bicolor is the ffh most widely grown cereal crop in the world, with the largest producers being Nigeria, India, USA, and Mexico. By studying genotypic diferences between sorghum species that are sensitive or resistant to aluminum, a MATE family transporter, SbMATE, was identifed via the positional cloning of the major sorghum Al resistance locus5 . SbMATE is highly upregulated in Al-tolerant sorghum, and in response to increased $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ levels in the soil, it underlies an increase in organic anion citrate exudation from roots into the surrounding rhizosphere, thereby chelating the free $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ , forming non-toxic complexes that are no longer taken up by the roots. Consistently, transgenic SbMATE was also found to confer Al-tolerance in barley, which is one of the most Al-sensitive cereal crop species6 .

Despite belonging to the MATE family of proteins that are known to transport multiple chemically-diverse compounds, SbMATE and other Al-resistance associated orthologues5,7–13 have been studied purely from the perspective of their organic acid anion (i.e. citrate) efux activity (Fig. 1A). Tus, a signifcant gap exists in our understanding of other classes of substrates that could potentially be transported. Furthermore, investigating the molecular mechanisms that govern SbMATE mediated transport is critical towards devising strategies that could improve aluminum tolerance traits in crops expressing SbMATE-type transporters in their roots.

Here, we have attained a broader understanding of SbMATE’s functionality by studying its transport characteristics in a series of biochemical and biophysical assays, using cell-based transport assays in two diferent heterologous expression systems, and also in detergent-purifed liposomal-reconstituted formulations. Additionally, we have used purifed SbMATE as a model, plant-derived, full-length integral membrane protein to discover single-domain antibody reagent tools that bind the native, folded conformation of SbMATE and afect its transport characteristics.

Almost half of the world’s arable land has acidic pH. Aluminum salts present in acid soils dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution that inhibit root growth causing severe loss in crop yields. Aluminium toxicity accounts for the second highest loss in plant productivity after drought. Aluminium in high doses causes damage to the plant cell wall, cytoskeleton and DNA. One of the ways by which plants alleviate aluminium toxicity is by the exudation of citrate from the roots that chelates the free $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ and prevents its entry into the plant. In several crop plants Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporters regulate citrate exudation from the roots. The MATE proteins are ubiquitously present in bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants. The origin and evolution of these membrane transporters in plants is not well known. Here, using protein sequence information we identify MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors. Our study indicates that the MATE family members expanded in number and functionally diverse among the land plants. We also identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade and a conserved aspartate residue that might regulate citrate exudation. This study can provide leads to engineer MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance in acid soils.
