The sessile lifestyle of plants makes them susceptible to multiple biotic and abiotic stresses. Abiotic stresses like high temperature, drought, flooding, nutrient scarcity, xenobiotics, drugs and metal toxicity in soil can severely affect plant growth and reduce yields. While the role of low or high temperature, water availability and nutrients has been studied a lot, an aspect that has comparatively received less attention is the role of soil $\mathrm { p H }$ on agricultural productivity. Almost $50 \%$ of the land used for food production is acidic in nature. Aluminium salts that are very abundant in the soil dissociate to release ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions in the soil solution, which inhibit root elongation and severely affect plant growth and productivity. This is known as Aluminium toxicity and accounts for the second highest loss in yields after drought (Kochian et al. 2004; Bojo´rquez-Quintal et al. 2017). Aluminium-mediated inhibition of root elongation primarily involves damage to the cell wall (pectin, hemicellulose), cytoskeleton elements (actin, microtubules) and also double stranded breaks in the nuclear DNA (Kar et al. 2021).

Plants adopt several morphological and biochemical modifications to counter different stresses. Plants enhance tolerance to aluminium toxicity by either sequestration or exclusion of aluminium. Several membrane-localized transporters play an important role in these tolerance responses. The ABC transporters, vacuolar ATPases and aquaporins mediate aluminium sequestration inside the vacuoles. Exudation of carboxylates like malate and citrate by the Aluminium Activated Malate Transporter (ALMT) and the Multidrug and Toxic Compound Extrusion (MATE) transporter respectively, helps the plant to exclude aluminium. The MATE proteins are ubiquitous in nature and present across all life forms including bacteria, archaea, fungi, animals and plants (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Here we have used the protein sequence information to identify the presence of MATE transporters in major groups of land plants and their algal ancestors (Fig. 2). While the MATE family members expanded in the land plants we identify motifs present across the streptophyte clade. We observed a conserved aspartate residue responsible for cation efflux one of the motifs that might play an important role in citrate exudation (Table 1, Figs. 2, 3). Future prospects of engineering MATE transporters to confer enhanced tolerance to $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + - }$ in acid soils are also discussed here.

MATE transporters play important roles in cellular detoxification mechanisms in several species. They belong to the multidrug transporter family consisting of the ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) superfamily, major facilitator superfamily (MFS), small multidrug resistance (SMR) family, resistance nodulation cell division (RND) family, and proteobacterial antimicrobial compound efflux (PACE) family (Putman et al. 2000). NorM from Vibrio parahaemolyticus and YdhE its homologue in $E$ . coli, were found to be topologically different from MFS transporters, and were identified as the first MATE transporters (Morita et al. 1998; Brown et al. 1999). In bacteria, MATEs were classified under multidrug/ oligosaccharidyl lipid/ polysaccharide (MOP) exporter superfamily (Hvorup et al. 2003). Since its discovery in bacteria, multiple research on this newly identified transporter family have identified the presence of MATE transporters in archaea as well as eukaryotes including fungi, plants and animals (Morita et al. 1998; Omote et al. 2006) (Fig. 1). Though these genes share a weak sequence similarity, they can be identified using the MatE domain (PF01554). The MATE proteins are membrane embedded and consist of about 400–700 amino acids residues generally forming 12 transmembrane helices. MATEs are further classified in terms of their structure into three distinct types, NorM, DinF and eukaryotic MATES (eMATEs). NorM and eMATE share conserved acidic residues at the C-terminal end whereas NorM and DinF share conserved acidic residues at the N-terminal end of the MATE proteins (Miyauchi et al. 2017). The ubiquitous presence of MATEs in unicellular and multicellular life forms might suggest its importance in the basic cellular processes. These membrane localized transporters primarily mediate cationic efflux (Morita et al. 2000). They regulate cation transport utilizing the $\mathrm { H ^ { + } / N a ^ { + } }$ electrochemical gradient as their driving force. Norfloxacin, ethidium bromide (EtBr), berberine, tetraphenylphosphonium, acriflavine are some of the cationic substrates transported by bacterial MATEs (Morita et al. 2000; Braibant et al. 2002; Chen et al. 2002).

In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, ERC1 type MATE transporter confers resistance to ethionine (Shiomi et al. 1991). In humans, presence of two MATE transporters hMATE1 and hMATE2 are involved in the transport of tetraethylammonium using proton gradient (Otsuka et al. 2005a). In plants they function in transport of secondary metabolites, phytohormones, organic acids along with roles in developmental processes and xenobiotic detoxification (Upadhyay et al. 2019).

We further looked at the expansion and distribution of MATE family of proteins in different bacterial and plant species (Fig. 1). We observed that the number of MATE genes per prokaryote species is less compared to eukaryotes especially plants resulting in a lower MATE sequence to species ratio in bacteria and archaea than eukaryote the N-terminal motif of citrate effluxing MATEs when mutated to N (indicated by downward arrow) affects cation transport (D) The distribution of the three motifs in the protein sequence of the AtMATE orthologs from red algae, green algae and land plants (color figure online)

(Fig. 1b). In Pseudomonas aeruginosa there are two MATE subtype transporters under MOP superfamily, while Escherichia coli has three. On the other hand, Arabidopsis thaliana and Glycine max contain 58 and 117 MATE transporters respectively. This might be correlated to the genome size. The small prokaryote genomes have relatively less number of genes coding for these transporters whereas the larger eukaryotic genomes have a greater number of paralogs resulting in expansion of the MATE family (Ren and Paulsen 2005). With the increasing cellular complexity, plants MATEs might have evolved to transport a broader range of substrates from cations to phytohormones, secondary metabolites, organic acids and anions. Regardless of the number of MATE proteins present, the evolutionary conservation of this group of proteins suggests its pivotal role in multidrug resistance and developmental roles across life forms (Fig. 1).

In order to understand better the expansion of the MATE family of proteins among different groups of land plants and their algal ancestors we used available genome sequences from red algae to angiosperms and identified the number of MATE genes in them. For each genome the retrieved genes were verified using a domain search in Pfam database. Only hits with the MatE domain (Pf01554) were considered as potential MATE genes. We observed the expansion of MATE family of transporters specifically in plants. There was an increase in the number of MATE genes from rhodophyta to flowering plants across the evolutionary timeline (Table 1). Red algae have 1–2 MATEs, while members of chlorophyta and charophyta have an average of 10 and 15 MATEs respectively. Chlamydomonas and Chara both have 16 MATE genes in their genome. Among the bryophytes, the first non-vascular land plants, Marchantia has 15 while Physcomitrella has 20 MATE proteins. The MATE family in the lycophyte Selaginella moelendorfii expands to 41 members and in the flowering plants the numbers are even higher. The expansion of the MATE family shows enormous variation both within the monocots and dicots. Rice and Wheat have 54 and 224 MATE proteins while Arabidopsis and Soybean have 58 and 117 of these transporters (Table 1). The change in habitat (movement of plants from water to land) exposed plants to multiple stresses inducing many developmental and genetic modifications. Whole genome duplications in plants might account for the rapid expansion of the MATE family across the evolutionary timeline. A report by Wang et al. (2016) suggests that the expansion of MATEs in Arabidopsis and rice might be a result of tandem and segmental duplication. The mapping of such tandem duplicated genes date back to the monocot dicot split (Wang et al. 2016). Despite a larger genome size, animal kingdom has not seen expansion of this family. Humans and rats have 2 MATE genes specifically involved in extrusion of toxic compounds from the body (Table 1). Hence, the expansion of MATE transporters in plants might be to allow plants to cope better while being sessile (Table 2).

MATE proteins in plants regulate a diverse array of functions, which involve transport of several substrates like secondary metabolites, xenobiotics, hormones, various cations and anions (Upadhyay 2019). A subset of MATE proteins regulates citrate efflux to promote aluminium detoxification. The organic acid exudation function of MATE transporters is well reported in plants like Arabidopsis, sorghum, barley, wheat, rice and soybean (Magalhaes et al. 2007; Liu et al. 2009, 2016; Yokosho et al. 2011; Zhou et al. 2013; Qiu et al. 2019). Although the primary function of the exuded citrate in several of these species is to alleviate aluminium toxicity, citrate might play other roles like phosphate mobilization especially in species that are inherently aluminium tolerant like rice. A citrate exuding motif has been identified in 28 MATE proteins in angiosperms that regulate citrate efflux in response to aluminium toxicity (Upadhyay et al. 2019). Furthermore, all the citrate exuding MATEs contain a conserved aspartate (D) residue within the motif (Doshi et al. 2017). Since we identified several MATE proteins in early land plants, we next wanted to examine the conservation of this D-containing motif in early plants. We retrieved the orthologs of AtMATE from the genomes of several early land plants and their algal ancestors including Micromonas pusilla, Physcomitrella patens, Selaginella moellendorfii, Amborella trichopoda using BLASTP in

Phytozome v13(Fig. 2). The hits with e- value 1e-8 cut off were selected. Since MATEs share a weak sequence similarity in the early plants the hits were checked for the presence of Pfam domain (PF01554) also. We then performed the motif scan in MEME with default parameters (number of motifs set to 3) using these orthologs, AtMATE, AtFRD3 and SbMATE (Bailey and Elkan 1994). Our search identified three motifs containing conserved D residues in all the AtMATE orthologs (Fig. 2). This included a N-terminal motif indicated in red and $2 \textrm { C }$ -terminal motifs indicated in blue and green respectively (Fig. 2). The D residue located within the N-terminal motif (red) that was conserved in citrate exuding flowering plants was found to be present from Chlamydomonacae $C .$ . reinhardtii) onwards (Fig. 3). The two C-terminal motifs containing the D residues were even found in the red algal lineages. The conservation of these motifs and the D residue across evolution of land plants suggests that citrate exudation might have a critical functional relevance in land plant adaptation. We further wanted to know if the position of this conserved motif and the D residue is similar in all AtMATE orthologs. We performed sequence homology modeling of these orthologs using Phyre (Kelley et al. 2015). The pdb structures were then opened using PyMOL and the D residue was selected to denote its position (Fig. 3b). The structural modeling of these orthologous proteins also showed a similar location of the motif and the conserved D residue suggesting similar mode of functioning. We further proceeded in obtaining clarity about the posirtion of this Asp residue. We used TOPCONS, a transmembrane helix predicting software to predict the number of transmembrane helices in these orthologs and also the exact amino acid distribution in the helix orientations (inside to outside or vice-versa) (Tsirigos et al.

2015). We looked for the MATEs from $P$ . patens to S.bicolor, and we identified 12 transmemebrane helices in all the transporters (Fig. 3d). The tool also predicted that the Asp residue is located in the outer loop of the first transmembrane helix of all the selected MATE transporters from bryophytes to angiosperms (Fig. 3c). This prediction suggests further conservation of the location of the Asp residue to retain its function throughout the evolutionary timeline.

Citrate permeable MATEs with a mutated Asp residue had a reduced organic cation efflux rate than the wild type allele (Doshi et al. 2017). This residue was homologous to NorM $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ driven MATE cation efflux transporter. In prokaryotes, the Asp36 from NorM of Vibrio chlorae is highly conserved among NorM and DinF types. Though Asp36 was not found to be directly involved in substrate transport using $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ gradient, mutation of this residue resulted in impaired transport activity (Otsuka et al. 2005b;

Jin et al. 2014; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Also, Asp41of Pyrococcus furiosus MATE $( P f M A T E )$ from DinF subtype is conserved among NorM and DinF types. This residue when mutated results in reduced drug and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport (Tanaka et al. 2013; Kusakizako et al. 2020). Hence, this ability of all citrate permeable MATEs to permit both efflux of cations and anions indicated the broad substrate specificity of this transporter family. In plants, the citrate permeable MATEs are generally localized at the cell membrane of roots. It is probable that the AtMATE orthologs in early plants might have undergone selection pressure when plants colonized land and started developing roots to anchor and assimilate nutrients at the same time exclude toxic substances. This study provides an insight on how MATE transporters retain some of the conserved function from their bacterial ancestors while expanding and diversifying in plants. In the future, studies involving mutations in some of the conserved residues can help elucidate the functional relevance of these traditional transporters. It would be exciting how we might be able to engineer the MATE transporters to enhance stress resilience in plants growing under acidic conditions. As (Kawasaki et al. 2021) has shown the effects of root exudates on root microbiome affecting the growth of plant by altering the expression of ALMT and MATE in O.sativa further transporter engineering can also be used to induce synthetic signaling approaches to alleviate the effects of abiotic stress created by enhanced anthorpogenic activity and changing climatic conditions.

Background: Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporters, which exist widely in plants, function as crucial regulators in plant resistance to aluminum (Al) toxicity by inducing citrate efflux. However, the functions of most MATE family members in soybean (Glycine soja) remain to be elucidated.

Results: Expression pattern analysis showed that GsMATE was constitutively expressed in different soybean organs, with the highest level in root compared with those in stem, leaf and cotyledon. In addition, Al stress induced expression of GsMATE in soybean. Temporal analysis indicated that GsMATE expression was greatly enhanced by increasing concentrations of aluminum $[ \mathsf { A } | ^ { 3 + } ]$ after short exposure, reaching the high levels detected in the BW69 (Al-resistant) and the JW81 (Al-sensitive) lines of Glycine soja of wild soybean at 6 h and $8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ respectively. Furthermore, transient GsMATE expression in Arabidopsis protoplasts showed that GsMATE protein localized to the plasma membrane. Overexpression of GsMATE on an Arabidopsis columbia-0 (Col-0) background resulted in increased Al tolerance in transgenic plants. Analysis of hematoxylin staining showed that the roots of GsMATE transgenic lines were stained less intensely than those of the wild-type exposured to the same $\mathsf { A l C l } _ { 3 }$ concentrations. Therefore, GsMATE enhanced the resistance of transgenic plants to Al toxicity by reducing Al accumulation in Arabidopsis roots.

Conclusions: In summary, our results indicate that GsMATE is responsive to aluminum stress and may participate in the regulation of sensitivity to Al toxicity in Arabidopsis. In addition, the GsMATE protein is an Al-induced citrate transporter of the MATE family and exerts an essential role in Al tolerance in Glycine soja.

Aluminum (Al) is the main limiting factor for crop production in acidic soils. Efflux of organic acids is one of the mechanisms that determine Al-tolerance, and an Al-activated citrate transporter (multidrug and toxic compound extrusion) MATE1 gene is involved in different species. The contribution of the rye MATE1 gene (ScMATE1) depends on the rye (Secale cereale L.) cultivars and the crosses analyzed; there is no information about different rye species. The cDNA sequences, phylogenetic relationships, Al-tolerance, citrate exudation, and expression of the ScMATE1 gene were analyzed in several cultivars and wild species/subspecies of the Secale genus. Genotypes highly tolerant to Al were found within this genus. For the first time, sequences of the cDNA of the ScMATE1 gene were isolated and characterized in wild ryes. At least two copies of this gene were found likely to be related to Al-tolerance. The sequence comparison of 13 exons of ScMATE1 revealed variability between species, but also inter- and intra-cultivars. Variations were found in the Al-induced expression of ScMATE1 gene, as well as its contribution to Al-tolerance. The pattern of citrate exudation was inducible in most of the species/subspecies studied and constitutive in few. The phylogenetic analysis indicated that ScMATE1 is orthologue of two genes (HvMATE1 and TaMATE1) involved in the Al stress response in barley and wheat, respectively, but not orthologue of SbMATE, implicated in Al-tolerance in sorghum. ScMATE1 is involved in the response to Al stress in ryes, but its contribution to Al-tolerance is complex, and like in other species, there are tolerant and sensitive alleles in the different cultivars and species studied.

Additional key words: Al-activated citrate transporter, citrate exudation, cultivated and wild rye.

Aluminum-activated root malate and citrate exudation play an important role in plant Al tolerance. This paper characterizes AtMATE, a homolog of the recently discovered sorghum and barley Al-tolerance genes, shown here to encode an Al-activated citrate transporter in Arabidopsis. Together with the previously characterized Al-activated malate transporter, AtALMT1, this discovery allowed us to examine the relationship in the same species between members of the two gene families for which Al-tolerance genes have been identified. AtMATE is expressed primarily in roots and is induced by Al. An AtMATE T-DNA knockdown line exhibited very low AtMATE expression and Al-activated root citrate exudation was abolished. The AtALMT1 AtMATE double mutant lacked both Al-activated root malate and citrate exudation and showed greater Al sensitivity than the AtALMT1 mutant. Therefore, although AtALMT1 is a major contributor to Arabidopsis Al tolerance, AtMATE also makes a significant but smaller contribution. The expression patterns of AtALMT1 and AtMATE and the profiles of Al-activated root citrate and malate exudation are not affected by the presence or absence of the other gene. These results suggest that AtALMT1-mediated malate exudation and AtMATE-mediated citrate exudation evolved independently to confer Al tolerance in Arabidopsis. However, a link between regulation of expression of the two transporters in response to Al was identified through work on STOP1, a transcription factor that was previously shown to be necessary for AtALMT1 expression. Here we show that STOP1 is also required for AtMATE expression and Al-activated citrate exudation.

Keywords: aluminum toxicity, aluminum tolerance, ALMT, multi-drug and toxic compound extrusion, transporter protein, plasma membrane protein, organic acid exudation.

Background The membrane transporters viz. multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) and aluminumactivated malate transporter (ALMT) are associated with aluminum (Al) tolerance by accelerating secretion of organic acids, which can infuence nutrient availability and stress response. However, such transporter families have not yet been reported in lentil under Al stress condition.

Method and results In this study, 90 MATE and 14 ALMT genes were identifed and clustered into four (MATE) and fve (ALMT) subfamilies/clades with smaller subgroups. All the MATE and ALMT genes were unevenly dispersed across lentil chromosomes. Duplication analysis suggested that LcMATE gene family has expanded primarily through tandem duplication event. Collinearity of lentil with soybean suggested a close relationship between the MATE genes. The MATE promoter regions harboured many stress responsive as well as Al resistance transcription factor 1 related cis-regulatory elements. Predicted 3D (three-dimensional) structure and molecular docking revealed that 5 LcMATE proteins could bind citrate and contain amino acids related to its secretion via citrate exuding motif and other neighbouring sites. Expression analyses of LcMATE and LcALMT genes were performed using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). Six genes namely, LcM1, LcM42, LcM46, LcM47, LcALMT8 and LcALMT14 responded to Al stress with varying levels of expression patterns at diferent time points (3, 6, 12 and 24 h).

Conclusion Our fndings ofer thorough details on the MATE and ALMT transporters in lentils and will aid in valuabl understanding for future functional studies of these transporters in generating Al tolerant cultivars.

Background: The yields of cereal crops grown on acidic soils are often reduced by aluminum (Al) toxicity because the prevalence of toxic $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ cations increases as pH falls below 5.0. The Al-activated release from the roots of simple organic acids such as malate and citrate confers resistance to Al in a many plant species including maize (Zea mays L.). The Aldependent release of citrate from resistant lines of maize is controlled by ZmMATE1 which encodes a multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporter protein. ZmMATE1 resides on chromosome 6 and its expression in roots is induced up to four-fold by Al treatment. ZmMATE6 is another member of this family in maize whose expression is also increased by Al treatment. We investigated the function of this gene in more detail to determine whether it also contributes to Al resistance.

Results: Quantitative RT-PCR measurements found that in the absence of Al ZmMATE6 was expressed in the roots and leaves of Al-resistant and sensitive in-bred lines, and that expression levels in the root tips were lower than in the rest of the root tissue. Treatment with Al induced ZmMATE6 expression in all tissues but several other divalent or trivalent cations tested had no effect on expression. This expression pattern and the induction by Al treatment was confi rmed in Arabidopsis lines transformed with $\beta$ -glucuronidase where the ZmMATE6 promoter was used to drive expression. While subcellular localization of the ZmMATE6 protein could not be determined with confi dence transgenic Arabidopsis lines expressing ZmMATE6 displayed a greater Al-activated release of citrate from the roots and were signifi cantly more resistant to Al toxicity than controls. This was associated with reduced accumulation of Al in the root tissues.

Conclusions: Our results demonstrated that ZmMATE6 expression is induced by Al and functions as a citrate transporter. While some fi ndings are consistent with ZmMATE6 contributing to Al resistance in maize, further research is required to confi rm this result.

Aluminum (Al) toxicity is a major agronomic problem on acidic soil, which comprise $3 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ of arable soils in the world (Vonuexkull and Mutert 1995). Increasing solubility of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ at low pH $\mathrm { ( p H } < 5 . 5 ) $ in acidic soil inhibits the plant root growth and function, which results in a serious loss of crop yields (Kochian et al. 2004; Delhaize et al. 2007). In plants, Al exclusion and internal tolerance are two main physiological mechanisms to tolerate Al toxicity (Kochian et al. 2004). Some membrane transporters, which either decrease Al concentrations in cytosol or transport compounds, such as organic acids, are the main contributors in exclusion mechanism. Recently, some genes from MATE gene family were identified that encode the transport proteins involved in Al activated citrate release to tolerate Al toxicity in several species (Liu et al. 2009; Maron et al. 2013; Sivaguru et al. 2013).

As a group of secondary active transporters, the MATE gene family consists of multiple genes that widely exist in bacteria, fungi, mammals and plants (Omote et al. 2006). The MATE gene was first reported in Vibrio parahaemolyticus named norM in 1998, which could export several $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ coupled antibacterial agents across the membrane (Morita et al. 1998). Since then increasing MATE members have been researched in a wide range of living organisms. Compared with a fairly small numbers of MATE members in the bacteria and animals, plants have a higher diversity of MATE genes (Omote et al. 2006). Since 56 MATE genes have been isolated in Arabidopsis thaliana and 52 in Oryza sativa (Li et al. 2002; Hvorup et al. 2003; Tiwari et al. 2014). MATE gene family has also been identified in other plant species, such as Sorghum bicolor (Sivaguru et al. 2013), Hordeum vulgare (Fujii et al. 2012), Triticum aestivum (Ryan et al. 2009), Secale cereale (Yokosho et al. 2010) and Lotus japonicus (Takanashi et al. 2013). MATE proteins are characterized by one or two highly conserved MATE domains and about 12 putative transmembrane helical segments (TMSs) (Tiwari et al. 2014). Plant MATE proteins that are regarded as $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ coupled antiporters are involved in the detoxication of endogenous secondary metabolites and exogenous agents (Omote et al. 2006). For example, Arabidopsis MATE protein, TT12 is responsible for the vacuolar sequestration of flavonoids in the seed coat endothelium (Debeaujon et al. 2001). ALF5, encodes a member of the MATE family of integral membrane proteins, which is required for protection of the roots from inhibitory compounds (Diener et al. 2001). Further, increasing reports reveal that MATE-type transporters are involved in Al detoxification in plants. For instance, HvAACT1, a barley MATE gene localized on the plasma membrane of epidermal cells of the roots is responsible for the Al-induced secretion of citrate (Furukawa et al. 2007).

Maize (Zea mays L.), is a major crop worldwide. As yet, only ZmMATE1 and ZmMATE2 have been identified in maize (Maron et al. 2010; Takanashi et al. 2014). With the completion of maize genome sequencing, an excellent opportunity is provided to conduct genomewide analysis of the maize MATE gene family and infer its evolutionary history (Schnable et al. 2009). In the present study, we identified MATE gene family in maize and conducted a relatively detailed research about the phylogenetics, gene structures, chromosomal localization, gene duplications and expression profiles. Our work is expected to pave the way for future cloning and functional studies of MATE proteins in maize and contribute to understand evolutionary history of MATE gene family.

A number of plant species, including rice, secretes citrate from roots in response to Al stress. Here we characterized the functions of a gene, OsFRDL4 (Os01g0919100) that belongs to the multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family in rice (Oryza sativa). Heterologous expression in Xenopus oocyte showed that the OsFRDL4 protein was able to transport citrate and was activated by Al. The expression level of the OsFRDL4 gene in roots was very low in the absence of Al, but was greatly enhanced by Al after short exposure. Furthermore, the OsFRDL4 expression was regulated by ART1, a C2H2-type zinc finger transcription factor for Al tolerance. Transient expression of OsFRDL4 in onion epidermal cells showed that it localized to the plasma membrane. Immunostaining showed that OsFRDL4 was localized in all cells in the root tip. These expression patterns and cell specificity of localization of OsFRDL4 are different from other MATE members identified previously. Knockout of OsFRDL4 resulted in decreased Al tolerance and decreased citrate secretion compared with the wild-type rice, but did not affect citrate concentration in the xylem sap. Furthermore, there is a positive correlation between OsFRDL4 expression level and the amount of citrate secretion in rice cultivars that are differing in Al tolerance. Taken together, our results show that OsFRDL4 is an Al-induced citrate transporter localized at the plasma membrane of rice root cells and is one of the components of high Al tolerance in rice.

Keywords: citrate, aluminum tolerance, multidrug and toxic compound excursion, transporter, rice.

Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) transporters contribute to multidrug resistance and play major determinants of aluminum (Al) tolerance in plants. Alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) is the most extensively cultivated forage crop in the world, yet most alfalfa cultivars are not Al tolerant. The basic knowledge of the MATE transcripts family and the characterisation of specific MATE members involved in alfalfa Al stress remain unclear. In this study, 88 alfalfa MATE (MsMATE) transporters were identified at the whole transcriptome level. Phylogenetic analysis classified them into four subfamilies comprising 11 subgroups. Generally, five kinds of motifs were found in group G1, and most were located at the N-terminus, which might confer these genes with Al detoxification functions. Furthermore, 10 putative Al detoxification-related MsMATE genes were identified and the expression of five genes was significantly increased after Al treatment, indicating that these genes might play important roles in conferring Al tolerance to alfalfa. Considering the limited functional understanding of MATE transcripts in alfalfa, our findings will be valuable for the functional investigation and application of this family in alfalfa.

Multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) family is the most recent categorized multidrug efflux transporter family, which is a secondary transporter family that couples the translocation of substrates with an electrochemical gradient of cations (such as $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ or ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ ions) across the membrane [1, 2]. The X-ray structure of the MATE transporter, NorM from Vibrio cholerae, reveals a unique topology of its predicted 12 transmembrane (TM) helices, which is distinct from any other known multidrug resistance transporter [3].

MATE transporters are widely distributed in bacteria, fungi, mammals and plants [4]. Hvorup et al. [5] found 203 sequenced proteins in the MATE family, which could be divided into 15 subfamilies. Omote et al. [4] identified 861 MATE transporters from Archaea, Eubacteria and Eukarya and classified them into three large subfamilies comprising 14 smaller subgroups. There are 56, over 40 and 53 putative MATE transporters in Arabidopsis thaliana [6], Medicago truncatula [7] and Oryza sativa [8], respectively.

The bacterial MATE transporters can export organic cations for multidrug resistance [9, 10]. In yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), the Erc1 MATE-type transporter confers resistance to ethionine [11]. The mammalian MATE transporters can excrete the metabolic waste and xenobiotic organic cations in the kidney and liver [12, 13]. The plant MATE family transports a broad range of substrates such as organic acids, plant hormones and secondary metabolites [14–16]. Recently, the functions of many MATE transporters have been illustrated in plants [17], including transport of secondary metabolites such as alkaloids [18], flavonoids [7, 19], and anthocyanidin [20–23], detoxification of toxic compounds or heavy metals [6, 24], regulation of disease resistance [25–27], efflux of plant hormones such as abscisic acid (ABA) [28], iron translocation [29–31] and aluminum (Al) detoxification [32–35], which indicates MATE transporters play important roles in a wide range of biological processes in plants.

Al toxicity is considered as the main factor limiting crop yield on acidic soils [36]. Under Al stress, root exudation of organic acids, such as malate, citrate, and oxalate, is an important mechanism in plant resistance to Al toxicity [37, 38]. The genes controlling organic anion efflux from roots have been isolated from several crop species [39, 40]. MATE transporters have been shown to mediate the citrate efflux to confer plant tolerance to Al toxicity [41]. The MATE transporters involved in detoxification of Al were first identified from sorghum (Sorghum bicolor, SbMATE) and barley (Hordeum vulgare, HvAACT1) by map-based cloning, respectively [14, 32]. Later study found that the function of HvAACT1 protein is to release citrate to facilitate the translocation of iron from roots to shoots, and the 1-kb insertion in the upstream of the

HvAACT1 coding region in the Al-tolerant barley variety enhances and alters its expression to root tips, which is important to detoxifying Al and adaptation to acidic soils in barley [33]. Overexpression of HvAACT1 increases citrate efflux and Al tolerance in wheat and barley [34]. BoMATE from cabbage (Brassica oleracea) requires ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ to activate citrate efflux, leading to enhanced Al tolerance in A. thaliana [35]. Several other MATE transporters, such as EcMATE1 (Eucalyptus camaldulensis), OsFRDL4 (O. sativa), and ZmMATE1 (Zea mays), are found localized to plasma membranes in the root tips and related to plant tolerance to Al toxicity [42–44].

Compared with other plant species, little work on MATE transporters has been done in soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.), which is an important oil crop worldwide. To date, only one MATE transporter, GmFRD3b $G .$ max ferric reductase defective 3b), was reported to play a role in iron efficiency in soybean [45]. With the public available whole genome sequence [46] and RNA-seq Atlas [47] of $G .$ max, it is possible to identify the genome-wide MATE genes in soybean and investigate their expression patterns and possible functions. Plant MATE transporters have been shown to be involved in diverse functions including Al tolerance. By comparing the sequences of soybean MATE family with the known MATE transporters from other plant species, the possible roles of soybean MATE transporters could be proposed and help us to further test their function. In this study, we performed a genome-wide search of all putative MATE transporters in soybean. Their chromosomal distribution, gene duplication, phylogenetic relationship, structures of genes and proteins, and expression patterns were analyzed. Soybean MATE genes related to Al detoxification/iron translocation were further investigated by promoter analysis and differential gene expression analysis between the root tips of Al-tolerant and Al-sensitive soybean cultivars in response to Al. This study would provide useful information on the research of MATE transporters in soybean.

Nitrate availability fluctuates greatly in soil because of the high turnover rate associated with leaching, denitrification and various seasonal edaphic factors (reviewed in Wolt 1994; Cameron et al. 2013). In order to adapt to these changes of nitrate availability, plants have developed several different transport systems (Siddiqi et al. 1990). Uptake of nitrate at high external concentrations is accomplished mainly by low affinity transport systems (LATS). LATS are encoded by members of the NRT1/PTR Family (NPF) genes, and in Arabidopsis thaliana NPF6.3 (NRT1.1) and NPF4.6 (NRT1.2) are major contributors to nitrate-inducible and constitutive LATS (iLATS and cLATS), respectively (Tsay et al. 1993; Huang et al. 1999). At concentrations below $0 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate, uptake from soil solution is achieved through high-affinity transport systems (HATS), of which there are both constitutive and nitrate-inducible systems, (cHATS) and iHATS, respectively (reviewed in Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998; Wang et al. 2012). The cHATS transporter is active without prior exposure to nitrate and is typically of higher affinity ( $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values $< 2 0 \mu \mathrm { M } ,$ but lower capacity $\left( V _ { \mathrm { m a x } } < 2 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 } \right.$ FW $\mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ ) than the iHATS transporters (Glass & Siddiqi 1995; Crawford & Glass 1998).

Net ${ } ^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake or $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx by the cHATS was first characterized in N-deprived barley roots (Behl et al. 1988; Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992). Siddiqi et al. (1990) found that the nitrate fluxes due to cHATS were saturable at ${ \sim } 0 . 2 \ \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ and exhibited $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values that were 27-fold and fourfold lower, respectively, than fluxes associated with iHATS in nitrate-induced plants. The noted high affinity for nitrate exhibited by cHATS transporters in barley and other species (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995) makes this transporter ideally suited to detect and respond to trace quantities of nitrate in the root environment. iHATS transport in Arabidopsis is achieved principally through the activity of AtNRT2.1, whose expression is strongly induced by nitrate, peaking at some hours after first exposure to nitrate (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001; Orsel et al. 2002; Okamoto et al. 2003; Li et al. 2007). In addition to this major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter, expression of a second nitrate-inducible protein (AtNAR2.1) is required for both cHATS and iHATS nitrate uptake (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Yong et al. (2010) have shown that the functional iHATS nitrate transporter is a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1, localized in the plasma membranes (PMs) of Arabidopsis roots. Bimodal patterns of nitrate influx into roots of nitrateinduced plants, when represented as Hofstee or Lineweaver– Burk plots, demonstrate that cHATS and iHATS contribute simultaneously to total nitrate uptake with distinct kinetic properties (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Aslam et al. 1992; Kronzucker et al. 1995). Behl et al. (1988) proposed that an important function of the cHATS system of nitrate uptake was to supply trace amounts of nitrate that would set in motion the transcriptional events leading to iHATS induction. In addition, many other genes are activated, including enzymes such as nitrate reductase as well as developmental changes associated with nitrate provision (Wang et al. 2000, 2003, 2004).

Wang & Crawford (1996) isolated an EMS-mutagenized Arabidopsis line that was impaired in cHATS activity. This mutant exhibited a delay in the expression of inducible HATS, and was resistant to $0 . 1 \mathrm { m M }$ chlorate, a toxic nitrate analogue. Electrophysiological studies showed that there was very little response to $0 . 2 5 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate in the uninduced nrt2 mutant compared with strong initial membrane depolarization in wild-type (WT) plants. However, the gene encoding this putative cHATS was not identified. cHATS is also reduced by $9 0 \%$ in Atnar2.1-2 mutants compared with WT (Okamoto et al. 2006), suggesting that the AtNAR2.1 gene is necessary for the function of the cHATS transporter as was demonstrated for iHATS (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006). Thus, one clue to the identity of the transporter responsible for cHATS is that it requires co-expression of NAR2.1 for physiological activity.

In an earlier communication we demonstrated that all members of the AtNRT2 family are capable of nitrate uptake in Xenopus oocytes when co-expressed with AtNAR2.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Furthermore, the most prominent $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ enrichment in oocytes was observed for NRT2.5/NAR2.1 co-expression, suggesting that AtNRT2.5 might function in nitrate influx as a PM complex with AtNAR2.1 as was demonstrated for NRT2.1 (Yong et al. 2010). Kechid et al. (2013) showed that AtNRT2.5 and AtNRT2.6 play an important role in plant growth regulation in response to growthpromoting rhizobacterium Phyllobacterium brassicacearum strain STM196. With respect to AtNRT2.5’s involvement in cHATS, Okamoto et al. (2003) demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was diminished by nitrate provision, while a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression increased continuously during N-starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Measurements of nitrate influx in N-deprived AtNRT2.5 mutants and in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 demonstrated a 30 and $9 3 \%$ reduction, respectively, compared with WT (Lezhneva et al. 2014), suggesting that NRT2.1/NRT2.2 plays a predominant role in nitrate influx in N-starved plants. However, the finding is surprising, given that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are strongly induced by nitrate and expressed at diminished levels following nitrate deprivation. Nevertheless, the present study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present in roots of Arabidopsis after $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ d ~ } }$ of nitrogen starvation.

To investigate the nature of the association between AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1, we have used biochemical methods to isolate and characterize a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex between these two polypeptides, as well as physiological assays of nitrate influx in mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 to evaluate the impact of this disruption upon the kinetics of cHATS influx.

Nitrate is unique among the essential inorganic nutrients in so far as its uptake from soil solution by the major nitrate transporters AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 and AtNPF6.3 (originally named NRT1.1), and subsequent assimilation by enzymes such as nitrate reductase, requires prior exposure to nitrate for several hours to induce expression of the encoding genes. In the absence of external nitrate, genes encoding these transporters and enzymes are not expressed or expressed at low abundance. An exception to this requirement for nitrate induction is the cHATS for nitrate uptake. Behl et al. (1988) suggested that the principal role of this cHATS was to enable roots previously deprived of nitrate to absorb this ion and initiate induction of nitrate-inducible genes. Thus, at low external nitrate concentration, the activity of cHATS represents the first step in the complex pathway of nitrate assimilation. In a recent study of AtNRT2.5 expression and nitrate influx under conditions of severe nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014), it was demonstrated that AtNRT2.5 expression was considerably enhanced, while nitrate influx measured at $0 . 2 \mathrm { m M }$ was reduced by up to $3 0 \%$ in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants. Nitrate influx in triple mutants disrupted in NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.5 was reduced by a further $6 3 \%$ suggesting that NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 are the major contributors to nitrate influx under these conditions. Li et al. (2007), however, found that the cHATS influx was reduced by only $3 5 \%$ in Arabidopsis nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutants, suggesting that $\mathrm { N R T } 2 . 1 / 2 . 2$ is not the major transporter responsible for cHATS influx. Indeed, a large contribution to constitutive nitrate influx by NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 is contrary to expectation, in so far as it has been presumed that after several days of nitrate deprivation, these genes are no longer expressed (Okamoto et al. 2003). Nevertheless, our study demonstrates that NRT2.1 is a long-lived membrane protein that is still present at low abundance even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ of $\mathbf { N }$ starvation (Supporting Information Fig. S3).

The influx data shown in Fig. 6 and Table 2 provide convincing evidence that in A. thaliana AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to the cHATS. The average reduction of influx ( $6 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the two T-DNA knockout mutants disrupted in AtNRT2.5 is of a similar order of magnitude as was observed for the reduction of iHATS influx ( $7 3 \%$ of WT influx) in the $n r t { 2 . } I n r t { 2 . } 2$ mutants (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). This finding is different in magnitude from results reported by Lezhneva et al. (2014) which indicated only a $3 0 \%$ reduction of influx in NRT2.5 mutants.The difference in present findings may result from the ‘severe starvation’ employed in the Lezhneva study.

Complementation of the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant with AtNRT2.5 cDNA resulted in a statistically significant increase of the cHATS compared with the mutant, but influx failed to reach $1 0 0 \%$ of WT influx (Table 3). Incomplete recovery of the influx in Atnrt2.5-35S:NRT2.5 may be a result of lower AtNRT2.5 mRNA expression in the complemented line compared with WT (Table 3) possibly due to partial gene silencing. Schubert et al. (2004) reported silencing of genes under 35S promoter control in Arabidopsis T-DNA transformants that is controlled by transcript levels of transgenes. Nevertheless, this partial complementation taken together with the documented reduced nitrate influx in two independent Atnrt2.5 mutants provides strong evidence that AtNRT2.5 represents the major component of cHATS influx with primary responsibility for nitrate uptake at low nitrate concentration in nitrate-deprived plants.

The observed reduction of influx resulted in reduced nitrate accumulation in the Atnrt2.5 mutants. Although roots and shoots of the mutants and WT plants contained similar nitrate concentrations after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without N, after $6 \mathrm { { h } }$ of induction by $1 \mathrm { m } \mathrm { ~ K N O } _ { 3 }$ , mutants contain significantly lower nitrate concentration than WT roots (Table 4). However, following short-term $\mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \prime } 5 \mathrm { \ m i n } )$ ) exposure to $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , no differences were observed in the proportion of tracer transferred to shoots in uninduced or induced plants. Thus, AtNRT2.5 plays an important role in nitrate uptake into roots but not in the transfer of nitrate to shoots of Arabidopsis (Table 2). With respect to the transfer of nitrate to shoots, similar conclusions may be drawn from results reported by Kechid et al. (2013) using plants supplied with $2 \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. Lezhneva et al. (2014) found that under conditions of extreme N deprivation (4 weeks without N) phloem nitrate concentrations of NRT2.4 mutants was reduced by $4 0 \%$ , although there were no differences in NRT2.5 single mutants. This is consistent with the pattern of mRNA expression of AtNRT2.5 that was more abundant in roots than in shoots of 6-week-old nitratedeprived WT plants (Fig. 3a). A similar expression profile of AtNRT2.5 during both vegetative and reproductive growth stages of Arabidopsis was observed previously by Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014). However, after $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ of exposure to nitrate in the present study, root AtNRT2.5 expression had decreased to such an extent (with virtually no change of shoot AtNRT2.5 expression) that AtNRT2.5 expression was more abundant in shoots than in roots. Thus, depending on the duration of nitrate deprivation or re-exposure both higher and lower levels of AtNRT2.5 expression may be observed in roots versus shoots. This may account for the apparent differences between reports from Orsel et al. (2002), Okamoto et al. (2003) and Lezhneva et al. (2014), and the reported higher levels of AtNRT2.5 expression in shoots than roots described by Mantelin et al. (2006) and Kechid et al. (2013). Recently,

Garnett et al. (2013) followed responses of nitrate transporters to nitrogen supply in Zea mays over the life cycle and found that ZmNRT2.5 is the only NRT transporter (besides NRT2.1) expressed at significant levels when plants were grown hydroponically in low concentration nitrate solution.

$^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx into roots of uninduced WT plants revealed that cHATS influx conformed to saturable Michaelis– Menten kinetics over the nitrate concentration range from 10 to $2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ $\mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 6a,b). We have calculated kinetic parameters for the difference flux (WT minus $A t n r t { 2 . 5 }$ mutants) as a measure of influx specifically due to the AtNRT2.5 transporter (Table 1). $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ were estimated to be $2 . 3 \mu \mathrm { m o l \ g F W ^ { - 1 } \ h ^ { - 1 } }$ and $1 1 \ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ , respectively, for the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant, and $1 . 7 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { g } \mathrm { F W } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { h } ^ { - 1 }$ and $7 ~ \mu \mathrm { { M } }$ for the Atnrt2.5-2 mutant. These results are consistent with the findings of Behl et al. (1988), Siddiqi et al. (1990), Aslam et al. (1992) and Kronzucker et al. (1995) where cHATS was found to be a low capacity uptake system that exhibited a significantly higher substrate affinity (lower $K _ { \mathrm { m } _ { \mathrm { \ell } } }$ ) than that of the iHATS. However, in these earlier studies, lacking specific mutants, it was not possible to differentiate components of the cHATS flux.

Nevertheless, a significant nitrate flux remains in the two knockout mutants under non-inducing conditions. As noted above, Lezhneva et al. (2014) reported a significant contribution of NRT2.1/NRT2.2 to nitrate uptake by nitrate-starved roots. We have demonstrated that NRT2.1 proteins have a long half-life even after removal of external nitrate, confirmed by Western blots that reveal the presence of traces of NRT2.1 protein even after $^ { 7 \mathrm { d } }$ without nitrate (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Although the iHATS nitrate influx has been attributed to the activities of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 (Zhuo et al. 1999; Filleur et al. 2001), while examining the double deletion (NRT2.1/NRT2.2) Arabidopsis nrt2 mutant, defective in iHATS, Cerezo et al. (2001) and Li et al. (2007) reported a residual high-affinity influx that was $2 7 \%$ of the WT flux. This remaining high-affinity nitrate uptake in the mutant is not nitrate inducible, is saturable and most likely the result of cHATS activity (Cerezo et al. 2001). Figure 3b shows that the expression of AtNRT2.5 is significantly higher in the double-mutant Atnrt2.1-nrt2.2 (described in Li et al. 2007) compared with WT plants both under induced and uninduced conditions. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in an $A t n r t 2 . I { - } I$ mutant disrupted in both NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 was reported earlier (Orsel et al. 2004, 2006). It is possible that up-regulation of AtNRT2.5 is a compensatory mechanism mitigating the loss of AtNRT2.1.

The reduced cHATS influx in Atnrt2.5-1 plants and diminished nitrate content of roots and shoots of the NRT2.5 mutant (Table 4) were associated with reduced induction/ expression of AtNRT2.1 (which is largely responsible for iHATS) and complete absence of the $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ oligomeric complex of NRT2.5/NAR2.1 in induced Atnrt2.5-1 mutants compared with WT plants (Fig. 4). Accordingly, nitrateinduced $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx (iHATS) was significantly reduced in the Atnrt2.5-1 mutants (Fig. 7b). These observations demonstrate the importance of AtNRT2.5 in optimizing nitrate uptake following resupply of nitrate.

AtNRT2.5 gene expression was strongly suppressed when nitrate or ammonium were supplied to N-starved plants (Fig. 3a, Supporting Information Fig. S1); after prolonged nitrate exposure, mRNA of AtNRT2.5 was almost undetectable. Likewise, Okamoto et al. (2003) observed that the provision of nitrate to WT Arabidopsis suppressed expression of AtNRT2.5. Elevated expression of AtNRT2.5 in roots under conditions of N-deprivation is consistent with its role as the transporter with the primary responsibility for nitrate uptake following a period of nitrate deprivation. Reduced expression of AtNRT2.5 following provision of nitrate is consistent with its principal function having been performed, that is, nitrate has been absorbed; induction of AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 is underway and subsequent nitrate uptake is now taken up by these higher capacity, lower affinity transporters (Siddiqi et al. 1990; Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). Noting that NRT2.5 is subject to downregulation following exposure to nitrate or ammonium raises the question as to the appropriateness of the term cHATS that has long been applied to this system, which is not truly constitutive.

The absence of AtNRT2.1 in Arabidopsis mutant lines has a strong effect on plant growth resulting in smaller plants, especially at low nitrate supply (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al.

2007). AtNRT2.1 also has an important role in morphological and physiological responses of the root system to nitrogen-limited conditions, having direct effect on initiation of lateral root primordia (Remans et al. 2006). In order to examine the effect of AtNRT2.5 mutation on growth, plants were grown on low and high nitrate prior to plant weight and root length measurements. There were no differences between WT and Atnrt2.5-1 root weights of 5-week-old plants or root length of 2-week-old plants (Supporting Information Fig. S2) as observed by Kechid et al. (2013), but shoot growth of the mutants was significantly reduced by comparison with WT plants grown under conditions of low $( 2 5 0 \mu \mathrm { u } )$ nitrate indicating that nitrate deprivation associated with disruption of AtNRT2.5 resulted in increased root to shoot ratio, a clear indication of N deprivation, in $A t n r t 2 . 5$ mutants (Supporting Information Fig. S2b). Under conditions of prolonged growth at limiting nitrate concentration, Lezhneva et al. (2014) also noted that AtNRT2.5 contributed to the maintenance of shoot growth.

AtNRT2.5 is located on chromosome 1 in the forward orientation, on the first half of the chromosome, close to the three most important Arabidopsis nitrate transporters NPF6.3, NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 and a nitrate reductase NR2. Phylogenetic analysis of the AtNRT2 family from different plant species reveals the existence of closely related AtNRT2.5 orthologues in both dicots and monocots (Fig. 1, red). The clade of NRT2.5 proteins is divergent from NRT2.1-like proteins in dicots and monocots, probably stemming directly from a common ancestral nitrate transporter (Fig. 1). Similarly, Plett et al. (2010) found that NRT2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6 genes from dicots sit on an entirely separate phylogenetic tree from grass NRT2s, while NRT2.5 is the only NRT2 gene that has clear orthologues among dicot and monocot species. Interestingly, out of all dicot and monocot species examined in this analysis, only S. tuberosum has no NRT2.5 orthologue. In a similar analysis that included sequences of another Solanaceae species, namely Solanum lycopersicum, the same absence of NRT2.5 orthologue was observed (Supporting Information Fig. S4). This observation is surprising given that S. lycopersicum appears to possess normal cHATS activity (Cárdenas-Navarro et al. 1999). As more plant genome sequences become available, it will be interesting to confirm this phenomenon and explore possible explanations.

Western blot analysis of protein complexes separated by the BN-PAGE indicates that AtNRT2.5 exists in root membranes only as a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex, that is absent in the Atnar2.1-2 mutant (Fig. 4).The complex was separated in the second dimension by denaturing SDS-PAGE, and both AtNRT2.5 and AtNAR2.1 monomers were detected and shown to be derived from the same $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex (Fig. 5). The corresponding complex with AtNAR2.1 was observed for the AtNRT2.1 nitrate transporter (Yong et al. 2010). Based on observed interactions of other NRT2 nitrate transporters with NAR2.1 in heterologous systems (Kotur et al. 2012), the oligomeric polypeptide complex $\left( { \sim } 1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a } \right)$ may be a universal model for NRT2/NAR2.1 interactions and function.

The evidence presented here strongly supports the hypothesis that AtNRT2.5 is a major contributor to cHATS in roots of $A$ . thaliana, and that this transporter has a critical role in the induction of iHATS in N-starved plants. Even though the Atnrt2.5 mutants are knockouts, a significant nitrate influx $( 3 7 \%$ of WT) remains in these mutants. The study by Lezhneva et al. (2014) indicates that AtNRT2.1/ AtNRT2.2/AtNAR2.1 is responsible for this remaining flux. The $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ complex in which NRT2.1 is expressed (Yong et al. 2010) and which is primarily responsible for the iHATS flux has a long half-life of around $3 5 \mathrm { h }$ (Supporting Information Fig. S5) and, in roots of plants deprived of nitrate for 1 week (a treatment that de-induces AtNRT2.1 expression), is still present at around $2 4 \%$ of the abundance found in nitrate-induced plants (Supporting Information Fig. S3). Moreover, cHATS was found to be reduced by $3 5 \%$ in the nrt2.1 nrt2.2 mutant compared with WT (Li et al. 2007), signifying a contribution of AtNRT2.1 and/or AtNRT2.2 to the constitutive nitrate influx under the same conditions used in experimental work presented in this paper. In NAR2.1 mutants, from which NRT2 (but not NPF) proteins are absent, $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx is approximately $4 \%$ of WT values. Hence, it is unlikely that the remaining $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ influx observed in $n r t 2 . 5$ mutants receives a significant contribution from NPF6.3 activity (Glass & Kotur 2013).

Clearly, the function of AtNRT2.5 is not limited to nitrate influx associated with cHATS activity. Thus, Kechid et al. (2013) have established that AtNRT2.5 and indeed AtNRT2.6 play an essential role in plant growth promotion induced by the rhizospheric bacterium P. brassicacearum. Interestingly, this effect is nitrate independent.

In summary:

1 AtNRT2.5 is predominantly expressed in roots of nitratedeprived WT plants and is present only as a $1 5 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ molecular complex with AtNAR2.1. Expression of AtNRT2.5 is down-regulated by exposure to nitrate and ammonium.   
2 cHATS influx into roots of nitrate-deprived (uninduced) Atnrt2.5 mutants is reduced by $6 3 \%$ of the corresponding values in WT plants.   
3 cHATS influx due to AtNRT2.5 (influx difference between the WT and Atnrt2.5-1 mutant) in uninduced plants conforms to a saturable rectangular hyperbola that has low $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values corresponding to earlier physiological estimates of these kinetics parameters.   
4 Disruption of AtNRT2.5 does not affect root growth of Atnrt2.5-1 plants, but under low-N supply results in a $2 3 \%$ reduction in shoot growth.This effect might be indirect and a consequence of lowered AtNRT2.1 expression in the Atnrt2.5-1 mutant.   
5 AtNRT2.1 expression is significantly reduced in Atnrt2.5-1 mutant compared with WT and correlates well with the lower tissue–nitrate concentration in the mutant.   
6 The remaining cHATS nitrate influx in Atnrt2.5 mutants appears to be the result of a residual contribution by a long-lived AtNRT2.1 transporter.

In the present study, we isolated an NRT2 family gene, BraNRT2.1, from non-heading Chinese cabbage, and we sought to characterize the expression pattern and the tissuespecific expression of the BraNRT2.1 gene as well as the subcellular localization of the protein encoded by

BraNRT2.1. We then performed functional experiments to analyze potential roles for BraNRT2.1 in mediating nitrate uptake.

Most steps in the nitrate assimilation pathway are nitrate-inducible (Cai et al. 2008). Changes in gene expression can be elicited by nitrate rapidly (within $5 { \mathrm { - } } 1 0 \ \mathrm { m i n } )$ ) for nearly $10 \%$ of the transcriptome (Krouk et al. 2010). In addition, it is well-known that according to the nitrogen demands of plant, inducible high-affinity nitrate transport system (iHATS) is subject to negative feedback from nitrate assimilation products. In the present study, following exposure of the plants to $0 . 2 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ , the transcription of BraNRT2.1 peaked rapidly and then decreased and stabilized. The increase in the expression of BraNRT2.1 demonstrates that BraNRT2.1 can be induced by nitrate, and the subsequent decrease in expression suggests that BraNRT2.1 is feedback-repressible by downstream metabolites. Similarly, after exposure to $2 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate, the maximum rate of high-affinity nitrate uptake was observed at $4 5 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ during the period of nitrate induction, with the rates then declining substantially. The downregulation of NRT2.1 by an elevated supply of nitrogen might result from the concerted action of two different signaling pathways: one pathway is the feedback repression caused by the accumulation of nitrate metabolites (Gansel et al. 2001; Gojon et al. 2009), and the other pathway is the inhibition of NRT2.1 by NRT1.1, which occurs through the local inhibition of transcript accumulation under high nitrate conditions (Krouk et al. 2006). A recent study showed that a 150-base pair region in the promoter of NRT2.1 mediates the induction and repression of the gene (Castaings et al. 2011), providing evidence that this region is a key factor of BraNRT2.1 gene expression.

The expression of NRT2.1 in Arabidopsis has been shown to be affected by fluctuations in the availability of sucrose and by variations in light exposure (Bartsch et al.

1988; Lejay et al. 1999; Vidal and Gutierrez 2008), and the diurnal regulation of nitrate uptake has been demonstrated in many plant species (Lejay et al. 1999; Delhon et al. 1995; Ono et al. 2000). In the present study, BraNRT2.1 was observed to be regulated by nitrate induction, but whether BraNRT2.1 can be regulated by other factors such as light exposure and sucrose availability remains to be examined.

Previous studies have demonstrated in barley (Palechar et al. 2004; Tong et al. 2005) and Arabidopsis (Okamoto et al. 2006) that some NRT2 proteins require a partner protein, NAR2, to mediate nitrate transport. The function of NAR2.1, a member of the NAR2 gene family, is not yet understood clearly, but in nar2.1 mutants, the attainment of nitrate through HATS is defective (Okamoto et al. 2006; Orsel et al. 2006), and the AtNRT2.1 protein does not localize to the plasma membrane (Wirth et al. 2007). It was then proposed that the active nitrate transporter is actually a complex of AtNRT2.1 and AtNAR2.1 localized together in the plasma membrane (Yong et al. 2010). Thus far, evidence suggests that NAR2.1 is required for the expression and/or the correct trafficking of NRT2.1. Although preliminary evidence suggests that NAR2.1 is a cofactor involved in the targeting of the NRT2.1 proteins to the plasma membrane in some species, whether the plasma membrane localization of BraNRT2.1 requires a NAR2 family protein will need to be examined.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrates that BraNRT2.1 is inducible by nitrate and is localized at the plasma membrane. In addition, we found that BraNRT2.1 is expressed primarily in the root and that it promotes nitrate uptake. Together, our results demonstrate that BraNRT2.1 is a high-affinity nitrate transporter which participates in nitrate uptake. These findings contribute to our knowledge of the functions and characteristics of the BraNRT2.1 gene and provide a foundation for future studies and plant breeding to improve the efficiency of nitrogen use and to reduce the accumulation of nitrates in vegetables.

NRT2 family of nitrate transporters normally require a partner protein, NAR2 (nitrate assimilation related protein), to transport nitrate to a high-affinity (high affinity nitrate transport system, HATS), although its role is still not well understood. In this study, the $C c N R T 2 . I$ and CcNAR2 cDNAs from of Capsicum chinense were cloned and characterized in terms of their structure, phylogeny, and their organ-specific transcriptional regulation, and by ligh/dark cycle, N and sucrose. CcNRT2.1 (putative molecular mass $5 7 . 5 \mathrm { k D a }$ and CcNAR2 $2 2 . 6 6 \mathrm { k D a } )$ retained the characteristic domains of NRT2 and NAR2 family, respectively. CcNRT2.1 is expressed exclusively in the root, and both western blot and protein immunolocalization, demonstrated its exclusive location in root epidermal and cortical cells. CcNAR2 is expressed mainly in the root, but also in fruits of 25 days postanthesis (DPA). The presence of two protein bands ( $\mathord { \sim } 6 0$ and ${ \sim } 8 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ ) detected in the western blot, suggested that CcNRT2.1 monomer and $\mathrm { C c N R T } 2 . 1 / \mathrm { C c N A R } 2$ heterodimer work together for nitrate transport function in roots. Both genes were induced by ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ , $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } ^ { + }$ and glutamate, and CcNRT2.1 was induced by sucrose. The co-expression of both genes in the specific zone of the root $2 \mathrm { - } 4 ~ \mathrm { c m }$ from the apex) in which the high-affinity nitrate transport occurs (evaluated by root $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ endogenous content, extracellular $\mathrm { p H }$ alkalinization, and $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ net flux by MIFE technique), strongly supports that $C c N R T 2 . I / C c N A R 2$ belong to a HATS, with a functional similarity to AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 of Arabidopsis. These are the first components of a HATS characterized in the Capsicum genus.
