## Cloning and Sequence Analysis of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 cDNAs


CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 cDNAs were obtained from total RNA of seedling roots subjected to the absence of N for $9 6 \mathrm { h }$ and subsequently treated with $1 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ . A sequence of a size of 1593 bp (Fig. S1a) was obtained which presented a high percentage of identity with the NRT2 family of transporters of Solanaceas, especially those of S. lycopersicum SlNRT2.1 $( 9 5 \% )$ and SlNRT2.2 $( 9 5 \% )$ , $N _ { \ast }$ . tabacum N t N RT 2 . 1 ( $94 \%$ ) a n d N t N RT 2 . 2 $( 8 9 \% )$ , a n d N. plumbaginifolia NpNRT2.1 $( 9 4 \% )$ . The greater identity of CcNRT2.1 with the members of this family in A. thaliana was presented with AtNRT2.1 $(78 \% )$ . Due to its identity with those previously reported, this sequence was named CcNRT2.1.

The deduced protein sequence CcNRT2.1 (Genbank accession number QDB63632) had a size of 530 amino acids, a molecular mass of $5 7 . 5 ~ \mathrm { { \ k D a } }$ and pI of 9.15. The hydrophobicity profile indicated that it is a hydrophobic protein with 12 transmembrane helices (HTMs), presenting an extensive cytosolic loop between the HTMs 6 and 7, and $\Nu _ { - }$ and C-terminal regions located towards the cytosolic side (Fig. S1b and Fig. S2a). The sequence A-G-W/L-G-N-M-G, characteristic of NNP protein family was detected in the HTM6, while the signature G-X3-D-X2-G-X-R of the NRT2s was found between the HTMs 3 and 4. The two arginine residues (R) involved in the transport of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ in these proteins were conserved in positions 115 and 332, respectively (Fig. S1b). The amino acid residues leucine 85 and serine 466 known to be important for interaction with the NAR2 proteins in A. thaliana and $H .$ . vulgare, were present in the primary sequence of CcNRT2.1 (Fig. S1b). The C-terminal had a length of approximately 71 amino acids and contained two conserved phosphorylation sites found in most of these proteins (S/T-X-R/ K). Another putative phosphorylation site of the NRT2s was also observed between HTMs 10 and 11. Besides, N-terminal region presented a 20 amino acids region found in most of the NRT2 and containing putative phosphorylation sites (Fig. S1b, and Supplemental Table S1).

A 609 bp cDNA sequence was cloned and sequenced. This sequence had a high identity with the NAR2 proteins of plants previously reported, especially with CaNAR2 of $C .$ . annuum $( 9 9 \% )$ , NtaNAR3.1 of tobacco $( 7 6 \% )$ and SlNAR3.2 of tomato $( 7 4 \% )$ . The identity of this clone with $A$ . thaliana proteins was of $54 \%$ with AtNAR2.2 and AtNART3.1, and $53 \%$ with AtNAR2. Due to these results, this sequence was named CcNAR2 (Genbank accession number MK879390) (Fig. S1c).

CcNAR2 encoded a deduced sequence of 202 amino acids (Genbank accession number QDB63631), with a predicted molecular mass of $2 2 . 6 6 ~ \mathrm { k D }$ , and $\mathsf { p I }$ of 8.73. In CcNAR2, the motifs K-(2)-K-(2)-LCY-(2)-S-(3)-Rx-WR-(3)-D-(4)-DK and YGQ were found, which relate to the members of the NAR2 protein family, as well as the aspartate residue (D) that has been shown to be essential for ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transport (Fig. S1d). The hydrophobicity profile indicated that CcNAR2 presented a transmembrane region that was located at the C-terminal region. The presence of a signal peptide of approximately 20 amino acids was detected in the N-terminal region (Fig. S1b and Fig. S2b).


## Phylogenetic Analysis of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 Proteins


In order to carry out the phylogenetic analysis of both proteins, the sequences of those proteins that have been previously studied and that have a molecular and/or functional characterization were selected. In addition, liverwort Marchantia polymorpha sequences with similarity to these $C .$ . chinense proteins ( $5 6 . 6 \mathrm { - } 6 3 . 6 1 \%$ and $3 7 . 3 { - } 4 5 \%$ of identity with CcNRT2 and CcNAR2, respectively) were included, considering the role of this species in the evolution of terrestrial plants (Bowman et al. 2017).

CcNRT2.1 was located in the same clade as SlNRT2.1 and SlNRT2.2 of S. lycopersicum and NpNRT2.1 of N. plumbaginifolia, close to other members of Solanaceas family such as NpNRT2.1 of $N .$ . plumbagilifolia, NtaNRT2 .1 and NtaNRT2.2 of $N .$ . tabacum, and SlNRT2.3 of S. lycopersicum. These proteins were grouped within the clade where NRT2.1, NRT2.2 and NRT2.4 families of previously characterized eudicotyledons are located (Fig. 1A).

Interestingly, 18 sequences with similarity to the NRT2 proteins in the genome of M. polymorpha were found, which were grouped in a single clade, and close to the 12 members of Physcomitrella patens, both belonging to briophytas.

The phylogenetic analysis of NAR2 proteins indicated that these proteins evolved according to the evolution of the species. CcNAR2 was grouped together with CaNAR2 from C. annuum, and close to SlNAR3.2 from S. lycopersicum and CmNAR2 from C. morifolium (Fig. 1B). The phylogenetic trees of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 suggest that these proteins are more closely related to higher plant proteins than to those of green algae and mosses (Fig. 1).


## In Silico Analysis of CcNRT2.1- CcNAR2 Protein Interactions


For in silico study of CcNRT2.1-CcNAR2 interaction, the StuNRT2 protein of S. tuberosum was used as a reference, since it exhibited the best values of bitscore (1051) and e- (1 e-0.0) presented with that of C. chinense (Fig. S3a). The same analysis was carried out for CcNAR2, where SlNAR3.2 of S. lycopersicum was used as a reference, considering that with CcNRT2.1, it was the best value of bitscore (317) and e- (1e110) presented with that of C. chinense (Fig. S3b).

The results suggest that CcNRT2.1 interacts with different proteins involved in N metabolism, such as NAR2 proteins, nitrate and nitrite reductase, and urease, among others (Fig. S3a). The highest interaction value was obtained with the NAR2 protein, followed by nitrate and nitrite reductase. On the other hand, CcNAR2 seems to interact with high and low affinity ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ transport proteins, manganese-dependent ADPribose proteins/CDP-alcohol diphosphatase and proteins that contain a U box domain (Fig. S3b). In both cases, the highest interaction score occurred between the protein pairs NRT2- NAR2.

Similarly, residues R90, D99 and N116, which are known to be important for the interaction with NRT2 in A. thaliana and $H .$ . vulgare, were conserved in the CcNAR2 sequence (Fig. S1d).


## 3-D Structure of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2


The best model provided for CcNRT2.1 by the I-TASSER platform was that using the glycerol-3-phosphate transport protein of $E$ . colli, GlpT (pdb: 1PW4A) as model ( $80 \%$ of CcNRT2.1 sequence was modelled with $100 \%$ confidence). For CcNAR2, the best modeled was that of the copperdependent polysaccharide monooxygenase protein PMO-2 of the fungus Neurospora crassa (4EIR) $41 \%$ of CcNAR2 sequence was modelled with $9 6 . 3 \%$ confidence).

CcNRT2.1 presented the typical form of MFS transporter family, which is characterized by 12 HTMs, with a long central cytosolic loop containing a short $\propto$ -helix close to the HTM7, which links the $\Nu _ { - }$ terminal (HTM1–6) with the Cterminal (HTM7–12) domains. The N- and C- terminals were presented towards the cytosol. This location presents them as possible target sites for post-translational modifications, such as phosphorylation, proteolysis and vesicle degradation (Fig. 2a–c and Supplemental Table S1). The HTMs 1, 2, 5, 7, 8 and 11 formed the pore through which the substrate passes. The residues R115 and R332, which are determinant for the transport of high-affinity $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , as well as substratebinding domain AGW/LGNMG, were located at a distance of 4.5, 4.8 and $5 \mathrm { \AA }$ with respect to the ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ molecule. The R115 was located within the HTM2, the R332 within the HTM8 and the substrate-binding domain in the HTM5 (Fig. 2d).

The three-dimensional modeling of CcNAR2 indicated that these proteins do not have a defined structure, since the transmembrane helix that predicts the secondary structure is not modeled (Fig. 3a). Only secondary structures, four $\propto$ -helices and three sheets $\beta$ are present, and most of their sequence was presented without modeling. It is necessary to mention that crystals of these proteins have not been made yet; therefore, there is no reference model to compare.

The server MotifScan was used to look for specific motifs present in CcNAR2 amino acid sequence related to the obtained structural model. This analysis supported the previous knowledge about the possible CcNAR2 interaction with membranes by identifying two possible myristoylation site in the protein. Putative phosphorylation sites were also found for this protein (Fig. S1b and Supplemental Table S1).

Interestingly, the structural motif predicted as $\beta$ -sheet structure in the 3D model was identified as a putative Forkhead-associated (FHA) motif near carboxyl termini. The

FHA structure reveals a four-stranded $\beta$ -sandwich architecture with strands long of $\beta 1$ and $\beta 2$ connected with a loop in an anti-parallel orientation (Fig. 3a). The residues arginine 134 and 168 located in this motif are giving a positive surface charge, in addition to the residue arginine 90 (Fig. 3b).


## Expression of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 in Different Organs of the C. chinense


CcNRT2.1 was expressed exclusively in $C$ . chinense roots, while CcNAR2 was expressed mainly in root, although it was barely observed in pericarp (Fig. 4a). Transcript levels were also analyzed in flower buds, flowers at the time of the anthesis, as well as during the development of the fruits. In none of these tissues, the expression for CcNRT2.1 was obtained; however, a very low expression of CcNAR2 was observed in flower and in fruits of 10 days post-anthesis (DPA), but the expression increased in fruits of 25 DPA. In the rest of the tissues, it was not possible to detect any expression of this gene (Fig. 4b).


## Immunodetection of CcNRT2.1 in the Different Organs of the C. chinense Plant


The results of CcNRT2.1 immunodetection indicated the presence of a band of ${ \sim } 6 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ , which coincides with the predicted molecular mass for $\mathrm { C c N R T } 2 . 1$ $\langle 5 7 . 5 \mathrm { \ k D a } \rangle$ , that was recognized by the antibody only in protein extracts from the root (Fig. 4c). In addition, a band of approximately $8 0 \mathrm { k D a }$ , probably corresponding to CcNAR2 $\sim 2 3 \ \mathrm { k D a }$ )-CcNRT2.1 heterodimer, was detected in the same protein extract. In the remaining organs of the plant, different bands with molecular masses between 70 and 90 kDa were detected (Fig. 4c).


## Regulation of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 Transcript Levels by Different Nitrogen Sources and $N O _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ Concentrations


When the seedlings were subjected for $9 6 \mathrm { h }$ to the absence of N (time 0), a low expression of CcNRT2.1 was observed. This did not occur for CcNAR2. This expression increased significantly until it reached a maximum for both genes at the first hour of being exposed to $1 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ , remaining high at $^ { 2 \mathrm { h } }$ and later decreasing at $4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ . At this time, transcript levels for CcNRT2.1 remained similar to plants of time 0 (Fig. 5A). Similarly, treatment with 1 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l }$ increased transcript levels of both genes, reaching the highest levels at $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of exposure and subsequently decreasing at $4 \textrm { h }$ . The effect of potassium glutamate on transcript levels was different between these genes; this amino acid produced an increase in CcNRT2.1 transcript levels at the second hour of exposure, which was maintained until $4 \textrm { h }$ of exposure. For CcNAR2, glutamate induced an expression at 1 h of exposure, but this decreased at $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ . However, a second induction was observed after $^ { 4 \mathrm { h } }$ of exposure (Fig. 5a).

The expression profiles of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 genes in response to the ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ dose show a concordance between them, being higher for CcNRT2.1 than for CcNAR2 at $0 . 1 \mathrm { m M }$ ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , but the maximum induction for both occurred at $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . At a dose of $1 \mathrm { \ m M \ N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ , CcNRT2.1 transcripts levels decreased drastically, while those of CcNAR2 still remained at slightly high levels although they had decreased at that time (Fig. 5b).


## Regulation of the Expression of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 during a Photoperiod Cycle, Sucrose and Light Intensity


At the beginning of the light cycle, the transcript levels of $C c N R T 2 . I$ were practically undetectable and these increased after $^ { 3 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of exposure to light, being highest at $1 1 \ \mathrm { h }$ . At the beginning of the dark cycle, transcript levels for this gene decreased drastically, with only a slight increase observed at $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 3 h }$ of darkness to decrease later at $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ . The behavior for CcNAR2 was very similar, although the decrease in transcripts was not as marked as that observed for CcNRT2.1 (Fig. 6A).

As can be seen in Fig. 6B, the transcript levels of CcNRT2.1 increased in the roots that were treated with sucrose, compared to those to which this carbohydrate was not added, and this behavior was visible at $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 3 h }$ of darkness. However, at $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ in the dark, there were no differences in the transcripts between the roots exposed to sucrose and those that were not exposed, which were much lower than at the beginning of the dark cycle. For CcNAR2, the presence of sucrose in the medium did not cause a significant effect (Fig. 6b).

In order to study the effects of light intensities on CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 expression, $C .$ . chinense plants were grown under different shadow nets and expression was checked after $^ { 7 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of ligh. In that case, a significant decrease in $C c N R T 2 . I$ transcript levels was observed from the reduction of light up to $30 \%$ $( 6 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } ,$ ), this decrease being much greater when this factor was reduced up to $10 \%$ $( 5 4 \ \mu \mathrm { m o l } \ \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } ,$ ). However, no significant effect of light intensity on the levels of CcNAR2 transcripts was observed (Fig. 6c).

The expression levels of CcNRT2.1 and CcNAR2 were evaluated in different regions of primary root (PR) in seedlings growing at $0 . 5 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N } 0 _ { 3 }$ (Fig. 7a). ## Localization of High Affinity Nitrate Transport Activity along the Primary Root of C. chinense

Nitrogen (N), which is an important component of biological macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, provides nutrients and energy for plant growth and development (Gojon 2017). Nitrate and ammonium are the most readily absorbed forms of N in soil by plant roots, especially nitrate, which is the preferred N source in soil for assimilation by most terrestrial plants (Kiba and Krapp 2016). The lack of $\mathbf { N }$ in the natural environment could lead to intense competition between plants and soil microorganisms (Norman and Friesen 2017). To further adapt to changes in diferent N levels, plants have evolved several absorption and transport systems to optimize the availability of nitrate for their own growth, including the low-afnity nitrate transporter system (LATS) and high-afnity nitrate transporter system (HATS) (Fang et  al. 2021). Among them, the NRT1/PTR family (NPF) and nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) are responsible for the functions of the LATS and HATS systems, respectively. The NRT2 family is responsible for the uptake of low nitrate from the soil by roots. Thus, understanding the functions of NRT2 members will be benefcial to the sustainable development of agriculture in the future.

NRT2 members have been isolated and characterized in many species, including seven NRT2 proteins in Arabidopsis (Okamoto et al. 2006), seven to ten NRT2 in barley (Vidmar et  al. 2000), and fve NRT2 in rice (Cai et al. 2008). Among the members of the NRT2 family, NRT2.1 plays a major role in nitrate uptake by roots in the HATS system. There was a strong association between HATS activity and NRT2.1 transcription, which was highly induced by nitrate depletion and repressed by abundant nitrate (Wirth et  al. 2007). OsNRT2.1 overexpression in rice signifcantly increased biomass and yield, and improved agricultural N use efciency (Yan et  al. 2011). Moreover, NRT2.1 played a key role in the regulation of nitrate signaling pathways by lateral root mediation, which was independent of its highafnity nitrate uptake function (van Gelderen et  al. 2021). Though the function of NRT2.1 has been thoroughly studied in herbaceous plants, it is still lacking in woody plants. Therefore, understanding more functions of NRT2.1 in diferent species could play a signifcant role in regulating N absorption.

Plant transporter genes have been well studied in mycorrhizal symbiosis processes. For example, some plant nitrate transporters have been induced by arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) colonization with the host plant. A study reported that one NRT gene (TC79437) was down-regulated with Funneliformis mosseae colonization in Medicago truncatula roots (Burleigh 2001). In addition, the expression of NRT genes was also afected by AM colonization in grapevine (Balestrini et  al. 2017), Solanum lycopersicum (Ruzicka et  al. 2012), tomato (Hildebrandt et  al. 2002) and Lotus japonicus (Guether et al. 2009a). Dark septate endophytes (DSEs) are a type of dematiaceous and septate fungal hyphae that are commonly found in the roots of host plants from natural environments (Jumpponen and Trappe 1998). Studies have reported that several DSEs are benefcial for their host plants’ N assimilation (Upson et al. 2009; Vergara et al. 2019; Wu et  al. 2021). However, the impacts of DSEs on plant $\mathbf { N }$ uptake through the regulation of NRT genes are poorly understood.

Sweet cherry (Prunus avium L.) is one of the most popular fresh fruits in the world. However, the molecular mechanism of its N uptake is poorly understood. A previous study found that the DSE fungus S16 could promote the growth of sweet cherry and upregulate the expression of nitrate transporters (Wu et al. 2021). Therefore, the aim of this study was to investigate the role of the nitrate transporter PaNRT2.1 during colonization by S16 and to determine the function of PaNRT2.1 in N uptake in sweet cherry. This would broaden our understanding of the molecular mechanism of $\mathbf { N }$ uptake with nitrate transporters in DSE symbiosis.

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ is a vital macronutrient essential for plant growth, development, and productivity. It is a structural component of amino acids, nucleic acids, and chlorophyll, and thus plays a central role in metabolic and physiological processes. Among the various forms of nitrogen available in the soil, nitrate $( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - } )$ is the primary source for most terrestrial plant species. Beyond its nutritional value, nitrate also functions as a critical signaling molecule, influencing gene expression, root architecture, and overall nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in plants (Crawford and Forde 2002). To cope with fluctuating soil nitrogen availability, plants have evolved specialized nitrate transport systems, broadly classified into low-affinity (LATS) and high-affinity (HATS) transport systems (Crawford and Glass 1998). In Arabidopsis thaliana, the NRT1 and NRT2 gene families encode the major components of these systems, respectively. Unlike NRT1, transporters belonging to NRT2 family operate in coordination with chaperone proteins, such as NRT3.1 (NAR2), to form functional two-component systems (Krapp et al. 2014). The NRT2 family in Arabidopsis thaliana comprises seven members (AtNRT2.1 to AtNRT2.7). Four of which (AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.4, and AtNRT2.5) are recognized as HATS. Among them, AtNRT2.1 has been studied extensively and is considered the principal component of inducible HATS, as it contributes to up to $7 5 \%$ nitrate uptake under low nitrate condition (Laugier et al. 2011; Cerezo et al. 2001). AtNRT2.2, though functionally redundant with AtNRT2.1, plays a supporting role (Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 are uniquely upregulated during nitrogen starvation and contribute to nitrate remobilization and phloem nitrate allocation (Xu et al. 2024). However, the recent work by Zhang et al. (2025) indicates that AtNRT2.4 is more than a passive transporter; it actively modulates nitrate signaling pathways and root system architecture (RSA), and thus, functioning as a sensor and transporter in the nitrate regulatory network.


## AtNRT2.4 in the Landscape of Nitrate Transporters


AtNRT2.4 has conventionally been classified as a high-affinity nitrate transporter, based on expression patterns and functional assays in heterologous systems like Xenopus oocytes (Kiba et al. 2012). It is primarily expressed in the lateral root epidermis and shoot vascular tissue and is induced under nitrogen starvation (Xu et al. 2024; Kiba et al. 2012). However, previous functional analyses showed that its loss does not affect plant biomass, nitrate influx, or total plant nitrate content, unlike AtNRT2.1, leading to speculation about its auxiliary role (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Indeed, Zhang et al. (2025) fundamentally shift this narrative by demonstrating AtNRT2.4’s responsiveness to both local and systemic nitrogen cues, suggesting its involvement in nitrate signal transduction rather than simple uptake.


## Sensing Local and Systemic Nitrate Signals


Through a well-designed split-root system experiment, Zhang et al. (2025) demonstrated the central role of AtNRT2.4 in nitrate sensing. They designed two homogeneous control treatment $\mathrm { { C . N a C l } }$ (both root compartments supplied with nitrogen-free medium containing $5 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l ) }$ and $\mathrm { C . N a N O } _ { 3 }$ (both sides supplied with 5 $\mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { , }$ and a heterogeneous split-root system (Sp. $\mathrm { N a C l / S p . N a N O _ { 3 } }$ ), in which one root half was placed in nitrogen-free medium supplemented with $5 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ (Sp. $\mathrm { N a C l } )$ and the other in medium containing $5 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a N O } _ { 3 }$ $\left( \mathrm { S p . N a N O } _ { 3 } \right)$ . This setup allowed the authors to differentiate between local and systemic nitrate signaling responses. Under homogeneous N-free conditions (C.NaCl), Wildtype plant (Col-0) roots exhibited stimulated root elongation, indicative of local nitrate deficiency signal perception. Conversely, $n r t 2 . 4$ mutants showed stunted root elongation under the same conditions, indicating impaired local nitrate deficiency signal sensing. More strikingly, in the split root heterogeneous configuration, wild-type plants displayed typical root foraging behavior, promoted lateral root (LR) growth on nitrate-rich side and inhibited LR growth on nitrate-depleted side. In contrast, the nrt2.4 mutant failed to respond appropriately on either side, indicating the necessity of AtNRT2.4 in systemic nitrate signal transduction. Gene expression data from roots further support this. Genes such as AtANR1, AtTCP20, AtCBL1 (calcineurin B-like proteins 1) and AtCIPK23 (CBL-interacting protein kinase 23), which are typically modulated by nitrate status and regulate root system architecture (RSA) in wild type plants, were significantly mis-regulated in $n r t 2 . 4$ mutants under these treatments. The largest transcriptional changes were noted for AtANR1, a key MADS-box transcription factor involved in LR foraging. Under local and systemic deficiency conditions, AtANR1 was severely downregulated in $n r t 2 . 4 _ { \cdot }$ , whereas in Col-0, its expression was upregulated, mirroring the RSA phenotypes. Thus, AtNRT2.4 is likely upstream of AtANR1 in nitrate-responsive signaling.


## Distinct from Canonical Nitrate Sensing Pathways


Nitrate signaling in plants is traditionally understood through three parallel modules:

1. Local sensing via AtNRT1.1 (CHL1), a dual-affinity transporter regulated through phosphorylation (T101) mediated by the CBL9-CIPK23 complex, a key component of a calcium-mediated signaling pathway in plants that plays crucial roles in ion homeostasis and adaptation to various environmental stresses (Ho et al. 2009). In their study, Zhang et al. (2025) found that AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT1.1 reciprocally regulate each other’s transcription. Under low nitrate (LN) growth condition, AtNRT2.4 expression was significantly downregulated in the nrt1.1 mutant, suggesting that AtNRT1.1 positively influences AtNRT2.4. Conversely, AtNRT1.1 was upregulated in nrt2.4, suggesting negative feedback from AtNRT2.4. Interestingly, the expression levels of CBL9 and CIPK23 were significantly elevated in nrt2.4 but not in nrt1.1, implying that AtNRT2.4 suppresses the dual-affinity regulatory module. This suggests a new model wherein AtNRT2.4 indirectly modulates AtNRT1.1 affinity by regulating upstream signaling kinases.

2. Systemic sensing via CEP-CEP receptor-CEP downstream loop, a peptide-based root-to-shoot-to-root communication mechanism under nitrogen starvation. C-terminally encoded peptide receptor 2 (CEPR2) and its downstream components regulate long-distance nitrate deficiency responses (Taleski et al. 2018; Ohkubo et al. 2017). Zhang et al. (2025) showed that AtNRT2.4 expression remained unchanged in cepr2 mutants, and vice versa, indicating that AtNRT2.4 does not participate in CEP signaling. Notably, in nrt2.4 mutants under normal nitrate (NN) conditions, AtCEPR2 was upregulated, hinting at negative regulatory feedback.

3. Intracellular nitrate sensing via NIN-like protein 7 (AtNLP7), AtNLP7 is a central transcription factor that binds nitrate and translocate to the nucleus to activate primary nitrate response genes (Liu et al. 2017). Although AtNRT2.4 is not a direct transcriptional target of AtNLP7 (based on datasets by Alvarez et al. (2020) and Konishi et al. (2021), Zhang et al. (2025) found that

AtNLP7 transcript levels were significantly elevated in the nrt2.4 mutant under both LN and NN conditions. This contrasts with nrt1.1, where AtNLP7 remained unchanged. This places AtNRT2.4 as a suppressor of AtNLP7 expression, potentially linking extracellular nitrate detection to intracellular response attenuation. This cross-talk might serve to prevent excessive activation of downstream nitrate-responsive genes under fluctuating conditions.


## Functional Independence from the NRT3.1 Pathways


The HAT, AtNRT2.1 is known to depend on the chaperone AtNRT3.1 (NAR2.1). In their study, Zhang et al. (2025) found that unlike AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.4 was unaffected in $n r t 3 . I$ mutants under both LN and NN conditions. Additionally, AtNRT2.4 could function independently of AtNRT3.1 in previous Xenopus oocyte assays (Kotur et al. 2012). Collectively, these data emphasize that AtNRT2.4 is functionally decoupled from the AtNRT3.1 pathways, suggesting a unique nitrate signaling branch. These findings indicate that AtNRT2.4 may represent a parallel or auxiliary nitratesensing module that provides robustness and specificity to the nitrate response network.


## Growth Promotion and Yield Enhancement Via AtNRT2.4 Overexpression


To probe physiological relevance, Zhang et al. (2025) generated two AtNRT2.4 overexpression lines (OE3 and OE16) and complementation lines in the nrt2.4 background (Com4 and Com9). Under (LN), none of the lines showed major differences in growth or biomass compared to Wild-type A. thaliana (Col-0), which is consistent with the observed redundancy in the NRT2 family (notably upregulation of AtNRT2.2 and AtNRT2.5 in nrt2.4). However, under normal nitrate (NN) conditions, overexpression lines accumulated significantly more ammonium in shoots and showed enhanced vegetative growth, silique number, and seed yield compared to Col-0 and the $n r t 2 . 4$ mutant. This suggests that AtNRT2.4 overexpression boosts nitrogen use and assimilation, possibly by modulating ammonium production pathways. The translational implication is clear: AtNRT2.4 could be a valuable genetic lever in improving nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) without increasing fertilizer input, an urgent need in sustainable agriculture.


## Role in Anthocyanin Biosynthesis: A Stress Marker Connection


A particularly striking findings of Zhang et al. (2025) is that AtNRT2.4 modulates anthocyanin accumulation under nitrate-deficient conditions. Anthocyanins serve as indicators of stress and protective agents against oxidative damage (Li and Ahammed 2023). Under LN conditions, nrt2.4 mutant leaves remained green compared to WT and accumulated less anthocyanin. AtNRT2.4 overexpression lines displayed enhanced anthocyanin biosynthesis, correlated with the upregulation of key biosynthetic genes such as AtPAP1 and AtGL3. This link suggests AtNRT2.4 may also participate in coordinating metabolic shifts in response to nutrient stress. This echoes earlier findings where nitrogen limitation led to anthocyanin buildup (Scheible et al. 2004), but AtNRT2.4 appears to offer a direct regulatory path, adding a novel layer to our understanding of nutrient-stress signaling crosstalk.


## Concluding Perspectives and Future Directions


Zhang et al. (2025) offer compelling evidence that AtNRT2.4 is more than a transporter, it is a key regulatory node in the nitrogen signaling network (Fig. 1 and Table 1). The independence from CEP and NRT3.1 pathways, the tight transcriptional crosstalk with other major nitrate sensors, and the dual influence on both root development and metabolic defense responses make AtNRT2.4 a potential target for breeding nitrogen-efficient crops.

Future research should focus on elucidating the molecular network surrounding AtNRT2.4. Identifying its protein interactors and post-translational modifications will clarify how it forms functional signaling complexes and responds to nitrogen fluctuations. Defining the upstream transcriptional regulators of AtNRT2.4 will further reveal how its expression is modulated under varying nitrogen conditions. Additionally, exploring the crosstalk between AtNRT2.4 and hormonal pathways such as auxin and cytokinin may uncover mechanisms linking nitrate signaling to root system architecture. Translational studies should extend to AtNRT2.4 orthologs in major crops like wheat and maize, including field evaluations of overexpression lines for nitrogen use efficiency and stress resilience. Finally, CRISPRbased fine-tuning of AtNRT2.4 expression holds promise for advancing sustainable nitrogen management in agriculture.

By bridging nitrate perception with root plasticity and metabolic resilience, AtNRT2.4 emerges as a promising candidate to address the grand challenge of improving nutrient efficiency in a climate-constrained world.

Background: High-affinity nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2) genes have been implicated in nitrate absorption and remobilization under nitrogen (N) starvation stress in many plant species, yet little is known about this gene family respond to various stresses often occurs in the production of rapeseed (Brassica napus L.).

Results: This report details identification of 17 NRT2 gene family members in rapeseed, as well as, assessment of their expression profiles using RNA-seq analysis and qRT-PCR assays. In this study, all BnNRT2.1 members, BnNRT2.2a and BnNRT2.4a were specifically expressed in root tissues, while BnNRT2.7a and BnNRT2.7b were mainly expressed in aerial parts, including as the predominantly expressed NRT2 genes detected in seeds. This pattern of shoot NRT expression, along with homology to an Arabidopsis NRT expressed in seeds, strongly suggests that both BnNRT2.7 genes play roles in seed nitrate accumulation. Another rapeseed NRT, BnNRT2.5 s, exhibited intermediate expression, with transcripts detected in both shoot and root tissues. Functionality of BnNRT2s genes was further outlined by testing for adaptive responses in expression to exposure to a series of environmental stresses, including N, phosphorus (P) or potassium (K) deficiency, waterlogging and drought. In these tests, most NRT2 gene members were up-regulated by N starvation and restricted by the other stresses tested herein. In contrast to this overall trend, transcription of BnNRT2.1a was up-regulated under waterlogging and K deficiency stress, and BnNRT2.5 s was up-regulated in roots subjected to waterlogging. Furthermore, the mRNA levels of BnNRT2.7 s were enhanced under both waterlogging stress and P or K deficiency conditions. These results suggest that these three BnNRT2 genes might participate in crosstalk among different stress response pathways.

Conclusions: The results presented here outline a diverse set of NRT2 genes present in the rapeseed genome that collectively carry out specific functions throughout rapeseed development, while also responding not just to N deficiency, but also to several other stresses. Targeting of individual BnNRT2 members that coordinate rapeseed nitrate uptake and transport in response to cues from multiple stress response pathways could significantly expand the genetic resources available for improving rapeseed resistance to environmental stresses.

Nitrogen is an essential element for nucleotide, amino acid, chlorophyll, and alkaloid metabolites [1]. It plays an important role in the construction of plant cells, and tissues, and in yield formation and is also the primary factor limiting plant growth and yield [2]. Potato is an important noncereal food crop and a highly heterozygous autotetraploid species [3, 4]. In China, the planting area is 4.67 million hectares per year, with an annual output of approximately 90 million tons. In actual production, the nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is less than $4 0 \%$ [5]. Cultivating varieties with high nitrogen use efficiency is an important way to improve nitrogen use efficiency, including nitrogen absorption, assimilation, and reallocation processes [2]. Nitrate is the main form of nitrogen absorbed by potato, which is taken up and transported by nitrate transporters in the roots. The NRT family (Nitrate Transporter and Peptide transporter family, NRT/NPF) plays an important role in the absorption, transport and distribution of nitrate nitrogen in plant cells and tissues [6]. It is one of the largest transporter families in the plant kingdom [7] and plays a crucial role in nitrogen use efficiency and crop production.

Various studies have focused on characterizing and cloning different members of this gene family in various plant species. In Arabidopsis, the NRT1.8 gene functions in nitrate removal from xylem sap and mediates cadmium tolerance [8]. Additionally, the NRT2.4 gene in Arabidopsis plays a dual role in the roots and shoots of nitrogen-starved plants [9]. The NRT2 gene family has been characterized in Arabidopsis, with studies showing interactions between different components of the nitrate uptake system. A total of fifty-three NPF genes, seven NRT2 genes, and two NAR2 genes were identified in Arabidopsis Thaliana [6, 10]. AtNRT1.1 is the first nitrate transporter identified and cloned in plants. It has the functions in nitrate absorption and transport, and auxin transport and regulates nitrate-mediated root development. AtNRT1.1 can respond to changes in the environmental nitrate concentration by changing its level of phosphorylation to regulate nitrate transport activity [11], and it is a receptor that senses nitrate signals [12]. Most NPFs have low nitrate affinity, whereas AtNRT1.1 and OsNRT1.1B have dual affinities [13]. In rice, 93 nitrate transporters were identified, including 70 NPFs. The OsNRT1.1A gene, a member of the nitrate transporter 1/peptide transporter family, has been identified as a key regulator of nitrogen utilization and flowering, leading to high yield and early maturation [14]. NRT1.1B participates in regulating the establishment of root microbial communities and promotes the mineralization of organic nitrogen, thereby mediating the interaction between plants and microorganisms. The rhizosphere of indica rice is richer in microbial communities involved in nitrogen metabolism than that of japonica rice is, resulting in higher nitrogen use efficiency in indica rice varieties than in japonica rice [15, 16]. The natural variation of the NRT1.1B protein is that the 327th amino acid of indica rice is methionine (Met), whereas that of japonica rice is threonine (Thr). The NPF family facilitates the transport of a multiple substrates, encompassing phytohormones such as abscisic acid (ABA) and gibberellins (GAs), as well as metabolites including jasmonic acid-isoleucine (JA-Ile), dipeptides, and polypeptides. OsNPF3.1 is an important low-affinity nitrate and plant hormone transporter gene, that is crucial for rice tillering and nitrogen use efficiency. This gene is strongly induced by nitrate, ABA and gibberellin 3 (GA3) in the roots, stems and leaves of rice and has a significant effect on rice tillering and nitrogen use efficiency. The expression of the OsNPF3.1 gene is positively correlated with the number of tillers. Its overexpression significantly promotes the accumulation of ABA in the roots and GA at the base of the plant, thereby inhibiting the growth of lateral buds and rice tillering, especially under high nitrate concentrations [17, 18]. Experiments have shown that OsNPF3.1 is a pH-dependent low-affinity nitrate transporter and is also a transporter of ABA and GA3. Most NRT2s are high-affinity nitrate transporters [6], and the high-affinity transport system is activated at low nitrate concentrations. NAR2 interacts with AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.5, OsNRT2.1 and $O s N R T 2 . 3 a$ on the cell membrane to improve nitrate transport efficiency [6, 19]. The overexpression of OsNAR2.1 can significantly improve nitrogen absorption and drought resistance in rice, whereas OsNAR2.1 knockout plants have the opposite effect [20]. Studies in tomato have shown that the expression of a cluster of genes encoding NPF members is downregulated in a mutant with a low-SGA phenotype, indicating the importance of these genes in plant growth and development [21]. Furthermore, 77 NPFs, 7 NRT2s, and 1 NAR2 were found in Solanum lycopersicum [22].

Overall, a comprehensive understanding the nitrate and peptide transporter (NRT/NPF) gene family is crucial for elucidating nitrogen metabolism and stress responses in various crops species, including potato. While Zhang et al. [23] identified 39 StNRT genes using PGSC DM v4.03 genome, our study significantly expands this number to 81 leveraging the SolTub_3.0 genome. The objectives of this research were (i) to conduct a more comprehensive identification of NRT genes in the potato genome; (ii) to systematically analyze gene structure, chromosomal distribution, promoter sequences, conserved protein domains and motifs; (iii) to perform a phylogenetic analysis of StNRT genes within potato species; (iv) to compare the homology and phylogenetic relationships of potato StNRT proteins with NRT proteins from other species; (v) to investigate the tissue-specific expression patterns of StNRT genes in potato; and (vi) to examine the expression dynamics of StNRT genes in response to nitrogen stress. To date, no comprehensive whole-genome analysis of the NRT gene family in potato has been reported. In this study, we used whole-genome analysis to identify members of the StNRT gene family. Through bioinformatics and expression analysis, our findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for further research on potato nitrate transporter genes and pave the way for functional studies of these genes. Further investigations into the regulatory mechanisms and functional roles of these genes will offer valuable insights into improving crop yield and nutrient utilization efficiency.

Genes encoding NRT2 or NAR2 proteins are present in many plant species2,10,19–21. According to degenerated primers, seven chrysanthemum NRT2 homolog CmNRT2 and one NAR2 homolog CmNAR2 were isolated by RT-PCR and RACE methods (data not shown). Here, we focus on the molecular characterization of one CmNRT2 gene and CmNAR2. The CmNRT2 sequence proved to be highly homologous with those of other NRT2 proteins, but conservation of the CmNAR2 sequence was less marked, although the LCYAP, WRK and YGQ motifs were still retained. AtNRT2.1 localizes mostly to the plasma membrane of root cortical and epidermal cells, and the BiFC assay has shown that an intact AtNRT2.1/AtNAR2.1 complex is formed within the A. thaliana plasma membrane29. CmNAR2 localized throughout the cell (Fig. 3). The natural hypothesis is therefore that CmNRT2 requires the presence of CmNAR2 to form a transporter unit. The effect on the rate of nitrate influx of constitutively expressing both chrysanthemum sequences as transgenes in A. thaliana simultaneously was much more positive than when either CmNAR2 or CmNRT2 on their own were expressed, underlining the importance of the CmNAR2/CmNRT2 interaction. In A. thaliana, AtNAR2.1 has been identified as chaperonin proteins, and AtNRT2.1–2.6 all require the presence of AtNAR2.1 to be effective (this dos not apply to AtNRT2.7)8 . In rice, the alteration in the influx of nitrate observed in an osnar2.1 knockdown mutant was taken to show that both HATS and LATS were impaired15. However, LATS was not affected using the different transgenic constructions in our results, which may be that CmNRT2 or CmNAR2 was responsible in HATS and CmNRT2 interacted with CmNAR2 at the protein level in HATS. Our work has further helped to confirm the proposed complementary roles of NRT2 and NAR2 proteins.

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ , as the essential element of amino acid, nucleic acid, chlorophyll, and among other biologically important molecules, is vital to plant growth and development. In aerated soils, plants take up nitrogen mainly in the form of nitrate due to intensive nitrification processes. In plants, nitrate can be absorbed and translocated through transmembrane proteins, which mainly consist of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF) and NRT2 (see excellent reviews by $\mathrm { X u }$ et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2018b). There are 53, 93, and 91 NPF genes in Arabidopsis, rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Leran et al. 2014). Most NPFs are responsible for low-affinity nitrate transporter activity $\mathrm { ~ ( > ~ 0 . 5 ~ m M } _ { \mathrm { ~ , ~ } }$ (Epstein et al. 1963; Noguero and Lacombe 2016), except for CHL1/NRT1.1/ AtNPF6.3, which was the first NPF to be found and cloned, displays a dual affinity property (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999). There are 7, 4, 7, and 5 NRT2 genes in Arabidopsis, rice, Brachypodium, and Sorghum, respectively (Orsel et al. 2002, Cai et al. 2008; Massel et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018a, b). In general, all of NRT2s are responsible for high-affinity nitrate transport $( < 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ). Additionally, a third family, named as NAR2/NRT3, requires interacting with most NRT2 members to transport nitrate (Zhou et al. 2000; Orsel et al. 2006; Yan et al. 2011; Kotur et al. 2012), except for AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al.

2012). There are 2, 2, and 3 NRT3 members in Arabidopsis, Rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Plett et al. 2010; Massel et al. 2016). Beside nitrate, NPF family transport diverse components as substrates, including dipeptides, glucosinolate, IAA, ABA, GA, and JA (Leran et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2018a). By contrast, NRT2 members have been only reported to transport nitrate so far.

Based on a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis from 31 fully sequenced plant genomes (Lee et al. 2011), NPF family can be classified into 8 unambiguous clades. Members from NPF1 subfamily have been shown to be involved in redistributing nitrate to developing tissues. For example, AtNPF1.1/NRT1.12 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.11 are expressed in companion cells (CC) of the primary vein, and their double mutant is deficient in remobilizing nitrate to younger leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013). Similarly, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7 is expressed in the phloem of the minor vein in mature leaves and is responsible for nitrate remobilization under nitrogen deficiency (Fan et al. 2009). Additionally, many other NPF2 family members (including AtNPF2.3, AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, OsNPF2.2, and OsNPF2.4) are involved in nitrate translocation from root to shoot (Wang and Tsay 2011; Li et al. 2015; Taochy et al. 2015; Xia et al. 2015). AtNPF2.12/NRT1.6 can mediate nitrate influx to premature embryos (Almagro et al. 2008). In addition to nitrate, two NPF2 members (AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5) are able to transport chloride (Li et al. 2016, 2017); five NPF2 members (AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, AtNPF2.10/ GTR1, AtNPF2.11/GTR2, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7, and AtNPF2.14) are able to transport glucosinolate, which is one of the important secondary metabolites for plant defense (Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). AtNPF3.1, originally identified as a nitrate/nitrite transporter, is found to be a GA transporter which is also affected by nitrate availability (Sugiura et al. 2007; Pike et al. 2014; David et al. 2016; Tal et al. 2016). AtNPF4.6/NRT1.2 has been characterized as a constitutive nitrate transporter (Huang et al. 1999), as well as an ABA transporter (Kanno et al. 2012). As the largest subfamily, three NPF5 members (AtNPF5.11, AtNPF5.12, AtNPF5.16) are responsible for nitrate efflux from tonoplast (He et al. 2017), AtNPF5.5 is involved in nitrate accumulation in embryos (Leran et al. 2015). Moreover, AtNPF5.2/PTR3 can transport dipeptide, which is important for plant pathogen defense (Karim et al. 2007). AtNPF6.3 is the most heavily studied member of the family, and it is a dual-affinity nitrate transporter (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999), auxin transporter (Krouk et al. 2010); it affects stomata opening (Guo et al. 2003) and also serves as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). Interestingly, indica rice OsNRT1.1B/OsNPF6.5, one of the closest orthologous genes of AtNPF6.3 with only a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) with japonica rice $O s N R T I . I B /$ OsNPF6.5, is responsible for better nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in indica rice (Hu et al. 2015). Recently, OsNRT1.1B is reported to facilitate Selenomethinone (Se) translocation in both roots and leaves, and the overexpression lines exhibit a higher Se accumulation in grains (Zhang et al. 2018b). AtNPF6.2/NRT1.4 is specifically expressed in leaf petiole, which is critical for nitrate storage in petiole (Chiu et al. 2004). AtNPF7.2/NRT1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 expressed in close proximity of xylem and their functions are antagonistic upon stress challenges (Li et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2014). The NPF8 subfamily (NPF8.1/PTR1, NPF8.2/PTR5, and NPF8.3/PTR2) in Arabidopsis transports dipeptide and has no detectable nitrate transport activity (Komarova et al. 2009), whereas OsNRT1/ NPF8.9 is a putative nitrate transporter in rice (Lin et al. 2000).

Compared to the large and complex NPF family, NRT2 and NRT3 families in plants are relatively small. There is a clear divergence between monocots and dicots of NRT2 family genes, suggesting NRT2 in monocots may function differently from heavily-studied AtNRT2 (Plett et al. 2010; Wang et al. 2018a, b). It has been well-documented that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are nitrate-inducible transporters, which are major components for high-affinity root nitrate uptake (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 are also involved in high-affinity root nitrate uptake but mainly upon nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Besides, AtNRT2.1 can serve as a signal transducer to regulate lateral root growth (Little et al. 2005). NRT2.7 is the only NRT2 member located on the tonoplast membrane and is responsible for nitrate transport in seeds (Chopin et al. 2007). In rice, OsNRT2.3b responds to pH changes and its overexpression leads to grain yield increase (Fan et al. 2016). Additionally, overexpressing OsNRT2.1 driven by the NAR2.1/NRT3.1 promoter is also able to enhance grain yield in rice (Chen et al. 2016). The importance of NRT3/NAR2 is underlined by their coexpression and interaction with NRT2 genes. All AtNRT2 members except for AtNRT2.7 can interact with NRT3.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Nevertheless, AtNRT3.1 is not indispensable for nitrate uptake mediated by AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al. 2012).

Sugarcane is one of the most productive crops in the world (FAOSTAT, 2016; http://www.fao.org/statistics/en/) and it accounts for $80 \%$ of world sugar supply and $40 \%$ of ethanol production (Zhang et al. 2013). N deficiencies can cause a decreased chlorophyll synthesis as well as a reduced biomass. Together with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, N makes up $90 \%$ of sugarcane dry matter (Brandes 1952). Sugarcane mainly absorbs N through $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilizers or biological nitrogen fixation owing to microbial nitrogen fixers (Boddey et al. 2003). Unfortunately, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is low for agronomic crops, especially for sugarcane, more than $50 \%$ of nitrogen is lost through surface run-off, leaching, denitrifications or volatilizations (Garnett et al. 2009). Only $20 \%$ (or less) of input N can be found in dry biomass of sugarcane at harvest (Franco et al. 2011). Therefore, understanding nitrogen uptake, translocation and utilization is key to improve NUE by conventional breeding and genetic engineering strategy. However, the genetic information for nitrate transporters is still missing in sugarcane, largely due to the lack of a complete genome information. Recently, an allele-defined genome of sugarcane Saccharum spontaneum L. became available (Zhang et al. 2018a), offering an excellent opportunity to identify nitrate transporter families at a genome-wide scale. In this study, we carried out a BLAST search using Arabidopsis and Sorghum NPF/NRTs against newly available sugarcane genome. Phylogenetic analysis, gene structure as well as protein motif analysis were conducted to understand molecular and evolutionary relationships between subfamilies and species. Moreover, RNA-Seq data were analyzed to investigate tissue-specific expression pattern across all NPF/ NRT genes in S. spontaneum. Our results presented a comprehensive characterization of sugarcane NPF/NRT genes, which laid the foundation for future investigations of these nitrogen transporters in sugarcane.

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ is an essential element for all plants. Higher herbaceous plants obtain the majority of their $\mathbf { N }$ from the assimilation of nitrate and subsequent reduction to ammonium. The first step of the nitrate assimilation pathway is the entry of nitrate into the cell, a process that is mediated by specific transporters. Based on their kinetics, nitrate uptake systems have been classified into two groups: the low-affinity transport system (LATS) and the high-affinity transport system (HATS). The LATS operates at high external nitrate concentrations and shows no evidence of saturation in planta, even at $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ concentrations as high as $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ . The HATS $( K _ { \mathrm { m } } < 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ operates at low external nitrate concentration, and has inducible (iHATS) and constitutive (cHATS) components (Siddiqi et al., 1989, 1990; Glass et al., 1992). Three plant gene families encode nitrate carrier proteins: the large PTR family (51 members in Arabidopsis), including the NRT1 and NAXT proteins (Segonzac et al., 2007), the NRT2 family, encoding HATS components (Miller et al., 2007), and the CLC family (Zifarelli and Pusch, 2010). NRT1 proteins have been identified in several species, for example Arabidopsis thaliana, Brassica napus, and Oryza sativa (for reviews, see Forde, 2000; Miller et al., 2007; Tsay et al., 2007). Compared with the large number of genes in these families, only a few members were functionally characterized as $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ transporters based on heterologous systems, for example in Arabidopsis AtNRT1.1, AtNRT1.2 (Tsay et al., 1993; Huang et al., 1999), AtNRT1.4 (Chiu et al., 2004), AtNRT1.5 (Lin et al., 2008), and AtNRT1.6 (Almagro et al., 2008), in rice OsNRT1 (Lin et al., 2000), and in B. napus BnNRT1.2 (Zhou et al., 1998).

The most studied NRT1 transporter is the Arabidopsis AtNRT1.1 protein (originally named CHL1). Its expression is inducible by nitrate (Huang et al., 1996), and functional characterization in Xenopus oocytes revealed its involvement in low- as well as high-affinity nitrate uptake, behaving both as a LATS and HATS component. This transporter is therefore currently considered as a dualaffinity nitrate transporter (Wang et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1999). AtNRT1.1 expression is also developmentally regulated, being mainly expressed in nascent organs, stems, leaves, flower buds, and roots (Guo et al., 2001). AtNRT1.1 was functionally linked to the stimulatory effect of nitrate on root growth (Walch-Liu et al., 2006; Walch-Liu and Forde, 2008). AtNRT1.1 has been shown to play a role in the nitrate-sensing system that stimulates root growth in nitrate-rich patches by promoting auxin fluxes in root apices (Ho et al., 2009; Krouk et al., 2010).

Nitrate transporters in legumes to date have received little interest, probably because these species are able to adapt to $\mathbf { N }$ starvation by promoting a specific response: the biological $\Nu _ { 2 }$ fixation in symbiotic nodules (Crespi and Frugier, 2008). Consequently, although nitrate also plays important nutritional and signalling roles in legumes, only few putative nitrate transporters were cloned in these species (Yokoyama et al., 2001) and none of them has been functionally characterized so far. Indeed, under N-limited conditions, legumes absorb mineral $\mathbf { N }$ and particularly $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ to fulfil their nutritional demand before functional symbiotic nodules are differentiated. In addition, nitrate is known to repress nodulation and ${ \bf N } _ { 2 }$ fixation activity (Streeter, 1985a, b; Barbulova et al., 2007), involving both local and systemic regulatory pathways (Jeudy et al., 2010). N supply was shown to modulate nodule initiation in Lotus japonicus by predisposing plants to successful or unsuccessful interactions with rhizobia prior to inoculation (Omrane et al.,

2009). The inhibitory effect of high exogenous $\mathbf { N }$ concentrations on the competence of plants to nodulate was maintained several days after transfer to low $\mathbf { N }$ concentration (Omrane et al., 2009).

Whether $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ repressive effects are due to the ion itself, to products of its assimilation, or both is not yet clearly demonstrated. Receptor-like kinases acting in legume shoots, HAR1 (Hypernodulation and Aberrant Roots) in L. japonicus, SUNN (Supernumerous Nodules) in Medicago truncatula, SYM29 (Symbiosis29) in pea, and NARK (Nodule Autoregulation Receptor Kinase) in soybean (Krusell et al., 2002; Nishimura et al., 2002; Searle et al., 2003; Schnabel et al., 2005), are involved in nitrate inhibition of nodulation (Okamoto et al., 2009).

Recent findings suggest that a protein belonging to the NRT1(PTR) family, encoded by the M. truncatula LATD/ NIP gene (lateral root organ defective/numerous infections and polyphenolics), regulates the legume root system architecture. LATD/NIP is expressed in the root apical meristem and elongation zones, as well as in the nodule meristem and infection zones (Liang et al., 2007; Yendrek et al., 2010). Accordingly, LATD/NIP is required for the establishment and maintenance of primary root, lateral root, and symbiotic nodule meristems (Yendrek et al., 2010). In addition, the latd mutant is not sensitive to the inhibition of primary root growth by nitrate.

In the present work, the first functional characterization of an $M .$ . truncatula nitrate transporter, MtNRT1.3, is reported. This transporter behaves as a dual-affinity nitrate transporter when expressed in Xenopus oocytes. Interestingly, unlike members of the NRT1 superfamily characterized so far, in roots the expression of MtNRT1.3 is locally stimulated by $\mathbf { N }$ starvation and repressed in medium supplied with $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ . The present data suggest that this transporter probably does not have a major role in overall root $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ acquisition but may rather be involved in the plant response to $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ starvation.

Nitrogen (N) is one of the most important nutrients for plant growth and development (Xu et al. 2012). As a major component of chlorophyll, nucleic acids, amino acids, and secondary metabolites, nitrogen (N) plays a significant role in the growth and improvement of plants (Amtmann et al. 2009). Nitrate $( \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } ^ { - } )$ is the primary supplier of N for plant development (Huang et al. 2016). As a signalling molecule, ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ regulates gene expression of several purposes, such as flowering time (Marín et al. 2011), seed dormancy, leaf growth and development (Urlić et al. 2017; Qiqige et al. 2017), and the development of root system architecture and plant growth (Araya et al. 2016). Plants absorb ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ and store it in vacuoles via a variety of transport channels (Yamamoto et al. 1998; Shitan et al. 2013), but are mostly carried out by multigene family-encoded nitrate transporters (NRTs) (Tavares et al. 2017). NRTs are classified into: the low-affinity transport system (LATS) via the nitrate transporter 1 family (NRT1) (Andrews et al. 2013) and the high-affinity transport system (HATS) through the NRT2 family of nitrate transporters (Vidmar et al. 2000); Cerezo et al. 2001). For efficient uptake, transport, and utilization of ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ nitrogen, plants utilize the NRT gene family that comprises three subfamilies: NRT1, NRT2, and NRT3. (Dechorgnat et al. 2011). NRTs play a significant role in ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transport and share diverse evolutionary origins in Arabidopsis thaliana (Orsel et al. 2002; Lezhneva et al. 2014), rice (Wang et al. 2018), poplar (Bai et al. 2013), and pineapple (Li et al. 2018a, b). NRTs responded significantly to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Zhang et al. 2020). In addition to ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transport, some NRTs responded to the drought stress (Pieczynski et al. 2018). NRT1 sub-family shared the largest number of genes and may comprise 8 to 10 clades during phylogenetic analysis (Wittgenstein et al. 2014). Gibberellin, nitrite, glucosinolates, peptides, amino acids, and abscisic acid are also transported by NRT1s (Amtmann et al. 2009). The NRT2 sub-family consists of seven members in A. thaliana, ranging from 1 to 7 (Orsel et al. 2002; Okamoto et al. 2003). Interestingly, NRT3 interacts with NRT2 at the protein level to increase the HATS activity (Yong et al. 2010). Another name for NRT3 is nitrate assimilationrelated gene 2 (NAR2). The distinct tissue expression patterns of NRTs revealed that these genes play vital roles in the absorption and transportation of nitrogenous molecules. For xylem nitrate ion loading, AtNRT1.5 is mostly expressed in the root pericycle cells (Lin et al. 2008). AtNRT1.9 enhances nitrate downtransport in the roots and encourages nitrate entry into the root phloem (Wang et al. 2011). According to reports, AtNRT1.11 and AtNRT1.12 control the redistribution of nitrate concentration in phloem and xylem (Hsu et al. 2013). NtAMT1.1/NRT1.1 were significantly upregulated at the roots, organs, leaves, and flowers (Liu et al. 2018). AtNRT2.1, AtNRT2.2, AtNRT2.4, and AtNRT2.5 played a significant role in root-mediated $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake from soil (Kant et al. 2018).

Furthermore, plenty of data suggest that nitrate transporter 1/peptide transporters (NPFs) have the capacity to transport nitrates with low affinity in various species, including rice, chrysanthemum, and Brassica campestris (Fang et al. 2017; Gu et al. 2016a, b; Hu et al. 2016). Concerning NRT2s, the epidermis of roots was the main point of expression for AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 to absorb nitrate (Li et al. 2007; Cerezo et al. 2001). On the root epidermal cells plasma membrane, AtNRT2.4 functioned as an extra protein for AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2. There was a consistent substantial inhibition of nitrate absorption in the $A t N R T 2 . I / 2 . 2 / 2 . 4$ triple mutation plants (Kiba et al. 2012). During nitrate remobilization, AtNRT2.5 participates in nitrate loading into the phloem and is mostly expressed in the epidermis and root hair zone cortex (Lezhneva et al. 2014). In vegetative organs, AtNRT2.6 is significantly upregulated and reacts to both biotic and abiotic stressors (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Furthermore, AtNRT2.7, which is found in the seed vacuolar membrane, may contribute to the buildup of nitrate in seeds at a later stage of development (Chopin et al. 2007). Other plants that have NRT2s as highaffinity NRTs include cucumber, chrysanthemum, cassava, and Brassica rapa (Gu et al. 2016a, b; Li et al. 2018a, b; Zou et al. 2019). The NAR2s (NRT3s) play a major role in nitrate transport and control the activity of proteins in the high-affinity transport system. In A. thaliana, AtNAR2 interacted with every AtNRT2 protein except AtNRT2.7 (Kotur et al. 2012). A high-affinity transport system’s nitrate transport activity was enhanced by the interaction between NRT2 and NAR2 (Wang et al. 2021; Yong et al. 2010).

Nitrogen has been identified in many studies of plant salt stress responses as a key nutritional component. There is a strong connection between plant salt stress responses and nitrogen absorption, metabolism, and transportation. Soil salinization affects one-fifth of the worlds agricultural area. Enhancing soil stress affects plant development and jeopardizes food security (Morton et al. 2019). In general, plants that are drought-stricken undergo physiological, morphological, biochemical, and molecular changes (Hossain et al. 2016). However, maize showed growth inhibition when exposed to high nitrate supplies (Wilkinson et al. 2007), whereas OsNAR2.1 positively regulated rice grain output and drought tolerance (Chen et al. 2019). The maizeZmNPF7.9 plays a significant role in seed development and grain weight by regulating $\mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ transport and metabolism (Wei et al. 2021). ZmAMT1. 1B and ZmAMT1.3 showed significantly higher expression in stems and roots at the vegetative $\left( \mathrm { V } _ { 7 } \right)$ and reproductive $\left( \mathsf { R } _ { 1 } \right)$ stages (Dechorgnat et al. 2019). $Z m N P F 6 . 6$ is strongly nitrate-inducible in the roots with negligible expression in shoots, whereas $Z m N P F 6 . 4$ is constitutively expressed in both roots and shoots irrespective of nitrate availability (Wen 2015). Although the roles of NRTs in transporting and accumulating $_ \mathrm { N }$ in various plant species have already been extensively studied, molecular mechanisms of how structural differences significantly affect functional properties of $Z { \mathrm { m N R T s } }$ have not been published yet.. Among the gene structural analyzes, phylogenetic relationship, three-dimensional (3D) protein modeling, syntenic relationship, gene ontology (GO), docking, protein–protein interaction (PPI), co-expression network, KEGG pathway, relative mRNA expression, subcellular localization analyzes guide an integrated molecular mechanism of how gene/protein act in real cellular system (Rabby et al. 2024; Zhai et al. 2019). Although extremely important, the above mentioned parameters are not evaluated among NRTs in maize that might consequence make the research on individual $Z { \mathrm { m N R T } }$ very challenging. Considering the importance of analyzing the above mentioned parameters, the current research was focused on precise analysis of the above mentioned parameters integrating a series of dry and wet lab data to enlighten how structural characteristics of ZmNRT affect functional properties in uptake, transport and accumulation of NRTs in maize. We lab validation of expression of major ZmNRTs under drought, nitrogen starvation, heat, and salinity stresses and subcellular localization might strengthen the validity of dry lab research. This in depth analysis might guide the plant biologists in understanding how evolutionary origin, structural characteristics, expression and subcellular localization affect functional properties of $Z { \mathrm { m N R T s } }$ . The critical findings of the research might guide the maize breeders in developing maize with high nitrate utilization efficiency.

Nonetheless, direct transport measurements from membranes prepared from H338N-expressing cells agreed with the growth phenotypes, i.e. the tolerant mutants had higher transport rates for $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ and $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ reflected in lower $K _ { m }$ values but reduced $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (Figs. 2 and 4). These experimental observations suggest that rather than destroying the filter, these mutants have altered ion selectivity. Our hypothesis is that the H338N variants have an increased $K _ { m }$ value for $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport; however, the negligible $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport measured in H338N-expressing cells makes precise measurements of changes in $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ kinetic parameters difficult.

The four amino acids at residue 338 that can confer calcium tolerance are similar in hydropathy (Fig. 7). This suggests hydropathy is an important determining factor for cation selectivity within the c-2 region. Despite the similar hydropathy of Asp and Glu to His, Lys, Asn, and Gln residues, these negatively charged amino acids at position 338 cannot confer calcium tolerance in yeast (Table II). Given that there is another Glu residue adjacent to $\mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ , we hypothesize that the H338D and H338E variants are nonfunctional because of an excess of negative charge within the filter domain (Fig. 1B ).

The selectivity of H338N for $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } > C a ^ { 2 + } }$ (Figs. 3–5) suggests that the putative filter domain of H338N appears to be able to discriminate between these similar ions (ionic radius for $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ is $9 7 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ whereas that of $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ is $9 9 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ ). However, extensive alterations in this region appear to inhibit completely the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ activity of the transporter (see above). The fact that H338N also has increased affinity for $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ is intriguing (ionic radius of

$7 4 \textup { \AA }$ and confirms that alterations in $\mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ affect the uptake of other metals, as indicated by our preliminary findings using the yeast growth assay and transport experiments (data not shown and Fig. 5). The observation that changes in hydrophilic residues within the transporter filter can change substrate specificity has been detailed with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels and other transporters (23, 24). For example, a Q103A mutation in the plant metal transporter IRT1 apparently eliminated zinc transport but did not alter the transport of other metals (25). Similarly, a T354A mutant of $O s \mathrm { C A X 1 }$ may increase $\mathrm { M n ^ { 2 + } }$ transport without altering $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport (8). However, the IRT1 and OsCAX1 studies utilized yeast growth assays to infer transport function, and thus the kinetic changes in these transporters can only be inferred.

The role of histidines can vary for different transporters and can also depend on the position of the residue within the protein sequence. For some channel proteins such as the guard cell inward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel, KST1, and the cardiac pacemaker channel NCN2, the histidine residues appear to be involved in a pH-sensing mechanism (26, 27). In the sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ cotransporter, SUC1, a histidine residue is implicated in substrate recognition and directly in the transport reaction (28). In human $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /peptide cotransporters, two different histidines play two different roles; one conserved histidyl residue appears to be important for translocation of protons (29), whereas the second seems to be responsible for the recognition of transportable peptide substrates (11). Although these are only some examples, such a diverse role of histidine residues is not surprising; histidine is capable of forming intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds. These bonds can have a variety of effects on the protein, from inducing conformational changes and changes in pore size to influencing activity and transport of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ and other ions (12).

This site-directed mutagenesis study will help future crystallography studies to define the quaternary structure of CAX1 and other $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /cation exchangers. The ability to manipulate the metal transport activity and selectivity of CAX transporters through simple mutations, as has been demonstrated in this study, holds promise that plants can be custom-engineered to become metal accumulators, enhancing characteristics needed when selecting plants to be employed as phytoremediators.
