The aim of this study was to characterize the role of histidine residues in the translocation of metal ions in the Arabidopsis CAX1 transporter. Like other CAXs from a variety of different organisms, analysis of the 463-amino acid sequence suggests that the protein has 11 TMs (Fig. 1A). CAX1 has an acidic motif in the cytosolic loop between TM6 and TM7 and repetitive domains between TM3 and TM4 and between TM8 and TM9 of 36 residues, 14 of which are identical (repeats c-1 and c-2 (8)). There are seven histidine residues in the CAX1 polypeptide at positions 35, 210, 259, 338, 412, 443, and 446. We initially generated a H35A variant of CAX1 to determine whether this would disrupt the autoinhibitory domain. Previously, we showed that the N-terminal domain (the first 36 amino acids) of CAX1 inhibits the ion transport activity in yeast assays (17). We cloned the H35A CAX1 open reading frame into a high copy yeast expression plasmid and expressed this plasmid in a yeast strain deficient in vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transporters and lacking functional calcineurin (5, 21). This strain (K667) lacks the endogenous vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -ATPase PMC1 and vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } /$ $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ antiporter VCX1 and thus is defective in vacuolar $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport, making it unable to grow on high $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ media such as $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ C a C l _ { 2 } }$ (21). The H35A mutant of CAX1 remained autoinhibited when expressed in yeast (unable to grow on the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -containing media; data not shown). For the remainder of our studies, we used a truncated CAX1 (sCAX1) that removed the first 36 residues from the full-length cDNA (CAX1). High level expression of sCAX1 suppresses the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -sensitive phenotype of K667 cells. When the six sCAX1 mutants (H210A, H259A, H338A, H412A, H443A, and H446A) were similarly expressed in K667 cells on $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -containing media, only the H338A mutant showed an altered phenotype compared with sCAX1. In H338A-expressing K667 cells, the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -sensitive phenotype was not suppressed, highlighting the importance of this residue in the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport of CAX1 (Fig. 1C). To demonstrate that the changes in transport were not due to alterations in protein expression or stability, we generated a c-myc tagged version of H338A and several of the other histidine mutants, and the tags were expressed in K667 cells. These tagged transporters retained the same growth phenotypes as the original sCAX1 variants. Immunoblotting of the crude membrane fractions prepared from the various CAX1 mutant expressing yeast cells demonstrated approximately equal accumulation of the tagged protein (Fig. $_ { 1 D }$ ; data not shown).

We confirmed the differences in calcium sensitivity of the mutants by measuring $^ { 4 5 } \mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ uptake activity using isolated membrane vesicles. In this system, the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient across yeast vacuolar membrane vesicles was generated by activation of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase. The vesicles of sCAX1-expressing cells took up $^ { 4 5 } \mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ from the medium in a pH- and time-dependent manner for up to $1 0 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ (Fig. 2, sCAX1). The accumulated $^ { 4 5 } \mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ was released after the addition of the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ ionophore A23187 (Fig. 2, $1 2 \mathrm { m i n }$ ). In the absence of ATP or in the presence of gramicidin, a protonophore that dissipates the $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient (6), no such activity was detected. Membrane vesicles of yeast cells expressing an empty vector or H338A had negligible activity (Fig. 2). These results corroborate that sCAX1 but not H338A could function as a $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } / H ^ { + } } }$ exchanger in yeast.

The $\mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ residue of CAX1 is part of the c-2 repeat that contains the consensus sequence GNAAE $\mathrm { H } X _ { 6 } \mathrm { A X D } X _ { 2 } \mathrm { L G } X _ { 3 } \mathrm { G S } .$ $X _ { 2 } \mathrm { Q } X _ { 3 } \mathrm { F } X$ found in various CAX transporters (Fig. 1B). This region has been proposed to function as a cation selectivity filter (8). In order to determine further the importance of $\mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ , this residue was changed to all possible amino acids by site-directed mutagenesis (Table I) (16), and yeast cells expressing these variants of sCAX1 were tested on a variety of media containing different metals. Yeast cells expressing 3 of the $1 9 \ \mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ variants and the wild type sCAX1 demonstrated tolerance to $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { C a C l _ { 2 } }$ . The cells expressing the wild type sCAX1 were the most tolerant to $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ in the media, but $\mathrm { H 3 3 8 N > H 3 3 8 Q > H 3 3 8 K }$ were all able to grow at low levels of $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ (Table II). To confirm the yeast growth phenotypes on $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ -containing media, we measured $^ { 4 5 } \mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ transport activity directly. Membranes isolated from yeast expressing the H338N mutant demonstrated ${ \sim } 2 5 \%$ of the $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport activity when compared with $\mathrm { H i s ^ { 3 3 8 } }$ -expressing cells (Fig. 2). Because of the limited sensitivity of the transport assay, we were unable to reproducibly detect $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ transport activity in the H338Qand H338K-expressing cells.

Yeast cells expressing the same four constructs (sCAX1, H338N, H338Q, and H338K) also conferred tolerance to $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ (Fig. 3 and data not shown). Vector controls and strains expressing other CAX transporters will not grow well in media containing 2 or $3 \ \mu \mathrm { M } \ \mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ (data not shown). Furthermore, ion competition studies suggest that sCAX1 is capable of transporting both $\mathrm { { C a ^ { 2 + } } }$ and $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ (6), discounting the possibility that other metal ions transported by CAX1 produce this metal tolerance.

To investigate further the difference in metal tolerance of H338N-expressing cells as compared with sCAX1, we studied metal-dependent $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -transport in isolated membrane vesicles from yeast vacuoles. The ability of H338N-expressing yeast cells to confer higher $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ and $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ tolerance suggested a greater transport capability of this mutant for these metals. Quinacrine fluorescence recovery was used to monitor the dissipation of a preset transmembrane $\mathrm { p H }$ gradient (generated by activation of the vacuolar $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase), following the addition of different metal ions. For both $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ and $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ ions, H338N demonstrated a higher metal $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -dependent transport activity than that measured in sCAX1 (Fig. 4, A and $B$ ). Other metal ions tested, including $\mathrm { N i ^ { 2 + } }$ , $\mathrm { C o ^ { 2 + } }$ , and $\mathrm { M n ^ { 2 + } }$ , showed no detectable $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -dependent transport activity in either sCAX1 or the H338N-expressing cells, confirming the growth phenotype observed on these metals (Fig. 5; data not shown). Furthermore, no $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ - nor $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ -dependent $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ transport was measured in the K667 vector control strain confirming that metal transport required the presence of sCAX1 (data not shown).

Michaelis-Menten kinetic analysis of the data showed that increased metal transport in the H338N-expressing yeast cells was a result of a decrease in the $K _ { m }$ value for the metals with little or no change in the $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ values. The $K _ { m }$ values for $\mathrm { C d ^ { 2 + } }$ decreased from a value of $2 3 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ in sCAX1 to a value of $1 8 7 \ \mu \mathrm { M }$ in the H338N mutant, whereas the $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ values increased slightly from $1 5 0 \% F \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 } { \mathrm { m g } ^ { - 1 } }$ protein to $\bar { 1 } 6 4 \% F \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { m g } ^ { - 1 }$ protein (Fig. 6A). In the case of $\mathrm { Z n ^ { 2 + } }$ , the $K _ { m }$ values decreased from a value of $2 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ in sCAX1 to a value of $1 6 2 \mu \mathrm { M }$ in H338N, whereas the $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ values showed little change; from $1 4 4 \% F$ $\mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { m g } ^ { - 1 }$ protein in sCAX1 to $1 4 9 \% F \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { m g } ^ { - 1 }$ protein in H338N (Fig. 6B).

$\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /cation antiporter activity has been described in numerous plant species and on several membranes, including the vacuolar, plasma, and chloroplast thylakoid membranes (Schumaker and Sze, 1985; Blumwald and Poole, 1986; Kasai and Muto, 1990; Ettinger et al., 1999; Shaul et al., 1999). This study was carried out to investigate the diversity of the genes that may confer these activities in plants. This study reports the identification and partial characterization of an Arabidopsis CAX gene, CAX4, which has greater than $5 0 \%$ identity to the previously characterized $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter CAX1. CAX4 has extensive sequence homology with all the previously characterized $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ antiporters (Ueoka-Nakanishi et al., 1999, 2000; Hirschi, 2001). The expression pattern of CAX4 in plants suggests that this gene is expressed at levels lower than CAX1, CAX2, or CAX3. Like the metal transporter CAX2, CAX4 RNA levels were not induced by exogenous ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al., 2000). Like CAX3 and CAX1, CAX4 levels increase with some ion imbalances (Fig. 2; $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ , and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment). Although the induction of CAX4 after these stimuli is less than 2-fold, this infers that CAX4 may be capable of adjusting specific cytosolic ion concentrations.

CAX4 appeared to be highly expressed in yeast and N-terminal HA-tagged versions of CAX4 localized at the yeast vacuole (Fig. 4). Furthermore, the plant vacuolar membrane location of CAX4 was shown by N-terminal HA-tagged CAX4 in tobacco cells (Fig. 5). This is a useful system for morphologically identifying the localization of proteins, although it should be noted that, in this experiment, the HA:CAX4 fusion protein was expressed under artificial conditions. The HA-tag was observed predominantly in the vacuolar membrane and not in the plasma membrane or nuclear envelope. This distribution was confirmed in immunoblot experiments and is consistent with the expression of sGFP-VCAX1 in mung bean (UeokaNakanishi et al., 2000).

Conceivably, the N terminus could target the CAX proteins to various membranes in yeast and plants, and the HA-tag or other modifications could perturb intracellular targeting and cause the transporters to localize by default to the vacuolar membrane. Several observations suggest that this is not the case. (a) Expression of chimeric constructs containing the N terminus of CAX3 fused to CAX1 suppress yeast mutants defective in vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport (J.K. Pittman and K.D. Hirschi, unpublished data). This strongly implies that the CAX3 N terminus is not localizing proteins to a membrane other than the vacuolar membrane. (b) Removal of the N terminus of CAX3 or CAX4 does not allow strong suppression of the vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport defects. This suggests that the N terminus is not directing CAX3 or CAX4 to a membrane other than the vacuole for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. (c) Expression of the full-length vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } /$ Ca2 transporter from mung bean, VCAX1, suppresses yeast mutants defective in vacuolar Ca2 transport. Given that the $_ \mathrm { N }$ terminus of VCAX1 is similar to CAX1, CAX2, CAX3, and CAX4, it is unlikely that this sequence targets the mung bean transporter to the vacuolar membrane and the Arabidopsis proteins are being targeted to a different membrane.

The CAX4 gene product does not suppress yeast defects in vacuolar $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. However, CAX4 expression weakly suppressed the $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitivity of an IRT1 harboring strain. Although this suppression was not strong, it suggests that CAX4 functions in providing $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance in this strain, indicating that CAX4 may transport $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ . The lack of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activity of CAX4 in yeast resembles CAX3 (Shigaki and Hirschi, 2000). Expression of CAX4 N-terminal truncations or CAX4 chimeric constructs containing the CAX1 ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ domain both very weakly suppress the yeast vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport defects. This suppression consists of only a few isolated colonies growing on the Ca2 containing media (Fig. 6A). When these two alterations are combined, expression of the chimeric CAX4 constructs strongly suppressed the yeast mutations. From these observations, it appears that removal of the $_ \mathrm { N }$ terminus or alterations of the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ domain alone are insufficient for high levels of CAX4 mediated ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. Juxtaposed with these observations was the finding that N-terminal amino acid additions alone were sufficient to mediate CAX4, CAX3, or CAX1 $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in yeast (Fig. 7). This suggests that repositioning of the $_ \mathrm { N }$ terminus relative to the native $\cot 2 +$ domain of CAX3 and CAX4 is sufficient to mediate $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport.

Most CAX genes appear to be expressed in all tissues. The biological significance of the fact that truncated forms of CAX1 and CAX2 can suppress yeast mutants defective in vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport is not immediately clear. A truncated version of CAX3 cannot suppress this phenotype, whereas truncated CAX4 variants weakly suppress the phenotype; however, both CAX3 and CAX4 can suppress this phenotype if N-terminal extensions are present (Fig. 7). Thus, CAX3 and CAX4 contain the necessary components to drive yeast vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport; however, we must now address the questions of how and when these transporters function as vacuolar ${ \mathsf { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters in plants.

Initial experiments utilized N. tabacum variety KY160 and the 35S promoter to drive expression of selected CAX genes. As shown in Table 1, maximal $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in isolated root-tonoplast, $\mathbf { M g A T P }$ -energized vesicles (after $2 3 \mathrm { m i n }$ post-addition of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ ) was found to be higher than that with vector control derived vesicles in all CAX variants tested. The $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport were also elevated in most cases. HA-sCAX1 is an $\mathbf { N }$ -terminal truncated form of CAX1 fused with the HA epitope at its N-terminus, which has been shown not to alter sCAX1 $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity (Pittman and Hirschi 2001). In agreement with a previous study (Hirschi et al. 2000), sCAX2 (N-terminal truncated CAX2) -expressing tobacco plants displayed strong root-tonoplast $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activities. The CAX3 is a full-length cDNA that was originally isolated as a homolog of CAX1 from the Arabidopsis genome. Preliminary analysis indicated that CAX3 did not signiWcantly alter ion-metal sensitivity when expressed in both wild type and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitive yeast mutant cells- (Shigaki and Hirschi 2000). However, the N-terminal addition of the HA epitope to CAX3 (HA-CAX3) modestly suppressed a yeast vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter deWcient mutant phenotype (Cheng et al. 2002). We note that in the case of sCAX11, sCAX11 line (2–2) and sCAX11 line (2–1) were high and low expressing lines, respectively. Results presented here demonstrate that all $C A X -$ encoded transporters studied are capable of transporting multiple divalent cations in planta.

Results of Table 1 suggest that increasing total CAX (endogenous tobacco CAXs plus the engineered Arabidopsis CAX) transporters in root tonoplast of transgenic plants increases divalent cation transport capability in root cell vacuoles. Six homologs of CAX genes have been detected in tobacco, thus far (A. Hayes et al., personal communication), but transport properties of these have not yet been studied. Results shown in Table 1 also indicate that transporters encoded by various CAX genes tested are not highly selective for the ions tested. However, some variation in e.g., $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ versus $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport was observed (Table 1). From these results, CAX4 and CAX2 appear to be relatively eYcient in enhancing root tonoplast $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. Since earlier CAX4 was found to show selectivity for $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in yeast (Cheng et al. 2002), and to be more highly expressed in roots (Hirschi et al. 2000), we chose CAX4 for further study using root-selective promoters (see below). Expression of CAX4 in KY160 and CAX2 in the variety KY14, both driven by the 35S promoter, produced similar results in vesicle transport assays (Fig. 2). As shown in Fig. 2, vector controls (hereafter as controls) with both KY160 and KY14 were similar. With KY160 expressing CAX4 driven by the 35S promoter (hereafter as line 35SCAX4 -6 and line 35SCAX4 -8) maximal $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport was increased over control by ${ \sim } 3 4 \%$ (Fig. 2a–35SCAX4 line 6 not shown). In KY14 expressing CAX2 driven by the 35S promoter (hereafter as line 35SCAX2 -2), maximal $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport was increased over control by about $5 3 \%$ (Fig. 2b). Initial rates of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in both 35SCAX4 and 35SCAX2 were somewhat increased over that in controls. Equivalent amounts of tonoplast vesicle protein were used in these measurements. From this point forward, all subsequent experiments were made using the variety KY14.

Thus, expression of CAX4 and CAX2 under the direction of the 35S promoter altered the kinetics of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. These changes occur both at the transport saturation level (maximal transport) and initial rates observed.

Next, we expressed CAX4 in KY14 using three promoters reported to be root-selective in plants. We observed that mannopine synthase (mas2) promoter from Agrobacterium tumefaciens (Ni et al. 1996) and the Arabidopsis thaliana late embryogenesis gene promoter (Atem6, Gauber et al. 1993) did not drive strong expression of CAX4 (produced only weak Northern signals, not shown) and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in vesicles from these plants were similar to controls (not shown). In contrast, a sub-genomic promoter (FS3) from the FMV, reported to be root-selective in tobacco (Bhattacharyya et al. 2002), showed relatively strong expression and high root-selectivity $( F S 3 { \mathrel { \mathop : } } { \mathrel { : } } C A X 4 .$ -expressing lines, hereafter as FSCAX4 lines). As shown in Fig. 3a, lines FSCAX4 ¡6, ¡24, and $- 3 1$ each had a copy number of one, and demonstrated low-to-medium/high-to-high expression in roots as assayed by Northern analysis. While CAX4 was expressed in roots of lines 24 and 31, none was found in leaves (Fig. 3b). Root-tonoplast cation transport was monitored in these lines and compared to control lines (Fig. 4). With increasing CAX4 expression (line $3 1 \geq 2 4 > > 6$ , respectively), the initial rate of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport increased (Fig. 4b–d, respectively) to exceed that of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in control (not shown). We had not previously observed a higher initial rate of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ over $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in root tonoplast vesicles in any non-transgenic or transgenic line. Also, the maximal transport of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ was highest in lines 24 and 31, which showed extraordinary $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ (and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ ) transport characteristics. We made no attempt to compare the relative promoter strengths of the 35S versus the FS3 promoter in these experiments. Furthermore, vesicles prepared from plants of diVerent age and growth-environment history are found to vary in their transport levels. In each experimental set (e.g., 35SCAX4 -8 and its control), plants were grown together to the same growth stage, and vesicles were prepared at the same time; however, quantitative diVerences in transport properties of vesicles are observed in some controls from diVerent experiment sets. We note here that the 35S promoter has been shown by GUS reporter experiments to be somewhat root and stem selective in tobacco (JeVerson et al. 1987). So, transgene expression using this promoter, generally considered to be a constitutive promoter, is shown to be root/stem-predominant. But, its leaf expression appears to be more pronounced than that of the FS3 promoter (JeVerson et al. 1987, and here). It was not possible to estimate the levels of AtCAX2 and AtCAX4 expression relative to endogenous tobacco CAXes because stringency used in Northern analyses here for CAX4 (Fig. 3) and earlier for CAX2 (Hirschi et al. 2000) was such that endogenous CAX transcripts were not detected.

The extent of acridine orange recovery (which represents maximal cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchange) and the initial rates of cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ exchange for control and FSCAX4 lines are illustrated in Fig. 5. As shown in Fig. 5a, the magnitude of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z _ { \mathbf { n } } { } ^ { 2 + }$ transport increased in lines 24 and 31 versus control and line 6, which had very low CAX4 expression. In contrast, maximum Ca2+ and Mn2+ exchange were not greatly altered. Initial rates of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { \bar { 2 } + }$ transport in FSCAX4 lines 24 and 31 were substantially higher than those of control and line 6 (Fig. 5b). We interpret these results to suggest that root speciWc expression of CAX4 results in higher and more ${ \bar { \mathrm { C d } } } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ selective transport in root tonoplast.

Alternatively, CAX4 may preferentially function in root tissues. Or, CAX4 may be more stable through posttranscriptional regulation, as has been shown for other ion transporters, such as IRT1, which is more active and stable in roots than shoots under ion stress (Connolly et al. 2002). Possibly, expression of CAX4 may shift ion selectivity of the cumulative tonoplast divalent-positivecation transport towards $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and away from $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ .

The cation selectivity of transport in CAX4 -expressing plants may be observed by comparing ratios of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C } \dot { \mathrm { d } } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z } \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in control versus CAX4 expressing lines. Table 2 lists the $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ratios observed in these studies. These results indicate that $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport selectivity is increased by about $3 7 \%$ in 35SCAX2-B versus control, but is increased more (by about $5 5 \%$ over control) in FSCAX4 lines 24 and 31. In contrast, $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ ratios are similar, suggesting that factors responsible for increasing ion transport selectivity do not distinguish between $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , but can distinguish $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ . This point is also seen from the $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ratio, which is similar to that of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ . The $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ ratio was also increased substantially in FSCAX4 line 31, but transport of this ion as measured in this assay is relatively low, making it diYcult to fully interpret this result.

In yeast studies, CAXs do not appear to predominantly transport one divalent cation versus another (Shigaki et al. 2003). However, earlier biochemical studies were able to distinguish between $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in root tonoplast proteoliposomes isolated from tonoplast vesicles of non-transformed oat seedlings and mature tobacco plants (Koren’kov et al. 2002). Reconstitution of root tonoplast vesicles resulted in complete loss of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, but retention of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport. Indeed, speciWc transport activity for $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ increased, reXecting reduction of vesicle total protein during reconstitution. To repeat, this phenomenon was observed for root tonoplast isolated from young, germinating oat seedling roots and root tonoplast from mid-age tobacco plants; so, it may reXect a general characteristic of tonoplast. Results of reconstitution studies suggested that either $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ selective enzymes were lost on reconstitution while $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ selective enzymes were retained, or perhaps $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ binding to a single transporter was altered while binding of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ was not. $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport were not monitored in these experiments. Also, in studies using oat root tonoplast vesicles, the inhibitor verapamil showed a much greater eVect on $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport than on $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport (Gonzalez et al. 1999). Verapamil is a phenylalkalamine type, so called $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ channel blocker that non-competitively inhibits binding of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ to channels (Striessing et al. 1998). Results of assays to test the ability of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ versus $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ to protect against verapimil inhibition of antiporter activity were consistent with separate, semi-selective transporters predominantly transporting $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (Koren’kov et al. 2002). Recently, Shigaki et al. showed that site directed mutagenesis of a gene encoding a CAX eYcient in transporting $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (sCAX1M) results in decreased $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity and enhancement of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity (Shigaki et al. 2005). Results presented here showing that enhancing CAX4 or CAX2 in root tonoplast increases tonoplast $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport add to the above evidence which suggests that individual CAX transporters may favor, to some extent, transport of one ion over another (e.g., $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ versus $\mathbf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ ). But, ultimately, answering the question of ion selectivity of CAX must await study of the ion preferences of isolated, individual CAX enzymes.

As shown in Fig. 6, $N .$ tabacum, cultivar KY14 seedlings of FSCAX4-31 and 35SCAX2 -2 lines when grown for 21 days with $0 . 0 2 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulated signiWcantly more $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ in roots than did respective control seedlings. Similar results were shown earlier for 35SCAX2 expressing $N .$ tabacum, cultivar KY160 grown for 50 days with $0 . 1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al. 2000). Thus, increased $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transport capability shown here for root tonoplast vesicles from 35SCAX2-2 and FSCAX4-31 is consistent with increased $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation in seedling roots of these lines. Shoot $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ was not diVerent from that of respective controls (Fig. 6). Nor was shoot $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ signiWcantly changed in earlier studies with 35SCAX2 expressing KY160 tobacco grown with $0 . 1 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al. 2000). We speculate that perhaps the level of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ exposure (concentration $\times$ time) used in these hydroponic experiments exceeds a level that allows root retention and reduction of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ translocated to the shoot. Preliminary results with 35SCAX2-2 grown in the Weld (no $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ amendment to the soil) indicate that 35SCAX2-2 plants accumulate less $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ in leaves than control, and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ levels in leaves was about $3 \%$ of that shown in Fig. 6 (unpublished). Further study is needed to conWrm this observation. Perhaps the Wnding here that both root and shoot $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ of solution cultured seedlings are higher in FSCAX4-31 and its control than in 35SCAX2-2 and its control is due to the fact that each pair was grown with $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ in a separate container. To summarize the results shown here, higher $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation in seedling roots of CAX4 and CAX2 lines versus respective controls is consistent with observed higher $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation characteristics of root tonoplast vesicles prepared from these lines.

Whatever the mechanistic basis of enhanced root tonoplast $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity in 35SCAX4 lines and even more enhanced $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity in root tonoplast of FSCAX4 lines as observed here, our results suggest that CAX4 (and also CAX2) expression in root tonoplast may serve the goal of retaining $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ taken up from the soil in root vacuoles so as to reduce its translocation to and accumulation in shoot tissues where it can contribute to the human $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ body burden. Experiments are underway to determine inorganic cation (and anion) accumulation, and growth characteristics of seedlings and Weld plants exposed to low $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ levels (as occur in agricultural soils). Also, grafting experiments are underway to determine if FSCAX4 root stocks retain $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ in roots to lower $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation to scions of non-transformed plants.

The vacuolar sequestration of metals is an important metal tolerance mechanism in plants. The Arabidopsis thaliana vacuolar transporters CAX1 and CAX2 were originally identified in a Saccharomyces cerevisiae suppression screen as $\bar { \mathrm { C a } } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters. CAX2 has a low affinity for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ but can transport other metals including $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ . Here we demonstrate that unlike cax1 mutants, CAX2 insertional mutants caused no discernable morphological phenotypes or alterations in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity. However, cax2 lines exhibited a reduction in vacuolar $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport and, like cax1 mutants, reduced V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase (V-ATPase) activity. Analysis of a CAX2 promoter $\beta$ -glucoronidase (GUS) reporter gene fusion confirmed that CAX2 was expressed throughout the plant and strongly expressed in flower tissue, vascular tissue and in the apical meristem of young plants. Heterologous expression in yeast identified an N-terminal regulatory region in CAX2, suggesting that Arabidopsis contains multiple cation $\mathrm { ~ H ~ } ^ { + }$ antiporters with shared regulatory features. Furthermore, despite significant variations in morphological and biochemical phenotypes, cax1 and cax2 lines both significantly alter V-ATPase activity, hinting at coordinate regulation among transporters driven by $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ gradients and the V-ATPase.

Cation $/ \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchangers (CAXs) mediate vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ sequestration and are critical for maintaining cytosolic $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ homeostasis in plants. Arabidopsis CAX1, a member of the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { C }$ ation Antiporter (CaCA) superfamily, features a modular architecture comprising two pseudosymmetrical domains separated by a cytosolic loop called the acidic motif. CAX1 is also regulated by a cytosolic N-terminal autoinhibitory domain. To define the structural basis of CAX1 activity, we characterized truncated constructs of the N-terminal half of CAX1, comprising a 6-transmembrane (TM) module lacking the autoinhibitory domain (½N-sCAX1), using yeast complementation, structural modeling, and protein interaction studies. The $\% \mathrm { N }$ -sCAX1 monomer folded into a stable topology but it failed to interact with itself or with full-length CAX1, or confer transport activity. Functional reconstitution required tethering two ½N-sCAX1 modules via the acidic motif or removal of TM1, which restored partial $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in yeast. Protein interaction assays revealed that the autoinhibitory domain contributes to ½N-CAX1 dimerization, while TM1 interferes with complex assembly. Structural models demonstrated that correct alignment of the conserved GNxxE motif across ½N-sCAX1 monomers, either by artificial tethering or potentially by higher order hexameric oligomerization, is essential to reconstruct a functional $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -binding pocket. These findings show that CAX1 functionality depends on specific topological constraints and modular interactions that guide formation of CAX1 halves. Our results highlight how architectural features such as TM1 and the autoinhibitory domain regulate transporter assembly and activity, offering insight into CaCA biogenesis and providing a framework for engineering transporters with tailored functional properties.


## Key message


We dissect the structure–function mechanisms of the Arabidopsis vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter CAX1 by analyzing its N-terminal half. Modular fragments alone are inactive but can assemble into tethered dimers that restore $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, revealing structural constraints on activity. The study unveils fresh perspectives on the evolutionary dynamics and functional diversity of CAXs, indicating broader implications for calcium transport across various organisms.

Agricultural soil contamination with heavy metals is one of the most widespread environmental issues which threatens the development and growth of plants and animals, as well as humans. Cd, as a non-essential and highly toxic element, can be released into the environment through human activities including agriculture, mining, textile and plastic manufacturing and the application of sewage sludge (Tamaddon and Hogland 1993; Wang et al. 2014). Moreover, absorption and accumulation of Cd into the crops owing to its solubility in irrigation water and mobility in the soil, interferes with many physiological and molecular processes of plants (Gzyl et al. 2015; Tang et al. 2012). A large body of evidence indicates the involvement of Cd in enzyme suppression, root and shoot growth inhibition, ions defciency, reduction in chlorophyll content and photosynthesis, as well as impairment of

cell division (Cui et al. 2017; Gzyl et al. 2015; Huang et al.   
2017b; Liu et al. 2009; Mohammad et al. 2009).

CAX genes encoding cation/proton exchangers play a crucial role in the sequestration of cations such as Mn, Na, Li, and Cd, as well as Ca, into the vacuole using proton gradients provided by $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ pumps such as $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase or $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (Korenkov et al. 2007; Pittman 2011; Shigaki and Hirschi 2006; Shigaki et al. 2010; Zhao et al. 2009). Six CAX genes have been identifed so far in the Arabidopsis genome (Shigaki and Hirschi 2006). CAX3, a tonoplastlocalized transporter, has been shown to participate in plant responses to excess levels of sodium and lithium and $\mathrm { p H }$ fuctuation (Zhao et al. 2008).

Many studies revealed the important roles of CAX genes in the plant response to various stresses. Brassica rapa CAX1a TILLING (Targeting Induced Local Lesions In Genomes) mutants grown in diferent Ca doses, exhibited lower total chlorophyll, higher accumulations of Ca, $\mathbf { M g }$ and Fe, as well as higher ROS levels (Navarro-Leon et al. 2018). Heterologous expression of AtCAX1 in tobacco and of SsCAX1 (Suaeda salsa) in Arabidopsis increased salt sensitivity (Han et al. 2011; Mei et al. 2007). Arabidopsis knock-out mutant cax1-1 showed a dramatic decrease in fresh and dry weight of shoots compared to wild-type in response to 3 weeks of waterlogging stress (Wang et al. 2016). Moreover, the reduction in primary root length and lateral root numbers in cax4 mutant and CAX4 RNAi Arabidopsis in response to auxin, Mn, and Cd have been reported (Mei et al. 2009). It has also been shown that the heterologous expression of N-terminally truncated AtCAX5 in K667 (a $\mathbf { C a / N i n }$ hypersensitive yeast mutant) can mediate Ca and Mn transport and confer Mn tolerance (Edmond et al. 2009).

In addition, the involvement of CAX genes in Cd tolerance has been demonstrated in several studies. Cd accumulation and transport in root tonoplast vesicles of tobacco have been shown to increase by heterologous expression of Arabidopsis CAX2 (Hirschi et al. 2000). The expression of SaCAX2 (Sedum alfredii), AtCAX2 and AtCAX4 in tobacco led to an increase in Cd tolerance, activity of tonoplast $\mathrm { { C a / H ^ { + } } }$ antiporter, and Cd accumulation, compared with control plants (Korenkov et al. 2007; Zhang et al. 2016). The Cd tolerance and content were enhanced in petunia expressing AtCAX1cd (CAX1 mutant) (Wu et al. 2011). The lower Cd tolerance was observed in the Arabidopsis cax1-1 mutant (Baliardini et al. 2015), and the over-expression of AhCAX1 (Arabidopsis halleri) promoted Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis (Ahmadi et al. 2018). Furthermore, a possible role of NtCAX3 in Cd tolerance has been postulated in transgenic tobacco that shows higher Cd tolerance (Bahmani et al. 2017, 2019; Lee and Hwang 2015c).

Ca concentration in the cell can be adjusted through the combined activity of various Ca pumps, channels and exchangers. The plasma membrane-localized Arabidopsis

ACA8 and ACA10 (auto-inhibited type IIB Ca-ATPase) have been shown to perform the function of expelling Ca from the cytosol using a K616 yeast strain lacking the Ca transporters PMC1 and PMR1 (Bonza et al. 2004; Schiott and Palmgren 2005). Regarding Ca importers, atcngc1 knockout Arabidopsis showed a slightly lower Ca accumulation in shoots compared to control plants (Ma et al. 2006). AtCNGC10 antisense lines also showed a lower Ca content in roots and shoots than that of wild-type, implying the involvement of AtCNGC10 in Ca uptake and translocation (Guo et al. 2010). The involvement of the MCA1 in Ca uptake has been shown by expressing MCA1 in yeast (Nakagawa et al. 2007). Moreover, MCA1-overexpressing transgenic Arabidopsis plants exhibited more cytosolic Ca accumulation than both wild-type and mca1-null mutants under moderate hypo-osmotic stress (Nakagawa et al. 2007). Expression of MCA1 in the plasma membrane of Xenopus laevis oocytes showed an induction in inward currents of Ca after hypotonic stimulation (Furuichi et al. 2012).

Ca has been demonstrated to regulate a variety of cellular functions, plant growth and development under diferent stress conditions, and to play an important role in plant signal transduction (Ahmad et al. 2015; Shi et al. 2014). Moreover, the Ca ion is able to infuence Cd absorption, translocation and accumulation, likely through uptake competition with Cd (Eller and Brix 2015; Huang et al. 2017a). Additionally, several studies have emphasized the importance of cross-talk between Ca and ROS, and suggested that regulation of ROS formation for the reduction of Cd-induced oxidative damages is one of the plant protection strategies by Ca (Mazars et al. 2010; Yuan et al. 2018). For example, exogenous application of Ca has been shown to mitigate the deleterious efect of Cd stress in chamomile, rice and mustard by reducing ROS production, thereby suppressing oxidative damage (Ahmad et al. 2015; Farzadfar et al. 2013; Srivastava et al. 2015).

Ca also can participate in the activation of antioxidant enzymes, which is required for reducing the oxidative burst in Zoysia japonica under drought stress conditions $\mathrm { { X u } }$ et al. 2013). Yang and coworkers reported that Ca increases the activities of antioxidant enzymes, aiding adaptation during heat stress in peanuts (Yang et  al. 2013). Similarly, other researchers showed that exogenous application of Ca induced GPX (glutathione peroxidase) and CAT (catalase) activity in the rice seedlings under arsenic stress conditions (Rahman et  al. 2015), as well as SOD (superoxide dismutase) and GST (glutathione sulfur transferase) activity in atrazine-treated Pennisetum (Erinle et al. 2016).

Given the role of CAX genes in Ca transport and the relationship between ROS generation and stress-induced Ca, the potential role of CAXs in regulating ROS levels under stress conditions has been considered. In this regard, lower Cd tolerance was ascribed to higher ROS accumulation in the Arabidopsis cax1-1 mutant (Baliardini et al. 2015). The over-expression of AhCAX1 promoted Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis, while AhCAX1-RNAi lines showed remarkable ROS accumulation in response to Cd in low Ca conditions (Ahmadi et al. 2018).

In our previous studies, we found that the expression of AtCAX3 and NtCAX3 was greatly enhanced in Cd-tolerant transgenic Arabidopsis and tobacco (Bahmani et al. 2017, 2019; Lee and Hwang 2015c). Therefore, these results raised the question of whether CAX3 can participate in Cd tolerance. To address this, we investigated the Cd tolerance and accumulation, ROS and Ca levels, and anti-oxidative enzyme activity in AtCAX3- and NtCAX3-expressing Arabidopsis. The presented results suggest that CAX3 is involved in promoting Cd tolerance by decreasing ROS generation via activation of anti-oxidative enzymes through enhancing the Ca level.

## The Expression of CAX1 Is Induced Transiently in Leaves in Response to Low Temperature


RCI4 was isolated by screening a cDNA library prepared from cold-acclimated $( 4 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ , 7 days) etiolated seedlings of Arabidopsis with a subtracted cDNA probe enriched in cold-induced transcripts. Comparison of the nucleotide sequence of RCI4 with sequences available in the databases revealed $100 \%$ identity with CAX1, a gene that encodes a vacuolar $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (Hirschi et al., 1996; Cheng et al., 2003).

The expression of CAX1 in response to low temperature was first characterized in etiolated seedlings of Arabidopsis. Because CAX1 is a component of a gene family (Maser et al., 2001), a specific CAX1 probe was obtained to avoid crosshybridizations. The specificity of this probe was determined by DNA gel blot analysis (data not shown). RNA gel blot hybridizations indicated that CAX1 expression was induced transiently in etiolated seedlings, reaching a maximum level after 12 to $^ { 2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ of cold treatment (Figure 1A). Expression analysis performed in Arabidopsis plants showed that CAX1 transcripts also were induced transiently in leaves when exposed to low temperature (Figure 1B). To determine the expression pattern of CAX1 in different organs of Arabidopsis, total RNA from roots, leaves, stems, flowers, and siliques from unstressed or stressed $( 4 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ , 24 h) plants were subjected to RNA gel blot hybridizations with the specific CAX1 probe. Results revealed that under unstressed conditions, CAX1 transcripts were present at low levels in all organs analyzed. In response to low temperature, CAX1 transcripts did not experience apparent changes in stems and flowers, whereas they increased in leaves and decreased in roots and siliques (Figure 1C). A probe that recognizes the KIN1 gene from Arabidopsis, the expression of which is induced by cold, dehydration, high-salt, and ABA treatments (Kurkela and Borg-Franck, 1992), was used as a positive control for low-temperature treatments. These data indicate that the expression of CAX1 is induced specifically in leaves in response to low temperature and that this induction is regulated transiently.


## CAX1 Expression Is Regulated Negatively by Dehydration and Not Affected by High Salt or ABA


Because many cold-inducible genes also are responsive to exogenous ABA and osmotic stresses (Thomashow, 1999), the effect of dehydration, high salt, and ABA on CAX1 mRNA accumulation was analyzed. Given the expression of CAX1 in response to low temperature (see above), this study was performed in leaves. Although CAX1 transcript accumulation was unaffected by NaCl and ABA treatments, it was reduced notably below control levels by dehydration (Figure 2A). KIN1 was used as a positive control for these treatments.

To determine whether the regulation of CAX1 expression by cold and dehydration is mediated by ABA, the accumulation of corresponding mRNAs in response to both stresses was analyzed in ABA-deficient (aba1) and ABA-insensitive (abi1) mutants. Figure 2B shows that the expression of CAX1 in response to low temperature and dehydration was identical in the mutants and in the wild type. Thus, the regulation of CAX1 expression by low temperature and dehydration was not mediated by ABA. KIN1 was used as a positive control for these experiments.

Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L., formerly Lycopersicon esculentum Mill.) is an important agricultural commodity and is widely consumed worldwide; however, most tomatoes contain little calcium $( \mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } )$ . Uptake and translocation of cationic nutrients including $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in plants plays an essential role in physiological processes such as signal transduction, growth, and development (Flowers and Colmer 2008; Wang et al. 2006). Among them, $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ plays a fundamental role in plant membrane stability, cell wall stabilization, and cell integrity (Hirschi 2004). Two Arabidopsis $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter genes, CAX1 and CAX2, can function in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) mutants as vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters (Hirschi et al. 1996). The transport properties of CAX2 suggested the potential for broad substrate specificity including $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , whereas CAX1 appeared to be a specialized $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter. Subsequent studies have demonstrated that CAX2 can also transport metallic ions such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al. 2000; Pittman et al. 2004; Schaaf et al. 2002; Shigaki et al. 2003). To identify the domains that determine $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ specificity in CAX2, six CAX2 variants without the N-terminal autoinhibitory domain (i.e., without the first 42 amino acids) (sCAX2s) were constructed by replacing the regions of divergent sequence in CAX2 with the corresponding regions from CAX1 (Shigaki et al. 2003). When the sCAX2 variant genes were expressed in yeast mutants defective in vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport, the yeast strains expressing sCAX2A and sCAX2B exhibited diminished growth on the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ - containing media, and completely failed to suppress $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitivity (Shigaki et al. 2003). These results imply that, among the six $\mathrm { s } C A X 2$ variants, sCAX2A and $\ s C A X 2 B$ are preferred candidates to genetically engineer a robust crop for its moderate but more specific ability of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport and diminished ability to accumulate metals such as $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ . Indeed, potato tubers expressing sCAX2B contained $5 0 \mathrm { - } 6 5 \%$ more $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ than wild-type tubers although these plants are as vigorous as controls, and did not show any significant increase of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Kim et al. 2006). In contrast, the transgenic crops ectopically expressing sCAX1 displayed alterations in plant development and morphology, including increased incidence of blossomend rot (BER) and tip-burn symptoms despite the elevated $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ levels (Hirschi 1999; Park et al. 2004, 2005). Our primary focus here was to evaluate the potential for increasing the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ levels of tomato fruits through expression of a variant cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter sCAX2A which has not been characterized on a mode-of-action in plant, and to analyze its potential impact on plant growth and development. This study also suggests that modulation of CAX transporters could make an important contribution toward increasing the value of various agriculturally important crops.

Phylogenetic analysis of NIP-type aquaporins from prokaryota and eukaryota

Our phylogenetic analyses using 366 bacterial, archaeal and plant NIP-type MIPs showed that the major prokaryotic MIP groups, which are AQPZs, AQPMs, AQPNs and GLPFs, formed well supported clades (Fig. 1). Six major AQPN clades (I–VI) with a full node support were detected. Two of these AQPN clades do not encode F–A–A–R-type SFs but display a wide variety of SF residue combinations: AQPN-I is mainly composed of archaeal and AQPN-II of bacterial sequences (Fig. 1).

The remaining four AQPN clades are characterised by a predominant occurrence of F–A–A–R-type SFs. All plant NIP-type sequences as well as three bacterial AqpNs formed together the AQPN-III clade (Figs 1, S1). Within this clade, algal NIPs (KnNIP6;1 and KnMIP) can be clearly separated from the NIP-I, NIP-II, NIP-III groups and the F–A–A–Rtype NIPs of land plants (Figs 1, S1). Interestingly, the F–A– A–R-type NIPs of land plants cluster closest with the NIP-III group members, which are crucial for Si transport in seed plants.

AQPN-IV clade is formed by sequences deriving mainly from Firmicutes but also Proteobacteria that are F–A–A–R-type SFdominated (Fig. 1). The AQPN-V clade is exclusively formed by cyanobacterial sequences, which all encode F–A–A–R-type SFs (Fig. 1). The member-rich AQPN-VI clade is formed by sequences from various bacterial phyla either encoding F–A–A– R-type or an W–A–A–R-type SFs (Fig. 1).

Two additional MIP groups, AQPNx and AQPZx cluster apart from other AqpZ and AqpN-like sequences. These sequences derive from various different bacterial and archaeal species, and encode MIPs with very diverse SFs and form a phylogenetically loose cluster. The overall backbone of the phylogenetic tree is unresolved.

## Occurrence of F–A–A–R-type NIPs in land plants


The prevalence of F–A–A–R residues constituting the SF in bacterial AqpNs and in early diverging plant NIPs such as S. moellendorffii and $P .$ . patens suggests that the last common ancestor to the plant NIPs encoded a F–A–A–R-type SF. To study the frequency and evolution of this SF composition, we screened various plant genome databases for NIPs with this SF composition. We identified a NIP with an F–A–A–R-type SF in the genome of the charophyte Klebsormidium nitens and thereby discovered the presence of NIPs also in green algae (Fig. 1). This finding suggests that the HGT of an aqpN happened before plants invaded the land and associate with the estimation of Zardoya et al. (2002). Additionally, we found such F–A–A–R-type NIPs in liverwort (Marchantia polymorpha), moss (Sphagnum fallax) and fern (Salvinia cucullata and Adiantum capillus-veneris) taxa (Figs 1, 2). These findings closed the knowledge gap on the NIP lineage throughout the phylogeny from bacteria, green plants, over land plants to vascular plants. Seed plants, both gymnosperms and flowering plants, encode various NIPs with SFs typical for the NIP-I, NIP-II and NIP-III group. However, the F–A–A–R SF-group has not been identified in seed plants in any of the analysed genome-rich databases.


## Identification of F–A–A–R-type MIPs allowing studying the functional evolution of NIP-type aquaporins


We subjected several MIPs to further analyses to resolve the functional evolution of F–A–A–R-type MIPs from bacteria along the plant lineage. KrAqpN is found in the aerobic, filamentous, nonmotile, Gram-positive bacterium Ktedonobacter racemifer belonging to the Chloroflexi phylum from which an aqpN gene may have been transferred via a HGT to plants (Fig. 1). Moreover, this F–A–A–R SF-encoding aqpN is located in a typical ars operon (Fig. 2). The F–A–A–R SF-carrying KnNIP6;1 is encoded by the filamentous terrestrial alga $K .$ nitens, which belongs to the Charophyta green algae group from which all terrestrial plants, the Embryophyta, emerged (Hori et al., 2014). The name KnNIP6;1 was adopted according to a detailed phylogenetic analysis (U. Johanson, per. commun.: H. I. Anderberg & U. Johanson, unpublished). PpNIP5;1, PpNIP5;2, and $\mathrm { P p N I P } 5 ; 3$ are encoded by the moss $P .$ patens and represent members of the F–A–A–R-type NIPs of early land plant lineages.

## Bacterial, algal and moss F–A–A–R-type NIPs are permeable to arsenous acid and boric acid when expressed in Xenopus oocytes


We determined the transport activity for arsenous acid in oocytes expressing KrAqpN, KnNIP6;1, PpNIP5;1, PpNIP5;2, PpNIP5;3, or the positive control OsLsi1 (Ma et al., 2006).

Expression of all MIPs resulted in a significant increase in As transport activity compared to water-injected oocytes quantified via ICP-MS analysis (Fig. 3b).

The permeability to boric acid was tested in direct uptake assays into oocytes in the presence or the absence of MIP expression. AtNIP5;1 which is physiologically important for the uptake of B into Arabidopsis roots was used as a positive control (Takano et al., 2006). Quantification of B levels in oocytes showed that the bacterial, algae and moss MIPs significantly increased the B uptake over that of water-injected oocytes (Fig. 3c,d).

## F–A–A–R-type PpNIP5 isoforms partially rescue the boron deficiency phenotype of the Atnip5;1 knock-down mutant


To test whether plant F–A–A–R-type NIPs are functional metalloidoporins in plants and to have an experimentally independent confirmation of the B transport ability, we performed an in planta growth complementation assay. We transformed Atnip5;1 knock-down Arabidopsis lines with genetic constructs in which PpNIP5;1, PpNIP5;2 and PpNIP5;3 were cloned behind the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter sequence. The Atnip5;1 plants were unable to take up sufficient amounts of B from the soil substrate under our standard growth conditions, resulting in a strong B-deficiency phenotype (Fig. 5b). This growth deficit was complemented when the Atnip5;1 mutant was transformed with the native AtNIP5;1 cDNA (Fig. ${ 5 } \mathrm { b , c } )$ . Independent PpNIP5;1 and PpNIP5;2 expressing lines also significantly complemented the Atnip5;1 mutant growth phenotype (Fig. 5b,c) and had a significantly higher B uptake ability, indicated by the higher shoot B concentrations, than the Atnip5;1 knock-down mutants, unambiguously demonstrating their ability to facilitate the uptake of B into plant roots (Fig. 5d). However, the PpNIP5;1 and PpNIP5;2 expressing lines exhibited still slight B-deficiency symptoms when compared to the wild-type (Fig. 5b). It was previously observed that the expression of functional NIP5 isoforms or the AtNIP5;1pro:AtNIP5;1 construct do not fully restore the shoot B concentrations of Atnip5;1 mutants compared to the wildtype (Diehn et al., 2019). All generated PpNIP5;3 harbouring lines spliced the PpNIP5;3 mRNA resulting in a cDNA sequence which is not encoding a full-length MIP (Fig. S3). Accordingly, PpNIP5;3 expression failed to complement the growth of the Atnip5;1 mutant. In P. patens, PpNIP5s transcript abundances were not regulated in response to varying metalloid feeding and exposure levels (Fig. S4).

The metalloids boron (B) and silicon (Si) are fundamental for the development of vascular plants not only because they ensure proper differentiation, structural support and elasticity of plant cell walls, but also because they contribute to pathogen defence and general stress tolerance (Ma et al., 2006; Bienert & Chaumont, 2011). Consequently, corresponding transport mechanisms for these elements are essential for sufficient plant B and Si nutrition. Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs) mediate B and Si transport and thereby sustain growth, fertility and yield of terrestrial plants. NIPs belong to the major intrinsic protein (MIP) superfamily (also termed as aquaporins, AQPs), which comprises channels for the diffusion of small neutral and mostly polar molecules across various biological membranes in all kingdoms of life. MIP channels possess six transmembrane helices connected by five loops and the two termini facing the cytoplasm. The so-called aromatic/arginine (ar/R) constriction region acts as an MIP selectivity filter (SF) and comprises four amino acids of transmembrane helices 2 and 5 (positions R1 and R2) and loop E (positions R3 and R4) representing the narrowest part of the channel pore and forming a size exclusion barrier conferring selectivity to particular substrates (Murata et al., 2000).

Phylogenetic analyses revealed the existence of four phylogenetically well supported prokaryotic MIP clades (Finn et al., 2014; Finn & Cerd-a, 2015). These are aquaporin Z-like proteins (AqpZ), aquaporin M-like proteins (AqpM), glycerol uptake facilitator-like proteins (GlpF), and aquaporin N-like proteins (AqpN). AqpZ proteins permeate water, AqpMs both water and glycerol, and GlpFs water, glycerol, urea and metalloids (Fu et al., 2000; Jensen et al., 2001; Kozono et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2005). Bacterial AqpN channels have not been functionally characterised to date. Eukaryotic MIPs evolved from bacterial and/or archaeal ancestor isoforms (Pao et al., 1991; Park & Saier, 1996; Zardoya et al., 2002). MIPs of higher plants group phylogenetically with AqpZs and the yet nonstudied AqpNs.

Sequences for NIP subfamily members have not been found in animal and fungal genomes and it has, therefore, been hypothesised that the first plant NIP was the result of a horizontal aqpN gene transfer (HGT) event during the origin of plant life forms (Finn & Cerd-a, 2015; Zardoya et al., 2002; Danielson & Johanson, 2010; Abascal et al., 2014). However, the exact origin of the plant NIP subfamily and the evolution and diversification of functions within early plant lineages are completely unclear and unresolved.

NIPs form one of the isoform-richest subfamily in plants with a high diversity regarding their amino acid sequences and substrate specificities. Besides their vast substrate spectrum (Bienert & Chaumont, 2011; Bienert & Bienert, 2017), the physiological relevance of NIPs in planta may be restricted to the transport of the essential and beneficial metalloids B and Si, but also to the extrusion of the toxic minerals arsenic (As), antimony (Sb), and germanium (Ge) (Pommerrenig et al., 2015; Bienert & Bienert, 2017). NIPs subdivide into three groups termed NIP-I, NIP-II and NIP-III (Wallace & Roberts, 2004; Mitani et al., 2008). This grouping is based on common substrate selectivities, sequence similarities and an amino acid composition consistency of their ar/R SF. The NIP-I and NIP-II subgroups are present in all higher plants, while NIP-III isoforms are largely, but not exclusively, confined to Liliopsida species (Ma & Yamaji, 2015; Trembath-Reichert et al., 2015; Deshmukh & Belanger, 2016).

Multiple NIP isoforms belonging to the NIP-II group (such as AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1, ZmNIP3;1, and OsNIP3;1) have been unambiguously demonstrated to be essential for the root uptake and translocation of B in various monocot and dicot plant species and therefore for B nutrition in seed plants (reviewed in Pommerrenig et al., 2015; Bienert & Bienert, 2017). NIP-III group isoforms are mainly found in plant species that are biosilicifying or which benefit from high Si concentrations in their plant body such as Poaceae or Cucurbitaceae species. Accordingly, NIP-III group members (such as OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2, HvNIP2;1, HvNIP2;2 and CmNIP2;1) were shown to be crucial for an efficient root uptake and translocation of Si and therefore for Si homeostasis in such plant species (reviewed in Ma & Yamaji, 2015; Bienert & Bienert, 2017).

NIPs differing from these three subgroups have been identified in the moss Physcomitrella patens and the lycophyte Selaginella moellendorffii (Danielson & Johanson, 2008; Anderberg et al., 2012). Those NIPs form a fourth NIP group (NIP-IV) and have a SF composition consisting of $\mathrm { F _ { R 1 } } { - } \mathrm { A _ { R 2 } } { - } \mathrm { A _ { R 3 } } { - } \mathrm { R _ { R 4 } }$ residues. As this SF layout is restricted to bacterial AqpNs and a few NIP isoforms found in extant members of early land plant lineages, it might represent the archetype SF layout of all plant NIPs and the original NIP channel selectivity (Finn & Cerd-a, 2015; Danielson & Urbanson, 2010; Abascal et al., 2014; Trembath-Reichert et al., 2015). It is unlikely that boric acid and silicic acid transport, the essential functions of modern seed plant NIP-IIs and NIP-IIIs, respectively, represent the ancestral function of bacterial AqpN proteins as neither B nor Si essentiality is common in bacteria. Initial analyses of seed plant NIPs identified glycerol as the first common substrate and suggested a role for bacterial AqpNs and NIPs in early nonvascular terrestrial plants in glycerol uptake and distribution (Zardoya et al., 2016; Roberts & Routray, 2017). However, the exact origin of plant NIPs and the evolution and diversification of functions within early plant lineages are completely unclear and neither bacterial AqpNs nor plant NIPs with a F–A–A–R-type SF composition have been characterised so far.

The present work sheds light into the functional evolution of NIPs. We combined intense sequence- and genetic context analyses with transport assays to resolve the functional evolution of NIPs within plants and reveal molecular features of bacterial AqpNs and algal and terrestrial plant F–A–A–R-type NIP channels. AqpN channels are permeable to arsenous acid and are frequently part of arsenic (As) resistance operons (ars operons) of diverse bacterial phyla. This suggests that an intrinsic function of the ancestors of plant NIPs namely the bacterial AqpNs resides in As detoxification processes and that modern NIP channels underwent subfunctionalisation and neofunctionalisation and turned from As effluxers into essential and beneficial plant nutrient channels. Permeability of ancestral plant NIPs was a premise for the ability of vascular plants to efficiently take up and translocate B and Si into and within the plant body. This transport ability first allowed plants to use these elements efficiently, a crucial prerequisite for terrestrial upright growth and stress tolerance.

Background: Arsenic is a toxic and highly abundant metalloid that endangers human health through drinking water and the food chain. The most common forms of arsenic in the environment are arsenate $( \mathsf { A } \mathsf { s } ( \mathsf { V } ) )$ and arsenite $( \mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } ) ) . \mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ is a non-functional phosphate analog that enters the food chain via plant phosphate transporters. Inside cells, $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ becomes reduced to As(III) for subsequent extrusion or compartmentation. Although much is known about As(III) transport and handling in microbes and mammals, the transport systems for $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ have not yet been characterized in plants.

Results: Here we show that the Nodulin26-like Intrinsic Proteins (NIPs) AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 from Arabidopsis thaliana, OsNIP2;1 and OsNIP3;2 from Oryza sativa, and LjNIP5;1 and LjNIP6;1 from Lotus japonicus are bi-directional $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ channels. Expression of these NIPs sensitized yeast cells to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ and antimonite (Sb(III)), and direct transport assays confirmed their ability to facilitate As(III) transport across cell membranes. On medium containing $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ , expression of the same NIPs improved yeast growth, probably due to increased As(III) efflux. Our data furthermore provide evidence that NIPs can discriminate between highly similar substrates and that they may have differential preferences in the direction of transport. A subgroup of As(III) permeable channels that group together in a phylogenetic tree required N-terminal truncation for functional expression in yeast.

Conclusion: This is the first molecular identification of plant $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ transport systems and we propose that metalloid transport through NIPs is a conserved and ancient feature. Our observations are potentially of great importance for improved remediation and tolerance of plants, and may provide a key to the development of low arsenic crops for food production.

Arsenic is widespread in the Earth's crust and is highly available in the biosphere. Arsenic is acutely toxic to all organisms and is rated as a group I human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research of Cancer [1]. Due to its high bioavailability and toxicity, arsenic is considered a global health hazard. Contaminated drinking water is the main source of arsenic intake in several parts of the world. In Argentina, Australia, Bangladesh, Chile, China, Hungary, India, Mexico, Peru, Thailand, and the United States of America, arsenic concentrations higher than the permissible levels have been reported and negative effects on human health have been documented [2]. The second largest source of arsenic for humans is through ingestion of food that has accumulated arsenic due to the irrigation of crop plants with polluted water [3]. In Argentina, arsenic concentrations of 300–400 parts per billion (ppb) were measured in soup and maize porridge [4] in villages where the drinking water was about 200 ppb [4,5], a concentration that is already considerably higher than the upper limit for drinking water of $1 0 \mathrm { p p b }$ as recommended by the World Health Organization [2]. It is estimated that, worldwide, $1 - 2 4 \%$ of the tolerable intake of inorganic arsenic is solely due to the consumption of arsenic-containing rice [6]. Consequently, a detailed understanding of arsenic uptake and detoxification in plants is of great interest and is important for strategies in plant biotechnology for designing safer crops as well as for generating plants for the use in phytoremediation [7].

Arsenate (As(V)) is the prevailing arsenic species in aerated soils. $\operatorname { A s } ( \mathrm { V } )$ is a non-functional phosphate analog that is taken up via plant phosphate transporters [8]. Inside the plant, most of the As(V) is reduced to arsenite (As(III)) via arsenate reductases [9,10]. As(III) reacts with sulfhydryl groups in cysteine residues and the imidazolium nitrogen in histidine residues leading to interference with general protein function [11]. To control As(III) levels in the cytoplasm, As(III) can be conjugated to phytochelatins [12] and probably sequestered into vacuoles by ABC transporters [13]. Most of the vacuolar arsenic however is inorganic As(III) [14,15]. In Arabidopsis, As(III) constitutes up to $7 0 \%$ of total arsenic and appears to be the main transported species [16]. Transporters involved in As(III) distribution and sequestration at the cellular level are still unknown. At the whole-plant level, arsenic can be transported from root to shoot via the vascular system. In the xylem sap, the predominant arsenic species are inorganic As(III) and As(V) [17,18] but methylated species are also present at low concentrations [17,19].

Recently, aquaglyceroporins from microbes and mammals have been shown to facilitate the movement of As(III) and the related metalloid antimonite (Sb(III)) across cell membranes (as reviewed in [20]). Moreover, in

Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa (rice), members of the Nodulin26-like Intrinsic Protein (NIP) subfamily of plant aquaporins, AtNIP5;1 and OsNIP2;1, have been localized to the plasma membrane in planta and were shown to play physiologically important roles in the uptake of the nutritionally important metalloids boron and silicon, respectively [21,22]. Finally, competition studies for the uptake of As(III) with glycerol in rice led to the suggestion that As(III) is also transported through members of the aquaporin family in plants [23]. Based on these observations and the fact that members of the NIP subfamily are believed to be the functional equivalents of aquaglyceroporins, we hypothesized that NIPs may be As(III) transporters. To test this prediction directly, we cloned various NIP isoforms from A. thaliana, Lotus japonicus, and O. sativa and expressed them in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (budding yeast) as a heterologous test system for metalloid transport. Our data demonstrate that the capacity to channel As(III) and Sb(III) is conserved in the NIPII subgroup in plants. Expression of specific NIPs was found to sensitize yeast cells to As(III) and Sb(III) and caused increased As(III) uptake into yeast. On medium containing As(V), expression of the same NIP isoforms improved growth, probably due to increased efflux of As(III) accumulating in the yeast cells upon As(V) reduction. Strikingly, a number of NIP isoforms proved particularly potent in releasing As(III) from yeast cells exposed to As(V), suggesting that specific NIPs could play a role in As(III) detoxification in plants.


## Results Expression of specific NIPs from Arabidopsis sensitizes yeast Δfps1 to As(III) and Sb(III)


To test whether plant aquaporin homologs transport As(III) and Sb(III), AtNIP1;1, AtNIP2;1, AtNIP5;1, AtNIP6;1 and AtNIP7;1 were heterologously expressed in the aquaglyceroporin deficient Δfps1 yeast mutant. As As(III) and Sb(III) enter yeast cells through Fps1p [24,25], Afps1 cells are characterized by low influx and enhanced resistance towards these metalloids. As positive controls, we used AQP9 from rat (rAQP9) and ScFPS1 that reverse metalloid tolerance of Δfps1 cells [24,26]. Yeast transformants were plated on medium containing various concentrations of As(III) or Sb(III) and growth was scored (Figure 1). Growth of yeast expressing rAQP9 was reduced on medium containing $2 \ \mathrm { \ m M }$ As(III) and completely repressed in the presence of $6 \mathrm { \ m M }$ As(III), whereas the control yeast transformed with the empty vector grew well at concentrations up to 9 mM As(III). Yeast transformed with ScFPS1 showed reduced growth at 6 and $9 \ \mathrm { \ m M }$ As(III) (Figure 1A). On medium containing Sb(III), growth of yeast transformed with rAQP9 was strongly affected whereas the control grew well at $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ Sb(III) (Figure 1B). Yeast cells expressing AtNIP7;1 were strongly Sb(III)-sensitive (Figure 1B) but only slightly As(III)-sensitive (Figures 1 and 2A). In contrast, none of the other plant aquaporin isoforms appeared to sensitize yeast cells to As(III) or Sb(III) (Figure 1). It was previously reported that, for functional expression of certain NIP isoforms in yeast, it is necessary to truncate parts of their hydrophilic N-terminal domain [27]. Therefore, we genetically engineered N-terminally truncated versions of several NIPs including Atnip1; $\cdot 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 4 4 } ,$ $A t n i p 2 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 3 7 } ,$ $A t n i p 5 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 7 } ,$ Atnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 9 }$ and $A t n i p 7 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 3 5 }$ . Importantly, yeast expressing the truncated $A t n i p 5 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 7 }$ and Atnip6; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 6 9 }$ showed strong sensitivity towards As(III) (Figure 1A) whereas growth of these cells was only slightly affected by Sb(III) (Figure 1B). On the other hand, expression of Atnip7; $1 \Delta _ { 2 - 3 5 }$ resulted in a very similar growth phenotype as expression of the full length AtNIP7;1, both on As(III)- and Sb(III)-containing plates (Figures 1 and 2A). Similarly, expression of AtNIP2;1 or $A t n i p 2 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 3 7 }$ (Figure 1), or a truncated version of AtNIP6;1 lacking only 28 aa of the N-terminal domain $\left( A t n i p 6 ; 1 \Delta _ { 2 - 2 9 } \right)$ , had no impact on metalloid sensitivity (discussed in the following).

## The capacity of NIP homologs to transport As(III) and Sb(III) is conserved across plant species


To gain more functional understanding of the NIP proteins, we first performed a phylogenetic analysis including $3 3 \mathrm { \ N I P }$ homologs from various species, using rat AQP9 as an out-group (Figure 4). The phylogenetic analyses support, and refine further, the subdivision of the NIP subfamily of the aquaporin superfamily into the two subgroups NIPI and NIPII [30-33]. Together, the phylogenetic analysis, transport assays, and phenotypic data presented above, suggested that the capacity to facilitate diffusion of As(III) and Sb(III) across membranes is associated with members of the NIPII subgroup. To substantiate our hypothesis, one isoform of subgroup I (OsNIP1;1) and three isoforms of subgroup II (OsNIP2;1, OsNIP2;2 and OsNIP3;2) from rice were expressed in yeast and tested for their permeability towards As(III). Expression of

OsNIP2;1 and OsNIP3;2 sensitized yeast to As(III) (Figure 5A) and Sb(III) (data not shown), whereas their expression improved growth of Δfps1 Δacr3 Δycf1 on As(V)-containing medium (Figure 5B). Expression of OsNIP2;2 produced moderate As(III) and Sb(III) sensitivities (Figure 5A and data not shown). In contrast, OsNIP1;1 expression did not affect growth at all (data not shown). Finally, direct transport assays confirmed that the increased sensitivity of cells expressing OsNIP2;1 towards As(III) was the result of increased influx into those cells (Figure 5C).

OsNIP2;1 and AtNIP5;1 were earlier identified as physiologically important $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ and $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ channels in rice [22] and Arabidopsis [21], respectively. When expressed in oocytes, AtNIP5;1 mediated the uptake of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ and OsNIP2;1 mediated the uptake of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ . Here we demonstrated that As(III) is an additional and common substrate for both proteins. To address whether there is selectivity for the uptake of one metalloid over another, we exposed yeast cells expressing OsNIP2;1 to As(III)

alone or together with various concentrations of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ . However, there was no significant difference in the uptake of As(III), even at a 10-fold higher concentration of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ over As(III) (data not shown). Higher concentrations of $\mathrm { S i ( O H ) _ { 4 } }$ in the uptake assay cannot be used because of polymerization of monosilic acid to polysilicic acid, and higher concentration of $\mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 }$ will lower the $\mathrm { p H }$ of the medium.
