## GsCHX19.3, a member of cation/H+ exchanger superfamily from wild soybean contributes to high salinity and carbonate alkaline tolerance


Bowei Jia1,2, Mingzhe Sun1,2, Huizi DuanMu1, Xiaodong Ding1, Beidong Liu 3, Yanming Zhu1   
& Xiaoli Sun2

Cation/H+ exchangers (CHX) are characterized to be involved in plant growth, development and stress responses. Although soybean genome sequencing has been completed, the CHX family hasn’t yet been systematically analyzed, especially in wild soybean. Here, through Hidden Markov Model search against Glycine soja proteome, 34 GsCHXs were identifed and phylogenetically clustered into fve groups. Members within each group showed high conservation in motif architecture. Interestingly, according to our previous RNA-seq data, only Group IVa members exhibited highly induced expression under carbonate alkaline stress. Among them, GsCHX19.3 displayed the greatest up-regulation in response to carbonate alkaline stress, which was further confrmed by quantitative real-time PCR analysis. We also observed the ubiquitous expression of GsCHX19.3 in diferent tissues and its localization on plasma membrane. Moreover, we found that GsCHX19.3 expression in AXT4K, a yeast mutant lacking four ion transporters conferred resistance to low $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ at alkali pH, as well as carbonate stress. Consistently, in Arabidopsis, GsCHX19.3 overexpression increased plant tolerance both to high salt and carbonate alkaline stresses. Furthermore, we also confrmed that GsCHX19.3 transgenic lines showed lower $\ N \widehat { \mathsf { e } } ^ { + }$ concentration but higher ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + } I { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ values under salt-alkaline stress. Taken together, our fndings indicated that GsCHX19.3 contributed to high salinity and carbonate alkaline tolerance.

Soil salt-alkalinity, one of the most important environmental stresses, not only reduces soil fertility, but also abates the amount of agricultural production. Salt-alkaline stress has severely limited the sustainable development of agriculture and economy. Also, with the growing population and increasing demand for food, soil salinization and alkalization has become one of the severest problems. Tus, it is necessary and urgent to study the molecular responses to salt-alkaline stress in crops.

As sessile organisms, plants have developed a variety of physiological and biochemical mechanisms to cope with saline-alkaline stress during their long-term evolution process. It has been well studied that under salt-alkaline stress, cation/proton antiporters (CPAs) serve to maintain lower cytoplasmic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and cellular pH homeostasis1 . Te CPA superfamily is structurally characterized by a conserved $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger domain, and could be divided into CPA1 and CPA2 subfamilies. Te CPA1 subfamily consists of NHAP and NHX clades, while CPA2 is composed of NHA, KEA, and CHX clades2 . Among them, CPA1 have been suggested to function in exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ , and maintaining pH balance under adverse conditions, such as ABA, salt and hyperosmotic stresses3, 4 . Compared with CPA1, research concerning the CPA2 family is very limited until now. Recently, studies of KEAs from the CPA2 family have been gradually begun. For instance, AtKEAs were functionally characterized as $\mathrm { K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters and functioned under high $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ stress5 . However, studies about CHXs are limited in plant growth and development6, 7 , while little is known about their function in response to salt and alkaline stress.

In Arabidopsis, the CHX family was divided into fve groups (Group I-V)8 . Group IV was the largest one, and consisted of 8 members (AtCHX15–21 and AtCHX23). Among them, AtCHX16–20 were all endomembrane transporters9–11. AtCHX 16–19 shared overlapping roles in reproduction and seed development11. AtCHX20 was highly expressed in guard cells, and functioned in osmoregulation of stomatal open by regulating $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ movement and pH homeostasis12. AtCHX21 was a putative $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporter, regulating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ balance in xylem and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in leaves13. AtCHX23 functioned in cytosol pH adjustment. In atchx21chx23 mutants, pollen tubes failed to target ovules, which resulted in impaired pollen fertility6 . However, date to now, studies on CHXs are mainly limited in Arabidopsis, the function of CHXs from other species, in carbonate stress responses is still unclear.

Glycine soja is a related species of Glycine max, which can survive in severely saline-alkaline areas14. In previous studies, from a total of 345 wild soybean lines, we screened out G. soja 07256, which showed the highest resistance to carbonate stress14. By using microarray and RNA-seq data, we constructed the gene expression profles in response to carbonate alkaline stress15, and further excavated several stress resistant genes, such as $\bar { G } s C B R L K ^ { 1 6 }$ , $G s S K P 2 l ^ { 1 7 }$ , GsACA118, GsGSTU1319 and so on. Considering the potential roles of CHXs in stress responses, in this study, we focused on the CHX family genes of G.soja. A total of 34 GsCHXs were identifed and clustered into fve groups. Expression profles of Group IVa members were investigated in detail, and one of them GsCHX19.3 was demonstrated to mediate $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and positively regulate plant responses to high salt and carbonate alkaline stresses.

Cells have evolved mechanisms to regulate ion and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis in order to respond to developmental cues and to adapt to a constantly changing environment. In prokaryotes, this feat is accomplished with a diverse array of transporters at the plasma membrane. In eukaryotes, cells have increased in size and contain more intracellular membranes, including organelles and various compartments of the secretory and endocytic pathways. Consequently, the number of ion transporters localized to endomembranes has increased considerably. As plant ancestors initially living in an aquatic or marine environment colonized land, we wondered how transport systems required for growth, reproduction, and adaptation evolved in their structure and function. The genomes of diverse plants have been sequenced in recent years offering the first opportunity to understand how plant transporters evolved over one billion years. Here we focus on the monovalent cation/proton antiporter (CPA) superfamily whose members are thought to regulate cation and pH homeostasis (Brett et al., 2005a) by exchanging $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { L i ^ { + } }$ , or $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ for $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ . Prokaryote and eukaryote CPA members fall into two major families designated as CPA1 (2.A.36) and CPA2 (2.A.37; Saier, 2000; Brett et al., 2005a). In plants, CPA1 includes the well-studied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } - }$ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchanger (NHX) family, and the relatively obscure CPA2 family that includes $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ efflux Antiporter (KEA) and Cation– $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ exchanger (CHX) families. The purpose of this study is to understand the evolutionary relationship of NHX, KEA, and CHX homologs from algae to flowering plants, to use comparative biology to infer functions of uncharacterized plant genes (Chang et al., 2004), and hopefully reveal new model systems to determine functions of KEA and CHX genes which remain largely uncharacterized.

Plant $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters function in maintaining cellular ion and $\mathtt { p H }$ homeostasis (Bassil and Blumwald, 2014; Isayenkov et al., 2020).These antiporters play an important role in a variety of cellular and physiological processes,including potassium nutrition, salt tolerance,auxin homeostasis,protein traficking,and growth and development (Bassil and Blumwald, 2014; Qiu, 2016; Fan et al., 2018; Sze and Chanroj, 2018).

Arabidopsis CHX gene family,which is predicated to encode cation/ proton exchangers,consists of 28 members (Chanroj et al.，2012; Isayenkov et al.，2O2O). Studies have shown that plant CHXs are involved in many aspects of growth and development, such as pHand $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ homeostasis,stomatal movement,male gametophyte development, pollen growth,and plant development (Chanroj et al., 2Ol2; Sze and Chanroj, 2018; Isayenkov et al., 2020). CHX23, which is located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER),is specially expressed in pollen (Lu et al., 2011; Sze and Chanroj, 2O18). CHX23 is critical for pollen ion and pH homeostasis and pollen growth (Lu et al., 2O1l). Studies have shown that CHX21 and CHX23 are involved in the reception or the transduction of female signals that target pollen tube to the ovule (Lu et al., 2011). Pollen of the double mutants chx21 chx23 develops into mature grains, but pollen tubes failed to reach the egg (Lu et al., 2Ol1). However, the mechanism underlying CHX23 function in regulating pollen growth remains to be studied.

Auxin plays an important role in plant growth and development (Mockaitis and Estelle, 2008; Adamowski and Friml, 2015). PIN proteins are auxin efflux transporters that are crucial for auxin asymmetric distribution in tissues (Krecek et al., 2009; Zhou and Luo, 2018). The PIN family contains eight members grouped into two subcategories:PM-PINs and ER-PINs (Viaene et al., 2O13). The PM-PINs, containing PIN1-PIN4 and PIN7,are located in the plasma membrane (PM) (Rakusova et al., 2015;Sauer and Kleine-Vehn, 2O19). The ER-PINs,containing PIN5, PIN6 (also acting at the PM; Simon et al.,2Ol6),and PIN8,are located in the ER (Friml and Jones, 201O; Grones and Friml, 2015).PIN8,which is more highly expressed in the male gametophyte,is critical for pollen growth (Dal Bosco et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2012). However, how PIN8 regulates pollen growth remains elusive.

Recently,progress has been made in understanding the mechanism underlying the regulation of the function of PIN5 and PIN6 in plant growth and development (Fan et al., 2018; Lv et al., 202O). Studies have shown that NHX5 and NHX6,endosomal $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporters in Arabidopsis,regulate the function of PIN5 and PIN6 and, consequently, cellular auxin homeostasis and plant development (Fan et al., 2O18; Lv et al.,2O2O).NHX5 and NHX6 co-localized in the ER with PIN5 and PIN6,and regulate the function of PIN5 and PIN6 with pH gradients created by their transport activity (Fan et al., 2O18; Lv et al., 2020). Since both CHX23 and PIN8 are localized in the ER,it is interesting to ask whether CHX23 regulates PIN8 function in pollen growth and development.

In this report,we studied the role of CHX23 in regulating PIN8 function and hence pollen growth.Genetic analyses found that the chx23 mutant was affected in pollen growth and pollen morphological development. The pin8 chx23 double mutant was decreased in pollen growth. CHX23 and PIN8 act jointly in maintaining pollen auxin homeostasis. CHX23 and PIN8 co-localized but did not interact.Both chx23 and pin8 chx23 were altered in pollen growth under KCl and NaCl treatments.We demonstrate that CHX23 and PIN8 act coordinately in regulating pollen growth.CHX23 may regulate pollen growth through regulating PIN8 function and hence auxin homeostasis by its transport activity.

The Arabidopsis genome contains many sequences annotated as encoding $\mathsf { H } ^ { \star }$ -coupled cotransporters. Among those are the members of the cation:proton antiporter-2 (CPA2) family (or CHX family), predicted to encode $\ N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / \hat { \Sigma } ^ { + }$ antiporters. AtCHX17, a member of the CPA2 family, was selected for expression studies, and phenotypic analysis of knockout mutants was performed. AtCHX17 expression was only detected in roots. The gene was strongly induced by salt stress, potassium starvation, abscisic acid (ABA) and external acidic pH. Using the $\beta$ -glucuronidase reporter gene strategy and in situ RT-PCR experiments, we have found that AtCHX17 was expressed preferentially in epidermal and cortical cells of the mature root zones. Knockout mutants accumulated less ${ \pmb { \ K } } ^ { + }$ in roots in response to salt stress and potassium starvation compared with the wild type. These data support the hypothesis that AtCHX17 is involved in ${ \pmb { \ K } } ^ { + }$ acquisition and homeostasis.

Keywords: Arabidopsis, salt stress, ${ \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ -starvation, $\ N a ^ { + } , K ^ { + } / \hat { \Sigma } ^ { + }$ antiporters, $\mathsf { K } ^ { \star }$ transport, CHX transporters.

## Growth conditions and ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ ‑specifc treatments


The certifed seeds of Panvel-3 (salt tolerant) and Sahyadri-3 (salt sensitive), widely grown popular cultivars (CVs) were procured from Saline Land Research Station, Panvel, India, and Regional Rice Research Station, Karjat, India, respectively. The selection of these CVs was based on their $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation abilities depicted in our previous studies (Khare et al. 2023; Kumar and Khare 2016). The seeds were initially surface sterilized with mercuric chloride $\mathrm { ( H g C l } _ { 2 }$ , $0 . 1 \%$ , w/v) for $4 { - } 5 \ \mathrm { m i n }$ with continuous shaking and were then washed with sterile distilled water several times to ensure complete removal of any residual $\mathrm { H g C l } _ { 2 }$ . Seeds were then placed in the Petri plate (10 seeds plate−1) containing moist flter paper and allowed to germinate in the dark at $2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . After $4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ , the equally grown seedlings were separated and used for pot experiments. The soil (clay loam, $3 5 \%$ clay, $3 0 \%$ silt, $3 5 \%$ sand) was sieved through $2 \mathrm { m m }$ mesh, autoclaved and completely air-dried before flling in pots. The nitrogen, phosphorous, and potassium levels, as well as the $\mathrm { p H }$ and EC of the soil, were measured. Plastic pots $( 1 5 \mathrm { c m } \times 3 0 \mathrm { c m } )$ were flled with approximately $2 \mathrm { k g }$ of airdried soil and fve equally grown seedlings were planted in each pot. After two weeks, the grown seedlings were thinned to one $\mathrm { p o t } ^ { - 1 }$ . The pots were watered regularly with halfstrength Yoshida’s medium for optimal growth, avoiding any undesired nutrient defciency.

The plants were allowed to grow till the initiation of the reproductive phase $\sim 6 5$ days after transplanting, 65 DAT). Salt treatments were applied to these plantlets after 65 DAT as it is considered as the completion of the vegetative stage and initiation of the reproductive stage of the rice (Kumar and Khare 2016). Three treatments resulting in an efective concentration of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ along with untreated control were applied in the soil, as follows:

(1) Control (only Milli-Q water, without the addition of any salt),   
(2) $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -dominant salts $( 4 0 \mathrm { m M N a N O _ { 3 } }$ , $1 5 \mathrm { m M N a _ { 2 } H P O _ { 4 } }$ and 15 mM $\mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } ,$ ),   
(3) $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -Gluconate $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M } )$ ,   
(4) NaCl ( $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M } )$ .

The sodium gluconate treatment represents the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ specifcity due to the impermeable nature of the gluconate anions, due to which they cannot enter the cell membrane (Tavakkoli et al. 2011). Hence the efects of this treatment can be solely attributed to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Treatments were applied at intervals of a day and continued till the EC of soil in all the pots (except control) reached $\sim 1 0 ~ \mathrm { d } \mathrm { S ~ m } ^ { - 1 }$ (equivalent to $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l ) }$ . The salinity levels were maintained till the plant harvesting stage. Reproductive tissues in the form of diferent stages of immature grains (post-anthesis grain flling) namely, early milk stage (97 DAT: $9 7 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day), milk stage (105 DAT: $1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day), and dough (112 DAT: $1 1 2 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) were harvested from plants with or without treatments and were used for biochemical analysis. Mature grains were harvested $( \sim 1 2 0 { - } 1 2 5 ~ \mathrm { D A T } )$ and used for the biochemical and agronomic evaluation.

## Reactive oxygen species (superoxide radical, hydroxyl radical and hydrogen peroxide)


Freshly harvested immature grain samples were immediately used for ROS estimation. The estimation of superoxide radicals $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - } )$ was done using the nitro-blue tetrazolium as per the method by Chaitanya and Naithani (1994) and expressed in terms of $\Delta _ { \mathrm { A 5 4 0 } } \mathrm { m i n ^ { - 1 } \ g ^ { - 1 } }$ FW. The hydroxyl radicals (˙OH) were estimated using the thiobarbituric acid (TBA) reagent and expressed in terms of the malondialdehyde (MDA) content (nmol MDA $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { F } \mathbf { W } )$ . The hydrogen peroxide $( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ content was evaluated as per the method by Loreto and Velikova (2001) using the potassium iodide reagent.


## Activity of antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase, peroxidase)


For enzyme extraction, fresh samples were ground fnely in liquid nitrogen, and homogenized with phosphate bufer $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M }$ , pH 7.5) containing $0 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ EDTA. The homogenate was centrifuged at $1 5 { , } 0 0 0 \ \mathrm { r p m }$ for $2 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ at $4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and the obtained supernatant was collected as a crude enzyme extract. Similar extracts were also used for the estimation of protein using the Bradford method (Bradford 1976) to express the enzyme activity in terms of $\mathrm { m g ^ { - 1 } }$ protein.

Superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity was calculated as per the reduction in absorbance of formazan by the superoxide-nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT) complex by SOD (Dhindsa et al.1981). One unit (U) of SOD equals the quantity of enzyme which reduced the absorbance by $5 0 \%$ in comparison with control (without enzymes). The catalase (CAT) activity was determined according to Aebi (1984) by measuring the rate of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ reduction at $2 4 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ . The one U of the enzyme was defned as $\bf { m M }$ of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ decomposed $\mathrm { m g ^ { - 1 } }$ protein $\operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ The peroxidase (POX) activity was calculated as the rate of oxidation of the guaiacol to tetra-guaiacol at $4 7 0 \mathrm { n m }$ (Castillo et al. 1984). One U of enzyme was defned as $\mu \mathrm { M }$ of tetraguaiacol formed $\mathrm { m g ^ { - 1 } }$ protein $\operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$

## Ion content


The immature grains were grinded using mortar and pestle and $1 0 0 \mathrm { m g }$ of the sample was digested in the concentrated nitric acid. The samples were further re-digested in a diacid mixture (nitric acid: perchloric acid; 10:4, 2 h) and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ contents were measured using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer (Shimadzu UV-1900, Tokyo, Japan)


## Nitric oxide and nitrate reductase activity


For the determination of nitric oxide (NO), the tissue homogenate was prepared in sodium acetate bufer ( $\mathrm { 1 0 0 m M }$ , $\mathrm { p H } 3 . 6$ ; with $4 \%$ zinc acetate). The obtained supernatant was mixed with the same volume of Griess reagent and after incubation $3 0 \mathrm { m i n }$ , room temperature) the absorbance of the developed pink color was measured at $5 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The NO content (nano mol $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { F } \mathbf { W } )$ was estimated using the standard $( \mathrm { N a N O } _ { 2 } ,$ ) curve (Zhou et al. 2005).

The nitrate reductase (NR) activity was assessed in terms of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 } ^ { - }$ production (Luo et al. 2006). One hundred mg samples were ground on ice in extraction bufer $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ potassium phosphate bufer with $1 0 \mathrm { m M }$ cysteine and $1 \mathrm { m M }$ EDTA; $\mathrm { p H } 8 . 7 , 5 \mathrm { m L }$ ). After centrifugation $( 1 2 , 0 0 0 ~ \mathrm { r p m }$ , $2 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ , $4 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ), $1 ~ \mathrm { m L }$ of supernatant was mixed with $2 ~ \mathrm { m L }$ of reaction bufer ( $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ potassium phosphate bufer, $1 0 0 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 }$ ; $\mathrm { p H } 7 . 5$ ) and $1 \mathrm { m L }$ of $2 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ NADH. After $3 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ of incubation at $2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , Nitrites produced were estimated after half $\mathbf { h }$ (at $2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ) using sulfanilamide ( $1 \%$ , in $1 . 5 \ : \mathrm { M } \ : \mathrm { H C l } \rangle$ and N-(1-naphthyl) ethylene diamine dihydrochloride $( 0 . 0 2 \%$ , in 0.2 M HCl) at $5 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The NR activity was expressed as n mol of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 } ^ { - }$ produced $\mathrm { m g ^ { - 1 } }$ protein $\operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ .


## Expression patterns of sodium and potassium transporters


Based on the level of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and oxidative and nitrosative response, the top $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stage (milk stage) was further considered for the assessment of expression patterns of sodium (OsNHX, OS11G0648000, Vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter) and potassium (OsHKT, OS04G0607600, Highafnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter) transporters. The RNA was isolated from the harvested tissue using TRIzol solution (TRI Reagent $\circled{8}$ , Merck). The isolated RNA was then subjected to cDNA synthesis using the M-MuLV reverse transcriptase (HiMedia, India) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. Further, the synthesized cDNA was used as a template for realtime quantitative PCR (RT qPCR) reaction. The reaction was performed using the Hi-SYBr master mix (HiMedia, India) and the gene-specifc primers (Supplementary Table S1). The rice ubiquitin gene was used as a house-keeping control gene and the RT qPCR reaction was performed as initial denaturation of $9 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $2 \mathrm { m i n }$ , 40 cycles of denaturation $( 9 4 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ for $3 0 \mathrm { ~ s ~ }$ , annealing for $4 5 \mathrm { ~ s ~ }$ , and extension $( 7 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ for $3 0 \mathrm { ~ s ~ }$ . The analysis was conducted with three biological replicates. The relative expression levels (RQ) of the genes were calculated as relative changes by the $2 ^ { - \Delta \Delta \mathrm { C t } }$ method.

Under the infuence of the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , the rice CVs with contrasting salt tolerance responded diferentially during the grain-flling phase. Similarly, the mature grain also displayed variabilities in the agronomic traits as well as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation. The following results confrmed the hazardous impacts of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ on grain development as well as grain quality.


## ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ ‑stress impacts on rice biomass


The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments caused a reduction in biomass in both CVs (Table 1). The reduction in shoot DW was evident in both the CVs under the infuence of all the treatments. A similar reduction trend was also observed in the case of the root DW. The extent of shoot biomass reduction was nearly equal under NaCl and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatments in Panvel-3 (1.2-fold) and Sahyadri-3 (1.3-fold). On the other hand, the reduction in root biomass was most pronounced under the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ gluconate treatment, in both the CVs. However, all the treatments reduced the shoot DW and root DW in the following manner: $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate ${ } > \mathrm { N a C l } > \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } .$ -dominant salts. The negative efect of excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the soil on plant growth is previously documented (Kumar and Khare 2016). The soil with high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration exerted a negative impact on rice growth (Momayezi et al. 2009; Khare et al. 2015, 2016; Feng et al. 2018). The current investigation is in coordination with these studies. Similarly, both the CVs showed reduced SL and RL under all the applied $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc stress treatments (Table 1). The reduction and SL and RL followed a similar trend as the DW reduction where the highest range of reduction was observed when the CVs were treated with $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate. In the case of SL, the degree of reduction was higher in Sahyadri-3 (1.4- and 1.3-fold reduction in response to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate and NaCl treatments) compared to the Panvel-3 (1.2-fold reduction in response to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate and $\mathrm { N a C l }$ treatments). Similarly, the RL decreased 1.3-fold in Sahyadri-3 and 1.2-fold in Panvel-3 in response to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate and NaCl treatments. The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -mediated salt stress has been previously reported to alter the SL and RL in Iranian rice genotypes (Momayezi et al. 2009). The current study also afrms the negative efect of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ on SL and RL.


## Rice yield and yield components under ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ stress


During the reproductive development and grain flling in rice, panicle development, booting, and fowering are considered the critical stages that eventually defne the number and size of the panicle as well as the number of spikelets per panicle. On the other hand, spikelet size and weight are determined during the spikelet flling event. Due to these important characteristics, the reproductive phase is considered crucial as it directly afects the crop yield. Unfortunately, the reproductive phase is highly sensitive to environmental stresses including salinity (Singh et al. 2021). Though there are reports focused on the impacts of salinity on the reproductive phase of rice along the altered yield components (agronomic characters), there is no such report on yield components concerning the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. Table 2 summarizes the efects of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments on the agronomic characters of the mature grains harvested from the 125-day-old plants.

The considerable impact of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress was observed on overall crop yield as well as the evaluated yield parameters including grain number, grain dimensions (length, width, thickness), grain weight, total yield, and grain flling percentage. The obtained variability in the yield parameters concerning the salt tolerance nature of the CVs as well as the treatments, with Sahyadri-3 delivering a higher yield. The imposition of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc stresses signifcantly afected the yield parameters. The shape and size of the grains are basic properties defning the quality of rice as well as the acceptance by consumers (Sreenivasulu et al. 2015) and soil salinity is known to impose notable negative impacts on these parameters. Overall, the impact of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts was lower than that of the $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatments on most of the parameters in both the CVs. The salinity-driven alterations in grain dimensions afect crop yield. This change in the agronomic characters can be linked with excessive salinity, especially the high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels (Rodríguez Coca et al. 2023). Also, a study by Abbas et al. (2021) revealed the sodium-induced reduction in the grain number and grain weight of the quinoa (Chenopodium quinoa). The current study has also confrmed the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress-mediated yield loss in rice with $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatments showing greater impacts on the overall agronomic characteristics.


## ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ stress impacts ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ and ${ \pmb { \ K } } ^ { + }$ content and their delicate balance


In the context of soil salinity, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ play major roles during plant growth and development. The optimum balancing between the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels during the salinityinduced regulatory interactions is a must to attain salt tolerance by plants (Chen et al. 2021a, b). During plant development, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is essential for most of the higher plants during the enzymatic interactions and osmoregulation. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is required at high concentrations in plant cells and it is primarily localized in the vacuole as an osmoticum. Interestingly, maintenance of vacuolar osmotic potential can also be achieved by $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in plants. Therefore, during salinity-induced interactions there is plentiful $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ availability in the cell, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ can be substituted by $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ for some of its vital functions (Wakeel 2013; Tayyab et al. 2023). Therefore, the knowledge regarding the cellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels may prove advantageous to depict the stress levels in plants (a high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio indicates higher stress levels). In the present study, the concentration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , and $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ is estimated from the mature grains from the 125-day-old plants (Fig. 1). In the mature grains of Panvel-3, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was highest in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment (1.4-fold more than the control) followed by $\mathrm { \bf N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts treatment. Sahyadri-3 followed the same trend of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation as Panvel-3 but the extent of accumulation was higher than that of the Panvel-3. Compared to the control, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate, $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts treatments caused 1.6-, 1.5-, and 1.4-fold more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation respectively, in grains of Sahyadri-3. On the other hand, the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content of the grain was highest in grains harvested from control plants. The greatest reduction in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content was observed in Sahyadri-3 under the infuence of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate and $\mathrm { N a C l }$ where each treatment caused a 2.9-fold reduction in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation. Though the Panvel-3 followed the same trend of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation under $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate, NaCl, and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts treatments, the extent of reduction was considerably lower than the Sahyadri-3 at the same treatments.

The characteristic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio also displayed higher values in Sahyadri-3 than in Panvel-3. The ability to maintain low cellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentrations is one of the reasons for the better growth of salt-tolerant plants in saline environments (Mahmood et al. 2024; Munns et al. 2012). Similarly, salt-tolerant plants maintain a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ homeostasis via the acquisition of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ (Hussain et al. 2021). Therefore, better maintenance of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio and lesser $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation can be attributed to the tolerance nature of Panvel-3.

The $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ was also estimated from the mature grains of both CVs. However, the increase in $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ was observed only under the infuence of $\mathrm { N a C l }$ , as it was the only treatment where excess $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ was available for plants for accumulation. However, it was previously established that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is more detrimental for rice than $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ during their individual as well as additive applications (Khare et al. 2015; Kumar and Khare 2016).


## ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ mediated deterioration of sugars, starch, and proteins in grains


Reproductive phases are regarded as crucial and crop yields and quality are heavily reliant on them. However, soil salinity is known to exert a negative impact on reproductive development and grain quality, mostly due to impaired photosynthate delivery to the grain-filling site (Kotula et al. 2015). Therefore, sugar metabolism is expected to be afected under stress condition. In the current investigation, the sugar (reducing and non-reducing) and starch content were estimated to check the efect of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress on the mature grains (Fig. 2). The reducing sugar content of the mature grains displayed no signifcant diference in response to all the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ specifc treatments. On the other hand, nonreducing sugars displayed reduction for all the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments. However, the extent of reduction was higher for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment and $\mathrm { N a C l }$ than that of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salt treatment. According to Hakim et al. (2014), salinity causes a decrease in non-reducing sugars in salt-sensitive rice CV than its tolerant counterpart. Soluble sugars are well known for their critical functioning in osmoregulation as well as their chelating properties to bind $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ ions with starch granules (Boriboonkaset et al. 2012). In the current study, the sugars were lower overall in the salt-tolerant CV (Panvel-3) than in the salt-sensitive CV (Sahyadri-3).

The saline environment has previously proved to be responsible for altered sugar levels in various crops. For instance, sugar levels were improved in itomato in response to salinity (Zahra et al. 2010). On the other hand, the sugar content pattern was variable in response to salinity across diferent rice CVs as per the report by Alamgir and Ali (1999).

Trends in the reduction of starch content were similar to the reduction observed for non-reducing sugars. Salinity stress has shown a signifcant impact on the biosynthesis and accumulation of starch in cereals as starch biosynthesis is dependent on efcient production and movement of photosynthates to the grains, both of which are hampered due to salinity (He et al. 2013). The current fndings are consistent with previous reports of lower starch content in plants exposed to salinity stress with a smaller decrease in tolerant genotypes (He et al. 2013; Surekha Rao et al. 2013; Hakim et al. 2014).

Under both normal and stressed conditions, Sahyadri-3 grains showed a greater protein content than Panvel-3 grains. However, all the treatments reduced protein content in the order $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate $> \mathrm { N a C l } > \mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ dominant salts, with Panvel-3 having a lesser impact than Sahyadri-3. Similar trends of salinity-mediated reduction in grain protein content were observed in rice by Hakim et al. (2014). Overall, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc stress treatments resulted in the qualitative deterioration of the mature rice grains in terms of decreased sugar and protein contents.


## Ion accumulation and expression levels of transporter genes in immature grains under ${ \pmb { \mathsf { N } } } { \pmb { \mathsf { a } } } ^ { + }$ stress


To determine the most prominent stage displaying the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation during the grain flling, the ion content $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { C l } ^ { - }$ ) was analyzed at the early milk stage $( 9 7 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day), milk stage $1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) and dough stage $1 1 2 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) (Fig. 3). In case of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content, the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was observed in response to the $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatments in both the CVs. Interestingly, out of the three considered grain-flling stages, a steep increase in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content was observed from the early milk stage $( 9 7 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) to the milk stage ( $1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) in both CVs. However, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content remained approximately the same in the dough stage ( $1 1 2 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day). This trend was equivalent in the immature grains of both the CVs but the degree of increase was comparably higher in salt-sensitive CV (Sahyadri-3). In the case of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , a slight reduction was observed in response to all the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments whereas immature grains from untreated plants displayed an increase. The characteristic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio was high in the immature grains at the milk stage $( 1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) which further remained alike in the dough stage ( $1 1 2 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day).

The highest elevation in $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ content was observed in response to $\mathrm { N a C l }$ treatment only, which was expected as the NaCl was the only treatment providing the additional $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ for the plants compared to the other treatments. Collectively, the ion content analysis revealed that the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was evident at the milk stage $1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) of the grain flling as from this particular stage the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content remained highest and constant from this stage onwards. The lower $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels as well as the high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ ratio at the milk stage also suggest the high level of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ mediated stress at this stage of grain flling.

The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content at the milk stage was further correlated with the expression patterns of the genes coding for their transport. In rice, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ Exchanger located on the tonoplast (OsNHX) works to maintain the low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels in the cytosol via vacuolar sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ (Fukuda et al. 2011). The expression of this gene has been reported in different parts including leaves, shoots, roots as well as panicles and actively compartmentalizes the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ under the salt stress and confers the salt tolerance in rice (Neang et al. 2020). On the other hand, the high-afnity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transporter (OsHKT) is also actively involved in preventing $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -over-accumulation, especially at the reproductive stage (Suzuki et al. 2016; Neang et al. 2020). In the current investigation, the OsNHX displayed elevated expression patterns in the immature grain (at the milk stage) of both cultivars in response to all three treatment conditions. However, the expression levels were comparably higher in the salt-tolerant cultivar. Compared to the untreated control, the expression levels of OsNHX were 1.3-, 2.8- and 2.9-fold higher in Panvel-3 (salt-tolerant CV) in response to the treatments of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts, NaCl, and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate, respectively (Fig. 4). In salt-sensitive CV, the OsNHX expression levels were 1.2-fold higher in response to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts’ treatments, whereas the $\mathrm { N a C l }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment caused two-fold higher expression. As per the study by Solis et al. (2021), the high expression levels of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / H ^ { + } }$ exchanger aided the sequestration of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and hence the salt-tolerance level of the rice CV. In the current investigation as well, the expression levels of OsNHX were higher in salt-tolerant CV compared to its counterpart. Further, these expression patterns can be well correlated with the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ sequestration and the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in the immature as well as mature harvested rice grains. The imposition of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress caused a nominal increment in expression levels of OsHKT in the immature grains of salt-sensitive CV ( $\sim 1 . 4$ -fold in response to all $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments). However, the expression levels of OsHKT in the immature grains of salt-tolerant CV were considerably higher (1.9-, 3.1-, and 2.7-fold higher in response to treatments of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ dominant salts, $\mathrm { N a C l }$ , and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate, respectively). The product encoded by OsHKT regulates the unloading of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem to the xylemparenchyma, reduce $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , and increases $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels during salt stress (Neang et al. 2020). The higher expression of OsHKT as well as OsNHX may indicate the high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and high $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ retention to maintain the cellular metabolism in the salt-tolerant CV. This may have contributed to the low $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ deposition in the cells in immature grains in a salt-tolerant CV than the salt-sensitive CV.


## Generation of reactive oxygen species in immature grains under ${ \pmb { \Lambda } } { \pmb { \alpha } } ^ { + }$ stress


It is now broadly accepted that plants crucially maintain a fne balance between ROS production and scavenging, mostly through enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant machinery. ROS have no detrimental efects on cells at lower levels, and can even act as signaling molecules (Chen and Yang 2020; Schieber and Chandel 2014). However, under stressful conditions such as a saline environment, this balance is disrupted, resulting in a sudden upsurge in intracellular ROS levels, which causes considerable cellular damage while also jeopardizing the functional capacities of cellular components (Hasanuzzaman et al. 2020; Gill and Tuteja 2010). The estimated levels of ROS [superoxide radicals $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { * - } } )$ , hydroxyl radicals (˙OH), and hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right) ]$ in the present investigation are presented in Fig. 5.

The frst prominent ROS entity generated as a response to the stress environment is $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ and about $2 \%$ of the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ consumed by plants is estimated to generate $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ via $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ reduction during electron transport (Puntarulo et al. 1988). The $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ generation is considered lethal as it triggers the formation of other free radicals including hydroxyl (˙OH), singlet oxygen $( ^ { 1 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ , and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ . In the current investigation, all the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc stress treatments led to the generation of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ in developing grains. The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment induced the highest production of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ in all the considered stages of immature grains (early milk, milk, and dough stage) in both the CVs. However, the generation of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ was maximum in the salt-sensitive CV (Sahyadri-3) compared to its salt-tolerant (Panvel-3) counterpart. For the developmental stages of the immature grains, the milk stage ( $1 0 5 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ day) displayed the greatest sensitivity as this stage exhibited the highest generation of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ in both the CVs.

Due to its persistence and capacity to traverse plant cell membranes, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ is regarded to be the most important ROS responsible for oxidative bursts in plants (Huseynova et al. 2014). It is generated from $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ via univalent reduction and its excess presence inside the plant cells results in oxidative stress (Gill and Tuteja 2010). The generation of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ in immature grains in response to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments followed similar trends as that of the $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ ; there the highest generation of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ was observed during the milk stage of the developing immature grains. Similarly, the salt-tolerant CV displayed a comparably lower rate of ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ generation than the salt-sensitive CV.

Hydroxyl radicals $\mathrm { ( \dot { O } H ) }$ are one of the potent ROS, which can be formed from $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ and ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ in the presence of transitional metals via $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ -driven Fenton reaction. These radicals are known for their signifcant role in mediating oxygen toxicity (Hasanuzzaman et al. 2020; Gill and Tuteja 2010) and they can react with any biological molecules and cellular elements. Excessive ˙OH production may eventually result in cell death (Hasanuzzaman et al. 2020; Vranova et al. 2002). In the current study, the generation of ˙OH was highest during the milk stage of the developing grain in both the CVs. Similarly, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment was responsible for the highest induction of ˙OH.

The analysis of ROS generation cumulatively represented that the milk stage (105th day) was the most afecting stage of immature/developing grains with the highest level of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \cdot ^ { - }$ , ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ as well as ˙OH generation. Besides, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ specifc treatments were responsible for the high ROS generation in both the rice CVs, with the lesser generation of ROS in salt tolerant (Panvel-3) CV than salt-sensitive (Sahyadri-3) CV.


## Status of enzymatic antioxidants in immature grains under ${ \pmb { \Lambda } } { \pmb { \alpha } } ^ { + }$ stress


The SODs, CATs as well as POXs are the antioxidant enzymes that have been shown a potential to detoxify the harmful ROS. These enzymes can be categorized as (1) those that react with ROS and maintain their low levels (POX, SOD, and CAT) and (2) those that regenerate oxidized antioxidants (ascorbate peroxidase, APX, and glutathione reductase, GR) to hold the redox balance (Kumar et al. 2009). SOD converts $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \mathrm { ^ { - } }$ to ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ , which is scavenged by POX in extracellular space and cytoplasm as well as by CAT in peroxisomes. In cellular components, APX decomposes ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ . By interacting directly or indirectly with ROS, these antioxidants play an important role in preserving the normal functioning of metabolic pathways and the integrity of cell structures (Hasanuzzaman et al. 2020; Gill and Tuteja 2010). One of the primary components of the tolerance mechanism against oxidative damage is the promotion of antioxidant defense, and salt tolerance of various plants is generally attributed to their greater antioxidant capabilities (Akyol et al. 2020). In the current investigation, the activities of ROS scavenging enzymes were calculated at diferent grain-flling stages (Fig. 5).

All the enzymes displayed higher activities in response to all three treatments in both the CVs. After comparing the enzyme activities at diferent grain-flling stages, the milk stage was found to show the highest activities of all the enzymes. Also, it was revealed that the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate treatment was responsible for the highest increment in all the enzyme activities. Additionally, the salt-tolerant (Panvel-3) CV exhibited considerably higher enzymatic activities compared to the salt-sensitive CV (Sahyadri-3).

Considering the generation of ROS (Fig. 5) and the activities of enzymatic antioxidants (Fig. 5), the ROS generation was highest during the milk stage as well as the activities of enzymatic antioxidants. This indicates that though there is a higher rate of ROS generation at the milk stage, the equivalent scavenging mechanisms are also activated at the same stage. This suggests the highest level of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -mediated oxidative interaction in the milk compared to the early milk and dough stage. The cellular $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation and the successive impacts of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity are regulated by the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transporters (Rao et al. 2021). Based on the activities of representative ion transporters in our studies (OsHKT and OsNHX), the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content and eventually the ion homeostasis are well-modulated in the immature grains of Panvel-3. This can be attributed to the lesser degree of oxidative damage observed in the immature grains of Panvel-3 compared to that of the Sahyadri-3. As a result, the salt-tolerant CV (Panvel-3) exhibited relatively lesser ROS generation than its salt-sensitive counterpart (Sahyadri-3); whereas, the activity of the ROS scavenging enzymes is higher in Panvel-3 than in Sahyadri-3. This can be attributed to the salt tolerance capacity of the Panvel-3 and the better performance of the Panvel-3 under the infuence of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress.


## Nitric oxide and nitrate reductase activity in immature grains under ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ stress


Nitric oxide (NO) is a reactive molecule known to interact with transcription factors (TFs), receptors, and messengers (Zhou et al. 2021). However, NO as a free radical, scavenges other reactive metabolic intermediates. It also functions as an antioxidant, able to inhibit self-propagating damaging chain reactions during lipid peroxidation (Ferreira and Cataneo 2010). The $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -mediated NO content and nitrate reductase (NR) activity in rice CVs are presented in Fig. 6.

The ROS-driven cytotoxic progressions in plants are inhibited by NO. NO’s role in reducing ROS-induced cellular damage under stress has been linked to either direct scavenging of ROS by NO to produce less harmful residues or functioning as a signaling molecule, modifying stress-related gene expression levels (Hasanuzzaman et al. 2012). NO is also known to increase the activity of nitrogen metabolism-related enzymes, particularly nitrate reductase (NR) and nitrite reductase (Manai et al. 2014). The current study has also displayed similar trends in both CVs. Both the NO content and NR activity were highest in the milk stage (105th day) which indicates the NR-dependent NO accumulation under the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stresses. These activities are also consistent with the increment in ROS generation, indicating the ROS-induced NO and NR stimulation to mitigate the ROS-driven damage. Similar trends were observed in cucumber in response to the salinity (Reda et al. 2018). However, the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments displayed inconsistent specifcity for the alleviation of NO and NR activity.

The overall correlation between $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress and all the considered parameters in the immature grains is depicted in Fig. 7.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the frst inclusive attempt to decipher the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress impacts on the reproductive development and tissues of the Indica rice grains. The investigation confrms that the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exposure triggers the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in rice grains. In addition, the highest $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was observed at the milk stage of the developing grains which remained fairly constant till the complete maturity. The expression levels of the OsNHX and OsHKT were elevated in response to the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . The milk stage exhibited the highest rate of ROS generation compared to the other two stages of immature grains under consideration. Similarly, the activity of the antioxidant enzymes was also highest at the milk stage. For most of the assessed parameters, the form of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ compound displayed increased toxicity as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ Gluconate $> \mathrm { N a C l } > \mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ dominant salts manner. In addition, the salt-tolerant CV displayed higher antioxidant activities and a lower rate of ROS generation in response to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. Our investigation concluded that the milk stage was the most $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ responsive stage. The study suggests the criticality of the milk stage of the rice reproductive development to the excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . This also recommends the necessity of deeper insights into the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -driven interactions during rice grain flling which may further contribute in developing stress resilience in crops.
