Key message Sodium treatment caused the sodium ion accumulation at the milk stage of immature rice grains which in turn triggered the overproduction of reactive oxygen species and oxidative damage. The tolerant cultivar showed an enhanced antioxidative response and induced expressions of OsNHX and OsHKT ion-transporters.

Abstract Sodium chloride- $\mathrm { ( N a C l ) }$ induced soil salinity is a major constraint hindering global rice production. Amongst its constituent ions, sodium $\mathrm { ( N a ^ { + } ) }$ is known to be the main driver of toxicity under salt stress. The present investigation aims to measure the impacts of excess $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ during rice grain flling using two Indica rice cultivars with opposite tolerances to salt (salt tolerant: Panvel-3, salt-sensitive: Sahyadri-3) mainly via oxidative and responsive antioxidative pathways. Plants were treated with $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -specifc treatments and $\mathrm { N a C l }$ with equimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels $\mathbf { \Pi } ^ { \mathrm { ' } } 1 0 0 \mathbf { \Pi } \mathbf { m } \mathbf { M } )$ at the initiation of the reproductive phase. Stressed and control plants were harvested at three diferent grain-flling stages- early milk, milk, and dough and assessed for ion accumulation and oxidative damage/antioxidant responses under $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ toxicity triggered reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and upregulated the responsive enzymatic antioxidants. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress also increased the nitric oxide (NO) levels and the activity of nitrate reductase in immature grains. Diferential expression levels of OsNHX and OsHKT transporters were observed in response to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. Mature grains displayed a high accumulation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ along with reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content and elevated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } / K ^ { + } }$ under high $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ availability. The alterations in mature grains’ sugar, starch, and protein content were also observed in response to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. Overall, the salt-tolerant cultivar displayed higher antioxidant activities and a lower rate of ROS generation in response to the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ stress. Results suggested a link between $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ -mediated stress responses via anti/-oxidant pathways, and the grain-flling process in both rice cultivars.

Keywords Agronomic yield $\cdot$ Antioxidants $\cdot$ Grain flling $\cdot$ Reactive oxygen species $\cdot$ Salinity $\cdot$ Sodium

Salinity and drought are two of the most common abiotic stresses that plants frequently encounter and cause a negative impact on their growth, development, and production due to ion toxicity and physiological drought (Munns and Tester 2008; Tang et  al. 2016). High-afnity potassium transporter (HKT) family proteins are anticipated to play an essential role in plant salt stress tolerance. HKTs were frst identifed as high-afnity potassium $( \mathrm { K ^ { + } } )$ transporters and were proven to transport sodium $\left( \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \right)$

via channels with other cations (Horie et al. 2009). HKTs are also responsible for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport as well as $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } { - } K ^ { + } }$ homeostasis in plants during plant development, making them potential goals for the development of salt tolerance in crops. Most of the research on the functional study of HKT family genes has focused on yeast and model plants such as Arabidopsis, as well as crops like wheat, maize, sorghum, barley, and eucalyptus (Liu et al. 2001; Rus et al. 2001; Haro et al. 2005; Munns et al. 2012; Ren et al. 2015; Li et al. 2019). However, a more thorough investigation needs to be into HKT family genes in rice.

In this study, we identifed nine HKT genes, whereas eight are functional depending on the japonica and indica cultivars from the rice genome database. Based on the conserved domain search, we confrmed that TrkH is conserved in all the HKT genes (Fig.  2). Te TrkH domain is a hydrophobic membrane protein vital in controlling $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ movement in higher plants, contributing to enhanced salinity tolerance (Horie et  al. 2009; Su et  al. 2015). All OsHKT proteins have similar physiological properties, comprising equal transmembrane helices, and are mainly localized in the plasma membrane (Table 1). Tese fndings indicate that HKT proteins have a close evolutionary connection with plants during biological evolution. Te paralogous pairs of OsHKT genes found in subfamily 1 and 2 of the monophyletic tree also indicate that each subfamily’s HKT genes undergo the same evolutionary process and serve the same functions, and potentially retain plant resistance to salt stress (Maser et al. 2002; Li et al. 2019). Furthermore, ten distinct motifs were discovered, and most of the motifs appeared in rice HKT proteins (Fig. 3B), suggesting that they are relatively conserved and have a strong evolutionary relationship (Singh et al. 2002). HKT genes have three exons and two introns (Fig. 4), demonstrating even more clearly that HKT genes in plants have been evolutionary conserved because the exon–intron arrangement has been utilized as supporting proof for developmental relationships between genes (Koralewski and Krutovsky 2011). In addition, gene duplication events are one of the critical factors that could provide a profound explanation for gene family expansion in plants (Moore and Purugganan 2005). Te chromosomal location ofers valuable information about tandem and segmental duplications of a specifc family gene. Two or more genes located on the same chromosome reveal the possibility of tandem duplication, while genes situated on diferent chromosomes indicate segmental duplication events (Zhu et  al. 2014; Nasim et al. 2016). Notably, two pairs of paralogous OsHKT genes (OsHKT1;4/OsHKT1;5 and OsHKT2;3/ OsHKT2;4) are segmentally duplicated, including OsHKT2;1/Po_OsHKT2;2 was discovered to be tandemly duplicated due to gene distributions on the same chromosome (Fig.  5). To understand functional sites and functional protein alterations, selective pressure investigations are generally required as they reveal selective benefts for changing amino acid sequences in the protein (Morgan et  al. 2010). Te $\mathrm { K a } / \mathrm { K } s$ value $< 1$ indicates the purifying selection, while the Ka/Ks ratio $> 1$ proposes the probability of a positive selection (Yang and Bielawski 2000; Bowers et al. 2003). Based on the $\mathrm { K a } / \mathrm { K } s$ values for both segmental and tandem, they indicated that rice HKT genes have undergone intense purifying selection pressure (Table  2). Te phylogenetic tree (Fig.  6) indicated that rice HKT proteins were related to monocot and dicot; however, they were more closely related to wheat and maize HKT proteins. Te highly conserved cluster of HKT genes provided evidence that they perform similar functions rather than being the result of a series of evolutionary events (Zhang et al. 2013). One pair of orthologous OsHKT genes with maize (OsHKT1;5/ Zm00008a011700) revealed the purifying selection and showed the same intron numbers, which means conserved gene organization (Table  2). Tese fndings suggest that the orthologous pair arose from the common inherited genes that existed before the divergence of the monocots and dicots. It is also mentioned that purifying selection played a vital role in the evolution of the HKT genes in other crop species (Zhang et al. 2019).

Transcription factors are pivotal in regulating the plant’s response to abiotic stress by modulating the gene expression (Lindemose et al. 2013). Regulatory elements are crucial for detecting gene expression patterns, as regulatory elements control the expression of many genes through distinct binding sites (Mariño-Ramírez et  al. 2009). WRKY, bHLH, bZIP, MYB, AP2/ERF, GATA, B3, Dof, and C2H2 type important binding sites that were highly distributed in all the promoter regions of OsHKT genes. TFs like WRKY, NAC, bHLH, bZIP, MYB, and AP2/ERF play vital roles in the responses to abiotic and biotic stress in many plant species (Lindemose et  al. 2013; Das et  al. 2019). Moreover, B3, a plant-specifc transcription factor, has a variety of roles in the growth and development of plants (Peng and Weselake 2013), GATA is involved in light responsiveness (Behringer and Schwechheimer 2015), C2H2 type transcription factor plays a diverse role in plant growth and development as well response to stress (Yin et al. 2020) and Dof transcription factor also participates in many plant development stages and the response to diferent environmental stressors (Khan et al. 2021). Te OsHKT genes possess a high abundance of stress-responsive cis-regulatory elements (CREs) such as MYB, MYC, MBS, W-box, ARE, STRE and DRE core. Te expression of MBS, which is a binding site for MYB TF, changes in many plants when exposed to salt, suggesting that these plants are responding to salt stress (Hua et al. 2006). Moreover, members of this TF also infuence the abscisic acid (ABA), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and SA-signalling pathways, which confer resistance to abiotic stresses (Ambawat et  al. 2013). TGACG, CGTCA-motif, ERE, and ABRE were also abundant in the rice HKT promoter region. Te next most common type of cis-acting elements were those that regulated growth and development, hormones, and light. Te GT1-motif, as1, G-box, TCCC, and Box-4 are more frequently present in rice HKT promoters that were responsive to light. On the other hand, TGACG and CGTCA-motif were responsive to methyl jasmonate, ERE was responsive to ethylene, ABRE was responsive to abscisic acid (ABA), TCA was responsive to salicylic acid, TGA was responsive to auxins and P-box and GAREmotif were responsive to gibberellin. Plant hormones and other signalling pathways are important for adequate and integrated stress responses (Ryu and Cho 2015). ABA, methyl jasmonate, and ethylene have been suggested as factors governing adaptive responses to abiotic stimuli, while auxin, salicylic acid, and gibberellin are essential in growth and development. Te presence of TGACG and CGTCA motifs suggests that methyl jasmonate may be involved in the regulation of the OsHKT gene. In line with this, a signifcant concentration of methyl jasmonate has been found in salt-tolerant rice cultivars (Kang et al. 2005). ERE-containing genes are regulated in the context of ethylene. It has been proposed that ethylene controls salt-responsive gene expression under salt stress (Verma et al. 2016). Most abiotic stress-responsive gene promoter regions comprise two cis-regulating elements, namely ABA-responsive elements (ABRE) and dehydration-responsive elements (DRE), both of which contain the core sequences ACGTGG/TC and TACCGA CAT or A/GCCGAC, respectively (Kobayashi et al. 2004; Yamaguchi-Shinozaki and Shinozaki 2006) and the ABRE motif participates in the ABA-dependent gene expression under high-stress situations (Finkelstein 2013). According to previous research, there are interactions between ABA and methyl jasmonate at the MYC2 transcription factor, which is implicated in the control of gene expression under salt stress (Moons et  al. 1997). Tus, cis-elements pertaining to ABA, ethylene, and methyl jasmonate suggest that these hormones have roles in OsHKTs in response to abiotic stresses. Various elements, such as W-box, WUN-motif, LTR, and TC-rich repeat also present in OsHKT promoter regions, are implicated in the salt stress response and defence (Gao et  al. 2010; Li et  al. 2013; Manimaran et  al. 2017). According to promoter analysis, OsHKTs may respond to environmental stress and stimuli to regulate plant growth and development. On the other hand, we have discovered that a wide range of transcription factors control OsHKT gene expression. Tese include C2H2 zinc fnger protein, Myb transcription factor, Dof zinc fnger domain-containing protein, DNA binding domain-containing protein, B3 domain-containing RAV and trihelix family-type protein, ARF, and dehydration-responsive transcription factors. Recent fndings have reported that the expression of OsHKT1;1 has been positively regulated by OsMYBc. It binds to specifc conserved DNA regions in the OsHKT1;1 promoter, modulating $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration and preventing sodium toxicity in leaf blades (Wang et al. 2015). Knocking out OsMYBc also led to a decrease in the salt-induced expression of OsHKT1;1, and modifcations in specifc promoter regions resulted in reduced OsHKT1;1 promoter activity. To increase the expression of OsHKT1;5, the stable complex of OsSUVH7, OsMYB106, and OsBAG4 binds to the promoter of OsHKT1;5 (Wang et  al. 2020). It has been shown that the bHLH transcription factor OsbHLH035 controls the expression of the genes OsHKT1;3 and OsHKT1;5. Tese fndings indicate that OsbHLH035 positively infuences the expression of OsHKT1;3 and OsHKT1;5 (Chen et al. 2018). Chen and his team identifed a popular TF, PalERF109, as a positive regulator of the PalHKT1 gene expression (Chen et  al. 2020b). In Arabidopsis, several TFs, such as AtbZIP24, ARR1, ARR12, and ABI4, have been found to regulate AtHKT1;1 expression (Yang et al. 2009; Mason et al. 2010; Shkolnik-Inbar et al. 2013). Te observation indicated that AtbZIP24, ARR1, and ARR12 are negative regulators of AtHKT1;1 gene expression. Additionally, ABI4 TF also negatively regulates AtHKT1;1 gene expression, and the involvement of the abscisic acid signal transduction pathway in salt responses in Arabidopsis suggests that OsHKT1;5 may play a similar function in rice. Te GT factors are a family of transcription factors found exclusively in plants and share a common DNA-binding trihelix domain. GT elements have A/T-rich core sequences and are highly degenerate ciselements. OsGTγ-1, OsGTγ-2, and OsGTγ-3 genes were upregulated in response to high salinity and other abiotic stimuli, suggesting a role for this subfamily transcriptional regulation of stress responses. At the vegetative stage, transgenic rice with an overexpression of OsGTγ- 1 demonstrated an improvement in their salt tolerance (Fang et al. 2010). On the other hand, DREB TFs, which mainly bind with C-repeat/DRE (A/GCCGAC), infuence the expression of several cold or drought-inducible genes in an ABA-independent route, enhancing plant abiotic stress tolerance (Chen et al. 2008). Tus, these TFs have roles in OsHKTs in response to abiotic stresses.

In our study, OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;5 had higher expression levels in both vegetative and reproductive tissues. On the other hand, OsHKT1;3, OsHKT2;1, and OsHKT2;4 had higher expression in the vegetative stage, while OsHKT1;4 had lower expression in the vegetative stage (Fig.  11A). Also, both salt-tolerant and salt-sensitive genotypes have higher expression of OsHKT1;5, OsHKT1;1, OsHKT1;3, and OsHKT2;1 (Fig.  11B). Our real-time PCR results have confrmed that OsHKT1;5, OsHKT1;1, OsHKT1;3, OsHKT2;1, and OsHKT2;3 are crucial genes responsible for rice salinity tolerance (Fig. 12). Te previous study on OsHKT1;4 also reported lower expression in a vegetative stage during stress (Suzuki et al. 2016). A rice QTL, SKC1, corresponded to OsHKT1;5 and maintained $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ion homeostasis under salt stress (Ren et  al. 2005), and OsHKT1;5 mutants also showed $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion and protected leaf blades under salt stress (Kobayashi et  al. 2017). OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT1;4 contribute to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ exclusion from leaf blades under salt stress (Cotsaftis et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2015; Suzuki et al. 2016). OsHKT2;1/2 is also involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ co-transport under high salt concentrations and has been reported to maintain an appropriate ionic balance in Nona bokra (Oomen et  al. 2012). Te previous report also suggested that HKT genes play a vital role in response to salt stress in many plant species like wheat (Munns et  al. 2012; Schachtman and Schroeder 1994), Arabidopsis (Sunarpi et al. 2005), maize (Ren et al. 2015) and barley (Mian et  al. 2011). Tus, HKT genes in rice may be excellent candidate genes for accelerating transgenic research for salinity stress management in plant growth and development.

Proteins rarely function alone. A protein’s activity can be activated, inhibited, or otherwise regulated through its interactions with other proteins or biological components. So far, no study has been disclosed identifying interaction partners for any HKT protein. Te protein– protein interaction exhibited exciting facts about the substantial contribution of OsHKT to numerous physiological functions (Fig.  13). Our fndings show that rice HKT genes (OsHKT1;1 and OsHKT2;1) interact with the P5CS, which participates in salt stress tolerance and plays a vital role in proline biosynthesis (Zhang et  al. 2014; Funck et  al. 2020). Likewise, the OsHKT gene interacted with NHX1 and NHX2, a sodium/hydrogen exchanger-related protein that plays a central role during plant exposure to $\mathrm { K ^ { + } }$ defciency and high salinity (Fukuda et al. 2011; Barragán et al. 2012; Teng et al. 2017); HAK1, HAK23, and HAK27 are related to high-afnity potassium transporters that also transport rubidium. Furthermore, Os01g0893400 is a putative BTB and TAZ domain protein, and TPKC is an inward-rectifying potassium channel family protein that is known to be important in plant growth and development (Bhattacharjee et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018). Interestingly, a small heat shock family protein, Hsp20/alpha-crystallin family protein, also interacts with rice HKT genes. Small HSPs are hypothesized to act as chaperones, protecting their targets against denaturation and aggregation when organisms are exposed to diverse biotic and abiotic stimuli. A recent study indicated that OsHSP20 exhibits molecular chaperone functions in  vitro, and overexpression has been shown to improve heat and salt stress tolerance in E. coli, $P .$ pastoris, and transgenic rice plants. It was also found that the N-terminal part of OsHSP20 is tightly linked to both in vivo stress tolerance and in vitro chaperone activity (Guo et al. 2020). Our results highlighted the signifcance of HKT transporters in rice salinity tolerance via their interactions with other proteins.

Plant cellular responses to abiotic stresses such as salinity, cold, and dehydration were revealed to be regulated by microRNA. Several miRNAs target genes that are actively involved in gene regulation or their associated transcription factors in response to stress. MiRNAs may play an essential role in reactions triggered by stress (Cheng and Long 2007; Sunkar et al. 2008). Fifteen OsamiR11339 (bona fde mRNAs from rice) found in rice HKT genes represent lipid metabolisms in rice by targeting the terpene synthase gene (LOC_Os07g11790) (Baldrich et  al. 2015) and also revealing the role in protein and starch metabolisms during grain flling under high day time temperature (HDT) stress (Payne et  al. 2023). Four Osa-miR11343 genes found in rice HKT genes are involved in biotic stress by targeting the MLO domaincontaining protein (LOC_Os10g39520) in rice. One novel Osa-miR5819 has three target sites found in rice HKT gene-targeted CPuORF -containing bZIP38 TF and lipid transfer protein (LTPL118) subject to translational control via regulation by sucrose (Baldrich et  al. 2015). Sucrose is a signal molecule that is involved in the activation of plant defense mechanisms. Another miR444 found in the rice HKT gene specifcally targets the MADS-box transcription factors, which play an essential role in the HDT-induced caryopsis development, (Payne et al. 2023). Evidence has also shown that heat stress has been demonstrated to induce an upregulation of miR444 in maize (He et  al. 2019). Interestingly, we found two microRNAs, Osa-miR1846 and Osa-miRN45, have several target sites in rice HKT genes. In both CDT and HDT, Osa-miR1846 was found to be strongly expressed during grain flling in the spikelets and its targeting of a heat shock factor (HSF) (Kushawaha et  al. 2021). HSFs may cause chalkiness by increasing the expression of heat shock proteins (Kaneko et al. 2016). Terefore, it is probable that increased amounts of Osa-miR1846 in the Cypress inhibit this HSF, resulting in less chalkiness. On the other hand, Osa-miRN45 has a particular function to play throughout the diferentiation process at the time of grain flling in rice (Peng et  al. 2013). Together, these fndings lay the groundwork for future genetic studies of OsHKT genes and facilitate the breeding of novel rice cultivars.

Cadmium (Cd) is a toxic metal that can accumulate in human body and cause diseases such as renal dysfunction, osteoporosis and cancers (Åkesson et al. 2014; IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) 1993; Nordberg 2009). Among different toxic metals, Cd has a relatively high mobility in the soil-plant systems and can readily accumulate in the edible parts of food crops. Humans are exposed to Cd primarily via food consumption, with cereal grains contributing a large proportion to the total dietary intake (Clemens et al. 2013; European Food Safety Authority 2009). The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food

Additives has recommended a tolerable daily intake (TDI) of $0 . 8 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { g } ~ \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ body weight (Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives 2010), whilst the European Food Standard Authority and The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry of the USA have recommended even lower limits (0.36 and $0 . 1 ~ { \mu \mathrm { g } } ~ \mathrm { k g } ^ { - 1 }$ body weight $\mathrm { d a y } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively) (Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) 2012; European Food Safety Authority 2012). The FAO/WHO limit is exceeded in subsets of populations in some countries including China, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka (Chen et al. 2018; Meharg et al. 2013; Zhao et al. 2015), raising concerns about the risk to human health. Rice is the most important dietary source of Cd for Asian populations, contributing $40 \%$ and $56 \%$ to the dietary Cd intake for the general population in Japan and China, respectively (Song et al. 2017; Watanabe et al. 2000). Subsistence rice farmers are particularly prone to Cdinduced diseases, because low levels of zinc and iron in polished rice can lead to elevated Cd bioavailability and toxicity (Chaney 2015). Whilst dietary intake of Cd in developed countries has decreased over the last decades due to stricter legislation of environmental protection (Nordberg et al. 2007), Cd intake appears to be increasing in some developing countries. For example, total diet studies in China have shown that the average dietary Cd intake for the general population has more than doubled during the 25 years from 1990 to 2015 (Song et al. 2017). It is therefore important to understand how Cd enters the food crops in order to develop mitigation strategies.

Among different cereal grains, rice often contains higher levels of Cd than other cereals. In a total diet study including tens of thousands of samples collected across China, Song et al. (2017) showed that the average Cd concentration in rice grains was 3 and 8 times those in wheat and other cereal grains, respectively. Similarly, a survey in Japan showed a 2.5 fold higher geometric mean of Cd concentration in polished rice than that in wheat flour (Shimbo et al. 2001). Because rice is typically grown under submerged conditions, which decrease Cd availability markedly (Arao et al. 2009; de Livera et al. 2011; Khaokaew et al. 2011), it might be expected that rice would accumulate less Cd than other cereals that are grown under upland conditions. To explain why rice apparently accumulates more Cd in the grain than other cereals, we hypothesize that rice plants have a greater ability for Cd uptake or translocation than other cereals. This hypothesis and the underlying molecular mechanism are tested in the present study.

As a toxic and non-essential trace element, Cd is taken up by plants inadvertently via transporters for essential elements, such as Fe, Zn and Mn (Clemens and Ma 2016; Uraguchi and Fujiwara 2013). In rice (Oryza sativa), Cd uptake into the root cells is primarily mediated by the Mn transporter OsNramp5 (Natural Resistance-Associated Macrophage Protein 5) (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Ishimaru et al. 2012; Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). This transporter protein is localized to the plasma membrane of root cells. Knocking out the OsNramp5 gene resulted in ${ > } 9 0 \%$ reduction in Cd uptake (Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). Mutation in the gene reduced Cd accumulation in rice grain markedly (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Tang et al. 2017a). The shared uptake pathway between Mn and Cd also explains why increasing Mn supply decreased Cd uptake by rice plants (Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). Other transporters, such as OsIRT1 (Iron-Regulated Transporter 1), OsIRT2 and OsNramp1, may also contribute to Cd uptake in rice, but their contributions are likely to be small (Nakanishi et al. 2006; Takahashi et al. 2011). Much less is known about the mechanisms of Cd uptake in other cereals. HvNramp5 is involved in Cd uptake in barley, but its relative contribution appears to be smaller than that of OsNramp5 in rice (Wu et al. 2016). It is not known if the Nramp5 orthologues in wheat and maize are able to transport Cd. The antagonistic effect of Zn on Cd uptake in wheat suggests that Cd may be partly taken up via Zn transporters (Hart et al. 2005; Hart et al. 2002).

Apart from root uptake of Cd, root-to-shoot translocation is another important step in controlling Cd accumulation in the above-ground tissues (Uraguchi et al. 2009). OsHMA3 $\mathrm { \Delta P _ { 1 B } }$ type Heavy Metal ATPase 3) is a tonoplast Cd transporter responsible for sequestering Cd into the vacuoles in rice (Miyadate et al. 2011; Ueno et al. 2010). The functionality of OsHMA3 is a strong determinant of Cd translocation. Rice cultivars possessing the loss-of-function or weak alleles of the OsHMA3 have low abilities to sequester Cd in the root vacuoles, leading to high Cd translocation to the shoots (Miyadate et al. 2011; Ueno et al. 2010; Yan et al. 2016). Other genes that can also influence Cd translocation in rice included OsHMA2 and OsCAL1 (Luo et al. 2018; Satoh-Nagasawa et al. 2012; Yamaji et al. 2013b). In durum wheat, a major locus controlling Cd translocation has been identified (Wiebe et al. 2010), but the causal gene remains unknown. Distribution of Cd from the vegetative tissues to the grain is also an important process controlling the accumulation of Cd in the grain. OsLCT1, a low affinity cation transporter, has been shown to be involved in the phloem-mediated Cd transport to the grain (Uraguchi et al. 2011).

In the present study, we compared Cd uptake and translocation in three major cereal species, rice, wheat and maize. We further cloned Nramp5 orthologues from wheat and maize, characterized their transport activities for Cd and Mn and quantified the absolute expression levels of Nramp5 genes in the three plant species. Our results provide mechanistic insight into the different abilities of Cd uptake between rice, wheat and maize.

Soil is a fundamental and indispensable resource for global agricultural production. However, not all soil conditions are suitable for crop growth and harvest. Soil contamination caused by toxic elements threatens food safety and poses signifcant risks to human health. Among inorganic contaminants, cadmium $\mathrm { ( C d ) }$ is one of the most toxic elements. The National Soil Pollution Survey report demonstrates that Cd is the most prevalent contaminant, with $7 \%$ of soil samples covering over $7 0 \%$ of land exceeding the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP) limit in China. In addition to its natural occurrence in the Earth’s crust, Cd in the environment originates from human activities such as metal mining, industrialization, and wastewater irrigation (Zhao et  al. 2015, 2022). Furthermore, nitrogen fertilizer application accelerates soil acidifcation, increasing Cd solubility and mobility in soil systems, which leads to higher uptake rates in cultivated plants (Zhao et  al. 2015). Cd poses serious risks to plants, animals, and humans. In plants, Cd accumulation inhibits plant growth by disrupting essential metabolic and physiological processes; In humans, Cd accumulation increases the incidence of severe diseases such as osteoporosis, kidney damage, and Itai-Itai disease, with efects reported even at the epigenetic level (Khan et  al. 2020; Lv et  al. 2017; Li et  al. 2021; Horiguchi et  al. 1994; Zhang et  al. 2023). Humans are mainly exposed to Cd via the food chain, particularly through the soil–plant-human continuum. Cd excess in soils is an evident threat to food safety (Clemens et  al. 2013; Zhao et al. 2015; Zhang et al. 2021b). In recent years, Cd contamination has worsened, with reports showing a 2.2-fold increase in the Chinese population’s exposure to Cd through the food chain compared to the 1990s (Song et al. 2017).

There is a real need to limit Cd transfer from soil to the food chain, and great efort is directed towards obtaining plants with lower Cd-accumulation rates in the edible parts. For this purpose, many studies have been conducted to reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying Cd absorption and translocation in rice and in the model plant Arabidopsis (Zhao et al. 2022). Primarily, Cd, as a non-essential metal, can enter plants through essential elements’ transporters, such as iron $\mathrm { ( F e ) }$ , zinc $( Z \boldsymbol { \mathrm { n } } )$ , manganese (Mn), and calcium $\mathrm { ( C a ) }$ transporters (Clemens and Ma 2016; Zhao et al. 2022). The zinc‐regulated transporter, and the iron‐regulated transporter-like proteins (ZRT-IRT-related protein, ZIP) are present in plants, animals, and microorganisms and are responsible for Zn and Fe translocation. In tobacco, it was reported that NtZIP4B was responsible for Zn and Cd transport (Barabasz et al. 2019). In Arabidopsis thaliana, Cd was found to be absorbed into roots via the broad-spectrum transporter AtIRT1 (iron-regulated transporter 1). Orthologue IRT1 proteins in wheat, Brassica. rapa (B. rapa), and rice also demonstrated Cd transport activity (Zhang et al. 2021a; Wu et al. 2021; Jiang et al. 2021).

Another relevant protein family associated with metal transport is NRAMPs (natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins), a family of proteins found in mammals, plants, and bacteria (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Nramp family members are generally composed of 11 or 12 transmembrane domains (TMs), with the frst 10 forming LeuT structures that contain complex but conserved metal ion-binding sites (Ehrnstorfer et al. 2014). Although NRAMPs are mainly involved in Mn and Fe absorption in plants, they may also contribute to Cd uptake. The presence of cysteine or methionine sulfur in the metal-binding site can even make Cd their preferred substrate (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Six Nramp transporters have been identifed in Arabidopsis thaliana. AtNramp1, $- 2 , - 3$ , and $^ { - 4 }$ participate in Cd, Mn, and Fe transport (Cailliatte et al. 2010; Lanquar et al. 2010; Gao et  al. 2018). AtNramp6 shows a high afnity for Fe and Cd and cooperates with AtNramp1 in Mn utilization (Li et al. 2022). NtNramp5 in Nicotiana tabacum also participates in Mn and Cd transport, while a cultivar possessing truncated NtNramp5 protein lost Cd/Mn transport activity (Tang et  al. 2017). In rice, it has been reported that OsNramp5 plays a major role in Cd uptake, and the mutant plants containing a defective OsNramp5 protein show decreased Cd uptake (Yang et  al. 2014; Sasaki et  al. 2012; Ishikawa et  al. 2012). Furthermore, changes in OsNramp5 expression levels can afect Cd uptake and translocation. For instance, OsNramp5 overexpression reduces Cd accumulation in rice grain by interfering with Cd transport into the stele and subsequent loading into the xylem (Chang et  al.

2020a). Considering that OsNramp5 activity is essential for Mn transport, it has been stated that the knockout of OsNramp5 largely decreases Mn and Cd absorption (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Ishimaru et al. 2012). On the other hand, OsNramp5 duplication in the rice cultivar Pokkali increases Cd and Mn uptake into root cells but simultaneously reduces Cd movement to the xylem (Yu et al. 2022). Kuramata et al. (2022) showed that a specifc amino acid change in the OsNramp5 protein can reduce Cd uptake without disrupting Mn absorption (Kuramata et al. 2022). In barley and buckwheat, HvNramp5 and FeNramp5 mediate Mn and Cd uptake in roots (Yokosho et al. 2020; Wu et al. 2016).

Green leafy vegetables are essential components of the human daily diet due to their high nutritional value and signifcant role in the diet of inhabitants in Asian countries. These vegetables are rich in minerals and vitamins and hold great potential for application in the feld of fortifed foods (Sarkar et al. 2023). While green leafy vegetables provide an adequate intake of essential trace elements, members of the Brassicaceae family are known to accumulate relatively high levels of Cd in their leaves (Kuboi et  al. 1986). Due to this distinctive ability, the B. rapa cultivar Beijingxiaoza 56 has been proposed as a promising plant for phytoremediation (Liu et  al. 2011). However, this characteristic presents a challenge, as leafy vegetable consumption accounts for $1 0 { - } 4 0 \%$ of dietary Cd exposure among the Asian population (Chen et al. 2018; Song et al. 2017; He et al. 2013).

In the present study, we characterized a Nramp orthologue in B. rapa, BrNramp1 (Bra003587), which is mainly expressed in roots and encodes a plasma membrane-localized protein playing an important role in Mn and Cd uptake. BrNramp1 overexpression in atnarmp1 mutant could accomplish Cd absorption. The present study suggests BrNramp1 participant in Cd and Mn accumulation of Brassica rapa, with a 17-amino-acid deletion in TM3 resulting in the loss-of-function in Cd and Mn transport.

Background and aims Cereals are the main dietary source of cadmium (Cd). Rice grains often contain higher levels of Cd than other cereals, but the reasons are unknown. The aims of this study were to compare Cd uptake, translocation and influx kinetics between rice, wheat and maize and to investigate whether the expression and functionality of Nramp5 genes differ between the three crop species.

Methods Two cultivars each of rice, wheat and maize were grown hydroponically and exposed to a range of Cd concentrations. Nramp5 genes were cloned from the three plants and their expression levels determined. The Cd transport activities of Nramp5 proteins were tested in yeast.

Results Under hydroponic conditions, Cd uptake in rice was 2.5–8.1 and 1.1–3.6 times that of wheat and maize, respectively. The maximum Cd influx velocity of rice was 6.5 and 2.2 times that in wheat and maize, respectively. Wheat showed the lowest Cd uptake but the highest Cd root-to-shoot translocation. The absolute expression level of OsNramp5 in rice roots was 4–5 times that of TaNramp5A and TaNramp5D in wheat or ZmNramp5 in maize. All Nramp5 proteins were localized to the plasma membrane. When expressed in yeast, OsNramp5 showed a greater Cd transport activity than wheat or maize Nramp5.

Conclusions Rice has a greater Cd uptake ability than wheat or maize, likely because OsNramp5 is more highly expressed and the protein has a higher Cd transport activity than wheat or maize Nramp5.

Keywords Cadmium $\cdot$ Maize $\cdot$ Nramp5 $\cdot$ Rice $\cdot$ Uptake . Wheat

Rice showed a higher Cd uptake than wheat and maize

After exposure to a range of Cd concentrations (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 and $1 . 5 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { \Omega }$ for $^ { 4 \mathrm { d } }$ , the roots of both rice cultivars accumulated much higher levels of Cd than maize or wheat, with wheat showing the lowest accumulation among the three plant species (Fig. 1a). There were no significant differences between either the two wheat cultivars or the two maize cultivars, but the japonica cultivar Nipponbare accumulated significantly higher Cd concentration in the roots than the indica cultivar 9311. On average of the two cultivars, rice roots accumulated 6.2–9.8 and $1 . 6 { - } 4 . 0$ times higher Cd concentrations than wheat and maize, respectively, with the difference being largest at the low concentrations of Cd (0.1 and $0 . 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ in the nutrient solutions. In the shoots, Cd concentrations were also significantly higher in rice than in wheat and maize in the two low Cd treatments (0.1 and $0 . 2 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ ) (Fig. 1b). In the treatments with higher Cd concentrations $( 0 . 5 \mathrm { - } 1 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , rice no longer had the highest Cd concentrations in the shoots. At $1 . 0 \mu \mathrm { M C d }$ , maize had the highest Cd concentrations in the shoots, whereas at $1 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, both maize and wheat became the higher accumulators of Cd in the shoots than rice, with the difference being significant when compared to Nipponbare. Between the two rice cultivars, 9311 accumulated higher Cd concentrations in the shoots than Nipponbare across all Cd treatments, a pattern that was opposite to the Cd concentrations in the roots.

Total Cd uptake in both roots and shoots was calculated and expressed on the basis of root dry weight (Fig. 1c). On average of the two cultivars per crop species, Cd uptake by rice was 2.5–8.1 times that of wheat and 1.1– 3.6 times that of maize. The difference was much more pronounced at the low levels of solution Cd than at the high concentrations of Cd. At 1.0 and $1 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, Cd uptake was comparable between rice and maize. The ratio of shoot to root Cd concentrations reflects Cd translocation from the roots to the shoots. This ratio showed a general pattern of wheat $>$ maize $>$ rice, particularly at the higher Cd concentrations in solutions (Fig. 1d). Whilst the ratios in rice and maize remained relatively stable across different Cd concentrations, the ratio in wheat increased more or less linearly with solution Cd. A similar pattern was observed in the shoot Cd content expressed as a percentage of the total Cd uptake (Supplementary Fig. S1). Among the three plant species, rice had the highest Mn concentrations in the shoots and highest Mn uptake per unit root weight (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Rice showed a higher Cd influx than wheat and maize

The above experiment was conducted with relatively long (4 days) exposure to Cd. An experiment was carried out to determine the short-term $2 0 \mathrm { m i n } )$ uptake kinetics of Cd, which reflect the influx of Cd into the root cells. One cultivar each of rice (Nipponbare), wheat (Jimai22) and maize (Zhengdan958) were selected for this experiment. At $4 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , Cd concentration in the roots increased slowly with the external Cd concentration, likely representing the apoplastic binding of Cd in the cell walls (Fig. 2a). There were no significant differences between the three plant species in root Cd accumulation at $4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ At $2 8 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , Cd uptake showed a hyperbolic pattern with increasing Cd concentration in the uptake solution. At this temperature, large differences between the three plant species were observed. Symplastic Cd uptake was estimated by subtracting the mean Cd concentrations at $4 { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ from those at $2 8 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and the resulting data of the net Cd uptake were fitted to a Michalies-Menten equation to derive the uptake kinetic parameters $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ (Fig. 2b). $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ for Cd influx in rice was 2.2 and 6.5 times that in maize and wheat, respectively, whereas $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values were comparable between the three plant species.

Phylogenetic and sequence analysis of Nramp5 in rice, wheat and maize

We first conducted a phylogenetic analysis on the Nramp family members from rice, wheat, maize and the model plant species Arabidopsis thaliana. There are 7, 8, and 6 Nramp members in the genomes of rice, maize, and Arabidopsis, respectively. The hexaploid wheat has three genomes (A, B and D) with 8, 11 and 8 Nramp members, respectively. Phylogenetic analysis reveals that two Nramp members in the wheat genomes A and D and one member in the maize genome have a close relationship with OsNramp5 (Supplementary Fig. S3); these are termed TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D, ZmNramp5, respectively. No close homologue of Nramp5 was found in the B genome of wheat. The other Nramp members are also named according to their relationship with the corresponding OsNramp members.

To analyze the sequences of Nramp5 from the three plant species, we cloned the Nramp5 genes from all cultivars of the three plant species used in the present study and determined their sequences by Sanger sequencing. There were no differences between the two cultivars of each plant species in the amino acid sequences encoded by Nramp5 genes (data not shown), but there were differences between the three plant species (Fig. 3). The coding sequences of Nramp5 genes among the three plant species shared $7 9 . 9 6 { - } 8 3 . 8 8 \%$ nucleotide similarity, and the protein sequences shared $8 2 . 9 0 { - } 8 5 . 3 7 \%$ identity (Fig. 3). There were 538, 540, 538 and 543 amino acid residues in OsNramp5, TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5, respectively. By alignment with ScaDMA, a Nramp transporter from Staphylococcus capitis for which the protein structure has been determined (Ehrnstorfer et al. 2014), putative transmembrane domains and metal binding sites could be identified in the four Nramp5 proteins from rice, wheat and maize (Fig. 3).


## TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5 are localized to the plasma membrane


OsNramp5 is localized to the plasma membrane (Sasaki et al. 2012). To observe the subcellular localization of TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5, we expressed these genes fused in-frame with enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) in tobacco (Nicotiana benthamiana) leaves. In the control expressing eGFP alone, the GFP signal was observed throughout the cells (Fig. 4). In contrast, the GFP signal in the leaves expressing TaNramp5A-eGFP, TaNramp5D-eGFP or ZmNramp5-eGFP was observed only at the plasma membrane, which overlapped with the signal from the plasma membrane marker dye FM4-64FX (Fig. 4). These results indicate that Nramp5 proteins from both wheat and maize are localized to the plasma membrane.

OsNramp5 showed higher Cd and Mn transport activities than ZmNramp5, TaNramp5A or TaNramp5D

To test the Cd transport activity of different Nramp5 proteins, we expressed four Nramp5 genes (two from wheat and one each from rice and maize) in wild-type yeast (Sey6210). The sensitivity of the transformed yeast cells to Cd was tested. In the absence of Cd, the transformed yeast cells expressing empty vector or different Nramp5 genes showed no difference in the growth curve (Fig. 5a). In the presence of $2 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd, growth of all transformed yeast cells was inhibited, but the inhibition was significantly larger in the cells expressing different Nramp5 genes than that in the vector control (Fig. 5a). Moreover, growth of the yeast cells expressing OsNramp5 was inhibited by Cd to a greater extent than those expressing either ZmNramp5, TaNramp5A or TaNramp5D. The uptake of Cd by transformed yeast cells was determined after exposure to $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd for $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ . Yeast cells expressing OsNramp5 accumulated $64 \%$ higher concentration of Cd $( P < 0 . 0 1 )$ )

than the empty vector control (Fig. 5b). Yeast cells expressing either ZmNramp5, TaNramp5A or TaNramp5D accumulated $1 3 \mathrm { - } 1 8 \%$ higher levels of Cd than the empty vector control, but the differences did not reach a significant level $P = 0 . 1 7 – 0 . 3 5$ ). These results suggest that OsNramp5 had a higher transport activity for Cd, whereas ZmNramp5, TaNramp5A or TaNramp5D had relatively weak transport activities for Cd.

OsNramp5 is a major transporter for Mn (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Ishimaru et al. 2012; Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). We tested if Nramp5 from wheat and maize could also transport Mn by expressing different Nramp5 genes in the Mn uptake deficient yeast mutant △smf1. In the absence of the Mn chelator EGTA, all transformed yeast cells grew equally well (Supplementary Fig. S4). Additions of 2 or $3 ~ \mathrm { \ m M }$ EGTA decreased the Mn availability in the medium and suppressed the growth of the vector control cells. Expression of Nramp5 genes reduced the growth suppression of EGTA, with the effect being more noticeable in the yeast cells expressing OsNramp5 t h a n t h os e e x p r e s s i n g e i t h e r Z m N r a m p 5 , TaNramp5A or TaNramp5D (Supplementary Fig. S4). These results suggest that Nramp5 proteins from wheat and maize have a weaker transport activity for Mn than OsNramp5.

The Nramp5 expression level was higher in rice than in wheat and maize

To compare the expression levels of Nramp5 genes in different plant species, we determined the absolute expression levels of Nramp5 genes in the roots using absolute quantification qRT-PCR. The results showed that the copy numbers of OsNramp5 in both rice cultivars were 4–5 times higher than those in wheat and maize (Fig. 6), indicating that OsNramp5 was expressed at a much higher level than TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D or ZmNramp5.

Compared with European and American populations, Asian populations generally have higher dietary Cd intakes (Wang et al. 2017), suggesting that rice, the staple food for the latter, may contain higher levels of Cd than other cereals. Nationwide surveys in China and Japan showed that this was indeed the case, with rice containing substantially higher levels of Cd than wheat and other cereals (Shimbo et al. 2001; Song et al. 2017). The difference could be due to soil or plant factors. To exclude soil factors, we compared Cd uptake in rice, wheat and maize under the same hydroponic conditions using a range of Cd concentrations. Our results showed that rice had a much greater ability to take up Cd than wheat and maize (Fig. 1). The difference was particularly large at the low concentrations of Cd $0 . 1 { - } 0 . 2 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ , which are environmentally more relevant because soil solution Cd concentrations are typically in the nM – sub $\mu \mathrm { M }$ range (Chaney 2015; Smolders and Mertens 2013). At the low Cd concentration range in the solution, not only root but also shoot Cd concentration was significantly higher in rice than in wheat and maize (Fig. 1). These results suggest that root Cd uptake is an important determinant of Cd accumulation in the shoots when different plant species are compared. In the short-term $( 2 0 \ \mathrm { m i n } )$ ) experiment examining the Cd influx kinetics, rice showed approximately 2–6 fold higher $V _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ for Cd influx than wheat or maize (Fig. 2), indicating a higher capacity for Cd transport in rice roots.

In order to understand why rice possesses a higher ability of Cd uptake, we cloned and characterized Nramp5 genes from the three cereal species, because OsNramp5 is known to be the main transporter mediating Cd uptake into rice roots (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Ishimaru et al. 2012; Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). Nramp5 proteins from wheat (TaNramp5A and TaNramp5D) and maize (ZmNramp5) share a high identity in the amino acid sequence to OsNramp5 in rice (Fig. 3). TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5 from wheat and maize were found to be localized to the plasma membrane (Fig. 4), as has been found for OsNramp5 (Ishimaru et al. 2012; Sasaki et al. 2012). However, there are two key differences between Nramp5s in the three plant species. First, TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5 were expressed at much lower levels in the roots of wheat and maize than OsNramp5 in rice (Fig. 6). Similarly, HvNramp5 was expressed at a lower level in barley roots than OsNramp5 in rice roots (Wu et al. 2016). Previous studies showed that the transcript abundance of OsNramp5 in rice roots was not affected by Mn supply or Cd treatments (Sasaki et al. 2012; Yang et al. 2014). Second, when expressed in yeast, TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5 showed lower transport activities for both Cd and Mn than OsNramp5 (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. S4). Although the four Nramp5 proteins are highly similar in their amino acid sequences, there also exist differences in the regions of the trans-membrane domains that could affect their transport activities for Cd and Mn (Fig. 3). For example, a number of amino acid residues in the transmembrane domains 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 were identical among TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5, but different from those in OsNramp5 (Fig. 3). Whether any of these differences cause different transport activities for Cd and Mn remain to be investigated. Taken together, the results from the present study suggest that different expression and transport activities of Nramp5 are likely to be important reasons for the different abilities of Cd uptake between rice and wheat or maize. Similarly,

Nramp5 probably also explains why rice was more efficient in Mn uptake than wheat and maize under the same hydroponic conditions (Supplementary Fig. S2). For wheat and maize, it is possible that other divalent metal transporters, e.g. those for Zn and Fe, may make greater contributions to Cd uptake. Knockouts of TaNramp5A, TaNramp5D and ZmNramp5 are needed to confirm whether they contribute to Cd uptake in wheat and maize.

Accumulation of Cd in the above-ground tissues depends not only on root uptake, but also on root-toshoot translocation. Despite a much higher ability of root Cd uptake, rice showed the lowest root-to-shoot translocation of Cd among the three plant species (Fig. 1). In contrast, wheat showed the lowest Cd uptake but the highest root-to-shoot translocation. In addition, the ratio of shoot to root Cd concentrations in wheat increased more or less linearly with increasing Cd concentration in the nutrient solution (Fig. 1), suggesting that wheat has a relatively low capacity to sequester Cd in the root cells. It has been shown that OsHMA3, a tonoplast Cd transporter, plays a crucial role in sequestering Cd in the vacuoles of root cells in rice (Miyadate et al. 2011; Ueno et al. 2010; Yan et al. 2016). Some rice cultivars possess OsHMA3 alleles that encode proteins with low or no Cd transporting activities, resulting in diminished Cd sequestration in the root cells and greatly elevated Cd translocation to the shoots (Miyadate et al.

2011; Ueno et al. 2010; Yan et al. 2016). Similarly, functional variation in HMA3 explains the variation in Cd translocation among natural accessions of Arabidopsis thaliana (Chao et al. 2012). It would be interesting to investigate the Cd-transporting functionality of HMA3 orthologues in wheat. Whether rice, wheat and maize differ in the redistribution of Cd from the vegetative tissues to the grain also require further investigation.

In conclusion, our results show that rice had a higher Cd uptake ability than wheat and maize under hydroponic conditions. This difference is likely due to a much higher expression level of OsNramp5 than the orthologues in wheat and maize. Additionally, OsNramp5 also showed higher transport activities for Cd and Mn than TaNramps and ZmNramp5. The higher Cd uptake ability in rice may explain why exceedance of the rice Cd limit is prevalent in rice grain produced in some parts of China even when soils are only moderately contaminated (Chen et al. 2018; Clemens and Ma 2016; Du et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2016; Zhao et al. 2015; Zhu et al. 2016). OsNramp5 is therefore a primary target for manipulating Cd uptake in rice. Knocking out OsNramp5 via mutation or gene editing has been shown to be highly effective at decreasing grain Cd concentration (Ishikawa et al. 2012; Tang et al. 2017a; Ueno et al. 2010), although mutating OsNramp5 may run the risk of inducing Mn deficiency in plants grown in soils with low Mn availability. Alternatively, increasing Mn availability can suppress Cd uptake via competition for the same transporter (Ueno et al. 2010; Yang et al. 2014). For wheat and maize, the contribution of Nramp5 to Cd uptake is likely to be smaller than in rice, and the measures targeting the $\mathrm { M n / C d }$ transporter would be less effective at decreasing Cd uptake. Wheat, in particular, has a high Cd translocation from the roots to the shoots, which should be the primary target for manipulation to decrease Cd accumulation in wheat grain.

## BrNramp1 shows high sequence identity with AtNramp1


The AtNramp1 protein sequence was used to retrieve homologs in the Brassicaceae  database (BRAD). Using the BLAST tool, three candidate orthologous proteins (ID: Bra003587, Bra035149, and Bra008437)

were identifed. Among these proteins, Bra003587 showed the highest sequence identity to AtNramp1 in A. thaliana $( 8 9 . 6 6 \%$ , Supplementary Fig. 1a). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that Bra003587 closely clusters with AtNramp1 from A. thaliana (Supplementary Fig.  1b). Regarding the protein sequence, 12 transmembrane domains were predicted (red-underlined), and structural motifs for metal recognition were also identifed (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Motif A in TM1 (DPGN) and motif B in TM6 (AMVM) in Bra003587 were identical to those reported for AtNramp1 (Lu et  al. 2018). Bra003587 matched the predicted protein with ID: XP_009104491.1 in the NCBI database. Based on these results, Bra003587 was named BrNramp1. The BrNramp1 gene contains 1584 nucleotides encoding 328 amino acids. The alignment of the genomic DNA and cDNA sequences of BrNramp1 showed that this gene consists of 11 exons and 10 introns (Supplementary Fig. 1c).


## BrNramp1 is expressed mainly in roots


To explore the expression pattern of BrNramp1, the expression level of BrNramp1 in the roots and shoots was determined by quantitative reverse transcriptase PCR. When $B$ . rapa plants were cultured in 1/2-strength Hoagland nutrient solution (control), BrNramp1 was mainly expressed in the roots, with a much lower expression level in the shoots. The addition of $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd or Mn defciency (no Mn was added in the nutrient solution) resulted in signifcantly higher BrNramp1 expression levels in roots and shoots compared to the control (Fig. 1).

BrNramp1 localizes in the plasmatic cell membrane

To identify the subcellular localization of BrNramp1, BrNramp1-eGFP was constructed under the control of the 35S promoter and inserted into N. benthamiana leaf mesophyll cells via Agrobacterium strain GV3101 injection. GFP fuorescence of $3 5 S { : : } e G F P$ in mesophyll cells was observed all around the cell components, including the cell membrane, the nucleus, and the cytoplasm, while the GFP fuorescence of 35S:: BrNramp1::eGFP product was observed only in the cell plasma membrane; OsNramp5 was used as the cell membrane marker. 35S::BrNramp1::eGFP and 35S::OsNramp5::RFP vectors were co-transformed into N. benthamiana mesophyll cells, confrming that BrNramp1 encodes a plasma membranelocalized protein (Fig. 2).

BrNramp1 shows transport activities for Cd and Mn when expressed in yeast

The BrNramp1 sequence was amplifed using cDNA of B.rapa accession Chiifu roots as template. Compared with BrNramp1 from Chiifu, Bra003587 from the BALST result in the BRAD database has a 51 base-pair deletion, resulting in a deletion of 17 amino acids in TM3 (Supplementary Fig.  2a, d). Secondary structure prediction showed that, despite the 17 amino-acid deletions, Bra003587 still has 12 transmembrane domains (green-underlined). However, diferences in protein sequence composition were observed: BrNramp1 consists of 275 alpha helixes, 20 beta turns, 157 random coils (Supplementary Fig.  2b), while Bra003587 consists of 272 alpha helixes, 18 beta turns, 157 random coils (Supplementary Fig.  2e). Tertiary structure prediction indicated that the 17 amino-acid deletion resulted in structural changes in TM3 (Supplementary Fig. 2c, f).

To determine the specifc function of the 51  bp fragment, we generated BrNramp1d (Bra003587) in which the 51  bp fragment was deleted based on the BrNramp1 sequence and then heterologously expressed BrNramp1 and BrNramp1d in the yeast INVScI and △smf1 mutant, which were further cultivated with two carbon sources (glucose and galactose). The assays were performed in the presence or absence of Cd and EGTA.

With glucose as the carbon source, no signifcant diferences were observed among yeast lines expressing the empty vector, BrNramp1 or BrNramp1d. When the carbon source was galactose, the GAL promoter was induced, and all yeast lines showed similar growth in the absence of Cd. However, in the presence of Cd, yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 displayed higher sensitivity to Cd compared with those expressing the empty vector, while those expressing BrNramp1d did not (Fig.  3a). The growth curve of yeast cells was determined in the presence and absence of $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd. No growth diferences were observed among yeast cultures in the absence of Cd, but the growth of yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 was signifcantly inhibited in the presence of $5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd. Yeast carrying the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed similar growth to those cultured without Cd (Fig. 3c). Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 accumulated signifcantly more Cd than those expressing the empty vector, while Cd accumulation in yeast cells expressing BrNramp1d showed no signifcant diference compared with the empty vector (Fig. 3d).

The growth of the △smf1 mutant showed no signifcant diferences among lines when glucose was used as the carbon source. However, when cultured with galactose, the △smf1 mutant expressing BrNramp1 showed signifcantly better growth on the solid medium containing EGTA, which chelates Mn and reduces its availability, than that expressing the empty vector, indicating the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1. Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1d exposed to EGTA showed similar growth sensitivity to those carrying the empty vector (Fig. 3b).


## The heterologous expression of BrNramp1 in the Arabidopsis complements Cd and Mn uptake


To further investigate the metal transport activity of BrNramp1 in plants, the A. thaliana atnramp1 mutant (SALK_053236) was transformed to express BrNramp1 under the control of 35S promoter. Three independent transgenic lines (OX-1, OX-2, OX-3) were selected and identifed (Supplementary Fig. 3). The relative expression levels of AtNramp1 and BrNramp1 were determined in Col-0, atnramp1 and the independent transgenic lines. Expression of AtNramp1 in atnramp1 and the independent transgenic lines was almost undetectable, while BrNramp1 showed much higher and similar expression levels in the transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 4).

To identify the Cd transport activity of BrNramp1, $0 . 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd was added in the hydroponic system to culture Col-0, atnramp1, and three independent transgenic lines. Transgenic atnramp1 plants overexpressing BrNramp1 showed a signifcant increase in Cd content. Cd concentrations in the independent transgenic lines were 2.59–3.09-fold in the shoots and 3.90–4.04-fold in the roots compared to the values found in atnramp1 (Figs.  4a,and b). The Cd contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were 3.84–5.42-fold that of atnramp1 (Fig.  4c). Overexpression of BrNramp1 also increased Mn concentrations in the independent transgenic lines, which were even higher than in Col-0. In the shoots, there was a 2.20–3.00-fold increase compared with atnramp1 and a 1.59–2.16- fold increase compared with Col-0. In the roots, Mn concentrations in the independent transgenic lines showed a 2.64–3.48-fold and 1.49–1.96- fold increase compared with atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Figs.  4d, and e). The Mn contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were 3.01–4.40-fold and 1.56–2.28-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig. 4f). Concentrations of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn were also detected, Fe, Zn and $\mathrm { C u }$ concentrations in the shoots, roots and contents of whole plants did not show signifcant diferences (Supplementary Fig. 5). The dry weight of Arabidopsis plants showed no signifcant diferences. The root-to-shoot translocation ratio (shoot content/whole plant content) of Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn and Cd also showed no signifcant diferences among

Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 6).

To identify the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1, Arabidopsis plants were exposed hydroponically to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M } \ \mathrm { M n C l } _ { 2 }$ and Mn defciency treatments, with both treatments showing a similar Mn distribution. When exposed to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M \ M n C l } _ { 2 }$ , Mn concentrations in the shoots of the independent transgenic lines were $4 . 2 6 { - } 5 . 0 1 $ -fold and 2.10–2.47-fold higher compared with those in atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5a). In the roots, Mn concentrations showed a 4.35–5.91-fold and 2.08–2.83-fold increase, respectively (Fig.  5b). The Mn content of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines was signifcantly higher, with 5.88–8.11-fold and 3.17–4.37-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5c). Fe and Cu concentrations in the shoots, roots and contents of whole plants did not show signifcant diferences, while Zn concentrations in the shoots of the independent lines were signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 (Supplementary Fig. 7). For the total content of Fe, Cu and Zn, similar results were observed, two transgenic lines (OX-1 and OX-2) showed no signifcant diferences, while OX-3 showed signifcantly higher contents of $\mathrm { C u }$ and Zn compared with atnramp1. The root-to-shoot translocation ratio of Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn showed no signifcant diferences among Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 8).

When exposed to Mn defciency solution, Mn concentrations in the shoots of the independent transgenic lines were 2.30–3.12-fold and 1.34–1.82-fold higher compared with those in atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5d). In the roots, Mn concentrations showed a 1.82–2.18-fold and 1.05–1.26-fold increase compared with atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig. 5e). The Mn contents of whole plants in the independent transgenic lines were signifcantly higher with 3.96–4.16-fold and 1.88–1.98-fold that of atnramp1 and Col-0, respectively (Fig.  5f). Zn concentrations in the shoots of two transgenic lines were also signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 and Col-0 (Supplementary Fig.  9c). However, when calculating the elemental contents of whole plants, all three independent lines showed higher accumulation of Fe, $\mathrm { C u }$ and Zn than atnramp1 and Col-0 (Supplementary Figs. $9 \ \mathrm { g - i } )$ . Analysis of dry weight showed that the dry weights of the three transgenic lines were higher than that of atnramp1(Supplementary Fig.  11). The root-to-shoot translocation ratio of Fe, Mn, Cu and

Zn showed no signifcant diferences among Col-0, atnramp1 and the three independent transgenic lines (Supplementary Fig. 10).

In the present study, we isolated and functionally characterized a Nramp member BrNramp1 in Brassica rapa. We characterized a homologue of AtNramp1 in B. rapa named BrNramp1, and determined the expression pattern and functional role of this protein in Mn and Cd uptake. Through RT-qPCR, we demonstrated that BrNramp1 is mainly expressed in B. rapa roots, and its relative expression level is induced signifcantly in the presence of Cd and the absence of Mn (Fig.  1). We also detected that BrNramp1 encodes a plasma membrane-localized protein (Fig.  2). Heterologous expression in both yeast and A. thaliana verifed Mn and Cd transport activity of BrNramp1 (Figs. 3,4,5).

It is well-known that plants can take up toxic and non-essential Cd cations through divalent metal ion transporters such as Fe, Mn, and Zn transporters (Verret et  al. 2004; Nakanishi et  al. 2006; Ishimaru et  al. 2012). A large body of evidence documents the role of Nramp proteins in the transport of essential divalent transition metals (including $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , and ${ \mathrm { C o } } ^ { 2 + }$ ) in many plant species (Bozzi and Gaudet 2021), and it is also known that they contribute to the uptake of toxic and non-essential metals such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { P b } ^ { 2 + }$ (Sui et  al. 2018; Chang et  al. 2022). The Nramp family members’ sequences are highly conserved, and they share homologous ion transport functions (Ehrnstorfer et  al. 2014), especially in rice and Arabidopsis thaliana: OsNramp5 and AtNramp1 have been shown to participate in Mn and Cd uptake in roots (Chang et  al. 2020a; Ihnatowicz et al. 2014). To explore the orthologous gene in Brassica rapa plants, we used the AtNramp1 protein sequence to perform a BLAST search in the BRAD database. The results demonstrated that three proteins showed high identity to AtNramp1 (ID: Bra003587, Bra035149 and Bra008437). Phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment indicated that Bra003587 has the highest identity and closely clusters with AtNramp1. Therefore, Bra003587 was named BrNramp1 in the present study. BrNramp1 sequence was amplifed to explore the gene structure (Supplementary Fig.  S1c). The expression pattern of BrNramp1 is also conserved, as reported previously. Through RT-qPCR, we demonstrated that BrNramp1 is mainly expressed in $B$ . rapa roots, and its relative expression level signifcantly increased in the presence of Cd and the absence of Mn (Fig.  1), resembling the behavior of the orthologous gene BcNramp1 (Bra008437) (Yue et  al. 2021). Interestingly, previous research showed that Mn defciency may induce the expression of AtNramp1(Cailliatte et al. 2010). This may be because Mn defciency triggers $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling, activating $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent protein kinases, CPK21 and CPK23, which could phosphorylate $\mathrm { T h r } 4 9 8$ of AtNramp1 to facilitate Mn uptake. The expression level of AhNramp1 in peanuts can be induced by Mn and Zn defciency in stems and roots (Wang et al. 2019). All of Arabidopsis thaliana, peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) and Brassica chinensis are dicotyledons. In monocots, the expressions of OsNramp1 and OsNramp5 in rice, showed no inducement by Mn defciency, but OsNramp1 could be induced by Cd addition and Fe defciency (Chang et al. 2020b). HvNramp5 in barley was not afected by Mn, Cu and Zn defciency (Wu et al. 2016). Transcriptional regulation between dicots and monocots showed both conservation and diferences. Based on the above researches, the response of Nramp family members to Mn defciency may be related to plant developmental pathways and their adaptation to environmental changes.

Conformational structure analysis of transmembrane proteins can help in understanding how these molecules recognize and bind their substrates and transport them into cells to fulfll plant nutritional requirements. The Nramp family encompasses proteins with 11 or 12 conserved transmembrane domains (TMs), with TMs 1–10 forming a LeuT fold, which is the structural core unit enabling the transport of a broad range of substrates (Bozzi et al. 2019). The role of these 10 TMs in metal transport has been extensively analyzed in bacteria (Bozzi et  al. 2016). Based on the sequence, we characterized BrNramp1 as consisting of 10 introns and 11 exons, encoding a protein of 328 amino acids (Supplementary Fig. S1). The predicted structure of BrNramp1, based on the amino acid sequence, indicates 12 transmembrane domains with positions similar to those of Nramp protein members in other species. By sequence alignment, we identifed in BrNramp1 the crucial motifs for Mn selectivity: motif A in TM1 (DPGN) and motif $\mathbf { B }$ in TM6 (AMVM), which are identical to those in AtNramp1 (Supplementary Fig.  S1). The full-length ORF of BrNramp1 obtained for $B$ . rapa accession Chiifu revealed a 51  bp diference compared with the Bra003587 sequence from the BRAD database, resulting in the deletion of a 17-amino-acid region in TM3. This deletion did not alter the number or position of transmembrane domains but caused changes in the secondary and tertiary structures of the protein (Supplementary Fig. S2).

Using a heterologous yeast-based expression system, in combination with Cd/Mn addition/depletion assays, we experimentally demonstrated that this 17-amino-acids protein component is necessary to retain Cd and Mn transport activities. Yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 showed growth inhibition when exposed to Cd treatment, demonstrating that BrNramp1 can transport Cd from the medium into yeast cells, while yeast expressing the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed no growth inhibition (Fig. 3). When cultured on a medium containing EGTA, which chelates Mn in the medium and prevents $\mathsf { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ mobility, yeast cells expressing BrNramp1 showed signifcantly better growth, demonstrating that BrNramp1 can transport Mn from the medium into yeast cells. In contrast, yeast expressing the empty vector and BrNramp1d showed growth inhibition, indicating that these yeast cells could not transport Mn (Fig. 3). These results demonstrate that BrNramp1 has Cd and Mn transport ability, whereas BrNramp1d, missing the 17-amino-acid component, lost the ability.

Previous studies suggested that the conserved metal-binding site, with methionine sulfur in TM1 and TM6, would prefer Cd as the coordinate substrate to Co and Fe (Bozzi et  al. 2016). It has also been indicated that TM1, TM5, TM6, and TM10 participate in the stage when the binding site switches from outward to inward during Mn transport (Ray S et al. 2023). A similar study indicated that in the TM3, positions E129, D131, and E134 are crucial points determining $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ transport and infuencing pH-dependent transport activity (Ehrnstorfer et  al. 2017). As for BrNramp1d, 17 missing amino acids in TM3 were detected in positions 131 to 148, and this may impair Mn transport by changing the protein structure of BrNramp1.

The overexpression of BrNramp1 in atnramp1 plants complemented Cd and Mn uptake, resulting in a higher accumulation of these ions in both shoots and roots compared with atnramp1 under Cd exposure. Similarly, three transgenic Arabidopsis lines expressing BrNramp1 accumulated signifcantly more Mn than the wild-type Col-0 under both Mnsufcient and Mn-defcient conditions, indicating the Mn transport activity of BrNramp1(Fig.  4). When exposed to $5 \ \mu \mathrm { M \ M n C l } _ { 2 }$ and Mn defciency conditions, Mn distribution was similar, but the independent transgenic lines accumulated signifcantly more Mn compared with atnramp1 and Col-0 (Fig.  5). Heterologous expression in Arabidopsis thaliana demonstrated the Mn and Cd transport activity of BrNramp1. In the present study, Zn concentrations in the transgenic lines showed no signifcant diferences under $0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Cd treatment (Supplementary Fig. S5). However, when cultured in Hoagland nutrient solution containing $5 \mu \mathrm { M } \mathrm { M n C l } _ { 2 }$ or under Mn defciency, Zn concentrations in the shoots of the independent lines were signifcantly higher than in atnramp1 and $\mathrm { C o l - 0 }$ (Supplementary Figs.  S6, S7). One possibility is that under Cd treatment, BrNramp1 preferentially transports Cd and Mn over Zn, while under Mn defciency or without Cd, BrNramp1 may prefer Zn as a substrate. Since Fe, Cu and Zn contents in the transgenic lines were higher than in atnramp1 and Col0, we analyzed dry weight and found that the shoot and root weights of the three transgenic lines were higher than those of atnramp1, resulting in higher Fe, Cu and Zn contents. The diferences in dry weight may explain that under Mn defciency, BrNramp1 expression in atnramp1 could promote plant growth. The dry weight of Arabidopsis is shown in Supplementary Fig.  11. Another possibility is that under Mn defciency, the expression of genes encoding Mn transporters may be induced in response to environmental changes, leading to higher absorption of divalent cations. Several Mn transporters have been reported to exhibit activity for multiple cations. For example, AtIRT1 shows transport activity for Fe, Mn, Zn, Co and Cd (Huang et  al. 2024; Barberon et  al. 2011; Vert et al. 2002), and AtNramp1 transports Fe, Mn and Cd (Cailliatte et  al. 2010). Members of the ZRT/IRT-related proteins (ZIPs) family also show transport activity for Fe, Mn, Zn and Cd (Spielmann et al. 2020). Recent studies have shown that Mn and Fe defciency may trigger $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ signaling, activating $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -dependent protein kinases such as CPK21 and CPK23, which could phosphorylate $\mathrm { T h r } 4 9 8$ and Ser149 of AtNramp1 and AtIRT1, respectively (Fu D et  al. 2022; Wang et  al. 2023). However, these phosphorylation sites specifcally enhance AtNramp1 uptake of Mn and AtIRT1 uptake of Fe, respectively. There may also be other genes responsible for Mn, Fe, Zn and $\mathrm { C u }$ uptake that are induced under Mn defciency. Both the expression pattern and heterologous expression assays indicate that BrNramp1 participates in Mn and Cd uptake in the roots of $B$ . rapa, with conserved functions similar to orthologous proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana, rice, wheat, barley and buckwheat (Cailliatte et  al. 2010; Sui et  al. 2018; Chang et al. 2022; Wu et al. 2016; Yokosho et al. 2020).

In conclusion, we identifed an ortholog of AtNramp1 in Brassica rapa named BrNramp1. This gene encodes BrNramp1, a plasma membrane-localized transporter functional for Mn and Cd. Heterologous expression of BrNramp1 in both yeast and Arabidopsis thaliana demonstrated its transport activity, and a 51 bp nucleotide missing in TM3 caused the loss of transport activity for both Cd and Mn. These fndings are particularly relevant, as BrNramp1 may serve as a valuable target for breeding low-Cd cultivars using molecular marker-assisted methods in the future.
