## Main conclusion The nitrate transporters, belonging to NPF and NRT2 families, play critical roles in nitrate signaling, root growth and nodule development in legumes.


Nitrate plays an essential role during plant development as nutrient and also as signal molecule, in both cases working via the activity of nitrate transporters. To date, few studies on NRT2 or NPF nitrate transporters in legumes have been reported, and most of those concern Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula. A molecular characterization led to the identification of 4 putative LjNRT2 and 37 putative LjNPF gene sequences in $L .$ japonicus. In M. truncatula, the NRT2 family is composed of 3 putative members. Using the new genome annotation of $M .$ . truncatula (Mt4.0), we identified, for this review, 97 putative MtNPF sequences, including 32 new sequences relative to previous studies. Functional characterization has been published for only two MtNPF genes, encoding nitrate transporters of $M$ . truncatula. Both transporters have a role in root system development via abscisic acid signaling: MtNPF6.8 acts as a nitrate sensor during the cell elongation of the primary root, while MtNPF1.7 contributes to the cellular organization of the root tip and nodule formation. An in silico expression study of MtNPF genes confirmed that NPF genes are expressed in nodules, as previously shown for $L$ japonicus, suggesting a role for the corresponding proteins in nitrate transport, or signal perception in nodules. This review summarizes our knowledge of legume nitrate transporters and discusses new roles for these proteins based on recent discoveries.

Keywords Lotus japonicus $\cdot$ Medicago truncatula $\cdot$ Nitrate signaling $\cdot$ NPF $\cdot$ NRT2

Nitrate is the preferred nitrogen source of higher plants and an essential nutrient for plant growth and development. Nitrate transporters (NRTs) play vital roles in the nitrate uptake and transportation. However, the NRT gene family in pineapple is still unexplored. In this study, we performed a genome-wide analysis of the pineapple genome and identified 48 NRT genes (AcNRTs) distributed unevenly across 9 chromosomes and 2 scaffolds. Phylogenetic analysis showed that these genes can be divided into three groups, namely, AcNRT1/PTR, AcNRT2 and AcNRT3/NAR1 with 44, 3 and 1 members, respectively. AcNRTs within the same phylogenetic group share similar gene structure and domain composition. In addition, syntenic and phylogenetic analyses identified 34 Arabidopsis NRT genes with 31 pineapple NRT genes as orthologs. By investigating the expression profiles of these genes in various tissues, we showed that the expression pattern of some AcNRTs genes is tissue-specific. Furthermore, we examined the expression of the AcNRT2s under nitrate starvation and found that AcNRT2.1 and AcNRT2.2 both have the strongest response in roots suggesting that AcNRTs may play a broad role in the pineapple in response to nitrate deficiency. Taken together, our data provide insights into the evolution and function of pineapple NRTs and pave a path for future functional investigation of pineapple NRTs genes.

Keywords NRT genes $\cdot$ Expression profile $\cdot$ Synteny analysis $\cdot$ RNA-Seq $\cdot$ Pineapple

To gain insight into the evolution of UMAMIT genes in plants, we utilized a total of 375 UMAMIT protein sequences (excluding pseudogenes) from the previous sixteen species to construct three phylogenetic trees for the UMAMIT protein family by MEGA-X and IQ-TREE v2.0.6 respectively. The results revealed that the topological structure of the three trees was similar, and the UMAMIT proteins were categorized into four subfamilies and nine clades (Fig. 1; Figs. S1–S3).

In the phylogenetic trees, it was observed that all UMAMIT members from green algae, bryophytes, and ferns clustered together in clade 9. This suggests that clade 9 may represent an ancestral lineage for UMAMIT proteins (Fig. 1; Figs. S1–S3). Furthermore, AtUMAMIT 01–03 and OsUMAMIT01-02 were also found in clade 9, indicating that these genes may be relatively ancient in their origin. UMAMIT proteins from eudicots, monocots, Amborellales, and gymnosperms were evenly distributed across the diferent clades, except for some variations. For example, UMAMIT members from gymnosperms (Ginkgo biloba and Gnetum montanum) were absent in clade 2 (Fig. 1; Figs. S1-S3). Interestingly, about half of the UMAMITs in Amborella trichopoda formed relatively independent expansions in clade 5. This fnding aligns with their evolutionary status and suggests that these UMAMITs in Amborella trichopoda have undergone specifc adaptations or diversifcations (Fig. 1; Fig. S4).

The distribution of UMAMITs from angiosperms in each clade suggests that these UMAMITs may share a common ancestor (Fig. 1). Synteny analysis is a useful tool for establishing both orthology relationships and functional linkages between genes. Gene synteny analysis was conducted among maize, rice, soybean, and Arabidopsis. The analysis revealed a general collinearity relationship among these species (Figs. S5 and S6).

In the phylogenetic trees (Fig. 1), we added the localization information for each UMAMIT protein. The results showed that more than $8 1 . 6 \%$ of UMAMIT proteins predicted to localize in chloroplast were clustered in Clades 1–4 and 9. Additionally, approximately $6 5 \%$ of UMAMIT proteins in subfamily I and subfamily II were predicted to localize in the plasma membrane. Interestingly, almost all members of Clade 8 were predicted to localize in the cytoplasm. Among them, AtUMAMIT05 (also known as WAT1) has been shown to promote auxin export and participate in plant immune responses and stress responses (Denancé et al. 2013; Ranocha et al. 2013). It is worth noting that AtUMAMIT05 was localized in the tonoplast (Ranocha et al. 2013). We further found that members of Clade 8 have motifs associated to the tonoplast (Zhao et al. 2021), which indicated that members of Clade 8 may localize to the tonoplast (Fig. S7).


## Conserved sequence and structure specifc to UMAMIT proteins


To gain a deeper understanding of the evolutionary changes in UMAMIT proteins, a multiple sequence alignment was performed using UMAMIT protein sequences from various species including Chlorokybus atmophyticus, Mesostigma viride, Mesotaenium endlicherianum, Spirogloea muscicola, Micromonas sp. RCC299, Physcomitrella patens, Marchantia polymorpha, Anthoceros angustus, Selaginella moellendorfi, Gnetum montanum, Ginkgo biloba, Amborella trichopoda, maize, rice, soybean and Arabidopsis. The analysis revealed that these sequences consisted of two similar parts which were identifed as EamA domains by Interpro and Hmmer searches (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/inter pro/, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/hmmer/). We also found two common core regions consisting of $\sim 7 0$ amino acid residues (Fig. 2).

We used the MEME software to identify ten motifs within the conserved regions of the UMAMIT proteins from the sixteen plant species (Fig. S8). Additionally, we employed TMHMM 2.0 to identify ten transmembrane domains (TMDs) in these proteins (Fig. 3). This fnding is consistent with previous reports that EamA is a $5 + 5$ transmembrane (TM) nucleotide sugar transporter found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Västermark et al. 2011). Notably, UMAMIT members from Anthoceros angustus were found to possess all ten transmembrane domains (Fig. 3a), suggesting that the integral EamA protein has existed in bryophytes. Among the eight algal sequences, only one had the $5 + 5$ TM pattern (Fig. 3), which difers from the complete ten transmembrane domains. This raises the question of why UMAMIT proteins exist in unicellular algae and whether they transport amino acids or other compounds to or from the environment. Furthermore, we observed one gene in maize that contains twenty transmembrane domains (Fig. 3; Table S4), which may have resulted from fragment replication events.

In our analysis of the phylogenetic trees, we found that incomplete $1 0 \mathrm { T M }$ UMAMITs distributed in diferent clades. For example, $4 3 . 8 \%$ of UMAMITs in Clade 9 lacked varying degrees of transmembrane domains. $3 3 . 3 \%$ of UMAMITs in Clade 6 were found to be unintegral EamA proteins. Clade 8 and Clade 7 contained $2 0 \%$ and $0 \%$ incomplete $1 0 \ \mathrm { T M }$ UMAMITs, respectively (Fig. 3; Table S4). These fndings suggest that UMAMIT initially consisted of incomplete 10 TM structures in aquatic life forms and gradually evolved to form complete $1 0 \mathrm { T M }$ structures, and then some TM was lost again to adapt to the complexities of terrestrial life.


## The switch of UMAMIT proteins for exporting amino acids was a four‑helix bundle


In order to gain insights into the function of UMAMIT proteins, we employed homology modeling and AlphaFold3 to predict their tertiary structure. The structure predicted by the two ways are similar and the resulting structure revealed that UMAMIT proteins have a basket-shaped conformation, with a large substrate-binding cavity located at the center of the basket (Fig. S9). This structure is composed of two inverted EamA domains, TM1-5 and TM6-10, which is similar to the structure of the bacterial inner-membrane protein YddG, which has a structural basis for amino acid export of DMT superfamily (Tsuchiya et al. 2016; Yan 2013). Similar to the outward-facing state of YddG topology, TM1-TM2, TM3- TM4, TM6-TM7, and TM8-TM9 are arranged alternately to surround the central cavity (Fig. 4a). TM5 and TM10, along with TM4 and TM9, form a four-helix bundle that seals one side of the central cavity (Fig. 4a). Within this structure, Pro109 (TM4) and Pro283 (TM9) might interact with other conserved residues to regulate the opening and closing of the central cavity towards the intracellular space (Fig. 4a). These two Pro residues are fully conserved in Arabidopsis, with $7 8 \%$ and $9 2 \%$ conservation across UMAMITs from all species, respectively (Fig. 4a). To investigate whether this highly conserved region is involved in amino acid binding, we performed molecular docking using the AtUMAMIT14 protein as the receptor and Trp as the ligand. The docking results showed that the ligand binds to Glu122 and Arg273

a b

on the intracellular side of the four-helix bundle (Fig. 4b), suggesting that the opening and closing of the four-helix bundle regulates the channel for exporting amino acids through binding to the amino acid ligand.

To investigate whether specifc amino acids are determined by each UMAMIT protein to binding substrates, we analyzed the tertiary structure predictions of AtUMAMIT18, AtUMAMIT01, and AtUMAMIT14. It has been reported that AtUMAMIT14 can export charged amino acids (His, Glu, Asp), polar amino acids (Gln, Asn, Ser, Thr), and nonpolar amino acids (Ala, Val, Ile, Leu, Phe) (Besnard et al. 2016). AtUMAMIT18 has been found to catalyze the efux of His and the uptake of Gln and Asp, while AtUMAMIT01 has been shown to take up Ala as an amino acid input vector when expressed in yeast 22Δ10α (Besnard et al. 2016; Ladwig et al. 2012; Zhao et al. 2021). The overall structures of the three proteins were found to be similar (Fig. 4c). However, there were specifc amino acid residues in each protein that may provide specifc binding environments for substrates. For example, Gly93 (TM3) and Gly280 (TM8) in AtUMAMIT01 may provide hydrophobic environments for substrate binding. Gln89 (TM3), Thr115 (TM4), and Tyr255 (TM8) in AtUMAMIT18 may provide hydrophilic environments for substrate binding. Phe113 (TM4) and Thr138 (TM5) in AtUMAMIT14 may provide both hydrophobic and hydrophilic environments for substrate binding (Fig. 4c). Based on these fndings, we speculate that the overall protein structures of UMAMIT family members are similar, the specifc amino acid residues involved in substrate binding may contribute to the transport of diferent amino acids by each protein.

To explore the specifc amino acids transported by each UMAMIT protein, we performed virtual screening using the four-helix bundle and complete sequence of UMAMIT family proteins from various species as receptors and 20 diferent amino acids as ligands via Autodock Vina1.1.2. Interestingly, the results showed that almost all members of UMAMIT in these eleven species (algae, bryophytes, ferns, Gnetum montanum and Arabidopsis) exhibited a high afnity for aromatic amino acids such as tryptophan, phenylalanine, and tyrosine (Fig. S10). Maybe this was caused by the limited accuracy of Autodock Vina1.1.2, and there could be some diferences in the protein structures compared to YddG (Tsuchiya et al. 2016). Surprisingly, the binding afnity of these UMAMIT proteins to the 20 amino acids showed a reverse pattern compared to the consensus order of amino acids that appeared during the formation of the Earth, as suggested in previous studies (Higgs and Pudritz 2009; Trifonov 2000). These fndings suggest that further investigations are needed to better understand the transport capabilities of UMAMIT proteins.

## The specifc amino acid sites of UMAMIT binding subtracts determined the subtracts specifcity


Amino acid synthesis occurs in various organelles within specifc tissues, such as chloroplasts, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and vesicles. For instance, aromatic amino acids (Trp, Phe, and Tyr), branched-chain amino acids (Leu, Ile, Val, Thr, Met, and Lys), His, Asp, and Arg are primarily synthesized in chloroplasts (Binder 2010; Jander and Joshi 2010; Lynch and Dudareva 2020; Maeda and Dudareva 2012; Slocum 2005; Yoo et al. 2013). These require amino acid transport proteins located at diferent sites to transport amino acids synthesized at diferent regions in the cell. In our study, we predicted the subcellular localization of UMAMITs from sixteen species and found that 314 UMAMIT proteins were localized in the cell membrane, 100 proteins in chloroplasts, 20 in the cytoplasm, 6 in the Golgi apparatus, 3 in the nucleus, and only 1 in the mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum respectively (Fig. 1; Table S3). This specifc subcellular localization information suggests the unique types of amino acids transported by diferent UMAMIT proteins. Protein structure predictions of UMAMIT14 and 18 also revealed that the amino acid binding sites of UMAMIT proteins are specifc, despite their overall structural similarity (Fig. 4). Zhao et al. (2021) also reported that mutations with the strongest efect are found in amino acids within both structural repeats, near or in TM5 or TM10 (Zhao et al. 2021). Analysis of expression patterns indicated that members of the same clade coordinate amino acid transport in various tissues and stages of plant growth and development (Fig. 5). This provides new insights into the transport of amino acids between cells and tissues.


## UMAMIT diferent from other amino acid transporters


Amino acid transporters can be classifed into three major families: ATF (Amino acid Transporter Family, also known as AAAP family), APC (Amino acid-Polyamine-Choline transporter family), and UMAMIT. These proteins share common characteristics such as broad expression patterns, wide substrate selectivity, and multiple physiological functions (Yang et al. 2020). Some members of the ATF and APC families, such as AAP1, AAP5, LHT1, LHT6, and ProT2, have been identifed as amino acid input vectors involved in root uptake. Additionally, AAP2, AAP3, AAP5, ProT1, CAT1, CAT6, and CAT9 contribute to phloem loading (Dinkeloo et al. 2018; Mechthild 2014; Rentsch 2010; Tegeder 2012). Unlike these two families, UMAMIT family members are exporter or bidirectional transporter proteins for amino acids. AtUMAMIT18 (SiAR1) is the frst amino acid transporter with clearly established export properties and and AtUMAMIT31 in subfamily I facilitate passive efux from the cytosol to the apoplast along the electrochemical gradient (Xu et al. 2023). Furthermore, the yeast expressing AtUMAMIT24 predominantly secretes Glu and Asp, while AtUMAMIT25 mainly secretes Glu and Arg. AtUMAMIT14 functions as an output protein for various amino acids when expressed in yeast. AtUMAMIT01 is responsible for ALA uptake, and AtUMAMIT18 catalyzes His efux and Gln and Asp uptake in yeast (Besnard et  al. 2016, 2018, 2021; Ladwig et  al. 2012; Zhao et  al. 2021). Further research on the mechanisms and regulation of these transporters will provide valuable insights into their roles in plant biology

bidirectional Gln transport in oocytes (Ladwig et al. 2012). Moreover, UMAMIT transporters also transport other substrates such as auxin (Ranocha et al. 2013; Xu et al. 2023). Our protein prediction of the UMAMIT family in amino acid transport has revealed potential molecular mechanisms and ofers insights into the transportation process of amino acids within plant tissues.


## Functional divergence and evolution of UMAMIT


Previous studies have examined the evolutionary analysis of 180 UMAMITs from 7 species including Arabidopsis, rice, M. truncatula, Selaginella moellendorf, Physcomitrella patens, Pinus pinaster, and Picea abies (Zhao et al. 2021). However, the study by Zhao et al. lacks UMAMITs from algae, which are essential for understanding the gene family’s origin, and gymnosperms, which are considered primitive seed plants. Furthermore, they did not explore the evolutionary history of the EamA structure, which is vital for comprehending its function. In this study, we conducted phylogenetic analysis of 375 UMAMITs across 16 key species in the evolutionary history of plants, ranging from algae to angiosperms. We found that UMAMITs may have originated from green algae and initially diversifed in bryophytes (Fig. 1), followed by a big expansion through gene duplication events in seed plants (Figs. 1 and 6). During evolution, the stabilization of the EamA structure was gradually completed in hornworts (Fig. 3). Our protein structure prediction revealed that the four-helix bundle motif is crucial in controlling the UMAMIT switch for exporting amino acid (Fig. 4). We hypothesize that the specifc amino acids in the amino acid binding region determine the type of amino acids being transported. Additionally, we have also compiled a summary of the functions of all identifed UMAMIT genes to date (Fig. 6; Table S5).

We have attempted to summarize the functions of UMAMIT genes in plant evolution in Fig. 6. In seeds, AtUMAMIT24 in subfamily I is known to transport amino acids such as Glu and Arg from the bead pore through the syncytial seed coat to the developing embryo (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT25 in subfamily I functions as an amino acid exporter, unloading amino acids from endosperm cells for use by the developing embryo (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT29, AtUMAMIT30, and AtUMAMIT31 in subfamily I are involved in exporting glucosinolates in seeds (Xu et al. 2023). AtUMAMIT28 and AtUMAMIT29 in subfamily I export amino acids like Ala and Glu from the phloem to the developing embryo (Müller et al. 2015). The high expression of these subfamily members in siliques, as indicated by the expression patterns analysis (Fig. 5), suggests their crucial role in seed nutrient storage and their potential application in molecular breeding. In subfamily II, AtUMAMIT18 and AtUMAMIT14 are involved in the radial transport of amino acids in roots, and AtUMAMIT14 also plays a role in phloem ofoading. In subfamily III, AtUMAMIT05 is responsible for determining secondary cell wall thickness in wood fbers and promoting growth hormone export from isolated Arabidopsis vesicles (Ranocha et al. 2013). AtUMAMIT05 and AtUMAMIT36 in subfamily III participate in plant immune responses and stress responses (Denancé et al. 2013; Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). The specifc subcellular localization of these subfamily members, as indicated by our data (Fig. 1; Table S3), suggests their specifcity in various activities. In subfamily IV (clade 9), all members are found in green algae, bryophytes, and ferns. Only AtUMAMIT01 was reported to uptake Ala in yeast cell (Zhao et al. 2021). Further research is needed to explore the functions and precise mechanisms of these genes in plants, with the goal of developing crop varieties that have improved nutrient use efciency. For example, multiple mutations within an evolutionary lineage could be constructed to study their function.

Expression pattern analysis is a valuable tool for understanding gene function. We performed a comprehensive expression analysis using RNA-seq data to explore the expression profle of the UMAMITs in Arabidopsis and rice (Fig. S11, S12). The expression level was estimated for all AtUMAMITs detected from 47 tissues during diferent stages, except for ten genes (AtUMAMIT16-psi, AtUMAMIT29, AtUMAMIT35, AtUMAMIT36, AtUMAMIT38, AtUMAMIT39-psi, AtUMAMIT40, AtUMAMIT43-psi, AtUMAMIT45 and AtUMAMIT46) (Fig. S11). Among the expressed AtUMAMIT genes, AtUMAMIT24 and AtUMAMIT25, which are involved in amino acid export from seeds and endosperm, showed high expression levels during seed stages and were grouped into subfamily I (Fig. S11) (Besnard et al. 2021, 2018). Similarly, the majority of OsUMAMIT genes in subfamily I also exhibited expression in seeds, suggesting their potential involvement in seed development (Fig. 1, Fig. S12).

We selected 14 genes for Quantitative real-time PCR analysis according to RNA-seq data (Fig. S11). The results showed that the expression level of AtUMAMIT10, 14, 17 and 20 grouped into clade 3, were higher in the inforescence and siliques which suggested members of this clade are involved in reproductive and embryo development. Studies have showed that AtUMAMIT11, 14, 24, 25 of clade 3 as amino acids exporters play a role in seed loading and phloem unloading during seed development (Besnard et al. 2016, 2018; Müller et al. 2015). AtUMAMIT07 and 08 clustered into clade 7, were highly expressed in the root, inforescence and siliques. AtUMAMIT02-03 clustered into clade 9, and AtUMAMIT33 -34 clustered into clade 5, were highly expressed in the leaves, roots, inforescence and siliques. AtUMAMIT11 belonged to clade 3 and AtUMAMIT30 belonged to clade 2 specifcally predominantly expressed in roots (Fig. 5). These results indicated that the expression patterns of members of the same clade were often similar and the UMAMITs coordinate to transport amino acids at various stages of plant growth and development.

Amino acids are synthesized, utilized, and degraded in different compartments within the cell such as chloroplasts, cytoplasm, mitochondria and vesicles, and therefore amino acid transporters are required for distributing amino acids within the cell compartments and between plant organs (Binder 2010; Jander and Joshi 2010; Maeda and Dudareva 2012; Slocum 2005; Yoo et al. 2013). UMAMIT (2.A.7.4 in TCDB)/MtN21/EamA-like is a class of transporters that can transport multiple acids in plants (Denancé et al. 2014; Gamas 1996). UmamiT had been originally described as MtN21-like nodulins (Medicago truncatula Nodulin 21,

MtN21) which was initially identifed to be induced by nodulation in M. truncatula, belonging to superfamily of drug/metabolite transporters (DMT) (Gamas 1996; Jack et al. 2001). It was later found that homologs of UMAMITs are also present in the genomes of non-nodulated plants (Denancé et al. 2014). Although UMAMITs are named "usually multiple acids move in and out transporter", most of the identifed UMAMITs have been characterized as uniporters that export amino acids (Zhao et al. 2021).

Only a few members of UMAMITs have been characterized, and their precise mechanism not fully understood. NODULIN 21 (MtN21) was initially identified through screening an M. truncatula nodule library and named "nodulin" (Gamas 1996). WAT1 (AtUMAMIT05) was later discovered as a tonoplast-localized auxin transporter in Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) (Ranocha et al. 2013). It was found that AtUMAMIT05 regulates disease resistance and secondary cell wall formation. Homologs of AtUMAMIT05, such as SlWAT1 in Solanum lycopersicum and GhWAT1 in

Gossypium hirsutum, are induced by auxin and promote lignin deposition and xylem diferentiation (Busov et al. 2004; Lee et al. 2021; Ranocha et al. 2013; Tang et al. 2019). Another member, 5NG4 in Pinus taeda, is also induced by auxin and promotes adventitious root formation (Busov et al. 2004). Inactivation of AtUMAMIT05 enhances broad-spectrum resistance to Ralstonia solanacearum, Xanthomonas campestris and Verticillium dahlia (Denancé et al. 2013). SiAR1 (AtUMAMIT18, Siliques Are Red1, SiAR1) is the frst amino acid transporter with clearly established export properties (Denancé et al. 2014). AtUMAMIT18 has been characterized as a bidirectional transporter of amino acids, playing a crucial role in the allocation of organic nitrogen, particularly in the accumulation of amino acids in seeds (Ladwig et al. 2012). AtUMAMIT11, 14, 24, 25, 28, and 29 act as amino acid exporters and are involved in seed loading and phloem unloading during seed development (Besnard et al. 2016, 2018; Müller et al. 2015). AtUMAMIT24 and AtUMAMIT25 are implicated in amino acid transfer within seeds (Besnard et al. 2018). AtUMAMIT14 and AtUMAMIT18 are also involved in phloem unloading in the roots (Besnard et al. 2016; Ladwig et al. 2012). UMAMIT14 and UMAMIT36 participate in plant immune responses and stress responses (Besnard et al. 2021; Denancé et al. 2013; Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). Overexpression of AtUMAMIT14 promotes the resistance to Hyaloperonospora arabidopsidis (Besnard et al. 2021). AtUMAMIT36 (Resistance to Phytophthora parasitica 1, RTP1) located in the endoplasmic reticulum, negatively regulates signaling pathways of plant resistance to biotrophic pathogens like Phytophthora parasitica, Golovinomyces cichoracearum, and Pseudomonas syringae (Pan et al. 2015; Qiang et al. 2021). AtUMAMIT29, 30, and 31 have recently been identifed as glucosinolate exporters, and loss-of-function mutants of these transporters show signifcantly reduced levels of seed glucosinolates (Xu et al. 2023). Glucosinolates are sulfur-containing compounds with important roles in plant defense against herbivores and pathogens. In addition, MtUMAMIT14 plays a role in nodule formation and nitrogenfxation in Medicago truncatula (Garcia et al. 2023). AtUMAMIT44 exports glutamate from chloroplasts, which is vital for controlling nitrogen availability within source leaf cells and for sink nutrition (Samantha et al. 2024). TaUMAMIT17 is an amino acid exporter which might promote to grain development in wheat (Fang et al. 2022).

Recently, UMAMITs has been identified at the genome level in some plant species. A total of 47 and 53 UMAMITs were found in Arabidopsis and rice transcriptomes, including 3 and 2 pseudogenes, respectively (Zhao et al. 2021). In wheat (Triticum aestivum), 213 UMAMITs were identifed (Fang et al. 2022). 88 UMAMITs from M. truncatula (MtUMAMITs), 53 from Oryza sativa (rice) (OsUMAMITs), 16 from Selaginella moellendorf, 8 from

Physcomitrella patens, 13 from Pinus pinaster, and 48 from Picea abies were used for phylogenetic analysis (Zhao et al. 2021). Despite the identifcation of UMAMITs in various plant species, their evolutionary history and functional diversity across the plant kingdom has not been fully explored.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the origins of the UMAMIT gene families. We utilized genomic and transcriptome data from numerous plant and algal species to explore the systematic evolution and classifcation of the UMAMIT gene family. By analyzing conserved motifs and predicting protein tertiary structures, we identifed key amino acids and motifs that control the switch of UMAMITs. Additionally, we examined gene expression patterns to gain insights into the potential functions of UMAMIT family genes. Our study also summarized the functions of all identifed UMAMITs, providing valuable information on the evolution of UMAMITs and their potential application in molecular breeding for developing crop varieties with improved nutrient use efciency.

The most recent report suggests that there are more than 100 annotated amino acid transporters in Arabidopsis thaliana (Table 1), although the number varies in other published reports [3]. Based on expression analysis, 22 of these amino acid transporters are expressed in siliques and seeds (Table 2). These transporters mostly belong to the cationic amino acid transporter (CAT) family, and usually multiple

amino acids move in and out transporter (UMAMIT) family, followed by the amino acid permease (AAP) family. Acquisition of amino acids in seeds can be influenced by any amino acid transporter expressed in the source and sink tissues or along the vascular transport path. However, the CAT, UMAMIT, and AAP families, with notable members expressed in seeds and siliques, appear to have significant importance in amino acid transport to seeds. There was a gap in understanding the amino acid export process in plants until the recent identification of the UMAMIT family. Members of this family are capable of both importing and exporting amino acids and are localized in both plasma and organelle membranes [22–24].

Amino acids are the primary form of organic nitrogen transported in plants and are essential for plant growth and development. Generally, amino acids are thought to be the constituents of proteins and precursors for the synthesis of nucleotides, chlorophyll, hormones, and secondary metabolites (Tegeder 2012). However, they fulfll many other functions in plants related to growth, development, adaptation to unfavorable conditions, and may also trigger defense signaling pathways (Toyota et al. 2018). Clearly, suggesting the importance of amino acid transport in plant growth. For the translocation of amino acids between cells and cellular organelles, transporters are needed. Amino acid transporters (AATs) are membrane-localized protein carriers involved in the movement of amino acids from the source to sink tissues in plants. The involvement of AATs has also been deciphered in leaf senescence and seed germination, for instance, in rice, the developing seeds receives $6 0 \%$ of their amino acid requirement from the amino acids retrieved from senescing leaves (Ortiz-Lopez et al. 2000). These transporters either act as importers or exporters, facilitating the redistribution of amino acids (Okumoto and Pilot 2011). The plant AATs have been categorized into three main families: (a) the ATF (amino acid transporter) family, also known as the amino acid/auxin permease (AAAP) family (b) the APC (amino acid polyamine choline facilitator) family (Su et al. 2004) and (c) the UMAMIT (usually multiple amino acids move in and out transporters) family (Denancé et al. 2014). The ATF superfamily of AATs (SLC38; pfam01490) has been reported to be eukaryote-specifc and found in plants, animals, and fungi. The members are either proton-coupled symporters or antiporters having 9–11 transmembrane domains with cytosolic $\mathbf { N }$ and extracellular C terminals (Wipf et al. 2002). This superfamily is further divided into six subfamilies based on their substrate specifcity: Amino acid permeases (AAPs), lysine and histidine transporters (LHTs), proline transporters (ProTs), aromatic and neutral amino acid transporters (ANTs), auxin transporters (AUXs), $\gamma$ -aminobutyric acid transporters (GATs). The APC family encompasses three subfamilies, namely cationic amino acid transporters (CATs), amino acid/choline transporters (ACTs), and polyamine $\mathrm { H } +$ -symporters (PHSs) subfamilies (Fischer et al. 2002). Members of the APC family (SLC7; pfam00324) have been reported in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes and possess 12–14 transmembrane domains (Wipf et al. 2002). The UMAMIT family belongs to the Drug/Metabolite Transporter (DMT) superfamily (Denancé et al. 2014). This family of transporters is unique to multicellular plants and no homologs are present in fungi and animals (Rodríguez-Ezpeleta et al. 2005). This family comprises 44 members and three pseudogenes in

Arabidopsis, possessing ten transmembrane domains. Most of the members of the AAAP and APC superfamilies are being characterized as amino acid importers (Tegeder and Rentsch 2010), with the exception being AtBAT1/AtGABP, which is described as a bidirectional transporter (Dündar and Bush 2009). Also, the UMAMIT family members such as AtUMAMIT11, 14, 18, 28, and 29 like AtGABP facilitate both import and export of amino acids (Ladwig et al. 2012; Müller et al. 2015). To date, only two AATs UMAMIT24 and UMAMIT25 are being reported to function as amino acid exporters (Besnard et al. 2018).

Additionally, Vacuolar Amino Acid Transporters (AtAVT) have also been identifed in Arabidopsis thaliana using the protein sequences of Saccharomyces cerevisiae AVT transporters (ScAvt1, ScAvt3, ScAvt4, and ScAvt6) as a query (Fujiki et al. 2017). These vacuolar amino acid transporters are reported to belong to the ATF superfamily. Homologs of these members are also present in animals and yeast, such as vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) from Caenorhabditis elegans UNC-47, the mammalian system A and N transporters of the SLC38 family, VGAT from rat, VIAAT from mouse, and AVT transporters from S. cerevisiae. A recent study suggests that the AATs localized in the vacuolar membranes enable plants to cope up with the changing environmental conditions by involving in the N storage, salinity tolerance, accumulation of toxic ions, maintenance of the cellular ion and $\mathrm { p H }$ homeostasis, calcium signaling and guard cell movements (Martinoia et al. 2007). However, the molecular identity of the majority of the vacuolar amino acid transporters is still unknown. AtANT1 is the frst member of the AtAVT3 family to be characterized molecularly and is reported to mediate the transport of auxin, aromatic and neutral amino acids. It is expressed in all organs, with the highest in cauline leaves and fowers (Chen et al. 2001). Recently, Fujiki et al. (2017) functionally characterized the other members of the AtAVT3 family of vacuolar amino acid transporters. Like yeast Avt3 and Avt4, the AtAvt3A-C also mediates proton-coupled amino acid transport in an ATP-dependent manner. Unlike other family members localized at the vacuolar membrane, AtANT1 is located at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (Fujiki et al. 2017). The functionality and substrate specifcity of the members of the other two subfamilies (AtAVT1 & AtAVT6) still needs to be explored. So far, only one member of the AtAVT1 family, AtAVT1A (AT2G41190) has been functionally characterized and was reported to be upregulated in response to water stress (Bray 2004). However, its exact role in helping the plant to overcome water defcit is not known. Some members of the CAT (cationic amino acid transporter) subfamily have also been identifed to be localized on tonoplast, such as AtCAT2, AtCAT4, AtCAT8, and AtCAT9 (Carter et al. 2004; Jaquinod et al. 2007).

A summary of amino acid transporter genes describing their inferred substrate specifcity, cell and tissue-specifc expression patterns, and roles in stress tolerance and plant development are detailed in Table 1. The substrate specifcity of amino acid transporters is studied using heterologous expression systems such as yeast mutants and Xenopus laevis oocytes or in plants (comparing wild-type and mutant plants lacking a functional transporter). For some transporters listed in Table 1 we have inferred their possible substrate based on their sequence similarity to functionally characterised family members. The data clearly depicts that the amino acid transporters exhibit complex expression patterns and are expressed diferentially in response to internal and external factors. Following this, a number of researchers are studying their transport properties and expression patterns, however, the regulatory elements localized in the promoter regions of these transporter genes, responsible for controlling the expression patterns are least explored. Thus, to understand the regulation and expression patterns of known and unexplored members in response to various developmental and environmental cues, the promoter regions of the transporter genes were analyzed. Reports to date strongly support the fact that functional signifcance is defned not only by the biochemical activity of the protein under study but also by its expression pattern, which in turn is controlled by various developmental programs, and by diferential responses to environmental conditions, such as alterations in nutrient availability, biotic and abiotic stresses, etc. (Liu and Bush 2006). In this review, regulation and expression patterns of amino acid transporter genes are discussed, and plausible candidates that could be targeted to improve plant stress tolerance and productivity for future research are detailed.

Members of large multi-gene families often display overlapping functions. Since many amino acid transporters act on the same substrates, specificity may derive from their expression patterns and their responses to environmental signals [14]. For example, the Arabidopsis AAP1 and AAP2 transporters display a preference for neutral and acidic amino acids. However, an analysis of promoter–GUS reporter lines revealed that AAP1 was expressed in the developing endosperm and cotyledons, thus strongly suggesting that AAP1 functions in the import of amino acids into the endosperm embryo. By contrast, AAP2 was highly expressed in the vascular tissue of stems and siliques, suggesting a role in amino acid retrieval and uptake into seeds. Moreover, although the Arabidopsis ProT1 and ProT2 proteins both transport the compatible solute proline, the expression pattern of their encoding genes responds differently to water and salt stress [63].

Nonetheless, not all related transporters share the same substrate specificity, as suggested by the characterization of selected amino acid transporters that differ both in their range of substrates and in their site(s) of action. Recently, Choi showed that Arabidopsis LHT2 can transport 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC), a biosynthetic precursor of ethylene, when expressed in Xenopus oocytes [112]. In addition, UMAMIT5, also called WALLS ARE THIN1 (WAT1), has been ascribed the function of indole-3-acetic acid exporter from the vacuole to the cytosol, unlike other UMAMIT members [18,109]. Seven members of the UMAMIT family have been suggested to play a role in the seed loading process, but their individual expression patterns differ during this process, suggesting that they play distinct roles in amino acid translocation from maternal to filial tissues. Indeed, the phenotypes associated with single umamit loss-of-function mutants are relatively benign, consistent with the involvement of multiple exporters in amino acid transport to developing seeds. Similarly, Arabidopsis LHT6 and AAP1 are expressed in root cells and display overlapping functions in root amino acid uptake. However, they also exhibit different substrate preferences. For example, Perchlik showed that LHT6 is involved in the uptake of acidic amino acids, such as glutamine and alanine, and probably phenylalanine, whereas AAP1 transports neutral amino acids and glutamate when amino acids are present at low concentrations [49]. In the feeding experiments, root uptake of the amino acids alanine, glutamine, proline, serine, glutamate, and phenylalanine significantly decreased in lht6 aap1 double mutant plants. Interestingly, the growth of the lht6 aap1 double mutant was not affected when grown on Murashige and Skoog medium, possibly because other amino acid transporters expressed in the root can compensate for their loss [49]. Similarly, Arabidopsis LHT1 and AAP5 assimilate neutral and acidic amino acids, respectively, and displayed non-overlapping specificity in their substrates, suggesting that they have separate roles in amino acid uptake [50].

Nitrogen (N) is an essential macroelement for plant growth and development. Plants mainly absorb inorganic N in the form of nitrate and ammonium from the soil, while organic N such as amino acids, can also be taken up by plants [1]. The absorbed inorganic N can be assimilated into amino acids in roots and/or leaves. Amino acids in roots are transported mainly to source leaves in the xylem transpiration stream [2]. As the main transport form of organic N in most plant species, amino acids synthesized in leaves or derived from roots are transported via phloem to developing sink organs to meet their N requirement [3]. Therefore, the transport and allocation of amino acids within plants is crucial for their growth, development and seed set.

Amino acids transport is generally mediated by transport proteins in plants. The first plant amino acid transporters were cloned mainly through functional complementation of yeast mutants deficient in amino acid transport [3–5]. Subsequently, amino acid transporters could be identified by bioinformatics analysis after the completion of genome sequencing of some plants [6,7]. Now, the presence of dozens, or even hundreds, of amino acid transporters are found in different plant species (Table 1). These transporters belong to three major families: ATF (amino acid transporter family, also called AAAP family), APC (amino acid-polyamine-choline transporter family) and the newly identified UMAMIT (usually multiple acids move in and out transporter family) [8]. The ATF family generally contains eight subfamilies: AAP (amino acid permeases), LHT (lysine and histidine transporters), ProT (proline transporters), GAT (γ-aminobutyric acid transporters), ANT (aromatic and neutral amino acid transporters), AUX (auxin transporters), ATL (amino acid transporter-like) and VAAT (vesicular aminergic-associated transporters) [9]. The members of the AUX subfamily usually transport auxin instead of amino acids [8,10]. The APC family consists of three subfamilies: CAT (cationic amino acid transporters), ACT (amino acid/choline transporters) and PHS (polyamine $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -symporters) [11]. UMAMITs belong to the nodulin-like gene family [12], and recently several members of this family have been reported to function as bidirectional amino acid transporters [13,14]. Among these families, of main attention in plants is the AAP family. With respect to the phylogenetic relationship of these transporters, readers are referred to other literature [7,15,16]. Despite belonging to different families, these amino acid transporters display some common properties such as broad expression pattern and substrate specificity. Here, we focus mainly on the amino acid transport processes and the other physiological roles mediated by these transporters. The potential applications of amino acid transporters for crop genetic improvement are also discussed in this review.

Here we have identified UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 as glucosinolate exporters with a key role in the accumulation of glucosinolates in seeds as evidenced by less than $6 \%$ of glucosinolates in seeds of umamit29 umamit30 umamit31 exporter mutants compared with the wild-type level. We previously identified the active high-affinity $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled glucosinolate importers (GTR1, GTR2 and GTR3) and showed that the elimination of seed glucosinolates in the gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 triple mutants was accompanied by altered accumulation patterns of glucosinolates in the rest of the plant8–12. The suppression of this phenotype in the umamit29 umamit30 gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 quintuple mutant provides genetic evidence that UMAMITs function as the exporters that deliver glucosinolates to the apoplast.

The biochemical and biophysical characterization of UMAMIT29–31 in oocytes shows that glucosinolates are exported passively along an electrochemical gradient. In Arabidopsis, in which the plasma membrane potential under physiological conditions is within the range of −100 to $- 1 5 0 \mathrm { m V }$ (ref. 31), UMAMIT29–31 are expected to facilitate efficient export of the monovalent anionic glucosinolates out of biosynthetic cells to the acidic apoplast. A recent theory-based study hypothesized that the mechanism for nutrient homeostasis aimed at reaching a desired cytosolic concentration of a given nutrient requires that at least two differently energized transporter types are involved13. The presence of passive UMAMIT exporters and $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled GTR importers fulfils this requirement. Accordingly, the $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled high-affinity GTR importers empty the apoplast for glucosinolates generating a strong outward chemical gradient (from the cytosol to apoplast), which— together with the strong negative membrane potential—promotes efficient export of glucosinolates through the passive uniport mechanism of UMAMIT29–31. Notably, the glucosinolate exporters as well as the exporters of sugars (SUGARS WILL EVENTUALLY BE EXPORTED TRANSPORTERS (SWEETs))32,33 and amino acids (UMAMITs)26,27 are all uniporters, which suggests the presence of a universal passive uniport mechanism for exporting compounds from symplasm in source tissues.

UMAMIT29–31 belong to UMAMIT clade I proteins (UMAMIT26–32) of which UMAMIT26–31 are brassicaceous-specific (Extended Data Fig. 9). This highlights the potential of transporter families involved in primary metabolism to evolve substrate specificity towards specialized metabolites as recently shown for the NPF family34–40. Analogously, the identification of UMAMITs as exporters of glucosinolates suggests that the UMAMIT family may represent a new family of exporters of specialized metabolites. Notably, the substrate specificity of the three UMAMITs exporters, with UMAMIT29 and UMAMIT30 having broad substrate specificity and UMAMIT31 being specific for indolic glucosinolates, is mirrored in the three GTR importers, with GTR1 and GTR2 having broad substrate specificity and GTR3 favouring indolic glucosinolates9 , indicating co-evolution of substrate preferences across these distinct transporter families. Previous studies on the amino acid export activity


## Article


of UMAMITs using Xenopus oocytes27 and Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells29 have reported different outcomes, which may reflect difficulties in measuring transport activity of primary metabolites that are concomitantly being metabolized by the heterologous host expressing the transporter. The minor alteration in free amino acid levels in seeds of various umamit mutants and myb28 myb29 (MYB28 and MYB29 are master regulators of aliphatic glucosinolates), as well as gtr1 gtr2 mutants41, merits future studies to investigate the relationship between glucosinolates and free amino acids in seeds.

On the basis of the overlapping presence of UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 with glucosinolate biosynthetic marker enzymes in the funiculus at the mature green stage, we propose that the funiculus acts as a major glucosinolate source tissue from where UMAMIT29, UMAMIT30 and UMAMIT31 export de novo synthesized seed-bound glucosinolates into the apoplast, and that the secondarily activated high-affinity $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled GTRs subsequently import them into the phloem through which the glucosinolates are translocated to the seeds. Generally, understanding the seed loading process has been hampered owing to a lack of tools, as transporter mutants of primary metabolites such as sucrose and amino acids—for which importers and exporters are already known—often have pleiotropic effects42–45. The latter is typically not the case for specialized metabolite transporters. The glucosinolate UMAMIT exporters, along with the GTR importers, are essential for seed accumulation and provide powerful molecular tools to dissect the process of seed loading to the embryo.

Transport engineering that uses altered expression of transporter genes to change metabolite distribution patterns has resulted in the development of improved agronomic traits2–5,46. Here we show that umamit29 umamit30 umamit31 exporter mutants do not alter the overall distribution of glucosinolates in the plant, which contrast with either reduction (roots, stems) or strong overaccumulation (rosette, cauline leaves, silique valves) in the gtr1 gtr2 gtr3 glucosinolate importer mutants. Thus, from an agricultural perspective, UMAMIT exporters have high biotechnological potential as molecular breeding targets for eliminating anti-nutritional glucosinolates in seed cake of brassicaceous oilseed crops through transport engineering without affecting glucosinolate defence in the rest of the plant.

Nitrogen (N) is one of the major mineral nutrients essential for plants growth and development. Plants absorb N mainly in the inorganic form (nitrate and ammonium) from soils, while the organic N such as amino acids could also be absorbed [1, 2]. Upon entering the plants, inorganic $_ \mathrm { N }$ is converted into amino acids in roots or leaves. The reduced $_ \mathrm { N }$ is transported mainly in the form of amino acids to developing vegetative or reproductive sink organs, where it is used for growth and development. The uptake and translocation of organic and inorganic N is mediated by a variety of transporters. Nowadays, the nitrate and ammonium transporters have been extensively studied in plants [3, 4], while the amino acid transporters are still poorly understood, especially in crop plants.

Physiological studies using isolated membrane vesicles and plant tissues have suggested the presence of multiple amino acid transporters with wide substrate specificity in plants [5–7]. Molecular methods have allowed the cloning of genes responsible for amino acids transport. The first plant amino acid transporters AAP1 and NAT2 were identified by functional complementation of yeast mutants defective in amino acid uptake from Arabidopsis cDNA libraries, both of which exhibited broad substrate specificity [8, 9]. Thereafter a multitude of amino acid transporters were reported from several plant species [10, 11]. In recent years, sequencing the full genomes of different plants gave us a chance to grasp the abundance of amino acid transporters in plant genomes.

At least 67, 85 and 189 genes have been identified to encode putative amino acid transporters in Arabidopsis, rice and soybean, respectively [12–14]. Based on sequence analysis, the amino acid transporters identified so far could be divided into two families: the amino acid/polyamine/choline (APC) family and the amino acid transporter (ATF) family. The ATF family was also referred to as AAAP (amino acid/auxin permease) family, and encompasses at least five subfamilies: AAPs (amino acid permeases), LHTs (lysine/histidine transporters), ProTs (proline transporters), ANTs (aromatics and neutral amino acid transporters) and AUXs (auxin transporters) [13, 15, 16]. These transporters generally differ in substrate specificity/affinity and tissue localization [17].

AtLHT1, the first member identified in LHT family, was initially viewed as a lysine (Lys) and histidine (His) selective transporter [18]. However, subsequent studies with other LHT members revealed that LHTs could transport a broad but distinct spectrum of amino acids [19–21]. LHT genes were expressed in various plant organs, including roots, leaves and flowers. They could mediate not only amino acids uptake from soil, but also translocation and partitioning of amino acids within plants [19–21]. However, it should be noted that the research on LHT transporters was mainly performed in Arabidopsis, while our understanding of LHTs in rice is generally scant. A genome-wide survey identified 6 LHT members in rice [14]. Liu et al. [22] isolated a LHT family member OsHT1 from rice by screening cDNA library, which could restore the growth of yeast mutant defective in His uptake. Due to highest identity with AtLHT1 among the 10 LHT family members in Arabidopsis, OsHT1 is referred to as OsLHT1 hereafter.

Although OsLHT1-mediated His transport was determined in yeast [22], it is not clear at present whether OsLHT1 could transport other amino acids. In this study, the substrate specificity of OsLHT1 was analyzed in Xenopus oocytes, and we found that OsLHT1 was able to transport a broad spectrum of amino acids with preference for neutral and acidic amino acids. Furthermore, to explore the role of OsLHT1 in rice growth and development, two oslht1 mutants were constructed using the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing technology. It is found that disruption of OsLHT1 significantly inhibited the rice growth and fecundity. Also, the expression pattern and subcellular localization of OsLHT1 was analyzed. This study will further our understanding of the substrate specificity of OsLHT1 and its roles in rice growth promotion and yield formation.

Owing to its pleasant flavor and multiple health benefits, tea is the second most popular nonalcoholic beverage worldwide, second only to water. Tea quality largely depends on the contents of polyphenols, caffeine, and theanine in the new shoots used for tea processing. Previous studies have shown that the biosynthesis of these metabolites is related to N (N) conditions1–3 , with highquality tea being produced from plants grown under adequate N levels1,4,5 . However, high $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilization accelerates soil acidification6 , which can lead to high accumulations of aluminum, fluorine, and heavy metals (e.g., lead and chromium) in tea leaves, posing potential risks to human health7 . In recent decades, tea produced from organic plantations has increased in popularity8,9 . For example, in China, during the past two decades, organic tea production has increased ${ \tt > } 4 5 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { f o l d } ^ { 9 }$ .

It has been shown that plants acquire N from the soil in the form of nitrate, ammonium, urea, and amino acids10, with amino acids representing a significant $_ \mathrm { N }$ pool in some soils11–13. Soil amino acids are derived mainly from exoenzymatic decomposition of proteins and peptides of decaying organisms14. Tea plants constitute perennial crops whose leaves are harvested and are periodically pruned $2 { \sim } 3$ times per year to maintain vigorous vegetative growth. In this regard, such tea plantation pruning has the potential to produce ${ \sim } 8 0 0 0 \mathrm { k g h a } ^ { - 1 }$ of pruned litter annually15. This pruned litter contains high levels of amino acids and proteins that can be recycled following its decomposition in the soil. These pruned litter-derived amino acids may serve as an important $_ \mathrm { N }$ source to be taken up by tea plant root systems.

Plant cells, including those of the roots, take up nutrients through a combination of passive and active transport mechanisms. Channels and permeases can participate in passive uptake when soil nutrient concentrations are high, whereas proton-coupled transporters engage in secondary active transport under low-nutrient conditions16–18. Given that soil amino-acid levels are much lower than those within the cells of roots, plasma membrane-localized transporters are generally required for amino-acid uptake from soils18. At present, many plant amino-acid transporters have been identified19–23 and are grouped into two superfamilies: amino acid/auxin permeases (AAAPs) and amino acid-polyamine-choline transporters (APCs)16,24. The AAAP superfamily includes six families, amino-acid permeases (AAPs), lysine and histidine transporters (LHTs), proline transporters (ProTs), GATs (γ-aminobutyric acid transporters), auxin transporters (AUXs), and aromatic and neutral amino-acid transporters (ANTs), whereas the APC superfamily includes members of the cationic amino-acid transporter (CAT) and L-type aminoacid transporter (LAT) families. Amino-acid transporters involved in uptake from the soil belong mainly to the AAP, ProT, and LHT families25–28.

In Arabidopsis, the LHT family members LHT1 and LHT6 have been shown to be critical for amino-acid uptake by plant roots25,29. AtLHT1 displays uptake activity for glutamine (Gln), Ala, Glu, and Asp but not for Arg or Lys. AtLHT6 is involved in the uptake of acidic amino acids (Gln, Ala, and probably phenylalanine) but does not seem to transport basic or other neutral amino acids25. Studies devoted to amino-acid transporters have generally been performed on annual plant species, with much less information available on the molecular mechanisms underlying amino-acid transport in perennial species30–33.

In this study, we measured the amino-acid composition in the soil at a normal (common) tea plantation and an organic tea plantation. Furthermore, we fed tea plants Glu, the most abundant amino acid detected in the soil and found that it was efficiently absorbed and utilized by these plants. We then cloned seven CsLHT genes and determined that CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 were able to transport a broad spectrum of amino acids. Arabidopsis lines overexpressing CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 were found to exhibit increased uptake of exogenously supplied amino acids. In addition, expression patterns and subcellular localization studies provided support for the hypothesis that CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 play important roles in aminoacid uptake into the roots of tea plants.

AtLHT1 is the first member identified in the LHT subfamily belonging to the amino acid transporter (ATF) family [18]. Uptake measurements in yeast suggested that AtLHT1 transported Lys and His most efficiently among the 13 different amino acids tested, and the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values for Lys $( 1 7 5 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ and His $( 4 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ were much lower than that for the third most-active substrate, Leu $( 1 1 \mathrm { m M } )$ , so it was regarded as a Lys and His selective transporter [18]. However, studies on the transport properties of other members of LHT family suggested that LHTs were able to transport a wide spectrum of amino acids, including neutral, basic and acidic amino acids, and exhibited preferential selectivity for neutral and acidic amino acids with high affinity [20, 21, 29]. For example, uptake analysis in yeast revealed that AtLHT2 transported aspartate and proline with high affinity $K _ { \mathrm { m } } = 7 2 ,$ ， $1 3 \mu \mathrm { M }$ , respectively), and competition experiments showed that other neutral and acidic amino acids, but not basic amino acids, act as efficient competitors for proline and aspartate uptake [20]. Furthermore, Perchlik et al. [21] studied AtLHT6 function in planta and found that knockout of AtLHT6 significantly reduced the uptake of acidic and some neutral amino acids, but not basic amino acids. There are 6 LHT members existing in rice [14], but their substrate specificity has not yet been determined until now. OsLHT1 has been reported as a His transporter previously [22], and its substrate specificity was analyzed in Xenopus oocytes in the present study. We found that OsLHT1 could mediate the transport of various amino acids with different characteristics (Fig. 1a, b). Different from AtLHT1 expressed in yeast [18], the Lys transport activity of OsLHT1 was very weak relative to His (Fig. 1a, b). Moreover, the neutral amino acid Asn, but not the basic amino acid His, was the best substrate for OsLHT1 among the amino acids tested (Fig. 1a, b), so the substrate profile of OsLHT1 resemble that of AtLHT2 and AtLHT6 [20, 21]. However, it should be noted that OsLHT1 and AtLHT2 differ in substrate specificity and affinity. The $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value of OsLHT1 for its best substrate Asn is $5 8 3 \pm 5 1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ (Fig. 1c), which is one order of magnitude higher than the values of AtLHT2 for Pro and Asp $K _ { \mathrm { m } } = 1 3 .$ , $7 2 \mu \mathrm { M }$ , respectively) [20]. The difference in $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ values between OsLHT1 and AtLHT2 may imply their different roles in planta, which will require further analysis in future study. Overall, given the substrate specificity of the LHTs identified so far, it could be concluded that the LHTs were not Lys and His selective transporters, but ones with broad substrate specificity and with preference for neutral and acidic amino acids.

The substrate profile of OsLHT1 was determined in Xenopus oocytes under $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 4$ condition. At $\mathrm { p H } 5 . 4 _ { \mathrm { i } }$ basic amino acids such as His are positively charged, while acidic amino acids such as Asp and Glu carry mainly negative net charges. However, all these amino acids with opposite charges could be transported by OsLHT1 (Fig. 1a, b). On the other hand, Lys and Arg carrying like charge as His were not efficiently transported by OsLHT1 (Fig. 1a, b). So it is supposed that net charge is not a major determinant of substrate recognition for OsLHT1. Besides charge, individual amino acids differ with respect to geometry, which might play a crucial role in substrate recognition by OsLHT1.

OsLHT1 was localized at the plasma membrane in rice protoplasts (Fig. 4b), which is consistent with its function as an amino acid transporter, and also agrees with previous work by Liu et al. [22] and Whiteman et al. [30]. In Liu’s study, the OsLHT1-GFP fusion construct was expressed transiently in onion epidermal cells, and green fluorescence was detected almost exclusively at the plasma membrane [22]. Whiteman et al. [30] isolated rice plasma membrane and tonoplast proteins, and found that OsLHT1 specific peptides were present in plasma membrane fractions but not in tonoplast.

OsLHT1 was expressed in roots (Fig. 4a, Additional file: Figure S4), and could transport amino acids both in yeast and Xenopus oocytes (Fig. 1a) [22], which implied that it might be capable of mediating amino acids acquisition from soil. However, given the facts that: (1) free amino acid concentrations found in the bulk soil solution vary greatly, and rarely exceed $5 0 \mu \mathrm { M }$ [31–34]; (2) the $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ value of OsLHT1 for the most active substrate, Asn, was $5 8 3 \pm 5 1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ (Fig. 1c), which is much higher than the free amino acid concentrations in most soil solution; (3) a large number of microorganisms exist in soil, which are the superior competitors for free amino acids in comparison to plant roots, especially at low soil amino acids concentrations [35–37], we reasoned that the main function of OsLHT1 in planta might not be to acquire amino acids from soil, which needs to be verified in future studies. On the other hand, the absorbed inorganic $_ \mathrm { N }$ was converted into amino acids in roots or mature leaves (source), which are the major transport forms of N within plants, and were transported to various metabolically active organs (sink) such as root tips, young leaves, flowers and seeds. The source-to-sink translocation of amino acids is involved in several processes such as phloem loading, import into sinks and xylem-to-phloem transfer, which require the mediation of multiple amino acid transporters [11]. The amino acid permeases (AAPs) have been reported to be involved in the source-to-sink transport of amino acids [38–40]. For example, AtAAP8 is expressed in the source leaf phloem, and loss-of-function of AtAAP8 reduced a broad spectrum of amino acid phloem loading and partitioning to sinks, which in turn led to decreased silique and seed numbers in ataap8 plants [40]. OsLHT1 was expressed in various shoot organs such as leaf, leaf blade, and localized to the plasma membrane (Fig. 4a, b), implying its function in amino acids translocation in planta. Furthermore, a lack of OsLHT1 function significantly inhibited plants development and reduced seed yields (Figs. 2e, 3a), so we supposed that OsLHT1 functions mainly in amino acids transport within plants, but the process it mediated will need further investigations in future.

## Amino-acid composition in tea plantation soils


Amino acids have been detected in many soil types11–13. However, there is little information on the amino-acid contents in tea plantation soils. In this study, soil samples were collected from control (common) tea plantation and an organic tea plantation to assess their amino-acid contents (Fig. 1a). Amino acids, including glutamate (Glu), alanine (Ala), valine (Val), leucine (Leu), threonine (Thr), serine (Ser), aspartate (Asp), glycine (Gly), and isoleucine (Ile), were detected in these soils (Fig. 1b). The levels of Glu, Ala, Val, and Leu were higher than those of the other amino acids. The total amino-acid content in the soils was $1 - 8 \mu \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { g }$ dry soil, with the amino-acid contents in the organic tea plantation soil being higher than those in the conventional tea plantation soil (Fig. 1b, c). These results confirmed the presence of amino acids in the soils of tea plantations, which is consistent with findings in other ecosystems, and implied a more important role of soil amino acids inorganic tea plantations.


## Glu feeding increases amino-acid levels in tea plant roots


Plant roots can take up various amino acids, such as Asp, Glu, and Gln, over a wide range of concentrations from $0 . 0 1 \mu \mathrm { M }$ to $5 \mathrm { m M } ^ { 3 7 , 4 3 }$ . Exogenous Glu can support seedling growth and increase the contents of Glu, Gln, Asp, Ala, Ser, Asn, and $\Upsilon$ -aminobutyric acid (GABA) in rice roots44,45. As shown in Fig. 1b, Glu was the most abundant amino acid in the soil of the organic tea plantations investigated in our study (Fig. 1b). We speculated that Glu is an important amino acid that can be directly utilized by tea roots. Therefore, we fed tea plants with Glu, as the sole $_ \mathrm { N }$ source, to test whether tea plants could use amino acids from the media. In this experiment, hydroponically cultured tea plant seedlings were first subjected to an N deficiency $( 0 \mathrm { N } )$ for $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 2 d }$ and then provided $1 \mathrm { m M }$ Glu for $5 ~ \mathrm { d } ,$ with $_ { 0 \mathrm { N } }$ for $^ \textrm { \scriptsize 5 d }$ serving as the control (Fig. 2a). The roots of these seedlings were collected for amino-acid analyses, and we found that $1 \mathrm { m M }$ Glu feeding increased the total amino-acid contents in these roots, especially Ala, GABA, tyrosine (Tyr), Ile, Leu, proline (Pro), Gly, phenylalanine (Phe), and Gln (Fig. 2b, c). These findings support the hypothesis that tea plants can acquire Glu from media as an $_ \mathrm { N }$ source and metabolize it to increase the synthesis of other amino acids.


## Absorption of $^ { 1 5 } \mathsf { N }$ -labeled Glu by tea roots and identification of CsLHT genes


To test whether tea plant roots can acquire amino acids from the soil, we fed hydroponically cultured tea plant seedlings $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -labeled Glu by adding $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { \dot { N } }$ -Glu to the nutrient solution. After $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ or $2 4 \mathrm { h } ,$ the $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ levels in the roots increased significantly compared with those in the control roots (Fig. 3a). These results indicated that tea seedlings can directly take up exogenously applied Glu.

As AtLHT1 and AtLHT6 can mediate amino-acid uptake from the soil25,38, we hypothesized that CsLHTs are involved in amino-acid uptake from the soil in the tea plant. To test this hypothesis, we first identified LHT family members in the tea plant. To this end, we searched for “lysine histidine transporter” in the gene annotations of transcriptome data for tea plant roots38 and identified 13 putative CsLHTs. We next downloaded AtLHT sequence information from The Arabidopsis Information Resource website (www.arabidopsis.org) and used it to identify CsLHT homologs via an online BLAST search39 (http://tpia.teaplant.org/). In this way, we identified two additional CsLHTs. We successfully cloned seven of these 15 CsLHT genes, and they were named CsLHT1-CsLHT7 based on their homologies to AtLHTs (Fig. 3b).


## Expression of CsLHT1, CsLHT2, and CsLHT6 in the roots was induced by Glu feeding


To investigate whether the expression of CsLHTs in the roots responds to amino acids in the soil, 100-day-old tea seedlings were transferred to N-deficient media supplemented with $2 \mathrm { m M }$ Glu for $^ { 6 \mathrm { h } }$ or $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ . Our results revealed that root expression of CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 was induced at both time points upon Glu feeding (Fig. 3c). Root expression of CsLHT2 was induced at $2 4 \mathrm { h }$ , whereas CsLHT3, CsLHT4, CsLHT5, and CsLHT7 did not respond to or were repressed by Glu feeding. Hence, these CsLHT genes respond differentially to amino acids within the root media, which may reflect various roles for these genes in tea root physiology. Based on these findings, we proposed that CsLHT1, CsLHT2, and CsLHT6 likely function in the root uptake of amino acids from the soil.


## CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 have the capacity to transport amino acids


To identify the CsLHT(s) responsible for amino-acid uptake, we next tested whether these CsLHTs could transport amino acids. The yeast mutant strain $2 2 \Delta 1 0 \alpha$ lacks 10 amino-acid transporter genes and cannot grow in media with amino acids (except arginine) constituting the sole N source46. Thus, we transferred the CsLHT genes individually into 22Δ10α and tested whether each transformant could grow in media with Glu, Gln, Ala, Pro, Asn, Asp or GABA as the sole N source. Interestingly, the expression of only CsLHT1 or CsLHT6 in this mutant enabled growth, indicating that CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 can transport these amino acids into yeast cells (Fig. 4a). Furthermore, according to these assays, yeast cells expressing CsLHT1 exhibited enhanced growth relative to that of cells expressing CsLHT6 (Fig. 4a). Similar findings were obtained from liquid culture assays (Fig. 4b). These results support the notion that CsLHT1 has a higher affinity for amino acids than does CsLHT6.


## CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 have different affinities for amino acids


To assess the CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 affinities for amino acids, we next analyzed their transport kinetics for $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ -Glu. Here, the yeast mutant $2 2 \Delta 1 0 \alpha _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , harboring CsLHT1 or CsLHT6, was fed $2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M } ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ -Glu, and the $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { \dot { N } }$ taken up into these cells was measured after a 0, 2, 5, 10, 20, or $3 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ incubation period (Fig. 5a). As expected, these transport assays demonstrated that $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu was absorbed and accumulated in the cells expressing CsLHT1 or CsLHT6. Importantly, $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ -Glu accumulation increased in the cells in a time-dependent manner. Moreover, $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N - G l u }$ accumulation in cells expressing CsLHT1 was much higher than that in cells expressing CsLHT6. These results provided further support for the notion that CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 can transport amino acids, albeit with different affinities.

A $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu concentration series (10, 20, 50, 100, 200, and $5 0 0 \mu \mathrm { M } )$ for CsLHT1 and one (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, and $2 0 \mathrm { m M } ,$ ) for CsLHT6 was also employed in our transport kinetics assays; $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ levels were measured in the cells after a $1 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ incubation. Concentration-dependent accumulation of $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ Glu in the cells was observed (Fig. 5b). The kinetic parameters calculated based on these $\mathrm { \bar { 1 } 5 _ { N } }$ -Glu assays indicated $K _ { m }$ values for CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 of $3 9 . 9 \mu \mathrm { M }$ and $2 . 5 \mathrm { m M }$ , respectively. These data indicated that CsLHT1 acts as a high-affinity-amino-acid transporter, whereas CsLHT6 is a low-affinity transporter.

To analyze CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 substrate specificities, competition experiments were next performed in which $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu uptake was measured in the presence of a 10-fold excess of unlabeled competitive amino acids. These assays showed that unlabeled Ala, Pro, Ser, Gln, Asn, Asp, and GABA significantly repressed $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ -Glu uptake by CsLHT1. In contrast, only Ala, Pro, and Ser significantly repressed $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu uptake by CsLHT6 (Fig. 5c). These findings indicated that, as a high-affinity-amino-acid transporter, CsLHT1 has broader substrate specificity than does the low-affinity-amino-acid transporter CsLHT6.

## CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 are $\mathsf { H } ^ { + }$ -coupled amino-acid transporters


To explore the mechanism through which CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 transport amino acids, we next performed $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } .$ - Glu uptake assays at $\mathsf { p H }$ levels of 4.0, 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0. These assays revealed that CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu transport activity was high at low $\mathsf { p H }$ levels but was significantly lower at neutral and alkaline pH levels (Fig. 6a). Moreover, the addition of the $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase inhibitor DES and the protonophore CCCP nearly abolished $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N }$ -Glu uptake by CsLHT1 and CsLHT6 (Fig. 6b).
