In peach, PpSUT2 overexpression improved cold and drought tolerance by modulating proline, soluble sugars, and oxidative stress markers (Zhao et al. 2022). More recently, SlSUT4 was shown to regulate sucrose partitioning between vacuole and cytosol, thereby afecting tomato drought responses (Liang et al. 2023).

Sugarcane (Saccharum spp. hybrids), a member of the grass family (Gramineae), is the world’s leading crop for sugar production and a key raw material for biofuel (Zhou et al. 2020, Ali et al. 2025). Commercial sugarcane cultivars are genetically complex, exhibiting allopolyploidy and aneuploidy, with large, highly variable genomes (Zhou et al. 2014; Healey et al. 2024). In China, the hybrid variety ROC22 (derived from $\mathsf { R O C 5 } \times 6 9 - 4 6 3 )$ has been the dominant cultivar over the past two decades, covering approximately $6 0 \%$ of the total sugarcane cultivation area (Su et al. 2019; Zhou et al. 2020). Previous studies have identifed numerous SUT family genes in sugarcane (Zhang et al. 2021a, b, c; Akbar et al. 2025) and examined their expression under various stress conditions; however, no such analyses have been reported for the Saccharum spp. Hybrid XTT22 (ROC22) genome. This study presents the first identifcation of ShSUT genes in the XTT22 genome, using bioinformatics to examine their physicochemical properties and evolutionary relationships. Transcription factors interacting with ShSUT4 were identifed through BiFC, and Y2H assays, and the expression of ShSUT genes was analyzed under Cold, Drought and Salinity, stressors. These fndings provide key insights into sugar transport, gene evolution, and the genetic basis for improving sugarcane through molecular breeding.

The world’s most planted grape species, Vitis vinifera, is susceptible to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, and waterlogging. It is also highly susceptible to several pathogens, including powdery mildew, caused by the ascomycete fungus Erysiphe necator (syn. Uncinula necator), and downy mildew, caused by the oomycete Plasmopara viticola. Furthermore, while abiotic and biotic stresses lead to disastrous losses in yields, elucidating the mechanisms by which plants adapt to adverse conditions can be challenging.

In higher plants, sugars (sucrose, monosaccharides, and polyols) not only are important metabolites but also act as nutrients and function as osmotic and signaling molecules. In numerous species, sucrose is the most prevalent form of carbon produced in photosynthetic organs (the source), and it is transported via the phloem over long distances to heterotrophic organs (the sink), a process that is dependent upon a constant supply of carbohydrates (Afoufa-Bastien et al. 2010a). Sucrose plays a variety of important roles in stress tolerance, serving as an osmolyte, a signaling molecule, and/or a nutrient (Gong et al. 2015; Gupta and Kaur 2005; Roitsch 1999; Ruan et al. 2010; Yu 1999), while sucrose transporters (SUTs) play key roles in the translocation of sucrose and in the export of photosynthetically-fixed carbon from leaves. Several studies that have analyzed the signaling functions of several SUTs, including Arabidopsis AtSUC2, AtSUC4, and AtSUC9 have demonstrated that SUTs are highly induced by exposure to salt, osmotic, and low temperature treatments (Gong et al. 2015; Jia et al. 2015). In addition, AtSUC3 was found to be induced by wounding (Meyer et al. 2004), while StSUT4 from the potato was shown to affect flowering, tuberization, and shade avoidance responses (Chincinska et al. 2008).

A search for V. vinifera open reading frames revealed the presence of four putative SUTs, three of which (VvSUC11, VvSUC12, and VvSUC27) were validated and the sucrose transport activity were verified (Afoufa-Bastien et al. 2010a; Ageorges et al. 2000; Manning et al. 2001; Zhang et al. 2008). VvSUC11 belongs to the SUT4 subfamily, including AtSUC4. VvSUC12 is encoded by a gene that spans more than $1 0 { \cdot } \mathrm { k b }$ and contains 14 exons and 13 introns. It has an extended N-terminal domain and an elongated central cytoplasmic loop that contains two structural characteristics specific to the SUT2/SUC3 subfamily, which includes AtSUC3. SUC27 is a SUT located at the plasma membrane (Cai et al. 2017) and belongs to the dicot-specific SUT1 subfamily, which includes the remaining AtSUCs. The expression patterns of SUTs in the organs of grapevines has been shown to be variety specific (Afoufa-Bastien et al. 2010a; Cai et al. 2017; Davies et al. 1999; Deluc et al. 2007); however, SUT expression patterns and physiological functions in biotic and abiotic stress tolerance, as well as the differences among the varieties are poorly known.

Sugar transporters and the enzymes involved in sucrose metabolism have been reported to play a role in plant stress responses (Albertazzi et al. 2009; Julius et al. 2017; Santi et al. 2013). The enzymes involved in the conversion of sucrose to hexoses are vacuolar invertase and sucrose synthase (SUS). Based on the genomic sequence of the PN40024 line of V. vinifera, there are only two predicted vacuolar invertase sequences in the grapevine genome, coding for $V \nu G I N I$ and $V \nu G I N 2$ (Davies and Robinson 1996). SUS of which there are at least five SUS isoforms in the grapevine has a dual role in producing both UDP-glucose and ADP-glucose (Baroja-Fernandez et al. 2012). Among them, VvSUS2 was shown to be highly induced in stolburinfected leaves (Hren et al. 2009; Santi et al. 2013) it shares 82 and $8 1 \%$ identity at the amino acid sequence level with Arabidopsis SUS4 and SUS3, respectively (Bieniawska et al. 2007).

Plant hormones regulate many plant responses to environmental stimuli, as well as the pathway downstream of sucrose metabolism in plants. It’s known that abscisic acid (ABA), salicylic acid (SA) (Seo et al. 2001), and jasmonates (JA) play major roles in mediating plant defense responses against pathogens and abiotic stresses. The roles of ABA in responses to abiotic stresses such as drought, salinity, cold, heat stress, and wounding have been well characterized (Verma et al. 2016). 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase (NCED), which catalyzes a key step in the regulation of ABA biosynthesis, has been identified. Of the two NCED genes (NCED1 and 2) identified in the grapevine, only the transcription of NCED1 can be potentially linked to ABA biosynthesis in leaves under stress conditions, whereas NCED2 is likely developmentally regulated (Hayes et al. 2010). Traditionally, SA and JA have been associated with resistance to biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens, respectively (Forcat et al. 2008). This generality is disputed when comes to grapevine, as JA signaling is related to resistance against biotrophs, such as powdery and downy mildews (Guerreiro et al. 2016; Hamiduzzaman et al. 2005). The catalysis of chorismate by isochorismate synthase (ICS) and that of phenylalanine by phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) are normally the two pathways responsible for increasing the levels of SA (Liu et al. 2016). JA are synthesized in plants via the octadecanoid pathway (Beale and Ward 1998; Creelman and Mullet 1997), where Allene oxide cyclase (AOC) and cis-OPDA reductase $3 \ : ( O P R 3 )$ are the key genes involved in the first step of JA biosynthesis (Guerreiro et al. 2016). Methyl jasmonate (MeJA) is a fragrant compound that was initially identified in the flowers of Jasminum grandiflorum and is formed from JA by jasmonic acid carboxyl methyltransferase (JMT) catalysis. MeJA has become a strong candidate for an airborne signal that mediates interplant communication during defense responses. The characterization of cellular component(s) that catalyze the formation of MeJA may help to clarify jasmonate-mediated plant responses (Seo et al. 2001), while recent studies have provided substantial evidence for hormonal crosstalk in the regulation of plant defense responses (Bari and Jones 2009).

Vitis amurensis, a wild grapevine species originating from East Asia, is characterized by its remarkable adaptive potential and the strong of resistance to adverse environmental conditions (Liu and Li 2013), in contrast to V. vinifera which has poor resistance. These findings triggered our interest in elucidating the physiological mechanisms underlying the response of V. amurensis to stress. In this study, we analyzed the differences in the expression patterns of SUTs and in their promoter regions between V. amurensis Ruper. ‘Zuoshan-1’ and $V .$ vinifera ‘Chardonnay’. We also investigated the involvement of SUTs in the adaptation to biotic and abiotic stresses and associated it with sucrose metabolism and synthesis of plant hormones (ABA, SA, and JA) in V. amurensis and V. vinifera to elucidate the mechanisms of SUT-mediated resistance to stress in V. amurensis.

Sucrose delivered from photosynthetic source organs to heterotrophic sink organs comprises the raw carbon for biosynthetic reactions that yield food as well as lignocellulose. Sucrose is loaded into, transported through and unloaded from the phloem in a series of steps underpinned by sucrose transporters (SUTs) (Slewinski and Braun, 2010). These processes differ in important ways between fastgrowing, herbaceous annual and slower growing, woodforming perennial species (Van Bel and Gamalei, 1992; Rennie and Turgeon, 2009). In Arabidopsis, many of the Solanaceous species and monocots, there is little symplastic continuity between the phloem companion cells and the photosynthetic mesophyll, and phloem loading occurs from the apoplast (Van Bel and Gamalei, 1992; Riesmeier et al., 1993; Stadler and Sauer, 1996; Barker et al., 2000; Knop et al., 2001; Schmitt et al., 2008). Proton-coupled Group I (monocot) and Group II (dicot) SUTs in the plasmalemma mediate apoplastic phloem loading, and they are essential for normal growth of these species (Riesmeier et al., 1994; Burkle et al., 1998; Gottwald et al., 2000; Hackel et al., 2006; Srivastava et al., 2008). In contrast, temperate tree species can exhibit high degrees of symplastic, plasmodesmatal connectivity between phloem companion cells and the mesophyll (Gamalei, 1989; Rennie and Turgeon, 2009). Phloem loading in these species is poorly understood, but is thought to occur at least partly via the symplasm, and to be energetically passive and comparatively inefficient for sucrose export (Van Bel and Gamalei, 1992; Korner et al., 1995; Rennie and Turgeon, 2009). Arguments for strict apoplastic phloem loading have been presented, but currently there is no consensus about whether SUT proteins have a role, or whether symplastic export is a significant contributor to

the process in these species (Russin and Evert, 1985;   
Turgeon and Medville, 2004; Rennie and Turgeon, 2009;   
Turgeon, 2010).

After phloem loading, differences in sucrose distribution between herbaceous and tree species can lie in the contrasting longevity, structural complexity and positioning of major sink organs relative to the transport path. Whereas the major sink organs in herbaceous annuals are terminal (e.g. seed and tuber), the major sinks in trees include lateral wood-forming and other specialized tissues that exhibit annual cycles of carbohydrate storage and re-mobilization for growth. SUT proteins, mode of phloem loading, and thermodynamic properties of the transport stream all interact during the distribution of photoassimilates to lateral and terminal sinks (Van Bel, 2003; Hafke et al., 2005; Srivastava et al., 2008). In the stems of woody species, symplastic as well as apoplastic exchange of various metabolites, including sugars, occurs across the cambium and between xylem and phloem (Van Bel, 1990, 2003; Fuchs et al., 2010), but SUT participation in that process has not been reported. The stem-specific, Group II walnut (Juglans regia) JrSUT1 is thought to have a role in the apoplastic distribution of sucrose within the xylem between the vessels and vesselassociated cells during seasonal freeze–thaw cycles (Alves et al., 2004; Decourteix et al., 2006). JrSUT1 also appears to have a role in mediating the export of sucrose from xylem to leaves emerging after winter dormancy (Decourteix et al., 2008). Seasonal redistributions of sucrose have also been reported in Populus and Salix species (Sauter, 1983, 1988).

Multiple SUT isoforms are responsible for phloem loading, transport and unloading of sucrose in herbaceous species as recently reviewed (Braun and Slewinski, 2009), but the understanding of plant-wide SUT function in species valued for wood production is much less comprehensive. In herbaceous species at least, certain source leafexpressed plasma membrane SUT proteins exhibit rapid turnover and are under tight transcriptional control as a function of sink demand (Kuhn et al., 1997; Vaughn et al., 2002). Tonoplast SUT proteins (Group IV) which can mediate subcellular compartmentation of sucrose (Endler et al., 2006; Reinders et al., 2008) are minor constituents in herbaceous species. Their regulation by sink-source relations has not been investigated, and their occurrence in woody perennials has not been reported. To date, gene silencing has been used in the functional analysis of one non-tonoplast Group IV transporter, the plasma/ER membrane-localized Solanum tuberosum (potato) StSUT4 (Chincinska et al., 2008). StSUT4-silenced plants displayed altered diurnal rhythms of sucrose accumulation, early flowering, increased tuber yield, and reduced expression of gibberellic acid and ethylene biosynthetic genes (Chincinska et al., 2008). No genetic characterization based on mutant or transgenic silencing has been reported for tonoplast-localized SUTs. To advance our understanding of

SUT function in sink-source relations in a woody perennial, we characterize the SUT gene family of Populus. RNAi was then used to investigate the importance of the most abundantly expressed SUT gene in Populus, PtaSUT4, encoding a Group IV tonoplast symporter, to sucrose efflux from source leaves, to biomass partitioning, and to the interface between carbohydrate and secondary metabolism.

Plant sucrose transporter (SUT) proteins are sucrose– $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ symporters, which mediate the active transport of sucrose across plasma membranes. Since sucrose is translocated from source to sink tissues through the phloem, plasma membrane sucrose transporters are believed to play important roles in mediating carbon partitioning in plants (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Over the last decade, genes encoding SUT proteins have been isolated from a wide range of both monocot and dicot plant species, from source and sink tissues and found to be localised in phloem and non-phloem tissues (see reviews by Williams et al. 2000; Truernit 2001; Lalonde et al. 2003).

In cereal species, SUT proteins mainly have been studied in developing grains. For example, in developing rice caryopses, OsSUT1 protein is present in the plasma membrane of the aleurone cell layer surrounding the endosperm (Furbank et al. 2001) and is essential for transport of assimilates into filling grains (Scofield et al. 2002). A similar role in grain filling has been proposed for HvSUT1 protein in barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and for TaSUT1 in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2002). However, cellular localisation of cereal SUT gene expression in vegetative tissues has been less well characterised despite the fact that SUT mRNAs are detectable in these tissues of rice (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000; Aoki et al. 2003), maize (Aoki et al. 1999), barley (Weschke et al. 2000) and wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). While in dicot plants there is considerable evidence that SUTs play a role in apoplasmic loading of sucrose into the phloem (see review by Lalonde et al. 2003), there is little evidence for this in cereal species. Indeed, there is some debate over whether phloem loading in cereals occurs via symplasmic or apoplasmic pathways (e.g. Russin et al. 1996, also see review by Lalonde et al. 2003). Significantly, antisense repression of OsSUT1 expression in transgenic rice did not appear to affect phloem loading (Ishimaru et al. 2001; Scofield et al. 2002).

Previously we reported the isolation of three cDNAs encoding SUT proteins from developing grains of hexaploid wheat (Aoki et al. 2002). The peptide sequences deduced from the three cDNAs showed $9 8 \%$ identity to one another, all with more than $8 5 \%$ similarity to SUT1 proteins from other cereal species. The three wheat SUT1 proteins were encoded individually by single-copy homeologous genes, designated TaSUT1A, 1B and 1D , which are represented once in each of the A-, B- and D-genomes. Northern blot analysis revealed that the TaSUT1 genes were highly expressed not only in developing grains but also in flagleaf blades, flag-leaf sheaths and culms (internodes) at the pre-heading stage.

As a major photosynthetic product, sucrose constitutes one of the primary carbohydrates, which is transported between source tissues and heterotrophic sink tissues (Lemoine 2000; Williams et al. 2000). Furthermore, as a signaling molecule, sucrose can significantly influence cellular processes of the plant, particularly with regard to metabolic activity and fruit development. Sucrose metabolism also plays a pivotal role in developmental processes, stress response, and yield formation, primarily by generating a series of sugar metabolites used for energy metabolism and the synthesizing of essential compounds, including proteins, cellulose, and starch (Kühn 2011; Ruan 2014). Sucrose transporters (SUTs) possess 12 transmembrane domains and constitute typical membrane proteins in higher plants. SUTs are responsible for sucrose transport across membranes, including phloem loading in source tissues and sucrose unloading into sink tissues (Kühn et al. 2010; Doidy et al. 2012a).

Since the first SUT gene SoSUT1 was discovered from spinach (Spinacia oleracea) (Riesmeier et al. 1992), numerous SUT genes have been identified and characterized both in dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous species (Aoki et al. 2003; Doidy et al. 2012b; Zanon et al. 2015a; Zhang et al. 2016). All the SUTs in plants can be categorized into five subfamilies (Kühn et al. 2010), of which SUT1, SUT2, and SUT4 subfamilies were identified in dicots, whereas SUT2, SUT3, SUT4, and SUT5 subfamilies were found in monocots. According to the phylogenetic analysis, SUTs were classified into three groups, including Type I, Type II (A and B), and Type III (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type I members, localized to the plasma membrane, are identified as high-affinity sucrose carriers, involving in phloem loading or sucrose import into sink cells (Gottwald et al. 2000; Sauer 2007; Slewinski et al. 2009). They have been detected across various sink organs, including tubers, pollen, flowers, and fruits, suggesting a complex role in sucrose partitioning (Kühn et al. 2010). The Type II group can be divided into two sub-groups, IIA and IIB. Type IIA contains both eudicot and monocot isoforms, whereas Type IIB only represents the monocot-specific SUTs (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type IIA members are characterized by an elongated central loop with an unclear function, and are localized to the plasma membrane, similar with Type I. Several Type IIB members are plasma membrane-localized, high-affinity, and participate in phloem loading (Reinders et al. 2012; Peng et al. 2014). Type III, comprising tonoplast SUTs from both monocots and eudicots, are thought to facilitate sucrose release from vacuoles into the cytoplasm (Schneider et al. 2012; Ruan 2014). Type III SUTs are expressed in various tissues, including the veins of sink and source leaves, roots, anthers, and fruits (Weise et al. 2000; Peng et al. 2011; Zanon et al. 2015a). Furthermore, they are targeted to the plasma membrane or tonoplast depending on the plant species. Dual localization with tonoplast and plasma membrane has been reported for some Type III SUTs in certain species, such as Arabidopsis AtSUT4, potato StSUT4, tomato SlSUT4, and poplar PtaSUT4 (Chincinska et al. 2013).

Heterologous expression in yeast indicated the ability of SUT4 (AtSUT4, LjSUT4, and PpSUT4) to catalyze sucrose uptake with low affinity (Weise et al. 2000; Reinders et al. 2008; Zanon et al. 2015a). The SUT4 homologs in Arabidopsis (AtSUT4), barley (HvSUT2), Lotus Japonica (LjSUT4), and peach (PpSUT4) function as sucrose proton symporters, suggesting that they are most likely involved in the sucrose efflux from the vacuole (Neuhaus 2007; Zanon et al. 2015a). SUT4 has been found to be participated in diverse biological processes in different plant species. In potato, inhibition of the StSUT4 expression results in early flowering, tuberization, and the reducing expression of gibberellic acid and ethylene biosynthetic genes (Chincinska et al. 2008). In poplar plants, PtaSUT4-silenced results in an increased leaf-to-stem biomass ratio with the decreased translocation of sucrose to the sink organs (Payyavula et al. 2010). In pear, PbSUT2 affected sucrose content in sinks and the overexpression of PbSUT2 leads to early flowering (Wang et al. 2016). Previous study showed sucrose not only improves fruit flavor but also relevant to lipid metabolism (Cui et al. 2016). Overexpression of AtSUT2 and/or AtSUT4 in combination with diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT) genes can increase seed oil production in both soybean and maize (Allen et al. 2015).

Jatropha curcas, well known as the “purging nut,” is a promising bio-energy perennial oilseed crop, in which the seeds can be processed to produce high-quality biodiesel fuel (Pereira et al. 2017). However, few transcriptome studies had mentioned the SUT genes in J. curcas (Jiang et al. 2012). Therefore, investigating the mechanism of SUTs might provide significant insight into the growth and development of J. curcas. In this study, we cloned JcSUT4 from J. curcas. JcSUT4 was mainly localized to plasma membrane and mediated the sucrose uptake by yeast complementation assay. JcSUT4 was highly expressed in mature source leaves, and gradually increased at early stages of fruit development. Our results identified the primary biological functions of JcSUT4, providing information for exploration of the mechanism that control sucrose accumulation in this bioenergy species.

Leaves capture atmospheric ${ \mathsf { C O } } _ { 2 }$ and ultimately convert it to starch for transient storage, and sucrose for long distance transport to developing sink tissues. In most plant species, carbon is transported throughout the plant as sucrose. After its synthesis in the mesophyll cells, sucrose moves toward the vascular bundle symplasmically via the plasmodesmata. In apoplastic phloem loading species, sucrose reaches the phloem parenchyma cells where it is unloaded into the cell wall space. Unloading from the parenchyma cells to the apoplast was hypothesized to be carried out by sucrose exporter proteins. Recently these proteins were identified as SWEET11 and SWEET12 in Arabidopsis (Chen et al., 2012). From the apoplast, sucrose is taken up into the phloem companion cells by sucrose transporter proteins such as AtSUC2 in Arabidopsis and ZmSUT1 in maize for allocation to sink tissues (Baker et al., 2016; Gottwald, Krysan, Young, Evert, & Sussman, 2000; Slewinski, Meeley, & Braun, 2009; Srivastava, Ganesan, Ismail, & Ayre, 2008; Stadler & Sauer, 1996). Export and delivery of sucrose to reproductive sink tissues is critical for sink formation, growth, and development (Kühn, 2003; Riesmeier, Willmitzer, & Frommer, 1994). Since most of the food for the world's population depends on sink tissues (seed, fruit, and tuber), it is critical to fully understand the process of sucrose allocation to these tissues.

Plant sucrose transporters belong to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS), also called the uniporter-symporter-antiporter family (Goswitz & Brooker, 1995; Marger & Saier, 1993; Pao, Paulsen, & Saier, 1998). MFS transporters, depending on the subfamily, can adopt either inward open, outward open, inward facing occluded, or outward facing occluded conformational states where the transition involves both rigid-body rotations, as in the rocker switch model for sucrose transporters, and structural changes in individual transmembrane helices (Quistgaard, Löw, Guettou, & Nordlund, 2016).

The SUC/SUT subfamily of MFS have been extensively studied in many plant species having different subgroups/types (Doidy, Vidal, & Lemoine, 2019; Reinders, Sivitz, & Ward, 2012). Evolutionary analysis of sucrose transporters from fission yeast, charophyte algae, red algae, non-vascular plants, early vascular land plants, and angiosperms show three transporter types (Reinders et al., 2012). Type I sucrose transporters are only found in eudicots, they are localized to the plasma membrane and are able to transport coumarin glycosides (for example esculin) in addition to sucrose. In contrast, Type II and III sucrose transporters only transport sucrose and noncoumarin glycosides (Gora, Reinders, & Ward, 2012; Reinders, Sivitz, Starker, Gantt, & Ward, 2008; Reinders et al., 2012; Sivitz et al., 2007). Type II sucrose transporters localize to the plasma membrane while Type III transporters are found in the vacuole membrane (tonoplast).

Sucrose transporters have been studied intensively in Arabidopsis. Specific expression patterns and localization to either the plasma membrane or tonoplast indicate specific, nonredundant functions for each transporter in the family (Endler et al., 2006; Kühn, 2003; Sivitz et al., 2007; Truernit & Sauer, 1995). For example, AtSUC1 is expressed in trichomes, pollen grains, and roots and is essential for normal pollen function (Sivitz et al., 2007; Sivitz, Reinders, & Ward, 2008). AtSUC2 is important for phloem loading of sucrose (Srivastava et al., 2008) while AtSUT4/SUC4 is localized to the tonoplast and transports sucrose from the vacuole into the cytoplasm (Endler et al., 2006; Schulz et al., 2011). In legumes, particularly in common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris), there are very few sucrose transporters functionally characterized to date. PvSUT1 along with a putative sucrose facilitator PvSUF1, which were isolated from the seed coat, were shown to allow growth of yeast on sucrose (Zhou, Qu, Dibley, Offler, & Patrick, 2007). Recently, Soltani, Weraduwage, Sharkey, and Lowry (2019) reported RNAseq analysis showing that expression of putative sucrose transporter Phvul.007G088200 is significantly reduced in leaves when exposed to elevated temperature. This gene is homologous to AtSUC2 and was named PvSUT2 (Soltani et al., 2019). In a more recent phylogenetic analysis of legume sucrose transporters, however, this gene was named PvSUT1.1, as a member of the Type I clade (Doidy et al., 2019). Common bean, like other plants, encodes a Type II sucrose transporter and thus to avoid confusion Phvul.007G088200 will be referred to as PvSUT1.1 in this study. PvSUT1.1 is grouped within the SUT1.1 subclade of the legume Type I sucrose transporter while PvSUF1 and PvSUT1 analyzed by Zhou et al. (2007) are from the SUT1.4 and SUT1.5 subclades and thus renamed PvSUT1.4 and PvSUT1.5 respectively (Doidy et al., 2019). At present, the function of PvSUT1.1 in sucrose uptake has not been demonstrated.

In this study we functionally characterized a sucrose transporter, PvSUT1.1, recently identified in common bean and implicated in high temperature resilience during common bean reproduction (Soltani et al., 2019). Because no functional study has reported that PvSUT1.1 is a sucrose transporter, we hypothesized that PvSUT1.1 is functioning in sucrose import into the cells. Predictive, biochemical, and molecular evidence reveal that PvSUT1.1 is a high affinity sucrose-proton co-transporter expressed in multiple tissues and is possibly involved in phloem loading of sucrose. Furthermore, the effect of elevated temperature on expression of PvSUT1.1 and the role of sucrose phloem loading in heat tolerance is discussed.

Active transport of sucrose across plant cell membranes is mediated by sucrose–proton symporter proteins. A number of sucrose transporters from dicot plant species have previously been identified, characterized and functionally analysed, most recently reviewed by Lemoine (2000) and Williams et al. (2000). Evidence from northern analysis, immunoblotting, cellular localization and functional analysis suggests that the principal role of many of these sucrose transporters (SUTs) is in the apoplastic loading of assimilate from the leaf mesophyll cells into the phloem. However, some SUTs are thought to be involved in pollen germination (Stadler et al. 1999), transport of sucrose into the dicot embryo (Harrington et al. 1997; Weber et al. 1997), and possibly in sugar sensing (Barker et al. 2000). Antisense suppression of gene expression has been used to determine the function of the dicot SUT1 sucrose transporter (Riesmeier et al. 1994; Kühn et al. 1996; Lemoine et al. 1996). These workers introduced antisense constructs of the potato SUT (StSUT) into potato with the result that transgenic plants showed retention of carbohydrate in the leaves and a subsequent inhibition of photosynthesis, along with a reduction in root development and tuber yield. Bürkle et al. (1998) also used antisense suppression to determine the function of the tobacco sucrose transporter NtSUT1. Again, accumulation of assimilates in the leaves and a reduction of photosynthesis was observed, along with reduction in root development and disrupted flowering. Similar data has recently been obtained using knockout mutants of Arabidopsis where SUC2, the gene encoding a similar SUT1-type transporter, was disrupted (Gottwald et al. 2000). These observations confirm the model of apoplastic phloem-loading transport mechanism of assimilates in the species examined, mediated by the SUT. However, to date, no such experiments have been done in cereal species.

In a previous study, we reported the isolation of a cDNA encoding the rice SUT, OsSUT1, the first to be identified from a monocot species (Hirose et al. 1997). Since then,

SUT genes have been isolated from other monocot species including maize and barley (Aoki et al. 1999; Weschke et al. 2000). Organ-specific mRNA expression patterns suggest that OsSUT1, unlike the dicot SUT1, does not play a major role in phloem loading of assimilate from the mesophyll cells of mature source leaves (Hirose et al. 1997). High expression levels of OsSUT1 in panicles after heading led us to propose that OsSUT1 is involved in transport of sucrose into the filling grain (Hirose et al. 1997), fulfilling a function analogous to SUT1 in Vicia faba (Harrington et al. 1997; Weber et al. 1997). This conclusion is supported by high-level expression of OsSUT1 mRNA and functional OsSUT1 protein in aleurone cell layers and in some of the maternal cell layers of developing grain (Furbank et al. 2001). The role of SUT1 in transport of sucrose to the filial tissue of developing grain has also been supported by studies in wheat (Bagnall et al. 2000) and barley (Weschke et al. 2000). In addition to its role in grain filling, OsSUT1 may have some role in the transport of sucrose remobilized from temporary starch reserves in the leaf sheath and stem during grain filling (Hirose et al. 1997, 1999). It also appears that OsSUT1 plays a role in loading remobilized carbohydrate into the phloem of young sink leaves during seed germination (Hirose et al. 1997; Matsukura et al. 2000).

While the data described above suggests that OsSUT1 encodes a protein involved in active transport of sucrose into the filling grain, the evidence is only correlative. In the present study, we probe the function of OsSUT1 using antisense suppression in transgenic rice plants. The effect of reducing OsSUT1 expression on plant growth, photosynthesis, grain filling and seed germination is examined.

Common wheat is one of the most important food crops worldwide, supporting $2 0 \%$ of the energy and protein requirements for human nutrition. However, the genome of common wheat is large (approximately 17,000 Mb, 40 times that of rice), which makes it difficult to carry out genetic and functional analyses. The diploid wild wheat $T .$ urartu is a progenitor species and is the donor of the wheat A genome for tetraploid and common wheat (Ling et al. 2013; Dvorak et al. 1993). Therefore, genetic improvements of $T .$ urartu have received much attention from scientists, as it would be helpful to ensure food security and the sustainable development of agriculture. The present study isolated two cation/ $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ antiporters, TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b, from T. urartu and described their functions for the accumulation and transportation of nutrient elements and heavy metals; this information provides an important genetic resource for the exploration of environment-related metal transporters.

The protein sequences of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b have high similarity with the homologous sequences in A. tauschii and H. vulgare, revealing that the genetic relationship of

TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b in T. urartu was consistent with the results of traditional taxonomy. In this study, TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b were mainly expressed in the internode and beard, respectively (Fig. 2a, b). The internode is the channel responsible for nutrient and cation transportation. The beard can increase the resistance of wheat to diseases and improve transpiration ability and ion transportation. The qRT-PCR showed that the expression levels of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b increased in shoots exposed to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , but decreased in the roots (Fig. 2), suggesting that TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b likely play a crucial role in regulating rootto-shoot metal translocation and the redistribution of trace elements in wheat shoots.

The process of removing heavy metals from the cytoplasm and segregating them into vacuoles is an effective tolerance mechanism in plants (Pittman et al. 2004). Studies have reported that the truncated NRR of Arabidopsis CAX1 resulted in better growth in yeast after $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment (Park et al. 2005; Shigaki et al. 2005). The antiporter activity of mung bean CAX1 with truncated NRR was approximately $7 0 \%$ higher compared with full-length CAX1 in yeast. Increased activity causes excess $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ to be segregated in vacuoles, reducing the amount in the cytoplasm (Pittman et al. 2004). NRR-truncated AtCAX2 (sCAX2) exhibited significant growth under $1 7 5 \mathrm { \ m M \ C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $5 { \mathrm { ~ m M ~ } } { \mathrm { M n } } ^ { 2 + }$ , and sCAX2 can accumulate more $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in root tissue vacuoles and inhibit excess $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ toxicity (Pittman et al. 2004; Shigaki et al. 2003; Schaaf et al. 2002). ∆NTuCAX1a transgenic Arabidopsis was significantly longer in root length than the WT and other transgenic lines under $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ stress; the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ contents in the shoots and roots and the translocation ratio were significantly higher than in WT (Figs. 3a, b, 4a, b). The TuCAX1a activity increased due to the deletion of NRR and translocation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ was promoted from roots to the shoots, resulting in excess $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in mesophyll vacuoles and decreased $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations in the cytoplasm. However, this study also found that the root growth in $\Delta C T u C A X I b$ transgenic Arabidopsis was best under $\mathrm { C a C l } _ { 2 }$ stress, and the deletion of CRR promoted rootto-shoot $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation (Figs. 3c, d, 4c, d). It is likely that TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b are regulated through different regions during $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation.

CAX1 was screened by quantitative trait locus mapping and identified as a candidate gene involved in $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance in Arabidopsis halleri (Baliardini et al. 2015). The truncated NRR of AtCAX1 exhibited obvious $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ transportation activity (Shigaki et al. 2005). In a previous study, a CAX isolated from Petunia hybrida (PhCAX) showed higher $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation than control lines (Wu et  al. 2011). Although the expression levels of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b were slightly higher than in the control shoots exposed to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ stress, plant growth and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation showed no significant differences with WT plants. Evidently, TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b are not involved in $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance and translocation in transgenic Arabidopsis (Figs. 2, 3, 4).

Preliminary biochemical analysis of AtCAX1 and AtCAX2 had suggested the translocation of these genes for various metals (Schaaf et al. 2002; Shigaki et al. 2003); Arabidopsis CAX2 transported $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ . Mutated atcax2 in Arabidopsis resulted in a reduction in $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ content in the vacuoles (Chen et al. 2016; Shigaki et al. 2003; Hirschi et al. 2000). According to root length analysis, the overexpression of the full-length TuCAX1a in Arabidopsis can improve the tolerance and translocation of $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ . Excessive $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ may be distributed in shoots and roots and stored in mesophyll and root vacuoles coincident with decreased concentrations of $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ in the cytoplasm. NRR-truncated TuCAX1b transgenic Arabidopsis showed enhanced root lengths and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation from roots to shoots (Figs. 3, 4), consistent with the suggestion that $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations in the roots would be transported to shoots. Therefore, $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ toxicity in the root was decreased, resulting in better root length. Moreover, redundant $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ could then be accumulated in vacuoles. These results also indicate that TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b have different transport regulatory mechanisms under $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments.

We examined whether TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b also played a role in the transportation of other metals under $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments because the transport of metal cations showed reciprocal promotion and restriction in plants. Under $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ stress, TuCAX1a transgenic plants prevented the translocation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from roots to shoots (Fig. S9a–d). In contrast, the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 }$ , $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ contents all increased in shoots exposed to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ in TuCAX1b overexpression lines (Fig. S10a–d). Additionally, the uptake and translocation of $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ was inhibited when exposed to $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , respectively (Fig. S10a, j), suggesting that TuCAX1b might be beneficial to the absorption and translocation of nutrition elements in soil and prevent the transport of toxic metals. Under $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ or $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment, the accumulation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in the shoots of TuCAX1b transgenic and truncated Arabidopsis lines was higher than in WT plants (Fig. S10a, i), suggesting that the overexpression of TuCAX1b can facilitate $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ translocation after the intake of other heavy metals.

In summary, the expression of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b can be induced by $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment in wheat seedlings. The heterologous expression of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b in transgenic Arabidopsis can improve the tolerance of plants to metal stresses and enhance the translocation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ or $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ from roots to shoots. In the soil, high contents of heavy metals, such as Cd2+, Co2+ and Al2+, reduce the absorption and translocation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ . These experiments showed that TuCAX1b transgenic plants enhanced the translocation of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , $Z n ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ from roots to shoots under $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ stress, but prevented $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ absorption and translocation under $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments, respectively. Therefore, TuCAX1b was favorable for crop growth and improved the microelement distribution in grains relative to TuCAX1a. Thus, studying metal tolerance and translocation of TuCAX1a and TuCAX1b helps to understand the regulatory mechanism for the translocation of metal ions in plants (Fig. 5). Overall, this study identifies novel candidate genes for enhancing crop tolerance to heavy metals and improving the accumulation of microelements in wheat.

Plants require various essential nutrients for optimal growth and development, including the macronutrients Ca2+, $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { \bar { g } } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , and the micronutrients $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ , $\mathrm { F e } ^ { \bar { 2 } + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ (Marschner, 1995). Although essential, all of these metals are toxic when present in excess. Furthermore, non-essential metals such as $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ can be taken up by plants and are extremely toxic if they accumulate above certain concentrations. Metal transporters have a critical role in maintaining the proper concentrations of metals in various cellular compartments. An ensemble of different transporters mediates metal homeostasis (Ma¨ ser et al., 2001; Maathuis et al., 2003); however, the regulation and functional diversity of these transporters is still poorly understood.

The removal of metals out of the cytoplasm, particularly sequestration into the vacuole, is an important tolerance mechanism against metal stress. Various types of transporters have been identified that mediate the movement of metals out of the cytoplasm including secondary-energised transporters such as cation $\mathrm { ~ H ~ } ^ { + }$ antiporters, driven by $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ gradients that are generated by $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ pumps (Hirschi, 2001; Gaxiola et al., 2002). For example, Arabidopsis thaliana has a large multigene family of cation exchanger (CAX) genes comprising multiple members (Ma¨ ser et al., 2001). The founding members of this family, CAX1 and CAX2 were originally identified as $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters in a yeast mutant $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ hypersensitivity suppression screen (Hirschi et al., 1996). Both CAX1 and CAX2 are localised at the tonoplast in Arabidopsis (Hirschi et al., 2000; Cheng et al., 2003). Biochemical and genetic analyses have confirmed that CAX1 is a high capacity, low affinity $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter and an important component of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ homeostasis in the plant (Hirschi et al., 1996; Cheng et al., 2003). However, CAX2 was shown to have a lower capacity and affinity for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport than CAX1, suggesting that it may have additional substrates (Hirschi et al., 1996), and subsequent characterization has demonstrated that as well as $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ , CAX2 can also transport $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ , and possibly $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al., 2000; Schaaf et al., 2002; Shigaki et al., 2003). A CAX transporter from rice, called OsCAX1a, is also able to mediate vacuolar transport of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and Mn2+ (Kamiya and Maeshima, 2004). Recently, we identified a molecular determinant of $\mathrm { ~ \dot { M } n ^ { 2 + } }$ specificity for CAX2, a 3-amino acid motif within the predicted transmembrane-spanning domain 4 (Shigaki et al., 2003). Ectopic expression of CAX2 in tobacco plants is able to mediate some modest tolerance to otherwise toxic concentrations of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al., 2000), indicating that CAX2 does have the potential to function as a $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in plants. This work, and previous analysis of the plant transport properties of transition metaltransporting cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters (Salt and Wagner, 1993; Gries and Wagner, 1998; Gonzalez et al., 1999), has demonstrated the importance of this mechanism of metal transport. However, plants deficient in these transporters have not been previously characterised.

Regulation at the level of metal transport is an important component of metal homeostasis. For example, metal homeostasis in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is tightly regulated (Radisky and Kaplan, 1999; Van Ho et al., 2002). In plants, the regulatory properties of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters have been well described (Sze et al., 2000; Pittman and Hirschi, 2003); however, much less is known about the regulatory properties of transition metal transport. Recent biochemical studies have shown that the N-terminal hydrophilic tail of CAX1 is involved in regulating $\dot { \mathrm { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity. Following heterologous expression in yeast, full-length CAX1 is inactive, possibly due to autoinhibition, unless the N-terminus is truncated or activated by interaction with another protein (Pittman et al., 2002a; Cheng et al., 2004). Other plant $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporting CAX transporters including VCAX1 from mung bean, appear to be regulated by a mechanism of N-terminal regulation (Pittman et al., 2002b). Similarly, a full-length version of CAX2 was recently identified that contains a long hydrophilic N-terminus and is unable to suppress a $\mathrm { \dot { M } n } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitive phenotype of yeast compared to N-terminal truncated versions (Schaaf et al., 2002). However, this potential mechanism of regulation was not analysed in any detail.

Recently, we identified and characterized CAX1 deletion mutants to give insight into the physiological function of this vacuolar $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter (Cheng et al., 2003). Biochemical analysis of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in cax1 indicated that a significant amount of the $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity in wild-type Arabidopsis was mediated by CAX1 as deletion of this gene caused a $50 \%$ reduction in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport, while the remainder of the activity was suggested to be due to other CAX transporters. Furthermore deletion of CAX1 resulted in a decrease in vacuolar V-type $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase (V-ATPase) activity. Despite these alterations in vacuolar transport activities, the effect of CAX1 deletion on plant growth was subtle. There was a slight delay by 5 to 7 days in bolting of the inflorescence stem, a small reduction in length of the primary root, and a reduction in total length and number of lateral roots. However, we did observe some interesting changes in ion tolerance of cax1 compared to wild-type. cax1 plants were more tolerant to the complete absence of $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ in the growth medium and were also more tolerant to excess concentrations of various metal salts including $\mathrm { { \bf M g C l } } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathbf { M n C l } _ { 2 }$ than wild-type. Whether these phenotypes are unique to CAX1 deletion or due to a general effect of CAX gene deletion remains to be determined.

In this report, we have analysed a knockout mutant of CAX2 and have examined alterations in V-ATPase activity and vacuolar metal transport in cax2 plants. We have also determined the wholeplant expression pattern of CAX2 . Furthermore we have characterised the regulation of CAX2 in yeast. Our findings in yeast suggest some similar regulatory mechanisms among the CAX transporters.

In this report we have further elucidated the function of the Arabidopsis CAX2 $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and transition metal transporter by identifying and characterising CAX2 insertional mutants. CAX2 has a low affinity and capacity for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport and it has been previously suggested that it may not be a major component in $\bar { \mathrm { C a } } ^ { 2 + }$ homeostasis unlike CAX1 (Hirschi et al., 1996; Cheng et al., 2003). When CAX1 was deleted by transposon insertion, a significant reduction in vacuolar $\dot { \mathrm { C a } } ^ { 2 + } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity was observed as well as upregulation of transcript expression for putative $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters CAX3 and CAX4 , but there was no significant change in CAX2 expression in the cax1 plants (Cheng et al., 2003). In this study, we observed no difference in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity in the cax2 mutant plants compared to wild-type (Figure 2), further suggesting that CAX2 is not the predominant $\mathrm { C a } ^ { \overline { { 2 } } + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { \overline { { + } } }$ antiporter in Arabidopsis. Similarly there were no changes in growth of cax2 plants on $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ -depleted media compared to wild-type unlike the changes observed for cax1. However, there was a slight increase in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity following sCAX2 overexpression. sCAX2 was expressed under the control of the high copy CaMV 35S promoter which may explain this increase in antiport activity; however, it is difficult to assess the potential physiological roles of a protein from such overexpression data, particularly when an artificial promoter is used. Yeast heterologous expression studies demonstrate that CAX2 certainly has the ability to transport $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and CAX2 may have a role in $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in the plant but this may be under specific physiological or developmental conditions that have yet to be determined. For example, in a recent microarray analysis of cation transporters it was shown that expression of CAX2 was significantly down-regulated upon $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ starvation (Maathuis et al., 2003), possibly suggesting that CAX2 may have a role in $\mathrm { \dot { C } a } ^ { 2 + }$ transport in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ conditions, although CAX2 expression was not found to be up-regulated upon high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ stress (data not shown; Hirschi et al., 2000).

Deletion of CAX1 mediated various morphological phenotypes such as delay in bolting and a slight reduction in root growth, and also caused increased tolerance in terms of plant growth in response to excess metal salts (Cheng et al., 2003). None of these phenotypes were seen for cax2, indicating alternative functions for both CAX transporters. These results are consistent with earlier studies that found that high-level expression of sCAX1 in tobacco mediated increased sensitivity to various abiotic stresses (Hirschi, 1999) while expression of sCAX2 in tobacco did not give these phenotypes (Hirschi et al., 2000). Another phenotype of the cax2 plants was the reduction in V-ATPase activity (Figure 3). We have previously observed a similar phenotype for the cax1 mutant plants (Cheng et al., 2003), and a similar phenotype has been seen in yeast. Yeast mutants defective in the vacuolar $\dot { Z } \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter ZRC1 , which encodes a putative $Z n ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter, also exhibit reduced activity of the V-ATPase (MacDiarmid et al., 2002). These results suggest that there is a conserved interplay between secondary energized transporters such as cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters and the $\mathrm { H \Omega ^ { + } }$ pump. For both cax1 and cax2, no significant reduction in V-PPase activity was observed. When sCAX1 was overexpressed in cax1 plants, the V-ATPase activity significantly increased by $2 6 \%$ (Cheng et al., 2003), while overexpression of sCAX2 conferred an $1 1 \%$ increase in V-ATPase activity (Figure 3A). Given the high expression of sCAX2 in the cax2 plant (Figure 1B), it might be expected that the up-regulation of the V-ATPase would be greater than observed. It is possible that there are additional regulatory factors that prevent excessive up-regulation of the V-ATPase so as to prevent too much acidification of the vacuolar lumen, which could be deleterious to the plant. Little is known regarding the effect of overexpression of the V-ATPase in plants, particularly as such studies are difficult because the V-ATPase is a multiple subunit protein complex (Sze et al., 2002). However, high-level overexpression of individual subunits of the yeast V-ATPase was lethal to the yeast cells (Curtis and Kane, 2002), indicating the importance of a properly regulated V-ATPase.

The ability of CAX2 to function as a $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ transporter has been demonstrated by its heterologous expression in yeast (Hirschi et al., 2000; Schaaf et al., 2002; Shigaki et al., 2003). Expression of sCAX2 increases the $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance of both wild-type and cnb1 mutant yeast strains, the latter strain having increased $\mathrm { M n } ^ { \dot { 2 } + }$ sensitivity due to the lack of functional calcineurin (Hirschi et al., 2000). Subsequently we have confirmed that the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ tolerance provided by sCAX2 is due to direct $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity at the yeast vacuolar membrane (Shigaki et al., 2003). Another recent study confirmed the role of CAX2 as an important component in $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ homeostasis. The minimal $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration that is toxic to the wild-type yeast strain BY4741 was determined and these conditions were used as a selection system for identifying Arabidopsis genes that confer tolerance to $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ (Schaaf et al., 2002). Following expression of an Arabidopsis cDNA library into the yeast, the only gene out of 120,000 transformants that was found to confer tolerance to the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ stress, was CAX2 . Two truncated variants of CAX2 were identified in this screen, a 399 amino acid protein identical to sCAX2, and a 349 amino acid protein in which translation started at Met-93 and therefore lacked the first predicted transmembrane spanning domain. Both variants could suppress the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ sensitivity of the wild-type yeast, but the suppression by the 349 amino acid variant was very weak (Schaaf et al., 2002). The authors argued that the ability of this shorter CAX2 variant to suppress the $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ sensitivity implies that the N-terminus of CAX2 does not play an important role in $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ specificity. This is largely in agreement with our previous results that identified a discrete amino acid region within the fourth predicted transmembrane spanning domain that is critical for CAX2 $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ specificity (Shigaki et al., 2003). Schaaf et al. (2002) also found that expression of sCAX2 slightly increased the sensitivity of the yeast towards hydrogen peroxide, possibly due to depletion in the concentration of cytosolic $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ that is known to cause increased sensitivity towards oxidative stress. CAX2 is predicted to have a low affinity for $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ transport (Shigaki et al., 2003) yet despite this, expression of sCAX2 in tobacco plants was able to confer increased accumulation of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ in root tissue, increased vacuolar $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + } /$ $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity and provide modest tolerance to high concentrations of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Hirschi et al., 2000). This suggests that CAX2 is able to function as a $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter in planta. $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ transport measurements into isolated vacuolar membrane vesicles from wild-type and cax2 Arabidopsis plants showed a significant reduction in vacuolar $\mathrm { \dot { M } n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H }$ antiport activity upon CAX2 deletion (Figure 2), demonstrating that CAX2 does have a critical role in vacuolar $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ accumulation. However no morphological phenotypes could be observed for the cax2 plants on various $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ growth conditions (data not shown). This could be due in part to genetic redundancy within the multigene CAX family and due to compensatory mechanisms for $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 \dot { + } }$ transport by other transport pathways at both vacuolar and other membranes that may prevent severe toxicity occurring (e.g. Wu et al., 2002).

Analysis of CAX2 promoter-driven GUS expression demonstrated that CAX2 was expressed in leaf tissue of both young (10 day) and older (30 day) plants, in the apical meristem of young plants, in the petiole, in the root including the root tip, and in mature floral tissue including pollen grains (Figure 4). This expression pattern is in agreement with previous northern blot analysis showing CAX2 expression in all tissues (Hirschi et al., 2000) and with the CAX2 expression pattern determined by microarray experiments (from analysis of the community-accessible microarray data). In addition, GUS expression was strongly observed in the vascular cells in most of these tissues. However, $C A X 2 { : : } G U S$ expression was not induced by any of the metal treatments tested, including $\mathrm { \dot { C } a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ despite the ability of CAX2 to transport these metals. In this respect, CAX2 varies from other CAX genes including CAX1, CAX3 and CAX4 , which are all up-regulated by various metal stress treatments (Hirschi, 1999; Cheng et al., 2002, 2003). The vascular expression of CAX2 may indicate a possible role of this antiporter in the long-distance distribution of metals, such as $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ , from the root to shoot tissues and flowers, maybe in regulating loading and unloading of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ from the vascular system. $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations have been determined in both xylem and phloem saps of various plant species (Loneragan, 1988; Rengel, 2000). $\mathrm { M n } ^ { \hat { 2 } + }$ is certainly transported in the xylem and may be partially mobile in the phloem sap. $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ accumulated into the roots is quickly transported to shoot tissues and seeds, although there is also evidence for remobilisation of $\mathrm { \bar { M } n } ^ { 2 + }$ from the leaves. As yet, the molecular mechanisms behind the control of long-distance transport of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ are unknown, as well as the mechanisms for regulating loading and unloading of $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ into and from the vascular system. The expression of CAX2 in the vasculature of root, leaf and flower tissues, certainly suggest a role of this transporter in both loading and unloading of cations such as $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ Many cation transporters have been shown to have specific vascular expression patterns, including the $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter SOS1, the $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } / H ^ { + } }$ antiporter AtMHX and the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { Z n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporter AtNramp3 (Shaul et al., 1999; Shi et al., 2002; Thomine et al., 2003). The expression of SOS1 is specific to parenchyma cells at the xylem/symplast boundary (Shi et al., 2002). This study also demonstrated differences between wild-type and sos1 knockout plants in shoot accumulation of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ and in $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ content in xylem sap, indicating a role of the SOS1 $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporter in long-distance transport of $\mathrm { N a } ^ { + }$ . Although expression of both AtMHX and AtNramp3 was demonstrated in vascular tissue, the potential role of these metal transporters in metal loading and unloading into the vascular system was not analysed any further. AtMHX and AtNramp3 are also vacuolar-localized transporters, although AtNramp3 is thought to mediate release of metals from the vacuole while AtMHX is likely to mediate vacuolar sequestration of metals, in a function similar to CAX2 (Shaul et al., 1999; Thomine et al., 2003). The potential role of CAX2 in regulating vascular metal distribution requires further analysis and the identification of the specific cell types in the vascular region in which CAX2 is expressed, such as xylem parenchyma cells, will be informative. Like CAX2, AtMHX is also highly expressed in meristematic regions (Shaul et al., 1999). Strong expression of CAX2 in the floral tissues and in the apical meristem of young seedlings may indicate a developmental role of this metal transporter.

Only a very few examples of plant transition metal transport regulation exist (Connolly et al., 2002; Magidin et al., 2003). A number of studies indicate that plant $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ transporting CAX transporters, including CAX1 and VCAX1, are regulated by a mechanism that involves the N-terminal hydrophilic tail (Pittman and Hirschi, 2001; Pittman et al., 2002a, 2002b). The yeast $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance screen that identified CAX2 as a suppressor, only identified truncated variants but not the full-length CAX2 cDNA (Schaaf et al., 2002). When the full-length CAX2 cDNA was expressed in a wild-type yeast strain, it was not able to confer growth on high concentrations of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ compared to the truncated sCAX2 , indicating that $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport activity for the fulllength CAX2 was abolished (Schaaf et al., 2002). Here we demonstrate that full-length CAX2 is unable to mediate yeast growth on high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ as well as $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ (Figure 5). This indicates that the N-terminal domain of CAX2 regulates cation transport activity for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { ~ M n } ^ { 2 + }$ rather than regulating the specificity of cation transport. Further studies are needed to confirm that the N-terminal region of the plant CAX transporters does indeed regulate antiport activity in planta. Interestingly, a shorter truncation of CAX2 (called mCAX2) in which translation started at Met-16 rather than Met-43, was still non-functional for $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ transport (Figure 5). Previously we found that only the full-length N-terminal tail of CAX1 was sufficient to allow inhibition of transport activity, as any truncation allowed activity (Pittman and Hirschi, 2001). This indicates that CAX1 and CAX2 differ in their mechanisms of N-terminal regulation.

The $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiport activity observed in the cax2 plants could be attributed to another Arabidopsis CAX transporter. Despite CAX1, CAX3 and CAX4 having no apparent function in $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ transport (Shigaki et al., 2003), a number of other putative CAX transporters exist (Ma¨ ser et al., 2001). Two additional Arabidopsis $C A X .$ -like genes, At1g55720 (CAX6) and $\operatorname { A t l } \operatorname { g } 5 5 7 3 0 ( C A X 5 ) .$ are highly similar to CAX2 , thus it is possible that either of these putative cation $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ antiporters may function as $\bar { \bf M } { \bf n } ^ { 2 + }$ transporters. In addition to CAX transporters, other transporter families are implicated in $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ homeostasis, including transporters that can mediate $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ uptake into the cell, vacuolar $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 ^ { + } }$ release, and endoplasmic reticulum and vacuolar $\mathbf { M } \mathbf { n } ^ { 2 + }$ sequestration (Vert et al., 2002; Wu et al., 2002; Delhaize et al., 2003; Thomine et al., 2003). Therefore, the relative contributions of each of these transporters in transition metal homeostasis at the cellular and whole plant level will need to be determined.

The observation that changes in hydrophilic residues within the transporter filter can change substrate specificity has been detailed with $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels and other transporters (23, 24). For example, a Q103A mutation in the plant metal transporter IRT1 apparently eliminated zinc transport but did not alter the transport of other metals (25). The role of histidines can vary for different transporters and can also depend on the position of the residue within the protein sequence. For some channel proteins such as the guard cell inward-rectifying $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel, KST1, and the cardiac pacemaker channel NCN2, the histidine residues appear to be involved in a pH-sensing mechanism (26, 27). In the sucrose $/ \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ cotransporter, SUC1, a histidine residue is implicated in substrate recognition and directly in the transport reaction (28). In human $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /peptide cotransporters, two different histidines play two different roles; one conserved histidyl residue appears to be important for translocation of protons (29), whereas the second seems to be responsible for the recognition of transportable peptide substrates (11). Although these are only some examples, such a diverse role of histidine residues is not surprising; histidine is capable of forming intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds. These bonds can have a variety of effects on the protein, from inducing conformational changes and changes in pore size to influencing activity and transport of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ and other ions (12).

This site-directed mutagenesis study will help future crystallography studies to define the quaternary structure of CAX1 and other $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ /cation exchangers. The ability to manipulate the metal transport activity and selectivity of CAX transporters through simple mutations, as has been demonstrated in this study, holds promise that plants can be custom-engineered to become metal accumulators, enhancing characteristics needed when selecting plants to be employed as phytoremediators.
