The role of AtHKT1;1 in the shoots is still unknown, as are the regulatory mechanisms that control AtHKT1;1 activity in response to salt stress.

It has been hypothesized that phytohormones play an important role in the response to salt stress (Munns and Tester, 2008), based on their ability to regulate the observed physiological changes, such as reduced shoot growth rate, that occur in response to salt. Cytokinin, auxin, gibberellin, abscisic acid and ethylene (Itai et al., 1968; Walker and Dumbroff, 1981; Seo et al., 2005; Albacete et al., 2008; Ghanem et al., 2008) have all been implicated in the response to salt stress. However, little is known about the mechanisms used by these hormones to regulate the salt stress response. To address this issue, we have focussed our efforts on understanding the role of cytokinin in response to salinity.

Several research groups have identified changes in cytokinin levels in response to elevated salinity. Itai et al. (1968) reported that the amount of cytokinin extracted from sunflower plants (Helianthus annuus) was inversely proportional to the NaCl concentration of the medium in which the plants were grown. In later studies, the changes in specific cytokinin species during salt stress were examined. Significant reductions in the levels of trans-zeatin riboside were observed in the leaves of tomato plants (Solanum lycopersicum) that were grown in 100 mM NaCl (Albacete et al., 2008; Ghanem et al., 2008). In another study of salt-treated tomato plants, cis-zeatin levels rapidly decreased within $2 4 ~ \mathrm { h }$ of salt treatment, but a small reduction in the levels of trans-zeatin was observed 8 days after salt treatment (Walker and Dumbroff, 1981). After the salt stress was removed, trans-zeatin and cis-zeatin levels increased, but that of trans-zeatin riboside remained unchanged. The regulation of cytokinin levels both during and in recovery from salt stress suggests that cytokinin plays a role in the response to salt stress.

In addition to changes in cytokinin levels, several studies have demonstrated that salt stress also affects the expression levels of several cytokinin response genes (reviewed by Argueso et al., 2009). In Arabidopsis, cytokinin salt-treated involves a set of three Arabidopsis histidine kinase (AHK) receptors that auto-phosphorylate upon binding of cytokinin. The phosphate is then shuttled from the AHK receptors via histidine-containing phospho-transfer proteins (AHPs) to type-B Arabidopsis response regulators (ARRs). The type-B ARRs are transcription factors that, together with the cytokinin response factors (CRFs) (Rashotte et al., 2006), regulate the transcription of cytokinin primary response genes, which include type-A ARRs (reviewed by To and Kieber, 2008). Expression of all three known cytokinin receptors (AHK2, AHK3 and AHK4), AHP4, CRF5, CRF6 and a number of type-A response regulators is affected by salt treatment (Jiang and Deyholos, 2006; Tran et al., 2007; Argueso et al., 2009). Consistent with these results, plants with loss-of-function mutations in any of the cytokinin receptor genes show reduced sensitivity to salt (Tran et al., 2007). These results suggest an intriguing association between cytokinin activity and salinity, although the mechanism behind these changes is unclear. In this study, we utilized cytokinin signalling mutants to clarify the role of cytokinin in the plant response to NaCl treatment. Our results reveal that cytokinin acts through a subset of type-B response regulators to regulate sodium accumulation in Arabidopsis, with regulation of AtHKT1;1 expression a likely component of this control.

HKT-type transporters appear to play key roles in $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ accumulation and salt sensitivity in plants. In Arabidopsis HKT1;1 has been proposed to influx $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ into roots, recirculate $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ in the phloem and control root : shoot allocation of $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + } .$ . We tested these hypotheses using $^ { 2 2 } \mathbf { N _ { A } } \mathbf { \Phi _ { + } }$ flux measurements and ion accumulation assays in an hkt1;1 mutant and demonstrated that AtHKT1;1 contributes to the control of both root accumulation of $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ and retrieval of $\mathbf { N a } ^ { + }$ from the xylem, but is not involved in root influx or recirculation in the phloem. Mathematical modelling indicated that the effects of the hkt1;1 mutation on root accumulation and xylem retrieval were independent. Although AtHKT1;1 has been implicated in regulation of $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ transport and the hkt1;1 mutant showed altered net $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation, $\mathbf { ^ { 8 6 } R b ^ { + } }$ uptake was unaffected by the hkt1;1 mutation. The hkt1;1 mutation has been shown previously to rescue growth of the sos1 mutant on low $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ ; however, HKT1;1 knockout did not alter $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ or ${ } ^ { 8 6 } { \bf R } { \bf b } ^ { + }$ accumulation in sos1.

Key-words: HKT1; salinity; salt tolerance; sodium transport.

## ${ \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + }$ and $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation in hydroponically grown plants


Control and mutant genotypes (hkt1-4, sos1-1, sos1-1- hkt1-1) were grown hydroponically and exposed to $5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ $\mathrm { \bf N a C l }$ or control solution for $1 0 \mathrm { d }$ . Root growth in $5 0 \mathrm { m M }$ NaCl was strongly reduced in sos1, and this inhibition was partially relieved in the sos1-hkt1;1 double mutant (Fig. 2a).

Although sos1 shoots showed visible symptoms of stress, shoot growth (DW) was relatively unaffected by $1 0 \mathrm { d } \mathrm { N a C l }$ treatment in all genotypes (Fig. 2b) and was unrelated to shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , as all mutant genotypes accumulated approximately threefold more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoot than the parental control line (Fig. 2c). In the roots, hkt1;1 plants accumulated less $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ than wild type (Fig. 2c), as observed in previous studies. sos1 plants accumulated a threefold higher root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration than wild type, and this hyperaccumulation was reduced to a twofold excess in sos1-hkt1;1 plants, suggesting that the salt sensitivity of sos1 mutants may be due to excessive root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation that is partially reduced by knockout of AtHKT1;1. Salt sensitivity was not related to tissue $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ content. Shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation (Fig. 2d) and total plant $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation was highest in sos1 and sos1- hkt1;1 plants, indicating that, at least in our conditions, excess $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ uptake did not inhibit $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition in sos1, as suggested by Qi & Spalding (2004). hkt1;1 plants accumulated slightly more root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ than controls; however, root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ of both sos1 and sos1-hkt1;1 plants was $5 0 \%$ lower than controls, indicating that knockout of AtHKT1;1 did not rescue sos1 root growth via enhancement of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation (Fig. 2d).


## Transport of $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + }$ (Rb+ ) fits a three-compartment model in Arabidopsis


To characterize the transport processes that underlie root and shoot accumulation of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , we first measured time courses of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ uptake. $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into Arabidopsis roots resembled typical measurements of cation uptake into excised roots and storage tissues. We therefore fitted a three-compartment model comprising the root cytosol, root vacuole and the shoot (as previously described in wheat, Davenport et al. 2005). The model was based on the classical ‘four-compartment’ model used to describe fluxes in algal cells and in roots with a xylem compartment, where uptake into an initial root compartment is followed by uptake in parallel into two compartments (in our model the vacuole and shoot) (Walker & Pitman 1976). The initial linear phase of uptake was attributed to unidirectional $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx across the plasma membrane of root cells, resulting in rapid labelling of the root cytosol. The second, slower linear phase of uptake was attributed to influx across the tonoplast to root vacuoles (which assumed a constant rate once the cytosol was approximately fully radioactively labelled). This model assumes that tonoplast fluxes of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ were much slower than fluxes across the plasma membrane, as is commonly assumed for plant cells. Alternatively the second linear phase could represent a second compartment within the root, such as the stele. We think that this is unlikely, given the relative sizes of the first and second compartments and the kinetics of uptake to the shoot. The first, rapidly saturating compartment was clearly small in volume compared to the slower compartment, which continued to fill over many hours (Fig. 3b). It is most likely that the first compartment represents the cytosol, or some portion of the cytosol that includes a stelar component, because it appears that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transported to the shoot derived from this compartment.

Transport of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ into the shoot occurred with a lag coinciding with the period required for labelling of the first compartment (Fig. 3a). Shoot uptake subsequently became linear (indicating full labelling of the compartment from which shoot loading occurred) and approximated the rate of unidirectional transfer from root to shoot. Root and shoot uptake continued for at least $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ with no evidence of saturation (Fig. 3b). The lag and then linearity in shoot uptake indicate that the first, rapidly exchanging compartment comprised the symplast from which xylem loading occurred, indicating that this compartment included a stelar component. The data also suggest that the second phase of root uptake did not contribute to shoot uptake, consistent with a vacuolar identity. A similar phenomenon was observed for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake in Spergularia marina (Lazof & Cheeseman 1986) and wheat (Davenport et al. 2005). It is of course possible that the apparently simple kinetics of uptake represented the summed contribution of many heterogeneous compartments; however, we think that there was a clear functional difference between the first ‘compartment’ that was in contact with the external medium and contributed to shoot uptake, and the second ‘compartment’ that did not have these characteristics. A similar model could describe $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -starved plants (Supplementary Fig. S1).


## AtHKT1;1 is not a ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ influx mechanism but affects root vacuolar $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ uptake


The rate of unidirectional influx into roots of intact control and $h k t l { ; } l$ plants (measured over the first $5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ of uptake) was similar in both genotypes (Fig. 4a). In contrast, the rate of vacuolar influx, estimated from the second linear component of root uptake $\left( { 2 0 - 6 0 \mathrm { m i n } } \right)$ , was much lower in hkt1;1 plants than controls (Fig. 4a).

Measurements of influx over $1 \mathrm { { h } }$ showed that the reduction of vacuolar accumulation in the hkt1;1 mutant was evident in low $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ but was more pronounced at high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ (Fig. 4b). The plants were exposed to different $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ levels with only $1 0 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ pre-treatment, so $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ effects were probably not mediated by changes in gene expression. Rus et al. (2001, 2004) have shown that hkt1;1 mutations were more effective in suppressing the sos salt sensitivity phenotypes in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ and attributed this to the lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake rates in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ conditions. $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ partially inhibits $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx into Arabidopsis roots, and this $\mathrm { C a ^ { 2 + } }$ -sensitive component has been attributed to influx via non-selective cation channels (Essah et al. 2003). One explanation of the present results is that the rate of vacuolar influx controlled by HKT1 was relatively constant (as suggested by the constancy of the absolute difference between control and hkt1;1 in the different $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments in Fig. 4b) and therefore comprised a larger fraction of vacuolar uptake in high $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ conditions, when total $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake and cytosolic $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were lower.

The inhibition of vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake in hkt1;1 roots led to an almost $5 0 \%$ difference in root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation over $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ (Fig. 4c) and was also evident in excised roots of hkt1;1 (data not shown). The lower rate of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx into root vacuoles was consistent with the lower root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ content of hkt1;1 plants measured after $1 0 { \mathrm { d } } ^ { \prime }$ exposure to NaCl (Fig. 2c).

It should be noted that there were some differences in fluxes between different experiments. It is our experience that Arabidopsis is a difficult plant for physiological experimentation compared to, for example, wheat. As a result, there was a degree of variation from experiment to experiment, possibly because of differences in growth rates between hydroponic batches and in experimental conditions such as humidity (which was not controlled). Despite this, we found the relative differences between hkt1;1 mutants and controls to be highly reproducible, although the absolute rates of transport varied between experiments.


## AtHKT1;1 affects xylem transport of ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ , not recirculation


The unidirectional flux of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ to the shoot was much more rapid in hkt1;1 plants than controls (Fig. 5a). Because the kinetics of initial root influx and saturation of the cytosolic phase of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ accumulation appeared similar in both hkt1;1 and control (Fig. 4a), it was assumed that the specific activity of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ loaded into the xylem (from the cytosolic phase) was similar in both genotypes, and therefore that the measured fluxes represented actual rates of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ translocation. hkt1;1 plants accumulated approximately five times more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the shoot within $1 \mathrm { { h } }$ , and this difference was maintained and did not increase significantly over $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ (Fig. 5b), indicating that shoot $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ hyperaccumulation in hkt1;1 was the result of processes occurring early in the pathway of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake. The difference in the rate of unidirectional transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot between genotypes was sufficient to explain the differences in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content (Fig. 2c), without recourse to explanations involving recirculation.

To test whether recirculation could contribute to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration, the plants were loaded for $4 0 \mathrm { h }$ with $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ and were then transferred to unlabelled solution of the same composition and sampled over $^ { 5 2 \mathrm { h } }$ . Shoot $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ content declined by only $1 3 \%$ over $^ { 5 2 \mathrm { h } }$ in the control plants (although this difference was statistically not significant), and showed little change in hkt1;1 plants (Fig. 5c). These results suggest that recirculation, if it occurs at all, does not significantly affect total shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in Arabidopsis. Certainly, the elimination of a possible recirculation rate of $5 \mathrm { - } 1 0 \%$ per day in hkt1;1 plants could not account for the fivefold difference observed in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation between hkt1;1 and control plants over $4 0 \mathrm { { h } }$ of labelling. Root $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ content was low compared to shoot $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ and did not change after $2 4 \mathrm { { h } }$ of rinsing; therefore, translocation of $^ { 2 2 } \mathrm { { N a } ^ { + } }$ from the roots to the shoot during the unlabelled rinse period could not have masked retranslocation.


## AtHKT1;1 affects ${ { \mathsf { N } } { \mathsf { a } } ^ { + } }$ retrieval from the xylem


The rate of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivery to the shoot depends on the rate of efflux of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ into the xylem from stelar cells, the rate of withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the transpiration stream back into root stelar cells, and the transpiration rate. The hkt1;1 mutant sas2 has been shown not to differ from control plants in transpiration rate under a range of humidity (Berthomieu et al. 2003). When only the apical portion of the root was exposed to $^ { 2 2 } \mathbf { N a } ^ { + } .$ -labelled solution (Fig. 6a), control and hkt1;1 plants exported approximately the same amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the apical root to the rest of the plant, suggesting that there was no difference in xylem loading, at least in this part of the root (Fig. 6b, ‘translocated’).

However, the amount translocated to the shoot was twofold greater in hkt1;1 compared with wild type (Fig. 6b, ‘shoot’) because twofold more $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was withdrawn into the upper root in the control compared with hkt1;1 (Fig 6c, ‘unlab root’). Control plants were able to withdraw $4 4 \%$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the xylem before it reached the shoot, compared to $2 1 \%$ in hkt1;1 mutants (Fig. 6c, ‘unlab/translocated’), indicating that hkt1;1 plants were defective in the retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem.


## Modelling $\mathsf { N a } ^ { + }$ fluxes in control and hkt1;1 plants


Knockout of AtHKT1;1 produced two effects on $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport; a reduction in root putative vacuolar uptake and a reduction in $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ withdrawal from the xylem, and these effects were sufficient to explain the hkt1;1 phenotype of low root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Because $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes are interdependent, it was not possible to judge whether these effects arose from alteration of a single transport process or were independent without modelling the total transport system. The root was modelled as two compartments, cytosolic and vacuolar, and the root cytosol exchanged $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ with a third compartment representing the shoot. To model xylem retrieval, it was necessary to add a compartment to the model to represent xylem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ (Fig. 7). It was assumed that the fluxes between compartments depended on the amount of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in the source compartment (e.g. root vacuolar influx represented the proportion of root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transported to the vacuole per unit time, in the range 0.01– 0.5). We first determined a number of sets of parameter values (‘control’ sets) that yielded estimates of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation that approximated the kinetics observed in control plants (Figs 3a & 8a,c).We then mimicked the effect of mutation by altering a single flux over a wide range of values and estimated the effect on the rates of other fluxes and the content of compartments for each control set of parameters to determine whether a ‘mutation’ affecting a single flux could produce the mutant phenotype.

The model indicated that alteration of root vacuolar influx did reduce root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ but had little effect on shoot uptake (Fig. 8a,b).This was because altering vacuolar fluxes did not cause root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to rise, which was required to raise the rate of xylem loading or decrease retrieval (the latter could occur if the xylem: cytosol gradient became unfavourable for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ re-uptake – this was not explicitly modelled because the lack of change in cytosolic $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ precluded this possibility). Cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ did not rise because a reduction in vacuolar influx reduced vacuolar accumulation and produced a corresponding reduction in vacuolar efflux. This is usually the case in real plants, where root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration is often fairly constant over time in high NaCl (Tester & Davenport 2003), and therefore vacuolar fluxes must be in balance.

Alterations of xylem loading, xylem retrieval and recirculation were all able to reproduce the mutant phenotype to some degree (Fig. 8c,d).A reduction in xylem withdrawal caused a large increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation but only a small reduction in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into root vacuoles, too small to account for the nearly $5 0 \%$ reduction in root uptake measured in hkt1;1 plants. Moreover, the phenotype of reduced root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was evident even in excised roots, where there would be no removal of root $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in the transpiration stream. The model therefore suggests that hkt1;1 mutations affected the two processes of vacuolar influx and xylem retrieval independently.


## AtHKT1;1 and SOS1 are not involved in root uptake of $\mathsf { K } ^ { + }$ (Rb+ )


The sos1 mutants have been reported to show inhibition of root growth in low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ on agar media and reduced $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake into whole seedlings fully immersed in $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ solution (Wu et al. 1996). Because AtHKT1;1 showed some evidence of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport activity (Uozumi et al. 2000), and because knockout of AtHKT1;1 rescued the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype (Rus et al. 2004), we compared $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation conditions in hydroponically grown control, sos1, hkt1;1 and sos1-hkt1;1 plants. There was no difference in uptake of $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ between genotypes from high or low RbCl solutions (Supplementary Fig. S2). It is possible that $\mathrm { { \mathbf { R } } { \mathbf { b } } ^ { + } }$ was not transported in a manner fully analogous to $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ; however, these data contradict the earlier report of reduced $^ { 8 6 } \mathrm { R b } ^ { + }$ uptake in whole sos1 seedlings $\mathrm { W u }$ et al. 1996). In our hydroponic conditions, $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ starvation for $^ { 5 \mathrm { d } }$ did not produce a clear sos1 phenotype (data not shown) and therefore it is possible that we missed an effect of sos1 and hkt1;1 mutations on $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport that is only exhibited under certain conditions. Qi & Spalding (2004) were also unable to reproduce the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype of sos1 on agar plates except in the presence of millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . We found that we could reliably reproduce the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype in sos1 mutants grown on agar plates only when we supplied sucrose in the medium (Supplementary Fig. S3), but that millimolar $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ and $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were not required to produce the phenotype.

## AtHKT1;1 controls root vacuolar uptake and withdrawal of $\mathbb { N } \bar { \mathbf { a } } ^ { + }$ from the xylem


AtHKT1;1 is a $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } } .$ -selective transporter that plays a central role in distribution of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ within the plant. While the hkt1;1 phenotype of low root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ is well established, the $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ transport processes causing this phenotype remain controversial. We used radioactive tracers to measure unidirectional fluxes of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ and $\mathbf { K } ^ { + } \left( \mathbf { R } \mathbf { b } ^ { + } \right)$ through intact plants, and found that hkt1;1 mutants showed two distinct differences in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes: reduced root vacuolar uptake and reduced root retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem. These defects in unidirectional $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ fluxes were consistent with the net $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation phenotype of the hkt1;1 mutant. There was no evidence to support the hypotheses that AtHKT1;1 was involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ uptake into roots or recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from shoots to roots. It appears that if recirculation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from shoot to root occurs at all in Arabidopsis, then it occurs at rates too low to contribute significantly to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ levels.We were not able to determine the function of AtHKT1;1 in the shoot using radioactive techniques; however, the role of AtHKT1;1 in the roots in controlling unidirectional transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot was sufficient to account for the net differences in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ between control and hkt1;1 plants.

The question then arose of whether AtHKT1;1 was involved in both vacuolar influx and xylem retrieval of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or whether perturbation of one of these processes was sufficient to cause the hkt1;1 phenotype. Net accumulation of ions depends on the sum of ion fluxes, but the fluxes themselves are interdependent, so alteration of one flux has effects both on net accumulation and on other fluxes.Therefore, it was necessary to model the movements of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ within the plant to estimate how alterations of single fluxes could impact on other transport processes. Our very simple model was able to describe the observed fluxes and, in conjunction with the experimental evidence, indicated that the effects of the hkt1;1 mutation on vacuolar uptake and xylem retrieval of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ were independent.

The dual effects of AtHKT1;1 on root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport support the hypothesis of Rus et al. (2004) that AtHKT1;1 functions to control ion homeostasis. How can these results be reconciled with those of Berthomieu et al. (2003), who found a fivefold elevation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the phloem of hkt1;1 (sas2) mutants compared to wild type and evidence for AtHKT1;1 localization to the phloem? Sunarpi et al. (2005) also found lower $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the phloem of hkt1;1 mutants, but found that the reduction in phloem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ between hkt1;1 and controls ranged between approximately sixfold and twofold depending on the hkt1;1 allelic mutant. A key question is whether the rate of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ export from the shoot in the phloem is high enough to have a significant effect on shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ concentration. Berthomieu et al. (2003) compared only relative amounts of phloem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ using the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ : glutamine ratio; however, Sunarpi et al. (2005) reported the amount of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ extruded from the phloem. They measured approximately $3 0 \mu \mathrm { m o l } \mathrm { N a } ^ { + } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ leaf DW, collected over a $^ { 4 \mathrm { h } }$ period, from plants exposed to $7 5 \ : \mathrm { m M } \ : \mathrm { N a C l }$ for $^ { 2 \mathrm { ~ d ~ } }$ . Xylem $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ content in the controls was approximately $6 \mu \mathrm { m o l }$ $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } m L ^ { - 1 } }$ xylem sap. The transpiration rate was not reported so it is difficult to compare these two measures. However, if we assume a transpiration rate of $0 . 3 \mathrm { m L g ^ { - 1 } }$ leaf fresh weight (FW) $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ (Hosy et al. 2003), then the delivery of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the leaf would be $2 \mu \mathrm { { m o l } \ N a ^ { + } / g ^ { - 1 } \ F W h ^ { - 1 } }$ . The retranslocation of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ via the phloem would be $0 . 7 5 \mu \mathrm { m o l }$ $\mathbf { g } ^ { - 1 }$ FW $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ (assuming a 10:1 leaf FW : DW ratio), suggesting that the phloem could remove as much as $4 0 \%$ of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivered in the xylem. This is much higher than indicated in the recirculation experiment presented in Fig. 5. If the average transpiration rate were $1 \mathrm { m L g ^ { - 1 } }$ leaf FW $\mathbf { h } ^ { - 1 }$ ,then the phloem would remove only $1 2 . 5 \%$ of xylem-delivered $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , closer to our estimates for control plants (Fig. 5c). However, even if the phloem removed as much as half the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ delivered in the xylem, a mutation causing a fivefold reduction in phloem export would result in only a 1.8-fold increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, which is too low to account for the three- to ninefold excess accumulation usually found in hkt1;1 mutants (Fig. 2c; Maser et al. 2002; Berthomieu et al. 2003; Gong et al. 2004). For a fivefold reduction in phloem export to cause a fivefold increase in shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation, phloem export would have to constitute around $8 5 \%$ of xylem import. We could find no evidence of such significant recirculation. By contrast, genotypic differences affecting xylem delivery would have a directly proportional effect on shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ . Although Berthomieu et al. (2003) measured only a statistically insignificant doubling of xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in the hkt1;1 (sas2) mutant, Sunarpi et al. (2005) found large and significant increases in xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in hkt1;1 mutants compared with wild-type controls, and concluded that withdrawal of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ from the xylem constituted the most significant function of AtHKT1;1 with respect to $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport in the shoot. While it is very likely that hkt1;1 mutants have lower rates of phloem transport of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ , the more critical effect on shoot $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ is the early effect of the hkt1;1 mutation in roots on unidirectional transfer of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the shoot in the xylem. There is little evidence for a significant contribution of recirculation to control of shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ content in any species (Tester & Davenport 2003).

The localization of AtHKT1;1 remains problematic. Berthomieu et al. (2003) presented evidence from RNA in situ hybridization and promoter fusion for phloem localization of AtHKT1;1 transcripts. While the images presented did not localize AtHKT1;1 unequivocally to the phloem, AtHKT1;1 transcripts appeared to be concentrated in cells around the phloem rather than the xylem (Berthomieu et al. 2003). However, using an antibody raised to AtHKT1;1, Sunarpi et al. (2005) demonstrated localization of the protein to the plasma membrane of xylem parenchyma cells in the shoot, commensurate with a direct role for AtHKT1;1 in withdrawal of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ from the xylem in the shoot. It remains unclear, therefore, whether AtHKT1;1 participates directly in retrieval of xylem $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in roots or controls the process indirectly. Plasma membrane localization of AtHKT1;1 is not compatible with a direct involvement in vacuolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ fluxes, and the effect of the hkt1;1 mutation in reducing vacuolar $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ influx is likely to be indirect (unless the AtHKT1;1 protein has several intracellular locations). Overexpression of AtHKT1 under control of its likely native promoter increased salt sensitivity (Rus et al. 2004), indicating that the role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport involves more than simply a reduction of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ transport to the shoot.


## How does hkt1;1 rescue sos1?


In hydroponic growth conditions, sos1 accumulated $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ to the same concentration as hkt1;1 and sos1-hkt1;1 mutants in the shoot, and showed little reduction in shoot growth in saline conditions (although the shoot displayed visible symptoms of stress). Therefore, high shoot $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ was not the cause of sos1 salt hypersensitivity, in accord with previous evidence (Ding & Zhu 1997; Shi et al. 2002). However, sos1 plants showed a strong reduction in root growth and hyperaccumulated $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ in roots. Root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation was partially reduced in the sos1-hkt1;1 double mutant relative to sos1, in conjunction with partial relief of growth inhibition. Because knockout of AtHKT1;1 caused a reduction in root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation (via inhibition of vacuolar influx), these results suggest that hkt1;1 mutations relieve sos1 salt sensitivity by reducing root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation.

The mechanism by which the hkt1;1 mutation rescues sos1 growth in limiting $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ conditions remains unclear. We found no evidence for a role of AtHKT1;1 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport.

We also found no evidence that the sos1 mutant was defective in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ acquisition $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ influx or net accumulation). This may have been because the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + } .$ -specific defect in sos1 is only evident in certain growth conditions. Qi & Spalding (2004) could not reproduce the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ deprivation phenotype except in the presence of millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ and speculated that excess root cytosolic $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ accumulation in sos1 plants inhibited $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake via $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channels. This would be compatible with our results showing that the hkt1;1 mutation reduced root $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ in sos1 and restored root growth. However, sos1 did not demonstrate reduced $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation under saline conditions (although $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ distribution was perturbed, with sos1 plants accumulating higher shoot $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ and lower root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ than controls) (Fig. 2d). Tissue $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ levels were not critical in determining salt sensitivity because the sos1-hkt1;1 mutant resembled sos1 in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ accumulation but was less salt sensitive. When we attempted to replicate previous studies using agar plates, we found no genotypespecific inhibitory effect of low millimolar $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ or $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ (which blocks high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake) on sos1 growth on low $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ agar plates, and could only reliably reproduce the sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ phenotype in the presence of sucrose (Supplementary Fig. S3). Qi & Spalding (2004) did not include sucrose in their media, whereas sucrose was always present in experiments demonstrating a clear sos1 $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ phenotype (Wu et al. 1996; Ding & Zhu 1997; Rus et al. 2001, 2004; Shi et al. 2002). $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is known to be important in sucrose transport (Deeken et al. 2002), and it is possible that indirect effects of mutations of SOS1 and AtHKT1;1 on intra-root $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ transport perturb phloem transport processes.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that AtHKT1;1 is not involved in $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ recirculation via the phloem and is not responsible for $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ influx into roots. Rather, AtHKT1;1 appears to control both retrieval of $\mathrm { { N a ^ { + } } }$ from the xylem and root vacuolar loading.This paper demonstrates the utility of measurements of unidirectional fluxes with radioactive tracers and the use of simple mathematical models to test intuitive descriptions of plant transport processes.

## Disruption of cytokinin signalling alters sodium accumulation


The level of total cytokinin in tomato plants has been reported to decrease when plants are grown in saline growth medium (Yurekli et al., 2001; Ghanem et al., 2008). To assess whether cytokinin has a role in regulating sodium ion homeostasis, both the shoots and roots of wild-type Arabidopsis (ecotype Columbia) and a cytokinin signalling mutant were treated with or without cytokinin and examined by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (Figure 1). The type-B ARR mutant arr1-3 arr12-1 (hereafter referred to as arr1,12) was used for this test, as it has been shown to be strongly cytokinin-insensitive in cytokinin root growth assays but is morphologically similar to wild-type plants when grown in the absence of exogenously supplied cytokinin (Mason et al., 2005; Argyros et al., 2008). Type-B response regulators function downstream of cytokinin receptors to mediate the primary transcriptional response to cytokinin. Exogenous application of cytokinin increased the sodium levels in the wild-type shoots by $4 6 \%$ $( P < 0 . 0 1 )$ , but the sodium levels in wild-type roots showed a small, non-significant, reduction of 54 ppm. In comparison to untreated wild-type plants, the cytokinin response mutant arr1,12 (Mason et al., 2005), was found to have $1 9 \%$ less sodium in the leaves $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ . Treatment of the arr1,12 mutant with cytokinin resulted in only a $2 1 \%$ increase in sodium levels in the shoots $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ , a significantly reduced response compared to that observed in cytokinintreated wild-type shoots. No significant change was observed in the roots of arr1,12 plants compared to wildtype. These results support a role for cytokinin, ARR1 and ARR12 in regulating sodium levels in Arabidopsis shoots.

To identify the key cytokinin signal transduction genes involved in regulating sodium levels in Arabidopsis, we examined the sodium levels in a number of Arabidopsis cytokinin signalling mutants that had been grown on soil under fully transpiring conditions (Figure 2). By growing the plants on soil, we are able to compare the sodium accumulation of multiple plants in close to ‘natural’ conditions and avoid the issues of altered plant morphologies that occur when plants are grown on agar plates and treated with and without cytokinin. Consistent with the cytokinin data obtained on agar-based media, the cytokinin-insensitive mutant arr1,12 showed significantly lower shoot sodium levels compared to wild-type. The arr1-3 arr10-5 arr12-1 mutant (hereafter referred to as arr1,10,12), which is almost completely insensitive to cytokinin (Argyros et al., 2008; Ishida et al., 2008), showed a similar reduction in shoot sodium levels compared to the arr1,12 mutant, but this was not significantly different from wild-type plants at the $P > 0 . 0 5$ level due to increased variation in the data, probably caused by its severe growth phenotype (Argyros et al., 2008). A number of other type-B ARR mutants were tested, including the single mutants arr1-3 and arr12-1, and the double mutants arr1-3 arr105, arr10-5 arr12-1 and arr2-4 arr12-1. All of these showed levels of sodium in their shoots that were close to those of the wild-type. Thus, ARR1 and ARR12 appear to be functionally redundant in their regulation of sodium accumulation as a mutation in only one of these genes was insufficient to significantly alter sodium levels under these conditions.

The cytokinin receptor mutant ahk3 ahk4 (ahk3,4) and the Arabidopsis histidine-containing phosphotransfer protein triple mutant ahp2 ahp3 ahp4 (ahp2,3,4) (Hutchison et al., 2006) showed a similar reduction in leaf sodium levels to that in the arr1,12 mutant, with both mutants showing significantly lower sodium accumulation than the wild-type (Figure 2). The similarity in the sodium accumulation phenotype between plant lines with defects in either the cytokinin receptors or type-B ARR genes was expected, as these genes have positive roles in cytokinin signal transduction. In contrast, the type-A ARRs are negative regulators of cytokinin signalling (To et al., 2004), and loss-of-function mutations in type-A ARR genes are predicted to result in greater sodium accumulation in the shoots. Indeed, a number of quadruple type-A ARR mutants, including arr3 arr4 arr5 arr 6, arr3 arr4 arr8 arr9 and arr5 arr6 arr8 arr9 (hereafter referred to as arr3,4,5,6, arr3,4,8,9 and arr5,6,8,9) (To et al., 2004) showed significantly higher levels of sodium in their leaves. Only higher-order loss-of-function type-A ARR mutants were used in this study due to the functional redundancy amongst these genes (To et al., 2004).

In addition to changes in sodium ions, some of the cytokinin mutants examined showed alterations in the levels of other ions relative to wild-type controls. This was not entirely unexpected as cytokinin has been reported to regulate gene expression in response to alterations in the levels of several nutrients, including sulfur, phosphate and nitrogen (Ei-D et al., 1979; Takei et al., 2002; MaruyamaNakashita et al., 2004; Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2005). Our data suggests that cytokinin may play a role in regulating the levels of both potassium and calcium (Figure S2), but further research is required to determine the exact nature of this association. The changes in sodium accumulation in the cytokinin mutants do not strongly correlate with changes in any other ion, including potassium, suggesting that the observed changes in sodium ions are likely to be a response to cytokinin rather than compensation for changes in other ions.


## The arr1,12 mutant is less sensitive than the wild-type to NaCl treatment


Sodium accumulation in the seeds was assessed to examine whether cytokinin influences sodium transport to other sink tissues. Despite lower sodium accumulation in the shoots, the arr1,12 mutant showed similar sodium accumulation in the seeds compared to wild-type controls (Figure S1). To test whether the mechanisms that cause decreased sodium levels in the leaves of the arr1,12 mutant also decrease its sensitivity to salt, seeds of wild-type and arr1,12 were germinated in the presence or absence of $1 5 0 \mathrm { \ m m } \mathrm { \ N a C l }$ (Figure 3a). Under these conditions, the arr1,12 mutant showed a higher germination rate relative to wild-type $( P < 0 . 0 5$ at $4 8 \ \mathrm { h }$ , Student’s t test), suggesting that ARR1 and ARR12 have a negative impact on the salinity tolerance of Arabidopsis germination processes. Similar results were also observed in three other independent experiments (data not shown). In contrast to the arr1,12 mutant, the type-A ARR mutants arr3,4,5,6, arr3,4,8,9 and arr5,6,8,9 all showed a significant reduction in the rate of germination relative to wild-type controls $( P < 0 . 0 5$ at $4 8 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ , Student’s t test) when examined on the same $1 5 0 \mathrm { \ m m \ N a C l }$ medium (Figure 3b). Similar results were also observed in independent experiments (data not shown).

The salt sensitivity of the arr1,12 mutant was also examined at the young seedling stage using a technique that has been successfully used on cytokinin receptor mutants (Tran et al., 2007). Wild-type, arr1-3, arr12-1 and arr1,12 plants were grown on standard ${ 1 \times 1 } \mathsf { M S }$ growth medium for 7 days, and then transferred to medium containing 200 mM NaCl (Figure 4a). Three days after transfer, plants of all four genotypes began to show bleaching of their first true leaves. After 4 days, the survival rate of each genotype had started to decline. Wild-type plants showed the quickest decline in survival rate, with $7 9 \%$ survival after 7 days on $2 0 0 ~ \mathsf { m m }$ NaCl. The survival rates of the arr1-3 and arr12-1 single mutants on $2 0 0 \ \mathsf { m m } \ \mathsf { N a C l }$ were similar to that of the wildtype over the first week of the experiment, showing a similar rapid decrease in survival rate after 3 days. However, the survival of these mutants did not appear to decline as rapidly as that of wild-type in the latter half of the experiment, although only arr12-1 mutants showed significantly higher survival on day 11 and 12 $( P < 0 . 0 5$ Student’s t test). The arr1,12 mutant was the least affected by the $2 0 0 \ \mathsf { m m } \ \mathsf { N a C l }$ treatment, showing a much slower rate of decline in survival than wild-type $\langle P < 0 . 0 5$ from day 7, Student’s t test). A similar result was also observed in an independent experiment (data not shown). Despite the phenotype of increased sodium accumulation of the type-A ARR mutants $( a r r 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ,$ arr3,4,8,9 and arr5,6,8,9), none of these mutants showed a significant difference in salt sensitivity compared wild-type controls (Figure 4b).


## ARR1 and ARR12 regulate salt stress-induced expression of the type-A response regulator gene ARR5


The type-A ARR genes are cytokinin primary response genes whose expression is directly and rapidly induced in response to cytokinin through action of the type-B response regulators (To et al., 2004). As such, studying the expression of these genes provides a convenient assay for cytokinin and type-B ARR activity. The expression of a cytokinin primary response gene (ARR5) was examined in hydroponically grown wild-type and arr1,12 plant lines in the presence and absence of NaCl (Figure 5a). Wild-type plants showed a 2.4-fold increase in ARR5 expression in their roots after saline treatment. Similar NaCl-induced expression of type-A ARRs has been reported previously (Urao et al., 1998; Jiang and Deyholos, 2006; Tran et al., 2007). No such increase was observed in the arr1,12 mutant, indicating that the NaClinduced increase in ARR5 expression is predominantly, or entirely, regulated through ARR1 and ARR12.

No significant changes in ARR5 expression occurred in shoots of either the wild-type or arr1,12 plant lines after 1 week in NaCl. This result is consistent with previous findings that showed no significant alteration in the levels of active cytokinin (zeatin) in the shoots of salt-treated tomato plants after a similar duration of NaCl treatment, despite a significant decline in total cytokinin levels (Albacete et al., 2008). ## ARR1 and ARR12 regulate AtHKT1;1 expression


ARR1 and ARR12 have previously been identified as transcription factors that play an important role in cytokinin signalling (Sakai et al., 2000, 2001; Mason et al., 2005; Rashotte et al., 2006; Argyros et al., 2008). Therefore, an expression study was performed to identify alterations in transcription that may explain how cytokinin regulates sodium homeostasis. AtHKT1;1 was used in this analysis as its product is known to play a vital role in regulating shoot sodium accumulation in Arabidopsis (Maser et al., 2002; Berthomieu et al., 2003; Sunarpi et al., 2005; Rus et al., 2006; Davenport et al., 2007). The arr1,12 mutant showed 6.2-fold higher expression of $A t H K T 1 ; 1$ in the roots compared to wild-type $( P < 0 . 0 1 )$ , but no significant change was observed in the shoots (Figure 5b). Similar results were observed in an independent experiment (data not shown). These results suggest that AtHKT1;1 is regulated by the ARR1 and ARR12 transcription factors in the roots in response to cytokinin. This conclusion is consistent with the overlapping expression patterns of AtHKT1;1 (Maser et al., 2002), ARR1 and ARR12 (Mason et al., 2004; Argyros et al., 2008) in the root vascular tissue.

The large difference in AtHKT1;1 expression between arr1,12 and the wild-type suggest a number of possibilities that are not necessarily mutually exclusive. It is possible that ARR1 and ARR12 restrict the tissue distribution of AtHKT1;1 expression, resulting in more AtHKT1;1-expressing cells in the arr1,12 mutant. Alternatively, ARR1 and ARR12 may induce the expression of one or more genes, potentially including a transcriptional repressor, that inhibit the expression of AtHKT1;1. Therefore, to further explore the effect of cytokinin on AtHKT1;1 expression, wild-type plants were treated with $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ 6-benzylaminopurine (BA) for 0,0.5, 1, 2 or 4 h. Cytokinin treatment resulted in a significant reduction in AtHKT1;1 expression after $\uparrow \ \mathsf { h }$ (Figure 5c). After $4 \textrm { h }$ of cytokinin treatment, AtHKT1;1 expression in wild-type plants had been reduced by $8 7 \%$ compared to the DMSO-treated controls. In comparison, the arr1,12 mutant showed only a $2 6 \%$ reduction in AtHKT1;1 expression at the same time point (Figure 5d). Thus cytokinin results in a rapid reduction in AtHKT1;1 expression, providing a direct link between cytokinin action and a gene whose product is instrumental in maintaining sodium homeostasis in plants. Examination of the roots of the type-A ARR mutants revealed that arr3,4,8,9 and arr5,6,8,9 showed $2 4 \%$ and $20 \%$ reductions, respectively, in AtHKT1;1 expression relative to wild-type controls $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ (Figure 5e). In contrast, there was no significant reduction in AtHKT1;1 expression in the arr3,4,5,6 mutant relative to wild-type. Similar results were observed in an independent experiment (data not shown).

The elevated expression of AtHKT1;1 in the arr1,12 mutant compared to the wild-type could explain the lower shoot sodium content of the mutant. To further explore this, wildtype and arr1,12 plants were grown hydroponically in the presence and absence of NaCl, together with the hkt1-4 loss-of-function mutant and an AtHKT1;1-over-expressing line. The over-expressing line was generated from a GAL4 promoter trap line (E2586) that specifically over-expresses AtHKT1;1 in root stelar cells (Møller et al., 2009). In the absence of applied NaCl, arr1,12 did not show a significant alteration in shoot sodium accumulation (Figure 6). This result was unexpected as the arr1,12 mutant showed increased shoot sodium accumulation when grown on both soil and MS medium (Figures 1 and 2). However, the similar lack of change in the shoot sodium content of the AtHKT1;1- over-expressing line grown under the same conditions suggests that an increase in AtHKT1;1 expression is not sufficient to alter shoot sodium content under the low sodium conditions used in this experiment.

Consistent with previous findings (Rus et al., 2004; Davenport et al., 2007), the elevated sodium content in the shoot tissue of the athkt1;1 mutant was accompanied by a decreased sodium level in its roots when grown in NaCl but not under control conditions (Figure 6). When grown under saline conditions $1 0 0 \ \mathrm { m m } \ \mathsf { N a C l } )$ , the arr1,12 mutant showed decreased shoot sodium accumulation compared to wildtype, which supports previous findings using soil- or plategrown plants. As expected, the AtHKT1;1 over-expressing line showed significantly lower sodium accumulation in its shoots compared to its control line (E2586) $( P < 0 . 0 5 )$ . No significant changes were observed in root sodium accumulation in either the $A t H K T 1 ; 1$ -over-expressing line or the arr1,12 mutant relative to their controls when grown under saline conditions. The similar reduction in sodium accumulation in the shoot tissues of arr1,12 and the AtHKT1;1-overexpressing line under saline conditions is consistent with the possibility that the elevated AtHKT1;1 expression observed in the arr1,12 mutant is at least partially responsible for the decreased sodium accumulation phenotype of the mutant. Furthermore, the differences in potassium levels in both of these mutants compared to their respective controls (Figure S3) do not correlate with the observed alterations in sodium levels, suggesting that ARR1 and ARR12 are not indirectly affecting sodium accumulation by regulating potassium levels.

## Cytokinin regulates sodium homeostasis via ARR1 and ARR12


In this study, we utilized Arabidopsis mutants with defects in cytokinin signalling to determine whether there is a connection between sodium levels and cytokinin signalling. A number of mutants with decreased sensitivity to cytokinin, including ahk3,4, ahp2,3,4 and arr1,12 (Higuchi et al., 2004; Mason et al., 2005; Hutchison et al., 2006; Riefler et al., 2006) had significantly lower shoot sodium levels compared to wild-type plants when grown on soil (Figure 2). Conversely, all of the cytokinin hypersensitive mutants with loss-offunction mutations in four type-A response regulator genes showed significantly higher levels of sodium in the shoots compared to wild-type plants. The lower shoot sodium accumulation phenotype of the arr1,12 double mutant was observed when the plants were grown in various growth media, demonstrating that the phenotype is not an artefact of any specific growth condition. Furthermore, wild-type plants grown in the presence of cytokinin accumulated significantly more sodium in their shoots (Figure 1). These results are consistent with a role for cytokinin in regulating sodium accumulation, possibly by modulating the transport of sodium ions to the shoot. The ability of cytokinin to regulate sodium accumulation is reminiscent of the previously described roles of cytokinin in regulating phosphate, sulfur and nitrogen levels by altering the expression of genes involved in their respective ion-specific starvation responses (Ei-D et al., 1979; Takei et al., 2002; Maruyama-Nakashita et al., 2004; Franco-Zorrilla et al., 2005). However, unlike phosphate, sulfur and nitrogen, sodium is not essential for the growth of C3 plant species such as Arabidopsis, although it is considered beneficial (Pilon-Smits et al., 2009).

Closer inspection of the type-B response regulator mutants showed that each gene does not contribute equally to the regulation of sodium accumulation (Figure 2). For example, the arr1,10, arr2,12 and arr10,12 mutants showed close to wild-type levels of sodium, whereas the arr1,12 mutant showed significantly lower sodium levels. These results indicate that ARR1 and ARR12 are functionally redundant in regulating sodium levels, and that ARR2 and ARR10 are either not significantly involved in this process or are functionally redundant with other transcription factors.


## Cytokinin acts through ARR1 and ARR12 to regulate AtHKT1;1 expression


Several studies have reported alterations in levels of cytokinin species in response to salt treatment (Itai et al., 1968; Walker and Dumbroff, 1981; Kuiper et al., 1990; Shakirova et al., 2003). In a recent study of salt-treated tomato plants, the concentrations of active zeatin-type cytokinins were found to increase in the roots in response to NaCl treatment despite a large decrease in the total cytokinin levels (Albacete et al., 2008), suggesting a salinity-induced cytokinin response. Consistent with this, the cytokinin primary response gene ARR5 was strongly induced by NaCl treatment specifically in the roots in wild-type plants but not the arr1,12 mutant (Figure 5a). Similar NaCl-induced up-regulation of type-A ARRs as well as the cytokinin receptors AHK2 and AHK3 has previously been observed (Urao et al., 1998; Jiang and Deyholos, 2006; Tran et al., 2007). However, it cannot be ruled out that the up-regulation of ARR5 in response to NaCl may occur via a cytokinin-independent signalling pathway. For example, it is plausible that NaCl stress activates the osmosensor AHK1 (Urao et al., 1999; Tran et al., 2007), which could potentially signal via ARR1 and ARR12 to regulate ARR5. However, these results clearly indicate that salt stress induces an ARR1- and ARR12- dependent signalling pathway in the roots of Arabidopsis plants.

The expression of AtHKT1;1 was examined in the arr1,12 mutant as its product is a major determinant of sodium accumulation and salt tolerance in Arabidopsis (Maser et al., 2002; Berthomieu et al., 2003; Sunarpi et al., 2005; Rus et al., 2006; Davenport et al., 2007). AtHKT1;1 showed 6.2-fold higher expression in the roots of the arr1,12 mutant compared to wild-type (Figure 5b). The findings that cytokinin results in a reduction in AtHKT1;1 expression (Figure 5c,d), and that the arr1,12 mutant shows elevated expression of AtHKT1;1, are consistent with cytokinin regulating AtHKT1;1 transcription through the action of the type-B ARRs. However, some cytokinin inhibition of AtHKT1;1 was also observed in the arr1,12 mutant (Figure 5d), suggesting that additional cytokinin transcription factors are involved in regulating AtHKT1;1. Whether the regulation of AtHKT1;1 by the cytokinin transcription factors is direct or indirect is not currently known. ARR1 and ARR12 appear to be able to repress, as well as induce, gene expression in response to cytokinin (Rashotte et al., 2006; Argyros et al., 2008) suggesting that ARR1 and ARR12 could directly repress AtHKT1;1 expression. The lower sodium accumulation in shoots of the arr1,12 mutant suggests that the phenotype is a result of a decrease in sodium transport to the shoot. The increased expression of the AtHKT1;1 gene in arr1,12 is consistent with this phenotype, and suggests that its altered expression is at least partially responsible for the sodium accumulation phenotype observed in the mutant, given the role of AtHKT1;1 in regulating sodium retrieval from the root xylem (Davenport et al., 2007). This conclusion is supported by the similar sodium accumulation phenotypes of the arr1,12 mutant and the AtHKT1;1- over-expressing line compared to their respective controls (Figure 6).

Arabidopsis mutants with defects in AtHKT1;1 show decreased tolerance to salt treatment (Maser et al., 2002; Berthomieu et al., 2003; Sunarpi et al., 2005; Rus et al., 2006; Davenport et al., 2007). In contrast, the arr1,12 mutant shows increased AtHKT1;1 expression, and is therefore predicted to have greater tolerance to saline conditions. Indeed, the arr1,12 mutant did perform significantly better than wild-type on 200 mM NaCl, with a $2 9 \%$ higher survival rate after two weeks (Figure 4a). Loss-of-function mutations in any of the three cytokinin receptor genes (AHK2, AHK3 and CRE1/WOL/AHK4) have also been reported to result in reduced sensitivity to salt (Tran et al., 2007), presumably due to the decreased activity of ARR1 and ARR12 observed here. Interestingly, the arr12-1 single mutant showed an increased survival rate on NaCl during the later stages of the experiment (Figure 4a), despite having wild-type levels of sodium in its leaves (Figure 2). This result may indicate the presence of NaCl-induced cytokinin signalling pathways that are not initiated under growth conditions such as those used to grow the plants for shoot sodium analysis.


## Complex roles for the type-A ARRs in the response to salt stress


We consistently observed phenotypes of the arr1,12 mutant that support a role for ARR1 and ARR12 in repressing AtHKT1;1 expression and enhancing sodium accumulation in wild-type plants. The type-A ARR mutants show a number of phenotypes counter to those observed for the arr1,12 mutant, including elevated sodium accumulation in mature shoots (Figure 2) and increased sensitivity to NaCl during germination (Figure 3b). These results are consistent with the commonly held hypothesis that type-A ARRs are cytokinin-induced antagonists of the primary cytokinin response pathway. Based on this hypothesis, it is predicted that the type A ARR mutants might also show a lower survival rate when grown on NaCl-containing medium, in contrast to that observed with the arr1,12 mutant; however, this was not the case (Figure 4). Similarly, the arr3,4,5,6 mutant did not show the predicted decrease in AtHKT1;1 expression observed in the arr3,4,8,9 and arr5,6,8,9 mutants (Figure 5e), potentially indicating that the previously reported antagonistic nature of ARR8 and ARR9 (To et al., 2004) may also play a role in the response of cytokinin to salt stress. Collectively, these results suggest that the role of the type-A ARRs in sodium accumulation and salt sensitivity is more complex than that of ARR1 and ARR12.

The apparent complexity of the role of the type-A ARRs in regulation of sodium accumulation, AtHKT1;1 expression and salt sensitivity most likely arises because the type-A ARRs are not part of the primary cytokinin signalling pathway. Type-A ARRs are not only regulated by cytokinin but also regulated by cytokinin-independent pathways. For example, it has been previously reported that the type-A ARR genes ARR5, ARR6, ARR7 and ARR15 are regulated by WUSCHEL in order to control the cytokinin responsiveness in specific regions of the shoot meristem (Leibfried et al., 2005). Differences in type-A ARR responsiveness to salt stress have also been observed previously. ARR4 and ARR5 (previously known as ATRR1 and ATRR2) are induced by NaCl stress whereas ARR8 and ARR9 (previously named ATRR3 and ATRR4) are not (Urao et al., 1998). Clearly, not all type-A ARR genes respond similarly to NaCl, and it is plausible that these differences are the result of additional regulation by cytokinin-independent signalling pathways. It is possible that these cytokinin-independent regulators of the type-A ARR genes may have a large impact on cytokinin responses throughout development and under various environmental conditions. Given that there are ten type-A ARR genes in Arabidopsis, which are potentially all uniquely regulated by a variety of signalling pathways, it is perhaps not surprising that the type-A ARR mutants have some unexpected phenotypes.

## Ion transport properties of OsHKT1;4 expressed in heterologous cells


${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ -selective transport mediated by some class I HKT (HKT1) transporters have been indicated to play a crucial role in ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ exclusion from leaves of salt-stressed plants [16, 19, 20, 24, 29–31, 33, 40]. The HKT1;4-A2 locus in durum wheat, which was derived from a wild wheat relative Triticum monococcum, was highlighted as a strong candidate for a salt tolerance QTL named Nax1 [27, 28, 33]. In rice, a role of OsHKT1;4 in controlling ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentrations in leaf blades was suggested by comparative analyses of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ contents in leaf blades and the level of OsHKT1;4 transcripts in sheaths using salttolerant indica rice varieties and a japonica rice cultivar Nipponbare [34]. However, the ion transport properties and physiological functions of OsHKT1;4 remain to be elucidated.

Stable and constitutive expression of OsHKT1;4 in a salt hypersensitive strain of S. cerevisiae G19 led to an increase in sensitivity to increases in extracellular $\mathrm { \Delta N a C l }$ concentration, with significant increases in ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ accumulation in the cells (Fig. 1). Plasma membrane-targeted OsHKT1;4 was found to elicit large currents stimulated by ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ in $X .$ . laevis oocytes with shifts in zero-current potentials toward a more depolarized status, dependent on increases in the ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentration in the bath solution (Fig. 2a-g). A 10-fold increase in the ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentration in the bath resulted in the shift of the reversal potential of $3 4 . 5 \pm 1 . 3 \mathrm { \ m V }$ on average (with the reversal potentials of $- 6 9 . 3 \pm 3 . 3 \mathrm { \ m V }$ and $- 3 4 . 8 \pm 0 . 7 \mathrm { \ m V }$ in the $2 \ \mathrm { m M }$ and $2 0 \mathrm { \ m M \ N a } ^ { + }$ solutions, respectively; Fig. 2g), which was smaller than the theoretical Nernstian shift of $5 8 { - } 5 9 ~ \mathrm { ~ m V }$ . Note however that the reversal potential shifts of OsHKT1;4-expressing oocytes can be less than the theoretical value because the cytoplasmic ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentrations of the oocytes may also shift due to the function of OsHKT1;4. Further experiments will be needed to characterize the ion selectivity of OsHKT1;4 in detail. In addition, investigation of monovalent cation selectivity of OsHKT1;4 expressed in oocytes bathed in solutions containing solo cation-chloride salts further revealed that this transporter is highly selective for ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ amongst ${ \mathrm { L i } ^ { + } }$ , $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ , $\mathrm { { R b } ^ { + } }$ , ${ \mathrm { C s } } ^ { + }$ , ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ , and $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } ^ { + } }$ (Fig. 3). These results indicate that OsHKT1;4 is a ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ transporter.

HKT proteins have been suggested to contain four selectivity-filter-pore (p-loop) domains that are distantly related to a bacterial $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel [41–44]. HKT1 transporters have been found to be highly selective for ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ , and in general a serine residue at the key amino acid position for $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ selectivity in the first p-loop domain is conserved instead of a glycine residue, which corresponds to the first glycine in the GYG motif of the shaker-type $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel [10]. Corresponding amino acid positions in the three other p-loop domains of OsHKT1;4 were reported to be glycine residues, resulting in a SGGG type for the p-loop domains of OsHKT1;4 as typical HKT1 transporters [10]. The property of ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ selective transport by OsHKT1;4 was consistent with the prediction of ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ selectivity of HKT transporters based on the p-loop hypothesis [10, 41, 42].

The role of OsHKT1;4 in salt tolerance mechanisms in rice QTL analyses for salt tolerance of durum wheat plants have led to the identification of the salt tolerancedetermining Nax1 locus, which was deduced to be the TmHKT1;4-A2 gene [27, 28, 33]. The Nax1 locusmediated xylem ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ unloading in roots and leaf sheaths of durum wheat plants has been suggested to avoid ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ over-accumulation in leaf blades during salinity stress [27]. Relatively steady expression in leaf sheaths throughout growth stages is a distinctive feature of the OsHKT1;4 gene in Nipponbare plants (Figs. 5, 6a and b). In 3-weekold Nipponbare plants, grown in hydroponic culture, the expression of OsHKT1;4 was also observed in roots (Fig. 6a). However, the level of OsHKT1;4 expression mostly showed significant decreases in tissues/organs of salt-stressed Nipponbare plants at the vegetative growth stage under salinity stress (Fig. 6a, Additional file 1: Figure S1). OsHKT1;4 RNAi plants in the vegetative growth stage did not show any noticeable difference either in visual phenotype or in ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ content after the imposition of $5 0 \ \mathrm { m M } \ \mathrm { N a C l }$ stress compared with Nipponbare wild-type plants (Additional file 2: Figure S2). These results suggested a possibility that OsHKT1;4- mediated ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ transport does not provide a profound contribution to vital ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis during the vegetative growth phase of the japonica rice cultivar during salinity stress.

Another characteristic feature of OsHKT1;4 gene expression was its high expression in the stem, including the peduncle and the internode II, of rice plants at the reproductive growth stage (Fig. 5). The observed expression profile of OsHKT1;4 was consistent with that found in the RiceXPro database, in which OsHKT1;4 is highly up-regulated in the stem of rice plants in heading and ripening stages (http://ricexpro.dna.affrc.go.jp/) [45]. Longterm salinity stress treatment with gradual increases in NaCl concentration in soil-grown Nipponbare plants from heading to ripening stages led to significant increases in OsHKT1;4 expression in the peduncle, with relatively steady expression levels in the flag leaf blade and internode II independent of salt treatments (Fig. 6b). Significant up-regulation of OsHKT1;4 expression was also observed in node I, although the basal expression level in this tissue was far less than that in the peduncle (Fig. 6b). Similar long-term salinity stress treatments of soil-grown OsHKT1;4 RNAi and wild-type plants resulted in significantly higher ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ contents in aerial tissues of RNAi plants, with the highest impact on the ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ content of flag leaf blades compared with wild-type plants (Fig. 7a). Together with ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ selective transport mediated by plasma membrane-targeted OsHKT1;4 (Figs. 1, 2, 3 and 4), these results suggested that OsHKT1;4 contributes to the prevention of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ over-accumulation in aerial parts, in particular leaf blades of Nipponbare plants that are in the reproductive growth stage, during salinity stress. HKT1;4 transporters in wheat have been suggested to function in xylem ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ unloading in roots and leaf sheaths upon salinity stress to reduce ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ transfer into leaf blades [27]. On the other hand, HKT1-mediated ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ recirculation via the downward stream of the phloem has been argued as a potential working model for HKT1 transporters [4, 14, 20, 27]. OsHKT1;4 RNAi plants in the reproductive growth stage accumulated more ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ not only in leaves but also in tissues of the stem investigated under salinity stress (Fig. 7a). The reason for the phenotype is not clear yet. In a previous study, analyses on athkt1;1 mutants of Arabidopsis indicated that the dysfunction of AtHKT1;1- mediated ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ unloading from xylem caused the impairment of ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ recirculation via phloem as well, which could together be attributed to ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ over-accumulation in shoots of athkt1;1 mutants upon salinity stress [20]. $^ { 2 2 } { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ -imaging analysis indicated a higher amount of the ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ transfer in peduncles of $O s H K T 1 ; 4$ RNAi plants than WT plants with an exception of an independent OsHKT1;4

RNAi-II plant (Additional file 4: Figure S4), suggesting that OsHKT1;4 mediates ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ unloading from xylem and reduced activity of OsHKT1;4 leads to an increase in ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ accumulation in this tissue. Together, ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ overaccumulation in aerial parts of OsHKT1;4 RNAi plants upon salinity might be due to the insufficient activity of OsHKT1;4 in ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ unloading from xylem, which in turn could also bring about inhibition of ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ recirculation.
