## Tonoplast-localized nitrate uptake transporters involved in vacuolar nitrate efux and reallocation in Arabidopsis


Ya-Ni He1,2,3, Jia-Shi Peng1, Yao Cai1,2, De-Fen Liu1,2, Yuan Guan1,3, Hong-Ying Yi1 & Ji-Ming Gong $\Phi ^ { 1 }$

A great proportion of nitrate taken up by plants is stored in vacuoles. Vacuolar nitrate accumulation and release is of great importance to nitrate reallocation and efcient utilization. However, how plants mediate nitrate efux from vacuoles to cytoplasm is largely unknown. The current study identifed NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 as vacuolar nitrate efux transporters in Arabidopsis. Histochemical analysis showed that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were expressed preferentially in root pericycle cells and xylem parenchyma cells, and further analysis showed that these proteins were tonoplastlocalized. Functional characterization using cRNA-injected Xenopus laevis oocytes showed that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were low-afnity, pH-dependent nitrate uptake transporters. In npf5.11 npf5.12 npf5.16 triple mutant lines, more root-fed $^ { 1 5 } { \mathsf { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ was translocated to shoots compared to the wild type control. In the NPF5.12 overexpression lines, proportionally less nitrate was maintained in roots. These data together suggested that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 might function to uptake nitrate from vacuoles into cytosol, thus serving as important players to modulate nitrate allocation between roots and shoots.

Nitrate is the major nitrogen source for most plants, especially those grown in aerobic soil conditions1 . Once taken up from soil, nitrate is either assimilated or stored in vacuoles. As the largest organelle in fully expanded plant cells, vacuoles are identifed as the major nitrate storage pools and contain up to $9 0 \%$ of the total cellular nitrate2, 3 . However, vacuolar nitrate is not readily accessible to NR (nitrate reductase), thus it has to be reallocated for metabolic use when necessary4, 5 . Vacuolar nitrate release helps to maintain the relative steady level of cytosolic nitrate when external nitrogen supply was limited6, 7 . During the dark-to-light transition, nitrate remobilization from vacuoles was also observed to comply with the new steady state caused by the increased NR activity4 . Terefore, vacuolar nitrate and its remobilization are important for the regulation of nitrogen assimilation and nitrogen use efciency5, 8, 9 .

Transport across the tonoplast is energized by the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -ATPase (V-ATPase) and the vacuolar $\mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ -pyrophosphatase (V-PPase), which create the proton gradient and the membrane potential10–12. For nitrate, its accumulation in vacuoles is probably mediated by the nitrate/proton antiport machinery13–16 and the nitrate/ proton symport system may serve to remobilize vacuolar nitrate16–18. However, only a few tonoplast localized nitrate transporters have been identifed up to date. AtCLCa and AtNRT2.7 are two transporters responsible for nitrate accumulation in vacuoles19–21. AtCLCa was a tonoplast localized $2 \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - } / 1 \mathrm { H ^ { + } }$ antiporter expressed in both shoots and roots20, 22. Disruption of AtCLCa led to approximately $5 0 \%$ decrease of vacuolar nitrate, suggesting an important role for AtCLCa in vacuolar nitrate accumulation19, 20. AtNRT2.7, however, was a tonoplast localized transporter expressed exclusively in seeds, which regulated the kinetics of seed germination by afecting nitrate storage in seed vacuoles21. AtCLCc was also supposed to be involved in vacuolar nitrate accumulation, because it was tonoplast localized and the related mutants showed lower nitrate contents22, 23. Regarding nitrate efux from vacuoles, however, indirect evidences imply that AtCLCb and OsNPF7.2 might get involved, as they both were tonoplast-localized, and heterologous expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes indicated that they mediated nitrate uptake, but no evidence showed that functional disruption of these genes led to nitrate accumulation in vacuoles24, 25. AtCLCa was also implied to get involved in vacuolar nitrate efux, because it mediated anion homeostasis in stomata movement26, while nitrate is one of the anions contributing to stomatal movement27, 28.

In the current study, three tonoplast-localized NRT1/NPF family members NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were identifed by bioinformatics analysis, and functional characterization was performed. Our data suggested that these three transporters were all tonoplast localized, and mediated nitrate uptake in a pH-dependent low-afnity manner when heterologously expressed in oocytes. Further analysis indicated that they possibly modulated nitrate allocation between roots and shoots via vacuolar nitrate release.

Signifcant progresses have been made in clarifying the nitrate uptake and transport in Arabidopsis by the characterization of the transporters in NRT1/NPF, NRT2, CLC and SLAC/SLAH families34. However, our current knowledge about nitrate transport across the tonoplast is quite limited though the signifcance of this process is widely recognized.

Te transporters responsible for vacuolar nitrate efux should be tonoplast-localized and uptake nitrate toward cytoplasm. Our data suggested that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were localized in tonoplast in Arabidopsis (Fig. 1) and plasma membrane in Xenopus laevis oocytes (Supplementary Fig. S2), and in oocytes they could elicit inward currents by external nitrate and uptake nitrate in a $\mathrm { p H }$ dependent way (Fig. 2). When these results were assigned to the topology of the plant tonoplast, the inward currents might represent $\mathrm { N O _ { 3 } } ^ { - } / \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ efux from the vacuole to the cytoplasm24, because the external medium for oocytes corresponds to the vacuole in planta35, 36 and the $\mathrm { p H }$ of vacuole in Arabidopsis is about $5 . 5 ^ { 3 3 , }$ 37. Tus we speculated that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 were responsible for vacuolar nitrate release in Arabidopsis.

Considering that NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and $\mathrm { N P F } 5 . 1 6$ are predominantly expressed in vacuole membrane of pericycle cells and xylem parenchyma cells in roots (Figs 1, 3). We proposed that they might be involved in the regulation of nitrate long-distance transport by modulating the vacuolar sequestration capacity (VSC) of nitrate in roots. Relationship between VSC and long-distance transport of metals in plant have been well documented38, and accumulating evidences indicated that VSC of essential anions including sulfate and nitrate also regulated their long-distance transport39, 40. Te vacuolar sulfate efux transporters SULTR4;1 and SULTR4;2 played an essential role in delivering sulfate to the xylem vessels by balancing storage and turnover of sulfate in the root vacuoles39. While Han et al., found that the decreased VSC of nitrate in roots would enhance nitrate transport to shoots and contribute to a higher nitrogen use efciency (NUE)40. Our hypothesis about the physiological role of NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 was supported by the observation that more proportion of $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ was translocated to shoots in triple mutant lines (Fig. 4) and overexpression of $N P F 5 . 1 2$ resulted in a lower nitrate contents in roots (Fig. 5c). In the triple mutant lines, root VSC increased but not too much was available to newly absorbed nitrate due to the impaired nitrate efux from vacuoles, resulting in less vacuolar nitrate sequestration and the consequent enhancement of $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ long-distance transport to shoots when fed with $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ for a short time $3 0 \mathrm { m i n } )$ ). In $N P F 5 . 1 2$ overexpression lines, the overall nitrate contents in roots decreased because of the lower VSC of nitrate, thus leading to the higher $\mathrm { S } / \mathrm { R }$ ratios in the overexpression lines (Fig. 5c, Supplementary Fig. S10b).

No signifcant diference of nitrate contents was detected between all the mutants and wild type under various growth conditions we tested (Supplementary Figs S5, S6, S7). We proposed that there might be other transporters or channels that function redundantly with NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16, as the reutilization of vacuolar nitrate is crucial to environmental adaption for plants. Te speculation is according with the observation that more $^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ^ - }$ was translocated to shoots in triple mutant but not in single mutant. Similarly, no obvious changes in nitrate allocation was observed in mutants of AtCLCb or $O s N P F 7 . 2 ^ { 2 \bar { 4 } , 2 5 }$ . In addition, considering their specifc tissue localization in roots (Fig. 3), we speculated that physiological efect of NPF5.11, NPF5.12 and NPF5.16 in nitrate allocation might be more noticeable specifcally in pericycle cells and parenchyma cells. Tus more defnitive evidences are needed in the future to demonstrate the working model for vacuolar nitrate efux.

Nitrogen (N), crucial to plant growth and development, is engaged in numerous physiological and molecular processes (Liu et  al. 2022b; Shi et  al. 2023). Nitrate, the primary N form in aerated soils, is recognized and transported by intricate sensors or transporters from environment into plants. Many transporters, such as nitrate transporter 1 (NRT1) /peptide transport family (NRT1/ NPF), nitrate transporter 2 (NRT2), chloride channel family (CLC), and slow anion channel-related homologues (SLAC/SLAH), have been confrmed to involve in nitrate transfer and utilization across various tissues and cells (von der Fecht-Bartenbach et al. 2010; Krapp et al. 2014; Maierhofer et al. 2014; Léran et al. 2014). As reported, NRT2 belongs to high-afnity transporter that is indispensable for nitrate uptake during environmental N defciency, i.e., $< 1 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ nitrate. For instance, NRT2s have been extensively verifed to promote nitrate uptake and utilization under nitrogen limitation in many plant species including but not limited to Arabidopsis (Wang et al. 2018), rice (Chen et al. 2016, 2020), wheat (Sigalas et al. 2023), barley (Guo et al. 2020), maize (Jia et al. 2023), and pea (Chen et al. 2024). Positive regulation on highafnity nitrate transporters improves plant adaptability to harsh environments and improves crop yields or nitrogenuse efciency under moderate nitrogen levels (Alam et al. 2023; Iqbal et al. 2023).

Over the past several decades, numerous studies have identified various regulators or transcription factors (TFs) involved in regulating NRT2s in plants (reviewed in (Vidal et al. 2020). Regulators or TFs modulate NRTs through binding to nitrate-responsive cis-elements (NRE) in NRT’s promoter (Choi et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2022a). For instance, the nitrate regulation master, nodule inception (NIN)-like proteins such as AtNLP7, ZmNLP5, MdNLP7, and HvNLP2, have been implicated in promoting NRT2.1/NRT2.2 via NREs binding (Castaings et al. 2009; Alvarez et al. 2020; Feng et al. 2022; Ge et al. 2020; Gao et al. 2022). Recently, AtNLP7 has been identifed to participate in nitrate transportation in Arabidopsis (Liu et al. 2022a). In addition, TGA1 and TGA4 directly bind to NREs in NRT2.1 or NRT2.2 promoter to infuence lateral root development and nitrate response in Arabidopsis (Alvarez et al. 2014; Zhong et al. 2015). TaNAC2 and OsSNAC1 regulate NRT2 via NRE to participate in seed vigor and nitrogen defciency adaptation (Li et al. 2020; Qi et al. 2023). PdGNC, induced by low nitrate levels, directly activates $P d N R T 2 . 4 b$ through NRE binding in poplar (Shen et al. 2022). AtBES1 enhances NRT2.1 and NRT2.2 through NRE under nitrogen defciency, linking brassinosteroid signaling and nitrate defciency in

Arabidopsis (Wang et  al. 2023). In apple, MdMYB10 transcriptionally activates MdNRT2.4–1 depending on NRE binding to enhance nitrate uptake (Liu et al. 2022c). Moreover, multiple regulators interact each other to modulate the same target gene through binding diverse NREs in promoter (Guan et al. 2017; Alvarez et al. 2020). For instance, TCP20 and NLP7&NLP6 bind to the diferent NRE of nitrate reductase gene (NIA1) and interacts to increase nitrate assimilation in Arabidopsis (Guan et al. 2017).

The presence of NREs in $_ 5 \cdot$ or $_ 3 \cdot$ terminal fanking regions is of utmost importance in advancing the regulation of regulators or TFs on their targets. NREs usually act as enhancer elements to improve the specifc binding, for instance, $\mathsf { S ^ { 3 } - T G A t / c C C N } _ { 1 2 } \mathrm { A a }$ L $/ \mathrm { t G g G a } - 3 ^ { \prime }$ in OsNRT2.1 and OsNRT2.3 (Wu et al. 2021), $_ 5 \cdot$ -CTATC/TGAGCTT $\mathrm { N _ { 1 0 } T / A A G G A } { - 3 } ^ { , }$ in ZmNRT2.1 and ZmNRT2.2 (Meng et al. 2020), and $\mathrm { 5 ^ { \circ } - G A C t C T T N _ { 1 0 } A A G - 3 ^ { \circ } }$ in AtNIA1 and nitrite reductase gene (AtNiR1) (Konishi and Yanagisawa 2014). However, motif analysis revealed that these putative NREs are not commonly conserved across plant species.

Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is a crucial tropical root crop that provides sustenance for over 800 million individuals worldwide, predominantly in South America and Africa. Starch from the root tubers are utilized in diverse applications, including food production to pharmaceuticals, textiles, plywood, paper, and adhesives, as well as a source of ethanol for biofuel production (Mohidin et al. 2023). In tropical regions, cassava thrives in marginal areas with erratic rain, acidic soils, poor native fertility, and challenging terrains, where other crops typically fail (Reinhardt Howeler and Thomas 2013). As previously reported, most MeNRT2 genes in cassava were induced by nitrate defciency, with MeNRT2.2 exhibiting the highest expression level. Moreover, MeNRT2.2-overexpressing Arabidopsis exhibited enhanced adaptation to low nitrate $( 0 . 3 \mathrm { m M } \mathrm { K N O } _ { 3 } )$ ) (You et al. 2022). However, the potential regulators on MeNRT2.2 and the putative NREs remain unexplored in cassava.

This study reveals MeZFP29 and MebZIPW influence MeNRT2.2 expressions by binding to adjacent NREs (TGCATT and CAGATG) in its promoter. Two regulators interact each other via conserved ANK repeat domains in vivo and in vitro. Interestingly, MeZFP29 and MeZFP29&MebZIPW exhibit a nitrate-dependent distribution, i.e., nitrate defciency results in extensive distribution in cytoplasm and nucleus, whereas sufcient nitrate restricts them to nucleus, although MebZIPW distributes in both compartments irrespective of nitrate conditions. Overexpression of MeZFP29 in seedlings notably enhanced plant growth under low nitrate, while MebZIPW did not, demonstrating their diferent roles in nitrogen utilization in plant.

Nitrogen $( \mathrm { N } )$ , as the essential element of amino acid, nucleic acid, chlorophyll, and among other biologically important molecules, is vital to plant growth and development. In aerated soils, plants take up nitrogen mainly in the form of nitrate due to intensive nitrification processes. In plants, nitrate can be absorbed and translocated through transmembrane proteins, which mainly consist of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF) and NRT2 (see excellent reviews by $\mathrm { X u }$ et al. 2012; Wang et al. 2018b). There are 53, 93, and 91 NPF genes in Arabidopsis, rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Leran et al. 2014). Most NPFs are responsible for low-affinity nitrate transporter activity $\mathrm { ~ ( > ~ 0 . 5 ~ m M } _ { \mathrm { ~ , ~ } }$ (Epstein et al. 1963; Noguero and Lacombe 2016), except for CHL1/NRT1.1/ AtNPF6.3, which was the first NPF to be found and cloned, displays a dual affinity property (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999). There are 7, 4, 7, and 5 NRT2 genes in Arabidopsis, rice, Brachypodium, and Sorghum, respectively (Orsel et al. 2002, Cai et al. 2008; Massel et al. 2016; Wang et al. 2018a, b). In general, all of NRT2s are responsible for high-affinity nitrate transport $( < 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M } )$ ). Additionally, a third family, named as NAR2/NRT3, requires interacting with most NRT2 members to transport nitrate (Zhou et al. 2000; Orsel et al. 2006; Yan et al. 2011; Kotur et al. 2012), except for AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al.

2012). There are 2, 2, and 3 NRT3 members in Arabidopsis, Rice, and Sorghum, respectively (Plett et al. 2010; Massel et al. 2016). Beside nitrate, NPF family transport diverse components as substrates, including dipeptides, glucosinolate, IAA, ABA, GA, and JA (Leran et al. 2014; Wang et al. 2018a). By contrast, NRT2 members have been only reported to transport nitrate so far.

Based on a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis from 31 fully sequenced plant genomes (Lee et al. 2011), NPF family can be classified into 8 unambiguous clades. Members from NPF1 subfamily have been shown to be involved in redistributing nitrate to developing tissues. For example, AtNPF1.1/NRT1.12 and AtNPF1.2/NRT1.11 are expressed in companion cells (CC) of the primary vein, and their double mutant is deficient in remobilizing nitrate to younger leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013). Similarly, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7 is expressed in the phloem of the minor vein in mature leaves and is responsible for nitrate remobilization under nitrogen deficiency (Fan et al. 2009). Additionally, many other NPF2 family members (including AtNPF2.3, AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, OsNPF2.2, and OsNPF2.4) are involved in nitrate translocation from root to shoot (Wang and Tsay 2011; Li et al. 2015; Taochy et al. 2015; Xia et al. 2015). AtNPF2.12/NRT1.6 can mediate nitrate influx to premature embryos (Almagro et al. 2008). In addition to nitrate, two NPF2 members (AtNPF2.4 and AtNPF2.5) are able to transport chloride (Li et al. 2016, 2017); five NPF2 members (AtNPF2.9/NRT1.9, AtNPF2.10/ GTR1, AtNPF2.11/GTR2, AtNPF2.13/NRT1.7, and AtNPF2.14) are able to transport glucosinolate, which is one of the important secondary metabolites for plant defense (Nour-Eldin et al. 2012). AtNPF3.1, originally identified as a nitrate/nitrite transporter, is found to be a GA transporter which is also affected by nitrate availability (Sugiura et al. 2007; Pike et al. 2014; David et al. 2016; Tal et al. 2016). AtNPF4.6/NRT1.2 has been characterized as a constitutive nitrate transporter (Huang et al. 1999), as well as an ABA transporter (Kanno et al. 2012). As the largest subfamily, three NPF5 members (AtNPF5.11, AtNPF5.12, AtNPF5.16) are responsible for nitrate efflux from tonoplast (He et al. 2017), AtNPF5.5 is involved in nitrate accumulation in embryos (Leran et al. 2015). Moreover, AtNPF5.2/PTR3 can transport dipeptide, which is important for plant pathogen defense (Karim et al. 2007). AtNPF6.3 is the most heavily studied member of the family, and it is a dual-affinity nitrate transporter (Tsay et al. 1993; Liu et al. 1999), auxin transporter (Krouk et al. 2010); it affects stomata opening (Guo et al. 2003) and also serves as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). Interestingly, indica rice OsNRT1.1B/OsNPF6.5, one of the closest orthologous genes of AtNPF6.3 with only a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) with japonica rice $O s N R T I . I B /$ OsNPF6.5, is responsible for better nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in indica rice (Hu et al. 2015). Recently, OsNRT1.1B is reported to facilitate Selenomethinone (Se) translocation in both roots and leaves, and the overexpression lines exhibit a higher Se accumulation in grains (Zhang et al. 2018b). AtNPF6.2/NRT1.4 is specifically expressed in leaf petiole, which is critical for nitrate storage in petiole (Chiu et al. 2004). AtNPF7.2/NRT1.8 and AtNPF7.3/NRT1.5 expressed in close proximity of xylem and their functions are antagonistic upon stress challenges (Li et al. 2010; Zhang et al. 2014). The NPF8 subfamily (NPF8.1/PTR1, NPF8.2/PTR5, and NPF8.3/PTR2) in Arabidopsis transports dipeptide and has no detectable nitrate transport activity (Komarova et al. 2009), whereas OsNRT1/ NPF8.9 is a putative nitrate transporter in rice (Lin et al. 2000).

Compared to the large and complex NPF family, NRT2 and NRT3 families in plants are relatively small. There is a clear divergence between monocots and dicots of NRT2 family genes, suggesting NRT2 in monocots may function differently from heavily-studied AtNRT2 (Plett et al. 2010; Wang et al. 2018a, b). It has been well-documented that AtNRT2.1 and AtNRT2.2 are nitrate-inducible transporters, which are major components for high-affinity root nitrate uptake (Filleur et al. 2001; Li et al. 2007). AtNRT2.4 and AtNRT2.5 are also involved in high-affinity root nitrate uptake but mainly upon nitrate starvation (Lezhneva et al. 2014). Besides, AtNRT2.1 can serve as a signal transducer to regulate lateral root growth (Little et al. 2005). NRT2.7 is the only NRT2 member located on the tonoplast membrane and is responsible for nitrate transport in seeds (Chopin et al. 2007). In rice, OsNRT2.3b responds to pH changes and its overexpression leads to grain yield increase (Fan et al. 2016). Additionally, overexpressing OsNRT2.1 driven by the NAR2.1/NRT3.1 promoter is also able to enhance grain yield in rice (Chen et al. 2016). The importance of NRT3/NAR2 is underlined by their coexpression and interaction with NRT2 genes. All AtNRT2 members except for AtNRT2.7 can interact with NRT3.1 (Kotur et al. 2012). Nevertheless, AtNRT3.1 is not indispensable for nitrate uptake mediated by AtNRT2.4 or OsNRT2.3b (Feng et al. 2011; Kiba et al. 2012).

Sugarcane is one of the most productive crops in the world (FAOSTAT, 2016; http://www.fao.org/statistics/en/) and it accounts for $80 \%$ of world sugar supply and $40 \%$ of ethanol production (Zhang et al. 2013). N deficiencies can cause a decreased chlorophyll synthesis as well as a reduced biomass. Together with carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, N makes up $90 \%$ of sugarcane dry matter (Brandes 1952). Sugarcane mainly absorbs N through $_ \mathrm { N }$ fertilizers or biological nitrogen fixation owing to microbial nitrogen fixers (Boddey et al. 2003). Unfortunately, nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) is low for agronomic crops, especially for sugarcane, more than $50 \%$ of nitrogen is lost through surface run-off, leaching, denitrifications or volatilizations (Garnett et al. 2009). Only $20 \%$ (or less) of input N can be found in dry biomass of sugarcane at harvest (Franco et al. 2011). Therefore, understanding nitrogen uptake, translocation and utilization is key to improve NUE by conventional breeding and genetic engineering strategy. However, the genetic information for nitrate transporters is still missing in sugarcane, largely due to the lack of a complete genome information. Recently, an allele-defined genome of sugarcane Saccharum spontaneum L. became available (Zhang et al. 2018a), offering an excellent opportunity to identify nitrate transporter families at a genome-wide scale. In this study, we carried out a BLAST search using Arabidopsis and Sorghum NPF/NRTs against newly available sugarcane genome. Phylogenetic analysis, gene structure as well as protein motif analysis were conducted to understand molecular and evolutionary relationships between subfamilies and species. Moreover, RNA-Seq data were analyzed to investigate tissue-specific expression pattern across all NPF/ NRT genes in S. spontaneum. Our results presented a comprehensive characterization of sugarcane NPF/NRT genes, which laid the foundation for future investigations of these nitrogen transporters in sugarcane.

Low nitrogen (N) use efficiency (NUE) is a serious problem impeding the sustainable development of bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) production worldwide (Zhang et al. 2015). Breeding wheat cultivars with a high N uptake ability is a promising option for improving N fertilizer use efficiency; however, breeding for improved N uptake cannot be achieved without a full understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying N uptake by wheat plants. Nitrate is the major N source in aerobic soils (Fan et al. 2017a). There are generally two nitrate transport systems in higher plants: the lowaffinity transport system (LATS) and the high-affinity transport system (HATS). LATS is the main nitrate uptake system at ${ \mathrm { N O } _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ concentrations ranging from 0.25 to $5 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ and HATS exhibits a Km of $1 0 \sim 2 5 0$ $\mu \mathrm { M }$ and is encoded by NRT2 family genes (Okamoto et al. 2003). LATS is encoded by NPF (nitrate transporter 1 and peptide transporter family) genes belonging to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS). Some NPF genes encode peptide transporters (Leran et al. 2014), but may not be able to transport nitrate due to the absence of the specific binding sites for nitrate in some of these proteins. In addition to nitrate and peptides, NPF genes were also involved in the transport of nitrite, chloride, glucosinolates, auxin (IAA), abscisic acid (ABA), jasmonates (JAs), and gibberellins (GAs). Some of these transporters are even capable of transporting more than one substrate (Corratge-Faillie and Lacombe 2017). In Arabidopsis thaliana, the AtNRT1.1 (AtNPF6.3) protein can act as a dual-affinity transporter when its affinity is altered by phosphorylation (Liu and Tsay 2003); in this way, AtNPF6.3 acts as a nitrate sensor (Ho et al. 2009). By contrast, NRT2 proteins are more specific to nitrate. Moreover, most NRT2 proteins require another protein, NAR2 (nitrate assimilation-related protein, also known as NRT3), to transport nitrate, with a few exceptions like AtNRT2.7 (Kotur et al. 2012), OsNRT2.3b (Liu et al. 2014) and OsNRT2.4 (Wei et al. 2018). In recent years, an increasing number of studies have shown that overexpression of NPF and NRT2 genes can significantly improve the yield, shoot biomass or NUE of crops (Fan et al. 2017b; Hu et al. 2015), suggesting great application potential of NPF and NRT2 genes during N-efficient wheat cultivar breeding.

NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat have been largely uncharacterized compared with those in model plants due to the large and complex genome of wheat and the difficulty of its genetic transformation (Paux et al. 2008). Some studies have investigated the responses of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat to $_ \mathrm { N }$ deficiency (Buchner and Hawkesford 2014), drought stress (Duan et al. 2016) and fungal colonization (Tian et al. 2017). TaNRT2.1, which was mainly expressed in the roots of wheat, can be induced by N starvation and ABA (Guo et al. 2014; Xiong et al. 2019; Yin et al. 2007; Wang et al. 2020), and may play a major role in post-flowering ${ \mathrm { N O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ uptake (Taulemesse et al. 2015). Recently, the overexpression of TaNRT2.5, which was mainly expressed in the tonoplasts of grain cells, increased grain nitrate uptake, seed vigor and yield (Li et al. 2020). Nevertheless, function of most of the wheat NPF and NRT2 genes have mainly been predicted based on DNA or protein sequence homology. Although basic phylogenetic analyses of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat have been conducted (Bajgain et al. 2018), the analyses were based on an old wheat genome version and some key information such as gene collinearity, detailed location on chromosomes, nitrate transport characteristics and evolution is still largely unknown.

It has been reported that the NAC transcription factor $T a N A C 2  – 5 \ A$ can positively regulate the expression of multiple NPF or NRT2 genes in wheat by directly binding their promoter regions (He et al. 2015). In rice, the NAC transcription factor OsNAC42 binds and activates the promoter of an elite NPF gene OsNPF6.1, and the NAC42-NPF6.1 signaling cascade is a strategy for high NUE and yield breeding in rice (Tang et al. 2019). A MYB transcription factor (AtMYB59) has been shown to directly bind to the promoter of the AtNPF7.3 gene and enable the regulation of its expression in Arabidopsis (Du et al. 2019). Members of other transcription factor families such as Dof, MADS-box, WRKY, ZFP, RWP-RK and bZIP may also regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in plants (Kumar et al. 2018; Mu and Luo 2019; Vidal et al. 2020). The overexpression of some wheat transcription factors, such as TaZFP593;l(Chen et al. 2017), TabHLH1(Yang et al. 2016) and TaNBP1(Liu et al. 2018), in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) led to differences in the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in tobacco, suggesting that the genes in wheat may also be regulated by these transcription factors. Nevertheless, direct evidence of the roles of these transcription factors in regulating NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat is lacking. In addition, it is unknown whether other unrecognized transcription factors may also regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat.

Natural variations in NPF and NRT2 genes may greatly alter the N uptake ability of plants; for example, in rice, a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) (T/C) of $\mathit { O s N P F 6 . 5 }$ contributes to the divergence in nitrate use between indica and japonica subspecies (Hu et al. 2015). The first green revolution beginning in the mid20th century led to a great increase in the production of wheat grain due to the introduction of dwarf genes into wheat cultivars and the application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. The dwarf trait, biotic or abiotic stress resistance and high quality have become the main target traits in wheat cultivar breeding since the first green revolution. It has been reported that the N utilization efficiency of wheat did not change significantly from 1958 to 2007 but that $_ \mathrm { N }$ uptake efficiency increased with the year of cultivar release (Sadras and Lawson 2013). The increase in N uptake efficiency may be due to the natural variation in NPF and NRT2 genes during the artificial selection of wheat cultivars in recent decades, which requires further investigation.

In the present study, we firstly identified putative NPF and NRT2 genes at the whole-wheat-genome level; and then verified the nitrate transport function of two NPF and one NRT2 genes via a heterologous expression system. We also investigated transcription factors that may regulate the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes in wheat via weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA). More specially, we analyzed polymorphisms of NPF and NRT2 genes in a natural wheat population composed of 254 wheat accessions collected worldwide. We aimed to test the following hypotheses: (1) just like some other gene families in wheat, duplication events are ubiquitous in NPF and NRT2 gene families in the wheat genome; (2) unrecognized transcription factors regulating the expression of NPF and NRT2 genes exist in wheat; (3) wheat orthologues of the previously characterized NPF or NRT2 genes reported in other plant species have similar characteristics in nitrate transport; and (4) cultivar selection is the main driver of polymorphism accumulation in NPF and NRT2 genes.

Nitrate is the major nitrogen for most terrestrial plants, which serves as both an essential nutrient and a signal molecule involved in plant metabolism, growth, development, and adaptation to various environments [1–4]. However, nitrate concentrations in the soil can vary by four orders of magnitude from the $\mu \mathrm { M }$ to mM range as nitrate ion is readily dissolved and very mobile in the soil [5]. Plants have evolved two nitrate uptake systems to counteract this fluctuation, including low-affinity transport system (LATS) and the high-affinity transport system (HATS). The absorbed nitrate is then transported to different parts of plants for further assimilation.

Diverse kinds of membrane proteins are found to be involved in absorption of nitrate from the external environment into plants, and its transportation and translocation between different parts of the whole plant. These transporters consist of NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1 (NRT1)/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER (PTR) family (NPF), NRT2, CHLORIDE CHANNEL (CLC) family, and SLOWLY ACTIVATING ANION CHANNEL and their homologs (SLAHs). In addition to nitrate, they can transport a diverse range of substrates, allowing their participation in diverse biological processes including plant growth, development, and adaptation to complicated environments. Detailed and comprehensive information regarding these nitrate transporters have been reviewed [6,7]. However, more and more evidence shows that a large portion of them take part in plants’ response to adverse environmental conditions. In this review, we specifically focus on nitrate transporters involved in plant abiotic stress tolerance and their physiological roles and regulation in the related processes (Table 1).

Fundamental studies to understand mechanisms that govern nitrate transport and signaling offer prospects to better control nitrogen use efficiency in plants. Mining of extant datasets enables identification of candidate genes and consideration of their possible roles in planta. To date, few studies of legume nitrate transporters have been undertaken, and thus much remains undiscovered, in particular the role of these transporters in nodules.

Experimental characterization of nitrate transporters is usually performed under optimal or at least unchallenging conditions. However, plants are continuously subjected to ever changing environmental conditions. Their sessile lifestyle exposes them to unavoidable frequent and severe climatic changes and attacks by herbivores and microorganisms. It is well known that legume plants adapt their root architecture and their metabolism to abiotic stress through signaling pathways involving ABA and NO (Planchet et al. 2011, 2014). Given that studies on both characterized nitrate transporters, MtNPF1.7 and MtNPF6.8, connect these NPFs with root architecture and ABA, it will be valuable to fully investigate the role of legume NPFs in response to challenging environmental conditions.

The two main sources of inorganic nitrogen for plants are nitrate and ammonium, and both are extremely important for plant growth and development (Chen et al. 2022a, 2022b). Nitrifcation is very rapid in well aerated soils, when nitrate nitrogen is the main source of nitrogen absorbed by plants (Jin et  al. 2015). Low nitrogen efficiency is frequently a signifcant limiting factor for crop output in the majority of nutrient-poor soils. The distribution and amount of nitrogen in plants are signifcantly infuenced by nitrate transporter proteins, which also function as a signaling molecule to awaken dormant seeds (Alboresi et al. 2005). Nitrate is transported to the leaves through the xylem when photosynthetic reducers are available, where it is reduced and assimilated (Lillo 2008). Therefore, in order to load and unload thin-walled xylem tissue for long-distance transport, nitrate transporter proteins are needed to import nitrate into the cytoplasm and store excess nitrate in vesicles. The siliques are additionally loaded by the nitrate transporter in order to remobilize nitrogen from older leaves (Fan et al. 2009).

Nitrate transport proteins including NRT1, NRT2, NRT3, NRT1s are essential for the uptake and transportation of nitrate in maize (Li et al. 2017; Xuan et al. 2017). In plants, peptide transporters (PTRs) are proton-dependent oligopeptide transporters (POTs) including dipeptide and tripeptide transporters, of which NRT1 is a member; NRT1 and the PTR family are collectively referred to as NPF because NRT1 and PTR are related; The NRT2 family is a family of transporters belonging to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS). Nitrate transport and distribution within the plant, as well as nitrate uptake by the root system, are all regulated by the nitrate transporter proteins NPF (previously known as low-afnity NRT1) and high-afnity NRT2 (Saf et al. 2021). AtNRT1.1, also known as CHL1, was the frst NRT member identifed in Arabidopsis thaliana. Studies show that the afnity of the Arabidopsis NRT1.1 protein for nitrate varies with soil nitrate concentration. When the soil nitrate concentration is low, the 101st amino acid Thr of the NRT1.1 is phosphorylated, giving it a high afnity for nitrate; when the soil nitrate concentration is high, the amino acids of the NRT1.1 transporter protein are not phosphorylated, thus the amino acids of the NRT1.1 transporter protein are not phosphorylated at high nitrate concentrations in soil, thus maintaining a low afnity for nitrate (Wang et al. 2020a, 2020b, 2020c; Tsay 2014). With regard to both high and low nitrate concentrations, the range of absorption for this dualafnity nitrate transporter is exceedingly large (Tsay et al. 1993). All organisms are thought to have PTR transporters (Daniel 2004). In higher plants, NPFs from diferent species share highly similar sequences as well as 12 putative TM that are connected by short peptide loops, with a big hydrophilic loop separating each of the six TM. A recent study has shown that mutations in all seven transcription factors of the Arabidopsis NIN-like protein (NLP) abolished plants’ primary nitrate responses. This study proposes that NLP7 was found to be an intracellular nitrate sensor, which is diferent from the plasma membrane extracellular nitrate transporter sensor NRT1.1 (Liu et al. 2022).

The NPF family, a star family, has been reported in several species. Among them, 53, 96, 331, 73, 51, 68 and 80 NPF genes have been identifed in Arabidopsis (Chiba et al. 2015), Oryza sativa (Yang et al. 2020), wheat (Wang et al. 2020a, 2020b), apple (Wang et al. 2018), Capsella rubella (Léran et al. 2014), poplar (Zhao et al. 2021) and Medicago truncatula (Pellizzaro et al. 2017) respectively.

For optimal nitrogen distribution in leaves, AtNPF1.1 and AtNPF1.2 transport nitrate between xylem and phloem when expressed more strongly in enlarged leaves (Hsu and Tsay 2013). The plant hormones ethylene and jasmine acid are some of the stressors that can control the expression of AtNPF7.2 and AtNPF7.3, leading to nitrate accumulation in the roots (Zhang et al. 2014). For the transportation of enough nitrate to growing seeds, AtNPF2.12 and AtNPF5.5 are both necessary (Léran et  al. 2015). The transporter protein NPF2.3 in Arabidopsis root columns facilitates the transport of nitrate to above-ground parts under salt stress (Taochy et al. 2015). The expression of MdNPF6.5 was increased by both low and high nitrate levels; 35S:MdNPF6.5 transgenic apple healing tissues were more tolerant to low nitrogen stress, indicating that the gene has a stronger nitrogen uptake capacity under low nitrogen stress (Wang et al. 2018). LjNPF8.6 has a positive efect on nodule function, and in African clawed toad oocytes LjNPF8.6 can take up nitrate at external concentrations of 0.5 and $3 0 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ and may act as a nitrate transporter in the control of nitrogen fxation nodule activity (Valkov et al. 2017a, 2017b). When OsNPF4.5 was expressed in the oocytes of African clawed toads, it was only found to be expressed in root cells that contained arbuscule and showed a low afnity for $\mathrm { N O 3 ^ { - } }$ transport activity. Additionally, when $\mathrm { N O 3 ^ { - } }$ was used as a nitrogen source, knockdown of ${ \cal O s N P F 4 . 5 }$ resulted in a $4 5 \%$ decrease in symbiotic $\mathbf { N }$ uptake and a signifcant decrease in the incidence of arbuscular, probably playing a crucial role in mycorrhizal ${ \mathrm { N O 3 ^ { - } } }$ acquisition (Wang et al. 2020a, 2020b, 2020c). Expression analysis of OsNPF4.5 direct homologues in Medicago truncatula (MtNPF4.5), maize $( Z m N P F 4 . 5 )$ and Sorghum bicolor (SbNPF4.5) revealed that in roots not inoculated with AMF, expression of all three NPF4.5 direct homologues was scarcely detectable; MtNPF4.5 expression in alfalfa was only marginally raised by AMF inoculation, in contrast to the substantial induction of ZmNPF4.5 in maize and SbNPF4.5 in sorghum (Wang et al. 2020a, 2020b, 2020c).

The vast majority of plants are able to collaborate symbiotically with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus (AMF) in natural soil environments to better withstand nutrient scarcity (Fu et al. 2021). In nature, plant-AMF symbiosis is a very common and mutually benefcial relationship, with around $8 0 { - } 9 0 \%$ of terrestrial plants able to symbiosis with AMF (Chen et al. 2022a, 2022b; Ho-Plágaro et al. 2022).

Maize is an important cereal crop worldwide. Maize is able to symbiosis with AMF in an aerobic environment, just like the majority of vascular fowering plants that can be colonized by AMF. A good model system is maize, which may be used to examine how mycorrhizal N uptake routes afect plant development and symbiotic relationships. In this study, we focus on the composition of the ZmNPF gene family and whether it plays a role in mediating nutrition under symbiotic with AMF. This is a useful reference for further exploration of the acquisition of nitrate nitrogen by maize through the AMF pathway.

8 named NRT1/PTR (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 1/PEPTIDE TRANSPORTER) and NRT2   
9 (NITRATE TRANSPORTER 2) (Nacry et al., 2013). According to the recent unified   
10 nomenclature, NPF is now the name to be used for the NRT1/PTR Family (Léran et al., 2014).   
11 Fifty three putative NPF genes were predicted from the genome sequence of Arabidopsis   
12 thaliana and ten were characterized as nitrate transporters (Tsay et al., 1993; Huang et al.,   
13 1999; Chiu et al., 2004; Almagro et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010;   
14 Wang and Tsay, 2011; Hsu and Tsay, 2013). All of the NPF transporters are located in the   
15 plasma membrane. Most of these nitrate transporters are low-affinity nitrate transporters,   
16 except AtNPF6.3 (AtNRT1.1), which is a dual-affinity nitrate transporter (Liu et al., 1999).   
17 Only AtNPF6.3 and AtNPF4.6 (AtNRT1.2) have been shown until now to participate in high   
18 nitrate concentration uptake by roots (Huang et al., 1999; Liu et al., 1999). In A. thaliana,   
19 seven members of the NRT2 family were identified and characterized as high-affinity nitrate   
20 transporters. Most of these AtNRT2 transporters are located in the plasma membrane, except   
21 AtNRT2.7 which is located in the tonoplast (Chopin et al., 2007). AtNRT2.1 is the major   
22 NRT2 transporter that participates in high-affinity nitrate uptake, while AtNRT2.2 and   
23 AtNRT2.4 have been shown to play a minor role in nitrate uptake (Li et al., 2007; Kiba et al.,   
24 2012).

Developmental plasticity allows a plant to respond to nutrient availability by changing the architecture of the root system (Zhang and Forde, 2000; Linkohr et al., 2002). Nitrate is one of the major nutrients known to act as a signal molecule involved in the control of root architecture through the regulation of primary root growth and in the emergence and development of lateral roots (LR), as part of an adaptive strategy (Zhang and Forde, 1998; Zhang et al., 1999; Zhang and Forde, 2000; Tian et al., 2008; Vidal et al., 2010b; CelisArámburo et al., 2011). The molecular nature of nitrate sensing and signaling has been extensively studied in A. thaliana in relation to the regulation of LR development. At high nitrate concentrations, a systemic response suppresses LR growth after initiation at the early LR emergence stage (Zhang et al., 1999). In addition, studies have shown that when a plant is subject to nitrate deficiency, followed by the application of a high local nitrate concentration, LR growth is locally stimulated towards this most abundant source of nitrate (Zhang and Forde, 1998; Zhang et al., 1999). The localized effect of nitrate on LR growth was shown to be mediated by the dual-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF6.3 (Remans et al., 2006) and ANR1, a transcription factor of the MADS box family (Zhang and Forde, 1998). Furthermore, the finding that AtNPF6.3 transports nitrate and auxin (indoleacetic acid; IAA), provides a model in which: (i) under low nitrate conditions, AtNPF6.3 transports auxin away from the LR tip and the low content of auxin in the tip inhibits the outgrowth of LR; (ii) under high nitrate conditions, nitrate stimulates LR emergence by inhibiting AtNPF6.3 dependent auxin basipetal transport, leading to auxin accumulation in the LR tip (Krouk et al., 2010). In nonnodulated Medicago truncatula, i.e. in the absence of rhizobia, the modulation of shoot-toroot auxin transport in response to nitrate availability was shown to reduce the density of LR and this effect was mediated by the SUNN (super numeric nodules) gene (Jin et al., 2012).

The effect of nitrate on primary root growth has been less well studied compared to LR growth, although nitrate has been shown in several species to inhibit primary root growth through the alteration of hormone transport or signaling. In maize seedlings, nitrate supply resulted in a decrease in auxin content in the phloem thus decreasing auxin shoot-to-root translocation (Tian et al., 2008). In A. thaliana, nitrate was shown to regulate primary root growth by a pathway involving the auxin receptor AFB3 (Vidal et al., 2010a). Nitrate treatment induced the accumulation of the small RNA miR393 which was shown to specifically direct cleavage of AFB3 transcripts (Vidal et al., 2010a). In M. truncatula, nitrateinduced inhibition of primary root growth was altered in a mutant affected in the high-affinity nitrate transporter MtNPF1.7 also known as LATD/NIP (LATeral root organ Defective/Numerous Infections and Polyphenolics) (Harris and Dickstein, 2010; Yendrek et al., 2010; Bagchi et al., 2012). As the root architecture phenotype of npf1.7 mutants was rescued by the application of exogenous abscisic acid (ABA) (Liang et al., 2007), it is possible that the control of root architecture by nitrate in M. truncatula might involve an interaction with an ABA signaling pathway. Accordingly, the A. thaliana low-affinity nitrate transporter AtNPF4.6 was shown to transport both nitrate (Huang et al., 1999) and ABA (Kanno et al., 2012). Three closely related proteins belonging to the NPF family (At1g27040 /AtAIT2 /AtNPF4.5, At3g25260 /AtAIT3 /AtNPF4.1 and At3g25280 /AtAIT4 /AtNPF4.2) were shown to transport ABA (Kanno et al., 2012).

In a previous study, we characterized the dual-affinity nitrate transporter MtNPF6.8 (MtNRT1.3) in M. truncatula (Morère-Le Paven et al., 2011; Léran et al., 2014). Based on

1 genetic analyses and co-localization of MtNPF6.8 with a peak of a major quantitative trait   
2 locus (QTL) for primary root growth, we put forward the hypothesis that this transporter is   
3 involved in the regulation of primary root growth by nitrate during seedling establishment   
4 (Morère-Le Paven et al., 2011). In the present study, we have tested this hypothesis by   
5 studying the effect of nitrate on the growth of primary roots of npf6.8 knockdown lines   
6 generated by RNA interference (RNAi). Our findings support the hypothesis that MtNPF6.8   
7 regulates primary root growth in response to nitrate availability by controlling the elongation   
8 of root cells. Our results also show that ABA is transported by MtNPF6.8 and is involved in   
9 nitrate inhibitory effect on primary root growth. Furthermore, analyses of short-term effects of   
10 nitrate $\mathrm { 3 0 ~ m i n }$ ) on nitrate-inducible genes support the proposal that MtNPF6.8 is involved in   
11 primary response to nitrate in M. truncatula.

## Wheat genes orthologous to rice group II HKTs


Full length cDNA (FL-cDNA) of the rice genes OsHKT2;1, OsHKT2;2, OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4 were used as query sequence in blastn and tblastx search of the IWGS survey sequence database in order to identify related wheat gene sequences. The four rice FL-cDNAs identified related wheat sequences on seven scaffolds (Table 1). The closely related FL-cDNA of OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;2, both identified hits on six wheat scaffolds, three on wheat chromosome 7AL, two on 7BL and one on 7DL with up to $7 6 \ \%$ DNA identity (Table 1) and in the same region as the known wheat group II HKT, TaHKT2;1. TaHKT2;1 had $7 5 \mathrm { - } 7 6 \ \%$ DNA identity to both OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;2. Similarly, FL-cDNA of OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4 both had $80 \%$ DNA sequence identity in the same region on three wheat scaffolds (Table 1). Therefore, a wheat group II HKT gene distinctly different to TaHKT2;1 had identity with both OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4. The wheat scaffolds having sequence similarity with OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4, #4510252; $\# 6 5 6 9 8 8 3$ and #3312548, on chromosomes 7AL, 7BL and 7DL, respectively, were selected for further investigation.

The wheat sequences with identity to OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4 on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL were analysed in multiple sequence alignments using the gene on 7AL as a reference to ascertain sequence variants that enabled design of gene specific reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) primer pairs (Table 2) to amplify FL-cDNA. The RT-PCR primers were strategically positioned against putative wheat exons assuming similar gene structure to OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4 (Fig. 1a). Since the scaffold on 7BL did not appear to contain sequence corresponding to the full length sequence of OsHKT2;3 or OsHKT2;4, the $3 ^ { \prime }$ -region of the gene on 7BL was amplified using primers designed from similar regions on 7AL and 7DL (Fig. 1a). Primer pairs showing sub-genome specificity were used to amplify partial but overlapping gene transcripts specifically from 7A, 7B and 7D and confirmed by nullisomic-tetrasomic (NT) analysis (data not shown). Subsequently, overlapping gene-specific cDNA from chromosome 7AL, 7BL and 7DL were amplified from root tissue, sequenced and assembled (Genbank accession numbers KR422354, KR422355 and KR422356 respectively). The FL-cDNA assembled for each gene on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL was aligned against the cognate genomic sequence from scaffolds #4510252; #6569883 and #3312548, respectively, to determine the intron-exon structure (Fig. 1b). The genes on chromosomes 7AL, 7BL and 7DL had similar structure to the OsHKT2;3 and OsHKT2;4 including 3 exons interrupted by 2 introns with intron splice sites having conserved motif GT and AG at the $5 ^ { \prime }$ and $3 ^ { \prime }$ boundaries, respectively. The cDNA of each gene had $6 4 \ \%$ DNA sequence identity with TaHKT2;1 gene family confirming that the two gene families were distinctly different. Therefore, the genes on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL were designated as TaHKT2;2 7AL-1, TaHKT2;2 7BL-1 and TaHKT2;2 7DL-1, respectively. When compared with TaHKT2;2 7AL-1, all variants within exons were SNPs, totalling 69 for TaHKT2;2 7BL-1 and 39 for TaHKT2;2 7DL-1 whereas the comparison between TaHKT2;2 7BL and TaHKT2;2 7DL identified 76 SNPs.


## Analysis of proteins encoded by TaHKT2;2 genes


Sequencing of FL-cDNA for TaHKT2;2 enabled the predicted translation and subsequent characterization of encoded proteins. Each TaHKT2;2 gene on chromosomes 7AL, 7BL and 7DL encoded a predicted protein of 508 amino acids. Combined analysis of hydrophobicity plots (Fig. 2a) and predicted 3D- structures (Fig. 2b) of the proteins encoded by TaHKT2 genes allowed identification of protein folding patterns and modelling of protein topology. Superimposing models identified a number of differences in folding structure between each respective proteins encoded by TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 genes (Fig. 2b). The proteins encoded by each gene modelled a topology consisting of four sequentially arranged membrane-pour-membrane domains resembling core protein structure typical of HKT proteins (domains I–IV in Fig. 2c). The protein encoded by each TaHKT2;2 gene was highly similar with $9 3 \mathrm { - } 9 7 \ \%$ amino acid identity and a high degree of sequence conservation in P-loops (Fig. 3). In each protein the conserved glycine molecules at Gly80, Gly221, Gly349 and Gly453 amino acid positions comprised the putative cation selectivity filter (Fig. 3). However, amino acid substitutions predicted variation in physical properties of the proteins including hydrophobic regions in the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ -terminus encoded by TaHKT2;2 7AL1 and TaHKT2;2 7DL-1 compared to TaHKT2;2 7BL-1 (Figs. 2a and 3).

The proteins encoded by TaHKT2;2 and TaHKT2;1 were compared to ascertain similarities and differences. The proteins encoded by TaHKT2;2 revealed less than $5 2 \ \%$ amino acid identity with the proteins encoded by TaHKT2;1 (Additional file 1: Figure S1), indicating that they are distinctly different. Although both protein families had a conserved structural core, protein topology and important functional domains, the protein encoded by TaHKT2;2 relative to TaHKT2;1 had truncated $\mathrm { N H } _ { 2 }$ -terminus, second cytoplasmic domain and carboxy-terminus, in addition to a four amino acid insertion in the third cytoplasmic domain (Additional file 1: Figure S1). Significant differences were identified in the carboxy-terminus whereby both hydrophobicity based analysis and in homology based 3D structures did not predict a transmembrane inner helix of 4th membrane-poremembrane structure but a membrane embedded carboxy end in the proteins encoded by TaHKT2;2 genes (Additional file 1: Figure S1). This is in contrast to the cytoplasm bound carboxy terminal in the proteins encoded by TaHKT2;1. In addition regions of amino acid variability in external and cytoplasmic caused distinct structural differences and these are depicted in Fig. 2c. Despite the different group II HKT proteins having conserved structural core and G-G-G-G type cation selectivity filter domains, variation in amino acid composition in the filter region (Additional file 1: Figure S1) and differences in cytoplasmic and external domains implied variability in functional characteristics.

TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 genes on chromosome 7AL, 7BL and 7DL were analysed for gene specific transcripts in roots, sheaths and leaf blade tissues of wheat seedlings (Chinese Spring). Significantly higher ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ levels in leaf $( \mathrm { c v } = 3 . 2 6 \%$ , $P < 0 . 0 0 0 1 _ { \cdot }$ ), root $( \mathrm { c v } = 3 . 3 5 \ \%$ , $P < 0 . 0 0 0 3$ ) and sheath $( \mathrm { c v } = 7 . 7 3 \ \%$ , $P < 0 . 0 0 1 5$ ) were observed for samples treated with $2 0 0 \ \mathrm { m M \ N a C l }$ for $^ { 7 2 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ compared with untreated control samples for each tissue (Fig. 4a) and, therefore, suitable for expression using quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR). Sub-genome specific primer pairs (Table 2) were designed based on unique polymorphic sites and specificity was confirmed by NT analysis (Fig. 4b). The qRT-PCR analysis showed that members of the TaHKT2;2 gene family and TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 and TaHKT2;1 7BL-1 were expressed in untreated root, sheath and leaf blade tissues and in the same tissue under $\mathrm { N a C l }$ stressed conditions (Fig. 4c). The exception, however, was TaHKT2;1 7DL-1 where transcripts were detected in both sheath and root samples but not in the detectable limits of the qRTPCR assay for the leaf blade in either the control or NaCl treated samples. Fold change between control and $\mathrm { \Delta N a C l }$ treatments $\left( \Delta \Delta \mathrm { C _ { T } } = - 1 \right)$ to $+ 1$ ) using TaActin as an internal reference showed no difference in expression of individual genes and it is likely that these genes were not salt responsive. However, a two-fold down regulation in TaHKT2;1 7DL-1 expression and up to three-fold down regulation in TaHKT2;2 7AL-1 expression levels indicated that these genes were differentially regulated in control and NaCl treated conditions (Fig. 4c).


## Physical mapping of wheat group II HKT genes and the promoter region of TaHKT2;2 gene family


Analysis of the pseudomolecule for rice chromosome 6L identified that OsHKT2;1 (Ordered Locus Name,

LOC_Os06g48810) and OsHKT2;4 (LOC_Os06g48800) were separated by a physical distance of 2441 base pairs (Fig. 5). Similarly, TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 were identified on the same sequence scaffolds from chromosome 7AL (scaffold #4510252) and 7DL (scaffold #3312548) with intergenic distances of 3154 base pairs and 3330 base pairs, respectively (Fig. 5). TaHKT2;2 7BL-1 and TaHKT2;1 7BL-1 genes were separated by an intergenic distance of 3302 base pairs, however, only partial sequence of TaHKT2;1 7BL-1, including the 3rd exon, 2nd intron and partial sequence of 2nd exon were identified on scaffold #6569883 (Fig. 5). Although a second copy of TaHKT2;1 7BL-2 was retrieved from contig $3 5 9 9 8 4 1 +$ assembled in two different scaffolds (#6657249 and #16748027), neither of the scaffolds identified TaHKT2;2 7BL-1, hence, the wheat genome survey sequence did not contain a single scaffold with the entire length of both TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 genes on 7BL. Nevertheless, it was evident that TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 genes in wheat are physically linked on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL with intergenic distances, comparable to OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;4 genes on rice chromosome 6L.

The similar size of the intergenic regions between the rice genes OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;4 and wheat genes TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 prompted a further comparison of the nucleotide sequences. The intergenic region on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL had $< 4 0 . 8 ~ \%$ DNA identity to the intergenic region between OsHKT2;1 and OsHKT2;4 in rice, indicating significant diversity in this region. A blastn and tblastx analysis in NCBI did not identify sequence similarity with any expressed genes in the intergenic regions for rice or wheat. However, a self-by-self blastn search identified direct, tandem imperfect repeats in the intergenic region (approximately 400 base pairs upstream of the translation start site of TaHKT2;2) of rice OsHKT2;4 and wheat TaHKT2;2 -7BL and TaHKT2;2 -7DL where each repeat motif was less than 70 base pairs in size (Fig. 5, Additional file 2: Figure S2). However, only one copy of two imperfect motifs was represented in the intergenic region on 7AL (Fig. 5, Additional file 2: Figure S2). Furthermore, a complete PIF/Harbinger type miniature inverted transposon element (MITE), DTH_Ors48, was identified in the $5 '$ region of the rice intergenic sequence and remnants of a DTC_Isidor type DNA transposon (TREP accession number TREP3425) in the central region (Fig. 5,

Additional file 2: Figure S2) but no transposon related elements were identified in the intergenic region of wheat 7AL, 7BL or 7DL.

The TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 intergenic region also represented the promoter region for TaHKT2;2 genes on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL and enabled comparative analysis of putative stress regulatory elements for genes on homoeologous chromosomes. The wheat TaHKT2;2 promoter region revealed 67–88 $\%$ sequence identity between promoters of genes on homoeologous chromosomes (Additional file 2: Figure S2). Conserved cis-acting regulatory elements (CRE) were identified including three major salt induced CREs, W-box, GT-box and AtMYC2 in the promoter regions on wheat chromosomes 7AL, 7BL and 7DL with similar elements also represented in the promoter region of rice OsHKT2;4 (Fig. 5, Additional file 2: Figure S2). Furthermore, the TaHKT2;2 promoter identified additional CRE including MYCATRED1 and ABRE on 7AL, 7BL and 7DL but were not evident in the promoter region of rice (Fig. 5, Additional file 2: Figure S2). Therefore, the CRE elements indicated a role for salt- activated transcription factors (TF) in regulation of TaHKT2;2 genes and orthologs in rice but with variable frequency of the individual elements.


## Functional Association of wheat group II HKT genes


An association of TaHKT2;2 genes with trait variation under salt stress was investigated using deletion and genetic mapping. Deletion line analysis showed that TaHKT2;2 genes were assigned to the distal end of chromosomes 7AL and 7DL and the proximal region of 7BL (data not shown) and the same chromosome bins as

TaHKT2;1 [13]. Therefore, functional analysis based on deletion line analysis previously reported [13] indicated that TaHKT2;2 is associated with similar phenotypes as TaHKT2;1 under salt stress. In order to further discriminate whether TaHKT2;1 and TaHKT2;2 were associated with specific trait variation under salt stress in different environments, QTL detected in response to low and high salt stress in Berkut/Krichauff DH mapping population [33, 37] were integrated onto the deletion map based on the chromosomal bin location of flanking markers. A total of six QTL were aligned to the distal bin on chromosome 7AL and in the same region as TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 and TaHKT2;2 7AL-1, however, neither TaHKT2;1 nor TaHKT2;2 genes were co-located with QTL in the same chromosomal bin on 7DL (Fig. 6) and QTL were not identified on 7BL. Therefore, the colocation of genes and QTL in the same chromosomal region indicated that TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 and TaHKT2;2

7AL-1 may contribute to variation for leaf/shoot ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ concentration, 1000 grain weight, grain number per $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ and seedling biomass on 7AL in response to specific saline environments.

The association of TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 and TaHKT2;2 7AL-1 with specific trait variation was further investigated using genetic mapping analysis. TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 and TaHKT2;2 7AL-1 were PCR amplified and sequenced from Berkut and Krichauff to identify polymorphism and to develop gene specific markers for mapping in the DH population. However, TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 identified 11

SNPs between Berkut (Genbank accession number KR422357) and Krichauff (Genbank accession number KR422358) (Fig. 7a). The TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 specific CAPS marker identified a 922 base pairs DNA fragment for Berkut and 1103 base pairs DNA fragment for Krichauff parents following digestion with Xmn1 (Fig. 7b). The Berkut/ Krichauff mapping population $1 5 0 ~ \mathrm { D H }$ lines) was genotyped for the TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 specific CAPS marker and the data was integrated into existing genetic map containing 34 markers on chromosome 7A.

TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 mapped on chromosome 7AL at a genetic distance of $1 3 6 . 4 ~ \mathrm { c M }$ and flanked by markers wpt-4744 $( 1 2 2 . 2 ~ \mathrm { c M } )$ and wpt-3992 $( 1 4 9 . 9 ~ \mathrm { c M } )$ and within the QTL intervals for shoot ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ concentration (Q.NaHY10.sar.7A) and grain number per $\mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ (Q.gnWT07.sar.7A, Q.gnGT08.sar.7A) detected under different saline environments (Fig. 6a). Since TaHKT2;2 7AL-1 did not show any differences in amino acid residues, the predicted proteins encoded by Berkut and Krichauff focused on TaHKT2;1 7AL-1 alleles and were further analysed to identify protein folding differences that may be related to trait variation. The encoded proteins were predicted from gene sequences derived from each parental allele and using FL-cDNA from Chinese Spring as a reference. Salinity tolerance is a complex polygenic trait and is regulated by several physiological mechanisms [3]. Salinity reduces plant growth through osmotic effects, which are experienced shortly after the addition of ${ { \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + } }$ to the external media, and ionic effects, which are experienced later in the stress as ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ accumulates in the leaves to toxic levels. The ability to maintain growth in saline conditions involves a suite of physiological mechanisms including osmotic adjustment, the exclusion of sodium from leaf tissues by sequestration in the root or leaf sheath, the storage of ${ \mathrm { N a } } ^ { + }$ into vacuoles or partitioning in tissues where the toxic effect of ${ { \mathrm { N } } { \mathrm { a } } ^ { + } }$ is reduced [3]. In this study, the complex polygenic nature of salinity tolerance in rice is evidenced by the large number of loci with small effects identified for shoot and root growth responses.
