## Boron transport under deficiency conditions


Boron is highly soluble and therefore it is easily leached from soil in high rainfall areas (Shorrocks 1997; Yan et al. 2006). The boron requirement for adequate plant growth is largely determined by the needs of the cell wall, notably the amount of pectin they contain (Matoh 1997; Hu and Brown 1994). Monocots tend to have only small amounts of pectin and generally grow with little B, whereas dicot cell walls are pectin-rich and require much more.

Most assays of boron deficiency focus on the nutrient solution or soil boron concentration required for early vegetative growth, and the tissue boron concentration at which maximum vegetative growth occurs. However the requirement for reproductive development can be an order of magnitude higher than for vegetative growth. For example in wheat (Triticum aestivum L), normal early vegetative growth occurs when tissue concentrations reach around $1 ~ \mathrm { m g ~ k g } ^ { - 1 }$ , but at this level in the anthers, grain set is negligible, requiring around

$1 0 ~ \mathrm { m g ~ k g ^ { - 1 } }$ (Rerkasem and Jamjod 2004). The higher requirement in reproductive tissue can be related to the very high concentration of the RG-II complex in the walls of pollen tubes (Matoh et al. 1998).

The importance of boron transporters for growth under deficiency conditions is best demonstrated by studies on Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana L). AtBOR1 was the first BOR transporter discovered in plants, and has subsequently been the most intensively studied. AtBOR1 transcripts accumulate most strongly in mature endodermal cells and also in all cells of the root tip, where a functional endodermis is absent. AtBOR2, a paralog of AtBOR1 is expressed in the epidermal cells but not in the endodermis (Miwa et al. 2013), thus complementing the distribution of AtBOR1. Mutants defective in AtBOR1 display impaired root to shoot transport of boron and grow poorly at low boron supply, but grow normally when boron is adequate. Despite this, expression of AtBOR1 does not increase under deficiency conditions. Instead, it is constitutively expressed but its activity is controlled by posttranslational degradation when boron supply becomes adequate (Takano et al. 2005).

In rice (Oryza sativa L), OsBOR1 appears to fulfil a similar role to AtBOR1, except that expression is seen in both endodermis and exodermis (Nakagawa et al. 2007). Under boron deficiency conditions, disruption of OsBOR1 results in severe growth retardation, which underlines its importance in boron uptake and distribution.

In addition to these efflux transporters, there is evidence in Arabidopsis for the involvement of a channel which is induced by deficiency. AtNIP1;5 is expressed most strongly in the surface layers of the root tip, and meristematic and elongation zones (Takano et al. 2010). Like AtBOR1 it is preferentially localised to one side of the cell, in this case in the plasma membrane facing the external solution (Fig. 3). It is hypothesised that AtNIP1;5 acts together with AtBOR1 to facilitate the radial transfer of boron from the root surface into the xylem, by providing a low resistance symplastic pathway. The activity of AtNIP1;5 is regulated through degradation of the mRNA in the presence of high boron (Tanaka et al. 2011).


## Boron transporters and reproductive development


The requirement for boron in reproductive tissues exceeds that in vegetative tissues, and as a consequence the reproductive cycle is more strongly affected by boron deficiency than is vegetative growth. Despite this, the activity of boron transporters in floral tissue has received comparatively little attention compared to root uptake and root to shoot transport. OsBOR4 is specifically expressed in floral tissue and its disruption leads to impaired reproductive competence, as a result of slower or reduced growth of pollen tubes (Tanaka et al. 2013). In grapes (Vitis vinifera L), poor fruit set is related to boron deficiency. The expression of VvBOR1 in floral tissue rises sharply at anthesis and expression can be directly linked to the accumulation of boron in berries during development (Pérez-Castro et al. 2012). The loading of boron into seeds also has important consequences for germination and early development. Uraguchi and Fujiwara (2011) showed that removal of the endosperm from rice seed greatly reduced growth of seedlings under low boron conditions but not under normal boron supply. They concluded that the endosperm is an important storage site for B.


## Transporters involved in tolerance to boron toxicity


In low rainfall areas, boron tends to accumulate in the upper soil layers and this exerts significant negative impacts on crop productivity in many areas of the world including southern Australia, parts of North Africa, Turkey, Syria, Iraq and the US (Yau and Ryan 2008). In other areas, high concentrations in irrigation water raise soil boron to levels sufficient to inhibit plant growth. While the range of tissue boron concentrations needed to overcome deficiency is quite broad, especially when considering differences between monocots and dicots, for toxicity the range is much narrower. Reid et al. (2004) compared toxicity in a monocot (barley), dicot (Arabidopsis) and an alga (Chara) and found that for all of these plant types, growth was inhibited by $4 0 -$ $60 \%$ when the soluble boron concentration reached

$1 0 \ \mathrm { m M }$ (approximately $1 5 0 { - } 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / g }$ DW). This is similar to the concentration range reported by Oertli and Kohl (1961) of $1 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / g }$ DW for the development of necrotic patches in leaves from a wide range of plants. This suggests that the target process for toxicity is similar in all plants, and independent of their minimum boron requirement for growth. There is some evidence that toxicity occurs through damage to DNA, by inducing double stranded breaks (Sakamoto et al. 2011).

The principal mechanism for avoiding boron toxicity revolves around activities that minimise tissue boron concentrations. Early studies demonstrated a strong correlation between boron tolerance and low tissue boron concentrations in wheat and barley, and attributed this to an ability of the tolerant cultivars to exclude boron (Nable 1988). Subsequent work established that lower tissue concentrations were not due to exclusion of boron per se, but to the active pumping of influxed boron back into the soil (Hayes and Reid 2004). Even though a number of membrane transporters have been linked to boron toxicity tolerance, it is arguable whether they are specifically synthesised for this purpose or whether by fortuitous mutation, their under or overexpression now contributes to a tolerant phenotype. In this respect, it is significant that none of these transporters is induced by toxicity, although TaBOR1.2 transcript levels increase in roots in high boron conditions (Leaungthitikanchana et al. 2013).

It is only recently that the identity of the efflux transporter responsible for boron tolerance in barley was revealed (Reid 2007; Sutton et al. 2007). The basis for tolerance was found to be a reduction in tissue boron resulting from the high expression of the efflux transporter HvBOR2 (also known as HvBot1) in both roots and leaves. It was hypothesised that this came about by accidental tandem duplication producing 4 copies of the gene and resulting in a 180-fold higher transcript level than sensitive barley varieties (Sutton et al. 2007). Natural variation in expression of HvBOR2 and TaBOR2 in cultivars of barley and wheat is correlated with differences in tolerance (Reid 2007).

It is not difficult to see how efflux transporters could reduce root boron concentrations by pumping boron back into the soil. Nor is it difficult to envisage how lower root concentrations could translate into reduced transport of boron to shoots, but how the increased expression of an efflux transporter in shoots could improve boron tolerance is less intuitive. Reid and

Fitzpatrick (2009) noted that toxicity symptoms in leaves of tolerant cultivars of wheat and barley occurred at local tissue concentrations that were significantly higher than in sensitive cultivars. They hypothesised that rather than this being due to an internal tolerance mechanism, it was due to greater efflux of boron from the intracellular phase into the cell wall, thereby protecting sensitive cytosolic metabolic processes. It was demonstrated that elution of boron from leaves of tolerant cultivars was much more rapid, as was predicted to occur if more of the leaf boron was located apoplastically.

The general concept of boron tolerance mediated by efflux transporters is reinforced by overexpression experiments on Arabidopsis. Miwa et al. (2007) showed that tolerance to high boron was increased with increasing expression of AtBOR4 in roots.

The contribution of boron-permeable channels to boron tolerance is enigmatic. If it is accepted that boron tolerance is due to the ability of efflux transporters to reduce intracellular boron concentrations below that of the surrounding solution or apoplast, then any boron flow through channels would have the effect of collapsing the concentration gradient established by the effluxers. Experimental evidence seems to support this conclusion. The role of AtNIP5;1 under deficiency conditions was mentioned above. Under normal circumstances high boron conditions result in the degradation of the mRNA which is mediated by a 5’UTR sequence. Tanaka et al. (2011) produced a variant of AtNIP5;1 lacking the a portion of the 5’UTR that is necessary for its degradation under high boron conditions. This alteration predisposed the plant to boron toxicity by increasing tissue boron levels at high boron levels. Conversely, Schnurbusch et al. (2010) proposed that tolerance to high boron in barley was in part mediated by reduced expression of HvNIP2;1, an aquaporin previously identified as having a role in Si uptake (Chiba et al. 2009).

Virtually all of the boron transport proteins so far identified appear to occur on the plasma membrane. However, Pang et al. (2010) have characterised a tonoplast intrinsic protein (TIP), AtTIP5;1 that was expressed in hypocotyl and leaf tissues, with increased expression under high boron conditions. In leaf mesophyll protoplasts, AtTIP5;1 was localised to the vacuolar membrane. Overexpression resulted in increased tolerance to high boron concentrations, with a slight increase in leaf boron accumulation. It was concluded that AtTIP5;1 was a boron-permeable channel that facilitated the movement of boron from the cytoplasm into the vacuole. It was noted above that membrane vesicles prepared from microsomal membranes were an order of magnitude less permeable to boron than those enriched with plasma membranes, possibly as a result of differences in lipid composition (Dordas et al. 2000). Potentially, low tonoplast permeability to boron retards the equilibration of boron within the cell, resulting in a higher concentration in the cytoplasm, and that tonoplast channels help reduce this concentration.


## Directional transport of boron in cells and tissues


Mention has already been made of the importance of xylem and phloem in the distribution of boron. In both these processes boron can be regarded as a passenger being swept along as one of many solutes in the transpiration stream, or because of its affinity for particular sugars in the phloem. However, this type of bulk flow has its limitations in meeting the demands of different tissues in the plant, since it is not specifically driven by tissue boron status. In the studies of boron transporters, it has frequently been observed that expression of the transporters occurs in patterns that would favour the directional, or polar, movement of boron. For example, the expression of AtBOR1 and AtBOR2 tends to be more prominent in regions of the cell membrane facing the vascular cylinder, with minimal expression on the outwardly facing membrane (Miwa et al. 2013) (Fig. 3). This is consistent with the directional pumping of boron towards the xylem to supply boron to the shoot. Polar localisation of AtBOR1 appears to depend on the presence of one or more tyrosine residues in a cytoplasmic loop of the protein. When these residues are substituted by alanine, expression becomes evenly distributed around cells of the epidermis and root tip (Takano et al. 2010).

Like AtBOR 1 and AtBOR2, AtNIP5;1 is preferentially localised to one side of the cell, in this case in the plasma membrane facing the external solution (Fig. 3). It is hypothesised that AtNIP5;1 acts together with AtBOR1 and AtBOR2 to facilitate the radial transfer of boron from the root surface into the xylem, by providing an inwardly directed low resistance symplastic pathway. In contrast AtBOR4, whose overexpression enhances tolerances to boron toxicity, is more concentrated on the outer (soil-facing) membranes of the epidermal cells, which is consistent with pumping of boron back into the soil. This is perhaps the best evidence yet for a specific B-tolerance gene. The polarity of HvBOR2 and TaBOR2, whose expression is linked to boron tolerance, is unknown but this would help to clarify whether these transporters are really expressed for the purpose of directional boron movement or whether they simply act at a cellular level.

Interestingly, the expression of HvNIP2;1 in cells of the stele, cortex and epidermis is more concentrated on the outer side (Chiba et al. 2009), which would tend to facilitate boron uptake rather than its efflux. Hence it is perhaps not surprising that boron tolerance is correlated with reduced expression of this gene (Schnurbusch et al. 2010).


## Prospects for improving crop productivity by manipulation of boron transporters


It will be obvious from the preceding sections that boron transporters play a crucial role in maintaining plant growth under conditions where the boron supply is sub-optimal or toxic. Quite probably, much of the genotypic variation in tolerance to both boron deficiency and boron toxicity is related to differences in transporter activity or characteristics. Potentially, manipulation of transporters, either by selective breeding or more direct molecular means, could deliver yield improvements in crops growing on soil with inadequate or excessive boron levels.

There are clearly two levels at which boron deficiency can affect crop yields. Since vegetative growth is less sensitive to low boron than reproductive performance, forage crops may grow adequately on low boron soils, especially monocots which are able to use boron more efficiently because of the lower requirement for normal cell wall integrity. However, since floral development requires a much higher boron level, grain and fruit production will be more severely affected than vegetative yield on low boron soils. The question is whether plants can be induced to make better use of a limited amount of boron. The evidence accumulated so far suggests that many plants have well-developed strategies for efficient uptake and distribution of boron. Deficiency results in the upregulation of genes for boron-permeable channels and strategically located efflux transporters to facilitate supply of boron to shoots and inflorescences. Inducible and constitutively expressed BOR-type transporters seem to be ubiquitous in plant tissues where their most likely role is to transfer boron from the cytoplasm into the cell wall where it is most needed. There is also some (limited) evidence that the tonoplast is less permeable to boron (Dordas et al. 2000), which would help to maintain boron in cytoplasmic and apoplastic compartments rather than being wastefully stored in the vacuole.

Although there may be some scope for tinkering with genes for these transporters, boron deficiency is easily corrected by boron fertilisation (Shorrocks 1997), so there is no real imperative. In contrast, boron toxic soils are difficult to remediate so plant-based strategies for coping with high boron have received greater attention. There is known to be a wide variation in tolerance to boron toxicity in many crop species and it is widely believed that this variation can largely be attributed to differences in the way in which boron is transported into, within and out of plant tissues. Considerable effort has been expended in trying to exploit the tolerance to high soil boron that is achieved by cereal cultivars with naturally high levels of expression of boron efflux transporters. Introgression of chromosome regions associated with high expression of boron efflux transporters from the highly tolerant barley cultivar Sahara into more agronomically important cultivars resulted in improved tolerance under glasshouse conditions but performance in field trials in southern Australia was much more variable (Emebiri et al. 2009; McDonald et al. 2009). The common problem is that high boron occurs in soils that are also high in salinity. Field trials with wheat and barley cultivars with varying salinity or boron tolerances grown in soil cores containing both boron and salinity at levels representative of calcareous soils showed that there was no significant yield advantage for improved boron tolerance where the soils also contained high salinity (Nuttall et al. 2010). This factor would seem to greatly diminish the potential for high or overexpression of boron efflux transporters for improvement of boron toxicity tolerance.

The involvement of boron-permeable channels in increasing tolerance to high boron is confusing. On the one hand, Schnurbusch et al. (2010) related the higher tolerance of a barley cultivar to the reduced expression of HvNIP2:1. In contrast, Kumar et al. (2014) found that OsPIP2;4 and OsPIP2;7 were strongly upregulated in roots in response to high boron, and that overexpression increased tolerance. It was proposed that the higher permeability induced by these channels facilitated efflux of boron from the roots but it is not clear how this could occur in the absence of outwardly directed boron efflux pumps.

The recent report of increased boron tolerance in Arabidopsis overexpressing the tonoplast channel AtTIP5;1 (Pang et al. 2010) perhaps deserves some further research. Little is known about the role of the vacuole and tonoplast boron transporters in the compartmentation of boron. If the tonoplast is indeed much less permeable to boron, this would tend to inhibit the equilibration of boron throughout the cell. Under deficiency conditions, low tonoplast permeability may be advantageous in keeping boron in the cytoplasm from which it can more easily be pumped into the cell wall where it is needed. However, under toxicity conditions, increasing boron movement into the vacuole through greater expression of boron-permeable channels would reduce the toxicity to the cytoplasm. Given that vacuoles generally occupy around $90 \%$ of plant cells, the impact of this redistribution could be significant.


## Concluding remarks


For such a simple and relatively unreactive molecule, boric acid demands an unusually high profile. Without it, plants cannot stand up because of their weak cell walls. Nor can they reproduce because of its critical importance in pollen tube growth. Yet a little too much can prove fatal. There is no real evidence that metabolic processes can be protected from its toxic effects. The only resort is to try to excrete it via efflux pumps or to reduce its uptake by shutting down leaky channels. The real weakness lies in the underlying high permeability to boric acid of the lipid bilayers that normally form the defensive barrier against other potentially hazardous solutes. Plants do their best, and for this they need a multitude of strategically placed boron transport proteins and an effective signalling system that alerts them to the presence or absence of a molecule that can be both friend and foe.

Boron (B) is a metalloid that is essential for plant growth and B deficiency is a worldwide problem affecting crop production (Shorrocks, 1997). B is present mainly as boric acid in solution at physiological $\mathrm { p H }$ in the absence of interacting molecules. Boric acid is a weak Lewis acid with a $\mathsf { p } K a$ of 9.24 $\left[ \mathrm { B ( O H ) } _ { 3 } \right. + \left. \right.$ $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } = \mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 4 } ^ { - } + \mathrm { H } ^ { + } ]$ (Marschner, 2012). B, as borate,crosslinks a pectic polysaccharide, rhamnogalacturonan II, and thus functions in the construction of cell wall structure (O’Neill et al., 2004; Kobayashi et al., 2011). On the other hand, excess-B is toxic to plants. In arid and semi-arid regions, B often accumulates in soil and is toxic to crop plants (Nable et al., 1997). The toxicity probably occurs via binding of borate to cis-diol-containing compounds such as ATP, NAD $^ +$ , and RNA, thereby inhibiting multiple cellular activities (Reid et al., 2004). In root tip cells of Arabidopsis, excess-B was shown to induce DNA double-strand breaks (Sakamoto et al., 2011).

Identification and characterization of boric acid channels and borate transporters revealed adaptive mechanisms of plants under low- and high-B conditions (Takano et al., 2008; Miwa and Fujiwara, 2010; Schnurbusch et al., 2010). In addition to the passive diffusion of boric acid across membranes (Dordas et al., 2000), facilitated transport of B by boric acid channels and borate exporters is required for normal growth under low-B conditions. Arabidopsis NIP5;1 is a boric acid channel localized in the plasma membrane with polarity toward the soil side in the outermost cell layers of roots (Takano et al., 2006, 2010). Arabidopsis BOR1 is a borate exporter localized in the plasma membrane with polarity toward the stele side in various types of root cells (Takano et al., 2002, 2010). The polarized localizations of NIP5;1 and BOR1 appear to be critical factors for the directional transport of B from soil solution to the xylem under low-B conditions. Importantly, the activities of NIP5;1 and BOR1 are down-regulated through post-transcriptional regulation under high-B conditions. NIP5;1 is down-regulated through mRNA degradation that is dependent on the $5 ^ { \prime }$ untranslated region (Tanaka et al., 2011). BOR1 is quickly down-regulated through endocytosis and degradation in vacuoles, dependent on the ubiquitination of the K590 residue under high-B conditions (Takano et al., 2005; Kasai et al., 2011; Yoshinari et al., 2012). These responses are important for preventing the accumulation of B to a toxic level in plant tissues. Polar localization and endocytic degradation have also been reported for other mineral transporters, including the iron transporter AtIRT1, and appear to be common factors controlling mineral transport (Zelazny and Vert, 2014).

In addition to the down-regulation of channels and transporters specifically required for the efficient uptake and translocation of B, B exclusion by borate exporters is an important mechanism for excess-B tolerance. At the single cell level, expression of a BOR1 homolog in yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae lowers cytosolic B concentrations by export at the plasma membrane, thereby conferring excess-B tolerance (Takano et al., 2007). In Arabidopsis, the mRNA levels of BOR4 were increased two-fold upon excess-B supply, which was dependent on the $5 ^ { \prime }$ untranslated region of BOR4 (Miwa et al.,

2014). BOR4 is localized on the plasma membrane with weak polarity toward the soil side in root cells (Miwa et al., 2007). In T-DNA insertion mutants of bor4, the B concentration in shoots was increased and shoot growth was decreased under excess-B conditions, suggesting that BOR4 is involved in B exclusion from roots or restriction of B translocation toward shoots (Miwa et al., 2014). Importantly, BOR4 orthologs in barley and wheat have been shown to function in B exclusion from roots and to be major genetic factors controlling excess-B tolerance among cultivars and landraces (Sutton et al., 2007; Pallotta et al., 2014). A recent phylogenetic analysis suggested that the common ancestor of vascular plants had already acquired BOR1- and BOR4-type transporters for low- and high-B tolerance, respectively (Wakuta et al., 2015).

To date, overexpression of borate transporters has been successfully applied to improve the efficiency of B utilization and excess-B tolerance. Overexpression of BOR1 under control of the cauliflower mosaic virus 35S RNA promoter (35S promoter) improved B translocation to shoots, increased shoot growth, and boosted fertility under low-B conditions in Arabidopsis (Miwa et al., 2006). This approach also improved the growth of tomato plants under low-B conditions (Uraguchi et al., 2014). Enhanced expression of NIP5;1 and the closest BOR1 homolog, BOR2, also improved growth under low-B conditions (Kato et al., 2009; Takada et al., 2014). Furthermore, overexpression of BOR4 decreased the B concentration in roots and shoots and conferred excess-B tolerance in Arabidopsis (Miwa et al., 2007; Miwa and Fujiwara, 2011). Therefore, molecular breeding using B transport proteins is a promising approach to improve crop productivity under variable B conditions.

In this study, we show that ubiquitous expression of a BOR1 variant with restricted polar localization and stable accumulation under high-B conditions confers plant tolerance to excess-B conditions.

Boron (B) is a micronutrient that is critical for crop growth and quality (Wimmer et al. 2020). It is required for the crosslinking of rhamnogalacturonan II, a pectic polysaccharide, during cell wall development (Funakawa and Miwa 2015). B defciency causes signifcant yield loss in many crop plants worldwide (BrdarJokanović  2020; Rerkasem et  al. 2020). It generally afects fower development and seed set. Low soil B is most prevalent in regions with high rainfall, including parts of China, India, Nepal, Bangladesh, and Brazil (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Shorrocks 1997). Excess soil B having detrimental efects on plants is also found in arid and semi-arid areas, including parts of India, the USA,

Pakistan, Malaysia, Chile, Peru, Hungary, Serbia, Italy, and the Middle East (Brdar-Jokanović 2020; Nable et al. 1997). Excess B concentrations cause double-strand breaks of DNA (Sakamoto et al. 2011) and afect cellular metabolism, likely through binding to ribose moieties of ATP, NADH, and NADPH in cells (Reid 2014). Binding to ribose, both as a free sugar and as an RNA constituent, can inhibit cell division and development (Reid 2014). Symptoms of B toxicity include chlorosis and necrosis, which spread from leaf tips, leaving brown lesions at the margins. Reductions in biomass and seed yield are commonly observed under prolonged B toxicity (BrdarJokanović 2020; Landi et al 2019).

Plant roots take up B mainly in the form of boric acid $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { B O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { ) }$ , which is a weak Lewis acid, with a pKa of 9.24 $[ \mathrm { B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 3 } + \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O = B } ( \mathrm { O H } ) _ { 4 } ^ { - } + \mathrm { H } ^ { + } ]$ (Power and Woods 1997). B is the only essential nutrient taken up in its uncharged form at physiological $\mathrm { p H }$ . Due to the theoretically high membrane permeability coeffcient of boric acid, it was once widely believed that B transport in plants was a mainly passive process. However, using the plasma membranes of giant internodal cells of the charophyte alga Chara corallina and plasma membrane vesicles isolated from squash roots, the membrane permeability of boric acid was determined to be higher than its theoretical value (Dordas et al. 2000; Stangoulis et al. 2001). Later, plants were found to facilitate the difusion of boric acid through major intrinsic protein (MIP) channels. Plants also use borate transporters (BORs) to export borate out of cells against a concentration gradient of soluble B (Yoshinari and Takano 2017). In this review, we describe the mechanisms of B transport, with an emphasis on membrane transport proteins and their regulation.


## B transport through MIPs


MIPs, including water channels (aquaporins), are universal to all kingdoms of life. Plant MIPs are channels for the bidirectional difusion of water and other small uncharged molecules (Bienert and Chaumont 2014). Based on sequence similarity and subcellular localization, MIPs in seed plants have been classifed into fve subclasses: plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs), tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs), small basic intrinsic proteins (SIPs), NIPs, and X intrinsic proteins (XIPs) (Maurel et al. 2016).

Plasma membrane intrinsic proteins (PIPs)

PIPs are plasma membrane-localized aquaporins that are mainly involved in water transport. They are further categorized into two subgroups, PIP1 and PIP2 (Bienert and Bienert 2017). PIP1 proteins possess an inherent capacity for water transport but require the help of PIP2s in plasma membrane trafcking in Arabidopsis and maize (Hachez et  al. 2013; Bienert et  al. 2018). Some PIP proteins have been shown to permeate boric acid in addition to water. In an early study, maize PIP1 expression in Xenopus laevis oocytes enhanced boric acid uptake into the cells (Dordas et  al. 2000). In a later study, the expression of barley (Hordeum vulgare) PIP1;3 and PIP1;4 in yeast led to increased B accumulation and enhanced sensitivity to high B (Fitzpatrick and Reid 2009). In rice roots, PIP expression was induced under high-B treatment (Kumar et  al. 2018). The expression of rice PIP1;3, PIP2;4, and PIP2;7 enhanced B infux and accumulation, and OsPIP2;6 enhanced B efux in yeast cells (Kumar et  al. 2014; Mosa et  al. 2016). Transgenic Arabidopsis plants overexpressing OsPIP1;3, OsPIP2;4, OsPIP2;6, and OsPIP2;7 enhanced plant tolerance to excess B concentrations (Kumar et al. 2014; Mosa et al. 2016). Tracer experiments using $^ { 1 0 } \mathrm { { B } }$ -enriched boric acid at 2.5 or $5 \ \mathrm { m M }$ showed that B uptake and efux from roots were both increased in transgenic plants. These results suggest the possible functions of PIPs in plant B tolerance of high B levels, although further studies using knockout plants are desired.

Tonoplast intrinsic proteins (TIPs)

TIPs function in water transport across the vacuolar membrane, turgor regulation, osmo-sensing, cell growth, and vacuolar diferentiation (Maurel et  al. 2016). TIP isoforms have highly variable sequences within the aromatic/arginine (ar/R) selectivity flter, to transport small molecules including urea, $\mathrm { N H } _ { 3 }$ glycerol, ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ , and boric acid (Sudhakaran et  al. 2021). The heterologous expression of grape TIPs (VvTnTIP1;1, VvTnTIP2;2, and VvTnTIP4;1) and maize TIPs (ZmTIP1;1 and ZmTIP1;2) in yeast led to higher sensitivity to toxic B conditions (Barzana et al. 2014; Sabir et al. 2014). Overexpression of AtTIP5;1 in Arabidopsis promoted hypocotyl elongation and increased silique production under excess B (Pang et  al. 2010). Transcription profling of B-efcient citrus rootstock showed the upregulation of TIP2;2 and TIP4;1 under B limitation, with diferent temporal patterns (Zhou et  al. 2015). However, the physiological signifcance of B transport across the vacuolar membrane and its relationship to TIPs remain obscure.

Nodulin 26-like intrinsic proteins (NIPs)

NIPs were frst reported to be localized in the symbiosome membrane of soybean (Glycine max L.) nodules, and to possess water and glycerol transport properties (Fortin et  al. 1987; Roberts and Routray. 2017). Phylogenetic analyses revealed that NIPs cluster together with aquaporin $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { Z } }$ or glycerol uptake facilitator proteins in bacteria (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). This close relationship supports horizontal gene transfer from the bacterial AqpN–aquaporin group to plant NIPs. AqpN is predominantly positioned in arsenic resistance operons of various prokaryotic phyla to contribute to the arsenic detoxifcation machinery (Pommerrenig et al. 2020). Ar/R selectivity flter residues of bacterial AqpN are conserved in NIPs in algae, liverworts, moss, hornworts, and ferns. Bacterial AqpN, KnNIP6;1 in the flamentous terrestrial alga Klebsormidium nitens, and PpNIP5;1, NIP5;2, and NIP5;3 in the moss Physcomitrella patens are impermeable to water and silicic acid but permeable to arsenite and boric acid in Xenopus oocytes. These fndings along with mutational analysis results suggest that bacterial arsenic efux channels are converted into silicic acid and boric acid channels for the efcient uptake and translocation of these nutrients in seed plants (Pommerrenig et  al. 2020). Plant NIPs are categorized as NIP-I (AtNIP1–4 s and others), NIP-II (AtNIP5–7 s and others), and NIPIII (OsNIP2;1 and others) based on similarities in their pore constriction regions, which consist of ar/R selectivity flters (Mitani-Ueno et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑Is in B transport


NIP-I proteins are aquaglyceroporins that mediate the transport of water and small neutral molecules such as glycerol (Roberts and Routray 2017). Although their physiological functions are unclear, Brassica napus NIP-Is (NIP2–4) transport B in Xenopus oocytes (Diehn et  al. 2019; see a later section on  Brassica napus for details).

Among NIP-Is in Arabidopsis, AtNIP4;1 is permeable to boric acid, ammonia, urea, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , as shown in Saccharomyces cerevisiae growth assays (Giorgio et  al. 2016). AtNIP4;1 and AtNIP4;2 are localized to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles of pollen tubes (Bock et  al. 2006; Giorgio et  al. 2016). In nip4;1 and nip4;2 mutants and amiRNA-mediated double knockdown plants, fertility was reduced, and pollen tube growth was afected under low B supply but normal under high B supply. These results suggest the roles of NIP4;1 and NIP4;2 in pollen tube growth via B transport.


## Roles of NIP‑IIs as major boric acid channels


The NIP-II protein AtNIP5;1 was the frst boric acid channel identifed to be involved in B uptake into roots, as the abundance of AtNIP5;1 mRNA increased after B starvation (Takano et al. 2006). In the plasma membrane of epidermal, cortical, and endodermal cells of roots, NIP5;1 showed polar localization towards the soil, increasing the efciency of boric acid uptake (Takano et  al. 2010; Wang et  al. 2017). B uptake and accumulation in roots and shoots of nip5;1  T-DNA insertion lines were signifcantly reduced when plants were grown under B limitation compared to wild-type (WT) plants. Due to defective B uptake, nip5;1 mutants showed severe root and shoot growth impairment under B limitation (Takano et al. 2006).

AtNIP6;1, the closest paralogue of AtNIP5;1, is involved in B xylem–phloem transfer for preferential translocation in shoots (Tanaka et  al. 2008). Unlike AtNIP5;1, the expression of AtNIP6;1 was confned to the phloem regions in nodes, including sieve elements (Tanaka et  al. 2008). The nip6;1 mutants showed inhibition of rosette leaf expansion and apical dominance under B limitation. Xenopus oocyte transport analyses indicated that NIP5;1 and NIP6;1 facilitate boric acid uptake into cells but difer in water transport activity (Takano et  al. 2006; Tanaka et al. 2008) with NIP5;1 but not NIP6;1, showing signifcant water permeability. The water-tight nature of NIP6;1 is likely important for phloem function.

AtNIP7;1 is a third member of the NIPII subclass; it plays a role in pollen development under B limitation and shows anther-specifc expression and localization in the plasma membrane of tapetum cells (Routray et  al. 2018). Loss-of-function nip7;1 mutants showed reproductive growth retardation characteristics including decreased fertility, petite siliques, and increased seed abortion compared to WT plants under B limitation (Routray et al. 2018). NIP-II subclass proteins such as AtNIP5;1 and AtNIP6;1 possess conserved ar/R pore-forming residues, including the transmembrane helix 2 (H2) region. Alanine at the H2 region is considered a characteristic residue for NIP-II boric acid channels including AtNIP7;1 (Wallace and Roberts 2004, 2005). However, AtNIP7;1 showed lower permeability to boric acid in Xenopus oocytes (Li et al. 2011). The substitution of tyrosine 81 in H2 with a cysteine residue (characteristic of AtNIP6;1) resulted in significantly higher boric acid transport than in WT NIP7;1 and NIP5;1 (Li et  al. 2011). Boric acid transport by AtNIP7;1 was proposed to be controlled by a channel gate function of the conserved tyrosine residue in the pore (Li et al. 2011).


## Roles of NIP‑IIIs in the transport of silicic acid and boric acid


The NIP-III proteins in rice (OsLsi1/OsNIP2;1) and barley (HvLsi1/HvNIP2;1) are silicic acid channels, facilitating its uptake (Ma et  al. 2007; Chiba et  al. 2009). In Xenopus oocytes, OsNIP2;1 and HvNIP2;1 showed signifcant boric acid transport activity along with silicic acid, germanic acid, arsenite, and water (Schnurbusch et  al. 2010; Mitani-Ueno et  al. 2011). The physiological functions of silicic acid channels in B transport in rice and barley are discussed in a later section.


## X intrinsic proteins (XIPs)


XIPs were frst identifed during whole-genome analyses of the moss Physcomitrella patens (Danielson and Johanson 2008). XIP proteins are present in a range of organisms, from unicellular eukaryotes to plants but absent in monocots and members of the Brassicaceae family (Abascal et  al. 2014), likely due to their functional complementation by other MIP subfamilies in these taxa. Based on amino acid residues of the ar/R flter, XIPs are predicted to form a wider and hydrophobic pore, similar to those in the NIP III group (Bienert et  al. 2011). Consistent with this prediction, the heterologous expression of Solanaceae XIP1;1s in oocytes $( \mathrm { S t X I P 1 } ; 1 \alpha$ and StXIP1;1β, SlXIP1;1α, and SlXIP1;1β) resulted in glycerol and urea transport. SlXIP1;1s expressed in yeast (S. cerevisiae) cells showed growth inhibition/sensitivity on media containing ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 }$ or excess boric acid, indicating $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } /$ boric acid infux activity (Bienert et  al. 2011). Grape $V \nu X I P I$ and tobacco $N b \mathrm { X I P 1 ; 1 \alpha }$ also showed increased sensitivity to excess boric acid media in the yeasts S. cerevisiae and Pichia pastoris (Ampah-Korsah et al. 2016; Noronha et  al. 2016). The expression of NtXIP1;1 under the control of the AtNIP5;1 promoter complemented a growth defect in an Arabidopsis nip5;1 knockout mutant under B limitation, demonstrating its function as a boric acid channel in planta (Bienert et  al. 2019). However, NtXIP1;1 overexpression in Nico‑ tiana tabacum and Arabidopsis under the En2pPMA4 or 35S CaMV promoter, respectively, resulted in B defciency symptoms such as diminished shoot apical meristem, sterile fowers, and contracted leaves. This result was probably caused by heterogeneous B distribution, prompted by the ectopic expression of NtXIP1;1. Further investigation of the physiological functions of XIP-mediated B transport is required.


## B transport through BORs


Under B limitation, plants use BOR-type borate exporters for efcient translocation of B (Takano et al. 2012; Yoshinari and Takano 2017). Borate exporters are also involved in lowering B concentrations in tissues for excess B tolerance (Miwa et al. 2007). Similarly, in S. cerevisiae, Bor1p functions as a borate exporter for excess B tolerance (Nozawa et al. 2006; Takano et  al. 2007). BOR transporters appear to be able to pump B out against a concentration gradient. For example, WT yeast cells maintained $< 2 5 \%$ of the intracellular B compared to bor1 deletion mutant cells in medium containing $0 . 0 5 { - } 1 \ \mathrm { m M }$ boric acid (Takano et al. 2007). Under these conditions, B concentrations in WT cells were estimated to be lower than in the treatment medium. Electrophysiological studies of Bot1, a BOR transporter in barley, in Xenopus oocytes and proteoliposomes showed electrogenic borate anion transport in a Nernstian manner (Nagarajan et al. 2016). The Km for borate was calculated to be $1 0 4 ~ { \mu \mathrm { M } }$ using patch-clamped proteoliposomes. Bot1 also transported chloride, phosphate, nitrate, and sulfate but with much lower afnity than borate. Therefore, it is most likely that BOR transporters are anion uniporters with high afnity with borate (Fig.  1). Boric acid taken up into cells via MIPs or passive diffusion is partly converted into borate anions in cytosol with higher pH, which are then exported by BORs dependent on the concentration gradient and negative membrane potential. In the acidic apoplasm, borate anions are converted back into boric acid, generating an uphill boric acid gradient across the plasma membrane.

The Arabidopsis genome encodes seven BORs (BOR1–7). In angiosperms, BORs are classifed into two separate clades (Wakuta et  al. 2015). It is likely that Clade I BORs (AtBOR1–3) and their homologs pH $( \sim 7 . 5 )$ . Then borate anions are exported by borate transporters (BORs) and converted into boric acid at lower $\mathrm { p H }$ $( \sim 5 \ – 6 )$ . Borate anions that are transported to secretion vesicles by AtBOR2 are hypothesized to form diester bonds with two RGII monomers to create B-RGII dimers in these small compartments. b.
