In pattern I, the secretion of organic acid anions immediately occurs when the plant is exposed to Al, as observed in wheat (Delhaize et al. 1993) and buckwheat (Zheng et al. 2005). Pattern II exhibits a significant lag phase until the onset of organic acid anion release, as in Cassia tora (Ma et al. 1997b), Sorghum bicolor (Magalhaes et al. 2007), and Zea mays (Maron et al. 2008). These results indicate that the genetically engineered protein that modulates the organic acid anion release in the plasma membrane is an effective way to enhance Al tolerance in plants. Although the function of ALMT1 from other plant species has been well studied, the regulatory role of CsALMT1 (Genbank accession number: KF021618) from Camelina in malate exudation remains unknown.

Camelina sativa L. is an emerging bioenergy crop that can be grown under harsh soil conditions (Knorzer 1978; Putnam et al. 1993; Vollmann et al. 1996; Zubr 1997; Park et al. 2014). Furthermore, Camelina ALMT1 (CsALMT1), which is a homolog of the Arabidopsis ALMT1, was isolated. This gene may mediate Al tolerance via malate exudation in Camelina roots under Al treatment. Therefore, overexpression of CsALMT1 in Camelina plants may improve the Al tolerance. In this study, we conducted tests to investigate the effect of CsALMT1 on the detoxification of aluminum toxicity by comparing with Camelina wildtype and CsALMT1 overexpressing transgenic plants.

Aluminum (Al) is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust (Tesfaye et al. 2001). In acidic soils $\mathrm { ( p H } < 5 . 5 $ , Al is present as phytotoxic ${ \mathrm { A l } } ^ { 3 + }$ ions, which are toxic to plants. Plants that show better growth in acidic soils have evolved resistance mechanisms in response to Al stress (Chen et al. 2012; Wu et al. 2012). The Al-activated release of organic acids (OAs, such as malate, citrate, and oxalate) from roots has been characterized as one of the most important Alresistant mechanisms in plants (Hoekenga et al. 2006; Sasaki et al. 2004a, b). The exudation of malate and citrate is mediated by membrane-localized transporters, and these proteins belong to two families, Al-activated malate transporter (ALMT) and multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) (Delhaize et al. 2007). However, the gene controlling oxalate efflux is still unknown. The Al-induced exudation of organic acids has been classified into two patterns. In pattern I, Al directly activates the plasma membrane OA transporters, and there is no discernible delay between the addition of Al and the onset of the release of organic acids. Wheat is a typical pattern I plant, in which the malate transporter encoding gene, TaALMT1, is constitutively expressed in roots but not induced by Al treatment. In pattern II, Al-induced organic acid secretion is delayed for several hours after Al stress. The lag phase may be involved in signal transduction, gene transcription, and protein synthesis. The OA exudation patterns in rape, Arabidopsis, and alfalfa belong to pattern II. In Arabidopsis, the expression of ALMT1 and MATE is controlled by a transcription factor, STOP1, which is a C2H2-type zinc finger protein (Liu et al. 2009).

To date, ALMT1 encoding genes have only been identified in Al-resistant and model plants. Overexpression of these ALMT1s was shown to be able to enhance malate exudation and Al resistance in transgenic plants (Delhaize et al. 2004; Pereira et al. 2010; Sasaki et al. 2004a; Ligaba et al. 2006). Recently, an ALMT1 encoding gene (MsALMT1, accession no. GU550122) was isolated in the roots of the Al-sensitive plant Medicago sativa L. cv. Yumu no. 1 (YM1) (Chen et al. 2011). Furthermore, the expression of MsALMT1 was upregulated in a time-dependent manner after Al treatment in YM1 (Chen et al. 2011). The induction of malate exudation from YM1 roots was triggered efficiently within $_ { 0 - 6 \mathrm { ~ h ~ } }$ following Al exposure (Chen et al. 2011). Thereby, we speculated that MsALMT1 plays an important role in the appearance of Al-activated malate in YM1 roots. The objective of this study was to further verify the function of MsALMT1 under Al stress conditions using transgenic plants. Overexpression of MsALMT1 under the control of the CaMV 35S (35S) promoter was generated in transgenic tobacco. Further investigation showed that overexpression of MsALMT1 significantly enhanced malate exudation and Al resistance in transgenic tobacco under Al stress conditions.

Aluminium is a common metal in the Earth’s crust that is usually found in insoluble forms when the soil $\mathrm { p H }$ is neutral or slightly acidic. However, when the soil $\mathrm { p H }$ drops below 5.0, the solubility of aluminium increases and toxic aluminium ions (especially the trivalent cation $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ ) can limit root growth and negatively interfere with water and nutrient uptake, consequently leading to reduced crop yields due to drought and mineral deficiencies (Kochian et al. 2015). Plant species have developed different mechanisms to cope with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity. The most studied mechanism is the exudation of organic acids from the root apex. Once in the rhizosphere, the organic acids chelate $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ , thereby reducing its toxicity (Ryan et al. 2001).

Although increments in organic acid production by plant cells have been associated with increased $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance in plants (de la Fuente et al. 1997; Barone et al. 2008), organic acid transport out of the root cells has a greater association with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance (Sasaki et al. 2004, 2006; Raman et al. 2008; Pereira et al. 2010; Zhou et al. 2013, 2014). In wheat (Triticum aestivum L.), two genes (TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B) that encode organic acid transporters were demonstrated to play a role in $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. TaALMT1 is located in chromosome 4D and encodes a malate transporter belonging to the ALMT (aluminium-activated malate transporter) family that is expressed in the wheat root tip (Sasaki et al. 2004). TaMATE1B is located on chromosome 4B and encodes a citrate transporter of the MATE (multi-drug and toxin extrusion) family that is expressed in the root tip depending on the allele (Ryan et al. 2009; Tovkach et al. 2013). Both genes exhibit a correlation between the level of expression, the amount of organic acid exudate by the roots and the level of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. The gene expression level is regulated by sequences in the promoter region (Sasaki et al. 2004, 2006; Ryan et al. 2009; Tovkach et al. 2013). For instance, the level of TaALMT1 expression is correlated with tandem repeats in the promoter (named here I to VII). Promoters containing a higher number of repeats (V and VI) have higher levels of gene expression and are usually $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistant, whereas promoters without repeats (I and II) have low levels of gene expression and are typically $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ sensitive (Sasaki et al. 2006; Raman et al. 2008). The TaMATE1B gene expression level is correlated with two polymorphisms in the promoter region (Tovkach et al. 2013). The first polymorphism is a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) that is responsible for a two-fold increase in gene expression and the second is a transposon-like insertion that is associated with a 20-fold increase in TaMATE1B expression. In fact, the transposonlike insertion not only increases but also changes the location of the expression to the root apex, thereby increasing the citrate efflux and consequently $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance (Tovkach et al. 2013).

The repeats located in the TaALMT1 promoter and the insertion in the TaMATE1B promoter can be easily detected by PCR. The allelic variations in these promoter regions have been studied in a number of genotypes and have revealed interesting aspects of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance in wheat (Sasaki et al. 2006; Raman et al. 2008; Han et al. 2013; Garcia-Oliveira et al. 2014; Pereira et al. 2015). For instance, wheat lines of Japanese origin do not show a clear correlation between the number of repeats in the TaALMT1 promoter region and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance; this finding is in contrast to the effects observed with lines of non-Japanese origin (Sasaki et al. 2006). An $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -tolerant Brazilian cultivar named Trintecinco was shown to possess TaALMT1 allele II (usually associated with sensitivity) (Raman et al.

2008), whereas the majority of the Brazilian wheat cultivars contains promoters V and VI (typically associated with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance) (Pereira et al. 2015). TaALMT1 allele V was less frequently identified in a collection of cultivars and landraces of Chinese wheat, whereas promoter VI was not detected and allele III was identified only in Chinese and Brazilian wheat to date (Han et al. 2013; Pereira et al. 2015). TaALMT1 promoter VII is rarely found; indeed, it has been detected in only three genotypes to date (Raman et al. 2008; Pereira et al. 2015). Moreover, the presence of the transposon-like insertion in the TaMATE1B promoter is less frequent in Brazilian wheat genotypes but is widespread among Portuguese wheat cultivars (Garcia-Oliveira et al. 2014; Pereira et al. 2015). This insertion appears to be important for the root growth of some genotypes analysed in short-term soil experiments. However, most genotypes presenting the insertion in the TaMATE1B promoter did not outperform the genotypes without the insertion that possessed the same TaALMT1 allele (Pereira et al. 2015). Therefore, evaluating the allelic distribution of the TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B promoters is crucial to increase our knowledge concerning the contribution of the different alleles to wheat $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. Moreover, the TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B alleles have been associated with only $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance in hydroponics or in short-term soil experiments to date. No correlation has been described between these alleles and wheat plants growing in acidic soils under field conditions.

Phenotyping using hydroponics is widely used to evaluate a number of traits including $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance because this method is fast, non-destructive and allows greater control over the environmental conditions (Shavrukov et al. 2012). Indeed, phenotyping for $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance in Brazilian wheat has typically been performed under hydroponic conditions (Camargo et al. 1987, 1998, 1999, 2006). Studies assessing $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance under field conditions for a large number of Brazilian wheat genotypes are rare (de Sousa 1998) even though field evaluation in acidic soils is more realistic. The downside is that soil evaluation presents issues related to non-uniform nutrient distribution, uncontrollable factors (i.e., drought or excess heat) and $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ toxicity occurring together with calcium deficiency and manganese toxicity. A high correlation for $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance phenotyping between field and hydroponic conditions has been reported for wheat (Baier et al. 1995); however, the genotypes evaluated under the field and hydroponic conditions differed in that study. To obtain a clear correlation, the same genotypes need to be used for the comparison of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance phenotyping between different methods.

In Brazil, acidic soils are predominant in wheat-growing areas (Echart and Cavalli-Molina 2001), and Brazilian wheat genotypes have been considered good sources of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. Some genotypes have been used in different breeding programmes worldwide to develop new lineages, including BH 1146, Carazinho, Cotiporã, Frontana, IAC 5—Maringá and Trintecinco (Hettel 1989). BH 1146, Frontana, IAC 5—Maringá, and Trintecinco are among the most common genotypes used by Brazilian breeders (de Sousa and Caierão 2014). Moreover, a number of the Brazilian cultivars exhibiting $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance have PG1 as a common ancestor. PG1 is a selection of Polyssú that is one of the parents of Fronteira, which is also used as a good source of $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance (de Sousa 1998). The constant use of the same or similar sources in breeding programmes can result in a lower genetic basis for $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance. Phylogenetic analysis using microsatellite markers revealed similarities among some of the Brazilian cultivars used as $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance sources, and these genotypes were most likely to share similar resistance/tolerance mechanisms (Pereira et al. 2015). Thus, the phenotyping of a large collection of wheat materials can result in the identification of sources containing potential new alleles/mechanisms that could be useful for breeders.

In this context, the goal of this work was to correlate the TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B allelic variability with wheat resistance to toxic aluminium under hydroponic and field conditions. We used a diverse wheat collection representing different countries and more than 90 years of breeding. Our goal also extended to the identification of resistant sources not commonly used by breeders, the comparison of hydroponic and field data and the evaluation of the TaALMT1 and TaMATE1B alleles over time to associate their frequency with $\mathrm { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ resistance over the past nine decades.

Aluminium (Al) toxicity is one of the primary factors limiting crop production on strongly acidic soils. At low $\mathrm { p H }$ values $\mathrm { ( p H } < 4 . 5 \mathrm { ) }$ , toxic forms of Al are solubilized into soil solution, inhibiting root growth and consequently reducing crop yields (Kochian et al. 2004). In response to Al toxicity, plants have evolved many strategies to overcome Al stress. Al-induced secretion of organic acid has been regarded as one of the important mechanisms for plant roots to ameliorate Al stress (Ma et al. 2001; Kochian et al. 2004). Many plants are reported to exude organic acid to detoxify Al toxicity such as citrate in soybean, common bean and rice (Yang et al. 2001; Shen et al. 2004; Yokosho et al. 2011), malate in wheat (Sasaki et al. 2004), and oxalate in buckwheat (Ma et al. 1997).

Genes encoding transporters for the Al-induced secretion of malate and citrate have been identified in sorghum, barley, Arabidopsis, wheat, rye, maize and rice (Sasaki et al. 2004; Furukawa et al. 2007; Magalhaes et al. 2007;

Liu et al. 2009; Ryan et al. 2009; Maron et al. 2010; Yokosho et al. 2010; Yokosho et al. 2011; Fujii et al. 2012). In wheat, an Al-activated malate transporter gene (TaALMT1) mediated the secretion of malate (Sasaki et al. 2004). Overexpressing TaALMT1 and SbMATE in Arabidopsis facilitated Al-activated malate and citrate efflux (Ryan et al. 2007; Magalhaes et al. 2007; Maron et al. 2010). Besides malate transporter gene (ALMT) and citrate transporter gene (MATE), several other genes such as citrate synthase gene, malate dehydrogenase gene, and plasma membrane $\mathrm { H ^ { + } } .$ -ATPase gene, etc. are also reported to mediate the secretion of organic acid and Al tolerance. For example, overexpression of a citrate synthase in tobacco, a mitochondrial ATP synthase in wheat, and a malate dehydrogenase in alfalfa and tobacco conferred an elevated Al tolerance (de la Fuente et al. 1997; Hamilton et al. 2001; Wang et al. 2010; Fan et al. 2011). A plasma membrane $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ -ATPase gene regulated the secretion of citrate from soybean roots via its transcriptional and translational process (Shen et al. 2005). Although several genes have been identified to mediate secretion of organic acid or Al tolerance in different plant species, it is still unclear how these genes coordinate to regulate the secretion of organic acid and root elongation in the same plant species.

Watanabe et al. (2005) performed root-split experiments, in which M. malabathricum roots were divided into part A roots growing in a nutrient solution, and part B roots growing in a calcium solution. When $0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m M }$ Al was applied to part A roots, citrate synthase activity was increased by fivefold in part A roots, while no variation in part B roots, suggesting that no Al signal was transmitted from part A roots to part B roots to stimulate the activity of citrate synthase. In a calcium solution, Yang et al. (2001) separated soybean roots into part A roots and part B roots. When Part A roots were exposed to $5 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ Al, the exudation of citrate from part A roots increased greatly, while citrate exudation was not observed in part B roots of the same plant, which received only calcium solution without Al. The results suggested that Al-induced exudation of citrate from soybean roots required the direct contact of Al. They further conducted a shoot-excised experiment, and found that Al-induced exudation of citrate decreased greatly when the shoot of soybean was excised, suggesting that shoots might play an important role in Al-induced secretion of citrate. However, it was unknown whether activation of gene expression and inhibition of root elongation were affected by shoots.

In this study, we investigated Al-activated secretion of organic acid, expression of genes (GmALMT1, GmMATE1, GmPHA1) and root elongation in soybean seedlings to better describe the interaction of these genes and processes to coordinate Al tolerance.

Aluminium-activated malate transporter1(ALMT1) was identified as an aluminium $( \mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + } )$ tolerant gene expressed in the root apex of wheat (Triticum aestivum) (Sasaki et al.，2OO4).Acidic soils limit crop production due to the toxicity of $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ (Kochian,1995).The ALMT1 protein is localized on the plasma membrane (Yamaguchi etal., 2005)

and acts as an $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -ligand-gated anion transport protein (Pineros, Cancado,& Kochian, 2008; Sasaki et al., 2004, 2014; W. H. Zhang et al.，2008). Heterologous expression of ALMT1 in tobaccosuspension cells (Nicotiana tabaccum),barley (Hordeum vulgare) and wheat conferred $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ -activated malate efflux and enhanced their tolerance to $A | ^ { 3 + }$ stress (Delhaize et al., 2OO4; Pereira et al., 2010; Sasaki et al.,2OO4；Sasaki， Tsuchiya,Ariyoshi,Ryan,et al.,2016).

Further studies have also revealed that the orthologous genes belonged to a previously uncharacterized gene family in diverse plant species； the first gene identified in wheat was named TaALMT1 (Delhaize et al., 2OO7).The ALMT-family genes are involved in many physiological functionsand properties；for example，stomatal movement (opening and closure),organic acid accumulation in fruit, pollen tube elongation,as well as $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ tolerance in many plant species (Barbier-Brygoo et al.,2011; Gutermuth et al., 2018;Pantoja,2021; Ryan et al., 2011).

Stomatal apertures primarily determine carbon dioxide uptake rate,a function essential for photosynthesis and transpirational water loss,and are regulated in response to myriad environmental stimuli, such as carbon dioxide concentrations,drought, temperature,and light conditions,as well as several plant hormones (Kim et al., 2010; Murata et al., 2015). Stomatal closure is mediated by two kinds of anion channels that are discriminated by their relaxation time to membrane voltage shifts,rapid (R)-type and slow (S)-type anion channels (Keller et al.,1989;Schroeder& Hagiwara,1989).Genes encoding S-type anion channels are known as‘Slow-Anion Channel Associated 1，SLAC1’ (At1g12480)in Arabidopsis thaliana (Negi et al.，2008;Vahisalu et al.,2008).AtSLAC1 is localized to the plasma membrane and is essential for stomatal closure in response to carbon dioxide,abscisic acid (ABA) and ozone (Negi et al., 2008; Saji et al.,2008;Vahisalu et al., 2008,201O).Furthermore,AtSLAC1- associated S-type anion channels are controlled by phosphorylation by Open Stomata 1 (OST1/SnRK2.6)，a type of sucrose nonfermenting-1 (SNF1)-related protein kinase 2， and calciumdependent protein kinases (CPKs).AtSLAC1-associated S-type anion channels are also inactivated by type-2C protein phosphatases (PP2Cs) via inhibition of OST1 kinase in response to ABA signalling (Geiger et al., 2009,201O; Lee et al., 2009). A SLAC1 homologue, SLAH3,is also involved in regulating stomatal movement-activated predominantly by phosphorylation with CPK21 (Demir et al., 2013; Geiger et al.,2011; Guzel Deger et al., 2015; Liu et al.,2019). SLAC/ SLAH anion channels are known to possess diverse physiological functions in shoots and roots in addition to their functions in guard cells (Dreyer et al.,2012; Hedrich & Geiger,2017).

The gene encoding R-type anion channels was found to be AtALMT12 (At4g17970).AtALMT12 is expressed in guard cells, contributes to stomatal closure in A. thaliana (Sasaki et al.,2O1O),and is functionallyactivated by extracellular malate (Meyer etal., 2010). The AtALMT12-encoded channel revealed features previously known from R-type channels； thus，AtALMT12 was also named 'quick anion channel 1, QUAC1' (Hedrich,2012; Meyer et al., 2010). AtALMT12/QUAC1-mediated stomatal closure is controlled by ABA signalling (Meyer et al.,201O; Sasaki et al.,201O). In addition to AtALMT12,several ALMT-family proteins (AtALMT4,AtALMT6 and AtALMT9 and HvALMT1) were reported to be the channels involved in stomatal movement (De Angeli et al., 2013; Eisenach et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015;W. Ye, Koya, et al., 2021).

Several distinctive features of AtALMT12 are known from analyses using Xenopus oocytes as an expression system；for example,(1)a bell-shaped current-voltage curve was observed,(2)

extracellular malate-activated channel function was identified,and (3) OST1 definitely stimulated AtALMT12 activity via protein-protein interaction,but the protein kinase was not always necessary for the production of malate efflux currents (Imes et al.，2013；Meyer et al.,201O;Mumm et al., 2013). In particular, the second feature is consistent with a previous report that an increase in apoplastic malate concentration caused stomatal closure in Vicia faba and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum） (Araujo et al.，2O11； Hedrich et al., 1994).

There are 16 ALMT-family proteins in tomato (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi，Nakano，et al.，2O16)．Two SIALMT genes (SIALMT4 $[ \mathsf { S o l y c O 3 g 0 9 6 8 2 0 } ]$ and SIALMT5 [Solyc03g119640]) are expressed mainly in the vascular bundles of fruit during tomato (cv.Micro-Tom) development，and both proteins possess malate efflux function. Notably，SlALMT5 is involved in the seed organic acid content (Sasaki, Tsuchiya, Ariyoshi,Nakano,et al., 2O16). J. Ye et al. (2017) performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) with 272 tomato accessions，revealing that tonoplast-localized SlALMT9 (a single gene from Solyc06g072910-Solyc06g072920) was involved in determining the malic acid content of fruit. SlALMT15 (Solyc11gO6897O) was found to be related to a stomatal density trait that functions in stomatal formation in tomato leaves,and further affects photosynthesis and drought tolerance in tomato (J.Ye,Wang, et al.,2021). Z.Wang et al. (202O) focused on the effects of WRKY transcription factors and jasmonic acid (JA) during $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress and found that six SIWRKY genes and SIALMT3 (Solyc01gO9614O) might be involved in inhibiting tomato root growth regulated by JA under $\mathsf { A l } ^ { 3 + }$ stress.In contrast，the SIALMT3 gene was reported to be negatively correlated with the sugar/organic acid ratio in tomato fruit (Li et al., 2021).The SlALMT genes involved in stomatal movement have not been identified in tomato.

Thisreport provides evidence suggesting that SlALMT11 (SolycO8g0o699O) expressed in tomato leaf guard cells is involved in stomatal closure induced by external malate,but not by abscisic acid.This study also highlights how the guard-cell-type ALMT proteins (SlALMT11 and AtALMT12)are activated by external organic acids and identifies the amino acid residues of the ALMT proteins involved in the voltage-dependent channel activity.

The plant genome has frequent repetitions of the aluminumactivated malate transporters (ALMT) genes, which is essential for transporting organic acids (OAs) across membranes (Zhang et al., 2014). OAs regulate plant metabolism and modulate adaptational (Sharma et al., 2016) activities like stomatal motion (Meyer et al., 2010a; Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010), aluminum tolerance, pH modulation, and stress response (Sharma et al., 2016). In the last few decades, multiple reports have suggested that the release of OAs (particularly, malic acid) can modulate plant tolerance to metal, while its improvs nutritional stress, ion transport, and cell turgor pressure (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010; Sharma et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2014).

Therefore, delineating the underlying mechanism of ALMTs action can provide us with tools to improve plant response to biotic and abiotic stressors.

Evolutionary analysis of ALMTs in bacteria (Takanashi et al., 2016), Arabidopsis (Kovermann et al., 2007), rice (Oryza sativa) (Liu et al., 2017), apple (Ma et al., 2018), and Chinese white pear (Xu et al., 2018) demonstrated that plants ALMTs have distinctive function, for example aluminum tolerance, and fruit acidity in plants. They have also been correlated with resistance response, ion transport, and opening and closing of the stomatal guard cells.

Based on a study on Arabidopsis thaliana, the ALMT family has 14 members, divided into three subgroups, according to their functions. The most representative family member is AtALMT1, which belongs to the first subgroup and is located in the root cell membrane. AtALMT9 represents member of the second subgroup and is primarily expressed in mesophyll cells. AtALMT12 belongs to the third subcategory and is primarily expressed in the plasma membrane and the intima of guard cells. Its function is related to the closure of guard cell type anion channels and stomata (Meyer et al., 2010b; Sasaki et al., 2010).

ALMTs were reported to function as anion channel proteins (Zhang et al., 2014). In particular, the activity and expression profile of the AtALMT12 gene was shown to have significant influence on the anion efflux. In stomatal guard cells, under drought stress, the gene was shown to accelerate guard cell cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, and vacuole anion discharge. A massive exudation of anions altered cell membrane polarity, activated $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ channel proteins, and resulted in the release of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ out of cells, causing reduction in cell turgor pressure, closure of the stomata and minimization of moisture loss.

Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum L.) is a highly profitable crop and the largest source of natural fiber for the global textile industry. The demand for enhanced fiber quality is increasing with the rapid growth of modern textile industries. Till now, little is known about the role of the ALMT gene family in upland cotton. Here, we screened the entire genome of the upland cotton ALMT gene family and predicted gene structure, chromosome distribution, cellular localization, and expression pattern. This work will offer new insight into the development of genetically enhanced stress-resistant cotton fiber.

For the past two decades, phytochelatins have been known to play a central role in the detoxification of diverse metals/ metalloids, including Cd(II), Hg(II) and As(III), in plants (Grill et al., 1987; Ha et al., 1999). However, it was uncertain whether a common transporter exists for PCs chelated to different metals/metalloids. In the case of fission yeast, the PC transporter SpHMT1 has a high substrate specificy; it can efficiently detoxify Cd(II) (Ortiz et al., 1995), but not As(III) (Preveral et al., 2009). We previously reported that the two ABC transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, which act as apo $\mathsf { P C } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathsf { P C } _ { 2 } \mathsf { - A s } ( | | | )$ transporters, play a central role in arsenic tolerance (Song et al., 2010). The aim of the present study was to investigate whether the same ABC transporters function in the detoxification of Cd(II) and Hg(II) in plants. The growth of atabcc1 and atabcc1 atabcc2 knockout plants was significantly more impaired in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II) than that of wild-type plants, suggesting that the same ABC transporters are responsible for the transport of all three phytochelatin complexes. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 play a major role in Cd sequestration, as vacuolar accumulation of Cd was decreased in atabcc1 atabcc2 protoplasts to $5 . 5 \%$ of wild-type levels (Figure 2). The remaining sequestration activity may result from the presence of other ABCC proteins, such as AtABCC3 and AtABCC6, which were previously implicated in Cd tolerance (Tommasini et al., 1998; Gaillard et al., 2008), or AtABCC11 and AtABCC12, which are the closest homologs of AtABCC1. AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 also play a crucial role in Hg (II) tolerance. The fact that both the PC synthase mutant and the transporter mutants (Figure 1f) exhibited such a high sensitivity to Hg(II) indicates that conjugation of Hg(II) to PCs and vacuolar sequestration of PC–Hg(II) are critical steps in Hg(II) detoxification.

AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 confer tolerance to As(III), Cd(II) and Hg(II), but not to Pb(II). The substrate specificity of AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 is distinct from that of ScYCF1, a well-characterized ABCC transporter, which confers tolerance to Pb(II) as well as to As(III), Cd(II) and Hg(II) in yeast and/or Arabidopsis (Li et al., 1997; Ghosh et al., 1999; Gueldry et al., 2003; Song et al., 2003). One explanation for this difference may be that ScYCF1 transports GS-conjugated metals (Li et al., 1997), whereas AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 transport PC conjugates (Song et al., 2010). In line with this explanation, the PC-deficient cad1 mutant did not exhibit decreased Pb(II) tolerance (Figure S1), suggesting that Pb tolerance in Arabidopsis does not depend on PCs. As the GSH-deficient cad2 mutant exhibited compromised Pb(II) tolerance (Figure S1), GSH appears to be important in Pb tolerance, either by facilitating Pb sequestration and/or functioning as an anti-oxidant.


## The importance of the ABC transporters in Cd(II) tolerance is different from that in Hg(II) and As(III) tolerance


Although the absence of the two ABC transporters rendered the plant nearly as sensitive to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { I I I } )$ or $\mathsf { H g } ( \mathsf { I I } )$ as plants lacking PC synthase, this was not true for Cd(II). The double knockout plant was hypersensitive to Cd(II), but to a lesser degree than the PC synthase mutant, cad1. What could cause the difference in sensitivity between Cd(II) and As(III)/ Hg(II)? One possible explanation is that the PC–metal/metalloid complexes have different stabilities at different pHs. In the case of Cd, it has been reported that the PC–Cd(II) complex is more stable at neutral pH and less stable under acidic conditions, while the PC–As(III) complex is most stable in an acidic environment (Delnomdedieu et al., 1994; Schmo¨ ger et al., 2000; Dorcˇa´k and Kre˛zel, 2003). In cases where a_ PC–metal/metalloid complex is more stable at acidic pH, efficient transport into the acidic vacuole is required to avoid release of the toxic metal/metalloid from the complexes in the cytosol. If a PC–metal/metalloid complex is more stable at a neutral or slightly basic pH, as is the case for Cd(II), release of the metal/metalloid ions would be lower within the cytosol, resulting at least partial detoxification even in the absence of vacuolar sequestration. Therefore, in atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout plants, Cd(II) toxicity may be attenuated by chelation to PCs, resulting in less severe sensitivity than for As(III) or Hg(II). This hypothesis is supported by Cd speciation analysis (Figure S8), which showed that Cd in the mutant is exclusively associated with sulfur detected at a retention time that corresponds with that of PCs.

Furthermore, the level of total low-molecular-weight sulfur compounds, including PCs and GSH, in the wild-type and the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant exposed to Cd(II) was very similar (Table S1). Since GSH concentrations remain constant during long-term exposure of Arabidopsis to Cd after a slight initial reduction (Xiang and Oliver, 1998), this result suggests that PC content in the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant does not differ much from that in the wild-type. This observation is in contrast to that made in a study of plants exposed to $\mathsf { A s } ( \mathsf { V } )$ , in which atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant plants contained a lower amount of PCs than the wild-type (Song et al., 2010). These contrasting results suggest again that Cd is more efficiently complexed to PCs at a cytosolic pH than As is. Tight binding of PCs and Cd in the cytosol may maintain apo PC at low levels, which cannot exert significant feedback inhibition of PC synthesis (Loeffler et al., 1989), even in the absence of vacuolar transport. In contrast, As is less efficiently complexed to PCs at cytosolic pH, and thus plant cells exposed to As may have a high level of apoPC in the cytosol, causing feedback inhibition on PC synthesis. This feedback inhibition is likely to be much higher in the atabcc1 atabcc2 mutant than in the wild-type, because the mutant plants lack the transporters that remove As–PC and apoPC from the cytosol.

When AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 were expressed in a yeast strain that produces PCs, resistance to Hg(II) was increased (Figure 3), but not resistance to Cd(II) (Figure S5). The difference in response to the two metals may be explained by the high stability of the PC–Cd(II) complex at cytosolic pH, as described above. Furthermore, the high concentration of

PCs produced in the yeast system could enable the cells to tolerate intracellular Cd even in the absence of the transporters. In a previous report (Song et al., 2010), we showed that SM7 yeast produced more PCs than Arabidopsis plants. Double knockout mutant plants grown in the presence of $1 0 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M }$ As contained 10–15 nmol PCs $\mathfrak { g } ^ { - 1 }$ FW, while SM7 yeast transformed with the empty vector control produced 3 nmol $\mathsf { P C s \mathsf { m } q } ^ { - 1 }$ protein. Assuming that, in the mutant plants and yeast, all PCs are localized in the cytosol [10 and $50 \%$ of the cell volume for plants and yeast, respectively, according to Winter et al. (1993) and Biswas et al. (2003)] and that yeast contain $5 0 ~ \mathsf { m g }$ protein per g FW $( 5 \% )$ , the cytosolic PC concentration is estimated to be $1 0 0 { - } 1 5 0 ~ \mu \mu \mu \mu$ in plants and at least $3 0 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ in yeast. As Cd is more efficient at inducing PC synthesis than As is, it is likely that SM7 yeast produces more PCs when grown in the presence of Cd(II) than in the presence of As. Such a high PC concentration could be enough to complex and detoxify Cd efficiently in the cytosol, in which case the presence of either ABC transporter would not enhance tolerance to Cd.


## Root-to-shoot translocation of Cd(II) is dependent on AtABCC1 and AtABCC2


Translocation of Cd from the root to the shoot was greater in the double knockout than in the wild-type (Figure 4). This suggests that vacuolar sequestration of the PC–Cd(II) complexes by AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 decreases the cytosolic concentration of the metal in root cells, and thereby reduces translocation to the shoot. In agreement with this explanation, several reports have demonstrated preferential accumulation of Cd and other non-essential heavy metals in the root, and have shown that translocation to the shoot is limited (Kim et al., 2002; Puig and Penarrubia, 2009; Verbruggen et al., 2009) and that xylem loading of Cd is an important factor in controlling shoot metal content (Uraguchi et al., 2009; Conn and Gilliham, 2010). The increased shoot-to-root ratio of Cd in the atabcc1 atabcc2 double mutant in this study is not as pronounced as that reported for rice plants (Oryza sativa) that have reduced OsHMA3 activity (Ueno et al., 2010). However, to our knowledge, the translocation ratio of the corresponding Arabidopsis mutant has not yet been investigated. Further studies are required to understand the relative importance of AtABCC1, AtABCC2, AtHMA3 and other candidate transporters, such as AtCAX2 and AtCAX4 (Hirschi et al., 2000; Korenkov et al., 2009; Ueno et al., 2010), in retaining Cd(II) in the root of Arabidopsis.


## Vacuolar sequestration can be engineered to increase heavy metal tolerance and accumulation


Over-expression of AtABCC1 driven by the 35S promoter enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation in Arabidopsis (Figure 5). This is probably the result of an increased vacuolar storage capacity, as shown for ScYCF1-expressing Arabidopsis plants (Song et al., 2003). However, this was different from the case of arsenic, in which tolerance was enhanced only upon over-expression of both AtABCC1 and PC synthase (Song et al., 2010), indicating that the transport and synthesis of PCs are both required for arsenic tolerance. This difference may originate from the different extents of induction of PC synthesis by different metals. Cd(II) is known to be a more efficient inducer of PC synthesis than As(V) or As(III), and results in a two- to four-fold higher level of PCs (Grill et al., 1989; Vatamaniuk et al., 2000; Oven et al., 2002). In plants over-expressing AtABCC1, it is likely that Cd(II) induces the production of sufficient amounts of PCs, such that transport of PC–Cd(II) determines the tolerance to Cd(II), rather than the PC synthesis.

Among several dozen AtABCC1 transgenic plant lines examined, we did not find any plants with transcript levels higher than $12 0 { - } 1 5 0 \%$ of the wild-type levels (Song et al., 2010). Increasing the expression level to above this level may improve the heavy metal tolerance of the plant further. To test whether a further increase in the level of PCs may have a synergistic effect on the Cd tolerance mediated by AtABCC1, we compared the Cd tolerance of plants over-expressing AtPCS1 alone or both AtABCC1 and AtPCS1, but did not find much difference between them (Figure S7). This may be due to the strong effect of AtPCS1 (an 8.6- to 32-fold increase in transcript level), which produces high levels of PCs that stabilize Cd in the cytosol, whereas AtABCC1 transcript levels were not increased much above wild-type levels.

Understanding the expression control mechanism of AtABCC1, and application of this knowledge may therefore be useful in phytoremediation projects that aim to produce plants with enhanced heavy metal accumulation and tolerance. The broad range of substrates transported by the ABC transporters is a further advantage of using these genes, because many sites are contaminated by a mixture of toxic ions (Vangronsveld et al., 2009). Furthermore, manipulation of these genes in a tissue-specific manner, e.g. in roots or stems, may reduce the accumulation of Cd in the edible parts of plants, such as fruits or grains.

The non-essential element cadmium (Cd) is toxic to both plants and animals.Excess Cd in soils can be absorbed by plant roots,which inhibits plant growth and diminishes crop yields [1].Importantly,the Cd absorbed by roots can be transported to the shoots and deposited in grains or friuts.Through the dietary intake,plant-derived Cd can enter the human body.Due to its long biological half-life,the Cd level in the body progressively accumulates by low-dose chronic exposure,which can cause various diseases such as renal dysfunction and osteoporosis [2, 3].Therefore,it is desirable to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of Cd detoxification and accumulation in plants,which will enable the development of low-Cd crops,thus reducing dietary intake of Cd by humans.

Cd enters root cells mainly through transport systems responsible for the uptake of essential elements [4,5],such as the manganese transporter OsNramp5 (natural resistance-associated macrophage protein 5) functioning as the major pathway for Cd entry into rice [6-8]. Once adsorbed into the root cels, Cd can cause serious cellular injuries [1,5]. Plants have evolved a series of strategies to cope with Cd toxicity, including extrusion,complexation with thiol-rich compounds such as glutathione (GSH) and phytochelatins (PCs),and vacuolar compartmentalization [5,9].During these biological processes,transporters from different families play important roles.For example,some efflux transporters localized in the plasma membrane can extrude Cd out of root cells [1O,11].AtPDR8(AtABCG36) has been identified as a Cd exporter in Arabidopsis.Its overexpression increases Cd extrusion and reduces the Cd content in the engineered plants,thus conferring resistance to Cd[11].Inaddition,Cd or its complexes can also be sequestered in vacuoles by transporters localized on the tonoplast. Several types of transporter, including HMA (Heavy Metal ATPases),ABC (ATP-binding cassette) and CAX (cation/proton exchanger) transporters,have been demonstrated to be involved in this process [12].In rice,OsHMA3 is the major transporter mediating Cd transport into root cell vacuoles,and the non-functional OsHMA3 fails to sequester Cd into vacuoles,consequently increasing the root-to-shoot Cd translocation [13,14]. Together, the extrusion and vacuolar sequestration of Cd in root cells can not only alleviate Cd toxicity,but also restrict Cd translocation and accumulation in shoots and seeds.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute a large,diverse gene superfamily found in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.Plant ABC transporters are grouped into eight major subfamilies (A-G,I) according to domain structure and evolutionary relationships [15].ABC proteins exhibit wide substrate profiles,including lipids,metals/metalloids,and phytohormones [16]. For example,OsABCC1 can sequester arsenic-PC conjugates in the vacuoles,thereby participating in arsenic detoxification and limiting its transport to the rice grains [17].Multiple ABC transporters have been reported to be capable of transporting Cd or Cd complexes [l2].The first ABC transporter that has been described as a Cd transporter is HMT1 in the fission yeast,which can transport PC-Cd complex into the vacuole for Cd detoxification [18,19]. Subsequently, additional ABC transporters involved in Cd (conjugate) transport have been found in various species [11,2O,21]．In Arabidopsis,besides AtABCG36 [11],three C-type ABC transporters,AtABCC1,AtABCC2 and AtABCC3,are also implicated in Cd tolerance by sequestering PC-Cd complexes into vacuoles [21,22].

133 genes have been annotated as ABC transporters in the whole rice genome [16],and two of them have been shown to participate in Cd tolerance so far. OsABCG43 is induced by Cd treatment in rice roots and confers Cd tolerance in yeast [23],but its exact function in rice remains unclear.Recently，involvement of another rice ABC transporter, OsABCG36,in Cd tolerance has been reported by Fu et al.[1O]. OsABCG36 can be induced in rice roots by brief Cd exposure and is localized to the plasma membrane.Heterologous expression of OsABCG36 in yeast showed an efflux activity for Cd, so itis thought to be required for Cd tolerance by exporting Cd or Cd complexes from the root cells in rice [1O].High-throughput analyses such as microarray and RNA sequencing have shown that OsABCC9 is also up-regulated by Cd treatment [24,25],suggesting its possible involvement in Cd tolerance in rice.However,it has not yet been established what role it plays in Cd tolerance in rice.In this study,we have investigated the role of OsABCC9 in Cd tolerance and accumulation in rice.The results showed that OsABCC9 was mainly expressed in the root stele under Cd stress,and was localized on the tonoplast.Disruption of OsABCC9 enhanced the Cd sensitivity of rice and the Cd content in the xylem sap and grains. Furthermore,its heterologous expression in yeast resulted in enhanced Cd tolerance along with a higher intracellular Cd content.We therefore propose that OsABCC9 is a vacuolar transporter that confers Cd tolerance and affects Cd accumulation in rice.

Heavy metals such as cadmium (Cd) and mercury (Hg) are toxic pollutants that are detrimental to living organisms. Plants employ a two-step mechanism to detoxify toxic ions. First, phytochelatins bind to the toxic ion, and then the metal–phytochelatin complex is sequestered in the vacuole. Two ABCC-type transporters, AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, that play a key role in arsenic detoxification, have recently been identified in Arabidopsis thaliana. However, it is unclear whether these transporters are also implicated in phytochelatindependent detoxification of other heavy metals such as Cd(II) and Hg(II). Here, we show that atabcc1 single or atabcc1 atabcc2 double knockout mutants exhibit a hypersensitive phenotype in the presence of Cd(II) and Hg(II). Microscopic analysis using a Cd-sensitive probe revealed that Cd is mostly located in the cytosol of protoplasts of the double mutant, whereas it occurs mainly in the vacuole of wild-type cells. This suggests that the two ABCC transporters are important for vacuolar sequestration of Cd. Heterologous expression of the transporters in Saccharomyces cerevisiae confirmed their role in heavy metal tolerance. Over-expression of AtABCC1 in Arabidopsis resulted in enhanced Cd(II) tolerance and accumulation. Together, these results demonstrate that AtABCC1 and AtABCC2 are important vacuolar transporters that confer tolerance to cadmium and mercury, in addition to their role in arsenic detoxification. These transporters provide useful tools for genetic engineering of plants with enhanced metal tolerance and accumulation, which are desirable characteristics for phytoremediation.

Keywords: vacuolar sequestration, heavy metal tolerance, phytoremediation, ABC transporter, phytochelatin transporter, heavy metal detoxification.

ABC transporters constitute a large superfamily of proteins described in all kingdoms of life. Some families have a restricted distribution, like the ABC subclass C (or multidrug resistance associated protein, MRP) which is limited to eukaryotes. In plants, ABCC/MRPs are subdivided in three phylogenetic clusters (Kolukisaoglu et al. 2002, Schulz and Kolukisaoglu 2006), two of which are fairly well characterized in Arabidopsis.

Cluster I contains four genes including AtMRP1 and AtMRP2 which are involved in cellular detoxification processes. These transporters display a ubiquitous expression in plants, mediate metal/metalloid tolerance and transport various compounds, such as phytochelatins (Song et al. 2010), glutathione conjugates (Lu et al. 1997), folate (AtMRP1), as well as chlorophyll catabolites (AtMRP2, Lu et al. 1998). The two other members of cluster I (AtMRP11 and AtMRP12) have been poorly investigated; they share transport properties of cluster I MRPs except for chlorophyll catabolites, which seems to be specific to AtMRP2 within this cluster (Frelet-Barrand et al. 2008).

Ten of the fifteen Arabidopsis ABCC/MRPs belong to cluster II. The AtMRP3 expression is induced in leaf and root under cadmium or several other metal treatments (Bovet et al. 2003), and confers tolerance to cadmium in yeast (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP3 exhibits glutathione S-conjugate transport activity, and as described for AtMRP1 and AtMRP2, chlorophyll catabolites transport activity has also been reported (Tommasini et al. 1998). AtMRP6 and AtMRP7 have the highest sequence similarity to AtMRP3 and are also upregulated by $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatments. In AtMRP6 mutants, leaf development is more sensitive to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment than in wild type. However, the expression pattern of AtMRP6 suggests that it is not only involved in $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ tolerance but also in developmental processes. Indeed, AtMRP6 is expressed during early seedling development, in root apical meristem and in lateral root initiation (Gaillard et al. 2008). AtMRP7 is constitutively expressed in roots and leaves and the protein was localized to both plasmalemma and tonoplast (Wojas et al. 2009). Overexpression of AtMRP7 in tobacco slightly enhances plant resistance to $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ treatment and modifies $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 2 + }$ rootto-shoot translocation. These observations suggest that AtMRP3 and its closest homologues may behave as cellular metal detoxifiers although additional functions in planta cannot be ruled out. AtMRP4 and AtMRP5, which also belong to cluster II, have a low sequence similarity, but their stomatal-specific expression patterns suggest a role in plant adaptation to water stress rather than cell detoxification. Indeed, AtMRP4 knock-out mutants display an increased water loss due to a larger constitutive stomata aperture. Considering its strong expression in guard cells and localization in plasmalemma, AtMRP4 is suggested to be involved in a stomata ion channel regulation (Klein et al. 2004). AtMRP5 is also expressed in guard cells but localizes to tonoplast (Nagy et al. 2009). Interestingly, Nagy et al. (2009) demonstrated that AtMRP5 is a high affinity inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) transporter, a molecule that modulates $\mathrm { C a } ^ { 2 \dagger }$ signaling and $\bar { \mathsf { K } } ^ { + }$ homeostasis in guard cells. AtMRP5 mutants are impaired in the export of InsP6 into vacuole resulting in constitutive stomata closure and a reduced water loss (Klein et al. 2003, Suh et al. 2007).

Cluster III genes have not been functionally characterized so far. In Arabidopsis (AGI 2000) it was revealed a single MRP/ABCC gene belonging to cluster III, AtABCC13/MRP11 $( \mathrm { A t } 2 \mathrm { g } 0 7 6 8 0 )$ . In this study, we investigated in-depth the expression pattern of AtABCC13 in Arabidopsis. The $\beta$ -glucuronidase (GUS) reporter gene approach revealed that the AtABCC13 expression was related to vascular elements, seed maturation, and seedling development.

ABC proteins are powerful transporters driving the exchange of compounds across many diferent biological membranes and the C-subfamily of ABC proteins is an important component77. In human, ABCC transporters have been studied extensively on substrate specifcity, tissue expression and transport kinetics to provide insights into cellular functions, drug discovery and development52,78. In plants, ABCC transporters are originally defned as vacuolar pumps of GS conjugates, and deemed to associate with detoxifcation, PTEs sequestration, chlorophyll catabolite transport and ion channel regulation76,79.

As a plant hyperaccumulating Cd, S. alfredii Hance harbors numerous genes related to metal transport or detoxifcation and requires intense attentions. Several characterized transporter genes include SaHMA334, $S a Z I P 4 ^ { 3 8 }$ and SaNramp636. Recent reports from Arabidopsis confer the roles of ABCC transporters as major detoxifers sequestering metal-chelators into the plant vacuoles57,58, suggesting that ABCC proteins might contribute to PTEs hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance. However, the physiological functions of ABCC proteins are still scarce in metal hyperaccumulators, and it is of great importance to address their roles in S. alfredii Hance. In the present study, the composition and diversifcation of ABCC subfamily in S. alfredii Hance were identifed using bioinformatics tools and their expression profles were characterized for their possible roles in Cd tolerance and accumulation.

Among the identifed ten proteins belonging to the ABCC subfamily, Sa45F39 is largest (1630 aa) and Sa48F96 is the smallest one (1024 aa). Similar size distribution is observed in Arabidopsis45, rice46 and wheat62. However, the number of ABCC genes in S. alfredii Hance is fewer than those reported species. For instance, there are

15 ABCC proteins in Arabidopsis45, 17 in rice45, 18 in wheat62, 26 in Vitis vinifera80 and 47 in Brassica napus81. Terefore, we presume that S. alfredii Hance may adopt a more economic strategy of assembling multi-functional genes rather than expanding gene family to cope with the external PTEs stress during the adaptive evolution. Tis phenomenon is also observed for leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinase (LRR-RLK) gene family which is also smaller in S. alfredii Hance than other plant species82. Nevertheless, these results are obtained from the transcriptomics rather than a complete genome sequencing data, which limits more precise evaluation of gene numbers especially for gene families composed by long proteins such as ABCC subfamily.

Te analysis on phylogeny and protein structure provides hints on the possible functions of SaABCC genes. Categorized into the division of AtABCC clade (Fig. 1), SaABCC genes are members of ABCC subfamily. All SaABCCs have similar distribution of TMD and NBD as that of AtABCCs, possessing similar protein length and spacer region (Fig. 2). However, it is worth noticing that members of SaABCCs and AtABCCs fall in diferent clades (I, II and III)76, and SaABCCs are only in clade I and II, suggesting the possibilities of multi-functionality in S. alfredii Hance. Additionally, SaABCCs have the identical numbers of MEME motifs and possess uniform distribution except for Sa23221 and Sa45F39 (Fig. 2C), demonstrating a higher conservation than AtABCCs. Tis may imply that under severe surroundings with PTEs stress, members of ABCC subfamily have prior functions to detoxify PTEs than other roles.

Te transcript abundance of ABCC genes across tissues helps in understanding their molecular functions. In the present study, six SaABCC genes exhibited tissue-specifc expression patterns in the absence of Cd, fve (Sa88F144, Sa23221, Sa48F96, Sa12F279 and Sa14F98) in roots and one (Sa14F190) in leaves (Fig. 3). Among them, Sa14F98 may participate in the plant growth and development as it is clustered with AtABCC6 which shows a similar root-specifc expression62. Sa14F190 showing the similar expression specifcity in leaves as TaABCC14 and $T a A B \bar { C } C l 5 ^ { 6 2 }$ may serve as candidate transporters in leaves. Although the clustering of SaABCCs and AtABCCs hints their functional similarity, there might be functional divergences as well. For example, though Sa88F144 and Sa13F200 are clustered together with AtABCC4, Sa13F200 was abundantly expressed in all three tissues and Sa88F144 exhibited a root-specifc expression pattern, neither consistent with the low expression level of AtABCC4 in all tissues83. ABCCs in wheat are reported to show preferential expression in specifc tissues, e.g., TaABCC3 in roots, TaABCC1 in stems, TaABCC14 and TaABCC15 in fag leaves62. As TaABCC3 clustered with AtABCC6 is a gene highly expressed at the initiation point of secondary roots84, it is suggested to play roles in root architecture development62. Such diferent expression patterns imply the possibilities of performing other functions apart from getting involved in the control of stomatal movements as $\bar { _ { A t A B C C } } 4 ^ { 8 3 }$ .

Cd-responsive expression of SaABCC genes hints their roles in Cd hyperaccumulation and hypertolerance in S. alfredii Hance. In the presence of Cd, Sa14F190 and Sa18F186 genes were mostly induced in roots (Fig. 4). Sa18F186 is segregated with AtABCC5 which is involved in $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake and salt stress tolerance85. Although AtABCC5 is regarded as a central regulator of guard cell ion channel59, guard cell signaling and phytate storage86, rare studies report the participation of AtABCC5 in Cd response. Te functional discrepancy between Sa18F186 and AtABCC5 may arise from the diferent leaf structures that S. alfredii has feshy leaves and Sa18F186 therefore might enroll to combat Cd stress rather than water loss. Sa14F190 gene falls into the same clade with AtABCC3 and AtABCC7, and AtABCC3 is important vacuolar transporters conferring Cd tolerance in Arabidopsis57. In addition, a Cd-responding cluster is found comprising AtABCC3, AtABCC6, AtABCC7 and SAT3 (serine acetyltransferase gene) on chromosome $\mathrm { I I I } ^ { 8 4 , 8 7 }$ . Although Sa45F39 did not respond signifcantly to Cd stress, it is clustered with AtABCC1/AtABCC2, which are reported to confer the tolerance to $\mathrm { A } s ^ { 5 6 }$ , Cd and $\mathrm { H g }$ in Arabidopsis55. AtABCC2 is particularly involved in vacuolar transport of chlorophyll catabolites58 and the uptake of cyanidin 3-O-glucoside (C3G)88. In rice, OsABCC1 closely related to AtABCC1/AtABCC2 does not confer Cd tolerance; instead, it is involved in As detoxifcation and reduces the allocation of As in grains63. Terefore, Sa45F39 is also speculated with roles in PTEs tolerance.

Han et al. proposed a comparative analysis of S. alfredii Hance transcriptomic datasets and characterized numerous hub genes strongly associated with Cd stress64. However, there are lack of details about SaABCC hub genes and their connections with other genes. In the present study, a co-expression network was reconstructed and uncovered fve SaABCC hub genes (Sa14F190, Sa13F200, Sa12F279, Sa23221 and Sa45F39). Te overlapping in the edge genes hints the internal connections among SaABCC hub genes. For Sa14F190 gene, the edge genes are associated with metabolic process, cellular process, biological regulation activity, transporter activity, response to stimuli and transcription factor (Fig. 5). To be more precise, the edge genes performing transporter activity include multidrug and toxic compound extrusion (MATE) efux family protein, zinc/iron transporter, ABC transporter B family member and sulfate transporter. Tose participating in metabolic process and cellular process consist of respiratory burst oxidase homolog protein D, CBL-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase (CIPK), plant cysteine oxidase, endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductin-1, phospholipid-transporting ATPase 1, GDSL esterase/lipase, and heavy metal-associated isoprenylated plant protein (HIPP). Representative transcription factors include bZIP and WRKY transcription factors. Among them, MATE efux family protein harbors multitasking abilities in encompassing regulation of plant development, secondary metabolite transport, xenobiotic detoxifcation, Al tolerance, and disease resistance89. Zinc/iron transporters difers in substrate range and specifcity, involved in the transport of $Z \mathrm { n }$ , Fe, Mn and $\mathrm { C d } ^ { 9 0 , 9 1 }$ . Members belonging to HIPP, CIPK and WRKY transcription factor are reported to confer Cd tolerance in yeasts92. Terefore, the functions of Sa14F190 are activated or magnifed through either direct or indirect interactions with these edge genes.

Taking Cd-responsive profles and co-expression network together, we chose Sa14F190 to further assess its roles in Cd tolerance and accumulation by heterologous expression in Cd-sensitive yeasts. Under Cd stress, Cd content in ∆ycf1_Sa14F190 was $3 5 . 4 8 \%$ higher than that in ∆ycf1_EV (Fig. 6), indicating the vital roles of Sa14F190 gene in Cd accumulation. However, Sa14F190 increased the sensitivity of transformed yeasts instead of enhancing Cd tolerance, evidenced by the retarded growth which may be due to more Cd accumulation. Similar fndings are observed for other transporters in S. alfredii Hance which all enhanced the Cd sensitivity and Cd accumulation of transformed yeasts, and the increase of cellular Cd content was $2 2 . 2 \%$ by SaNramp636, $2 5 . 2 \%$ by $S a H M A 3 ^ { 3 4 }$ and $1 6 . 4 \%$ by $S a \dot { C } A X \mathcal { 2 } h ^ { 3 9 }$ . It has been reported that AtABCC3 could confer Cd tolerance in yeast cells, but not Cd accumulation93, consistent with another study on AtABCC3 in Arabidopsis57. Tese fndings suggested that members of ABCC subfamily closely located in the phylogenetic tree might have functional divergence, and Cd tolerance and accumulation are mediated by diferent pathways.

In summary, the ABCC transporter Sa14F190 gene is responsible for Cd hyperaccumulation and other SaABCCs might have diverse roles in the tolerance or accumulation of PTEs. Members of ABCC transporter are a genetic pool of candidates encompassing strong ability to transport, tolerate or accumulate Cd and other PTEs for phytoremediation. Tis work applies bioinformatic analysis to provide a preliminary study uncovering the interesting functions of ABCCs members in S. alfredii Hance, and these functions need further experimental evidence to enrich our knowledge.

ABC super families of transporters are expressed in microorganisms and mammals and are involved in the transport of chemically diverse compounds across membranes. ABCC (MRP) is a subfamily among the ABC transporters shown to have important functions across evolution. Mutations in ABCC1 (MRP1) cause drug resistance and immune response in humans. In plants, Arabidopsis thaliana ABCC1 is present in vacuolar membranes and is known to transport glutathione (GSH) conjugate and folates (Rea, 2007;

Raichaudhuri et al., 2009). Early studies with AtMRP1 showed MgATP-energized, vanadate-inhibitable, uncoupler-insensitive uptake of several glutathione (GSH) conjugates (GS-conjugates) like N-ethylmaleimide-GS (NEM-GS), S-(2,4-dinitrophenyl)-GS (DNP-GS), glutathionylated chloroacetamide herbicides, (metolachlor-GS), folates and antifolates (methotrexate MTX) mediated by this protein in isolated vacuoles (Martinoia et al., 1993) or in vacuolar membrane vesicles purified from plants (Li et al., 1995; Rea, 2007; Raichaudhuri et al., 2009). In addition, AtMRP1 was shown to have a role in tolerance and detoxification of heavy metal and metalloids (Rea, 2007; Song et al., 2010). MRP proteins are classified based on the presence of one or two ATP-binding cassettes or nucleotide binding domains (NBDs). Each NBD encompasses \~200 amino acid residues and contains three idiotypic sequence motifs. These are a Walker A motif $\cdot G X _ { 4 } \mathrm { G K } ( \mathrm { S T } ) )$ and a Walker B motif $( \mathrm { R K } ) X _ { 3 } \mathrm { G } X _ { 3 } \mathrm { L }$ (hydrophobic)3), that are separated by \~120 amino acid residues (Walker et al., 1982), and an ABC signature (alias C motif, ((LIVMFY)S(SG)GX3(RKA)(LIVMYA)X(LIVFM)(AG)) (Bairoch, 1992).

In addition to two NBDs, AtMRP transporters contain two or three hydrophobic integral membrane spanning domains (MSDs), each of which contains multiple (usually four to six) transmembrane $\pmb { \mathscr { L } }$ -helices. The MSDs form the pathway for solute amovement across the phospholipid bilayer.

In south Asia, particularly in parts of Indian subcontinent, arsenic in ground water is a hazardous environmental pollutant. Arsenic content in water used for drinking and irrigation has been reported to cross the accepted limits of $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { g / L }$ proposed by the mWorld Health Organization in several areas of South Asia. Arsenic is taken up by plant roots and is sequestered in plant vacuoles. Two transporters in Arabidopsis, from ABCC (MRP) family AtABCC1 and AtABCC2, were shown to contribute to arsenic tolerance via vacuolar sequestration of As (III)-phytochelatin conjugates. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Yeast Cadmium Factor 1 (Ycf1), an ABC transporter localized to the vacuolar membrane originally identified for its role in vacuolar cadmium sequestration, was shown to detoxify arsenic by transporting As(glutathione $) _ { 3 }$ complexes into vacuoles (Szczypka et al., 1994; Li et al., 1996; Ghosh et al., 1999). AtMRP1 is the Ycf1 homolog in A. thaliana. AtMRP1 is localized at the vacuolar membrane and transports substrates to the vacuolar lumen thereby effectively sequestering them from cytosol (Li et al., 1997; Rea et al., 1998). Over expression of Ycf1 (35S::ycf1) was shown to confer both accumulation and enhanced resistance to lead and cadmium in Arabidopsis plants (Song et al., 2003). The most common forms of arsenic available in the environment for uptake by plants are arsenate (AsV) and arsenite (AsIII). Arsenate is acquired by plant roots through endogenous transport systems for phosphate and is reduced to the thiol-reactive form As III inside the cell (Asher and Reay, 1979). At equimolar concentrations, AsIII is more toxic than AsV.

Ycf1p (the yeast homolog of AtMRP1) shows several potential phosphorylation sites. Genetic evidence in yeast suggested that yeast casein kinase $_ { 2 \alpha }$ (Cka1p) may regulate Ycf1p function athrough phosphorylation of $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 2 5 1 }$ either directly or indirectly (Paumi et al., 2008). Ycf1p phosphorylation at $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 9 0 8 }$ and $\mathrm { T h r } ^ { 9 1 \bar { 1 } }$ was found to be required for cadmium detoxification (Eraso et al., 2004), and phosphorylation at $\mathsf { S e r } ^ { 2 5 1 }$ negatively regulated transport activity (Paumi et al., 2008). Six additional sites of phosphorylation were identified within the linker region by studies aimed at examining the complete yeast phosphoproteome via highthroughput analysis (Li et al., 2007; Smolka et al., 2007; Albuquerque et al., 2008).

The experiments described here were directed towards understanding the role of phosphorylation events controlling AtMRP1 transporter function both under AsIII stress as well as under antifolate treatment. There are several potential phosphorylation sites in AtMRP1. Using mutational analysis and heterologous expression in yeast, the role of phosphorylation, especially in the serine triad, has been investigated.

The data presented here shows that AtMRP1 C-terminal NBD2 phosphorylation is important in the presence of As III and antifolate MTX. A potential signaling event in response to As III is also indicated.

ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters are one of the largest known superfamilies of membrane transporters in all living organisms [1,2]. ABCC transporters, which belong to one subclass of the ABC transporter superfamily, are well known for their roles as multidrug resistance-associated proteins (MRPs), which are found in all eukaryotic organisms [3–7]. These proteins shuttle substrates as diverse as glutathione conjugates, xenobiotic compounds, intermediate metabolites and hormones across a variety of biological membranes [2,5,8,9].
