Several Pht1 family members were investigated in the past two decades, yet only a few members of the Pht2 family were functionally characterized. Daram et al. (1999) identified a Pht2 family PT gene designated as $P H T 2 ; I$ in Arabidopsis. Sequence comparison analysis suggested that PHT2;1 shares homologous identity with yeast PT family member PHO84. Expression analysis revealed that PHT2;1 is predominantly expressed in green tissues, with transcripts located in cells of the leaf blade, where they possibly participate in the transport of phosphate into leaves (Daram et al. 1999). Localization analysis of a PHT2;1– GFP fusion indicated that it is present in the chloroplast envelope. Furthermore, the phenotype of a PHT2;1 null mutant, pht2;1-1, is consistent with reduced Pi transport in the chloroplast, which links PHT2;1 and Pi distribution within the plant (Versaw et al. 2002). These findings suggest that $P H T 2 ; I$ is an important component in the mediation of Pi translocation from the cytosol to the chloroplast in Arabidopsis.

Sequence search analysis suggested a subset of uncharacterized Pht2 family members and cDNA sharing homologous identity to Arabidopsis PHT2;1 (data not shown). However, their molecular characterizations and their putative biological functions on mediation of Pi translocation are largely unknown. In this study, we functionally characterized a wheat PT member referred to as TaPHT2;1. This wheat PT gene shared high similarity to an array of Pht2 family members characterized in diverse plant species (Supplemental Fig. 2), in addition to its homologous relation to Arabidopsis $P H T 2 ; I$ and $B$ . distachyon PT2-1. Gene expression patterns, subcellular location, and acquisition of Pi in mutant yeast with lowaffinity biochemical kinetics suggest that TaPHT2;1 is a member of the Pht2 family in wheat and putatively plays an important role on mediation of Pi translocation in plants.

Pi transport across the chloroplast envelope is attributed to members of the plastidic phosphate translocator (pPT) family (Knappe et al. 2003). The PTs, such as the Pht2 family members, are important components in the Pi translocation system (Versaw et al. 2002). In this study, transgenic plants with knockdown expression of TaPHT2;1 were generated to evaluate the roles of the target gene in the mediation of Pi translocation and in the regulation of plant growth under various Pi supply conditions. In accordance with its potential functions presumed from its subcellular location and its biochemical kinetics of $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ on acquisition of Pi, TaPHT2;1 has an essential role in controlling Pi concentrations in chloroplasts under sufficient and deficient Pi conditions. Compared with WT, the knockdown expression of TaPHT2;1 in the transgenic lines (Lines 2 and 5) caused pronounced reductions in chloroplast Pi (Fig. 5b). This finding confirms that this wheat PT member is an essential component that mediates Pi translocation from the cytosol to the chloroplast. The plants with dramatically down-regulated expression of TaPHT2;1 exhibited lower levels of photosynthesis parameters such as photosynthetic rates and photochemical efficiencies of PSII (Fig. 6a, b), and worse growth behaviors in terms of plant phenotypic features (Fig. 7a, b). All findings indicate that TaPHT2;1 is critical in the regulation of photosynthetic organ functions and plant growth under various $\mathrm { P i }$ supply conditions through its role on mediation of Pi translocation at the subcellular level. These results are also in accordance with the concept that Pi concentration in the chloroplast stroma is closely coordinated with environmental conditions, such as external Pi supply status and circadian rhythm, which modulates photosynthesis and the subsequent partitioning of fixed carbon (Sharkey 1985; Walker et al. 1986).

There are distinct features of the expression pattern across Pht families. Most Pht1 family members are more abundantly expressed in roots than in shoots, and the transcripts are enhanced in response to Pi deprivation in most cases (Leggewie et al. 1997; Liu et al. 1998). Previous studies have revealed that a cis-regulatory element, referred to as PIBS (motif sequence of ATATGCA), plays crucial roles in PT genes in response to low Pi stress. For example, the low Pi induction effects of HvPht1;1 (AF543197) and HvPht1;2 (AY187019), two high-affinity PT members in barley, are directly associated with the P1BS-like motifs located at the promoter region (Schu¨nmann et al. 2004a, b; Glassop et al. 2005). Mutations in two out of three P1BS elements in the HvPht1;1 promoter can completely abolish low Pi induction (Schu¨nmann et al. 2004b). In this study, two cis-regulatory elements of PIBS were found in the TaPHT2;1 promoter at positions 1,218 and 1,384 bp upstream of the translation start codon (ATG), respectively (Supplemental Fig. 4). This finding indicated that these PIBS elements are possibly involved in TaPHT2;1 response to low Pi in the leaves. However, the potential roles of PIBS cis-regulatory elements in responding to the low Pi stress in roots were blocked due to unknown reasons. The molecular mechanism of the differentially spatial expression pattern of TaPHT2;1 in response to low Pi stress needs to be further investigated.

Endogenous oscillators control the diurnal rhythmic phenomena in prokaryotic cyanobacteria and in almost all eukaryotes (Sweeney 1987; Kondo et al. 1993; Hall 1995; Dunlap 1996). In vascular plants, photosynthesis is one of the representative phenomena regulated by circadian clocks at the metabolic (Sweeney and Haxo 1961; Hennessey and Field 1992) and gene expression levels (Kloppstech 1985; Giuliano et al. 1988; Nagy et al. 1988). Along with photosynthesis and photoperiod progression, ATP and NADPH, two energy molecules that use Pi as the chief component, are consumed more by Calvin and photorespiratory cycles. By contrast, less ATP, NADPH, and Pi are consumed by plants in the dark phase in the absence of accumulated photosynthetic $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ assimilates (Farquhar et al. 1980; Yamori et al. 2011). The diurnal rhythmic phenomenon on carbon metabolism and Pi consumption in plants, especially in the photosynthetic organs, implies that distinct PT members are involved in these biological processes. Some members in PT families of $\mathrm { P h t } 2$ and Pht4 display variable expression patterns with changes of light intensity in a photoperiod. For example, Arabidopsis PHT2;1 exhibits rapidly increased transcript levels after exposure to light (Rausch et al. 2004). Three Arabidopsis Pht4 family members of PHT4;1, PHT4;2, and $P H T 4 ; 4$ that putatively target the Golgi apparatus are expressed in a typical rhythmic expression pattern (Wang et al. 2011). A cis-regulatory element designated as CIRCADIAN CLOCK ASSOCIATED 1-binding site (CBS, motif sequence of AAAAATCT) was suggested to play essential roles in morning-specific circadian expression in PHT4;1 (Wang et al. 1998). In the current study, TaPHT2;1 showed a rhythmic expression pattern similar to that of the Arabidopsis PHT4 members mentioned above (Fig. 2a, b). However, no CBS motif was identified in the TaPHT2;1 promoter, which is similar to PHT4;2 and PHT4;4, two Pht4 family members that show typical diurnal rhythm expression patterns in the absence of CBS motif. Exploration of other cis-regulatory elements involved in the regulation of rhythm expression pattern in TaPHT2;1 and in other PT members can improve our understanding of the molecular mechanism of Pi translocation in wheat and in other vascular plants.

Under sufficient and deficient Pi conditions, the plants with knockdown expression of TaPHT2;1 (Lines 2 and 5) displayed reduced Pi concentrations in the chloroplast, total P contents in the leaves and roots, and accumulated phosphorus amounts in plants (Figs. 5b, 8b, c). Given that TaPHT2;1 is located at the envelope of plastids, especially in the chloroplast, and functions mainly as the Pi translocator to mediate Pi translocation from the cytosol to the chloroplast, the reduced phosphorus amounts (total $\mathrm { \bf P }$ contents and accumulated phosphorus amounts) in the plants with knockdown expression of TaPHT2;1 possibly resulted from some distinct PT members with functional blocking on Pi acquisition from the external environment and Pi translocation within the plants. In the past decade, Pi starvation signaling and regulatory system have been well documented in Arabidopsis (Bari et al. 2006; Schachtman and Shin 2007). A defined Pi signaling pathway consisting of MYB transcription factor PHR1, a small plant ubiquitinlike modifier (SUMO) E3 ligase SIZ1, PHOSPHATERESPONSIVE2 (PHO2), and miR399 has been posited (Bari et al. 2006). In this Pi starvation signaling, PHR1 acts as a key regulator (Rubio et al. 2001; Nilsson et al. 2007), and sumoylation is controlled by SIZ1 (Miura et al. 2005). As the target gene of PHR1, the low Pi-induced miR399 negatively regulates PHO2 expression through mRNA degradation (Fujii et al. 2005; Chiou et al. 2006). The downstream component PHO2 regulates several Pi starvation-induced genes such as Pht1;8, Pht1;9, AtIPS1, and AT4 (Bari et al. 2006). In this study, down-regulated expression analysis suggested that there are distinct P signaling pathways associated with TaPHT2;1. Some distinct PT members, possibly acting as the downstream components in the signaling pathways involved in various external Pi supply conditions, are involved in the regulation of Pi acquisition and translocation in plants. In the signaling pathways, variations of Pi in the chloroplast and cytosol associated with expression level modifications, as well as the circadian rhythm expression pattern of TaPHT2;1, are presumed to act as the signaling mechanisms. The signaling pathway components, their interaction mechanism, and the mechanism through which TaPHT2;1 initiates the signaling cascade need to be investigated.

P is an essential macronutrient for plant growth, development, and productivity in crops. P deficiency in cereal crops is widespread and causes significant yield reductions (Elliott et al. 1997; Gahoonia and Nielsen 2004). Therefore, a large amount of Pi fertilizers is applied to achieve high crop yields. Reports show that wheat and barley production consumes approximately $46 \%$ of the $\mathrm { \bf P }$ fertilizers in all cultivated cereals (FAO Fertilizer and Plant Nutrition Bulletin 17; http://www.fao.org). However, extensive fertilization with $\mathrm { \bf P }$ has led to rapid depletion of nonrenewable $\mathrm { \bf P }$ resources and contributed largely to environmental pollution (Vance et al. 2003). The improvement of P efficiency in wheat and in other cereals through molecular breeding approach is crucial for sustainable agriculture and worldwide food security (Godfray et al. 2010; Parry and Hawkesford 2010). In this study, we found that the wheat PT member TaPHT2;1 has a potential use on genetic improvement of plant phosphorus usage efficiency and is beneficial for high biomass production owing to its pronounced role on mediation of Pi remobilization in plants.

## Identification and characterization of OvPHTs in O. violaceus


A total of 22 OvPHT genes were renamed based on the homology with AtPTs. The detailed physicochemical properties of the OvPHT proteins were analyzed, including sequence IDs, protein characteristics and chromosomal locations (Table S1). The amino acid lengths and molecular Weights of the 22 OvPHT proteins ranged from 351 (OvPH3;1) to 584 (OvPHT2;1) and from $3 6 . 4 3 \mathrm { \ k D a }$ to 63.61  kDa, respectively. Additionally, the isoelectric points ranged from 8.81 to 9.53. The GRAVY index analysis revealed that all the OvPHT proteins were hydrophilic. The information of chromosomal location showed 22 OvPHTs were randomly distributed on nine chromosomes in O. violaceus. In addition, the subcellular localization of OvPHTs were predicted using the WoLF PSORT online website. Overall, the subcellular localization of OvPHTs was comparable to those observed for PHTs in other plant species. OvPHT1 and OvPHT4 subfamily members were localized in the plasma membrane. Whereas OvPHT2s and OvPHT3s were localized in the chloroplasts and mitochondria, respectively.


## Phylogenetic analysis of PHT genes in O. violaceus


As shown in Fig.  1, the 22 OvPHTs can be categorized into four subfamilies (PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, PHT4). As the largest group, the OvPHT1 subfamily contains 14 members, and all OvPHT1 genes exhibit high homology with the PHT1 genes in Arabidopsis, with the exception of OvPHT1;11 and OvPHT1;12. PHT2 subfamily was the smallest group and comprising only two OvPHT2 members. Both the PHT3 and PHT4 subfamilies contain three members each.

To further uncover the evolutionary history of the PHT gene family, we selected 28 species to construct a time tree and list the numbers of PHTs in each subfamily of these species (Fig.  2). No members of the PHT1 and PHT2 subfamily were found in Volvox carteri and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, while PHT4 subfamily contain the majority of PHT genes. The number of PHT1 family gene members in the Vitales, Amborellales, Solanales and Cucurbitales ranges between 6 and 9, whereas  significantly higher numbers, ranging between 9 and 14, are found in Polales and Fabales. A similar evolutionary distribution pattern is also evident in the PHT3 gene family. Interestingly, the number of PHT2 subfamily members remained highly conserved among diverse land plants, hinting at a limited degree of functional diversification within this subfamily. Additionally, the expansion pattern of the PHT gene was inconsistent with different plant families. For instance, the number of PHT1 and PHT4 genes in Eucalyptus grandis had three times compared with those in Psidium guajava. But in Brassicales species, the expansion of PHT1 subfamily plays a major role in the difference of total gene numbers between Arabidopsis thaliana and O. violaceus.


## Gene structure, conserved protein domain and motif analyses of OvPHTs


All PHT1 genes contain the phosphate- $\cdot \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporter domain (pfam00083). PHT3 subfamily members contain two mitochondrial carrier domains (pfam00153). Besides, PHT2 and PHT4 have a phosphate/sulfate permease domain (COG0306) and major facilitator superfamily domain (cd17380), respectively. These distinct conserved domains within each subfamily of OvPHT genes in O. violaceus likely underlie their unique responses to phosphorus-deficiency stress, highlighting the diverse roles these genes play in P homeostasis.

The intron–exon structure of OvPHT genes showed that most OvPHT1 and OvPHT2 genes contained $1 \sim 3$ exons, with the exception of OvPHT1;5, which uniquely possesses 4 exons (Fig. 3c). OvPHT3 subfamily had $5 \sim 6$ exons. Furthermore, OvPHT4 genes had the most exons, such as OvPHT4;1 and OvPHT4;1 contained 11 and 12 exons, respectively. It is noteworthy that the exon lengths of OvPHT3;1 and OvPHT3;3 were highly conserved, similar gene structure was also found in OvPHT2;1 and OvPTH2;2. Furthermore, we identified and characterized 15 conserved motifs to further elucidate the functional characteristics of OvPHT proteins. The results showed OvPHT1 subfamily members contained more motifs than other PHT subfamilies, and motif 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 14 were present in all OvPHT1 members (Fig. 3d, Table S2). In addition, all OvPHT proteins, except OvPHT1;3, OvPHT3;1, OvPHT3;2, OvPHT3;3, had motif 1. Motif 11 was found in OvPHT2, OvPHT3 and OvPHT4 subfamilies, but not in OvPHT1. Although OvPHT3 subfamily members contained two to three motifs, motif 15 was present only in this subfamily, underscoring its unique functional properties. Combining the characteristics of conserved domain, motif and intron–exon structure of the OvPHTs, we further confirmed the reliability of the phylogenetic analysis and clustering in O. violaceus.


## Collinearity analysis of PHTs between O. violaceus and other plants


Investigating gene duplication events is crucial for understanding the expansion of PHT gene families in O.

violaceus. As shown in Table 1, nine segmental duplications and two tandem duplications were identified in the OvPHT gene family, implying that segmental duplication has a dominant contribution to the expansion of $O \nu P H T$ gene family. The Ka/Ks ratio was calculated to further estimate the evolutionary selection pressure on duplication gene pairs. Except for two duplication gene pairs (OvPHT1;3; OvPHT1;11) and (OvPHT1;11; OvPHT1;12), for which the Ka/Ks ratio was not available, the $\mathrm { K a } / \mathrm { K } s$ values of segmental and tandem duplicated gene pairs ranged from 0.03 to 0.1921, suggesting that $O \nu P H T$ genes underwent purifying selection throughout their evolutionary history (Table 1).

In addition, to better understand the evolutionary relationships among PHT genes across different plant species, we conducted a collinearity analysis comparing OvPHT genes with their homologues in A. thaliana and G. max. Our findings revealed that the highest number of collinear gene pairs (18 pairs) was observed between O. violaceus and A. thaliana, which can be attributed to the close evolutionary relationship between these two species (Fig.  4). Additionally, 14 collinear gene pairs were identified between A. thaliana and G. max, 8 pairs between O. violaceus and $G .$ . max. Notably, the majority of these collinear gene pairs belonged to the same subfamily, while OvPHT1;9 had two homologous genes from PHT4 subfamily in G. max, including GmPHT4;4 and GmPHT4;6, indicating that the GmPHT4 subfamily has undergone an increased functional diversity during the whole genome duplication event in G. max.

Phosphorus (P) is an essential element of phospholipids and nucleic acids, which plays a crucial role in energy transfer reactions and signal transduction processes that are vital for all life forms on Earth [1]. Although soils generally contain abundant $\mathrm { { P } } ,$ only a small fraction is accessible for crop use [2]. It is bound to incompletely weathered mineral particles, adsorbed on mineral surfaces, or forms occluded $\mathrm { P }$ through secondary mineralization [2]. Therefore, roots obtain phosphate (Pi) against a huge concentration gap between plant cells $( \mathrm { m M } )$ and soil $( \mu \mathrm { M } )$ [3, 4]. So, efficient Pi acquisition from soil and translocation within plants are necessary to maintain general levels of cellular Pi [5]. Root cell absorption of Pi from the soil is energy-dependent. The PHT1 family of plant Pi transporters are known to be the primary facilitator of this process [6, 7].

The first Pi transporters (PTs) identified were AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 in higher plant [7]. So far, 9 AtPHT1s have been found in Arabidopsis thaliana [8]. 13 OsPHT1s have been discovered in rice (Oryza sativa) [9]. These PHT1s have distinct functions in the absorption, movement, and storage of Pi. In Arabidopsis, disruption of AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 leads to Pi uptake to reduce to $5 7 \%$ of the wildtype under Pi deficiency, and $7 0 \%$ of the wild‐type under Pi sufficiency [10]. AtPHT1;8 and AtPHT1;9 mediate inorganic phosphate acquisition during Pi starvation [8]. In rice, mutation of OsPHT1;2, OsPHT1;3, OsPHT1;6, or OsPHT1;8 reduces Pi uptake under low Pi regimes [9, 11, 12], and mutation of OsPHT1;1, OsPHT1;4, or OsPHT1;8 reduces Pi uptake under Pi sufficiency [11, 13, 14]. OsPHT1;9 and OsPHT1;10 redundantly function in Pi uptake under both high- and low-Pi conditions [15]. GhPHT1;4 and GhPHT1;5 were responsible for Pi uptake under Pi-starvation conditions in cotton [16]. The transgenic plants overexpressing MtPT5 in M. truncatula showed larger leaves, higher biomass and Pi enrichment compared with wild type [17]. Expression of PnPht1;1 or PnPht1;2 in mutant strains could enhance the uptake of Pi in Panax notoginseng [18]. Collectively, these studies confirm that PHT1 proteins play important roles in Pi acquisition from the rhizosphere into plant roots under different Pi supply.

Commonly, PHT1 family members are highly conserved among the different species [19]. 36 TaPHT1s have been found in wheat (Triticum aestivum), among which TaPHT1.1/1.9, 1.2, and 1.10 were expressed especially in roots [20]. There are 14 PHT1s in soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merr.), which are expressed differently not only in responding to Pi availability but also in other nutrient deficiencies, including N, K, and Fe, in the different tissues [21]. 8 PHT1s showed diverse roles and genetic redundancy responding to Pi deficiency in tomato [22]. Genome-wide analysis has identified 12

PHT1s in Gossypium hirsutum [23]. 9 CsPHT1s were identified in tea plants (Camellia sinensis L. O. kuntze), which play crucial roles in selenite homeostasis [24]. 201 PHT1 homologs were identified and analyzed from three diploids and two allotetraploids Brassica species, which were induced by heavy metal stress [25]. However, the characterization of PHT1 gene family and the stressresponsive patterns are still unknown in melon.

Melon is an important crop for its unique flavor and nutritional value worldwide [26]. Pi uptake and transport mediated by PHT1 play an important role in melon plant growth, fruit growth and quality formation, especially sugar accumulation. Furthermore, current melon cultivars have a narrow genetic base and are vulnerable to both biotic and abiotic stresses due to prolonged domestication and artificial selection for high yields and desirable traits [27, 28]. Therefore, breeders are facing the arduous work of improving melon resistance with conventional and/or modern breeding approaches. Our previous research revealed that three CmPHT1s positively participated in Pi uptake under Pi-deficiency [29]. We speculated that there should be other PHT1s in melon. Are CmPHT1s involved in the other stress responses in melon? Further, what factors regulate the transcription of these PHT1 genes? In the current study, 7 CmPHT1 genes were identified and systematically analyzed based on the updated melon genome and their characteristics were analyzed including gene structure, conversed motif structure, chromosomal location, evolutionary relationship, synteny relationship, and cis-elements in the promoters. 14 cis-element categories were identified in CmPHT1 promoters. The stress-responsive expression patterns of CmPHT1s in melon were surveyed under low-phosphate stress (LP) and other stresses. Combining the bioinformatical analysis, three CmWRKYs regulated CmPHT1;5 expression by binding to its W-box element. This research shed light on the characterization and stress-regulatory elements of CmPHT1s, which contribute to clarify further the functional mechanisms under biotic and abiotic stress in melon.

In the present study,we showed that SNX1 is a negative modulator of Pi uptake by facilitating PHT1;1 protein degradation in Arabidopsis. How plants modulate SNX1- mediated PHT1;1 protein degradation under different Pi conditions remains unclear.We examined the expression of SNX1 in plant seedlings treated with sufficient or deficient Pi by qRT-PCR,and found that low Pi treatment significantly downregulated SNX1 expression,consistent with increased PHT1;1 protein stability in low Pi-treated plants. Our result showed that the phr1 mutant had comparable levels of SNX1 expression to the wild type (Figure S5)，revealing that SNX1 expression is not affected by PHR1. How plants modulate SNX1 expression to fine-tune PHT1;1 protein stability remains elusive,and extensive experiments are required to explore the underlying mechanism.We speculate that identification of the upstream factors of SNX1 may shed more light on how plants coordinate mechanisms to increase and reduce Pi uptake under different Pi availabilities.

Endosomal traficking controls the localization,degradation,storage,or reutilization of membrane proteins,thus playing a fundamental role in plant membrane protein turnover and responses to environmental stimuli.ALiX in Arabidopsis interacts with the ESCRT-Il component SNF7 and mediates PHT1;1 trafficking from the plasma membrane to the vacuole for degradation through MVBs. Thus, the alix mutant displays reduced vacuolar degradation of PHT1;1 and increased Pi content compared to wild-type plants.Similar to the alix mutant,our study showed that the snx1-2 mutant also has increased PHT1;1 stability and Pi content,raising the possibility that SNX1 acts upstream of ALIX in the endosomal trafficking of PHT1;1 as SNX1 acts in the sorting center for protein trafficking.We speculated that the cytoplasmic PHT1;1 protein is recognized by SNX1 via their interaction,subsequently sorted into ALIXassociated MVBs,and finally degraded in the vacuole in the plant response to sufficient Pi.

In addition to PHT1;1，a series of proteins have been identified as ALIX cargos，including the ABA receptor PYL4/RCAR10 and the brassinosteroid receptor brassinosteroid-insensitive 1，which are modulated by ALIX-mediatedvacuolardegradation(Cardona-Lopez et al., 2015; Garcia-Leon et al., 2019). Thus,alix null mutation can retard plant growth and even result in lethality,in contrast to the snx1-2 mutant,which exhibits relatively normal growth and development, suggesting that ALIX and SNX1 have common as well as different target cargos involved in plant growth and stress responses.The complicated relationship between SNX1-mediated protein sorting and ALIX-mediated protein degradation in diverse plant biological processes remains to be further experimentally elucidated.

It has been reported that the microtubule-associated protein CLASP interacts with SNX1 to mediate an association between endosomes and microtubules; clasp-1 mutant plants exhibit enhancedPlN2 degradation (Ambrose et al., 2013)，indicating that CLASP represses PIN2 degradation via SNX1. Another previous report also documented that both BLOC-1 complex components BLOS1 and BLOS2 interact with SNX1 on sorting endosomes and that BLOS1 knockdown lines exhibit increased PIN2 protein levels (Cui et al., 2010),revealing that BLOS1 promotes PIN2 degradation via SNX1. These reports imply that SNX1 lies at the switch point of the two routes, retrograde transport for protein recycling and protein vacuolar degradation (Cui et al.,2010). The present study demonstrates that SNX1 negatively modulates plant Pi uptake under Pi deficiency by sorting PHT1;1 into endosomes for vacuolar degradation，suggesting the possible involvement of BLOS1 in SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation in plants.Unraveling the role of BLOS1 in the plant response to limited Pi conditions shall shed more light on how SNX1 functions in Pi uptake through modulating PHT1;1 protein stability. Previous reports also showed that SNX1 facilitates iron acquisition by suppressing IRT1 degradation and increasing its plasma membrane localization (Brumbarova & lvanov,2016; lvanov et al.,2014). Considering the antagonistic interaction between iron and P in plantnutritionacquisition， wewonderedwhether increased Pi content in the snx1-2 mutant was partially due to altered iron uptake. However,we noticed that compared to wild-type plants, the snx1-2 mutant has similar ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under ironsufficient conditions and lower ITR1 protein accumulation and ion content under iron-deficient conditions (lvanov et al.,2014). Thus,we speculate that increased Pi uptake in the snx1-2 mutant is independent of IRT1 under low Pi but suficient iron conditions. In addition,these reports show distinct effcts of SNX1 on its targets， suggesting that SNX1 differentially affects sorting and stability of the target proteins in an environmental stimuli-dependent manner via complicated mechanisms.

We previously reported that SNX1 functions in plant salt stress tolerance by affecting NO accumulation and the activities of antioxidant enzymes (Li et al., 2018). It is widely reported that NO significantly affects plant root development and responses to environmental stresses by inhibiting primary root elongation but promoting lateral root and root hair development in plants (Lombardo et al.,20o6; Schlicht et al.,2013),similar to the effect of low Pi on plant root architecture (Liu et al., 2009,2017),suggesting a possible role of NO in the plant response to low Pi conditions.

A recent study documented that low Pi restrains SNX1 accumulation in the cytoplasm but stimulates its plasma membrane localization in a PA-dependent manner (Lin et al.,2020). Combined with our observations,we further speculated that under sufficient Pi,SNX1 interacts with PHT1;1 in cytosolic vesicles to promote its protein degradation, thereby reducing root Pi uptake,while low Pi facilitates SNX1 localization at the plasma membrane in a PAdependent manner and also represses SNX1 expression, thus relieving SNX1-mediated PHT1;1 degradation and increasing root Pi uptake.

Phosphorus (P) is an essential nutrient for plant growth and development, contributing about $0 . 2 \%$ of the dry weight. It serves as an important component of many biological macromolecules, such as nucleic acids, membrane lipids, and ATP. Meanwhile, multiple plant biological processes, including photosynthesis, respiration, and glycolysis, require this element [1]. In plants, P is mainly taken up from the soil by the roots in the form of inorganic phosphate $( \mathrm { P i } )$ , including $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { - }$ and $\mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 2 - }$ . Although $\mathrm { P }$ is abundant in the soil, the form of $\mathrm { P i } ,$ available for plant uptake, is relatively rare $( 0 . 1 { - } 1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { M } )$ . However, in the cytoplasm of plant cells, the $\mathrm { P i }$ concentration is generally about $5 { - } 1 0 \mathrm { m M }$ [2,3]. Thus, the uptake of P from the soil to the plant roots is an active process and requires special transporters.

Phosphorus uptake from soil and translocation between plant tissues and organs is facilitated by phosphate transporters (PHT), which are $\mathrm { P i } { \cdot } \mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ symporters. The first PHT protein identified in higher plants was AtPT1 from Arabidopsis thaliana [4]. Since then, many genes encoding PHTs have been identified and characterized from a series of plant species, including Arabidopsis thaliana [5,6], Oryza sativa [7], Triticum aestivum [8], and Solanum tuberosum [9]. In addition, genome-wide identification of plant PHT family genes has also been reported in Populus trichocarpa [10,11], Arabidopsis thaliana [12,13], Triticum aestivum [14], Solanum lycopersicum [15], Oryza sativa [16], Solanum tuberosum [17], and Malus domestica [18].

There are two Pi uptake systems in plants: a low-Pi-inducible high-affinity system and a constitutive low-affinity system [3]. The former is inducible by and responsible for low Pi concentrations, whereas the latter is constitutively expressed. The plant genes encoding Pi transporters are classified into five families, PHT1, PHT2, PHT3, PHT4, and PHO, the first four of which are reported to localize in the plasma membrane, plastid inner membrane, mitochondrial inner membrane, and Golgi compartment, respectively [2,9]. Among the four families, the PHT1 family is relatively well characterized. Most PHT1 family members are high-affinity Pi transporters. Although the majority of PHT1 genes are expressed in roots and responsible for Pi uptake from the soil under Pi-limited environments [5], many of them are also located in the leaves, stems, and flowers, suggesting that they may be involved in Pi translocation inside the plant [19,20]. In Arabidopsis, there are nine PHT1 family genes (AtPHT1;1-9), some of which are regulated in response to changes in Pi availability [21]. In rice, 13 members of the PHT1 family (OsPT1-13) contribute to Pi uptake from the soil and internal translocation [19,22]. In maize, ZmPht1;1-5 are expressed both in roots and in shoots, and are induced by Pi starvation [23]. In soybean, the PHT1 family is composed of 14 members (GmPT1-14), encoding high-affinity transporters and contributing to Pi uptake in roots under low-Pi conditions [24]. In Medicago truncatula, five PHT1 genes are also induced by low Pi and are responsible for Pi uptake and translocation [25,26]. In contrast to the PHT1 family, the other families are less investigated and mainly contribute to Pi distribution within subcellular compartments [3]. The PHT2 family only has one member in many species, such as rice, Arabidopsis, and maize. AtPHT2;1 is a low-affinity transporter located in chloroplasts, responsible for phosphate-starvation responses in Arabidopsis [27]. In addition, there are 11 members of PHO1 gene family in Arabidopsis, required for Pi translocation [6,12,28].

Aside from the PHT2 family, the other families are composed of more than one member. The Pi-affinity and expression pattern within the family vary greatly. For instance, AtPHT1;6 is mainly expressed in floral organs, revealing the role of PHT1 transporters in flower development [5]; the other eight AtPHT1s are all at least expressed in the roots, in line with their major role in Pi uptake from the soil [29]. AtPHT1;1 and AtPHT1;4 are two high-affinity transporters and contribute to Pi uptake under both normal and low-Pi conditions [30]. In addition, AtPHT1;5 is required for Pi translocation from roots to shoots [31]. The expression of AtPHT1;8 and AtPHT1;9 is inducible by low-Pi concentrations and functions in Pi translocation within plants [32,33]. Taken together, most PHT1 members in Arabidopsis are detected in diverse tissues or organs and share overlapping expression patterns with other PHT1 transporters, suggesting the functional redundancy and complexity of roles [5,29,34].

Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench) is a C4 crop with high photosynthetic efficiency and environmental adaptability. As compared with its closely-related species maize, Sorghum is more resistant to harmful environments, including drought, high temperature, high salinity, and sterile soil. Although the whole-genome sequence of Sorghum has been published [34], the PHT family genes in Sorghum have not been systematically investigated yet. In this study, we identified 27 potential SbPHT family members via sequence alignment, classified these proteins into subfamilies, and further analyzed their sequences and expression patterns.

Plant SUT proteins were originally classified into three phylogenetic groups according to Aoki et al. (2003), and later into four distinct classes by Sauer (2007). An expanded phylogenetic analysis of SUT orthologs from 10 sequenced genomes (six dicots and four monocots) supports the latter classification (Figure 1 and Table S1), with Group I and aPtaSUT4 is mapped to three partial gene models in the JGI poplar genome v2.2 release.

Group II representing monocot- and dicot-specific branches, respectively. PtaSUT1 and PtaSUT3 belong to Group II, and cluster with SUT isoforms from other perennial species (e.g. Ricinus, Vitis, Juglans and Citrus). This subclade also includes SUT proteins from herbaceous species, but is distinct from the Arabidopsis- and legume-specific subclades (Figure 1). PtaSUT5 and PtaSUT6 fall into the dicot subclade of Group III, clustering with other perennial SUT orthologs. Group IV also forms monocot- and dicot-specific subclades, with the dicot group divided into a legume-specific branch and a non-legume branch that includes PtaSUT4. In dicots, plasma membrane-localized SUT proteins that mediate apoplastic loading generally fall into Group II, as for example, Arabidopsis AtSUC2 (Chandran et al., 2003) and tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) SlSUT1 (Hackel et al., 2006). Tonoplast-localized isoforms are found in Group IV, exemplified by Arabidopsis AtSUC4 (Endler et al., 2006) and lotus (Lotus japonicus) LjSUT4 (Reinders et al., 2008). The function of Group III SUTs remains less clear (Braun and Slewinski, 2009).


## Expression of PtaSUT genes in Populus


The Group IV transporter PtaSUT4 was ubiquitously expressed based on QPCR, and its transcripts were more abundant than those of the other PtaSUT genes in every tissue examined (Figure 2). PtaSUT4 transcript levels were highest in mature source leaf (ML) and developing xylem. Transcripts of the Group III members, PtaSUT5 and PtaSUT6, were also readily detected, and at similar levels across all tissues sampled from greenhouse plants. Their level was much lower than that of PtaSUT4 in most tissues, but was comparable in shoot tips (ST). Transcripts of Group II PtaSUT1 and PtaSUT3 were detected mainly in roots and stems, respectively. PtaSUT3, PtaSUT4 and PtaSUT5, were selected for in situ transcript localization (Figure 3). With their strong sequence and expression-pattern similarity, PtaSUT5 and

PtaSUT6 transcripts contributed equally to in situ hybridization signal. PtaSUT1 and PtaSUT3 sequences are also highly similar; however, PtaSUT3 was the predominantly expressed Group II member in shoot organs.

PtaSUT4 transcripts were present in epidermal cells, spongy mesophyll and lower layers of the palisade mesophyll in lamina of source leaves, but not in the upper palisade layer (Figure 3b, yellow arrowheads). Hybridization was also evident in minor phloem traces (red arrows) in source leaves. PtaSUT3 transcripts were observed in minor veins of source leaf lamina, but were barely detected in the mesophyll (Figure 3a). PtaSUT5/6 expression was detected in all cell types, but at lower levels than PtaSUT4 (Figure 3c). By comparison, RuBisCO transcripts were abundant in all mesophyll layers, but not in vascular traces (Figure 3d). In stems, PtaSUT4 transcripts were readily detected in mesophyll and conducting cells of phloem, and in ray parenchyma, fibers and vessels of the secondary xylem (Figure 3g). Vascular cambium and dividing xylem cells also yielded clear hybridization signals. In conducting cells of primary stem internodes, PtaSUT4 signals were also strong (Figure 3j). Hybridization of PtaSUT3 was much more evident in xylem vessel and fiber cells than in adjacent phloem tissues (Figure 3f). Weak PtaSUT5/6 signal was also detected in phloem tissues, including phloem fibers where PtaSUT3 and PtaSUT4 transcripts were not detected. In contrast to PtaSUT4, hybridization signals of PtaSUT3 and PtaSUT5/6 were weaker in the primary internodes than in secondary internodes (Figure 3f–k).


## PtaSUT4 exhibits sucrose transport activity and is localized to the tonoplast


Function of the Populus SUT proteins was verified using the Saccharomyces cerevisiae SUSY7/ura3 mutant strain. This mutant is deficient in sucrose transport activity and unable to grow on media containing sucrose as the sole carbon source (Riesmeier et al., 1992). Ectopic expression of PtaSUT3, PtaSUT4 and PtaSUT5 complemented the mutant phenotype on sucrose-containing media (Figure 4a). Active sucrose transporter rather that passive sucrose facilitator function is supported for all three Populus isoforms by their capacity to rescue growth of the mutant on media supplemented with only $2 \%$ sucrose (Zhou et al., 2007). Unlike the Group II and Group III members, PtaSUT4 was strongly expressed in both source and sink organs. As a first step toward detailed functional analysis, membrane-targeting of PtaSUT4 protein was determined. Group IV SUT proteins are localized to the tonoplast in several species (Endler et al., ${ 2 0 0 6 }$ ; Reinders et al., 2008), but have been found in the plasma membrane in potato and, according to one proteomic survey, in Populus (Chincinska et al., 2008; Nilsson et al., 2010). Therefore, to confirm localization of PtaSUT4, N. benthamiana leaves were infiltrated with Agrobacterium carrying the GFP–PtaSUT4 construct and protoplasts were isolated for visualization of GFP targeting. Targeting of PtaSUT4 protein to the tonoplast was supported by localized GFP signal along the perimeter of a large structure, presumably the tonoplast surrounding the major vacuole, and interior to the chloroplasts (Figure 4b).


## Transgenic manipulation of PtaSUT4 by RNAi altered biomass partitioning


The abundance of PtaSUT4 transcripts coupled with the near absence of Group II SUT transcripts in exporting leaves marks a clear difference between Populus and apoplasticloading species. In the apoplastic-loading species, Group II transporters that mediate phloem-loading are the predominantly expressed isoforms in source leaves, and Group IV SUT transcripts are rare. In an effort to determine whether sucrose export depends on PtaSUT4 function in Populus, RNAi-mediated gene silencing was performed. PtaSUT4 transcript levels were reduced by $5 0 \mathrm { - } 9 0 \%$ in different tissues of four independent transgenic poplar lines (Figure S2a). Transcript levels of PtaSUT5 were not systematically affected in transgenic plants, confirming specificity of the PtaSUT4 silencing (Figure S2b). Based on these results, and on preliminary measurements showing that all four lines exhibited higher source-leaf sucrose contents than wild-type (WT) controls (Figure S2c), transgenic line G exhibiting the strongest overall suppression of PtaSUT4 was propagated for further analysis.

Plant growth was monitored under hydroponic conditions where N supply could be conveniently and uniformly varied to alter plant-wide patterns of carbon use. Suppression of PtaSUT4 had no obvious effect on plant appearance or growth. However, the ratio of leaf area to stem volume proxies was greater in transgenic than WT plants under the two N regimes tested (Figure 5a). Leaf and stem dry masses per unit area and volume, respectively, were identical in transgenic and WT plants. The difference in leaf:stem ratio was consistent with shorter stem height and greater summed leaf area (in the leaf expansion zone) of transgenics compared with WT (Figure 5b,c). In N-replete plants, the leaf area differential was largest in non-exporting leaves, LPI-0 and LPI-1 (Figure S3a), smaller in source leaves reaching full size, and not evident in fully mature source leaves (LPI-8). During N-limitation, importing leaves were smaller in the transgenics, but sink-source transitional and source leaves expanded to a larger size in transgenic than WT plants (Figure S3b). The RNAi effect on early leaf expansion and shoot growth of N-replete plants was robust, and similar trends were observed in all four transgenic lines when they were grown in soil (Figure S3c,d).

During N-replete growth, the predominant SUS (SUS2) and SPS (SPS6) isoforms exhibited lower transcript levels in ML of transgenic than of WT plants (Figures 6a and S4).
